title.rendered: Dahal urges people to help Budhigandaki flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

Nepali Communist Party (NCP) Coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal has urged people to join in the rescue, relief and safety of those affected by the Budhigandaki flood.

The flash flood in the Budhigandaki River in Gorkha district has caused extensive physical damage. The flood, which came with black silt, has damaged permanent bridges, suspension bridges, houses and market areas.

Areas including Chumnubri, Dharche and Arughat have suffered damage, with bridges and houses washed away.

Writing about the situation on social media, Prachanda urged people to take part in rescue, relief and safety efforts for those affected.

“I sincerely urge everyone to join in the rescue, relief and safety of the affected citizens. I also request citizens living from the Budhigandaki to the banks of the Trishuli to stay safe with utmost caution,” he wrote on social media. “Let us unite in support of the affected citizens in this hour of disaster.”

title.rendered: Budhigandaki flood: 10 people go missing; six bridges swept away

content.rendered:
Gorkha, October 11

Ten people have gone missing in the Budhigandaki flood that occurred early this morning today. The flood also swept away six bridges- two motorable and four suspension bridges.

Assistant chief district officer in Gorkha, Netra Prasad Sharma, told RSS that the flood swept away the motorable bridges of Arughat, Tripurasundari and Soti-Manbu.

The disaster also swept away a Bailey bridge connecting wards No. 1 and 3 of Dharche Rural Municipality in Gorkha. Other damaged footbridges include those connecting Machhikhola to Karauja; Thadobharyang to Jagat; and Ghattekhola to Philim in Gorkha district.

The flood washed away nearly 35 houses from Painyu and Bagar of Chumnubri Rural Municipality-3. It also damaged settlements at Jagat, Salleri, Dovan and Ghattekhola.

—RSS

title.rendered: Bada Dashain kicks off with Ghatasthapana today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

The “Navaratri,” a nine-night festival celebrated as Bada Dashain, has officially begun today, marking a significant occasion for Hindus across the world. Ghatasthapana takes place on Ashwin Shukla Pratipada, which is the first day of the bright half of the lunar month Asoj or Kartik.

As per the Nepal Calendar Determination Committee, the auspicious moment for Ghatasthapana this year is set for 11:47 am today. During this sacred hour, devotees worship the deity Shailaputri. The festival is a time to honour various deities, including Bhramacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri, and Siddhidatri.

The first day is dedicated to worshipping Shailaputri through Vedic rituals and preparing for Jamara (barley shoots) by sowing maize and barley seeds in a jar filled with soil and cow dung to encourage germination. Additionally, prayers are offered to Durga Bhavani, the goddess of power, today.

The germination of the auspicious “Jamara” also begins at Hanumandhoka Dashain Ghar, following Vedic traditions. The committee has designated 10:26 am as the most favourable time for Dashain tika on October 21 (Kartik 4) this year.

—RSS

title.rendered: Road department says Soti Khola bridge and 22-metre RCC section of Arughat bridge swept away

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

The flood in the Budhigandaki River has damaged two bridges in Gorkha district.

According to preliminary damage details released by the Department of Roads, the Soti Khola bridge connecting Arughat Rural Municipality-2 and 3 has been completely washed away.

The flood also swept away a 22-metre RCC section of the Arughat bridge connecting Gorkha and Dhading. The bridge has a total of 60 metres of truss and a 25-metre RCC structure, and its truss section still appears to be standing.

The department said it is studying whether a Bailey bridge could be placed on the remaining truss structure to restore traffic.

It said a detailed technical assessment of the bridge’s condition is underway, and that the full extent of the flood damage will become clear after that assessment.

title.rendered: Scenes from the Budhi Gandaki flood-affected areas (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

A sudden flood carrying black mud and debris has caused extensive damage along the Budhi Gandaki River in Gorkha, sweeping away bridges, houses and parts of a hydropower project.

The full extent of the damage is yet to be determined. Preliminary reports say a mud house belonging to Ram Bahadur Gurung in Sirdibas, Ward 3 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality, was swept away, while floodwater entered another house.

A suspension bridge connecting Machhikhola in Ward 5 of Dharche Rural Municipality with Kerauja was also swept away. Floodwater entered the lower settlement of Machhikhola.

The flood destroyed an iron concrete bridge at Soti connecting Wards 2 and 3 of Aarughat Rural Municipality. It also swept away the under-construction Sahaj Urja powerhouse in Salleri, Ward 3 of Chumnubri, along with seven or eight houses in the surrounding area.

The flood also washed away one of the three sections of the motorable bridge connecting Aarughat in Gorkha with Dhading at Nayapul in Ward 9 of Aarughat Rural Municipality, completely blocking the road.

Meanwhile, around 20 to 22 houses in Salleri, Ward 3 of Dharche Rural Municipality, are reportedly at risk.

Cause of flood remains unclear

The cause of the flood has not yet been established. Binod Parajuli, a senior hydrologist at the Flood Forecasting Division under the Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research, said there had been no recorded rainfall in the upper reaches of the Budhi Gandaki River.

Authorities suspect that a landslide may have temporarily blocked the river before releasing a sudden surge of water, or that an ice avalanche may have triggered the flood.

“The flood appears to have originated in the Himalayan region above human settlements,” Parajuli said. “We are investigating the overall cause, including whether the river was blocked by a landslide or whether the flood originated in the Himalayan region.”

A Nepali Army helicopter has been deployed from Kathmandu to the affected areas. Nepal Police personnel have also been mobilised to evacuate settlements and move residents to safer locations.

Authorities have warned that the flood could affect areas extending from Gorkha and Dhading to Tanahun, Muglin and Chitwan, urging residents in potentially affected areas to remain alert.

title.rendered: Gandaki provincial health ministry releases preliminary details of Budhigandaki flood damage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

The Gandaki Province Ministry of Health has released preliminary details of the damage caused by the flash flood in Gorkha’s Budhigandaki River.

The details say houses, bridges and a hydropower project were damaged.

The ministry said health institutions in Philim, Salleri, Jagat and Machhikhola are at lower risk because they sit at higher elevations.

It added that the district-level Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) of Gorkha, Lamjung and Tanahun, along with the Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) of the provincial hospitals, have been placed on standby.

Preliminary details of damage received from Gandaki’s health ministry

  • Chumnubri Rural Municipality-3, Nyakchet: The old suspension bridge connecting Nyakchet to Sirdibas was washed away.
  • Chumnubri-3, Sirdibas: One mud-built house belonging to Ram B. Gurung was washed away and floodwater entered one house.
  • Dharche Rural Municipality-5: The suspension bridge connecting Machhikhola to Keroja was washed away.
  • Dharche-5, lower settlement in Machhikhola: Floodwater entered five to seven houses and five to seven sheds.
  • Dharche-3, Salleri: 20 to 22 houses are at risk.
  • Arughat Rural Municipality-2 and 3: The steel permanent bridge at Soti connecting the two wards was washed away.
  • Chumnubri-3, Sallery: The Sahaj Urja power house under construction and seven to eight houses around it were washed away.
  • Arughat-9, Nayapul: One of the three sections of the permanent bridge connecting Arughat and Dhading, the one on the Gorkha side, was washed away. The road is completely blocked.

title.rendered: 570 kg of marijuana seized from vegetable-laden vehicle in Morang

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, October 11

Marijuana has been seized from a pickup van that was carrying vegetables toward India.

The Armed Police Force took control of 570 kg of marijuana, hidden among the vegetables, from a vehicle heading to India via Jahada in Morang on Saturday night.

A team deployed from the Armed Police Force Nepal’s Border Outpost (BOP) in Nocha recovered the marijuana at Ramchowk in Jahada Rural Municipality-4 at around 11 pm on Saturday.

According to the Armed Police, the driver of the van, numbered Pra 1-01-00 Cha 7422 and bound for India, abandoned the vehicle and fled when the force tried to stop it. A search then turned up 19 packets of marijuana hidden between chayote and cabbage, said Superintendent of Police Gehendra Bahadur Bhandari, chief of the Armed Police Force in Morang.

The seized marijuana weighed 570 kg in total. The marijuana and the pickup van have been handed over to Nepal Police for investigation and action. Police said a search for the driver is underway.

title.rendered: Budhigandaki flood washes away Times Energy buildings, 18 employees flee to safety

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

The flash flood in the Budhigandaki River has caused heavy physical damage at Times Energy Pvt Ltd, Gorkha. The company’s 18 employees escaped with their lives by fleeing.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, preliminary information indicates that the flood swept away nine blocks and six public buildings belonging to the company.

The 18 employees working on the project escaped after locals warned them that a flood was coming. They went to a high, safe place on their own.

Authority Chief Executive Officer Dr Dharma Raj Upreti said preparations are underway to rescue them by Nepali Army helicopter.

“Security personnel of Nepal Police, the Nepali Army and the Armed Police Force Nepal have been mobilised in their respective areas,” Dr Upreti said. “The most important thing right now is to protect human life.”

The Nepali Army said its team has airlifted six people from the Jagat area.

A Nepali Army air team has been mobilised from Kathmandu. Teams from the Army, the Armed Police and Nepal Police have also been deployed on the ground.

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has expressed grief over the severe flood in the Budhigandaki River, which caused heavy damage in Gorkha’s Chumnubri area and washed away two bridges.

In a Facebook post, Thapa urged people living along the riverbanks, from the Budhigandaki down to the Trishuli, to exercise extreme caution.

Noting that the flood swept away the bridge connecting Nyakchet and Philim and the bridge linking Dhading and Gorkha, he asked people living along the river to stay in safe places and follow the directives issued by local administrations.

He appealed to all Congress leaders and cadres to take an active part in rescue, relief and other necessary support for those affected during this time of disaster.

With further risks possible in the flood-affected areas, he asked riverside residents to stay alert and take the necessary precautions against possible danger.

title.rendered: What triggered the devastating flood in the Budhi Gandaki river?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

A devastating flood carrying black mud and debris has struck the Budhi Gandaki River in Gorkha, damaging bridges and market areas just a month and a half after the Rasuwagadhi–Bhote Koshi flood.

The full extent of the damage is yet to be determined. Home Minister Sudan Gurung, who was elected to Parliament from Gorkha, described the disaster as another devastating flood for Nepal.

Residents of northern Gorkha have told Onlinekhabar that they have never witnessed such a severe flood before.

The flood swept away part of the motorable bridge connecting Aarughat in Gorkha with Dhading. Videos shared on social media show one span of the bridge on the Gorkha side being washed away.

It also destroyed an old suspension bridge connecting Nyakchet and Sirdibas in Ward 3 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality, a suspension bridge linking Machhikhola in Ward 5 of Dharche Rural Municipality with Kerauja, and an iron concrete bridge at Soti connecting Wards 2 and 3 of Aarughat Rural Municipality.

Ice avalanche suspected as cause

The exact cause of the flood, which carried away large boulders, has not yet been established. However, officials suspect that an ice avalanche in the northern region may have triggered the disaster.

Dr Dharmaraj Upreti, executive director of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), said preliminary information suggested that an ice avalanche may have sent snow, mud and other debris into the river, triggering the flood.

“This information was obtained through telephone contact with locals. However, the actual cause of the flood has not yet been confirmed,” he said.

Binod Parajuli, a senior hydrologist at the Flood Forecasting Division of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, said there had been no recorded rainfall in the upper reaches of the Budhi Gandaki River. Therefore, the flood could not be attributed to rainfall based on the available records.

Four people missing, rescue efforts underway

According to NDRRMA, no human casualties had been confirmed at the time of reporting. However, the National News Agency (RSS) reported that four people had gone missing from the area along Ungilung Khola in Ward 6 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality.

A Nepali Army helicopter has been deployed from Kathmandu to the affected region. However, rescue operations have faced difficulties because conditions have not yet allowed the helicopter to land, NDRRMA said.

Nepal Police personnel have also been mobilised to evacuate settlements and move residents to safer locations.

Authorities have warned that the flood could affect areas extending from Gorkha and Dhading to Tanahun, Muglin and Chitwan, urging residents in potentially affected areas to remain alert.

title.rendered: Home Minister urges residents along Budhi Gandaki to move to safety

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

Home Minister Sudan Gurung has urged residents living along the Budhi Gandaki River to immediately move to safer locations and remain on high alert following a massive flood in the area.

In a post on Facebook, Gurung specifically appealed to residents of Sirdibas, Jagat, Salleri, Kholbesi, Machhikhola, Soti, Arkhet and Aarughat to evacuate areas along the riverbank.

Gurung said he was seriously concerned by reports of the flood, which had swept away a bridge connecting Nyakchet and Philim Bazaar in Ward 3 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality in his home constituency of Gorkha. He also said muddy floodwaters had entered some houses in the Ghattikhola area and that the river’s flow continued to rise.

Calling the incident another major flood disaster for Nepal, Gurung said helicopters had been mobilised to the affected areas following the incident.

He added that the Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and local administration had been deployed for rescue, relief and evacuation operations.

The home minister urged residents to remain calm and prioritise their safety. He also asked those in need of emergency assistance to contact the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The bridge was washed away by the flood that struck the river on Sunday morning, said Anil Shrestha, inspector at the Area Police Office in Aarughat.

The flood also swept away several other bridges in the region, including an old suspension bridge connecting Nyakchet and Sirdibas in Ward 3 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality.

Additionally, an iron concrete bridge at Soti connecting Wards 2 and 3 of Aarughat Rural Municipality was swept away.

title.rendered: Four missing after flash flood in Gorkha; 15 yaks swept away

Four people have gone missing after a flood from Ungilung Khola in Chumnubri Rural Municipality-6, Gorkha, surged into the Budhi Gandaki River.

According to the National News Agency (RSS), the flood swept away four cattle sheds along the banks of Ungilung Khola, along with 15 yaks and nak (female yaks). The four missing people had been staying at the sheds to look after the animals.

The flood also swept away the Machhikhola bridge connecting the area to Dharche Rural Municipality and caused damage in Machhikhola Bazaar, said Assistant Chief District Officer Netra Prasad Sharma.

A bridge connecting Soti and Manbu in Aarughat Rural Municipality was also swept away, he added.

title.rendered: Budhi Gandaki flash flood sweeps away more than 35 houses in northern Gorkha

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

A debris-laden flash flood in the Budhi Gandaki River swept away more than 35 houses in several locations in northern Gorkha on Sunday morning, according to local officials.

Houses were swept away in Salleri, Bagar and Ghattikhola, among other places, said Nima Lama, chairperson of Chumnubri Rural Municipality.

The full extent of the damage has yet to be determined. Lama also said five cattle sheds in Chumchet had gone out of contact following a landslide in Churi.

The flood damaged a hydropower project under construction in Salleri and swept away a motorable bridge connecting Manbu and Soti.

It also destroyed a suspension bridge linking Nagchet and Sirdibas in Ward 3 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality with Machhakhola and Kerauja in Ward 5 of Dharche Rural Municipality, according to Police Inspector Akash Kadel.

A concrete bridge at Soti, which connects Wards 2 and 3 of Aarughat Rural Municipality, was also swept away, Kadel said.

Residents have fled their homes and moved to higher ground in search of safety.

“We have climbed up to the hills and are staying there,” said Ganesh Karki, a resident of Jagat. “There is nothing we can do except watch our houses being swept away.”

Karki said he had never witnessed such flooding in the Budhi Gandaki River. He said the floodwaters had subsided briefly before surging again suddenly.

Kumari Gurung, a resident of Sirdibas, said the flooding had not stopped and locals remained frightened.

The flood is believed to have occurred after Syarl Khola, a tributary of the Budhi Gandaki River, was temporarily blocked by a landslide and then suddenly burst open.

Chief District Officer Dharmendra Kumar Mishra said authorities were collecting details of the damage. No human casualties had been reported as of Sunday morning, he added.

Both aerial and ground teams have been mobilised in the affected areas.

Kathmandu, October 11

Former King Gyanendra Shah will observe this year’s Dashain in a simple manner. The Communication Secretariat at Nirmal Niwas said there will be no programme for him to put tika and jamara on the general public on Vijaya Dashami.

According to a notice issued by the secretariat, the former king decided to keep this year’s Dashain simple in view of the heavy loss of life and property, and the displacement of thousands of people, caused by August’s avalanche-triggered flood and the incessant rain in September.

The secretariat said there will be no programme to put tika and jamara to the general public on Vijaya Dashami this year.

title.rendered: Flood recalls Bhotekoshi disaster, says Chumnubri Deputy Chair Gurung

content.rendered:
Gorkha, October 11

A large flash flood carrying silt and gravel has hit the Budhigandaki River, which flows through Gorkha’s Chumnubri Rural Municipality.

Chumnubri Rural Municipality Deputy Chair Laxmi Gurung said the flood that hit the Budhigandaki this morning is reminiscent of the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa.

In a brief conversation with Onlinekhabar, she likened the Budhigandaki flood to the devastating flood that hit the Bhotekoshi in Rasuwa on August 26.

“The Budhigandaki flood is reminiscent of the Bhotekoshi flood,” she said. “It has washed away dozens of houses. It is not possible to say the exact extent of the damage right now.”

title.rendered: Nepal to take on Canada in League 2 cricket

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

Nepal are playing Canada today in the ODI series being held in Oman as part of the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2.

The match between Nepal and Canada will begin at 11:15 am at Oman Cricket Academy Turf 1.

This is the final series of League 2, and it matters for both teams. Oman beat Canada in the first match of the series.

Oman’s win over Canada ended Nepal’s chances of finishing in the top four. Nepal’s focus will now on retaining their ODI status.

In the League 2 standings, Nepal are seventh with 24 points from 32 matches, while Canada are sixth with 25 points from 33 matches.

Nepal squad: Sandeep Lamichhane (captain), Dipendra Singh Airee, Rohit Paudel, Aasif Sheikh, Arjun Kumal, Ishan Pandey, Dev Khanal, Sundeep Jora, Basir Ahamad, Gulsan Jha, Karan KC, Nandan Yadav, Lalit Rajbanshi, Shahab Alam, Sher Malla

title.rendered: Flash flood in Budhigandaki puts areas down to Arughat at risk

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

A flash flood carrying silt and gravel has hit the Budhigandaki River in Gorkha’s Chumnubri Rural Municipality.

The flood is feared to cause damage downstream as far as Arughat. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has urged people living along the riverbanks to stay alert.

According to the authority’s Chief Executive Officer, Dharmaraj Upreti, the flood could cause damage as far as Sirdibas, Jagat, Yari, Tatopani, Machhikhola, Soti, Aarukhet and Arughat. He said residents of these areas should be alert.

The Flood Forecasting Division of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has also sent SMS alerts to residents along the riverbanks. Flood expert Binod Parajuli of the division said the flood is expected to take about three hours to reach Arughat, and the SMS urges people to stay alert all the way to Arughat.

The flood joined the Budhigandaki through a local stream from the Chumchet area of Ward 6 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality in Gorkha. The Budhigandaki flows along the eastern face of Mount Manaslu.

The cause of the flood has not yet been established. There is no record of rainfall in the upper catchment. The disaster authority said the preliminary assessment is that a landslide may have blocked the flow and the dam later burst, triggering the flash flood.

title.rendered: Flood in Budhigandaki washes away 35 houses in Chumanubri

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

A flood in the Budhigandaki River, which flows through Gorkha’s Chumanubri Rural Municipality, has washed away 35 houses in Paiyu and Bagar villages.

According to Chumanubri Rural Municipality Deputy Chair Laxmi Gurung, there was extensive damage in Dobhan, Ghattekhola, Jagat and Sallery villages.

Locals fled to safety after floodwaters entered the villages at around 4 am on Sunday.

She said the bazaar in Chumanubri-3 suffered heavy damage from the flood.

Considering the flood risk, residents of Khorlabeshi, Machhakhola, Soti, Arkhet and Arughat in Sirdibas and Dharche rural municipalities have been asked to move to safer places, said Police Inspector Aakash Kandel of the District Police Office, Gorkha.

No details of human casualties have been received so far, and a detailed account of the damage is still awaited.

title.rendered: Flash flood in Gorkha’s Chumnubri, river suspected to be blocked

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 11

A flash flood has hit Chumnubri Rural Municipality-6 in Gorkha.

Gorkha Chief District Officer Dharendra Kumar Mishra said he received information of a major flood at 4:35 this morning. According to him, there is no information so far of any human casualties.

He said preparations are underway to deploy a Nepali Army helicopter to assess the situation.

Rural Municipality Chair Nima Lama said a landslide blocked the Chumke Khola in Chumanubri-6, and the flood came afterwards.

Locals said Sallery and Jagat Bazaar, in the lower riparian area, are at risk. Some people have been displaced because of the danger.

The Flood Forecasting Division has sent out an SMS alert urging caution because of the flash flood.

title.rendered: Blood donation should not depend on desperation

content.rendered:
An appeal for blood asks strangers to act quickly. A patient needs help, and the family has little time to consider why finding blood has become so difficult.

Such appeals deserve a generous response. They should also prompt a broader question: what would reduce the need to search in a panic in the first place?

For Nepal, part of the answer lies in building a more dependable relationship between voluntary donors and organised blood services. The Nepal Red Cross Society already plays a central role in providing blood services. Strengthening this work means looking beyond the visible success of individual donation campaigns to the less visible task of maintaining a safe and reliable blood supply.

In a June 2026 assessment, the World Health Organization reported persistent inequalities in access to safe blood and called for stronger financing, quality assurance and donor engagement. Although its findings reflect global trends rather than Nepal’s specific circumstances, the underlying principle is relevant: generosity needs a system that can turn it into reliable care.

A family with an extensive network of contacts can circulate an appeal widely. Another may have fewer people to call, limited internet access or relatives unable to travel. When finding blood depends heavily on the reach of personal networks, access to care can become unequal before treatment even begins.

The goal should be a system in which families receive clear, verified guidance from clinical teams and authorised blood services. Public appeals can support this process, but they cannot replace professional decisions about a patient’s requirements, the availability of suitable blood products or the arrangements needed to supply them safely.

Regular voluntary donors are central to achieving this goal. Yet encouraging people to donate is not enough if they do not know when a centre is open, whether appointments are available or what to expect when they arrive. Every invitation to donate should make the next step clear.

Blood centres and authorised donation organisers can help by publishing reliable schedules, explaining procedures in accessible language and providing straightforward ways to ask confidential questions about eligibility. Trained staff must determine whether someone can donate. No campaign should pressure people to withhold health information or make them feel that medical deferral reflects a personal failing.

Someone who cannot donate on a particular day should be treated with the same respect as someone who can. Where appropriate, staff can explain whether and when they may return. A respectful first experience can encourage long-term participation; an embarrassing one can discourage it.

Schools, colleges, workplaces and community organisations can also help people connect with authorised donation services at convenient times. The aim should be sustained participation, supported by consent-based reminders, rather than collecting phone numbers to circulate an endless stream of urgent appeals.

What happens after collection matters just as much. Testing, storage, transport and coordination require trained personnel, reliable infrastructure and adequate resources. Counting how many people attend a donation camp measures participation, but it does not establish whether patients ultimately receive the blood products they need.

Planning must also extend beyond major urban centres. Hospitals and blood services serving smaller towns and remote communities need arrangements that account for travel times, local capacity and the practical challenges of maintaining supplies. Nepal needs a clearer understanding of where shortages and service gaps occur and how blood services can coordinate to address them. Technology may help with communication and coordination, but no single application can resolve the underlying logistical and clinical challenges.

Information must be handled responsibly, too. Publishing a donor’s phone number or a patient’s personal details should not become an automatic condition of seeking help. Contact information should be shared only with permission and for a clearly defined purpose. The urgency of a request does not remove the need to protect privacy.

Families also deserve clear explanations of the process and any applicable service charges. Uncertainty about what they are paying for can undermine trust, even when testing, storage and handling involve legitimate costs. The responsible service should explain these requirements transparently.

None of this diminishes the importance of individual appeals. Those who respond to them can make an extraordinary difference. But a dependable blood service should reduce the burden on families to organise that response while frightened, exhausted and worried about a loved one.

The strongest tribute to a generous donor is a system that uses that generosity safely, efficiently and fairly. Nepal must prepare for the next patient while the phone is still quiet.

title.rendered: How many floods will it take for Nepal to act?

content.rendered:
Disaster risk reduction is rarely a priority until a disaster strikes close to home. Yet even the destruction caused by the Bhote Koshi flood on July 8, 2025, was not enough to spur the state into taking meaningful action to reduce future risks. Thirteen months later, disaster struck the same corridor on a much larger scale.

On August 26, 2026, an ice avalanche triggered a massive flood that swept through the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor. More than 1,400 people were killed, more than 5,000 were reported missing, and approximately 7,570 homes were damaged or destroyed. Roads and hydropower projects also suffered severe damage.

This was not the first time Nepal had experienced such a disaster. In 1985, an ice-related event in the Khumbu region caused major flooding along the Dudh Koshi River. In 2012, an ice avalanche in the Annapurna region contributed to a devastating flood along the Seti River, killing people and damaging settlements and infrastructure. Nepal has also experienced at least 24 glacial lake outburst flood events.

How many disasters will it take before we learn to reduce their consequences? What assurances can we offer people who continue to live along Nepal’s high-risk, snow-fed rivers? And what answers can we give those who will never see their loved ones again, including the grandmother recovered from a flooded house in Betrawati after 11 days and the baby pulled alive from a mud-filled house in Timure three days after the disaster?

We cannot prevent an ice avalanche by producing a flood of articles and expert commentary on glacial disasters. Such an event could happen today, tomorrow or the day after. What we can control is how effectively we protect lives, settlements and development projects along Nepal’s snow-fed rivers.

This article draws lessons from the experiences of Bhote Koshi flood survivors and the destruction of settlements, roads and hydropower infrastructure. These lessons fall into three broad areas: human resilience, development resilience and institutional resilience.

Human resilience

Six-year-old Zoyal Tamang from Timure ran uphill from his school, climbed a tree and survived the flood. Sushant Lamichhane from Rasuwagadhi escaped from his room as the flood approached. His laptop and phone fell to the ground, but he did not stop to retrieve them. He ran uphill and survived.

Kishor Gauli, an employee of Prabhu Bank in Timure, was not as fortunate. Instead of immediately seeking safety, he spent valuable time closing the bank’s cash vaults. Similarly, Suroj Dangol, the principal of a school in Betrawati, was swept away after staying behind too long to instruct school staff to evacuate.

Ramesh Thapa, a security guard at the Upper Trishuli Hydropower Project, was swept away while trying to rescue others. He survived by drawing on diving skills acquired through training. Suman Lama from Betrawati said his previous experience swimming in rivers helped him save himself and his wife. As the flood reached them, he managed to hold on to a tree and survive.

These experiences reveal both the importance and the limits of individual preparedness.

Lessons: In an emergency, escape first and retrieve belongings later. Prioritise life over property. Help others when it is safe to do so, but do not put yourself at unnecessary risk.

Where appropriate, vegetation and trees can provide footholds or places to hold on to during an escape. Swimming and water-safety education should be expanded, including for schoolchildren, alongside practical guidance on escaping flash floods. Buildings, fences and other structures should not obstruct evacuation routes. Communities need clearly marked escape paths leading to higher ground.

Development resilience

Development resilience in the affected corridor was extremely weak because settlements, roads and hydropower projects were highly exposed to flood hazards.

Timure, the nearest settlement to the China customs office, occupies a narrow strip of land between the Bhote Koshi riverbank and a steep hillside. This geography leaves residents with few escape options during a major flood. The settlement was reportedly only about eight metres above the riverbed, while floodwaters rose more than 20 metres.

In Betrawati, buildings are situated along a bend in the Bhote Koshi River. The force and momentum of the fast-moving flood drove water into the settlement, causing extensive damage. Other severely affected areas, including Trishuli Bazar, Devighat and Dhunge Bazar, are located on low-lying land shaped by previous major floods.

The Bhote Koshi road corridor is squeezed between the river and steep hillsides. During a flood of this magnitude, sections of the road are highly vulnerable to damage and collapse. At several hydropower projects, tunnel entrances face directly towards the river, exposing them to boulders and debris that can block access and trap workers inside.

Lessons: Settlement planning must account for extreme flood levels, not just the river’s normal flow. Where feasible and supported by detailed hazard assessments, settlements such as Timure and Syabrubesi should be considered for relocation to safer, higher ground. An increase in elevation of around 40 metres could be explored as a preliminary option, but the appropriate height and location must be established through technical assessments.

The fact that some settlements at higher elevations in Syabrubesi reportedly escaped damage offers an important lesson. The flood’s high-water marks should be documented and used alongside historical records and hazard modelling to guide future land-use decisions.

In Betrawati, relocation away from the exposed river bend should be considered. A distance of at least 300 metres could be assessed as a starting point, subject to detailed flood modelling and local topography. Development on high-risk floodplains, including areas around Trishuli Bazar, Dhunge Bazar and Devighat, should be strictly controlled. Where risks cannot be reduced to an acceptable level, planned relocation to safer land must be considered, with adequate support for affected households and businesses.

The entire Bhote Koshi corridor needs a risk-sensitive land-use plan that clearly identifies areas where development should be prohibited, where it can be encouraged under appropriate safeguards, and where existing settlements and infrastructure may need to be relocated.

Road investments should also be guided by long-term risk assessments rather than a commitment to existing alignments. Where necessary, safer alternatives should be explored instead of repeatedly rebuilding vulnerable road sections. Hydropower projects must be designed and retrofitted to reduce the risk of tunnel blockages, worker entrapment and structural damage during extreme floods.

Institutional resilience

Institutional resilience is the final line of defence for communities and infrastructure in highly exposed locations. Effective early-warning systems may not prevent property damage, but they can save lives by giving people time to reach safety.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) was active during the Bhote Koshi disaster, issuing alerts and coordinating with disaster risk reduction agencies. However, the event exposed serious weaknesses in the ability to detect the hazard, communicate warnings and reach people in time.

According to the reported timeline, the ice avalanche began at its source at 8:37 a.m., while the Flood Forecasting Division became aware of the event at 9:00 a.m. Nepal Telecom and Ncell sent 679,295 warning text messages at 9:15 a.m. By then, the flood had reportedly reached Betrawati after devastating Timure and Syabrubesi. When NDRRMA issued its warning at 9:28 a.m., the flood had already damaged Trishuli Bazar and was moving towards Devighat.

Around noon, NDRRMA was reportedly sending letters to various agencies, including the Army, requesting helicopter support. In an emergency where every second matters, relying on formal written requests and waiting for responses can cost valuable time.

Lessons: Establish a system of continuous river monitoring near Rasuwagadhi and other strategic locations. Trained observers could monitor river conditions in shifts from safe vantage points, supported by automated sensors and remote monitoring wherever possible.

A network of sirens connected through strategically placed towers could provide rapid alerts from Timure to Devighat. Unusual changes in water levels or flow should trigger warnings through established protocols. Sudden drops in river levels may also indicate upstream blockages or other hazards and should prompt immediate investigation. Sirens should be backed by mobile alerts, local communication networks and clearly understood evacuation procedures so that warnings reach people even when one communication channel fails.

NDRRMA and other responsible agencies should establish emergency response protocols that do not depend on lengthy written correspondence. Dedicated response teams, with access to helicopters and other appropriate equipment, should be positioned or mobilised rapidly for major snow-fed river corridors. They should have clearly defined authority to act immediately within established emergency procedures, rather than waiting for multiple layers of approval.

Early-warning systems must be integrated with evacuation planning, regular drills, clear lines of responsibility and reliable communication between agencies. A warning is useful only if it reaches people in time and they know what to do.

There is nothing wrong with studying ice avalanches, debating the science of glacial hazards or arguing that Nepal, despite contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions, deserves international support and compensation for climate-related losses. But these discussions must not distract us from the measures we can take ourselves. Installing and maintaining effective early-warning systems, for example, is a practical step that Nepal can pursue while continuing to seek international assistance.

The United Nations Green Climate Fund (GCF) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) have reportedly committed US$35.5 million to reducing glacial disaster risks, including plans to install early-warning systems. This raises an important question: why did the government fail to make sufficient progress in putting these resources to work after the 2025 Bhote Koshi disaster?

The lessons of this disaster must not fade once the immediate public attention subsides and the festival season passes. Authorities must be willing to enforce risk-sensitive land-use policies, even when doing so is politically difficult or faces resistance from communities and businesses.

Reconstruction must not mean rebuilding the same vulnerabilities in the same places simply because there is public pressure to restore what was lost. It must mean creating safer settlements, more resilient infrastructure and a stronger economy.

Ultimately, disaster risk reduction is not just about responding to the next catastrophe. It is about making the decisions today that will prevent tomorrow’s disaster from becoming another tragedy of avoidable loss.

title.rendered: The case for rumble strips on Nepal’s highways

content.rendered:
A road crash can happen in seconds. A momentary lapse in attention, excessive speed, poor visibility, a sudden change in road alignment or an unsafe overtaking manoeuvre can turn an ordinary journey into a dangerous situation.

On the Mugling–Pokhara Highway, drivers encounter sharp curves, bridges, intersections, settlements and mixed traffic amid changing terrain and visibility. Recognising hazards early and adjusting speed accordingly are therefore essential to safe travel.

Rumble strips installed at selected locations provide an additional warning. As vehicles pass over them, the resulting sound and vibration can alert drivers, draw their attention back to the road and prompt them to adjust their speed or driving behaviour before reaching a potential hazard.

Although simple in design, rumble strips can serve as an important layer of protection alongside speed management, road signs, markings, barriers and other safety measures. They cannot prevent every crash, but they can provide drivers with an additional opportunity to respond to danger.

A warning built into the road

Rumble strips are textured or raised road-surface treatments designed to produce audible and tactile feedback when vehicles pass over them. The resulting sound and vibration signal that drivers may need to pay closer attention, reduce speed or adjust their driving.

They do not replace sound road design, clear signage, traffic enforcement or responsible driving. Instead, they provide an additional warning that may interrupt the sequence of events leading from driver inattention to a crash.

This is particularly relevant on the Mugling–Pokhara corridor, where mountainous terrain, curves, intersections, settlements and variable visibility create different driving risks. Department of Roads design documentation for the highway improvement works identifies hazards including run-off-road, head-on and side-swipe crashes, as well as unsafe overtaking where visibility is restricted. Rumble strips and other audio-tactile treatments form part of the wider range of safety measures intended to address such risks.

The principle is straightforward: a road should not merely carry traffic; it should also communicate potential hazards to those using it.

Why a few seconds matter

When a vehicle approaches a hazardous location at an inappropriate speed, the time and distance available to respond safely may be limited. A rumble strip can provide an additional sensory warning before the vehicle reaches the hazard, prompting the driver to slow down, maintain lane position or make another appropriate adjustment.

The effectiveness of this warning depends on several factors, including the strip’s location and design, the vehicle’s speed, road conditions and the driver’s response. Rumble strips should therefore be understood as a supporting safety measure, not a guarantee against crashes.

Assessing their effectiveness also requires more than counting accidents. A reduction in crashes may indicate improved safety, but establishing whether rumble strips contributed to that improvement requires systematic monitoring. Useful evidence includes vehicle-speed measurements, crash and near-miss records, field observations, road-safety audits and before-and-after assessments.

This is an important distinction in preventive road safety. When a driver notices a warning, slows down and negotiates a curve safely, the intervention may leave no visible trace. However, the absence of a crash alone does not prove that a rumble strip prevented one. Its contribution must be evaluated alongside other safety indicators and changes in road conditions.

Better roads require better safety management

The Mugling–Pokhara Highway improvement project involves upgrades to pavement, drainage, structures, alignment and roadside safety. As a strategically important corridor connecting Kathmandu and Pokhara and serving communities, businesses and travellers along the route, the highway’s safety depends on both infrastructure quality and road-user behaviour.

Improved road surfaces and geometry can make journeys smoother and more comfortable. However, they may also encourage drivers to travel faster. Without appropriate speed management and clear warnings, better infrastructure does not automatically translate into safer journeys.

This is especially important at curves, junctions, settlements and other locations where terrain, visibility and roadside activity demand greater caution. Road design must work alongside measures that encourage drivers to recognise changing conditions and respond appropriately.

A safe highway should help drivers understand where they can travel efficiently and where they need to slow down, pay closer attention or change their driving behaviour. Rumble strips are one way to reinforce that message.

One treatment, multiple layers of protection

Rumble strips are most useful as part of an integrated road-safety strategy. Their effectiveness depends on appropriate placement, design, spacing and maintenance, as well as coordination with other interventions.

Depending on local conditions, these may include speed-limit and warning signs, road markings, delineators, protective barriers, lighting, safer intersections, pedestrian facilities, traffic enforcement and public-awareness campaigns.

This layered approach recognises that crashes rarely have a single cause. Speed, road geometry, visibility, weather, vehicle condition, driver behaviour and roadside activity can combine to create dangerous situations. A resilient road-safety system seeks to prevent one mistake or unsafe condition from resulting in a serious crash.

Rumble strips can contribute to that system, but they cannot compensate for inadequate road design, missing safety infrastructure or unsafe driving.

Measuring what does not happen

Evaluating preventive road-safety measures presents a particular challenge. Crashes leave visible evidence, including damaged vehicles, injuries, fatalities and police records. Successful prevention, by contrast, may amount to little more than a driver slowing down and continuing safely.

Nevertheless, the contribution of rumble strips can be assessed through changes in vehicle speeds, crash frequency and severity, near-miss reports, observed driving behaviour and road-safety assessments. Comparing conditions before and after installation, while accounting for changes in traffic volume, road geometry and other safety interventions, can help establish whether the measures are working as intended.

Monitoring can also identify locations where rumble strips need maintenance or where additional interventions are necessary. On the Mugling–Pokhara corridor, such assessments will become increasingly important as traffic volumes, vehicle types, roadside development and travel patterns evolve.

The objective should not simply be to install safety features, but to determine whether they are delivering measurable benefits and to improve them where necessary.

A small intervention with a larger purpose

Compared with bridges, tunnels, retaining walls and widened road sections, rumble strips may seem like a minor addition to a highway. Their purpose, however, is significant: to give drivers an additional warning at moments when a timely response can make a difference.

Highway safety depends on sound engineering, appropriate speed management, clear signs and markings, roadside protection, responsible driving, enforcement and continuous monitoring. No single intervention can eliminate crashes, but well-designed measures working together can reduce risks and provide multiple opportunities to prevent serious incidents.

A driver may encounter a rumble strip, slow down and safely negotiate a hazardous section without giving the warning a second thought. Passengers may notice only that the vehicle has reduced speed. No crash occurs, no emergency response is needed, and nothing appears in official records.

That is the purpose of preventive road safety: not merely to respond when crashes happen, but to create road conditions in which they are less likely to occur.

title.rendered: Nepal wants more babies. Will longer maternity leave help?

content.rendered:
The government is preparing to extend paid maternity leave to six months, and paternity leave to 42 days, presenting the move partly as a response to Nepal’s declining population growth rate.

A bill registered in the House of Representatives proposes amending the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2018, which currently provides 98 days of maternity leave and 15 days of paternity leave.

Under the proposed amendment, women working in government, non-governmental and private organisations would be entitled to six months of paid leave before or after childbirth. Male employees in these sectors would receive 42 days of paid leave before or after their wives give birth if the bill is passed without changes.

The government says the proposed extension is intended to encourage population growth.

“According to Nepal’s latest national census, the country’s population growth rate has been on a continuous downward trend. It is therefore necessary to amend the law to introduce measures, including incentives through leave provisions, to encourage population growth,” Health and Food Hygiene Minister Nisha Mehta wrote, explaining the rationale behind the bill.

Defending the proposal in the House of Representatives, Mehta argued that maternity leave should be understood as more than an employment benefit.

“We should not understand six months of maternity leave merely as a benefit or a period of leave granted to employees. It is an important issue connected to respect for motherhood, the health and nutrition of mothers and newborns, and the state’s long-term investment in human capital,” she said.

Extending leave, she added, should be viewed as an investment in the country’s future.

“When making laws, we should not look only at today’s needs. We must also consider what kind of society we want to build for tomorrow,” Mehta said. “We want to build a healthy, capable and productive workforce. Investing in the health of mothers and children is an investment in the human capital of tomorrow.”

But can longer maternity and paternity leave reverse a demographic trend that has been decades in the making? Nepal’s experience with population control, together with the difficulties other countries have faced in encouraging people to have more children, suggests there are no easy answers.

A population growth rate in decline

Nepal began conducting national censuses in 1911. More than a century later, its population growth rate has fallen below one per cent for the first time in eight decades.

The rate was negative in the country’s earliest censuses, standing at minus 0.13 per cent in 1921 and minus 0.07 per cent in 1931. It subsequently remained positive for decades, reaching 1.16 per cent in 1941, 2.27 per cent in 1951, 1.64 per cent in 1961, 2.05 per cent in 1971 and 2.62 per cent in 1981.

The rate then fell to 2.08 per cent in 1991 and 2.25 per cent in 2001, before dropping to 1.35 per cent in 2011 and 0.92 per cent in 2021.

The 2.62 per cent growth rate recorded in 1981 remains the highest in Nepal’s census history, according to records maintained by the National Statistics Office.

The decline is not confined to the national level. Thirty-four districts and 319 local governments have recorded negative population growth.

Concerned about the trend, some local governments have introduced incentive payments and other programmes to encourage people to have children.

The national government is now considering longer maternity and paternity leave as part of its response. Yet the declining growth rate is not simply the result of recent social changes. It also reflects decades of policies that encouraged smaller families, as well as broader transformations in society.

Understanding whether the trend can be reversed requires looking back at how population growth came to be treated as a problem in the first place.

How population control became a policy priority

Long before Nepal conducted its first national census, British economist Thomas Robert Malthus had published An Essay on the Principle of Population, outlining a theory that would influence population debates for generations.

Malthus argued that population grows geometrically while food production increases only arithmetically. In his formulation, population grows from 1 to 2, 4, 8 and 16, while food production rises from 1 to 2, 3, 4 and 5. Over time, he concluded, the imbalance would lead to crises such as famine.

He identified two ways of checking population growth: natural and artificial. Floods, landslides, earthquakes, epidemics and diseases were examples of natural checks. The artificial alternative was to limit reproduction by marrying late, remaining unmarried, choosing not to have children after marriage, or having fewer children.

In 1968, seven decades after the turn of the century and long after Malthus’s death, American biologist Paul Ehrlich published The Population Bomb. He warned that rapid population growth would trigger famine, food shortages and a crisis of natural resources, arguing that the Earth might struggle to sustain everyone if its population continued to expand too quickly.

Ehrlich’s ideas gave further impetus to debates about contraception, family planning and population control.

The influence of Malthus and Ehrlich soon spread across Asia, where governments adopted increasingly aggressive measures to curb population growth.

In India, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi’s government introduced an aggressive sterilisation programme. Experts say the state of emergency declared in 1975 was used to carry out the programme, with millions of people forcibly sterilised.

A few years later, China introduced its one-child policy in 1979. Demographers say families who had more than one child faced fines and, in some cases, forced abortions.

Yet population control was never solely about balancing numbers against food supplies or natural resources. It was also shaped by ideas about which populations should grow and which should not.

One of the starkest examples was the eugenics movement in Europe and the United States. Eugenics promoted discouraging reproduction among marginalised or targeted communities while encouraging it among groups considered to be of supposedly superior ancestry.

The ideology reached its most extreme expression in Nazi Germany’s population policies. Eugenics was subsequently criticised for seeking to improve what its proponents called genetic quality while effectively eliminating the populations of other groups.

After the Second World War, population politics became increasingly consequential for countries in the Global South, including Nepal. Their populations were often portrayed as causes of poverty, political instability and other social problems. These countries were frequently labelled the “Third World” by those who considered themselves part of the First World.

Nepal, too, came under the influence of international non-governmental organisations promoting population control.

Nepal’s long campaign for smaller families

When Nepal launched its first five-year plan in 1956, a decade had passed since the end of the Second World War. From the outset, the country took a position against rapid population growth.

In 1959, before the first five-year plan had even ended, the Family Planning Association of Nepal was established. The Nepali term niyojan, used in the association’s name, means planning or control and can refer to measures taken to prevent conception.

The name itself reflects the emphasis placed on controlling reproduction at the time. For at least three decades, Nepal appears to have pursued a population control policy.

“The first through the fifth five-year plans emphasised migration, family planning, and maternal and child health programmes,” states the National Population Policy, 2014.

From the 1960s onwards, the government pursued aggressive policies to reduce birth rates for three consecutive decades. Public messaging repeatedly associated having many children with being uncivilised, uneducated, poor and backward. Smaller families, by contrast, were presented as a sign of development and prosperity.

The effects began to emerge after three or four censuses. Nepal’s population growth rate peaked at 2.62 per cent in 1981 before falling to 2.25 per cent in 2001, 1.35 per cent in 2011 and 0.92 per cent in 2021.

Following Nepal’s political transformation in 1990, the Family Planning Association of Nepal began to describe its purpose in terms of reproductive health rather than population control.

The shift reflected a broader change in international thinking. In particular, following the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development in Cairo, greater attention was paid to individual reproductive rights, women’s empowerment, healthcare and voluntary family planning.

Dr Bal Krishna Mabuhang, a retired population expert from Tribhuvan University, argues that Nepal had also absorbed the influence of eugenics, including the idea that people from wealthy backgrounds and certain geographical regions were more civilised than others.

“Caught in the trap of eugenics, we too adopted a policy that essentially said having too many children was a problem, while having few was just right,” Mabuhang says. “The eugenicist argument that European and American ancestry was superior while Asian and African ancestry was inferior has already been discredited.”

Mabuhang believes Nepal followed prevailing international thinking without sufficiently examining whether the traditional aspiration for children to populate the country’s hills and mountains was appropriate.

His criticism raises a broader question: did Nepal’s population policies adequately consider the long-term consequences of encouraging smaller families, or did the country simply follow the prevailing international consensus?

Can governments persuade people to have more children?

Nepal is not alone in confronting declining population growth. Governments around the world have introduced measures to encourage people to have children, including maternity and paternity leave, financial incentives, tax breaks, fertility treatment subsidies and guarantees relating to children’s education, healthcare and employment.

Some have also offered employment support to parents.

But reversing a decline that has developed over decades is considerably more difficult than introducing incentives.

Various studies and population experts generally conclude that policies intended to increase population growth have had limited success. Incentives may influence family decisions, but they do not necessarily reverse the long-term decline in fertility associated with social, economic and cultural change.

The United Nations has also acknowledged the difficulty.

Its report World Population Policies 2021: Policies Related to Fertility states: “Although various approaches and initiatives to reduce fertility rates have produced results globally, reversing the long-term downward trend in total fertility rates driven by social, economic and cultural transformations has proved extremely difficult.”

The experience of countries that have tried to encourage larger families illustrates the challenge.

Dr Yogendra Bahadur Gurung, a professor of population studies, says increasing a population growth rate that has already declined is an extremely difficult task.

“Nevertheless, incentive programmes introduced to increase fertility rates may help stabilise the population growth rate,” Gurung says.

Countries such as France, Germany and Hungary appear to have had some success in preventing further declines in their population growth rates. However, experts caution that maintaining those rates over the long term remains difficult.

Gurung believes improved employee benefits are worthwhile, but should not be treated as a comprehensive solution to declining population growth.

“In an open and free society like ours today, it is not good to formulate manipulative policies dictating whether the population should increase or decrease,” he says.

The challenge is that decisions about having children are shaped by much more than government incentives. Sociologists say more people are choosing to marry later, remain unmarried, or have no children or fewer children after marriage.

These are broader social changes that cannot necessarily be reversed by extending leave entitlements alone.

From population control to population growth

Nepal’s policy thinking has gradually shifted alongside these changes.

In 1992, the country’s eighth five-year plan began explicitly recognising the importance of population in national policy. Following the 1994 Cairo conference, Nepal introduced a 20-year long-term plan covering 2067–2087 in the Nepali calendar.

More recent population policies, as well as the maternal protection bill now registered in Parliament, suggest that the government is increasingly interested in encouraging population growth rather than merely controlling it.

The question is whether this shift in policy can produce the intended results.

The National Statistics Office projects that Nepal’s fertility rate will range between 1.13 and 2.1 over the next 15 years. According to its Population Projections for 2021–2051, the country’s total population could reach 33.5 million within the next 25 years.

These projections offer a picture of the country’s possible demographic future, but they do not settle the question of what population Nepal should aim for.

Mabuhang argues that the issue cannot be reduced to a single ideal number.

“There is no such thing as a country having too many people, too few people or just the right number of people in absolute terms,” he says. “The population a country needs depends on the resources, opportunities and other conditions available within that country.”

That distinction matters as Nepal considers extending maternity and paternity leave. Paid leave can be defended on its own merits, particularly in relation to maternal health, newborn care, nutrition and the well-being of families. Whether it can also reverse the country’s declining population growth rate is a separate question.

The government may hope that better support for parents will encourage people to have more children. But Nepal’s own history shows how deeply population trends can be shaped by public policy, while international experience suggests that changing those trends is rarely straightforward.

Population policy affects far more than the number of people in a country. It intersects with reproductive rights, gender equality, public health, economic opportunity and access to resources.

For that reason, experts argue, decisions about population growth require sustained public debate and careful consideration of the country’s circumstances, rather than an assumption that either a larger or a smaller population is inherently better.
