title.rendered: With his rivals gone, Gagan Thapa faces his biggest test yet

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Gagan Thapa has spent much of his political career challenging the power structures of the Nepali Congress. At the party’s 13th General Convention, he entered the leadership race through Krishna Prasad Sitaula’s third faction. At the 14th convention, he joined Shekhar Koirala’s panel to challenge the established Deuba camp.

Now, as the Nepali Congress concludes its 15th General Convention, Thapa is on the verge of becoming the party president with virtually no organised rival left standing. The irony is difficult to miss.

The politician who once had to find space between the Nepali Congress’s established factions has now become the centre of a new establishment. On Wednesday evening, as he closed the convention’s closed session, Thapa declared that the party’s old factional divisions were over.

“From today, all the formal factions that existed for a long time—the 74, 36, Deuba group, Koirala group, Poudel group, special and non-special groups—are finished,” Thapa said. “This is the biggest achievement of this General Convention.”

His declaration came just after former joint general secretary Kishor Singh Rathore withdrew his candidacy for party president. Shyam Krishna Khadgi is now the only remaining candidate challenging Thapa.

That means Thapa is effectively assured of the presidency even before the vote. But removing rivals may prove easier than managing the party once there are no factions left to absorb political tensions. That is the challenge now confronting Thapa.

The end of the old Nepali Congress order

For decades, leadership contests in the Nepali Congress were structured around competing camps.

Deuba had his organisation. Koirala had his. Poudel and other senior leaders had their own networks. Candidates for party positions generally emerged through these groups, and a leader who failed to secure the backing of a faction often had little incentive to contest independently. Thapa himself has argued that this was one reason earlier conventions produced fewer candidates.

That system has now been disrupted.

At the 15th convention, even though the party has increased the number of office-bearer positions to 24, there is no major faction organised against Thapa.

Rathore’s withdrawal was particularly significant. He was among the senior leaders who had left Deuba and was expected to provide an alternative platform for that section of the party. But that effort did not materialise.

Thapa also called on other aspirants, including Dr Minendra Rijal, Min Bishwakarma, Dev Raj Chalise, Yogesh Gauchan and Min Bham, to withdraw their candidacies.

He asked parliamentary party leader Bhishma Raj Angdembe not to contest for an office-bearer position, saying Angdembe was leading a separate political front.

The response to those appeals tells the story of how much the balance of power inside the Nepali Congress has changed. General Secretary Gururaj Ghimire had already referred to Thapa as the party president while addressing the closed session.

The 15th convention is therefore ending very differently from previous conventions. There is no comparable contest between rival power centres.

Thapa has become the centre of the party. And that makes his next challenge fundamentally different.

He has already dismantled the old factions

Thapa’s rise to this position did not happen overnight. After emerging as a prominent youth leader during the anti-monarchy movement, he entered the Central Working Committee at the age of 34 at the 12th General Convention.

His popularity allowed him to win without depending heavily on an established faction. But moving from the central committee to the party’s executive leadership was more difficult.

The traditional factions were controlled by senior leaders, and none was initially prepared to make Thapa its principal candidate for an office-bearer position.

At the 13th convention, Thapa therefore aligned himself with Sitaula and contested for general secretary from his panel. Sitaula and Thapa emerged as the third force behind the main Deuba and Ram Chandra Paudel camps.

At the 14th convention, Thapa changed his alignment again. He joined Shekhar Koirala’s panel and contested for general secretary. Koirala lost the presidential race, but Thapa won the general secretary election.

Bishwa Prakash Sharma emerged as another young leader through a similar route. He contested as part of Prakash Man Singh’s panel but won the general secretary election despite Singh’s poor showing in the presidential contest.

The result was the emergence of the Gagan-Bishwa partnership.

From there, the two leaders began challenging the existing balance of power inside the party. The culmination came with the special convention.

The Gen Z uprising changed the balance

The political upheaval following the Gen Z movement created the circumstances in which Thapa and Sharma were able to challenge the established Congress leadership.

As the Deuba-led leadership faced mounting pressure, the demand for a special convention gained momentum within the party.

The Thapa-Sharma camp claimed that more than 56 percent of convention representatives had supported the demand, well above the 40 percent threshold required under the party statute.

The special convention ultimately produced a new leadership team headed by Thapa.

Bishwa Prakash Sharma and Pushpa Bhusal became vice presidents, while Pradeep Paudel and Gururaj Ghimire became general secretaries.

Farmullah Mansoor, Dila Sangraula, Bahadur Singh Lama, Karna Bahadur Budha, Yogendra Chaudhary, Uday Shumsher Rana, Prakash Rasaily and Mukta Kumari Yadav became joint general secretaries.

The significance of the new team was that many of these leaders had previously been associated with the old establishment.

Mansur and Sangraula had won their positions from Deuba’s panel at the 14th convention. Paudel had contested for general secretary from the Deuba camp. Deuba himself had appointed Bishwa Prakash Sharma as party spokesperson.

Others had been closer to the Koirala camp.

Thapa and Sharma had therefore done something more consequential than simply defeating Deuba.

They had begun bringing leaders from different factions into a new political arrangement.

When the Election Commission recognised the special convention and the Supreme Court later upheld Thapa’s legitimacy, the old power structure weakened further.

The old rivals were brought inside

Thapa then moved to bring former rivals into the new establishment. On May 10, he nominated 19 leaders associated with Deuba and Koirala to the Central Working Committee.

Among those associated with Deuba were Mahendra Yadav, Umesh Shrestha, Ramesh Rijal, Ajay Kumar Chaurasia, Laxmi Pariyar, Angelu Sherpa, Dinesh Kumar Yadav, Rajib Dhungana, Nagina Yadav, Jeevan Rana and Sita Thapaliya.

Leaders associated with Koirala, including Jeevan Pariyar, Sujata Koirala, Dilendra Prasad Badu, Chandra Bhandari, Rajiv Koirala, Govinda Pokharel and Dinesh Koirala, were also brought into the Central Working Committee.

Thapa even appointed Umesh Shrestha as treasurer, the same position he had held under Deuba.

But the process did not end there. As the 15th convention approached, leaders who had continued to operate separately from Thapa increasingly began joining the new establishment.

A group led by Purna Bahadur Khadka initially maintained its own position. Later, Shashank Koirala emerged as another reference point for leaders outside Thapa’s immediate camp.

But on September 12, 31 Central Working Committee members led by Khadka announced that they would participate in the convention.

They said Thapa had agreed to address their eight demands, including bringing 111 former Central Working Committee members into the party structure.

By the time the convention arrived, only four of the 13 office-bearers elected at the 14th convention—Deuba, Khadka, Badri Prasad Pandey and Umakanta Chaudhary—had stayed out.

The old factions had not simply lost an election. They had largely lost their organisational identity.

From fighting factions to becoming the establishment

This is where Thapa’s current position differs from the one he occupied only a few years ago.

He once needed a faction to reach the party’s executive leadership.

Now other leaders need to decide whether to align themselves with him.

A senior Nepali Congress leader who left Deuba’s camp and joined the current convention says many leaders eventually had little choice.

“Many leaders understood that it is impossible to do Congress politics by abandoning the tree symbol and the party’s four-star flag,” the leader said. “But once Gagan prevented us from maintaining group-level unity, we had no option left.”

According to the leader, Thapa ensured that the old groups could not retain a separate organisational identity by bringing their leaders into his camp individually.

Rathore’s withdrawal was the clearest demonstration of that process.

“Those of us who left Deuba could not even build a separate group and participate in the convention. We kept hoping until the end that the court would intervene, but that did not happen,” the leader said.

The former rebel has therefore achieved something unusual in Congress politics. He has not merely defeated the factions that once kept him outside the centre of power. He has absorbed much of them.

But can he keep the Nepali Congress together?

This is where Thapa’s declaration that factionalism has ended becomes a test rather than simply an achievement.

The Nepali Congress has historically been a party of powerful individuals, competing networks and senior leaders with independent political bases.

Thapa now has to manage many of those same leaders without allowing new factions to form around them.

Political analyst Jainendra Jeevan says Thapa’s own declaration will ultimately have to be tested by his ability to manage the people around him.

“Congress has suffered from the disease of factionalism for a long time. Gagan Thapa has recognised that and that is why he has said this,” Jeevan said. “If the central leadership can accommodate everyone, and if he can manage leaders who have the capacity and qualifications to form factions of their own, Gagan Thapa has an opportunity to create a record.”

Jeevan points to BP Koirala’s leadership as an example.

BP led a party containing powerful figures such as Subarna Shumsher, Surya Prasad Upadhyaya and Ganesh Man Singh, as well as leaders from the Madhes including Ram Narayan Mishra and Mahendra Narayan Nidhi.

“There were so many people capable of forming factions, but BP kept everyone together,” Jeevan said.

Thapa has also acknowledged that managing the senior leaders around him will be a major responsibility.

At the convention, he noted that many of the leaders on the stage were senior to him and that the Congress now includes politicians from as many as five generations.

“As president, it will be my responsibility to do whatever is necessary to bring everyone together,” Thapa said.

For Jeevan, the key will be how decisions are made.

“He has to listen to everyone, move forward by taking everyone along, make the right decision at the right time and avoid favouritism,” he said. “Even those who do not get an opportunity should feel that the person who got it was more deserving than them.”

Whether Thapa can create that kind of political balance remains to be seen.

For now, however, the transformation is clear.

The young leader who once challenged the Congress establishment from within has become the establishment himself. His old rivals have either withdrawn, joined his camp or lost the organisational strength to mount a separate challenge.

Thapa may therefore enter the presidency without a meaningful rival. But with the old factions gone, he can no longer blame them for the divisions inside the party. That may be the biggest test of his leadership yet.

title.rendered: Yeti Air suspends upper-class fares on outbound Dashain flights

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Yeti Airlines has suspended its upper-class fares on flights departing Kathmandu during the Dashain festival, citing high passenger demand for outbound flights.

The airline said the decision was taken despite the likelihood of empty return flights and higher fuel costs during the festive period.

Yeti said it is offering fares at the lowest available rates on flights returning to Kathmandu.

The airline said aviation fuel prices have surged from Rs 127 to Rs 249 per litre this year due to wars in different parts of the world, making fuel the most expensive it has been so far.

Yeti said the sharp rise in fuel prices has made it difficult to offer fares at the affordable rates it provided last year and expressed regret over the situation.

The airline also extended Dashain greetings to its passengers and well-wishers, wishing them happiness, peace, prosperity and good health.

title.rendered: Where Nepal’s deities live: A journey through lore, legend and living faith

content.rendered:
Step into the Nepal Art Council in Babar Mahal and the familiar rhythm of Kathmandu begins to recede. The traffic and noise of the city remain outside, while inside, another kind of landscape unfolds—one populated by gods, goddesses, myths, rituals, legends and the spiritual imagination that has shaped Nepal for centuries.

This is the world of Deities of Nepal III: Lore and Legends, the third edition of the deity-themed exhibition organised by the Nepal Art Council, which began on September 17. Curated by Swasti Rajbhandari Kayastha (Lead Curator) and Pranab Man Singh (Co-Curator), assisted by Rajani Sinkhwal and Rashmi Manandhar, the exhibition brings together 285 artworks by 157 Nepali artists, creating a broad visual account of the ways deities are worshipped, imagined and represented across Nepal.

Rather than presenting the works simply as a collection of paintings and sculptures, the exhibition takes visitors through different layers of religious and cultural experience. Its arrangement across the floors of the Nepal Art Council creates something resembling a visual pilgrimage, beginning with the tangible world of household and communal rituals and gradually moving towards mythology, meditation and the cosmos.

A visual journey where Nepal’s sacred world unfolds

The exhibition also carries a strong generational dimension, featuring works by 22 veteran artists aged 65 and above. Alongside these living masters are works by a few artists who are no longer alive, allowing their artistic legacies to remain part of this wider conversation on Nepal’s sacred imagery.

The exhibition unfolds floor by floor, creating a gradual movement through Nepal’s religious imagination. On the ground floor, it begins with representations of Lord Ganesh, Lord Bhairav, Uma Maheswor and more. These works establish the exhibition’s initial connection with deities who are deeply embedded in Nepal’s everyday religious and cultural life.

In the exhibition, the Ganesh series unfolds with artist Sharda Man Shrestha’s Ganesh Chauthi, where he has used mixed media on plywood, creating his unique blend of 2D and 3D features. Next to his artwork, Palistha Manandhar’s ‘The Golden Divine’ in impasto on canvas gives a different feel to a painting because of the texture and the brushstrokes on canvas. Using surrealistic technique, artist Naresh Sainju has created ‘Cheethu Ganesh Dhoka Kirtipur’ in acrylic on canvas. Likewise, artist Sunita Rana, in her painting ‘Nostalgic Dream ’, creates a semi-realistic landscape where a peepal tree has engulfed the Ganesh temple, with details like pigeons and other stone statues, and the background is blurry, giving a hint of eerie greenery around. Then, in Mithila style, artist Ranju Yadav created ‘Mangalkarta’ in acrylic on paper.  

The next room shifts from the deities themselves to the rituals and practical dimensions of religious life among different communities across Nepal. Here, visitors encounter traditional block art, also known as Punh Jya, alongside works related to Ihi, Jitiya Parba, Dashain and other rituals and festivals. The section demonstrates how religious traditions are not limited to images of gods and goddesses but are expressed through ceremonies, festivals, community practices and everyday life.

As visitors walk upstairs, they encounter Nepal’s longest festival, Bunga Dyo Jatra, before entering the main gallery. The works trace the lore and stories associated with Bunga Dyo, creating the sense of following the deity’s journey through the festival and its cultural memory.

Inside the gallery, the narrative expands into the traditions surrounding Indra Jatra, with representations of the Asta Matrika, Navadurga and other deities and ritual traditions. The exhibition then moves into one of the foundational myths of the Kathmandu Valley—the story of Manjushri cutting through the gorge at Chobhar and draining the primordial lake. Nearby are works related to Swayambhunath, Harati Ajima and Namasangati. In this section, the sound of flowing water combined with blue waves creates a particularly calming and immersive atmosphere, bringing a sensory dimension to the sacred imagery.

As visitors continue through the gallery, the exhibition moves into a wider range of Hindu mythology and cultural narratives. Works related to Samudra Manthan lead into representations of Hanuman and stories from the Mahabharata, before the exhibition opens into aspects of Limbu culture and other cultural dance forms. The narrative also reaches towards Kailash, expanding the exhibition’s geographical and spiritual landscape.

On the upper floor, the focus shifts towards Buddhist traditions. Works depicting Buddha, Green Tara, Arya Tara and other Buddhist deities are placed alongside representations of Milarepa and Himalayan caves and sacred spaces associated with meditation and spiritual practice.

The floor above takes the exhibition beyond individual deities and sacred narratives altogether. Dedicated to the Universe and cosmic energy, it brings the exhibition to its most expansive point. After moving through gods, rituals, festivals, myths, cultural traditions and Buddhist imagery, visitors arrive at a space where divinity is no longer confined to a particular figure or form, but is imagined as part of the larger cosmos and the energy that permeates it.

Weaving diverse faiths and artistic traditions into one narrative

The third edition brings together senior artists, art students and artists who have been practising different forms of art for years. Works by former chancellor of the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts Kiran Manandhar, including Avatar; academy chancellor Erina Tamrakar’s Third Eye series; veteran late artist Krodhakala Shiromani Kalu Kumale’s large copper sculptures of Astamatrikas, senior artist Jimmy Thapa’s Taramandal and Brahmanda; and Rajendra Shakya’s large copper sculpture of Vajrayogini, Late artist Tej Chitrakar’s ‘Dakshinkali’, Lok Chitrakar’s ‘Namasangati’ are among the highlights of the exhibition.

“From this year, we have dedicated space for two veteran artists. This year the exhibition highlights the artwork of Jimmy Thapa and Tenzin Norbu,” says Manandhar. Moreover, talk shows were also part of the exhibition and these veteran artists shared their experiences with the audience.

Ultimately, the exhibition becomes more than an exhibition of religious imagery. It creates a space where the distinction between traditional and contemporary art begins to dissolve. Paubhas, sculptures, ritual objects and traditional representations of deities stand alongside contemporary paintings and interpretations without one being presented as more important than the other. Different generations of artists, diverse religious traditions and varied artistic languages come together within the same visual narrative.

In doing so, the exhibition offers a compelling model of coexistence—not only between different faiths and traditions, but also between different ways of making and understanding art. Rather than separating Nepal’s artistic heritage into the categories of old and new, traditional and modern, the curatorial approach allows them to speak to one another. The result is a living exhibition in which tradition is not frozen in the past and contemporary art is not detached from its cultural roots, but both continue to evolve side by side.

If you want to witness it on your own, visit the exhibition, which continues till October 10.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Three ordinances recommended by the government have reached the President’s Office.

The ordinances arrived at around 5pm on Thursday, according to Krishna Bahadur Shahi, spokesperson for the President’s Office.

The Cabinet meeting held on Wednesday afternoon had recommended that President Ram Chandra Paudel issue the three ordinances.

According to government spokesperson Sasmita Pokharel, the ordinances seek to amend certain Nepal laws related to land, forests and disaster management.

The disaster-related ordinance has been proposed in response to the Bhotekoshi floods. It includes a provision to shorten the period for declaring missing persons dead in disaster-related cases. Under the existing law, a person missing for 12 years can be declared dead, while the proposed provision would allow a person to be declared dead after 45 days in cases related to disasters.

The ordinance amending land-related laws includes provisions to provide land to landless Dalits, squatters and unorganised settlers.

The provisions of the ordinances will come into effect once they are issued by the president.

Shahi said the ordinances had reached the President’s Office but had yet to be formally presented to the president.

“Three ordinances have arrived. They arrived at around 5pm today. They are yet to be presented to the president,” Shahi told Onlinekhabar.

title.rendered: Buddha Air says fares being misrepresented through AI-generated content

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Buddha Air has warned that misleading screenshots and other content created using Photoshop and artificial intelligence are being circulated on social media and some online media outlets regarding its airfares.

The airline said it has taken serious note of the circulation of such misleading content.

In a statement issued on Thursday, Buddha Air said it has been offering one-way flights from Kathmandu to Dhangadhi for Rs 10,800.

The airline said tickets on most flights have already been sold out on many days because of the availability of tickets at the minimum fare.

Road transport was disrupted for an extended period after the Rasuwa floods and landslides caused extensive damage to highways. In response to the disruption, Buddha Air had announced that it would offer tickets at the minimum fare from Dashain to Tihar, until road transportation became easier.

The airline said it has been implementing the fare arrangement accordingly to provide passengers with affordable and convenient air services during the disruption.

Buddha Air also warned that if any individual, travel agency or other party is found selling tickets at prices higher than those listed through its official booking and sales channels, it will take legal action in accordance with the law.

The airline urged passengers not to form opinions about airfares based on misleading information or screenshots circulated through social media and other unauthorised channels.

Passengers have been advised to check Buddha Air’s official website, mobile application and authorised sales channels for accurate information on fares and ticket availability.

The airline said the number of passengers travelling out of Kathmandu is currently higher than those flying into the capital. It has also introduced a promotional-code offer for passengers travelling to Kathmandu at minimum fares.

The promo code can be obtained through Buddha Air’s website and mobile application.

Buddha Air said it remains committed to providing convenient, safe and affordable air services to passengers and the general public during times of disaster.

title.rendered: Inam Sapkota’s remand extended as money laundering investigation moves forward

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Police have launched a money laundering investigation against Inam Sapkota, a controversial figure whose connections have been traced to suspended Armed Police Force AIG Banshiraj Dahal and former chief justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana.

Sapkota, who is currently in the custody of the Kathmandu District Police Range, has been remanded for investigation into an alleged money laundering offence, according to police sources.

The Kathmandu District Court had granted police a one-day remand for investigation on Wednesday. After the remand expired, police took Sapkota to the court again on Thursday seeking an extension.

“We have taken him to court for an extension of the remand. It remains to be decided how many more days will be granted,” a source said.

Sapkota was arrested by a Special Bureau team at Tribhuvan International Airport while he was preparing to travel to Delhi. After keeping him in custody for a day for investigation, the bureau handed him over to the Kathmandu District Police Range.

Police sources say further investigation into Sapkota uncovered his links with AIG Dahal. Dahal was subsequently suspended and an investigation launched over his alleged connections with Sapkota, including allegations that he met a person under police custody without informing others.

Police had earlier detained former chief justice Rana after receiving information about alleged attempts to influence proceedings in court cases. A Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office team arrested Rana from his residence late at night and released him after questioning him for around 12 hours. Police also took control of his mobile phone during the detention.

The investigation subsequently brought Sapkota into focus, with police alleging that he had acted as an intermediary to facilitate arrangements.

According to sources, investigators found potentially sensitive information on Sapkota’s mobile phone. Police are also investigating alleged exchanges of information between Sapkota and Dahal, including claims concerning the activities of Prime Minister Balendra Shah and financial transactions.

Sources say the investigation was taken seriously after investigators allegedly found conversations involving specific amounts of money and other financial details.

Rana had come under scrutiny after authorities received information about alleged unusual meetings and attempts to influence cases pending before the courts. Police had also received information about alleged attempts to intervene in cases involving businessmen Deepak Bhatta and Sulav Agrawal, who are in custody in cases related to money laundering, insurance, securities and banking offences.

Meanwhile, the Department of Money Laundering Investigation on Wednesday raided the residences of Rana, his relatives and close associates and seized documents as part of its investigation.

title.rendered: UML to hold national gathering in November

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The CPN-UML has decided to hold a national gathering in Kathmandu in November, the party’s secretary Mahesh Basnet said.

The decision was taken at the party’s Standing Committee meeting on Thursday after completing gatherings at the lower levels of the party.

“We will hold the national gathering around mid-November,” Basnet said after the Standing Committee meeting.

According to Basnet, provincial and district office-bearers, rural and municipal chairpersons and vice-chairpersons, as well as elected representatives from the federal, provincial and local levels, will participate in the gathering.

The party has also decided to hold ward-level conventions on December 12 and local-level conventions on December 19. Provincial-level gatherings will be held after the local and ward conventions, Basnet said.

The Standing Committee meeting will continue at 1pm on Friday.

Former president Bidya Devi Bhandari also attended Thursday’s meeting and took the oath as a senior leader of the party.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Once, someone said to me, “Feminists wreck their own homes.” I was stunned, not just by the words, but by the logic beneath them. A woman who knows her rights, speaks against violence, refuses humiliation, or leaves an abusive relationship is labelled a “home wrecker.” Strangely, the person who committed the violence is rarely given the same title. The woman who exposes the home’s brokenness is blamed for breaking it. But a home is not saved simply because a woman remains silent inside it. If maintaining a family requires a woman to tolerate violence, surrender her dignity, or remain silent about abuse, then it needs to be clear that the violence wrecked the home, not feminism.

According to an annual factsheet on gender-based violence published by Nepal Police, the majority of sexual offence victims were children (0-18 years) at 64%, followed by 35% women aged 19-59 years and 1% of elderly women 60 years and above. Among the child victims, 63.33% were in the 11-16 age group. 88.06% of offenders were men, followed by 11% boys. The most concerning fact is that 67.53% of offenders had basic literacy, 12.89% had school-level education, and 8.82% had a +2 qualification.

The educational profile of offenders is worth examining. It tells us something extremely concerning: literacy and certificates alone do not automatically dismantle misogyny. A person may be academically educated and remain deeply uneducated about consent, dignity and equality.

Yet public discussion often becomes fascinated with exceptional cases involving women accused of manipulating, falsely accusing or “trapping” men. The phrase “honey trap” is quickly introduced, and suddenly an entire conversation about sexual violence becomes a conversation about supposedly dangerous women. Fraud, extortion and false accusations, where established by evidence, should of course be investigated and punished. Gender justice cannot mean abandoning due process for anyone. Therefore, exceptional cases cannot be allowed to swallow the larger reality.

This is precisely why the phrase “boys will be boys” deserves scrutiny. It has been used for generations to excuse behaviour in boys and men that would never be tolerated from girls: sexual remarks, aggression, disregard for boundaries, public displays of sexual entitlement and irresponsible behaviour.

Small habits that build rape culture

Rape culture is not created by only rape offences. It is sustained through smaller ideas that make larger violations easier to excuse. It exists when harassment is called flirting. It exists when a man’s persistence is romanticised even after a woman has said no. It exists when daughters are told to protect the family’s honour while sons are rarely told that the dignity of women is not theirs to control.

It exists when boys are exempted from housework because domestic responsibility is considered feminine. It exists when a woman who has multiple relationships is degraded while a man with the same history is admired. It exists when women in sex work are treated as morally polluted while the men who create the demand remain socially invisible.

None of these behaviours automatically produces a sexual offender. That distinction matters. But together, such practices can reinforce a gender hierarchy in which men are associated with authority, freedom and entitlement while women are associated with service, restraint and accommodation.

Consider something as ordinary as a family gathering. Women who enter another person’s home as guests may still find themselves moving towards the kitchen, helping prepare food or cleaning afterwards. Men from the same gathering may remain seated, eating and talking. An individual dinner does not creates sexual violence the real problem is the repeated social rituals influences children in a different direction. They teach who serves and who is served. Who adjusts and who expects adjustment. Who has authority and who carries responsibility? When these messages are repeated for years, male entitlement seemingly increases. 

In ‘Why Men Rape: An Indian Undercover Investigation’, writer Tara Kaushal investigates the social conditions surrounding sexual violence through interviews with men accused of or associated with serious forms of sexual violence, survivors and experts. Her work repeatedly returns to patriarchy, masculinity, entitlement and the ways everyday social behaviour can communicate who is permitted to occupy space and whose body must remain controlled. Kaushal mentions the provocative idea of “penis privilege” to question something many of us barely notice: boys and men are often granted bodily freedoms in public spaces.

The importance of this argument is not that a man urinating publicly or scratching himself somehow becomes a rapist. That would be an absurd causal claim. The deeper issue is entitlement. Who is taught that public space belongs to them? Who is expected to adjust? Who is told to sit properly, dress properly, return home early, lower their voice, protect their reputation and constantly anticipate danger? And who is rarely given equivalent lessons about respecting another person’s boundaries?

Re-victimisation and imagination of perfect victim

A recent Indian series, ‘Hunkkaar: The Roar’, captures another dimension of this problem particularly well. The drama follows 17-year-old Meenu Rawat after she accuses a powerful spiritual leader of sexual assault. The series moves through police investigation, media pressure and courtroom proceedings, while repeatedly questioning what happens when the credibility of the complainant becomes more intensely examined than the conduct being alleged.

One of its most powerful ideas emerges when the girl questions why she must repeatedly narrate what happened to her. She has already experienced the alleged violence once. Yet the justice process requires her to return to it again and again, before investigators, lawyers, doctors and the court repeatedly. Outside those institutions, society conducts another much more brutal trial altogether.

Why was she there? What was she wearing? Why did she not scream? Why did she wait to report? Why did she continue talking to him? Why does she appear calm? Why is she crying too much? Why is she not crying enough? The fictional scene resonates because the problem is not fictional.

There remains an imagined picture of what a “real victim” should look like. She must behave in a particular manner, remember trauma perfectly, report immediately, possess an uncomplicated personal history and display the amount of emotion society precisely expects. If she departs from that script, suspicion shifts towards her. What society does not understand is that trauma, however, does not perform for an audience.

But we have so many laws

Nepal does not lack legal provisions. Article 38(3) of the Constitution of Nepal expressly prohibits physical, mental, sexual, psychological and other forms of violence or exploitation against women and provides that such conduct is punishable by law, with victims entitled to compensation. The National Penal Code criminalises rape and sexual assaults. Nepal’s Crime Victim Protection Act goes further, guaranteeing victims respectful and dignified treatment during the criminal justice process and specifically recognising privacy protections for victims of offences including rape and sexual harassment.

On paper, therefore, the victim has rights. But formal equality and substantive justice are not the same thing. A beautifully drafted law cannot protect a woman if the police station humiliates her. A constitutional right cannot restore dignity if society publishes her photograph, questions her character or forces her family into hiding. A criminal prohibition cannot produce equality if girls are raised to fear shame more than offenders are raised to fear consequences. Law is essential. But law cannot do the cultural work alone.

Does Patriarchy only harm women?

No! Patriarchy creates different burdens for everyone, although those burdens are neither identical nor equal. Men are taught that masculinity requires dominance, financial success, sexual confidence, emotional toughness and the ability to “protect” women. Many boys learn that crying is weakness, domestic work diminishes masculinity and asking for emotional support makes them less of a man. Ironically, the same man who insists that the women in his own family must be protected from other men seems to participate in objectifying someone else’s daughter, sister or wife.

That contradiction tells us something important: the problem is not protection, but the real problem is ownership. Gender justice does not require women to exchange dependence on “bad men” for dependence on “good men.” It demands that women be recognised as autonomous human beings with rights over their bodies, choices and lives.

Patriarchy also carries an enormous national cost. A society cannot systematically restrict the opportunities of more than half of its population and then claim to be using its human resources efficiently. The World Economic Forum’s ‘Global Gender Gap Report 2026’ ranks Nepal 120th out of 145 economies, with an overall gender parity score of 0.669. Nepal has made significant long-term progress, but substantial gaps remain, particularly in economic participation and leadership.

Gender inequality therefore is not just a “women’s issue.” It is a development issue, an economic issue, a justice issue and a question about what kind of society we want to become.

From Nirmala Pant to Jane Doe

And then there is Nirmala Pant, thirteen years old. Even after being brutally raped and murdered, eight years later, her killer has still not been identified. More than 1,000 people have reportedly been questioned and more than 100 DNA samples tested. In March 2026, Nepal Police formed yet another investigation committee to examine the case. Her mother still waits for an answer that should never have taken eight years. Thousands of kilometres away, another name is now echoing through a very different society: ‘Jane Doe’.

In the United States, a Cornell University student using the legal pseudonym Jane Doe has filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The allegations remain subject to legal proceedings, and the accused are entitled to due process. But after renewed scrutiny of how the matter was handled, New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor and the criminal investigation was reopened. Then something extraordinary happened. As attempts were reportedly made online to uncover the woman’s identity, women began posting under the hashtag #IamJaneDoe. Some did it in solidarity. Some shared their own experiences. Others deliberately used the name so that identifying the actual complainant became harder. The point was larger than one lawsuit. “I am Jane Doe” became a refusal to allow shame to isolate one woman.

Nirmala Pant and Jane Doe are not equivalent cases. One concerns the unresolved rape and murder of a child in Nepal. The other concerns serious allegations that remain under investigation in the United States. Gender justice requires us to respect that distinction. Supporting survivors must never mean abandoning evidence, fair investigation or due process.

But the stories meet at one disturbing point. They reveal the extraordinary burden placed on women and girls around sexual violence. One family waits eight years for the state to identify a perpetrator. Another woman fights to keep her own identity from becoming the subject of public punishment. And between those two stories are countless others whose names we will never know. Jane Doe and Nirmala Pant are often treated as exceptional names attached to exceptional cases. I perceive them differently; I see Jane Doe in every woman who calculates whether speaking will cost her more than remaining silent. I see Nirmala in every girl whose safety depends upon institutions and adults taking her seriously.

I see fragments of their stories whenever a victim covers her face while an accused person walks before cameras without shame, whenever a woman’s character is investigated before the allegation itself, whenever families are advised to remain quiet to protect their “honour”, and whenever society asks what a woman did to invite violence before asking why someone believed the offender had the right to violate her.

Perhaps that is what makes these stories so uncomfortable. Jane Doe is not simply one anonymous woman. Nirmala Pant is not simply one unsolved case. They are reminders of what happens when sexual violence meets power, silence, stigma and institutional failure. So when someone tells me that “feminists wreck their own homes,” I say, a woman who refuses violence is not destroying a home. A girl who reports abuse is not destroying a reputation. A survivor who demands accountability is not destroying society. What destroys homes and societies is violence, entitlement and the culture that protects them. The question is no longer why women are speaking so loudly. The question is why they still have to scream before we listen!

title.rendered: PM Balendra Shah takes note of soaring airfares during festive season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Prime Minister Balendra Shah has taken note of growing complaints over high domestic airfares during the festive season.

According to sources close to Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Minister Khadga Raj Paudel, Shah’s concern over rising airfares prompted the minister to direct the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN) to take steps to address the complaints.

Following the prime minister’s concern and the minister’s direction, CAAN held discussions with representatives of domestic airlines on Thursday.

According to a source at the Prime Minister’s Office, the meeting agreed that airlines would sell tickets at fares lower than the approved maximum rates where possible and publish information about the fares on their respective sales and distribution platforms.

The government’s intervention comes as demand for domestic flights rises during the festive season, with passengers complaining about expensive air tickets.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress leadership election postponed to Friday after voting fails to start

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Voting to elect the new leadership of the Nepali Congress has been postponed to Friday after the voting process failed to begin on Thursday.

Voting was initially scheduled for 10am but was postponed three times, eventually being scheduled for 2:30pm. However, voting could not begin even by the revised time, and the Central Election Committee did not announce another time for Thursday.

According to Election Committee coordinator and senior advocate Prem Bahadur Khadka, voting will now begin at 7am on Friday.

The Election Committee has attributed the delay to the late arrival of election materials from the printing press.

The 15th General Convention is being held to elect the party’s new Central Working Committee, including the president, vice-presidents, general secretaries, joint general secretaries and Central Committee members.

title.rendered: Prakash Man Singh says special convention was aimed at splitting Congress

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Nepali Congress leader Prakash Man Singh, who is aligned with the Sher Bahadur Deuba faction, has claimed that the party’s special general convention was held at the behest of “unseen forces” seeking to divide the party.

Singh made the statement while addressing the inaugural ceremony of the Kathmandu Metropolitan City convention of the Deuba faction on Thursday.

“This did not happen at the demand of the Congress. The special convention was held to divide the Congress at the behest of the ambitions of certain individuals and the interests of some unseen forces—forces seeking to weaken nationalism and democracy,” he said.

Describing those who organised the special convention as people who had “made a mistake”, Singh urged party members not to follow them.

He questioned whether party members should strengthen those who had made mistakes by supporting them or instead follow the path shown by their leaders and make every effort to oppose what is wrong and support what is right.

Singh said he was holding the regular general convention in line with that effort.

He added that the party would move ahead under the leadership of Sher Bahadur Deuba and the Central Working Committee by making necessary decisions in accordance with the party statute and rules.

title.rendered: Police arrest 25 people with drugs from across country

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Police have arrested 25 people with drugs from various parts of the country during routine patrols.

According to the Central Police News Room, two people were arrested from Nakkhu Dobato in Lalitpur Metropolitan City-4, one from Chambas in Gajuri Rural Municipality-2, Dhading, two from Pipra Tole in Siraha Municipality-21, four from Khotang Hotel in Mamachowk, Damak Municipality-1, Jhapa, and two from Bodebarsain Municipality-5, Saptari.

Similarly, two people were arrested from Jamuni Bazaar in Badhaiyatal Rural Municipality-2, Bardiya; three from Alka Marg in Biratnagar Metropolitan City-11, Morang; one from Nadipur in Pokhara Metropolitan City-3, Kaski; one from Amaha Chowk in Itahari Sub-Metropolitan City-19, Sunsari; three from Nayabasti in Barahachhetra Municipality-3, Sunsari; two from Sagarpath in Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City-11, Makwanpur; and two from Birendranagar Municipality-11, Surkhet.

Police said they recovered brown heroin, marijuana and nitrazepam, a drug that can be purchased only on a doctor’s prescription, from those arrested.

title.rendered: Man arrested for making firearms at home in Morang

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, October 8

Police have arrested a man for allegedly making firearms at his home in Letang Municipality-7, Warangi Kolaghar, Morang.

Police arrested 45-year-old local Purnalawati Limbu from his residence. He had set up a workshop at home to manufacture muzzle-loading firearms and was also selling the weapons, according to police.

Police said they found one muzzle-loading firearm in his room during a search of his house on Thursday morning.

District Police Office, Morang spokesperson DSP Makendra Kumar Mishra said police also recovered one percussion firearm and parts used in muzzle-loading firearms from another room where Limbu had set up the workshop.

The Area Police Office, Letang, is investigating Limbu, who was arrested with illegal firearms and materials used to manufacture them.

title.rendered: Nepal Congress convention turns into a sea of posters despite code of conduct

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The venues of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention have been covered with campaign materials despite the party’s Election Committee imposing a complete ban on printed and physical publicity.

Voting for the new Central Working Committee is taking place on Thursday, with hundreds of candidates contesting for the posts of president, vice-presidents, general secretaries, joint general secretaries and Central Committee members.

The Election Committee had prohibited candidates from using flashy and extravagant campaign materials, citing the need to keep the convention dignified, economical and disciplined in the aftermath of recent disasters.

Election Committee member-secretary Raju Katuwal had said all forms of extravagant campaigning would be completely prohibited.

Party president Gagan Thapa had also instructed candidates and delegates not to put up campaign materials around the convention venues.

“Let’s not put up campaign materials or paste leaflets around the convention venue. Some have been seen doing so. Let’s remove them. If you do not remove them, our volunteers will,” Thapa said during Wednesday’s closed session.

However, the situation on Thursday was markedly different. Khula Manch, Rastriya Sabha Griha and the Bhrikutimandap area were covered with campaign posters, leaflets and banners.

Posters and pamphlets were pasted across walls and roads, while campaign materials were scattered on the ground as delegates walked over them.

The Election Committee’s code of conduct had completely prohibited the use, display, distribution or pasting of flexes, banners, posters, pamphlets and other printed campaign materials at or around the convention venues.

It had also prohibited physical campaigning outside the convention venue, including in surrounding areas, public roads and other nearby spaces.

The code allowed candidates to use only digital and technology-based methods for campaigning.

Despite these provisions, physical campaign materials have continued to be displayed extensively around the convention venues, contrary to the rules set by the Election Committee.

title.rendered: Nepal Tourism Board unveils Rs 1.7 billion budget

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The Nepal Tourism Board has introduced a budget of Rs 1.7 billion for the current fiscal year 2026/27. The board has unveiled the new budget in the third month of the current fiscal year.

The board had implemented a budget of Rs 1.59 billion in the last fiscal year but managed to spend only Rs 894.7 million, or 56 per cent of the allocated amount. The budget for the current fiscal year is Rs 110 million higher than last year’s allocation.

In fiscal year 2024/25, the board had spent Rs 1.16 billion. The board had remained without leadership after the incumbent government scrapped all appointments. In the absence of a new chief executive officer, the board has been unable to carry out strategically important activities and has remained focused on routine operations.

This year, the board expects to generate the largest share of its revenue, Rs 1.17 billion, from tourism service fees. It has estimated revenue of Rs 46.6 million from the Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal (TAAN) Management System (TIMS) fee.

The board also expects revenue from various other sources, including participation contributions, hall rentals and interest, as well as its accumulated funds, accumulated TIMS funds and the balance in the joint TIMS account.

Of the board’s projected expenditure, Rs 156.3 million has been allocated for employee expenses and Rs 102.1 million for office expenses.

title.rendered: Malaysia row pushes foreign employment agencies’ association towards split

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies is on the verge of a split following a dispute over the listing of 275 manpower agencies in Malaysia’s Foreign Worker Centralized Management System (FWCMS).

The association has suspended the agencies included in the list. The Department of Foreign Employment is also investigating the agencies and has halted their pre-approval to send workers abroad.

The association initially suspended 25 manpower agencies after they were included in the list. It later suspended an additional 250 agencies and sought clarifications from them.

The agencies included in the list are preparing to form a separate association. One of the manpower entrepreneurs said they had no option but to unite to protect their rights and interests after the existing association took action against them and expelled them.

“We have already moved ahead with the initiative to form an association. They expelled all 25 of us, and now that we have been expelled, we have to fight for our rights and interests,” the entrepreneur said. “Even now, more than 80 per cent of the manpower agencies sending workers are with us.”

The entrepreneur accused the association of suspending member agencies, vandalising and padlocking their offices instead of holding discussions and dialogue after their names were included on the list.

“We did not submit our names from Nepal, but our names appeared on the list from Malaysia. Malaysia included our names in the system based on the C-license,” he said. “But the association treated us like criminals. Since there was no place for us in the association, we concluded that we had to form another one.”

Malaysia has listed 25 Principal Recruitment Agencies (PRAs) and 250 Associate Recruitment Agencies (ARAs) from Nepal through which Nepali workers will be allowed to travel to Malaysia under the FWCMS. A deadline has been set for sending workers through these agencies from November 5.

The doctors raised concerns about the college administration, citing excessive pressure on students and a lack of a conducive learning environment. They urged the government to ensure a peaceful and respectful environment at the college so that they can resume their studies without disruption.

Shailendra Jha, adviser to the Education Minister, and other senior ministry officials were present at the meeting.

The resident doctors expressed confidence that the government would address their concerns and hoped for a positive intervention to resolve the issues.

title.rendered: Janakpur hospital director transferred after snakebite patient dies amid ICU shortage

content.rendered:
Janakpur, October 8

The director of Janakpur Provincial Hospital has been transferred to the Madhesh Ministry of Health and Population following the death of a snakebite patient who was reportedly referred elsewhere after the hospital could not provide ICU care.

Dr Jamun Prasad Singh, a 10th-level senior consultant paediatrician and director of the hospital under the Madhesh Institute of Health Sciences, has been transferred to the ministry for work duties.

The Chief Minister and Council of Ministers’ Office transferred Singh to the ministry and assigned Dr Indrajit Kumar Rajak, a 10th-level medical superintendent currently working at the ministry, to take charge of the hospital.

The action follows the death of 25-year-old Mahesh Yadav of Mujeliya, Janakpurdham Sub-Metropolitan City-14, who reached the provincial hospital after being bitten by a snake on the night of September 29.

Yadav had ridden his scooter to the hospital himself after the snakebite. He was treated with 10 doses of anti-snake venom, but his condition later became critical and he required intensive care.

Hospital authorities reportedly referred him elsewhere after saying that no ICU bed was available.

Yadav was subsequently taken to two other hospitals, but treatment could not be provided there either. He was eventually taken to the Snakebite Treatment Centre in Bardibas, where doctors declared him dead.

The incident has drawn widespread criticism of Janakpur Provincial Hospital over its handling of the case and lack of ICU capacity.

title.rendered: No decision yet on holding local and provincial elections together: EC chief

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Chief Election Commissioner Man Bahadur Karki has said the Election Commission is carrying out internal preparations for the upcoming local-level elections.

Speaking informally to a delegation from the National News Agency (RSS) at the Election Commission on Thursday, Karki said the commission was preparing for the elections, as it always remains ready for electoral processes.

“The government decides the election date. The commission is responsible for conducting the election fairly and without disputes on the date set by the government, and we are committed to that,” he said.

Asked about reports that the government was preparing to hold the local elections in March, Karki said the commission was not in a position to announce a date.

“The government announces the date in consultation with the Election Commission, in accordance with the constitutional provisions,” he said. “We are of the view that local governments should not remain vacant for a long period. Our preparations are being made accordingly.”

Karki said the elections would be held in accordance with the constitutional provisions, around the time the current terms of local governments expire in May 2027.

Asked whether the commission had begun preparations to hold local and provincial elections simultaneously, Karki said no decision had been made on that.

“Elections will be held in accordance with the constitutional and legal provisions. There are also practical considerations for us. Therefore, it cannot be said at this point that the elections will be held simultaneously,” he said. “We will work according to the date announced by the government.”

Karki also said the commission was ready to continue cooperating with RSS, noting its role in creating a positive and election-friendly environment during previous elections.

Election Commissioners Sagun Shumsher JB Rana and Dhruvaraj Wagle were also present during the discussion, which covered cooperation between the commission and RSS and other contemporary issues.

title.rendered: 73 per cent of electricity customers still pay bills at counters

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Around 73 per cent of electricity customers in Nepal still pay their electricity bills by physically visiting payment counters.

A total of 655 electricity tariff collection counters are currently operating under the branches of 129 distribution centres of the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA). The NEA collects electricity payments from customers through these physical counters.

The operation of the counters costs around Rs 597.9 million annually.

Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has urged customers to pay their electricity bills through digital platforms, saying a large number of people still have to visit payment counters.

He said digital payments would save customers time and transportation costs while reducing cash transactions and improving financial transparency and security.

The minister also said the resources and human resources currently used to operate payment counters could be utilised for other essential customer services.

According to Shrestha, around 73 per cent of electricity customers still visit physical counters to pay their bills. Shifting to digital payments would reduce the cost of operating counters and allow the staff involved to be assigned to other tasks.

“Digital payments save citizens’ time and transportation costs. Reducing cash transactions increases financial transparency and security, while the resources and human resources used to operate counters can be utilised for other essential customer services,” he said.

Shrestha urged people to inform, teach and encourage their family members, relatives, neighbours and acquaintances to use digital payment services for electricity bills.

Aryan Majhi, the alleged leader of a robbery group who was arrested after police opened fire in Kathmandu’s Kageshwori Manohara area, has been found to be a defendant in 27 cases.

According to police, Majhi had previously been arrested in 27 robbery and theft cases by the District Police Range, Bhaktapur; Area Police Office, Banepa, Kavre; and District Police Range, Kathmandu, on different dates.

title.rendered: Windstorm damages tomato crops in Gulmi

content.rendered:
Gulmi, October 8

A windstorm accompanied by rainfall has damaged tomato farms in Thulolumphek of Satyawati Rural Municipality-3, Gulmi.

Of around 400 commercial plastic tunnels built in the area, 80 were damaged by the strong winds.

According to Ward Chairperson Jit Bahadur Tramu Magar, the tomato crops were damaged after the plastic coverings of the tunnels were torn by the wind.

Farmers grow tomatoes, cabbage, cauliflower, beans, cucumber, bell peppers and bitter gourd in the tunnels. Farmers said each tunnel produces around 400 to 500 kilograms of tomatoes. The damage to the plastic coverings has affected tomatoes as well as other vegetables.

The area is known for its high tomato production, and vegetables produced in Thulolumphek are sold in local markets as well as transported to Butwal.

Magar said more than Rs 800,000 worth of tomatoes were damaged by the windstorm. Tomatoes are sold for Rs 50 to Rs 60 per kilogram in local markets and Rs 35 to Rs 40 per kilogram at wholesale.

Farmers including Indra Bishwakarma, Lils Rahadi, Hemraj Thapa, Motiprasad Shris and Chetman Rahadi are engaged in commercial vegetable farming in the area.

Road disruptions during the monsoon have also made it difficult for farmers to transport their produce to markets. They currently have to use an alternative road for about an hour to reach the collection centre.

Satyawati Rural Municipality has rented a shop at the Agricultural Produce and Vegetable Wholesale Market in Butwal to help farmers market their produce. Rural Municipality Chairperson Tikaram Pandey said the local government has been paying the shop rent and facilitating vegetable sales for the past three years.

He said the municipality also provides production-based subsidies to promote self-reliance among farmers, including Rs 2 per kilogram to farmers and Rs 20 per quintal to groups involved in managing the produce.

title.rendered: Police urge public to report suspicious activities during festive season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Nepal Police has urged the public to immediately report any suspicious or criminal activities observed during the festive season instead of keeping such information to themselves.

Using the message “If You See Something, Say Something” as a key component of its festival security plan, police said timely information from citizens could help prevent major crimes and accidents.

Nepal Police spokesperson DIG Abhi Narayan Kafle said information received from the public in a timely manner is crucial for preventing and investigating potential crimes during the festive period.

“If you receive information that any suspicious or criminal activity is about to take place or is taking place, do not keep it to yourself. Inform the nearest police office,” he said. “A small piece of information can help us protect a community or a place from a major accident or crime.”

According to police, information provided by citizens will be used as a basis for immediate mobilisation, and the confidentiality of informants will be maintained. Citizens can call the police emergency number 100 free of charge, with calls answered round the clock by the concerned district police offices.

Police said the “If You See Something, Say Something” campaign also covers digital crimes. It is monitoring misinformation, disinformation and deepfake content through its social media monitoring desk.

Kafle said legal action would be taken against activities that spread crime or misinformation.

The security plan also covers online fraud involving artificial intelligence. Police have warned the public about fake online shopping and festival offers, fake lottery and gift messages, fraudulent investment and profit schemes, mobile banking and digital wallet fraud, and phishing aimed at stealing OTPs, PINs and passwords.

Kafle urged people not to immediately trust unusual requests for money made through AI-generated voices or videos, or messages sent in the name of relatives or officials, warning that they could be scams.

title.rendered: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to French and Japanese scientists

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry this year will be jointly awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japanese scientist Kenzo Soai.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Wednesday that the two scientists would receive the prize for their discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

The scientists discovered a method that allows chemists to produce only one of two mirror-image forms of molecules during chemical reactions.

What was the century-old mystery?

Some molecules, including amino acids, exist in two different forms in nature that are mirror images of each other, much like the left and right hands. However, only one of these forms is found in proteins in living organisms. Scientists refer to this phenomenon as “homochirality.”

For a long time, this was a major mystery for chemists. When they attempted to produce such molecules in laboratories, chemical reactions typically produced equal amounts of both forms. However, when developing molecules that interact with living organisms, such as medicines, one mirror image can be effective while the other may not be. Scientists therefore sought ways to produce only one form.

The two scientists helped solve this mystery. In 1986, Kagan of Université Paris-Sud in France discovered a new way to control chemical reactions, making it possible to significantly increase the proportion of one mirror image.

Soai of the Tokyo University of Science in Japan subsequently took the work further. In 1995, he designed the first chemical reaction capable of producing a homochiral outcome and achieved success in 2003.

He demonstrated a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror-image forms was produced. This was the first time such a result had been achieved in a laboratory outside natural biological processes.

Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said Kagan and Soai had solved a more than century-old chemical mystery of how homochirality can arise spontaneously. He described the chemical reactions they developed as “excellent.”

Their discovery has been particularly significant for chemists involved in pharmaceutical development.

The laureates will receive a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately $1.2 million.

The Nobel Prize announcements began on Monday with the prize in physiology or medicine, followed by physics on Tuesday. The prizes for literature, peace and economic sciences are scheduled to be announced on Thursday, Friday and Monday, respectively.

Last year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to three scientists for developing new molecular structures capable of storing large amounts of gas.

title.rendered: Consumers in Kathmandu Valley can exchange LPG cylinders across brands for free during Dashain

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Consumers in Kathmandu Valley will be able to exchange empty LPG cylinders of one brand for filled cylinders of another brand without paying any additional fee during the festive season.

Gas industry operators are preparing the arrangement to ensure consumers do not face shortages simply because they own a cylinder of a particular brand.

The arrangement is being coordinated among the Nepal Oil Corporation, LPG gas companies, dealers and security agencies, particularly ahead of Dashain.

NOC Executive Director Nagendra Sah said the corporation itself had asked gas companies to introduce the system to make it easier for consumers to obtain LPG.

“If someone has only one cylinder and is having difficulty getting gas because it belongs to a different company, even when gas is available in the market, we asked the gas companies to make arrangements to provide relief to the public,” Sah told Onlinekhabar.

He said consumers would not have to pay any additional charge for exchanging cylinders.

In the past, there had been complaints that dealers charged consumers up to Rs 300 when exchanging cylinders belonging to different companies.

“That will not happen now. The arrangement will be completely free of charge,” Sah said.

Joint sales counters planned

Shiva Prasad Ghimire, a former president of the Nepal LPG Gas Industry Association and a gas entrepreneur, said the industry is planning to operate joint sales counters at around 15 to 20 major locations across Kathmandu Valley.

“We will exchange cylinders internally between the companies. For a limited period, we want to ensure that people do not have to return empty-handed simply because they cannot find gas. They should be able to exchange whatever cylinder they have,” Ghimire said.

He said discussions were underway to operate such counters in places including the Nepal Army headquarters area, Chhauni and Sitapaila, in coordination with gas companies, NOC, the Federation of Nepal Petroleum Transport Entrepreneurs and security agencies.

Gas companies will later manage the empty cylinders collected from different brands among themselves.

Service limited to genuine consumers

Ghimire said the facility is intended only for consumers facing difficulties obtaining gas, rather than dealers or other businesses.

To prevent misuse, consumers will have to provide identification details at the counters before receiving gas.

“We will not provide this facility to dealers or businesses. We will provide gas only after keeping a copy of the consumer’s citizenship certificate or another form of identification and their mobile number,” Ghimire said.

He said the system would also allow government agencies to monitor the distribution and ensure the facility reaches consumers genuinely affected by shortages.

NOC prefers exchange through regular dealers

The Nepal Oil Corporation said it would issue a formal notice within a day or two once the participating locations are finalised.

Sah said it would be even more convenient for consumers if cylinders could be exchanged across brands directly through regular dealers instead of requiring them to visit designated joint counters.

The exact locations where consumers will be able to exchange cylinders have not yet been finalised. Gas companies are discussing the arrangements internally and are expected to announce the details within the next one or two days.

LPG consumption in Kathmandu Valley typically falls by around 40 percent during Dashain as millions of people leave the Valley.

However, officials expect the cross-brand exchange arrangement to provide relief to consumers who remain in the Valley, particularly those with only one cylinder who otherwise have to visit multiple shops when their gas runs out.

title.rendered: El Niño expected to peak in December, raising risks of heavy rain and drought

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

El Niño is expected to strengthen further towards the end of 2026 and reach its peak around December, potentially affecting temperature and rainfall patterns in different parts of the world.

According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are likely to remain unusually high between October and December, increasing the likelihood of a strong El Niño event.

Sea surface temperatures in the Niño-3.4 region were about 1.6 degrees Celsius above average in June and rose to around 2.5 degrees Celsius by August. They are forecast to reach an average of up to 3.7 degrees Celsius above normal between October and December. If temperatures rise further in December, the event could become one of the strongest El Niño episodes on record.

The WMO said El Niño is likely to persist until February 2027.

A strong El Niño could raise global temperatures and increase the risk of extreme heat, drought, heavy rainfall and flooding. While some regions, including the eastern and central Pacific, parts of the Greater Horn of Africa, Central Asia and coastal East Asia, could receive above-normal rainfall, below-normal rainfall is expected in the western Pacific and the Indian subcontinent.

The reduced rainfall outlook for the Indian subcontinent could affect agriculture, water resources and related economic activities in South Asia.

The WMO has also noted unusually warm conditions in the Indian and Atlantic oceans, which could further complicate global weather patterns. However, local weather systems and other climate factors will also influence actual conditions, and individual extreme events cannot be attributed to El Niño alone.

title.rendered: Government attorney’s office reviewing CIB report on ANFA alleged match-fixing, fraud

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The District Government Attorney’s Office in Lalitpur is reviewing an investigation report submitted by the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) concerning alleged match-fixing and fraud within the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA).

The CIB on Wednesday submitted its investigation report recommending prosecution of four people, including ANFA President Pankaj Bikram Nembang and General Secretary Kiran Rai, to the District Government Attorney’s Office, Lalitpur.

According to the CIB’s investigation, the four individuals were involved in financial irregularities amounting to Rs 6.65 million.

District Attorney Ganesh Poudel said the office received the report on Wednesday and is currently studying its findings.

“We received the report on Wednesday and are studying it. We will make a decision by tomorrow,” Poudel told Onlinekhabar.

The office is expected to decide by Friday whether to file a case based on the CIB investigation.

The CIB raided the ANFA headquarters on September 18 and arrested Treasurer Rabindra Joshi and accountant Sanjiv Pandey as part of the investigation.

Following the arrests, ANFA President Nembang and General Secretary Rai have reportedly been out of contact.

The investigation began following complaints alleging serious financial irregularities, corruption and abuse of authority within ANFA.

The complaints alleged that ANFA sold home-game rights in a manner contrary to national interests and the country’s reputation, defied directives from the National Sports Council, distributed illegal allowances, and engaged in commission-related irregularities and corruption involving hotel rates during the Women’s SAFF Championship.

The complaints also alleged unauthorised foreign trips, misuse of grant funds and unnecessary appointments.

Investigators were also asked to examine alleged irregularities in tenders conducted at different times and alleged corruption in awarding marketing, digital, broadcasting and ticketing rights for various competitions.

Meanwhile, FIFA has suspended ANFA since June 24, citing third-party interference in the football body.

title.rendered: 788 climbers obtain permits to scale 31 peaks this autumn

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

A total of 788 climbers from 70 countries have obtained permits to climb 31 Himalayan peaks in Nepal during the autumn 2026 season.

According to the Department of Tourism, the climbers are part of 91 expedition teams. Of them, 582 are men and 206 are women. The department has collected Rs 247.21 million in royalties from the climbing permits.

Mt Manaslu (8,163 metres) has attracted the highest number of climbers, with 500 climbers from 43 teams obtaining permits. The department has collected Rs 225.86 million in royalties from Manaslu expeditions.

Similarly, 36 climbers from five teams have obtained permits to climb Mt Dhaulagiri-1, generating Rs 8.24 million in royalties. Another 34 climbers from three teams have received permits for Himlung Himal, with the department collecting Rs 2.09 million in royalties.

Nineteen climbers from two teams have obtained permits for Ama Dablam, generating Rs 2.91 million in royalties.

Permits have also been issued for peaks including Putha Hiunchuli, Danga Hiunchuli, Baruntse, Makalu, Gangapurna West (Langchenel), Thorong Peak, Norbu Khang, Annapurna IV, Chamlang, Lamjung Himal, Pumori, Saribung, Thapa Peak (Dhampus), Pokhar Khang, Ardang and Peri.

Department information officer Suraj Ghimire said climbers from China accounted for the largest group, with 118 permits. Other climbers include 65 from Russia, 60 from France, 52 from the United States, 45 from the UK, 25 from Poland, 23 from Nepal, 18 from India, 23 from Italy and 25 from Japan.

The department said it collected $1.63 million in royalties, equivalent to Rs 247.21 million, from the permits.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

World Sight Day is being observed today with various programmes under the theme “Love Your Eyes, Protect Your Vision.”

World Sight Day is observed every year on the second Thursday of October.

This year’s theme not only encourages individuals to take care of their eyes but also urges the government and stakeholders to ensure accessible and quality eye health services for everyone. It also highlights the importance of expanding eye check-ups and awareness activities in schools, workplaces and policymaking forums.

It may be noted that the prevalence of blindness in Nepal was 0.84 per cent in 1981. According to the 2022 RAAB survey, the figure has dropped to 0.28 per cent. However, the decline in blindness does not mean that all eye health problems have been addressed.

According to Dr Shailesh Kumar Mishra, executive director of the Netra Jyoti Sangh, issues such as glaucoma, corneal diseases, diabetes-related vision problems, age-related eye diseases and refractive errors have also become growing challenges.

Increasing life expectancy, the burden of non-communicable diseases, changing lifestyles and the widespread use of digital devices are creating new risks to eye health.

The Netra Jyoti Sangh has provided treatment services to more than 50.2 million people and performed eye surgeries on 5.65 million people.

It currently provides eye care services to Nepali citizens as well as foreign nationals through 28 eye hospitals, 44 district branches and 226 treatment centres.

title.rendered: CIB recommends filing case against four ANFA officials

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The Nepal Police Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) has recommended filing cases against four officials of the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) after concluding its investigation into financial irregularities and match-fixing.

The investigation found financial irregularities amounting to more than Rs 6.65 million. The CIB submitted its report to the Attorney General’s Office on Wednesday, recommending that the officials face charges.

CIB spokesperson Anupam Shumsher JB Rana said ANFA President Pankaj Bikram Nembang, General Secretary Kiran Rai, Treasurer Rabindra Joshi and Accountant Sanjiv Pandey have been recommended as defendants.

“The study of the evidence and documents obtained during the investigation showed irregularities of Rs 6.65 million. Based on that, it has been recommended to make them defendants and file cases,” said spokesperson Rana.

The CIB focused its investigation on ANFA’s financial transactions, decision-making processes and activities related to various competitions.

“We have already sent the investigation report to the Attorney General’s Office. Now, based on the facts, evidence and legal provisions mentioned in the report, a necessary decision will be made,” Rana said.
