title.rendered: Tribhuvan University proposes Rs 30.87 billion budget for 2026/27

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Tribhuvan University has proposed a budget of Rs 30.87 billion for the fiscal year 2026/27, an increase of 9.77 percent from the previous fiscal year.

According to TU Registrar Rabindra Shivakoti, the proposed budget has been divided into regular, internal and development programmes.

Of the total proposed budget, Rs 15.24 billion, or 49.38 percent, is expected to come from TU’s internal sources, while Rs 15.63 billion, or 50.62 percent, is proposed to be financed through the Nepal government’s budget.

TU has projected that 86.14 percent of the total budget will be spent on recurrent expenditure, while 13.86 percent will go towards capital expenditure.

The Nepal government has allocated Rs 7.31 billion in grants to TU for the 2026/27 fiscal year.

Shivakoti said the government’s allocation is Rs 4.8 billion lower than last year.

At the same time, TU faces additional financial obligations following a 10 percent salary increase for government-service teachers and employees, along with a 10 percent incentive allowance on the increased salary amount.

As a result, TU is expected to face a funding shortfall of Rs 8.32 billion, Shivakoti said.

He warned that if the university does not receive the required amount from the government, it could struggle to meet even its mandatory financial obligations.

Shivakoti said the government has been informed about the university’s financial situation and that the process of arranging funds for mandatory obligations is underway.

He also urged Prime Minister and TU Chancellor to make arrangements for the shortfall in the university’s proposed budget.

title.rendered: Passenger traffic surges on Pokhara-Jomsom air route

content.rendered:
Gandaki, October 8

Passenger traffic on the Pokhara-Jomsom air route has surged following the blockage of the road connecting Mustang with Beni in Myagdi due to flooding.

Jomsom Airport chief Bishwanath Sharma said the limited number of flights has made it difficult to accommodate the increased passenger demand. Twin Otter aircraft operated by Tara Air and Summit Air have increased their flights from five to seven a day to meet the demand.

The ongoing tourist season has further contributed to the rise in air travel, particularly as tourists visit Mustang during Sohra Shraddha, also known as Pitri Paksha or Mahalaya. Sohra Shraddha is a 16-day Hindu ritual period dedicated to honouring and remembering deceased ancestors. Pilgrims from Nepal and India are also travelling to Kagbeni to perform the rituals, further increasing passenger numbers.

The airlines prioritise the transportation of sick and disabled passengers, while local authorities assist in facilitating their travel alongside foreign tourists.

Sharma said passenger traffic is expected to decline once the road is reopened, easing pressure on air services.

title.rendered: Education Minister Pokharel directs TU that results be made public within one month

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Minister for Education and Sports Sasmit Pokharel has directed that students’ results at the university be made public within one month.

Speaking at the meeting for Tribhuvan University’s (TU) 67th anniversary, Minister Pokharel, who is also the university’s pro-chancellor, said the ministry often receives complaints that exams and results are not held on time.

“The Chancellor, the Prime Minister, has also directed that results be brought out within one month,” Minister Pokharel said.

He urged the university to implement the academic calendar. He also called for decentralising the university’s powers.

“It will be even more effective if decentralisation can be achieved,” he said.

He said convocation ceremonies should also be held in other provinces.

Minister Pokharel said the government is working on education reform.

“We are set to reform education. But we have not been able to tell the university and the school apart. The university is a think tank,” he said. “We are drafting an Education Act. We are working on curriculum reform. We are in the process of making a new education policy. The university’s role in this should be greater.”

He urged the university to build infrastructure at TU’s constituent campuses and to attract foreign students. He stressed a transparent university, digital systems, life-relevant education and a research-friendly university.

In earlier assemblies, the TU Assembly was chaired by the Chancellor, who is the Prime Minister. This time, in the Chancellor’s absence, Pro-Chancellor Pokharel chaired the TU Assembly.

title.rendered: Foreign Minister Khanal meets Australian counterpart Wong

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal and Australian Foreign Minister Senator Penny Wong have held talks. In the meeting, both sides expressed satisfaction with the long-standing friendly relations between Nepal and Australia and stressed further expanding cooperation in the days ahead.

According to Minister Khanal’s secretariat, the meeting, held in Melbourne on Thursday, discussed further strengthening ties between the two countries and expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest.

During the meeting, Australian Foreign Minister Wong expressed sorrow for the families and communities affected by the recent floods in Nepal and said Australia stands with Nepal in post-disaster rescue, early recovery and reconstruction.

She announced an additional AUD 15 million in assistance for flood- and disaster-affected Nepal. The amount will be added to the AUD 11 million Australia had earlier announced for the emergency response. The new assistance will focus on relief and early recovery work, it was said.

Minister Khanal thanked the Australian government and the Australian people for the humanitarian support received during the disaster. He said the assistance received in a time of crisis has further strengthened the long-standing friendly relations between the two countries.

Cooperation on climate change and COP31

The meeting also discussed the common risks that Nepal and Pacific countries face because of climate change.

Khanal urged Australia to use its leading role in the international arena to raise, more effectively before the world at the upcoming COP31, the unequal and severe impact of climate change on Himalayan ecosystems.

He stressed expanding Nepal-Australia cooperation in climate adaptation, early warning systems, disaster risk reduction, disaster preparedness and the building of climate-resilient infrastructure.

Discussion on opening campuses of Australian universities in Nepal

The meeting also discussed expanding educational cooperation.

Both sides discussed the possibility of moving forward with initiatives to establish Australia-accredited technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutions in Nepal and potential satellite campuses of Australian universities in Nepal.

Citing the contribution that Nepali students and the Nepali diaspora have made to Australia’s multicultural society and economy, Khanal asked that favourable and fair arrangements be made for eligible Nepali students amid policy changes on student visas.

From trade and investment to direct air connectivity

Expanding the Nepal-Australia economic partnership was also a priority in the meeting. Discussions covered possibilities for expanding cooperation in areas including trade and foreign direct investment, technology transfer, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, tourism promotion and labour mobility.

The two sides also talked about establishing direct air connectivity between Nepal and Australia. Direct flights are expected to make tourism, trade, investment and people-to-people ties easier.

Wong said Australia remains committed to further strengthening its partnership with Nepal in the days ahead. She also expressed a commitment to continued cooperation in the priority areas.

Both sides agreed to continue regular high-level exchanges and to work closely to turn the understandings reached in the meeting into concrete outcomes. They also expressed a commitment to making Nepal-Australia relations stronger and more multifaceted for the mutual benefit of the people of the two countries.

title.rendered: 95,540 students to graduate from TU this year, preparations underway for convocations in all seven provinces

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

A total of 95,540 students are set to graduate from Tribhuvan University (TU) this year.

Presenting figures on the 64th grace list at the meeting marking TU’s 67th anniversary, Registrar Rabindra Adhikari said a total of 95,540 students who completed various levels between June 15, 2025 to July 16, 2026 are eligible for convocation.

Of the total, 15.10 percent are in technical programs and 84.90 percent in general programs. There are 253 in MPhil, 184 in PGD (postgraduate diploma) and 166 in PhD programs.

By faculty, the Faculty of Management produced the most graduates, with 43,142. The Faculty of Education has 19,533, the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences 15,441, and the Faculty of Law 3,001.

In addition, 6,688 students from the Institute of Science and Technology, 5,160 from the Institute of Engineering, 1,920 from the Institute of Medicine, 463 from the Institute of Agriculture and Animal Science, and 192 from the Institute of Forestry are eligible for convocation.

According to Registrar Adhikari, the plan is to hold the main convocation ceremony in Kathmandu in December.

He also said preparations are underway to hold convocation ceremonies in all seven provinces for the students’ convenience.

title.rendered: 300 Nepalis stranded in Tibet’s Purang as Hilsa-Simkot road blocked, demand rescue

content.rendered:
Surkhet, October 8

Around 300 Nepali citizens who went from Humla to China are stranded in Purang, Tibet, after heavy snow accumulated on the Hilsa-Simkot road section and blocked movement. With the road still closed, they cannot return home and have been forced to stay on the Chinese side.

According to information provided online by Sam Chen, who is in Purang, around 300 citizens from various local levels of Humla are currently stranded there. He said more than 150 of them are from Namkha Rural Municipality alone.

Chen said that because snow has closed the road from Hilsa towards Simkot, they cannot return home and need to be rescued.

He said some people from India are also stranded in Purang along with citizens from various municipalities of Humla.

Snow blocks the way home

Purang County, in the Ngari Prefecture of China’s Tibet Autonomous Region, is a major trading area linked to Humla’s Hilsa border point.

Nepalis who had gone to Purang from Humla for trade, employment and other work have been stranded there since the road was blocked.

Heavy snow on the road returning to Simkot via Hilsa has prevented vehicles from operating. With travel on foot also becoming risky, the Nepali citizens have been forced to stay in Purang.

According to the stranded citizens, it is impossible to return to Nepal until the snow is cleared and the road reopens.

They say the prolonged blockage has begun to affect their accommodation, food and other daily needs.

Return possible only after snow is cleared

Chief District Officer of Humla Bholanath Guragain said that traders and residents who went to the Chinese side are stranded there because of the snow on the Hilsa-Simkot road.

According to him, the way back to Humla via Hilsa will open only after the snow that has accumulated in the Purang area is cleared.

“Traders and locals have been stopped towards Taklakot because of snow on the road from Hilsa to Simkot. For now, there is a problem until the route opens,” he said.

The road blockage has also affected trading activity and local movement in northern Humla. Nepali citizens who reached Purang in China, in particular, are waiting for the road to open.

Coordination needed for rescue

If heavy snowfall keeps the road closed for long, the problem of the Nepali citizens stranded in Purang could become more complicated. With the information that more than 150 of them are from Namkha Rural Municipality alone, coordination appears necessary among the local level, the district administration and the concerned agencies regarding their situation.

The stranded citizens have demanded that the road be opened immediately and, if that is not possible, that they be rescued by alternative means. Continuous snowfall in the high Himalayan region is expected to make clearing the road take time.

Because the Hilsa-Simkot road is the main route of travel for the people of Humla, its closure by snow directly affects daily life, trade and movement. If the road does not reopen soon, the problem for the Nepali citizens stranded in Purang is likely to drag on.

title.rendered: Veteran actor Nana Patekar passed away

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Veteran Bollywood actor Nana Patekar has died at the age of 75, Indian media outlets have reported. According to the reports, he died of cardiac arrest.

He is reported to have died at 5:20 am today. CPR was administered continuously for 45 minutes in an attempt to save him.

Patekar was one of the best-known actors of Hindi and Marathi cinema. He was born on January 1, 1951, in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra. He was not only an actor but also active as a film producer, director and writer. Counted among the most influential actors in Indian cinema, he carved out a distinct place through his unique acting style and dialogue delivery.

Patekar entered Hindi cinema with the 1978 film Gaman. In his early career, he worked in both Marathi and Hindi films. His work in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! in 1988 won praise.

The 1989 film Parinda then became an important turning point in his career. He won the National Film Award and a Filmfare Award for his role as a gangster in the film.

Over his long career, Patekar played a wide range of roles. Among his well-known films are Ankush, Pratighaat, Prahaar, Tirangaa, Krantiveer, Agni Sakshi, Khamoshi: The Musical, Ab Tak Chhappan, Apaharan, Raajneeti, Welcome and Welcome Back.

Having proved himself in serious and powerful roles, he also made an equally strong impression in comedy and commercial films. His role as Uday Shetty in Welcome made another side of him popular with audiences.

Patekar was last seen in Vishal Bhardwaj’s romantic action thriller O’Romeo, which starred Shahid Kapoor and Triptii Dimri in the lead roles. In the film, released in February 2026, Patekar played Ismail Khan, head of the Mumbai Intelligence Bureau.

Banke, October 8

Wednesday’s rain has caused heavy damage to the paddy crop in Banke. In many places, the paddy has been flattened, causing problems for farmers.

Jaman Singh Bali, manager of the Sakar Agriculture Cooperative in Rapti Sonari, said the rain, accompanied by strong winds, severely damaged the ripened seed paddy.

According to him, the rain has damaged seed paddy that farmers had planted on 150 bigha of land. As the damage came just when the crop needed tending, there will be a shortage of paddy seed for next year.

The cooperative distributes seed to farmers for seed paddy cultivation. Farmers produce the seed paddy and sell it back to the cooperative, Manager Bali said.

He complained that although the paddy had grown well this year thanks to good rainfall, the rain caused damage at the crucial time of tending.

Sujita Sharma, information officer at the Agriculture Knowledge Centre, Banke, said the rain, which came just as the crop was ripening and ready to be stored, caused major damage to the paddy.

She said that while reports of rain damage to the paddy crop have come in from various parts of Banke, exact details of the losses have yet to be collected.

Of Banke’s 54,526 hectares of arable land, paddy is usually planted on 33,570 hectares. This year, paddy was planted on 33,503 hectares, Sharma said.

title.rendered: Govt begins preparations to build temporary homes for Bhotekoshi-Trishuli flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The government has begun preparations to build temporary homes for people affected by the devastating Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods of August 26.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has called on non-governmental organisations willing to construct temporary homes to provide details of how many houses they plan to build and in which local governments.

The authority has asked organisations to specify the number of temporary homes they intend to construct, their locations and the names of the respective local governments. They have also been asked to submit work plans indicating the estimated time required for construction and the deadline for completion.

Organisations that have already signed agreements to construct temporary homes in flood-affected areas have also been asked to provide details of those agreements.

NGOs will be allowed to construct the temporary homes in coordination with the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction and the concerned local governments.

According to Prakash Aryal, deputy director general of the department, proposals submitted by organisations will be assessed against basic building code requirements. Designs meeting the required standards will be approved and organisations will then be permitted to proceed with construction.

“Since these are temporary homes, the same design cannot be applied to every geography, location and district,” Aryal said. “But we will assess whether the proposed structures meet the minimum safety standards required for the particular location.”

The government’s own temporary housing programme will also follow the same standards, he said.

Aryal said the government was prioritising safety because it was unclear how long families would need to remain in the temporary homes.

“We do not know exactly when families will leave temporary housing,” he said. “Therefore, the structures will be built to provide safe accommodation and minimise the risk of being affected by another disaster.”

The government is generally preparing to build two-room temporary houses covering around 320 square feet for each family.

The 37th meeting of the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Executive Committee, held on September 30, had approved model designs for temporary housing. The meeting decided that the designs would be used as reference materials for construction.

The meeting also decided to identify potentially safe locations for temporary settlements based on a report submitted to the government by a committee formed by the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation and the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration.

Local governments will identify suitable locations from those listed in the report. The Department of Mines and Geology or geological experts will then conduct geological assessments of the identified sites.

Based on the assessment, the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development will coordinate with district administration offices and the authority to construct temporary settlements, with partner organisations also being mobilised.

Relevant government agencies will arrange essential infrastructure such as roads, electricity, drinking water, sanitation and communications at the sites. The meeting also decided that relevant ministries would amend existing legal provisions if necessary to facilitate these arrangements.

400-500 families may need temporary homes initially

The Department of Urban Development and Building Construction had earlier conducted a survey in coordination with local governments to determine the number of flood-affected families requiring temporary housing.

The initial assessment indicates that around 400 to 500 families may require temporary homes.

“Some affected families are currently living in rented accommodation, while others are staying with relatives,” Aryal said. “At the first stage, we have identified a need to build temporary homes for around 400 to 500 families. This number could increase as the work progresses.”

The state will also have a responsibility to provide temporary housing to affected families currently living in rented accommodation if they wish to move into such homes, he said.

According to the latest figures, 17 holding centres are still operating in the flood-affected areas. Four centres in Nuwakot are housing 121 people, while nine centres in Rasuwa are accommodating 843 people. Another 121 people are staying at four holding centres in Dhading.

The government has decided to provide families unwilling to remain in holding centres with up to six months of accommodation and livelihood support until alternative housing is arranged.

A family of up to four members will receive Rs 15,000 per month. Families with more than four members will receive an additional Rs 2,000 per additional member.

The authority said the procedure for receiving the assistance has been finalised and sent to the concerned local governments for implementation.

Temporary homes could cost up to Rs 500,000

According to the department, the cost of a temporary home could range from Rs 200,000 to Rs 500,000.

The houses will not follow a single model across all locations. Organisations will also propose designs based on their available budgets, which could result in differences in construction costs.

Aryal said the estimated cost was necessary to provide safe accommodation with basic facilities.

The government has yet to prepare a detailed reconstruction plan for the flood-affected areas.

However, Minister for Physical Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal has already informed a parliamentary committee about plans to develop a new smart city in the affected areas.

Such permanent arrangements will take considerable time to develop, meaning affected families are expected to rely on temporary housing in the interim.

The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods affected a total of 32,936 people, according to authority data.

A total of 8,317 households were affected, while 7,570 private buildings were damaged in the disaster.

title.rendered: Lumbini candidates line up for Congress office-bearer and central member posts

content.rendered:
Butwal, October 8

Seven people from Lumbini Province are competing for various central office-bearer posts at the Nepali Congress’s 15th General Convention. Three are contesting for party vice-president: Deepak Giri of Dang, Chandra Kant Bhandari of Gulmi, and Binod Chaudhary of Nawalparasi. Chaudhary has filed his candidacy for the inclusive vice-president post.

Kishor Singh Rathaur of Bardiya registered his candidacy for president but withdrew on Wednesday, saying his candidacy could appear to lack support for Gagan Thapa.

Pushpa Bhusal of Arghakhanchi was elected unopposed as women’s vice-president. She had become vice-president at the party’s special general convention. A former deputy speaker, she was in the Sher Bahadur Deuba camp before the special convention.

For general secretary, Amar Singh Pun of Rolpa is in the race. For joint general secretary, Abhishek Pratap Shah of Kapilvastu, Yogendra Chaudhary of Dang, and Devendra Raj Kandel of Nawalparasi are contesting.

Pun, chosen by consensus as a convention delegate from Rolpa, is currently the party’s president of Lumbini Province. He is one of the leaders who have openly and consistently stood outside the Deuba camp. Pun said he is contesting for general secretary with the aim of reaching the party’s central leadership.

Yogendra Chaudhary, who is contesting for joint general secretary, became joint general secretary at the special general convention. Abhishek Pratap Shah and Devendra Raj Kandel have announced their candidacies for joint general secretary for the first time. Shah is also a member of the House of Representatives. Kandel was previously a central member.

A total of 1,009 convention delegates from Lumbini Province are taking part as voters.

Who is contesting for central member?

Dozens from Lumbini Province are competing for central member posts.

In the provincial open category, nine candidates are contesting three posts: Amar Prasad Bhandari, Kamal Prasad Bhusal, Kamal Kishor Ghimire, Dhanendra Karki, Prachanda Bikram Neupane, Pradip Raj Sharma, Motilal Bhandari, Bishnu Prasad Khanal, and Hira Bahadur Khatri.

Karki and Neupane are former provincial ministers. Hira Khatri is a former mayor of Devdaha Municipality.

For the one central member post reserved for young women under 35, five candidates are in the race: Kamala Hamal, Babita Shahi, Sanchita Gyawali, Sushma Pandey, and Susmita Dhungana.

For the one open central member post for youth under 35, seven candidates are competing: Anukul Regmi, Anurag Khadka, Kumar Acharya, Dipendra Regmi, Rakesh Yadav, Shambhu Regmi, and Sudan Kumar Wali.

Wali of Rolpa is an economist and a former member of the provincial planning commission.

Candidates in the central member open category also include Lumbini provincial lawmakers Nima Giri and Jamuna Dhakal; Prof. Govinda Raj Pokharel; former minister Janma jaya Timilsena; former state minister for finance Bharat Kumar Shah; former provincial lawmaker Nirmala Khetri; Amrit Gyawali; Himal Dutta Shrestha; Butwal Mayor Khelraj Pandey; Bijay Gurung; Sushil Gurung; Ganga Shahi; and Rita Sen Oli.

Kathmandu, October 8

The election to choose the Nepali Congress’s new Central Working Committee, which was to begin at 10 am today, has been postponed until 1 pm.

Raju Katuwal, member secretary of the Central Election Committee, said the vote was pushed back to 1 pm because preparations were not complete.

The voting schedule had earlier been announced for 7 am on Thursday. Citing rain and some technical issues, the committee then moved the start to 10 am. It has now been delayed again, to 1 pm.

A total of 7,255 delegates to the general convention will vote to choose the party’s next leadership.

Voting at three locations

Seven polling stations have been designated at three locations in Kathmandu. Separate polling stations have been arranged by province and by category of representation for the delegates’ convenience.

The Election Committee has designated polling stations at the Rastriya Sabha Griha, Khulamanch, and Pragya Bhawan.

Delegates from Bagmati Province will vote at the Rastriya Sabha Griha.

The polling station for delegates from Gandaki and Lumbini provinces is at Pragya Bhawan.

Delegates from Koshi, Madhesh, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces will vote at Khulamanch.

Delegates of each province or group must go to their designated polling station to vote. Voters will be allowed to cast their ballots only after their identity and the voter list have been verified.

title.rendered: Transport operators warn against charging passengers above festive fare

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

The Federation of Nepalese National Transport Entrepreneurs has urged transport operators not to charge passengers more than the government-approved fare during the upcoming festive season.

Federation General Secretary Deknath Gautam said vehicles found charging fares above the prescribed rates would face action.

The government has decided to open advance ticket bookings for passenger vehicles across the country from October 9 ahead of Dashain.

The decision was taken following discussions among the Department of Transport Management, the federation, transport workers’ unions, Nepal Police and the Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office to ensure smooth, organised and safe transportation of passengers and goods during the festive period.

The federation said it has issued necessary instructions to its seven provincial committees, district committees, member organisations and branch chiefs and staff working at Gongabu Bus Park in Kathmandu.

Staff working at advance ticket booking counters will be required to wear designated uniforms and identity cards. They have also been instructed to treat passengers politely, make ticketing convenient and help ensure safe travel.

To manage the increased traffic during Dashain, trailers and other heavy vehicles will be barred from operating on the Narayangadh-Kathmandu road section from Ghatasthapana on October 11 until October 25.

The restriction will not apply to vehicles carrying food, medicines, fruits and other essential goods, in accordance with existing laws.

The federation said long- and medium-route permits for passenger vehicles across the country will remain open from Ghatasthapana until November 6. However, restrictions on certain types and sizes of public vehicles imposed because of the nature of specific roads will remain in place.

The Department of Transport Management will deploy teams, including designated focal persons, to monitor and facilitate passenger assistance desks set up at major entry and exit points of Kathmandu Valley.

The federation has assigned representatives to Gongabu Bus Park, Kalanki, Koteshwor, Gaushala and Chabahil for the same purpose.

Vehicle fitness testing has also been prioritised ahead of the festive rush. Technical staff from the department’s Vehicle Testing Office in Teku will be deployed to Gongabu Bus Park to provide free fitness tests for passenger vehicles.

title.rendered: Singer, composer and playwright Ratna Behoshi dies at 91

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

Veteran singer, composer, lyricist and playwright Ratna Behoshi, also known as Ratna Bajracharya, has died at the age of 91.

Behoshi, who made significant contributions to Nepali and Nepal Bhasa music for more than six decades, died on Wednesday, according to Surajbir Bajracharya, former president of the Newa: Journalists’ Association and a media professional.

Behoshi was active as a singer, composer, lyricist and playwright and is remembered as an important figure in both Nepali and Nepal Bhasa music.

He was among the pioneering singers associated with the early history of Radio Nepal. In 1956, he passed the radio station’s voice audition and was given the opportunity to sing live on air on the same day.

He was selected as a solo singer from among 17 contestants, marking the beginning of a career that would remain closely connected with the development of Nepali radio music.

Among his best-known songs are Malai Mero Deshko Sindoor Launa Man Chha, which he sang with Bharati Upadhyay, and the popular Nepal Bhasa song Su Madugu Taak Swoya Wa, which he performed with Tirath Kumari Thapa.

Born and raised in Bhimchhal, Patan, Ratna Behoshi later lived in Bhol Dhoka.

He is survived by two sons, Anand and Chetan, and daughter Munu Bajracharya.

His final rites were performed at Pashupati Aryaghat on Wednesday. Before the cremation, his body was kept at Nepal Bhasa Manka Khala in Tyagal for people to pay their final respects.

title.rendered: Training children and students against future disasters

content.rendered:
Mudslides and floods disrupted Central Nepal on August 26, 2026, with children being one of the most affected ones. The devastating flood served as an alarming reminder of Nepal’s evolving disaster scenario. It signalled that familiar monsoon floods and landslides are not the only concern of Nepal. We must now prepare for complex and rapidly developing hazards originating in its high mountains. In this scenario, strengthening infrastructure, monitoring glaciers and improving forecasting are essential. Nepal’s preparedness strategy should also focus on its people, particularly children and students.

Disaster risk reduction gets limited attention in Nepal’s school curriculum. A small amount of information is included in social studies, science, and other subjects, but much of it remains theoretical and disconnected from the hazards surrounding individual communities. A definition of a landslide in a textbook cannot prepare a student to respond when a slope starts eroding. Reading about floods does not teach children how to identify a safe evacuation route, react to an early warning, help a younger student, or communicate with family members after phone networks fail. Preparedness must therefore extend beyond classrooms and examinations. Students need regular simulations and drills based on the hazards in their own communities. Schools along riverbanks should practice flood evacuation.

Some private and community schools conduct simulation drills in partnership with NGOs, humanitarian organisations and donor agencies in Kathmandu Valley, and a few cities. However, activities supported through temporary projects may stop when funding ends. Whether a child learns how to survive a disaster should not depend on whether their school happens to have an external partner. Teaching DRR to children and students is very important because they are vulnerable during disasters. In fact, it’s a long-term investment in Nepal’s collective knowledge, behaviour and resilience. A child who learns about landslide warning today might be a teacher, engineer, health worker, journalist, business owner, government officer or minister tomorrow. He/She will carry risk awareness into consideration while making future decisions about where houses will be built, how roads should be designed, how public funds must be spent and how communities must respond to warnings.

Students trained in preparedness can also carry knowledge from school to their homes. Furthermore, they can encourage family members to identify evacuation routes, prepare emergency contact information, store essential medicines safely and avoid crossing flooded roads. In many communities, children may be among the first family members to receive organised information about disaster risks. Communities will respond calmly and quickly to early warnings. Children should not be expected to replace government agencies or emergency responders. The responsibility for reliable early warning systems, safe infrastructure, organised evacuation and emergency relief remains with public institutions. Nevertheless, warnings can save lives only when people understand, trust, and know what action to take.

An inventory prepared by ICIMOD alongside UNDP identified around 2,070 glacial lakes in Nepal. It has classified 21 lakes as potentially vulnerable and in need of regular monitoring. This does not imply that all 2,070 lakes are likely to burst. Each of them has different levels of stability and risk. The inventory reinforces the urgency to educate students about the hazards affecting Nepal’s mountains and river basins. A glacial lake assessment carried out by ICIMOD found that the changing climate is contributing to glacier retreat and the formation and expansion of glacial lakes.

A normal student does not need to become a glaciologist to understand these risks. They must simply be able to differentiate between a normal seasonal flood, a flash flood and a glacial lake outburst flood. They should understand warning signals, safe locations and trusted sources of information. Nepal government has recently tabled a bill in parliament through the National Service Corps (NCC) focusing on secondary level students (Grade 8-12). If approved, it will set up the legal framework for training students as cadets and, if needed, deploying them as volunteers for national duty, mostly in times of war and disaster.

Nepal already has a Comprehensive School Safety Framework in action. It covers disaster risk reduction, resilience education, safe learning environments, and school disaster management. On paper, it gives a strong foundation for improving school safety and ensuring that classes continue in the case of an emergency, but implementation is the biggest challenge. This framework is part of the School Sector Development Plan (SSDP) 2016–2023 and the CSS Master Plan. It covers the minimum activities that are to be implemented to achieve a minimum level of safety in schools. Many schools lack updated hazard maps, comprehensive emergency plans, qualified focal teachers, preparedness kits, and clearly marked evacuation routes.

Children in Nepal are not well prepared for hazards. There is no curriculum in Nepalese schools that teaches what should be done in times of disaster, when evacuation should be done, and how preparedness should be carried out. In a few schools, networks such as Junior Red Cross and Scouts teach students about first aid, simulation drills, etc.

In Kathmandu Metropolitan Municipality, Lalitpur Metropolitan Municipality and other big cities, schools that are financially and resource-rich have DRR education somewhat implemented at the school level through programs like Book Free Friday, Training of Teachers on DRR education, etc. But this education system is also not an accessible, accepted education system in the context of Nepal overall. We need a more inclusive, learnable education system applicable to all students and children of Nepal. More resources must be allocated for integrating both theoretical and practical aspects of DRR.

The school children are highly vulnerable to disasters. A very large number of Nepal’s public schools are sited along riverbanks or near rivers and pond areas, narrow valley floors, and unstable slopes without multi-hazard zoning or climate-resilient construction and infrastructure. The vulnerability is higher in the upper Himalayan region, as it has very weak access to standard roads and basic amenities to combat disasters and post-disaster effects.

While DRR topics are now somewhat formally included in the national curriculum, the delivery remains theoretical. It also heavily lacks practical execution, including disaster practice sessions: regular multi-hazard drills are very rare, teachers receive minimal actionable emergency response training, and curricula seldom address local risks. Age- and context-specific DRR education should be started in the early grades and continue through secondary and higher education. Small children can learn basic warning signs, emergency contacts, and safe behaviour.

Elder students can study local hazard maps, climate risks, first aid, evacuation processes, and responsible communication. Universities and colleges should integrate DRR into the curriculum. Then, future engineers, teachers, health workers, planners, journalists, and public officials can make decisions that influence disaster risk. Therefore, preparing each student is more than a school safety program. It’s an effort to create a culture of risk awareness.

Not every disaster can be rendered harmless by a drill. However, skilled people are better able to identify danger, comprehend warnings, evacuate more efficiently, and make safer choices across their lifespans. Soon, students in Nepal’s schools will be governing towns, managing municipalities, creating buildings, and instructing the next generation. They are better able to defend the nation and themselves if they are raised with an awareness of disasters, preparedness, and resilience. Thus, training children and pupils involves more than just keeping them safe. It is about preparing Nepal for future calamities.

title.rendered: Complaint alleging increased movement of ‘apple boxes’ led to raids

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 8

A complaint alleging that “apple boxes” were increasingly being used to transport bribes led the Department of Money Laundering Investigation to conduct searches at the residences of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana and several people close to him, according to sources familiar with the investigation.

The department’s special team searched the residences of Rana in Bansbari, his brother Prabhu Shumsher Rana in Mandikhatar, former High Court judge Navaraj Thapaliya in Ranibari, Narayan Dahal in Dhumbarahi, Deepak Timalsena nearby, and Navin Basnet in Bhaktapur.

The department seized documents, electronic devices and other materials from the residences, according to sources.

Officials said Basnet’s residence was searched on the same day by coincidence and that his investigation is unrelated to his association with Rana.

Prabhu Shumsher is the former chief justice’s brother. Thapaliya, who was dismissed as a High Court judge over conduct-related issues in February 2024, is considered close to both Rana and current Chief Justice Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma.

Dahal, who runs Barnan monthly magazine, has long been known in Supreme Court circles for his interest in cases pending before the court and for maintaining contacts with people involved in judicial matters.

Timalsena, who built his career in the Supreme Court’s information technology sector, was recommended for a ministerial position during the Sher Bahadur Deuba government when Rana was chief justice. He has since been involved in the telecommunications sector.

According to a source at the Prime Minister’s Office, the investigation into Rana’s contacts began after security concerns surrounding the former chief justice led authorities to examine his interactions with various intermediaries and other individuals.

Rana was taken into police custody at midnight on September 26 citing security concerns. A few days later, police arrested Inam Sapkota in Jhapa.

Government agencies investigating phone communications involving Rana and Sapkota subsequently provided information and correspondence to the government. Following this, Armed Police Force AIG Banshiraj Dahal was suspended and an investigation was launched against him.

The money laundering department subsequently expanded its investigation and searched the residences of several individuals, according to department sources.

The teams were deployed around noon on Wednesday and remained at the residences until the afternoon. The searches resulted in the seizure of documents, electronic gadgets and other materials.

A department source said some materials expected to be obtained from Rana had already been collected, with Wednesday’s search being conducted partly as a formal procedure.

Complaint over ‘apple boxes’

According to sources, the department received a complaint through the government’s Hello Sarkar grievance mechanism alleging that “apple boxes” were being used to transport bribes.

The term “apple boxes” was reportedly used symbolically by complainants to refer to cartons commonly used to transport apples and other fruits. The complainants alleged that such cartons were being used to carry bribes because they are relatively sturdy and less likely to be damaged by minor external impacts.

The department gathered additional information while examining the complaint. Sources said the searches were carried out after investigators received further information indicating that the movement of such boxes had increased.

“The complaint contained details of several incidents involving the transportation of bribes in apple boxes,” a department source said.

The source claimed that the searches were conducted after the department collected additional information and obtained agreement from the team at Prime Minister Balen Shah’s office.

Rana-Thapaliya connection

Thapaliya had remained largely inactive after being dismissed as a High Court judge in February 2024. However, according to sources, he became active again following the appointment of Manoj Kumar Sharma as chief justice.

Sources said information about Thapaliya’s renewed activities reached the Prime Minister’s Secretariat.

Thapaliya is known to have a close relationship with former Chief Justice Rana. Sources at the Supreme Court claimed that he had recently increased his meetings with people involved in cases pending before the court.

According to the sources, Thapaliya also had access to senior judicial administration officials and some Supreme Court judges.

The Nepal Bar Association had previously raised questions about the relationship between Rana, Sharma and Thapaliya during the parliamentary investigation into Rana.

In a memorandum submitted to the Federal Parliament Secretariat in March 2023, the Bar Association referred to alleged communications between Sharma and Thapaliya concerning efforts to influence case decisions through Rana. The Bar had requested that call details and communications involving the judges concerned be examined.

According to Supreme Court sources, a complaint filed through Hello Sarkar alleged that Rana and Thapaliya had again become active in a similar manner and that their activities were beginning to have an impact on cases at the Supreme Court and other courts.

The complaint was subsequently forwarded to the Department of Money Laundering Investigation and reportedly included details of several cases.

The department has also begun investigating the assets of Rana and his brother Prabhu Shumsher. Rana had previously acknowledged as his own certain land purchased by his brother and loans taken against the property.

Dahal, Timalsena and Basnet

Dahal has faced allegations of taking an interest in court cases and using such connections to gain access to judges. He became particularly active during the tenures of former chief justices Ram Kumar Prasad Shah and Damodar Sharma, according to sources.

His activities around the courts were later discouraged during the tenure of Chief Justice Kalyan Shrestha and continued to be restricted during Sushila Karki’s tenure.

Dahal became active again during the tenure of Chief Justice Dipak Raj Joshee but was subsequently less visible in court-related matters.

The department had increased its monitoring of Dahal following correspondence from the Prime Minister’s Office, according to sources.

Timalsena, who had risen through the Supreme Court’s IT section, left the court after becoming embroiled in a dispute over equipment procurement during Kalyan Shrestha’s tenure. He subsequently continued working in the information technology sector outside the court.

Timalsena had appeared before the Parliamentary Hearing Committee when Rana was being considered for chief justice. He was later reportedly being prepared for appointment as a minister in the Deuba government on Rana’s recommendation, but the appointment was halted after questions were raised by various political leaders.

A few weeks after Timalsena’s proposed appointment was halted, Gajendra Bahadur Hamal was appointed Industry Minister in October 2021.

After learning that the department’s team had arrived at his residence, Timalsena himself went to the department’s office in Pulchowk. A department source said he was warned that he could be arrested and charged with misconduct if he obstructed the investigation, after which he left the office.

No one whose residence was searched has been arrested so far, according to the department.

title.rendered: NHRC recommends action against four security officials over Tinkune protest

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has recommended departmental action against four senior security and administrative officials over their handling of the pro-monarchy protest in Kathmandu’s Tinkune area on March 28, 2025.

In a report made public on Tuesday, the commission recommended action against then-Kathmandu SSP Bishwo Adhikari, who is now a DIG, SP Apilraj Bohara, Armed Police Force SP Shailendra Shrestha, and then-Kathmandu Chief District Officer Rishiram Tiwari.

The NHRC has recommended action under Article 249(2)(b) of the Constitution, which provides for departmental action against officials responsible for preventing human rights violations if they fail to perform their duties or show negligence in carrying out their responsibilities.

Failure to implement security plan

The commission said the officials failed to properly assess the activities of the protest organisers, formulate and implement an adequate security plan, and mobilise security personnel in accordance with the Integrated Special Security Plan approved by the District Security Committee.

It said the failure contributed to the inability of the security agencies to maintain peace and security during the March 28 protest.

The NHRC has also recommended that the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers’ Office, Ministry of Home Affairs, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force be alerted about the findings, in accordance with Section 5(1) of the National Human Rights Commission Act, 2012.

Expired tear gas used

The commission has also called for security agencies to be provided with adequate resources and equipment after finding that expired tear gas was widely used during the Tinkune protest.

According to the report, statements recorded during the investigation revealed that security agencies lacked adequate resources and that procurement of essential equipment had not been carried out for a long time.

The NHRC has therefore recommended ensuring sufficient resources and strictly preventing the use of expired tear gas.

NHRC flags statements by Oli government

The commission has also decided to draw the attention of former Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli and members of his cabinet over hate speech directed at political parties and groups holding different beliefs and views.

The NHRC concluded that the then prime minister and ministers had made statements against groups with differing political beliefs and ideologies.

During its monitoring, the commission found that such statements had been published and broadcast by various media outlets. It warned that such remarks could have a negative impact and contribute to hostility toward groups holding different views.

However, the commission has not disclosed the names of the ministers who made the controversial statements.

The NHRC investigated the March 28, 2025 Tinkune protest, during which clashes and violence were reported as a pro-monarchy demonstration escalated in Kathmandu.

title.rendered: CIB recommends prosecution of ANFA president, general secretary and 2 others

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Nepal’s Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) has recommended prosecution of All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) President Pankaj Bikram Nembang, General Secretary Kiran Rai and two other officials over alleged match-fixing and financial fraud.

The CIB submitted its investigation report to the Office of the Government Attorney on Wednesday, recommending that Nembang, Rai, Treasurer Rabindra Joshi and accountant Sanjiv Pandey be made defendants, CIB spokesperson Anupam Shamsher Rana told Onlinekhabar.

According to the CIB, its investigation found irregularities amounting to Rs 6.653 million.

The CIB raided the ANFA headquarters on September 18 and arrested Treasurer Joshi and accountant Pandey. ANFA President Nembang and Secretary-General Rai have been out of contact since the arrests.

The investigation followed complaints alleging serious financial irregularities, corruption and abuse of authority within ANFA.

The complaints included allegations of selling home-game rights in a manner contrary to national interests and the country’s reputation, defying instructions from the National Sports Council, distributing unauthorised allowances, and taking commissions and engaging in corruption in hotel arrangements for the Women’s SAFF Championship.

ANFA officials were also accused of undertaking foreign trips without approval, misusing grant funds and making unnecessary appointments.

The complaints further alleged that ANFA failed to follow prevailing laws while awarding various tenders and committed financial irregularities in awarding marketing, digital, broadcasting and ticketing rights for different competitions.

The CIB launched its investigation after complaints called for action over alleged corruption, serious irregularities and misuse of authority within the football governing body.

ANFA has been suspended by FIFA since June 24 over alleged third-party interference.

title.rendered: Nepal, US near agreement to extend MCC Compact by one year

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Nepal and the United States are moving closer to an agreement to extend the implementation period of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC Compact) in Nepal by up to one year, according to sources at the Ministry of Finance.

The extension is being considered after the implementation of MCC-funded projects was disrupted for several months amid a US review of foreign assistance following Donald Trump’s return to the White House, as well as delays caused by major floods in the Trishuli River.

The MCC Compact normally requires projects to be completed within five years of entering into force. Nepal’s Compact entered into force on August 30, 2023, meaning the projects are currently scheduled to be completed by August 2028.

According to ministry sources, the proposed extension would be a “no-cost extension”, meaning the project timeline would be extended without increasing its cost.

“Work is underway to extend the implementation period by up to 12 months without increasing the project cost,” a ministry source said.

The issue was also discussed during Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle’s recent visit to the United States, when he met Jason Small, MCC’s acting vice president. According to the ministry source, both sides agreed in principle that the projects should be completed successfully, even if an extension is required.

“There is an in-principle understanding between the two sides that the project should be implemented as an exemplary programme and that its deadline should be extended if necessary to ensure successful completion,” the source said.

The Millennium Challenge Account Nepal (MCA-Nepal) has already submitted a proposal to the Ministry of Finance seeking an extension. The ministry will need to take the proposal to the Cabinet, which would then formally communicate Nepal’s decision to MCC.

The MCC Board could consider Nepal’s request at its meeting scheduled for December, according to the ministry source. However, the Ministry of Finance has not yet submitted the extension proposal to the Cabinet.

The source said the possibility of extending the Compact has already been incorporated into this year’s US appropriations legislation, meaning the process can move forward once Nepal makes a formal decision.

Seven-month suspension also affected implementation

The MCC Compact entered into force on August 2023, more than six years after Nepal and the United States signed the agreement.

Implementation was subsequently halted after US President Donald Trump launched a review of foreign assistance on January 20, 2025. The US government recommended continuing the MCC programme in Nepal in late July 2025, resulting in an interruption of around seven months.

The projects have also faced delays because of major floods in the Trishuli River last year and again this year.

In March, while the US was still reviewing its foreign assistance programmes, MCC wrote to Nepal allowing certain essential procurement and office-operating activities to continue.

Projects worth $747 million

Nepal and the United States signed the MCC Compact on September 14, 2017, to develop electricity transmission infrastructure and improve road infrastructure.

The original agreement provided for a $500 million US grant. The United States later added another $50 million, bringing its total contribution to $550 million.

Nepal initially committed $130 million to the programme. As project costs increased, the government committed an additional $67 million in May 2023.

The total programme cost therefore stands at $747 million, comprising $550 million from the United States and $197 million from Nepal.

The programme includes the construction of electricity transmission lines and substations, as well as road upgrades.

An 18-kilometre transmission line from the New Butwal substation to the Indian border has already been completed. Construction of another 297 kilometres of transmission lines and three substations has also been contracted.

A contract has also been awarded for upgrading the East-West Highway section between Dhanakhet in Dang and Lamahi.

MCA-Nepal completed the 18-kilometre New Butwal–Indian border transmission line within nine months of its groundbreaking. The project was completed on September 14.

The MCC programme is also constructing 400 kV substations in Damauli, Tanahun; Ratmate, Nuwakot; and Nawalparasi.

Why the deadline needs to be extended

The transmission-line component has itself experienced delays. A tender launched three years ago for the construction of a total of 315 kilometres of transmission lines was cancelled after the lowest bid submitted was about 60 percent higher than the estimated cost.

Following a reassessment of the transmission-line project, the previously allocated budget was found to be insufficient. The US Congress subsequently approved an additional $50 million grant, equivalent to around Rs 7 billion.

The 18-kilometre section to the border was then tendered separately, while the remaining 297 kilometres were divided into three packages and awarded to contractors.

The contracts for these projects extend beyond the current MCC Compact deadline, making an extension of the Compact necessary if the projects are to be completed under the programme.

What is MCC?

The Millennium Challenge Corporation is a US government foreign assistance agency established by the US Congress in 2004. It provides time-bound grants aimed primarily at reducing poverty and supporting economic growth and institutional development.

MCC says its programmes are intended not only to promote stability and prosperity in partner countries but also to advance US interests.

MCC began showing interest in Nepal in 2011 and selected Nepal as eligible for its programme in 2014. Following continued efforts by the Nepali government, the US agreed to provide Nepal with a $500 million grant.

The programme is being implemented by the Nepali government through the Millennium Challenge Account Nepal, or MCA-Nepal, an organisation established under the Development Board Act 1956 through a government formation order.

title.rendered: Law to be amended to declare missing persons dead after 45 days

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The government is preparing to amend the law to significantly reduce the period after which a missing person can be legally declared dead.

A Cabinet meeting on Wednesday recommended that President Ram Chandra Paudel issue an ordinance to amend certain Nepal laws related to disasters.

According to government spokesperson Sasmit Pokharel, the existing law requires a person to have been missing for 12 years before they can be declared dead.

The proposed amendment would reduce the period to around 45 days.

“The change is quite significant. The 12-year period is being reduced to around 45 days,” Pokharel said.

The proposed change is expected to address situations in which people remain unaccounted for following major disasters and other emergencies, where waiting 12 years to establish their legal status can create difficulties for their families.

Nepali Congress to begin voting at 10 am Thursday after three-hour delay

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Voting to elect the new Central Working Committee of the Nepali Congress will begin at 10 am Thursday, with 7,255 general convention delegates set to cast their ballots for the party’s new leadership.

Voting had originally been scheduled to begin at 7 am, but the election committee has delayed the process by three hours due to rainfall and technical issues.

Prem Bahadur Khadka, coordinator of the Central Election Committee and senior advocate, said preparations were underway to begin voting at 10 am.

Seven polling stations have been set up at three locations in Kathmandu to facilitate voting.

The National Assembly Hall will serve as the polling centre for delegates from Bagmati Province.

Delegates from Koshi, Madhes, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces will vote at Khulamanch. Delegates representing the party’s sister organisations, affiliated organisations and overseas liaison committees will also cast their ballots at Khulamanch.

The Pragya Pratishthan building has been designated as the polling centre for delegates from Gandaki and Lumbini provinces.

Delegates must vote at the polling centre assigned to their respective province or group.

The election committee said delegates will be allowed to vote only after their identity and names on the voter list have been verified.

The voting will determine the leadership of the Nepali Congress at its 15th General Convention, with delegates choosing the party’s new Central Working Committee.

title.rendered: How a dispute over the Constitutional Bench exposed deeper tensions at the Supreme Court

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The names on Wednesday’s cause list contained an unusual addition.

Since Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma became chief justice, Justice Hari Phuyal had not been included in any of the Constitutional Benches formed by the Supreme Court. But on Wednesday, his name appeared alongside those of Chief Justice Sharma and Justices Sapana Pradhan Malla, Nahakul Subedi and Abdul Aziz Musalman.

After the cause list was published, Phuyal went to the chief justice’s chamber, where all five judges were present.

According to one of the judges who took part in the discussion, Phuyal questioned the process by which the Constitutional Bench had been formed. He said he would be willing to sit on the bench only if the matter was discussed at the full court meeting the following day and a clear procedure was agreed upon for forming Constitutional Benches in the future.

Chief Justice Sharma responded that selecting the four judges to sit with the chief justice on the Constitutional Bench was his authority and did not require discussion at the full court.

That response prompted a sharper question from Phuyal.

“If that is the case, why was I not needed in the past, and why am I needed today? Why have you included me in the Constitutional Bench?” Phuyal said, according to the judge present at the meeting. “I cannot sit on a bench that is formed in such a subjective manner.”

The exchange continued.

Sharma reportedly pointed out that a similar practice had been followed during the tenure of former Chief Justice Prakash Man Singh Raut.

Phuyal responded that there was no comparison between Raut and Sharma.

“How can you compare Raut with you? You are not the same,” he reportedly told Sharma.

When Phuyal made clear that he would not sit on the bench, the other three judges also declined to proceed.

“If that is the case, then we cannot sit either,” they reportedly said before leaving the chief justice’s chamber.

The Constitutional Bench therefore did not sit on Wednesday. Phuyal, Malla, Subedi and Musalman returned to their respective chambers instead.

What lies behind the confrontation?

The dispute over Wednesday’s bench formation has brought to the surface deeper tensions that have been building at the Supreme Court since Sharma became chief justice about four and a half months ago.

Sharma was appointed chief justice despite being fourth in the seniority ranking at the time. According to several Supreme Court judges, more than half of the judges were dissatisfied with his appointment, while judges who had ranked ahead of him were particularly unhappy.

Some judges say the tensions that first emerged over the formation of Constitutional Benches gradually began spilling into the Supreme Court’s full court meetings.

A senior Supreme Court official said Sharma had failed to bring the dissatisfied judges into his confidence.

“He needed to work by taking those judges into confidence, but he did not appear to have the confidence to do that,” the official said. “Instead, he seemed comfortable within a small circle of judges and officials. The disagreement that began there appears to be widening.”

According to judges familiar with the matter, Sharma has not been able to win the confidence of some of the senior-most judges who would traditionally be expected to serve on Constitutional Benches.

Instead, they say, he began selecting judges according to his own preference.

That approach has also begun to affect the functioning of the bench, according to those judges.

At the time Sharma was appointed chief justice, judges senior to him included Sapana Pradhan Malla, Kumar Regmi and Hari Phuyal, along with Nahakul Subedi. Sharma was said to have shown little inclination to include some of them on Constitutional Benches, while judges such as Sharanga Subedi and Binod Sharma were selected instead.

Differences among judges also began emerging over whether interim orders should be issued in petitions challenging government decisions.

According to sources, the Constitutional Bench gradually became a more difficult environment for Sharma, leading to changes in its composition. In subsequent benches, judges such as Subedi and Sharma were increasingly selected.

Sources familiar with the Supreme Court’s full court say Sharma began altering the composition of Constitutional Benches and including senior judges after the Nepal Bar Association started publicly objecting to the practice.

But even after those changes, sources say Sharma never placed Malla, Regmi and Phuyal together on the same Constitutional Bench.

Indeed, Phuyal had not appeared on any Constitutional Bench since Sharma became chief justice — until Wednesday.

Discontent spreads beyond the Constitutional Bench

According to Supreme Court judges, the disagreement over Constitutional Bench formation was not the only source of tension.

Dissatisfaction also grew over other administrative and judicial decisions, including the appointment of High Court Butwal judge Basudev Acharya as chair of the Special Court and the promotion of District Judge Himlal Belbase to the High Court just four days before his retirement.

Both Acharya and Belbase had, in one way or another, been involved in orders concerning cases against Rabi Lamichhane, according to the source.

The decisions further contributed to unease among some judges, sources said.

Was Wednesday’s confrontation planned or coincidental?

The timing of Phuyal’s appearance on the Constitutional Bench has also attracted attention.

On Tuesday, the Judicial Council recommended four judges for appointment to the Supreme Court. The nominees were High Court Chief Judge Dr Ratna Bahadur Bagchand and High Court judges Chandra Bahadur Saru, Janak Pandey and Gokarna Dangi.

A source close to the Judicial Council said Bagchand’s recommendation had become almost unavoidable because of an order he issued from the Pokhara High Court on May 15.

High Court Judge Janak Pandey is also a former classmate of Supreme Court Justices Sharanga Subedi and Sunil Pokharel, according to the source.

The source said Subedi’s support had helped clear the way for Pandey’s recommendation.

Dangi, a lawyer from Dang, had previously been appointed to the High Court with the backing of former Judicial Council member Padam Baidik. He has now been recommended for the Supreme Court.

Against this backdrop, the dispute over Wednesday’s Constitutional Bench has triggered another confrontation between the Supreme Court and the legal profession.

The Nepal Bar Association called an emergency meeting after the incident and sharply criticised Sharma’s working style, describing it as resembling the “Cholendra tendency” associated with former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana.

There is another interesting detail.

All four names recommended by the Judicial Council had been proposed by Damodar Bhandari, who became a council member on the recommendation of the Nepal Bar Association. During the council meeting, Sharma himself reportedly responded to the nominations by saying he was “under compulsion” regarding them.

Sharma was already facing pressure over the Bar’s repeated objections to Constitutional Bench formation, while two members of the Judicial Council had also expressed dissent on council matters.

At the same time, posts began appearing on social media questioning why Phuyal had not been included in any Constitutional Bench since Sharma became chief justice.

According to sources, it was against this backdrop that Sharma decided to include both Sapana Pradhan Malla and Hari Phuyal on Wednesday’s Constitutional Bench, apparently in an effort to ease the growing dissatisfaction.

But instead of defusing the dispute, Phuyal’s inclusion triggered a fresh confrontation over the very process used to select the bench.

His refusal to sit ultimately meant that the Constitutional Bench could not convene.

Bar calls for objective criteria

Following the incident, the Nepal Bar Association renewed its demand for a clear and predictable system for forming Constitutional Benches.

The Bar said benches should be constituted on the basis of seniority. If objective circumstances make that impossible, it said, a lottery system should be adopted.

The association argued that a Constitutional Bench should neither be treated as a private list of preferred judges nor as an area of personal discretion for the chief justice.

“Constitutional Bench formation is neither anyone’s private list of choices nor an area of personal privilege for selecting judges,” the Bar said in a statement. “Voluntary selection without clear, objective and predetermined criteria raises serious questions not only about judicial impartiality but also about the institutional credibility of the judiciary.”

The Bar also said the controversy had created the impression that practices seen during Rana’s tenure — when bench formation and judicial administration were widely criticised as discretionary and opaque — were beginning to re-emerge.

But on Wednesday, his name appeared alongside those of Chief Justice Sharma and Justices Sapana Pradhan […]

title.rendered: Malaysia to introduce new system for recruiting Nepali workers from November 5

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Malaysia has announced that it will recruit workers from Nepal through a new system starting November 5.

Malaysia has set November 5 as the final date for recruiting workers through the Foreign Worker Centralised Management System (FWCMS).

Bestinet Sdn Bhd, which operates the recruitment system for foreign workers on behalf of the Malaysian government, issued a memo on October 6 stating that the new system would be implemented for Nepal from November 5.

Bestinet said it had set the date based on a letter from Malaysia’s Ministry of Human Resources and informed medical centres and manpower agencies accordingly.

Under the FWCMS, recruitment from Nepal will be conducted through 25 Principal Recruitment Agencies (PRAs) and 250 Associate Recruitment Agencies (ARAs). The memo states that the recruitment process will operate through the network of 275 agencies, comprising 25 PRAs and their 250 affiliated ARAs.

Bestinet said new biomedical registrations would begin through the 25 PRAs under the new arrangement.

October 15 deadline for biomedical registration under existing system

October 15 has been set as the deadline for biomedical registration under the existing system before the new arrangement takes effect.

According to Bestinet, workers’ biomedical registrations must be successfully submitted to and recorded in the FWCMS by October 15. New biomedical registrations will not be allowed under the existing arrangement after that date.

However, Bestinet clarified that the closure of biomedical registration under the existing system does not mean that the service will be suspended indefinitely.

The memo states that biomedical registration and related procedures will continue under the new system based on official system guidelines.

Processes for VDR applications to be completed by October 31

Bestinet has also instructed medical centres and recruitment agencies to complete the procedures for workers already in the recruitment process under the existing system.

Medical centres have been asked to identify workers whose identification or biometric registration, health examinations, laboratory reports, re-examinations, medical reviews or correction of details remain pending and complete the necessary procedures.

Bestinet has instructed them to submit medical examinations and results by October 31 so that eligible workers can proceed with the Visa With Reference (VDR) application process.

PRA system training on October 26

Before the new system is implemented, registration and account activation for the PRA system will begin. Bestinet has scheduled training on PRA system registration and account activation for October 26.

The training will cover document preparation, registration requirements and system operation procedures. An official link for PRA registration will be provided on November 4, after which system registration and account activation will proceed, according to the memo.

The recruitment of workers from Nepal for Malaysia will then proceed under the new PRA/ARA arrangement from November 5.

Bestinet said its role under the new system would be limited to system operation, technical arrangements, technical support and training.

It said the authority to approve or recognise recruitment agencies and make decisions regarding VDR applications would remain with the relevant government authorities.

Therefore, registration in Bestinet’s system or activation of an account alone will not mean that an agency has been officially approved or appointed by the government.

Bestinet has also instructed medical centres and recruitment agencies to preserve records of workers during the transition, avoid duplicate registrations and not charge additional fees or require fresh medical examinations solely because of the transition.

Any worker transfer, re-registration, repeat medical examination or additional payment required under the new system must be carried out only in accordance with official instructions, it said.

Bestinet said it has been operating the FWCMS and providing technical support to the Malaysian government. Its memo states that it will also manage the transition and provide technical facilitation through the system under the new PRA/ARA arrangement.

Nepal has objected to the integration of Nepali manpower agencies into the FWCMS and sent a diplomatic note to Malaysia. Nepal has maintained that any action leading to a monopoly or undermining fair competition is unacceptable and that recruitment should proceed in accordance with the labour agreement between the two countries.

Malaysia, however, has proceeded with implementation, saying the decision was made in accordance with a decision of its Cabinet.

title.rendered: 341 kg of marijuana found in crashed vehicle, one arrested

content.rendered:
Dhankuta, October 7

Police have recovered 341 kg of marijuana from an SUV that met with an accident in Bhedetar, Sangurigadhi Rural Municipality-6, Dhankuta.

The SUV, bearing registration number Ba 13 Cha 6275, was travelling from Dhankuta towards Bhedetar when it crashed. Police reached the site after receiving information about the accident and found the vehicle about 15 metres below the road.

Police said they arrested one person after finding marijuana during a search of the vehicle. According to the District Police Office, Dhankuta, the marijuana had been concealed in sacks inside the vehicle.

The arrested person has been identified as 39-year-old Amit Bishwakarma of Biratnagar Metropolitan City-9, Morang, who currently resides in Dharan Sub-Metropolitan City-10, Sunsari.

Hemant Bhandari Chhetri, information officer at the District Police Office, Dhankuta, confirmed the arrest.

title.rendered: Party president has no greater right than a grassroots worker: Gagan Thapa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has said the party president has no greater rights or status within the party than an ordinary grassroots worker.

Addressing the closed session of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention in Kathmandu, Thapa said the party should be viewed as a single family, with the current contest being about who takes on responsibility rather than about winning or losing everything.

“Congress is a family. Within a family, our competition is over who will take responsibility. The person who wins does not win everything, and the person who loses does not lose everything,” he said.

Thapa said the presidency or any other party position is simply a responsibility assigned for a specific period, rather than a permanent status or privilege.

“The right and status I have in this party is equal to that of the colleague sitting on the floor of the party,” Thapa said. “The party president is not someone to be revered or treated as superior. It is simply a responsibility entrusted to someone for a specified period.”

His remarks come as the Nepali Congress prepares to elect its new leadership during the ongoing general convention, with several leaders competing for key positions.

title.rendered: Congress must remain united as country faces uncertain situation, says Angdembe

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Nepali Congress parliamentary party leader Bhishmaraj Angdembe has called for unity within the party, warning that the country is going through a complex situation in which national interests could face serious challenges.

Addressing the Nepali Congress general convention, Angdembe said the party should not split at a time when the country could face circumstances that could destabilise it.

“We do not know when they might turn the country into Ukraine, so the Nepali Congress must not break apart or split,” he said.

Angdembe said party leaders should focus less on competition for leadership and instead build trust in the leadership and move forward together. He said people ranging from 18-year-old youths to citizens above 80 had placed their trust in the party’s leadership.

He also argued that the Nepali Congress should not limit itself to being a party focused solely on forming governments.

“There now needs to be a debate on whether the Nepali Congress is merely a party that forms governments or a party that builds the country,” he said. “If the party is made merely a means of gaining power, we will return to the same situation again.”

According to Angdembe, the party has drifted away from its political principles and ideology by repeatedly aligning itself with different forces and tendencies in pursuit of power.

He said the party needed to learn from the consequences of putting power at the centre of its politics.

“We should not merely change faces; we should provide direction to an era,” Angdembe said.

He called on the Congress to engage more seriously with national issues and connect its political agenda with nationalism and the country’s pressing problems.

Angdembe also expressed his commitment to inclusive leadership and said all factions and groups within the party should be taken forward together.

“Bhishma Angdembe is committed to taking everyone along,” he said.

He stressed the need to unite party leaders and cadres across all districts to strengthen the organisation and its leadership.

Angdembe expressed hope that the Congress would emerge from the general convention with renewed energy and ideas, while urging the party not to deviate from its core political principles and ideology.
