title.rendered: Nepali Congress closed session begins ahead of leadership election

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The closed-door session of the Nepali Congress general convention has begun, with delegates set to endorse four reports before the party moves to the election of its new leadership.

The closed session will discuss and pass reports presented by the party president, vice president, general secretary and treasurer.

Once the reports are endorsed, the main task remaining will be the election of the new party leadership.

According to the election schedule, voting is scheduled to begin at 7 am on October 8.

The general convention will elect 24 office-bearers, including one president, one senior vice president, four vice presidents, three general secretaries, 15 joint general secretaries and one treasurer.

Of these, 19 office-bearers will be elected by the general convention.

The party’s statute provides for the president to nominate four joint general secretaries and one treasurer, meaning five of the 24 office-bearer positions will be filled through nomination.

The closed session is therefore the final major organisational process before delegates cast their ballots to select the party’s new leadership.

title.rendered: Why climate disasters must now be seen as a national security threat

content.rendered:
The flood that struck Nepal on the morning of August 26, triggered by the collapse of a glacier in the Himalayas, has caused billions of dollars in damage. So far, more than 1,450 bodies have been recovered, while more than 6,000 people remain missing.

Unlike conventional floods, where forecasts can provide time for evacuation and rescue efforts, this disaster struck suddenly and with little warning. What Nepal witnessed that day was, in many ways, a Himalayan tsunami.

The terrifying wall of water travelled at an estimated speed of 167–193 km per hour and reached a height of around 100 metres. Recent studies have linked the disaster to climate change. Australian tunnel expert Arnold Dix described the Bhotekoshi flood as an unprecedented disaster and one of the toughest challenges he has faced, as multiple rescue operations had to be carried out simultaneously.

The first responders, including the Nepal Police and Armed Police Force, are often the first to reach disaster sites, working around the clock to save lives. One poignant incident occurred when Armed Police Force personnel rescued a child from the rubble after hearing his cries, highlighting the human side of disaster response.

These two security agencies form the backbone of Nepal’s disaster management system. However, when a disaster grows beyond the immediate emergency and begins to affect critical infrastructure, the economy and cross-border connectivity, it becomes a matter of national security.

As climate change warms the mountains, the risks of avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods are increasing. Their consequences extend far beyond immediate loss of life. Sudden floods can destroy strategic roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure. In the recent disaster, 13 hydropower projects and a 25 MW solar plant in Devighat, Nuwakot, were destroyed.

This requires Nepal to adopt a broader understanding of national security — one that encompasses not only military defence but also disaster preparedness and climate resilience.

The role of the Nepali Army as a “force of last resort” therefore becomes indispensable. Article 267(4) of the Constitution of Nepal allows the government to mobilise the Nepali Army for development and disaster management. When the Army constructed a bridge in five days in flood-affected Nuwakot, it was widely praised by the public.

The growing challenges posed by climate change raise fundamental questions about national security and require a reassessment of its traditional definition.

The recent floods have caused extensive devastation and widespread damage to property worth trillions of rupees, creating a serious humanitarian crisis. The government has declared 15 local levels as disaster-prone areas. Many people have been left without their families, homes or basic necessities and are now dependent on the state for shelter and support.

The right to live with dignity has been severely affected. Thousands of children have also been deprived of their right to education and a healthy environment.

The strategically important Kerung border area along the Nepal-China border has suffered severe damage, with significant consequences for the national economy. At the same time, Nepal is taking steps on the climate front, maintaining around 46 percent forest cover, developing a clean energy system based largely on renewable hydropower, and emerging as one of the world’s leading importers of electric vehicles.

Yet Nepal continues to bear the heavy costs of a climate crisis it played little role in creating.

According to an ICIMOD report, glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalayan region are melting rapidly, with the rate of snowmelt having doubled since 2000. To protect citizens from the growing risks, national security must therefore extend beyond military readiness. It should include proactive measures to mitigate the effects of climate change, timely emergency communication, protection of critical infrastructure and stronger rescue capabilities.

The Nepali Army’s initiatives provide examples of this expanded role. Its “Operation Sankat Mochan” during the 2015 earthquake, the draining of the highly vulnerable Imja glacial lake in the Himalayas, and the use of drones to deliver relief to remote areas during recent floods demonstrate how the military can contribute to disaster preparedness and response.

During the 2015 earthquake, nine out of every ten Army personnel were mobilised for search, rescue and relief operations. Similarly, the draining of Imja glacial lake, located at an elevation of 5,010 metres in Solukhumbu district, took more than six months. The project was part of a United Nations initiative aimed at helping Nepal cope with the effects of climate change.

Nepal still has 21 highly vulnerable glacial lakes that could cause severe damage to downstream communities and the national economy. As the government works to address these risks, it must maintain a strong focus on innovation in disaster preparedness and response.

Greater coordination among government agencies, greater involvement of the military in disaster preparedness and stronger support for resilient communities will be essential to strengthening national security in the face of climate change.

Nepal, situated in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region between China and India and characterised by a fragile and dependent economy, must increasingly view disasters through the lens of national security.

This broader understanding must go beyond traditional military concerns. The growing threat of climate-induced disasters is a wake-up call for Nepal. Protecting citizens from the catastrophic effects of climate change will require rapid response mechanisms, resilient infrastructure and effective strategies to minimise damage and preserve lives.

title.rendered: Supreme Court bars Gandaki government from taking long-term decisions until writ is settled

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The Supreme Court has ordered the Gandaki provincial government not to take decisions or carry out activities of long-term significance until the final resolution of a writ petition challenging the government’s failure to seek a vote of confidence.

A division bench of Justice Shreekanta Paudel issued the interim order on Wednesday while hearing a writ petition filed by Lil Bahadur Thapa against the Office of the Gandaki Province Chief and other authorities.

The court directed the Gandaki chief minister not to make decisions or undertake activities concerning matters of long-term significance until the petition is finally settled.

The order comes after the petitioner argued that the constitutional requirement under Article 188(2) for a chief minister to seek a vote of confidence within 30 days had not been implemented.

The petitioner has also submitted a letter showing that the CPN-UML had withdrawn from the Gandaki provincial government and informed the province chief of the decision on August 26.

The Supreme Court said the petition raised a question over the implementation of the constitutional provision requiring the chief minister to seek a vote of confidence within 30 days. Taking into account the sensitivity of the balance of convenience, the court issued the interim order restricting long-term decisions and actions until the writ is resolved.

The court has ordered the defendants to submit written responses, along with the grounds, reasons and evidence showing why the interim order should not be continued, by October 28.

The written response from the province chief is to be submitted through the Office of the Attorney General, while responses from the other defendants are to be filed through the Office of the Chief Attorney of Gandaki Province.

Given the sensitivity of the matter, the court has accorded the case priority and ordered that it be presented during the week following October 28.

The Supreme Court has not yet made a final determination on whether the Gandaki chief minister was constitutionally required to seek a vote of confidence. That question will be decided after considering the written responses and hearing the parties at the next stage of the proceedings.

Senior advocates Ramesh Badal, Raman Kumar Shrestha, Tikaram Bhattarai, Shreekanta Baral and Ram Narayan Bidari represented the petitioner.

content.rendered:

The stock market index NEPSE fell 6.38 points on Wednesday and closed at 2,572.

Turnover improved, rising to Rs 3.74 billion from Rs 3.13 billion the previous day. Prices rose for 99 companies and fell for 167, while 13 were unchanged.

title.rendered: Nepal Police delays transfers of senior officers beyond one-year tenure

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Transfers of several senior Nepal Police officers have been delayed despite them completing the one-year tenure normally prescribed for command positions, with some officers continuing in the same posts for 13 to 14 months.

Under the Nepal Police Regulations, senior officers are generally transferred after completing one year in a command position. The provision applies to officers serving as district police chiefs, battalion and traffic chiefs, provincial police chiefs, training centre heads and commanders of other police units.

However, transfers of inspectors, deputy superintendents of police (DSPs), superintendents of police (SPs) and some senior superintendents of police (SSPs) have not been carried out even after their one-year terms ended.

The latest large-scale transfer of SPs took place on September 16 last year, when 48 SPs were transferred and assigned to command positions in districts and police units. The officers are now approaching 13 months in their current assignments, but the Police Headquarters has yet to announce their replacements.

New SPs have not been assigned to districts including Banke, Morang, Tanahun, Bhaktapur, Kaski, Kailali, Udayapur, Dang and East Nawalparasi.

The tenure of several battalion commanders has also crossed the one-year mark. These include commanders of Nepal Police Armed Police Battalion No. 1 in Naxal, the Nepal Police Special Security Battalion in Sunwal, Rupandehi, the Madhesh Province Police Battalion in Dhanusha, the Special Security Battalion in Ratamate, Makwanpur, the Special Security Battalion in Janakpur and the Special Security Battalion in Tanahun.

The situation is similar among DSPs.

DSPs serving as district and area police chiefs, as well as heads of police circles in the Kathmandu Valley, have also remained in their positions beyond one year. DSPs in districts including Darchula, Dadeldhura, Mugu, Pyuthan, Kalikot and Panchthar have completed their one-year tenure but have not yet been transferred.

Delayed transfers raise career concerns

Police administration experts say prolonged postings can affect officers’ career development and limit their exposure to different types of assignments.

They argue that keeping an officer in the same post for several years can leave them without experience in other areas of police work. Such experience becomes important when officers are later transferred to battalions or headquarters, where they may be expected to handle different responsibilities.

Regular transfers are also considered important for preparing officers for senior leadership roles. Exposure to different assignments allows officers to gain experience dealing with different operational and administrative challenges.

From an administrative perspective, transfers are also viewed as a way of ensuring a “distribution of equal opportunity” within the organisation. Timely and transparent transfers allow officers to receive opportunities across different types of assignments.

The Inspector General of Police has the authority under the regulations to transfer officers up to the rank of SP. Although the IGP can technically make such decisions, police officials say transfers have traditionally not been carried out without the Ministry of Home Affairs giving the go-ahead.

Police Headquarters says transfers are coming soon

Nepal Police spokesperson DIG Abinarayan Kafle said preparations were underway to transfer officers whose tenure had expired.

“Generally, transfers are made after one year. Sometimes there are variations due to various reasons. We are preparing to issue the transfers soon,” Kafle told Onlinekhabar.

He attributed part of the delay to the deployment of a large number of police personnel for search and rescue operations following the Bhotekoshi floods.

“Personnel have still been focused on flood-related search and rescue operations, which has caused some delay in the transfers. Those who have completed their tenure will be transferred soon,” he said.

However, some police officials say the delay cannot be attributed solely to flood-related deployments. According to them, uncertainty over who will take command of key districts has also contributed to the delay, particularly as decisions on the new postings have yet to be finalised.

title.rendered: New draft of meat inspection regulations makes 12 hours of rest mandatory for animals before slaughter

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment has made public a draft of the “Animal Slaughterhouse and Meat Inspection (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2057 BS.”

In a notice, the ministry has sought opinions, suggestions and feedback on the draft from the general public and stakeholders under Section 6(2) of the Legislation Act, 2081.

According to the summary released, the main aims of the draft are to simplify the process of obtaining a licence to sell meat, update the physical standards for meat shops and slaughter sites to current needs, and cover the work of technical staff in meat inspection.

Under the proposed provisions, meat shops and slaughter sites must be completely separate. Before animals are slaughtered, a roofed shed capable of letting them rest for at least 12 hours must be built.

The draft also proposes special arrangements for cleaning animals before slaughter, conducting health checks and keeping sick animals, or those suspected of disease, separate. Areas for skinning, removing hair or feathers, cleaning and cutting meat, and for inspection and sale and distribution must also be properly organised.

With consumer health in mind, meat shops must have an adequate supply of clean water as well as hand-washing facilities for customers. The draft also proposes that sales areas have a chiller or freezer for the cold chain, to maintain meat quality and hygiene.

The draft tightens the conditions that people who slaughter animals and cut meat must follow. A new Rule 8 (A) provides that meat suspected of disease, or showing marks or spots, as well as materials attached to the meat such as the serous membrane, may not be removed or erased in any way without the order of a meat inspector.

If an animal has to be slaughtered in an emergency, prior notice with reasons must be given to the meat inspector. Cloths, tools or weapons used on the meat of a diseased animal are completely barred from reuse without disinfection, and after the inspector has examined the meat of a slaughtered animal, work must proceed only according to the inspector’s instructions.

The amendment widens and clarifies the powers and responsibilities of meat inspectors. Inspectors can verify whether a slaughterhouse or slaughter site meets the standards and give operators the necessary directions.

Inspectors are given full authority to decide whether an animal is fit for slaughter and whether the meat is fit for human consumption, to destroy unhealthy meat, and to stamp meat as fit, unfit or suspect according to its condition. Once an inspector has stamped or marked the meat, the slaughterhouse or slaughter site operator, the transporter and the meat seller bear full responsibility for its safe transport, storage and quality.

To make the system modern and transparent, the draft also adds a provision allowing the department to operate an “integrated digital system” to keep records on slaughterhouses and meat inspection.

To reduce administrative hassle, the legal wording has been revised so that certain recommendations previously made in consultation with the ward office and the village or municipal executive will now be handled by the “livestock section or division.”

The ministry has asked all stakeholders and the general public to send their constructive opinions and suggestions to the ministry’s address or email within one week of the notice’s publication.

title.rendered: Why a Russian lab worker’s death has raised plague concerns

content.rendered:
Conflicting information about the death of a lab worker at a Russian plague research institute has fuelled fears about the possibility of pneumonic plague spreading.

Nearly 200 people are in quarantine in Siberia after 28-year-old Darya Shipilova fell ill at work and later died on October 2.

The exact circumstances of her death are unknown. A senior Russian official posted on social media last week that Shipilova “had died from the plague” – before editing the post to add “possibly”. Russia’s health watchdog has since stated she died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology”.

Local media reports suggested she was infected following an accident at the lab where she worked, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. But these have not been confirmed.

So, what is plague, and how does it spread? Should we be worried?

What is plague? Are there different types?

Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The bacteria generally live in ground-dwelling rodents such as rats and prairie dogs, but can also infect humans.

The same Y. pestis bacteria can cause three different types of plague.

Bubonic plague is spread from animals to humans by fleas, and causes swelling (called buboes) in the lymph nodes. Other symptoms include fever, headache, chills and weakness.

Bubonic plague can kill within a few days if antibiotics are not used. Between 30–60% of people who contract this form of plague will die.

Septicemic plague occurs if bubonic plague is left untreated, or it can occur directly if the disease enters the bloodstream. Septicemic plague causes bleeding into the organs; the name refers to the serious blood infection, septicemia, that this form of the disease can cause.

Pneumonic plague – the suspected but unconfirmed cause of Shipilova’s death in Siberia – can occur when bubonic plague spreads to the lungs. But pneumonic plague can also spread from person to person via tiny respiratory droplets.

Pneumonic plague is the rarest but most severe form. The fatality rate is up to 100% if left untreated.

In addition to the other symptoms, pneumonic plague also includes severe pneumonia – an infection of the lungs, in this case caused by bacteria.

Isn’t plague a medieval sickness?

Bubonic plague was responsible for the death of tens of millions of people in the western Mediterranean between 541–750CE (the Plague of Justinian) and killed up to half of Europe’s population in the middle ages (the Black Death).

But there have been outbreaks since medieval times.

A third pandemic spanning the end of the nineteenth century and beginning of the twentieth killed up to 12 million people.

Plague is still endemic to Central Asia, Africa, the Americas and Siberia, where the Russian lab worker died last week. This means it is present at a steady, consistent level in these regions.

Cases typically occur in rural and agricultural areas which makes a potential lab leak in an urban area unusual.

Can it be treated?

Yes. A 10–14-day course of antibiotics (either oral or intravenous) treats the plague – as long as they are taken soon after infection.

However, since 1995, several antibiotic-resistant strains have been detected in the wild.

In the 1980s, Soviet Union scientists also engineered resistant strains – this history forms the basis of hypothetical scenarios involving biological warfare.

However, there is no evidence the strain alleged to have killed Shipilova could not be treated by antibiotics or that the lab is researching biological weapons.

How worried should we be?

There has only been one documented major outbreak of the pneumonic plague, in the 1910s in China.

We still don’t know much about the case in Siberia. But at this stage, there’s little evidence to cause concern about potential for an epidemic (which is localised) or a pandemic (which involves multiple countries).

In a statement on Monday, the World Health Organization (WHO) said it was aware of reports a laboratory worker in Irkutsk had “died of severe pneumonia” but no cause of death had been officially confirmed.

The WHO statement also said: “Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low. The risk assessment will be updated once more information is available.”

To assess this risk, access to transparent information about how Shipilova fell ill and died will be essential.

title.rendered: Rana says he can bring all sides into the mainstream as general secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Nepali Congress leader and former Tarun Dal president Udaya Shamsher Rana has said his leadership is needed to make the party more dynamic.

Rana has filed his candidacy for general secretary at the ongoing 15th General Convention.

Speaking at a programme in Kathmandu on Wednesday, Rana said he is in the race for general secretary representing the entire younger generation rather than out of personal interest. He based his claim on his past performance.

“I have not come forward just as Udaya Shamsher. I have filed my candidacy as the former president of Tarun Dal and a representative of the youth. The support and backing of my young colleagues is my main strength,” Rana said.

Recalling the party’s electoral success in Lalitpur when he led Tarun Dal, he claimed his image is clean and effective. Addressing the factional discontent and disagreements visible within the party, Rana said he has the ability to bring all sides into the mainstream.

“When I was president of Tarun Dal, I had a record of delivering a clean sweep for the Congress in Lalitpur. With that experience and confidence, I am ready to take on the responsibility of general secretary,” he said.

title.rendered: Top End cricket series raises $4,269 for flood-affected children in Nepal

Kathmandu, October 7

The Top End T20 series in Australia has raised US$4,269 for flood-affected children in Nepal.

The organisers said the money raised during the series will be handed over to UNICEF Australia. It will be spent to support children affected by the flash floods in Nepal.

Through UNICEF Australia, the funds will be used to provide affected children with life-saving health services, nutrition and safe drinking water, the organisers said.

The organisers thanked the Nepali community that supported the campaign, the Study NT ambassadors who helped run the raffle, and everyone who bought tickets, took part in the raffle or donated directly.

The Nepal A cricket team took part in the Top End T20 series in Australia. While the series was underway, devastating floods struck districts of Nepal including Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

At the time, Cricket Australia expressed solidarity with the Nepali people affected by the floods and also appealed for support for UNICEF Australia’s Nepal emergency relief campaign.

title.rendered: Parliamentary committee may form separate team to investigate ambassador complaints

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The Parliamentary Hearing Committee is considering forming a separate team to investigate some of the complaints filed against Nepal’s 13 proposed ambassadors, after committee members concluded that certain allegations may require a deeper fact-checking process.

Committee Chair Bodh Narayan Shrestha said some of the complaints could not be addressed through a routine review and might require the committee to conduct a more detailed investigation.

“Some complaints may require us to look into how serious they actually are, rather than simply taking them at face value. We may have to form a committee or a small team to investigate them,” Shrestha said during Tuesday’s meeting.

Shrestha did not disclose which nominees were the subject of the complaints that may require further investigation.

The committee received seven complaints against the 13 ambassadorial nominees. Two complaints challenge the nominations as a whole, alleging that the government did not follow the prescribed ambassador appointment guidelines. The remaining five complaints concern individual nominees and raise issues related to their conduct, qualifications and personal or professional backgrounds.

The complaints were distributed among committee members on Tuesday for detailed study.

Among the individual complaints, Japan’s proposed ambassador Jigyan Kumar Thapa faces three complaints. One alleges that he gave up his Nepali citizenship and obtained permanent residency abroad, while another questions his eligibility for the ambassadorial position. A third complaint raises questions about his property, business interests, investments, bank loans and professional liabilities in Japan.

Saudi Arabia nominee Giribahadur Sunar faces two complaints, including allegations concerning violence against women and involvement in economic and criminal activities. The allegations remain claims contained in the complaints and have yet to be established by the committee.

A committee member said the allegations should be determined before the committee decides whether to endorse or reject the nominations.

“If we approve or reject someone without determining what the complaints are about, it would send the wrong message,” the member said.

The committee has scheduled hearings on the complaints and the nominees for October 12, 13 and 14.

The Cabinet had recommended ambassadors to 13 countries on September 18. The nominees include Nischal Nath Pandey for India, Kalyan Raj Sharma for China, Chiran Jung Thapa for the United States, former Army chief Gaurav Shumsher Rana for the United Kingdom, Jigyan Kumar Thapa for Japan and Giribahadur Sunar for Saudi Arabia, among others.

title.rendered: Finland orders Google to halt data centre construction over environmental concerns

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Finnish authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on two proposed data centres over environmental concerns, alleging that more than 300 hectares of forest were cleared during pre-construction activities.

According to Finland’s Supervisory Agency (LVV), environmental impact assessments were mandatory for the proposed data centres in Kajaani and Muhos, but pre-construction work had begun at least at one site without the assessment.

The agency has ordered activities that could cause “significant changes” to the environment to stop until October 23.

The activities included tree clearing, removal of topsoil, construction of access roads and storage areas, and alterations to drainage ditches, said Tommi Muilu, the agency’s head of environment.

Tuike Finland, the company responsible for the projects, has been asked to explain the incident and submit a plan for further action by October 14. The agency warned that enforcement action could follow if the order is not complied with.

Google acknowledged that it had failed to meet its own environmental standards but said it had acted in good faith under the Forestry Act and taken measures to protect areas of high environmental value.

Google plans to invest at least 13 billion euros in Finland in 2027 and 2028, including new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala.

Kathmandu, October 7

The Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene has discussed making telemedicine services more effective, better organised and sustainable.

Those taking part included Health Secretary Dr Bikas Devkota, the acting director general of the department, representatives of Patan Hospital and Bir Hospital, and the head of the Curative Service Division.

The discussion covered the budget, human resources and institutional management needed to run telemedicine on a sustainable basis. It also considered managing the staff required for the service separately so that it can run continuously and effectively.

Participants also discussed organising the records and documentation of services provided through telemedicine, keeping patient details secure, and systematically recording consultation information.

The meeting stressed the need to identify problems and challenges that could arise as telemedicine expands, and to prepare in advance to address them. In particular, it gave priority to making identity verification of service users reliable and well organised, and to increasing public trust in telemedicine.

Minister Mehta said telemedicine should be developed not merely as a technology-based service but as an effective means of expanding citizens’ access to health care. He stressed the need to make arrangements that maintain the service’s credibility and quality.

The meeting also discussed taking forward the next action plan by improving the policy, technical and management aspects needed to make telemedicine more effective.

title.rendered: New notes easier to get for Dashain, Rs 100 notes available from bank ATMs

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Targeting Dashain and other festivals this year, Nepal Rastra Bank has directed banks and financial institutions to make new Rs 100 notes available through ATMs.

Following the central bank’s directive, some banks and financial institutions have begun distributing Rs 100 notes from newer-model ATMs.

Rastra Bank spokesperson Gurus Prasad Paudel said that, with the Bhotekoshi flood having caused heavy loss of life and property, arrangements have been made for the public to get crisp, clean notes from Rastra Bank and commercial banks without unnecessary publicity about new notes, with a focus on the festival season.

“On the one hand, exchanging money is a daily routine task. There is no need to issue a notice for it,” he said. “With the Bhotekoshi flood causing heavy loss of life and property right at the start of the festival season, it is also not appropriate for Rastra Bank to issue a notice about celebrating Dashain. This is how we have decided to go about it.”

Paudel said that since September 17, crisp and clean notes have been distributed from Rastra Bank’s Thapathali office, its provincial offices and commercial banks.

He added that, for the past four to five years, Rastra Bank has been gradually trying to reduce the practice of bringing new notes into the market specifically for festivals.

“Up to September 16, currency in circulation stood at Rs 794 billion,” he said. “We estimate that around 8 to 10 percent of this amount will increase during Dashain.”

title.rendered: Former NSU leaders dominate Nepali Congress leadership race

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Former leaders of the Nepali Congress-affiliated Nepal Student Union (NSU) are playing a prominent role in the party’s ongoing leadership contest, underscoring the student organisation’s long-standing role as a training ground for future Congress leaders.

In its 56-year history, the NSU has had 21 presidents, including both elected and ad hoc leaders. Its history began in 1970 with the election of founding president Bipin Koirala and has now reached the tenure of its current president, Karuna Katuwal.

The NSU has long been regarded as an organisation that produces political leaders for the Nepali Congress. The current 15th General Convention provides another illustration, with a significant number of former NSU presidents contesting key party positions.

Kishor Singh Rathore, who is contesting for the post of party president, previously led the NSU representing the Nepali Congress (Democratic) faction during the party split. Rathore entered mainstream party politics through the student organisation and served as the Free Student Union president at Tri-Chandra Campus on an NSU ticket.

Party president Gagan Thapa also rose through student politics and served as NSU general secretary, although he never became the organisation’s president. Another candidate for party president, Shyam Krishna Khadgi, did not have a background in student politics.

Senior Vice President-elect Bishwa Prakash Sharma is also a former NSU president. He was elected president at the organisation’s eighth general convention in 2000.

Two other candidates for vice president, Dhanraj Gurung and Govinda Bhattarai, are also former NSU presidents.

Gurung, who was elected vice president of the Nepali Congress at the previous general convention, is seeking another term in the same position. He took over the NSU leadership in 1996 and led the organisation for seven months. Later that year, the NSU’s seventh general convention elected Govinda Bhattarai as president. Bhattarai is now contesting for vice president of the Nepali Congress.

Ranjit Karn, another vice presidential candidate, also has a history in the student organisation. He led the NSU as president of an ad hoc committee in 2012.

The contest for general secretary also features three former NSU presidents. Pradip Paudel, Gururaj Ghimire and Nain Singh Mahar are all running for the post.

Paudel, who currently serves as Nepali Congress general secretary, is seeking another term. He was elected NSU president at the organisation’s 10th general convention in 2007.

Ghimire was elected NSU president at its ninth general convention in 2002, while Mahar was elected president at the 11th general convention in 2016.

Former NSU president Rajiv Dhungana is also contesting for joint general secretary. He led the organisation as president of an ad hoc committee in 2018.

Several other former NSU presidents are participating in the general convention without contesting for office. Former presidents Balkrishna Khand and Gyanendra Bahadur Karki are among them. Khand was elected NSU president at its fifth general convention in 1987, while Karki became president in 1982.

Meanwhile, the legacy of the NSU is also reflected in the competing convention plans within the Nepali Congress. A faction led by former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba, who was the NSU’s second president, is preparing to hold a separate general convention.

Former NSU presidents Bimalendra Nidhi and NP Saud have openly backed the Deuba faction’s convention plans. Former NSU president Dujang Sherpa, however, has said he will not participate in either faction’s convention. Another former president, Kalyan Gurung, has so far maintained silence over the competing conventions.

The large presence of former NSU leaders in the current leadership race highlights the organisation’s enduring influence within the Nepali Congress, with decades of student politics continuing to serve as a pathway into the party’s senior leadership.

title.rendered: More than 500 containers stranded from Lete to Korala

content.rendered:
Mustang, October 7

Around 500 containers have been found stranded in queues at various locations along the road from Lete in Mustang to the Korala border point.

The containers have been stranded at different locations in the district for the past week after floods, landslides and snowfall following rainfall from Asoj 8 to 11 obstructed the road.

Road repairs are underway at Pokharebagar, Kunaute, Baisari and other locations in Myagdi, which were affected by the heavy rainfall. Technicians involved in the road project said it could take another week for the road to fully reopen.

As the road remains closed, more than 70 containers and over 100 electric vehicles have been parked at the bus park in Jomsom.

Although the Beni-Jomsom road remains blocked, some containers carrying goods have been brought to Jomsom from the Korala border point. The containers were transported after the Kaligandaki Corridor Road Project repaired blocked sections along the Jomsom-Korala stretch. They had been stranded at the Mustang Customs Office.

Earlier, hundreds of containers had remained stranded in the border area as customs clearance of goods imported from China could not be completed due to electricity and internet disruptions caused by floods and landslides.

The central 33-kV electricity transmission line and internet services in Mustang had remained disrupted for a week after floods, landslides and river erosion damaged power poles at dozens of locations in Myagdi.

The disruptions have affected regular services at the Upper Mustang Customs Office.

Gobinda Gurung, a container driver stranded at the Korala border point, said around 300 containers carrying imported goods and more than 200 electric vehicles were still awaiting customs clearance.

As goods imported from China through the Korala border and intended for the Dashain and Tihar festivals cannot be delivered to their destinations on time, traders and consumers have been affected. Consumers have been unable to purchase the goods they want, while the disruption has also affected economic activity in the Nepali market.

title.rendered: When will Nepal’s ODI World Cup dream become reality?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Every cricketing nation has its own set of dreams. After entering international cricket, the first goal is to establish an identity, followed by playing regularly in international competitions, defeating bigger teams and gradually reaching the biggest stage in world cricket.

These dreams are no different for Nepal. Since entering international cricket, Nepal has passed through several stages. Having established its own identity as an Associate nation, Nepal has now reached a level where it competes against Test-playing nations. But one dream remains unfulfilled—the ODI World Cup.

Nepal have yet to play in a men’s ODI World Cup. The country has already appeared three times on the biggest stage in T20 cricket. But reaching the 50-over World Cup has become an even longer wait for Nepali cricket.

Playing in a World Cup is not simply about participating in a tournament. It is the result of years of hard work, infrastructure development, player production, domestic cricket and international performances.

Nepal has also demonstrated its growing stature in international cricket in recent years. From playing against teams such as India and Pakistan in the Asia Cup to appearing in the T20 World Cup, Nepal has strengthened its presence on the world cricket map.

But the door to the ODI World Cup remains closed. Nepal has come close several times in the World Cup qualification process. It has played the ODI World Cup Qualifier three times—in 2014, 2018 and 2023—but has failed to progress to the World Cup.

This leaves one question hanging: How much longer will Nepal have to wait to play in an ODI World Cup?

Retaining ODI status is the first challenge

While Nepal continues to dream of reaching the World Cup, another important challenge at present is retaining its ODI status. Nepal is currently struggling to maintain that status, making the World Cup an even more distant prospect for now.

For an Associate nation, ODI status itself is a significant achievement. But maintaining it requires consistent international performances.

Nepal’s ODI performances have fluctuated in recent years. The team has produced impressive victories at times but has also delivered performances below expectations, preventing it from achieving consistency. Its ODI victories have often been isolated successes rather than part of sustained progress.

If Nepal wants to play in the World Cup, winning a few big matches will not be enough. It needs to become a team capable of performing consistently over a long period. Therefore, the immediate priority is not only the dream of reaching the World Cup but also establishing a permanent place in ODI cricket.

For this, Nepal needs to focus not only on T20Is but also on ODI cricket. Former Nepal captain Pawan Agrawal shares this view.

“There is no alternative to improving the domestic structure if we want to play in the 50-over World Cup. Because players play so much T20 cricket, they struggle to cope with the demands of the longer format,” Agrawal said. “Our development starts more with T20 cricket, which is why playing 50-over cricket has become difficult.”

Nepal have also struggled to perform consistently in overseas conditions. To play in a 50-over World Cup, the team needs to perform well not only at home but also in different conditions abroad.

“Wickets abroad are somewhat challenging. Nepal has also become accustomed to playing on relatively flat pitches, so the team has struggled to bat well on wickets overseas,” said another former captain, Raju Khadka.

As a result, Nepal has performed well at home in ODI series under the World Cup League 2 but has struggled overseas. This has had a direct impact on the points table and made the World Cup route more difficult.

Recent performances have already demonstrated that Nepal has talent. The question now is not simply about talent but about developing a structure capable of sustaining that talent at the international level.

A harder road for Associate nations

The reasons behind Nepal’s failure to reach the World Cup cannot be sought only within Nepal. The structure of Associate cricket itself presents significant challenges.

Fewer teams participate in the ODI World Cup than in the T20 World Cup. Ten teams played in the 2023 ODI World Cup, while the 2019 edition also featured only 10 teams. Fourteen teams participated in the 2015 and 2011 editions.

The number of participating teams was reduced from 2019, making it even more difficult for Associate nations to reach the ODI World Cup.

Fourteen teams are set to participate in the 2027 World Cup, but the main competition will effectively involve 12 teams. Hosts South Africa and Zimbabwe will qualify automatically, while India, Australia, New Zealand, England, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan and Bangladesh will also qualify directly based on rankings.

The remaining teams will be decided through the World Cup Qualifier. Of the teams finishing in the top four in the qualifier, the top team will qualify directly for the World Cup, while the remaining three will compete against each other for one additional World Cup spot.

This means that although 14 teams are officially listed as participants, two teams will see their campaigns end before reaching the main tournament. The limited number of World Cup spots therefore continues to make qualification difficult for Associate nations.

Full-member nations, meanwhile, have regular opportunities to play Test, ODI and T20I cricket. Their players compete consistently in high-level international competitions. Associate nations have far fewer opportunities to play at that level.

Nepal has faced the same problem. In a major qualification process, one poor performance can affect years of hard work.

For now, the main pathway to the World Cup for Associate nations is the Cricket World Cup League 2, in which the top eight Associate teams play 36 ODIs over a period of three to four years.

The route from League 2 leads to the World Cup Qualifier and potentially from there to the World Cup. The top four teams in League 2 qualify directly for the World Cup Qualifier, while the remaining four can also reach the qualifier by progressing through the playoffs.

Therefore, Nepal’s journey to the World Cup is not simply about winning matches on the field. Adequate international exposure, a strong domestic structure, regular high-level competition and an appropriate qualification system are equally important.

Test status: another big dream

What could be the next major target for Nepali cricket after the ODI World Cup? The answer is obvious—Test status.

Achieving Test status is one of the biggest accomplishments for any cricketing nation. But reaching that level requires even greater structural preparation than qualifying for the ODI World Cup.

Domestic first-class cricket needs to be strengthened. Players need opportunities to play four-day cricket. Regular high-level competitions are essential. Infrastructure, the player pool and cricket administration all need to develop together.

Test status, therefore, is less an immediate target than a long-term destination for Nepali cricket. At the ICC annual conference, Cricket Association of Nepal Secretary Paras Khadka said Nepal would soon become a Test nation.

“We have fans, and we have the support of the government and the ICC. We are playing a series against the West Indies for the first time. Nepal will soon become a Test nation, it is not just our dream, but our commitment,” Paras said.

At one time, even playing in the T20 World Cup and gaining ODI status seemed like distant dreams for Nepal. Today, Nepal has achieved both.

Nepal therefore has every right to dream bigger. Nepali cricket has demonstrated time and again that it can compete with major teams when given the opportunity.

But reaching the World Cup will require more than occasional victories over bigger teams. Nepal will have to establish itself as a team that consistently merits a place in major international tournaments.

A single World Cup qualification will not solve all the problems facing Nepali cricket. But earning that place could give the next generation of Nepali cricketers a foundation on which to build even bigger dreams.

The current generation has witnessed the T20 World Cup. The next generation could witness Nepal playing in an ODI World Cup. After that, the dream of Test cricket may no longer seem impossible.

But the question is no longer whether Nepal can play in the World Cup. The question is simply: When will Nepal’s dream of playing in the ODI World Cup finally come true?

The answer will have to be found on the field. And it will not be determined by one match, but by years of sustained performance.

title.rendered: Snowfall, rainfall affect life in Humla

content.rendered:
File

Humla, October 7

Normal life has been affected in Humla district due to sudden rainfall, and snowfall has occurred since Tuesday night. The higher reaches of the district have been witnessing snowfall, and incessant rainfall is taking place in the lower areas. Snowfall is taking place at mountainous areas and high-hilly areas including Namkha and Simkot while lower area including Adanchuli and Tajakot have been experiencing light rainfall from Tuesday night. Daily life of the locals has been affected due to the chilly conditions following rainfall and snowfall.

Problems have also surfaced in movement due to muddy roads following incessant rainfall. Dipak Karki of Sarkegad-1 shared that vehicular movement has been disrupted following road obstruction at some places. Farmers are worried, thinking the rainfall might damage their paddy crop as well as vegetables planted in their farms. Locals are concerned after water flow in streams has started increasing.

The problem is so severe that they cannot even take out the cattle for grazing due to snow. Locals have been urged to remain alert towards possible damage as snowfall and rainfall are taking place in the district along with the sudden change in weather, said Deputy Superintendent of Police at the District Police Office, Shankar Khadka.

A landslide has buried a Bolero jeep at Sanata Khola in Chhayanath Rara Municipality-12, Mugu. The jeep, with registration number Lu 1 Cha 1211, was buried on Wednesday morning while returning after going from Gamgadhi towards Sanata.

According to police, officers from the temporary police post in Rowa, Mugu, were sent to the scene after information was received that the landslide had come down at 10:30 am and buried the jeep. The police team reached the site at 1:20 pm.

On reaching the spot, police found that there were no passengers in the jeep and that no one had been hurt.

Police said the jeep is completely buried and efforts are underway to recover it. The site lies about two hours south of the Rowa temporary police post.

title.rendered: Medical teams mobilised for providing health checkups to climbers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The Himalayan Rescue Association (HRA) has dispatched a team of doctors to the mountain areas. HRA stated that a team of doctors has been deployed to provide information about health issues like altitude sickness, diarrhoea, and fever that may occur during trekking and mountaineering in the Himalayan region, as well as to offer treatment services if required.

The chief executive officer of the HRA, Govinda Basyal, shared that teams of local and foreign volunteer doctors and staff have been sent to health posts in Manang and Pheriche, Solukhumbu. A team comprising Dr Robert James Edward Dixon from Australia and Dr Victoria Jane Robertson from the UK, along with supporting staff, has been deployed at Manang Health Post.

Similarly, a team including Dr Mary Abercrombie from the UK and Dr Matthew Alex McAlpine from Australia has been deployed at the Pheriche Health Post. Emergency health services will be available 24 hours a day at Manang and Pheriche Health Post.

HRA’s Chief Executive Officer Basyal said that coordination and support for running the health post were received from the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, the Department of Tourism, the Department of Health Services, the Labour Department, the Department of Immigration, the Nepal Medical Council, the National Trust for Nature Conservation, Nisyang Rural Municipality of Manang, and Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality.

According to him, the service will be running until the end of November. During that time, a team of volunteer doctors and support staff will be operating in the Himalayan region.

title.rendered: A ward where chronic patients don’t have to worry about medicine costs

content.rendered:
Sitaram Paudel was walking down the stairs of the Lamsure Basic Health Centre, a packet of medicines in his hand.

His wife, Krishnamaya, has been taking medication for high blood pressure for the past 12 years and is also suffering from cancer. For an ordinary family with a chronically ill member, the cost of regular medicines can be difficult to manage.

But for Sitaram, finding money for his wife’s medicines is no longer a monthly worry. “I came to get blood pressure medicine for my wife. She also has cancer. We have been receiving medicines worth up to Rs 1,000 every month from the ward,” he said. “We elderly people don’t have to go anywhere else. We can get check-ups and medicines here.”

For Sitaram, the health concerns within his family remain, but the burden of having to arrange money for regular medicines has eased. Eighty-year-old Annapurna Adhikari and 65-year-old Sita Khatiwada were also preparing to return home from the health centre with medicines in their hands. Like Sitaram, they have been receiving medicines free of charge. “We have been getting our medicines from here for a long time. We have never had to pay for them,” they said.

This is the experience of residents of Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City-9, where people with chronic illnesses do not have to arrange money every month for their regular medicines. Health check-ups and laboratory tests are also provided free of charge. Residents have been receiving these services for the past four and a half years, after the ward began prioritising healthcare and developing the Lamsure Basic Health Centre under the concept of a “village hospital” in 2079 BS.

According to Auxiliary Health Worker Anjita Rimal, 40 to 50 people visit the centre each day for treatment, health check-ups and medicines for chronic illnesses. Over the past four and a half years, around 13,000 people have received free treatment and medicines from the health centre. The centre provides 98 types of medicines supplied by the government. The ward office adds another 82 types of medicines purchased through its own budget.

Medicines required by prostate patients and relatively expensive medicines such as RotaCap and Asthalin used by asthma patients are also provided free of charge. The health centre provides medicines for people suffering from hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, mental illness, high cholesterol, arthritis and thyroid disorders, among other conditions.

“Some patients have been receiving medicines worth Rs 5,000 to Rs 8,000 a month from here,” said Ward Chairperson Sukaram KC. “That is not a small amount. We have been able to provide free medicines and treatment to families who cannot afford to spend Rs 5,000 a month on medicines.”

From Rs 500,000 to Rs 2 million

The ward’s initiative to expand free health services began in 2079 BS with a budget of Rs 500,000. The budget was increased to Rs 1 million the following year, and by 2083 BS, the ward had allocated Rs 2 million for health services, according to KC.

The initiative has also received support from the provincial government and the private sector. The Ministry of Health of the Bagmati Province government provided Rs 1 million in the fiscal year 2082/83, which was used to purchase medical equipment. The ministry has also allocated another Rs 1 million for the current fiscal year, 2083/84, KC said.

Berger Paints Pvt Ltd, based in the Hetauda Industrial Area, provided Rs 500,000 to purchase equipment for health check-ups of pregnant women.

The ward office also provides Rs 1 million annually to the central office of Manav Sewa Ashram in Hetauda-9. The amount is used for the medical treatment of hundreds of elderly people staying at the facility.

Healthcare at home

The ward’s health services are not limited to people who can reach the health centre. Health workers also visit the homes of people who are unable to walk, persons with disabilities and patients with chronic illnesses. Patients requiring oxygen also receive services at home.

“There are many chronic patients who remain at home. We visit and treat those who cannot come to the health centre,” Rimal said. “For patients who need oxygen, we even take an oxygen plant to their homes to provide the service.” Four female community health volunteers have been assigned to provide home-based services.

The health centre has one senior auxiliary health worker, one auxiliary health worker, one auxiliary nurse midwife, one lab assistant and one office assistant. Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City covers the salaries of the other employees, while the ward office pays for the office assistant and community health volunteers from its own resources. The ward also operates two community clinics at Shiv Panchayan Temple and Kalimai Temple. The clinics are held twice a month.

Using household data to set health priorities

Behind the ward’s investment in healthcare is a painful reality. According to KC, 20 residents of Hetauda-9 died of cancer between 2079 and 2083 BS. “It is unbearable to see ward residents die of cancer every year,” KC said. “That is why we have been investing in health and education to the best of the ward’s capacity.”

In 2079 BS, the ward office conducted a household survey covering 24 tole development organisations. The survey collected information on the number of patients in each household, the types of illnesses they suffered from and the most common health problems in the community.

The data helped the ward identify its health priorities. Records at the health centre currently show a significant number of patients with hypertension and diabetes. There are 108 newly diagnosed hypertension patients and 1,161 receiving follow-up treatment. Similarly, 64 patients are newly diagnosed with diabetes and 474 are receiving follow-up treatment.

Seven new patients have cardiovascular diseases and 84 are receiving follow-up treatment. There are 16 new patients with lung diseases and 82 receiving follow-up treatment. Similarly, there are 24 new thyroid patients and 78 receiving follow-up treatment. Two new cancer patients are in the 30–69 age group. There are also nine new patients with other non-communicable diseases and 57 receiving follow-up treatment.

Bringing specialists closer to patients

The ward recognised that medicines alone are not enough for people living with chronic illnesses. It has therefore been arranging specialist consultations at the health centre twice a month.

Through an annual agreement with the Madan Bhandari Academy of Health Sciences under the Bagmati Province government, specialist doctors are brought to the health centre.

According to Rimal, two physicians from the academy visit the centre twice a month, while a gynaecologist and a radiologist visit once a month. As a result, patients who need specialist consultations can receive the service within their own ward rather than travelling elsewhere.

The health centre also operates a laboratory offering 20 types of health tests. Patients do not have to pay for these tests. For residents such as Sitaram, the significance of these services is perhaps simplest to measure in the money they no longer have to find each month.

His wife still needs regular treatment, and his family still has to live with the uncertainty that comes with chronic illness. But when he walks out of the health centre carrying her medicines, one burden has been lifted: the need to worry about how to pay for them.

title.rendered: Justice Phuyal refuses to sit on Constitutional Bench, questioning its formation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Supreme Court Justice Hari Phuyal refused to sit on the Constitutional Bench, questioning what he described as the Chief Justice’s arbitrary discretion in forming the bench. As a result of Phuyal’s stance, the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Bench could not convene on Wednesday.

Chief Justice Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma had previously not included Justice Phuyal on the Constitutional Bench. However, after Phuyal was included in Wednesday’s bench, he met the Chief Justice and refused to sit.

Phuyal questioned why he had not been included in the bench previously and why his presence was needed on Wednesday.

After Phuyal declined to sit, the other justices also refused to proceed, preventing the Constitutional Bench from convening. The bench consists of five justices, including the Chief Justice.

Phuyal has maintained that there should be a scientific method for forming benches, either based on seniority or through a lottery system. He has argued that the Constitutional Bench should not be formed at the discretion of the Chief Justice.

Discontent has recently emerged within the Supreme Court over the formation of benches and the allocation of responsibilities among justices. There have also been publicly reported instances in which justices have differed in their opinions on the Constitutional Bench.

title.rendered: Buying meat in Kathmandu Valley is about to change

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The next time you buy meat in Kathmandu Valley, the government wants to make sure it has already passed a health check.

Starting November 17, the government will begin enforcing the Animal Slaughterhouse and Meat Inspection Act, 1999 across all 21 local levels of Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur.

The law has existed for 28 years but has never been implemented effectively across the country. This time, the federal government, provincial agencies and local governments are preparing to enforce it as a public health measure.

The government says the system is intended to address the widespread practice of slaughtering animals in open spaces, along roadsides and riverbanks, as well as the sale of meat without inspection.

Such practices can increase the risk of zoonotic diseases — infections that can pass from animals to humans.

227 inspectors headed to the Valley

The government has begun preparing the machinery needed to enforce the law. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment has assigned 227 veterinarians and meat inspectors to Kathmandu Valley. Kathmandu will receive 137 inspectors, Lalitpur 56 and Bhaktapur 34.

The deployment has been divided among local governments according to population, the number of meat shops and the volume of slaughtering activity.

Kathmandu Metropolitan City will have the largest team, with 53 inspectors. Budhanilkantha will have 16, while Kirtipur and Chandragiri will each have 13. Tarakeshwar will have 10, Tokha eight and Nagarjun seven. Gokarneshwar will have six, Kageshwori Manohara five, Shankharapur four and Dakshinkali two.

In Lalitpur, 33 inspectors will be stationed in Lalitpur Metropolitan City. Mahalaxmi will have 12 and Godawari eight. Konjyosom, Bagmati and Mahankal rural municipalities will each have one.

In Bhaktapur, Madhyapur Thimi will have 12 inspectors, Bhaktapur and Suryabinayak will each have eight, and Changunarayan will have six.

From the animal to the butcher shop

The new system will introduce checks at two points — before and after slaughter. Inspectors will first determine whether an animal is healthy before it is slaughtered. The meat will then be examined to establish whether it is fit for human consumption. Only meat approved by inspectors and bearing an official stamp will be allowed to reach retail outlets.

Dr Umesh Dahal, director general of the Department of Livestock Services, said the purpose was not to shut down existing meat businesses.

“The implementation of this law does not mean displacing existing meat businesses or taking away their livelihoods,” Dahal said. “It is about bringing traditional businesses into a more organised, dignified, modern and legal framework.”

According to Dahal, previous attempts to enforce the law in isolated wards or smaller areas failed to produce lasting results. The government has therefore decided to implement it across the entire Kathmandu Valley at the same time.

He acknowledged that enforcing the law simultaneously across the Valley would be difficult but said the government would continue adjusting its approach based on what it learns during implementation.

13 task forces to support local governments

The government has also created a separate monitoring and coordination structure for the rollout. Eight technical joint-secretary-level officials have been assigned to oversee implementation in the three districts.

In Kathmandu, the responsibility has been assigned to Dr Binay Kumar Karn, Dr Hemraj Awasthi and Dr Sujan Rana. Dr Barun Kumar Sharma, Dr Sulochana Shrestha and Dr Pragya Koirala will oversee Lalitpur, while Dr Bikash Shrestha and Dr Jagadish Pandey will be responsible for Bhaktapur.

The Department of Livestock Services has also formed 13 task forces made up of under-secretary-level officials. The task forces will work with the 227 inspectors and local governments to provide technical support and monitor implementation.

They will map meat shops and slaughtering locations, assess slaughterhouses against required standards and recommend improvements where necessary. The teams will also meet meat traders and other stakeholders to explain the law and discuss the changes businesses will need to make.

Their field reports will be sent regularly to the department, allowing officials to identify problems and adjust the implementation strategy.

The plan does not stop at Kathmandu

The Valley is only the first step. From January 15, 2027, the government plans to extend the law to all metropolitan cities, sub-metropolitan cities and municipalities outside Kathmandu Valley.

From July 17, 2027, it will be extended to all rural municipalities.

The government’s stated goal is to bring meat production and sales under a system in which animals are inspected before slaughter, meat is checked afterwards, and only approved meat reaches consumers.

After 28 years on the books, the government is now attempting to turn the meat inspection law into a system that consumers can actually see — from the slaughterhouse to the kitchen.

title.rendered: US recalls B-1 bombers from UK base amid alleged terrorist threat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The United States has recalled dozens of B-1 bomber aircraft stationed at the Royal Air Force Fairford base in the UK amid an increased risk of a possible terrorist attack. US President Donald Trump has claimed that Iran was behind the security threat as well as a recent alleged attack attempt involving a flydubai aircraft.

The US abruptly returned B-1 Lancer bombers deployed at PCS Fairford Air Base in Britain.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said the move was part of a routine diplomatic and military rotation and was not linked to any direct threat. However, within hours, President Trump contradicted Rubio, saying the aircraft had been withdrawn because of a security threat allegedly backed by Iran.

“The planes did not leave suddenly. There was a real threat there,” Trump told reporters. Asked about an alleged Iranian plan to launch an attack from British territory using drones or other means, Trump warned, “If they have the audacity to do that, they will pay a big price.”

Arrests in Britain and Israeli intelligence

British security authorities last week arrested several British-Iranian dual nationals suspected of planning an attack near Fairford Air Base. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had provided Britain with intelligence about the alleged attack plot.

When asked about the alleged terrorist attack attempt on a flydubai flight, Trump also accused Iran of being directly involved or having encouraged the incident.

On September 30, flydubai co-pilot Hammam Al-Hammami, an Omani national, allegedly attacked the aircraft’s captain in the cockpit with a “Crash Axe” while the plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

Following the attack, the co-pilot reportedly put the aircraft into a steep descent, causing it to lose around 16,000 feet of altitude in 30 seconds. He allegedly intended to crash the aircraft into Ben Gurion Airport or a tower in Tel Aviv in a suicide attack.

The incident was brought under control after the injured captain, two retired pilots and courageous passengers entered the cockpit and restrained the attacker. The aircraft was later diverted for an emergency landing at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

The Pentagon has said its strategic B-1, B-2 and B-52 bombers remain fully capable and ready to conduct precision strikes anywhere in the world after taking off from bases within the United States.

title.rendered: Relief materials provided to flood-affected families in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Relief materials have been provided to 60 flood-affected households at Dandagaun of Uttargaya Rural Municipality-2 in Rasuwa.

The materials were distributed through the Integrated Humanitarian and Early Recovery Programme with support from Start Fund Nepal, according to Lubh Raj Neupane, executive director of Rural-Oriented Youth Movement (ROYM) Nepal.

Neupane said the assistance was aimed at providing immediate support to single-woman households affected by the Bhotekoshi flood and those at high risk. Winter essentials, drinking water and sanitation materials were distributed in the first phase.

Relief materials will also be distributed in wards 1 and 5 of the rural municipality next week, he said.

ROYM Nepal has also been facilitating community kitchens at three locations in Rasuwa and Nuwakot for the past month with financial support from UN Women. The kitchens provide breakfast, lunch, snacks and dinner to flood-affected and displaced families.

According to Goma Bista, administrative and financial assistant at ROYM Nepal, disaster-affected families have also been provided employment opportunities at the community kitchens in coordination with ward offices.

The organisation plans to provide financial assistance to at least 300 households to support their livelihoods. It is also preparing to distribute blankets, quilts, thermals, thermoses and hot-water bags to 1,000 households ahead of winter.

ROYM Nepal is also repairing flood-damaged water supply pipelines in Bidur Municipality of Nuwakot and Uttargaya Rural Municipality of Rasuwa.

title.rendered: Nepal slips one spot in Economic Freedom of the World report

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Nepal has dropped one place in the Economic Freedom of the World: 2026 Annual Report, released today by the Prosperity Foundation in collaboration with Canada’s Fraser Institute. Nepal ranks 90th out of 165 countries, down from 89th last year. This is the 19th consecutive year the foundation has released the report in Nepal.

Nepal scored 6.59 out of 10, up slightly from 6.58 in 2025. The raw data show its score has fully recovered from the Covid-19 dip, when it fell from 6.52 in 2019 to 6.31 in 2020.

Nepal’s rankings on the report’s five main indicators were mixed. On size of government, it fell from 49th (7.29) to 51st (7.25), and on legal system and property rights, it dropped from 91st (4.92) to 96th (4.82). On sound money, it slipped from 96th to 101st even though its score rose from 7.37 to 7.57. Nepal did improve on freedom to trade internationally, rising from 126th (6.21) to 117th (6.39), but fell on regulation from 37th (7.12) to 50th (6.90).

Of the 24 sub-indicators, Nepal improved on seven, declined on six and held steady on 11.

Hong Kong ranks first globally, followed by Switzerland, Singapore, New Zealand, the United States, Ireland, Denmark, Australia and Mauritius. Finland, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom share the final top-10 position. Venezuela ranks last. Among other countries, Japan is 13th, Germany 19th, France 39th, India 88th, China 110th and Russia 143rd.

According to the report, people in countries with higher economic freedom tend to be more prosperous and live longer. Countries in the top quartile had an average per capita income of $65,596 in 2024, compared with $9,552 in the bottom 20 percent.

title.rendered: Burn treatment service standards come into effect, setting out which hospitals will provide what care

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The government has prepared the “National Burn Treatment Service Standards” to bring uniformity to the treatment of burn patients across the country.

Prepared by the Curative Service Division under the Department of Health Services, the standards cover everything from initial burn treatment to specialist care, referral, rehabilitation and training of health workers.

The standards classify burn treatment services in Nepal into four levels. Level 1 is basic burn care, Level 2 is general burn care, Level 3 is specialist burn centres and Level 4 is super-specialist burn centres.

The standards also treat training of health workers as an important part of the treatment system. Health workers at the local level and in communities must be trained in initial burn treatment, patient classification, fluid management, pain control, wound dressing, monitoring, record-keeping and referral where necessary.

Under the standards, where a higher-level treatment centre is more than two hours away, the local hospital must develop the capacity to provide resuscitation care to burn patients for the first 24 hours. Level 3 and Level 4 centres have also been made responsible for further specialist and advanced treatment and training related to burns.

For first aid, the standards recommend cooling the burnt area under cool running water for 30 minutes where possible, and then covering it with a clean cloth or dressing. They also state clearly that toothpaste, soil, ghee, oil, butter, herbal pastes, and ice or ice water should not be applied to burns.

The standards also provide that systemic antibiotics should not be given routinely to all burn patients, and should be used only on the basis of medical evaluation when there is clear evidence of infection.

The standards link burn treatment with initial care, stabilisation, specialist treatment, surgery, infection control, nutrition, rehabilitation, psychosocial support and the referral system.

The Ministry of Health said the standards will ensure timely treatment and referral of burn patients at appropriate health institutions according to their condition, maintaining the quality and uniformity of burn care across the country.

title.rendered: Rabin Mahato files candidacy for Nepal at Youth Parliament Forum

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

The 153rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) is underway, with House of Representatives member Rabin Mahato participating as Nepal’s young parliamentarian.

Mahato represented Nepal at the Youth Parliament Forum on the conference’s second day.

He has registered his candidacy at the forum on Nepal’s behalf. While doing so, he called on parliamentarians from all countries to support his candidacy.

The IPU conference is being held in the city of Arusha in Tanzania, Africa.

Addressing the conference, Mahato noted that young people are very poorly represented in parliaments around the world and described the composition of Nepal’s current House of Representatives. He said 43 percent of the members of Nepal’s parliament are young parliamentarians.

Speaker Dol Prasad (DP) Aryal also spoke about parliamentary inclusion in Nepal when he addressed the 153rd IPU Assembly.

According to Aryal, Nepal’s House of Representatives has 35 percent women, 51 percent from various inclusive groups, five persons with disabilities and 37 percent young parliamentarians under 40.

He added that gender and sexual minority communities are also represented in parliament, and said that in this sense too Nepal’s federal parliament is progressive on inclusion.

Aryal said proportionate, meaningful and effective representation of different communities, classes and groups strengthens citizens’ sense of ownership of state institutions and public trust in the democratic system.

Mahato also described the current state of the federal parliament at the forum.

He also raised the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli floods in Nepal and the risks they posed to the health sector.

He also drew the attention of young parliamentarians to issues including the role young people should play in crisis management.

title.rendered: Rain continues in Karnali, warning issued for all districts

content.rendered:
Surkhet, October 7 – Most parts of Karnali Province have been receiving rain for the past 24 hours. Because rain is still falling in districts including Humla, Jajarkot, Dailekh, Surkhet and Western Rukum, a weather warning has been issued for all districts of the province for today.

With rain continuing across most of the province, people have been asked to carry out daily activities only after checking updated weather information and forecasts. Residents have been told to stay alert, as the rain could trigger landslides on hilly and sloping terrain, block roads and raise water levels in rivers and streams.

Rain is likely in various parts of Karnali tomorrow and the day after as well, and people have been asked to take extra care in risk-prone areas. High alert is needed especially in settlements at risk of landslides and in areas along roads, rivers and streams.

As transport could be disrupted by the rain, people have been asked to check weather and road conditions before long-distance travel and to avoid unnecessary trips along risky road sections. The authorities concerned have also urged people not to try to cross rivers and streams when the water level is high. Snowfall has been reported in Humla.

title.rendered: 7 in 10 Nepalis struggle to pay housing costs

content.rendered:
Photo: Habitat for Humanity International

Kathmandu, October 7

Seven in 10 people in Nepal frequently struggle to pay housing-related costs, while an equal proportion fear an unexpected setback could threaten their housing security, according to a new global study by Habitat for Humanity International.

The “Home at What Cost?” research, based on nationally representative surveys in 22 countries and responses from more than 30,000 people, found that 70 per cent of respondents in Nepal have difficulty meeting housing-related expenses, compared with 34 per cent globally.

The study also found that 28 per cent of respondents in Nepal had delayed or avoided medical care because of housing-related financial pressures, while 36 per cent had postponed necessary home repairs and 21 per cent had relied on food assistance.

Extreme weather is another major concern. Seventy-two per cent said extreme weather makes it difficult to feel safe where they live, while 70 per cent expect such conditions to make living where they currently reside more difficult within the next three years.

The report said 68 per cent of respondents considered their housing situation one of the biggest sources of stress in their lives, compared with 35 per cent globally.

Eliza Sthapit, national director of Habitat for Humanity Nepal, said the findings highlighted the need for safer, more affordable and resilient housing.

According to the organisation, Nepal needs an estimated 136,000 housing units, with an annual gap of around 34,000 units between homes built and those required.

The state-owned Dairy Development Corporation (DDC) and the Nepali Army have signed an agreement for the purchase and sale of milk and dairy products.

Under the agreement, the Nepali Army will regularly purchase milk from DDC for its barracks in 32 districts across the country.

According to the agreement, DDC will supply 10,251 litres of processed milk daily, amounting to 3.74 million litres annually, to the Army’s barracks.

The agreement also covers the supply of other dairy products. The Army will receive 365 kg of curd daily, or 133,522 kg annually, along with 37 kg of paneer daily, or 13,240 kg annually.

Similarly, DDC will supply 21 kg of whole milk powder daily, totalling 7,441 kg annually, and 15 kg of cheese daily, amounting to 5,278 kg annually.

The purchase agreement was signed on behalf of the Nepali Army by Brigadier General Sanjay Kumar Ranjit, Director of the Directorate of Supply and Transport, and on behalf of DDC by General Manager Dr Sharan Kumar Pandey.
