title.rendered: The femininity we celebrate, and the femininity we condemn

content.rendered:
I was thinking about Suman Sen’s film Elephants in the Fog recently, specifically about how it captures the delicate, dangerous space trans women are forced to navigate simply to exist on their own terms. Watching it felt like opening a door to my own memory.

I remember the women around the Blue Diamond Society and their midnight parades. I was fourteen, wearing skimpy clothes, carried by that clubbing-girl confidence, and I was completely enraptured. Yet, according to everything I had been taught, that was not how a respectable woman was supposed to look.

Society actively shamed what I was seeing, leaving me deeply confused because all I saw were people following the exact trends that would have been celebrated if worn by white influencers online.

Still, they lived a life I wanted: that audacity, that confidence, wearing dresses without my mother policing them. Even as society called them provocative and dangerous, there they were, prevailing. They sat in a nearby canteen, gossiping, laughing, and flaunting a style I would never have learned from my mother’s sense of class. They taught me femininity, and then they taught me what femininity was not. They taught me survival.

Their flawless makeup was what I admired most, yet that same art was used by others as a reason to condemn them. Growing up, my fourteen-year-old brain was constantly trying to solve the puzzle of what it meant to be a “correct” woman.

On one side, I had a massive fascination with Miss Nepal. I remember watching Nikita Chandak on screen and thinking, maybe that could be me. Miss Nepal sold the idea of the ultimate woman: intelligent, graceful and, above all, respectable. But her expression had to remain safe, sanitised so it would not agitate anyone.

On the other side, drag queens expressed femininity without restriction: loud, exaggerated and entirely on their own terms. I felt torn between the safety of the sanitised standard and the genuine freedom of the exaggerated one.

By 2016, the mainstream beauty world had exploded with pouty, over-lined lips, cut creases and heavy contouring, all celebrated as modern female empowerment. But these techniques had been built directly on the backs of drag queens and trans women. Mainstream culture took the very aesthetic it had once used to shame queer performers, rebranded it as a trend and stripped away credit from its creators.

Eventually came the Pride movement, and social acceptance expanded among my Gen Z peers. Being gay became tied to new social hierarchies and specific circles, like Thames College. Yet I did not rejoice simply because it had become fashionable. I thought of creators like Stan, who spoke about being treated like dirt in his home country despite his style. While mainstream gay culture became polished and digestible, I wondered whether the divas from Lazimpat were ever taken into consideration.

Before you are allowed to be a woman or a queer person in this society, you are expected to be palatable.

Mainstream culture embraces rich, polished figures who look “cleaner” while forgetting the raw predecessors who built the movement. Just as traditional femininity is policed, the LGBTQIA+ community is sanitised to be small, agreeable and easy to consume, reducing complex human beings to the “gay best friend” or a gender-fluid trend.

This sanitisation is not progress; it is control.

The same men who enforce rigid moral standards on women are often drawn to the very trans and queer identities they publicly shame, seeking out marginalised sex workers in the dark while demanding that their wives cover up at home. They accept queer people only when they have been sanitised for public consumption, revealing an inability to reconcile femininity when it operates outside their control.

When drag makeup or trans expression exaggerates femininity, it demands that you see art outside accepted rules. Beauty stops being merely soft or effortless. It becomes excessive, theatrical, angry, sexual, absurd and imperfect. That exaggeration proves femininity does not have to be quiet to be legitimate.

Yet when those same silhouettes appear on marginalised bodies, they are labelled cheap or vulgar. The same skirt is fashionable on one body and provocative on another. The same makeup is art on a stage and evidence of bad character on the street.

What changes? The clothes, or the person wearing them?

Transgender people are expected to be pitch-perfect symbols or figures of pity, but rarely complex human beings. Women face the exact same trap. They are placed on pedestals as symbols of beauty while being stripped of the right to be angry, flawed or absurd.

True empowerment is not a forced performance for the spectator. It is the simplicity of embodying your true mood without asking for permission.

My beautiful midnight ballerinas of Lazimpat Street still don their art. While mainstream society watches drag shows on television, sex workers on the street are rarely acknowledged in the light of day.

I remember one night, dressed more boldly than usual, when I gained the confidence to say a quick hello to them. Walking away, I realised how deeply women’s experiences mirror one another.

We divide women into those we admire and those we are afraid to become.

I used to resent those street divas. Now I realise that resentment was admiration. I wanted their colour, confidence and audacity to be seen without asking permission.

Femininity is not supposed to be one singular, polished aesthetic or the next social media trend. It is simply existing.

The greatest freedom would be to stop turning people into symbols long enough to let them simply be people.

Femininity was never supposed to be a prison made beautiful, and beauty was never supposed to be the price of being allowed to exist.

title.rendered: Repairs intensified on flood-damaged Beni-Jomsom-Korala road

content.rendered:
Myagdi, October 7

Repair and reconstruction work has been intensified along several sections of the Beni-Jomsom-Korala road under the Kaligandaki Corridor after floods and landslides triggered by heavy rainfall disrupted the route.

The 202-kilometre road connecting Pang of Kushma Municipality-1 in Parbat with the Korala border point in China via Beni, Myagdi and Mustang was disrupted at 55 locations. The Kaligandaki River flood washed away or damaged 10 sections following heavy rainfall from September 24 to 27.

Tejaswi Sharma, chief of the Beni-Jomsom-Korala Road Project, said preliminary repairs had been completed at all affected sites except Kunauta in Raghuganga Rural Municipality-2 and the bridge approach road at Pokharebagar in Annapurna Rural Municipality.

The Maldhunga-Kunauta and Korala-Pokharebagar sections have been restored for heavy vehicles. Landslide clearance and alternative routes have also been completed at Ratopani, Dhirchyang, Bhirkate, Mahabhir, Tiplyang and Begkhola.

About 250 metres of road was washed away at Kunauta, where four excavators and tippers are being deployed. A gabion wall is being built at Pokharebagar.

Narendra Subedi, head of the Federal Road Supervision and Monitoring Office in Pokhara, said efforts were underway to reopen the remaining sections by Monday.

The Department of Roads estimates that about Rs 3 billion will be required for reconstruction.

title.rendered: Early weather warnings ease paddy harvesting for Kanchanpur farmers

content.rendered:
Kanchanpur, October 7

Early weather warnings have made it easier for farmers in Kanchanpur to decide when to harvest paddy and protect their crops from rain and floods.

For years, farmers relied on the sky and their own judgment to determine when to harvest. Now, many check weather forecasts before entering their fields. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology provides information on the likelihood and amount of rainfall and other weather conditions. Farmers can also call the department’s toll-free number 1155 for updates.

Nilam Karki of Saraswati Tole in Krishnapur Municipality-2 grows paddy on five katthas of land. She said the forecasts have made harvest decisions easier.

“Earlier, we had to look at the clouds and make our own judgment about when to harvest. Now, weather forecasts have made it much easier,” Karki said.

Nirmala Badu of the same municipality, who grows paddy on four katthas, also checks the forecast before harvesting.

Farmers also receive siren and mobile phone alerts when river levels rise and flood risks increase.

Bisan Pant of Bedkot Municipality-7 said timely warnings have helped reduce flood-related crop losses.

According to the Agriculture Knowledge Centre, Kanchanpur, paddy is cultivated on 48,496 hectares of the district’s 56,363 hectares of cultivable land.

title.rendered: Narayani flood damages 1.15 km of embankment in Chitwan

content.rendered:
Chitwan, October 7

The Narayani River flood has damaged around 1.15 km of embankment along the Chitwan side of the river. Of the 35-km stretch from the Narayani Bridge westward to Golaghat in Bharatpur Metropolitan City, embankments have been constructed along about 20 km. The recent floods damaged 600 metres of embankment in the Siddhiganesh forest area, 300 metres in Majhuwa forest, 100 metres in Hirapur, and 50 metres each in Gareshwar, Ganjipur and Katero forest area.

According to Sagar Paudel, information officer at the Irrigation and Water Resources Management Project in Bharatpur, the embankments helped limit flood damage in Chitwan despite some inundation. However, the situation was more difficult on the Nawalparasi side, where embankment construction remains limited.

Floodwaters caused extensive erosion in several areas, including Amaltari, Nandapur, Sitapur, Serai, Parsauni, Tamaspur, Baguwa and Susta, Paudel said. Only about nine kilometres of embankment have been constructed along the 98-km stretch below the Narayani Bridge in Nawalparasi, leaving unprotected areas more vulnerable to river erosion.

title.rendered: Kishor Singh Rathore accuses Gagan Thapa of failing to do enough to unite Nepali Congress

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Nepali Congress presidential candidate Kishor Singh Rathore has accused party president Gagan Thapa of failing to make sufficient efforts to unite the party.

Speaking to journalist Nimesh Banjade on Himalaya Television’s Yaksha Prashna, Rathore said Thapa did not appear to have made the level of effort required to bring different factions of the party together.

“The effort that should have been made to unite the party was not visible,” Rathore said. “The intensive effort that was needed was not seen. We can only see things from outside; we do not know what happened internally.”

Rathore also accused Thapa of failing to ensure fairness in the distribution of election tickets during his tenure as party president.

He further questioned Thapa’s ability to maintain the party’s dignity, alleging that some of his supporters have recently resorted to abusive language.

“He cannot make this party dignified. His supporters are now engaging in verbal abuse. Abusing others is not the culture of the Nepali Congress,” Rathore said, adding that he considered such behaviour to be associated with communist politics.

Rathore said he has a plan to improve the party’s internal culture and bring it back to what he described as the traditional values of the Nepali Congress.

title.rendered: Snow cuts off Limi as residents face shortages and isolation

content.rendered:
Surkhet, October 7

Heavy snowfall has cut off the northern parts of Namkha Rural Municipality in Humla from the road network, leaving residents of the Limi and Hilsa areas struggling to travel and access essential supplies.

Up to three and a half feet of snow has accumulated at Nyalu and Nara La, blocking roads leading to Limi since the first week of October. With the routes closed, residents needing urgent medical treatment or other essential services have been forced to consider chartering helicopters.

The road to Limi through Nyalu in Ward 5 and Nara La in Ward 6 has been buried under thick snow. Paljor Tamang, ward chair of Namkha-6, said the snowfall has also made it difficult for residents of Humla staying in Taklakot to return home ahead of Dashain and Tihar.

“If someone falls sick in the village, there is no road to take them out immediately. We have to charter a helicopter,” Tamang said. “The snow needs to be cleared and the road reopened as soon as possible.”

Three feet of snow covers Tumling

Tumling Bazaar, a high-altitude settlement in Namkha-6, has been buried under heavy snow following snowfall about 10 days ago.

The settlement, located at an altitude of around 4,000 metres, received heavy snowfall from October 9 to 11, with locals reporting up to three feet of snow on the ground.

Kunjok Tamang, a resident of Halji village in Limi, said hotel operators, yak herders and other residents in Tumling have been struggling even to leave their homes.

“There is so much snow that even walking outside has become difficult,” he said. “People have been forced to stay indoors.”

The snowfall has turned the entire Limi area white, while thick layers of snow on roads and surrounding paths have disrupted daily activities.

Four-hour walk now takes two days

The journey from Tumling to Jang, which normally takes about four hours on foot, now takes local residents up to two days.

With roads and foot trails covered in snow, vehicles cannot operate and residents have been forced to travel on foot. Since Tumling also lacks communication services, residents have to reach Jang to establish contact with the outside world.

The disruption of both transport and communication has added to the difficulties faced by people living in the remote settlement.

Water sources frozen

The cold has also frozen water taps in Tumling, leaving residents without their regular supply of drinking water. With no alternative source available, locals have been melting snow to meet their daily water needs.

Residents say the need to melt snow for drinking water has made everyday life even more difficult. This year’s snowfall has also arrived unusually early compared with previous years.

Essential supplies difficult to transport

The closure of roads has disrupted the supply of food, firewood and other essential goods to Limi. With vehicles unable to reach the area, residents have been forced to carry supplies on foot.

Local hotel businesses have also been affected. Eighteen hotel operators in Til, 90 in Halji, three in Jang and 11 in Tumling are reportedly affected, while two hotels are operating in Takchi.

Nyalu La, located at an altitude of around 5,000 metres, is one of the main entry points into Limi. Heavy snowfall has covered the road there, preventing vehicles from operating.

Police post also struggling under snow

The snowfall has affected daily life at the police post in Sunkhani, Limi, where around three feet of snow has accumulated after three consecutive days of snowfall.

The lack of firewood has made cooking difficult, while frozen water pipes have created a shortage of drinking water. Firewood and food are being carried from Halji village to the police post.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Shankar Khadka of the District Police Office, Humla, said the Sunkhani police post was also facing difficulties due to the snowfall.

Communication services in Sunkhani are weak. Police personnel stationed there have to walk for about four hours once a day to reach Halji, where 4G service is available and information can be exchanged.

Ten police personnel, including an assistant sub-inspector, are stationed at the post.

Road through Nara La needs heavy machinery

Nara La, located at an altitude of 4,670 metres, has received up to three and a half feet of snow, blocking the Hilsa-Simikot road section.

According to Armed Police Force Inspector Kedar Sapkota of the border security post, clearing the accumulated snow manually would be extremely difficult and a JCB excavator would be required to reopen the road.

Pema Lama, operator of Mansarovar Hotel in Hilsa, has urged the Hilsa-Simikot Road Project to clear the snow and resume transport services.

The road closure has affected Armed Police Force and Nepal Police personnel stationed in Hilsa, as well as employees at the Yari border customs and immigration offices, hotel operators and local traders.

Heavy snowfall arrives unusually early

Local residents say Hilsa has experienced heavy snowfall from September 26 this year for the first time in around 15 years. In previous years, heavy snowfall generally began only after November.

Residents have attributed the unusually early snowfall to changes in weather patterns. With roads blocked just ahead of Dashain and Tihar, Humla residents staying in Taklakot are also struggling to return home.

Residents of Limi and Hilsa have urged the concerned authorities to immediately clear the accumulated snow and restore road connectivity to the region.

title.rendered: Roads remain blocked in several districts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 7

Roads in several parts of the country remained fully or partially blocked on Tuesday due to floods and landslides, according to police.

The main highways in Rasuwa remain completely obstructed. The Beni-Jomsom road at Baisari in Raghuganga Rural Municipality-2 of Myagdi has also not yet reopened.

In Manang, the Khangsar-Besisahar road section has resumed operation on only one side. The road was damaged by a flood on the night of September 25, affecting the route from Besisahar towards Khangsar.

Meanwhile, a landslide at Janti in Baudikali Rural Municipality-3 of Nawalparasi East has reduced the Kaligandaki Corridor to one-way traffic. Large vehicles are currently unable to pass through the affected section.

The highways in Rasuwa have remained closed since August 26 following floods. The Beni-Jomsom road has been affected by a landslide since September 26, while the Janti section of the Kaligandaki Corridor has been operating one-way since September 30.

Authorities have advised travellers to check road conditions before starting their journey, particularly along routes affected by recent floods and landslides.

title.rendered: Tears and tributes as Messi bids farewell to Argentina

content.rendered:
Buenos Aires, October 7

Lionel Messi has brought his 21-year international career to an emotional end, making his final appearance for Argentina in front of more than 85,000 fans at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires.

The 39-year-old captain signed off in style, scoring once and providing two assists as Argentina defeated Benin 3-0 in a match that was as much a celebration of Messi’s career as it was a football fixture.

Playing his record 208th international for Argentina, Messi set up veteran defender Nicolás Otamendi for the opening goal before Nico Paz doubled the lead. Messi then completed the farewell in the 71st minute, converting a penalty for his 126th international goal.

The occasion had been billed as “The Last Tango”, and the emotional significance of the night was evident long before kick-off.

Messi wiped away tears as the Argentina team bus made its way through streets packed with supporters. He later walked onto the pitch with his three children, while his wife Antonela Roccuzzo and mother Celia Cuccittini watched from the VIP box.

A giant Argentina shirt bearing Messi’s famous No. 10 and the word “Gracias” was laid out on the pitch before the match, prompting a huge roar from the crowd.

Messi became emotional again during the national anthem as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana performed alongside a banner reading “The Malvinas are Argentine.”

The match was stopped in the 10th minute in honour of Messi’s iconic shirt number, with the entire stadium joining in a minute-long ovation.

But the biggest moment came in the 71st minute, when Messi stepped up to take a penalty and scored to complete his final international appearance.

‘I gave it my all’

At the final whistle, the celebrations continued as a drone show lit up the sky above the Monumental, forming an image of Messi and paying tribute to the eight-time Ballon d’Or winner.

“It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told the crowd after the match.

“Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.”

Despite the emotion, Messi said he had no regrets about his decision.

“Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through,” he said.

His farewell came around two and a half months after Argentina lost the World Cup final to Spain 1-0 in New Jersey. Messi left that match in tears after a difficult performance.

“I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote after that defeat.

The end of an era

Messi’s journey with Argentina has spanned more than two decades, taking him from a young player carrying enormous expectations to the captain who finally delivered the World Cup.

He led Argentina to the 2021 Copa América title before guiding the team to victory at the 2022 World Cup, ending the country’s 36-year wait for a third world title.

Argentina also won the Copa América again in 2024.

During Messi’s international career, Argentina won one World Cup, finished runners-up in 2014 and 2026, and claimed two Copa América titles.

Before his final match, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate at a ceremony held at the Argentine Football Association headquarters.

“To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!” Messi joked after receiving the honour.

Outside the AFA headquarters, supporters displayed a giant Argentine flag featuring Messi’s image and the words “The joy of my life.”

Former Barcelona teammate Neymar also paid tribute to Messi on X.

“It’s not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more,” Neymar wrote.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, meaning his retirement from international football does not necessarily mark the end of his playing career.

However, following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, Messi has suggested that he could also bring his club career to an end earlier than expected.

For Argentina, though, the farewell at the Monumental marked the closing chapter of one of the country’s most celebrated football careers.

After 21 years, 208 appearances, 126 goals and a World Cup triumph, Messi has finally said goodbye to the Argentina shirt.

title.rendered: Seven complaints filed against 13 proposed ambassadors

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The parliamentary hearing process for 13 ambassadors proposed by the government has begun, with the Parliamentary Hearing Committee distributing the complaints filed against the nominees among its members on Tuesday.

The committee also distributed the proposed ambassadors’ work plans for review.

According to the committee, two complaints have been filed against the proposed ambassadors as a group, while three individual complaints have been filed against Jigyan Kumar Thapa, who has been proposed as Nepal’s ambassador to Japan. Two complaints have been filed individually against Giribahadur Sunar, the nominee for Saudi Arabia.

The Cabinet had recommended ambassadors for 13 countries on September 18. The nominees are Dr Nischal Nath Pandey for India, Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma for China, Chiran Jung Thapa for the United States, and former army chief Gaurav Shumsher Rana for the United Kingdom.

Other nominees are Jigyan Kumar Thapa for Japan, Suresh Kumar Karn for Israel, Prapti Sherchan for Spain, Saru Joshi for Germany, Dr Padmakshi Rana for Oman, Chudamani Kharel for Malaysia, Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha for South Korea, Dr Manchala Jha for Sri Lanka and Giribahadur Sunar for Saudi Arabia.

The Parliamentary Hearing Committee had decided on October 24 to invite complaints against all 13 nominees. Seven complaints were filed within the 10-day period.

Questions over ambassador appointment guidelines

One of the complaints calls for the rejection of all 13 nominations, alleging that the government did not follow the Ambassador Appointment Directive, 2018.

The directive sets criteria for ambassadorial appointments and calls for a balance between career diplomats and political or other distinguished professionals.

Under the directive, at least 50 per cent of ambassadorial appointments are to be made from among gazetted first-class or higher-ranking officials of the Foreign Service. The remaining 50 per cent can be appointed from the political sector or among distinguished and specialised individuals from other fields.

The complaint alleges that these provisions were not followed in the latest nominations.

Complaints against nominees for Saudi Arabia and Japan

Giribahadur Sunar, the nominee for Saudi Arabia, faces two individual complaints. One alleges involvement in violence and mistreatment of women, as well as an extramarital relationship. Another alleges involvement in financial and criminal activities.

The complaints have called on the parliamentary committee to investigate the allegations and examine Sunar’s personal and professional background before approving his nomination.

Sunar is a PhD researcher in sociology at Tribhuvan University and has more than 25 years of experience in international development, policy advisory work and multi-stakeholder governance. He has also worked in social protection, gender equality, social inclusion and community-based climate adaptation.

Jigyan Kumar Thapa, the nominee for Japan, faces three individual complaints. One alleges that he renounced Nepali citizenship and obtained permanent residency in a foreign country. Another questions his eligibility for the ambassadorial position, while a third alleges that he owns property and has business, investment, bank loan and other commercial interests in Japan.

Thapa has postgraduate qualifications in international relations and law from Yokohama National University and a bachelor’s degree in international cooperation from Sumei University. He has worked in Japan on Nepal-Japan bilateral programmes, international cooperation and public policy and has been involved in high-level exchanges between the two countries.

No individual complaints against 11 nominees

No individual complaints have been filed against the remaining 11 nominees, including those proposed for India, China, the United States and the United Kingdom.

Dr Nischal Nath Pandey, proposed as ambassador to India, is an academic specialising in Nepal’s foreign policy and South Asian affairs. He has previously served as executive director of the Institute of Foreign Affairs and as an adviser to the National Planning Commission.

Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma, nominated for China, is an economist and scholar of China-related affairs. He has more than two decades of experience in academia, institutional governance and Nepal-China policy cooperation.

Chiran Jung Thapa, proposed for the United States, is a specialist in national security and international affairs with two decades of experience in security policy, crisis management and diplomacy.

Former army chief Gaurav Shumsher Rana has been nominated as ambassador to the UK. He served as chief of the Nepali Army during Nepal’s transition to a federal democratic republic and led military rescue and relief operations following the 2015 earthquake.

The government has presented the other nominees as professionals with expertise in fields including information technology, banking, international development, gender equality, sustainable development, public administration, climate resilience, water diplomacy and public policy.

The parliamentary hearing committee will now examine the complaints, qualifications and work plans of the nominees before deciding whether to endorse their appointments.

title.rendered: A midnight meeting led to a phone trail. Now an AIG faces suspension and a probe

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The suspension of Armed Police Force (APF) Additional Inspector General (AIG) Banshiraj Dahal has raised questions inside Nepal’s security establishment, with investigators looking into his alleged links with individuals under investigation and the possible leakage of sensitive state information.

The Home Ministry announced Dahal’s suspension on Monday evening, saying he had allegedly leaked sensitive security-related information and acted in breach of official conduct. The ministry, however, did not say what information Dahal allegedly disclosed.

What has brought the serving AIG under scrutiny appears to be a chain of events that began with a former chief justice being taken into police custody in the middle of the night.

The midnight visit

On September 26, police went to the residence of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana late at night and took him to the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office in Teku at around 2 am. About an hour later, Dahal arrived at the same office.

According to sources, the AIG reached Teku at around 3am, met Rana and remained there for roughly two hours before leaving at around 5am.

The timing of the visit drew attention because Rana was in police custody and Dahal had allegedly gone to meet him without informing the relevant authorities.

Dahal and Rana are related by marriage, with Rana being Dahal’s father-in-law. Dahal is said to have gone to the crime investigation office after learning that Rana had been taken into custody. But investigators have also questioned whether a serving AIG should have visited a person in police custody in the middle of the night without going through the chain of command.

The incident was reportedly brought to the attention of both the Home Ministry and the Prime Minister’s Office. It later became one of the issues surrounding Dahal’s suspension.

Then came the phone trail

Rana was kept at the crime investigation office for around 12 hours. During that period, police examined his mobile phone and messages. Investigators reportedly found contacts and conversations that led them to another person, identified as Inam Sapkota.

Sapkota was subsequently placed under investigation.

The Nepal Police Special Bureau arrested him at Tribhuvan International Airport several days ago while he was preparing to travel to Delhi. He was reportedly questioned for a day before being handed over to the Kathmandu District Police Range.

Kathmandu Police spokesperson SP Dan Bahadur Thapa said Sapkota is currently being investigated for alleged indecent behaviour after police obtained a detention extension from the Kathmandu District Administration Office. But investigators are looking beyond that charge.

According to sources, examination of Sapkota’s phone revealed connections with Rana, Dahal and several other security officials.

It was the alleged frequency of communication between Sapkota and Dahal that reportedly brought the AIG further under the government’s scrutiny.

What information was allegedly exchanged?

This is where the investigation takes a more serious turn.

A senior source claimed that investigators found exchanges between Dahal and Sapkota concerning information about the activities of Prime Minister Balen Shah. The source also claimed that information relating to the prime minister’s activities and financial transactions was found on the phone.

Investigators are said to have found conversations that allegedly referred to specific amounts of money.

“These matters are being investigated seriously,” the source said.

However, the government has not publicly disclosed the specific information Dahal is accused of leaking, nor has it publicly confirmed the details of the alleged exchanges. The allegations therefore remain part of an ongoing investigation.

The timing makes the suspension more significant

Dahal’s suspension comes just as his tenure as AIG was nearing its end. He was appointed AIG on May 11, 2022 and was due to complete his four-year term on October 13.

Under the APF Rules, an AIG normally serves a four-year term. However, the government can extend the tenure by one year on the recommendation of the APF inspector general.

APF headquarters had already recommended that Dahal’s tenure be extended. The suspension now leaves that recommendation in doubt.

Instead of preparing for a possible extension, Dahal is facing a departmental investigation that could potentially end with serious disciplinary action.

Why was he suspended before the investigation?

The decision to suspend an AIG before completing the investigation is itself significant. Under the APF Rules, suspension can be used when there is a risk that allowing an officer to remain in office could affect the investigation, allow evidence to be destroyed or manipulated, cause financial loss to the government, affect organisational morale or damage the reputation of the force.

Rule 90 also prohibits APF personnel from disclosing confidential information obtained in the course of their official duties to unauthorised individuals or the media without government approval.

Depending on the findings, violations of these provisions can result in removal or dismissal from service.

The Home Ministry has assigned AIG Anjanikumar Pokharel, who works at APF headquarters’ Human Resources Department, to investigate the allegations. He has been given three days to submit his report.

A rare move against a serving AIG

Former APF AIG Narayan Babu Thapa said he could not recall a previous case in which an AIG had been suspended specifically over allegations of leaking confidential information.

“This is a completely new development,” Thapa said, adding that while internal investigations and disciplinary actions are routine, the allegation of leaking confidential information makes the case unusual.

The decision by the Home Ministry to publicly announce the suspension has also attracted attention. A former APF inspector general said the public statement could be understood as a warning that access to sensitive state information comes with responsibility. Home Minister Sudan Gurung has made that message explicit.

“Sensitive state information is not anyone’s private property; it is a public responsibility,” Gurung said. “A position gives access to information, but it does not give anyone the right to misuse it.”

He said anyone who deliberately breaches the confidentiality entrusted to them by the state would face legal action.

For now, the central question remains unanswered: what exactly did AIG Dahal allegedly disclose, and to whom?

The three-day investigation is expected to provide the first official answers.

title.rendered: Former CAAN chief Sanjiv Gautam to remain in custody in Pokhara airport corruption case

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Former director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN), Sanjiv Gautam, has been ordered to remain in custody pending trial in a corruption case related to the procurement of consultancy services for the construction of Pokhara Regional International Airport.

A joint bench of Supreme Court justices Dr Nahakul Subedi and Tek Prasad Dhungana upheld an earlier order of the Special Court, ruling that Gautam should remain in custody while the case is heard.

The corruption case concerns allegations that public funds were caused to be lost or misused during the procurement of consultancy services for the airport project.

Under an agreement between CAAN and China CAMC Engineering Co., Ltd. for the construction of the Pokhara airport, the cost of consultancy services was to be covered under a “provisional sum”. However, according to the case, the consultancy services were procured in violation of the agreement. A separate cost estimate was prepared for a higher amount, allowing expenditure from a budget outside the terms of the original agreement.

The prosecution alleges that Gautam, while serving as CAAN director general, approved the proposal on September 2, 2016, and subsequently entered into the consultancy services procurement agreement on May 7, 2018.

The Special Court had ordered Gautam’s detention on June 16, 2026, stating that he appeared to be the main official responsible for the decision based on the evidence available at the preliminary stage.

The Supreme Court has now ruled that the Special Court’s order was issued in accordance with legal procedure and found no grounds to overturn it.

Gautam will therefore remain in custody while the corruption case proceeds to trial.

title.rendered: UML directive bars public criticism of party leadership, warns of disciplinary action

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The CPN-UML has issued an inter-party directive tightening party discipline and barring leaders and cadres from publicly criticising the party leadership, policy or decisions.

The directive, issued by party chair KP Sharma Oli following the UML’s third Central Committee meeting held in September, warns that anyone who publicly criticises, opposes, denounces or insults the party leadership, engages in factionalism or carries out “anarchic and undisciplined activities” will face disciplinary action.

The directive states that past conduct will be treated as a closed chapter, with the latest Central Committee meeting serving as the cut-off point.

It also gives the Central Disciplinary Commission greater authority to take action against those violating party discipline. The Central Organisation Department will also be authorised to initiate disciplinary proceedings where necessary.

The directive comes after the UML suffered a major defeat in the March 5 election, following growing calls within the party for leadership restructuring.

The party had collected suggestions from 13 groups after the election, with most calling for changes in the leadership structure. Senior leaders including Bishnu Prasad Paudel, Prithvi Subba Gurung and Shankar Pokhrel had also led calls for organisational restructuring after the election.

However, the restructuring task force’s report was not discussed at the Central Committee meeting. Instead, Oli presented his own report, whose conclusions have been incorporated into the latest inter-party directive.

Oli accepts responsibility but says he will not step down

In the directive, Oli says he accepts moral responsibility for the election result as party chair but rejects the argument that accepting responsibility means resigning.

“I accept moral responsibility for the election result as party chair,” Oli says in the directive, while arguing that responsibility and leaving the field are not the same thing.

He says the election defeat had multiple causes and should not be attributed solely to the party chair.

“Self-reflection is not a practice of removing the leadership. It is a process of making the leadership more responsible,” the directive states.

The document also compares the election defeat to a multi-causal event, arguing that those placing all blame on the party chair are simply looking for an easy target.

Ten reasons cited for election defeat

The directive identifies 10 reasons for the UML’s election defeat, most of which relate to shortcomings within the party organisation and its cadres.

The reasons include the party’s failure to reach people at the grassroots, weak engagement with young people, failure to effectively counter opposition attacks, an oversized party structure, unmet ambitions among party members and shortcomings in delivering services to the public.

It also cites the growing distance between central and local leadership, mistakes in candidate selection and the party’s failure to effectively communicate its ideology to voters.

The directive says the party failed to adequately explain how its ideology relates to the lives of a new generation, while its achievements were also overshadowed by negative campaigning and misinformation.

It does not identify a specific failure by the party leadership among the 10 reasons for the defeat. Instead, it places much of the responsibility on the wider party organisation for failing to communicate the leadership’s work and respond effectively to public concerns.

The directive outlines two major tasks for the party — protecting the Constitution and democracy and preparing for the next election — along with 15 organisational tasks for party cadres.

Bidya Devi Bhandari given senior leader role

The directive also formally brings former president Bidya Devi Bhandari into an active political role in the UML, assigning her the position of senior leader.

Bhandari will hold the second-highest position in the party hierarchy after the chair and participate in meetings of the Central Committee, Politburo, Standing Committee and Secretariat.

According to the directive, she will assist the party chair and contribute to timely and appropriate decisions for the party.

title.rendered: Nepal Tourism Board to install traditional swings at tourist destinations for Dashain

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The Nepal Tourism Board is set to install and operate traditional swings (linge ping) at various tourist destinations across the country during Dashain, linking Nepal’s traditional culture and festivals with tourism promotion.

The board’s Tourism Heritage and Tourism Development Division will install the swings in collaboration with local governments and tourism-related organisations, including in the Kathmandu Valley and other popular tourist destinations.

The board has partnered with Lalitpur Metropolitan City, Kirtipur Municipality, Changunarayan Municipality, Bhaktapur Tourism Development Committee, Thamel Tourism Development Committee, Himalayan Rescue Association, Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal (TAAN), Hotel Association Nepal (HAN), the Hotel Entrepreneurs Federation and hotel and tourism associations in various provinces.

Under the agreements, the linge ping will be constructed at selected tourist destinations and operated throughout the Dashain period. Priority will be given to locations with high tourist footfall and those suitable for cultural activities.

The agreements require the concerned local governments and organisations to ensure safety, manage crowds and take measures to minimise the risk of accidents while operating the swings.

They will also be responsible for removing the swings after Dashain and restoring the sites to their original condition.

The Tourism Board said the initiative aims to preserve and promote Nepal’s traditional culture and festivals while using them to further develop cultural tourism.

The government has banned the operation of trailers and other large cargo vehicles on the Narayangadh-Kathmandu road section during the Dashain festival.

The decision was taken at a meeting of stakeholders held at the Department of Transport Management on Tuesday, as passenger vehicles are expected to face heavy traffic during the festival period.

The restriction has been introduced to ease traffic movement and facilitate the transportation of passengers during the peak Dashain travel period.

title.rendered: Bidsbazar launches pre-owned auction marketplace in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Bidsbazar, a brand of Darshika Ecommerce Pvt. Ltd., has launched as a pre-owned auction marketplace, offering a structured digital platform for buying and selling second-hand and resale goods.

The platform was officially launched at Dees Boutique Hotel in Kathmandu. It connects individual sellers, households, resellers, small traders, collectors and second-hand shoppers through a digital marketplace.

According to the company, eligible listings offer buyers three purchasing options: direct purchase at the displayed price, bargaining within applicable rules and timeframes, and bidding in an active auction.

Sellers can choose the selling method appropriate for their listings and, where applicable, set minimum acceptable prices. The platform also targets businesses and eligible sellers seeking to sell resale, surplus and stock-clearance inventory.

Bidsbazar said it has introduced user verification and account controls, seller ratings, activity monitoring, reporting and support mechanisms to promote trust and reduce scams, fake inquiries and suspicious activity.

The platform also features a Seller Points and Tier system under which successful sales contribute to sellers’ points and progression through different tiers. Higher tiers provide access to different platform benefits and a larger share of the applicable Variable Pool.

Bidsbazar said it acts as a technology facilitator rather than buying, selling or owning products listed on the platform.

Election Commissioner Dr Rajib Subba said it would be necessary to map the ICT-related knowledge, skills, human resources and technical capacity available not only at the Election Commission but also across various government agencies when implementing an internet voting system.

He said identifying and utilising the technical human resources, expertise and institutional capacity required to move towards implementing an internet voting system would provide a basis for its implementation.

title.rendered: What it takes to build the next generation of Nepali entrepreneurs

content.rendered:
For Nepal to become truly prosperous, we need to create more opportunities. We need quality jobs, modern infrastructure and, more importantly, strong entrepreneurial ecosystems. Entrepreneurs are drivers of economic growth. They inspire people, create jobs and transform societies. Nepal can no longer rely primarily on a traditional agriculture-based economy, remittance income and labour migration. We need businesses, and businesses are built on more than ideas. Scaling a business requires discipline, execution and resilience, not luck.

Entrepreneurial ventures and startups are becoming an increasingly important part of Nepal’s urban economy. For these businesses to succeed, they must embrace certain principles. Here are eight lessons that can help Nepali entrepreneurs build and scale sustainable businesses.

1. Put the problem first, not the product

Successful businesses identify a genuine problem and then develop an effective solution. In contrast, many entrepreneurs create a product first, fall in love with it, and only later discover that there is little market demand or a limited customer base.

A real problem is the true reason for a venture to exist. A product that does not solve a meaningful problem is a solution to a question no one asked.

Nepali platforms such as eSewa and Khalti did not succeed simply because they used sophisticated technology. They addressed real problems. People were tired of standing in long queues, carrying cash and having limited access to convenient financial services. These platforms understood customer pain points and built businesses around them.

For an entrepreneur, removing obstacles from customers’ lives is more important than building a flashy product.

2. Make speed a competitive weapon

Speed matters in a competitive world. Many ventures fail because of slow execution, hesitation and perfectionism. There should not be a large gap between “we should build this” and “we built this.”

The faster a product reaches the market, the sooner customers can interact with it and the sooner the business can test its assumptions. This increases the potential for success.

It is often wiser to learn from a real market than from a whiteboard. Startups can test, learn and pivot after receiving market feedback, reducing the risk of wasting significant amounts of time and capital on an idea that does not work.

3. Monitor your cash flow and track ROI closely

Startups typically operate under tight financial constraints. Nepal also has relatively high interest rates, a strong reliance on bank lending and limited access to venture capital. This makes careful cash-flow management particularly important.

If expenses consistently exceed incoming cash, a business can become unsustainable even when its revenue is growing.

Businesses must also be prepared for unexpected setbacks and maintain sufficient working capital to withstand them. At the same time, entrepreneurs need to track their Return on Investment (ROI) carefully so that underperforming channels do not continue consuming valuable resources.

Monitoring ROI also helps evaluate operational efficiency. It can provide early warning signs and allow entrepreneurs to take corrective action before problems become more costly.

4. Think from first principles: innovate rather than imitate

First-principles thinking involves breaking a complex problem down into its fundamental components and then using those fundamentals to develop a solution.

Many businesses in Nepal are built by copying competitors and assuming that “this is how things have always been done.” But imitation rarely leads to meaningful innovation.

Innovation often begins with better questions rather than better answers.

Take cafés in the Kathmandu Valley. Instead of simply opening another conventional café, an entrepreneur could identify an unmet customer need and build a business around it. The same principle applies to software companies. Rather than developing another conventional website, mobile app or software product, they should ask what new or underserved problems they can solve.

The objective should not be to build what already exists slightly better. It should be to rethink what needs to exist in the first place.

5. Use reverse benchmarking: win by exploiting neglect

Reverse benchmarking means identifying what competitors do poorly or consistently overlook and then excelling in those areas.

Whatever competitors treat as untouchable is worth questioning.

Nepal can be fertile ground for this strategy because many sectors still operate through traditional business models. Agriculture, for example, offers significant opportunities. Much of the industry continues to rely on multiple layers of intermediaries, yet there is considerable scope for businesses that build more direct relationships between farmers and international buyers.

Reverse benchmarking works by identifying competitors’ blind spots. While established businesses may focus on volume, for instance, a new entrant could focus on premium positioning, quality and higher margins.

The opportunity is often not where everyone is looking. It can be where everyone else has stopped looking.

6. Harness the power of technology and AI

Technology can remove constraints that once limited businesses. Artificial intelligence can reduce operating costs, improve customer service and increase productivity.

AI has also made it possible for businesses with relatively small teams to perform tasks that previously required much larger workforces and, in some cases, compete in international markets.

Strategic use of AI can provide an advantage that was previously unavailable to small businesses. Technology has increasingly become a leveller, allowing smaller companies to access tools and capabilities that were once largely available only to larger organisations.

The opportunity for entrepreneurs is not simply to use AI because it is fashionable. It is to identify where technology can fundamentally improve the way a business operates, serves customers or creates value.

7. Align with the macroeconomic tide; don’t swim against it

Entrepreneurs rarely succeed by fighting broader economic trends. They need to understand the direction in which the economy is moving and adapt their business models accordingly.

Nepal is seeing growing opportunities in areas such as hydropower, digital trade and tourism. Globally, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, quantum computing and industrial automation are likely to reshape industries and economies.

Demographic trends matter too. A country’s median age, for example, can influence consumer demand, labour markets and the types of products and services that businesses need to provide.

Founders should therefore think beyond the immediate market. They should ask where Nepal’s economy and the global economy are likely to be five or ten years from now, and position their businesses accordingly.

8. Think beyond Nepal’s borders

Nepal is home to roughly 30 million people, with relatively low average incomes. Our domestic market is not large enough to support every ambitious founder seeking to build a large-scale company.

Nepal should be treated as a base, not a ceiling.

Export-oriented thinking and globally competitive digital products should become a larger part of Nepal’s entrepreneurial culture. Founders should ask themselves, “Can this business compete anywhere in the world?”

This shift in perspective — from building for Nepal to building from Nepal for the world — can help Nepali businesses become globally relevant.

Nepal needs more entrepreneurs who are willing to think beyond the limitations of the domestic market, challenge conventional ways of doing business and build companies that can compete internationally.

The opportunity is there. What matters now is whether we have the discipline, ambition and willingness to seize it.

title.rendered: Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to Francis Halzen

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics to scientist Francis Halzen.

Halzen was awarded the prize for establishing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and detecting high-energy neutrino particles from space.

Halzen developed the concept of using ice at the South Pole to track neutrino particles. He first proposed the idea in 1988.

Neutrinos are found throughout the universe. These particles can easily pass through the Earth and the human body. Only occasionally do neutrinos collide with an atomic nucleus.

When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, sensors placed in clear ice record the flash of light produced by the interaction. Based on this principle, the IceCube Observatory, covering an area of one cubic kilometre, was built at the South Pole in 2011.

title.rendered: ‘The Nepali Congress needs to break free from factional politics’

content.rendered:
The Nepali Congress has significantly expanded its organisational structure through its 15th General Convention, increasing the size of its Central Working Committee from 231 to 297 members and adding more office-bearer positions. The decision has drawn criticism from within and outside the party, with questions being raised over whether the Congress has created an unnecessarily large or “jumbo” leadership structure.

Party president Gagan Thapa, however, argues that the expansion is driven by the need to make the party more inclusive, broaden opportunities for leadership and create space for groups that have traditionally had limited representation in the party’s top decision-making body.

Thapa says the new structure is intended to bring more young people, professionals, workers and Nepalis living abroad into the Central Committee, while also protecting the proportional representation of different communities. He argues that expanding the number of office-bearers will also help address internal divisions following the special General Convention and provide greater opportunities for women and members of historically underrepresented communities to rise to senior leadership positions.

At the same time, Thapa says the changes are not simply about creating more positions. The revised statute assigns specific responsibilities to office-bearers and Central Committee members, including the newly created position of senior vice president, which he describes as being similar to a co-president in terms of handling the party’s internal affairs. He says the objective is to free the party president to focus more on national politics, public engagement and the broader direction of the party.

Thapa also outlines a series of longer-term organisational reforms he wants to pursue. These include ending factional control over candidate selection, introducing a “one person, one executive responsibility” principle, digitising the party and eventually allowing ordinary Nepali Congress members across the country to directly elect the party leadership rather than relying on General Convention representatives gathered in Kathmandu.

With the nomination process for the General Convention underway, Thapa also addresses the unusually large number of candidates seeking positions in the Central Committee and argues that the absence of factional gatekeeping has opened the door to a much wider pool of aspirants. He explains why he has chosen not to form a panel of his own and why he has privately urged some experienced leaders not to contest for office-bearer positions, arguing that the party needs their experience regardless of whether they hold a formal leadership post.

In this interview with Onlinekhabar’s Lilu Dumre, Thapa discusses the thinking behind the expanded Central Committee, the new distribution of responsibilities, the future of party leadership and the reforms he believes are necessary to transform the Nepali Congress into a more inclusive, democratic and functional organisation. Excerpts:

Political parties have long faced criticism for having unwieldy structures and oversized committees. Yet the Nepali Congress has increased its Central Committee from 231 to 297. Why?

Under the previous statute, the Central Committee had 231 members. This time, we realised that without special provisions for young people, it would be difficult for them to get elected because of the party’s existing structure and membership composition. So we created a separate youth cluster and added 21 positions.

We also wanted representation for Nepalis living abroad. Although the party has organisational structures overseas, they had never been represented in the Central Committee. We also wanted to bring in professionals and workers, who otherwise had very little opportunity to enter the Central Committee.

The party had become inclusive in terms of communities, but the same people who had been working in the party for years were continuing to come to the top, regardless of which cluster they represented. Young people, professionals, workers and Nepalis living abroad were largely missing.

The new positions were open to everyone, however, which meant the proportional representation of Dalits, Madhesis, Muslims, Janajatis and other communities would have declined. So we also had to adjust their representation. That was one reason the Central Committee became larger.

What was the reason for increasing the number of office-bearers?

The Nepali Congress has come through a special General Convention, and I have been trying to unite the entire party. If we had kept the number of office-bearers unchanged, there was a risk that the division between those associated with the special General Convention and those outside it would become permanent.

By creating more space, everyone can compete. This time, I am not forming a panel or team. The competition is open to everyone. If we had kept the old structure, those currently in the committee could have effectively formed one team and those outside it another.

There is also a leadership-development aspect. We want to increase women’s participation. Women had been able to enter through the joint general secretary level, but the path to vice president or general secretary was largely closed. By opening those positions to women, we have also opened a path for a woman to eventually lead the Nepali Congress.

Similarly, inclusive representation at the vice-president level creates a path for Dalits, Janajatis, Madhesis and other communities to reach the party’s higher leadership.

Why was the new position of senior vice president created?

There has been a lot of discussion about creating more positions, but less attention has been paid to the fact that the revised statute also assigns specific responsibilities to them.

Previously, the general secretaries had essentially the same broad responsibility of overseeing the central office. Now their responsibilities are differentiated. One will oversee the office, another the organisation, while others will handle specific areas. The vice presidents will also have clearly defined responsibilities.

The idea is that the party president should focus more on external and political matters. At present, too much of the president’s time is spent managing internal party affairs.

In a sense, the senior vice president is like a co-president. The senior vice president will oversee the party’s broader internal affairs, while the general secretaries will handle day-to-day organisational and office work.

This allows the president to focus on connecting the party with the people and on national politics and national issues. That is what the president of the Nepali Congress should be thinking about.

There are now 15 joint general secretaries. How will you ensure they do not remain without responsibilities as happened in the past?

That will not happen this time. The previous statute gave the president the authority to assign responsibilities, but the problem was that this was not done.

Under the new statute, every elected Central Committee member must be assigned a specific responsibility according to a defined terms of reference. They must also report on their work.

We have introduced three broad categories of responsibility — someone can be assigned a particular level of the organisation, a party body or department, or a specific issue.

Someone may be responsible for a province, someone for a municipality, and someone else for a particular issue. But no one will simply be left without a responsibility.

The nomination process has seen a very large number of candidates. Does this suggest the new structure has become unmanageable?

No. The number of candidates was similar in the past. The difference is that factions used to control who could contest. If you belonged to a faction, you could become a candidate; if you did not, your chances of winning were almost zero.

This time, we decided not to distribute lists telling people whom to vote for and whom to defeat. That removed the gatekeeping. Anyone with the ability and desire to contest could do so.

That is a positive development, although it has also created a challenge because many more people are now competing.

What major reforms do you want to introduce next?

The first is that, by the next General Convention, we should end the current system of selecting the party president and Central Committee through General Convention representatives.

By then, we will have digitised the party and established a strong technological system. Ordinary Congress members across the country should be able to directly vote for the party leadership.

The second is the principle of “one person, one executive responsibility.” Someone serving on the Central Committee should not simultaneously seek a mayoral position or contest a direct provincial or parliamentary election.

I have told colleagues that if they want to seek a mayoral ticket in the future, they should not join the Central Working Committee now. Membership of the Central Committee itself will carry substantial responsibilities under the new system.

There is also another issue. After the Central General Convention, we will hold provincial and district elections. Anyone who contests for the Central Committee here should not then go down and contest at the provincial or district level.

We have around 7,000 General Convention representatives and a Central Committee of around 300 members, but nearly 1,500 people are competing. The 1,200 or 1,300 who do not make it are also capable people with political aspirations. We need to think carefully about how to retain and utilise that talent within the party.

There has been speculation that increasing the number of office-bearers was intended to accommodate particular leaders.

That is not the case. The first objective was to create more space and opportunities to promote unity within the party. The second was to ensure that people from different sectors and communities can reach the higher levels of leadership.

There are also many capable leaders contesting for office-bearer positions who are extremely important to the Nepali Congress.

Our system is different from the CPN-UML’s. Here, if you contest for an office-bearer position, you either win or lose. You cannot then remain as a Central Committee member.

At this critical juncture, some leaders are particularly important to the party. For example, I have seen reports that Dr Minendra Rijal is contesting for vice president. If I had the opportunity to tell him directly, I would say that the Nepali Congress needs an intellectual and experienced leader like him.

I have also asked leaders such as Min Bishwakarma not to contest for office-bearer positions because we need to work with them in the organisation. We need their experience to help connect the new generation with the previous generation.

Becoming an office-bearer is not everything. Some leaders have a stature and importance within the Central Committee that they have earned through their own work.

There is speculation that panels will be formed during the election. Will you form one?

If someone else wants to form a panel, that is their choice. But I will not form one.

I am a candidate for president, and others are free to contest or form panels. But I will not have my own panel because the colleagues entering the race all want to work with me. I cannot form a panel based on who I like or dislike.

I have also told some leaders, including Dr Minendra Rijal, that they do not necessarily need to contest for office-bearer positions because the party needs them. Not everyone has to contest an election.

So I am clear on this — I will not form a panel.

title.rendered: Nepal in talks with China to reopen Tatopani border point: Minister Lamsal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal said the government is in continuous dialogue with China to reopen the Tatopani border point.

Lamsal made the statement at a meeting of the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Impact of Climate Change in the Himalayas, Climate Justice and the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster held at Singha Durbar.

“We are also working on how to reopen the Rasuwagadhi border point. There is currently no problem on the Nepali side at the Tatopani border point. The Nepali side has already restored the road for operating the Tatopani border point,” Lamsal said. “We are ready even now. We face no difficulty in operating the border point. We are also in regular dialogue with the Chinese side. Discussions are taking place almost daily.”

He said although disasters had caused problems in operating the border points, the government was working to immediately restore roads and other infrastructure. He said the Nepali side was ready to operate the Tatopani border point but had yet to receive permission from the Chinese side.

“They are not ready yet. Our dialogue is continuing. It appears that the Chinese government remains somewhat reluctant to operate the border point under such circumstances, citing floods and other disasters,” he said. “They have not yet given the ‘green signal’ to operate the border point during the disaster situation. We are making efforts. I believe we will succeed in reopening the border point soon.”

Minister Lamsal said the government was also making plans to resume operations at the Rasuwagadhi border point, as it is a major trade route with China.

title.rendered: SC scraps provision requiring widows to return property if they remarry

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The Supreme Court has scrapped a legal provision requiring a widow to return property inherited from her deceased husband if she remarries.

A Constitutional Bench struck down Sub-section 2 of Section 214 of the National Civil Code, 2017, following a writ petition filed by three organisations, including the Forum for Women, Law and Development (FWLD).

The provision stated that if a widow remarried, property she had received as her share from her deceased husband’s estate would go to her children from the previous marriage or, in the absence of such children, remain with her.

The bench comprising then Acting Chief Justice Sapana Pradhan Malla and Justices Kumar Regmi, Hari Phuyal, Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma and Dr Nahakul Subedi scrapped the provision on May 4.

The petitioners argued that the provision curtailed rights previously guaranteed to widows under the existing law on partition of property.

The Supreme Court examined the provision against constitutional guarantees of the right to live with dignity, equality and property rights under Articles 16, 18 and 25 of the Constitution.

The court concluded that the provision was inconsistent with these constitutional rights and could discourage widows from remarrying by making them financially vulnerable.

“The requirement to return property received as a share would economically weaken single women and discourage them from remarrying,” the full text of the verdict states.

The court said requiring women to return property solely because they remarried amounted to an unreasonable restriction on their property rights.

It further held that once ownership of the property had been legally established, it should not be taken away merely because a woman’s marital status changed.

The court also found the provision inconsistent with Nepal’s obligations under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.

The court said a subsequent law cannot take away, remove or reduce rights or benefits already granted by previous laws and that such a provision cannot be given constitutional validity.

title.rendered: Nepal, WWF agree to cooperate on post-disaster reconstruction, biodiversity conservation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Nepal and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) have agreed to cooperate on post-disaster reconstruction, biodiversity conservation, climate resilience and human-wildlife conflict management.

Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary held a courtesy meeting with delegations from WWF-US and WWF Nepal at the ministry on Sunday. They discussed the recent floods and landslides in Nepal, post-disaster reconstruction, biodiversity conservation, climate resilience and management of human-wildlife conflict.

During the meeting, WWF-US Chief Executive Officer Laura expressed her organisation’s commitment to continuing cooperation with the Nepali people and government during the difficult situation caused by the disasters.

She stressed the need to advance post-disaster reconstruction in a more sustainable, nature-based and climate-resilient manner than in the past. She also said her organisation would provide full support in mobilising international technology, knowledge and resources according to Nepal’s needs.

Minister Chaudhary thanked WWF for its support during the disasters and briefed the delegation on damage caused to agricultural land and forests by the floods and landslides, as well as the challenges of reconstruction.

She said long-term climate and disaster resilience should be prioritised alongside reconstruction.

The minister also expressed concern over the growing human-wildlife conflict. She said modern technology and scientific management were needed to address increasing human-tiger conflict following the rise in the tiger population, the problems caused by wild elephants and monkey-related problems reported in around 55 districts.

The meeting also discussed the possibility of using sterilisation technology for monkey management, implementing a special project for elephant management and establishing special conservation areas to control man-eating tigers.

Representatives of WWF Nepal said substantial investment was needed for reconstruction, conservation, tourism, nature-based solutions and community resilience in Nepal. They said cooperation with development partners, including the World Bank and the European Union, would be made more effective.

A WWF Pakistan representative shared successful experiences of wetland restoration and nature-based solutions implemented in Pakistan following the 2022 floods and suggested that similar programmes tailored to local needs could be implemented in Nepal.

The meeting also discussed the possibility of mobilising international environmental and climate finance, including through the ninth phase of the Global Environment Facility, for elephant and human-elephant conflict management.

WWF-US committed to facilitating the mobilisation of world-class technology, knowledge and resources based on Nepal’s priorities.

The ministry said both sides agreed to make future cooperation more result-oriented by integrating nature conservation, community resilience and sustainable economic development.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The Matatirtha-Chobhar section of the Thankot-Chapagaun-Bhaktapur 132 kV transmission line project has been completed, a key development aimed at strengthening and improving the reliability and quality of electricity supply in Kathmandu Valley.

The approximately six-kilometre 132 kV transmission line from the Matatirtha substation to the Chobhar substation will be charged from Friday. Once charged, the Matatirtha-Chobhar section will be connected to the national transmission system and begin regular power transmission.

Nepal Electricity Authority Managing Director Dirghayukumar Shrestha said the operation of the Matatirtha-Chobhar transmission line and Chobhar substation would make it easier to balance electricity demand and supply in Kathmandu Valley and surrounding areas.

Shrestha said construction of an approximately 4.5-kilometre 132 kV underground transmission line from the Chobhar substation to Patan was also being advanced on a high-priority basis.

The authority had decided on September 24 to charge the Matatirtha-Chobhar transmission line within 15 days to manage the growing electricity demand in Kathmandu Valley during the upcoming winter. Two bays have been constructed at the Chobhar substation as part of the infrastructure required to charge the line.

The Thankot-Chapagaun-Bhaktapur transmission line project was initiated to build a 132 kV transmission-line ring covering Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur to ensure an adequate, safe, reliable and quality power supply to the valley.

However, construction of the transmission line was affected by local opposition in Khokana, Bungamati, Harisiddhi and Lamatar areas of Lalitpur. As an alternative, construction of a 132/11 kV substation at Chobhar was taken forward.

The Chobhar substation has nine 11 kV feeders for local power distribution. It will supply electricity to areas including Kirtipur, Pharping, Pulchowk and Ekantakuna.

The operation of the substation is expected to improve voltage and make electricity supply more reliable and stable in these areas.

Electricity generated by hydropower projects mainly in the Trishuli and Marsyangdi river basins is currently supplied to Kathmandu Valley through the Matatirtha substation.

The operation of the 132 kV transmission line between Matatirtha and Chobhar will provide an additional alternative route in the valley’s electricity supply system.

An approximately 4.5-kilometre 132 kV underground transmission line from Chobhar through the Ring Road to the Lagankhel (Patan) substation in Lalitpur is under construction. The Patan substation is also being upgraded to operate at the 132 kV level.

The Thankot-Chapagaun-Bhaktapur 132 kV transmission line project was initiated in fiscal year 1998/99 with investment from the Nepal government and the Nepal Electricity Authority.

Under the project, transmission-line construction on the Kathmandu and Bhaktapur sides has already been completed. The completed section on the Kathmandu side, up to Chobhar, is now being prepared for charging.

Construction of the Lalitpur section, however, has not progressed after residents in Khokana, Bungamati, Harisiddhi and Lamatar obstructed the work, demanding a change in the transmission-line route.

As a result, the plan to operate Kathmandu Valley’s 132 kV transmission system as a complete ring network has continued to face delays.
