title.rendered: Rasuwa floods to cut Nepal’s economic growth to 3.7 per cent: World Bank

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The World Bank has projected that Nepal’s economic growth will slow in the current fiscal year due to the Rasuwa floods on August 26. It has estimated that disruptions in the industrial and services sectors caused by the floods will bring economic growth down to 3.7 per cent.

According to the World Bank’s latest Nepal Development Update, economic activity is expected to receive a boost once reconstruction and rehabilitation activities begin. The bank has projected economic growth to rise to 5.2 per cent in fiscal year 2027/28.

The Nepal Development Update, titled “Building Back Differently for the Future”, states that Nepal’s economic growth and industrial sector are expected to be significantly affected by the widespread damage caused by the floods.

Extensive damage to hydropower, solar energy, electricity transmission and transport infrastructure will directly affect power generation, manufacturing activities and the movement of goods, the report says.

The services sector is also expected to be affected by disruptions to trade, transport, tourism and financial activities. Although damage to the agriculture sector is expected to have a limited impact on overall production, it could have a significant effect on the livelihoods of people in affected areas.

“The Rasuwa floods have caused significant human and economic losses. They also provide Nepal with an opportunity to rethink its infrastructure, roads, communications, energy, water supply and sanitation, health and education services,” said David Sislen, World Bank Division Director for Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

He said resilience and alternative arrangements should be given greater priority in infrastructure planning and investment, particularly in the context of climate change and changing risks. He added that the World Bank was ready to support the Nepal government in investing in systems and implementing appropriate policies to put Nepal on a more resilient and sustainable development path.

As Nepal moves from rescue and relief towards reconstruction, the report recommends that the recovery process should go beyond restoring damaged structures and include updated assessments of multi-hazard risks.

It also recommends careful consideration of the location and design of infrastructure and ensuring additional alternatives for critical transport, energy and communication networks.

The report also highlights the importance of strengthening disaster early warning systems. It calls for an integrated social protection system to provide the basis for rapidly delivering post-disaster assistance to vulnerable households.

The Nepal Development Update is a related report to the South Asia Economic Update, which is published twice a year and analyses economic developments and prospects in the South Asia region.

The latest South Asia Economic Update has projected the region’s economic growth at 6.9 per cent this year. The region’s economies are expected to remain resilient to global shocks due to strong domestic demand, while growth is projected to slow to 6.7 per cent in 2027.

The report also examines how strategic use of artificial intelligence can create new sources of economic growth. Although AI adoption is increasing in South Asia, its use remains significantly lower than in advanced economies. Despite this gap, AI adoption is growing rapidly, with businesses using it to identify new market opportunities.

“AI offers the potential to transform South Asia’s development trajectory by raising labour productivity, expanding export opportunities and improving public service delivery,” said Franziska Ohnsorge, World Bank Group Chief Economist for Asia. “But to realise these benefits, governments need to address the underlying weaknesses that hinder AI adoption.”

The report recommends policy measures to strengthen workforce skills, create a business-friendly environment and improve physical and digital infrastructure. It also calls for removing barriers faced by small businesses in adopting AI, promoting AI-related innovation at the local level and establishing clear regulatory frameworks.

Such regulatory frameworks should reduce uncertainty while ensuring data security and privacy, the report says.

title.rendered: UML says Oli should not be singled out for election defeat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The CPN-UML has concluded that its defeat in the March 5 election should not be viewed as a personal failure of party Chairman KP Sharma Oli.

In the political document issued after the party’s third Central Committee meeting, the UML said the election defeat should be analysed in the context of the overall political and organisational situation.

“The defeat was not only the result of external attacks. It was also a result of our internal weaknesses. But the defeat is not the personal failure of the chairman,” the document states.

According to the document, the election result was a combined outcome of the party’s organisational weaknesses, the prevailing public mood, external environment, digital attacks and the overall electoral situation.

Oli has acknowledged responsibility for his share of the defeat but has maintained that he will not step down as party chairman.

“As chairman, I accept the responsibility that falls on my part. But I also say this — this is not the time to run away, nor is it the time to remain caught up in blame games,” Oli said in the document.

The 26-page political document also includes Oli’s remarks and various decisions taken by the Central Committee, including decisions on nominations.

title.rendered: NRB eases foreign exchange rules, raises limits for medical treatment and imports

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) has eased its foreign exchange policy by increasing the foreign currency exchange limits for medical treatment abroad, telecommunications services and the import of aircraft equipment and spare parts.

Issuing a new directive, the central bank has doubled the annual foreign exchange facility available to Nepali citizens travelling abroad for medical treatment.

Nepali citizens can now exchange up to US$30,000 per year for treatment at hospitals abroad and for purchasing medicines and medical equipment. The previous limit was US$15,000.

The central bank has also increased the limit for advance payments by Nepali airlines importing aircraft engines, spare parts and other equipment. Banks and financial institutions can now make advance payments of up to US$500,000 based on the required documents, including a recommendation from the concerned regulatory authority.

Previously, the limit for such advance payments was US$100,000. A bank guarantee from a foreign bank will no longer be required for the facility.

Similarly, Nepali telecommunications service providers can make payments of up to US$500,000 annually through banks and financial institutions for leasing or using satellite services from foreign service providers under an agreement.

The central bank has also introduced new requirements for imports from China. Importers seeking foreign exchange facilities must provide a commitment that the goods have not already been imported. They must also make a payment of at least 10% of the import value before shipment.

The full payment must be made before the goods are cleared through customs, according to the new provision.

For imports through drafts or telegraphic transfers, banks must submit monthly details of partial payments made before shipment within 15 days of the end of each month.

The NRB has also increased the foreign exchange facility for payments for services imported from countries other than India. Commercial banks can now provide up to US$30,000 or an equivalent convertible currency per transaction, based on approval, agreement or a foreign exchange recommendation from the concerned regulatory authority. The previous limit was US$15,000.

For services imported from India, the limit has been increased to INR 6 million per transaction, from INR 4 million previously. A recommendation from the concerned authority will be required for the facility.

The central bank has also introduced provisions concerning payments between travel and tour agencies. If an agency purchases services from another travel or tour agency and provides them to customers, the agency selling the service must issue a foreign currency invoice. The purchasing agency must receive the foreign currency in its bank account and make payment without exceeding the amount received for the particular purpose.

The NRB has further allowed Class A banks to issue foreign currency bank guarantees for Nepali firms and companies seeking to bring foreign loans into Nepal from foreign institutions.

The provision applies to companies involved in information technology, commercial agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure development, tourism and energy-related industries. Previously, energy-related industries were not included under the provision.

The central bank has also introduced provisions for foreign currency earned through exports of services using electronic cards. Such foreign currency must be credited to the card, and at the request of the cardholder, the amount can be transferred to their domestic or foreign currency bank account.

If the balance on a card exceeds US$10,000 or its equivalent in convertible foreign currency, the excess amount must be deposited into the cardholder’s domestic or foreign currency account.

title.rendered: Dashain shopping slows as floods and transport costs push prices up

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Dashain begins four days from now with Ghatasthapana. As in previous years, shopping activity has already picked up in Kathmandu’s major markets, including New Baneshwar, New Road, Asan and Bhrikutimandap.

Consumers typically begin buying clothes, shoes, bags and other goods for Dashain during the week leading up to the festival. But while the markets are busy this year, neither traders nor consumers appear particularly happy.

The damage caused by the flood in Rasuwa on August 26, particularly to the northern border routes to China, and the sharp increase in transportation costs are now being felt everywhere from roadside markets to large shopping complexes.

On Sunday evening, Sita Ghimire of Shantinagar was browsing for Dashain clothes for her 10-year-old son and seven-year-old daughter at an open market in New Baneshwar.

After visiting several shops, she complained that she could not find clothes at the prices or quality she was looking for.

“Clothes have become more expensive compared to last year,” she said. “Last Dashain, I bought my son a pair of trousers and a T-shirt for Rs 1,500. Now, they are asking Rs 2,200 to Rs 2,500 for a single set. The price of kurta-suruwal for my daughter is also far too high. With prices rising so much, it has become difficult to buy clothes for the children this year.”

Sumi Thapa, who had come to the same market to buy a kurta-suruwal, trousers and shoes, also found prices considerably higher than last year.

“Last year, I bought clothes for myself and my sister from here. A pair of trousers that cost me Rs 1,000 then now costs Rs 1,400 even after a lot of bargaining,” she said. “I still have to buy a kurta set for my mother, and the traders say those prices have also gone up. It doesn’t look like we will be able to buy clothes without spending a lot this year.”

The rising cost of Chinese garments, which have long made it easier for Nepalis to maintain the tradition of wearing new clothes during Dashain, is now putting thousands of consumers and traders like Sita and Sumi under pressure.

Gautam Sah, who has been selling clothes at an open market in New Baneshwar for the past three years, says there are plenty of inquiries but very little actual business.

“Compared to last year, there simply aren’t as many customers. People come, ask the price and leave saying it is too expensive,” he said. “People also don’t seem to be in much of a festive mood this year. The country has suffered such a major disaster.”

Sah said traders have been forced to raise retail prices because wholesale prices have increased.

“Cheap goods have become Rs 25 to Rs 50 more expensive at the wholesale level, while more expensive items have gone up by Rs 100 to Rs 200,” he said. “We also have to keep a small profit margin.”

Kurta sets are imported from India. Traders say clothes imported from India are already relatively expensive, but transportation problems have made the situation even worse this year.

Another trader, Binod Oli, has had a similar experience. He sells kurta sets, tops and other clothing and says Chinese goods are in short supply, while the prices of whatever has reached the market have risen sharply.

Oli says it has become difficult to satisfy customers after having to buy goods at higher wholesale prices.

“A kurta-suruwal set that used to cost us Rs 1,500 to Rs 1,700 is now costing us Rs 2,200 to Rs 2,500,” he said. “Wholesalers say transportation costs have increased because the roads have been damaged. When we add Rs 200 or Rs 300 as profit and sell the goods, customers complain that they are too expensive and walk away. Business is in terrible shape.”

Prices of footwear have also risen along with clothing compared to last year.

Ramesh Thapa of Koteshwor was bargaining with a shopkeeper over a pair of shoes he liked because of its higher price.

“I was looking at a pair of Samba shoes for Dashain. Last year, they cost Rs 1,200, but now the seller won’t let them go for less than Rs 1,500,” he said. “I still have to buy other things, so it looks like my budget won’t be enough.”

The trader trying to sell the shoes, Mukesh Bishwakarma, said he could not reduce the price because the shoes themselves had become more expensive.

“The goods are stuck on the way, so we haven’t been able to provide customers with what they are looking for,” he said. “The limited goods that have reached the market have become more expensive because of transportation costs.”

Archana, who has been trading at the open market in Baneshwar for two and a half years, has a similar complaint. She said the new stock she ordered for Dashain is stuck in transit, forcing her to sell old stock.

“The new designs have not arrived. A heavy set that cost Rs 2,400 last year now costs us Rs 2,600,” she said. “Customers first bargain over the price and, if they find it expensive, they leave saying they will check two or three other places.”

The root of the current shortage and price increase lies at the northern border crossings.

The flood in the Bhotekoshi River last month damaged roads leading to the Rasuwagadhi and Tatopani border points, leaving billions of rupees worth of goods ordered by traders for Dashain stranded along the routes.

Some goods have also been imported through the Korala border point, but that route is currently closed after continuous rainfall a week ago damaged roads and bridges. Reconstruction work is under way.

The government is making diplomatic efforts to reopen the Tatopani border crossing, but it appears that it will take some time.

Traders in New Road, one of the capital’s main commercial hubs, also say prices have increased because transportation charges have doubled.

Ratna Shrestha, a New Road trader, said customer traffic has increased as Dashain approaches, but most people are not actually buying.

“Not much stock has reached the wholesale market either. Retailers are reluctant to take goods because they cannot sell them at such high prices, although some are still buying,” he said.

He said even Dashain discounts and special offers have failed to attract much interest from customers.

Parshuram Dahal, chairman of the RB Complex Business Association in New Road, says the entire increase in prices currently seen in the market is due to the disruption at the northern border points and the doubling of transportation costs.

“No new goods have arrived in the market. All the routes are closed,” Dahal said. “I have always said that these northern border points have become an ambush for traders. We bring goods in, and then they get stuck there.”

He said the financial losses suffered by traders when festival goods are stranded in transit are impossible to quantify.

“Nearly 200 trucks and containers carrying goods from China were swept away by the floods. So much money has been lost, but nobody seems to care,” he said. “Goods coming from China are not insured, so traders themselves have to bear the entire loss when goods are swept away or rot on the way.”

Dahal believes the main reason for the increase in prices is not the traders but the higher transportation charges imposed by transport operators.

“Container transporters have doubled their charges. Transportation alone has increased the price of goods by 5 to 7 percent,” he said. “When transport costs rise, traders cannot simply pay the difference out of their own pockets. They have to raise prices. But there is no monopoly in the market now; it is competitive. Whoever offers the lower price will sell, so traders are not making excessive profits.”

Business owners say they have grown frustrated with the recurring problems at the northern border points, where floods and landslides or unofficial restrictions disrupt supplies almost every festive season. They are now calling on the government to take serious measures to address the problem.

During the festive season, ordinary consumers visit roadside stalls and open markets hoping to find good-quality goods at affordable prices. But this year, natural disasters, rising prices and government shortcomings have left neither traders nor consumers satisfied.

In previous years, traders would barely have time to eat during Dashain because of the crowds. This year, many say they are sitting in their shops, scrolling through their phones and waiting for customers.

title.rendered: Nepal’s Hora and T2K Esports drawn in same group for PMGO

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Nepal’s two esports teams, Hora Esports and T2K Esports, have been drawn into the same Group A for the PUBG Mobile Global Open (PMGO).

The draw, held on Monday night, placed the two Nepali teams in Group A for the tournament, which is scheduled to take place in Pakistan from October 20.

Both Hora and T2K qualified for the main event through the South Asia Finals held in Kathmandu.

Group A also includes Foke, Al Ula, Geek, S2G, SP, BTR, AKG, SLB, ROW, INF, RA, Old Not, HC and the top team from the PUBG Mobile Pakistan Open (PMPO).

Group B consists of 18 Esports, RAT, CS, iKurd, VPE, AE, REG, BUF, ULF, Alpha7, MGLJ, VCS, Four Thrives, Next and the second-placed team from the PMPO.

Four Thrives Esports of Pakistan won the South Asia Finals held in Nepal. The Pakistani team topped the standings with 209 points, while T2K finished second and Hora third.

Another Nepali team, Hidden Leaf Esports, finished fourth, while TGB, another team from Nepal, secured eighth place.

The Global Open will bring together teams from across the region, with Hora and T2K now set to face each other as well as some of the region’s leading PUBG Mobile teams in the group stage.

title.rendered: Dashain advance ticket booking to open from October 9, two drivers mandatory on long routes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Advance ticket booking for public transport for the upcoming Dashain, Tihar and Chhath festivals will open from October 9.

The decision was taken at a high-level meeting held at the Department of Transport Management on Tuesday among representatives of relevant agencies.

The meeting, organised by the department, brought together representatives of the Federation of Nepalese National Transport Entrepreneurs, transport workers’ organisations, Nepal Police, Traffic Police and Lhotse Multipurpose Pvt Ltd, the operator of the New Bus Park. Dipak KC, president of the All Nepal Transport Workers’ Organisation, said the participants agreed to open advance ticket booking from October 9 to facilitate passengers leaving Kathmandu Valley during the festive season.

More than one million passengers are expected to leave Kathmandu Valley during Dashain this year. The decision is expected to ease uncertainty among passengers caused by the lack of an advance booking system, with only some transport companies currently offering online booking.

The meeting also made several decisions to improve passenger safety, convenience and transport management. Long-distance vehicles will now be required to have two drivers. Ticket-counter staff must wear uniforms and identification cards, while passengers’ names and contact numbers must be recorded when tickets are issued.

The department warned that anyone charging fares above the prescribed rates, engaging in black marketing or committing irregularities in ticket sales would face legal action. The government, transport entrepreneurs and security agencies will coordinate to ensure a transparent ticketing system.

According to KC, a central information centre will also be operated to facilitate information sharing on safe travel and road blockages or accidents. All passenger vehicles must carry first-aid supplies, fire extinguishers, drinking water and other essential facilities.

Participants also stressed the need for effective mobilisation of security personnel to manage heavy crowds at bus parks and ticket counters and prevent passengers from facing difficulties due to a lack of tickets.

title.rendered: Speaker Aryal and Australian counterpart Dick hold talks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal and Milton Dick, Speaker of the Australian Parliament, have held talks.

Speaker Aryal is in Arusha, Tanzania, to attend the 153rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU). According to Aryal’s secretariat, the two speakers discussed a range of topics at today’s meeting, including the friendly relations between Nepal and Australia and parliamentary cooperation.

On the occasion, Speaker Aryal said that since diplomatic relations were established between Nepal and Australia in 1960, ties based on friendship, mutual respect and shared democratic values have continued to strengthen.

He thanked the Australian government for the humanitarian assistance and search and rescue support it provided after the flood in the Bhotekoshi area. Expressing condolences to the families of the Australian citizens who went missing in the flood, he praised the solidarity Australia showed during the disaster.

Noting that Himalayan countries, including Nepal, are being seriously affected by climate change, Speaker Aryal expressed hope for Australia’s support and solidarity in international debates and initiatives on climate change.

Aryal said the formation of the Nepal-Australia Parliamentary Friendship Group is an important foundation for further strengthening parliamentary ties between the two countries.

He expressed the view that bilateral relations can be strengthened further through regular interaction among parliamentarians, exchange of experience and parliamentary diplomacy.

During the meeting, Australian Speaker Dick expressed Australia’s willingness to further strengthen parliamentary and bilateral relations with Nepal, the secretariat said.

title.rendered: Intermediary linked to suspended APF AIG Dahal remains in police custody

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Inam Sapkota, an intermediary allegedly linked to suspended Armed Police Force (APF) AIG Banshiraj Dahal, remains in police custody as investigators look into the alleged leakage of confidential and sensitive information.

Sapkota is currently being held at the District Police Range, Bhadrakali, Kathmandu. Dan Bahadur Thapa, superintendent of police and spokesperson for the Kathmandu police, confirmed that Sapkota remains in custody.

“He is in our custody. We have been investigating him for the past three to four days,” Thapa told Onlinekhabar.

According to Thapa, police obtained a remand from the Kathmandu District Administration Office to investigate Sapkota on a charge of indecent behaviour. However, sources said the investigation is primarily related to the alleged leakage of information rather than indecent behaviour.

Sources have claimed that Sapkota has connections ranging from former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana to businessman Deepak Bhatta.

Rana was taken into police custody and released about 12 hours later. At the time, police had also seized and examined his mobile phone.

Following the incident, Sapkota, who has been described as an intermediary, came under the radar of the police. He was initially detained by the police’s Special Bureau and later handed over to the Kathmandu police.

The Kathmandu police are currently investigating Sapkota.

Meanwhile, APF AIG Banshiraj Dahal has been suspended, and an investigation has been initiated over allegations that he leaked confidential information through WhatsApp, including information allegedly shared with Sapkota.

title.rendered: AIG Pokharel tasked with investigating suspended AIG Dahal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

A committee has been formed to investigate Armed Police Force (APF) Additional Inspector General (AIG) Banshiraj Dahal, who was suspended on allegations of leaking confidential information.

The Ministry of Home Affairs said AIG Anjanikumar Pokharel, who works at the Human Resources Department of the APF Headquarters in Halchowk, has been assigned responsibility for the investigation. He is the sole member of the committee.

“A responsibility has been assigned to conduct the investigation in accordance with the relevant provision of the APF regulations,” a Home Ministry source said.

Dahal had gone to meet former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana when the latter was arrested and taken to the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office in Teku. Dahal is also alleged to have had connections with another middleman from Jhapa and to have leaked confidential information.

He has been given three days to complete the investigation. The ministry said further action would be initiated based on the report submitted within the deadline.

Dahal, who has been suspended, was serving as chief of the APF Border Security Department. Had his tenure not been extended by the government, he would have been due to retire at midnight on October 13.

Under Section 65(c) of the Armed Police Force Regulations, 2015, the tenure of an APF AIG is four years. Dahal was promoted to AIG on May 11, 2022. Under this provision, he was scheduled to retire at midnight on May 10, 2026.

However, Sub-rule (2) of Section 65(c) of the regulations allows the government to extend an AIG’s tenure by one year beyond the four-year term on the recommendation of the IG of the APF.

Accordingly, the APF Headquarters had recommended to the Home Ministry that Dahal’s tenure be extended by one year. In the meantime, he was suspended over allegations of leaking confidential information.

title.rendered: Two held with 63 mobile phones without invoices

content.rendered:

Police have arrested two people with 63 mobile phones allegedly being sold or supplied without invoices.

According to the District Police Office, Chitwan, Dipak Prasain was arrested on a tip-off that he was selling mobile phones without official trade records. He was arrested from Hakimchowk in Bharatpur Metropolitan City-10.

Similarly, 28-year-old Umnand Bhusal was arrested for allegedly supplying mobile phones without invoices. He was arrested from Ramnagar in Bharatpur Metropolitan City-1, and five mobile phones were seized from him.

Prasain and Bhusal were arrested two days ago.

Both have been handed over to the Birgunj Customs Office for further legal action. The seized mobile phones and accessories have also been handed over to the customs office.

title.rendered: Province government selects 11 community schools for STEAM labs

content.rendered:
Kaski, October 6

The Gandaki Province government has selected 11 community schools to receive grants for establishing and operating STEAM laboratories to make science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics education more practical and technology-friendly.

The Education Development Division under the Ministry of Social Development, Youth and Sports selected the schools under its annual programme for operating STEAM labs targeting secondary-level education.

The schools were selected on Monday based on proposals submitted for the grants. Each school will receive Rs 400,000, with a total of Rs 4.4 million allocated for the programme, according to Division chief Ghanshyam Poudel.

“The establishment of STEAM labs will help link the teaching of science and technology-related subjects with experiments, tests and practical activities. It will foster skills beyond theoretical knowledge,” Poudel said.

The selected schools are Dhanubas Kalika Secondary School in Madi Rural Municipality-7, Kaski; Suryodaya Secondary School in Dharche Rural Municipality-5 and Tara Secondary School in Gorkha Municipality-10, Gorkha; Shiva Secondary School in Byas Municipality-10, Tanahun; Saraswati Sanskrit Secondary School in Hupsekot Rural Municipality-3, Kumarawati Secondary School in Gaindakot Municipality-3, Krishna Gandaki Secondary School in Nawalpur and Suryajyoti Secondary School in Hupsekot Rural Municipality-9, Nawalpur; Purushodaya Secondary School in Barahkot, Baglung; Balmandir Secondary School in Kalipul, Myagdi; and Chandidanda Secondary School in Mattikhan, Syangja.

The grants will be used to purchase necessary materials and equipment and develop infrastructure for the laboratories.

title.rendered: Passenger help desk set up at Jamunaha border point

content.rendered:
Banke, October 6

The district administration has set up a passenger help desk at the Jamunaha border point to facilitate the return of Nepalis from India ahead of Dashain and Tihar.

With the major festivals approaching, the number of Nepalis returning home from India has been increasing. Banke Chief District Officer Dil Kumar Tamang said the help desk was established to prevent possible incidents of robbery and fraud targeting Nepalis returning home to celebrate the festivals.

He said the facility at the border point would help ensure the safe return of Nepalis.

“We’ve kept the safety of citizens at the centre and implemented a security plan after identifying possible risks,” he said, adding that the help desk would establish contact with relevant agencies and provide information to people passing through the border point.

Chief of the District Police Office, Banke, Angur GC, said the desk would also help curb criminal activities that could take place by taking advantage of the festive season.

Similar help desks will also be operated at bus parks in Nepalgunj and Kohalpur to provide information and assistance to Nepalis returning from India for Dashain.

Personnel from the Nepal Police and Traffic Police have been deployed at the help desks.

title.rendered: The British College holds 12th graduation ceremony for Class of 2026

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The British Education Group (BEG) organised a joint graduation ceremony for its Class of 2026 at The Soaltee Kathmandu on October 2.

The 12th graduation ceremony of The British College brought together graduating students from four institutions under the group — The British College, British International College, British Model College and British Professional College.

Graduates from programmes ranging from A Levels and professional qualifications to undergraduate and postgraduate degrees in business, computing, information technology and accountancy received their awards during the ceremony.

The programmes included Executive MBA, MBA, MSc IT, MSc Advanced Computer Science, MSc Professional Accountancy, ACCA, BBA, BSc (Hons) Computing, BSc (Hons) Cyber Security and Digital Forensics, and A Levels.

The ceremony was held in two sessions, with graduates receiving their qualifications from the group’s international academic partners, including Leeds Beckett University, the University of the West of England, Keele University, the University of London, ACCA and Cambridge International Examinations.

The programme began with an academic procession, followed by the national anthems of Nepal and the United Kingdom. British Education Group CEO Rajen Kandel formally opened the ceremony by lighting the traditional Panas.

Addressing the graduating students, Kandel congratulated them on completing their academic journeys and thanked their families, faculty members and the wider college community for their support.

He said the Class of 2026 would join a growing alumni network of more than 4,000 graduates of The British College and more than 10,000 graduates across the British Education Group. He encouraged the graduates to remain connected with the college and one another as they move into further studies and professional careers.

Paul Cleves MBE, advisor to The British College, and Michael Rutland OBE, first honorary consul of Bhutan to the UK and former advisor to the college, also addressed the graduates.

Dave Chesley, senior lecturer and link tutor at Leeds Beckett University, attended the ceremony as a representative of the university’s academic partnership with The British College.

Video messages were also delivered by Professor Steve West CBE, vice-chancellor and president of the University of the West of England, Professor Kevin Shakesheff, vice-chancellor of Keele University, and Simon Cleary of the University of London.

The ceremony also featured Excellence Awards recognising outstanding student achievements. Representatives from different programmes shared their experiences and reflections on their academic journeys.

The event concluded with a vote of thanks from Arun Kandel, country director of The British College, followed by photographs and celebrations involving graduates, families, faculty members and guests.

Amardeep Mandal, chief growth officer of British Education Group, said the graduation marked the first time all four institutions under the group had come together to celebrate their graduating students on a single platform.

He said the joint ceremony reflected the group’s shared vision and commitment to providing education and opportunities for students in Nepal and abroad.

title.rendered: ‘Art for Humanity’ exhibition begins to support Bhotekoshi flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

A special art exhibition titled ‘Art for Humanity’ began at the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA), Naxal, on Monday to raise funds for relief and rehabilitation of families and communities affected by the Bhotekoshi River floods.

The exhibition has been organised to collect donations for the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support relief, assistance and long-term rehabilitation of those affected by the devastating flood that struck the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

Artists, art galleries, artist groups, art and cultural organisations, art institutions, students, curators, art collectors, art enthusiasts and foreign artists have participated in the exhibition.

Of the proceeds from the sale of artworks, 70 per cent will be deposited in the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund and 10 per cent in the Artists’ Relief Fund. The remaining 20 per cent will go to the artists.

More than 200 artworks by over 160 artists are on display, representing traditional and folk art, painting, drawing, sculpture, ceramics, photography, printmaking, installation, mixed media, digital art and other forms of visual art.

The exhibition will run through October 14.

NAFA has called for participation and support for the initiative, which seeks to connect the creativity, sensitivity and social responsibility of artists with humanitarian service during the disaster.

title.rendered: Govt to amend two laws to facilitate death registration of missing persons

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The government is preparing to amend two laws to facilitate the registration of deaths of people who went missing in the devastating Bhotekoshi–Trishuli disaster. The amendments will be pursued through a “fast-track” process.

Home Ministry Secretary Kedar Nath Sharma and Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Ministry Joint Secretary Subash Kumar Bhattarai provided the information at a meeting of the parliamentary special committee formed to study the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli disaster at Singha Durbar on Tuesday.

Bhattarai said the existing legal procedures were making it difficult for families of missing persons to access relief, compensation and other legal benefits.

The Law Ministry is preparing to prioritise proposals from the Home Ministry to amend the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act and the National Identity Card and Registration Act.

“As the existing legal provisions are not sufficient for declaring the death of missing citizens and registering their deaths, the process of amending the relevant laws has been initiated in coordination with the Home Ministry,” Bhattarai said. “We are preparing to move the process forward through a fast-track procedure as necessary.”

The ministry said the death declaration and registration procedure under the existing Civil Code is lengthy and cumbersome. Bhattarai said discussions were also underway on how to expedite the amendment process even when Parliament is not in session.

Long-term legal reforms for climate-related disasters

Bhattarai said legal reforms were also needed to address the long-term impacts of climate-related disasters.

He said the government would discuss with the Ministry of Forests and Environment whether to amend the Environment Protection Act or enact a separate law on climate change.

He also said the Land Use Act and laws related to infrastructure safety needed revision to ensure risk-based land classification and use.

The special committee, coordinated by the Minister for Law, is holding discussions with representatives of various ministries on these reforms.

Bhattarai said reforms were necessary not only to address the immediate consequences of climate-related disasters but also to reduce future risks through stronger laws on disaster management, environmental protection, land use and infrastructure.

Home Secretary Sharma described the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli disaster as one of the most devastating and unprecedented disasters Nepal has experienced, saying it had also raised questions about the government’s preparedness.

He said search, rescue and relief operations had been carried out through the joint efforts of federal, provincial and local governments, security agencies and other bodies. The government has now shifted its focus to rehabilitation and reconstruction.

13,795 rescued, 1,457 bodies recovered

Sharma said 13,795 people had been rescued by land and air following the disaster.

A total of 1,457 bodies have been recovered. Of these, 1,334 have been managed, while 112 have been identified and handed over to their families.

DNA samples have been collected from 2,066 people to identify the bodies. Sharma said the government was working to obtain DNA test results before Dashain and had sought the assistance of foreign experts where necessary to expedite DNA matching.

He said search and rescue operations initially faced difficulties because of challenging terrain and adverse conditions, but government agencies, security forces and local governments were now working in coordination.

Damage estimated at Rs 723 billion

Sharma said the National Planning Commission’s Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment had estimated the initial damage from the disaster at Rs 723 billion.

The government has completed the search and rescue phase and entered the rehabilitation and reconstruction phase, he said. A decision to provide affected families with Rs 15,000 to Rs 19,000 per household for rent is being implemented.

Around Rs 170 million has been sent to local governments and district disaster management funds for relief. Sharma said some technical delays had occurred because payments could only be processed after beneficiaries were identified.

A detailed assessment of damaged public infrastructure is underway, with rehabilitation and reconstruction being advanced in coordination with the concerned ministries and the Ministry of Finance.

Sharma also said work had begun to identify land and develop infrastructure for the long-term resettlement of people currently staying at holding centres.

title.rendered: Gas vendors write to Oil Corporation, demand end to retail sales from industries

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The Gas Dearler Federation Nepal has drawn the attention of the Nepal Oil Corporation, saying the shortage of cooking gas in Nepal is worsening and consumers are suffering.

The federation submitted a memorandum to the corporation’s executive director, Nagendra Sah. It demanded an immediate end to retail gas sales by industries and arrangements for sales and distribution only through dealers.

Federation president Gyaneshwar Aryal said the main cause of the shortage is that there are more cylinders in the market than needed.

Ignoring this, various gas industries are selling new cylinders at Rs 2,500 to Rs 2,700 each, and the federation has strongly objected. It said the Nepal Oil Corporation and the government remain silent spectators even as industries sell new cylinders, and it expressed doubts about the conduct of industry owners, the corporation and the government.

The federation said that instead of refunding deposits for the unnecessary cylinders already in the market, industries plan to sell new 5 kg, 19 kg, 50 kg and 450 kg cylinders in the coming years with the aim of fleecing ordinary consumers. It warned that such a plan would not be acceptable to a civilised society.

To make gas distribution transparent and orderly, the federation urged the corporation mainly to stop the continuing retail sales by industries immediately and arrange for gas to be sold only through dealers.

It also asked the corporation to identify the cause of the shortage correctly, ensure smooth supply in consultation with stakeholders, and properly manage the 14.2 kg cylinders currently used by the public.

title.rendered: Fast track to be adopted to amend laws for disaster-affected people

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs will move ahead with amending laws through a “fast track” to resolve legal complications in registering the deaths of people who went missing in climate-induced disasters.

Joint Secretary Subhash Kumar Bhattarai told a meeting of the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Impact of Climate Change in the Himalayas, Climate Justice and the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli Disaster at Singha Durbar on Tuesday that amending the law is essential to address the hardship procedural hurdles in current law have caused disaster-affected families.

He said the ministry is coordinating with the Home Ministry to resolve problems related to the legal status of disaster victims and the registration of deaths.

The procedure in the current National Civil Code is long and cumbersome, making it hard for families of the missing to get relief and other legal benefits. In view of this, the Law Ministry is preparing to prioritise proposals received from the Home Ministry to amend the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act and the National Identity Card and Registration Act. Bhattarai said discussions are under way on how to settle this quickly even when Parliament is not in session.

“Existing legal provisions are currently inadequate for declaring and registering the deaths of missing citizens, so the process to amend the relevant Acts has begun in coordination with the Home Ministry,” he said. “We are preparing to move this ahead through the fast track as needed.”

According to Bhattarai, managing the long-term effects of climate change requires legal reform in coordination with various ministries. For this, discussions will be held with the Ministry of Forests and Environment on amending the Environment Protection Act or, if needed, creating a separate climate change law.

He also said the ministry will coordinate with the relevant ministries to reform the Land Use Act and laws related to infrastructure safety, so that land can be classified and used according to risk.

A special committee formed under the law minister’s coordination is currently holding discussions with representatives of various ministries on legal reform.

The government has committed to playing a coordinating role in lawmaking and finding a permanent legal solution to problems caused by climate-related disasters.

title.rendered: Tenders for flood-damaged structures before Dashain, efforts to rehabilitate displaced people, says Minister Lamsal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal has said bids will be invited before Dashain to rebuild structures damaged in the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli flood, and that efforts will be made to rehabilitate displaced people. He also said the process of amending existing laws is moving ahead so that infrastructure is built in a way that natural disasters cannot damage.

“The present practice is exactly the opposite, and we are now departing with a major paradigm shift,” he said. “The government is taking that forward.”

From now on, he said, bridges must be designed to withstand even high floods.

Minister Lamsal said current designs are based on estimates of how high floodwater will reach, but pay no attention to the stones, gravel and sand that pile up every year. He said bridges will be built with that in mind.

“Compared with the hills, the Tarai has much more deposition. But existing law does not allow extraction from forest and national park areas,” he said. “When we extract more than the allowed amount, it causes erosion problems, and when we don’t extract, it damages infrastructure too. In the new law, we have started the process of amending the law to solve this problem.”

Contracts and rehabilitation before Dashain

He said the process of awarding contracts to rebuild damaged bridges, roads and other physical infrastructure will start before Dashain.

He also said work is underway with the aim of arranging safe housing soon for those who lost their homes.

“We are working to the target of providing housing before Dashain,” Minister Lamsal said. “As far as possible, we want to rehabilitate people and create a festive atmosphere.”

He also committed to working to solve the drought problem in the Tarai.

He said the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli flood was unusual and beyond what the early warning system could keep pace with, and that the government will pay attention to this in the future.

title.rendered: Tiger sanctuary to be built in Nepal to resolve human-tiger conflict

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The government has begun the process of establishing a “tiger sanctuary” (tiger conservation) centre to resolve the human-tiger conflict that has grown along with the rise in the tiger population.

The National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC) has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US-based organisation The Wild Animal Sanctuary (TWAS).

The agreement was signed by NTNC member-secretary Dr Chiranjibi Prasad Pokharel on behalf of the trust and TWAS executive director Pat Craig.

With Nepal’s tiger population more than doubling, tigers have been entering human settlements and causing human casualties. After “conflict tigers” are taken from their natural habitat, they are currently kept in various cramped cages.

The Ministry of Agriculture said it has advanced international partnerships under the plan, since a separate sanctuary for long-term care, modern housing and scientific management has become essential.

Under the agreement, a modern tiger sanctuary with an open, natural-environment-friendly design will be built on at least 50 hectares in Nepal. Using its more than 46 years of experience and expertise, TWAS will raise the financial and technical resources needed for the sanctuary’s physical infrastructure, natural habitat design, veterinary hospital and enclosure.

The land will remain owned by the Government of Nepal or the NTNC. The agreement says the sanctuary will be developed not only as a lifelong safe habitat for problem tigers but also as a centre for public awareness and conservation education.

Tigers inside the sanctuary may not be used for any commercial entertainment, photo sessions, games or breeding purposes. The project is expected to reduce human-wildlife conflict and ensure the conservation of the endangered Bengal tiger.

title.rendered: Disaster damage to infrastructure Rs 227 billion, Rs 63 billion sought immediately for reconstruction

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Recent floods, landslides and climate-related disasters have caused preliminary damage worth Rs 227 billion to the country’s infrastructure.

Padma Kumar Mainali, secretary at the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, gave the figure at a meeting of the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Impact of Climate Change in the Himalayas, Climate Justice and the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli Disaster, held at Singha Durbar. He said Rs 63 billion is needed immediately for reconstruction.

Secretary Mainali presented a detailed account of the damage, saying housing, the road network, bridges and drinking water infrastructure were badly hit.

According to Mainali, housing (private and public) suffered the most damage. Damage to 7,570 private and 48 public buildings totals Rs 103.54 billion.

The preliminary estimate also puts damage at Rs 20 billion for the road network, Rs 13.80 billion for motorable bridges, Rs 2.65 billion for suspension bridges and Rs 87.87 billion for drinking water and sanitation.

Mainali said the total damage reaches US$1.48 billion (nearly Rs 227 billion), and that this raises serious questions about foreign assistance for climate justice.

“According to the Ministry of Infrastructure Development’s preliminary assessment, damage to buildings, roads, motorable and suspension bridges and drinking water is estimated at Rs 227 billion,” he said. “This is a preliminary figure, and exact details will come later.”

He added, “Prioritising restoration of connectivity, 12 of the 20 damaged suspension bridges have been repaired. A Bailey bridge is being built in the Betrawati area, and work is moving ahead to restore road links gradually through Dhunche and Syafrubesi up to Rasuwagadhi. Land has been identified for resettlement. Design and construction are being prepared with a target of building about 300 transitional shelters immediately.”

About Rs 63 billion is needed immediately for overall reconstruction, he said. Given the scale of the damage, he said relief and reconstruction must proceed with a long-term plan.

Mainali claimed the ministry is working at war footing to improve connectivity, with the blocked road in the Trishuli corridor and Bailey bridge construction made priorities.

He said preparations are underway to build about 300 transitional shelters (temporary housing) for victims before the coming Dashain. The government has sought a budget of Rs 63 billion for the initial phase of disaster response and rehabilitation.

title.rendered: How pond algae led to a Nobel prize and a new way to study the brain

content.rendered:
Scientists who worked out how to control brain cells with light have won this year’s Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were honoured for their research into “light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.

Peter Hegemann, at Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel, at the University of Würzburg, wanted to understand how a tiny, single-celled alga called Chlamydomonas senses light. Light-sensing is not unique to animals with eyes: organisms throughout the living world use light to detect their surroundings and respond to changes in their environment. Even single-cell organisms have proteins that respond to light. These proteins are used to move towards or away from light, to generate energy and to respond to the various demands of a 24-hour day.

Hegemann and Nagel discovered that Chlamydomonas has a beautifully ingenious mechanism of light detection that relies on a single protein called channelrhodopsin.

Channelrhodopsin is built into the outer membrane of the algal cell. Part of the protein faces the water outside the cell and part faces the inside. The protein also contains a small molecule called retinaldehyde, which is able to absorb light.

When light hits the retinaldehyde inside channelrhodopsin, it changes shape. This makes the channelrhodopsin protein change shape too. That change opens a tiny passage through the cell membrane. Positively charged particles, including sodium, can then flow from the water outside the alga into the cell. This movement of charged particles sends a signal inside the alga that helps it swim.

How fantastic to have solved such an interesting biological question, but why the Nobel prize in physiology or medicine? The answer lies in the way nerve cells work. Nerve cells use the movement of charged particles (called “ions”) across their membranes to control their activity. When positively charged particles flow into a nerve cell, they can make it more active.

The researchers realised that if they could put channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, they might be able to switch those cells on simply by shining a light on them. That is exactly what Hegemann, Nagel and the third Nobel-prize winner, Karl Deisseroth, a psychiatrist and bioengineer at Stanford University in California, went on to do.

Switching on nerve cells with light

The ability to control nerve cells with light is called optogenetics. It has become a powerful research tool because scientists can use it to switch specific groups of nerve cells on and off and see what happens.

First, scientists deliver the gene for channelrhodopsin to the nerve cells they want to study. The gene is usually carried into the cells by a virus that has been altered so that it cannot cause disease. The cells then make the channelrhodopsin protein, which makes them respond to light.

In animals such as mice, scientists can shine light into the brain through a thin optical fibre. When the light reaches the cells, channelrhodopsin opens and the cells become active. Nearby nerve cells that do not contain the protein are unaffected.

Light can be aimed at a very small part of the brain and switched on and off extremely quickly. This makes optogenetics a powerful way to investigate how the brain works. For example, if scientists want to know whether a particular group of nerve cells is involved in memory, sleep, sensation or movement, say, they can switch those cells on with light and see what happens.

In one experiment in 2012, a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology gave mice a mild electric shock in a particular cage. They used optogenetics to tag the nerve cells in the brain’s memory centre that were active during that the fear-conditioning experiment. Days later, in a different cage, they switched those cells on with light. The mice froze in fear, as if they remembered the shock.

Mice that were not shocked did not freeze, which showed that the light was reactivating a specific memory. Deisseroth was one of the study’s authors.

Optogenetics has transformed scientists’ ability to investigate how the brain and nervous system work. It may also have a future as a treatment. Optogenetics is already in early-stage clinical trials for people with retinal degeneration. In these trials, researchers introduce light-sensitive proteins into nerve cells that remain in the retina after the cells that normally detect light – called rods and cones – have been lost. This can make surviving cells respond to light and restore some vision.

Researchers are also investigating whether optogenetics could eventually be used to treat neurological conditions, including Parkinson’s and epilepsy.

This year’s Nobel prize celebrates work that started with a question that may sound esoteric: how do Chlamydomonas swim toward light? This question has no obvious practical importance. It doesn’t address an urgent need in human health, nor is it a clear route to riches. The success of optogenetics is an illustration of the importance of continuing to ask questions simply to understand the world around us because it’s impossible to predict where knowledge will take us.

title.rendered: Man’s body found in pond in Janakpurdham

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, October 6

The body of a man has been found in a pond in Janakpurdham.

The body of a man aged about 55 was found in Dasharath Talau pond in Janakpurdham Sub-Metropolitan City-8.

Locals saw the body in the pond at around 9:45 am today, and police went to the site and pulled it out.

title.rendered: Flood damage to Maldhunga Bridge cuts off western Nepal, thousands affected

content.rendered:
Pokhara, October 6

Landslides have occurred at several locations from Kushma Bazaar to Maldhunga and Beni Bazaar. In some places, landslides have swept away sections of the road, while in others, piles of rocks and soil have accumulated along the roadside. Rocks on the cliffs appear precariously poised to fall.

Vehicles have begun operating along the damaged sections of the road at Sahasradhara in Kushma Municipality of Parbat and along the Maldhunga–Beni road. However, passengers continue to travel while looking up anxiously at hillsides that appear ready to collapse overhead.

The floods and landslides triggered by incessant rainfall since September 24 caused extensive loss of life and property across Gandaki Province. Flooding in the Kaligandaki River swept away the old Farse Bazaar in Jaljala Rural Municipality. The river has also eroded land at several locations between Beni, the headquarters of Myagdi, and Kushma, the headquarters of Parbat.

Conservation activist RK Adipta Giri believes the scale of the erosion along the Kaligandaki River suggests that an even greater disaster was narrowly avoided.

“Kaligandaki has eroded settlements and land to such an extent that it seems our settlements survived by a whisker. A major loss of human lives was averted,” Giri said while observing the damaged areas. Unusual and almost unbelievable scenes can still be seen all the way from Kushma to Jaljala.

Damage to Maldhunga Bridge approach road affects western region

The flood in the Kaligandaki River on September 27 washed away the approach road to Maldhunga Bridge, which connects Parbat and Baglung. Erosion on the Parbat side of the bridge has caused major problems for residents of western Parbat as the festive season approaches.

With the Kaligandaki eroding the approach to Maldhunga Bridge, road connectivity from Baglung and Burtibang to Rukum East, Rukum West, Jajarkot, Dailekh, Achham and all the way to Baitadi (Jhulaghat) in Sudurpaschim has been disrupted.

The highway had provided a direct connection to western and mid-hill districts, including Rukum East, Rukum West, Rolpa, Jajarkot and Dolpa, mainly through the Burtibang area of Baglung. Baglung Chief District Officer Krishna Prasad Acharya said thousands of people had been affected by the loss of the approach road at Maldhunga just before the festive season.

Maldhunga Bridge is Nepal’s first arch bridge. The bow-shaped bridge was constructed in 1991 with Chinese assistance. Similar arch bridges have since been built at Muglin, Bijulibazar over the Dhobikhola and Ramdi over the Kaligandaki River.

In an arch bridge, the load is transferred not only directly to the pillars but through the curvature of the arch to strong foundations on both sides. A key feature of such bridges is that they do not require pillars in the middle of the river.

Experts say the ability to construct long spans without pillars reduces the risk of damage to the pillars or the bridge itself from logs, gravel and debris carried by floods.

Damage to approach road linked to river exploitation

However, the Kaligandaki, which floods almost every year, has this time eroded a section of the road beside the arch bridge. Engineers say the erosion of the section is linked to the exploitation of the river.

“The flood on September 27 caused extensive damage at several locations. There has also been encroachment along the river in various places, as well as riverbed exploitation by crusher operators,” said Dhurba Pokhrel, information officer at the Road Division Office, Pokhara. “It appears that changes in the river’s course have damaged the approach road. This needs to be studied, and it should be.”

Excavators can still be seen operating in the river, while tipper trucks and bulldozers are being used to extract and transport riverbed materials. Locals are concerned that crusher operators have continued extraction activities despite the scale of the disaster.

The claim that businesses are misleading the administration is also reflected in the remarks of Parbat Chief District Officer Gangabahadur Chhetri.

“Locals have complained that settlements and structures, including bridges, along the riverbank have been eroded because of river exploitation. Extraction also appears to have contributed to the river changing course and entering settlements,” CDO Chhetri said. “We will strictly monitor the situation, determine what is legal and illegal, and take action accordingly. However, it appears that the businesses here have arranged everything through some kind of setting. We are still studying the matter.”

Target to repair before Dashain

When an Onlinekhabar team reached Maldhunga Bridge on Sunday, a bulldozer was being used to level the soil at the eroded section. With Dashain approaching, locals remained uncertain about when the bridge would be restored.

Engineer Pokhrel said the Road Division Office, Pokhara, was working through the emergency fund with the aim of reopening the road before Dashain.

“When the river eroded the road and we began emergency construction, it was difficult during the initial days because the water level at some locations was as high as 8 to 10 metres. We are now preparing a suitable platform for construction,” Pokhrel told Onlinekhabar. “The foundation work is also in its final stage. The structure now needs to be raised to a height of 18 metres. Preparations are underway to open it at least before Dashain.”

With Maldhunga Bridge out of operation, people have been unable to travel to major cities such as Pokhara, Narayangadh and Kathmandu. Although vehicles have resumed operation after landslides were cleared at several locations between Kushma and Beni, locals remain fearful, saying the risk of accidents has not been eliminated, according to local Ganesh Acharya.

The bridge, which connects to the Mid-Hill Highway, has affected daily life across western Nepal. The Beni–Jomsom road has also been severely damaged by floods and landslides, leaving Mustang district cut off by road. The Korala border point, which had emerged as an alternative to the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, has also been brought to a standstill because of road damage.

As the bridge is expected to take some more time to reopen, locals say shortages of food, petroleum products and cooking gas have begun to emerge. Baglung resident Hari Khadka said people were concerned that they might face shortages during Dashain.

Residents of Baglung and Parbat are currently using the Gandaki Golden Suspension Bridge, claimed to be the longest suspension bridge in Asia, which connects Baglung and Parbat, as well as other high suspension bridges in Kushma as alternatives. Passengers are crossing the river on foot using these bridges, reaching the Parbat side and then taking other vehicles to continue their journeys.

title.rendered: UK university’s licence suspended, Nepali students among those affected

content.rendered:
Hundreds of students, including Nepalis, have been affected after the UK Home Office suspended Buckinghamshire New University’s student sponsor licence on September 30.

The suspension took effect immediately, and the government has removed the university from the register of licensed sponsors. The university, which has campuses in High Wycombe, London and Nottingham, says most of the issues raised relate to past international student recruitment.

The Home Office has given it 20 days to respond. If the university cannot provide enough evidence to justify reinstating the licence, it will be revoked.

Nepali students affected

Pramod Adhikari, director of Ample International Education, a consultancy in the UK and Nepal, said about 250 Nepali students are enrolled, many of them studying nursing at what is seen as a relatively cheap university. His agency has also recommended students there. He said there is no need to panic.

Students remain worried, however, as the government is getting tougher on sponsors.

“The university says it is working on it, but with so little time left, I fear what the outcome will be,” said one nursing student.

Students with valid visas can continue studying during the suspension. If the licence is revoked, they must find a new sponsor within 60 days of their visa being cancelled, get a new Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS) number and apply for a new visa, paying the application fee and health surcharge again. Otherwise they must leave the UK.

Tighter rules

On August 5, the Home Office revoked the sponsor licence of London’s Bloomsbury Institute after it failed the Basic Compliance Assessment, an annual check of visa refusal, enrolment and course completion rates. It needed to keep visa refusals below 10 percent, enrolment at 90 percent or more and completion at 85 percent or more.

Since June 1, 2026, the thresholds have been tightened to visa refusals below 5 percent, enrolment of at least 95 percent and completion of at least 90 percent.

The government says the tougher measures cut asylum claims by students by 30 percent in a year. Asylum claims by people on work, study and visit visas had risen more than threefold to 37 percent under the previous government, with foreign students the largest share.

Universities under pressure

Home Office data show student visa applications up to the end of July were 11 percent lower than a year earlier. Some fear international enrolment could fall by as much as 30 percent. University leaders warn of financial trouble and have urged the government to rethink the levy on international student fees introduced under Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

King’s College London vice-chancellor Prof Shitij Kapur told The Guardian that every five international students support one university job, so the fall will affect finances and staffing.

Madhu Acharya is set to contest for the post of vice-president at the ongoing 15th General Convention of the Nepali Congress.

Nomination registration for the general convention is taking place today. Nomination forms are currently being distributed, while registration will be open from noon to 4 pm.

title.rendered: Finance Minister Wagle and World Bank President Banga meet in the US

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga held a high-level bilateral meeting.

Minister Wagle, who travelled to the United States leading a delegation at the World Bank president’s invitation, met Banga in Washington, DC.

During the meeting, Minister Wagle discussed rebuilding the physical and economic infrastructure damaged by the recent flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, macroeconomic reform, and mobilising resources worth about US$1 billion for insurance and social protection, according to the minister’s private secretariat.

Expressing sadness over the damage from the flood disaster in Nepal, Banga committed the World Bank to providing significant support in reconstruction.

Praising the steps the new government has taken for policy and institutional reform, he stressed the need to expand investment in infrastructure and create jobs within the country.

Banga said the World Bank would take a new initiative to expand joint investment in Nepal’s priority sectors by coordinating with development partners including the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.

According to David Sislen, the World Bank’s country director for Nepal, this is the first direct bilateral meeting between a World Bank president and a Nepali finance minister in the past three decades.

Senior officials, including World Bank vice presidents Johannes Zutt and Junaid Ahmad, took part in the meeting.

title.rendered: Nepal returns from Asian Games with two bronze medals, falls short of double-digit target

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Before leaving for Japan to participate in the 20th Asian Games (Asiad), Nepal had hoped to win a double-digit number of medals, including gold.

The government had launched ‘Mission-26’ in Magh 2080 with the same target. However, Nepal not only fell short of its goal but returned home with just two bronze medals.

Nepal sent 135 athletes to compete in 21 sports at the Asiad but had to settle for two bronze medals. Karateka Tenzing Sherpa and the women’s kabaddi team saved Nepal’s reputation.

The women’s kabaddi team retained the bronze medal it had won at the 19th Asiad, while Tenzing won Nepal’s first-ever bronze medal in karate. However, karateka Arika Gurung, who had won a silver medal at the 19th Asiad, failed to win a medal this time. Nepal also failed to achieve the expected results in other sports in which it had medal hopes.

Nepal has been participating in the Asian Games for 75 years. However, it has yet to win a single gold medal. Over the past 75 years, Nepal has won three silver and 25 bronze medals. The country remains in a situation where merely participating in the Asiad is considered an achievement rather than winning medals.

Nepal’s performance raises the biggest question about its preparations. Although the government had set a target of winning double-digit medals, athletes’ training was affected for around four months during preparations for the Asiad due to a lack of budget.

Major competitions such as the Asiad require clear planning years in advance, continuous training and adequate funding. However, Nepal has yet to overcome the tendency to intensify preparations only when a major competition is approaching.

Even during the final preparations, athletes did not receive adequate sports equipment and diets. Training alone is not enough for high-level performance; international exposure is equally important. However, some Nepali athletes competed in an international tournament for the first time at the Asiad itself.

India’s women’s kabaddi team, which was preparing for the Asiad, invited Iran to India for a practice match. The Indian team later faced Iran in the Asiad final, where India defeated Iran to win the women’s kabaddi gold medal.

The Nepali women’s kabaddi team prepared for the Asiad in India. During their preparations, the Nepali team played practice matches against Indian state teams and local clubs. India became Nepal’s opponent in the Asiad semi-final.

Nepal lost to India in the match and had to settle for bronze. The confidence India had developed by playing practice matches against strong teams was evident. The lack of experience against stronger opponents was also apparent in the Nepali team. This highlights the significant gap between Nepal’s international preparations and those of countries competing for medals.

Regular competition and match exposure against strong nations are essential when preparing for international competitions. This Asiad has demonstrated that simply arranging overseas training or a few practice matches shortly before a tournament is not enough to expect a high-level performance.

For the 20th Asiad, athletes in most sports were not selected through a systematic process starting from the grassroots level. The tendency to form teams from the available pool of athletes was repeated. Had the 10th National Games been held on schedule, outstanding performers there could have been selected and prepared for the Asiad.

National competitions are an important foundation for identifying and selecting athletes and preparing them for competition. The delay in holding the National Games therefore directly affects preparations for international competitions, as this Asiad has demonstrated.

Nepal now needs to be clear about whether it wants to regard mere participation in competitions such as the Asiad as an achievement or develop a strategy aimed at winning medals.

Rather than spending large amounts of resources on sports with little medal potential, the need of the hour is to identify sports with realistic medal prospects and provide them with adequate funding, training and international exposure. The government must be clear about which sports should participate, and why, and which should not.

Successful sporting nations around the world invest in athletes from a young age. Athletes are developed through talent identification, grassroots training, regular competitions and long-term planning. In Nepal, however, such a system remains weak.

The government and sports associations have failed to adequately identify talent at an early age and provide continuous training and opportunities. Many athletes have made significant contributions to Nepali sports through their individual efforts and struggles. However, individual efforts alone cannot create a sustainable foundation for winning international medals. That requires long-term state investment and an institutional system.

Another problem in Nepal is weak coordination between the government and sports associations. The government needs to effectively monitor what activities each association is conducting, how individual athletes are performing, how much investment each sport requires and what preparations are being made for international competitions. Due to disagreements between a sports association and the government, Nepal’s PUBG team, which was considered a medal contender, was selected but was unable to participate in this Asiad.

The preparations and facilities provided to athletes participating in international competitions also need to be reconsidered.

While government employees and representatives receive substantial daily allowances when travelling abroad, athletes at this Asiad had to manage their food, accommodation and preparations within limited daily allowances. If athletes are being sent abroad to win medals for the country, priority must be given to their food and accommodation, as well as training, medical treatment and other essential facilities.

Athlete selection, grassroots development, regular national competitions and international exposure must be integrated into a single plan. Nepal must also adopt available technologies to make athletes’ training more effective.

title.rendered: Hearings for 13 proposed ambassadors begin today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The Parliamentary Hearing Committee of the House of Representatives begins hearings today for ambassadors proposed to 13 countries.

According to the Parliament Secretariat, the committee will meet at 11:15 am today. Complaints received against the proposed ambassadors will be distributed to committee members at the meeting.

The agenda for today’s meeting also includes distributing the work plans submitted by the proposed ambassadors to committee members.

Seven complaints have been filed against the 13 proposed ambassadors. Two complaints are against all of them, while five name individuals.

A Cabinet meeting held on September 18 decided to recommend ambassadors to 13 countries.

The government has recommended Dr Nischal Nath Pandey for India, Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma for China, Chiran Jung Thapa for the United States, and former Chief of the Army Staff Gaurav Shamsher Jung Bahadur Rana for the United Kingdom.

It has also recommended Jigyan Kumar Thapa for Japan, Suresh Kumar Karna for Israel, Prapti Sherchan for Spain, Saru Joshi for Germany, Dr Padmakshi Rana for Oman, Chudamani Kharel for Malaysia, Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha for South Korea, Dr Manchala Jha for Sri Lanka and Giri Bahadur Sunar for Saudi Arabia.

title.rendered: 36 bills in Parliament, preparations to register 14 more

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The government has taken the process of registering 14 more bills in Parliament to its final stage.

There are currently 36 bills pending in the federal Parliament. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs said work is moving ahead to register another 14 bills soon.

According to Ekram Giri, joint secretary and spokesperson at the Parliament Secretariat, 12 bills passed in the last two sessions have been passed by both houses. Eleven have been certified by the President, and one is in the process of certification.

Of the 36 bills pending in the federal Parliament, 24 are under clause-by-clause discussion in parliamentary committees. One is in the National Assembly. The rest are still in the House.

The Law Ministry said the government has taken the process of registering 14 more bills to its final stage.

Among the bills close to registration are the bill to amend the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority Act and a bill to amend the Act related to the National Vigilance Centre.

A bill to amend the Companies Act and five bills to amend various codes are also being brought. A bill on industrial property is also moving ahead for registration soon.

The Ministry of Finance is bringing bills related to public debt management and foreign exchange.

The Ministry of Energy has advanced a bill related to renewable energy and a bill to amend the Act related to water resources.

A bill related to an infrastructure tribunal and a bill related to agriculture are also moving ahead.

A bill related to animal slaughterhouses is also moving ahead to be registered in Parliament soon.

The Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Ministry is tracking where each bill stands. It said the process of registering 14 more bills soon is moving ahead.

Several roads across the country remain fully blocked today as well.

Police said roads in Rasuwa, Myagdi, Manang and Nawalparasi East are blocked.

According to police, Rasuwa’s main highway remains completely blocked, and the blockage on the Beni–Jomsom road in Myagdi has not been cleared.

The Khangsar–Besisahar road section in Manang is also fully closed. A flood on the night of September 25 fully cut the road that runs through Besisahar to Khangsar. This road has also not yet been repaired.

In Nawalparasi East, a landslide has reduced the Kaligandaki Corridor road at Janti, Baudikali Rural Municipality-3, to one lane. Large vehicles cannot use this section.

Rasuwa’s highways have been closed since August 25 because of floods, while the Beni–Jomsom road has been blocked by a landslide since September 26. The road at Janti on the Kaligandaki has been one-way since September 30.
