Rijal informed leaders and cadres close to him of his decision during a discussion at his residence on Monday morning.

Rijal was elected a general convention representative from Morang Constituency No. 2. Since then, there had been speculation that he would contest for the post of vice-president. However, Rijal himself had said that he had no ambition for any party post.

title.rendered: Annapurna Circuit trek route opens after snow cleared

content.rendered:
Mustang, October 6

Snow has been cleared from the Annapurna Circuit trek route.

The Thorong La Pass trail in the Annapurna Conservation Area, which links Manang and Mustang, reopened on Monday after 20 people cleared the snow on the initiative of the Muktinath Hotel Association.

Foreign tourists trek from Besisahar in Lamjung through Manang over Thorong La Pass to reach Muktinath. Muktinath Hotel Association president Suraj Gurung said the trek has been made easier by clearing the thick snow on the Thorong La Pass trail linking Manang and Mustang.

Heavy snowfall from September 24 to 27 had fully blocked the Thorong La Pass trail and halted tourist movement.

Thorong La Pass is the most suitable place for adventure trekking from October to November. Tourist trekking on the Manang–Mustang Annapurna Circuit takes place for only five months each year.

Foreign tourists prefer the Thorong La Pass section of the Annapurna Circuit, which has established itself as one of the world’s best-known trekking routes, for adventure trekking.

The Muktinath Hotel Association said trekkers travelling from Manang over Thorong La Pass to Mustang will face no problems.

title.rendered: Crowds return home through Jamunaha border point to celebrate Dashain

content.rendered:
Banke, October 6

Numbers of people are returning home from India through the Jamunaha border point in Nepalgunj to celebrate Dashain.

The number of Nepalis returning home is rising daily as the festival nears, said Chief Police Inspector Rajan Prasad Bhattarai, head of the Area Police Office, Jamunaha, Banke.

More than 50,000 Nepalis have returned home through the Jamunaha border point for Dashain in the past five days, he said. “Queues of Nepalis returning home from India for Dashain are forming from morning till evening now. More than 10,000 citizens come through the Jamunaha border point every day,” he said. “Nepal Police has been coordinating to prevent criminal incidents such as robbery against them in the border area.”

Nepalis who work in New Delhi, Mumbai and various cities in Himachal Pradesh are returning home for Dashain.

Banke Chief District Officer Dilkumar Tamang said a passenger help desk has been set up at the Jamunaha border point to ensure Nepalis returning from India for the festival are not robbed, cheated or left stranded in the border area, and are taken safely to their destinations.

“We have put a security plan in place by putting citizens’ safety first and identifying possible risks,” CDO Tamang said. “The passenger help desk is operating right at the Jamunaha border point so that Nepalis returning from India do not face problems such as fraud and robbery along the way.”

He said the help desk will provide the necessary information, coordination and help for the convenience and safety of the large number of passengers who go to India for work and return home at festival time.

Banke’s police chief, Senior Superintendent of Police Angur GC, said a special security plan has been put in place to control criminal activity during the festival, with arrangements to take Nepalis returning from India safely to their destinations.

Police Superintendent GC said passenger help desks will also operate from Tuesday at the Nepalgunj and Kohalpur bus parks, aimed at the rush of Nepalis returning from India.

title.rendered: Congress begins distributing candidacy forms as 7,114 delegates prepare to choose leadership

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Candidacies for the new working committee are being filed today under the Nepali Congress’s 15th General Convention. A total of 7,114 convention delegates will choose the new leadership.

The Election Committee has set up an office at the National Assembly Hall (Rastriya Sabhagriha) to distribute candidacy forms and register candidacies. According to Election Committee member-secretary Raju Katwal, nomination forms have been distributed to candidates since 10 am.

The delegates’ list is posted on the wall of the hall. Candidates will get a form after paying the prescribed fee to Prabhu Bank staff inside the hall.

Nominations for candidacies will be registered from 12:30 pm to 4 pm. The Congress has increased the size of its Central Working Committee from 167 to 297 members. The amended statute passed on Monday raises the number of office-bearers from 14 to 26.

Under the new arrangement, one senior vice-president and one woman vice-president have been added, bringing the number of vice-presidents to four. The number of general secretaries has been raised to three, with one woman general secretary made mandatory.

Two open joint general secretaries have been added, taking the number of joint general secretaries to 11. A spokesperson post has also been added. The party said the number of joint spokespersons may be increased further as needed.

At the 14th General Convention, the Congress Central Working Committee had 167 members and 14 office-bearers.

The Congress said it has increased the size of the Central Working Committee and the number of office-bearers because the number of delegates and inclusive participation have grown this time.

title.rendered: Congress general convention to elect new committee in 80 clusters

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The new working committee of the Nepali Congress will be elected from 80 clusters, including inclusive categories, at the party’s 15th General Convention.

The amended statute passed at Monday’s closed session has 80 categories (clusters), covering the president, office-bearers and central members. Central members will be elected from separate categories including open, women, Dalit, Indigenous Peoples (Adivasi Janajati), Madhesi, Muslim, Khas Arya, province, diaspora and youth.

Nominations for the new working committee are being filed today. After all the processes that follow nomination are complete, voting is scheduled for 7 am to 5 pm on October 8.

Under the amended statute, the Central Working Committee will have 297 members. It will include one president, one senior vice-president and four vice-presidents. One of the vice-presidents must be a woman.

There will be three general secretaries, two from the open category and one from the women’s quota.

There will be 15 joint general secretaries. Two will be elected from the open category. One each will be elected from the Indigenous Peoples (Adivasi Janajati), Dalit, Madhesi, Khas Arya, Tharu, Muslim, backward areas, and minority/disability quotas.

The treasurer will be nominated from among the central members. There will be one spokesperson and one joint spokesperson.

Among central members, 45 will be elected through open competition. Fifteen will come from the women’s open category. Eight will be elected from Indigenous Peoples women, 12 from Indigenous Peoples open, five from Dalit women, one from Madhesi Dalit and eight from Dalit open.

Eight each will come from Madhesi women and Khas Arya women, and 10 from Khas Arya open.

There will be two central members from Tharu women, four from Tharu open, two from Muslim women and three from Muslim open.

One central member each will be elected from backward areas women, backward areas open, minority and disability quotas.

One central member each will come from democracy fighters, martyrs’ families and conflict-affected families.

Central members will also be elected from all seven provinces from among women and open candidates under 35. One central member each will come from the Kathmandu Valley from women and open categories.

Quotas for central members have been set aside for the Nepali Public Relations Committee Europe region, Oceania–America region, Nepali Public Relations Committee Middle East region, Asia Pacific region and the Nepali Public Relations Committee India. Central members will also be elected for professional and thematic areas and labour, including a women’s open seat.

The statute also provides for the Central Working Committee to nominate 66 more members later.

title.rendered: Home Minister Sudan Gurung warns action against those leaking sensitive information

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Home Minister Sudan Gurung has said that anyone found leaking confidential information will face action.

Gurung made the statement on Tuesday through a post on Facebook.

He said that no one would be granted immunity for deliberately betraying the country or their organisation by violating the confidentiality entrusted to them by the state. He added that such individuals would be brought to justice.

The government on Monday suspended Armed Police Force AIG Banshiraj Dahal on allegations of leaking sensitive information. The Home Ministry accused Dahal of violating official conduct and leaking sensitive information.

Gurung wrote, “I have been closely observing for a long time the tendency of officials and employees working at the Ministry of Home Affairs and its subordinate agencies to forget their official responsibilities and leak confidential or sensitive information to unauthorised individuals or organisations.”

He further wrote, “Sensitive state information is not anyone’s private property; it is a public responsibility. Holding a position gives one access to information, but it does not give one the right to misuse it. Even the smallest piece of information, tip-off or intelligence obtained here can play a decisive role in preventing crime, advancing investigations or establishing the truth about a serious incident in the future.”

title.rendered: AIG Banshiraj Dahal suspended over sensitive information leak

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The government suspended Armed Police Force AIG Banshiraj Dahal from his post on Monday afternoon on allegations of leaking sensitive information.

According to a statement issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Dahal was suspended for engaging in conduct contrary to official protocol and for leaking sensitive information.

According to information provided to Onlinekhabar by sources, two reasons have emerged behind his suspension.

The first concerns his “connection” with former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana.

According to Home Ministry sources, AIG Dahal had reached the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office in Teku on the night of September 27. Police had brought former Chief Justice Rana there shortly after taking him into custody from his residence.

“It appears that he reached Teku shortly after Rana was brought to the police station,” the source said. “After he arrived at the police office in the middle of the night without regard for official protocol, further investigation into him was initiated.”

According to the source, Dahal had gone to Teku without informing anyone and had also bypassed the chain of command.

The source said that while investigating why AIG Banshiraj Dahal had gone to Teku, a second reason came to light.

That was his “connection” with a person named Inam Sapkota from Jhapa.

An investigation conducted by the Police Special Bureau found that AIG Dahal had been in contact with Sapkota, whom the police investigation regarded as suspicious.

According to the source, Dahal appears to have shared sensitive information concerning former Chief Justice Rana through Sapkota.

Following the investigation, police also took Inam Sapkota into custody. He was released after being held for a day.

A source at the investigation bureau said investigators found that Dahal had been sharing information through Inam’s mobile phone.

A meeting of the Ministry of Home Affairs held today also decided to appoint an investigation officer and proceed with a formal inquiry. The appointed officer has been given a mandate to complete the investigation and submit a report to the ministry within three days.

The government is preparing to include in the report the findings concerning the connection between Rana, Dahal and Sapkota.

On the night of September 27, the government took former Chief Justice Rana into custody from his residence, citing a security threat.

Police kept him in custody for around 12 hours before releasing him. At the time, the manner in which he was taken from his home in the middle of the night had also drawn criticism.

title.rendered: 13 proposed ambassadors face parliamentary hearing from today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

The parliamentary hearing process for 13 individuals recommended as ambassadors to various countries will begin on Tuesday.

According to the Federal Parliament Secretariat, a meeting of the Parliamentary Hearing Committee scheduled for 11:15 am will distribute the complaints filed against the proposed ambassadors among committee members. The work plans submitted by the nominees will also be distributed to the members.

Seven complaints have been filed against the 13 proposed ambassadors. Two complaints have been filed against all 13 nominees, while five complaints have been filed against individual nominees.

The government had recommended the 13 ambassadors at a Cabinet meeting held on September 18. The Parliamentary Hearing Committee subsequently initiated the process for their hearings.

The government has recommended Dr Nischal Nath Pandey as ambassador to India, Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma to China, Chiran Jung Thapa to the United States and former army chief Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana to the United Kingdom.

Similarly, Jijyan Kumar Thapa has been recommended as ambassador to Japan, Suresh Kumar Karn to Israel, Prapti Sherchan to Spain, Sharu Joshi to Germany, Dr Padmakshi Rana to Oman, Chudamani Kharel to Malaysia, Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha to South Korea, Dr Manchala Jha to Sri Lanka and Giri Bahadur Sunar to Saudi Arabia.

The Parliamentary Hearing Committee is responsible for conducting hearings on individuals recommended for appointment as ambassadors under Article 292 of the Constitution.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s Facebook post about Khula Manch has sparked an open debate in Nepali society.

With the opening of the Nepali Congress general convention at Khula Manch on Sunday, the venue’s old role as a public space for political rallies and gatherings has been revived after nearly a decade. But a debate is also underway over who deserves credit — or blame — for closing and reopening the venue.

The vast Tundikhel area, which was used during the Rana era for military parades and displays of state power, was gradually adopted by pro-democracy activists as Khula Manch, or “Open Stage.”

After the 1951 democratic revolution, the northeastern section of Tundikhel was transformed into a major centre for political rallies and civic dialogue. On February 19, 1951, King Tribhuvan declared democracy from there.

Following the 1959 general election, the policies and programmes of Nepal’s first elected government, led by BP Koirala, were also presented from this very stage. But after King Mahendra staged a coup in 1960 and imposed the Panchayat system, the area was placed under strict surveillance and Tundikhel was gradually divided into different sections. In the process, Khula Manch was reduced to the northern section after being separated from the military area.

Khula Manch witnessed the student movement of 1979, the 1990 democratic movement and the 2006 republican movement. A central platform for democratic consciousness and civic resistance, Khula Manch was eventually closed even under a democratic system.

The situation became particularly complicated after a multi-storey commercial building project began at the old bus park adjacent to Khula Manch. From 2014, the bus park was moved into Khula Manch.

A market was also established inside Khula Manch, with commercial shutters installed alongside the bus park. Jaleshwar Swachchhanda Bikoi Builders, which had won the contract to construct a 29-storey tower at the old bus park, encroached on Khula Manch and rented out the shutters to businesses. No one appeared willing to put a “brake” on the activities of businessman Manoj Bhetwal, owner of Swachchhanda Builders, which was collecting rent from the shops at Khula Manch.

However, the issue led to a public dispute in 2017 between then-Kathmandu Metropolitan City Mayor Bidhya Sundar Shakya, elected from the CPN-UML, and Deputy Mayor Hari Prabha Khadgi.

Khadgi, who is now a Bagmati provincial assembly member, recalls that while serving as deputy mayor, she had to launch a campaign against her own metropolitan city’s decisions to protect Khula Manch.

“The mayor at the time did not stop even when 52 shutters were being constructed. The subsequent mayor, Balen, also tried to turn it into a parking area,” she says.

Following widespread public opposition, then-Deputy Mayor Khadgi supported the activists. In April 2019, the federal government used bulldozers to demolish the commercial shutters.

Shakya says Khula Manch was opened during his tenure

However, Shakya claims that Khula Manch was actually cleared during his tenure.

“The old bus park was moved to Khula Manch after the decision to construct the multi-storey building. At the same time, the new Bir Hospital building was under construction, as was Durbar High School, which had been damaged by the earthquake. Construction materials for those buildings could not be stored on the roads, so they were placed at Khula Manch. But once the Bir Hospital and Durbar High School buildings were completed, Khula Manch was cleared,” he says.

But why, then, were political programmes not held there until now?

“That is something you should ask the organisers. But there was no obstruction,” Shakya says.

In the 2022 local elections, Balendra Shah was elected mayor and Sunita Dangol deputy mayor. Soon afterwards, the metropolitan city began the process of preparing a detailed project report for constructing a triple-basement parking facility at Khula Manch.

The decision taken by the metropolitan city’s 10th executive meeting on November 15 that year came under widespread criticism.

According to activist Sushan Vaidya, had the metropolitan city’s plan succeeded, Khula Manch would no longer have remained Khula Manch.

He says the metropolitan city was planning a concrete structure similar to the one at Chandni Chowk in New Delhi, with commercial activity on top.

“I cannot understand why every mayor wants to turn Khula Manch into a milking cow,” Vaidya says. “It was the people who saved Khula Manch. Activists and the media supported them.”

During Balen’s tenure as mayor, Kathmandu Metropolitan City carried out work at Khula Manch under its “Sports Infrastructure Maintenance, Improvement and Upgrading Programme,” including planting grass, constructing walking paths around the area and painting.

“Planting grass, painting or constructing pathways cannot be called saving Khula Manch,” says Vaidya, one of the activists involved in the campaign to protect the site.

Vaidya stresses that protecting Khula Manch also means preserving its spirit. He is also president of the Nepali Congress Kathmandu Metropolitan City committee.

“Even now, it is fenced off with railings and kept locked. The spirit of Khula Manch can only be preserved if it is actually open to everyone,” he says.

“Khula Manch was already good, Prime Minister. You did some painting. Thank you for your colourful efforts,” Gen Z activist Majid Ansari commented on social media.

Balen’s Facebook post targeted at Gagan?

Many believe Prime Minister Balen Shah’s Facebook post — “Thankfully, Khula Manch has been made better, so the new party can hold programmes there and abuse others!” — was aimed at Congress President Gagan Thapa.

The prime minister’s post came as a response to comments Thapa had made about him during the opening session of the Congress’s 15th General Convention on Sunday.

Speaking at Khula Manch, Thapa said: “Today, Nepal needs many more Khula Manchs like this. Where is the first Khula Manch needed? It is needed inside Parliament. Parliament is not open. Parliament is closed. The prime minister who was made by this very Parliament needs to be present for both the lawmakers who supported him in becoming prime minister and those who did not, and for the dignity and functioning of Parliament. Until the prime minister is present there with respect, Parliament cannot be considered open. We need a Khula Manch inside Parliament.”

Public land linked to Khula Manch ‘sold’

Thapa’s remarks were clearly directed at what he sees as the prime minister’s disregard for a Parliament in which the Rastriya Swatantra Party has 182 lawmakers.

But was it appropriate for the leader of the main opposition party to make such comments from the platform of his own party’s general convention?

Analyst Neelambar Acharya says, “Not only was it appropriate, he had to do it. If the opposition does not speak about the prime minister’s lack of accountability to Parliament, who will? Gaganji has not done anything excessive. He has said what needed to be said.”

Meanwhile, media scholar Bhanu Bhakta Acharya wrote in a comment on social media:

“Thank goodness Mark Zuckerberg created the Facebook chautari, allowing us to read the whimsical status updates of prime ministers, ministers, lawmakers and everyone else.”

title.rendered: Did Gagan Thapa change Nepali Congress’s ideology — or merely reinterpret it?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 6

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa had previously signalled a departure from democratic socialism. In November 2021, when he was preparing to contest for the post of general secretary, he had presented a document that continued to shape his position until the party’s recent special general convention.

However, in the 46-page political document he presented at the 15th General Convention, Thapa has largely stood for the development and continuity of the party’s traditional ideology, with the term “social democracy” appearing only once, in passing.

Discussing the ideological debates across different societies in Europe and Asia, Thapa writes on page 25, “In different societies, including Europe and Asia, the traditions of democratic socialism and social democracy, despite their historical differences, are engaging in dialogue around shared questions of freedom, social justice, inclusion, economic opportunity and democratic accountability.”

Thus, five years ago, when he was contesting the 14th General Convention as a candidate for general secretary, Thapa forcefully promoted the agenda of social democracy. Today, however, in the political proposal he has presented as party president, he has returned to democratic socialism. Whatever terminology he uses, the substance of the two programmes appears broadly similar.

While the terminology Thapa used in the past generated considerable discussion and ideological debate, the political path he has proposed now as party president makes clear his effort to reconcile ideological ambition with the responsibilities of organisational leadership. When writing the main document for the convention, he appears to have clearly recognised the responsibilities that come with leading the party.

Questioning BP’s ideas

At the 14th General Convention five years ago, when Thapa was contesting for general secretary, he had presented a 60-page document arguing that the party should move from “democratic socialism” towards “social democracy.” At the time, he questioned the relevance of BP Koirala’s documents and argued that new thinking was needed to respond to a new era.

His argument then was that Nepali society in BP Koirala’s time and Nepali society today were not the same. The economy had changed, the middle class had expanded, the character of the state had changed and the role of the private sector had grown.

Thapa stated clearly at the time, “Democratic socialism seeks an alternative to the capitalist economic system. Social democracy, on the other hand, accepts that a capitalist economy will remain and seeks competition, reform and social justice within it.”

In that document, Thapa argued that individual freedom and a capitalist economy could coexist. Although capitalism produced negative consequences, he argued that the path of competition and reform should be pursued within that system. Rather than completely rejecting the market economy, his proposal embraced a welfare-oriented approach in which markets would be regulated through a democratic state, social security, equal opportunity and quality public services.

Thapa’s political line was not adopted at the time, but he was elected general secretary by a large margin. Some leaders within the Congress opposed him, arguing that he had abandoned BP Koirala’s socialist ideas.

Thapa had stated clearly at the time, “Democratic socialism seeks an alternative to the capitalist economic system. Social democracy, on the other hand, accepts that a capitalist economy will remain and seeks competition, reform and social justice within it.”

His document proposed advancing individual freedom alongside a capitalist economy while ensuring equal access to state resources and services through appropriate policy interventions.

He argued that the Congress could not answer the questions of a new society simply by repeating BP Koirala’s ideas word for word.

Thapa said at the time that he had been inspired by Chaitanya Mishra’s debates on social democracy. According to him, there was a tendency within the Congress to complain that BP’s agenda had been abandoned, but little effort had been made to reinterpret it in light of changing times. That, he argued, was why he wanted to clarify the idea of social democracy.

His document sought to connect markets and democracy with social justice rather than treating them as contradictory. This provides a clear picture of Thapa’s ideological position five years ago.

That position included markets, private initiative and individual freedom, but not an entirely unregulated market. The state was expected to ensure education, healthcare, social security and equal opportunity.

In other words, Thapa sought to move the Congress away from the traditional definition of socialism and towards a political project that pursued social justice within a market economy.

He had delivered a clear ideological message at the time: I want to shift the Congress’s ideological identity from BP’s democratic socialism towards modern social democracy.

In informal meetings with close associates, he used to identify former British Prime Minister Tony Blair as a political model and emphasise the need for an ideological shift within the party.

Socialist after becoming president

But in the political proposal titled “National Renaissance and Prosperity”, presented by Thapa as party president at the 15th General Convention, the term “social democracy” has not been put forward as an ideological identity. As mentioned above, it appears only in passing.

Instead, the document defines its ideological foundation in terms of nationalism, democracy and socialism, and advances it through the language of “democratic socialism.” In substance, describing the programme previously referred to as democratic socialism in slightly different democratic terminology amounts to much the same thing.

Thapa writes in the political proposal that the Congress’s ideological foundation has evolved through its glorious history, struggles, social experiences and debates, and has continually been refined through new knowledge.

“Nationalism, democracy and socialism are the fundamental pillars of this ideological tradition of the Congress. Their revival and effective implementation require both steadfastness towards core values and necessary changes in practice,” Thapa writes.

Thapa also offers an extensive explanation of democratic socialism.

“Democratic socialism creates the social, economic and human foundations necessary to enjoy freedom. Hunger, illiteracy, ill health, unemployment and discrimination restrict the enjoyment of rights,” he writes. “Easy and equal access to education, healthcare, nutrition, entrepreneurship, social security and justice enables citizens to make their own choices and develop their inherent creativity. Its purpose is not to make citizens permanently dependent on the state, but to make them independent, capable and creative.”

His conclusion is that nationalism separated from democracy becomes state-centric, socialism separated from freedom becomes controlling, and democracy without social and economic capacity is reduced to formal equality.

“The ideological strength of the Congress lies in maintaining a balance among these three,” he writes.

Thapa thus presents socialism not as a fixed slogan but as an idea that must engage with changing times. Having moved closer to Blair’s thinking along the path charted by Girija Prasad Koirala after 1990, Thapa has ultimately returned to BP.

But he has not simply stopped at BP’s ideas. He writes, “The democratic socialism developed by BP placed the life, human dignity, participation and opportunities of ordinary citizens at the centre of development, rather than merely statistical economic growth. While embracing BP’s historic symbol of the farmer ploughing the land, we have placed at the centre of economic development policy the reality of young people standing with passports in their hands or searching for opportunities within the country.”

It is important to remember that, in the meantime, the Rastriya Swatantra Party had developed its own interpretation of social democracy and adopted a document at its first general convention in June.

Now, as the Congress’s principal rival, the RSP presents one challenge, while communist parties continue to interpret socialism in their own ways. Thapa appears to be trying to find a balance in the language of his document so that the Congress can maintain a clear identity and distance from both.

On one hand, there is the need to listen to the voice of a changing society and changing times. On the other, there is the responsibility of carrying the party’s legacy on his own shoulders. To balance the two, Thapa has chosen a subheading for his ideological interpretation: “Permanent Ideals, Changing Times and a Dynamic Society.”

Thapa says the Congress’s political and ideological journey is inseparably linked to the fundamental ideals of nationalism, democracy and socialism.

“These three ideals are not merely political slogans of a particular period. They are permanent principles that define the relationship between the nation, citizens and society. In its own ideological tradition, the Nepali Congress has understood these three principles not separately, but as interconnected foundations of a single democratic vision,” he writes.

Thapa discusses how society, citizens’ aspirations, the economy and forms of production change over time, while technology transforms relations of power and consequently the challenges facing nations.

“In such circumstances, the ability to keep core values effective under changing conditions is the defining characteristic of a living political ideology. The society envisioned by the Congress is not only just, free and egalitarian, but also dynamic,” he writes.

In this way, Thapa has attempted in 2026 to restore within the historical language of Nepali Congress’s “democratic socialism” the ideological reinterpretation he had sought in 2021 under the banner of “social democracy.”

A strategic compulsion?

A natural question now arises: Has Thapa retreated from his ideological position? Why did Thapa, who proposed social democracy when seeking to become general secretary, return from the chairmanship to strongly advocate BP’s democratic socialism? Is this an ideological shift or a strategic compulsion?

The answer requires examining the substance of the document.

Thapa has not advocated a political system fundamentally different from social democracy under the banner of democratic socialism. In presenting a framework for ideological renewal, he identifies nationalism, democracy and socialism as the Congress’s core ideological foundations.

The document states clearly, “Nationalism, democracy and socialism are the fundamental pillars of this ideological tradition of the Congress. Their revival and effective implementation require both steadfastness towards core values and necessary changes in practice.”

By the time of the 15th General Convention, Thapa had become party president. A remarkable generational transition was taking place within the party. The faction led by former president Sher Bahadur Deuba, which had opposed this transition, had become considerably weaker and was looking towards the Supreme Court with hope as it talked about holding its own general convention in November.

Thapa is now in a position where he must provide answers rather than ask questions. He is responsible for bringing the party together rather than leading a rebellion.

A Congress office-bearer says Thapa therefore faces certain constraints.

“It appears that Gagan has paid attention to two things this time — his base within the party and the compulsions created by the circumstances,” the office-bearer said.

The leader argues that at a time when the party is moving towards a possible split, Thapa could not send the message that “I am the one carrying BP’s legacy” by introducing an entirely new ideology. He interprets this as a strategic compulsion rather than an ideological contradiction on Thapa’s part.

“To send this message, Gagan had to strongly invoke the slogan of democratic socialism. He also needed to convince the party’s traditionalist ranks and leaders who had left the Deuba faction that he had not moved outside the Congress’s mainstream ideological tradition,” the office-bearer said. “That is why it appears that he has emphasised democratic socialism.”

Ideological change is not easy in a political party built around a legacy. Ideas there are not merely theories. They are history, leaders, movements and emotional bonds shared across generations.

Thus, while one generation may see a new interpretation of BP’s socialism as natural ideological development, another may view it as a departure from the legacy.

Thapa may have recognised the risk of proudly standing in BP’s shoes while simultaneously challenging BP’s ideas and giving an advantage to a faction already preparing for the next convention.

So, has Thapa inserted a new ideology within the old terminology?

To answer that question, one must closely examine both the discussion under the document’s section on ideological direction and the broader political and economic programme contained within it.

Whatever the name, the substance is the same

Although Thapa has titled the ideological framework “democratic socialism,” the substance of the document appears to be a more refined interpretation of social democracy.

The document says the purpose of democratic socialism is neither for the state to make all economic decisions itself nor to treat the market as synonymous with freedom.

“Education, healthcare, nutrition, skills, employment, opportunities for entrepreneurship, social security, legal protection and a dignified life are not merely separate headings in economic policy. They are the social and economic foundations of citizens’ freedom,” the proposal states.

In presenting his economic roadmap, Thapa has also accepted the market economy. He identifies a liberal, pro-private-sector economy as one of the major pillars and seeks to establish the private sector as a major driver of prosperity.

The policy document envisions the government acting as a transparent regulator rather than becoming a trader or controller itself.

In principle, his economic proposals differ from the traditional objective of democratic socialism, which sought to replace capitalism and establish state ownership over the means of production. Thapa’s document instead places its economic approach within the concept of a “social market economy,” based on the idea that the market and the state are not necessarily in conflict.

“The state itself should not become a trader or owner. It should become an impartial regulator, guardian of good governance, builder of modern infrastructure and provider of quality public services,” the document states.

Seen in this light, the ideological debate Thapa sparked through his advocacy of social democracy at the 14th General Convention has, by the 15th General Convention, been brought under the cover of BP’s democratic socialism and reinterpreted for the present context.

Whatever the name, democracy ultimately means the inseparable connection between sovereignty vested in citizens and the mechanisms through which that sovereignty is exercised.

Today, political parties around the world are generally struggling not against non-democratic systems but against the consequences of democracy’s own shortcomings. Democratic institutions are becoming internally hollow and weakened as they contract. When state power becomes concentrated within circles of a limited power elite, institutions lose their genuine democratic legitimacy.

Our elections are increasingly becoming processes that merely legitimise the powerful. As a result, elections first lose their ability to produce governments that citizens actually want and eventually lose their legitimacy as well.

The depoliticisation created by the consumerist mindset and lifestyle promoted by neoliberalism is pushing traditional political mechanisms beyond citizens’ reach. Citizens are becoming little more than a vote — able to cast a ballot but unable to make their voices heard where it matters.

In the 21st century, refreshing the debate on democracy also requires changes to some of democracy’s basic grammar.

The question of how to bring economic power under the control of political power remains a question of enduring importance. The document does not appear to give sufficient attention to answering these questions.

Opening the general convention, Thapa had said, “History is glorious, but history does not give us power; it gives us lessons.”

In other words, history can provide political power only when the lessons it offers are transformed into action in the present.

Just as BP interpreted socialism by reading the society of his time, can today’s Congress read today’s society and provide new political answers?

The proposal put forward by Gagan Thapa will now be tested in practice.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah’s UN speech and the missing link in Nepal’s climate response

content.rendered:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s address to the United Nations makes a legitimate case for climate justice, grant-based recovery and stronger Himalayan cooperation. Recent scientific evidence supports important parts of his warning. Yet the speech also invites a second reading from within Nepal.

If the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster is evidence of a changing Himalayan climate, it is also evidence of how settlements, infrastructure, institutions and development decisions shape the consequences of that climate. The speech therefore raises a question that goes beyond international responsibility. Can Nepal seek more integrated regional climate action while climate science, disaster-risk institutions, spatial planning and infrastructure decisions at home remain only partially connected?

The concerns of a vulnerable country

Prime Minister Balendra Shah spoke at the United Nations General Assembly while the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was still painfully fresh in Nepal’s collective memory. His speech moved from lives lost, missing family members and destroyed infrastructure to a larger argument about climate justice. He noted Nepal’s negligible contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions, the instability of Himalayan systems and the repeated destruction of roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms and clean-energy infrastructure. He also argued that a poor country should not have to repeatedly borrow to rebuild losses from a crisis to which it contributed little.

There is considerable evidence behind this position. The World Bank has warned that Nepal’s economy could be at least 7 percent smaller by 2050 under severe climate impacts if effective action is not taken. Nepal’s Third Nationally Determined Contribution, or NDC 3.0, similarly recognises that adaptation cannot eliminate all climate risks and includes loss and damage, resilience and international climate finance within its policy framework. The Prime Minister’s demand for international responsibility should therefore not be dismissed as a post-disaster emotional appeal.

Yet the speech makes another statement that deserves equal attention. Nepal, the Prime Minister argued, must move from ad hoc response towards preparedness, stronger infrastructure and institutions, early-warning systems and resilience. This is where the international argument meets domestic development practice. Climate change can alter the probability or severity of a hazard, but it does not decide where a road, hydropower project, settlement, dry port or other major infrastructure is located. Climate injustice and domestically produced risk can therefore coexist.

Climate change matters, but disaster causation remains more complex

The Prime Minister argued that warming is destabilising the Himalaya through glacier retreat, permafrost degradation and increasingly unstable mountain slopes. A World Weather Attribution assessment supports important parts of this warning. It concluded that warming and degrading permafrost likely contributed to weakening the source rock wall at Langtang Lirung. Human-induced climate change was estimated to have increased July and August temperatures near the failure site by about 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with a pre-industrial climate.

The same study, however, does not reduce the disaster to climate change alone. Geological conditions remained fundamental, while the 2015 earthquake may have contributed to longer-term instability. The researchers explicitly state that they did not determine whether this particular rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change. Climate change therefore belongs within the chain of causation, but it cannot replace all other explanations.

More important for planning is the study’s conclusion about exposure. Immediate impacts were almost entirely dependent on what lay in the hazard path. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD, similarly describes how limited flatter terrain around Rasuwagadhi accommodated the Friendship Bridge, customs yard, dry port, truck park and hydropower works. These developed areas were in the flood path.

This does not mean that Nepal can withdraw development from Himalayan valleys. In a mountainous country, such locations are often among the few feasible places for transport, trade, settlements and energy infrastructure. The planning question is how to distinguish unavoidable exposure from exposure unnecessarily increased through development decisions. Kathleen Tierney’s work on the social roots of risk is useful here because it shifts attention from disaster as a physical event towards the institutional, economic and political processes operating before the event. A warning about a river or unstable slope has limited preventive value if it enters the planning system after buildings, roads and infrastructure have already been located.

Policy exists, but risk has not fully entered spatial development

Nepal does not lack legislation for risk-sensitive development. The Local Government Operation Act gives local governments substantial responsibilities for land use, settlement development, building regulation and local planning. It specifically requires land-use standards to consider geo-risk sensitivity and allows building approval only within those standards. The problem is whether these legally grounded responsibilities consistently become enforceable, risk-informed spatial development decisions.

Current urban programmes illustrate both progress and the remaining institutional gap. The Asian Development Bank-supported Urban Resilience and Livability Improvement Project cover seven municipalities, including Pokhara Metropolitan City, and is helping strengthen risk-sensitive and low-carbon urban planning. One of its institutional outputs is the preparation of decarbonisation and risk-sensitive urban development plans, together with stronger enforcement of development control.

The fact that a major current urban programme is explicitly investing in the preparation and operationalisation of such plans also suggests that these approaches have not yet become routine development practice across urban Nepal. The project is therefore important not only for what it delivers in participating municipalities, but also for what it reveals about the wider need to mainstream risk-sensitive spatial planning within Nepal’s urban development system.

This should now be a central concern of the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, the renamed former Ministry of Urban Development, together with the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction and local governments. The question is not simply whether municipalities possess annual plans, building-permit systems or land-use classifications. It is whether they have an integrated spatial framework in which multi-hazard information influences where settlement growth, infrastructure, densities and major public investment should occur before development becomes difficult to reverse.

The Nepal Disaster Report 2024 reveals a related contradiction. All 753 local governments have laws or policies on Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, or DRRM. More than 400 operate Local Emergency Operation Centres and 419 have prepared Local Disaster and Climate Resilience Plans. Yet the same report acknowledges continuing limitations in coordination, research, education and financing. More significantly, it notes that DRRM financing remains secondary to development expenditure, particularly infrastructure development.

This is more than a conventional implementation gap. It points to an institutional separation between organisations expected to reduce risk and those whose decisions can create future exposure. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, or NDRRMA, coordinates disaster-risk management under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, or DHM, under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, generates hydrological, meteorological, glaciological and early-warning information. National climate-change coordination is centred in the Climate Change Management Division of the Ministry of Forests and Environment. Settlement planning, building regulation and much of urban infrastructure are institutionally located elsewhere again.

Specialisation itself is not the problem. The test is whether knowledge produced in one institution changes decisions taken in another. A flood forecast produced by DHM is not a land-use decision. A climate vulnerability assessment does not determine where a municipality permits urban expansion. NDRRMA does not select every road alignment or infrastructure investment. Sumit Vij and colleagues have shown how response, disaster-risk management, climate adaptation and federalised disaster-governance paradigms continue to coexist in Nepal. More recent research led by Anshu Ogra, examining DHM and the Department of Mines and Geology, shows how institutional and disciplinary structures shape what knowledge is produced and how it enters policy.

The implication extends beyond the organisation of scientific departments. A disaster such as Bhotekoshi passes simultaneously through hydrology, geology, land use, settlement, infrastructure, energy, social vulnerability and emergency management. Yet these dimensions do not pass through a single institutional chain. Greater scientific capacity is necessary, but so is a system through which different forms of knowledge can influence development before risk becomes fixed into the landscape.

Climate policy and the geography of exposure

The administrative location of climate change within the Ministry of Forests and Environment requires careful interpretation. Its Climate Change Management Division is formally a national nodal body with a mandate to coordinate federal ministries, provinces and municipalities and to mainstream climate change into development planning. It would therefore be inaccurate to suggest that Nepal’s climate policy is concerned only with forests.

At the same time, institutional location can influence how a problem is framed and operationalised. Much of the exposure revealed by recent disasters lies in settlements, roads, hydropower facilities, trade infrastructure and expanding urban areas. Climate adaptation therefore has to be equally embedded within the institutions that determine where these systems are built. Climate change cannot remain an environmental consideration added to sectoral development after major spatial and investment decisions have already been taken.

Nepal’s National Adaptation Plan 2021-2050 recognises this problem more clearly than is sometimes assumed. Its programmes for rural and urban settlements include integrated settlement and urbanisation models for climate-risk reduction, climate-resilient building practices and physical development plans based on geographic information systems and hazard mapping. It also includes programmes for industry, transport and physical infrastructure. The issue is therefore not policy neglect. It is the uneven translation of national adaptation intentions into municipal spatial plans, capital investment decisions and enforceable development controls.

This is where the Ministry of Infrastructure Development needs a stronger integrative role. Climate policy does not need to be transferred away from the Ministry of Forests and Environment. Rather, adaptation has to become as firmly institutionalised within spatial and infrastructure planning as it is within environmental policy and climate reporting. Otherwise, human settlements may continue to appear in climate documents as an adaptation sector while decisions that create future exposure remain only weakly connected to the climate-governance system.

Climate duty and the consequences of development

The Prime Minister’s speech also places climate justice within a wider argument about development and a fairer international order. Nepal’s climate commitments can be viewed through two ethical perspectives. From a deontological, or duty-based, perspective, Nepal should conserve forests, reduce emissions, promote renewable energy and honour the climate commitments it has voluntarily undertaken because these actions are environmentally responsible in themselves. A country asking historical emitters to meet their responsibilities also strengthens its position by taking its own commitments seriously.

A teleological, or consequence-based, perspective asks another question. What do those commitments actually produce for Nepalese society and the economy? Do they increase employment, productive capacity, energy security and resilience? Who bears the costs of transition, and who receives the benefits? These questions matter because Nepal still faces substantial development deficits and must expand infrastructure, employment, productive capacity and reliable energy while pursuing a low-carbon transition.

NDC 3.0 makes this tension visible. Nepal estimates that meeting quantified mitigation targets through 2035 will require about USD 73.74 billion, with about USD 62.92 billion, or 85 percent, expected from international climate finance. Around 96 to 97 percent of targeted emission reductions are conditional on international support. These are nationally determined commitments rather than externally imposed development limits, but their implementation depends heavily on a financial architecture Nepal does not control.

Hydropower illustrates the same tension. Nepal needs electricity for domestic consumption, industry, electrified transport and regional trade. At the same time, research across 12 run-of-river hydropower sites in the Gandaki basin has shown how projects serving national sustainable-development objectives can produce uneven local social and political consequences. A project can therefore be low-carbon without automatically being socially just or physically resilient.

Climate finance, forests and social value

The Prime Minister defines climate justice not only through responsibility between countries but also through distributive justice, concerning who bears the costs, and procedural justice, concerning who has a voice. That distinction is equally useful within Nepal.

In November 2025, Nepal received USD 9.4 million from the World Bank’s Forest Carbon Partnership Facility for approximately 1.88 million tonnes of verified emission reductions under the REDD+ Emission Reductions Program in the Terai Arc Landscape. REDD+ refers to reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, together with conservation, sustainable management of forests and enhancement of forest carbon stocks. This creates a genuine opportunity to attach economic value to forest conservation.

A forest, however, is not only a carbon stock. It also supports fuel, fodder, livelihoods, identity, community institutions and social relations. Research led by Poshendra Satyal on Nepal’s REDD+ pilots found gains in recognition and empowerment but continuing problems of distributive, procedural and recognition justice across caste, gender, ethnicity, class and location. A 2024 study led by Hari Prasad Pandey also reported poor overall understanding of REDD+ among local stakeholders at about 29 percent.

This does not make carbon finance undesirable. It shows why carbon value and social value cannot be assumed to be identical. The Prime Minister’s own definition of climate justice therefore provides a useful standard for examining Nepal’s domestic climate transition.

International climate commitments under strain

The Prime Minister’s appeal is directed at an international climate system that is itself becoming less predictable. In January 2026, the United States moved to withdraw from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and immediately withdrew from the Green Climate Fund, following its renewed withdrawal from the Paris Agreement. For Nepal, the significance lies less in American domestic politics than in the asymmetry this creates. Vulnerable countries are expected to strengthen mitigation targets, reporting and adaptation systems while part of the international architecture expected to mobilise collective responsibility and finance is becoming less stable.

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage illustrates the scale problem. Its Barbados Implementation Modalities initially allocated USD 250 million for the 2025-2026 start-up period and have since been increased to USD 342 million, with at least half reserved for Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States. Such finance is important, but remains modest compared with the scale of climate-related losses faced by vulnerable countries. The Prime Minister’s call for grant-based support therefore addresses a genuine structural constraint.

Regional cooperation also requires integration at home

One of the more constructive parts of the speech is the proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China. The Prime Minister proposed sharing satellite information and expertise, monitoring dangerous glacial lakes, strengthening joint early-warning systems and coordinating cross-border disaster assistance. The physical logic is clear because Himalayan hazards do not stop at national boundaries.

ICIMOD already provides a regional platform linking eight Hindu Kush Himalayan countries, including Nepal, India and China. A new trilateral mechanism would therefore need to clarify the institutional gap it intends to fill and how it would complement existing arrangements.

The proposal also raises an important question at home. Satellite information received from another country still has to move through Nepal’s own institutional system. It must reach DHM, disaster authorities, sectoral ministries, provincial governments and municipalities, and eventually influence land-use regulation, infrastructure design and settlement development. Regional integration cannot compensate for weak domestic integration. The value of a cross-border warning is ultimately determined by whether it changes a decision on the ground.

From climate justice to development practice

The Prime Minister’s six words, “Relief, Rehabilitation, Reconstruction, Responsibility, Reparation, Resilience”, deliberately shift the discussion from humanitarian response towards responsibility. The term “reparation”, however, is politically and ethically stronger than the present legal architecture of the Paris Agreement. Decision 1/CP.21 states that Article 8 on loss and damage does not provide a basis for liability or compensation. Reparation in the speech is therefore better understood as a normative and political claim for climate justice rather than an existing legal entitlement within the Paris framework.

That distinction does not weaken Nepal’s argument. It clarifies the different levels at which responsibility operates. Global emissions influence climatic hazards. National institutions shape development choices. Provincial and local governments influence land, settlement and infrastructure. Markets distribute costs and benefits. Social structures influence who is most exposed and who has the capacity to recover.

The central challenge raised by the speech is therefore not only whether the international community accepts responsibility for climate loss. It is whether Nepal can connect climate science, spatial planning, infrastructure investment, disaster governance and social justice before risk becomes loss.

The Prime Minister was right to present the Himalayan disaster as a warning to the international community. The same warning asks Nepal whether the institutional integration it proposes across international borders is sufficiently developed within its own borders. If that question remains relevant after the immediacy of Bhotekoshi fades, the speech may achieve something more than bringing Nepal’s tragedy before the United Nations. It may help move climate justice from a claim made abroad towards a principle through which development itself is examined at home.

title.rendered: Nepal fields Sangeeta Mishra for WHO Southeast Asia chief

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Nepal is preparing to contest the top post of the World Health Organization’s South-East Asia Regional Office (SEARO), with the government planning to nominate Additional Secretary at the Ministry of Health and Food Safety, Dr Sangeeta Kaushal Mishra, for regional director.

The post became vacant after former regional director Saima Wazed of Bangladesh resigned.

According to sources at the Ministry of Health, the government has decided to put forward Mishra’s candidacy and has already started diplomatic efforts to secure support from member states.

The WHO is preparing to announce the official schedule for the election of the new regional director. According to sources, nominations are expected to open on October 12, with the election scheduled for January 24.

Nepal is not the only country preparing to field a candidate. Bhutan, the Maldives and Sri Lanka are also expected to put forward candidates.

WHO’s South-East Asia Region has 11 member states. However, only 10 countries are expected to participate in the voting this time. Myanmar will be excluded from the voting process due to United Nations sanctions imposed following the military coup in 2021.

Nepal, India, Bhutan, North Korea, the Maldives, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Timor-Leste are among the countries whose votes are expected to be significant in the election.

Health sector experts say India’s position could have a major influence on the outcome.

“Cabinet has also decided to nominate her as a candidate for regional director. We have now started preparations to secure votes and support from member states,” a Health Ministry official said.

Mishra had previously been proposed for appointment as health minister during the interim government led by Sushila Karki. Her name was also sent to the Office of the President for approval.

However, Karki withdrew the decision to appoint her after being informed that a case against Mishra was under investigation at the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority.

The Special Court acquitted Mishra in the case on June 15.

Nepal had previously fielded senior public health expert Dr Shambhu Acharya, who works at WHO headquarters, in the 2023 election for the SEARO regional director. Saima Wazed received eight votes in that election, while Acharya received two.

Wazed was later suspended following political changes in Bangladesh, corruption allegations against her and an internal WHO investigation. She subsequently resigned from the regional director position on September 9.

title.rendered: Nepal face crucial Oman series to preserve ODI status

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Nepal’s cricket team now faces another major challenge after winning the ACC Premier Cup — performing strongly in the final series of the ICC World Cup League 2 to preserve its ODI status.

Nepal’s route to directly qualifying for the World Cup Qualifier has become extremely difficult. Although a mathematical possibility remains, Nepal would need an unlikely sequence of results to finish among the top four in League 2 and secure direct qualification.

Even if Nepal fails to finish in the top four, it still has a chance to reach the World Cup Qualifier through the playoff route. For now, however, Nepal’s immediate priority will be to secure its ODI status.

The upcoming series in Oman will therefore be crucial in determining whether Nepal can remain an ODI team. It will also have a major bearing on whether Nepal can keep its hopes of reaching the World Cup Qualifier alive.

Nepal, Oman and Canada will compete in the final League 2 series in Oman, making it important for all three teams. For Nepal, however, the series carries much greater significance.

Nepal currently has 24 points from 32 matches and sits seventh in the League 2 standings. While finishing in the top four has become highly complicated, Nepal still has an important target within reach — retaining its ODI status.

“The team’s momentum has changed. Our goal will be to save our ODI status and take the team to the World Cup Qualifier,” captain Sandeep Lamichhane has said.

That makes the Oman series much more than an ordinary bilateral series for Nepal. If Nepal fails to finish among the top six by the end of League 2, it could finish seventh or eighth and face the serious possibility of losing its ODI status.

The ICC has not yet issued a final and explicit provision on ODI status in this particular context. But under the current scenario, finishing among the top six appears to be the safest position for Nepal, according to the Cricket Association of Nepal.

Points table and the equation

The points table shows the scale of Nepal’s challenge.

Scotland leads the standings with 45 points from 36 matches and has completed all its games. The United States is second with 43 points from 32 matches, while the Netherlands is third with 38 points from 32 matches. All three are assured of finishing in the top three.

Oman is fourth with 31 points from 28 matches. Namibia is fifth with 29 points from 33 matches, while Canada is sixth with 25 points from 32 matches.

Nepal is seventh with 24 points, while the UAE is eighth with 19 points from 29 matches.

Nepal is therefore only one point behind Canada. But closing that one-point gap alone will not be enough. The remaining matches, results involving other teams and the final points-table equation will all have to work in Nepal’s favour.

The United States is currently hosting a series involving the US, Namibia and the UAE. Those results will make the equation clearer by the time Nepal, Oman and Canada take the field in Oman.

The final League 2 series will then be played between the UAE, Netherlands and Oman. Nepal will therefore have a clearer picture of its position before it begins its Oman campaign.

If Nepal wins three or all four of its matches against Oman and Canada, it will reach between 30 and 32 points. That would at least take Nepal past Canada. If Namibia fails to move ahead significantly in its remaining matches, Nepal could also overtake Namibia.

Even if Namibia remains ahead of Nepal, the latter would still have a chance of finishing sixth depending on the final results.

If Nepal beats Canada in both matches but loses both games against Oman, it would finish with 28 points. If Nepal beats Canada twice and Oman also beats Canada at least once, Canada would remain behind Nepal.

Therefore, winning both matches against Canada and reaching at least 28 points appears to be one of the safest routes for Nepal to retain its ODI status.

The most straightforward scenario for Nepal would be to win all four matches in the upcoming series. If Nepal fails to beat either Canada or Oman, its chances of finishing in the top six will become considerably more dependent on results elsewhere.

If Nepal reaches 28 or 30 points and the UAE wins all its remaining matches, Namibia would still not necessarily move beyond the relevant points threshold, leaving Nepal in contention for a top-six finish.

If Nepal finishes on 26 or 28 points, however, it will have to rely more heavily on results involving other teams.

New captain, same challenge

Nepal suffered defeats in all four matches during its previous League 2 series in the Netherlands. The team has since undergone changes, including a change in captain.

Sandeep Lamichhane replaced Rohit Paudel as captain. Under Lamichhane, Nepal has since won the ACC Premier Cup.

Nepal’s form in League 2, however, has not been strong. The challenge now is to improve its performance in the competition and collect crucial points.

The squad had only recently returned from Japan after participating in the Asian Games in T20 cricket, following its Premier Cup triumph. Most of the players from the Premier Cup-winning squad remain in the team for the Oman series, giving the side confidence and momentum.

“The team’s momentum has changed. Our goal will be to save our ODI status and take the team to the World Cup Qualifier,” Lamichhane said.

Head coach Stuart Law also understands the importance of the series. For him, the focus is not simply on talking about winning but on putting the right process and plan into practice.

“It is easy to say we will win, but we also need to know the process required to do that and perform accordingly,” Law said.

The squad

Nepal has made only limited changes to the squad that won the ACC Premier Cup, adding two players.

Nandan Yadav has returned to the squad in place of Hemant Dhami, while left-arm spinner Shahab Alam has also been included.

Sompal Kami, Kushal Bhurtel and Bhim Sharki are not part of the squad for the series. They were also absent from Nepal’s Premier Cup campaign.

Asif Sheikh and Arjun Kumal are expected to continue as the opening pair. Ishan Pandey, Dev Khanal and Rohit Paudel provide options in the top order, while Dipendra Singh Airee, Gulshan Jha, Sandeep Jora and Basir Ahmed are among the middle-order options.

In the lower order, Nepal has Karan KC and Nandan Yadav, along with captain Lamichhane, Lalit Rajbanshi, Sher Malla and Shahab Alam.

Nepal has more options in spin than pace bowling. Karan and Nandan are the main pace options, with Gulshan also capable of contributing as a part-time seamer.

In spin, Nepal has captain Lamichhane, Lalit, Shahab, Sher and Basir, while Dipendra and Rohit can also provide additional options.

It remains difficult to predict the final playing XI. Nepal could opt for a combination featuring Asif, Arjun, Ishan, Rohit, Dipendra, Basir, Gulshan, Karan, Nandan, Lalit and Lamichhane.

For Nepal, the equation is now straightforward in principle, even if difficult in practice — win matches, collect points and stay inside the top six.

title.rendered: Govt report recommends withdrawing some Gen Z protest cases, not violent crime cases

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

A government-formed study committee has recommended that criminal cases against people involved in violent and criminal activities during the Gen Z movement should not be withdrawn.

The Cabinet decided on Monday to implement the report submitted by a three-member committee led by former Special Court chairperson Baburam Regmi.

The Cabinet decided to forward the report to the Ministry of Home Affairs for necessary action. The committee was formed to investigate cases filed in connection with the Gen Z movement and recommend which cases could be withdrawn.

According to the report, cases filed against those involved in violent attacks on security personnel, attacks on police posts and the looting of weapons should not be withdrawn under any circumstances.

Sources at the Home Ministry said the committee had also recommended against withdrawing cases involving people accused of vandalising and setting fire to the Supreme Court, Federal Parliament and Singha Durbar.

Around 400 cases have been filed in connection with the incidents of September 9, 2025. According to Home Ministry sources, the committee has classified around 100 of these cases as cases that should not be withdrawn.

The committee has made a separate recommendation regarding cases involving the vandalism of private institutions and personal property.

According to the recommendation, such cases could be withdrawn if those accused admit their offences and agree to compensate for the damage caused.

The report also states that cases could be withdrawn if the owner of a damaged house or property chooses to forgive those involved. However, the committee has recommended that the consent of the complainant or victim must be obtained before such cases are withdrawn.

The committee also found that cases had been filed against some people who merely came onto the streets during the Gen Z movement, participated in demonstrations or chanted slogans, but were not found to have been involved in other criminal activities.

The committee has recommended that cases of this nature should be withdrawn.

The study committee has also advised the government to follow the Criminal Procedure Code and the Government Cases Withdrawal Procedure, 2020, when withdrawing cases.

If the government decides to withdraw a case, the Office of the Attorney General must submit an application through the relevant government attorney’s office to the concerned district court. A case can only be withdrawn after the district court grants permission.

The committee studied cases pending before various district courts in Kathmandu Valley. It classified the cases into three categories — those that cannot be withdrawn, those that can be withdrawn with the consent of the complainant, and those that can be withdrawn unconditionally.

“The committee’s position appears to be that if someone was prosecuted simply because they participated in the Gen Z movement or the events of the following day, that amounts to political prejudice and such cases should be withdrawn,” a Home Ministry source said.

“However, the report makes it clear that those who participated in the movement but were involved in attacks serious enough to cause deaths, arson targeting sensitive state institutions or the vandalism of private property should not be granted immunity.”

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah takes aim at Nepali Congress over 7-decade-old promise on land to the landless

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Prime Minister Balen Shah has criticised the Nepali Congress, saying that although the party promised in its 1959 election manifesto to distribute land to landless farmers, the problem remains unresolved even after seven decades.

In a Facebook post on Monday evening, Shah said successive governments had spent significant state resources trying to address the landlessness problem, but had failed to deliver the expected results.

“The Nepali Congress, then the country’s largest political party, had written in its manifesto for the 1959 parliamentary election that land obtained by clearing forests or fallow land, as well as surplus land resulting from the determination of a maximum landholding limit, would be distributed with priority to landless farmers,” Shah said.

“Since then, the country has gone through different political systems. There have been Panchayat governments, multiparty democracy, republican governments, majority governments, two-thirds majority governments and coalition governments. Yet a problem mentioned in a political manifesto seven decades ago remains one of the country’s major national issues that needs to be resolved.”

Shah said political parties had continued to seek votes for decades by promising to resolve the problem and provide land ownership certificates, but the situation remained largely unchanged.

He said previous governments had established various commissions and structures in the name of resolving land-related problems, resulting in substantial expenditure of state resources.

“More than Rs 2 billion appears to have been spent on such structures between 2020 and last year alone. But the expected results were not achieved in proportion to the expenditure,” he said. “The structures that were supposed to solve the problem themselves became obstacles to solving it.”

Shah said his government had changed the approach in line with its pre-election commitment and had started working on the issue through a different model.

“Instead of political distribution and unnecessary layers, we have chosen a path based on expertise, coordination with local governments and clear responsibilities,” he said. “We are trying to make the process streamlined, transparent and less burdensome for the state.”

Shah said that after the formation of the Land Problem Resolution Committee, data from across the country was being collected and processed through an integrated system.

“So far, 1,311,197 applications have been entered into the system. The process of reviewing and verifying these applications has already begun, and we are now moving towards prioritisation and resolution,” he said.

According to Shah, 5,737 families have received land ownership registration certificates since the current government came to power.

“Land ownership registration certificates have already been distributed to 5,737 families across different districts, including landless people without certificates, landless Dalits, landless squatters and people living in unplanned settlements,” he said. “This is only the beginning. We have now entered a phase of rapidly expanding this work across the country.”

He said the government had also begun the process of relocating landless squatters living in public-interest areas and high-risk locations to safer places.

For families displaced from the Kathmandu Valley, the government has started the process of managing land in their respective permanent home districts, Shah said.

He added that the government had begun the process of verifying records and taking legal action against people who falsely claimed to be landless.

Shah said the government was also moving to amend the Land Act, Forest Act and other relevant laws to accelerate the process.

“Legal, procedural and structural obstacles that are preventing solutions are being changed as necessary to open the way for resolution,” he said.

Shah said the government had made a clear election pledge to resolve the problem of landless squatters within 1,000 days and that the commitment had been adopted as a specific performance target of the Rastriya Swatantra Party-led government.

He said the government was working towards resolving the problem district by district and eventually declaring districts free of the landless squatter problem.

“After seven decades of promises, citizens will now receive land ownership certificates,” Shah said. “We are working towards that.”

title.rendered: Accessible, friendly toilets being made mandatory at highway rest areas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities and Social Security has begun an initiative to ensure safe, dignified and accessible toilets and the necessary infrastructure at highway rest areas for women, children, persons with disabilities, senior citizens, and gender and sexual minorities.

In a letter to the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, the Ministry has asked that accessible, friendly toilets and necessary infrastructure be built for everyone at temporary and permanent rest areas where public vehicles stop passengers on highways and road sections across the country.

The Ministry said passengers on long journeys should be able to get basic services at rest areas easily, but that many places lack minimum facilities, including toilets and accessible infrastructure.

The Ministry’s letter says this particularly causes additional problems for women, children, persons with disabilities and senior citizens, so rest-area infrastructure needs to be made inclusive and accessible.

The Ministry has also asked that the necessary toilet facilities be ensured at rest areas already built, and that arrangements be made so public vehicles stop only at places with toilet facilities.

It stressed that when new rest areas and other road infrastructure are built, accessible structures friendly to women, children, persons with disabilities, senior citizens, and gender and sexual minorities must be built from the start.

The Ministry sent the letter to put into practice the rights guaranteed by the Constitution of Nepal, the Act Relating to the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, the Senior Citizens Act and the Sustainable Development Goals.

It also asked the Ministry of Infrastructure Development to give the necessary directions to, and coordinate with, the relevant infrastructure development offices, and said it would provide the necessary support, partnership and coordination in this work.

As the festival season approaches, passenger numbers on long-distance public vehicles will rise, so the need for basic services and accessible infrastructure at highway rest areas will grow further, the Ministry said.

The Ministry has taken the initiative to create an environment in which passengers can rest and get the services they need in a safe, clean and dignified way, and to make highway rest areas safe and accessible for women, children, persons with disabilities, senior citizens, and gender and sexual minorities.

Russian House Kathmandu, the venue partner since the first edition, is again providing the festival venue this year.
