title.rendered: Ranjit Karna announces candidacy for Congress general secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Leader Ranjit Karna has announced his candidacy for general secretary of the Nepali Congress. He made the announcement at a press conference in Kathmandu.

The party’s 15th General Convention is under way. Karna, a former president of the party’s student wing, the Nepal Student Union, has announced his candidacy for general secretary.

Karna, currently a member of the National Assembly, said in announcing his candidacy that the Congress has not become weak. Rather, he said, the organisational energy within the party has been declining.

“It is not that the Congress has no history of ideas. The effort to connect those ideas with today’s generation has become weak,” he said. “It is not that the Congress has no leaders. The door to bring the new generation into leadership is not open enough.”

He also spoke about what his own role would be.

“Today I have not come merely to ask for the post of general secretary. I have come to start a new debate within the Congress,” he added. “The time has come for us to ask ourselves serious questions. Why is Congress membership becoming only a number? Why are workers made to wait for instructions instead of being partners in decisions?”

title.rendered: AA Films to release Nepali film Himalayan Gold across India

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Nepali film Himalayan Gold has signed a deal with the Indian distributor AA Films for a release across India, the film’s team said.

The agreement was signed in Mumbai with AA Films founder Anil Thadani. The film, directed by Dhiraaj Rajbanshi, is scheduled to open in theatres on November 20. According to the team, it is the first time a Nepali film has secured a nationwide Indian release through a distributor of this stature.

AA Films has distributed films including Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, Baahubali, RRR, KGF: Chapter 2, Pushpa and Kantara in India.

“Himalayan Gold is a film with exceptional content that audiences across India deserve to experience,” Thadani said. “It is a privilege for us to associate with the talented team behind it, and we are confident that audiences will break language barriers to embrace and love this film.”

Rajbanshi, for whom this is a debut feature, thanked Thadani and AA Films for backing the film.

“I cannot even begin to put into words how huge this is, not just for me but for the entire Nepali film industry,” he said. “With their backing, this film will now reach audiences everywhere. This is exactly the kind of motivation our industry is constantly seeking, and to receive this level of support for my debut film honestly means everything to me.”

The cast includes Sunil Thapa, Rahul N. Mukhia, Parikshya Limbu, Sajan Thapa and Karma Shakya in lead roles.

The film is the last of veteran actor Sunil Thapa’s career, Rajbanshi said. Taking his final performance to audiences in Nepal and India is a fitting tribute to his legacy, the director said.

The trailer is due to be released on Monday, the team said.

title.rendered: Homework underway to review interest rates to manage Nepal Airlines debt, says Tourism Minister Paudel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel has said the government is holding the necessary consultations on reviewing the interest rates on loans to manage the financial liabilities of Nepal Airlines Corporation.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives’ International Relations and Tourism Committee on Monday, Minister Paudel said the corporation’s loans from two large financial institutions cannot be called unmanageable. He said talks are moving forward with the prime minister and the finance minister to facilitate a solution.

At the committee meeting, he said policy-level efforts are under way to make the interest rates and instalment payment process more practical on the loans taken from the Employees’ Provident Fund and the Citizen Investment Trust.

Both institutions hold the savings of the general public and employees, so the government has a duty to find a balanced way out that does not put their investments at risk, he said.

Minister Paudel claimed that the corporation’s present liabilities, worth about Rs 50–56 billion, are not at an impossible or “unmanageable” level for an institution with a large brand and assets such as the national flag carrier.

“Nepal Airlines Corporation is not a profit-oriented institution, but it needs to be made financially capable and orderly. The corporation’s main problem is related to the management of its present loans and interest rates,” he said. “Discussions are under way on the government’s side to review the interest rates on the loans taken from the Employees’ Provident Fund and the Citizen Investment Trust. Talks are also taking place with the prime minister and finance minister on this matter.”

Minister Paudel said he believes that if the loan interest rates can be modified somewhat, the corporation can make further progress by using internal resources or alternatives.

He said that if funds are not enough to buy new aircraft immediately, the corporation can operate them on lease, or increase income by making the flight schedules of existing aircraft more scientific.

“If we can ease the loan restructuring and interest rates somewhat, the corporation’s cash flow will improve. After that, it looks possible to run the corporation more effectively by improving aircraft purchase, leasing and flight management,” he said.

He told the committee that inter-ministry coordination has been stepped up to free the corporation from crisis, since it is a public body with a national responsibility rather than just a profit-seeking one.

title.rendered: Govt decides to adjust prices of public construction contracts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The government has decided to provide special price adjustments for public construction contracts.

According to the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development, the decision has been made to implement special price adjustments under Section 55(1a) of the Public Procurement Act, 2007.

The ministry said special price adjustments will be provided for petroleum products, bitumen, HDPE pipes, cement and steel, whose prices have risen abnormally due to international conflicts and disruptions in the supply chain. The adjustment will apply to public construction contracts that remained under implementation with a valid performance period even after March 29, based on actual and verified consumption.

Contracts that are executed annually and those without a price-adjustment provision will also be covered if they meet the prescribed criteria. For contracts that already have a price-adjustment provision, the amount payable under the existing arrangement and contract will be deducted, and only the remaining eligible amount will be provided as a special price adjustment.

The ministry said the provision will address price increases caused by extraordinary circumstances rather than normal market fluctuations. Payments will be determined based on actual consumption, verified quantities and applicable prices to prevent double benefits or unnecessary payments.

The decision aims to prevent construction works from being halted, ensure continuity of ongoing development projects and address imbalances in the construction sector fairly, the ministry said.

Construction entrepreneurs had been demanding price adjustments for a long time. The government had also announced the provision in the current fiscal year’s budget.

title.rendered: Saugat Thapa announces candidacy for Nepali Congress central committee member

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Businessman Saugat Thapa has announced his candidacy for a central committee member of the Nepali Congress.

Thapa has filed his candidacy in the under-35 category at the party’s 15th General Convention, which is currently underway at Bhrikutimandap in Kathmandu. He is a general convention representative from Kaski-2.

Thapa said greater participation of young people in the party’s leadership would help transform the Nepali Congress into a more modern and dynamic political organisation.

“This time, young people are entering the central leadership, and that is a matter of happiness for us,” Thapa said. “The general convention should understand the aspirations and concerns of young people and formulate clear policies on ideology, organisation and programmes. There should also be provisions for an exit alongside entry. This will make the party more dynamic.”

He said the party’s policy of creating greater space for young people following the Gen Z movement was beginning to be reflected in party conventions.

“The general convention should bring programmes and plans that allow the younger generation and the generation that has carried the legacy of long political movements to move forward together,” he said. “The Gen Z movement has increased young people’s direct interest in politics. The party should therefore connect this development with its ideological framework.”

Thapa also said the party leadership should make efforts to bring people with expertise in various professions and businesses, who have not previously been involved in politics, into the political mainstream.

He said the provision ensuring representation from different groups from the ward level to the central level had sent a positive message. He argued that a similar approach should also be adopted when selecting candidates for local and provincial elections.

Thapa holds a Master of Business Studies degree from Infomax College. He was recently elected the vice president of Pokhara Chamber of Commerce and Industry. He is also involved in the tourism business and serves as a director of Ansuvara Group.

He has previously served as president of the Nepal Students’ Union in Pokhara Metropolitan City and has been a regional representative twice. He was also elected as a representative at the Nepali Congress’s 14th General Convention.

Thapa has served as a member of the Pokhara Chamber of Commerce and Industry twice. He was elected as a general convention representative from the under-35 youth category from Kaski-2 for the 15th General Convention.

Surendra Silwal, managing director of Saras Beverage, the Red Bull distributor in Nepal, said the company has partnered with a world-class platform like The Voice to promote Nepali music by producing new talent and original songs.

title.rendered: Govt prepares to revise road and bridge designs after flood disasters

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The government has begun preparations to revise road and bridge designs following major flood and landslide disasters in Rasuwa, Bhotekoshi and Kaligandaki.

Officials from the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development said the government is preparing to establish a Maintenance and Disaster Resilience Unit and revise design codes for roads and bridges.

Speaking at a programme organised by the Nepal Infrastructure Journalists Society on Monday, ministry Joint Secretary Bhimarjun Adhikari said floods and landslides have caused billions of rupees in annual damage to road and bridge infrastructure. He said climate change has made the nature and scale of disasters increasingly difficult to predict.

Adhikari said recent disasters have shown the need to review existing design codes, as floods now carry large amounts of sediment and debris. He said roads and bridges in upper catchment areas need designs suited to such conditions.

He stressed that future infrastructure must be climate-resilient and that safety and resilience should be incorporated from the design stage.

Road Department Director General Dr Bijay Jaisi said the department restored basic road connectivity within 15 days of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster. He said a temporary road at Krishnabhir was designed within three days and brought into operation within weeks.

He also said taller and longer bridges may be required in areas affected by high flood levels, depending on need.

title.rendered: Supreme Court orders government not to restrict children of Bhutanese refugees from leaving Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Supreme Court has ordered the government not to restrict the children and family members of Bhutanese refugees from leaving the country.

The court said preventing refugee children from travelling abroad obstructs their legal resettlement, family reunification and safe movement. It issued a mandamus order directing the government to facilitate their departure.

Hearing a writ petition filed after a refugee family was denied permission to travel abroad, the Supreme Court said freedom of movement and family reunification are protected principles in the international refugee protection framework.

“Standards that prevent unnecessary, disproportionate or arbitrary barriers to the free movement and family reunification of refugees have been established as binding norms,” the court said. “Nepal, like any other state, has a duty to facilitate rather than obstruct the resettlement process.”

The court also said preventing children of refugees from reuniting with their parents disrupts family unity and is contrary to the principles of international protection.

“Such action must be regarded as contrary to the inaction of responsible authorities and the principle of the rule of law,” the court said. “Where the state has a responsibility, the government cannot remain a mere spectator. Appropriate and necessary facilitation must be provided to remove obstacles to refugee family reunification.”

Sonika Ankari, Sandhya Ankari and Srijan Ankari are siblings born at the Beldangi refugee camp in Jhapa. Their father, Monikumar, came to Jhapa as a refugee after fleeing repression and human rights violations in Bhutan in the 1990s.

Under the UN refugee agency’s third-country resettlement programme, Monikumar travelled to the United States in 2015. Their mother, Gita Giri, also travelled to the United States in 2024.

The three children then applied to the District Administration Office in Jhapa in May for a recommendation to obtain travel documents.

The District Administration Office refused to issue the recommendation, saying the children were not registered in the refugee management information system.

According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, Monikumar’s refugee status had been removed from the records after he was resettled in a third country. Since their mother was not a registered refugee, the ministry argued that the children could not be granted exit permission as refugees.

The Supreme Court, however, questioned the decision after finding that the children had birth registration records, DNA tests had confirmed their relationship with their parents, and both parents had travelled to the United States in connection with their refugee status and family relationship.

The court said the District Administration Office should have examined the application submitted after completion of the required legal procedures and made an immediate decision on whether to grant permission.

Questioning the failure to make such a decision despite the available evidence, the court said, “Such acts amount to a constructive violation of the right of refugee families to leave the country and the right to family life.”

The Supreme Court held that the children should not have been prevented at the administrative level from obtaining exit permission when their father had reached the United States as a refugee and their mother had also travelled there through their marital relationship.

“Denying refugee children permission to leave the country means obstructing their legal resettlement, family reunification and safe movement,” the court said.

The court issued a mandamus order directing the authorities to provide the children with exit permits so that they could be resettled in the United States.

title.rendered: We celebrate their remittances, but do we respect their labour?

content.rendered:
We often talk about brain drain, emigration and the steady stream of Nepali students and workers leaving the country in search of better opportunities. But what really drives them to leave?

It is not simply the absence of jobs. It is the absence of better jobs.

For many Nepali workers, a better opportunity means higher pay. But wages are only part of the equation. Workers also want security, fair treatment, social respect and the assurance that their labour will allow them to live with dignity. Too often, Nepal’s labour market provides none of these adequately.

The consequences are visible in the scale of labour migration. More than 1,500 Nepali migrant workers died abroad in a recent fiscal year. Many work in difficult conditions, particularly in the Gulf and Malaysia. Yet even these risks rarely outweigh the disadvantages of returning to a domestic labour market where wages remain low and working conditions are often insecure.

When work abroad carries more dignity

The decision to migrate is not always driven by money alone. Social attitudes also matter.

A Nepali worker earning money abroad through housekeeping, cleaning, construction or retail is often treated with a degree of respect because of the sacrifice associated with overseas employment. A person doing essentially the same work in Nepal can be looked down upon.

We regularly see street vendors, footpath sellers, domestic workers and other informal-sector workers treated as though their occupations make them less worthy of respect.

This creates a contradiction.

We celebrate the remittances generated by workers performing these jobs abroad, while often failing to recognise the dignity of the same work when it is performed at home.

Why should cleaning a hotel in Dubai be considered respectable but cleaning a hotel in Kathmandu be viewed differently?

Exploitation does not stop at the border

The difficult reality facing Nepali migrant workers is well documented. Recruitment agencies can charge excessive fees, workers can fall victim to fraudulent contracts, and some foreign employers subject migrants to exploitative working conditions.

But exploitation is not exclusively a problem of foreign employment. It is deeply embedded in Nepal’s domestic labour market, particularly in the informal sector.

A joint study by ActionAid Nepal, Nepal Mahila Ekata Samaj and Truth Advocacy Nepal found that 66.2 percent of surveyed informal-sector workers in construction, agriculture, domestic work and brick kilns did not receive their legally prescribed full wages.

The brick industry provides a particularly stark example. Workers, including marginalised communities and migrant families, can become dependent on advance payments or loans that effectively tie them to arduous work across successive seasons in order to repay their debts.

These conditions are not simply economic problems. They are questions of rights and dignity.

Nepal has laws intended to protect workers and prevent exploitation. The Human Trafficking and Transportation (Control) Act provides a legal framework against trafficking, while the government’s National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights for 2024–2028 seeks to promote responsible business practices and fair recruitment.

But legislation alone cannot protect workers. Enforcement remains the crucial test.

What does the Constitution promise?

Nepal’s Constitution recognises labour as a fundamental right. Article 34 guarantees workers the right to appropriate remuneration, facilities and appropriate working conditions. Article 51 also directs the state towards policies relating to labour and employment.

The question is how much of this promise reaches the workplace.

Are workers receiving fair pay? Are overtime rules enforced? Are workplaces safe? Do workers have meaningful protection from dismissal, harassment and exploitation? And perhaps most importantly, are workers treated with dignity?

These questions should not be reserved for policymakers. They should also concern employers, professionals and ordinary citizens.

There is growing public discussion about toxic workplace culture, exploitation and poor management. But it is worth asking whether we are willing to confront exploitation when we benefit from it.

It is easy to condemn an abusive corporate culture when we are the employee. It is harder to examine our own behaviour when we become the employer.

If businesses try to maximise profits by cutting wages, denying overtime, avoiding contracts or shifting risk onto workers, they are contributing to the same culture of exploitation they may publicly criticise.

Labour is not disposable

Labour is one of the foundations of any economy. Nepal needs engineers, doctors, architects, managers and entrepreneurs. But it also needs construction workers, cleaners, drivers, farmers, domestic workers, factory workers and countless others whose labour keeps the economy and society functioning.

A labourer is not simply someone who lifts heavy materials. They build our houses, roads, bridges and workplaces. They clean our offices and care for our homes. They produce and transport the goods we consume.

We expect our buildings to be safe and our bridges to stand. We should expect the people who build them to be safe as well.

A worker’s life should not collapse under the weight of inflation, insecure employment, unpaid overtime, unsafe conditions or social discrimination.

Enforcement must begin at home

The government has an important role to play in changing this reality. Labour laws must be enforced consistently and promptly. Overtime must be properly compensated. Employers who violate labour standards must face consequences, while workers need accessible mechanisms through which they can report exploitation and seek remedies.

The government has also taken steps to examine recruitment practices in foreign employment, including restrictions and arrangements affecting migrant-worker recruitment. Similar scrutiny is necessary within Nepal’s domestic labour market.

Informal employment cannot remain an excuse for weak enforcement.

Employment creation is also about more than establishing industrial parks or opening factories. It means creating workplaces where people can earn a living safely and securely, without having to surrender their dignity in exchange for a wage.

Dignity must be part of the job

Nepal’s labour problem cannot be solved by the government alone. Employers must respect labour rights. Law-enforcement and regulatory agencies must enforce the rules. Consumers and citizens must recognise the value of work that society often takes for granted. And workers themselves must have meaningful avenues to organise, negotiate and seek justice.

The choice facing Nepali workers should not be between low-paid insecurity at home and exploitation abroad. A genuinely successful labour market would give people a reason to stay—not because they have no alternative, but because they can find decent work at home.

Ultimately, employment is about more than earning a wage. It is about being able to work safely, support a family, plan for the future and live with dignity.

Nepal does not merely need more jobs. It needs better jobs—and a society that respects the people who do them.

title.rendered: Congress’s resolve: No pre-election alliances; will contest alone under its own ‘Tree’ symbol

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Nepali Congress has proposed a clear policy of not forming alliances with other political parties before any future elections.

In the political proposal presented by party President Gagan Thapa at the ongoing 15th General Convention in Kathmandu, the party has made a firm commitment to contest elections independently under its own tree symbol.

The Congress concluded that alliances with other parties in past elections weakened its identity and connection with voters, prompting it to adopt a policy of contesting elections on its own.

The document states, “We remain firmly committed to contesting elections without pre-election alliances, with our own candidates and programmes under the tree symbol.”

The section on political conduct, which outlines what the party will and will not do, also makes clear that the party will not allow its identity to depend on pre-election alliances or electoral arithmetic. The Congress has declared that it will compete with its own symbol, programmes and candidates and strive to become capable of winning elections.

No power-sharing for government positions

The Congress has adopted a policy of cooperating with other political parties on national issues without turning such cooperation into a transaction for power.

The document states that cooperation may be necessary on issues such as protecting the Constitution, disasters, national security, justice and public interest, but such cooperation should not be turned into the sharing of government power or institutional positions.

The party has committed not to treat the exchange of positions, influence or privileges as political cooperation.

Right to reject and voting from abroad

For electoral reform, the Congress has proposed bringing into public debate the option of “no vote”, allowing voters to reject all candidates or indicate that they do not wish to vote for any candidate.

The proposal also calls for reforms aimed at ensuring clean and less expensive elections and improving voting access for citizens living abroad or outside their permanent electoral constituencies. The party has also said it will bring issues such as rotating reserved constituencies and improvements in representation into public debate.

title.rendered: Congress proposes state funding for parties based on votes received

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Nepali Congress has proposed strict financial discipline to make the party’s financial system transparent and end the influence of interest groups.

In the political document presented by party President Gagan Kumar Thapa at the 15th General Convention, the Congress has proposed that all levels of the party operate according to approved annual and programme-based budgets.

The proposal states that decisions concerning the party’s funds will no longer depend solely on the personal discretion of party leaders. The same discipline will also apply to spending on primaries and internal elections.

Addressing public concerns that political parties have not maintained transparent financial practices in elections and organisational operations, the Congress has also proposed providing financial assistance to political parties from the state coffers.

The document states, “A proposal to provide political parties with a certain amount of financial assistance from the state based on the votes they receive will be advanced alongside strict financial discipline and public audits. The party plans to initiate necessary legal and financial discussions with the objective of making political spending transparent and accountable.”

The Congress has also committed to maintaining verified records of its movable and immovable assets, adopting a uniform accounting policy, operating economically and conducting regular public audits.

The document also states that the sources and conditions of financial contributions, as well as potential conflicts of interest, will be examined.

title.rendered: Binod Chaudhary announces candidacy for Nepali Congress vice-president

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Nepali Congress Binod Chaudhary has announced his candidacy for the post of party vice-president at the ongoing 15th General Convention.

Chaudhary said he decided to contest the election to help establish younger leadership in the party and begin a new chapter in Nepal’s economic transformation.

“The country is currently looking for young leadership. The Nepali Congress must establish young people in leadership through this general convention. At the same time, leaders with a clear vision for economic prosperity must be brought into the leadership to begin a new chapter in economic transformation,” he said.

Chaudhary said he believed such leadership could lead the country’s economic transformation in the coming years.

He also said his participation, from the party’s special general convention to the ongoing 15th General Convention, was aimed at helping establish younger leadership.

Binod Chaudhary said his candidacy was not merely about securing a party position, but about bringing economic development to the centre of political discourse and addressing the aspirations of young people.

“My candidacy is to bring economic development agendas to the centre of politics, address the aspirations of young people, demonstrate through action that the Nepali Congress can lead the country’s development through economic transformation, and make the Congress stronger, more modern and people-oriented by connecting it with the new generation,” he said.

He said political change alone could not bring transformation without clear plans for economic prosperity.

“Doing politics simply for the sake of politics cannot transform the country. For that, it is necessary to work on clear plans for economic prosperity. I am ready to take responsibility for economic prosperity,” Chaudhary said.

title.rendered: Nepathya to perform live in Kirtipur on October 10

content.rendered:
Lalitpur, October 5

Nepathya, one of Nepal’s popular musical groups, will perform live in Kirtipur on October 10.

Organised by Ramailo Event Management Pvt. Ltd., the “Nepathya Live in Kirtipur” concert will be held at the ground of Kirtipur Laboratory School. The concert will begin at 6 pm, with audience entry opening at 4:15 pm through Gates 1 and 2.

According to the organisers, Nepathya will perform some of its popular songs and long-time audience favourites at the concert.

The event will also feature the formal launch of Gaurabta Nepal, a digital platform aimed at promoting Nepal’s tourism, culture, heritage and national identity to national and international audiences.

The organisers said the platform will operate under the concept of a “Digital Gateway to Nepal” and seek to connect Nepal’s identity, potential and cultural heritage with the younger generation and the global community.

The concert will bring together Nepathya’s music with Kirtipur’s historical and cultural identity, according to the organisers.

NTORQ 150 is the title sponsor of the event, while Proton is the “In Association With” partner. Thuprai Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is the ticketing partner and Nepalaya is the production partner.

title.rendered: Government suspends Bhotekoshi-Trishuli flood search and rescue, except urgent operations

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The government has decided to suspend, for the time being, the search and rescue phase following the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, except for urgent operations.

The 21st meeting of the National Council for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, held today at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers under the chairmanship of Prime Minister Balen Shah, decided to direct the concerned agencies to expedite reconstruction and rehabilitation work while continuing only essential search operations.

The decision was taken based on recommendations from the District Security Committees, District Disaster Management Committees, the Executive Committee of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, as well as on-site observations.

The meeting also decided to recommend to the Ministry of Finance the approval of a budget of Rs 559.17 billion for 504 plans and programmes submitted by various ministries and agencies for the reconstruction and rehabilitation of affected areas.

Resources for the approved plans will be managed through the Ministry of Finance in accordance with the Financial Procedures and Fiscal Responsibility Regulations, 2020.

The meeting also directed the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority to recommend the necessary budget allocation to the Ministry of Finance after receiving details of projects whose cost estimates have not yet been determined and which have yet to be prioritised.

At the meeting, Prime Minister Shah said disaster management efforts were being carried out in coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments, and that reconstruction and rehabilitation would also be carried out in the same manner. Opposition parties, the Nepali Congress parliamentary party leader, and the chief ministers of Bagmati, Gandaki, Madhesh and Koshi provinces expressed their full support for the efforts.

The meeting expressed sorrow over the loss of lives and property caused by the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods and monsoon-related disasters, paid heartfelt tribute to all those who died and expressed condolences to the bereaved families.

The council also highly appreciated and extended heartfelt thanks to security personnel, elected representatives, civil servants, the private sector, volunteers and media workers involved in search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts under difficult circumstances, as well as donor countries and development partners that assisted.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress proposes councils for young and senior leaders to connect five generations

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has proposed forming two new councils as part of his pledge to build a party that brings five generations together.

In the political proposal presented by Thapa at the ongoing 15th General Convention in Kathmandu, he has proposed forming a Youth Council comprising young people aged 18 to below 21 to listen to the experiences and aspirations of the younger generation.

He has also proposed forming a Wisdom Council to draw on the experience and knowledge of the older generation.

Both councils will engage directly with the party president in dialogue and consultation. According to the document, the recommendations of both councils will be linked to the party’s decision-making process in accordance with its statute, facilitating dialogue and the transfer of experience between generations.

33 per cent women officers at every level

To promote meaningful inclusion within the party, the Nepali Congress has proposed a firm policy of ensuring 33 per cent representation of women among party office-bearers.

The proposal states, “Structural reforms will be advanced to ensure that women make up at least one-third of office-bearers at every level.”

The Congress has also said it will ensure meaningful participation of youth, workers, Madhesis, Dalits, Indigenous Nationalities, Tharus, Muslims, persons with disabilities, and gender and sexual minorities.

The proposal states that the representation of these historically marginalised communities will no longer be limited to presence or token representation within the party, but that mechanisms will be established to incorporate their experiences into policymaking.

title.rendered: Digital technology should be promoted: Chief Justice Sharma

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Chief Justice Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma has said the use of digital technology should be promoted to ensure transparency, accountability and public trust.

Speaking at a programme organised by the Internet Governance Institute in Kathmandu on Monday, Chief Justice Sharma said that although technological development has increased interdependence, risks and challenges are no longer confined to the borders of any single country, making collective efforts necessary to address them.

He said natural and human-induced crises have exposed the vulnerabilities of overall infrastructure, including digital and technological infrastructure.

He said the importance of secure digital records, reliable backups and effective disaster recovery systems has increased, as any loss of access to court records could seriously affect the functioning of the judiciary.

He noted that the use of technology in the judiciary has been increasing in areas including case management, electronic filing, evidence management and judicial hearings. He said the primary objective of digital transformation should be to strengthen access to justice and ensure speedy, cost-effective and citizen-centred delivery of justice.

He also stressed that internet governance should be firmly based on risk management, preparedness and resilience.

He said the “Judicial Information and Communication Technology Policy 2026” recently formulated by the Supreme Court has established information security as a key foundation of digital transformation.

title.rendered: Ruling issued against MPs addressing each other by name in parliamentary committee

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Law, Justice and Human Rights Committee of the House of Representatives has ruled that lawmakers should not address other MPs by name during committee meetings.

Committee chairperson Samiksha Baskota issued the ruling to ensure that committee meetings are conducted in an orderly manner.

Opening Monday’s meeting, Baskota said, “Let us not refer to individuals by name during discussions. Let us not interrupt others while they are speaking or try to speak before it is our turn. It is the responsibility of all of us to conduct the meeting in an orderly manner.”

The committee’s agenda includes a briefing by the committee secretary on bills received by the committee and a general discussion on the Mediation (Second Amendment) Bill, 2083.

According to the committee secretariat, besides the Mediation (Second Amendment) Bill, the Nepal Law Commission (First Amendment) Bill and the Free Legal Aid Bill are also under clause-by-clause discussion.

A total of 66 amendment proposals have been registered by 12 lawmakers on the Mediation (Second Amendment) Bill introduced by Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam.

The bill aims to make the mediation process more inclusive, transparent and effective; ensure representation and protection of women, Dalits and vulnerable parties; introduce strict provisions to invalidate mediation conducted under fear, intimidation, threats or pressure; and give greater authority to judicial committees at the local level, among other provisions.

The Nepal Law Commission Act (First Amendment) Bill, 2083, proposes that the Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs serve as the chairperson of the commission.

Currently, the chairperson of the commission is required to be a person qualified for appointment as a Supreme Court justice. The proposed bill provides that the Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs would serve as the chairperson.

title.rendered: Meeting called for Tuesday to discuss advance ticket booking for public transport

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Department of Transport Management will hold discussions with transport operators on Tuesday regarding advance ticket booking for Dashain.

The department has scheduled a meeting for Tuesday morning to discuss the issue. Passengers planning to leave Kathmandu during the festival season remain uncertain as advance ticket booking has not yet officially opened.

However, some companies have already started online ticket bookings, adding to confusion among the general public.

Passengers continue to face difficulties securing tickets during the festival season and are often forced to wait in long queues at bus parks. The department has called a meeting of stakeholders for Tuesday to discuss the matter.

Representatives from the Highway and Security Division of Nepal Police Headquarters, Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office, Federation of Nepalese National Transport Entrepreneurs, Nepal Transport Independent Workers’ Organisation, All Nepal Transport Independent Workers’ Organisation, Nepal Transport Workers’ Association, Nepal Truck Transport Entrepreneurs’ Association and Lhotse Multipurpose Cooperative Association have been invited to the meeting.

More than one million passengers are estimated to leave the Kathmandu Valley during this year’s Dashain festival.

title.rendered: Preparations underway to restructure 3 major health sector institutions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The government has begun preparations to restructure key regulatory and public health institutions in the health sector.

The government has moved forward with a concept to establish a Centre for Disease Control (CDC) for disease control and surveillance, a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to regulate medicines, food and other health-related materials, and a National Health Accreditation Authority (NHAA) to assess and certify the quality of health institutions.

Secretary at the Ministry of Health and Food Safety Dr Bikash Devkota said the government plans to develop the new institutions based on the changing needs of the health sector and international practices.

There is a concept to modernise the existing Department of Health Services. Along with disease control and surveillance, the new structure would focus on research, studies, academic activities, national and international coordination, and evidence-based health policy formulation.

“CDC is another form of the existing Department of Health Services,” Devkota told Onlinekhabar. “We are seeking to develop it in a modern and scientific way, making the implementation of existing achievements more effective and strengthening national and international coordination.”

According to him, various divisions and structures currently under the Ministry of Health and the department could be integrated within the CDC. Preparations are also underway to establish a separate structure and develop capacity for research and investigative work.

The issue of establishing a CDC in Nepal is not new. Although it has been discussed for a long time, the structure has not been established. Devkota said the government has now moved ahead with the work with confidence that it can be implemented.

“We have been discussing doing this for a long time. It is not a new concept, but it has not happened so far,” Devkota said. “This time, however, we have moved ahead with the confidence that it will happen.”

Although Nepal’s public health system is based on primary healthcare and public health, there is a need to develop institutional capacity in line with the changing disease burden, epidemics and health challenges.

“The principle is based on moving forward from the current public health and primary healthcare system. But it has not been fully achieved,” Devkota said. “The disease burden, health challenges and needs are changing. A scientific and modern model is needed for that.”

He said the health system has so far been operated according to the available resources and human resources capacity, adding that a new structure could make more effective use of even limited resources.

The debate over establishing a disease control centre in Nepal in line with international standards began soon after the promulgation of the Constitution in 2015. However, the proposal has repeatedly remained stalled due to opposition from ministry employees and groups seeking to retain senior positions.

According to senior officials at the Ministry of Health, establishing the CDC would mean abolishing the existing Department of Health Services and various divisions and centres under it and creating an integrated structure. Currently, each of these bodies has a separate director. Officials have been obstructing the proposal because merging all of them into a single centre would eliminate the posts of 10 to 12 senior officials and leave only one director.

The issue of establishing a CDC was also included in the policy and programme for fiscal year 2020/21, presented by then-President Bidya Devi Bhandari. At the time, the ministry had formed a committee under the coordination of Dr Dipendra Raman Singh and moved the work forward. There was pressure to establish the centre at the time due to fears surrounding the coronavirus pandemic. However, the plan remained limited to paper after efforts were made, under bureaucratic pressure, to retain the existing large and cumbersome structures.

At the time, a proposal was made to abolish the existing department and merge the functions of divisions and centres that duplicated the ministry’s work, including the Epidemiology and Disease Control Division, Curative Service Division, Management Division, Nursing and Social Security Division, National Centre for AIDS and STD Control, National Tuberculosis Control Centre, National Public Health Laboratory, National Health Training Centre, and National Health Education, Information and Communication Centre, into a single powerful disease control centre.

The structure of the centre had already been prepared with six divisions and 195 positions, but it was shelved due to concerns over power and positions. The proposal included divisions for non-communicable disease control, communicable disease control, HIV/AIDS, leprosy and sexually transmitted disease control, tuberculosis control, health and biomedical training, and health promotion and communication.

It was proposed that the centre would have a single director, with staff assigned accordingly to the divisions. It was expected that bringing all the structures together would significantly reduce the number of administrative, accounting and other staff currently working separately in different centres and divisions. This concept has now been brought forward again.

The policy and programme for fiscal year 2026/27 included the CDC, FDA and NHAA. The ministry is currently holding discussions with relevant agencies on developing the structures.

Regulation to cover food and medical devices, not just medicines

Another important structure proposed by the government is the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The Department of Drug Administration currently mainly regulates medicines. The proposed structure, however, would cover food products, cosmetics, medical devices and other areas in addition to medicines.

According to Secretary Devkota, the FDA concept includes making the structures currently responsible for food and drug regulation under the Ministry of Health more organised and scientific.

“The structures related to food and drug administration are also under the Ministry of Health,” he said. “There is a need to make these structures more scientific, research-based and effective.”

The proposed FDA would not be limited to medicines. Discussions are underway to create a structure that would extend regulation to food, medicines, cosmetics and medical devices. He said there are also discussions about bringing tobacco products and alcohol within its regulatory scope.

“FDA can oversee food, drugs, cosmetics and medical devices,” Devkota said. “Tobacco products and alcohol, among other things, can also be included.”

However, no final decision has been made on the exact form of the FDA structure. Options under discussion include placing the Department of Drug Administration and the food-related structure under a single higher authority or creating a new structure encompassing both.

“These can be taken forward as two branches under a single higher authority. Alternatively, a new structure can be created by merging the two,” Devkota said. “A model can also be developed by expanding their scope and adding various divisions and branches.”

The ministry plans to study practices in different countries to develop a structure suitable for Nepal.

Separate authority proposed to assess health institution quality

Another important concept put forward by the government is the National Health Accreditation Authority (NHAA).

At present, the Ministry of Health assesses health institutions on the basis of certain standards and checklists when granting operating permits and conducting monitoring. However, the ministry has concluded that a separate independent body is needed for international-level quality certification and for measuring the actual quality of health institutions.

The NHAA would be responsible for measuring, certifying, grading and accrediting the quality of health institutions.

“Currently, we prepare a checklist to assess the quality of an institution. Government employees go and inspect it, and if it meets the standards, we grant permission to operate,” Devkota said. “But a separate authority is needed to certify the level of quality of each institution.”

Hospitals and other health institutions could be classified and certified at different levels in line with international practices. A concept has also been put forward to grade institutions based on their quality, service capacity, human resources, infrastructure and other standards.

“Just as there are international-level quality certifications such as ISO and MSO, there is a need for an authority to certify and grade quality in the health sector as well,” Devkota said.

The ministry plans to develop the NHAA as a body that operates differently from the monitoring and operating-permit functions currently carried out by health divisions.

‘The ministry alone cannot make the decision’

The ministry says it will not make a hasty decision on the three structures because they would bring major institutional changes to the health system. According to Devkota, national and international practices will be studied and discussions held with experts, stakeholders and other ministries. The ministry has already conducted an initial workshop on the issue. It now plans to build a common understanding through further workshops and discussions.

“We have held a general workshop for now. We will now conduct a series of workshops,” Devkota said. “We will hold discussions with all concerned parties. We will look at international and national practices and move forward to determine what model is suitable for Nepal.”

According to him, creating the new structures is not a matter that can be decided solely by the Ministry of Health. Since the structures would need to encompass other government agencies and various stakeholders in the health sector, the government plans to move forward by developing a common understanding.

“This is a major issue. The ministry alone cannot create such a structure and say it has been established,” he said. “We will move forward by developing a common understanding so that other ministries and all concerned agencies can also accept it and the structure can be effective.”

The government aims to clarify the concepts for these structures and prepare drafts of the necessary legal provisions within the current fiscal year. According to Devkota, the immediate priority is not to establish the structures at once but to advance the legal and institutional preparations required for them.

“We will hold further workshops, meetings and discussions after Tihar. Within this fiscal year, we will prepare the concept paper and move ahead with drafting the law for the necessary policy arrangements,” he said.

He said laws should be formulated to give the three structures autonomous roles.

title.rendered: Beni-Jomsom-Korala road to remain closed for another week

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Beni-Jomsom road connecting to the Korala border point between Nepal and China will remain closed for about another week, despite partial progress in reopening the route.

According to the Department of Roads, two-way traffic has resumed along the Ghansa-Korala section of the Maldhunga-Beni-Jomsom-Korala road.

In the Tatopani area, traffic has been resumed after back-cutting and construction of retaining walls at damaged sections of the road. Work on the approach to the Pokharebagar bridge is also underway. However, several sections of the road remain severely damaged.

At two locations in Ratopani and near Bhirkate, the road has been cut off to the extent that even pedestrians cannot pass. Around 100 metres of road near Begkhola has completely sunk, according to the Department of Roads.

A major landslide at a location called Baiseri has also blocked the road. The road from Rahughat to Sirubari has been reopened for one-way traffic. The department said a track has also been opened near Ratopani in the Pokharebagar area. Work to fill and stabilise the road at a location known as Kuneto is ongoing.

The department said work on the major road cuts and landslide-affected sections will begin from Monday.

Overall, the department estimates that it will take another six days to reopen the entire section for regular traffic. The Korala border point is an important trade and transit route between Nepal and China. The disruption of the Beni-Jomsom-Korala road has affected road connectivity towards the border and the Mustang region.

title.rendered: Dr Dilli Harijan begins hunger strike again after agreement remains unimplemented

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Dr Dilli Harijan has begun his second hunger strike, saying that an agreement reached with the government to address the demands of interns and resident doctors has not been implemented.

Dr Harijan began the hunger strike on Monday at the office of the Medical Education Commission in Sanothimi, Bhaktapur. He had previously led protests over issues including working hours, stipends and safe working conditions for interns and resident doctors.

Following his previous hunger strike, the government had reached a five-point agreement with Dr Harijan. However, he has accused the government of failing to implement the agreement even after two months.

He said he was forced to resume the hunger strike after repeated requests for implementation received no response from the government.

Dr Harijan said interns and resident doctors are still working under extremely difficult conditions. He said being required to work continuously for up to 36 hours could affect doctors’ health and performance, as well as the quality of patient care.

“It is unfortunate that despite repeatedly raising concerns about doctors’ working hours, stipends, safe working conditions and other legitimate issues, there has been no expected improvement,” he said.

He has called for an end to the practice of making interns and resident doctors work for long hours without providing appropriate facilities, safety and due recognition of their labour. He said it is the state’s responsibility to ensure that doctors can work in a safe and dignified environment.

Dr Harijan said they had already adopted democratic and peaceful means, ranging from street protests to raising the issue in parliament and from dialogue to hunger strikes, to have their demands addressed. However, he said the problem has persisted because repeated commitments have not been implemented in practice.

He urged the government to implement the agreement and immediately address the legitimate demands of interns and resident doctors. He said the issues he has raised are not personal but concern the working conditions and rights of interns and resident doctors across the country.

He said he would continue the hunger strike until his demands are fulfilled.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah says government continues disaster response without compromise

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Prime Minister Balen Shah has said disaster management efforts have been continuing through coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments since August 26.

Addressing the 21st meeting of the National Council for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management held at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers in Singha Durbar on Monday, Shah said the government has been continuously working on disaster response without compromising on its efforts.

Chief ministers of Gandaki, Bagmati, Madhesh and Koshi provinces also attended the meeting.

Addressing the chief ministers, Shah said the government was mobilising available resources and human resources to complete disaster management and response work as quickly as possible.

“We are mobilising the available resources and human resources to complete disaster management work as soon as possible, so I urge you to remain assured on this matter,” Shah said.

Shah said the government was also assessing the damage caused by floods and landslides in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli and Gandaki areas, as well as other affected regions, and was working on their management and recovery.

He said the government was preparing to further strengthen the early warning system as part of efforts to reduce disaster risks.

Shah also said the government was carrying out necessary work to reduce the risks posed by avalanches.

The prime minister expressed gratitude to civil servants, security personnel, volunteers, representatives of political parties and others who have continued working in disaster response operations, putting their own lives at risk.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress to have 15 joint general secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Nepali Congress will increase the number of joint general secretaries to 15.

Of the 15 joint general secretaries, nine will be elected under the inclusive representation system, two through the open category and four will be nominated by the party president.

One joint general secretary will be elected from each of the women, Indigenous Nationalities, Dalit, Madhesi, Khas Arya, Tharu, Muslim, backward region and minority/persons with disabilities categories.

The minority/persons with disabilities category was not included during the previous general convention. The party has also decided to elect deputy general secretaries through the open category, with two positions allocated for it.

The party president will nominate four joint general secretaries. The party statute has been amended to allow the president to appoint four additional joint general secretaries, including at least one woman.

title.rendered: World Egg Day being observed for a week

content.rendered:
Chitwan, October 5

The Nepal Layers’ Poultry Farmers Association is observing World Egg Day this year through a week-long series of events aimed at raising public awareness about the nutritional and health benefits of eggs. The theme for this year’s World Egg Day that falls on October 9, is “Protein that Powers and Protects.”

According to the Association’s Central President, Binod Pokharel, programs are being conducted in various schools across the country to educate students and parents about the nutritional value of eggs, their role in health, and their importance in a balanced diet. Special programs are being organized under the lead of the Association, with support from the U.S. Soybean Export Council (USSEC) and collaboration between the government and private sectors.

On October 9, an “Egg Walk” is being held to start from the premises of the Chitwan Industries Association and conclude at Shahid Chowk in Narayangarh. The walk aims to raise public awareness regarding egg nutrition, its positive impact on health, and its importance in the daily diet.

A panel discussion involving stakeholders will also be organised on the same day. The program will feature discussions on egg production, nutrition, health, consumption, marketing, and the role of eggs in Nepali society. According to physician Dr. Bhojraj Adhikari, a single egg contains approximately 6 grams of high-quality protein, along with essential nutrients such as vitamins A, B, and B12. The protein found in eggs aids in building and repairing body tissues and muscles, while also playing a crucial role in the growth and development of children.

title.rendered: Tourist numbers rise at Annapurna Base Camp as roads reopen

content.rendered:
Pokhara, October 5

The number of tourists heading to the world-famous Annapurna Base Camp (ABC) trekking route has increased significantly in recent days after roads disrupted by floods and landslides were reopened.

Tourism entrepreneurs say the improvement in weather and disruptions on trekking routes in the Manang and Manaslu regions have also diverted tourists towards the Annapurna Base Camp, increasing visitor numbers in the area.

According to Dilip Gurung, secretary of the Chhomrong Tourism Management Committee, around 300 tourists are currently reaching Annapurna Base Camp each day.

There are six hotels and lodges at the base camp with a combined capacity to accommodate up to 350 tourists.

“There are currently no domestic tourists, but the number of foreign and South Asian tourists has increased. All the roads leading here have now reopened, making the trek easier,” Gurung said.

The tourism sector in the Annapurna region had been badly affected after continuous rainfall, floods and landslides disrupted roads and trekking routes at several locations.

The road at Birethanti and Syauli Bazaar along the Annapurna route had remained blocked for an extended period after the Modi River eroded sections of the road. The rural municipality reopened the road in the first week of October after working on it for nearly one and a half months.

Gurung said tourists who had planned to travel to Manang and Manaslu were increasingly choosing ABC as an alternative after roads and trekking routes in those areas were affected by landslides.

“Among Manang, Manaslu and Annapurna, the route towards Annapurna Base Camp is comparatively easier. That is one reason why tourists from South Asian countries are increasingly choosing ABC. We expect Nepali tourists to start arriving after Dashain,” he said.

Travel to the starting points of the trek from Pokhara has also become easier after roads disrupted by floods and landslides in different parts of the Annapurna region were reopened.

Himbahadur Gurung, ward chairperson of Annapurna Rural Municipality-11, said the road from Pokhara through Ghandruk to ABC is currently open.

He said trekking routes have also been reopened in some places through temporary arrangements.

“Birethanti and Syauli Bazaar are open. There are no major problems above Ghandruk either. Both permanent and temporary routes to ABC are now open. Tourists can come through Nayapul, Ghandruk and Chhomrong,” he said.

Meanwhile, a trekking route that had been disrupted after the Kimrung River swept away a suspension bridge two months ago has also been reopened after a temporary wooden footbridge was constructed across the river.

Annapurna Base Camp is located at an altitude of around 4,130 metres above sea level. The trek is considered one of the world’s renowned trekking destinations, offering visitors close-up views of the Annapurna mountain range and Machhapuchhre.

The route is particularly popular for its sunrise views from close to the mountains, mountain scenery, and opportunities to experience local culture and lifestyles.

During the ABC trek, visitors can experience Gurung culture, local lifestyles, mountain settlements, forests, waterfalls, rivers and Himalayan landscapes.

The route through Machhapuchhre Base Camp to Annapurna Base Camp is one of the area’s major attractions. Trekkers can also see Machhapuchhre, Annapurna South and Annapurna I from close range.

With the number of domestic and foreign tourists increasing in the Annapurna region, the rural municipality has also recently started operating a first-aid centre with a focus on tourist health.

The centre has been established at Machhapuchhre Base Camp and provides immediate basic medical treatment to tourists and local residents experiencing common health problems or emergencies in the ABC and Machhapuchhre Base Camp areas.

Tourists trekking to ABC have previously fallen ill, with some deaths reported due to altitude sickness at high elevations.

title.rendered: Successful completion of Zipline and Sky Cycling trials at Resunga

content.rendered:
Gulmi, October 5

The final testing phase for the zipline and sky cycling facilities aimed at boosting adventure tourism has wrapped up successfully at Garjura, a well-known tourist hotspot in the district. With the trials yielding positive results, Resunga Municipality has announced that all preparations for the adventure tourism infrastructure are now complete.

This ambitious project includes a 568-metre zipline and a 110-metre sky cycling setup. Around 40 participants took part in the hands-on testing of both facilities during this morning’s trial sessions. Lakshmi Khanal, one of the trial participants, described the zipline experience as smooth and visually stunning.

She mentioned that it took her about 58 seconds to glide down the 568-metre zipline. Prakash Bhalami, another participant, shared his satisfaction with how well the infrastructure is functioning, especially considering some earlier scheduling hiccups. Khildhwaj Panthi, the chief administrator of Resunga Municipality, highlighted that the primary goal of the zipline and sky cycling is to promote tourism in the region.

He anticipates that this new adventure tourism infrastructure will attract more visitors to Resunga. Binod Marasini, the administrative officer of Resunga Municipality, announced that regular operations will kick off within the next week. He also noted that the municipality will take charge of managing and coordinating the operations for both the zipline and sky cycling. The pricing has been set at Rs 600 for the zipline and Rs 400 for sky cycling.

From Resunga’s impressive height of 2,300 meters above sea level, visitors can enjoy breathtaking views of various snow-capped mountain ranges and picturesque landscapes, including Machhapuchchhre and Dhaulagiri. The project was contracted by Khanal Infra Pvt Ltd for Rs 12.5 million.
