title.rendered: Gagan Thapa’s 29 proposals to reshape the Nepali Congress

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa has presented his political report for the party’s 15th General Convention at the Central Working Committee meeting.

The report outlines the party’s political, ideological, organisational and economic direction for the next four years. It includes a review of the party’s past performance, a stronger opposition role, a policy against pre-election alliances, organisational restructuring, greater cooperation with the private sector, increased youth participation and the concept of a “Prosperous Nepal, Respected Nepali.”

The report acknowledges that the Nepali Congress has prioritised positions and power over its core political objectives over the past two decades.

It says coalition management, power-sharing, factionalism and transactional politics have weakened the party’s moral standing. It also says the tendency to protect people associated with the party in cases of corruption and irregularities has weakened the autonomy of public institutions.

The report further acknowledges that the party has grown increasingly distant from younger generations and has failed to understand changing expectations among citizens. It says the party has sought to apologise to the people through the second special general convention and pledged to reform itself.

Congress to remain in opposition

The report describes the Congress’ defeat in the February 21 election as a result of the growing distance between the party and citizens, as well as political weaknesses that have accumulated over the past two decades.

With 38 seats, the party has proposed playing a responsible role as the main opposition and effectively monitoring the government.

The report calls for the party to question government actions based on evidence and facts, speak out against corruption, rights violations and poor governance, and present alternative policies rather than limiting itself to criticism.

It also proposes a “shadow government” mechanism to monitor ministries at the federal and provincial levels, while giving greater priority to long-term national issues over day-to-day political disputes.

No pre-election alliances

Thapa has proposed that the Nepali Congress should not form electoral alliances with other parties before the next election.

The party would contest elections under its own tree symbol, with its own candidates and agenda. Candidate selection would prioritise qualifications, contribution and performance over factional affiliation, access and political patronage.

The report proposes considering primary elections, public opinion surveys and direct voting by party members in candidate selection. It also proposes that membership rules should not be changed at the last minute to influence conventions or candidacies.

Ideological renewal

The report proposes retaining nationalism, democracy and democratic socialism as the party’s core ideological foundations while updating its political thinking to reflect the needs of the 21st century and changing socioeconomic conditions.

It proposes linking nationalism not only to geography and slogans but also to national capacity in energy, food, technology and finance.

Democracy, it says, should not be limited to elections but should include meaningful citizen participation in decision-making and the exercise of public power.

The report also proposes connecting BP Koirala’s socialist vision with a modern social-market economy and incorporating Pradeep Giri’s emphasis on study, debate, self-criticism and the concerns of marginalised communities into the party’s ideological tradition.

‘Prosperous Nepal, Respected Nepali’

The report says economic growth alone should not be the measure of prosperity.

Education, health, nutrition, skills, capabilities and people’s real freedom should form the foundation of development, it says.

It proposes pursuing development through cooperation among citizens, communities, the private sector, cooperatives, universities and experts rather than relying solely on the government.

The report also calls for clear outcomes and accountability in major decisions taken by the state.

Five-question accountability system

The report proposes a five-question accountability system for major government and public decisions. It asks what decision was made, why it was made, who is responsible, what the outcome was and what was done if the expected outcome was not achieved.

These five questions would form the basis of public accountability under the proposed system.

Open-source citizen dashboard

The report proposes developing a digital system through which citizens can monitor development projects, budget expenditure and the officials responsible for them.

Information on the progress of projects, spending and responsible officials would be made publicly available to facilitate real-time monitoring and institutionalise citizen oversight of government work.

Private sector and economy

The report proposes treating the private sector not merely as a source of tax revenue but as a key engine of wealth creation, production, innovation and employment.

It calls for protection of private investment and policy stability, along with a business-friendly environment. The relationship between the government and private sector should shift from regulation and tax collection towards cooperation and partnership, it says.

Production, entrepreneurship and job creation would be placed at the centre of economic policy. The report also proposes directing remittances towards productive investment in agriculture, industry, tourism and technology.

Hydropower and clean energy would be promoted as a foundation for industrialisation and green-energy exports.

Jobs and foreign employment

The report proposes making the expansion of productive and dignified employment within Nepal a national priority.

Foreign employment, meanwhile, should be made safer, better managed and rights-based rather than treated solely as an economic compulsion.

It also calls for policies to protect the rights and social security of Nepalis working abroad and for creating an environment in which remittances can be invested productively.

Migration and population

The report calls for different approaches to declining populations in the hills, increasing migration towards the Madhes and highway corridors, and growing pressure on major cities.

It proposes designing development plans based on actual settlement patterns, mobility and demand for services rather than administrative boundaries alone.

Education, healthcare, housing, transport and social security policies should also reflect changing lifestyles and family structures, it says.

Agriculture, industry and production

The report proposes shifting Nepal from an economy dependent on imports and remittances towards one driven by production.

Agriculture, hydropower, energy, tourism, industry and digital technology have been identified as major pillars of economic growth.

The report calls for agriculture to be connected with modern technology, markets and entrepreneurship, while remittances should be channelled into agricultural and industrial investment.

Climate change and green development

Climate change should be treated not only as an environmental issue but also as an economic and national security concern, according to the report.

It calls for disaster risks to be incorporated into development plans, infrastructure and settlement planning, while promoting sustainable use of natural resources.

The report also proposes linking green energy, hydropower and environmental protection with economic opportunities and emphasises intergenerational justice.

Technology and artificial intelligence

The report notes that artificial intelligence and digital technology are changing employment, education, knowledge and competition.

It proposes preparing Nepal not only to use new technologies but also to take advantage of opportunities created by them.

Education and skills systems should be adapted to new technologies, while media literacy and fact-based public dialogue should be promoted to counter misinformation and hate in the digital age.

Social sector

The report proposes linking the Congress with continuing social campaigns against caste discrimination, child marriage, gender-based violence and malnutrition.

Public education and healthcare should serve as foundations for equal opportunity, while social security for senior citizens, children, women and vulnerable communities should be strengthened.

Mental health, loneliness and changing family structures should also be incorporated into long-term state policy, the report says.

Federalism and the Constitution

The report acknowledges that although the federal structure has been established, its effectiveness remains weak.

It calls for better coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments, along with improvements in administrative capacity and fiscal federalism.

The debate on constitutional amendments, it says, should be based on national consensus rather than immediate political power equations.

Transitional justice

The report calls for completing the remaining tasks of the peace process and ensuring truth, justice and reparation for conflict victims.

Transitional justice should not be used as a tool for political bargaining or power-sharing, it says, arguing that the trust of victims and the credibility of institutions should remain central.

National sovereignty and foreign policy

The report proposes understanding national sovereignty not only in terms of formal independence but also in terms of national capacity in energy, food, finance, technology and knowledge.

It calls for maintaining Nepal’s independent decision-making capacity amid changing geopolitical competition and expanding diplomatic options based on national interests.

It also stresses the need to view domestic economic capacity and external relations as interconnected.

New concept of national reconciliation

The report proposes developing BP Koirala’s concept of national reconciliation beyond a political settlement and as a basis for social and cultural unity.

It calls for strengthening a shared Nepali identity among people from the mountains, hills, Madhes and the diaspora, while promoting coexistence, dialogue and democratic culture among different communities, religions and cultures.

Organisational reform

The report proposes transforming the Congress into an organisation that remains connected with citizens throughout the political cycle rather than becoming active only during elections.

It calls for greater transparency in membership, participation and internal democracy, while creating an institutional mechanism for leadership transition between generations.

The report proposes establishing a Leadership Training Institute for cadres and young leaders, a Policy Institute for research, an Election Bureau for election preparations and a Governance Institute to assist elected representatives on policy, budgeting and good governance.

Internal anti-corruption measures

The report proposes high ethical standards for party officials and elected representatives, along with financial transparency and mandatory public audits.

It calls for no protection for party members accused of corruption, a clear suspension process for those facing corruption allegations and an independent internal ombudsman to investigate conduct and corruption-related complaints.

What Congress says it will not do

The report proposes a public commitment that the Congress will not engage in partisan appointments or power-sharing in the judiciary, constitutional bodies, universities and administration.

It also proposes not using public property and authority for the benefit of a party, faction or individual, and not giving opportunities based on money, access or proximity to party leaders.

The party would also commit to treating corruption allegations against its own members consistently and not changing rules at the last minute to delay conventions or influence candidacies.

Two-term limit for prime minister

The report proposes initiating efforts for a constitutional provision preventing anyone from serving as prime minister for more than two terms.

It says a term limit would help prevent long-term concentration of power and leadership in an individual.

Electoral reforms

The report proposes introducing primary elections for candidate selection and exploring a “none of the above” option.

It also calls for legal and constitutional initiatives to enable Nepalis living abroad to vote.

The report proposes discussions on alternatives such as rotating reserved constituencies to make the electoral system more participatory, transparent and representative.

Rs 100 million endowment fund

The report proposes establishing a Rs 100 million endowment fund to support the education and healthcare of families of martyrs, injured party workers and displaced activists.

It also calls for long-term protection for families who contributed to the party’s political movements.

Special measures for young people

The report proposes forming a special task force comprising independent young experts to study the concerns and demands of the Gen Z generation.

Its recommendations would be incorporated into party policymaking, while youth participation and leadership development would be placed at the centre of party renewal.

The report also proposes increasing youth participation in policymaking and party decisions through digital platforms.

Timeline for implementing ‘prosperity’

The report sets out a timeline for implementing its concept of prosperity.

During the first 100 days, it proposes reviewing the party’s political and organisational performance from 2006/07 to 2025/26, beginning the review process in all seven provinces, publishing the first “Prosperity Policy Paper” and preparing a record of community contributions.

During the first year, provincial task forces would be formed on education, nutrition, employment, good governance and green development. Citizen dialogue and public-service monitoring would also begin.

Before elections, the party would publish clear criteria for candidate selection and advance a primary election process, with community work, ethical conduct and performance considered in selecting candidates.

The report also proposes internal reviews every three months, an annual public “Prosperity Report” and an assessment of the four-year leadership based on the implementation of policies and commitments.

A broader restructuring agenda

The political report links the Congress’ proposed renewal not only to leadership or organisational changes but also to political culture, economic policy, private-sector cooperation, employment, social security, federalism, good governance, youth participation, technology, climate change and national sovereignty.

Its central concept is “national renewal and prosperity.” The report seeks to acknowledge past weaknesses, reduce the party’s distance from citizens, strengthen democratic institutions, expand production and employment through cooperation with the private sector, and establish measurable outcomes for party policies and commitments.

Thapa has proposed regular reviews of policies, organisation and programmes throughout the four-year leadership period, with performance assessed on the basis of results. The broader objective is to transform the Congress from an election-focused organisation into a political institution that remains continuously connected with citizens.

title.rendered: 2 killed, one rescued after being buried under landslide in Baglung

content.rendered:
Baglung, October 5

Two workers were killed, and another was injured after a mound of soil suddenly collapsed on them during road construction in Nisikhola Rural Municipality-3, Bohoragaun, Baglung, on Sunday morning.

According to District Police Office Chief SP Phanindra Prasai, the deceased have been identified as 28-year-old Lal Bahadur Budhathoki of Salyan and 32-year-old Raju Thapa of Gaighat, Udayapur.

The three workers were buried when the soil mound collapsed at around 7:30 am while they were working on the Kapra-Bohoragaun-Chhapakhani-Pyuthan road section. Two of the buried workers died at the scene while rescuers were trying to recover them.

The third worker, Krishna Gharti Magar of Rolpa, was rescued in critical condition and taken to Provincial Hospital Burtibang for treatment, said Ramesh Bikram Shahi, ward chair of Nisikhola Rural Municipality-3.

The workers were buried when a mound of soil suddenly collapsed as an excavator, registration number Lu 1 Ka 3446 and operated by driver Bhadra Malla, was being used to upgrade the road.

title.rendered: Which posts is Nepali Congress adding?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The Nepali Congress is preparing to amend its statute to ensure that at least one woman is elected as vice-president and one as general secretary of the party.

Under the proposed amendment, the number of vice-presidents will be increased to four. One of the four posts will be designated as senior vice-president.

The party will also increase the number of general secretaries from two to three, with one of the three posts reserved for a woman.

All vice-presidents and general secretaries will have to be elected, according to the proposed amendment.

The number of joint general secretaries will also be increased. The party is preparing to raise the number from 11 to 13.

Of the 13 joint general secretaries, eight will be elected under the inclusive category, two through the open category and three will be nominated by the party president.

The previous general convention had introduced a provision for eight joint general secretaries under the inclusive category.

With the proposed changes, the number of office-bearers in the Nepali Congress will rise to 21.

The party is also preparing to increase the number of central committee members elected from the open category. The number is proposed to be increased from 35 to 45.

A senior party leader said there have been demands to increase the number of central committee members under other clusters as well if the number of open-category members is increased.

According to the leader, an agreement has already been reached to increase the number of vice-presidents, general secretaries, joint general secretaries and central committee members. However, discussions are still underway to determine the final number of central committee members.

The Nepali Congress had previously amended its statute to form a 231-member Central Working Committee. The party is now preparing another amendment that would further increase the size of the central committee.

title.rendered: Misbehave should never be considered a part of governance reform

content.rendered:
Governance reform is about changing and improving the systems of government so that they better serve citizens. It requires institutional accountability, transparency, professionalism and a willingness to challenge practices that no longer work.

The governance reform agenda was a major component of the Rastriya Swatantra Party’s manifesto for the House of Representatives election of 2082. The single-party government led by Balendra Shah has also unveiled a 100-point agenda for governance reform, demonstrating the priority the government places on changing the way the state functions.

But the government’s enthusiasm for radical reform risks being undermined if reform is confused with aggressive behaviour. In recent months, the conduct of some ministers, lawmakers and political appointees has raised an important question: Is intimidation being mistaken for accountability?

Holding public officials accountable is essential to good governance. But accountability does not require humiliation, intimidation or threats.

Accountability is not intimidation

Whether in the House of Representatives, the National Assembly or during official monitoring visits, public officials and elected representatives are expected to question, scrutinise and demand answers. They are also expected to do so within the norms of democratic institutions.

Aggressive and threatening language cannot simply be justified as part of a reform agenda. When criticism turns into personal attacks, intimidation or humiliation, it risks becoming bullying rather than accountability.

The conduct of the Home Minister has attracted criticism on several occasions for the way he has responded to questions from lawmakers, including members of opposition parties. Rather than addressing criticism through substantive political debate, aggressive exchanges and personal remarks can shift attention away from the issue being raised.

Similar concerns have emerged in the National Assembly. The use of threatening language towards the media over criticism of the government raises another concern. A government committed to reform should be able to tolerate scrutiny, including uncomfortable questions from journalists and political opponents.

Reform cannot mean creating an environment in which criticism is treated as disloyalty.

Ministers must also be accountable for their conduct

Similar concerns have been raised about the conduct of other ministers.

The Minister for Industry, Commerce and Supplies has faced criticism after making allegations against employees over alleged collusion with businesspeople and threatening action against gas industries, including the possibility of revoking licences. Serious allegations involving businesses and public officials require evidence, due process and appropriate institutional mechanisms.

Threatening businesses or individuals from a position of political authority does not strengthen governance. If wrongdoing is suspected, the proper response is investigation, evidence and action under the law.

The Minister of Finance has also faced criticism over his responses to opposition lawmakers questioning budget information leaks, tax-rate adjustments and changes to the Finance Bill. Threatening to expose alleged past scandals involving political opponents from the parliamentary rostrum does little to strengthen public confidence in parliamentary oversight.

The same principle applies when ministers respond to journalists. Questioning a journalist’s professional or technical ability in a way that appears intended to humiliate them does not advance public accountability.

Governance reform does not give those in power a licence to vent anger at others.

Power must come with restraint

Threatening language from ministers has increasingly appeared to be treated as normal political behaviour.

The problem extends beyond Singha Durbar. A statement by the Minister for Infrastructure Development about breaking the legs of a contractor over delays in completing a project drew criticism for its threatening nature. Instructions to cancel contracts may be legitimate when supported by law and contractual provisions, but intimidation is not a substitute for due process.

A government seeking to reform public administration should be especially careful about the distinction between authority and coercion.

The same applies to lawmakers.

There have been several instances in which lawmakers from the ruling party have been criticised for their conduct in public places. Reports of lawmakers scolding a school principal for not coming out to welcome an MP, berating an army officer over road expansion, or confronting members of a hospital management committee and threatening action have raised questions about the understanding of governance reform among some elected representatives.

An elected representative has considerable authority. But that authority comes from the public and is exercised within the limits of law and institutional responsibility. It does not provide a licence to humiliate public servants or other citizens.

Parliament must protect institutional credibility

A recent incident involving an MP making allegations against the Inspector General of Police during a meeting of the Public Accounts Committee also attracted considerable attention.

Questions raised by lawmakers about the functioning of security institutions are legitimate and necessary. But allegations against senior officials, particularly those responsible for national security, must be handled carefully and through appropriate parliamentary procedures.

When accusations are made without sufficient regard for institutional process, they can damage the credibility of both the individual being questioned and the institution conducting the oversight.

These are not isolated concerns. They form part of a wider pattern in which the language of reform risks becoming associated with confrontation, humiliation and the public display of power.

Political appointees are not above institutional norms

The issue also extends to political appointees.

Reports that advisers to the Prime Minister used threatening language towards officials of the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA), including commissioners, in connection with the e-passport controversy have raised questions about the independence of constitutional bodies.

If political appointees attempt to pressure constitutional officials into taking immediate action, that would raise serious concerns about institutional independence and the limits of political authority. Such allegations should be investigated through appropriate channels rather than dismissed or normalised as part of a reform-oriented government.

Similarly, the reported presentation of a farewell certificate to the Chief Secretary by the Prime Minister’s Political Advisor was criticised as inconsistent with established administrative norms. Even lawmakers from the ruling party questioned the appropriateness of the incident.

Institutional reform cannot succeed if informal political authority begins to replace established administrative procedures.

Reform requires rebuilding trust

The RSP-led government came to power with significant public support and high expectations for political and administrative transformation.

That mandate carries both opportunity and responsibility.

Strong public support does not mean that ministers, lawmakers or political appointees can disregard their roles, responsibilities or limits of authority. Opposition lawmakers do not lose their right to ask questions simply because they belong to parties associated with the old political establishment.

Similarly, civil servants do not become legitimate targets for humiliation simply because the government wants to demonstrate that it is different from previous administrations.

Nepal’s recent Gen Z movement has already brought profound political and social change. The destruction of police stations, government offices, Singha Durbar, courts, media houses, Bhat-Bhateni outlets and other public and private property caused not only physical damage but also affected the morale of many people working in public institutions.

At such a moment, the government has an opportunity to rebuild confidence in the state.

That requires working with Parliament rather than treating political disagreement as an obstacle. It requires restoring the morale of civil servants rather than intimidating them. It requires engaging the private sector through rules and institutions rather than threats. And it requires protecting constitutional bodies from political pressure.

Reform must be institutional

A government does not achieve governance reform simply by adopting the word “reform” as a political slogan.

Real reform is institutional. It means improving procedures, strengthening accountability, clarifying responsibilities, enforcing laws fairly and ensuring that decisions are made through established mechanisms.

It also requires political leaders to demonstrate the behaviour they expect from the institutions they seek to reform.

There is nothing inherently wrong with being firm. Ministers and lawmakers should be able to demand answers, challenge officials, investigate wrongdoing and take action when laws or procedures have been violated.

But firmness is not intimidation. Accountability is not humiliation. Political authority is not a licence to threaten.

The RSP-led government has been given an opportunity to demonstrate that governance in Nepal can be different. That change will ultimately be measured not by how loudly leaders speak or how aggressively they confront opponents, but by whether institutions become more accountable, professional and trustworthy.

Governance reform should reinforce institutional accountability, professionalism and adherence to rules and procedures. It should not normalise intimidation or humiliation.

Misbehaviour is not reform. And a government serious about reform should be the first to understand the difference.

title.rendered: Sher Bahadur Deuba’s absence and the end of an era in Nepali Congress

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

The stage at the Nepali Congress’s 15th General Convention was filled with leaders from across Nepal’s political spectrum.

Almost all of the office-bearers elected at the party’s 14th General Convention were present, with only four exceptions. Photographs of the party’s late presidents and prominent leaders were placed at the front of the stage. But one face was missing.

Former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba was not there.

According to Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa, a chair had been kept for Deuba in his honour. His photograph was also included in the logo of the 15th General Convention. The party had formally invited him to attend the opening ceremony as chief guest. But the invitation never reached him.

Leaders including General Secretary Yogendra Chaudhary were turned back by security personnel when they attempted to deliver it.

Even shortly before the opening ceremony began, some Nepali Congress leaders, including Vice President Pushpa Bhusal, were still holding on to a faint hope that Deuba might appear.

He did not.

For a politician who has spent nearly six decades at the centre of Nepal’s democratic movement, Deuba’s absence from the Congress convention was more than the absence of a former president.

It marked the growing distance between Deuba and the party he once dominated.

Deuba had established a separate office to organise activities around the 15th General Convention and had been conducting political activities across the country. Some within Congress therefore expected that he might make a last-minute decision to attend.

He chose not to.

Instead, Deuba has continued on an uncertain political path, refusing to recognise the leadership elected by the party’s special convention as legitimate. In doing so, he has also gradually lost many of the political companions who stood beside him for years.

The people who once formed his closest political circle are no longer walking the same path.

The roots of the split lie in the questions raised about Deuba’s leadership following the Gen Z movement. Gagan Thapa and other Congress leaders openly challenged his leadership.

Deuba appears to have failed to recognise how quickly those questions were gaining strength.

The special convention eventually removed him from the party leadership.

For a politician with a six-decade history in the democratic movement, the more significant question was not simply that he lost the leadership. It was that he was unwilling to accept questions raised against him through a democratic process.

Thapa appeared to allude to this when he used Khulamanch as a metaphor during Sunday’s convention.

“The special feature of Khulamanch is that it brings different people together. But coming to Khulamanch does not mean all differences disappear. We need many more such open forums. People should not be expelled from the party simply for asking questions,” Thapa said.

Thapa himself had once been expelled from the party by Deuba after demanding a special convention under the party’s constitutional provisions.

Thapa also offered Deuba a difficult reminder about what it means to honour a political leader.

“Sher Bahadur Deuba’s honour will not be determined by how many times people salute at his door. It will be determined by how much they expand the party that Sher Bahadur Deuba built,” he said.

Thapa said Congress respected Deuba’s history and that was precisely why a chair had been reserved for him on the convention stage. But the symbolism went further.

The 15th General Convention was set to bring the party its largest-ever number of representatives and potentially make significant changes to its leadership and political direction.

By staying away, Deuba may have lost an opportunity to shape the final chapter of his political career.

Deuba is not an ordinary figure in Nepali politics.

He has been jailed for his political activities, won elections repeatedly, served as home minister and become prime minister five times. He split the Nepali Congress in 2059 BS, later returned to the party and eventually transformed himself from an outsider into one of the central figures of the party establishment.

But near the end of his political career, he now finds himself in a role that appears increasingly difficult to justify.

His final political battle is no longer against a rival at an election, an opponent in Parliament or even a monarch.

It is against his own time.

Deuba has based his claim to political legitimacy on a case currently pending before the Supreme Court. But even if the court eventually restores that legitimacy, it may not be enough to restore his political relevance.

The mood at Khulamanch suggested that the party’s energy had moved elsewhere.

The new expectations and enthusiasm were directed toward a Congress that was trying to transform itself.

The party’s leaders were also sending a broader message—that Congress could continue without Deuba and some of the second-tier leaders who have remained close to him.

Thapa put it bluntly.

“I do not know where the sons of BP Koirala and Ganesh Man Singh are. But the spirit of BP and Ganesh Man is here,” he said.

RSP Chair Rabi Lamichhane added his own interpretation.

Sometimes, he said, instead of continuing to persuade people inside a party who constantly complain, create trouble and drain the organisation’s energy, it may be better to let them go.

It was a veiled political message, but its target was not difficult to identify.

Deuba’s absence has cost Nepali Congress the presence of several second-generation leaders associated with him, including Shashank Koirala, the son of BP Koirala; Prakashman Singh, the son of Ganesh Man Singh; Bimalendra Nidhi, the son of Mahendra Narayan Nidhi; and Shekhar Koirala.

Some older party workers have also been left outside the new Nepali Congress arrangement. But for Deuba himself, something more consequential may have been lost.

An important chapter of his nearly six-decade political history is missing. There was little left for Deuba to prove in conventional political terms.

He had served as prime minister five times. He had led Nepali Congress twice. He had split the party and eventually become part of its establishment. He had overtaken many of his contemporaries to reach the top.

He had fought against the monarchy and challenged the dominance of the Koirala family within Nepali Congress.

He had repeatedly won elections and secured the support of voters.

Had he voluntarily handed over leadership in the final phase of his career, he might have achieved another kind of victory—the victory of knowing when to leave.

He could have done so at the special convention.

Even if that opportunity had been missed, he could have used the 15th General Convention as a chance to correct course, particularly after the Supreme Court had already provided legal recognition in the matter he had been contesting. He chose not to. And that decision has left his political ground increasingly unstable.

Deuba’s political character does not require a great deal of documentation to understand. His five terms as prime minister tell much of the story.

Few contemporary politicians have understood the psychology of power as instinctively as Deuba.

He knows the arithmetic required to reach government. He knows when to remain silent, whom to bring into an alliance and when to make a decision.

But the question now is whether he has recognised that the question facing him is no longer simply who controls power.

It is whether he remains politically relevant.

There were also substantive achievements during his time in government.

The Mahakali Treaty, implementation of value-added tax, the declaration of the liberation of bonded labourers, efforts to strengthen the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority, and policy attempts to bring women, Dalits, indigenous communities, Madhesis and people from historically marginalised regions into the mainstream were among them.

Yet the central thread running through Deuba’s political career remained power.

In recent years, he was also seen as trying to position his wife, Arzu Deuba, as his political successor.

That further damaged his public standing.

The depth of the public anger became visible during the Gen Z movement, when the situation deteriorated to the point that Deuba himself faced a physical attack.

For decades, Deuba’s greatest political strength was the network of people around him.

Ministers, lawmakers and political appointees who benefited from his patronage helped sustain his influence. That network is now weakening.

Many of his closest political allies have already moved away.

For now, one thin thread of hope remains—the case pending before the Supreme Court.

But even a favourable verdict may not answer the larger question confronting Sher Bahadur Deuba.

The question is no longer whether he can reclaim a position he once held. It is whether the political era in which that position mattered has already passed.

title.rendered: Nepal’s politics has changed. Its political culture has not

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Had Sher Bahadur Deuba arrived to occupy the chief guest’s chair at the Nepali Congress general convention, Gagan Thapa might have had one less thing to worry about.

As he began addressing the gathering, the newly elected Nepali Congress president briefly appeared unsure about whom to acknowledge first. Then he seemed to remember that he was no longer simply one of the party’s leaders. He was its president, and the responsibility of managing the moment was now his.

The small hesitation was symbolic of a larger transition underway in Nepali politics.

Thapa was presiding over a Nepali Congress convention at which the party’s old leadership was conspicuous by its absence, while leaders of newer political forces were on the stage questioning the party’s legacy, its relevance and even its claim over its own voters.

Rastriya Swatantra Party President Rabi Lamichhane, who spoke before Thapa, captured that tension with a carefully chosen line.

“You have become party president at the age of 50. If you had taken the inspiration to become president at 40, I might have become a Nepali Congress member too,” he said.

The remark was delivered almost poetically, and Lamichhane returned to the phrase several times. It was both a compliment and a provocation.

He was speaking at the convention of a party that had dominated Nepali politics for decades, while leading a party that has emerged as one of the strongest challengers to that political order.

Lamichhane then offered perhaps the most telling assessment of Nepali Congress.

“Nepali Congress’s strength is its history. But its weakness is also its history.”

There was little need to explain the contradiction.

Nepali Congress’s history is inseparable from Nepal’s democratic struggles. But the same history carries the weight of its years in power, its compromises, its failures and the public frustrations that have helped create space for parties such as the RSP.

Lamichhane pushed that point further by telling the Congress gathering that some of those present may have voted for the RSP’s election symbol, the bell.

The message was clear. No political party owns its voters.

If a party does not perform, voters can leave.

That was more than a jab at Nepali Congress. It was a statement of the political philosophy that helped bring the RSP into existence in the first place.

Yet Lamichhane’s speech also revealed the limits of the new politics he represents.

He was at a Congress convention, criticising an old party for its history, while leading a party that is itself now part of the establishment. His remark, “Jai Nepal. But not for the party, for the country,” was another attempt to draw a line between national politics and partisan politics.

But the line is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain.

Political movements that begin by challenging the establishment eventually acquire establishments of their own.

That may explain some of the unusual chemistry between Lamichhane and Thapa.

The two have been allies at times and fierce opponents at others. Their disagreements, particularly during the cooperative fraud controversy and its political fallout, were public and bitter.

Yet there remains a sense of familiarity between them.

Lamichhane has previously pushed Thapa to take a more assertive leadership role. At that time, Thapa was not ready to make that leap, and Lamichhane himself had not yet decided to establish a new political party.

Now the political landscape has changed dramatically.

Thapa leads the Congress. Lamichhane leads the RSP. Balendra Shah, the RSP-backed prime minister, occupies the centre of government.

And yet neither Thapa nor Lamichhane appears entirely comfortable with where they have arrived.

Nepali Congress has lost electoral ground despite its enormous political legacy. The RSP has demonstrated extraordinary electoral strength but has also become part of the very system it once challenged. Lamichhane has helped bring a prime minister to power but does not himself hold the government.

Their exchange at the Congress convention therefore felt less like a battle between two political winners and more like two leaders negotiating the pressures created by their own success.

Thapa’s response to Lamichhane made that particularly clear.

When Lamichhane suggested that some people at the Congress convention had voted for the RSP, Thapa reminded him that Congress had also sent many people into the RSP—including office-bearers and lawmakers—and had, in his words, trained them.

It was a clever retort, but hardly a knockout blow.

Neither man truly defeated the other.

Instead, their exchange exposed the insecurity running beneath both political projects.

That insecurity was also visible in the symbolism of Khulamanch.

Thapa has repeatedly used the open ground as a metaphor for the kind of politics he believes Nepal needs. Khulamanch has historically been a place where anger, dissent, questions and political demands could be expressed openly.

His criticism of Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s absence from Parliament was therefore not merely about attendance.

For Thapa, a Parliament that does not have the prime minister appearing before lawmakers cannot truly function as an open political forum. The absence becomes symbolic of a wider closing of political space.

He extended that argument to political parties themselves.

Questions must be allowed. Leaders must be challenged. Party members should not lose their membership simply because they disagree with their leaders.

In other words, democracy cannot be demanded from the state while being denied inside political parties.

That argument is particularly significant coming from a new Congress president who has inherited one of Nepal’s oldest political organisations.

Thapa’s speech also carried a personal dimension that was less visible in his earlier appearances.

When he recalled the two Congress workers swept away in the Rasuwa floods, his voice became emotional. For a moment, the political contest disappeared and the new Congress president sounded less like a party leader delivering a carefully managed address and more like a politician confronting the human cost of the country’s continuing crises.

Lamichhane, meanwhile, took a different opportunity.

Thapa had strongly criticised the prime minister for not attending Parliament. Lamichhane was even more pointed about Deuba’s absence from the Congress convention.

His message was that the absence of one or several individuals should not determine the fate of a political institution.

For Thapa, that argument may have offered some relief. The Congress convention did not collapse because Deuba was absent.

But it also exposed the irony of the moment.

The RSP was born by questioning the relevance of old political leadership. Yet its own rise has now placed it in a position where its leaders must answer questions about institutional responsibility, government performance and the conduct of power.

This is perhaps where Pushpa Kamal Dahal “Prachanda’s” intervention becomes interesting.

Prachanda looked back at the political journeys of leaders who had once served under him and spoke of “breaking the pattern.”

“There was a time when I used to break the pattern. The kind of pattern-breaking I used to talk about has been done by Gaganji. Now Ravi-ji should do it too,” he said.

The phrase was deliberately vague.

What exactly is the next pattern Lamichhane is supposed to break?

Prachanda did not say.

Perhaps the answer is power. Lamichhane helped disrupt the old party system but has yet to translate his personal political influence into formal power within government.

But there was another irony in Prachanda’s call.

A leader who once built his political identity around breaking established political patterns was now asking the leaders of other parties to do the breaking.

That may say as much about the present state of his own party as it does about Congress or the RSP.

Prachanda also urged Thapa not to leave behind those who had been separated from him, telling him to move forward while taking them along.

His emphasis on respecting history was understandable. But political change has always involved questioning history.

Every major political movement in Nepal has, in one way or another, challenged the order that came before it.

Prachanda himself knows that better than most.

The question now is whether the new generation of politicians will merely inherit that history or genuinely challenge it.

That question was also present in UML General Secretary Shankar Pokharel’s remarks.

Pokharel recalled the days when he and other student leaders stood against the Rana regime, the Panchayat system and King Gyanendra’s rule.

“We stood together against the Rana regime, the Panchayat and Gyanendra’s rule. Now is the time for us to stand together again so that we do not allow frustrated young people to become even more frustrated,” he said.

It was an appeal for political cooperation at a time when the traditional parties are under increasing pressure from younger voters.

But Pokharel also acknowledged that simply changing faces would not be enough.

“Simply changing faces will not solve anything. The need for a new political revolution still remains,” he said.

That may have been one of the most important lines delivered at the Congress convention.

Because the political debate in Nepal is no longer simply about who should lead Congress, who should lead the RSP or who should become prime minister.

It is increasingly about whether changing political faces can produce a fundamentally different political system.

Congress is attempting to renew itself under Thapa without abandoning its history. The RSP is attempting to remain a force of disruption while exercising the responsibilities of power. The UML is arguing for cooperation while confronting the demand for generational change. And Prachanda, once the great disruptor himself, is urging others to break the patterns that he once claimed as his own.

The contradictions are obvious. But perhaps that is precisely what made the Congress convention revealing. The speeches were full of history, rivalry, nostalgia, criticism and political theatre. Beneath them, however, was a common recognition that Nepal’s political order is no longer as stable as it once appeared.

The old parties cannot rely on history alone. The new parties cannot rely on novelty alone. And changing faces, as Pokharel himself acknowledged, may not be enough. The real test is whether any of them can change the political habits that produced the frustration in the first place.

title.rendered: Gandaki Chief Minister Pandey to run for Nepali Congress vice-president

content.rendered:
Pokhara, October 5

Gandaki Province Chief Minister and Nepali Congress central member Surendra Raj Pandey has announced his candidacy for vice-president at the party’s 15th General Convention.

Pandey was previously close to outgoing president Sher Bahadur Deuba and vice-president Purna Bahadur Khadka. After the special convention, however, he renewed his active party membership under the leadership of president Gagan Thapa.

He joined Thapa’s camp after the Election Commission and the Supreme Court recognised Thapa’s leadership.

Announcing his candidacy, Pandey said he would move forward with unity within the party, a stronger organisation and ideological clarity.

title.rendered: Fire breaks out at scrap shop in Suryabinayak

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

A fire has broken out in Kapali Tole, Suryabinayak Municipality-8, Bhaktapur.

According to the Police Circle, Jagati, Bhaktapur, the fire started at around 6:30 am today at a scrap shop run by Nawaraj Bhatta.

DSP Deepak Karki said the fire may have been caused by a short circuit in the electrical wiring.

“The scrap shop is built of tin sheets and iron, and the information is that the fire started from a short circuit in the electrical wire. Further investigation into the incident is under way,” he said.

Police and locals have worked together to put out the fire.

title.rendered: Chitwan National Park preparing to reopen jeep safari from Friday

content.rendered:
Chitawan, October 5

Chitwan National Park is preparing to reopen the jungle safari, which was closed inside the park because of the monsoon, from Friday, October 9.

The park had closed the jeep safari from July 1. It is now rushing to repair roads damaged by monsoon flash floods and clear fallen trees.

Floods in August damaged the jungle safari routes, which delayed the reopening, said Abinash Thapamagar, the park’s information officer.

“We had planned to start the jeep safari in the second week of Asoj, but heavy rain at that time sent floods through various streams and rivers inside the park and damaged the routes. We are repairing them,” Thapamagar said. “We are now working to resume from October 7.”

The flood in the Riu Khola in August did the most damage to the route to the park’s Tiger Tops area, Thapamagar said. Work is underway to prepare the route by laying gravel.

Although the jeep safari is closed inside the park, jeep and elephant safaris have continued as usual in the buffer zone and community forests.

Elephant safaris are not allowed inside the park at other times of the year. Jungle walks continue even during the three monsoon months when the jeep safari is closed.

The park earns tens of millions of rupees from the jeep safari every year.

Most foreign tourists visiting the park take the jeep safari, and it is just as popular with Nepalis.

Data show that more than 200,000 domestic and foreign tourists visit Chitwan National Park a year on average.

The park charges Rs 5,000 per jeep. Entry fees are Rs 2,000 for foreign tourists, Rs 1,000 for tourists from SAARC countries and Rs 150 for Nepalis.

Thirty jeeps from the Sauraha area, 10 from Kasara, seven from Meghauli and five from Amaltari run inside the park. Each jeep carries up to 10 people.

title.rendered: VIP prisoners being pushed out of Dillibazar jail

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Businessman Deepak Bhatta, held at Nakkhu jail, has been transferred to Sindhupalchok jail. Nakkhu sent Bhatta to Sindhupalchok on Saturday following a letter from the Department of Prison Management.

Bhatta was arrested and prosecuted for offences under the money laundering law, the Insurance Act and securities law. He was sent to jail over the money laundering charge.

A bench of Kathmandu District Court judge Shiva Prasad Acharya, had ordered Bhatta released on bail of Rs 15 million for the Insurance Act offence and Rs 10 million for the securities offence. But he remained in jail after the Special Court ordered him to be held in custody on the money laundering charge.

He was first sent to Dillibazar jail, considered to be a facility with better amenities. Bhatta and Sulabh Agrawal of Shankar Group were remanded in a case filed over money laundering and related offences. The case against Bhatta puts the amount involved at Rs 26.63 billion, and the case against Agrawal at Rs 25.59 billion.

Following the Special Court’s order, they were sent to jail on June 17. Dillibazar is usually the first choice of VIPs and high-ranking figures remanded in custody pending trial. They often ask the judge, through their lawyers, to be sent there.

Bhatta and Agrawal were also sent to Dillibazar, known as the jail where VIPs are held, probably at their own request. Once a person is remanded, prisoners are generally sent to the jail of their choice where possible, and Bhatta and Agrawal ended up at Dillibazar on that basis.

Within 15 days of Bhatt’s arrival at Dillibazar, however, he was transferred out. On that occasion too, he was moved to Nakkhu jail in Lalitpur after a sudden letter from the Department of Prison Management.

Bhatta was moved to Nakkhu overnight on July 4. Another VIP, Pradip Adhikari, then director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, was transferred at the same time. Adhikari was moved to Central Jail, Sundhara. Both men had chosen to go to Dillibazar.

Jail officials say prisoners are crammed into other jails, while Dillibazar has open spaces, which makes it a popular choice. They claim facilities are the same wherever a prisoner is held.

Open space, easy access for visitors and its location in the heart of Kathmandu have also made Dillibazar the jail of choice for prisoners.

Former Armed Police Force DIG Ranjan Koirala spent eight years and six months in Dillibazar after being sentenced to life imprisonment with confiscation of all property for murdering his wife. He was released from Dillibazar on July 23, 2020, after a Supreme Court bench of then Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana and Justice Tej Bahadur KC overturned the district court’s verdict and reduced the sentence.

Koirala was arrested again after that order was reversed and the district court’s verdict upheld. He asked, through his lawyer, to be sent to Dillibazar, but was sent to Sundhara jail instead.

Prisoners who attract controversy in custody or are reported to be pulling strings are now being moved out of Dillibazar. Koirala, who had earlier stayed there, was not given Dillibazar when he asked for it later. He was sent to Sundhara jail.

Another VIP, Pradip Adhikari, also ended up at Sundhara. Bhatta went to Sindhupalchok via Nakkhu.

Past inmates of Dillibazar include former Speaker Krishna Bahadur Mahara, former ministers Shyam Sundar Gupta and Khum Bahadur Khadka, former lawmaker Balkrishna Dhungel, former Inspectors General of Police Om Bikram Rana and Hem Bahadur Gurung, Durga Prasai and Deepak Manange.

Several VIPs are still at Dillibazar. They include former Madhesh Province chief Rajesh Ahiraj, CPN-UML leader and former minister Top Bahadur Rayamajhi, and former lawmaker Ichha Raj Tamang. Sunil Poudel, Bikal Poudel and former Civil Aviation Authority director general Sanjiv Gautam are also still there.

title.rendered: Kathmandu Climate Week concludes with 16-point call for climate justice

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Kathmandu Climate Week 2026 concluded on Sunday with a declaration setting out 16 commitments and calling on the international community and the Government of Nepal to take “immediate, effective, and results-oriented action” on climate justice, the organisers said.

The three-day conference ran from October 2 to 4 under the theme “Climate Justice for Climate Resilience: From Local Action to Global Climate Diplomacy.”

According to the organisers, it was meant to bring local experiences, national policy priorities, and international climate diplomacy onto one platform.

Diksha Thapa Magar presented the “Kathmandu Call for Climate Justice” on behalf of the organising committee.

Opening and sessions

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal gave the inaugural address on October 2. The opening session featured a dialogue between children and young people affected by the Rasuwa Himalayan Tsunami and representatives of various organisations.

The second day had 29 thematic sessions and three outdoor sessions at venues across Kathmandu. Topics included loss and damage, climate diplomacy, research and policy, the circular economy, and mobilising private-sector climate finance. Participants also discussed the impacts of the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Himalayan Tsunami on affected communities.

Participants included scientists, researchers, parliamentarians, policymakers, senior government officials, civil society representatives, children and young people, Indigenous Peoples, Dalits, women, sexual and gender minorities, persons with disabilities, private-sector leaders and representatives of frontline communities.

Concluding day

Two high-level sessions were held on the final day. The special session on climate justice featured Member of the House of Representatives Dhananjay Regmi and Ganesh BK, a member of the International Relations and Tourism Committee. It was moderated by Apekshya Subedi.

A second session, “Amplifying Nepal’s Voice for Climate Justice through Action and Climate Diplomacy,” was facilitated by Sushmita Mishra. Speakers were Member of Parliament Anushka Shrestha; Abhishek Shrestha, adviser to the Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment; former Foreign Minister Dr Bimala Rai Paudyal; and media entrepreneur Samriddhi Gyawali.

At the closing session, Dr Rajendra Prasad Mishra, Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment, stressed the role of multi-stakeholder collaboration in strengthening Nepal’s climate policymaking and global representation.

Kalpana Tamang, a young girl from an area affected by the Rasuwa Himalayan Tsunami, called for justice and spoke about the experiences and demands of communities bearing the consequences of climate-related disasters.

Plans

Advocate Arnab Chaudhary, a member of the organising committee, said future editions would broaden the scope of sessions and deepen partnerships with government bodies and regional institutions. Organiser Binod Parajuli said the long-term aim is to expand Kathmandu Climate Week to the regional level and establish Kathmandu as a leading regional hub for climate advocacy and action.

As a continuation of the conference, a public screening of the film Elephants in the Fog is scheduled for October 5.

The event was jointly organised by Creasion, Climate Risk and Resilience Lab, All In Foundation, Nepal Climate Centre, Nepal Peacebuilding Initiative, Institute for Rural Development, Wind Power Nepal, Nepal Bar Association, Youth Alliance for Environment and Dignity Initiative, among others.

title.rendered: Absconding accused in banking offence case Dipendra Ale arrested

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Dipendra Ale, who had been absconding in a banking offence case, has been arrested. He was taken into custody about nine months after the District Court Kathmandu granted permission to arrest him.

Ale was arrested on Sunday while hiding in Mandikatar, said Inspector Devi Ram Bhandari of the Metropolitan Police Circle, Singha Durbar.

The District Court Kathmandu issued the arrest permission on January 14. Ale had been absconding since the arrest warrant was issued.

Ale had taken Rs 500,000 from the victim, a woman, through a bank account, promising to send her to Europe. He deceived her by taking her as far as India instead.

The woman first filed a complaint against Ale with the Nepal Police Human Trafficking Investigation Bureau. After the Bureau summoned and questioned him, Ale gave the victim a cheque for the amount he had taken. The cheque bounced, and she then filed a complaint under the banking offence law. The court granted the arrest permission on the basis of that complaint.

Ale had remained in hiding after the court granted the arrest permission.

According to Inspector Bhandari, further investigation against Ale is ongoing.

title.rendered: Rainfall to increase in the coming days

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 5

Although the monsoon has begun withdrawing from Nepal, meteorologists say rainfall activity will increase in the coming days. They say rain is likely to be somewhat heavier from today until the day after tomorrow.

According to Dr Binod Pokharel, associate professor at Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, the monsoon system remains over eastern Nepal, and moisture-laden air is arriving from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, which is why rainfall activity is set to rise.

“Going by the current situation, rain is likely in many places until roughly the day before Ghatasthapana of Dashain,” Pokharel said. He expects rainfall to ease somewhat on Ghatasthapana itself.

Madhavi Sigdel, a meteorologist at the Meteorological Forecasting Division of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, also said scattered rainfall will continue in various parts of the country from today.

The division issues forecasts for only three days at a time, and Sigdel said rain will continue throughout the next three days. She added that rainfall is likely to increase particularly in the western region in the coming days.

Rain likely today too

Meteorologists say rain is possible again today. According to Sigdel, moderate rain is likely this afternoon in a few places across the hilly and mountainous regions, including the Kathmandu Valley, and in some parts of the Tarai.

Pokharel said many places in the hilly region could see rain on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, the day after tomorrow, rain is likely in even more places from west to east. Pokharel said one or two places in Sudurpaschim could also see heavy rainfall on the same day.

Rain from Karnali to Koshi in the past 24 hours

Rain fell across the country from Karnali to Koshi in the past 24 hours. Moderate to heavy rain was recorded in some places in Koshi, Madhesh, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces in particular.

Rain has also been falling for the past hour in Bargadha in Bardiya, Simalpani in Arghakhanchi and Gadhawa in Dang, all in Lumbini Province.

According to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, skies are generally cloudy in Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces, and partly cloudy in Madhesh, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces. The forecasting division said fog has also set in at some locations.

The division’s bulletin says moderate rainfall is likely in a few places in the Tarai areas of Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki, and in one or two places in the Tarai areas of Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces.

title.rendered: Nepal’s C-section generation is growing. What does it mean?

content.rendered:
I am the father of two children. My elder child was born through vaginal delivery, while my younger child was delivered by Caesarean section.

Watching both children grow has made me think more closely about childbirth than I might otherwise have done. The two experiences were very different, but both ultimately brought home the same lesson: the way a child is born is not simply a personal choice. It is also a matter of medical necessity, access to care, health-system capacity and, increasingly, the way families and health providers understand childbirth.

In Nepal, Caesarean section rates have risen sharply over the past decade. National survey data indicate that the proportion of births delivered by C-section increased from 10.2 percent in 2016 to 18.2 percent in 2022. Data from the Routine Health Management Information System also indicate a substantial increase in C-section deliveries in recent years.

The increase is not, in itself, a problem.

Caesarean delivery is one of modern medicine’s most important life-saving interventions. When complications make vaginal delivery unsafe, timely access to surgery can save the lives of both mother and child.

The challenge is finding the balance between ensuring that every woman who needs a C-section can get one and avoiding unnecessary surgery when it is not medically indicated.

That distinction matters for Nepal’s health system.

More women are giving birth in health facilities

Nepal has made considerable progress in maternal and newborn health.

Each year, more than 600,000 women become pregnant, and nearly 91 percent of births now take place in health facilities. Yet significant disparities remain. In Madhesh Province, for example, the proportion of births occurring in health facilities is lower than the national average, while women from the poorest households continue to face greater barriers to accessing institutional delivery.

There are also important differences in newborn care. Only around 38 percent of babies are breastfed within the first hour of birth.

Nepal’s progress in reducing maternal mortality has been supported by the expansion of emergency obstetric and neonatal care, including through the Aama Programme and the training and deployment of skilled birth attendants. Greater access to C-section services has been an important part of this progress, particularly for women experiencing high-risk pregnancies or obstetric complications.

The policy challenge now is different.

Nepal needs to ensure that the expansion of C-section services does not turn into a system where surgical delivery becomes the default option for women who could safely give birth vaginally.

The public-private divide

Government-supported Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal Care services are now available through facilities across the country, while a large and growing private sector provides maternity services, particularly in urban areas.

Research suggests that women giving birth in private hospitals in several provinces, including Koshi, Bagmati, Madhesh and Lumbini, are more likely to have a C-section than those delivering in public facilities.

There are many possible reasons.

Women and families may perceive private hospitals as offering better or more responsive care. Private facilities may have greater availability of specialists, operating theatres and diagnostic services. Differences in staffing, referral systems and the perceived quality of care can all influence where women choose to give birth and how childbirth is managed.

But the difference in C-section rates between facilities deserves closer examination.

It is important to distinguish between medically necessary C-sections and procedures that may be avoidable. Without reliable data on the indications for each procedure, however, it is difficult to determine how much of the increase reflects genuine medical need and how much reflects differences in clinical practice, patient preference or institutional incentives.

That is an area where Nepal needs better evidence rather than assumptions.

The financial cost of Caesarean delivery

A C-section is also considerably more expensive than an uncomplicated vaginal delivery.

During a recent visit to Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital in Kathmandu, I observed a family spending more than NPR 30,000 on a Caesarean delivery. Similar procedures in private hospitals can cost considerably more.

Even a rough estimate illustrates the scale of the issue.

If around one-quarter of births were delivered by C-section and more than half of those procedures took place in private hospitals, the combined annual expenditure could run into billions of rupees. The exact figure requires more systematic costing, including differences between public and private facilities and between uncomplicated and complicated procedures.

For families, particularly those with limited incomes, these expenses can be substantial.

For the health system, increasing reliance on surgical delivery also means greater demand for operating theatres, anaesthesia, surgical teams, medicines, blood supplies, hospital beds and post-operative care.

The financial consequences therefore extend well beyond the cost of the operation itself.

When one C-section leads to another

The consequences of rising C-section rates do not necessarily end with one delivery.

A previous Caesarean can affect decisions in subsequent pregnancies. Depending on the circumstances of the previous surgery and the woman’s current pregnancy, vaginal birth after Caesarean, or VBAC, may be an option. But many women ultimately undergo repeat C-sections.

This can create a cycle in which an increase in primary C-sections contributes to more repeat procedures in the future.

A 2018 study at Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital found that elective C-sections accounted for 25.6 percent of all C-section deliveries during the study period. More than two-thirds of those elective procedures were reported to have occurred because women declined vaginal birth after a previous C-section.

This finding points to an important part of the conversation.

A woman’s preference matters. But preference is shaped by information, previous experiences, fear of labour pain, advice from health professionals, family expectations and perceptions about the safety of different modes of delivery.

Women need to be able to make these decisions with accurate information and appropriate clinical counselling.

What does a C-section mean for the child?

There is no simple answer to whether vaginal birth or Caesarean delivery is “better” for every child.

A planned C-section can avoid some complications associated with difficult labour and may be medically preferable in certain pregnancies. But it is major abdominal surgery and carries risks for the mother and newborn.

For newborns, planned C-section can be associated with a higher risk of certain short-term respiratory problems, particularly when performed before the onset of labour and without a medical indication.

Research has also found associations between Caesarean birth and some longer-term outcomes, including childhood obesity, asthma and certain immune-related conditions. However, these relationships are complex. It is difficult to separate the effects of Caesarean delivery itself from the medical or social conditions that led to the procedure in the first place.

This distinction is important.

We should not frighten parents by suggesting that a C-section automatically causes poor health outcomes. Nor should we present vaginal birth as universally safer.

The appropriate mode of delivery depends on the individual pregnancy and the circumstances at the time.

The goal should be safe birth, not a particular birth method at all costs.

Choice must come with information

Around the world, Caesarean rates are rising. The World Health Organization has warned that both underuse and overuse can occur within the same health system — some women do not have timely access to life-saving surgery, while others undergo C-sections without a clear medical indication.

Nepal faces both challenges.

In some parts of the country, women still struggle to reach facilities capable of providing emergency obstetric care. In urban areas, meanwhile, the concern may be the opposite: whether surgical intervention is being used more often than necessary.

This makes the question of choice particularly important.

A woman should be able to discuss the benefits and risks of vaginal birth and Caesarean delivery with a qualified health professional. Fear of labour pain, previous birth experiences and concerns about complications should be addressed through counselling and childbirth preparation rather than allowing fear alone to determine the mode of delivery.

Family members also matter. In Nepal, husbands and other relatives can have considerable influence over decisions about where and how women give birth. They therefore need access to the same accurate information.

Informed choice cannot be the responsibility of the woman alone.

Reducing unnecessary C-sections

Nepal does not need to reduce C-sections simply for the sake of reducing the national rate.

It needs to reduce unnecessary C-sections while ensuring that every woman who needs one can receive it quickly.

That requires action at several levels.

First, preventing unnecessary primary C-sections should be a priority. Every first C-section can influence the options available in future pregnancies.

Second, hospitals should strengthen clinical audit systems. Reviewing the indications for primary C-sections and providing feedback to clinicians can help identify variations in practice and encourage adherence to evidence-based guidelines.

Third, where clinically appropriate and safely supported, hospitals should offer women the option of vaginal birth after Caesarean. VBAC can reduce the need for repeat surgery for appropriately selected women.

Fourth, Nepal should strengthen midwifery-led care and ensure that women with low-risk pregnancies are not unnecessarily medicalised. Better-designed birthing spaces, continuous support during labour, appropriate labour-monitoring tools and reliable referral mechanisms can all contribute to safer maternity care.

Finally, women and families need balanced information.

They should understand both the benefits and risks of vaginal birth and Caesarean delivery. Counselling should address concerns about pain, complications and previous birth experiences without presenting either option as inherently superior in every situation.

The question Nepal needs to ask

The rise of C-sections is not simply a story about doctors, hospitals or mothers making the “wrong” choice.

It is a story about a health system in transition.

More women are reaching health facilities. Emergency obstetric care is more available. Private hospitals have expanded. Families have changing expectations. Medical technology has improved. At the same time, Nepal continues to face major inequalities in access to quality maternal care.

All of these factors are shaping how children are born.

As a father of two children who experienced both vaginal and Caesarean delivery, I do not believe one experience should be held up as the correct model for everyone.

What matters is that women have access to safe, respectful and evidence-based maternity care, wherever they live and whatever their economic circumstances.

Nepal has spent decades working to ensure that women who need Caesarean delivery can get it.

The next challenge is more nuanced.

We must make sure that every C-section is driven by the best interests of the mother and child — not by lack of alternatives, inadequate information, institutional habit or financial incentives.

The goal should never be fewer Caesareans simply because the number looks high.

The goal should be the right care, at the right time, for every mother and every child.
