title.rendered: Why climate security must matter to Nepal’s diplomacy

content.rendered:
The Trishuli valley has been a trade and pilgrimage route for centuries, linking Nepal with China. On August 26, it became the path of one of the most devastating mountain disasters in recent years.

A rapid slope failure involving a glacier near the Nepal-China border triggered an ice-rock avalanche, sending water, ice and debris down the Lhende Khola and into the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. The resulting flood travelled nearly 100 kilometres, damaging communities and critical infrastructure, including roads and hydropower facilities.

Nepal then received little respite. In late September, persistent heavy rain triggered floods and landslides across the country, killing at least 12 people between September 24 and 27, with more people missing and thousands affected.

The pattern is difficult to ignore. A country that has contributed little to historical global greenhouse gas emissions is confronting hazards that are becoming more complex, interconnected and difficult to manage.

This is where science meets politics. The immediate disaster may be geological and hydrological, but the ability to prepare for the next one depends heavily on cooperation among governments.

A warning from the mountains

Scientists are still examining exactly how the August disaster unfolded. USGS describes it as a catastrophic debris flow and flood likely triggered by rapid slope failure involving a glacier. ICIMOD has referred to it as an ice-rock avalanche originating on Langtang Lirung. The event was powerful enough to generate seismic energy equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake.

The precise contribution of climate change to this individual event requires careful scientific attribution. A single disaster rarely has a single cause.

But the broader context is clear. The Hindu Kush Himalaya is warming, glaciers are changing and permafrost and mountain slopes are becoming increasingly unstable. The August disaster is therefore part of a wider risk landscape that Nepal and other Himalayan countries must prepare for.

The lesson is straightforward: preparing for one predictable hazard at a time is no longer enough. High-mountain disasters can be compound, cascading and transboundary.

A glacier does not recognise a political boundary. When ice, rock and water move across a frontier, neither should disaster preparedness.

Climate security is also diplomacy

The international environment in which Nepal must seek assistance is increasingly complicated. Wars, trade disputes, sanctions, energy insecurity and geopolitical rivalry compete for governments’ attention. Development and climate priorities can easily be pushed down the agenda when security concerns dominate.

The consequences are practical.

Mountain early-warning systems require satellite imagery, glacier monitoring, seismic information, weather forecasting and rapid communication across borders. Suspicion or a lack of institutional cooperation can prevent or delay the sharing of information. In the mountains, hours can matter.

Climate finance faces a similar challenge. Vulnerable countries need resources for adaptation and loss and damage, but competing global priorities can make those resources harder to secure.

This is why climate diplomacy cannot be treated as separate from security diplomacy. Climate-related disasters can destroy infrastructure, disrupt energy systems, displace communities and place additional pressure on already fragile institutions.

What Nepal and the Himalaya should do

First, build a Himalayan hazard compact.

Nepal and China already cooperate on trade, transit and hydropower. Disaster-risk reduction should become another area of practical cooperation. This could include real-time data exchange, glacier and slope monitoring, joint early-warning protocols and coordinated search and rescue.

India, Bhutan, Pakistan and other countries across the Hindu Kush Himalaya should be part of a wider regional effort. Institutions such as ICIMOD can provide scientific expertise and a platform for cooperation.

Disaster management is one of the few areas where countries with difficult political relationships can find common ground. It can also build the trust needed for wider cooperation.

Second, treat early-warning systems as essential infrastructure.

The August disaster demonstrated the importance of understanding what is happening high in the mountains before hazards reach populated valleys. Closing the gap between observation and action requires sensors, satellite analysis, trained local observers, community alert systems and clear evacuation protocols.

Villages need drills, not just dashboards.

The cost of an effective early-warning network is small compared with the economic and human cost of a destroyed valley.

Third, rebuild for the hazards of the future.

The August disaster damaged roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and telecommunications infrastructure. Nepal and other Himalayan countries depend heavily on hydropower and mountain connectivity for development, yet these systems are highly exposed to floods, landslides and other cascading hazards.

Future projects should incorporate hazard mapping into site selection, strengthen design standards and account for changing climatic and geological risks. Reconstruction financing should prioritise resilience rather than simply replacing what was destroyed.

Fourth, turn climate justice into a concrete diplomatic agenda.

Nepal has a strong case for greater international support because its contribution to global emissions is small while its exposure to climate and mountain hazards is high.

But the argument must be backed by evidence, financing proposals and alliances.

The International Court of Justice’s 2025 advisory opinion on climate change confirmed that states have obligations under international law relating to climate harm, environmental protection and international cooperation.

Nepal should work with other mountain and least-developed countries to push for stronger support for mountain adaptation, glacier monitoring and early-warning systems.

COP31, scheduled for November 9–20 in Antalya, Türkiye, provides another opportunity to put these concerns on the international agenda. Nepal should arrive with evidence of losses and damages, specific funding requests and a coordinated position with other Himalayan countries.

Fifth, keep climate cooperation alive despite geopolitical tensions.

Nepal and other climate-vulnerable countries cannot afford to wait for global political tensions to disappear.

Regional data-sharing arrangements, bilateral resilience funds, technology partnerships and other smaller-scale agreements can move forward even when larger international negotiations are slow. Such initiatives should complement, rather than replace, the multilateral climate system.

Nepal must also put its own house in order

Diplomacy will only be credible if Nepal strengthens its domestic disaster-management capacity.

Disaster agencies need stable funding, technical expertise and clear authority across federal, provincial and local levels. Nepal needs a well-equipped national institution with strong scientific capacity, adequate personnel and resources for both disaster response and research.

Land-use regulations must also be enforced along river corridors where settlements and infrastructure have expanded into high-risk areas. Local governments need personnel capable of interpreting hazard maps and using them in planning decisions.

Transparency matters too. How relief and reconstruction funds are managed will influence public trust as well as the confidence of international partners.

A government that demonstrates credible stewardship at home strengthens its case abroad.

The mountains will not wait

There is a temptation, at a time of war, economic uncertainty and geopolitical rivalry, to treat climate adaptation as a problem that can be addressed when international conditions improve.

Nepal’s experience should make that approach difficult to sustain.

The glacier did not wait for a peace settlement. The heavy rains did not check the diplomatic calendar. Floods and landslides do not wait for governments to resolve their differences.

The real test of international cooperation will not be the number of speeches delivered at the next climate summit. It will be whether Himalayan valleys have functioning early-warning systems before the next monsoon; whether critical data can cross borders without political delay; whether reconstruction finance reaches affected communities; and whether the countries of the Himalaya are working together to manage risks they cannot manage alone.

Nepal has told the world what it is losing. The mountains have made their argument in the clearest language possible.

What remains is for governments to listen—and to act before the next mountain moves.

title.rendered: Nepal worships animals but still has no law to protect them

content.rendered:
Every year on October 4, the world marks World Animal Day. It is a day to celebrate animals. It should also be a day to remember how much of our own story they carry, and to ask what we owe them in return.

Long before we built cities, wrote laws or drew borders, we shared our fires with animals. Wolves that drifted towards human camps became our first domesticated companions at least 15,000 years ago, before we had even learned to farm. Around 10,000 years ago, goats, sheep and cattle turned wandering foragers into settled farmers, and with them came villages, surplus and civilisation itself. Horses, donkeys and, on the high plateaus, yaks carried people, goods and ideas across mountains and continents.

The relationship did not only change how we lived. It changed who we are. Many human populations evolved the ability to digest milk well into adulthood, a genetic trace of thousands of years spent alongside cattle, goats and buffalo. Dogs, in turn, evolved a small facial muscle that lets them raise their inner eyebrows, the “puppy eyes” that wolves barely have, and extra copies of a gene that helps them digest the starchy leftovers of our meals. We did not simply use animals. We evolved together.

Nowhere is this clearer than in Nepal. The ox ploughs the terraced hillside. The buffalo feeds the household. The mule and the donkey carry bricks, rice and gas cylinders to places no road can reach. The chauri and the yak make life possible in the high Himalaya. And the dog waits at the doorstep of almost every home.

Gods who ride animals

Our faith knows this too. In the Hindu tradition that shapes so much of Nepali life, almost every deity is accompanied by an animal. Ganesh rides a mouse. Shiva has Nandi, the bull, who sits facing his shrine at Pashupatinath. Durga rides a lion. Vishnu flies on Garuda. Saraswati has her swan, Lakshmi her owl, Kartikeya his peacock, Indra the elephant Airavata, Yama the buffalo. Bhairav is followed by a dog. During Tihar we worship the crow, the dog, the cow and the ox, each on its own day.

Have we ever stopped to wonder why? Why would the divine choose to be carried by a mouse, a bull or a bird? Perhaps it was never only symbolism. Perhaps it was a lesson: that even the gods do not stand apart from the living world, that power is meant to be shared, and that the world belongs to all who live in it. Read this way, our traditions describe an ecocentric world, one where humans are part of a web of life and not its owners, and where loving and conserving the diversity of nature is a sacred duty.

Buddhism, born here in Lumbini, takes the same truth further and makes it a path. The Buddha’s teaching begins with the precept to avoid harming living beings and asks us to extend loving-kindness to all sentient beings, not just to our own kind. The Jataka tales tell of the Buddha’s earlier lives as a hare, a monkey king and a deer. At Namo Buddha, a short drive from Kathmandu, we remember the story of a prince who gave his own body to a starving tigress so that she and her cubs might live. Emperor Ashoka, inspired by these teachings, recorded in his edicts that medical care should be provided for animals as well as for people.

Compassion for animals is not a foreign idea that Nepal must import. It is written into our temples, our festivals and our scriptures.

The pyramid we chose

And yet, somewhere along the way, we chose a different picture of the world. Instead of a circle of life, we built a pyramid, with humans at the very top ruling over animals, plants and the rest of the natural world beneath them. This is anthropocentrism: the belief that humans are the centre and measure of all things, and that everything else exists to serve us.

It is an egocentric illusion, and it shapes far more than our attitudes. It shapes our economy, our institutions and our laws. In the pyramid, a buffalo is not a being who can feel pain, fear and comfort. It is a unit of milk or meat. A donkey is a load capacity. A dog is a nuisance or a possession. Once animals are seen only as resources, their suffering becomes invisible, or, at best, a cost to be managed.

We garland dogs during Kukur Tihar and then look away when they are poisoned, beaten or left to die on the same streets the next week. We bow to Nandi at the temple gate and say nothing about bullocks overloaded on the highway or buffalo packed into trucks bound for slaughter with no water and no rest. The gap between what we worship and what we permit has never been wider.

An economy carried on animals’ backs

This gap is all the more striking because Nepal depends on animals so heavily.

The livestock sector contributes roughly 13 per cent of Nepal’s national GDP and around 24 per cent of agricultural GDP. Against a national economy of about USD 49 billion, that is roughly USD 6.4 billion, or more than NPR 850 billion, generated every year by animals.

Animal-related exports crossed NPR 15 billion in just the first seven months of the fiscal year. Wool carpets alone brought in NPR 6.4 billion and raw wool another NPR 3.4 billion. Animal feed earned NPR 2.5 billion. Chhurpi, the hardened yak and cow cheese now sold abroad as dog chews, earned NPR 2.3 billion, a fast-growing market built on the milk of Himalayan animals. Leather and leather products earned NPR 254 million, and dairy, honey, live animals, meat and fish added more.

At home, the numbers are larger still. Nepal produces more than 2.68 million metric tons of milk a year; raw buffalo milk alone accounts for over 7 per cent of agricultural GDP and cow milk almost 4 per cent. Net meat production stands at around 447,767 metric tons, led by buffalo and goat. Our hens lay some 1.64 billion eggs a year. And the manure of these animals fertilises our fields and fuels our kitchens.

Behind every one of these figures is a living, feeling animal. Our national income is, quite literally, carried on their backs. A country that earns this much from animals and does not legally guarantee their welfare is not just failing them. It is failing its own farmers, its consumers and its standing in international markets, where animal welfare is fast becoming a condition of trade, not a courtesy.

None of this is news to our leaders. For more than a decade, Animal Nepal and our partners in the animal welfare movement have asked for one thing: a standalone Animal Welfare Act that recognises animals as sentient beings and makes their welfare the purpose of the law.

We did not just ask. Around four years ago, together with some 20 organisations, we drafted Nepal’s first Shadow Animal Welfare Act, built through research, technical expertise and wide consultation, and submitted it to every relevant government body. We presented it to the Parliamentary Committee on Agriculture, Cooperatives and Natural Resources, which directed the Department of Livestock Services to prepare a draft law within six months. On July 2, 2025, we brought government, parliamentarians, experts and civil society together for a national consultation on the gaps in our laws and the need for a comprehensive Act.

Successive governments have nodded along. Ministers have acknowledged the importance of animal welfare in speeches and meetings. But when it came to action, very little followed.

A draft that misses the point

Then, recently, the government circulated its draft Animal Services and Animal Welfare Bill for comment by civil society. After years of waiting, it was a profound disappointment to us and to everyone who has worked on this issue.

The draft is not an Animal Welfare Act. It is, at its core, a law about animal production: livestock development, breeding, genetic improvement, animal health administration, disease control, commercial regulation and production management. Animal welfare appears as one chapter among many, an add-on to a law whose real purpose lies elsewhere.

This is the pyramid, written into legislation. It treats welfare as something that matters only insofar as it does not interfere with output. It places the duty to protect animals in the same framework designed to maximise their productivity, a conflict of interest that will always be resolved in favour of production. And after three years of consultations, recommendations and technical inputs from the animal welfare community, very little of what we offered is reflected in it.

That is why Animal Nepal has formally rejected this draft as a substitute for a standalone Animal Welfare Act.

A genuine Animal Welfare Act would begin from a simple, scientifically settled truth: animals are sentient beings who can feel pain, fear and suffering, and who can also experience comfort and positive emotions. From that foundation, it would protect every animal whose life we touch: companion and street animals; farmed animals, in housing, nutrition, handling, transport and slaughter; working animals, with proper equipment, reasonable workloads, rest, water and veterinary care; captive wildlife and animals used in entertainment; and animals used in research, under ethical approval. It would set humane standards for transport, provide for rescue, rehabilitation and adoption, and include animals in disaster preparedness, something the floods and landslides of recent years have shown we can no longer ignore. And it would be enforced by trained animal welfare officers with powers of inspection and seizure, by meaningful penalties, and by education for schools, police, the judiciary and the public.

Animal welfare cannot be confined to one chapter. It must guide every chapter of the law.

The law we choose

On this World Animal Day, we ask the Government of Nepal to withdraw the current draft as the country’s animal welfare legislation, to sit down in good faith with the animal welfare community, and to enact a genuine, standalone Animal Welfare Act, one that reflects international best practice, modern science and the compassion our own traditions have taught for thousands of years.

Our gods chose to be carried by animals. Our economy is carried by them still. The least we can do is carry their welfare into law, not as a footnote or a single chapter, but as the purpose of the law itself.

The law we choose defines who we are. Nepal’s animals have waited long enough. Until they have the protection they deserve, we will not stop asking.

title.rendered: Girl missing for 37 hours found in forest; suspected abductor shot and arrested

content.rendered:
Rupandehi, October 4

A 10-year-old girl who went missing from her home in Tilottama Municipality-10, Rupandehi, has been rescued after 37 hours, while police have arrested a man suspected of abducting her.

The girl had been sleeping with her five-year-old brother and grandparents at their home on the night of October 1. At around 3am, her grandfather woke up to use the toilet and went to cover the children with a blanket.

That was when he realised the 10-year-old was missing from the bed.

Alarmed, he woke his wife and began calling for his granddaughter. The family searched around the house, while neighbours who heard the commotion also joined the search. Police at the Area Police Office, Mangalapur, were informed during the night.

A team led by Inspector Gyanendra Chand reached the house and began searching with local residents. They searched nearby houses, bushes, fields and surrounding areas through the night, but found no trace of the girl.

Police teams from Butwal and the district were subsequently mobilised. A team led by DSP Nishant Srivastava also joined the investigation, while the provincial police leadership deployed additional personnel, including a PIT team.

According to Deputy Inspector General Bhupendra Khatri, around 150 police personnel were involved in the search operation.

The girl had returned home from India with her grandparents only the previous day. Given the circumstances of her disappearance, police investigated the possibility that someone known to the family could have been involved.

During the investigation, police began focusing on a local man known as Bishal, identified as Yuvraj Tharu. Police searched areas where he was believed to frequent, including forests, fields and ponds.

Police later learned that Tharu often stayed in the forest. This prompted investigators to expand their search operations in forest areas.

After about 37 hours, information was received that the suspected man might be in the Chakrahawa forest in Tilottama-10. Police launched a larger search operation involving 55 personnel, with assistance from local residents.

Tharu was not found during the operation. The missing girl, however, was found alone in the forest at around 3pm on October 2.

Police said she was found in a condition in which she was unable to speak. She was immediately rescued and taken to Lumbini Provincial Hospital. She was later kept overnight at a safe house operated by the Area Police Office, Butwal, before being handed over to her relatives the following day.

The suspected abductor remained at large.

Police continued searching for Tharu and located him early on October 4 in a paddy field in Darakhsawa, Tilottama-17.

Police shot him below the knee before arresting him. He is currently receiving treatment at Lumbini Provincial Hospital. Police said they recovered a knife and an iron rod from him.

According to police, villagers told investigators that Tharu frequently ate and slept in the forest.

Police said their investigation so far indicates that he kept the girl alone in the forest for the 37 hours she was missing. Further investigation into the circumstances of the abduction is underway.

title.rendered: CAAN warns against flying kites, drones and balloons near airport

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The Tribhuvan International Airport office of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN) has warned that kites, drones and balloons being flown around the airport could pose serious risks to flight safety.

In a statement issued on Sunday, the airport office said such activities, which are prohibited by law, could create serious safety challenges during aircraft operations.

The warning comes as kite-flying activities increase with the start of the Dashain festival.

According to the airport office, kites, kite strings, balloons and drones entering aircraft take-off and landing areas can obstruct the safe operation of flights and create risks during take-off and landing.

The office said legal provisions prohibit such activities in areas around the airport and that the public has repeatedly been informed not to engage in them.

However, it expressed concern that such activities have continued despite the warnings.

“Flight safety is not only the responsibility of the airport and concerned authorities but a shared responsibility of all citizens,” the statement said.

The airport office called for public cooperation and responsible behaviour to ensure safe flight operations and the safety of passengers.

The National Sports Council (NSC) has nominated Gunjan Shah Thakuri as a member of the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN).

The decision was taken at the level of the NSC member secretary.

According to Clause 3, Sub-clause 4 of Chapter 2 of the Cricket Association of Nepal Statute 2055, the NSC has the authority to nominate an ex-officio member to the cricket governing body.

Thakuri has been nominated to the vacant position under the same provision.

The position became vacant after the NSC recalled Chhumbi Lama from CAN membership following the formation of the new government.

Thakuri previously served as personal secretary to then Minister for Industry, Commerce and Supplies Gauri Kumari Yadav.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa says Nepal’s political culture needs more openness

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Standing before a large gathering at Khulamanch, Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa used the historic public space to make a broader argument about the state of democracy in Nepal.

His message was that the country needs more places where people can question those in power, disagree openly and be heard.

Addressing the inaugural session of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention on Sunday, Thapa said the decision to hold the convention at Khulamanch was not simply about choosing a venue. For him, the space represented the kind of openness he believes is missing from Nepal’s political life.

“Khulamanch does not mean that differences disappear. It is a place where differences can be brought together on a common platform,” he said.

Thapa recalled the political history associated with Khulamanch, noting that leaders including BP Koirala, Ganesh Man Singh and Girija Prasad Koirala had addressed people from the same space.

“Khulamanch has opened after 10 years. It is not merely a ground in Kathmandu,” he said. “Big political parties were built here, and smaller ones also emerged from here.”

But Thapa’s focus was less on the history of the venue and more on what he said Nepal needs now.

He argued that the country needs “open forums” not only in public spaces but also inside Parliament, political parties, communities and even on social media.

His first target was Parliament.

Thapa questioned the absence of Prime Minister Balendra Shah, saying Parliament could not truly be considered open if the prime minister was not present to face lawmakers and listen to their questions.

“Parliament is not open. Parliament is closed,” he said.

For Thapa, the issue was not simply the prime minister’s physical presence. He linked it to the dignity of Parliament and the relationship between the executive, lawmakers and the people.

He said the prime minister should be present for both the lawmakers who supported him and those who did not, as well as for the dignity of the parliamentary system and the people.

Thapa then extended the argument beyond Parliament.

He said political parties also needed spaces where members could question their leaders without fear of losing their membership.

“There should be an open forum within the party too. Party membership should not be cancelled simply because someone questions a leader,” he said.

He argued that the right to disagree, criticise and question leadership should become part of the internal culture of political parties.

For Thapa, this was not separate from the larger question of democracy.

“Democracy cannot be sought only outside. Political parties themselves must also have democratic structures and practices,” he said.

He also warned against treating Nepal’s current problems lightly.

Thapa said the country’s difficulties could not be solved simply by assuming that a new person in power would make everything disappear.

“Our problems cannot be taken lightly — nor can they be solved as if someone has arrived today and will make everything disappear with a magic wand,” he said.

He also pointed to the influence of international developments on Nepal, asking whether the country could remain insulated from global conflicts.

“Isn’t Nepal affected by the Russia-Ukraine war? Can Nepal remain unaffected by what is happening in the Middle East?” he asked.

Thapa said the challenges facing Nepal therefore needed to be understood in a wider context, rather than treated as problems that could be solved through quick political fixes.

He said the country needed open spaces from the hills to the Tarai, from physical public spaces to digital platforms, where citizens could raise questions and leaders could respond.

That, he suggested, was the larger message behind bringing the Congress convention back to Khulamanch after a decade.

The convention, he said, should not be treated merely as an event to choose party leaders. It should also be an opportunity for the party to reflect on what kind of political culture it wants to build.

“Parliament is closed, parties are closed, and that is why the country needs open forums,” Thapa said.

title.rendered: Rabi Lamichhane says he might have joined Congress if it valued loyalty over wealth

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) President Rabi Lamichhane on Sunday reflected on both the strengths and weaknesses of the Nepali Congress, saying he might have become a Congress member had the party placed greater value on political loyalty than material wealth.

Addressing the inaugural session of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention at Kathmandu’s Khula Manch, Lamichhane said the Congress could have attracted him if it had given greater importance to people committed to the party rather than those with financial resources.

“I might have been a Congress member if the party had valued those who considered loyalty their capital, rather than giving importance to those with material capital,” Lamichhane said.

He also criticised the party’s approach to proportional representation and ticket distribution, saying opportunities should not be concentrated among people who are already privileged.

“I might have been a Congress member if, while talking about proportional representation for people from remote and disadvantaged areas, the Congress had not prioritised the most privileged and those who had already received the most opportunities when distributing election tickets,” he said.

Lamichhane also praised the election of a 50-year-old party president, referring to Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa, but suggested the party could have encouraged younger leadership much earlier.

“You feel proud to have a 50-year-old president today. If you had taken inspiration from the idea of having a president at 40, I might have been a Congress member,” he said.

He also referred to the Congress’ electoral decisions, saying he might have joined the party had it not instructed its supporters to vote for other parties instead of its own candidates.

“Nothing is lost. We have to move the country forward together,” Lamichhane said.

Parties should unite on national issues

Lamichhane said political parties should maintain unity on matters concerning the country, the constitution and national interests.

He stressed that questions of nationality and major national issues should rise above partisan differences.

“When it comes to the country, when it comes to the Constitution, when it comes to the federal democratic republic, and when it comes to people’s livelihoods, there are no different parties,” he said. “There are no different flags or slogans. There is only one thing — the country, the country and the country.”

Lamichhane said it was in this spirit that he had attended the Congress’ convention opening ceremony.

He also said the country had reached a point where a son of Madhes had become prime minister, highlighting the importance of inclusion and representation in national politics.

Lamichhane further stressed the need for political parties to ensure proportional and inclusive representation while working together on issues of national importance.

title.rendered: Prachanda urges Gagan Thapa and Rabi Lamichhane to ‘break the pattern’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Nepali Communist Party coordinator and former prime minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’ has urged Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa and Rastriya Swatantra Party President Rabi Lamichhane to continue what he described as a “break from the established pattern” in Nepali politics.

Speaking at the inaugural session of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention at Khulamanch in Kathmandu on Sunday, Prachanda said Thapa had already taken a step in that direction and encouraged both leaders to continue doing so.

Prachanda recalled his own political career, saying he had repeatedly made such breaks in the past, from moving the country from war to peace, from the peace process to constitution-making and from the Constitution to the establishment of a republic.

“I used to break the pattern before. I would take peace towards war, war towards peace, peace towards the Constitution and the Constitution towards a republic,” he said.

He said it had now become more difficult for him to make such political shifts.

“Perhaps it has become a little difficult for me to break the pattern now. It is Gaganji’s turn. Keep breaking the pattern. Now it is Raviji’s turn as well. You still have some breaking of the pattern left to do. You should do it too, and then Nepal will be built,” Prachanda said.

Prachanda also recalled that both Thapa and Lamichhane had served as ministers in his cabinet.

He praised both leaders for their political awareness and said he continued to hold them in equal regard.

“Whether you are RSP President Raviji or Nepali Congress President Gaganji, or the ministers from my cabinet standing in line here, I have equal affection for everyone,” he said.

Prachanda said he had equal trust and respect for them and expressed hope that all political leaders would contribute to building a prosperous Nepal.

title.rendered: Constitution amendment shouldn’t be a matter of numbers alone: Bishwa Prakash Sharma

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Nepali Congress Vice President Bishwo Prakash Sharma has said the issue of constitutional amendment should not be treated merely as a matter of parliamentary numbers.

Addressing the inaugural ceremony of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention at Khulamanch in Kathmandu on Sunday, Sharma said constitutional amendment should be approached as a matter of national concern.

He said the Nepali Congress would support the government if it moved ahead with constitutional amendment in an organised and mature manner, in line with the principles envisioned by the Constitution.

“Constitutional amendment should not become merely a matter of the desires of the ruling and opposition sides. It should not be reduced to a matter of arithmetic,” Sharma said.

He stressed that any process of amending or drafting constitutional provisions should go beyond parliamentary calculations and reflect broader national unity and public sentiment.

Sharma also urged the government to take into account the spirit and demands of the Gen Z movement, the Madhesh movement and the concerns raised by different groups and communities across the country while pursuing constitutional amendments.

He called on the government to ensure that the amendment process addresses these issues in a comprehensive manner.

title.rendered: UML General Secretary warns of Nepal’s future amid geopolitical rivalry

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

CPN-UML General Secretary Shankar Pokharel has raised concerns about the impact of geopolitical rivalry on Nepal’s future, calling it an important issue facing the country.

Addressing the inaugural ceremony of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention at Khulamanch in Kathmandu on Sunday, Pokharel said Nepal’s future had come into question because of geopolitical tensions.

“What will happen to Nepal’s future because of geopolitical conflict? That question has arisen,” he said.

Pokharel said the government should move forward by holding dialogue on all major national issues.

He said Nepal’s political parties needed to stand together on issues concerning the country’s identity, sovereignty and national interests.

“The situation has arisen where Nepal’s political parties must stand together in defence of national interests and sovereignty,” he said. “We need to reassure the Nepali people and also reassure our neighbouring countries.”

Pokharel also said the government should take steps to address young people’s aspirations for a future in Nepal, noting that many youths want opportunities to build their lives in the country.

He urged political leaders to learn from history and move forward accordingly.

Pokharel, however, did not elaborate on the specific geopolitical challenges or conflicts he was referring to.

title.rendered: Resham Chaudhary says Gagan Thapa can lead Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Resham Chaudhary, founder of the Nagarik Unmukti Party, has expressed confidence that Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa can lead the country.

Speaking at the inaugural ceremony of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention in Kathmandu on Sunday, Chaudhary said Thapa, who played a role in the struggle for the establishment of a republic, could now play a leading role in building the country.

“Gagan can lead this country. I have faith in him,” Chaudhary said. “The person who played a role in bringing the republic will certainly play a role in building this country as well.”

Chaudhary also said the Nepali Congress had played an important role in drafting the Constitution and that recent changes within the party had strengthened his confidence in it.

However, he criticised the implementation of constitutional rights for marginalised communities, including the Tharu community.

He said rights had been written into the Constitution but had not been delivered in practice.

“Rights were written into the Constitution, but they were not given. Identity cannot be traded away,” Chaudhary said.

title.rendered: Baburam Bhattarai calls for directly elected executive president, fully proportional ststem

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Former prime minister Baburam Bhattarai has suggested that Nepal’s political parties consider a directly elected executive president and a fully proportional electoral system as an alternative to ensure political stability.

Speaking at the inaugural session of the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention at Khulamanch in Kathmandu on Sunday, Bhattarai said political stability was necessary for faster economic development.

He said Nepal’s governments have generally remained in office for only around three years, creating challenges for political stability and long-term development.Bhattarai also urged the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) government to complete its five-year term.

“Please sustain the current government. I wish you well and hope it lasts,” he said. “But given our political tendencies, I cannot say what will happen.”

He then suggested that political parties reach an agreement on a different system of government.

“Either build a consensus and move towards a directly elected executive president and a fully proportional legislature. Reform the federal structure accordingly as well,” Bhattarai said.

Bhattarai argued that changes to the political and electoral system could provide an alternative framework for achieving greater political stability and supporting economic development.

title.rendered: What I learned about leadership as a woman

content.rendered:
From being a young district officer in Nepal to taking on community leadership in the United States, my journey has taught me something I did not fully understand when I began my career: women do not lack the ability to lead. Too often, we are simply asked to prove it.

When I look back, I realise I never consciously set out to prove that a woman could lead.

I simply wanted to do my work well.

Yet at different points in my career, I found myself having to demonstrate that I could handle responsibility, make decisions, lead people and have a voice at the table.

It started when I was very young.

During the final year of my bachelor’s degree, I began working as a District Program Officer with ECARDS-Nepal under the Multi-Stakeholder Forestry Program. I was young and suddenly responsible for working with communities and managing a team of almost 20 people across field and office settings.

It was a lot of responsibility for someone just beginning her career.

And I knew people were watching.

Would this young woman really be able to manage the work? Would the community listen to her? Could she make the right decisions?

I understood the hesitation, so I did not try to force anyone to accept me as a leader.

I worked.

I listened to the community. I learned from the people around me. I made mistakes and learned from them. When things did not go as planned, I took responsibility.

Slowly, people began to trust me.

That experience taught me one of the most important lessons of my career: trust takes time, particularly when people are not accustomed to seeing someone like you in a particular role.

I remain grateful for those early years. They taught me how to work with people, manage a team, solve problems and, perhaps most importantly, understand what leadership looks like on the ground.

Choosing public service

After working with NGOs and development projects, I began thinking about what I wanted from the next stage of my career.

I wanted stability, but that was not the only reason I considered government service. I wanted to contribute through public institutions and understand how decisions and policies were made.

So I applied for the civil service. I was fortunate to pass and was posted as an officer in the Ministry of Forests and Environment.

It was another important chapter of my life.

It also made me more aware of something I had experienced before but had not fully understood — the way gender can influence how people perceive authority.

I remember situations where a man in a lower position would be addressed as Sir, while I would be called sister.

To be clear, being called sister never offended me. It is a normal and often affectionate way of addressing someone in our culture.

What stayed with me was the difference in how people sometimes responded to us.

People would enter a room and instinctively approach the male officer first. There were occasions when I had to review files, make decisions and sign documents, only for people to look surprised when they realised I was the person responsible.

It was never one dramatic incident. It was a series of small moments.

And sometimes those small moments tell you a great deal.

They made me realise that people can see age and gender before they see the person, the position or the qualifications.

I could have spent my energy being frustrated by that. Instead, I decided to keep doing my work.

Starting again in America

Eventually, my life took me to the United States. Like many immigrants, I had to begin a new chapter.

I continued my education, completed my higher studies and began working as a Business Analyst and Data Analyst. It was a very different environment from the one I had known in Nepal.

I continued learning, building my career and finding my place professionally.

But after some time, I felt that something was missing.

I wanted to contribute to my community. I wanted to do something beyond my professional work. I wanted to remain connected to Nepal, to Nepali people and to the community around me.

So I began getting involved.

Eventually, I was elected Secretary of the NRNA NCC Colorado Chapter.

That experience gave me a completely different kind of education.

Community work is not the same as a regular job. People volunteer their time. Everyone brings different expectations, personalities and opinions. There are no simple job descriptions, and sometimes there is no clear line between personal relationships and organisational responsibilities.

But I enjoyed it.

I learned a great deal, met wonderful people, worked with committed teams and developed in ways that a corporate job alone could not have offered.

Today, I serve as Secretary of NRNA NCC USA.

And once again, I encountered something familiar.

Under the NRNA NCC USA bylaws, my position is designated Secretary (Women) for election and representation purposes. The designation exists to ensure women’s representation in the election process. It does not create a hierarchy between the Secretary (Women) and Secretary (Open) positions. The two positions have equal rights and responsibilities.

Yet I have still encountered people who interpret the word Women as though it means the position comes second.

That raises a question worth asking.

Why should a designation intended to ensure representation be interpreted as a reason to diminish authority?

Women’s representation should not become women’s marginalisation.

If an organisation believes women should have a place in leadership, that place must come with equal respect, responsibility and recognition. Otherwise, representation risks becoming symbolic rather than meaningful.

We also need to look at ourselves

There is another part of this conversation that we do not discuss enough.

Women need to support women.

I have seen women-led organisations and events where male guests are introduced with their professional titles and recognised prominently, while women who organised, contributed to and led the programme receive much less acknowledgement.

That should make us pause.

If we want young women to believe that leadership is possible, we have to demonstrate that belief through our own actions.

Recognise her work.

Give her credit.

Introduce her with the same respect.

Recommend her for an opportunity.

Listen when she speaks.

And when another woman succeeds, we should not see her success as taking something away from us.

Her success does not make our success smaller.

Her seat does not take away our seat.

Her voice does not silence ours.

A personal reflection

This is my experience, and I know that things have changed and continue to change.

I have met many men and women who genuinely support women in leadership. I am grateful for the people who have encouraged me, trusted me and supported me throughout my journey.

But some old attitudes remain in our communities — in how women are recognised, whose voices are heard and whose contributions receive acknowledgement.

Sometimes supporting another woman is as simple as saying, I see your work. Keep going.

Those words can mean more than we realise.

What I want to leave behind

When I look back at my journey — from a young district officer in Nepal, to a government officer, to an immigrant professional in the United States and now an elected community leader — I can see how each chapter prepared me for the next.

My years in NGOs and development projects taught me how to build trust.

Government service taught me institutional responsibility.

My professional career taught me adaptability and continuous learning.

Community leadership taught me service.

And being a woman in leadership taught me resilience.

But perhaps the most important lesson is this:

Leadership is not simply about earning a seat at the table. It is about making sure the table has room for others.

I want young women to enter leadership without first asking whether people will accept them.

I want them to be judged by their work.

I want them to be able to disagree without being labelled difficult.

I want them to be ambitious without being questioned for it.

I want women to recognise and support the contributions of other women.

And I want men to understand that supporting women in leadership does not diminish men’s leadership.

It strengthens the organisations and communities we all belong to.

Ultimately, leadership should not be measured by who speaks the loudest or who occupies the most visible position. It should be measured by service, accountability, competence and contribution.

That is the kind of leadership I have tried to practise.

And it is the kind of leadership I hope to make easier for the women who come after me.

title.rendered: Disaster relief is not climate justice

content.rendered:
When a disaster strikes, the first duty is obvious: save lives, rescue the missing, provide shelter and ensure that affected families have food, medicine and security. But once the immediate emergency is over, a more difficult question begins: is relief enough?

Nepal’s catastrophic August 2026 glacier-related disaster has made that question painfully relevant. Recent scientific analysis indicates that climate change likely contributed to the conditions that destabilised the glacier and surrounding terrain, although scientists have also identified other contributing factors. The disaster has left more than 1,300 people dead and thousands missing, while destroying homes, roads, hydropower infrastructure and livelihoods. If a disaster of this scale is increasingly connected to a changing climate, should our legal and policy response remain limited to distributing relief after the destruction has already occurred?

The first legal question should be directed inward: what does the State owe its citizens before a disaster occurs? Nepal’s Constitution guarantees the right to live in a clean and healthy environment under Article 30 and provides a right to compensation, in accordance with law, for injury caused by environmental pollution or degradation. Nepal also has the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, 2074, which establishes a legal framework for disaster-risk reduction, preparedness, response and recovery. So, when authorities know that glaciers are retreating, rivers are changing, settlements are exposed to floods and landslides, and climate-related hazards are increasing, what preventive responsibility follows? Who is responsible for maintaining monitoring stations? Who must ensure that early-warning systems reach communities? Who decides whether a road, bridge, hydropower project or settlement is sufficiently safe to proceed? A legal system concerned only with compensation after death has occurred is addressing the consequence, not necessarily the duty that preceded it.

This is where the distinction between disaster relief and climate justice becomes important. Relief is immediate and necessary. It may provide food, temporary accommodation, medical assistance or financial support to affected families. Climate justice asks a much broader question: why are particular communities repeatedly carrying the greatest burden of a crisis they did little to create? Nepal’s NDC 3.0 recognises the country’s high vulnerability to climate change and identifies loss and damage as a major concern, including economic and non-economic impacts. The document also recognises the need to strengthen Nepal’s framework for addressing climate-induced loss and damage. This changes the character of the debate.

The affected farmer is not merely someone waiting for relief; the displaced family is not merely a beneficiary of a government program. Their losses form part of a wider question of rights, public responsibility, climate finance and international cooperation.

The international question is even harder. If Nepal contributes only a very small share of global greenhouse-gas emissions, yet faces severe climate-related losses, who should bear the cost of adaptation and recovery? Nepal has now placed climate justice at the centre of its international appeal following the 2026 disaster and has sought substantial external support for recovery. But as lawyers, we should resist the temptation to turn a morally powerful argument into an over-simplified legal claim.

It is one thing to establish that human-induced warming has increased climate risks; it is another to prove that a particular state or corporation is legally responsible for a particular disaster. Questions of scientific attribution, causation, state responsibility, jurisdiction and applicable international law remain complex. That does not weaken Nepal’s case for climate finance and loss-and-damage mechanisms. Rather, it tells us that Nepal needs evidence, not merely rhetoric: systematic records of deaths, displacement, infrastructure damage, livelihood losses, ecological damage and the scientific relationship between climate change and particular hazards.

There is another question that Nepal cannot avoid: when international climate money arrives, does justice actually reach the people who suffered the loss? Nepal’s NDC 3.0 estimates substantial financial requirements for implementing its climate commitments, with a significant portion dependent on international support. But who decides where that money is spent? How much reaches local governments and vulnerable communities? Who audits it? Can affected citizens obtain information about climate-finance allocations? Can they challenge a project that is described as climate-resilient but fails to protect the community for which it was designed? These are not merely questions of administration. They concern transparency, accountability and access to remedies. From the perspective of a law firm in Nepal, climate finance should therefore be viewed not simply as an economic resource but as an area requiring legal oversight, contractual accountability, public procurement scrutiny and meaningful community participation.

The question of equality is equally unavoidable. Does a family that loses its only farmland suffer the same kind of loss as a business that loses a commercial building? Can a person living in a remote mountain settlement recover as quickly as someone with insurance, savings and access to government institutions? And when reconstruction funds are distributed, should every victim be treated identically when their vulnerability and capacity to recover are radically different? Climate justice requires us to look at these differences. Nepal’s climate policy already recognises that climate-related loss is not limited to destroyed physical property; it can involve livelihoods, displacement, social systems, cultural heritage and other non-economic losses. The law therefore needs to move beyond the simple calculation of how many houses were destroyed and ask what was actually lost, who lost it, and whether the proposed remedy is capable of restoring a dignified life.

Ultimately, Nepal needs to change the language of disaster governance. Relief is necessary, but relief cannot be the final measure of justice. The real test begins after the helicopters leave, the temporary shelters close and the headlines disappear. Were vulnerable communities protected before the disaster? Were warnings adequate? Were known risks incorporated into development decisions? Was reconstruction carried out in a way that reduces future risk rather than reproducing the same vulnerability? Were climate funds transparently used? And when a loss cannot realistically be prevented, what mechanism exists to ensure that the affected person is not left to bear the cost alone? Nepal’s climate response must therefore connect constitutional environmental rights, disaster law, scientific evidence, climate finance and international loss-and-damage mechanisms.

A victim should not have to rely solely on charity to rebuild a life destroyed by a climate-related disaster. Relief addresses immediate suffering; climate justice asks who is responsible, who pays, who decides and what must change before the next disaster. That is the legal conversation Nepal can no longer postpone.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa proposes sweeping political and organisational reforms in NC report

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has proposed a broad overhaul of the party’s political culture, ideology, organisation and economic policies in the political report prepared for the party’s 15th General Convention.

The report reviews the Nepali Congress’s past performance and acknowledges that the party has grown increasingly distant from the public because of a political culture centred on power, positions, factions and access.

Thapa has proposed a new political culture and working style aimed at rebuilding the party’s relationship with citizens.

The report also calls for the political developments following the protests of Bhadau 23 and 24 to be understood beyond the framework of conspiracy theories. It says the demands raised during the movement — including good governance, opportunity, justice and equality — must be addressed.

It proposes an impartial investigation into the use of force, violence and damage caused during the protests, followed by legal action against those responsible and justice and compensation for victims.

The report also calls on the Congress to undertake a self-assessment of the results of the Falgun 21 elections, describing them as a reflection of the party’s two-decade-long growing distance from citizens.

Nepali Congress to play stronger opposition role

Thapa has proposed establishing the Nepali Congress as an effective principal opposition party following the election.

The report calls for fact-based monitoring of government activities, scrutiny of corruption and violations of rights, and the presentation of alternative policies.

It proposes establishing a “shadow government” at both the federal and provincial levels to monitor governments and develop alternative policy options.

For future elections, the report proposes that the Congress should not enter into pre-election alliances.

Instead, it should contest elections under its own election symbol, with its own candidates and agenda.

Thapa has also proposed changing the way candidates are selected. Rather than giving priority to factional affiliation, access or financial influence, the party should select candidates based on qualifications, contribution and performance.

The report proposes mechanisms such as primary elections, referendums or direct voting by party members for candidate selection.

Rethinking Nepali Congress’s ideology

The report proposes a 21st-century reinterpretation of nationalism, democracy and democratic socialism.

It links nationalism not only to political sovereignty but also to the country’s capacity in areas such as energy, food, technology, finance and knowledge.

Similarly, it argues that democracy should extend beyond voting in elections to include continuous citizen participation and involvement in decision-making.

The report proposes a development model based on the idea of “Prosperous Nepal, Respected Nepali”, arguing that economic growth alone is not enough.

It calls for equal access to education, healthcare, nutrition, skills, capabilities and opportunities.

Thapa has also proposed the concept of “pre-distributive justice”, which focuses on creating equal opportunities from the beginning through access to education, healthcare, skills, finance and employment.

Private sector and remittances

The report proposes establishing the private sector as a key partner in employment generation, production, investment and innovation.

It calls for stronger investment protection, policy stability and a better business environment.

The report also proposes creating conditions for remittances to be invested in agriculture, industry, tourism and technology.

Hydropower and clean energy are to be linked with industrialisation and green exports as part of a broader strategy to build a production-oriented economy.

Agriculture, energy, water, tourism, industry and digital technology have been identified as key foundations of that economy.

Focus on youth and migration

The report places particular emphasis on creating dignified employment opportunities for young people within Nepal.

It also proposes making foreign employment safer and more rights-based, while strengthening social security for Nepalis working abroad and directing remittances towards productive sectors.

Thapa has argued that development planning should respond to changing patterns of population and migration.

Rather than relying solely on administrative boundaries, planning should take into account where people actually live and where they need public services.

The report also proposes forming an independent panel of young experts to study youth dissatisfaction and the demands raised by Generation Z.

Its recommendations would be required to be incorporated into policymaking, according to the proposal.

Climate change, technology and social protection

The report treats climate change as both an economic and national security issue.

It proposes making disaster risk assessment mandatory in infrastructure, settlement and development planning.

Thapa has also called for restructuring Nepal’s education and skills systems in response to changes brought about by technology and artificial intelligence, particularly in employment, education and knowledge.

On the social front, the report prioritises issues including caste discrimination, child marriage, gender-based violence, malnutrition and access to education and healthcare.

It also calls for stronger social protection for senior citizens, children, women and other vulnerable groups.

Stronger federalism and institutional independence

The report proposes stronger coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments and calls for administrative and fiscal federalism to be strengthened.

It says constitutional amendments, if necessary, should be pursued on the basis of national consensus.

The report also calls for transitional justice to be concluded through truth, justice and reparation rather than being used as a subject of political bargaining.

Thapa has proposed ending political appointments and factional sharing in institutions including the judiciary, constitutional bodies, universities and the civil administration.

The report also commits the Congress to not protecting its own leaders or cadres accused of corruption.

Changes to elections and party governance

Among the proposals are a constitutional provision limiting a prime minister to two terms and the introduction of a “none of the above” option in elections.

It also proposes voting rights for Nepalis living abroad and reforms aimed at making the electoral system more participatory and transparent.

Within the party, Thapa has proposed greater financial transparency, regular audits and a code of conduct, along with mechanisms to investigate leaders facing corruption allegations.

The report proposes a 100-day review of the Congress’s political and organisational performance over the past two decades.

In the first year, provincial task forces would be formed to implement programmes focused on education, nutrition, employment, good governance and green development.

The party would also publish an annual “Prosperity Report” to assess progress.

A five-generation party

Thapa has proposed restructuring the Nepali Congress around cooperation among five generations.

He has called for institutional structures focused on leadership development, policy, elections and good governance, alongside greater investment in political and organisational training.

The report also proposes establishing a Rs 100 million endowment fund for families of martyrs, those injured in political movements and displaced families, with long-term support for education and healthcare.

Overall, the report presents the Nepali Congress’s future direction as something broader than a change in party leadership.

It proposes a transformation of the party’s political culture and organisation alongside reforms in the economy, employment, private-sector investment, youth policy, technology, social protection, federalism and governance.

The central challenge, the report suggests, is to rebuild the Congress’s relationship with citizens while creating a party capable of responding to a changing political and social landscape.

title.rendered: Two killed in motorcycle accident in Tanahun

content.rendered:
Damauli, Tanahun, October 4

Two people were killed in a motorcycle accident in Bhanu Municipality-10, Tallomailan, Tanahun, on Sunday.

The deceased have been identified as 45-year-old Shankar Pandey and 65-year-old Tankaniti Pandey, both from the same locality, according to the District Police Office.

The accident occurred when the motorcycle, with registration number Ga 19 Pa 8065, travelling from Hatiya towards Chisapani, lost control and fell about 10 metres off the road.

Both victims sustained serious injuries and were taken to separate hospitals for further treatment. They died during treatment, according to Police Inspector Manoj Pandey of the District Police Office.

Shankar, who was riding the motorcycle, died at Chitwan Medical College, while Tankaniti died at Provincial Hospital, Lamjung, Inspector Pandey said.

—RSS

title.rendered: Which political leaders attended the Nepali Congress convention opening?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The opening ceremony of the Nepali Congress’s 15th General Convention has brought together senior leaders from several political parties at Khula Manch in Kathmandu.

The convention began on Sunday under the slogan “Respect tradition and resolve for change — a strong Congress for a prosperous Nepal.”

Among the political leaders attending the opening ceremony were NCP coordinator and former prime minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’, CPN-UML General Secretary Shankar Pokharel, Rastriya Prajatantra Party Chair Rajendra Lingden, Nagarik Unmukti Party Nepal patron Resham Chaudhary and Janata Samajbadi Party Nepal co-chair Sharat Singh Bhandari.

Leaders and representatives from other political parties and organisations have also been invited to the opening ceremony. The closed session and other programmes of the general convention will be held on Monday and Tuesday. The Central Election Committee has scheduled the party’s election process for October 7 and 8.

The Nepali Congress registered its general convention representatives on Friday and Saturday ahead of the convention.

title.rendered: 10th National Games preparations stepped up, 21 teams to compete in 32 sports

content.rendered:
Surkhet, October 4

Preparations for the 10th National Games have been stepped up, with the main organising committee deciding to delegate authority to an executive committee to oversee the event’s operation, management and preparations.

The decision was taken at a meeting of the main organising committee held in Birendranagar on Sunday. Officials said the delegation of authority would make it easier to take and implement decisions as it would be difficult for the main committee to meet frequently.

The National Games will be held in Surkhet and other districts of Karnali Province.

The meeting decided that 21 teams will participate in the Games, including teams from all seven provinces, three departmental teams, three other teams and representatives of the relevant national sports associations.

Competitions will be held in 32 sports disciplines.

The meeting was chaired by Education and Sports Minister and National Sports Council Chair Sasmita Pokharel. Karnali Chief Minister Mangal Bahadur Shahi attended as the chief guest.

Around 50 to 55 people participated in the meeting, including Karnali Social Development Minister Jit Bahadur Malla, Minister for Economic Affairs and Planning Tek Raj Pachhai, National Planning Commission member Renu Dhungana, senior federal and provincial government officials, security officials, representatives from the sports sector and other stakeholders.

Executive committee given wider responsibilities

The meeting authorised the executive committee to issue necessary directions and oversee preparations, management and the operation of the National Games in accordance with the National Games Operation Directive 2083.

The committee will also be responsible for forming and mobilising various subcommittees required for the Games, managing expenditure according to prescribed budgetary standards and overseeing the operation and management of the first Para National Games.

The main organising committee said the delegation was necessary to ensure that preparations could move forward efficiently.

Focus on public-private partnership

The meeting also decided to increase the participation of government agencies, the private sector and other stakeholders in order to make the Games more effective.

It agreed to work with sponsors under a public-private partnership model and move forward with the necessary agreements and arrangements.

Officials informed the meeting that preparations were already underway through the executive committee, various subcommittees and a separate monitoring committee formed under the main organising committee.

The meeting also discussed further coordination between the federal and Karnali provincial governments to make preparations more systematic.

The main organising committee welcomed the government’s decision to hold the 10th National Games in Karnali and passed a resolution thanking the federal government.

The National Games are held every two years with the objective of identifying and developing sporting talent from the local level and expanding sports activities across the country.

The meeting concluded that close coordination and cooperation among government agencies, security bodies, sports associations, the private sector and other stakeholders would be essential for the successful organisation of the Games in Karnali.

title.rendered: India police investigate sexual harassment allegations during protests against election commission

content.rendered:
New Delhi, October 4

Indian police have launched an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment against police officers during protests in New Delhi against the country’s Election Commission.

Protests began on Friday, with demonstrators demanding the resignation of Election Commission of India (ECI) chief Gyanesh Kumar. Opposition groups have accused the commission of wrongdoing during a large-scale revision of voter rolls that they say has resulted in millions of names being removed from electoral lists.

The ECI has rejected the allegations. Kumar has not publicly commented on the claims.

The sexual harassment allegations emerged on Saturday after police detained dozens of protesters near Jantar Mantar, the government-designated protest site in central New Delhi.

Delhi Police said in a statement that three female journalists had made allegations of sexual harassment against police officers.

The police said they would conduct a “fair and impartial enquiry” into the allegations.

In a video posted on social media, one of the complainants alleged that a police officer pushed her and touched her inappropriately.

Protests are expected to continue in the capital on Sunday, with left-wing groups and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) also planning demonstrations.

The CJP began as a satirical online movement in May and later campaigned for the removal of India’s then education minister.

CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke, who had criticised the police response and detentions on Saturday, called for the immediate arrest of the officer accused of misconduct.

Meanwhile, Neha Bora, an activist affiliated with a left-wing student organisation, called on protesters to march towards India Gate in central New Delhi.

“From Streets to Protests, Women Are NOT SAFE!” she wrote on social media.

Opposition parties have accused the ECI of acting in favour of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the election body has rejected.

Opposition leaders have announced plans to march to the Election Commission in New Delhi on Tuesday, followed by “Save Democracy” rallies across the country.

The CJP has also called for a “massive mobilisation of young Indians” in New Delhi on October 10.

title.rendered: Speaker Aryal to address international forums in Nepali

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal will address international forums in the Nepali language.

Aryal is leaving today to lead a Nepali parliamentary delegation to the 153rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), being held from October 5 to 9.

At the assembly in Arusha, Tanzania, Aryal will address the general debate on “Advancing good governance and empowering communities through inclusion, trust and opportunities.”

Nepal has also selected “Urgent Parliamentary Action” as an emergency agenda item. Its main theme is “Addressing climate-related disasters and strengthening resilience in the Himalayan region and other vulnerable areas.”

Nepal will present a proposal on the issue. Such proposals require support from other countries as well.

According to Aryal, the proposal has already received support from 50 countries. Preparations have also been made for around 28 sideline meetings.

Speaking about his visit last Friday, Aryal said he planned to promote the Nepali language at international forums.

“Since I became Speaker, and throughout my tenure, I have tried to promote Nepali, my mother tongue. I have conducted all programmes in Nepali,” Aryal said.

He said he had conducted all diplomatic meetings he held in Nepal through dialogue and interaction in Nepali. He said he would follow the same policy abroad.

“I will communicate in my mother tongue abroad as well,” he said.

Aryal said that although he had spoken in English when he was a minister and was capable of communicating well in English, he had made Nepali the language of communication with all sides since becoming Speaker.

“We have held around 40, 50 or 60 meetings here. No one has ever told me that I should speak in English. They have been happy that I spoke in Nepali. That is why I am also informing you about this [decision to address international forums in Nepali],” he said.

After participating in the 153rd IPU Assembly and related meetings, Speaker Aryal will travel to Kenya.

title.rendered: Affordable, low-speed internet packages will no longer be available

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The Internet Service Providers’ Association of Nepal (ISPAN) has announced that it will no longer offer affordable, low-speed internet packages.

According to a statement issued on Sunday in the name of ISPAN President Sudhir Parajuli, internet service providers will stop offering affordable, low-speed packages from Monday, October 5.

The association said the packages are being withdrawn because several factors have made it difficult for providers to operate, and even to keep operations running. It cited price increases in previous years, fuel prices pushed up by Middle East tensions, soaring fibre prices, high inflation, and a sudden rise in electronics and chipset prices driven by the rapid growth of AI, among other reasons.

Apologising for the inconvenience to customers, the association has directed all providers to continue striving for the dream of a digital Nepal by delivering better-quality service. It has also directed all providers to display the rates approved by the Nepal Telecommunications Authority prominently on their websites.

The association has also urged all customers to make sure they get a VAT bill.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Singer Shiva Pariyar and singer Samikshya Adhikari will perform in a dozen American cities for Dashain.

Under the “Dashain Tihar Dhamaka USA Tour”, they will take part in shows organised from the East Coast to the West.

The tour, organised by Three-E Entertainment of Virginia, will run for about a month and a half. The two are reported to have gone to the US on P-3 category visas.

The tour has been in the works for a year. After the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa caused loss of life and property, it was decided to give the money raised from the tour to flood victims.

On the initiative of Suresh Sapkota, chairman of the organising company, up to $500 raised from the tour will be sent to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

Pariyar and Adhikari will perform in New York on Sunday. They have already performed in Akron on October 2 and in Columbus on October 3.

It is Adhikari’s first trip to the US.

title.rendered: Prachanda says understanding reached to cooperate with UML and CPN (Masal)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Nepali Communist Party (NCP) coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’ has said an understanding has been reached to work together with the CPN-UML and Masal.

Speaking at a programme organised by the NCP Bagmati Province Contact Committee in Kathmandu on Sunday, Prachanda said discussions were also underway with other leftist and patriotic forces on possible cooperation.

“We have already reached an understanding to move forward by coordinating with the CPN-UML and Masal,” Prachanda said. “We are also continuing discussions with other patriotic and leftist forces.”

Prachanda said his party was also taking initiatives to strengthen cooperation with the international community.

He said people’s lives had not become easier even after the election, arguing that the constitution and republican system were facing attacks.

According to Prachanda, political forces need to come together to defend the Constitution, the federal democratic republic and the rights achieved through past political struggles.

He said the current situation required all those committed to these achievements to unite and move forward together.
