title.rendered: Speaker Aryal leaves for Tanzania to attend IPU Assembly

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal is leaving for Tanzania today to lead a Nepali parliamentary delegation to the 153rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU).

The assembly is being held from October 5 to 9 in Arusha, Tanzania.

Aryal is scheduled to leave for Tanzania via Doha at 7 pm on Sunday on Qatar Airways flight QR645. The delegation includes his wife Ambika KC, House of Representatives member Rabin Mahato, National Assembly member Jhakku Prasad Subedi and Anjan Shakya.

Federal Parliament Secretary-General Padma Prasad Pandey, House of Representatives Secretary Prakash Adhikari, Federal Parliament Secretariat Joint Secretary Rekha Upadhyay Khanal and Speaker Aryal’s private secretary Madhu Mijar are also part of the delegation.

At the assembly, Aryal will address the general debate on the theme “Advancing good governance and empowering communities through inclusion, trust and opportunities.”

An “Urgent Parliamentary Action” has also been set as an emergency agenda item. Its main theme is “Addressing climate-related disasters and strengthening resilience in the Himalayan region and other vulnerable areas.” Nepal is preparing to table a proposal on the issue.

National Assembly member Jhakku Prasad Subedi will participate in the Asian Parliamentary Assembly under the IPU. Anjan Shakya will participate as a co-rapporteur from the Asia-Pacific region in the Standing Committee on Sustainable Development and in the Forum of Women Parliamentarians. Rabin Mahato will participate in the Forum of Young Parliamentarians.

The Nepali delegation is also scheduled to hold sideline meetings with delegations from various countries participating in the assembly.

Federal Parliament Secretary-General Padma Prasad Pandey will make a presentation at the meeting of the Association of Secretaries General of Parliaments on parliamentary system structures, funds and capacity building.

After participating in the 153rd IPU Assembly and related meetings, Speaker Aryal will travel to Kenya.

The Nepali delegation will make an official visit to the Kenyan Parliament at the invitation of Kenyan Speaker Moses Wetang’ula.

The delegation is scheduled to return to Kathmandu on October 13 after completing the Kenya visit.

title.rendered: CK Raut re-elected Janamat Party chair, Sanjay Yadav elected general secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Dr CK Raut has been re-elected chair of the Janamat Party.

Raut was elected chair with 958 votes in the election held during the party’s general convention in Birgunj.

A total of 99 candidates contested 26 office-bearer positions. Although Raut was the only candidate for the chairperson’s post, party members also voted for him because the party statute requires a candidate to secure at least 20 per cent of the total valid votes to be elected.

Anitakumari Mandal of Siraha, Anitadevi Sah of Dhanusha, Narendra Prasad Chaudhary of Kapilvastu, Basant Kumar Kushwaha of Rautahat, Dr Jayakant Raut of Saptari, Rajay Kumar Yadav of Siraha and Madhav Prasad Singh of Parsa were elected vice-chairs.

Eleven candidates had contested for the seven vice-chair positions. Parmeshwar Murmu, Harpal Singh Sodi, Manohara Devi Baitha and Roshan Khatun were defeated.

Sanjay Kumar Yadav elected general secretary

Sanjay Kumar Yadav of Siraha was elected general secretary with 618 votes.

Mamata Jha and Chandan Kumar Singh had also contested for the post. Jha received 220 votes and Singh 165 votes. According to the Janamat Party, they failed to cross the 20 per cent threshold.

Nirmal Kumar Mandal of Siraha was elected deputy general secretary with 501 votes. His rival Lalit Chandra Mallik received 414 votes.

Surendra Sharma, Paras Prasad Sah, Santosh Raj Sahani, Anjani Devi, Radhakumari Yadav, Harendra Chaudhary and Bal Govinda Chaudhary were elected secretaries.

Nine candidates had contested for seven secretary positions. Birendra Mahato (Jeevan Tyagi) and Rambabu Sah were defeated.

title.rendered: 540 middlemen arrested in six months, 170 charged

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

A total of 540 middlemen have been arrested in the past six months, and 170 of them have been charged, according to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.

The office has made public a summary of the government’s achievements in its first six months. Point 3 of the summary details work related to peace, security and good governance.

Under the heading “Middlemen control and monitoring”, it says: “540 middlemen have been taken into custody and cases filed against 170.”

The government says that in the six months since, it has arrested 540 middlemen and prosecuted 170 of them. But it has not given details on what kinds of middlemen were arrested or who has been charged.

The summary also lists other work related to peace, security and good governance. Under control of illegal activities, 26 betting apps and more than 305,663 betting domain links have been shut down.

According to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, a separate Narcotics Control Department has been established to curb the growing drug trade and abuse.

Under protection of public land, a campaign against encroachment has removed 4,226 illegal structures nationwide, including 3,457 in the Kathmandu Valley.

The summary says industrial and business security has also been prioritised.

“A Rapid Response Team (RRT) and District Industrial Security Coordination Committees have been formed to ensure the security of the industrial and banking sectors. A total of 7,669 CCTV cameras have been installed in major markets and highways,” it says.

The summary also says that in the past six months, the National Vigilance Centre has monitored 1,117 offices in 32 districts and recommended action against 10,621 employees.

title.rendered: China tops Asian Games with 341 medals, Nepal limited to two bronzes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

China finished first at the 20th Asian Games in Japan with 341 medals.

All events at the Games, which began on Asoj 3, concluded on Sunday. China maintained its dominance with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals.

Host Japan finished second with 39 gold, 95 silver and 91 bronze medals. South Korea was third with 150 medals, including 39 gold, and India fourth with 85 medals, including 21 gold.

Nepal was limited to two bronze medals. The Nepali women’s kabaddi team won bronze for the second consecutive time, and karateka Tenzing Sherpa also won a medal.

Nepal won only two bronze medals, with 135 Nepali athletes taking part.

title.rendered: Chinese ambassador arrives in Lomanthang with seven-member team

content.rendered:
Mustang, October 4

Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming and a seven-member team reached Lomanthang in Upper Mustang on Saturday via the Korala border point.

Mustang’s Chief District Officer Ajita Sharma said, “The Chinese ambassador has come to Mustang from Korala. We have not received detailed information about the visit.”

The ambassador is on a three-day visit to Lomanthang. Five members of the team are Chinese. They are scheduled to leave Lomanthang today and head toward China via the Korala border point.

According to Tashi Norbu Gurung, chair of Lomanthang Rural Municipality, the Chinese ambassador has come to Mustang to assess the situation at the Korala border point.

The ambassador’s visit is seen as significant at a time when there are demands to reopen Korala. The Kerung Bhotekoshi route, which had become an alternative to the long-closed Tatopani border point, has been turned into a riverbed by flooding.

Since the closure of the Rasuwa and Tatopani border points, the Mustang Customs Office has been collecting about Rs 300 million in revenue daily.

title.rendered: 700 police deployed for Congress convention, from sniffer dogs to drones

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The 15th General Convention of the Nepali Congress begins today, Sunday, at the Khulamanch, Kathmandu. The convention venue has been decorated, and delegates continue to arrive. Supporters of declared candidates, along with delegates, are already asking for votes.

The inauguration session is scheduled for 2 pm. Heads of other political parties and representatives from various countries are arriving at the Khulamanch for the opening.

A large number of police have been deployed to secure the convention. According to SSP Dilip Ghimire of the District Police Range, Kathmandu, 700 police personnel have been mobilised to provide security.

Both plainclothes and uniformed police are on duty. Ghimire said surveillance is also being carried out by drone. Trained police dogs have also been deployed, and sniffer dog checks are underway.

A command post has been set up under the command of the Metropolitan Police for security. Police said they are also managing traffic in coordination with the Traffic Police.

The organisers have said they will hold the convention peacefully and without extravagance.

title.rendered: Police raid gambling den in Kanchanpur at midnight, 5 arrested

content.rendered:
Dhangadhi, October 4

Police have raided a gambling den in Kanchanpur in the middle of the night. Gamblers scattered after the raid, and some fled, leaving behind their cars and motorcycles at the scene.

A joint team from the Provincial Police Office and the Area Police Office, Tribhuvanbasti, carried out the raid at around 2 am. Acting on information that high-stakes gambling was under way on a tarpaulin spread over a dirt road section at Purainaa in Punarbas Municipality-1, the team moved in.

According to police, five people were taken into custody during the raid. Many other gamblers fled when they learned the police team had arrived.

DSP Tek Bahadur Rawat, spokesperson for the District Police Office, Kanchanpur, said the five are in custody and an investigation into the incident is under way.

Those arrested are Jagat Bahadur Dhami of Rajipur in Gauriganga Municipality-4, Kailali; Bikram Bista of Dhangadhi Sub-Metropolitan City-4; Prem Bahadur Singh of Jugeda in Dhangadhi-12; Krishna Bahera of Bungal Municipality-11, Bajhang; and Suresh Tamang of Balabhadrabasti in Punarbas Municipality-1.

Police said they recovered Rs 20,910 in cash from the five. They are being held at the Area Police Office, Tribhuvanbasti.

Police also found four cars, two scooters and nine motorcycles at the gambling site. Police said the other gamblers abandoned their vehicles at the scene and fled after the team arrived.

title.rendered: Finance Minister Wagle arrives in US to seek support for reconstruction and economic reforms

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle arrived in the United States on Sunday night, leading a two-member delegation.

Wagle was received in Washington, DC, by Nepal’s Acting Ambassador Sharad Raj Aran and officials from the Nepali Embassy.

During his visit, Wagle is scheduled to meet US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga on Monday.

The meetings are expected to focus on strengthening Nepal’s economic partnership and cooperation with the United States and the World Bank.

According to officials, discussions will cover ways to enhance bilateral cooperation, support Nepal’s efforts to exit the Financial Action Task Force’s grey list, and advance broader economic reforms.

The Nepali delegation will also seek additional assistance for the reconstruction of physical and economic infrastructure damaged by the recent floods in the Bhotekoshi area.

Wagle is expected to discuss support for reconstruction and resilient development with representatives of the World Bank and the US government.

The visit will also focus on attracting greater investment from development partners and the private sector in key infrastructure projects, including roads and electricity transmission lines.

The government aims to use such investment to create jobs and expand economic opportunities within Nepal.

During his visit, Wagle is also scheduled to meet senior officials of the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and leading private-sector investors.

The visit is aimed at strengthening Nepal’s economic partnerships, mobilising development assistance and investment, and supporting the country’s broader economic reform agenda.

title.rendered: Why was Bikal Paudel sentenced to only 2.5 years for Rs 419.4 million corruption?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The Special Court has convicted Bikal Paudel, former executive director of the Security Printing Centre, in a corruption case.

A bench comprising Special Court Chairperson Basudev Acharya and members Umesh Koirala and Bidur Koirala found Paudel guilty of corruption involving Rs 419.4 million.

The court ordered the confiscation of property worth Rs 419.4 million and imposed a fine of the same amount.

Although the Special Court has determined the largest-ever amount of assets and fine in a case involving illegal acquisition of property, it sentenced Paudel to only two and a half years in prison.

He was sentenced to an additional six months for committing corruption while holding a position equivalent to a special-class government post. Since he is already in custody and has been ordered to pay a substantial amount in damages and fines, he can remain in custody while appealing the verdict to the Supreme Court.

Before the illegal property acquisition case was filed, three corruption cases had already been filed against Paudel. The Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) filed a case in 2080 BS over alleged irregularities in the construction of the Security Printing Centre’s building and other structures.

A second case was filed against him for allegedly obtaining an appointment in Nepal after acquiring permanent residency (PR) in the United States and concealing information about it. In the third case, the CIAA filed charges against Paudel and five others for alleged corruption in the procurement of equipment for the Security Printing Centre.

After filing the illegal property acquisition case, the CIAA also filed another corruption case against Paudel and then-Chief Secretary Dr Baikuntha Aryal.

What were the allegations?

The CIAA filed a case against Paudel at the Special Court on May 22, 2024, accusing him of illegally acquiring property worth Rs 621.9 million.

According to the CIAA, suspicious amounts of money had been deposited into accounts belonging to Paudel and his relatives, while the amounts were highly disproportionate to his known income.

The CIAA accused Paudel of illegally acquiring assets worth Rs 620 million, claiming that he had concealed money in Singapore and the United States. It alleged that he had received commissions from suppliers while working in the information technology sector and that the money had subsequently been channelled through accounts in the names of different individuals.

The CIAA also alleged that money held by Paudel in accounts at United Overseas Bank in Singapore and Bank of America in the United States had been acquired through corruption.

Paudel served as executive director of the Security Printing Centre for around five years. Before that, he worked as an engineer at the National Information Technology Centre.

The CIAA alleged that Paudel had taken bribes from foreign companies involved in transactions with various companies contracted by the Security Printing Centre.

The CIAA claimed that Paudel had Rs 289.5 million in Singapore alone in accounts held in his name.

To make the income appear legitimate, Paudel allegedly prepared documents showing that he had been appointed as a consultant at two Singapore-based companies, Bankotex and Instasef.

During its investigation, the CIAA determined that Paudel had illegally acquired property worth Rs 621.9 million. However, it said that only Rs 445.2 million could be traced, and sought the confiscation of property worth Rs 176.6 million that it claimed had been concealed.

Why was he sentenced to only two and a half years?

The Special Court convicted Paudel in the illegal property acquisition case.

An investigation into his assets covered the period from March 28, 2005, to April 12, 2023. During this period, Paudel was found to have received Rs 3.092 million in salary and allowances.

The Special Court deemed his salary and allowances, as well as assets acquired from the sale of shares, to be legitimate. It also declared more than Rs 300 million deposited into his accounts and received through remittances to be legitimate.

According to the Special Court’s verdict, Paudel’s net legitimate income amounted to only Rs 41.6 million.

A total of Rs 289.5 million was found in various accounts at United Overseas Bank in Singapore and in his wife’s Bank of America account in the United States. Of this amount, the Special Court deemed only Rs 37.2 million held in the account of Paudel’s wife, Elina Basnet, to be legitimate. It declared the remaining amount to be illegally acquired through corruption.

A total of Rs 461.1 million in assets belonging to Paudel was traced, but the source of only Rs 41.6 million could be established. According to the Special Court, the remaining amount had been acquired through corruption.

In its brief verdict, the Special Court stated that Paudel had committed an offence under Section 20(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 2002. Under Section 20(2) of the same Act, it sentenced him to two years in prison and imposed a fine of Rs 419,473,282.85, equivalent to the amount of illegally acquired property. It also ordered the confiscation of property equivalent to the same amount.

Although the Special Court found that Paudel had illegally acquired nearly Rs 420 million, the largest amount determined in a case involving illegal acquisition of property, it sentenced him to only two years in prison.

The Prevention of Corruption Act, 2002, was amended to add a provision under Section 20 that treats the acquisition of property through unlawful means as corruption. The law provides for one to three years in prison for acquiring disproportionate or unusually large assets through illegal means.

At the time the corruption case over illegal acquisition of property was filed against Paudel, the law provided for a two-year prison sentence. The Special Court imposed the sentence under the provision contained in Section 20(1) of the Act.

The additional six-month sentence was imposed for corruption committed while Paudel was holding a special-class government position.

Section 24 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 2002, provides for an additional prison sentence of up to three years for officials holding special-class positions, equivalent to the rank of secretary, if they are found guilty of corruption.

Under this provision, the Special Court imposed an additional six-month sentence on Paudel, who served as executive director of the Security Printing Centre.

Although the law allows the court to impose up to three additional years in prison, the Special Court imposed the minimum additional sentence of six months.

title.rendered: Former Congress chief whip Ishwari Devi to run for joint general secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Ishwari Devi Neupane, a former chief whip of the Nepali Congress parliamentary party and former chair of the State Affairs and Good Governance Committee, has announced her candidacy for joint general secretary at the party’s 15th General Convention.

Neupane has long been active in the party’s organisation building, democratic movements and parliamentary politics. She announced her candidacy with a commitment to develop the party into a stronger, more popular organisation connected with the people. She has served three times as a central member of the Nepali Congress and has also held important parliamentary responsibilities alongside her organisational work.

Announcing her candidacy, Neupane said she would play a significant role in making the party more popular, strong and trusted by the people.

“I will have an important role in the campaign to build the Nepali Congress into a popular party, strengthen the organisation further and establish it as the country’s number one party. I therefore sincerely appeal to all convention delegates to give me this opportunity by voting for me,” Neupane said.

Neupane said the party’s organisation needs to be made more orderly and effective from the village level to the centre, and that a new generation must be brought into the Congress mainstream.

According to her, her candidacy is focused on party unity, strengthening the organisation, respecting cadres and building closer ties with the public, so that the Congress can become a more effective political force.

Her candidacy is seen as a strong representation of women’s leadership at the 15th General Convention. She has also made it a priority to make women’s participation and role in the party’s central leadership more effective.

Announcing her candidacy for joint general secretary at the convention, which began on Sunday, Neupane expressed her commitment to use her political experience, her experience in organisation building and her continued contribution to the party more effectively in the coming term.

title.rendered: India played Brazil. Nepal is losing the chance to play at all

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The scene in Kolkata on Saturday was one Nepali football fans could only watch from a distance. More than 51,000 people packed Salt Lake Stadium as India took on Brazil. Vinicius Junior and his teammates walked onto the pitch, the Brazilian national anthem played and Indian players stood opposite one of the most decorated teams in international football.

Brazil won 4-0. But for India, the significance of the evening went beyond the score.

The match gave Indian players the chance to test themselves against the five-time world champions. It gave supporters the chance to watch one of football’s biggest teams play on Indian soil. It also showed what international football can offer even when the result does not go the home team’s way.

India will play Uruguay on October 6, having drawn with Panama on September 25. There is a full international programme ahead.

Nepal, by contrast, has no such programme.

Its national team should have been preparing for the SAFF Championship. Instead, Nepal will not even be at the tournament. For the first time in its history, Nepal has missed the SAFF Championship because of FIFA’s suspension of the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA). And that absence says more about the state of Nepali football than the loss of one tournament.

A tournament Nepal should have been playing

The SAFF Championship has traditionally been one of the biggest occasions on Nepal’s football calendar.

By this stage, the national team should have been assembling its squad, beginning preparations and building towards another campaign in South Asia.

Instead, there was no squad announcement, no training camp and no national-team buildup.

FIFA suspended ANFA on June 25, citing third-party interference in the association’s internal affairs. The suspension prevented Nepal’s national team and clubs from participating in international competitions.

When FIFA’s September 30 deadline for resolving the issues passed without a breakthrough, Nepal’s absence from the SAFF Championship became unavoidable.

For the players, that meant losing an important international tournament without ever getting the chance to compete for it.

It also meant another missed opportunity to play together, gain international experience and represent Nepal at home and abroad.

The damage, however, extends beyond the national team.

The crisis goes beyond FIFA

The dispute between the government and ANFA has gradually turned into a wider crisis for Nepali football.

The government has argued that ANFA has not done enough to address the issues surrounding the suspension. ANFA, on the other hand, has maintained that government intervention is at the centre of the dispute.

Neither side has been able to produce a solution acceptable to FIFA.

FIFA has reportedly set a number of conditions for lifting the suspension, including withdrawal of the National Sports Council’s March 25 decision, reinstatement of the existing ANFA executive committee and continuation of ANFA’s electoral process.

Repeated discussions have failed to resolve the disagreement.

The situation has also become more complicated because of separate investigations into ANFA treasurer Rabindra Joshi and accountant Sanjiv Pandey.

Both were arrested by the Central Investigation Bureau of Nepal Police and are being investigated over allegations including match-fixing and financial irregularities. The Supreme Court has not ordered their immediate release in response to habeas corpus petitions filed by the two.

While the institutional dispute continues, football activity has been disrupted.

The national league, women’s competitions and youth competitions have all been affected, leaving players and coaches uncertain about when the normal football calendar will resume.

More than 100 days without a solution

At one stage, the sports minister had indicated that discussions with FIFA were progressing and that the suspension could soon be lifted.

That optimism has not translated into a resolution. The suspension has now crossed the 100-day mark.

Nepal last played an international match on March 31, when it faced Laos. Six days earlier, the National Sports Council had suspended ANFA. Since then, Nepal’s international programme has effectively stalled.

The government is now considering whether it can continue domestic football even while the FIFA suspension remains in place.

Following discussions with former footballers, National Sports Council Member Secretary Ramcharitra Mehta said there had been an understanding to develop a plan to continue domestic leagues.

That may keep some form of football going at home. But it cannot replace international competition.

A domestic match cannot provide the same experience as a national-team game. It cannot replace the opportunity to play against teams from other countries. And it cannot undo the loss of tournaments that players should have been preparing for.

The cost is being paid on the field

This is where the institutional dispute becomes a football problem. The arguments are taking place between officials, government agencies and football administrators. The consequences, however, are being felt by players.

A generation of Nepali footballers is losing opportunities to play international matches at a time when regular competition and exposure are crucial to their development.

Players who should have been preparing for the SAFF Championship are instead playing domestic football or continuing their careers abroad.

The national team has no clear next opponent. Supporters have no clear next fixture to look forward to.

And young players have no clear indication of when they might get their chance to step into the national setup.

What happens next?

The contrast with India is difficult to ignore. India lost to Brazil. But India played Brazil.

Its players experienced the pressure of facing a world-class opponent. Its supporters filled a stadium. Its football system created an opportunity for its players to compete at the highest level available to them.

Nepal did not lose a match this weekend. It simply did not have one. That is the deeper concern.

The issue is not whether Nepal can compete with India, Brazil or any other team. It is whether Nepali football can create the conditions necessary for its players to compete at all.

Every missed international window means fewer opportunities. Every cancelled tournament means less experience. Every month spent in institutional uncertainty makes the return to normal football more difficult.

The SAFF Championship is already gone. The next challenge is making sure the same thing does not happen again.

For now, the players are waiting, the supporters are waiting and Nepali football is waiting for its administrators to find a way forward.

Brazil came to Kolkata and played. Nepal is still waiting for its next match.

title.rendered: Let me live in my present, says Eleena Chauhan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Singer Eleena Chauhan has urged the media and journalists to stop repeatedly linking her past and former relationship in news reports and commentary.

After social media comments began pairing her name with her ex-husband’s, Chauhan asked on Facebook that her present not be defined by past relationships.

“Let me live, let me live in my present,” she wrote. “Sometimes I see things in the news that I have never even imagined.”

Saying she has moved far ahead and left the past behind, Chauhan said that repeatedly tying old photographs and relationships to news stories reopens old wounds.

“I have put my old wounds behind me like a bad dream. Each time that past is dug up and old photos are pasted into a story, the wound is reopened,” she wrote.

She says the past is one chapter of her life, not her entire life. Please close that chapter.

She also said she does not need anyone else’s name to establish her identity.

“I say this not out of arrogance but with confidence. I do not need to lean on anyone’s name to build my identity,” she wrote.

Chauhan further warned of legal action if misleading content or material that harms her dignity is published or broadcast.

“I will now take legal action under the prevailing law against media outlets and individuals who keep spreading such misleading news that damages my self-respect,” she wrote.

title.rendered: CESCA sets up child-centred safe space for disaster-affected children in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The Center for Economic, Social and Climate Advancement (CESCA) has launched a 12-day safe space for children affected by recent disasters in Belkotgadhi, Nuwakot.

Called “Milan Aangan – A Child-Centered Post-Disaster Safe Space,” the initiative aims to support children’s emotional well-being, creativity and social connection. A team of seven volunteers is running activities including creative arts, painting, games, group activities, dancing and storytelling.

The initiative seeks to give children a safe and welcoming environment to play, express themselves, interact with peers and regain a sense of normalcy after difficult experiences. Alongside the activities, the team is observing children’s participation, interaction and emotional expressions through indirect and participatory approaches. It aims to better understand their psychosocial well-being and the kinds of support they may need.

“Milan Aangan is not simply about organising activities for children,” said Susan Sapkota, founder and chair of CESCA. “We believe that creating a safe space where children can play, express themselves, create and feel heard is an important part of supporting their well-being, particularly after a disaster. These seemingly small moments can contribute to confidence, connection, creativity and resilience.”

During the camp, children have taken part in mosaic art, painting, colouring, games such as hot potato, dancing and mindfulness sessions. CESCA said the activities are designed to encourage expression, teamwork, confidence and positive social interaction.

The initiative is supported by the Karmayog Foundation, with CESCA working alongside Setu Nepal and Nepal Rapid Action Team. The team has also brought medical supplies, humanitarian essentials, stationery and learning materials, sanitation supplies, menstrual hygiene materials and diapers to support the children and the community.

CESCA describes Milan Aangan as part of its broader Project Resilient Minds, which seeks to strengthen community resilience and promote child-centred psychosocial support after disasters. The organisation works at the intersection of climate change, social development, community resilience and youth engagement.

title.rendered: Manchester City supporters have been gaslit. What happens now?

content.rendered:
The Premier League has published the core findings of the independent commission investigating Manchester City Football Club. It finds the club guilty of all charges relating to serious financial breaches across nine seasons, from 2009-10 to 2017-18.

Among its findings were that City used “sham” commercial arrangements to inflate revenues and reduce costs, misstated its accounts and concealed its true financial position from auditors and regulators. The commission concluded that the club had intended to circumvent Premier League rules.

Manchester City has said it is “disappointed and surprised” by the decision, stating that it is “innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League”. It will pursue the appeal avenues open to the club.

It’s impossible to overstate the potential impact of this case on English football. Indeed, the findings have unleashed something approaching open season, as rival supporters, pundits and commentators are already demanding everything from points deductions and relegation to the stripping of titles. Arguments rage over whether an entire era of English football has now been irreparably tainted.

But amid the swirling mass of bloodlust surrounding Manchester City, it is worth considering the impact of this case on a group which is receiving less attention: the club’s supporters.

What the findings mean for fans

For City fans, the past few days have brought an uncomfortable reckoning. The ownership that transformed the club they love has now been found to have disgraced it.

Over the 18 years since Sheikh Mansour purchased Manchester City, the distinction between club and owner has become – perhaps understandably – increasingly blurred. City’s Abu Dhabi-backed ownership transformed perennial underachievers into a global powerhouse, while investing heavily in the club and its surrounding East Manchester community. In doing so, they accumulated enormous goodwill among supporters.

But in the context of the findings against City, it is clear that has also left a powerful sense of dissonance among the City fanbase.

For years, repeated denials and assurances created a fog of obfuscation around the allegations. Within it grew an increasingly conspiratorial impulse among people who should have known better, including claims that regulators and rival clubs were conspiring to keep City down. This has led to an extraordinary inversion through which some of the richest and most powerful owners in world football could be recast as victims of a system they have now been found to have systematically circumvented.

As recently as three days before the final findings were published, chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak wrote directly to fans insisting that Manchester City’s confidence in proving its innocence remained undiminished. He invoked key moments in the club’s recent history, such as victories in Istanbul and at Wembley. He warned of those seeking to “undermine” the club, and appealed to the strength of the “Manchester City family”.

That language is significant precisely because it is a blatant exploitation of the inherited relationship between supporters and Manchester City – its memories, loyalties and sense of collective belonging – in support of the current ownership. The commission’s findings make that exploitation impossible to ignore.

And there is a temptation here to offer Manchester City supporters an easy consolation. Whatever happened in the boardroom, nobody can take away the goals, trophies and memories. But I am not sure that is good enough.

Professional football depends upon a simple bargain. Supporters invest extraordinary quantities of time, money and emotion because they believe that, however unequal the resources available to different clubs might be, the competition itself has meaning.

Systematically circumvent those rules and the damage extends far beyond Manchester City. Other clubs competed for the same trophies, European places and prize money. Their supporters invested their own lives in those competitions too. Sporting integrity is not some bureaucratic technicality. It underpins the emotional meaning of football itself.

That makes what happens next vitally important. City supporters have been placed in an invidious position. Accepting the findings means confronting the possibility that one of the most glorious periods in their inherited story has been profoundly compromised. Anger, denial and even defiance are understandable responses to that rupture.

But the evidence now requires Manchester City supporters to make the distinction their owners have spent years blurring: Manchester City is not its ownership.

If this really is their club – an institution inherited through generations of families and communities – then supporters now have a responsibility to defend it. That means refusing to direct their anger exclusively towards the Premier League, rival supporters, journalists or some imagined external conspiracy. It means turning that anger towards the people who have brought their club into disrepute.

The same tribal loyalty that has been mobilised in defence of Manchester City’s owners can be mobilised against them. City supporters should demand accountability from an ownership that has exploited their trust, appropriated the heritage of a wonderful football club and, according to the commission’s findings, systematically circumvented the rules of the competition in which that club exists.

The question now is not whether Manchester City supporters still love their club. It is what their love for it requires them to do next.

title.rendered: Congress to increase number of office-bearers, including a senior vice president and central members

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The Nepali Congress is set to enlarge its central committee, including the number of office-bearers. The move follows suggestions from party ranks to the statute drafting committee to increase the number of office-bearers and central members.

The statute is being amended to accommodate more aspirants seeking party leadership. The leadership has come under pressure to include differing factions within the party, which is why it is adding positions.

Under the current provision, the party has 231 central members. The provision of 17 office-bearers will also be amended.

According to party sources, the amendment will make it mandatory for one of the vice presidents to be a woman. The current provision of two vice presidents will be amended to add one more.

The statute will be amended to reserve a quota for women among the vice presidents. The party also plans to create the post of senior vice president among them.

The party has not previously had a senior vice president. The post of general secretary will remain at two.

The party also plans to add the post of joint general secretary to the office-bearers.

According to top party leaders, a new provision will allow open competition for joint general secretary.

One of the leaders told Onlinekhabar, “Under the current provision, joint general secretaries are chosen based on inclusion, and the president nominates three. There has been discussion on amending this to add an open category for joint general secretary as well.”

Under the existing provision, candidates compete in eight clusters: Janajati, Madhesi, Tharu, Muslim, women, Khas Arya, backward regions and Dalit. The plan is to add an open category alongside the inclusive clusters for joint general secretary.

The party also plans to create additional central member posts. The current provision of 35 open-category members will be amended to increase the number. Leaders said how many will be added is still under discussion.

The statute amendment drafting committee, led by General Secretary Pradip Paudel, had drafted a statute under which the party president nominates 61 of the 231 central members.

That number will now increase. The drafting committee is still discussing the total once the senior vice president, joint general secretaries and central members are added.

The provisions for 21 members from among those under 35, seven chosen from professionals and intellectuals, and six chosen from the public relations committee will not be amended.

The statute prepared by the drafting committee will be presented to the party. After the Central Committee endorses it, the general convention hall will pass it.

Besides General Secretary Paudel, the statute amendment drafting committee includes Jiwan Pariyar, Ishwari Neupane and Rajiv Dhungana as members, with Pratap Paudel as member secretary.

title.rendered: 6 construction companies blacklisted for contract violations

content.rendered:
Jumla, October 4

Six construction companies contracted to build and upgrade roads along the Karnali Highway have been blacklisted for violating their contracts.

The companies were also contracted to maintain roads linking Jumla with the Manang and Mustang districts. The Public Procurement Monitoring Office took action against the companies following reports submitted by the Road Division Office, Jumla.

Road Division Office Chief Shravan Kumar Mahatara said the office had initiated action against the construction companies and forwarded the reports to its head office in Kathmandu.

Binamra Construction Service of Surkhet, which was contracted for road construction from fiscal year 2075/76 to 2079/80, has been blacklisted for three years.

Dhruba Building Service of Birendranagar has been barred from participating in public procurement for two years, while Abinash Construction Service of Chhayanath, Mugu, has been blacklisted for one year.

According to Sub-Engineer Birendra Rawal of the Road Division Office, Shankar Mali Construction Service of Kathmandu and Man Shahi Construction Service of Kalikot have each been blacklisted for three years, while Kashyap Contractors Service of Kathmandu has been blacklisted for two years.

The action was taken under Clause 63 of the Public Procurement Act, 2007. The companies are barred from participating in public procurement during their respective periods of blacklisting.

Industry closures rise in Jumla

Meanwhile, the number of industries being closed in Jumla has been increasing. According to Tanka Prasad Neupane, chief of the Industry and Consumer Protection Office, 180 industries were closed in fiscal year 2082/83, while 188 were registered and 334 renewed their registration.

In the commerce sector, 61 firms were registered, 58 renewed their registration, and 52 were closed. The office collected around Rs 1.6 million in revenue during the fiscal year, Neupane said.

In the first two months of the current fiscal year, 43 firms have been registered, while 119 have renewed their registration and five have been closed. Eleven firms were registered under the commerce sector during the period.

Neupane said the registration of new industries has been declining for the past four years, while closures have been increasing. Newly registered businesses are engaged in production, agriculture and forestry, services, tourism, construction and information technology.

title.rendered: Gauthali earns Rs 260 million by 75th day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The film ‘Gauthali’ has completed 75 days in theatres. Released on July 17, it entered its 76th day on Thursday.

Producer Suman Giri said the film has collected Rs 260 million so far. It has sold 943,331 tickets in that time.

According to the Film Development Board’s Cinepah data released last Monday, ‘Gauthali’ had grossed Rs 259,584,640 as of September 27.

Already the second-highest-grossing film in the Nepali film industry, ‘Gauthali’ trails only ‘Purna Bahadur Ko Sarangi’.

Directed by Dr Kapil Rijal, the film stars Arun Chhetri, Simran Khadka, Madan Krishna Shrestha, Prakash Ghimire, Loonibhat Tuladhar, Rabindra Jha, Ishwari Baral, Sanjog Rasaili, Sita Devi Timilsina and Laxminath Timilsina, among others.

Produced under the banners of Bhola Rijal Production and Suman Giri Production, the film has Sarala Rijal as executive producer. Suman Giri and Dr Kapil Rijal are the producers.

A 22-year-old man was injured after a gun went off at a house in Devdaha Municipality, Rupandehi, on Saturday.

According to the District Police Office, Rupandehi, the incident occurred when a man showed a pistol to a person who had arrived at the house.

Ryan Khatri Chhetri of Devdaha-7 was injured after the pistol held by Dipak Kharel accidentally discharged at Kharel’s house.

Toronto Sixers, featuring Nepal women’s cricket team captain Indu Barma, won the women’s title at the Canada Super 60 on Sunday.

Toronto defeated Vancouver Warriors by six wickets in the final, completed on Sunday morning. Chasing a target of 86 runs, Toronto reached the target with three balls to spare.

title.rendered: RSP to launch organisational expansion campaign from Lumbini provincial capital

content.rendered:
Dang, October 4

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) is set to launch an organisational expansion, public outreach and election-focused campaign from Maurighat, the capital of Lumbini Province, in Dang.

The party will inaugurate its provincial office in Maurighat after relocating it from Lamahi. RSP General Secretary Bipin Acharya and all party lawmakers elected from Dang are scheduled to arrive in Deukhuri today to participate in the office inauguration and campaign activities.

RSP Dang Chair Kiran Khanal said the campaign would begin at the provincial level and expand to local levels, electoral constituencies, wards and neighbourhoods.

In its first phase, the party plans to expand its organisation to ward and neighbourhood levels, engage directly with local residents and link local problems and needs with its political agenda.

Acharya, who is also a lawmaker, is scheduled to meet all government office chiefs in Dang on Sunday to discuss the state of development projects and the government’s work and priorities.

Tourism Minister Khadkaraj Paudel is also scheduled to visit Dang on October 8 to inspect Tarigaun Airport in Tulsipur, among other activities.

The RSP has been expanding its organisation across the country in preparation for local-level elections. The party plans to mobilise lawmakers and central members across all 753 local levels in 77 districts for the campaign.

The party said the campaign will include discussions with citizens on local government performance, policy initiatives and its candidate selection process for upcoming elections.

title.rendered: Homlal and Sunsari win Asia Trail Master titles

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Nepali runners Homlal Shrestha and Sunsari Rokaya won the Asia Trail Master (ATM) Championship titles on Saturday.

The fifth edition of the ATM Mu Cang Chai Ultra Trail was held in Mu Cang Chai, Vietnam. Nepal’s Gopal Tamang finished second, while Kieu Suelo of the Philippines came third in the men’s race.

Forty-two-year-old Homlal became the first Nepali runner to win the Asia Trail Master title.

In the women’s race, 24-year-old Sunsari faced a strong challenge from 19-year-old fellow Nepali runner Kalpana Budha. Kalpana finished just a few seconds behind Sunsari to take second place, while Hong Kong’s Celine Louibire finished third.

Nepali runners dominated the top 10 in both the men’s and women’s races. Dhir Bahadur Budha finished eighth, and Bishal Rai finished 10th.

title.rendered: Nepal must put agrobiodiversity at the centre of regenerative agriculture

content.rendered:
Nepal’s agricultural future may depend on something it already has in abundance — diversity.

Across the country’s mountains, hills and plains, farmers have cultivated crops and raised livestock adapted to very different climates, soils and landscapes. Over generations, they have selected seeds, developed farming practices and preserved knowledge suited to the places where they live.

That diversity is more than an agricultural inheritance. It is a resource for dealing with some of the biggest challenges facing Nepal’s food system — climate change, declining soil health, changing diets, rising production costs and increasingly unpredictable weather.

If regenerative agriculture is to become more than a new label for sustainable farming, agrobiodiversity needs to be at its centre.

Diversity is a form of resilience

Agricultural diversity gives farmers choices.

A farming system that relies heavily on a single crop variety can be highly productive under the right conditions, but it can also be vulnerable when those conditions change. Drought, floods, new pests, diseases or shifts in temperature can quickly turn uniformity into a liability.

Genetic diversity provides a buffer.

Nepal’s agricultural genetic resources include crops, livestock, forages, agro-insects, microorganisms and aquatic species. They are spread across the country’s extraordinary ecological range, from around 60 metres above sea level to more than 5,000 metres in the Himalayas. According to the source material, these resources account for nearly 28 percent of Nepal’s total biological diversity.

But their value cannot be measured only in biological terms.

Local crops and livestock are tied to what communities eat, how food is prepared, local festivals and traditions, household incomes and the knowledge passed from one generation to the next. A local seed variety may carry traits that allow it to survive in poor soils, tolerate drought or mature within a short growing season.

Those traits may become increasingly valuable as Nepal’s climate changes.

The cost of becoming more uniform

Despite its agricultural diversity, Nepal’s research and development system remains heavily reliant on genetic material from outside the country. An estimated 95 percent of the germplasm used in agricultural research and development is sourced externally.

At the same time, the widespread promotion of uniform, high-performing varieties has contributed to the marginalisation of local landraces.

There is nothing inherently wrong with using improved varieties or introducing genetic material from elsewhere. Agricultural research depends on the exchange of genetic resources, and improved varieties can bring important gains in productivity and farmer incomes.

The concern arises when diversity is lost in the process.

A variety that performs exceptionally well under one set of conditions may be less useful when those conditions change. Once a local landrace disappears from farmers’ fields, the loss is not simply a loss of a seed. It can mean losing a collection of traits, farming knowledge and cultural practices that may be difficult or impossible to recover.

The increasing dependence on external inputs can add another layer of vulnerability. Intensive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides can place pressure on soils and ecosystems, while replacing locally adapted practices with standardised technologies can weaken the systems that have traditionally maintained agricultural diversity.

The question, therefore, should not be whether Nepal should modernise its agriculture.

It should be what kind of modern agriculture Nepal wants.

Conservation cannot stop at a seed bank

Protecting agricultural biodiversity does not mean simply collecting seeds and putting them into storage.

Seed banks are essential for safeguarding genetic resources, particularly when varieties are at risk of disappearing. But conservation is most meaningful when diversity continues to be grown, eaten, exchanged and improved.

This is the idea behind “conservation through use”.

Local varieties need to remain part of living agricultural systems. Farmers should be able to grow them in their fields, sell them in markets and pass them on to the next generation.

That requires a different relationship between farmers, researchers, government agencies, businesses and consumers.

It could mean supporting the continued cultivation of landraces, developing agroecological production systems, improving local varieties through participatory breeding and establishing community seed banks. School and community field gene banks, agro-gene sanctuaries, crop-specific conservation parks and seed exchanges could also help keep agricultural diversity visible and active.

In some cases, lost or neglected crop varieties could even be reintroduced into the communities where they once grew.

The principle is simple. Conservation should not freeze agricultural diversity in the past. It should allow it to evolve.

Farmers will conserve what they can make a living from

There is also an economic reality that conservation programmes sometimes overlook.

Farmers cannot be expected to maintain varieties that have little economic value simply because they are culturally or biologically important.

If a local crop takes more work to produce but earns less in the market than a commercially promoted alternative, farmers will naturally face pressure to switch.

That is why markets matter.

Native crops and products can create new income opportunities if they are supported by better processing, packaging, branding, quality standards and market development. Protecting geographical indications and other forms of intellectual property can also help communities retain value from products associated with particular places and traditions.

Local markets can play a role too. Raithane haat bazaars, homestays, farm stays and programmes that bring local foods into tourism and hospitality can connect agricultural diversity with consumers.

The aim should not simply be to turn every traditional crop into a premium product.

Commercialisation needs to be done carefully, with community rights protected and farmers and knowledge holders recognised for their contributions. Traditional knowledge and genetic resources should not become commodities that can be appropriated without consent or fair benefit-sharing.

What regenerative agriculture could mean for Nepal

Regenerative agriculture is often discussed in terms of soil health, biodiversity, natural processes and reducing dependence on harmful external inputs.

These ideas have obvious relevance to Nepal.

But there is a danger in treating regenerative agriculture as a single package that can be applied in the same way everywhere.

A farmer in Mustang does not face the same conditions as a farmer in the mid-hills or the Tarai. Growing seasons, water availability, soils, crops, livestock and climate risks vary enormously.

Nepal therefore needs a regenerative approach rooted in its own landscapes.

That means recognising farmers not simply as recipients of agricultural programmes, but as custodians and innovators. Their knowledge can complement scientific research in areas such as seed selection, soil management, pest control, food processing and climate adaptation.

The most effective solutions may emerge when these two forms of knowledge work together.

Lessons from Mustang and Manang

Some of the work taking place in Mustang and Manang offers an indication of what this could look like.

Community-led initiatives in these mountain districts have included collecting and repatriating diverse crop accessions and working with farmers to improve local landraces.

Such efforts matter beyond the communities where they take place.

Mountain crops have evolved under difficult conditions — short growing seasons, cold temperatures, limited water and high elevations. The traits that allow them to survive in these environments could become increasingly valuable as climate change alters growing conditions elsewhere.

Ideas such as a Himalayan Seed Vault, a Mountain Agro-Gene Sanctuary and community gene banks for safety duplication could strengthen long-term conservation.

But storage alone is not enough.

The most useful conservation systems will be those that maintain a living connection between genetic resources and the communities that have developed and used them.

From local diversity to wider markets

Nepal has the raw material for a distinctive agricultural identity.

Its native crops, livestock, foods, seeds and farming practices could find wider markets. But simply promoting them as “traditional” or “indigenous” will not be enough.

Farmers and local enterprises need access to research, processing facilities, quality improvement, certification, branding and reliable markets.

Scientific research can play an important role here. It can help improve varieties, understand nutritional properties, develop better processing methods and identify new markets.

But scientific improvement should complement local knowledge rather than replace it.

That requires a policy shift.

Nepal should strengthen farmers’ rights and community knowledge, support local seed enterprises and community seed banks, create incentives for cultivating landraces and invest more in research on native genetic resources. Public institutions could also use procurement policies to create demand for diverse, locally produced foods.

Conservation could be linked more deliberately with nutrition, tourism and rural enterprise.

And perhaps most importantly, farmers need fair prices and dependable markets if they are expected to maintain diversity that benefits society as a whole.

A strategic choice for Nepal

Agrobiodiversity should not be treated as a niche environmental issue.

It is connected to food security, climate resilience, rural livelihoods, nutrition and cultural continuity.

For too long, agricultural success has often been measured primarily through productivity — how much a particular variety can produce, how quickly it grows or how efficiently it responds to external inputs.

Those measures matter. But they do not tell the whole story.

A resilient agricultural system should also be judged by whether it maintains genetic diversity, protects soil health, produces nutritious food, supports farmers and retains the knowledge that allows communities to adapt to changing conditions.

Nepal has an opportunity to build an agricultural model around what it already possesses rather than continually looking elsewhere for the next solution.

That does not mean rejecting improved varieties, modern science or international research. It means bringing them into a system where local genetic resources, farmer knowledge and ecological conditions are treated as assets rather than obstacles to modernisation.

The future of Nepalese agriculture will not be secured by replacing diversity with uniformity.

It will depend on whether we can conserve that diversity, continue to improve it and create a future in which farmers have good reasons to keep growing it.

That is where regenerative agriculture should begin.

title.rendered: Top party leaders set to attend Nepali Congress general convention opening

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The opening ceremony of the Nepali Congress’s 15th General Convention is being held at Tundikhel in Kathmandu today. The Nepali Congress has invited senior leaders from various political parties to attend the ceremony. However, not all of the invited leaders will be attending.

Similarly, Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’, coordinator of the Nepali Communist Party, is expected to attend the event. Party spokesperson Prakash Jwala said Prachanda himself will address the opening ceremony. According to Prachanda’s chief personal secretary, Govinda Acharya, attending the Nepali Congress general convention is included in his schedule for today.

Rastriya Prajatantra Party Chair Rajendra Lingden will also attend the ceremony. Party spokesperson Mohan Shrestha said Lingden, who is currently in his home district of Jhapa, will travel to Kathmandu today to attend the event.

Janata Samajbadi Party Nepal Chair Upendra Yadav will not attend. According to his secretariat, Yadav has asked Co-chair Sharat Singh Bhandari to represent the party at the opening ceremony.

title.rendered: More than 732,000 people enrolled in health insurance in Sudurpaschim

content.rendered:
Sudurpaschim, October 4

More than 732,000 people in Sudurpaschim Province have enrolled in the health insurance programme, according to the Health Insurance Board’s Sudurpaschim office.

As of the end of Bhadra, 732,752 people had been enrolled in the programme, according to data entered into the Health Insurance Management Information System.

Province coordinator Janak Bahadur Saud said Kailali has the highest number of beneficiaries, with 361,979 people enrolled. Kanchanpur has 87,087 beneficiaries, followed by Achham with 67,308, Bajhang with 52,211, Bajura with 45,454, and Baitadi with 34,270.

Similarly, 33,378 people in Dadeldhura, 27,862 in Doti and 23,203 in Darchula have enrolled in the programme.

The health insurance programme was launched on March 25, 2016, as a social security scheme aimed at ensuring affordable and quality healthcare and reducing the financial burden of major medical expenses. The Health Insurance Board was established under the Health Insurance Act 2017 and Health Insurance Regulations 2018 to manage the programme.

Under the scheme, a family of up to five members pays an annual contribution of Rs 3,500, while each additional member pays Rs 700. An insured family of up to five members is entitled to healthcare services worth up to Rs 100,000, with Rs 20,000 added for each additional member, up to a maximum of Rs 200,000.

People enrolled in the programme can receive outpatient, emergency, laboratory and general surgical services at designated government hospitals.

title.rendered: Lamichhane Foundation donates over £51,000 for flood relief

content.rendered:
London, October 4

The Lamichhane Foundation has donated NPR 1.07 crore (£51,727) to support victims of the recent floods in Nepal’s Bhote Koshi region.

The UK Charity Commission-registered foundation, chaired by UK-based entrepreneur and philanthropist Rabindra Jung Lamichhane, transferred the donation directly to the official bank account of the Embassy of Nepal in London.

The embassy said the funds will be transferred to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

During a ceremony at the embassy, Lamichhane handed over the cheque to Bipin Duwadi, Chargé d’Affaires at the Embassy of Nepal in London, and Vidushi Rana, a member of parliament from the Rastriya Swatantra Party.

Calls for diaspora support

Speaking at the event, Rana thanked Lamichhane for the contribution and said support from the Nepali diaspora would be important for post-disaster rehabilitation and reconstruction.

She said Nepalis living abroad, including those in the UK, had responded generously following the floods.

Rana also said she had met British parliamentarians during her visit to the UK to seek support for Nepal’s post-flood reconstruction efforts.

According to Rana, Nepal could need to spend nearly 10 percent of its GDP on reconstruction, making international support important.

Former British Labour Party MP Virendra Sharma also praised Lamichhane’s contribution, saying he had been involved in humanitarian initiatives as well as efforts to strengthen UK-Nepal relations.

Duwadi expressed gratitude to the foundation and recalled Lamichhane’s support during the 2015 earthquake and the COVID-19 pandemic.

He said the Nepal government is currently focused on rehabilitation and reconstruction following the latest disaster.

‘I cannot remain a passive bystander’

Lamichhane said supporting Nepal during times of crisis was a moral responsibility.

“I love my country. When disaster strikes, I cannot remain a passive bystander,” he said. “Seeing the devastation caused by the recent floods broke my heart, which motivated me to raise these funds.”

He also thanked donors and friends of Nepal who contributed through the foundation.

Lamichhane, who founded London-based fashion businesses Genie London and Ravi Famous Ltd, has been involved in various humanitarian and community initiatives in Nepal and the UK.

The foundation said his previous support has included relief following the 2015 earthquake and assistance during the COVID-19 pandemic.

During the 2015 earthquake, Lamichhane provided relief materials through the Nepal Army and Nepal Police and donated NPR 51 lakh to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

During the second wave of COVID-19, he donated NPR 15 lakh to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund and helped provide 33 portable oxygen concentrators to Nepal in cooperation with a UK-based organisation.

The foundation also said Lamichhane has supported education and youth development through scholarships and sports initiatives, while contributing to cultural and community projects in Nepal and the UK.

He currently supports scholarships for 55 students through the Ravichandra Trust in Nepal.

Lamichhane is also involved in UK-Nepal trade and investment initiatives and has facilitated several meetings and engagements involving Nepali and British political and business leaders.

content.rendered:

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

Westerly winds are partially affecting various areas in the Karnali and Sudurpashchim Provinces, as well as the western parts of the Gandaki and Lumbini Provinces. Meanwhile, the monsoon winds are also making their presence felt across all regions of Koshi, Madhesh, and Bagmati Provinces, along with the remaining areas of Gandaki and Lumbini Provinces.\

According to the meteorological forecasting division, the Himalayan and hilly regions of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini Provinces are expected to have generally overcast skies today. In contrast, the Himalayan and hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpashchim Provinces are likely to see partly cloudy conditions.

The Terai regions throughout the country are expected to remain partly cloudy as well. Moderate rainfall or even some snowfall is anticipated in certain spots within the Himalayan and hilly regions of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini Provinces, with isolated showers also possible in the Himalayan and hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpashchim Provinces.

Light precipitation is on the horizon for some isolated locations in the Terai regions of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini Provinces.

title.rendered: 300 families displaced by landslides in Parbat

content.rendered:
Parbat, October 4

Landslides have displaced 300 families in Parbat district, with 170 houses completely destroyed and another 131 partially damaged.

According to the District Administration Office, six of the district’s seven local levels have been affected. Jaljala Rural Municipality has been hit the hardest, with 113 houses damaged and 58 others at risk of landslides. A total of 171 families in Jaljala have been displaced.

Other local levels have also reported significant damage. Two houses in Kushma Municipality, 20 in Falebas Municipality, nine in Bihadi Rural Municipality, two in Mahashila Rural Municipality and 15 in Modi Rural Municipality have been destroyed.

Chief District Officer Ganga Bahadur Chhetri said 131 houses across the district have sustained partial damage.

The landslides and floods have also damaged five school buildings, an agricultural farm, a temple, a health centre and a police station. The Maldhunga Bridge along the Mid-Hill Highway and a suspension bridge connecting Parbat and Baglung have also been damaged.

Rural roads in the district remain blocked. CDO Chhetri said it would take a few more days to reopen the Falebas-Bihadi and Lungkhudeurali-Huwas roads along the Kaligandaki Corridor.

Meanwhile, the local administration, local governments, the Nepal Red Cross Society and other social organisations are providing tents, food, utensils, clothing, and hygiene and medical supplies to the affected families.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress to use paper ballots for 15th General Convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The Nepali Congress will not use electronic voting machines to elect its new leadership at the party’s 15th General Convention.

The party has decided to conduct the election using traditional paper ballots after concluding that electronic voting would not significantly reduce the time required to announce the results.

The 15th General Convention is being held at Kathmandu’s Khula Manch on Sunday. According to the election schedule, registration of candidacies for the new party leadership and central working committee will begin on Monday.

Voting will be conducted at three locations — Khula Manch, the National Assembly Hall and Nepal Academy in Kamaladi.

A Congress leader said discussions had been held with Ram and Laxman about the possibility of using electronic voting machines. However, the party was informed that announcing the results within a day or two would not be possible given the participation of more than 7,000 convention representatives.

“We discussed the electronic voting machines with Ram and Laxman. But they said that with more than 7,000 representatives, it would not be possible to produce the results within one or two days. So, we concluded that voting should be conducted using the traditional paper ballot system,” the leader said.

The Congress is expecting more than 7,500 representatives to participate in the convention, which will elect the party’s leadership and central committee for the next term.

title.rendered: Where have all the fireflies gone?

content.rendered:
There was something magical about a power cut during the monsoon when I was growing up.

Once the lights inside the house went out, we would often wander outside. The darkness did not feel empty. Fireflies flickered among the bushes, along streams and over the edges of rice fields. Sometimes there seemed to be hundreds of them, blinking on and off without any obvious rhythm.

You did not need to know anything about ecology to be fascinated by them.

For many Nepalis who grew up before the rapid spread of concrete and artificial lighting, fireflies are part of that childhood landscape. They were simply there.

But I wonder how many children growing up in Nepal today will have the same memory.

The places where fireflies once appeared are changing quickly. Fields are being built over. Streams are being narrowed or polluted. Bright LED lights have replaced much of the darkness around homes, roads and public spaces.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, the fireflies are becoming harder to find.

We have become very good at noticing the disappearance of large animals. Nepal rightly celebrates the recovery of tigers and greater one-horned rhinos. These are remarkable conservation achievements, and they deserve the attention they receive.

But conservation is not only about animals large enough to appear on a wildlife poster.

There is an entire world of insects around us that we know surprisingly little about. Fireflies are one small part of that world, and their decline should make us pause.

We barely know what we have

One of the problems is that we do not have a good picture of Nepal’s fireflies to begin with.

There are roughly 2,200 described firefly species around the world, but Nepal’s own diversity remains poorly documented. Historical records go back to the 1830s, yet only a small number of species have been formally recorded in the country.

Even basic identification can be a problem. Local reports have at times identified Nepalese fireflies as Luciola cruciata, a species associated with Japan. Errors like these may sound minor, but they point to a larger problem. If we cannot reliably identify the species living here, it becomes much harder to know where they occur, how their populations are changing or what is causing those changes.

That matters because fireflies are not particularly resilient creatures.

Their lives begin on the ground. Firefly larvae can spend months or even years in soil, leaf litter and damp places, where they hunt small organisms and pests. They depend on the kind of moist, relatively undisturbed environment that is becoming increasingly difficult to find.

Pesticides add another pressure.

Agricultural chemicals are widely used across Nepal, and their effects do not necessarily stop at the crop they are intended to protect. Chemicals that enter soil and water can affect organisms that were never the target.

For a firefly larva living in that soil, the consequences can be serious.

Then, once the firefly finally reaches adulthood, there is another problem waiting above the ground.

Light.

When the night is no longer dark

Fireflies use their flashes to communicate, including to find mates. That simple exchange becomes much harder when the surrounding environment is flooded with artificial light.

Streetlights. Vehicle headlights. Buildings that remain brightly lit through the night.

All of them change the darkness that fireflies evolved to navigate.

It is easy to think of light pollution as a problem for astronomers who can no longer see the stars. But artificial light changes the behaviour of living organisms too.

And fireflies are particularly vulnerable because their entire courtship depends on being able to see one another.

This is becoming an increasingly important question for Nepal as places that still have fireflies begin to attract visitors.

Pokhara is one example. Firefly-watching has been promoted around areas near Phewa Lake as a form of night-time tourism. There is obvious appeal in it. People are willing to travel to see something that has become increasingly rare.

But that creates a strange contradiction.

The more successful firefly tourism becomes, the greater the pressure on the places where fireflies live.

Visitors walking along stream edges and lakeshores can disturb vegetation and soil where larvae live. Flashlights and cameras can disrupt the darkness. More buildings and decorative lighting can make the habitat less suitable in the first place.

If fireflies are going to become a tourism attraction, their habitat cannot simply be treated as a backdrop.

The fireflies have to come first.

A blind spot in conservation

There is also a bigger question here about how we think about conservation in Nepal.

Our laws have historically been designed around the animals we can easily see and name. The National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act, 1973, for example, was built around specific groups of protected wildlife, with its schedules focusing on mammals, birds and reptiles.

Insects are largely absent from that framework.

That does not mean Nepal has no laws that can protect them. Environmental and pesticide legislation provides tools that could help. The Environment Protection Act, 2019, for example, provides a broader framework for environmental protection, while the Pesticides Management Act, 2019 and Pesticide Management Regulations, 2024 provide mechanisms for regulating agricultural chemicals.

The problem is often less about having a law on paper than about what happens afterwards.

A stream can be important habitat for countless small organisms, but if its edges are steadily built over, lit up and polluted, the damage is not necessarily going to make headlines.

A rhino disappearing from a national park would rightly trigger an alarm. A population of insects disappearing from a wetland may not even be noticed. That is partly because we have not done enough work to find out what is there.

Start by looking

There is no single solution to the disappearance of fireflies.

But the first step should be surprisingly simple.

We need to start looking.

Universities and researchers could work together to document the firefly species found across Nepal and establish where populations remain. Citizen-science projects could allow people to record sightings using their phones. Such projects would not replace scientific research, but they could help researchers understand where fireflies are still being seen and where they are disappearing.

There are also practical things communities can do.

If firefly-watching becomes part of local tourism, visitor numbers should be controlled. Flashlights and flash photography should be restricted. Important breeding areas should be protected from people walking through them. And unnecessary lighting around known habitats should be reduced.

Farmers and local authorities also have a role to play in reducing the unnecessary use of pesticides and protecting streams, wetlands and other damp habitats.

None of this is as dramatic as counting tigers.

There is no single photograph of a firefly that will generate the same excitement as a tiger emerging from the forest.

But perhaps that is precisely why they are easy to overlook.

A firefly does not announce that an ecosystem is changing. It simply stops appearing.

One summer there are fewer of them. Then fewer again. Eventually, a child grows up without ever seeing the night filled with those tiny flashes.

By then, we may realise that we have lost much more than a childhood memory.

Fireflies are part of the ecosystems around us. Their lives depend on clean water, healthy soil, vegetation and darkness. When they disappear, they may be telling us something about the condition of those environments too.

Perhaps the next time we talk about Nepal’s conservation success, we should look beyond the animals that make the biggest headlines.

And perhaps, on a warm monsoon evening, we should turn off a few lights, step outside and look carefully.

There may be a world disappearing in the darkness that we have not yet learned to notice.

title.rendered: Chyangra from Dolpa head to Pokhara and Kathmandu for Dashain

content.rendered:
Surkhet, October 4

Chyangra brought from Upper Dolpa for Dashain sales have begun making their way towards Pokhara and Kathmandu via Mustang.

The goats were brought from Chharkatangsong Rural Municipality in Upper Dolpa to Mustang by crossing the Himalayan terrain on foot.

Traders from Tripurasundari Municipality in Dolpa are now transporting the chyangra through Mustang towards markets in Pokhara and Kathmandu.

According to trader Shivananda Giri of Tripurasundari, traders are aiming to bring more than 1,000 chyangra to the market this year in response to consumer demand.

“We are bringing the chyangra down to the markets after crossing the mountains. We have started bringing them down based on consumer demand,” Giri said.

A difficult journey from the highlands to the market

Bringing chyangra from Upper Dolpa to the market is far from an easy journey.

The mountainous terrain means the animals have to be herded on foot over long distances. The chyangra are brought down towards Mustang after crossing high-altitude areas, including the Bhyarol region, before being transported onwards through Pokhara to other markets.

Their journey connects the high Himalayan grazing grounds with consumers’ kitchens in the cities.

Demand for chyangra traditionally rises during Dashain, prompting traders to collect the animals from Upper Dolpa and transport them to major markets for sale during the festival.
