title.rendered: New bill proposes subsidised loans, tax breaks for smart homes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The government has proposed a new legal framework aimed at helping citizens aspiring to build their own homes, with provisions for subsidised loans, tax exemptions and affordable instalment plans.

The Ministry of Infrastructure Development has tabled a bill in the Federal Parliament seeking to amend the Building Act, 1998. The proposed legislation would facilitate financial packages in coordination with banks and financial institutions for the construction of modern, safe, earthquake-resistant and smart homes.

Once the bill is enacted, procedures to be introduced under the law could allow subsidised housing loans with down payments of as little as Rs 500,000 and monthly instalments of around Rs 11,000.

Legal provision for subsidised loans and instalments

Clause 16J of the proposed bill introduces special provisions for the “construction and promotion of smart homes.”

The provision allows all three levels of government to coordinate with banks and financial institutions, insurance companies and cooperatives to provide subsidised loans for the development of safe and technology-friendly housing aimed at improving citizens’ quality of life.

The government may also provide grants, tax exemptions and other financial incentives to encourage the construction of such homes.

The provision is intended to make it possible for low- and middle-income families to build or purchase homes without having to arrange a large amount of capital upfront, instead paying a minimum down payment followed by regular monthly instalments.

Free map approval and full exemption from fees

The bill also seeks to reduce the cost and administrative burden involved in home construction.

Clause 8 classifies residential structures based on standard designs that are safe and earthquake-resistant as “smart homes.”

Under sub-clause 11(2), local governments would be required to provide a 100 percent exemption from map preparation and map approval fees when applications are submitted for the construction of such smart homes and buildings using traditional technologies.

Local governments would also be required to provide standard house designs free of charge.

Cash grants for low-income families building their first home

The bill also proposes financial assistance for extremely poor families building their first residential home for their own use.

Under the proposed citizen housing provision, local governments would provide free technical consultation, standard designs and locally available construction materials.

In addition, extremely poor families recommended by local governments would be entitled to direct cash grants of at least Rs 50,000 from the federal government and Rs 25,000 from the provincial government.

The exact mechanism for implementing the subsidised loans, instalment plans and other financial incentives would be determined through guidelines and financial procedures to be introduced after the bill is passed.

The proposed framework is expected to make safe housing more accessible to low-income citizens by combining low upfront payments, affordable monthly instalments, fee exemptions and direct government support.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress 15th General Convention starts today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 4

The 15th General Convention of the Nepali Congress will begin on Sunday, with the party set to hold its opening ceremony at Kathmandu’s Khula Manch.

The convention is being held under the slogan, “Respect tradition, resolve for change — a strong Nepali Congress for a prosperous Nepal.”

The opening ceremony will begin at 2 pm on Sunday. The closed session and other convention activities will be held on Monday and Tuesday.

According to the Central Election Committee, elections for the party’s new leadership and other positions have been scheduled for October 7 and 8.

The party registered convention representatives on Friday and Saturday. Congress spokesperson Devraj Chalise said each representative was required to pay Rs 3,500 for registration.

Registered representatives have been provided with a bag containing the party statute, a diary, a ballpoint pen, food and snack coupons, and an identity card.

More than 7,500 representatives to participate

More than 7,500 convention representatives are expected to participate in the general convention, according to spokesperson Chalise.

“This time, more than 7,500 representatives are participating, which is the largest convention in the history of the Nepali Congress,” Chalise said at a press conference held at Khula Manch on Saturday.

He said the party would seek to make the convention more about policy than simply selecting party leaders.

“We will try to turn this convention into a convention for policy selection rather than merely leadership selection,” he said.

RSP, UML and other parties invited

The Nepali Congress has invited the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), as well as opposition parties including the CPN-UML and the Nepal Communist Party, to the opening ceremony.

Guests have also been invited from India, China, the United States and more than half a dozen other countries.

However, the Congress said the number of foreign guests attending could be limited because of changes to the date of the opening ceremony.

Closed session from Monday

Following Sunday’s opening ceremony, the closed session will begin on Monday.

Party spokesperson Chalise said the convention would discuss the party’s future policies, programmes and various reports on contemporary issues.

Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa will present a policy paper outlining the party’s political, economic, production, employment and foreign policy perspectives for the next five years, according to Chalise.

Hotels booked for representatives, accommodation costs to be borne by delegates

The Congress has arranged hotel accommodation in several parts of Kathmandu, including Gaushala, Koteshwor, Lazimpat, Thamel, New Bus Park, Sundhara, Balaju and Kalanki.

According to Lilaprasad Dhakal, president of the Nepal Democratic Small Hotel Entrepreneurs Association and a member of the accommodation management committee, hotels have been booked to accommodate around 10,000 representatives and supporters.

Representatives from Koshi and Madhesh provinces have been allocated hotels in Gaushala and Koteshwor, while those from Bagmati will stay in Lazimpat and Thamel.

Representatives from Gandaki and Lumbini will be accommodated in Balaju and New Bus Park, while those from Karnali and Sudurpaschim will stay in Sundhara and Kalanki.

Representatives from Nepali Congress sister organisations abroad will be accommodated in Lazimpat and Thamel.

The party said district-level representatives, representatives of overseas Nepali Congress chapters and representatives of sister organisations will have to cover their own accommodation and hotel expenses.

The party will cover accommodation expenses for foreign guests attending the convention.

According to spokesperson Chalise, the party will provide breakfast and lunch to convention representatives at Bhrikutimandap throughout the convention.

Health desk set up with 30 health workers

The Congress has established a health desk at the convention venue to provide medical services to representatives.

According to Dr Kedar Narasingh KC, coordinator of the convention’s health committee, the health desk has been set up on the western side of Khula Manch.

The facility will have five service counters and will provide basic health checks and emergency medical services.

Dr KC, who is also a central committee member, said the health desk would operate in two shifts, with doctors, paramedics and nurses providing services.

Representatives will have access to free blood pressure and blood sugar checks, paracetamol, oral rehydration solution and medicines for minor injuries.

Arrangements have also been made to transfer patients requiring emergency treatment to Bir Hospital, the National Trauma Centre and BP Smriti Hospital in Basundhara.

Two ambulances will remain on standby at the convention venue. An on-call service will also be available at night if medical assistance is required.

Dr KC said arrangements had also been made to provide medical assistance at hotels where representatives are staying if necessary.

Parking arrangements made from Dharahara to Durbarmarg

The Congress has also made parking arrangements for representatives attending the convention at Khula Manch in coordination with traffic police.

According to Vijay Bahadur Swar, coordinator of the convention’s transport management committee, parking has been arranged at the underground parking facility at Dharahara, along the one-way section of the road between Maitighar and Bhadrakali, and at the premises of Annapurna Hotel in Durbarmarg.

The party is also coordinating with traffic police to arrange additional parking around the Old Bus Park and inside Bhrikutimandap.

The 15th General Convention is expected to bring together thousands of Nepali Congress representatives for discussions on the party’s policies and programmes, followed by the election of its new leadership.

title.rendered: 7 destinations to explore in Sudurpaschim during Dashain

content.rendered:
If you are planning to explore somewhere new during the long Dashain holiday, Sudurpaschim could be an option worth considering. The province offers an unusual mix of landscapes and experiences, from mountains and hills to forests, lakes, wildlife, religious sites and distinctive local cultures.

From the high-altitude landscapes of Khaptad and Api-Nampa to the lowland areas around Shuklaphanta and Ghodaghodi, a trip through Sudurpaschim can offer a variety of experiences in a single journey.

The Nepal Tourism Board lists Khaptad, Shuklaphanta, Badimalika, Api-Nampa, Ghodaghodi and Ramaroshan among the province’s major natural and religious destinations.

If you are planning a Dashain trip, here are seven destinations to consider.

1. Khaptad — Meadows, forests and mountain tranquillity

Khaptad is one of the first destinations that comes to mind when talking about Sudurpaschim. Situated at elevations ranging from around 1,400 to 3,300 metres above sea level, the Khaptad region is known for its natural, religious and spiritual attractions.

According to the Khaptad Area Tourism Development and Management Committee, the area is home to around 270 species of birds and 224 species of medicinal plants.

What to see

Khaptad Lake, Triveni, Sahasralinga, Khaptad Baba’s Ashram, Nagdhunga, dense forests and mountain and hill landscapes are among the attractions.

Khaptad Baba’s Ashram is located at an elevation of around 3,160 metres. The Khaptad Area Tourism Development and Management Committee says Khaptad Baba spent more than five decades meditating in the area.

According to the Nepal Tourism Board, 20 species of mammals and 175 species of birds have been recorded in Khaptad.

Hiking, nature observation, birdwatching and meditation or spiritual tourism are among the main activities here.

2. Ramaroshan — A landscape of 12 lakes

For those looking for lakes, greenery and open mountain landscapes, Ramaroshan in Achham is another option.

Ramaroshan is locally associated with five traditional areas. Its lakes, green meadows and surrounding hills are among its main attractions. The Nepal Tourism Board also identifies Ramaroshan as one of Sudurpaschim’s major natural destinations.

What to see

Visitors can explore the lakes, green meadows, mountain landscapes, local settlements, forests and different species of birds.

Conservation work is also being carried out in the Ramaroshan-Badimalika area, which has biological and cultural significance. A project of the National Trust for Nature Conservation has focused on biodiversity conservation, nature tourism and the participation of local communities.

Visitors can walk around the lakes, hike, observe nature and birds, and experience local culture. Its combination of lakes, mountains and quiet surroundings can also make it an appealing destination for photography.

3. Shuklaphanta — Looking for tigers and swamp deer on safari

If you are not interested in high-altitude trekking, Shuklaphanta National Park can offer a different kind of nature experience during Dashain.

The park is particularly known for its vast grasslands and swamp deer. According to the Nepal Tourism Board, wildlife found in the park includes Bengal tigers, wild elephants, spotted deer, nilgai, wild boar and leopards. More than 350 species of birds have also been recorded there.

What to see

Visitors can look for swamp deer, Bengal tigers, wild elephants, spotted deer, nilgai, mugger crocodiles and various species of birds.

Jungle safaris and wildlife observation are the main attractions.

Dashain also falls around a period considered suitable for visiting the park. The Nepal Tourism Board considers October to March an appropriate season for Shuklaphanta.

4. Ghodaghodi — Lakes, birds and Tharu culture

If you want to combine nature with local culture, the Ghodaghodi Lake area in Kailali is another destination to consider.

Ghodaghodi is recognised by government tourism sources as an important wetland and natural destination in Sudurpaschim.

What to see

Visitors can explore Ghodaghodi Lake, the surrounding wetlands and forests, and observe birds and other natural features. The area also offers an opportunity to experience Tharu villages and culture.

Nature observation, birdwatching and cultural experiences linked to the local community can be enjoyed around the lake, particularly in the morning and evening.

For those looking for a shorter and more relaxed trip with family, Ghodaghodi can be an option.

5. Dadeldhura — Hills, temples and history

Dadeldhura can be made one of the main stops on a longer Sudurpaschim trip during the Dashain holiday.

Cool hill weather, expansive views of the surrounding landscape, historic forts, temples, lakes and local lifestyles give the district a range of attractions.

The Sudurpaschim provincial government lists Ugratara Temple, Amargadhi Fort, Ajayamerukot, Alital, Parshuram Dham and Ghatal Baba, among others, as sites of tourism and religious importance.

What to see

Those looking to combine religious, historical and hill tourism can include Dadeldhura in their itinerary.

Ugratara Temple, Amargadhi, Ajayamerukot, hill markets and villages, as well as mountain and hill views from the surrounding areas, are among the places to explore.

The province’s official tourism information also identifies Ajayamerukot, Alital and Ugratara among Dadeldhura’s major tourist attractions.

Dadeldhura can be suitable for those who want to experience the hill climate, history, religious sites and local food without undertaking a long trek.

6. Badimalika — A Himalayan trek with a religious journey

Badimalika in Bajura is known for both its religious significance and natural beauty.

Located at an elevation of around 3,800 metres above sea level, the Badimalika Temple is dedicated to Goddess Kali and is regarded as a Shakti Peetha. According to the Nepal Tourism Board, Badimalika lies in the high hills around the Budhiganga and Karnali rivers.

If you have a long Dashain holiday and enjoy trekking, Badimalika can offer a very different experience. The journey combines a religious pilgrimage with a high-altitude trek.

What to see

The Badimalika Temple and the vast meadows surrounding it are the main attractions.

As the altitude increases, the landscape changes, with open grasslands, green hills and distant mountain views adding to the experience. The Nepal Tourism Board also lists the Himalayan views from Badimalika among its major attractions.

The meadows become particularly colourful when flowers bloom during spring and the monsoon season.

The Badimalika Temple itself is the centre of the religious journey. According to Hindu belief, a part of the body of Sati Devi is believed to have fallen here, and the site is revered as a Shakti Peetha.

The Nepal Tourism Board says large numbers of pilgrims visit Badimalika, particularly during Janai Purnima.

7. Api-Nampa — Face to face with the Himalayas

For those looking for a more adventurous journey, the Api-Nampa Conservation Area in Darchula offers a high-altitude experience.

The Nepal Tourism Board lists Api-Nampa among Sudurpaschim’s major natural destinations, with Api Himal as one of its main attractions. The provincial government’s tourism information also includes Api Himal and the Api-Nampa region among the province’s major tourist sites.

What to see

The Api-Nampa Conservation Area is a Himalayan landscape known for its mountains and natural beauty. The Api and Nampa mountain ranges, high-altitude landscapes, mountain settlements and local culture are among its main attractions.

During treks, visitors can experience mountain views along with Himalayan forests, medicinal plants, wildlife and different species of birds.

The area also offers an opportunity to observe the landscapes around Kaladhunga, Sitola and the Byas region, as well as the lifestyles of local mountain communities.

With its rich biodiversity, Api-Nampa can also be an attractive destination for those interested in rare Himalayan plants and wildlife.

title.rendered: Mothers, muscles and making space for themselves

content.rendered:
At first glance, they are simply three women at the gym.

They arrive, work out, lift weights and leave. But spend a little more time talking to them and the story becomes something else.

They are mothers. They carry children, run households, worry about their families and navigate the expectations that often come with being a woman. And now, for about an hour at a time, they are choosing to carry something else too — weights.

I met three mothers at my gym who had been working out consistently for about a month. Each came for a different reason. One was concerned about her physical health. Another was encouraged by a doctor. The third was influenced by her friends and supported by her husband.

What they had in common was not simply a desire to become fitter. It was the decision to make a little time for themselves.

For many mothers, carrying a baby is just one of the many things they carry every day. There are household responsibilities, family expectations, worries and the needs of others. Somewhere between all of these responsibilities, finding time for themselves can become difficult.

So I wanted to know what happens when a mother decides that her own health and happiness deserve some space too.

The first woman I spoke to was Chandrakala Gajurel, 53.

Her journey to the gym began with concerns about her physical health. Her daughter encouraged her to take better care of herself. Before joining the gym, Chandrakala had undergone physiotherapy rather than exercising regularly. She had tried being physically active before, but had eventually stopped because of financial difficulties.

Now, after about a month at the gym, she is working towards becoming fitter and healthier.

But it was not just her decision to start exercising that caught my attention. It was how she had managed to make the gym part of her life.

Chandrakala has not told her husband that she joined the gym because she expects it would lead to a lot of questions. Her mother-in-law knows that she goes, but does not really pay much attention to it.

For Chandrakala, the gym has quietly become something of her own. It is a place to exercise, but it is also a small break from her usual responsibilities — a little time in the day that belongs to her.

Then there is Kabita Khatiwada, 42.

Kabita has a rather different relationship with the gym. When she talks about going, there is an enthusiasm that is hard to miss. She told me that coming to the gym sometimes feels like going to play school. She waits for her gym time and gets excited about going. At the same time, she wishes the gym opened earlier than 3pm. With the responsibilities she has at home, the timing is not always convenient.

Kabita is a mother of two, a son and a daughter, whose daughter is currently in Grade 8. Like many mothers, finding time for herself is not always easy.

She first came to the gym after a doctor suggested that she exercise. But her story is about more than fitness.

Kabita got married while she was still studying for her undergraduate degree, even though she did not want to get married at that time. That experience has stayed with her and shaped the way she thinks about the expectations placed on women.

She told me that she does not want to pass those same traditions and expectations on to her daughter or, one day, her future daughter-in-law.

She wants the women in her family to have more choice and freedom than she had.

Perhaps that is why the gym means something more to her than exercise. It is something she genuinely looks forward to. It is a small part of her day where she gets to make a choice for herself.

The third woman I spoke to was Muna Baskota, 56, who lives in Balkot with her family.

Muna’s decision to join the gym was mainly influenced by her friends, while her husband also encouraged her to go.

After about a month, she says she is enjoying it. She feels fitter and fresher, and believes the gym has helped both her mental and physical wellbeing. Before joining, Muna had been experiencing back pain. She felt that medical treatment had not been particularly effective. Since starting at the gym, however, she feels that her health has been improving.

She says she has experienced less pain and has also noticed that her sleep has become more regular after previously being disturbed. Her husband encouraged her to try the gym, and she has been happy with the change.

For Muna, as with the other women, the gym has become more than a place to exercise. It is time away from her usual responsibilities and time she can spend focusing on herself.

Listening to these three women, I began to realise that this was not really a story about women who had started going to the gym. It was about women making space for themselves.

Motherhood is often associated with caring, sacrificing and putting others first. A mother is expected to take care of her children, her husband, her home and the people around her.

But somewhere between all those responsibilities, the woman herself can become invisible.

The gym does not erase any of their responsibilities. Chandrakala is still a mother. Kabita is still a mother. Muna is still a mother. But for an hour, they are also simply women taking care of themselves.

That made me think about the way we understand femininity, too.

Femininity is often associated with being gentle, caring, delicate and self-sacrificing. But why can’t strength be feminine too? Why can’t a woman be soft and strong at the same time? Why can’t a mother care deeply for her family while also caring about her own body? And why should taking time for herself be considered selfish?

These women do not necessarily answer all of these questions directly. But their presence in the gym makes us ask them.

The idea for the title, “From Carrying Babies to Lifting Weights”, started as a playful thought. But after listening to these women, it began to mean something more.

Mothers have always carried things.

They carry babies, responsibilities, expectations and, often, the emotional weight of their families. Now, these women are choosing to lift weights too. Not because they are leaving their responsibilities behind, but because they are making room for themselves alongside them.

The dumbbell they lift is not replacing the baby they once carried. It represents something different — their health, their strength, their confidence and their right to have time for themselves.

Maybe being a strong mother does not mean carrying everything alone. Maybe sometimes, strength means knowing that you deserve to be carried too — by your own choices, your own confidence and the time you give yourself.

From carrying babies to lifting weights, these mothers are not simply becoming stronger physically. They are reminding us that being a mother is one part of a woman’s identity, not the entirety of it.

title.rendered: Beyond reconstruction, building a settlement where people choose to live

content.rendered:
Gumsipakha, in Laprak of Dharche Rural Municipality, Gorkha, is more than a remote mountain settlement. It is an ancestral homeland of the Gurung community, shaped by generations of social relationships, cultural traditions, agriculture, livestock, natural resources and collective life. Its homes, landscape, cultural practices and community institutions remain central to local identity and belonging.

Yet an important question is emerging. Why are younger and economically active residents increasingly reluctant to live permanently in Gumsipakha despite their strong ancestral, cultural and family ties?

The answer cannot be explained by migration, housing conditions or declining attachment alone. Settlement decisions are increasingly shaped by livelihoods and employment, education, healthcare, connectivity, basic services, disaster and environmental safety, digital access, household needs and changing aspirations.

People may remain deeply connected to Gumsipakha while living elsewhere because the settlement does not yet provide the opportunities, services, security and quality of life they require.

The challenge, therefore, is not simply to retain the population. It is to create conditions that allow people to choose to stay, return, invest and build a secure and dignified future in Gumsipakha.

The changing meaning of permanent settlement

In traditional agrarian societies, permanent settlement was closely tied to land, agriculture, family, culture and community networks. Today, residential decisions are increasingly shaped by livelihood opportunities, education, healthcare, connectivity, basic services, safety, mobility and aspirations for personal and professional development.

A household may own a house and farmland in Gumsipakha, participate in cultural and community life, and maintain strong ancestral ties while living elsewhere for employment, education, healthcare or other opportunities.

Migration or temporary residence, therefore, does not necessarily indicate weakened attachment. It may simply reflect changing household needs and aspirations.

Permanent settlement cannot be measured by housing or land ownership alone. A sustainable settlement must enable people to live safely and with dignity, secure livelihoods, access essential services and opportunities, maintain social and cultural connections, and adapt to changing economic and environmental conditions.

For Gumsipakha, the priority is not merely to preserve houses and infrastructure, but to create a safe, inclusive, economically viable, culturally vibrant and environmentally resilient community for present and future generations.

Livelihoods: The foundation of settlement

Reliable and diversified livelihoods are essential to Gumsipakha’s long-term viability. Agriculture and livestock remain central to household food security and income, but limited and fragmented land, steep terrain, high transport and input costs, weak market access, labour shortages and climate variability constrain their profitability.

Traditional farming may support household consumption and supplementary income, but often does not generate sufficient and predictable cash income to meet growing needs for education, healthcare, transport, communication and other services.

Limited economic diversification further encourages working-age residents to migrate. Opportunities in high-value agriculture, livestock, agro-processing, tourism and homestays, small enterprises, construction, services and digital or remote work remain limited.

This can create a reinforcing cycle: fewer working-age residents reduce local economic activity and demand, which limits jobs and services and further increases incentives to migrate.

Breaking this cycle requires a diversified, market-linked local economy that builds on agriculture and livestock while expanding value addition, tourism, entrepreneurship, skills, digital connectivity, financial services and access to wider markets and employment.

The objective is not to prevent migration, but to create viable choices to live, work, invest, return and build sustainable livelihoods in Gumsipakha.

Migration: Opportunity and challenge

Migration should not be viewed inherently as a negative development. For many households, migration and foreign employment provide essential income, improve living conditions, support education and healthcare, and strengthen household resilience.

However, prolonged out-migration can alter the demographic and economic structure of Gumsipakha. When working-age people spend much of their productive years elsewhere, older residents may increasingly bear responsibility for households, agricultural land and community affairs. This can contribute to labour shortages, declining agricultural activity and weakening local institutions and social networks.

Migration also changes aspirations. Exposure to urban environments, higher education, technology, new occupations and different lifestyles can reshape younger generations’ expectations of life and opportunity.

The objective should therefore be to expand meaningful choices rather than prevent migration. Gumsipakha should provide conditions that enable people to stay, return, invest or work while maintaining strong connections with their ancestral community.

Migrants can also be an important resource, bringing skills, savings, professional networks, technology and investment back to the settlement.

Education and healthcare

Education and healthcare are fundamental to long-term settlement viability. Families make residential decisions largely around the wellbeing and future prospects of their children and dependants.

Limited access to quality secondary education, technical and vocational training, higher education and specialised learning can encourage families to relocate closer to educational centres. Over time, children’s education, employment and social networks established elsewhere may further weaken a household’s residential connection with Gumsipakha.

Healthcare is equally important, particularly for older people, women, children, people with disabilities and households requiring regular or specialised care. Limited access to reliable primary healthcare, essential medicines, emergency services and timely referral can make remote settlement increasingly difficult.

For Gumsipakha to remain viable, residents need reasonable and dependable access to quality education and essential healthcare, including emergency and referral services. These are not simply social priorities; they are conditions that influence whether families remain, return and invest in their community.

Accessibility and connectivity

Physical accessibility is another fundamental determinant of rural settlement viability. A road can improve access to services, markets and economic opportunities, but the presence of a road alone does not guarantee effective accessibility.

Road quality, year-round reliability, maintenance, travel time, transport availability, affordability and seasonal disruptions all shape actual mobility. Poor or unreliable connectivity increases the cost of agricultural inputs, food, construction materials, healthcare and other essential goods and services. It can also limit market access and reduce the competitiveness of local products.

Digital connectivity is becoming equally important. Reliable mobile networks and internet access can expand opportunities for education, information, financial services, markets, government services, remote employment, entrepreneurship and social interaction.

For younger generations, digital exclusion can reinforce the disadvantages of physical remoteness.

Settlement viability therefore depends not only on improved roads, but on reliable and affordable physical and digital connectivity linking residents to essential services, markets, institutions and wider economic opportunities.

Disaster risk and confidence to stay

The 2015 Gorkha earthquake underscored the importance of settlement safety and disaster resilience in mountain communities. Gumsipakha remains exposed to multiple hazards, including earthquakes, landslides, slope instability, intense rainfall, floods, road failures and other climate- and terrain-related risks.

Reconstructing or strengthening individual houses alone is not sufficient. Long-term settlement viability depends on residents’ confidence that the settlement as a whole is safe, accessible and resilient to future hazards.

This requires risk-sensitive land-use planning, hazard-informed site selection, resilient housing and public infrastructure, stable access roads, reliable water systems, effective drainage, emergency preparedness, early warning where appropriate, and functional disaster-response and evacuation arrangements.

A permanent settlement requires more than a physical place to live. It requires a safe and resilient environment that gives households confidence to remain, return and invest in their future.

Changing families and social relationships

Family structures and social relationships in rural communities are changing. Traditional extended households are increasingly influenced by nuclear families, migration, intergenerational separation, education and changing employment patterns.

A household may have parents living in Gumsipakha, children studying elsewhere and working-age members employed in Kathmandu or abroad. Such families may retain strong emotional, cultural, social and economic ties to the settlement without maintaining year-round residence.

This highlights an important distinction between belonging and habitation.

People may continue to identify with Gumsipakha, maintain property and social relationships, participate in community affairs and return periodically without permanently residing there.

Recognising this distinction is essential for realistic settlement planning. The future of Gumsipakha should be understood not only in terms of permanent residence, but also through continuing community affiliation, cultural identity, family connections, periodic residence and engagement from outside the settlement.

Cultural attachment is not enough

Gumsipakha’s cultural heritage is a major source of identity, continuity and community cohesion. Its language, traditions, rituals, architecture, social institutions and ancestral practices reflect generations of cultural knowledge and collective life.

However, cultural attachment alone does not guarantee permanent residence.

Younger generations may retain a strong emotional and cultural connection to Gumsipakha while seeking education, employment, healthcare and other opportunities elsewhere. If this pattern continues across generations, traditional knowledge, language, cultural practices and community institutions may gradually weaken.

Cultural preservation should therefore be integrated with broader economic and social development. A culturally vibrant settlement must also be a socially, economically and physically viable place to live, work, raise families and maintain intergenerational connections.

From reconstruction to sustainable settlement

The central lesson is clear: reconstruction and sustainable settlement are not synonymous.

Rebuilding houses restores physical assets, but does not by itself ensure that households will return, remain or invest in the community. Houses may remain vacant where employment and livelihood opportunities are limited, essential services are inadequate, transport and digital connectivity are unreliable, or households continue to face disaster risks and uncertainty about the future.

Sustainable settlement requires an integrated approach combining safe and resilient housing, reliable infrastructure, essential services, viable livelihoods, quality education and healthcare, physical and digital connectivity, disaster-risk reduction, cultural continuity and opportunities for future generations.

The focus must therefore shift from a predominantly house-centred reconstruction model to a people-centred and settlement-based development strategy.

What could make Gumsipakha more livable?

A long-term strategy for Gumsipakha should focus on a mutually reinforcing package of interventions rather than isolated projects.

The local economic base could be strengthened through high-value agriculture, livestock development, agro-processing, local products, cooperatives, small enterprises and stronger market linkages. The emphasis should be on commercially viable production, value addition, income diversification and reliable market access.

Young people also need opportunities through vocational and technical training, entrepreneurship support, digital skills, remote employment and skills-based enterprises. This would provide alternatives to permanent out-migration while enabling young people to participate in the local economy.

Essential services should be treated as core settlement infrastructure. Quality education, primary healthcare and emergency referral services, safe drinking water, sanitation, electricity, telecommunications and reliable internet are fundamental to household wellbeing and influence decisions to remain, return or relocate.

Reliable all-season roads, regular maintenance, affordable transportation and dependable links to nearby service and market centres are equally important for households, producers, students, businesses and patients.

Disaster resilience should be integrated into settlement planning through hazard assessment, risk-sensitive land-use planning, slope management, resilient housing and infrastructure, effective drainage, early warning, emergency preparedness and response arrangements.

Gumsipakha and the wider Laprak area could also benefit from carefully planned community-based tourism centred on homestays, local cuisine, traditional architecture, handicrafts, cultural experiences and local products. Such development should remain consistent with community capacity, environmental limits and local priorities.

Cultural preservation should similarly be integrated with social and economic development. Local language, traditions, festivals, architecture, crafts, traditional knowledge and community institutions should be documented, transmitted across generations and incorporated into education and appropriate cultural initiatives.

Meaningful community participation is equally important. Residents should be involved in identifying priorities, planning investments, implementing activities, monitoring results and maintaining infrastructure. Locally informed planning can strengthen relevance, ownership, accountability and long-term sustainability.

People living outside Gumsipakha should also be recognised as potential contributors. Migrants and the wider diaspora can provide skills, knowledge, investment, professional networks, technology and social support. A structured engagement mechanism could help mobilise these resources while maintaining strong economic, social and cultural connections with the settlement.

Finally, Gumsipakha’s natural resource base must be protected. Forests, water sources, agricultural land, biodiversity and fragile mountain ecosystems should be managed sustainably, with development aligned with environmental conservation, climate adaptation and disaster-risk reduction.

Together, these measures can help create a more economically viable, socially connected, service-supported, environmentally sustainable and disaster-resilient Gumsipakha.

Planning must start with people

Effective settlement planning should begin with a clear understanding of why different households choose to stay, migrate, return or maintain seasonal residence.

This requires evidence-based assessment through household surveys, community consultations, focus-group discussions, demographic analysis, livelihood assessments and participatory settlement planning.

Needs will vary across population groups. Young people may prioritise employment, skills and digital connectivity. Families may place greater emphasis on education, healthcare and basic services. Older residents may require accessible services and social support. Farmers may prioritise irrigation, agricultural inputs, transport and market access, while vulnerable and disadvantaged households may require targeted support and inclusive services.

Settlement development should therefore not rely on a single standardised package of interventions. Planning should be evidence-based, locally informed, inclusive and responsive to the different needs, capacities and aspirations of households.

A new vision for Gumsipakha

The long-term objective should not be to prevent migration or compel people to remain in Gumsipakha. Individuals and families should have the freedom to pursue education, employment and other opportunities wherever they choose.

The development challenge is to ensure that remaining in, returning to or investing in Gumsipakha is a viable and meaningful choice.

This requires a settlement where people can earn sustainable livelihoods, access quality education and healthcare, benefit from reliable physical and digital connectivity, live in a safe and resilient environment, participate in community life, and maintain their cultural identity and social connections.

The vision should therefore be to make Gumsipakha not simply a place of ancestral belonging, but a viable, resilient, inclusive and forward-looking community for present and future generations.

The reluctance of local people to maintain permanent residence in Gumsipakha is a multidimensional settlement challenge shaped by livelihoods, migration, education, healthcare, accessibility, infrastructure, disaster risk, changing household structures, cultural and social dynamics, environmental conditions, governance and evolving aspirations.

Gumsipakha’s strong ancestral identity, cultural heritage and community networks provide an important foundation for its future. But cultural attachment alone cannot ensure permanent habitation.

Long-term settlement viability depends on whether households have practical and sustainable conditions to remain, return and invest in the community.

The future of Gumsipakha should therefore not be assessed solely by the number of houses reconstructed or residents returning. It should be assessed by whether the settlement provides sustainable livelihoods, essential services, safety and resilience, reliable connectivity, dignity, social inclusion, cultural continuity and opportunities for future generations.

Sustainable development consequently requires a shift from physical reconstruction towards an integrated, people-centred settlement strategy combining local economic development, resilient infrastructure, quality public services, disaster-risk reduction, cultural preservation, environmental sustainability and participatory governance.

The ultimate objective is not simply to bring people back to their ancestral homes, but to create conditions in which people have a genuine and sustainable choice to live, work, return, invest, participate, belong and prosper in Gumsipakha.

title.rendered: Use AI. But never hand over your judgment

content.rendered:
On September 8, a 27-year-old British researcher sat on a park bench in San Francisco and quit his job. Jacob Coxon had spent three years training AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic, and his resignation post claimed that neither company was acting responsibly and that both were racing toward self-improving superintelligence. Within 36 hours, roughly 153 million people had seen it.

Fear of new machines is nothing new. English weavers smashed looms in the 1810s, and teachers panicked when calculators arrived in classrooms in the 1970s. Each time, work changed instead of disappearing. What makes this moment strange is who is sounding the alarm. Some of the loudest warnings are coming from the people building the technology.

The builders ask for brakes

Coxon was not alone for long. Four days later, Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei published a long essay arguing that the risks justify a slowdown. On September 14, OpenAI’s Sam Altman said no amount of competitive pressure should excuse recklessness or let AI’s abilities race ahead of our ability to monitor them. By September 23 he was at the UN Security Council, warning that humanity could lose control of AI’s future and that the biggest decisions should not be left to San Francisco labs alone.

Both men came with proposals. Altman asked for international standards to measure what AI can do and whether safeguards are enough. Amodei suggested narrow global bans, such as one on AI-made bioweapons, along with ways for countries to verify each other’s promises and a shared system for reporting AI incidents.

The trap: Who slows down first?

Good ideas are one thing, and getting rivals to adopt them is another. President Trump has called fears of AI destroying humanity a hoax and argued that aggressive regulation would only help China. Vice President Vance said the administration wants to manage the risks without weakening America’s position in the race. Meanwhile, about 20 countries led by Finland and Norway backed a global oversight declaration. The United States and China, the two front-runners, stayed out, and experts see little chance that either will accept major limits soon.

This is a classic arms-race trap. If one country slows down and its rival does not, the slow one falls behind, so both keep sprinting even if both would rather stop. Countries have escaped this trap before, most famously with nuclear weapons, and it was not trust that got them out. It was inspections and verification. That is why Amodei’s proposal for countries to check one another matters more than any dramatic warning. A rule nobody can verify is only a promise.

Should we trust the messengers?

Fair enough, but should we trust the people delivering the warnings? Suspicion runs in both directions. Critics of Coxon, including former White House AI adviser David Sacks, note that it was his first ever post, that safety groups boosted it within minutes, and that he offered no hard data. A later report said a communications firm linked to AI-safety figures had helped arrange his media appearances, though it did not show that his claims were false. On the other side, skeptics of Altman argue that a company that built the technology may be asking for rules mainly to protect its lead.

Endorsements from inside the industry cut both ways too. Anthropic’s Evan Hubinger publicly backed Coxon and put the odds of AI killing all humans within a decade above 10 percent. That is one researcher’s estimate, not a scientific consensus.

Motives are worth checking, but they do not settle the question. Who says something has no bearing on whether it is true. The better test is whether the claim rests on evidence that others can examine.

What the evidence shows today

So let us look at some evidence. The extinction debate is about the future, but the research already available paints a steadier picture. AI is powerful, uneven, and remarkably easy to over-trust.

Take programmers. In one randomised trial, experienced developers believed AI made them 20% faster, when in fact they were 19% slower. It was a small study, but the gap between feeling and fact is the point. Consultants show a similar pattern. In a study of 758 of them, AI made people faster and better on tasks within its ability. On a task just beyond it, AI users were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the right answer, because the wrong answers looked so convincing.

Classrooms tell the same story with a twist. In Turkey, students given an unrestricted ChatGPT-style tool scored 17% worse on the exam than students who never had AI, and they did not realise they had learned less. In Nigeria, a World Bank trial used AI with teacher supervision and prompts designed to encourage reasoning, and the results were striking: roughly 1.5 years of typical learning in six weeks. The tool was similar, but the outcomes were opposite, and the difference was how it was used.

Jobs may be where the effects show up first, and they are landing at the bottom rung. Stanford economists found that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is now 19% below where it would have been, while experienced workers show no comparable gap. The same researchers see no widespread, economy-wide job loss, and other economists argue that a general hiring slowdown explains part of the pattern. Even so, the risk may not be that AI takes your job tomorrow. It may be that fewer beginners get the first one.

Across all of these studies, the lesson is that “human oversight” is not only a job for governments and labs. Every user needs to practise it: check the answer, and keep learning without the machine.

What Nepal should take from this

Nobody will write AI rules with Nepal in mind, and the stakes here are high. Unemployment among 15- to 24-year-olds stood at 22.7 per cent in 2022-23, and around a million young Nepalese leave the country each year. AI has to become a tool for them, not another closed door.

Three steps follow from the evidence. First, schools should teach students to check AI’s work, not just use it. Second, classrooms should favour guided, teacher-led AI, as in the Nigeria trial, over a free-for-all. Third, Nepal should push for proper Nepali-language support, since researchers testing Nepali have found it takes more tokens, the units of text AI tools charge for, than the same content in English. A small country lacks power, but it can join coalitions, as those 20 nations did.

The bottom line

AI may be genuinely dangerous, and the people warning us may have motives of their own. Both can be true. The race with China means no country wants to break alone, so the real question is whether countries can build ways to check one another. Until they do, the sensible rule for everyone is a simple one: use AI, but never hand over your judgment.

title.rendered: Why civil service morale matters for better governance

content.rendered:
The civil service is the permanent institution of the state and a foundation of democratic governance. Regardless of which political party comes to power, civil servants are responsible for implementing the government’s policies and programmes. Yet the morale of Nepal’s civil servants appears to have declined significantly in recent years. This has implications not only for administrative performance but also for the quality and timeliness of services received by citizens.

The issue has become particularly relevant under the current government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah. In the March 2026 general election, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) secured 182 of the 275 seats in the House of Representatives, giving it a clear parliamentary majority. Shah was subsequently appointed prime minister on 27 March.

The election created significant expectations among the public. The RSP’s election symbol, the bell or ghanti, became closely associated with the prospect of a new political leadership, including Shah as the party’s prime ministerial candidate. The new government consequently assumed office with considerable public expectations for change, particularly in governance and service delivery.

While the programmes announced after the formation of the government initially generated hope, sustaining those expectations has proved challenging. Doubt and uncertainty have gradually replaced some of the optimism that accompanied the government’s formation.

One of the government’s central priorities appears to be improving public service delivery. The effectiveness of any government is closely linked to the bureaucracy because civil servants are responsible for translating political decisions into administrative action. In Nepal, where many administrative processes are still not fully digitised, improving service delivery will inevitably require time, institutional reform and adaptation.

The roots of declining morale

The working culture of the bureaucracy has long been criticised for being slow, hierarchical and resistant to change. There is also a widespread public perception that government employees are vulnerable to corruption and personal interests. Although political changes and movements have repeatedly sought to improve governance, many citizens continue to experience delays and difficulties in accessing public services.

However, it would be unfair to assume that all civil servants are resistant to reform or committed to poor service. Many employees entered the civil service through competitive examinations and continue to believe in providing quality and timely services to the public. Treating the entire civil service as corrupt, inefficient or incapable of reform risks further demoralising the very institution expected to deliver that reform.

The working habits and attitudes that have developed within the bureaucracy over many years cannot be changed overnight. Reform requires time, institutional support and a working environment in which employees are expected to perform but are also treated with dignity and fairness.

For this reason, attempts to reform the bureaucracy through threats or intimidation are unlikely to strengthen democratic governance. Ministers and senior officials need to be able to hold employees accountable while maintaining their professional dignity and self-respect.

There are several factors contributing to declining morale among civil servants.

Political and managerial pressure

One major concern is the working style of departmental ministers and the pressure placed on civil servants in day-to-day operations.

Ministers may have political authority, but they do not necessarily have detailed knowledge of the policies, rules and administrative procedures governing their respective ministries. At times, employees may therefore come under pressure to complete tasks outside established procedures or to bypass prescribed administrative channels.

Such pressure can create uncertainty among civil servants and undermine their confidence in the system. Ministers should provide political direction while allowing professional administrators to carry out their responsibilities within the framework of existing laws and procedures.

Inadequate flow of information

Another important problem is insufficient information flow within public administration.

The civil service is often described as the permanent mechanism of the state, yet employees are not always adequately informed about government decisions, priorities, methods of implementation or changes in policy.

It is difficult to expect employees to perform effectively and remain motivated when they are uncertain about the objectives they are expected to achieve or the procedures they are required to follow.

A systematic and regular mechanism for communicating government decisions, policies and priorities is therefore essential.

Transfers and postings

The use of transfers and postings as a form of political reprisal can also damage morale.

There is a perception among civil servants that employees appointed or posted during a previous government may be viewed with suspicion by a new administration. If employees believe that their professional future depends on their perceived political affiliation rather than their competence and performance, an atmosphere of insecurity develops.

Transfers and postings should instead be based on professional competence, performance, institutional needs and transparent criteria. A predictable and fair system would reduce anxiety and help strengthen professionalism within the civil service.

Digitalisation and technological insecurity

The government’s emphasis on digitalisation is intended to make public services more efficient and accessible. However, technological change can also create uncertainty among employees who feel they lack the necessary skills or fear that their existing roles may become less relevant.

This concern should not be addressed by blaming employees for being unfamiliar with technology. It should be addressed through timely training, reskilling and institutional support.

Digital transformation should be viewed as an opportunity to strengthen the capacity of civil servants rather than as a threat to their employment.

The role of civil service unions

The government’s plans concerning civil service unions have also contributed to uncertainty among employees.

Representative organisations can provide employees with a mechanism to raise concerns about workplace conditions, unfair treatment and professional rights. At the same time, unions must also operate within a framework that protects public service delivery and professional standards.

The challenge is to maintain a balance between employees’ legitimate right to representation and the need for an efficient, politically neutral and accountable civil service.

Restructuring and job security

Recent government efforts to improve the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of the civil service have created another source of uncertainty.

Proposals to reduce the number of federal and provincial ministries, restructure government departments and potentially reduce the number of government employees have raised concerns about job security. Discussions around mandatory retirement, as well as possible changes to entry and retirement age limits, can further contribute to uncertainty about career stability and future opportunities.

Even where such reforms may be intended to improve the efficiency of government, uncertainty surrounding their implementation can affect employee motivation and morale.

What can be done?

Addressing declining morale requires more than a single intervention. It requires changes in management, communication, professional development, personnel administration and institutional culture.

First, there needs to be a fundamental improvement in the working relationship between ministers and civil servants. Undue pressure on employees should be minimised, while legitimate performance expectations should remain clear.

Questioning the qualifications of ministers would not be appropriate, but ministers may not always be familiar with the detailed legal and procedural frameworks governing their ministries. Orientation programmes could therefore help ministers understand the institutional, legal and administrative systems within which they are expected to operate.

Second, employees must be properly informed about government priorities, the nature of their tasks and the procedures for implementation. A systematic and regular information-flow mechanism would allow civil servants to understand not only what is expected of them, but also why particular decisions have been taken.

Third, transfers and postings should be based on transparent and professional criteria. Employees should not be evaluated or transferred simply because they served under a previous administration. Professional competence, performance and institutional requirements should be the primary considerations.

Fourth, the government should invest in training to support digital transformation. Employees who feel insecure because of limited information-technology skills should be given opportunities to acquire new skills. Refresher and reskilling programmes can improve technical capacity while reducing anxiety about technological change.

Institutional change also requires patience. Changes in individual behaviour and organisational culture take time. Sudden changes to systems and working environments established by previous governments can naturally create confusion and uncertainty. The current government should therefore manage the transition carefully, providing clear guidance and allowing employees time to adapt to new expectations.

Finally, job security and career stability remain important concerns for civil servants. Employees need a professional environment in which they can carry out their responsibilities without fear of arbitrary punishment, transfer or dismissal. At the same time, job security should go hand in hand with accountability and performance.

A civil service that feels secure but is not accountable cannot deliver effective public services. Likewise, a civil service that feels constantly threatened is unlikely to perform at its full potential.

From confrontation to partnership

The decline in civil service morale is not the result of a single factor. It reflects a combination of structural, managerial, political and policy-related pressures.

The government should not treat civil servants as either puppets or enemies. They are part of the machinery through which government policies are implemented.

If the government treats the bureaucracy as a partner in reform — while maintaining clear standards of accountability and performance — it can create a more constructive environment for change.

Ultimately, better public services require effective coordination between political leadership and the professional bureaucracy. Ministers provide the political direction; civil servants provide institutional knowledge and administrative continuity. Neither can deliver lasting improvements in governance by working in isolation.

If Nepal’s current reform agenda is to translate into better services for citizens, improving the morale, professionalism and capacity of the civil service must be part of that effort.

title.rendered: 450 TU professors, employees found to have misused study leave; only 17% repay

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 3

Tribhuvan University has recovered Rs 167.1 million from professors and employees found to have misused study leave.

According to a report submitted to TU Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Bhola Thapa on Friday by the Study Leave Management Implementation Committee, the university has recovered the amount from 77 people.

The report states that the accounts of 18 people, involving Rs 44 million, have been calculated but the amount has yet to be recovered. Around 40 professors and employees are currently in the process of returning the money, according to the university.

The university has identified around 450 professors and employees as having misused study leave. So far, only around 17 percent have returned the money, while 83 percent have yet to do so.

The government has considered the recovery of the money an achievement. However, TU has yet to recover the remaining amount from those who misused study leave.

The committee submitted its report after its term expired.

The university had formed a committee under Dr Jeevan Kafle after an Onlinekhabar report published on November 22, 2024, reported that TU professors who had gone abroad on study leave were staying there instead of returning to the university.

The committee found that 450 professors and employees had misused study leave. The committee had initially investigated 398 cases before around 50 additional files were subsequently found.

After the committee submitted its initial report, the university formed the Study Leave Management Implementation Committee under Kafle to recover the money from those who had misused study leave.

The committee was formed on August 13, 2025, and was given a one-year mandate. It began the recovery process after its formation.

According to the committee, around 250 professors and employees who went abroad on study leave did not return, while another 200 returned without completing their studies.

Committee coordinator Kafle said the amount recovered was relatively low partly because the university had not made a decision on how to deal with employees who returned without completing their studies.

“The executive body did not make a decision regarding those who returned without completing their studies, so the process could not move forward. There was no clarity on how much should be recovered or how it should be recovered,” Kafle said.

He said the committee had been given a one-year term and had therefore submitted its report. Further action can now be taken through the Registrar’s Office, he said.

“The committee believes that since study leave is an ongoing matter, it can now be managed through the regular administrative system,” the report states.

The committee concluded that collecting current information on teachers and employees who took study leave but failed to fulfil their service obligations, verifying their financial records and preparing the necessary documents remained challenging.

Under TU’s Teachers and Employees Service Rules 2050 BS, teachers who take study leave for more than three years and up to five years are required to serve the university for at least five years after returning.

Those who take three years of study leave are required to serve the university for at least three years after returning.

Employees who fail to return after their study leave are required to repay the salary and allowances received from the university during the leave period, along with 10 percent interest, under an undertaking signed before taking leave.

However, the university has found that many teachers and employees resign without repaying the money and remain abroad.

Many teachers have gone to countries including the United States, Australia and Canada on study leave. Some have gone on scholarships, while others have travelled at their own expense. Some have obtained permanent residency in those countries after their study leave expired.

The university said it would give professors and employees who have not been in contact until mid-January to repay the remaining amount.

“We will give them time until mid-January. We will recover the university’s money by whatever means necessary,” TU Registrar Rabindra Shiwakoti said.

He said the remaining work would now come under the Registrar’s Office following the submission of the committee’s report.

“We have set up a help desk at the Registrar’s Office and assigned four employees. They will look after both teachers and employees,” he said. “Until now, a committee was handling the matter. Now the work will come under the Registrar’s Office.”

The committee has also recommended policy decisions to make the study leave system more systematic.

“Policy decisions are necessary to manage study leave. We have recommended measures to make the system more systematic,” Kafle said.

Tribhuvan University provides paid study leave to help produce qualified academic staff. However, the misuse of study leave has resulted in financial losses, academic difficulties and other institutional costs for the university, particularly as the number of employees who fail to return after completing their leave has increased.

title.rendered: 100 days under FIFA suspension, Nepal football remains in limbo

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

It has been 100 days since FIFA suspended the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA), but there is still no clear indication of when the ban on Nepali football will be lifted.

FIFA suspended ANFA indefinitely on June 25, citing third-party interference in the affairs of the football governing body. The suspension has prevented Nepal’s national teams and clubs from participating in FIFA and Asian Football Confederation (AFC) competitions and cut ANFA off from FIFA and AFC funding, development programmes and training opportunities.

The prolonged suspension has become more notable when compared with recent cases involving Nepal’s neighbours.

India was suspended by FIFA in August 2022 over third-party interference after the country’s Supreme Court appointed a Committee of Administrators to take over the functions of the All India Football Federation (AIFF) executive committee.

FIFA suspended India on August 16 and lifted the ban after the committee was dissolved and the AIFF administration regained full control of its daily affairs. FIFA announced the lifting of the suspension on August 27, meaning the ban lasted 11 days by calendar dates.

Pakistan, meanwhile, was suspended by FIFA in February 2025 for a different reason. FIFA said the Pakistan Football Federation (PFF) had failed to adopt constitutional amendments required to ensure democratic elections.

The suspension was lifted on March 2 after the PFF Congress unanimously approved the constitution validated by FIFA and the AFC.

Nepal, however, remains suspended 100 days after FIFA’s decision.

What FIFA wants from Nepal

FIFA has set conditions for lifting the suspension.

One requires the complete revocation of the National Sports Council’s March 25 decision concerning ANFA and the reinstatement of the current ANFA Executive Committee.

The second requires ANFA to complete the electoral process it had already initiated, as soon as possible and in accordance with its statutes and regulations.

The dispute dates back to the conflict between the National Sports Council and ANFA over the football association’s election process.

On March 25, the NSC suspended ANFA for three months, citing violations of the Sports Development Act. ANFA had planned to hold its election in Jhapa on March 27, but the election was postponed after the NSC’s decision.

The government later revoked the three-month suspension on May 15. However, the dispute over the election process and the extent of state involvement was not fully resolved.

FIFA subsequently concluded that the continued involvement of state authorities amounted to third-party interference and suspended ANFA indefinitely.

A dispute with no clear exit

The central disagreement now remains between the government and ANFA.

The government has maintained that ANFA must comply with the decisions and directives of Nepal’s sports authorities, while ANFA has argued that it must operate independently in line with FIFA and AFC regulations.

FIFA’s position is that member associations must be able to manage their affairs independently and without undue third-party influence.

The football body had already warned Nepal about the issue before imposing the suspension. According to FIFA’s account, it had repeatedly sought assurances that ANFA would be allowed to conduct its affairs and complete its electoral process without interference.

The consequences of the suspension are not limited to the national team’s international fixtures.

ANFA and its member bodies have lost access to FIFA and AFC funding and development programmes, while Nepal’s national teams and clubs cannot participate in competitions organised by the two bodies for as long as the suspension remains in place.

The suspension has also already affected Nepal’s participation in continental competitions. The AFC had informed ANFA that Nepal’s youth teams could take part in upcoming qualifiers only if FIFA lifted the suspension before specified deadlines.

What happens next?

There is currently no indication that the two sides have reached an agreement that would satisfy FIFA’s conditions.

The longer the dispute continues, the greater the uncertainty for Nepali football.

The immediate issue is no longer simply when FIFA will lift the suspension. It is whether the government and ANFA can resolve their disagreement over the football body’s autonomy and electoral process in a way that meets FIFA’s requirements.

Until then, Nepal remains outside international football — 100 days after the suspension that brought an unprecedented disruption to the country’s football administration.

title.rendered: After weeks of searching, focus shifts to recovery of missing workers and hydropower projects

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

More than a month after the Bhotekoshi flood swept through hydropower projects in Rasuwa and neighbouring districts, the search for missing workers and employees has entered a new phase.

The government has shifted from a regular search-and-rescue operation to what it calls a “search and recovery” effort, as the possibility of finding missing people alive has diminished after prolonged searches.

The 37th meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Executive Committee decided to continue search and rescue in critical and highly sensitive locations, while prioritising the recovery of bodies and damaged structures in other areas.

The change has also affected the way hydropower projects are conducting searches.

According to Bijay Mohan Bhattarai, secretary of the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal (IPPAN) and manager of the Langtang Khola Hydropower Project, most of the immediately accessible areas have already been searched.

“Wherever we needed to look, we have already looked. After discussions with the security agencies, it has been decided not to continue the search in the same way,” he said.

The focus is now shifting towards relief, reconstruction and restoring infrastructure damaged by the flood.

But before hydropower companies can begin rebuilding their projects, they face another major obstacle — getting back to their project sites.

First the roads and bridges, then the projects

The flood severely damaged access roads leading to hydropower projects. In several locations, roads were completely washed away, while bridges will have to be rebuilt before equipment and workers can reach the sites.

The government is working on roads and bridges up to Betrawati, but additional infrastructure will be needed to reach projects further upstream, Bhattarai said.

“A Bailey bridge still needs to be installed at Betrawati, and there is no road beyond that,” he said. “Around a kilometre of road in the Bhotekoshi area beyond Chilime has been completely destroyed and needs to be rebuilt.”

Another Bailey bridge will also be required further along the route, meaning it could take considerable time before some project sites become accessible again.

“Until the road reaches the sites, nobody can move forward,” Bhattarai said.

Projects around the Chilime area may become accessible relatively sooner, but reaching those located further upstream could take much longer. Bhattarai estimates that access to some projects could take as long as a year.

Search operations give way to reconstruction planning

An official at the Ministry of Energy said the ministry is no longer directly coordinating daily search-and-rescue operations as it did immediately after the disaster.

Relevant hydropower projects, the Nepal Electricity Authority and security agencies are continuing necessary work, while the ministry has begun focusing on how reconstruction should proceed.

“Our focus is now on how to move ahead with rehabilitation. Planning is under way,” the official said. “We are preparing a matrix to determine which issues require political decisions and which can be handled under the existing arrangements.”

The shift reflects a broader change in the government’s response — from immediate rescue operations towards long-term recovery and reconstruction.

Rebuilding projects while displaced families wait

Hydropower companies say reconstruction cannot be separated from the problems facing families affected by the flood.

Many residents around the project areas have lost their homes and remain in difficult circumstances, according to Bhattarai.

“First, there is the issue of resettling people. Some have lost their homes altogether,” he said. “We may not be in a position to enter the project areas until their problems and those of other affected people are addressed.”

He said relief and resettlement programmes for affected communities and reconstruction of hydropower projects should therefore move forward together.

Projects face billions in reconstruction costs

The flood directly affected hydropower projects including Chilime, Langtang and Rasuwagadhi in Rasuwa. Some were nearing completion, while others were already generating electricity.

For project developers, the challenge is not only how long reconstruction will take but also how to finance the additional costs.

The impact is particularly significant for projects that were about to begin generating electricity or had only recently entered operation.

“Our project was hit just two or three days before it was due to start generating electricity,” Bhattarai said. “Now, after having to spend again, the project itself has reached a point where its financial viability is under pressure.”

Private developers are seeking policy measures including extensions to licence periods, adjustments to bank interest and loan repayment schedules, and provisions to account for a new generation period following reconstruction.

Waiting for government support

Private hydropower developers say they are prepared to rebuild, but they are waiting for the government to restore access infrastructure and introduce measures to ease the financial burden.

“There is no alternative to rebuilding the projects. They have to be rebuilt,” Bhattarai said. “But the government needs to facilitate a few things. Otherwise, it will be difficult.”

Discussions are under way between the private sector and government on issues including access roads, licence periods, bank interest and the period of electricity generation following reconstruction.

“We cannot move forward with vague assurances,” Bhattarai said. “The government says it will move ahead with relief and policy measures. We are waiting for that.”

The government’s decision to move towards a search-and-recovery phase comes as the number of people still missing following the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi floods and subsequent monsoon-related disasters remains high.

According to government data cited by officials, 5,285 people remain missing.

For the hydropower sector, rebuilding will depend heavily on what happens outside the project sites — when roads and bridges are restored, how affected families are resettled and what financial and regulatory support the government provides.

Until those pieces fall into place, many of the hydropower projects damaged by the Bhotekoshi flood remain inaccessible — and reconstruction cannot fully begin.

title.rendered: Bailey bridge installation begins along flood-damaged Galchhi-Betrawati road

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Installation of a Bailey bridge has begun at Betrawati along the flood-damaged Galchhi-Betrawati road section in Rasuwa after an alternative temporary track was opened.

According to Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal, work on the foundations required for the Bailey bridge had already begun alongside construction of the temporary track.

The foundations on both sides of the proposed bridge have now been completed, Lamsal said.

With the temporary track operational, authorities have accelerated the transportation of bridge components and other construction materials to the site. The materials are being delivered while the bridge installation work proceeds, according to Lamsal.

Once the Bailey bridge is completed, the main road connection to Rasuwa, which was disrupted by the floods, will be formally restored.

The bridge is expected to ease transportation to and from Rasuwa and restore road connectivity affected by the flood damage.

Lamsal said temporary arrangements have been made to resume traffic immediately, while long-term reconstruction of the damaged road infrastructure is being carried out simultaneously.
