title.rendered: Disney layoffs ‘extremely painful’ but necessary, says president Dana Walden

content.rendered:
Los Angeles, October 2

Walt Disney Company President Dana Walden has described the company’s recent layoffs as “extremely painful” but necessary as the entertainment giant faces intensifying competition in streaming and rapid technological changes.

Speaking at the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles on Thursday, Walden said Disney had recently parted ways with employees she had worked with for much of her career.

“We’ve exited colleagues who I’ve worked with for most of my career. It is in many ways a harsh reality,” Walden said. “It is extremely painful.”

More than 300 Disney employees were laid off on Tuesday, according to US media reports. Most of those affected reportedly worked in human resources and information technology.

The latest cuts came after Disney eliminated around 1,000 positions in April, primarily in its marketing division, following the appointment of Josh D’Amaro as the company’s new chief executive, according to trade media reports.

Disney has undertaken several rounds of cost-cutting in recent years as it seeks to compete in the increasingly crowded streaming market. The entertainment industry is also undergoing rapid technological change, including the growing use of artificial intelligence tools in production.

Walden said the company had also offered some executives the option of deciding whether they wanted to leave or remain with the company through a voluntary retirement programme.

It remains unclear whether the latest round of layoffs included employees who participated in the programme.

“There is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured,” Walden said, referring to Disney and its competitors in the technology sector.

“Technology set their sights on our business, and we must survive and thrive and grow. And that’s what we’re going to do,” she said.

The Walt Disney Company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title.rendered: Committee begins probe into public bus driver’s self-immolation in Tripureshwor

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

A committee formed to investigate the self-immolation of public bus driver Arjun Dong Tamang in Tripureshwor has held its first meeting.

The meeting was held on Friday under the coordination of Rajiv Pokharel, director general of the Department of Transport Management.

The committee has made four decisions as part of its investigation.

It will first study investigation reports previously prepared by agencies under the Ministry of Home Affairs and request the concerned authorities to implement recommendations made in those reports.

The committee will also proceed with collecting and analysing evidence related to the incident.

It has decided to invite representatives of insurance companies to its next meeting to discuss relief and compensation for those affected by the incident.

The committee will also seek suggestions from transport entrepreneurs and transport workers’ unions on measures to prevent similar incidents in the long term.

A committee member said the meeting held detailed discussions on the circumstances that led Tamang to self-immolate, the actual background of the incident, facts and evidence related to the sequence of events, and actions taken by the concerned authorities.

The committee is expected to examine the circumstances surrounding the incident and recommend measures based on its findings.

title.rendered: Australia’s rental crisis deepens as vacancy rates fall and rents rise

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Australia’s rental housing crisis is deepening as rents continue to rise while the availability of homes remains limited, putting growing financial pressure on international students, new migrants and low- and middle-income households.

A September 2026 analysis by Commonwealth Bank found that Australia’s national rental vacancy rate had fallen to around 1.8 percent, compared with an average of about 2.8 percent between 2015 and 2019. Advertised rents across the eight capital cities were increasing at an annual rate of 5.7 percent.

The shortage is particularly visible in major cities such as Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide, where tenants face intense competition for relatively affordable accommodation.

International students are among those facing significant pressure. A 2026 analysis by global property consultancy CBRE estimates potential unmet demand for around 185,000 purpose-built student accommodation rooms across Australia. Even if all planned projects proceed, the country is expected to add around 34,000 student accommodation beds between 2026 and 2029.

The shortage is particularly pronounced in Sydney and Melbourne. CBRE estimates unmet demand for about 25,000 student accommodation beds in central and inner-west Sydney and around 10,000 in Melbourne City and inner-north Melbourne.

Student accommodation rents in Sydney currently range from around A$700 to A$900 per week, according to CBRE. The corresponding range is A$550 to A$650 in Melbourne and A$500 to A$600 in Brisbane.

The high cost of accommodation has forced some students to share rooms, live farther from their universities or allocate a substantial portion of their income to rent.

The situation is also difficult for newly arrived migrants and refugees.

ABC News recently reported the case of Jay Biayi, a refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo, who spent almost six months looking for a rental property in Adelaide. He attended more than 100 inspections and had his applications rejected before eventually securing a home in Adelaide’s northern suburbs.

Adelaide’s rental vacancy rate stood at 0.4 percent in June, while the median weekly house rent had reached A$650, according to figures cited by ABC News from Domain.

The shortage is expected to remain a challenge as construction costs rise and the supply of new apartments remains constrained.

Recent CBRE projections indicate that average apartment rents could rise by as much as 26 percent over the next five years if construction costs and cancellations of private projects continue to constrain supply. The analysis also projects that 40 percent of two-bedroom apartments could have rents above A$1,000 per week.

The Australian government has set a target of building 1.2 million new, well-located homes over five years from July 2024 under the National Housing Accord. The government has also introduced measures intended to address planning and infrastructure constraints and increase housing construction.

However, the housing shortage continues to pose challenges for renters, particularly in major cities where population growth and demand for accommodation remain strong.

Australia’s housing pressures are also being felt by the country’s large Nepali student and migrant community. Nepalis arriving in Australia for study or employment often have to manage rental payments, upfront bonds and other housing costs while competing in a tight market.

For those searching for accommodation, community representatives and housing advocates advise prospective tenants to inspect properties before making payments, use written rental agreements and ensure that bond payments are officially registered through the relevant state or territory system.

With rents continuing to rise and vacancy rates remaining low, access to affordable accommodation is likely to remain a major challenge for international students, migrants and other renters across Australia.

title.rendered: NC General Convention won’t have panels; delegates to vote independently: Bishwa Prakash Sharma

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Nepali Congress will not form panels for its upcoming 15th General Convention, and delegates will be free to vote for candidates of their choice, party Vice President Bishwa Prakash Sharma has said.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar at the convention venue at Khulamanch, Sharma said the convention would seek to institutionalise the changes initiated by the party’s special general convention held last December.

“The difference this time is that there will not be the situation of saying this is one group and that is another group,” Sharma said. “There is no control over who gets to become a candidate through a group ticket. There will be no panels.”

He said all candidates would be treated equally and delegates would be allowed to vote according to their own judgment.

“We will not discourage anyone from contesting for any position,” he said. “All our colleagues are respected. Everyone is equal. Delegates will find it easier to vote independently and according to their own judgment.”

More than 7,000 delegates are expected to participate in the convention, which is scheduled to be held at Kathmandu’s Khulamanch.

Sharma said the convention was being organised at a time when the Nepali Congress was undergoing a transition, with the party seeking both ideological and organisational change.

He compared the special convention to a “force landing” and said the 15th General Convention would take the party toward a “safe landing”.

“The special general convention was a kind of force landing. The 15th General Convention will take the Nepali Congress towards a safe landing,” he said.

According to Sharma, the convention will also examine the party’s ideological position and identify areas where it needs to change.

He said the party should acknowledge its mistakes while clearly communicating the positive contributions it has made to the country.

“The convention will discuss how the ideas and principles we have carried from the past should be modified according to the present context,” Sharma said.

Party President Gagan Kumar Thapa is expected to present a document containing ideological and theoretical issues, including how the country should move forward over the next decade.

Sharma said his own document would examine the erosion of democratic culture and the need for reforms suited to the changing times. Other documents, including those from General Secretary and Deputy Speaker-level party leadership, will also be presented.

Sharma said the convention would also reflect changes in the composition of the party, including greater representation of younger members and groups previously not adequately recognised by the party statute.

The party has created a separate representation category for members below the age of 35, with around 600 delegates from that age group expected to attend the convention, according to Sharma.

He said more than 35,000 members below the age of 35 had also reached party committees from the ward level to the central level under the new provisions.

“Politics should be based on agendas, not age,” Sharma said. “That does not mean an older person becomes irrelevant simply because of age. What matters is how many times they have led, whether they still have creativity and whether their agenda remains relevant.”

He said the Nepali Congress was attempting to present a model in which experienced and younger leaders could work together.

The convention will also use digital systems for distributing documents and recording discussions, Sharma said.

Documents will be made available digitally, while speeches will be audio- and video-recorded. A separate team will take notes and incorporate suggestions made during discussions before the documents are finalised.

Sharma said three halls had been prepared at Khulamanch, each accommodating more than 2,500 delegates. The arrangement is intended to allow around 150 delegates to speak during a day while ensuring that documents presented in one hall are broadcast to the others.

He said the stage had been positioned facing east so that sound would not disturb patients at nearby hospitals.

Sharma acknowledged that political conventions often focus heavily on leadership contests and candidate support rather than substantive discussion of documents.

“It would be unrealistic to say that we will be completely free from that,” he said. “But our entire effort is to make the convention better.”

The Nepali Congress has also decided to limit the use of elaborate promotional displays across Kathmandu during the convention.

Unlike previous conventions, there will be no large gates, banners and decorations across areas such as Maharajgunj, Lagankhel, Jorpati, Koteshwar, Nagdhunga and Bhaktapur, Sharma said.

He said the decision was influenced by the recent disasters in the country, in which many people lost their lives and thousands remain missing.

“There is no need to make the entire city colourful at a time when we are holding a convention after a major disaster,” he said.

Promotional activities will instead give greater priority to digital platforms, while normal decorations will be allowed within the convention venue.

The Nepali Congress is also discussing the use of electronic voting machines for the leadership election.

Sharma said electronic voting would be used if the system could process more than 7,000 votes within a single day. If that is not possible, the party would have to use a manual voting system.

He rejected concerns that manual voting and counting would significantly delay the conclusion of the convention.

“The counting will not take a month,” Sharma said. “The Nepali Congress’ vote counting will not prevent people from celebrating the festivals.”

Sharma also recalled the historical significance of Khulamanch for the Nepali Congress, referring to a speech delivered there by party founder BP Koirala in 2036 BS, when Koirala was suffering from throat cancer and had undergone surgery.

He said the convention should not be seen only as an internal Nepali Congress event but as an opportunity to generate hope across the country.

“We have come here to awaken a new hope across the country, not just for the Nepali Congress,” Sharma said. “The country should move forward on the foundation of that hope and confidence.”

title.rendered: Speaker Aryal says he does not feel Parliament has become weaker

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal has said he does not feel that Parliament has become weaker.

Speaking to journalists on the occasion of the conclusion of the budget session of the House of Representatives, Aryal said there had been no decline in the dignity, pace of work or accountability of Parliament towards the people.

Aryal recalled his previous experience as a member of the House of Representatives for three years, as well as his interest in parliamentary affairs even before entering politics.

He said that even when comparing the current Parliament with previous ones, he did not feel that it had become weaker under his leadership.

“I have not felt at all that Parliament has become weaker. I also worked as a member of the House for three years in the past. Even before entering politics as a citizen, I had been observing Nepal’s Parliament,” he said.

Aryal said it was natural to experience fatigue while working for nearly 30 million Nepalis, but such fatigue had not affected the role of Parliament.

Speaking about parliamentary proceedings and the government’s delivery, Aryal said holding the executive accountable and pressing it to perform was a shared responsibility of lawmakers, citizens and journalists.

He said the current Parliament had instead introduced several new practices.

According to Aryal, unlike in previous sessions, both the ruling and opposition sides had held intensive discussions on issues concerning people’s livelihoods and other important matters.

He said top political leaders had also been given time twice a month to raise issues concerning the people directly from the rostrum.

Such new practices had made Parliament more effective, he said.

Aryal is also preparing to participate in an Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) assembly as Nepal’s representative.

He said Nepal was preparing to present the impact of climate change and compensation-related issues as an emergency agenda at the forum.

According to Aryal, the proposal has already received support from around 50 countries, while preparations are underway for around 28 side meetings.

Aryal also said he had given special priority to using Nepali, the country’s mother tongue, at meetings with diplomatic missions and international forums during his tenure, saying the practice had helped strengthen Nepal’s identity.

Journalists also raised questions about the construction of the new federal Parliament building.

Responding to the concerns over delays in the construction of the building, Aryal said he was confident that future parliamentary meetings would be held in the new building.

title.rendered: Nepal asks Malaysia to remove 25 foreign employment firms from foreign worker recruitment system

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

The Nepal government has asked Malaysia to remove 25 Nepali foreign employment companies registered under Malaysia’s Foreign Worker Centralized Management System (FWCMS).

The request comes amid a dispute over Malaysia’s decision to designate 25 Nepali foreign employment companies as “principal” agencies and another 250 companies as “supporting” agencies for recruiting Nepali workers.

The 25 companies registered under the FWCMS have themselves asked the Nepal government to remove them from the system, saying they do not want to remain part of the arrangement.

Based on their request, the Ministry of Youth and Employment has sent a letter to the Malaysian government through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

However, while Nepal has asked Malaysia to remove the listed foreign employment companies from the system, Malaysia has instructed employers to recruit foreign workers only through foreign employment companies registered under the FWCMS.

Initially, Malaysia had listed only 25 of the around 1,200 licensed Nepali foreign employment companies as registered recruitment agencies under the FWCMS. After the arrangement faced opposition in Nepal, another 250 foreign employment companies were brought under the 25 companies as supporting agencies.

The Nepal government has said it does not accept the structure of 25 principal and 250 supporting foreign employment companies. Nepal’s position is that all licensed foreign employment companies have equal status under Nepali foreign employment laws and that the Nepal-Malaysia labour agreement does not provide for a principal and supporting agency arrangement.

Amid the dispute, the 25 foreign employment companies included in Malaysia’s list submitted an application to the government in the first week of September, seeking to withdraw from the FWCMS.

During an earlier discussion at the ministry, the companies had also agreed to seek their removal from the system.

Hari Bahadur Dangi, general secretary of the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies, said the companies wanted to withdraw because they did not accept an arrangement that would connect only a limited number of foreign employment companies with Malaysian employers.

The government has also begun an investigation into the involvement of the 25 foreign employment companies in the FWCMS.

The Department of Foreign Employment has sought details on their transactions, the basis on which they were selected, their previous involvement in recruiting workers for Malaysia and the process through which other foreign employment companies were brought under them.

The department has also asked the 25 principal foreign employment companies to submit their business and financial details for the past five fiscal years.

The information sought under Section 34 of the Foreign Employment Act 2007 includes details of transactions, the number of workers recruited, service charges, taxes and audited financial statements.

Earlier, the department had also stopped issuing new pre-approval for Malaysia-bound workers to the 250 foreign employment companies affiliated with the 25 principal companies under the FWCMS.

A decision was taken not to issue new pre-approval to those companies until the investigation is completed.

Nepal has maintained that it will not accept an arrangement under which workers are sent to Malaysia through only a limited number of foreign employment companies.

Labour Minister Ramji Yadav had also urged Malaysia’s Human Resources Minister during a telephone conversation to provide equal opportunities to all licensed foreign employment companies in Nepal in the process of sending workers to Malaysia.

The two countries had also held discussions at the prime ministerial level earlier. The Ministry of Labour said efforts were being made to resolve the dispute over the selection of foreign employment companies through high-level political and diplomatic channels.

“We are trying to resolve the complexities in Nepal-Malaysia labour relations at the highest level. We have sent through the Foreign Ministry the list of foreign employment companies that want to withdraw from the system,” said Labour Ministry spokesperson Mira Acharya.

Nepal has been maintaining that all licensed Nepali foreign employment companies should be given an opportunity to participate in the FWCMS.

Malaysia, meanwhile, has said the system is intended to streamline the recruitment of foreign workers under government oversight and control illegal fees, middlemen and fraud.

The FWCMS facilitates employer registration and the recruitment process for foreign workers in Malaysia. The system also provides for workers to be selected through recruitment agencies in source countries.

Employers in Malaysia are required to obtain prior approval from the relevant authorities before hiring foreign workers. The FWCMS has been used in this process.

Malaysia’s Labour Department has also linked the verification of demand letters for Nepali workers to the Nepal-Malaysia labour agreement.

The Nepali Embassy in Kuala Lumpur, however, said it was not aware of the letter sent by Nepal to Malaysia.

An embassy official said the letter had not been received by the embassy so far. The official said the letter may have been sent directly because discussions between the two countries are currently taking place at the prime ministerial and ministerial levels.

“Direct discussions are currently taking place at the prime ministerial and ministerial levels, so there has not been much communication through the embassy,” the official said.

Nepal had earlier also initiated diplomatic discussions with Malaysia after rejecting the arrangement involving 25 principal and 250 supporting foreign employment companies.

The dispute has continued to affect the verification of new demand letters from Malaysian employers and the recruitment process for workers bound for Malaysia.

title.rendered: Pernod Ricard contributes Rs 5 million to Prime Minister’s Relief Fund

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Pernod Ricard has announced a contribution of Rs 5 million to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund to support relief and recovery efforts for communities affected by recent natural disasters in Nepal.

The company said the contribution would be used to assist families affected by the disasters.

Pernod Ricard expressed sympathy to those affected and said its thoughts were with the affected communities as well as those involved in relief and recovery efforts.

Saurav Bhattarai, Business Development Manager-Nepal at Pernod Ricard, said the company hoped its contribution would provide support to relief efforts and people facing difficulties.

“Our hearts go out to everyone affected by these devastating events. We stand in solidarity with the people of Nepal and hope this contribution can provide some support to relief efforts and to those facing the greatest hardship,” Bhattarai said.

He also expressed gratitude to government authorities, security forces, emergency responders, volunteers and local communities involved in rescue, relief and recovery operations.

Pernod Ricard said it has maintained a presence in Nepal through its local partner SPG Trading and remains committed to supporting communities where it operates.

The company said it would continue to contribute where possible during extraordinary circumstances affecting communities in Nepal.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress bans banners, posters and pamphlets for 15th General Convention campaign

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

The Central Election Committee of the Nepali Congress has introduced a code of conduct for its 15th General Convention.

Committee member-secretary Raju Katuwal said in a statement on Friday that the committee had decided to enforce the code of conduct for candidates contesting the general convention.

“The Central Election Committee has decided to introduce additional and stricter provisions, along with the existing provisions of the election code of conduct, for aspirants and candidates contesting various posts in the general convention,” the statement said.

According to Katuwal, flamboyant and ostentatious campaigning will be completely prohibited. He said all forms of extravagant campaign activities have been banned to ensure that the general convention is conducted in a dignified, economical and disciplined manner while respecting the situation following the disaster.

The committee has completely banned printed and physical campaign materials. It said candidates will not be allowed to place, paste or distribute flexes, banners, posters, pamphlets or any other printed campaign materials at or around the general convention venue.

Similarly, campaigning outside the convention venue will not be allowed. The committee has strictly prohibited the placement or display of any type of physical campaign material in the outer premises of the convention venue, public roads or surrounding areas.

Katuwal said only digital and technology-based campaigning would be permitted. Candidates will be allowed to communicate their agendas and details of their candidacies only through digital means, including social media, online platforms and other electronic media.

title.rendered: More than 700 arrested at Jantar Mantar during protest in India

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

More than 700 people have been arrested by police during protests in India demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

More than 700 people were reportedly arrested from Jantar Mantar in Delhi alone. The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) launched the protest on Thursday demanding Kumar’s resignation. Other established opposition parties had also been staging protests earlier.

Those arrested include students as well as several opposition leaders. According to BBC Hindi, Aam Aadmi Party leader and former Delhi Chief Minister Atishi, and former minister Saurabh Bharadwaj were among those arrested.

Rashtriya Janata Dal lawmaker Manoj Jha was also arrested by police at Jantar Mantar in Delhi. Meanwhile, Indian Communist leader MA Baby was also arrested.

title.rendered: Oli says UML can overcome current setback by strengthening party

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

CPN-UML Chair KP Sharma Oli has said the party can rise well above its current setback if it moves forward by strengthening itself.

Oli made the remarks while administering the oath of office to newly nominated central committee members at the party’s central office in Chyasal on Friday. He said a party pursuing the great goal of national prosperity could face setbacks from time to time, but it could rise well above the current setback by strengthening itself and moving forward.

He said forces opposed to development had attempted to obstruct the UML, which was advancing the country’s development campaign.

Oli expressed confidence that although the country had experienced regression and the party had suffered a setback, the party could recover from where it had fallen and move further ahead than before if its members avoided getting caught up in minor issues and moved forward with an open mind.

He said the newly sworn-in central committee members should play a leading role and establish themselves in society as role models. He urged them to abandon improper conduct and demonstrate integrity, discipline, communist decorum and humility.

He also stressed that party leaders and cadres should understand modern technology and the contemporary context and move forward accordingly, as the current era is one of “IT war.”

title.rendered: ACC president Naqvi to skip Asian Games cricket final in Japan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Asian Cricket Council (ACC) President Mohsin Naqvi will not travel to Japan to watch the cricket final of the 2026 Asian Games.

India and Pakistan will face each other for the men’s cricket gold medal on Saturday. Before that, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh will compete for the bronze medal.

The ACC said in a statement on Friday that Naqvi would not travel to Japan for the final. The statement said Naqvi extended his best wishes to all four teams competing for the gold and bronze medals.

Naqvi said he would be unable to travel to Nagoya due to his busy schedule. He wished all the participating teams the best for the gold- and bronze-medal matches and said he was looking forward to watching an exciting contest.

Naqvi is also the chairperson of the Pakistan Cricket Board.

title.rendered: Legal reforms, clear policies needed for infrastructure development: Chamber

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Kamalesh Kumar Agrawal, president of the Nepal Chamber of Commerce, has said necessary legal and policy reforms are needed by prioritising infrastructure development to enhance Nepal’s competitiveness and promote economic development.

Agrawal made the remarks at a workshop on legal reforms for investment and development organised by the Ministry of Infrastructure Development on Friday.

He stressed the need to make legal procedures for infrastructure development simple, clear and transparent. He said modern and reliable infrastructure is essential to advance investment, technology, production, trade, tourism, employment and economic activities amid rapid changes in the global economy.

Agrawal said infrastructure development should encompass not only roads, bridges and physical structures but also digital infrastructure, information technology, cybersecurity, energy, communications, smart infrastructure and new technologies.

He said the government’s ongoing legal amendment process should consider technical and financial capacity, project requirements, and environmental and social impacts rather than selecting projects solely based on the lowest cost.

He also said clear, time-bound and transparent arrangements are needed for environmental approvals, land acquisition and forest-related procedures for infrastructure projects.

“Infrastructure development is not solely a matter of budget; legal provisions also affect it,” he said. “Simplifying procedures attracts investment, ensuring respect for agreements and transparency mobilises private capital, and maintaining accountability increases public trust.”

title.rendered: Lawmakers draw government’s attention to flood-damaged roads, bridges ahead of festivals

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Lawmakers drew the government’s attention during the zero hour of the National Assembly meeting on Friday to damaged roads and bridges and disruptions to daily life caused by continuous rainfall across the country.

They sought answers from the government over the hardships faced by people as transport services remained disrupted on the eve of major festivals such as Dashain and Tihar.

Lawmakers prominently raised the impact of floods in the Bhotekoshi and Mahakali rivers and damage to road infrastructure in various parts of the country.

Lawmaker Gomadevi Timilsina drew the government’s attention to containers swept away by the Bhotekoshi flood and cargo vehicles stranded at the Korala border point in Mustang. She called for roads to be repaired and relief to be provided to traders.

Similarly, lawmaker Jagat Bahadur Parki called for the immediate reconstruction of a damaged suspension bridge in Dodhara Chandani, Kanchanpur, saying more than 50,000 people had been deprived of access to the bridge.

Speaking on infrastructure, lawmaker Nar Bahadur Bista sought a clear response from the government over the Baddichaur-Kholighate road, which he said had remained incomplete for seven years. He also questioned the contractor’s negligence and the disruption of road networks during the festive season.

Lawmaker Rajendralaxmi Gaire expressed concern over damage to bridges along the Kaligandaki Corridor and to farmers’ paddy crops and urged the government to introduce a compensation package.

During the meeting, lawmaker Madankumari Shah objected to a statement attributed to Prime Minister Balen Shah. She said Shah’s claim that Indian territory had also encroached on Nepal’s land was false and against national pride, and demanded that the statement be removed from the parliamentary record.

Lawmaker Suresh Kumar Ale Magar called for the date and month to be included when Nepal Sambat is listed on the National Assembly’s agenda. He also urged the government to speed up repairs of damaged roads ahead of the festivals.

title.rendered: When Sudurpaschim comes alive on stage

content.rendered:
The sound of a folk melody fills the theatre. Somewhere in the landscape of Sudurpaschim, a young girl calls out to her cattle as the first scene unfolds. There is something immediately familiar yet distant about the setting, a glimpse into a way of life, a culture and a region that rarely finds such space on the Kathmandu stage.

The girl is Gauri, played by Sushmita Kunwar, and her appearance marks the beginning of Shree Bijoo Bhoot, currently being staged at Mandala Theatre.

Written by Diwas Nath and directed by Akash Nepali, the play revolves around the socio-political dynamics of Sudurpaschim. It tells the story of a daughter who is on the way to Bombay, India, in search of her father, who left for work there but has not returned home for the past two decades.

The play draws on a reality that remains familiar to many families in Sudurpaschim. Many people from the region have travelled to India in search of employment, and some, like Gauri’s father, have remained away from home for years without returning.

Because of this, people from Sudurpaschim can closely relate to the play and its story.

The conversations among the characters, about their families, jobs, businesses and everyday challenges, also offer an insight into the daily lives and social realities of people in Sudurpaschim.

The conversations between Gauri and her mother (played by Barsha Bhandara) reveal the difficulties of being a single mother. The conversation also shows how women who raise their children alone are often subjected to unfair judgment and social scrutiny.

In one scene, a woman visits Gauri’s mother to ask whether Gauri would marry her brother, who is a government officer. Gauri’s mother then suddenly begins pressuring her daughter to get married. The scene reflects the reality of young women being pressured to marry once they enter their twenties. Rather than focusing on empowering their daughters, many families across Nepal continue to mount pressure on women to marry at a young age, and Sudurpaschim is no exception.

Art is a powerful medium through which we can learn about diverse cultures, and Shree Bijoo Bhoot is a fine example of this. The play not only tells a specific story but also gives audiences an opportunity to learn about the language, dance, music and food of Sudurpaschim.

The technical aspects of the production, particularly the acting and music, are remarkable. The makers have made a thoughtful choice by bringing both actors and musicians from Sudurpaschim into the production. This gives the actors a natural familiarity with the dialect used in the region, allowing the dialogue to feel effortless and authentic.

Singer Harina Nath, who is making her theatre debut, has done an outstanding job. Her voice adds another layer of authenticity to the play. When she sings, particularly when she reaches the high notes, her performance can send shivers down the spine.

Shree Bijoo Bhoot is actually the name of a deity. In Ningla village of Dadeldhura, there is a belief that nothing bad can happen in a place where Shree Bijoo Bhoot (Da) is present. Interestingly, a goat appears as a character in the play. The goat can be understood as someone sent by Shree Bijoo Bhoot or as a character in whom the deity dwells.

According to the belief that nothing bad can happen in the presence of Shree Bijoo Bhoot, the goat brings back two characters who have looted the other characters in the play. Before carrying out the robbery, the two characters make the others consume food that causes them to lose consciousness. The goat later finds the two robbers, ties them up with ropes and brings them back.

While the play revolves around serious issues, it also has a strong comedic side. The character of Hari, played by Aaditya Mishra, is particularly entertaining. Hari works in Bombay and has returned to the village, and his actions and interactions frequently make the audience laugh.

Shree Bijoo Bhoot is a play that can be appreciated by audiences regardless of where they come from. People from Sudurpaschim can relate closely to its story and perhaps experience a sense of home away from home. For audiences from outside the region, meanwhile, the play offers an opportunity to learn about a culture they may not be familiar with.

However, the use of the Sudurpaschim dialect in some parts of the play may make it difficult for audiences unfamiliar with the language to understand certain conversations.

Finally, the title of the play could perhaps have been more closely connected to its broader narrative, as the connection between the title and the central context of the play does not always feel immediately apparent.

More than a story, Shree Bijoo Bhoot offers a glimpse into the culture, struggles and lived realities of Sudurpaschim.

Shree Bijoo Bhoot will run daily (except Mondays) through October 11 at 5:30 pm at Mandala Theatre in Kathmandu. An additional show will run on Saturdays at 1:30 pm.

title.rendered: Government will not make laws to benefit middlemen: Minister Lamsal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal has said the government is seeking to create an environment conducive to development and investment by reforming existing laws.

Lamsal made the remarks while addressing a workshop on “Legal Reforms for Investment and Development Related to Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026” organised by the Ministry of Infrastructure Development on Friday.

He said the government is focused on creating citizen-friendly laws, arguing that the state system should operate in accordance with the law and produce tangible results. He said laws reflect a country and that the kind of laws a country makes determines the kind of nation it becomes.

“An Act is the mirror of a country. The kind of laws we have, determines the kind of nation we are. If we look at our current urban laws, our cities are also like that. Our schools are also shaped by the kind of education laws we have. The results also seem to correspond to the laws we make. The laws we are now seeking to amend are being reformed accordingly,” he said.

Lamsal said the government had studied suggestions from stakeholders during the process of amending the Public Procurement Act but could not incorporate them because they did not meet the required policy objectives.

He said the workshop would play an important role in identifying reforms needed to make infrastructure development more dynamic and effective. He added that the government was clear that laws should not be drafted in a way that allows middlemen to benefit.

“We need to study the draft we have prepared word by word and think about how to make the law better. When we were passing the Procurement Act, the construction entrepreneurs’ association brought forward a suggestion. But we did not accept it because their suggestion did not provide a policy departure,” he said. “We studied their suggestions as well as our own preparations. We wanted to provide them with many things, but it also seemed that they were unwilling to accept them. The government is specifically seeking a public-centric policy departure.”

title.rendered: Minister Pun pledges to modernise National Forensic Laboratory

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun has said the government is committed to modernising the National Forensic Laboratory, highlighting the need for the National Forensic Laboratory (Establishment and Operation) Bill, 2081.

Speaking at Friday’s meeting of the National Assembly, Pun said the laboratory, which had long operated largely as a nominal institution under a government formation order, would now move towards a structured system under an Act.

During the extensive discussion on the bill, Pun informed the House about the laboratory’s current poor condition. He said its limited capacity became evident when DNA testing of victims was required following the Bhotekoshi floods. As the tests could be conducted only with assistance from foreign teams at the time, he stressed the need to strengthen domestic capacity.

Pun said forensic laboratories had so far been operating in temporary structures and rented buildings. With the passage of the Act, he said, the government would now be able to acquire land and construct its own buildings.

He said design work had begun for a modern building within the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology (NAST) premises in Kathmandu.

The ministry has also begun preparations to modernise the forensic laboratory using this fiscal year’s budget. Rs 200 million has been allocated for equipment, while additional funds will be arranged for construction of the building. The government also plans to modernise existing small laboratories across the country and establish laboratories in the remaining provinces.

Recalling detailed discussions in the parliamentary committee on DNA security, Pun said DNA testing was highly sensitive in the administration of justice, and there would be no compromise on its security and accuracy.

title.rendered: Popular Hollywood franchise ‘Fast & Furious’ to become a TV series

content.rendered:
Los Angeles

The popular Hollywood franchise Fast & Furious is set to return as a new scripted television series. Streaming platform Peacock announced Thursday that it has officially greenlit a new series based on the franchise.

The series was first announced as being in development earlier this year at NBCUniversal’s Upfronts event. At the event in May, actor Vin Diesel said a scripted Fast & Furious series was being developed.

Diesel will also serve as an executive producer. Other executive producers include Sam Vincent of One Race, Neal H. Moritz and Pawan Shetty of the original films, Jeff Kirschenbaum, and Chris Morgan of Chris Morgan Productions.

Mike Daniels, known for Sons of Anarchy, Shades of Blue and The Rockford Files, and Wolfe Coleman, associated with Shades of Blue and 9-1-1: Lone Star, will serve as co-showrunners. They will write the pilot episode and also serve as executive producers.

According to Peacock, the series is targeted to premiere by 2028. Its premiere is expected to coincide with the release of the franchise’s upcoming film Fast Forever, which is scheduled to hit theatres on March 17, 2028.

Universal Television, part of Universal Studio Group, will serve as the studio behind the series.

At the May Upfronts event, Diesel said fans had been asking for more content from Fast & Furious over the past decade, particularly expanded stories involving established characters.

The franchise has previously appeared on television. Netflix aired six seasons of the animated series Fast & Furious: Spy Racers from 2019 to 2021.

The Fast & Furious franchise marks its 25th anniversary this year. According to NBCUniversal, Universal Pictures released the first film, The Fast and the Furious, on June 22, 2001.

Set against the backdrop of Los Angeles street-racing culture, the film starred Vin Diesel as Dominic Toretto, Paul Walker as Brian O’Conner, Jordana Brewster as Mia and Michelle Rodriguez as Letty. The story that began with the film later expanded into a global cultural phenomenon.

—Variety

title.rendered: MP Rana Magar urges government to address wild elephant, land issues in Jhapa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Indira Rana Magar has drawn the government’s attention to the problems faced by people in Jhapa due to wild elephants and unresolved land issues affecting landless settlers.

Speaking at the House of Representatives meeting on Friday, she urged the government to take immediate and effective measures to control damage caused by elephants during the harvest season and to provide land ownership certificates to citizens who have already received land ownership slips.

Rana Magar said farmers in Jhapa have been forced to stay awake throughout the night to protect their crops from elephants as Dashain approaches.

She said land-related problems were equally serious. She expressed concern that landless settlers who have already received land ownership slips were being subjected to further hardship in the name of re-surveying their land.

“Farmers are currently forced to give up their sleep and keep watch over their crops throughout the night because of elephants, but there has been no assurance of concrete relief from the government. Those who have already received land ownership slips should receive their land ownership certificates soon. They should not be made to suffer by adding more procedures,” she said.

Rana Magar said she had received complaints that some local governments were spreading confusion by claiming that they had received “orders from above”. She called on the concerned ministry to clarify the matter.

She urged the government to immediately announce an action plan to provide relief to farmers affected by wild elephants and ownership certificates to those waiting for them.

title.rendered: Traffic police discover driver with 729 violations in six years

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

There was an unusual conversation at the Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office on Thursday. A traffic police officer sat down with a driver and began asking questions that went far beyond the usual traffic violation.

What do you drive? How long have you been a driver? Where do you usually drive? What do you carry? How do you transport it? Who is in your family?

For nearly half an hour, the officer listened as the driver answered. The reason for the unusual conversation was a number that had caught the traffic police by surprise: 729. That was the number of times the driver had been penalised for traffic violations over the past six years.

The driver was Ram Bahadur Bista from Makwanpur. He drives a goods vehicle with the registration number Ba 16 Cha 8064.

Traffic police had begun noticing Bista because he kept turning up at their office. After learning that the same driver was repeatedly being brought in for violations, Traffic Police Superintendent Naresh Raj Subedi asked his staff about him.

The answer surprised him.

“He is a driver who repeatedly faces action. We were told that he might have been fined 700 or 800 times,” Subedi told Onlinekhabar.

The police checked the records. The figure was not 700 or 800. It was 729.

Subedi then asked Bista to come to the traffic police office at Ramshahpath.

“We were surprised to hear that he had already been penalised 729 times. We wanted to understand how he was driving and why this kept happening, so we called him in and listened to him,” Subedi said.

So, instead of simply issuing another fine, the traffic police decided to talk to him.

Bista was asked about his work, the vehicle he drove, the routes he took and the goods he carried. Officers also asked about his personal and family circumstances.

They wanted to understand the person behind the extraordinary traffic record.

What was he doing wrong?

Bista drives a vehicle used to transport hardware materials, particularly metal goods. According to traffic police, most of his violations were related to the way he transported those goods. He would sometimes carry metal rods and other materials beyond the vehicle’s body. At times, the rear side of the vehicle would be left open so that the goods could extend outside. His number plate was also found to have been covered while carrying goods.

Most of his traffic tickets were issued for operating a public goods vehicle without displaying the required identifying signs properly. He was also penalised for other offences, including running red lights and crossing lanes. But there was another reason Bista apparently did not take the repeated fines particularly seriously. His company usually paid them.

Bista had paid fines ranging from Rs 500 to Rs 1,000 over the years, but fines related to transporting hardware goods improperly were generally paid by the company.

As a result, he had not realised that repeatedly breaking traffic rules could eventually have consequences for him personally.

By Thursday, however, the message was clear. Police told him that continuing to accumulate violations could eventually put his driving licence at risk.

“He was not aware that repeated traffic violations could affect his professional record,” Subedi said. “We explained the traffic rules to him and told him not to repeat such offences.”

One violation every three days

The numbers make the record even more striking. Bista has been penalised 729 times in six years. That means an average of about 122 penalties every year. Or roughly one traffic violation every three days.

He has already paid the fines for 728 of those violations. The latest fine is still outstanding.

Traffic police say there is at least one thing Bista was not doing during those incidents. He was not driving under the influence. Police records show that he has not been found driving after consuming alcohol or drugs. In some periods, however, the records show that he was penalised on consecutive days.

An unusual record

Traffic police officials say they are not aware of another case in Nepal in which a single driver has been penalised as many as 729 times in six years.

For the traffic police, however, Bista’s case is about more than an unusual record.

It also raises a question about what happens when repeated fines fail to change a driver’s behaviour.

Traffic police have continued awareness campaigns and enforcement drives, but Bista’s record suggests that some drivers may require a different approach when repeated violations become a pattern.

For now, Bista has been sent home with a warning that his next mistake could cost much more than a fine.

title.rendered: UML nominated central committee members take oath

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Nominated central committee members of the CPN-UML took their oath of office on Thursday.

Party Chairperson KP Sharma Oli administered the oath to the newly nominated members at the party’s central office in Chyasal.

The UML Central Committee meeting, which began on September 21 and concluded on September 24, nominated 33 people as central committee members, including 13 who joined the party from other political parties.

The nominations were made in accordance with the party statute, which allows 10 per cent of the central committee members to be nominated.

The UML has also nominated seven members to its Standing Committee.

Former President Bidya Devi Bhandari has been appointed as a senior leader of the UML.

title.rendered: Over 800 historical Nepali documents returned from German private collection

content.rendered:
Photos: Aryan Dhimal

Kathmandu, October 2

More than 800 important historical Nepali documents dating from the 13th to the 20th century have been handed over to Nepal’s National Archives after being held in the private collection of German national Josef Peter Rindfleisch.

The documents were jointly handed over to Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal by Professor Axel Michaels of the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities under Heidelberg University, Dr Manik Bajracharya and Rajan Khatiwada at a programme held at the National Archives on Friday.

Professor Michaels was a friend of Rindfleisch’s son, Walter Rindfleisch. Walter had handed over his father’s collection to Michaels with the intention of returning the documents to Nepal. Michaels subsequently facilitated their return to Nepal through Heidelberg University.

The documents were repatriated through collaboration among the Nepali Embassy in Germany, Heidelberg University, the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, the Sharaf Foundation and the National Archives.

Foreign Minister Khanal said the return of the historical documents had restored Nepal’s cultural integrity and sovereign ownership over its civilisational heritage.

“Our art, literature, traditions and sacred texts are not merely physical remains. They are the living soul of our civilisation. They carry centuries of philosophical thought, political governance, legal knowledge and spiritual life,” he said.

“The return of each historical document to its homeland is a restoration of cultural rights and a renewed commitment to sovereign ownership of our civilisational heritage,” he added.

Khanal recalled that the late Josef Peter Rindfleisch had expressed his wish to return the more than 800 important Nepali documents in his private collection and praised his respect for cultural heritage and his foresight.

He also expressed gratitude to Walter Rindfleisch for honouring his father’s wishes by handing the documents over to Professor Axel Michaels of Heidelberg University’s South Asia Institute.

“This extraordinary archive includes ancient palm-leaf manuscripts, royal decrees, court orders, Sanskrit texts and historical travel accounts. These documents are indispensable sources for understanding Nepal’s political, legal and intellectual development,” he said.

Khanal also praised Professor Michaels and his research team for their role in identifying, cataloguing and repatriating the documents, saying their academic integrity, research and sustained efforts had made the return possible.

The collection, which was gathered from Nepal between the 1780s and the 1990s, includes more than 800 royal and official documents, including palm-leaf manuscripts, rukka and lal mohar documents.

The collection was preserved and catalogued by the Heidelberg University Library and the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities before being returned to Nepal in coordination with the Nepal government.

According to the catalogue of the collection, it includes 465 palm-leaf manuscripts from the Malla period, including palm-leaf documents and lal mohar records, as well as 312 legal decrees and royal documents from the Shah and Rana periods bearing clay seals.

The collection also includes 18 handwritten texts and travel diaries from the offices of Rana prime ministers and 11 handwritten manuscripts on various subjects.

Khanal said Nepal and Germany are both parties to the 1970 UNESCO Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property.

He said the handover demonstrated a shared commitment to the spirit and principles of the international convention.

“Today’s handover is an important example of our shared international commitment. We highly appreciate the active support provided by the German government, the German Embassy in Kathmandu and Heidelberg University for the smooth return of these documents,” he said.

Khanal also recalled that Professor Michaels had formally handed over the documents to the Nepali Embassy in Berlin on April 24, 2026.

He praised the coordination among the Nepali Embassy, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the National Archives throughout the repatriation process.

title.rendered: Legal stability essential for investment and development: Minister Gautam

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam has said legal stability is essential for creating an investment-friendly environment and promoting development in the country.

Speaking at a workshop on “Legal Reforms for Investment and Development” organised by the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport in connection with the Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026 on Friday, Gautam said the government was working to ensure that investors could trust their agreements would be honoured regardless of which government comes to power.

She said the government had declared the current fiscal year as the “Year of Legal Reform” and had already begun the process of drafting new laws and amending existing ones as necessary.

Gautam said Nepal should develop its own model of development rather than simply copying models from other countries, taking into account the country’s social, cultural and economic context.

She said around 54 bills had been approved by the Cabinet since the government was formed and were in the process of being registered in Parliament.

Gautam stressed that the three-day workshop should identify practical legal challenges faced during infrastructure development and investment and find solutions to them.

She also said the government was preparing to establish an infrastructure court to prevent disputes between the government and private sector from remaining unresolved for long periods.

title.rendered: Lal Babu Sah Kanu wins Rs 1 million in taxpayer incentive draw

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Under the Taxpayer Incentive Gift Program, the government on Friday announced the prizes for 1 to 15 Asoj.

According to the new announcement, Lal Babu Sah Kanu of Parsa has won the 15-day bumper prize of Rs 1 million.

Kanu was selected based on a Rs 21,000 lube oil purchase.

At an event held at the Ministry of Finance, Sumnima Udas, chair of the House of Representatives’ International Relations and Tourism Committee, along with House members Ganesh Karki and Santosh Rajbanshi, jointly announced the prizes for the first 15 days of Asoj.

The Finance Minister’s Secretariat said Bhishma Kumar Bhushal, Director General of the Inland Revenue Department, called Kanu immediately to congratulate him and asked him to contact the nearest tax office to claim the prize.

According to the Inland Revenue Department, 31,818,286 transactions (3 crore 18 lakh 18 thousand 286) made between Asoj 1 and 15, in which consumers took bills for online and cash purchases, were eligible for the gift program.

Of these, 247,979 were cash transactions with bills, while 31,570,307 were purchases paid online or by card.

title.rendered: Nepali ‘Australian dream’ needs a more honest conversation

content.rendered:
The photograph is familiar to almost every Nepali family.

A young person stands at Tribhuvan International Airport, passport in hand, tika on the forehead and a khada around the neck. Parents press close. Siblings make room for one more picture. There are blessings, hurried instructions and tears that someone tries to hide.

Call when you land. Eat properly. Look after yourself.

Within hours, the photograph appears on Facebook. Congratulations arrive from relatives and friends. A new life in Australia has begun.

What happens after that photograph receives far less attention.

Where will this young person sleep? What happens if work does not materialise? Who will notice if they stop attending classes or answering calls? And will they feel able to tell their family that the life everyone is celebrating has become difficult?

As a Nepali-born immigration and family lawyer in Australia, I believe these questions belong at the centre of our migration conversation.

A successful visa application matters. So does the life a person can build after it.

The distance between a dream and a crisis

Bikram Lama came to Australia as an international student in 2013. His family sold land to help fund his education. Years later, he was sleeping rough in Sydney.

The Australian government-funded ABC reported that his body was found near St James station in December 2025, having gone unnoticed for more than a week. His family reportedly discovered only after his death that he had been homeless.

In July 2026, The Guardian reported that preparations were finally under way to return his body to Nepal after months of delay.

There is much we cannot know about Bikram’s private struggles. We should resist filling those gaps with assumptions about his decisions, his family or his mental health.

But we can ask what his story requires of us.

How do we make help accessible to someone who has become isolated? How do we support people who cannot easily explain what has happened to them? How do we ensure that a person who arrived with aspirations does not become invisible when those aspirations unravel?

Our community knows how to come together after a tragedy. The harder task is building support that reaches someone before the emergency becomes a headline.

A family’s investment can become a child’s silence

For a Nepali student, the cost of Australia may be measured in much more than tuition. It may be the land their parents sold, the loan a relative guaranteed or the savings intended for another child’s education.

That sacrifice can inspire extraordinary determination. It can also make an ordinary admission — “I am struggling” — feel almost impossible.

Imagine the conversation from the student’s side. The family has celebrated. Neighbours have congratulated the parents. Everyone asks about work, earnings and permanent residence.

How does the student explain that the rent is overdue?

This is a situation families should discuss before departure. It becomes harder when financial difficulty is treated as evidence that someone has not worked hard enough.

A budget needs room for delayed employment, unexpected expenses and a period of adjustment. A family’s expectations need the same flexibility.

The question should be asked plainly: if this plan becomes unaffordable, what will we do together?

That final word matters. A young person should not feel solely responsible for rescuing a decision the whole family helped make.

The first address matters as much as the admission letter

Accommodation often enters the conversation late. A friend knows someone. There is a room advertised in a Facebook group. Arrangements can be made after landing.

Yet safe, stable housing is fundamental to studying, working and staying well.

The warnings are longstanding. In Living Precariously, a 2019 report by Laurie Berg and Bassina Farbenblum, half of the 2,440 international students who answered housing questions reported at least one housing problem. Reported experiences included misleading offers, withheld bonds, overcrowding and unsafe conditions. Among Nepali respondents, one in five reported paying for accommodation that did not exist.

These were findings from that survey, not a current estimate for all Nepali students.

The implications are practical. Before money changes hands, students need help understanding what they are renting, from whom, on what terms and with what recourse if the arrangement goes wrong.

Education providers should make that assistance easy to find. Recruiting a student creates a relationship that should continue when that student needs help securing somewhere safe to live.

An Australian address is no guarantee of a safe marriage

As a family lawyer, I also believe we must examine the assumptions surrounding migration through marriage.

A prospective partner’s Australian citizenship, permanent residency or overseas income may reassure a family. Those facts reveal little about how that person will behave within a relationship.

In June, ABC’s 7.30 reported the account of a Nepali woman identified as Shree. She described pressure to marry, followed by abuse, isolation and restrictions on her independence in Australia. The report described her reliance on refuge accommodation while seeking security for her future.

Her account deserves attention without being used to stereotype arranged marriages or our community. The issue is whether a person has genuine choice, independence and support.

Before a marriage, families should ask about compatibility and expectations with the same seriousness they bring to questions about immigration status. After a disclosure of abuse, their first concern should be the person’s safety.

Advice to “adjust” can have serious consequences when the behaviour being described is intimidation or violence.

Immigration uncertainty can make leaving feel especially frightening. Here, legal accuracy matters: a spouse cannot personally cancel someone else’s visa. That power belongs to the minister or a delegated official. Family violence provisions may allow eligible applicants to continue towards permanent residence after a relationship ends, depending on their circumstances.

Someone facing threats about deportation needs independent advice. Their understanding of the law should never depend entirely on the person threatening them.

Preparing for Australia means preparing for daily life

Safety also extends beyond the home.

Sachet Bimali, a Nepali student undertaking a master’s degree in information technology at Macquarie University, drowned at Wattamolla Lagoon in January 2021.

In January 2019, SBS reported that Nepalis in Adelaide gathered to remember Nischal Ghimire, whose body was found at Glenelg after he went missing the previous December.

These deaths occurred in circumstances different from Bikram’s. They do not establish that financial or visa pressures caused these tragedies. They remind us that student preparation must encompass everyday safety.

We devote considerable attention to English tests, admission documents and visa applications. Water safety, emergency assistance, healthcare and knowing where to seek help deserve attention too.

A capable, well-educated person can still be unfamiliar with local risks. Practical orientation should continue beyond a welcome email and the first week of classes.

A pathway is a possibility, not a promise

The need for honest advice begins before anyone boards a plane.

On 9 September, ABC reported that Australia’s student visa refusal rate had reached a decade high. Drawing on Department of Home Affairs data, it reported that more than 51 percent of student visa applications from Nepal were refused in 2025–26. The department said applications were not assessed on nationality.

That figure cannot predict an individual decision. It should, however, make families cautious about anyone presenting an outcome as virtually assured.

Admission, a visa, graduate employment and permanent residence are separate stages. The word “pathway” can make them sound more continuous and predictable than they are.

As professionals, we must explain where uncertainty lies. What requirements can the applicant meet today? What depends on future employment, policy or personal circumstances? What happens if the preferred option becomes unavailable?

Families should receive those explanations before committing substantial sums of money.

Education also needs to have value beyond a migration outcome. Students should ask whether a qualification suits their abilities and would support a career in Australia, Nepal or elsewhere.

A course chosen solely for a predicted immigration advantage can become a costly commitment if that advantage disappears.

Care must continue when the success story becomes complicated

Responsibility is shared, but it is not vague.

Education providers should connect recruitment with housing assistance and accessible welfare services. Advisers should explain costs, limitations and alternatives in writing. Governments should address gaps in crisis support for temporary residents rather than leave frontline organisations to manage them without adequate resources.

Nepali community organisations can help through confidential mentoring and referral networks. Someone should be able to seek assistance without fearing that their circumstances will become community gossip.

Families have an equally important role.

During Dashain or Tihar, a cheerful video call may conceal a difficult week. Ask about meals, sleep, friendships and how life actually feels. Leave space for an answer longer than “Everything is fine.”

And make clear that returning to Nepal, changing direction or needing help will not erase the family’s pride in them.

For some people, returning is complicated by children, safety concerns or other circumstances. They need practical support and proper advice. For those who can return, coming home should remain a legitimate choice.

The promise we should make before departure

Australia can offer an excellent education, meaningful careers and lasting belonging. Nepali families are right to see opportunity there.

We can honour that ambition while preparing more carefully for uncertainty. We can celebrate a visa grant while asking about housing. We can value a marriage while defending a person’s right to safety. We can hope for permanent residence without making it the measure of someone’s worth.

Before the next farewell photograph at Tribhuvan International Airport, there is one more conversation worth having.

Tell the person leaving that they can speak honestly if life becomes difficult. That help will not depend on maintaining appearances. That a change of plans will not mean a loss of love.

The tika will fade and the khada will be folded away.

The assurance should remain: “Whatever happens, you can tell us.”

title.rendered: Festival security plan in Kathmandu: Over 3,500 police to be deployed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Nepal Police has launched a security plan for the festival season. Police say they will deploy 3,506 personnel for it.

The Metropolitan Police Range, Kathmandu, says it has made the plan after identifying security challenges.

Police have listed the following challenges and say the plan was designed with them in mind: murder, rape, human trafficking, kidnapping, threats, pickpocketing, theft, gambling, robbery, foreign currency fraud, and spiking drinks with intoxicants.

Police have also divided the places in Kathmandu that need protection into several categories: religious, cultural and traditional sites; food grain and goat markets; crowded public places; bus parks and traffic management points; offices, banks and financial institutions; shopping malls; and jewellery shops.

title.rendered: Stock market falls double digits, turnover tops Rs 4 billion

content.rendered:
The stock market fell in double digits on Friday, the week’s final trading day. NEPSE said the market fell 11.90 points to close at 2,587.25.

The market fell 0.45 percent today. Friday’s turnover exceeded Rs 4 billion. A total of 1,19,12,550 shares were traded through 43,685 transactions across 356 listed securities.

These transactions amounted to turnover worth Rs 4,29,37,74,181. All sub-groups except mutual funds and trading fell in price today, driving the overall market down. The production and processing sub-group lost the most, down 0.73 percent.

NMB debenture gained the most on Friday, up 14.29 percent. SBL debenture rose 8.80 percent. Mandu Hydropower, Laxmi Unnati Fund and NIBL Growth Fund were among other securities with sizable gains.

Sindhu Bikas Bank’s investors lost the most today, with its price falling 8.55 percent. Dhaulagiri Laghubitta Financial Institution’s price fell 4.95 percent.

Besides these, Muktinath Krishi Company, Apollo Hydropower and Sarbottam Paints also saw large declines. SBL debenture saw the highest turnover by value.

Although the Ministry of Finance announced various measures last week to improve the stock market, their positive effect was not seen in the market this week. The market’s trend suggests investors remain in a wait-and-watch mode.

title.rendered: Market monitoring not aimed at intimidating businesses, says Minister Sah

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Minister for Industry, Commerce and Supplies Deepak Kumar Sah has clarified that market monitoring is not intended to intimidate businesses.

Speaking at a discussion of the National Assembly’s Development, Economic Affairs and Good Governance Committee on Friday, Sah said businesses would be fined if irregularities were found during market monitoring, regardless of whether they were government-owned or private.

“Market monitoring is not about intimidating businesses. It is about ensuring fair competition in the market and protecting consumer rights,” he said.

Sah said the law would be applied equally to anyone found violating it.

“Just yesterday, I would like to mention that Salt Trading Corporation Limited was fined Rs 300,000,” he said. “The message is clear. Whether it is a government or private entity, large or small, the law applies equally when consumer interests are compromised.”

Sah said the government was also preparing to conduct market monitoring on a data-driven and risk-based basis.

“We are working to develop a system under which monitoring can be carried out whenever necessary based on information, particularly in areas where there is a higher likelihood of problems,” he said.

Sah also said the government was working to ease the supply of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), which he described as one of the most pressing supply-related issues at present.

“The major problem that ordinary citizens have directly experienced recently is the supply of LPG. I have not viewed this issue simply from the perspective of how many gas bullets arrived today,” he said.

“We have viewed the entire supply chain — from gas loading to transportation, storage, refilling and distribution through dealers to consumers’ kitchens — as a single system,” he added.
