title.rendered: Govt begins initial work to implement Kathmandu Valley Urban Transport Master Plan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

The government has begun preliminary work to implement the Kathmandu Valley Urban Transport System Master Plan, a long-term strategy aimed at addressing traffic congestion, road safety, air pollution and inadequate public transport in Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur.

As part of the initial process, the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport has prepared a Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) report for the master plan.

The plan has been prepared with technical assistance from the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and sets out a long-term transport strategy for the Kathmandu Valley through 2050.

The government expects the plan to help transform Kathmandu Valley’s transport system by improving public transportation, upgrading roads and strengthening traffic management.

Traffic congestion and air pollution among key concerns

The master plan comes amid growing pressure on the Valley’s transport infrastructure.

Rapid urbanisation, a growing number of vehicles and the physical limitations of the historic city have made large-scale road expansion increasingly difficult.

The government says the strategy therefore focuses not only on road improvements but also on strengthening public transport and institutional capacity.

Air pollution is another major concern. Kathmandu’s air quality frequently deteriorates to hazardous levels, particularly during winter and before the onset of the monsoon. Vehicle emissions are considered one of the major sources of air pollution in the Valley.

Noise pollution, unsafe roads and inadequate public transport have also been identified as major problems.

The proposed improvements are expected to reduce traffic congestion and travel times while improving road safety and access to employment, education and public services.

According to the latest census, Kathmandu’s population stands at around 2.94 million. The master plan has been developed based on projections that the population could exceed 4.2 million by 2050.

Fourth transport master plan in three decades

This is the fourth major transport master plan prepared for the Kathmandu Valley.

Similar plans were prepared in 1993, 2012 and 2017, but previous plans were not fully implemented.

The latest master plan is estimated to require an investment of more than Rs 200 billion for implementation.

The strategy aims to establish a transport system that is safer, more inclusive, climate-resilient and capable of supporting the Valley’s economic growth.

Stronger road network across the Valley

The plan proposes strengthening east-west connectivity between Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur.

It also seeks to improve the efficiency of the inner and outer ring road systems and upgrade transport links in heavily congested northeastern parts of the Valley.

Since constructing large roads through the central areas of Kathmandu is difficult, the plan proposes shifting commuters from private vehicles to high-capacity public transport.

Implementation has been divided into three phases, with targets set for 2032, 2040 and 2050.

Junction upgrades and new road infrastructure

The master plan proposes several measures to reduce existing bottlenecks and improve road safety.

These include upgrading major intersections and introducing a coordinated traffic signal system.

New river crossings are also proposed, while elevated or semi-underground roads could be developed along corridors where road expansion is severely constrained.

The plan also calls for completing missing links in the inner ring road and upgrading river corridors.

An emergency road network is proposed to improve the Valley’s ability to respond to disasters and other emergencies.

Historic and tourist areas such as Thamel and Kathmandu Durbar Square are also proposed as potential no-vehicle zones.

Public transport to become the backbone

The master plan identifies buses as the primary mode of public transport for the Valley.

It proposes restructuring and integrating bus operators to improve operational efficiency and accountability.

Bus routes would also be reorganised to reduce congestion in central areas and improve connectivity across the network.

Bus parks, terminals and bus stops would be upgraded, with designated operating zones and clearer passenger information.

On high-demand corridors, the plan proposes measures such as dedicated bus lanes, Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) and Public Transport Priority Systems (PTPS).

The strategy also includes gradual vehicle replacement, improved vehicle maintenance standards, expanded driver training and GPS-based fleet management.

Real-time passenger information systems and information and communication technology infrastructure would also be developed to support an integrated transport system.

Metro rail proposed for Ratnapark–Bhaktapur corridor

The master plan recognises that buses alone may not be sufficient to meet the Valley’s long-term transport demand.

It therefore proposes developing higher-capacity transport systems, including BRT, Mass Rapid Transit and Automated Guideway Transit.

Three potential high-capacity public transport corridors have been identified — a ring corridor, a north-south corridor and an east-west corridor.

Among these, the Ratnapark–Bhaktapur east-west corridor has been prioritised for a pre-feasibility study for metro rail.

The proposed metro would be integrated with BRT services at various locations to create a more accessible and efficient public transport network.

The plan also proposes underground sections in parts of the inner city and the Jadibuti-Koteshwor area.

The proposed metro route would be approximately 14.6 kilometres long.

Major infrastructure projects proposed

The master plan includes a number of major road and transport infrastructure projects.

Maharajgunj underpass

An underpass has been proposed at Maharajgunj to ease traffic congestion at the busy junction.

Chabahil–Gaushala underground tunnel

The Chabahil–Gaushala section is considered one of the most challenging parts of the proposed ring road expansion because of the Pashupati area, which is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site.

With limited options for surface-level road expansion, the master plan proposes a two-level underground tunnel with four lanes of road capacity.

Chabahil–Bagmati elevated highway

A two-lane elevated road has been proposed along the busy Chabahil–Bagmati corridor.

The area includes important heritage sites, including the Boudhanath Stupa. The plan also proposes redesigning Chabahil junction and introducing improved traffic signal systems.

Bishnumati River elevated highway

A four-lane elevated road has been proposed along the Bishnumati River corridor, connecting it with the Ring Road.

Three design options have been proposed, with the project expected to help ease traffic pressure in northwestern Kathmandu.

Gausala–Tinkune Ring Road expansion

The Gausala–Tinkune section, which serves as an important gateway to Tribhuvan International Airport, has also been included in the proposed Ring Road expansion.

The master plan identifies the expansion as necessary to prevent additional bottlenecks arising from other projects around Koteshwor.

Thapathali–Tripureshwor river corridor

The plan proposes developing the Thapathali–Tripureshwor section of the river corridor to connect the remaining gap with the existing Bagmati River corridor.

New bridges and utility corridors

The plan also proposes new bridges at several locations.

A new bridge is proposed near the existing UN Park bridge, which has been identified as a major traffic bottleneck.

Additional bridges have been proposed around the New Bus Park area and across the Bishnumati, Dhobikhola, Karmanasa and Bagmati rivers.

The master plan also proposes developing utility corridors alongside roads to accommodate infrastructure such as underground services.

Historic areas of Kathmandu and Lalitpur are proposed to be developed as car-free zones, while cycling lanes would also form part of the transport strategy.

Existing traffic signal systems would be restructured, and additional parking capacity would be developed in congested areas.

The plan also proposes restructuring the bus industry as part of the broader effort to create a more integrated and efficient public transport system by 2050.

title.rendered: Three arrested for allegedly abusing health workers, security personnel at Teku hospital

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Kathmandu Police have arrested three people for allegedly abusing health workers and security personnel on duty at Sukraraj Tropical and Infectious Disease Hospital in Teku.

According to the District Police Range, Kathmandu, those arrested are 41-year-old Ram Kumar Budhathoki, 23-year-old Ayush Budhathoki and 27-year-old Sachin Budhathoki, all residents of Kirtipur Municipality-4.

Police said the three allegedly entered the hospital’s emergency department at around 1 am on October 1 and verbally abused, threatened and physically assaulted health workers and security personnel on duty.

The District Police Range said it received information that the three had abused and threatened the staff and were involved in physical assault.

A police team deployed from Kalimati Police Circle reached the hospital and conducted an investigation. Police found that the three had allegedly been involved in the incident, said Kathmandu Police Range spokesperson SP Dan Bahadur Thapa.

The three have been arrested on charges of indecent behaviour, according to police.

Police have obtained a five-day remand from the Kathmandu District Administration Office and are investigating the case, Thapa said.

title.rendered: National Assembly passes National Forensic Laboratory Bill

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

The National Assembly has unanimously passed the National Forensic Laboratory Establishment and Operation Bill, 2081.

The bill, returned by the House of Representatives with several amendments, was presented in the National Assembly by Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation, Mahabir Pun.

At Friday’s meeting, following detailed discussions on the bill, Minister Pun moved a proposal to pass it by accepting the amendments made by the House of Representatives.

With the passage of the bill, both houses of the federal parliament have reached agreement on moving forward with the legislation, which had been under consideration for a long time.

The passage of the bill has established the necessary legal framework for the establishment and operation of a forensic laboratory in Nepal.

The legislation is expected to strengthen access to scientific evidence in criminal investigations.

Informing the House about the significance of the bill, Minister Pun expressed confidence that its implementation would open up new avenues in scientific research.

title.rendered: House panel forms subcommittee to probe election police uniform procurement

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

The Public Accounts Committee of the House of Representatives has formed a subcommittee to study the procurement of uniforms for election police.

A meeting of the Public Accounts Committee on Friday formed a nine-member subcommittee led by Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Manish Jha. The subcommittee has been given two months to complete its study.

Lawmaker Ain Mahar, Yogesh Gauchan Thakali, Aren Rai, Khagendra Sunar, Khushbu Oli, Ramesh Kumar Malla, Ganesh Dhimal and Mahendra Bahadur Shahi are members of the subcommittee.

Nepal Police procured uniforms for election police last Magh. Lawmaker Khagendra Sunar has repeatedly raised questions, alleging irregularities in the procurement process.

For the House of Representatives election held on Falgun 21, 2082 BS Nepal Police recruited 133,980 election police, while the Armed Police Force recruited 15,110. A total of 149,090 election police were recruited by the two forces.

The government allocated between Rs 50,954 and Rs 86,484 per election police, depending on their deployment location. The amount covered 40 days of remuneration, food, transportation and snacks.

The government also allocated Rs 11,500 for uniforms for personnel deployed in the mountainous region, Rs 7,945 for those in the hills and Rs 6,170 for those deployed in the Tarai.

According to police officials, around Rs 1 billion was released under the election police uniform budget.

Complaints had been filed with various agencies at the time, alleging that substandard uniforms were supplied to police personnel recruited for only about one and a half months.

title.rendered: 50-plus containers halted at customs after Korala road disruption

content.rendered:
Mustang, October 2

Containers laden with goods imported from China have been halted at Nhechung Customs in Lomanthang Rural Municipality-4, Korala, with the Beni–Jomsom–Korala road, a national pride project, blocked at various points after heavy rainfall. The floods, landslides and river erosion caused by heavy rainfall since last Saturday night inflicted damage to the Beni–Jomsom–Korala route in 46 different places.

It has completely affected trade from northern Korala. According to Bidur Chudal, head of the Mustang Customs Office, containers with goods brought into Nepal from Korala have been cleared by customs but cannot move to their destination due to road blockage. “More than 150 containers are stuck at the customs yard in Korala. Out of these, customs clearance for 90 per cent has been completed,” said Customs Chief Chudal. “Some containers are still undergoing customs clearance, which should be completed within the next two days.”

After the complete closure of Tatopani and Rasuwagadhi checkpoints, the only alternative route via Korala has also been affected due to the rains, it is stated. Chudal further said the state had to suffer a loss in revenue collection due to roads being blocked by floods, landslides, and river erosion, especially while importing goods from China targeted for Dashain and Tihar. With the Korala checkpoint blockage, around 200 electric vehicles are not reaching their destinations.

Among them, more than 100 vehicles have been stuck at Jomsom Bus Park for five days without being able to go down from Jomsom, according to Armed Police Force 33, Gulmi, Jomsom.

title.rendered: MP Rai wishes RSP government to complete full 5-year term

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Dhrubraj Rai has wished the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) and the government to remain in power and govern for the full five-year term without bringing down their own government.

Reviewing the monsoon session of the federal parliament, Rai said lawmakers were not in a position to return to their constituencies with enthusiasm.

Speaking at the House of Representatives meeting on Friday, Rai drew the attention of Prime Minister Balen Shah to the situation in which lawmakers had been forced to question the performance of a government with a two-thirds majority.

He urged the prime minister to ensure that a situation in which lawmakers could not find him in parliament despite repeatedly seeking his presence would not recur in the next session.

“As I understand it, the session is coming to an end. It feels like only yesterday that I was jumping around calling for the prime minister to come, but four or five months have already passed,” he said.

“Things went as they did during this session. May the bad things we did, the bad things done by our government and the bad things done in the House all flow away with the festival,” he added.

Referring to the upcoming Nepali festivals, Rai said lawmakers had raised the people’s concerns throughout the session but had not received answers from the head of government.

“Like in Deusi, I say this year went this way. When we come next year, we will have to offer blessings, saying, may you have a golden roof. As a lawmaker standing as a member of the opposition, I wish that the government will be able to properly engage with the opposition, move forward while managing us, and respond to the people’s voices. I want to say this to the government and the ruling party members as the next session approaches,” he said.

Rai also said he had heard that there were disputes within the RSP and wished the party and government to complete the full five-year term.

Saying that he was a student of political science, Rai recalled that the Nepali Congress had secured a two-thirds majority in 1959 and the then CPN (Maoist) had won a majority in 2008.

“It is equally powerful now. This is said to be a country cursed by its own strength. You young colleagues, be careful. You and I have nothing to gain, but if you preserve the power and the government and keep it going for five years, it will be what we and the people have hoped for. I wish you well in this House and hope you move forward positively,” he said.

Rai said ministers had answered some questions, but the prime minister had failed to respond to questions raised in parliament.

“We did not receive many answers to the questions directed to the head of government. We raised many issues concerning the people, but we did not receive answers,” he said. “As the session ends, I am compelled to say that I am returning to the people empty-handed from this honourable House. I am returning to the doorsteps of the people of Bhojpur, but I am not returning with enthusiasm.”

He reiterated that the government was close to a two-thirds majority only in terms of the number of lawmakers it had.

“I am worried about what happened during the protests of September 8 and 9 last year. Houses were set on fire at that time because of the activities of leaders of the old parties, who were accused of corruption and making large amounts of money. Now, I fear it may be difficult for us to prevent our own houses from being set on fire,” he said.

He said activities during the ongoing parliamentary session had created such fears.

“Do not take this multiparty competition and the practice of a multiparty system lightly. This is how parliament works. The opposition and the ruling side put forward their positions, while the ruling side must remain alert and move forward in a way that facilitates the government’s functioning,” he said.

Rai again wished that the government would improve its conduct by the time the next session begins.

“Through the Speaker, I want to tell the head of government and the government that I hope we meet again in three months. Please do not bring down your own government,” he said. “With these wishes, I say again: when the next session begins, there should be no need to create a situation in which the honourable Speaker has to call for such things as are happening now. There should be no statements that force us to proceed in such a manner.”

title.rendered: Foreign Minister Khanal to visit Fiji and Tuvalu for Pre-COP Leaders Event, then Australia

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal is set to depart for Fiji to participate in the Pre-COP Leaders Event on climate change. His secretariat said his schedule has him departing for Fiji on Saturday.

The secretariat said a four-member Nepali delegation led by Minister Khanal will travel to Fiji and Tuvalu to take part in the event, which will be held on October 5 and 6.

According to a press release issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday, Minister Khanal will address the Leaders Plenary session being held on October 6.

Ahead of that session, he will also take part in a press question-and-answer program being jointly organized with the President of Palau and the prime ministers of Australia and Fiji.

Nepal’s participation in the Pre-COP Leaders Event, organised to advance global dialogue and cooperation on climate change, is expected to offer an opportunity to raise the impacts of climate change, climate justice, and issues of concern to mountain nations on the international stage.

After taking part in the events in Fiji and Tuvalu, Foreign Minister Khanal will travel to Australia.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said he has a bilateral meeting scheduled with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong on October 8.

The meeting is expected to cover Nepal-Australia relations, bilateral cooperation, and various matters of mutual interest.

During his visit to Australia, Minister Khanal will also take part in separate programs organised by the Nepali Embassy in Canberra and the Nepali diaspora in Sydney.

Through these programs, he will interact with the Nepali community in Australia.

Minister Khanal is scheduled to return to Nepal on October 12.

title.rendered: MP Ansari alleges fake-patient scam at National Medical College

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Rahbar Ansari has drawn the government’s serious attention to an ongoing protest by postgraduate (PG) students at National Medical College in Birgunj.

Speaking at Friday’s House of Representatives meeting, Ansari, a Birgunj resident, said PG students have been protesting for the past 10 days and claimed they have been barred from vacating their hostel, from protesting, and even from entering through the college gate.

According to him, the college administration tried to restrict the students after they raised their voices against irregularities taking place at the medical college.

Ansari also alleged that National Medical College had obtained around 25 PG seats by listing “fake faculty members,” meaning professors who are not actually working there. He further claimed that during an inspection by the Medical Education Commission, the college management had dressed up security guards as fake patients and placed them in the emergency hall.

“At that medical college, around 25 PG seats have been obtained by showing fake professors, faculty members who don’t actually work there,” Ansari said. “When the Medical Education Commission went for inspection, the college management forced the guards there to pose as patients in the emergency hall and act as though they were receiving IV fluids.”

Drawing the government’s attention to this, he said, “The state cannot allow colleges running such a racket in the name of fake patients, fake teachers and fake inspections to leave the future of its students in uncertainty.”

Ansari also claimed such activities had been going on for a long time, and alleged that pressure and influence on state bodies was the reason action had not been taken against the college concerned.

He made clear that his remarks were not an accusation against any single institution, but a call to end the broader malpractice visible in medical education.

He further alleged that when students raised these issues and began protesting 10 days ago, the college administration forced them to vacate the hostel and barred them from entering through the gate.

Noting that roughly half of the protesting students are currently in Kathmandu, Ansari urged the government to pay attention and resolve the matter by meeting the protesting students’ demands.

title.rendered: NOC projects Rs 7.5 billion loss in 3 months as global fuel prices rise

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) has projected a net loss of around Rs 7.5 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year as international crude oil and refined fuel prices continue to rise.

The corporation says its inability to fully implement an automatic fuel pricing system in the domestic market has added to the financial pressure.

NOC estimates that it will incur a net loss of around Rs 7.5 billion between mid-July and mid-October, with liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) emerging as the biggest source of losses.

The corporation has been selling LPG at a substantial loss per cylinder, while imports have also increased sharply.

NOC reviews its profit and loss position every 15 days based on the latest purchase prices received from the Indian Oil Corporation (IOC).

Losses have grown every two weeks

The corporation began the fiscal year on a positive note. During the first half of Shrawan, NOC recorded a profit of Rs 710 million.

However, losses increased in every subsequent two-week period.

In the second half of Shrawan, NOC recorded a loss of Rs 1.49 billion. The loss stood at Rs 313.5 million in the first half of Bhadra and rose to Rs 1.24 billion in the second half.

The financial pressure intensified further in Asoj.

NOC recorded a loss of Rs 1.9169 billion between September 17 and October 1. For the following 15-day period, from October 2 to October 16, it has projected a loss of Rs 3.2038 billion.

Overall, NOC is expected to incur losses of around Rs 8.1679 billion from the second half of Shrawan through the end of Asoj. After accounting for the Rs 710 million profit recorded at the beginning of the fiscal year, the corporation’s net loss for the three-month period is projected to reach around Rs 7.46 billion.

Geopolitical tensions and LPG losses

NOC spokesperson Manoj Thakur said fluctuations in international crude oil prices and geopolitical developments have put significant pressure on the corporation’s finances.

“We have no option but to accept international market prices, which are beyond our control,” Thakur said. “The biggest challenge at present is the high loss per LPG cylinder and the growing demand for LPG.”

According to Thakur, NOC is currently incurring a loss of Rs 493 on every LPG cylinder it sells.

The corporation is also selling petrol at a loss of around Rs 26.50 per litre and diesel at a loss of around Rs 48.50 per litre, he said.

NOC attributed the growing LPG losses to rising international prices, the decision not to increase domestic prices and a sharp increase in demand during the festive season.

Despite increased imports, however, consumers continue to report shortages of LPG in the market.

LPG imports surge

NOC data show a significant increase in LPG imports compared with previous months.

In Shrawan alone, Nepal imported 57,316 tonnes of LPG, equivalent to around 4.036 million cylinders.

In Shrawan last year, the country had imported around 3.121 million cylinders. This means imports increased by roughly 900,000 cylinders compared with the same month last year.

Similarly, Nepal imported 3.355 million cylinders in Bhadra last year. By September 13 this year, imports had already reached 3.713 million cylinders, or 52,737 tonnes. Total imports for Bhadra were estimated at around 59,833 tonnes.

By September 30, NOC said 25,688 tonnes of LPG had already been imported in the new month.

Thakur said Nepal needs to gradually reduce its dependence on imported LPG by increasing domestic electricity consumption. However, he said the corporation currently has little choice because of consumers’ continued dependence on LPG.

NOC says it will absorb losses during the festive season

NOC Executive Director Nagendra Sah said the corporation is increasing LPG imports from India and will ensure that supplies are maintained.

Sah said NOC was currently absorbing the losses to protect consumers from an immediate increase in fuel prices.

He attributed the recent increase in international crude oil prices to developments in Saudi Arabia and said the corporation was facing growing financial pressure.

“If we increase the price of diesel now, fares for buses and other transport will increase from the next day,” Sah said. “Similarly, an increase in aviation fuel prices would push up airfares. During the festive season, the government and the board have decided to keep prices stable, taking consumer interests into consideration.”

According to Sah, the corporation will use its Price Stabilisation Fund to manage the losses for the time being.

“We have Rs 4.7 billion in the Price Stabilisation Fund. We can use this fund to maintain smooth supplies for a month or two,” he said.

Sah said NOC was hoping international prices would fall within the next 15 days or month.

“If prices fall, we will return to a normal situation. If they do not, we will have to approach the government to increase fuel prices,” he said.

Sah also recalled that NOC had previously borrowed Rs 7 billion from the government by pledging land during the Russia-Ukraine war, but said the corporation currently did not face a similar immediate situation.

Transport disruptions add to LPG supply problems

Regarding the LPG shortage reported in the market, Sah said supplies from India had not been halted.

He said heavy rainfall and strong winds in recent days had disrupted vessel loading and unloading operations in India, while transportation routes had also been affected.

“LPG supplies from India have not stopped. Heavy rain and strong winds over the past four days caused some problems with vessel loading and unloading in India,” Sah said.

He added that supplies arriving through Haldia, Paradip and Durgapur can also face occasional disruptions.

Road disruptions within Nepal have further delayed the movement of LPG tankers, particularly due to flooding in the Bhotekoshi area, the Krishnabhir landslide and continuous rainfall.

“There is some congestion on the roads, but vehicles are continuing to arrive as sand and landslides are cleared,” Sah said. “These three factors have caused some difficulties, but IOC is supplying us with an average of 55,000 to 60,000 tonnes of LPG a month. So, even if there are disruptions for a day or two, supplies should remain manageable.”

Fuel prices to remain unchanged for now

NOC plans to keep petroleum prices unchanged during the upcoming Dashain, Tihar and Chhath festivals.

The corporation has said an immediate increase in fuel prices would directly affect transport fares for people travelling home during the festive season. Transport operators have already indicated that they would seek fare increases if fuel prices rise.

Higher fuel prices could also increase transportation costs for everyday goods, potentially adding to broader inflationary pressure.

NOC last adjusted petroleum prices from the night of August 2. At the time, petrol became Rs 3 more expensive per litre, while diesel and kerosene increased by Rs 5 per litre. The price of aviation fuel for domestic flights was increased by Rs 20 per litre.

Since then, petrol has remained at Rs 200 per litre, diesel and kerosene at Rs 200 per litre and domestic aviation fuel at Rs 249 per litre.

NOC’s decision to absorb losses could provide temporary price stability for consumers during the festive period. However, if international fuel prices remain elevated, the corporation could face increasing pressure to either raise domestic fuel prices or seek other measures to address its deteriorating finances.

title.rendered: Snowfall disrupts Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route

content.rendered:
Humla, October 2

Heavy snowfall has disrupted travel along the Hilsa-Taklakot route in northern Humla, leaving 41 Nepali nationals stranded at Hilsa.

Immigration Officer Bimal Paudel said the stranded people are residents of Namkha Rural Municipality-1, 2 and 3, most of whom are engaged in business in Taklakot. They had reached Hilsa last Friday but were unable to proceed after snowfall began.

The Chinese side has closed the route for the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage due to heavy snowfall. Immigration staff member Pema Lama said the border is expected to reopen on Oct. 4. Although efforts are underway to clear the road on the Chinese side, it is expected to take longer to reopen the route on the Nepali side.

According to Armed Police Force DSP Nanda Bahadur Saud, around 2 to 2.5 feet of snow has accumulated in Hilsa. Lama said clearing the route would take longer as travellers have to cross Nara Lake to reach Hilsa.

Locals and security personnel are working to clear the snow and resume traffic.

A total of 6,010 people have travelled to Kailash Mansarovar through Hilsa this year. Most are Indian nationals, followed by visitors from the UK, US and Nepal. The snowfall has also affected local trade and daily life in the border area.

title.rendered: Musician Jibesh Chamling Rai passed away

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Senior musician Jibesh Chamling Rai has passed away. Family sources said he died Wednesday night while undergoing treatment at Hams Hospital in Kathmandu.

Rai, 65, had been receiving treatment at the hospital for a brain tumour.

Known as a music guru, Rai was also the father of the two well-known singers Melina Rai and Junu Rai. Both daughters were inspired to pursue music by their father’s own musical dedication.

Rai was not only a music teacher but a composer as well. He set music to numerous songs, many of them children’s songs. According to his contemporary, musician Shanti Ram Rai, Jibesh worked as a music teacher at 12 schools across Kathmandu.

“Much of his life was spent teaching children to sing in schools. He made his living working as a teacher in schools,” Shantiram said.

“He was a musician with deep knowledge of music. He was sociable. He was a dear friend. But in recent times, he had started talking in a pessimistic way,” he said.

Musician Basanta Sapkota said Jibesh, whose birthplace was Ramite in Miklajung Rural Municipality, Morang, had been immersed in music since childhood.

Jibesh is survived by one son, two daughters and two wives. His funeral will be held at his birthplace on Friday afternoon.

title.rendered: One killed in tiger attack in Kailali

content.rendered:
Kailali, October 2

A person was killed in a tiger attack this morning. According to Ramesh Bahadur Shahi, Sub Inspector at Chaumala Police Station, the jungle cat killed 40-year-old Krishna Chaudhary at Bhairav Women Community Forest located in Gauriganga Municipality–6, Moyas, in Kailali.

Chaudhary, along with two others, had moved to the community forest to pick mushrooms. The tiger attacked Chaudhary while he was picking mushrooms. The two others had managed to narrowly escape the wild cat’s attack. Sub-Inspector Shahi said that Chaudhary died on the spot due to the tiger attack.

The gates of India’s Dhauliganga hydropower project dam in Uttarakhand are set to open for 48 hours.

The District Administration Office, Kanchanpur, said the dam’s gates will be opened for silt clearance from 1 am on Saturday, October 3, until 1 am on Monday, October 5.

With the water level in the Mahakali River expected to rise once the gates are opened, the administration has urged residents of riverside areas to stay alert.

The District Administration Office has asked people living along the Mahakali River’s banks, as well as those travelling on the river, to take precautionary measures in advance.

Since the water level in the Mahakali is likely to rise during the period the gates are open, the administration has requested people not to enter the river or go near its banks, and to stay safe from potential risk.

The administration has also urged riverside residents to remain cautious, since the water level in the Mahakali may stay elevated for some time even after the gates are closed.

title.rendered: Tourism Minister Paudel calls for major reforms at Nepal Airlines

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadkaraj Paudel has said that the current financial and managerial condition of Nepal Airlines is extremely fragile. He said there would be no point in adding more aircraft to Nepal Airlines without carrying out structural reforms.

Speaking at a meeting of the International Relations and Tourism Committee under the House of Representatives on Friday, Minister Paudel said adding aircraft alone would not restore the airline’s reputation unless improvements were made to its existing administrative structure and managerial weaknesses.

He said that if a private company were in the same condition, it would have already been forced to shut down. “The situation of Nepal Airlines is extremely serious. If it were a private company, it could have reached the point of liquidation. However, it was not established solely to make profits. As the national flag carrier, it is linked to tourism, employment, the private sector and national prestige. Therefore, major reforms and restructuring are necessary at the corporation,” he said.

Minister Paudel said Nepal Airlines is not merely a profit-making organisation but also a matter of national pride and the country’s flag carrier. He said the time had come to take tough decisions to save the airline.

title.rendered: Repairs begin on flood-damaged transmission line in Myagdi

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Repairs to the transmission line have begun to restore electricity supply in Annapurna Rural Municipality in flood-and-landslide-affected Myagdi, and in Mustang.

Rain that fell continuously from September 24 to 27 caused flooding in the Kaligandaki River, which brought down four towers of the 220kV Dana-Khurkot transmission line at Pokharebagar and Dhirchyang in Annapurna Rural Municipality, and at Bhirkate in Dovan, Myagdi. The fallen towers severed the line, cutting off power supply to Mustang district and Annapurna Rural Municipality.

Likewise, six hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 176 megawatts in Myagdi and Mustang have been unable to connect to the central power system, resulting in losses worth tens of millions of rupees. Power shortages have also disrupted communication services and affected residents’ daily lives.

Hemraj Chapagain, chief of the Nepal Electricity Authority’s Tatopani Distribution Centre, which covers wards 2, 3, 4 and 5 of Annapurna Rural Municipality and all of Mustang district, said that since the transmission line problem makes it impossible to restore power supply immediately from the Dana substation, preparations are underway to operate an alternative line.

“Since supply from the Dana substation isn’t immediately possible, we’ve started repairing the 33kV transmission line from Milanchowk through Dana to Kowang in Mustang,” he said. “Since that transmission line has also sustained extensive damage in its Myagdi section, we’ve mobilised authority staff as well as labourers through contractors for the repair work.”

Chapagain said he had returned from a site inspection confirming there was no problem with Mustang’s transmission and distribution lines.

Work to plant fallen poles and replace severed and sagging wires with new ones has been completed from Tatopani to Pokharebagar, the centre of Annapurna Rural Municipality. One pole has fallen at Gharma, and four poles on the transmission line connecting Rakhu to Begkhola have also fallen.

Between Begkhola and Tiplyang, poles and wires have been completely swept away by the Kaligandaki flood over a 1.5-kilometre stretch. With road transport not operating, there have been difficulties transporting materials for the power line repairs.

Materials are being brought from the authority’s provincial office, transported by vehicle via Beni to Rakhu, and from there carried by porters to the Begkhola area.

Distribution centre chief Chapagain said the transmission line repair work is being carried forward at a rapid pace.

title.rendered: Baa: Ek Yoddha picks up pace as it enters second week

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

The film “Baa: Ek Yoddha,” which has been running since last Friday, has gradually been gaining momentum. After earning Rs 600,000 on its opening day, the film has now grossed Rs 1.11 crore by Thursday.

It has been watched by 40,823 viewers over seven days. With audience flow in theatres steadily increasing, the film enters its second week today.

With audience affection growing and shows filling up, the production team believes the box office will climb steadily as well.

“The business is growing every single day. Viewers who’ve watched the film say they’re sending every member of their family to see it,” said director Hari Lamsal. “We’re confident the number of viewers will keep rising every day from here.”

He says strong word of mouth has been driving growing audience turnout for the film each day.

According to distributors, the film has secured more than 100 shows nationwide. As demand grows, various theatres are adding more shows.

The film’s story centres on the sacrifices, struggles and lifelong challenges a father endures for his children’s future in Nepali society. It focuses on the lengths parents go to fulfil their children’s wishes, as well as the neglect and hardship they often face in old age.

The cast includes Divya Dev, Jharana Thapa, Suhana Thapa, Maotse Gurung, Anil Budhathoki, Sagar Khanal, Shishir Sivakoti, Suprajna Sharma and Shobi Thapa.

Written and directed by Hari Lamsal, “Baa: Ek Yoddha” is produced under the Artistic Entertainment banner. The story and screenplay are also by Lamsal.

The film is produced by Basanta Lamsal, with Anil Budhathoki as executive producer. Arjun Paudel is line producer and Krishna Kafle is co-producer.

Nepali Congress former president Sher Bahadur Deuba has been selected as a regional representative to the 15th general convention from the establishment-outside group.

He was unanimously selected as regional representative at the ward convention of the Congress establishment-outside group held in his home district of Dadeldhura, in Ganyapadhura Rural Municipality-1.

However, Deuba has instead sought to win a regional representative seat from the ward level through electoral competition, rather than arriving as a convention representative automatically.

Former president Deuba has, in past conventions as well, been among the leaders who have competed from the ward level.

Deuba’s personal secretary, Bhanu Deuba, was also selected as a regional representative from the Ganyapadhura-1 ward convention.

title.rendered: Wild elephant terrorises Parsa’s Thori, two injured while fleeing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

A wild elephant has been terrorising Thori Rural Municipality-4 in Parsa.

Buddha Pakhrin, chair of the Kusumbatika Buffer Zone Users’ Committee, said an elephant that strayed in from Parsa National Park has been causing terror in Thori Rural Municipality-4.

Pakhrin said the elephant entered the village last night and tried to break into a local’s house, injuring two people as they fled.

According to him, those injured are 72-year-old Panchmaya Syangbo of Thori Rural Municipality-4 and her granddaughter. He said that after seeing the elephant come straight toward their house at night, they ran to a neighbour’s house for safety and were injured in the process.

“The elephant was following them. As they were entering the neighbour’s house, the elephant knocked down the house’s veranda, injuring the grandmother and granddaughter,” he said.

According to him, the elephant entered the village twice last night alone.

The elephant also damaged one local house. Pakhrin said that after breaking into the house, it damaged stored food grains and a sugarcane crop.

He said the wild elephant causing the disturbance in the village appeared extremely agitated and aggressive.

He said that over the past several days, wild elephants entering villages at night and causing disturbances have left residents living in fear.

title.rendered: Nepal’s monsoon expected to withdraw by Dashain

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Nepal’s monsoon season is nearing its end, with meteorologists saying it is likely to withdraw from the country by Dashain.

According to meteorologists at the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, the monsoon could completely withdraw from Nepal by the Dashain festival. The monsoon entered Nepal through the eastern region on June 19 this year.

Meteorologist Binu Maharjan said there is currently no significant weather system capable of bringing heavy rainfall to Nepal. The monsoon has already withdrawn from most parts of neighbouring India.

The monsoon is now expected to begin withdrawing from western Nepal as well.

“Based on the current indications, there is a possibility that the monsoon will withdraw by Dashain,” Maharjan said.

This year, Ghatasthapana falls on October 11, while Dashain’s main Tika festival will be observed on October 20.

Normally, Nepal’s monsoon season begins around June 13 and withdraws by October 2. However, the withdrawal date can vary from year to year.

Meteorologists have cautioned that the end of the monsoon does not necessarily mean an immediate end to rainfall. Light rain could still occur during Dashain.

Meteorologist Binod Pokharel has also said on social media that there could be occasional drizzle during Dashain, which may bring a noticeable chill to the weather.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress at 80: A party shaped by change, now facing the question of its own transformation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

The Nepali Congress has spent eight decades helping shape Nepal’s political history. It fought to overthrow the Rana regime, led the struggle against the Panchayat system, helped restore multiparty democracy, played a central role in the peace process with the Maoists, supported the transition from monarchy to a republic and took a leading role in drafting the Constitution.

Yet the party that repeatedly helped transform Nepal has itself struggled to transform at the same pace.

From BP Koirala to Gagan Thapa, the leadership of the Nepali Congress has changed many times. The political system has changed many times. So have the expectations of voters and the society the party seeks to represent.

As the Nepali Congress moves towards its 15th general convention, those changes have brought a fundamental question into focus: how much has the party itself changed?

The answer requires looking back at the party’s journey from the days of BP Koirala to its current leadership under Thapa, and examining how its role in power, opposition and political transformation has evolved.

The Nepali Congress remains one of Nepal’s oldest political parties, and much of the country’s modern political history is intertwined with its own. At different points, it has been the principal force behind political change and, at other times, struggled to adapt to changes it helped bring about.

Its eight-decade history has included periods of extraordinary political influence as well as moments of organisational weakness and internal division.

Today, the question is no longer simply how large or powerful the Congress is. It is whether the party can adapt to a political environment that is itself changing rapidly.

BP Koirala’s Congress: A movement for political change

The origins of the Nepali Congress date back to 1946, when the Nepali National Congress was formed under the initiative of BP Koirala and other leaders. The Nepal Democratic Congress was formed separately in 1948, and the two parties merged in 1949 to form the Nepali Congress.

The new party sought to end the Rana regime and establish representative government.

The 1951 revolution became its first major political test. The Rana regime fell, opening the way for a new political order. The party later won 74 of the 109 seats in the first general election in 1959, giving it a two-thirds majority, and BP Koirala became Nepal’s first elected prime minister.

But the party’s internal divisions emerged early. A dispute between BP Koirala and his elder brother Matrika Prasad Koirala contributed to a split in the party, with Matrika later forming the Rastriya Praja Party.

The democratic experiment was short-lived.

On December 15, 1960, King Mahendra dismissed the elected government and parliament, banned political parties and introduced the Panchayat system. BP Koirala and other Nepali Congress leaders were imprisoned or forced into exile.

For the next three decades, the Congress was defined largely by two struggles: its confrontation with the monarchy and its own recurring leadership disputes.

From the 1990 movement to the politics of power

The 1990 People’s Movement brought the Congress together with left-wing forces against the Panchayat system. Ganesh Man Singh became the movement’s supreme commander, and the Panchayat system was eventually replaced by multiparty democracy.

The Nepali Congress won a majority in the 1991 general election and formed a government under Girija Prasad Koirala.

The post-Panchayat period brought significant economic and institutional changes. The Nepali Congress government pursued economic liberalisation, expanded the role of the private sector and advanced infrastructure and local development.

But the party also entered a new phase in which internal factionalism and the struggle for political power became increasingly prominent.

The tension between the Congress’s historical image as a democratic movement and its behaviour as a governing party became increasingly visible.

Political appointments, competition over ministerial positions and factional disputes contributed to growing criticism of the party.

In 1994, the Nepali Congress government failed to complete its five-year term after internal divisions within the parliamentary party led to an early election. The party fell to second place.

The episode became an enduring example of the difficulty political parties can face when internal competition overwhelms the mandate received from voters.

The 1999 victory and another split

The Nepali Congress returned to power after winning a parliamentary majority in the 1999 election. Krishna Prasad Bhattarai initially became prime minister, but internal tensions again surfaced and Girija Prasad Koirala eventually returned to the premiership.

The rivalry between Koirala and Sher Bahadur Deuba subsequently became one of the defining conflicts within the party.

In 2002, amid the Maoist insurgency, disagreements over the dissolution of parliament, the state of emergency and elections deepened the conflict between Deuba and Koirala. Deuba eventually broke away and formed the Nepali Congress (Democratic).

The split came at a particularly unstable moment in Nepal’s history. Parliament had been dissolved, elections were not held as scheduled and King Gyanendra later assumed direct political power.

The episode demonstrated another recurring feature of Nepali Congress politics: a party with a long history of fighting for democratic institutions was repeatedly challenged by its own inability to maintain internal unity.

Girija Prasad Koirala and the transformation to republicanism

Girija Prasad Koirala’s political legacy cannot be understood solely through the lens of his internal battles for power. He also became a central figure in one of the most consequential transformations in Nepal’s modern political history.

The 2006 People’s Movement, the 12-point understanding between the seven parliamentary parties and the Maoists, and the subsequent peace process fundamentally altered Nepal’s political system. Koirala played a central role in the peace process and in the transition towards a republic. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement formally ended the decade-long Maoist conflict.

For the Nepali Congress, this represented a major political transformation.

BP Koirala’s Nepali Congress had fought against the Panchayat system while retaining a commitment to constitutional monarchy. Girija Prasad Koirala’s Nepali Congress eventually worked with the Maoists to end the monarchy and establish a federal democratic republic.

The party also moved towards accepting federalism, secularism and a more inclusive constitutional order. The transformation was not merely institutional. It represented a significant shift in the party’s political identity.

The Constitution and a new political order

The promulgation of the Constitution in 2015 marked another major chapter in the Nepali Congress’s history. Under the leadership of Sushil Koirala, the Congress worked with other major parties to complete the constitution-writing process. The Constitution was promulgated on September 20, 2015. The Congress subsequently played a role in implementing the new federal system and organising elections at the federal, provincial and local levels.

But the completion of the Constitution did not resolve the party’s internal problems.

Nepal had moved from a unitary monarchy to a federal democratic republic. Representation and inclusion had become central elements of the new constitutional framework.

The Nepali Congress, however, faced the challenge of adapting its own organisation to that transformed political landscape.

The state had changed faster than the party’s internal structures.

The question was no longer simply whether the Congress supported federalism, inclusion and democratic institutions. It was whether its organisation, decision-making structures and political culture could evolve accordingly.

The Deuba era and the politics of continuity

Sher Bahadur Deuba emerged as one of the Nepali Congress’s most influential leaders of the post-1990 era. He served as party president twice and as prime minister five times.

Under Deuba, the Nepali Congress remained a central player in coalition politics, working at different times with the Maoists, the UML and other parties.

That flexibility allowed the party to remain close to the centre of power, but it also generated questions about its political direction and organisational renewal.

The repeated movement between government and opposition, and the frequent changes in political alliances, contributed to a perception that the party’s immediate political calculations often overshadowed questions about its longer-term identity.

The tensions became particularly acute after the rise of a younger generation of leaders and the growing demand for internal reform.

Deuba’s leadership was eventually challenged by a faction led by Gagan Thapa and Bishwa Prakash Sharma. A special general convention held in January 2026 elected Thapa as party president. The Deuba faction challenged the change, but the Supreme Court later recognised the Thapa-led faction as the official Nepali Congress.

The dispute, however, did not disappear.

The party is now preparing for its 15th general convention, while the Deuba-aligned faction has also been preparing for a separate convention. The Congress had initially scheduled its convention for October 2–5, 2026, but preparations were affected by floods and landslides, prompting discussions about postponement.

Gagan Thapa and the question of generational change

The rise of Gagan Thapa marks a new phase in the Nepali Congress’s history.

Thapa emerged from student politics and became associated with a younger generation of Congress leaders. His rise has coincided with a broader generational shift in Nepali politics, as younger voters increasingly demand changes in political culture, governance and leadership.

His election as party president through the special general convention represented a sharp break from the leadership pattern dominated by the older generation.

But generational change alone does not guarantee organisational transformation.

Thapa now faces questions over how the Nepali Congress will change its internal decision-making, organisational structure, financial transparency, factional culture, management of party cadres and relationship with voters.

These questions are particularly important because the political environment surrounding the Congress is no longer the same one in which earlier generations operated.

A party with a long history facing a different Nepal

The Nepali Congress’s historical record is inseparable from Nepal’s political transformation.

BP Koirala led the party through the struggle against the Rana regime and into Nepal’s first experiment with elected government.

Ganesh Man Singh led the 1990 democratic movement in cooperation with the left.

Girija Prasad Koirala helped move the Nepali Congress from opposition to the monarchy towards cooperation with the Maoists and the establishment of a republic.

Sushil Koirala led the government during the final stage of constitution-making.

Deuba became one of the central figures in Nepal’s coalition-driven parliamentary politics.

Now Thapa represents a generational transition within the party.

The question facing him, however, is larger than leadership succession.

Nepal itself has changed dramatically since the Nepali Congress was founded. The country is more urban, more connected and more diverse. A younger generation has grown up with different expectations of politics, government and public institutions.

The political struggles that defined earlier generations are now history. The questions facing voters are increasingly about employment, migration, economic opportunity, public services, governance and the performance of institutions.

For the Congress, historical legitimacy can provide a foundation, but it cannot by itself guarantee continued relevance.

The party’s 15th general convention therefore carries significance beyond the election of office-bearers.

It will also be a test of whether a political organisation that repeatedly helped transform Nepal can now transform itself.

The Congress has a long history of adapting when the country’s political order changed. The end of the Rana regime, the restoration of multiparty democracy, the peace process, the abolition of the monarchy and the adoption of a federal republican Constitution all required the party to change its political position.

The challenge now is different.

The political system is no longer the principal question. The question is whether the organisation can renew itself within that system and respond to a society whose expectations have moved well beyond the political struggles of its past.

BP Koirala took the Congress into the struggle for democracy. Ganesh Man Singh helped lead it through the restoration of multiparty politics. Girija Prasad Koirala helped take it from constitutional monarchy to republicanism. Sushil Koirala oversaw the completion of the Constitution.

Deuba’s era was defined largely by coalition and power politics.

For Thapa, the next chapter will be defined by whether he can turn generational change into broader organisational and political renewal.

The Nepali Congress has spent much of its history helping change Nepal. Its next test is whether it can change itself.

title.rendered: How can the same El Niño cause drought in one part of the world and floods in another?

content.rendered:
The Pacific Ocean is warming unusually quickly, and this year’s El Niño has already surpassed previous records. Forecasters expect it to strengthen even further before approaching its usual peak around December.

El Niño, the warm phase of a natural fluctuation in the Earth’s climate system, can reshape weather thousands of miles away, bringing drought to some regions while increasing the risk of heavy rain and flooding in others. To understand why, you need to follow what happens to the Pacific’s warm water – and the air above it.

Usually, winds over the tropical Pacific blow from east to west, pushing warm surface water towards the western Pacific, where it piles up around Indonesia and nearby regions. These are the trade winds. As warm water moves westward, colder water from deeper in the ocean rises to replace it in the east — a process called upwelling. This is why the western Pacific is usually much warmer than the eastern Pacific.

Warmer water means more evaporation, much like heating water on a stove makes more of it turn into vapour. The warm western Pacific therefore feeds more moisture into the air above it. The ocean also warms that air, making it less dense than the cooler air around it, so it rises.

As the air rises, there is less air above it pressing down, so the pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands in this lower-pressure environment and cools. The water vapour then condenses into clouds and rain. When this happens, the energy carried upwards by the water vapour is released as heat into the atmosphere.

High above the Pacific, the rising air spreads out. Some of it moves eastward before sinking again over the cooler eastern Pacific. Near the surface, air flows back westward as the trade winds, completing the large circulation loop known as the Walker circulation.

This is one reason places around Indonesia and the western Pacific receive so much rainfall, while the eastern tropical Pacific and much of coastal Peru are normally far drier. In fact, some parts of Indonesia can receive more rain in a single month than Lima receives in an entire year.

The same ocean–atmosphere pattern also helps keep itself going. The warm western Pacific encourages air to rise, while cooler conditions in the east favour sinking air. This helps maintain the east-to-west trade winds. Those winds then keep pushing warm water westward and bringing colder water to the surface in the east, preserving the temperature contrast that helped drive the winds in the first place. In this way, the ocean and atmosphere reinforce each other – a process scientists call the Bjerknes feedback.

How El Niño changes the tropical Pacific:

So what changes during El Niño?

Some years, the tropical Pacific stops following its usual script. The east-to-west trade winds weaken, so less warm surface water is pushed towards the western Pacific. More warm water remains in the central and eastern Pacific, while the western Pacific can become relatively cooler. This is El Niño.

Once the warm water shifts eastward, the atmosphere above it begins to shift too. Think of moving the stove: the region of strongest evaporation, rising moist air, cloud formation, and rainfall also moves farther east into the central and eastern Pacific. This is why El Niño can bring much wetter conditions to parts of the eastern Pacific and nearby regions, including coastal Peru.

But that shift has consequences elsewhere. With more air rising over the central and eastern Pacific, air higher in the atmosphere spreads outward, and some of it sinks over the western Pacific. Sinking air makes cloud formation more difficult, so places such as Indonesia and the surrounding region near the western Pacific can become much drier than usual – conditions that can also increase the risk of forest and peatland fires in Indonesia.

At the same time, the temperature difference between the western and eastern Pacific becomes smaller. That weakens the pressure contrast that helps drive the trade winds, so the winds can weaken even further. The whole Walker circulation therefore becomes weaker and shifts eastward.

How El Niño reaches around the world

But El Niño’s influence does not stop at the Pacific. It can affect weather thousands of kilometres away through what scientists call teleconnections.

Remember the heat released when water vapour condenses into clouds? As the main zone of rising moist air shifts eastward during El Niño, so does this atmospheric heating. That can warm the middle and upper tropical atmosphere far beyond the Pacific.

In places such as the Sahel – the southern fringe of the Sahara – this makes it harder for warm, moist air near the surface to keep rising, suppressing rain-producing clouds and favouring drier conditions. Fewer clouds can also allow more sunlight to reach the surface, further warming and drying the land. Scientists refer to this as the tropospheric temperature mechanism.

That is one pathway. Another involves huge ripples in the atmosphere, triggered when the main zone of rising air and rainfall shifts eastward. These ripples can travel far from the Pacific, changing winds and storm paths along the way. Even Britain can feel the effects: El Niño can increase the chance of wetter and stormier weather in autumn and early winter, and also raise the risk of colder spells later in winter. But these links are less certain than many tropical impacts, because UK weather is also shaped by several other atmospheric influences.

A third route involves El Niño altering conditions in other oceans. These changes can interact with the Indian Ocean dipole, for instance, a see-saw in temperatures between the western and eastern Indian Ocean that strongly influences rainfall over East Africa and parts of India.

But El Niño alone does not determine the weather on any given day. For example, Thailand generally tends towards drier conditions during El Niño, yet parts of it, including Bangkok, experienced heavy rainfall and flooding this September. India also has shown a similar contrast: the monsoon has been unusually dry overall this year, while some regions have still experienced intense rainfall and flooding. El Niño shifts the odds, but local weather systems can still produce extremes in the opposite direction.
