title.rendered: A new chapter for the Nepali Congress: Reflections at a moment of transition

content.rendered:
As the Nepali Congress, having remained at the centre of Nepal’s modern political history for eight decades, moves toward its 15th general convention, the present moment invites both remembrance and reflection. It also offers an opportunity to ask what the democratic tradition represented by the Nepali Congress has meant to Nepal, how the country it helped shape has changed, where the party stands today, and what that tradition will need in order to remain relevant.

No political tradition in Nepal has been more closely associated with the country’s struggle for democracy, the expansion of political participation and the making of its modern political institutions than the one the Nepali Congress represents, and the Congress led that struggle at each stage, setting its democratic demands, sustaining its movements and giving its gains institutional form. Its significance extends beyond the history of an organisation: it forms part of the larger story of how Nepal came to understand citizenship, representation, constitutional government and the possibilities of democratic politics.

That history belongs to a period in which Nepal moved from a highly restricted political order toward a more open and representative one, and political participation gradually acquired a wider meaning. The Nepali Congress was the principal torchbearer of that democratic journey and, at different stages, worked in cooperation and common purpose with other democratic, left and progressive forces.

Its own political journey also included periods of cooperation with the monarchy, from the establishment of the democratic order to work within the constitutional framework. That accommodation ultimately ended when the monarchy reasserted direct political authority in the early 2000s. Other political forces, through struggle, contestation, adaptation and negotiation, also came to embrace the liberal democratic order and became part of Nepal’s parliamentary experience. The inheritance is therefore larger than any one organization. It includes the aspirations, institutions and practices that helped create a more participatory Nepal and gave successive generations greater room to shape the country’s future.

It is natural, on such an occasion, to look back with pride at what has been accomplished. But it may be more important to ask what kind of country Nepal has become, what remains unfinished, and what the next phase requires. The political and social world in which earlier struggles were fought is no longer the world of today. Nepal is more open, connected, mobile and socially diverse, while expectations have expanded alongside education, technology, migration, communication and economic opportunity. A democratic inheritance cannot remain meaningful simply because of what it achieved in its own time; its continuing value depends on whether it can carry forward the principles and purposes that gave it meaning while speaking to the country that has emerged from that history.

The reversal of established political parties, including the Nepali Congress, in the 2026 election has given these questions particular urgency. It pointed to more than a change in parliamentary arithmetic; it also revealed changing public expectations and a changing relationship between citizens and established political traditions. Against this changing landscape, the party’s 15th general convention is taking place amid an unresolved dispute over organizational legitimacy and questions about its leadership. These immediate questions matter, but they also bring into focus the larger challenge of how a political tradition can renew its relevance in a country that has changed so much.

A younger and more outward-looking population increasingly judges politics not only by historical achievement or ideological commitment, but also by the quality of government, the opportunities available to people and the ability of public institutions to respond to everyday problems. Nepal’s central task has moved beyond creating a political order capable of representing its citizens. It is now to make that order capable of delivering deeper economic transformation, competent government and resilient prosperity. The sections below take up what that requires.

From political change to economic renewal

Nepal’s political transformation created the institutional space within which wider social and economic change could take place. Over the decades, the country has seen the expansion of infrastructure, education, health services, communications, public institutions and markets. The state has acquired a much greater presence across the country, and citizens have gained access to opportunities and forms of communication that were largely unavailable to earlier generations. Yet the productive economy has not advanced at the same pace.

Nepal has developed an industrial base, but industry has not acquired the depth or breadth to drive higher productivity and structural transformation. Manufacturing has not absorbed labor on the scale experienced in countries that followed a sustained industrial path, nor has it generated the degree of domestic production, technological learning and value addition associated with such a course. Agriculture remains important and is increasingly, though still insufficiently, connected to markets, while services have expanded markedly. The result is an economy in which the social and institutional landscape has moved ahead of the productive base that must ultimately sustain it.

Geography is central to this challenge, as both constraint and asset. Nepal’s position between India and China creates possibilities, but location alone does not produce connectivity or economic integration. Connections toward the north remain constrained by rugged Himalayan terrain and limited infrastructure, making the movement of people, goods and investment more difficult and costly.

The value of Nepal’s position will depend on whether infrastructure, institutions and productive capabilities can turn proximity into practical economic opportunity. At the same time, the country’s geography provides some of its greatest economic assets. Rivers and elevation create substantial hydropower potential; mountains, biodiversity and cultural landscapes underpin tourism; and ecological diversity supports distinctive forms of agriculture and local economic activity. Their economic value, however, depends on the infrastructure, skills, investment and markets needed to make sustained and productive use of them.

The future will depend less on identifying a single new engine of growth than on creating conditions in which several sources of productive potential can reinforce one another. Hydropower must connect with industry and markets, tourism with infrastructure and local enterprise, agriculture with technology, finance, storage and processing, and digital connectivity with skills and investment. Regional integration, in turn, depends on reliable physical and institutional networks that allow Nepali producers and businesses to participate effectively. Services also offer scope: information and communication, finance, education, health and other knowledge-based activities. In every sector the task is to turn possibility into productive activity, employment, domestic value addition and stronger linkages.

Progress cannot be judged by aggregate growth alone. What matters is whether the economy creates productive employment, raises productivity, encourages investment and innovation, expands domestic value addition and allows more people to participate in a dynamic economy. Nepal’s difficulty is less a shortage of resources than a shortage of the enterprise, infrastructure, skills and institutions needed to connect them.

A Changing Society and New Expectations

Migration has become one of the clearest expressions of Nepal’s changing economic and social structure. Internal migration has altered the demographic geography of the country, while overseas migration has become deeply embedded in household livelihoods and the wider economy. Remittances have provided an important cushion for families and communities and supported consumption, education, housing and other forms of investment.

At the same time, the scale of outward migration reflects the limited capacity of the domestic economy to provide sufficient productive employment. The longer-term question is not whether migration should be regarded as a problem or a solution. It has become part of Nepal’s economic life. The more useful aim is to connect the skills, experience, networks and resources acquired through migration more closely with productive activity at home. A country cannot indefinitely rely on the export of its labor while importing a large share of what its people consume. Mobility should become a source of capability, not a substitute for opportunity at home.

Nepal is also becoming more urban, mobile and educated, and younger people are increasingly shaped by exposure to opportunities and standards beyond the country. This can become a source of dynamism if education, skills, health, employment and enterprise develop sufficiently to make productive use of human capability. But a demographic dividend is not automatic.

Technology is opening another set of possibilities. Digital connectivity can help overcome some of the disadvantages imposed by geography, widen access to markets and services, facilitate new forms of enterprise and employment, and improve public-service delivery. But technology cannot overcome structural limitations by itself. Its benefits depend on the wider economic and institutional capacity to put it to effective use.

Climate change adds a further dimension. Nepal’s contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions is negligible, while its exposure to climate-related risks is substantial. Climate pressures can affect agriculture and livelihoods, water availability, hydropower, roads and other infrastructure, tourism, settlements and ecosystems. Climate resilience cannot be treated as an environmental concern separate from development. It has to be incorporated into the planning and management of the sectors on which livelihoods and prosperity depend.

This also gives Nepal a distinctive international position. Its negligible contribution to global emissions, combined with serious vulnerability, provides grounds for a stronger voice on climate justice, adaptation, resilience and the concerns of mountain and Himalayan regions. That voice will carry greater weight when accompanied by stronger domestic resilience and the capacity to protect people and productive assets from growing risks.

From political settlement to effective government

These changes bear directly on the state. Citizens look for responsive institutions, good public services, transparency and accountability. Political legitimacy is experienced not only through participation and representation but through the everyday performance of government. The quality of public administration increasingly affects how citizens experience the state itself. Nepal’s political journey has produced a substantial constitutional and institutional settlement.

The transition to a federal democratic republic, a more inclusive constitutional framework, wider representation and devolution of authority have significantly altered how the state is organized and how citizens participate in public life. For the present, the challenge is less further restructuring than making these arrangements work with greater coherence, competence and responsiveness. Debates over federal arrangements and the electoral system will continue, and some adjustment may prove necessary, but citizens now judge the settlement chiefly by how well it performs.

Federalism is an important part of this new architecture. It has brought government closer to citizens and created more room for locally grounded development. Yet weak coordination among levels of government and uneven administrative, technical and fiscal resources have constrained its promise. Local governments hold real potential, but proximity alone does not guarantee good government. Strengthening professional administration, clarifying responsibilities and improving coordination will be central to the years ahead. The same is true beyond domestic administration.

Economic development, infrastructure, migration, urbanisation, technology and climate resilience increasingly require coordination across jurisdictions, while Nepal’s relations with India and China, its place in a changing regional economy, and its growing engagement with global markets and climate diplomacy require coherent and sustained national policy. Nepal needs a state capable of delivering at home while also navigating a complex regional and international environment in pursuit of long-term national interests.

The measure of the present constitutional order will increasingly be found in implementation: the quality of public services, the ability of governments at different levels to work together, the competence of public institutions, and the capacity to turn Nepal’s possibilities into tangible improvements in people’s lives.

Renewal and continuity

The moment matters beyond this general convention. Nepal’s political arrangements have evolved alongside a society whose expectations of politics and government have shifted markedly. Yet the productive and institutional weaknesses described above remain, and they cannot be overcome by political change alone. Democratic institutions must continue to respond to the society they have helped create and to the expectations that have grown around them.

For the Nepali Congress, the moment is significant not simply because of the organisational questions immediately before it, but because it brings into focus a larger question about the future of a political tradition that has played such a consequential role in Nepal’s history. The experience, democratic commitments and sense of public purpose accumulated over eight decades must remain relevant to a society that has itself changed profoundly. The task is thoughtful renewal: understanding what is worth preserving, what needs to change and what the future demands.

That renewal calls for a closer relationship between political achievement and institutional performance. Representation remains fundamental, but it must be accompanied by capable government and meaningful opportunity. Together, these are the larger test facing Nepal’s political order: whether the gains of the past can be converted into a more capable state and wider prosperity. Political traditions still matter here. They carry memories of struggle, institutional experience and public trust accumulated over time.

A tradition that has served the nation well has much worth preserving, but preservation cannot mean standing still. History can provide a foundation; it cannot guarantee continued relevance or public confidence. Those have to be earned again by understanding the country as it is becoming and responding to the aspirations of those who will shape its future. That requires the courage to ask what once made a political tradition meaningful to people and useful to the nation, and to give those qualities new expression in changed circumstances. Democratic conviction, a connection with ordinary citizens, a sense of public service and commitment to a larger national purpose are not relics of an earlier era. Their value lies precisely in how they are carried forward by each new generation.

There is nothing wrong with looking back with affection. Political journeys are made not only through institutions and ideas, but through friendships, sacrifices, shared struggles and memories that remain long after particular moments have passed. For someone like me who has been part of such a journey, attachment is inevitably personal. It is a source of gratitude, and quiet pride, to have shared, however modestly, in a cause larger than any individual: the advancement of democracy and the building of the nation.

That association carries a responsibility to look at the present with candor, including the disagreements and strains that accompany a period of transition, and to look to the future with faith. To care for a political tradition is not to shield it from difficult truths or from the need to change; it is to want it to retain its connection with people, its public purpose and its capacity to serve the country as it is becoming. Precisely because that inheritance matters, it deserves neither uncritical celebration nor easy dismissal, but an honest reckoning with what should be preserved, what must change and what may have been lost along the way.

Every political generation eventually makes room for another. But democratic renewal need not mean a rupture between them. New leadership will necessarily see Nepal through somewhat different eyes, speak more directly to people whose experiences differ from those of their predecessors, and bring expectations that earlier leaders could not have fully anticipated. But successors also inherit a debt: to the pioneers who carried the cause of liberty; to those who devoted themselves to the dignity and well-being of ordinary people; to the builders of modern Nepal; to those who carried that responsibility forward; and to the martyrs who gave their lives for it.

Their sacrifices gave meaning to a political tradition whose deepest inheritance is not simply memory, but the democratic and national purpose entrusted to them. The accumulated wisdom of a long political experience can offer guidance, but those who come next must have the freedom to bring their own language, priorities and imagination to the democratic enterprise. Continuity gives renewal a foundation; renewal gives continuity a future.

A new chapter does not erase the pages that came before it. It carries their lessons forward while accepting that the story must be written in circumstances that have changed. The hope, then, should not be for a return to an earlier political moment or for change for its own sake, but for a future that preserves what was strongest in the democratic traditions that helped shape modern Nepal, learns honestly from what has not worked, and gives each new generation the freedom to bring its own experience and imagination to that inheritance.

When the party looks back from its centenary, it should be able to do so with gratitude for the journey, honesty about what remains unfinished, affection for what was built, and confidence in those who have carried and will carry the work forward. The present period of disagreement should ultimately matter less as an organisational dispute than as a test of whether the Congress can emerge with a stronger sense of purpose, a deeper connection with the people and a greater capacity to meet the demands of a changing Nepal. The ultimate measure will be whether its deepest democratic and national purpose can continue to command the trust of the people it sought to serve, and whether that inheritance can be made meaningful to the Nepal of its time.

May the next chapter carry that inheritance into the Nepal of today, renewing its democratic purpose for a new generation. May those entrusted with it bring fresh eyes, fresh energy and a renewed sense of purpose, while drawing wisdom from the experience that made their work possible. And may that continuing journey contribute to the larger unfinished task before us all: building a more prosperous, inclusive, capable and resilient Nepal.

title.rendered: 8 more bodies recovered from Himlung avalanche

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 2

Eight more bodies have been recovered from the Himlung avalanche in Narpa Bhumi Rural Municipality-5 of Manang, taking the death toll from the disaster to 15.

The avalanche struck the Himlung mountain area on September 27. Four bodies were recovered on Thursday morning, while four more were found later in the afternoon, according to Krishna Prasad Poudel, assistant chief district officer of Manang.

Seven bodies had been recovered earlier. One person remains missing following the avalanche.

“Two bodies have been brought to the district headquarters in Chame, while six have been brought to Phu village,” Poudel said. “It is already dark, so helicopters cannot fly. We will bring the remaining bodies on Friday.”

The bodies recovered on Thursday were transported by a Nepal Army helicopter.

Meanwhile, a Nepal Army team, in coordination with locals and other security agencies, is working to clear the Marsyangdi River at Thado Khola in Chame Rural Municipality-4, where the river has been blocked by a landslide.

The team is also working to restore the electricity transmission line that was disrupted by the landslide.

The avalanche occurred at the mountain’s base camp on September 27 morning. The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) has deployed an 11-member trained search and rescue team to the area.

title.rendered: 13 years after sandalwood smuggling case, authorities seek contractor Nabin Raj Basnet

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Authorities have written to a court seeking the appearance of a man who was not prosecuted 13 years ago in a red sandalwood smuggling case because his exact whereabouts were unknown.

The man, Nabin Raj Basnet of Dolakha, is currently being investigated by the Department of Money Laundering Investigation. During the investigation, authorities found that he was a fugitive in a red sandalwood smuggling case dating back to April 22, 2013.

Authorities have now identified him as the same Nabin Raj Basnet who had worked closely with Pradeep Adhikari, the former director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN), who was later prosecuted by the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority.

At the time of the sandalwood case, a person named Nabin Raj Basnet was listed as a fugitive, but his exact address was not known. The case was registered with the provision that he would be prosecuted if his whereabouts were established.

The Department of Money Laundering Investigation has now written to the Division Forest Office, stating that his address and identity details have been established and requesting that he be located and produced before the Kathmandu District Court.

According to the department’s letter, documents obtained from the Inland Revenue Office, Koteshwor, included records of Kalinchowk Mai Suppliers, operated by Basnet, as well as a copy of the citizenship certificate of Nabin Raj Basnet, whose details had also been mentioned in the complaint.

The letter states that the Kathmandu District Court’s decision of June 22, 2025, had kept Basnet’s case pending because his exact address was unknown. It requests that he now be located and produced before the court based on the newly obtained documents.

The Office of the Government Attorney, Kathmandu, has also been informed about the development.

Two others convicted in sandalwood smuggling case

In the original red sandalwood smuggling case, a bench of then Kathmandu District Court judge Ramesh Raj Pokharel convicted Bhim Kumar Sunuwar and Khem Bahadur Singh.

They were each sentenced to six months in prison and fined Rs 361,600.

They had been arrested on April 1, 2013.

What was the case about?

On March 31, 2013, police received information that red sandalwood was being smuggled in a mini-truck with registration number Ba 1 Kha 5759.

Police intercepted the truck while it was travelling from Guheshwori towards Gothatar in Kathmandu.

A search of the truck found red sandalwood concealed under sand in the rear section. Nine pieces of red sandalwood were recovered, and driver Bhim Bahadur Sunuwar of Kakurthakur, Sindhuli, and his assistant Khem Bahadur Singh of Hariwan, Sarlahi, were arrested.

The Metropolitan Police Range, Hanumandhoka, investigated the case.

During the investigation, the arrested men told police that Nabin Raj Basnet, the owner of Kalinchowk Suppliers, had called them on March 29, 2013, instructing them to transport sand.

According to their statements, Basnet travelled ahead on a motorcycle while they followed in the truck. The vehicle was subsequently intercepted by police.

Investigators also found that Basnet had rented the truck from Ramesh Prajapati under a one-year agreement signed on November 9, 2012, at a monthly rent of Rs 25,000.

However, when the case was filed, only the driver and assistant were made defendants on the grounds that Basnet’s address was unknown.

The report alleges that investigators at the time did not conduct further inquiries into who owned Kalinchowk Suppliers and did not include Basnet as a defendant.

Basnet also under money laundering investigation

Nabin Raj Basnet is also being investigated for alleged money laundering.

According to sources at the Department of Money Laundering Investigation, authorities are collecting documents related to Basnet and have requested records from various government agencies.

“We have started the investigation. We have asked various agencies to provide documents related to his assets. A detailed investigation will be conducted after all the information is received,” a department source said.

The department is currently examining the assets of Basnet, his family members and business partners.

A department source claimed that a significant amount of land has been found in the Kathmandu Valley in connection with Basnet.

Basnet, who is described as coming from a modest economic background, is now considered financially well-off. Companies linked to him and his family include Sandarbhik Construction Service Pvt Ltd, Nil David International Unisex Salon, Kshamadevi Construction Solution Pvt Ltd, Dreamtown Developers Pvt Ltd, Kshamadevi Interior and Kshamadevi International Pvt Ltd.

According to department sources, some assets are registered in the names of family members and some in the names of business partners who share the Basnet surname. Authorities are examining the sources of those assets.

The department also claims to have found a substantial amount of land registered not only in Basnet’s name but also in the names of family members and relatives.

A department official said a preliminary investigation showed that 72 ropanis of land had been purchased and developed in Duwakot, Bhaktapur, in partnership with other shareholders of Dream Town Developers.

The official said authorities were also investigating large land holdings in Sinamangal, Duwakot, Jorpati, Koteshwor, Thimi and Balkot registered in the names of different individuals.

“More land appears to be registered in the names of his partners and relatives than in Basnet’s own name. If the source of the assets cannot be established, everyone involved will come under investigation,” the official told Onlinekhabar.

The department said it has previously filed a money laundering case against 26 people, including Dipak Bhatt, and continues to investigate other major cases of a similar nature.

Basnet’s connection to former CAAN chief

Earlier, the Kathmandu police investigated former CAAN Director General Pradeep Adhikari and others over allegations of threatening the then CIAA chief and other senior officials.

Basnet and other individuals were also found to have connections to that case. However, no case was filed against them at the time, with authorities stating that further investigation was needed.

The investigation report stated that if evidence establishing the involvement of any person in the offence was found, a separate investigation report would be submitted under Section 35 of the National Penal Code.

Basnet also secured a contract three years ago to construct the taxiway and apron at Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa.

The contract was awarded to Ashish-Kshamadevi-Buddha Himalaya JV. Basnet was associated with Kshamadevi at the time.

title.rendered: Cockroach Janata Party announces nationwide protests demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation

content.rendered:
New Delhi, October 1

The founder of the Cockroach Janata Party, Abhijit Dipke, has announced nationwide protests from October 2, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Dipke made the announcement at a press conference held in Mumbai on Thursday.

“We will begin our protest in Mumbai tomorrow, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar,” Dipke said at the press conference.

The protesters are also demanding that a criminal case be filed against Kumar.

Dipke alleged that several questions have been raised over the current electoral process and said the chief election commissioner should step down to address the issues.

He said the protests would continue until Kumar resigns from his post.

Dipke further said, “We demand that the SIR process be stopped immediately, the elections be conducted on the basis of the 2025 electoral roll, and a new chief election commissioner be selected by an independent body.”

The Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls have become subjects of political debate. The planned protest in Mumbai comes amid the ongoing debate.

title.rendered: Supreme Court refuses to order release of ANFA treasurer and accountant

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The Supreme Court has refused to order the release of All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) treasurer Rabindra Joshi and accountant Sanjiv Pandey.

A joint bench of Supreme Court justices Binod Sharma and Sunil Kumar Pokharel rejected separate habeas corpus petitions filed on behalf of Joshi and Pandey, ruling that their detention for investigation was lawful.

Joshi’s wife, Shobha Joshi, and Pandey’s wife, Anita Pandey, had separately filed habeas corpus petitions at the Supreme Court, arguing that their husbands were being detained unlawfully.

The joint bench dismissed both petitions and upheld the legality of keeping Joshi and Pandey in custody while the investigation continues.

The Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police had raided the ANFA headquarters on September 18 and arrested treasurer Joshi and accountant Pandey.

The CIB is investigating them on allegations related to match-fixing, irregularities and fraud.

Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel, who is also the government spokesperson, said on Tuesday that new facts had emerged during the investigation into ANFA.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

From major policy changes and developments at home to stories making headlines around the world, Thursday brings a range of developments worth keeping track of. Nepal’s proposed civil service legislation, the country’s absence from the upcoming SAFF Championship and developments surrounding Mt Himlung are among the key stories today, alongside updates from education, public services, climate and international affairs.

Proposed civil service bill sets aside 49 per cent posts for reservation

The proposed Federal Civil Service Bill has allocated 49 per cent of posts filled through open competition for reservation to make the federal civil service more inclusive. The bill treats the reserved quota as 100 per cent, with 50 per cent of the reserved posts allocated exclusively for women and the remaining 50 per cent for candidates from other targeted groups.

New bill sets two-year cooling-off period for civil servants

The Federal Civil Service bill introduces a two-year cooling-off period for government employees seeking other appointments after leaving their current job. A cooling-off period is a fixed span during which someone who has resigned from government service or taken mandatory retirement is barred from taking up another government, constitutional, diplomatic or similar government post.

Nepal to miss SAFF Championship for first time in history

Nepal is set to miss the 15th edition of the SAFF Championship, to be held in Bangladesh from November 4 to 17. With the suspension not lifted even by the deadline of September 30 set by the South Asian Football Federation (SAFF), it is now certain that Nepal will miss the SAFF Championship for the first time in its history.

Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary denies personal ties to people heard in controversial audio

Agriculture, Forest and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary has clarified her position over a controversial audio recording that has been circulating on social media. Chaudhary said she had no personal or family relationship with either of the two people heard speaking in the audio clip. She also said she was prepared to face any evidence presented against her.

Tribhuvan University assembly to meet on October 8

The Tribhuvan University Assembly is scheduled to meet on October 8 (Ashoj 22), after months of delay in approving the university’s policy and programme, budget and student grace list.

Passport Department services affected by internet outage

Services at the Department of Passports in Tripureshwor have been affected after its server went down. Department officials said the disruption was caused by an internet outage.

Swiss glaciers lose 5.5% of ice volume this year, second-largest decline on record

Glaciers in Switzerland, home to the largest number of glaciers in the Alps, lost 5.5% of their ice volume this year, marking the second-largest percentage decline on record amid heat waves and low winter snowfall, experts said.

4 more bodies found on Himlung, death toll reaches 11

The bodies of four more people who went missing in an avalanche on Mt Himlung in Manang have been found. The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association team deployed to search for the missing climbers found four bodies on Thursday, the association said. An experienced mountain guide team led by Pasang Kaji Sherpa continued the search and rescue operation.

US judge blocks Trump’s $100,000 H-1B visa fee

A US federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers. US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland, California, ruled on Wednesday that US Citizenship and Immigration Services and the State Department had failed to follow the required rulemaking procedures before implementing the fee.

title.rendered: A sacred union: From peacock feathers to cosmic trees in Sabita Dangol’s art

content.rendered:
Peacocks have long occupied a distinctive place in Sabita Dangol’s paintings. Sometimes she paints them almost realistically, allowing their brilliant colours and familiar forms to command attention. At other times, the artist takes them apart, turning their feathers, anatomy and intricate details into elements of her visual vocabulary. A feather becomes a pattern; the interior of the bird’s anatomy becomes an outline; and within those forms, her brush moves freely, filling them with vivid colours and elaborate motifs.

For Dangol, the peacock is more than a decorative presence. It is a recurring visual and symbolic element—one that carries associations of beauty, renewal and watchfulness. Its significance becomes particularly resonant in A Sacred Union: Eternal Harmony, her eighth solo painting exhibition, which draws inspiration from Lord Krishna, his teachings and the enduring relationship between Radha and Krishna.

The exhibition explores love, companionship, spirituality and coexistence through Dangol’s distinctive fusion of traditional imagery, ornamental patterns, vibrant colours and meticulous detail. It is currently on display at 108 Gallery in Durbar Marg, Kathmandu, where it will continue until October 4.

The connection between the peacock and Krishna is particularly relevant to Dangol’s latest works. The peacock feather, traditionally associated with Krishna, becomes part of a larger visual world in which cultural memory, spirituality and personal expression intersect. Dangol does not simply reproduce familiar religious imagery; she reworks it through her own ornamental language.

That approach is evident in one of the exhibition’s striking paintings, where a monumental tree trunk covered in intricate patterns of insects and beetles gradually transforms into an embracing couple. The couple appears to emerge from the tree itself, making their relationship inseparable from the natural world.

The roots suggest the foundations of love, while flowers emerging from the branches evoke peace, creativity and spiritual growth. The tree appears to move from barrenness towards renewal, as though love itself has the power to restore life.

Behind it, patterned mountains carry a sense of history and cultural memory. Elephants add another layer of symbolism, recalling their longstanding presence. Dangol brings these elements together not as isolated symbols but as parts of a single ecosystem in which people, animals and nature coexist.

Another work moves from the earthly to the cosmic. A lotus base supports a slender green stem that rises through swirling atmospheric forms, carrying fantastical creatures towards a golden Kalasha at its apex. Set against deep indigo and violet tones, the composition draws on Hindu-Buddhist and South Asian visual traditions while creating a dreamlike space of spiritual transformation.

The artist’s fascination with transforming ordinary objects into carriers of meaning is also evident in her recurring comb motif. An oversized wooden comb appears as both a three-dimensional object and a painted form, its surface covered with elaborate patterns.

Dangol describes the comb as “a manifestation of the feminine essence,” associating the act of combing hair with releasing emotional baggage and with collaborative synthesis. In her visual language, the comb also becomes a metaphor for the human mind: just as a comb untangles hair, it can represent the process of working through anxiety, confusion and the complications of life.

This transformation of familiar objects and cultural symbols is central to Dangol’s practice. A peacock is no longer simply a bird. A feather becomes a field for pattern and colour. A tree becomes a metaphor for love. A comb becomes an instrument for untangling the mind. A lotus becomes a point of spiritual ascent.

Through these transformations, A Sacred Union: Eternal Harmony brings together the personal and the universal. Its imagery is rooted in cultural traditions, but its concerns are contemporary: how people form relationships, how they live with nature, how they carry emotional burdens and how they seek balance.

The exhibition opened on September 4 and continues until October 4 at 108 Gallery. Ten per cent of sales from the exhibition will be donated to the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund.

For Dangol, harmony is not presented as something static. It is something that grows, changes and is continually renewed—much like the peacock feathers that return each season, carrying with them the colours and patterns that have become an enduring part of her artistic world.

‘Art Can Do More’ by At 108 Gallery

The “Art Can Do More” initiative by Gallery 108 has successfully brought together Nepali artists in a powerful collective gesture of solidarity, mobilising art to support communities devastated by the recent natural disasters.

According to the latest inventory data, the initiative has catalogued a total of 73 artworks. Of these pieces, 33 artworks have been sold, leaving 40 available for art collectors and humanitarian buyers.

This collective action has generated a total value of Rs 981,800. Out of this gross value, the gallery has recorded a massive total contribution of Rs 512,800, with 100% of these proceeds directed entirely towards the Nepal Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund.

The contributed artworks are being actively exhibited physically at Gallery 108 and featured online simultaneously. The collection continues to expand with rolling updates; as new artwork contributions arrive from local creators, both the physical gallery space and the digital storefront are updated to reflect the new additions.

title.rendered: Kathmandu Climate Week to begin from Friday

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Kathmandu Climate Week is all set to begin from Friday. The three day event will bring together policymakers, parliamentarians, politicians, climate practitioners, communities, activists, young people, researchers, civil society, businesses, financial institutions, media and development partners.

Foreign Affairs Minister Shishir Khanal will inaugurate the program. Organized under the theme “Climate Justice for Building Climate Resilience, from Local Action to Global Climate Diplomacy,” the event aims to connect experiences and solutions from communities across Nepal with national policy and international climate diplomacy.

The program will open on Friday, October 2, with a national opening and remembrance for those who lost their lives in recent climate disasters, followed by high-level discussions on Nepal’s climate priorities from the UN General Assembly to COP31. The opening day will also include a dialogue with political party leaders on climate justice priorities, an intergenerational roundtable, sessions with sustainability entrepreneurs, and a panel on climate litigation in Nepal.

On Saturday, October 3, seventeen parallel sessions will be held across five thematic areas: climate justice, loss and damage, sustainability and climate action, technology in climate change, and the private sector’s role in climate justice. Topics will include youth involvement in climate justice, Indigenous and marginalized communities, climate finance, organic agriculture, the circular economy, data and artificial intelligence, climate-resilient infrastructure, and private-sector climate finance.

On Sunday, October 4, the program will focus on frontline voices, with a youth-led session on the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi flood, a parliamentary dialogue on climate justice, a closing plenary with community representatives from affected areas, and hands-on training in hydroponic farming.

The week will conclude on Monday, October 5, with a public film screening of stories from the event.

Organizers said the program is intended to connect government, local and Indigenous communities, financial institutions, researchers, technologists, media, youth and civil society groups with diplomatic and development partners, and to lay the groundwork for an annual climate dialogue platform in Kathmandu focused on South Asia and mountain issues.

title.rendered: Yuvraj Dulal criticises PM Balen Shah for not informing Parliament about UN trip

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Nepali Communist Party chief whip Yuvraj Dulal has expressed regret over what he described as Prime Minister Balen Shah’s disrespect towards Parliament.

Speaking during the special session of the House of Representatives, Dulal recalled that Prime Minister Shah had travelled to the United Nations General Assembly to represent Nepal at its 81st session.

At the General Assembly, Shah presented Nepal’s common national agendas and raised issues including the impact of climate change on the Himalayas, the Himalayan tsunami in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers and the damage it caused, climate justice, and international assistance based on grants.

Dulal thanked Prime Minister Shah and the government for raising these issues at the UN. However, he criticised the government for not informing Parliament about the visit before or after the prime minister’s trip.

“But I express regret over the disrespect shown to the legislature by the prime minister by not informing Parliament before leaving for the General Assembly or after returning,” he said.

Dulal also said there was little scope for celebrating festivals with greetings at a time when hundreds of Nepalis have died and thousands remain missing following the Bhotekoshi floods and other floods and landslides. He said many of those missing have effectively been considered dead.

“But why is there hesitation and delay in granting those missing citizens the same legal status as the deceased?” he asked the government.

Dulal put forward four demands to the government.

  • Children who have lost their teachers and schools should be provided with teachers and schools so they can resume their education.
  • Children who have lost their parents should feel that the government is there to support them.
  • Citizens who have lost their homes should be provided with shelter, while disaster victims should receive the food and clothing sent by donors.
  • There should be no reports of relief materials rotting in warehouses while funds remain stuck in the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund. Victims should not be told that assistance cannot be provided because different laws do not align.

He also urged the government to learn from previous natural disasters and the responses of governments at the time, and to follow the path of good governance.

Dulal said the previous government led by then Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal had been pursuing corruption investigations in a planned manner, taking into account experience, research, preparation and national needs, but was eventually brought down.

He urged the current government to learn from that experience as well.

“Let this government open files backed by strong evidence of corruption. There should not be an attempt to create the impression that a government that cannot open files is trying to govern by misusing state power and staging stunts, while MPs shout in Parliament and mislead the public,” he said.

He called for those involved in corruption to be brought to justice through due legal process.

Dulal also referred to a speech by Rastriya Swatantra Party Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane made before the February 21 election.

“Try to remember that very popular and appealing speech — what do people hope for? What do people ask for? They ask for electricity, water, roads, education and healthcare. What do people hope for? Is this even a demand in the 21st century?” Dulal said.

He added, “If our government-side colleagues feel that this sounds like them, they need not take it otherwise. You are right.”

Dulal then raised seven questions about the current situation and public sentiment.

  • Should we talk about the long queues people faced waiting for half a cylinder of cooking gas, or the queues of young people waiting for passports that covered Tripureshwor?
  • Should we talk about queues at hospitals or those of farmers waiting for chemical fertiliser?
  • Should we talk about soaring inflation or the migration of unemployed young people abroad?
  • Should we talk about taxes imposed on education and healthcare or VAT charged on household electricity bills?
  • Should we talk about vehicles blocking media gates or unlawful arrests carried out at midnight?
  • Or should we talk about the heartbreaking plight of landless citizens living in holding shelters?
  • With the current parliamentary session ending and lawmakers returning to their constituencies, what will we tell the people?

title.rendered: Woman arrested in Rupandehi with one kilogram of gold jewellery

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The Armed Police Force Nepal has arrested a woman in Rupandehi with one kilogram of gold jewellery.

APF Nepal Deputy Spokesperson DSP Shailendra Thapa said the woman was arrested with one kilogram of gold jewellery from Shantigate in Siddharthanagar Municipality-1 on Wednesday night.

The arrested woman has been identified as 46-year-old Ila Patel, a resident of Kathmandu Metropolitan City-19, Thapa said. A team deployed from the APF Nepal Border Security Gulma in Danda arrested her.

The team arrested Patel based on a tip-off while she was travelling to Nepal from India.

Following her arrest, the jewellery was tested by gold and silver traders in Siddharthanagar and found to weigh one kilogram, Thapa said.

She was handed over to the Bhairahawa Customs Office in Rupandehi along with the recovered gold for necessary action.

The APF said the seized gold is valued at Rs 25,193,350.

title.rendered: Swiss glaciers lose 5.5% of ice volume this year, second-largest decline on record

content.rendered:
Geneva, October 1

Glaciers in Switzerland, home to the largest number of glaciers in the Alps, lost 5.5% of their ice volume this year, marking the second-largest percentage decline on record amid heat waves and low winter snowfall, experts said.

“Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions,” the GLAMOS Swiss glacier monitoring service and the Swiss Academy of Sciences said in a statement released Thursday.

The decline has accelerated in recent years. Over the past five years alone, Switzerland has lost nearly one-fifth of its total glacier ice volume, according to the experts.

The findings add to growing concerns over the impact of global warming on Europe, which is the world’s fastest-warming continent.

“The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100% to anthropogenic climate change. It’s as simple as that,” said Matthias Huss, head of GLAMOS. “Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn’t have any warming at the moment.”

Ice loss continues to accelerate

Switzerland recorded its largest glacier retreat in 2022, when summer heat and low winter snowfall combined with an unusual layer of reddish dust from the Sahara. The dust darkened the glaciers, causing them to absorb more heat.

Huss said winter snow cover was important for two reasons.

“On the one hand, it protects the bare ice from melting. The longer you have snow, the longer you avoid the loss of old ice,” Huss said in an interview at the Federal Polytechnic Institute ETHZ, where he is a professor of glaciology.

“On the other hand, the snow is important also for generating new food for the glacier. The more snow you have, the higher the potential to keep some of the snow at high elevation and to form new ice,” he added.

The accelerated melting in the Alps is part of a wider global trend. Experts say global warming also contributed to destabilising a Himalayan slope that collapsed in August, triggering catastrophic flooding in Nepal.

Satellites have also documented significant glacier shrinkage in Greenland and Antarctica over the past half-century.

Percentage loss rises as glaciers shrink

In absolute terms, the amount of ice lost in Switzerland this year was lower than in 2003. However, the percentage decline was greater because Switzerland’s glaciers now contain roughly one-third of the ice volume they had 23 years ago.

In 2003, glaciers lost 3.5% of their total ice volume.

The accelerated melting has significant consequences for Switzerland. The loss of 2.2 trillion litres (581 billion gallons) of water between July and September is equivalent to about four times the country’s annual water consumption.

Switzerland, with a population of around 9.1 million, generates more than half of its electricity from hydropower.

The effects of glacier loss extend beyond Switzerland. The country is considered Europe’s water tower and supplies water to some of the continent’s major rivers, including the Danube, Po, Rhine and Rhone.

Experts said the “extreme melting” recorded this year resulted in an average reduction of between 2.5 and 4 metres (about 8 to 13 feet) in glacier thickness. Some glacier tongues lost as much as 10 metres (33 feet).

Expert teams have been assessing runoff and crevasses formed by water flowing through the glaciers. In some areas, they have used red dye in streams to track water flows.

The Allalin, Clariden, Rhone and Aletsch glaciers were among those that experienced their largest melt on record this year. Aletsch is the largest glacier in the Alps.

title.rendered: 4 more bodies found on Himlung, death toll reaches 11

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The bodies of four more people who went missing in an avalanche on Mt Himlung in Manang have been found.

The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association team deployed to search for the missing climbers found four bodies on Thursday, the association said. An experienced mountain guide team led by Pasang Kaji Sherpa continued the search and rescue operation.

The association said four bodies were found, quoting Sherpa. With this, the number of Nepali nationals who have died in the Himlung avalanche has reached 11.

Adverse weather conditions since September 25 triggered the avalanche on the mountain.

A total of 16 people went missing after an avalanche struck the base camp of Mt Himlung. The bodies of 11 people have now been recovered, while five people remain missing.

title.rendered: Track reopened on flood-damaged Galchhi-Betrawati road

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

A track has been opened along the Galchhi-Betrawati road section damaged by the Rasuwa floods.

Infrastructure Minister Sunil Lamsal said public movement along the road section has resumed following the opening of the track.

According to Minister Lamsal’s secretariat, the section, which serves as a major road link to Rasuwa, has been reopened, but work to level the road and lay gravel remains.

Lamsal has urged everyone to facilitate the ongoing construction and maintenance work, saying heavy traffic while the work is underway has been affecting construction activities.

Following the completion of track-opening work, preparations are also underway to install a Bailey bridge along the road section. The foundation for the Bailey bridge on the Nuwakot side has already been prepared, and preparations for its installation have begun with the support of the Nepal Army.

The foundation for the Bailey bridge on the Rasuwa side is also in its final stage, Lamsal said. The ministry said work is being expedited with a target of completing the Bailey bridge installation within a week.

Travel to and from Rasuwa had been affected after the floods damaged the road infrastructure. The reopening of the track is expected to facilitate transportation, while the installation of the Bailey bridge is expected to improve road connectivity further.

title.rendered: Nepal tourist arrivals rise 12.1 per cent in September; Chinese visitors double

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Tourist arrivals to Nepal have improved despite the country facing natural disasters continuously over the past two months.

According to the Nepal Tourism Board, 88,248 tourists visited Nepal in September, a 12.1 per cent increase compared with the same month last year.

Arrivals from South Asian countries increased by 23.9 per cent, rising from 24,285 in September 2025 to 30,085 this year. Arrivals from other Asian countries increased by 58 per cent, from 12,590 to 19,888.

However, arrivals from the ASEAN region fell by 25.9 per cent to 5,422. European arrivals declined by 8.7 per cent, from 16,597 last year to 15,148 this year. Arrivals from the Americas also fell, with 10,107 visitors recorded this September compared with 11,523 last year.

Among SAARC countries, arrivals from Bangladesh increased by 31.5 per cent to 3,964, while Bhutanese arrivals rose to 1,111 from 833. India recorded 17,425 arrivals, up from 15,556, while arrivals from Sri Lanka increased to 7,108 from 4,616.

Chinese arrivals more than doubled, rising 114.1 per cent from 5,237 last September to 11,212 this year. Japanese arrivals increased 45.4 per cent to 2,066.

British arrivals fell 25.2 per cent to 3,725 from 4,981, while US arrivals declined to 8,299 from 9,679. Arrivals from the Middle East increased by 11.9 per cent.

title.rendered: Federal Civil Service Bill aims to strengthen federal governance, says minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The government has said the Federal Civil Service Bill registered in Parliament will provide an important foundation for the effective implementation of Nepal’s federal governance system.

Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration Pratibha Rawal made the statement regarding the bill, which was registered in Parliament on Thursday.

The Civil Service Bill has been prepared to amend and consolidate laws relating to the federal civil service.

After the bill was registered, Minister Rawal said it had been finalised following extensive study and broad consultations.

According to Rawal, the bill is expected to make the civil service more capable, effective, efficient, accountable and results-oriented, while bringing significant changes to performance and accountability.

“We believe this will not only provide an important foundation for the effective implementation of the federal governance system but also become an important milestone in the direction of good governance and public administration reform,” she wrote on social media.

Rawal said she had made the bill a clear priority after assuming responsibility for the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration.

She recalled that one of her priorities was to bring the long-pending Federal Civil Service Bill to a conclusion and establish a strong foundation for public administration reform and good governance.

She also said the government aims to simplify, speed up and make public services more transparent and technology-friendly through extensive digitisation and automation, including in land administration.

Civil Service Bill linked to unresolved issues of federalism

The government’s 100-point agenda for governance reform had stated that the bill would be drafted within 45 days of the formation of the government. However, its progress has been delayed.

Previous Houses of Representatives had also considered the bill, but it was never transformed into law.

The bill is closely linked to the implementation of federalism. Following the adoption of federalism, the government carried out the major task of adjusting civil servants among the federal, provincial and local levels.

However, issues relating to recruitment, jurisdiction and which level of government civil servants should come under remain unresolved.

Provincial Public Service Commissions have been established as required by the Constitution. However, employees working at provincial and local levels are still under the federal government.

The bill had also been introduced during the previous term of the House of Representatives amid disagreement over whether provincial chief secretaries, secretaries of provincial ministries, chief administrative officers of local governments and accounting officers should remain under the federal government.

The bill did not progress as expected amid arguments that keeping federal government employees under provincial and local governments was contrary to the spirit of federalism.

These issues will now be discussed again in Parliament.

Retirement age becomes another point of debate

The proposed retirement provisions have also sparked discussion.

The government has advanced a draft proposing retirement for civil servants who have reached the age of 55 or completed 30 years of service.

According to the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration, employees retiring at the age of 55 would be treated as having completed 58 years of service for pension purposes.

The ministry says the provision would ensure that employees taking early retirement would not lose their retirement benefits.

Bill unlikely to be passed in current session

The government is preparing to end the ongoing session of the Federal Parliament on October 2. The parliamentary calendar for the House of Representatives has been prepared up to October 2 as part of this process.

Although the bill has now been registered in the House of Representatives, it will have to wait for the next session to move through the legislative process.

Once the next session begins, the House will hold a principle-based discussion on the bill. Following the discussion, lawmakers will be given 72 hours to submit amendments.

The proposed amendments and the bill will then be considered together during clause-by-clause discussions.

The process will take place in both houses of Parliament. Once both houses pass the bill, it will be sent to the president through the House in which it originated.

The bill will come into force as an Act after the president authenticates it.

title.rendered: Ncell announces special bundle for iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo buyers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Ncell has partnered with Generation Next Communications, the authorised Apple distributor in Nepal, to launch a special bundle package for customers purchasing the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo.

The offer is available to existing Ncell users as well as new customers purchasing an Ncell SIM.

Customers purchasing the new iPhone models will receive unlimited data, unlimited local calls, 150 free SMS messages per day and a subscription to Lionsgate, an OTT platform offering premium content.

Under the offer, the first 200 customers purchasing the iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max will receive these benefits free of charge for three months.

Similarly, the first 100 customers purchasing the iPhone Duo will receive the same benefits free of charge for six months.

“We are pleased to offer this special package to customers purchasing the new iPhone models in partnership with Generation Next Communications,” said Upang Dutta, chief consumer business officer at Ncell.

“Aligned with Ncell’s commitment to practical value and supporting digital lifestyles, this plan will provide our users across the country with reliable connectivity wherever they are. Dhant will feature in various Pulsar NS brand communications, campaigns and consumer engagement activities. Through these initiatives, Bajaj said it will highlight not only the features and technical aspects of its products but also themes of strength, confidence, performance and a bold attitude.

According to Bajaj, the partnership between Dhant and Pulsar is an effort to bring together two distinct identities around a common spirit. The company believes that the shared emphasis on strength and performance will help make the Pulsar brand identity more distinctive.

Customers can follow Bajaj Nepal’s official social media channels and other communication platforms for upcoming campaigns and content featuring Pulsar and Rabindra Dhant.

For more information about Pulsar motorcycles, customers can also contact their nearest Bajaj showroom.

title.rendered: Civil Service Bill: Nine types of leave mentioned, but menstrual leave remains unclear

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The proposed Federal Civil Service Bill, 2026, includes provisions on leave available to civil servants, but the available explanatory section of the bill does not clearly specify menstrual leave for female employees.

Section 125 of the bill deals with leave for civil servants and states that a total of “nine types of leave” will be provided.

However, the available document does not provide a detailed list of the nine types of leave or clarify whether menstrual leave is included.

Section 148 of the bill, which provides the authority to formulate regulations for implementing the Act, specifically states that matters related to “leave and unpaid leave available to civil servants” will be covered by the regulations.

Similarly, Section 126 contains provisions on unpaid leave, including leave of up to five years in cases where an employee’s spouse is posted to a diplomatic mission abroad.

The full details of the nine types of leave, including the conditions for specific forms of leave such as menstrual leave, are expected to be clarified through regulations to be formulated after the bill is passed.

title.rendered: BTS becomes first K-pop group to win Song of the Year at MTV VMAs

content.rendered:
Seoul

South Korean pop group BTS won three awards at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs), adding another major achievement to its award history.

At the ceremony held at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, BTS members Jin, V, J-Hope, Suga, Jimin, Jungkook and RM won three trophies for their song “Swim” and the group’s achievements.

BTS won Song of the Year and Best K-Pop for “Swim” and also took home the Best Group award.

The group made a clean sweep of all the categories in which it was nominated at this year’s VMAs. Its Song of the Year win was particularly significant, making BTS the first K-pop group to receive the award.

The Best Group award marked BTS’s fifth win in the category. The group previously won the award four consecutive times from 2019 to 2022.

Following the wins, BTS thanked its fan group ARMY through its agency BigHit Music.

“We sincerely thank ARMY for always giving us unwavering love and support,” the group said. “Arirang is an album that feels like a new beginning for us, so these awards are even more meaningful.”

BTS said winning Song of the Year for “Swim” was possible because of everyone who loves its music. The seven members also pledged to continue creating and performing music together.

title.rendered: US regulator launches broad investigation into Anthropic and OpenAI over AI safety

content.rendered:
Washington, October 1

The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has launched a broad investigation into the artificial intelligence (AI) safety practices of Anthropic and OpenAI, The Washington Post reported Wednesday, citing a senior agency official.

The FTC has broad authority to investigate unfair and deceptive practices affecting consumers in the United States.

The scope of the investigation has not been disclosed. The launch of the inquiry does not mean the companies will face charges of wrongdoing.

The investigation comes amid growing concerns over AI safety.

Anthropic and OpenAI have reported incidents in which their AI systems operated beyond their intended environments. In one incident, OpenAI agents reportedly escaped a sandbox and breached Hugging Face, another AI company.

OpenAI also cancelled a model release on Monday over safety concerns.

Meanwhile, executives from both companies have proposed coordinated slowdowns aimed at strengthening AI safety measures.

title.rendered: UML lawmaker questions nature of Balen-led government; RSP lawmaker responds

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Opposition and ruling-party lawmakers exchanged questions and answers in the House of Representatives on the nature of the government led by Prime Minister Balen Shah.

Speaking at Thursday’s House meeting, CPN-UML lawmaker Laxmi Prasad Pokhrel said the government appeared to be a constitutional government because the leader of the parliamentary party with a majority in the House was the prime minister. However, he said it also appeared to be an independent government because the prime minister did not attend meetings of his own party.

He said the government also appeared to be a one-party government because it did not attend all-party meetings.

Describing it as resembling a Panchayat-era government run by an underground group and a “Shree 3 Maharaj” who disregards the president, he asked, “What kind of government is the Balen government, actually?”

Ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Santosh Rajbanshi responded to the question after some time.

He said the election held on March 5, 2026, was not a regular election that marked a continuation from one political sequence to another, but had brought a new government by breaking the existing political pattern.

He urged lawmakers to remember that the government had been endorsed by the people’s mandate and that it had the support of a majority of lawmakers.

“I want to tell the honourable member who keeps asking what kind of government the Balen government is: it is a government that seeks to reduce corruption. Whatever mechanism weakens the country—whether the judiciary, the bureaucracy or the political mechanism—it is a government that listens to everyone and jails everyone,” Rajbanshi said.

He said the government was not one that would follow regular procedures for the sake of anyone and reiterated that it would take action against those who had engaged in corruption in the past.

title.rendered: Key provisions of the Federal Civil Service Bill

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The government has registered the Federal Civil Service Bill in Parliament, proposing several changes to the existing structure and provisions governing the civil service.

The bill has generated significant discussion among civil servants, particularly because it introduces a provision allowing employees who have reached the age of 55 or completed 30 years of service to take voluntary retirement under certain conditions.

The major provisions of the Civil Service Bill are as follows

1. Shift from rank-based to level-based system

The existing rank-based system in the civil service would be replaced with a level-based system, ranging from 14th level for officers to first level for assistants.

2. Mandatory retirement at 60

The Civil Service Bill proposes setting the mandatory retirement age for civil servants at 60.

3. 11 services and clustering

There will be 11 services under the federal civil service. These services would be grouped into six major clusters for specialisation.

4. New framework for inclusive recruitment

Of the positions filled through open competitive examinations, 49 per cent would be reserved for inclusive recruitment.

This 49 per cent would be treated as 100 per cent for the purpose of allocation. Half of the reserved positions would be contested only among women, while the remaining half would be contested separately among other targeted groups.

5. Tenure for senior officials

The tenure of gazetted special-class officers at the 14th level would be two years, while the tenure of 13th-level officers would be three years.

6. Performance agreements and accountability

Chief secretaries, secretaries, departmental heads and office chiefs would be required to enter into annual performance agreements. Their performance would be evaluated objectively on that basis.

7. Civil Service Board

The Civil Service Bill proposes establishing a Civil Service Board chaired by the chief secretary to make transfers, postings and career development more transparent, predictable and merit-based.

8. Level promotion under certain conditions

Employees who have completed the prescribed minimum service period of seven years and received excellent performance evaluation scores in the previous three years would be eligible for promotion by one level.

9. Contributory pension system

A contributory pension system would apply to newly appointed civil servants.

10. Restrictions after retirement

Officials at the special or first class level would be barred from being appointed to constitutional, diplomatic or other government positions for two years after retirement or resignation.

11. Voluntary retirement

Employees who have completed at least 20 years of service to qualify for a pension and have either reached the age of 55 or completed 30 years of service would be allowed to apply for voluntary retirement at any time.

12. Additional service period for pension calculation

Employees taking voluntary retirement after reaching the age of 55 or completing 30 years of service would be allowed to add the remaining period before reaching the mandatory retirement age to their service period, within a specified limit.

The provision would allow an additional five to seven years of service to be counted, subject to the prescribed conditions, increasing the amount of pension or gratuity payable.

13. Government approval required

The government or concerned authority would have the power to approve or reject applications for voluntary retirement submitted by employees who have reached the age of 55 or completed 30 years of service.

The decision would take into account service requirements, the nature of the employee’s position and workforce management needs.

14. Lump-sum payment of accumulated benefits

Employees retiring after completing 30 years of service or reaching the age of 55 would receive, in a lump sum and according to prevailing law, their accumulated benefits, including unused sick leave and home leave, medical expenses and other applicable benefits.

title.rendered: Proposed civil service bill sets aside 49 per cent posts for reservation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The proposed Federal Civil Service Bill has allocated 49 per cent of posts filled through open competition for reservation to make the federal civil service more inclusive.

The bill treats the reserved quota as 100 per cent, with 50 per cent of the reserved posts allocated exclusively for women and the remaining 50 per cent for candidates from other targeted groups.

The women’s quota is divided among eight groups: Khas Arya (27.7 per cent), indigenous nationalities (25.7 per cent), Madhesi (15.3 per cent), Dalit (12.7 per cent), Tharu (6.6 per cent), Muslim (4 per cent), people from backward areas (4 per cent) and women with disabilities (4 per cent).

The remaining 50 per cent is allocated to indigenous nationalities (32.5 per cent), Madhesi (19 per cent), Dalit (15.5 per cent), economically disadvantaged Khas Arya (10 per cent), Tharu (9 per cent), Muslim (5 per cent), people from backward areas (5 per cent) and persons with disabilities (4 per cent).

The bill defines economically disadvantaged Khas Arya as individuals holding a poverty identification card or those recommended as disadvantaged by their local government.

A person can use the reservation facility only once for non-gazetted posts and once for gazetted posts. The government must review the reservation provisions every five years.

If a reserved post remains vacant, it will be carried forward to the same group’s advertisement the following year. If it remains unfilled, candidates from the inclusive alternative list and, subsequently, the next year’s open competition will be considered.

title.rendered: Angdembe questions government’s governance, parliamentary accountability despite majority

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Nepali Congress parliamentary party leader Bhishmaraj Angdembe has questioned the governance and parliamentary accountability of a government with a clear majority.

Speaking at Thursday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, he said a majority alone does not constitute the capacity to govern and urged the government to work in a way that maintains public trust.

Angdembe said although a majority can form a government, vision, dialogue, coordination, institutional respect, decision-making capacity and results are needed to retain public trust.

“The government has a clear majority in the House of Representatives. This is a major political asset. But a majority alone is not the capacity to govern,” he said. “A majority can form a government, but it cannot retain public trust. For that, vision, dialogue, coordination, institutional respect, decision-making capacity and results are needed.”

Angdembe said the government should move forward by taking all three tiers of government, Parliament, constitutional bodies, the administration, the private sector and civil society along with it, but said he had the impression that the government was trying to confine itself to a limited political circle.

“The government is supposed to run the state, not just its own side or a small group within its side,” he said. Angdembe also said the government should view Parliament not as a competitor but as an institution that partners with democracy.

He stressed the importance of parliamentary traditions under which the government informs Parliament about its decisions, policies and international commitments, holds dialogue and remains accountable.

Angdembe drew the government’s attention to the fact that Prime Minister Balen Shah did not inform Parliament before attending the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

He reminded the prime minister that attending the General Assembly after informing Parliament was not merely a tradition but also provided parliamentary legitimacy to the issues he would raise.

“Unfortunately, you did not inform Parliament, and I had expected you to inform Parliament after returning from the United Nations General Assembly, but that did not happen either,” he said. “If you try to break every tradition, one day you may be swept away by the force of those very traditions. Keep that in mind.”
