title.rendered: The inflation problem hiding in your savings account

content.rendered:
Imagine filling a bucket with water while it is slowly leaking from the bottom. That is what can happen to your money when it sits in a regular savings account while inflation rises. The leak is called inflation.

You may have done everything right. You worked hard, spent carefully and put your money in a bank savings account because that is what you were taught to do. But there is an uncomfortable truth: while your money may be sitting safely in your account, its purchasing power can be declining over time.

Not because the money was stolen. Not because the bank failed. But because of something silent and largely invisible — inflation.

A typical savings account in Nepal may offer an interest rate of roughly 2.75 to 4 percent a year, while inflation can be higher. When that happens, the real value of your savings declines even though the number in your bank account increases.

Consider a simple example. Suppose you deposit Rs 100,000 in a savings account. If the bank pays you 3.5 percent interest over a year, your balance will grow to about Rs 103,500. That sounds like good news — until you look at what happens to prices.

If prices rise by around 6 percent over the same period, goods that cost Rs 100,000 today could cost roughly Rs 106,000 a year from now. You therefore have more rupees in your account, but those rupees can buy less than they could before.

This is one of the psychological traps of inflation. Because the number in our bank account goes up, it feels like our money is growing. But the more important question is not how many rupees we have. It is what those rupees can actually buy.

Think about our mothers and grandmothers, many of whom spent years putting small amounts of money into a piggy bank, a cupboard or some corner of the house. When the savings became substantial, they moved the money into a bank account, believing that it would remain safe and gradually grow.

They saved for their children’s education, weddings, medical emergencies and other important needs. Putting those savings in a bank provided security and peace of mind. But if those savings earn less interest than the rate at which prices are rising, their purchasing power can gradually erode.

This affects more than one generation or one type of household. Government employees, small-business owners, homemakers, retirees and families trying to build a financial cushion can all face the same problem. Many of us are simply following financial habits passed down from our parents and grandparents without considering whether those habits still work in today’s economic environment.

The problem may seem small when viewed month by month. Over several years, however, the difference can become significant.

The good news is that you do not need to be a financial expert to start thinking about it differently.

Fixed deposits

A fixed deposit can be one of the simplest steps for people looking to earn more on money they do not need immediately. Depending on the bank, term and prevailing interest rates, fixed deposits can offer higher returns than ordinary savings accounts.

A fixed deposit, however, does not automatically protect your money from inflation. If the inflation rate is higher than the interest earned after considering taxes and other factors, your money may still lose purchasing power in real terms.

Its advantage is that it can provide a relatively predictable return while keeping the money within the banking system.

Gold

Gold is another asset that many Nepali households already understand and trust.

For generations, gold has been more than jewellery in Nepal. It has also been a way of storing wealth and passing assets from one generation to another. Even households with relatively modest incomes have often tried to accumulate small amounts of gold over time.

Gold is also widely viewed internationally as an asset that can provide some protection against inflation and economic uncertainty. However, that does not mean its price always rises with inflation or that it is guaranteed to outperform other investments. Gold prices can fluctuate significantly, and buying jewellery also involves costs that do not necessarily translate into investment returns.

For someone considering gold as part of their savings strategy, it is therefore important to distinguish between buying gold as jewellery and investing in gold as an asset.

Stocks and mutual funds

Shares listed on the Nepal Stock Exchange and mutual funds offer another potential avenue for long-term investors, but they also come with considerably more risk.

Stocks can generate higher returns over time, but their prices can also fall sharply. Economic conditions, company performance, investor sentiment and political developments can all influence the market.

Mutual funds may be an option for people who want exposure to the market without selecting individual stocks themselves. These funds are managed by professionals, although they still carry investment risk and charge fees.

Investors can also use licensed portfolio management or asset management services, where professionals manage investments on their behalf for a fee.

But there is one important principle worth remembering: do not invest money that you may need urgently, and avoid investing borrowed money simply in the hope of earning a higher return.

Diversification

For people who want to manage risk rather than place all their savings in one option, diversification can be useful.

Instead of keeping all your money in a savings account, you can consider dividing your savings across different assets according to your financial needs, risk tolerance and time horizon. For example, some money could remain readily accessible in a savings account, some could go into a fixed deposit, and a portion could be allocated to investments such as mutual funds, shares or gold.

There is no single formula that works for everyone. The right balance depends on factors such as income, expenses, emergency needs, investment horizon and willingness to accept losses.

The reason diversification can help is simple: different assets behave differently. If one performs poorly, another may perform better, reducing your dependence on a single investment.

That does not eliminate risk. Bank deposits can fail to keep pace with inflation. Fixed deposits lock money away for a specified period. Gold prices can fluctuate. Stock markets can fall sharply. Mutual funds are also subject to market risk.

Diversification is therefore not about finding a way to avoid losses altogether. It is about avoiding the risk of putting all your financial eggs in one basket.

Stop the leak

Coming back to the leaking bucket, you may not be able to stop every leak.

Inflation is influenced by forces far beyond the control of an individual household. But you can think more carefully about how you protect the purchasing power of your savings.

The goal is not to abandon bank accounts or chase the highest possible return. A savings account serves an important purpose, particularly for emergency funds and money you need to access quickly.

The goal is to understand the difference between saving money and preserving its purchasing power.

For years, many of us have been taught that putting money in a bank is the safest thing we can do. In terms of protecting the money from theft or keeping it accessible, that remains true in many circumstances. But safety from loss of principal is not the same as safety from inflation.

Even small changes in how we think about our savings can make a difference over time. You do not need a large amount of money or deep financial knowledge to start. You simply need to ask a different question:

Is my money only increasing in number, or is it also retaining its ability to buy the things I will need in the future?

title.rendered: ‘I am an average-capacity engineer, trying to become extraordinary’: RSP General Secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Bipin Kumar Acharya, general secretary of the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) and a member of the House of Representatives, has said that he is trying to become “extraordinary.”

He made the remark while speaking during the zero hour in the House of Representatives on Thursday.

“I may be an engineer of average ability, which is perhaps why people who excel in ability, intent and facts in every field seem extraordinary to me. I am also trying to become extraordinary myself,” he said.

Acharya did not name Prime Minister Balen Shah in his remarks. However, Shah had held a discussion with lawmakers from engineering backgrounds only on Wednesday. During the meeting, Shah had described lawmakers with engineering backgrounds as “extraordinary” lawmakers.

Seventeen lawmakers attended the meeting held at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. Mohan Acharya, a Nepali Congress lawmaker from Rasuwa, was the only participant from the Nepali Congress, while the others were RSP lawmakers.

The lawmakers initially presented their views, after which Prime Minister Shah addressed the meeting.

During his address, Shah explained the types of issues raised by different lawmakers and classified lawmakers into three categories based on their expressions: average, below average and extraordinary.

Shah described lawmakers with engineering backgrounds as “extraordinary” lawmakers.

“Engineers are extraordinary. Ordinary people talk about events. Those below that level tell me to do this or that. Since you are extraordinary, you should raise ideas and talk about creativity. The country will develop if this is done. The country will develop through your ideas,” a lawmaker quoted Shah as saying to Onlinekhabar.

During the discussion, Shah asked lawmakers with engineering backgrounds to provide ideas on what could be done for industrialisation.

He also assured them that they could directly contact the Prime Minister’s Office with ideas and that he would readily meet those who came with ideas.

Against this backdrop, RSP General Secretary Acharya said without naming Prime Minister Shah that he was an engineer of average ability and was trying to become extraordinary.

After making the remark, Acharya raised the issue of the Nepali currency.

“All the powerful currencies in the world have their own symbols. The dollar, euro, pound and even the Japanese yen, as well as the currencies of neighbouring countries such as the Chinese yuan and Indian rupee, have their own symbols,” he said.

He said having a distinct symbol for Nepal’s currency would make things easier in the current global fintech era.

He drew the attention of the Ministry of Finance and Nepal Rastra Bank to the need to create a currency symbol reflecting the originality of Devanagari script and the country’s national pride.

title.rendered: Annapurna local government calls for climate action amid rising risks

content.rendered:
Kaski, October 1

Annapurna Rural Municipality has called for climate justice and urgent measures to address growing climate-related risks in the mountain region from the Annapurna Base Camp (ABC).

The rural municipality held a special village executive meeting at the ABC, located at an altitude of 4,130 metres, on Wednesday to draw attention to the impacts of climate change and the need to strengthen local resilience.

Annapurna Rural Municipality Chairperson Bishnu Bahadur KC said floods, landslides and river erosion during this year’s monsoon had damaged infrastructure, agriculture, transportation and tourism. Floods in the Modi Khola and Kimrung Khola damaged hotels and roads, while Birethanti and Syauli Bazar remain at risk. The washing away of a paved road also disrupted road connectivity between Ghorepani and Pokhara for 40 days.

The meeting called for federal and provincial support through policies, technical assistance, adequate funding, climate finance, research and stronger intergovernmental coordination.

According to spokesperson Bharat Man Gurung, the municipality will prepare an Annapurna Climate Resilience Action Plan and assess climate risks and vulnerabilities across all 11 wards.

The meeting also decided to develop an early warning and emergency communication system, introduce climate-resilient infrastructure criteria and maintain regular records of loss and damage from climate-induced disasters.

title.rendered: Nepal to miss SAFF Championship for first time in history

content.rendered:
Nepal is set to miss the 15th edition of the SAFF Championship, to be held in Bangladesh from November 4 to 17.

With the suspension not lifted even by the deadline of September 30 set by the South Asian Football Federation (SAFF), it is now certain that Nepal will miss the SAFF Championship for the first time in its history.

FIFA had suspended the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) indefinitely on June 24, citing third-party interference in the association’s affairs.

Since the suspension, Nepal has been losing one international competition after another. With this, it is now certain that Nepal will not participate in SAFF for the first time in the tournament’s 33-year history.

SAFF had earlier released a fixture list including Nepal, contingent on the suspension being lifted by September 30. But with the suspension not lifted within that deadline, Nepal is set to miss out.

This year’s SAFF Championship will have six participating countries. Group A includes hosts Bangladesh, along with Sri Lanka and Bhutan. Group B has India, Pakistan and the Maldives. Had the suspension been lifted, Nepal would have played in Group A.

Nepal had participated in all 14 previous editions of SAFF, finishing runners-up once and third once, besides reaching the semifinals five times.

At SAFF, Nepal would present its case as a contender, and players would also get a chance to showcase their ability. But missing out this time means that opportunity is lost.

Former Nepal national team captain, coach and former ANFA vice-president Upendra Man Singh says players have lost a platform to prove themselves by not participating in SAFF.

“This tournament comes every two or three years; playing it is also an opportunity for players to get contracts in professional football abroad, a platform for South Asian players. Now that’s being denied too,” he said. “I’ve felt that a political fight at the top is taking a huge toll on players today.”

Singh believes Nepali football has reached this point because of an arrogance born from the belief that leadership belonged to them alone.

“It’s that arrogance, pride, and the misuse of political power that led to this accident happening in football,” he said.

Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel, who is also the government’s spokesperson, hinted on Tuesday that Nepal’s participation in SAFF was no longer possible. He said it was already too late for SAFF and that preparations were underway to run the domestic league instead.

Asked when ANFA’s suspension might be lifted, Minister Pokharel said, “It’s already too late for SAFF. We’ve discussed with various players what to do if the suspension isn’t lifted. We need to run the domestic league. Since players have told us it’s been years since they played in a domestic league, we’re preparing for that.”

Marking his remarks, there is little likelihood of Nepal’s FIFA suspension being lifted anytime soon. Minister Pokharel had earlier said publicly that talks with FIFA had been positive and that the suspension would be lifted soon. But with no positive response from FIFA, the government has moved toward advancing domestic football activities instead.

Nepal Police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) has arrested ANFA treasurer Rabindra Joshi and accountant Sanjiv Pandey on match-fixing charges. With the investigation under way, ANFA officials are currently unreachable, pushing Nepali football further into uncertainty.

title.rendered: 648 mountaineers from 69 countries obtain climbing permits for autumn season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

A total of 648 mountaineers from 69 countries have obtained permits to climb various mountains in Nepal during the upcoming autumn season.

According to the Department of Tourism, permits were issued to 648 mountaineers from 69 countries to climb 20 different peaks in the country. The permits cover 71 teams comprising 485 men and 163 women, said the department’s information officer, Suraj Ghimire.

The mountaineers include 17 from Australia, 16 from Canada, 21 from Japan, 18 from India, 41 from the USA, 38 from the UK, 15 from Spain, 13 from Switzerland, 57 from Russia, 19 from Poland, 20 from Nepal and 118 from China.

Similarly, mountaineers from Germany (34), France (51), Belgium (7), Bulgaria (5), the Czech Republic (16) and Argentina (7), among others, have also obtained climbing permits.

The department collected US$1,571,659, equivalent to Rs 238,964,298, in royalties from the permits.

Among the peaks for which permits were issued, Mount Manaslu (8,163 metres) attracted the highest number of climbers, with 500 mountaineers from 43 teams obtaining permits.

Climbing permits were issued to 34 climbers from four teams for Dhaulagiri I, 20 climbers from two teams for Putha Hiunchuli, 16 climbers from two teams for Danga Hiunchuli and 10 climbers from one team for Baruntse Himal.

Similarly, the department issued permits for peaks including Makalu, Gangapurna West (Langchenel), Thorong Peak, Norbu Khang, Annapurna IV, Chamlang, Lamjung Himal, Pumori, Saribung, Thapa Peak (Dhampus), Pokhar Khang, Ardang and Peri.

title.rendered: Drinking water restored for 180 flood-affected households in Dhading

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Drinking water services have been restored for 180 flood-affected households in Baireni, Galchhi Rural Municipality-6, Dhading, after repairs to the Maheshkhola-Bhattatar-Jintetar deep-boring water supply scheme were completed.

The Nepal Red Cross Society, Dhading District Chapter, carried out the repair project under its Rasuwa Flood Response Program, with financial assistance of Rs 446,680.

Galchhi Rural Municipality Chairperson Kedarnath Khatiwada inaugurated the restored water supply scheme at a programme held after the completion of the repairs. He commended the Red Cross for helping restore access to drinking water for residents affected by the floods.

Durlabh Kumar Tamang, chairperson of the Nepal Red Cross Society Dhading District Chapter, said restoring essential services such as drinking water was an important part of humanitarian response during disasters.

Red Cross District Program Coordinator Saroj Thapa said the restoration would help residents overcome the severe water shortage caused by the floods and return to normal life.

Nepal Red Cross General Secretary Rishi Raman Khanal said flood-response activities were continuing, including shelter and food assistance, WASH services, health and psychosocial support, family reunification and cash assistance. Over the past month, WASH services have reached 2,200 affected households, while 18 water tanks have been installed.

title.rendered: Stakeholders call for stronger implementation of National Climate Change Policy 2083

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Stakeholders have called for making the proposed National Climate Change Policy 2083 more implementation-oriented.

They have drawn the government’s attention to the need for clear institutional structures, human resources, funding and inter-agency coordination, saying the policy cannot be effectively implemented unless these requirements are clearly addressed.

At a discussion organised by Prakriti Resources Centre with representatives of various organisations working in the climate and energy sectors, participants said the draft incorporates many positive provisions but needs clearer institutional, financial and legal foundations for implementation.

They also called for giving special priority to climate justice, loss and damage, the role of local governments and mobilisation of climate finance in the changing context. They expressed concern that climate justice has not been given adequate priority in the draft despite Nepal suffering significant losses from climate-induced disasters in recent years.

They suggested that climate justice should not be limited to issues Nepal raises at the international level but should be mainstreamed into every policy, strategy and action plan.

Climate justice and implementation aspects need to be strengthened: Sherchan

Pragya Sherchan, programme coordinator at Prakriti Resources Centre (PRC), said the draft addresses more issues than previous policies but its implementation aspects need to be further strengthened.

She said although the draft identifies issues including coordination among the three levels of government, the need for skilled human resources and the lack of climate finance, it needs to provide a clearer roadmap for mobilising the climate finance Nepal requires.

Noting that it is positive that gender diversity and sexual and gender minorities have been included in policy formulation, she stressed the need for clear provisions to ensure their participation.

“Many issues left out of the previous policy have been incorporated this time, and existing gaps in climate governance have also been identified. But having a good policy alone is not enough. It needs to be clearer on how to ensure the finance, skilled human resources, institutional coordination and legal structures required for effective implementation,” she said.

She added, “If the policy itself clearly states how representation, quotas or other institutional mechanisms will be ensured, the implementation gaps seen in the past can be reduced.”

Sherchan stressed that climate justice should be incorporated into every policy, strategy and action plan rather than being treated as a separate issue.

“Although climate justice has been mentioned in the draft, it does not appear to have been given adequate priority. Climate justice should not be limited to issues Nepal raises at the international level; it should be mainstreamed into every policy, strategy and action plan,” she said.

She also said the policy should include provisions to enforce the “polluter pays” principle at the national level, rather than applying it only at the international level.

Separate provision needed for loss and damage

Stakeholders have suggested that loss and damage, which has emerged as a major issue in international climate discussions alongside climate adaptation and mitigation, should be clearly addressed in the policy.

Kushal Gurung, a climate and energy expert, said the proposed National Climate Change Policy 2083 needs a separate provision to clearly address loss and damage caused by climate-induced disasters.

He said systematic accounting of loss and damage, evidence-based data and a responsible mechanism should be made important foundations for policy implementation.

“Compared with the previous policy, the draft is broader, but greater clarity is needed on implementation and the management of loss and damage,” he said.

He said the new draft also includes strategies and an action plan, making it necessary to clearly define responsibilities and monitoring mechanisms for implementation.

He particularly warned that it would be difficult for the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Environment alone to implement and monitor the policy because it covers sectors including food security, forests, hydropower, energy, transport, physical infrastructure and health.

Although the draft states that the Climate and Environment Protection Council and the National Planning Commission will be responsible for monitoring, Gurung said their participation in the policy-making process and the provision of adequate human resources and other resources would be important.

“The draft is much broader and more inclusive than the previous policy. The roles of various stakeholders, including the private sector, have been clearly identified,” he said. “Gender equality and social inclusion have also been incorporated. But the main challenge now is implementation.”

Experts said the issue of loss and damage arising from recent climate-induced disasters, particularly in Rasuwa and other areas, needs to be clearly addressed in a separate section of the policy.

Gurung said although the draft mentions climate finance, it should not be limited to international loans and grants but should be linked with the government’s own resources and financial mechanisms. He said international climate finance, the domestic financial system, green investment and carbon finance should be viewed in an integrated manner.

Gurung said systematic records of damage caused by disasters in areas including Melamchi, Kagbeni and Humla should be prepared to support claims for funding from international sources.

He said although the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has been identified as the lead agency for disaster management, changes in institutional structures and coordination are also needed because separate recognition and mechanisms are required to access international climate finance.

“Policy should be clear on localisation and resource management”

Representatives of organisations working on climate action also suggested that the proposed National Climate Change Policy 2083 should clearly address the role of local governments, private-sector investment and climate finance mobilisation in reducing and adapting to the impacts of climate change.

Badri Baral, national director of Winrock International Nepal, said the draft is more comprehensive and broad than the previous policy, but some aspects need to be clarified for implementation.

He said that as Nepal has adopted a federal structure, the policy should place local governments, which directly face the impacts of climate change, at the centre of climate action. He said the policy should clearly provide for the resources, authority and human resources needed by local governments to address climate-related risks.

“Important issues such as climate justice, youth, local governments and loss and damage have now been incorporated, and the government should be appreciated for that. But the main requirement now is to make it implementation-oriented and localise it,” he said.

He added, “In line with the federal structure, the policy should provide clear guidance on strengthening local governments to address climate change issues, providing them with the necessary resources and human resources, and making their roles more effective.”

He also stressed the need to mobilise private-sector investment and introduce incentives for such investment alongside public resources and international climate finance. He said the green finance taxonomy introduced by Nepal Rastra Bank could be linked with the climate policy to create a clear basis for encouraging the private sector to invest in climate-resilient activities.

Stressing that climate change education should be incorporated scientifically and systematically from the school level, he said, “It is equally necessary to develop the human resources and capacity required to formulate and implement climate-related plans at the local level.”

“Regarding loss and damage, a separate procedure or regulation should be formulated to mobilise international resources. The measurement, verification and documentation of damage should be made reliable, while ensuring that disaster-affected communities themselves receive resources in a fair manner,” Baral said.

Baral also stressed the need for the policy to provide guidelines for integrated mobilisation of public resources from the federal, provincial and local levels, as well as private-sector investment, alongside international resources.

He said a system should be established not only to provide resources but also to monitor whether the available authority and resources are being used effectively, reward agencies that perform well and hold accountable those that fail to fulfil their responsibilities.

Baral argued that if the proposed policy provides clear guidance on financial resource mobilisation, effective use of authority and localisation of climate policy, it would facilitate the development of necessary procedures, regulations and other legal and institutional structures.

After the government published the draft of the National Climate Change Policy 2083 and sought suggestions from civil society and stakeholders, PRC organised the discussion among organisations working in climate change, renewable energy and rights-based advocacy to discuss the positive aspects of the draft and areas requiring improvement.

The draft of the climate change policy includes 15 thematic areas, 55 strategies and around 288 action plans. It incorporates many issues that were absent from the previous policy.

The suggestions received during the discussion will be submitted to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Environment. The government published the draft of the National Climate Change Policy 2083 on October 2 and requested suggestions within 10 days.

— News Agency Nepal

title.rendered: Australia’s largest medicinal cannabis farm now under Chinese ownership

content.rendered:
Sydney, October 1

Tasmanian Botanics, one of Australia’s largest medicinal cannabis producers, has now come under almost complete Chinese ownership.

Ownership of the company’s holding company, Pigeon, based at Pontville north of Hobart, changed hands after Chinese-owned Yongji Health purchased its remaining shares for around AU$31 million.

Yongji Health, a subsidiary of China’s Guizhou-based Yongji Printing, already held a major stake in Tasmanian Botanics. The latest purchase has now raised its indirect ownership of the company to around 96.5 percent.

Tasmanian Botanics has long produced, processed and packaged medicinal cannabis. More than 150 employees work at the company’s Pontville facility, which includes a large state-of-the-art greenhouse alongside roughly 2.5 hectares of outdoor cultivation.

Company CEO Craig Knight made clear that, despite the ownership change, no major immediate changes are planned for employees or customers. He said there is no concern over job security and that the company plans further expansion in the coming period.

title.rendered: Government recommends ending current Parliament session

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The government has recommended ending the Federal Parliament’s current session effective midnight tomorrow.

The Cabinet meeting held on Tuesday decided to end the session and sent a letter to the President’s Office accordingly. Under the system, the President ends the parliamentary session on the government’s recommendation.

The recommendation to end the session has been made by the government on this basis.

The Federal Parliament’s current session began on May 11. During this session, the government’s budget and budget-related laws were passed. Ordinances the government had brought while Parliament was not in session were also approved during this period.

Ordinance-replacement bills covering matters amended by the approved ordinances were brought to Parliament, passed, and became law.

A direct question-and-answer program with ministers was held, and ministers addressed contemporary issues on the government’s behalf, among other activities. However, a direct question-and-answer program with the Prime Minister could not be held.

title.rendered: New bill sets two-year cooling-off period for civil servants

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The Federal Civil Service bill introduces a two-year cooling-off period for government employees seeking other appointments after leaving their current job.

A cooling-off period is a fixed span during which someone who has resigned from government service or taken mandatory retirement is barred from taking up another government, constitutional, diplomatic or similar government post.

The bill, brought to Parliament by the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration, provides for a two-year cooling-off period for government employees before they can take another appointment after leaving their job.

The Cabinet meeting held on September 29 had earlier decided to approve submitting the Federal Civil Service bill to the Federal Parliament. Before that, the Cabinet meeting of September 10 had decided to send the bill’s draft to the Public Service Commission for feedback, and the bill reached the commission that same day. The Public Service Commission has not objected to the two-year cooling-off provision for those who resign or take mandatory retirement from government service.

The government believes that if the proposed provision becomes law, it will stop the practice of moving straight from retirement or resignation from government service into constitutional, diplomatic or other government appointments.

Attempts to bring in a cooling-off period for government employees have been made before, but earlier versions of the Federal Civil Service bill also failed to become law. A version of the bill registered in the House of Representatives in 2080 B.S. (later rendered inactive) also contained a two-year cooling-off provision.

The House’s State Affairs and Good Governance Committee passed and advanced that bill in May 2025, with a two-year cooling-off provision in its report, under which civil servants or other government employees who resigned or retired could not take a constitutional or government post until two years had passed.

Although the House of Representatives passed the bill on June 29, 2025, a dispute arose over the cooling-off provision. A question was raised that the two-year provision set by the parliamentary committee did not align with another subsection of the bill, prompting the House to form a special inquiry committee to study the matter.

Based on that committee’s recommendations, the National Assembly’s Legislation Management Committee corrected the discrepancy found in the House version and advanced the bill with the two-year cooling-off provision retained. Under the version passed by the National Assembly, chief secretary, secretary and joint secretary-level employees would have been barred from constitutional, diplomatic and government appointments for two years after retirement or resignation.

However, that bill did not become law. Although the House of Representatives had passed it and the National Assembly had returned it with amendments, the House had yet to decide on those amendments. In this situation, the House of Representatives was dissolved on September 12. 2025, rendering the bill inactive, and with it, the earlier effort to apply a post-service cooling-off period for civil servants also failed to become law.

The government has now again included a two-year cooling-off provision for employees seeking other appointments after their job in the Federal Civil Service bill.

title.rendered: Who is Indian pilot Smit Machchhar at the centre of Flydubai cockpit incident?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Indian pilot Captain Smith Machchhar has come into the international spotlight following an extraordinary incident aboard Flydubai flight FZ-1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday.

The Boeing 737 MAX 8 was carrying 174 people when a serious confrontation broke out between the two pilots in the cockpit during the flight. The aircraft subsequently lost around 14,000 feet in altitude before making an emergency landing at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

Flydubai said all passengers and crew members on board were safe.

At the centre of the incident was Machchhar, an Indian captain whose actions after he was attacked have drawn international attention.

Who is Smit Machchhar?

According to The Times of India, Machchhar is from Ghatkopar in Mumbai, Maharashtra.

He is an experienced commercial pilot who has spent years flying professionally, based in Mumbai. Public professional profiles and reports in Indian media indicate that he has extensive experience in commercial aviation.

Machchhar began his professional flying career with SpiceJet, joining the airline in 2011. He worked there for around 11 years and rose to the position of senior captain.

From November 2020, he also served as a line training captain. In that role, pilots are responsible for training other pilots, assessing their flying skills and ensuring that required standards are followed during commercial operations.

In June 2022, Machchhar joined Flydubai as a direct-entry captain. This meant he joined the airline as a captain based on his previous command experience rather than starting as a new pilot.

His public LinkedIn profile lists around 9,750 hours of flying experience on Boeing 737-800 and 737 MAX aircraft. Publicly available details also indicate that he had logged more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command while at SpiceJet.

What happened on September 30?

Flydubai flight FZ-1073 was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. According to Reuters, there were 174 people on board.

During the flight, a serious confrontation took place in the cockpit between Captain Machchhar and his co-pilot. Initial reports indicate that the co-pilot attacked Smit Machchhar with a sharp weapon.

During the incident, the aircraft rapidly lost altitude. Reuters reported that the plane descended by around 14,000 feet. The aircraft later transmitted an emergency signal.

However, the exact sequence of events, the motive for the attack and everything that happened inside the cockpit remain under investigation.

Flydubai has also said that no conclusions should be drawn yet about the cause or motive of the incident.

Machchhar opened the cockpit door despite being injured

One of the most notable aspects of the incident was Machhar’s actions after he was seriously injured.

According to reports, Smit Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door despite being wounded in the attack. Passengers and crew members were then able to enter the cockpit and help restrain the attacker.

Other Flydubai pilots who were on board subsequently took over responsibility for the cockpit.

The aircraft was then diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia and landed safely before reaching its destination in Tel Aviv.

International media reports have highlighted Machchhar’s actions and his response under the circumstances. However, reports also indicate that the safe landing involved the efforts of passengers, crew members and other pilots on board.

What is Machchhar’s condition?

After the emergency landing, Smit Machchhar was taken to a hospital in Tabuk.

Recent reports said he underwent surgery and remains in stable condition. Flydubai and Indian officials are reported to be in contact with his family.

The co-pilot involved in the incident was also arrested, according to reports, and authorities are investigating the case.

Various reports have identified the co-pilot as an Omani national. However, the full details of the incident and its motive remain subject to the outcome of the official investigation.

Modi, Trump and Netanyahu praise Machchhar

Following the incident, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised Smit Machchhar.

Trump praised the Indian pilot who was attacked during the incident and called Machchhar a “hero.”

Netanyahu also praised Machchhar for opening the cockpit door despite suffering serious injuries, allowing passengers and crew members an opportunity to intervene.

Indian media reports said Modi also called Smit Machchhar a “hero” and praised the courage he displayed during the crisis.

title.rendered: Fertiliser subsidy to cost Rs 59 billion, says ministry secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment has said it is committed to preventing a chemical fertiliser shortage in the coming season, but that budget management poses a major challenge.

Ministry Secretary Dr Rajendra Prasad Mishra said the burden of the current subsidy is difficult for the state to bear, and that a new approach to managing it is being sought.

Briefing the Federal Parliament’s Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee on Thursday, Secretary Mishra said that at current market prices, a subsidy of up to Rs 120 per kg is needed. Around Rs 59 billion is estimated to be required to meet this, and raising such a large sum is proving challenging for the government even as it coordinates with the Ministry of Finance.

He said a plan for smooth fertiliser supply, to take effect after mid-February to mid-March, is being advanced. Since demand peaks during the main season from Baishakh through mid-April to mid-August, preparations are being made accordingly.

“We’ve prepared to ensure timely purchase and supply so there’s no fertiliser shortage after February. But the subsidy burden has grown because of rising fertiliser prices,” Mishra told the committee.

He added, “At current prices, DAP alone requires a subsidy of about Rs 120 per kg. Since the estimated requirement for the coming period is around Rs 59 billion, managing this has become challenging. Discussions are under way with the Ministry of Finance on this.”

He said that although the government has been providing farmers large sums in fertiliser subsidies, the benefit has not reached all farmers effectively, and the supply and distribution system needs to be made more orderly so farmers see the real benefit.

Farmers have complained that, due to flaws in the distribution system, genuine farmers have not received fertiliser even as the government spends large sums meant to help them.

Mishra said the ministry is making maximum effort for farmers’ benefit despite the budget shortfall, and that the distribution system needs to be made more transparent and orderly. He said discussions are also under way on increasing private-sector participation, incentivising producer companies, and developing new supply and distribution methods.

title.rendered: Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary denies personal ties to people heard in controversial audio

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Agriculture, Forest and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary has clarified her position over a controversial audio recording that has been circulating on social media.

Chaudhary said she had no personal or family relationship with either of the two people heard speaking in the audio clip. She also said she was prepared to face any evidence presented against her.

The audio, which was recently made public on social media, features two people discussing financial transactions while mentioning the names of Agriculture Minister Chaudhary, Home Minister Sudan Gurung and Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Thakursingh Tharu, among others.

One of the people speaking in the audio is heard referring to Minister Chaudhary as his “maternal uncle’s daughter.”

Members of the Federal Parliament’s Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee had sought an explanation from Minister Chaudhary over the audio during the committee meeting on Thursday.

Responding to the questions, Chaudhary said, “I do not know the people speaking in the audio. I have no personal or family relationship with them.”

She said the matter had already entered a legal process and that an investigation was underway, making it inappropriate for her to comment further.

Chaudhary said she had been fighting for good governance for a long time and had also contributed to the Gen Z movement. She urged people to raise questions based on evidence rather than making unnecessary comments.

“We have come for good governance. Rather than making comments, if there is evidence, I am ready to face it,” she said.

She also urged journalists to verify the facts and understand the truth before publishing or making the issue public.

title.rendered: Lawmakers question Agriculture Ministry over fertiliser shortage and distribution system

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Lawmakers have drawn the attention of the agriculture minister and secretary to the shortage of chemical fertilisers, irregularities in the distribution system and a controversial audio recording linked to the ministry.

Expressing dissatisfaction with the ministry’s performance over the past six months, lawmakers sought answers over the apparent contradiction between farmers struggling to obtain fertilisers and ministry data showing that supplies are sufficient.

Lawmaker Khagendra Karna pointed to delays in the ministry’s work despite what he described as increased ministerial activity. He said farmers were being affected by delays in the tendering process and leakages in the distribution system.

He urged the ministry to ensure a transparent fertiliser distribution system in the coming fiscal year.

Lawmaker Gyanendra Singh Mehta sought written responses on the problems faced by farmers in districts including Sudurpaschim and the difficulties in marketing agricultural produce.

He raised 13 questions covering issues including how to attract young people to agriculture, the impact of climate change on the agricultural sector and the failure to bring technologies developed by the Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC) to farmers’ fields.

Lawmakers Poonam Agrawal and Laxmi Prasad Pokharel sought clarification from the committee over the audio recording linked to the Agriculture Ministry that recently went viral on social media.

They also questioned the appointment of NARC’s executive director, asking the minister why there was a need to reappoint a person who had become controversial.

Lawmaker Suresh Kumar Chaudhary expressed concern that the agricultural sector was shrinking due to the lack of a clear land-use policy and irrigation framework.

Although the government has decided to prioritise organic fertilisers, he said the ministry had shown little commitment to implementing the decision. He stressed the need to reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers.

At the meeting, lawmaker Sagar Dhakal stressed that the committee should focus on policy-level issues and urged members to concentrate on long-term agricultural reforms rather than becoming preoccupied with minor matters.

title.rendered: US judge blocks Trump’s $100,000 H-1B visa fee

content.rendered:
Washington, October 1

A US federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers.

US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland, California, ruled on Wednesday that US Citizenship and Immigration Services and the State Department had failed to follow the required rulemaking procedures before implementing the fee.

Gilliam, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama, granted a request by a coalition of unions, employers and nonprofit organisations to prevent the government agencies from enforcing the fee until a final ruling is issued in a lawsuit filed in October.

The ruling is the latest in a series of legal challenges to the fee.

In June, a federal judge in Boston temporarily blocked the fee in a separate lawsuit filed by 20 states. The Boston-based appeals court declined to overturn that decision in July.

In August, the Department of Homeland Security began the process of imposing a permanent fee of about $103,000. That fee could also face a legal challenge once the rule is finalised.

However, that case would involve different legal issues from the lawsuits challenging Trump’s fee. The current cases are focused on the president’s authority to impose such a fee unilaterally.

The $100,000 fee was initially set to expire on September 21, but Trump recently extended it for another year.

The White House did not immediately comment on Wednesday’s ruling.

Democracy Forward, a left-leaning legal organisation representing the plaintiffs, welcomed the decision in a statement.

“Today’s decision … protected a system that had been thrown into chaos overnight,” said Steve Bressler, an attorney with the organisation.

The US Chamber of Commerce, the country’s largest business lobbying group, has also filed a third lawsuit challenging the fee. The chamber is appealing a judge’s decision that rejected its claim that Trump lacked the authority to impose the fee.

What is the H-1B visa programme?

The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers trained in specialised fields. Technology companies, in particular, rely heavily on workers who obtain H-1B visas.

The programme provides for 65,000 visas annually, along with an additional 20,000 visas for workers with advanced degrees. Visas are generally granted for periods ranging from three to six years.

Trump’s order significantly increased the cost of obtaining an H-1B visa. Previously, fees generally ranged from around $2,000 to $5,000, depending on various factors.

In imposing the fee, Trump invoked presidential authority under federal immigration law to restrict the entry of certain foreign nationals whose admission he said could harm US interests.

He has also claimed that businesses have abused the H-1B programme by replacing American workers with cheaper foreign labour.

The Trump administration has additionally ordered tighter screening of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would give preference to highly skilled and higher-paid workers.

title.rendered: Red Bull named title sponsor for NPL broadcast on Himalaya Sports TV

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Red Bull has been named the title sponsor for the live broadcast of the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) on Himalaya Sports Television.

Himalaya Sports announced Red Bull as the title sponsor at an event held on Wednesday.

Bajaj Pulsar, Prostyle, Nepal Life Insurance, Proton, Asian Paints, Soyum and Himstar have joined the NPL broadcast as sponsors.

Bajaj Pulsar is the association partner, while Prostyle, Nepal Life Insurance and Proton are the “Powered By” partners. Asian Paints, Soyum and Himstar have joined as co-sponsors.

Speaking at the broadcast sponsorship signing ceremony, Himalaya Television Network Chair Dharma Raj Bhusal said the partnership would provide brands with a platform to connect with consumers.

“We are not simply selling advertising slots through a sporting event. We have created meaningful partnerships that allow brands to reach consumers through a platform,” he said.

Bhusal described the NPL broadcast as both a challenging responsibility and an opportunity.

“Investment in the sports sector is not an investment made on an ad hoc basis. We have taken it as a strategic part of our long-term business plan,” he said.

Surendra Silwal, managing director of Sarash Beverages Pvt Ltd, which represents Red Bull Nepal, said the company was excited to join Himalaya Television as the title sponsor for the broadcast.

He said Red Bull had supported the NPL since its inception.

“Sports and energy are Red Bull’s core principles. A major share of our investment in sports goes into cricket,” he said. “Red Bull began this partnership with the NPL from its very beginning with a long-term commitment.”

Nepal Cricket Association (CAN) Secretary Paras Khadka said Nepali sports and cricket were gradually becoming more professional and sophisticated.

“The love and support that the corporate sector has shown towards Nepali cricket in recent times has been encouraging. We expect that this support will not remain limited to cricket but will extend to sports as a whole,” he said.

Himalaya Sports had secured the broadcast rights for the third edition of the NPL after paying a record amount of nearly Rs 172.4 million, including taxes.

The investment is among the most significant made so far in the broadcasting of Nepali sports.

Himalaya Television Executive Director Shyam Kandel said the company had made the investment after assessing market conditions.

Suraj Giri, CEO and director of Himalaya Sports, said the broadcaster aimed to do more than simply show the matches and would work to bring fans closer to the players.

“Our job is not just to show the game. It is to bring the game closer, tell good stories and connect players with fans. We want Nepalis living abroad to feel, even for a few moments, that they are closer to home,” he said.

title.rendered: Kathmandu public vehicles may soon be required to carry fire extinguishers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office is preparing to make fire extinguishers mandatory in public passenger vehicles, alongside route permits, as part of efforts to make public transport safer and more passenger-friendly.

The traffic police office plans to strengthen regular inspections of public vehicles and tighten enforcement of requirements directly related to passenger safety.

In coordination with the relevant authorities, police will regularly inspect the condition of public vehicles, required documents, route permits and safety equipment.

Although public vehicles are required to obtain permits to operate on designated routes, police say they continue to receive complaints about vehicles operating without necessary documents or outside their authorised routes. Authorities are preparing to tighten enforcement of route permit requirements to address such practices.

Suresh Prasad Kafle, chief of the Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office and Senior Superintendent of Police, said preparations were underway to make fire extinguishers mandatory in all public passenger vehicles.

He said vehicles can catch fire at any time due to electrical or technical problems, fuel leaks and other causes, making it necessary to have equipment on board that can be used to control a fire at an early stage.

“The rule will be strictly implemented in all public vehicles,” Kafle said.

He said the fire extinguishers installed in public vehicles would have to be in working condition and suitable for use.

Traffic police spokesperson Naresh Raj Subedi said authorities would regularly monitor the condition of public vehicles, drivers’ competence, required documents, route permits and the condition and usability of fire extinguishers.

“Vehicles that fail to meet standards, including requirements for fire extinguishers, will be brought under action during inspections,” he said. “Passenger safety is our first priority. Meeting requirements including route permits is a mandatory condition for ensuring passenger safety.”

Subedi said effective implementation of safety standards was particularly important during festivals and other periods when passenger numbers and vehicle movement increase, raising the risk of accidents and other incidents.

The traffic police have urged public vehicle owners and operators to fully comply with existing laws and safety standards.

They have also urged operators not to be negligent on matters directly affecting passenger safety and to conduct regular inspections and maintenance of their vehicles.

title.rendered: Deuba vows to strengthen Nepali Congress through General Convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Former Nepali Congress president Sher Bahadur Deuba has pledged to resolve the differences within the party through the 15th General Convention and further strengthen the organisation.

Deuba made the commitment in a Facebook post on Thursday morning.

The Deuba faction is beginning ward-level conventions today as part of preparations for the party’s 15th General Convention.

In his message, Deuba appealed to party leaders and cadres to participate enthusiastically in the ward conventions beginning today.

He said the 15th General Convention is particularly important given the Nepali Congress’s nearly eight-decade history.

According to Deuba, the convention will be important for further strengthening the party’s contributions, sacrifices and struggles for a democratic republican system of governance, full press freedom and the rule of law.

He also urged party leaders and cadres to participate enthusiastically in the ward conventions being held across all 6,743 wards of the country and ensure that they are completed by following the required procedures.

The Deuba faction has informed the Election Commission that it plans to hold the 15th Central General Convention in Kathmandu from December 7 to 9.

title.rendered: Govt recommends ending current federal Parliament session on October 2

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

The government has recommended to President Ram Chandra Paudel that the ongoing session of the federal Parliament be prorogued on October 2.

The Cabinet meeting held on Tuesday decided to recommend ending the session on Ashwin 16, which falls on October 2, to the President.

Under the Constitution, the President summons and prorogues a session of the federal Parliament on the recommendation of the Cabinet.

The current session began on May 11. During the session, Parliament passed and endorsed the government’s policies and programmes, the annual budget and bills replacing ordinances.

It also passed and endorsed the Alternative Finance Mobilisation Bill and a bill to revive the previous provisions of the Nepal Special Service Act, 1985.

The Shaheed Dasharath Chand National Health Sciences University Bill was also authenticated during the session.

title.rendered: Nearly a dozen leaders vie for Nepali Congress general secretary post

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

Nearly a dozen Nepali Congress leaders are preparing to contest for the post of general secretary at the party’s 15th General Convention, scheduled to begin on October 4.

Current and former office-bearers, as well as current and former central committee members, have expressed interest in the post as district-level conventions continue to determine the delegates who will participate in the general convention.

Some potential candidates have already publicly announced their intentions, while others have informed their close associates about plans to contest.

The party’s incumbent general secretaries, Pradeep Paudel and Gururaj Ghimire, both want to retain the position.

Paudel said he plans to contest for general secretary again.

“We are trying to transform the Nepali Congress under the leadership of party president Gagan Thapa,” he told Onlinekhabar. “I will try to present myself again for the responsibility of general secretary.”

Ghimire has also begun preparing for another term.

“I have thought about retaining my current position. It is a natural aspiration as well,” he said. “If there is an election, I will contest for general secretary. If there is consensus, I will move forward after consultation.”

Ghimire said he wanted to serve another term, recalling that reforms to the party’s internal system, evaluation mechanism, electoral and decision-making processes, as well as efforts to increase public trust in the party, had been presented as key themes during the special general convention.

Paudel had contested for general secretary at the 14th General Convention but was defeated. Ghimire had contested for the post of Koshi Province party president at the same convention and also lost.

Several office-bearers enter the race

Congress spokesperson Devraj Chalise and joint general secretaries Uday Shumsher Rana, Prakash Rasaily ‘Snehi’ and Dr Dila Sangraula are also said to be interested in the general secretary post, according to leaders close to them.

All four have told Onlinekhabar that they are aspirants for the position. At the same time, they have indicated that their final candidacies will depend on consultations with party president Thapa.

Other leaders are also preparing for the contest.

Jeevan Pariyar, who was elected joint general secretary at the 14th General Convention, has expressed his intention to contest for general secretary. Nain Singh Mahar, Ramhari Khatiwada and Aangeltu Sherpa, who recently left former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba’s faction, are also seeking the position.

“I have already served two terms as a central committee member. I have also served as joint general secretary,” Pariyar said. “This time, I will compete for general secretary.”

Mahar has been travelling to different districts as part of his preparations for the general secretary race.

Khatiwada, who is currently in his home district of Okhaldhunga for the regional convention, has also confirmed his interest.

“The regional convention is currently underway and I am in the district,” he said. “I will have a claim to an office-bearer position. I am an aspirant for general secretary.”

Sherpa, a member of the Congress Working Committee, has already announced his candidacy.

“I will contest for general secretary at the upcoming 15th General Convention,” he told Onlinekhabar.

Amar Singh Pun, president of the party’s Lumbini Province chapter, has also announced that he will contest for the post. He was unanimously selected as a general convention delegate from Rolpa on Sunday.

“I will contest for general secretary,” Pun said. “After being selected as a general convention delegate, I have already come to Kathmandu from the district and further discussions are underway.”

Pun said he wanted to work in the party’s leadership and expressed confidence that party leaders and cadres would support him. He was among the leaders involved in preparations for the special general convention held last December.

Central committee member Madhu Acharya is another aspirant. Acharya, who is also deputy head of the party’s Policy Academy, played a leading role in the special general convention.

Why is the general secretary position important?

The general secretary plays a key role in the Nepali Congress, particularly in running the party organisation, implementing policies, coordinating party activities and overseeing its day-to-day political operations.

The party statute places the central party office under the general secretary.

The general secretary is responsible for overseeing and operating the central office and implementing decisions taken by the Central General Convention, Central General Committee, Central Working Committee, Central Executive Committee and other central committees.

The post also carries responsibility for strengthening the party’s organisational structure, keeping party bodies informed about organisational activities, and implementing and supervising party decisions and programmes.

The general secretary can also, under the direction of the party president, deploy representatives or form committees and subcommittees for party-related work.

The position is responsible for presenting reports and proposals to the Central Working Committee, Central General Committee and General Convention, as well as maintaining the party’s official records.

The party statute also gives the general secretary authority to grant party membership, including active membership, in cases where an eligible individual needs to be enrolled immediately.

Could the number of general secretaries increase?

Under the Nepali Congress statute, two general secretaries are elected by the General Convention.

However, party leaders say discussions are underway about increasing the number of office-bearers, including general secretaries.

Some leaders believe the party could add another general secretary position to accommodate leaders who have recently left former president Sher Bahadur Deuba’s faction and joined the mainstream party leadership ahead of the convention.

Vice-president Bhusali confirmed that the issue of increasing the number of office-bearers is under discussion.

“There is discussion about whether to increase the number of office-bearers,” she said. “No meeting has been held yet.”

General Secretary Ghimire said a committee has been formed to draft amendments to the party statute.

“A draft amendment has been prepared regarding increasing the number of office-bearers,” he said. “We are still discussing it.”

Spokesperson Chalise also confirmed that the issue remains under discussion.

“This issue is still being discussed. Nothing has been finalised,” he said.

title.rendered: Displaced Syabrubesi residents seek a way home after Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, October 1

It has been more than a month since Singi Dhindup Tamang, 58, of Syabrubesi in Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-5, Rasuwa, arrived at Yellow Gumba in Swayambhu, Kathmandu.

Tamang was among those displaced by the Bhotekoshi floods and brought to Kathmandu for shelter. Living alone in the monastery, he says memories of Syabrubesi keep returning.

“When I walk around alone, I realise that I am in the monastery; my house was swept away by the flood and my property is gone,” he said.

The monastery has provided them with food and a place to stay. But for Tamang and others displaced from Syabrubesi, the memories of their homes, relatives and neighbours lost in the disaster remain.

According to Tamang, around 300 displaced people from 137 families of Syabrubesi are currently staying at the monastery.

“We are 137 households who have been completely displaced,” he said. “One hundred and twenty-six people have died. Five hundred and twenty of us are alive.”

The survivors were rescued by the government and taken through Dhunche to Batar in Nuwakot. They were later brought to the monastery in Kathmandu with support from Rasuwa Samaj.

Almost every surviving family has lost someone in the floods. Tamang, who narrowly survived, lost his daughter-in-law.

“There is no one here who has not lost a relative,” he said.

They have nowhere to return to

Along with their relatives, the people of Syabrubesi lost their homes and their settlement.

“When we ran uphill and looked back, there was nothing left of the market or the village. The flood wiped out three villages,” Tamang said. “The areas where the rural municipality and police post stood have been turned into a riverbed. We could not take any money or even our mobile phones from our homes.”

The monastery has given them shelter, but they do not know how long they can remain there.

The monastery initially provided beds and bedding. The displaced people slept on the floor at first, before bringing in essential belongings. Others also provided items such as fans.

“We are comfortable here for now. But there is no certainty about how many days we can stay. We may stay for a month, or we may have to stay for two months,” Tamang said.

Returning to Syabrubesi, however, is also not an option yet. There is nowhere to live, the roads are not accessible and they have no food supplies.

“If we were to farm and live off it, it would take six months before we could produce anything. We have been businesspeople from the beginning,” he said. “What would we eat if we went back? Where would we live? We have nothing.”

They want to return to Syabrubesi

The displaced residents are waiting for temporary accommodation, even if it is only a basic shelter.

“The state could build us temporary huts in Syabrubesi and let us live there. Later, it could build a permanent house with up to four rooms for each family,” Tamang said. “We can earn and add to it ourselves later. Large families need houses of up to four rooms.”

They say they have no land elsewhere and therefore want to return to their ancestral home.

“We are thinking of going back there. Where would we go and live elsewhere? We are people from that place. We have our faith, our geography, our culture and all our relatives there,” Tamang said. “In Kathmandu, an organisation may support us for a few days, but we do not know what will happen after that.”

Tamang says they are willing to repay money provided by the state if it is given to them without interest.

“If the government makes arrangements for us to return the money after earning it ourselves, we are willing to run businesses and support ourselves,” he said.

Collective funeral rites, but no money to pay for them

With little hope of finding those swept away by the floods alive, the displaced residents have begun conducting collective Ghewa funeral rites according to Buddhist tradition.

The rites would normally be conducted separately for each deceased person. But because the survivors have lost their homes and are living together, they are conducting collective prayers and funeral ceremonies.

According to Pratima Lama, Buddhist rituals are performed every seven days, with a major Ghewa ceremony held on the 49th day.

“According to our Buddhist tradition, prayers have to be performed every seven days. A major Ghewa has to be held on the 49th day. Until the Ghewa is completed, we are not supposed to go anywhere or move to another place,” she said.

“But we cannot conduct them separately. We are conducting a collective ceremony for 76 people in one place. Other monasteries are also holding collective funeral rites, for around 10 people in some places and seven in others.”

The survivors, however, say they are struggling to pay for the ceremonies.

“Money is needed to conduct Ghewa. Money is needed to light the lamps. According to our religion, we have to provide food and make offerings to the lamas,” Tamang said. “Our gold is gone, our money is gone, our silver is gone, our diamonds are gone. Our houses are gone. Everything is gone. We only have our lives left. We are facing financial difficulties even to conduct the Ghewa.”

The government has issued cards stating that the displaced people will receive Rs 15,000 a month, but the survivors say they have not yet received the money.

“These days, you need money as soon as you step outside. So the government needs to identify and officially declare the dead as soon as possible and distribute relief,” Tamang said. “That is our only hope.”

Crowded holding centre takes a toll

Pratima Lama, 40, from Syabrubesi, is visually impaired. She says staying at the holding centre has begun to affect her mental wellbeing.

“We want to leave this place as soon as possible. Staying here for so long has already affected our mental state,” she said. “We are all living together here. We need separate accommodation. We have been here for a month and it has been painful.”

She said financial assistance from the government would allow them to find rooms and move out.

“If the government simply tells us to start managing on our own and provides us with financial support, we could find rooms and move elsewhere,” she said.

Kami Gyalpo Tamang, 65, described similar difficulties.

“I feel like we will fall sick if we keep staying here. There are too many people. It is noisy. We have not been able to sleep,” he said. “We are becoming unwell because we are not getting enough sleep. The government should quickly provide us with small plots of land somewhere and settle us.”

The displaced residents want to leave the holding centre after completing the Ghewa if temporary accommodation can be arranged.

For now, they have no choice but to live together.

“When four or five people sleep in the same place, it is difficult even to breathe. Some have fractured legs. Some have colds and coughs. Others are sick with different problems,” Kami Gyalpo said.

“We cannot stay here forever.”

Finding rented rooms in Kathmandu is also difficult.

“When we go looking for a room, they ask who we are. When we say we are disaster victims, they tell us there are no rooms available. Perhaps it is also because we have nothing,” Tamang said.

They say they feel as though they are living like refugees.

“Some people do not even have their documents. We are living like refugees. How long are we supposed to stay here?” asked Karsang Tamang.

Residents seek an integrated settlement

The displaced residents of Syabrubesi want the government to establish an integrated settlement for them.

“We want all the people from Syabrubesi to be provided with an integrated settlement in one place,” Pratima said.

They say living together is also important for preserving their religion, culture and traditions.

“We have an emotional and spiritual connection with the soil and land there. We want to be settled in a safe place higher up from the original settlement,” said Chhiring Tenzing Lama.

The floods also destroyed cultural heritage in the area, he said.

“Our monastery was swept away. There were inscriptions carved into stones. Things that represented the identity of the Tamang community have disappeared. They need to be restored,” he said.

Some households missing from official data

Some displaced residents at the holding centre have also complained that their households were left out of official data collection.

Karsang Tamang is among them. His house was also damaged, but he says his household was not included in the data.

“It appears that the data of around 30 to 40 households was missed. We have also lost relatives and suffered physical damage. The data should not leave anyone out,” he said.

Karsang works as a guide and was in Kerung, Tibet, on the 10th. Because he was delayed in returning, his name was left out of the household count.

He said he also lost around 100 to 150 fellow guides at the border.

“Guide friends from Rasuwa and Sindhupalchok are still out of contact,” he said. “I survived because I had already crossed the border.”
