title.rendered: Kathmandu Valley braces for Dashain exodus of up to 1 million passengers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Up to 1 million passengers are expected to leave Kathmandu Valley for their home districts during this year’s Dashain festival, according to a report submitted to the government by the House of Representatives’ Infrastructure Development Committee.

The committee submitted its report on public transport management for Dashain to Prime Minister Balen Shah and Minister for Physical Infrastructure and Transport Sunil Lamsal. A team led by committee chair Ashish Gajurel handed over the report.

The committee estimates that between 600,000 and 1 million people will travel outside the Kathmandu Valley during the festival. However, transport entrepreneurs believe the actual number could be higher.

According to the report, passenger movement will begin to surge around Ghatasthapana, with the biggest rush expected on Phulpati.

The committee estimates that between 45,000 and 68,000 passengers will leave Kathmandu on Ghatasthapana. The number could rise to as many as 113,000 on Phulpati, when more than 7,000 vehicles are expected to operate.

An estimated 13 to 20 per cent of Dashain-bound passengers are expected to leave the Valley on Phulpati. The figure is projected to fall to around 4 per cent on Dashami.

The projections are based on historical data from the traffic police. Committee chair Gajurel said the committee had studied previous years’ practices and prepared a detailed report to help agencies involved in managing the Dashain travel rush.

Large buses expected to carry nearly half of passengers

Large buses are expected to carry the largest share of Dashain passengers, accounting for around 47.8 per cent of travellers, according to a survey conducted at the Nagdhunga checkpoint.

Microbuses are expected to carry around 42.9 per cent of passengers, while minibuses are projected to carry 9.2 per cent.

Public transport leaving Kathmandu generally sees two major rush periods. The morning peak runs from 6am to 9am, with 7am to 8am being the busiest hour. The evening peak is between 6pm and 9pm, with the highest traffic recorded between 8pm and 9pm.

Pokhara route expected to see highest traffic

Among vehicles leaving the Valley through the Nagdhunga checkpoint during Dashain, those heading towards the Pokhara section are expected to account for the largest share.

Around 27 per cent of vehicles are expected to travel along the Muglin-Pokhara corridor, covering destinations including Kaski, Syangja, Baglung, Myagdi, Parbat, Gorkha, Lamjung and Tanahun.

The second-highest traffic volume is expected on the Butwal route towards western Nepal, including Dang, Banke, Surkhet, Kailali, Kanchanpur and the far-western districts.

The third-highest volume is expected on routes heading east via Narayangadh towards Birgunj, Janakpur, Dharan, Biratnagar and Jhapa.

The fourth-highest volume is expected on routes heading towards Muglin and districts including Dhading, Naubise, Malekhu, Trishuli and Nuwakot.

Vehicles travelling via Muglin and Butwal towards Nawalpur, Rupandehi, Kapilvastu, Palpa and Arghakhanchi are expected to account for another significant share.

The report estimates that around 55 percent of vehicles leaving through Nagdhunga eventually reach Narayangadh, from where they split towards eastern and western Nepal along the Mahendra Highway.

Up to 65,000 vehicles may be needed

The committee estimates that up to 65,000 vehicles may be required to transport passengers during the Dashain travel period.

Large buses are expected to remain the backbone of the system as they are projected to carry nearly half of all passengers.

According to transport entrepreneurs, around 150,000 vehicles are normally operated from the Kathmandu Valley.

Last year, an average of around 10,000 vehicles carried passengers out of the Valley each day from Shasthi to Navami. On Phulpati alone, 19,671 vehicles left the Valley.

Based on the availability of vehicles this year, the committee expects sufficient seats to be available to meet passenger demand.

Why do passengers still struggle to get tickets?

Despite the availability of a large number of vehicles, passengers often struggle to obtain tickets during Dashain.

The report attributes this partly to the fact that demand is not evenly distributed across different destinations, days or exit routes. Problems arise when vehicles cannot be deployed according to changing demand.

Poor road conditions also contribute to the problem. Vehicles may fail to reach their destinations on schedule, meaning they cannot return in time to carry another group of passengers.

The report also notes that complaints may arise when passengers are unable to get the particular seats they want.

Agencies prepare for Dashain travel rush

The parliamentary committee has itself become involved in efforts to improve Dashain travel management. It has launched an online portal to collect passengers’ experiences, complaints and suggestions.

The committee plans to use complaints received through the portal to issue directions to the relevant authorities.

The Department of Transport Management has already held an initial discussion on advance ticket booking, although a date for opening bookings has not yet been fixed.

The department has also instructed transport operators to facilitate ticket bookings primarily through online platforms.

Transport operators have been asked to provide identification cards to drivers and staff and prevent ticket sales through unauthorised locations, counters and individuals.

Authorities have also been instructed to ensure that passengers receive tickets and to monitor drunk driving. Long-distance services have been told to deploy two drivers and arrange vehicles according to passenger demand.

The Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office is preparing to mobilise more than 1,300 personnel during the festival period. Passenger assistance desks are planned at 10 locations across the Valley, while police will maintain regular checks at other major exit points.

The Department of Roads will keep emergency response and disaster rescue teams on standby. Fifty-three heavy machines will also be kept ready for emergency operations.

This year, transport management faces additional challenges following the Bhotekoshi floods, which swept away several vehicles and left some employees missing. The government also halted vehicle registration for an extended period following the disaster.

Committee calls for long-term reforms

The parliamentary committee has also recommended long-term measures to address the travel problems that recur during Dashain each year.

It has called for better collection and use of transport data, greater use of technology in public transportation, and the introduction of digital ticketing and digital challan systems.

The committee has also recommended developing a reliable system for providing travel information, increasing public awareness and providing adequate training to people directly involved in transport operations and service delivery.

It has further suggested establishing a Public Transport Authority to address the structural problems facing the sector.

title.rendered: Three more bodies recovered from avalanche on Himlung Himal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

The bodies of three more people who went missing after an avalanche on Himlung Himal in Narpa Bhumi Rural Municipality-5, Manang, have been recovered.

According to Manang Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal, the bodies of Aash Gurung of Kerauja in Dharche Rural Municipality-2, Gorkha, Suraj Rai of Aiselukharka Rural Municipality-3, Khotang, and Kalam Budha of Hukam, Rukum, were recovered on Wednesday.

All three were affiliated with a travel company called Himalayan Holidays, according to the Manang administration.

Four bodies had been recovered earlier. With the recovery of three more bodies on Wednesday, the total number of bodies recovered has reached seven, while nine people remain missing, Khanal said.

Among those still missing, seven are associated with Himalayan Holidays and two with Imagine Nepal.

The bodies of Birendra Gurung and Ghanshyam Rai were recovered on Monday, while the bodies of Chhebi Bhote and Pasang Bhote were recovered on Sunday.

Search and rescue teams have been deployed in the Himlung area to locate those still missing and recover the remaining bodies.

According to the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, a rescue team led by IFMGA mountain guides Pasang Kaji Sherpa and Bikram Karki is currently at Himlung.

title.rendered: Power cuts planned in Kathmandu as underground electricity system work begins

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Electricity supply will be disrupted in several parts of Kathmandu Valley between October 1 and 12 as the Nepal Electricity Authority carries out technical work to operate the underground electricity distribution system and prepare for winter power demand.

According to the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), areas under the Kuleshwor, Baneshwor, Jorpati and Kirtipur distribution centres will experience scheduled power cuts during the period.

Electricity supply will generally be cut from 10 am to 3 pm in the affected areas. The NEA said scheduled outages may be cancelled if weather conditions are unfavourable.

According to the authority, electricity will be cut in Satungal-Bauthali on October 1, Machhegaun-Dobhan Chowk and Khusi Chowk on October 2, Mulpani on October 3, Gurjudhara on October 4 and Mulpani again on October 6.

Similarly, power supply will be disrupted in Balambu on October 7, Koteshwor-Balkumari on October 8, Siphal on October 10, Satungal-Dhaulagiri residential area on October 11 and Dhobikhola on October 12.

The NEA is carrying out the work as part of its plan to make Kathmandu Valley’s electricity distribution system underground, strengthened and automated.

The first phase of the project began in areas under the Ratnapark and Maharajgunj distribution centres in Kathmandu. The second phase covers other urban areas of Kathmandu, while the third phase will cover urban areas of Lalitpur and Bhaktapur. The fourth phase is planned for Pokhara and Bharatpur metropolitan cities.

Under the project, 33 kV, 11 kV and 400-volt electricity lines will be placed underground, along with optical fibre cables.

The NEA expects the underground system to improve the reliability and safety of electricity supply and gradually help automate the distribution network.

The system is also expected to reduce problems caused by the haphazardly placed electricity, telephone and internet cables in urban areas, while improving the visual appearance of Kathmandu Valley and supporting a more modern and organised electricity distribution system.

title.rendered: Woman killed while resisting midnight robbery in Parsa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

A 62-year-old woman was killed in Parsa while resisting a group of robbers who broke into her house at around 2:30 am, police said.

Lakharjiya Devi of Dhobini Rural Municipality-5 was found dead in a room on the second floor of her two-storey house at around 8am on September 21. Police initially suspected murder based on the condition of her body and launched an investigation.

The District Police Office, Parsa, has arrested three 18-year-old men in connection with the robbery and murder. They have been identified as Chandan Kumar Patel, Raj Kapoor Baitha, also known as Ghalathariya, and Ramu Paswan, all from Dhobini-5.

According to police, the suspects entered the house through a window after climbing over the rear wall. They broke open a steel cupboard and stole cash and jewellery. Lakharjiya became aware of the theft while the suspects were breaking open a tin box in another room.

Police said she went upstairs and resisted the robbers, who attacked her, resulting in her death.

Police have recovered two gold bangles, Rs 760 in cash, a knife, pliers and a vehicle spring leaf. The suspects had allegedly divided the stolen cash and jewellery among themselves.

Police have obtained a seven-day remand to investigate the suspects on murder charges.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

A lot can happen in a day, and keeping track of it all can be difficult. From major developments in Nepal to stories shaping conversations around the world, the Daily Digest brings together the key news and developments you may have missed.

Today’s roundup covers the government’s response to the Bhotekoshi disaster, developments in Parliament and the judiciary, climate and energy concerns, a major global wealth report, and a food safety alert involving a popular noodle brand. Here are the stories making headlines today.

Parliamentary climate committee begins work under Ganesh Parajuli

Ganesh Parajuli has been unanimously elected chair of the parliamentary special committee formed to study the impact of climate change in the Himalayas, climate justice and the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster. Parajuli was elected during a meeting on Wednesday and has since assumed responsibility for the committee.

PM Shah holds two-hour discussion with MPs from engineering backgrounds

Prime Minister Balendra Shah held a two-hour discussion with lawmakers from engineering backgrounds. On Wednesday afternoon, Shah discussed issues raised in Parliament with them and reviewed them.

Bhotekoshi flood: 1,454 bodies recovered, 4,718 still missing

A total of 1,454 bodies of people reported missing in the August 26’s Bhotekoshi flood have been recovered as of Tuesday, according to the Nepal Police. According to data released by the Police Headquarters, 236 bodies were recovered in Rasuwa district, 24 in Nuwakot, 72 in Dhading, 369 in Chitwan, 79 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 232 in Nawalparasi East and 222 in Nawalparasi West.

Half of global wealth held by 1.5% of richest, concentrated in US and China

Although personal wealth continues to rise worldwide, the gap between the rich and poor is widening. According to the Global Wealth Report 2026 published by Swiss bank UBS, nearly half (48.4 per cent) of the world’s total personal wealth is concentrated in the hands of just 1.5 per cent of the wealthiest people.

Government works to manage winter electricity in Kathmandu

The devastating Bhotekoshi River flood damaged various hydropower projects, taking 430 megawatts of electricity off the national transmission system. The government has since moved to arrange alternative management, officials at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said.

Supreme Court seeks reasons for arrest of Durga Prasai

The Supreme Court has ordered the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau to explain the reasons for the arrest of activist Durga Prasai. A bench of Justice Hari Phuyal issued a show-cause order directing the Cyber Bureau to submit the reasons for Prasai’s arrest within 48 hours. Prasai was most recently arrested on September 28.

Rara noodles found below quality standards, department orders recall

Rara, a popular instant noodle brand sold in Nepal, has been found to be below the required quality standards, according to the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control. The department has directed the company producing the noodles to recall the products already distributed in the market and completely stop their further sale and distribution.

title.rendered: Government seeks reconstruction model for flood-damaged hydropower projects

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

The devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26 caused extensive damage to hydropower projects in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

A month later, floods and landslides triggered by incessant rainfall since September 25 also affected hydropower projects under construction and in operation in districts including Kaski, Myagdi, Baglung and Tanahun.

According to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, the August 26 flood alone damaged 14 hydropower projects with a combined capacity of around 783 MW.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said electricity generated by projects with a combined capacity of around 190 MW has been disconnected from the national grid due to the recent floods and landslides.

Along with collecting detailed data on the damage caused by the floods, the government has begun preparations to develop financial and regulatory models for the reconstruction and resumption of affected projects.

Energy Ministry spokesperson Mohan Dev Shakya said detailed damage data is being collected through the Post Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), led by the National Planning Commission.

He said the assessment covers various subsectors of the energy sector, including electricity generation, irrigation and embankments.

“Work is currently being carried out in coordination in the energy sector. Teams from various subsectors have been mobilised in the field under the leadership of Dr Sudan Jha, the National Planning Commission member overseeing the energy sector,” he said. “Detailed data is currently being collected.”

According to the ministry, the teams deployed for the PDNA are expected to complete data collection within a few days. This will provide greater clarity on the actual damage caused by the floods, the resources required for reconstruction and the condition of the affected projects.

A rapid assessment conducted earlier had estimated damage to the energy sector at around Rs 134 billion. However, as that was only a preliminary assessment, more detailed figures will emerge after the PDNA, said ministry spokesperson Shakya. “A rapid assessment was conducted. The details will become clearer once the PDNA report is released,” he said.

Question of whether to rebuild projects

It is not certain that all projects will be rebuilt in their original form once the damage assessment is completed.

The floods have not only damaged project structures but also raised questions about the future financial viability of the projects. Therefore, technical, financial and climate-related risks will need to be addressed simultaneously during reconstruction.

According to Energy Ministry spokesperson Shakya, the PDNA will not provide the final assessment of the damage alone; additional project-specific studies will also be required.

“We are only at the initial stage of discussions on how to facilitate individual projects and what measures should be taken,” he said. “Which projects will be reconstructed and which will be shut down is also a matter for further discussion.”

He said project-specific technical studies would have to be conducted after the PDNA. Consultants and expert teams would need to be mobilised to ensure that damaged structures are redesigned so that they do not suffer similar damage in the event of another disaster.

“We should not rebuild them in the same way and allow them to be destroyed again if a similar flood occurs,” he said. “The technical improvements that need to be made will be considered afterwards.”

Higher reconstruction costs: Who will bear the burden?

Managing financial resources appears to be the biggest challenge in reconstructing damaged projects. According to Prajesh Bikram Thapa, executive director of Hydroelectricity Investment and Development Company Limited (HIDCL), the financial model for damaged projects is currently at the preliminary concept and exercise stage.

This is because the affected projects are not all of the same type. Projects owned by the Nepal Electricity Authority, its subsidiary companies, publicly listed companies, foreign-invested projects, private-sector projects and solar projects have all been affected.

“The financial framework is complex because all types of projects are involved,” Thapa said. “Technically, everyone’s costs have increased, and it is not clear whether they will be able to generate the same amount of power. Another question is whether the developers will rebuild them.”

Reconstructing damaged projects while taking climate and disaster risks into account will require stronger structures. This will also increase project costs.

According to Thapa, once additional costs are added, it may be difficult to reconstruct the projects under their existing financial models.

“We have to make them capable of withstanding disasters, and such a design inevitably adds to the cost,” he said. “Once that additional cost is added, the question arises of how the financial model will cover it.”

Therefore, the government may need to decide on various concessions and incentives for damaged projects.

Thapa said discussions could also be held on extending loan repayment periods, extending the generation period or providing other financial concessions.

“It is currently 35 years, while our Electricity Act has a provision allowing it to go up to 50 years,” he said. “There are many technical issues involved, such as how long it should be extended.”

However, the form and extent of government concessions have not yet been finalised. Energy entrepreneurs have also been demanding concessional loans and an extension of the generation period from 35 to 50 years, among other measures.

Reviewing old standards, introducing new ones

Following the floods, the Electricity Regulatory Commission has also begun work on developing a new regulatory framework to manage risks to hydropower projects.

According to commission chairperson Dr Ram Prasad Dhital, work is underway to develop a regulatory framework for “disaster-resilient energy infrastructure.”

The commission plans to address this in three phases: before, during and after a disaster.

Technical and safety standards that projects must meet before a disaster will be reviewed. Dhital said the commission would study whether the technical standards of the Department of Electricity Development, provisions of the Nepal Electricity Authority and regulatory conditions required during the commission’s approval process are adequate.

“We will evaluate the existing standards and see whether anything needs to be added or removed,” he said. “Before granting approval, we will certify whether those standards have been met.”

Safety measures to be adopted at projects and structures during disasters will also be included in the regulatory framework. The standards are also expected to cover issues such as sirens and information systems at tunnels and powerhouses, as well as coordination with relevant disaster management agencies.

However, the most important question in post-disaster reconstruction will be who bears the cost.

According to Dhital, the commission is studying the issue of not placing the entire burden of natural disasters solely on developers or consumers.

“The developer should not be made to bear the cost of a mistake it did not make, or the authority for a mistake it did not make, when the cause was natural,” he said.

The commission is also working on the concept of setting insurance premiums according to risk. It believes a risk-based insurance system should be developed under which projects facing higher risks would pay higher insurance premiums and those facing lower risks would pay lower premiums.

The study also covers how much insurance would cover of the total reconstruction cost, how much support would come from government relief or other funds, how much would be provided through concessional loans and how much of the eventual burden would be passed on to electricity tariffs.

“The costs have to be verified. If the cost is Rs 100, we need to examine how much insurance will pay, how much will come from the relief fund, how much will be provided through soft loans and how much impact there will be on consumers’ electricity tariffs,” Dhital said.

Efforts to develop a common framework from South Asian experience

Energy infrastructure in other South Asian countries is also facing disaster risks. Therefore, Nepal is preparing to incorporate the experiences of other countries into its regulatory framework, according to the commission.

As the Electricity Regulatory Commission is also a member of a group of South Asian regulators, efforts are underway to prepare a common technical and regulatory document incorporating experiences from countries including India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Bhutan, Dhital said.

“Disasters are not limited to Nepal. Similar situations exist in India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Bhutan,” he said. “We are trying to prepare a common document by incorporating the experiences of other countries as well.”

The commission is preparing to mobilise experts on the issue. Dhital said experts would be consulted on the regulatory role before, during and after disasters.

Scientific study and naming of Bhotekoshi flood

The Energy Ministry has formed a seven-member committee to conduct a scientific study and determine a name for the unusual flood that occurred in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

The committee, coordinated by water policy and governance expert Devesh Belbase, includes hydrologist Dr Narendra Man Shakya, glaciologist Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, remote sensing expert Dr Uttambabu Shrestha, geologist Dr Meghraj Dhital, hydropower infrastructure expert Dr Hari Pandit and disaster risk reduction expert Anil Pokharel.

According to Tika Baral, joint secretary at the Water and Energy Commission Secretariat, names including “glacier rock avalanche,” “ice-rock avalanche/landslide” and “Rasuwa Bhotekoshi Great Disaster” have emerged during preliminary discussions. However, he said the name of the event would not be finalised until the scientific study is completed.

“This is a rare event globally. We cannot conclude without a detailed study,” Baral said. “An appropriate name will be given after all scientific bases and evidence of the climate disaster have been collected.”

According to ministry spokesperson Shakya, preparations are also underway to facilitate the study by forming a technical committee within the government alongside the scientific committee. He said decisions would be made by the ministry, while implementation and coordination would be handled by the Water and Energy Commission Secretariat.

Challenge is to reduce risks, not just count losses

The recent floods and landslides, including the Bhotekoshi flood, have exposed both the risks facing hydropower infrastructure and the challenges of reconstruction. Although the government is currently collecting detailed damage data, an even bigger question will follow: how should the damaged projects be rebuilt, and how can they be protected from similar disasters in the future?

The government’s preliminary preparations indicate that reconstruction is being considered not simply as restoring damaged structures to their previous condition, but in connection with technical risks, insurance, financial resources, electricity tariffs and regulatory arrangements.

According to HIDCL Executive Director Thapa, the financial model can be finalised only after there is clarity on the actual damage and the future of individual projects.

“Once the exact loss figure is available, it may not be possible under the existing financial model,” he said. “The issue of what incentives the Nepal government should provide to make the projects financially viable will come afterwards.”

The reconstruction of flood-damaged hydropower projects is likely to be effective in the long term only if the government can integrate the PDNA, scientific studies, financial models and a new regulatory framework into a single process.

title.rendered: Controlling floods and landslides using Chepang knowledge

content.rendered:
Bharatpur, September 30

There was a time when residents of Chandisthan in Ichchhakamana Rural Municipality-7, Chitwan, would become fearful whenever they saw clouds gathering in the sky. Landslides, both small and large, were frequent.

Soil and rocks would wash downhill, forming gullies and exposing farms and settlements below to risk. Whenever clouds gathered in the sky, residents would routinely check the lake formed by water being blocked uphill.

The situation has now changed. The soil has stabilised, while grass and other vegetation have begun to grow.

Amrit Gurung, chairperson of Chandisthan Community Forest, says soil erosion has been reduced by around 95 per cent in an approximately 80-metre-long landslide-prone area where soil had continuously been washed away until three years ago.

Before discussing the measures taken to control the landslide, it is important to look at what happened in Chandisthan three decades ago.

A devastating flood in Ashwin 2054 BS caused extensive damage in Chandisthan. Water became blocked in the Ghade Khola area, forming a large lake and creating fear among settlements downstream. Locals remained awake throughout the night.

Had the lake burst at the time, nearby settlements, houses and agricultural land would almost certainly have been swept away. Tek Bahadur Chepang, then a ward member of Ichchhakamana-7, informed ward chairperson Bhaktaman Gurung about the situation. The matter was subsequently reported to the District Coordination Committee.

A team of around 300 soldiers from Bharatpur Barracks was deployed to safely drain the lake. However, the problem was not resolved.

After no solution was found, 194 households were relocated to a safer area. But relocation did not completely resolve the problem, as landslides continued. Various attempts to control the landslides failed.

The community then began looking for a long-term solution together with locals, according to Community Forest Chairperson Gurung. Instead of relying solely on external technology, discussions were held with the local community. Particular importance was given to the practical knowledge the Chepang community had developed over generations on landslides and soil conservation.

Discussions focused on which plants could hold the soil, how water flow could be reduced and how locally available bamboo, stones and other materials could be used. The work was then taken forward through consultations with engineers and technical experts, says Shiva Subedi, programme coordinator of the Nature-based Solutions Programme. He says landslide control was carried out using bio-engineering methods that combined local knowledge with modern technology.

According to Subedi, the team learned that the local Chepang community had been effective in controlling landslides. The possibility of using their knowledge and skills along with technology to control landslides was tested, and the trial proved successful.

The Chepang community, which lives in landslide-prone settlements, has long been working to prevent floods and landslides by using local resources and traditional knowledge.

Bhim Bahadur Chepang of Thulo Syangdi worked for two months on prevention efforts in the area. According to him, Chepang people have been levelling soil and working to control landslides since they were young.

“Because our houses are located in landslide-prone areas, landslides have always caused us problems,” Chepang said. “If plants survive, landslides can also be stopped, and it becomes easier to graze buffaloes and goats. That is why we plant broom grass, Datiwan and other plants.”

Chepang said locals use bamboo in areas affected by large landslides. He said bamboo and broom grass help hold the soil and prevent landslides from expanding.

“In a landslide-prone slope, we tie three bamboo poles together, cover them with soil from above, and let them sprout from below. After planting broom grass above them, it holds the soil,” he said.

Chepang said he had never received formal training in landslide-control techniques. Instead, different methods were developed through generations of experience dealing with landslides and flash floods.

“No one taught us. Landslides had occurred here before, and later there was a major landslide. When a landslide occurs, there is no place to graze goats. So we plant vegetation immediately,” Chepang said.

At the time, 36 Chepang people from Thulo Syangdi worked for around one and a half months to control the landslide. Landslides and flash floods are not new problems for them.

“We grew up dealing with landslides and flash floods. We have succeeded by doing what we know,” he said.

The Chepang community, which has long faced natural disasters, has been practising landslide control by using locally available resources and knowledge passed down through generations. Their practices demonstrate the role that traditional knowledge and local technology can play in disaster prevention.

What is bio-engineering?

One of the key approaches used in Chandisthan is bio-engineering. The method combines vegetation and natural materials with engineering structures to control soil erosion, landslides and rapid water flow, and it has proved effective.

Bamboo, grass, shrubs, plants and other locally available biological materials have been used to control landslides. Stones, gabions and other structures have also been built where necessary, according to Programme Coordinator Subedi.

The objective is not to stop water completely but to reduce its speed, prevent soil from being washed away and create an environment in which vegetation can grow, says Bishnu Acharya, chief of the Division Forest Office, Chitwan. As plant roots spread through the soil, they help hold it together, while landslide-affected areas gradually become green, he said.

Therefore, he said, bio-engineering structures can be understood not simply as physical structures but as a combination of nature and engineering.

Work has been carried out in different phases on a landslide-affected hill in Chandisthan measuring around 380 metres in length and 180 metres in width.

“Locally available bamboo and stones have been used to control the landslide,” said Community Forest Chairperson Gurung. “Bamboo crib walls have been constructed, along with stone pitching and walls. Gabion walls have also been installed at the bottom of the stream to prevent water flow from eroding and carrying away the ground.”

These structures have helped control water flow and reduce the speed of soil erosion. Grass and other vegetation have now begun to grow in the area. Soil has stabilised in places where soil and rocks previously washed downhill.

Locals have been able to see the impact of the landslide-control measures themselves.

“Previously, soil would wash downhill from the landslide during the monsoon,” said resident Maya Tamang. “The landslide had created gullies. Now the soil has stabilised, and plants have started growing in those areas. Perhaps there will be no more landslides.”

The experience of Chandisthan shows that disaster-related problems can be addressed by understanding nature, respecting local knowledge and working together with communities.

The Nepal women’s kabaddi team, which won a bronze medal at the 20th Asian Games held in Japan, has returned home.

The Nepali team arrived home via Thai Airways on Wednesday afternoon. It had been scheduled to return two days earlier, but its flight was disrupted by floods in Thailand, forcing the team to remain there.

Nepal defeated Thailand and Sri Lanka to reach the semifinals and secure the bronze medal. However, Nepal lost to India in the semifinals.

The Nepali women’s kabaddi team had also won a bronze medal at the 19th Asian Games.

title.rendered: Scrub typhus spreads to seven local units in Salyan, expert team to study outbreak

content.rendered:
Surkhet, September 30

An expert team is set to visit Salyan to study the rapid spread of scrub typhus in the district. Initially confined to Darma Rural Municipality, the infection has now spread to seven local units.

More than 2,400 people were tested during health camps organised by the District Health Office, with 472 testing positive for scrub typhus. As the infection has begun spreading as an outbreak in the district, a team including additional experts is preparing to visit Salyan, according to Chief District Officer Bandana Kumari KC.

Eight people have died from the infection in Darma Rural Municipality alone. The deceased include one woman, one child and six men. Health workers said most of those who died were elderly people or had underlying chronic illnesses.

KC said a research team from the Epidemiology and Disease Control Division in Teku is preparing to visit Salyan after the infection spread to several parts of the district.

“A team is being mobilised to conduct further study and analysis of the infection situation in different parts of the district, high-risk areas and the reasons behind the spread of the disease,” she said.

Infection spreads as fever cases rise

The infection has now spread to seven local units in Salyan: Darma, Kapurkot, Kumakh, Chhatreshwori, Kalimati, Bagchaur and Bangad Kupinde. As the number of patients with fever increased in these areas, health camps were organised at various locations, and rapid diagnostic kits were used to test for scrub typhus.

According to the District Health Office, Salyan, 116 people in Darma, 65 in Kumakh, 175 in Bagchaur, eight in Chhatreshwori, two in Kalimati, 53 in Kapurkot and seven in Bangad Kupinde have tested positive.

Similarly, 46 of the 785 people tested at Salyan District Hospital were found to have the infection.

Health workers urge caution as rural residents remain at risk

Health workers have been urging people to protect themselves from tick bites while working with grass, firewood and in agricultural activities by wearing full-body clothing, gloves and footwear that covers the legs up to the knees. They have also urged residents to keep bushes and vegetation around their homes cleared.

However, health workers say it is difficult for rural residents to take adequate precautions because their daily agricultural and livestock-related activities require frequent contact with forests, bushes and grass.

According to Pratibha BK, acting chief of the Health Service Office, Salyan, the infection is spreading because people fail to take necessary precautions while working in grassy and bushy areas. She said most patients recover with regular medication once the disease is diagnosed, but problems arise when people take medicines randomly without being diagnosed.

Risk of death when infection goes undiagnosed

According to Yagya Bahadur Basnet, chief of the health section of Darma Rural Municipality, deaths from the infection have stopped recently after health camps accelerated testing and treatment. However, due to a lack of health awareness, some patients with fever continue to take medicines purchased from medical shops without getting tested at health facilities.

“No one has died recently after attending the camps, being diagnosed with the disease using test kits and taking medication,” Basnet said. “Patients with mild symptoms are being treated within the local unit, while only those with complications are referred elsewhere.”

He said that as the infection has not yet been brought under complete control, health workers are visiting fever-affected settlements to test and treat suspected patients and raise health awareness.

Rural livelihoods increase exposure

According to Dr Jagat Kiran Oli of Salyan District Hospital, controlling the infection has become challenging because the daily lives of rural residents bring them into frequent contact with the mites that transmit scrub typhus.

“Rural residents depend on agriculture and livestock farming. Their daily activities involve grass and firewood,” Oli said. “As they need to go near forests two or three times a day, they sometimes fail to take precautions while working in haste.”

He said the risk of infection increases through tick bites while working in forests and bushy areas. Therefore, he said, people should keep bushes around their homes clear and wear full-body clothing, gloves and shoes while collecting grass and firewood.

title.rendered: Anupam Foodland operator Krishna Paudel arrested

content.rendered:

title.rendered: Congress convention: Fight breaks out in Morang-6, acting president injured

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

A clash has broken out during the regional convention of the Nepali Congress’s Morang constituency No. 6. The clash occurred over active-membership issues at the convention held in Sundarharaicha on Wednesday.

Wednesday’s agenda was to nominate candidates. But before the convention could even open, vandalism and violence broke out, and the convention fell apart.

Regional acting president Chuma Narayan Tabdar and leader Chet Raj Regmi, among other activists, were injured in the incident. They have been admitted to Nobel Medical College.

Deputy general secretary Dr Dila Sangraula was also assaulted. Earlier, the ward convention had not been held on time either due to the active-membership dispute.

Morang-6 is Dr Shekhar Koirala’s constituency. He is not participating in the Congress general convention. However, the Congress establishment faction claims that activists close to Koirala were behind the disruption of the convention.

Leader Dev Raj Tamang, close to Koirala, had earlier held the responsibility of regional president. After he failed to cooperate with the central leadership, the responsibility for holding the convention was given to former MP Tabdar.

Tamang was also present at the convention venue on Wednesday. He said dissatisfied members had caused the disruption even before the convention began, and said the claim that those responsible were close to him was false.

“There was an active-membership dispute here, and dissatisfied ward representatives created the dispute over that very issue,” he said. Asked about the claim that people close to him had carried out the attack, he said, “Those making that allegation need to prove it.”

Tension reportedly escalated at the convention venue over a dispute that arose during the distribution of active memberships and online form submissions at the ward level. According to eyewitnesses, the dispute escalated into an altercation and vandalism between leaders and activists.

Congress leader Ramesh Jung Rayamajhi said efforts are underway to calm the situation and resolve the dispute.

title.rendered: Parliamentary climate committee begins work under Ganesh Parajuli

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Ganesh Parajuli has been unanimously elected chair of the parliamentary special committee formed to study the impact of climate change in the Himalayas, climate justice and the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster.

Parajuli was elected during a meeting on Wednesday and has since assumed responsibility for the committee.

Thanking lawmakers and others involved for entrusting him with the responsibility, Parajuli pledged to make the committee’s work meaningful through cooperation, impartial study and results-oriented efforts.

He said the committee would seek to strengthen Nepal’s position on climate justice through scientific evidence, systematic research and practical recommendations.

“The committee’s efforts will focus on strengthening Nepal’s voice raised at the global level and our position on climate justice through scientific evidence, systematic study and implementable recommendations,” Parajuli said.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah recently addressed the 81st United Nations General Assembly, where he highlighted Nepal’s climate crisis, the vulnerability of the Himalayas and the need for international cooperation.

Parajuli said the committee would study the impact of climate change across the country, including the Himalayas, and work to strengthen Nepal’s case for climate justice while developing concrete measures to reduce future human and physical losses.

He also pledged to implement the committee’s mandate through a clear work plan, division of responsibilities and a timetable, with fact-based work completed within the stipulated period.

The House had formed the 15-member parliamentary special committee at its meeting on September 21.

The committee members are Achyutam Lamichhane, Anushka Shrestha, Gangadevi Shrestha, Ganesh Parajuli, Dhananjaya Regmi, Dhruvaraj Rai, Nisha Dangi, Pushparaj Kandel, Mohan Acharya, Mingmagyabu Sherpa, Ramesh Kumar Malla, Rabindra Patel, Saraswati Lama, Sujata Tamang and Sita Thapaliya.

The committee has been tasked with studying the impact of climate change in the Himalayas, including changes in Himalayan temperatures, snowfall, glaciers, glacial lakes and watersheds.

It will review available studies and data on emerging risks, identify gaps in research and monitoring, and recommend measures to strengthen scientific research and regular monitoring.

The committee will also study the causes and impacts of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster, including its origins, sequence of events, immediate causes and factors that intensified the risks. It will examine the possible links with climate change, the impact of transboundary river basins and the effects on downstream areas.

Its mandate also includes reviewing search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts following the disaster.

The committee will assess the status of missing citizens, relief distribution, temporary shelter, basic services and livelihood restoration, and recommend immediate and medium-term measures based on the needs of affected communities.

It has also been tasked with developing recommendations for sustainable and safer reconstruction, studying disaster risk reduction and early warning systems, exploring opportunities for climate diplomacy and cross-border cooperation, and recommending legal and institutional reforms.

title.rendered: Prakash Sharan Mahat says he expects justice in Nepali Congress dispute

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 30

Nepali Congress leader Dr Prakash Sharan Mahat has said he believes his faction will receive justice from the court in the ongoing dispute within the party.

Mahat, who is aligned with former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba, was speaking at an event in Pokhara about the dispute surrounding the Nepali Congress special general convention and its leadership.

He said his side had chosen judicial review after disagreements over the party’s 15th General Convention could not be resolved internally.

Mahat argued that an earlier court ruling had been flawed and that the Supreme Court’s decision to allow a review had strengthened their case.

“We have stood on the side of truth. Truth will certainly prevail,” Mahat said. “The court has already said that there was an error. We still believe that justice has not died in Nepal. We will get justice.”

Mahat said the Nepali Congress’s 15th General Convention should be held fairly and transparently, with respectful participation from all sides.

He said the failure to reach an agreement on these issues had led his side to seek judicial intervention.

Mahat also dismissed reports that former party president Deuba would attend the opening ceremony of the general convention scheduled to begin on October 4, saying there was no possibility of his participation.

title.rendered: Rara noodles found below quality standards, department orders recall

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Rara, a popular instant noodle brand sold in Nepal, has been found to be below the required quality standards, according to the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control.

The department has directed the company producing the noodles to recall the products already distributed in the market and completely stop their further sale and distribution.

The department collected samples of Rara noodles during routine market monitoring and inspection under the Food Hygiene and Quality Act 2081.

Laboratory tests conducted at the department’s official laboratory found that the sampled product did not meet the prescribed standards for food products and was therefore classified as substandard.

The product is the 60-gram Rara instant noodles manufactured by Himgiri Foods Pvt Ltd, based in the Pokhara Industrial Area of Kaski.

The affected product carries batch number REG 01 and has a production date of February 5, 2026.

Although the manufacturer has set a shelf life of 12 months from the date of production, the department said all packets from this particular batch must be removed from the market after the product was found to be substandard during testing.

The department has instructed that all food products bearing the affected batch number be immediately recalled and warned against selling or distributing them under any circumstances.

Consumers have also been advised not to purchase or consume Rara noodles bearing the specified production date and batch number in order to protect their health.

Both sides have signed the written agreement. The complaint filed with the bureau alleged the song demeans and insults the Brahmin community, and demanded it be taken down immediately.

Following the complaint, police called both sides in for discussion on Tuesday. Since Tuesday’s talks didn’t reach a conclusion, they were called in again on Wednesday.

Hindu activist Sagar Thapa, among others, had filed the complaint with the bureau. The activists objected to a specific line in the song referencing the eating of pork.

The song, released three weeks ago, has been viewed more than 6.5 million times on YouTube.

title.rendered: PM Shah holds two-hour discussion with MPs from engineering backgrounds

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Prime Minister Balendra Shah held a two-hour discussion with lawmakers from engineering backgrounds.

On Wednesday afternoon, Shah discussed issues raised in Parliament with them and reviewed them.

Seventeen MPs attended the discussion, held at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. Nepali Congress MP Mohan Acharya of Rasuwa was present, while the rest were RSP lawmakers.

The Prime Minister’s Office said MPs with engineering backgrounds were not invited from UML or the Nepali Communist Party, since those parties have no such lawmakers.

The discussion ran from noon to 2:15 pm. MPs first spoke about the situation following the floods and landslides, after which PM Shah addressed the group.

Shah went on to classify lawmakers into three categories based on how they express themselves: average, below average, and extraordinary, describing which type of MP tends to raise which kind of issue.

Shah described MPs with engineering backgrounds as “extraordinary.” One MP told Onlinekhabar that the Prime Minister said ordinary people talk about events, those below average tell him what to do, and since engineers are extraordinary, they should be raising ideas and creativity, adding that their ideas are what will build the country.

During the discussion, Shah asked the engineering-background MPs to contribute ideas on industrialisation. He said the concerned ministries, ministers, and the Prime Minister’s Office are following up on issues raised in Parliament, and assured the MPs they could contact the Prime Minister’s Office directly with any idea and would be given easy access to meet.

Shah also noted that new bills are forthcoming and said MPs’ input would be reflected in them, based on what they have seen and experienced, and asked for their support and cooperation.

RSP MP Dr Ram Lama confirmed the meeting with the Prime Minister, saying Shah discussed with engineering-background MPs and gathered their experience and ideas.

Lama said he told the Prime Minister that Nepal’s existing laws need reform for the country’s development, citing the need for a forest-related law and supportive legislation for major development projects, as well as programs that would increase electricity consumption. He said Shah responded that the government is conscious of this and committed to moving ahead accordingly. He further said that government policy is focused more on increasing power consumption than on selling electricity.

Shah also told the MPs the government is moving forward on opening a chemical fertiliser factory in Nepal. Lama quoted Shah as saying the government would soon call for proposals to open the factory, and that necessary facilities would be provided for such projects and programs, including the fertiliser factory and those aimed at increasing power consumption.

title.rendered: Two-way traffic resumes on Ghasa-Korala road after landslide clearance

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Two-way traffic has resumed on the Ghasa-Korala road after the Department of Roads cleared landslides blocking the route, paving the way for the reopening of the Korala border point with China.

The Korala border point had been closed following recent rains, floods and landslides that damaged roads and bridges in the Mustang area.

According to the Department of Roads, the Ghasa-Korala section has now been cleared and is ready for two-way traffic.

However, several sections between Mustang and Beni remain damaged after roads were washed away. The department is working to clear these sections by cutting into hillsides and constructing retaining walls where necessary.

The department said it expects to restore traffic along the affected sections by Thursday evening.

Work is also underway to repair road damage caused by erosion in the Tatopani area, with traffic expected to resume by Wednesday evening.

The approach roads to the Pokhare Bazaar bridge are expected to be completed by Thursday evening. Similarly, road damage near the Raghu Ghat Hydropower Project is being repaired through back-cutting and construction of retaining walls, with traffic expected to resume by Thursday evening.

The Department of Roads is also working along the Maldhunga-Beni-Kerabari section to open a track along the hillside and construct retaining walls to restore traffic.

The Korala crossing is currently the only one of Nepal’s three major border points with China where the road on the Nepali side is being restored after recent weather-related disruptions. Rasuwagadhi was damaged by floods in Bhadra, while Tatopani has been closed by the Chinese side.

title.rendered: Opposition lawmakers revive questions over PM Shah’s border remarks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Opposition lawmakers in the House of Representatives have once again raised questions over Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s remarks that Nepal had also encroached on Indian territory.

Several lawmakers stood before Wednesday’s House meeting had formally begun. Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal told them that the session had not yet started.

After the speaker formally opened the meeting, some lawmakers stood again. Aryal allowed one lawmaker to raise the issue.

Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Ambika Devi Sangraula demanded a response from the government over Shah’s controversial remarks on the Nepal-India border.

“From this respected rostrum on May 31, the respected prime minister made what we consider a treasonous statement that our country has also encroached on India’s border,” Sangraula said. “We have been demanding for a long time that this statement be corrected from this House.”

She also demanded that the statement be removed from the parliamentary record if the government does not provide clarification.

“As this demand has still not been addressed, when will this question and demand be addressed? When will we receive an answer? I would like to draw the government’s attention through the speaker,” she said.

Shah had responded to questions from lawmakers on May 31, including on the Nepal-India border dispute.

He told Parliament that Nepal had officially sent a diplomatic note to India regarding Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura and had received a response.

According to Shah, the two governments had discussed resolving the issue through talks involving historians, surveyors and people with knowledge of the respective territories.

He also said Nepal had discussed the issue with a third country.

“We have spoken not only with India and China but also with the British government,” Shah had said. “Our position is that since the issue dates back to the time British India left, Britain should also have an interest in it.”

He said the issues would be resolved through diplomatic discussions.

Shah’s response, including his reference to discussions with the British government, had drawn attention both inside and outside Parliament.

The issue was also raised by Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Aaren Rai, who asked when citizens would feel that the government was present on the border.

“The problems of Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura have continued for a long time, and there are problems along other parts of the border as well. When will ordinary citizens feel that there is a government at the border?” Rai asked.

In response, Shah repeated that the border issues would be resolved through diplomatic table talks.

It was during this response that Shah said he had learned after becoming prime minister that Nepal had also encroached on Indian territory.

“You may find one thing surprising. I also learned only after becoming prime minister that India has not only encroached on Nepali land, but Nepal has also encroached on Indian land at many places,” Shah said.

He said both countries should study the issue and resolve it through discussions as friends.

Shah’s statement that Nepal had also encroached on Indian territory was subsequently questioned in Parliament and outside it, with opposition parties raising the issue for an extended period.

The issue had recently received less attention from opposition lawmakers. On Wednesday, however, they revived it and demanded either clarification and evidence regarding the statement or its removal from the parliamentary record.

title.rendered: Ramesh Lekhak calls for swift reconstruction of historic suspension bridge over Mahakali

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Nepali Congress leader Ramesh Lekhak has expressed concern over the collapse of the suspension bridge over the Mahakali River connecting Dodhara Chandani and Bhimdatta Municipality in Kanchanpur and urged the government and concerned authorities to begin reconstruction work as soon as possible.

Expressing concern over the difficulties caused to the daily lives and transportation connectivity of people in Dodhara Chandani following the collapse, Lekhak stressed the need to repair and reconstruct the bridge.

He made the remarks in a Facebook post on Wednesday. Lekhak said the bridge was not only important to Kanchanpur but also a historic structure in the development of suspension bridges in Nepal.

“This bridge, which directly connected Dodhara Chandani with the rest of the country at a time when the area had no road connectivity with other parts of the country, and people faced extremely difficult living conditions, is historic not only for Dodhara Chandani or Kanchanpur but for the entire country,” he wrote.

Lekhak also recalled that after he was first elected to the House of Representatives from Kanchanpur in 1999, he raised the issue in Parliament of constructing a suspension bridge over the Mahakali River to connect Dodhara Chandani with the rest of the country.

He recalled that some people had mocked the proposal at the time, saying that constructing a suspension bridge over the Mahakali River was impossible.

However, he said work on the bridge moved forward during the same period, resulting in the construction of a historic long suspension bridge with funding from the Government of Nepal and the involvement of Nepali technicians and contractors.

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 30

Larkya La, popularly known as Larke Pass, has been completely blocked following heavy snowfall from Thursday to Saturday, disrupting movement between northern Gorkha and Manang.

The pass, located at an altitude of 5,106 metres along the border of northern Gorkha and Manang, has been covered by thick snow, affecting daily life in the region.

Nima Dorje Lama, a hotel operator from Samdo in Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1, said the closure has disrupted the transportation of essential supplies.

According to Lama, floods and landslides during the monsoon prevented daily necessities from being transported from markets in the lower areas. As a result, supplies began being transported to northern Gorkha from Bhimthang in Manang through Larkya La.

But the heavy snowfall has now erased the trail, making travel between the two areas impossible.

“Mules that went from here to collect supplies are stuck in Manang. Those that came from there are stranded here,” said Lama, a former ward member. “If the route remains closed for a few more days, a food shortage could develop in Samagaun and Samdo.”

The Manaslu trekking trail has also been obstructed at several points by floods and landslides. Bridges along the trail were swept away, preventing horses and mules from travelling through the area. Temporary wooden bridges have been built for local residents and tourists.

Because floods and landslides destroyed the bridges, horses and mules could not be used to transport goods from the lower parts of the district to Samagaun and Samdo during the monsoon. Residents have therefore been relying on Bhimthang in Manang for essential supplies.

Karma Chhewang Lama, chair of Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1, said movement to Manang had also come to a complete halt after snowfall blocked Larkya La.

“The Manaslu trail is already blocked, and Manang was the only route for transporting food to Samagaun and Samdo. Now that route has also been blocked by snow, creating further problems,” he said.

The closure of Larkya La has also affected trekking along the Manaslu-Larkya-Chum route, according to local resident Nima Lama.

“This is the tourist season. Hundreds of domestic and foreign tourists who came to cross Larkya La are now stranded in Samagaun and Samdo because the pass is blocked,” he said. “Tourists, tourism businesses, local hotel operators, guides and porters have all been affected.”

Lama said locals had written to the Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal, Manaslu Conservation Area Project, the rural municipality and the Chumnubri Hotel Entrepreneurs Association, requesting that Larkya La be reopened and made safe for travel.

Larkya La has been blocked by heavy snowfall in the past as well. Last year, local youths cleared the route, but Nima Dorje Lama of Samdo said that would not be possible this year.

“The snow is extremely thick this year. It is not possible for locals to clear it on their own,” he said.

title.rendered: RSP to launch local election campaign, visit all 753 local units from October 6

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) is set to launch a local election-focused campaign from October 6, with party leaders visiting every local unit across the country. The campaign will begin after the ongoing session of the Federal Parliament concludes. Teams comprising members of the House of Representatives and central party members will visit local units as part of the campaign.

According to RSP Co-General Secretary Nisha Dangi, the party intends not only to listen to citizens but also to communicate its own plans and views. “We are coming to your doorstep this time not only to listen to you but also to share and explain some of our views. All central members and lawmakers will be coming to your local unit,” she said in a video message.

Two objectives of the local-level campaign

According to Dangi, the campaign has two main objectives. First, the party will explain the functioning of local governments and its process for selecting candidates for the upcoming election. Second, it will inform citizens about the initiatives taken through Parliament and the government during the six months since the current government was formed.

As local governments are the institutions most closely connected to citizens’ daily lives and development, the party said it aims to explain the democratic process for selecting local leaders. Dangi said another key objective was to explain how the RSP plans to promote capable, honest and willing leaders for the local-level elections scheduled for February.

Under its previously announced candidate-selection framework, the RSP has said candidates will be selected through a Candidate Club, Leadership Academy and a fully democratic selection process.

Party to publicise government’s work

The RSP said the current government is nearing six months in office and that the campaign will provide detailed and transparent information on policy initiatives taken by Parliament and the government, the status of implementing promises made to citizens and the party’s plans for the coming days.

“Our lawmakers and central members will visit all 753 local units in 77 districts from October 6 as part of the campaign,” Dangi said. “This campaign is not merely preparation for the election. It is also an important democratic exercise to make local governments more accountable and establish the right leadership with citizens’ participation.”

title.rendered: Roads not an obstacle to reopening Tatopani border point, says official

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Narayan Datta Bhandari, chief of the Division Road Office in Charikot, has said the road on the Nepali side is not an obstacle to reopening the Tatopani border point with China.

He said there was currently no need to stop vehicle movement because of the condition of the road.

China has closed the Tatopani border point citing road conditions on the Nepali side. A joint team comprising representatives of the Chinese side, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Finance, customs officials, the Department of Roads, Sindhupalchok District Administration Office and security agencies inspected landslide-affected sections of the road.

During the inspection, Bhandari said vehicles could continue to operate on the road and that there was no condition requiring a complete halt to traffic.

He said any necessary improvements could be completed within one or two days, allowing the border point to resume operations.

According to Bhandari, vehicles had continued operating one-way on the Nepali side even during the monsoon. With the rains now easing, work has begun to improve the road for two-way traffic.

He said the Chinese side had stopped vehicle movement citing difficult road conditions on the Nepali side, but the actual situation was not as serious as claimed.

Bhandari said a joint inspection involving a Chinese technical team was carried out after concerns were raised that the condition of the Nepali road was the reason for the border closure.

He said the road would not obstruct vehicle movement once the border point reopened.

“From the road’s perspective, there is no situation where vehicles cannot pass. If some improvement is needed, we can complete it within one or two days. Until now, it was the monsoon season and we were operating one-way traffic. There is no problem with that even now. Once the rains have stopped, we can allow two-way traffic,” he said.

“We will clear everything within two or three days. We will make the necessary preparations to allow all types of vehicles to pass from here. Once the border is opened, vehicles will not have to wait even for an hour. They can pass directly. The road will not be an obstacle if the border is reopened,” he added.

Bhandari said 57 containers measuring 45 feet had already been allowed to pass from the Nepali side. He also said loaded vehicles that had been stranded along the road had been sent to their destinations.

Bhandari said the Department of Roads had made the Nepali side of the road ready for vehicle movement.

The Tatopani border point has remained closed since a landslide occurred along the Kodari Highway. The Kerung border point has also been closed following floods in Rasuwa on August 26, while the Korala border point in Mustang has been affected by recent floods and landslides.

With the major border points with China closed, the government has been making efforts to reopen the Tatopani border point.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi flood: 1,454 bodies recovered, 4,718 still missing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

A total of 1,454 bodies of people reported missing in the August 26’s Bhotekoshi flood have been recovered as of Tuesday, according to the Nepal Police. According to data released by the Police Headquarters, 236 bodies were recovered in Rasuwa district, 24 in Nuwakot, 72 in Dhading, 369 in Chitwan, 79 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 232 in Nawalparasi East and 222 in Nawalparasi West.

DIG and the central Spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle informed that 1,334 of the recovered bodies have so far been managed after completing necessary procedures, including the collection of DNA samples for identification. A total of 7,975 police personnel have been mobilised for post-disaster response efforts, including rescue and search operations, relief distribution and management of recovered bodies in the flood-affected areas.

Meanwhile, search operations are continuing for 4,718 people who remain missing, according to the Police Headquarters. It may be noted that the devastating Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa claimed scores of lives and caused extensive damage to property across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and other districts.

—RSS

title.rendered: ‘The Everest Dream’ wins Special Jury Award in Shimla

content.rendered:
Kathmandu

Nepali documentary film The Everest Dream has won the Special Jury Short Documentary Award at the 12th International Film Festival of Shimla in India.

Directed and produced by filmmaker and media professional Ganesh Pandey, the film won the award after competing with international documentaries from around the world.

At the award ceremony in Shimla, Himachal Pradesh Governor Kavinder Gupta and festival director Pushpraj Thakur presented the award to Pandey. The festival was held from September 25 to 27 at the historic Gaiety Heritage Complex in Shimla, featuring films from 33 countries.

The Everest Dream tells the story of a British citizen who faces various challenges in life after suffering a serious brain injury and embarks on an adventurous journey to Everest Base Camp. The documentary captures the team’s challenging training in Scotland and their journey to the Himalayas in Nepal.

The film focuses on the journey of a seven-member team led by James Lamb, including five brain injury survivors, to Everest Base Camp. It conveys an inspirational message that people can achieve their dreams despite physical and mental challenges.

According to director Pandey, the film’s central message is that “even after a serious injury or hardship in life, people can dream new dreams and achieve them.”

The Everest Dream had previously won the Best Documentary Film Award at the KAB International Film Festival in Georgia, USA. With the international award in Shimla, the Nepali documentary has further strengthened its presence at international film festivals.

title.rendered: Parliamentary special committee to hold first meeting

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

The parliamentary special committee formed to study climate change in the Himalayas and the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster is scheduled to hold its first meeting today.

The meeting will be held at Singha Durbar and will elect the committee chairperson.

Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Ganesh Parajuli has already filed the sole nomination for the chairperson. Lawmaker Mohan Acharya has proposed his candidacy, while Nisha Dangi, Pushparaj Kandel, Ramesh Kumar Malla, Dhruv Rai and Saraswati Lama have supported it.

The House of Representatives had formed the 15-member special committee at its meeting on September 21. As Parajuli is the only candidate, he is expected to be declared elected unopposed at today’s meeting.

The committee members are Achyutam Lamichhane, Anushka Shrestha, Gangadevi Shrestha, Ganesh Parajuli, Dhananjay Regmi, Dhruvraj Rai, Nisha Dangi, Pushparaj Kandel, Mohan Acharya, Mingmagyabu Sherpa, Ramesh Kumar Malla, Rabindra Patel, Saraswati Lama, Sujata Tamang and Sita Thapaliya.

The committee’s terms of reference include studying the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.

It will review available studies and data on changes in Himalayan temperatures, snowfall, glaciers, glacial lakes and watersheds and the risks arising from such changes. It will also identify gaps in research and monitoring and recommend measures to strengthen scientific research and regular monitoring.

The committee will study the causes and impacts of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster, including its origin, sequence of events, immediate causes and factors that intensified the risks, based on expert and scientific evidence. It will also review its possible links to climate change, the impacts on transboundary watersheds and the effects on downstream areas.

The committee will also review search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts.

It will assess search and rescue operations, the status of missing citizens, relief distribution, safe temporary shelter, basic services and livelihood restoration to ensure an appropriate response to the needs of disaster-affected people. It has also been authorised to recommend immediate and medium-term measures based on the needs of affected communities.

The committee has been tasked with proposing a roadmap for sustainable and safe reconstruction.

It will also study disaster risk reduction and early warning systems and make recommendations.

The committee will explore possibilities for climate diplomacy and cross-border cooperation and has been authorised to recommend legal and institutional reforms.

SP Sagar Bohara, chief of the District Police Office, said Bogati was found dead in the toilet.

The district hospital, however, said Bogati was found unconscious in the toilet and died while undergoing treatment.

Further investigation into the incident is underway.

title.rendered: Half of global wealth held by 1.5% of richest, concentrated in US and China

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Although personal wealth continues to rise worldwide, the gap between the rich and poor is widening. According to the Global Wealth Report 2026 published by Swiss bank UBS, nearly half (48.4 per cent) of the world’s total personal wealth is concentrated in the hands of just 1.5 per cent of the wealthiest people.

According to the report, 58 million adults with more than US$1 million in wealth control US$250.59 trillion in assets.

In contrast, 42.1 per cent of the world’s adult population, or around 1.62 billion people, have net wealth of less than US$10,000. They account for just 0.6 per cent of global wealth, or US$3.22 trillion.

This highlights the reality that a large proportion of people in least developed and developing countries such as Nepal remain at the bottom of the global wealth pyramid.

India has 944,000 dollar millionaires

UBS analysed 56 major markets that together account for more than 92 per cent of global wealth in this year’s report. Nepal is not included among these 56 markets.

India is the only South Asian country covered by the report and has 944,000 dollar millionaires. The total number of dollar millionaires across the 56 markets tracked by UBS is around 57.5 million.

Nearly one million new dollar millionaires were added worldwide in 2025 alone, meaning an average of around 2,680 people became dollar millionaires every day.

Wealth concentrated in two major powers

The report shows that global wealth is concentrated in a handful of major economies. Among the markets analysed, the United States and Greater China, which includes China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, together account for more than half of the world’s personal wealth.

The United States accounts for 35.7 per cent of total global wealth, while Greater China accounts for 18.5 per cent.

Western Europe accounts for another 21.9 per cent of global wealth. In terms of average wealth per adult, Switzerland ranks first globally at US$910,382, followed by the United States at US$696,277.

Emerging markets account for 26.2 per cent of global wealth, down from 28.8 per cent in 2022.

Wealth rises, but distribution remains highly unequal

According to UBS, total personal wealth in the markets covered by the study increased by 10.8 per cent in 2025. The increase in wealth also highlights significant differences between various wealth brackets.

According to the report’s wealth pyramid, 1.62 billion adults with less than US$10,000 in wealth hold a combined US$3.22 trillion. Another 1.58 billion adults with wealth between US$10,000 and US$100,000 hold US$63.16 trillion.

Some 588 million adults with wealth between US$100,000 and US$1 million hold US$200.72 trillion. At the top of the pyramid, 58 million adults hold US$250.59 trillion in wealth.

Financial assets and real estate

The composition of wealth varies significantly by country, particularly in terms of the share held in financial assets. According to UBS, financial assets account for 83.6 per cent of total personal wealth in Sweden, 80.8 per cent in Taiwan and around 79 per cent in the United States.

However, being a dollar millionaire does not mean having US$1 million in cash in a bank account. According to UBS, for typical dollar millionaires with wealth between US$1 million and US$5 million, their primary residence is often their largest asset.

As property values rise, an individual’s total wealth can increase and make them a dollar millionaire even if their income or cash holdings do not increase. However, that wealth becomes cash or an immediately usable asset only after the property is sold and the proceeds are realised.

UBS generally defines liquid assets as cash, bank deposits, voluntary pension savings, collective investment schemes and direct investments in financial instruments such as shares. Mandatory pension savings and real estate are not included as liquid assets.

The report shows that while global wealth continues to grow, there are significant disparities in both its distribution and composition.
