title.rendered: Ghising urges government to prioritise energy security, infrastructure reconstruction

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Ujyalo Nepal Party Chairperson Kulman Ghising has urged the government to expedite the restoration of electricity and road infrastructure damaged by floods and landslides.

Ghising made the call in a Facebook post on Tuesday.

He urged the government to prioritise the reconstruction of the power transmission system along the Trishuli and Kaligandaki corridors.

Ghising said the government should immediately introduce a clear action plan and provide necessary facilitation to maintain the confidence of domestic and foreign investors.

“This is not just a problem of one sector; it is a serious national challenge linked to the lives of citizens, national energy security and Nepal’s development journey. I draw the government’s attention to the need to take this issue seriously,” he wrote.

Saying that damage to transmission lines along the Trishuli and Kaligandaki corridors had put pressure on the overall electricity generation, transmission and supply system, Ghising said the government should give high priority to identifying and rebuilding transmission structures that can be restored immediately, as managing electricity demand could become challenging in the coming winter.

“During a crisis, we should not get caught up in minor issues. The country’s energy security, the lives of affected citizens and the restoration of damaged infrastructure must be given the highest priority,” he said.

title.rendered: Technical study begins into damage to suspension bridge linking Dodhara Chandani

content.rendered:
Kanchanpur, September 30

The government has begun a technical study into the damage to the suspension bridge over the Mahakali River connecting Dodhara Chandani and Bhimdatta Municipality in Kanchanpur.

The bridge has been completely closed to traffic after one of its spans and the central tower collapsed this morning.

Kanchanpur Chief District Officer Madan Koirala inspected the damaged bridge this morning and said a technical study would be carried out to determine how the bridge was damaged.

According to Koirala, security personnel were deployed, and movement across the bridge was immediately halted after authorities received information early this morning that the bridge had become “unbalanced.” At around 8 am, one section of the bridge collapsed into the river. The bridge is currently not usable.

“One span of the bridge and one of its central towers have collapsed. It is not possible to cross the bridge at present,” Chief District Officer Koirala said.

Koirala said a technical team from the Infrastructure Directorate under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development of Sudurpaschim Province has been called in to identify the technical cause of the damage. The team will conduct an on-site inspection and analyse how the bridge was damaged.

He said the necessary process for repairing and reopening the bridge would begin after the technical team completes its study. If the problem can be addressed within the jurisdiction and capacity of the provincial government, work will be carried out at the provincial level. If it cannot be resolved at the provincial level, the federal government will be approached for coordination and support.

“If the technical analysis shows that the provincial government can address the issue, we will proceed accordingly. If it is a technical problem that cannot be resolved by the provincial government, we will coordinate with the federal ministry to determine how the bridge can be repaired and reopened as soon as possible,” Koirala said.

He said the process of reopening the bridge as soon as possible would be taken forward in coordination with the concerned agencies once the technical team’s report is received.

Koirala also urged the general public not to visit the site, including to inspect the bridge or record videos, as the damaged structure remains dangerous.

title.rendered: Neer Shah’s Paleti becomes a fusion of memories and music

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Lyricist Neer Shah’s Paleti was held last weekend at Nepalaya’s R Sala. The event, coordinated and hosted by musician Aavaas, was divided into three segments.

The first segment featured songs Shah wrote close to themes of life and philosophy, sung by Abhigya Ghimire and Rupak Chaudhary. Seated centre stage, Shah shared memories of working with past artists, growing especially reflective while recalling his association with Narayan Gopal.

He recounted travelling with Narayan Gopal to the Golden Kite World Song Festival, where they learned Narayan Gopal had received the Jagadamba Shree award.

Shah also recalled his friendship with singer-composer Deep Shrestha from their early struggling days performing in restaurants, noting they still address each other by a nickname from that time. He spoke fondly of past televised talent-discovery programs and their role in launching several artists’ careers, and remembered composer Natikaji, calling him a “melody king.”

He recalled singer Prem Dhoj Pradhan’s shy nature, and actor-musician Shiv Shankar. When the host noted the next segment would feature romantic songs, Shah joked about feeling nervous around the word “romantic,” before revealing the next song was one he’d written during his honeymoon, drawing laughter from the audience.

Later, discussing the song written at Danny Denzongpa’s request to reflect the bond between Nepalis at home and abroad, Shah shared a vivid memory of an evening at Narayan Gopal’s home, where Ambar Gurung, Bhupi Sherchan, Bishwambhar Pyakurel and Shah gathered for a dinner honouring singer Aruna Lama.

Shah described the night’s music-filled atmosphere, with Gurung on harmonium and Narayan Gopal on tabla as Lama sang, recalling neighbours gathering at their windows to listen until 4 am, a night Shah called an unforgettable moment in his life.

The program moved through film songs, memories of the “Sangeet Sangam” and “Pratibhako Dabali” talent shows, and closed with a song from the film “Ke Ghar Ke Dera,” with Shah joking that people often wrongly credit him with another song from that soundtrack.

The evening’s musicians included Mohan Rana Magar on keyboard, Buddha Lama on flute, Prabin Pulami Magar on lead and rhythm guitar, Kripesh Lohani on bass, Milesh Tandukar on tabla, and Sundar Kumar Maharjan on percussion.

title.rendered: Historic Pharse Bazaar swept away by Kali Gandaki flood

content.rendered:
Parbat, September 29

When the Kali Gandaki River surged after days of heavy rain on September 27, residents of Pharse in Jaljala Rural Municipality-8, Parbat, faced a disaster they had never imagined.

The river, which had long been part of everyday life in the settlement, suddenly began cutting into the old Pharse Bazaar.

Residents who had remained relatively untroubled even during previous floods watched helplessly as the river swallowed one house after another.

“People in Pharse have faced a disaster they never imagined in their lifetime. The Kali Gandaki, which had always made life easier, came as a destructive force this time,” local resident Ganesh Acharya said. “No one lost their life, but house after house was swept away. Residents could only watch helplessly.”

Hundreds of people were left without homes as the river continued to erode the settlement.

A market with more than a century of history

Pharse was once an important trading point in the Dhaulagiri region, long before roads connected the settlement to the rest of the country.

According to historian and researcher Chandraprakash Baniya, a Madan Puraskar winner who has studied the history of the former Parbat state and the Dhaulagiri region, Pharse was already a bustling market 70 years ago, despite having no road connection.

A suspension bridge built at least a century ago connected Pharse with Baglung. At the time, Beni was the main trading gateway in the region, and travellers using the Annapurna route would stay overnight in Pharse before continuing their journey.

Baniya recalls seeing houses surrounded by traditional grain storage structures in Pharse seven decades ago. Some were thatched, while the settlement served as a stop along an old pilgrimage route to Muktinath.

“Pharse Bazaar is one of the oldest markets in the Dhaulagiri region. It was a trading gateway,” Baniya said. “Goods were carried by mules from Pharse to Baglung and Myagdi. The historic trade route to Muktinath, and along the Kali Gandaki through Triveni and Batouli towards Mustang and the Tibetan border, passed through Pharse.”

According to Baniya, the old Parbat and Galkot districts were merged during the Rana period in 1952 to form Baglung district, with Baglung made its headquarters. At the time, areas west of the Modi River belonged to Parbat while areas to the east belonged to Syangja.

A bridge at Pharse became important for connecting the western part of Modi with Baglung.

“The area west of Modi needed a road to Baglung. There was a crossing at Beni, but not here. So a suspension bridge was first built at Pharse. It must be more than a century old,” Baniya said. “That historic bridge has also now been swept away by the flood.”

As Pharse became connected to Baglung and parts of Beni, the settlement grew into a trading centre.

Small shops and shelters stood along the riverbank, serving not only traders but also travellers looking for a place to stay. Similar settlements existed in Beni, where a suspension bridge was also built across the Kali Gandaki around 200 years ago, Baniya said.

Locals say the settlement of Pharse expanded through the efforts of former local officials Purnachandra Sharma and Colonel Chakrapani Sapkota. Engineer Ramchandra KC said an inscription records the construction of a Shiva temple in Pharse 105 years ago.

Residents still remember traders and travellers carrying goods by mule and horse and stopping overnight in the market.

Pharse’s Shiva Secondary School, health post, community building and agricultural produce collection centre have also been damaged, according to KC.

Before the Maldhunga-Beni road opened in the early 1990s, travellers used Pharse as a major route. The settlement was historically connected to markets in Parbat, Baglung and Beni.

80 houses swept away, 24 at high risk

The September 27 flood has devastated the old Pharse Bazaar.

The Kali Gandaki has damaged or swept away around 80 houses, while another 24 houses are considered too dangerous to live in.

Jaljala Rural Municipality Vice Chairperson Deepak Acharya said residents were not only worried about the immediate danger but also about the future of the historic settlement.

“Until the other day, this was a peaceful settlement. Now it has become a riverbed, and the houses are damaged,” Acharya said. “No one lost their life, but generations of property have been swept away.”

Parbat Chief District Officer Ganga Bahadur Chhetri said the river had not merely damaged around 80 houses but had swept some of them away completely. Three more houses were washed away on Monday.

Residents remain anxious despite the river level falling.

“The risk remains even though the Kali Gandaki is not currently flooding. Damage is continuing even after the sun comes out. Continuous rainfall has caused springs to emerge, and the ground and roads from Pharse towards Beni have cracked,” Chhetri said. “People have now been moved to safer locations.”

The disaster has completely altered the daily lives of residents who had spent generations engaged in trade, business and agriculture.

Some now spend their days staring at the remains of their homes. Others look at the land where their houses once stood.

“People have been living in Pharse for at least 150 years, but they had never experienced such a disaster,” local engineer Ramchandra KC said. “Houses built by carving and shaping stone have now been reduced to ruins. The disaster has put the history of old Pharse Bazaar itself at risk.”

Pharse Bazaar, located in one of Jaljala Rural Municipality’s more densely populated wards, had continued to grow as people from surrounding hills migrated into the lower and upper parts of the settlement.

“Pharse Bazaar had been becoming increasingly vibrant. Now there is silence,” KC said.

Locals blame riverbed extraction

Residents also blame the extensive extraction of materials from the Kali Gandaki for worsening the damage.

They say crushers and both legal and illegal extraction activities have continued along the river from Kushma to Galeshwor, including during periods when extraction is prohibited.

They argue that Pharse residents have now suffered the consequences.

The suspension bridge linking Baglung and Parbat, believed to have been built more than 100 years ago, has also been swept away.

With 24 houses now considered unsafe and around 100 families affected, temporary accommodation has been prepared for 27 families through coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments.

According to CDO Chhetri, the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police and local residents worked together to set up tents for the 27 families.

“An immediate arrangement had to be made for 27 families, and a temporary camp was prepared with the province also taking the lead,” Chhetri said. “The remaining families are staying with relatives or in vacant houses in the area.”

Gandaki Province Chief Minister Surendra Raj Pandey inspected Pharse Bazaar and directed authorities to ensure there was no shortage of relief, rescue and temporary accommodation for those affected.

title.rendered: Pokhara to host ‘Dashain Tourism and Cultural Festival’ on October 25

content.rendered:
Kaski, September 30

A ‘Dashain Tourism and Cultural Festival’ will be organised in Pokhara with the aim of giving visitors a closer experience of Nepali culture and traditions. The festival, themed ‘Tika, Jamara and Kite Flying-Celebrating Dashain with Tourists in Pokhara,” will be held on October 25, the day of Kojagrat Purnima, at Barahi Ghat ground in Lakeside, according to event coordinator Uma Bhandari.

Organised by the Women Tourism Entrepreneurs Forum (WOTEF), the festival seeks to take Dashain beyond a family celebration and create an opportunity for domestic and international tourists to experience Nepali customs, food, culture and lifestyle. Tourists visiting Pokhara will be welcomed with tika and jamara (traditional paste made of vermillion and sacred barley shoots). Visitors can also take part in a kite-flying competition. The festival will also feature traditional cultural performances representing different ethnic groups and communities.

Visitors will also have an opportunity to taste traditional Nepali cuisines and explore local products, handicrafts, cultural items and tourism-related businesses. Pokhara Tourism Council Chairperson Hari Bhujel said linking Dashain with tourism would help promote both Pokhara’s cultural heritage and its tourism sector.

WOTEF Founding Chairperson Jamuna Parajuli described the festival as an opportunity to showcase Pokhara’s culture and identity as part of its tourism experience. WOTEF Chairperson Mamata Neupane said the festival would allow visitors to experience not only Pokhara’s natural beauty but also its art, culture and traditions.

title.rendered: Tourists stranded in Manang as floods, snowfall disrupt Annapurna Circuit

content.rendered:
Manang, September 30

Tourists on the Annapurna Circuit have been stranded in Manang district after incessant rainfall triggered flooding in lower Manang and heavy snowfall in upper Manang. According to Dhak Bahadur Bhujel, Chief of the Annapurna Conservation Area Project (ACAP) unit in Manang, tourists in both upper and lower Manang have been unable to continue their journey. Bhujel said some tourists attempting to cross the Thorong La Pass have also returned due to heavy snowfall.

“Some 226 foreign tourists have been registered in upper Manang, while 44 have returned. More than 150 tourists attempting to cross the Thorong La Pass have returned due to heavy snowfall,” Bhujel informed. He said all tourists currently in Manang are safe. However, tourists who have fallen ill and those whose visas have expired have been evacuated by helicopter, he added. Other tourists attempting to cross the Pass have been allowed to proceed, with helicopter evacuation available from Mustang if necessary.

Meanwhile, ACAP tourism education assistant Bhupendra Gurung mentioned that 590 foreign tourists were registered at the Dharapani checkpoint from September 22 to 28. Of them, 146 have returned due to rain, floods and landslides, he said. Flood and river erosion have washed away sections of roads at several places, disrupting transportation. Alternative tracks are being constructed, but transporting heavy equipment to the affected areas remains a challenge.

title.rendered: Finance Minister returns home after attending AIIB annual meeting

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle returned home today after attending the annual meeting of the Board of Governors of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB).

He returned to Kathmandu on a Qatar Airways flight at 8:45 am today. The visit proved productive for expanding the bank’s investment in Nepal’s key infrastructure development, technology transfer and further cooperation among member countries.

He had left for Doha, Qatar, on September 26 to attend the meeting. The annual meeting elected Wagle, in his capacity as finance minister and AIIB governor for Nepal, as vice-chairperson of the Board of Governors for 2026-27.

Nepal was elected vice-chairperson from among the bank’s regional member states. During a governors’ business roundtable at the meeting, Wagle said capital formation through infrastructure is a key source of economic growth for less-developed countries, and stressed the need to invest in key means of production such as roads, electricity, communications and information technology.

He also shared views on ways to make the bank’s lending as concessional as possible to match the needs of countries like Nepal, and on making finance available in ways that attract domestic and foreign private capital. During the meeting, he held discussions with the AIIB president and with the finance ministers of member states including Qatar, India, Bangladesh, Armenia and Georgia, on bilateral interests, economic cooperation, expanding investment, and support for Nepal’s reconstruction after the natural disaster it has faced.

With Nepal elected vice-chairperson of the AIIB for the first time, there is hope this will further pave the way for expanded bank investment, technology transfer and cooperation in the country’s key infrastructure development.

title.rendered: Government seeking alternative after Bhotekoshi flood knocks out 430 MW power

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

The government has been making alternative arrangements after 430 MW of electricity was disconnected from the national transmission system following the damage caused by the Bhotekoshi flood at different hydropower projects. The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation has started the homework for alternative management after the power brought from the Trishuli corridor to Balaju and Chapali in Kathmandu was disconnected.

Following the disruption of power supply from the Trishuli corridor, the Balaju and Chapali transmission lines have been under pressure. Ministry Spokesperson Mohan Kumar Shakya shared that the ministry has forwarded homework to develop an alternative supply system, and the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has been carrying out activities to form a task force.

The Ministry on Tuesday held a discussion with the Department of Roads and the Kathmandu Metropolitan City for the construction of additional underground grids. NEA has forwarded the construction of additional underground grids as an alternative arrangement for winter, and a discussion was held for collaboration with the Department of Roads and Kathmandu Metropolitan City for this purpose, added Shakya. Similarly, Kathmandu Division Chief of the Department of Roads, Subodh Devkota, expressed commitment to necessary support and cooperation from the side of the Department in the construction of underground grids.

Likewise, Chief of the Department of Public Works of KMC, Suresh Kumar Rai, stated that there would be necessary collaboration by laying underground cables in the footpath. Chief of the Bagmati Distribution and Customer Service Directorate, Munindra Thakur, made a presentation about load management of Kathmandu and necessary activities and shared that the NEA has been forwarding activities for the management of winter demand of power by forming a task force. NEA Board Member Anshu Kiran Shahi pointed out the need for high cooperation and collaboration of all bodies in the management of winter demand for power in Kathmandu.

title.rendered: NSU president Katuwal elected as general convention representative

content.rendered:
Dhankuta, September 30

Nepal Students’ Union (NSU) president Karuna Katuwal has been elected as a general convention representative from her home district, Dhankuta.

Katuwal received the highest number of votes, 690, in the youth-open category, where each voter could vote for up to two candidates.

Gobinda Limbu, who placed second, has also been elected as a convention representative, with 305 votes. Katuwal received 385 more votes than Limbu.

In the youth-open category, Kranti Raj Paudel received 243 votes, Chiranjibi Kongren 184, and Abhinav Guragain 139.

Katuwal received the highest number of youth-open votes in her home district, with around 70 percent of the participating representatives voting for her.

title.rendered: Beni-Babiachour road reopens after four days

content.rendered:
Myagdi, September 30

The Beni-Babiachour road section has reopened, four days after rain disrupted it.

The road connects three local units in western Myagdi to the district headquarters, Beni Bazaar, easing residents’ daily life since reopening.

The Infrastructure Development Office repaired 16 km of road from Beni to Babiachour, the centre of Mangala Rural Municipality, to Panabagar, restoring traffic from Tuesday evening.

On the Gandaki provincial road, repairs also progressed on the 24-km Beni Darbang-Bangepahiro stretch, connecting Dhaulagiri, Malika, Mangala and Tamankhola (Baglung) rural municipalities.

The road had been blocked since Asoj 10, affecting life across western Myagdi.

Provincial Assembly member Resham Bahadur Jugjali said machinery had been mobilised to reopen Beni-Panabagar, and repairs are now underway from both ends on the Panabagar-Ranabang-Dukhu-Ratodhunga-Tolabang-Bangepahiro stretch. He said coordination with the chief minister and the physical infrastructure ministry aims to restore traffic as quickly as possible.

Chief District Officer Ganesh Gairhe said all three tiers of government are coordinating to repair their respective roads and restore traffic.

Separately, the Kaligandaki has damaged the Beni-Jomsom-Korala road, Nepal’s main trade route to China, at several points, cutting transport links to Mustang and affecting cross-border trade and apple and chyangra exports.

title.rendered: Government works to manage winter electricity in Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

The devastating Bhotekoshi River flood damaged various hydropower projects, taking 430 megawatts of electricity off the national transmission system. The government has since moved to arrange alternative management, officials at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said.

With the flood blocking power coming through the Trishuli corridor to Balaju and Chabahil in Kathmandu, ministry officials said work on alternative arrangements is under way.

Ministry spokesperson Mohan Kumar Shakya said that after the Bhotekoshi flood disrupted power from the Trishuli corridor, pressure has built on the Balaju and Chabahil transmission lines. He said the ministry has moved ahead with work to develop an alternative supply system, and that the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has formed a task force to work on it.

Talks held with KMC

The ministry held discussions on Tuesday with the Department of Roads and Kathmandu Metropolitan City on building additional underground grids. The NEA has moved ahead with building more underground grids as part of its alternative winter management plan.

Spokesperson Shakya said the discussions covered improving the reliability of the underground alternative power grid in certain areas, building additional underground grids, and winter electricity management with a fixed timeline, in coordination with the Department of Roads and Kathmandu Metropolitan City.

At the meeting, Department of Roads Kathmandu Division chief Subodh Devkota pledged the necessary support and cooperation from the department’s side for building the underground grid.

Kathmandu Metropolitan City’s Public Construction Department chief Suresh Kumar Rai also said he would extend the needed cooperation while managing underground wiring within footpaths.

NEA Project Directorate chief Durgananda Badiyat said the authority would further streamline the underground wiring work under way within Kathmandu Valley, and work closely with the Distribution and Customer Service Directorate to meet winter demand-management needs.

Bagmati Distribution and Customer Directorate chief Munindra Thakur made a presentation at the discussion on Kathmandu’s load management and related tasks, saying the NEA has formed a task force to carry forward winter demand-management work.

NEA board member Anshu Kiran Shahi said high-level cooperation and support from all agencies is needed to manage Kathmandu’s winter power demand. She said coordination with the ministry is continuing to address winter power pressure through smooth management.

title.rendered: The drivers swept away by the Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 30

At 86, Homnath Lamichhane spends much of his time talking to himself.

It does not matter whether anyone is beside him. Since the Bhotekoshi flood, the elderly man has been restless, repeatedly talking about what happened.

“He keeps talking even throughout the night. He has not really been able to come back to his senses since the incident,” said Yamuna Dhakal, Homnaths’ second daughter-in-law.

When we visited his home in Dharapani, in Kalika Rural Municipality-3, on September 23, Homnath was sitting on the stairs, wiping tears from his eyes.

For a man who is in the later stages of his life, the scale of the loss he has endured makes his condition difficult to regard as surprising.

After having five daughters, Homnath had three sons in succession.

“He was especially attached to his sons”, Yamuna said. “But the flood took away two sons whom he loved very much, at the same time.”

Homnath’s sons, Balram, 38, and Krishna, 35, disappeared in the flood on August 26. Both were drivers. Balram, the elder son, had been travelling from Kathmandu towards Kerung.

“He was apparently heading from Betrawati towards Syabrubesi,” Yamuna said. “The other friends who reached Dhunche survived. But Balram, who was behind them, disappeared.”

Balram had been driving for 16 years and owned his own large freight truck, locally known as a ‘dibba’. In Dharapani, owning such a truck was more than a means of earning a living. It was also a marker of status and identity.

Krishna, on the other hand, worked transporting vehicles across the Kerung border.

“The Chinese bring the vehicles up to Kerung, and drivers from Rasuwa take the vehicles brought by the Chinese to other Nepali drivers,” said local resident Navaraj Lamichhane. “Krishna did the same work.”

Young drivers from Rasuwa had increasingly found opportunities in this cross-border trade. Krishna, who had also been driving for 16 years, had started working as a cross-border driver only six months earlier.

When the flood struck, he was at Rasuwagadhi.

“We were talking on the phone. He said he was getting work and that he would come home once he had some free time,” his wife, Yamuna, said. “But the phone has not connected since the flood. Everyone says he was swept away by the flood.”

Krishna leaves behind a son and a daughter. Balram leaves behind three daughters and a son.

“The children are still very young. The person who were the main breadwinners are gone,” Yamuna said. “Where do we even go to look for them?”

She has been sitting and crying alongside her elderly father-in-law.

“The grandchildren are still small, and I am old,” Homnath said. “Who will raise them?”

A village of missing drivers

The Bhotekoshi flood swept away the Rasuwagadhi border crossing and sections of the Pasang Lhamu Highway running through Ghattekhola, Timure and Syabrubesi. Dharapani, too, has been left in mourning.

“Seven drivers from our own Lamichhane family were caught in the flood,” Navaraj said. “Twenty-seven people from Dharapani village are missing.”

The Lamichhane family is not an isolated case.

During reporting trips to Rasuwa, Nuwakot and other areas affected by the flood, we encountered a large number of families who had lost drivers.

Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal’s major border crossings with China. On the day of the flood, the Pasang Lhamu Highway was carrying large numbers of drivers.

Some were driving passenger vehicles. It was the season for trips to Mansarovar and Gosainkunda, and drivers were carrying tourists. Foreign visitors heading for the Langtang trekking route were also travelling through the area.

Large freight trucks carrying goods between Kerung and Kathmandu were also on the road. Their drivers came from different parts of Nepal, but a significant number were from Rasuwa itself.

Being local offered drivers advantages at the border, residents said.

The facilities available to local people from the Chinese side had also helped make driving an attractive profession for young people in Rasuwa.

“Our brothers became drivers because the income was attractive. The flood swept them all away,” said local resident Gomadevi Ghimire.

Four of Gomadevi’s brothers, all drivers, are missing. One of them, Kumar Lamichhane, 38, was her biological brother.

“After Kumar was caught in the flood, our dream of having a home has disappeared,” she said

Kumar had been driving for eight years and had only recently bought his own ‘dibba’. He had used the family’s savings and borrowed money to buy the truck. He was the main breadwinner for his family.

“Don’t worry too much. I am here,” his wife, Prasuna, recalled him telling her.

Kumar had been at home until August 24, the day before the flood. He drove between Kathmandu and Rasuwagadhi. After hearing that his vehicle would clear customs, he left for Rasuwagadhi on August 25.

“The customs clearance was done that day, but because it happened at night, the checkpoint did not let him leave,” Prasuna said. “Apparently, he left at 6am the next morning.”

That morning, Kumar video-called his wife.

“When I asked him why he had left so early, he said the gate had opened early,” Prasuna recalled. During the call, he also told her that he was stuck in a traffic jam because of a landslide.

“I spoke to him for about 15 minutes,” she said. “A little later, I heard that the flood had come. When I called him, his phone was already switched off.”

After hearing that there was little left at Rasuwagadhi, Ghattkhola and Timure, Prasuna called again.

“The phone does not connect. Where do I go to look for him?” she said. “There is neither a body nor a breath.”

Prasuna learned that seven of the nine people who had eaten together at the same mess were drivers who had gone missing.

With her husband gone, responsibility for her elderly in-laws and her children has fallen on her.

Her father-in-law, Diwakar, 72, and mother-in-law, Chetakumari, 65, are ill and need regular medication. Her 16-year-old daughter and nine-year-old son are still in school.

“We probably have more than Rs2m in debt,” she said. “I have to regularly buy medicine for my in-laws and educate the children.”

A wedding that will not happen

Prasuna’s neighbour, Sita Lamichhane, is living through a similar uncertainty.

Her son Sagar Lamichhane, 32, has been missing from Rasuwagadhi. The family had been preparing for his wedding in November.

Sagar was the eldest son. His mother had long been worried that he had not married despite his age. This time, he had finally agreed.

“Once my son said yes, we started preparing for the wedding,” Sita said. “But they say Sagar was caught in the flood.”

The family had been thinking about arranging his marriage for several years. But Sagar had also been trying to bring his younger brother Santosh home from prison. Santosh is being held on a rape allegation.

“Sagar was working hard because he believed his brother had been framed and that he would prove him innocent,” Sita said.

Sagar had arranged his sister’s wedding. She now lives in Japan, while her seven-month-old son is being cared for by his grandmother, Sita.

“My daughter went to Japan when her baby was four months old, and one son is in prison,” Sita said, wiping away tears.

Sagar had returned home only a week before the flood. He had been driving for 16 years and stayed home for three days before leaving for Rasuwagadhi on 21 August.

“He used to say he would not go abroad to earn money. He would earn here and look after us,” Sita said.

How driving became a way of life

Local residents say one reason the death toll was so high in Kalika Rural Municipality, an area that was otherwise comparatively safe apart from Ward No 1 of Ramche, is that so many people there work as drivers.

According to Gomadevi, this is not unique to Kalika. Across Rasuwa, it is common to find a driver in almost every household, and sometimes more than one male member of the same family works as a driver.

Driving has become almost a culture in the district. The Lamichhane settlement was no exception.

Residents remember Bhim Prasad Lamichhane as the person who first drew members of the Lamichhane family towards the profession. Around 1990, Bhim Prasad started driving, and young people in the village began hearing about his work.

“When the border opened, people started saying that the lives of those who drove vehicles would change. Like other young people, my brother and I also became drivers,” Navaraj said. “Young people were attracted by the facilities local drivers received at the border.”

According to Navaraj, drivers can earn up to Rs7,500 when taking vehicles from China into Nepal.

With that kind of income available, he said, young people in Rasuwa began competing to become drivers. Like other villages in the district, young people in Dharapani gradually joined the driving trade.

“Almost every household had a driver. Brothers drove, fathers and sons drove. It became a culture,” Navaraj said. “Today, that same wave swept everyone away at once.”

Navaraj himself drove on the same route until five years ago.

On March 7, 2019, his brother died while driving a vehicle across the Kerung border.

“The vehicle got stuck in the snow. While trying to get it out, the cold got into him and my brother died,” Navaraj said. “After that, I stopped driving on that route.”

The decision eventually saved Navaraj’s life. He now drives an autorickshaw on local routes.

“I survived. But my friends, brothers and uncles were all swept away,” he said. “I might have been among them in this very flood.”

Who will speak for the drivers?

Among the families affected by the devastation caused by the Bhotekoshi flood, a large number are families of drivers.

Rasuwa is a geographically remote Himalayan district, and residents say driving has consequently become one of the preferred professions there. But after the flood, affected families say the rescue and search for missing drivers, and the concerns of their families, have not received enough attention.

“I hear the hydropower companies talking about their employees and workers,” Gomadevi said. “We hear about the suffering of the army, police and armed police and their families. But I have not heard anyone say that drivers also have families.”

She said the state appeared to have forgotten that drivers pay road taxes to operate their vehicles.

“Drivers pay money to the state to operate on these routes, but when they disappear, the state did not make them a priority,” she said.

Navaraj also argues that drivers have been overlooked.

“We must not forget that drivers had lives and families too,” he said. “Some do not have a union, and some may not even have licences. Who will speak for them? Who will do something for the drivers?”

Affected families say government agencies have not yet collected even basic figures on how many drivers disappeared in the flood.

An initial estimate from informal sources puts the number of missing drivers at more than 500. More than 300 of them are believed to have been driving freight vehicles along the Pasang Lhamu Highway.

PM Shah to make result-oriented India visit at appropriate time: Foreign Minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has said Prime Minister Balendra Shah will make a result-oriented visit to India at an appropriate time, although no formal date has been fixed yet.

Speaking to reporters at Tribhuvan International Airport on Wednesday after returning from the 81st United Nations General Assembly, Khanal said India had formally invited Shah soon after the new government was formed.

“We have been saying from the beginning that the Prime Minister received an invitation as soon as the government was formed, and we took it positively,” Khanal said. “We are preparing for a result-oriented visit at an appropriate opportunity.”

Asked about the timing of the visit, Khanal said no date had been finalised so far.

“As of today, it is not certain when the visit will take place. But both sides expect and want the visit to be as fruitful and result-oriented as possible,” he said.

Khanal also said Prime Minister Shah’s address to the 81st UN General Assembly had attracted significant attention from the international community.

He said there had been considerable international interest in how Nepal’s youngest prime minister following the country’s recent political changes would present Nepal on the global stage.

“After his address, headlines around the world were about his speech,” Khanal said. “The video of the Prime Minister’s address is also the most-watched speech from this year’s UN General Assembly. This clearly shows the level of interest around the world.”

Khanal said foreign representatives and diplomats had openly praised Shah’s address during various formal and informal meetings in New York following the speech.

According to the foreign minister, the international community also expressed strong solidarity with the issues and concerns raised by Shah at the global forum.

Khanal further said the international community had shown strong interest in supporting Nepal’s reconstruction efforts following the Bhotekoshi floods and in helping the country address the climate crisis.

title.rendered: International community keen to support Nepal after Bhotekoshi flood: Foreign Minister Khanal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has said the international community has shown strong interest in supporting Nepal’s reconstruction efforts following the Bhotekoshi floods and in helping the country address the climate crisis.

Speaking to reporters at Tribhuvan International Airport on Wednesday after returning from the 81st United Nations General Assembly, Khanal said the international community had expressed concern and solidarity over the damage caused by the Bhotekoshi floods during his meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

“During the meetings, the international community expressed concern about the damage caused by the Bhotekoshi floods and solidarity with Nepal over the suffering caused by the disaster,” Khanal said. “In almost all my formal and informal meetings, there were questions and discussions about how they could support Nepal in this difficult situation.”

Khanal said various countries and international organisations had shown interest in supporting Nepal’s post-flood reconstruction efforts.

He also said the international community was concerned about the broader climate crisis affecting Nepal.

“Overall, Nepal is facing disasters brought about by the climate crisis, and I found that the international community stands in solidarity with us on this issue as well,” Khanal said. “I found that there was particular interest in the issues Nepal raised about its difficulties on the international stage.”

According to Khanal, the Prime Minister’s address to the UN General Assembly and the high-level meetings held by the Nepali delegation helped strengthen Nepal’s position on national interests and climate justice at the international forum.

title.rendered: Mahakali flood destroys part of suspension bridge linking Dodhara Chandani and Bhimdatta

content.rendered:
Kanchanpur, September 30

A suspension bridge connecting Dodhara Chandani with Bhimdatta Municipality in Kanchanpur has been damaged after flooding in the Mahakali River.

A section of the bridge was completely destroyed at around 8am on Wednesday after floodwaters damaged a pillar in the middle of the river, according to eyewitnesses.

Police said the sixth section of the bridge from the Bhimdatta Municipality-13 side and the third section from the Dodhara Chandani side were damaged.

The damaged section fell into the river after the central pillar collapsed, according to eyewitnesses.

Jagat Prasad Joshi, director of the Sudurpaschim Province Transport Infrastructure Directorate, said preparations were underway to send a technical team to assess the damage.

“I was also informed about the damage to the suspension bridge by the chief district officer. As soon as I received the information, preparations were made to send a technical team,” Joshi told Onlinekhabar. “The extent of the damage can only be determined after a detailed assessment by the technical team.”

Bridge built in 2004

The suspension bridge connecting Dodhara Chandani and Bhimdatta was completed in 2004.

According to Khadak Rawal, manager of Mahakali Online, local residents travelling across the bridge at around 4-5am on Wednesday noticed that one section of the bridge had risen unusually high.

Police were informed about the unusual condition of the bridge, Rawal said. However, at around 8am, the raised section collapsed into the river, he said.

Following the collapse, the direct route between Dodhara Chandani and Bhimdatta has been closed.

Rawal said people travelling between the two areas will now have to take a route around two kilometres upstream to cross the Mahakali River using a concrete bridge.

title.rendered: China border closures disrupt Nepal’s pre-Dashain trade as all three major crossings shut

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Nepal’s land-based trade with China has come to a complete halt after three days of continuous rainfall and natural disasters disrupted all three major border crossings with the northern neighbour.

With just two weeks remaining until Dashain, the closure of the Tatopani-Khasa, Rasuwagadhi and Korala crossings has disrupted the land-based supply chain between Nepal and China.

According to Department of Customs data, Nepal imported goods worth more than Rs 76.40 billion from China in the first two months of the current fiscal year alone. But damage to roads and infrastructure leading to all three major crossings has now made large-scale trade through these routes impossible.

China had already closed the Tatopani-Khasa border crossing over concerns about landslides. The Rasuwagadhi crossing was then severely damaged after flooding in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

With both major crossings closed, the Korala crossing in Mustang had emerged as an alternative route for Nepal-China trade. However, flooding in the Kali Gandaki River has now severed road access to Korala as well.

Floodwaters washed away approach roads to key bridges along the Kaligandaki Corridor and the Mid-Hill Highway, blocking the route to the Korala border. While the Korala border point and customs office remain safe, damage to bridges along the Beni-Jomsom road has halted the movement of cargo vehicles.

Billions of rupees worth of trade stuck on the roads

Trade pressure at the Korala crossing had increased sharply after Tatopani and Rasuwagadhi were closed.

In just 15 days, from September 10 to 25, 434 containers and 641 electric vehicles entered Nepal through Korala. By the last week of Bhadra, Mustang Customs had already collected more than Rs 2.31 billion in revenue in the current fiscal year.

The crossing handled imports worth Rs 14.41 billion and more than 3,000 electric vehicles last fiscal year. With the road now cut off, billions of rupees worth of trade have been brought to a standstill.

Only 30 percent of goods reach Kathmandu, prices expected to rise

The border closures have halted the movement of clothes, footwear, bags, electronics and electric vehicles from China, raising concerns among both traders and consumers.

Parshuram Dahal, president of the RB Complex Business Association, said only around 20 to 30 percent of goods brought in for Dashain have reached Kathmandu so far.

“Dashain-targeted goods are stuck on the roads. We tried to divert the goods in warehouses through the Korala border, but that has also stopped,” Dahal said. “At most, only 30 percent of the goods have arrived so far.”

He said customs procedures were not the main problem, but the rising US dollar exchange rate and transportation costs were pushing up prices.

“The dollar has risen sharply, and transportation costs have also increased after the roads were blocked,” Dahal said. “Because of the higher transport costs, the prices of goods arriving now are expected to increase by 25 to 30 percent.”

With large cargo trucks unable to operate, some traders have started bringing goods from India in smaller vehicles. But Dahal said Indian goods are more expensive than Chinese goods and transportation costs are higher when using smaller vehicles.

He said existing stocks and locally produced goods had provided some relief despite the disruption in Chinese imports.

Wholesale trade has also been affected as traders from outside Kathmandu have been unable to travel to the capital to collect goods after roads were damaged by several days of rain.

Some traders are taking orders through WhatsApp and social media, but business remains slow.

“It has been three consecutive years that roads are damaged and trade is disrupted by rain in September,” Dahal said. “Traders are always the ones who suffer. Everyone is now forced to bear the impact of this disaster.”

Traders call for infrastructure and diplomatic efforts

Manoj Babu Shrestha, president of the Federation of Nepalese National Businessmen, said the closure of all three crossings with China had severely affected traders, markets and the supply system.

He accused the government of failing to make sufficient diplomatic efforts while Chinese authorities had cited various reasons for keeping the crossings closed.

He said billions of rupees had been spent on infrastructure at the Tatopani border, including a dry port and parking facilities, but the crossing remained closed.

“We have already told the government that diplomatic efforts should be made to reopen the Tatopani border immediately. Lawmakers also raised the issue in Parliament yesterday,” Shrestha said. “But we have not been able to understand why the government does not want to reopen the border.”

Shrestha also pointed to delays in customs clearance and inadequate infrastructure at Korala.

He said the crossing had initially been clearing customs for around 50 containers a day during its first 15 days of operation, but the process had slowed.

“The government’s physical infrastructure at Korala is not adequate, and there is also a shortage of staff,” he said. “There have been major problems with software and networking. Sometimes the server goes down and sometimes there is no network. This problem has continued for a year, but the government has not been able to fix it.”

Transportation from Korala is also expensive because of the geographical distance.

According to Shrestha, trucks travelling from Kerung to Korala have to take a route of around 1,200 kilometres on the Chinese side, while the road from Korala into Nepal includes around 200 kilometres of heavily damaged road.

“Because of transportation costs, the price of a pair of shoes or a jacket increases by around Rs 100 to Rs 150,” Shrestha said. “Even if goods were more expensive, the market would at least have a regular supply. But now everything is blocked.”

He said the border closures had disrupted the market at a time when business activity normally increases ahead of Dashain.

“Traders are suffering greatly. The market should be picking up and showing excitement ahead of Dashain, but that is simply not happening,” he said.

What is happening at the border?

According to Bidur Chudal, chief customs officer at Mustang Customs Office, more than 150 cargo vehicles and containers are currently stranded at the customs point, including vehicles awaiting customs clearance.

Around 300 to 400 electric vehicles, along with empty and loaded containers, are also stranded in the yard and at the border.

“Although the flow of vehicles from the Chinese side has increased, traders are not in a hurry to complete customs clearance because the road on the Nepali side is blocked,” Chudal said.

He said the Department of Roads was working to repair the damaged road and that goods could be transported to Kathmandu once the route reopens.

title.rendered: Bangladesh has lost 900 children to measles – a warning to other countries where vaccine rates have slipped

content.rendered:
Almost 900 people in Bangladesh are suspected to have died in a measles outbreak that began in March. Most of those affected are children.

Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. It can spread rapidly when vaccination rates fall, and the Bangladesh outbreak shows how quickly years of gaps in protection can turn into a serious public health crisis.

The country had hoped to eliminate measles and rubella by 2020. Instead, the pandemic disrupted routine childhood vaccinations, leaving pockets of children vulnerable to the virus. Now other countries where vaccination rates have fallen face a similar risk.

Vaccine hesitancy is probably part of the story here too. During the COVID pandemic, almost half of Bangladesh’s population were wary of getting vaccinated. That same wariness may well have carried over to the measles-rubella jab, with many parents simply refusing to let their children be vaccinated.

Measles has its own set of drivers, too. Poverty, education levels, and how often mothers attend antenatal check-ups all shape whether children in a community end up vaccinated. Add it all up, and childhood vaccination coverage has been sliding for years – down to just 87%.

Between March 15 and September 6 2026, Bangladesh reported 92 suspected measles cases per 100,000 population and 11 confirmed measles cases per 100,000 population, based on an estimated national population of 178 million.

In March 2026, Bangladesh’s vaccine advisory group approved an emergency measles-rubella vaccination campaign for children aged six months to five years, with extra provisions for infants aged six to eight months.

Children normally get two doses of the measles vaccine. During this outbreak, however, the World Health Organization (WHO) advised giving one additional dose to all children in the target age group, regardless of whether they had been vaccinated before, to slow transmission and prevent severe illness. This built a rapid wall of immunity.

The vaccination campaign began in early April in 30 sub‑districts across 18 priority districts, then rolled out nationwide later in the month. It was the first national measles campaign since 2020. In the intervening years, routine vaccination services were badly disrupted by the pandemic and political instability, leaving many children without full protection.

Alongside vaccination, every child with suspected or confirmed measles was given vitamin A, a simple supportive treatment for active and suspected infections that lowers the risk of severe illness and death. A nationwide vitamin A drive had already taken place in 2025, and the advisory teams built on that experience for this 2026 outbreak.

Bangladesh’s Directorate General of Health Services activated district rapid response teams, and hospitals added isolation beds and tightened infection control measures. Paediatric wards in some hospitals quickly filled with children with high fever, rash and breathing difficulties.

Operational teams began producing weekly situation reports, and health authorities issued new national and divisional guidelines covering vaccination, patient care and vaccine supply. This helped local authorities across all eight administrative divisions to coordinate their response as the outbreak spread.

Unicef, the WHO and Gavi (global vaccine alliance) worked with the government to back the response. Organisations such as Save the Children ran community awareness drives, including door-to-door visits and work with mothers’ groups and schools, to encourage families to register their children and bring them for vaccination.

Even with this large‑scale national campaign, risks remain. If children miss their routine booster shots, or if large gatherings continue, or if rumours keep parents away from vaccination centres, another wave of infections is back knocking the door.

Measles is highly contagious – one infected person can pass it on to dozens of others if the people around them aren’t protected. It travels through the air in a cough or a sneeze, and can hang there, invisible, long after the person who sneezed has left the room. That’s why vaccination can’t be patchy – it has to be active, widespread, and reach every corner of a community to break the chain of infection.

Herd immunity

The COVID pandemic introduced many people to the term “herd immunity” – the idea that once enough of a community is immune to a disease, it becomes hard for the infection to spread. For measles, that threshold is high: around 95% of a community needs to be vaccinated to keep the disease under control.

Even a small dip in vaccination rates can leave pockets of unprotected children. A single imported case is then enough to spark an outbreak, and Bangladesh’s recent experience shows how those small pockets can grow over several years. Similar patterns have played out in other countries where coverage has slipped.

Some countries have managed to eliminate measles and rubella altogether – a significant public health milestone. Cabo Verde, Mauritius and Seychelles were the first in sub-Saharan Africa to reach it.

Zimbabwe faced a large measles outbreak in 2022. Intensive vaccination campaigns helped contain the virus, prevent hospitalisations and save lives.

In 2016, the Americas became the first WHO region to stop measles spreading continuously on its own. That status didn’t last: Venezuela recorded cases in 2018, followed by Brazil in 2019.

The region regained its elimination status in 2024, then lost it again in November 2025 after cases emerged in Canada. Elimination is a major achievement, but holding on to it depends on sustained routine vaccination, strong surveillance and the ability to respond quickly when outbreaks occur.

Bangladesh’s outbreak is a reminder that vaccines only work if people actually receive them. The science has already done its job: measles vaccines are safe, effective, and have protected children for decades. What’s missing is trust, access, and the urgency needed to close the gap – until that changes, outbreaks like this one won’t be the last.

title.rendered: Australia tightens temporary visa rules, international students among those affected

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

The Australian government has announced new measures to tighten its temporary visa system as part of efforts to manage immigration levels.

The government has set a target of limiting net overseas migration (NOM) to 245,000 in the current financial year.

Under the new measures, international students already studying in Australia will face additional restrictions if they apply for another student visa and seek to move to a course at a lower level than their current qualification.

The government said the measure is aimed at curbing the use of student visas to switch courses primarily as a way of extending long-term stays in Australia.

Australia has also proposed introducing a ballot system for second- and third-year visas under its Working Holiday Maker programme.

Under the proposal, 45,000 places would be allocated annually for second-year working holiday visas and 5,000 for third-year visas. Eligible applicants would be selected through a ballot.

Applicants would still need to meet the existing requirement of completing the specified period of work in eligible areas. For a second-year visa, the current requirement of completing 88 days of specified work would generally remain in place.

The government also said it would tighten the pathway through which people enter Australia on visitor visas and then seek to move to another type of visa.

Some visitor visas will include conditions preventing holders from extending their stay, according to the government.

The Australian government said the changes are intended to better manage the temporary visa system, reduce visa misuse and keep immigration levels within the targeted range.

The new measures will not apply uniformly to all visa holders. Their application will depend on the type of visa, nationality and individual circumstances under the relevant Australian immigration rules.

title.rendered: All vehicles to operate on Prithvi Highway from 1pm today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 30

Traffic along the Prithvi Highway is expected to return to normal from 1pm Wednesday, provided there are no further landslides or road obstructions.

The Dhading District Administration Office said Tuesday that efforts were underway to clear landslides and repair sections of the highway that were damaged or had subsided following continuous rainfall.

Currently, vehicles are operating on the affected sections on a one-way basis.

According to the administration, all types of vehicles will be allowed to operate along the Prithvi Highway from 1pm Wednesday if no further landslides or other obstructions occur.

Although the rain has stopped, the risk of landslides remains at several points along the highway, and the administration warned that landslides could occur at any time.

Authorities have urged drivers, passengers and the general public to travel with caution and strictly follow traffic rules and road safety guidelines.

title.rendered: Shankar Agrawal sent to custody despite Supreme Court bail order

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Businessman Shankar Agrawal, who had been ordered released on bail by the Supreme Court, has been sent to custody by the Special Court.

A bench of Supreme Court justices Balkrishna Dhakal and Nrip Dhwaj Niraula had ordered Agrawal’s release on bail of Rs 1 million in a banking offence case.

On September 16, the bench overturned the detention order issued by the Patan High Court and ordered Agrawal’s release on bail.

However, a joint bench of Special Court chairperson Basudev Acharya and members Hemant Rawal and Bidur Koirala on Tuesday ordered that Agrawal be kept in custody while the case proceeds to trial.

In its order, the Supreme Court had said there was no direct evidence of Agrawal’s involvement in the alleged offences. It also took his age and health condition into consideration while ordering his release.

The Supreme Court further noted that Agrawal had not signed the documents related to the disputed loan and that there was no evidence of his direct involvement in decisions concerning the purchase of land and payment of advance money.

title.rendered: How a residential visa was allegedly shifted from one foreigner to another

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

A computer operator at the Department of Immigration has been charged with forgery after investigations by the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police and the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA).

The CIAA has filed a case against 31-year-old Rajiv Mahato of Durgabhagwati Rural Municipality-2, Rautahat, accusing him of illegally altering immigration records, manipulating documents and failing to account for revenue collected for a visa.

Mahato has been charged under Section 276(1) and (2) of the National Penal Code, 2017, which prohibits forgery of documents. If convicted of forging government or public documents, he could face up to seven years in prison and a fine of up to Rs 70,000.

Mahato is currently giving his statement before a bench of Kathmandu District Court Judge Sudarshan Lamichhane. A detention hearing will be held after his statement, following which the court will decide whether to release him on general date or bail, or send him to prison pending trial.

Residential visa allegedly transferred between two foreigners

According to the charge sheet, Mahato is accused of transferring a residential visa issued in the name of Luxembourg citizen Paul Christian Pierre Geditz to US citizen Dean Jay Robinson.

The incident dates back to February 2024.

Records show that Geditz had been issued seven visas since 2019, including six residential visas and one tourist visa. Robinson, meanwhile, had received 10 tourist visas, two study visas and one residential visa since 2021.

Investigators found that the residential visa most recently issued in Geditz’s name was altered and issued in Robinson’s name.

Geditz had obtained a residential visa through a secretary-level decision dated June 8, 2014. The Department of Immigration had subsequently renewed the visa.

On January 1, 2024, the Department issued a residential visa under the same visa number on Geditz’s passport and generated a revenue payment of $1,200 through the RIMS portal. The required documents were also submitted.

The equivalent of Rs 159,408 was deposited at Global IME Bank as the visa fee after the payment was processed through the user ID of immigration assistant Prem Kumar Jha.

However, investigators later found that the same residential visa had been issued under Robinson’s passport number and attached to his passport.

Robinson had previously applied for a residential visa three times but had not received one. He had obtained a study visa on May 31, 2023, and applied for a residential visa after his study visa expired.

The Home Ministry had not made any decision approving Robinson’s residential visa, according to the investigation.

Investigators allege that Mahato, who was then working in the department’s non-tourist section, abused his access to the government system and used the Travel Centralisation function to merge Geditz’s visa records with Robinson’s details.

The charge sheet alleges that Mahato removed documents attached to Geditz’s record and merged Robinson’s documents with the existing visa record, making it appear that the residential visa belonged to Robinson.

The visa was subsequently printed and attached to Robinson’s passport.

Travel Centralisation is normally used to merge visa records when there are errors in a person’s passport or visa records and information belonging to the same individual needs to be consolidated.

The CIAA alleges that Mahato misused the system to transfer a residential visa belonging to one foreign national to another.

Mahato has denied knowing how the changes occurred. In his statement, he claimed that the Travel Centralisation option was not available in the department’s system at the time.

He also claimed that staff at the assistant level did not have access to the visa printer, visa stickers or the relevant system functions.

Investigation into alleged Rs 23,000 bribe continues

Meanwhile, the CIAA is also investigating a separate incident involving an alleged Rs 23,000 bribe at Tribhuvan International Airport.

On September 21, a man identified as Manish Bista reportedly travelled to Kuwait on a labour visa without obtaining the required labour approval. The incident is being investigated after suspicious activity was detected in the Department of Immigration’s Nepali Port system and CCTV footage.

According to Director General Ram Chandra Tiwari, the department began investigating after noticing the suspicious activity at around 6:30 am.

CCTV footage showed Bista entering immigration at the airport at around 6:30 am and speaking with immigration official Tek Bahadur Sejuwal for around 30 minutes.

Sejuwal allowed Bista to depart at around 7:10 am.

According to the investigation, Sejuwal provided Bista with the phone number of his brother-in-law, Dipak Malla, who was in Japan. Bista subsequently contacted Malla, and a deal for Rs 23,000 was allegedly agreed.

The QR code for the payment was reportedly shared through WhatsApp, after which Bista paid Rs 23,000 and travelled to Kuwait without labour approval.

Investigators have found that Sejuwal himself provided the QR code. The Rs 23,000 was later returned after the department became aware of the payment.

The CIAA is currently investigating the alleged bribery case.

title.rendered: Police chief Dan Bahadur Karki meets Chief Justice Manoj Sharma

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Nepal Police Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki met Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma at the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon.

According to Supreme Court sources, Karki arrived at the Supreme Court at around 4 pm and held a meeting with Chief Justice Sharma in his office for nearly 45 minutes.

The subject of their discussion has not been disclosed.

The meeting comes days after police took former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana from his residence to a police station overnight, citing a security threat.

The government has said Rana was taken into protective custody after threats against him increased.

However, the Supreme Court’s full court meeting had expressed objections to Rana being kept in police custody for around 10 hours on Sunday.

Karki’s meeting with Chief Justice Sharma took place after the full court issued a statement on the matter.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress announces revised schedule for 15th general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The Nepali Congress Central Election Committee has announced a revised schedule for the party’s 15th General Convention.

According to the revised schedule released through a press statement on Tuesday, the opening ceremony of the general convention will be held on October 4.

The opening ceremony will begin at 2 pm at the Khula Manch, according to the statement issued by committee member-secretary Raju Katuwal.

The closed-door session and other programmes will be held on October 5 and 6.

The election process has been scheduled for October 7 and 8.

“Other programmes related to the election process and the detailed schedule will be published later,” the statement said.

The Election Committee has asked the party to complete regional conventions by October 1 and submit the list of delegates to the general convention.

Registration of general convention delegates has been scheduled for October 2 and 3.

title.rendered: CIB found new facts in ANFA investigation: Minister Pokharel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The government has said the investigation into the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) is still ongoing after new facts emerged during the probe.

Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel, who is also the government spokesperson, said the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police was continuing its investigation into ANFA.

“After two people were taken into custody and investigated, additional information came to light, so the CIB has become more active in the investigation,” Pokharel said. “The investigation will proceed through the normal process.”

Pokharel also said the government was preparing to resume domestic football leagues after football activities were disrupted following ANFA’s suspension.

“We are preparing to operate the domestic leagues,” he said.

The minister said Nepal’s inability to win medals at the international level was partly due to insufficient investment in grassroots sports.

“The reason we have not been able to win medals is that we have not invested properly at the grassroots level,” he said. “Even today, our sports infrastructure is not adequate. There are not enough places to play football or cricket, and there are not enough covered halls.”

He said the lack of investment by the state, rather than a lack of effort by athletes, was a major problem.

Pokharel said the government had moved ahead with a plan to build sports infrastructure at 27 locations across the country’s seven provinces as part of its efforts to develop sports from the grassroots level.

title.rendered: Supreme Court justices raise serious concerns over Chief Justice Manoj Sharma’s leadership

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

At an emergency meeting of Nepal’s Supreme Court on Monday, nearly all of the country’s senior judges turned their criticism on Chief Justice Manoj Sharma, raising questions about the direction of the judiciary and its declining credibility.

The meeting was called to discuss the arrest of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana. But the discussion quickly widened into a broader examination of the leadership of the Supreme Court and developments in the judiciary in recent months.

Three of the five judges who spoke to Onlinekhabar compared some courts to a supermarket, where, they suggested, anything could be obtained for the right price.

“Some courts have become like superstores during this period. Pay money and you can buy anything,” one judge said, according to a source familiar with the meeting. “How did our courts reach this situation within just three months of your arrival?”

Almost all of the judges, except for Justice Sharanga Subedi and Chief Justice Sharma, questioned what they described as the capacity and working style of the judicial leadership.

Justice Binod Sharma, considered close to the chief justice, was not present. He was visiting courts in Nepal’s far-western region.

The judges who spoke with Onlinekhabar did not want their individual comments identified. They said, however, that the meeting addressed several contentious issues, including Rana’s arrest, the composition of the Constitutional Bench, the relationship between Rana and Chief Justice Sharma, problems at the Special Court and the increasingly open activity of intermediaries around the judiciary.

The chief justice’s secretariat said it could not comment on the substance of the meeting. Amit Upreti, head of the secretariat, said they did not know what had been discussed.

Supreme Court spokesman Arjun Koirala also declined to elaborate, saying the matters the full court had decided to make public were already included in its statement.

The arrest of a former chief justice

The immediate trigger for the meeting was the arrest of Rana, a former chief justice.

According to judges who spoke to Onlinekhabar, seven justices had urged Chief Justice Sharma to convene a full court after he remained silent following Rana’s arrest.

The judges questioned why the court had not met “even in such a situation,” according to one account. Chief Justice Sharma subsequently called the emergency meeting.

One judge said the judges raised the view that the government had been wrong to arrest Rana.

Those who agreed with that view said three aspects of the arrest were particularly problematic: that Rana had been taken into custody without an arrest warrant, that he was released the following day without an adequate explanation, and that police had brought a former chief justice to a police office citing public security and peace.

The judges agreed that the full court should take a position on the matter, the judge said. That position was reflected in the statement issued after the meeting.

According to the judge, Chief Justice Sharma appeared enthusiastic during the discussion over Rana’s arrest.

But the judges also wanted the court’s statement to address what they described as Rana’s recent activity and attempts to influence the judiciary, rather than simply opposing his arrest.

The final paragraph of the statement said that actions taken or to be taken in the administration of justice should not be portrayed or communicated by linking them to any former officeholder.

It also said the full court wanted to assure the public that no internal or external influence would be given any space in the administration of justice.

Questions about intermediaries

The judges also questioned why intermediaries — people who act between litigants and the courts — appeared to have become active again.

According to the judges, after Rana left office, there had been few complaints about interference or the activities of intermediaries in the judiciary.

After Rana, Deepak Kumar Karki served as acting chief justice, followed by Harikrishna Karki, Bishwambhar Prasad Shrestha and Prakash Man Singh Raut.

“Why did intermediaries become active and influential as soon as you came, when the judiciary had been functioning normally during their terms?” one judge asked Chief Justice Sharma, according to a source.

The judges also questioned why Rana, who they said had remained silent during the terms of the previous chief justices, had suddenly become active.

During the same period, a writ petition against Rana was dismissed, opening the way for him to receive a pension certificate.

The judges said intermediaries outside the courts had become increasingly active, that people had begun openly discussing cases and that individuals who had been inactive for a long period had returned.

“What are we supposed to do if we do not hear cases simply because we have heard rumours?” one judge was quoted as saying. “But if we hear the cases, someone else outside has already finished the work using our names. How can we work in such a situation?”

‘Special Court or superstore?’

The Special Court was another source of concern. Some judges raised what they described as serious irregularities and problems at the court, according to a source familiar with the meeting.

The comparison to a superstore resurfaced in discussions about the Special Court, with judges questioning whether it had begun to be seen as a place where outcomes could be obtained according to one’s financial means.

Three Special Court judges had previously met Chief Justice Sharma and told him they were having difficulty working.

Four other judges, excluding chairman Basudev Acharya and member Hemant Rawal, later met Sharma and some senior-most Supreme Court justices. They said either those involved in the alleged irregularities should be removed or they themselves should be transferred elsewhere.

Some judges subsequently asked Sharma why, if he had known controversy could arise, he had not appointed a capable chairperson to the Special Court.

According to the source, Sharma replied, “Sometimes things turn out this way even when we try to avoid them.”

The judges called for the problems at the Special Court to be taken seriously. They said that if there were problems, its leadership should be changed; if the leadership was considered appropriate, those complaining about it should be transferred elsewhere.

Sharma responded that he would make some changes after returning from China, according to the source.

Judges also raised concerns about people allegedly approaching court users with assurances that they could arrange outcomes in cases.

They questioned how even police officers assigned to court duty had gained the confidence to go around trying to “fix” cases.

The judges said the chief justice had failed to demonstrate leadership at the Special Court and some other courts.

Dispute over the Constitutional Bench

The judges also questioned Chief Justice Sharma over the way the Constitutional Bench was being formed.

They called for the four other members of the bench to be selected according to seniority, as had been the previous practice.

The judges alleged that judges were being selected according to the chief justice’s preference and that politically sensitive or interest-related cases were being brought before the Constitutional Bench.

They also called for the concerns repeatedly raised by the Nepal Bar Association to be addressed.

The Bar Association has been demanding that the four other members of the Constitutional Bench be selected either according to seniority or through a lottery process.

Under Nepal’s constitutional arrangement, the chief justice leads the Constitutional Bench and selects its other four members.

According to the report, except during the terms of Chief Justices Cholendra Shumsher Rana and Prakash Man Singh Raut, the practice of selecting the other members according to seniority had not been set aside.

Since becoming chief justice, Dr. Manoj Sharma has selected judges in a way that departs from that seniority-based practice, according to the judges.
