The meeting was called to discuss the arrest of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana. […]

title.rendered: Oli warns of action against UML leaders violating party discipline

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

CPN-UML chair KP Sharma Oli has said the party will strictly enforce discipline and take action against those who violate its policies or make statements that please opposition parties.

Addressing a virtual party meeting on Tuesday, Oli said the party would no longer tolerate what he described as growing indiscipline and disorder within the UML.

“Growing disorder and indiscipline within the party will no longer be tolerated. We have taken the Central Committee meeting as the cut-off date,” Oli said. “Anyone who goes against the party’s policy and discipline, spreads disorder or speaks in a way that pleases the opposition will face strict action.”

Oli also described attempts to remove him from the party leadership in the name of party restructuring as “criminal activity.”

“There was talk of removing the chairperson in the name of restructuring. This is a criminal activity,” he said.

Oli said the party had forgiven such activities that took place before the Central Committee meeting, but warned that such leniency would not continue.

“We have said all those things that happened before the Central Committee meeting are forgiven. But there will be no forgiveness now,” he said.

He also ruled out moving towards a representative council meeting, saying the party should focus on the upcoming elections rather than internal confrontation.

“We are not moving towards any representative council meeting. This is the time to prepare for the election. This is not the time for fighting among ourselves,” Oli said.

Oli said the party’s main priorities are restoring democracy and preparing for the local-level elections scheduled for next Baisakh.

“The party will decide when to focus on which of these two tasks. We will focus on the election and win,” he said.

title.rendered: Govt says threat to former CJ Rana came from unidentified group

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The government has said former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana was threatened by an unidentified group, rejecting reports that the threat came from the Gen Z group.

Speaking to journalists at Singha Durbar on Tuesday, government spokesperson Sasmita Pokhrel said Rana received the threat through a text message sent by an unidentified group.

According to Pokhrel, Rana was moved to a secure location after receiving the threat.

“There was no statement from the government or police that the security threat came from Gen Z. That was something reported in the media,” Pokhrel said. “The threat did not come from the Gen Z group. He received a threat through a text message from an unidentified group, after which he was taken to a secure location.”

Pokhrel also said Rana’s family reported that he continued to face security threats even after he had been moved to a secure location.

“The threats had already been received initially. After the threats, he was moved to a secure place. Even after that, his family reported that there was still a security threat,” she said.

title.rendered: Cabinet approves federal civil service bill, accepts $20.7m US health grant

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The Cabinet has taken six key decisions, including approving the Federal Civil Service Bill for submission to the Federal Parliament.

Government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmita Pokhrel made the decisions public following the Cabinet meeting held on Tuesday afternoon.

According to Pokhrel, the Cabinet decided to accept a $20.7 million grant from the US government for health service improvement.

The meeting also approved the use of national forest areas for the Kamala-Dhalkeshwar-Pathlaiya section of the East-West Highway, the Garjan Khola Small Hydropower Project and the Balefi Khola Hydropower Project. Permission was also granted to use national forest areas for the construction of training academy units and border security posts of the Armed Police Force, Nepal.

The Cabinet approved the submission to Parliament of a bill to amend the Animal, Slaughterhouse and Meat Inspection Act. It also approved the Federal Civil Service Bill for submission to the Federal Parliament.

Similarly, the Cabinet approved a bill to amend the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act for submission to Parliament.

The meeting also decided to promote Joint Secretary Awas Shrestha Karna to the gazetted special class of the Nepal Administration Service and appoint him as chief secretary at the Office of the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers of Gandaki Province.

Likewise, Dr Jagadishwar Karmacharya was promoted to the gazetted special class of the Nepal Engineering Service and appointed secretary at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation.

title.rendered: Parajuli set to chair Parliamentary Special Committee on Bhotekoshi–Trishuli Disaster

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Ganesh Parajuli, leader of the Rastriya Swatantra Party parliamentary group, is set to chair the Parliamentary Special Committee on Climate Change in the Himalayas and the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster after he filed the sole nomination for the post.

With no other candidate, Parajuli is certain to become the chair of the special committee. The election for the committee chair is scheduled for 2 pm Wednesday.

Parajuli has received the support of lawmakers from all parties represented in the House of Representatives. Nepali Congress lawmaker Mohan Acharya has proposed his candidacy, while CPN-UML lawmaker Pushpa Raj Kandel, CPN lawmaker Ramesh Kumar Malla, Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Dhurvaraj Rai, Rastriya Prajatantra Party lawmaker Saraswati Lama and RSP lawmaker Nisha Dangi have supported it.

The parliamentary special committee was formed on September 21 against the backdrop of the devastating flood in Rasuwa on August 26.

The 15-member committee comprises Achyutam Lamichhane, Anushka Shrestha, Gangadevi Shrestha, Ganesh Parajuli, Dhananjay Regmi, Dhurvaraj Rai, Nisha Dangi, Pushpa Raj Kandel, Mohan Acharya, Mingmagyabu Sherpa, Ramesh Kumar Malla, Rabindra Patel, Saraswati Lama, Sujata Tamang and Sita Thapaliya.

The committee has been given a three-month term, with a provision allowing its tenure to be extended later.

The committee’s mandate includes studying the impact of climate change in the Himalayas. It will review available studies and data on changes in Himalayan temperatures, snowfall, glaciers, glacial lakes and watersheds, as well as the risks arising from such changes. It will also identify gaps in research and monitoring and recommend measures to strengthen scientific research and regular monitoring.

The committee will study the causes and impacts of the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli disaster, including its origin, sequence of events, immediate causes and factors that intensified the risks, based on expert and scientific evidence. It will also review its possible links to climate change, the effects on transboundary watersheds and the impacts on downstream areas.

The committee will review search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts, including the status of missing citizens, relief distribution, safe temporary accommodation, basic services and livelihood restoration. It has been tasked with recommending immediate and medium-term measures based on the needs of affected people.

The committee will also suggest a roadmap for sustainable and safe reconstruction, study disaster risk reduction and early warning systems, explore possibilities for climate diplomacy and cross-border cooperation, and recommend legal and institutional reforms.

title.rendered: Bhandari calls for resolving industrial hurdles to expand businesses in Lumbini

content.rendered:
Butwal, September 29

Former President and senior CPN-UML leader Bidhya Devi Bhandari has called for resolving problems facing the industrial sector to promote the expansion of industries and businesses in the Lumbini region.

Speaking at a welcome programme held in Butwal, Rupandehi, on Tuesday, Bhandari said the government and stakeholders should consult industrialists and businesspeople and focus on addressing the problems affecting the sector.

Bhandari also said the construction of an international airport, international convention centre and road infrastructure in the Lumbini region were important achievements.

Recalling her political association with the region, Bhandari said she was first given the responsibility of UML vice-chairperson at the International Convention Centre in Lumbini.

“I was first given the responsibility of party vice-chairperson here at this International Convention Centre. At the time, we had discussed the need to develop this place with an international convention centre, sports ground and other infrastructure. Today, all of that has been completed. It is a matter of happiness for all of us,” she said.

Bhandari said Lumbini, which was already internationally renowned, had gained further prominence following the development of major infrastructure in the region.

“Now that an international airport and international convention centre have been built and good roads have also been constructed, the question is how to take industries and businesses forward. We need to consult our friends involved in industry and business and move ahead by resolving the problems in the industrial sector,” she said.

Bhandari also expressed happiness over being nominated as a senior leader of the UML, while saying that the process for formally assuming the responsibility had yet to be finalised.

The UML Central Committee meeting held recently nominated Bhandari as a senior leader of the party.

title.rendered: Work begins to clear blocked Marsyangdi River

content.rendered:
Manang, September 29

Authorities have begun efforts to clear the Marsyangdi River after it was blocked at Ghattkhola on Sunday by large rocks, gravel, sand and mud following continuous rainfall.

Assistant Chief District Officer Krishna Prasad Poudel said that the lake formed by the blockage had started draining after the river’s course was diverted.

“The river is partially flowing. Some work has begun using excavators and other equipment available here,” Poudel said. “Large rocks need to be broken, and preparations are underway for this.”

The river changed course above a bridge, inundating some houses in the area, he said.

Chame Rural Municipality Chair Lokendra Bahadur Ghale said residents could return home soon if the river was cleared using locally available resources.

He said authorities must assess the risks to settlements along the Marsyangdi before using explosives to break the rocks. Removing some of the obstructing rocks with excavators could reduce damage to the riverbank, he said.

Poudel said authorities were studying the use of explosives to restore the river to its original course without damaging surrounding areas.

Floods and landslides have disrupted electricity and drinking water supplies, telephone and internet services, and completely blocked roads in the area. In Nisyang Rural Municipality-4, Humde, floodwater and mud have entered houses in nearby settlements.

Electricity supply has also been disrupted after the powerhouse of a micro-hydropower project at Sabje Khola was damaged.

Floods in Ghattkhola, Thado Khola and the Marsyangdi River had previously caused extensive physical damage in Manang in 2021.

title.rendered: Damaged suspension bridge disrupts life in Manakamana area

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 29

Around 150 households in and around Manakamana of Shahid Lakhan Rural Municipality-3 have been facing difficulties travelling after floods triggered by recent rainfall damaged the suspension bridge connecting Silingtar and Cheres.

According to Ward Chair Deepak Pandey, residents of three settlements and pilgrims have been affected after the suspension bridge linking Silingtar in Shahid Lakhan Rural Municipality-3 with Cheres, the lower station of the Manakamana cable car, was damaged.

“The residents of Silingtar, Kevarpani and Manakamana Hatiya are having difficulty reaching the highway after the bridge was damaged,” Pandey said. “More than 50 students travelling to schools and colleges in Kurintar and Muglin are also facing problems. Farmers are unable to easily take their vegetables to market or purchase essential goods.”

He said residents now have to make a detour of one and a half to two hours to reach Theuwatar and cross another bridge.

Previously, pilgrims who could not or did not want to use the cable car would cross the bridge to reach Silingtar and then take buses or jeeps to the temple.

“The pilgrims are also facing difficulties,” Pandey said. “This time, the bridge has been damaged so badly that there is not even enough space to park a jeep.”

The bridge had also been damaged by floods two years ago.

title.rendered: 462 children sheltered in 13 child-friendly centres in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 29

Thirteen child-friendly centres have been set up in different parts of the district to protect children affected by disasters and support their psychosocial development. The Nepal Red Cross Society has established and facilitated these centres with support from UNICEF.

These centres were set up to provide a safe, comfortable, and child-friendly environment for the children affected by the Bhotekoshi flood disaster. Out of the centres set up so far, nine are fully operational, while the remaining four are in the process of being operated.

Currently, 462 children are being taken care of in the operational centres. Activities related to sports, entertainment, learning, creativity, and psychosocial support are conducted according to the age and needs of the children kept in the centres. The centre has given children a great opportunity to express their feelings, mingle with friends, and take part in creative activities in a safe and positive environment after the disaster.

Currently, there are 219 boys and 243 girls in those centres. Based on age groups, 88 children are under five years old and 374 are above the five-year age group. Among the children sheltering in the centres, one child is disabled, according to the Nepal Red Cross Society, Rasuwa branch.

—RSS

title.rendered: Kanti Lokpath reopens for one-way traffic

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The Kanti Lokpath, which had been completely closed for several days due to landslides triggered by continuous rainfall, has reopened for one-way traffic from Tuesday.

Heavy rainfall from September 24 to 27 damaged several sections of the road, disrupting transportation services.

The rainfall in the second week of September triggered major landslides at various locations along the Kanti Lokpath. The road blockage directly affected passengers and vehicles travelling along the short route connecting Kathmandu and Hetauda.

Following the disruption, the Road Division Office mobilised technical teams and equipment to clear the landslides. After prolonged efforts, the landslide debris was removed and the road was made passable. One-way traffic has now been allowed on the affected section.

However, authorities have urged travellers to exercise extreme caution as several sections of the road remain risky due to continued rainfall. Further maintenance work is underway to restore two-way traffic at full capacity.

title.rendered: Search for 12 missing in Himlung avalanche suspended

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The search for people missing in the Himlung avalanche has been temporarily suspended, according to the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA).

The association said 12 kitchen staff members are still missing following the avalanche. The bodies of four people have so far been recovered.

An experienced search and rescue team led by the association was deployed immediately after the avalanche. The association said a massive avalanche at the Himlung Base Camp had covered the camp with snow up to 14 feet deep.

An eight-member rescue team led by Mingma G. carried out search and rescue operations despite the difficult conditions. However, the team has now suspended the operation as there is no longer a possibility of rescuing anyone alive from the avalanche.

The association said excavation work will resume depending on the condition of the snow and the mountain.

title.rendered: Stock market falls 9 points, trading declines

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The stock market’s benchmark index fell 9.62 points on Tuesday. Following the decline, NEPSE stood at 2,603 points.

Trading volume also declined. Turnover fell from Rs 5.38 billion the previous day to Rs 4.65 billion today. Prices of 69 companies rose while 199 declined. Ten companies’ prices remained unchanged.

By sub-index, trade fell the most, down 1.87 percent. Banking fell 0.13 percent, development banks 0.45 percent, finance 0.32 percent, hotels and tourism 0.65 percent, hydropower 0.52 percent, investment 0.22 percent, life insurance 0.37 percent, manufacturing and processing 0.50 percent, and microfinance 0.55 percent. Non-life insurance rose 0.11 percent and other groups rose 0.12 percent.

Today’s top gainers included Sayapatri Hydropower, up 6.79 percent; Sarbottam Paints, up 6.29 percent; Hathway Investment Company, up 3.46 percent; and Menchhiyam Hydropower, up 3.40 percent.

Top losers included Dhaulagiri Laghubitta, down 4.23 percent; Apollo Hydropower, down 4.14 percent; Shikhar Power, down 4.08 percent; Mandu Hydropower, down 3.72 percent; and Kalinchowk Darshan, down 3.01 percent.

Companies with the highest turnover today were, in order, Himalayan Distillery, Shivam Cement, Siddhartha Bank, Garima Bikas Bank, Hathway Investment Company, Reliance Spinning Mills, and Mountain Energy.

Kathmandu, September 29

Former Gandaki Province minister Rajiv Gurung, popularly known as Deepak Manange, has joined the Nepali Congress.

Gurung joined the party’s establishment-opposition faction led by former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba on Tuesday.

According to the secretariat of Shashank Koirala, coordinator of the faction’s committee preparing for the Nepali Congress’ 15th general convention, Koirala formally welcomed Gurung into the party.

Gurung has also been given responsibility as the coordinator of the faction’s preparations in Manang, according to Koirala’s secretariat.

Gurung was previously elected to the Gandaki Provincial Assembly from Manang as an independent candidate. He also served as a minister in the Gandaki provincial government.

title.rendered: Hollywood film Tenzing gets special screening in Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu

The much-anticipated Hollywood film Tenzing, produced by technology company Apple, received its Nepal premiere at a special screening organised by the British Embassy on Monday evening.

The screening was held at the QFX multiplex at Civil Mall and attended by members of the House of Representatives, diplomats from the United Kingdom, the United States and European countries, celebrities, filmmakers, mountaineering figures, and the film’s producers, director and cast.

Actress Manisha Koirala and Tenzing actress Thinley Lhamo also attended the event.

Director Jennifer Peedom and representatives of New Zealand-based film production company See-Saw Films were present at the screening. The British Embassy said proceeds from the event would be deposited into the Natural Disaster Rescue Fund established by the government for flood relief.

The two-hour film received a positive response at the special screening. It was filmed in Nepal’s Everest region, Patan, Bandipur and Mustang. Nepali technicians involved in the production, including location manager and cinematographer Bishnu Kalpit, also attended the event.

The film tells the story of Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay Sherpa’s historic first ascent of Mount Everest in 1953. It follows the life of Tenzing Norgay, played by Genden Phuntsok, and portrays his courageous journey as he joined a British mountaineering expedition and led the climbing team.

Phuntsok plays Tenzing, while Thinley portrays Norgay’s wife. Tom Hiddleston plays Edmund Hillary, and Willem Dafoe portrays the leader of the mountaineering team.

The film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival last week. It is scheduled for a limited theatrical release in the United Kingdom and the United States on October 9 and will be available on Apple TV from October 16.

Kathmandu, September 29

Police have arrested a fugitive convict who had been sentenced to 20 years in prison for murder.

The Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police arrested 60-year-old Rajkumar Shrestha of Kathmandu.

Shrestha had been sentenced to 20 years in prison for the murder of a person. He had been serving his sentence when he escaped from Sundhara Prison during the Gen Z movement.

CIB spokesperson Anupam Shumsher JBR said Shrestha has been sent back to prison following his arrest.

title.rendered: Himalayan Airlines resumes direct Kathmandu-Shanghai flights

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Himalayan Airlines has resumed regular direct flights between Kathmandu and Shanghai, with services between Tribhuvan International Airport and Shanghai Pudong International Airport restarting on Monday.

Himalayan Airlines flight H9780 departed Kathmandu for Shanghai at 7:11 pm on Monday and landed at Shanghai Pudong International Airport at 2:36 am Tuesday, Chinese time. The aircraft landed at Tribhuvan International Airport at 8:13 am Tuesday, Nepal time.

With the resumption of the service, Himalayan Airlines has become the only airline operating regular direct flights on the Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu route. The service restores an important air link between Nepal and Shanghai, one of China’s major global cities.

The airline is initially operating two flights a week on the route. Flights from Kathmandu to Shanghai will depart every Monday and Friday, while return flights from Shanghai to Kathmandu will operate every Tuesday and Saturday. The company said it may increase the number of flights based on passenger demand and load factors.

The Kathmandu-Shanghai service provides passengers with direct air connectivity between Nepal’s capital and Shanghai, China’s largest city and a major global financial centre.

The company said the resumption of the service at the beginning of Nepal’s main tourism season would further enhance the strategic importance of the route. It expects the service to significantly increase the number of Chinese tourists visiting Nepal and contribute positively to the hospitality and tourism sectors, as well as support Nepal’s economic recovery and growth.

Himalayan Airlines Vice President Bijay Shrestha said the company was committed to strengthening trade, tourism and people-to-people ties between Nepal and China. He said the airline was continuously exploring new destinations in China and operating regular flights accordingly.

title.rendered: Indian Ambassador Srivastava makes farewell call on PM Shah

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava paid a farewell call on Prime Minister Balen Shah on Tuesday as he prepares to complete his tenure in Nepal.

Srivastava met Prime Minister Shah at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers earlier in the day.

During the meeting, Shah congratulated Srivastava on successfully completing his tenure and thanked him for his role in further deepening and diversifying Nepal-India relations.

Shah also expressed gratitude to India for its support during recent disasters in Nepal, including the floods in Rasuwa.

Srivastava is scheduled to return to India in the coming days after completing his tenure as ambassador to Nepal.

title.rendered: Schools, community buildings turned into shelters for flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Schools, mothers’ group buildings and disaster holding centres in flood- and landslide-affected areas have become temporary shelters for people who were rendered homeless by floods and landslides caused by continuous rainfall.

According to a report by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, around 2,000 people have been relocated from high-risk areas to safer places across the country, while 1,082 families have been directly affected.

625 displaced people sheltered at BP Secondary School in Susta

Hundreds of residents in Susta Rural Municipality-5, Nawalparasi, have been forced to leave their homes. According to the authority, 625 displaced people are staying at BP Secondary School, while 45 others have taken shelter at a disaster holding centre. Other affected people are staying with relatives.

The local Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the rural municipality are coordinating efforts to manage the displaced people, while the Red Cross has provided tents. Although there is no immediate food shortage, the report states that 70 households need rehabilitation.

Schools and mothers’ group buildings used as shelters in Myagdi

In Myagdi, residents of settlements at risk of landslides and river erosion have also been relocated to safer areas and sheltered in schools and mothers’ group buildings. Forty families rescued from Paudwar in Annapurna Rural Municipality-5 have been sheltered at a school.

Similarly, seven families in Malika, 22 in Mangala, 45 in Raghuganga, 40 in Annapurna and 10 in Beni have been relocated to safer areas and provided shelter in schools and mothers’ group buildings.

With support from the provincial government, food and non-food items have been distributed to 40 families, while food worth Rs 50,000 has been delivered locally. Arrangements have also been made to send relief supplies by helicopter for an additional 65 people.

Ward offices arrange food in Baglung

According to the authority’s report, 46 displaced people in affected local units of Baglung are staying in schools and with relatives. Local ward offices have arranged food for them.

As road links have been disrupted, food, tents and blankets have been sent by helicopter. The provincial government has also been requested to provide an additional 300 tents.

Disasters have completely destroyed 227 houses across the country and partially damaged 142 others. Having lost their homes, affected people are currently relying on public buildings for temporary shelter.

title.rendered: Four injured as rock falls on moving bus in Kapilvastu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Four passengers were injured after a rock fell onto a moving bus at Chorkhola in Kapilvastu on Tuesday morning.

According to Armed Police Inspector Dil Kumar Shrestha, the rock fell on the bus, registration number Su Pa Pra 01-001 Kha 3770, at around 1:30 am at Chorkhola in Shivraj Municipality-1. The bus was travelling from Chitwan to Bardiya.

The injured have been identified as 37-year-old Dwarika Prasad Tharu and 35-year-old Suresh Lal Tharu of Gorakha Rural Municipality-2, Bardiya; 20-year-old Salina Sunar of Bharatpur Metropolitan City-11, Chitwan; and 40-year-old Bhagawati Kandel of Bhimdatta Municipality-10, Kanchanpur.

Shrestha said the injured passengers were trapped by the seats after the rock struck the bus. They were rescued and taken to Bhalubang Hospital in Dang for treatment.

A team of the Armed Police Force, Nepal, No. 29 Jwalamai Battalion, Dang, led by DSP Baburam Thapa, carried out the rescue after receiving information about the incident.

There were 30 people travelling on the bus.

title.rendered: Nepal selected as AIIB vice president for next year

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Nepal has been selected as vice president of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB).

Nepal was selected as vice president representing non-regional member countries for the coming year during the 11th annual meeting of the AIIB Board of Governors, currently underway in Doha, the capital of Qatar. Ireland has also been selected as a vice president alongside Nepal.

Under the AIIB’s organisational structure, the bank has one president and vice presidents representing regional and non-regional member countries.

Finance Minister and Nepal’s governor to the AIIB, Dr Swarnim Wagle, formally assumed the position during the annual meeting.

Addressing the Governors’ Business Roundtable held on the second day of the meeting, Minister Wagle emphasised that capital formation through infrastructure is a major source of economic growth for least-developed countries.

He stressed the need to expand investment in key means of production, including roads, electricity, communications and information technology. He said the bank’s investments should be made as concessional as possible to match the needs of developing countries such as Nepal.

Wagle also said financing should be provided in a way that attracts domestic and foreign private capital.

title.rendered: MPs question bill to restore provisions scrapped by ordinance

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Members of the House of Representatives have questioned a bill seeking to restore provisions of 85 laws that were rendered inactive by an ordinance issued by the government.

During the discussion on the bill, lawmakers questioned why the ordinance was introduced to remove public officeholders if the previous legal provisions were to be restored later.

CPN-UML lawmaker Pushpa Raj Kandel questioned the necessity of the bill, saying it was unnecessary because the Supreme Court had already interpreted that the previous legal provisions would automatically come into effect once an ordinance became inactive.

He also questioned the government’s commitment to stability, good governance and establishing a system of governance. Kandel said the government had removed provisions from laws for a specific purpose three months earlier and was now restoring them for its own interests.

The Special Provision Ordinance on the Removal of Public Officeholders was issued. It amended 110 existing laws and resulted in the removal of 1,534 public officeholders.

No new appointments have been made to the vacant positions. The government has now introduced the bill to restore the previous provisions in 85 of the 110 laws amended by the ordinance.

Nepali Congress Whip Nishkal Rai also questioned the move, asking why the previous provisions were scrapped if they were appropriate.

Nepali Communist Party lawmaker Balawati Sharma said the government had removed officeholders without justification.

title.rendered: MPs question government over delay in federal civil service bill

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Lawmakers have questioned why the Federal Civil Service Bill, which the government had listed as a priority under its 100-point programme and promised to introduce within 45 days, has not yet been presented to Parliament.

Some lawmakers have also raised concerns that the government may be preparing to end the ongoing session of the Federal Parliament and introduce legislation on the federal civil service through an ordinance.

Parbati BK, a lawmaker from the Nepali Communist Party, questioned why the government was seeking to bring the civil service law through an ordinance instead of Parliament.

“The civil service law is reportedly being brought through an ordinance. This is very problematic. Why is the government trying to bypass Parliament and bring the civil service law through an ordinance?” she asked.

The current parliamentary session is expected to end this week.

The parliamentary calendar had initially been set until October 1, but was extended by one day to October 2. Parliament is expected to complete work on pending business by then and hold either the same day’s or an additional meeting before concluding the session.

The ongoing session began on May 11. During the session, Parliament passed the budget and legislation related to it. It also endorsed ordinances introduced by the government while Parliament was not in session. Bills replacing those ordinances were subsequently passed and converted into laws.

Parliament also conducted direct question-and-answer sessions with ministers and allowed ministers to address contemporary issues on behalf of the government. However, a direct question-and-answer session with the prime minister has not yet been held.

The absence of the Federal Civil Service Bill and the School Education Bill was also raised by NCP lawmaker Balawati Sharma.

CPN-UML lawmaker Gurupasad Baral questioned the government’s priorities, while fellow UML lawmaker Pushparaj Kandel accused the government of seeking to govern through ordinances.

Kandel also questioned the government over an earlier ordinance that removed more than 1,500 public officeholders and alleged that the government was attempting to restore previous provisions to facilitate political appointments.

The Special Provisions Ordinance on the removal of public officeholders was issued on May 2. It amended 110 existing laws and resulted in 1,534 public officeholders losing their positions.

No new appointments have yet been made to all the vacant positions. Meanwhile, the government has introduced a bill seeking to restore provisions from 85 of the 110 laws that had been amended or repealed by the ordinance.

Speaking during the discussion, Kandel alleged that both the earlier ordinance and the current bill were motivated by partisan interests.

“This was brought purely in the party’s interest. The earlier ordinance was also brought for the same reason, and so is the current bill. If the old provisions are being restored, then restore the previous appointments as well,” Kandel said.

The questions raised in Parliament come amid preparations to conclude the current parliamentary session and concerns among lawmakers that the government could again use ordinances to introduce legislation on important issues.

title.rendered: CAN president Chand vows to push for better playing conditions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

After all four Asian Games cricket quarter-finals were washed out due to continuous rain, Nepal Cricket Association (CAN) president Chatur Bahadur Chand has said the body will work to correct the tournament’s playing conditions in the days ahead.

In an interview with Himalaya Television, Chand said no one had anticipated that all four quarter-finals would be “washed out” by rain. He said the matter was not taken seriously enough at the time, since the process of drawing up the playing conditions involves the Full Member nations.

“It was never imagined that all four quarter-finals would be washed out. Since the people who draw up the playing conditions are the Full Members, we didn’t take it seriously back then; it wasn’t done properly,” Chand said.

According to him, CAN had already accepted the tournament’s playing conditions beforehand. So rather than disputing the matter now, he said, it makes more sense to push for the necessary corrections ahead of future tournaments.

He said any shortcomings found in the playing conditions need to be fixed.

“There’s no option but to accept it for now. Since we had already accepted the playing conditions, there’s no point disputing it now. It will be corrected from next time; we will lobby for it,” Chand said.

Continuous rain at the Asian Games led to all four quarter-finals being cancelled, including the one between Nepal and Sri Lanka.

With the matches unable to be played, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, who ranked higher under the pre-determined playing conditions, advanced to the semi-finals.

title.rendered: Music video for Jabunik Rukhwa released on YouTube

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

A music video for Jabunik Rukhwa (Jamun Tree), an Indigenous Tharu song, was released on YouTube on Saturday.

The song is traditionally performed after Hareri Puja, a significant Indigenous Tharu ritual for agricultural land, usually held in August. The celebration opens with rituals led by Gurwa shamans, as the village gathers at the chief’s home, known as the Barghar, where all the mandra drums are brought together and blessed. The first ceremonial beat, called Trasan, marks the start of a new cycle of singing and dancing and permits the mandra to be played through the year.

Historically, such jhumra songs were performed to comfort families who had lost loved ones to diseases like diarrhoea, fever and smallpox. Over time, the tradition also became a celebration of resilience and community. Since August also marks the end of an intensive planting season, jhumras give villagers a chance to gather, rest, sing, dance and reconnect after the farming season. The song is customarily performed by male dancers dressed in women’s attire, a distinctive and enduring Tharu cultural practice.

Ujjwal Sagar of Odaar Studio directed the music, while Lavkant Chaudhary of Karkha Charkha served as creative director. Lalta Chaudhary and Somati Tharu are the vocalists, with Arzoo Chaudhary, RK Tharu, Anju Chaudhary and Urmila Gamwa Tharu on backing vocals. Manzil Bikram KC handled audio engineering. The musicians include Kiran Baral on flute, Naren Moktan on guitar and ukulele, and Nandu Chaudhary on percussion.

Chabilal Kopila worked as field producer, with Lavkant Chaudhary, Dirgha Chaudhary and Newraj Chaudhary as videographers. Sushil Khanal was the colourist, and Sunil Chaudhary choreographed the video.

Kavrepalanchok, September 29

The BP Highway, which had been closed since September 25 due to continuous rainfall, has reopened. However, only small vehicles are currently allowed to operate on the highway.

Suman Yogesh, chief of the Road Division Office, Bhaktapur, said traffic resumed after temporary diversions were constructed at locations washed away by floods in the Roshi River.

According to him, floods in the Roshi River had washed away temporary diversions at Chaukidanda in Namobuddha-6, Ghumawane in Roshi-7, and Mamti in Roshi-11 and 12. Landslides had also occurred at Chaukidanda in Namobuddha-6, Charsaybesi in Roshi-7, Gimdibesi in Roshi-8 and Mamti in Roshi-11.

The Road Division Office said two diversions have been constructed at Chaukidanda—one across the river and another above the river.

The office said all types of vehicles are expected to resume normal operation from the afternoon. However, six-wheel cargo vehicles, buses and minibuses will have to wait for a few more hours before being allowed to operate.

content.rendered:

The Nepali Congress is preparing to finalise a new date for its 15th general convention today.

An office-bearer said the Central Office team will hold an informal meeting today to finalise the new date.

The office-bearer told Onlinekhabar this morning, “We are consulting on a new date for the convention; the Central Office team will meet and finalise it today.”

Congress had earlier decided to hold the 15th general convention from October 2 to 5. Invitations had already been sent to leaders of various political parties for the event.

However, continuous rain, floods and landslides from September 24 to 27 affected lower-level conventions. Preparations are underway to push the general convention back by a few days.

With major festivals such as Dashain, Tihar and Chhath approaching, leaders of the Congress establishment faction say a decision on whether to hold it before or after those festivals will be finalised today.

However, another leader said, “There is informal discussion in the party over whether to push it back by just a day or two, not many days.”

The Sher Bahadur Deuba-led faction outside the establishment has also begun preparing to hold a separate 15th general convention of its own in the coming month of Mangsir.

title.rendered: 4 days of heavy rain trigger 542 disasters, kill 27

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

At least 27 people have died, and four remain missing in 542 disaster incidents triggered by heavy rainfall across Nepal from September 24 to 27, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

Eight people were injured, and 1,082 families were affected during the period, while 114 livestock were killed or damaged.

Landslides accounted for 304 incidents, killing 20 people, leaving four missing and injuring seven. Floods caused 87 incidents and four deaths, while 151 incidents related to heavy rainfall claimed three lives and injured one person.

The rain completely destroyed 227 houses and partially damaged 142 others. Floods and landslides also damaged 31 bridges.

The NDRRMA said more than 100 mm of rainfall was recorded at 186 rain-monitoring stations during the four days. The highest rainfall was recorded at Dedhgaun in Nawalparasi East at 544.2 mm, followed by Panchase in Kaski at 500.2 mm and Atraulitar in Tanahun at 472 mm.

The authority said a low-pressure system developed over the Bay of Bengal caused heavy rainfall in various parts of the country.

Around 980,000 people received flood warning SMS messages, while nearly 2,000 people at risk were evacuated to safer locations. Helicopters were used to rescue people stranded by floods and landslides in remote districts, including Myagdi, Jajarkot and Baglung.

title.rendered: Regulation needed to prevent racial bias and hate speech in AI, says Foreign Minister Khanal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has said that regulation is needed to control racially biased algorithms and hate speech seen in artificial intelligence and other new technologies.

Minister Khanal shared this view while addressing a high-level meeting in New York marking the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action (DDPA), held during the UN General Assembly’s 81st session.

Speaking at the meeting, held under the main theme of mobilising worldwide public support for the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, he said the Durban Declaration represents the international community’s shared resolve to fight racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and the legacies of colonialism and apartheid.

In his address, Foreign Minister Khanal emphasised four priorities for ending racial discrimination and injustice. He stressed the strict enforcement of anti-discrimination laws at both the legal and civic levels, and empowering marginalised communities in society. He also called for regulating racially biased algorithms and hate speech in emerging technologies, including AI, to eliminate them, and for advancing principled multilateralism to end systemic intolerance prevalent around the world.

Foreign Minister Khanal, in New York with the Nepali delegation led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah to attend the General Assembly, is presenting Nepal’s positions at various high-level UN sessions and sideline meetings.

title.rendered: Nepal collects Rs 238.5 million in royalties from autumn mountain expeditions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

A total of 637 climbers have obtained permits to climb 18 mountains in Nepal during the autumn season of 2026.

According to the Department of Tourism, 637 climbers from 68 teams have received permits to climb various mountains in the country this autumn. Of them, 474 are men and 163 are women, said the department’s information officer, Suraj Ghimire.

The department has collected Rs 238.51 million in royalties from the climbers for issuing climbing permits.

Among the mountains for which permits have been issued, Mt Manaslu (8,163 metres) has attracted the highest number of climbers. A total of 500 climbers from 43 teams have obtained permits to climb Manaslu, generating Rs 225.86 million in royalties.

According to the department, 34 climbers from four teams have obtained permits for Dhaulagiri I, while 20 climbers from two teams have received permits for Putha Hiunchuli. Similarly, 16 climbers from two teams have obtained permits for Danga Hiunchuli and 10 climbers from one team for Baruntse.

The department has also issued permits for Makalu, Gangapurna West (Langchenel), Thorong Peak, Norbu Khang, Annapurna IV, Chamlang, Lamjung Himal, Pumori, Saribung, Thapa Peak (Dhampus), Pokhar Khang, Ardang and Peri, among others.

The permits issued for these mountains have generated $1.57 million, equivalent to Rs 238.51 million, in revenue, according to the department.

title.rendered: National Defence University bill presented in House of Representatives

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The National Defence University bill, proposed with a main role for the Nepali Army, has been presented in the House of Representatives. Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sobita Gautam presented the bill in the House on behalf of Prime Minister Balendra Shah (Balen).

Presenting the bill at Tuesday’s sitting, she said its purpose is to protect, strengthen and promote national interest through advanced study, teaching and research on national security, defence, international relations and strategic affairs.

The National Defence University bill has been drafted with the aim of producing capable, skilled and responsible human resources, both Nepali and foreign, in this field.

The main reason for establishing and running the university is to set up a specialised academic centre at home to provide higher education and training to military and non-military officials, in order to address geopolitical sensitivities and changing security challenges.

The bill also aims to help the government by providing evidence-based advice when it formulates security and strategic policy, and to make an important contribution to strengthening the country’s security diplomacy.

Minister Gautam said the bill had to be introduced in the Federal Parliament because, with the construction of the National Defence University’s infrastructure in its final phase, a permanent and clear legal framework is needed to operate it and grant it academic autonomy.

Under the proposed bill, the Prime Minister will be the university’s chancellor.

This provision is contained in Section 19 of the bill, registered in the House of Representatives on Tuesday by Prime Minister and Defence Minister Balen Shah.

It states: “The Prime Minister shall be the chancellor of the university.” The chancellor will be the head of the university.

The university’s supreme body will be the “Assembly.” The Nepali Army’s Chief of the Army Staff will be an ex officio member of it. The chancellor will preside over Assembly meetings and the university’s convocation ceremonies. The Prime Minister will be chancellor and the defence minister pro-chancellor. The university’s Assembly will approve policy, rules, the budget and the annual program.

The Nepali Army’s Director General of Military Training will be an ex officio member of the university’s Academic Council. The council will handle tasks such as setting the curriculum and prescribing admission standards. The Nepali Army will also have a role in selecting the university’s executive leadership.

Recommendations for appointment to key posts such as the university’s vice-chancellor and registrar will be made by a committee led by the Chief of the Army Staff. The Nepali Army’s Director General of Military Training will serve as member-secretary of the appointment recommendation committee.

A legal provision is proposed under which a serving Major General of the Nepali Army would be posted as the education officer heading the National Defence College under the university.

There is a provision allowing Nepali Army personnel to be deployed on deputation to meet the university’s staffing needs. The university’s central office will be located at Perungedanda in Banepa Municipality, Kavrepalanchok district, Bagmati Province.

Under Section 4 of the bill, the university will be an autonomous, self-governing and organised institution. Sub-section 1 of Section 4 states: “The university shall be an autonomous, self-governing and organised institution with perpetual succession, and it shall acquire legal personality.”

As a legal person, the university will exercise rights, perform duties and discharge liabilities in accordance with prevailing law.

title.rendered: MPs sign up for zero hour, then skip the chamber when called

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

As soon as a House of Representatives sitting begins, “emergency time” runs first, in which a few lawmakers speak. Zero hour then begins.

MPs sign up to speak during this zero hour, but are not in the House when the Speaker calls their names. This scene has repeated itself in Parliament.

The same scene repeated on Tuesday. During emergency time, Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Dhrubaraj Rai was the only one to speak. Zero hour then began.

During zero hour, Jagat Prasad Joshi and Jagadish Kharel (Lalitpur) spoke. Speaker Dev Prasad Aryal then called the third name, Jagadish Kharel (Dolakha), to speak. But he was not present. The Speaker called his name three times. He was not in the chamber.

The Speaker then called other names, and lawmakers took their turns raising their subjects. Next came the turn of another House member, Dharma Raj KC. He, too, was not in the chamber. The Speaker called his name three times.

The Speaker called another MP’s name, and other lawmakers kept speaking. Next came the turn of MP Pukar Bam. The Speaker called his name. He, too, was not in the chamber and did not speak.

The lawmakers who signed up to speak during zero hour in the House of Representatives on Tuesday but were absent from the chamber, Kharel, KC and Bam, are all lawmakers of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party.

Parliamentary practice allows the Speaker to call a lawmaker’s name up to three times to let them speak. If they do not respond after three calls, that turn ends, and the Speaker lets another person speak or moves the House’s agenda forward.

Rule 15 of the House of Representatives Rules of Procedure covers provisions on zero and special time, under which the Speaker may set aside zero and special time to raise contemporary issues.

If a member seeks time by pressing the buzzer over a serious incident or issue arising between the previous sitting and the one about to begin, the Speaker may make emergency time available.

There is a provision requiring the concerned minister to respond within seven days in the House to issues raised during emergency, zero and special time. However, some lawmakers sign up to speak in the House but do not show up.

title.rendered: MP Dangi demands government protect Nepali jute industry

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Nisha Dangi has drawn the government’s attention to India’s unfair tax policy on Nepali jute products, saying it has pushed Nepal’s jute industry toward collapse.

At Tuesday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, she demanded immediate diplomatic initiative to protect the jute industry.

Speaking in the House, MP Dangi said the anti-dumping duty India has imposed on Nepali jute, along with an ongoing countervailing duty investigation, has directly hit domestic industries.

She warned that if the industries run into trouble, thousands of workers will lose their jobs, and farmers’ jute will have to be thrown away on the street for lack of a market. She said this would seriously affect the overall agriculture sector and industrial output.

“It is positive that the government is taking steps to reopen the Biratnagar Jute Mill, but, unfortunately, it cannot protect the industries that are currently operating,” she said. “The government should not limit itself to a policy of reopening closed industries; it needs to formulate a sustainable industrial policy that can sustain the industries currently in operation.”

MP Dangi stressed that the process of reviving the jute industry should be accelerated in keeping with the spirit of the Industrial Enterprise Act, 2076 B.S.

She pointed to the need for Nepali jute products to gain easy entry into the Indian market, and for the necessary diplomatic and commercial talks toward that end to be intensified.

title.rendered: When rain decides the winner, what is cricket really measuring?

content.rendered:
There was no bad shot. No dropped catch. No tactical mistake. There was not even a toss.

Nepal’s Asian Games campaign ended without its quarterfinal against Sri Lanka producing a single ball of cricket. Persistent rain washed out the match, and Sri Lanka advanced to the semifinal because it held the higher ICC T20I ranking.

For Nepal, that meant the work done to reach the quarterfinal suddenly counted for little.

Nepal had beaten Afghanistan in the group stage and finished top of Group A. It had earned its place in the knockout stage on the field. But once the quarterfinal was abandoned, the tournament’s playing conditions turned to a different measure — ranking.

That is not a new feature of Asian Games cricket. It was already visible at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games.

When the final was decided by a ranking

India and Afghanistan were playing for gold in the men’s cricket final. Afghanistan had reached 112 for five after 18.2 overs when rain stopped play.

The match never resumed.

Instead of the bat and ball deciding the gold medal, the ICC T20I rankings came into play. India, the higher-ranked side, was declared the winner. Afghanistan, despite reaching the final and putting itself in a position to compete for gold, took silver.

The same pattern appeared elsewhere in Hangzhou.

In the women’s quarterfinal, India had scored 173 in 15 overs against Malaysia, which had faced only two balls before rain intervened. India progressed to the semifinal on the basis of its higher ranking.

The Pakistan-Indonesia and Bangladesh-Hong Kong quarterfinals were also abandoned because of rain. Pakistan and Bangladesh advanced because they were higher ranked.

So what happened to Nepal in 2026 was not an isolated incident. It was the continuation of a system already seen at the previous Asian Games.

The same rule, a different tournament

This time the setting was Japan.

In the women’s competition, China and Bangladesh never even reached the toss in their quarterfinal. The match was abandoned because of rain, and Bangladesh progressed because it was higher in the women’s T20I rankings.

Then came the men’s quarterfinals.

India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had been placed directly into the quarterfinals based on their ICC T20I rankings. Nepal, Afghanistan, Japan, Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman had to play the preliminary stage for the remaining four quarterfinal places.

Once those teams reached the knockout stage, however, the ranking advantage did not disappear.

The Asian Games cricket playing conditions contain a specific provision for this situation. Under Rule 16.10.2(b), if a knockout match is completely abandoned because of rain and no result is possible, the higher-ranked team is declared the winner and advances.

That rule allowed India to progress without playing Afghanistan and Pakistan to advance without playing Hong Kong. And then Nepal’s quarterfinal met the same fate.

The paradox for teams outside the top rankings

This is where the structure becomes difficult to ignore.

Nepal had to play its way into the quarterfinal. So did the other teams competing for the four available places.

The higher-ranked teams, meanwhile, entered the competition at the quarterfinal stage.

That in itself is a tournament-format decision based on ranking.

But the same ranking can become decisive again when rain prevents a knockout match from being played.

For a team such as Nepal, that creates a narrow path.

It must first earn its way through the competition on the field. Then, once it reaches the knockout stage, it can still lose the opportunity to compete if weather prevents the match from taking place.

Nepal’s group-stage performance could not overcome Sri Lanka’s higher ranking once the quarterfinal was abandoned.

The same happened to Malaysia against Bangladesh.

The rule therefore does not affect only associate nations. Higher-ranked full members benefit from it as well. India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh all progressed from rain-affected quarterfinals without completing those matches.

But the consequences are particularly significant for teams that spend much of their cricket outside the higher reaches of the rankings.

A rainout does not give them the chance to show what they can do against a higher-ranked opponent.

Who made this rule?

That leads to another question: whose rule is it?

The Asian Games are governed by the Olympic Council of Asia. Cricket at the Games operates within the competition regulations established for the event.

The ICC can provide advice and recommendations on cricket-related matters, but the final decision on the Asian Games playing conditions rests with the OCA.

The available official material shows that the 2026 men’s tournament structure was built around ICC T20I rankings. India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka were given direct quarterfinal places on that basis.

The ICC’s description of the tournament structure also explained that those four teams would enter at the quarterfinal stage while the remaining teams competed for the other places.

What is less clear is whether the ICC specifically advised that abandoned knockout matches should be decided by ranking.

There is therefore an important distinction.

The ICC rankings are clearly being used as part of the Asian Games structure. But there is not enough publicly available official evidence to conclude that the ICC itself instructed the Asian Games to use the ranking as the winner-determining rule for rain-abandoned knockout matches.

Why use the rankings at all?

There is a practical reason. The Asian Games are not a standalone cricket tournament. Cricket has to fit into a much larger multi-sport schedule.

In the 2026 men’s competition, the quarterfinals were scheduled for September 28 and 29, the semifinals for October 1, and the gold and bronze medal matches for October 3.

That leaves little room for a series of reserve days.

If one quarterfinal is postponed, another match cannot simply be pushed back indefinitely without affecting the rest of the tournament.

So a competition needs a predetermined way of deciding who advances when a knockout match cannot be played.

In this tournament, that mechanism is the T20I ranking.

It is clear. It is known to the teams before the match. And it allows the schedule to continue.

But clarity does not remove the competitive question.

A rule problem, or a structural problem?

The ranking rule is straightforward on paper.

If rain completely prevents a knockout match and there is no result, the higher-ranked team advances.

The difficulty is what that rule means in practice.

For Nepal, the journey to the quarterfinal required performances on the field. The team beat Afghanistan and topped its group.

But in the quarterfinal, there was no opportunity to repeat that performance.

The outcome was determined before Nepal and Sri Lanka could compete.

That raises a broader question about the balance between tournament practicality and sporting opportunity.

There is also the question of infrastructure.

Japan is highly developed in many areas, but cricket remains an emerging sport there. The facilities available for cricket are not necessarily comparable with those found in countries where the sport has a much deeper infrastructure.

In the matches affected by rain, there was no provision to completely cover the playing surface. Once the rain arrived and the ground became wet, the possibility of restarting the match became even more difficult.

That means the problem cannot be reduced simply to whether the ranking rule is fair or unfair.

The tournament format, the limited schedule, the playing conditions and the infrastructure all intersect.

When the weather becomes part of the competition

There is an unavoidable irony in what happened to Nepal.

A team can beat a higher-ranked opponent in the group stage, finish first in its group and reach the knockout stage. But if rain prevents the next match from taking place, the earlier performance may no longer be enough.

The ranking, established before the tournament, can suddenly become more important than what happens during the tournament itself.

That may be an efficient way to keep a multi-sport event on schedule.

But it also means that, in a knockout competition, sometimes the decisive moment does not happen with a bat or ball in hand.

For Nepal, it happened when the rain came. And there was nothing left to play.

Khanal, who is in New York to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, held the meeting with his Sri Lankan counterpart on the sidelines of the assembly, according to his secretariat.

The two ministers discussed ways to further strengthen Nepal-Sri Lanka bilateral relations.

During the meeting, Khanal expressed sympathy and solidarity with communities affected by Nepal’s recent devastating climate-related disasters. He also thanked the Sri Lankan government and people for providing economic and humanitarian assistance to Nepal.

The two ministers exchanged views on various aspects of the friendly and cooperative relations between Nepal and Sri Lanka.

They emphasised the need to convene meetings under existing bilateral mechanisms and expressed their commitment to expanding and strengthening cooperation in areas of mutual interest, including trade, tourism, education, culture, connectivity and people-to-people relations.

title.rendered: 246 foreign tourists turn back from Manang as bad weather disrupts Annapurna Circuit

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Foreign tourists trekking to Manang along the Annapurna Circuit have started cutting their journeys short and returning towards Lamjung as persistent rainfall has worsened weather conditions and increased risks along the trekking route.

Many of the tourists had planned to cross the Thorong La Pass and continue towards destinations including Mustang and Pokhara. However, deteriorating weather and growing risks on the trail have prompted them to turn back from Manang.

According to Bhupendra Gurung, chief of the Annapurna Conservation Area Project (ACAP) office in Dharapani, 246 foreign tourists returned from Manang towards Lamjung over the past week.

Of those who returned, 151 were men and 95 were women. The figures cover the period from September 22 to 28.

Until a few days ago, around 100 to 150 foreign tourists were passing through Dharapani towards Manang every day. Tourist movement has declined sharply with the worsening weather.

“At least 100 to 150 tourists were heading towards Manang almost every day until a few days ago. Now, we see only one or two tourists heading towards Manang, while most have started turning back,” Gurung said.

Tourists who had planned to cross Thorong La Pass and continue towards Mustang and other destinations have shortened their journeys due to continuous rainfall, poor weather and increased risks along the trekking route.

The Annapurna Circuit begins from Besisahar Municipality-7 in Lamjung and passes through Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, Myagdi and Kaski. The highest point of the trekking route is Thorong La Pass, which stands at an altitude of 5,416 metres.

The route has long remained a popular destination among foreign tourists because of its natural and cultural diversity.

title.rendered: Efforts to blast blocked Marsyangdi River in Manang remain unsuccessful

content.rendered:
Chame, September 29

Efforts to clear the blocked Marsyangdi River in Chame, Manang, by blasting have not yet succeeded.

According to Krishna Prasad Poudel, assistant chief district officer of Manang, a technical team from the Nepal Army arrived in Chame from Pokhara on Monday to carry out the blasting operation. However, work has not yet begun.

“The technical team arrived in Chame yesterday, but the problem is that they have not found a suitable place for the blast,” Poudel told Onlinekhabar.

According to him, a large rock formation is needed to carry out the blasting. However, no suitable rock has been found around the point where the river is blocked.

“The river has been blocked by gravel, sand, trees, soil and other debris. Because of this, a suitable location for blasting could not be identified,” he said.

As blasting is not immediately possible, authorities have started clearing the blockage using two heavy machines, Poudel said.

The Marsyangdi River was blocked after continuous rainfall caused mud, rocks, gravel and sand from the local Ghattekhola to accumulate in the Chame area.

Water has started flowing partially from the lake formed by the blockage. However, according to Poudel, the lake is still around 400 metres long and 80 metres wide. The water level could be as deep as 20 feet, he said.

Four days of continuous rainfall have also disrupted electricity, telephone and road networks at various locations across Manang.

title.rendered: Questions remain over former CJ Cholendra Rana’s midnight detention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

The government has yet to officially explain why former Chief Justice Cholendra Rana was detained by police late Saturday night and released about 12 hours later.

Police took Rana into custody from his residence in Basbari shortly before midnight. According to his family members, police said they had to take him into protective custody because of a security threat from Gen Z protesters. However, police did not present an arrest warrant.

The absence of a warrant has raised questions over the legal basis for Rana’s detention. The main opposition Nepali Congress and other opposition parties have questioned the government over the incident.

The government has not publicly clarified the matter, while the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which leads the government, has largely remained silent.

According to a lawmaker, there was an understanding at the leadership level that the issue would not be raised in Monday’s House of Representatives meeting. No formal circular was issued to lawmakers, but there was an informal understanding among senior leaders to remain silent on the matter, the lawmaker said.

Two RSP central members and lawmakers, Ranju Darshana and Rajiv Khatri, have publicly raised concerns about Rana’s detention, while senior party leaders have not commented.

Khatri criticised the manner in which Rana was detained, questioning how the alleged security threat had suddenly disappeared.

“How was the security threat against Cholendra resolved? We do not know,” Khatri said. “If a citizen feels insecure, it is the state’s responsibility to provide security. But the way the police picked him up from his home, almost like an abduction, was not right.”

Khatri said Rana’s past conduct could be questioned and investigated if there were legal grounds to do so.

“If there are questions about his conduct, ethics or finances, he should be investigated. Others accused of similar wrongdoing should also be investigated. But taking someone into custody at midnight without even providing an arrest warrant was wrong,” he said.

Khatri also compared the incident with the way former RSP chairman Rabi Lamichhane had been arrested by the previous government, saying the current government had displayed a similar approach in Rana’s case.

RSP central member Ranju Darshana also expressed dissatisfaction with the manner of Cholendra Rana’s detention.

“The law allows a person to be arrested when an offence has been committed. But even when making an arrest, the procedure has to be followed,” Darshana said.

“Even if the offence is not immediately visible, the law requires evidence. An allegation alone is not enough. There must be a basis and evidence to establish the offence. That is what the rule of law means. Powers can be exercised, but not without due process and evidence.”

RSP had previously questioned government actions

RSP lawmakers and leaders have previously criticised government actions through Parliament and social media, including the displacement of squatters and the use of vehicles outside media houses and residences of political leaders.

After vehicles were found parked outside media houses, political leaders’ residences and business premises in what were described as suspicious incidents, RSP general secretary Bipin Kumar Acharya had criticised the government.

The party said suspicious and unexplained activities aimed at intimidating media organisations and journalists or creating psychological pressure on them were a direct violation of democratic norms.

The RSP had called on the government to identify those involved and bring them within the scope of the law. Although the owners of some of the suspicious vehicles were identified, the government did not take legal action against anyone, according to the report.

RSP lawmakers had also criticised the government after squatters temporarily housed in Kirtipur were affected by flooding.

Chief whip Krantishikha Dhital had questioned the government at the time, asking whether the action was consistent with the party’s election manifesto and whether this was what a responsible state should look like.

Lawmakers including Indira Rana Magar and Ranju Darshana had also raised the issue.

However, lawmakers who had previously been vocal in questioning the government have largely remained silent over Rana’s detention.

Dhital did not raise the issue during Monday’s parliamentary meeting either. Instead, she praised Prime Minister Shah’s address to the United Nations General Assembly and the government’s preparedness ahead of recent floods and landslides.

Other lawmakers who spoke in the House on Monday, including RSP chief whip Kabindra Burlakoti, Manish Khanal, Ashish Gajurel, Khagendra Karn, Karishma Kathariya and Ashok Chaudhary, also did not raise the Cholendra Rana case.

RSP says Rana was taken into custody for his security

RSP spokesperson Jagadish Kharel said Rana was taken into custody because of a security threat and that Rana himself had subsequently requested additional security.

“After being taken home, he asked for additional security. The party’s understanding is also that security personnel took him into custody for his own protection,” Kharel told Onlinekhabar.

Kharel said he expected the Home Ministry to provide further clarification.

“The government needs to explain how and why he was detained. The Home Ministry can provide you with further clarification,” he said.

Opposition demands legal basis for detention

Opposition parties have strongly questioned the government over Cholendra Rana’s midnight detention.

The Nepali Congress, the main opposition party, has demanded an official explanation from the government and said it should make public the legal basis and justification for the detention.

Congress spokesperson Devraj Chalise said conflicting statements from government officials about the detention were a matter of serious concern.

“If the arrest was lawful, necessary and justified, the government should be able to make its clear legal basis and justification public,” Chalise said.

The Congress said that if Cholendra Rana was detained because of a specific security threat, the need for an investigation or another extraordinary circumstance, the state should provide credible grounds for such action.

The CPN-UML also said detaining the former chief justice without evidence or charges would constitute a serious violation of existing law and the justice system.

UML general secretary Shankar Pokhrel said the detention was contrary to the Constitution, democratic system and rule of law.

UML deputy general secretary Yogesh Bhattarai also questioned the legality of the midnight detention.

“The arrest of former Chief Justice Cholendra Rana is illegal and unjustified. The government must step back from such bizarre actions,” Bhattarai said.

Nepali Communist Party chair Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’, another opposition leader, warned that the government would have to pay a heavy political price if it continued detaining prominent individuals without sufficient grounds.

Speaking to journalists at the Federal Parliament building in Singha Durbar on Monday, Prachanda said the government’s intentions could ultimately prove damaging to itself.

“The facts will gradually come out. Such intentions will be harmful to the government itself,” he said.

Prachanda also argued that citing a security threat as the reason for Rana’s detention was merely an excuse by the government.

The Rastriya Prajatantra Party has also demanded an explanation from the government.

RPP parliamentary party leader Gyanendra Shahi questioned why Cholendra Rana was released if he was guilty and why he was detained if he was not.

“If the former chief justice is guilty, why was he released? If he is innocent, why was he arrested?” Shahi asked Home Minister Sudan Gurung. “The Home Minister’s position is not for personal ego, anger or political arrangements. State power is not a children’s game.”
