title.rendered: Who does Nepal’s police serve — power or the law?

content.rendered:
There was a time when seeing the police made me nervous. These days, I find myself feeling sorry for them.

I used to assume that anyone being led away by the police must have been a thief, a fraudster, a thug or a criminal. Now the instinct is almost reversed. When someone is arrested, I wonder whether they might emerge from custody with more public sympathy, greater political standing and a stronger claim to victimhood than they had when they went in.

That is an extraordinary position for a police force to find itself in.

So here is a question for Nepal Police, offered with a smile but not without seriousness: where exactly did you fail – in following orders, or in following the law?

The immediate occasion is the arrest of former chief justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana. But Rana is only the latest case in a pattern that should concern anyone who cares about the credibility of state institutions.

The issue is not whether Rana should be above scrutiny. He should not.

His record is well known. His tenure as chief justice was marked by controversy and ended in an impeachment process. His conduct before and during his time at the top of the judiciary has been extensively debated.

He was widely regarded as a powerful political operator, capable of influencing not only the judiciary but also the executive and legislature. Allegations about his political reach, including claims that he had a say in ministerial appointments, are hardly new.

None of this, however, answers the question the police had to answer.

What crime was committed? What evidence exists? What procedure was followed?

Those are not technicalities. They are the foundations of a democratic state. If there is evidence against Rana, investigate it. If there is a case, prosecute it. If the law requires that he be detained, then detain him. But the state does not get to substitute suspicion for evidence, or political instruction for due process.

That is where this story becomes much bigger than one former chief justice.

The strange logic of protection

The explanation surrounding Rana’s security makes the episode still more difficult to understand.

Reports suggested that he needed protection from threats associated with the Gen Z movement. If that was the case, the obvious response would have been to provide protection.

If someone threatened Rana, investigate the threat. Find those responsible. Take action against them. Instead, the person allegedly under threat was himself taken into custody.

Was the security threat real for only 11 hours? If so, what changed after that? And if there were people threatening him, why were they not the ones being pursued?

A written request for security has since emerged publicly.

There is something deeply unsettling about the image this creates: a man allegedly taken from his bed in the middle of the night now appealing to the same state apparatus for protection.

The absurdity is difficult to miss.

‘We were only following orders’ is not enough

There is a reason democratic policing places such emphasis on the rule of law, accountability and procedural fairness.

The police possess enormous coercive power. They can deprive people of their liberty. They can enter homes, conduct searches and initiate criminal proceedings.

That power is legitimate only when it is exercised within a legal framework.

Perhaps the order to arrest Rana came from the Prime Minister’s Office. Perhaps it came from the Home Ministry. Perhaps the police were simply instructed to act. But “we were following orders” cannot be the end of the conversation.

In a democracy, the law is the limit of state power. And when an order conflicts with the law, the police face their most important professional test.

Not when they arrest someone powerless. Not when they act against a suspect who has no political connections. The real test comes when the order comes from above.

Can the police still say no?

The real test for the police

This is why the question to the inspector general is not whether the police can arrest people.

Of course they can. Nepal Police has decades of experience investigating crimes, making arrests and pursuing prosecutions. It is not an institution that needs to be taught how to investigate.

The question is whether it can maintain professional independence when the political stakes are high.

Several recent high-profile arrests have raised questions about the evidence and legal grounds presented by the Home Administration. When arrests appear to be driven by political impulse rather than transparent procedure, the consequences can be precisely the opposite of what the government intends.

Politicians who might otherwise have struggled to attract sympathy can suddenly become victims.

KP Sharma Oli, Ramesh Lekhak and Bishnu Paudel, among others, have benefited from the public sympathy generated by confrontational state action, while several business figures have also found themselves caught up in similar episodes.

So, IGP sir, is something wrong with the system? Because the purpose of policing is to establish facts, not to manufacture martyrs.

Nepal has seen this before

There is an uncomfortable familiarity to all of this. Nepal’s political history is full of moments when rival factions have attempted to turn state institutions against one another.

When KP Sharma Oli and Madhav Kumar Nepal fought, when Pushpa Kamal Dahal and Baburam Bhattarai fell out, when Girija Prasad Koirala and Sher Bahadur Deuba were locked in political battles, the machinery of the state was repeatedly drawn into those struggles.

Cases were threatened. Police machinery was mobilised. Investigations appeared and disappeared with the political weather. People who might otherwise have faced prosecution sometimes found shelter behind political power.

The personalities change. The temptation does not.

Today, tensions between Rastriya Swatantra Party chair Rabi Lamichhane and prime minister and senior party leader Balen Shah have created another political faultline. Rana now appears to have become entangled in it.

Perhaps there is a perfectly legitimate case against him. If there is, the answer is straightforward. Produce the evidence. Follow the law. Follow the procedure. Make the process transparent. If the evidence justifies 11 hours in custody, so be it. If it justifies 11 years, so be it. But show the evidence.

That is the difference between the exercise of lawful power and the arbitrary exercise of power.

The silence of a party built on good governance

There is another striking feature of the current moment. The Rastriya Swatantra Party has rarely been shy about expressing an opinion. Its political voices have spoken on subjects ranging from the melting of the Himalayas to storms at sea.

Yet when an episode directly touches the party’s central promise of good governance, the response has been remarkably quiet. That matters.

Good governance is not a slogan to be deployed against one’s opponents. It is a principle that becomes meaningful precisely when applying it is politically inconvenient.

If the state is acting lawfully, explain why. If it is not, say so. Silence is not a substitute for accountability.

The question is bigger than Cholendra Rana

Nepalis have already made their demand clear. They want good governance.

The Gen Z uprising last year and the government formed after were products of that demand. Citizens who placed their hopes in a new political order are entitled to expect more than a change in the people operating the machinery of the state.

They should not have to watch one form of political influence being replaced by another. And the police should not be pulled into the personal ambitions, rivalries or calculations of politicians.

The principle is simple. The police must enforce the law. They must not become the servants of whoever happens to hold power.

A police force derives its immediate power from its weapons and its uniform. But that is not what gives it legitimacy. Legitimacy comes from public trust.

And trust is lost when citizens begin to suspect that the police do not ask whether something is lawful, but whether someone powerful has ordered it.

Cholendra Rana may be the latest example. But the real issue is not Rana. It is the police themselves.

When power gives the order, whom will the police obey? That is the question on which their credibility will ultimately depend.

title.rendered: Nepal knocked out of Asian Games cricket after quarterfinal against Sri Lanka washed out

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 29

Nepal’s campaign in the men’s cricket tournament at the 20th Asian Games in Japan has ended in the quarterfinals after their match against Sri Lanka was abandoned due to rain.

The third quarterfinal between Nepal and Sri Lanka was scheduled to begin at 5:45 am local time, but persistent rain prevented the match from getting underway.

With the match cancelled, Sri Lanka advanced to the semifinals on the basis of their higher ranking.

Nepal’s Asian Games campaign therefore came to an end at the quarterfinal stage.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress factions set different rules for 15th general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Disputes between the establishment and rival factions of the Nepali Congress over the party’s 15th General Convention have intensified, with the two sides adopting different provisions on delegate nominations, election procedures and nomination fees.

The party statute amended after the 14th General Convention had allowed the party president to nominate 40 general convention representatives. However, a subsequent special convention amended the statute and increased the number to 75.

The rival faction preparing to hold a separate general convention has set a different provision in its election directive, allowing the party president to nominate 300 general convention representatives.

As the two factions move ahead with separate convention processes, differences have emerged not only over the party statute, election directives and delegate selection procedures, but also over nomination fees for candidates.

Nepali Congress, led by President Gagan Thapa, who was elected at the special convention, has fixed the nomination fee for the central president at Rs 40,000.

The fee has been set at Rs 30,000 for vice-president and general secretary, Rs 20,000 for joint general secretary and Rs 11,000 for central committee members.

The rival faction led by Sher Bahadur Deuba has proposed lower fees in its election directive. Candidates for central president will have to pay Rs 30,000, while the fee for vice-president and general secretary has been fixed at Rs 25,000.

The nomination fee for joint general secretary is Rs 20,000 and Rs 10,000 for central committee members.

This means candidates contesting for central president under the Deuba faction’s convention would pay Rs 10,000 less than those contesting under the Thapa-led convention. The difference is Rs 5,000 for vice-president and general secretary and Rs 1,000 for central committee members.

The two factions have set the same Rs 20,000 nomination fee for candidates seeking the post of joint general secretary.

Differences in nomination fees also extend to lower levels of the party.

Under the Thapa-led convention, the fee has been set at Rs 20,000 for provincial president, Rs 15,000 for district president, Rs 10,000 for House of Representatives constituency president and Rs 7,000 for provincial assembly constituency president.

The Deuba-led faction has proposed Rs 10,000 for provincial president, Rs 5,000 for district president, Rs 3,500 for House of Representatives constituency president and Rs 2,500 for provincial assembly constituency president.

The differences are even wider at the local level.

The Thapa-led convention has fixed nomination fees of Rs 1,000 for ward president, Rs 5,000 for rural municipality and municipality presidents, and Rs 7,000 for sub-metropolitan and metropolitan city presidents.

The Deuba-led faction has set the fee at Rs 250 for ward president, Rs 1,000 for rural municipality president, Rs 2,000 for municipality president and Rs 2,500 for sub-metropolitan and metropolitan city presidents.

The Thapa-led establishment faction has scheduled its 15th General Convention for October 2, while the Deuba-led faction has set its central general convention for December 7 to 9.

The establishment faction is also preparing to postpone its convention by a few days.

title.rendered: Nepal to import 1,154 MW of electricity for winter

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) plans to import 1,154 megawatts of electricity from India between January and May to meet rising winter demand and offset losses in hydropower generation caused by recent floods and landslides.

NEA Managing Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha said domestic generation during the dry season would not be sufficient to meet projected demand.

According to Shrestha, Nepal is expected to have around 1,218 MW of electricity available from domestic generation during the dry season, while winter peak demand is projected to reach 2,272 MW.

The NEA plans to meet the shortfall through imports from several points in India.

Under the plan, 600 MW will be imported through the Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur transmission line, 54 MW through Tanakpur-Mahendranagar, 350 MW from various points in Bihar and 150 MW through the Real-Time/RTC mechanism, bringing total planned imports to 1,154 MW.

Shrestha said imports would be necessary because domestic generation alone would not be able to meet winter demand.

Focus on Kathmandu Valley

The NEA said strengthening the transmission and distribution systems has been prioritised to ensure reliable electricity supply during the coming winter.

Last winter, peak electricity demand in Kathmandu Valley reached around 700 MW. The NEA expects demand to increase by about 10 percent this year.

“Load is higher in Kathmandu Valley during winter. We recorded a peak demand of 700 MW last year, and we estimate it will increase by around 10 percent this year,” Shrestha said. “We are preparing to meet that additional demand.”

The authority plans to shift some of the load from older substations in the Kathmandu Valley to newly charged or soon-to-be-charged substations.

It plans to transfer loads from heavily loaded feeders and transformers through substations including Chobhar, Futung and Mulpani.

The NEA has also formed a four- to five-member task force led by the head of its Bagmati Provincial Office to study and manage the distribution of electricity loads. The team has already begun its work, according to Shrestha.

The authority also plans to charge the 11 kV underground cables installed in the Kathmandu Valley before the winter begins. Some of the load from heavily loaded substations will be shifted through these cables.

Repairing flood-damaged transmission infrastructure

The NEA is also working to restore the 220 kV transmission infrastructure damaged by the Bhotekoshi floods.

A 220 kV transmission line running from the Chilime Hub through the 3B Hub towards the upper areas was damaged in the floods. However, Shrestha said rebuilding the 3 B Hub at its previous location immediately would not be possible.

The flood swept away the 3B Hub substation itself, he said, adding that a new substation will have to be constructed in the area. Since the NEA owns land in the Chilime area, the authority plans to build a new 3B Hub there.

The NEA also plans to use the Kulekhani reservoir as an important source of electricity during the winter. Shrestha said water storage at Kulekhani is currently sufficient.

The authority plans to manage winter demand through a combination of domestic generation, electricity imports from India, hydropower reservoirs such as Kulekhani, and improvements to the transmission and distribution network.

“Whatever it takes, our responsibility is to provide electricity to the public,” Shrestha said. “But providing electricity alone is not enough. We have to provide electricity that is reliable and of good quality.”

title.rendered: Supreme Court refuses to order release of two ANFA officials

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The Supreme Court has refused to order the release of All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) treasurer Rabindra Joshi and accounts officer Sanjiv Pandey, who are in police custody in connection with an ongoing investigation.

A joint bench of Justices Abdul Aziz Musalman and Balkrishna Dhakal declined to order Joshi’s release.

Similarly, a separate joint bench comprising Justices Mahesh Sharma Paudel and Sunil Kumar Pokharel refused to order Pandey’s release.

The court also ordered that both cases be kept with the respective case files and dealt with according to law.

Joshi’s wife, Shobha Joshi, and Pandey’s wife, Anita Pandey, had separately filed habeas corpus petitions at the Supreme Court, claiming that their husbands were being unlawfully detained.

The Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police arrested Joshi and Pandey on September 18 after raiding the ANFA headquarters in Satdobato.

The two are being investigated over alleged match-fixing, irregularities and fraud. The Lalitpur District Court had previously granted the CIB permission to keep them in custody for further investigation.

Police have also been investigating allegations related to ANFA’s financial and administrative activities, including match arrangements and World Cup ticket sales. The allegations remain under investigation.

The Kathmandu District Court has granted police permission to keep businessman Durga Prasai in custody for three days while investigating a cybercrime case.

Police have not disclosed further details about the specific cybercrime allegations under investigation.

title.rendered: ‘Shark Tank Nepal’ Season 2 to air after Dashain

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The second season of Himalayan Television’s popular reality show Shark Tank Nepal will begin airing shortly after Dashain.

At a press conference held at Hotel Everest in Kathmandu on Monday to announce the new season, Dharma Raj Bhusal, chairman and managing director of Himalayan Television, said Season 2 would be bigger and more refined than the first season.

“The size of the business has grown by 60 to 65 per cent compared to Season 1,” Bhusal said. “Everyone involved in the show has shown much greater maturity this time. In terms of storytelling and business evaluation, Season 2 has become bigger and better.”

The show will air two episodes a week on Himalayan Television at 8 pm and will conclude within around two and a half months.

Preparations for Season 3 will begin as soon as Season 2 starts airing, he said.

Shyam Kandel, executive director of Himalayan Television, said he felt emotional recalling the commitment he made four years ago to bring the Shark Tank format to Nepal.

“The show has millions of viewers not only in Nepal but also outside the country,” Kandel said. “Deals worth around Rs 600 million have been made in Season 2, which clearly shows how much bigger and more successful the second season has become.”

The event also featured the signing of sponsorship agreements between Himalayan Television and companies associated with Season 2.

Same sharks return for Season 2

All five sharks from Season 1 have returned for the second season.

They are Ananda Bagaria, managing director of Nimbus Group; Cabinet Shrestha, co-founder and chairman of Agni Group; Saurabh Jyoti, investor at Padma Jyoti Group and chairman of Syakar Trading Company; Ritu Singh Vaidya, managing director of Vaidya’s Organization of Industries and Trading Houses; and Hemraj Dhakal, co-founder and managing director of IME Group.

The sharks shared their experiences from the first season and discussed various aspects of the new season.

Bagaria said the sharks had been nervous during the first season because they had little experience or practice in evaluating businesses.

“After completing Season 2, I feel this is the beginning of an economic revolution,” he said.

Shrestha said he was excited about the platform that Shark Tank Nepal has created for entrepreneurs.

“I was amazed to hear the business model of a 17-year-old in Season 2 who did not have even a single rupee to invest,” he said. “New business models are getting new opportunities through a new platform.”

Jyoti said Himalayan Television had taken a significant risk by bringing the show to Nepal in its first season.

“Now the results can be seen in Season 2,” he said. “Shark Tank is not just a television show. It has also made a valuable contribution to the economy and inspired people to believe that their ideas can be good and that they too can become entrepreneurs.”

Vaidya described Shark Tank Nepal as an effective platform that has brought the programme closer to the economy and business sector.

“It was a new experience to evaluate new business models and concepts,” she said. “Because of this programme, many people have been able to start new businesses.”

Dhakal said sitting in a position where he had to make investment decisions despite being nervous during Season 1 had been a new experience.

“Season 1 succeeded in bringing hope, confidence and ideas to people who wanted to start businesses, and Season 2 has become even better,” he said. “Shark Tank has become a unique source of inspiration and encouragement for startups.”

content.rendered:
The most expensive consequence of Bhotekoshi was not the flood itself. It was the bill it created.

The government-led Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment placed direct physical damage and economic losses at Rs408.29 billion and estimated Rs723.31 billion for recovery, reconstruction, livelihood restoration, risk reduction and more resilient rebuilding. The second figure is not an invoice already payable by the government. It is an economy-wide estimate. Yet its scale shows how quickly a mountain disaster can become a national public-finance problem.

The comparison with Nepal’s budget makes the burden visible. The Rs723.31 billion recovery estimate is roughly one-third of the federal budget for 2026/27 and more than half of its recurrent expenditure. The Rs408.29 billion disaster impact is close to the entire annual capital budget.

It is also more than three times the revised cost of the Kathmandu–Tarai/Madhesh Fast Track, one of Nepal’s largest national-priority transport projects. Put differently, the estimated recovery requirement could finance more than three expressways at today’s revised project cost, although reconstruction needs and highway costs are not directly interchangeable. The comparison shows opportunity cost, not a claim that the government must immediately pay the full amount.

Reconstruction will arrive through many projects and funding sources over several years, but it can consume fiscal space, administrative attention and development time on that scale. Every rupee redirected to restore a bridge, grid or settlement is a rupee unavailable for a planned school, hospital, irrigation scheme or new road unless revenue, grants or borrowing expand.

The comparison with debt is equally important, but it must be made carefully. Nepal was assessed at low risk of external and overall debt distress before the disaster, with public debt at 48.1 percent of GDP in 2024/25.

Bhotekoshi did not create an automatic debt crisis. The warning is cumulative. Every emergency allocation, revenue interruption, guarantee, distressed public enterprise and delayed development project narrows the room available for the next shock.

The disaster therefore tested whether the state can distinguish private loss from public obligation before political pressure turns one into the other. It also tested whether Nepal can finance reconstruction without repeatedly sacrificing planned development or rebuilding the same exposure.

How physical destruction enters the budget

Every budget tells two stories. One records today’s expenditure. The other hides tomorrow’s liabilities.

Nepal’s bridges, mountain highways and hydropower plants appear in government accounts as completed assets. Increasingly, they should also be understood as contingent fiscal liabilities whose cost becomes visible only when rivers reclaim them.

A destroyed government bridge is a direct public loss. Rescue, temporary shelter and restoration of essential services demand immediate spending. Damage to a state-owned electricity asset can create obligations through ownership, lending or guarantees. A public-private project can return risk to the government through contracts, renegotiation or pressure to maintain an essential service. These costs enter the budget through identifiable channels.

The harder liabilities are implicit. Government may have no prior legal duty to rebuild private homes, rescue uninsured firms or compensate hydropower investors. But support becomes difficult to avoid when households lose shelter, employers cannot restart, banks face impaired loans, electricity supply is disrupted, or local governments cannot restore basic services. A private loss can then migrate onto the public balance sheet through relief, subsidies, credit support, recapitalisation, guarantees or reconstruction grants.

Disasters also weaken the revenue side. Interrupted trade, tourism, transport, power generation and business activity can reduce customs duties, taxes, royalties and local revenue just as public expenditure rises. Government must then draw on reserves, reallocate the budget, mobilise grants and concessional finance, or borrow.

The fiscal cost is therefore not one reconstruction number. It is the combined movement of expenditure, revenue, public assets, guarantees, state enterprises, financing needs and postponed priorities.

Nepal’s missing fiscal architecture

Nepal does not lack climate institutions. It lacks a coherent fiscal architecture that connects them.

Today, disaster funds, the Climate Budget Code, the Climate Change Financing Framework, contingent credit, fiscal-risk reporting and investment appraisal through the National Project Bank largely operate as parallel mechanisms. The next phase of reform is not creating another institution. It is making the existing ones function as one system.

That system should begin with a common view of exposure: what government owns; what federal, provincial and local bodies are responsible for; which guarantees and contracts exist; what support may become politically unavoidable; and which financing instrument responds at each level of loss.

Hazard information must reach project approval, asset registers, annual budgets, debt strategy and the Fiscal Risk Statement. The National Project Bank should then serve as the front door of this architecture. A project that cannot demonstrate its exposure, resilience standard, maintenance plan and lifecycle cost should not enter the budget merely because its construction financing is available.

At the other end, fiscal-risk reporting should show the stock of vulnerable assets and the liabilities attached to them. Between those two points, budget codes and financing frameworks should track whether spending reduces exposure or simply replaces damaged structures.

Otherwise, Nepal will continue identifying physical risk in technical reports while discovering its fiscal meaning only after disaster.

International practice offers bounded lessons. New Zealand links infrastructure risk with investment and asset-management decisions. Japan’s river-basin approach combines prevention, exposure reduction, land use, infrastructure and preparedness rather than treating each damaged structure separately. Fiji uses layered disaster-risk financing, including contingent credit, while recognising that finance cannot substitute for prevention.

Nepal does not need to copy these systems. It needs to connect risk information, investment decisions and pre-arranged finance with equal discipline.

Immediate reforms

First, strengthen fiscal-risk disclosure. The annual Fiscal Risk Statement should include a climate- and disaster-risk annex separating direct public losses, explicit guarantees, contractual obligations, implicit support expectations, revenue effects, public-enterprise and public-private partnership exposure, and provincial and local risks. Scenario ranges would be more credible than a single headline figure and would clarify which losses remain private, which are shared and which may reach the state.

Second, make resilience an investment gate. The National Project Bank already filters and prioritises major public investments; climate-risk screening should become an approval condition rather than an optional technical review. Roads, bridges, energy facilities, irrigation systems and public buildings should not advance to budget approval without documented hazard exposure, resilient design, maintenance responsibility and climate-adjusted lifecycle cost.

Rebuilding the same vulnerability is not reconstruction. It is the creation of another public liability.

Reconstruction creates visible political rewards. Prevention creates invisible success. That is the political economy behind Nepal’s repeated preference for repairing assets after failure rather than financing resilience before it. An investment gate matters because it shifts prevention from ministerial discretion to a condition for receiving public money.

Medium-term reforms

Third, complete layered disaster finance. Frequent, lower-cost shocks should be covered through predictable contingency appropriations and disaster funds. Severe events require pre-arranged concessional credit and rapid grant mobilisation. Insurable assets need carefully designed risk-transfer mechanisms.

The objective is not to socialise every loss, but to decide in advance which instrument responds, at what threshold and who retains the remaining risk.

Fourth, connect intergovernmental responsibility to fiscal capacity and asset ownership. Cost sharing among federal, provincial and local governments should reflect who owns the asset, who controlled its design and maintenance, who can finance recovery and whether resilience standards were followed.

Reliable asset registers and transparent assessments are essential. Without them, fiscal federalism can distribute money after disaster without distributing responsibility before it.

Bhotekoshi did not prove that Nepal is entering a debt crisis. It demonstrated something more useful: physical destruction can move rapidly into expenditure pressure, revenue loss, contingent liabilities and difficult budget choices.

The policy response should therefore extend beyond relief and engineering. Nepal must decide how risk is recorded, priced, financed and prevented across the entire public-investment cycle.

The next river will not ask whether Nepal created another policy. It will ask whether today’s assets were designed to survive tomorrow’s climate.

title.rendered: Traffic police step up vehicle monitoring ahead of festive season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Traffic police have intensified vehicle inspections and monitoring across Kathmandu Valley as the major festive season approaches, citing increased passenger movement and the risk of ticket fraud and traffic violations.

Naresh Raj Subedi, superintendent of police and spokesperson for the Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office, said monitoring has been stepped up as passenger movement across the country is expected to increase significantly during the festive period.

He said unauthorised individuals without identification could sell bus tickets, charge passengers excessive fares, issue more tickets than the vehicle’s seating capacity or sell multiple tickets for the same seat.

Traffic police are also concerned about violations arising from speeding, overloaded vehicles and unhealthy competition between vehicles on the roads.

Passenger help desks at key locations

Subedi said passenger help desks will be established at major locations across Kathmandu Valley to prioritise passenger safety and facilitate joint inspections and monitoring.

Help desks will be set up at bus parks, Chabahil, Koteshwor, Chapagaun, Balkhu, Pulchowk, Nagdhunga, Kalanki, Bhimdhunga and Sankhu, among other locations.

Vehicles will undergo mechanical inspections as part of the monitoring drive, while pollution checks will also be carried out.

Traffic police said the legal requirement for long-distance vehicles to have two drivers will be strictly enforced.

Monitoring of drunk driving will also be intensified during the festive season, with traffic police using breathalysers to check drivers.

Traffic police will maintain a presence on major roads during both daytime and nighttime to strengthen road safety and provide assistance to commuters.

Parking management at temples

Traffic police will also be deployed around temples and other religious sites where large crowds of devotees are expected during the festive period.

Parking arrangements will be managed at such locations to help prevent congestion and maintain smooth traffic flow.

The traffic office said a coordinated mechanism involving civil police, traffic police, the Department of Transport Management, Department of Roads and the metropolitan police will be mobilised for the festive-season traffic management drive.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

From a proposed change to abortion rules for minors to widespread damage to the country’s power and road infrastructure, several major developments are shaping today’s news.

Floods and landslides have disrupted around 1,000 MW of electricity generation, while rescue efforts continue after an avalanche on Himlung Himal claimed two lives. Police have also arrested medical businessman Durga Prasai again, while another man has been detained over alleged claims of ties to people associated with Home Minister Sudan Gurung.

Elsewhere, the government has proposed six months of paid maternity leave as a population-growth incentive, the FNCCI has called for the withdrawal of VAT on electricity tariffs, and authorities are working to reopen the flood-blocked BP Highway ahead of the festive season.

Proposed abortion law for minors sparks concerns among gynaecologists

The government has proposed allowing girls under 18 who become pregnant through rape or incest to undergo abortion at any stage of pregnancy. The proposed provision seeks to remove the existing 28-week limit and allow abortion “at any stage” of pregnancy.

Floods, landslides disrupt around 1,000 MW of power generation

Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has said floods and landslides this year have disrupted around 1,000 MW of electricity generation in Nepal’s national power system.

Two from Sankhuwasabha killed in avalanche on Himlung Himal

Two men from Sankhuwasabha district have died after being caught in an avalanche on Himlung Himal in Manang district. The deceased have been identified as Chhebi Bhote of Bhotkhola Rural Municipality-3 and Pasang Bhote of Bhotkhola-2, according to Wangchhedar Bhote, chairperson of Bhotkhola Rural Municipality.

Durga Prasai arrested again

Medical businessman Durga Prasai has been arrested. The Central Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police at Bhotahiti arrested Prasai. The bureau took him into custody from Bhaktapur. It has not said anything about the reason for the arrest. Prasai has repeatedly been arrested and released. Most of the time, he has been arrested on cyber offences.

Man arrested over alleged claim of ties to Home Minister’s aides

Police have arrested a man accused of claiming close ties with people associated with Home Minister Sudan Gurung and using those alleged connections in phone conversations to negotiate deals. The arrested man has been identified as 37-year-old Dharmaraj Malla, also known as Ashish Malla, of Nepalgunj Sub-Metropolitan City-4, Banke. A team from the Kathmandu District Police Range arrested him.

6-month paid maternity leave proposed to boost population growth

Minister for Health and Food Hygiene Nisha Mehta has said incentives through maternity leave are also being proposed to encourage population growth.

She made the statement while presenting the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights (First Amendment) Bill, 2026 in the House of Representatives on Monday

FNCCI calls for withdrawal of VAT on electricity tariff

The Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI) has called on the government to withdraw the value-added tax (VAT) imposed on electricity tariffs from the current fiscal year 2026/27, saying it has increased production costs.

Efforts underway to reopen flood-blocked BP Highway

Efforts are underway to reopen the BP Highway, which has been blocked by landslides and flood-induced road erosion. The highway was completely obstructed by landslides at Chaukidanda in Namobuddha-6, Charsaybesi in Roshi-7, Gimdi Besi in Roshi-8 and Mamti in Roshi-11.

Transport operators ask government not to raise fuel prices during festive season

Transport operators have called on the government not to increase petroleum prices during the festive season. Saroj Sitoula, president of the Nepal National Federation of Transport Entrepreneurs, said transport operators would also refrain from raising fares if fuel prices were kept unchanged.

title.rendered: Floods, landslides disrupt around 1,000 MW of power generation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has said floods and landslides this year have disrupted around 1,000 MW of electricity generation in Nepal’s national power system.

Speaking to journalists at the Parliament building in Singha Durbar on Monday, Shrestha said floods and landslides had caused significant damage to hydropower infrastructure, affecting generation, transmission and distribution systems.

He said around 1,000 MW of generation capacity has been disrupted due to damage to electricity infrastructure caused by the disasters.

Shrestha also said around 370 MW of electricity generated by 13 hydropower projects has been affected after the Kaligandaki Corridor transmission line was disrupted by the recent rainfall.

According to him, the disruption has highlighted the difficulty of evacuating electricity when transmission infrastructure is not available alongside generation capacity.

Shrestha said charging the Hetauda-Dhalkebar transmission line would make it easier to transmit electricity generated in the east to the west and vice versa, helping address the challenges of connecting the country’s eastern and western power systems.

He said the government is prioritising domestic generation to manage the power system and is importing electricity from India to cover any shortfall.

title.rendered: Man arrested over alleged claim of ties to Home Minister’s aides

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Police have arrested a man accused of claiming close ties with people associated with Home Minister Sudan Gurung and using those alleged connections in phone conversations to negotiate deals.

The arrested man has been identified as 37-year-old Dharmaraj Malla, also known as Ashish Malla, of Nepalgunj Sub-Metropolitan City-4, Banke. A team from the Kathmandu District Police Range arrested him.

An audio recording had surfaced in which Malla and another person allegedly claimed to have connections with people close to the home minister while negotiating a deal.

According to Dan Bahadur Thapa, superintendent of police and spokesperson for the Kathmandu District Police Range, Malla was also found to have six cases registered against him.

Thapa said Malla was arrested after police questioned him about the authenticity of the audio recording and he allegedly behaved indecently toward the police during the inquiry.

Police have obtained a two-day remand to investigate him on a charge of indecent behaviour.

According to police, a case has been filed against Malla in Banke under the Telecommunications Act, in which he is a fugitive.

Police said three other cases of indecent behaviour, one fraud case and one banking offence case have also been registered against him in Banke.

title.rendered: Two from Sankhuwasabha killed in avalanche on Himlung Himal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Two men from Sankhuwasabha district have died after being caught in an avalanche on Himlung Himal in Manang district.

The deceased have been identified as Chhebi Bhote of Bhotkhola Rural Municipality-3 and Pasang Bhote of Bhotkhola-2, according to Wangchhedar Bhote, chairperson of Bhotkhola Rural Municipality.

They died after an avalanche struck the Himlung Himal area on Sunday, September 27.

The two were in the area for mountaineering and other activities around Himlung Himal when they were caught in the avalanche.

The avalanche occurred in Narpa Bhumi Rural Municipality-5 of Manang.

According to the rural municipality chairperson, the bodies of both men were brought to Kathmandu by Kailash Helicopter for postmortem at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.

Both Chhebi and Pasang were working as tourist guides.

Chairperson Bhote said the bodies will be cremated in Kathmandu after the postmortem.

title.rendered: Proposed abortion law for minors sparks concerns among gynaecologists

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The government has proposed allowing girls under 18 who become pregnant through rape or incest to undergo abortion at any stage of pregnancy. The proposed provision seeks to remove the existing 28-week limit and allow abortion “at any stage” of pregnancy.

The provision has been proposed in a bill to amend the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2018. Health and Food Hygiene Minister Nisha Mehta registered the bill at the House of Representatives on September 21, seeking to change the existing provisions and definition related to safe abortion.

Experts have described the proposal to allow abortion at any stage without adequately considering technical and practical aspects as insensitive and inhumane. They argue that the provision could legalise the termination of pregnancies involving fetuses capable of surviving outside the womb. They say that if the bill is passed in its current form, it could allow the termination of pregnancies involving potentially viable babies.

Doctors say a fetus is fully developed by 26 weeks. Senior obstetrician and gynaecologist Dr Jageshwar Gautam said the proposal to allow abortion after 22 weeks was problematic from both ethical and practical perspectives. “A baby after 26 weeks can cry and move,” Gautam said. “After 22 weeks, it is not abortion but delivery. How can a doctor kill a living baby?”

According to the World Health Organization, a pregnancy before 22 weeks or involving a fetus weighing less than 500 grams is classified as an abortion. Experts say a baby born after that stage is considered premature. Gautam said he had treated and saved hundreds of babies born at 26 weeks and argued that a baby capable of being born alive at that stage should not be killed in the name of abortion.

“I have saved many babies born at 26 weeks. Allowing abortion at any stage directly means killing a baby,” Gautam said. “We cannot implement a law to kill a baby.” Dr Padam Raj Pant, president of the Nepal Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, said the proposed provision was unacceptable.

“We completely reject abortion after 22 weeks. These days, babies born at 26 weeks are also surviving. Such a baby cannot be killed after birth,” Pant said. “Such a provision could encourage abortions, which would pose risks to women’s health.” Gynaecologists say the proposed provision could create various health risks as well as ethical dilemmas for healthcare workers.

“In cases of pregnancy resulting from rape or incest, family members sometimes pressure women to undergo abortion, saying they do not want to pursue a legal case and that the matter has already been settled,” Pant said. “Some babies are born breathing even after 22 weeks. In such cases, there is no question of killing a baby after birth. That is not abortion; it is delivery.”

Doctors say the risks associated with delivery increase as pregnancy progresses from 22 to 28 and 30 weeks. If normal delivery itself carries risks, inducing an abortion with medication could pose additional risks to the mother’s life, they said. Gynaecologists argue that abortion at any stage should be permitted when necessary to save the mother’s life in an emergency, but that such a provision should not apply under normal circumstances.

Gautam objected to the proposal to allow abortion at any stage, arguing that it could result in the killing of babies capable of surviving outside the womb. “If a woman comes at 28 weeks and asks a doctor to abort her baby, which doctor can kill it?” Gautam asked. “That would be like strangling the baby to death.” He said the right of a baby to survive should not be disregarded regardless of how the pregnancy occurred. “The baby does not know whether the pregnancy resulted from rape or consensual sex. The baby has a right to live,” he said.

Who will assume responsibility for a baby born alive?

Senior obstetrician and gynaecologist Dr Kirtipal Subedi said the proposed legal provision on abortion should be viewed from two different perspectives. He said the issue of allowing abortion at any stage for girls under 18 who become pregnant through rape or incest was highly sensitive and should not be decided hastily.

Some girls may be unable to disclose that they have been raped, while families may only discover the pregnancy at a late stage. If the pregnancy is detected only at 28 or 30 weeks, the existing time limit can create difficulties, he said. “In some cases, a girl may not be able to say that she was raped. By the time the pregnancy becomes visible, it may already be 28 or 30 weeks,” Subedi said.

In such cases, he said, not only the condition of the fetus but also the girl’s social and family circumstances could become complicated. He said lawmakers should also consider the possibility that a girl who becomes pregnant through rape could face rejection by her family or social exclusion. However, Subedi said another complication could arise if the pregnancy is detected only after 26 or 27 weeks.

Since a baby born after that stage may have a chance of survival, the law should also clearly address what happens to a baby born alive following an attempted abortion, he said. “If it is detected and an abortion is carried out after 26 or 27 weeks, the baby could survive,” Subedi said. “The family may refuse to take responsibility, and the perpetrator may be unknown or unavailable. The law should make it clear in advance whether the state or the family will assume responsibility after the baby is born.”

Dr Shree Prasad Adhikari, director of Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital in Thapathali, also said that babies born at 28 or 30 weeks may survive and that the state should introduce clear legal provisions concerning their rights and future care. Gynaecologists said the law should clearly specify where a baby born alive would be placed, who would provide medical treatment, who would be responsible for care and education, and how parental, property and other legal rights would be ensured after the child reaches adulthood.

“Babies after 26 weeks can be born alive. Doctors cannot kill them. The state must establish in writing provisions concerning their right to live, education, parental rights, property rights and other rights,” Adhikari said. He said situations in which the mother’s life is at risk should not be treated under the same legal provision as pregnancies involving minors who have become pregnant through rape or incest.

According to Adhikari, the problems and responsibilities arising from these two situations are different and therefore require separate analysis. He said the proposed provision allowing abortion at any stage when the mother’s life is at risk was appropriate. However, he said the social, legal and health complications arising from allowing abortion at any stage for minors who become pregnant through rape or incest should be studied.

“There needs to be a major debate on what should be done in cases involving the rape of a minor after 28 weeks,” Adhikari said. “If the state does not clearly determine what responsibilities it will have in the future and how they will be managed, a hasty decision could create another complication.”

Dr Padam Raj Pant also agreed with the concerns raised by other experts. He said that if the proposed provision allows abortion at any stage, the law must clearly establish responsibility for the treatment, protection, care and civil rights of a baby born alive. “A family may be unable to take responsibility after a child is born following a rape-related pregnancy,” he said. “Who will be responsible for the child’s upbringing, citizenship and other rights? This issue must be addressed by law.”

The Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2018, currently allows abortion up to 28 weeks in certain cases. The government is seeking to relax the provision by allowing abortion at any stage in specified circumstances. However, regulations under the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act have still not been formulated eight years after the law was enacted, partly due to opposition from medical experts.

The Act states that a woman has the right to safe abortion up to 28 weeks, with her consent, if the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest. After the Act was passed, the Ministry of Health also held discussions with obstetricians and gynaecologists on the necessary directives and regulations.

However, doctors could not reach an agreement on the issue. They have been strongly calling for the time limit for abortion in pregnancies resulting from rape to be reduced to 22 weeks. Nepal first introduced a law on safe abortion in 2002. In general, the existing provision allows a pregnant woman to obtain a safe abortion, with her consent, up to 12 weeks of pregnancy.

title.rendered: Aloft Kathmandu Thamel named Nepal’s Leading Hotel 2026 at World Travel Awards

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Aloft by Marriott Kathmandu has been named Nepal’s Leading Hotel 2026 at the World Travel Awards.

The award was announced during the World Travel Awards Asia, Oceania & Indian Ocean Gala Ceremony held on September 27 at CROSSROADS Maldives.

The recognition highlights the hotel’s focus on contemporary design and guest experiences, as well as its contribution to Kathmandu’s tourism sector.

Operating since 2019, the 167-room lifestyle hotel combines contemporary spaces with elements of Nepali art, music and cuisine.

“Being named Nepal’s Leading Hotel 2026 by the World Travel Awards is a proud moment for our entire team,” said Vikram Singh, general manager of Aloft by Marriott Kathmandu Thamel.

Commenting on the current tourism environment, Singh said that despite the impact of recent floods in parts of the country, tourism services in much of Nepal continue to operate normally.

“We hope this recognition further highlights the resilience of Nepal’s tourism industry and the many destinations that continue to welcome visitors,” he said.

Established in 1993, the World Travel Awards recognises achievements across the global tourism and hospitality sectors.

Aloft Kathmandu Thamel is operated by Chhaya Devi Complex Ltd. under a licence from Marriott International, Inc.

title.rendered: The 3Cs that hold a cooperative together

content.rendered:
The story of cooperatives in Nepal is not particularly old. It began on April 2, 1957, when Bakhan Cooperative Society was established in what was then Bakhanpur, now Sharadanagar, Chitwan, becoming the country’s first cooperative institution. Given this history, cooperatives may appear, at first glance, to be built around money: savings, loans, investment, interest and returns. But look more closely, and the real story of a cooperative begins not with money, but with people and trust. That trust is sustained, day after day, by three simple yet powerful elements: information, timing and understanding.

Most urban cooperatives that have emerged over the past two or three decades were founded by people who came to the cities to run businesses, take up jobs, work as daily wage earners or pursue other professions. They were bound not by capital, but by a shared purpose. Some may not have had much money, but they shared a common goal. This is why a cooperative is never merely an economic institution; it is also an institution of shared trust.

At monthly Board of Directors meetings, discussions naturally arise over whether loans have been disbursed, where investments have been made and what decisions have been taken. Yet if even one small thing goes wrong—if information is not exchanged in time—it can breed suspicion, misunderstanding and tension. The real question, then, is not simply, “Who failed to call whom?” It runs deeper: have we, as an institution, built a system that ensures the right information reaches the right person, at the right time, in the right way?

The first “C” is Communication, the foundation of any functioning institution. The communication model developed by Shannon and Weaver describes communication as a process involving a sender, a message, a medium and a receiver, with “noise” or disruption potentially distorting the message along the way. Later scholars such as Berlo and Schramm added the importance of feedback and a shared field of experience, recognising that communication involves not only what is said but also how it is interpreted and how the receiver responds.

This is why the statements “I already told them” and “I never got any information” can both be sincerely believed. The gap between them is a textbook example of communication “noise”. In a cooperative, managerial communication takes this basic process to the institutional level through the systematic sharing of plans, decisions, responsibilities and results among the appropriate people and levels of the organisation.

The International Cooperative Alliance (ICA) defines a cooperative as a member-owned and democratically controlled institution. It links active member participation and the accountability of elected representatives to the foundational principles of cooperatives. When Board members are left out of the information loop on important decisions, the administrative outcome may still be that “the work got done”. But that does not necessarily build the institutional trust that comes from people knowing, understanding and moving forward together.

The second “C” is Chronology, or timing. This is not simply about the clock. It is also about choosing the right medium at the right time. Daft and Lengel’s Media Richness Theory suggests that high-risk or ambiguous information is better communicated through “richer” channels, such as telephone calls or meetings, while low-risk and straightforward information can be conveyed through “leaner” channels such as text messages or notices.

Consider a decision involving significant risk and multiple stakeholders, such as the disbursement of a loan. If the relevant information does not reach everyone at the appropriate time, questions can quickly arise: “Why were we not told?” or “How was this decision made?” Research on the banking sector in Kathmandu Valley has also found a significant positive relationship between managerial communication and decision-making.

The lesson is straightforward: making the right decision is not enough. The information needed to make and understand that decision must reach the relevant people through the appropriate medium and at the appropriate time. Responses such as “I did not call, so they were not informed” or “The phone was not picked up, so I could not inform them” point to a failure to establish an appropriate communication process. Neither should be considered an adequate institutional response.

Ensuring that information reaches the right people at the right time requires a system. But a system alone cannot complete institutional communication. If something is discussed in a meeting but no written record is made, different memories and interpretations can emerge afterwards. This is another way Shannon and Weaver’s “noise” can manifest at the institutional level.

A simple communication protocol can therefore be valuable for cooperatives. It can clarify which information must be shared immediately and through which medium, which decisions must be tabled at meetings, and which decisions must be documented in writing. The ICA has also noted that modern mobile and internet technologies can facilitate democratic participation, while emphasizing that the value of in-person discussion and participation remains important.

WhatsApp, Viber and email are not solutions in themselves. The real solution is a culture in which the right information travels through the right medium at the right time.

But even when information and timing are right, a third “C” is necessary: Comprehension. Without mutual understanding, trust cannot be sustained.

Mayer, Davis and Schoorman’s organisational trust model identifies three important attributes of trust: ability, or confidence in a person’s competence to perform their responsibilities; benevolence, or confidence that they care about the interests of others; and integrity, or confidence that they will follow agreed principles and procedures.

When a decision is questioned, the concern may not always be about the decision-maker’s competence. It may instead be about integrity and process. “Why wasn’t I told about it?” can gradually become “Why wasn’t I trusted to hear it?”

Research on cooperative governance has similarly found a significant relationship between members’ perceptions of their involvement in governance and their confidence in directors. The purpose of communication, therefore, is not to involve everyone in every minor detail. It is to ensure that each person receives the information relevant to their role and responsibilities. That is what allows ability, benevolence and integrity to be demonstrated in practice.

Ultimately, the future of a cooperative is not determined by an impressive office or an attractive financial scheme alone. It is also determined by how its people communicate with one another.

The three dimensions—clarity of information, appropriateness of medium and timing, and understanding built on ability, benevolence and integrity—work together to build institutional trust. A single “seen” mark is no proof of comprehension. A single phone call does not fulfil the full responsibility of transparency. And a single meeting does not end the conversation.

A healthy cooperative culture should instead routinely ask four simple questions: Who needs this information? By when do they need it? How should it be delivered? And how should feedback be gathered once a decision has been made?

The founders of Nepal’s cooperative movement planted the seeds of collective trust more than seven decades ago. It is now up to today’s generation to nurture that trust through these three elements. The real strength of a cooperative is not found in its ledger alone, but in the trust among its members.

And perhaps the most valuable investment in protecting that trust is also the simplest: timely, clear and responsible communication.

title.rendered: 3-crane operation underway to free cruise ship from Narayani Bridge

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Efforts are underway to remove the Rhino cruise ship that was swept away by flooding in the Narayani River and became stuck against the Narayani Bridge using three cranes.

The administration said efforts were being made to pull the cruise towards the riverbank with the help of the cranes.

The three cranes are being used to tow the cruise towards the Gaindakot side of the river.

The cruise was swept away from in front of Hotel River Crown by a powerful flood in the river on Sunday evening and carried towards the bridge. It became stuck against a pillar on the Gaindakot side of the bridge.

The three-storey cruise becoming lodged against the bridge pillar increased the risk of damage to the bridge.

The company said the Rhino cruise ship had been secured to trees using two 20-mm ropes, but the powerful floodwaters broke the ropes. It said the ropes had been secured according to international standards.

The company said the ropes broke after two trees became lodged at the site where the cruise was moored and pushed against it.

The cruise weighs more than 70 tonnes, but the company said its effective weight is much lower when it is floating in water. The cruise had been brought to a location upstream of the Narayani Bridge only one and a half years ago.

The 100-foot-long and 25-foot-wide cruise can accommodate up to 180 passengers at a time. Built with an investment of around Rs 150 million, it is Nepal’s first cruise ship.

title.rendered: 10 Humla residents missing while collecting medicinal herbs

content.rendered:
Humla, September 28

Ten residents of Thehe village in Simkot Rural Municipality-2, Humla, have gone missing while collecting medicinal herbs. Their relatives said they have been out of contact for a week.

The missing individuals have been identified as residents Baliban Bohara, Juna Bohara, Gorasingh Bhandari, Dhanpuri Bhandari, Dhanman Singh Bohara, Piuli Bohara, Punna Bohara, Nar Bhandari, Khim Bhandari and Laxmi Bohara, according to locals.

They had gone to collect medicinal herbs in a forest area along the border between Khadpunath Rural Municipality-5 and Chankheli Rural Municipality-5 in Humla. However, they have not been in contact for a week, said local resident Gwam Singh Bhandari.

He said their relatives had informed the local administration, provincial government and federal government about the incident and requested search and rescue efforts.

Chief District Officer Bholanath Guragain said a meeting of the District Security Committee was underway following reports that the 10 people had gone missing.

He said the provincial government and the Ministry of Home Affairs were also being informed about the incident.

title.rendered: Human Rights Commission summons SSP Santosh Khadka over Cholendra Rana’s detention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has summoned Santosh Khadka, chief of the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office, for questioning over the detention of former chief justice Cholendra Rana.

NHRC spokesperson Dr Tikaram Pokharel said Khadka was summoned to the commission on Tuesday through the Nepal Police headquarters.

“He has been summoned for discussions regarding the detention of the former chief justice on Sunday and the commission team being prevented from monitoring the detention,” Pokharel said.

The NHRC team had gone to the Crime Investigation Office in Teku on Sunday to monitor Rana’s detention after he was taken into police custody.

However, police made the commission team wait for around an hour before turning them away from the gate.

The NHRC had expressed its objection to the incident through a statement issued on Sunday.

The commission is now seeking clarification from Khadka regarding the circumstances surrounding Rana’s detention and why its monitoring team was not allowed to enter the police office.

title.rendered: Vehicular movement resumes on Banbasa Bridge as Mahakali River flow recedes

content.rendered:
Kanchanpur, September 28

Vehicular movement of four-wheelers has resumed on the Banbasa Bridge after the water level in the Mahakali River in Kanchanpur began to recede.

Four-wheeler traffic on the bridge connecting Nepal and India had been halted since Sunday as a precaution after the river’s water level rose due to flooding.

Vehicles resumed operating on the bridge from Monday afternoon as the river’s flow decreased.

According to Tek Rawat, information officer at the District Police Office, Kanchanpur, the flow of the Mahakali River has now reached 98,272 cusecs.

Traffic on the Banbasa Bridge had been affected after the river’s flow increased following continuous rainfall.

Police said vehicular movement on the bridge has now returned to normal as the river’s flow has receded.

title.rendered: Rhino swept away by Narayani River reaches Susta

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

A rhinoceros believed to have been swept away by the Narayani River from Chitwan National Park and its buffer zone has reached Susta in Nawalparasi (Bardaghat-Susta West).

The rhino, estimated to be around five years old, was spotted in Susta Rural Municipality-4 on Monday morning.

Abinas Thapa Magar, information officer at Chitwan National Park, said park officials began monitoring the rhino after receiving information that it had been swept downstream.

“We are carrying out reconnaissance of the rhino and preparing for its rescue,” Thapa Magar said.

He said the rhino would likely have to be darted and sedated before being transported back either by boat or through Indian territory. As Susta lies in Nawalparasi, reaching the area by land requires passing through India.

Floods sweep rhino downstream

The rhino is believed to have been swept away during the major flooding in the Narayani River on Saturday and Sunday.

Thapa Magar said other rhinos and wildlife may also have been swept into India by the floodwaters.

A similar incident occurred in 2017 when major flooding in the Rapti and Narayani rivers swept several rhinos downstream towards Susta and into Indian territory. According to Ram Chandra Kadel, who was then the chief conservation officer of Chitwan National Park, 12 rhinos that had reached Indian territory were rescued and brought back to Nepal.

He said coordination with officials of India’s Valmiki Tiger Reserve helped facilitate the rescue operation at the time.

Officials suspect that some rhinos may have reached India this year as well because of the scale of the flooding.

The park said rhinos swept away by the Rapti River in areas including Meghauli and Khairahani during this weekend’s floods have managed to return to land on their own. A deer was also rescued from Shishuwar in Bharatpur Metropolitan City-17.

The latest rhino census recorded 694 rhinos in Chitwan National Park. Officials believe the unusually large volume of water in the Narayani this year, combined with the growing rhino population, may have resulted in more animals being swept away.

title.rendered: Efforts underway to reopen flood-blocked BP Highway

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Efforts are underway to reopen the BP Highway, which has been blocked by landslides and flood-induced road erosion.

The highway was completely obstructed by landslides at Chaukidanda in Namobuddha-6, Charsaybesi in Roshi-7, Gimdi Besi in Roshi-8 and Mamti in Roshi-11.

The Roshi Khola has also washed away a diversion at Chaukidanda. Kavre Chief District Officer Gopal Kumar Adhikari said various efforts were being made to reopen the highway, which has been obstructed at several points due to landslides and erosion caused by the Roshi River following recent rainfall.

He said efforts to clear the obstructions on the Khurkot-Bhaktundebesi section were ongoing and that the road could reopen from Tuesday afternoon. Although landslides have been cleared at some locations, more time may be needed in the Chaukidanda area, he said.

Adhikari said technicians from the Road Division Office had reported that the road had been extensively washed away by floods in the final section on the Kavre side under the Japanese-funded contract, and that the work could take until Tuesday to complete.

Chief District Officer Adhikari and representatives of the security agencies also conducted an on-site inspection of the blocked BP Highway.

title.rendered: NEPSE falls 16.47 points, turnover exceeds Rs 5 billion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The share market fell by double digits on Monday, the first trading day of the week.

The Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index fell 16.47 points to close at 2,613.33 points on Monday, a decline of 0.62 per cent. However, daily turnover exceeded Rs 5 billion.

A total of 13,178,128 shares of 357 securities were traded in 58,500 transactions on Monday. The total turnover stood at Rs 5.385 billion.

All sub-indices except the trading sub-index declined on Monday, weighing on the overall market. Investors in non-life insurance companies suffered the biggest loss, with the sub-index falling 1.20 per cent.

KBL Debenture posted the highest gain of 12.17 per cent on Monday, followed by Laxmi Sunrise Debenture, which rose 10 per cent. Prime Bank Debenture gained 8.83 per cent.

Hathway Investment Nepal Limited recorded the biggest decline, falling 10.58 per cent.

Emerging Nepal Limited, Global IME Balanced Fund and Dhaulagiri Laghubitta Financial Institution were among other securities that posted significant declines.

Himalayan Distillery recorded the highest turnover, while Hathway Investment Nepal Limited recorded the highest number of transactions.

title.rendered: Cockroach Janata Party announces ‘Jail Bharo Andolan’ in India

content.rendered:
India’s Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has announced a new protest movement. CJP founder Abhijit Dipke announced the move on Monday.

In a poster shared on X, Dipke said the CJP would stage a “Jail Bharo Andolan” (fill the jails movement) at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on October 2.

Through his post, Dipke reiterated the party’s demand for the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The CJP had previously announced that it would launch the protest from October 2 if Kumar did not resign from his post.

However, the CJP has not been granted permission to stage the protest in Mumbai.

Responding to the denial, Dipke said attempts to suppress the voice of the people would not be acceptable.

title.rendered: 69 inmates at Chitwan prison suffering from chronic, complex diseases

content.rendered:
Narayangarh (Chitwan), September 28

Sixty-nine of the 761 inmates at the Chitwan Prison Office in Bharatpur are suffering from various chronic and complex diseases, according to prison authorities.

The patients include those suffering from hypertension, diabetes, tuberculosis, mental health conditions, cancer and HIV/AIDS.

Inmates have died of cancer at the prison every year. The prison office said cancer patients from various prisons are referred to the BP Koirala Memorial Cancer Hospital in Bharatpur for treatment, and some patients in advanced stages of the disease die during treatment.

According to prison records, one inmate died of cancer in the current fiscal year 2026/27, said Chetanath Dhungana, information officer at the prison office.

One inmate died of cancer in each of the fiscal years 2025/26 and 2024/25. Dhungana said three inmates are currently suffering from cancer, with two receiving treatment inside the prison and one at a hospital.

Hypertension and diabetes account for the largest number of chronic and complex disease cases among inmates. According to the data, 42 inmates have hypertension and 22 have diabetes.

Dhungana said two inmates—one with cancer and another with a different illness—are currently hospitalised for treatment. He said health workers conduct daily health checkups and provide necessary medication to inmates receiving treatment inside the prison.

Five HIV-positive inmates are regularly taking antiretroviral therapy (ART) medication.

The Chitwan District Prison currently houses 717 men, 42 women and two dependent minors.

—RSS

title.rendered: Floods disrupt power, internet services in Mustang for 36 hours

content.rendered:
Mustang, September 28

Electricity and internet services have been completely disrupted in Mustang for the past 36 hours after floods and landslides damaged power and internet infrastructure in the district.

The services were disrupted on Saturday night following continuous rainfall, floods, landslides and river erosion.

San Prasad Thakali, chief of the Nilgiri Consumers Cooperative Society, the electricity distributor based in Jomsom, said the 33-kilovolt transmission line supplying electricity from Dimukha in Parbat was disconnected after floods and river erosion damaged its poles.

He said power infrastructure in Parbat and Myagdi was also damaged, preventing the Dana substation in Myagdi from being charged and forcing it to shut down.

A team from Jomsom has headed towards the area to assess the condition of the 33-kV transmission line and the Dana substation. Thakali said technicians were also repairing damaged power poles in Thasang Rural Municipality-3 after trees fell on them.

Meanwhile, Nepal Telecom’s Jomsom office said the optical fibre network was damaged at dozens of locations in Parbat and Myagdi, disrupting internet services in Mustang.

Nepal Telecom Jomsom chief Hum Bhujel said repair work was underway in Baisari of Myagdi and Lete of Thasang. He said telephone and 4G services were still operating in some parts of Mustang through radio links.

Officials said efforts were underway to restore both services by Monday evening.

—RSS

title.rendered: Rekha Paudel’s Phnom Penh Crown win Cambodian Women’s League title

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Phnom Penh Crown Women FC, featuring Nepal women’s national team forward Rekha Paudel, have won the Cambodian Women’s League title.

Phnom Penh Crown defeated Visakha FC 3-0 in the final at the Olympic Stadium on September 27 to clinch the championship.

Paudel played an important role in Phnom Penh Crown’s title-winning campaign. Following the victory, she said she was proud to represent the club’s women’s team and described the hard work, improvement and experience gained throughout the season as an important achievement.

Eight teams competed in the league, with Phnom Penh Crown finishing at the top of the league standings to reach the semifinals.

In the semifinal, Phnom Penh Crown defeated Preah Khan Reach Svay Rieng FC, featuring fellow Nepali player Preeti Rai, 3-2 in a penalty shootout.

Paudel also scored on her debut for Phnom Penh Crown.

The title is Phnom Penh Crown’s fourth consecutive Cambodian Women’s League championship.

Paudel had previously won the UAE Women’s League First Division title with Abu Dhabi Country Club while playing in the UAE.

title.rendered: Transport operators ask government not to raise fuel prices during festive season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Transport operators have called on the government not to increase petroleum prices during the festive season.

Saroj Sitoula, president of the Nepal National Federation of Transport Entrepreneurs, said transport operators would also refrain from raising fares if fuel prices were kept unchanged.

Speaking at a meeting of the Infrastructure Development Committee on Monday, Sitoula said the government should not increase petroleum prices even if it has to bear losses.

“We are ready to transport passengers from Mechi to Mahakali at the current fare,” he said. “But if petroleum prices are increased, it will not be possible for us to operate the vehicles.”

He also urged the authorities to take into account the one-way surge in passenger traffic during the festive season.

Sitoula said the transport business was not a seasonal business like tourism in Mustang and that vehicle operators did not make such high profits.

title.rendered: SSB personnel beat Nepali youth near Biratnagar border

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

A team of India’s Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) allegedly beat a Nepali youth in the border area of Biratnagar on Saturday.

The incident took place in Darauna, a border area near Biratnagar, where SSB personnel allegedly assaulted 28-year-old Anuj Kamat of Biratnagar Metropolitan City-2.

According to police, a dispute broke out between Kamat and SSB personnel as he was returning to Nepal from India. During the confrontation, Kamat allegedly threw a stone at an SSB personnel, hitting the security officer.

After Kamat crossed into Nepal, SSB personnel reportedly pursued him, pulled him back towards the no-man’s land area and beat him before taking him towards the Indian side.

Nepal’s Armed Police Force and Nepal Police personnel were also present at the scene when the incident occurred.

A video of the incident circulated on social media shows Nepali security personnel initially attempting to stop Kamat. However, they appear to take no further action when SSB personnel begin beating him. Several people who had gathered at the scene can also be seen holding Kamat as he attempted to flee.

The video shows SSB personnel taking Kamat into custody and beating him with batons before taking him towards India. After keeping him in custody and assaulting him for some time, the SSB handed him over to Nepal Police.

The Area Police Office, Rani, kept Kamat in custody for a day before releasing him to his family on Sunday.

Police said Kamat is a drug user and was not in a normal state when the dispute with the SSB personnel occurred.

Makendra Kumar Mishra, deputy superintendent of police and spokesperson for the Morang District Police Office, said Kamat was released in the presence of his wife on Sunday and sent home.

Kathmandu, September 28

Xtreme Energy Drink has launched a special activation campaign ahead of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) Season 3, aiming to build excitement among cricket fans even before the tournament begins.

Xtreme, which is sponsoring seven of the eight teams participating in NPL Season 3, has set up seven dedicated gates outside the Tribhuvan University International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur, the tournament’s main venue.

The gates have been designed around the identity of each of the seven teams, along with Xtreme’s branding, giving supporters an opportunity to connect with their favourite teams even before entering the stadium.

The company said Xtreme is the first brand to launch an activation of this scale before the start of the NPL.

Xtreme has sponsorship partnerships with Kathmandu Gorkhas, Biratnagar Kings, Chitwan Rhinos, Janakpur Bolts, Karnali Yaks, Pokhara Avengers and Lumbini Lions.

The company said it is further expanding the NPL experience through pole banners, hoardings, gate branding and television advertisements.

NPL Season 3 is scheduled to run from October 26 to November 21.
