title.rendered: RSP lawmakers silent in Parliament over Cholendra Rana’s detention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Opposition lawmakers have questioned the government over the detention and subsequent release of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana, but lawmakers from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) did not raise the issue in Parliament.

During the emergency hour of Monday’s parliamentary session, RSP lawmakers raised issues concerning public life, including the damage caused by floods and landslides and the need for greater preparedness.

But they remained silent on the detention of Rana, who was taken from his residence late Saturday night and released into the custody of his family on Sunday afternoon.

Rana was taken to the Criminal Investigation Office in Teku after police arrived at his Maharajgunj residence at around midnight.

Police initially described the action as an arrest but later said Rana had been taken to a safe place because of a security threat. Authorities have not publicly disclosed the nature of the alleged threat or clarified the specific legal basis for taking him from his home. Police also did not present an arrest warrant to Rana, according to reports.

The National Human Rights Commission team that went to the Teku office to meet Rana was also not allowed to see him. The team waited for around 45 minutes before leaving. The commission later criticised the police conduct, saying it was contrary to its constitutional and legal rights.

While RSP lawmakers did not raise the matter in Parliament, some party lawmakers have expressed concerns about the police action on social media.

Ranju Darshana questions the procedure

RSP lawmaker Ranju Darshana said that although the law allows a person to be arrested when there is evidence of an offence, the legal procedure and evidentiary basis for an arrest must also be respected.

“Even when an offence is evident and a person can be arrested, the process of arrest must follow the law,” Darshana wrote on Facebook.

She said an allegation alone was not sufficient and that there must be grounds and evidence to establish an offence.

According to Darshana, the essence of the rule of law is that state authority must be exercised in accordance with proper procedure and evidence.

“Authority can be exercised, but not without procedure and evidence,” she wrote.

Darshana described Rana’s detention as an action taken to temporarily move him to a safe place and urged the authorities to strengthen security around him.

She also said the state should ensure that no “generation” is in a position to threaten him.

Her remarks came after police said Rana had been taken into custody because of a security threat.

Police have not publicly explained what the threat was, who posed it or why Rana needed to be removed from his residence rather than provided additional security there.

Rajiv Khattri questions how the security threat disappeared

Another RSP lawmaker, Rajiv Khattri, also questioned the police explanation.

“Police said there was a ‘security threat’ to Cholendra,” Khattri wrote on social media.

“But the reason for the detention was kept secret and he was released. It is still not clear how the security threat to Cholendra disappeared.”

Khattri used sarcasm to question the official explanation.

He compared the situation to a hypothetical scenario in which Rana’s house was supposedly at risk of flooding, forcing authorities to move him to safety, only for the rain to stop and the authorities to return him to his family once the sun came out.

The point, he suggested, was that the government had not provided a convincing explanation for what happened.

‘The state should guarantee security’

Khattri said the responsibility of the state is to guarantee security when a citizen feels threatened.

But he questioned the manner in which police removed Rana from his home.

“If a citizen feels unsafe, it is the state’s responsibility to provide security. But the way the police picked him up from his home, almost in the style of an abduction, was not right,” he wrote.

Khattri also recalled the arrest of RSP chair Rabi Lamichhane.

He said the manner in which Lamichhane was previously arrested was wrong and argued that the same criticism applies to the action against Rana.

“If the former chief justice has done something wrong, he can be prosecuted. But the proper method and procedure must be followed,” Khattri wrote.

He said there could be “a thousand questions” about Rana’s conduct and that if there were grounds to prosecute him over alleged moral or financial wrongdoing, the state should do so.

“Cholendra’s actions can raise a thousand questions. If there has been moral or financial wrongdoing, he should be held accountable. Other leaders facing similar allegations should also be investigated,” Khattri wrote.

“But taking him in the middle of the night without even providing an arrest warrant was wrong.”

Questions over the government’s explanation

The police have maintained that Rana was taken to the Criminal Investigation Office after authorities received information about a security threat.

SSP Santosh Khadka of the Crime Investigation Office said Rana was brought to the office because police believed something could happen to him. Police later handed him over to his relatives and said security would be provided at his residence.

However, police have not explained the nature of the threat or identified who or what posed it.

The ambiguity has also raised questions over whether Rana was formally arrested or was placed in protective custody.

A senior police official initially confirmed that Rana had been detained. Later, the Crime Investigation Office described the action as a security measure and said there was no plan to file a case against him.

The lack of a clear explanation has drawn criticism from lawyers, opposition politicians and human rights officials.

RSP’s silence in Parliament

The issue was particularly notable in Monday’s parliamentary session because RSP lawmakers did not raise the detention during the emergency hour.

They instead spoke about damage caused by floods and landslides, public safety and the need for preparedness.

The silence is notable because two RSP lawmakers have publicly questioned the manner in which Rana was detained.

While Darshana and Khattri have raised concerns on social media, the party’s lawmakers as a group have not yet raised the issue in Parliament.

For now, the government has maintained that the action was taken because of a security threat.

But with no public explanation of the alleged threat, no clear disclosure of the legal basis for taking Rana from his home and no explanation of why he was released hours later, questions over the episode remain.

title.rendered: Parliamentary special committee chair election set for Wednesday

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The election for the chairperson of the Parliamentary Special Committee on Climate Change in the Himalayas and the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Disaster has been scheduled for Wednesday.

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal announced the election date during Monday’s meeting of the House of Representatives. According to him, the election will be held at 2 pm on September 30.

The 15-member special committee was formed on September 21 in the aftermath of the devastating flood in Rasuwa on August 26.

The committee members are Achyutam Lamichhane, Anushka Shrestha, Gangadevi Shrestha, Ganesh Parajuli, Dhananjaya Regmi, Dhruvaraj Rai, Nisha Dangi, Pushparaj Kandel, Mohan Acharya, Mingmagyabu Sherpa, Ramesh Kumar Malla, Rabindra Patel, Saraswati Lama, Sujata Tamang and Sita Thapaliya.

The committee has been given a three-month term, with a provision allowing its tenure to be extended later.

The committee’s terms of reference include studying the impact of climate change in the Himalayan region.

It will review available studies and data on changes in Himalayan temperatures, snowfall, glaciers, glacial lakes and watersheds, as well as the risks arising from such changes. It will also identify gaps in research and monitoring and recommend measures to strengthen scientific research and regular monitoring.

Regarding the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster, the committee will study its causes and impacts, including the origin and sequence of events, immediate causes and factors that intensified the risks, based on expert and scientific evidence. It will also review the possible links with climate change, the impact of transboundary watersheds and the effects on downstream areas.

The committee will also review search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts.

It will assess search and rescue operations, the status of missing citizens, relief distribution, safe temporary housing, basic services and livelihood recovery to ensure a fair response to affected people. It has been authorised to recommend immediate and medium-term measures based on the needs of affected citizens.

The committee has also been tasked with proposing a roadmap for sustainable and safe reconstruction.

It will study disaster risk reduction and early warning systems and make recommendations.

The committee has also been tasked with exploring possibilities for climate diplomacy and cross-border cooperation and recommending legal and institutional reforms.

title.rendered: FNCCI calls for withdrawal of VAT on electricity tariff

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI) has called on the government to withdraw the value-added tax (VAT) imposed on electricity tariffs from the current fiscal year 2026/27, saying it has increased production costs.

The federation said electricity is a basic infrastructure for industrial production, trade and tourism, and that imposing an additional tax on it directly affects production costs, operating expenses, cash flow and overall business competitiveness.

According to the federation, businesses have complained that the additional VAT has increased costs, particularly for energy-intensive industries, businesses involved in VAT-exempt transactions, small and medium-sized enterprises, and hotels and tourism businesses.

Although the law provides for input tax credit, businesses have complained that not all enterprises are able to adjust the VAT paid on electricity immediately or in full due to the nature of their transactions and the tax adjustment and refund procedures.

The federation said this has put pressure on working capital and affected new investment, industrial expansion and job creation. It said the provision could also increase costs for consumers and add further pressure on overall prices.

At a time when industrialisation should be accelerated through increased domestic electricity consumption, import substitution and export promotion, the policy of increasing energy costs has added challenges to private-sector investment and production expansion, the federation said.

The federation has also called for a regular, quality and reliable electricity supply to industries and measures to minimise production losses and damage to machinery caused by voltage fluctuations, sudden power outages and other technical problems.

The federation urged the government to review the VAT provision on electricity, hold extensive consultations with the private sector, and simplify and make the tax adjustment and refund process transparent and time-bound.

It called on the government to withdraw VAT on electricity, arguing that electricity should be treated not merely as a source of revenue but as essential infrastructure for industrial production, tourism development, job creation and economic growth.

title.rendered: RSP Lawmaker Khagendra Karn draws government’s attention to flood, elephant damage in Saptari

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Khagendra Karn has urged the government to provide relief to residents of Saptari affected by flooding and wild elephants.

Speaking during the zero hour of the House of Representatives meeting on Monday, Karn said more than 500 houses in Saptari had been inundated.

“Due to continuous rainfall over the past three days, farmers’ fields in Hanumannagar, Kankalini Municipality and Tilathi Koiladi Rural Municipality of Saptari have been inundated. More than 500 houses have been affected,” Karn said. “People are suffering. Similarly, crops planted by farmers in Kamalpur of Saptakoshi Municipality and Bastipur of Kanchan-Rup Municipality have been destroyed by elephant attacks. I urge the government to make arrangements for necessary relief and compensation.”

Karn praised the government for its work in Madhesh. He claimed that the government led by Prime Minister Balen Shah had initiated development-oriented politics in the province.

He said the government was working on the Kamala-Kanchanpur road and preparing to operate the Ram Raja Prasad Singh Health Sciences Academy, a medical college and an engineering college.

title.rendered: 6-month paid maternity leave proposed to boost population growth

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Minister for Health and Food Hygiene Nisha Mehta has said incentives through maternity leave are also being proposed to encourage population growth.

She made the statement while presenting the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights (First Amendment) Bill, 2026 in the House of Representatives on Monday.

Presenting the bill, she said, “According to Nepal’s latest census, the country’s population growth rate has been continuously declining. Therefore, it is necessary to amend the law to introduce provisions, including leave incentives, to encourage population growth.”

Minister Mehta registered the bill in the House of Representatives on September 21.

According to the proposed bill, women working in government, non-government or private organisations would be entitled to six months of paid maternity leave before and after childbirth. It also proposes 42 days of paid paternity leave for male employees whose wives give birth.

The existing law provides mothers with 90 days of maternity leave. The bill proposes increasing it to six months, while paternity leave would be increased from 15 days to 42 days.

Mehta said the bill has also been introduced to ensure safe, quality, affordable and accessible maternal and reproductive health services and to respect, protect and fulfil women’s constitutional rights to safe motherhood and reproductive health.

The bill also includes provisions requiring childbirth services to be provided by trained birth attendants, prohibiting refusal to provide maternity services and banning violence against women during childbirth.

It also proposes additional and amended provisions concerning abortion in special circumstances, as well as provisions concerning forced abortion. The proposed amendments would classify newly added offences as criminal acts and prescribe penalties for them.

title.rendered: Nikhil Upreti and Divya Dev Pant urge viewers not to gamble with producers’ investments as film piracy spreads

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Films currently in theatres are being hit by copyright violations (piracy). Just two days after its release, scenes from Nikhil Upreti’s action-heavy film “Acharya” are all over social media.

Not only that, key scenes from another film currently showing, “Ba: Ek Yoddha,” have also been posted on TikTok and Reels.

Clips of 10 to 20 minutes have been found uploaded by social media users. Producers have expressed concern that audiences recording and uploading key scenes in this way will hurt business.

Producers, actors and distributors are making public appeals on social media not to do this.

Upreti, the director, producer and actor of “Acharya,” said that recording the film and posting it on social media is a betrayal of the producer’s dream. He has asked people to stop putting footage on TikTok for entertainment and to boost views.

Releasing a video message on Facebook, Nikhil said, “It is a betrayal of the dream of a producer who has invested with so much hardship. For a little entertainment and to increase their own views, 10, 15, even 20 minutes of the film’s footage is put on TikTok. What a painful incident. Let this not be done to any film, not just mine.”

Saying that Nepali films need to become strong within the country, he said, “We need to become much stronger within our own country. Let us cooperate. Please do not play with the producer’s investment and business. Let us all come together to oppose this piracy.”

Divya Dev Pant, an actor in the film “Ba: Ek Yoddha,” which is currently running in theatres, has urged people to stop recording footage and posting it on social media. While saying they are happy about the audience’s love and response, Divya Dev asked people to respect the right of viewers to watch the film in the darkness of the theatre.

He writes, “Sharing a favourite scene is natural, but it can spoil key moments for others. Behind every film are months of hard work by hundreds of people. Review it, recommend it, even criticize it, but please don’t record and post the film, whether it’s ours, Nikhil dai’s, or anyone else’s. Let others experience it first in the darkness of the theater, just as you did.”


US distributor Suresh Darpan Pokhrel has expressed concern that this kind of piracy is also damaging the overseas market. He has given suggestions, including the need to build a strong system.

This piracy problem is not new for Nepali films. Although the problem has existed for a decade, measures to prevent it have not been implemented. The Film Development Board has repeatedly issued public notices urging people not to record films inside theatres.

The board has also sent a letter with directives to the Film Association, the exhibitors’ body, in the past. However, it has not been implemented. The board’s Cinema Hall Monitoring Committee appears inactive lately. The Film Association also appears to be ignoring the issue.

title.rendered: How much damage have recent floods caused to Nepal’s infrastructure?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Floods since September 25 have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, including roads, bridges, drinking water projects and energy facilities.

According to the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development, rainfall and floods have washed away approach roads to bridges along the Kaligandaki Corridor at Myagdi Pokharebagar, Baglung Maldhunga and Dedaun in Tanahun-Nawalparasi. A concrete bridge over the Kaligandaki River has also been washed away.

Preliminary details show that several sections of the Kaligandaki Corridor, as well as the Dumre-Besisahar-Chame road section, have suffered extensive damage.

On the Dumre-Besisahar-Chame road, around 40 metres of road at Rambazar-Syange in Lamjung has completely collapsed due to erosion by the Marshyangdi River. The road has been blocked by a landslide carrying rocks at Naso-Khotro in Manang. At Naso-Bagarchhap in Manang, around 50 metres of road has completely collapsed due to erosion by the Marshyangdi River.

Three temporary wooden bridges in Chame, Manang, have been washed away by floods. Floods and landslides have also damaged more than a dozen roads in the district, including the Prithvi Highway, BP Highway and Kanti Lokpath connecting the district with the Kathmandu Valley.

Floods and landslides have completely damaged the Nathigad suspension bridge in Rukum East and the Baglung-Parbat Jaljala-Forse suspension bridge. Partial damage has been reported to the suspension bridges connecting Tanahun’s Ghiring Karuwatar with Bulingtar-Machedi in Nawalpur; Syanja’s Galyang-Belchaur with Ramba Naugaun-Sathibazar in Palpa; Kasiban in Palpa with Atrauli in Tanahun; Parbat with Syanja through Setibeni; and Myagdi’s Beni with Jaljala in Parbat.

Preliminary details show that 31 drinking water projects have been damaged by floods and landslides. According to the ministry, efforts to reopen the roads began on Sunday, and work is underway on various sections today.

According to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, floods have also caused extensive damage to hydropower projects. Preliminary estimates put the damage to hydropower projects at Rs 134.69 billion.

The floods have affected hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 783 megawatts. Of these, the Kaligandaki Hydropower Project is scheduled to resume operation today.

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal held discussions on Sunday with elected representatives from areas affected by damage caused by continuous rainfall. As floods and landslides disrupted daily life across the country, Minister Lamsal discussed the rehabilitation of affected residents and reconstruction of damaged physical infrastructure with local representatives from the affected areas, along with the Prime Minister’s adviser Sudip Dhakal.

The meeting discussed arrangements for temporary housing for families displaced by the floods and the immediate reconstruction of damaged structures.

Minister Lamsal said the government would assess the damage to bridges, roads, suspension bridges, drinking water projects and other infrastructure affected by the floods and rainfall over the past three days, immediately arrange the necessary budget and proceed with reconstruction through the tendering process. He pledged to begin reconstruction work within September.

title.rendered: Madan Bhandari Cup International Men’s Volleyball Tournament begins

content.rendered:
Butwal, September 28

The second edition of the Madan Bhandari Cup International Invitational Running Shield Men’s Volleyball Tournament begins in Butwal today. The trophy was unveiled at the Butwal International Conference Centre on Monday morning ahead of the tournament.

Butwal Sub-Metropolitan City Deputy Mayor Sabitra Aryal, who unveiled the trophy, said the international volleyball tournament would help promote Butwal as a sports tourism destination.

According to Dhruv Acharya, president of the Madan Bhandari Sports Academy, former President Bidhya Devi Bhandari will inaugurate the tournament at 3 pm today. The tournament will run until October 3 and feature eight teams—five from Nepal and three from abroad.

From Nepal, Nepal Police Club, APF Club, Manimukunda Volleyball Club, Sabhapokhari Volleyball Club and Galkot Volleyball Club will compete. The foreign teams are Gujarat State Volleyball Association and Khaira Club Punjab from India, and the Sri Lankan Police team.

The winner will receive the running shield and Rs 700,000, while the runner-up will receive Rs 350,000. The third-place team will receive Rs 175,000, and the fourth-placed team will receive Rs 75,000, along with cups, medals and certificates.

The best player will receive Rs 15,000, while the best spiker, setter, server, blocker, defender and coach will each receive Rs 8,000 in cash. The organisers said the Player of the Match in each game will receive Rs 5,000.

Nepal Volleyball Association Vice President Bharat Shah, Madan Bhandari Sports Academy Vice President Mohan Regmi, Ganesh Thagunna and other officials were present at the trophy unveiling ceremony.

title.rendered: Dedgaun in Nawalpur records highest rainfall of 544.2 mm in four days

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Over the past four days, continuous rainfall across the country has brought total rainfall of more than 100 millimetres at 186 rain gauge stations nationwide.

The highest rainfall, 544.2 millimetres, was measured at Dedgaun in Nawalpur (East Nawalparasi).

According to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, the data covers the period from 8:45 a.m. on September 23 to 8:45 a.m. on September 27.

After Dedgaun in Nawalpur, the next highest was 500.2 millimetres at Panchase in Kaski.

The department said Atraulitar in Tanahun recorded 472 millimetres, Tansen in Palpa 458 millimetres, and Panchamul in Syangja 431.8 millimetres.

Likewise, 397.4 millimeters was measured at Darbang in Myagdi, 396 millimeters at Madi Kalyanpur in Chitwan, 388.6 millimeters at Mainar in Kapilvastu, 366.6 millimeters at Bhagwanpur in Kapilvastu, and 365.6 millimeters at Deurali Nawalpur in Nawalpur.

According to the department’s data, 233 rain gauge stations recorded up to about 175 millimetres of rainfall in the same period. Of these, 186 stations recorded more than 100 millimetres.

Simikot, the district headquarters of the Himalayan district of Humla, had earlier recorded record-breaking rainfall within 24 hours.

According to Dr. Indira Kadel, head of the Meteorology and Climate Science Office, Surkhet, 114.8 millimetres of rainfall was measured at Simikot between 8:45 a.m. on September 25, 2083 and 8:45 a.m. on September 26.

This is the highest 24-hour rainfall on record for the period from June 1, 1978 to September 26, 2026. Previously, 110 millimetres had fallen in 24 hours at Simikot on October 19, 2021, and that was considered the record.

Meteorologists had already made public forecasts of extremely heavy rainfall in Gandaki and Lumbini provinces due to the effect of a low-pressure system that developed in the Bay of Bengal.

At least 21 dead in four districts

Continuous rainfall has also caused loss of life and property through floods and landslides in various districts of Nepal.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, data from September 24 to 6 p.m. on September 27 shows that at least 21 people have died in various districts, while five are missing and five are injured. A total of 747 families have been directly affected.

Districts including Baglung, Parbat, Manang, Nawalparasi East, Chitwan, Palpa and Dhanusha, and surrounding areas, have been the most affected.

title.rendered: Women-friendly blue bus service yet to be implemented

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The issue of the government’s failure to launch the women-friendly blue bus service, which was included among its 100-day priorities, has been raised in Parliament.

The issue was raised by Ashok Kumar Chaudhary, a lawmaker from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).

“A few days ago, while travelling on public transport from Koteshwor to Maitighar, a woman recognised me and asked, ‘What happened to the government’s plan to operate safe public transport for women?’” he said.

He said the question was not merely that of one woman but the voice of thousands of women who face insecurity, inappropriate touching and harassment while travelling on public transport every day.

“But the sad thing is that instead of questioning the person responsible for the harassment, the victim is still questioned. They are told that such things happen after getting on a bus,” he said.

Stating that safe travel is every citizen’s right, Chaudhary said an environment should be created in which women can travel on public transport without fear.

He also recalled the women-friendly blue bus service included in the government’s 100-day priorities.

“I therefore strongly urge the government to immediately implement the women-friendly blue bus service included in its 100-day priorities,” he said.

The 100-point action plan approved by the Cabinet had set a target of operating free blue bus services for women in all seven provinces and launching at least 25 buses within the first 100 days.

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle had also announced in the budget statement for fiscal year 2026/27 that blue bus services equipped with CCTV cameras would be operated for women.

The government had assigned the Department of Transport Management and Sajha Yatayat responsibility for operating the blue buses. However, the service has yet to be implemented.

The issue was raised in Parliament by Chaudhary, a lawmaker from the ruling RSP.

title.rendered: Deuba faction sets Rs 10,000 lower fee than Gagan’s for party president candidacy

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

As the establishment faction led by Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa and the faction led by former president Sher Bahadur Deuba prepare separately for the party’s 15th General Convention, they have set different nomination fees for candidates.

The Nepali Congress led by Thapa, who was elected president through a special general convention, has fixed the nomination fee for the post of central president at Rs 40,000 for the 15th General Convention.

The nomination fee has been set at Rs 30,000 for vice president and general secretary, Rs 20,000 for joint general secretary and Rs 11,000 for central committee member.

However, the election guidelines prepared by the faction led by Deuba have set relatively lower nomination fees. According to the guidelines, candidates for central president will have to pay a nomination fee of Rs 30,000.

Similarly, the fee has been fixed at Rs 25,000 for vice president and general secretary, Rs 20,000 for joint general secretary and Rs 10,000 for central committee member.

A candidate contesting for central president will have to pay Rs 10,000 less at the convention organised by the Deuba faction than at the convention led by Thapa. The Deuba faction has also set the nomination fee Rs 5,000 lower for vice president and general secretary and Rs 1,000 lower for central committee members.

Both factions have fixed the nomination fee for candidates seeking the post of joint general secretary at Rs 20,000.

The difference in nomination fees is not limited to central-level positions. The two factions have also set different fees for positions at lower levels of the party.

The Thapa-led convention has fixed the nomination fee at Rs 20,000 for provincial president, Rs 15,000 for district president, Rs 10,000 for House of Representatives constituency president and Rs 7,000 for provincial assembly constituency president.

The Deuba-led faction, meanwhile, has set the fees at Rs 10,000 for provincial president, Rs 5,000 for district president, Rs 3,500 for House of Representatives constituency president and Rs 2,500 for provincial assembly constituency president.

There is also a significant difference in the fees at the local level. The Thapa-led convention has set the nomination fee at Rs 1,000 for ward president, Rs 5,000 for rural municipality and municipality presidents, and Rs 7,000 for sub-metropolitan and metropolitan city presidents.

The Deuba-led faction has set the nomination fee at Rs 250 for ward president, Rs 1,000 for rural municipality president, Rs 2,000 for municipality president and Rs 2,500 for sub-metropolitan and metropolitan city presidents.

title.rendered: Former Chief Justice Rana’s letter seeking protection was received, says DIG Thapaliya

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

A letter in which former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana has requested police protection for his life has been made public on social media.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar, SSP Somendra Singh Rathore of the Kathmandu Valley Police Office, Ranipokhari, said that the letter from Cholendra Shumsher had not been received at the office.

However, DIG Gobinda Thapaliya of the same office said the letter had been received.

“The letter was received yesterday, on a holiday. Since it was a holiday, some colleagues may not have known. After receiving the letter regarding peace and security, we have made arrangements for protection,” Thapaliya told Onlinekhabar.

In the application addressed to the Kathmandu Valley Police Office, Ranipokhari, submitted on Cholendra’s behalf by his son Sachindra Shumsher Rana, a request was made to arrange the necessary security for the residence and family members.

A team from Nepal Police’s Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office had taken Rana into custody at midnight on Saturday, citing information about a “security threat,” and released him on Sunday afternoon.

Police say the application seeking peace and security was received yesterday, Sunday, the same day he was released.

title.rendered: Riverbank settlements need to be relocated: RSP Chief Whip Burlakoti

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chief Whip Kabindra Burlakoti has said that settlements along riverbanks need to be relocated and managed.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives, he said the government faced strong criticism when it removed settlements from riverbanks.

“The government was heavily criticised when it removed settlements along riverbanks. The government also endured the criticism. There may have been some shortcomings in the process of relocating the settlements, and there may be areas that need improvement,” he said. “But looking at the Bhotekoshi flood of August 26 and the floods of September 26 and 27, everyone has now realised that settlements along riverbanks need to be relocated.”

He said many settlements still remain along riverbanks and need to be managed.

“There are still many settlements along riverbanks. If they are not managed in time, we will face a major risk again,” he said. “We have also built our bridges too low, apparently under the influence of commissions. I urge the government to reassess all these issues and move forward accordingly.”

title.rendered: Prayashna Gurung becomes Miss Universe Nepal, Binita Oli takes Miss Earth Nepal crown

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The winners of two prestigious beauty pageants have been announced this year. The Miss Universe Nepal and Miss Earth winners were declared at the grand finale held on Sunday evening.

Prayashna Gurung won the Miss Universe Nepal 2026 title, while Binita Oli was crowned Miss Earth 2026. Fourteen contestants competed for the title.

Former Miss Universe India and Bollywood actress Celina Jaitly was the chief judge at the finale. Gurung is a non-resident Nepali based in Britain and runs women’s empowerment programs.

She is running a project called “The Dignity” to support entrepreneurship and empowerment among Nepali women. Oli, the 27-year-old Miss Earth Nepal, is reported to have had a few years of experience as an international air hostess.

The Hidden Treasure, the organisation that has long run Miss Nepal, had been organising Miss Earth for a long time. It gave up the event a few years ago.

Now, the same organisation, which holds the license for Miss Universe Nepal, has organised Miss Earth as well.

title.rendered: 10 dead, one missing in landslide in Baglung

content.rendered:
Baglung, September 28

A tragic landslide in Baglung has claimed the lives of 10 people, with one individual still unaccounted for, following relentless rainfall in the area. The past couple of days have seen a significant toll on life in the district, with nine fatalities reported just on Sunday and one more on Saturday.

Phanindra Prasai, the chief of the District Police Office in Baglung, shared that four people lost their lives in Tamankhola Rural Municipality on Sunday, while one person is missing, and five others perished in Nisikhola Rural Municipality. Among the victims were 80-year-old Buddhiraj Gharti and 66-year-old Bhimdevi Gharti, who tragically died when their home was swept away in Tamankhola Rural Municipality-3 Dharnasuk.

The landslide also obliterated eight houses in that area. In another heartbreaking incident, 50-year-old Hastabir Sripali and 65-year-old Udisara Sripali were killed when their house was destroyed in Tamankhola Rural Municipality-4 Santar, and Hastabir’s wife is currently missing.

In Nisikhola Rural Municipality-3 Jugjakhola, four family members lost their lives when their home was engulfed by a landslide. The deceased include 36-year-old Shyam Kumari BK, along with her son Manoj, and two others named Mukesh and Nishan. Additionally, 50-year-old Surya Bahadur Gharti died when a landslide took down a cowshed in Nisikhola Rural Municipality-6 Rangil.

On Saturday, 59-year-old Man Bahadur Roka was also a victim, as a landslide destroyed his house in Tarakhola Rural Municipality-5 Dhasmar. Krishna Prasad Acharya, the chief district officer of Baglung, noted that more lives were likely saved thanks to timely warnings.

A rescue team, including security personnel and a helicopter from the Nepali Army, has been deployed to the affected areas. In related news, floods and landslides have wreaked havoc in Tanahun, damaging 24 houses across six localities due to the recent heavy rains. Deputy Superintendent of Police Dwarika Prasad Ghimire from the District Police Office in Tanahun reported that five houses were affected in Byas Municipality, with additional damage in other areas.

title.rendered: National Digital Literacy Campaign for digital transformation of hotels and restaurants

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

‘National Digital Literacy Campaign’ has been launched for the digital transformation of hotels and restaurants. The ‘National Digital Literacy Campaign’ has been launched for the digital transformation of the hotel and restaurant sector in a programme organised by the Hotel Entrepreneurs Federation Nepal on the occasion of the 47th World Tourism Day.

TR Bhandari, president of the federation, informed that the aim of connecting hoteliers and restaurateurs of all seven provinces with digital technology and artificial intelligence is through the campaign, which will be conducted for one year. As part of the campaign, practical training on Google Business Profile, Google Maps, online booking, hotel management system, digital marketing, social media, customer review management and digital security will be conducted, he said.

In the programme, Dipendra Subedi, secretary of the Ministry of Tourism, Transport, Industry and Labour of Bagmati province, expressed the commitment of the ministry to support the campaign, saying that it is necessary to increase the capacity of small and medium hoteliers and use technology. Naresh Lal Shrestha, vice president of the Federation of Nepal Industry and Commerce, expressed his commitment to cooperate in making the campaign nationwide. The campaign aims to connect hotels and restaurants in rural areas, highways and new tourist destinations with the digital market

title.rendered: Snowfall and rain affect life in Humla

content.rendered:
File

Humla, September 28

Snow and rain have been causing quite a stir in Humla lately. The relentless downpour and snowfall have hit life in the district hard. Most areas, including the district headquarters in Simkot, are experiencing disruptions in telephone and internet services.

The solar systems that power the communication towers in the higher regions have failed, leading to these outages. This communication breakdown is making it tough to coordinate with local authorities, security agencies, and other offices to assess the damage. Reports indicate that rain has damaged several school buildings, and many roads are now impassable.

In addition to the rain, Simkot has also seen snowfall, and the Hilsa route is completely blocked due to the heavy snow.

title.rendered: Congress invites political parties from India to America to its convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The Nepali Congress has guests from various countries to the opening ceremony of its 15th general convention.

Along with its northern and southern neighbours, the Congress has guests from more than half a dozen countries, including the United States.

For the opening ceremony of the convention, which begins in Kathmandu on October 2, ruling and opposition parties from countries including India, China, the United States, Britain, Germany and Bangladesh have been invited.

One of the leaders given responsibility for inviting foreign guests to the ceremony said that India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the opposition Indian National Congress have been invited.

According to him, an invitation has also been sent to the Communist Party of China. The Congress has also sent invitations to the Republican and Democratic parties of the United States.

Likewise, Britain’s ruling Labour Party and main opposition Conservative Party, and Germany’s ruling Social Democratic Party, have been invited.

The leader said an invitation was also sent to Bangladesh’s ruling party, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).

“We have also invited the democratic socialist parties of Europe, the Socialist International, and the International Conference of Asian Political Parties (ICAPP),” he said.

He said the short notice and adverse weather could affect the presence of foreign guests at the opening ceremony.

Congress acting chief secretary Krishna Dulal said the guests who have been invited to previous conventions of the party have been invited this time as well.

“We have sent invitation letters to the guests we have been calling to the convention,” he told Onlinekhabar. “Confirmation from the other side has not yet come.”

title.rendered: Dammed Marsyangdi River resumes normal flow

content.rendered:
Manang, September 28

The Marsyangdi River, which was dammed at the Tatopani area after the deposition of debris comprising stones, gravel, and sand brought down by the flooded Ghattekhola stream following incessant rain, has now started to flow normally. The police have reported that water has started flowing partially from the lake formed by the dammed river.

According to Lokendra Bahadur Ghale, the chairperson of Nason Rural Municipality, electricity, telephone, and road networks in various parts of the district have been disrupted due to four days of continuous rain. “We are cut off from telephone, electricity, and road networks due to the rain-triggered disaster. The local government is making the most of the limited resources available. At times like this, the provincial and federal governments should make us feel like they are our guardians,” he said.

According to him, as the flooding has decreased, residents who had taken shelter in the Nepali Army barracks, community buildings, and other public places started checking the damage to their homes and villages early this morning. Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal said that the flow of the previously blocked Marsyangdi River is gradually reopening.

He informed that discussions are going on about using an excavator to restore the water flow since the road connection in that area has been cut off. The flood has damaged the Tal Bazaar area on the border of Lamjung and Manang. “We urge the residents in the riverside area of Marsyangdi to remain alert,” CDO Khanal said. Due to continuous rain, floods in Thadokhola and Khattre Khola have caused erosion and damaged houses, bridges, and roads in the area. On May 28 and June 15, 2021, floods in the Ghattrekhola, Thadokhola streams, and Marsyangdi River also caused significant physical damage in Manang.

title.rendered: Two more bodies found in Himlung avalanche

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Two more bodies have been found in the Himlung avalanche.

The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) recovered the two additional bodies.

According to the NNMGA, the bodies of Birendra Gurung and Ghanashyam Rai were found today. Earlier, on Sunday, the bodies of Chhabi Bhote and Pasang Bhote were found.

With this, the number of people killed in the Himlung avalanche has reached four.

The association also said the search and rescue operation will continue.

title.rendered: Deuba faction sets candidacy fees for general convention, Rs 30,000 for president

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

The faction of former Nepali Congress president Sher Bahadur Deuba has set candidate nomination fees for the conventions at various levels under the 15th general convention.

The election directive prepared by the Central Election Committee sets nomination fees for aspirants seeking candidacy in committees at all levels, from the centre down to the ward.

The directive sets a nomination fee of Rs 30,000 for president of the Central Working Committee, and Rs 25,000 each for central vice-president and general secretary.

A nomination fee of Rs 20,000 has been set for joint general secretary aspirants and Rs 10,000 for candidates for central member.

For central convention delegates, who are counted as voters for selecting the Central Working Committee, the directive sets a nomination fee of Rs 2,500.

A nomination fee of Rs 3,000 has been set for aspirants for membership of the Central General Committee, to be elected from among convention delegates.

For the election of provincial constituency representatives, Rs 500 has been set, and for the election of provincial convention delegates, Rs 1,000.

For provincial conventions under the other group’s general convention, the nomination fee is Rs 10,000 for provincial committee president, Rs 6,000 for vice-president, general secretary and joint general secretary, and Rs 3,000 for member.

For districts, the fee is Rs 5,000 for president, Rs 3,500 for vice-president and secretary, Rs 3,000 for joint secretary and Rs 1,500 for member.

The election committee has set nomination fees of Rs 250 for village and city ward presidents, Rs 1,000 and Rs 2,000 for rural municipality and municipality presidents, respectively, and Rs 2,500 for sub-metropolitan and metropolitan city presidents.

Likewise, the directive says aspirants for president of a provincial constituency committee must pay Rs 2,500, and aspirants for president of a House of Representatives constituency committee must pay Rs 3,500.

In the convention being run by the leadership elected by the special general convention, nomination fees have been set at Rs 30,000 for central president, Rs 30,000 for vice-president and general secretary, Rs 20,000 for joint general secretary and Rs 11,000 for central member.

The election directive prepared by the establishment-side Central Election Committee says fees of Rs 1,000 will be charged for ward presidents, Rs 5,000 for rural municipality and municipality presidents, and Rs 7,000 for sub-metropolitan and metropolitan committee presidents.

title.rendered: Opposition MPs demand answers on why ex-Chief Justice was detained and freed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Questions have been raised in Parliament over the taking into custody and subsequent release of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana.

Nepali Communist Party chief whip Yubaraj Dulal, UML chief whip Ain Bahadur Mahar and Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Dhrubaraj Rai, among others, raised the issue.

“Without an arrest warrant, without any reason, the government has once again shown an example of a lawless state, and in the middle of the night it has shown a new stunt,” Chief Whip Dulal said.

He asked whether the country is moving ahead as a state of law or is in a lawless state. If there is a security threat, he asked, should the person making the threat be arrested, or someone else?

UML chief whip Mahar said, “It was arrested in the style of thuggery, in the style of abduction. It presented a blatant specimen of state terror.”

They protested that he was taken into custody and released as if “I am the state.”

Shram Sanskriti Party’s Dhrubaraj Rai sought answers from the government on the arrests of Bharat Dahal and Cholendra Shumsher Rana.

The government had arrested political analyst and writer Bharat Dahal a few days earlier. A Supreme Court bench of Justice Kumar Regmi later ordered that the written reasons for Dahal’s arrest be submitted.

Lawmaker Rai linked this to the police taking former Chief Justice Rana into custody and releasing him.

Police took Rana into custody from his home on Saturday night. However, police have not clearly stated which offence or on what grounds he was held. Government bodies have also said nothing officially about it.

In the meantime, Rana, taken into custody at night, was released during the day.

The Shram Sanskriti Party has demanded that Prime Minister Shah himself answer on these matters.

“One moment Bharat Dahal is arrested, they do it, and release him. Then Cholendra Shumsher is picked up and released,” Rai asked. “At least if the matter is serious, treat it seriously. If not, how exactly is this government working?”

title.rendered: Gold falls Rs 5,000 per tola in one day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Gold and silver prices have fallen in the Nepali market again today, Monday.

According to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association, gold fell by Rs 5,000 per tola and silver by Rs 145 on Monday.

Gold, which traded at Rs 299,300 per tola on Sunday after falling Rs 700 from Friday, fell further on Monday and is now priced at Rs 294,300.

Silver has also declined. The federation said silver is trading today at Rs 4,510 per tola. On Sunday, silver traded at Rs 4,655 per tola.

title.rendered: Finance Minister Wagle meets AIIB President Zou, urges more investment in reconstruction and infrastructure

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, who has travelled to Doha to attend the 11th annual meeting of the Board of Governors of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), has held talks with the bank’s president, Zou Jiayi.

In the meeting, Minister Wagle asked President Zou to expand AIIB investment in Nepal, support reconstruction after natural disasters, and widen access to concessional financing.

President Zou expressed deep condolences for the human and material losses Nepal has suffered from the recent devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River. She pledged the bank’s fullest possible support for resilient reconstruction after the disaster.

She said the bank will provide grant assistance for project preparation through the Project Preparation Specialised Fund.

She also said that by using grants under the Specialised Fund window, the loans AIIB provides to Nepal could be kept at the most concessional interest rate possible. She reiterated the bank’s commitment to continued cooperation in the economic development of Nepal, a founding member of the AIIB.

On the occasion, Minister Wagle congratulated the new president and thanked the bank for the support it has extended to Nepal as a founding member.

He asked for the early completion of the Power Distribution System Improvement and Expansion Project, currently running with AIIB financing, and of the study for the expressway.

Under medium- and long-term assistance, Minister Wagle also asked the bank to mobilise its own resources, along with those of other donor agencies, for developing green energy, cross-border electricity transmission lines, road infrastructure and digital infrastructure.

During the discussion, Minister Wagle also invited President Zou to visit Nepal within 2026.

title.rendered: Heavy snowfall in northern Humla, Nara and Nyalu roads blocked

content.rendered:
Humla, September 28

Heavy snowfall has hit Namkha Rural Municipality in northern Humla, along with three days of incessant rain.

The snowfall has blocked the road at Nyalu Lek in Namkha Rural Municipality-6 and at Nara Lek in Ward 5.

Ward Chair Paljor Tamang of Namkha-6 said travel to and from Til, Jang and Halji in Limi has been cut off. He said about 3 feet of snow has accumulated, far more than is usual even in the winter season.

Vegetables and other crops planted in the village’s fields have been buried under the snow.

Tamang said the yaks grazing in the forest could not be brought home, and that, fearing landslides, residents are staying safely in a community building.

With Nyalu Lek closed, domestic and foreign tourists travelling to and from Limi-Lapcha for Mansarovar-Kailash darshan have also been left stranded.

title.rendered: Win over Sri Lanka would send Nepal into semi-final against India

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Nepal is set to play against Sri Lanka in the men’s cricket quarter-final at the 20th Asian Games on Tuesday. If Nepal win, they will make history by reaching the semi-finals for the first time, where they will face India.

India advanced to the semi-finals on higher seeding on Monday after their quarter-final against Afghanistan could not be played because of rain. Pakistan have also reached the last four after their match against Hong Kong was abandoned.

Nepal reached the quarter-finals as winners of Group A. After beating Afghanistan in the group stage, Nepal secured top spot when their match against Japan ended with no result because of rain.

However, there is again a high chance of rain in Japan on Tuesday. If the quarter-final between Nepal and Sri Lanka is also washed out, higher-seeded Sri Lanka will go through to the semi-finals and Nepal’s campaign will end at the quarter-final stage.

Nepal have never progressed beyond the quarter-finals at the Asian Games. At the previous edition, Nepal lost to India in the quarter-finals.

title.rendered: Bill proposes jail, Rs 500,000 fine for attacks on health workers

content.rendered:
The government is preparing to end the legal provision that lets people who assault health workers escape by paying a fine. A bill has been advanced to amend the law so that anyone who beats or physically injures a health worker can be jailed for up to five years.

Health and Food Hygiene Minister Nisha Mehta has registered the bill, which amends the Health Workers and Health Institutions (Protection) Act, 2066 B.S., in the House of Representatives.

Under current provisions, such assaults carry a fine. The proposed amendment provides two to five years’ imprisonment and a fine of Rs 200,000 to Rs 500,000, or both. Offenders will no longer escape by paying a fine alone; depending on the nature of the offence, the court can impose both imprisonment and a fine.

The bill also treats displaying criminal force with a weapon as a serious offence. Beating, assaulting or physically injuring a health worker, health institution staff member or student, or displaying criminal force with a weapon, would carry up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to Rs 500,000.

“Health workers work in fear, wondering when they will be beaten,” said Dr Badri Rijal, president of the Nepal Medical Association. “We hope the proposed law will create an environment where they can serve patients without worry.”

A law born of rising attacks

The government chose to tighten the law as assaults on health workers, hospital vandalism and mob attacks increased. Doctors’ long-standing demand for “jail without bail” has advanced in this context. People in the sector say attacks are sometimes carried out by mobs or hired people acting as a third party, and that some private hospitals pay whatever patients’ relatives demand just to avoid escalation, which has failed to deter such incidents. Lacking workplace security, health workers are increasingly quitting and going abroad.

Dr Amit Rijal, a former senior medical officer at Om Hospital and Research Centre in Kathmandu, decided two decades ago to leave the country after mistreatment by a patient’s relatives.

“I treated the patient even though I wasn’t on duty, but I had to endure humiliation,” he told a media outlet. “That incident deeply wounded my self-respect. So I eventually quit the profession.”

“Earlier, people got off by paying a fine. The proposed provision at least opens the way to imprisonment,” said Dr Locha Karki, a former association president. “It could instil fear of the law.”

Dr Karki said assaults began rising after the 2062/63 B.S. people’s movement. After pressure from the association, the government enacted the 2066 Act, with regulations in 2069, but the fines were weak. Offenders typically paid Rs 2,000 to 5,000 and were released on bail.

Demands for “jail without bail” intensified in 2073 B.S., after locals and police made health workers line up and apologise at the Charikot Primary Health Centre. A committee led by Dr Pushpa Chaudhary drafted an amendment, but the process halted when the House of Representatives was dissolved. The issue resurfaced after an attack on health workers at Bheri Hospital in Banke during the COVID-19 pandemic. The government then issued an amendment ordinance in 2079 B.S., which tightened the law but did not make attacks fully non-bailable.

Dr Karki said the amendment largely ended out-of-court settlements after arrests, since cases now go through the government attorney’s office to court. Suspects were taken into custody on this basis in Chitwan and Karnali. The new provision goes further: earlier the court could impose “a fine or imprisonment,” while imprisonment and a fine are now more explicit and binding.

Experts say tougher laws raise the question of negligence by health workers, but adequate avenues already exist, including the Nepal Medical Council, the courts and consumer courts.

“There is no shortage of avenues when health workers err,” Dr Rijal said. “So there is no need to assault them.”

He said the law alone will not end hospital violence, and that public awareness and accurate information are also needed.

What offence carries what punishment?

Arson at a health institution would carry two to five years’ imprisonment and a fine of Rs 200,000 to Rs 500,000, both mandatory (currently imprisonment or a fine, or both).

Vandalism or other damage, or beating and physically injuring staff, would carry up to three years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to Rs 300,000.

Lockouts or sieges, obstructing treatment, abuse or indecent behaviour, or inciting others to do so, would carry up to one year and a fine of up to Rs 100,000 (currently up to one year or a fine of Rs 100,000, or both).

The bill also expands the definition of health worker to include interns and adds economic security to the definition of security.

title.rendered: Roads in five Karnali districts remain blocked

content.rendered:
Surkhet, September 28

Incessant rain has blocked road sections in five districts of Karnali Province, disrupting transport services.

On the Karnali Highway, the road has been blocked since Sunday at Tribeni Danda in Tilagufa Municipality-4 and at Bhattadi in Raskot Municipality-8, both in Kalikot. The blockages were caused by landslides and rain.

Likewise, a section of the Karnali Corridor blocked at Khachha in Sarkegad Rural Municipality-1, Humla, has yet to reopen. In Mugu, the blocked road at Talcha in Chhayanath Rara Municipality-7, on the Nagma-Gamgadhi section, has also not been restored.

In Western Rukum, the Mid-Hill Highway is blocked at Sisne in Sanibheri Rural Municipality-2. The concerned road division office said continuous rain is making it difficult to clear the road.

In Dolpa, the Bheri Corridor has been blocked by a landslide at Abbedula in Tripurasundari Municipality-5. Efforts are underway to clear the debris and reopen the road, officials said.

The respective road division offices said they will move ahead with the necessary work to reopen the blocked roads as soon as the weather improves.

Mukunda Prasad Rijal, chief of the Nepal Police Highway Safety and Traffic Management Office, Surkhet, said the weather is improving and the necessary coordination is underway to clear the blocked roads.

title.rendered: Ranju Darshana questions former CJ Rana’s detention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Ranju Darshana has questioned the police’s detention of former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana.

In a Facebook post on Monday, Darshana said that while a person can be arrested if an offence is evident, legal process and evidentiary grounds are crucial in carrying out the arrest.

“The law itself provides that a person can be arrested if an offence is evident. But even when arresting, the tune and rhythm must match,” she wrote. “Even if the offence is not visible, the law demands evidence. Allegation alone is not enough; grounds and evidence to establish the offence are also needed.”

She said the core of the rule of law is that authority must be exercised in accordance with method, procedure and evidence.

“That is exactly what the rule of law is. Authority can be exercised, but not without procedure and evidence,” Darshana said.

In her status, Darshana also described the action as “an arrest made to relocate him to a safe place for some time,” and urged heightened vigilance for his security. She said conditions must be created in which no “generation” can threaten him.

The Crime Investigation Office of Nepal Police at Teku took former Chief Justice Rana into custody at midnight on Saturday. Police did not even allow a team from the National Human Rights Commission to meet him. He was kept at the office for almost a day on Sunday and handed over to relatives in the afternoon.

Police have argued that he was placed in a safe location after a “security threat” was identified. Lawyers and political party leaders have criticised this approach by the police. The National Human Rights Commission also issued a statement criticising the police.

title.rendered: Man beaten to death after dispute at Kailali feast, body thrown off cliff, police say

content.rendered:
Dhangadhi, September 28

Police say a man was beaten to death during a dispute at a rice weaning ceremony in Nigali, Churey Rural Municipality-1, Kailali, about a week ago, and his body was then taken to a cliff and thrown off to hide the incident.

A police officer at the Area Police Office, Malakheti, informed that a preliminary investigation shows that 52-year-old local Yagya Bahadur Bohara died after being beaten, and his body was dumped off a cliff to conceal the incident.

The incident took place on September 21. That day, Yagya Bahadur had gone to attend the rice weaning ceremony of the grandson of a relative, Dhan Bahadur Bohara, and afterwards went missing. During the search, his body was found at the bottom of a cliff in Tulikhet forest.

For the investigation, police have arrested eight people who had been drinking with him at the ceremony. Those arrested are Dhan Bahadur Bohara, the head of the household hosting the pasni, along with Man Bahadur Bohara, Govinda Bohara, Yagya Bahadur Bohara, Dilip Dhami, Ram Bahadur Bohara, Gambhir Bohara and Tilak Jethara.

Based on a complaint filed by the victim’s son, a murder case has been registered against all eight, and an investigation is under way, said DSP Hira Singh Mahara, chief of the Area Police Office, Malakheti.

According to police sources, a dispute broke out between Yagya Bahadur and Man Bahadur while they were drinking at the ceremony. The quarrel, which began the previous day over the abuse of a wife, turned into a physical assault, and Yagya Bahadur fell to the ground unconscious.

A video of the unconscious Yagya Bahadur after the beating has also surfaced. In it, one man is heard saying, “If he dies, I’ll go to jail,” and another replies, “You did wrong.”

Police involved in the investigation said Yagya Bahadur died from the beating that same night. They found that his body was then carried to the cliff and thrown off so that it would appear he had fallen.

Police sources said some of those arrested have told police that he died at the scene and that they dumped the body over the cliff out of fear of being caught.

Although the dispute and beating were initially between two people, police said they are investigating further whether others were involved in, or had planned, the disposal of the body.

DSP Mahara said that because the case is still under investigation, he could not comment on details at this stage. According to him, the incident is being investigated from various angles.

title.rendered: Kaligandaki ‘ A ‘ shut after floods, to resume operations today

content.rendered:
Syangja, September 28

The 144-megawatt Kaligandaki ‘A’ hydropower project in Beltari, Syangja, will resume electricity generation today after water levels in the Kali Gandaki River fell.

The project, located in Beltari, Kaligandaki Rural Municipality-5, had halted generation after four days of continuous rain pushed the river to high levels.

According to Atmesh Paudel, chief of the Kaligandaki ‘A’ Hydropower Station, production was stopped to avoid risk while the river was running high. With the water level now receding, the project is clearing silt that has built up inside the tunnel and inspecting the condition of the powerhouse before restarting generation, he said.

Paudel said a technical team has already assessed the post-flood situation, and production can be resumed.

After the Kali Gandaki flooded, the project opened all the gates of its dam at Mirmi to release the water into the river.

Incessant rain has also inundated Setibeni Bazaar, the meeting point of Syangja, Parbat and Gulmi districts. Residents of 26 households in the bazaar have been sheltered in a nearby school.

Separately, the flood in the Kali Gandaki on Sunday morning swept away the motorable bridge linking Syangja and Gulmi, located a short distance downstream of the project’s dam site.

title.rendered: Two decades on, Nepal’s conservationists search for new ‘dream’ generation

content.rendered:
In September 2006, Nepal’s then Minister of Forests and Soil Conservation Gopal Rai and a contingent of conservation leaders flew to a remote village in eastern Nepal to hand over a conservation area to the people living there.

On the evening of Sept. 22, Rai handed over management of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area (KCA) to the community, hailing it as a milestone in Nepal’s conservation history. “For the community, this was the beginning,” Ghana Shyam Gurung, now WWF’s country representative, tells Mongabay.

The next day, minutes after take-off, the contingent’s Russian-built Mi-8 helicopter crashed, killing all 20 passengers and four crew. Among the dead were the forest minister, his spouse, senior officials, a Finnish diplomat, a senior USAID official and WWF staff. Bad weather hampered rescue efforts for two days. No one in the capital Kathmandu could confirm what had happened until searchers reached the wreckage.

Two decades later, the community-based approach to conservation pioneered by “dreamers” such as Harka and Chandra Gurung and Mingma Norbu Sherpa, all of whom were killed in the crash, still drives Nepal’s wildlife and forest recovery. The country’s tiger population has more than tripled and its forest cover has grown by six percentage points since the crash. But conservationists say progress has since stagnated.

A generation lost

The crash left empty seats at Nepal’s key conservation institutions. Conservationist Sarita Jnawali, then with the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC), remembers the day the deaths were confirmed. “When people like that weren’t there, we felt a huge sense of vacuum,” she tells Mongabay. “It felt like there was nothing left in conservation.”

At the forest ministry, then Joint Secretary Krishna Chandra Paudel lost his minister and Acting Secretary Damodar Parajuli. At the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, ecologist Shiv Raj Bhatta lost his supervisors, director general Narayan Poudel and former director general Tirtha Man Maskey. The two were of such international stature, Bhatta says, that there was no one to replace them, “I wondered how we would ever produce people of that height again.”

WWF lost seven staff, “the single greatest loss of life in WWF’s 45-year history.” Among the dead was Mingma Norbu Sherpa, who had helped establish the Annapurna Conservation Area and led WWF Nepal at the time. “I’m a tough person,” Ghana Shyam Gurung from WWF says. “I could never endure that. That was hard..The hardest thing for me was meeting Mingma sir’s wife — meeting his widow. I haven’t cried that much even for my own mother. That was the first time.”

A wound that left scar

Paudel, who later served as the forest ministry’s secretary before retiring, describes the 20 years as a wound that left a deep scar. “It’s like when parents die suddenly, the family finds some comfort, and carries the ordinary rhythm of life forward,” he tells Mongabay. “But the old loss is never truly fulfilled.”

For Jnawali, the story of the past two decades is one of replacement, not continuity. “The vacuum I imagined didn’t happen, because people from a new generation took over,” she says. “They don’t remember the old story, but the vacuum still got replaced.”

Visionaries and people who dream a dream and see it through have grown scarcer, she says. This could be a result of government instability and weakening individual commitment as much as of the crash itself, she adds.

“In the absence of dreamers who could shift paradigms, what came after 2006 was largely the same work repeated,” she says, referring to the shift from strict, exclusionary conservation to community-based management pioneered and led by the people on the helicopter.

‘Have we stopped dreaming?’

Gurung says the difficult question to answer now is: Have we stopped dreaming after 2006? “We keep talking about the same things, redoing the same work,” he says. “So what’s next? Why aren’t we looking for new green areas?”

Conservation needs a breakthrough on the scale of the 1990s shift to community-based management, he says — one built around climate and water. He points to a model of coexistence suited to a landscape that now holds far more wildlife and far fewer farming families than it did in 2006. “The world ahead is about water,” he says.

Paudel disagrees with Gurung and Jnawali. Forest for Prosperity, the policy vision he says he pushed as secretary to tie conservation to household income, is a new dream by his own account. It aimed at prosperity rather than protection for its own sake. WIt was conservation becoming highly politicized that slowed the sector down, he argues, not that his generation stopped dreaming.

Missed opportunities

Jnawali counts the cost of the crash in missed opportunities for Nepal. Had the 2006 delegation lived, she says she believes that protected areas such as Annapurna and Manaslu might have followed Kanchenjunga into full community management, and new areas might have opened. “We didn’t just lose people that day,” she says. “We lost the pace we were moving at.”

Ecologist Bhatta traces the sector’s shortcomings to a failure of collaboration more than to the crash itself. Nepal’s community-based model won international recognition for biodiversity outcomes, he says. That model included the Terai Arc Landscape approach, a transboundary corridor of protected forests linking Nepal and India. But it delivered less on livelihoods, he says, because other ministries never fully joined in.

He says he wants devolution and to hand more control from the government to local communities. Buffer zones, areas around national parks, should be transferred more completely to community control, he says, with the park warden no longer the central authority. “The core was always local people,” he adds. That handover, in his view, is unfinished business.

Success in numbers

Nepal’s tiger population has grown from 121 in 2010 to a record 429 this year. Its rhino population has grown from 645 in 2015 to 752 in 2021. “We’ve increased tigers, we’ve increased rhinos,” former Secretary of the Ministry of Forests Paudel says. “That’s a result of the dream that generation was dreaming at the time.”

Part of that recovery rests on the community forestry system that the 2006 generation helped build. Nepal’s forest cover has grown from about 40% in the 1990s to more than 46% today — one of the sharpest reversals of deforestation anywhere. More than 23,000 community forest user groups now manage roughly 2.5 million hectares (6.2 million acres), and about a third of Nepal’s population belongs to one.

The cost of success

The recovering wildlife itself has become part of the strain. As tiger and rhino numbers have climbed, so has the toll of people killed or injured by the animals brought back by conservation efforts.

A 2026 study of Nepal’s Terai Arc Landscape documented 245 tiger attacks on humans between 2010 and 2024 with 141 fatalities. The study also found a sharp surge in attacks in the Banke-Bardia complex between 2019 and 2023 — Bardia’s tiger population roughly doubled over the same period. Attacks declined after park authorities captured and relocated 21 tigers responsible for repeated conflicts, the study says.

Meanwhile, in the hills, people are abandoning their villages. In Taplejung, the district where the 2006 helicopter went down, data from officials in its Phungling Municipality reportedly say 245 to 330 families leave hill settlements every year with most citing crop losses due to monkeys.

A memory fading

In 2006 after the last rites of the deceased were performed and work resumed, the government instituted the National Conservation Day and a National Conservation Award to commemorate the memory of the deceased. WWF set up memorial scholarships that have since supported around 200 students, many of them women from underserved communities. More than 20 memorial scholars have gone on to pursue master’s degrees in New Zealand, according to WWF’s Gurung.

Two decades on, even the memory of the crash is fading unevenly. In Taplejung, a memorial features statue of the 24 deceased. In Kathmandu, the government-built statue park in Ramkot is overgrown and dilapidated, some names faded or gone. Paudel says observance of the disaster, once marked at the highest level of government, has all but lapsed. “Twenty years have passed and we have almost abandoned it for the last 10,” he says.

Local problems demand local solutions

Paudel says some progress has been made in tackling the challenges, but the measures don’t address the challenges completely. He points to compensation schemes for human-wildlife conflict deaths and insurance programs, both introduced since 2006, but argues that the answers Nepal needs next won’t come from Kathmandu. “Local governments should look for local solutions,” he says. “People know better.”
