title.rendered: Trump and Xi face an AI security dilemma – but face‑to‑face diplomacy could be a start in mitigating it

content.rendered:
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping’s Washington summit has been billed as a discussion of major issues surrounding the development and possible regulation of artificial intelligence (AI), as well as trying to find common ground over Taiwan and trade. What everyone wants to know is whether – and how – the leaders of the two biggest world powers can get over their rivalry through face-to-face diplomacy to achieve a positive outcome in what is surely the most urgent question facing global leadership.

The importance Beijing attaches to such encounters was underlined on September 17 when, in a call with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi declared that “head-of-state diplomacy is the anchor of China-US relations”.

For this diplomacy to bear fruit, Trump and Xi have to develop what is known as “security dilemma sensibility”. This is the ability to recognise that an adversary may be acting out of fear and not predatory intent and to appreciate how one’s own state’s actions have contributed to that fear. If Trump and Xi can do this, it could create an opening for policies of reciprocal reassurance.

In our new book we argue that face-to-face diplomacy offers leaders an opportunity to examine these questions directly and explore what reassurance could involve.

Each of the two leaders need to acknowledge how their own country’s actions contribute to the other’s insecurity. Trust may develop out of such a shared understanding, but recognising an adversary’s fears does not require accepting their claims. What it does do is open the path to new policies of reassurance and restraint.

This summit is an important opportunity for the US and Chinese presidents to show each other that they are exercising security dilemma sensibility, especially in relation to those issues (Taiwan and AI) that could if left unmanaged plunge the two sides into deeper confrontation.

Reagan and Gorbachev’s nuclear rapport

There are lessons to be taken from the relationship between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev in the late 1980s. When the two leaders met for their first summit in Geneva in November 1985, it was against the backdrop of a tense superpower relationship in the first part of the 1980s, especially Soviet fears that the United States was planning to launch a nuclear attack on the Soviet Union under the cover of Nato’s November 1983 Able Archer exercise.

Gorbachev came to power as general secretary of the Soviet Union in March 1985. He had a reputation as a pragmatist and reformer who wanted to reduce global tensions and curb the expensive nuclear arms race.

In their first private conversation, Reagan proposed examining the suspicions driving the arms race. Gorbachev argued that cooperation did not require either country to change its political system and that it was possible to advance one superpower’s interests without undermining that of the other.

On the all-important nuclear question, their joint statement declared that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”. Crucially, and often overlooked, they also pledged that: “They will not seek to achieve military superiority.”

These commitments publicly acknowledged a common interest in preventing nuclear war. Their statement agreed to “study the question at the expert level of centers to reduce nuclear risk” and “took satisfaction in such recent steps in this direction as the modernization of the Soviet-US hotline”.

This led to the development of the Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers (NRRCs) in 1987. These were described by the US Department of State as “specialized 24/7 government communications hubs … to lower the risk of accidental nuclear war”.

So while the Geneva summit did not eliminate superpower competition, it established a framework on which further cooperation could build.

Could AI provide a similar opening?

While nuclear fears were at the top of the agenda for Reagan and Gorbachev, AI is the burning issue for Trump and Xi. There have already been some positive steps. On September 21, US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Washington and Beijing had agreed to establish a formal AI dialogue, including an incident line. Further talks are planned in Shenzhen later in the year.

It’s a start. But agreeing to establish a channel, or “AI hotline” as some have called it, is no guarantee as to how it will work. We know that the US fears that if it constrains its development of AI, China may cheat and surge ahead. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, said exactly this when he wrote: “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance.”

It’s reasonable to assume that China feels the same way. This is going to make cooperation very difficult.

The security dilemma arises when each side’s efforts to protect itself intensify the other side’s feelings of insecurity. When it comes to AI, our argument is that recognising the common danger is only part of the task. Each side also needs to consider whether its efforts to avoid falling behind will encourage the other to accelerate, potentially at the expense of safety.

The incident line will go some way to addressing this by establishing common tests for dangerous AI capabilities and procedures for warning one another about serious incidents.

The real test of the summit

A summit need not resolve fundamental disagreements or produce personal trust to make cooperation possible. Rather, the test of the summit is whether each can recognise the other’s security fears, especially in relation to AI, and acknowledge how their own actions have contributed to them.

The summit and new AI dialogue provides an opportunity to explore potential common ground on AI safety that can limit the dangers of US-China competition.

For outside observers, the evidence would lie less in declarations of personal rapport than in specific reciprocal commitments, responsibilities assigned to officials and arrangements for follow-through.

An operational incident-reporting channel would not prove that trust had developed, but it would provide a way to examine whether the leaders’ commitments were being put into practice.

title.rendered: RTI exists in law. Now it must work for citizens

content.rendered:
Today should be an important day for ordinary citizens. The United Nations has recognised September 28 as the International Day for Universal Access to Information since 2019. In July 2011, the UN Human Rights Committee also confirmed that the right of access to information is an inherent part of freedom, placing an obligation on states both to respond to requests, with limited exceptions, and to proactively publish information of public interest.

The right to information (RTI) is therefore a foundation of democratic governance. It empowers citizens to hold governments accountable and participate meaningfully in decision-making. In Nepal, the right to information was recognised as a fundamental right in the 1990 Constitution and is guaranteed under Article 27 of the 2015 Constitution. The Right to Information Act, 2007 (2064 BS), and the Right to Information Regulations, 2008 (2065 BS), were enacted to operationalize this constitutional guarantee, while the National Information Commission (NIC) was established in 2008 as the primary regulatory and adjudicatory body.

Despite these progressive legal foundations, however, the gap between legal entitlement and practical exercise remains wide. Nepal has the laws and institutions needed to protect RTI, but the right has yet to become a routine part of citizens’ daily lives.

Nepal’s RTI architecture is robust on paper. Article 27 of the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to seek and obtain information on matters of personal or public importance. The RTI Act, 2007, requires public bodies across all three tiers of government, as well as public institutions, political parties and certain non-governmental organizations, to respect this right and proactively disclose information. Section 4(1) requires public bodies to respect citizens’ right to information, while Section 3(2) requires every public body to appoint an Information Officer.

The NIC serves as the primary body responsible for protecting, promoting and implementing RTI. It hears appeals from citizens whose information requests have been denied and can issue binding orders requiring information to be disclosed. The RTI Implementation Monitoring Directive, 2015, further established monitoring mechanisms at the federal, provincial and district levels to support implementation nationwide.

Yet laws and institutions alone do not guarantee effective implementation. The NIC’s own Handbook for Information Seekers acknowledges that, despite more than a decade of constitutional and legal provisions, public awareness of the right to information remains inadequate.

The number of citizens actively exercising their RTI remains low. Awareness is not uniform across society, and many citizens, particularly those at the grassroots level, remain unaware of how RTI can be used to access information and hold public bodies accountable.

The NIC itself operates under significant constraints. Its limited budget restricts its ability to conduct promotional activities and fulfil its responsibilities across federal, provincial and local governments and other public bodies. Although the Commission has instructed public bodies to appoint Information Officers, compliance remains uneven.

Information classification is another concern. Government agencies have historically been reluctant to disclose information, sometimes citing its “classified” status without adequate justification. A culture of secrecy continues to persist in many public offices.

Perhaps the most deeply rooted challenge is a bureaucratic culture that treats information as a source of power to be guarded rather than a public good to be shared. The NIC itself has recognised that when officials responsible for upholding the Constitution and the law do not follow those same laws, citizens are less likely to do so either. Ensuring good governance, transparency and accountability therefore requires officials to understand the law and be willing to follow it.

This resistance can take many forms, including delays in responding to requests, unnecessary procedural requirements and, in some cases, intimidation of RTI activists and information seekers. Such intimidation can discourage civic participation and undermine the very purpose of the RTI law.

There are, however, encouraging signs. The NIC’s growing caseload suggests increasing public awareness and willingness to use the appeals mechanism. In fiscal year 2080/81, 1,265 appeals were filed, the highest number in the Commission’s history, before falling to 1,049 appeals in 2081/82, according to the NIC’s annual report. This represents a significant increase from just 12 appeals in the Commission’s first year. The Commission has disposed of more than 95 percent of appeals each year, demonstrating its commitment to timely adjudication. Notably, 72 percent of appeals originated at the local level, suggesting that citizens are increasingly using RTI to monitor local governance and development activities.

The NIC has also launched an RTI Management System to digitize and streamline the information request and appeal process. Such initiatives can make the system more accessible, but technology alone cannot bridge the gap between legal rights and their practical use.

The first priority must be greater citizen awareness. RTI needs to be brought into civic education at schools and universities, including practical guidance on filing information requests and appealing denials. Community radio and local media can also play a greater role, particularly in communities where access to official information remains limited. Civil society organizations such as Freedom Forum, Open Knowledge Nepal and Accountability Lab Nepal have demonstrated how RTI can support open budgets and local development monitoring. Their grassroots outreach should be expanded, particularly among women, Dalits and other marginalized communities where awareness remains low.

At the institutional level, the NIC needs adequate resources to fulfil its mandate. Public bodies should also be required to submit regular RTI compliance reports, with meaningful consequences for non-compliance. The appointment of Information Officers must be systematically monitored and enforced.

Protection for information seekers is equally important. Section 29 of the RTI Act provides protection for whistleblowers, but information seekers themselves can face intimidation. Such cases should be promptly investigated and those responsible held accountable. Citizens cannot meaningfully exercise a legal right if doing so exposes them to fear or retaliation.

Proactive disclosure should also become a much stronger part of government practice. The RTI Act already requires public bodies to publish certain categories of information without waiting for individual requests. This is one of the most effective ways to empower citizens because it reduces the need for formal applications and eases the burden on both information seekers and public bodies. Study and investigation reports of public interest should be routinely disclosed. It is particularly concerning when governments that come to power promising better governance withhold important investigation reports.

Ultimately, however, legal and institutional reforms will not be enough without a change in bureaucratic culture. The prevailing attitude that information is a privilege to be guarded must give way to a service-oriented understanding of information as a public right. Public officials, particularly office chiefs and Information Officers, should receive mandatory training on RTI and their constitutional obligations. The NIC’s handbooks for public bodies and information seekers provide useful resources that should be systematically incorporated into such training.

Political parties and their leaders at all levels must also demonstrate a visible commitment to RTI, including through parliamentary oversight of implementation. At the same time, public bodies that demonstrate exemplary transparency should be recognised and rewarded, creating positive incentives for others to follow.

The transformative potential of RTI is best demonstrated through concrete examples. Investigative journalists have used RTI to uncover irregularities in public bodies, while citizens at the local level have used it to monitor development and governance. These successes should be documented and shared more widely so that similar practices can be replicated elsewhere.

Nepal’s RTI legal framework provides a strong foundation for transparent and accountable governance. The constitutional guarantee, the comprehensive RTI Act and the establishment of the National Information Commission have created the necessary legal and institutional framework. The challenge now is implementation.

Bridging the gap will require sustained citizen awareness campaigns, stronger institutions, greater protection for information seekers and RTI activists, proactive disclosure and a fundamental shift from a culture of secrecy to one of transparency.

Empowering Nepali citizens through RTI is not merely a matter of legal compliance. It is a foundation for participatory democracy, good governance and inclusive development. The time to act is now, before the promise of the right to information remains confined to the pages of legislation instead of becoming a reality in the daily lives of Nepali citizens.

title.rendered: Why was Cholendra detained? What we know about the former chief justice’s midnight detention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 28

Former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana was taken from his Maharajgunj residence in the early hours of Sunday and released into the custody of his family roughly 12 hours later.

Police initially confirmed that Rana had been detained. Later, however, they said he had not been arrested and had instead been taken to a safe place after receiving information about a security threat.

The government and police have not publicly disclosed the nature of the threat, who allegedly posed it or why Rana had to be taken from his home.

SSP Santosh Khadka of the Criminal Investigation Office, Teku, said police had received information that Rana could be at risk.

“After learning that there was a security threat to him, we brought him to our office at night because something could happen,” Khadka told Onlinekhabar.

Rana’s brother, Prabhu Shumsher, gave a different account of the circumstances. He said police told Rana that there was a threat to him from Gen Z protesters.

According to Prabhu Shumsher, Rana did not know about any such threat and instead asked police to strengthen security at his residence.

Police nevertheless took him to the Criminal Investigation Office in Teku.

The National Human Rights Commission also sent a team to the police office to check on Rana. The team waited for around 45 minutes but was not allowed to meet him. The NHRC later objected to the police conduct, saying it was contrary to its constitutional and legal authority.

The episode therefore raises an immediate question: why was Rana taken from his home, and what exactly was happening behind the police operation?

The plan was made before midnight

According to sources familiar with the developments, the decision to take Rana into custody had already been discussed on Saturday evening.

A police team from the Crime Investigation Office reached his residence at around 12:30am.

Rana initially refused to accompany the officers.

According to police sources, officers spent around an hour and a half trying to persuade him. A team of about a dozen plain-clothes personnel had reached the residence under the command of a DSP.

Rana was eventually taken to the Crime Investigation Office in Teku at around 2am, where he was kept in the office of SSP Santosh Khadka.

Police have said no criminal case was being pursued against him and that the purpose of taking him into custody was his own protection.

But another question remains unanswered.

If Rana was being protected, why was he taken away from his residence rather than provided additional security there?

That question has been raised by legal professionals as well as Rana’s family.

No arrest warrant

Sources familiar with the matter said police had not obtained a court-issued arrest warrant before taking Rana away.

The legal basis for holding him therefore became an immediate issue.

Onlinekhabar’s reporting found that police had not publicly disclosed any criminal charge against Rana. Police have also not identified the specific security threat or the person or group believed to have posed it.

Nepal Bar Association president Professor Dr Bijay Prasad Mishra also questioned the government’s decision.

The Bar, he said, does not support corruption or wrongdoing, but that does not mean the state can ignore legal procedures.

The question, therefore, is not whether Rana should be investigated if there are grounds for doing so. It is whether the state followed the law in taking a former chief justice from his home in the middle of the night.

Why was the government watching Rana?

The immediate security explanation is only one part of the story.

In recent weeks, Rana had become increasingly active after the Supreme Court effectively cleared the way for him to emerge from the shadow of his long-running impeachment dispute.

Sources close to the government say his activities had attracted growing attention.

According to sources, Rana was becoming active on two fronts.

The first was political.

The second was judicial.

Sources claim that Rana had begun taking an unusual interest in political developments and had started discussing the possibility of a future political role.

They also allege that he was meeting people connected to cases pending before the courts and attempting to influence judicial proceedings from behind the scenes.

These are allegations from government and judicial sources and have not been established by a court.

But they help explain why Rana’s movements and political contacts had become a concern within Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s team.

Bansbari becomes a meeting point

After the Supreme Court ruling that removed the immediate legal obstacle to his return to public life, Rana’s residence became increasingly active.

People from different political camps were reportedly visiting him.

RSP leaders and lawmakers were among those visiting Rana. He was also reportedly meeting leaders associated with the Nepali Congress and CPN-UML chair KP Sharma Oli.

Sources close to the government claim that the number of visitors to Rana’s residence had increased significantly and that his political activity was being monitored.

According to one source, the government became concerned that Rana was attempting to influence the judiciary while simultaneously expanding his political contacts.

An RSP source cited in the reporting went further, saying the detention was intended to send a message to RSP leaders that the government knew whom they were meeting.

That claim could not be independently established.

But it reflects the growing tension surrounding Rana’s political contacts.

Rana and the RSP

Rana’s relationship with the Rastriya Swatantra Party appears to have been one of the issues that particularly concerned people around the Prime Minister.

According to sources, Rana had begun referring to the RSP as “our party”.

He was also reportedly presenting himself as a possible future presidential candidate.

At the same time, his contacts were not limited to the RSP.

He was meeting members of the Sher Bahadur Deuba camp in the Nepali Congress and was also in contact with UML chair KP Sharma Oli.

This placed Rana in an unusual position.

A former chief justice who had spent years at the centre of a bitter political and judicial controversy was once again meeting leaders from different political camps at a time when Nepal’s political system was undergoing another major realignment.

The Congress connection

Rana’s meetings with Congress leaders also became significant in the eyes of government sources.

According to the reporting, Rana had increased his meetings with leaders outside the Congress establishment before a Supreme Court full bench headed by Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma issued an order allowing a review of a case concerning the Nepali Congress’s special general convention.

Sources viewed the timing of Rana’s meetings and developments in court with suspicion.

There is, however, no established evidence that Rana influenced the court’s decision.

The significance of these meetings lies in the perception within political circles that Rana was attempting to regain influence over both politics and the judiciary.

The Oli connection and the idea of restoring Parliament

Rana was also reportedly discussing the political possibility of restoring the House of Representatives.

According to the reporting, he had been in contact with UML chair KP Sharma Oli and had discussed a concept paper concerning the restoration of Parliament.

Oli later spoke publicly about the possibility of restoring the House.

Whether there was a direct political understanding between Rana and Oli remains unclear.

But sources close to the developments viewed Rana’s political activity as part of a broader attempt to shape the country’s political direction.

Some sources also claimed that Rana was trying to persuade Nepali Congress leader Sher Bahadur Deuba to support such a political course.

These claims remain part of the political accounts surrounding Rana and have not been independently established.

Why Rana’s return mattered

To understand why Rana’s recent activity attracted so much attention, it is necessary to go back to his time as chief justice.

Rana became a permanent Supreme Court justice in 2014 after a controversial parliamentary hearing process.

His judicial record had already attracted criticism.

In 2001, while serving at the Biratnagar Appellate Court, Rana was part of a bench that acquitted defendants in a gambling case. The bench held that the card game involved was based on skill and therefore did not amount to gambling.

In 2006, while serving at the Special Court, Rana was part of a bench that dismissed a corruption case against former Home Minister Govinda Raj Joshi on the grounds of limitation.

The Supreme Court later overturned that decision, and the corruption case against Joshi was ultimately established.

Rana went on to become chief justice in January 2019.

His tenure coincided with some of Nepal’s most consequential constitutional and political disputes.

The dissolution battles

During the political crisis surrounding the dissolution of the House of Representatives, the Supreme Court under Rana became one of the central institutions in the political struggle.

The court restored the House in February 2021.

It later issued another landmark ruling ordering the appointment of Sher Bahadur Deuba as prime minister.

Rana’s role in these cases became a subject of intense political debate.

His critics accused him of becoming too closely involved in political bargaining, while his supporters maintained that the court was simply exercising its constitutional authority.

The controversy eventually reached Rana’s own position as chief justice.

The Hamal episode

In October 2021, Deuba appointed Gajendra Hamal as Industry, Commerce and Supplies Minister.

Hamal was related to Rana by marriage.

The appointment triggered immediate controversy.

Hamal resigned roughly 40 hours later.

The episode further intensified pressure on Rana, with the Nepal Bar Association beginning protests against him.

Judges at the Supreme Court also stopped appearing before his benches.

By then, Rana’s position as chief justice had become increasingly untenable.

The impeachment motion

On February 13, 2022, lawmakers from the Nepali Congress and CPN-Maoist Centre registered an impeachment motion against Rana.

He was suspended from his position.

But Parliament never completed the impeachment process.

The motion remained unresolved for years, even as parliamentary terms changed.

This created an unusual constitutional situation.

Rana had retired while the impeachment motion remained pending, but Parliament had not either removed him or acquitted him.

For years, his legal status remained contested.

The Supreme Court ruling that changed everything

The issue returned to the Supreme Court this month.

A Constitutional Bench led by Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma dismissed petitions challenging the Federal Parliament Secretariat’s position on Rana’s suspension.

The ruling cleared the way for Rana to receive pension benefits and other facilities and effectively removed the legal obstacle that had kept his status in limbo.

That decision changed Rana’s position dramatically.

After years of suspension and political isolation, he was once again free to move publicly and engage with political actors.

And according to sources, he did exactly that.

Manoj Sharma and Rana

There is another layer to the story.

Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma had been nominated to the Supreme Court while Rana himself was chief justice.

The Nepal Bar had previously raised questions about an alleged discussion involving Rana, Sharma and then High Court judge Nawaraj Thapaliya concerning a case.

The allegations were disputed and did not establish that Sharma had acted improperly.

Nevertheless, the relationship between the two became part of the political and judicial speculation surrounding Rana’s return.

The Supreme Court’s recent decision concerning Rana’s impeachment dispute was delivered under Sharma’s leadership.

That coincidence has also become a subject of political discussion.

Why Balen’s team became concerned

According to sources close to the Prime Minister’s Office, several developments increased concern about Rana’s activities.

These included Supreme Court orders involving property investigations, constitutional matters and a pension-related case concerning Rana.

Government sources also claimed that Rana was attempting to influence the judiciary through personal contacts.

Separately, concerns were reportedly raised after judges at the Special Court complained to Chief Justice Sharma and Supreme Court judges about difficult working conditions.

According to a Supreme Court source, the concerns eventually reached the Prime Minister’s secretariat.

The allegations are significant because they suggest that the government’s concern about Rana was not limited to his political contacts.

It also extended to what officials believed he was attempting to do through the judiciary.

A history of political influence

Rana’s critics have long argued that his career cannot be understood separately from Nepal’s political establishment.

His appointment to the Supreme Court, his decisions during the parliamentary dissolution disputes, the appointment of Gajendra Hamal and the subsequent impeachment motion all became part of a wider debate over the relationship between political leaders and the judiciary.

The current dispute therefore has a long history.

What has changed is that Rana, after years of being suspended and politically sidelined, has once again begun appearing at the intersection of political and judicial affairs.

That is why his Bansbari residence had become significant.

Some in political circles have even described it as a new centre of influence, comparing it with the old political and legal influence associated with former Chief Justice Kalyan Shrestha’s residence in Kupandole.

The phrase “power has shifted from Kupandole to Bansbari” is essentially political commentary, but it captures the perception that Rana’s residence had become an important meeting point.

The question of the RSP and judicial cases

Sources associated with the RSP also claim that there had been increased activity around Rana’s residence by people seeking help in cases involving allegations of money laundering.

They allege that some of those meeting Rana were interested in securing the release of people facing such accusations.

These claims have not been independently established.

But they add to the government’s stated concern about Rana’s recent activities.

The question is therefore not simply why Rana was detained on Sunday morning.

It is also why a former chief justice, after years away from public life, had once again become important enough to attract attention from political parties, government officials and people involved in court cases.

Why was he taken—and why was he released?

This remains the biggest unanswered question.

Police say Rana was taken into protective custody because of a security threat.

But they have not explained the nature of the threat.

They have not publicly identified who posed it.

They have not explained why additional security could not have been provided at Rana’s home.

And they have not clearly explained the legal basis on which police removed him from his residence and held him at the Criminal Investigation Office.

By afternoon, the same police authorities had handed him back to his family.

SP Rameshwar Karki said Rana would be provided security at his residence going forward.

That raises another question.

If the threat was serious enough to require taking a former chief justice from his home in the middle of the night, what changed within those few hours?

The human rights question

The National Human Rights Commission’s experience at the Teku police office has added to the controversy.

The commission sent a team to meet Rana but police prevented the team from entering and meeting him.

The NHRC later said the police conduct was contrary to its constitutional and legal responsibilities and called for an impartial investigation into the incident.

For the Nepal Bar, the issue is equally straightforward.

The Bar has said it does not oppose investigation into allegations against Rana.

But it has also questioned whether a former chief justice can simply be taken from his home without proper legal procedure.

A former chief justice once again at the centre of power

Rana’s latest episode cannot be separated from his history.

He was once the most powerful figure in Nepal’s judiciary.

His tenure as chief justice became entangled with the country’s political crises.

He was suspended following an impeachment motion.

For years, he remained caught in a legal and political limbo.

Then, earlier this month, the Supreme Court ruling effectively cleared the way for his return.

Within weeks, he was once again meeting political leaders, receiving visitors at his residence and, according to sources, discussing the country’s political future.

Then, in the early hours of Sunday, police came for him.

The official explanation is a security threat.

The political background suggests a more complicated picture.

Rana’s reported contacts with the RSP, Nepali Congress and UML, his alleged interest in judicial cases and his reported discussions about the country’s political direction had made him a person of renewed interest to the government.

But whether those activities had anything to do with his detention remains unproven.

What is clear is that the government has yet to provide a full explanation for the operation.

And until it does, the questions surrounding Rana’s brief detention will extend beyond the issue of security.

They will touch the larger question that has followed Rana throughout his career: where does the boundary lie between judicial power, political influence and executive authority in Nepal?

title.rendered: Marsyangdi River blocked by flood debris near Chame in Manang

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The Marsyangdi River has been blocked near Chame in Manang after a flood carrying mud and debris from Ghatte Khola entered the river.

Mukti Prasad Khanal, Chief District Officer of Manang, confirmed that the river had been obstructed by the debris-laden flood.

“The river has been blocked by the flood carrying mud and debris from Ghatte Khola,” Khanal said. “The river flow is increasing, so the risk is also rising.”

A warning siren installed along the Marsyangdi River is currently sounding as authorities monitor the situation.

title.rendered: Floods and landslides kill 14 across Gandaki Province, hundreds displaced

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 27

At least 14 people have died and hundreds have been affected by floods and landslides across Gandaki Province after three days of continuous heavy rainfall.

According to preliminary figures from the Gandaki Province Police Office, three people are injured and two remain missing, while 179 houses have been completely destroyed and 28 partially damaged. Another 295 houses are considered at high risk.

A total of 512 households, involving 1,684 people, have been displaced or affected by the disasters. Twelve livestock sheds have also been destroyed and 44 livestock have died.

Four members of family killed in Baglung

In Nisi Khola Rural Municipality-3 of Baglung, a landslide buried a house at around 3:45am on Sunday, killing a mother and her three children.

The victims have been identified as 39-year-old Shyam Kumari BK and her sons Manoj, 12, Mukesh, 9, and Nisan, 5.

The family was asleep when the debris came down from above the house, leaving them no opportunity to escape.

Shyam Kumari’s 14-year-old daughter, Muskan, survived because she had gone to her grandparents’ home on Saturday.

According to Kuvir BK, ward chair of Nisi Khola Rural Municipality-2, the family had built their house on a hillside and had not anticipated a landslide or flood despite the continuing rain.

The four bodies were recovered, post-mortems were conducted in the presence of relatives and the funerals were held on Sunday, according to ward chair BK.

Flooding has also damaged at least 10 to 12 houses in Jhiwa Khola Bazaar in ward 4. Because the flooding occurred around 10:30am, many residents had already moved to safer locations and no further loss of life was reported there.

Another person died in Talakot Rural Municipality-10 of Baglung after a landslide buried a house while he was sleeping. The victim was identified as 59-year-old Man Bahadur Roka.

Baglung Chief District Officer Krishna Prasad Acharya said landslides had blocked several roads and damaged electricity and telecommunications towers.

“We are still collecting details of the damage. Our first priority is to restore electricity and network services,” Acharya said. “There is no electricity or network across much of the district, and major roads are also blocked.”

Three killed and four missing in Myagdi

Myagdi has suffered the second-highest human and physical losses in Gandaki Province after Baglung.

Three people have died in landslides in the district, while four others remain missing and several people have been injured.

Myagdi Chief District Officer Ganesh Gaire said Annapurna and Malika rural municipalities and Beni have reported casualties and significant damage.

Four people are missing in Annapurna Rural Municipality, where one body has been recovered. In Malika Rural Municipality, two people were reported missing, with one rescued unconscious. Another person was reported buried in Bhamkini of Beni-3.

Kumari Wali BK, estimated to be around 35, died in a landslide in Beni-3.

In Ghiwang of Annapurna Rural Municipality-5, 75-year-old Sukumari Garbuja and another woman, estimated to be around 55-year-old Domaya Garbuja, were reported dead.

Kiran Pun, who had gone missing in Aula of Malika Rural Municipality-3, was found unconscious and rescued. The search for two others is continuing, according to local journalist Santosh Gautam.

Two people from Annapurna Rural Municipality-3 were rescued by a Nepal Army helicopter and brought to Beni.

Floods and landslides have also damaged several hydropower projects in Myagdi.

According to Deputy Superintendent of Police Rajan Karki, search operations are continuing for those still missing. Electricity and telecommunications services have also been disrupted in the district.

Rising Kali Gandaki raises concerns

The water level of the Kali Gandaki River began rising on Saturday and turned into a major flood by Sunday morning.

The river has eroded parts of Beni Bazaar, putting settlements along its banks at risk.

Floodwaters also eroded the land connecting the Beni-Jomsom bridge at Pokhare Bagar, cutting off road access to Jomsom.

The Kali Gandaki has caused damage from Mustang and Myagdi through Parbat and Syangja and as far as Devghat in Tanahun.

67 houses swept away in Parbat

In Farse of Jaljala Rural Municipality-8, Parbat, the Kali Gandaki River has swept away an entire settlement.

Parbat Chief District Officer Ganga Bahadur Chhetri said 67 houses had been completely swept away and another 23 were at high risk.

“Sixty-seven houses in Farse Bazaar, which lies along the Kali Gandaki, appear to have been completely destroyed, while another 23 are at high risk,” Chhetri said. “The river erosion has taken away those houses.”

Residents had moved to safer locations after authorities warned from September 24 that continued heavy rainfall could trigger floods and landslides.

“They are currently staying with relatives or neighbours,” Chhetri said. “The Gandaki Province government and district administration are providing essential supplies for the time being.”

A suspension bridge connecting Parbat and Baglung has also been swept away.

Flooding from the Kali Gandaki has inundated houses in Bihadi Rural Municipality-6 of Parbat and Galyang Municipality-5 of Syangja. Initial reports suggested around 30 houses were flooded, although officials are still assessing the damage.

Manang cut off as floods damage houses and bridges

Manang has also suffered damage from floods, with houses, bridges and causeways swept away.

Communication with several parts of the district has been disrupted because electricity and mobile network services are down, making it difficult for authorities to collect information.

Manang Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal said around 10 houses had been completely destroyed and another 10 were inundated following flooding in local streams.

All four local levels in the district — Chame, Narpa Bhumi, Nasong and Manang Ngisyang — have reported varying degrees of damage.

Narpa Bhumi remains without road connectivity, while authorities have been unable to establish communication with Narpa Bhumi and Manang Ngisyang.

“Electricity has been out since the day before yesterday. There is no mobile network,” Khanal said. “We have also been unable to determine where trekkers who had gone to the area are, although their agencies have been calling.”

Two wooden bridges and two causeways in Chame have been swept away.

Five houses in Chame have been completely damaged. Khanal said there were no reported casualties there because residents had moved to safer areas before the situation worsened.

Around 10 houses in Tal village have been inundated. A suspension bridge over the Marsyangdi River in Nasong Rural Municipality has also been swept away, while roads in Nising Rural Municipality remain blocked.

Authorities say even excavators cannot currently reach several affected areas.

A micro-hydropower project in Narpa Bhumi is also reported to have been damaged.

163 houses inundated in Nawalpur

Flooding of the Narayani River has also affected Nawalpur, where 163 houses were inundated after the river rose above the danger level.

Several areas of Gaindakot were flooded, while Madhyabindu and Binayi Tribeni rural municipalities were also affected.

According to Assistant Chief District Officer Rana, some displaced residents are staying with relatives, while many have been accommodated in schools.

While low-lying areas of Gaindakot, Madhyabindu and Binayi Tribeni were inundated, floods and landslides also damaged roads and bridges in the hill municipalities of Bungdikali and Bulingtar.

Other districts including Kaski, Gorkha, Lamjung and Tanahun have also been affected by the prolonged rainfall.

In Kaski, the water level of the Seti River rose and formed a temporary pool at Ramghat in Pokhara, although the level has now started to decline. Landslides have blocked several roads, but no major loss of life has been reported there.

title.rendered: 2 bodies recovered after avalanche leaves climbers missing in Himlung

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Two bodies have been recovered after an avalanche struck Himlung Himal in Narpa Bhumi Rural Municipality-5 of Manang, leaving several people missing.

According to Manang Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal, a rescue team brought the two bodies to Chame by helicopter on Sunday.

“Two bodies have just arrived by helicopter. It is no longer possible to continue searching and rescuing the others today. It is already dark, which makes rescue operations difficult,” Khanal said. “The rescue operation will resume tomorrow.”

Khanal said the area had been hit by multiple hazards, including the avalanche and flooding in the Thado Khola. Communication has also been affected in Manang due to disruptions to electricity and network services.

He added that another group of 10 people who had travelled toward Himlung Himal had made contact and were being moved to a safe location.

Meanwhile, Krishna Prasad Poudel, assistant chief district officer of Manang, said debris brought down by flooding in Thado Khola had formed a temporary blockage in the Marsyangdi River at Chame. However, he said there was no immediate indication of a major threat.

A warning system installed along the Marsyangdi River is currently sounding an alarm.

Floods cause widespread damage in Manang

Continuous rainfall has also caused significant damage in different parts of Manang.

Floods in streams around Chame swept away two wooden bridges and two causeways, while five houses were completely damaged, according to CDO Khanal.

Around 10 houses in Tal village have been inundated.

A suspension bridge over the Marsyangdi River in Nasong Rural Municipality has also been swept away, while roads in Nising Rural Municipality remain blocked.

Authorities say heavy debris and difficult conditions have made it impossible for excavators to reach the affected areas.

Mountain guides among those missing

The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said a total of 16 people were initially reported missing in the Himlung Himal incident, of whom two have now been found dead.

According to the association, 14 kitchen staff and two mountaineering guides were missing after the avalanche. They had travelled to the mountain as members of different expedition companies.

The association said the two mountaineering guides were found dead, although their identities have not yet been released.

An association rescue team reached the avalanche site by Prabhu Helicopter and has been carrying out search and rescue operations.

Rescuers including Mingma G, Pasang Kaji Sherpa, Ashish Gurung and Pemba Chhiring Sherpa have reached the site, while four additional rescuers are preparing to join the operation.

title.rendered: Flood sweeps away cruise ship in Narayani River, crashes into bridge

content.rendered:
Chitwan, September 27

A cruise ship stationed in the Narayani River in Chitwan was swept away by floodwaters on Sunday afternoon and crashed into a pillar of a bridge over the river.

Superintendent of Police Rameshwar Poudel confirmed that the cruise ship had become lodged against the bridge pillar on the Gaindakot side.

“It is stuck against the pillar on the Gaindakot side. The water level is rising, and the risk is also increasing,” Poudel said.

He said the river’s flow was continuing to increase.

According to Poudel, vehicular movement across the bridge has currently been suspended as a precautionary measure.

title.rendered: Landslides disrupt Kathmandu’s LPG supply, 125 gas bullets stranded

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Continuous rainfall since Wednesday night, followed by floods and landslides, has disrupted Nepal’s supply network, with Kathmandu Valley facing growing concerns over cooking gas, vegetables and other daily essentials.

The Prithvi Highway and the Nagdhunga-Muglin road section, considered key lifelines connecting the federal capital with the Tarai, have been obstructed at multiple locations.

According to the Nagdhunga-Muglin Road Project, landslides occurred at more than 10 locations on Sunday. Large landslides at Krishnabhir, Jamireghat, Chaukibhir, Ghoptebhir and Simaldhara in Dhading and Chitwan have completely blocked the road in both directions.

Road sections at Shitalbazar, Gomti Khola, Hugdi Khola-Jawang Khola, Fishling, Chumlingtar and Dharapani are operating only on a one-way basis because of landslides.

The Department of Roads says it is prioritising the reopening of key lifeline routes and is working to clear the blockages across the country.

The disruption has prevented gas bullets and other freight trucks carrying supplies from India from entering Kathmandu Valley. Nepal Oil Corporation says no new LPG bullet has entered the Valley since rainfall began on Wednesday.

The situation has revived concerns over a possible LPG shortage in Kathmandu. A similar shortage occurred around three weeks ago after a landslide at Krishnabhir blocked the main highway connecting the Valley.

Although supplies had begun returning to normal after the highway reopened, the latest disruption has once again affected the movement of LPG and other essential goods.

Around 150,000 gas cylinders stuck on the road

Nepal Oil Corporation has urged consumers not to panic, saying a significant volume of LPG is already on its way to Kathmandu and can be brought into the market once the roads reopen.

NOC Executive Director Nagendra Sah said around 125 LPG bullets loaded for 16 gas brands operating in Kathmandu Valley are currently stranded at different locations.

The bullets have already cleared customs at Birgunj and are being held at safe locations in coordination with local administrations, including Ramnagar in Chitwan and Hetauda.

“About 125 gas bullets are currently stuck on the road,” Sah said. “They have already cleared customs at Birgunj. Some are at Ramnagar in Chitwan, some in Hetauda and others at safe locations.”

A gas bullet carries enough LPG to fill an average of 1,250 cylinders. Based on that figure, the stranded consignments contain enough gas to fill roughly 150,000 cylinders for Kathmandu Valley.

Sah said the corporation could quickly increase market supplies once the roads reopen.

“Once the road opens, we can send 50,000 to 60,000 cylinders to the market each day for three or four consecutive days,” he said. “That would help us normalise the market.”

He said there was no difficulty in bringing LPG from India, with gas already loaded from locations including Barauni, Paradip and Haldia and brought close to Chitwan and Hetauda.

“The main issue now is clearing the landslides at Krishnabhir and other locations in Dhading,” Sah said.

According to Sah, gas industries also released around 17,000 to 18,000 cylinders from their existing stocks on Sunday.

He said there could be some short-term inconvenience and it could take time to meet 100 percent of demand, but the corporation was working to prevent a repeat of the severe shortages seen previously.

More than 63,000 cylinders supplied in three days

Although no new gas bullets have entered Kathmandu since Wednesday, NOC and gas companies have continued supplying LPG from their existing stocks.

According to NOC data, 63,256 LPG cylinders were distributed in Kathmandu Valley and surrounding districts over the three days from Friday to Sunday.

The highest daily distribution was recorded on Friday, when 37,986 cylinders were sent to the market through various dealers.

Sagar Gas supplied 6,234 cylinders on Friday, followed by Nepal Gas with 4,640. STC Gas supplied 3,138 cylinders, Everest Gas 2,645, Shriram Gas 2,520, Sitashree Gas 2,513, Shree Gas 2,409 and Himal Gas 2,345.

Other companies also continued distribution, including HP Gas, Sai Baba, Shrimaya, Om, Sugam and Bhanu.

Distribution was lower on Saturday because of the public holiday, with 6,399 cylinders sent to the market.

On Sunday, 18,871 cylinders were distributed through 320 dealers and shops operated by 10 gas companies across Kathmandu, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur and Kavre.

Sagar Gas recorded the highest distribution, supplying 4,576 cylinders through 102 dealers. Nepal Gas distributed 3,360 cylinders through 34 dealers, while STC Gas supplied 2,832 through 38 dealers.

No immediate problem with petrol, diesel and aviation fuel

NOC says supplies of petrol, diesel and aviation fuel are not currently facing the same disruption.

The corporation has enough petrol and diesel stocks at Thankot to meet demand for around seven to 10 days.

Pradeep Yadav, chief of NOC’s aviation fuel office in Sinamangal, said there was also enough aviation fuel for domestic and international flights for around 10 days.

“We will not face any problem for the next 10 days,” Yadav said. “If the main road remains blocked for a longer period, we can use alternative routes to prevent shortages.”

Why LPG faces a bigger supply challenge

Long-term road blockages generally create a greater challenge for LPG than for petrol and diesel because of the different ways the fuels are transported.

Petrol and diesel imported through the pipeline are stored at the Amlekhgunj depot. From there, smaller tankers can transport fuel to Kathmandu using alternative routes, including the BP Highway.

LPG, however, requires large specialised bullets for transport. These vehicles cannot easily use narrow and winding alternative roads, making it difficult to bring gas into Kathmandu when the main highways are blocked.

During previous prolonged road closures, gas companies have had to collect empty cylinders from dealers in Kathmandu, transport them to gas plants in the Tarai using ordinary cargo trucks, fill them and then bring the cylinders back through alternative routes.

The process is time-consuming, cumbersome and significantly more expensive.

If the main highways remain closed for an extended period, gas companies could again be forced to resort to this costly alternative.

With the Muglin-Nagdhunga road currently blocked, the Valley Traffic Police Office says the Tribhuvan Highway has been opened on a limited basis to facilitate the movement of essential food, vegetables and fuel.

However, the route is narrow and considered risky, making it unsuitable for large freight vehicles and LPG bullets.

title.rendered: Narayani River reaches record water level of 11.94 metres

content.rendered:
Chitwan, September 27

The water level in the Narayani River rose to a record 11.94 metres at Devghat on Sunday, the highest level recorded since measurements began at the station.

According to the Narayani Basin Field Office in Bharatpur, the water level was measured at the Devghat hydrological station.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology recorded the water level at 11.94 metres at 2:10pm. At Devghat, 7.30 metres is considered the warning level, while 9 metres is the danger level.

The water level had fallen to 11.75 metres by 3:40pm. Although it is now declining, the river remains significantly above the danger level.

Sumit Adhikari, chief hydrologist at the Narayani Basin Field Office, said Sunday’s measurement was the highest water level recorded since hydrological measurements began at Devghat.

He said the water level could fluctuate further as rainfall continues in the hills.

According to office records, the previous highest recorded level was 11.6 metres on October 12, 2024.

The river reached 8.33 metres on August 14, 2023, 9.52 metres on October 6, 2022, and 10.50 metres on June 17, 2021.

Hydrological measurements at Devghat have been conducted since 1963.

title.rendered: RN Joshi Museum of Modern Art established in Lalitpur

content.rendered:
Lalitpur

The R N Joshi Museum of Modern Art has been established at the former residence and studio of renowned artist Ramananda Joshi (1938–1988) in Pulchowk, Lalitpur, with the aim of preserving, studying and promoting modern Nepali art.

The museum, established through the initiative of the RN Joshi Museum of Modern Art and the Ramananda Joshi Art Trust, will be formally inaugurated with an exhibition titled Imbricated: R.N. Joshi and the Making of Nepali Modern Art.

The exhibition is curated by Art historian Pranab Man Singh, who also teaches at Kathmandu University. It traces the development of modern Nepali art while highlighting Joshi’s contribution to the field.

The museum houses Joshi’s artworks alongside photographs, personal documents, correspondence, publications and other archival and historical materials. These resources will provide visitors with an opportunity to explore the development of modern Nepali art from the 1950s onward.

Trust Chairperson Nabin Joshi said the museum was established to honour Ramananda Joshi’s contribution to Nepali art and preserve the country’s artistic heritage.

Singh said the museum was envisioned not merely as a venue for displaying artworks but as a centre for art archives, history and research. The inaugural exhibition explores Joshi’s work alongside his contributions to teaching, writing and cultural activities.

The museum also plans to organise archival and educational programmes alongside exhibitions to promote research, dialogue and public participation. It will be formally inaugurated in the coming days.

title.rendered: NHRC objects to police conduct during visit to check on Cholendra Rana

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has objected to the conduct of police after its team was stopped from meeting former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana at the Criminal Investigation Office in Teku.

NHRC spokesperson Dr Tikaram Pokharel said in a statement that the commission’s team had gone to the office to monitor Rana’s situation but was not allowed to enter and meet him.

The team waited at the gate for around 45 minutes before returning after it was denied access to Rana.

Expressing concern over the incident, the commission said it regretted the conduct of Nepal Police, describing it as contrary to the NHRC’s constitutional and legal rights.

“The commission regrets this kind of conduct by Nepal Police, which is contrary to constitutional and legal rights,” the statement said.

The NHRC has also drawn the government’s attention to taking legal action against police personnel who obstructed the commission from carrying out its constitutional and legal responsibilities.

The commission called for an impartial investigation and urged the government to ensure that its constitutional and legal powers are respected.

“Therefore, the commission draws the attention of the Government of Nepal to conduct an impartial investigation, bring police personnel who obstructed the fulfilment of its constitutional and legal responsibilities within the scope of law, and respect the constitutional and legal powers granted to the commission,” the statement said.

The NHRC has also expressed concern over the police detention of former Chief Justice Rana.

Police took Rana from his Maharajgunj residence late Saturday night and brought him to the Criminal Investigation Office, citing a “security threat.” The circumstances and legal basis of the detention have drawn questions from legal experts and human rights authorities.

title.rendered: Hetauda-Kathmandu route closed as Indrasarovar water level rises

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Authorities have banned vehicular movement along the Hetauda-Kathmandu short route after the water level in the Indrasarovar reservoir of the Kulekhani Hydropower Project continued to rise.

The District Administration Office, Makwanpur, has urged passengers and vehicle operators using the short route to exercise caution.

Administrative officer Santosh Subedi said vehicles will not be allowed to operate on the Deurali-Sisneri-Kathmandu and Palung-Sisneri-Deurali-Hetauda routes from 4pm Sunday until 5am Monday.

The administration said the water level in Indrasarovar is continuing to rise. Based on an assessment of rainfall in the reservoir’s catchment area, the Nepal Electricity Authority may sound the warning siren and open the reservoir gates at any time after completing the required safety procedures.

As a precaution, all types of vehicles have been prohibited from operating along the affected road section from 4pm Sunday until 5am on Monday.

Passengers and drivers travelling to Kathmandu from Hetauda or to Hetauda from Kathmandu for essential purposes have been advised to use the Tribhuvan Highway during the restriction period.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Ten people have gone missing after an avalanche struck Himlung Himal in Narphu, Manang, on Sunday morning.

According to Manang Assistant Chief District Officer Krishna Prasad Poudel, the avalanche occurred on Sunday morning. All 10 people reported missing are Nepali nationals.

“We received information that 10 people went missing after being caught in the avalanche,” he told Onlinekhabar. “We have received information that all those reported missing are Nepali. A helicopter has also been deployed. It dropped rescuers at the reported site of the avalanche and returned. Another helicopter is heading there again.”

The District Administration Office, Manang, said the group had travelled to the area through Alpine Trek and Travels.

title.rendered: ACAP urges trekkers to hire guides amid flood and landslide risks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The Annapurna Conservation Area Project (ACAP) has urged tourists heading on trekking routes to travel with licensed guides, except for short-distance routes.

ACAP issued the request after floods and landslides increased risks in several parts of the conservation area.

Tourists have been advised to undertake trekking and travel within the conservation area with authorised guides. However, guides are not mandatory for travel to Jomsom, Muktinath and Ghandruk.

According to ACAP, entry permits for the Annapurna, Manaslu and Gaurishankar conservation areas have started being issued from noon today.

However, ACAP said entry permits will be issued only after assessing road conditions and weather conditions in the respective areas.

The project has urged tourists to check local conditions and follow safety instructions before travelling to trekking destinations affected by recent floods and landslides.

title.rendered: Flood damages 40 MW Rahughata Hydropower Project in Myagdi

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Floods have damaged structures and transmission line towers of the 40 MW Rahughata Hydropower Project in Myagdi, which was recently completed and connected to Nepal’s national power grid.

The project, located in Raghuganga Rural Municipality, suffered damage after the Rahughanga River swelled following heavy rainfall.

According to the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), the flood also damaged transmission line towers. A technical team has been deployed to assess the extent of the damage and begin restoration work.

The project was built by RaghuGanga Hydropower Limited, a subsidiary of the NEA, and had only recently been connected to the national grid.

The project began generating electricity through its two 20 MW units and started supplying power to the national grid from September 24.

The damage to the project and transmission infrastructure could affect its test generation and preparations for commercial operation. However, the extent of the damage and its impact on power generation will be determined after the technical team completes its assessment.

The Rahughata Hydropower Project is located in Raghuganga Rural Municipality and uses water from the Rahughanga River to generate 40 MW of electricity.

The project’s major structures are located on the left bank of the Rahughanga River, while its powerhouse is situated in the Galeyshwar area on the right bank of the Kali Gandaki River.

The project includes a 25-metre-high dam, two spillways, an undersluice, an 80-metre-long two-bay desander, a 6.27-kilometre headrace tunnel, a 53.2-metre surge tank, a 1,026-metre pressure shaft and two penstocks that carry water to the powerhouse.

The project is designed to generate around 247.9 million units of electricity annually. The generated electricity is connected from the project’s switchyard to the Dana-Kushma transmission line through a roughly 600-metre-long 220 kV transmission line.

RaghuGanga Hydropower Limited, which is wholly owned by the Nepal Electricity Authority, developed the project with concessional financing from India’s EXIM Bank also involved in the investment.

The project was completed after a process spanning nearly two decades. Physical construction and equipment installation were completed in August, after which both units underwent testing before being connected to the national grid.

The technical team is currently assessing which structures were damaged, which transmission line towers were affected and how long restoration could take.

The NEA said the actual impact on power generation and transmission will become clear only after the assessment is completed.

title.rendered: Kathmandu skies clear after four days of rain (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Kathmandu’s skies began clearing on Sunday afternoon, with sunshine now visible over the valley after four consecutive days of rain.

According to meteorologist Sanjib Adhikari of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology’s forecasting division, the low-pressure area near India’s Uttar Pradesh has weakened, reducing rainfall activity in Nepal, including over the Kathmandu Valley and the wider Bagmati region, where the monsoon has also weakened.

Moisture-laden winds from the Bay of Bengal had moved toward central Nepal overnight, but with the low-pressure system now gradually fading, only limited residual rain activity is expected today.

Rain is still forecast in various parts of the country this afternoon, though heavy rain is expected in only one or two locations.

title.rendered: Narayangadh-Muglin road reopens after landslide cleared

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The Narayangadh-Muglin road section has resumed operation after a landslide and mudflow blocking the Namsi Khola bridge were cleared.

Vehicles and freight carriers travelling between Narayangadh and Pokhara have started moving after the debris was removed from the road.

According to the Chitwan Division Road Office, a mud-laden landslide fell near the Namsi Khola at around 7:55am. Information officer and engineer Krishna Acharya said the road was reopened at around 12:15pm.

Vehicles travelling from Pokhara to Narayangadh and Narayangadh to Pokhara are now moving towards their destinations.

11 landslide sites along Malekhu-Muglin section

Meanwhile, continuous rainfall has triggered landslides at 11 locations along the Malekhu-Muglin section of the Prithvi Highway, disrupting traffic at several points.

Sachindra Mishra, information officer of the Nagdhunga-Muglin Road Project’s western section, said a landslide carrying mud and trees fell at Shitalbazar, while part of the road edge has also subsided.

Near Benighat Bazaar, a mud-laden landslide at Gomti Khola has reduced traffic to one-way operation. A landslide from above Krishnabhir has also blocked the road.

Mishra said rocks and mud have blocked the road at Jyamireghat and Chaukibhir, while smaller rockslides have occurred at several locations between Hugdi Khola and Jawang Khola.

Around 200 metres of road at three locations near Fishling has been covered by landslides carrying rocks, mud and trees. Around 30 metres of the road has also developed cracks, with about half of the road affected.

A rock-laden landslide has occurred at Chumlingtar, while around 50 metres of road has been damaged at two locations in Dharapani.

Work is underway to clear a blocked culvert in the area. Large rocks and mud have also blocked the road at Ghoptebhir and Simaldhara.

Mishra said teams are working to clear landslides at all affected locations. If there are no further major landslides, efforts are expected to clear the road and resume traffic by evening.

Equipment belonging to the contractor responsible for the road construction is being used to remove the landslide debris.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The sixteen-day ancestral rites, known as Sohra Shraddha or Pitri Paksha, began today. Observed every year from the first day of the waning fortnight of the month of Ashwin, the period began today. The calendars approved by the Nepal Panchanga Nirnayak Development Committee have stated that Shraddha for the first lunar day should be performed today. Prof Dr Devmani Bhattarai, a former member of the committee and scholar of religious scriptures, said the offering of pindas for the first lunar day should be performed after noon.

The period is called Sohra Shraddha because offerings of water, sidha and pindas are made with reverence to deceased ancestors on the 16 lunar days from the first day of the waning fortnight of Ashwin to the first day of the waxing fortnight of Ashwin. The period is also known as Apar and Preta Paksha.

According to the Vedic Sanatan Hindu scriptural tradition, Sohra Shraddha is observed to remember and pay respects to ancestors before festivals, yajnas and other major religious activities.

There is a scriptural belief that ancestors wait for offerings during this period. It is also a religious belief that observing Sohra Shraddha fulfils one’s duty towards one’s ancestors and frees one from ancestral debt.

Prof Dr Ramchandra Gautam, a religious scholar and former chairperson of the committee, said Shraddha is performed based on scriptural teachings that failing to perform the rites during this period results in an unforgivable religious fault.

He also said that scriptures prescribe performing Sohra Shraddha in the afternoon. Religious scholar Gautam said Sohra Shraddha should not be skipped except in cases of birth-related impurity, death-related impurity or when one’s wife is menstruating.

The scriptures provide several alternatives if Sohra Shraddha cannot be performed for some reason. There is a provision for performing the ritual on the lunar date of one’s father. Religious scholars say that under the rules applicable during emergencies, if the ritual cannot be performed for any reason, it can be performed from the new moon day of the waning fortnight of Ashwin to the fifth day of the waxing fortnight of Ashwin.

If Sohra Shraddha still cannot be performed during this period, it can be performed on the new moon day of the waning fortnight of Kartik, which is also Lakshmi Puja. If it cannot be performed even on the new moon day of Kartik, it can be arranged and performed by the time of Vrishchik Sankranti, or Mangsir, according to the religious scripture Dharmasindhu.

Prof Dr Bhattarai, a committee member and head of the Department of Dharmashastra at Valmiki Vidyapeeth of Nepal Sanskrit University, said religious scriptures including Nirnayasindhu and Dharmasindhu also provide an option to perform the postponed Sohra Shraddha on Ashtami, Dwadashi or Amavasya after the fifth day of the waxing fortnight of Ashwin, regardless of the lunar date, as well as on days falling under the Bharani Nakshatra and Vyatipat Yoga.

He said that if the ritual still cannot be performed, those who are able to do so themselves, and those who cannot through a Brahmin, may chant 108 mantras daily as another scriptural option. Such chanting should be performed according to the prescribed procedure for 10 months. There is a religious belief that ancestors also attain satisfaction through this practice.

Religious scholars say that they have received information that some priests have been instructing people to perform Sohra Shraddha in the morning according to their convenience, despite scriptures prescribing that it be performed in the afternoon on the lunar date of the father. They say such practice is not in accordance with the scriptures.

People whose lunar date fell today visited various Shiva temples, including the Pashupatinath Temple in Kathmandu, to make offerings and perform Shraddha. With the end of Pitri Paksha, Durga Paksha, or Bada Dashain, begins. According to religious scriptures, Sohra Shraddha is performed to satisfy the ancestors before celebrating Bada Dashain. It is a Vedic Sanatan tradition to perform rituals for the satisfaction of ancestors before celebrating major festivals.

title.rendered: NEA steps up preparedness as floods and landslides disrupt power supply

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has intensified preparations and coordination to maintain electricity supply and quickly restore services in areas affected by damage to power transmission and distribution infrastructure caused by continuous rainfall, floods, landslides, strong winds and lightning.

The authority is continuously monitoring electricity supply across the country, the condition of transmission and distribution infrastructure and the situation in affected areas.

It has kept the necessary manpower, equipment and materials ready to respond to possible damage and power disruptions and has begun mobilising resources where required.

NEA Managing Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha held a virtual meeting on Sunday with the heads of all seven provincial offices and two division offices, along with officials from the Distribution and Customer Service Directorate and Grid Operations Department.

The meeting reviewed the impact of rainfall, floods and landslides on electricity infrastructure in different provinces, the current state of power supply and potential risks.

Shrestha instructed office chiefs to immediately mobilise the necessary personnel, equipment and materials to restore electricity services in affected areas.

He also directed officials to restore supply through alternative lines and feeders wherever possible and to assess damaged infrastructure before carrying out safe repair and restoration work without delay.

The NEA said it would continue monitoring affected areas and mobilise additional manpower, equipment and technical resources as needed.

All relevant offices and technical teams have been mobilised to restore disrupted services as quickly as possible and maintain supply through alternative arrangements wherever feasible.

The authority has also instructed its offices to prioritise the safety of employees and technical personnel while carrying out repair and restoration work in areas affected by natural disasters.

The NEA said the power supply system is being continuously monitored and coordinated at the central level, with all necessary measures being taken to maintain regular electricity supply and restore disrupted services as soon as possible.

1,303 MW of power system affected

Floods and landslides following continuous rainfall have affected transmission and distribution systems in several parts of the country.

Faults have developed in transmission lines, while equipment at power generation plants and substations has also been affected, disrupting electricity supply in several areas.

According to the NEA’s latest assessment, major disruptions have been reported in the power systems of Pokhara, Butwal, Hetauda and Kathmandu.

Disruptions affecting various transmission lines, generation facilities and loads have impacted around 1,303 megawatts of the power system, according to the authority.

title.rendered: Public Service Commission gives opinion on Civil Service Bill

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The Public Service Commission (PSC) has submitted its opinion on the Federal Civil Service Bill to the government.

Lokhari Basyal, joint secretary at the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration, confirmed that the commission’s response was received last Thursday.

However, the ministry has not yet reviewed or discussed the recommendations.

“We received the opinion, but I have not reviewed it yet. It also needs to be discussed within the ministry,” Basyal told Onlinekhabar. “The discussion has been pending due to holidays and other reasons.”

The Cabinet meeting held on September 11 had decided to send the draft bill to the PSC for consultation. The draft was sent to the commission the same day.

At the time, Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration Pratibha Rawal had said the government would move ahead with the bill after receiving the PSC’s recommendations.

The Civil Service Act requires the government to consult the PSC while preparing legislation concerning the terms and conditions of civil servants.

The bill had already received approval from the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs to move forward.

Following the PSC’s consultation, the government can now study the recommendations and proceed with the bill. Once the Cabinet authorises the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration to register the bill in the Federal Parliament, it can be formally introduced.

Bill linked to federalism implementation

The Federal Civil Service Bill is considered important for implementing Nepal’s federal structure.

Although the country has already undergone civil servant adjustment following the transition to federalism, questions remain over recruitment, authority and the administrative relationship among federal, provincial and local governments.

Provincial Public Service Commissions have also been established constitutionally. However, federal government employees continue to serve in provincial and local governments.

In previous attempts to pass the bill, the government had proposed keeping provincial chief secretaries, provincial ministry secretaries, local-level chief administrative officers and accounting officers under the federal government.

The proposal faced objections that retaining federal employees in provincial and local governments would run contrary to the spirit of federalism.

The government has not yet made public how these issues have been addressed in the latest draft.

Debate over retirement age

The proposed bill also includes a controversial provision on the retirement age of civil servants.

The government has prepared a draft proposing mandatory retirement at the age of 55 or after 30 years of service.

The PSC’s opinion on the proposed retirement provision has also not been made public.

According to the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration, employees retiring at 55 would be treated as having completed 58 years of service for pension purposes. The ministry says this would prevent a reduction in pension benefits for those taking early retirement.

However, officials within the ministry have reportedly not provided a clear explanation for why the provision has been proposed.

Could the bill come through an ordinance?

There is also speculation that the government could introduce the civil service legislation through an ordinance.

The current session of the Federal Parliament is expected to end around October 2 or 3, with the House of Representatives’ parliamentary calendar prepared up to October 2.

If the government chooses to introduce the Civil Service Act through an ordinance, it could do so soon after the parliamentary session ends. If it proceeds through the regular bill process, implementation could take several more months.

The government is preparing to call the next parliamentary session only in January after ending the current session in October.

Once a bill is registered in Parliament, it must go through principle-level discussion, followed by a 72-hour period for lawmakers to submit amendments. The bill and proposed amendments then undergo clause-by-clause discussion.

The process must take place in both houses of Parliament. After both houses pass the bill, it is sent to the President for authentication and comes into force as an Act after promulgation.
