title.rendered: Former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana released, handed over to family

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana has been handed over to his family.

SP Rameshwar Karki of the Crime Investigation Office said Rana, who was taken from his residence at midnight on Saturday, was handed over to his family a short while ago.

SSP Santosh Khadka of the Crime Investigation Office had earlier said that Rana had been sent to a “safe place”. However, he did not disclose where the “safe place” was.

A team from the Crime Investigation Office took Rana from his residence in Maharajgunj last night.

A team from the National Human Rights Commission that reached the office to meet Rana was also not allowed to meet him by the police. The commission team returned after waiting at the gate for around 45 minutes without being allowed to meet him.

The government has not disclosed the reason for taking Rana into custody.

SSP Khadka told Onlinekhabar that Rana had to be brought to the office overnight because of a “security threat”.

After a team from the Crime Investigation Office in Teku arrived at his residence last night, Rana called his brother, Prabhu Shumsher, and informed him about the situation.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar on Sunday morning, Prabhu Shumsher said, “The police told my brother that there was a threat to him from Gen Z and took him away.”

Legal experts, however, have questioned the manner in which the police handled the matter.

title.rendered: Man missing while bathing in Kamala River in Siraha

content.rendered:
Siraha, September 27

A 47-year-old man went missing while bathing in the Kamala River at Bhokraha in Kalyanpur Municipality-6, Siraha.

The missing man has been identified as Gobindaraj Dulal, 47, the son of Dinnanath Dulal of Makwanpurgadhi Rural Municipality-5, Makwanpur.

According to police, Dulal was working as a Bolero driver for Elite Construction, which is constructing a concrete bridge over the Kamala River in Bhokraha.

Ramesh Bahadur Pal, spokesperson and DSP at the District Police Office, Siraha, said Dulal was swept away by the river’s strong current at around 9:55 am on Saturday while he was bathing in the river.

Immediately after the incident, five police personnel led by Police Inspector Bikash Paswan from the Area Police Office, Mirchaiya, along with a team from a temporary police post, were deployed to search for him.

Additional teams from nearby police units were also mobilised, police said.

On Saturday, 24 personnel from the Disaster Management Team of the Armed Police Force Nepal Security Base in Kalyanpur, under the command of Armed Police Inspector Raju Singh Bhandari, were also deployed for the search and rescue operation.

The search resumed on Sunday morning, with Dulal’s family members also joining the search effort.

title.rendered: 27 killed in 2 separate shootings in South Africa

content.rendered:
Johannesburg, September 27

At least 27 people have been killed and 26 others injured in two separate shootings in South Africa.

Seventeen people were killed and 15 others injured in a shooting at a bar in western Johannesburg on Saturday night, police said. The victims included 13 men and four women.

According to police, around eight gunmen carried out the attack. After searching some customers and taking their mobile phones, the attackers fled in two unidentified vehicles. The incident took place at around 7:30 pm local time on Saturday.

Police said the motive for the attack remains unclear. The suspects reportedly set fire to the two vehicles before fleeing. Investigators and specialised police teams have been deployed to arrest those involved.

Meanwhile, another shooting at an entertainment venue in a township outside Cape Town on Sunday morning left 10 people dead and 11 others injured.

Both legal and illegal firearms are widely used in South Africa. Shootings are frequently linked to gang disputes and competition among informal businesses.

South Africa, with a population of around 62 million, has one of the highest murder rates in the world. Statistics cited in reports indicate that around 60 people are killed in the country each day on average.

In March this year, the military was deployed to assist police in combating crime in violence-hit areas of Johannesburg. President Cyril Ramaphosa has described rising crime as one of the country’s major challenges.

—RSS/AFP

A team from the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has returned after police refused to allow it to meet former Chief Justice Cholendra Rana, who was taken into custody overnight.

title.rendered: Nepal needs prevention systems before tragedy strikes

content.rendered:
Nepal has witnessed several deeply disturbing incidents involving suicide and self-immolation in recent months. In July, the deaths of Ganesh Nepali and Ashwin Raut generated significant public attention, followed by the case of Suresh Chandra Shrestha. On September 21, another incident occurred in Tripureshwar involving 25-year-old bus driver Dawa Lama, who set fire to the bus he was driving while it was empty. Police said an investigation was underway into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

These cases are not identical. Their backgrounds, circumstances and personal histories differ. It would therefore be inappropriate to reduce them to a single explanation. However, their recurrence raises an important question: What happens when an individual tragedy becomes part of a broader social narrative, particularly when vulnerable people are repeatedly exposed to such incidents? For a country already struggling with limited access to mental-health services, this is a question that deserves serious public discussion.

Looking beyond the final trigger

Public discussions surrounding suicide often focus on the event immediately preceding a person’s death: a financial dispute, family conflict, relationship breakdown, legal problem, humiliation or another acute crisis.

Such events can certainly be significant. However, psychologically, a triggering event should not automatically be treated as the sole cause of suicide. A person may already be experiencing financial stress, loneliness, family conflict, trauma, hopelessness, social pressure, relationship difficulties or previous suicidal thoughts. An additional crisis may then become the immediate trigger within a much longer history of distress.

The World Health Organisation describes suicide as a complex phenomenon influenced by interacting psychological, social, economic and cultural factors. It cannot generally be explained by one event or one characteristic of an individual.

This distinction is important because focusing only on the final incident can prevent society from recognising the suffering that existed before it. If we ask only, “What happened that day?”, we may fail to ask the more important question: “What was happening in this person’s life before that day?”

The risk of imitation and contagion

There is another issue that deserves attention: the possibility of suicide contagion and imitation.

This does not mean that one person simply decides to copy another person’s actions. Rather, research has identified circumstances in which exposure to suicide, particularly repeated, sensationalised, or highly detailed exposure, can increase risk among vulnerable individuals.

This makes the role of the media and social media particularly important. A tragic incident can quickly move from a news report to a social-media post, then to a short video, a discussion thread and thousands of comments. In the process, the person who died can become a symbol, while the circumstances of the death can become a dramatic public narrative.

This creates an ethical responsibility for journalists, content creators and social-media users. The World Health Organisation recommends avoiding sensational reporting, explicit descriptions of suicide methods and unnecessary repetition, while encouraging reporting that promotes hope, recovery and help-seeking. The purpose of journalism should be to inform the public, not unintentionally romanticise or amplify a person’s final act.

The message we send through our response

The response that follows a death also deserves examination.

Following the death of Ganesh Nepali, his family and authorities reached a nine-point agreement that included measures such as an independent investigation, employment support for his wife, educational support for his daughter and financial assistance.

Supporting a grieving family is necessary and humane. Families should not be abandoned because they have lost someone. However, such responses also raise a broader policy question: Are comparable forms of support available before a person reaches a point of severe crisis? The concern is not that families should receive less support after a death. Rather, the concern is whether sufficient support exists before the death occurs.

A person facing financial hardship should not have to reach a point of irreversible crisis before assistance becomes visible. A family experiencing severe distress should not have to lose a member before institutions respond. The message of prevention should therefore be clear: People should be able to access support while they are still alive and asking or even struggling, to be heard.

Suicide prevention cannot consist only of slogans such as “Suicide is not the solution.” For someone experiencing severe psychological distress, a slogan does not address the circumstances that have made life feel unbearable. Nepal needs stronger systems of early intervention.

Local governments and municipalities are closest to communities and therefore have an important role in prevention. Accessible psychological first-response services could provide people experiencing severe emotional, family, financial or occupational distress with an immediate point of contact. Mental-health support should not be treated as a luxury available only to those who can afford private counselling.

Training frontline workers

Police officers, teachers, health workers, community workers, ward representatives and employers frequently encounter people experiencing distress.

They do not need to become psychologists. However, they can be trained to recognize warning signs, communicate safely, de-escalate difficult situations and connect individuals with appropriate professional services. Sometimes recognizing that a person’s apparent anger is actually a sign of severe distress can become an important opportunity for intervention.

The media has a particularly important role in suicide prevention. Repeatedly displaying graphic images, describing methods in unnecessary detail or turning a person’s final moments into viral content can create risks beyond the original tragedy. Responsible reporting does not mean avoiding the subject. It means reporting it carefully. Journalists can discuss the circumstances surrounding an incident while avoiding unnecessary details that may contribute to sensationalism. They can also include information about available mental-health and crisis-support resources.

Psychologists should not be limited to private counselling rooms. Their expertise can contribute to schools, universities, workplaces, municipalities, police training, community programmes and public-health campaigns. Mental-health education should also extend beyond discussions that occur after a suicide.

Communities need opportunities to learn about emotional regulation, coping with failure and humiliation, problem-solving, interpersonal conflict, financial stress, help-seeking and crisis management before an emergency occurs.

From reaction to prevention

Every major tragedy generates public concern. Statements are released. Investigations are announced. Political discussions follow. Social media becomes active. Then, eventually, public attention moves elsewhere. Prevention requires more than this cycle of reaction.

Nepal needs better data and systematic research into the circumstances surrounding suicide and suicidal behaviour. Which populations are most vulnerable? What circumstances commonly precede a crisis? Where are people seeking help? Where are they unable to access it? How does social-media exposure affect vulnerable individuals? Which interventions are effective in Nepal? These questions require sustained research rather than temporary attention following individual tragedies.

It is important not to judge people who die by suicide. None of us can know the complete psychological experience of another person, and reducing a death to a single argument, financial problem, government decision or family conflict oversimplifies an extremely complex phenomenon.

At the same time, acknowledging complexity should not prevent us from examining the possibility of social influence.

When suicide receives repeated and sensational public attention, vulnerable individuals may be affected by what they see and hear. This is why responsible reporting and preventive mental-health systems must be considered together.

Perhaps the most useful question is therefore not simply:

“Who is to blame?”

It is:

“What could have happened earlier that might have changed the outcome?”

Could someone have recognised the warning signs?

Could a family member have known how to respond?

Could a police officer have de-escalated a crisis?

Could a local government have provided immediate psychological support?

Could the media have reported the incident differently?

Could professional help have been accessible before the crisis became overwhelming?

These questions shift the conversation from reaction to prevention.

Suicide prevention is not about predicting who will die. It is about creating enough opportunities for a person experiencing a crisis to find another path. Nepal’s response must therefore move:

From reaction to prevention, from blame to understanding, from sensational coverage to responsible conversation. And from asking only “Why did this happen?” to asking “What could have been done before it happened?”

By the time a society is discussing compensation, investigations, protests and accountability, a life may already have been lost. The greater responsibility is to build systems that intervene while there is still time to save it.

Prevention must begin before tragedy becomes the only reason we pay attention.

title.rendered: Authorities urge caution as water level rises in Kamala River

content.rendered:
Siraha, September 27

Security personnel have been using loudspeakers in vulnerable areas to urge residents to remain alert after the water level in the Kamala River, which separates Siraha and Dhanusha districts, rose due to continuous rainfall.

Following a weather warning of heavy rainfall and strong winds from September 24 to 27, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and the Nepali Army have been deployed in potentially vulnerable areas of Siraha.

According to Assistant Chief District Officer Chet Raj Baral, the District Administration Office, Siraha, has also issued a notice urging residents to exercise high caution. He said 83 Armed Police Force personnel have been deployed in the field, while another 200 have been kept on standby.

Similarly, 250 Nepali Army personnel have been kept on standby for immediate deployment if necessary, Baral said.

He added that Nepal Police personnel are also regularly deployed in the field.

According to Baral, the rising water level in the Balan River in Lahan could affect Sakhuwanankarkatti Rural Municipality-5 and Siraha Municipality-6.

He said security personnel have been deployed and public announcements are being made along rivers and in other vulnerable areas as a precautionary measure.

Baral urged people living along riverbanks and in other vulnerable areas to remain alert and take necessary precautions.

title.rendered: Shram Sanskriti Party proposes visa system for Nepal’s open borders

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The Shram Sanskriti Party has proposed tightening Nepal’s open borders and introducing a visa system as part of amendments to a bill aimed at controlling human trafficking and smuggling.

Party chair Harka Raj Rai, popularly known as Harka Sampang, and party lawmaker Aren Rai have proposed the amendment to the Human Trafficking and Transportation (Control) (First Amendment) Bill, 2083.

The proposed bill adds a new provision requiring the government to establish surveillance mechanisms at international borders, international airports and locations considered vulnerable to human trafficking and transportation.

Under the provision, if officials deployed for surveillance suspect that an offence of human trafficking or transportation has been committed or is about to occur, they must immediately inform an authorised investigating officer or the nearest police office.

The Shram Sanskriti Party has proposed adding a specific provision to this section requiring the government to tighten controls at open borders and introduce a visa system.

The proposed amendment states that the law should include a provision to “tighten open borders and implement a visa system.”

The government introduced the bill with the stated objective of protecting the dignity, freedom and fundamental rights of people affected by human trafficking, which has developed into an organised crime operating across countries.

Minister for Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities and Social Security Sita Badi registered the bill in the House of Representatives on August 30. The House has already held a principle-level discussion on the bill, after which lawmakers submitted amendment proposals.

According to Minister Badi, the bill aims to ensure access to justice for people at high risk of trafficking and those who have been trafficked, bring individuals accused of trafficking offences in Nepal or abroad within the scope of the law, and expand the range of punishments for such offences.

The bill also seeks to establish mechanisms at all three levels of government in line with Nepal’s federal structure and make all three levels of government responsible for controlling human trafficking and transportation.

It also proposes clearer legal provisions for the rescue and rehabilitation of victims and affected persons.

The government has further sought to incorporate into national law provisions from the supplementary protocol under the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime concerning the prevention, suppression and punishment of trafficking in persons, particularly women and children.

A total of 111 amendment proposals have been registered on the bill. Lawmakers have submitted the amendments in 28 groups, including the Shram Sanskriti Party’s proposal to tighten Nepal’s open borders and introduce a visa system.

title.rendered: Filmmaking workshop held in Kathmandu, led by industry professionals

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Presented by Kym Rapier Foundation in collaboration with Shanta Nepali Productions and Shanta Foundation, a free, immersive filmmaking workshop was organised on Saturday, September 26, giving participants the chance to learn directly from industry practitioners.

The workshop featured Emmy-nominated directors, an experienced cinematographer, and other professional filmmakers as instructors, including Burt Gregory, Luke Cormack, Jovan Sales, Zachary Tidmore, Christian Palladino, and Matthew Venezio.

Participants got hands-on experience with professional filmmaking equipment, covering cinematography, camera operation, composition, lighting, and visual storytelling. The session also explored how to shoot and tell stories in tough terrain and extreme conditions, with a focus on real-world challenges, problem-solving, and adapting filmmaking techniques to unpredictable environments.

According to the organiser, the main objective behind the workshop was to exchange knowledge with filmmakers from across the world.

“Whenever a team of international filmmakers visits Nepal, only certain people have access to them, resulting in only a few gaining knowledge from them,” said Shanta Nepali, founder of Shanta Nepali Production and Shanta Foundation. “This time, we wanted to break that practice and conduct the workshop for a relatively larger number of people.”

Rather than a classroom-based session, the workshop was built around learning by doing. Participants handled equipment, shot scenes, experimented with techniques, and received guidance and feedback from experienced filmmakers.

The workshop was held at Hotel Yak and Yeti from 1 pm to 3 pm on September 26. Participation was free for everyone, offered on a first-come, first-served basis.

title.rendered: Floods and landslides damage power infrastructure, affecting up to 1,303 MW of system

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Floods and landslides triggered by continuous rainfall have affected electricity transmission and distribution systems in various parts of the country.

Power supply has been disrupted in several areas after floods caused faults in transmission lines and problems with equipment at power generation plants and substations.

According to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, major disruptions have been reported in the electricity systems in Pokhara, Butwal, Hetauda and Kathmandu. The ministry said disruptions affecting various lines, generation facilities and loads have impacted a total of around 1,303 MW of the system.

However, this does not represent the amount of electricity disrupted at a single time. It is the combined total of disruptions to transmission lines, generation and loads recorded at different times and locations.

Pokhara worst affected

The Pokhara area has been the worst affected. A fault in the Kusma-New Butwal 220 kV transmission line affected around 200 MW of electricity. Similarly, disruptions in the RauGhat-Dana lines 1 and 2 affected around 155 MW.

Floods have also affected the generation and supply of several hydropower projects, including Kaligandaki, Upper Madi, Super Madi, Sikles-Namrjung, Seti River-Karuwaseth, Upper Dordi and Modi. More than 400 MW of capacity from various projects in the Pokhara area alone has been affected.

In the Raughat area, a fault in the New Butwal-Kusma 220 kV line affected around 110 MW. The line was expected to resume operation at 9:50 am.

In the Butwal area, a tree fell onto the New Bharatpur-New Butwal 220 kV transmission line, causing a fault. According to the report, the line was charged at 9:51 am. When the Chapar-Pathlaiya 132 kV line went out of service, load shedding of around one hour was carried out at the Kawasoti substation.

The Hetauda area has also been affected by floods. Around 32 MW was affected at the Mandu 66 kV system due to flooding. Supply was also disrupted after a CVT at the Bharatpur substation under the Kawasoti-Bharatpur 132 kV line was damaged by fire.

Around 20 MW at the Simara substation, around 80 MW supplied to industries in Amlekhgunj, Parwanipur and Birgunj, and around 25 MW at the Kamane substation and industries have been affected.

Kathmandu Valley also affected

In the Kathmandu Valley, electricity supply was briefly disrupted in Patan and Teku. The outages occurred from 9 am to 9:10 am in both areas.

According to the report, the problem in Patan occurred after the Pathlaiya line and the KL-1 Syuchatar 66 kV line became overloaded simultaneously. An emergency supply from the MRS was used after floods disrupted regular supply.

Load reduction at several substations

Load reduction has also been carried out at several substations due to flooding and transmission-line problems.

At the Kawasoti substation, 20 MW of load was reduced from 8 am to 9:15 am, while 25 MW was reduced at the Hardi substation during the same period.

Similarly, around 50 MW of load was reduced at industries in Sunwal-Mainiya and the Butwal area from 6:02 am. At the Simara substation, 20 MW was reduced from 6 am to 10 am, while around 80 MW was reduced at industries in Amlekhgunj, Parwanipur and Birgunj from 6:01 am.

Western and central Nepal significantly affected

The main causes of disruption to the electricity system include damage to transmission lines and generation facilities caused by floods, line faults, problems with substation equipment and subsequent overloading.

Disruptions along the Pokhara-Butwal 220 kV transmission corridor and the 132 kV transmission lines around Pathlaiya have particularly affected electricity supply in western and central Nepal.

Nepal Electricity Authority Managing Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha said technical and maintenance teams had been deployed to affected areas to collect preliminary details of the damage, identify areas where electricity supply has been disrupted, operate alternative supply arrangements and carry out immediate repairs to damaged infrastructure.

NEA says restoration is a high priority

Shrestha said arrangements had been made to restore electricity supply to areas experiencing outages through alternative feeders and available transmission and distribution infrastructure wherever possible.

He said the authority was assessing the condition of damaged infrastructure and mobilising the necessary equipment, materials and personnel to gradually restore electricity supply.

Despite damage to electricity infrastructure caused by the natural disasters, the authority is giving high priority to restoring power supply to consumers as soon as possible, Shrestha said.

The NEA said heavy rainfall, floods, landslides and blocked roads have made it difficult for technical teams to reach some affected areas. Shrestha said additional technical teams and necessary equipment would be mobilised to accelerate repairs and restoration as soon as roads and access routes are reopened.

The authority said all available resources were being mobilised to maintain electricity supply through alternative arrangements where possible and restore regular supply in the shortest possible time, despite disruptions caused by damage to power infrastructure.

The NEA has urged consumers to remain cautious during the disaster and avoid approaching damaged electrical structures, fallen wires or poles.

title.rendered: Stripped titles? Compensating rivals? How the Manchester City cheating scandal could play out

content.rendered:
One of the biggest cheating scandals in world sports history has erupted in England: Manchester City has reportedly been found guilty of 114 of the 115 alleged breaches of English Premier League financial rules brought against the club in 2023.

The charges relate to the club’s incredibly successful spell between 2009 and 2018 when they won seven major titles, headlined by three Premier League championships.

Manchester City was bought in 2008 by the Abu Dhabi United Group, led by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan – a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family.

The group now owns or has a stake in 13 football teams across the world, from New York to Melbourne, meaning there may be ramifications well beyond England.

But Manchester City is expected to appeal, having long protested its innocence – so this case is not over yet.

What are the charges?

The guilty findings are a potentially seismic development in a case that has hung over English football for more than three years.

The charges cover several areas, including:

  • the accuracy of financial information supplied to the Premier League
  • player and manager remuneration
  • compliance with Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) and Premier League financial regulations
  • cooperation with the league’s investigation.

But there are important caveats. The independent commission’s decision has not yet been published, no sanction has been announced, Manchester City has consistently denied wrongdoing – which is why an appeal is expected.

Until the written decision is available, any assessment of precisely what City did and what should happen next would be premature.

What could happen to Manchester City?

Recent Premier League cases demonstrate how breaches of financial rules can result in sporting sanctions.

In recent years, Everton was initially deducted ten points (reduced to six points on appeal) for breaching the league’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules, while Nottingham Forest was deducted four points. Both sides narrowly avoided relegation after the sanctions.

But these cases provide limited guidance for Manchester City. They concerned relatively discrete breaches of spending rules, whereas the charges against City cover multiple categories of alleged misconduct over almost a decade.

So any attempt to extrapolate a likely points deduction for City from Everton or Forest would be speculative.

More severe possibilities – including relegation or expulsion from the Premier League – have inevitably been discussed, as has the prospect of retrospectively stripping City of titles.

Little precedent exists for the latter in English professional team sport. Saracens were relegated from rugby union’s Premiership following salary-cap breaches in 2020, but their previously won titles were not removed.

Australian sport, however, provides precedent. The National Rugby League (NRL) stripped the Melbourne Storm of their 2007 and 2009 premierships, three minor premierships, and all their 2010 competition points after it uncovered systematic salary cap breaches.

Those cases illustrate possible sporting sanctions. But they cannot establish what City’s penalty should be before the commission publishes its reasoning.

Could the consequences spread beyond Manchester?

The shockwaves from this case could also spread overseas.

The City Football Group owns or has a stake in 13 clubs worldwide – including Melbourne City, New York City and Italy’s Palermo.

For example, Melbourne City joined City Football Group in 2014 and is now wholly owned by it.

A Premier League sanction against the English team would not automatically apply to the Melbourne club.

Yet if the published findings concern governance, financial reporting or transactions within the wider ownership structure, they may prompt scrutiny of how the group oversees its international clubs.

That would not establish wrongdoing at Melbourne City or any other City Football Group club. It would test whether rules and oversight built around individual clubs adequately address shared ownership and decision-making across borders.

Beyond any official Premier League sanctions, there could be more ramifications. Many rival Premier League sides are reportedly considering legal action for compensation, claiming they have been impacted by City’s alleged cheating.

Winning Premier League titles, qualifying for and winning major European championships can earn clubs hundreds of millions of dollars.

But a league penalty and a compensation claim are separate matters.

No rival club is automatically entitled to compensation. Each would need to show a proven breach caused a measurable loss, despite the many results and decisions that shape a season.

Why this is far from over

Whatever sanction ultimately follows, the dispute is unlikely to end there. Manchester City are expected to appeal the commission’s findings, meaning any final resolution could still be some way off.

A successful appeal could substantially alter, or even overturn, the significance of the initial ruling. Until that process is exhausted, both the findings and their consequences should therefore be treated as unresolved.

The case reaches beyond football. The Financial Times has described the verdict as the latest test of United Kingdom–United Arab Emirates relations, with the British government seeking closer economic ties with the UAE and greater investment from Abu Dhabi.

These wider political and economic considerations illustrate how the ownership of modern football clubs can intersect with international investment, politics and diplomacy.

The commission’s full decision remains unpublished. Until its reasons and any sanction are known, we cannot say which of these consequences will follow.

The case already asks a broader question: can football’s rules keep pace with the financial and governance structures that now connect clubs across leagues and countries?

title.rendered: Why has the govt kept silent on the reason behind Cholendra Rana’s arrest?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana was taken from his Maharajgunj residence late Saturday night, in an unprecedented episode involving a former head of Nepal’s judiciary.

But more than the detention itself, questions have been raised over why Rana was taken into custody, under what legal authority, and whether he was actually arrested or taken into protective custody.

Police have not publicly disclosed any criminal charge against Rana.

Senior Superintendent of Police Santosh Khadka of the Criminal Investigation Office, Teku, told Onlinekhabar that Rana was brought to the office after police received information about a security threat.

“After learning that there was a security threat to him, we brought him to our office at night because something could happen,” Khadka said.

Another police account reported by Kantipur said Rana was being kept in a safe place because of a perceived security challenge and that there was no plan to pursue a criminal case against him.

Why was Rana taken from his home?

The exact nature of the alleged security threat has not been publicly disclosed.

Rana’s brother, Prabhu Shumsher, said police told Rana that there was a threat to him from Gen Z protesters when they arrived at his residence.

Rana was subsequently taken to the Criminal Investigation Office in Teku.

Reports say police did not provide Rana with an arrest warrant when they took him from his residence.

The distinction is significant because police have described the action as being linked to Rana’s security, while the initial reports described it as an arrest.

Legal questions over the procedure

The manner in which Rana was taken from his residence has prompted questions among legal professionals.

Senior advocate and Nepal Bar Association President Professor Dr Vijay Prasad Mishra said the government should clearly explain the basis and purpose of its action.

“The government must clearly answer on what basis and for what reason this step was taken,” Mishra said. “It is necessary to immediately clarify the government’s intention and objective.”

Mishra said that if the purpose was to address a security threat, the state could have increased security around Rana rather than taking him away from his residence.

Senior advocate Tikaram Bhattarai also questioned the procedure.

According to Bhattarai, regardless of a person’s background or alleged conduct, the state must remain transparent in its treatment of citizens.

“Even if the alleged offence is serious, the government itself cannot become mysterious. The state must guarantee the constitutional rights and legal protection of every citizen,” Bhattarai said.

He argued that if police had genuinely received information about a threat to Rana’s safety, security personnel could have been deployed at his residence and the alleged threat investigated.

What does the law say about urgent arrests?

Legal experts have also referred to the Supreme Court’s previous interpretation of circumstances in which an urgent arrest order may be issued.

According to that interpretation, an urgent arrest authorisation may be justified in circumstances where there is an immediate risk that evidence could be destroyed, the person could abscond, or failing to take the person into custody could lead to another serious offence.

Bhattarai said it was not clear whether any of those circumstances existed in Rana’s case.

“If the state has taken him into custody citing a security challenge, he could have been provided security at his own residence,” Bhattarai said.

He added that any action taken without a clear legal basis and proper procedure would raise questions about the rule of law.

Rana had already been a controversial figure

Rana’s detention comes against the backdrop of his controversial tenure as chief justice.

An impeachment motion was registered against him in Parliament in February 2022, after which he was suspended from his position.

The impeachment process was never brought to a final conclusion during his tenure, and the issue continued to generate legal disputes.

Earlier this month, the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Bench ruled that the impeachment motion against Rana had lost its purpose and dismissed four writ petitions related to the dispute.

Allegations of political and judicial involvement

Separately, government and judicial sources have claimed that Rana had recently become increasingly active in political and judicial affairs.

Sources have alleged that complaints had been lodged at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers accusing him of attempting to influence governance and judicial proceedings.

According to those sources, Rana’s activities fell broadly into two areas.

One involved alleged political activity and interest in a possible future political role. The other involved his reported interest in cases pending before the courts.

Sources have also claimed that people associated with sensitive cases had continued visiting Rana after his retirement.

Government sources have alleged that Rana met stakeholders before hearings in several high-profile cases, including the Teramox case involving the Nepal Telecommunications Authority and the case involving Birgunj Mayor Rajeshman Singh.

However, Singh has rejected that claim, telling Onlinekhabar that he has never met or even seen Rana and that he was being unnecessarily linked to the matter.

The allegations remain claims from sources and have not been established as the reason for Rana’s detention.

What happens next?

For now, the central question remains unresolved.

Police have cited a security threat as the reason for bringing Rana to the Criminal Investigation Office, while authorities have not publicly identified the nature of the threat or the person or group allegedly responsible.

At the same time, questions have been raised about why Rana was taken from his home rather than being provided security there, and what legal procedure was used to bring him to Teku.

The latest police account indicates that Rana was expected to be released and that the matter was not necessarily linked to a criminal case.

As a result, the circumstances surrounding the former chief justice’s late-night detention remain unclear, with both the security explanation and the legal procedure used by police now under scrutiny.

title.rendered: Woman dies after landslide buries house in Dhanusha

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, September 27

A woman died after a landslide buried a house in Dhanusha district on Sunday morning.

The landslide struck the single-storey house of Rajan Shrestha in Aampagachhi Tole of Mithila Municipality-11 amid rainfall, police said.

According to police, 42-year-old Kamala Shrestha died after the house was buried by the landslide.

Four other members of the family managed to escape safely, police said.

title.rendered: Kaligandaki floods submerge 50 houses in Setibeni

content.rendered:
Syangja, September 27

Flooding on the Kaligandaki River has submerged 50 houses in the Setibeni area, spanning both Syangja and Parbat districts.

Following four straight days of continuous rain, rising water flow in the river submerged 30 houses in Bihadi Rural Municipality-6, Parbat, and 20 houses in Galyang Municipality-5, Syangja.

The flood also swept away the concrete bridge connecting Mirmi, in Kaligandaki Rural Municipality-7, Syangja, to Harmichaur, in Kaligandaki Rural Municipality-1, Gulmi.

The bridge had already been damaged by rising water levels before it was fully washed away this morning, according to the District Administration Office, Syangja. Its loss has disrupted travel and transportation between Syangja and Gulmi.

Locals say this is the largest flood on the Kaligandaki River in the past 30 years, the first of this scale since the Kaligandaki “A” Hydropower Project was built.

Due to the high water flow, power generation at the 144-megawatt Kaligandaki “A” Hydropower Project in Beltari, Syangja, was halted from 8:45 pm Friday.

According to project chief Atmesh Paudel, this marks the first time since the plant began operations that generation has had to be suspended for an extended period. All three gates of the project’s dam at Mirmi have been fully opened since Friday night due to the high water flow.

With water levels also rising in smaller streams across the district, the District Administration Office, Syangja, has urged residents living along riverbanks in the Ridi, Ramdi, Malunga, and Chapakot areas to remain alert, and said it is continuously issuing warnings and using loudspeaker announcements about the potential risk.

title.rendered: Nepal could receive $20 million from loss and damage fund: Foreign Minister Khanal

content.rendered:
New York, September 27

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has said Nepal could receive $20 million (Rs 3.65 billion) immediately from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.

Khanal, who is in the United States to attend the United Nations General Assembly, made the statement in an interview with Onlinekhabar.

“We have now requested $20 million immediately. I think we may be able to receive that amount,” he said.

He said such a decision could be made at the fund’s upcoming board meeting.

“Given the current situation, based on my discussions with the leadership of the Loss and Damage Fund, the letter our colleagues sent to the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Environment, and our continued campaign, I think we could receive $20 million by the time of the upcoming board meeting,” Khanal said.

The 10th meeting of the fund’s board is scheduled to be held in Manila, the Philippines, in December 2026.

Khanal acknowledged that the amount would be small compared with the loss of lives and property caused by the Rasuwa floods.

“$20 million is not a very large amount. When we are talking about $5 billion, $20 million is a very small amount,” he said.

However, he said securing the amount would still be a symbolic victory for Nepal.

Nepal had sent a letter to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage on August 31, seeking emergency financial assistance, arguing that the Rasuwa floods of August 26 were linked to climate change.

On September 9, the fund’s board said it was holding discussions and coordinating to respond to Nepal’s request for immediate assistance as soon as possible.

title.rendered: Kaligandaki flood update: 80 houses washed away in Parbat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Flooding on the Kaligandaki River has washed away 80 houses in Farse settlement, located in Jaljala Rural Municipality-8, Parbat district.

Shailendra Thapa, co-spokesperson for the Armed Police Force, said 80 houses were swept away after floodwaters entered the settlement.

Residents began moving to safer locations after floodwaters started entering the settlement on Saturday night. The Armed Police Force said no information on human casualties has been received so far.

After receiving reports that other houses in the area were also at high risk, a joint team from Armed Police Force Nepal No. 25 Chandika Company, Parbat, and Nepal Police relocated remaining residents and their belongings to safer ground.

Further details are still awaited, as the area is currently facing power outages and phone connectivity issues.

title.rendered: Aayo Gorkhali to stage in Kathmandu on September 28-29

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

A theatrical production titled Aayo Gorkhali will be staged at Sarwanam Theatre, Kathmandu, on September 28 and 29, beginning at 5:15 pm both days.

The play is directed by Mamunur Rashid, with the script written by playwright Mok Chiu Yu.

Aayo Gorkhali traces the history of Gorkhali soldiers, exploring their wartime experiences, sacrifices, and the broader themes of humanity, identity, discrimination, justice, and the pursuit of peace.

Spanning a narrative arc from the First World War through the Second World War and the Malayan Emergency to Hong Kong, the production frames war not simply as a soldier’s story, but as one intertwined with human suffering, identity, and the search for peace.

title.rendered: Weather set to improve from tonight as low-pressure area weakens

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Meteorologists say the low-pressure area near Uttar Pradesh, India, is gradually weakening, which will cause rainfall activity in Nepal to decrease progressively. Still, rain is forecast across various parts of the country this afternoon, with heavy rain expected in only one or two locations.

According to meteorologist Sanjib Adhikari of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology’s forecasting division, the low-pressure system positioned south of Nepal’s Lumbini and Sudurpashchim provinces has concentrated rainfall activity in those areas. Combined with moisture-laden winds from the Bay of Bengal that moved toward central Nepal overnight, this caused heavy overnight rain in several parts of central Nepal.

Adhikari said the low-pressure system is now gradually weakening, though some residual rain activity is expected today. With continued moisture from the Bay of Bengal, clouds have also formed over Madhesh, Bagmati, and the western part of Koshi Province, raising rain chances there too. Western Nepal remains cloudy in many places, but no major rainfall is currently occurring there.

Heavy rain expected around Chitwan and Gandaki

Adhikari said moderate rain is expected this afternoon across many mountainous, hilly, and Tarai areas of Sudurpashchim Province, with comparatively less rain in eastern Koshi Province. Rain is expected to continue across areas from Karnali eastward to Madhesh, though heavy rain is unlikely in most places, except possibly one or two locations.

He said heavy rain remains possible in one or two spots in Madhesh Province, the lower Bagmati region and around Chitwan, the lower and hilly areas of Gandaki, mountainous regions, the southern part of Lumbini Province, and parts of Sudurpashchim’s mountains, hills, and Tarai.

However, Adhikari said heavy rain is unlikely tonight, and overall weather conditions are expected to improve significantly.

title.rendered: What my mother taught me about womanhood

content.rendered:
“Have you figured out what it means to be a woman?” I look at Aama (mother), her slightly wrinkling eyes, the adornment on her nose, and the tika between her eyebrows.

I have been asking these questions lately—to myself, to the women around me, to the women who seem to know the answer, to the women who pretend to know the answer. I had never asked the question to Aama.

Usually, we talk about how I like fried Parwal for dinner and have forbidden her to cook it otherwise. Some days, we talk about books that she reads, the kind of character that inspires her, the linguistic magic that moves her. Some days, we talk about how we never take vacations and how this Dashain is the one time we have to go somewhere as a family. Most days are filled with complaints.

“You did not finish your meal properly.” “For once, fix your bed without me telling you to.” “Don’t be such a spendthrift. Save money!” and “How will you ever live without me?”

All my fondest memories with my Aama are bittersweet: a tad bit of love, a weeny little fret, lots of life advice, and even more of tsk tsk tsk.

But we never had the chance to just sit down and talk about what it means to be a woman.

 I have read feminist writers explain it to me word by word. I have heard advocates fight for it. But what did the woman I knew even before I came into this world think about womanhood?

“Why are you bothering me in broad daylight?” She looked at me, brushing off a few grey strands of hair that blocked her eyes.

“Aama, let’s talk sometime.”

“All you do is talk. Look at your wardrobe. Don’t come asking me where your green pants are tomorrow.”

My Aama is the life of a room in any gathering. She is always beaming, always the one with the lame jokes. Her outlook on life has never been dull. However, every time I push her beyond “normal” conversations, she seems to build a wall.

It is not that she has not taught me anything—she does it in silence. Whenever I panic over the slightest inconvenience, she gives me the simplest yet most rational answers. Whenever I come home tired, angry, and frustrated, she gives me the space I crave. She has single-handedly taken care of two daughters—to feed them, raise them, support them, embrace them, and hold them.

Yet the words never get enunciated.

I remember being 13 or 14 and watching Sushmita Sen answer her Miss Universe 1994 question: “What is the essence of being a woman?”

The winning answer always rang through my head. To show a man what loving, caring, sharing is all about. Is that the essence of being a woman? Well, it made her win the coveted title. I used to think maybe that was it—a beauty queen stamped the answer.

I always looked at my Aama and saw her have a very conventional life as a woman—what society dictates it to be: raise kids, stay home, domesticate.

Yet she never let those shackles strangle me.

“I don’t want to get married.”

“First, learn to wash your socks. Marriage is not in the cards any time soon,” she would say.

She took care of her in-laws when she could have easily chosen not to. She chose to stay home when she could have easily opted out. She cooks and cleans, exercises and writes. There is nothing abnormal about the frontiers of womanhood that my Aama drew for herself.

“Are you a feminist, Aama?”

“Feminists cook their own meals. Learn to cook one meal for yourself, and I will tell you.”

Her answers are never direct, never precise—always full of metaphors, riddles, idioms. You have to read between the lines, dig between the sighs, and look for the truth in the stack of indirectness.

“I don’t have a room of my own. You always have to come into my room, don’t you?”

Every time I disturb my mother when she is writing, she complains. She wants to breathe sometimes. Her fingers slowly type words in Preeti font. The speed with which she cuts parwal in chulesi without even looking is completely opposite to the way she types. She looks at the keyboard—every letter, every key, every click is calculated. Every click holds meaning. She is not used to technology. She is not a digital native. But she learns and adapts, like she adapted when she had to shift to a home that was not her own.

“Go do Aarati today. Tell God to give you Buddhi,” She looks at her shrine and taunts me sometimes.

“Aama, I am an atheist.”

My Aama did not have answers to many of my questions or my disagreements. She was a woman of a different generation. Yet I wanted to know what her thoughts on womanhood were.

“Do you see yourself being a grandmother someday?”

“Are you planning to elope?”

“Why not? I might elope and adopt a child.”

“Liberate yourself first.”

“But I am free. Are you?” I ask her.

My mother wrinkles her forehead. Little hills like Chure grow between her eyebrows.

“A woman has to be free. From within. From what defines her. From what limits her. From what destroys her. From what builds her. A woman has to learn when to hold on and let go. A woman has to surrender and conquer. A woman has to bleed and break, build and become. A woman has to be free.”

“But are you free, Aama?”
 
“The world has never let me be.”

 “Why?”

 She looks at the persimmon tree outside, its branches brushing against our windowpane.
 
“I am like this tree. The branches long to wander, but the roots hold them back. The leaves stretch to explore, yet the trunk must stand still. Rooted, reaching, but never leaving.”

As she oils my hair with Bhringaraaj oil before I take a bath, she tells me, “Take good care of your hair.”

“I am thinking of going bald.”

“Do it. But while you have hair, take care of it.”

Every morning, when I leave my messy, unkempt bed, she shouts, “Neem Karoli Baba says those who leave their beds unmanaged will have an unmanaged life.”

I don’t know what my Aama thinks of being a woman. I have never known. She has led me to believe that a woman is just a name, a tag. You could call an apple an orange if you want—nothing would change.

But she has shown me what being beyond a woman is like. How womanhood is making compromises but also handling consequences. Womanhood is taking responsibility but also handling the wreckage. Womanhood is a cocktail of emotions. Womanhood is preaching and praying but also daring and doing. Womanhood is wailing and whispering but also weaving and withstanding.

It is a process. It is a journey.

“Aama, am I woman enough?”

She touches the persimmon tree outside.

“Woman enough? Look at this tree, child. You are its leaves. Reaching, daring, unstoppable.”
 
“But I feel like being a tree is not enough.”

“Then be the forest and the forest fire!”

She picks up her broom and starts cleaning the staircase.

As I look at her doing the most mundane tasks with absolute sincerity, I feel like maybe that is it! That is being a woman.

title.rendered: After an hour and a half of consultation, Cholendra Rana was taken to the police office

content.rendered:
At 12:30 am police arrived at former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana’s residence in Maharajgunj. A team from the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office reached the house at midnight, causing a stir in the area; the local police circle (Maharajgunj) was also informed given the location.

A team led by a DSP told Rana to accompany them to the police office, which he initially refused outright. Police claimed at the time that he faced a “security threat” and needed to be taken along, but he continued to refuse. According to police sources, it was only after roughly an hour and a half of persuasion that officers were able to bring him out of the house.

About a dozen plainclothes police officers, under a DSP’s command, had arrived at the Rana’s residence from the Crime Investigation Office. Rana was brought to the Crime Investigation Office in Teku around 2 am and questioned in the office of SSP Santosh Khadka, who reportedly stayed at the office through the night in anticipation of needing to act.

Police say they received a “Gen Z” attack threat against him

It remains unclear why a former Chief Justice would be arrested in the middle of the night. Police confirmed no arrest warrant had been issued against Rana. SSP Khadka claimed Rana was brought in due to a “security threat,” saying information had been received suggesting a possible physical attack on him overnight, and that he was brought in for his own safety.

However, questions have been raised about this explanation, since providing additional security at his residence would have been a more standard option than removing him at night.

Khadka said that the information reached police late at night, necessitating immediate action. Police have claimed the threat information involved potential attackers linked to “Gen Z” groups. This marks the first time in the Supreme Court’s history that a former Chief Justice has been arrested in this manner, though again, no formal arrest warrant was issued.

title.rendered: Power supply disrupted in 10 local units after Malangawa substation flooded

content.rendered:
Sarlahi, September 27

Electricity supply has been disrupted in 10 local units after water entered the Nepal Electricity Authority’s substation in Malangawa, Sarlahi, following continuous rainfall.

According to the NEA’s Malangawa Distribution Centre, electricity supply to areas served by the substation has been cut off since around 4 am on Sunday.

Technical engineer Saurav Shah said electricity had to be shut off after water entered the substation’s switchyard and control room due to the continuous rainfall.

He said the substation area remains inundated, making it impossible to immediately resume power supply. Efforts are underway to drain the water using motor pumps. Electricity will be restored only after the water level falls and technical tests are completed, he said.

Madhavendra Yadav, chief of the NEA’s Malangawa Distribution Centre, said efforts to drain the water were being expedited. According to him, holes have been made in the wall surrounding the substation premises to facilitate water drainage. He said the drainage process has been hampered by a blocked external drain.

“The water has already been removed from the control room. Fans are now being used to dry the equipment,” Yadav said. “Electricity supply may resume within the next two to three hours after technical tests are completed.”

Consumers in 10 local units, including Malangawa, have been affected by the power outage. The NEA said electricity supply would be restored after the water is drained and technical tests are completed.

title.rendered: Four-wheelers banned on Sharda Barrage as Mahakali River crosses danger level

content.rendered:
Kanchanpur, September 27

Four-wheeled vehicles have been barred from crossing the Sharda Barrage after the water level in the Mahakali River crossed the danger mark following continuous rainfall.

According to police, vehicle movement was halted after the river’s water flow reached 197,774 cusecs.

The restriction applies to vehicles travelling in both directions between Nepal and India via the Sharda Barrage.

The Mahakali River has been rising steadily following continuous rainfall in the hilly districts of Sudurpaschim Province since Thursday night.

Authorities have also restricted the operation of short- and long-distance vehicles in the hill districts of Sudurpaschim due to the continued rainfall.

With weather conditions showing no significant improvement, the restrictions on vehicle movement have been extended until Monday morning.

Authorities have urged the public to remain cautious and avoid unnecessary travel in areas affected by heavy rainfall and rising river levels.

title.rendered: Heavy rainfall disrupts roads in 6 districts of Karnali

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Continuous rainfall has disrupted road transportation in six districts of Karnali Province after landslides and debris blocked several road sections.

According to the Provincial Police Office, the Karnali Highway has been obstructed by a landslide at Gagane Khola in Shubhakalika Rural Municipality-1 of Kalikot.

The Rapti Highway has also been blocked after landslides occurred at Kharkhola in Kapurkot Rural Municipality-1 and at Aringale in Wards 3 and 4 of the rural municipality in Salyan.

Police said the Jumla-Nagma section of the Karnali Highway has been obstructed by a landslide at Ranka in Tatopani Rural Municipality-1 of Jumla.

Several sections of Karnali Corridor affected

The Karnali Corridor has been affected at several points. A landslide and mudflow blocked the road at Khachcha in Sarkegad Rural Municipality-1 of Humla, disrupting the Karnali Corridor. Police said the accumulation of mud and debris on the road has affected transportation.

Similarly, the Nagma-Gamgadhi road has been obstructed by a landslide along the Pina-Talcha section in Wards 7 and 8 of Chhayanath Rara Municipality in Mugu. The road section is also part of the Karnali Corridor.

Police said transportation services have also been affected along several road sections in Jajarkot due to continuous rainfall.

The ongoing rainfall has increased the risk of landslides, mudflows and road erosion in hilly areas, affecting the movement of passengers and vehicles.

Karnali Province Police said coordination is underway with the concerned authorities to clear the blocked roads.

Karnali Province Police spokesperson SSP Santosh Singh Rathore said authorities are assessing the condition of roads affected by the rainfall and taking necessary steps to resume transportation.

title.rendered: What PM Balen Shah’s UNGA speech could mean for the world

content.rendered:
At the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen, said what he needed to say.

At its core, his message was about the vulnerability of countries that have contributed relatively little to many of the crises confronting the world today, yet continue to bear their consequences.

Small island developing states, landlocked developing countries and least developed countries are increasingly exposed to shocks originating far beyond their borders and largely outside their historical responsibility. At the same time, they must contend with inflation, fuel and fertilizer shortages, food-price volatility and supply-chain disruptions resulting from conflicts over which they have little influence.

Nepal may appear geographically distant from the centres of global power, but what is happening in the Himalayas is not a distant problem.

Balen spoke not only for Nepal but, in many ways, for the wider Hindu Kush Himalaya region, which contributes a negligible share of global greenhouse gas emissions but sustains ecosystems, rivers and livelihoods for nearly two billion people.

The consequences of a rapidly destabilising Himalayan ecology will travel far beyond Nepal’s borders.

“I am told I am the youngest Head of Government to address this Assembly this year. I did not come here to make that the story.”

Instead, he made the story one that matters to humanity as a whole. Three years ago, standing in the shadow of Mount Everest in Nepal, UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned of “the madness of an impending climate disaster.”

But Balen was not there “to blame any country or continent.”

He argued that what vulnerable countries such as Nepal are looking for is “shared responsibility and solidarity.” Countries that carry a heavier historical burden for greenhouse gas emissions must take greater responsibility and “must do more”, in line with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.

But his speech was not only about climate change.

It was about what it means to be a small state in today’s international order.

Alongside the climate impacts that claim lives and “erase years of development”, he spoke about the uncertainty of global supply chains, the impact of wars on people who have nothing to do with them, and the continuing relevance of multilateralism for small states such as Nepal.

“A world that can deliver a weapon anywhere in seventy-two hours has no excuse for leaving a farmer without means for a decent livelihood.”

Balen’s speech exposed one of the uncomfortable realities facing small states like Nepal: the structural inequalities built into the international system.

When catastrophic disasters strike, vulnerable countries are told to seek climate justice and turn to international climate-financing mechanisms for support.

Yet the very system designed to help them has become, in Balen’s words, a “bureaucratic maze”, forcing countries already grappling with devastation “to spend years proving that they need help.”

“When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms. We act. That is what climate justice must mean.”

Nepal has sought around US$20 million from the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage following the devastating “Himalayan tsunami” that left at least 1,400 people dead and more than 6,000 missing, while causing billions of dollars in infrastructure losses that are still being assessed. Balen said in his UN address that rapid assessments had put Nepal’s physical recovery needs at about 10 percent of GDP.

Claims from affected countries have already reached $2.8 billion, while only a fraction of that amount has been pledged by developed nations.

Countries most exposed to climate disasters are often those with limited institutional, financial and technical capacity to navigate complicated international financing mechanisms. For countries like Nepal that face these consequences repeatedly, climate finance that arrives years after a catastrophe cannot build resilience in time.

This leads to an important question.

How can a small state like Nepal access international financing mechanisms, influence decisions made within them, and develop the institutional confidence and capacity to claim what those mechanisms promise?

Scholars of international relations have long identified recurring characteristics in the behaviour of small states. They tend to possess limited political, economic and administrative capacity, depend more heavily on external actors for security and resources, and frequently find themselves on the weaker side of asymmetric relationships.

Their material limitations constrain their ability to independently shape the behaviour of larger powers. Indeed, one influential strand of small-state scholarship defines smallness not simply by territory or population, but by limited capacity to influence the security interests of great powers or defend against them.

Nepal fits many elements of this structural dilemma.

It cannot influence global emissions through economic power. It cannot independently develop every satellite, climate model or monitoring technology it needs. Its negotiating teams and technical institutions cannot match the resources available to major powers.

But smallness may limit certain forms of power without eliminating agency.

A country’s strategy is shaped not only by the constraints of its external environment, but also by the material and human resources it can mobilise within those constraints.

Research on Small Island Developing States, for example, shows that states conventionally regarded as structurally weak have nevertheless used international organisations to advance development interests and institutionalise their concerns. Scholars have even described how small states can act as “norm entrepreneurs”, transforming vulnerability from merely a weakness into a basis for collective diplomatic action.

For Nepal, that points towards a strategy built around agency rather than simply vulnerability.

The first element is coalition-building — pooling diplomatic resources, technical expertise and negotiating capacity. But coalitions will mean little without domestic capacity.

Institutional competence must be developed over time to conduct regional negotiations, undertake assessments, gather scientific evidence and negotiate continuously with multilateral institutions. For this, Nepal needs real-time satellite data, technology and technical expertise.

In climate negotiations, financing is justified through evidence and its links to climate change. Yet small states often depend on information produced elsewhere.

This is where Balen’s proposal for a “Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism” becomes significant. He proposed a mechanism involving Nepal, India and China that would facilitate scientific research, satellite-data exchange, joint monitoring and early-warning systems, real-time hydrological information, and coordinated cross-border disaster preparedness and response.

That may be what it means to turn the Himalayas into a “laboratory of international cooperation” — recognising that some threats transcend border disputes and are too interconnected to be managed within national borders.

Multilateral engagement is equally important.

Historically, small states have been among the strongest supporters of international institutions precisely because institutionalised multilateralism can substitute, to some extent, for the power resources they lack. Through multilateralism, they can find niche opportunities to exercise comparative advantages.

For Nepal, this means that vulnerability need not be the end point of its diplomacy. It can also be a basis for coalition-building, institutional innovation and agenda-setting.

That was perhaps the larger significance of Balen’s message from Nepal. A distant country in the Himalayas may indeed be carrying a very close warning for humanity.

title.rendered: Nepali community in Melbourne celebrates Indra Jatra

content.rendered:

The Nepali community living in Melbourne, Australia, celebrated Indra Jatra with great festivity on Saturday. Organised by Newa: Guthi Victoria, the event gave Nepalis living abroad a glimpse of Kathmandu’s Durbar Square.

Held at the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre in Diggers Rest, the celebration featured a vibrant procession including the living goddess Kumari, the White Ganesh, and Lakhe dances. A traditional chariot and a backdrop resembling Kathmandu’s Durbar Square were set up at the venue to give participants a feel of being in Nepal.

The event, themed “Let’s celebrate culture, let’s support the community, together let’s respect, preserve and promote our culture,” was free to attend.

Running from 10 am to 4 pm, the event drew a significant turnout of Newa community members and other Nepalis living in Victoria. Attendees said such programs play an important role in preserving traditional culture abroad and passing it on to the next generation.

Organiser Newa: Guthi Victoria thanked all volunteers, supporters, and participants who helped make the event a success.

title.rendered: World Tourism Day 2026: Nepal’s richness deserves a place in the AI economy

content.rendered:
This World Tourism Day, the official theme, “Digital Agenda and Artificial Intelligence to Redesign Tourism”, asks the sector to consider how artificial intelligence can support smarter, more inclusive and sustainable tourism. It also carries an important warning: digital progress matters only if its benefits reach travellers, workers, enterprises and communities.

For Nepal, this should be more than another global slogan. As travel planning increasingly moves from search boxes towards conversations with AI assistants, it raises a question of national competitiveness: Are we preparing tourism for the AI economy, or merely digitising old practices?

Imagine a traveller asking an AI assistant to design a ten-day journey through Nepal — culture rather than crowds, regional cuisine, comfortable walking, a spiritual experience, reliable accommodation and a destination suitable for winter. Will the answer include Badimalika, Rara, Dhorpatan or Humla? Will it introduce community homestays, pilgrimage routes, traditional food, wellness experiences and living cultural landscapes? Or will it return only the Nepal that is already internationally familiar?

The answer may depend not only on what Nepal offers, but on what the digital world can find, understand and trust.

A new gateway to travel

Nepal Tourism Board recorded 1,158,459 international visitor arrivals in 2025, about 96.8 per cent of the 2019 level. That recovery is important. But recovering visitor numbers does not necessarily mean Nepal is prepared for the next transformation in how journeys are imagined, compared and purchased.

That transformation is already visible. A 2025 Amadeus study of 9,500 travellers across seven markets found that the use of generative AI for travel planning had risen sharply. Travellers valued time savings, personalised recommendations and the discovery of new destinations. Yet one-quarter had also encountered outdated or inaccurate information.

Adobe’s 2026 analysis of US travel websites reinforces the direction of change. Traffic arriving from AI services increased substantially, while travellers used AI for research, inspiration, transport planning and itinerary creation. Adobe also found that parts of many travel websites were not readily interpretable by machines, weakening their visibility in AI-generated results.

These findings are not Nepal-specific, and they do not show that conventional search has disappeared. But they do demonstrate that AI is becoming an additional gateway through which destinations are discovered, evaluated and recommended.

In that environment, digital invisibility is a new form of remoteness.

This is an emerging challenge rather than an established statistical category. Geographic remoteness will continue to matter: roads, flights, communications, health facilities and emergency services remain fundamental. But a second form of remoteness is emerging. A destination can exist physically, possess extraordinary cultural and natural value, and still be absent from the digital systems through which travellers increasingly make decisions.

Nepal is more than its famous icons

Everest, Annapurna, Kathmandu, Pokhara, Chitwan and Lumbini are central to Nepal’s tourism identity. The challenge is not their visibility. It is whether the rest of Nepal can also be responsibly discovered.

Dhorpatan brings together protected landscapes, wildlife, walking and village-based accommodation. Badimalika links natural beauty with sacred geography and pilgrimage. Rara offers trekking, boating, birdlife and mountain scenery. Humla represents another dimension of Nepal whose experiences can be difficult for potential visitors to discover and assess through reliable digital information.

This is not an argument for promoting every destination immediately. Digital attention must be matched by safe access, conservation, sanitation, reliable services, community consent and credible visitor information. A destination can become visible on a screen much faster than it can develop the capacity to receive visitors responsibly.

Visibility, therefore, is not merely a marketing function. It is part of destination governance. Nepal must decide which places are promoted, what information accompanies that promotion, who verifies it, whether the destination is ready and how local people benefit when attention becomes visitation.

Nepal’s Tourism Policy 2025 already provides important direction. It identifies religious circuits, indigenous cuisine, cultural heritage, rural and community tourism, meditation, yoga, wellness, health tourism and multi-season experiences as areas for diversification. It also proposes multilingual digital promotion, classification-based destination profiles, structured tourism information and integrated digital services.

Nepal is not starting from a policy vacuum. The unresolved question is implementation.

Trust still comes before technology

AI can inspire travel, but trust determines whether a destination is chosen. A traveller considering Nepal may need answers to practical questions: Is the road open? Is the trail operational? Is a permit required? What accommodation is available? Where is the nearest health facility? Who should be contacted during an emergency? When was the information last verified?

The Tourism Policy acknowledges many of these needs through proposals for an integrated digital trekking-permit system, tourist assistance centres, a 24-hour helpline, improved signage, updated tourism information and public tourism services delivered through digital platforms.

The task is not simply to build another application. It is to connect these functions from the traveller’s perspective and establish clear responsibility for the information behind them. National agencies, provincial and local governments, protected areas, operators and communities should each maintain the information for which they are accountable.

Technology must also complement rather than replace human knowledge. An AI assistant cannot inspect a landslide, assess changing mountain conditions, repair a road, evacuate an injured traveller or determine whether a community is ready to receive guests. Guides, residents, local authorities, transport providers, accommodation operators and rescue services remain indispensable.

AI should help reliable local knowledge travel further. It should not create the illusion that local expertise is no longer necessary.

Begin with Governance, Not Software

Nepal’s digital tourism strategy should begin with trustworthy information and institutional capability. Destinations need verified profiles, multilingual content and consistent information on access, trails, permits, accommodation, events, safety and services. Information that changes quickly — weather disruptions, closures, road conditions or emergency contacts — must be updated, attributable and time-stamped.

Small tourism enterprises, homestays, guides and community organisations should not be expected to manage this transition alone. Digital transformation should expand their ability to communicate, maintain information and access markets without erasing their identity or transferring control over cultural representation to distant platforms.

Responsible AI also requires boundaries. Personal information must be protected. Digital systems must be secure. Recommendations should be transparent enough to examine for error or bias. Cultural knowledge should not be extracted, simplified or commercialised without respect for the people to whom it belongs. Human accountability must remain clear when automated information affects travel, safety or community reputation.

Success should therefore not be measured by how much content Nepal publishes or how many platforms it launches. The real tests are whether travellers receive more reliable answers, whether lesser-known destinations become responsibly discoverable, whether small enterprises can participate, and whether increased visibility creates fair local benefit.

AI will not replace Nepal’s mountains, cultures, hospitality, guides or communities, nor should it. Its significance lies in shaping the doorway through which travellers first encounter them.

Just as Nepal has spent decades reducing geographic remoteness through roads, airports, trails and communications, it must now address digital remoteness with equal seriousness.

On this World Tourism Day, the question is no longer only whether the world wants to visit Nepal. It is whether, when a future traveller asks an AI assistant where to go, the world’s algorithms can discover the full richness of Nepal — or only the Nepal that is already famous.

title.rendered: 1 dead, 3 missing as landslides bury houses in Palpa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

One person has died, and three others are missing after landslides buried houses at separate locations in Palpa district.

Seventy-five-year-old Sher Bahadur Chidi was injured after a landslide buried his house in Rupse of Mathagadhi Rural Municipality-2 on Saturday night. He was rescued and taken to a health post for treatment, where doctors declared him dead, according to ward chairperson Bom Bahadur Thada Magar.

Chidi’s wife survived the incident as she had gone outside to use the toilet when the landslide struck, he said.

Meanwhile, continuous rainfall triggered a landslide that buried two houses in Bhaisakatta of Mathagadhi Rural Municipality-3. Police said three people are missing after the landslide buried a house.

The landslide struck the house of Lil Bahadur Gharti Magar at around 4:30 am on Sunday.

According to police, 75-year-old Lil Bahadur Gharti Magar, his 17-year-old daughter Dina Gharti Magar, and 15-year-old Jharana Gharti, the daughter of their neighbour Motilal Gharti, are missing.

Ward Chairperson Tej Bahadur Gharti Magar said local representatives, the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police personnel have reached the site to carry out rescue operations.

Mathagadhi Rural Municipality Chairperson Yam Bahadur Chidi said the rescue operation could take time due to the large size of the landslide.

Further details of the incident are awaited.
