On Saturday night, a Scorpio vehicle that met with an accident near the Oil Corporation area in Biratnagar Metropolitan City-3 was found carrying 398 kg of marijuana.

title.rendered: Leopard found dead after being electrocuted in Chitwan

content.rendered:
File

Chitwan, September 27

A leopard was found dead after becoming stuck to an electrical transformer on the premises of the Agriculture Campus in Rampur, Chitwan.

A post-mortem conducted on Saturday confirmed that the leopard died from electrocution.

According to Deviprasad Paudel, information officer at the Division Forest Office, the leopard was an approximately 10-month-old female. Its body was found stuck to the transformer.

A team of veterinarians and technical staff from the Biodiversity Conservation Centre in Sauraha, under the National Trust for Nature Conservation, examined the carcass and conducted the post-mortem. Dr Amir Sadaula, a veterinarian at the centre, said the examination confirmed that the leopard had died after receiving an electric shock.

A mother leopard and her cubs had been spotted in the Rampur settlement area in June and July. Following the sightings, the Division Forest Office and the Biodiversity Conservation Centre launched efforts to control the leopards. One of the two male cubs was captured and is currently being kept at the conservation centre.

Leopard activity had increased in the area since June, particularly in Wards 15 and 5 of Bharatpur Metropolitan City.

The Division Forest Office stepped up efforts to capture the leopards after they were spotted in bushes and around poultry farms near the Agriculture and Forestry University.

Paudel said drones were flown during the daytime and CCTV cameras, cage traps and leg traps were used as part of the efforts to control the leopards.

Of the two cubs, one was captured from bushes near Rampur and taken to the National Trust for Nature Conservation. The mother leopard continued to be spotted in settlement areas with the other cub.

Dr Sadaula said the leopard found dead could possibly have been the other cub from the same group.

—RSS

title.rendered: Floods, landslides and rain disrupt Nepal Telecom services

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Nepal Telecom’s services have been disrupted in various parts of the country due to continuous rain, windstorms, floods and landslides. The company said the disruption has been ongoing since September 24, caused by persistent rainfall and windstorms across multiple locations.

According to the company, heavy rain and landslides have made it difficult for technical teams to reach affected areas, and optical fibre lines have also been damaged. Power supply disruptions, along with reduced efficiency of solar sites due to snowfall, rain and cloud cover, have further hampered service operations.

Nepal Telecom said repair work that can be handled remotely through the system is ongoing, and physical repairs are being carried out wherever possible. The company has technical teams on standby, ready to be deployed to affected sites once weather conditions improve.

Nepal Telecom apologised for the inconvenience caused to customers and thanked them for their patience during the difficult conditions caused by floods, landslides and continuous rain.

title.rendered: Weather update: moderate rainfall across country

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The latest weather update indicates the monsoon trough is positioned normally, with the country experiencing monsoon and westerly winds, along with a significant low-pressure area in Uttar Pradesh, India. The meteorological forecasting division predicts generally cloudy conditions nationwide, with moderate rain and snowfall expected in various regions, particularly the Himalayan and hilly areas of Sudurpashchim, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, and Karnali Provinces.

Thunder and lightning are also anticipated in these areas. In the Terai regions, moderate rainfall accompanied by thunder and lightning is likely in Sudurpashchim, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini Provinces, with heavy rainfall possible in select locations within Gandaki and Sudurpashchim Provinces, as well as the Terai areas of Madhesh and Bagmati.

Gusty winds may occur in parts of the Terai regions of Lumbini and Sudurpashchim Provinces. Overall, cloudy conditions are expected to dominate, particularly in Sudurpashchim and the Himalayan areas of other provinces, while partly cloudy weather will be observed in the remaining regions.

title.rendered: Cholendra Rana’s overnight detention raises questions as police cite security threat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

Former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher JB Rana was taken into custody from his residence in Maharajgunj on Saturday night, with police saying he was brought to the Criminal Investigation Office in Teku following a reported security threat.

Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Santosh Khadka of the Criminal Investigation Office, Teku, said Rana was taken to the office after police received information that he could be at risk.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar on Sunday morning, SSP Khadka said the decision was taken as a precautionary measure.

“After learning that there was a security threat to him, we brought him to our office at night because something could happen,” Khadka said.

No arrest warrant obtained

Sources familiar with the matter said police had not obtained an arrest warrant from any court before taking Rana into custody.

According to sources close to the judiciary, if police need to take someone into custody without first obtaining a court-issued warrant, they are required to seek an emergency arrest authorisation under the applicable legal procedure.

Police have not yet provided further details about the nature of the alleged security threat or identified who may have posed the threat.

Rana informed his brother

When police arrived at his Maharajgunj residence on Saturday night, Rana reportedly called his brother, Prabhu Shumsher, and informed him about the situation.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar on Sunday morning, Prabhu Shumsher said police told Rana that there was a threat to him from Gen Z protesters.

“The police said there was a threat to you from the Gen Z [group] and took my brother with them,” Prabhu Shumsher said.

According to Prabhu Shumsher, Rana is currently being kept at the Criminal Investigation Office in Teku.

A source close to Rana said he has not been allowed to meet visitors. His son has reportedly gone to the Teku office seeking to meet him.

Police yet to clarify further details

Rana was taken into custody by a team from the Criminal Investigation Office, Teku, late Saturday night.

While police have confirmed that he was brought to the office because of a reported security threat, authorities have not publicly provided further details about the nature of the threat or whether Rana is being investigated in connection with any criminal case.

The circumstances surrounding his detention, including the legal basis for taking him into custody without a court-issued arrest warrant, remain unclear.

title.rendered: Flydubai’s Pokhara-Dubai flights see strong passenger numbers on fourth day

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 27

Flydubai’s regular Dubai-Pokhara-Dubai service continued to see encouraging passenger numbers on its fourth day of operation on Saturday.

The Flydubai aircraft landed at Pokhara International Airport at 6:05 pm on Saturday with 156 passengers on board. It then departed for Dubai carrying 83 passengers from Pokhara, according to airport information officer Binod Singh Rawat.

The airline began its regular service on Wednesday.

On Thursday, 122 passengers arrived in Pokhara from Dubai, while 143 passengers flew from Pokhara to Dubai.

The flight scheduled for Friday was cancelled due to bad weather.

On the first flight on Wednesday, 113 passengers arrived in Pokhara from Dubai, while the return flight carried 152 passengers from Pokhara to Dubai.

Tourism sector encouraged by initial response

Tourism entrepreneurs and other stakeholders in Pokhara, who have been working to make the new international service effective and sustainable, say the initial passenger numbers are encouraging.

Former president of the Pokhara Tourism Council, Pomanarayan Shrestha, said the initial response to the Pokhara-Dubai service was positive.

“Bookings are good, and tour and travel businesses are also happy,” Shrestha said. “Hotels and restaurants have introduced discount schemes targeting passengers arriving through this flight.”

According to airport information officer Rawat, Flydubai’s aircraft is scheduled to land in Pokhara every day at 6:15 pm and depart for Dubai at 7:15 pm.

Flydubai has started the service using a Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft with a capacity of 165 passengers.

It is the first airline to operate regular commercial international flights from Pokhara International Airport. Some airlines had previously operated international charter flights from the airport.

Dubai connection opens access to international destinations

With the start of the service, passengers from several countries can travel to Pokhara more conveniently by using Dubai as a transit point.

Tourism and business stakeholders expect the new international connection to support tourism, business activity, employment and the broader local economy in Pokhara.

Pokhara International Airport came into operation in January 2023, but had not previously been able to establish regular international flights.

The government had recently announced plans to make diplomatic efforts to attract international airlines to Pokhara International Airport as part of its policies and programmes for the current fiscal year.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal granted Flydubai permission to operate the Dubai-Pokhara-Dubai service on June 8.

Government offers incentives to attract international airlines

The government has provided various fee incentives to encourage international airlines to operate from Pokhara International Airport.

Until September 2028, the airport has waived parking, landing and navigation charges for international flights.

The government has also decided to provide a 50 percent discount on ground-handling charges for international airlines operating from the airport.

title.rendered: Narayani River flood level crosses danger mark at Devghat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 27

The water level in the Narayani River at Devghat has crossed the danger mark, raising the risk of flooding in surrounding areas.

According to the Flood Forecasting Division, the water level in the Narayani River had reached 10.8 metres at the time of reporting.

The danger level at Devghat is 9 metres, while the warning level is 7.4 metres.

As the river has already crossed the danger level, authorities have urged residents and concerned agencies in vulnerable areas to remain alert due to the high risk of inundation.

The water level is still rising, and stakeholders have urged people to maintain caution throughout the evening.

Water levels also above danger mark in other rivers

Water levels have also crossed the danger mark at several other monitoring stations.

These include the Kali Gandaki River in Parbat, Chepe Khola in Lamjung, Mangalghat in Myagdi and Riu Khola in Chitwan.

According to the Flood Forecasting Division, all of the stations currently reporting water levels above the danger mark are located within the Narayani River basin.

Authorities have urged people living near rivers and flood-prone areas to remain alert and follow updates from the flood forecasting authorities.

title.rendered: Why was former Chief Justice Cholendra Rana arrested?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

Former Chief Justice Cholendra Rana has been arrested amid allegations that he was attempting to influence judicial proceedings and was becoming increasingly involved in political activities.

Authorities have not publicly disclosed the detailed grounds for his arrest. However, sources say repeated complaints had been lodged with the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers over Rana’s alleged involvement in governance-related matters and judicial affairs.

According to sources, Rana had become active on two fronts in recent months.

One was political. Sources say he had begun increasing his political activities and was showing interest in a possible future political role.

The other was judicial. He was allegedly taking an unusual interest in cases pending before the courts and meeting people connected to sensitive cases.

Increased activity from his Bansbari residence

Sources associated with the Ministry of Home Affairs say intelligence agencies had been monitoring Rana after the number of visitors to his residence in Bansbari increased.

“Surveillance was increased after there was a noticeable rise in people visiting Rana’s residence,” a source said.

According to sources, Rana’s activities increased particularly after Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma became Chief Justice.

Rana had reportedly told people who came to meet him that he could help facilitate matters if they were facing difficulties. He had also claimed that he had played a role in Sharma becoming Chief Justice, according to sources.

Alleged interest in sensitive cases

Sources claim Rana met with stakeholders ahead of hearings in several high-profile cases.

Among the cases mentioned are the Teramox case involving the Nepal Telecommunications Authority and the case concerning Birgunj Mayor Rajeshman Singh.

The allegations have raised questions about whether a former chief justice was attempting to influence ongoing judicial proceedings.

Special Court judges had also raised concerns

A senior Supreme Court source said that around two weeks ago, Special Court judges Narayan Paudel, Umesh Koirala and Bidur Koirala met Chief Justice Dr Sharma and several Supreme Court judges.

According to the source, the judges complained that the working environment at the Special Court had become extremely difficult.

The information was reportedly communicated to Prime Minister Balen Shah’s secretariat.

A Supreme Court source said Rana’s arrest appears to have been linked to a combination of factors, including his alleged political ambitions and his growing involvement in judicial affairs.

Arrest after Prime Minister’s return

Rana was arrested just hours after Prime Minister Balen Shah returned to Nepal following his participation in events related to the United Nations General Assembly.

Authorities have yet to publicly provide a detailed explanation of the legal basis for Rana’s arrest.

The allegations against Rana are based on claims by government and judicial sources, and further details are expected to emerge as the authorities disclose the grounds for the arrest.

title.rendered: Conserving Nepal’s indigenous crops is an insurance policy against climate change

content.rendered:
Nepal’s agricultural heritage is preserved not only in its fields and forests, but also in the seeds passed down through generations of farmers. From kodo (finger millet) and phapar (buckwheat) in the hills and mountains to traditional rice, pulses, taro, yam and other locally adapted crops, Nepal holds a remarkable diversity of agricultural genetic resources.

But that diversity is gradually disappearing.

At a time when climate change is making farming increasingly uncertain, losing indigenous crops could also mean losing some of our options for adapting to the future.

More than traditional crops

Indigenous crops are often viewed simply as traditional or subsistence crops. That overlooks their genetic and ecological importance.

Over generations, farmers have selected varieties suited to particular local conditions. Some landraces have traits associated with tolerance to drought, temperature variation, poor soils, pests and other environmental stresses. Not every indigenous variety is automatically climate-resilient, but the genetic diversity they contain provides valuable material for research, breeding and adaptation.

Nepal’s National Agriculture Genetic Resource Centre (NAGRC) considers agricultural genetic resources fundamental to food, nutrition, business and environmental security. The National Genebank has collected more than 14,000 accessions representing about 100 crop species from across Nepal.

A seed maintained by a farmer may therefore be more than a crop for the next season. It may contain genetic traits that become valuable under future climatic conditions.

Climate change and disappearing diversity

Nepalese farmers are already facing changing rainfall patterns, rising temperatures, drought, water shortages, pests and diseases.

A 2025 study of 229 Tharu households in western Nepal found that farmers were combining modern agricultural technologies with landraces and traditional practices as climate adaptation strategies. The researchers also highlighted the importance of maintaining landraces as a way of conserving valuable genetic resources.

Research from Lamjung offers another warning. A study in Pasagaun documented climatic changes and found that traditional varieties of rice and foxtail millet (kaguno) had disappeared from cultivation in the community studied. It also reported declines in rice and millet yields during the period examined.

The contradiction is clear. As climate change increases the need for agricultural diversity, that diversity may itself be declining.

Diversity is a form of resilience

A farming system based on a single crop variety can be highly vulnerable to one drought, disease or pest. A system containing different crops and varieties spreads that risk. Damage may still occur, but the entire system is less likely to fail in the same way.

This is one of the fundamental contributions of agrobiodiversity. Crop diversification can distribute risk, while genetic diversity within crops provides options for future breeding and adaptation.

Indigenous crops can therefore contribute to resilient farming systems alongside irrigation, soil management, weather information, improved varieties and other climate-smart practices.

But traditional crops should not be romanticised. They may have lower yields, limited markets or vulnerabilities of their own. Their value lies partly in the diversity of traits and adaptation options they preserve.

The farmer’s field matters too

Conserving indigenous crops does not mean simply placing seeds in a genebank.

Nepal has developed both ex-situ conservation through seed banks and genebanks, and on-farm conservation through community seed banks, household genebanks, field genebanks and farmer seed networks. The National Genebank reports conservation through seed, field, tissue and DNA banks, alongside community-based initiatives.

These institutions provide an essential safety net. But a seed stored in a genebank is different from one that is continuously grown, selected and exchanged by farmers.

The field is where genetic diversity meets the real environment. Farmers observe how varieties perform, select seeds and pass knowledge from one generation to another. In doing so, they keep both crop diversity and agricultural knowledge alive.

Community seed banks can help connect conservation with production by giving farmers access to locally adapted planting material while maintaining varieties that might otherwise disappear. Their value is greatest when farmers themselves participate in deciding which varieties should be conserved and how they should be used.

Conservation must also make economic sense

Farmers cannot be expected to conserve indigenous crops indefinitely if growing them provides little economic benefit.

This is where agricultural science, entrepreneurship and markets become important. Millet, buckwheat, traditional rice, pulses and other indigenous crops can be developed into value-added products through better processing, packaging, branding and market connections. Tourism can also create opportunities by promoting traditional foods as part of local culinary identity.

The National Genebank has highlighted product diversification, market development, geographical indications, recognition of agrobiodiversity-rich farmers and promotion of native agricultural products.

Conservation should therefore not simply ask farmers to save seeds. It should give them reasons to keep growing them.

Connecting science with traditional knowledge

Agriculture students and researchers have an important role to play. They can document local crop varieties and farmers’ knowledge, identify endangered landraces and study their agronomic, nutritional and economic characteristics.

Universities and research organisations can also evaluate indigenous germplasm for traits such as drought and heat tolerance, disease resistance, nutritional quality and adaptation to different agro-ecological conditions.

This creates an opportunity to connect traditional knowledge with modern agricultural science. NAGRC itself emphasises the use of native agricultural genetic resources in research and education.

Nepal should now strengthen this connection by documenting and characterising endangered crops, strengthening community and household seed banks, supporting farmer-to-farmer seed exchange and evaluating indigenous varieties for climate-resilient traits. Valuable traits can be used in participatory breeding, while farmers conserving rare landraces should have greater economic incentives.

At the same time, Nepal needs better processing and markets for indigenous crops, stronger protection of agricultural knowledge and greater collaboration among farmers, universities, NARC, local governments and the private sector. Agrobiodiversity should also be incorporated into local climate adaptation plans.

NAGRC already operates conservation programmes, including community-based conservation, local crop projects and indigenous seed initiatives. The challenge now is to connect these efforts more directly with farmers’ livelihoods and climate adaptation.

From heritage to the future

Nepal does not have to choose between traditional and modern agriculture.

Modern science can help identify useful traits in indigenous crops. Plant breeding can combine desirable characteristics. Improved agronomic practices can increase productivity, while better markets can create income. At the same time, farmers’ knowledge can guide scientists towards varieties and practices that have survived generations of environmental change.

The goal should not be to replace indigenous diversity with modernity, but to use modern science to understand, conserve and make better use of that diversity.

Climate change has made agricultural resilience a necessity. In this changing environment, the diversity preserved by farmers over generations may become one of Nepal’s most valuable agricultural resources.

A seed of kodo, phapar or a local rice variety may look ordinary. But within it can lie genetic diversity, cultural history, farmer knowledge and possibilities for the future.

Conserving indigenous crops is therefore not simply about protecting the past. It is about keeping choices open for the future.

Nepal’s indigenous crops should not become specimens preserved only in museums or genebanks. They should remain living crops in living fields, cultivated by farmers, studied by scientists and valued by consumers.

If biodiversity is the foundation of agricultural resilience, every indigenous crop we conserve today is an option we preserve for tomorrow.

title.rendered: Where can I refill my bottle?

content.rendered:
A person can buy bottled water almost anywhere in Kathmandu. Finding a place to refill a bottle is much harder. That difference shapes behaviour. Students buy another bottle between classes. Office workers do the same on their way home. Visitors at parks, bus stops and public offices often have no idea whether safe drinking water is available nearby.

At a time when Kathmandu is already struggling with waste and water quality, public drinking-water points deserve more attention.

Recent testing has again raised concerns about drinking-water safety in the Valley. Public health officials have found contamination in samples from households and public taps, particularly during the monsoon. Any refill system must therefore begin with water quality, not simply the installation of more taps.

Safe water, clearly marked

A public refill point should answer three basic questions immediately: Is the water safe to drink? Who maintains it? When was it last tested?

A simple sign can provide all three.

Kathmandu does not need hundreds of new fountains at once. It could start with places where people already gather or spend time, such as major parks, bus terminals, municipal offices, libraries, hospitals and busy pedestrian areas.

Existing public taps should also be mapped and tested. Some may already provide suitable water after treatment. Others may need repairs or should be clearly marked as non-potable.

The worst situation is uncertainty: a tap exists, but nobody knows whether the water is safe to drink.

Make refilling easier than buying another bottle

Convenience shapes habits. If clean refill water is hidden behind an office gate while bottled water is available on every corner, people will continue buying bottles. Public refill points need to be visible, accessible and easy to use.

Schools and colleges can play an important role. Students are among those most likely to carry reusable bottles, but a bottle is useful only if it can be refilled during the day. Campuses should provide accessible drinking-water stations and maintain them properly.

Businesses can also participate. Cafes, banks and shopping centres with filtered water could display a simple “refill available” sign. Some may offer it free, while others could charge a modest amount for treated water. The important thing is that people know where to go.

A citywide digital map could bring these points together. Platforms that already list toilets, ATMs and restaurants could also identify verified refill stations.

Maintenance matters

Kathmandu has seen public facilities installed with good intentions and then left without proper maintenance. Drinking-water stations cannot follow the same pattern.

Filters need replacing, tanks need cleaning, water needs testing and broken taps need repairing. Most importantly, someone must be responsible.

That responsibility should be clearly displayed at each station. If a ward office, school or business maintains it, the sign should say so and provide a contact number for complaints.

The public has a role too. Refill points should not become places for washing vehicles or dumping waste. Clear design, proper drainage and nearby bins can help protect them.

Safe drinking water should also become part of the planning checklist for public events. Fairs, sports programmes and festivals often provide toilets, security and waste bins. When people spend hours outdoors, access to safe drinking water should be just as basic.

There is also a simple economic benefit. People should not have to keep buying bottled water throughout a day in the city because no safe public alternative is available. Free or low-cost refill points would make hydration easier for students, delivery workers, street vendors and others who spend long hours outside.

This is not a grand infrastructure project. It is a small public service that could be used many times a day.

People will continue to buy bottled water, particularly when travelling. The goal is not to eliminate that option. It is to make reuse realistic.

Kathmandu often talks about reducing plastic. Asking people to carry reusable bottles is easy.

The more practical question is this: Where are they supposed to fill them?

title.rendered: How I unlearned my need for a cigarette

content.rendered:
There was a time when I never thought I would become a smoker.

Until I was 21, smoking and drinking had simply never been part of my life. I was not interested in either, nor did I feel the need to join in because others were doing it. In fact, long before I ever touched a cigarette, I had written about why I had never been fond of alcohol and why I had chosen to stay away from it.

Life has a way of taking us places we never imagined we would go.

When I began travelling to other countries, I was introduced to new cultures and people who lived differently from me and belonged to social circles very different from my own. Those experiences broadened my thinking and enriched my understanding of the world. They also exposed me to choices and situations that were new to me.

One of them was smoking.

I do not look back on that period with either pride or regret. It is simply part of my journey. I write about it to explain how someone who never intended to become a smoker could become one, remain one for years and eventually quit.

I am not writing to glorify smoking or to judge those who smoke. I am writing as someone who knows first-hand how a habit can begin, and I hope others can take something positive from my experience.

When I arrived in South Africa at the age of 21, I entered a world very different from the one I knew.

I had never been particularly interested in smoking. It was simply not for me. I did not hate smokers or judge them, but I certainly never imagined that I would become one.

South Africa changed my surroundings, and slowly, it changed my thinking.

What first attracted my attention was how common smoking was. It did not seem limited to a particular class, race, profession or age. It crossed all those boundaries. Whether someone was white or non-white, male or female, young or old, rich or poor, smoking seemed to belong to everyone.

It was part of celebrations and moments of sadness. People smoked during conversations, during breaks, after work and in moments of stress. Some smoked to relax. Others smoked to relieve tension. For almost every occasion and every mood, there seemed to be a cigarette.

As a young man trying to understand this new world, I quietly observed it. Day after day, those images became part of my surroundings and, without me realising it, began to influence the way I thought.

Looking back, I can see how my psychology slowly changed. I began to associate smoking with personality. Whenever I saw well-dressed, confident or attractive people with cigarettes in their hands, my mind created an association: smoking made them look cool.

I began to feel that I was missing something they had. It was not really the cigarette that fascinated me. It was the image I had attached to it.

The influence was not limited to strangers. Some of the Nepali friends I was closest to, including Raj brother, were smokers. They were good people and I enjoyed their company. Smoking was therefore part of the environment around me, and slowly it began to feel normal.

No one forced me to smoke. No one pressured me into it. But when something is constantly around us, it can gradually become normal.

There was another influence I did not think much about at the time.

At work, smokers would often take five-minute breaks, sometimes every hour. They would use those breaks to relax, chat with colleagues, laugh and briefly escape the boredom of work. As a non-smoker, I remained at my desk until they returned, seemingly refreshed.

It sometimes felt as though I was missing out on something.

These were small things, but together they influenced me. The environment around me gradually conditioned me to believe that smoking was somehow special.

Today, I know that a cigarette could never give anyone personality. But at the time, my young mind had begun to believe that it could.

That conditioning eventually led me to make a decision that would change the course of my life.

Raj brother and I worked for the same employer, although we managed different shops. After work, I would often meet a few Nepali friends before going home.

Raj brother would usually buy six small bottles of beer for the group. I would have a bottle of Coke or some fruit juice and enjoy the company of my friends. Cigarettes were always part of the gathering.

I was not drinking or smoking, but my mind had already been conditioned.

After weeks of seeing people smoke in the streets, at work, in restaurants, at celebrations and during stressful moments, I had begun to believe that smoking was somehow connected to personality. Somewhere in my mind, I had started to believe that I was missing something.

One evening, as we sat together, curiosity got the better of me.

“I want to know what it feels like to smoke,” I said.

Nobody criticised me or tried to argue with me. I had simply said what was on my mind.

Raj brother smiled, handed me a cigarette and said, “Go ahead, give it a try.”

I held a cigarette for the first time in my life.

I lit it clumsily and tried to imitate what I had seen so many people do before me. I took a puff and almost immediately began coughing uncontrollably.

The smoke burned my throat and lungs. My eyes watered and I could barely catch my breath. Everyone laughed while I wondered why millions of people around the world voluntarily subjected themselves to something so unpleasant.

If someone had told me then that this miserable first puff would eventually become a habit, I would not have believed them.

But bad habits do not usually arrive all at once.

The next day, I took another puff. A day later, perhaps two.

One puff became two. Two became three. Three became half a cigarette. Eventually, half a cigarette became a whole one.

For a long time, I did not even buy cigarettes. I would take a puff from Raj brother or one of my other friends whenever we met after work. Because I was not smoking regularly, I convinced myself it was harmless.

Looking back, I understand how easily a habit can develop. It does not always begin with a conscious decision. Sometimes it grows quietly through repetition until we realise that we are no longer making the choice we thought we were making.

There was no particular day when I decided to become a smoker. There was no dramatic event, emotional crisis or unbearable pressure that pushed me towards cigarettes.

I was simply becoming one.

Fortunately, it did not stay that way forever.

As time passed, I began questioning the associations I had created around smoking. The more I questioned them, the more I began to see how little they had to do with reality.

I started asking myself a simple question:

What was I smoking for?

When I first experimented with cigarettes, I had somehow imagined that smoking might help me relax. Perhaps, subconsciously, I thought it could help me think better, cope with difficult moments or make me feel more confident and composed.

Eventually, I began to see the difference between the power I had imagined a cigarette possessed and the power it actually had.

It had none.

What made me smoke was not that cigarettes made me happy. The reality was almost the opposite. They made me cough, irritated my throat and lungs and made my eyes water.

But the first unpleasant experience was not what made me stop. By then, the habit had already taken hold.

Then I began to ask myself another question.

Why had I become so dependent on a cigarette when what I actually needed in difficult moments was a person? When I am in pain, don’t I need someone to talk to? When I am stressed, don’t I need someone to listen? When I am confused, don’t I need someone to advise me? When I am struggling, don’t I need someone to help me?

A cigarette could do none of those things.

It could not listen to me, understand me, advise me or reassure me that everything would be all right. Yet I had somehow convinced myself that it could make me feel better.

That was when I began to understand something important.

Sometimes we believe in something not because it is true, but because we have convinced ourselves that it is.

I had conditioned myself to believe that a cigarette could make me feel better. Once I began questioning that belief, the cigarette began to lose its hold over me.

There was no dramatic morning when I woke up after hearing shocking news and decided never to smoke again. No doctor stood before me and told me I had to quit immediately. I did not make a grand promise to myself.

I simply began to understand that cigarettes were doing nothing positive for me.

They were not healing my pain. They were not making me stronger or more creative. They were not solving my problems or giving me personality.

The personality I had imagined I was gaining from smoking was something I already possessed, or something I could develop through my actions, confidence, work and relationships.

A cigarette could never give me that. So, slowly and almost quietly, I quit.

That is perhaps the most interesting part of my experience with smoking. Neither the beginning nor the end was dramatic.

I did not crush my final cigarette, throw away a packet and declare, “That’s it. No more.”

I simply began reducing the number of cigarettes I smoked.

When I felt the urge, sometimes I would smoke. But I also began paying closer attention to what I was feeling and asking myself why I wanted a cigarette.

Sometimes I gave in. Sometimes I did not.

Gradually, I began ignoring the cravings. Whenever the urge came, I reminded myself of what I had already understood. A cigarette was not going to heal my pain, remove my stress, make me more creative or solve my problems.

So why should I depend on it?

I did not declare war on the cigarette. I did not fight myself. I simply kept reminding myself that I was stronger than the habit I had unknowingly created. Gradually, the number of cigarettes I smoked decreased.

Then the occasions on which I smoked became fewer. Then the cravings began to disappear. And slowly, smoking disappeared from my life as quietly as it had entered it. That is how I quit.

Not with a final puff. Not with a dramatic promise. Not with a date marked on a calendar.

I kept reducing, questioning, resisting and reminding myself that I did not need it.

Until one day, I realised something very simple. I had stopped smoking.

Perhaps that is the most important thing I learned from my relationship with cigarettes. I did not quit because I had suddenly become a different person. I quit because the person I already was understood that I did not need a cigarette to become the person I wanted to be.

The habit began with a single puff.

But it ended not with a single decision, but with many small decisions to say:

I don’t need this.

title.rendered: Nepal cannot afford to leave its medicine supply to chance

content.rendered:
When a country cannot reliably produce or procure essential medicines during a crisis, the problem is not simply commercial. It becomes a matter of health security. Nepal learned this painfully during the 2015 border disruption, when medicine shortages and interruptions to health services showed how quickly treatment can become hostage to logistics.

The lesson should have changed the way Nepal thinks about pharmaceuticals. A decade later, the country has made progress, but the underlying vulnerability remains.

Nepal has dozens of pharmaceutical manufacturers, skilled pharmacists and technicians, and a domestic industry that has historically supplied roughly 45–46% of the medicines market by value. Yet the chemistry behind that production is still overwhelmingly imported. A Department of Industry study found that 80% of pharmaceutical raw materials came from India, 15% from China and 5% from other countries.

For many products, Nepal handles formulation, manufacturing and packaging. But it remains dependent on external suppliers for the active ingredients and other critical inputs that make production possible.

That distinction matters. A tablet made in Nepal from imported chemistry is genuine local manufacturing and creates real value. But it is not full medicine security. If an API shipment stops, a factory in Nepal can stop just as surely as an imported finished medicine can disappear from a warehouse.

The national debate therefore needs to move beyond the old binary of “local versus imported”. The real question is how much strategic capability Nepal needs to guarantee continuous access to priority medicines at an acceptable quality and cost when borders, freight routes, currency markets or geopolitics become unstable.

Nepal is not starting from a policy vacuum. Its National Medicines Policy already speaks of making the country self-reliant in pharmaceutical manufacturing. It calls for incentives for essential medicines, encourages production of active ingredients, excipients and packaging materials, supports technology transfer and exports, and gives priority to national industries in public purchasing in accordance with financial rules.

The problem is not the absence of policy. It is the absence of a sufficiently funded, time-bound and coordinated system for putting that policy into practice.

Nepal now needs a National Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Medicine Security Strategy. It should not be a slogan, nor a shield for inefficient firms. It should be an industrial and health compact with clear targets, budgets, accountability and a public scorecard.’

The case is constitutional as well as economic. Article 35 of Nepal’s Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to free basic health services and protection from denial of emergency health care. The Ministry of Health’s own sector review has acknowledged medicine stock-outs, limited domestic production, weaknesses in pharmacovigilance and quality control, and the need to reform procurement and supply chains while increasing domestic production of quality medicines.

A right to health cannot be delivered reliably if the medicine supply system is chronically fragile.

But domestic production is valuable only when quality is beyond doubt. The regulatory side of the equation matters just as much as industrial capacity.

The Department of Drug Administration’s own WHO Global Benchmarking Tool self-assessment placed Nepal’s regulatory functions at maturity level 1, with major gaps in vigilance, market surveillance, marketing authorisation and laboratory capacity. In March 2026, the Ministry of Health, DDA and WHO held a strategic dialogue to develop time-bound roadmaps for stronger regulation and national quality-control capacity.

That work should become a central part of the industrial strategy rather than remain a separate conversation.

Nepal should reject the false choice between industrial promotion and rigorous regulation. Protection without quality can create complacency. Quality regulation without industrial strategy can leave a small country permanently dependent on imports.

Nepal needs both: a regulator capable of removing substandard products and a manufacturing base capable of producing medicines that can compete internationally.

The international direction is already clear. The World Health Assembly’s resolution WHA74.6 calls for an all-of-government approach to sustainable local production, including stronger regulation, financing, skilled workers, technology transfer, research and development, demand aggregation and private investment.

WHO has already worked with Nepal to strengthen local producers in current Good Manufacturing Practice and WHO prequalification. Nepal should use that support to build export-grade capability rather than simply increase the number of factories or brands.

Bangladesh offers a useful regional lesson, although Nepal should learn from it rather than attempt to copy it. Bangladesh’s investment authority reports that its pharmaceutical industry meets about 98% of domestic medicinal demand and exports to more than 150 destinations.

The 1982 policy era helped create space for domestic production. But Bangladesh’s success also reflects market scale, sustained industrial learning and the intellectual-property flexibilities available to least developed countries. Even today, Bangladesh imports large volumes of APIs.

The lesson is not that one restrictive policy can produce a miracle. It is that decades of coordinated policy can change what a country is capable of producing.

Nepal’s own transition out of the LDC category makes this more urgent. The country is currently scheduled to graduate from the UN LDC category on 24 November 2026, although the government has requested an extension until 2029 and the matter awaits final UN action.

WTO rules provide LDCs with special pharmaceutical patent transition arrangements only while they remain in the category. Whether Nepal graduates in 2026 or later, it needs a post-LDC medicines and intellectual-property strategy now.

That should include patent-examination capacity, lawful public-health flexibilities, technology-transfer pathways and an assessment of which products could become commercially or legally harder to manufacture after graduation.

None of this means Nepal should try to manufacture every API itself. That would be economically unrealistic and could create environmental risks.

The country should instead identify a Strategic Medicines and Inputs List covering essential medicines, APIs, excipients, packaging materials and devices whose disruption would cause the greatest health harm. Nepal could then select a limited number of high-volume or high-risk inputs for domestic or regional production, diversify suppliers for the rest, and maintain strategic buffer stocks where local production is not viable.

An API and pharmaceutical-inputs cluster could form part of that strategy, but only after serious feasibility analysis.

India’s bulk-drug parks show why shared infrastructure can matter. Common effluent treatment, solvent recovery, testing facilities, utilities and waste management can reduce the cost and environmental burden of chemical manufacturing.

Nepal should not build an “API park” as a prestige project. It should build only what the demand, environmental assessment and commercial case can justify.

Public procurement may be the state’s most powerful industrial tool.

Nepal buys medicines for basic health services, hospitals and public programmes every year. The goal should not be to give automatic preference to locally made products. Procurement should reward verified quality, reliable delivery, resilience and genuine local value addition.

Multi-year framework contracts for priority medicines could give efficient local producers the certainty they need to invest in better plants, validation, bioequivalence, laboratories and skilled staff while preserving competition and price discipline.

The market itself also needs reform.

Nepal’s health-sector review notes that the Public Health Service Act requires prescribing by generic name, but implementation remains weak. Instead of arbitrary limits on the number of brands, Nepal should move towards transparent generic-name registration, stronger dossier requirements, bioequivalence requirements for selected high-risk or narrow-therapeutic-index products, electronic product and price databases, removal of inactive or non-compliant products, and risk-based post-market surveillance.

The aim should be to shift competition away from promotional intensity and towards quality, price and therapeutic value.

The final test is whether Nepal can become an exporter.

A resilient industry cannot be built by permanently insulating companies from competition. Firms that receive public support should be required to climb a quality ladder, from national GMP to stronger cGMP capability, validated analytical systems and pharmacovigilance, and eventually to WHO prequalification or registration in demanding export markets for selected products.

Public support should buy capability, not dependency.

The government should therefore publish a 10-year Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Medicine Security Strategy, backed by a 100-day launch programme, three-year milestones and annual public reporting.

It should be jointly owned by the ministries responsible for health, industry, finance and commerce, with the Department of Drug Administration, National Medicines Laboratory, public procurement bodies, universities, hospitals, professional councils, patient representatives and manufacturers involved.

No single ministry can solve a supply-chain problem that crosses health, trade, taxation, intellectual property, skills, energy, environment and regulation.

The strategy should begin with a clear map of Nepal’s pharmaceutical vulnerabilities. Essential medicines and critical inputs should be classified according to clinical importance, import concentration, lead times, substitutability and stock-out risk. That would help determine what Nepal should produce, what it should diversify, what it should stockpile and what it should secure through regional arrangements.

Backward integration should then be selective, not symbolic. Nepal should commission commercial and environmental feasibility studies for a limited number of APIs, excipients and packaging inputs. Shared utilities, solvent recovery, effluent treatment, analytical laboratories and warehousing should be considered only where the scale justifies them.

Public purchasing should be designed to buy resilience as well as medicines. Multi-year agreements for selected essential medicines could assess suppliers on quality history, delivery reliability, local value addition, supply resilience and total lifecycle cost rather than simply the lowest price.

At the same time, the DDA and National Medicines Laboratory need to be treated as critical infrastructure. Nepal needs a ring-fenced plan to strengthen regulation and move towards WHO maturity level 3, with enough inspectors and assessors, stronger pharmacovigilance, risk-based market surveillance, modern laboratories, digital systems and transparent recall procedures.

Industrial incentives should be tied to measurable improvements. Tax relief, concessional finance, matching grants and customs support should depend on milestones such as cGMP upgrades, validation capability, data integrity, accredited testing, bioequivalence, WHO prequalification or successful export registration.

The country also needs a pharmaceutical research and skills compact linking universities, pharmacy schools, chemistry and biotechnology departments, hospitals and industry. The focus should include formulation science, analytical chemistry, process engineering, biostatistics, regulatory science and biomanufacturing, supported by competitive, milestone-based research grants.

And if Nepal wants to export, it must solve quality first. An export-regulatory desk could help companies identify target markets, understand dossiers and inspections, and use WHO prequalification or regional reliance pathways. Support should focus on products where Nepal can develop reliable and sustainable competitiveness.

Nepal does not need pharmaceutical autarky. No serious country produces everything it consumes.

What Nepal needs is strategic resilience: the ability to keep critical treatment available when one supplier fails; the regulatory capacity to know that medicines are safe and effective; the bargaining power to buy intelligently; and enough domestic capability to prevent every external shock from becoming a national health emergency.

The next crisis should not teach Nepal the same lesson again.

The country already has the policy language. It has manufacturers. It has skilled people. It has WHO support for quality local production.

What is missing is execution at national scale.

Medicines should be treated as critical national infrastructure, alongside food, energy, digital systems and disaster preparedness.

The work should begin now.

Medicine security is not the ability to manufacture everything. It is the ability to keep essential treatment available, affordable and quality-assured when one border, one supplier or one geopolitical shock fails.

title.rendered: Rethinking road safety through the safe system approach

content.rendered:
For a long time, especially in Nepal, the general public and elected policymakers have operated under the assumption that human error is an inevitable cost of mobility. If someone on the road speeds, misjudges a turn, or steps off a footpath at the wrong moment, the resulting injury is often framed as a consequence of individual fault. We know of a history in which transportation companies measured their success and efficiency by the amount of steel moved from one point to another, while the human losses along the way were treated as collateral damage.

That framework is no longer viable. As our cities struggle with climate change, rapid urbanisation and social inequality, road safety can no longer be managed from a single perspective. It is not merely an engineering problem; it is a human rights issue, an environmental imperative and a central pillar of sustainable development.

If we intend to build equitable, low-carbon societies, our approach to road policy must fundamentally change. We must abandon the old habit of prioritising speed over survival.

Why the old model won’t work

To understand where policy goes wrong, we must first look at who is most vulnerable on our roads.

The World Health Organization reports that more than 1.1 million people die on the world’s roads each year. But those numbers hide a stark imbalance. More than half of all traffic deaths involve people who are not occupants of four-wheel vehicles. They are vulnerable road users — pedestrians, cyclists, and motorcycle and scooter riders. In rapidly urbanising nations, that proportion can rise sharply.

The global fatality rate, with fewer than 40% of deaths involving four-wheel vehicle occupants and more than 60% involving other road users, illustrates this disparity.

This disparity reveals a clear policy failure. For decades, urban design has prioritised car ownership as an engine of economic progress. Highways have not been kind to lower-income neighbourhoods, pedestrian crossings have been lengthened or sometimes eliminated to keep traffic flowing, and public transport has received minimal funding. In the Nepali context, funding has also not always reached where it was intended to go.

The result is a gap in mobility. The poorest citizens — those who walk or use two-wheelers out of economic necessity — bear the greatest physical risk so that others can commute quickly.

When a family’s primary breadwinner is killed or disabled in a traffic crash, the economic shock can propagate through generations. Children may be pulled from school, medical debts can mount, and household stability can collapse. Road violence does not just occur on infrastructure; it also undermines Sustainable Development Goal 1, No Poverty, and Goal 10, Reduced Inequalities.

Moving from “Safe Drivers” to “Safe Systems”

Where should modern transport policy go from here?

The answer lies in a paradigm shift that began in Scandinavia and has since gained global momentum: the Safe System Approach, often operationalised through Vision Zero.

Traditional road safety policy spent decades attempting to make human beings better road users through public awareness campaigns and punitive fines. The Safe System framework flips that logic entirely.

The core premise is simple: humans are inherently fallible. They will make mistakes, miscalculate speeds and experience moments of distraction. A truly sustainable transportation system must therefore be designed so that when human error inevitably occurs, it does not result in death.

Under a Safe System model, responsibility shifts from the individual road user to the system designers — planners, civil engineers and lawmakers who set speed limits and shape streetscapes.

If a driver hits a pedestrian at 50 km/h (31 mph), the pedestrian’s chances of survival are less than 20%. Drop that speed limit to 30 km/h (18 mph) through narrow lanes, raised crosswalks or speed tables, and survival rises to more than 90%. Such interventions rely on street design rather than a driver’s goodwill.

Climate action and road safety

Historically, environmental policy and traffic safety were treated as completely separate fields. Environmental writers covered emissions and green spaces; transport analysts covered asphalt projects and crash statistics.

Today, those two worlds are inseparable. Transport accounts for roughly 14% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Decarbonising this sector requires more than swapping petrol- and diesel-powered cars for battery-electric ones. Replacing a million gasoline-powered sedans with a million electric sedans may reduce tailpipe emissions, but it leaves urban gridlock, spatial inefficiency and pedestrian deaths largely unaddressed.

True sustainability requires a structural shift in how people travel — most importantly, moving away from single-occupancy vehicles towards mass transit, active travel and micromobility.

However, people will not walk or cycle if they believe doing so puts their lives at risk.

The relationship works like this:

Safe, protected infrastructure
↓
Higher rates of walking and cycling
↓
Reduced vehicle miles and air pollution
↓
Healthier, more equitable communities

A government that builds wide, high-speed roads while encouraging people to cycle for the climate is sending a contradictory message. On the other hand, when a municipality redesigns a corridor to include protected bike lanes, wide sidewalks and dedicated bus lanes, it can achieve two goals at once.

Direct safety: Physical separation protects vulnerable users from heavy vehicular traffic.

Climate action: Reduced car dependency directly lowers urban carbon footprints and local air pollution.

Overcoming policy resistance

Implementing these changes is rarely straightforward. Technical solutions are of little use if they cannot survive political debate.

Reallocating street space away from motorised vehicles will often trigger public pushback, particularly from those who currently benefit most from that space. Small business owners may worry that removing street parking will hurt foot traffic, despite evidence that pedestrian- and cyclist-friendly environments can support local businesses over time. Commuters may resist lower speed limits, viewing them as deliberate inconveniences rather than life-saving measures.

To bridge this gap, policymakers must reframe road safety as a broad public health issue rather than a series of isolated traffic rules.

Consider how societies have approached smoking or seatbelt use. Meaningful change does not happen purely through individual choices; it requires clear legislation, public health messaging and structural changes that make the safer choice the natural one. The same approach applies to city streets.

Rethinking modern streetscapes

The modern road cannot remain an arena where speed takes priority over human life.

As we move towards the Sustainable Development Goals, which specifically call for halving global road deaths and providing safe, accessible transport for all, policy must align with reality. A street that is unsafe for a nine-year-old child to walk alone or for an elderly resident to cross confidently is not a finished piece of infrastructure. It is a system failure.

As future policymakers, urban designers and transport scholars take on these challenges, the guiding principle must remain straightforward: mobility should never demand human sacrifice.

When we design streets that protect the most vulnerable, we do more than reduce crash statistics. We create quieter, cleaner and more resilient cities where everyone can move freely and safely.

title.rendered: Connecting disaster relief and social protection in Nepal

content.rendered:
Nepal is highly exposed to natural and non-natural disasters, including floods, landslides, earthquakes, inundation, fires, epidemics and other hazards. Their impact extends far beyond the immediate humanitarian emergency. Disasters can destroy homes and productive assets, interrupt livelihoods, reduce household income, disrupt children’s education, create health risks and increase the financial burden on already vulnerable families.

For this reason, disaster response cannot end with immediate relief. It must also consider how affected households’ circumstances change over time and how social protection can support them through response, recovery and reconstruction.

The Disaster-Sensitive Social Protection and Relief Distribution Standard, 2081 provides an important policy context for this discussion. It creates an opportunity to view disaster relief and social protection not as separate interventions, but as complementary mechanisms for supporting people whose circumstances change because of a shock.

The challenge now is to translate this policy direction into practical arrangements that can identify affected households, understand their changing needs, coordinate appropriate assistance, track delivery and support recovery.

Nepal already has a broad range of social protection, social assistance and disaster-response programmes covering social security allowances, disaster relief, health, education, agriculture, employment, insurance, housing, rehabilitation and reconstruction. These programmes are managed by different ministries, departments, agencies, funds, development partners and local governments.

Over time, many institutions have also developed information systems and databases to support their responsibilities. These systems contain valuable information and have improved service delivery in many areas. However, much of this information remains within individual institutional systems. When a disaster occurs, this separation can make it difficult to develop a complete picture of what has happened to a particular household.

This is one of the central challenges of Shock-Responsive Social Protection (SRSP). A household affected by a flood, for example, may need emergency relief, healthcare, temporary shelter, agricultural support, livelihood assistance, education support and eventually housing or reconstruction assistance.

Relevant information about these needs may already exist within different government systems. The challenge is therefore not necessarily a lack of information, but the ability to connect and use relevant information securely, lawfully and at the right time so decision-makers can understand a household’s circumstances and coordinate an appropriate response.

Traditional social protection programmes generally focus on determining who is eligible for a particular benefit. A shock-responsive approach requires an additional perspective: what happened to the household when the shock occurred, how has its situation changed, and what additional support does it now require?

A family may have been receiving social protection before a disaster, but a flood, landslide or earthquake may subsequently destroy its home, reduce its income, damage agricultural production or affect access to health and education. Assistance that was adequate before the disaster may no longer be sufficient afterwards.

Understanding this change requires information about the household both before and after the disaster. Existing government information may already indicate household composition, location, social protection status, livelihood characteristics and other relevant vulnerabilities. Following a disaster, damage and needs assessments, local government records and sectoral systems may provide information about new losses and requirements.

If these sources can be appropriately connected, government can develop a better understanding not only of which households have been affected, but also of how their circumstances have changed.

This does not mean Nepal needs to create a single, massive database containing all government information. Institutions should continue to own and manage the information for which they are responsible. Health information can remain within the health system, education information within education systems, agricultural information within agricultural systems and disaster information within disaster-management systems.

The objective should instead be to establish trusted mechanisms through which authorised information can be exchanged when there is a legitimate and clearly defined purpose.

The principle should be straightforward: information should be shared because it is necessary, authorised and relevant — not simply because it exists.

This is particularly important because social protection and disaster-response systems may handle personal, financial, health and other sensitive information. Strong access controls, authentication, encryption, audit trails and clear rules governing information use are therefore essential. Interoperability should strengthen cooperation between institutions without weakening the privacy and rights of citizens.

A household-centred approach provides a practical way to connect these different systems. The process can begin by identifying the individual and household, understanding where they live and their situation before the disaster, identifying the disaster event and determining whether the household has been affected. This can then be followed by damage and needs assessment, connection with appropriate relief and social protection programmes, tracking of assistance and payments, grievance management and continued support through recovery and reconstruction.

The central idea can be expressed simply as “One Person. One Household. One Location. One Shock Event. One Connected Case.”

This does not mean creating a new database for every disaster. Where legally permitted and technically feasible, existing information can be securely reused so that an affected household does not have to repeatedly establish the same basic information with every government programme.

A connected case can also help authorities understand what assistance a household has already received and what important needs remain unresolved.

This is particularly relevant because the impacts of a disaster are often interconnected. A flood may damage a family’s home, destroy crops, interrupt employment and create health and education challenges at the same time. If each issue is addressed independently, different programmes may struggle to understand the household’s overall circumstances.

A coordinated household view can allow different programmes to contribute their respective forms of support while each institution retains responsibility for its own mandate and information.

The same principle should apply to payment and service delivery. Approval of assistance does not necessarily mean that it has actually reached the affected household. A responsive system should, where possible, allow authorised users to determine whether support has been approved, scheduled, delivered, paid, delayed or unsuccessful.

This can help identify failed payments and unresolved cases. Digital and banking-based payments can improve efficiency and transparency, but alternative arrangements remain important for people who lack adequate banking access or face difficulties using digital services.

Grievance management should also be treated as part of the assistance journey. An affected household may be excluded from an assessment, experience a payment problem or believe that its damage has been incorrectly recorded. A grievance mechanism connected to the relevant household case can help authorities follow an issue from submission and review through action and resolution. This can strengthen accountability and provide affected citizens with a clearer pathway for seeking correction or assistance.

The role of local government is particularly important. Local governments are often closest to affected communities and are well placed to understand the actual conditions of households, neighbourhoods and communities following a disaster.

Their role should therefore extend beyond data collection. They can be important partners in identifying affected households, validating information, assessing needs, coordinating services and managing grievances. Effective coordination among federal, provincial and local levels will be essential for translating national policy into practical support.

At the same time, SRSP should not be treated simply as a technology project. Connecting computer systems is only one component of a broader institutional challenge. Government agencies need to agree on information ownership, access rights, data quality, responsibilities, information-sharing arrangements and accountability.

Legal and institutional frameworks must provide clarity about when information can be shared and how it can be used. Technology should support this cooperation rather than create another institutional boundary.

Proposed national SRSP interoperability architecture

The 2026 Bhotekoshi flood could provide a practical opportunity to test this approach. Rather than attempting to connect every government system across Nepal immediately, a geographically focused pilot could examine how the complete household journey can be supported in an actual disaster context.

Such a pilot could explore how available information about households before the disaster can be appropriately connected with information about affected locations, damage, needs, relief, social protection, payments, grievances and recovery.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority is already maintaining disaster information and situation-reporting systems, providing an institutional base from which such an approach could be explored. The recent Bhotekoshi disaster has also generated substantial damage and needs information across affected districts.

The success of such a pilot should not be measured only by how much relief is distributed or how many households receive assistance. It should also examine whether affected households can be identified more quickly, whether their needs can be assessed more effectively, whether different programmes can coordinate better, whether payments reach households on time, whether unresolved needs can be identified and whether families can be followed through the recovery process.

These lessons could provide practical evidence for developing a broader national approach.

Nepal does not need to transform every information system at the same time. A gradual approach may be more practical.

The first step could be to map existing systems related to identity, social protection, disaster management, payments, health, education, agriculture, employment, insurance, housing, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

This could be followed by agreement on common definitions, identifiers and data standards that allow institutions to understand and exchange relevant information consistently. Secure information-sharing mechanisms could then be established and tested through practical pilots before being gradually expanded.

The broader objective is to move from programme-centred intervention towards more coordinated support around the affected household. This does not require replacing existing social protection programmes or creating a single institution responsible for every aspect of disaster response. Instead, it requires enabling existing institutions to work together more effectively when a household experiences a shock.

The Disaster-Sensitive Social Protection and Relief Distribution Standard, 2081 provides an important policy foundation for this direction. The opportunity now is to connect that policy foundation with institutional coordination, responsible information sharing, practical interoperability and household-centred case management.

If these elements are developed together, Nepal can strengthen the link between disaster relief, social protection, recovery and reconstruction.

Ultimately, a responsive system should help government answer a simple set of questions: Who was affected? What was the household’s situation before the disaster? What changed? What does the household need now? What support has it received? What remains unresolved? And how can it be supported through recovery?

The answers do not require every government system to become one system. They require trusted institutions, appropriate information sharing, common standards and a shared commitment to putting affected households at the centre of the response.

Nepal therefore has an opportunity to move beyond a model in which disaster relief and social protection operate largely as separate programmes. By building on the policy direction of the 2081 Standard and connecting existing institutional and information resources in a secure and accountable manner, Nepal can gradually develop a social protection system that is better able to respond when households face major shocks.

The ultimate vision is simple: One Person. One Household. One Location. One Shock Event. One Connected Case.

The purpose is not to build another database. It is to ensure that when a disaster changes a family’s life, government has the ability to understand that change, coordinate the right support and continue following the household until the path to recovery becomes clearer.
