title.rendered: National Defence University: Should it be military-led or academically driven?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

A bill to establish a National Defence University under the Ministry of Defence has been registered in the House of Representatives.

The National Defence University Bill, originally drafted when KP Sharma Oli was prime minister, was registered in Parliament on September 21.

The bill has drawn attention because, unlike most legislation concerning the establishment of universities, it has been introduced by the Ministry of Defence rather than the Ministry of Education.

People familiar with the process say disagreement over whether the proposed university should fall under the Education Ministry or the Defence Ministry delayed the bill’s registration.

“There was no disagreement over the need for a defence university. But while discussions were underway over whether it should be led by the Ministry of Education or the Ministry of Defence, Parliament was dissolved,” said Girirajmani Pokharel, who was education minister when the bill was being drafted.

Under the proposed legislation, the defence minister will serve as co-chancellor of the National Defence University.

The bill also proposes a recommendation committee chaired by the chief of the Nepali Army to recommend candidates for the positions of vice-chancellor and registrar.

The committee would include members nominated by the chancellor from the Academic Council, while the director general of military training of the Nepali Army would serve as its member-secretary.

Prime Minister and Defence Minister Balendra Shah has said the National Defence University is being proposed with the objective of producing skilled and responsible human resources through higher-level study, teaching and research in national security, defence, international relations and strategic affairs.

“Establishing a specialised academic centre within the country to provide higher education and training to military and civilian officials, in order to address geopolitical sensitivities and changing security challenges, is the main reason for establishing and operating this university,” Shah states in the bill.

While there appears to be little disagreement over the need for a defence university, there are differing views over what kind of institution it should be — primarily military in character or primarily academic.

Educationist Dr Bidya Nath Koirala says the first priority should be to clearly define the purpose of the university.

“A university performs three functions — teaching, research and service to society. We need to be clear about what kind of university we are trying to establish,” Koirala said. “The main debate is whether to make the National Defence University academic in nature or military-oriented.”

Although the bill has only recently reached Parliament, the process of establishing a National Defence University dates back several years.

The government issued the National Defence University Infrastructure Development Committee Formation Order in 2019. In accordance with the order, a committee was formed under the leadership of retired Lieutenant General Balananda Sharma.

Former lawmaker and security expert Deepak Prakash Bhatta, who has been involved in efforts to establish the National Defence University from the beginning, says such an institution is essential.

“It should become an institution for professional security and defence officers, as well as civilians who are interested in the field and capable of contributing and conducting research,” Bhatta said. “Senior officers should not have to travel to other countries for education and training.”

During Girirajmani Pokharel’s tenure as education minister, proposals were also put forward to establish Madan Bhandari University, Yogmaya Ayurveda University, Nepal Open University, National Defence University and Tourism University.

The proposals for the latter two institutions, however, failed to move forward after it was proposed that they be placed under the respective ministries of Defence and Tourism.

The Ministry of Education is also regarded as the ministry responsible for human resource development. Proposals concerning the technical aspects of universities are sent to the University Grants Commission for consultation.

Pokharel, the former education minister, argues that allowing individual ministries to establish separate universities is not appropriate as a matter of policy.

“It is not right, in terms of policy, for other ministries to establish separate universities. If every ministry is going to open its own university, then why do we need a Ministry of Education?” he said.

Pokharel maintains that the Cabinet should determine how much human resources are required in different sectors and that the establishment and development of universities should be carried out through the Ministry of Education.

Former Tribhuvan University Vice-Chancellor Kedar Bhakta Mathema, meanwhile, says the government should not rush to establish universities without first considering whether the necessary resources are available.

“It is not that a university should never be established if the resources can be arranged,” Mathema said. “But if a college, academy or institute can provide the degrees we want to teach, then there is no need to establish a university.”

Officials involved in the establishment of the National Defence University say the idea initially emerged around the concept of a National Defence College (NDC).

The Nepali Army has been sending officers abroad for defence-related training.

The bill itself cites Sri Lanka as an example, where a defence academy exists. Sri Lanka enacted the Sir John Kotelawala Defence Academy Act in 1981.

The bill registered in Parliament also cites Pakistan’s National Defence University Act, 2011, as another example.

However, Bhatta, a former lawmaker who holds a doctorate on civil-military relations, says Pakistan should not be used as a model.

“There was no need to cite Pakistan as an example. I do not think it is necessary to convince society by presenting such an example,” he said.

Bhatta has suggested that the proposed university should have more than one co-chair, citing the example of Shaheed Dasharath Chand Health Sciences University, where the education and health ministers serve as co-chairs.

He said the education minister should serve as a co-chair alongside the defence minister, while the health minister’s role could be represented in the university’s council or senate.

Former defence minister Bhimsen Das Pradhan, however, says Nepal needs its own university to produce human resources capable of conducting study and research on national security and strategic affairs.

“There are defence universities in various countries around the world. There should be nothing objectionable about establishing one in our country,” Pradhan said.

Retired Lieutenant General Balananda Sharma, Professor Dr Yubraj Sangroula and Brigadier General Bishnu Raut were involved in drafting the bill.

Sangroula says some provisions of the proposed university differ from those of other universities because of the institution’s specialised nature, including the provision for the defence minister to serve as co-chair.

“This is a university primarily for security professionals rather than fresh students,” Sangroula said. “In particular, it is intended for the education and training of military professionals.”

title.rendered: Balen Shah takes Nepal’s climate justice message to UNGA

content.rendered:
New York, September 25

As evening fell outside the United Nations headquarters on the banks of the East River along 42nd Street, the cold wind grew sharper.

Inside, however, the General Assembly Hall was the scene of heated debate, with heads of government and heads of state from around the world making their cases before the global community.

On Thursday afternoon, as Prime Minister Balen Shah travelled from the Hyatt Hotel at Grand Central to the UN headquarters to deliver his address, Nepalis gathered along the route chanting slogans in his support.

By the time evening set in, the number of participants inside the main chamber of the General Assembly Hall had begun to thin. But the Nepalis waiting in the balcony for Shah were still there.

For those attending in person and those following the prime minister’s address through various platforms, there was one common expectation — that Nepal, having just suffered the devastating impact of a Himalayan climate disaster, would make its voice heard on climate justice before the international community.

Onlinekhabar had reported the previous day that Shah was expected to raise the issue of the suffering faced by people in smaller countries due to climate disasters and wars imposed by powerful nations.

That is precisely what unfolded during Thursday’s special session of the General Assembly.

The applause and occasional cheers heard as Shah spoke suggested that many of those watching felt the prime minister had addressed the concerns they had come to hear.

Around 130 heads of state, heads of government and foreign ministers are scheduled to address the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. Among the heads of government and heads of state participating, Shah is the youngest by age.

He made a point of acknowledging that himself.

“I am the youngest head of government to address this Assembly this year. But I am not here to tell that story,” Shah said.

Shah’s participation in this year’s General Assembly was decided relatively late.

He travelled to New York after the devastating Bhotekoshi flood killed thousands of people and destroyed property worth trillions of rupees, with the aim of drawing greater international attention to Nepal’s situation.

At the UN, Shah spoke about what he presented as two distinct tragedies facing Nepal.

The first was a disaster caused by a climate that Nepal did little to heat. The second was the consequences of wars that Nepal itself did not wage.

He connected the two through a narrative that focused on the unequal burden borne by countries and communities with limited responsibility for the problems affecting them.

“A country that wants to pay [for climate change compensation] should be allowed to pay, and a world that can deliver weapons anywhere within 72 hours cannot leave farmers helpless simply to live a normal life,” Shah said.

He spoke emotionally about the devastation caused by the Bhote Koshi flood.

“I want to speak about those families who are waiting for their loved ones who will never return home, who are searching for their people beneath mud, rocks and water, whose bodies may never be found,” he said at the beginning of his address.

During the opening session of the General Assembly, UN Secretary-General António Guterres had recalled that nearly three years ago, while standing in the Everest region, he had warned that the roof of the world was collapsing, but that his warning had not received sufficient attention.

Shah echoed that message.

“We heard that warning in Nepal. Our communities heard it. Scientists around the world heard it. They kept repeating it with evidence. But we, the political leadership of the world, ignored it,” he said.

At times, Shah’s voice sounded slightly subdued. But his descriptions of the injustices Nepal has faced because of climate change did not lose their force.

While speaking out for Nepal, Shah did not portray another country as a criminal or single out any particular nation for blame.

Instead, he thanked those who had openly supported Nepal in its time of suffering.

Climate justice discussions often involve assigning responsibility to wealthy countries and large corporations. Shah took a different approach, calling instead for countries around the world to build a common campaign against climate change and to take seriously the warnings emerging from the Himalayas.

Nepal, he said, would require resources equivalent to 10 percent of its gross domestic product for physical reconstruction.

He called for the kind of solidarity and support Nepal received during the reconstruction following the 2015 earthquake.

“A poor country like Nepal, despite contributing negligibly to climate change, is being forced to take on significant debt to compensate for the damage,” Shah said.

“We are not here to blame any country or continent. We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battleground. We are here to call on everyone to recommit to their responsibility and solidarity.”

Shah argued that “climate justice” should not remain merely a beautiful phrase in UN documents.

He particularly warned that the commitments made by the international community to mitigate climate change have not been fulfilled.

He also proposed the establishment of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region, with Nepal, China and India taking the lead.

Shah then highlighted Nepal’s progress towards becoming a carbon-neutral country.

He pointed to the expansion of forest cover, hydropower as a source of clean energy and the increasing use of electric vehicles as areas where Nepal has made progress.

During his address, Shah also asked the United Nations to pay particular attention to six words beginning with the letter “R.”

“Relief.” “Rehabilitation.” “Reconstruction.” “Responsibility.” “Reparation.” “Resilience.”

The first three, he argued, are needed immediately after a disaster, while the remaining three are necessary for a lasting solution.

Several world leaders who spoke before Shah also referred to the climate devastation in Nepal.

UN Secretary-General Guterres spoke about it, as did General Assembly President Annalena Baerbock and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, who spoke immediately before Shah.

Earlier, activists gathered outside the UN headquarters had also raised slogans demanding that Nepal receive climate justice immediately.

Not loans, but grants

Shah said large loans or fragmented grants would not be enough to rebuild after climate-related losses and damage.

“We need sufficient grant-based support from the international community,” he said.

He argued, however, that existing mechanisms, including the Loss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other relevant financial mechanisms, remain inadequate and that additional resources must be mobilised.

He also called for the process of accessing climate finance to be simplified.

The poor bear the cost when powerful nations go to war

Shah also turned his attention to the consequences of wars involving powerful nations, arguing that poor people once again bear the costs when the world shifts from peace to conflict.

“When poor farmers in Nepal tried to sow seeds in their fields this monsoon, they could not get fertiliser on time. When we tried to pave highways, we could not get bitumen. When families wanted to cook their evening meal, there was no cooking fuel,” he said.

He questioned the global supply chain in which weapons can cross borders and reach battlefields on time while fertiliser and food face obstacles.

“We have created a world where it is easy to supply the things needed for war but extremely difficult to supply food,” Shah said. “This is not Nepal’s misfortune alone.”

Shah concluded with a call for changes to the existing global order.

“Let us reform the current world order in which the weak are the most powerless,” he said.

Guterres’ affection for Nepal

As UN Secretary-General António Guterres approaches the end of his tenure, he has continued to express strong affection for Nepal.

He displayed the same sentiment during his meeting with Prime Minister Balen Shah on Thursday evening.

Guterres told Shah that the United Nations stood with Nepal on climate issues. He also recalled visiting Nepal as a tourist in 1978 and said he would continue supporting Nepal even after retiring from his position at the United Nations.

title.rendered: Kabir Maharjan discharged after surviving 10 days trapped inside hydropower tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

Kabir Maharjan, the mechanical supervisor who was rescued alive after spending 10 days trapped inside a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3-A Hydropower Project in Rasuwa, has been discharged from hospital.

Maharjan was discharged on Friday after his health improved significantly. He was welcomed at his residence in Lalitpur following his release.

Maharjan had been trapped inside the hydropower project’s tunnel after a devastating flood struck the area on August 26. His rescue became a subject of widespread attention both in Nepal and internationally.

After spending 10 days trapped in the darkness of the tunnel, battling uncertainty and difficult conditions, Maharjan was brought out alive by a joint rescue team comprising personnel from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force.

He was admitted to hospital following the rescue, where doctors closely monitored his condition.

According to hospital sources, Kabir Maharjan gradually recovered after enduring prolonged physical and psychological stress.

When he was discharged on Friday, he appeared fully conscious and in good health.

As Maharjan travelled from Kathmandu towards his residence in Lalitpur after leaving the hospital, local residents in several places welcomed him with flower garlands and wished him a speedy recovery.

Maharjan expressed his gratitude to the rescuers who, he said, gave him a new lease on life, as well as to the health workers involved in his treatment.

title.rendered: Narayangadh-Muglin, Prithvi Highway sections remain blocked by landslides

content.rendered:
Chitwan, September 25

The Narayangadh-Muglin road section and the Chitwan section of the Prithvi Highway remain blocked due to landslides triggered by rainfall.

Both roads were obstructed by landslides from around 8pm on Thursday.

According to Chitwan District Police Office chief SP Rameshwar Poudel, continuous landslides at several locations have prevented the roads from being fully reopened.

Vehicles heading towards Pokhara and those travelling towards Narayangadh that had been stranded on the roads were allowed to pass on Friday afternoon.

However, the roads remain unsafe for regular traffic as landslides carrying rocks and mud continue to fall at several points, Poudel said.

Vehicles arriving since Thursday have been stranded along the affected sections. The local administration has restricted traffic movement considering the risk posed by the continuing landslides.

title.rendered: Deuba group deploys central representatives for 15th general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

The group led by former Nepali Congress president Sher Bahadur Deuba has deployed central representatives across the country as part of preparations for the party’s 15th general convention.

The group has appointed representatives for 76 of the country’s 77 districts, with no representative yet assigned to Rukum West. The representatives will coordinate convention-related activities at the district level.

The Deuba group is preparing to hold its 15th general convention from December 7 to 9, following ward-level conventions scheduled to begin on October 1.

Former general secretary Dr Shashank Koirala, who heads the 15th Central General Convention Preparation Committee, has been coordinating the process. The committee has also appointed district coordinators in several districts.

The Deuba group has been pursuing a separate convention schedule from the Nepali Congress establishment faction. The group has said it decided to move ahead with its own process after disagreements over the convention schedule and the party’s internal arrangements.

title.rendered: Flood-hit students in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading to continue studies in residential schools

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

Students who lost their parents or homes in the Rasuwa floods are being accommodated at schools so they can continue their education.

Residential arrangements have also been introduced for children affected by the floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts.

“Students have started staying in hostels and continuing their studies. Those who remain in Rasuwa have been accommodated at Nilkantha Secondary School,” said Durga Silwal, chief of the Education Development and Coordination Unit in Rasuwa.

Some students from Rasuwa have reached Kathmandu and Batār in Nuwakot. “Students who have reached Kathmandu and those staying in Batār have started attending schools there. Those who are in Rasuwa have also started going to school,” Silwal said.

According to Madhav Lamichhane, principal of Neelkantha Secondary School, 80 students are currently staying in the hostel.

“We have also brought students from across the river. There are no bridges or houses, and students who cannot travel from one side to the other have also been accommodated in the hostel,” Silwal said.

Lamichhane said students staying at the holding centre in Batār have not yet been brought to the school because the roads are inaccessible.

“The aim is to ensure that no child is deprived of education. But we have not been able to bring those staying in Batār because there is no road,” he said.

According to the Education Development and Coordination Unit in Rasuwa, 285 students in the district remain unaccounted for following the floods. Of the 17 teachers reported missing, the body of one has been recovered. Both parents of 39 students are also reported to be missing.

Four schools in Rasuwa have been completely destroyed. Students from those schools are being accommodated in hostels so they can continue their education.

A residential school has also been established in Nuwakot.

“Twenty-nine students have been accommodated at Annapurna Panchakanya School. The school has been converted into a residential facility and classes have begun,” said Surya Bahadur Chhetri, chief of the Education Development and Coordination Unit in Nuwakot.

Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, which was completely damaged, has also resumed classes.

“About 80 percent of students have returned to school,” Chhetri said. “Three schools in Bidur-10 were completely damaged. Their students are attending nearby schools.”

In flood-hit Nuwakot, 224 students and 11 teachers remain unaccounted for. According to Chhetri, 10 schools have been damaged, including two institutional schools.

Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, Ramchandra Basic School, Chetana Basic School, Ganeshman Singh Basic School, Trishuli Boarding School and Uttargaya Boarding School in Nuwakot have been completely destroyed. Chandeshwari Secondary School and Kshetrapal Basic School have sustained partial damage.

A residential school is also operating in Dhading.

“Two schools were completely destroyed. Classes have resumed after alternative locations were arranged,” said Krishna Kumar Shrestha, chief of the Education Development and Coordination Unit in Dhading.

He said students from Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Chitwan have also been arriving in Dhading.

“There are around 37 students at present, and more are arriving. Data collection is ongoing,” he said.

Three teachers remain unaccounted for in Dhading. According to the Education Development and Coordination Unit, the body of one teacher has been recovered. The bodies of four former teachers have also been recovered, while two remain unaccounted for.

Shrestha said authorities are collecting data on the whereabouts of students. Ten schools in Dhading have been damaged. Schools have said classes are being conducted only after providing psychosocial counselling to students.

Some schools that were completely destroyed by the floods have yet to resume operations. Officials at the district education units said arrangements have been made for students from those schools to attend nearby schools.

However, there is still no confirmed data on how many students have moved to which schools. Officials said the process of collecting the data is ongoing.

The government has also directed schools to regularly assess students’ psychosocial condition, as the floods may have caused fear, anxiety, stress and other psychological effects.

More than 9,000 students were affected by the floods, according to a Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment report prepared by a joint technical team from the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

title.rendered: Nepal avenge 2014 Asian Games defeat with five-wicket win over Afghanistan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

Twelve years ago, Afghanistan handed Nepal one of the most painful defeats in the country’s Asian Games cricket history.

In the 2014 Asian Games quarterfinal, Nepal fell eight runs short while chasing Afghanistan’s modest target of 120. The defeat ended Nepal’s hopes of a historic medal and remained a bitter memory for Nepali cricket fans.

Twelve years later, on the same Asian Games stage, Nepal finally changed the story.

Nepal defeated Afghanistan by five wickets in a much-anticipated encounter, not only settling the score from the 2014 defeat but also moving within touching distance of a place in the quarterfinals.

Nepal and Afghanistan had also met earlier in 2014, at the T20 World Cup, where Nepal emerged victorious. But it was Afghanistan’s win at the Asian Games that proved costly for Nepal’s medal campaign.

This time, Nepal made sure history did not repeat itself.

Afghanistan won the toss and elected to bat first, but Nepal’s spin attack quickly took control. Afghanistan managed only 102 runs for seven wickets in their allotted 20 overs.

Faisal Shinwari top-scored with 33 runs, while experienced batter Najibullah Zadran made 30. The rest of the Afghan batting lineup struggled against Nepal’s bowlers.

Kushal Bhurtel produced the best bowling figures of his career, taking four wickets, while Lalit Rajbanshi claimed three. Their combined spell dismantled Afghanistan’s middle order and restricted them to a below-par total.

Nepal chased down the 103-run target in 17.2 overs, losing five wickets.

Sundeep Jora top-scored with 34 runs, while captain Rohit Paudel remained unbeaten on 33. Dipendra Singh Airee contributed 15 runs to steady the innings.

The victory has put Nepal in a strong position to reach the quarterfinals, where they will face either India or Sri Lanka. The opponent will be determined after Nepal’s final group-stage match against Japan on Saturday.

If Nepal defeats Japan, it will finish top of the group and face Sri Lanka in the quarterfinals. Even if Nepal loses to Japan, it is still likely to qualify as runners-up and face India, provided the defeat is not by an unexpectedly large margin.

Bhurtel and Rajbanshi put Afghanistan under pressure

Nepal had been invited to bowl first after losing the toss, while Afghanistan opted to bat after assessing the conditions.

Lalit Rajbanshi immediately put Afghanistan under pressure. Bowling the opening over, he bowled Hasan Eisakhil and then dismissed Mohammad Akram in the third over.

Rajbanshi struck again in the fifth over, bowling experienced batter Karim Janat to leave Afghanistan struggling at 16-3.

Afghanistan then began rebuilding through a partnership, but Kushal Bhurtel broke it.

Introduced in the 11th over, Bhurtel dismissed the well-set Faisal Shinwari. He then struck twice in the 15th over, removing Mohammad Ishaq and Darwish Rasooli off consecutive deliveries.

Bhurtel completed his four-wicket haul in the 17th over by dismissing Najibullah Zadran.

With Nepal’s spinners continuing to trouble the Afghan batters, Afghanistan finished on 102-7 after 20 overs. Although the conditions made the total somewhat competitive, Afghanistan had still been expected to score more.

After the match, Dipendra said Nepal had planned from the outset to rely heavily on its spinners.

“We believed the spinners would do well. Lalit and Kushal bowled exceptionally well. Once we restricted them to a low total, the chase became easier,” he said.

Middle order steadies Nepal after poor start

Nepal also struggled early in the chase.

Kushal Bhurtel was dismissed without scoring on the second ball of the innings, while Asif Sheikh followed in the fourth over after making just two runs.

Batting at No. 3, Sandeep Jora provided stability. He scored 34 off 35 balls and helped Nepal recover from its difficult start.

Nepal, however, continued to lose wickets through run-outs. Kushal Malla was dismissed for nine, while Jora himself was eventually run out while attempting to push for an additional run.

When Jora departed, Nepal was 56-4 after 10 overs.

Captain Dipendra Singh Airee and Rohit Paudel then put together a crucial 46-run partnership to take Nepal close to victory.

Their running between the wickets was particularly effective. They capitalised on fielding mistakes and picked up twos without taking unnecessary risks.

Nepal eventually completed the chase in 17.2 overs to secure a five-wicket victory over Afghanistan, 12 years after their painful Asian Games defeat.

Bhurtel, who contributed little with the bat but played a decisive role with the ball, said he was pleased to make an impact.

“I couldn’t do much with the bat today, but I’m happy that I was able to contribute with the ball. I have enjoyed cricket since I was young, so it is always satisfying to contribute wherever I can,” he said.

Nepal almost certain to reach quarterfinals

Nepal will play Japan in its final group-stage match on Saturday, with the top two teams advancing to the quarterfinals.

Even a defeat against Japan could be enough for Nepal to reach the last eight, but a victory would see Nepal finish as group winners and set up a quarterfinal against Sri Lanka.

Dipendra said the Japan match remains important and that Nepal’s medal ambitions are still alive.

“The team is boosted and we also have the experience. We will give 100 percent from our side to bring home a medal,” he said.

Twelve years ago, Afghanistan ended Nepal’s medal hopes at the Asian Games. This time, Nepal’s victory over the same opponent has strengthened its hopes of writing a different chapter in its Asian Games story.

title.rendered: RSP leader meets UK Conservative Party official in London

content.rendered:
London, September 25

Hikmat Jung Karki, a member of the International Relations and Diplomacy Department of Nepal’s Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), has met Amit Jogia, international relations director of the UK’s Conservative Party, in London.

The meeting focused on strengthening Nepal-UK relations and exploring possibilities for dialogue, cooperation and exchange of experience between the two political parties.

During the meeting, Karki briefed Jogia on the devastating floods that hit Nepal on August 26 and the situation that followed. He provided information about the loss of life and property, rescue and relief efforts, and the long-term impact on affected communities.

Jogia expressed a positive view of Nepal-UK relations and said the Conservative Party was interested in expanding relations, dialogue and cooperation with the RSP in the coming days.

The two sides also discussed the possibility of establishing institutional and formal party-to-party relations.

Karki said he would consult with the RSP’s central leadership after returning to Nepal and take the necessary initiatives on the matter.

The RSP has assigned Karki to its International Relations and Diplomacy Department, where he has been involved in international relations and diplomatic affairs.

title.rendered: Ameet Jogia and Hikmat Jung Karki
Families of missing Ukrainians still awaiting word a month after Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

A month after devastating floods struck the Nepal-China border area, families of more than 50 Ukrainian nationals are still waiting for information about their missing loved ones.

36-year-old Olena Kalinichenko was part of a group of 56 people, most of them Ukrainian, who had travelled to Mount Kailash in Tibet for a spiritual retreat. They went missing after the August 26 flood struck as they were making their way back from China into Nepal.

Kalinichenko was last seen leaving a Chinese border checkpoint roughly 15 minutes before the flood hit. She had bought chrysanthemum tea in China, planning to share it with a friend once she returned home.

Her friend Oles Vysych has been waiting a month for news of her.

“She said we’d drink tea made from the Chinese flowers together once she got home,” he said.

According to the Nepal government, more than 1,400 people have died in the floods, with over 6,000 still missing, most of them on the Nepali side of the border. Nepal says 636 foreign nationals remain missing, including 54 Ukrainians. China has reported 261 foreign nationals missing on its side, including one Ukrainian.

Nepal says it has recovered 1,451 bodies so far, but only 112 have been returned to families. The government says it has collected DNA samples from 2,035 relatives, though it has not disclosed how many bodies have been identified.

Because immigration offices and records on the Nepali side were destroyed in the floods, it has become difficult to confirm whether some individuals who left China ever entered Nepal. Chinese officials have told some families that their relatives had already left Chinese territory before the flood struck.

The group, led by spiritual teacher Irina Blonskaya, had planned to travel by bus from Tibet to Kathmandu before flying home to their respective countries. A massive surge of ice, rock, mud, and water from the mountains caused extensive damage at the Kerung border crossing used by pilgrims heading to Kailash.

Families of the missing have complained that the search and identification process has been very slow. Vladyslava Horlova, based in Norway, has been contacting the Ukrainian embassy, Norwegian police, and the Red Cross in search of her mother, and has even provided a DNA sample to police.

Even though a month has passed since the disaster, some families still hold out hope of finding their relatives alive. Vysych, Kalinichenko’s friend, says he too is trying to stay positive.

title.rendered: New Zealand Government, Nepali leaders discuss flood reconstruction and bilateral cooperation

content.rendered:
Wellington, September 25

Senior officials from New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade met with representatives of the Nepali community in Wellington to discuss relief, reconstruction, and bilateral cooperation following the devastating flood in Bhotekoshi.

At Friday’s meeting, New Zealand officials spoke of the special bilateral relationship between Nepal and New Zealand, noting that the assistance New Zealand provided immediately after the disaster reflected that friendship. Ministry officials said recent talks at the prime ministerial and foreign ministerial level between the two countries had further strengthened this warm relationship.

The meeting explored possible areas of cooperation between the two countries during the reconstruction phase. Discussions touched on how New Zealand’s world-class knowledge and expertise in disaster management could benefit Nepal, with such support to be tailored to Nepal’s specific needs.

The two sides also discussed opportunities for cooperation in key sectors such as education, engineering, and trade. Ministry officials praised the important role the Nepali community has played in strengthening people-to-people ties between the two countries. Nepali representatives, in turn, expressed their commitment to deepening bilateral relations for the shared benefit of both countries and their peoples.

Earlier, New Zealand’s Foreign Minister Winston Peters and Climate Change Minister Simon Watts had expressed solidarity over the flood disaster and sent a personally signed letter to the Nepali delegation.

The Nepali delegation at the meeting included Prof. Dr Rajesh Dhakal of the University of Canterbury, Christchurch; Dr Achyut Aryal, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) New Zealand; and Raj Maharjan and Mandira Rimal, president and vice-president respectively of the New Zealand Nepal Chamber of Commerce.

Chamber president Maharjan said the meeting at this level between the Nepali community and the New Zealand government would prove fruitful in promoting trade and business interests between the two countries.

title.rendered: 9 families from Patrakhalla moved to safer places after flooding in Jogbuda

content.rendered:
Kanchanpur, September 25

After the Weather Forecasting Division predicted heavy rainfall in various parts of the country from September 25 to 27, Kanchanpur has also stepped up precautions in light of the potential risk.

Rain is currently falling in parts of the hill districts across Sudurpashchim, including Kanchanpur. Tek Rawat, information officer at the Kanchanpur District Police Office, said the water flow in the Mahakali River currently stands at only 34,000 cusecs.

According to Rawat, 9 families from Patrakhalla in Dodhara Chandani Municipality-3 have been moved to safer locations due to the risk of rising water in the Jogbuda River entering the settlement.

They have been relocated to the nearby ward office and Jamunaghadi School. With the help of the Armed Police Force and residents, family members, along with essential food supplies and livestock, are being moved to safety as a precaution.

Patrakhalla is a settlement at risk from the Jogbuda River, which has flooded the area in the past when water levels rose. Since further rain is forecast in the coming days, residents living along riverbanks and in low-lying areas have been urged to remain alert.

title.rendered: Rain system shifts west, 38 districts face high flood risk

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

A low-pressure system that developed over the Bay of Bengal continues to bring rain to most districts of Nepal. The persistent rainfall has raised water levels in rivers and streams, while landslides have blocked highways at several locations.

According to meteorologists, the system is gradually shifting from the eastern part of Nepal toward the west, and rainfall is forecast to increase in western areas as a result.

“Rainfall in the eastern region is expected to ease somewhat tomorrow, Saturday,” said meteorologist Rojan Lamichhane. “Rain is likely to intensify in western areas starting tonight.”

Districts in Lumbini and Gandaki have already been experiencing rain since Wednesday. Meteorologists forecast that rainfall will now extend further, reaching as far as Sudurpashchim.

A risk map issued by the Weather Forecasting Division of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology marks districts from Bagmati Province eastward in yellow, while districts in the higher hill and mountain regions from Gandaki westward are marked in red.

Yellow indicates that people should stay alert and keep track of weather updates, while red indicates a risk of floods and landslides requiring precautionary action.

High flood risk in 38 districts

Due to the continuous rainfall, the Flood Forecasting Division under the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has also forecast rising water levels in small rivers and streams across various districts over the next two days, along with the possibility of flash floods.

The Flood Forecasting Division reported a high flood risk today in Gorkha, Lamjung, Kaski, Manang, Mustang, Dang, Banke, Bardiya, Surkhet, Dailekh, Kailali, and Kanchanpur.

The area at high flood risk will expand further tomorrow, September 25.

According to the division, high flood risk is forecast for Nawalparasi East, Nawalparasi West, Rupandehi, Kapilvastu, Arghakhanchi, Palpa, Gulmi, Syangja, Tanahun, Gorkha, Lamjung, Kaski, Manang, Parbat, Baglung, Pyuthan, Rolpa, Salyan, Dang, Banke, Bardiya, Surkhet, Doti, Dadeldhura, Kailali, and Kanchanpur.

The division also said flash flooding could occur in small rivers flowing through all seven provinces starting Sunday.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has additionally urged people in low-lying and flood-prone areas along the Saptakoshi River to remain on high alert through the day after tomorrow, as water levels there continue to rise.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

Nepal has climbed two places to 14th in the ICC’s T20 International rankings.

According to the updated rankings released by the ICC on Friday, Nepal moved up two spots to reach 14th position.

The improvement came after Nepal beat Afghanistan by 5 wickets on Friday in the ongoing Asian Games competition in Nagoya, Japan.

Nepal restricted Afghanistan to 102 runs for the loss of 7 wickets in 20 overs, then chased down the 103-run target in 17.2 overs.

Kushal Bhurtel took 4 wickets and Lalit Rajbanshi took 3, while Sandeep Jora scored 34 and Rohit Paudel finished unbeaten on 33.

title.rendered: 31 gates opened at Koshi Barrage as water flow rises

content.rendered:
Sunsari, September 25

Thirty-one gates at the Koshi Barrage have been opened as water flow in the river continues to rise.

Chief District Officer Ishwori Prasad Aryal said the barrage is currently under a “red alert” status. According to him, the flood discharge at the Koshi Barrage has reached 240,000 cusecs.

The flow, however, remains below levels recorded in previous years, when the Koshi River saw floods exceeding 500,000 cusecs.

“The Koshi Barrage is currently under a red alert. However, flood levels of up to 500,000 cusecs have been recorded in previous years,” Aryal said. “There is no need to panic at this point, but we are on alert.”

Vehicle movement across the Koshi Bridge has not been halted.

“There is no situation requiring us to stop vehicles at present. If the flood level rises further, we will take a decision as necessary,” Aryal said.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has urged residents in downstream and flood-prone areas to remain highly alert until the day after tomorrow, as the water level in the Saptakoshi continues to rise.

title.rendered: Janakpur residents protest Guthi land eviction drive

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, September 25

A protest has been held in Janakpurdham against the campaign to clear land encroached upon Guthi trust property. The Guthikutti Ghar-Jagga Management Struggle Committee staged demonstrations in various parts of Janakpurdham.

The committee submitted memoranda to the Guthi Sansthan (Guthi Corporation), Janakpurdham Sub-Metropolitan City, and the District Administration Office.

Committee chairperson Santosh Sah said they had submitted memoranda to the government multiple times in the past, but since the government had not addressed their demands, they had taken to protest.

He said 30,000 to 35,000 people have built homes and lived for generations on Guthi and “kutti” land in Janakpurdham. He argued that the government, without preparing accurate data of its own, has labelled them encroachers and moved to demolish their homes, which is why they have taken up the protest.

He said their demand is for the government to properly assess the land occupied by these residents, provide compensation, and convert it into regular registered (raithane numbari) land in their names.

Chairperson Sah warned that if the government fails to address their demands and proceeds with efforts to clear the “encroached” land, they will launch a larger movement.

title.rendered: Hunting season begins in Dhorpatan; permits issued for 10 blue sheep and 7 Himalayan tahr

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

The first hunting season of the year has begun in the Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve. This season, running from September to December, permits have been issued for the hunting of 10 blue sheep (naur) and 7 Himalayan tahr (jharal).

Chief Conservation Officer Ananath Baral said arrangements are underway with the company awarded the contract by the Department of Wildlife Conservation to bring in licensed foreign hunters. Wealthy hunting enthusiasts from around the world regularly travel to Dhorpatan for hunting.

Over the past few decades, hunters from countries including Russia, the United States, Spain, Denmark, various African nations, and France have come to Nepal to hunt. The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, under the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment, had invited competitive bids from companies last Bhadra to organise the hunts.

Last year, 21 blue sheep and 11 Himalayan tahr were hunted in the reserve across two seasons, generating revenue of Rs 41.7 million. Revenue collection for this year’s first season is currently underway.

Chief Conservation Officer Baral noted that a single blue sheep fetched Rs 2 million last year, and said a count of the blue sheep and tahr population within the reserve will be conducted this year.

Foreign hunters typically travel directly into the reserve area by helicopter. The reserve has designated seven hunting blocks: Surtibang, Phagune, Barse, Seng, Dogadi, Ghustung, and Sundaha.

During hunts, reserve staff are deployed alongside Nepali support personnel to accompany the foreign hunters. The department sets an annual quota for blue sheep and tahr hunting each year, and foreign hunting groups must complete their hunt within the designated block within 15 days.

According to the department, the second season, running from February to May, will also be open for permitted hunting. Established in 1987 (2044 BS), the reserve spans Eastern Rukum, Baglung, and Myagdi districts, with its office located in the Dhorpatan valley in Baglung.

The reserve office reported that around 37,000 domestic and international visitors came to the Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve for sightseeing last year.

title.rendered: Nepal defeats Afghanistan in Asian Games cricket

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

In the men’s cricket competition at the 20th Asian Games underway in Japan, Nepal has defeated Afghanistan.

Nepal beat Afghanistan by 5 wickets in the match played at Korogi Sports Park in Nishin, Aichi, Japan.

Nepal chased down Afghanistan’s target of 103 runs, reaching it in 17.2 overs for the loss of 5 wickets.

Sundeep Jora top-scored for Nepal with 34 runs, while Rohit Paudel finished unbeaten on 33 and Dipendra Singh Airee added 15.

title.rendered: Roshi River crosses danger level as flood risk rises across Nepal

content.rendered:
Kavre, September 25

The water level in the Roshi River has crossed the danger level, with the river rising to 4.51 metres against the danger threshold of 4.5 metres.

The water level was stable at the time of reporting. However, the Flood Forecasting Division sounded a warning siren after the river crossed the danger level.

Flooding has also been reported in the Trishuli River in Nuwakot and the Hanumante River in Bhaktapur. According to the Flood Forecasting Division, water levels in both rivers have reached the warning threshold.

The division has forecast rising water levels in several major rivers and river basins across the country over the next five days, with some rivers likely to cross their alert levels.

Hydrologist engineer Saraswati Bista of the division urged people to remain highly alert, particularly over the next 24 to 48 hours, as sudden rises in water levels are possible in small rivers and streams in several districts.

According to Bista, measurements taken on Friday morning showed water levels in the Koshi, Narayani, Kankai and Kamala rivers and their tributaries at or above alert levels. Water levels in the West Rapti, Babai, Karnali and Mahakali rivers remained below their alert thresholds.

Rising water levels expected in Koshi basin

In the Koshi basin, water levels are expected to rise on Friday in the Saptakoshi at Chatara, Tamor at Majhitar and Triveni, Arun at Turkighat and Simle, as well as the Sunkoshi, Tamakoshi, Likhu and other tributaries.

Some locations could cross their alert levels, according to the Flood Forecasting Division.

The risk level in these areas is expected to remain moderate on Friday, while river flows are forecast to fluctuate normally from Saturday.

Special caution advised in Narayani and Kaligandaki

In the Narayani basin, water levels in the Narayani at Devghat, Trishuli at Betrawati, Budhigandaki at Arughat, Marsyangdi and Seti at Damauli are expected to reach around alert levels on Friday and Saturday.

The Narayani at Devghat is expected to remain at moderate risk through Sunday.

The risk will be high on Friday and Saturday in the Badigad at Rudrabeni and Kaligandaki at Kumalgaun. Although the risk is expected to fall to moderate on Sunday, people living along riverbanks and those travelling through these areas have been urged to exercise particular caution on Friday and Saturday.

High risk forecast for Karnali on September 27 and 28

The Karnali at Chisapani is expected to remain at normal risk on Friday, with moderate risk forecast for Saturday. The river flow could rise significantly on September 27 and 28, bringing a high risk of flooding.

The Karnali at Asarghat is expected to remain at moderate risk from Friday through Sunday, with rising river flows forecast.

The Thulibheri at Rimna is expected to pose moderate risk on Friday, while significantly higher flows are forecast for Saturday and Sunday, requiring heightened vigilance.

In the western region, the Seti at Dipayal could reach around its alert level from Friday through Sunday, with moderate risk expected.

The Mahakali at Parigaun is forecast to see a significant rise in flow on Friday, followed by moderate risk on Saturday and Sunday.

Kankai, Kamala and Bagmati also expected to rise

The Kankai at Mainachuli is forecast to face high risk on Friday. Although river flow is expected to rise significantly on Friday, it is forecast to gradually return to normal from Saturday.

The Kamala at Belsot is expected to face moderate risk on Friday, with a significant rise in flow possible. From Saturday, the flow is expected to fluctuate normally.

The Bagmati at Padhera Dobhan is forecast to face moderate risk on Friday and Saturday, with rising water levels possible.

At Khokana, the Bagmati is already above its alert level and is considered at high risk on Friday. River flow is expected to fluctuate normally from Saturday.

The East Rapti at Rajaiya is forecast to face moderate risk on Friday and Saturday.

Moderate risk and rising flows are also forecast on Friday in the Tinau at Dobhan, Butwal, Banganga, Bardaghat, West Rapti at Kusum and Babai at Chepang.

The division has advised heightened caution on the 11th and 12th, after which river flows are expected to gradually return to normal.

Sudden flooding possible in small rivers and streams

The division said many small rivers and streams across the country could experience sudden rises in water levels over the next 24 hours.

While most areas are expected to face moderate risk, some districts are at high risk of sudden flooding.

From Friday morning through Saturday morning, there is a high risk of sudden rises in small rivers and streams in districts including Mustang, Manang, Kaski, Lamjung, Gorkha, Dang, Banke, Bardiya, Surkhet, Dailekh, Kailali and Kanchanpur, according to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

Surkhet, September 25

With heavy rain continuing, long-distance vehicles operating in Karnali Province have been completely suspended. The ban was imposed to protect passengers and vehicles from potential accidents, given the high risk of floods, landslides, and road blockages.

According to the Karnali Province Police Office, long-distance vehicles operating toward Surkhet, Nepalgunj, Jumla, Humla, Kalikot, Jajarkot, Dolpa, Salyan, and Rukum have been suspended.

Karnali Province Police spokesperson Santosh Singh Rathore said short-distance local vehicles are still operating depending on road conditions.

Landslides, road subsidence, and rising water levels in rivers and streams have been reported at various points along the Bheri Corridor, Karnali Highway, Rapti Highway, and Mid-Hill Highway in particular. Rain has been falling steadily across Karnali since early Friday morning.

Transport has been suspended because of the risk that long-distance vehicles could get stranded mid-route if the roads are blocked. Since hill districts typically lack immediate alternative routes once a road is blocked, even a minor obstruction can turn into a transport problem lasting hours or even days — which is why the suspension was ordered.

title.rendered: Kulekhani dam will not be opened, local official says

content.rendered:
Makwanpur, September 25

A local government official has said reports claiming that the Kulekhani hydropower project’s reservoir dam is being prepared for opening are false.

Bhimfedhi Rural Municipality Chairperson Hidam Lama said the water level at the Kulekhani reservoir has not risen to a point where the dam needs to be opened.

He also urged the public not to create confusion by sharing old photos and videos from two years ago on social media.

According to Lama, citing information provided by the chief of Kulekhani First Hydropower Project, the water level stood at 1,522.38 metres on Wednesday. It had fallen to 1,522.18 metres by Friday.

The Kulekhani dam was previously opened on October 12, 2024, when the release of water caused significant loss of life and property.

The Kulekhani reservoir has a maximum capacity of 1,530 metres. If the dam gates are opened, the resulting flow could affect riverbank areas in Bhimfedhi, Indrasarovar and Bagmati rural municipalities in Makwanpur, as well as parts of Sindhuli, Sarlahi and Rautahat.

“Please do not be alarmed by misleading reports,” Lama said. “If the water level at the Kulekhani dam rises to a point where it needs to be opened, residents in downstream areas should remain alert based on the notice issued by the Nepal Electricity Authority. But there is no such risk at present.”

The Kulekhani First Hydropower Centre of the Nepal Electricity Authority said it has a system to issue warnings through sirens if a rise in the reservoir’s water level creates a safety risk.

According to the authority, one siren means the first warning, two sirens mean the second warning, and three or continuous sirens indicate an emergency.

In such a situation, residents in downstream areas have been advised to move to safer locations.

title.rendered: Nepal’s resilience highlighted at St. Xavier’s College International Conference

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

Nepal has built a bold and deep faith in resilience despite a series of disasters, including the Himalayan Tsunami-2026 and the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, said Professor Fr. Xavier Savarimuthu SJ, keynote speaker at the International Conference organised by St. Xavier’s College (ICSXC-2026), which began today.

“Nepal taught the rest of the world that resilience is the order of the day,” Prof. Savarimuthu told around 300 delegates from across the world. He praised the country for remaining “happy” despite repeated natural calamities, noting that Nepal ranks above India on the global happiness index.

Prof. Savarimuthu, an environmental expert and climate justice advocate who has spoken at forums in Stockholm, the Philippines, the University of Oxford, and UN climate summits in Paris and Bonn, also warned that a Super El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon, could pose a threat to countries including Nepal. Describing Nepal as a country of “excessive beauty and risk,” he urged the country to join hands with others in demanding climate justice.

Calling young people the “rays of hope,” he stressed the need for Nepal to focus research on seismic and mountain engineering, food security, and silent toxicology.

The conference’s second keynote speaker, Rev. Fr. Dr Thomas V. Thennadiyil, SJ, said university education should also focus on building learners’ character rather than concentrating solely on knowledge and skills.

Fr. Dr Augustine Thomas, SJ, Chief Patron of ICSXC-2026, said new knowledge is needed to better understand today’s youth.

“The future cannot be reimagined without listening to the young people who will inherit it,” he said, adding that the widening technological gap has created an even greater gap in understanding and ways of thinking. He said academia has a responsibility not only to generate new knowledge but also to develop the wisdom to understand, accompany, and engage the younger generation, calling ICSXC-2026 “an invitation to bridge that gap through dialogue, interdisciplinary reflection, and shared learning.”

The third edition of ICSXC-2026, themed “Reimagining the Global Future with Youth at the Crossroads of Change,” is examining the transformative role of early-career scholars in shaping the digital era. More than 300 research students, scholars, and academicians from the Philippines, Japan, India, Spain, Slovakia, the UK, Nepal, and other countries are attending.

Held once every two years, the conference is co-hosted by Ritsumeikan University, Japan; Universitat Politècnica de València, Spain; Web Consortium Asia Pacific, Spain; and Women’s Christian College, India. The event opened with dance performances from five countries and runs from September 24-25, featuring 75 scientific paper presentations across multiple plenary and parallel sessions.

title.rendered: High alert at hydroelectric projects in the Gandaki basin after heavy rain forecast

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

Following a forecast of heavy rainfall from September 25 to 27, hydroelectric projects in the Gandaki basin have been placed on high alert.

After the Weather Forecasting Division projected that the Gandaki region would be heavily affected by the rains, the Department of Electricity Development under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said all hydropower plants in the basin have been put on high alert. Director General Sagar Raj Gautam said heightened precautions are in place at both Nepal Electricity Authority projects and those run by the private sector.

He said the Authority has directed all its projects to monitor weather updates continuously and take safety measures accordingly, while the Independent Power Producers’ Association (IPPAN) is coordinating on behalf of the private sector.

At a Nepal Electricity Authority board meeting held Thursday evening, Minister of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Birat Bhakta Shrestha, citing lessons from the Bhotekoshi flood, directed that weather updates be tracked continuously and that safety precautions be taken at hydropower plants and power infrastructure in the Gandaki region and other vulnerable areas.

Authority Executive Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha said all projects in the Gandaki basin have been placed under round-the-clock high alert. He said the Authority is coordinating continuously, and that IPPAN has deployed a representative to coordinate from the private-sector side.

Energy Ministry spokesperson Mohan Kumar Shakya said that after the Bhotekoshi flood damaged power infrastructure, hydropower projects, and substations, knocking out 10 percent of the power system, the government is now paying special attention to preparedness and early warning for any disasters that may follow.

Naresh Raj Subedi, spokesperson for the Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office, Ramshahpath, said monitoring had been increased in areas along the rivers.

“As water levels in Kathmandu’s streams and rivers have risen, we have also increased monitoring of riverside areas. Announcements are being made asking people not to travel along the corridors,” Subedi said.

He said traffic police have also asked people to remove vehicles parked along roads near rivers and streams. Police personnel have been deployed at Chyasal Bridge and other vulnerable locations, he added.

According to meteorologists at the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, rainfall in Nepal is being caused by a low-pressure system that developed over the Bay of Bengal.

However, for transporting essential food and fuel supplies to Kathmandu, only the Tribhuvan Highway remains open — and only in one direction.

title.rendered: Government moves to restore provisions of 85 laws repealed through ordinance

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 25

The government has introduced a bill seeking to restore the original provisions of 85 laws that were repealed through an ordinance issued to facilitate the removal of public office-holders.

The Bill to Restore Provisions of Some Nepal Acts was registered in the House of Representatives on September 21. Its stated objective is to restore the legal provisions that were in force before the ordinance was issued, after the ordinance became inactive.

The move follows the lapse of the Special Provisions Regarding the Removal of Public Office-Holders Ordinance, 2026, which amended provisions in 110 existing laws and resulted in the removal of 1,534 public office-holders. Parliament’s records show that the ordinance subsequently became inactive under Article 114(2)(g) of the Constitution.

No new appointments have yet been made to all of the positions left vacant following the removals. The government has now sought to restore the original provisions of 85 of the 110 laws affected by the ordinance.

The proposed bill contains only two sections. The first specifies its name and provides that it will come into force immediately after being enacted into law.

The second section states that the provisions that existed before the ordinance will be deemed to have been restored. It lists the 85 laws whose provisions are to be revived.

The bill also contains a one-line explanatory note, stating that the provisions amended or repealed by the Special Provisions Regarding the Removal of Public Office-Holders Ordinance, 2026 are being restored to their previous form.

Its preamble similarly states that Parliament is enacting the law because it is considered desirable to restore the provisions that were amended or repealed by the ordinance.

The wording of the preamble has drawn attention because it explicitly says that restoring the previous legal arrangements is desirable.

Questions over use of ordinance power

Constitutional expert Bipin Adhikari has described the bill as an example of what he considers an excessive use of the executive’s ordinance-making authority.

He questioned the need to amend 110 laws through a single ordinance.

“There was nothing that would have immediately happened if such an ordinance had not been issued,” Adhikari said. “Issuing an ordinance to amend so many laws through a single instrument was intentional. It was something that should not have been done, but it was done.”

Adhikari argued that using an ordinance to achieve a political objective and subsequently introducing legislation to restore the previous legal provisions represents, in his view, an extreme misuse of executive authority.

“The declared powers under which the ordinance was issued can be exercised,” he said. “But the objective of this ordinance was political. Therefore, it was a misuse.”

Article 114 of the Constitution allows the President to issue an ordinance on the recommendation of the Council of Ministers when immediate action is necessary while Parliament is not in session. An ordinance has the same force as an Act but must be presented to both houses of the federal parliament.

If both houses do not accept it, the ordinance automatically ceases to operate. Under the constitutional process, a replacement bill must be enacted within the stipulated period for the changes introduced by the ordinance to continue.

The Shah government issued eight ordinances between April 30 and May 5. All eight were subsequently presented in Parliament.

Four of them were successfully replaced by legislation, covering cooperatives, public procurement, anti-money laundering and certain laws relating to health science academies. The other ordinances, including the one concerning the removal of public office-holders, did not complete the replacement process.

The public office-holders removal ordinance was specifically designed to remove politically appointed officials from public institutions. Contemporary reporting said it was part of a broader government effort to remove officials appointed or nominated by previous governments.

What happens when an ordinance expires?

Adhikari said the constitutional purpose of an ordinance is to address situations in which immediate legal action is necessary and waiting for Parliament could leave a legal gap.

“The intention of the Constitution is to ensure the law through an ordinance when an emergency situation cannot be addressed because of the absence of law, or when the existing law cannot function,” he said. “That intention is not visible here.”

He said the sequence of events suggested that the ordinance was primarily used to remove public office-holders and that the government’s decision to restore the previous provisions after the ordinance expired strengthens that interpretation.

“Bringing an ordinance, doing what you want and then bringing a bill to return to the previous arrangement does not correspond with the spirit of the Constitution,” he said.

The Supreme Court has previously examined questions surrounding the use of ordinances. In a 2021 case concerning a citizenship ordinance, the Constitutional Bench said ordinances should not be used as an instrument for achieving political objectives and warned that bypassing Parliament for political purposes could improperly interfere with the legislature’s authority.

In another ruling in November 2025 concerning changes made through an ordinance to the Political Parties Act, the Supreme Court held that an ordinance cannot permanently displace, amend or repeal provisions of a permanent law enacted through the legislative process.

The court’s ruling stated that a temporary power with a limited lifespan cannot permanently replace a law passed after broader parliamentary deliberation.

No direct challenge to removal ordinance

According to Supreme Court spokesperson Arjun Prasad Koirala, no petition has been filed directly challenging the Special Provisions Regarding the Removal of Public Office-Holders Ordinance, 2026.

“There are around three [petitions] concerning individuals,” Koirala told Onlinekhabar.

Constitutionally, an ordinance has the force of law while it remains in effect. Therefore, officials removed under the ordinance are considered to have been legally removed under the provisions that were then in force.

However, Adhikari said the ordinance’s constitutional validity and purpose could still become subjects of judicial scrutiny.

“The question of its justification arises once the ordinance fails to be replaced by an Act within 60 days,” he said. “And after the government itself brings a bill to restore the provisions repealed by that same ordinance, those questioning it or arguing before the court have additional grounds.”

He said the court could potentially invalidate the ordinance or interpret the circumstances surrounding its use when considering related disputes.

Nepal’s long history of ordinance use

Nepal has had constitutional provisions allowing the executive to issue ordinances for decades. The power was first provided for under the Government of Nepal Act, 2004, although that constitutional arrangement was never implemented.

The Interim Government of Nepal Act, 2007 provided greater clarity on ordinances, while their use became more established after the Constitution of the Kingdom of Nepal, 2015 came into force.

According to a study conducted by the Federal Parliament Secretariat, five ordinances were issued in 1959 and two in 1960. Three of the five issued in 1959 were related to taxation.

After the Constitution of Nepal, 1962, 64 ordinances were issued.

Under the Constitution of the Kingdom of Nepal, 1990, 182 ordinances were issued between 1990 and 2006. The number rose sharply in the final years of that period, with 27 ordinances issued in 2003, 33 in 2004 and 79 in 2005.

After the Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2006 came into effect, 39 ordinances were issued up to 2015.

Following the promulgation of the current Constitution in 2015, three ordinances were issued in 2017, five in 2018, 11 in 2020, 28 in 2021, nine in 2022, two in 2023 and seven in 2024.

The use of ordinances continued in 2025, including during the political transition following the Gen Z movement.

The interim government led by Sushila Karki issued ordinances concerning the Nepal Special Service Act, elections to the House of Representatives and the voter list. It also sent a Constitutional Council-related ordinance to the president, who did not issue it.

The Balendra Shah government has continued the practice in 2026, issuing eight ordinances. Four have since been converted into Acts, while the remaining measures have been dealt with through other legislative processes.

The latest bill to restore the previous provisions of 85 laws therefore represents another stage in the legal aftermath of the government’s use of ordinances earlier this year.

title.rendered: Gabion wall collapses at Krishnabhir, putting new track at risk

content.rendered:
Dhading, September 25

A gabion wall built to protect the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir has collapsed following continuous rainfall, putting a newly constructed road track at risk.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Prakash Dahal of the District Police Office, Dhading, said the gabion wall supporting the old section of the highway gave way due to the persistent rain.

Part of the wall along the old road has slipped downhill, raising concerns about the safety of the new track constructed at Krishnabhir.

“The gabion wall along the old road, just below the newly opened track, has collapsed. This could affect the new track,” Dahal said.

The Department of Roads has also confirmed that the gabion wall on the river side of the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir has shifted downhill.

According to the department, there is currently no visible problem with the slope above the road currently in operation.

The department said the project team is monitoring the condition of the road.

Kumar Basnet, ward chair of Benighat Rorang Rural Municipality-7, said the gabion support built to stabilise the new track had collapsed because of the continuous rainfall.

“The support section of the gabion built for the new track has collapsed. It is extremely dangerous. Since the lower section has already given way, the risk is very high. I request people not to travel along this road,” Basnet said.

Floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26 and 30 damaged the highway section at Krishnabhir, leaving the road closed for an extended period.

After the floods cut away part of the highway, a new track was constructed at the damaged section, allowing traffic to resume on September 17.

title.rendered: Australian PM Albanese pledges support to Nepal after devastating floods

content.rendered:
New York, September 25

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has expressed deep sorrow over the devastation caused by the recent floods in Nepal and pledged continued Australian support for rescue and reconstruction efforts.

Albanese made the commitment during a meeting with Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen, in New York on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

Sharing details of the meeting on social media, Albanese said Australia stands with the Nepali people during the disaster.

“Today at the UN, I met with Prime Minister Balen Shah and expressed Australia’s deepest condolences to those affected, and provided an update on Australia’s assistance efforts to date,” Albanese said.

Albanese also referred to the fact that several Australian citizens remain missing following the floods, saying his thoughts are with their families and loved ones.

He pledged that Australia would continue working closely with Nepal to provide assistance wherever it is most urgently needed.

Prime Minister Shah, who is in New York to attend the UN General Assembly, has begun holding meetings with heads of state and government from various countries on the sidelines of the gathering.
