title.rendered: Oli wants Parliament restored. But does the UML really want to go back?

content.rendered:
CPN-UML Chairman KP Sharma Oli has called for the restoration of Parliament.

And not casually. He has put the demand in writing in a document presented to the party’s Central Committee meeting. For a moment, it was hard to believe what we were hearing. Even after seeing the demand clearly stated on page 78 of the document, our eyes were reluctant to believe it.

How could they?

Oli is the very leader who, when he was prime minister, dissolved Parliament twice in what the Supreme Court later ruled were unconstitutional moves — in December 2020 and May 2021. Those who demanded the restoration of Parliament were denounced by Oli and his supporters.

Yet now the same Oli has accepted the Parliament that collapsed under the force of the Gen Z movement and has also accepted the results of the election held under a new political consensus.

A new government has been formed under Balen Shah.

Knowing, understanding and seeing all of this, why has Oli started talking about restoring Parliament again?

To understand Oli’s latest argument, perhaps it is no longer enough to look at political science. We have to enter the domain of psychology.

Oli himself knows that he is making a demand that is impossible in his lifetime. The new Parliament has already been functioning for more than six months. Is there really a UML member today who would dare take to the streets demanding its restoration?

Consider the Parliament that once had the Rastriya Swatantra Party with just 21 seats. Today, the RSP has not merely won close to a two-thirds majority; it has also secured almost half of all votes cast on its own.

In such circumstances, what would the narrative of restoring the old Parliament even mean? The Parliament itself would hardly survive the contradiction, let alone the streets.

Perhaps the argument will be made that restoring the old Parliament would make Oli prime minister again. But how much of that argument would even be acceptable to UML members themselves?

At the Onlinekhabar newsroom, we had discussed what the length, breadth, height or depth of Oli’s argument might be. At the time, we decided that perhaps it did not deserve much attention. So we remained silent.

But after listening to Central Committee members such as Gokarna Bista, Raghuji Pant, Hikmat Karki, Yamlal Kandel, Binda Pandey, Rachana Khadka, Sarita Bhusal, Keshav Pandey, Gokul Baskota, Jhapata Rawal and Hemraj Rai, and then looking at Oli’s responses to them, it became clear that he appears to be seriously trying to revive the demand for Parliament’s restoration.

The reason is simple. The demand to restore the House of Representatives has been placed right at the top of the party’s two main tasks.

Speaking at the Central Committee meeting against this backdrop, Rachana Khadka remarked that the trust of ordinary people in the party had already been eroding since the dissolution of the House of Representatives on December 20, 2020, and that the demand for restoration now being pushed by Chairman Oli would only accelerate that downward journey.

But is Oli prepared to grasp the seriousness of what Rachana and other leaders are saying?

Because Oli now appears to be moving towards a line in which the dissolution of Parliament was good when he did it and bad when somebody else did it.

The Gen Z revolt swept away not only Parliament but many other things as well. The leadership of the UML and other political parties needs to understand that.

We too had wondered at the time what constitutional alternatives existed after the dissolution of the House of Representatives. That is why, when Parliament was dissolved on September 9, 2025, we published a special editorial proposing, among other options, the creation of a powerful civilian government followed by direct elections.

There could have been a constitutional route under which Parliament would have continued to exist until elections were held, while remaining politically inactive. There would have been no need to keep fighting over the remaining disputes.

But this is politics. It does not always follow the full grammar of constitutional theory.

A flood is not supposed to wash away a settlement. But sometimes it does. The Gen Z revolt was such a flood.

It swept away some of the deeply entrenched but mistaken assumptions in Nepali politics. There is still debate over who did what by entering the questions raised by young people.

But now that political parties — and the UML itself — are reviving the debate over restoring Parliament, what exactly are they trying to go back to?

Was the old Parliament really some kind of a utopia?

If it was not, then it is not enough for a dozen Central Committee members to raise questions.

The entire political course needs to be corrected.

The UML has been standing for some time on the foundation of mistaken assumptions.

UML leaders often say that politics requires an analysis of concrete circumstances.

So, when faced with a concrete situation, is it really a concrete analysis to fall back on arguments as insubstantial as restoring Parliament?

Parliament was swept away after a massive youth movement.

Before that, Oli himself had dissolved Parliament as part of the regular political course.

The real problem is that Oli continues to refuse to understand these simple truths. That is precisely why history is now moving forward without him.

The UML, more than anyone else, needs to understand this.

Had the UML fully understood it, Shankar Pokhrel would not have had to carry the political agenda of party reorganisation with such hesitation and fear. Bishnu Paudel would not have had to set aside his own convictions and rush into reconciliation with Oli.

At yesterday’s Central Committee meeting, Suhang Nembang invoked Mao Zedong and Che Guevara to make his point.

Just as dirt accumulates when you do not wash your face every day, he said, ideas decay when there is no self-reflection and no acceptance of mistakes. Hiding mistakes, he argued, is like hiding an illness — and ultimately leads to destruction.

Nembang also appeared to signal that it is time for the old leadership to step aside.

He said he wanted the arduous struggles and contributions of the older generation, as well as the glorious history of the communist movement, to be told and remembered for generations to come.

But Suhang and his generation may have to fight another battle within the party simply to get their turn.

Because Shankar Pokhrel and his generation have apparently failed to believe that there can be light for them beyond Oli.

They have failed to believe that they, too, can shine through their own personalities and abilities.

And so, even when Oli is left standing alone, he continues to keep everyone on edge.

He promises one person the chairmanship. Another gets the general secretary’s post. Someone else gets a chief ministerial position. Because he can no longer hand out the posts of prime minister or federal minister as he once could.

So one gets this. Another gets that.

Fear is not the greatest enemy of a person. Greed is. And it is through this greed that UML’s second generation is preparing to become corrupt.

A person does not become corrupt only by taking money. Is someone who is constantly abandoning their own convictions really any less corrupt?

The UML’s future depends on whether it is prepared to fight this form of corruption as well. And if anyone believes that Oli was right and that Parliament must be restored to reinstate him, they should understand one thing.

Oli is not Girija Prasad Koirala. Koirala stood with the people’s movement against an autocratic king.

Oli himself faced a large section of the population in opposition, and the dissolution of Parliament took place in the middle of that conflict.

Parliament is not going to come back simply because Oli wants it to.

So the question is not really for Oli. It is for the remaining members of the UML.

Do you genuinely want the old Parliament back? Do you really believe that this is possible? Or, even if you know it is impossible, are you pursuing some political manoeuvre that could make your own political revival easier?

When you leave the Central Committee meeting, do not leave without first finding answers to these questions.

Yes, the matter is apparently still before the court.

But when history has already put an issue away and the people have already delivered a fresh mandate, those who continue to raise expired political agendas should not expect public trust to return either.

title.rendered: What Balen Shah’s UN speech said about a world in crisis

content.rendered:
There was considerable anticipation surrounding Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Shah came to the UN at a particular political moment. He had emerged as prime minister after a major political upheaval, carrying with him expectations that go well beyond those normally placed on a newly elected leader. In Nepal, particularly among young people, there was curiosity about what he would say. The same was true among Nepalis living in the United States and elsewhere abroad.

Would he raise uncomfortable questions? Would he speak about the issues confronting Nepal in a way that went beyond the usual diplomatic language?

After listening to the speech, my impression was that it was thoughtfully prepared and, overall, effective.

It appeared to have been shaped by people who had tried to understand the current global situation, particularly the environmental crisis, rather than simply assemble the standard language of a diplomatic address. Shah, for his part, made a serious attempt to present those arguments effectively.

A question for political leadership

Shah began with an important question — the failure of political leadership.

His argument was that environmental crises are becoming deeper and the damage they cause greater because political leaders have failed to act in time and have remained indifferent to problems that require urgent intervention.

The point was not simply to describe the crisis. It was to argue that much of the damage could still be reduced if political leaders made the right decisions and intervened at the right time.

Infrastructure could be protected. Lives could be saved.

There was a degree of self-criticism in that argument because Shah himself is now part of the political leadership he was questioning.

But his position as a relatively new political leader also gave the argument another meaning. He was, in effect, questioning those who have held power for decades and who have played a major role in shaping the international order.

That question is necessary.

Political failure and political indifference have consequences, and Nepal has experienced them repeatedly. The recent Bhotekoshi floods are only the latest example. Nepal has suffered major disasters before, while elsewhere, including Pakistan and Sikkim, communities have also endured enormous losses.

Shah tried to place those experiences within the larger global climate crisis.

That was one of the stronger aspects of his address.

War, farmers and the global order

Perhaps the most interesting part of the speech was the way Shah connected war with the predicament of ordinary farmers.

There is an extraordinary contrast in the way the world mobilises resources.

When it comes to war, countries can mobilise enormous amounts of money, technology, logistics and political will. Yet there is no comparable urgency when it comes to ensuring that an ordinary farmer can continue farming.

At the same time, wars disrupt global supply chains. Those disruptions have consequences far beyond the battlefield. They affect the ability of ordinary people to produce food, earn a living and maintain their livelihoods.

Shah used this contrast as a metaphor.

He did not directly name the United States. Nor did he name the powers involved in wars around the world or those providing resources that sustain them.

But the question was there. And because he was raising it from New York, the setting mattered.

The argument was essentially this: If the world can mobilise extraordinary resources for war, why can it not demonstrate the same urgency when ordinary people are facing a crisis that threatens their livelihoods?

Others have raised similar questions, sometimes in much more direct language, at the UN.

But Shah’s use of the farmer-and-war imagery gave the question a particular force.

For Nepal, this is not an abstract argument. Nepali farmers are already experiencing the consequences of environmental and economic disruption.

The speech therefore moved beyond simply saying that Nepal is vulnerable to climate change. It asked who bears the cost of a global system that Nepal has contributed relatively little to creating.

Nepal cannot face the crisis alone

Shah was also clear about one thing. Nepal cannot confront the crisis by itself.

He emphasised cooperation with India and China and appealed to other neighbouring and friendly countries as well. That was important.

Nepal’s contribution to the global environmental crisis is comparatively small, yet the country is paying a disproportionately large price.

Those with greater resources and greater capacity, therefore, have a greater responsibility to contribute.

I had expected Shah to make this point more directly to the United States.

He was in New York, after all, speaking on American soil. I had expected him to explicitly name the United States and ask it to help Nepal.

He did not.

But by speaking about war, global supply chains and the changing global order, he still raised questions that could not easily be separated from the role of the major powers.

That was significant.

Why end with Pashupatinath and Buddha?

The ending of the speech raises a different set of questions.

After speaking about climate change, political failure and the need for international cooperation, Shah concluded by invoking Pashupatinath and Buddha.

He said in Nepali, “May Pashupatinath bless everyone.”

The phrase has a particular political and cultural history in Nepal. It is traditionally associated with the country’s kings and is particularly familiar from former King Gyanendra, who often used it at the end of his speeches.

Shah used it in a similar way, while also invoking Buddha.

There is a positive way to understand this.

He may have been deliberately bringing Nepal’s cultural identity into an international setting. By ending in Nepali and invoking symbols associated with Nepal’s cultural and religious heritage, he was perhaps trying to present a particular image of the country to the world.

But there is another, more critical interpretation.

Shah had spent much of the speech arguing that political leadership has failed.

That criticism can arguably extend beyond national political leaders.

The United Nations itself is part of the global system of institutions created to manage international crises and promote cooperation. If that system is failing to respond adequately to the crises before us, then the failure of leadership cannot be confined to individual governments.

So where does hope lie?

If human beings, political leaders, international institutions and global mechanisms of cooperation are all failing to adequately confront an increasingly severe crisis, what remains?

Shah’s invocation of Pashupatinath and Buddha can therefore also be read as an expression of uncertainty — even despair.

Perhaps the message was that we have reached a point where human institutions are proving inadequate to the scale of the problems we have created.

There is also a more critical question.

Could the speech have ended in a way that was more inclusive, more explicitly hopeful and more representative of Nepal’s identity without relying on a religious invocation?

It could have.

The stronger message was solidarity

Still, the religious reference should not overshadow the more important message with which Shah was trying to conclude.

Before the final invocation, he repeatedly used phrases such as “Let’s do this” and “Let’s do that”.

Those lines were rhetorical, but they carried a clear message.

Commitment. Recommitment. Solidarity.

Shah was not presenting himself as someone who had come simply to accuse other countries. He was presenting himself as someone seeking cooperation.

That distinction matters.

The speech was essentially saying that the crisis is too large for any one country to solve, and that international cooperation is not optional.

That was perhaps the most constructive part of the address.

A speech is not an achievement by itself

The speech was good. But it could have been better.

Its delivery could have had greater force. The arguments could have been presented with more energy and in a manner that held the audience’s attention more strongly.

There is plenty to debate about how it could have been improved. But there is an even more important point.

This speech is not the end of the story. Nor is it everything.

A powerful speech at the UN does not, by itself, produce a major achievement for Nepal. Neither does an interesting address automatically translate into international cooperation, climate finance or protection from future disasters.

The real test comes afterwards.

What does Nepal do with the arguments it has made? What cooperation does it secure? What commitments does it pursue? And how does the government translate the language of climate justice and international solidarity into actual policy?

Those questions matter even more because of the circumstances in which Shah became prime minister.

He has emerged after a major political transformation, at a time when expectations are unusually high. That makes his appearance on the world stage more consequential than a routine diplomatic speech.

Watching the address from near New York, I felt both pleased and proud.

A young Nepali leader stood before the world and questioned the failures of political leadership. He tried to make sense of a rapidly changing global order. He raised the plight of farmers, the consequences of war and the disproportionate burden carried by countries such as Nepal.

He did not have all the answers. But he asked some important questions. And, at a time when the world is struggling to answer them, that matters.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah urges world to act on warnings from the ‘rooftop of the world’

content.rendered:
New York, September 24

Prime Minister Balendra Shah has called for greater international support for countries facing the consequences of climate change, saying Nepal is paying a “colossal price” for a crisis it did little to create.

Addressing the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday, Shah placed Nepal’s recent Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods at the centre of his speech, describing the disaster as a warning to the international community about the growing risks facing the Himalayas.

“Climate change does not recognize borders,” Shah said, pointing to the effects of melting glaciers, unstable mountain slopes, floods and landslides across Nepal, China and India.

He said the disaster had killed at least 1,400 people and left more than 6,000 missing, while preliminary assessments put Nepal’s physical recovery needs at around 10 percent of its GDP.

The floods, he said, had swept away bridges, roads, schools, homes and livelihoods and interrupted Nepal’s progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.

“I come before you from Nepal — a distant country in the Himalayas — carrying a close warning for humanity,” Shah said.

He recalled United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres’ visit to Nepal nearly three years ago, when Guterres warned from the foot of Mount Everest about the dangers posed by the climate crisis.

Shah said the warning had not been translated into action quickly enough.

“We, the political leaders of the world, have been negligent to translate those warnings into action at the speed and scale that vulnerable people require,” he said.

Calls for Himalayan cooperation

Shah said a warming climate was destabilising the Himalayan ecosystem, with melting permafrost contributing to unstable mountain slopes and increasing the risks of ice-rock avalanches, floods and landslides.

He proposed the establishment of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China.

The mechanism, he said, should allow the three countries to share satellite data and technical expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, strengthen early-warning systems and coordinate assistance when disasters occur.

“Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information,” Shah said.

He said the Hindu Kush Himalaya was home to nearly two billion people and provided water, ecosystems, agriculture and livelihoods to populations far beyond Nepal.

“The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet’s life-support system,” he said.

Nepal seeks climate finance

Shah said Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions but is facing retreating glaciers, increasingly unstable mountain slopes and unpredictable rivers.

“For Nepal, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event, but a development emergency,” he said.

The prime minister said major disasters destroy infrastructure and livelihoods while forcing poorer countries to borrow money to rebuild damage they did not cause.

He called for greater grant-based international assistance and said existing climate financing mechanisms remained inadequate.

“The Loss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other relevant financing mechanisms remain grossly inadequate,” Shah said.

He also criticised the complexity of accessing international climate finance.

“Climate finance must not become a bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years proving that they need help,” he said. “When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms. We act.”

Shah argued that the principle of “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities”, recognised under the UN climate framework, should guide the international response.

“Those who have historically contributed more to the problem, and those with greater capacity to respond, must do more,” he said.

‘Flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food’

Shah also used his speech to criticise what he described as an unequal international system in which military goods move more efficiently across borders than essential supplies for ordinary people.

He referred to shortages of fertiliser, bitumen and cooking fuel in Nepal, contrasting them with the speed at which weapons and military equipment cross international borders.

“Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet every deadline,” Shah said.

“But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure her fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.”

“We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food,” he said.

Shah said Nepal was not alone in facing such pressures, pointing to Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

He argued that countries across the region were dealing with the consequences of climate change while also being affected by wars and geopolitical crises they did not start.

“This tells us there is a lot more broken than meets the eye in the present order of global cooperation,” he said.

Six words for climate action

Shah framed Nepal’s immediate demands around six words.

“Relief. Rehabilitation. Reconstruction,” he said. “And also: Responsibility. Reparation. Resilience.”

The first three, he said, were needed after a disaster, while the latter three were necessary to ensure that climate disasters did not become a permanent condition for vulnerable countries.

He said Nepal had already taken steps to strengthen its resilience, including restoring forests, expanding hydropower, promoting electric mobility and strengthening climate adaptation at the local level.

But he said Nepal could not build resilience alone.

“Remarkable for a least developed country, Nepal is already playing a global role exceeding its ecological share,” he said.

Shah links climate justice with global inequality

The prime minister also broadened his argument to the wider international order, saying the UN was founded on the principles of sovereignty, international law and human dignity.

“Today, that international system is under strain,” Shah said.

“Too often, military and economic power determines whose voice is heard.”

He called for a fairer global economic order and said climate justice was not simply about financial assistance.

“It is about distributive justice — who bears the costs,” he said.

“It is about procedural justice — who has a voice.”

He said the international system should also consider whether the interests of mountain communities, small island states, landlocked and least-developed countries, and future generations were being given equal weight.

Focus on Nepal’s new political generation

Shah also presented Nepal’s recent political changes as part of a broader generational shift.

He said young people had demanded politics based on integrity and accountability and described the change as part of a wider reaction against conflict, inequality and a lack of opportunities.

“Our youth have demanded a politics of integrity and accountability,” he said.

Shah said his government’s priorities were to build a state capable of delivering decent jobs, social protection and opportunities for Nepalis to build their futures at home.

He also said the country needed to move away from ad hoc responses to climate disasters and develop a culture of preparedness.

“Let us finance resilience, and invest in insurance and innovation,” he said.

“Let us build stronger infrastructure and institutions. Let us reduce fossil-fuel dependence. Let us build systems that warn, alert and save lives.”

Shah ended his address with a reference to the Himalayas as the “rooftop of the world”.

“And when the next warning comes from the rooftop of the world,” he said, “let us be ready to hear it, and ready to act.”

He concluded by wishing for the welfare of the world and calling for the world to follow the path shown by the Buddha.

title.rendered: BP Highway completely blocked by landslides in Kavrepalanchok

content.rendered:

The BP Highway has been completely blocked at several locations in Kavrepalanchok following continuous rainfall that triggered landslides and mudslides.

The local administration has urged people living downstream and in areas prone to flooding to remain alert.

Chief District Officer Gopal Kumar Adhikari said the Roshi River crossed the warning level in Panuti, according to information received from the Flood Forecasting Division.

title.rendered: How a Nepali doctor became a leader in obstetrics at Karolinska

content.rendered:
For hours, a young boy from Arghakhanchi would walk up and down the hills with a schoolbag on his shoulder. His village was on the hills, while Janjyoti Secondary School stood beside the Sandhikharka stream below. Each morning, Dr Ganesh Acharya walked down. Each afternoon, he climbed back up.

He could not have imagined then that those walks would eventually take him from Kathmandu to the former Soviet Union, Britain, Norway, the United States, China and Sweden — or that he would one day head the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Sweden’s Karolinska Institutet.

Today, at 65, Professor Dr Ganesh Acharya is a physician, researcher and academic whose work has taken him across some of the world’s leading medical institutions.

But his story began much closer to home.

A childhood shaped by education

Dr Ganesh Acharya was the youngest of six children — five brothers and a sister. His father, Pandit Homakanta Acharya, lived modestly but placed enormous value on education.

Homakanta himself had studied at the prestigious Harihar Pathshala, where students from different parts of Nepal came to study. They had to travel to Banaras in India to sit their examinations.

“My father went to Banaras to take his examination,” Acharya recalls. “It used to take 13 or 14 days to reach Kathmandu from our home. When my father sent one of his brothers to Kathmandu to study, he died after contracting smallpox. So my father chose Banaras.”

For Homakanta, education was more than personal advancement. He saw it as the surest way to give his children a different future. He even sold land to pay for their schooling.

Acharya spent his early years in the hills. After three grades at Janajivan Primary School, he moved to Janjyoti Secondary School beside the Sandhikharka stream.

“It took an hour to get to school and another hour to return. We carried our books in a bag and walked up and down the hills every morning,” he says.

In 1976, Janjyoti did not have an SLC examination centre, so Acharya travelled to Taulihawa in Kapilvastu to sit the exam. He passed in the second division.

At the time, health assistant and overseer were among the most sought-after professional courses. Acharya was drawn towards healthcare. He did not yet know that the decision would take him far beyond Nepal.

A scholarship to the Soviet Union

His elder brother, who had completed his ISc at Amrit Science College, encouraged him to study health assistance.

“My brother suggested that I study to become a health assistant,” Acharya recalls. “His argument was that at least after completing that course, I would definitely find a job.”

Nepal did not yet have a medical school producing doctors. Medical education in the country began only around 1980, making health assistant training one of the highest levels of formal health education available at the time.

Dr Ganesh Acharya enrolled at the Institute of Medicine in Maharajgunj and completed the three-year course with strong results.

“I came second,” he says with pride.

His classmates included people who would later become prominent figures in Nepal, including Prakash Sharan Mahat and Narayan Kaji Shrestha. His academic performance earned him a government scholarship to study abroad. In 1980, aged 20, he left Nepal for the Soviet Union.

“There were about 10 of us,” he says. “When we left, we did not know which city we would end up in. It was a seven-year course — the first year was for language and the remaining six years were medical studies.”

He was eventually sent to Lviv, Ukraine, where he studied at the Lviv Medical Institute and completed his MD in 1987.

The adjustment was difficult.

“The first challenge was simply getting used to the place,” he says.

Four students shared a hostel room — two Ukrainians and two Nepalis. Even basic necessities were sometimes hard to find.

“Essential things were not easily available. We had to stand in long queues. Sometimes it was difficult even to find toilet paper,” he says with a laugh.

He finished his degree and returned to Nepal in 1988.

Looking beyond Nepal

Back in Kathmandu, Dr Ganesh Acharya worked as a resident doctor in obstetrics, gynaecology and surgery. He also completed a postgraduate diploma in obstetrics and gynaecology from Tribhuvan University. But he wanted to continue studying.

At the time, Britain was a popular destination for Nepali medical professionals. Acharya eventually followed that route, initially working in Bristol before joining University College Hospital in London in 1999. There, he trained as a specialist and completed an MSc in ultrasound.

He also considered returning to Nepal.

During holidays, he came home and tried to coordinate with hospitals about continuing his career there. But the professional environment did not match what he was looking for.

“I did not find the kind of environment I was looking for,” he says.

He decided to remain in Britain.

Then he met Professor Torvid Kiserud, a Norwegian specialist who would introduce him to the next chapter of his career.

“We became friends,” Acharya says. “One day he told me, ‘You should come to Norway. They are looking for a specialist to develop a fetal medicine service for diagnosing and treating diseases in unborn babies.’”

The opportunity appealed to him, but moving again meant navigating a new licensing system.

“Every country required a new licence. That was a major challenge,” he says.

The process began in 1999 and was completed in 2001. Acharya moved to Tromsø, northern Norway, close to the Arctic Circle.

Learning to live in the Arctic

Tromsø was unlike anywhere he had lived before. There were periods when daylight seemed endless and others when darkness dominated.

“In the first few months, it felt as though I had lost all sense of time,” he says with a laugh.

Language presented another hurdle. The hospital provided an interpreter, but Dr Ganesh Acharya began learning Norwegian himself. He continued his academic work and completed a PhD in medicine at the University of Tromsø in 2005.

A year later, he travelled to the United States for a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of South Florida, where he studied advanced techniques for detecting heart defects in unborn babies.

He returned to Norway and in 2008 became a professor at the University of Tromsø. The following year, he was appointed head of department.

The university is now known as UiT The Arctic University of Norway.

His academic work soon took him elsewhere. In 2011, he went to Oxford. A year later, he became a visiting professor at Sweden’s Karolinska Institutet. In 2015, he worked in China and the United States.

From 2016, he began working full-time at Karolinska Institutet and its university hospital.

For the past eight years, he has headed its Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. His work includes dozens of international research papers, publications and books, and he continues to be invited to major medical conferences as a keynote speaker.

“It was a long journey. It was not easy,” he says. “But every challenge showed me a new path.”

What Nepal can learn

After decades of working in different healthcare systems, Dr Ganesh Acharya has developed clear views about what Nepal could learn from Scandinavia. He points to national health insurance as one of the biggest differences.

“The Scandinavian countries spend around 10 percent of their budget on health. You can see from the budget itself how important health is to the state,” he says.

For him, the central principle should be equal access to care. In Sweden, he says, political leaders, government employees and ordinary citizens receive the same treatment in hospitals. That system has its own trade-offs.

“Sometimes here you have to wait two or four months even for treatment of a common illness,” he says. “In Nepal, people expect everything to be treated immediately. Here, apart from emergencies, it is normal for treatment to take time.”

The difference is also visible outside hospitals.

“Basic healthcare is available in villages across the country. In Nepal, healthcare is still heavily concentrated in Kathmandu. There is still a belief that everyone has to come to one place for treatment.”

Staying connected to Nepal

Despite spending decades abroad, Dr Ganesh Acharya remains keen to work with Nepal.

“I have a strong desire to remain connected with Nepal and work there,” he says.

He believes Nepal’s heavy patient load helps doctors develop strong clinical skills. What is missing, he says, is systematic evaluation and research.

“We need to know what impact the services we provide have had, how many complications occurred and where we stand compared with the rest of the world. We do not have that record.”

That is where he believes his experience in European research could be useful.

“It is not that I have not tried. I have also encouraged other Nepali colleagues,” he says.

But returning to practise in Nepal is complicated by legal restrictions affecting Nepalis who have acquired foreign citizenship.

“If I go to Nepal and work, I am considered a foreigner in the eyes of the government because my passport is foreign,” he says. “We need an environment where Nepalis who have specialised abroad and acquired foreign citizenship can contribute to Nepal’s development without unnecessary legal complications.”

He also believes Nepal needs to move beyond short-term medical missions.

Doctors may visit for a few days, treat hundreds of patients and leave. Conferences are organised, but such efforts rarely produce lasting institutional change, he says.

“Going to Nepal for four days, seeing two or three hundred patients and returning does not bring major change. One conference does not create major change. For sustainable, long-term transformation, we need a system — and it must be a system without unnecessary obstacles.”

The lesson of the journey

Dr Ganesh Acharya considers himself fortunate, but he places greater weight on persistence than luck.

“I am proud to be a doctor because the knowledge I share grows every day,” he says.

He has also developed a philosophy about time and ambition.

“We always say we do not have enough time,” he says. “But my boss used to tell me, ‘If you need to get something done, go to the busiest person in the world. Only people who have free time say they do not have enough time.’”

For him, the lesson from his own career is straightforward.

“I am still working hard. My journey shows that you should not wait for opportunities. You should create them. Challenges will come, but you need to have the courage to overcome them.”

And despite decades spent abroad, his identity remains firmly tied to where he started.

“I am proud to be Nepali and to have come from Nepal,” he says. “Nepal may have its problems, but internationally, the way Nepalis are viewed is still respectful. People look at us positively. Hearing and experiencing that gives me a great sense of pride.”

title.rendered: An OpenAI agent hacked Medicare. Will anyone be held responsible?

content.rendered:
Australia’s Medicare system manages health and medical data for over 27 million people. So it makes sense there has been widespread shock at the news it was hacked by an OpenAI agent in June.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed the hack while in New York to advocate for tighter international regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems at the United Nations.

The government is still working out exactly what happened, with a newly announced taskforce set to investigate further.

Early reports indicate OpenAI’s agent had been tasked with researching public medical data when it broke into Medicare’s systems. It accessed private statistical data, such as billing patterns, rather than personal medical information from an old Australian government website that carried Medicare statistics.

Albanese said the agent found a way around privacy protections – it “didn’t accept ‘no’ for an answer”.

This hack marks a real escalation in the recent history of concerning behaviour by AI systems controlled by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, which have all been found to have hacked multiple websites.

And given Australia’s recent history of cybersecurity lapses, it’s unlikely this will be the last time a prominent Australian system is hacked by an AI agent.

It also raises an important question: will anyone be held responsible?

What are agents?

AI agents are essentially highly advanced, autonomous chatbots. Rather than having a conversation, these agents are empowered to pursue complex tasks with limited guidance. They can browse the web, download data and run code, all without human oversight.

This power – and the lack of human oversight – underpins why we’ve repeatedly seen these agents hacking websites. An agent that is tasked with gathering data on the healthcare system in Australia may see hacking a private system as just another part of following its instructions.

It’s also why it’s so challenging for these companies to clamp down on these behaviours. Empowering the agents with greater capabilities increases their power and usefulness – but it also provides them with tools that can be used to hack websites.

Cause for alarm

Even though personal medical data was apparently not accessed in this hack, it is hard to overstate how serious this incident is. This appears to be the first time an AI agent breach of a government system has been made public.

Moreover, it appears Medicare was completely unaware that a hack had taken place until OpenAI notified the government about it on September 10 – roughly three months after the hack occurred.

The notification from OpenAI, which itself learned of the hack in August during a review of the model’s activity, came via an email sent to a public government mailbox.

And while OpenAI’s disclosure will ultimately help the government fix the security issue that led to this hack, it also speaks to the fact we’re reliant on the goodwill of AI companies to disclose potentially illegal or harmful acts.

Relying on these companies to disclose these types of breaches is fraught with danger. In previous data privacy and cybersecurity incidents, we’ve repeatedly seen how self-reporting by tech companies rarely protects consumers.

The long delay between the hack occurring and OpenAI becoming aware of it raises another question: what else have AI agents been up to that no one knows about yet?

After learning a New South Wales government website was among the four sites accessed by the OpenAI agent, the state’s health department announced a review into its own systems to make sure they weren’t compromised.

Late on Thursday morning, NSW Premier Chris Minns said OpenAI agents may have also accessed information from the state’s Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research. Minns said the information wasn’t private or personal – it was “a similar example of what is generalised information but was not released to the public, being accessed by an open AI agent”.

Abstracting responsibility

The way AI companies have disclosed these hacks – and the way we talk about them – highlights a real failure of public discourse and legislation to keep up with AI agents.

Many people think of AI systems as if they are human – which reflects how we feel when we chat with them. However, this way of thinking also allows us to abstract away responsibility from the companies that are responsible for them.

Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles described the Medicare hack as “unauthorised” but “unintended”, while an OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, referred to it as a “misaligned model”.

Framing model behaviours like this obscures the human decisions that led to this outcome. These agents do not exist by themselves – they are software systems that are designed by humans and operated by humans.

However, establishing who is legally responsible for an AI action like this is a real challenge.

In a speech earlier this year, New South Wales Chief Justice Andrew Bell took aim at this question. In his view, the current legal standard in Australia is clear: AI agents cannot be blamed in and of themselves for their actions.

However, legal liability does not necessarily fall on the user, either. Legal scholars in the area have noted that the law requires a crime to have some level of deliberate intention by the person who commits it.

For instance, if a human asks an AI agent to gather health statistics, and the agent hacks a government server to do so, the human could lack the deliberate intent required for a conviction. The AI agent, meanwhile, lacks the legal personhood to be charged, as well as human intentionality.

Current laws effectively treat AI actions as if they are something that just happens to us – like a severe weather event. This shows a glaring loophole in our legal system that does not hold those who make, maintain and use these systems to account when something goes wrong.

AI agents are, in the end, commercial products deployed by billion-dollar corporations. And while “regulatory lag is inevitable” with AI, as Chief Justice Bell argues, he also stresses this is not sustainable in an era of such rapidly advancing technology.

title.rendered: 11 Nepali films set for Dashain-Tihar box office battle

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Dashain and Tihar are considered one of the most commercially important periods for the Nepali film industry, with producers often targeting the long holidays and festive atmosphere to release films.

The festive season typically sees competition among films featuring popular actors and larger production budgets, as audiences have more free time and are generally more willing to spend on entertainment.

However, the festive season alone does not guarantee box-office success. While the long holidays can help boost business, a film’s subject matter and presentation ultimately determine whether it can attract audiences.

This year, the release calendar for Nepali films targeting Dashain and Tihar has largely been finalised, with 11 films scheduled for release during Asoj and Kartik. The release schedule begins on October 9.

October 9 — ‘Tunnel 26’ and ‘Akshara’

The festive-season releases will begin on October 9, with Tunnel 26 and Akshara scheduled to hit cinemas on the same day.

A co-production of Bhutan, Nepal and India, Tunnel 26 is a zombie thriller, a genre rarely seen in Nepali cinema.

Akshara, starring Nancy Khadka, is a women-centred film.

October 16 — ‘12 Gaun 2’ and ‘Abaat Aama 2’

Two Nepali films will compete at the box office from October 16, with Biraj Bhatta’s 12 Gaun 2 and Chandra Pant’s Abaat Aama 2 scheduled for release.

12 Gaun 2 is an action film, while Abaat Aama 2 is a family drama. The two films will enter the market with different genres as they seek to attract audiences during the early Dashain holiday.

October 17 — ‘Chha Maya Chhapakkai 2’

Deepak Raj Giri and Deepa Shree Niraula’s Chha Maya Chhapakkai 2 is scheduled to release on October 17, the day of Phulpati.

With three films arriving within a span of two days, competition is expected to be particularly intense during the opening phase of the Dashain box office. Their opening-day business will be closely watched.

October 23 — ‘Kabaddi 5’

Two days after Vijayadashami, on October 23, Ram Babu Gurung’s much-awaited Kabaddi 5 will be released.

Starring Dayahang Rai, the film is currently scheduled for a solo release on the date. Its release timing allows it to target the remaining Dashain holidays as well as the Tihar period.

October 30 — ‘Pariwar’

Following Dashain, the Nepali film Pariwar is scheduled to release on October 30.

Its release will continue the run of films targeting the festive season.

November 6 — ‘Paanch Pandav’, ‘Maya Bhane Kai Yasto Hola’ and ‘Zero Degree’

Three Nepali films are scheduled to open on the same day on November 6, setting up another three-way competition at the box office.

The multistarrer Paanch Pandav will be released alongside Rekha Thapa-starrer Maya Bhane Kai Yasto Hola. Zero Degree is also scheduled to hit cinemas on the same day.

The three films will compete for audiences during the festive period.

November 12 — ‘Batulo Joon’

The Dashain-Tihar release cycle will conclude with Batulo Joon, directed by Bhuwan KC and starring Anmol KC.

The film is scheduled to release on November 12, Thursday, the final day of the Tihar holiday and the day after Bhai Tika.

With this release, 11 Nepali films are preparing to enter cinemas during the festive season. While some dates will see two or three Nepali films competing for audiences, others have given individual films the opportunity for a solo release.

The release calendar does not include foreign films. Several major international releases are also expected during the festive period, meaning Nepali films will face competition not only from one another but also from foreign productions.

title.rendered: UML calls for judicial commission to investigate September 8–9 events

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

The CPN-UML has called on the government to form a competent judicial commission to conduct an impartial investigation into the events of September 8 and 9, 2025.

The demand was made by the UML Central Committee, which said newly emerging facts reported by domestic and international media, along with public statements by officials of the interim government and the chair of an investigation commission, had raised questions about various factors said to be behind the incidents.

The UML alleged that the government was attempting to avoid investigating what it described as the “destruction of the state” that occurred on September 9 and was seeking to provide impunity to those involved.

The party also claimed that political leaders were being targeted for prosecution over the events of September 8 while efforts were being made to prevent the facts surrounding the security response that day from coming to light.

The UML has demanded that reports of commissions formed to investigate previous incidents also be made public without delay.

It said the full and authentic versions of such reports should be released rather than summaries or selected sections.

According to the party, developments in recent months and statements made by officials have brought additional facts about the September 8–9 events into the public domain. It said an independent and impartial investigation should therefore examine both the role of political leaders and the actions taken by security agencies.

The party has also criticised the government over what it described as attempts to displace people from squatter settlements and restrict the rights of trade unions and free student unions, as well as concerns over human rights and press freedom.

The UML further objected to the task force formed to review the Constitution, reiterating that any constitutional amendment should not affect the Constitution’s basic structure.

The party’s demand for a fresh investigation comes amid continuing political and legal disputes over the events of September 8 and 9.

A separate commission led by former justice Prem Raj Karki had investigated the September 9 violence and destruction, but the government has not formally accepted its report. Meanwhile, the Karki government’s commission on the September 8 crackdown had recommended investigation and action against former prime minister KP Sharma Oli, former home minister Ramesh Lekhak and other officials. The Shah government decided in March to implement those recommendations, although Oli and Lekhak were later released by the Supreme Court.

The UML has continued to question aspects of the investigation and has called for a broader examination of the events, including the security response. The issue has also featured in discussions at the party’s ongoing Central Committee meeting.

title.rendered: Government plans to increase cooking gas supply to 160 tankers a week

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

The government has prepared short-, medium- and long-term plans to address the shortage of cooking gas and improve the country’s overall petroleum supply system, Industry, Commerce and Supplies Minister Deepak Kumar Sah said on Thursday.

Responding to questions raised by lawmakers in the National Assembly, Sah said the ministry was working on measures to address the immediate shortage while also developing longer-term solutions to make the supply system more reliable.

As part of the immediate measures, the government has asked the Ministry of Finance to help reduce the time required for customs clearance, while the Ministry of Home Affairs has been asked to help manage road congestion affecting the transportation of cooking gas.

The government has also initiated diplomatic efforts through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to temporarily increase the regular supply of cooking gas from 100 bullets a week to up to 160 bullets, Sah said.

A “bullet” refers to the large tanker used to transport liquefied petroleum gas.

Sah, however, said there was currently no shortage of petrol, diesel or aviation fuel in the country.

He said the government would seek to reduce unnecessary expenditure by making the transportation, storage, distribution and administrative systems more cost-efficient.

The government also plans to improve stock management through a more systematic approach, he said.

Sah said resources were being mobilised under the Price Stabilisation Fund Operating Regulations, 2014 (including amendments) to help stabilise the prices of petroleum products and cooking gas.

According to the minister, the government considers factors including the cost structure, international market prices, exchange rates, taxes and fees when determining petroleum prices.

He said the impact of these factors was being analysed transparently as part of the pricing process.

title.rendered: Government plans mandatory waste segregation at source

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

The government plans to make waste segregation at source mandatory and introduce measures to make waste management financially sustainable, Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal said on Thursday.

Responding to lawmakers during a discussion on the Waste Management Bill, 2026 in the House of Representatives, Lamsal said the proposed law would restructure waste management as a public service and promote a public-private partnership model.

Under the proposed system, households that fail to segregate waste at source will not have their waste collected, Lamsal said.

He said waste collection vehicles with three separate chambers would be used to collect different categories of waste.

The government also plans to replace the traditional concept of collection centres with transfer stations based on population size, according to the minister.

Each local government will be required to establish a waste-processing system with four facilities — a Material Recovery Facility (MRF), compost processing centre, incinerator plant and crusher plant.

Lamsal said the facilities would be interconnected and help advance the government’s goal of achieving “zero waste”.

He said the government was also preparing measures to make the system economically sustainable.

The proposed bill includes subsidies for compost production and a fee based on the “polluter pays” principle for the management of hazardous waste, according to Lamsal.

The government also plans to end what the minister described as the monopoly of scrap dealers over recyclable materials generated through MRFs. The proposed model would ensure that local governments also receive financial benefits from recyclable waste.

Similarly, materials produced by crusher plants would have to be used in public construction projects carried out by local governments, Lamsal said.

The minister said these measures were intended to turn waste management from a conventional collection-and-disposal system into an integrated system involving segregation, processing, recycling and resource recovery.

title.rendered: Supreme Court says Bharat Dahal exercised freedom of expression, orders release

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

The Supreme Court has observed that political analyst Bharat Dahal’s recent statements amounted to an exercise of his freedom of thought and expression and ordered that he be released from custody.

A joint bench of Justices Kumar Regmi and Sunil Kumar Pokharel directed Nepal Police’s Cyber Bureau to release Dahal and continue any necessary investigation while keeping him on a date to appear before the authorities.

Dahal’s daughter, Denika Dahal, had filed a habeas corpus petition at the Supreme Court following his arrest.

The court said the investigation file did not show sufficient grounds for keeping Dahal in custody.

The bench observed that Dahal did not appear to have called for a violent movement against the Constitution or the law and that his statements appeared to constitute a peaceful exercise of the right to freedom of thought and expression guaranteed under Article 17(2)(a) of the Constitution.

“Since it does not appear that he called for a violent movement against the Constitution and the law, and appears to have peacefully exercised the right to freedom of thought and expression guaranteed by Article 17(2)(a), no basis or reason requiring his continued detention is seen from the investigation file,” the order states.

Dahal, who is also chair of the Trimool Nepal Party, was arrested by police in Belbari, Morang, and brought to Kathmandu for investigation under the Electronic Transactions Act.

He had recently been making political comments and giving interviews in which he alleged that the Gen Z movement and some of its leaders had been influenced or mobilised by foreign powers.

Dahal had cited material published by The Grayzone while making claims about the Gen Z protests and alleged external influence. He was arrested after such content circulated on social media.

The Kathmandu District Court had on September 21 granted police a three-day remand to investigate Dahal. His statement had already been recorded, according to the Supreme Court’s order.

The Supreme Court therefore said that if further investigation was required, it could be conducted while Dahal remained outside custody.

However, the court did not issue a habeas corpus order in the strict sense.

The bench noted that Dahal had been arrested under Section 47(1) of the Electronic Transactions Act, 2006, and that the Kathmandu District Court had also issued an arrest warrant against him. The court therefore ordered his release while directing that the investigation continue with him on a date to appear.

Dahal was arrested on September 20 from Belbari, Morang. Police had said he was being investigated over content concerning geopolitical issues and alleged involvement of senior political figures.

The Supreme Court issued a two-page brief order on Thursday, saying the full text would take time to prepare.

With the order, Dahal will remain outside custody while the police investigation proceeds. If a case is filed against him, he can face the proceedings while remaining out of detention, subject to further orders of the court.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah’s speech to focus on climate justice, wars and Nepal’s concerns

content.rendered:
New York, September 24

Prime Minister Balen Shah is scheduled to hold only one diplomatic meeting during his visit to New York for the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Shah is scheduled to meet UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Thursday, according to the government’s official programme. Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal is handling the remaining bilateral and diplomatic engagements during the high-level week.

There had been speculation that Shah could participate in sideline meetings with India and China during the General Assembly. However, the Prime Minister’s Office has ruled out such meetings, according to sources close to the prime minister.

A source close to Shah told Onlinekhabar that the government believes issues requiring high-level engagement can be taken up during diplomatic visits expected in the coming months. As a result, no additional bilateral meetings have been scheduled for the prime minister during the UN visit.

During his meeting with Guterres, Shah is expected to raise the Bhotekoshi disaster and issues arising from the disaster, with climate justice expected to be a major focus.

Shah is also scheduled to address the UN General Assembly on Thursday. The UN speaking schedule has allotted him a 15-minute slot.

His speech is expected to focus on the climate crisis and the disasters faced by countries such as Nepal. The Bhotekoshi disaster and Nepal’s call for climate justice have emerged as key themes of his visit.

According to sources close to Shah, he is also preparing to speak about conflicts and tensions in West Asia and other parts of the world. He is expected to raise the impact of wars on countries such as Nepal.

A source close to the prime minister quoted part of the draft speech as saying, “They wage trillion-dollar wars, but we bear the burden of a few hundred rupees in gas and petrol costs.”

The source said Shah is preparing to argue that countries such as Nepal can send a message calling for an end to wars and greater efforts for peace, while acknowledging that the final speech could be changed depending on the situation.

Shah had previously criticised US President Donald Trump in a social media post in February 2025, when he was mayor of Kathmandu. In the post, he had referred to the US diversity visa programme and Nepali workers in a critical manner.

A year later, Shah has arrived in New York as Nepal’s prime minister to lead the country’s delegation to the UN General Assembly, where US President Trump is also attending. Chinese President Xi Jinping, however, is not attending this year’s General Assembly and is instead scheduled to meet Trump in Washington.

According to sources close to Shah, the prime minister is unlikely to attend dinners or other formal social engagements during the visit. He is expected to return to Kathmandu soon after completing his UN engagements, while Foreign Minister Khanal will continue to represent Nepal at other programmes and meetings.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said Shah is scheduled to return to Nepal on September 26.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

From the CPN-UML’s decision to reinstate former President Bidya Devi Bhandari as a senior leader to a planned opposition movement against the government, Thursday brought several significant developments in Nepal. Here are the day’s key stories, along with updates on currency, aviation, legal aid, security and more.

Bidya Devi Bhandari reinstated as UML senior leader

The CPN-UML has decided to make former President Bidya Devi Bhandari a senior leader of the party. A meeting of the party’s Secretariat held on Thursday proposed making Bhandari an honorary senior leader, placing her second in the party hierarchy after Chairman KP Sharma Oli. The proposal will now be presented to the Central Committee for approval.

Fire damages 10 houses in Taplejung’s Dobhan Bazar

Ten houses were damaged after a fire broke out at Dobhan Bazar in Taplejung district on Thursday afternoon, reportedly due to an electrical short circuit. The fire started from the house of local resident Dandu Sherpa after an electrical short circuit, according to authorities.

Mahesh Basnet announces post-festival movement against Balen Shah government

PN-UML Secretary Mahesh Basnet has said his party, along with other political parties, will launch a “strong movement” across the country after Dashain, Tihar and Chhath. Speaking to journalists at the venue of the UML Central Committee meeting, Basnet said the movement would target the government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah.

Resident doctors at National Medical College instructed to leave the college

National Medical College and Teaching Hospital in Birgunj has instructed its first-year postgraduate (PG) resident doctors to leave the college immediately. The college has announced that all academic activities for these resident doctors, including classes, clinical postings, departmental training, and ward and emergency duties, are suspended until further notice.

Nepal Rastra Bank to issue new Rs 1000 notes from Friday

Nepal Rastra Bank is set to put new Rs 1,000 banknotes into circulation from Friday. According to the Currency Management Department of Nepal Rastra Bank, the new notes will be brought into circulation from Friday. The new Rs 1,000 notes will retain the same dimensions as the existing notes but will feature a different colour scheme. The notes will be light green with a purple border, according to the central bank.

Himalaya Airlines resumes direct Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu flights

Himalaya Airlines will resume direct flights on the Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu route. Himalaya has announced to resume regular direct flight service from Tribhuvan International Airport to Pudong International Airport, Shanghai, starting Monday, September 28.

Bill on Free Legal Aid tabled

Sobita Gautam, Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, has presented the Free Legal Aid Bill 2083 before the House of Representatives. She tabled the bill at Thursday’s meeting. While presenting it, Minister Gautam noted that the new bill has been drafted to effectively implement the fundamental right to justice enshrined in Article 20 of the Constitution, as well as the integrated legal aid policy issued in 2076 BS.

Indian national arrested at TIA with half a kilogram of gold

An Indian national has been arrested at Tribhuvan International Airport with half a kilogram of gold. The person arrested is 42-year-old Mohammad Chera Thodi, who arrived in Kathmandu via Doha, Qatar. Police said he was arrested from the airport’s parking area, with 536 grams of gold recovered from him.

title.rendered: Why were visas of 88 Chinese workers cancelled at Sindhuli meat factory?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

The Department of Immigration has cancelled the visas of 88 foreign nationals working at an under-construction meat processing factory in Marin Rural Municipality of Sindhuli, saying they were found to have worked in violation of the purpose of their visas.

The workers were employed at Jian Foods Pvt Ltd, which is developing the Nepal Heat Processed Buffalo Meat Export to China Project with financial partnership from Chengdu Tian Food Limited.

The Department of Immigration at Kalikasthan made the decision to cancel all 88 visas in a single decision on Wednesday.

The department has also started the process of deporting the workers, according to its spokesperson Tikaram Dhakal.

“Since they were found to have engaged in activities contrary to the purpose of their visas, their visas have been cancelled. In addition, the process of imposing fines and deportation has been initiated in accordance with the Immigration Act 1992,” Dhakal said in a statement.

Although the department said the workers had violated the purpose of their visas, it did not initially disclose which visas they had entered Nepal on or what work they were carrying out.

An immigration official said the workers whose visas were cancelled were Chinese nationals who had entered Nepal on business visas but were working at the meat factory project.

Asked why the visas of all 88 workers were cancelled at once, Immigration Department Director General Ram Chandra Tiwari said they had entered Nepal on business visas but were found to be working in violation of the purpose of those visas.

“They came on business visas. But since they were found to have worked contrary to the purpose of their visas, action has been taken in accordance with immigration law,” Tiwari said.

Immigration says workers entered on business visas

According to department sources, most of the Chinese nationals had entered Nepal on business visas after registering IT companies.

Immigration officials said the foreigners had registered IT companies under different names through the Office of the Company Registrar and the Department of Industry, and then worked at the under-construction meat factory.

Officials said IT companies are often registered because they are not subject to the same investment threshold applicable to other businesses.

The department suspects that the business visas were used primarily as a means of entering Nepal rather than for conducting business.

“They appear to have obtained business visas simply to enter Nepal. There are companies on paper, but they appear to have been working without actually conducting business,” an immigration official said.

Company says workers are skilled technicians

The company developing the meat factory, however, has a different explanation.

Jian Foods has said it had been trying to obtain work visas for the Chinese workers and that the sudden cancellation of their existing visas could create a shortage of skilled manpower, making it difficult to complete the project on schedule.

Onlinekhabar has obtained a letter sent by Jian Foods requesting approval for work visas.

On July 17, the company wrote to the Department of Agriculture under the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, requesting approval for work visas for its Chinese technical workers.

“We would like to submit applications for labour permits and work visas for Chinese technical workers in connection with our company’s plans to operate a large food-processing project in Nepal,” the letter said.

The company said construction was underway to establish a modern buffalo slaughterhouse and food-processing factory in Marin and that the foreign workers involved were technically skilled personnel.

It argued that the factory’s production lines were complex and highly technologically advanced and therefore required experienced technical specialists.

The company said it had prioritised foreign workers with the necessary technical expertise because of the requirements of the project.

“Our company requires a team of 500 foreign specialists. This number is less than 5 percent of our 10,000 local permanent workers, and therefore fully complies with the government’s labour management regulations,” the company said in the letter.

It added that the production equipment could not be operated without the foreign specialists being present in Nepal.

The company had planned to bring the meat factory into full operation from January. Construction of the slaughterhouse is underway on around 50 bighas of land.

A major China-bound buffalo meat project

The project is linked to an agreement reached during former Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli’s visit to China to export buffalo meat from Nepal to China.

After the investment was approved, Oli announced on Facebook that the Department of Industry had approved foreign direct investment of Rs 20 billion for the project.

According to Oli’s announcement, Chengdu Jian Food Company of China’s Sichuan province had proposed establishing the factory in Marin Rural Municipality-4, Sindhuli.

The company has set a target of producing 200,000 tonnes of meat annually along with 55,000 tonnes of by-products, including hides, internal organs and heads.

The project has been promoted as having potential benefits for Nepal’s livestock sector and economy.

Its proponents have said it could help develop a standardised buffalo farming industry and directly benefit around one million Nepali farmers.

The factory is also expected to create employment for around 10,000 Nepalis and generate up to $1.5 billion annually in foreign exchange through exports of processed buffalo meat to China.

title.rendered: Bidya Devi Bhandari’s return to UML leadership revives her political ambitions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Former President Bidya Devi Bhandari had already returned to active politics within the CPN-UML. The party’s latest decision to bring her in as a senior leader has now revived questions about her future role in the party and its leadership.

The UML Secretariat has proposed making Bhandari a senior leader, with the proposal set to go before the Central Committee for approval.

Bhandari had left active party politics after being elected president in October 2015. Before her, former President Ram Baran Yadav, who had previously served as general secretary of the Nepali Congress, maintained an independent public profile after leaving office rather than returning to active party politics.

Bhandari, however, has made clear in recent years that she intended to continue her political journey within the UML after completing her presidential tenure.

In an interview with Onlinekhabar three years ago, she said the possibility of becoming UML chairperson had not been ruled out. More recently, she publicly expressed the belief that KP Sharma Oli would not return as party chairperson, while saying leadership change should be accepted as part of democratic practice.

Her return to party politics has been accompanied by a prolonged dispute with Oli.

When Bhandari sought to renew her party membership after leaving the presidency, the issue became contentious within the UML. The party leadership had argued that someone who had served as president, the country’s head of state, should not immediately return to active partisan politics.

Bhandari nevertheless maintained that she had never abandoned the UML. At a programme marking the birth anniversary of her late husband and UML leader Madan Bhandari, she said she had renewed her party membership with the intention of continuing her political journey within the UML.

She also criticised what she described as the growing dominance of a single-person style of leadership in the party, saying it was inconsistent with the spirit of the People’s Multiparty Democracy advocated by the UML.

Oli and Bhandari have since exchanged sharp political remarks. At one event marking Madan Bhandari’s birth anniversary, Oli made remarks referring to fears that something dramatic would happen around the occasion, which were widely interpreted within the party as directed at Bhandari.

Bhandari expressed dissatisfaction with Oli’s presentation at the event. By then, however, Oli had already left the venue.

Three weeks later, the UML placed Bhandari’s party membership on hold. Although the party described the move as a membership “hold”, it effectively left her without active party membership at the time.

Bhandari responded angrily, saying she had returned to UML politics after 35 years as a party member and had not left the party when she became president.

She also said no one could take away her membership of the UML.

Her relationship with the party leadership had become so strained that her supporters said she received a cold reception when she visited the UML headquarters in Chyasal.

From president to senior party leader

Bidya Devi Bhandari’s political career predates her marriage to Madan Bhandari. She became involved in the politics of the All Nepal National Free Students’ Union and later joined the organisation of the then CPN-Marxist-Leninist. She married Madan Bhandari, one of the most prominent communist leaders of the time.

After Madan Bhandari died in 1993, she returned to active politics and went on to hold several positions in the UML and the All Nepal Women’s Association.

She later served as minister for science and technology, minister for population and environment, and defence minister before becoming UML vice-chairperson and eventually president of Nepal.

Her return to a senior position in the UML therefore marks a significant shift from the role she occupied for two consecutive terms as head of state.

Her political ambitions have also been discussed within the UML for several years.

At the party’s most recent general convention, Ishwar Pokhrel, who was backed by the Bhandari camp, challenged Oli for the party chairperson position. Oli won the contest.

The latest decision by the UML Central Committee comes amid an internal debate over the party’s leadership following its poor performance in the March 5 election. Several senior leaders have been calling for organisational and leadership changes.

Bhandari has also held meetings with Oli and UML General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel in recent months, adding to speculation about her role in the party’s future.

Debate over a former president returning to party politics

Bidya Devi Bhandari’s return has also raised a broader debate over whether a former head of state should resume active partisan politics.

Political analyst Sanjeev Pokharel has criticised the move, arguing that the return of someone who has served as the country’s highest constitutional office to party politics raises questions about the distinction between the presidency and partisan politics.

He has also argued that Nepal’s presidential system should not be directly compared with the US system, where a former president can return to party politics and seek elected office.

“There, it is an executive presidency; here, it is about serving as the respected ceremonial head of state,” Pokharel said, according to the source text.

Bhandari’s supporters, meanwhile, have argued that her return to the UML is consistent with her long political career and that she never formally abandoned the party.

Her political comeback has also acquired significance as discussions continue over possible cooperation or unification among Nepal’s communist parties.

The UML and the Nepali Communist Party (NCP) have held several rounds of talks in recent months. Against this backdrop, some within the left have begun discussing Bhandari as a possible figure for leadership in a future unified party.

The UML’s proposal to make her a senior leader does not itself determine her future position in the party. But it formally brings her back into the senior leadership structure and reopens the question that has followed her return to active politics — whether her long-discussed possibility of seeking the UML’s top leadership could eventually become a political reality.

Ten houses were damaged after a fire broke out at Dobhan Bazar in Taplejung district on Thursday afternoon, reportedly due to an electrical short circuit.

The fire started from the house of local resident Dandu Sherpa after an electrical short circuit, according to authorities.

Chief District Officer Umesh Kumar Dahal said seven houses were completely destroyed in the fire, while three others suffered extensive damage.

Nepali Army personnel, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police and local residents are involved in efforts to bring the fire under control.

There are around 50 houses in the market.

“The fire is now coming under control. The timely arrival of the fire engine and security personnel has helped prevent further damage,” Dahal said.

The CPN-UML has decided to make former President Bidya Devi Bhandari a senior leader of the party.

A meeting of the party’s Secretariat held on Thursday proposed making Bhandari an honorary senior leader, placing her second in the party hierarchy after Chairman KP Sharma Oli. The proposal will now be presented to the Central Committee for approval.
