title.rendered: Trump and Xi head into Washington summit with both believing time is on their side

content.rendered:
Washington, DC, September 24

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet at the White House on Thursday with a long list of difficult issues on the agenda, from trade and artificial intelligence to Taiwan, Iran and critical minerals.

Despite the tensions, both leaders appear to believe they have time on their side as Washington and Beijing prepare for what is expected to remain one of the world’s most consequential economic and national security rivalries.

China has resisted pressure from the Trump administration to use its influence over Iran to push Tehran towards US terms for ending the nearly seven-month war. Beijing, meanwhile, wants Washington to permanently halt arms sales to Taiwan and ease restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductor technology.

The two countries also agreed on Wednesday to extend their one-year trade truce for another two months, postponing a broader agreement.

Edgard Kagan, a former senior State Department official responsible for East Asia policy under Trump and former President Joe Biden, said Trump believes the US economy will strengthen over time, while the country continues to advance in artificial intelligence and technology and develops alternative sources of critical minerals and rare earths.

Xi, meanwhile, believes the US is in decline and that time is working in China’s favour, Kagan said.

Trump puts on a show of hospitality

Trump has placed considerable emphasis on the ceremonial aspects of Xi’s visit.

The US president personally greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, when they arrived near Washington on Wednesday evening.

Trump has also made efforts to ensure the White House is ready for the visit, including completing construction of a new helicopter landing pad on the South Lawn.

He has openly expressed disappointment that a planned White House ballroom was not completed in time to host the state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening.

The guest list includes Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, bringing some of the world’s most prominent technology executives into a meeting where artificial intelligence is expected to be an important topic.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two leaders could consider establishing a new “notification mechanism” for AI-related incidents that could pose national security risks.

However, it remains uncertain whether the summit will produce progress on AI or other major disputes.

Trade truce extended, but bigger deal remains uncertain

Bessent announced shortly after Xi arrived in Washington that the two countries had agreed to extend the trade truce reached last year in Busan, South Korea.

He said Trump and Xi could potentially reach a broader agreement by January, or could decide to extend the truce again.

Both governments have strong reasons to avoid a renewed trade confrontation.

Trump’s Republican Party faces a difficult political environment ahead of the November midterm elections, while another major economic disruption could add pressure.

China, meanwhile, is dealing with an uneven economy, with weakness in domestic demand alongside strong exports of high-tech products.

During last year’s trade war, US tariffs on Chinese goods reached as high as 145%, while China imposed retaliatory tariffs of up to 125%.

After Trump and Xi met in South Korea last year, the average US tariff rate fell to about 47%, while China’s average tariff rate was in the mid-30% range.

The US Supreme Court later overturned many of Trump’s tariffs in February, resulting in greater variation in the tariff rates applied to Chinese goods.

The latest extension is shorter than the timelines previously discussed by both sides.

China had indicated that it wanted the truce to remain in place until the end of Trump’s current term in January 2029. Trump administration officials, however, had suggested an extension of between three and six months, citing China’s slow progress on commitments involving rare-earth exports, US soybean purchases and aircraft imports.

Ryan Hass, a senior China policy adviser in the Obama administration who is now with the Brookings Institution, said a major breakthrough may not emerge from the summit.

Instead, he said, both sides are likely to focus on securing limited gains while avoiding a broader confrontation.

Iran unlikely to produce a breakthrough

Iran is another major issue where expectations for a breakthrough remain limited.

Trump has argued that China has a strong incentive to use its influence over Tehran because Beijing is considerably more dependent on Gulf oil than the United States.

China, however, has been critical of the US and Israeli military action and has expressed concern over the conflict.

Xi has described the developments as evidence of a return to what he called the “law of the jungle.”

Beijing has also been unsettled by the US military operation against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, which Trump ordered to remove Maduro from power and bring him to New York to face federal narcoterrorism and drug-trafficking charges.

Trump has since urged Latin American countries to reduce their economic and political ties with China and has cited Chinese and Russian influence as a reason for greater US involvement in Venezuela’s oil industry.

Jake Werner, director of the East Asia Program at the Quincy Institute, said Beijing is concerned about what he described as the “19th-century imperialist cast” of Trump’s geopolitical approach.

At the same time, Werner said China considers its relationship with the US to be decisive and does not want to take steps that could cause the relationship to deteriorate sharply.

Taiwan remains a central issue

Taiwan is expected to be another major point of contention during the summit.

China considers Taiwan part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring the island under its control.

Under US law, Washington is required to provide Taiwan with sufficient defence equipment to help deter an armed attack from China.

Beijing has repeatedly called on Washington to end arms sales to Taiwan permanently, including during Trump and Xi’s previous meeting in Beijing in May.

Following that meeting, Trump said he had delayed final approval of a proposed $14 billion arms package for Taiwan. He also described US arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.

Analysts say Trump may have an incentive to maintain the pause at least until the end of the year.

Trump has also viewed direct meetings with Xi as important for maintaining stability in the relationship. He wants Xi to attend the Group of 20 summit in December at his resort in Doral, Florida.

Xi, meanwhile, wants Trump to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November.

Hass said maintaining the current situation, with the Taiwan arms sales still delayed, could be seen by Beijing as a favourable outcome from the talks.

title.rendered: Bill on Free Legal Aid tabled

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Sobita Gautam, Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, has presented the Free Legal Aid Bill 2083 before the House of Representatives.

She tabled the bill at Thursday’s meeting. While presenting it, Minister Gautam noted that the new bill has been drafted to effectively implement the fundamental right to justice enshrined in Article 20 of the Constitution, as well as the integrated legal aid policy issued in 2076 BS.

She said the bill broadens the scope of parties eligible for free legal aid on economic or other grounds, and extends such assistance beyond the courts to all judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.

She added that the bill guarantees eligible parties the right to free services at every stage — from initial legal consultation and advice through to case proceedings, hearings, and the final implementation of the verdict.

title.rendered: RSP lawmaker Bipin Acharya calls for autonomous board to oversee civil servant transfers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) General Secretary and lawmaker Bipin Acharya has called on the government to establish an autonomous board to oversee the transfer and promotion of civil servants through a predictable, rules-based system.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives on Thursday, Acharya said pressure over the transfer and promotion of government employees was one of the biggest pressures he had faced since entering politics.

He said even people who otherwise speak about good governance and transparency approach him seeking transfers and promotions based on personal connections and influence.

“The biggest pressure I face after entering politics is over transfers and promotions,” Acharya said. “Even friends and relatives who talk about good governance and transparency come to me seeking nepotism and favouritism for transfers and promotions.”

He said some people even question his political standing when he is unable to arrange a transfer.

Acharya said he has been telling people that transfers and promotions under the government should be carried out according to established procedures and rules, rather than through personal recommendations.

He also referred to point eight of the RSP’s election manifesto, which proposes an autonomous transfer board to establish a predictable, procedure-based system for civil servant transfers. The party’s manifesto includes the formation of such a board as part of its proposed civil service reforms.

“I have been telling people that there will be no recommendations and that transfers and promotions will be carried out according to rules and procedures,” Acharya said.

He urged the government to form the proposed board soon.

“If this board is not formed, I fear that I may not receive tika and blessings from my own relatives this Dashain. Instead, I may receive curses for not getting their work done,” he said, making a humorous reference to the pressure he faces.

Acharya was elected to the House of Representatives from Dang-2 in the March 5 general election and is currently a member of the Public Accounts Committee.

title.rendered: RPP lawmaker Khushbu Oli draws government attention to problems faced by Nepalis in Russia

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) chief whip Khushbu Oli has drawn the government’s attention to the problems faced by Nepali citizens living in Russia.

Speaking during a special session of the House of Representatives on Thursday, Oli called for immediate policy initiatives on issues including bilateral banking arrangements with Russia, no-objection certificates (NOCs) for scholarship students, recognition of medical education and labour approvals.

Oli identified the difficulty Nepalis in Russia face in legally sending their earnings back to Nepal as one of the most serious problems.

She said Russian banks have been affected by restrictions on the international financial system following the Russia-Ukraine war, forcing Nepali citizens to carry cash back to Nepal.

She warned that the situation could encourage informal money transfer channels such as hundi and urged Nepal Rastra Bank to explore alternative mechanisms, similar to the banking arrangements Nepal has with India.

Raising concerns over education, Oli said some Nepali students who have received full scholarships from the Russian government were at risk of losing their opportunities because they were unable to obtain NOCs.

She also called for the Nepal Medical Council and the Medical Education Commission to prepare an “equivalent matrix” to address difficulties related to the registration and internships of doctors who have completed medical education in Russia.

On labour approvals, Oli said the government’s restriction on employment in the Russian military sector was appropriate, but suggested that labour approvals for non-military sectors should be reopened gradually.

title.rendered: From the “Pakhe” disposition to inner restoration and global resilience

content.rendered:
Every monsoon, Nepal’s hills collapse into devastating landslides, and riverbanks swallow entire downstream settlements. Globally, we witness rising temperatures, erratic weather patterns, and accelerating climate collapse. It is convenient to dismiss these recurring tragedies as uncontrollable environmental crises or acts of God. Yet, on closer inspection, environmental degradation and climate collapse are not merely external phenomena; they are the direct physical manifestation of a deeper human crisis unfolding now: the erosion of our internal root systems, the fragmentation of our homes, and a society driven by the “Pakhe” disposition of superficiality.

Historically, the Nepali term Pakhe referred geographically to steep mountain slopes (Pakho) or rural settlements outside urban centres. Over generations, urban elites transformed it into a derogatory label implying someone uncultured or rustic. Evaluated through modern sociology, psychology, and philosophy, Pakhe is not a geographic identity, but a state of spiritual and intellectual poverty. It manifests as the supreme delusion of modern isolation, with humans acting selfishly as if they are the sole inhabitants of the universe, operating under the dangerous illusion that they can survive in isolation. In truth, existence is an inextricably interconnected and interdependent web of life.

​A person can hold elite university credentials, wear luxury brands, and command high-achieving professional status, yet remain fundamentally Pakhe when they ignore this interdependence. Living purely on the surface, chasing external validation, adopting superficial trends, and neglecting internal self-awareness, which leaves us unrooted. This internal detachment from our core values (Svadharma) drives the reckless exploitation of everything around us, from the food we consume and the people who love us to our personal health and the natural world.

​The inner universe: Microcosm of the gut-brain axis

​When we live superficially, destruction begins within our biology. Science reveals an astonishing truth: a human being is not a solitary organism, but a walking universe carrying over 38 trillion microscopic creatures. We are over 50% microbe by cell count, harbouring an entire inner universe of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and archaea inside our gastrointestinal tract and imagine these microbes having their own galaxy within.

​This internal cosmos functions as an intricate biological society where millions of microbial species coexist in precise balance to regulate immune cells, synthesise essential vitamins, and communicate directly with the central nervous system via the Vagus Nerve, where 80% of signals travel upward from gut to brain. Microbes inside this cosmos produce up to 95% of the body’s serotonin and vital calming neurotransmitters like GABA.

​To nourish this living galaxy, the microbiome requires diversity, whole foods, fibre, complex carbohydrates, and fermented foods, while suffering under ultra-processed foods, refined sugars, artificial additives, and chemical preservatives. A useful guideline for grocery shopping is to choose products that an insect has already nibbled, because bugs avoid heavily poisoned food, a telling metaphor for navigating our artificial world, according to my dad.

Furthermore, aligning meals with circadian rhythms allows the gut lining to repair itself during natural fasting windows, preventing metabolic disruption and systemic inflammation. Digestion itself begins in the mind and mouth, where eating in a state of stress or distraction inhibits digestive enzymes, whereas eating mindfully and chewing thoroughly activates the parasympathetic nervous system for optimal nutrient absorption.

​When this inner universe falls into dysbiosis due to poor diet, chronic stress, or unaddressed emotional trauma, the systemic consequences are severe. Modern neuro-gastroenterology links gut breakdown directly to systemic inflammation, cognitive fragmentation, severe anxiety, major depression, complex personality disorders, and psychotic spectrum illnesses like schizophrenia. An unanchored gut creates an unstable, reactive, and restless mind, trapping an individual in survival mode. Consider this simple reality: when you are constipated for days, you cannot think clearly or maintain deep focus because your gut lining is compromised and leaking toxins throughout your body. This is precisely what we are doing to our environment. Chronically congested and overburdened, the Earth is now suffering from a disease spreading through it, much like malignant cells destroying a host. Without an inner biological foundation, we cannot cultivate peace or emotional intelligence, leaving us unable to maintain harmony within ourselves, our partners, or our families.

Our internal ecosystem reflects the external ecosystem. Humans often act as though non-human life exists merely for human consumption or convenience, failing to see that every living organism holds up a pillar of our shared existence. Consider the humble honeybee, a single insect species that quietly sustains our world through pollination. If pollinators like bees were to vanish, global agriculture would collapse within years, triggering a catastrophic domino effect of lost crops, failing livestock feed, and severe global famine.

The bee does not seek recognition, status, or dominance; it simply fulfils its Svadharma, keeping human civilisation alive in the process. From soil microbes and forest fungi to street animals and pollinators, every creature is part of a delicate web, and when we harm animals or poison habitats, we sever the very lifelines that keep humanity alive.

​Unhealed Parents: The First Bully and the Roots of Personality Pathology

​An unstable mind in the home transforms domestic space into a breeding ground for generational trauma. Long before a child steps into a classroom, their emotional reality is shaped by their domestic environment, where an unhealed parent is often a child’s very first bully.

When parents carry unaddressed emotional wounds, chronic stress, or unexamined toxicity, they unconsciously project their insecurity onto their children through criticism, emotional withdrawal, unpredictable outbursts, or conditional love.

​Through this early conditioning, children learn the mechanics of power, fear, and vulnerability. They absorb this dynamic and adapt in one of two ways: they either learn to become the bully to protect themselves from feeling powerless, or they adapt to being bullied, carrying a subconscious template of victimhood into adulthood as chronic people-pleasers. Tragically, many children raised in these environments develop severe personality pathology, turning outward as narcissists, emotional manipulators, or gold diggers who perpetuate the cycle.

However, a conscious few utilise this pain differently by deeply understanding the nature of their wounds, choosing to transmute trauma into empathy, and growing up to dress the wounds of others rather than inflicting them.

​The chain reaction

​Human consciousness operates as an interconnected ecosystem where an unanchored mind and gut dysbiosis ripple outward into unhealed parenting and dysfunctional homes. This domestic breakdown fosters an unconscious generation characterised by narcissism, bullying, and personality pathologies.

As these individuals step into society, their internal disconnection manifests as short-sighted exploitation of nature and humanity through deforestation, toxic food systems, and systemic corruption. Ultimately, this macrocosmic reflection of micro-cosmic internal disorder produces ecological disasters, landslides, accelerated global warming, and traumatised families, perpetuating the cycle endlessly.

​When individuals lack emotional processing and internal grounding, domestic life breaks down. Marriages crumble under unhealed childhood trauma, communication failures, and the normalisation of infidelity or superficial distractions, which is hugely in trend these days, pursued under the guise of being modern. This leads to Pakhe individuals, Pakhe family roots, and ultimately a Pakhe nation.

Children raised in trauma-heavy homes, where emotional, mental, financial, or psychological abuse is present, absorb this instability, fracturing their developing nervous systems. When these children grow into leaders, engineers, policymakers, and citizens, they make decisions from disconnection. They build roads without ecological foresight, strip hillsides of native roots for short-term profit, and consume resources either from nature or from other human beings mindlessly to escape reality, directly driving criminal mindsets, cheaters, corrupt individuals, professionals and systemic collapse, leading to a corrupt society and corrupt nation. Global warming and natural disasters are simply the macrocosmic mirror of humanity’s micro-cosmic internal disorder.

The foundation of the “Grihastha Yogi”

​Real, enduring transformation begins only when we understand truth at a fundamental level and choose to change ourselves. We align our energy through deliberate internal steps, beginning with periods of solitude and self-observation to quiet external noise, introspect, and understand our internal landscape. This is paired with a systemic lifestyle shift in what, when, and how we eat, aligning our thought processes (Bichara) to generate love within and release regulating hormones from the gut that spread harmony outward.

​Furthermore, we must treat the home as a sanctuary by actively choosing to build and rebuild our marriage every day through accountability, honest communication, quiet dedication, surrender and exposing each other to mutual vulnerability and trusting that we are protected despite the exposure. Continuously nurturing a partnership quiets a reactive mind, pulls us out of survival mode, and lowers cortisol to promote physical health. Spiritually, true commitment is a practice of surrender and unconditional love that reflects the divine cycle of creation, preservation, and transformation [GOD: Brahma ( Generator ) , Vishnu ( Operator ) , and Maheshora ( destroyer/ transformer ) ]. Socially, a secure home creates a healthy baseline that allows us to interact with the world with empathy, clear boundaries, and deep-rooted confidence.

​When we intentionally build our domestic foundation, we give future generations a template of stability, emotional intelligence, and self-love. Ego must stay out of marriage for a simple reason: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Just as a country suffering from civil war is powerless to make progress nationally or internationally, a family torn apart by ego loses its capacity to thrive or heal or be able to get out to the world and do something great. The home is our first nation, and peace within these four walls is the prerequisite for all outer strength. By establishing ethical boundaries, mastering the discipline of saying no, and protecting our homes from internal enemies like ego, anger, rage, revenge, etc., we become a Grihastha Yogi. We raise conscious, grounded individuals who do not need to exploit people, animals, nature or partners with wandering eyes and cheating tendencies to feel complete. We consciously breed an individual who understands the responsibility that leaves no room for excuses once we choose to bring children into the world.

​A paradigm shift in education

​To sustain this shift across generations, we must reimagine how we educate our children. Addressing Honourable PM Balendra Shah and Honourable Education Minister Sasmit Pokhrel, education must transcend job preparation to cultivate the whole human being by integrating foundational wisdom with modern science.

​A reimagined 12-pillar curriculum must introduce age-appropriate psychology and nervous system regulation early in life, while restoring the essentials of childhood through unstructured play, restorative sleep, and nutrient-dense whole foods. It must teach children how to think through deep introspection rather than what to think through rote memorisation.

Linguistic architecture should be taught through Sanskrit as a precise mathematical and acoustic science that sharpens cognitive processing and neuroplasticity. Ecological literacy must be grounded in farming, soil science, and the lesson of the honeybee to teach fundamental interdependence. Sound therapy and Nada Yoga through music and intentional prayer can harmonise brain hemispheres and stimulate the vagus nerve.

​Ayurvedic functional nutrition will teach children how food (Aahar) affects their microbiome and innate healing capacity, while daily Yoga practice regulates the nervous system through conscious breath and somatic awareness (Bichara and Aacharan). Rigorous Bigyan (modern science) and mathematics will build analytical logic, while Jyotish (astrology) and Vastu introduce awareness of cosmic cycles, spatial balance, and karmic choices.

Finally, financial education must reframe money as an energy of exchange, ethical earnings and responsibility, and abundance rather than an instrument of greedy hoarding or superficial status. Equipping children with this integrated wisdom cultivates conscious, responsible individuals capable of facing real-world challenges with resilience, ultimately providing them with true liberation and non-attachment.

​Realising “Aham Brahmasmi”

​This integrated approach culminates in the realisation of the Vedic Mahavidya: Aham Brahmasmi (I am the Divine Infinite Consciousness).

When an individual recognises that the divine source of life resides within themselves, within their family, within the microscopic bacteria in their gut, within the honeybee pollinating a flower, and within nature as a whole, the desire to destroy or exploit another being vanishes. They no longer seek superficial validation, nor do they treat their homes, animals, or the Earth as disposable.

This is how we cultivate a conscious child, society, and world.

​In the end

​We cannot repair our climate, prevent landslides, or build a resilient nation while our internal lives and domestic foundations remain fractured. The journey back to sustainability begins within our intimate internal and external environments. Nature’s law remains immutable: only trees anchored by deep, unyielding roots endure the storm.

By shedding the superficiality of modern Pakhe living, Pakhe thoughts and actions, we restore our physical health, shield our children from trauma, honour all living beings, and heal the world within and around us, ultimately guiding us toward true liberation (Moksha).

​Crucially, liberation does not require renouncing the world as a Sadhu or abandoning worldly duties. True liberation is achieved by stepping fully into our responsibilities: growing, evolving, and sharing wisdom from every moment of existence. Human life is a continuous dynamic evolution where the person you were at ten should not be who you are in your twenties, and the mindset you held in your thirties must evolve before you reach your forties and fifties.

​If we remain stagnant, refusing to learn, adapt, expand our consciousness, and cultivate wisdom, we squander the precious gift of human birth. Even the Divine manifests in human form (Avatara) to restore balance and drive systemic change, because the human incarnation alone is uniquely blessed with the higher cognitive capacity to discern right from wrong, exercise free will, and reap the karmic fruits of those choices. Yet, for this higher brain to function with clarity and moral courage, we must return to where consciousness takes root: our gut health. When we heal the inner microbiome cosmos and anchor the Gut-Brain Axis, we clear the biological fog, allowing the human mind to fulfil its highest cosmic purpose.

​This profound reality exposes the core of our modern turmoil, illuminating the path forward: where human effort ceases, we bow before a greater, absolute truth, knowing that when logic stops, the extraordinary takes over. To truly liberate is the ultimate meaning of love, and within that love, we experience GOD: the eternal cycle of the Generator (Brahma), the Operator (Vishnu), and the Destroyer or Transformer (Maheshar). Through this divine alignment, we make the conscious choice to choose love, transform, heal, outgrow our limitations, and set ourselves, our environment, and our loved ones free. This is how we and let our loved ones achieve Nirvana and Moksha. And this is the ultimate goal/ truth of any living or non-living beings that reincarnate on earth.  You, me, dogs, crocodiles, snakes, trees, etc.

title.rendered: 29 trainees successfully climb 6,355-metre Danga Peak after mountaineering training

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Twenty-nine trainees and six instructors from the Nepal Mountaineering Association (NMA) have successfully climbed 6,355-metre Danga Peak in the Kanchenjunga region after completing professional mountaineering guide training.

The team completed the association’s regular training programme, titled ‘Summer Skills for Professional Mountain Guides’, before making the successful ascent of the peak.

The Nepal Mountaineering Association, which has contributed to Nepal’s mountain tourism sector for the past 53 years, has been conducting various mountaineering-related training programmes for many years.

For the past three years, the association has been conducting the summer skills training based on a 1,696-hour curriculum approved by the Council for Technical Education and Vocational Training (CTEVT).

The second phase of the programme requires trainees to undergo practical training on a mountain at an altitude of 6,000 metres or above.

This year’s training was conducted at Danga Peak in partnership with the Sustainable Tourism Project (STP). A total of 33 trainees, including one foreign participant, took part in the programme.

The trainees first completed rock-climbing and other theoretical classes in Kathmandu before travelling to Danga Peak for glacier training in a real mountain environment.

After more than a week of glacier training at the peak, the trainees and instructors successfully climbed Danga Peak.

Trainees lead the climb

According to chief instructor Sarki Sherpa, trainees take the lead during the mountain expedition after receiving around 40 days of theoretical and practical training in Kathmandu and on the relevant mountain.

“After teaching practical and theoretical skills for around 40 days in Kathmandu and on the mountain, the trainees are taken for the summit. The entire ascent is led by the trainees themselves,” Sherpa said.

He said instructors observe and assess the trainees’ work and skills during the climb and intervene only when they make a mistake.

“Their proficiency is reflected in the results of the skills they demonstrate during the training and ascent,” he said.

The association considers mountain climbing an important component of the training programme. Trainees are required to apply the skills they have learned while leading the ascent.

The programme is designed to prepare them to work professionally as mountain guides on other mountains in Nepal.

Training linked to employment

Instructor and NMA central executive committee member Dawatasi Sherpa said the programme aims to produce skilled human resources for Nepal’s mountain tourism industry.

“We have been organising this training with the objective of producing skilled manpower for Nepal’s mountain tourism. It is a major achievement for us that such a large number of trainees successfully climbed the mountain,” he said.

He said the success of the trainees could help meet the demand for skilled workers in Nepal’s mountain tourism sector and contribute to making mountain tourism safer and more reliable.

The training programme is also directly linked to employment opportunities for Nepali youths.

Mountain guides working on Nepal’s mountains require the black, blue or red books issued by the association. Trainees who successfully complete this programme are eligible to obtain the blue book directly.

The qualification enables them to work as professional mountain guides on mountains across Nepal.

Another instructor, Sanjeev Gurung, said the programme was important from several perspectives, particularly because of its connection to employment and the development of Nepal’s mountain tourism sector.

“The most visible outcomes are employment for all trainees who successfully complete the programme and the strengthening of Nepal’s mountain tourism sector,” Gurung said.

He added that the association should continue the programme and that support from all stakeholders was necessary.

Multiple stages to become a professional mountain guide

The government-recognised training curriculum covers several components.

Only trainees who have successfully completed the basic skills training are eligible to participate in the summer skills programme.

Those who complete the summer skills training can then participate in the winter skills programme.

They must also complete training in areas including long-line rescue, heli-marshal operations and first aid before receiving certification as professional mountain guides.

In a notice issued Thursday by the college’s principal and hostel superintendent, it was stated that, due to the current academic and institutional situation, a formal request had been made to the Institute of Medicine (IOM) and Tribhuvan University to recall the first-year PG resident doctors of the 2082 academic session from the college.

They have been directed to hand over any college property in their possession to the hostel administration or the administrative office.

Similarly, the notice states that resident doctors must complete the necessary handover process within the specified period and remove their personal belongings from the residential premises.

title.rendered: The first international flight from Pokhara brings home a long-awaited change

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 24

For decades, residents of Pokhara had waited for the day when they could fly abroad from their own city. That day arrived on Wednesday evening, when a Flydubai Boeing aircraft from Dubai landed at Pokhara International Airport, beginning the airport’s first regular international commercial service.

The aircraft touched down at 6.18pm carrying 113 passengers. It was welcomed with a water salute as a large crowd gathered outside the main terminal building.

Some had come to welcome relatives returning from abroad. Others were there to see off family members beginning journeys overseas. For many, the arrival meant they would no longer have to travel to Kathmandu to begin or end an international journey.

The aircraft, operated by a crew that included Nepali pilot Sarbajit Yadav, departed for Dubai at 7.54pm with 152 passengers on board.

According to the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, the flight from Dubai to Pokhara took four hours and 30 minutes, while the return journey took four hours and 50 minutes.

The service establishes a direct air connection between Pokhara and the United Arab Emirates, giving the city access to Dubai, one of the world’s major aviation hubs.

But at the airport on Wednesday, the significance of the new route was most apparent in the experiences of the passengers and their families.

A shorter journey home

Tara Sinjali Magar, from Myagdi, had spent five years working in Dubai. When she walked out of the international arrivals hall and saw the crowd waiting outside, she was surprised. Returning to Nepal was already a source of happiness. But being able to land at an airport in her own province meant even more.

“I have returned to the country after five years. I am extremely happy to be able to land at Pokhara airport,” she said.

For Raju Parajuli, from Syangja, the new route offered a different kind of relief. Parajuli has spent 30 years working in Bahrain. During those years, he used Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu dozens of times. After landing there, he would still have to find a hotel, travel to his village and wait to meet his family.

“When I landed in Kathmandu from Bahrain, I had to find a hotel. It was difficult for my family to come from the village,” he said.

He remembered wanting to see his mother as soon as he arrived but being separated from her by the journey from Kathmandu.

“As soon as you land at the airport, you want to see your mother. At that time, if I told my mother to come, she would wait there while we travelled by car. There were no telephones. There were difficulties with so many things.”

Now, he said, that experience had changed.

“I am extremely happy to be able to land at my own place of residence now,” he said.

He hopes the international service will continue.

“Pokhara will develop now too. This must operate regularly,” Parajuli said.

Suman Gharti, from Tanahun, arrived from Romania via Dubai. His relatives were waiting for him at the airport.

Naresh, who had returned home after working in Dubai, was preparing to go abroad again. This time, he said, he wanted to begin his journey from Pokhara rather than Kathmandu.

“International flights must now operate regularly. I will return from here,” he said.

Rugi Timilsina, from Malepatan in Kaski, arrived from Norway via Dubai after spending time with her children. She had not expected that she would be able to arrive on an international flight at an airport in her own district.

“I was very happy. I had never thought I would come on this very flight,” she said.

Passengers arriving through Dubai from Europe, the United States and the Gulf countries expressed a similar hope: that the service would continue.

Arrivals and departures

The excitement in the arrivals hall was matched by a different emotion in the departures area.

Devka Gautam was preparing to travel to Britain via Dubai to study. Her grandmother had come to the airport to see her off and broke down in tears.

Family members tried to comfort her. Devka was fed yoghurt before departure, and photographs were taken with the name of Pokhara International Airport visible behind them.

For the family, the photograph marked the beginning of a new journey.

Nabin Gurung, from Lekhnath, has worked in Dubai for 15 years. He was home on holiday and had deliberately waited for the first international flight from Pokhara to return to Dubai.

“I had been waiting specifically to take the first flight from Pokhara,” he said.

Regina Kumal, from Rupa Rural Municipality, was travelling to Britain for her studies. For her, being able to travel from Pokhara to Dubai and onwards was a matter of convenience.

Vivek Shrestha, lead singer of the band Kandara, and musician Sunil Thapa had also arrived on the first international flight after returning from the United States, where they had completed a musical programme.

They had waited for the first international flight to return to Pokhara and saw the occasion as part of a much larger change for the city.

“This was a dream for the people of Pokhara. We had the historic opportunity to witness that dream,” Shrestha said.

A five-decade project

The idea of flying directly abroad from Pokhara is not new.

Discussion of an international airport in the city dates back nearly five decades. Pokhara International Airport was inaugurated on January 1, 2023, by Pushpa Kamal Dahal, who was then prime minister.

But for a long period after its inauguration, the airport did not have regular international commercial flights.

There were charter flights. Himalaya Airlines attempted to operate commercial services to several cities in China, while charter flights also operated from Pokhara to China and Bhutan.

Without a regular international service, questions continued to be raised about the airport’s future.

There had also been repeated concerns over India’s refusal to grant the necessary air routes for flights serving Pokhara. Some residents feared the airport might remain largely limited to domestic services.

The Flydubai route has changed that situation, at least for now.

What the flight could mean for tourism

Local officials and tourism businesses see the new connection as an opportunity to expand Pokhara’s links with international visitors and Nepalis working abroad.

Pokhara Mayor Dhanraj Acharya, who was at the airport to welcome passengers from Dubai, described the service as a historic beginning.

“There has been a historic beginning that has dispelled the uncertainty over whether international flights would operate or not,” he said.

Although charter flights had previously operated, he said, there had been no regular commercial international service.

“The pilot of Flydubai is also Nepali. Another 153 people are now going from here. It is a matter of happiness. We are all happy. Congratulations to everyone,” Acharya said.

Tourism entrepreneurs and representatives of various organisations also gathered at the airport under the leadership of the Pokhara Tourism Council to welcome the arriving passengers.

Santosh Pokharel, a member of the Nepal Tourism Board, said the regular service followed continued efforts by the Nepal government, Tourism Minister Khadkaraj Paudel ‘Ganes’, Pokhara Metropolitan City and local organisations and stakeholders.

For tourism entrepreneur Gopi Bhattarai, the flight removed some of the uncertainty surrounding the airport.

“There had been doubts about whether international flights would operate from Pokhara at all, and whether large aircraft would even be able to come here,” he said. “Today is a breakthrough day for the entire Gandaki region.”

Tourism, he said, depended on air and other forms of connectivity.

“The hope of tourism is connectivity. This flight must operate regularly, and everyone must contribute from their respective positions to make that happen,” Bhattarai said.

Pomanarayan Shrestha, president of the Pokhara Tourism Council, said the direct connection with Dubai had expanded the city’s possibilities.

Dubai is connected by air to more than 250 destinations around the world, he said, potentially making it easier for people travelling from Pokhara to reach other countries.

“There is a large workforce from Gandaki and surrounding areas in the Middle East. We can bring tourists from there and Nepali people living abroad to Pokhara,” he said.

Regular flights could benefit tourism businesses as well as passengers, he said.

The question of continuity

The airport’s history makes the question of what happens next particularly important.

During its construction, industrialists, businesspeople, civil society groups and local residents organised protests and pressure campaigns.

The airport was built by a Chinese construction company at a cost of more than 22 billion rupees. Although it eventually came into operation, the absence of regular international flights led to continuing questions about the use of the investment and infrastructure.

Residents have also followed issues including geopolitical complications, international air routes, operational challenges at the airport and the federal government’s role in international coordination.

The experience of Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa, where international flights began but failed to continue regularly, has added to those concerns.

Flydubai has opened bookings for daily flights from Sept. 7 for at least six months, according to the information provided. Hotels, restaurants and adventure tourism businesses in Pokhara have also announced discounts and promotional schemes to attract passengers and support the new service.

Flydubai is offering passengers travelling to Pokhara a fare discount of up to 5,000 rupees compared with Kathmandu, according to the information provided.

The first flight brought 113 passengers to Pokhara. Another 152 left for Dubai that evening.

For a city that had spent decades waiting for a direct international connection, the significance of the day was clear.

But whether Wednesday’s flight becomes the beginning of a sustained international service will depend on its continuity, government efforts, passenger numbers, tourism promotion and the airport’s ability to connect with more international destinations.

title.rendered: AI: A food of knowledge, a drought of wisdom

content.rendered:
Some stories in human history do more than reflect their own time. They continue to speak to generations that follow because they capture something enduring about human nature.

One such story is The Sorcerer’s Apprentice.

The apprentice brings a broom to life and orders it to carry water, hoping to make his work easier. The broom neither tires nor complains. Delighted, the apprentice believes he has freed himself from repetitive labour.

But that is where the problem begins. He has learned how to make the broom start, but not how to make it stop. The water keeps rising, the situation slips beyond his control, and every attempt to stop the broom only makes things worse. In the end, the power he has created proves greater than his ability to govern it.

This centuries-old story has an unexpectedly close connection to today’s debate about artificial intelligence.

Every transformative technology arrives with two competing narratives.

The first is one of hope. AI could accelerate medical breakthroughs, compressing decades of research into years. It could help teachers personalise education, help farmers increase yields and help doctors identify illnesses earlier.

The second is one of fear. AI could displace millions of jobs, allow misinformation to spread at unprecedented scale, centralise power in the hands of a few and eventually produce systems whose behaviour we do not fully understand.

There is truth in both narratives.

The printing press democratised knowledge. Electricity expanded productive capacity. The internet connected billions of people. Every transformative technology has reshaped society while creating new problems. AI will probably be no different.

A few weeks ago, I had the opportunity to use Claude AI at work. Tasks that had sat on a “one day” list for years were completed within two weeks. Work I had expected to take months moved much faster. Research accelerated, drafts improved and analysis became more structured.

My first reaction was amazement. I had not imagined so much could be done with so little time and effort. But the excitement did not last.

I had assumed that becoming more productive would mean I could finally sit back. Instead, I found myself asking different questions.

Productivity had risen, but so had a subtle unease. If AI can compress months of work into weeks, what is my real contribution? Is expertise about possessing information, or about knowing what to do with it? Is value created by producing an answer, or by making the right decision in the right context?

These are not merely personal questions. Millions of knowledge workers may be wrestling with the same uncertainty.

For much of human history, knowledge was scarce. Those who possessed more of it held greater influence. Expertise was limited, research was slow, and gathering information was itself a competitive advantage.

That world is changing. Today, anyone with access to generative AI can retrieve, organise and synthesise the equivalent of thousands of pages within minutes. The question is no longer simply who has information. The question is where value lies when information becomes abundant.

There is a related challenge. When generative AI is this accessible, almost anyone can sound like an expert. A few well-phrased questions can produce answers that appear authoritative, confident and complete.

But AI answers the question it is asked. It does not necessarily know the situation behind the question. It does not know why a decision matters, who it will affect or which constraints were never included in the prompt. It can produce a polished answer without knowing whether that answer actually fits the context.

The danger, therefore, is not simply that people will stop knowing things. It is that fluency will be mistaken for understanding.

A calculator can perform mathematics, but it cannot make life decisions. GPS can show a route, but it cannot choose the destination. AI can present options, but the responsibility for choosing between them remains human.

That may make judgement one of the most valuable skills of the AI age.

The ability to ask the right questions in complex situations, make decisions despite incomplete information, understand human context and recognise consequences may matter more as machines become better at producing information and possible answers.

This shift is not limited to individuals. It is already playing out at the level of organisations.

Every organisation is asking the same basic question: will AI make us more effective? The answer, in many areas, is clearly yes.

Reports, code, analysis, legal drafting and customer service can increasingly be produced faster and at lower cost. If one employee can use AI to accomplish work that previously required several people, organisations will have strong incentives to rethink how work is organised.

The change may not happen overnight. It could begin with AI acting as an assistant, making individual workers more productive. Over time, however, organisations may ask whether they still need the same number of employees, whether vacancies need to be filled, whether teams can be smaller and whether some processes can operate with minimal human involvement.

The outcome is not predetermined. Technology has repeatedly eliminated some forms of work while creating others. Telephone operators largely disappeared, while software engineers emerged. Typewriter specialists faded, while the digital economy created entirely new professions.

Something similar may happen with AI, although its scale and speed could make the transition different from previous technological shifts.

The implications extend beyond individual jobs and organisations. The same capabilities are now shaping how nations compete.

AI itself is neither inherently good nor bad. Fire can cook food or destroy a home. The same technological capabilities that help protect a hospital can also be used to identify vulnerabilities. Systems that strengthen national infrastructure can also expose ways to compromise it.

AI is therefore no longer merely a commercial asset. It is increasingly a strategic one.

A technology that can accelerate scientific research, strengthen cybersecurity, increase economic productivity and support national decision-making can influence economic, scientific and geopolitical power for decades to come.

The United States, China, Europe and countries in the Middle East are all investing heavily in AI. That creates another dilemma. “Let’s stop and think” may sound like the obvious response to a technology this powerful, but it is difficult to put into practice when companies and countries fear that moving more slowly could leave them behind.

The result is a familiar tension. The greater the potential of AI becomes, the stronger the incentive to develop it. And the stronger the incentive to develop it, the more important it becomes to consider how that power will be governed.

Does more intelligence automatically mean a better future? Perhaps not.

AI can analyse information, solve complex problems and operate at unprecedented speed. But intelligence does not automatically provide compassion, morality or purpose. A highly capable system can pursue the wrong objective just as efficiently as the right one.

Intelligence and wisdom are not the same thing.

That may be one of the most important lessons the AI age teaches us.

In The Sorcerer’s Apprentice, the problem was never the broom itself. Nor was it simply the power the apprentice had discovered.

The problem began when his ability to create power outgrew his ability to control it. That is where the real question about AI begins.

Not simply whether we can build systems that are more capable, faster and more intelligent, but whether our ability to govern them, understand their consequences and exercise judgement can keep pace.

The challenge of the AI age may therefore be less about whether machines can produce more answers.

It may be about whether humans can continue to ask the right questions. In the age of AI, information is no longer scarce. Clear thinking is.

title.rendered: Minister Badi urges respect for dignity and privacy of disaster-affected citizens

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Minister for Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, and Social Security Sita Badi has urged that the dignity and privacy of disaster-affected citizens be respected.

Speaking at Thursday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, Minister Badi called for a stop to the practice of photographing or filming victims without their consent in the name of relief distribution and then publicising it on social media, and directed special attention to the rights and protection of children.

Minister Badi said that, so far, 6,459 people affected by the floods have received psychosocial first aid.

According to her, 155 personnel and security staff deployed for rescue work have been given stress management training, while an additional 102 people have been oriented for affected-friendly service delivery.

Speaking on the role of non-governmental organisations in disaster response, Minister Badi said the Social Welfare Council’s project approval process has been made faster. Since Bhadau 15, 149 new projects have been approved. The ministry said relief materials worth roughly Rs 504.2 million from international NGOs and over Rs 205.7 million from national organisations have been mobilised.

Minister Badi cautioned against activities during relief distribution that could humiliate victims.

“When helping victims, we shouldn’t be rubbing salt in their wounds; we need to create an environment that helps heal those wounds,” she said.

She urged everyone in particular not to publish material that reveals children’s identities, and not to use demeaning language targeting women and victims.

To reduce the risk of human trafficking and gender-based violence that could arise from treating disaster risk as an opportunity, monitoring has been increased at border points and holding centres in coordination with the Home Ministry and Nepal Police.

The ministry said it has not limited its priorities to relief and rescue alone, but has also prioritised programs for the rehabilitation, livelihoods, and long-term social protection of those affected.

title.rendered: Civil society urges government to publish comprehensive disaster action plan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Members of civil society and human rights activists have demanded that the government immediately make public a detailed action plan for rehabilitating flood victims, rebuilding damaged infrastructure, and reducing loss of life and property from future disasters.

In a joint statement, they expressed sorrow over the damage caused in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading by flooding that followed a glacial collapse in the Lirung area of the Langtang Himal on Bhadau 10, with the flood traveling through Tibet’s Kyirong area via the Lhende Khola.

The statement notes complaints of delays from affected communities during search, rescue, relief, temporary shelter, and rehabilitation efforts following the flood, and claims there was insufficient coordination among government mechanisms. It also urges the government to make the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority’s role more effective.

Citing the Authority, the statement says the flood affected 32,936 people, killed 1,451, left 5,745 people unaccounted for, and left 1,200 children having lost both parents.

Civil society members and human rights activists said that, given the rising risk in the Himalayan region due to climate change, early warning systems, information dissemination, and risk-reduction programs must be prioritised. The statement also notes an assessment by international organisations that 47 glacial lakes in the Himalayan region remain at risk of bursting.

They have called on the government to publish a comprehensive action plan, including an early warning system, for rehabilitating those affected by the flood, rebuilding physical infrastructure, and reducing loss of life and property from future natural disasters.

Call for PM to raise the disaster issue at the UN

The statement urges that, when Prime Minister Balendra Shah addresses the UN’s 81st General Assembly, he present to the international community the disasters Nepal has faced, along with efforts on search and rescue, relief, rehabilitation, and reconstruction.

It also notes that Nepal has claimed USD 20 million in compensation from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage for damage caused by the flood and climate change, and urges the government to push for a fair resolution of that claim.

The statement also calls for an appeal, through the General Assembly, for international grant support for victim rehabilitation, establishing information centers, building a cross-border information network, and rebuilding damaged physical infrastructure.

It states that Nepal’s climate-related compensation claim should be presented on the basis of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, and that the international community should be reminded of the outcomes of Nepal’s various national climate initiatives, including the Rio Earth Summit, the Kyoto Protocol, and the Paris Agreement.

The statement is signed by 17 people, including Abhishek Adhikari, Ayush Baral, Indu Tuladhar, Krishna Gautam, Dinesh Tripathi, Nitu Pokharel, Bhagawati Adhikari, Monika Niraula, Ramesh Adhikari, Riyav Bania, Savitri Thapa, Shiva Khakurel, Shyam Kumari Sah, Sushil B.K., Sushil Pyakurel, Som Niraula, and Shobhakar Budhathoki.

title.rendered: Himalaya Airlines resumes direct Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu flights

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Himalaya Airlines will resume direct flights on the Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu route.

Himalaya has announced to resume regular direct flight service from Tribhuvan International Airport to Pudong International Airport, Shanghai, starting Monday, September 28.

With the resumption of this service, Himalaya Airlines will become the only airline operating regular direct flights on the Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu route. This will also restore a strategically important air link between Nepal and Shanghai, one of China’s major global metropolises.

The Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu flight will offer passengers convenient, direct air travel between Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, and Shanghai, China’s largest city and a leading global financial centre.

The company says the Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu route will further strengthen Himalaya Airlines’ commitment to providing convenient, safe, and efficient travel services to passengers. It also says the route will make an important contribution to strengthening Nepal-China bilateral relations and people-to-people contact and exchange between the two countries.

The resumption of the service at the start of Nepal’s main tourism season will further enhance the route’s strategic importance. The company says the route is expected to bring a notable increase in the number of tourists coming to Nepal from China, contributing positively to the overall hospitality and tourism sector, and will also support Nepal’s economic recovery and growth goals.

Himalaya Airlines will initially operate two flights a week on this route. Kathmandu-Shanghai flights will depart every Monday and Friday, while return flights from Shanghai to Kathmandu will operate every Tuesday and Saturday. The airline has said it will increase the number of flights in the future depending on passenger demand and load factors.

Himalaya Airlines Vice Chairman Bijay Shrestha said regular flights are set to resume on the Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu route. He said Himalaya Airlines remains committed to strengthening trade, tourism, and people-to-people ties between Nepal and China.

He said, “We have always sought out new destinations in China and continued to operate regular flights. This resumption of the Kathmandu-Shanghai-Kathmandu flight supports our airline’s goal of strengthening citizen-to-citizen relations between the two nations and promoting tourism and trade.”

Himalaya Airlines is an international airline established as a joint venture partnership company between Nepal and China. It was founded in 2014. Himalaya Airlines currently operates 4 aircraft.

Himalaya Airlines currently operates passenger flights to the United Arab Emirates, Malaysia, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bangladesh, and China in the Middle East and South Asia.

title.rendered: Tomato prices rise to 15 percent in a single day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Tomatoes have become more expensive in the market. According to data released Thursday by the Kalimati Fruits and Vegetables Market Development Committee, prices for all types of tomatoes have risen.

Today, the price of large Nepali tomatoes rose the most, up 15.38 percent. Large Nepali tomatoes, which had an average wholesale price of Rs 65 per kg on Wednesday, reached Rs 75 per kg on Thursday.

Similarly, the price of large Indian tomatoes also rose by 13.33 percent. The price of large Indian tomatoes, which stood at Rs 75 per kg the previous day, has now risen to Rs 85.

The increase was not limited to large tomatoes; small tomatoes saw a similar rise in price. The average price of local small tomatoes rose from Rs 47 per kg to Rs 55 per kg, a 15.30 percent increase.

Likewise, the committee reported that the price of tunnel-grown small tomatoes rose 12 percent, from Rs 61 per kg to Rs 68. This data from the Market Development Committee shows that tomato prices rose by Rs 7 to Rs 10 per kilogram in a single day.

title.rendered: Parliamentary hearing process begins for 13 ambassador nominees

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

The Parliamentary Hearing Committee under the Federal Parliament has begun the parliamentary hearing process for ambassadorial nominees recommended by the government for 13 countries.

A meeting of the committee held at Singha Durbar on Thursday decided to move forward with the hearing process for the proposed ambassadors.

Committee Chair Bodh Narayan Shrestha said complaints against the nominees have been invited for 10 days.

According to Shrestha, members of the public can submit information or complaints regarding any of the proposed ambassadors within 10 days from the date of publication of the notice. Complaints can be submitted electronically or through any other means, provided they include clear grounds and supporting information.

The committee has invited complaints to inform the public about the individuals nominated for the diplomatic posts and to gather any relevant information concerning their suitability.

The Cabinet, at its meeting last Friday, had recommended ambassadors for 13 countries, including India and China.

title.rendered: RSP MP demands probe after customs officer’s threats to APF SP, Home Minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

A question has been raised in parliament regarding a Kanchanpur customs officer who allegedly threatened an Armed Police Force (APF) Superintendent of Police (SP) from Kailali over the impounding of a vehicle.

Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Tika Sangroula raised the issue in the House of Representatives.

She raised the matter in parliament after it emerged that the officer had used extremely low-level, threatening language while reprimanding the SP over the vehicle’s impoundment at customs.

“That employee has openly disregarded the law, discipline, and chain of command, saying he would ‘smack’ his own departmental director-general, the Inspector General of the Armed Police Force, and even the Home Minister himself,” Sangroula said. “What does this ‘smack’ mean? Does it mean calling to threaten, meeting in person to hit, or taking away your position?”

She also asked, “If a customs officer has the capacity to threaten the Home Minister, then what exactly are we doing here in parliament?”

Saying the incident has tarnished the image of the entire state apparatus, she demanded an investigation into the audio clip in question.

title.rendered: Congress conventions concluded in 12 municipalities of Kavre; Khanikhola remains

content.rendered:
Kavrepalanchok, September 24

The Nepali Congress has completed its municipal-level conventions in 12 of Kavrepalanchok’s 13 local units. The convention in Khanikhola Rural Municipality is yet to be held.

According to Congress, Wednesday’s completed convention elected Ram Joshi as chair of Banepa Municipality. He defeated his competitor Sudhir Baidya.

Similarly, Sanjay Tamang was unanimously chosen for a second term as chair of Panchkhal Municipality.

Likewise, Ramhari Sapkota was elected unanimously as chair of Mandandeupur Municipality, while Rupak Mahat was chosen unanimously as chair of Panauti Municipality and Bidur Basnet as chair of Dhulikhel Municipality.

Similarly, Manju Shah was elected unanimously as chair of Bhumlu Rural Municipality.

Shah, the only woman elected chair among the 13 local units, had previously been a general convention delegate.

Digman Tamang was elected chair of Bethanchok Rural Municipality; Khajenchi Lama was his competitor there.

Bikulal Tamang was chosen as chair of Temal Rural Municipality, Dorje Lama as chair of Roshi Rural Municipality, Sagar Moktan for a second term as chair of Mahabharat Rural Municipality, Krishna Lama Bomjan as chair of Namobuddha Municipality, and Rajesh Gautam as chair of Chaurideurali Rural Municipality.

title.rendered: Deuba faction appoints coordinators in 56 districts for general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 24

Nepali Congress former President Sher Bahadur Deuba’s faction has appointed coordinators in 56 districts for the party’s 15th General Convention.

Dr Shashank Koirala, coordinator of the 15th Central General Convention Preparation Committee formed for the convention, has appointed coordinators across 56 districts in the seven provinces.

According to Deuba faction’s Chundevi contact office, coordinators have so far been appointed in 9 districts of Koshi Province, 11 of Bagmati Province, 8 of Gandaki Province, 12 of Lumbini Province, 8 of Karnali Province, and 8 of Sudurpashchim Province.

In Koshi, responsibility for coordinating the convention has been given to Dekendra Kumar Tamang in Panchthar, Krishna Humagain in Jhapa, Ramkumar GC in Sankhuwasabha, Dharmaraj Rai in Bhojpur, Subhash Poudel in Morang (co-coordinator Binayak Panta), Rojan Rai in Khotang, Balgovinda Rajbhandari in Okhaldhunga, and Basant Basnet in Udayapur.

The contact office also said Govinda Chamling has been given the co-coordinator role in Udayapur. The Deuba faction still needs to appoint coordinators in Taplejung, Ilam, Terhathum, Dhankuta, Sunsari, and Solukhumbu in Koshi Province.

In Bagmati Province, coordinators appointed include Tarakumar Khadka in Dolakha (co-coordinator Jayaraj Shrestha), Jit Bahadur Magar in Ramechhap, Upendra Lamsal in Rasuwa, Gopal Bik in Dhading, Shriram Shrestha in Nuwakot, Lalkaji Tamang in Sindhupalchok, Milan Shrestha in Chitwan, Bhim Lama in Makwanpur, Durlabh Thapa in Bhaktapur, Sudarshan Ghimire in Lalitpur, and Jaikrishna Maharjan in Kathmandu.

Coordinators are yet to be appointed in Sindhuli and Kavrepalanchok in Bagmati Province. The Deuba group has not appointed coordinators in any district of Madhesh Province.

In Gandaki Province, Bhugol Thapa in Gorkha, Ram Krishna Kandel in Lamjung, Rishiram Kafle in Kaski, Nachong Gurung in Manang, Ramkrishna Malla in Parbat, Hira Bahadur Pun Magar in Myagdi, Sagar Chhantyal in Baglung, and Ashok Bastakoti in Nawalpur have taken on convention responsibilities for the Deuba group. Coordinators have not yet been chosen for Tanahun, Mustang, and Syangja in Gandaki Province.

In Lumbini Province, Bikas Ghimire in Nawalparasi, Gunakhar Bhurtel in Rupandehi, Abdul Mannan Khan in Kapilvastu (co-coordinator Khursed Ahmad Khan), and Madhav Nepal in Palpa have been given responsibility.

Similarly, Laxman Pandey has been made coordinator in Arghakhanchi, Bed Bahadur Thapa in Gulmi, Datta Bahadur Basnet in Rukum East, Man Bahadur Khatri in Rolpa, Ishwori Singh Bista in Pyuthan, Gopal Raj Sharma in Dang, Krishna Karki in Banke, and Jagga Prasad Pande in Bardiya.

In Karnali Province, coordinators have been appointed as follows: Deu Prasad Budha in Dolpa, Hem Budhathapa in Jumla, Karna Rawal in Mugu, Surya Bahadur Shahi in Humla, Matrika Singh in Kalikot, Raj Jung Shah in Jajarkot, Minbahadur Bishwakarma (Milan) in Dailekh, and Lalit Bhattarai in Surkhet. Coordinators are yet to be appointed in Rukum West and Salyan.

title.rendered: Asian Games women’s kabaddi: Nepal loses to Chinese Taipei

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Nepal lost its second match of the women’s kabaddi competition at the 20th Asian Games, falling to Chinese Taipei.

In the match held Wednesday afternoon at Tokai Citizen Gymnasium in Japan, Nepal was defeated by Chinese Taipei 37-18.

The first half ended level at 13-13. However, Nepal’s performance dropped off badly in the second half, conceding the half 24-5 and losing the match 37-18.

Nepal had defeated Thailand in its first match, while Chinese Taipei had beaten Sri Lanka.

The 8-team kabaddi competition is divided into groups of 4 nations. Nepal’s group includes Thailand, Sri Lanka, and Chinese Taipei.

Nepal will now play its final group-stage match against Sri Lanka on Thursday, after which its qualification for the semifinals will be determined.

title.rendered: Congress leadership unanimous in 9 municipalities of Rolpa

content.rendered:
Rolpa, September 24

The Nepali Congress has completed its conventions in 9 of Rolpa’s 10 local units. In the remaining one, the convention could not be completed within the scheduled time.

Election Officer Sudip Gautam said that in all 9 municipalities, 21-member working committees, including the chair, women’s and men’s vice-chairs, secretary, joint secretary, and other members, were elected unanimously.

“We have completed conventions in about 90 percent of Rolpa’s local units. Only 10 percent, meaning one local unit, was unable to hold its convention,” he said.

Chair in the 9 municipalities

Ram Bahadur Budhathoki was elected chair in Rolpa Municipality, Roshan Giri in Sunilsmriti Rural Municipality, Mati Pun in Lungri Rural Municipality, Harka Ram Budha Magar in Sunchhahari Rural Municipality, Chetlal Khatri in Runtigadhi Rural Municipality, Prem Prakash Pun in Triveni Rural Municipality, Krishna Wali in Ganga Dev Rural Municipality, Pashupati Gharti Magar in Madi Rural Municipality, and Kul Bahadur Gharti Magar in Paribartan Rural Municipality.

However, the convention could not be held in Thabang Rural Municipality. Nepali Congress Rolpa Secretary Sher Bahadur Thapa said the convention in Thabang could not take place due to certain problems. “We completed conventions in about 90 percent of local units on Wednesday. In the 9 completed units, the chair and other office-bearers were elected unanimously. In one local unit, the convention could not be held within the scheduled time due to problems,” Thapa said.

It has been said that the convention in Thabang will be held by Thursday or Friday.

Under the Congress’s 15th General Convention process, the regional convention is scheduled for September 26.

title.rendered: Koshi Province on high alert as heavy rain warning triggers flood preparedness

Physical Infrastructure Development Minister Jeeban Acharya said instructions had been given for effective coordination with local levels and other stakeholder agencies for rescue and relief work that might be needed in the event of natural disasters caused by the rain.

Minister Acharya directed increased monitoring of at-risk roads, bridges, and infrastructure, readiness of personnel, machinery and equipment, and immediate mobilisation in case of any disaster. He also urged the general public to remain highly alert.

Koshi Province’s Minister for Internal Affairs and Law, Gombu Sherpa, said the provincial mechanism had adopted high alert. He called on the public to stay safe and aware.

He said the provincial government had begun preparations in advance, keeping the risk of heavy rain in mind. Minister Sherpa said the concerned local administration and security mechanisms had stepped up efforts to deliver warnings to at-risk settlements.

Following the flood warning, all 14 district administration offices in the province and at-risk local levels have made preparations with caution. Biratnagar Metropolitan City is using loudspeaker announcements to alert people in flood-prone areas.

title.rendered: High alert urged in Syangja after possibility of heavy rain

content.rendered:
Syangja, September 24

Given the possibility of heavy to very heavy rain in Syangja, the District Administration Office has urged people to remain highly alert.

The administration has requested the public to take precautions, saying continuous rainfall could raise water levels in rivers and streams and increase the risk of flash floods, landslides, inundation, and riverbank erosion.

The District Administration Office, Syangja, issued the notice based on a weather bulletin from the Weather Forecasting Division of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

According to the notice, a low-pressure system developing over the Andaman Sea region of India is strengthening and moving in a west-to-northwest direction, raising the possibility of heavy to very heavy rain, along with thunder, lightning, and windstorms, in Syangja and surrounding areas from Thursday, September 24, through 27.

The administration said continuous rain could increase the natural flow of rivers and streams, raising water levels. This carries a high risk of flash floods, surges, inundation, and landslides near rivers and streams.

Because dry landslides can occur even after strong sunshine following rain, and mudslides carrying debris can flow down from upper sections of rivers and streams, residents living along riverbanks have been urged to take special precautions.

The administration has asked people not to fish, swim, bathe, wash clothes, collect firewood, sand or gravel, or carry out any other activity along riverbanks during periods when flooding is possible. People have been asked not to go near riverbanks to retrieve belongings during flooding and not to allow family members to go to such places either.

Similarly, the administration has requested that people avoid grazing or watering livestock, and avoid playing volleyball, football, cricket, or other outdoor games near riverbanks. Parents have been asked to keep watch over children and prevent them from going to risk-prone areas.

Residents living along riverbanks and in low-lying areas have been told to continuously monitor water flow and to be ready to move immediately to safe locations if water levels rise. Drivers have been asked not to stop or park vehicles on roads and in market areas along riverbanks.

To stay safe from lightning, the administration has asked people to remain safely indoors and not to stand under trees, electric poles, towers, or other tall structures. People have also been asked to stay away from ponds, rivers, and streams, and not to stay on hilltops or elevated ground.

The administration has requested that people regularly follow official weather forecasts, advisories, and warnings issued by the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, the federal government, provincial government, local administration, local levels, and security agencies, and comply with directives from the relevant bodies.

The administration has also urged relevant federal and provincial government bodies, local levels, security agencies, volunteers, and other stakeholders to remain on alert with necessary preparations, and to relocate at-risk residents to safe locations in time.

For information related to rain and floods, the District Administration Office said people can contact 1155, the disaster helpline 1234, Nepal Police at 100, or the Armed Police Force, Nepal at 1114.
