title.rendered: Lawmakers urge government to address rising prices ahead of festivals

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Lawmakers have drawn the government’s attention to rising prices, delays in post-disaster recovery and problems facing the communication sector.

They called for immediate government action over price increases ahead of the festival season and the difficult living conditions of flood-affected people.

Lawmaker Balawati Sharma questioned the government’s approach, saying prices of daily consumer goods had surged. She also questioned the government’s preparedness to protect citizens from floods in view of seasonal weather forecasts.

“Prices of vegetables and meat have risen unusually ahead of Dashain and Tihar, but the government has been avoiding responsibility by citing external factors,” she said.

Lawmaker Buddharatna Maharjan said disaster-affected families were still being forced to live in temporary shelters and demanded the announcement of a comprehensive relief and rehabilitation package.

Lawmaker Bharat Prasad Parajuli said the government should clarify the status of those missing in the floods and provide relief arrangements equivalent to those for deceased victims.

Raising concerns about the communication sector, lawmaker Buddhiprasad Pant expressed solidarity with the Federation of Nepali Journalists’ protest over cuts in government advertising. He accused government policies of pushing independent media into crisis and called for strengthening the independent media sector.

Lawmaker Bishwaraj Pokhrel renewed the demand for an Area Administration Office, while lawmaker Bina Gurung urged the government to address teacher shortages and poor infrastructure in community schools.

Similarly, lawmaker Bharat Giri suggested conducting safety audits of major highways and strictly testing vehicle fitness to reduce road accidents during the festival season.

title.rendered: Nepal’s public debt nears Rs 3 trillion, while debt payments outpace capital spending

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Nepal’s public debt has reached nearly Rs 3 trillion, even as the government’s total debt burden declined slightly in the first two months of the current fiscal year.

According to the Public Debt Management Office, Nepal owed Rs 2.973 trillion by the end of Bhadra, the second month of the fiscal year 2026/27. The figure is slightly lower than the Rs 2.981 trillion recorded at the end of the previous fiscal year.

The decline came because the government repaid more debt than it borrowed during the period.

By the end of Bhadra, the government had borrowed Rs 61.05 billion while repaying Rs 70.13 billion in principal, excluding interest. A loss arising from exchange-rate movements, however, added Rs 436.3 million to the debt burden.

Of the total debt, Rs 1.361 trillion was domestic debt and Rs 1.611 trillion was external debt. They represented 20.63 percent and 24.41 percent of gross domestic product respectively, putting total public debt at 45.05 percent of GDP.

The Public Debt Management Office publishes monthly government debt statistics, including reports through Bhadra 2083.

Government plans to borrow Rs 658 billion

Despite the slight decline in the first two months, the government plans to raise Rs 658.28 billion in public debt during the current fiscal year.

By the end of Bhadra, it had raised Rs 61.05 billion, or 9.28 percent of the annual target.

The government plans to raise Rs 400 billion through domestic borrowing this fiscal year. It had already raised Rs 50 billion by the end of Bhadra, equivalent to 12.20 percent of the annual target.

It has set a target of raising Rs 248.28 billion in external loans, of which Rs 11.05 billion had been received by the end of Bhadra, or 4.45 percent of the annual target.

Domestic borrowing accounted for 81.89 percent of total borrowing during the first two months, while external borrowing accounted for 18.11 percent.

The government raised Rs 20 billion in domestic debt in Shrawan and increased borrowing to Rs 30 billion in Bhadra. External borrowing rose from Rs 3.84 billion in Shrawan to Rs 7.21 billion in Bhadra.

More money going to debt than development

The figures become more striking when government expenditure is examined alongside debt servicing.

By the end of Bhadra, the government had spent Rs 85.01 billion on servicing public debt, including principal and interest. Capital expenditure during the same period stood at just Rs 7.66 billion.

The government has allocated Rs 417.88 billion for public debt servicing in the current fiscal year. By the end of Bhadra, it had already spent 20.34 percent of that allocation, equivalent to 1.29 percent of GDP.

During the period, the government repaid Rs 63.54 billion in domestic principal and Rs 13.25 billion in domestic interest.

For external debt, it repaid Rs 6.59 billion in principal and Rs 1.61 billion in interest.

In total, principal repayments amounted to Rs 70.13 billion, while interest payments stood at Rs 14.87 billion.

The pattern raises a broader question about how much of Nepal’s borrowing is contributing to new capital formation and how much is being absorbed by existing liabilities.

The Office of the Auditor General has also raised concerns about the use of public debt and whether borrowed funds are being directed towards productive capital formation. Its 63rd annual report is the latest annual audit report published by the office.

Public debt has nearly doubled in seven years

Nepal’s debt burden has increased sharply over the past seven years.

According to government figures, public debt stood at Rs 1.43 trillion in fiscal year 2019/20. It has since increased to nearly Rs 3 trillion.

As a share of GDP, public debt has risen from 38.05 percent in 2019/20 to around 45 percent now.

The increase has come amid rising government expenditure, declining foreign grants and weaker-than-expected revenue mobilisation.

Economists generally distinguish between borrowing used to create productive assets and borrowing used to finance recurrent expenditure. Debt can generate future economic capacity when it is invested in projects that increase production, employment, income or infrastructure.

The concern arises when borrowing does not generate sufficient returns to meet future repayment obligations.

A high-level Economic Reform Recommendation Commission formed by the government in 2024 also warned about this issue.

Its report noted that GDP and revenue mobilisation had not increased in line with the growth in public debt, increasing the burden of principal and interest payments.

The commission warned that if public debt is not properly utilised and fails to generate returns, the risk of the country falling into a debt trap could increase.

It also noted that rising debt-servicing obligations can leave fewer resources available for essential government functions such as education, health and security.

Commission calls for tighter rules on domestic borrowing

The National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission has recommended that domestic borrowing should not be used to finance recurrent and administrative expenditure.

While setting the ceiling for domestic borrowing by the federal, provincial and local governments for fiscal year 2083/84, the commission recommended that domestic borrowing be directed towards projects capable of creating employment, generating long-term benefits and contributing to capital formation.

The commission has set the federal government’s domestic borrowing ceiling at no more than 5.5 percent of GDP, consistent with its annual recommendations.

It has specifically recommended that domestic borrowing be strictly prohibited for recurrent and administrative expenditure.

According to the commission, net domestic borrowing in fiscal year 2081/82 amounted to only 1.41 percent of GDP. Much of the domestic borrowing, it said, was effectively absorbed by repayment of existing debt because debt-servicing costs have been rising.

The commission has therefore called for domestic borrowing to be concentrated on projects that can increase production, employment and income, develop infrastructure and create capital.

It has also recommended conducting cost-benefit analysis, net present value calculations and internal rate of return analysis before directing domestic borrowing towards projects.

For projects financed through borrowing, the government should ensure that future returns will be sufficient to repay both principal and interest, according to the commission.

It has further called for an integrated electronic information, accounting and reporting system covering domestic borrowing and overall public debt across all three levels of government.

Auditor General raises concerns over use of borrowed money

The Auditor General has also questioned whether public debt is being used sufficiently for capital formation.

Its 63rd annual report says borrowed funds have also been used for recurrent purposes, including employee expenses, services and consultancy and office operations.

The report also points to foreign-exchange risks associated with external debt and recommends that borrowing be directed towards productive sectors while considering financial instruments that can help manage currency risk.

The Auditor General has additionally noted pressure on domestic resources as total revenue collection remains below the government’s target.

With debt-servicing obligations increasing, the government faces a growing need to borrow to finance other expenditures, creating a cycle that could further increase the debt burden.

The Auditor General has recommended keeping recurrent expenditure within desirable limits and directing borrowed funds towards projects capable of generating returns.

The bigger question is not simply how much Nepal owes

Nepal’s public debt has not yet reached Rs 3 trillion, but it has moved close enough to that mark to highlight a larger fiscal question.

The government borrowed Rs 61.05 billion during the first two months of this fiscal year while repaying Rs 70.13 billion in principal. Yet it spent Rs 85.01 billion on debt servicing during the same period, compared with only Rs 7.66 billion in capital expenditure.

The numbers underline the growing weight of past borrowing on the government’s current budget.

The central question for Nepal, therefore, is not simply how much more debt the government can raise.

It is whether the money borrowed today can create enough economic activity, revenue and productive assets to repay that debt tomorrow.

title.rendered: Government will not interfere in Citizen Investment Trust: Finance Minister Wagle

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle has said the government has given high priority to transparency, professional discipline and risk management in the operation of the Citizen Investment Trust.

Responding to questions raised during Wednesday’s meeting of the House of Representatives on the Citizen Investment Trust (Third Amendment) Bill, 2083, Wagle said the government valued the common concerns and relevant suggestions raised by lawmakers and claimed that the bill would further strengthen the fund.

Wagle said the Citizen Investment Trust is a sensitive institution linked to the future of Nepali citizens and needs to be updated in line with changing circumstances.

“Our national savings alone cannot fill the large investment gap, so mobilising both domestic and external sources is essential,” he said. “We will not interfere in these institutions as we do in private banks, but they are instruments for implementing the government’s financial and monetary policies.”

Summarising the issues raised by lawmakers into five key points, Wagle said the government was positive about expanding the scope of investment and carrying out institutional reforms.

Although some lawmakers claimed that domestic savings were sufficient, he pointed out that the country needed large-scale investment given its revenue and expenditure situation. He also said the concerns raised by lawmakers regarding risk management had been taken seriously.

Warning of the risk of “privatising profits and socialising losses,” Wagle said limits would be set on risky investments by public institutions and conflicts of interest would not be allowed.

He said government control and regulation of public institutions were necessary for implementing government policies and that the government would pay particular attention to making appointed officials accountable.

title.rendered: Raju Lama Foundation and Small World provide relief and health services to flood victims in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

The Raju Lama Foundation, a charitable organisation run by singer Raju Lama, and the social organisation Small World have distributed relief supplies in Tetangche village, Amachhodingmo Rural Municipality, in Rasuwa, an area affected by Bhotekoshi flooding.

The two organisations have also provided health services to those affected. Singer Lama said 3,500 kg of food grains and medicine were distributed to affected residents of the village, which had been cut off from the road network after the flood.

A four-hour health camp was also run there with the participation of senior physician Ganesh Gurung. After road access was severed, the two organisations arranged to fly relief supplies to Tetangche by helicopter, with nine shuttle flights used for the purpose, Lama said.

Lama, who has since returned to Kathmandu from the affected area, said delivering relief supplies had been extremely difficult.

“There’s no road at all above Dhunche, which makes distributing relief supplies difficult. A helicopter is the only way to get there,” he said. “It took us 17 hours just to get the relief supplies there.”

Lama said the shortage of food and other problems in the affected area remain severe.

“Even those who have money aren’t able to buy things. People can manage with the clothes they have, but victims told us they don’t know how to survive without food,” he said. “Crops haven’t grown either, and without crops it’s hard to sustain life. They’ve asked that other organisations help as well.”

Meanwhile, Small World has rescued a 9-year-old boy from Amachhodingmo Rural Municipality and brought him to Kathmandu. The boy, who lost all his family members in the flood, is currently sheltering at Yellow Gumba, and the organisation has also taken responsibility for his education.

Small World is also preparing to provide relief supplies and other services to 200 more families in Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot, another flood-affected area. Plans include distributing gas stove sets, clothing, and kitchen supplies to these families.

Both Small World and the Raju Lama Foundation are active in social and charitable work.

title.rendered: Egg prices rise again, large eggs cost Rs 600 per crate

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Egg prices have increased again in the market. The Nepal Layers Poultry Farmers Association said the price of eggs has increased by Rs 10 to Rs 15 per crate, effective from Tuesday.

According to the price list issued by the association, the depot and dealer price for extra-large eggs has been set at Rs 4,300 per box, while the price of large eggs has been fixed at Rs 4,200 per box.

Accordingly, an extra-large egg will now cost Rs 615 per crate, while a large egg will cost Rs 600 per crate.

Previously, the association had fixed the prices effective from September 4. At that time, extra-large eggs were priced at Rs 605 per crate, large eggs at Rs 590 and medium eggs at Rs 550. The price of small eggs was fixed at Rs 3,200 per box.

The association said that although wholesale and farm-gate prices have been increased, the retail prices paid by consumers have not been raised.

According to association secretary Madan Pokhrel, consumers will continue to buy large eggs at Rs 25 per piece and two medium eggs for Rs 45.

title.rendered: Waste Management Bill tabled in House of Representatives

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

The Waste Management Bill, 2083, was tabled in the House of Representatives on Wednesday.

Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal presented the bill after the House granted permission to introduce it for deliberation.

No member submitted a notice of opposition to the proposal seeking permission to introduce the bill, following which the Speaker allowed Minister Lamsal to present it.

Presenting the bill, Lamsal said it was necessary to further clarify the roles and responsibilities of the federal, provincial and local governments in waste generation, collection, disposal and overall waste management.

He said the bill was essential to establish effective coordination among the three tiers of government and create a clean and healthy environment.

The main objective of the bill is to minimise the adverse effects of waste on human health and the environment.

It also aims to establish a legal framework for processing waste and using it as a resource by adopting the concept of a circular economy.

title.rendered: China provides equipment and technology for DNA testing of Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

The Chinese government has provided the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology (NAST) with equipment, materials and technology required for DNA testing.

China has transferred the necessary technology to Nepal for DNA profiling to identify people who died or went missing in the Rasuwa floods.

At a programme held on Wednesday in the presence of Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun, Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming handed over the materials and technology required for DNA profiling to NAST.

Dr Ram Chandra Paudel, senior scientist and spokesperson for NAST, said DNA testing is also being conducted at NAST’s laboratory after the National Forensic Science Laboratory and Nepal Police’s Forensic Laboratory alone were unable to handle all the samples following the floods.

According to Paudel, NAST’s laboratory has so far received around 807 samples. He said NAST most recently received 12 samples from the Nepal Police Forensic Laboratory.

He said work had been divided among different laboratories to speed up sample testing after preliminary reports indicated that a large number of people had gone missing following the floods.

Experts from India are also assisting the National Forensic Science Laboratory, while foreign experts are supporting the Nepal Police Forensic Laboratory, he said.

“Scientists at our laboratory are currently working in coordination with the relevant experts. They are training us, helping build our capacity and generating the necessary data,” Paudel said.

He said some bone and tooth samples received by the National Forensic Science Laboratory, as well as samples excavated to identify missing people, are being tested by the experts themselves, while some are being sent to NAST.

According to Paudel, NAST prepares profiles of the samples it receives and provides them to the concerned forensic laboratories.

“We officially receive those samples, but the legal responsibility does not lie with us; it lies with the concerned forensic institutions. We send the data we prepare to them,” he said. “The forensic laboratory and the relevant police mechanism then analyse the data. They also have access to international databases, where the data we send is incorporated.”

According to Paudel, NAST’s work is contributing not only to the immediate DNA testing process but also to building the capacity of Nepali scientists. He said Chinese experts were providing training and technical assistance to Nepali scientists using their own equipment.

title.rendered: Fair-price shops open for festive season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Government-owned enterprises have started selling daily consumer goods at subsidised prices targeting the upcoming Dashain, Tihar and Chhath festivals.

Salt Trading Corporation and Food Management and Trading Company Limited have opened fair-price shops at various locations across the country. However, the government will not sell goats, sheep and mountain goats at subsidised prices this year, a practice it has followed during Dashain to help control market prices.

Salt Trading offers discounts at 45 locations

Salt Trading Corporation has been operating fair-price shops through 38 sales centres across the country, including the Kathmandu Valley, since September 17. It is providing discounted food items through 13 stalls and three mobile vans in the Kathmandu Valley and 25 locations outside the Valley.

According to the corporation’s information officer Kumar Rajbhandari, consumers will receive discounts of Rs 5 per kilogram on sugar, Rs 2 on salt and Rs 7 per kilogram on edible oil, rice, beaten rice, flour and other products. Sugar is available at Rs 100 per kilogram, with a limit of two kilograms per person.

“We have started the fair-price shops from September 17 until the end of Kartik (Chhath festival), as in previous years,” Rajbhandari said. “At present, sales are being made through our own counters in the Valley, while three vans have been arranged to supply goods to other locations where there is demand.”

Food company offers discounts in 44 districts but no livestock sales

Food Management and Trading Company Limited has also been operating fair-price shops since the last week of Shrawan with the objective of providing subsidised goods to consumers throughout the year.

With an approved government budget of Rs 35 million, the company is operating the shops through provincial offices, main branch offices, branch offices and depot offices in 44 districts, including 26 remote districts.

According to the company’s information officer Madhav Mishra, consumers are receiving discounts of Rs 5 per kilogram or litre on rice, lentils, edible oil, sugar, pulses and local crops such as chino, kaguno and buckwheat. The fair-price shops, which started on September 13, are being operated in coordination with local governments.

However, the company will not sell goats, sheep and mountain goats at subsidised prices during Dashain this year, citing a lack of budget. The company has sold livestock at subsidised prices during the festival every year to prevent unusual increases in meat prices.

“Although we are providing discounts on daily food items and local crops through our sales centres across the country, no budget has been allocated this year to purchase goats, sheep and mountain goats. Therefore, we have decided not to bring subsidised livestock to the Kathmandu Valley,” Mishra said.

Last year, the company had also opened online bookings for goats, sheep and mountain goats. The company said it had to cancel the bookings after roads were blocked by continuous rainfall and has decided not to offer the service this year from the outset.

Traders have said that around 35,000 to 40,000 goats, sheep and mountain goats are in demand in the Kathmandu Valley alone during Dashain.

title.rendered: Transport operators urge public to avoid long-distance and night travel amid rain forecast

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Transport entrepreneurs have urged the public to avoid long-distance and night travel from Thursday as the country faces the possibility of heavy rainfall and increased risks of floods and landslides.

The Federation of Nepal National Transport Entrepreneurs issued a statement urging transport operators to obtain updated information about road conditions and weather before operating services from Thursday through September 28.

The federation has also asked the public to avoid long-distance travel unless it is necessary.

It has specifically urged people not to travel at night from Thursday, citing the increased risks posed by adverse weather and road conditions.

The federation said it was issuing the appeal in line with an earlier request from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, which had urged stakeholders to take precautions amid the forecast of continuous rainfall this week.

The government has warned that prolonged rainfall could increase the risk of floods and landslides in several parts of the country.

The transport federation has accordingly instructed its members to assess weather and road conditions before operating vehicles and to take necessary precautions.

Authorities have also urged the public to remain alert and avoid unnecessary travel in areas vulnerable to flooding and landslides.

title.rendered: What should Balen say at the UNGA beyond asking for aid?

content.rendered:
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah (Balen) is set to speak at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on September 24, in the aftermath of the Bhotekoshi floods.

If Balen steps down from the UNGA podium having simply asked for aid, Nepal will remain what Nepal has always been: a tragic headline. 

I propose the following national stance in Balen’s speech at the 81st UNGA. 

“Your Excellencies, my country Nepal experienced a mountain bedrock collapse followed by a ‘Himalayan Tsunami’ that claimed over 1,451 lives, with another 5,745 still missing, including approximately 600 foreigners from 35 countries. We did not cause the mountain bedrock to collapse, yet we are facing disproportionate consequences.

I am not here today to present a bill for our collective dead, and I am not here to ask for your pity. For far too long, vulnerable nations have been patient in dealing with transnational polycrises. 

There is an ecological crisis underway in the Himalayas. The delicate Himalayan ecosystem is interconnected with livelihoods in both lower riparian and upper riparian regions, including the global economy.  

I am here to tell you that Nepal is retiring the quiet and passive posture of waiting for action.

Nepalis have a long history of persevering in the face of extreme adversity. We come from the roof of the world, Sagarmatha (Mt. Everest), the land of the fierce Gurkhas, and the land of the Sherpa guides hauling mountaineers through death zones. 

Starting today, Nepal is putting forward our mountains not as a hazard zone or merely a tourist attraction fading away from the ecological disaster currently underway. To the UN member states and global funds: we want to tell you that we do not want to pour temporary concrete that washes away with the next monsoon. 

Today, we begin to take on a more challenging task. We call upon all UN member states to deal with the global ecological crisis at hand to ground our hopes for a greener and sustainable future.  

To this end, Nepal is here to negotiate a global partnership for structural resilience against the crisis we collectively face. 

We are opening a Special Himalayan Economic Zone that will feature a world-class disaster tech university along with an international legal and financial corridor. The goal will be to develop novel intellectual property in disaster tech, including alpine drone logistics, early-warning systems, and predictive terrain modelling to strengthen disaster response mechanisms.

The government of Nepal invites the UN member states and all global funds to co-endow and co-create the International University of Disaster Risk Reduction, Prevention, and Management (IUDRRPM), headquartered in the Himalayas in the Special Himalayan Economic Zone dedicated to disaster-resilient technology, public administration, environmental governance, and environmental diplomacy.

We will offer the world’s researchers frontline data and invite you to bring capital, research prowess and collaborative spirit to join us in taking definitive long-term measures for structural resilience against disaster scenarios. 

Our promise is disaster technology designed in Nepal, manufactured and scaled in India & China, our neighbours with whom we share the common ecological and cultural heritage of the Himalayas.

We want to develop green, affordable and sustainable technology to export to every climate-vulnerable country on Earth, along with the most advanced search, rescue, and relief operations capacity. Nepal wants climate-vulnerable countries to be positioned to thrive rather than barely survive in the face of the crisis.

As a non-aligned state between two Asian giants, we want to offer a neutral institutional home for an International Court of Arbitration for Environmental Disputes, International Carbon Clearing-house/Exchange, and an International Innovation Hub for Sustainability.

Let us end the era of waiting for climate justice. 

I call upon all UN member states to begin the era of building the tools necessary to deliver climate justice.

The Himalayas are calling, and this time for a different kind of adventure. The partnership to deliver climate justice is open, and the choice is yours to join us.”

The Prime Minister Balendra Shah can either deliver a conventional diplomatic eulogy. Or he can redefine Nepal’s identity and posture at the global stage. 

Why? Strategic autonomy without structural capacity is a pipe dream. Nepal needs to retire the posture of passive “resilience” without structural capacity. 

Thus, Balen must not read from the default diplomatic playbook at the UN General Assembly. The traditional plan to point to melting glaciers, showcase the dead and the debris, and present the bill for loss and damage as reparations fundamentally relies on the moral conscience of the very actors who have been strategically inactive in solving the root causes of the global polycrisis facing planet Earth, leaving vulnerable countries to borrow their way out of economic losses.    

Nepal must proactively pivot to become a coalition-based structural power for the changes that it wants in the future. The sample speech above reimagines a new global identity of Nepal suited to this purpose.

The old international identity

Nepal is the land of tall mountains with extensive gorges. Historically, Gurkhas are renowned for their bravery and participation in various wars, fighting in the security forces of the UK, Hong Kong, India, and Singapore. Currently, Nepali soldiers are among the top contributors to UN peacekeeping forces. And the Sherpas of Nepal, or mountain guides, are experts at scaling the peaks of the world. 

Economically, Nepal is in poverty (others call it poor). Nepal cannot provide employment or higher education to its young people in their own country, so the Nepalis migrate. The state institutions are in perpetual disarray, forever under construction, just like the infrastructure. Back-to-back natural and political crises every decade or so haven’t helped the state, but they have tested the identity of Nepalis as resilient people.

In brief, Nepal’s perceived international identity can be categorized into the following: the first is the territorial identity as the people of the mountains and second as the brave ones capable of being deployed in the most treacherous of conditions to fight, to labor and to do really the impossible.

Vision 2050 AD: Who are the Nepali people? 

Imagine a historian in 2050 AD looking back at how Nepal responded to the 2026 crisis with developed structural capacity.

Nepali people are the most technologically advanced disaster experts in the world. They save lives the fastest when deployed in crises. They can reach the most treacherous of places with courage. And they apply themselves most thoughtfully. They are the humanitarian spirit and brain of the world, enabled by cutting-edge science, research, engineering and robust public policy.

Nepalis simultaneously manage search, rescue and relief operations in the most efficient manner. They are swift in saving people, getting food, shelter and medicine where it is needed the quickest and in ensuring minimum risks for the most vulnerable. They are experts not just in disaster technology but also in administration, management and risk reduction.  

Essentially, Nepalis rejuvenated their state identity by honouring and building on their ecological and socio-cultural heritage.”

There has never been a more pressing moment to redefine Nepal’s identity and posture on the global stage. As the outgoing Secretary-General António Guterres said, one alternative to a networked multipolar world is a world with fragmentation and transactionalism rife with shrinking cooperation, rising tensions and deepening mistrust. This is a world Nepal cannot afford. 

Can PM Balendra Shah rally the global community to break the ritual of vulnerable nations describing suffering and waiting until structural powers decide on a course of action? 

PM Balendra Shah’s speech needs to deliver a powerful vision in New York, and his government needs to operationalise it in the coming decades.

title.rendered: Typhoon Dujuan kills 9 in Japan, 4 still missing

content.rendered:
Tokyo, September 23

At least nine people have died and four remain missing after floods and landslides triggered by heavy rainfall brought by Typhoon Dujuan in eastern Japan.

Heavy rainfall in the Kanto region on Monday caused flooding and landslides in several areas around Tokyo. According to local media reports, six deaths have been confirmed in Chiba Prefecture alone.

Among the deceased was a man in his 50s who reportedly fell into a bamboo grove while operating heavy machinery to clear mud and debris from a landslide. The body of another man was found inside a submerged vehicle.

Three people also died in Kanagawa Prefecture. A woman in her 60s reportedly died after a landslide struck her house and buried it under mud.

Police and firefighters are continuing search and rescue operations for those still missing.

After Typhoon Dujuan reached Japan’s eastern Pacific coast on Monday, record rainfall was recorded in the Kanto region and the Izu Islands. The heavy rain triggered landslides and caused rivers to overflow, affecting areas around Tokyo.

More than 500 buildings in Chiba, Kanagawa and Ibaraki prefectures have so far been destroyed, damaged or affected by flooding. As of before 6 am Wednesday, more than 24,700 households in Chiba and Kanagawa prefectures remained without electricity.

—RSS/Xinhua

title.rendered: Advance ticket booking to continue for Dashain, Tihar and Chhath

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

The government will continue the system of advance ticket booking for the upcoming Dashain, Tihar and Chhath festivals. This is among the decisions outlined in a 15-point directive sent by the Department of Transport Management to stakeholders.

However, the department has not yet specified when advance ticket booking will open.

According to the department, public transport operators should make arrangements for online ticket booking as far as possible and operate vehicles only with travel documents containing passengers’ identifying details.

The department has also directed transport operators, companies and institutions to issue mandatory identification cards to employees involved in ticket sales. It has instructed them to completely control ticket sales from unauthorised counters and by individuals without identification cards or uniforms.

It has also called for coordination among the Department of Transport Management, Nepal Police, traffic police, Nepal Railway Company and other concerned agencies to effectively monitor passenger vehicles entering and leaving the Kathmandu Valley.

The department said passengers must travel on public vehicles only after obtaining tickets. It has urged passengers not to travel after consuming alcohol and to purchase tickets only from authorised counters or employees and individuals carrying identification cards.

Drivers and transport staff must arrange for passengers to have meals and snacks at designated locations in accordance with government standards and ensure that there is no overcrowding during such stops.

Focus on road maintenance and traffic management

The department has directed concerned agencies to continuously inspect and carry out necessary maintenance on major roads and highways used by passenger vehicles during the festival period.

It has requested the Department of Roads to make arrangements for landslide control and prevent traffic congestion, while continuously providing information to the public about road conditions.

Transport operators will also have to arrange additional vehicles required during the period.

The department has said it will hold further discussions and consultations with stakeholders on opening route permits for passenger vehicles, advance ticket booking and the movement of large vehicles, and issue a notice specifying the date and duration of transport operations.

Drivers to undergo mandatory health tests

The department has directed authorities to conduct health tests on drivers operating under the influence of alcohol or drugs at major entry and exit points of the Kathmandu Valley and across the country. If a driver is found to have consumed alcohol or drugs, the concerned transport operator must arrange another driver.

Likewise, long-distance passenger vehicles must undergo mandatory checks, including inspections of their mechanical condition, before departing for their destinations.

The department has also directed operators of long-distance public passenger vehicles to have at least two drivers and arrange for them to take turns driving. Concerned authorities will monitor whether this arrangement is in place.

The department has clearly instructed transport operators not to employ children under 18 as drivers or in other jobs.

As the number of passenger vehicles is likely to increase significantly as the festivals approach, raising the risk of road accidents, the department has directed concerned authorities to ensure effective monitoring and surveillance accordingly.

title.rendered: How bad could the coming rains get for Kathmandu?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

A low-pressure system developing over the Bay of Bengal is gradually strengthening, and meteorologists have been monitoring it and issuing updated bulletins.

As of this writing, it has not yet taken the form of a cyclone. If it does become a cyclone, its strength will be clearer and its impact more predictable. Even if it stays as a low-pressure area rather than becoming a cyclone, it still carries considerable energy, and it is likely to bring widespread rain across Nepal.

According to meteorologists, systems that develop over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea generally affect Nepal indirectly rather than directly.

The system is currently moving from the Andaman-Nicobar region toward Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. While over the sea, it can gain more energy and moisture and grow stronger.

Once it moves onto land in India, friction with the terrain will gradually weaken it. However, the clouds, moisture, and rain system it generates will still travel through India and reach Nepal.

The system’s eventual path and strength will determine its impact on Nepal. Since its path could still shift, it remains difficult to say exactly how much rain will fall or what effects it will have.

What impact could Kathmandu see?

According to Madan Sigdel, associate professor at Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, current projections suggest the system may move through Jharkhand in India, then Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh, and on toward Bihar.

“If it comes in around Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces could see higher risk,” Sigdel said. “Current estimates suggest it’s more likely to move via Gorakhpur. If that holds, Kathmandu Valley, the eastern part of Bagmati, and Lumbini and Gandaki could be affected more.”

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has also forecast greater impact in Lumbini and Gandaki provinces.

He said that because Kathmandu is heavily urbanised, hemmed in by waterways, and has poor drainage, even a sustained 50 to 80 mm of rainfall could cause flooding there.

“Whereas it takes 100–150 mm of rain to cause risk in areas like Lumbini, in Kathmandu even around 50 mm can be enough to create risk,” Sigdel said. “So, looking at past flooding in areas like Nakkhu, it’s necessary to prepare to avoid such risk.”

Main risk from Friday

The effects of this weather system have already begun appearing in Nepal since this morning, with continued cloud cover and rain. Forecasts indicate the area and volume of rain and cloud will increase further from Thursday, with the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology forecasting the greatest impact from September 25 to 27. 

According to department spokesperson Bibhuti Pokharel, the system’s effects will bring rain or snow across Nepal, with strong winds in some places. However, current estimates suggest comparatively heavier rain and snowfall in districts of Lumbini and Gandaki provinces.

Since the impact could bring flooding in the Tarai, landslides in the hills, and snowfall in the mountains, meteorologists say vigilance is needed nationwide.

Professor Madan Sigdel of Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Hydrology and Meteorology also said caution is needed from east to west and from the mountains to the Tarai.

According to him, the first major risk from heavy rain is flooding in the Tarai. As water levels rise in rivers and streams, riverbank and low-lying settlements could be affected.

In hilly areas, the risk of landslides is greater. Because the ground in many areas has already been saturated recently, and roads and infrastructure have already been weakened by earlier disasters, additional rain could raise the risk further.

“Since we’re in the latter half of the monsoon, the ground is already soaked and weakened, so even a short spell of rain can carry high risk. If we prepare for the big one, we can handle the smaller ones,” Sigdel said.

“Red alert” for high mountain areas

In the risk map of the special bulletin issued by the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, high-mountain districts are also marked in red, indicating high risk. Spokesperson Pokharel explained the reason: “There’s a possibility of a snowstorm in the mountain regions, which is why the risk there is estimated to be somewhat higher.”

Meteorologists therefore advise that those trekking or mountaineering in high-altitude areas manage their travel according to weather conditions. 

“It’s best not to go trekking right now, and if already out there, to move to a safe location,” Sigdel said.

Even 150 mm of rain could be risky

Some independent meteorologists have written on social media that the system could bring up to 400 mm of rain over its duration.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, Nepal’s official weather authority, has not released a rainfall estimate but has forecast heavy to very heavy rain in some areas.

According to the department, more than 50 mm but less than 100 mm of rain is classified as “heavy rain”; more than 100 mm but less than 200 mm as “very heavy”; and more than 200 mm as “extremely heavy” rainfall.

Sigdel said that with the ground already saturated, even 100–150 mm of rain in 24 hours could bring risk of landslides, flooding, and road damage.

“Overall, heavy rain plus weakened ground can create risk. In the current situation, even 100–150 mm of rain in a day could be risky,” Sigdel said.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung and Energy Minister Birajbhakta Shrestha visited the department on Tuesday to learn about the possible risks and preparations for risk reduction.

He said that although the system may weaken as it moves through India, its potential to bring prolonged heavy rain to Nepal should not be dismissed, and preparation is needed to guard against the risk.

Meteorologists specifically advise against night travel during this period, saying it would be particularly risky. Even during the day, they suggest travelling only based on actual rainfall in the area, road conditions, and official advisories.

Since heavy rain could affect both road transport and air services, Sigdel said the relevant authorities should manage transportation according to the risk. 

“Given the possibility of heavy rain, it would be best to avoid long-distance travel between September 25 and 27 if possible,” he said.

Caution and preparation

Since heavy rain in watershed areas affects river systems downstream, he suggested that those living near rivers and streams take special precautions for the next few days.

“The provincial, local, and federal governments each need to prepare in their own way and get accurate information to at-risk areas in time,” Sigdel said. “If early warnings are taken seriously and precautions are taken in time, loss of life and property can be reduced.”

He also said that identifying potential landslide-prone areas, restricting movement through them during heavy rain, monitoring river conditions, and warning at-risk settlements in time were necessary.

Sigdel suggested that local governments identify areas prone to landslides and flooding, step up monitoring of rivers and streams, issue early warnings to at-risk communities, and prepare to relocate people to safe areas if needed.

With heavy rain expected, farmers too should make immediate necessary preparations. Meteorologists advise paying attention to the timing of harvesting ripening paddy and to weather conditions, and storing harvested paddy in a safe place.

Follow official information, not rumours

Weather systems keep changing, so forecasts are updated regularly as the system’s direction and intensity shift.

Experts therefore caution against forming opinions based on unverified information and exaggerated claims circulating on social media.

Experts stress that decisions regarding weather and disasters should be based on official information issued by the relevant government agencies of Nepal.

title.rendered: The flood took Syabrubesi. Its survivors are still waiting to return

content.rendered:
Syabrubesi, September 23

Twenty-seven days after a devastating flood tore through Syabrubesi, Phurba Maya Tamang and Kanchhi Tamang were finally crossing the Bhotekoshi River. They had been stranded on the western bank of the river after the flood swept away the bridges connecting Syabrubesi to the rest of the area.

Then, last week, on September 14, a lifeline appeared. With the initiative of security personnel and local residents, a tarping cable crossing, or tuin, was put into operation across the Bhotekoshi.

It is no replacement for a bridge. But for people who had been unable to move around for 19 days, it has brought some relief.

When the Onlinekhabar team arrived, Phurba Maya and Kanchhi were taking turns crossing the river using the tuin. A joint team from the Nepal Police and Armed Police Force also helped carry across sacks of consumer goods the women had brought from Dhunche, the district headquarters.

“Of course, a tuin cannot provide the convenience of a road and a bridge,” said Assistant Sub-Inspector Rampravesh Patel, who leads the team operating it. “But people who could not move around for 19 days can now travel back and forth.”

Police operate the crossing from 9am to 4pm every day.

“Because this is a geographically difficult area, we are helping operate the tuin ourselves,” Patel said.

The need for it is visible in the people gathered around the crossing.

According to police, up to 40 people cross the Bhotekoshi by tuin every day. The number is significant given that the flood swept away a large part of the area, including the Syabrubesi market, and many displaced residents have already been moved to Kathmandu and elsewhere.

Near the tunnel of the Chilime Hydropower Project, workers were also building an iron staircase to make it easier for people to get on and off the tuin.

“We are working to make it easier to get on and off the tuin,” said an employee of the Nepal Electricity Authority.

For residents who have spent weeks cut off by the loss of roads and bridges, the crossing has offered a small return to movement.

But beyond it lies a landscape that is almost unrecognisable.

Where Syabrubesi once stood

After crossing the river, Phurba Maya, Kanchhi and the Onlinekhabar team walked along the Bhotekoshi riverbed towards a rough road that had been opened through the area.

“We never imagined something like this could happen. It is unbelievable,” Phurba Maya said as she carried a sack.

Until August 26 — the day the flood struck — Syabrubesi had looked very different.

“People in Syabrubesi earned more than the average Nepali,” said Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, chairman of Gosainkunda Rural Municipality. “There probably wasn’t a household that did not earn several hundred thousand rupees a year.”

The village lies on major routes to the Kerung border point, Mansarovar and Gosainkunda, which had helped make it relatively prosperous.

The rural municipality office was also located there, making Syabrubesi an administrative centre.

“Administratively, Syabrubesi was the centre,” Tamang said. “The hotel business was the main identity of this place.”

Foreign tourists travelling to Manasarovar, Gosainkunda and the Langtang trekking route also passed through the settlement, prompting significant investment in hotels.

According to Tamang, some individuals had invested tens of millions of rupees in the hotel business.

“No one could have imagined that everything would be destroyed all at once,” he said. “We kept investing, dreaming big.”

Then, on the morning of August 26, the flood arrived. It was something Syabrubesi had never imagined.

‘Everyone was shouting, run’

Tara Ghale, 54, was preparing food when she heard a sound that reminded her of a landslide.

“I was cooking when I heard a sound like the cliff had collapsed,” she said. “When I came outside, everyone was shouting, ‘Run, run.’ I ran too, and I survived.”

Other residents who survived the flood described similar moments to the Onlinekhabar team.

Today, only a few houses remain in one corner of Syabrubesi.

The Bhotekoshi, once a river running through the settlement, now appears in places like a small stream beneath a huge waterfall. In other places, the remains of houses can be seen. Much of the land has been turned into a riverbed.

For those who escaped, the landscape is a reminder of how quickly everything disappeared.

Deju Ghale, 80, still does not feel safe sleeping at night.

“We are afraid to sleep here at night. Everyone goes up to the school, the holding centre,” she said. “No one is willing to stay even in the houses that survived.”

Deju was picking vegetables from the kitchen garden that survived the flood when she recalled the night.

“Everyone ran. My husband and I could not run,” she said. “We survived only by chance at night. They picked us up and took us to the school.”

Everything below her house has now become a riverbed.

Deju and her husband were rescued after the flood, surviving almost by coincidence. Many others in Syabrubesi who escaped the disaster have similar stories.

But for weeks, there were few people around to hear those stories.

The bridges had been swept away, making it difficult even for journalists and others to cross the Bhotekoshi and reach the survivors.

“No media had come until today,” said local resident Buddhiman Tamang. “I am happy to see you. We could not tell our story. We had no one to tell it to.”

‘At first, we did not even know it was a flood’

When the flood struck, Buddhiman was at his shop with his young son.

His wife, Kanchhi Tamang, a teacher, called him and urged him to run.

“I was filming with my phone after seeing what looked like smoke. Then I saw the water coming,” Kanchhi recalled.

“At first, I did not even realise it was a flood. When I saw the frightening flood, I told my husband. He did not believe me. He said it might be a flood, but it would not reach our shop.”

The Bhotekoshi had also flooded in October last year, causing extensive damage in Rasuwagadhi and Timure and killing several people.

Kanchhi believes that memory may have contributed to the tragedy this time.

“I estimate that many people were swept away because they were misled by last year’s flood,” she said. “Many did not run in time because they thought it would be similar to the flood last year.”

But after Kanchhi repeatedly urged him to leave, Buddhiman took their son and ran, also telling others to escape.

“If I had stayed at the shop, I would have been swept away,” Buddhiman said. “So many people were swept away.”

The ward chairman and deputy chair remain missing

Among those still missing are Dawa Mingmar Tamang, ward chairman of Syabrubesi in Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-5, and rural municipality deputy chair Pratima Tamang.

According to local residents, ward chairman Tamang was caught in the flood while running to help save others.

“He was telling everyone to run and was heading towards the police station when he was swept away,” said Tara Ghale.

“He was riding his motorcycle because he thought that if he informed the police, more people could be evacuated.”

According to the rural municipality office, 176 people from Syafru alone remain missing.

The 2021 census put the population of the area at around 450.

More than 400 houses have been reduced to riverbed.

The rural municipality office, ward office, army barracks and health post are among the structures that were swept away.

Life now depends on helicopters

The Komin Syamewangphel Basic School, located near the hillside along with a few surviving houses, remains standing.

It has now become a holding centre for people displaced by the flood.

The centre is in one of the highest parts of Rasuwa, and displaced people are still living there.

People displaced from Rasuwagadhi and Timure have been moved to Kathmandu and other places. Those who remain here, however, continue to depend on helicopters.

Even with the tuin operating, large quantities of food and other supplies cannot be transported across the river.

“So far, helicopters have been bringing us food,” said local resident Dupsang Tamang, 54. “Even if we need to go somewhere, we have to depend on helicopters.”

The tuin may have restored a limited form of movement, but it has not restored the road network that once connected Syabrubesi to the outside world.

From relief to rebuilding

Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, chairman of Gosainkunda Rural Municipality, says Syabrubesi could move away from its dependence on helicopters once a Bailey bridge is built across the Bhotekoshi.

“At the moment, we are using helicopters to keep the displaced people alive. But this cannot continue for a long time,” he said. “A bridge over the Bhotekoshi has to be built as soon as possible.”

A Bailey bridge, he said, would also help bring Gosainkunda Rural Municipality’s Syabrubesi, as well as wards of Aamachhodingmo and Uttargaya rural municipalities, out of the current state of isolation.

For now, relief supplies are being transported not only by helicopter but, on a limited basis, by drones operated by the Nepal Army.

But for residents, relief is only the immediate need.

They are already thinking about what happens after the relief stops.

“Food is arriving,” said local resident Pasang Tamang. “But people are scattered in different places. It would be better if everyone could be provided with a place to live together.”

Twenty-three members of Pasang’s family and relatives are missing.

After so many of her relatives disappeared, she was left devastated. But she has slowly begun returning to everyday work.

When the Onlinekhabar team visited, she was taking several goats towards the shed.

The flood had spared her goat shed.

“I graze the goats during the day and go to the school in the evening,” she said.

For Pasang and the other survivors of Syabrubesi, life has begun moving again in small ways.

A tuin now carries people across the Bhotekoshi. Helicopters bring food to those still stranded. Farmers and residents have started returning to small daily tasks.

But beneath that fragile return to routine is a settlement that has lost its roads, bridges, homes and livelihoods — and hundreds of people who remain missing.

The immediate emergency is being met with relief.

The harder question is how Syabrubesi will rebuild what the flood took away.

(All photos: Chandra Bahadur Ale)

title.rendered: Growing tiger population raises human-wildlife conflict concerns in Chitwan

content.rendered:
Bharatpur, September 23

Kalpana Bote lives in a small thatched house on the edge of Chitwan National Park. Forest surrounds her home, and her family’s life remains closely connected to it. But the same forest that sustains them has also become a source of fear and pain.

Inside her house, children still cry as Kalpana goes about her daily chores. She has no one to help her. Her greatest pain is the memory of her mother-in-law, Umadevi Bote. The memory becomes even more painful when the children cry.

In 2022, Umadevi was attacked by a tiger while she had gone near the forest to collect grass and fiddlehead ferns. She died at the scene. The family received Rs 1 million in relief within 20 days. The money helped ease the immediate financial burden, but it could not bring Umadevi back or end the family’s dependence on the forest.

Kalpana’s family still needs to enter the forest for grass, firewood, fiddlehead ferns and other forest products.

Her story is shared by many families living around Chitwan National Park and its buffer zone.

Conservation success, growing challenge

The number of tigers in and around Chitwan National Park has reached 145. According to the National Tiger Survey 2025, Nepal has 429 tigers, an increase of 74 in four years.

The growth in tiger numbers represents a major achievement in conservation. But alongside that success, human-tiger conflict has emerged as a growing challenge. Ten people were killed in tiger attacks across Nepal in the last fiscal year.

Tigers are increasingly being seen not only inside national parks and buffer zones but also near and inside settlements, increasing fear among locals.

A recent incident in Meghauli, Bharatpur-28, illustrates the risk. On August 9, 65-year-old Mangle Bote was attacked by a tiger in the Rapti Hariyali and Bethari Buffer Zone Community Forest. He had gone for a morning walk at around 8 am and disappeared after the attack. His body was found at 4:20 pm following a search by the national park, Nepal Army, police and residents.

A few days later, a tiger attacked 60-year-old Thakur Adhikari in Dipat settlement of Rapti Municipality-1. Adhikari was injured in the thigh. The same tiger also attacked a cow tied in the shed of resident Dilakumari Tamang.

Since the beginning of the current fiscal year, tigers have entered settlements and attacked people and domestic animals in Chitwan. One person was killed and another injured in August alone.

When the forest is both livelihood and risk

The risk of human-tiger conflict is not the same for all communities. Those directly dependent on national parks and buffer zones face greater exposure.

For poorer families, the forest is not simply a source of employment but a means of meeting daily needs. Collecting grass, firewood, fiddlehead ferns and other forest products requires them to enter the forest, turning their dependence into a potential risk.

Wildlife expert Baburam Lamichhane says not all tigers pose a threat to settlements. Some old, injured or physically weak tigers that struggle to hunt in the forest may move towards settlements in search of easier prey, including domestic animals, and can also attack people.

He says the number of problem tigers is small compared with the total tiger population. However, failure to identify and manage them in time can increase losses of human lives and livestock and fuel resentment towards tiger conservation.

Chitwan National Park has recently captured some tigers that entered settlements and posed risks. On June 23, an incapacitated tiger that had entered Lakshmaniya village in Madi Municipality-1 and killed livestock was captured.

A study conducted in Chitwan identified 22 problem tigers between 2007 and 2016. Of them, 13 had killed people, six had repeatedly killed livestock and three were considered a risk to human safety.

Research covering human-tiger conflict in Chitwan National Park and its buffer zone from 2007 to 2014 also found that conflict was influenced not only by tiger behaviour but also by human entry into forests, dependence on forests, the location of settlements and forests, and the time and place of encounters.

Seven holding cages and a new proposal

Chitwan National Park has seven holding cages in different areas for tigers that enter settlements or become problematic. But with tiger numbers and activity increasing, these facilities are considered insufficient.

According to park information officer Abinash Thapa Magar, weak, injured or old tigers, as well as tigresses raising cubs, may sometimes leave the forest in search of food and security.

The park is now considering a “tiger sanctuary” concept for problem tigers, with the aim of keeping them in a managed setting that provides as natural a habitat as possible.

Thapa Magar says the plan would combine natural habitat management with conservation of tiger prey species. The park is also preparing to increase funding for programmes ranging from improving holding cages to managing prey species.

For communities such as Kalpana’s, however, the challenge goes beyond compensation after an attack. Their dependence on the forest remains unchanged.

According to data from the National Trust for Nature Conservation, 10 people were killed by tiger attacks across Nepal in the fiscal year 2025/26—four in Banke, three in Parsa, two in Bardiya and one in Chitwan. Over the past eight years, 85 people have died in tiger attacks.

The growing tiger population marks a conservation success, but for families living alongside forests, that success also depends on whether both tigers and the people whose lives are tied to the forest can remain safe.

Biratnagar, September 23

Police have seized an ambulance carrying 450 kg of marijuana in Itahari, Sunsari. Police recovered the marijuana, packed in plastic bundles, from the ambulance in a forest area along the Koshi Highway.

At around 11:30 pm on Tuesday, police attempted to stop an ambulance belonging to Triveni Cultural Group, bearing registration number Ba 2 Cha 9573, near Panipiya forest in Tarahara, Itahari Sub-Metropolitan City-20. The driver fled after police attempted to stop the vehicle.

Police pursued the ambulance, but the driver abandoned the vehicle and fled. Police have taken the ambulance and the 450 kg of marijuana into custody and kept them at the Area Police Office, Itahari.

According to police data, more than 72,000 kg of marijuana has been seized in Koshi Province over the past five fiscal years. Police seized 10,420 kg in fiscal year 2023/24; 26,705 kg in 2024/25; and 27,671 kg in 2025/26.

title.rendered: Guterres points to Nepal disaster as evidence of worsening climate crisis

content.rendered:
New York, September 23

UN Secretary-General António Guterres has said the recent disaster in Nepal has demonstrated the reality of the climate risks he warned about three years ago from the foot of Mount Everest.

Addressing the opening of the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Guterres recalled his visit to Nepal in 2023, when he warned that the world’s glaciers were melting at an alarming rate.

“Three years ago, from the mountains of Nepal, I warned that the roof of the world was collapsing,” Guterres said, referring to the rapid melting of glaciers.

He said some had dismissed such warnings as exaggerated, but recent events in Nepal showed that the severe impacts of climate change were emerging sooner and spreading more widely than many had expected.

Guterres said the risks posed by climate change had become a reality, while the countries least responsible for global emissions were bearing some of the greatest costs.

“Polluters must pay. Vulnerable countries suffering the impacts must receive justice,” he said, calling for greater climate justice and financial support from wealthy countries.

He also criticised the limited resources available to address climate-related loss and damage.

The loss and damage fund has “shamefully little money”, Guterres said, arguing that it needs to be adequately financed and that vulnerable countries should not face further exploitation. He called on developed countries to honour their climate finance commitments, triple adaptation finance and scale up the loss and damage fund.

Guterres said the impacts of climate change were falling most heavily on those least responsible for causing it.

“One generation is consuming the future of another, while one group is making profits,” he said.

He also criticised major fossil fuel companies, saying the industry had treated the atmosphere as an “open sewer” while profiting from the consequences.

Guterres said the contrast between fossil fuel profits and climate finance available to developing countries demonstrated the inequity at the heart of the climate crisis.

‘Faultlines in the world are widening’

Guterres also warned that international rules and institutions were under growing pressure.

“The faultlines in our world are widening. Cracks have become canyons,” he told the General Assembly.

He said conflicts in the Middle East, Ukraine, Sudan and Myanmar reflected a world in which power was increasingly escaping established international constraints.

Guterres described Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine as a clear violation of the UN Charter and called for international law to be upheld consistently. He also stressed the need to comply with orders of the International Court of Justice.

He called for reforms to the international financial system to ease the debt burden facing developing countries.

On emerging technologies, Guterres said technology itself was not inherently dangerous, but warned that technology without accountability could be.

“Life and death decisions must never be handed to machines,” he said, calling for a complete ban on lethal autonomous weapons.

Guterres is in the final year of his term as UN secretary-general. He said he would continue working to defend the UN Charter, international law and peace.

The general debate of the 81st UN General Assembly began in New York on Tuesday and is being held under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.”

The General Assembly is scheduled to continue its high-level debate through September 28.

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Thursday. Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal, Foreign Secretary Amrit Rai and Nepal’s Permanent Representative to the UN Lok Bahadur Thapa are also participating in the high-level week.

title.rendered: Congress ward conventions held in 69 of Rolpa’s 72 wards

content.rendered:
Rolpa, September 23

Ward-level conventions of the Nepali Congress have been completed in 69 of the 72 wards in Rolpa under the party’s 15th General Convention.

The conventions, held on September 19 and 20, elected ward committees unanimously in all 69 wards, according to the Nepali Congress Rolpa. Conventions could not be held in the remaining three wards within the scheduled timeframe.

Sudeep Gautam, Rolpa district election officer for the 15th General Convention, said 24 regional representatives, along with ward presidents, were also elected unopposed from the 69 wards.

According to Gautam, around 97 per cent of the ward conventions in Rolpa were completed in a peaceful and cordial environment.

“We have completed around 97 per cent of the ward conventions in Rolpa. Conventions could not be held in only three wards, or around three per cent,” he said.

The ward presidents elected in Rolpa Municipality are Karnapal Gharti in Ward 1, Bhuwaneshwar Acharya in Ward 2, Lil Bahadur Roka Magar in Ward 3, Jamalal Roka Magar in Ward 4, Rak Bahadur Mahara in Ward 5, Deusin Gharti Magar in Ward 6, Kumarsingh Budha Magar in Ward 7, Padam Wali in Ward 8, Jhakku Prasad Wali in Ward 9 and Giriraj Thapa in Ward 10.

In Sunil Smriti Rural Municipality, Mohan Bhandari, Rajendra Singh Thakuri, Tularam Bisht, Narayan Bisht, Shuklal Thapa, Shalikram KC, Reshamlal Seti Mahar and Bhuma Pun were elected ward presidents in Wards 1 through 8, respectively.

In Lungri Rural Municipality, ward presidents were elected in Wards 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7. Jhakamn Gharti Magar, Rajendra Khadka, Dor Bahadur Bisht, Tilak Bahadur Bisht, Anjana Malla Thakuri and Thaman Bahadur Gharti Magar were elected, respectively.

Ward presidents were also elected in all seven wards of Sun Chhahari Rural Municipality.

In Thabang Rural Municipality, Dumey Roka Magar, Ramkaji Roka and Kulman Roka Magar were elected ward presidents in Wards 3, 4 and 5, respectively.

Likewise, ward-level conventions were completed in all wards of Parivartan, Madi, Gangadev, Triveni and Runtigadhi rural municipalities.

3 wards could not hold conventions

Although the party had scheduled ward conventions for September 19 and 20, conventions could not be held in three wards of Rolpa.

Nepali Congress Rolpa Secretary Sher Bahadur Thapa said the convention could not be held in Lungri Rural Municipality-3 due to internal and technical problems. He said conventions in Thabang Rural Municipality-1 and 2 could not be held because of the low number of active party members.

“We have completed around 97 per cent of the ward conventions. In all the wards where the conventions were held, ward presidents and other office-bearers were elected unopposed. Conventions could not be held in three wards within the scheduled timeframe due to some problems,” Thapa said.

Thabang Rural Municipality-1’s Thulo Gaun and Ward 2’s Jhakebang are also known as places associated with the origins of the communist movement.

The next phase of the Nepali Congress’s 15th General Convention, involving rural municipalities, municipalities, sub-metropolitan cities and metropolitan cities, is being held on Wednesday.

content.rendered:

Police have arrested two people accused of extorting money by instilling fear and issuing threats while claiming to be police officers.

Upon receiving this information, police deployed from the District Police Range, Kathmandu, arrested the two individuals involved.

Police have obtained a four-day remand extension from the Kathmandu District Court to investigate them on charges of extortion (fraud), and further investigation is underway.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Nepal has won its first medal at the 20th Asian Games underway in Japan. Karateka Tenzing Sherpa won bronze in the men’s kumite over-84kg weight category.

Tenzing lost 5-0 to Iran’s Mahmoud Nemati in the semifinal held at Toyohashi Gymnasium on Wednesday. After losing the semifinal, he competed for the bronze medal.

In the bronze-medal bout, Tenzing defeated Laos’s Vathana Xayasane 9-1.

With this, Nepal has opened its medal account at the ongoing Asian Games.

title.rendered: Temple donation theft case in Dolpa deepens as money found twice

content.rendered:
Dolpa, September 23

The case involving the alleged theft of donation money from the Bala Tripurasundari Temple in Tripurasundari Municipality-1, Dolpa, has become more complicated after money was found at the temple on two separate days.

Donation money kept at the temple’s main worship area went missing at around 9:30 am on Saturday, September 19. The incident was not immediately made public and came to light on Sunday through social media.

Following the disclosure, a police team led by DSP Anilraj Giri and Chief District Officer Junu Hamal Dhakal reached the temple and began an investigation.

On Monday evening, the Shri Bala Tripurasundari Shusankadari Yogini Udyan Peeth issued a statement saying around Rs 55,000 in donation money had been found tied to a timur tree on the western side of the temple. The money was handed over to priest Ram Prasad Upadhyay by police head constable Indra Bahadur GC, who heads the temple security post.

However, around Rs 54,000 was reportedly found again inside the temple premises on Tuesday afternoon. According to locals, the second amount was made public by the priest as the temple’s money.

The discovery of nearly identical amounts on two different days has raised questions about how much money was actually stolen and whether either amount was the money reported missing on Saturday.

Police said they are investigating the source and authenticity of both amounts and the people involved. One person is currently in police custody, although police said the person’s name would be made public on Wednesday afternoon.

The temple is equipped with CCTV cameras covering its interior and surrounding areas. Police are examining the footage and other evidence as part of the investigation.

title.rendered: Flydubai begins regular flights from Pokhara International Airport

content.rendered:
Kaski, September 23

Flydubai is beginning regular flights on the Dubai-Pokhara-Dubai route from Pokhara International Airport from Wednesday.

The launch of regular international flights has generated excitement among tourism entrepreneurs, industrialists and the general public in Pokhara, as the airport, which began operations on January 1, 2023, had not been able to sustain regular international services.

Airport General Manager Jagannath Niraula said all preparations and infrastructure required for international flights had been completed. According to him, a Flydubai aircraft will land at Pokhara at 6:15 pm and depart for Dubai with passengers at 7:15 pm. The aircraft will be given a water cannon salute upon arrival.

The airport is fully prepared to provide immigration, customs, cargo and other services, Niraula said.

Tourism entrepreneurs and businesspeople in Pokhara are also preparing to welcome and bid farewell to passengers and tourists arriving from and departing for Dubai with khadas and garlands.

Pokhara Customs Office Chief Hari Bhandari said all preparations required for customs procedures, including revenue collection, facilitating legitimate trade, and passenger clearance and import-export procedures, had been completed.

Former president of the Pokhara Tourism Council Pomanarayan Shrestha said the regular flight could help make Pokhara’s international air connectivity sustainable, as Dubai is a major global transit hub and Flydubai operates flights to more than 120 destinations.

Chief District Officer Kuman Singh Gurung said necessary security arrangements had also been made at the airport.

title.rendered: Preparations for winter electricity management, five-member committee formed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

The Nepal Electricity Authority has begun necessary preparations to manage the rising electricity demand expected in Kathmandu Valley and other areas during the upcoming winter.

A meeting held at the Authority on Tuesday to discuss winter electricity demand and supply management decided to accelerate the required studies and work.

The preparations come after flooding along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Rasuwa district damaged hydropower stations operating in that area, halting power generation.

The meeting, chaired by Authority Executive Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha, was attended by deputy executive directors of the Project Management and Transmission directorates, department heads, and project chiefs.

The meeting formed a five-member committee, convened by the director of the Bagmati Provincial Office, to carry forward the necessary studies and work for managing winter electricity demand. The committee has been instructed to submit daily progress reports to the executive director and to promptly report any problems arising during implementation.

At the meeting, Executive Director Shrestha said that although the halt in generation from power stations in the Trishuli River basin has put some pressure on demand and supply management. There would be no need for load-shedding this coming winter.

He said preparations for managing power supply were already being carried forward.

The meeting also set a deadline for completing ongoing transmission and distribution projects under construction in and around Kathmandu Valley.

Likewise, it decided to discuss various options for making power supply more reliable in flood-affected Nuwakot and Rasuwa and to proceed with the necessary process. A team has also been mobilised to conduct a field study on the possibility of bringing the flood-damaged Devighat substation back into operation.

title.rendered: Siddhababa Tunnel to open for traffic by mid-November

content.rendered:
Palpa, September 23

Preparations are underway to open the under-construction Siddhababa Tunnel to traffic by mid-November.

The Siddhababa Tunnel Project Office in Butwal has expedited work to bring the main tunnel and other required infrastructure to the final stage of construction.

Project chief Navaraj Bastola said preparations were being made to allow vehicles to operate through the tunnel by mid-November, as road construction and other civil works inside the tunnel have been completed.

“Construction was pushed back by a month due to delays in the delivery of construction materials caused by the monsoon and the Bhotekoshi floods. Once the materials arrive in the next few days, we will proceed with the remaining work inside the tunnel. We will operate vehicles by December 1,” Bastola said.

The planned opening was affected after the Bhotekoshi floods swept away electrical equipment brought for the tunnel project, he said.

Paving inside the tunnel has been completed, and painting is underway. Finishing work on the technical building is also in progress. Civil works, including lining and concrete works on the floor and walls, have already been completed. Electromechanical works remain to be completed.

According to the project information officer and engineer Saumya Anand, the project has achieved 69.70 per cent physical progress and 63.55 per cent financial progress so far.

Excavation and lining of the main and bypass tunnels, construction of 14 culverts and installation of precast structures inside the tunnel have been completed, Anand said. Three bypasses have been constructed.

Once the internal works are completed, work will begin to secure the road section outside the tunnel. Rock sheds, rockfall barriers and slope protection measures will be installed to protect the tunnel’s external section from landslides.

The 1,126-metre tunnel was awarded under a contract signed in February 2022, with construction beginning in April 2022. China State Construction Engineering Corporation is constructing the project under a contract worth Rs 7.342 billion.

The tunnel is being constructed along the landslide-prone section of the Siddhartha Highway between the lower Siddhababa Temple and Dobhan in Palpa. The section is also prone to dry landslides during the dry season, prompting the government to build the tunnel to improve road safety.

Once operational, the government-funded tunnel is expected to reduce the risks posed by landslides and falling rocks in the Siddhababa area.

Residents of Gulmi, Arghakhanchi, Palpa and Pyuthan in Lumbini Province, as well as Syangja, Parbat, Baglung and Myagdi in Gandaki Province, are expected to benefit directly from the project.

title.rendered: 10 bills registered in parliament in 7 days

content.rendered:
