The government has registered 10 different bills in the federal parliament over the past seven days.

Three bills were registered on Tuesday alone: the Ramraja Prasad Singh Health Science Academy Bill, a bill to activate provisions of certain Nepal Acts, and a bill to amend certain Nepal Acts related to women, children, gender and sexual minorities, and social security.

Before that, five bills were registered on September 21: the Diploma Engineering Council Bill, the National Defence University Bill, and the bill on the security of health workers and health institutions (second amendment).

The Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights (first amendment) Bill and the bill on breast-milk substitutes (sale and distribution control) (first amendment) were also registered.

On September 18, the bill on free legal aid was registered, and on September 17, the Solid Waste Management Bill was registered.

According to Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sobita Gautam, the government is moving to speed up the lawmaking process.

She said, “This year we aim to enact 166 laws, and more than 40 have already been registered so far.”

A person who had gone missing from home in Kailali has been found dead.

DSP Hira Singh Mahara of the Area Police Office, Malakheti, said that while searching for Bohara, who had gone missing from home, he was found dead on a forest hillside in Tulikhet, Chure Rural Municipality-1.

According to him, it has come to light that Bohara and seven others had been drinking alcohol together at the same location before the incident.

Police also said a video was found showing those present threatening to kill Bohara.

Police said they are being brought to the Area Police Office, Malakheti, for further investigation.

A cap, mobile phone, and slippers believed to belong to the deceased were also found at the scene.

Police say further investigation is underway and detailed information is yet to come.

title.rendered: Wildlife conservation must go beyond administrative boundaries, says minister Chaudhary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Geeta Chaudhary has said wildlife conservation should not be confined solely to the administrative boundaries of protected areas but should be broadened.

Speaking on the occasion of the 20th National Conservation Day held in Lalitpur on Wednesday, Minister Chaudhary said that a strong partnership among all three tiers of government, local communities, and stakeholder bodies is essential for nature conservation and human-wildlife coexistence.

Chaudhary pointed to the need to move beyond simply prioritising human-wildlife conflict management and instead advance the concept of “coexistence.”

She said the Nepal government has, from this fiscal year, incorporated a “Human-Wildlife Coexistence Program” into the national budget system, and that a strategic plan is being implemented based on the report of the conflict-reduction task force.

Nature and wildlife do not recognise administrative boundaries, she said, adding that nature’s contribution, through clean air and water, climate regulation, and agricultural production, is indispensable to the national economy.

Noting that the government has declared the current year as the “Year of Legal Reform,” Minister Chaudhary stressed that conservation and development must be complementary rather than opposed to each other.

“Alongside wildlife conservation, cooperation among all stakeholders is essential to ensure the life, livelihood, and safety of local communities,” Chaudhary said. “Our goal should be to focus not just on managing human-wildlife conflict but on programs that establish sustainable coexistence.”

She also said that policies on zoo management, wildlife rescue standards, and animal welfare are being updated to keep pace with the times.

title.rendered: For Tetangche, the flood has become a crisis of food, work and survival

content.rendered:
Tetangche, September 23

The kitchen in Selkar Tamang’s home has gone quiet. Tamang lives with six other members of his family in Tetangche, a remote settlement in Ward 5 of Aamachhodingmo Rural Municipality in Rasuwa district.

Since the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26 cut off the road connection to the village, no food supplies have reached Tetangche. The rice, cooking oil and salt in Tamang’s home have run out.

“We have been surviving on nettles and potatoes,” he said.

His family is not alone.

Across the village, households are struggling to find food. Some families have 10 to 12 members, and even those who have money cannot buy what they need because there is no way to bring supplies into the settlement.

“It has become difficult to keep the stove burning,” he said.

After the flood, the government provided each household with a sack of rice as relief. But that supply has already been exhausted.

“What good can one sack of rice do to a family this big. The times are tough,” said Tamang.

Nepal’s last settlement before Tibet

There is no settlement beyond Tetangche on the Nepali side. It is the country’s last settlement in that direction. Tibet lies beyond the village.

For years, food supplies reached Tetangche from Syafrubesi and Hakubesi. But the August 26 flood swept away Syafrubesi itself, severing one of the main routes through which supplies reached the remote settlement.

“There is no settlement, no road and no bridge. There is no way to bring food,” said local resident Mingmar Tamang. “The food shortage in Aamachhodingmo Rural Municipality is because the roads and bridges are gone.”

The crisis is not only about food.

Around 19 people from Tetangche who worked in areas including Timure were caught in the flood. Those who remain in the village are still dealing with uncertainty over their relatives. Even materials needed to carry out funeral rites have become difficult to obtain.

“The 49th-day funeral rite has to be performed, but there are no materials,” Mingmar said. “A small funeral rite for the fourth week is going on. We are struggling to figure out where to get the materials.”

A village that now depends on the market

Tetangche once produced grain. That is no longer the case.

Mingmar said agricultural production declined with the development of hydropower projects, leaving residents dependent on markets for their food.

“We used to grow grain before. That is no longer possible because of hydropower,” he said. “There is no grain. We all depend on the market for our food.”

Some residents from the village worked at the Timure border point, while others were employed by hydropower projects.

Some of those who were caught in the flood have still not made contact.

“We are suffering twice over,” Mingmar said. “On one side, our relatives have been caught in the flood. On the other, there is nothing here.”

Five wards cut off

The broken roads and bridges have affected five wards of Aamachhodingmo Rural Municipality. Buchung Tamang, chairman of the rural municipality, said the lack of road access has made it impossible to transport essential goods into the affected areas.

“There is no way to take supplies there because there are no roads,” he said. “Around 5,000 people from 1,701 households have been affected.”

There is food being produced in some parts of the municipality, but getting it to market has become another problem.

Cabbage farmers previously sold their produce and used the income to buy food. Now, with the roads blocked, they have lost access to the market.

“There is no market where we can sell the cabbage now,” chairman Tamang said. “Local production is not enough to feed people throughout the year. The federal government needs to give this priority.”

The municipality has provided one sack of rice and oil to each household, but Tamang said the relief would not last long.

Cabbages are rotting as farmers lose their market

The flood has created a strange contradiction in Aamachhodingmo.

Farmers have crops, but they cannot get them to the market. At the same time, villagers are running short of food.

Cabbage produced by farmers in the municipality is now at risk of going to waste because there is no market to sell it.

Last year, farmers in the municipality sold cabbage worth around Rs 30 million. This year, they had expected the trade to reach Rs 60 million.

“This was the time to take the cabbage to market, but the flood blocked the roads,” chairman Tamang said. “Since there is no way to take it to market, farmers will suffer.”

For many farmers, selling cabbage was not simply a way of earning money. It was how they bought food for their families.

But with the roads and bridges damaged, even that source of income has been cut off.

Food may have to come by helicopter

Dawa Gombo Tamang, chairman of Ward 5, said the lack of road access means food may now have to be transported by helicopter.

“Syafrubesi has not reopened. There is no other option but to bring food here by helicopter,” he said. “It would become easier if the roads and bridges were rebuilt quickly.”

The flood has affected 198 people from Aamachhodingmo Rural Municipality, according to rural municipality chairman Buchung Tamang.

They include residents who were in Timure, Syafru and other areas for work when the flood struck.

“The largest number are from Ward 1,” he said.

Children have classrooms, but no notebooks

The disruption has reached the village school as well.

At Shree Saraswati Basic School in Chilime, Ward 5, students are struggling to find even basic stationery because shops in the area have run out of supplies.

“Classes are continuing, but there are no notebooks and pens,” Mingmar said.

The school has 50 students up to Grade 8, according to teacher Pasang Tamang. It also has a hostel.

But the flood has prevented food supplies from reaching the hostel, while stationery has also become scarce.

“There is a hostel at the school,” she said. “Food has not arrived because of the flood. There is also a shortage of stationery.”

For the people of Tetangche, the flood has therefore become more than a disaster that destroyed roads and bridges.

It has cut off the routes through which food arrives, the markets where farmers sell their crops and the places where many villagers work.

For families such as Selkar Tamang’s, the consequences are being felt at the most basic level — at home, around a stove that is becoming increasingly difficult to light.

Local residents are calling for immediate relief and the rapid reconstruction of roads and bridges.

title.rendered: Gautam Buddha’s lessons for Pokhara as Flydubai begins regular flights

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 23

Flydubai’s daily scheduled flights between Dubai and Pokhara have brought a fresh sense of optimism to Nepal’s third international airport.

But as the first regular international service begins, Pokhara also faces a question that has proved difficult for Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa: how can an international airport attract airlines and, more importantly, keep them flying?

Under the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal’s summer schedule, Flydubai has been approved to operate one flight a day on the Dubai-Pokhara-Dubai route from September 23 to October 24.

The service is the second scheduled international service to Pokhara by a foreign airline. Himalaya Airlines had previously operated regular flights to Lhasa, China, but withdrew the service after low passenger numbers made the route financially unsustainable.

That experience offers an early lesson for Pokhara. Getting an airline to operate a route is one thing. Generating enough passengers to keep it commercially viable is another.

Former Nepal Tourism Board chief executive officer Deepak Raj Joshi says sustaining international flights at a relatively new airport requires coordination between the government, airlines and tourism stakeholders.

“Airports cannot be sustained by the government alone, airlines alone or the private tourism sector alone,” he said. “Airlines need enough passengers to make their operations viable.”

What happened in Bhairahawa?

The experience of Gautam Buddha International Airport provides perhaps the clearest example of the challenge Pokhara now faces.

The Bhairahawa airport saw a sudden increase in international flights after maintenance work at Tribhuvan International Airport reduced its operating hours from November 2024.

International airlines, facing limited operating windows in Kathmandu, shifted some services to Gautam Buddha International Airport.

Flydubai, Jazeera Airways, Nepal Airlines, Qatar Airways and Thai AirAsia were among the airlines operating scheduled flights from Bhairahawa during that period.

The airport became busy and appeared to have finally found the international traffic it had been waiting for.

But the momentum did not last.

Once maintenance at Tribhuvan International Airport was completed in March, airlines returned to Kathmandu and the activity at Gautam Buddha declined again.

For Joshi, the episode demonstrates a basic problem: an airport cannot depend on circumstances that temporarily force airlines to use it.

“Foreign tourist arrivals need to be ensured for an airport to operate,” he said. “But that alone is not enough to provide airlines with sufficient occupancy. Domestic passenger demand also needs to increase.”

Bhairahawa has two major potential sources of passengers. It is close to Lumbini, which has the potential to attract Buddhist pilgrims and tourists from countries across Asia. It also serves a large population of Nepalis travelling abroad for employment.

Yet those potential passengers have not been sufficiently converted into sustained traffic, Joshi said.

The government could have used diplomatic channels to make it easier for migrant workers from western Nepal to complete labour, medical and other procedures without travelling to Kathmandu, he said.

The private sector, meanwhile, could have worked directly with airlines to generate tourist traffic.

The broader problem, according to Joshi, was a lack of coordinated effort.

The airspace problem

Bhairahawa also faced a problem that Pokhara does not face to the same extent: international flight routes and airspace access.

Former Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal deputy director general Devanand Upadhyay said repeated discussions between Nepal and India had not produced agreements on additional entry routes or sufficient facilitation for aircraft using Indian airspace during take-off and landing at Gautam Buddha International Airport.

Aircraft approaching Nepal from the west are largely required to enter through the Simara route. That creates an unusual situation for airlines flying towards Bhairahawa.

Even aircraft travelling close to the Nepal-India border on the western side may have to enter Nepal through Simara before heading back towards Bhairahawa.

“This increases the cost for airlines,” Upadhyay said. “Airlines do not want to take on that additional risk.”

He said allowing aircraft to enter Nepal through points such as Nepalgunj or Mahendranagar would make Bhairahawa more attractive to international carriers.

“Singapore-bound flights enter Malaysian airspace soon after take-off, but the two countries have facilitated this through agreements,” he said. “Nepal and India should also have reached such an agreement quickly.”

Unlike Bhairahawa, Pokhara does not face the same route and airspace constraints, according to Upadhyay.

That gives airlines operating from Pokhara a potential advantage. But easier airspace access alone will not guarantee the airport’s success.

Pokhara has another lesson to learn

There is another lesson from Bhairahawa: passengers need more than an airport.

Gautam Buddha International Airport has the infrastructure to handle the types of international flights operating from Kathmandu. But connecting the airport to its potential passenger base has remained a challenge.

Road connectivity was particularly poor when efforts were being made to increase flights to Bhairahawa.

The Butwal-Narayangadh road was in poor condition, while traffic jams around Daunne could last five or six hours.

“If someone lands in Bhairahawa and then has to travel to Jhapa, how much difficulty will that person face?” Upadhyay asked.

For Pokhara, he said, reliable and safe road connections with other parts of the country will be important if international flights are to be sustained.

That means the success of Flydubai’s Pokhara service will not depend only on what happens at Pokhara International Airport.

It will also depend on how easily passengers from other parts of Nepal can reach the city.

Pokhara already has one advantage

Pokhara has, however, demonstrated that there is international demand for the destination.

Before the launch of scheduled Flydubai flights, the city received more than two dozen charter flights operated by Sichuan Airlines from China.

There have also been charter flights from Bhutan.

These services were facilitated through cooperation between airlines, the private sector and local government.

For tourism stakeholders, that experience offers a possible model for attracting more international flights.

Joshi says the Nepal Tourism Board should incorporate both Pokhara and Bhairahawa airports into its international tourism promotion rather than promoting the destinations alone.

“We cannot simply promote Pokhara anymore. We also need to promote Pokhara International Airport,” he said. “When the private sector is enthusiastic, the state needs to work alongside it.”

Can Dubai make the difference?

Flydubai’s route gives Pokhara something that previous services did not have to the same extent: direct access to Dubai, one of the world’s major aviation hubs.

Dubai also has a large South Asian population and serves as a transit point for passengers travelling to destinations beyond the UAE.

That gives the Pokhara-Dubai route the possibility of drawing passengers not only from the UAE but also from other international markets.

But that potential will have to translate into actual passengers.

The airline’s current approval covers daily flights from September 23 to October 24. The longer-term question is whether passenger demand will be strong enough for the service to continue beyond the initial period.

Joshi believes the government should consider appropriate incentives to help airlines establish and sustain international routes during their early stages.

A successful route could also help demonstrate demand to other airlines and create conditions for additional international connections.

The services passengers need

Upadhyay says Pokhara has an advantage over Bhairahawa when it comes to international routes and airspace.

But he stresses that the airport must be supported by services that make international travel genuinely convenient.

“If passengers flying from Pokhara to Dubai are still required to travel to Kathmandu to complete other documentation, the effort will not be sustainable,” he said.

That, he argues, is one of the key lessons Pokhara should take from Bhairahawa.

An international airport cannot be sustained simply by building a runway, opening a terminal or persuading an airline to operate a route.

It needs passengers, tourism promotion, road connectivity, convenient government services, airline cooperation and private-sector participation.

Flydubai’s arrival therefore gives Pokhara an opportunity. But the experience of Gautam Buddha International Airport shows that the real test begins after the first aircraft lands.

For Pokhara, the challenge is no longer simply getting international flights.

It is making sure there are enough reasons — and enough passengers — for those flights to keep coming.

title.rendered: Indra Jatra begins with ceremonial erection of Indradhwaja at Hanumandhoka

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 23

Indra Jatra, one of Kathmandu Valley’s major traditional festivals, has begun at Basantapur Durbar Square with the ceremonial erection of the Indradhwaja, a sacred wooden pole, in front of Hanumandhoka.

The pole is traditionally erected on the 12th day of the bright fortnight of Bhadra, marking the beginning of the eight-day festival.

The ritual is known as Indradhwajotthan. A religious ceremony is performed at the base of the pole, where Bhairav is worshipped.

Indra Jatra is traditionally associated with the celebration of victory after defeating enemies. It is also regarded as a festival centred on worshipping Indradhwaja to invoke and demonstrate strength.

The festival features various traditional dances, chariot processions and worship of deities over eight days.

A major attraction of the festival is the chariot procession of the living goddess Kumari, along with Ganesh and Bhairav. The President traditionally attends the procession from the Gaddi Baithak at Hanumandhoka.

Various traditional dances are performed throughout the festival, including Bhakku, Mahakali, Lakhe and Dashavatar. Pulukisi, a dance representing Airavata, the elephant believed to be the vehicle of the Hindu god Indra, is also performed.

The festival concludes with Indradhwaja Patan, the ceremonial lowering of the sacred pole, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Ashwin, eight days after it is erected.

Indra Jatra is primarily celebrated by the Newar community and is observed with various traditional ceremonies and festivities in Kathmandu as well as Lalitpur, Bhaktapur, Dhulikhel and Dolakha.

title.rendered: Why is the United Nations losing the trust it once commanded?

content.rendered:
New York, September 22

The Second World War killed an estimated 70 million to 85 million people, with civilians accounting for a large share of the dead. Hundreds of cities across Europe and Asia were reduced to ruins.

After two devastating world wars, humanity sought to ensure that such destruction would never be repeated. Representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to draft the United Nations Charter. The Charter was signed on June 26, 1945, and came into force on October 24 that year, marking the formal birth of the United Nations.

Bringing large and small states, victors and vanquished, under one roof at a time of fear and distrust was itself an extraordinary act of international confidence. The idea was simple but ambitious — disputes should be settled through dialogue and diplomacy rather than force.

The General Assembly was built around the principle of one country, one vote. The Security Council was established as the principal body responsible for maintaining international peace and security. UN agencies and programmes, including the World Health Organization, UNICEF and the Food and Agriculture Organization, began working on issues ranging from public health and hunger to development and reconstruction.

For smaller, weaker and newly independent countries, the UN offered something the balance of military and economic power could not — a forum where sovereignty was recognised and their voices could be heard.

In its early decades, the organisation built considerable moral and political legitimacy from the ruins of war.

But this is not 1945.

And the confidence once placed in the United Nations is under strain.

Khalilur Rahman, Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister and president of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, has placed the issue at the centre of this year’s session. The official theme is “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.”

Rahman has argued that trust cannot simply be demanded. It has to be earned continuously.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres has similarly identified rebuilding confidence in multilateralism as one of the major challenges facing the international system.

World leaders gathering at UN headquarters in New York this week are therefore speaking at a time when the organisation is confronting a basic question — can the institution created after the Second World War still deliver on the expectations placed upon it?

Why has trust in the United Nations declined?

The crisis of confidence did not emerge overnight.

For decades, the UN has struggled to prevent wars and conflicts in different parts of the world. Its ability to uphold a rules-based international order has also come under increasing pressure.

That has consequences for countries such as Nepal, which lack the military, economic and political weight of major powers.

The problem is also visible in the slow progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals. The world remains behind schedule on many of the targets set for 2030, while displacement has reached record levels and development assistance is under pressure.

The organisation itself is also facing serious financial constraints.

The UN General Assembly approved a regular budget of $3.45 billion for 2026, about 7 percent lower than the approved 2025 budget. The UN has also confirmed that 2,900 positions were abolished as part of the organisation’s restructuring and budget pressures.

Peacekeeping has been affected as well. UN Peacekeeping has warned that financial shortfalls are forcing missions to reduce operations by around 25 percent, affecting their ability to protect civilians and support peace efforts.

For Nepal, this is particularly significant.

Why Nepal has a stake in UN peacekeeping

Nepal has been one of the major contributors to UN peacekeeping for decades.

UN records show that Nepal had more than 6,000 uniformed personnel serving in UN peacekeeping operations in July 2025, making it one of the organisation’s largest contributors.

Any reduction in peacekeeping operations therefore has direct implications for Nepal.

It is also an issue Bangladesh has a particular interest in raising. Bangladesh has long been among the largest contributors of troops and police to UN peacekeeping operations.

For countries such as Nepal and Bangladesh, peacekeeping is not simply an international responsibility. It is also one of the clearest areas where smaller developing countries make a tangible contribution to global security.

Nepal therefore has a strong interest in ensuring that the financial crisis facing the UN does not undermine its peacekeeping capacity.

Rules-based multilateralism is a lifeline for smaller states

For countries such as Nepal, the international system works most predictably when it is based on rules rather than raw power.

The United Nations remains one of the few global institutions where a small country formally has the same vote as a major power in the General Assembly.

That does not mean all countries have equal influence in practice. The structure of the Security Council, particularly the veto power held by its five permanent members, gives major powers considerable influence.

But the principle remains important for smaller states.

When multilateral institutions weaken, countries with less military, economic and political power can find themselves more exposed to the decisions of larger states.

The World Trade Organization offers another example of the broader strain on multilateralism. As trade becomes increasingly shaped by protectionism and bilateral bargaining, smaller economies can find it harder to compete on equal terms.

A 2026 Munich Security Report has also warned about the risks of a more transactional international order, in which powerful states can use economic and political leverage to secure advantages.

At the same time, the threats facing the world — conflict, nuclear proliferation, poverty, inequality and climate change — are increasingly international in nature.

Guterres has repeatedly argued that this makes multilateral cooperation more important, not less.

The challenge is rebuilding faith in institutions that many countries increasingly believe are failing to deliver.

The climate crisis exposes another gap

For Nepal, the credibility of the international system is also closely tied to climate change.

The country is highly vulnerable to climate-related disasters despite contributing very little to global greenhouse gas emissions.

The gap between climate commitments and delivery has therefore become a central concern for developing countries.

Developed countries had pledged in 2009 to mobilise $100 billion a year in climate finance for developing countries. According to the OECD, that target was exceeded for the third consecutive year in 2024, with $136.7 billion in climate finance provided and mobilised.

But the figures remain contested.

Oxfam has argued that the headline figures significantly overstate the actual value of climate finance received by developing countries. Its 2026 analysis estimated the “true value” of the finance provided in 2024 at between $33 billion and $45 billion, noting that a large proportion was delivered through loans rather than grants.

That disagreement illustrates the wider problem.

Climate justice is frequently discussed at UN-led negotiations, but developing countries continue to question whether the financial support promised to them is actually reaching them at the scale and terms required.

For countries facing increasingly severe climate impacts, the distinction between a promise and its implementation is not merely technical.

It can determine whether communities receive the resources needed to recover from a disaster.

Can the UN restore trust?

Rahman has placed conflict prevention and peacebuilding, civilian protection, development and stronger engagement with civil society among the priorities of his presidency.

His programme for the 81st General Assembly is built around six pillars, including peace and security, development, climate action, rights and protection, innovation and greater engagement with people and civil society.

The question is whether these ambitions can translate into meaningful institutional change.

Reforming the Security Council has been discussed for decades, but the permanent members have shown little willingness to give up their existing privileges.

That makes fundamental reform difficult.

The financial crisis presents another obstacle. The UN approved a smaller regular budget for 2026 and abolished thousands of positions as part of its restructuring process.

Peacekeeping missions are also operating under financial pressure, while geopolitical divisions continue to make consensus on major conflicts difficult.

The climate crisis presents a similar contradiction. The UN has helped establish a global framework for climate action, but the delivery of finance and support remains disputed.

The debate over restoring trust in the United Nations is therefore important in itself.

After 80 years, the organisation is confronting questions that go to the heart of its original purpose — whether it can prevent conflict, protect vulnerable populations, support development and ensure that international rules apply beyond the interests of the most powerful states.

For least developed countries such as Nepal, the stakes are particularly high.

A world governed primarily by power and transactions leaves smaller countries with fewer safeguards. A functioning multilateral system, even with all its shortcomings, gives them a forum in which their voices can be heard.

As Rahman has put it, trust cannot simply be requested.

It has to be earned, day after day.

The 81st General Assembly now faces the harder part — demonstrating that the United Nations can still earn it.

title.rendered: As war raged in Ukraine, a Nepali restaurant in Bratislava became a refuge

content.rendered:
On 24 February 2022, one breaking news story dominated television channels, radio stations and news websites around the world. Russia has launched an invasion of Ukraine.

Hundreds of kilometres away, the news sent shockwaves through Nepali communities across Europe. Phones began ringing almost immediately.

Nepali students and workers trapped in Ukrainian cities were frightened. Some were desperate to get home. Others were already moving towards the borders, unsure where they could go or how they would get there safely. Amid the sound of bombs over Ukrainian cities, one question kept returning.

Where do we go now? How do we survive?

At the time, Jaya Prasad Siwakoti, originally from Panchthar in eastern Nepal, was living in Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia. Then his phone began ringing repeatedly. The people on the other end were Nepalis stranded in Ukraine.

“We are stuck. Is there anyone who can rescue us?”

Their voices stayed with Siwakoti.

He had his own business and his own responsibilities, but suddenly those seemed less important. Slovakia shared a border with Ukraine, and he felt that living so close to the unfolding crisis gave him a responsibility to act.

He did not yet know how. But he decided to try.

The first journey to the border

“I was confused,” Siwakoti recalls. “What should I do? How many Nepalis were there in the war zone? What condition were they in?”

The calls began coming in from around 11am.

Many were from relatives living outside Nepal, asking him to help family members trapped in Ukraine.

“They called with hope,” he says. “But I had no answers. Should I say I could help or that I couldn’t?”

Then four or five calls came one after another.

“That was when I thought, this can’t continue like this.”

Siwakoti contacted Ram Kaji Khadka, who was then Nepal’s ambassador to Germany. Khadka told him to go ahead.

A volunteer rescue team began taking shape, bringing together Nepalis and volunteers based in several countries.

Nepalis inside Ukraine started contacting the team directly. They were given information and guidance on possible routes out of the country.

By February 26, many of those trying to escape had reached the borders with Poland and Slovakia.

But the situation at the Polish border was becoming increasingly chaotic. Large crowds were gathering, and confusion and fear were spreading.

Some began looking for another route. Slovakia became the alternative.

Siwakoti was able to contact organisations including Human Rights groups and the International Organization for Migration because of his previous experience working in the health sector in both Nepal and Slovakia.

That network soon proved crucial.

On the evening of February 26, the first eight Nepalis managed to cross into Slovakia.

At that stage, the border was primarily being opened for Ukrainian citizens. The eight were placed in shelter provided by the International Organization for Migration. The following day, February 27, Siwakoti called them.

“Come to Bratislava. I’ll receive you.”

They travelled by train from about 600 kilometres away.

“They came simply because they trusted that I was here and that they had my contact,” he says.

A restaurant becomes a home

On the morning of February 27, the first group of eight Nepalis arrived in Bratislava. There was a woman among them. Siwakoti took them to the Nepal Restaurant, the business he was running.

“There was no other option at the time,” he recalls.

The restaurant normally opened at 11am. They arrived shortly before 9am. The kitchen was still closed, but the dining area was warm. Siwakoti made tea himself and served it to the exhausted travellers. Then something happened that he still remembers vividly. As they talked, some of them suddenly fell asleep in their chairs.

“They had escaped the war and finally entered a safe place,” he says. “It felt as though they could finally relax enough to sleep.”

He made a decision. The restaurant would not just help them that day. It would become a rescue centre.

At first, the exhausted travellers used cushions from the chairs as pillows. Siwakoti brought mattresses from his own furniture business and laid them out so they could sleep properly.

“They had walked through forests to reach the border,” he says. “They were exhausted.”

More groups were on their way.

Siwakoti soon found himself trying to manage three things at once — looking after those already in the restaurant, preparing for incoming groups and answering a steady stream of calls from Nepalis still trapped in different parts of Ukraine.

So he formalised the restaurant as a rescue centre.

Those who arrived were given a place to rest. But there was another idea behind the arrangement. When a new group arrived, those who had already been through the journey could help them.

The restaurant had only two toilets and no proper bathroom. But Siwakoti arranged first-aid supplies, essential items for women and Wi-Fi.

“At least I wanted to create an environment where they could stay comfortably for two nights,” he says. “I thought being able to contact their families would also give them some mental relief.”

The restaurant had become something very different from the business it had been only days earlier.

For people who had crossed a war zone, it was a temporary home.

When the border became another source of fear

Not everyone who tried to leave Ukraine initially headed towards Slovakia.

Around the seventh or eighth day of the war, some Nepalis reached the Polish border. But what they found there was frightening.

The crowds were growing. People were pushing and struggling to get through.

Then, according to the Nepalis who later told Siwakoti what happened, unfamiliar people suddenly began firing shots and looting started amid the crowd.

“According to the Nepalis, some unknown people fired shots and started looting,” Siwakoti says. “The border itself had become another scene of terror.”

Those who had gone there hoping to enter Poland were forced to turn back. They abandoned that route and eventually headed towards Slovakia. But the journey was still far from safe.

“One group of around 22 to 25 people had travelled together,” Siwakoti says. “But only 13 eventually got in touch with me. We didn’t know what had happened to the others.”

They spent two days travelling through forests.

They moved at night, afraid of what might happen in the darkness and uncertain of whom they could trust.

“They told us very painful stories,” Siwakoti says. “They had to spend nights in the forest, moving forward while worrying about whether someone might shoot at them or rob them.”

When they finally reached his restaurant, the relief was palpable. For Siwakoti, giving them somewhere safe to sleep was one of the few things he could do.

Building a rescue network

By February 29, Siwakoti realised that the rescue effort needed something more organised. He developed what he called a “chain information system”. His idea was simple.

If groups travelling through different parts of Europe could communicate directly with one another, information could move faster and the rescue effort would become easier to manage.

He connected Nepalis staying at his restaurant with groups that had already reached Portugal or France.

Those groups were then connected with people crossing the border.

The people crossing the border were linked with Nepalis still trapped in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine.

A network began to form.

“I created a system like a chain,” Siwakoti says. “It made it easier for people to help one another.”

The system reduced the pressure on the small team coordinating the rescue.

Each group could guide the next.

Another team was then formed to help manage Nepalis who had reached different European countries.

Siwakoti and his colleagues held discussions with Nepali associations and diplomatic representatives in five countries.

The aim was to make sure people arriving from the war zone received reliable information and practical advice.

The network eventually helped Nepalis travelling towards countries including Portugal, France and Spain.

“It helped people who had just come out of the war get the right information and advice,” Siwakoti says.

On February 27, 2022, the Nepal Restaurant had officially become a rescue centre.

For the whole of March, Siwakoti closed the restaurant and devoted himself to the rescue effort.

By the final week of March, the number of arrivals had begun to fall.

Only two or three people were arriving each day.

“They would eat and leave,” he says. “They didn’t want to stay. They just wanted to continue on their journey.”

The additional accommodation arranged with the help of the International Organization for Migration was eventually closed as well.

On 1 April, the Nepal Restaurant reopened. Siwakoti returned to his business. But the experience had left its mark.

More than a place to sleep

During the rescue operation, the restaurant sheltered not only Nepalis but people from other countries as well.

Around 15 foreign migrants, including Indians, Bangladeshis and Senegalese, also found temporary refuge there.

Siwakoti helped move 78 Nepalis from his restaurant to another accommodation facility and kept a record of all of them.

More than 100 others spent nights at the restaurant before continuing their journeys.

He did not keep records of everyone who passed through. But he remembers their faces.

“I still feel as though all of this happened in a dream,” he says.

“When they arrived, some were afraid even to speak. But after staying for two nights, they would rest their heads on my shoulder and talk comfortably. When I took them outside and said goodbye, it was very difficult for me.”

Many stayed in touch for months. Some continued calling for as long as six months. But, over time, those connections faded.

“Ninety-five per cent have changed their phone numbers,” he says. “Many no longer use their old Facebook accounts. I don’t have contact with most of them now.”

Some, however, still remember. And occasionally, they call.

The rescue ended. The problems did not.

Once the immediate rescue effort was over, Siwakoti returned to running his business.

But he soon realised that helping people escape the war had solved only one part of a much larger problem.

Nepalis living in Slovakia were facing difficulties of their own.

There is no reliable official figure for how many Nepalis currently live in Slovakia, he says.

Siwakoti estimates the number at around 1,000, with many living without proper documentation.

Many come from central and western Nepal.

They typically work in car factories, hospital cleaning services and agriculture.

But finding stable work is not always easy.

“About 40 per cent of the Nepalis who come here are unemployed,” he says.

A common route is to pay a large sum of money in Nepal for a one-year work contract.

But when that contract expires, problems can begin if the company does not renew it or provide continued documentation.

Some do not want to return to Nepal.

They try to move to another European country or end up living in Slovakia without legal status.

A few months ago, Siwakoti says, a Nepali who had arrived from Cyprus died in Slovakia.

“He didn’t have proper documents here,” he recalls. “We somehow managed to arrange for his body to be taken care of.”

The episode underlined a problem that Siwakoti believes is still poorly understood in Nepal.

He continues to contact companies in Slovakia and try to find jobs for Nepalis.

But he is concerned about the way migration to Slovakia is being promoted in Nepal.

“People are being told there is a huge demand for workers here without properly understanding the reality,” he says. “It is still not clear where the problem lies.”

From emergency rescue to a longer responsibility

The Ukraine war forced Siwakoti into a role he had never planned to take.

His restaurant became a shelter.

His phone became a lifeline.

And a network built almost spontaneously became a way for hundreds of people to find information, accommodation and a route to safety.

But the experience also exposed the deeper vulnerabilities faced by Nepalis who migrate to Europe in search of work.

Today, Siwakoti is also leading the Non-Resident Nepali Association in Slovakia.

He has formally registered the NRNA in Slovakia, creating a legal and organisational platform through which he hopes to address the longer-term problems facing Nepalis there.

The war may have moved out of the restaurant.

The mattresses have been put away. The kitchen has reopened. The tables once again serve customers rather than exhausted travellers arriving from a war zone.

But for Siwakoti, the responsibility that began with a phone call on 24 February 2022 has not entirely ended.

The emergency was temporary.

The questions it revealed — about migration, legal status, employment and the safety of Nepalis abroad — remain.

title.rendered: Ed Sheeran, Macklemore and the myth of being apolitical

content.rendered:
Headlines this week have been inundated with news of artist Macklemore being dropped from Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour, following Macklemore’s onstage calls to “free Palestine”.

The rap artist said Robert Kraft, owner of New England Patriots and the Gillette Stadium, barred him from playing in his stadium, and rallied other stadiums to join the boycott.

In response, Sheeran’s remaining support acts also withdrew. Sheeran has attempted to distance himself from the decision, suggesting it was the promoter’s and not his. He has taken an “apolitical” stance, referring back to his history of avoiding public political statements.

But the resulting condemnation from fans and commentators suggests forcing neutrality in such situations isn’t straightforward.

What does it mean to be ‘apolitical’?

Politics isn’t limited to government. In a more general sense, it refers to the relationships of power in society and between members of society, and efforts to change them.

This seems to be what Ed Sheeran’s recent statements are reaching for. He claims to be apolitical in the sense that he keeps his political views separate from his work as an artist:

People buy my records to put on while they make out. I’m not Mr Political. I vote the way I feel I should, but won’t tell somebody else what to do.

Importantly, Sheeran’s recent statement doesn’t just claim he is apolitical on the issue of Palestine, but that he is apolitical in general. This would require never expressing any views in relation to the arrangement of power and control in society.

It doesn’t seem Sheeran has done this. He has previously supported campaigns against Brexit and far-right racism, has supported Jermey Corbyn, and played a Concert For Ukraine in 2022. These are political positions.

So, if Sheeran is not apolitical at all times, this means he chooses to be apolitical on specific issues. In this case the issue is Palestine.

Is apolitical the same as neutral?

Being apolitical is not the same as being “neutral” on political issues, especially in cases where significant injustice is taking place.

Some argue attempts at neutrality on such issues entrench, or at least permit, the injustice.

Beyond the entertainment industry, neutrality has often been a question in the context of wars. Here, the importance of weighing intention against outcomes become especially clear. The Red Cross argues its political neutrality allows it to assist more people affected by conflict.

On the other hand, mercenary soldiers – who are politically neutral and fight purely for wages – are generally seen as much less ethical. Many current conflicts in the world are fought by such soldiers.

The 17th century philosopher Grotius argued that because mercenaries fight for pay, without regard for the justice of their cause, “there is no course of life more abominable and to be detested”.

Yet some advocates argue that if mercenaries result in faster ends to a conflict, that outcome may make their actions ethical – though their intentions may not be ethical.

Is it unethical to be apolitical?

Not always. Being apolitical is defensible based on some philosophical perspectives, but context matters.

Greek philosopher Epicurus argued politics is best avoided. He believed we should aim for “tranquility of the soul”, retired from the affairs of the world, and living one’s life in peace.

It seems possible to be “neutral” – to not hold views – on specific political issues. Yet many philosophers, including Aristotle and Italian philosopher Antonio Gramsci, have held that humans are unavoidably political creatures. As such, some issues seem to demand a response from us.

Philosopher Hannah Arendt showed it was a kind of “thoughtlessness” that facilitated the evils of the Nazi regime: a failure to pay attention to serious ethical wrongs.

In Sheeran’s cases, perhaps from a personal perspective he does think he is being “apolitical”. However, his decision takes place in a broader context, wherein it appears to have been influenced or made by wealthy individuals with well-stated political stances on Palestine.

He has gone beyond simply refusing to express his own political beliefs. He has allowed Macklemore’s political views to be removed at the behest of another party acting in its own political interest, thereby favouring one over the other.

Action through inaction

Another problem with choosing not to “take sides” on a particular issue is that it is often a response reserved for those who are privileged enough to not be affected by the injustice or power relationship under discussion.

At the same time, the more privileged we are, the more ability we have to affect change. This is one of the justifications Macklemore offers for his support of Palestine.

Sheeran’s removal of Macklemore from his tour is a statement on whose interests count, and who has the power in this situation. And that’s political whether he wants it to be or not.

title.rendered: Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal attends UN General Assembly opening session

content.rendered:
New York, September 22

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal attended the opening session of the high-level general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday.

The high-level segment began at the UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday.

Khanal attended the session as part of the Nepali delegation, which included Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai, Nepal’s Permanent Representative to the UN in New York Ambassador Lok Bahadur Thapa and Joint Secretary Krishna Prasad Dhakal, among other officials.

According to the Foreign Minister’s Secretariat, Khanal is scheduled to attend various high-level meetings, ministerial-level discussions and side events during the week-long high-level segment.

He will also hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from various countries and senior UN officials.

Nepal is also organising a side event titled ‘Sagarmatha to Sea’ during the General Assembly.

The event will highlight the impacts of climate change on the Himalayan region and the challenges created by climate-induced disasters, according to officials.

Khanal is also scheduled to participate in ministerial-level meetings of the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries, Non-Aligned Movement, and the Group of 77 and China.

The high-level general debate of the 81st UN General Assembly will continue until September 28.

Prime Minister Balen Shah is scheduled to address the high-level general debate on September 24.

Shah left for New York on Tuesday evening to lead the high-level Nepali delegation to the UN General Assembly.

Foreign Minister Khanal, Prime Minister’s Chief Adviser Kumar Byanjankar, Foreign Secretary Rai and other members of the delegation are accompanying Shah.

title.rendered: Speaker reminds lawmakers of rules on mobile phones and parliamentary conduct

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal on Tuesday reminded lawmakers of the rules governing conduct inside the House of Representatives, including a provision prohibiting the use of mobile phones for calls, photography and audio or video recording during parliamentary meetings.

Concluding Tuesday’s House meeting, Aryal drew lawmakers’ attention to Rules 20 and 21 of the House of Representatives Rules, 2083, and urged them to help make parliamentary proceedings more orderly and dignified.

“I draw the attention of all honourable members to Rules 20 and 21 of the House of Representatives Rules. I would particularly draw your attention to clause (t) of Rule 20,” Aryal said.

Rule 20 sets out 11 provisions governing the conduct of lawmakers during House meetings. Clause (t) states that members must keep their phones on silent and must not make calls, take photographs or record audio or video inside the meeting hall.

The Speaker’s reminder comes amid concerns over lawmakers using mobile phones during House proceedings. Aryal, however, did not name any particular lawmaker while drawing attention to the provision.

Rule 20 also requires lawmakers to stand and show respect when the Speaker enters the meeting hall, remain seated while the Speaker is addressing the House, speak only after being given time, and refrain from actions that disrupt proceedings or undermine the dignity of the House.

Rule 21 contains five provisions governing lawmakers participating in debates. Among other things, it prohibits members from criticising the Speaker’s conduct except during a motion concerning the Speaker’s conduct, discussing matters barred under Article 105 of the Constitution, and using indecent, obscene, insulting or offensive language.

It also prohibits remarks that demean or adversely affect any person, caste, religion, language or gender, as well as the use of unparliamentary language.

The rules further state that lawmakers must not misuse their right to speak with the intention of obstructing House business.

Reminder comes after dispute over comments on judiciary

Aryal’s reminder came a day after a dispute in the House over comments made by Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Yagyamany Neupane about the judiciary.

During Tuesday’s proceedings, Neupane said recent developments had given him the impression that the courts had not embraced change.

“Looking at recent developments, it feels as though the courts have not embraced change,” Neupane said.

He went on to criticise the justice system, saying that even people who had won cases and held court verdicts in their hands would say that the courts do not deliver justice.

CPN-UML lawmaker Guru Prasad Baral raised a point of order over Neupane’s remarks.

Baral said the Constitution clearly provides for separation of powers and assigns distinct roles to the executive, legislature and judiciary.

He also questioned what he described as attempts to interfere with the judiciary, referring to attacks on the Supreme Court and other courts during the Gen Z movement.

Article 105 of the Constitution bars discussions in either House of the Federal Parliament on matters concerning cases under consideration by a court if such discussion could adversely affect the administration of justice. It also bars discussion of judicial acts performed by judges in the course of their duties, except when discussing an impeachment motion concerning a judge’s conduct.

Against this backdrop, Aryal reminded lawmakers that maintaining the dignity and quality of parliamentary proceedings is a shared responsibility.

“I urge all honourable members to recognise that everyone has a duty and responsibility to make each day’s House meeting dignified and exemplary,” he said.

The Federal Parliament’s official website lists the House of Representatives Rules, 2083, as the current rules governing the House.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

PM Shah leaves for the USA for the UN General Assembly

Prime Minister Balen Shah has left for the USA today, leading a high-level Nepali delegation to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. PM Shah’s delegation members are his chief advisor Kumar Byanjankar, chief personal secretary Subash Sharma, private secretary Pradeep Pariyar and photographer Binay Shakya, among others.

SC upholds pardon granted to Resham Chaudhary

The Supreme Court has upheld the pardon that President Ramchandra Paudel granted to Resham Chaudhary, the founding leader of the Nagarik Unmukti Party.

Malaysia recruitment dispute reaches prime ministerial level

The dispute over Malaysia’s plan to limit Nepali worker recruitment to a small group of manpower companies has now reached the prime minister’s level. Prime Minister Balendra (Balen) Shah, speaking by phone with his Malaysian counterpart Anwar Ibrahim on Tuesday morning, urged an end to the syndicate and middleman system seen in Malaysia’s employment sector.

Foreign Minister Khanal holds talks with Bhutanese PM, EU vice-president in New York

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal held separate meetings with Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay and European Union Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera in New York on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

Bus driver dies after suffering severe burns in Tripureshwor fire

The driver injured in a bus fire at Tripureshwor on Monday has died while undergoing treatment at Kirtipur Hospital, also known as Burn Hospital. According to police sources, the bus driver died on Monday night while receiving treatment.

Transport unions demand probe, compensation over Tripureshwor bus driver’s death

Transport entrepreneurs and workers’ organisations have demanded an investigation and compensation over the death of bus driver Arjun Dong, who died after attempting self-immolation in Tripureshwor on September 21.

Climbers begin returning from Manaslu due to heavy snowfall

Climbers attempting to scale Mount Manaslu have begun returning home midway through their expeditions as heavy snowfall and continuous rainfall have made weather conditions unfavourable for mountaineering.

title.rendered: Cooperative operators, CEOs barred from renting own homes for offices

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Cooperative operators and chief executive officers (CEOs) will not be allowed to operate cooperative offices from houses owned by themselves or their relatives, according to a directive issued by the National Cooperative Regulatory Authority.

The authority has prohibited cooperatives from renting houses owned by their operators, CEOs or their family members for office operations. Cooperatives found violating the provision must relocate their offices within six months.

The authority has also made prior approval mandatory for savings and credit cooperatives seeking to register or change the objectives of institutions whose main business is savings and credit transactions. Cooperatives must submit an application to the authority for such approval.

Under the amended Regulatory Standards for Operating Cooperatives Engaged Mainly in Savings and Credit Transactions, proposed cooperatives must declare that their members are not members of other cooperatives of a similar nature. The proposed area of operation must also have geographical continuity.

The standards require cooperatives to submit a business plan covering at least five years and a commitment to maintain the prescribed qualifications of directors, accounting supervision committee members, managers and employees.

Applications for prior approval must also include a recommendation from the concerned local level. The authority will assess the feasibility of implementing the proposed business plan and conduct on-site inspections covering office infrastructure, security of savings, market conditions and potential investment areas.

title.rendered: Aravind Kumar Jha elected secretary of International Kabaddi Federation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Aravind Kumar Jha, general secretary of the All Nepal Kabaddi Association, has been elected secretary of the International Kabaddi Federation (IKF).

According to the All Nepal Kabaddi Association, Jha was elected to the post at the IKF General Assembly held in Japan.

Jha said his election would make it easier for Nepali players to gain international exposure and contribute to the development of kabaddi in Nepal.

“It will make it easier to gain international exposure and will support the development of kabaddi. Two international events are now being held in Nepal, and this will also help those events,” Jha said.

He said both international competitions to be held in Nepal were also approved by the General Assembly. The Four Nations Cup is scheduled to be held in Nepal in November, while the Asian Women’s Championship will be held in March.

The All Nepal Kabaddi Association said the election of a Nepali representative as secretary of the International Kabaddi Federation was an important achievement for Nepali sports.

The All Nepal Kabaddi Association congratulated Jha and wished him success in his new term.

title.rendered: Galchhi-Syabrubesi road to resume traffic by Dashain

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

The Department of Roads is working to resume traffic along the flood-damaged Galchhi-Syabrubesi road section within the month of Ashoj, ahead of Dashain.

According to the department, traffic has already resumed at most locations after road repairs. Director General Dr Bijay Jaisi said work was underway to restore traffic along the entire Galchhi-Syabrubesi section by Dashain.

Temporary repairs have been completed at Kolpu Khola, connecting Dhading and Nuwakot, and traffic has resumed. The department has also completed the contract process for permanent repairs, and the contractor has started work.

At Ratomate, around 200 metres of road damaged by the flood has been reopened after back-cutting. In Nuwakot’s Devighat, the Nepal Army has installed a Bailey bridge, allowing traffic to operate from Galchhi to Bidur.

Of the approximately 10-km Bidur-Betravati section, nine kilometres have been reopened. Around 300 metres remains blocked by a landslide, where the Nepal Army has started blasting from both sides to open a track. Traffic is expected to resume there within a few days.

After that, Bailey bridges will need to be installed at Betravati and Syabrubesi. A 72-metre Bailey bridge will be installed at Betravati, while a 76-metre bridge is planned for Syabrubesi.

The road from Betravati through Dhunche to Syabrubesi is otherwise accessible. The approximately 15-km Syabrubesi-Rasuwagadhi section, however, has been severely affected by the flood, and a survey has begun.

—RSS

title.rendered: RSP lawmaker calls for psychological training for drivers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Ashish Gajurel has called for providing psychological training to drivers.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives, Gajurel, who said he had studied transport engineering, said drivers needed psychological knowledge, referring to Monday’s incident in Tripureshwor.

He said the subject of transport and psychology was given significant priority during his university studies, particularly the psychological aspects that drivers should understand.

Referring to practices in developed countries, he said significant investment was made in public awareness programmes and in efforts to have a positive impact on drivers’ psychological well-being. Such initiatives, he said, were not visible in Nepal.

He also said traffic management in developed countries relied heavily on technology, with fewer traffic police required on the roads.

“Currently, around 1.3 to 1.4 million vehicles are operating in Kathmandu alone, while there are not even 1,000 traffic police to manage them,” he said. “Drivers appear to use the roads fearing that they might be penalised, while traffic police are also under pressure to manage transportation by working around the clock.”

Gajurel said the government also needed to reconsider its approach to enforcement.

He said the government appeared to prioritise imposing penalties and fines and taking action against traffic violations as a means of reducing road accidents and making traffic management easier.

“Where are the public awareness programmes? Where are the classes to provide psychological knowledge to drivers?” he said.

He also said regulations prohibit drivers from driving for more than six hours a day, but the provision has not been effectively implemented.

In such circumstances, he said, road safety and safe travel could not be ensured through enforcement alone.

title.rendered: Home, energy ministers visit Meteorological Department ahead of heavy rain forecast

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Home Minister Sudan Gurung and Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Biraj Bhakta Shrestha visited the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology to inquire about the rain and snowfall forecast from September 25 onward.

They went to the department’s office in Baburmahal and met Director General Archana Shrestha, spokesperson Bibhuti Pokharel and others, and discussed the possible risks and necessary preparations.

During the discussion, the department’s meteorologists said that due to the effect of a low-pressure system developing over the Bay of Bengal, heavy to very heavy rainfall is forecast in various parts of Nepal, along with heavy snowfall in the high Himalayan region.

The rain-bearing system is likely to spread across the whole country. Heavy to very heavy rainfall in the hills and Tarai, and snowfall in the high Himalayan region, may also bring risk.

Department spokesperson Pokharel said that based on the current outlook, the highest rainfall is likely in Lumbini and Gandaki provinces. She said the rain carries the risk of flooding, riverbank erosion and landslides, so people have been advised to exercise high caution in identified risk areas and to avoid travel toward the Himalayan region.

She also said the department is continuously exchanging updated information with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and officials of the concerned ministries.

“We are in regular contact with the Disaster Authority; necessary preparations are also under way at the concerned agencies,” spokesperson Pokharel said.

Advised not to travel long distances or at night

According to the department’s Weather Forecasting Division, the low-pressure area that developed over the North Andaman Sea and surrounding areas has now reached the middle of the Bay of Bengal and has intensified further into a “deep depression.”

As this system is moving in a west-northwest direction, rainfall activity will increase from Wednesday in Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces as a result.

According to the division, from September 25 to 27, some places in Gandaki and Lumbini provinces will see heavy to very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunder, lightning and windstorms, with the possibility of extremely heavy rainfall in one or two places.

Similarly, a few places in Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati and Sudurpashchim provinces may see heavy to very heavy rainfall, and a few places in Karnali province may see heavy rainfall.

Following the special bulletin the Meteorological Department issued on Monday, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority also issued a notice urging all stakeholders and the general public to exercise high caution.

The Authority has urged people not to travel long distances or at night during this period unless necessary. It has also asked the concerned federal ministries, provincial governments, local levels, all three security agencies and volunteers, among others, to keep the public informed and remain ready to respond. It has directed that equipment such as dozers, excavators and loaders be kept ready along at-risk highways and roads.

content.rendered:
Mustang, September 22

An apple-picking festival has been underway since Sunday at the Marpha-based Temperate Horticulture Development Center, at Gharpojhang rural municipality-2 in Mustang. The festival will run till October 1.

According to the Centre’s Chief Prakash Pantha, the festival offers visitors an opportunity to harvest and enjoy a juicy and sweet taste of fresh apples. Mustang, the district known as beyond the Himalaya, is famous for apple production in the country. According to the organiser, the event has attracted a good number of visitors.

The district has now entered the main harvesting season for apples, with farmers harvesting fruit and supplying produce to the market. The entry fee to the festival is Rs 200 per person.

Visitors are prohibited from damaging or tearing branches from the plants, and anyone found doing so will be fined Rs 1,000. The centre, established in 2033 BS, produces and sells supplies of fruits, vegetables, and other crops.
