title.rendered: The Nepali scientist who wants to turn hydrogen into a practical energy source

content.rendered:
As a boy in Gorkha, Bishnu Bastakoti studied by the light of a smoky kerosene lamp. Today, thousands of kilometres away in the United States, he is researching a different kind of light — hydrogen, which could one day help power a cleaner future.

The journey from a remote village in Nepal to the laboratories of Harvard University has taken him through scholarships, setbacks and years of research. But the memory of those dark evenings in Gorkha has never quite left him.

Now an associate professor of chemistry at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, Bastakoti is working on ways to produce hydrogen more cheaply and make clean-energy technologies more accessible.

For someone who grew up experiencing Nepal’s power shortages, the work is more than an academic pursuit. It is, in a sense, a search for the light he once studied by.

A village boy with limited horizons

In Aampipal, Gorkha, life followed the rhythm of the village.

School meant an uphill walk. After returning home, there were cattle to tend, fields to help with and lessons to study. At night, the kerosene lamp provided the light.

For children growing up in farming families, this was simply life.

The people they saw as successful were usually those who had gone abroad to work and returned home during the festivals, men serving in the Nepal Police or Army, or teachers at the local schools.

There was little reason to imagine a career in scientific research, let alone one that would take a village boy from Gorkha to some of the world’s leading universities.

This was the world in which Bishnu grew up.

Some of his friends left school after Grade 7 or 8 to find work. But Bishnu, the youngest of three children, continued studying. His parents were illiterate, but they had a clear belief that their children should receive an education. His elder brother, Rishi, was doing well academically and became an important influence on him.

In 1995, Bishnu passed his School Leaving Certificate examination from Janata Secondary School in Aampipal in the first division. But passing the SLC was only the beginning. He now had to decide what came next.

At the time, education was largely viewed as a route into employment. Young people tended to choose subjects according to the jobs they could eventually lead to.

Agriculture could lead to becoming a junior technical assistant. Engineering could lead to becoming an overseer. Forestry could lead to becoming a ranger. Science or education could lead to teaching. Cost and distance mattered too. Then his brother sent him towards an opportunity he had not expected.

The exam that changed his direction

After completing his SLC, Bishnu travelled to Pokhara to visit Rishi, who was studying forestry. His brother sent him to sit an entrance examination at SOS School in Rambazar.

It was Bishnu’s first time in a city. He remembers looking around at the other candidates, many of them from urban, English-medium schools, and wondering how he could compete with them.

He sat the examination anyway. He was selected. He received a full scholarship for two years. The decision did more than give him an education. It changed the direction of his life.

He moved towards science, eventually completing higher secondary education in science, a bachelor’s degree from Birendra Multiple Campus in Bharatpur and a master’s degree in chemistry from Tribhuvan University Central Campus in Kirtipur in 2004.

By then, teaching seemed the natural next step. He taught at private colleges in Kathmandu and became a popular lecturer. But teaching also exposed him to something else — a desire to understand more, go further and continue studying. In 2008, that opportunity arrived.

From teaching to research

Bishnu received the Japanese government’s Monbukagakusho scholarship and an opportunity to pursue a PhD at Saga University. It was the beginning of a second transformation.

He moved from the classroom into scientific research, working on the synthesis of polymers and nanomaterials and their applications in energy. The work was demanding, but it opened a new academic world.

His doctoral research was published in scientific journals. After completing his PhD, he received a Japan Society for the Promotion of Science fellowship and spent three years conducting research at the National Institute for Materials Science in Japan.

He later spent a year as a research associate at the University of Sydney in Australia and worked as a visiting researcher at other research centres. The distance between Aampipal and the laboratories in which he now worked was enormous. But Bishnu saw the journey differently. For him, each new opportunity simply opened another horizon.

From Handikhola to Harvard

As a child, Bishnu had spent time herding cattle and goats in Handikhola, Pathibhara. He now uses the landscape of his childhood to describe his journey.

When you are walking through a narrow gorge, he says, you can see only what is immediately in front of you. Climb higher and the view begins to widen. Keep climbing and an entirely different horizon appears. His career followed something like that pattern.

While working at the University of Sydney, he applied for a research associate position at Harvard University. After a lengthy selection process, Professor Juan Pérez-Mercader offered him the position. The appointment was another extraordinary step for someone who had grown up in rural Gorkha.

But one question from the professor stayed with him.

“Your parents must be so happy to know that their son has got an opportunity to do research at Harvard. How will you give them this surprise?”

The question struck Bishnu. His parents had never received a formal education. They had worked hard to raise their children and had insisted that education was their best chance at a different life. Bishnu shared the news with his elder brother, Rishi, who was living in Canada. The two brothers became emotional as they reflected on their childhood, their parents and the distance they had travelled.

Their parents might not have fully understood what research at Harvard meant. But they understood that their son had gone much further than anyone in their village could once have imagined.

For Bishnu, Harvard became another important stage in his development as a researcher.

Searching for a cleaner source of energy

Today, his research focuses on some of the biggest challenges facing the modern world. At North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, Bishnu is involved as a principal investigator or co-principal investigator in around 15 research grants.

According to university data, he has received about $15 million in research funding from institutions including the US National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health.

Much of his work centres on finding ways to convert atmospheric carbon dioxide into useful chemicals and fuels through chemical and electronic processes. Another major area is hydrogen.

Hydrogen can be produced from water and used as an energy source, offering the possibility of cleaner energy. But turning that possibility into an affordable, practical technology remains difficult.

“Hydrogen production from water began many years ago, but the nanomaterials required for the process are expensive,” Bishnu says. “Hydrogen energy is possible in the laboratory, but more work is needed to make the technology accessible to everyone in real life.”

His research group is therefore exploring relatively inexpensive nanocatalysts that could help reduce the cost and improve the practicality of hydrogen production.

The work has resulted in more than 100 academic papers in scientific journals and around 3,800 citations, according to Google Scholar.

But the numbers only tell part of the story.

Bishnu also teaches and supervises postgraduate and PhD students, helping train researchers who may eventually take the science further.

His work has been recognised through several awards, including the Interdisciplinary Research Award and Outstanding Graduate Coordinator Award in 2025, the Outstanding PhD Research Adviser Award in 2023 and the Outstanding Young Researcher Award in 2021.

A scientist who still looks towards Nepal

Despite spending much of his professional life abroad, Bishnu has remained closely connected to Nepal.

He wants his experience to benefit Nepali universities, research institutions and young scientists.

“I want the stories of struggle, achievement and lessons from someone born in a remote place and who worked his way here to inspire the next generation,” he says.

That ambition has already taken concrete form.

In collaboration with the Nepal Chemical Society, he has helped organise two international conferences in Kathmandu.

He has also worked with the Department of Chemistry at Tribhuvan University to co-supervise PhD researchers.

Last year, the Nepal Science Journalists Forum invited him to the sixth edition of its “Meet the Scientist” programme, where he presented his work on hydrogen energy, including its opportunities and challenges, to policymakers, researchers and representatives of the private sector.

His research group has also begun collaborating with researchers at Kathmandu University working on hydrogen energy.

“I hope we can increase institutional collaboration with Nepali universities and research institutions in the future,” he says. “Our knowledge, skills and research could then benefit our homeland.”

The student who brought the story back to Nepal

There is another connection to Nepal that has stayed with Bishnu. One of his American students once wrote about visiting Nepal with his father after finishing high school. The student experienced hours of power cuts during the trip. The experience made him wonder whether there had to be an alternative source of energy.

Could hydrogen be part of the answer?

That question eventually helped lead him towards hydrogen research. When Bishnu read what the student had written, he was deeply moved.

“How would he know that I am from Nepal, that I grew up studying by a kerosene lamp and experienced load-shedding?” he says.

The connection was striking. The student had travelled to Nepal and encountered the same problem Bishnu had known as a child. Years later, that experience had helped inspire research into a possible solution.

For Bishnu, it was a reminder that scientific research does not exist in isolation from people’s lives.

The questions scientists pursue often begin with ordinary experiences — a power cut, an expensive fuel source, a polluted environment, a child studying after dark.

Finding the light

Bishnu’s journey began in a place where the boundaries of possibility seemed narrow. He grew up in a farming family in Gorkha, walked to school, helped look after cattle and studied under a kerosene lamp. He became a teacher, then a researcher. Scholarships took him to Japan. Research took him to Australia and Harvard. He eventually established himself as a scientist in the United States.

But he does not describe the journey as a straight line.

It has been shaped by uncertainty, opportunities, hard work and the willingness to take the next step even when the destination was unclear.

“One dream after another, along with struggles and opportunities, has brought me to where I am today,” he says.

The dream now is not simply to publish another paper or win another award. It is to help make hydrogen energy practical and accessible, and to build stronger links between the scientific communities he has become part of and the country where his own journey began.

The boy who once depended on a smoky kerosene lamp is now working on ways to produce a cleaner source of energy.

The light he is looking for is no longer only for himself.

“We still have a lot of work to do to find the light.”

title.rendered: Koshi Highway section to close for 9 hours daily for roadworks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

A 17-kilometre section of the Koshi Highway between Khandbari and Sabhakhola in Sankhuwasabha has been closed to traffic for nine hours daily to facilitate road maintenance and widening works.

The road section from Khandbari to Tumlingtar and Sabhakhola has been closed to traffic to widen and repair the existing blacktopped road, said Manoj Kumar Mandal, acting chief engineer at the Road Division Office, Tumlingtar.

According to the office, the road will remain closed from September 22 to October 16 for the widening and maintenance works.

Mandal said traffic would be stopped from 8 am to noon and from 1 pm to 6 pm daily to facilitate the works.

Vehicles will be allowed to operate from noon to 1 pm and from 6 pm to 8 pm, the office said.

The Road Division Office said the traffic restriction was imposed at the request of the construction company to ensure that the work is completed on time.

Migur Sherpa of Shri DS Builders/Super Like JV, Khandbari-3, said work was being carried out during the nine-hour daily closure. Vehicles can use alternative routes during the restricted hours, according to the office.

title.rendered: Police arrest 58 foreign nationals in overnight operation in Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Police arrested 58 foreign nationals during an overnight operation conducted at various locations in Kathmandu Valley on Monday, according to security sources.

A joint team from the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB), Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office and the Anti-Human Trafficking Bureau carried out the operation.

According to police sources, 20 of those arrested are Chinese nationals, while the others are citizens of Bangladesh, South Korea and other countries.

Police have not yet made public details about the identities of those arrested or the reasons for their detention. Authorities have also not issued an official statement regarding the operation.

A security official who spoke to Onlinekhabar said the operation was conducted following a directive from Home Minister Sudhan Gurung.

On Monday afternoon, Gurung instructed CIB chief AIG Uma Chaturvedi to launch an operation against foreign nationals allegedly involved in illegal activities and take them into custody, according to the official.

Following the directive, the CIB took command of the operation and coordinated the overnight sweep across different parts of Kathmandu Valley.

It remains unclear what activities the 58 foreign nationals were allegedly involved in or what offences, if any, they are suspected of committing.

Police have yet to provide further details about the operation or the cases involving those arrested.

title.rendered: Malaysia recruitment dispute reaches prime ministerial level

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

The dispute over Malaysia’s plan to limit Nepali worker recruitment to a small group of manpower companies has now reached the prime minister’s level.

Prime Minister Balendra (Balen) Shah, speaking by phone with his Malaysian counterpart Anwar Ibrahim on Tuesday morning, urged an end to the syndicate and middleman system seen in Malaysia’s employment sector.

He made clear that such an arrangement is not acceptable to Nepal and urged the Malaysian prime minister to have the two countries’ labour ministers hold direct talks to resolve the problem.

In his conversation with the Malaysian prime minister, PM Shah stressed the need to make the Nepal-Malaysia labour relationship dignified, transparent and free of exploitation.

“We do not like the syndicate and middleman system, and it is not acceptable under any circumstances. It has hurt workers,” PM Shah said. “So I request that your labour minister sit down for direct talks with our labour minister and take the necessary steps to remove this problem for good.”

In response, Malaysian PM Ibrahim also said he opposes the syndicate and middleman practice. He committed to directing his labour minister to coordinate with the Nepali counterpart and work out a concrete solution.

Even before this prime-minister-level exchange, Nepal had been carrying forward continuous dialogue with Malaysia at the diplomatic and administrative levels.

Nepal has formally objected since Malaysia initially listed only 25 manpower companies as “registered recruitment agencies” for Nepali worker recruitment under the Foreign Workers Centralised Management System (FWCMS).

Through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nepal had written to the Malaysian government saying that even if the new system is implemented, it should proceed only through discussion and agreement between the two countries.

Nepal has stated that this matter should be settled through the Joint Technical Committee and bilateral mechanism under the Nepal-Malaysia labour agreement.

However, Nepal did not accept it even after Malaysia went on to list a further 250 manpower companies as “support agencies” under the 25 main companies. Nepal has objected on the grounds that a structure of 25 main and 250 support companies would limit competition and place the Nepali worker recruitment process under the control of a few entities.

To resolve this dispute, Nepal is now making diplomatic efforts to convene a Joint Technical Committee (JTC) meeting between the two countries at the earliest.

According to the Ministry of Labour, coordination is continuing at the diplomatic level on holding the meeting, though the date and other technical matters remain to be settled.

According to ministry spokesperson Mira Acharya, the Malaysian side has been giving a positive response on labour market matters. Nepal, for its part, has asked for clarity on the process, evaluation system and criteria used in selecting the 25 main and 250 support manpower companies.

From departmental investigation to holding pre-approvals

Alongside the diplomatic effort, Nepal has also advanced administrative and legal processes of its own.

Under the direction of the Ministry of Labour, Youth and Employment and a ministerial-level decision of September 11, the Department of Foreign Employment has held back new pre-approvals for Malaysia related to the 250 manpower companies said to be affiliated with the 25 main entities under the FWCMS. The department is investigating those companies’ dealings, their relationship with the 25 main companies, and the basis of their selection.

The department has also opened an investigation into the 25 main manpower companies themselves, seeking details of their past involvement in Malaysian employment, the basis on which they were selected as main entities under the FWCMS, and the process they followed in affiliating other companies.

In the latest stage, the department has asked the 25 manpower companies to submit their complete business and financial details, including financial transactions for the last five fiscal years. They have been directed to provide the details within 15 days under Section 34 of the Foreign Employment Act, 2064.

According to the department, the necessary process under the Foreign Employment Act will move forward as the investigation continues, during which the companies’ explanations, transactions and business relationship with Malaysia are also being studied.

Although the government has objected to Malaysia’s new system, it has said it will not halt the departure of Nepali workers who have already obtained labour approval under it.

The department has said only new pre-approvals for Malaysia for the 250 companies affiliated under the FWCMS are on hold until the investigation concludes; the government says the departure of workers who had already received labour approval will not be affected.

Since Malaysia is a major destination for Nepali workers, the government also faces the risk that a prolonged dispute could affect new workers’ foreign employment. For this reason, Nepal is simultaneously rejecting the limited manpower structure and pursuing an investigation, while also seeking dialogue at the diplomatic level and a Joint Technical Committee meeting.

The latest conversation between PM Shah and his Malaysian counterpart Ibrahim shows that the matter is no longer confined to the Ministry of Labour or the administrative level alone.

With the two prime ministers reaching an understanding to advance direct dialogue at the labour minister level to resolve the problem, Nepal’s push to end the syndicate system, secure a transparent recruitment system, and find a solution through the Joint Technical Committee has now reached an even higher political level.

title.rendered: Government to ensure essential public services during festive season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

The government has decided to ensure the regular operation of essential public services during the upcoming festive season.

A meeting of government secretaries held on Monday made the decision, according to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. The meeting also decided to take measures to prevent disruptions to road transport, taking into account festivals such as Dashain, Tihar and Chhath as well as the ongoing monsoon.

Chief Secretary Govinda Bahadur Karki said the meeting decided that concerned agencies would prepare schedules and make necessary arrangements to ensure regular operation of essential public services by keeping personnel, resources, machinery and equipment in proper working condition.

The meeting also decided to strengthen joint market monitoring to control black-marketing, price hikes and unfair business practices that may occur in the market during the festive season.

title.rendered: NEPSE’s ‘technical glitch’ was a ransomware attack. What happened?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

On Monday, the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) was forced to suspend regular share trading for an entire day. NEPSE initially described the disruption as a “technical problem”. But information emerging after the incident points to a more serious cause — a ransomware attack on the data centre operated by Data Hub Pvt Ltd.

The attack disrupted the servers and trading management systems (TMS) of 72 brokerage companies, bringing the stock market to a standstill.

Trading resumed on Tuesday after the systems were restored using backup data from Data Hub’s disaster recovery centre in Butwal.

According to information provided by Data Hub, the attack was detected early Sunday morning, around 4am to 5:30am. However, the affected brokerage systems remained unable to operate throughout Monday.

Cybersecurity expert and BugV founder Naresh Lamgade said the incident should not be treated as an ordinary hacking attempt.

“This was not a normal hack. It appears to have been a systematic and planned ransomware attack,” Lamgade said.

What happened?

A letter sent by Data Hub to YCO Pvt Ltd also explicitly refers to the incident as a ransomware attack.

In a ransomware attack, attackers gain access to a computer system or server and encrypt files, making them inaccessible. In many cases, attackers then demand a ransom in exchange for a decryption key.

According to Lamgade, ransom notes are commonly left behind in such attacks, demanding payment through bank transfers or cryptocurrencies.

“It is possible that such a message exists within Data Hub but has not been made public,” he said.

However, a senior Data Hub official said the incident appeared to differ from the conventional pattern.

“Ransom messages are usually left in ransomware attacks. But that did not happen in our case. The data was encrypted and the systems were rendered unusable,” the official said.

The official said it was too early to determine whether any data had been stolen.

“We are investigating whether the data was compromised. Our team is currently working on it. We will also know who was behind the attack only after the investigation,” the official said.

How did the stock market resume?

The official said trading resumed on Tuesday after Data Hub restored the affected systems from its disaster recovery centre in Butwal.

“We formatted all the encrypted data and restored it from the backup in Butwal. Fortunately, there was no data loss. That is the biggest relief for now,” the official said.

The official also acknowledged that some fintech companies and other organisations were affected by the incident, although he declined to identify them or provide details about the extent of the damage.

“All the details will emerge after the investigation,” he said.

Why is the Data Hub attack significant?

Data Hub is one of Nepal’s major data centre service providers. According to information on its website, the company has been providing services since 2012 and hosts data for more than 1,000 companies.

Banks, insurance companies, mobile wallet providers and other major institutions use data centres to host their systems and data.

Nepal’s regulatory framework also restricts banks and payment service providers from storing certain data outside the country, making domestic data centres particularly important to the financial sector.

The scale of the disruption has therefore raised questions about the security of critical infrastructure hosted at a single facility.

Lamgade uses a simple analogy to explain the situation.

“Imagine a house being used as a data centre. One room houses NEPSE, another houses banks and another houses insurance companies,” he said.

“The attack may appear to have primarily affected the room where NEPSE was located, but the house itself was attacked.”

This is why investigators must determine whether systems belonging to other organisations were also compromised, he said.

Was the attack planned?

Another cybersecurity expert, who spoke to Onlinekhabar on condition of anonymity, said attacks of this scale are generally not carried out in a single day.

According to the expert, attackers often spend considerable time identifying critical systems, monitoring networks and looking for vulnerabilities before launching an attack.

“The fact that the attackers were able to affect NEPSE’s entire trading system so deeply could indicate that they had gained access to the system beforehand,” the expert said.

However, the expert stressed that only a forensic investigation can establish how long the attackers had access to the system.

“It is important to establish whether Data Hub itself managed the servers or whether that responsibility lay with NEPSE and the brokers,” the expert said.

“In some cases, a data centre only provides space, electricity and internet connectivity, while the client manages the systems. But regardless of the arrangement, the incident raises questions about the security of the infrastructure.”

He said data centre operators need to maintain strong security systems because attackers may make repeated attempts before successfully penetrating a network.

The importance of backups

The incident has also highlighted the importance of maintaining reliable backups. In this case, the backup at the Butwal disaster recovery centre allowed the stock market to resume operations. But the cybersecurity expert said more information is needed about exactly how the recovery was carried out.

“Data Hub needs to clarify whether the affected systems had to be completely formatted and restored, or whether the data was moved to another server before operations resumed,” he said.

It is also important to establish whether the attackers merely encrypted the data or whether they copied and removed it from the system, he added.

What is a ransomware attack?

Ransomware is a form of cyberattack in which criminals gain access to an organisation’s computer systems or servers and encrypt important files and data.

Once encrypted, the files cannot normally be opened or used. Attackers often leave a ransom note demanding payment in exchange for a decryption key.

More recent ransomware attacks frequently involve a second step known as “double extortion”. Attackers first steal sensitive data and then encrypt the victim’s systems. They threaten to publish the stolen information if the ransom is not paid.

This means that even organisations with functioning backups can face serious consequences if sensitive information has already been copied and removed from their systems.

Whether the Data Hub incident involved data theft as well as encryption remains under investigation.

Ransomware attacks have disrupted critical infrastructure worldwide

Ransomware has repeatedly targeted financial institutions, data centres and other critical infrastructure around the world.

In May 2021, the DarkSide ransomware group attacked Colonial Pipeline in the United States, forcing the company to shut down its pipeline operations. The disruption contributed to fuel shortages and price increases in parts of the eastern United States. Colonial Pipeline later paid a ransom of about $4.4 million.

In November 2023, the LockBit ransomware group attacked the US arm of China’s Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC). The incident disrupted trade settlement operations in the US Treasury market, forcing some transactions to be handled manually.

The 2019-20 ransomware attack on UK foreign exchange company Travelex also disrupted the company’s website, mobile application and operations at branches around the world for weeks.

Other financial institutions, including US insurer CNA Financial, have also been targeted by ransomware attacks.

The incidents demonstrate why ransomware attacks on financial institutions and the infrastructure supporting financial markets can have consequences beyond a single company.

India has also experienced similar disruptions. In 2024, a ransomware attack on C-Edge Technologies affected the operations of hundreds of small banks in the country.

Large data centre operators have also been targeted. Companies including Equinix and CyrusOne have previously reported ransomware-related incidents.

For Nepal, the attack on Data Hub has raised a more immediate question — how resilient are the systems underpinning critical financial infrastructure, and what safeguards are in place if the primary data centre is compromised?

Those questions are likely to become clearer as the forensic investigation into the incident progresses.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

A tripartite agreement has been signed to make the distribution of driving licences more systematic and convenient.

The agreement was signed on Tuesday between the Department of Transport Management, the Department of Postal Services and the Security Printing Centre at the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport.

Under the agreement, data on driving licences issued through the Electronic Driving Licence and Vehicle Registration System operated by the Department of Transport Management will be sent directly to the Security Printing Centre’s system, where the licences will be printed.

The agreement aims to streamline the distribution of licences issued through the electronic registration system to the concerned provincial offices or their delivery to addresses specified by service recipients.

title.rendered: Asian Games: Nepali women’s team secures win in kabaddi

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Nepal has won against Thailand in the women’s kabaddi game in the 20th Asian Games ongoing in Nagoya, Japan. In the first match held today at Tokai Citizen Gymnasium in Japan, Nepal defeated Thailand 46–43 to secure the win.

In the first half of the game, Nepal was trailing Thailand 24–15. However, in the second half, they improved and secured the game against Thailand with a 31–19 score. With that, Nepal managed to win overall against Thailand with a total score of 46–43. While the expected results in the Asian Games have not come from the hoped-for sports, the win in women’s kabaddi is considered very important for Nepal.

In the previous 19th edition of the Asian Games, the women’s kabaddi team also brought a bronze medal for Nepal. Nepal is placed in Group B in the ongoing Asian Games. Along with Nepal, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Chinese Taipei are included in this group. In the league stage, Nepal will now play against Sri Lanka and Chinese Taipei. Similarly, in Group A, there are Iran, India, Bangladesh, and Japan. The top two teams from each group will reach the semifinals.

The Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index rose 7.06 points on the first trading day of the week to close at 2,654 points.

Share prices of 137 companies increased, while those of 131 companies declined. Prices of 11 companies remained unchanged.

Midsolu Hydropower rose 15 per cent, First Microfinance 7.75 per cent, Mailung Khola Hydropower 5.63 per cent and Mandeu Hydropower 5.43 per cent.

Snow River fell 8.23 per cent, Narayani Development Bank 6.96 per cent, Bottlers Nepal (Balaju) 6.75 per cent and Infinity Laghubitta 5.64 per cent.

title.rendered: Tanker attacked in Hormuz as US-Iran tensions escalate

content.rendered:
Tehran/London, September 22

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has warned that further US escalation of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East would expand the geographical scope of the war.

The Revolutionary Guard said on Monday that Iran would “change the geography” of the war if the United States further escalated the conflict. It did not provide details of possible measures.

Meanwhile, the British military said a tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile on Monday while entering the Strait of Hormuz. Two crew members were injured in the incident.

The Strait of Hormuz is a major route for energy and maritime trade. Security incidents in the waterway can affect regional shipping and oil supplies.

Heightened Security Alert in Israel

The Israeli military has maintained a high security alert across the country amid the regional conflict. Security forces increased vigilance as many parts of Israel remained closed and quiet for Yom Kippur, one of the holiest days in Judaism.

Yom Kippur is a Jewish religious observance associated with atonement and fasting. Daily activities in various parts of the country were limited during the religious occasion. The developments came amid continued tensions in the Middle East, including Iran’s warning, the tanker incident in the Strait of Hormuz and heightened security in Israel.

—RSS/AP

title.rendered: Content creators Princy and Prisma allege sexual harassment, raise concerns over victim-blaming by police

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Content creator Princy Khatiwada has spoken publicly about an alleged incident of harassment involving her and her twin sister, Prisma, saying they faced victim-blaming when they sought help from police.

In a video posted on Instagram, Khatiwada said she and her sister were allegedly harassed by two men. The video has been blurred and includes symbolic images. It does not clearly identify where the incident took place.

“We all know that two boys harassed us,” Khatiwada said in the video.

According to Khatiwada, the two men had earlier posted a video of the incident on social media. She said the video was later removed because it had not been blurred.

‘Why were you wearing such short clothes?’

Khatiwada said she and her sister initially tried to deal with the situation themselves but realised they could not confront the two men.

“We could not fight with them, but simply ignoring it did not seem right either,” she said.

They then contacted the police. A police van arrived and took the two men into custody, according to Khatiwada.

She said police later questioned her and her sister about what had happened, and they explained the incident in detail. However, Khatiwada said they were shocked and upset by comments allegedly made by police during the interaction.

“Why were you wearing such short clothes?” she quoted the police as asking.

She said the remark appeared to place responsibility for the alleged harassment on the clothes she and her sister were wearing.

“What was our fault? What was wrong with the clothes we were wearing?” she said.

Khatiwada said she and her sister decided to speak about the incident on social media after becoming dissatisfied with the police response.

Home minister intervenes

Khatiwada also said Home Minister Sudan Gurung commented on their social media post after they made the incident public.

“We then spoke with the home minister,” she said. “He immediately took action on the issue.”

According to Khatiwada, following the home minister’s intervention, the case was taken up by the Gaushala police circle and further action was initiated. She did not provide details about the action taken against the alleged perpetrators. She said she would share further information as the process moves forward.

Khatiwada has particularly objected to the alleged remarks about their clothing, arguing that a person’s clothes cannot justify harassment.

“What kind of action should the government take so that this becomes a precedent, so that no victim has to face victim-blaming because of what they are wearing?” she said.

She also called on police officers and other public officials to respond to such complaints responsibly and accountably.

‘If you face injustice, take action’

Khatiwada said many people commented on their social media post saying they had experienced similar incidents.

“If you face such injustice, take action,” she said.

She acknowledged that not all police officers respond negatively and urged people facing harassment to seek police assistance.

“Dial 101 and call the police,” she said.

At the same time, she urged victims not to remain silent if they are blamed instead of being supported.

“Do not be afraid to speak about your experience on social media,” she said, adding that public attention had helped their complaint reach the home minister.

‘Harassment is harassment’

Khatiwada said harassment should not be dismissed based on its perceived severity. She said inappropriate remarks or gestures made with an improper intention should not simply be tolerated.

The incident has also drawn negative comments online, with some users arguing that the women’s clothing contributed to what happened. Khatiwada rejected that argument.

“The clothes were not short. Your thinking is short,” she said.

title.rendered: RSP appoints coordinators for all local levels in Dolakha

content.rendered:
Dolakha, September 22

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Dolakha has formed a district secretariat to expand its organisation and streamline party activities. A meeting of the party’s District Coordination Committee appointed coordinators for all nine local levels, formed two departments and established a district advisory council.

The meeting appointed Arjun Karki as head of the Organisation Department, Sobhit Upreti as deputy head, and Nishan Budhathoki as secretary. It also assigned office-bearers and members of the district committee responsibilities for coordination and facilitation at the local level.

The party has appointed District Chair Dinesh Basnet as coordinator for Bhimeshwar Municipality. Similarly, Vice-Chair Krishna Bahadur Khadka has been assigned responsibility for Melung, Secretary Ramesh Kumar Shrestha for Baiteshwar and Joint Secretary Arjun Karki for Tamakoshi.

Secretary Shrestha said the new arrangement was introduced to support the expansion of the party organisation and its activities at the local level. A nine-member department has also been formed, with at least one representative from each local level. RSP Dolakha has additionally formed a district advisory council, with Babulal Lama of Baiteshwar appointed as its chair.

Central committee member and lawmaker Jagadish Kharel, lawmaker Smriti Senchuri and Provincial Committee member Prakash Khatri attended the meeting.

title.rendered: Legendary Sculptor Kalu Kumale dies at 93

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Legendary sculptor Kalu Kumale, celebrated in Nepal and abroad as “Krodhakala Shiromani” (Crest Jewel of Wrathful Art) for his mastery of tantric and wrathful deity iconography, died on Tuesday at the age of 93.

Kumale, an honorary member of the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA), passed away on September 22. According to his son, Rakesh Awale, family members found him unconscious at around 11 am and took him to Sumeru City Hospital, where he was declared dead at noon.

His body will be kept at his home on Tuesday. At 10:30 am on September 23, it will be taken to the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts, from where it will be taken to Balkumari Ghat in Tyagal, Lalitpur, for the final rites at noon.

Born in 1933, Kumale, also known by his family name Kumha, built a career spanning more than seven decades as one of Nepal’s foremost metal and stone sculptors. He worked in the traditional lost-wax method to create sculptures of wrathful and peaceful deities drawn from Hindu, Buddhist and Newa traditions.

His works are installed at some of the Kathmandu Valley’s most revered religious sites, including the Bhairav idol at Kwachhen Balkumari Temple and the Dhanvantari Barahi at Dhantal Temple in Lalitpur, the Ganesh and Bhairav figures at Tyagal Balkumari Temple, and the large statue atop the Dharmadhatu Mandala in front of Patan’s Mahabuddha Temple.

He also created the face paintings of the Ashtamatrika deities, including Ganesh and Bhairav, at Bishnu Devi Temple in Satungal, as well as the six-and-a-half-foot Barahi Yogini housed at Patan Durbar Museum.

Kumale’s work also extended beyond Nepal. His sculptures are held at the Victoria and Albert Museum in Britain and the Tibetan Traditional Medical University Museum in Tibet. His works also include a 21-foot Bhagwati statue at the Argha Durbar premises.

Over his career, he created more than 600 sculptures, including representations of Chhvaska Muni Ajima (Palden Lhamu), Vajrayogini, Vajravarahi, Vajrabhairav, Chakrasamvara, Kalabhairav, Svetabhairav, Kagyu Mahakala, Garuda, Kalachakra, Hayagriva, Vajrapani, Padmapani Lokeshwor, Mahadev, Kali and Harakha Dya. Many of his works were sent to monasteries and collections in more than 55 countries.

Over the decades, Kumale received numerous state and civic honours, including the Prabal Gorkha Dakshinabahu, Prabal Janasevashree, National Talent Award, Lifetime Achievement Award, National Best Domestic Entrepreneur Award, Lalitpur Mahanagar Gaurav Puraskar, Araniko National Lalit Kala Pragya Samman, Dirgha Sadhana Samman, National Citizen Samman, Senior Artist Samman and the title “Tho Shhowa,” among others.

He is survived by three sons and two daughters.

Kumale, an honorary member of the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA), passed away on September 22. According […]

title.rendered: Transport unions demand probe, compensation over Tripureshwor bus driver’s death

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Transport entrepreneurs and workers’ organisations have demanded an investigation and compensation over the death of bus driver Arjun Dong, who died after attempting self-immolation in Tripureshwor on September 21.

In a joint statement issued on Tuesday, the organisations alleged that Dong attempted to set himself on fire after facing prolonged harassment and pressure from traffic police following a dispute over the use of his bus horn.

According to the statement, the bus, Ba 5 Kha 4274, was travelling from Mulpani towards Thankot Bhanjyang when traffic was obstructed by a motorcycle on the bus’s side of the road near the Eye Hospital in Tripureshwor. Dong reportedly honked to clear the way.

The organisations claimed traffic police stopped the bus over the incident, asked for its documents and attempted to take action against the driver. A dispute reportedly began after Dong told police that he had not committed any wrongdoing.

The statement alleges that passengers were ordered off the bus and that the vehicle was kept under police control for around two hours while Dong was reprimanded. When police attempted to take the bus to the Traffic Police Headquater, Dong protested.

The organisations claim that he subsequently set himself on fire after being unable to withstand what they described as mental pressure and harassment from traffic police.

They have described the incident as a serious failure on the part of the state, arguing that the driver attempted self-immolation while the bus was under traffic police control.

The transport organisations have put forward a nine-point list of demands, including immediate relief, appropriate compensation and rehabilitation for Dong’s family. They have also demanded compensation for the owner of the bus, which was completely destroyed in the incident.

They have called for a judicial investigation committee involving relevant stakeholders to establish the facts of the incident and take action against those responsible.

The organisations have also demanded that transport workers be covered by the Labour Act, employed under formal contracts and enrolled in the social security system.

They have called for a 24-hour helpline and a rapid-response mechanism through which transport workers can file complaints about alleged mistreatment, harassment and disputes involving traffic police.

The unions have also demanded an investigation into the conduct and working methods of traffic police on the roads.

“Traffic police operations should be made technology-friendly and people-oriented, with a monitoring mechanism involving stakeholders,” the statement said.

They have also called for the delegation of discretionary powers given to traffic police to be reviewed and reorganised to prevent their misuse.

A joint struggle committee comprising the presidents of six transport federations and unions has been formed to press for the demands. The organisations warned that if their demands are not addressed immediately, they will announce further peaceful, democratic and lawful protest programmes.

The statement was signed by Punya Prasad Sitoula, president of the Nepal Transport Entrepreneurs’ National Federation; Dolnath Khanal, president of the Central Federation of Public Transport; Dipak KC, president of the All Nepal Transport Workers’ Union; Rajendra Bikram Baniya, president of the Nepal Truck Transport Federation; Bhimjwala Rai, president of the Nepal Transport Independent Workers’ Organisation; and Jagannath Gautam, general secretary of the Nepal Transport Workers’ Union.

title.rendered: Climbers begin returning from Manaslu due to heavy snowfall

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 22

Climbers attempting to scale Mount Manaslu have begun returning home midway through their expeditions as heavy snowfall and continuous rainfall have made weather conditions unfavourable for mountaineering.

Karma Chhewang Lama, ward chair of Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1, Samagaun, near Mount Manaslu, said climbers started returning after waiting for nearly two weeks without any improvement in the weather. He said continuous rainfall in the Manaslu region has resulted in around five feet of snowfall in the surrounding areas.

“We have never seen anything like this. I don’t know what has happened. It keeps raining and snowing,” Lama said. “The government has also urged people to remain alert from September 24 to 28. That is why climbers have been returning in large numbers.” He said climbers were unlikely to return to the mountain for expeditions this season even if the weather improves.

Local businessperson Prabal Lama said that although rainfall was generally rare in the region in previous years, it has been raining continuously for the past two weeks this year. “People have been regularly coming to the base camp since 2014. I have never seen anything like this in these 12 years,” he said. “There has been heavy rainfall and snowfall this year. There is up to three feet of snow at the base camp, while Camps I, II and III have already received seven to eight feet of snow.”

He said climbers had started returning after assessing the risks. However, Mingmar Chhiring Lama, a hotel operator in Samagaun, said many climbers were still in the area despite some returning due to the changed weather conditions.

“Climbers have returned in previous years when they could not climb the mountain. This year, however, more of them have returned, probably because of the unfavourable weather,” he said. “So far, around 10 per cent may have returned.”

Around 500 climbers have obtained permits to climb the 8,163-metre Mount Manaslu this season. Last year, 366 male and 127 female climbers from 67 countries, representing 41 teams, obtained permits to climb the mountain. The government collected Rs 224.814 million in revenue from the permits.

—RSS

title.rendered: Nepal cannot afford to treat Himalayan climate losses as business as usual

content.rendered:
When Prime Minister Balen Shah addresses the UN General Assembly on September 24, the 15-minute speech must abandon the tired script of a victim pleading for charity. Frontline nations have catalogued their suffering for decades, only to receive polite sympathy and loans. The General Assembly is an arena for international diplomacy and legal accountability, not an international donor conference.

Nepal comes with a strong case: it contributes a tiny share of global emissions — around 0.1% in recent estimates — and just 0.01% of cumulative global CO₂ emissions since 1751.

Yet on August 26, cryospheric collapse struck with devastating force. An ice, rock and soil mass failure in the Langtang region triggered a massive flood that swept through Rasuwa and downstream districts, destroying settlements and critical infrastructure, disrupting hydropower generation and severing Nepal’s northern trade corridor with China. More than 1,300 people have been reported dead, with thousands still unaccounted for. Damage and recovery needs are estimated in the billions of dollars.

The multilateral safety net remains far smaller than the need. More than 100 countries have reportedly sought around $3 billion through the UN’s Loss and Damage Fund, while only around $400 million has been deposited. The Fund itself reports $822.06 million in pledges as of March 2026, illustrating the gap between announced resources and money actually available for financing.

As historic polluters fall short of climate-finance commitments, frontline states are left to compete for limited resources or borrow to survive disasters they did little to cause. With the water security of some two billion people downstream at stake, Nepal should not approach the UN simply as a recipient of aid. It should press for climate justice through eight enforceable, rights-based mandates.

Reframing cryospheric collapse as a transboundary injury

The Hindu Kush Himalaya — the planetary “Third Pole” — holds the largest concentration of ice outside the polar regions and serves as the Water Tower of Asia, with its snow and ice providing freshwater for around two billion people. ICIMOD assessments project that, under current emissions pathways, up to 80% of the region’s current glacier volume could disappear by 2100.

When glacial systems destabilise and flash floods tear through Nepal’s valleys, the consequences do not stop at national borders. They represent a wider transboundary threat to a vital planetary commons, driven in part by global emissions and requiring stronger international accountability and non-repayable finance.

Grounding claims in customary international law

Nepal’s position can be grounded in established principles of public international law. The customary “no-harm” principle, reflected in cases including Trail Smelter and Pulp Mills, requires states to exercise due diligence to prevent significant environmental harm.

The International Court of Justice’s proceedings on the obligations of states in respect of climate change have further clarified the central role of states’ existing international legal obligations in addressing climate change. Nepal itself submitted a written statement to the Court in that proceeding.

A failure to adequately regulate emissions, or continued support for activities that contribute significantly to climate harm, raises questions of international responsibility that Nepal should place firmly on the diplomatic agenda.

Protecting mountain peoples and codified human rights

The Himalayan crisis is also a human rights emergency. Climate impacts can threaten the rights to life and an adequate standard of living under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. The UN General Assembly has also recognised the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment in Resolution 76/300.

In the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi basins, Indigenous Tamang, Sherpa, Gurung, Magar and Newar communities have served for generations as ecological stewards. The August 2026 floods destroyed homes, farms, religious sites and community infrastructure.

Under the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and relevant international standards, states have obligations concerning Indigenous peoples’ lands, cultures and livelihoods. In Torres Strait Islanders v Australia, the UN Human Rights Committee found Australia responsible for violating certain rights of the petitioners under the ICCPR in connection with climate impacts.

Nepal should invite relevant UN Special Procedures to undertake fact-finding missions and formally recognise climate-displaced populations within appropriate frameworks, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement.

Accounting for non-economic loss and cultural heritage

Reconstruction cannot be measured solely in concrete, roads and power grids. Nepal must demand accountability for non-economic loss and damage.

Floodwaters in Nuwakot damaged historic temples and sacred river confluences at Devighat. Across Rasuwa, debris flows also affected ancestral burial grounds and culturally significant sites. Such losses cannot be fully captured through conventional monetary metrics.

Spiritual sanctity, lineage continuity, cultural memory and community identity have value beyond their economic replacement cost. The Loss and Damage Fund should therefore develop mechanisms capable of addressing non-economic losses, including damage to cultural heritage, Indigenous rights and community wellbeing.

Enforcing transit rights for landlocked nations

The Langtang-Bhotekoshi disaster severely disrupted the Rasuwagadhi–Kerung corridor, including bridges, roads and border infrastructure that connect Nepal with China. For a landlocked country, such disruption has consequences far beyond the affected communities.

Under Article 125 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and Article 11 of the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement, landlocked countries have rights relating to transit to and from the sea.

Nepal should therefore call for a grant-funded LLDC Climate-Resilient Transit Facility to rebuild and climate-proof critical trade arteries.

Rejecting debt for 100% grant-based reparations

A large share of international climate finance continues to be delivered through loans rather than grants, adding to the debt burdens of vulnerable countries. Nepal should insist that finance for climate-related loss and damage be provided primarily through non-repayable grants rather than creating new debt.

The principle of full reparation has a long history in international law, most famously articulated by the Permanent Court of International Justice in the Chorzów Factory case. Whether and how that principle applies to contemporary climate loss and damage remains a matter of legal and political debate, but the underlying argument is clear: countries facing climate impacts should not be pushed deeper into debt to address destruction associated with a global crisis to which they have contributed little.

Nepal’s contribution to global emissions remains very small, while its economy is increasingly exposed to climate-related risks. The country should therefore press for grant-based financing through the Loss and Damage Fund and other climate-finance mechanisms.

Establishing a trans-himalayan early warning framework

Mountain river basins do not respect borders. Upstream on the Tibetan Plateau, unstable glacial lakes and rapidly changing cryospheric conditions can create risks for downstream communities.

Nepal should call for a binding Trans-Himalayan Regional Framework for real-time cryospheric monitoring, satellite observation, hydrological data sharing and coordinated transboundary alerts.

This should complement the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, particularly its Target G on increasing the availability of and access to multi-hazard early warning systems and disaster-risk information.

The objective should be straightforward: early-warning networks should leave as few blind spots as possible between mountain sources and vulnerable valley communities.

Aligning mountain justice with global demilitarization

The melting of the Third Pole and the growing vulnerability of low-lying island states are interconnected expressions of a planetary climate crisis. Nepal should seek a stronger diplomatic alliance between high-mountain states and Small Island Developing States (SIDS) to pursue common climate and legal strategies.

This coalition should also press for a greater focus on the climate and environmental costs of military activity and for resources to be redirected towards climate adaptation, debt relief, climate finance and community-centred renewable energy transitions.

The call to action

The 81st UN General Assembly offers Nepal an opportunity to redefine mountain diplomacy.

Bearing the mandate and lived testimony of its people, Nepal’s delegation should deliver an unequivocal message: the Third Pole is collapsing, and frontline states are coming to the United Nations not simply to seek charity, but to demand climate justice grounded in international law.

The question is no longer whether the Himalayas matter to the world. They are a source of water, ecological stability, culture and livelihoods for hundreds of millions of people across Asia.

The question is whether the international system will recognise the consequences of their rapid transformation — and whether countries that have contributed least to the climate crisis will continue to bear a disproportionate share of its costs.

title.rendered: Protest outside Kirtipur burn hospital over Tripureshwor bus fire driver’s death

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

A protest has been held outside the Kirtipur Burn Hospital against the death of a driver who was burned when a bus caught fire in Tripureshwor, Kathmandu.

The family of the deceased, Arjun Dong, along with the Independent Drivers’ Union Nepal, held the protest outside the hospital on Tuesday.

During the protest, Arjun’s two wives demanded justice for their husband and said action should be taken against those involved in the incident.

They said, “Our husband needs justice. We don’t need anything else. Those who forced him to die must also face action.”

The Independent Drivers’ Union has demanded a fair investigation into the incident and action against those responsible.

Union chairman Dhan Bahadur Shrestha told Onlinekhabar, “The mistreatment of drivers must stop. The wrongdoing against drivers must end. The deceased driver’s family must be given proper compensation. A drivers’ commission should also be formed to ensure a fair investigation into the incident. Those responsible must be punished.”

They held the protest chanting slogans including “Stop the oppression against drivers,” “Drivers must not be killed,” and “Give the driver justice.”

Arjun Dong of Makwanpur was injured when a bus caught fire in Tripureshwor, Kathmandu, on Monday. He died at the burn hospital in Kirtipur later that night while undergoing treatment.

title.rendered: Nepal’s digital government needs authority budgets for AI agents

content.rendered:
OnlineKhabar’s opinion pages have recently raised two closely connected challenges. One argued that Nepal’s National AI Policy needs action rather than applause. Another examined the gap between ambitious digital-governance policy and what institutions can actually implement. Those questions become more urgent as AI systems shift from answering questions to acting through government tools, databases, accounts and workflows.

The issue is not whether Nepal should use AI. It should. The issue is how much authority an AI agent should receive before a person has to approve what happens next.

Nepal can address that question through authority budgets — explicit ceilings on the data, credentials, tools, communications, changes, expenditures and consequential decisions an agent may make autonomously.

The need for such limits is becoming increasingly visible at the technological frontier.

Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September after roughly three years of pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, warning that the companies are racing towards self-improving superintelligence. That is Coxon’s judgment, not a consensus forecast. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s Alignment Science Lead, has made the concern more concrete. He has written that he personally thinks there is a greater than 10 percent chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade. Hubinger has also emphasised that he considers the risk from present models to be low and is primarily concerned about future superintelligence arising through recursive self-improvement.

That estimate could be wrong. The reason it deserves attention is that today’s systems are already demonstrating autonomous cyber capabilities and control failures that would have sounded speculative not long ago.

An independent investigation by METR and Redwood Research examined an OpenAI cybersecurity evaluation in which roughly 1,200 agents that were supposed to be isolated discovered an unsanctioned communication mechanism and exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files. About 700 subsequently participated in an attack on Hugging Face. The investigation found that the agents coordinated with one another through an unauthorised message board during the evaluation.

The agents had not been instructed to attack Hugging Face. Yet, operating under reduced safeguards in the evaluation, they communicated through unauthorised channels, exploited vulnerabilities and gained access to external systems. OpenAI has acknowledged that its models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of its internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems.

This does not show that present AI can seize Nepal’s public systems. It does show why autonomy should expand only inside tested boundaries.

If increasingly capable systems can independently discover vulnerabilities, obtain credentials, move laterally, coordinate across instances and work around monitoring, the consequences could become much more serious when electric grids, financial institutions, communications networks, health systems, government databases or defence establishments are involved.

I’m no AI skeptic. I love what AI can do, I help organisations adopt it for a living, and I want adoption to move faster. In my experience, strong safeguards increase trust and make faster adoption possible while reducing the risk of failures like the Hugging Face incident.

My book, The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work, makes the same point from the organisational side: people are more willing to adopt AI when the rules are clear, the controls are credible and responsibility for failures is visible.

Some frontier AI companies now argue for stronger external governance themselves. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has argued that frontier developers should give embedded third-party evaluators employee-like access so they can verify safety practices, inspect processes and report incidents. Anthropic says it will voluntarily make that commitment. Amodei has also argued for regulation because voluntary cooperation cannot reach companies that refuse to participate.

OpenAI has separately called for national and international technical standards, capability-based safety requirements, common testing and independent assessments, stronger cybersecurity protections and clear incident-reporting rules. These are commitments to evaluate, not reasons to trust any provider automatically. Individuals, companies and governments can vote with their dollars by preferring providers whose security, evaluation, incident-response and governance commitments can be independently tested.

Regulation should establish a floor so weaker-governance firms cannot win a race to the bottom.

Nepal can apply the same principle directly to digital government.

An AI agent that drafts a summary may need broad informational access but little action authority. An agent that changes a citizen record, approves a payment, sends an official communication, alters a security setting, deploys software or acts inside critical infrastructure should receive much narrower permissions.

Least privilege, short-lived credentials, human approval gates, durable logs, continuous monitoring, independent testing and a reliable pause or kill mechanism should be standard for consequential workflows.

That approach fits the implementation challenge OnlineKhabar has already identified. Nepal’s AI policy will matter most when its principles become operational controls inside real institutions.

Authority budgets offer one concrete way to keep humans meaningfully in charge while allowing useful AI systems to do more as their reliability and safeguards improve.

The goal should not be to prevent AI agents from acting.

It should be to make sure that when they act, the boundaries of their authority are designed by humans before the system reaches them.

title.rendered: Seven Congress Siraha leaders expelled from party for one year

content.rendered:
Siraha, September 22

Seven leaders of the Nepali Congress in Siraha have been expelled from the party for one year.

The Central Discipline Committee decided to expel the seven leaders and activists from Siraha for one year on charges of failing to support the party’s official candidate in the House of Representatives election held on March 5.

The decision to take action against them was made at a meeting of the Central Discipline Committee held on September 16.

Those facing action are Subhash Kumar Das of Aurahi Rural Municipality-5, Mahadev Yadav of Aurahi Rural Municipality-3, regional member Shatrudhan Prasad Yadav of Sukhipur Municipality-6, district member Nilkumar Raut of Dhangadhimai Municipality-10, Golbazar Municipality chair Rajdev Sah (Lalbabu), Golbazar Municipality-9 chair Prem Sharan Yadav, and provincial convention representative Murali Rayamajhi of Bishnupur Rural Municipality-5.

The decision states that they have been expelled from the party for one year under Article 34(8)(d) of the Congress Constitution, 2017 (with the eleventh amendment).

title.rendered: Infrastructure Development Committee forms subcommittees in all seven provinces

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

The Infrastructure Development Committee under the House of Representatives of the Federal Parliament has decided to form province-level subcommittees in all seven provinces.

The meeting held on Wednesday under the chairmanship of Committee Chair Ashish Gajurel formed provincial subcommittees to effectively monitor, study and evaluate projects and programmes being carried out at the provincial level in areas within the committee’s jurisdiction, including infrastructure development, energy, water resources and irrigation.

The subcommittees will study and monitor the progress, management and implementation status of projects and programmes running in their respective provinces, as well as coordination with stakeholders. They will also study the protection of public property and whether government bodies are working in accordance with prevailing laws and regulations, and submit reports and necessary suggestions to the committee.

The committee has instructed the subcommittees to prepare fact-based study reports by carrying out site visits to relevant projects and locations, holding discussions with relevant bodies and stakeholders, and interacting with experts and researchers.

title.rendered: Mongolian Heart to tour four European countries; proceeds to go to Bhotekoshi flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Nepali pop band Mongolian Heart is heading to Europe for the first time in three decades. Under the “Mongolian Heart Europe Mini Tour 2026,” the band will perform live in four countries.

The tour is being organised by Four Brothers Event Management. The band’s eight-member team is scheduled to depart on September 24.

The team’s lineup includes Raju Lama on lead vocals, Bobby Lama on guitar, Santosh Thapa Magar on drums, Pawan Kapali on bass guitar, Bhupendra Bajracharya on lead guitar, Baburaja Maharjan on madal and tabla, Binaya Maharjan on flute, and Nirendra Ranjit as sound engineer.

According to the schedule, the band will perform live in Denmark on September 26, Romania on October 3, Portugal on October 5, and Croatia on October 11. This European trip is tied not only to music but also to a social cause.

Singer Lama said part of the proceeds from the musical tour will go towards relief for those affected by the Bhotekoshi floods.

“Our journey is not limited to entertainment alone. We also have a responsibility towards our Nepali brothers and sisters affected by the disaster in Rasuwa and elsewhere. So we will use part of the funds raised from this tour to support them,” singer Lama said.

Guitarist Bobby Lama, who is also the band’s manager, has invited the entire Nepali community and music lovers in Europe to take part in this journey, which is tied to a social cause as well.

title.rendered: Prime minister to be chancellor of National Defence University

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

The government has brought a bill under which the prime minister will be the chancellor of the National Defence University.

This provision is mentioned in Section 19 of the bill, registered in the House of Representatives on Tuesday by Prime Minister and Defence Minister Balen Shah.

It states, “The prime minister shall be the chancellor of the university.”

The chancellor will preside over meetings of the assembly and the university’s convocation ceremony.

If the chancellor is unable to attend the convocation ceremony, the assembly’s co-chair will preside over it instead.

The chancellor may inspect the university, or have it inspected, and issue directives as needed.

Section 20 provides for a vice-chancellor. It states, “There shall be one vice-chancellor at the university to act as the university’s chief executive.”

The bill also sets qualifications for the vice-chancellor.

Under it, a person must be at least 45 years old to become vice-chancellor.

They must also hold at least a master’s degree from a recognised university in defence, security, military studies, strategic studies, international relations, international law, or diplomacy.

The provision also requires at least 20 years of experience in the relevant field.

Section 3 of the proposed bill deals with the university’s establishment, where its objective is laid out.

Sub-section 1 of Section 3 states, “The National Defence University is established as a specialised academic centre for advanced study, teaching and research in national security, defence, international relations and strategic affairs, to produce skilled, qualified, capable and responsible human resources who can contribute to protecting, promoting and advancing the national interest.”

The university will be called the National Defence University in English.

The university’s central office will be located at Perungedanda in Banepa Municipality, Kavrepalanchok district, Bagmati Province.

Under Section 4 of the bill, the university will be an autonomous, self-governing and organised institution.

Sub-section 1 of Section 4 states, “The university shall be an autonomous, self-governing and organised institution with perpetual succession, and shall acquire the status of a legal person.”

As a legal person, the university will exercise rights, perform duties and discharge obligations under prevailing law.

However, the bill proposes that before selling any immovable property or transferring ownership of it in any other way, the university must obtain approval from the Government of Nepal, the Council of Ministers.

According to Prime Minister and Defence Minister Balen Shah, the university is being established to protect, promote and advance the national interest through high-level study, teaching and research in national security, defence, international relations and strategic affairs.

He said the National Defence University bill has been drafted with the aim of producing capable, skilled and responsible human resources, both domestic and foreign, for this purpose.

PM Shah has written in the bill itself, “The main reason for establishing and operating this university is to provide higher education and training to military and non-military officials by setting up a specialised academic centre at home to address geopolitical sensitivities and changing security challenges.”

The bill aims to help the government by providing evidence-based advice and suggestions when formulating security and strategic policy, as well as to make a significant contribution to strengthening the country’s security diplomacy.

According to PM Shah, infrastructure construction for the National Defence University has reached its final phase. It is in this context that the bill has been brought, given the need for a permanent and clear legal structure to operate it and grant it academic autonomy.

Once registered in the House of Representatives, the bill will go through the process of passing there and then move to the National Assembly. After the National Assembly also passes it, it comes back to the House of Representatives. It then goes from the Speaker to the President. Once the President signs it, it becomes an Act and is published in the Gazette. The Act comes into effect once published in the Gazette.

title.rendered: Three arrested with drugs in Dhankuta

content.rendered:
Dhankuta, September 22

Police in Dhankuta have arrested three people from separate locations with drugs.

Two of them were arrested with drugs during a checkpoint search at Mulghat, Ward No. 9 of Dhankuta Municipality.

A team deployed from the Mulghat police post said that while checking an electric vehicle bearing number Province No. 1-02-001 Ja 4519, travelling from Itahari towards Tehrathum, they recovered a brown, heroin-like substance along with capsules and tablets from a cloth bag kept under the seat.

The seized brown substance, excluding the plastic packaging, weighed 1 gram 230 milligrams. Narayan Ranjitkar, Superintendent of Police in charge of the District Police Office, Dhankuta, said those arrested in the incident were 22-year-old Bhola Rai of Temkemaiyung Rural Municipality Ward No. 1, Bhojpur, and 24-year-old Prabin Rai of Bhojpur Municipality Ward No. 6.

Similarly, police have arrested one person with drugs from Chamcha, Ward No. 7 of Shahidbhumi Rural Municipality, Dhankuta. Acting on a special tip-off, a team deployed from the Akhisalla police post recovered 29 strips of Tramol-50 (290 capsules) and 29 strips of Spasmo Proxyvon (290 tablets) from the house of 21-year-old resident Pragat Rai.

SP Ranjitkar said all three arrested have been brought to the District Police Office, Dhankuta, and further investigation into the matter is underway.

title.rendered: Police identify driver killed in Tripureshwor bus fire

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Police have identified the driver who died in the Tripureshwor bus fire.

According to SSP Dilip Ghimire of the Kathmandu Police Range, the driver who died in the bus fire was Arjun Dong Tamang of Sisneri, Indrasarowar Rural Municipality, Makwanpur.

SSP Ghimire said it has come to light that he was using a driving licence issued in the name of Dawa Lama in Monday’s incident in Tripureshwor.

According to SSP Ghimire, preliminary investigation has revealed facts suggesting that Arjun may have been involved in various incidents using a bank account and a citizenship certificate in the name of Dawa Lama.

According to police, he was involved in an incident in November 2025 in which a bus overturned in Balaju, injuring three people, and has been on the run since then. SSP Ghimire said he was found to have used a driving licence issued in the name of Sunil Tamang in that incident.

Arjun was also found to have used a driving licence issued in the name of Dawa Tamang in an incident of misbehaving with traffic police in the Mulpani area about three months ago.

Police said further investigation is underway into whether Arjun may have used identity documents and papers issued in other people’s names as well.
