title.rendered: The crisis after the flood: What Nepal’s flood survivors face next

content.rendered:
File

When disaster strikes, the first questions are necessarily about survival: Who is missing? How many people have been affected? How many have been rescued? How many lives have been lost?

But once the immediate rescue operation begins to wind down, a different set of questions emerges—questions that are less visible but equally critical. Where will displaced families live? Will they have access to safe drinking water and healthcare? What happens to children whose schools have been destroyed? Can families recover their livelihoods? And, most importantly, can people rebuild their homes and communities in genuinely safe places?

Following the catastrophic flash flood that struck Nepal’s northern central region on August 26, these questions are becoming increasingly urgent. The disaster tore through mountain settlements, displaced thousands and damaged the physical systems on which communities depend. For survivors, the crisis did not end when floodwaters receded.

The recovery ahead is likely to be long and complex. Rebuilding cannot simply mean clearing debris and replacing damaged buildings. It must address the social and economic vulnerabilities that existed before the disaster while ensuring that reconstruction does not reproduce the same risks. The task, therefore, is not merely to restore what was lost, but to create safer and more resilient communities.

A public health crisis beyond the debris

One of the most immediate challenges after a major flood is protecting public health. Floodwaters can contaminate drinking-water sources with mud, waste, sewage, dead animals, human remains and hazardous materials released from damaged infrastructure. If debris and contaminated materials are not managed properly, they can accumulate around residential areas and increase the risk of waterborne diseases such as cholera, dysentery and typhoid.

The problem extends beyond contaminated water. Large quantities of silt deposited across agricultural valleys also require systematic removal and management. Without proper clearance, the accumulated material can affect soil health and create longer-term environmental problems.

Sanitation is another urgent concern, particularly for women and girls living in temporary shelters or crowded displacement centres. Access to functional toilets, privacy, bathing facilities and menstrual hygiene products can become severely restricted after a disaster.

These are sometimes treated as secondary concerns during an emergency. They are not. Inadequate sanitation directly affects physical health, personal safety and psychological wellbeing. Recovery planning must therefore treat dignified sanitation as a basic necessity rather than an optional addition to emergency relief.

A health system under strain

The damage to healthcare infrastructure creates another layer of vulnerability. The affected communities need more than temporary medical camps. People living with chronic illnesses may require uninterrupted access to medication and regular treatment. Pregnant women need prenatal care, emergency obstetric services and safe delivery facilities. Infants and older people can be particularly vulnerable to respiratory infections, cold temperatures and the difficult conditions of temporary shelters.

Temporary health camps can provide essential emergency assistance, but they cannot substitute for functioning district-level healthcare systems. The disruption also has a profound psychological dimension. Children who have lost parents, people who witnessed deaths and families waiting for information about missing relatives may experience prolonged trauma. For them, recovery cannot be measured only by the reconstruction of roads, bridges or buildings.

Mental health support must form part of the longer-term recovery process. Restoring permanent health facilities, reconnecting communities to healthcare services and ensuring access to psychological support will be essential if the disaster is not to develop into a secondary health crisis.

Where will survivors rebuild?

Perhaps the most difficult question facing displaced communities is where they will live permanently. Temporary shelters can provide immediate protection, but they do not resolve the question of long-term resettlement. In areas exposed to floods and landslides, simply rebuilding houses where they previously stood may expose families to the same dangers again.

Any relocation effort therefore needs to examine whether proposed settlement areas are vulnerable to changing river channels, unstable slopes, landslides or other hazards. The availability of roads, drinking water and basic civic infrastructure must also be considered.

Long-term reconstruction needs to incorporate disaster-risk reduction into physical planning. High-risk riverbeds and active floodplains should not simply be rebuilt without assessing the hazards. Buildings may need stronger foundations and designs that can better withstand high-velocity water and unstable slopes.

Infrastructure itself must also become more resilient. Decentralised systems for communication, water supply and sanitation can provide alternatives when central infrastructure fails during another emergency. The distinction is important: restoring physical access is not necessarily the same as restoring human safety.

The people most at risk

Disasters do not affect everyone equally. Women, children, older people, persons with disabilities, displaced families, daily wage workers and low-income households can face heightened risks following sudden displacement. These may include family separation, unsafe shelter conditions, gender-based violence, labour exploitation, human trafficking and exclusion from relief distributions.

The design of temporary and transitional shelters can play a significant role in preventing such risks. Safe facilities require adequate lighting, separate and secure sleeping arrangements, lockable gender-segregated toilets and accessible bathing facilities. Seasonal conditions make the challenge even more urgent. With winter approaching in the high-altitude areas of northern central Nepal, temporary shelters need to be adapted to colder conditions through insulation, appropriate heating arrangements and the distribution of warm clothing and blankets.

But physical shelter alone is not enough. Survivors also need a clear understanding of what happens next. They need transparent timelines and identifiable institutional mechanisms for moving from emergency tents to transitional or permanent housing. The central question should remain: Are survivors being moved to genuinely safe places, or are they simply being transferred from one unsafe environment to another?

Women’s losses and invisible burdens

The economic impact of disasters on women is often less visible in conventional assessments. Women may lose livelihoods while simultaneously taking on greater responsibilities at home. After a disaster, they may spend more time cooking, collecting water, caring for children, looking after injured relatives and supporting older family members.

Many women also work in informal employment, small-scale agriculture or unpaid care work. Because they may not formally own land or other assets, their losses can remain poorly documented. Recovery programmes therefore need to ensure that women can directly access cash assistance, livelihood support and replacement documentation. Their participation in community relocation and recovery committees is equally important.

For displaced families, the loss of documents can create another obstacle. Citizenship certificates, land deeds and other forms of identification can be essential for accessing compensation, services and legal claims. Replacing these documents must be simple, accessible and fast. Accurate records of people living in temporary shelters are also important. Registration can support family tracing and reunification while helping authorities protect separated children and vulnerable individuals from trafficking and exploitation.

Children need schools, not just classrooms

The consequences of the flood extend deeply into education. Schools have been destroyed or damaged, while surviving school buildings may be used as emergency holding centres or temporary medical facilities. This can keep children away from formal education at a time when they are already coping with displacement, trauma and, in some cases, the loss of family members.

Returning children to school is therefore about much more than continuing lessons. A classroom can restore routine and a sense of normality when almost everything around a child has become uncertain. Temporary learning centres can provide an immediate bridge until permanent schools are rebuilt.

These spaces can also serve as platforms for psychosocial support. Teachers, working with trained caseworkers and mental health professionals, can help identify children showing signs of severe anxiety, trauma or behavioural changes and refer them for specialised care.

Structured play, creative activities and psychological first aid can help children process traumatic experiences and rebuild a sense of safety. Yet there is a further risk: some children may never return to school. Girls, children with disabilities and children from historically marginalised communities may face additional barriers even after schools reopen. Recovery planning must therefore include targeted educational support and active community outreach to prevent disaster-related displacement from becoming permanent educational exclusion.

Rebuilding livelihoods

For affected families, rebuilding a home without rebuilding a livelihood will not constitute genuine recovery. The floods have destroyed or disrupted the productive assets on which local communities depend. Livestock have been lost, seed stocks destroyed, agricultural tools washed away, stored grain ruined, and irrigation systems damaged.

Farmers are not the only ones affected. Micro-traders, tourism workers, transport operators and daily wage earners may also have lost their primary sources of income almost overnight. Emergency food assistance can prevent immediate hunger, but long-term recovery requires people to regain the ability to earn.

Agricultural recovery may require seeds, organic fertilisers, livestock feed and other essential inputs. At the same time, local markets need to be restored so that farmers, traders and service providers can begin earning again. This is where recovery policy needs to move beyond traditional relief models.

Unconditional cash assistance can give households greater control over their own recovery priorities while allowing money to circulate through local markets. Rather than assuming that every family has identical needs, cash support enables survivors to decide what matters most for their household.

Reconstruction itself can also become a source of employment. As roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure are repaired, displaced local workers can be employed in reconstruction projects. This can provide immediate income while allowing communities to participate directly in rebuilding their own surroundings.

From recovery to resilience

Nepal’s challenge after the flood is therefore much larger than reconstructing damaged infrastructure. The real test will be whether recovery can reduce the vulnerabilities that made communities more exposed in the first place.

A successful recovery will require resilient infrastructure, safe resettlement, functioning healthcare, restored education, protection for vulnerable groups and the revival of local livelihoods. It will also require women and marginalised communities to have a meaningful role in decisions that determine where and how their communities are rebuilt.

The temptation after a disaster is to restore what existed before as quickly as possible. But returning to the previous situation may simply recreate the same vulnerabilities. For the survivors of the August 26 flood, recovery must mean more than returning home. It must mean returning to safety, dignity, opportunity and a functioning community.

The flood may have destroyed houses, roads, schools, livelihoods and essential services. But the reconstruction that follows can determine whether those losses remain a source of long-term vulnerability or become the starting point for a safer future. Nepal now has an opportunity to make recovery more than reconstruction—to rebuild communities with greater resilience, stronger local systems, and a clearer commitment to inclusion.

The crisis after the flood is only beginning. How Nepal responds to that second crisis will determine what the future looks like for the people who survived the first.

title.rendered: Balen urges Malaysian PM to end syndicate and middleman practices in employment

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Prime Minister Balendra Shah (Balen) has urged Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to stop the syndicate and middleman practices in Malaysia’s employment sector.

He drew attention to the many problems in employment in Malaysia, resulting in the suffering of Nepali workers, urging that the problem be resolved.

According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, PM Shah spoke with his Malaysian counterpart Ibrahim by phone on Tuesday morning.

“We do not like the syndicate and middleman system, and it is not acceptable under any circumstances. It has hurt workers,” the Secretariat quoted PM Shah as telling his Malaysian counterpart. “So I request that your labour minister sit down for direct talks with our labour minister and take the necessary steps to remove this problem for good.”

PM Shah stressed the need to make foreign employment between Nepal and Malaysia dignified, transparent and free of exploitation.

He made clear to his Malaysian counterpart that he and his government do not favour the syndicate and middleman practices present in Malaysia’s employment sector.

Making clear that such impractical and unjust practices are unacceptable, he stressed the need for a joint initiative to resolve the problem permanently.

Malaysian PM Ibrahim also said he stands against such practices.

“I am also completely opposed to this wrong and exploitative system. I will immediately direct our labour minister to discuss this matter with his Nepali counterpart and work out a concrete solution,” the Malaysian prime minister said.

title.rendered: Dr Poudel appointed acting director general of the Department of Health Services

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Dr Krishna Prasad Poudel has been appointed acting director general of the Department of Health Services.

Health Minister Nisha Mehta gave Dr Poudel the responsibility of acting director general of the department in a ministerial-level decision made last Friday. He has formally taken up the role since Tuesday.

“I have taken charge of the department’s responsibility from today,” Dr Poudel told Onlinekhabar.

Dr Poudel was previously posted at Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Rajbiraj, Saptari.

The role of acting director general of the department had previously been held by Dr Anuj Bhattachan.

Bhattachan, who was also serving as director of the Epidemiology and Disease Control Division (EDCD) alongside leading the department, will now remain only as director of that division.

The post of director general of the Department of Health Services is a 12th-level position.

With Dr Sangita Mishra having moved to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, Dr Shree Krishna Shrestha is now the only 12th-level physician remaining at the Ministry of Health.

title.rendered: Oli on the defensive, but not ready to give an inch

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

For leaders who have attended CPN-UML Central Committee meetings for years, Monday’s meeting was unlike anything they had seen before.

Traditionally, the party’s general secretary would open Central Committee meetings, invite the chair to preside over them and then hand over the floor to the chair for his opening remarks. Once the chair had spoken, the meeting would proceed according to the rules agreed for the session.

On Monday, however, KP Sharma Oli changed the script.

The UML chair opened the meeting himself, delivered the opening remarks, laid down detailed instructions on how members would be allowed to participate and then read out his own political report. He subsequently ended the meeting and left.

In the past, the general secretary would conduct the meeting, while Oli would have another leader present his report. This time, there was little room for that kind of arrangement.

The change in style became apparent when leader Krishna Gopal Shrestha challenged the procedure from inside the meeting. Referring to the party’s established practice, Shrestha argued that the general secretary should be conducting the meeting. Oli did not allow him to continue.

Instead, he told Shrestha to “speak after looking at the statute”. According to leaders present at the meeting, Shrestha subsequently left the meeting.

There was no attempt to soften the atmosphere.

Oli also laid down strict instructions on how Central Committee members would speak. Members would have to seek the chair’s attention before speaking and would be given three minutes. The chair could interrupt a speaker if he felt it necessary, while the speaking time could also be changed in special circumstances.

From the following day, members were told they would have to leave their mobile phones outside. Phones could not be kept in recording mode. Members would need the chair’s permission before leaving their seats. Oli also instructed volunteers to maintain complete neutrality.

They were not to make any gesture, sign or signal. Even if, as political beings, they had feelings about what was being discussed, he said, those feelings should not be reflected on their faces.

The instructions were striking enough for one Central Committee member to describe the situation as something they had never witnessed before.

The change in procedure, however, was not simply about how one meeting was conducted. It reflected the much bigger fight now unfolding inside the UML over Oli’s leadership.

Oli is under pressure from within the party to step aside and allow the UML to be reorganised. But he has shown no willingness to do so.

Instead, Monday’s meeting suggested that he intends to hold his ground.

The Central Committee is a larger body than the party’s office-bearers, and Oli has comparatively greater support among its members. In that setting, he appeared determined to keep control of the proceedings rather than allow the discussion to be shaped by other senior leaders.

That may help explain why he chose to conduct the meeting himself rather than allow the general secretary and other office-bearers to take the lead.

Oli has a formal basis for doing so.

The party’s statute convention last year strengthened the authority of the chair, including giving the chair the authority to conduct meetings. On Monday, Oli exercised that power directly.

The result was a meeting in which other office-bearers, including the general secretary, remained largely on the sidelines.

One leader summed up the significance of the change by pointing to the decision at the statute convention to concentrate authority in the chair.

Monday, that leader said, showed the consequence of that decision.

No sign of retreat

Oli’s political report made his position even clearer.

He has received a report prepared by a task force led by Ram Bahadur Thapa after demands for a change in leadership grew inside the party. But he did not present that report at Monday’s meeting.

Instead, the meeting will focus on the political report presented by Oli himself. And that report leaves little indication that he intends to surrender the leadership question.

In the opening session, Oli accused what he described as fascist forces of attacking him and the UML, while also accusing people within the party of attempting to weaken the chair.

His anger was also evident in the way he addressed the demand for party reorganisation.

Oli questioned whether replacing the leadership should itself be considered reorganisation.

He pointed to previous episodes of reorganisation in the communist movement, from the period involving Keshar Jung Rayamajhi and the Jhapa movement to the reorganisation of the party in 2018, and argued that the present situation was fundamentally different.

Party reorganisation, he argued, should not be a matter of desire or impulse.

For Oli, the answer is not to remove the old leadership but to transform how the party works.

He described transformation as changing working methods, changing the language used to communicate with the public, making decision-making more efficient and turning party committees from formal meeting structures into centres for solving people’s problems.

He also rejected the idea that leadership transfer should mean simply vacating a position.

Instead, he argued for a planned transfer of responsibility, knowledge, experience, institutional understanding, political culture and decision-making capacity.

His argument on generational transition followed the same line.

Youth alone, he said, should not be treated as qualification, just as age alone should not be treated as disqualification. What is needed is a combination of energy and experience.

To reinforce the point, Oli turned to the image of a tree. A new shoot, he argued, does not require cutting the roots.

“The history of UML is the root, and the new generation is the new shoot,” he wrote in his report.

The metaphor neatly captures the position Oli is taking in the current dispute. The pressure inside the party is for change. Oli’s response is that change does not require changing him. And Monday’s meeting showed that, at least for now, he intends to make that argument from the chair — and on his own terms.

From Tuesday, Central Committee members will be allowed to speak on his political report, with three minutes allocated to each speaker.

The debate will therefore move from Oli’s presentation to the wider Central Committee. But the first day has already established the tone.

Oli is not preparing to step aside. He is preparing to defend his position — with the authority of the chair, control over the proceedings and a political argument that says the party can transform without replacing its roots.

title.rendered: ‘Many international donors fail to identify the real, ground-level needs’

content.rendered:
American philanthropist Kym Rapier, Founder of the Kym Rapier Foundation, is currently in Nepal with her team for the first time. With over two decades of social work experience, Rapier focuses on empowering underfunded, community-led initiatives rather than top-heavy organisations.

Onlinekhabar spoke with Rapier about her lifelong journey in giving, the purpose behind her visit to Nepal, and how international donors can better support local communities.

Excerpts: 

Firstly, could you share the primary purpose behind your visit to Nepal?

About 15 years ago, my dentist in Montana began telling me about the challenges children in Nepal face in accessing education, getting to school, funding their studies, and pursuing primary, secondary, and university education. He had helped establish schools here. We planned this trip to visit those schools, assess how we can help improve them, and explore how our foundation can offer long-term support to Nepali children. 

As part of this trip, we already visited a school based in Helambu and have decided to support its infrastructure development.

You have been involved in philanthropy for over two decades. What first motivated you to step into social work?

It actually started when I was six years old. My friend was diagnosed with muscular dystrophy, and I started fundraising to help her get doctor’s appointments and support. Even with the innocence of a child, I believed I could make a difference in her life, and I did. That early experience stayed with me, and I knew as I grew up that I wanted to keep helping people for the rest of my life.

Through your foundation, you focus heavily on grassroots support. Why is working with locally led organisations so important to you?

Going to communities, meeting people face-to-face, and directly listening to their problems is essential. Many grassroots organisations are underfunded; they aren’t big groups that spend huge amounts of money on overhead. They know what works, but they just need resources. Needs vary from community to community based on culture, religion, and local dynamics. You cannot simply duplicate solutions from one place to another; you have to support what specifically works for that local community.

How do you ensure accountability and transparency in the organisations you support?

Accountability and transparency are very important to us. Before supporting an organisation, we take the time to understand their work, how funds will be used, and the impact they hope to achieve. We stay in communication, ask for updates and reporting, and whenever possible, visit the programs ourselves. For us, it’s about building trusted partnerships and making sure our support is creating meaningful impact.

Philanthropists are sometimes criticised for providing short-term relief without addressing root causes. How do you ensure your projects create lasting, sustainable change?

We go in directly to speak with community members and leaders to understand their long-term needs. Sustainable change comes from supporting areas like education and child welfare. Local leaders already know what solutions are required; our role as a foundation is to listen, identify those needs, and allocate the necessary resources so local communities can drive their own progress.

What do you think international donors often misunderstand about communities in developing nations?

Many international donors fail to identify the real, ground-level needs. They overlook the fact that a strategy that works in one location won’t necessarily work in another. Every country has unique cultural and contextual differences. Understanding and respecting what works for a specific community is always the best approach.

Nepal was recently hit by severe flooding. As a humanitarian, what goes through your mind when a disaster of this scale hits, and what can organisations learn about long-term preparedness?

My immediate thought goes to the basic survival needs of the affected people: shelter, hospital care, clean water, and food. Disasters underline the need for resources, government foresight, and unified coordination. 

Everyone must come together to assess the real ground needs and prepare communities before the next disaster strikes.

Given your foundation’s focus on children’s support, how do you plan to address the challenges faced by children displaced or orphaned by the floods?

Our priority is to help support displaced children and get them back into schools. However, as a foundation visiting Nepal for the first time, we are being very cautious not to jump in with assumed solutions. We are consulting with well-established local partners on the ground who understand the immediate relief and hospital rescue efforts to see exactly where our support can be most meaningful.

title.rendered: Pokhara International Airport faces uncertain future despite new hope

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 22

In daylight, the main terminal building of Pokhara International Airport is an attractive landmark. Visitors often stop to take photographs with the building in the background. But after sunset, the same structure tells a very different story.

The western section of the terminal glows with lights, while the eastern section remains dark. The illuminated side serves domestic passengers, with people moving through its arrival and departure halls. The eastern side, designated for international passengers, remains closed. Its doors are locked, its lights are switched off, and there is little sign of the international activity for which the airport was built.

For Pokhara, the contrast has come to symbolise the airport itself: half bright and half dark. Built after decades of pressure, agitation and lobbying for an international gateway, the airport was expected to connect Pokhara directly with cities beyond Nepal. Instead, regular international flights failed to materialise, leaving the airport largely dependent on domestic operations. The grand opening brought celebration, but the absence of international flights soon turned that excitement into disappointment—not only among Pokhara residents but also among those who had fought for the airport and businesses that had invested in anticipation of increased international tourism. Now, nearly four years after its inauguration, a new possibility is beginning to change that mood.

On September 23, Flydubai is scheduled to begin a daily flight between Pokhara and Dubai, with ticket bookings open for at least six months. The planned service has generated renewed enthusiasm among residents, tourism entrepreneurs and business organisations. For a city that has spent years waiting for its international airport to function as intended, the flight is being viewed as a possible turning point.

The optimism is not simply about Dubai. Dubai is seen by local business leaders as a major international transit point and a potential gateway to destinations across the world. According to former Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry president Anand Raj Mulmi, if the Dubai connection can be sustained, it could eventually create opportunities for connections with India, China and other South Asian countries.

He describes the Flydubai service as a small but important step toward overcoming the obstacles that have prevented Pokhara from achieving international connectivity. Dubai, he argues, can serve as a link between Pokhara and a major international city.

Flydubai has also been actively promoting the Pokhara route. It has opened an office in Pokhara and has been holding discussions and promotional activities in partnership with local stakeholders. The airline has opened ticket bookings from September 23, with daily flights planned. The airline’s Nepal general manager, Navaraj Shahi, says fares from Pokhara are at least Rs 5,000 lower than those from Kathmandu and that Flydubai and Emirates view Pokhara as a long-term opportunity.

The first flight is scheduled to land at Pokhara International Airport at 6:15 pm on September 23 and return to Dubai an hour later. The government granted permission for the daily service on May 25, and airport authorities say the flight schedule will remain the same each day.

Local tourism officials are preparing to welcome the first passengers with a water salute. Tourism entrepreneurs say the initial flights are already showing strong interest, with information that tickets for the first few flights of the 166-seat aircraft have been sold out. Hotels, restaurants, trekking agencies and ticketing companies are preparing packages aimed at supporting the new service and attracting visitors.

A long-awaited international gateway

The anticipation surrounding Flydubai has to be understood against the long history of Pokhara’s airport dream. The idea of an international airport in Pokhara dates back to around 1974, when land at Chhinedanda was acquired under the leadership of then-zonal administrator Shankar Raj Pathak. Yet it took more than five decades for the city to see the airport become a reality. In the intervening years, the project was affected by political debates, investment questions, competing interests and allegations of corruption and geopolitical complications.

In 2012, Pokhara residents, businesspeople, industrialists and social workers intensified their campaign for an international airport. The movement included a relay hunger strike, with local stakeholders putting pressure on the federal government to move the project forward.

Construction eventually took shape after the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal signed an agreement with China CAMC Engineering in 2014. In 2016, Nepal and China Exim Bank agreed on a $216 million loan for the airport, while CAMC was tasked with constructing it as a turnkey project. The foundation stone was laid by then Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli in 2016, with completion initially targeted for July 2021. The COVID-19 pandemic delayed the project. The airport was finally inaugurated on January 1, 2023, by then Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal.

But the opening did not bring the international traffic that local businesses had expected. Some international charter flights operated after the inauguration. Sichuan Airlines connected Chengdu with Pokhara through 26 charter flights. Bhutan Airlines and Druk Air also operated charter flights. Himalayan Airlines conducted flights between Pokhara and Lhasa, completing 52 arrivals and 52 departures—104 movements in total—but the service was eventually suspended because of insufficient passengers. A Chinese military aircraft also landed in Pokhara carrying relief supplies during the Jajarkot earthquake.

These flights demonstrated that international aircraft could use the airport. What remained elusive was a sustained commercial connection. The airport had received more than Rs 22 billion in Chinese investment, according to the report, making the absence of regular international operations a source of continuing frustration.

The lesson from Bhairahawa

For local stakeholders, the arrival of Flydubai brings excitement, but also caution. They have watched international services at Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa begin with similar expectations and subsequently struggle to become sustainable.

Jazeera Airways started a direct Kuwait-Bhairahawa service on May 16, 2022, the first foreign airline to operate there, but the service did not become regular. Himalayan Airlines, Nepal Airlines, Thai AirAsia, Flydubai and Qatar Airways also operated or announced services linking Bhairahawa with international destinations under different circumstances, including periods of maintenance at Kathmandu’s Tribhuvan International Airport and government incentive packages. Yet Bhairahawa failed to sustain the expected international traffic.

Mulmi says Pokhara must learn from that experience. He has warned against a situation in which Flydubai begins operating and later stops because the route cannot sustain itself commercially. For him, the challenge is not merely bringing one international airline to Pokhara but creating conditions under which the airline can cover its costs and continue operating.

That requires more than enthusiasm. It requires improvements in airport services and facilities, sustained promotion of Pokhara and active efforts to attract passengers, he says. Pokhara should also promote itself in Dubai rather than simply wait for passengers to discover the destination.

Can Dubai become Pokhara’s gateway?

The attraction of the new route lies partly in its potential reach. Through Flydubai and Emirates, passengers travelling via Dubai could potentially connect with 250 destinations. For a city whose international airport has struggled to establish its first regular overseas route, that network is being viewed locally as an opportunity to expand beyond a single destination.

For Pokhara’s tourism industry, the possibilities are particularly significant.

Tourism entrepreneurs point to the city’s natural and adventure attractions, including its proximity to high mountains and trekking routes. Tourism Council Pokhara president Hari Bhujel says the city can market the opportunity to visitors who would be able to travel directly to Pokhara and experience the mountains from the city.

The tourism industry is also looking towards visitors from the Gulf. Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal Gandaki president Krishna Acharya says Dubai has adventure-oriented visitors who may be attracted to activities such as cycling, motorbike riding and paragliding. The direct connection could make it easier to market Pokhara as an adventure destination.

The hotel industry is watching closely. Hotel Association Pokhara president Laxman Subedi says businesses invested in the city partly with the expectation that the international airport would bring more visitors. Pokhara has around 1,200 hotels and more than 15,000 people employed in the sector, according to the report. Yet businesses have faced difficulties, including the effects of recent disasters and uneven tourist seasons.

For Subedi, the success of the Flydubai service will depend on whether businesses and other stakeholders are prepared to support it. His warning is direct: businesses cannot continue operating at losses. If the new service is not sustained, he says, Pokhara could face a situation similar to Bhairahawa.

Restaurant and Bar Association of Nepal Pokhara president Basanta Gautam also sees the flight as significant beyond Pokhara itself. With Nepal relying heavily on a single international airport, he says the opening of another international gateway could strengthen visitors’ confidence. Pokhara already has international-standard hotels, restaurants and tourism services, but international flight connectivity has remained a missing component.

Preparing the airport for international passengers

Authorities say preparations for the Flydubai operation have been completed. The Civil Aviation Authority has made arrangements for the necessary services. Nepal Airlines has completed preparations for ground handling, while Solti Hotel has received permission and certification to provide flight catering services. Around 200 Civil Aviation Authority employees, including service providers and permanent staff, are working at the airport. Nepal Police has deployed 104 personnel and the Nepal Army 80 personnel for security. Customs and immigration offices have also deployed the required staff.

Local tourism organisations have also been preparing. The Nepal Association of Tour and Travel Agents Gandaki says it has trained 163 member companies in connection with the Flydubai service. Businesses are working together to develop tourism packages, while travel companies have been encouraged to bring their relatives and visitors to Nepal through Pokhara.

The broader business community is similarly calling for government involvement. Pokhara Chamber of Commerce and Industry president Shobha Gautam, who recalls the earlier campaigns for an international airport, says the government needs to take the issue seriously if the Dubai connection is to lead to further international routes. She says the chamber will continue coordinating with stakeholders and putting pressure on the government to maintain the service.

One immediate issue raised by Mulmi is visa access. If passengers travelling from Pokhara have to go to Kathmandu to obtain visas, he argues, the inconvenience could discourage potential travellers. He has called for mechanisms that would allow passengers in Pokhara to obtain the necessary visa-related services locally.

A test of whether hope can become habit

The optimism surrounding Flydubai is therefore tempered by an understanding that the first flight is not the destination. For Pokhara, September 23 represents the possibility of turning an international airport from a largely unrealised promise into an operating gateway. But sustaining that gateway will depend on passengers, tourism promotion, business cooperation, airport facilities and continued government support.

Tourism Council president Bhujel describes Flydubai as a potential milestone after years of struggle. Yet he also acknowledges the central challenge: ensuring that the service remains regular in the long term and using its success to attract other airlines.

Former tourism council president Pomanarayan Shrestha similarly sees Flydubai as only a beginning. Dubai has a large Nepali workforce, a significant Indian population and attracts wealthy international visitors. If Pokhara can bring some of those visitors directly to the city, he believes the benefits could extend across Gandaki Province and the wider Nepali tourism sector.

For years, the international terminal at Pokhara’s airport has remained a physical reminder of an unfulfilled promise: a building designed for international passengers but often left without them. Now, as Flydubai prepares to land, the dark eastern half of the terminal may finally begin to see more activity.

Whether that light remains on, however, will depend on what happens after the welcome ceremony, after the first flight and after the initial excitement fades.

For Pokhara, the real measure of success will not be that an international aircraft lands once. It will be whether the city can keep its international gateway open, active and connected and turn a long-awaited flight into a sustainable link with the wider world.

title.rendered: PM Shah leaving for USA today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Prime Minister Balen Shah is leaving for the USA today, leading a high-level Nepali delegation to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. PM Shah’s delegation members are his chief advisor Kumar Byanjankar, chief personal secretary Subash Sharma, private secretary Pradeep Pariyar and photographer Binay Shakya, among others. PM Shah is leaving for the USA from Tribhuvan International Airport, Kathmandu, on a Qatar Airways flight at 4:15 pm.

He is scheduled to address the high-level session of the UN General Assembly on September 24. Even the Foreign Minister, Shisir Khanal, is in the PM-led delegation to the UN General Assembly.

PM Shah is scheduled to meet UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in New York. Shah will return home on September 26. It is the first foreign visit of PM Shah.

—RSS

title.rendered: Foreign Minister Khanal holds talks with Bhutanese PM, EU vice-president in New York

content.rendered:
New York, September 22

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal held separate meetings with Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay and European Union Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera in New York on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

During his meeting with Tobgay, the Bhutanese prime minister expressed deep sorrow over the loss of life and destruction caused by the recent floods in Nepal.

Tobgay conveyed Bhutan’s solidarity with the Nepali people and expressed hope that reconstruction and recovery in the affected areas would proceed soon.

Khanal thanked the Bhutanese government for its generous support following the floods, saying that the Nepal government and people highly appreciated Bhutan’s assistance.

The two sides also discussed ways to further strengthen bilateral relations, including expanding cooperation in trade, aviation and other areas of mutual interest.

The meeting also covered climate change and the increasing frequency and intensity of natural disasters faced by mountainous countries such as Nepal and Bhutan. Both sides discussed the need to strengthen cooperation on climate-related issues.

Separately, Khanal met EU Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera at the UN headquarters in New York.

The meeting focused on various aspects of the Nepal-EU partnership and ways to deepen cooperation between the two sides.

Khanal expressed gratitude for Ribera’s message of sympathy and solidarity following the Bhotekoshi floods and discussed Nepal’s difficult situation after the disaster.

The two sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation, particularly in the recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction of areas affected by the Bhotekoshi floods.

Khanal and Ribera also exchanged views on broader areas of Nepal-EU cooperation, according to the foreign minister’s secretariat.

title.rendered: NEPSE resumes regular trading after data centre issue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

Regular share trading at the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) will resume today after a technical problem at Data Hub Pvt Ltd, the data centre hosting the servers of 72 NEPSE trading member companies, was resolved.

According to NEPSE, the technical issue at Data Hub has been fixed, allowing regular trading to resume.

The problem was first reported on the morning of September 20, prompting NEPSE to suspend regular trading the following day, Monday.

The Stock Brokers Association of Nepal had requested the suspension, citing concerns that continuing trading while the data centre problem remained unresolved could potentially affect NEPSE’s trading system.

Based on the request, NEPSE suspended trading on Asoj 5 under Rule 21(1) of the Securities Listing and Trading Regulations, 2018.

After trading was halted for one day and Data Hub confirmed that the technical problem had been resolved, NEPSE announced that regular trading would resume from today.

title.rendered: Bus driver dies after suffering severe burns in Tripureshwor fire

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 22

The driver injured in a bus fire at Tripureshwor on Monday has died while undergoing treatment at Kirtipur Hospital, also known as Burn Hospital.

According to police sources, the bus driver died on Monday night while receiving treatment.

The hospital said around 90 percent of his body had been burned. He was taken to the hospital at around 1pm following the incident.

The fire broke out at a bus stop at Tripureshwor Chowk around noon on Monday. The bus, operated by Riddhi Siddhi Yatayat, was numbered Ba 5 Kha 4274.

Police have preliminarily concluded that the driver himself set the bus on fire. According to the preliminary investigation, the incident followed a dispute between the driver and traffic police over a fine.

A committee has been formed to investigate the incident further. The circumstances surrounding the fire and the events leading up to it are being investigated.

title.rendered: Inside Chhong Norbu Sherpa’s journey From Dolakha to IRO Sushi

content.rendered:
Sixteen thousand kilometres from the village where he grew up, Chhong Norbu Sherpa was watching one plan after another fall apart.

First came his failed attempt to join the British Gurkhas. Then he prepared for the IELTS exam, hoping Australia might offer another way out. He passed, began the process of applying, and then Australia changed its immigration rules. The consultancy returned his application.

One disappointment followed another.

For Sherpa, who grew up in Dolakha, confidence was beginning to give way to frustration. There were few opportunities at home, and now even the prospect of leaving Nepal seemed to be slipping away.

Then Britain relaxed its immigration rules and introduced the Tier 4 student visa route.

In July 2009, Sherpa finally got his visa.

“I was one of thousands of Nepali students who came to Britain in that wave,” he recalls. “But the beginning was extremely difficult.”

For eight months after arriving in Britain, he could not find a job. He survived by borrowing money from friends.

Sixteen years later, the contrast is striking.

When we met him in Woolwich one weekend, the 38-year-old arrived in a Ferrari Portofino worth around £150,000.

The journey from a young man who once thought twice before taking a public bus to a businessman arriving in a Ferrari is dramatic. But Sherpa’s story is less about the car than what happened in between.

Today, the sushi business he started in 2014 has grown into IRO Sushi, with around 30 outlets across the UK. The business operates on a franchise model and employs around 200 Nepalis, according to Sherpa.

He says the business generates monthly revenue of around £1 million and annual turnover of about £20 million. The name IRO means “colourful” in Japanese. It is an apt description, at least of the life Sherpa has built for himself. But the business did not begin in a glossy restaurant.

It began with a £5,000 investment, a rented kitchen and a man who was working another job during the day.

From sushi chef to business owner

Sherpa arrived in Britain to study IT at Maritime Greenwich College, where the programme was run for Nepali students. When the college closed, he changed courses and moved into business management.

But studying was only one part of his life.

From April of the year after he arrived, he began working as a sushi chef with the help of a friend. He was working two jobs while studying, all while trying to repay the debts he had accumulated.

“There was a lot of pressure,” he recalls.

In 2014, he took the first real step towards building his own business.

He rented a kitchen near an industrial area that was already being used to supply sandwiches to hotels and airlines. He could use it from 5pm to 10pm.

During the day, he worked elsewhere. In the evening, he made sushi and sold it online. There were just two employees and a driver. That was IRO Sushi’s beginning.

The following year, as the business gained momentum, Sherpa opened his first shop on a high street.

In 2015, he completed a postgraduate degree in hospitality management at Westminster College. By then, his attention was increasingly turning towards business rather than employment.

He opened a second IRO Sushi outlet in Fulham in 2018, followed within months by a third in Greenwich and then another at Tower Bridge.

It was while working with a friend on the Greenwich outlet that Sherpa says he discovered the idea of franchising.

“I didn’t even know what a franchise concept was when I started,” he says.

The model would eventually become central to the company’s expansion.

The pandemic that changed the business

For many restaurant businesses, the Covid-19 pandemic was devastating.

For Sherpa, it became a period of expansion.

New IRO Sushi outlets opened in Highgate and South Norwood during the pandemic. The chain has since expanded into numerous locations across London and beyond, including Welling, Purley, Camden, West Hampstead, Stratford, Reading, Slough, Croydon, Dartford, Palmers Green, Bromley, Chingford, Orpington, Sidcup, Stockwell, Woolwich, Eltham, Penge, Tonbridge, Sevenoaks, Maidstone, Tunbridge Wells, Guildford and Newbury.

Sherpa says he plans to add more outlets and eventually take IRO Sushi to cities across the UK.

His ambition does not stop there. He says the company is also looking towards Europe and the United States.

“Once the system is in place, you mainly have to maintain it,” he says.

IRO Sushi currently operates through two models. In one, Sherpa partners with investors. In the other, the investor finances the entire outlet.

Opening a franchise, he says, requires an investment of roughly £120,000 to £150,000.

The company provides support with location, property setup, administration, legal work, accounting and marketing. Sherpa says experienced sushi chefs and restaurant operators can also become partners, while those who want to invest can participate through the franchise model.

For franchisees operating independently, he says there is a franchise fee and a 5% royalty on turnover.

Sherpa claims that franchise businesses have a 98% success rate, although that figure is his own claim rather than an independently verified industry statistic.

The expansion of IRO Sushi has also taken Sherpa beyond restaurants. Through IRO Property, he is involved in property, and he has recently started another fast-food venture, Momo & Company.

He says he is willing to share what he has learned with others without charging them. His philosophy is straightforward. Determination matters. Hard work matters. And, he says, a little luck helps.

The village he came from

For all the scale of his business today, Sherpa’s childhood was a long way from London’s high streets. He grew up in Chilankha, in Bigu rural municipality of Dolakha. Basic necessities were not readily available. To buy salt, oil and rice, his family sometimes had to walk for two days to either Khasa or Charikot.

Getting to school took two hours on foot. Luxury was not something he remembers thinking about. His family kept yaks and made churpi, and as a child he helped his parents with the work.

“My childhood was very difficult,” he says. “We never had the chance to think about luxury.”

Today, his parents, Tenzing Sherpa and Sangmo, live in Kapan, Kathmandu, along with his sister. One brother lives in Australia and another sister lives in Britain. Sherpa lives in Greenwich, London, with his wife, Dichenla Lama, and their two children.

The distance between Chilankha and Greenwich is measured not only in kilometres. It is also measured in the life Sherpa has built.

He says becoming a millionaire has not changed his preference for a relatively simple lifestyle.

Money, he believes, is ultimately a tool for solving problems.

“I don’t feel that money makes me something special,” he says. “But when other people tell me how far I have come, I feel proud of what I have achieved professionally.”

For Sherpa, that achievement is also tied to a lesson he believes many Nepalis in Britain overlook.

He says many migrants arrive with the immediate goal of finding a job, but are reluctant to take the risks involved in starting a business.

“Progress requires the willingness to take risks,” he says. “You also need ambition.”

For someone whose own path began with one failed plan after another, it is a lesson shaped less by theory than by experience.

The Gurkha attempt did not work. Australia did not work. Even Britain began with eight months without a job.

What eventually changed his life was not a single stroke of luck, but what he did after each setback.

The young man who arrived in Britain looking for a way forward ended up building a sushi business with dozens of outlets — and a life far removed from the one he had imagined as a boy walking two hours to school in Dolakha.

title.rendered: Nepal could show the world how to recover sustainably from a major disaster

content.rendered:
With chances of further sensational hydropower tunnel rescues dimming, the devastating ice-rock avalanche in August at the Nepal-Tibet border and catastrophic floods downstream are no longer making global headlines.

But now is the time to pay careful attention to community-centred lessons from past disasters as complex planning decisions are made about recovery and reconstruction that will shape long-term outcomes.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority recently released a Rapid Disaster Needs Assessment (RDNA) highlighting many of the challenges facing disaster-affected Nepalis, including the approximately 33,000 who have lost their homes.

As Nepal prepares long-term recovery and risk-reduction strategies, we offer insights from our collaborative research about post-disaster reconstruction and displacement following Nepal’s 2015 earthquake, as well as ongoing mountain hazards, to highlight areas of concern for the country’s affected communities.

Policies and funding must protect people’s livelihoods and rights while the global community must meet Nepal’s demands for climate justice and reparation. A focus on the climate impact may help reduce long-term risk and vulnerability, but must proceed in tandem with in-depth engagement with affected communities, including many Indigenous Peoples, to determine what their immediate future will look like.

Rebuilding livelihoods amid risk

The destruction of entire villages, road-bridge networks and economic hubs raises major reconstruction challenges for Nepali communities and households.

After the 2015 earthquake that left more than 800,000 houses in need of reconstruction, most homeowners received small grants to rebuild through an “owner-driven reconstruction” model.

But families affected by the current disaster may find little point in rebuilding their homes if there are no nearby roads, schools or economic opportunities. For many farmers, the land that underpins their agricultural livelihoods has been washed away.

The RDNA rightly states that “household recovery … depends on the restoration of connected services and access,” which in turn requires viable terrain.

Some households may find that upcoming technical assessments deem their land too hazardous to rebuild on. As in past disasters, “integrated settlements” are being discussed to collectively resettle displaced communities.

But our research has shown that integrated settlements set up after the 2015 earthquake struggled most when livelihood needs and caste-ethnic relations among resettled communities weren’t prioritized.

Relocation away from hazards like landslides and floods may reduce exposure, but it doesn’t address other forms of risk, including economic precarity and inequality.

Any approach to rebuilding will first require beneficiary identification: who is entitled to compensation or support, and on what basis? The RDNA acknowledges that “building ownership alone does not identify all households requiring assistance” and notes the challenges with verification, especially when documents are permanently lost.

These are important lessons from the post-earthquake experience, when property ownership was the primary criteria for reconstruction grants, leaving many affected people ineligible. This created additional vulnerability through a disaster recovery process that was meant to help them.

Governance and local autonomy

Nepal’s 2015 constitution devolved significant legal responsibility for disaster risk-reduction and management to provincial and municipal governing bodies.

But in the initial days after the recent flash floods, affected local authorities understandably had limited capacity to oversee disaster response, with the Nepal army leading search-and-rescue efforts directed by the central government. It’s now time to refocus on local capacity and aspirations.

Each municipality will likely have different preferences and priorities for reconstruction, relocation and restoration. These will depend on the specific disaster impacts experienced in their jurisdictions and the cultural and economic dynamics of their constituencies.

A one-size-fits-all recovery approach mandated by the federal government following a “one-door” policy is unlikely to succeed fully. Instead, needs-based, municipality-specific plans should be negotiated carefully in relation to relevant federal, provincial and municipal policies.

The RDNA says “no household survey, key informant interviews, focus groups, structured community consultation, or detailed engineering assessment was undertaken” to prepare its initial report three weeks after the flood.

Such person-to-person learning is the necessary next step. Affected Indigenous Peoples and local communities must not be treated as simply informants for central government programs, but rather as political entities with the capacity to lead assessment and craft policy.

The dangers of riverside development

The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods swept over homelands of the Tamang community and other Indigenous Peoples whose identities are deeply connected to place. Indigenous nationalities comprise approximately 38 to 90 per cent of the population in nine of the 15 affected municipalities.

Even when relocation would offer greater physical safety, many Indigenous participants in our post-earthquake research said they didn’t want to move away from their ancestral territory.

At the same time, many communities in Nepal have long histories of mobility. The populous, disaster-affected market towns on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli riverbanks reflect historic downhill and river-centred migration trends linked to national development planning and hydropower investment.

The disastrous consequences of ad hoc, river-centric development in the Himalayas cannot be clearer.

When rivers are conceived only as corridors for economic development, roads, services and opportunities become concentrated in flood- and landslide-prone areas. People migrating for work find themselves exposed to levels of risk they cannot mitigate.

It remains an open question what responsibility Nepal’s hydropower sector will take for worker compensation and regional rebuilding.

Rather than reconstruction in the same risky locations, there should be a systems-wide rethink of settlement and development patterns.

Those who moved to take advantage of riverside economies might consider moving uphill once again if connectivity and collective needs are appropriately addressed and resourced. Ultimately, people should not have to choose between place-based attachment and safety, or between traditional territory and economic opportunities.

Ways forward

Rampant development in known hazard zones is creating untenable risks for communities globally.

With financial support from the international community and private sector corporate social responsibility, Nepal has an opportunity to show the world how to reconsider economic development in relation to climate and geohazard risks and in consultation with communities and local governments. This will also require a reframing of transboundary geopolitical relationships.

Rather than “building back better,” as the mantra goes, Nepal can build back differently by upholding human-centred values, emphasizing sustainability, recognizing the inequitable distribution of risk and its causes, and prioritizing communities’ autonomy over their futures.

title.rendered: Nepal Airlines cancels Kathmandu-Narita flights as both wide-body aircraft remain grounded

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Nepal Airlines has cancelled its scheduled Kathmandu-Narita and Narita-Kathmandu flights for Tuesday as one of its wide-body aircraft remains grounded in Japan for repairs.

The airline had planned to bring the aircraft back to Kathmandu after completing maintenance in Narita. However, the repair work was not completed as planned, forcing the cancellation of the flights.

The cancellation has left hundreds of passengers who had booked tickets for travel during the festive season in uncertainty.

Nepal Airlines has another wide-body aircraft, which has been taken to Italy for scheduled maintenance.

The national flag carrier operates four international aircraft — two wide-body and two narrow-body planes.

With both wide-body aircraft currently grounded, the airline has so far been forced to cancel nearly a dozen flights, resulting in losses running into millions of rupees.

Nepal Airlines uses its narrow-body aircraft mainly for shorter international routes, while wide-body aircraft are required for long-haul destinations such as Japan.

The airline has yet to restore both wide-body aircraft to service, raising concerns over further flight disruptions during the upcoming festive travel season.

title.rendered: Supreme Court upholds passport contract awarded to German company

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

The Supreme Court has ruled that the contract awarded by the Department of Passports for printing e-passports was in accordance with the law.

A joint bench of Justices Kumar Regmi and Shrikanta Paudel dismissed three writ petitions filed by French company IDEMIA, clearing the way for the contract awarded to German company Veridos.

The court also issued a directive in a separate writ petition seeking to have passports printed at Nepal’s Security Printing Centre.

The Department of Passports had awarded the contract for the production and supply of e-passports to German companies Veridos GmbH and Muehlbauer ID Services after an international competitive bidding process. IDEMIA, which had been supplying passports to Nepal, challenged the decision through the public procurement review process and later moved the Supreme Court.

The two German companies were selected for separate packages. Muehlbauer was awarded the package covering the eMRTDS system, including enrolment, data management and delivery, while Veridos was selected for the production and personalisation of e-passports. The combined contract was valued at around Rs 7.66 billion.

The Public Procurement Review Committee had earlier upheld the Department of Passports’ decision and rejected IDEMIA’s objections. IDEMIA subsequently challenged the committee’s decision at the Supreme Court.

Dispute over corruption claim

The passport procurement has also come under scrutiny in a separate corruption case investigated by the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA).

The CIAA has treated the total contract amount as the amount involved in corruption rather than limiting the alleged loss to the amount actually paid, according to the allegations cited in the case.

The anti-graft body has sought a combined recovery of Rs 10.13 billion from the accused. However, the amount it has identified for recovery and an equivalent fine is around Rs 184.4 million, according to the case details.

Questions have also been raised over the basis for calculating the claimed loss. The CIAA has acknowledged that around Rs 184.4 million had actually been paid, while its charge sheet sought recovery of more than Rs 10 billion.

In the case against Manindra Raj Malla, the Nepali agent of Muehlbauer, the CIAA has sought Rs 1.90 billion in damages, equivalent to the contract amount.

The Supreme Court’s latest ruling on the procurement contract, however, concerns the legality of the Department of Passports’ tender process and the Public Procurement Review Committee’s decision. It is separate from the issues raised in the CIAA corruption case.
