title.rendered: ‘Nepali leaders understand India better than India understands itself’

content.rendered:
Nepal’s political landscape has undergone a generational change. For decades, its relationship with India was shaped by political leaders who shared deep personal, ideological and historical ties with New Delhi. That familiarity is now giving way to a younger political generation that grew up in a globalised Nepal, shaped by migration, technology, social media and new expectations of the state.

For India, the change presents both a challenge and an opportunity. Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s government has entered office without the traditional political relationships that defined Kathmandu’s engagement with New Delhi, while India itself is navigating a rapidly changing South Asian geopolitical landscape.

How should New Delhi understand Nepal’s new political leadership? Is the historically close relationship between the two countries changing, or simply taking a different form? And what does the rise of youth movements across South Asia say about the region’s political future?

Manjeev Singh Puri, who served as India’s ambassador to Nepal from 2017 to 2019, spoke to Onlinekhabar about Nepal’s generational transition, the changing nature of India-Nepal relations, Kathmandu’s understanding of New Delhi, the shifting geopolitics of South Asia and the growing aspirations of its younger generation. Edited excerpts:

As soon as a new government is formed in Kathmandu, speculation begins about what its relationship with India will look like. It is relatively easier to make such assessments based on a political party’s legacy. But this time, the government has no traditional political baggage or legacy in its relationship with India. How do you see the relationship between this new government and India developing?

Thank you for this very interesting question. Let us look at it from a somewhat historical perspective. Until now, Nepal’s major leaders — Oli, Deuba, Prachanda and others — were products of their respective times. They were leaders who fought against the monarchy for democratic rights. Prachanda-ji is perhaps the most interesting example. His objective was to fundamentally transform the structure of Nepal, and he did so.

But let us consider the backgrounds they came from. Prachanda came somewhat later. Apart from him, all of them are now above 75 and belong to the generation shaped by India’s independence and the end of the Rana regime in Nepal.

But now, you are witnessing a genuine generational transition. You have a 36-year-old prime minister, the youngest prime minister in the world. The average age of the Cabinet is around 40, and the oldest member was 52, although Mahabir has since been added.

This is not simply a change in age. It has come at a time when Nepal is fully connected to globalisation.

With the beginning of constitutional monarchy in 1990, Nepal started opening up to the rest of the world. People began going abroad for education and employment. Today, a large Nepali population is spread across the world, including the United States, Europe, the Gulf countries, Southeast Asia and India, and remittances account for a significant share of the country’s GDP. All of this is a consequence of that openness.

So, apart from the transformation brought about during Prachanda’s time, the previous political movements were largely continuations of what had come before. This is the first real qualitative change since then.

It is a clear message of generational transition: ‘We already had democracy, we formed governments, and now it is our turn.’ That is why they came out onto the streets.

What you mean by the absence of a legacy is correct in terms of party or personal relationships. Leaders of the old parties knew India’s political leadership closely. But why do people talk about the legacy of relationships? Because its fundamental basis lies in people-to-people ties, history and civilisational proximity.

Look at what happened when Nepal suffered a major flood. Our Prime Minister Modi-ji directly called Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah. That was not a political stunt. It was civilisational and instinctive warmth. It comes naturally.

That is also why relief materials could reach Nepal from India that very evening, while it would take a day or two for them to arrive from elsewhere — because we are the closest neighbours.

That said, I was pleased to hear both the foreign minister and the finance minister, speaking at the NDTV conference in Kathmandu, say that there should be a high-level bilateral visit before the end of this year. That is a positive signal.

It is natural that a new government without the legacy of previous relationships would need some time initially to settle its internal affairs. But the experience of relief and rescue following the floods has itself reminded the government that Nepal is part of the global system and that continuous dialogue with its neighbours is necessary.

In my view, the most important aspect of any relationship is continuous dialogue.

Once you are neighbours, you have a border, and with borders, some problems or misunderstandings are inevitable. That is why continuous contact needs to be maintained at the technical level, between people, in trade, between the militaries and security agencies, and, most importantly, at the highest political level.

Dialogue is what opens the way to solutions. We have been doing this for centuries, and we should continue doing so.

India also appears to have maintained a flexible and positive approach towards the new government from the beginning. Prime Minister Modi himself congratulated the RSP leadership on its victory. But our prime minister introduced a protocol regarding meetings with foreign diplomats and officials. The Indian foreign secretary was reportedly preparing to visit Kathmandu to formally invite our prime minister to India on behalf of Prime Minister Modi, but the visit was called off because a meeting could not be confirmed. How exactly is New Delhi viewing this?

I am not the official spokesperson for the government. I know no more about the foreign secretary’s visit than what has appeared in the media. So it would not be appropriate for me to comment on that. But I would say this: let us remember the context of 2008. We made it clear that the people of Nepal themselves would decide Nepal’s future.

We have more than two and a half centuries of historical relations between us. That is one part of the story. There is also the roti-beti relationship. But modern nation-states have to adapt to changing times and interact with other nations accordingly.

The prime minister here has said that he will initially focus on domestic priorities. That is understandable. But the expectation is that once the internal preparations are complete, the old dynamism of the relationship will return.

Another point is that Nepal’s current prime minister studied in India. That is not merely a coincidence. It reflects a deeper cultural relationship that goes beyond ordinary educational ties.

So it was natural to expect his visit to India — possibly his first foreign visit — because we have all grown up with this tradition and pattern.

Circumstances change; change is the rule of the world. But just because technology and globalisation have changed the way relationships work does not mean we should completely forget the fundamental foundations of the past.

I hope he will visit India by the end of this year, and that it will send a positive message.

My understanding is that because this is a new situation, people are still trying to understand the landscape. Since a different style is emerging compared with the past, it is natural for people to wonder whether something unusual is happening.

But ultimately, the people of Nepal will decide Nepal’s destiny and future.

We have cultural, social and economic ties, as well as formal government-to-government relations. Those relationships should move forward according to the wishes of the Nepali people.

I think the relationship is on the right track.

Our prime minister has made some concessions to the protocol he initially established. He has met the ambassadors of India and China. There have also been reports that our prime minister’s chief political adviser, Kumar Ben, informally travelled to India and met some Indian officials. Our prime minister appeared keen to attend the BRICS summit, but no formal invitation came. Does this indicate that Singha Durbar’s approach towards India is changing?

If such initiatives are genuinely taking place, they are welcome. I would call it an ‘effort to expand relations’ rather than a ‘correction’. As for BRICS, I do not know much about its internal diplomacy. What I do know is that the invitation for Prime Minister Balendra Shah to visit India is always open.

A formal state visit carries both ceremonial and diplomatic significance. It reflects a shared understanding and trust between the two countries. Personal relationships or ‘chemistry’ between leaders can make a major difference. It is one thing to say that relations are good at the bureaucratic level. But when top leaders meet face to face, talk and untangle difficult issues, that is when a genuinely friendly relationship is built. Even though national interest is paramount in diplomacy, personal warmth can be extremely helpful in resolving complex problems.

I hope that visit will take place soon.

In the past, Indian ambassadors had relatively easy informal access to the prime minister’s office. They could even reach the prime minister’s residence in Baluwatar with ease. You have your own experience from your time as ambassador in Kathmandu. That no longer appears to be the case. How do you view this changing nature and style in Kathmandu?

Nepal’s previous prime ministers had a different kind of closeness with India. Most of them were in our age group, and sometimes even the same age as the ambassador. So many interactions were naturally informal.

I remember meeting Girija Prasad Koirala. Our conversations were not limited to formal matters. We would sit around a private dining table and talk even about our food preferences because our lifestyles and cultures are so similar.

Balen Shah-ji is much younger. He is an engineer by profession and studied in Bangalore. He has seen India from a somewhat different perspective — differently from my generation: a modern India connected to technology, IT and artificial intelligence.

So it is natural that the nature of the relationship should change.

Whenever a new government is formed in Kathmandu, a great deal of time is spent understanding one another and building an atmosphere of trust. As a result, fundamental development and bilateral issues are often pushed into the background. How can this be improved so that the relationship becomes more stable and predictable?

The current government in Nepal has emerged from a particular historical situation and a wave of generational transition. They believe there were flaws in the structures of the past and that these need to be corrected.

The government has been saying, ‘We will spend the first 100 to 150 days on internal reforms.’

What that means is that while the government is fully focused on internal management, there may be some slowdown in important bilateral trade, economic agreements and projects with neighbouring countries.

But this is a transitional phase. Four or five months have passed now, and the government is moving towards greater stability.

I believe cooperation with neighbours and diplomatic engagement will naturally become priorities.

There are possibilities for high-level visits. Continuous dialogue and warm relations are what remove misunderstandings and make a relationship more mature and predictable.

To put it bluntly, from Kathmandu’s perspective there is not one India but ‘many Indias’ operating through different centres of power: the BJP’s political India, the RSS’s cultural India, the bureaucratic India, the mysterious India of the agencies, the India of the military, and various other Indias represented by different lobbies. Nepal’s establishment often seems confused about which ‘India’ to deal with and how. Sometimes it appears exhausted by it. Don’t you see this difficulty in Kathmandu?

Umesh-ji, you have forgotten the most important aspect — where is the relationship created by cricket? What about Nepali artists working in Indian cinema and music? What about films, the warmth between ordinary citizens and commercial relationships? These are also parts of India. I do not think the Nepali establishment is confused.

Nepali leaders understand India better than we understand ourselves.

Why? Because despite all our diversity, there is a common ground.

All right, let us accept your argument that many ‘Indias’ are active in Nepal. Even then, Nepali politics knows very well how to balance its dealings with all these ‘Indias’.

A senior Nepali leader told me in Kathmandu a few days ago that his father, who was himself a major political leader, used to say, ‘My father knew India, understood Bharat and knew Hindustan — and he knew the art of negotiating and cooperating with all three.’

So you have understood India much more deeply than we have.

It is natural to think that Kathmandu’s centres of power may become tired while coordinating with all these different institutions.

But that is how large and diverse countries work.

When you deal with the United States, do you deal with just one person or one institution? Of course not.

India itself is a vast and complex society. If that is a challenge, it is also an opportunity. If one door closes, another 10 doors open.

To be honest, someone looking from outside can sometimes see things more clearly because someone living inside a house can be confined by their own surroundings.

I, too, continue to try to understand Nepal in all its diversity.

For a long time, it was believed that the United States viewed South Asia, particularly Nepal, through India’s eyes or effectively ‘outsourced’ the region to India. But that dynamic appears to be changing. The US has appointed a special envoy specifically for South Asia, and India-US relations also no longer appear as smooth as they once did. How is India viewing this changing situation in South Asian affairs?

I firmly believe that India-Nepal relations are sui generis — distinctive and unique in nature. As for the ‘outsourcing’ of international affairs, I would not describe it that way.

In this era of globalisation, it is natural for Nepal to expand its relations with countries large and small around the world, whether in Southeast Asia, Japan, Australia or the United States.

Your border is connected to China, an emerging global power, so it is natural that Nepal should be a country of interest to the international community.

We view every relationship on the basis of mutual interests. We are neighbours, but we are also sovereign nation-states with our own national and security concerns. These include issues such as border management, cross-border crime and the fight against extremism.

Where our interests converge, cooperation becomes deeper. We are a large country. China is equally large, while the United States and Europe are major global players. In such a situation, balancing relationships requires considerable diplomatic skill.

When India, China and Nepal were all at an early stage of development, the situation was different. Today, much greater maturity and openness are required.

In this modern era, flexibility and strategic skill are certainly necessary, but serious maturity is equally important.

Given Nepal’s progress economically and demographically, and its ongoing graduation from the least developed country category, I am confident that Nepal will be able to deal intelligently with the challenges arising from its geopolitical position.

Nepal’s five-time former prime minister Sher Bahadur Deuba and his wife, former foreign minister Arzu Rana, were attacked by protesters during last year’s protests and had to spend nearly a year in Hong Kong after leaving Kathmandu. They went to Hong Kong because, according to reports, they were neglected even by their old friends. How do you view this?

I was deeply saddened to see those unpleasant images of Sher Bahadur-ji and Arzu-ji. No one can feel comfortable seeing such scenes. But during periods of intense political upheaval, such tragic incidents occur in many parts of the world.

In Nepal’s case, however, one beautiful aspect is that you have managed major political transformations with relatively little violence.

This time, there was some disorder and property damage, and there was also some humiliating behaviour. Amid intense anger, they became targets and perhaps thought it appropriate to stay away for some time.

Sher Bahadur-ji has now returned home and is active in politics again. In my view, this is a sign of the great strength and tolerance of Nepali society. You can express strong disagreement and protest, but after a change you again make space for everyone to play a constructive role in society and politics. That is an admirable characteristic of Nepali society.

I do not think external powers have much of a role in this. It is something Nepali society itself has determined.

Two ‘Hindu’ voices are currently being heard prominently in Kathmandu — Shashi Tharoor, author of Why I Am a Hindu, and Sher Bahadur Deuba. Tharoor’s book has been translated into Nepali, while Deuba recently asserted his Hindu identity strongly at a public gathering. Has his message travelled across the border to India? Could it have any impact there?

As I understand it, both are Hindus and are expressing their respective views. Shashi Tharoor’s book is intended for intellectual discussion. What Sher Bahadur-ji said may have been part of his own political strategy, depending on the context in which he said it.

The fundamental point is that Nepal is a Hindu-majority country. That is part of its historical identity. A large proportion of India’s population also follows Hinduism.

This shared cultural and religious faith strongly connects the people of our two countries.

Whether it is Indian pilgrims visiting Pashupatinath or Nepali devotees travelling to Kashi, Gangasagar and Tirupati, these are living realities between our societies.

Politics tries to make use of such sentiments and issues.

Some people think politics is purely an ideological debate, like the Oxford Union. But in practice, politics works somewhat differently.

Take Donald Trump as an example. He raised issues that resonated with ordinary people rather than focusing on complex economic theories, and the people elected him for a second time.

The same thing is happening in developed democracies across Europe.

Ultimately, it is the people who decide how influential a particular message becomes.

Let us turn to a somewhat different subject — India-Bangladesh relations. Over the past decade, relations between the two countries were considered very close, but following the recent youth uprising, Bangladesh’s politics has changed completely. Ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has taken refuge in India, and there is anger towards India among sections of the Bangladeshi population. How is India managing this new situation?

At the time, Sheikh Hasina’s life was at risk. She came to India and is currently safe. I do not accept the idea that ‘the entire Bangladeshi population’ is against India. Some groups or elements may have tried to create such an atmosphere.

I believe politics will return to a normal rhythm as circumstances evolve. India has remained a democracy continuously since independence. When crises have occurred in neighbouring countries, political leaders from different countries have sought refuge in India. We have examples ranging from Nepal’s top political leaders to the Dalai Lama.

Although India is not a signatory to certain technical aspects of international refugee conventions, it has always given priority to humanitarian considerations and protection.

Of course, serious dialogue on both sides is necessary to resolve misunderstandings. Foreign policy is shaped by both domestic needs and the international environment. Emotional politics may exist on one side, but ultimately the livelihoods of people, trade and economic cooperation are the real foundations of relationships.

Neighbours cannot be changed, so there is no alternative to moving forward pragmatically.

Finally, how do you assess the Gen Z movements and youth discontent seen across South Asia and around the world? We have seen young people take to the streets in Nepal, Bangladesh and even India. How should governments respond to the aspirations of the younger generation?

We need to recognise one thing. Because of the information and communications revolution, young people in the modern world are immediately connected to developments taking place across the globe.

This has created high aspirations among them. This is not just a phenomenon in Nepal. It is a global phenomenon. The resources and capacities available to states and governments have their own limits.

In India’s case, when voices of youth discontent emerged, the state engaged in dialogue in time and addressed their demands. Mature democracies must listen to the voices on the streets and public discontent in time and respond to them.

Nepal now has the youngest and most youthful government in its history. In a sense, this leadership has come to power representing the anger and aspirations expressed on the streets.

But the new generation should not forget that while bringing in modern technology and new ideas is valuable, the institutions and traditions of the past also had their own historical reasons and accumulated experience behind them.

So there needs to be a balance between the experience of the older generation and the energy of the new generation.

As the English saying goes, ‘Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater.’

When making changes, we should not lose sight of ourselves to the point of destroying the very foundations on which everything stands.

title.rendered: Heavy to very heavy rain forecast across Nepal from Friday

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall in several parts of the country from Friday to Sunday, warning that the weather system could disrupt daily life.

According to a special monsoon weather bulletin issued Monday evening, the rainfall is expected from September 25 to 27, with some areas also at risk of extremely heavy rain.

Weather system

The Meteorological Forecasting Division said a low-pressure system that developed over the northern Andaman Sea and adjoining areas has moved into the central Bay of Bengal and intensified into a deep depression.

The system is expected to move west-northwestwards, increasing rainfall activity in Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces from Wednesday.

From September 25 to 27, some parts of Gandaki and Lumbini provinces are likely to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms, lightning and strong winds. One or two places could receive extremely heavy rainfall, the division said.

A few places in Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati and Sudurpaschim provinces are also likely to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall, while some areas of Karnali province could receive heavy rain.

Authorities urge people to avoid unnecessary night travel

Following the weather department’s bulletin, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) issued a separate notice Monday urging authorities and the public to remain highly alert.

The authority warned of possible floods, landslides, debris flows and inundation in urban and Tarai areas due to heavy rainfall.

It urged people to avoid long-distance travel, particularly at night, unless absolutely necessary during the forecast period.

Federal ministries, provincial governments, local governments, security agencies and volunteers have also been asked to keep the public informed and remain prepared for emergency response.

Authorities have been instructed to keep equipment such as bulldozers, excavators and loaders ready along roads and highways considered vulnerable to weather-related disruptions.

District security committees, local governments and security agencies have been asked to relocate people and families living in high-risk areas to safer locations before disasters occur, based on early warnings.

Residents living near rivers, streams and areas vulnerable to landslides have also been urged to remain particularly alert.

The authority has asked people to call 1149 for information on rainfall and floods, 1234 for disaster assistance, 100 for Nepal Police and 1114 for the Armed Police Force.

Agriculture and tourism sectors also at risk

The weather department said rising water levels in major and minor rivers could affect daily life, agriculture, health, tourism, construction activities, roads and air transport.

As the rice harvesting season has begun in some areas, farmers have been advised to carry out related activities only after consulting agricultural experts.

The department has also warned that the weather system could bring heavy snowfall in mountainous areas and urged mountaineers and others in the region to exercise heightened caution.

title.rendered: The flood has gone. For Nepal’s children, the fear remains

content.rendered:
“I don’t need anything.”

The boy stood among other children at a relief distribution centre and watched them choose what they could carry.

Some were looking through piles of clothes. Others were reaching for food. A child who had received a new toy had already begun playing with it.

The boy wanted none of it.

“What’s the point of taking it?” he said. “There’s nowhere to keep it.”

It was an unusual response to a relief distribution, but it made sense once you understood what the flood had taken from him.

His home was gone. So was his family. The place he once knew as somewhere he could return to was no longer there. For him, a bag of clothes could not replace that.

The roads were beginning to reopen. Relief was reaching the affected areas. The immediate crisis was slowly giving way to the long work of recovery. But for the boy, the flood had not ended. He was still living in it.

That is what psychosocial counsellors working with children in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading are beginning to understand.

At a distance, many of the children look as though they are recovering. They play. They laugh. They queue for food. Some run around holding new toys.

Then someone sits down beside them and starts talking. The difference can be startling.

Some children barely speak. Some keep looking for their parents. Some are frightened by water or loud noises. Others have trouble sleeping. And some are still waiting for people who may never return.

A rapid assessment by the National Child Rights Council found 1,233 children in 30 holding centres across the three districts. At least 102 had lost both parents, while 439 had been separated from their parents. Another 691 were living with either their mother or father.

There were 21 children with disabilities.

Those numbers provide a measure of the disaster. But they do not explain what it means for a child to wake up without knowing where their mother is.

They do not capture the child who no longer knows where home is. And they do not explain why a 14-year-old girl continues to believe that her younger sister will come back.

‘My sister will come’

The sisters were together when the flood came. Then their hands were separated. The younger girl disappeared. The 14-year-old does not know where she is. She is also unsure where her father is. Yet she keeps saying the same thing.

“My sister will come.”

During counselling, she explained why.

“My father will save my sister.”

For adults, the reality of a disaster often becomes clear quickly. For children, it can be different. They may hold on to an explanation, a person or a promise because they need something familiar in a world that has suddenly become unfamiliar.

That is why counsellors do not necessarily begin by asking children to talk about the flood. They give them something else to do. They play. They draw. They make space for children to decide what they want to say and when they want to say it. Sometimes the story emerges on paper.

One child drew a house and looked at it for a while.

“Our house was swept away by the flood,” she said. “Maybe our house will become like this again.”

Another drew a large river.

Others drew their parents carrying children.

For children who cannot find the words, a drawing can become a way of saying what happened without having to describe it.

Tara Bhandari, a psychosocial counsellor and chairperson of Bishwas Nepal, saw another expression of that fear when teams tried to move children to a temporary safe place.

Some refused.

“If you take us down, the flood will sweep us away,” they said. “A big river will come again.”

The river had stopped rising. The children’s minds had not.

When safety does not feel safe

For Bhandari, that moment illustrates why simply moving children to a physically safe place is not enough. A child has to feel safe too. Food, water, clothing and shelter remain essential. But so is listening to what children are afraid of.

Grishma Paneru, who works in psychosocial support, says the children she has encountered have reacted to the disaster in very different ways.

“Some have become withdrawn. Some are afraid. Some prefer to be alone. Some cannot sleep at night,” she said.

Water can trigger memories of the flood. So can rain. So can a sudden loud noise.

Others continue to play.

That can be reassuring, but it should not be taken as proof that everything is fine.

“A child playing does not mean they are okay,” Paneru says.

What matters is the change in the child — whether their sleep, appetite, behaviour, relationships or ability to concentrate have changed.

Child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr Utkarsh Karki says such reactions are common after disasters and should not immediately be treated as signs of mental illness.

A child may become unusually quiet or unusually talkative. They may cling to their parents, cry suddenly, have nightmares or struggle to sleep.

Most children gradually return to normal. But some do not.

In some cases, children may develop acute stress reactions, anxiety, depression, behavioural changes or post-traumatic stress disorder.

They may repeatedly relive the flood, have nightmares, become intensely afraid of water or rain, avoid reminders of the disaster or remain constantly alert to danger.

They may also struggle to concentrate or withdraw from friends.

The important distinction, Karki says, is time and severity.

Symptoms that persist for four to six weeks, worsen or interfere with eating, sleeping, playing or studying need greater attention.

But the first response to a traumatised child is not necessarily psychiatric treatment.

It is safety. A safe place. Food and water. A familiar routine. And, where possible, a family to return to.

The children who are no longer where they were

That last part is becoming increasingly difficult.

As the emergency phase passes, one of the most troubling questions is not only how children are coping, but where they are.

Bhandari recalls one day when 65 children were placed in a safe holding centre.

The following day, only 37 remained.

The whereabouts of the others were not immediately clear.

Some children were reportedly being taken into private homes by people who said they were relatives. In some houses, several children were being kept together.

But not every claim of kinship had been verified.

For children already separated from their families or left without parents, that uncertainty creates another danger.

They can become vulnerable to trafficking, child labour, child marriage and sexual abuse.

Tilottam Paudel, a child-rights activist and chair of Jagriti Child and Youth Concern Nepal and the Child-Friendly Peace Zone Campaign, says children should not be moved elsewhere without information from and approval of their families or relevant local authorities.

The problem is made harder by the loss of documents.

Birth certificates and other records may have been swept away with homes.

Without those records, even establishing who a child is and where they belong can become difficult.

The scale of the uncertainty is visible in the figures coming from the affected districts.

In Rasuwa’s Uttargaya Rural Municipality, at least 57 children are reported to have lost their parents and could not be found in the camps. Around 200 children are reportedly missing there.

In Nuwakot’s Bidur Municipality, 614 children have been affected. Twenty-seven have lost both parents and 203 have been separated from their parents.

In Belkotgadhi, 52 children are reported to have been left without parents.

The numbers are still being established.

And that is part of the problem.

‘How many people do we have to tell our story to?’

There is another danger in the rush to understand what happened. Children are being asked to tell their stories repeatedly. One organisation arrives with relief. Another arrives to provide counselling.

Someone asks what happened. Someone else asks the same question. Photographs are taken. Then the visitors leave.

For the adults involved, each visit may serve a different purpose.

For the child, it is the same flood. Again, and again, and again.

At one point, a girl asked a counsellor a question that captures the exhaustion of being repeatedly made to revisit the worst moment of her life.

“How many people do we have to tell our story to?”

The question has implications beyond counselling.

Children who have experienced trauma need support, but they also need privacy.

Their stories cannot become material to be repeatedly photographed, recorded or shared simply because adults want to document the disaster.

Psychosocial support, counsellors say, works through trust. And trust takes time.

The person who has earned a child’s confidence may need to keep showing up long after the first relief distribution has ended.

Then there is school

For many children, school could become one of the simplest ways of beginning to rebuild that sense of normality. But schools remain closed in affected areas, leaving children without one of the basic structures of their daily lives. Some have little to do.

Others are helping retrieve belongings from damaged houses and shops. Some are entering dangerous areas in search of possessions. The longer that continues, the more difficult it becomes to separate recovery from risk. Reopening schools, therefore, is about more than education.

A functioning school provides routine. It gives children a place to see friends, play and interact with trusted adults. It can also help authorities answer basic questions.

Who has returned? Who is absent? Who is missing? Who has moved elsewhere?

But schools themselves must first be safe. Buildings and access routes need to be assessed. Psychosocial support needs to be available. And where floodwaters have destroyed school records, local governments, schools and child-protection organisations will have to work together to reconstruct them.

The second wave of the disaster

The most difficult part of a disaster may not always be the moment when the water rises.  For some children, it comes later.

When the relief queues become shorter. When the roads reopen. When schools resume. When families return to the places where their homes once stood.

That is when the enormity of what has happened may finally become clear.

A child who was too busy surviving to grieve may begin to grieve.

A child who kept waiting for a parent may begin to understand that the parent is not coming.

A child who remained silent may begin to speak.

Karki says children who have lost parents, been separated from their families, lost contact with relatives or lost their homes entirely may require psychosocial support for months or longer.

“One or two counselling sessions cannot heal such deep trauma,” he says.

“They need continued relationships, a safe environment, school, places to play, friends and reunification with their families. Where necessary, they need access to specialist mental health services.”

But perhaps the most important thing is also the simplest.

They need to know that someone will listen.

From relief to rebuilding

In the first days after the flood, relief is measured in food, clothes, water and shelter.

Those things are still needed.

But for children, recovery will demand something much larger.

Paudel says the focus must now begin moving beyond immediate relief.

“We need reliable information on missing children,” he says. “We need family identification and reunification. Children without parents need safe protection. They need protection from trafficking, child marriage, child labour and sexual abuse.”

Birth certificates and other records need to be restored.

Schools need to reopen safely.

Psychosocial support needs to continue.

Families need to be reunited where possible.

And children need places where they can play without being afraid of the next sound of rushing water.

The boy at the relief centre was right about one thing.

Another bag of supplies could not give him what he had lost.

The harder work begins after the relief trucks leave — finding the missing, rebuilding families, restoring routines and helping children believe that the world around them can become safe again.

The flood has gone.

For many of Nepal’s children, the work of surviving it has not.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

Oli rejects calls for leadership change, says UML reorganisation is not about replacing leaders

CPN-UML Chair KP Sharma Oli has made clear that he has no intention of stepping down as party chairman, arguing that replacing the leadership cannot by itself be described as party reorganisation. Presenting his political report at the UML Central Committee meeting on Monday, Oli argued that the debate over party reorganisation should be understood in its proper historical and organisational context and should not be treated as a matter of impulse.

Probe committee formed to investigate Tripureshwor bus fire

A committee has been formed to investigate the bus fire incident in Tripureshwor, Kathmandu. The Kathmandu Valley Police Office, Ranipokhari, formed the investigation committee, according to AIG Sushil Singh Rathour of the office. The committee is headed by SSP Ramesh Basnet and has been given five days to complete its investigation

Gas supply easing, no need to worry about shortages during festive season: Minister Sah

Industry Minister Deepak Kumar Sah has said the supply of cooking gas in the market is gradually becoming easier. Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives, he said the government’s continuous efforts had helped restore two-way traffic on the road obstructed at Krishnabhir from September 17.

100 billion needed for post-disaster reconstruction, says Minister Lamsal

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal has said that around Rs 100 billion is needed for post-disaster reconstruction and infrastructure management following the Bhotekoshi disaster. Speaking at a meeting of the Infrastructure Development Committee held at Singha Durbar on Monday, Minister Lamsal said this amount would be required for a plan covering the current disaster damage and future preparedness.

Ransomware attack shuts stock market as investors raise security concerns

Nepal’s stock market was abruptly shut down on Monday after a ransomware attack targeted the infrastructure of Data Hub Pvt. Ltd., which hosts the Trading Management System (TMS) servers of 72 brokerage companies. According to Data Hub, the attack on its TMS hosting infrastructure was detected at around 5:30 am on Bhadra 4. Data Hub hosts the servers used by 72 trading member, or brokerage, companies.

39 dead, 439 missing at Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project

Thirty-nine people working at the 216 MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa have been found dead, while 439 others remain missing following the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

Petition seeks transfer of Nepali Congress dispute to Constitutional Bench

A petition has been filed at the Supreme Court seeking to transfer the case concerning the Nepali Congress’s special general convention from the full bench to the Constitutional Bench.

VAT on electricity to be scrapped, energy and finance ministers agree in principle

The government is preparing to scrap the value-added tax (VAT) it has levied on electricity tariffs since the current fiscal year. The move comes just two months after VAT took effect at 5 percent for household consumers and 13 percent for industrial and other non-household consumers.

Deposits in government-run relief funds reach near Rs 15 billion

Monetary contributions to the Prime Minister Natural Disaster Relief Fund have continued to pour in following the floods that struck the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system on August 26. Around Rs 15 billion has been collected so far in the Prime Minister Natural Disaster Rescue Fund and the Prime Minister Relief Fund, both operated by the government. According to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the combined balance in the two funds presently stands at Rs 14,889,038,871.

title.rendered: Nepal’s climate message to the world at UN General Assembly

content.rendered:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s participation in the 81st United Nations General Assembly is an important opportunity for Nepal. He is scheduled to address the General Debate on September 24. At a time when climate change is becoming crucial, Nepal is facing floods, landslides, droughts and other extreme weather events with growing frequency.

The recent floods and landslides in the Bhotekoshi area have once again shown Nepal’s vulnerability to climate-related disasters. According to Our World in Data, Nepal accounted for only about 0.05 percent of global CO₂ emissions in 2024. Yet the country is facing serious consequences from a crisis to which it has contributed very little.

Climate change is no longer only an environmental issue. Its impacts are being felt in agriculture, food and water security, energy, health, infrastructure, livelihoods and the economy. Nepal’s dependence on agriculture and natural resources makes many communities particularly vulnerable to changing rainfall, droughts, floods, landslides and rising temperatures.

The Himalayan climate challenge

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is vital to millions of people but highly vulnerable to climate change. Rising temperatures are rapidly reducing snow and ice, threatening water systems, ecosystems and mountain communities. The 2019 Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment warned that even if global warming is limited to 1.5°C, the region could lose about one-third of its glacier volume by 2100.

The situation is becoming more serious. An ICIMOD assessment published in 2023 found that glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalaya lost ice 65 percent faster during 2011–2020 than in the previous decade. Nepal has 3,808 glaciers, making it particularly exposed to these risks. If current warming and glacier-loss trends continue, the consequences for water, ecosystems, livelihoods and communities will be severe. A UNDP report also notes that Nepal spends around 1.5 to 2 percent of its GDP each year on climate adaptation and disaster management.

The consequences extend far beyond Nepal. Rivers originating in the Hindu Kush Himalaya provide water to hundreds of millions of people across Asia. Changes in glaciers, snow and rainfall can affect water supplies, agriculture, energy and livelihoods across the region. Protecting the Himalayas is therefore not only Nepal’s responsibility but a regional and global concern.

Climate justice for vulnerable countries

These realities make climate justice an important issue for Nepal’s international engagement. Countries that have contributed relatively little to global emissions should not have to bear a disproportionate share of climate-related losses and damage.

For Nepal, climate justice is not simply about receiving support after a disaster. It also means fair access to climate finance, appropriate technology, scientific knowledge and resources needed to adapt to climate change and build resilience.

The UN General Assembly provides Nepal with an important platform to highlight these concerns. Nepal can call on major emitting countries to strengthen climate action and fulfill their commitments under the Paris Agreement, including stronger climate plans, adaptation support, climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building. Nepal can also work with other climate-vulnerable countries to ensure that their concerns receive greater attention and that global climate commitments lead to meaningful action.

Building climate partnerships

Nepal can strengthen partnerships with Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries, Small Island Developing States and other mountain countries. Although their circumstances differ, many share a common challenge: high vulnerability to climate change despite relatively small contributions to global emissions. Cooperation can strengthen their collective voice on adaptation, loss and damage, climate finance and resilient development.

Climate diplomacy should therefore become an important part of Nepal’s foreign policy. Through bilateral meetings and multilateral dialogue, Nepal can seek stronger cooperation in renewable energy, disaster risk reduction, climate research, sustainable mountain development and climate-resilient infrastructure.

Nepal should also strengthen cooperation with research institutions, development partners, multilateral organizations and countries across the Himalayan region. Scientific information, early warning systems and regional cooperation are especially important because rivers, glaciers and ecosystems cross national boundaries.

Turning climate finance into climate action

Nepal’s National Adaptation Plan estimates that the country will need about Rs. 6.3 trillion for climate adaptation by 2050, or nearly Rs. 280 billion a year. For a country that collects around Rs. 1.2 trillion in annual revenue, meeting this need is a major financial challenge.

International mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund, Least Developed Countries Fund, Adaptation Fund and Loss and Damage Fund can provide important support. However, there is still a wide gap between Nepal’s needs and the resources available. Nepal requires about US$2.1 billion annually for adaptation in agriculture, water resources, infrastructure and disaster management, while the funding secured so far remains much smaller.

Nepal therefore needs to strengthen its capacity to develop quality projects, access international finance and ensure effective implementation. Priority should be given to disaster preparedness, early warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure, ecosystem protection and support for communities affected by climate-related disasters.

Climate finance should not be used only to rebuild roads, bridges, schools, hydropower projects and settlements after disasters. It should also help reduce future risks and build safer, stronger and more resilient communities and infrastructure.

A clear message from Nepal

The 81st UN General Assembly offers Nepal an important opportunity to present the realities faced by its people and the wider Himalayan region. Nepal’s message should be clear: the climate crisis is not only an environmental challenge. It is also a challenge to development, livelihoods, food and water security, infrastructure and human well-being.

Nepal should use this global platform to advocate for climate justice, improve access to climate finance and technology, strengthen international partnerships and highlight the global importance of the Himalayas. At the same time, Nepal can showcase its own contributions through hydropower, forest conservation, biodiversity protection and sustainable mountain management.

The General Assembly is therefore more than a diplomatic event. It is an opportunity for Nepal to make its climate concerns heard, build stronger international partnerships and call for collective action to protect vulnerable communities and mountain ecosystems.

title.rendered: Gas supply easing, no need to worry about shortages during festive season: Minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Industry Minister Deepak Kumar Sah has said the supply of cooking gas in the market is gradually becoming easier.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives, he said the government’s continuous efforts had helped restore two-way traffic on the road obstructed at Krishnabhir from September 17.

“With this, the supply of gas in the market has been gradually becoming easier,” he said.

He said the government had been coordinating with the Ministry of Industry, local administration and security agencies to facilitate the transportation of gas in the Kathmandu Valley.

He said 1,000 gas cylinders that had been hidden at various locations were seized and distributed to consumers.

The minister said the government would take action against those involved in wrongdoing and that such action would continue.

He said consumers should not have to remain uncertain about whether they would be able to obtain gas during the upcoming festive season.

He said the government’s responsibility regarding gas supply should not be measured by the number of meetings held or announcements made, but by concrete results, including whether cylinders reach consumers on time, whether prices remain transparent and how quickly complaints are addressed.

“We want to reassure all consumers that you do not need to remain uncertain about whether you will get gas during the upcoming festive season. The government will resolve this problem before the festive season,” he said.

He added that along with addressing the immediate problem, the government was also working on a long-term plan.

title.rendered: Samsung Nepal launches Galaxy S26 FE at Rs 119,999

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Samsung Nepal has launched the Galaxy S26 FE, the latest addition to its Galaxy S26 series and the first smartphone in the series to come with One UI 9.

The company said the Galaxy S26 FE features a slim and lightweight design, with a focus on camera capabilities, image processing and Galaxy AI features.

The phone comes with several features designed to make everyday photography, video recording, editing and other tasks easier, according to Samsung.

Pranay Ratna Sthapit, Senior Director and Head of MX at Samsung Nepal, said the Galaxy S26 FE was designed to make a meaningful difference in users’ daily lives through its features.

He said the phone would make premium features from the Galaxy S series accessible to a wider range of customers.

New camera and video features

The Galaxy S26 FE features an upgraded triple rear camera system and enhanced image processing technology, Samsung said.

The company said the camera is designed to capture both still images and moving subjects clearly, while also offering improved photo-editing capabilities.

The My Fan Cam feature, previously introduced on Samsung’s new foldable phones, is also available on the Galaxy S26 FE.

According to Samsung, the feature automatically tracks a selected person and keeps them in the centre of the frame, adjusting the framing according to the movement of the subject or scene.

The phone also comes with Super Steady with horizontal lock, which is designed to keep fast-moving footage stable and level while recording.

It offers up to 3x optical zoom, while Samsung’s Nightography feature is designed to capture brighter and clearer images in low-light conditions.

More personalised Galaxy AI features

The Galaxy S26 FE comes with One UI 9 and a range of Galaxy AI features.

Samsung said the features are designed to provide information based on users’ daily activities and needs and help them organise their tasks.

The Now Brief feature, first introduced with the Galaxy S25 series, has also been made more personalised.

Users can select briefing cards based on information they want, including weather and health-related updates. Samsung said users can also create their own cards using simple instructions.

Priced at Rs 119,999

Samsung Nepal has priced the Galaxy S26 FE (8GB/256GB) at Rs 119,999.

The phone is available in three colours — Pistachio, Graphite and Blueberry.

The company has also announced several launch offers. Customers can receive an exchange bonus of up to Rs 8,000 and a six-month Google AI Pro subscription worth Rs 18,351 at no additional cost.

Samsung is also offering a 24-month EMI option for the Galaxy S26 FE. According to the company, monthly instalments start at Rs 3,256, while the 12-month EMI option costs Rs 6,000 per month.

title.rendered: Dispute over fine preceded bus fire in Tripureshwor

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

A dispute reportedly took place between a bus driver and traffic police on duty in Tripureshwor, Kathmandu, shortly before the bus caught fire.

A video clip of the argument circulated on social media captures the driver saying, “I am ready to die, but I will not pay the fine.”

Shortly afterwards, a Riddhi Siddhi Yatayat bus, Ba 5 Kha 4274, caught fire. Bus driver Dawa Lama, 25, from Kavre, was seriously injured in the fire. Police rescued him and took him to a burn hospital in Kirtipur. Doctors involved in his treatment said his condition was critical.

The video of the argument appears to show traffic police attempting to issue the driver a fine for allegedly violating traffic rules. The driver, however, insists that he had not committed any offence and refuses to pay the fine.

“I am being fined without committing any offence,” he is heard saying in the video.

The video shows the driver inside the bus and traffic police officers on the road. People wearing Armed Police Force uniforms and others in civilian clothes are also seen. They appear to be asking the driver to move the bus to the side, saying that stopping it in the middle of the road was affecting traffic movement.

During the argument, the driver says he respects the traffic police and has apologised, but complains that they are still trying to fine him.

As the traffic police insist that he must pay the fine and the driver refuses, the argument escalates. The driver becomes more agitated and says, “We are working people. I am ready to die.”

He repeats that he had not committed any offence but had still apologised, saying, “Despite showing them so much respect, they are being careless. Do whatever you can.”

A short while later, flames were seen coming from the rear of the bus.

title.rendered: The journalist giving the Himalayas a voice

content.rendered:
At 16, Navin Singh Khadka was already teaching English to children in Kathmandu.

He was still a student himself.

Money was tight, so he taught during the day and studied when he could. At Adarsha Vidya Mandir, where he later taught, he began putting together a small school magazine. He collected stories, poems and essays written by the children and turned them into something that looked, to him, like a real publication.

Then something unexpected happened. Some of those children’s pieces were picked up by The Rising Nepal and Gorkhapatra. Khadka had found his way into journalism without quite realising it.

More than three decades later, his work appears on the BBC World Service, where he reports on climate change, biodiversity and environmental crises for an international audience.

He has reported from United Nations climate conferences, travelled to around 50 countries and covered some of the most consequential environmental stories of the past two decades.

But when he talks about his work, he rarely begins with London. He talks about the mountains.

“The mountains are coming down,” he says.

It is an arresting way of describing what he has watched happen across the Himalayas.

Snow and ice are disappearing. Springs are drying. Rainfall is becoming less predictable. A farmer can face drought when water is needed and flooding when it is not. And beneath all of that, Khadka sees a story that is still not being told loudly enough.

The story of what climate change looks like from the mountains themselves.

The boy who learned English from war stories

Khadka’s path to becoming an international journalist began with a language. His father, the late Puran Singh Khadka, had served in the army and was determined that his son should learn English. He brought home comics and stories about the Second World War.

“He taught me in a way that would keep me interested and stop me from getting bored,” Khadka recalls.

The lessons stuck. After the family returned to Kathmandu from India, Khadka continued teaching himself. He watched English films, read newspapers and wrote his college answers in English. When people spoke in Nepali, he would often make notes in English.

He did not know it at the time, but he was building the foundation for a career that would eventually depend on moving between languages and audiences. His own education followed a less straightforward path.

He completed his schooling at Nandi Ratri Secondary School in Naxal and went on to study management at Public Youth Campus, followed by a bachelor’s degree at Shanker Dev Campus and a master’s at Ratna Rajya Campus.

Journalism was not his subject. Survival, however, was.

“I started teaching when I was 16,” he says.

His first job was at Deep Shishu Niketan in Bishalnagar. He later taught at Adarsha Vidya Mandir and became head of the English department at Gyanodaya Bal Batika.

At the same time, something was beginning to pull him towards journalism. The school magazine was the first clue. The newspapers that later published the children’s work were the second. Soon, he wanted to know how the people who wrote those newspapers actually did their jobs.

Jumping into the swimming pool

Khadka enrolled in a 10-month journalism course at the Nepal Press Institute.

Even that was difficult. Classes were held in the morning, but he was also teaching and attending college.

“I could only go on Sundays, so I couldn’t attend all the classes,” he says.

After completing the course, he needed an internship.

He wanted The Kathmandu Post. Instead, veteran journalist Sushil Sharma offered him a place at Spotlight, the weekly he edited.

“If you want to work at Spotlight as well, you’re welcome,” Sharma told him.

Khadka took the offer. For the next few years, he lived two professional lives. Teacher by day, journalist alongside it. Eventually, he realised he could not keep doing both.

“If journalism was what I wanted to do, I felt I had to jump into the swimming pool,” he says.

So he did and left teaching.

What followed was a tour through Kathmandu’s media landscape — Spotlight, The Rising Nepal, The Himalayan Times, SpaceTime, Nepali Times, Radio Sagarmatha and Channel Nepal.

His beat was initially tourism. But Khadka was less interested in telling people where to go than in asking what was happening behind the industry.

He began looking at civil aviation, government projects, money and power.

Where was the money going in Melamchi? What happened to the money connected to Lauda Air? What really happened during the privatisation of Butwal Power Company?

“I always gave importance to the story,” he says. “I didn’t have an ambition to reach a big media organisation. But I believed that only strong stories could bring about change.”

That attitude would eventually take him somewhere he had not expected – The BBC.

The BBC had one problem with him

When Khadka joined the BBC Nepali Service in March 2002, he had a problem. He could speak English. He could report. But he had never worked as a Nepali-language news reporter.

The timing was unforgiving.

Nepal was deep in a conflict. Political confrontation between the seven-party alliance and the monarchy dominated the headlines. News had to be written, translated, recorded and delivered quickly.

Khadka had to learn on the job. Again, Sharma became his teacher.

“He would keep a clock in front of me and say, ‘You have to finish this in this many minutes,’” Khadka recalls.

“It wasn’t just about writing. I had to read it, send it and record it as well.”

There were people who doubted him. Some dismissed him as an English-speaking journalist who could only read what somebody else had written. He kept going.

“I give all the credit to the late Sushil Sharma,” he says. “He believed I could do it more than I believed in myself.”

In 2005, Khadka travelled to London to work on a BBC special programme. It was the first glimpse of the world that would eventually become his professional home. But something else was happening at the same time.

Khadka was becoming increasingly convinced that environmental journalism mattered. Not as a specialist niche. As one of the defining stories of the future.

The story he could not leave alone

His interest in the environment had started years earlier.

When the 1992 Rio Earth Summit was taking place, the internet was barely accessible in Nepal. There were no social media feeds delivering the latest developments to a phone.

So Khadka went to the British and American libraries in Kathmandu. He read newspapers. He followed the international debate. And he began to understand that environmental issues were becoming inseparable from global politics.

“I realised even then that this issue would not only matter to our generation,” he says. “It would be even bigger for the generations that followed us.”

He began looking at environmental stories wherever he went. Eventually, he told the BBC that he did not want to remain only a producer in the Nepali Service. He wanted to report.

There was a larger argument behind that decision.

Climate change was increasingly being discussed on the world’s biggest stages, but much of the conversation was still being shaped by people in powerful countries and institutions.

What happened when the story was told from the Himalayas? What did climate change look like to people living at altitude? What happened when a farmer, rather than a government minister or scientist, became the starting point of the story?

Khadka thought those questions mattered.

The BBC agreed to give him a one-year pilot opportunity to develop environmental reporting from the Himalayan perspective. Then came two stories that changed the course of his career.

The plants that travelled illegally from the Himalayas

One began with flowers.

Rare Himalayan plants growing above 4,000 metres were being targeted for their seeds. The seeds were being collected and sold in Europe. Khadka began investigating.

The trade was not as straightforward as it appeared. He found allegations that plants were being taken without proper permission, while local people were being misled about how those permissions had been obtained.

He followed the trail. The story eventually reached major public gardens and attracted the attention of authorities.

In India’s Sikkim state, arrest warrants were issued against people allegedly connected to the case. For Khadka, the significance went beyond the headlines.

“I investigated the story properly and when I saw the impact it had, I felt that our work could actually bring about change,” he says.

It was proof of something he had believed since his days chasing stories in Kathmandu. A journalist did not have to be powerful to make a story powerful. Then came the glacier story. And this time, the mistake was much bigger.

The number that was wrong

In 2009, a scientist told Khadka that if the existing trend continued, glaciers could disappear by 2300. But somewhere in the process of publication, the date became 2030.

A mistake of almost three centuries.

The incorrect figure later appeared in an IPCC report and became ammunition for people challenging climate science. The claim travelled rapidly through the international media. But Khadka was not convinced.

He began looking at the evidence. There was a problem with treating the Himalayas as one uniform system. Glaciers in parts of the eastern Himalayas were retreating. But in the Karakoram region to the west, some glaciers were behaving differently.

The story was more complicated than a single dramatic number. Khadka reported the contrasting trends, using scientific evidence and images to show what was actually happening. The reporting impressed the BBC.

His pilot period ended with the organisation creating a new position for him. He had found his place.

Not simply as a Nepali journalist working for an international broadcaster, but as an environmental journalist bringing stories from a part of the world that was often talked about without being heard directly.

What does “normal” mean to a farmer?

Today, climate change remains at the centre of Khadka’s work. But he is sceptical of stories that stop at statistics. Take the monsoon. A meteorological department might describe a season as “normal”. A farmer might tell a completely different story.

“If you ask the meteorological department, they might say the monsoon was normal this year,” Khadka says.

“But if you ask a farmer, they might say, ‘Drought damaged my crops when I needed rain, and then three months’ worth of rain fell in a week and washed everything away.’ “Why don’t the department’s understanding and the farmer’s experience match? That’s where journalists need to go.”

For Khadka, that gap is where climate journalism becomes human.

In Nepal’s hills, he says, springs are drying. Snow is becoming less predictable. Farmers can be left without water when they need it and overwhelmed by it when they don’t. And the consequences are spreading beyond farms.

Roads, bridges, hydropower projects and settlements are increasingly exposed to unstable slopes, landslides and floods. Khadka worries particularly about what happens when melting ice and changing rainfall destabilise mountain slopes. Snow and ice, he says, once helped bind the mountains together.

“It was almost like cement holding a house together,” he says.

When that ice disappears, the landscape changes. Heavy rainfall can then bring down soil, rocks and debris. The danger is not limited to visible glacial lakes.

“The more dangerous ones can be the hidden lakes,” he says. “If lakes form inside mountains or beneath rock and then suddenly break through, there may be no way of predicting it.”

A journalist caught between two worlds

Khadka now works across four languages — English, Nepali, Hindi and Urdu.

He appears on BBC television, radio and online platforms and contributes analysis to the BBC’s Pashto and Persian services, where his comments are translated for audiences in those languages.

He has travelled to almost every continent. He has reported from some 50 countries. Yet his journalism keeps bringing him back to Nepal.

Perhaps because the country’s environmental story contains the contradiction that has defined so much of his career.

Nepal is one of the countries most exposed to the consequences of a changing climate, while also being a country racing to build roads, hydropower projects and other infrastructure.

Development is urgently needed. So is caution.

“Where we should be more careful, we are becoming even more careless,” Khadka says. “That is a path towards destruction.”

It is a strikingly blunt conclusion from a journalist whose career has otherwise been built around asking questions rather than delivering answers. But perhaps that is the point. Khadka’s job is not to tell the world what to think about the Himalayas.

It is to make sure the Himalayas are part of the conversation. The teenager who once filled a school magazine with children’s stories eventually found himself reporting to a global audience. The teacher became a journalist. The journalist became a broadcaster.

And the broadcaster became, almost by accident, one of the international media’s recurring voices on a region undergoing profound environmental change.

His career has taken him a long way from that school magazine in Kathmandu. But the instinct remains the same.

Find the story. Follow it. And, if it matters, make sure people hear it.

title.rendered: High-level efforts underway to lift ANFA suspension, says Minister Pokharel

content.rendered:
Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel has said high-level efforts are underway to lift the suspension that FIFA, the world football governing body, imposed on the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA).

Minister Pokharel gave the information while speaking at Monday’s meeting of the House of Representatives.

He said the National Sports Council had directed ANFA to amend its statute and hold tiered elections in line with the National Sports Development Act, 2077 and the National Sports Development Regulations, 2079.

According to Pokharel, ANFA went ahead with its general assembly and election process without following the Council’s directive. After repeated warnings, it was suspended under the executive committee’s decision on March 26.

“FIFA sent a notice of suspension, treating the Council’s directive to ANFA as third-party interference. The period of suspension has not been specified, and the Government of Nepal is making high-level efforts to lift it, so the suspension may be lifted soon. I would also like to inform the House that no international competition has been held since the suspension,” he said.

He also said the government is working to improve the country’s community education, and expressed a commitment to issue an Education Act incorporating stakeholders’ suggestions to resolve problems in school education.

title.rendered: House of Representatives passes National Service Corps Bill

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

The House of Representatives has passed the National Service Corps Bill, 2083, paving the way for changes to the structure and operation of the National Service Corps currently run under the Nepal Army.

Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam presented the proposal seeking passage of the bill at Monday’s House meeting.

The bill aims to instil patriotism, public service and a sense of national unity among school students while promoting discipline. It also allows individuals and institutions beyond students to receive training based on national needs.

A key change in the bill is the removal of a provision requiring serving military officers to provide training. The State Affairs and Good Governance Committee removed the mandatory arrangement, although the Nepal Army will retain a role in selecting trainers.

Under the revised provision, the Director General of the National Service Corps will be a retired lieutenant general of the Nepal Army. The Chief of Army Staff will recommend three names, from which the government will appoint one.

The bill also allows the government to mobilise trained individuals as volunteers for national service based on national needs. The Cabinet will determine what constitutes a national need, while the government must inform both houses of Parliament after mobilising such volunteers.

The bill will now be sent to the National Assembly for consideration.

title.rendered: 100 billion needed for post-disaster reconstruction, says Minister Lamsal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal has said that around Rs 100 billion is needed for post-disaster reconstruction and infrastructure management following the Bhotekoshi disaster.

Speaking at a meeting of the Infrastructure Development Committee held at Singha Durbar on Monday, Minister Lamsal said this amount would be required for a plan covering the current disaster damage and future preparedness.

According to Lamsal, the government has already moved ahead through an “emergency tender” process to quickly repair damaged structures and restore connectivity after the disaster. He said work has gathered pace in places with complex geography, including Krishnabhir, with the support of geotechnical experts and the swift action of the Department of Roads.

The Disaster Authority recently submitted an initial demand of Rs 90 billion. This includes reconstruction of damaged roads and bridges, construction of two alternative routes, and work to reduce future risks.

“The Disaster Authority has presented a requirement of about Rs 90 billion for reconstruction. Including additional damage such as buildings and drinking water, the total requirement is estimated to reach about Rs 100 billion. The government has adopted a policy of managing the necessary resources so that work does not stop,” he said. “Where detailed project reports have been prepared, structures such as bridges will be tendered immediately under the design-and-build model and rebuilt quickly. Drinking water has also been prioritised as an essential service.”

Lamsal said that with the costs of drinking water and other infrastructure added, the total requirement is estimated to reach Rs 100 billion. On managing financial resources, he said coordination with the Ministry of Finance is under way and made clear that work will not stop for lack of budget.

“Reconstruction work is being advanced in phases. In the first phase, priority was given to clearing damage and restoring connectivity, and emergency tenders were opened in phases on the 12th, 16th and 17th,” Lamsal said. “The emergency provision in the Public Procurement Act has helped move this along faster. In areas of complex geography, including Krishnabhir, designs were prepared immediately on the advice of geotechnical experts and work has advanced. The Department of Roads is carrying out blasting and other work in parallel at many places.”

On drinking water, he said a temporary arrangement has been made for now, but there are plans to purify river water and distribute it, keeping in view the dry season that will begin in two months.

title.rendered: Indian envoy Srivastava pays farewell call on Speaker Aryal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava has paid a farewell call on Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal.

During the meeting, Speaker Aryal congratulated and wished Ambassador Srivastava well on completing his tenure as India’s ambassador to Nepal. He said Srivastava had made an important contribution to strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation between Nepal and India during his tenure.

Speaker Aryal expressed special gratitude for the support the Indian government extended, as a first responder and trusted neighbour, during the devastating disaster Nepal has faced recently.

Noting that relief and rescue materials were brought to Nepal on Indian Air Force aircraft and that technical support was provided, including a team of experts for tunnel rescue and forensic specialists, he said the assistance received in a difficult time of disaster further reflected the deep ties of friendship, goodwill, solidarity and cooperation between Nepal and India.

The meeting also discussed the Nepal-India Parliamentary Friendship Group, formed after the constitution of the new House of Representatives, and the inter-parliamentary cooperation that could be advanced through it.

Speaker Aryal said parliamentary diplomacy plays an important role in strengthening relations between the two countries, and that it would help expand mutual understanding, exchange of experience and cooperation among lawmakers of both countries.

Noting that Nepal holds the Indian Parliament in high regard as a strong institution of democracy, he stressed the need to continue exchanging democratic practices, parliamentary experience and best practices.

At the meeting, Ambassador Srivastava said the damage in Rasuwa was unimaginable and that India was continuing to support the relief and rescue work. He expressed India’s commitment to always stand with Nepal in times of crisis.

Speaker Aryal thanked Srivastava for his tenure in Nepal and wished him happiness, peace and good health in his personal life and success in his next responsibilities.

Srivastava took charge as India’s ambassador to Nepal on June 25, 2022.

He joined the Indian Foreign Service in 1993. He previously served at Indian missions in Hong Kong, Beijing and Washington DC, and held the posts of Consul General of India in Shanghai, Indian Ambassador to Cambodia, and a position at the New Development Bank in Shanghai.

title.rendered: Questions raised over lack of Dalit representation in parliamentary special committee

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Questions have been raised in Parliament after no Dalit member was included in a special parliamentary committee formed to work on post-disaster issues.

Member of Parliament Ganesh Bahadur Bishwakarma raised the issue while speaking in the House of Representatives.

“We have just formed a special parliamentary committee. Perhaps it was difficult to ensure inclusiveness when a party sending only one representative sent one. But when eight members are being sent, we should at least keep in mind that there should be at least one Dalit member in the committee. Or let us make it mandatory,” he said.

He urged that the inclusive clusters represented through the proportional electoral system be taken into consideration.

The House of Representatives meeting held on Monday formed the 15-member special parliamentary committee to work on post-disaster issues. Its members are Achyutam Lamichhane, Anushka Shrestha, Gangadevi Shrestha, Ganesh Parajuli, Dhananjaya Regmi, Dhruv Raj Rai, Nisha Dangi, Pushparaj Kandel, Mohan Acharya, Mingma Gyabu Sherpa, Ramesh Kumar Malla, Rabindra Patel, Saraswati Lama, Sujata Tamang and Sita Thapaliya.

The committee will select its coordinator at its first meeting.

The committee has been given a three-month term, with a provision allowing its tenure to be extended later.

The committee was formed against the backdrop of the devastating floods in Rasuwa. While Parliament has formed the committee to carry out post-disaster work, MP Bishwakarma questioned the lack of consideration for inclusiveness in its composition.
