title.rendered: Oli rejects calls for leadership change, says UML reorganisation is not about replacing leaders

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

CPN-UML Chair KP Sharma Oli has made clear that he has no intention of stepping down as party chairman, arguing that replacing the leadership cannot by itself be described as party reorganisation.

Presenting his political report at the UML Central Committee meeting on Monday, Oli argued that the debate over party reorganisation should be understood in its proper historical and organisational context and should not be treated as a matter of impulse.

Oli said leadership cannot be displaced without considering the condition of the party and the broader circumstances surrounding it.

His report covers national politics, problems within the party and the tasks ahead, while also citing three major instances of reorganisation in the history of Nepal’s communist movement.

He referred to the period following Keshar Jung Rayamajhi’s move towards the palace, the Jhapa movement and the party’s reorganisation in 1960, and the reorganisation carried out after the split of the Nepal Communist Party in 1962.

Oli argued that each of those reorganisations took place under circumstances in which the party and movement faced serious organisational or political crises.

“What is reorganisation? Under what circumstances does it take place? Is replacing the leadership what we call reorganisation? We need to properly understand how many times and when reorganisation took place in our political movement. Party reorganisation is not a matter of desire or impulse,” Oli said in the report.

Three examples of reorganisation

According to Oli, the first major reorganisation took place after Keshar Jung Rayamajhi, then the party’s general secretary, openly moved towards the monarchy following King Mahendra’s 1960 coup.

Oli said Rayamajhi welcomed the royal takeover and moved towards supporting the Panchayat system while holding a majority in the party’s Central Committee.

He argued that the party had to be reorganised because the leadership and majority had moved towards the right and there was no other way to protect the movement.

Oli said the party’s minority subsequently organised zonal committees and held the Third General Convention, leading to the first reorganisation.

He described the second reorganisation as having taken place in 1970, when the party had become organisationally weak and fragmented under Panchayat repression.

According to Oli, the Jhapa movement and subsequent formation and expansion of new communist organisations were part of an effort to rebuild the movement with a clear objective of establishing a people’s democratic republic.

He said the process eventually developed through the Jhapa movement, Appeal, the Coordination Committee, CPN (Marxist-Leninist) and eventually the CPN-UML.

Oli said the third reorganisation took place after the communist movement had reached a strong position through organisational expansion, party unification and electoral success, but internal conflict later led to the split of the Nepal Communist Party.

He said his leadership was again involved in reorganising the UML after the split.

“These and similar major organisational steps taken under compelling circumstances and which had a positive impact on the life of the movement were reorganisation,” Oli said.

He argued that the current calls for reorganisation do not fit that historical definition.

“The talk of reorganisation being carried out at this time carries neither the literal nor the substantive meaning of the term and does not match its justification, necessity or context,” he said.

‘Transformation does not mean erasing history’

Oli also sought to distinguish between transformation, handover of responsibility and generational transition.

He said transformation should not mean erasing the party’s history or rejecting its political struggle, ideology, sacrifices and organisational traditions.

“Transformation means changing the working style; changing the language used to speak with the people; making the decision-making process more efficient; turning committees from formal meeting structures into centres for solving people’s problems; and changing leadership from a level that gives orders to one that listens, understands and delivers results,” Oli said.

He used the metaphor of a tree to argue that organisational renewal does not require cutting off its roots.

“New shoots do not grow on an old tree by cutting its roots. The roots must be nourished so that new shoots can grow. UML’s history is the root and the new generation is the shoot,” he said.

Oli also argued that leadership handover should not be treated as a sudden or arbitrary decision.

He said responsibility, knowledge, experience, institutions, political culture and decision-making capacity should be transferred in a planned manner, warning that a handover without preparation could create a vacuum.

He further said generational transition should not be reduced to age.

“Generational transition is not merely the arithmetic of age. It is a process of giving the new generation responsibility, training, experience, opportunities and a place in decision-making. Being young is not qualification in itself, and being older is not disqualification in itself. A combination of energy and experience is necessary,” Oli said.

Oli’s position comes amid an ongoing dispute within the UML over party reorganisation and leadership.

title.rendered: Ransomware attack shuts stock market as investors raise security concerns

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Nepal’s stock market was abruptly shut down on Monday after a ransomware attack targeted the infrastructure of Data Hub Pvt. Ltd., which hosts the Trading Management System (TMS) servers of 72 brokerage companies.

According to Data Hub, the attack on its TMS hosting infrastructure was detected at around 5:30 am on Bhadra 4. Data Hub hosts the servers used by 72 trading member, or brokerage, companies.

The company has explicitly described the incident as a ransomware attack in a letter sent to YCO Pvt. Ltd.

A ransomware attack can restrict access to data and systems, potentially leaving them unusable. Data Hub said the attack may have spread to other connected networks and systems, prompting it not to bring the affected systems back online immediately.

The company said it was conducting an investigation and forensic analysis to assess the full impact of the incident while taking necessary security and recovery measures.

“We isolated the affected infrastructure to prevent the ransomware attack from reaching NEPSE’s system after the problem occurred within Data Hub’s infrastructure,” NEPSE spokesperson Murahari Parajuli said.

NEPSE said trading would resume only after Data Hub fully resolves the problem.

Data Hub said the latest backup of its entire infrastructure before the incident had been taken at around 4 am on Bhadra 4 and was stored securely in an isolated location.

The company said the affected systems had not yet been brought back online because of the possibility that the ransomware could have affected or spread to other connected networks and systems.

Since the TMS is connected to other related systems, Data Hub had requested additional time to conduct forensic analysis and implement necessary corrective measures before restoring the system, leading NEPSE to suspend all trading on Monday.

Data Hub said it was working to restore the system as quickly as possible.

NEPSE said it suspended trading because operating under the circumstances could potentially expose its own trading system to damage.

In a notice, NEPSE said the decision was taken under Rule 21(1) of the Securities Listing and Trading Regulations, 2018. The rule allows NEPSE to suspend or close regular share trading in the event of special circumstances, technical problems or systemic risks.

NEPSE spokesperson Parajuli said measures had been put in place to protect the NEPSE Online Trading System (NOTS), which is under NEPSE’s control.

“Cyberattacks cannot be reduced to zero anywhere in the world. However, adequate arrangements have been made to minimise the potential damage from such risks,” Parajuli said.

Investors raise concerns

Investors, meanwhile, have expressed concern over repeated disruptions to share trading and accused the regulatory authorities and government of failing to take the issue seriously.

“Sometimes it is a server outage, sometimes an attack on the server. When such problems shut down trading, our assets effectively remain locked,” said Tulsiram Dhakal, president of the Nepal Investors’ Forum.

He said it was unfortunate that NEPSE, the Securities Board of Nepal and the Ministry of Finance had not taken the recurring problems seriously.

“This is also an attack on our assets. Some investors may have to sell shares and arrange money on the same day, but when trading is halted, we are the ones who suffer,” Dhakal said.

He said around eight million investors are involved in Nepal’s capital market and argued that the Ministry of Finance should take the lead in adopting secure technologies used by major stock markets around the world.

“One of the reasons we have repeatedly called for a new stock exchange is the expectation that new technology would be introduced and problems like these could be avoided,” he said.

Nepal’s capital market is currently worth around Rs 4.553 trillion. Dhakal said investors are repeatedly worried that an incident involving the market’s infrastructure could put such a large pool of assets at risk.

“We investors have put our entire earnings into the capital market. Incidents like these keep frightening us from time to time,” he said.

Securities Board of Nepal spokesperson Niranjay Ghimire said the board was currently seeking information from the concerned parties about the incident.

title.rendered: 39 dead, 439 missing at Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Thirty-nine people working at the 216 MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa have been found dead, while 439 others remain missing following the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

According to Nepal Water and Energy Development Company, the project promoter, around 1,433 Nepali and foreign workers were at the project site when the flood occurred. Of them, 877 people have been safely rescued, while 78 others have since made contact. The company confirmed the deaths of 39 people and said 439 remain missing.

The company said the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police, Korean experts and project teams have been conducting search and rescue operations since the flood. The search is being carried out inside underground structures as well as on the surface around the project site, cliffs, villages and other possible locations.

Teams with trained search dogs, mountain rescue personnel and other skilled workers have also been mobilised. As roads leading to the project site were damaged by the flood, helicopters are being used to transport necessary equipment for search and rescue operations.

The main tunnel area has suffered extensive damage from the flood. The company said excavators are being used to remove mud and debris accumulated in the upper section of the project’s access tunnel. Excavators and other equipment required for rescue operations have also been transported to the site by helicopter.

Bodies recovered from the project site are being transported by Nepal Army helicopters to the Nepal Army camp in Bidur, Nuwakot. The company said it is coordinating with the families and relatives of the deceased to facilitate identification and final rites.

The company said potential search areas are identified based on information received from families, details provided by rescued employees and other reliable sources, and the information is then provided to rescue teams.

The company is also coordinating regularly with the government-formed war room, the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and electricity development-related agencies.

The company said it is making maximum use of all available resources, equipment, technology and human resources for the search and rescue of those still missing.

title.rendered: Typhoon disrupts flights, transport and Asian Games in Japan

content.rendered:
Tokyo, September 21

A powerful typhoon named Dujuan has intensified its impact across eastern Japan, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to Tokyo and surrounding areas and disrupting air and rail services, public events and the Asian Games.

Japanese authorities have raised alerts in several areas as the typhoon moves towards Japan’s eastern coast. Although the centre of the storm is expected to remain offshore, winds of more than 90 kilometres per hour are forecast along the eastern coast of Honshu and up to 75 kilometres per hour in Tokyo. Winds around the typhoon’s centre are estimated at 130 kilometres per hour, with gusts reaching 194 kilometres per hour.

Nearly 500 flights from Tokyo’s Haneda and Narita airports have been cancelled, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24. Some bullet train services have also been suspended.

The typhoon has also affected events, with Monday’s programme of the Rock in Japan music festival in Chiba and Monday’s programme of the Tokyo Game Show cancelled.

The Asian Games, being held in Nagoya and Aichi Prefecture, have also been affected. An equestrian event scheduled for Monday has been postponed to Tuesday. Around 4,000 Asian Games participants are staying aboard the cruise ship Costa Serena, which may have to be moved to a safer location if the typhoon affects the area.

Japan’s Meteorological Agency has warned of heavy and continuous rain in the Kanto region, with rainfall of up to 250 millimetres possible in some areas. Authorities have warned of rising river levels, flooding and landslides.

A Level-4 warning has been issued in Tokyo’s Meguro area for flooding and landslides, while a Level-3 warning is in effect in central Tokyo. The Izu island chain and Oshima have been placed under the highest Level-5 warning.

In Chiba, a woman in her 40s was slightly injured in a landslide, while several roads have been flooded. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has urged residents to follow government instructions on evacuation and safety.

title.rendered: Nine agenda items set for UML Central Committee meeting

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Nine agenda items have been set for the CPN-UML Central Committee meeting. The meeting, which begins today, will include the presentation of Chairman KP Sharma Oli’s report, among other items.

The other agenda items are nominating members to the Central Committee, forming departments, forming the Politburo, forming the Standing Committee, and forming the Advisory Council and the Senior Communist Forum. The Central Committee will also discuss forming a Disciplinary Commission and other contemporary issues.

Vice-Chairman Bishnu Paudel, Gokarna Bista and General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel have been given the responsibility of writing the minutes of the meeting. Deputy General Secretary Yogesh Bhattarai, Secretary Padma Aryal, Surya Thapa, Niraj Acharya and Khimlal Bhattarai have been assigned to the committee to take notes on the discussion.

title.rendered: Ishwar Pokhrel asks KP Oli to make way for new UML leadership

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

CPN-UML leader Ishwar Pokhrel has urged party Chairman KP Sharma Oli to make way for new leadership, calling for a “respectful departure” in response to the sentiments of party cadres.

In a letter addressed to Oli on the occasion of the UML Central Committee meeting that began on Monday, Pokhrel argued that the party needs institutional reform, collective leadership and a change in leadership to regain momentum.

Pokhrel, who is currently in New Delhi for the medical treatment of his wife Mira Pokhrel, said he was unable to attend the Central Committee meeting. He sent the letter outlining his views on the party’s current situation and its reorganisation.

He said the UML needed to strengthen collective leadership and restore institutional decision-making processes.

According to Pokhrel, party cadres have increasingly raised concerns over the weakening of established procedures and methods within the party.

He argued that the principles of checks and balances, institutional decision-making and internal democracy should be strengthened rather than weakened.

Pokhrel also criticised what he described as a decline in collective ownership of party decisions and said the party’s relationship with working people had weakened as a result.

He said the ongoing debate over “reorganisation, transition and transformation” should be carried out strictly according to party procedures.

“Whatever needs to be done, let us do it only according to the established method and process,” he wrote.

He also called on party leaders and cadres to accept decisions reached through institutional processes, regardless of whether those decisions matched individual preferences.

“Let us all abandon the feeling that ‘the party cannot function without me’ or that ‘I alone am everything’,” he wrote.

‘Respectfully make way for new leadership’

Pokhrel made his strongest appeal to Oli towards the end of the letter, referring to remarks he had made at the closed session of the UML’s 11th General Convention.

He recalled telling Oli at the time that he had already served as party chairman for 11 years and had been prime minister for six years during the decade since the Constitution was promulgated.

Pokhrel said Oli’s tenure had produced both achievements and shortcomings, but argued that the shortcomings had been increasing.

He warned that failing to address them could cause damage to Oli personally, to the UML, to Nepal’s communist movement and to the country.

“The cycle of damage must now be stopped,” Pokhrel wrote, adding that a “respectful departure” for Oli and an institutional transition to new leadership based on Oli’s own plan and proposal was necessary.

Pokhrel said the situation had become increasingly difficult despite several opportunities for the party to make a fresh start.

He referred to the developments following Bhadra 23–24, the UML’s 11th General Convention and the results of the Falgun 21 general election as opportunities that the party had failed to use.

“These were not only setbacks for us, but also challenging opportunities to make a new beginning. Unfortunately, we could not accept them,” he wrote.

He then directly urged Oli to step aside.

“Whatever happened in the past, happened. At this point, there is no other option that can inspire hope than your respectful departure and moving towards new leadership through the established process,” Pokhrel wrote.

He added that Oli’s own positive role in facilitating the transition was necessary.

Criticism and internal democracy

Pokhrel also called for greater space for criticism and self-criticism within the party.

He said rejecting criticism outright was wrong and argued that a party committed to a particular political ideology needed an active culture of critical debate.

Pokhrel said the absence of such debate could lead to an “intellectual drought” within the party.

He also questioned why many leaders who had played important roles in the party’s history and development had become increasingly inactive.

“Either one had to speak in support, or one had to come under a hostile gaze or face punishment,” he wrote, asking Oli to reflect on whether this had happened within the party.

Pokhrel said the reorganisation process should not be reduced to a question of whether individuals wanted or did not want a particular change.

He argued that reorganisation should encompass the party’s ideology, procedures, organisational structure, leadership, working style and decision-making process.

He described the process as an opportunity to move the party forward.

The UML has been engaged in an intense internal debate over reorganisation following the party’s poor performance in the March 5 election. A task force formed to review the election and recommend party reorganisation collected views from leaders and cadres across the country.

The task force subsequently produced differing views on Oli’s leadership. General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel’s report called for leadership change, while Vice Chairman Ram Bahadur Thapa prepared a separate report arguing that Oli should remain chairman.

The dispute has now reached the Central Committee, which began its meeting in Lalitpur on Monday.

title.rendered: Woman rescued 11 days after Rasuwa flood to undergo skin grafting

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

A 63-year-old woman who was rescued 11 days after being swept away by the Rasuwa flood is undergoing treatment at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu.

Chandika Shrestha is receiving treatment in the hospital’s Plastic Surgery Department after she was rescued from her own house, which had been swept away by the flood.

Doctors involved in her treatment said Shrestha sustained injuries to her right knee and thigh. She is scheduled to undergo skin grafting on Monday to cover the wounds on her body.

“Her health condition is currently normal. Since the injured areas need to be covered with skin, we are planning to perform skin grafting on Monday,” a doctor involved in her treatment told Onlinekhabar.

The doctor said Shrestha may need to remain in the hospital for another one to two weeks even after the grafting procedure.

According to the doctor, the transplanted skin may take around seven to 10 days to properly attach to the wound.

“After the operation, the grafted skin needs time to settle. It can take at least seven to 10 days for it to properly take. So she may have to stay in the hospital for another one to two weeks,” the doctor said.

Shrestha was rescued on September 5, 11 days after she was buried inside the house that had been swept away by the flood.

Her house was originally located around 70 metres behind the location of another house in the area. The flood swept her house away and carried it another 50 metres downstream, where she was eventually rescued from the remains of the house.

title.rendered: 40 injured in monkey attacks in Nepalgunj in 45 days

content.rendered:
Banke, September 21

Forty people have been injured in monkey attacks in Nepalgunj over the past 45 days. Many of them were injured while trying to chase the monkeys away. Dr Badri Chapagain, who is studying cases of snake and animal bites at Bheri Hospital in Nepalgunj, said 40 people injured in monkey attacks had sought treatment at the hospital during the past one and a half months.

He said cases of people arriving at the hospital after being injured by monkey bites were a new phenomenon in Nepalgunj. “People have long been coming to the hospital after being injured by dog, cat and snake bites,” Dr Chapagain said. “But it is surprising that monkeys are now entering homes and biting people.”

He urged people to remain cautious as monkey activity has increased in the city and to seek immediate medical treatment in case of an attack. Bheri Hospital has recently seen an increase in cases involving snake and animal bites. According to data provided by Dr Chapagain, who is studying such cases at the hospital, 1,036 cases of animal bites were recorded at Bheri Hospital over the past 45 days.

The highest number involved dog bites, with 865 cases, followed by cat bites with 110, monkey bites with 40 and rat bites with 21 cases. During the same period, 118 snakebite patients also received treatment at Bheri Hospital. Four people were treated for insect bites, while 19 patients were treated after being bitten by unidentified animals.

Dr Navin Darnal, chief medical superintendent of Bheri Hospital, said monkey bites had previously been reported among farmers in rural areas, but cases in the market area were a new development. He said patients injured by monkey bites were treated as victims of wild-animal attacks and provided anti-rabies vaccines, with necessary arrangements made to ensure they received treatment as required.

title.rendered: Parliamentary Committee directs NARC to focus research on local needs

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

A parliamentary committee has directed the government to make the working approach of bodies under the Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC) more results-oriented and focused on local needs.

Ashok Kumar Chaudhary, chairperson of the Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee, issued the directive during the committee’s meeting held at Singha Durbar on Monday.

He said policy initiatives would be taken to ensure the effective use of research findings and the transfer of technology.

The meeting discussed the priorities of research bodies under NARC, human resource management, infrastructure development and budget utilisation.

Chairperson Chaudhary said the agricultural research system would be restructured based on suggestions received from regional directors and findings from field research.

During the discussion, Chaudhary stressed that research activities should not be limited to paperwork but should be linked to farmers’ needs.

“We need to give high priority to the use of research findings and technology transfer. We are preparing to provide the ministry with necessary policy directives while incorporating the suggestions made at today’s meeting,” he said.

Committee members said the lack of inter-institutional cooperation had prevented research activities from progressing as expected. They called for greater attention to the proper mobilisation of resources and capacity development of human resources.

The committee directed NARC to broaden the scope of its research and focus on addressing agricultural problems at the local level.

title.rendered: We need to rethink what an early warning system is

content.rendered:
When we talk about early warning systems, much of the discussion focuses on the dissemination of warning information: a hazard is detected, a warning is issued, people receive it and they evacuate. This is an important part of early warning, but it is not the whole story.

A warning does not arrive in an empty space. People receive information with previous experiences, expectations and assumptions about what a hazard means. They have to make sense of what they are hearing and decide whether the situation unfolding in front of them is familiar or whether something is different this time. This is particularly important for rare, rapidly evolving or unfamiliar events — what scientists describe as “uncertain events”.

The experience of Rajendra Dawadi during the recent flood in Rasuwa, Nepal, illustrates this human side of warning. Dawadi, the principal of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, managed to evacuate around 1,200 students to higher ground before the school itself was washed away by the flood. His account shows that, during a rare and uncertain event, receiving a warning is only the first step. The life-saving difference comes from how multiple uncertain signals are interpreted, discussed, judged and transformed into action.

It is therefore important to distinguish between two sides of warning: warning dissemination and warning interpretation for action. That distinction matters for how we understand risk communication and how we design future early warning systems.

The warning did not arrive as one warning

Dawadi’s account describes information arriving incrementally. At around 9:25 on Wednesday morning, he was teaching in a classroom. It was a normal morning and there was no rain. Hundreds of students were inside the school, studying in the morning shift, when one of his staff members came running into the school and shouted, “The flood is coming! The flood is coming! Everything has been swept away from upstream! Everything has been swept away!”

Dawadi came down to the ground floor to see what had happened outside. At first, he thought nothing would happen because everything appeared normal. Then another staff member, a social studies teacher, reported that there was flooding.

He came shouting, “Sir, I have left the classroom. There is a huge flood upstream and everything has been swept away.” He also stressed that his elder brother had told him not to stay there: “The Trishuli is not safe.”

The staff member then got on his motorcycle and left. After he had gone, Dawadi began thinking about the hundreds of students still inside the school.

Just as the teacher was leaving, another colleague called and said, “Sir, the flood has come from upstream.”

A colleague standing with Dawadi began asking, “What should we do now?” Then a parent entered through a nearby gate on a scooter. He told Dawadi, “Sir, the flood is very large. I have come to collect my child. I don’t know whether the flood will reach the school or not, but apparently everything upstream has already been swept away.”

By then, Dawadi had heard several different reports. His phone was ringing continuously and he was becoming increasingly worried. The colleague with him also said, “Sir, this might actually be serious.” Dawadi realised that he had to make a decision. As he explained:

“I thought: if someone had exaggerated the situation and the flood was not actually severe, then we would simply lose one day of teaching. But if the flood really had arrived, then we had to act.”

None of these pieces of information, considered individually, necessarily provided a complete picture of what was about to happen. The warning did not arrive as a single, formal message. Instead, information emerged through staff reports, telephone calls, a parent’s account and discussion among colleagues. Each signal was uncertain on its own, but together they changed Dawadi’s understanding of the situation and prompted him to weigh the consequences of acting against those of waiting.

His decision to evacuate was therefore not based on certainty. It was based on interpreting multiple signals and recognising that the potential cost of waiting was far greater than the cost of a false alarm. The warning did not simply turn into action. It emerged through interpretation, judgement and collective sensemaking.

Dawadi and his colleagues therefore did something fundamental to risk communication: they interpreted information in context. They considered whether the information was credible, discussed it with colleagues and weighed the consequences of acting on information that might turn out to be wrong. The challenge was not simply to communicate what was happening. It was to decide what the information meant and what should be done about it.

Risk communication is not information communication

This is where Dawadi’s experience challenges a conventional understanding of risk communication. A warning does not move directly from a scientific or monitoring system into human action. Between information and action sits interpretation.

People ask: What does this information mean? How credible is it? Is it relevant to us? How serious could the consequences be? What happens if we act and the warning is wrong? What happens if we do not act and the warning is right? What should we do now?

These questions become particularly important when hazards are rare, rapidly evolving or difficult to predict. In such situations, waiting for certainty can itself become a dangerous decision. Dawadi did not need certainty that the flood would reach the school. He and his colleagues needed to determine whether the available information was sufficiently credible and consequential to justify action. That is a fundamentally different way of understanding risk communication.

From information to meaning

Dawadi’s account shows that a warning is not simply transmitted from a technical system to a person. It develops through a chain of interpretation and action.

Signal: A signal is an individual piece of information suggesting that something may be happening, but it does not yet provide a complete or certain picture.

In Dawadi’s case, the signals included:

  • the accountant running in and saying, “The flood is coming!”;
  • a teacher reporting a huge flood upstream;
  • the teacher’s brother warning that the Trishuli was not safe;
  • telephone calls from colleagues saying the flood had come from upstream; and
  • a parent arriving on a scooter and reporting that everything upstream had been swept away.

Interpretation: Interpretation is the process of asking: What does this signal mean?

Dawadi initially looked outside and thought nothing would happen because everything appeared normal. This shows that the same signal can be interpreted differently depending on what people can see and what they already expect.

As further information arrived, his interpretation began to change. The question shifted from, “Is there really a flood?” to, “Could this be serious enough to threaten the students?”

Sensemaking: Sensemaking goes beyond interpreting one piece of information. It is the process of putting multiple pieces together to develop an understanding of what is happening.

This is particularly visible in Dawadi’s account. He had heard several reports from different people, his phone was continuously ringing and he was discussing the situation with colleagues. The individual reports gradually formed a larger picture: destruction upstream, a parent’s confirmation and continuing calls pointed to something potentially much more serious than a normal flood. Sensemaking was therefore collective and cumulative rather than simply Dawadi receiving one authoritative message.

Decision on evacuation: Once Dawadi had developed an understanding of the situation, he had to decide what to do despite the remaining uncertainty. This is where his reasoning becomes particularly important.

If the information was wrong, they might lose one day of teaching. If it was right, people could lose their lives. He did not know exactly how high the flood would be or when it would reach the school. But he could compare the consequences of two choices: waiting for greater certainty or acting despite uncertainty. He decided that the potential consequences of waiting were too serious.

Trust is part of the warning system

Dawadi’s story also raises an important question about trust. The information became actionable partly because it was embedded in relationships. Staff members communicated with one another, colleagues consulted each other and a parent arrived with information from outside the school. Telephone calls provided further reports as the situation developed.

Dawadi was therefore not responding to an anonymous message from a distant warning system. He was making sense of information within a network of people he knew, trusted and could consult. Those relationships helped him assess whether different signals were credible and whether, taken together, they pointed to a situation serious enough to require action.

Trust and relationships, then, are not peripheral to risk communication infrastructure. They are part of it. A technically sophisticated warning system may detect a hazard and disseminate information quickly, but detection alone does not guarantee that people will recognise its significance, trust the information or know when to act. In uncertain situations, trust can allow fragmented information to become credible enough to support a decision.

The problem is not uncertainty or rare events

Dawadi’s decision also illustrates something central to my thinking about risk communication: disaster decisions do not necessarily fail because uncertainty exists. They can fail when the meaning of uncertainty for action is poorly communicated.

The information available to Dawadi was incomplete. He did not know precisely what would happen. But uncertainty did not prevent action. Instead, uncertainty became part of the decision. The question was essentially one of consequences:

What is the consequence of acting when the information is wrong, compared with the consequence of not acting when it is right?

This is particularly important for low-frequency and rapidly evolving hazards, where prediction may never provide the level of certainty that decision-makers would ideally like. Risk communication should therefore not be designed around the assumption that uncertainty must first be eliminated. It should help people interpret uncertainty in relation to decisions and consequences.

A warning system is more than sensors and messages

This has implications for how we invest in early warning systems. It is tempting to define an effective warning system through its technical components: sensors, monitoring networks, forecasting models, communication channels and alert technologies. These are essential. But Dawadi’s experience suggests that another form of infrastructure is equally important: the capacity to interpret information and turn it into action.

The lesson from Dawadi’s experience is therefore not simply that warnings need to be faster. It is that we need to think more carefully about what happens between receiving information and taking action. An early warning system should not be judged only by whether it successfully detects a hazard or issues an alert. We should also ask whether it creates the conditions in which uncertain information can be recognised and interpreted for action.

Alongside warning delivery, we need to focus on action capacity. This changes how we understand risk communication.

Risk communication is not simply about getting the right information to the right people at the right time. It is about enabling people and institutions to determine what information means, what it requires them to do and when that judgement needs to change.

Dawadi’s story is powerful precisely because he does not describe himself as a hero. He describes himself and his colleagues as doing their duty. That may be the most important lesson of all.

Effective risk communication does not necessarily depend on extraordinary individuals making extraordinary decisions. It depends on ordinary people having the relationships, information, judgement and institutional capacity to make consequential decisions before certainty arrives.

The warning is not the end of communication. It is the point at which interpretation has to become action.

title.rendered: 1.5 million children in Pakistan at risk of online sexual exploitation

content.rendered:
Islamabad, September 21

About 1.5 million children in Pakistan fall victim to online sexual abuse every year, according to a report by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). Most victims do not tell anyone what they faced, for fear of social stigma, shame, and the reaction of their family and society.

Zara Shah, 17 (name changed for her safety), was also targeted for sexual abuse after coming into contact with a stranger while playing an online game. According to her, the man acted friendly to win her trust, then asked to meet her and demanded nude photographs. She said that when she refused, he threatened to show their conversations to her family.

According to UNICEF, in about 85 percent of cases the perpetrator is someone the victim knows. The report says perpetrators win children’s trust through online games, friendly conversations, gifts, money or promises of love. About 71 percent of victims tell no one, and none of the survey participants had filed a formal complaint through the police, a helpline or a social worker.

According to Mehak Naeem, director of the child rights organisation Pehchaan, about 44 percent of reported cases take place entirely online, with Snapchat and WhatsApp among the most-used platforms. About 74 percent of children aged 12 to 17 in Pakistan use the internet, which makes online safety even more challenging.

Meanwhile, the Punjab government has proposed banning children under 16 from using social media. Digital rights activist Usama Khilji said such a ban would be difficult to enforce and could affect children’s freedom of expression.

Tahira Afrasiab, a spokesperson for Muslim Hands, said Pakistan has legal provisions to prevent the misuse of technology against children, but they have not been implemented effectively. Human rights lawyer Salman Afridi said people are exploiting economic vulnerability to sexually exploit children, using technology to win their trust, lure and threaten them, and even to produce and distribute material.

Shah said her experience, which began with an online game, has left her living in fear. “I was scared, and I am still scared,” she said.

(RSS/AFP)

title.rendered: Petition seeks transfer of Nepali Congress dispute to Constitutional Bench

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

A petition has been filed at the Supreme Court seeking to transfer the case concerning the Nepali Congress’s special general convention from the full bench to the Constitutional Bench.

A member of the Deuba faction has filed the petition, seeking to transfer the dispute currently under consideration by a three-member full bench to a five-member full bench led by the chief justice.

The petitioner has argued that the dispute over the leadership of the Nepali Congress involves a “serious question of constitutional interpretation” and has requested that the case be referred to the Constitutional Bench.

Supreme Court spokesperson Arjun Koirala confirmed that the petition had been filed but said no decision had been made on it. “The petition was filed, but no decision has been made on it yet,” he told Onlinekhabar. According to him, the petitioner later took back the copy of the petition.

However, another senior Supreme Court official said the petition had been attached to the main case file and submitted to the chief justice for an administrative decision.

“The case file was submitted to the chief justice’s chamber after the Deuba faction filed the petition,” a Supreme Court source said. “The file is in the chief justice’s chamber, and no further decision has been made.”

Chief Justice Dr Manoj Sharma is currently in Guangzhou, China, on a four-day visit.

The Supreme Court had previously determined the judges who would hear the case through the lottery system during the review process.

If it is decided that the case should be heard by a full bench, the Constitutional Bench led by the chief justice will hear it. The other four judges on the bench will be selected by the chief justice rather than through the lottery system.

Agaraj Pokharel, senior advocate and coordinator of the election committee formed by the Deuba faction, said no such petition had been officially filed. “If someone filed a petition individually, we are not aware of it,” he said.

Article 137(3) of the Constitution provides that if a case pending before the Supreme Court involves a serious question of constitutional interpretation, the chief justice may refer it to the Constitutional Bench. The petition has sought to use this provision to transfer the Nepali Congress dispute to the Constitutional Bench.

Dispute following special general convention

On January 16, the Election Commission decided to recognise the Nepali Congress special general convention and update its records with the newly elected office-bearers. Following the decision, Sher Bahadur Deuba and his working committee automatically lost recognition.

Deuba, the then party president, and Purna Bahadur Khadka, the acting president, subsequently filed a writ petition at the Supreme Court challenging the Election Commission’s decision. As the election date was approaching, the case reached final hearing without even a discussion on an interim order. On April 17, the Supreme Court rejected the demands of leaders from the Deuba faction and upheld the Election Commission’s decision.

After the full text of the verdict was made public, Deuba and Khadka filed petitions seeking a review of the verdict. They claimed that the decision had been made contrary to judicial principles and precedents.

On August 6, a bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma and Justices Nityananda Pandey and Shrikant Paudel issued an order granting permission for a review of the verdict.

The order stated that the Election Commission’s decision should be subject to judicial review again on the grounds that the Deuba faction had not been given an opportunity for a hearing before the decision on the special general convention was updated.

Following the Nepali Congress special general convention, the Gagan Thapa faction had applied to the Election Commission to update the details of the new leadership.

On February 12, the Election Commission recognised the decision of the special general convention and officially recognised the new working committee led by Gagan Thapa. On April 17, a joint bench of the Supreme Court upheld the Election Commission’s decision.

The three-member bench led by Chief Justice Sharma on Thursday granted permission to review the Supreme Court’s earlier verdict in light of two precedents. Following the order, the revived Nepali Congress dispute is pending before a three-member full bench. A hearing date has not yet been scheduled.

title.rendered: Safe motherhood bill tabled in Parliament, proposes hospitals must serve women who reach them

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

A bill to amend the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2075 BS has been registered in Parliament. Minister for Health and Food Hygiene Nisha Mehta has brought the bill.

According to her, maternity and reproductive health services must be made safe, quality, affordable and accessible to respect, protect and fulfil women’s constitutional right to safe motherhood and reproductive health.

The Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2075 is currently in force to make the necessary provisions in this regard. However, the new bill has been brought because Nepal’s population growth rate has been steadily declining, according to the latest census, and the law needs to be amended to include provisions such as leave incentives to encourage population growth.

According to Mehta, the proposed bill covers matters including delivery services by trained birth attendants, a bar on refusing delivery services, and a ban on violence against women in the postpartum period.

The bill provides six months of paid maternity leave, before and after delivery combined, for women working in government, non-governmental or private bodies. It proposes 42 days of paid maternity care (paternity) leave for male employees when their wife gives birth.

It also revises the rules on abortion in special circumstances and on forced abortion, and makes the new provisions punishable offences.

Under the bill, violence during pregnancy and the postpartum period is prohibited. It adds a provision that no physical, mental or sexual violence may be committed against women from pregnancy through the postpartum period, and that anyone doing so will be liable to punishment.

The bill also bars services from being refused on grounds of money. It proposes that a hospital must provide services to a pregnant woman who reaches it even if she has no money.

Under the bill, no health institution may refuse to provide pregnancy or delivery services for financial or any other reason.

Babita Paswan, 30, of Parsahi in Rajbiraj-14 was forced to give birth on the roadside pavement in front of a hospital because she had no money. She gave birth on the pavement in front of Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Rajbiraj.

The bill comes amid a debate over the Constitution and existing laws, sparked by a woman who gave birth on the street for lack of money.

Article 35 of the Constitution guarantees the right to health. It states: “Every citizen shall have the right to free basic health services from the State, and no one shall be deprived of emergency health services.”

Article 38 guarantees women’s rights. It states: “Every woman shall have the right to safe motherhood and reproductive health.”

The Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2075 was enacted to implement this constitutional right.

Regulations were framed in 2077 to implement the Act, and the Mother and Newborn Safety Programme Guidelines, 2078 were brought in to implement the regulations.

The government allocates more than Rs 3 billion annually for the mother safety programme alone. Under the Constitution, the law, the regulations and the Mother and Newborn Safety Programme, no fees can be charged at government hospitals for delivery or for treatment of the mother and newborn.

In practice, however, women have not been able to exercise their right to safe motherhood and reproductive health because of financial hardship. The Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene said the bill has also been brought to address this.

caption.rendered: A newborn being fed breastmilk within the first hour of delivery. Photo Courtesy: UNICEF

image_meta.caption:
On 9 August 2022, at the Paropakar Maternity and Women's Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, Sunita Rai uses a spoon to feed her newborn son breastmilk. Sunita had come to the hospital to seek treatment after her son was born prematurely. Seeing that Sunita was unable to breastfeed her child, healthworkers quickly referred her to the hospital’s newly-launched 'Amrit Kosh', the first human milk bank to be established in the country, which provided Sunita’s baby with breastmilk donated by other mothers.  

In Nepal, only 42 per cent of children under 2 years of age are breastfed within one hour of birth and 62 per cent of children under six months are exclusively breastfed.

When expressed breast milk is not adequate or available, these newborns are usually given infant formula milk. However, feeding formula milk can often lead to a high risk of developing an infection (sepsis) as well as necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious disease that affects the intestines of premature infants. It typically happens within the first 2 weeks of life in babies who are fed formula instead of breast milk. Donor human milk, if made available to these babies, can save them from the adverse effects of formula milk.

The ‘Amrit Kosh' has the facilities to collect, pasteurize, test and store safe donor human milk from lactating mothers and then provide it to infants in need. The centre has been established in partnership with the European Union and UNICEF.  

Nepal’s Multi-Sector Nutrition Plan (MSNP) seeks to improve maternal, adolescent, and child nutrition throughout Nepal by promoting healthy, nutritious, and diversified diets for adolescents, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, infants, and young children. Since 2013, UNICEF has been supporting the Government of Nepal in implementing MSNP, with funding support from the European Union. Nepal.

title.rendered: Driver himself set bus on fire (photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Police have reached a preliminary finding that the driver himself set fire to the bus in front of the bus stop at Tripureshwor Chowk, Kathmandu.

Police’s preliminary understanding is that the driver was inside the bus when it caught fire and did not flee, so he must have set the fire himself.

SSP Dilip Ghimire of the District Police Range, Kathmandu, also suspected that the driver may have set the fire and said an investigation is under way.

“The exact cause will be known only after a full investigation, but our conclusion from the investigation so far is that the fire was set by the driver,” he said.

The bus Ba 5 Kha 4274 caught fire. Police said the driver is Dawa Lama, 25, of Kavre. He has been sent to Kirtipur Hospital for treatment.

The Armed Police Force has put out the fire with the help of fire engines.

title.rendered: Made in Mind Series III exhibition concludes today

content.rendered:
Photos: MCube Gallery

Kathmandu

Made in Mind Series III: Narratives of the Contemporary, a group exhibition featuring 15 multidisciplinary artists, explores contemporary realities through themes including personal experience, memory, culture, identity, politics, society, ecology and technology.

Curated by artist Manish Lal Shrestha, the exhibition at MCube Gallery, Chakupat brings together works in painting, sculpture, installation, photography, printmaking, textiles, video, sound, performance and mixed media.

The exhibition examines how narratives change through personal memories, history, imagination and everyday experiences. It also focuses on the Nepali context, where traditional cultural practices intersect with technological change, migration, urbanisation, changing lifestyles and global influences.

According to the gallery, the exhibition does not seek to present a single perspective on contemporary life but brings together diverse voices and viewpoints. The artworks are intended to encourage dialogue, reflection and engagement rather than offer fixed answers.

Participating artists include Bidhata KC, Bijay Maharjan, Kailash K. Shrestha, Kapil Mani Dixit, Kaushal Joshi, Manish Lal Shrestha, Nirvita Shakya, Roshan Bhandari, Roshan Mishra, Roshan Pradhan, Samana Rai, Sarita Dangol, Sanjeep Maharjan, Saurganga Darshandhari and Sushma Shakya.

Amid the impact of floods in Nepal, the exhibition also encourages visitors to support affected communities through donations and essential supplies, particularly for children and girls.

The exhibition that began on September 4 concludes on September 21.

title.rendered: Bhatbhateni reopens Tangal store, shoppers say no more running around for basic goods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

The Tangal branch of Bhatbhateni Supermarket, which suffered serious physical damage from arson during last year’s Gen Z movement, reopened today.

With repairs and reconstruction complete, the store formally opened to customers at 10 am on Monday.

Bhatbhateni Chairman and Managing Director Min Bahadur Gurung inaugurated the store himself.

According to Gurung, 12 stores across the country were damaged during the movement. Ten of them, including Tangal, have been repaired and are back in operation. The Damak and Hetauda branches are in the final phase of reconstruction and are preparing to open soon.

‘We rose by risking our lives’

Gurung said he felt deep pain watching assets worth billions burn before his own eyes, but took it as a challenge and moved forward.

Saying it is as hard to build anew as it is easy to destroy, he added that the reconstruction had also seriously affected his health.

“I have tried to rebuild this by putting my life on the line. My haemoglobin had dropped to 4; it has improved now,” Gurung said. “We Nepalis are courageous, and we are Gorkhalis on top of that. The courage of Gorkhalis is different. So we made one resolve: we will rise again from the ashes.”

Gurung said Bhatbhateni is not just his personal property but the “nation’s property”.

“This is not only my property, but it is also Nepal’s property. Thousands of Nepalis are employed here,” he said. “We pay 30 percent of the money from our revenue. Nobody would set fire to their own property!”

Recalling that he started the business 42 years ago from a rented room of 120 square feet, with just Rs 35,000 raised by selling his wife’s jewellery, he said his blood and sweat had gone into it.

‘This is where we work, and where we die’

Gurung said he is very hopeful that Nepal can become a developed country within 15 years if it gets honest leadership. He urged those disheartened by the lack of a business-friendly environment not to panic and to keep at their work.

“Why panic? This is where we work, this is where we die. The private sector plays a big role in the country’s development,” he said. “May such an incident never happen again in my country. The government must protect the private sector and the nation’s property.”

He extended special thanks to the engineers and staff who worked around the clock on the reconstruction, partner organisations, the media, and all well-wishers at home and abroad who offered encouragement.

The company has committed that customers will continue to receive modern and quality service.

Happy customers

A significant crowd of shoppers had gathered since Monday morning. Customers who had been left disappointed by the long closure of their regular shopping destination appeared very excited at the reopening.

Bishnu Bhandari, a regular customer who lives in Mulpani and works in Tangal, said she came to Bhatbhateni as soon as she learnt the store had opened.

She said the arson had left them very sad.

“Without this store, it had become very difficult for us to buy things. We were fed up running to one place for one item and another for the next,” she told Onlinekhabar. “I feel very happy today that it has opened.”

Bhandari, who had not expected the store to reopen so soon, congratulated the operator and all the staff for recovering quickly. She said she expects lower prices than outside, offers, and quality goods that have not passed their expiry date.

Govinda Regmi, another regular customer since Bhatbhateni began, described it as a proud “shopping complex” that has introduced Nepal to the world.

He said that rising from the ashes so quickly and returning in a new form sends the message that anything can be achieved if people have courage.

“Bouncing back in such a short time even in such circumstances is exemplary and a matter of pride,” Regmi said, praising Gurung’s courage. “It is a good example that if people have courage, they can do anything in a short time.”

title.rendered: Rukum East Hospital’s oxygen plant remains nonfunctional 5 years after installation

content.rendered:
Rukum East, September 21

An oxygen plant installed at Rukum East Hospital to address oxygen shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic has failed to operate as expected even five years after its installation.

Although the hospital has an oxygen production plant, it currently has to bring oxygen cylinders from other districts, including Pokhara and Bhairahawa, whenever patients require oxygen. The plant, installed at a cost of millions of rupees, has raised questions over the return on government investment as it has not been operating regularly.

The Ministry of Health and Population allocated Rs 7.5 million in the fiscal year 2021/22 to install the oxygen plant at Rukum East Hospital. According to hospital records, the plant was installed through a tender process at a cost of around Rs 7.2 million.

At the time of installation, the plant was said to have the capacity to fill 30 to 32 cylinders, each with a capacity of 40 litres, per day. However, the hospital now has to bring cylinders from outside whenever patients require oxygen.

Acting Medical Superintendent Dr Krishna Kharal said producing oxygen at the hospital would make it easier to provide treatment services.

“It would be much easier if we could produce oxygen here,” he said. “The number of patients is increasing, and we have to bring cylinders from outside when needed.”

Plant damaged by landslide

The oxygen plant was damaged by a landslide triggered by continuous rainfall on July 5. According to Dr Kharal, stones and soil stockpiled during road construction in Sisne Rural Municipality-5 were washed away by rainwater and damaged the plant.

He said the landslide completely damaged the plant’s booster and partially damaged other components. As the plant was damaged by stones and soil stockpiled during road expansion, the hospital has initiated the necessary process to seek compensation from the agencies and construction company involved in the road project.

He said the hospital had also coordinated with the District Police Office, Rukum East, regarding compensation and that the police had initiated the necessary process.

Dr Kharal said the plant is currently unable to produce oxygen because of the damage caused by the landslide.

“I have been here for around 15 to 16 months. We produced oxygen from the plant for about five to six months, but we could not continue production because the electricity supply was not regular,” he told Onlinekhabar. He said the hospital also lacked a skilled technical team to operate the plant.

“Operating the plant using a generator is expensive. It is cheaper to bring oxygen from outside than to produce it this way,” he added. Local Krishna Khadka said the oxygen production equipment, pipelines and pressure-system structures at the hospital premises were lying unused. “Not being able to regularly operate a plant built by spending such a large amount of money means wasting public property,” he said.

Administration preparing to relocate plant

After the oxygen plant at the hospital was damaged by runoff from the road connecting Sisne Rural Municipality-5 and Rumalbara, the hospital submitted an application to the District Administration Office. Chief District Officer Kopila Rai said the administration subsequently wrote to Sisne Rural Municipality.

According to her, preparations are underway to relocate the oxygen plant from the risky location to a safer site and bring it back into operation. She said coordination was being carried out for the required electricity supply and technical manpower.

“The oxygen plant is located in a risky area, so preparations are underway to relocate it to a safer location and bring it into operation,” Rai told Onlinekhabar. “We are coordinating with the concerned technical team for the required electricity supply.”

Rural municipality pledges support

Sisne Rural Municipality Vice-Chairperson Gopal Reule said the plant had not been completely destroyed by the runoff during the monsoon.

According to him, the plant had not been in regular use for several years. “It is not that the runoff during the rainy season completely destroyed the plant,” Reule told Onlinekhabar. “The plant had not been in use regularly for the past few years. I understand that the police prepared a report regarding the damage caused after runoff came down from the road.”

He said the rural municipality would provide necessary support because the oxygen plant was not only hospital property but also connected to healthcare services throughout the district. “This is not something that the rural municipality alone can build or look after; it is a shared responsibility,” he said. “Therefore, the rural municipality has mobilised workers to remove the soil accumulated around the plant.”

Cleanup underway

According to Dr Kharal, cleanup work at the oxygen plant, which was damaged by the landslide, has been ongoing for the past few days.

He said stones and gravel accumulated around the plant were being removed.

According to him, the concerned parties are removing the soil and debris deposited around the oxygen plant by the landslide, and the cleanup work is expected to be completed within a few days.

title.rendered: VAT on electricity to be scrapped, energy and finance ministers agree in principle

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

The government is preparing to scrap the value-added tax (VAT) it has levied on electricity tariffs since the current fiscal year. The move comes just two months after VAT took effect at 5 percent for household consumers and 13 percent for industrial and other non-household consumers.

Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha and Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle reached an agreement in principle on Sunday evening to remove VAT on electricity, according to a source at the Ministry of Energy.

The source said the two ministries reached the understanding after the prime minister also appeared positive about scrapping the tax. The process will move ahead once the Cabinet makes a decision at the upcoming meeting.

The government introduced VAT on electricity services through the budget for the current fiscal year 2026/27. Under the provision, household consumers using more than 50 units a month pay 5 percent VAT, while all other consumers pay 13 percent.

VAT that was supposed to apply from July was deducted earlier, even in the June bills. The Nepal Electricity Authority then sought clarification from the Inland Revenue Department, which replied that the tax would apply only from July. The authority updated its billing system accordingly.

The levy, however, had faced opposition, with critics saying it would raise costs for industries and businesses as well as household consumers. Industrialists in particular had argued that 13 percent VAT on electricity would increase production costs and push up the prices of goods and services.

According to the Energy Ministry source, once the decision is implemented, the VAT collected on electricity tariffs since July will also be reconciled. The plan is to adjust the amount collected earlier in upcoming electricity bills. After the Cabinet makes a formal decision, the arrangement of no VAT on electricity tariffs will come back into effect.

title.rendered: Gandaki health secretary removed amid bribery allegations against former minister

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 21

The Gandaki provincial government has launched an investigation into allegations that former Health Minister Laxman Bahadur Pandey and Health Secretary Dr Yuva Nidhi Basaula engaged in bargaining over a bribe while granting permission to increase the number of beds at a hospital.

The allegations surfaced in connection with the approval to upgrade Padma Nursing Home in Pokhara from a 50-bed to a 100-bed hospital. It was alleged that then-Minister Pandey, his secretariat and the ministry secretary negotiated a payment in connection with the approval.

Journalist Apil Tripathi claimed in a video published on the ‘Gandaki Chhadke’ YouTube channel on Friday that a Rs 3 million bribe deal had been negotiated in the case. Pandey has denied receiving any bribe. However, it has been claimed that the former minister and his secretariat did not explicitly deny the alleged bribe negotiations.

Meanwhile, the Gandaki provincial government has removed Health Secretary Dr Yuva Nidhi Basaula from his responsibilities. According to government spokesperson and Finance Minister Jit Bahadur Sherchan, the Cabinet decided to relieve Basaula of his duties at the Health Ministry and assign him to the Office of the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers until further arrangements are made.

The government will also investigate the legal provisions and practices concerning hospital approvals and upgrades granted by the Health Ministry over the past two years. A three-member investigation committee has been formed under the coordination of an undersecretary at the Office of the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers. The committee has been given 15 days to submit its report.

The provincial government has also decided to write to the Pokhara office of the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) seeking an investigation into the case.

As an investigation into the alleged bribery case is underway, the Cabinet has decided to suspend implementation of the permission granted to Padma Nursing Home to upgrade its hospital until the allegations of irregularities are clarified.

UML also forms investigation committee

The CPN-UML Gandaki provincial assembly parliamentary party has also expressed concern over the allegations involving former minister Pandey, who is a UML leader. It has formed a separate committee to investigate the facts of the case.

The committee, coordinated by Chief Whip Devka Pahari Tripathi, has been instructed to investigate the case and submit its report within 15 days.

The committee members are Bed Bahadur Gurung, a UML Gandaki provincial assembly member and secretary of the parliamentary board, and Dhananjay Dawadi, secretary of the party’s provincial committee.

Pahari said the committee would investigate the facts of the case and submit its report.

Pandey was appointed health minister on April 15 during Chief Minister Surendraraj Pandey’s Cabinet reshuffle. He, along with three other UML ministers, resigned on September 10. Before Pandey, Krishna Pathak of the UML had served as health minister.

According to him, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority will instead be strengthened. He said the government has no plan to establish a new authority and that a bill to strengthen the existing authority through legal reforms is being drafted.

“We will strengthen the Disaster Authority through legal reforms,” he said. “A bill to that effect will be introduced soon.”

Lamsal said around Rs 100 billion would be required for infrastructure reconstruction alone.

He said the government plans to begin reconstruction by reallocating funds from other projects and later reimburse those projects once the reconstruction budget is secured.

title.rendered: Dengue infection high in Koshi Province, with Jhapa being most at risk

content.rendered:
Jhapa, September 21

The rate of dengue infection is increasing in Koshi Province. Jhapa district appears to be at the highest risk for dengue. According to Smriti Luintel, a public health officer at the Koshi Province Health Directorate, 793 people in the province have been confirmed with dengue as of September 19.

The infection has spread across 13 districts in the province. She said that so far 228 people have tested positive in Jhapa alone. The second most affected district is Sunsari, where 203 people have tested positive. According to the directorate, 122 people in Okhaldhunga and 82 in Khotang have been infected with dengue.

Similarly, 18 people in Sankhuwasabha, 44 in Panchthar, 34 in Udayapur, 31 in Bhojpur, four in Dhankuta, 20 in Morang, three in Solukhumbu, three in Tehrathum, and one in Taplejung have tested positive for dengue.

Luintel informed that 51 potential and two suspected dengue cases were reported in hospitals across different districts during the same period. Considering the increasing risk of infection, she mentioned that it is necessary to run campaigns to search for and destroy mosquito breeding sites.

title.rendered: Government studies tunnel, viaduct options for long-term Krishnabhir solution

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

The government has begun studying a tunnel or viaduct as a long-term solution to landslides and road disruptions at Krishnabhir along the Prithvi Highway.

Speaking at a meeting of the Infrastructure Development Committee on Monday, Department of Roads Director General Dr Bijay Jaishi said technical studies were underway on two options for addressing the recurring problem at Krishnabhir.

According to Jaishi, the options being studied are to construct a tunnel through the Krishnabhir area or build a viaduct further ahead to connect the road. He said the technical study had already begun and a technical report was expected within about two months.

The Department of Roads plans to begin the tendering process for construction after the technical report is prepared.

“Studies have already begun on two long-term options at Krishnabhir—digging a tunnel through the area or connecting the road by constructing a viaduct further ahead,” Jaishi told the committee. “The technical report will come in about two months. After that, we will proceed with the tendering process.”

Traffic along the Prithvi Highway has repeatedly been disrupted by landslides at Krishnabhir. Most recently, the road was damaged by the impact of the Bhotekoshi-Rasuwa flood on Bhadra 10. A section of the road at Krishnabhir was damaged on Bhadra 14.

As an immediate measure, authorities have opened a track above the damaged section to allow vehicles to pass. Jaishi said the department was also working on an alternative road to reduce the risk in the long term while addressing the immediate problem.

He said work had already begun on an alternative route that would take the road across the bridge towards Fishling and Benighat. According to him, work to cut through about 1.5 kilometres of hillside towards Fishling has started.

The department expects the alternative route to allow traffic to operate even when problems occur along the main section of the Prithvi Highway.

“Work to cut through 1.5 kilometres of hillside towards Fishling has already started,” Jaishi said. “Once this section is completed, the route can be brought into operation quickly if the highway continues to cause problems.”

title.rendered: Nepal aim to break Asian Games quarter-final barrier

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

Nepal’s national cricket team has repeatedly found its Asian Games campaign ending at the quarter-final stage. This time, however, the team is heading to the 20th Asian Games in Japan, determined to rewrite that history and open a new chapter.

After failing to progress beyond the quarter-finals in their previous three appearances, Nepal has set a clear target of reaching at least the semi-finals and putting itself in contention for a historic medal.

Nepal secured its place in the Asian Games after winning the Asian Games qualifying tournament in Singapore. The team has been drawn in Group A alongside Afghanistan, one of Asia’s established cricketing sides, and hosts Japan.

Afghanistan will present the biggest challenge in the group. Nepal is set to face Afghanistan at the Asian Games after a gap of exactly 12 years. The two sides previously met in the quarter-finals of the 2014 Asian Games and later that year at the T20 World Cup in Bangladesh.

Japan, meanwhile, is a more familiar opponent than it might initially appear. Nepal recently faced Japan during the global qualification process for the T20 World Cup, giving the Nepali side an opportunity to assess the hosts’ strengths and weaknesses.

While both opponents are familiar to Nepal in terms of recent or past experience, the challenge remains significant. Afghanistan has not sent its full senior side, but its squad remains competitive. Japan, meanwhile, is expected to field its regular team.

With only three teams in the group, one victory could be enough to put Nepal in a strong position to reach the quarter-finals.

Captain Dipendra Singh Airee says the team is travelling to Japan with a medal in mind.

“Everyone is experienced, the team is good and our practice sessions have also gone well. We are going with the target of returning with a medal,” Airee said.

Head coach Stuart Law has also set his sights beyond simply participating.

“We are not going there just to be present. We also want to prove what level we are at. We will have to beat some very good teams, so we will play with high confidence,” Law said.

The team and its preparation

Nepal did not have a separate, specialised preparation programme specifically for the Asian Games. Instead, the team planned to use the various competitions and series played in the lead-up to the Games as part of its preparation.

Nepal participated in the Top End T20 Series in Darwin, Australia, although it was the A team that represented Nepal rather than the senior side. Nepal won two of its six matches in the competition.

Three players who featured in the Top End series are part of Nepal’s Asian Games squad — Kushal Bhurtel, Kushal Malla and Lokesh Bam.

The senior team was busy competing in the ODI-format Premier Cup at the time.

As a result, most members of the Asian Games squad will arrive in Japan having recently played ODI cricket. Bhurtel was the standout performer among the three players who featured in the Top End series, while Malla and Bam were unable to make the same impact.

The fact that most of the squad has been playing ODIs could present a challenge when switching to the T20 format. However, captain Dipendra believes the players are coming into the tournament in good rhythm.

“Kushal [Bhurtel] also played well in the Top End. Aasif scored a century in the Premier Cup. The bowlers have also been doing well. I feel everyone is in good rhythm, so the preparation has been good,” he said.

The experience of playing against strong teams in overseas conditions could also prove useful for Nepal at the Asian Games.

Three Asian Games appearances, three quarter-finals

Nepal first participated in cricket at the Asian Games in 2010. At the Games in China, Nepal lost to Hong Kong in the group stage but defeated the Maldives to reach the quarter-finals. Its campaign ended with a defeat against Sri Lanka in the last eight.

At the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon, South Korea, Nepal defeated Kuwait and the Maldives in the group stage to reach the quarter-finals.

Nepal then lost to Afghanistan by eight runs in the last eight. Chasing Afghanistan’s target of 120, Nepal scored 111 for seven in its 20 overs.

Nepal again reached the quarter-finals at the 2022 Asian Games in China after defeating Mongolia and the Maldives in the group stage. Its campaign ended with a defeat against India in the quarter-finals.

Three appearances, three quarter-final exits.

Breaking that pattern will therefore be Nepal’s first major objective this time.

Captain Dipendra says the team is aiming to return with a medal.

“We have been playing good cricket. If we cannot win gold, our target is to return with some other medal,” he said.

Coach Law acknowledges that progressing beyond the quarter-finals will be difficult, but sees it as an opportunity to test Nepal against the best.

“In T20 cricket, anyone can produce a good result. We have to play our best on the day. To progress, we will have to beat some excellent teams,” Law said.

One win could be enough to reach the quarter-finals

Nepal is in Group A alongside Afghanistan and Japan. With three teams in the group, winning at least one match could put Nepal in a strong position to reach the quarter-finals.

But facing Afghanistan and Japan will not be straightforward. Even with the possibility that one win could be enough to progress, Nepal will need consistent performances throughout the group stage.

The immediate priority will be to secure a place in the quarter-finals. From there, Nepal will look to reach the semi-finals for the first time in its Asian Games history.

If Nepal reaches the quarter-finals, it could face either India or Sri Lanka.

Nepal also faced India in the quarter-finals at the previous Asian Games, where its campaign came to an end.

To win a medal at the Asian Games, Nepal will have to compete against teams of this calibre. Reaching the quarter-finals, therefore, would represent only one stage of the journey.

In recent years, Nepal has increasingly had opportunities to compete against teams such as India, Pakistan and Bangladesh in international cricket.

The experience gained from those encounters could help Nepal compete against stronger opposition in Japan.

A chance to rewrite history

Nepal’s cricket journey at the Asian Games has so far ended at the quarter-final stage on all three occasions. This time, the team has an opportunity to go beyond that barrier.

The challenge will be considerable — from facing strong opposition in the Top End T20 Series to taking on Afghanistan and Japan in the group stage and potentially meeting another major cricketing nation in the quarter-finals.

For Nepal, however, progressing beyond the quarter-finals would mark a new chapter in its Asian Games cricket history.

Nepal squad: Dipendra Singh Airee (captain), Rohit Kumar Paudel, Sompal Kami, Karan KC, Sandeep Lamichhane, Aarif Sheikh, Aasif Sheikh, Kushal Bhurtel, Lalit Rajbanshi, Gulshan Jha, Nandan Yadav, Lokesh Bam, Sandeep Jora, Sher Malla and Kushal Malla.
