title.rendered: Youth suspend hunger strike at Manaslu Base Camp after govt assures action on demands

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 21

A group of youths who had been staging an indefinite hunger strike at the Manaslu Base Camp since Friday has suspended their protest after the Gandaki provincial government and the Manaslu Conservation Area Project (MCAP) pledged to take necessary steps to address their demands.

The youths had launched the hunger strike under the leadership of Dhawa Nurbu Lama of Samagaun in Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1, Gorkha, raising various demands including measures to mitigate the impacts of climate change.

On Sunday, the Office of the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers publicly appealed to the protesters to suspend the hunger strike and come to the negotiating table, saying their demands could be addressed through discussions and dialogue.

The provincial government said it was positive about coordinating with the federal government, local governments and other concerned agencies to ensure appropriate action on the issues raised by the protesters.

MCAP also urged the youths to withdraw their hunger strike and seek solutions through dialogue. It pledged to take the necessary initiative to address their demands.

The protesters had warned that the risks posed by climate change, including the possibility of glacial lakes bursting, were increasing and urged the government to take timely measures to reduce such risks.

A team of 10 youths had been staging the hunger strike at the Manaslu Base Camp since Friday.

title.rendered: A river, a mountain and a boy who wanted to understand them

content.rendered:
At one end of Dingla, Bhojpur, the Arun River once ran noisily past the village. Above it, Mount Makalu glimmered in the distance, while clouds drifted between the river valley and the mountains.

For Dr DB Kattel, those surroundings were more than a childhood landscape. They became the beginning of a lifelong curiosity about how the natural world worked.

“I used to wonder how it was possible,” Kattel recalls. “The river was flowing below, the mountain was above, and clouds were moving between them. Those questions eventually led me to become a scientist.”

Kattel grew up in an environment where education was valued, even if the infrastructure was limited. He passed his School Leaving Certificate from Arun Secondary School in 1990. Getting to school meant walking uphill and downhill for about an hour every day.

Across the river, Khandbari had already begun to glow with electricity. In Dingla, Kattel still remembers studying by the dim light of a traditional oil lamp.

The circumstances were not unusual for students growing up in rural Nepal at the time. But Kattel was drawn to learning from an early age, influenced by educated people around him and by his own curiosity.

That curiosity eventually took him far beyond the Arun Valley.

After completing his SLC, Kattel moved to Kathmandu for higher education. He studied science, completing his ISc at Patan Multiple Campus and his BSc at Tri-Chandra Campus before earning a master’s degree in hydrology and meteorology from Tribhuvan University.

But science was not the only path he explored.

For a period, Kattel worked in journalism, writing about science and technology for newspapers and presenting science programmes on television. He worked for Nepal Television on Environment World and later at Image Metro TV.

It was another way of pursuing the same curiosity.

“My goal since childhood was to become a scientist,” he says. “I changed tracks several times along the way, but academically, I never left the path towards becoming a scientist.”

Like many middle-class students trying to survive in Kathmandu, Kattel found different ways to support himself while studying. But the desire to conduct research remained.

Eventually, he left the media and joined the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology (NAST), where he secured a position as a technical officer.

He stayed for about three years.

The job gave him experience, but not the research environment he had hoped for. Kattel wanted to study, experiment and pursue scientific research. Gradually, he began looking beyond Nepal.

An opportunity came when he travelled to Beijing to participate in a programme at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Then came an offer to pursue a PhD.

For DB Kattel, it felt like the opportunity his childhood dream had been waiting for.

He did not hesitate. He applied for study leave from NAST. But instead of receiving approval, he received a letter at his home address asking why disciplinary action should not be taken against him for being absent from work.

“I had applied for leave, but before the leave was approved, the administration sent a letter to my village asking why I should not be punished,” he says. “I had no choice but to send in my resignation.”

China became the place where his scientific career began to take shape.

The theoretical knowledge he had acquired at Tribhuvan University was complemented by the technical training and research experience he gained there. Before he had even completed his PhD, he received an offer for postdoctoral research in Germany.

He went.

He later spent time in Pakistan, teaching at universities in both Germany and Pakistan before returning to China in 2016.

“We studied at universities in Nepal and our theoretical knowledge is good,” Kattel says. “But I gained the technical knowledge here.”

That experience also shaped his view of what Nepal needs to do differently.

He believes Nepal must invest more heavily in technical and practical education, rather than relying primarily on theoretical learning.

There was one missed opportunity along the way.

Kattel had an opportunity to conduct climate-related research through the academy, but the work required a consent letter from Nepal’s then Ministry of Science and Technology. He applied, but the ministry secretary at the time did not provide the required approval.

The opportunity passed.

When he later received a fellowship, China opened its doors again. In 2016, Kattel returned.

“Initially, because I did not get consent from the science secretary, I could not come,” he recalls. “But after I received the fellowship award, I returned to China in 2016.”

He remembers the episode with some bitterness.

“I was told not to resign, that they would approve two years of leave and even provide a salary for a certain period,” he says. “But because I could not get a simple letter from my own country, I lost the opportunity.”

Since 2019, Kattel has been an associate professor at the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the institution where he had studied.

His work focuses primarily on climate research.

The region he studies is known as the Third Pole, the high-altitude area encompassing the Tibetan Plateau and surrounding Himalayan region. It is considered a major source of water for much of Asia and plays an important role in the continent’s climate system.

His research has examined how climate change is altering the region.

Temperatures are rising. Glaciers are melting faster. The risk of glacial lake outbursts is increasing.

“These areas are experiencing rising temperatures, causing glaciers to melt and increasing the frequency of glacial lake outbursts,” Kattel says. “This has a major impact on environmental balance.”

Nepal, he says, cannot separate itself from these changes.

Heavy rainfall has always been part of the Himalayan environment. Floods and landslides are not new phenomena. Nor is snow melting in the mountains.

What is changing is the speed and scale.

“Snow melting in the mountains is not new,” he says. “But it is melting faster. Night-time temperatures are also increasing in our region. When rainfall becomes heavier, the possibility of glacial lakes bursting also increases.”

But Kattel is wary of attributing every environmental problem in Nepal to global warming.

In Kathmandu, for example, he believes human behaviour and poor urban planning are major contributors to rising heat.

“We say global warming is responsible whenever Kathmandu becomes hot,” he says. “But Kathmandu has no trees, no soil. We have made the impact even worse ourselves. We have to take this seriously.”

Research that could benefit Nepal

Between January 2023 and December 2024, DB Kattel received a research fellowship worth around Rs 13 million to study climate change in the Himalayan region and its consequences.

He won the fellowship after competing against scientists from across the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The research brought together an integrated study of the Himalayan regions of Nepal, Pakistan, Bangladesh, India, Bhutan and Tibet.

One of his areas of focus has been the underlying causes of increasing pollution in the Himalayan region and its effects on the mountains.

His research has also contributed to a growing body of scientific work examining how pollution affects the rate at which Himalayan snow and ice melt.

“There are already high-level studies and research showing how pollution affects the melting of snow in the mountains,” he says. “There are more than 100 studies related specifically to Nepal.”

DB Kattel believes the scientific evidence is increasingly available. What is missing, he argues, is stronger policy action.

“Scientists provide research findings,” he says. “We have provided them.”

He is concerned that Nepal has largely confined its response to climate change to international conferences rather than translating scientific findings into concrete policy.

“Now it is the state’s responsibility to formulate policies and move towards action,” he says. “I do not think we have been serious enough. It is already late.”

For Kattel, the issue is also deeply personal.

He grew up in the Arun Valley, beneath Makalu, in a place whose landscape first made him curious about nature. He still carries a connection to that part of Nepal, even as his career has taken him thousands of kilometres away.

In 2020, he had an opportunity that few Nepali scientists get. He was among 17 scientists from countries including Nepal, India, the United States and Russia who met with then Chinese Premier Li Keqiang at Beijing’s Great Hall of the People.

He says he felt proud to have been there as a Nepali scientist.

But international recognition has not erased his desire to contribute to Nepal.

“No matter how much respect you receive abroad, it does not give you the same satisfaction as working for your own country,” he says.

Sometimes, he thinks about returning.

“I sometimes remember that I am from the Arun Valley, that I grew up in the lap of Makalu,” he says. “Who would not want to go back and work in a place like that?”

Then comes the harder question.

Where would he go?

Kattel wants to bring back the knowledge and research experience he has gained in Beijing. But he worries that Nepal’s academic institutions do not yet offer the environment needed to make that possible.

“I cannot make everything happen simply because I want it,” he says.

For now, he takes some comfort in the belief that his work abroad still carries a connection to home.

“I work here as a Nepali,” he says. “If I do well, it is ultimately for my country.”

His concern extends beyond his own career.

Young Nepalis, he notes, are increasingly leaving the country soon after completing school.

“Now young people do not even stay in Nepal after completing Grades 10 or 12,” he says. “Policies should be designed to help fulfil their dreams and support them in the future. Other countries support their people. We need that kind of environment here too.”

What troubles him most is the role of politics in Nepal’s academic institutions.

“I have not seen politics affecting creative fields in the same way elsewhere in the world,” he says. “In Nepal, when you go somewhere, people ask which political party you belong to.”

He still wants to return.

But after a career built around research, curiosity and scientific opportunity, one question remains unresolved.

“I want to return to Nepal,” he says. “But the question is, where do I go?”

title.rendered: The health governance gaps in Madhesh Province

content.rendered:
Nepal’s 2026 federal election verdict reflects a clear public demand for better public service delivery. While the ballot has changed the face of political representation at the federal level, a more fundamental question remains unanswered: will provincial and local governments finally become capable of delivering the services citizens are entitled to?

Much of Nepal’s dysfunction in public service delivery is rooted in bureaucracy and procedural failures. But nowhere are the consequences more immediate than in basic health care and education—both enshrined as fundamental rights in Nepal’s Constitution. These sectors face persistent challenges in access, quality and implementation, despite being central to human development and among the issues that most directly shape people’s aspirations after an election.

Addressing these inequities should be among the new government’s most immediate priorities.

The recent case of Babita Paswan, who gave birth on the footpath outside a federally managed hospital in Rajbiraj, is a particularly stark illustration of how people-centred development—and basic public health—has been pushed to the margins.

The contradiction is difficult to ignore. Nepal’s federal structure has transferred substantial responsibility for operating, managing and delivering health and education services to provincial and local governments. Yet the institutions entrusted with these responsibilities continue to struggle with some of the most basic functions of governance.

The big leap forward is often made through small but meaningful adjustments. Fixing how health and education services are delivered could be one of them.

Lessons from the work of alternative political movements and governments elsewhere in South Asia, including India and Sri Lanka, could offer useful examples for Nepal’s new government to consider.

Health governance at a crossroads

In the center of Golbazar, just steps away from the municipality’s newly built executive office, stands a modest structure that doubles as a birthing centre.

Every year, more than 300 women—many of them Madhesi Dalits, daily wage earners and among the poorest members of society—come to this dark and poorly maintained building for emergency obstetric care. For many, it is their only lifeline during childbirth.

Yet despite the federal government’s Aama Programme, which provides transportation support and incentives for antenatal care, only about half of these women receive the support they are entitled to by the time they are discharged. The rest leave empty-handed, forced to bear the cost themselves.

The reason is not particularly complicated. It is a failure of governance and bureaucratic accountability.

More troublingly, routine Health Management Information System (HMIS) data does not necessarily reflect this reality. Health workers prepare reports that present performance as satisfactory, while the experience on the ground tells a very different story.

Further investigation suggests that the problem extends beyond a single facility. Similar patterns are found in birthing centres and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (CEONC) sites managed by both local and provincial governments.

This is the uncomfortable gap between what exists in the government system and what exists on the ground. On paper, the system works. In practice, people are left waiting.

Who bears the greatest responsibility for this failure is a legitimate question. But perhaps more striking is the silence surrounding it.

Local and provincial executives, health managers and frontline workers rarely acknowledge the delayed provision of transportation support as a systemic problem. What should be treated as an administrative failure has quietly become routine, with only rare exceptions across Madhesh Province.

For the women who are already among the most underserved and neglected in Madhesh, this is not simply about money. It is about dignity at one of the most vulnerable moments of their lives.

Committees without capacity

Governance is ultimately about who makes decisions, how those decisions are made, who participates in the process and whether citizens actually experience the benefits of those decisions.

When institutions repeatedly fail to meet public expectations, dissatisfaction is inevitable.

The unfinished birthing centre in Bishnupur, Mahuhai, along with 22 other basic health service centres in Siraha district alone, is a stark reminder of the provincial government’s failure to translate plans into functioning services.

Every political leader leaves behind a blueprint. Every government announces plans. But too many of those plans remain trapped on paper.

This is not fundamentally a question of ideology or political identity. Whether a government is left-leaning or right-leaning, national or regional, the real test is execution.

The issues that matter to citizens are far more basic: respectful maternity care, vaccination, protection from the vicious cycle of malnutrition and access to meaningful, skill-based education.

Federalisation was supposed to bring decision-making closer to citizens. Instead, in Madhesh, the transfer of responsibilities has often exposed a different problem: authority has been devolved, but capacity and accountability have not followed.

Provincial and local governments have established—or been required to establish—various committees and governance structures, including Social Development Committees, Immunization Coordination Committees and Health Facility Operation and Management Committees.

These bodies are supposed to strengthen decision-making and improve public health delivery.

But committees alone do not deliver health services.

Without the capacity to make decisions, the resources to implement them and mechanisms to hold decision-makers accountable, decentralisation risks becoming little more than the redistribution of administrative responsibility.

The long-recognised gaps in capacity and accountability within Madhesh’s decentralised health system have not been adequately addressed. The consequences are not abstract. They are reflected in maternal and newborn deaths, recurring vaccine-preventable diseases and repeated outbreaks of diarrhoeal disease.

Federalisation cannot be considered a success simply because responsibilities have been transferred. The real test is whether people receive better services because of it.

Accountability, planning, budgeting and auditing

Nepal’s Auditor General has painted a troubling picture of fiscal accountability among local governments in Madhesh.

Local governments were envisioned as engines of bottom-up planning, accountability and citizen participation. Yet the absence of routine audits has left more than Rs 200 billion in unsettled financial irregularities.

These are not merely numbers in an audit report.

They represent resources that could have funded health insurance premiums, hospitals, schools, medicines and basic services that citizens are still waiting for.

More than 20 local governments in Madhesh have also repeatedly failed to submit budgets for approval by their respective local assemblies.

The failure to approve plans and budgets is not simply an administrative inconvenience. It can directly paralyse basic service delivery.

Shortages of essential medicines and supplies, difficulties in operating health facilities and failures to implement conditional-grant public health programmes have all undermined the ability of local governments to deliver what those programmes were designed to achieve.

The consequences are visible in Madhesh’s persistent maternal mortality, fragile neonatal survival and the continuing cycle of malnutrition.

When planning fails, budgets remain stuck, audits are ignored and no one is held accountable, it is ultimately the citizen—not the bureaucracy—who pays the price.

The way forward

The lived reality of mothers, newborns, adolescents and marginalised communities in Madhesh remains one of unmet promises and institutional neglect, despite the constitutional and policy guarantees designed to protect them.

The problem is not that Nepal chose federalisation.

The problem is that we devolved responsibility without adequately equipping the governments expected to carry it.

There is no solution in turning back the clock. The answer is to make federalisation work.

That means putting all hands on deck to build the capacity of provincial and local governments while embedding real accountability into the system. It means ensuring that technically sophisticated health services are delivered to the people who need them most—not merely recorded as delivered in government reports.

The path forward requires more than another blueprint, another committee or another annual plan.

It requires political commitment, institutional capacity and the skills to implement, monitor and deliver basic health and education services with integrity.

The health sections of local governments need more than experienced personnel. They need professionals who understand not only how the system operates, but also health governance, public policy and the needs of the communities they serve.

Madhesh does not lack plans.

What it lacks is consistent execution, accountability and the political urgency to turn those plans into services.

For the mothers waiting outside health facilities, the newborns who need emergency care and the families who depend on public services, that distinction is not theoretical.

It is the difference between a right guaranteed on paper and a right experienced in real life.

title.rendered: Rainfall likely to intensify as low-pressure system develops, impact remains uncertain

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

A low-pressure system developing over the North Andaman Sea and adjoining areas of the Bay of Bengal is expected to increase rainfall activity in Nepal from September 24 to 28, but its potential impact cannot yet be determined, according to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

The department said it is continuously monitoring the system. While the system is expected to cause rainfall in Nepal, it said it is too early to determine the level of risk and the possible impacts.

According to the Meteorological Forecasting Division, the system is expected to strengthen and move west-northwest. Current projections suggest it could intensify into a depression around September 23 before moving inland near the coastal areas of southern Odisha and northern Andhra Pradesh.

The department said it will continue monitoring the system and issue further updates as necessary.

However, independent meteorologists have urged authorities and the public to remain alert, citing projections from various weather models.

Tribhuvan University hydrologist and meteorologist Dr Binod Pokharel said some models have projected between 400 mm and 741 mm of rainfall in Nepal between September 24 and 28.

He said the rainfall would not necessarily be uniform across the country and could be concentrated in certain areas. He stressed that information was being provided in advance to allow for preparations.

Meteorologist and environmentalist Ujjwal Upadhyay said the available models were indicating potentially serious conditions from September 24 to 27, with some models suggesting particularly significant risk on September 26.

He advised people, except those in Sudurpaschim, to consider postponing long-distance travel on September 24, 25 and 26. He also urged the public not to panic but to remain highly cautious.

Upadhyay said there was still a possibility that the system could weaken before reaching Nepal, similar to a cyclone system seen last year, but preparations should not be reduced.

Farmers urged to remain alert

Heavy rainfall could have a significant impact on the agricultural sector, particularly on mature paddy crops.

Meteorologists have urged farmers to remain alert as heavy rain could damage ready-to-harvest paddy.

The system, which has moved from the northern Thailand and Myanmar region, is currently progressing towards the central Bay of Bengal. If it develops into a cyclone, it would become the first tropical cyclone of 2026 in the North Indian Ocean region.

According to the World Meteorological Organization’s naming list, the system would be named Arnab, a name proposed by Bangladesh, if it develops into a cyclone.

title.rendered: Jhalanath Khanal calls for ideology-based left unity amid political uncertainty

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Former Prime Minister and senior Nepal Communist Party leader Jhalanath Khanal has called for left-wing forces to unite on the basis of common policies and principles, saying the country is facing serious instability and uncertainty.

Speaking at the launch of Sahakari Thagiko Jaal (The Cooperative Fraud Network), a book written by Rastriya Janamorcha General Secretary Manoj Bhatta, Khanal said the country’s crisis had deepened as the left-wing movement weakened.

He said there was also a lack of a culture of even minimal unity among left-wing forces to move forward together.

“The communist movement has claimed from the beginning that it is the most patriotic movement, but because of our own mistakes and compromises, nationalism has reached a serious juncture,” Khanal said.

Khanal stressed the need to establish a clear basis for political unity, arguing that simply bringing leaders together would not create a lasting alliance.

“Unity cannot be achieved simply by bringing heads together. It can be sustained only when it is built on the basis of policy, principles, ideals and the right ideological and political direction,” he said, urging left-wing forces to make efforts towards unity.

He said there was no alternative to bringing left-wing forces together to strengthen national interests, protect Nepal’s 5,000-year-old cultural heritage and pursue socio-economic transformation.

Khanal calls for cooperative law reforms

At the same event, Khanal called for immediate amendments to existing policies and laws to address the crisis and alleged fraud in the cooperative sector.

He said the cooperative sector could not be taken to a new level under its existing structure and regulatory framework.

Khanal stressed the need to establish a new policy and legal framework to make the cooperative sector stronger and more secure.

title.rendered: Tourism can be a force for climate justice in Nepal

content.rendered:
Since the floods hit Nepal on August 26, we have heard repeatedly that Nepal has contributed little to the climate crisis yet faces some of its harshest consequences. That reality should force us to rethink more than how we respond to disasters. It should also force us to rethink how we develop and benefit from tourism.

Nepal’s tourism industry depends on the mountains, rivers, forests, biodiversity, heritage and communities that make the country such a compelling destination. If tourism benefits from these places, it should also help protect them.

Tourism can become a practical instrument of climate justice if every trip, trek and holiday contributes not only to Nepal’s economy but also to the resilience of the destinations and communities that make those journeys possible.

For many international travellers, Nepal first appears through an aircraft window — green hills rising through the clouds, the Kathmandu Valley below and, on a clear day, a horizon lined with snow peaks.

Travellers arrive to stand beneath Everest, trek through the Annapurna region, experience Kathmandu’s living heritage, seek spiritual reflection in Lumbini or explore the country’s forests, rivers, wildlife and mountain cultures.

But the country they are arriving in is changing.

Nepal has made only a negligible contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet its geography leaves it highly exposed. Rising temperatures, glacier loss, expanding glacial lakes, floods, landslides, extreme weather and pressure on water systems are already affecting lives, livelihoods and infrastructure.

In mountain regions, these are no longer distant projections to be discussed at international conferences. They are realities shaping how communities live and how tourism operates.

This is not simply an environmental challenge. Communities that have contributed least to the climate crisis increasingly bear the costs of protecting water sources, restoring damaged infrastructure and access routes, preparing for disasters and sustaining landscapes valued by visitors from around the world.

The Himalaya is paying a price for a crisis it did not create. It is time for those who benefit from the Himalaya to play a greater role in protecting it.

Tourism’s climate paradox

The paradox is difficult to ignore. People travel across the world to experience the Himalaya while the landscapes they admire face growing pressure from a warming planet.

Nepal’s tourism appeal rests on mountains, glaciers, rivers, biodiversity, heritage sites, sacred places and living traditions. Yet a trek is never simply a walking route. It depends on functioning trails and bridges, reliable water supplies, local knowledge, communications, transport services and communities able to host visitors.

When climate risk increases, tourism risk increases with it.

Damage to infrastructure, water shortages, floods and landslides affect residents and visitors alike. They disrupt access, damage services, undermine visitor confidence and threaten the quality of the tourism experience.

The consequences extend across the entire tourism economy. Guides, porters, lodge owners, homestay operators, drivers, farmers, craftspeople and tourism businesses all depend on destinations remaining functional and attractive.

Protecting ecosystems and communities is therefore not a burden imposed on tourism. It is an investment in tourism itself — in employment, local income and the long-term resilience of Nepal’s tourism sector.

We should stop treating environmental protection and tourism development as competing priorities. In Nepal, they are increasingly the same priority.

Beyond climate guilt

Tourists are not the problem. Tourism, however, can be part of the solution.

The answer is not to discourage people from travelling to Nepal or turn holidays into an exercise in guilt. For most international visitors, aviation remains the practical gateway to the country. We should be honest about that reality.

But the conversation cannot end with how travellers arrive. We also need to ask what their visit leaves behind.

Once in Nepal, visitors can make choices that reduce environmental pressure and increase local benefits. They can employ local guides and porters, stay in locally owned accommodation, purchase Nepali products, respect designated routes, minimise waste and choose operators that treat communities and ecosystems as integral to the visitor experience.

These may seem like small decisions. Collectively, they can determine how much value tourism retains in local communities and how much pressure it places on fragile destinations.

Tourism businesses also have responsibilities. Airlines, hotels, lodges and trekking companies should be expected to take seriously their use of energy and water, their waste, their sourcing and their relationship with local communities.

Cleaner energy, efficient water use, responsible sourcing, low-waste operations and stronger local supply chains should not be treated as optional extras for environmentally conscious businesses. They should become part of what responsible tourism means in Nepal.

Government, meanwhile, must provide the standards, information and accountability needed to distinguish genuine action from greenwashing.

The goal is not climate guilt.

The goal is climate justice.

A Climate Justice Fund for the Himalaya

Nepal should consider establishing a transparent and accountable Climate Justice Fund linked to tourism.

This is a proposal, not an existing policy. The principle is straightforward: a small share of the value generated by tourism should help strengthen the resilience of the people and places that make that tourism possible.

Contributions could remain voluntary while being conveniently integrated into the visitor journey through airline tickets, visas, permits, accommodation bookings or tourism packages.

Airlines, hotels, trekking operators and booking platforms could provide contribution channels, while the government, tourism institutions, local representatives and an independent governing body would safeguard the integrity of the mechanism.

But there is an important line that must not be crossed.

These contributions should not be marketed as carbon offsets. They cannot neutralise a flight or make a holiday impact-free. Pretending otherwise would simply give travellers a more comfortable story about the environmental consequences of travel.

Instead, contributions should be presented honestly as climate-justice investments that support communities and landscapes facing risks they did little to create.

Carbon offsetting asks whether an environmental impact can somehow be cancelled elsewhere. Climate justice asks a more fundamental set of questions: Who bears the risks? Who benefits from the destination? Who decides how resources are used? And where should resilience finance go?

The purpose of the fund should not be to purchase moral innocence. It should be to finance visible protection and adaptation.

Keeping the benefits local and visible

If such a fund is created, its benefits must be visible where tourism happens.

Resources generated through tourism should support clearly identified priorities within tourism destinations. These could include watershed restoration, protection of drinking-water sources, trail and bridge conservation, waste management, renewable energy, disaster preparedness and community-led ecosystem restoration.

Such investments would strengthen both local resilience and tourism systems.

Protecting a water source benefits residents and accommodation providers alike. Renewable energy can support lodges while reducing pressure on forests. Local procurement can help farmers, cooperatives and rural enterprises retain more of the money visitors spend.

Resilience financing could also enable tourism SMEs, community organisations, guides, homestay operators and young people to participate directly in destination stewardship.

But there is a fundamental principle that must guide the system: communities should be decision-makers, not merely project locations.

Too often, development projects arrive with decisions already made. That cannot be the model here.

Local priorities should guide project selection. Tourism workers, women, small businesses and climate-exposed households should have meaningful representation.

Funding decisions should also reflect the very different needs of trekking regions, heritage cities, protected areas and emerging rural destinations. A single national formula imposed from Kathmandu will not work everywhere.

Neither the fund nor visitor contributions should replace international climate finance obligations. A tourism-linked mechanism would instead create an additional channel through which visitors and the tourism industry participate directly in protecting the destinations from which they benefit.

Trust must be designed into the fund

There is little point creating another fund if people cannot trust it.

A Climate Justice Fund will succeed only if travellers and communities know where the money goes and can see what it achieves.

Every contribution should be traceable. Every supported project should be publicly listed. All spending should be independently audited. Selection criteria should be transparent, and results should be reported in language that both visitors and communities can understand.

A public reporting system could show how much funding was collected, where it was directed, who participated in decisions, what activities were completed and what outcomes were achieved.

Tourism businesses should not control project selection. Communities should not be consulted only after decisions have already been made.

Transparency cannot be an annual publicity exercise designed to produce a glossy report. It must connect contributions directly to outcomes.

A traveller should be able to see the relationship between a payment and a protected spring, restored trail, safer crossing, cleaner energy system or preparedness initiative.

That is how trust is built.

It would also allow Nepal to tell a different story about tourism — one in which visitors are not simply consumers of spectacular landscapes, but participants in protecting them.

A new contract between travellers and the Himalaya

Nepal cannot solve global warming through tourism. Electric transport, solar-powered lodges, low-waste treks and restored watersheds cannot substitute for deep reductions in global emissions.

But that is no reason for Nepal’s tourism sector to wait for the rest of the world to act.

Climate resilience is built through practical decisions that reduce vulnerability, protect essential systems and strengthen community capacity.

Nepal now has an opportunity to rethink what responsible tourism should mean.

A climate-just tourism model would create a new contract between visitor and destination.

Travellers would continue to come for adventure, culture, spirituality and rest, but their journeys would also help sustain the places they enjoy. Tourism businesses would compete not only on price and comfort but also on credible responsibility. Government would provide oversight, while communities would have meaningful influence over resilience investments.

This is not about making tourism perfect. It is about making it more responsible.

If these responsibilities come together, Nepal can offer more than a conventional holiday. It can offer trips and treks that acknowledge their footprint, reduce avoidable harm, retain more value locally and help protect the mountains, cultures and livelihoods that make travel meaningful.

The Himalaya is changing. Nepal cannot change that reality alone.

But it can decide how its tourism industry responds.

A journey to Nepal should create lasting memories. It should also contribute to securing the future of the places and people that make those memories possible.

That is the promise of tourism as a pathway to climate justice.

title.rendered: Smriti Mandhana becomes highest run-scorer in women’s T20 international cricket

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

India vice-captain Smriti Mandhana has become the highest run-scorer in women’s T20 international cricket.

Mandhana set the record while scoring 37 runs off 19 balls against Bangladesh in the semifinal of the Asian Games, surpassing New Zealand’s Suzie Bates.

The 30-year-old, who made her international debut for India in 2013, is regarded as one of the most successful batters in women’s cricket. She has scored 4,751 runs in women’s T20 internationals so far.

Mandhana had previously become the highest run-scorer in women’s international cricket while playing against Hong Kong in the 2026 Women’s Asia Cup. She has now scored 10,950 international runs across all three formats.

The left-handed opener has scored 14 centuries in One-Day Internationals and two in T20 internationals. She is currently ranked No. 1 in the ICC Women’s ODI batting rankings and fifth in the T20I batting rankings.

title.rendered: Sabita Rai finishes 10th in Wushu at Asian Games

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Nepal’s Sabita Rai finished 10th in the women’s Taijiquan and Taijijian events in wushu at the ongoing 20th Asian Games in Japan.

Rai finished 10th among 12 competitors at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall, scoring 9.183 points.

China’s Qin Tong won the gold medal with 9.783 points. Japan’s Shiho Saito claimed silver with 9.740 points, while Singapore’s Jian Zhi Ning Lau and Brunei’s Basma Lachkar won bronze medals with 9.740 and 9.720 points, respectively.

Nepal has fielded 10 athletes in various wushu events at the Asian Games. Along with Rai, Nepal’s Vijay Sinjali has also been eliminated from the competition after competing in the men’s Changquan event.

title.rendered: The Nepali chef reshaping Portugal’s Italian food culture

content.rendered:
At five years old, Tanka Sapkota began walking 45 minutes to school.

There were no cars waiting for him, no easy shortcuts. School was simply another part of a childhood spent working.

Before and after classes, he and his siblings worked in the fields. At 11 or 12, he was raising chickens. A little later, he began keeping goats. During Maghe Sankranti fairs, he sold lemons.

At 13, he helped dig an irrigation canal from Thuldhunga to Pokhari, about a kilometre away, to bring water to his village.

It was a childhood shaped by necessity.

More than four decades later, the 51-year-old Sapkota has built a very different life.

He lives in Portugal, where he has become a prominent name in Italian cuisine. His four restaurants attract political leaders, footballers, artists and other international visitors. His cooking has earned international awards, while his experiments with pizza, gold ovens and truffles have made him a distinctive figure in Portugal’s food scene.

Yet Sapkota still traces much of what he has achieved back to those early years in Baglung.

“We worked in the fields from morning to evening while continuing our studies,” he recalls. “Life taught me to work hard and keep working.”

A restless young man

Tanka Sapkota grew up in Damek, in what is now Jaimini Municipality-2 of Baglung, with seven brothers and two sisters.

His parents, Jagupati and Kalawati Sapkota, shaped his understanding of work in different ways. His mother was known for completing any task quickly and efficiently. His father was a community-minded man.

When his father died, Sapkota says, the number of people who came to pay their respects showed him how much his father had contributed to the community.

At school, he considered himself an average student. He completed his education from Grade 1 to 10 at Suntalachaur Secondary School.

But academic success was never the only measure of ability in his eyes.

Looking back, he believes creativity and the willingness to work mattered more to the life he eventually built than rote learning.

After completing his SLC, he began thinking seriously about becoming financially independent.

It was the era of watches, radios and cassette players. He watched people in Baglung bazaar making a living repairing them and became interested in learning the trade.

He did not know where to learn. So he decided to go to India with his elder brother Hemlal. The family did not approve. The brothers left home at 3am. They were robbed on the way. Still, they made it to India.

Sapkota initially found work cleaning a house for 280 Indian rupees. He soon left and found another job at a shop where he hoped to learn how to repair watches, radios and tape recorders.

The opportunity never quite materialised.

He was expected to clean the house and deliver tea to the shop. He was told he would be taught the technical work during winter, but that time never came.

Four months after arriving in India, he received a letter from his father asking him to return. He went home. Then came another worry.

His elder brother was getting married. On the day of the wedding, a guest mentioned Germany.

Sapkota immediately asked whether he could go too.

He made his father a promise.

“Send me to Germany. I will serve you for the rest of my life and I will never claim any share of the property,” he told him.

Eventually, his father agreed.

Germany and the kitchen

At the time, travelling to Germany did not require a visa in the way it does today. A traveller needed a ticket and travel cheque, although there was always a risk of being sent back.

Tanka Sapkota spent around Rs 150,000 and left Nepal. He was about 18.

Germany was another world. The language was unfamiliar. The culture was different. The technology and lifestyle he encountered made him realise how far behind Nepal was at the time.

He also made a personal decision there.

Back in Nepal, politics had been part of everyday life. Sapkota had been a member of the Nepali Congress, but his experience in Germany changed his perspective.

“I realised that in our country people are involved in politics from birth until death,” he says.

He decided to leave politics behind. From Berlin, he travelled by train to Stuttgart. He arrived at 9am. By 5pm that same day, he was at work.

The 18-year-old, thin and inexperienced, was not initially taken very seriously by his employer. That changed quickly.

His work ethic and willingness to learn earned him an opportunity at another restaurant, where he spent four years.

It was there that his relationship with food began to take shape. He worked 14 to 15 hours a day. For six months, he did not take a single day off. Not because his employer demanded it, he says, but because he wanted to work.

Within his first three years, he learned almost every part of the restaurant business — washing dishes, helping in the kitchen, making pizza, working behind the bar, serving customers and eventually cooking as a chef.

The restaurant owner became more than an employer.

“I still consider him like my father,” Sapkota says. “He also loves me like his own son.”

Those years gave him something that formal training could not easily provide — an intimate understanding of European kitchens and the discipline required to run them.

A new life in Portugal

After four and a half years in Germany, a school friend, Laxmi Sapkota, suggested Portugal. Sapkota arrived there in 1996. Two years later, his brother Hemlal also returned from Germany. For Sapkota, it felt like a turning point.

In 1999, the brothers opened their first restaurant. Their cousins Krishnaprasad Sapkota and Laxmiprasad Sapkota also played an important role in helping them get started.

The restaurant filled up within its first week. It never looked back.

Today, Tanka Sapkota has four restaurants. But expansion for its own sake has never been his goal.

“My aim is not simply to increase the number. It is to achieve excellence in quality,” he says.

The four restaurants are all within a two-kilometre radius, yet each has its own identity.

For Sapkota, food is inseparable from culture.

Italian, Portuguese and Nepali cuisine may look different, he says, but underneath the differences are fundamental similarities. In one place, the food itself may take centre stage; in another, spices may be more important.

His approach to cooking has grown from that idea.

The pizza experiment

One of Sapkota’s most important culinary experiments began during a trip to Venice with his wife, Sita. At the time, he told Sita that his life had become about flour. He began experimenting with Neapolitan-style pizza.

In Portugal at the time, the style was relatively unfamiliar. People were more accustomed to thin-crust pizza. Sapkota took the risk anyway. The experiment worked.

Today, Neapolitan-style pizza has become common in restaurants across Portugal.

“I am naturally proud of it,” he says. “The path I started is now being followed by thousands.”

Then came another idea that sounded even more improbable. A gold oven.

Tanka Sapkota once told a friend he wanted to build one. The friend laughed and suggested the idea sounded arrogant. Sapkota had another way of looking at it.

“If temples, mosques, monasteries and churches can be built in gold, why shouldn’t the temple where I do my work be made of gold?” he recalls saying.

He began making pizza in a gold oven.

The idea eventually became popular too.

His restaurants also follow another principle — seasonal ingredients.

He believes food prepared with ingredients when nature provides them produces better results in both health and flavour.

Searching for Portugal’s truffles

His next ambition was more difficult. He wanted to find truffles in Portugal. He told his wife that he wanted their oldest restaurant to become known for truffles. But there was a basic question.

Could truffles actually be found in Portugal?

An unexpected connection helped. At an awards ceremony where Sapkota had won a prize, Portugal’s agriculture minister was the chief guest. Through the minister, Sapkota was able to collaborate with scientists from the country’s agriculture and environment ministries.

The search began.

For five weeks, a 12-member team and two dogs investigated potential locations. Eventually, they found truffles in four places. Tanka Sapkota calls them the “diamonds of the kitchen”.

Truffles are among the world’s most sought-after and rare culinary ingredients.

News of the discovery spread nationally.

Sapkota appeared in interviews and television discussions, and his reputation grew.

Today, more than half the dishes at his oldest restaurant are based on truffles.

His name has become closely associated with the ingredient in Portugal.

In 2018, he publicly introduced a rare white truffle brought from Italy — the first time such a truffle had been presented in Portugal. A year later, in 2019, he was awarded the title “Cavaliere delle Tartufi Bianchi”, or “Knight of the White Truffle”, in Alba, Italy.

In 2024, he discovered Portugal’s first black summer truffle.

His ambitions have grown with the discoveries.

He now wants Portugal to develop into a centre for truffle tourism and cultivation, seeing the potential for a business worth tens of millions, as has happened in Italy and Spain.

When restaurants became a refuge

The pandemic changed the way Tanka Sapkota viewed his business. While restaurants and businesses around the world struggled simply to survive, he decided to use his kitchen for something else. His message was simple.

“We cannot change the world alone, but we can help change the world.”

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Tanka Sapkota distributed pizzas free of charge, delivering them directly to people’s homes.

In total, he says, 10,500 pizzas were distributed. The campaign attracted national attention.

Portuguese television channels reported on his efforts, highlighting the restaurant owner who had turned his kitchen into a source of food and reassurance during a period of fear and uncertainty.

“COVID gave me an opportunity to look at my work from a new perspective,” he says. “I focused on what I could do.”

From presidents to footballers

Sapkota’s restaurants have now become part of Portugal’s food landscape. His journey began with Come Prima, which recently marked 25 years. His restaurants Forno di Oro and Come Prima have appeared on lists of the world’s leading Italian restaurants.

Casa Nepalesa, meanwhile, offers another part of his identity, bringing Nepali dishes and flavours to an international audience.

After nearly three decades in Portugal, his restaurants have become meeting places for prominent figures.

Presidents and prime ministers of Portugal have visited. International artists and footballers have also stopped by while travelling through the country.

But Tanka Sapkota does not describe his success as the result of one dramatic breakthrough.

He sees it as the accumulation of small changes.

“Small improvements, continuous effort and high-quality service are what ensure business success,” he says.

A life on screen

His three decades in the food industry have now been turned into a six-part documentary. Taste of Italy was broadcast on Portugal’s TVI channel. The documentary explores Italian cuisine, its ingredients and techniques, as well as Tanka Sapkota’s nearly 30 years of experience in the industry.

Filming took place across different parts of Italy over two months.

Directed by filmmaker Tiago P. de Carvalho, the documentary was produced to mark the 25th anniversary of Come Prima.

“I wanted the documentary to show how deeply I immerse myself in Italian cuisine,” Sapkota says.

It is a long way from the boy who walked barefoot to school in Baglung.

The child who sold lemons, raised chickens and goats, and once left home at 3am to learn how to repair watches in India could hardly have known where those decisions would lead.

But the thread running through his life has remained remarkably consistent.

Work. Curiosity. And the refusal to waste what he has been given.

Tanka Sapkota has a simple philosophy about food: throwing it away is one of the greatest crimes a person can commit.

His career has followed a similar principle.

He has taken difficult beginnings, failed plans, uncertain journeys and unexpected opportunities — and found a way to make something from each of them.

title.rendered: Preparations underway for Indra Jatra at Basantapur Durbar Square (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Preparations are underway for the annual Indra Jatra festival at Basantapur Durbar Square. Work is currently being carried out to construct chariots and clean the area. Painting and maintenance work is also underway at heritage sites within the Durbar Square complex, including Kasthamandap, Kumari Ghar and the Shiva-Parvati Temple, along with the replacement of the red cloth banner.

Indra Jatra, celebrated primarily by the Newa community, is observed with much fanfare in Kathmandu as well as in Lalitpur, Bhaktapur, Dhulikhel, Dolakha and other places.

A ceremonial pole, known as the Indradhwaja, is erected during the festival. The base of the pole is worshipped as Bhairav. Indra Jatra is traditionally celebrated as a festival of victory following the defeat of enemies and is also regarded as a festival of worshipping the Indradhwaja to gain and display strength.

During the festival, the President traditionally observes the chariot procession of Kumari, Ganesh and Bhairav, regarded as living deities, from the Gaddi Baithak at Hanuman Dhoka.

Various traditional dances, including Bhakkunach, Mahakali dance, Lakhe dance, Dashavatar and Pulukisi, representing Indra’s elephant Airavata, are performed throughout the festival.

On the eighth day after the Indradhwaja pole is erected, it is ceremonially brought down on the fourth day of the waning fortnight of Ashwin.

title.rendered: Nepal Academy to launch ‘Katha Dabali’ with Indra Jatra stories

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The Nepal Academy is set to launch a special series, ‘Katha Dabali’, aimed at documenting and digitally archiving old myths, stories and legends of cities for future generations.

The first edition, ‘Katha Dabali-1’, will feature stories and legends associated with Indra Jatra. The event will be held on September 24 at the Dabali of the Nepal Academy in Kamaladi.

The programme will begin at 2 pm on Thursday, with Nepal Bhasa Academy Chancellor and senior cultural expert Malla K. Sundar presenting the stories, according to the Nepal Academy.

The Academy said Sundar will narrate written stories about centuries-old tales, myths and legends associated with Indra Jatra, as well as the origins of Kathmandu and its cultural heritage.

Traditional dances will also be performed during the programme, titled ‘Indra Jatra: The Autumn Festival’. Deepak Sapkota, head of the Academy’s Poetry, Culture and Digitalisation Department, said artists will perform the valley’s famous Lakhe Pyakha (Lakhe dance) and Kumari dance.

Sapkota said the ‘Katha Dabali’ series, which aims to preserve and archive cultural stories, will be organised continuously in different cities and villages across Nepal.

title.rendered: Government sets new quality standards for edible oils

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The government is preparing to enforce stricter rules on the production, packaging and distribution of edible oils in Nepal, with a focus on quality, purity and consumer health. The Department of Food Technology and Quality Control under the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies has prepared the final draft of new quality standards for mustard, soybean and sunflower oils.

The new standards clearly classify edible oils into those suitable for direct consumption and those that are not. They also prohibit misleading advertisements and the reuse of previously used containers.

Mustard oil

The department’s technical committee has prepared specifications for mustard oil under Nepal Standard 03:2035 (Second Amendment: 2083). Under the standard, mustard oil is divided into two categories based on the production process: express and solvent-extracted. All oils extracted through the express process — refined, virgin and expeller — as well as refined oil produced through the solvent process, will be considered suitable for direct human consumption.

However, Grade 1 oil produced through the solvent process cannot be consumed directly and must undergo further processing before use. Such oil cannot be sold in consumer packets. Its container must carry the words “Not for direct edible consumption” in English in letters at least 50 millimetres high. In terms of purity, the oil must not contain the harmful weed Argemone mexicana or any other inedible oil. The maximum peroxide value has been set at 10 milliequivalents. Strict limits have also been set for toxic metals, with lead and arsenic capped at 0.1 milligrams per kilogram, cadmium at 1 milligram per kilogram and mercury at 0.25 milligrams per kilogram.

Soybean oil

The department has prepared new standards for soybean oil under Nepal Standard 103:2042 (First Amendment: 2083). Under the new provision, soybean oil extracted through the solvent extraction process will be classified as refined, degummed and Grade 1. Only refined oil will be considered suitable for direct consumption.

Degummed and Grade 1 oils are considered raw materials for producing vegetable ghee or refined oil and therefore cannot be sold in retail packets. Their containers must also carry a warning in letters at least 50 millimetres high stating that the oil is not intended for direct consumption. The oil must be extracted only from healthy soybeans of the Glycine max species of the Leguminosae family. Aflatoxin content must not exceed 30 micrograms per kilogram. For refined oil, the limit for hexane has been set at 5 ppm and phosphorus at a maximum of 12 ppm.

Sunflower oil

The department has prepared a draft first amendment to regulate the quality of sunflower oil. Sunflower oil has also been divided into express and solvent-extracted categories. Refined oils from both processes and Grade 1 oil produced through the express process will be considered suitable for direct consumption.

However, Grade 1 oil produced through the solvent extraction process cannot be consumed directly and cannot be sold in consumer packets. Its container must carry a warning against direct consumption in large letters using indelible ink. The oil must be free from artificial colours and flavours. Its peroxide value must not exceed 10, while aflatoxin content must be below 30 micrograms per kilogram. Strict limits on toxic metals, including lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury, will also apply.

Restrictions on misleading advertising and reuse of containers

One of the key aspects of the new standards is stricter regulation of advertising and packaging. Producers will no longer be allowed to use misleading or exaggerated terms on oil packets or in advertisements. The use of terms such as super-refined, extra-refined, micro-refined, double-refined, ultra-refined, anti-cholesterol, cholesterol fighter, heart soothing, cholesterol friendly and saturated fat free will be completely prohibited.

Similarly, only Nepal Standard-certified tins or plastic containers can be used for packaging. The reuse of previously used tins or plastic containers for packaging edible oil will be completely prohibited in the interest of public health. The manufacturer’s name and address, batch number, month or year of production and net weight must be clearly displayed in English or Nepali on the outside of the container.

Only producers meeting the standards will be allowed to use the Nepal Standard certification mark. The department expects the new scientific and stringent standards to help ensure the purity of edible oils available in the Nepali market and play an important role in protecting consumers’ health.

title.rendered: Gandaki government urges Manaslu Base Camp hunger strikers to join talks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The Gandaki Province government has urged youths on an indefinite hunger strike at the Manaslu Base Camp to suspend their protest and join talks to address their demands concerning the safety of communities in the Himalayan region.

In a public appeal issued on Sunday, the Office of the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers said the demands would be best addressed through dialogue and discussions involving all three levels of government and civil society.

The provincial government said it was positive about coordinating with the federal government, local governments and other relevant agencies to address the issues raised by the protesters.

The office said the demands were sensitive and directly related to public safety, adding that the provincial government was serious about the concerns raised by the youths.

A 10-member group led by Dhawa Nurbu Lama, a resident of Samagaun in Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1 of northern Gorkha, began an indefinite hunger strike at the Manaslu Base Camp on Friday.

The group has put forward several demands related to mitigating the impacts of climate change and reducing risks to Himalayan communities.

The protesters have warned the government that the risk of glacial lake outburst floods has increased due to climate change and urged authorities to take preventive measures.

They have called for the measurement and risk assessment of vulnerable glacial lakes in northern Gorkha, including Birendra Lake in Samagaun, Kal Lake in Prok and Hariyo Lake in Pugen, to assess the possibility of future outbursts.

They have also demanded arrangements for joint monitoring by the mechanisms of Nepal and China of glacial lakes on the Chinese side located near human settlements in Nepal.

The group has called for aerial monitoring of glacial lakes in the Manaslu region and Chum Valley and the installation of warning sirens near vulnerable settlements to provide early warnings in the event of a disaster.

The provincial government has urged the protesters to immediately suspend the hunger strike and come to the negotiating table to seek solutions to their demands.

title.rendered: Mahesh Basnet criticises government over Bharat Dahal’s arrest

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

CPN-UML Secretary Mahesh Basnet has criticised the government over the arrest of analyst Bharat Dahal.

Speaking to journalists on Sunday, Basnet objected to Dahal’s arrest, alleging that it was carried out at the direction of Prime Minister Balen Shah’s secretariat.

He challenged the authorities to refute reports published by ‘Grey Zone’ media, saying Dahal was arrested merely for commenting on publicly reported news that mentioned the prime minister.

“Regarding Bharat Dahal’s arrest, he was arrested while having tea at the direction of the prime minister’s secretariat. Why was he arrested? Because he provided somewhat extensive commentary on the ‘Grey Zone’ issue. This is like the saying that when a thief is told to cut off the thief’s leg, the thief raises his own leg. Balen and his people are raising their legs,” Basnet said.

“If the report is false, they should prove that it is false and provide clarification and an explanation. They cannot act like a cat secretly stealing milk and then arrest Bharat Dahal and others who raise questions about the ‘Grey Zone’ reports. This shows their authoritarian, autocratic and vindictive style,” he said.

Basnet also claimed that reports published by Grey Zone had clarified who played what role in the Gen Z movement on September 8 and 9 last year. He said Rabi Lamichhane, Balen Shah and others should respond to the reports.

title.rendered: Oli urges journalists to seek permission before posing questions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Former Prime Minister and CPN-UML Chairman KP Sharma Oli has advised journalists to be mindful of journalistic norms and practices when asking questions.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday as he left a meeting of the UML’s election review and restructuring task force at the party’s central office in Chyasal, Oli suggested that journalists follow the international practice of asking permission before posing a question, and also informing the person before publishing what they said.

Oli said that the standard convention in journalism worldwide is to first ask whether a question can be posed, and afterwards to check with the person before publishing their remarks. He then added, more informally, that reporters shouldn’t shove a microphone right up into someone’s face or mouth.

Oli said that questions should not be put to someone by thrusting a microphone at them without first asking permission.

title.rendered: 9 local govts join hands to expand night bus service in Kathmandu Valley

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Nine local governments in Kathmandu Valley have joined a common programme to expand night-time public bus services in the Valley.

Led by Kathmandu Metropolitan City, the local governments have partnered with Sajha Yatayat to expand the night bus service that was launched on a trial basis from April 14.

Under the agreement, the participating local governments will share financial responsibilities based on the requirements for expanding and operating the service.

The agreement was signed with Sajha Yatayat on Constitution Day, with the aim of providing convenient, safe and reliable transportation at night for commuters, businesspeople, entrepreneurs, workers, patients travelling to hospitals and domestic and international tourists.

The local governments signing the agreement are Kathmandu Metropolitan City, Lalitpur Metropolitan City, Budhanilkantha Municipality, Godawari Municipality, Chandragiri Municipality, Kirtipur Municipality, Bhaktapur Municipality, Suryabinayak Municipality and Madhyapur Thimi Municipality. Sajha Yatayat Chairman Sushil Raj Pyakurel signed the agreement on behalf of the transport company.

Following the agreement, 30 buses have begun operating on six routes.

Kathmandu Metropolitan City Deputy Mayor Sunita Dangol said the night bus service was being expanded as part of efforts to improve access to basic services guaranteed to citizens by the Constitution.

She said four additional buses had been added to the two routes operated during the trial period, increasing the total number of buses from seven to 30. The number of municipalities involved has also increased from four to nine.

Lalitpur Metropolitan City Mayor Chiribabu Maharjan said local governments had begun collaborating on a locally operated transport system after the federal government failed to move ahead with plans for a metro system in the Valley.

Sajha Yatayat Chairman Pyakurel said the expanded service would provide a reliable option for people travelling safely at night.

Which routes will the night buses operate on?

Under the expanded service, six buses will operate between Jagati-Suryabinayak and Thamel, while another six will run between Godawari and Thamel via Lagankhel and Budhanilkantha.

Eight buses will operate along the Ring Road in both clockwise and anticlockwise directions.

Four buses will run between Kirtipur and Jamal, two between Takhel and Thamel, and four on the existing Nagdhunga-Airport route.

Previously, seven buses operated a trial night service between Lagankhel and Budhanilkantha and between Nagdhunga and the Airport from 8 pm to 11 pm.

How will the service be funded?

Under the agreement, if ticket revenue is insufficient to cover the operating costs, the seven municipalities will jointly bear 50 percent of the shortfall.

The remaining 50 percent will be covered according to the population of the participating municipalities. Kathmandu Metropolitan City and Lalitpur Metropolitan City will each contribute 18.55 percent, while the other seven municipalities will contribute 9 percent each.

If additional funds are required to operate the service, Sajha Yatayat will submit a quarterly request for the necessary amount.

The participating municipalities will determine bus boarding and drop-off points along the routes. Sajha Yatayat has been assigned responsibility for installing digital signage and developing and operating digital bus stops by the end of fiscal year 2026/27.

With the night bus service available around the Ring Road, passengers will be able to reach different parts of the Valley by changing buses at designated points. The maximum fare for such journeys will be Rs 80.

Sajha Yatayat has also been developing a digital ticketing system since September 17 to reduce revenue leakage. Passengers will be able to purchase tickets either by QR payment or cash.

The Government of Nepal holds shares worth Rs 3 billion in Sajha Yatayat, while Kathmandu Metropolitan City has invested Rs 150 million. Sajha Yatayat currently operates 111 buses.

Police say DNA samples have been collected from the recovered bodies for identification purposes, and 1,292 bodies have been processed so far.

title.rendered: As floods damage hydropower projects, what happens to public investments?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Six of the 13 hydropower projects damaged by the floods of August 26 are owned by companies listed on the secondary share market, meaning thousands of public investors are exposed to the losses caused by the disaster.

The affected listed companies are Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Company, which operates a 111 MW project; Chilime Hydropower Company (22 MW); Trishuli Jal Vidhyut Company (37 MW); Mailung Khola Hydropower Company (5 MW); Upper Mailung Khola Hydropower Company (14.8 MW); and Sanjen Hydropower Company, which operates the 42.5 MW Sanjen and 14.8 MW Upper Sanjen projects.

The companies have been among the hardest hit in the stock market since the floods, with the share prices of some falling by more than 30 percent.

Rasuwagadhi, Chilime and Trishuli Hydropower have suffered particularly extensive damage. Initial reports indicate that dams, tunnels, powerhouses, machinery and transmission infrastructure have been severely damaged or destroyed.

As a result, share prices of the six companies have fallen by between 4.25 percent and 30.48 percent since August 26.

Source: NEPSE

Debt remains even as projects are destroyed

The damage has created a difficult financial situation for the companies. While investors have already suffered losses from falling share prices, the bigger challenge is how the projects can be rebuilt.

Many of the affected companies still have billions of rupees in outstanding bank loans. With projects either severely damaged or destroyed, they may have to borrow additional money to rebuild while continuing to service existing debt.

This could leave companies paying interest on previous loans for years while taking on new debt for reconstruction. At the same time, electricity generation and associated revenues could remain at zero for several years.

The cost of rebuilding is also expected to be higher than the original project cost.

“Some of the equipment may no longer be usable, and equipment has become more expensive now. Therefore, rebuilding the project could cost more than it did originally,” said Narnath Neupane, company secretary of Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Company.

The companies also face a separate problem: their electricity production has been disrupted while the remaining period of their generation licences continues to run down.

The average cost of developing a hydropower project is currently around Rs 200 million per megawatt and has been rising, according to energy-sector officials. Some of the losses at insured projects will, however, be covered by insurance.

Insurance assessment could take time

The extent of the insurance payouts will depend on detailed damage assessments.

Mohan Dangi, president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), said insurance companies would first send surveyors to assess the damage.

“Only after the surveyors complete their assessment will we have a detailed picture of the losses. In some projects, surveyors have not even been able to reach the site yet,” Dangi said.

Once the damage has been assessed, the insurance claim process will move forward.

Typically, once a project is completed, annual depreciation is calculated by dividing the project cost by the number of years remaining on its licence. Insurance compensation is generally calculated after deducting depreciation.

Dangi said the government should introduce a package of measures for the affected projects, including customs exemptions on replacement equipment, access to low-interest loans and extensions to electricity generation licences.

He said government and insurance-sector support would help give project developers the confidence to rebuild. The government could also consider using various financial instruments to help manage the reconstruction, he said.

Access itself remains a challenge at some projects, with flood damage destroying or disrupting roads leading to project sites.

Rasuwagadhi faces the biggest challenge

The 111 MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project appears to have suffered the most extensive damage among the listed projects.

The project had already been damaged by last year’s floods, and reconstruction had not yet been completed. The company had taken on additional debt to complete the rehabilitation when this year’s floods caused extensive new damage.

“The powerhouse has been buried, the tunnel is filled with mud and debris, and none of the external structures remain,” Neupane said.

The company is currently focused primarily on managing the human impact of the disaster rather than its financial situation, he said.

According to the company’s financial statement for the last fiscal year, Rasuwagadhi had long-term debt of Rs 14.78 billion as of the end of the fiscal year.

Trishuli project damaged before generating revenue

The 37 MW Upper Trishuli-3B project, operated by Trishuli Jal Vidhyut Company, also faces a difficult future.

The project suffered major damage while it was still under construction and had not yet begun generating revenue.

The company has outstanding debt of around Rs 3.75 billion. Servicing that debt while finding the financing required to rebuild the project will be a major challenge.

A company linked to the project will also have to deal with the fact that revenue generation had not yet begun before the disaster.

Chilime hit directly and through its investments

Chilime Hydropower’s 22 MW project was directly affected by the floods, with preliminary assessments indicating significant damage around the powerhouse.

The impact on Chilime extends beyond its own project. The company has invested in Rasuwagadhi Hydropower, whose project has been severely damaged, as well as Sanjen Hydropower.

Damage to transmission infrastructure at Sanjen has also affected electricity evacuation.

As a result, Chilime’s shareholders face exposure not only to damage at Chilime’s own project but also to losses and delays at projects in which the company has invested.

Damage at Mailung Khola comparatively limited

The 5 MW Mailung Khola Hydropower Project has suffered damage to its powerhouse, penstock and switchyard, according to preliminary assessments.

The damage is considered relatively limited compared with some of the other affected projects. Initial estimates put the damage at around Rs 50 million.

The company has informed the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) that the project was damaged by the floods and that electricity generation has been affected.

Upper Mailung Khola hit mainly in transmission infrastructure

The 14.8 MW Upper Mailung Khola Hydropower Project has mainly suffered damage to its switchyard and transmission line.

A preliminary assessment has estimated the damage at around Rs 28.6 million.

Sanjen projects largely intact, but unable to evacuate power

Sanjen Hydropower Company’s 14.8 MW Upper Sanjen and 42.5 MW Sanjen projects have also been affected by the floods.

According to IPPAN’s preliminary assessment, the projects themselves have not suffered major physical damage. However, electricity evacuation has been disrupted because of extensive damage to the 220 kV substation and transmission structures at the Trishuli-3B hub.

With no clear timeline for the reconstruction of the damaged grid and transmission infrastructure, the company is facing continued uncertainty despite its generation facilities remaining largely intact.

For investors, the damage therefore extends beyond the immediate physical destruction of hydropower infrastructure. Companies must now contend with reconstruction costs, existing debt obligations, potentially higher equipment prices, lost generation revenue and uncertainty over how quickly damaged transmission networks can be restored.

title.rendered: Bullet removed from body of person injured in Dewanganj incident

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, September 20

A bullet has been removed from the body of a young man who was injured Saturday evening in a clash between two groups in Madhya Harshahi, Dewanganj Rural Municipality-1, Sunsari.

A group of 8–9 people opened fire in Madhya Harshahi, injuring 24-year-old resident Niraj Kumar Yadav. He was admitted to Nobel Medical College, Biratnagar, immediately after the incident. Sunsari District Police Office spokesperson, Deputy Superintendent of Police Chandra Khadka, said the bullet was removed from his body through surgery Sunday morning.

According to him, the bullet removed from the body appears to be from a homemade (locally-made) pistol, but the type of weapon used will only be confirmed after ballistic testing.

Yadav was shot on the right side of his lower back. Since neither the weapon nor a shell casing was found, police had earlier said it would only become clear after surgery whether he had been shot or injured some other way. Police said a medical team removed the bullet through surgery.

Police said an investigation is underway against 18-year-old Bishnu Kumar Yadav and 26-year-old Jay Krishna Yadav, also known as Lali, both of Dewanganj Rural Municipality-2, who were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the incident. After the shooting near the village, locals had overpowered Bishnu and Jay Krishna and tied them to a tree; they were handed over to police upon arrival. Their motorcycle was also set on fire. DSP Khadka said police are searching for other individuals believed to be involved.

Niraj was shot Saturday evening while returning home on a motorcycle with his neighbour Bibek Kumar Yadav from Harinagar Bazar. The group that opened fire also assaulted Bibek.

“There are reports that this may also be linked to an old rivalry and a dispute over a young woman,” Khadka said. “We are investigating this angle.”

On July 26, three people were killed and seven injured when police opened fire during a clash between two groups in Kaptanganj, Dewanganj Rural Municipality-3.
