title.rendered: NCP rethinks convention schedule after Rasuwa flood disruption

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The Nepali Communist Party’s (NCP) previously set schedule for its conventions has been disrupted. Party spokesperson Prakash Jwala said the schedule was affected due to the situation following the Rasuwa flood.

“Earlier, the party’s Central Coordination Committee had drawn up a timeline for the conventions and general convention,” he said. “But because of the devastating flood that hit Rasuwa on August 26 and related factors, the planned schedule couldn’t be carried out.”

He said the party now needs to discuss the matter and set a new schedule. A meeting of the Central Coordination Committee held last April had decided to hold the general convention in Kathmandu from December 26 to 30.

That plan had included conducting a membership renewal and new membership drive through the end of June and July.

The schedule called for ward-level conventions to be completed by August 30, municipal-level conventions from September 1 through the end of the month, district-level conventions by the second week of October, and provincial conventions by November 1.

However, spokesperson Jwala said that because conventions and the general convention could not proceed according to that schedule, the party now needs to discuss the matter and come up with a new one.

To hold this discussion, the NCP has called a meeting of its Central Coordination Committee.

Jwala said the meeting has been called for 1 pm Tuesday at the party’s central office in Parisdanda.

“The Central Coordination Committee meeting will discuss the general convention and the conventions, as well as the matter of membership renewal,” he said.

According to party leaders, lower-level committees have complained that although the centre made the general convention schedule public, the procedures needed to actually hold the conventions were not in place, causing problems.

The upcoming Tuesday meeting will also discuss bringing in convention procedures. Leaders say preparations are underway to introduce a new schedule that would, if possible, still allow the general convention to take place in November-December.

title.rendered: Free legal aid for those injured in the Gen Z movement

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The government is set to provide free legal aid to those injured in the Gen Z movement. To that end, the Act relating to free legal aid is being amended.

A provision in Section 4 of the bill registered by Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sobita Gautam in the House of Representatives on Friday addresses the categories of people entitled to receive free legal aid, a list that includes those injured in the Gen Z movement.

The Gen Z movement took place on September 8–9 last year. During the movement, 76 people died nationwide. The government initially declared 45 of them martyrs. On the first day of the movement, 19 people lost their lives.

More than 422 people were seriously injured nationwide during the movement, with the total number of injured exceeding 450.

The Act is being amended to provide free legal aid to these individuals.

Nine categories of people eligible for free legal aid

(a) Socially or educationally disadvantaged women, Dalits, Indigenous nationalities, Madhesi, Tharu, minorities, marginalised groups, Muslims, backward classes, gender and sexual minorities, economically disadvantaged Khas Arya, labourers, farmers, and citizens from oppressed or backward regions

(b) Economically disadvantaged citizens

(c) Victims of domestic or gender-based violence

(d) Children, senior citizens, persons with disabilities, or helpless individuals

(e) Martyrs and victims of the armed conflict, those injured, disabled, or incapacitated during various people’s movements, including the Gen Z movement, democracy fighters, and displaced citizens

(f) Victims of offences related to caste-based or other social untouchability and discrimination

(g) Persons arrested in criminal cases who state at the time of arrest that they are unable to retain legal counsel

(h) Detainees or prisoners held in custody

(i) Parties to a case for whom a court has ordered that free legal aid be provided

The proposed bill significantly widens the scope of who qualifies as unable to afford legal help, and extends free legal aid services to all courts as well as judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.

The bill establishes that an eligible party’s right to legal aid covers everything from free legal consultation and advice through case proceedings, hearings, and even execution of the verdict.

For individuals arrested in criminal cases who are unable to arrange their own legal counsel, the bill ensures the right to free legal aid begins from the moment of arrest.

The bill also includes provisions requiring the use of sign language when providing free legal aid to individuals with hearing or speech-related disabilities, and mandates psychosocial counselling services for eligible parties as needed.

According to the bill, legal aid for eligible parties will be coordinated across all three levels of government: federal, provincial, and local.

Agencies providing legal aid are required to deliver services in an integrated manner. To make free legal aid more effective and centrally coordinated, the Ministry is tasked with developing and implementing an electronic system for free legal aid.

To improve the quality of free legal aid, the bill also includes provisions for providing legal aid services through subject-matter experts.

The proposed bill establishes the structure for a National Legal Aid Council, an Executive Committee, and provincial and district-level legal aid committees.

title.rendered: Environment diplomacy section established at Foreign Ministry

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The Foreign Ministry has set up an environment diplomacy section in a bid to institutionalise and make effective the diplomatic endeavours on climate and environment. The section was established for the first time at the Foreign Ministry in view of the increasing impact of climate change in Nepal and the urgency of proper and adequate responses, according to the Foreign Minister’s secretariat.

Based on the Organisation and Management Survey, the section comes under the division looking after the UN and specialised agencies. Nepal has been actively attending the national, regional and international forums dwelling on climate change and environmental conservation. The facility is expected to advance coordination and institutional measures.

In addition to facilitating climate diplomacy in international conferences and events, the section builds coordination with the national bodies. In this connection, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said climate diplomacy should not be limited to international conferences and events but should be advanced in a long-term and institutional manner.

title.rendered: Crisis Connect Nepal launched to build nationwide disaster volunteer network

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Crisis Connect Nepal (CCN), a new non-profit organisation aimed at strengthening Nepal’s disaster response capacity, was formally established following its preliminary assembly held Saturday at Sagarmatha Hall, Techspire College.

Twenty-one Charter Members took their oath of office at the assembly, officially chartering the organisation and laying the groundwork for a nationwide, technology-enabled network of disaster-trained volunteers.

Suraj Raj Pandey was elected President of Crisis Connect Nepal during the assembly. The organisation will be run by a seven-member Board of Directors, a Chief Executive Officer, and five standing committees overseeing areas ranging from technology architecture to field volunteer deployment.

According to the organisation, Crisis Connect Nepal has been formed to address critical gaps in Nepal’s emergency management system. By combining a centralised digital command system with a network of certified volunteers, CCN aims to enable rapid, independent deployment during emergencies, from small, localised incidents to national-scale disasters.

“Crisis Connect Nepal is founded out of a fundamental need to bridge the critical first-hour gap when disasters strike,” said Pandey. “Our focus is to build a reliable, tech-enabled network of certified volunteers across Nepal who deploy autonomously and deliver life-saving search, rescue, and relief operations alongside local authorities.”

The organization’s governance structure includes the 21 voting Charter Members, an executive Board of Directors, and a non-executive Advisory Board covering seven strategic areas, among them disaster risk reduction, emergency medicine, GIS technology, resource mobilisation, and non-profit governance.

title.rendered: Government to spend Rs 136.76 million annually on free legal aid

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The government is estimated to spend Rs 136.76 million annually to implement the proposed Free Legal Aid Bill, 2083.

Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sobita Gautam registered the bill in the House of Representatives on September 18. The bill proposes providing legal aid to disadvantaged people through coordination among the federal, provincial and local levels.

It provides for the establishment of the National Legal Aid Council, an executive committee, and provincial and district legal aid committees. The proposed law would expand the existing scope and structure of free legal aid services, resulting in an additional financial burden on the government.

Of the estimated annual expenditure, Rs 43.72 million has been allocated for salaries of non-gazetted first-class employees in 65 districts and officer-level employees in all 77 districts through district legal aid committee offices. Additional expenses will be incurred for office operations and salaries of office assistants.

An estimated Rs 56.36 million will be spent on managing paid legal practitioners, while Rs 7.5 million has been allocated for meetings of the National Legal Aid Council. The council, chaired by the Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, is expected to meet 15 times a year.

Similarly, Rs 4.5 million has been estimated for meetings of the executive committee and Rs 1.5 million for the secretariat expenses of the council and executive committee.

The Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs said Rs 104.45 million is currently being spent on legal aid committees and paid legal practitioners. Implementation of the proposed bill would therefore increase the annual financial burden by an estimated Rs 48.71 million.

The ministry said the estimate does not include expenses for legal aid provided under the Senior Citizens Act, 2063, Domestic Violence (Offence and Punishment) Act, 2066, and Act Relating to Rights of Persons with Disabilities, 2074. It also excludes legal aid costs covered by the Nepal Bar Association and non-governmental organisations.

The estimate does not include office rent, as legal aid offices are currently housed in existing government and legal institutions in some districts.

title.rendered: Two lawsuits filed alleging copyright infringement against songwriters

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The government has filed a lawsuit at Kathmandu District Court against music company Sagarmatha Digital Pvt. Ltd., alleging that the copyright of two songwriters was infringed.

The Office of the Government Attorney, Kathmandu, filed two separate copyright-related cases against the company, seeking 9.5 million rupees in damages and other compensation.

According to the charge sheet filed by the Government Attorney’s Office, the company is accused of infringing the copyright of songwriters Saroj KC and Shashi Sharma Majgaiyan. The complaint seeks damages of 3.5 million rupees for KC and 6 million rupees for Majgaiyan.

The two songwriters have accused the company’s director, Hira Bahadur KC, of taking unauthorised control over their songs, using and commercially exploiting them without permission, and concealing income earned from their creative work, amounting to fraud. The case was filed following an investigation into their complaint.

Songwriter KC stated in his complaint that the company failed to disclose any earnings from several songs he wrote, including one referenced in the complaint, claiming there was no income at all, and that he had repeatedly been deceived and defrauded.

Songwriter Majgaiyan stated in his complaint that several songs he wrote were used and controlled without his permission, and alleged that the accused company earned income from them without authorisation. He has sought damages and compensation on that basis.

In this case, the Government Attorney has recommended that the defendant be punished according to law, in line with the complainants’ demands.

title.rendered: Spain’s Nepali and Spanish communities unite in tribute to flood victims

content.rendered:
Barcelona, September 20

Nepali and Spanish communities across several Spanish cities have come together in memory of those killed or missing in Nepal’s flood disaster. From Benidorm, a tourist town in the Costa Blanca region, to Barcelona, residents and elected officials joined tribute events.

More than a hundred Nepalis and local Spanish residents took part in a candle-lighting ceremony organised Thursday evening by the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) Spain in Benidorm.

Local officials in attendance included Benidorm Mayor Antonio “Toni” Pérez and Social Welfare Councillor Ángela Zaragozí, among others.

Participants lit hundreds of candles in tribute to those killed or gone missing in Nepal.

Benidorm Municipality to provide €8,000 aid

Expressing solidarity with the Nepali community, Benidorm’s municipal government also decided to contribute €8,000 (NPR 14,07,272) to support those affected by the disaster.

The day after the Benidorm event, a tribute program was also held in Barcelona with participation from both the Nepali and Spanish communities.

The Barcelona event took place in two parts. In the first part, members of the Nepali and Spanish communities jointly performed kirtan (devotional chanting), with Spanish residents joining alongside the Nepali community. This was followed by a lamp-lighting ceremony in the second part.

Over 2 million rupees collected

Members of the Nepali and Spanish communities lit lamps together in tribute to the deceased. Participants prayed for the eternal peace of the departed souls and expressed condolences to the grieving families.

NRNA Spain President Santosh Shrestha said that while there had been plans to hold part of the event outdoors with placards drawing attention to the rising frequency of such disasters in Nepal due to climate change, delays in getting local permits meant the program had to be held indoors instead.

Shrestha said NRNA Spain has collected more than 2 million rupees for those affected by the disaster and is preparing to send the funds to Nepal soon. He added that Nepalis in Spain, along with various organisations, are also continuing to raise funds both individually and institutionally.

title.rendered: Free Legal Aid Bill registered in Parliament

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The Free Legal Aid Bill, 2083 BS, has been registered in the House of Representatives.

Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam registered the bill in the House of Representatives on September 18.

Article 20 of the Constitution of Nepal guarantees the right to justice as a fundamental right. An Integrated Legal Aid Policy was issued in 2019 under this provision. The Ministry of Law said the bill has been introduced to implement the policy.

The proposed bill broadens the scope of disadvantaged people eligible for free legal aid. It also expands free legal aid services to all courts, judicial bodies and quasi-judicial bodies.

The bill provides for the right of disadvantaged people to receive free legal consultation and advice, as well as legal assistance during case proceedings, hearings and the implementation of court decisions.

It also guarantees free legal aid from the time of arrest to people arrested in criminal cases who cannot afford to hire a lawyer themselves.

The bill requires sign language to be used when providing free legal aid to people with hearing, speech or communication-related disabilities. It also provides for psychosocial counselling services to disadvantaged people as needed.

According to the bill, legal aid services for disadvantaged people will be operated through coordination among the federal, provincial and local levels.

It states that agencies providing legal aid must provide such services in an integrated manner. The ministry will develop and implement an electronic system for free legal aid to make the service more effective and integrated.

The bill also provides for legal aid services from subject-matter experts to improve the quality of free legal assistance.

The proposed bill establishes the National Legal Aid Council, an executive committee, and provincial and district legal aid committees.

It also proposes encouraging lawyers to provide voluntary free legal aid, or pro bono services. Non-governmental organisations willing to provide free legal aid will be able to do so after registering with the concerned district committee.

Minister Gautam has stated in the bill, “As these issues cannot be addressed merely by amending the existing law, I have presented this bill as it is necessary to enact a new law concerning free legal aid.”

title.rendered: Nepal’s flood survivors need homes, not holding centres

content.rendered:
Through years of working alongside land-poor and displaced communities, I have learned that recovery is measured not by the relief we hand out, but by whether families can live again with dignity, security and hope.

The flash floods that struck Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading on August 26 took far more than homes and roads. In the worst-affected settlements, many people have died or remain missing.

Survivors have lost their homes, land, livelihoods and, in many cases, several members of their families. People are still searching along riverbanks and in forests, hoping that even a body can be recovered so that final rites can be performed with dignity.

A different kind of humanitarian crisis

The usual approach to delivering relief — reaching one household at a time and assessing each family’s losses — does not fully fit what has happened here.

In Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, families themselves have been scattered. Some members have died or are missing. Others have moved in with relatives, while some are staying in holding centres. In some places, the population has been dramatically reduced.

Many displaced families are sheltering in schools that are now serving as holding centres. As schools prepare to reopen, the question is becoming increasingly urgent: where will these families go?

Two weeks on, many still have no answer. In some places, even a verified list of those affected has yet to be drawn up.

This is why the first priority should be people and families — not only relief commodities.

One affected family member staying at the holding centre at Bhimsensthan Basic School in Uttargaya asked a simple but critical question: “You are bringing relief to us, but where will we put it? Where will we go when the school reopens?”

From holding centres to dignified living

The government and humanitarian agencies have distributed significant amounts of relief assistance. Food, water, hygiene supplies, blankets and other essentials remain vital in the immediate aftermath. But relief alone cannot resolve the current crisis.

People cannot remain in holding centres indefinitely.

One practical option would be to provide rental assistance for six months to one year to families who can safely find accommodation in nearby communities or cities. This could help many of those now living in holding centres move quickly into more stable family surroundings.

But rental support is only the first step.

Many of the families hit hardest had little or no land of their own even before the flood. Some had been resettled on these very riverbanks after losing their homes in earlier disasters. For them, real recovery will depend on secure land — safe plots where they can rebuild with proper tenure, rather than return to ground the river has already taken.

For those who cannot access rental housing, temporary shelters will be necessary. But these arrangements should not become permanent camps. They should be connected to a clear recovery plan built around secure land and housing, while also addressing livelihoods, education, health and protection.

With strong coordination between the government, humanitarian organisations, development partners and local communities, there is a realistic possibility of supporting many families to move towards more permanent housing within a year.

But this requires a common mission, clear responsibilities and coordinated resources rather than fragmented interventions.

Cash is a humanitarian need too

Another major gap is cash assistance.

People who have lost everything need more than food and blankets. They need clothes, medicines, transportation and other basic necessities. Families searching for missing relatives or recovering bodies may have to travel from one location to another. People who have lost access to regular medicines need immediate access to them.

Cash assistance gives affected people the flexibility and dignity to address their needs according to their own priorities.

During our visit, some elderly women told us they were not comfortable with the clothes distributed as relief because they were different from what they normally wore. They wanted to buy the traditional clothes they were accustomed to wearing, but they had no cash to do so.

A young man shared another deeply painful reality: “Today is the 13th day since the death of my family member, but I do not have even a single rupee to buy incense (dhup) for the ritual and prayers.”

These experiences show that cash is not simply financial assistance. It gives affected families the choice and dignity to meet their immediate needs in ways that external relief cannot always anticipate.

Yet many affected families have not received direct cash support. This creates additional hardship at a time when people are already experiencing enormous emotional and financial stress.

Humanitarian assistance should restore dignity and choice, not only provide commodities.

Listening to affected families

Perhaps the most important lesson is that recovery cannot be designed entirely from outside affected communities.

Affected families and local governments must be directly involved in recovery and reconstruction decisions. These people know their land, settlements, livelihoods, risks and priorities better than anyone sitting outside the disaster area.

Consultation must go beyond simply informing people about decisions that have already been made. Their views must influence the decisions themselves.

Solutions developed by people who have not experienced the disaster, without properly listening to survivors, are unlikely to respond to the realities on the ground.

We need to listen to affected families — not only through technical assessments, but with empathy and from the heart.

Recovery should not be something that is done for affected people. It should be done with them.

From relief to resilient recovery

The international community and Nepal’s development partners have an important role beyond the immediate relief operation.

The financial resources already mobilised must reach affected families effectively and transparently. But resources should also support the longer-term recovery of housing, land, livelihoods and community infrastructure.

At the same time, this disaster requires serious study. We need to understand what happened, why the consequences were so severe, which early-warning and preparedness mechanisms worked or failed, and how similar risks can be reduced in the future.

The findings should form a strong case for greater international investment in disaster preparedness, early-warning systems, climate resilience, risk reduction and safer infrastructure.

The tragedy in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading reminds us that disasters destroy far more than buildings. They can tear apart families and livelihoods, erase memories and undermine people’s sense of security.

Therefore, the recovery response must be measured not by how many relief packages are distributed, but by whether affected people can once again live safely, with dignity, security and hope.

The immediate task is to find the missing, support the survivors and provide safe and dignified living conditions.

The larger task is to rebuild lives, restore livelihoods and ensure that communities are better prepared for the next disaster.

title.rendered: Environmental Diplomacy Section established at Ministry of Foreign Affairs

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has established an Environmental Diplomacy Section for the first time, aimed at institutionalising and strengthening diplomatic efforts related to climate and the environment.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal’s secretariat said the ministry decided to establish the section in response to current needs, given the impact of climate change.

Based on the ministry’s Organisation and Management (O&M) survey, the section will operate under the “Economic, Social Development and Environmental Diplomacy Section” structure within the UN and Specialised Agencies Division.

Nepal has continuously and actively participated in national, regional, and international forums on climate change and environmental protection. The section has been established to advance these efforts in a coordinated and institutionalised manner. The new section will facilitate international diplomatic initiatives on climate and environmental issues and coordinate with relevant national bodies.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said climate diplomacy should not be limited merely to participation in international conferences and events, but should instead be pursued as a long-term, institutional priority.

He said that focusing only on participation in UN climate change conferences or similar events would not strengthen the country’s climate diplomacy capacity.

title.rendered: License printing begins under new system

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Printing of vehicle driving licenses has begun through the Electronic Driving License and Vehicle Registration System (EDLVRS), which the government implemented on June 15.

The Department of Transport Management, under the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, launched the printing process through the new system to address service-seeker congestion and the long-standing problem of license printing delays.

The new system will make both new license issuance and renewal faster, smoother, and more service-oriented. Under the arrangement, applicant details uploaded to the EDLVRS go directly to the Security Printing Press, which prints the licenses and sends them via postal service to the respective Transport Management Service Office.

The ministry says this will resolve the long-standing problems with license printing and distribution.

In the first phase, 3,081 driving licenses from Madhesh Province have been printed and sent through the postal service to the relevant Transport Management Service Office for distribution. Provincial governments have also been given the option to sign their own agreements with Surakshan Mudran to handle printing independently.

Accordingly, the Madhesh Province government has signed such an agreement with Surakshan Mudran and is managing its own license printing. Similarly, the Lumbini Province government also signed an agreement with Surakshan Mudran on Friday and has begun printing driving licenses.

In provinces that have not signed agreements with Security Printing Press, license printing is being coordinated between the Department of Transport Management and Surakshan Mudran directly, taking into account service-seeker congestion and related issues.

With license printing now underway through the new system, responsibility for printing is being managed province-wise, putting into effect a system meant to provide driving licenses to service seekers more conveniently, quickly, and on time.

content.rendered:

Bang Chan, a member of the K-pop group Stray Kids, has donated 200 million won (about $144,295). JYP Entertainment announced on Saturday that the funds will go toward rehabilitation care in South Korea and recovery efforts following the devastating flood in Nepal.

Bang Chan donated 100 million won each to Seoul Rehabilitation Hospital and the Korean Committee for UNICEF.

The donation to Seoul Rehabilitation Hospital will be used to establish specialised rehabilitation centres tailored to patients’ age and health conditions. The funds given to UNICEF Korea will go toward recovery efforts for communities affected by the recent major flood in Nepal.

In a statement released through JYP Entertainment, Bang Chan said, “I wanted to offer even a small measure of comfort to those going through an exhausting and difficult time.” He added, “I sincerely hope as many people as possible can return to a peaceful daily life as soon as possible.”

Bang Chan has continued to donate steadily in recent years.

Last year, on October 3, to mark his birthday, he donated 100 million won to Samsung Medical Centre to cover treatment costs for pediatric patients, along with another 100 million won to UNICEF Korea for children worldwide.

In 2024, he donated 100 million won to the Community Chest of Korea for people with disabilities, becoming a member of the organization’s major-donor group, the “Honour Society.”

title.rendered: Oral cholera vaccination campaign launched in flood-affected areas

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 20

An oral cholera vaccination campaign has been launched in Nuwakot following the recent floods and the increased risk of cholera in the affected areas.

The campaign has vaccinated more than 50,000 people so far, with a target of reaching more than 77,000 residents in the affected areas.

The campaign, led by the Public Health Office in coordination with the Epidemiology and Disease Control Division, aims to prevent the spread of cholera and other water-borne diseases amid worsening drinking water and sanitation conditions following the Bhotekoshi floods on August 26.

Dr Anju Karki, chief of the Public Health Office, stressed the need for safe water practices, personal hygiene and a clean environment alongside vaccination efforts.

The floods have displaced many people from their homes, increasing the risk of cholera, particularly in holding centres where maintaining proper sanitation is difficult. The detection of E. coli in local water sources has further raised concerns over water-borne diseases.

Recent water testing in Bidur Municipality found E. coli contamination in five of 15 local water samples following the floods.

In response, the emergency vaccination campaign is targeting everyone above the age of one. The vaccine is being provided free of charge at health facilities and holding centres.

Health officials said 40,291 people have already been vaccinated in municipalities, and efforts are underway to reach residents in remote areas who face higher risks.

The vaccination programme will continue for seven days. Health officials have urged residents to get vaccinated and seek prompt medical attention if they develop symptoms of cholera.

They have also advised residents to boil or purify drinking water, keep food preparation areas clean and maintain hygienic living conditions to prevent the spread of water-borne diseases in the aftermath of the floods.

title.rendered: Meteorologists warn of heavy rain nationwide from Thursday

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

Some meteorologists have forecast that rainfall activity could increase across Nepal from September 24 to 28, due to a low-pressure system developing in the Bay of Bengal. They say certain areas could see extremely heavy rainfall and have stressed the need for preparation and caution.

Binod Pokharel, a hydrologist and meteorologist at Tribhuvan University, said his study of various forecast models suggests a strong likelihood of rainfall nationwide from September 24 to 28.

He noted on social media that some models project over 400 mm of rainfall during that period, with certain scenarios showing as much as 741 mm. However, he expects this rainfall to be concentrated in specific areas rather than spread evenly across the country.

“I’m making this forecast public only after looking at many forecast models,” Pokharel wrote. “This isn’t meant to scare anyone; it’s meant to help everyone prepare quickly.”

According to Pokharel, as the monsoon begins withdrawing from northwestern India, dry winds from that region could affect the movement of the low-pressure system coming from the Bay of Bengal. He said this could push its impact toward Nepal, raising the risk of heavy rainfall in some areas.

Bigger impact around September 24-28

Meteorologist and environmental expert Ujjwal Upadhyay also said the weather system developing in the Bay of Bengal needs close watching. He noted that most currently available forecast models show a serious situation from September 24 to 28.

According to Upadhyay, indications point to September 26 as the day of highest risk. However, he cautioned against treating the current forecast as final.

“I’m still hopeful the potentially severe rain of September 24 to 26 might ease somewhat,” Upadhyay wrote on Facebook, ” but measured against nearly all currently available models, the situation looks alarming.”

He also pointed to last year’s example as a reason forecasted risk could diminish by the time it plays out. He noted that the “Montha” cyclone in November last year, despite being powerful along India’s eastern coast, had weakened into a low-pressure system by the time it reached Nepal, resulting in far less damage than anticipated. “I’m hoping for a similar kind of fortune this time,” he wrote.

He urged the public not to panic over the potential risk, but to remain highly alert. “Let’s not fear, let’s not panic, let’s stay aware, let’s be as careful as possible,” he said.

Upadhyay also suggested it may be wise to postpone long-distance travel on September 24, 25, and 26 in areas outside the Far West. However, he said the actual intensity of the rain and which areas would be most affected isn’t yet clear.

Meteorological Department says it’s monitoring closely

Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology said it is closely monitoring the weather system developing in the Bay of Bengal.

“Systems like this sometimes fade into a depression and change direction,” senior department meteorologist Barun Paudel told OnlineKhabar. “But we’re watching it very closely and with real concern.”

He said the department would have more clarity on its impact in the coming days.

He said that once there is more clarity about the system’s effect on Nepal, the department will share the necessary information through an official notice.

He added that although there’s growing discussion on social media about heavy rain from September 24 to 28, it will take a few more days before a conclusion can be drawn about the exact amount of rainfall, its geographic spread, and the level of risk. According to him, how the low-pressure system develops, and any changes in its direction and strength in the coming days, will determine its actual impact on Nepal.

Meteorologists say that if the rainfall occurs as forecast, it could also affect the agriculture sector, particularly ripened paddy crops, and have urged farmers to stay alert.

If it becomes a cyclone, it will be named “Arnab”

India’s Meteorological Department has said that a system formed over northern Thailand and adjoining Myanmar is likely to develop into a low-pressure area over the north Andaman Sea within the next 48 hours.

The system is then expected to move toward the central Bay of Bengal and could develop into a depression or deep depression by September 22.

Since a weather system forming in the Bay of Bengal could also affect India’s eastern coastal region, monitoring has been increased in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, and West Bengal.

If the system developing in the Bay of Bengal turns into a cyclone, it will be the first tropical cyclone of the 2026 North Indian Ocean season.

In that case, according to the World Meteorological Organization’s North Indian Ocean cyclone naming list, it will be named “Arnab”, a name contributed by Bangladesh.

title.rendered: Mustang sees drop in tourist arrivals after Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Mustang, September 20

Tourism in Mustang has witnessed a slowdown in the aftermath of the floods that struck the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system on August 26.

The District Police Office, Mustang, said the district saw a significant decline in arrivals of both domestic and foreign tourists in the month of Bhadra (August 17 to September 16) compared to the corresponding period last year.

The district welcomed a total of 31,989 tourists in Bhadra, a decline of 29,274 from the corresponding period last year and a 47.78 per cent drop from the previous month.

The ongoing challenges posed by blocked roads along the Kaligandaki Corridor due to flooding and river erosion have further worsened the situation.

In the month of Saun, Mustang welcomed 61,263 tourists, including 30,655 domestic tourists, 31,575 from SAARC countries and 193 from other countries.

However, the number dropped to 31,989 in Bhadra, including 16,503 domestic visitors, 15,138 from SAARC countries and 348 from other countries.

Tourist arrivals have declined following the Rasuwa floods, with the number of domestic tourists dropping by 46.16 per cent and arrivals from the SAARC region decreasing by 52.05 per cent.

However, the number of tourists from other countries increased, with 348 tourists visiting the district this year compared to 193 in the previous season, an increase of 155.

Overall, the District Police Office reported that 93,252 tourists have so far visited Mustang this year, including 47,158 domestic tourists, 46,713 from SAARC countries and 441 from other countries.

title.rendered: ‘Shared Dreams Woven by Struggle’, documenting struggles of 13 women leaders launched

content.rendered:
Lalitpur, September 18

A research book documenting the lives, struggles and contributions of 13 women leaders involved in Nepal’s social movements was launched in Lalitpur on Friday.

Titled Shared Dreams Woven by Struggle, the book brings together personal stories of women who challenged discrimination, organised communities and fought for rights, dignity and social justice.

The book features the story of Umadevi Badi and her struggle for land, rights and dignity as part of the Badi community’s rights movement. It also documents the journey of Muskan Khatun, an acid attack survivor who has continued her struggle for justice and dignity.

Some of the stories focus on the Sino Bahishkar Movement, which has gradually faded from public memory. The experiences of Mahari Devi, Bhola Devi and Chandeshwori Sada, who were involved in the movement, document women’s efforts to challenge caste-based discrimination and demand equality and dignity.

Speaking at the launch, Sunita Dangol, acting mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, said documenting women’s experiences was an important part of the struggle for women’s rights. She said recording such histories would help establish women’s own narratives in a society where their struggles and voices are often questioned.

Following the launch, a panel discussion titled “Women Leaders and Social Movements: Reflections and Practices” was held with activists, academics, researchers and representatives from different fields.

The book, published by Voices of Women Media, seeks to preserve the histories of women involved in Nepal’s social movements and highlight their contributions to social change.

title.rendered: NPL awaits ICC sanction as CAN prepares for first-ever DRS

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 20

The Nepal Premier League (NPL) could feature the Decision Review System (DRS) for the first time this season, with the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) currently assessing available technology.

The schedule for the third edition of the NPL was announced on Saturday, while franchises have already begun signing overseas players ahead of the tournament.

Kathmandu Gorkhas have completed the biggest signing in NPL history by bringing in former Australia captain David Warner. Other international names, including Jimmy Neesham, Shakib Al Hasan, Sikandar Raza and Charith Asalanka, have also been confirmed for the upcoming season.

The arrival of high-profile overseas players has increased interest in the tournament, with excitement also growing among Nepali cricket supporters.

CAN Secretary Paras Khadka said preparations were underway to introduce DRS in the NPL for the first time.

According to Khadka, the association has already tested technology from two companies and will make a final decision after evaluating its accuracy.

“We have tested systems from two companies. Now, once we get the final assessment of their accuracy, we will decide which company to work with. If the technology is found to be reliable, we can start DRS from this edition,” Khadka said.

He said a full-scale DRS system similar to the one used in international tournaments such as the World Cup would require significant resources, but CAN was exploring a reliable system suitable for a domestic league.

“The DRS used in the World Cup requires considerable resources. But if there is a reliable system that can be used for the first time in Nepal, we are in favour of implementing it,” he said.

DRS allows teams to challenge certain umpiring decisions and have them reviewed using available technology.

ICC sanction process nearing completion

Khadka also said the process of obtaining ICC sanction for the NPL has reached its final stage.

He said several international players, including Warner, Shakib Al Hasan, Sikandar Raza and Ravi Bopara, have already been signed, while further high-profile names will be announced after the tournament receives ICC sanction.

“There is a lot of interest, so various names have emerged. But it would not be appropriate to speculate until the official announcements are made. Once the sanction is received, the franchises will gradually announce all their players,” Khadka said.

If the NPL receives ICC recognition, players’ performances could be officially recorded in their careers, depending on the classification granted to the tournament.

Khadka said it could receive List A or T20 status.

Performances from the first two editions of the NPL have not been counted in players’ official career records.

ODI status and Test nations among CAN’s priorities

Khadka said Nepal’s upcoming four matches in the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 are currently the association’s biggest priority.

He said Nepal needs strong results to retain its ODI status, while CAN is also preparing for a possible push towards the playoffs.

Meanwhile, the process for a series involving India A and Bangladesh has already moved forward, while proposals have also been sent to other Test-playing nations for bilateral series.

“Our cricket calendar for 2027 is almost ready. We will make it public once the formal decisions are made,” Khadka said.

Khadka also urged Nepali supporters to continue backing the national team.

“Whether we lose by one run or win by one run, no one is more concerned about it than the players themselves. Nepali cricket has reached this point through this struggle, so trust and support are our greatest strength right now,” he said.

title.rendered: Thanks, Trump: Why Canada may become the European Union’s first ever ‘associate member’

content.rendered:
Can a country change continents? Canada seems set to try.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced an intention to seek some novel form of associate membership in the European Union. It’s no mere flight of fancy, either, as Ursula von der Leyen, president of the EU Commission, has already endorsed the idea.

It’s a proposal that manages to be both absurd and eminently logical, depending on how you frame it. Geographically, Canada remains firmly affixed to North America, sharing a border with its increasingly unpredictable neighbour to the south, the United States.

In other important ways, however, Canada clearly has much more in common in recent months with European countries than the unstable U.S. That’s because in the space of a year, America has gone from Canada’s most important friend and ally on the world stage to the clearest threat to Canadian sovereignty.

By deepening links with other European democracies, Carney clearly hopes to buy Canada a degree of insurance against continuing American intervention and hostility from U.S. President Donald Trump. There’s a logic to the argument.

Middle powers coming together

In fact, in many ways this proposal is very much in keeping with Canada’s multilateral approach to international politics since the Cold War era. This is a history Carney clearly invoked when he spoke about the need for middle powers to forge their own path together in his landmark speech to Davos earlier in the year.

Canada, then as now, is not a match for the greatest powers in the world. But working with other like-minded states, it can find ways to defend itself and amplify its power. The difference, of course, is that now the U.S. is no longer one of those allies but, instead, Canada’s biggest threat.

That threat cannot be underestimated, either. While observers like myself have been warning of the danger ever since Justin Trudeau’s ill-fated mission of supplication to Mar-A-Lago prompted Trump’s 51st state joke, the scale and severity of the problem has become impossible to ignore.

The latest trade negotiations have made that clear. From ugly jokes and offensive maps, the Trump administration has proceeded to make more concrete demands of fealty.

Even before taking office, Trump was inventing border drug-trafficking problems for Canada to solve — a grievance the president continues to return to.

More recent trade negotiations included demands that amounted to the surrender of Canadian sovereignty. They included a veto over who Canada trades with internationally, an entrenched dependency on the U.S. for defence procurement and security provision and, incredibly, even an attempt to interfere with official Canadian bilingualism.

Looking for help elsewhere

Along the way, Canada has watched figures close to Trump pumping up the idea of Alberta’s secession and the U.S. ambassador treating Canadians with utter contempt. Worst of all, Canada has had precious little in the way of support even from Americans who are sympathetic.

The message is clear: Americans have been cowed by a bullying administration with no respect for Canada or Canadians. If Canada wishes to defend its sovereignty, it must look for help elsewhere. No country is more vulnerable than the one without allies.

That brings us back to a more European-allied Canada.

The European Union is the world’s foremost club of democracies and economic force in the world. When European states can co-operate politically — not always a given — they are a force to rival the other great powers of the world.

Canada also has long ties to Europe, not only cultural connections in the form of a shared heritage for many — though far from all — Canadians, but through diplomatic and defence collaboration in numerous international institutions. Those organizations include NATO, the United Nations, the G7, la Francophonie and many others.

As democracies that are facing shared vulnerabilities from increasingly assertive authoritarian regimes, Canada and EU member states have a mutual interest in protecting one another and collaborating to defend democratic values and institutions.

Potential risks, drawbacks

There are many unanswered questions about Canada becoming an associate member of the EU, and some real risks associated with the idea as well. European Union membership is not without its drawbacks, as Brexit clearly demonstrated just a decade ago.

The United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, and while that was an economically problematic decision, it was not without its logical arguments in favour. EU membership remains controversial because pooling sovereignty requires sacrifice: nations trade away unilateral control in exchange for shared, broader gains.

This is not a minor point. The loss of control over decision-making is, in no small measure, what Canada is objecting to in trade negotiations with the U.S. While it’s far too early to know what goes into associate membership, Carney will need to be careful to ensure steps are taken to prevent Canadian populists from finding a new distant target in Brussels.

Harmonizing policy with European allies would also likely become a further barrier to trade with the U.S. While it’s clear Canada can no longer rely on a trusting relationship with its southern neighbour, the two countries will remained joined at the hip, and the U.S. will likely remain Canada’s biggest trading partner as a function not only of geography, but decades of investment and policy.

As much as Canada needs friends, it’s important for the country to proceed in a way that does not blow up its relationship with the U.S.

Asian trade

Finally, Canada must be careful not to lose sight of the fact that millions of Canadians trace their heritage to places far beyond Europe.

The Pacific Rim remains Canada’s largest source of trade outside the U.S., and the democracies of the region are in many ways caught in a situation more analogous to Canada’s own than the countries of the EU.

Japan, South Korea, Australia and Taiwan are, like Canada, caught between U.S. and Chinese influence and must find a way to walk that line. Accordingly, in its search for friends, Canada cannot be too narrow-minded or historically oriented. Europe is Canada’s past, but the Pacific Rim looms large in its future.

One thing is clear, however. Canada’s prime minister understands that the world has changed; the old normal is not coming back. Canada is in a fight for its existence and is acting accordingly.

title.rendered: A Nepali teacher’s long road into America’s healthcare system

content.rendered:
When Dr Dharma Padhyaya first arrived in the United States, he did not begin with a prestigious job in data engineering. Like many Nepalis, he began behind the counter of a 7-Eleven.

The store in Boston sold vegetables, tea, coffee and everyday groceries. For five months, Padhyaya worked there, learning how American workplaces functioned and trying to find his footing in a country where almost everything was unfamiliar.

It was a modest beginning for someone who would go on to work with some of the largest healthcare organisations in the United States.

Today, Padhyaya is a data engineer and analytics specialist whose career has taken him through cancer research and treatment, hospital systems, health insurance and public health. He has worked in senior data roles and, at one point, secured a position with the US Department of Health and Human Services after competing against around 5,000 applicants.

But the path to that position began much earlier, in a remote corner of Nepal.

From Bajhang to Boston

Dharma Padhyaya was born on November 23, 1985, in Sutiya, in what is now Jayaprithvi Municipality-7 of Bajhang district in far-western Nepal.

His formal education began in his village.

After studying up to Grade 8 at Sunipapal Secondary School, he moved to Dhangadhi, where he completed Grades 9 and 10 at Sharada Secondary School. He then studied at Kailali Multiple Campus before completing a master’s degree in science at Siddhanath Science Campus in Kanchanpur.

He had been drawn to teaching from an early age.

After completing his SLC, he began teaching and went on to work at Stepping English Boarding School and Stone Bridge in Dhangadhi, as well as Gyanodaya English School in Dadeldhura.

For roughly a decade, teaching was his profession. America, however, was becoming his ambition.

Every year, he applied for the US Diversity Visa programme. In 2013, while he was still pursuing his postgraduate studies, his name was selected.

In September that year, he left Nepal for the United States with his wife.

The dream had finally acquired a destination. The reality, he soon discovered, would require considerably more work.

Starting again

Dharma Padhyaya had studied science in Nepal, and he knew that working in a convenience store could support him but was unlikely to take him where he wanted to go.

So while working at 7-Eleven, he began studying information technology.

He completed a three-month course in data engineering. That led to his first opportunity in the field, with CoGent Data Solutions, a communications-related company.

He worked on data collection and business reporting and, in 2014, spent six months working for two companies at the same time.

By the end of that year, another opportunity took him to California.

At City of Hope National Medical Center, a cancer treatment and research centre, he joined as a senior data engineer.

It was a significant shift.

His work was no longer simply about managing information. He was working with data related to patient treatment, service effectiveness and patient satisfaction, using that information to help improve healthcare delivery.

He stayed there for around five years.

During the same period, he continued building his academic qualifications.

He completed a Master of Project Management from the American Academy of Project Management, a Master of Science from the University of Phoenix and a Master of Science in Information Technology from the same university.

His career was moving in parallel with his education.

When data became a healthcare tool

After five years at City of Hope, Dharma Padhyaya moved to Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, a healthcare system operating more than 25 hospitals across the state.

He joined as director of data management and analytics.

The scale of the job was considerably larger.

His responsibility was to bring together data from hospitals across the network and use it to analyse treatment systems, identify problems, help doctors act proactively and assess how effectively hospital services were being delivered.

“At least 25 hospitals were under my direct responsibility for monitoring and analysing data and implementing plans based on that analysis,” Padhyaya says.

He worked there until 2021, continuing to build both his professional and academic credentials.

Over two and a half years, he completed a PhD in Information Technology Systems as well as a postgraduate degree in Business Administration. He received a full scholarship for his MBA.

Then another offer arrived.

Padhyaya joined UnitedHealth Group in Minnetonka, Minnesota, a company involved in health insurance and healthcare services and one of the world’s largest companies.

Again, his work centred on data.

But the role was broad. Alongside data analysis, he worked across data science, data engineering, reporting, writing and business analytics. His work also included cardiovascular analytics and neurological studies.

The thread running through all of it was the same — using large amounts of information to understand healthcare systems and make them work more effectively.

A race against 5,000 applicants

One of the most significant stages of Padhyaya’s career came with the US Department of Health and Human Services.

He secured a position as an IT specialist and head of data architecture management and analytics after an open competition involving around 5,000 people.

The job brought together the two fields that had shaped his American career — technology and healthcare.

His responsibilities included managing data and analysing information, as well as work related to evaluating the quality of medicines and approving pharmaceutical products. He was also involved in reviewing and approving biological products and medicines and in improving the efficiency of services.

Dharma Padhyaya says his work helped the organisation reduce unnecessary expenditure and save around $20 million.

His experience in data analysis, he says, was central to that work.

But even after reaching a position that many immigrants spend years trying to attain, Padhyaya did not stop moving.

After completing his PhD last year, he left the organisation and joined another healthcare-related institution working in the field of eating recovery, mood and anxiety.

Based in Denver, Colorado, the organisation provides AI-based behavioural health services and has expanded to 40 US states.

Padhyaya took on the role of head of data science and advanced analytics.

His work there involved analysing data related to eating disorders and human behaviour and using evidence and information to develop programmes related to mental healthcare.

Building something of his own

Dharma Padhyaya’s career in the US has not been confined to large institutions.

He also owns Lamanya Group, through which he works in data engineering. He serves as an adviser to various organisations in the United States.

Over the years, his work has increasingly centred on the intersection of data and healthcare — from electronic medical records to patient safety and treatment systems.

For him, data is not simply a technical resource.

Used properly, it can help identify problems in healthcare systems, measure whether services are working and guide decisions that affect patients.

His experience has also given him a more complicated view of the American dream.

The United States, he says, offers opportunities, but those opportunities come with intense competition.

“It is a land of opportunity,” he says. “But in such a competitive environment, opportunities can only be secured through competition. Anyone coming here from anywhere in the world has to change not only their surroundings but also their mindset.”

For Nepalis, he says, adapting is particularly important.

“People have to leave behind their natural way of doing things. You have to keep playing on a field of constant struggle. My struggle is still continuing.”

Looking back towards Nepal

More than a decade after arriving in America, Padhyaya’s ambitions have begun to point in the opposite direction.

He wants to use what he has learned in the United States to contribute to Nepal.

His particular interest is healthcare.

Years of working with American hospitals and healthcare organisations have given him experience in using data to develop plans, analyse services and improve healthcare systems. He believes some of those lessons could be useful in Nepal.

“I have worked in the American healthcare system through data for many years,” he says. “I feel I have played a significant role in improving the health system through different plans and strategies.”

Now he wants to see whether that experience can travel home.

“I would like to work on improving Nepal’s healthcare sector based on what I have learned here. If circumstances allow, I believe it will certainly be possible one day.”

The boy who began his education in a remote village of Bajhang, the teacher who spent years in Nepali classrooms, and the immigrant who once worked at a 7-Eleven have travelled a long way.

His next destination, he hopes, may be home.

title.rendered: Infectious disease risks rise in Rasuwa flood-hit areas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

The risk of infectious diseases has increased in areas affected by the Rasuwa floods, with 81 people diagnosed with diarrhoea at various holding centres over the past three weeks.

Dr Sameer Adhikari, spokesperson for the Ministry of Health, said the risk of infection has increased because of problems with drinking water and sanitation, a lack of properly managed toilets and overcrowding at temporary shelters and holding centres.

“Cases of diarrhoea have been reported among people staying at the holding centres. It has not spread to the extent of a major outbreak or epidemic,” Adhikari told Onlinekhabar. “However, the risk of infection is higher because of the temporary living conditions, so we are taking precautions.”

The risk of infectious diseases typically rises in areas affected by floods and landslides. Public health experts say floodwaters can contaminate water sources and food, increasing the possibility of waterborne diseases.

Diarrhoea, cholera, flu, typhoid, dengue, leptospirosis, viral hepatitis and various skin infections are among the diseases that can become more common following such disasters.

Fever cases also reported

Some flood-affected people staying at Shivalaya Basic School in Uttargaya Rural Municipality of Rasuwa have also developed fever.

Prakash Nepal, a teacher at Nilkantha Secondary School, said the number of people with fever has increased in recent days.

“Five to seven people at the holding centre have developed fever,” Nepal told Onlinekhabar. “Uttargaya-5 Ward Chairperson Eknath Acharya became seriously ill with fever and was airlifted to Kathmandu for further treatment.”

Infectious disease specialist Dr Sher Bahadur Pun said the possibility of waterborne disease outbreaks can remain for months following a natural disaster.

“When water sources become contaminated, diseases such as diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid can spread easily,” Pun said. “The risk of cholera becomes particularly high after floods and inundation because drinking water can become contaminated.”

Public health experts say waterborne infections are among the most immediate health threats after a disaster. Besides cholera, diarrhoea and fever caused by various bacteria and viruses can also occur, making continuous disease surveillance necessary.

“Cholera can make many people seriously ill. If one or two cases appear, there is a possibility of it spreading to many others,” Pun said. “If symptoms such as diarrhoea or fever are identified and treated immediately, the spread of infection can be prevented to a large extent.”

Cholera can cause persistent diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps. Doctors say symptoms can appear anywhere from 12 hours to five days after infection, usually within two to three days.

They therefore recommend that ensuring safe drinking water and proper water treatment should be a priority in flood-affected areas.

Overcrowding increases transmission risk

The collective accommodation of displaced people at holding centres also increases the risk of person-to-person transmission.

Respiratory infections such as flu and Covid-19 can spread more easily in crowded conditions, particularly through coughing.

Pun pointed to international experience showing that infectious disease risks can persist long after a disaster itself has passed.

He cited Haiti, where a major cholera outbreak emerged several months after the devastating earthquake in 2010.

“The earthquake occurred in January, but the major cholera outbreak appeared in October,” Pun said. “The risk of infection does not end when the disaster ends. As long as displaced people do not have organised accommodation, drinking water, sanitation and other necessary infrastructure, the risk of infectious diseases remains.”

Dengue and leptospirosis risks

Experts also warn that the risk of dengue can increase after floods because stagnant water provides suitable breeding grounds for mosquitoes.

Flooding can leave pools and pits of standing water, including relatively clean water, where dengue-carrying mosquitoes can breed.

Flood debris can also contaminate water sources. Various infectious diseases can spread through contaminated water and food.

Doctors are also concerned about leptospirosis, a bacterial infection whose risk can increase after disasters.

The disease can be transmitted through contact with water or soil contaminated by the urine of infected animals. The risk is higher when people have cuts or open wounds on their skin.

“An infection can spread quickly if someone has a wound, an open cut or drinks contaminated water,” Pun said. “There have been cases of this disease spreading after floods and landslides.”

Symptoms of leptospirosis can generally appear between two and 30 days after infection. They may include fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, red eyes, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and rashes.

In severe cases, doctors say the disease can cause jaundice and problems affecting the kidneys and nervous system and can even be fatal.

Typhoid and skin infections

Public health expert Dr Baburam Marasini says typhoid could also become a major health challenge in flood-affected areas.

Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water, making people displaced by floods particularly vulnerable.

“Houses have been destroyed and there are no toilets. People are forced to use whatever water is available,” Marasini said. “In such circumstances, the risk of typhoid increases further.”

If not diagnosed and treated on time, typhoid can cause intestinal perforation, bleeding and complications affecting other organs.

Skin infections are another concern among flood-affected people. Some people have already developed skin-related problems, while animal and human remains in affected areas have also contributed to foul odours and unhygienic conditions.

Dermatologist Dr Prajjwal Pudasaini said skin problems tend to increase in such circumstances.

“Problems such as itchy skin, burning sensations and rashes increase,” he said. “Fungus becomes active in damp environments and can attach to and affect the skin.”

Ministry says response is being coordinated

The Ministry of Health says it is coordinating with relevant agencies to identify and treat diseases in affected areas and improve sanitation in response to the infection risks.

Health Ministry Secretary Dr Bikash Devkota said preparations and precautionary measures had been taken to prevent diarrhoea from spreading in flood-hit areas.

He said the ministry had not assessed the cases reported so far as a major outbreak.

“Health workers are being deployed. Necessary medicines, treatment and other supplies have also been kept ready,” Devkota said. “There are health workers at the holding centres. Local governments and relevant agencies also need to pay attention to sanitation.”

He said preparations had been made to immediately mobilise health workers if diarrhoea begins to spread.

The government has also made cholera vaccines available in the affected areas, treating them as potentially high-risk zones, according to Devkota.

Safe water and food key to preventing outbreaks

Experts say immediate coordination among local governments, health institutions and government agencies is necessary to prevent infectious diseases from spreading in flood, landslide and inundation-affected areas.

They recommend prioritising safe drinking water, waste management, disease surveillance and expanding health services in high-risk areas.

Marasini said local governments and health institutions should identify areas where infectious diseases are likely to spread and immediately implement preventive measures.

“Potential areas for the spread of infectious diseases should be studied and preventive measures taken immediately,” he said. “If local governments actively work on disease control along with public awareness, the spread of infections can be prevented to a large extent.”

Experts have also recommended health camps, disease surveillance and psychosocial counselling where necessary, alongside the provision of safe drinking water.

Doctors advise people in flood-affected areas to drink only boiled or properly treated water, eat fresh food, use toilets for defecation and urination, and wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water after using the toilet and before preparing food.

Raw vegetables and salads should also be washed thoroughly with clean water before consumption.

“If hands, food and water are kept clean, most infectious diseases can be prevented,” Pun said. “Many diseases spread through waste. So people should use clean, boiled water and fresh food.”

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi flood reveals the growing danger of Himalayan cascading hazards

content.rendered:
The catastrophic flood which took place in the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river area in August 26 has left Nepal facing one of the worst mountain disasters in recent times. Starting in the glacierized Himalayan region, the situation quickly turned into a destructive sequence involving ice, rock, debris and water, which moved downstream through Rasuwa and then into Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan, Tanahun and Nawalparasi. As a result of the disaster, settlements, bridges, roads, hydropower facilities and the Rasuwagadhi–Kerung trade route were destroyed, together with a huge loss of human life and livelihoods.

The incident was caused by a major failure of an ice-and-rock mass in the upper Lhende Khola catchment, north of the Langtang-Lirung peak. Analysis using satellite data indicates that an area of about 2.10 square kilometres of glacier and the surrounding land from 5,200 m elevation have collapsed, with an additional 3.05 square kilometres being greatly eroded at an elevation of about 3,800 m, part of which is debris-covered glacier. The total estimated volume of ice, rock, sediment and debris that was moved could have exceeded 74.43 million cubic metres, though these figures need to be confirmed by further studies.

This is unlike a typical monsoon flood or even a glacial lake outburst flood in that the Bhote Koshi event seems to have developed very quickly, with little or no heavy rainfall having occurred previously in the immediate source area, the northern side of the Langtang-Lirung Peak. The steep terrain of the Himalayas sped up the flow of ice, rock and water, thus giving rise to a highly powerful flood wave.

The effects have been huge. As of writing this articl , there had been 1,410 confirmed deaths, some 6,145 people missing and nearly 93,000 people affected. Initial estimates by NDRRMA suggested that the total damage amounted to about USD 2695.33 million, comprising 1,812.01 million in physical damage and 883.32 million in economic losses. The cost of reconstruction would be 4,774.99 million USD. It was reported that fourteen hydropower projects, 68 bridges and approximately 40 to 45 kilometres of major roads had been damaged or destroyed. Additionally, the disaster disrupted electricity generation and the main northern trade route with China.

The Bhote Koshi disaster, starting in the high mountains of Nepal, the ice-and-rock failure and the flood wave it caused had a catastrophic impact on the area near the Nepal-China border around Rasuwagadhi–Kerung and then continued down through Nepal. What initially was a high-altitude cryospheric hazard eventually became a large-scale cascading disaster, influencing the populations and critical infrastructure in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and in several local municipalities downstream in the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system. This incident serves as a clear indication that mountain hazards do not respect political boundaries and that effective disaster risk reduction in the Himalayan region must include stronger cross-border monitoring, the sharing of information, early warning systems and coordinated emergency preparedness between neighbouring countries.

The increase in temperature in recent years in Nepal’s high Himalayas has led to major changes in its glaciers, snow and permafrost. The rapid warming is accelerating the retreat of glaciers, greater melting, degradation of the frozen ground and the destabilisation of mountain slopes. On the other hand, extreme precipitation and other hydro-meteorological events are becoming increasingly important parts of disaster risk. Climate change is modifying the environmental conditions in which these hazards take place; glacier retreat and the degradation of permafrost can reduce previously stable slopes, while changes in precipitation can increase the chance of extreme runoff, landslides and debris flows.

The direct cause of the Bhote Koshi incident seems to have been a large ice-and-rock failure rather than a typical flood triggered by rainfall or breach of glacial lakes. There is a broader interaction between warming, glacier retreat, slope instability, snow and ice conditions, river processes, and exposure downstream. These interactions are capable of causing a series of hazards, one process setting off another and, in the end, resulting in an effect much greater than that of the original event.

Nepal has for a long time suffered from floods, landslides, debris flows, avalanches, earthquakes, droughts, forest fires and glacial lake outburst floods; what is becoming more worrying is the idea that these hazards might interact. The fact that the 2021 Melamchi disaster, the repeated floods and landslides that have occurred all over the country, the more recent hazards associated with glaciers and rainfall, and the flooding in the same Bhote Koshi area in 2025 show that mountain hazards can occur again and change quickly is contrasted by the 2026 disaster, which brings out a different aspect: a high-altitude cryospheric failure can cause a devastating flood many tens of kilometres downstream, putting at risk communities and infrastructure which may not at first seem to be directly affected by a glacier hazard.

The growing extent of Nepal’s infrastructure is at the same time altering the level of possible losses. Increasingly, roads, hydroelectric power stations, transmission lines, settlements, tourism facilities and trade infrastructure are situated in the narrow river valleys. Although these areas are of economic importance, they also serve as natural routes for floods, debris flows and landslides. As seen in the Bhote Koshi flood, one extreme event can at the same time cause a humanitarian, energy, transport, trade and environmental crisis.

Nepal is trying to strengthen disaster preparedness, climate adaptation, hydrometeorological monitoring and early warning systems, but in the high mountain area these measures are still generally insufficient because of the rapidly changing cryospheric and geological conditions which are causing hazards that are becoming more complex and interconnected. There is an urgent need for the government to give greater attention, make more investment and improve institutional coordination if sustained high-altitude monitoring through university research, early warning is to be strengthened, and community preparedness is to be enhanced, and if infrastructure development is to be based on risk assessments that take account of climate conditions and hazards.

The key lesson from Bhote Koshi is that merely rebuilding what has been destroyed is not sufficient; if roads, bridges, hydropower projects, settlements and public facilities are reconstructed in the same dangerous locations and built to the same standards, then it will just end up with the same conditions that led to the previous disaster.

Future development in the Himalayan region must therefore be based on risk assessment and be resilient to the effects of climate change. Hazard assessments should be made a mandatory part of major infrastructure planning, especially in the high mountain river valleys. Glacier, permafrost, snow, glacial lake, landslide and river monitoring should all be incorporated into a national mountain hazard observatory. Continuous monitoring and rapid assessment can be supported by the use of satellite imagery, UAV surveys, numerical modelling and artificial intelligence, greatly backed by field measurements.

Hazards do not regard political boundaries. Nepal, China, India and the other countries of the Himalayas need more effective mechanisms for sharing real-time information on glacier movement, avalanches, glacial lakes, rainfall, river discharge and newly emerging hazards. The information sharing should be linked to action at institutional and community levels. Early warning should lead to early action by means of timely and locally understandable alerts, regular evacuation drills, safe evacuation routes, designated shelters, and site-specific emergency plans for communities, schools, hydropower projects, transport operators and local governments.

The Bhote Koshi disaster is therefore not merely a tragic incident in the sequence of Nepal’s disasters; it is a message coming from a Himalaya that is changing rapidly. While climate change is not causing all the hazards in the Himalayas, it is altering the conditions in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, slopes and rivers interact. As temperatures continue to rise, disasters may become less predictable, more interconnected and more destructive.

The Bhote Koshi flood shows how important it is to carry out continuous monitoring of glaciers, glacial lakes, slopes, and river systems, especially in high-mountain regions where observations are still limited. Research should be directed at understanding the connections between climate change, instability of glaciers and permafrost, cascading hazards, and the effects of floods downstream, using field observations, remote sensing, and modelling. Disaster risk reduction has to improve multi-hazard early warning systems, the sharing of real-time data, risk mapping, and the clear communication that goes from warning to early action. Most important of all, the results of monitoring and research must be turned into practical preparedness measures, evacuation planning, resilient infrastructure, and regular community-organised disaster drills.
