title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

Government recommends ambassadors to 13 countries

The government has recommended ambassadors for 13 countries, including India, China, the United States and the United Kingdom. A Cabinet meeting held on Friday decided to recommend the names for ambassadorial appointments.

PM Shah urges Gen Z lawmakers to create jobs and lead by example

Prime Minister Balen Shah has held discussions with lawmakers from the Gen Z age group, urging them to lead by example and create employment opportunities in Nepal for their generation through innovative thinking.

6 bodies recovered from Upper Trishuli 3A tunnel

Six bodies have been recovered from a tunnel of the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project. According to the Nepal Army Headquarters, six bodies were found entangled in the reinforcement steel mesh installed for concreting the tunnel. Security personnel and representatives of the project have been deployed inside the tunnel and are working at the site.

CIB raids ANFA headquarters in Lalitpur

The Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police has raided the headquarters of the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) in Satdobato, Lalitpur. CIB SSP and spokesperson Anupam Shamsher JBR confirmed on Friday that the bureau conducted the raid at the ANFA headquarters.

Prachanda says NCP preparing for new movement against government

Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’, coordinator of the Nepali Communist Party (NCP), has said they are preparing to launch a movement against the government. Addressing a gathering of the farmers’ federation affiliated with the NCP, he accused the government of starting repression and excesses.

ANFA warns of independent activities from Monday if suspension isn’t lifted

The All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) has said that if the government does not make a firm decision to lift its suspension, it will resume its activities from Monday in line with FIFA’s directive.

Sipradi Yatri announces price of locally made Yatri P2 electric scooter

Sipradi Yatri has officially announced the price of its new locally engineered and manufactured electric scooter, the Yatri P2. The launch marks another milestone in Sipradi Yatri’s efforts to develop electric mobility products that are engineered and manufactured in Nepal.

New York tops 2026 global cities index, Kathmandu ranks 687th

New York has been ranked the world’s best city in the 2026 Global Cities Index published by Oxford Economics. London ranks second and Paris third. According to Oxford Economics, the overall ranking was prepared by evaluating 1,000 major cities worldwide on five criteria: economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance.

title.rendered: Nepal receives Rs 215.05 billion in remittances in first month of fiscal year

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Nepal received remittances worth Rs 215.05 billion in the first month of the current fiscal year, according to Nepal Rastra Bank.

Remittance inflows in the month of Shrawan increased by 21.2 percent compared with the same period last fiscal year. Nepal had received Rs 177.41 billion in remittances in Shrawan of the previous fiscal year.

Nepal received a total of Rs 2.363 trillion in remittances during the last fiscal year, the central bank said.

In US dollar terms, remittance inflows increased by 10.2 percent to $1.40 billion in Shrawan. Such inflows had increased by 25 percent during the same period of the previous fiscal year.

Net secondary income, or net transfers, stood at Rs 229.98 billion in the first month of the current fiscal year, up from Rs 193.85 billion during the same period last fiscal year.

Meanwhile, 42,693 Nepalis received final labour approval for foreign employment in Shrawan, while 27,748 obtained re-entry labour approval.

During the same month last fiscal year, 44,466 Nepalis had received final labour approval and 23,644 had obtained re-entry approval.

title.rendered: In Vienna, a Nepali classroom keeps language, culture and memory alive

content.rendered:
In a quiet classroom at the University of Vienna, Nepali words fill the air. Students from different countries practise Nepali, Sanskrit, Limbu and Nepal Bhasa. But this is not simply a language class.

Alongside vocabulary and grammar, they learn about Nepal’s politics, society, history and literature. They write poems, sing Nepali songs, perform dances and stage plays. Sometimes, the classroom becomes a small theatre; at other times, it turns into a celebration of Nepali culture.

At the centre of it all is Dr Alka Atreya Chudal.

A writer, researcher and linguist, Chudal has spent nearly two decades teaching Nepali language and literature at the University of Vienna. She holds a PhD in the intellectual history of South Asia, with a particular focus on Indian scholar and writer Rahul Sankrityayan.

Her journey to Vienna, however, began long before she entered a European university classroom. It began at home, with a father who believed education was not optional.

Learning at home

Chudal was born on July 6, 1976, in Taulihawa, Kapilvastu. Her father, Prof Dr Vishnu Raj Atreya, was a scholar who carried on the traditions of the gurukul system. Her earliest education took place at home.

“I was taught by my father at home. There was an atmosphere of education in our family. My aunts and uncles had studied at least up to the Acharya level. We were not financially well-off, but education was considered essential. The belief was that everyone, sons and daughters alike, had to study,” she recalls.

Her father was working at Banaras Hindu University in India, where he served as the Nepal Chair, and the family lived in university quarters. Every morning, he taught his daughter before leaving for the university. He brought home old examination papers and gave her assignments.

“That is how I learned self-study,” she says.

At the time, India allowed students to sit private examinations from Grade 8 onwards. Chudal prepared for her exams at home and appeared for them once a year.

She was also had to look after her younger siblings.

“My brothers and sisters were very young, so I was almost like their guardian,” she recalls.

Her education was heavily focused on Sanskrit grammar, literature and philosophy. She did not have the usual pressure to study subjects such as mathematics and science. That early immersion in language would shape the rest of her life.

She passed the Purva Madhyama examination at the age of 10. She later completed an Acharya degree in Sarvadarshan from Nepal Sanskrit University and a master’s degree in Nepali from Tribhuvan University.

By the time she was 18, she had already completed postgraduate studies in three subjects. And before she was even 18, she had begun teaching as an assistant professor at Nepal Sanskrit University.

“I owe all of this to my father’s inspiration and guidance,” she says.

Not having attended a conventional school occasionally made her feel that she had missed something. But teaching soon filled that gap.

“At first, it felt strange teaching students who were much older than me. But I began to enjoy it. Teaching itself became my inspiration,” she says.

From the classroom to the microphone

There was another childhood dream.

Growing up in Banaras in the 1980s, Chudal would sometimes visit friends’ homes to watch television because her family did not have one. She was fascinated by the newsreaders appearing on the black-and-white screen.

As a child, she imagined herself doing two things — teaching and becoming a newsreader. The second dream came true remarkably early.

In 1987, at just 11 years old, she began presenting a children’s programme called Sanskritam on Nepal Television. A few years later, she became a newsreader.

She presented news in three languages — Nepali, Sanskrit and Hindi.

From 1996 to 2006, she remained associated with Nepal Television. Her radio career began in 1994, when she was contacted by phone about a plan to broadcast Sanskrit news. Her love of Sanskrit made the decision easy. Soon, her voice became familiar to audiences on both radio and television.

“Even during festivals such as Dashain and Tihar, there was no real possibility of taking a holiday. We had to work day and night,” she recalls.

At the time, professors and highly educated people were more visible in the media. Later, as FM radio stations expanded, a younger generation entered broadcasting and many of the older voices gradually disappeared from the mainstream.

Chudal, however, never saw broadcasting as the final destination. Her deeper interest remained teaching and research. Even today, she has strong views about the way news is presented.

She believes the increasingly loud style of television newsreading is at odds with the character of the Nepali language.

“Newsreading has increasingly become a shouting style. But the beauty of Nepali is that it should flow gracefully, like a river. Sometimes it feels as if we are copying Aaj Tak rather than maintaining our own style,” she says.

For her, language should be heard as naturally as it is written.

A new chapter in Vienna

Around 18 years ago, Chudal’s life took another turn. She moved to Austria and joined the University of Vienna. The university, founded in 1365, is the oldest university in the German-speaking world and has a long tradition of Sanskrit studies. Chudal became part of its Department of South Asian, Tibetan and Buddhist Studies, a field closely connected to Nepal and India.

Language is central to the department’s work. Chudal remembers entering the application process without personal connections or recommendations.

“I didn’t know anyone there. I had no recommendation. They were looking for someone who understood both Nepal and India and was proficient in Sanskrit, Nepali and Hindi,” she says.

After a demanding application process, she reached the final stage and received an email informing her that she had been selected.

She was invited to Vienna for an interview. After the interview, she was offered the position.

The move gave her something she had long wanted — the opportunity to pursue higher research while working with languages and cultures she had studied since childhood.

At the University of Vienna, she went on to complete her PhD on the intellectual history of South Asia, focusing on Rahul Sankrityayan. But Vienna also gave her something else.

It gave her a platform from which to introduce Nepal to students who might otherwise never encounter its language, literature and culture.

“Perhaps if I had stayed in Nepal, I would not have been able to do as much for the Nepali language. But coming abroad gave me an opportunity to present Nepali language and literature in a much broader way. That makes me extremely happy,” she says.

Bringing Nepal into the classroom

Chudal’s classroom is therefore about much more than learning Nepali words.

“We don’t only teach the Nepali language,” she says. “Students learn about Nepal’s history. They understand the development of its literature. They become interested in what is happening in Nepal today. They are just as curious about its politics, society and culture as people living in Nepal.”

Her teaching reflects that philosophy. A lesson might move from grammar to a song, from a discussion of history to a poem, or from language practice to a performance. Students sing Nepali songs, write poems, dance and sometimes write and perform their own plays. They are also introduced to languages such as Limbu and Newari.

Interestingly, Chudal herself learned Newari and Limbu after moving to Austria.

“I learned Newari here in Austria. I learned Limbu here as well,” she says.

Most of her students are Austrian, but students from other parts of Europe and the United States also travel to Vienna to study Nepali. She says the University of Vienna is currently the only university where Nepali is formally taught as part of an academic curriculum. Keeping students engaged is central to her approach. Even numbers can become a song.

When teaching numbers, for example, she uses familiar Nepali lyrics and wordplay to make students remember them.

For grammar and verbs, she often uses songs. One of her examples is Ani Choying’s Chitta Shuddha Hos, Mero Boli Buddha Hos.

The method allows students to encounter pronunciation, rhythm, grammar and culture at the same time.

“This is my way of teaching. You have to consider both the students’ interests and the curriculum. It makes learning easier, enjoyable and more lasting,” she says.

Why language matters

For Chudal, language is closely connected to the way people think.

A limited vocabulary, she argues, can limit the range of ideas a person is able to express and explore. Learning another language, meanwhile, can expand the way we understand the world. But she is equally wary of the idea that anyone can ever become completely finished with learning a language.

Language, she believes, is something people continue learning throughout their lives.

That is also why she is concerned about children from Nepali families growing up abroad without learning their parents’ languages.

She gives the example of a Limbu-speaking couple living in Spain who speak Nepali at home but do not teach either Nepali or Limbu to their children. The children grow up speaking only Spanish.

The consequence, she says, goes beyond language.

It can make communication with grandparents and other relatives more difficult and weaken a child’s connection with Nepal.

“If parents made an effort to teach their children their mother tongue, the children could participate in family conversations,” she says. “So teaching a mother tongue is not only about language skills. It is also a foundation for intellectual development and maintaining cultural connections.”

A book that became personal

Chudal’s work has also taken her beyond the classroom and into translation. One of the most emotionally significant projects of her career was her Nepali translation of Of Salt and Rice, a book by Swiss anthropologist Dr Hanna Rauber about the lives and businesses of the Bhote-Khampa community.

Rauber had spent decades studying and developing a deep affection for Nepal. She wanted her work to be available in Nepali. At the age of 82, she sent Chudal her first email.

“I’m already very old. I want to see this English book translated into Nepali,” she wrote.

The sentence stayed with Chudal.

Rauber had already tried to have the book translated elsewhere, but the results had not satisfied her. The two women began communicating by email and later by phone. Chudal started translating the book afresh.

Translation was unfamiliar territory for her. Understanding every sentence and capturing its precise meaning took time. Her other responsibilities repeatedly pushed the project back. Then came unexpected news.

Rauber had been diagnosed with cancer.

From that point, the translation became more than a literary project. It became a personal responsibility. In September 2024, Chudal travelled to Switzerland to meet Rauber in person. Despite her illness, Rauber remained remarkably energetic.

She walked with a cane, but still had a smile on her face and a sparkle in her eyes.

For 15 days, the two women worked almost continuously, from 7 in the morning until 11 at night. They went through the book line by line, revisiting words and sentences.

At times, Chudal urged her to rest.

“You are unwell. We shouldn’t work like this,” she would tell her.

Rauber would smile and reply, “I want to keep working until I die.”

Their intense collaboration brought the two women closer. Doctors had told Rauber that she might have only a week left. Yet even from her hospital bed, she continued checking every line of the book. She had one wish — to hold the book in her own hands.

Eventually, Chudal was able to place a dummy copy of Nun Ra Chamal (Salt and Rice) in her hands. For Chudal, the moment was deeply emotional. It also brought back memories of her own father, who had died of cancer. In his final days, she had placed a dummy copy of his work Vararuchi in his hands.

“I had the opportunity to introduce two people who were dear to me to their own creations in the final moments of their lives,” she recalls.

Rauber passed away in January 2025. But her wish was fulfilled. Salt and Rice was eventually published in Nepali.

For Chudal, the book remains a tribute to Rauber’s lifelong love for Nepal and a reminder of how translation can carry not only words, but relationships and memories across languages.

Returning Nepal’s forgotten voices

Her work with language and culture has also led her into historical research.

Chudal has collected and published folk songs and stories associated with Nepali Gurkha prisoners of war who were held abroad more than a century ago. She began researching the material in 2015.

As she searched through archives and historical collections, she gradually discovered more stories, voices and details. Much of the material had been preserved in a museum in Germany. For Chudal, it raised a simple question — why should the voices of Nepalis remain locked away in a foreign archive?

“We often think of a country’s wealth as physical structures and money,” she says. “But language, literature and culture are also national wealth.”

She wanted those voices to return to Nepal.

“I strongly felt that the voices of these Nepalis needed to come back home,” she says. “That is why I also felt that this book should be published in Nepal.”

The resulting work is more than a collection of wartime stories. According to Chudal, it offers a window into history, society, language and literature. Readers can learn how the prisoners lived, what communities they came from, what they thought and how they expressed themselves through songs, poems and stories.

“For me, it is really a historical document,” she says.

A life in language

Chudal’s own writing has followed many different paths. She has written two books in German, including work developed with a colleague. She has also written Ramro Nepali, a book designed particularly to help German-speaking students learn Nepali.

She has written the long poem Ninad Vallari and, around 18 years ago, published her autobiography Balyakal Sanga Lobhindai Balyakal. More recently, she completed an English translation of Swasthani with a friend.

She continues to work on presenting the stories and folk songs of Nepali Gurkha prisoners of war to English-speaking audiences.

Her research interests also include Nepali political consciousness, the history of Nepali women, and the linguistic and cultural development of Nepali society.

Across all these projects, however, there is a common thread. Language is never merely language for Chudal. It is history. It is memory. It is culture. It is a way of connecting generations and allowing one society to be understood by another.

Nearly two decades after arriving in Vienna, she continues to bring Nepal into classrooms thousands of kilometres from home — through its words, songs, stories, history and literature.

“My goal is to take Nepali identity to the world,” she says.

And that work continues, one word, one book and one classroom at a time.

title.rendered: What has Nepal done to adapt to climate change?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

A week has passed since the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, established under the UN climate change framework, pledged to make the “earliest possible and meaningful response” to the devastation caused by the Rasuwa floods.

Nepal had written to the fund on September 1, arguing that climate change was a contributing factor behind the disaster, which killed 1,410 people and left 5,130 missing.

In its response 10 days later, the fund said it had recommended that its board consider various options within the limits of its existing mandate, structure, policies and procedures.

The response has renewed an important question for Nepal. If climate change is contributing to increasingly severe disasters in a country that contributes very little to global emissions, what should Nepal be entitled to under the principle of climate justice?

International research has strengthened Nepal’s argument that climate change played a role in creating the conditions for the Rasuwa disaster.

A group of international researchers who conducted a disaster analysis for World Weather Attribution, an initiative that studies the role of climate change in extreme weather events, said climate change could have contributed to the Rasuwa flood.

Climate scientist Dr Friederike Otto, one of the researchers involved in the study, told the BBC that there was no doubt human-induced climate change had played a role in creating the background conditions for the disaster.

National Geographic reported that a huge mass of glacier ice and rock covering around two square kilometres fell from the Langtang Lirung mountain area in Rasuwa into the valley below.

The report said climate change had been weakening the slope in the days, weeks, months and years before the collapse, leaving it vulnerable to landslides.

For Nepali officials, the scale of the disaster is particularly significant because the country’s contribution to global climate change remains extremely small.

But there is another side to the story.

Nepal’s emissions have increased sixfold

There is little dispute that Nepal’s contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions is negligible. Its per capita emissions are not only far below those of the world’s biggest emitters but also substantially below the global average.

The global average annual carbon emissions per person stand at 4.67 tonnes. Nepal’s figure is just 0.54 tonnes.

That, however, does not mean Nepal can simply sit back because its emissions are low, experts say.

Nepal became a party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in 1994. Over the three decades since then, the country has sought to reduce emissions and strengthen its ability to adapt to climate change.

But World Bank data show that per capita emissions have actually increased.

In 1994, Nepal’s annual per capita emissions stood at 0.0873 tonnes. By 2024, the figure had risen nearly sixfold to 0.5360 tonnes.

The increase has continued in recent years. Per capita emissions stood at 0.5063 tonnes in 2022 and 0.5197 tonnes in 2023.

Compared with 1970, Nepal’s per capita emissions have increased roughly 20-fold. In 1970, the figure was only 0.02683 tonnes per person per year.

These figures, however, do not mean that Nepal has done nothing to reduce emissions or adapt to climate change.

Forests and climate adaptation

Nepal signed the Convention on Biological Diversity during the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. The convention covers the conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources.

Nepal says its forest coverage has also increased significantly. Forests covered around 40 percent of the country in 2000, while the figure has now reached 46 percent.

Government officials attribute part of this increase to community forestry and the implementation of the national REDD strategy, arguing that the expansion of forest cover has also contributed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Nepal says it has been working on climate management and balance since becoming a party to the UN climate convention in 1994.

Even before climate change became a central policy issue, the country’s Millennium Development Goals and Sustainable Development Goals indirectly addressed several climate-related concerns, officials say.

Nepal began its National Adaptation Programme in 2008 with the aim of strengthening climate adaptation capacity and reducing risks faced by vulnerable households and communities. Reducing the risk of floods caused by glacial lake outbursts was identified as one of its priority areas.

A year later, the government established the Climate Change Council under the prime minister, with experts included, as well as a Climate Change Coordination Committee involving various stakeholders to coordinate climate-related plans and programmes.

The Climate Change Division at the Ministry of Forests and Environment was designated as the focal point for coordinating climate-related issues.

Hydrologist Madhukar Upadhya says Nepal has repeatedly told international climate forums that it is suffering the consequences of a problem it did little to create.

According to Upadhya, Nepal has prioritised climate concerns not only through the Millennium Development Goals and Sustainable Development Goals but also through the national budget.

He says 81 budget headings are related to activities that contribute to climate balance, with Nepal beginning to track such spending from the 2012 budget.

“Annual spending itself shows how Nepal can address the issue of climate change,” Upadhya says.

From policy to Paris

The government formulated a climate policy in 2010. The same year, a framework for Local Adaptation Plans of Action was prepared to integrate climate concerns into local development planning.

The plans were subsequently developed in areas considered vulnerable to climate-related risks, according to government officials.

Nepal signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 and subsequently made commitments through its Nationally Determined Contribution.

A new National Climate Change Policy was introduced in 2019.

In November 2021, the Cabinet approved the 30-year National Adaptation Plan for 2021–2050. The same meeting also approved the Long-Term Net-Zero Emission Strategy and the National Framework on Climate Change-Induced Loss and Damage.

The international loss and damage mechanism itself was established by the Conference of the Parties to the UN climate convention and the meeting of parties to the Paris Agreement.

Its purpose is to support developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. Its mandate covers support for developing countries dealing with both economic and non-economic losses and damages associated with climate change.

Nepal wants climate leadership, but faces a growing risk

Last year, Nepal organised the Sagarmatha Sambaad under the theme “Climate Change, Mountains and the Future of Humanity”.

The conference concluded in May 2025 with the adoption of a 25-point “Sagarmatha Call for Action”, outlining measures aimed at maintaining the 1.5-degree Celsius temperature limit.

Through the Sagarmatha Sambaad, Nepal also sought to position itself as a leading voice on climate issues on the international stage.

But climate change is no longer simply an international environmental issue for Nepal.

Experts say it has increasingly become intertwined with development, energy, forests, agriculture, infrastructure, the economy and, most directly, disasters.

Arjun Dhakal, who works as a consultant in environmental economics and policy, says Nepal initially failed to take climate change seriously enough.

“Climate change was at times treated as an issue for NGOs or a foreign agenda,” he says. “Initially, we said it was an environmental issue. Later, we considered it a development issue. But we did not look at it as an economic issue that could create a major crisis like the one now seen in Bhotekoshi.”

Dhakal says he had been warning about the potential risks to hydropower projects for years.

“I have been saying this, but nobody seemed to care. There are no measures to reduce risks in major projects like Melamchi,” he says.

At the very least, he argues, Nepal now needs to recognise that climate change can affect the country’s infrastructure and livelihoods on a much larger scale.

That may be the central challenge behind Nepal’s demand for climate justice.

The country remains a very small contributor to global emissions, yet its emissions have risen over the decades. At the same time, it has expanded forest cover, introduced climate policies, invested in adaptation and sought a stronger role in international climate diplomacy.

The Rasuwa disaster has brought these two realities into sharp focus: Nepal is asking those responsible for the bulk of global emissions to help bear the cost of climate-related losses, while it must also confront the growing climate risks — and its own rising emissions — at home.

title.rendered: Meet the 13 people proposed as Nepal’s new ambassadors

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

The government has recommended 13 individuals for appointment as Nepal’s ambassadors to different countries, including India, China, the United States and the United Kingdom.

A Cabinet meeting held on Friday recommended the names of individuals with backgrounds in diplomacy, academia, security, development, business, public policy and other fields.

The recommended names will now be sent to the Parliamentary Hearing Committee. Following parliamentary hearings, the government will seek agrément from the respective countries. Once agrément is received, the President will formally appoint the nominees as ambassadors.

Here is a look at the backgrounds of the 13 proposed ambassadors.

1. Dr Nischal Nath Pandey — India

Dr Nischal Nath Pandey is an academic and foreign policy expert who currently serves as director of the Centre for South Asian Studies (CSAS).

He previously served as executive director of the Institute of Foreign Affairs under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from 1998 to 2006 and as an adviser to the National Planning Commission on tourism and civil aviation from 1996 to 1997.

Pandey also served as an expert with Nepal’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 2016 and as a member of a high-level foreign policy task force formed by the government in 2017.

He holds a PhD in political science and an LLB from Tribhuvan University. He has also served as an honorary associate professor at the National Institute of Advanced Studies in Bengaluru and as a non-resident senior fellow at the Institute of South Asian Studies at the National University of Singapore.

Pandey has completed visiting fellowships at Germany’s SWP in Berlin and the University of Hull in the UK. He has also served on the board of the Regional Centre for Strategic Studies in Colombo.

He has authored three books published by SAGE and Manohar Publishers, along with numerous edited works on Nepal’s foreign policy and regional cooperation. In 2015, he completed the South Asia Leadership Executive Program at Harvard Kennedy School.

2. Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma — China

Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma is a Nepal-China affairs expert, sinologist and economist with more than two decades of experience in academia, institutional governance and bilateral policy cooperation.

He holds a PhD in economics from Fudan University, where his research focused on foreign direct investment, trade and tourism financing.

Sharma is currently chairman of the Fudan University Alumni Association Nepal, the Nepal-China Friendship Forum and the Council of Sinologists-Nepal. He also serves as a visiting scholar at Kathmandu University School of Management, where he developed and teaches a course on doing business in China.

He is managing director of Adventure Outdoor Excursion and has been involved in promoting Himalayan and cross-border tourism. He also serves as an independent board director at Apex Funds and several hydropower and energy companies.

For his contribution to Nepal-China relations, Sharma received the Nepal Bhushan from the President of Nepal in 2016 and the Silk Road Friendship Award in 2021.

3. Chiran Jung Thapa — United States

Chiran Jung Thapa is a national security and international affairs expert with more than two decades of experience in security policy, crisis management and diplomacy.

He holds a master’s degree in international affairs from Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, which he completed on a full academic scholarship, and a bachelor’s degree in international relations from SUNY Geneseo.

Since 2017, Thapa has served as Oxfam’s regional security adviser for Asia, where he has led risk and crisis management work across 15 countries.

Previously, he worked as regional security and justice adviser for Asia at Saferworld from 2013 to 2016 and as an adviser on security sector and civil-military relations at The Asia Foundation from 2010 to 2013.

During his career, he has advised Nepal’s Ministry of Defence, National Security Council, Nepal Army and Nepal Police. He also developed the Nepal Army’s first civil-military relations course.

Earlier, he worked with the permanent missions of Singapore and Nepal to the United Nations in New York.

Thapa completed Harvard Kennedy School’s Leadership in Homeland Security programme and has worked in Nepal, the United States, the United Kingdom and several countries in South and Southeast Asia.

4. Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana — United Kingdom

Former Chief of Army Staff Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana has more than four decades of experience in the Nepal Army and served as chief of army staff from 2012 to 2015.

During his tenure, he oversaw the integration of former Maoist combatants into the Nepal Army under the Comprehensive Peace Agreement. He also led the army during Nepal’s transition to a federal democratic republic.

Rana was involved in implementing the army’s 10-year long-term plan and Military Doctrine 2013.

Following the 2015 earthquake, he led the Nepal Army’s disaster response operation, Operation Sankat Mochan, and coordinated the involvement of 18 foreign military teams in relief efforts.

He previously served as chief of staff, director general of the Directorate General of Military Operations and commander of Nepal’s UNIFIL battalion in southern Lebanon.

Rana holds a master’s degree in defence and strategic studies from Quaid-i-Azam University in Pakistan and a bachelor’s degree in history and political science from Tribhuvan University. He is also a graduate of the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, the US Army Command and General Staff College at Fort Leavenworth and Pakistan’s National Defence University.

5. Jigyan Kumar Thapa — Japan

Jigyan Kumar Thapa has more than two decades of experience working to strengthen Nepal-Japan relations.

He holds a master’s degree in international relations and law from Yokohama National University and a bachelor’s degree in international cooperation from Shumei University.

Since 2009, he has worked at the Kanagawa International Foundation as an expert on international cooperation, public policy and multicultural affairs.

Since 2005, he has also coordinated high-level Nepal-Japan bilateral programmes, facilitating visits and exchanges involving presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers of both countries.

Thapa organised the Nepal-Japan Business Dialogue during the Nepali president’s official visit to Japan in 2026.

He has worked closely with JICA, UNICEF and Japanese local governments on international cooperation and migration governance initiatives. He has also served as an adviser to the Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Nepal, former general secretary of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan and former president of the Nepali Students Association in Japan.

He has taught as an associate professor at several Japanese universities and is proficient in Japanese, having passed JLPT Level 1.

6. Suresh Kumar Karn — Israel

Suresh Kumar Karn is a senior professional with more than 30 years of experience in information technology, banking and economic policy.

While serving as chief information and marketing officer at Kumari Bank from 2003 to 2015, he developed and launched Kumari Mobile Cash, described as Nepal’s first mobile wallet.

He later served as chief operating officer of Nepal Bank from 2015 to 2019, where he led the bank’s transition to an integrated core banking system.

Since 2024, Karn has chaired Kumo Labs, a Japanese technology investment established under Nepal’s Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act.

He has also served two consecutive terms as president of the Computer Association of Nepal Federation and was a member of Nepal’s IT Council and the High-Level Commission for Information Technology.

Karn contributed to drafting Nepal’s first national IT policy in 2000. He holds an MBA in international trade, investment and infrastructure economics from Beijing Normal University’s Belt and Road School.

He began his career as an inspector in the Nepal Police and has also received the National ICT Excellence Award.

7. Prapti Sherchan — Spain

Prapti Sherchan is an international development and partnership professional with 15 years of experience across South Asia, Southeast Asia and Africa.

She has worked at the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, since 2015 and currently serves as an operations officer for gender solutions and impact.

She has led IFC India’s gender country programme and previously served as the Asia lead for IFC’s women’s insurance programme, helping expand inclusive finance partnerships across Asia and Africa.

The programme has covered more than 1.3 million women and contributed to the creation of 9,500 jobs, according to the profile provided by the government.

Sherchan has also led multi-country research initiatives involving Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka and a 10-country regional study with the ASEAN Insurance Council.

She holds an MBA in sustainable international development from Brandeis University’s Heller School and a bachelor’s degree in sociology from the National University of Singapore.

She has represented IFC at high-level international forums, including the World Bank-IMF Spring Meetings. She is also co-chair of the US board of Women Lead Nepal and co-founder of the IFC Millennial+ Resource Group.

8. Saru Joshi — Germany

Saru Joshi is a senior policy expert with more than 25 years of experience in foreign employment governance, gender equality and international cooperation.

She has contributed to the development of Nepal’s migration framework, including the Foreign Employment Act 2007, Foreign Employment Rules 2008 and Foreign Employment Policy 2012.

Joshi worked at UN Women for a decade, serving as regional programme manager for South Asia and head of labour diplomacy from 2002 to 2012.

She later served as a programme specialist and head of the Women’s Economic Empowerment Unit at UN Women Nepal, followed by a role as strategic partnership specialist.

Since 2018, she has worked as an independent senior policy and international relations consultant. Her work has included advising UN Women, the World Bank and the Global Forum on Migration and Development.

She has represented Nepal at international forums including COP28.

Since 2024, Joshi has served on the executive board of the Nepal Policy Institute and has been involved in advocacy for voting rights for Nepali migrant workers.

She holds master’s degrees in women and development from the Institute of Social Studies in The Hague and political science from Tribhuvan University. She is also the author of the book Euta Sinko Bhachera Herdā and has published more than 60 articles on foreign employment and gender issues.

9. Dr Padmakshi Rana — Oman

Dr Padmakshi Rana is a development and entrepreneurship professional with more than 15 years of experience in sustainable development, inclusive innovation and international cooperation across Nepal, Asia and Europe.

Since 2022, she has served as executive director and co-founder of Impact Hub Kathmandu, representing Nepal within the Impact Hub Global Association and its Asia-Pacific regional network.

She has developed partnerships with organisations including UK Aid/FCDO, the European Union, UNDP, UNICEF, UNESCAP, the World Bank and the Royal Academy of Engineering.

Rana holds a PhD in corporate social responsibility in food production from the University of Cambridge’s Institute for Manufacturing. She also holds an MPhil in environment, society and development from Cambridge and an MBA from Webster University Thailand.

Before joining Impact Hub, she held research and teaching positions at Cambridge and co-founded a sustainability innovation consultancy in Singapore.

Her research has focused on sustainable business models in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region and post-disaster tourism recovery.

10. Chudamani Kharel — Malaysia

Chudamani Kharel has an academic background in humanities, English, political science and law and has worked in education and public administration.

He holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in English, a master’s degree in political science and an LLB from Tribhuvan University.

Kharel is currently general secretary of the Nepal Yoga Sports Association. He previously served as general secretary of the Nepal Skating and Skateboarding Association and as member-secretary of the 7th National Games subcommittee under the National Sports Council.

His academic career includes several years as a lecturer in English at Cosmos College and John Bauer College.

11. Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha — South Korea

Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha is an academic and global policy expert with more than 25 years of experience in international cooperation, climate resilience and water-security diplomacy.

He is currently a professor at the School of Engineering and Technology at the Asian Institute of Technology in Thailand and a former dean of the school. He is also founding co-director of the Global Water and Sanitation Center.

Shrestha has worked with the Asian Development Bank, World Bank, Gates Foundation, UN agencies, European Union, FAO and UNESCO on international grants and cooperation.

He has worked with governments and diplomatic missions in more than 30 countries.

He holds a PhD in integrated river basin management from Yamanashi University in Japan and has published more than 200 research papers.

He has also served as a visiting professor at Beijing Normal University and the National University of Laos and has supervised more than 20 PhD students and over 150 postgraduate students across Asia.

12. Dr Manchala Jha — Sri Lanka

Dr Manchala Jha is a governance and public policy expert who served as a commissioner at Nepal’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission from 2015 to 2019.

During her tenure, she represented the commission at international transitional justice forums and presented Nepal’s experience with truth, justice and reconciliation in Sri Lanka.

She is an associate professor at Tribhuvan University and taught in its master’s programme on governance and corruption control from 2021 to 2024.

Jha holds a PhD in Hindi literature from B.R. Ambedkar University in India and master’s degrees in political science, with a specialisation in foreign policy and diplomacy, and Hindi literature from Tribhuvan University.

She has also served as an invited expert on Nepal’s national implementation and monitoring committee for the United Nations Istanbul Programme of Action.

Jha has provided training to government and civil society stakeholders on women, peace and security under UN Security Council resolutions 1325 and 1820.

She has worked as an election observer and media analyst on Nepali politics and governance and is proficient in Nepali, Hindi, English and Maithili.

13. Giribahadur Sunar — Saudi Arabia

Giribahadur Sunar is a sociologist and development professional with more than 25 years of experience in international development, policy advice and multi-stakeholder governance.

His areas of expertise include social safeguards, gender equality and social inclusion, community-based climate adaptation and grievance redress mechanisms.

He has applied this expertise to major infrastructure and water-sector programmes supported by the World Bank and Asian Development Bank.

Sunar is pursuing a PhD in sociology at Tribhuvan University and completed an MPhil in 2019.

He is the author of Empowering Women Through Self-Defense, published by Scholars Press in Germany, and has written more than 100 policy articles for Nepali newspapers including The Himalayan Times, The Annapurna Express and Republica.

He also serves as secretary of Social, Environment and Rural Development Nepal (SERD-Nepal) and has appeared as a public diplomacy commentator on national television.

title.rendered: United School inaugurates second KUMON Lab

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

United School has inaugurated its second KUMON Lab at its premises in Imadol, Lalitpur, expanding its capacity to offer the KUMON self-learning programme in mathematics and English.

The facility was inaugurated on September 15 by United School Founder Director Nara Hang Rai in the presence of Yusuke Yoshikawa, CEO of Colorbath, Japan, and Bikash Lama, CEO of IGC Holdings.

The KUMON Lab is designed as a structured learning space where students develop mathematics and English skills through independent study and personalised worksheets. The programme is available to students from Year 2 and is intended to strengthen numeracy, literacy, problem-solving and independent learning skills.

According to the school, the second lab will accommodate students already enrolled in the programme and create additional space for new learners.

The KUMON programme will operate alongside the school’s regular academic curriculum, with a dedicated teacher overseeing the lab.

United School Principal Manoj Bishwokarma said the new facility was aimed at promoting independent learning among students by combining technology with the KUMON learning approach.

KUMON, founded in Japan by Toru Kumon in 1958, is a self-learning method focused on mathematics and reading. The school said its KUMON programme is part of its broader efforts to provide students with exposure to STEM education and hands-on learning.

title.rendered: At least 16 killed, 30 injured in Pakistan’s Kohat explosion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

At least 16 people were killed and more than 30 injured in an explosion near a former police lines building in Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa IGP Zulfiqar Hamid said preliminary reports indicated that a vehicle loaded with explosives had rammed into the old police lines. He said an exchange of fire with armed militants was underway following the explosion.

According to the provincial police chief, preliminary details indicated that a suicide attacker detonated himself near the Special Branch following the explosion.

According to BBC Urdu, one militant was killed in the exchange of fire. Local police said the explosion occurred at around 1:15 pm local time on Friday.

Fourteen ambulances and more than 40 personnel have been deployed at the site for rescue operations.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the Kohat explosion and expressed grief over the incident, in which a large number of people were injured.

According to a statement issued by Pakistan’s Prime Minister’s Office, Sharif directed authorities to ensure immediate treatment for the injured.

He also sought a report from the concerned authorities on the cause of the explosion and directed them to expedite relief and rescue operations and provide all necessary facilities to those affected.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also condemned the Kohat explosion and expressed grief over the loss of life and property.

According to Peshawar police, 11 civilians and five police officers were killed in the explosion.

title.rendered: PM Shah urges Gen Z lawmakers to create jobs and lead by example

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Prime Minister Balen Shah has held discussions with lawmakers from the Gen Z age group, urging them to lead by example and create employment opportunities in Nepal for their generation through innovative thinking.

According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, Shah urged the lawmakers to go beyond addressing basic livelihood problems and take the lead in making their generation self-reliant.

For this, he suggested conducting field-based studies and research, making maximum use of information technology, adopting a problem-solving approach and abandoning outdated and impractical thinking.

He also urged them not to make politics a profession but to establish an independent source of income and become self-reliant and a source of inspiration in the long term.

According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, the lawmakers who participated in the interaction took Shah’s suggestions as parental guidance and expressed their commitment to working to make their generation self-reliant and create opportunities within the country.

Kathmandu, September 18

The government has recommended ambassadors for 13 countries, including India, China, the United States and the United Kingdom.

A Cabinet meeting held on Friday decided to recommend the names for ambassadorial appointments.

The government said the proposed ambassadors include individuals with expertise in various fields, academic and research backgrounds, and experience in leadership and other areas.

The recommended names will now be forwarded to the parliamentary hearing committee for approval. Once the parliamentary hearing process is completed, the government will seek agrément from the respective countries.

The President will appoint the ambassadors after receiving approval from the host countries.

Who has been recommended?

The government has recommended the following individuals for ambassadorial appointments

  • Dr Nischal Nath Pandey — India
  • Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma — China
  • Chiran Jung Thapa — United States
  • Former Army Chief Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana (retired) — United Kingdom
  • Jigyan Kumar Thapa — Japan
  • Suresh Kumar Karn — Israel
  • Prapti Sherchan — Spain
  • Sharu Joshi — Germany
  • Dr Padmakshi Rana — Oman
  • Chudamani Kharel — Malaysia
  • Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha — South Korea
  • Dr Manchal Jha — Sri Lanka
  • Giribahadur Sunar — Saudi Arabia

The government had been preparing ambassadorial recommendations after inviting applications for several vacant diplomatic posts. More than 4,400 applications were received during the open application process, with the number later reduced after incomplete and duplicate applications were removed.

The ambassadorial appointments have been delayed for months, leaving a number of Nepal’s diplomatic missions without ambassadors. The latest recommendations cover only part of the vacant missions, with several posts still requiring appointments.

The nominees will have to go through parliamentary hearings before their names can be forwarded to the respective countries for agrément. Only after receiving consent from the host country can the President formally appoint them as ambassadors.

title.rendered: Six soldiers killed in roadside bomb blast in Pakistan

content.rendered:
September 18, Islamabad

Six soldiers were killed when a roadside bomb exploded, targeting a security forces vehicle in northwestern Pakistan, Pakistani military and police said Friday. Ten suspected militants affiliated with the Pakistani Taliban were also killed in separate operations carried out by security forces following the incident.

Local officials said the bomb targeted a security forces vehicle in Hangu district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Thursday. Six soldiers were confirmed killed in the blast.

According to the military, security forces raided locations where suspected militants were hiding during intelligence-based operations conducted in North Waziristan and Hangu districts on Thursday. The military said in a statement that 10 suspected militants were killed in the operations.

The military referred to those killed as “Khawarij,” a term used by the Pakistani government for members of Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Although the TTP is a separate organisation from the Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021, the two are said to have ties.

Soldiers have also been killed in various attacks targeting security forces in Pakistan this year. In June, three soldiers of the Pakistan Rangers were killed and four others injured in an encounter with militants.

Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Taliban government in Afghanistan of providing shelter to the TTP and failing to take adequate measures to prevent cross-border militant attacks. The government in Kabul has repeatedly rejected the allegations.

—RSS/AP

title.rendered: Manpower firms told to submit updates on Nepali workers abroad

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

The Department of Foreign Employment has directed manpower companies to submit details on the status of Nepali workers they have sent abroad for employment.

The department has instructed the companies to provide the required details by October 7. In June, the department had directed licensed agencies to submit progress reports on the status of Nepali workers they had sent abroad every three months. The latest directive is a follow-up to that instruction.

The department said licensed agencies must submit the relevant details to its Monitoring Section, keeping the rights, interests and safety of workers in mind.

According to the department, information on whether each worker who has gone abroad for employment has safely reached the respective destination country must be obtained within 15 days. For this, manpower companies must contact the workers and collect the necessary details.

Similarly, the department has directed the companies to directly contact workers and collect information on whether they are receiving the work, salary and other services and facilities specified in their foreign employment contracts.

Licensed agencies must submit the collected information on workers’ status to the department’s Institution Monitoring Section by email within 20 days of the workers’ departure.

The department has also warned that licensed agencies that fail to comply with the directive or fail to update information on the status of Nepali workers will face action under the Foreign Employment Act, 2007.

title.rendered: Transport Department seeks details of flood damage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

The Department of Transport Management has sought details of damage caused by floods from stakeholders.

The Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport has formed a committee to collect details of damage to the transport sector. The department has issued a public notice seeking the information required by the committee.

Government agencies, non-governmental organisations, media outlets, private institutions, researchers and the general public can submit details of disaster-related damage to the transport sector.

The details can be submitted via the department’s email or in writing.

title.rendered: New York tops 2026 global cities index, Kathmandu ranks 687th

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

New York has been ranked the world’s best city in the 2026 Global Cities Index published by Oxford Economics. London ranks second and Paris third.

According to Oxford Economics, the overall ranking was prepared by evaluating 1,000 major cities worldwide on five criteria: economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance.

New York ranks first, followed by London in second and Paris in third.

Seattle ranks fourth, San Francisco fifth and Dublin sixth. Boston ranks seventh, San Jose eighth, Tokyo ninth and Zurich 10th.

Where does Kathmandu rank?

Nepal’s capital Kathmandu ranks 687th overall. Kathmandu ranks 670th in economics, 562nd in human capital, 840th in quality of life, 639th in environment and 635th in governance.

According to Oxford Economics, the overall assessment combines all five criteria to measure the condition of a city. It covers the city’s overall performance in economic conditions, human resources, housing and quality of life, environment and governance rather than focusing on any single aspect.

New York tops the list with a score of 100, followed by London with 98.8 and Paris with 93.4. Canberra, the capital of Australia, has been ranked the world’s best city for quality of life. It ranks 45th overall.

The quality-of-life assessment considers factors including people’s income, income inequality, rent and housing costs, life expectancy, crime and access to recreational and cultural facilities.

Seven of the top eight cities in the economics index are in the United States. London ranks seventh, while New York, Los Angeles, San Jose, Seattle, San Francisco, Dallas and Washington occupy the other positions.

In the human capital index, London, Dubai, Tokyo, Riyadh, New York, Abu Dhabi, Paris and Shenzhen rank first to eighth, respectively.

In the environment index, Honolulu, Fortaleza, Bergen, Wellington, Aracaju, Suva, Stockholm and Santa Cruz de Tenerife rank first to eighth, respectively.

Similarly, Copenhagen, Aarhus, Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Helsinki, Tampere and Oslo rank first to eighth, respectively, in governance.

title.rendered: Sipradi Yatri announces price of locally made Yatri P2 electric scooter

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Sipradi Yatri has officially announced the price of its new locally engineered and manufactured electric scooter, the Yatri P2.

The launch marks another milestone in Sipradi Yatri’s efforts to develop electric mobility products that are engineered and manufactured in Nepal.

The P2 has been developed with Nepal’s diverse and challenging road and geographical conditions in mind. The company says the scooter is not designed solely for urban commuting, but also for uphill roads, winding routes, daily city traffic and longer-distance travel.

According to Sipradi Yatri, the starting price of the Yatri P2 is Rs 329,900.

Customers can customise the scooter according to their needs and preferences by choosing from different battery capacities, colours and other comfort and connectivity options.

Engineered for Nepal’s roads

One of the key features of the Yatri P2 is its PMSM mid-drive motor, which has been designed to deliver performance across different road and riding conditions.

The motor produces 315 Nm of torque at the wheel. An actively cooled high-power controller is also designed to help maintain consistent and reliable performance, particularly on uphill roads.

The P2 uses a high-strength steel chassis, long-travel suspension and 14-inch wheels to provide stability and control across different road conditions in Nepal.

The scooter is equipped with dual disc brakes and a combined braking system, which the company says provides greater confidence while braking.

Three battery options

The Yatri P2 is available with three battery options to suit different daily travel requirements.

The 3 kWh battery provides a range of up to 90 km in urban conditions, while the 3.7 kWh battery offers up to 112 km. The 5.2 kWh battery provides a range of up to 157 km, according to the company.

For riders requiring additional range, an extender pack can provide up to another 50 km.

Sipradi Yatri says the P2’s battery systems were developed specifically for the platform and tested according to operating conditions in Nepal.

The scooter comes with a battery warranty of up to eight years or 80,000 kilometres, which the company says reflects its focus on building customer confidence for long-term use.

Connectivity and riding features

The Yatri P2 comes with an installed onboard charger and a 7-inch TFT display.

Other features include 4G connectivity, multiple riding modes, smart charging mode, multiple levels of regenerative braking, hill hold and cruise control.

The scooter is also equipped with Class D headlamps, a regen-responsive tail light, anti-theft notification and motor lock features.

title.rendered: Prachanda: Preparing for new movement against government

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’, coordinator of the Nepali Communist Party (NCP), has said they are preparing to launch a movement against the government.

Addressing a gathering of the farmers’ federation affiliated with the NCP, he accused the government of starting repression and excesses.

“There is a need to form a broad united front and launch a movement against the repression, excesses and atrocities being committed by the so-called new government. We are also preparing for that,” Prachanda said.

He further told party leaders and cadres that they were holding continuous discussions with various political parties, intellectuals and civil society as part of the preparations. He said the discussions were moving in a positive direction.

“I want to make it clear to all the comrades and leaders that we are continuously holding discussions with various political parties, intellectuals and civil society as part of the preparations. Things are moving forward in a positive direction,” Prachanda said.

He also said everyone should resolve to defeat counter-revolution and take the revolution to a new height.

“There is a need for all of us to make a new resolve to defeat counter-revolution and take the revolution to a new height. We are currently in that process,” he said.

Prachanda said a new movement should be launched after the festivals, taking into account the situation in the country at that time.

title.rendered: Inside the DNA and fingerprint effort to identify Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
More than 6,000 people remain missing following the devastating flood on the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa. Most of the bodies recovered so far cannot be identified.

According to the latest figures, 1,403 bodies have been found. Of these, only 103 have been identified and handed over to relatives. The remaining 1,300 unidentified bodies have been buried underground.

Some families of the missing have already given up hope of finding their loved ones alive and have performed final rites using effigies (kush bodies).

DNA testing has now become the main basis for establishing links between unidentified bodies and missing persons. Samples collected from the bodies are being tested at the National Forensic Science Laboratory in Khumaltar and the Police Forensic Science Laboratory in Samakhushi.

Nirajan Thapa, head of the DNA branch at the National Forensic Science Laboratory, told OnlineKhabar that if work continues at its current pace, completing the identification process, testing samples from both bodies and relatives, could take around two and a half months.

The National Forensic Science Laboratory alone has received 1,660 samples so far: 837 collected from bodies (mainly teeth and bone) and 823 from blood samples given by relatives of missing persons, collected from various districts. Collection of relatives’ blood samples is still ongoing.

Of the 823 relative blood samples received, DNA profiles have already been prepared for 551. Since extracting DNA from blood is comparatively straightforward, Thapa said the remaining samples could be completed within one to one and a half weeks.

Testing bone and teeth samples from bodies, however, is more complex and time-consuming. Of the 837 body samples received, results have so far been obtained for only about 195.

An additional roughly 200 samples are being tested by a Chinese team at NAST’s laboratory, and the rest are being processed at the Police Forensic Science Laboratory as well.

According to Thapa, extracting DNA from bone and teeth, building a profile, and matching it against relatives’ samples is a lengthy process. 

 “The DNA extracted from a body has to be compared against the DNA extracted from a relative’s blood. Only then can a biological relationship be established,” he said. “It won’t be an exact match. But DNA passes genetically from one generation to the next, and traits are passed from parents to children accordingly. Relationships are identified on that basis.”

Profiling first, then matching

Thapa said DNA profiling of bodies recovered from the flood is proceeding rapidly, alongside blood sample collection and DNA work for relatives of the missing. Since so many people are missing, DNA profiles are being built for both the bodies and the relatives. First, the unknown DNA from bodies is compared with known DNA from relatives to check for a biological link. Matching happens only after that. 

One body’s DNA profile is matched simultaneously with a large number of samples submitted by families of the missing.

 “In an ordinary case, comparing one unknown sample against one likely candidate is enough. Here, the bodies can’t be identified visually,” Thapa says. “So a single body’s DNA has to be checked with every sample collected from relatives of missing persons.”

Software will be used for this to generate a ranked list of which relatives’ samples are most likely related to a given unknown DNA sample. Experts then finalise identification through statistical analysis of relationships such as parent-child and sibling ties.

“If we test and match 20 samples now and test the remaining hundreds two months later, the identification process becomes more complicated,” Thapa says. “So we wait until a large number of DNA profiles are ready, then run the matching through software.”

Profiles will be built from DNA extracted from relatives’ blood and from bone and teeth recovered from bodies, a process Thapa estimated could take one to one and a half months. 

Bodies found in the flood are fragmented, with some individuals possibly represented by three or four separate remains.  524 of the total recovered are partial remains, making profiling from bone or teeth comparatively more complex, experts say.

Fingerprint matching also underway

Alongside DNA testing, police are also trying to identify the dead by matching fingerprints. The work is being carried out at the Police Forensic Science Laboratory. 

Nepal Police spokesperson Abinarayan Kafle said fingerprints collected from bodies are being compared against fingerprints individuals previously submitted for various purposes.

“We’ve been able to lift fingerprints from more than 290 bodies. We’re trying to match them against records in government databases, including the national ID system,” Kafle told OnlineKhabar. “We’re coordinating with the Ministry of Home Affairs on this. Bodies that get matched this way can be handed over to relatives more quickly.”

He said Singapore has provided equipment for fingerprint identification, and a team from Singapore is helping with the work, alongside equipment already available with Nepal Police.

 Facial detection technology is also being used. A police team is exploring whether AI-based comparison of photographs of missing persons against the faces of bodies could aid identification.

“Some DNA matches will need to be re-tested. Sample collection is ongoing and the numbers could still rise. We’re working to deliver results as quickly as possible,” Kafle says.

US software used for DNA testing

Advanced software is being used to analyse DNA data. Separate databases have been maintained, one for DNA samples from relatives of missing persons, another for DNA samples from bodies. The software calculates the most likely matches between the two databases to help identify probable family relationships.

According to Thapa, the matching software used is CODIS (Combined DNA Index System), a system used by the US FBI for criminal investigations, personal identification, and familial searching. The Police Forensic Science Laboratory is now using it to help identify missing persons.

China, India, South Korea, and Singapore have sent equipment and personnel to Nepal to assist with body identification. 

Kafle said that using only Nepal’s own machines and staff, testing such a large number of samples would take a long time, but with the help of foreign experts and additional machines and manpower, the pace of testing has increased.

The National Forensic Science Laboratory has five DNA experts and three support staff. Eight forensic DNA experts have come from India, and 15 from China. The Chinese team is working out of NAST. Teams from South Korea and Singapore are working at the Police Forensic Science Laboratory.

Establishing ties when an entire family is missing

In some cases, entire families are missing. On how identification is possible in such cases, Thapa said unknown samples (from bodies) can also be compared against each other to determine whether a biological relationship exists between them.

For example, once a grandfather is identified from a family, that same sample can be used to test relationships with subsequent generations. Once a child’s identity is confirmed, that sample can then serve as the basis for testing relationships with grandchildren and other family members.

Comparing unknown samples against each other allows preliminary conclusions about which individuals may belong to the same family or share a biological relationship. But Thapa noted that final confirmation still requires a known sample from at least one family member, a grandparent or one or two relatives, as a reference point for tracing relationships with others.

The most straightforward and reliable samples for DNA testing are those of a parent or child, since roughly 50% of genetic material passes from each parent to a child, allowing biological relationships to be confirmed with up to 99.99% certainty, Thapa said. 

If a parent’s or child’s sample isn’t available, full siblings’ samples can be used instead, or half-siblings’ samples if that too is unavailable.

 The more distant the relationship, the weaker DNA’s ability to confirm it. Between a grandparent and grandchild, genetic similarity is only around 25%.

 “Parents and children share roughly half their genetic traits, which makes confirming the relationship easier,” Thapa says. “But moving toward grandparents, uncles, aunts, or more distant relatives, that identifying power decreases. So we need samples from as many family members as possible.”

Extracting DNA from bone is itself a challenge

Not every sample yields a complete DNA profile, Thapa says; some produce only a partial profile. 

Generally, 70–80% of bone samples yield a usable profile; for the remaining roughly 20%, DNA of sufficient quality may not be obtained, resulting in “no profile” or “partial profile” outcomes. 

Some samples with unclear DNA results need to be re-tested using a different method, adding further time.

Thapa estimated that completing all testing could take two to two and a half months at current projections. The actual timeline also depends on how much additional equipment becomes available and how much it speeds up testing.

“The real challenge right now is extracting a DNA profile from the body itself. With teeth and bone, one attempt doesn’t guarantee a result; bone contains less DNA,” Thapa says. “Out of 100 samples, we might get results for around 40 in the first round. The rest have to be tried again using another method. Repeating the process takes time.”

Blood samples, by contrast, tend to yield results in a single attempt and in less time.

Thapa said there isn’t a major technology gap between Nepali and foreign expert teams currently working on this. The methods used by Indian and Chinese experts who came to Nepal after the disaster are largely similar to those already in use here.

Dr Kamal Chauhan, assistant director at the Central Forensic Science Laboratory in Delhi, said Nepal’s DNA-testing technology and setup are comparable to India’s.

 “The equipment here is similar to what’s used in India,” Chauhan says. “The challenge here is operational capacity. With fewer machines, fewer samples can be tested at a time.”

According to Thapa, the main challenge right now isn’t technology but managing the large volume of incoming samples in an organised way.

title.rendered: Janaki Temple declared protected monument zone

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

The government has declared the Janaki Temple a protected monument zone. According to the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, the Cabinet made the declaration under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1956.

Ministry Secretary Mukunda Prasad Niraula said the monument zone was declared by defining its four boundaries.

The eastern boundary has been set along the Parikrama Path, stretching from Bhanu Chowk and Kadam Chowk in Janakpur past the District Administration Office and Land Revenue Office towards the south.

Similarly, the western boundary has been set along the Parikrama Path from Bhamarpura Chowk towards the west, passing through Yagyavalkya Sanskrit Secondary School, Gyan Kupa and Hanuman Temple before turning north.

The northern boundary has been set along the Parikrama Path from Hanuman Temple and Pidari Chowk, where the Raja Janak Memorial is located, through the Madhes Province government building and Mills Area to Bhanu Chowk.

The southern boundary has been set along the Parikrama Path from Murali Chowk in Janakpurdham, where the Vidyapati Memorial is located, to Bhamarpura Chowk.

The ministry informed the public about the decision by publishing a notice in the Nepal Gazette.

Nepal has set a goal of listing the Janaki Temple as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. For this, the heritage site needs to be declared a protected monument zone. The government made the decision accordingly.

With the declaration, specified standards, including those governing the construction of buildings around the protected area, will now apply.

The government has also included the plan to list the Janaki Temple as a World Heritage Site in the budget for the current fiscal year.

title.rendered: CK Raut elected unopposed as Janmat Party president, 14 candidates vying for vice president

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Dr. CK Raut has been elected national president of the Janmat Party. As part of the party’s second general convention, nomination filings took place on Thursday, and since Dr. Raut was the only candidate for president, he was declared elected unopposed.

While the president’s post was uncontested, elections are expected for other positions. The party’s second general convention will be held in Birgunj on September 25–26.

According to the preliminary list of candidates, 14 people have filed for the 7 vice president posts.

Candidates for vice president include Basant Kumar Kushwaha (Rautahat), Anita Sah (Dhanusha), Anita Mandal (Siraha), Dr. Jaykant Raut (Saptari), Narendra Prasad Chaudhary (Kapilvastu), and Madhav Prasad Singh (Parsa).

Also contesting for the same post are Raj Kumar Yadav Tyagi (Siraha), Dr. Kamrullah Ansari (Bara), Sanjay Kumar Mishra (Rupandehi), Madhnesh Kumar Chaudhary (Saptari), Parmeshwar Murmu (Morang), Rosan Khatun (Bara), Harpal Singh Sodhi (Banke), and Manohari Devi Baitha (Sarlahi).

According to Rajesh Kumar Mandal, member secretary of the Janmat Party Central Election Committee, three candidates, Mamata Jha (Saptari), Chandan Kumar Singh (Mahottari), and Sanjay Kumar Yadav (Siraha), are contesting for the single general secretary post.

For the single deputy general secretary post, Nirmal Kumar Mandal (Siraha) and Lalitchandra Mallik (Rautahat) are contesting.

For the 7 secretary posts, 10 candidates have filed nominations: Santosh Kumar Sahani (Dhanusha), Surendra Sharma Madhesi (Saptari), Harendra Chaudhary (Rautahat), Anjani Devi (Mahottari), Rohit Mahato (Siraha), Paras Prasad Sah (Bara), Radha Kumari Yadav (Banke), Bal Govind Chaudhary (Nawalparasi), Birendra Mahato (Jeevan Tyagi) (Mahottari), and Rambabu Sah (Bara).

title.rendered: Korean ambassador discusses Bhotekoshi rescue and AI cooperation with Communications Minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Nepal Park Jae Kyung paid a courtesy call on Minister for Information and Communications Dr Bikram Timilsina on Thursday, with discussions focusing on the Bhotekoshi flood response and Nepal-Korea cooperation in technology.

The meeting, held at Minister Timilsina’s office at Singha Durbar, covered Nepal-Korea relations, rescue and rehabilitation of people affected by the Bhotekoshi flood, and Korean assistance for relief and reconstruction.

The two sides also discussed cooperation in information technology, the digital economy and artificial intelligence.

Minister Timilsina thanked the Korean government for its support and solidarity with Nepal following the Bhotekoshi flood.

He expressed gratitude for Korea’s mobilisation of a disaster management team for search and rescue operations, as well as its commitment to supporting flood-affected communities and reconstruction and rehabilitation efforts.

Timilsina stressed the need to further strengthen Nepal-Korea relations based on mutual respect, understanding and cooperation.

Ambassador Park said South Korea would continue its support for rescue and rehabilitation efforts in the flood-hit areas.

He also enquired about the condition of Korean nationals reported missing in the Bhotekoshi flood.

According to Park, a Korean security team rescued 10 Korean citizens from the flood-hit area, while nine Korean nationals remain out of contact.

Nepal to participate in Global ICT Leadership Forum

During the meeting, Ambassador Park also informed Minister Timilsina about Nepal’s participation in the 12th Global ICT Leadership Forum, scheduled to take place in South Korea from September 30.

The forum will bring together representatives from Nepal and other countries for high-level discussions on cooperation in information technology and artificial intelligence, as well as future strategies in the sector.

The forum is being organised by South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT in coordination with the National Information Society Agency.

title.rendered: Two arrested for alleged hundi transactions worth Rs 1.57 billion

content.rendered:
Sunsari, September 18

Police have arrested two people in Biratnagar on suspicion of conducting hundi transactions worth more than Rs 1.57 billion.

Shambhu Prasad Sah, 56, of Rani in Biratnagar Metropolitan City-15, and Suraj Prasad Sah, 35, of Biratnagar-17, were arrested on Thursday by a police team deployed from the District Police Office, Sunsari.

According to Chandrabahadur Khadka, information officer at the District Police Office, police analysed the banking transactions of individuals suspected of involvement in hundi dealings based on information received about such activities. The analysis showed that Shambhu Prasad and Suraj Prasad, in collusion with other individuals, had used personal and firm bank accounts to conduct hundi transactions amounting to Rs 1,576,439,340.

Khadka said the two were arrested for investigation into offences related to hundi transactions under the National Penal Code, 2017, as well as offences under the Organised Crime Prevention Act, 2010, and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2008.

Police said both arrested individuals have been kept at the District Police Office, and further investigation is underway.
