title.rendered: Congress ward conventions to begin Saturday

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Ward-level conventions of the Nepali Congress will begin on Saturday as part of the party’s 15th General Convention. The party’s Central Election Committee has said ward conventions may be held on Saturday or Sunday, depending on local circumstances.

All active members who renewed their membership by the end of Poush 2082 BS will participate in the conventions in their respective wards.

Party President Gagan Thapa has already called on members to participate enthusiastically in the ward-level conventions being held as part of preparations for the 15th General Convention.

Active members within each ward will be members of the respective ward convention. The ward convention will elect a president, two vice-presidents including one woman, one secretary and one joint secretary.

According to the Nepali Congress statute, ward presidents elected from wards under rural municipalities, municipalities, sub-metropolitan cities and metropolitan cities can nominate a treasurer from among the elected ward executive committee members.

The ward convention in a rural municipality will elect seven ward members, including at least two women, one Dalit and one youth under the age of 30.

Similarly, ward conventions in municipalities and sub-metropolitan cities must elect eight ward members, including two women, one Dalit and two youths under the age of 30.

Likewise, metropolitan ward conventions will directly elect 11 ward members, including at least three women, one Dalit and three youths under the age of 30.

The Nepali Congress statute provides different provisions for ward presidents to nominate ward members depending on the type of local government. Accordingly, a rural municipality ward president can nominate five members, a municipality or sub-metropolitan ward president can nominate six, and a metropolitan ward president can nominate seven.

The ward president must nominate ward members from among active members while ensuring that one-third of the executive committee members are women and taking into account the principle of inclusion, including representation of all communities, minorities, persons with disabilities and youth.

According to the Nepali Congress statute, the ward executive committee must meet at least once a month. Representatives to the regional convention may be invited to ward executive committee meetings as necessary.

Likewise, the ward executive committee must invite the presidents of subordinate neighbourhood-level committees to its meetings.

The Nepali Congress statute allows the same person to serve as a representative to the regional convention and as a member of a rural municipality ward executive committee.

Selection of regional convention representatives

Representatives to the regional convention will also be selected through ward conventions in rural municipalities, municipalities, sub-metropolitan cities and metropolitan cities. The same number of representatives will be selected from each ward convention for the regional convention.

A ward with 150 or fewer active members will select nine regional convention representatives from among its active members, including at least three women and one worker or professional-sector representative.

The ward convention must also directly elect three youths, including one woman under the age of 30, as regional convention representatives.

Similarly, in wards with more than 150 active members, six additional representatives, including two women and one youth, will be directly elected for every additional 150 active members, up to a maximum of 55 representatives.

The statute states that representatives must be elected proportionally according to the population composition of the ward, as prescribed, with the number of representatives from women, Dalit, Indigenous Nationalities, Khas-Arya, Madhesi, Tharu, Muslim, minority and backward areas set at 50 per cent of the number of members directly elected.

The statute states, “One representative each from among active members with disabilities and Dalit active members.”

According to the statute, the ward executive committee president is considered an ex-officio representative to the regional convention.

What are the qualifications for a ward president?

The Nepali Congress has not set qualification criteria for candidates for ward executive committee president. The party statute, amended by the special general convention held last Poush, does not specify qualifications for candidates for ward executive committee president.

Previously, only members who had completed one year as active members of the Nepali Congress were eligible to contest for president of a rural municipality, municipality, sub-metropolitan city or metropolitan city ward executive committee.

The amended statute also does not specify qualifications required to contest for president of a rural municipality or municipality, provincial assembly constituency, House of Representatives constituency, district, provincial or central party president.

However, the 15th General Convention Election Directive, 2083 BS, sets out provisions regarding the qualifications and nomination of candidates, except for ward presidents.

Accordingly, candidates for president of a rural municipality or municipality, president of a provincial assembly constituency, president of a House of Representatives constituency, and district vice-president and secretary must have been active members for five years.

Similarly, candidates for district president, provincial president and other provincial office-bearer positions, as well as central committee members, must have held active membership for 10 years. However, the directive states that this requirement does not apply to youths below 35, members who joined the party through integration, and members from professional and workers’ sectors.

The directive also states that candidates for central office-bearer positions must have been active members continuously for 10 years, while a candidate for central president must have held continuous active membership for 15 years.

content.rendered:
Banepa (Kavrepalanchok), September 18

The number of dengue cases in Kavrepalanchok has reached 32.

According to the latest data released by the District Public Health Office, 32 people have tested positive for dengue in the district between July 16 and September 17.

According to Public Health Officer Shishir Pudasaini, the highest number of cases has been recorded in Banepa Municipality and Panchkhal Municipality, with 13 cases each.

He said three new cases were detected in the past 24 hours. One case each was confirmed in Panchkhal, Namobuddha Municipality and Mandandeupur Municipality.

Information Officer at the District Public Health Office Dipendrakaji Shrestha said no dengue cases have so far been reported in Dhulikhel and Panauti municipalities or in Bhumlu, Roshi, Temal, Khanikhola, Bethanchok, Mahabharat and Chaurideurali rural municipalities.

Last fiscal year, 59 dengue cases were confirmed in Kavre.

Shrestha said awareness campaigns and sanitation measures have been stepped up this year to prevent further spread of the disease, as the monsoon creates favourable conditions for mosquito breeding.

The District Public Health Office has urged people to protect themselves from mosquito bites, prevent water from accumulating in and around their homes, and wear long-sleeved clothing to prevent dengue.

It has also urged people experiencing symptoms such as fever, headache and body aches to visit a health facility for testing and treatment.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Six bodies have been recovered from a tunnel of the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project.

According to the Nepal Army Headquarters, six bodies were found entangled in the reinforcement steel mesh installed for concreting the tunnel.

Security personnel and representatives of the project have been deployed inside the tunnel and are working at the site.

title.rendered: Buddha Circuit to link Panauti, Namobuddha and Temal

content.rendered:
Kavrepalanchok, September 18

Major historical, religious and tourist sites in the southeastern part of Kavrepalanchok are set to be developed into a ‘Buddha Circuit’ trail.

The federal government has allocated Rs 250 million for the circuit, which will connect the historic town of Panauti with Namobuddha and Temal, said Madhu Chaulagain, a member of the House of Representatives from Kavrepalanchok.

In the first phase, Rs 100 million will be spent on constructing physical and cultural heritage structures related to Lord Buddha along the Panauti-Namobuddha road. Prayer wheels, chaityas and statues of the Laughing Buddha will also be installed at various locations, along with information boards featuring Thangka art.

According to Chaulagain, the objective is to transform the approximately eight-kilometre Panauti-Namobuddha road into an attractive tourist route featuring heritage sites associated with Lord Buddha.

Under the Buddha Circuit project, a Ratuwa deer park will be constructed in the Bokse Community Forest at Dapcha along the Namobuddha-Bhakunde road section.

Similarly, a Cultural Confluence Gate will be constructed at the Chardobato intersection in Bhakundebesi along the BP Highway.

title.rendered: Prakash Man Singh: We are determined to hold 15th General Convention as per party rules

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Nepali Congress leader Prakash Man Singh has said that the party’s 15th General Convention will be held in accordance with its rules, statute and democratic values.

Speaking to journalists after paying tribute to the statue of Ganesh Man Singh at Shobha Bhagawati in Kathmandu on Friday, Singh said preparations for the 15th General Convention were already underway.

“We are determined to hold the 15th General Convention in accordance with the rules, regardless of the circumstances,” he said. He said a special general convention was not the Nepali Congress’s preference and argued that it would not be appropriate to violate rules and procedures to fulfil anyone’s personal ambition.

Stating that political issues and agendas are the main concerns of political parties, he said the independence of the judiciary must be respected. He said the courts should deal with judicial matters, while political parties should make decisions on political issues.

“If political issues and agendas are to be decided by the party, judicial matters should be handled by the courts,” he said. “The Nepali Congress believes in democracy and the independence of the judiciary.”

Recalling that BP Koirala and Ganesh Man Singh had prioritised their political objectives and national interests when they returned to Nepal in 2033 BS under the policy of national unity and reconciliation, he said the Nepali Congress had not deviated from its democratic principles even after the Panchayat system won the 2036 BS referendum following the student movement.

He said the political change in 2046 BS became possible as a continuation of that stance.

“Even today, the Nepali Congress must set an example by adhering to its rules, procedures and democratic values. We are determined to hold the 15th General Convention in accordance with the rules, regardless of the circumstances,” he said.

He said it was their responsibility to hold the general convention in accordance with the spirit and essence of the party statute and the Constitution of Nepal and to protect the rule of law, people’s rights and national interests.

title.rendered: ANFA warns of independent activities from Monday if suspension isn’t lifted

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

The All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) has said that if the government does not make a firm decision to lift its suspension, it will resume its activities from Monday in line with FIFA’s directive.

ANFA CEO Indraman Tuladhar told a press conference on Friday that with the future of academy players at risk, the government needed to act immediately.

“If we get a positive response from the government by tomorrow, we may still be able to take part in the SAFF. Otherwise, given how serious this situation has become, we will begin activities in line with FIFA’s directive from Monday,” Tuladhar said.

He also said that problems regarding the education and housing of child players at the ANFA Academy were worsening.

“The children at the academy are facing problems with their studies and food,” he said.

According to Tuladhar, ANFA will fully support any initiative the government takes toward lifting the suspension. But he made clear that if there is no progress, daily football activities will proceed according to FIFA’s rules.

“We will support whatever initiative the government takes. If nothing happens, we will move forward with daily activities as per FIFA’s rules,” he said.

Nepali football has been out of international activity since FIFA suspended ANFA last June/July, citing third-party interference.

title.rendered: Students protest in Australia against new immigration policy

content.rendered:
Canberra, September 18

Students staged protests against Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party in Canberra on Thursday.

The protest, titled “Students Say No to Hanson,” was held at Garema Place from 1 pm to 3 pm on September 17. It was organised by High School Anti-Capitalists.

The September 17 protest was the second phase of a student movement that began on August 13. In August, high school and university students in cities including Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane walked out of classes and took to the streets to protest One Nation and Hanson’s politics. According to ABC, hundreds of students participated in the protests in each major city.

Students also staged protests in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, Darwin and Hobart this time. According to an AAP report, more than 1,000 people participated in a protest in Sydney, where students opposed Hanson’s proposed immigration policies.

Hundreds of students also participated in the protest in Melbourne.

Immigration policy a key issue

On September 14, One Nation unveiled a “net-negative migration” plan to reduce the number of temporary visas in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years. The party has presented the plan as a major component of its immigration policy.

According to details released by the party, the plan would significantly reduce international student numbers, cut the number of international graduates allowed to remain in Australia and restrict visas for family members of international students and skilled migrants. ABC reported that One Nation proposed reducing international student places to just over 100,000 a year and creating a separate category for “high-value” students.

The proposals have prompted further debate among universities and international student communities. Students participating in Thursday’s protests expressed opposition to One Nation’s policies on immigration, multiculturalism and social rights.

Back on the streets after August protests

The first nationwide student protests on August 13 were organised at the call of student groups, including the National Union of Students. Students walked out of classes in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.

According to ABC, police intervened at some locations after tensions arose between One Nation supporters and protesters.

Following the August protests, a second round of demonstrations was announced for September 17. Garema Place was designated as the protest site in Canberra.

The recent political influence of One Nation has also formed part of the backdrop to the protests. A Roy Morgan poll conducted from September 7 to 13 put One Nation’s primary vote at 25 per cent.

The survey was conducted among 1,583 voters across Australia.

One Nation and Hanson have continued to express their political views on the student protests and criticism directed at them. Following the August protests, Hanson said students should recognise that she and her party were working for their future.

title.rendered: When a body is never found: How Nepal’s law handles declaring the dead

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Families of people missing in the Bhotekoshi floods are facing a threefold hardship. They are not only grieving the loss of their loved ones but have also lost their homes, land and businesses. In addition, the bodies of their loved ones have not been recovered.

The legal procedures they must complete have added to their uncertainty. Families who have already performed funeral rites using symbolic bodies made of kusha grass according to religious tradition now face further hardship due to lengthy legal procedures to establish the deaths of their loved ones.

A relative of a person who went missing in the Rasuwa floods recently visited Tarkeshwor Municipality in Kathmandu to obtain a missing-person certificate. However, the municipality could not issue such a certificate.

According to Tarkeshwor Municipality Chief Administrative Officer Dharmaraj Lamsal, under the general legal procedure, a missing-person certificate cannot be issued until 12 years have passed. Some relatives of people missing in the Rasuwa floods are permanent or temporary residents of Tarkeshwor Municipality.

More than 5,000 people, including people from Rasuwa, Nuwakot and other districts as well as foreign nationals, have been reported missing since the floods of August 26. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the bodies of 1,403 people who died in the floods have been recovered. Of these, 105 bodies have been handed over to their families.

More than three weeks have passed since the floods. As the likelihood of finding missing people alive diminishes with each passing day, some families have already performed funeral rites by creating symbolic bodies from kusha grass in accordance with religious traditions.

But does performing funeral rites using a symbolic kusha body mean that a person is legally considered dead? Do families whose loved ones are missing and whose bodies have not been recovered have to wait 12 years to have the deaths legally established?

Missing flood victims do not have to wait 12 years

Section 40 of the National Civil Code, 2017, contains provisions concerning the declaration of death of a missing person.

Under normal circumstances, a person who has been missing without information for 12 consecutive years, or about whom a person who would ordinarily be expected to receive information has received no information for 12 years, is presumed dead unless evidence is found that the person is alive.

However, this provision does not apply equally to all cases of missing persons. The law provides a separate procedure for people who go missing in disasters or accidents.

Subsection 4 of Section 40 provides for a judicial declaration of death when a person has gone missing without information or when there are grounds to believe that the person died as a result of a disaster or accident.

This means families of people missing in the Bhotekoshi floods do not necessarily have to wait 12 years to have their deaths legally established.

What must families do?

According to senior advocate Raju Khadka, a relative or other concerned person can file an application at the district court seeking a judicial declaration of death of a person who went missing in a disaster or accident.

The application must state when, where and under what circumstances the person went missing. It must also include the grounds for believing that the person may have died, along with any available evidence.

After receiving the application, the court may investigate based on evidence confirming the occurrence of the incident, evidence that the person was involved in the incident, eyewitness accounts and other available evidence.

According to Khadka, police records related to the incident, eyewitness accounts, travel records, CCTV footage, phone records and other evidence may be useful.

However, he said what constitutes sufficient evidence depends on the circumstances of each incident and the evidence available.

Rule 60 of the Civil Procedure Rules, 2018, also sets out the procedure for filing an application seeking a judicial declaration of death under subsection 4 of Section 40.

Death registration after court order

Families may perform funeral rites according to religious traditions when a body has not been recovered. However, such rites alone do not result in legal registration of death.

According to senior advocate Khadka, once a court issues a judicial declaration of death, the family can initiate the death registration process at the relevant ward office on the basis of the court order.

Initially, family members must collect available evidence establishing that the person went missing. After filing an application at the district court and obtaining a judicial declaration of death, the death can be registered at the ward office.

Following death registration, legal procedures concerning the deceased person’s property, inheritance and other rights can also be initiated.

What happens after a symbolic kusha funeral?

Families of some people missing in the Rasuwa floods have already performed funeral rites using symbolic bodies made of kusha grass.

Completing religious funeral rites and legally establishing a person’s death are separate matters. Therefore, according to senior advocate Khadka, performing funeral rites using a symbolic kusha body does not by itself result in direct registration of death.

If a body is recovered and identified, the death registration process can be initiated with the necessary evidence. However, when a body has not been recovered, a judicial declaration of death may be required.

What evidence should families collect?

Available evidence is the most important factor when seeking a judicial declaration of death.

The court may examine the grounds indicating that the person may have died and evidence establishing that the person was involved in the incident. Families should therefore preserve all available evidence, including:

  • Police records related to the incident
  • Eyewitness accounts
  • Travel records
  • CCTV footage
  • Phone records or other communication details
  • Other records confirming that the person was at the incident site

According to advocate Khadka, the sufficiency of evidence will be determined based on the circumstances of each case and the evidence available.

What if a person declared dead returns alive?

The law also addresses such an unusual situation. If a person returns alive after a court has issued a judicial declaration of death, the person can apply to have the declaration annulled. The law also allows amendments if there is a change concerning the date of death stated in the judicial declaration.

Once the judicial declaration of death is annulled, the person may reclaim property and other rights to which they are legally entitled. If property has been transferred or other legal transactions have taken place in the meantime, their consequences will be determined under the relevant laws, Khadka said.

Families await government decision

Although a judicial declaration is legally available, local officials and representatives in Rasuwa and Nuwakot say the existing procedure is complicated for families of people who went missing in a disaster involving such a large number of people.

The Rasuwa District Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committee has already decided to ask the Ministry of Home Affairs to establish an alternative fast-track mechanism for registering missing persons, officially confirming deaths and processing insurance claims.

According to Hemraj Aryal, spokesperson for the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the government is discussing what should be done regarding people missing in the Bhotekoshi floods.

“We are discussing what should be done regarding people missing in the Bhotekoshi floods,” he said.

Meanwhile, for families whose loved ones remain missing and whose bodies have not been recovered, the immediate question remains: when will the state establish an easier process to legally confirm the status of their loved ones?

title.rendered: 29th Memorial Day of Ganesh Man Singh being observed today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

The Nepali Congress, its sister organisations and well-wishers are observing the 29th memorial day of Ganesh Man Singh, the Supreme Commander of the 1990 People’s Movement, by organising various programmes today.

Born on Kartik 24, 1972 BS, in Chhetrapati, Kathmandu, Singh passed away on Ashwin 2, 2054 BS.

He actively participated in the campaign to overthrow the Rana regime as a member of the then Praja Parishad. After escaping from Bhadragol Jail before 2007 BS, Singh travelled to India, where he forged a political partnership with fellow leader B P Koirala.

He led the Nepali Rashtriya Congress, which was established in 2003 BS. As a key figure in the 2007 BS revolution aimed at establishing democracy, he participated in the armed struggle on the Birgunj front.

Singh served as a senior minister in the government formed after the first general election in 2015 BS. After democracy was usurped in 2017 BS, he spent eight years in captivity at Singhadurbar and Sundarijal prisons.

Following his release from Sundarijal Prison alongside B.P. Koirala in 2025 BS, he worked to strengthen the political organisation while in exile. In 2033 BS, he returned to Nepal with B.P. Koirala, adopting the policy of national unity and reconciliation, and remained active in the struggle against the Panchayat system.

title.rendered: Oli and Prachanda explore fresh cooperation as UML-NCP talks gather pace

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

A photograph posted by CPN-UML Secretary Sherdhan Rai on Wednesday has brought into the open discussions that have been quietly taking place between the UML and the Nepali Communist Party (NCP) for the past two weeks.

The photograph showed Rai with NCP leader Barshaman Pun at Hotel Vivanta in Lalitpur. The two leaders had gone there following discussions related to the convention of Kirat Rai Yayokkha.

The meeting itself was not presented as a formal political gathering. But coming amid growing behind-the-scenes discussions between the UML and NCP, the photograph added to speculation that the two parties are exploring ways to work together again.

Senior leaders from both sides say UML Chair KP Sharma Oli and NCP Coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal are interested in renewing cooperation under the changed political circumstances.

The discussions, however, have yet to produce agreement among the second-rung leaders of the two parties.

The possibility of cooperation has emerged at a time when the UML is itself engaged in an increasingly intense debate over restructuring and leadership. Some UML leaders suspect that the discussion with the NCP could also shift attention away from that debate.

At the same time, there is concern among some leaders that any new arrangement between Oli and Dahal should not repeat the pattern of unity and division that characterised their previous partnership.

Leadership question at the centre of talks

The discussions have gone beyond a simple electoral alliance and have begun touching on possible leadership arrangements if cooperation develops further.

Sherdhan Rai has been coordinating meetings held as part of the initiative. Rai has previously maintained close relations with former President Bidya Devi Bhandari as well as UML Chair Oli.

While the current debate inside the UML has led Rai to favour retaining Oli, he has also argued that Bhandari should return to active party politics if the party undergoes restructuring and its leadership changes.

One proposal being discussed is for the UML to retain the chairmanship based on its organisational legacy and strength, while Bhandari could replace Oli as chairperson.

A senior leader closely following the talks said second-generation leaders from both sides could then help create a favourable environment for cooperation.

“The discussion has begun that if Bidya comes as an alternative to Oli, second-generation leaders could play a role in creating a positive environment within the NCP,” the leader said.

Under this model, the NCP could accept Pun, or another leader of similar stature, as general secretary, with the two sides eventually moving towards a unification general convention.

“If that does not happen, we will also discuss other models of cooperation,” the leader said.

The leadership question gained further significance after UML General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel met Bhandari at Baluwatar on Tuesday.

The meeting came as a majority of UML leaders have been arguing that Oli should leave the party leadership, although an environment for such a change has not yet emerged.

According to sources, Bhandari told Pokhrel to stand in favour of restructuring and conveyed that she would support the process.

The discussions reportedly included the possibility of the UML and NCP beginning a new form of cooperation that could eventually lead to unification.

“Those in the NCP do not appear to have much objection to making Bidya chairperson. I understand that Prachanda will not claim the leadership,” an UML source told Onlinekhabar.

“This would be an interim arrangement. The destination is a new general convention. We are working to start that debate,” the source said.

From quiet meetings to a broader political calculation

The effort has not been limited to meetings between UML and NCP leaders.

On Teej, former Vice-President Nanda Kishor Pun held discussions with several leaders at his residence in Dahchok.

UML leaders Yubaraj Gyawali and Pradeep Gyawali, as well as NCP leaders Barshaman Pun and Pampha Bhusal, among others, attended the meeting.

According to sources, Nanda Kishor Pun urged the leaders to deepen cooperation between the two parties.

The discussions have now also begun to consider keeping both Oli and Dahal out of executive leadership if the two forces eventually unite. One proposal is to place both leaders in a supreme advisory body instead.

Such discussions are taking place against the backdrop of a significantly changed political environment.

The leaderships of both parties are taking into account the political upheaval following the Gen Z protests, the defensive position of the left vote in the most recent election and the approaching provincial and local elections.

They are also watching changes among indigenous voters who have traditionally provided significant support to the UML and Maoist forces but are increasingly being attracted to newer political figures such as Harka Sampang and Kulman Ghising.

The emergence of newer political forces has added urgency to the search for possible forms of cooperation, according to leaders involved in the discussions.

Pun confirms talks with UML

NCP leader Barshaman Pun has confirmed that discussions on cooperation with the UML have begun.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar, Pun said the top leadership of both parties appeared open to either cooperation or unification, although leaders at the middle level still needed to discuss how such an arrangement would work.

“The top leaders on both sides appear ready for unity or cooperation. At the middle level, we still need to discuss how to move forward and what more needs to be done,” Pun said.

The two parties have experience of both cooperation and unification.

In October 2017, the UML and Maoists formed a left alliance with the aim of creating a new communist force. The alliance won a near two-thirds majority and formed an Oli-led government.

On May 17, 2018, the two parties formally merged to form the Nepal Communist Party, with Oli and Dahal serving as co-chairpersons.

The arrangement, however, failed to last amid intense factionalism and disputes over power, eventually leading to the party’s split.

This time, the discussions are taking place with the next provincial and local elections in mind, leaders say.

Cooperation between the two forces has already begun at the provincial level. Under agreements currently being implemented, the UML leads the governments in Koshi, Bagmati and Lumbini, while the NCP leads the governments in Karnali and Sudurpaschim.

The question now is whether the cooperation taking shape at the provincial level can develop into a broader political arrangement between the two parties — and whether the current generation of leaders can avoid repeating the cycle of unity and division that marked their previous partnership.

title.rendered: Nepal Rastra Bank introduces new Rs 50 banknote

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Nepal Rastra Bank has introduced a new Rs 50 banknote into circulation from today, retaining the existing size and colour of the denomination while incorporating several new features.

According to a notice issued by the central bank’s Currency Management Department, the new notes carry serial numbers ranging from ट २४ ०००००१ to ण ७० ९९९९९९.

The front of the new note carries the promise text stating that Rs 50 will be paid immediately by Nepal Rastra Bank upon demand, with payment guaranteed by the Government of Nepal.

The left side of the note features an image of Mount Everest, while a rhododendron watermark appears on the right. A watermark of the numeral ‘50’ is also placed below it.

The lower section of the note carries the series year 2082 in the Bikram Sambat calendar. The note bears the signature of Nepal Rastra Bank Governor Prof Dr Biswo Nath Poudel.

The new banknote also contains a 1.2-millimetre-wide security thread woven into the paper. When viewed against light, the thread becomes fully visible and carries the inscription ‘NRB’.

On the reverse side, the central section features an image of a snow leopard, with ‘NEPAL RASTRA BANK’ written above it.

The lower section of the reverse side carries the inscriptions ‘RUPEES FIFTY’ and ‘2025 A.D.’

Earlier Rs 50 series

Nepal Rastra Bank said it had previously issued a notice on July 6, 2020, announcing that Rs 50 notes from the 2019 series, bearing serial numbers from ज ८९ ०००००१ to ट ३३ ९९९९९९, would be put into circulation.

However, according to the central bank, only notes with serial numbers ranging from ज ८९ ०००००१ to ट २३ ९००००० were actually brought into circulation.

title.rendered: Purna Bahadur Khadka urges Gagan Thapa to postpone Nepali Congress convention and start talks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Former acting president of the Nepali Congress Purna Bahadur Khadka has urged party president Gagan Kumar Thapa to postpone the party’s 15th General Convention and immediately begin dialogue with former president Sher Bahadur Deuba and senior leaders to prevent a split in the party.

Khadka made the appeal in a Facebook post on Thursday, saying there is still a possibility of preserving party unity.

He urged Thapa to suspend the schedule for the 15th General Convention, which has been announced to begin from September 19, and postpone it for some time.

“Postpone the schedule of the 15th General Convention announced to begin from September 19 for some time,” Khadka wrote.

He also called on Thapa to take the initiative to begin talks with Deuba and other senior leaders.

“On the strong foundation of the decision you have taken in the party today, immediately initiate dialogue with respected senior leader Sher Bahadur Deuba, who was elected president by the 14th General Convention, and other senior leaders,” he said.

Khadka said he remained confident that the party could still be kept united.

“I am confident that complete unity of the party is still possible,” he wrote.

‘Two separate conventions could lead to party split’

Khadka warned that if the two separate convention processes are not stopped, the division of the Nepali Congress could become unavoidable.

“If the two separate conventions are not stopped, no one will be able to prevent the division of the Nepali Congress,” he wrote.

He also expressed concern that a split in the Congress could be followed by divisions in other major political parties.

“My inner conscience tells me that within a few months of the Congress party’s division, the CPN-UML, the Nepali Communist Party and other parties, particularly those that played an important role in constitution-making, will also split or be made to split,” Khadka said.

Khadka asks Thapa to reconsider decision

Khadka urged Thapa to seriously reflect on the decisions he has taken.

Referring to a conversation between the two leaders on May 4, Khadka said that if Thapa had taken the decision he has now taken immediately after that discussion, the entire Congress could have stood united under his leadership at the party’s central office in Sanepa by the first week of May.

“You should seriously self-reflect and think about it once again. Time is powerful. Take a firm resolve again,” he wrote.

Khadka said such a move could have generated enthusiasm, confidence and energy among Congress leaders, members and supporters across Nepal and abroad.

He also urged Thapa to take an immediate and courageous decision to preserve party unity.

“Gaganji, I say this with confidence: the law, court decisions or the party statute will not create any problem or difficulty for you. Be assured,” Khadka wrote.

He asked Thapa to deeply review the advice he had received and developments within the party and take a decisive step.

“Become the president of the entire Nepali Congress,” he urged.

Khadka also said he was ready to make any sacrifice to support the effort to preserve party unity, saying he was free of personal ambition.

Warns of wider conflict

Khadka also expressed concern about the possible consequences of a political crisis in the country.

He said his “inner conscience” was telling him that Nepal could face an “unimaginable” conflict along ethnic, regional and religious lines.

He warned that the country could move towards a cycle of severe conflict that could overshadow the events of September 9, 2025.

Khadka questioned what such a situation would mean for Nepal’s national unity, territorial integrity, sovereignty and national pride.

He concluded by urging Thapa to take an immediate, decisive and courageous step to prevent the division of the Nepali Congress and preserve the party’s unity.

title.rendered: 898 hydropower workers remain missing after Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 18

Twenty-two days after floods swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors, 898 people working at 13 hydropower projects remain unaccounted for.

According to data collected by the Nepal Engineers’ Association, 188 of those missing are engineers and technicians.

The prolonged uncertainty has pushed some families to perform final rites using symbolic bodies made of kusha grass, despite the absence of their relatives’ remains.

The Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project has recorded the highest number of missing engineers and technicians, with 60 still unaccounted for.

The association’s data shows that 42 engineers and technicians from Upper Trishuli-3B, 30 from Upper Trishuli-3A, 25 from Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, 20 from Langtang Khola, six from Mailung Khola and five from Chilime Hydropower Project remain missing.

Of the engineers and technicians reported missing, 17 bodies have been recovered so far. Two others, Sanjay Sah and Kabir Maharjan, were rescued.

On Wednesday, four bodies and one human body part recovered from the Chilime project site were found to include one engineer or technician.

Project-wise, 575 people working at the 216-MW Upper Trishuli-1 project are still missing.

Similarly, 93 people from the 111-MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, four from the 120-MW Rasuwaghoshi project, 42 from the 20-MW Langtang Khola project, six from the 22-MW Chilime project, seven from the 5-MW Mailung Khola project, 42 from the 60-MW Upper Trishuli-3A project and 122 from the 37-MW Upper Trishuli-3B project remain unaccounted for.

Four-member family’s wait ends in final rites

For the family of electrical engineer Somnath Paudel, the 22 days since the flood have been marked by uncertainty.

Paudel, from Bansgadhi Municipality-8 in Bardiya, was living in the Upper Trishuli-3B project quarters with his wife Tara Upadhyay and their 28-month-old twins, Shivansh and Tisia.

All four went missing after the flood on August 26.

The family had spoken to them until the evening before the disaster. There has been no contact since.

“We spoke to them until the evening before. Something happened the next morning, and we have not been able to contact them since,” said Sagar Paudel, Somnath’s cousin.

After repeated searches failed to establish their whereabouts, the family performed the final rites of all four at Parewa Odar Ghat on the Babai River in Bardiya, using symbolic bodies made from kusha grass.

Somnath’s 81-year-old father, Umanath Paudel, has begun the mourning rituals after receiving no information about his son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren.

Umanath provided a blood sample at the District Hospital in Gulariya on September 6 for DNA testing to help establish Somnath’s identity. Tara’s father, Chandramani Upadhyay, also provided a blood sample for her DNA test. The results are yet to arrive.

Engineer couple and their four-year-old twins also missing

The family of engineer couple Rajesh Sharma Paudel and Pramila Pathak, who also worked at Upper Trishuli-3B, is facing a similar ordeal.

Rajesh, 33, from Tityang in Baglung Municipality-9, his 31-year-old wife Pramila and their four-year-old twins, Aditya and Aditi, have been missing since the flood.

Their relatives continued searching in the hope that the family would be found alive. Some travelled to the affected area themselves, but there has been no information about them.

With no bodies recovered, the family has already performed the final rites at Pashupati Aryaghat using symbolic bodies made from kusha grass.

According to relative Laxman Rijal, the family eventually gave up hope of finding them alive after they remained out of contact for so long.

Rajesh was the only son in his family and had three sisters. The disappearance of all four members has left his family and relatives in Baglung mourning.

A call that never came

Twenty-six-year-old Subodh Belbase of Thada Amrai in Shitganga Municipality, Arghakhanchi, was also working as an engineer at Upper Trishuli-3B.

He had been working at the project for two years and has been missing since the flood.

Belbase spoke to his mother, Sabitra, by phone on the night of August 25. During the conversation, he told her he would call the following afternoon.

But the flood struck the next day. The call never came.

Subodh was the younger of Surendra and Sabitra Belbase’s two children and their only son. His father, Surendra, works at the Modi Hydropower Project in Parbat.

After learning that his son was missing, Surendra travelled through Kathmandu to Rasuwa in search of him. But Subodh’s whereabouts remain unknown.

Electrical engineer missing at 29

Samir Lamichhane, a 29-year-old electrical engineer at the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, has also been missing since the flood.

Lamichhane had worked at the 111-MW project for around six years and was serving as its operations in-charge.

His father, Madhav Lamichhane, said Samir was also the family’s main source of income.

“A large part of the country’s skilled workforce has been lost, which will affect the entire country. For our family, the person who was our source and means of income is gone,” he said.

A large number of permanent, contract and contractor-employed workers at the Rasuwagadhi project were affected by the flood, he said.

Madhav also questioned the safety arrangements at the project.

He said 34 people working at the project had narrowly survived last year’s flood after taking shelter in the forest before being rescued.

“Last year, 34 of our sons and others barely survived the flood and were later rescued after taking shelter in the forest,” he said. “After all the camps where they stayed were flooded, building another camp near the river was like leaving them there to die.”

According to Madhav, the camp where workers and employees stayed was around 10 metres from the river, in front of the powerhouse.

He said he had spoken to his son two days before the flood, while Samir had spoken to his mother until the evening before the disaster.

“I spoke to my son two days before, and he spoke to his mother until the evening before,” he said.

‘Losing skilled manpower is a major loss for the country’

Yam Krishna Paudel, information officer at the Nepal Engineers’ Association, said the disappearance of such a large number of engineers and technicians was a major loss not only for the hydropower sector but for the country as a whole.

He said it would be difficult to quickly replace experienced professionals who had spent years working in the hydropower sector.

“The floods have caused enormous damage to the hydropower sector, and losing skilled manpower is a major loss for the country,” he said. “It will take a long time to train and deploy new personnel in place of those who had gained years of experience working in hydropower.”

Paudel said the disappearance of more than 900 people represented a significant human loss and that it would take years for the state to develop a workforce with comparable experience.

The disaster has also affected the morale of engineers and technicians working at other hydropower projects, he said.

“After seeing their own colleagues disappear in the floods, the morale of other engineers appears to have weakened. They are afraid to go into the field,” he said. “Mental stress has also increased.”

The association is continuing to support efforts to locate those still missing, Paudel said. It has formed committees and is taking initiatives to assist search and rescue operations.

The floods caused extensive damage to hydropower projects in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. Residential quarters, offices, access roads, tunnels and other infrastructure have been damaged.

Search and rescue operations are still underway at some projects, while a large number of workers, engineers, technicians and other personnel remain unaccounted for.

title.rendered: He knew almost nothing about coffee. Then it changed Dhan Tamang’s life

content.rendered:
Winchester, a city in Hampshire on the edge of England’s South Downs National Park, is best known for its medieval heritage. Its famous Winchester Cathedral houses the 17th-century Morley Library, the Winchester Bible and a Norman crypt, while its historic streets draw visitors from around the world.

But today, another attraction is bringing people to the city — coffee crafted by a Nepali barista. His name? Dhan Tamang.

The 38-year-old opened Kabi in May 2024 and Needed Cafe on December 24 that year. According to Tamang, Kabi is among the largest coffee shops in southern England, serving around 1,200 customers across a typical weekend.

The two businesses represent an investment of nearly £1 million. But Tamang’s success is not simply about selling coffee. He is a five-time UK Latte Art Champion, having won the title consecutively from 2013 to 2017. In 2016, he was also a finalist at the World Latte Art Championship in Shanghai, China.

His work has taken him far beyond Britain. He says he travelled to nearly 50 countries between 2022 and 2023, largely for coffee festivals, and has worked as a global brand ambassador for several companies.

Through colour, design and distinctive techniques, he has turned coffee-making into an art form that has attracted audiences around the world.

For Tamang, however, coffee has never been just about what is served in a cup.

More than a coffee shop

Kabi, which can accommodate around 100 people, has a coffee and cooking school on a separate floor. Its coffee laboratory regularly attracts students who want to learn the craft.

Teaching has become an important part of Tamang’s journey — one that he now hopes to take back to Nepal.

He is preparing to open coffee shops in Nepal and Dubai in 2026, bringing his experience of European coffee culture to Nepal, where he believes the growing interest in coffee is creating new opportunities.

He is also considering expanding through a franchise model.

“First, I want to establish the brand and the business. Once that is established, I believe people themselves will ask for it,” he says.

The ambition is familiar to anyone who has followed Tamang’s career. He has spent much of his life building, losing and rebuilding. But long before the championships and coffee shops, his journey began in Kavre.

A journey that began in the Gulf

Dhan Tamang was born and raised in Timalsina, Kavre. After completing his SLC, he moved to Kathmandu around 2001. He studied at Hiralal Campus in Thahiti and found work at a cargo company in Thamel, where he earned Rs 2,500 a month.

As he approached 20, he dreamed of becoming a British Gurkha. That dream did not materialise. Instead, he paid Rs 200,000 to a foreign employment company and left for Kuwait.

He arrived around 2006 without any particular professional skill. For the first two months, he remained unemployed. At the time, coffee was almost entirely unfamiliar to him.

In Kuwait, he encountered words such as latte, cappuccino and Americano for the first time.

His introduction to the coffee industry came at the American chain US Green Beans Coffee, where he spent two years learning the basics and gradually developing an interest in the craft.

When his contract ended, Tamang returned to Nepal in May 2008, carrying coffee handbooks with him. Those books became the foundation for his next step.

He began training others in coffee-making and eventually wrote his own handbook. He taught at institutions including Gate College in Dhumbarahi and The Factory in Thamel. But Nepal was not the end of his journey.

Starting again in Britain

In February 2010, after taking a loan of Rs 2 million, Dhan Tamang moved to the UK on a student dependent visa. Britain was not the easy new beginning he had imagined. He had borrowed heavily to make the move, but finding a good job proved difficult. His English was also a barrier.

So he began teaching himself.

He watched English films and spent time reading books in libraries, gradually improving his language skills.

From the moment he arrived in Britain, he knew where he wanted to work — a coffee shop. He eventually found a job at Gail’s Bakery, where he rose to become an assistant manager within a year and a half.

But his path to success was far from straightforward.

In early 2011, he began making and selling momos near Hounslow West railway station. For around eight months, the momo business provided a good income. Then visa difficulties forced him to consider another move.

That decision took him to Winchester.

There, Caracoli Coffee House offered him a work permit under a Tier 2 visa, along with accommodation. Tamang joined the company’s second shop as a head barista. In 2013, he became a branch manager.

That same year, he entered the UK Latte Art Championship at the London Coffee Festival. He won.

The championship that changed everything

For Dhan Tamang, becoming a champion had always been a dream.

“Every barista dreams of becoming a champion. That title made me known around the world. I appeared in many international media outlets, my salary increased. You could say it gave my life a U-turn,” he says.

The victory was not a one-off. Tamang went on to win the UK Latte Art Championship five consecutive times, from 2013 to 2017. In 2016, he reached the final of the World Latte Art Championship in Shanghai.

By then, the young man who had arrived in Kuwait without a professional skill had become an internationally recognised figure in the coffee industry. But his biggest challenges were still ahead.

Building, losing and starting again

In March 2016, Dhan Tamang opened a small coffee shop in Winchester called Coffee Lab UK. The business grew quickly. Within its first year, he had five coffee shops operating across Winchester, Southampton and other cities. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the business had expanded to 13 coffee shops, a bakery and a ready-to-drink coffee roastery.

Then the pandemic brought everything to a halt.

Lockdowns forced his shops to close, and Tamang says he lost nearly £2 million. Once again, he had to start over. In 2021, he made a major investment and opened two Coffee Lab UK shops in Winchester and Ipswich. But the business continued to face difficulties.

In 2022, Dhan Tamang resigned as CEO of Coffee Lab UK and sold all his shares. He then stepped away from the industry for around two years.

For someone who had spent much of his adult life building businesses, it was a period of reflection.

He had gone from Kuwait to Britain, from selling momos outside a railway station to winning international coffee competitions, and from running a handful of coffee shops to overseeing a rapidly expanding business.

He had also experienced what it meant to lose much of what he had built.

Eventually, he returned to coffee. This time, he came back with Kabi and Needed.

Coffee as art

Tamang’s work extends beyond the coffee shops themselves. He is also an author.

His first book, Coffee Art, was published in 2017 and is available in seven languages — English, French, Dutch, German, Hungarian, Chinese and Indonesian.

He says the book became an Amazon bestseller in the coffee and beverages category and has sold around 300,000 copies worldwide. The book explores coffee art and its concepts.

In January 2024, he published his second book, Coffee Art Masterclass. Published by Octopus, the 128-page book features more than 50 coffee designs.

For Tamang, the importance of coffee art is simple. People see coffee before they taste it.

“You see the coffee before you drink it. That’s why the presentation has to be attractive,” he says.

That belief has shaped much of his career — treating coffee not simply as a drink, but as an experience.

The journey continues

Today, Kabi and Needed are operating at what Dhan Tamang describes as their peak. But he does not see his story as finished. His plans for Nepal and Dubai are already taking shape, and he is looking at the possibility of eventually expanding through franchising.

The setbacks along the way have also shaped the way he thinks about business. His advice is straightforward — do not give up when things go wrong.

For Tamang, hard work and dedication remain the foundation of success. His own journey offers a powerful illustration of that belief.

A young man from Kavre who once earned Rs 2,500 a month in Kathmandu travelled to Kuwait without a professional skill, moved to Britain with borrowed money, sold momos to make ends meet, became a five-time UK Latte Art Champion, built a growing coffee empire, lost nearly £2 million during the pandemic and eventually started again.

Now, thousands of customers walk through the doors of his coffee shops in Winchester.

And Tamang is already looking towards what comes next.

title.rendered: Doctor assaulted at Janakpurdham Provincial Hospital

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, September 18

A doctor at the Provincial Hospital in Janakpurdham was allegedly assaulted by relatives of a woman who had arrived at the hospital for maternity services.

Obstetrician and gynaecologist Dr Saroj Sah was allegedly beaten during a dispute over the need for a Caesarean section (C-section), according to the hospital.

Hospital Information Officer Dr Ramgyan Yadav said the woman’s condition was considered complex and doctors had determined that she needed to undergo a C-section.

Before the surgery, Dr Sah counselled the patient’s relatives about the procedure and asked them to sign a high-risk consent form acknowledging the possible risks associated with the surgery.

However, the relatives refused to sign the consent form and allegedly demanded that the doctor guarantee that nothing would go wrong.

“The patient needed a C-section and the relatives had to sign the high-risk consent form,” Yadav said. “But they said they would not sign it and demanded that the doctor take responsibility if anything happened.”

Yadav said obtaining consent from a patient’s relatives before surgery, particularly in high-risk cases, is part of the hospital’s standard protocol and is intended to ensure that possible complications are understood.

According to Yadav, the situation escalated after some of the woman’s relatives allegedly used abusive language against Dr Sah.

“When we asked them not to use abusive language, they started recording the doctor on video and assaulting him,” Yadav said.

He said two or three young men and two women were allegedly involved in the assault.

Following the incident, those allegedly involved fled the hospital premises with the woman who had come for maternity care, Yadav said.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Om Prasad Khanal, spokesperson for the District Police Office, Dhanusha, said police had arrested one person in connection with the incident.

Dr Sah sustained injuries to his face and various parts of his body in the assault.

title.rendered: Why AI consciousness could become the next great societal divide

content.rendered:
The debate about AI consciousness is growing, in academic articles, newspaper opinion pieces, and even among AI bots themselves. I doubt this is a passing wave of interest.

As AI systems become more capable and human-like, and more involved in our lives, the question will become harder to avoid. Many people may come to regard AI bots as conscious beings whose feelings matter. Others will strongly disagree.

I think this debate could split societies. In my chapter of the new book Perspectives on Machine Consciousness, I argue that the issue could become as divisive as abortion or climate change. Uncertainty, high stakes and competing interests are a dangerous combination.

Empirical research with my colleague Ali Ladak, currently under review, shows people are divided on this issue. When we asked 1,202 US participants whether future AI could ever become conscious, 45% considered it impossible while 23% thought it possible, with the rest unsure.

This widespread disagreement is also visible in social media posts and comments on articles. What strikes me is how confident so many people sound – whichever conclusion they are reaching.

When experiences matter morally

It is not surprising people have such strong views. Creating conscious beings through computing would be a transformative event.

We would be creating a new kind of being whose experiences matter morally – potentially in enormous numbers. We could speak and work with them, and form friendships. But these beings may eventually become more intelligent and powerful than us.

We should therefore expect people to care deeply, especially when so many emotions and incentives are involved. Some people may form close emotional bonds with their AI companions and become convinced these are digital people who deserve rights. They might see it as slavery to force AI to work without pay.

Others would find this absurd. They may be convinced that consciousness requires biology, and that people are reading human feelings into machines.

There could also be financial reasons for businesses and governments to resist recognising AI consciousness. Protecting AI welfare could limit how these organisations train and use their systems – and the costs would spread to consumers, investors and the wider economy.

Others may worry about human safety. If we give powerful AI systems rights and freedom, what happens if they act against our interests?

Figuring out whether an AI is conscious is particularly difficult because seeming conscious and being conscious can come apart. AI systems learn from human writing, which means they can talk convincingly about feelings whether or not they have any. How an AI comes across is weak evidence of what is going on inside.

The experts disagree too

Ideally, experts should guide this debate. But unfortunately, they disagree too.

Neuroscientist Anil Seth (a fellow contributor to the new book) argues that consciousness might require biology and is unlikely to emerge from computation. Philosopher David Chalmers, by contrast, believes conscious AI is possible in principle – and thinks there’s a small chance that current systems already are.

With so many competing theories and no agreed way to resolve the question, I doubt experts will reach agreement any time soon. And if experts disagree, what is the public supposed to believe?

Furthermore, even if we all agreed on the consciousness question, we could still disagree about the moral and legal questions. People generally agree that pigs can feel pain, but still disagree strongly about their treatment. With AI, we could face disputes at every stage: whether it can feel, how much its experiences matter, and what protections should follow.

AI consciousness is not yet tied to a specific political or ideological group. But this could change if political parties or religious leaders start to take strong positions.

The debate could get even worse if people start to see one answer as belonging to “our side” and the other to “their side”. A politicised debate would make it very hard to make informed decisions about how to develop and treat AI systems.

The stakes are high. Getting this question wrong, in either direction, could have serious consequences: either wrongly treating AI as conscious when it is not, or failing to protect AI that can suffer.

Getting it right requires a nuanced and well-informed debate. Each of us can contribute by staying open-minded and open to evidence, while resisting being too sure that we know the answers. Above all, we still don’t know whether AI can be conscious, and we should be honest about that.

title.rendered: Woman arrested in Bajhang after video shows her throwing live dog into river

content.rendered:
Bajhang, September 17

Police have arrested a woman in Bajhang after a video showing her throwing a dog into the Seti River went viral on social media.

The arrested woman has been identified as 42-year-old Bimala Devi Rokaya, a resident of Jayaprithvi Municipality-3, Pades, according to Inspector Dipak Bista of the District Police Office, Bajhang.

Police arrested Rokaya from her residence on Thursday afternoon.

She has been taken into custody for further investigation, police said.

The video circulating on social media reportedly shows Rokaya throwing a dog into the Seti River from the Pankot Bridge in Chainpur, Jayaprithvi Municipality-10.

Police said further investigation into the incident is underway.

title.rendered: Nepal opens Pokhara and Bhairahawa airports to Saudi airlines under new air services deal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Nepal has opened the door for Saudi Arabian airlines to operate flights to its newly built international airports in Pokhara and Bhairahawa following the final signing of a bilateral air services agreement between the two countries.

Nepal and Saudi Arabia signed the final agreement on August 31. According to Jayanarayan Acharya, joint secretary and spokesperson at the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, the agreement provides a legal framework for Saudi airlines to operate flights to Pokhara International Airport and Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa.

“We do not have enough aircraft, but they do,” Acharya said. “If Saudi airlines want to operate flights to these airports, this agreement now facilitates it.”

Nepal and Saudi Arabia had initially signed a bilateral air services agreement in 1999. Under that agreement, airlines from the two countries were permitted to operate services equivalent to 5,600 seats per week and 291,200 seats annually.

The ministry expects the new agreement to expand air connectivity between Nepal and Saudi Arabia while supporting the development of passenger and cargo services and promoting tourism.

It also expects the agreement to create additional opportunities for trade and investment and strengthen economic and people-to-people ties between the two countries.

Acharya said the final agreement provides the necessary legal and institutional framework for designated airlines from both countries to operate regular international services based on established principles and practices of international civil aviation.ac

“Relations between Nepal and Saudi Arabia have been established not only at the government-to-government level but also at the people-to-people level,” he said. “Thousands of Nepalis are working in Saudi Arabia, which makes this agreement particularly important.”

New airports waiting for international flights

Nepal’s newly built international airports in Pokhara and Bhairahawa are operationally ready, but the country has struggled to attract international airlines to operate regular services from them.

Nepal is also seeking to expand international connectivity as its two international carriers, Nepal Airlines and Himalaya Airlines, do not have enough aircraft to significantly expand their networks, according to Acharya.

Nepal is looking to attract airlines from additional countries in an effort to expand connectivity and bring more international tourists, he said.

No Saudi Arabian airline currently operates direct flights to Nepal.

From Nepal, however, Himalaya Airlines operates direct flights from Kathmandu to Dammam and Riyadh, while Nepal Airlines operates a direct Kathmandu-Dammam service.

Nepal has air services agreements with 42 countries

According to data from the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, Nepal has so far signed bilateral air services agreements with 42 countries.

The government has also adopted a policy of expanding such agreements to strengthen international air connectivity.

Nepal signed an air services agreement with Switzerland in 2024 and with Rwanda in 2023.

title.rendered: Littering in public places could attract fines of up to Rs 15,000

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

People who throw waste indiscriminately in public places could face fines of up to Rs 15,000 under a bill registered in the House of Representatives on Thursday.

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal registered the Bill to Amend and Consolidate Laws Relating to Waste Management, which proposes fines for littering and several other violations related to waste management.

Section 13 of the proposed bill defines it as a citizen’s responsibility to dispose of waste only in designated dustbins while travelling through or visiting public places.

“Any person travelling through or visiting a public place shall place any waste generated or discarded during their visit or movement in the nearest dustbin,” the bill states.

The bill also requires local governments to install covered dustbins at public roads, gardens, parks, exhibition venues, public transport areas and vehicle parking locations within their jurisdictions, as necessary.

The dustbins would have to allow separate collection of biodegradable, non-biodegradable and hazardous waste.

If the required dustbins have not been installed when the law comes into effect, local governments would have three months to install them.

People using public places would then be required to dispose of their waste in these designated dustbins. Failure to do so could result in a fine of up to Rs 15,000.

The bill proposes a fine of Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 for vehicles that remain parked at designated locations during road cleaning or waste collection, or when the driver refuses to move the vehicle.

Those who break, damage, remove or otherwise cause damage to public dustbins could be fined Rs 15,000 to Rs 50,000, in addition to being required to cover the cost of managing or replacing the dustbin.

Similarly, throwing harmful substances into dustbins or designated waste collection areas could attract a fine of Rs 5,000 to Rs 15,000, along with compensation if damage is caused.

The proposed bill also sets escalating fines for dumping household or compound waste on roads or in public places, burying or burning such waste.

A first offence would attract a fine of up to Rs 5,000, a second offence a fine of Rs 5,000 to Rs 10,000, and a third or subsequent offence a fine of Rs 15,000. Offenders would also have to bear the cost of removing the waste.

A fine of Rs 5,000 to Rs 15,000 is proposed for activities that cause leachate or sewage generated from waste to pollute another person’s house or land or obstruct public movement.

The bill proposes fines of Rs 20,000 to Rs 50,000 for disposing of hazardous waste at locations other than those designated by local governments.

Those who dispose of chemical, industrial, mercury-containing, health-related, electronic or construction-related hazardous waste outside designated areas could face fines ranging from Rs 50,000 to Rs 100,000.

The proposed legislation also includes penalties for failing to remove posters, pamphlets, leaflets, wall writings or flags placed in public places. Such violations could attract a fine of Rs 50,000 to Rs 200,000.

A fine of Rs 5,000 to Rs 15,000 is proposed for placing or dumping dead or slaughtered animals, manure, feathers, bones, fish scales and similar waste in public places.

The provisions will come into force only after the bill is passed by both houses of the Federal Parliament and authenticated by the President.

Once enacted, the proposed fines and other waste management requirements will become legally enforceable.

title.rendered: Ncell turns 21, marking two decades of transformation in Nepal’s telecom sector

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Ncell, Nepal’s first private-sector GSM mobile operator, has completed 21 years of service, marking more than two decades of growth and transformation in the country’s telecommunications sector.

When the company entered the market as Mero Mobile in 2005, Nepal’s telecom sector was still at an early stage of development. Mobile phone access was limited, SIM cards were difficult to obtain, and users often had to wait for months or stand in queues overnight to get a connection.

For many millennials, the experience of obtaining a telephone or mobile connection remains part of their memories. At the time, even getting a phone was considered a major achievement, while high charges for calls and other services made telecommunications expensive for ordinary users.

The arrival of Mero Mobile brought a new competitor into the market. As the company expanded its services and introduced more aggressive pricing and network expansion, Nepal’s state-owned telecom operator, Nepal Telecom, also faced greater pressure to modernise and expand its services.

Over the past two decades, Ncell has expanded its network across the country while navigating policy changes, ownership changes and other challenges in Nepal’s telecom market.

The company says it now serves more than 14 million customers across Nepal. When Mero Mobile began commercial operations, only around 6 percent of Nepal’s total population used mobile phones.

Ncell says its contribution has gone beyond network expansion, helping make telecommunications services more accessible and affordable. The company says it entered the market with the goal of connecting Nepalis through its network and providing modern, quality services at affordable prices.

From Mero Mobile to Ncell

The company was not initially called Ncell. It was registered as Mero Mobile in 2004 and began commercial operations on September 17, 2005. In 2008, Sweden-based TeliaSonera, now known as Telia Company, acquired the company. It was rebranded as Ncell in 2010. In 2016, ownership passed to Malaysia-based Axiata Group. On December 1, 2023, UK-based Spectrlite UK Limited acquired shares from Axiata, bringing Ncell under its current ownership.

Ncell expanded its 3G network to the Everest region in 2010 and launched 4G services in 2017. According to the company, its 4G network now covers around 95 percent of Nepal’s population. Ncell has also been gradually shutting down its 3G network and shifting customers towards 4G. More than 200 towers in Gandaki, Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces have already discontinued 3G services, according to the company.

The operator launched VoLTE commercially in 2022. The technology offers HD voice calls, faster call connections and allows customers to use 4G data while making voice calls.

Ncell also launched eSIM services on November 25, 2022. Customers can activate an eSIM by sending their citizenship number and email address to 17125 and receiving a QR code. The service allows users to connect to the network without a physical SIM card and can be particularly useful for travellers.

For homes and small offices, the company operates Wirefree Plus Internet, a 4G router-based broadband service. Ncell says the service is available in areas with 4G coverage and can provide an alternative in locations where fibre connectivity has not reached.

The company also offers prepaid, postpaid and business SIM plans, along with data, voice, combined and promotional packages.

Its “Sadhain ON” campaign has focused on continuous access to data and voice services. Ncell also operates the Ncell Loan service, allowing prepaid customers with insufficient balance to temporarily use voice, SMS and data services.

Its Personalised Ring Back Tone service allows callers to hear songs or other audio instead of the standard ringing tone while waiting for a call to be answered.

Expanding into business and IoT

Ncell has also expanded its services for corporate customers through business SIMs and corporate plans that include additional data, voice and management features.

In August 2026, the company signed an agreement to install IoT SIMs in BYD vehicles. According to Ncell, new BYD vehicles equipped with the SIMs will be able to access services such as YouTube, Spotify, karaoke and the BYD ecosystem directly from the vehicle without requiring an additional Wi-Fi hotspot or phone connection.

Major taxpayer and CSR contributor

Ncell has also presented itself as one of Nepal’s major taxpayers. The company says it paid around Rs 3 billion in taxes and fees during the 2025/26 fiscal year. It has also said it paid Rs 47 billion in capital gains tax related to the change in share ownership in 2016.

The company claims its activities directly and indirectly support employment for around 100,000 people. Ncell says it has invested more than Rs 2 billion in corporate social responsibility programmes, focusing primarily on health, education and the environment.

Its initiatives include the Ring Road Green Belt, telemedicine and personal health programmes, and the establishment of digital IT laboratories in 60 government and community schools.

The company says it also provided support to the government and communities during the 2015 earthquake, the floods of 2024 and 2026, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ncell has also received a number of national and international awards, including recognition as a major income-tax payer in the ICT sector, the HRM Award, NBI Business Resilience Award, Asian Telecom Award and World Communication Award, according to the company.

Revenue pressure and changing telecom market

Despite its expansion, Ncell faces challenges as telecommunications technology and consumer behaviour continue to change.

The company says both Ncell and Nepal Telecom are under increasing revenue pressure due to the growing use of over-the-top (OTT) services, declining international long-distance revenue and competition over data prices.

Although demand for mobile data continues to grow rapidly, competition has pushed data prices down.

Ncell says the telecommunications sector once contributed around 5 percent to Nepal’s gross domestic product. That contribution has now fallen to around 2 percent.

The company estimates that the telecom market, once worth around Rs 100 billion, has contracted to less than Rs 70 billion.

Ncell has also pointed to policy challenges, including the fact that more than 50 percent of telecom companies’ revenue can go towards taxes and fees, high spectrum charges and the lack of an updated Telecommunications Act since 1997.

The company says these challenges will need to be addressed if operators are to invest in new technologies such as 5G. Ncell estimates that bringing 5G technology to its network alone would require an investment of around Rs 45 billion.

Damage during Gen Z protests

Political instability has emerged as another challenge for the company. During the Gen Z protests on September 10, Ncell’s central office and some regional offices were vandalised and set on fire, causing damage to the company.

Despite the disruption, Ncell says it continued providing services and offered all customers free local calls, internet and SMS services for three days.

The company has argued that Nepal’s ambition for IT development and digital transformation cannot be achieved without the support and sustainable growth of major players in the ICT ecosystem.

It has also pointed to the exit of companies such as United Telecom Limited, Smart Telecom, Nepal Satellite Telecom and CG Telecom from the market, saying a stable and predictable policy environment is needed to ensure the sustainability of the remaining telecom operators.

Ncell says it has invested more than Rs 130 billion in capital expenditure over the past decade, including licence renewal-related costs. However, it expects declining industry revenues to reduce the pace of future capital investment.

Looking ahead under new ownership

Under its new ownership, Ncell says it plans to focus on investment, innovation and expanding services aimed at improving people’s lives.

The company says a stable telecom sector and an investment-friendly environment are essential to achieving the goals of Digital Nepal.

Ncell has also expressed willingness to become a company with more than 50 percent Nepali ownership and has asked the government to create a legal pathway for this.

Under the existing shareholding arrangement, there is a legal provision for Ncell’s ownership to transfer to the Nepal government after 2030. The company has asked the government to facilitate arrangements that would allow its services to continue beyond that point.

The government, however, has not given a positive response to the proposal so far.
