title.rendered: Kuber Rai finds his voice again on paper

content.rendered:
A short walk from the Bouddha Dham in Ilam, there’s a small house. From inside, you can hear a tanpura playing. This is where singer Kuber Rai lives.

I saw Rai practising music alone. But his voice wasn’t the same as before. His body wasn’t the same either. Somewhere along the way, something in his life had broken. What had happened to him?

There was a time when he performed at almost every event in the district: fairs, festivals, football matches, and Phulpati celebrations. Announcers would call his name with excitement, “And now, here comes Kuber Rai.”

He’d walk on stage with folded hands, get wrapped in a khada, and sing a few songs.

He never turned down an invitation. He’d show up everywhere, even while still managing farm chores like feeding the cattle. In return, he’d get gifts like a shawl, a token of appreciation, sometimes an envelope of cash.

He’d keep the money and ride his motorbike home to his village, Shreeantu.

Back then, the village was lively. Every evening you’d hear harmonium, tabla, madal, guitar. Students would come to his hillside house to learn music from him.

In exchange for lessons, they’d help him dig roads. He was determined to build a proper road to Shreeantu, Salleri. He badly wanted to see a vehicle reach his home someday.

Nepali migrants abroad would also invite him to perform. He’d pack a bag, arrange his visa, and fly off. So far, he has performed in the UK, Hong Kong, and Australia. These yearly trips kept him busy, often pulling him away from farm work back home.

Abroad, people welcomed him like family. He’d talk warmly with everyone and perform solo evening shows.

As soon as he returned from the shows, he’d be back in the fields, weeding maize, cutting grass, carrying manure. In the evenings, he’d pick up his harmonium and riyaz. 

That was his life before. Now, things are different.

When life fell out of tune

One day, at a memorial gathering, he felt thirsty and someone gave him sweetened coffee. He drank it and went home.

While working in the field, his face suddenly felt like it was burning. Someone splashed water on him, but he still felt unwell. He went home, lay down, and when it didn’t improve, his daughter and son-in-law took him to hospital.

After a long stretch of treatment, he came home with the left side of his body paralysed. He’d had a stroke; on top of existing high blood pressure and diabetes, it affected his hand, leg, mouth and eye on that side.

After that, everything changed. The busy life of performances, friends, recordings and concerts came to a stop.  

But from that low point, something new began. Alongside yoga, breathing exercises and therapy, he started writing the story of his life, as if this pause had given him time to finally tell it.

Finding his own story again

Back in 1981, he left his hillside home in Shreeantu, Salleri, to “become a singer.”

Now, sitting near the Bouddha Dham, he’s going through that whole journey, page by page.

He writes about winning first place in Ratna Recording’s National Youth Song Competition and Radio Nepal’s singing contest. 

He writes about hard evenings when he survived on bread bought with money borrowed from musician Dinesh Subba. He writes it all down carefully, telling his present self, “You’re not someone who gives up.”

That same stubbornness is helping him recover from paralysis. He’s regaining strength, standing, walking and writing.

Through this recovery, one thing has helped him most: creativity. When his voice failed him, his fingers took over, keeping his mind active. That’s how he started writing his own story.

As he fills the pages of his diary, his energy keeps growing  and that same energy now brings him back to music practice every morning and evening.

As mist settles around his quiet house near the Bouddha Dham, his voice rises again with the tanpura, sa re ga ma…

title.rendered: LPG distributors asked to sell cylinders at Rs 2,060 amid alternate-route transport costs

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

The Nepal LP Gas Industry Association has urged LPG industry operators to sell cooking gas cylinders at the existing price of Rs 2,060 per cylinder.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the association asked gas companies to comply with the price fixed by the Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) from last Friday.

LPG companies supplying the Kathmandu Valley had been charging an additional Rs 105.38 per cylinder to cover increased transportation costs after the Prithvi Highway was obstructed by floods in the Bhote Koshi River.

Following the disruption, companies supplying cooking gas to the Kathmandu Valley began refilling cylinders at plants in Makwanpur, Parsa, Bara, Chitwan, Nawalparasi and Dhanusha from August 30.

They then transported the cylinders to Kathmandu through alternative routes, resulting in additional transportation expenses.

The association, however, has now asked industry operators to sell the cylinders at the NOC-fixed rate of Rs 2,060 per cylinder.

title.rendered: ANFA leadership says FIFA suspension does not mean dismissal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

The leadership of the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) has claimed that FIFA still recognises its committee as the official football governing body in Nepal, despite its suspension.

Speaking at a press conference organised by ANFA on Thursday, General Secretary Kiran Rai said the association had been suspended by FIFA but had not been dismissed.

“FIFA recognises Pankaj Bikram Nembang’s committee as the official one. In that sense, we are suspended, not dismissed. There will be discussions,” Rai said.

Rai also said the salaries of players and employees had been withheld following the suspension and the government’s directive.

He said the government should provide clear instructions on how the situation should be handled.

“Either the government needs to give us clear instructions and tell us not to operate, or we need to decide whether the children should be handed over to their families or whether the government will take responsibility,” Rai said.

“We also need to clearly inform the employees. Otherwise, I believe we need to move ahead by resolving the problems we are facing,” he added.

Rai said talks held between the government and ANFA President Nembang on Wednesday had not produced a positive outcome.

He said a three-way meeting involving the government, FIFA and ANFA could be proposed if discussions with the government continue.

“If there are discussions with the government, we can propose a tripartite meeting involving FIFA,” Rai said.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

Gagan Thapa urges Deuba to inaugurate Nepali Congress general convention

Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa has urged former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba to attend and inaugurate the party’s 15th general convention, saying his participation would be a matter of honour for the party.

Bodies of five Chilime Hydropower employees handed over to families

The bodies of five employees who were trapped at the Chilime Hydropower Station have been handed over to their respective families. Chilime Hydropower Company Managing Director Baburaja Maharjan said the bodies of engineer Santosh Pandey, electrical supervisor Minraj Moktan, security guards Shyam Bahadur Thapa Magar and Tilak Bahadur Thapa Magar, and Nepal Electricity Authority employee Lakpa Tamang were identified and handed over to their families.

Himalayan glaciers melting 65 per cent faster amid growing climate risks

The Himalayas are undergoing rapid changes, with the rate of glacier melting increasing by 65 per cent compared with a decade ago, according to a new report. The report highlights growing risks from glacial lakes, melting snow and unstable mountain slopes. It also points to black carbon as a major contributor to glacier melt. Black carbon originating from South Asia accounts for about one-third of glacier melt, while industrial sources, particularly brick kilns, contribute 32–42 per cent of the human-generated black carbon accumulating in the Himalayan region.

Sadak Sujhav App launched to report damaged roads

The ‘Sadak Sujhav’ app has been officially launched to make the repair of damaged federal roads in Kathmandu Valley more effective. The Road Division Kathmandu under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development formally launched the app following a successful trial. Citizens in Kathmandu Valley can now register complaints and provide suggestions through the app regarding the repair of damaged roads under the federal road network.

Bill proposes mandatory dustbins in public places within 3 months

The government is drafting legislation that would require dustbins to be installed in public places.Under a bill registered in the House of Representatives that revises and consolidates existing waste management laws, any person, group, organisation or body generating waste would be responsible for managing that waste itself. Local governments would be required to arrange for its collection within their jurisdiction.

Australia tightens visa rules, most international students to be barred from bringing families

Australia is tightening visa rules for international students and other temporary migrants, with most foreign students set to be barred from bringing their partners and children to the country while they study. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced the migration reforms on Thursday as the government seeks to reduce net overseas migration and tighten controls on temporary visa holders.

Singaporean climber dies while attempting to climb Mt Manaslu

A foreign climber died while attempting to climb Mt Manaslu in Samagaun of Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1, Gorkha. According to police, 50-year-old Singaporean national Lau Wee Seng died on Thursday. District Police Office Gorkha DSP Raj Kumar Shrestha said Seng died while returning to the base camp from Camp II after he had difficulty walking and sat down at the spot.

24-year-old arrested after CIB uncovers Rs 1.34 billion in alleged hundi transactions

A 24-year-old man has been arrested in Dhanusha on suspicion of involvement in hundi transactions worth more than Rs 1.34 billion over the past two years. Ajay Kumar Mukhiya of Shahid Nagar Municipality-4 is currently in the custody of the District Police Office, Dhanusha. A joint team from the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police and the District Police Office arrested Mukhiya from Shahid Nagar-4 at around 5:20 pm on Tuesday.

title.rendered: Nepal lose to Indonesia, crash out of Asian Games volleyball quarterfinal race

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Nepal suffered a second consecutive defeat in women’s volleyball at the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, losing 3-0 to Indonesia on Thursday.

Nepal needed a victory to keep its hopes of reaching the quarterfinals alive but was beaten in straight sets.

Nepal lost the opening set 25-12 before putting up a stronger fight in the second. However, Indonesia held its nerve to win the set 25-21.

Indonesia maintained its momentum in the third set, taking an early lead and eventually sealing the match with a 25-20 victory.

Nepal had also lost its opening Group A match against hosts Japan in straight sets.

With only three teams in Group A, Nepal’s second successive defeat means Japan and Indonesia have secured their places in the quarterfinals with one group match still to play. Their meeting will determine the group winner.

Nepal’s two defeats have ended its hopes of reaching the quarterfinals. The team will now compete in the classification matches for ninth to 14th place.

Nepal’s next opponent will be determined after the remaining group-stage matches are completed.

A total of 14 of Asia’s top teams are competing in the women’s volleyball tournament at the Asian Games.

The official opening ceremony of the 20th Asian Games is scheduled for September 19, but competitions in several sports began before the ceremony.

Basketball, football, volleyball and modern pentathlon competitions are already underway, while women’s cricket and teqball also began on Thursday.

title.rendered: Army helicopter sent to rescue woman injured in cliff fall in Bajhang

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

A Nepal Army helicopter has been mobilised to rescue a woman critically injured after falling from a cliff near Nyuna village, Saipal Rural Municipality-5, in Bajhang.

The rescue effort is moving forward through an initiative by the Minister for Infrastructure Development, in coordination with disaster management agencies.

The woman suffered spinal injuries in the fall and is in critical condition. Since carrying her by stretcher to the district headquarters, Chainpur, could have taken up to two days, resident Ain Mahar requested Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal to help arrange a helicopter rescue instead.

A Nepal Army helicopter has been mobilised from its Surkhet base for the rescue, with preparations underway to bring the woman to Nepalgunj.

Earlier, the District Administration Office, Bajhang, had written to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority requesting a helicopter for the rescue.

title.rendered: She left her village to support her family. Along the way, she found her own path

content.rendered:
In the village of Ibhang in Ilam, surrounded by green tea gardens, Ayusha Shrestha grew up carrying responsibilities that most children her age never had to think about.

Her mother shouldered the burden of running the family, while Ayusha took on responsibilities from a young age. She did not have the carefree childhood her friends enjoyed. She was already thinking about her younger sister’s education, household expenses and her own future.

“I felt from a young age that my life would not change if I simply stayed at home. I had to dream big,” says 42-year-old Shrestha, looking back.

Poverty had placed a heavy burden on her shoulders early in life. She was not prepared to carry it, but circumstances left little room for innocence.

Eventually, those circumstances pushed her towards a difficult path — and eventually, towards opportunities she could not have imagined at the time.

The hardships of Lebanon

At 19, Ayusha left Nepal in search of foreign employment.

A foreign employment agency had presented Lebanon as an opportunity to work as a doctor’s assistant. Having little knowledge of foreign employment, she left for Lebanon in 2006. But what she found there was completely different from what she had been promised.

She did not know the language. The culture was unfamiliar. She had no experience in the work she was expected to do. For the first three years, she endured humiliation, unequal treatment and emotional distress.

“I went to Lebanon to work as a personal secretary. But the job was not what I had been told. I had also been misled by the foreign employment agency. I suffered a lot. I didn’t even know the language,” Ayusha recalls.

“I was very young and did not have a mature understanding of things. After facing many difficulties, I returned to Nepal in 2009.”

Yet those painful experiences would eventually make her stronger.

“That was when I understood what it meant to face humiliation abroad without education and skills,” she says.

Qatar: Opportunity and confidence

After returning to Nepal, Ayusha Shrestha went back to her village in Ilam and stayed there for some time.

But being in Nepal only made the weight of her responsibilities feel heavier. The entire responsibility of her family was on her shoulders.

“I couldn’t stay in Nepal because the responsibility of my entire family was on me,” she says. “The situation in Nepal was also not good. Because of the circumstances in Nepal, I accepted foreign employment again and went to Qatar.”

She left for Qatar in 2010, this time to work as a sales executive.

She joined Apparel Qatar as a sales executive after being selected from among 150 to 200 applicants. One of only a small number of Nepali women selected for the opportunity, she began working with the Nine West brand.

The beginning was not easy.

Her English was weak, and the environment was completely unfamiliar. But continuous hard work helped her move forward.

Soon, she was recognised as a “top performer” within the company. She went on to perform strongly with brands including Skechers and Inglot, gradually establishing herself in the industry. Her performance was often better than that of people who had already been working in the field for 12 to 15 years. As a result, she was promoted within a year and given the opportunity to move to another company.

Becoming a makeup artist

The company then gave Ayusha the responsibility of becoming a makeup artist. She had no experience. But she refused to give up.

Through her own practice and learning, she built her confidence within three months. Within six months, she had become a makeup artist. Within seven years, she had taken on the responsibilities of store manager and trainer.

Her clients eventually included Qatari sheikhs and international celebrities.

“I felt proud when customers would ask, ‘Where is Ayusha?’” she says.

As she continued working, the country manager of the company one day asked her if she would join the Inglot brand. Inglot was a Polish brand specialising in professional makeup and training professional makeup artists.

Ayusha asked what her position would be if she moved to another company, given that she was already in a senior position at her current workplace. She did not have a strong educational background or extensive experience at the time. But when the opportunity with the Polish brand came, she decided to take it.

She was given the opportunity to receive training there. At the time, no other Nepali woman in Qatar was receiving training of that kind. The company was not even willing to train Nepali workers, she says.

“I learned to do my own makeup within three months. I learned about selling products, but I also learned how to do makeup myself. Within six months, I became a makeup artist,” Ayusha says.

“Then, gradually, during the seven years I worked there, I became a makeup trainer and a makeup store manager.”

Entering the luxury world

Her career took another step forward when she joined the luxury brand Salup Group with a monthly salary of 12,000 Qatari riyals, equivalent to around Rs 468,000.

She began appearing at VIP events and international masterclasses. But as her career progressed, another question began to occupy her mind.

“How long will I keep working only for others?”

In 2018, she decided to leave her secure job and become a freelancer. At first, she travelled from house to house, hotels and weddings carrying makeup equipment in a bag and providing services wherever she was hired. She had started her career in Qatar earning 1,600 Qatari riyals a month. Later, she was earning up to 12,000 riyals in the luxury sector. As her income improved, so did her confidence. She began to feel that it was time to build something of her own. After working as a freelancer for around two years, she took another major step.

In 2020, she bought Dana Salon in Maidar. She paid 400,000 Qatari riyals for the salon, equivalent to around Rs 15.6 million. By the time she completed the decoration and setup, her total expenditure had reached around 700,000 riyals, equivalent to approximately Rs 27.3 million.

Starting her own salon was particularly challenging because she had only recently given birth. Despite being postpartum, she worked as much as 18 hours a day.

“I opened Dana Salon in Maidar in 2020. It was the time of Covid. I had no money in my pocket and my son was still very young,” Ayusha says.

“I had just given birth, there were so many challenges. I bought the salon without having enough money and there were no staff.”

She had taken on debt to enter the salon business, making her even more determined.

She had always been deeply committed to her work while working for others. Now that the business was her own, there was even less reason for her to stop.

“I didn’t even get the chance to think of myself as someone who had just given birth. I didn’t have time to say, ‘I’m pregnant’ or complain about the difficulties. I drove, carried bags, ran around and worked,” she recalls.

“I brought whatever I earned and invested it in the salon. After doing that for six months, I hired staff and completed the salon.”

Building her own business

Ayusha’s hard work, dedication and constant activity gradually began to pay off. She bought a house in Kathmandu and built another good house in Damak, Jhapa. She also bought a good car, continuing to strengthen her financial position.

Throughout the journey, she received support from her husband.

While Ayusha worked outside throughout the day, her husband stayed home and looked after their infant. He also continued with his own work while taking care of the child.

In 2021, Ayusha opened another salon under her own name, Ayusha Makeup Salon.

She opened her second branch in Mandala Royal Gorkha, known as a popular Nepali area in Qatar.

Today, her two salon branches employ 32 people, including Nepali, Filipino and Indian workers.

She has also given responsibilities to her own daughter and continues to prioritise Nepali workers in the management of her salons.

She has purchased property in Dubai and plans to expand her business around the world.

“Dubai is the city of dreams. I want to turn dreams into reality,” she says firmly.

Turning struggle into a lesson

When Ayusha reflects on her struggles, she often returns to the painful experience she had in Lebanon.

“I experienced what it means to face humiliation abroad when you do not have education and skills,” she says. “That is why I always advise the younger generation to study, learn and prepare themselves.”

Her approach to work has also remained different. She does not sit in a chair simply because she is the owner.

“I am hungry for work. I take the lead myself in every task,” she says.

Today, Ayusha is not only a successful businesswoman but also a source of inspiration.

Her journey began in a small village in Ilam and took her through Lebanon and Qatar before expanding into an international business.

Over two decades of working abroad, she has turned difficult circumstances into opportunities through determination and courage.

Her story is an example of how an ordinary girl from a small village can build an identity beyond her own country.

She also encourages other Nepalis to consider starting businesses of their own whenever possible.

For that, she emphasises the importance of money, knowledge and teamwork.

“If you struggle for a few years, understand the market, gain knowledge and have the money, then it is better to start your own business,” Ayusha says.

“But money alone is not enough. You need teamwork, knowledge and skills.”

She believes Qatar and other Gulf countries offer relatively accessible opportunities for people seeking to earn money. She says the Gulf can be safer for this purpose because taxes are higher in places such as Europe and the United States.

Ayusha now also plans to return to Nepal and create employment opportunities for Nepali women.

title.rendered: Startups selected by Koshi government fail to receive seed capital

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, September 17

Entrepreneurs selected under the Koshi provincial government’s ‘Startup Enterprise Seed Capital Mobilization Programme’, introduced last fiscal year to encourage new businesses, have not received the promised seed capital.

A total of 32 entrepreneurs selected for the programme were denied the seed capital due to errors in the procedures prepared by the government.

The Ministry of Industry, Agriculture and Cooperatives had selected 32 enterprises for the programme. However, as the ministry failed to provide the seed capital, the entrepreneurs have faced both financial and mental distress.

The ministry had issued a 21-day notice on Chaitra 25, 2082 BS seeking applications for the startup seed capital programme. Based on the applications received, 32 enterprises were selected on Jestha 21.

Under the programme, each enterprise was to receive up to Rs 1 million in seed capital depending on the nature of its project. The provincial government had allocated Rs 10 million for the programme last fiscal year.

The ministry had prepared the ‘Startup Enterprise Seed Capital Mobilization Procedure, 2082’ to distribute the funds. It had planned to provide the seed capital through government-owned banks, with the government itself standing as guarantor.

However, the ministry did not coordinate with government-owned banks while preparing the procedure. The banks were therefore not prepared to implement the programme.

After the programme was halted, entrepreneurs who reached the ministry in Jestha to sign agreements were forced to return disappointed. As the allocated budget has already been frozen without being spent, there is little possibility that they will receive the seed capital from last fiscal year.

Despite this, the selected entrepreneurs continue to visit the ministry.

“We were selected and called to sign the agreement, but we did not receive the seed capital,” said one of the selected entrepreneurs. “It felt as if we had been cheated by the government itself.”

Prakash Marasini, spokesperson for the Ministry of Industry, Agriculture and Cooperatives, acknowledged that the programme could not be implemented due to procedural errors. He said discussions were underway to include the affected entrepreneurs from last fiscal year in the programme for the current fiscal year, as the previous budget had already been frozen.

The ministry has allocated Rs 20 million for the startup seed capital programme in the current fiscal year.

According to the procedure, entrepreneurs receiving the seed capital would have to repay it within two to five years, with the government guaranteeing the bank guarantee.

However, the entrepreneurs were affected because the programme was introduced without adequate preparation.

Chandrabahadur Karki, an officer at the Industry and Cooperative Development Division, said preparations were underway to amend the procedure after holding necessary discussions with banks. He said the process would be made easier this time after coordination with banks was not carried out previously.

According to Karki, entrepreneurs who were selected for seed capital but did not receive it are being considered for priority when a new call for applications is issued.

The ‘Udaya Project’ is also being implemented in Koshi Province with support from the Swiss government. Under the project, loans are provided to entrepreneurs with the provincial government standing as guarantor.

The Koshi provincial government has selected Rastriya Banijya Bank and Global IME Bank for investment under the project.

Small and medium-sized young entrepreneurs can obtain concessional loans ranging from Rs 3 million to Rs 30 million from these banks.

title.rendered: Nepal is paying the price for a climate crisis it did not create

content.rendered:
As I met with survivors at a shelter in Nuwakot district, one of the areas most affected by the catastrophic flash flooding which struck on August 26, and heard their stories of loss, the sheer scale of the disaster felt almost incomprehensible.

Nearly every household has lost someone. Whole communities are in mourning; entire schools are grieving for students who will never return to class. People have lost their homes and the land they depend on for their livelihoods. 

Essentials like food, blankets and sleeping bags are urgently needed, but recovery will take more than just relief supplies. Nepal’s disaster authorities estimate that $2.56 billion worth of property, housing and infrastructure has been damaged. The immediate cost of early recovery alone is expected to be around $53 million.

Behind these numbers lies a question the international community can no longer avoid: who pays when countries that are least responsible for the climate crisis suffer catastrophic losses?

The Himalayas are on the climate crisis frontline 

Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of the world’s annual global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet it is among the most climate-vulnerable countries due to its geographical location in the Himalayan mountains, where the warming climate is accelerating glacier melt and increasing the risks of glacial lake outburst floods, ice avalanches, and glacier collapse. 

Nepal has known about these risks for years. The disaster appears to have been triggered by a major collapse of glacier ice, rock and bedrock, setting off a cascading flood and debris flow through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems. Scientists are still establishing the precise sequence of events, including the role of glacial and temporarily dammed water. What is already clear is that the disaster exposes the growing risks posed by a warming climate and an increasingly unstable Himalayan environment.

A critical test for the loss and damage fund

Countries like Nepal cannot be expected to shoulder the cost of rebuilding after climate-related disasters alone. Nepal should not have to choose between recovery and investing in schools, healthcare or development. Nor should it be pushed further into debt to recover from climate impacts it did little to cause.

This is why the international community established the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. The principle is straightforward – when climate change causes losses that adaptation cannot prevent, vulnerable countries are owed financial support to recover and rebuild.

Since the fund was established in 2022, it has been inundated with requests amounting to around $2.8bn, from around 119 countries, including Nepal, which submitted three separate proposals. Yet the fund only has around $350m in cash actually available for disbursement and to date, it has not yet released any of it.

Nepal has now formally asked the Fund for emergency assistance following the Bhotekoshi disaster. Members of the Fund’s board have called for an extraordinary meeting to consider the request. This is the moment when the Fund must prove it can be more than another international mechanism that promises action while communities wait.

If a catastrophic climate-related disaster of this scale does not trigger rapid support, what exactly is the Loss and Damage Fund for? The answer cannot simply be another expression of solidarity.

Nepal needs money urgently. It needs support to restore essential services, rebuild, recover livelihoods and prepare for the next disaster. And that funding must be provided as grants, not loans that leave already vulnerable countries carrying yet more debt.

Climate finance is moving far too slowly

Nepal should not have to wait. Yet previous experience has proven just how slow the global climate finance system can be. For example, a Green Climate Fund (GCF) project to reduce the risks from glacial lake outburst floods and climate-induced flooding in Nepal was in the pipeline for seven years before being approved in July 2025. It entered implementation only in March this year.

The geographical focus does not overlap with the site of the August 26 disaster, and earlier implementation would not have stopped that tragedy from unfolding. But its seven-year journey through the climate finance system illustrates a much bigger problem: finance is moving far too slowly for a country facing multiple, known and escalating climate-related risks.

For communities living beneath increasingly unstable mountains, seven years is not an administrative inconvenience, it is a lifetime in which the risk continues to grow. Our demand is clear: climate finance must be issued promptly, and it must flow beyond national governments to the local communities facing immediate risks, particularly women’s organisations and grassroots groups leading local preparedness, livelihood protection, and recovery.

Nepal needs justice, not charity

The people of Nepal are not asking for charity. They are asking for justice. Countries and companies that have benefited most from fossil-fuel-driven economic growth have far greater resources and historical responsibility for the emissions that have warmed our planet. Meanwhile, countries such as Nepal are being asked to absorb the economic and human costs.

That is not inevitable: it is a political choice. The international community can continue with a system in which vulnerable countries wait years for adaptation finance and then scramble for humanitarian assistance when disaster strikes. Or it can recognise that climate justice requires finance that is adequate, predictable, accessible and disbursed speedily to match the risks people face. Nepal’s disaster should be a test for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, and for those who have promised to support it.

Nepal must not simply be presented as a case study of climate vulnerability. Countries around the world must stand with Nepal in solidarity and support the resources needed to build resilience. Nepal did not create this crisis; it should not be left to pay the bill for it alone.

title.rendered: Accounts of 12 local units in Dhanusha remain inoperative

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, September 17

The financial accounts of 12 local units in Dhanusha have not yet become operational even though two months of the fiscal year 2026/27 have passed.

As of September 16, the accounts of only six of the district’s 18 local units had become operational, according to the Treasury and Controller Office, Dhanusha.

The local units whose accounts have become operational are Janakpurdham Sub-Metropolitan City, Ganeshman Charnath Municipality, Laxminiya Rural Municipality, Janaknandini Rural Municipality, Dhanauji Rural Municipality and Aurahi Rural Municipality.

The office said the accounts of the remaining local units have not become operational because they have failed to complete the required procedures.

Under the law, local units must have their budgets approved by their village or municipal assemblies, along with an appropriation act, authorisation, approved annual programme and inventory inspection to operate their accounts.

However, the remaining local units have not yet completed these procedures.

The municipalities whose accounts remain inoperative are Mithila, Chhireshwarnath, Mithila Bihari, Dhanushadham, Kamala, Nagarain, Hanspur, Sabaila, Shahidnagar and Videha.

Similarly, the accounts of Bateshwar and Mukhiyapatti Musaharnia rural municipalities have also not become operational, according to the office.

title.rendered: Bill proposes mandatory dustbins in public places within 3 months

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

The government is drafting legislation that would require dustbins to be installed in public places.

Under a bill registered in the House of Representatives that revises and consolidates existing waste management laws, any person, group, organisation or body generating waste would be responsible for managing that waste itself. Local governments would be required to arrange for its collection within their jurisdiction.

Under Section 12(2), the specific procedures for waste collection would be determined by the relevant local government.

Under Section 13, local governments would be required to publish a notice in the local gazette and install closed-lid dustbins as needed at public places under their jurisdiction, including public roads, gardens, parks, exhibition venues, public transport, and vehicle parking areas, for waste collection. These dustbins would need to allow separate collection of biodegradable, non-biodegradable and hazardous waste.

Under Section 13(4), any public place that does not already have such dustbins in place when the law comes into force would need to install them within three months of that date. The bill also specifies that anyone passing through or visiting a public place must dispose of any waste in the nearest dustbin.

The bill was registered in the House of Representatives on Thursday by Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal. He said the bill aims to clearly define the roles and responsibilities of the federal, provincial and local governments in waste generation, collection, disposal and overall management.

Minister Lamsal noted that the bill seeks to minimise adverse effects on human health and the environment, and to enable waste processing and reuse in line with circular economy principles.

Article 30 of Nepal’s Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to live in a clean and healthy environment, along with the right to compensation from polluters for environmental damage. Article 35 guarantees citizens access to clean drinking water and sanitation. The Constitution places drinking water and sanitation under the concurrent list of federal and provincial powers, basic health and sanitation under local government authority, and environmental matters under the concurrent list of all three tiers.

The government believes that once passed, the bill will enable co-investment, public-private partnerships and development assistance in waste management among the different levels of government.

title.rendered: Australia tightens visa rules, most international students to be barred from bringing families

content.rendered:
Sydney, September 17

Australia is tightening visa rules for international students and other temporary migrants, with most foreign students set to be barred from bringing their partners and children to the country while they study.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced the migration reforms on Thursday as the government seeks to reduce net overseas migration and tighten controls on temporary visa holders.

Under the new arrangements, most future international students will no longer be able to attach their spouses, partners or dependent children to their student visas.

There will, however, be exemptions for students from Pacific and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries, as well as those enrolled in certain courses, including PhD programmes. Students who are already in Australia with their families will not be affected.

The changes are part of a broader package aimed at reducing Australia’s net overseas migration to 225,000 by 2028. Net overseas migration had fallen to 292,100 in the year to March, according to figures released on Thursday, but remains above the government’s target.

Student families face new restrictions

Currently, partners of international students can accompany them to Australia and may be allowed to work, subject to conditions linked to the student’s course. Students can also bring dependent children under certain conditions.

The new rules will significantly restrict these arrangements for future student visa holders.

Burke said the changes would not break up families already in Australia and would apply to future visas.

The government says the measures are intended to give it greater control over the temporary migration programme and reduce pressure associated with high migration levels.

The reforms have prompted concern in Australia’s international education sector. Universities Australia chief executive Luke Sheehy warned that restricting students from bringing family members could affect Australia’s appeal as a study destination.

Visitor visas and ‘visa hopping’ targeted

The government is also moving to prevent temporary visa holders from repeatedly switching between visa categories to extend their stay in Australia.

A “no further stay” condition will be applied across visitor visas, meaning people entering Australia on visitor visas will generally be prevented from applying for another substantive visa while remaining in the country.

The government will also increase enforcement against people who remain in Australia after their visas expire.

It plans to appoint 100 additional compliance officers as part of efforts to identify and deal with visa overstayers.

Working holiday visa changes

The government is also changing arrangements for backpackers seeking to remain in Australia beyond their initial working holiday period.

For those seeking a third year of the working holiday programme, places will be allocated through a ballot, with the number of places significantly restricted.

Under the new arrangements, the second-year programme will also have a cap of 45,000 places, down from 57,000 people who qualified this year. The third-year programme will be limited to 5,000 places through the ballot system.

The government is also targeting “visa hopping” among international students, including cases where students repeatedly move from one course to another in order to remain in Australia.

Migration has fallen from post-pandemic peak

Australia’s migration numbers surged after international borders reopened following the COVID-19 pandemic.

Net overseas migration reached a peak of about 518,000 in 2023 but has since declined. The latest figure of 292,100 for the year to March is substantially lower than that peak.

The government has nevertheless maintained its target of bringing net overseas migration down to 225,000.

Burke has rejected suggestions that the changes are politically motivated, saying the government is seeking greater control over who enters Australia temporarily, who stays and who leaves.

International education remains a major export

The reforms come as Australia continues to rely heavily on international education as an economic sector.

International education was worth around A$55 billion to the Australian economy, making it Australia’s fourth-largest export sector, according to ABC.

Education sector representatives have warned that restrictions on students and their families could make Australia less attractive compared with other study destinations.

The government, however, says the reforms are necessary to bring migration back towards more manageable levels while ensuring temporary visas remain genuinely temporary.

title.rendered: Sadak Sujhav App launched to report damaged roads

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

The ‘Sadak Sujhav’ app has been officially launched to make the repair of damaged federal roads in Kathmandu Valley more effective.

The Road Division Kathmandu under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development formally launched the app following a successful trial. Citizens in Kathmandu Valley can now register complaints and provide suggestions through the app regarding the repair of damaged roads under the federal road network.

The app also allows citizens to track the status and progress of their registered complaints. The Road Division Kathmandu said users will also receive information through the app once their complaints have been addressed.

Currently, citizens can register complaints and suggestions regarding around 472 kilometres of federal roads in Kathmandu Valley through the ‘Road Suggestion App’. For roads that do not fall under the federal road network, the app will also provide information on which agency is responsible for those roads, according to the Road Division Kathmandu.

Preparations are also underway to expand the app nationwide to make the management of road maintenance complaints more effective. The Road Division Kathmandu plans to include Lalitpur and Bhaktapur in the app within the next two weeks and gradually expand the service across the country.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa urges Deuba to inaugurate Nepali Congress general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa has urged former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba to attend and inaugurate the party’s 15th general convention, saying his participation would be a matter of honour for the party.

Addressing the party’s Central Working Committee meeting on Thursday, Thapa appealed to Deuba to inaugurate the convention scheduled to begin on October 2.

“My respected leader and former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba, I would like to make an appeal to you,” Thapa said. “Some colleagues have said that if the former party president inaugurates the convention on the day it begins, it would be a matter of honour for us.”

Thapa also said the party statute does not allow Deuba to seek another term as party president.

“The party statute also says the same. He is not going to become the party president again,” Thapa said.

The Nepali Congress is scheduled to begin its general convention at Khulamanch on October 2. Ward-level conventions are scheduled for September 19 and 20, followed by municipal, district and provincial conventions.

Thapa said the party should focus on maintaining unity as it moves through the convention process.

“We will begin the convention at Khulamanch on October 2. Ward conventions will be held on the 19th and 20th, followed by the municipal convention,” he said. “There has been pressure regarding the district and provincial conventions, but there will also be an opportunity for further discussions with party colleagues. As far as possible, we should stand together for party unity.”

‘We are one family’

Thapa also urged party leaders and members not to take sharp remarks made during internal discussions personally.

He acknowledged that leaders may sometimes make harsh comments about one another but said such remarks should not be allowed to damage relations within the party.

“I may have made a sharp comment about someone at times, and someone may have made a sharp comment about me. We have never taken such things personally,” Thapa said.

Describing the Nepali Congress as a family, Thapa said disagreements and occasional friction were natural in a political organisation.

“Our party is a family. We are one family. When a family lives together, sometimes there are bumps along the way,” he said. “There may have been such instances from me, and there may have been such instances from other colleagues. These are normal things. We should discuss them in a cordial manner and move forward.”

Thapa’s remarks come as the party prepares for its general convention amid internal differences and efforts to bring different factions together around the convention process.

title.rendered: Payments to PM Relief Fund ruled ineligible for taxpayer incentive gift

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The Inland Revenue Department has run into a technical snag after someone who donated to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund won the department’s “taxpayer incentive gift” draw.

Under the procedure the department has set for the programme, only those who purchased goods or services and obtained a bill are eligible to take part. However, a person who contributed Rs 1,000 to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, set up after the September flooding, was among the one lakh winners selected through the lottery.

According to department director Keshav Raghubanshi, since a payment to the fund isn’t a payment for goods or services purchased, it doesn’t actually qualify under the taxpayer incentive scheme. He said such fund payments shouldn’t normally have been included in the draw, calling it a technical lesson the department will now correct, and added that the department would consult the Ministry of Finance on what to do about draws that have already been held.

The government introduced the scheme at the start of the current fiscal year to encourage the practice of billing and receiving bills. Payments made directly to the government are not eligible for the incentive under the scheme’s rules.

title.rendered: Police searching for woman who threw dog into Seti River

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Police say they are searching for a woman who forcibly pushed a helpless dog into the Seti River. Widespread public outrage followed after a video of the incident went viral on social media, with many calling for her arrest.

The woman has not yet been located, according to police. Deepak Bista, information officer at the District Police Office, Bajhang, said police received information about the incident and have begun searching for those involved.

He said the incident appears to have taken place on the Pankot Bridge over the Seti River, between wards 10 and 11 of Jayaprithvi Municipality. Bista said police have received the report and launched an investigation, and are now working to establish the identity of the person seen in the video and verify what actually happened.

Police say they are gathering further details about the location and those involved based on the video footage.

“Such incidents can be reported to police”

Senior advocate Padam Bahadur Shrestha says that expressing outrage on social media alone isn’t enough when animal cruelty is witnessed, such incidents can and should be reported to the relevant authorities.

He said anyone who witnesses abuse against dog or other animal can file a complaint at a police office. If police decline to register it, a complaint can also be filed with the District Administration Office or the District Government Attorney’s Office.

In this case too, the video’s spread on social media has given police an initial basis to investigate. What remains to be established is who the woman in the video is, why the dog was thrown from the bridge, and what became of the dog afterward.

What penalty applies for cruelty to animals?

Following the video, there have been social media calls for action against the woman. However, Shrestha noted that police need to establish the facts through investigation rather than reaching conclusions based on the video alone.

Before 2017, there was no specific law on this matter, but since the Muluki Criminal Code came into effect that year, such acts are treated as a criminal offence, punishable by up to three months in jail, a fine of Rs 5,000, or both, according to Shrestha.

title.rendered: Himalayan glaciers melting 65 per cent faster amid growing climate risks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

The Himalayas are undergoing rapid changes, with the rate of glacier melting increasing by 65 per cent compared with a decade ago, according to a new report.

The report highlights growing risks from glacial lakes, melting snow and unstable mountain slopes. It also points to black carbon as a major contributor to glacier melt. Black carbon originating from South Asia accounts for about one-third of glacier melt, while industrial sources, particularly brick kilns, contribute 32–42 per cent of the human-generated black carbon accumulating in the Himalayan region.

The report was jointly released by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and the G B Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment.

Glacier retreat is also affecting the economy. As glaciers retreat, new glacial lakes are forming behind weak natural dams made of snow, loose rocks and debris. If such dams fail, large volumes of water can flow downstream, causing major destruction.

The Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa on August 26 caused loss of life and property, as well as damage to people’s livelihoods.

ICIMOD remote sensing expert Sudan Bikash Maharjan presented details of the changes in the Himalayas to the International Relations Committee of the House of Representatives. According to him, Nepal’s glacier area declined by about 31 per cent between 1980 and 2020.

The Yala Glacier has lost about 66 per cent of its area over the past 50 years, while its lower section has moved about 800 metres higher. Since 1982, the glacier has experienced significant loss of area and thinning, with its thickness declining by about 0.8–0.9 metres a year.

A 2014 study of the Langtang Valley showed a clear relationship between glacier changes and rising temperatures. The rate of glacier change in Langtang is about 25 per cent higher than the overall rate in Nepal. Temperatures in Langtang are rising by about 1.7 degrees Celsius per decade, nearly three times Nepal’s average.

The glacier area in the Langtang Lirung catchment has declined by about 35 per cent over the past 45 years. Between 1990 and 2026, the decline was about 25 per cent.

A recent large landslide and flood in the Langtang Lirung area involved an estimated total mass of 109 million cubic metres. Of this, about 38 million cubic metres came from the glacier and about 12 million cubic metres from the debris-covered glacier.

Joint Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment Dr Maheshwar Raj Dhakal said rising temperatures and melting snow had caused snow masses to fall along with the ground, resulting in the destructive August 26 flood in Rasuwa and the Bhotekoshi area.

According to Dhakal, the initial speed of the flood was 180 kilometres per hour. It later became more destructive after combining with flows from the Kerung, Langtang and Mailung rivers. Greater damage was reported in Betravati and Devighat markets, while a large section of the mountain above Trishuli Bazaar also collapsed.

According to the latest figures cited by the government and the Ministry of Home Affairs, 1,395 people have died, 5,130 are missing and 9,358 have been injured in the August 26 disaster.

The Hindu Kush-Himalaya region is estimated to have around 40,000 glaciers, but only 0.1 per cent are regularly monitored. The report states that future disasters will be difficult to predict without regular monitoring, risk mapping and early warning systems.

Glacier water is the foundation of water security for a large population in South Asia. Most Himalayan river basins are expected to reach “peak water” by the middle of this century, after which river flows are expected to decline as glacier ice diminishes.

If current trends continue, up to 80 per cent of the present glacier ice could be at risk by the end of the century. This could affect agriculture, drinking water, hydropower, industries and cities.

The report says black carbon can be controlled more immediately than global climate change. It calls for a shift from petrol, diesel and coal to green energy and for reductions in black carbon emissions from sources such as brick kilns and petrol- and diesel-powered vehicles.

The report identifies 10 priority areas for action, including reducing black carbon, increasing glacier and permafrost monitoring, strengthening early warning systems, reviving drying water sources and improving forest management. It also calls for tourism to be developed according to carrying capacity.

According to the report, every rupee invested in these measures could generate an average benefit of about Rs 8 when economic, social and environmental benefits and avoided disaster losses are taken into account.

ICIMOD Director General Dr Pema Gyamtsho said the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region is changing rapidly, with glaciers retreating and permafrost and high-altitude slopes becoming increasingly unstable. He said this was creating complex and recurring disaster risks downstream.

According to Gyamtsho, such risks do not respect national borders. He stressed the need for cross-border monitoring, sharing of risk information, early warning systems and joint investment.

Grantham Research Institute Chair Lord Nicholas Stern has described the Himalayas as the “third pole.” Unlike the Arctic and Antarctic, tens of millions of people live around the Himalayan region. He said protecting glaciers is therefore directly linked to water, food, the economy and human security.

The report stresses the need to view glacier melt, unstable glacial lakes, unstable slopes, drying springs and disasters as parts of a connected system. Their impacts can extend to agricultural fields, water supplies, electricity and livelihoods in the plains.

Maharjan said the August 26 disaster was extremely large and difficult to predict, although similar floods had occurred in the Bhotekoshi area in the past.

He said lessons from an earlier disaster had led to the Kodari bridge being raised. He stressed the need to link rising temperatures, glacier decline, changes in permafrost, and the risks of landslides and floods with development planning.

According to him, infrastructure and settlement planning should require assessments of climate and mountain-related risks.

Kathmandu, September 1

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Bodhanarayan Shrestha has called for a comprehensive plan to excavate structures buried by the floods in Rasuwa.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives on Thursday, Shrestha said he had received numerous calls from relatives in Trishuli seeking the excavation of houses where they believed their family members’ bodies were buried.

He said search and rescue operations were currently underway but had slowed, suggesting that the government should now revise its approach.

According to Shrestha, excavation should be carried out at private houses as well as public buildings, including schools, health facilities and local government offices. He also called for the excavation of archaeological structures, monasteries, temples, religious sites and buildings belonging to financial institutions.

“I urge the Ministry of Home Affairs and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority to prepare a separate comprehensive plan and launch excavation operations simultaneously across all these areas and all affected districts,” he said.

Shrestha also said cooperation between the government and the private sector would be necessary to carry out the excavation work.

title.rendered: UML leaders continue talks at Oli’s residence over party reorganisation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

A meeting of CPN-UML leaders continued at Chairman KP Sharma Oli’s residence in Gundu on Thursday, with discussions focused on the party’s proposed reorganisation and the growing dispute over its leadership.

The meeting is being attended by Vice Chairs Ram Bahadur Thapa and Bishnu Paudel, General Secretary Shankar Pokharel, and leaders Pradeep Gyawali, Prithvi Subba Gurung, Bhanubhakta Dhakal and Bishnu Rimal, among others.

The meeting is taking place at Oli’s residence even as some leaders have been pushing for his removal from the party leadership as part of the proposed reorganisation.

Thapa, who is considered close to Oli, had earlier proposed holding the meeting in Gundu, but some leaders had initially opposed the idea. They have returned to Gundu citing Oli’s health and other reasons, according to party sources.

According to sources, Oli has indicated that he is prepared to accept most of the proposals related to party reorganisation but has made it clear that he will not relinquish the chairmanship.

Dispute over task force report

The latest discussions follow disagreements over a report prepared by an UML task force on party reorganisation.

Although an editing committee was formed to resolve differences over the task force report, leaders failed to reach an agreement.

Thapa is the coordinator of the task force, while General Secretary Pokharel is its member-secretary. Pokharel prepared the report based on the mandate given to the task force.

However, differences emerged after Pokharel maintained his position on the report’s conclusions, including the proposal that Oli should step down as party chairman.

Thapa had proposed that Pokharel’s report be withdrawn, but other leaders did not agree to the proposal.

Paudel appears softer on Oli’s leadership

After several rounds of discussions with Oli in Gundu, Vice Chair Bishnu Paudel has reportedly taken a softer position on the proposal to retain Oli as chairman, according to party sources.

The push for party reorganisation has gained strength within the UML, but Oli has not agreed to step aside.

Leaders are now discussing how to proceed with the Central Committee meeting scheduled for September 21 to 23, particularly how to settle differences over the task force report before the meeting begins.

Some UML leaders told Onlinekhabar that there is a possibility the Central Committee meeting could be postponed if the leadership fails to resolve the remaining disagreements.

One office-bearer said the ongoing discussions were important because the party leadership had yet to resolve its internal crisis.

“The Central Committee meeting may not begin until the chairman’s crisis is resolved,” the leader said. “In that sense, today’s meeting is important.”

After the Gundu meeting, the task force is also expected to meet again on Thursday.

Pokharel refuses to withdraw report

Pokharel has maintained that he will not withdraw his report, arguing that he prepared it in accordance with the mandate given by the party secretariat and the task force.

The report explicitly proposes that Oli should step down as party chairman.

However, some leaders close to Oli have argued that if Oli is required to take responsibility and leave the leadership, other office-bearers who came into the party leadership alongside him should also accept moral responsibility and step down.

“Some leaders have taken the position that not only Oli but other leaders should also leave their posts,” another leader said. “Otherwise, one cannot write a fabricated report to portray oneself as blameless while targeting others.”

Thapa has submitted a written rebuttal to Pokharel’s report. Pokharel and other leaders have demanded that Thapa withdraw the rebuttal, warning that otherwise a response to the rebuttal would also be attached to the report submitted to the Central Committee.

The leaders had earlier held a three-day residential meeting in Balthali in an attempt to resolve disputes and differences over the report.

Leaders divided over Oli

According to party sources, General Secretary Pokharel, Vice Chairs Gokarna Bista and Raghujii Pant, Deputy General Secretaries Yogesh Bhattarai and Raghuvir Mahaseth, and Secretaries Khagaraj Adhikari, Chhabilal Bishwakarma, Rajan Bhattarai and Hikmat Karki are among those supporting the proposal for Oli to step down.

Vice Chair Thapa and Secretaries Sherdhan Rai and Mahesh Basnet have stood clearly in Oli’s defence, according to the sources.

Paudel is now also understood to be leaning towards supporting the continuation of Oli’s leadership.

title.rendered: Waste Management Bill registered in Parliament

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

A bill seeking to amend and consolidate laws related to waste management has been registered in Parliament.

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal registered the bill in the House of Representatives on Thursday.

According to Lamsal, the bill has been introduced to clarify the roles and responsibilities of the federal, provincial and local governments in waste generation, collection, disposal and overall management.

The bill aims to ensure effective coordination among the three levels of government and maintain a clean and healthy environment through proper and effective waste management.

Lamsal stated in the bill that it was presented to the Federal Parliament to minimise the adverse impacts of waste on human health and the environment and to provide for processing waste and using it as a resource in line with the concept of a circular economy.

Article 30 of the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to live in a clean and healthy environment and the right to compensation from the polluter for damage caused by environmental pollution or degradation.

Article 35 guarantees every citizen the right to access clean drinking water and sanitation.

The government expects the bill, if passed, to facilitate co-investment among the different levels of government, public-private partnerships and the mobilisation of development assistance for waste management.

It also aims to create a basis for research, technological development and transfer, inter-local and intergovernmental partnerships, and the exchange of knowledge, skills and experience.

The government believes the bill will clarify the responsibilities of different levels of government and help achieve constitutional goals related to waste management and environmental cleanliness while promoting the use of processed waste as resources under the circular economy concept.

title.rendered: 24-year-old arrested after CIB uncovers Rs 1.34 billion in alleged hundi transactions

content.rendered:
Dhanusha, September 17

A 24-year-old man has been arrested in Dhanusha on suspicion of involvement in hundi transactions worth more than Rs 1.34 billion over the past two years.

Ajay Kumar Mukhiya of Shahid Nagar Municipality-4 is currently in the custody of the District Police Office, Dhanusha.

A joint team from the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Nepal Police and the District Police Office arrested Mukhiya from Shahid Nagar-4 at around 5:20 pm on Tuesday.

According to CIB Senior Superintendent of Police Anupam Shamsher Rana, police began investigating Mukhiya after receiving information that he was involved in large-scale hundi transactions.

Police examined transactions in his personal and business bank accounts and found that he had carried out transactions worth Rs 1.347 billion through hundi, based on preliminary investigation.

The amount was identified from transactions conducted through the banking system alone. Police believe the total amount could be significantly higher because hundi transactions are also carried out in cash.

Rs 1.5 billion in two years

The CIB launched a detailed investigation after receiving information about Mukhiya’s alleged involvement in hundi transactions.

Police arrested him after collecting evidence that they said corroborated the information.

“Preliminary investigation shows that he has been involved in hundi transactions for the past two years. We have found evidence of large-scale hundi transactions during this period,” SSP Rana said.

According to investigators, the group primarily conducted hundi transactions linked to Malaysia. Transactions targeting other Gulf countries have also been identified.

Allegedly hired to carry out transactions

Police say Mukhiya was not the owner of the hundi operation despite the large volume of transactions linked to him.

An investigation officer said Mukhiya appeared to have been used as a hired person to carry out transactions on behalf of others.

“Preliminary investigation shows that Mukhiya was not the owner but was being used on a hired basis. It appears that he carried out hundi transactions in return for a fixed payment,” the officer said.

Police suspect that other individuals own and operate the hundi network. However, those alleged owners have not yet been arrested.

The CIB said its investigation is continuing to identify other people involved in the operation and trace the alleged owners of the funds.

How does hundi work?

Hundi can involve both domestic and cross-border transactions. Authorities consider cross-border hundi particularly challenging because it can prevent foreign currency that should enter Nepal from being recorded through formal channels.

Such transactions can contribute to discrepancies in remittance flows and can facilitate the illegal transfer of capital out of the country.

In some cases, money transferred abroad through illegal channels can later enter Nepal through other routes, including as purported foreign investment, potentially providing a channel for money laundering.

Hundi can also be used to facilitate financial transactions linked to criminal activities and to conceal the movement of illegally obtained money.

What does the law say?

Section 125 of Nepal’s National Penal (Code) Act prohibits hundi transactions.

The law defines hundi-related transactions as transferring or settling money or value between Nepal and foreign countries, or receiving or making payments through individuals, instruments or channels other than institutions or payment instruments recognised under prevailing law.

The law also prohibits receiving or making payments in a manner that conceals the actual accounts of a commercial transaction.

A person convicted of conducting hundi transactions can face confiscation of the amount involved and any property acquired or increased through the proceeds, along with imprisonment of up to one year.

title.rendered: Foreign Minister Khanal updates PM Shah on climate justice efforts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has said the government is working on a long-term plan to advance Nepal’s agenda for climate justice, including by consolidating existing research and developing new studies on climate-related risks.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives’ International Relations and Tourism Committee on Thursday, Khanal said the government was looking beyond short-term discussions and was considering institutional mechanisms that would allow Nepal to pursue the issue consistently.

“This should not remain merely a subject for discussion. I have also been drawing the attention of the prime minister to these issues,” Khanal said. “We need to work on longer-term institutions and design, keeping the timeline in mind.”

The remarks come in the aftermath of the devastating Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa on August 26, which caused extensive damage along river corridors in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan.

The government has linked the disaster to the broader risks posed by climate change. A government expert committee formed this week is also studying the scientific causes and sequence of the flood, including the possible role of climate change.

Khanal said the government was examining how Nepal could respond to such risks in a sustainable manner.

“We need to rethink governance as well,” he said, adding that he had been raising issues highlighted by experts and lawmakers in his briefings and discussions with the prime minister.

Building a national climate position

The parliamentary committee meeting focused on Nepal’s vulnerability to climate change, climate justice, international cooperation and access to climate finance.

Experts also discussed how Nepal could present its climate-related concerns more effectively on international platforms.

Khanal said one of the immediate priorities should be to strengthen Nepal’s knowledge base.

“The issue we need to think about now is study, research and knowledge creation,” he said.

He said studies conducted in Nepal and abroad on the Himalayan region should be brought together and reviewed collectively.

“Bringing together the studies and research conducted in Nepal and outside Nepal on the Himalayan region and developing a consistent national position from them is an important aspect,” he said.

Khanal said Nepal needed to develop a stronger evidence-based position so that it could present its concerns clearly at international forums.

Nepal has already sought international support following the Rasuwa floods. The government submitted an initial claim of $20 million to the UN-backed Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, arguing that the disaster was linked to climate change.

The fund’s board has since said consultations are under way to consider options for responding to Nepal’s request for emergency assistance.

Climate diplomacy ahead of UN General Assembly

The discussion in the parliamentary committee comes as Prime Minister Balendra Shah prepares to lead a Nepali delegation to the United States to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly next week.

The Rasuwa disaster is expected to form an important part of Nepal’s international climate agenda.

Khanal said Nepal’s participation in the General Assembly would provide an important opportunity to present the country’s diplomatic and international priorities.

He also said suggestions raised by experts and lawmakers during the committee meeting would be conveyed to Prime Minister Shah.

“I will draw the prime minister’s attention to the suggestions received today,” Khanal said.

He added that he would also consult former prime ministers and hold further discussions on the issues raised.

Nepal has increasingly sought to frame climate change not only as an environmental issue but also as a question of justice, given the country’s relatively small contribution to global emissions and its exposure to climate-related risks.

Khanal has previously called for stronger international action, including support for countries facing disproportionate impacts from climate change.

He has also stressed the need for long-term institutional structures to ensure that Nepal’s climate diplomacy does not depend solely on individual international conferences or short-term initiatives.

The government is now looking to consolidate research, strengthen its institutional capacity and develop a consistent national position as it prepares to take Nepal’s climate justice agenda to international forums.

title.rendered: Parliamentary special committee to be formed to address Rasuwa flood and climate issues

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

A parliamentary special committee is set to be formed to address issues related to the disaster caused by the Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa and the broader challenges posed by climate change.

Leaders from political parties represented in Parliament, including parliamentary party leaders, deputy leaders and chief whips, are holding discussions on the formation of the committee.

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chief Whip Kabindra Burlakoti said the discussions were based on an agreement reached at an all-party meeting on Wednesday.

The all-party meeting had agreed to establish two separate mechanisms to work on disaster response, recovery and long-term disaster risk reduction.

One is a high-level political mechanism comprising parties both inside and outside Parliament, while the other will be a parliamentary committee comprising parties represented in Parliament.

Lamichhane-led political mechanism

According to RSP spokesperson Jagadish Kharel, a high-level political mechanism has been formed under the leadership of RSP chair and ruling party leader Ravi Lamichhane.

The mechanism includes the Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, Nepali Communist Party, Shram Sanskriti Party, Rastriya Prajatantra Party, Janamat Party and Janata Samajbadi Party Nepal.

Kharel said a decision had also been taken to request the Rastriya Janamorcha to join the mechanism.

“The decision is to keep this high-level political mechanism, coordinated by RSP chair Ravi Lamichhane, in place to discuss sustainable disaster risk reduction and management as well as overall development and reconstruction issues,” Kharel said.

The mechanism is intended to work beyond the immediate response to the Rasuwa floods, with a focus on long-term disaster risk reduction, reconstruction and policy reform.

Parliamentary committee to be formed within a week

The second mechanism will be established within Parliament.

According to Kharel, the parties have agreed to form the parliamentary committee within a week, with representation based on the number of seats held by each party.

“The decision is to take the initiative to form the parliamentary committee and request the Speaker to facilitate its formation,” Kharel said.

The proposal will now be taken forward through the Speaker and Parliament.

CPN-UML Parliamentary Party Deputy Leader Padma Aryal said discussions were also under way on who would lead the parliamentary special committee.

“The issue of leadership of the parliamentary special committee is being discussed,” Aryal told Onlinekhabar.

The terms of reference for the committee are also expected to be discussed before its formation.

Proposal came after Rasuwa disaster

The move follows a proposal made by Lamichhane immediately after the devastating Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa.

A day after the disaster, Lamichhane called an all-party meeting and proposed forming a mechanism involving political parties to support the government from rescue and relief through rehabilitation.

“Let’s form an all-party, parliamentary or broader committee from rescue and relief to rehabilitation. It would make it easier for the government to take decisions,” he had said.

Representatives of the RSP, Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, Nepali Communist Party, Shram Sanskriti Party, Rastriya Prajatantra Party, Janata Samajbadi Party Nepal and Janamat Party participated in the initial discussions.

The all-party meeting subsequently adopted a 10-point commitment that included agreement to form a parliamentary committee to monitor government efforts and provide advice on post-disaster reconstruction, climate adaptation and improvements to national disaster policy.

The proposed parliamentary mechanism is expected to have a broader mandate than immediate flood response, including disaster preparedness, sustainable infrastructure, early warning systems and climate-related policy.

The development comes amid continuing calls from political parties for a parliamentary mechanism to oversee rescue, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction following the Rasuwa floods. Opposition parties had also urged the government to establish such a committee earlier this month.
