title.rendered: Bagmati prepares to expand Cabinet, Rama Ale set to become agriculture minister

content.rendered:
Hetauda, September 17

The Bagmati provincial government is preparing to expand its Cabinet, with Chief Minister Kiran Thapa Magar preparing to appoint Rama Ale Magar as minister for Agriculture, Livestock, Forest and Environment on Thursday.

Ale Magar has arrived in Hetauda and is expected to take the oath of office and secrecy on Thursday evening. She previously served as youth and sports minister in the government led by Shalikram Jamarkattel.

Of the two ministries allocated to the CPN in the Bagmati government, Saral Sahyatri Poudel, who comes from the CPN (Maoist Centre) background, was appointed minister for Economic Affairs and Planning, while the other ministry was allocated to the then CPN (Unified Socialist), the Madhav Nepal faction.

According to the earlier agreement within the CPN, preparations have been made to appoint and swear in Ale Magar on Thursday.

The coalition government of the CPN-UML, CPN and Rastriya Prajatantra Party has seven ministries besides the Office of the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers. Six ministers were appointed on August 20, while the ministries of Internal Affairs, Law and Cooperatives and Agriculture remained vacant. UML’s Gyan Bahadur Tamang was appointed minister without portfolio.

Under the power-sharing arrangement, UML has three ministries, including the chief minister; the CPN has three ministries along with the provincial Assembly speaker, and RPP has three ministries.

The CPN has Saral Sahyatri as minister for Economic Affairs; UML’s Bharat KC is minister for Physical Infrastructure; and RPP’s Gir Bahadur Tamang is minister for Health and Social Affairs, Raju Bisht is minister for Water Supply, Energy and Irrigation, and Rajendra Prajapati is minister for Industry, Tourism, Labour and Transport.

CPN seeks additional ministry

During the Cabinet expansion, the faction led by Ganga Narayan Shrestha and Krishna Prasad Sharma Khanal within the CPN has strongly demanded the appointment of another minister from the party.

The lawmakers have demanded that the vacant Internal Affairs, Law and Cooperatives Ministry, which was previously allocated to UML, should also be given to the CPN.

According to a CPN lawmaker, the party has already proposed to Chief Minister Thapa that it should receive another ministry due to growing pressure within the party. However, Thapa has not agreed to the proposal. The chief minister is under pressure to appoint his party’s minister without a portfolio, Gyan Bahadur Tamang, to the Law Ministry.

The ruling coalition has agreed not to increase the number of ministries beyond eight.

“Party leadership has instructed us to first have Rama Ale Magar sworn in. There has been no agreement yet on taking another ministry. We are still discussing it,” the CPN lawmaker said.

title.rendered: Foreign Minister calls Rasuwa flood a “Himalayan tsunami”

content.rendered:
Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has described the devastating flood in Rasuwa as a “Himalayan tsunami.”

He remarked while speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives’ International Relations and Tourism Committee on Thursday. He said he has taken to calling the current flooding a “Himalayan tsunami,” adding that the disaster has shaken the narrative of prosperity Nepal has been building for the past 20–25 years.

The devastating flood hit Rasuwa on August 26, causing damage along riverside areas stretching from Rasuwa and Nuwakot to Dhading and Chitwan.

The government has concluded that climate change is behind the damage, and Minister Khanal said further studies are underway on the matter.

According to Khanal, Nepal’s prosperity is closely tied to river corridors, particularly the Himalayan river corridor, with major north-south road plans envisioned around them. He noted that a bridge project being planned jointly with two neighbouring countries also depends on connectivity along this river corridor as a key lifeline.

He added that over the past 30–40 years, Nepal’s settlement and market development has also clustered around river-corridor basins, and that hydropower, central to the country’s prosperity ambitions through power generation and export, is likewise ultimately tied to the Himalayan river corridor.

A Nepali delegation led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah is set to travel to the United States next week to attend the UN General Assembly. It was against this backdrop that the parliamentary committee held discussions with climate change experts.

At the meeting, experts shared their views on the climate risks facing Nepal, climate justice, international cooperation, and climate finance, along with how Nepal can more effectively present climate issues on the international stage.

Minister Khanal said Nepal’s participation in the General Assembly would be an important opportunity to present the country’s international relations and diplomatic priorities. He added that a key priority now is consolidating research and studies conducted on the Himalayan region, both within Nepal and abroad, into a single, consistent national position.

title.rendered: ‘The technology and setup in Nepal are equivalent to ours in India’

content.rendered:
In the aftermath of the devastating Rasuwa flood, identifying disaster victims has presented a significant forensic challenge for Nepal. To bolster local efforts, an Indian forensic team was deployed to Kathmandu to assist with DNA profiling and victim identification. 

Onlinekhabar spoke with Dr Kamal Chauhan, Assistant Director at the Central Forensic Science Laboratory, Delhi, about his team’s operations in Nepal, the technical aspects of forensic identification, and what grieving families should expect from this complex process.

You and your team have been in Nepal for over two weeks now. What have been some of your primary forensic challenges while examining the bodies?

Actually, we are not directly examining the bodies here; our focus is on lab work, specifically DNA profiling. We process reference samples from relatives of the deceased, alongside post-mortem samples received from doctors following autopsies. By generating DNA profiles for both groups, we can match them to establish identifications.

In terms of challenges, our primary bottleneck is operational capacity. The local machinery processes eight samples at a time, whereas equipment capable of handling 24 samples per run would significantly increase our output. Beyond that constraint, the technical infrastructure here is solid, featuring modern machinery comparable to what we use in India.

Having conducted DNA profiling for various disaster scenarios in the past, how does your work in Nepal compare to previous operations?

The sample types are essentially identical, primarily molar teeth and dense bone fragments, which yield the best DNA results. However, the context creates different challenges. In events like air crashes, passenger manifests make victims known, allowing us to source reference samples from families relatively quickly. In a flood disaster, many victims are initially unknown or swept away, making it much harder to gather corresponding reference samples from missing persons’ families.

Why is DNA profiling so crucial in flood disaster recovery?

Because the bodies are often severely decomposed or fragmented, visual identification becomes impossible. DNA provides an objective, foolproof method because everyone possesses a unique genetic profile. Since a child inherits 50% of their DNA from their mother and 50% from their father, direct lineage matching can definitively confirm an identity.

What happens if a victim’s parents are no longer alive? How do you establish a match?

When parents aren’t available, we utilise lineage-specific testing. For male victims with surviving male relatives, such as brothers, paternal uncles, or paternal cousins, we perform Y-STR profiling. Because the Y-chromosome passes intact along the paternal line, male relatives share the same Y-STR profile. For female relatives or maternal lines, we employ equivalent marker systems like X-STR profiling.

How has the experience been collaborating with the Nepalese forensic team?

The experience has been very smooth. We have been working closely with local officials and their team, who have been extremely cooperative. Our primary contribution as an international team of around 14 to 15 DNA experts is scaling up testing throughput. To date, our lab operations have processed over 500 reference samples and approximately 300 post-mortem samples.

Many families are anxiously awaiting news regarding missing loved ones. What should they know about this process, and how long will it take?

First and foremost, families searching for missing relatives must come forward to submit reference samples at designated medical centres; without a reference sample, a DNA profile generated from a body cannot be matched to anyone.

Given the scale, where thousands may be affected, and individual bodies may yield multiple fragmented samples, this process requires immense patience. At our current pace, completing the primary laboratory profiling will likely take around a month, though overall operational timelines remain subject to government directive.

title.rendered: Fiji declares national emergency as HIV cases surge

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Fiji has declared a national emergency over a sharp rise in HIV infections that has placed significant pressure on the country’s health system, with the government planning to expand testing, treatment and prevention services.

The Pacific island nation now has an estimated one in every 60 adults living with HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago. Fiji recorded 2,016 new HIV infections in 2025 alone, according to the report.

UNAIDS estimates that about 9,100 people were living with HIV in Fiji in 2025. Only 39 per cent knew their HIV status, while 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment, compared with a global treatment coverage rate of 78 per cent.

Health authorities have linked the spread to increasing drug use, unsafe sex, needle sharing and a practice known as “bluetoothing” or “hotspotting,” in which blood from a person under the influence of drugs is transferred to another person.

The government plans to introduce a needle and syringe programme and is preparing legislative amendments to facilitate its implementation. Health Minister Antonio Lalabalavu has urged people to come forward for HIV testing, saying social stigma is keeping some people away from healthcare services.

Jason Mitchell, head of Fiji’s National HIV Response Taskforce, said controlling the outbreak could take at least five years and warned that the epidemic was placing additional pressure on an already strained health system.

Four pistols and six rounds of ammunition have been recovered from an abandoned Indian-registered car in Birgunj, Parsa.

The team recovered two locally made pistols, two sixer pistols and six rounds of 7.62mm ammunition used in the pistols.

The APF said the recovered weapons, ammunition and the abandoned vehicle have been handed over to the District Police Office, Parsa, for further investigation.

title.rendered: Probe committee recommends action against health workers over childbirth outside hospital

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

A probe committee has recommended departmental action against doctors, nurses, paramedics and other staff on duty when a pregnant woman gave birth outside Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Rajbiraj after reportedly being unable to pay for services.

Babita Paswan gave birth on a roadside on September 10 after visiting the hospital for maternity services. The committee found that the health workers failed to properly counsel her, ensure that she remained at the hospital for treatment and monitor her condition after she left the facility.

The committee also identified shortcomings in the hospital administration and the implementation of the government’s Safe Motherhood Programme. It said hospital staff had insufficient knowledge about the programme and failed to clearly inform the woman about the services available to her.

According to the committee, poverty, illiteracy and a lack of awareness about healthcare also contributed to the incident. However, it said responsibility should not be placed solely on the service recipient and raised questions about the hospital’s service delivery and staff responsibilities.

The committee recommended clarifying the scope of services covered by the Safe Motherhood Programme, including necessary laboratory tests, to ensure women are not denied maternity care due to financial constraints.

The team, led by Nepal Medical Council Registrar Dr Suprabhat Shrestha, conducted an on-site investigation from September 10 to 12 and has submitted its report to the Ministry of Health.

title.rendered: Cooperatives’ maximum lending rate cut to 13 per cent

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

The maximum interest rate that cooperative institutions can charge on loans to their members has been reduced to 13 per cent, effective Wednesday.

The Office of the Cooperative Registrar revised the reference interest rate based on the recommendation of a committee formed under Section 51 of the Cooperatives Act, 2017. The maximum lending rate was previously capped at 16 per cent.

Under the new provision, cooperatives cannot charge more than 13 per cent interest on loans. However, they may set a lower rate after assessing their financial condition, needs and justification.

The difference between the interest rate offered on savings and the rate charged on loans has also been capped at six percentage points.

The office has directed cooperatives to comply with the legal provision prohibiting them from capitalising interest accrued on loans into the principal and charging further interest on the capitalised amount.

If a cooperative imposes a penalty, it cannot charge more than five per cent of the outstanding interest amount.

The office also said all costs associated with loans must be included in the interest rate, barring cooperatives from charging additional amounts under administrative, service, renewal, application or similar fees.

Cooperatives must publicly disclose their interest rates through their websites or other means. They are also prohibited from discriminating among members, directors, committee members, managers and employees when setting rates for similar savings or loan products.

title.rendered: Nepal records historic recovery in vulture population

content.rendered:
Arghakhanchi, September 17

Nepal has become the first country in South Asia to halt the decline and achieve a sustained increase in its vulture population following conservation measures, restrictions on harmful veterinary drugs, protection of habitats and provision of safe food.

Vulture populations across South Asia began declining sharply in the 1990s. Research later identified diclofenac, a painkiller used in veterinary treatment, as a major cause of vulture deaths. Vultures feeding on carcasses of livestock treated with the drug suffered kidney failure and usually died within two days.

Nepal, India and Pakistan banned veterinary use of diclofenac in 2006, while Bangladesh introduced a ban in 2010. Safe feeding sites known as Jatayu Restaurants, habitat conservation and efforts to reduce the use of other harmful drugs have since supported vulture recovery.

A recent scientific study found that the population of the critically endangered Oriental White-rumped Vulture has increased by an average of 12.7 per cent annually in Nepal since 2012-13, with the trend continuing through 2025.

Satellite tracking of 70 vultures found annual survival rates of 94.7 per cent for adults and 95.5 per cent for immature birds. Researchers also monitored 6,410 nests between 2007 and 2025, recording an average nesting success rate of about 69 per cent.

Researchers said the recovery is mainly attributable to improved survival and breeding within Nepal, rather than an influx of vultures from India. However, conservationists cautioned that populations remain well below their pre-1990s levels and urged continued monitoring of veterinary drugs harmful to vultures.

title.rendered: Bishwokarma puja, Vastu Diwas being observed today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Artisans are observing Vastu Diwas and Bishwokarma Parba today by worshipping and paying homage to Lord Bishwokarma.

Bishwokarma Parba, or the Bishwokarma festival, is observed every year on Ashwin Sankranti, the first day of the month of Ashwin according to the lunar calendar. On this occasion, workshops, artisans and members of the general public formally worship images of Lord Bishwokarma to mark the festival.

Bishwokarma is considered the divine architect of the universe and the personification of divine creativity in the Rigveda. He is credited with constructing the city of Ved Dwaraka for Lord Krishna and the palace of Indraprastha for the Pandavas, as well as creating various weapons for Hindu gods, including Vishnu’s Sudarshana Chakra, Shiva’s trishula and Kartikeya’s lance.

Bishwokarma is also regarded as an expert in architecture, or Vaastu. He is believed to have authored the Sthapatya Veda, which deals with architecture, mechanics and related sciences. He is considered the patron deity of craftspeople, who traditionally worship their tools and equipment in his honour on Bishwokarma Puja.

Artisans decorate their workshops and celebrate the festival with grandeur. They worship the tools, machinery and other implements used in their professions. There is a religious belief that worshipping these tools on Bishwokarma Puja will ensure their longevity, prevent them from breaking during work and help artisans perform their tasks well.

Vastu experts also observe the day as Vastu Diwas or Vastu Day in memory of the authors and scholars who contributed to Vaastu Shastra literature.

In recent years, there has also been a revival of interest in Vastu knowledge in Nepal. The Atharvaveda, one of the four Vedas, contains references to architecture. The number of people building houses and other structures based on traditional architectural principles has also begun to increase. As a result, the importance of Vastu Shastra has grown in recent years.

title.rendered: Nepal collects Rs 184.58 billion in revenue in first two months of fiscal year

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Nepal collected Rs 184.58 billion in revenue during the first two months of the current fiscal year despite the devastating September 25 floods and disruptions along the northern border points.

According to the Ministry of Finance, revenue collection in the first two months of fiscal year 2026/27 has increased compared with the same period last fiscal year.

Nepal had collected Rs 158.71 billion in revenue by the end of Bhadra in fiscal year 2025/26.

Revenue collection was particularly higher in Bhadra this year. The government collected Rs 91.38 billion during the month, compared with Rs 73.61 billion in Bhadra last year.

Revenue collection last year was affected in the final week of Bhadra by the Gen Z-led protests.

Despite the year-on-year increase, revenue collection remains below the government’s target.

The government had set a target of Rs 214.81 billion for the first two months of the current fiscal year. By the end of Bhadra, it had achieved 85.93 percent of the target.

For Bhadra alone, the revenue target was Rs 96.88 billion. Collection stood at Rs 91.38 billion, or 94.33 percent of the monthly target.

The government collected Rs 5.58 billion in revenue on Bhadra 31 alone.

In the same period last fiscal year, the government had set a target of around Rs 218 billion but collected only Rs 158 billion.

The government has set a total revenue collection target of Rs 1.58 trillion for the current fiscal year.

However, the floods in Rasuwa and along the Bhotekoshi corridor are expected to affect revenue collection in the coming months, particularly due to disruptions at the northern border points.

title.rendered: 191 vehicles operated under FNNTE damaged, 344 employees missing in Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

As many as 191 vehicles operated by nine companies affiliated with the Federation of Nepalese National Transport Entrepreneurs (FNNTE) were damaged in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor floods on August 26, with 344 people reported missing.

FNNTE General Secretary Deknath Gautam said the missing included drivers, helpers and passengers travelling in the affected vehicles. According to the federation, 19 buses, one minitruck, two jeeps and four containers operated by Nepal Araniko Transport Service Pvt. Ltd. were damaged, with 50 people missing. Similarly, 19 buses operated by Namaste Pasang Lhamu Transport Pvt. Ltd. in Balaju were damaged, with 21 people missing.

Two drivers went missing after two containers operated by Bhaktapur New Vision Transport Pvt. Ltd. were washed away. Likewise, 10 drivers went missing after four trucks, 16 containers and one Sumo jeep operated by Himalayan Transport Company were washed away and damaged. Seven tippers, 22 containers, 23 trucks and one trailer operated by the Nepal Tipper and Truck Entrepreneurs Committee were damaged, leaving 45 drivers missing.

Similarly, 59 trucks and containers operated by Narayani Transport Entrepreneurs Company Pvt. Ltd. were damaged, with 70 people missing. Nine microbuses operated by Nepal Micro Company were also damaged. One driver and 22 passengers went missing after a bus operated by Prithvi Highway Transport Operator Company was swept away by the floods. Likewise, Gautam said one driver and 25 pilgrims went missing after a bus operated by Dhading Mandali Transport Pvt. Ltd. was damaged in the floods.

title.rendered: Home is still waiting for the people of Timure

content.rendered:
The prayers begin quietly.

Some people sit with their heads bowed, murmuring mantras. Others are silent. Families who have lost relatives gather for Buddhist rituals, while children and older people sit among the iron beds and mats spread across the floor.

There is grief everywhere, but little certainty about what comes next.

At Mustang Gumba in Swayambhu, Kathmandu, around 250 people from Timure, a settlement near Nepal’s border with China, have found temporary shelter after the Bhotekoshi floods swept through their village on August 26.

They came here after losing homes, possessions and, in many cases, family members.

For 67-year-old Lakpache Ghale, survival came down to chance.

She had gone to a nearby settlement to look after a woman who had recently given birth and her baby. While she was away, the flood tore through Timure.

“Those who could run fled towards the forest. Those who could not were swept away. Many people from Timure were swept away,” she says. “It was something we never imagined. We have suffered such a tragedy.”

Ghale says she has cried so much that her eyes have swollen.

“We are here now, but we do not know where we will go tomorrow,” she says. “Those who were supposed to leave have already gone. We, the survivors, must perform the religious rites for those who have gone.”

That responsibility has become one of the first tasks for the survivors. But even mourning has become difficult.

A village without a village

Before the flood, Timure was a busy settlement on one of Nepal’s important routes to China.

According to the 2021 census, 163 households and 550 people lived there. But the number of people who were actually present when the flood struck was much higher.

Phurpu Dorje Ghale, principal of Nepal Rastriya Basic School in Timure, estimates that more than 250 local residents were in the settlement.

Only about 95 rescued people, he says, made it out.

“Around 145 people are still missing,” he says.

The village had around 200 houses.

“Now they are gone.”

A few houses escaped the full force of the flood, but even those are no longer considered safe to live in.

And Timure was not only home to its permanent residents. It was a border hub crowded with workers, traders, security personnel, tourists and truck drivers. There were seven banks in the settlement, as well as customs and immigration offices, quarantine facilities and offices belonging to Nepal’s three security agencies.

“There must have been around 2,000 people there,” Ghale says.

Tourists travelling towards Kailash had been passing through. Between 700 and 800 container trucks were in the area, he estimates, bringing with them drivers and helpers. Hotels were full. There were four or five large hotels in nearby Ghattekhola and another three or four in Timure itself.

“Everyone who was between Timure and the customs office did not survive,” Ghale says.

His own school has been devastated. Twenty-five students and six teachers remain unaccounted for.

“Only 10 students managed to escape and survive,” he says.

The scale of the destruction has made the question of exactly how many people were caught in the flood difficult to answer. But for those now sheltering in Kathmandu, the numbers are personal. Every missing person has a family waiting.

49 days

Inside the monastery, the survivors have begun the traditional Buddhist rituals for those who died. They intend to remain there for 49 days.

“We will stay here for 49 days and perform ghewa for those who died, according to our customs, religion and traditions,” Ghale says.

But they have brought almost nothing with them. Their homes are gone. Their possessions are gone. Many of their relatives are gone. And they say they do not even have enough money to carry out the rituals properly.

“We have to light incense every day and every week. We have to perform prayers. We have no money for that,” Ghale says.

The timing matters, he says.

“If we are given funeral expenses after 49 days, it will have no meaning. If we do not receive support when it is needed, it will be of no use later.”

The government, he says, should take responsibility.

“We can even survive by begging and eating on the streets of Swayambhu,” he says. “But we cannot leave those who have died without performing our religious duties.”

The survivors say the government should provide funeral expenses immediately.

“It has already been three weeks. Only four weeks remain. The funeral expenses should be provided as soon as possible.”

Even the dead remain trapped in bureaucracy

There is another problem, less visible than the destruction of Timure but just as immediate. The missing people left money in bank accounts. Their families cannot easily access it.

“Death registration is required to withdraw the money,” Ghale says. “Our relatives have died. We need money to perform the rituals and meet expenses, but we have not received death registration certificates.”

Without official death registration, he says, families cannot access their relatives’ funds. The survivors are therefore asking the government to create a way to register the deaths of people who disappeared in the disaster. For people who have lost almost everything, the money is not an abstract legal issue. It can mean food, shelter, travel and the ability to perform the rituals that their religion requires.

They do not want Kathmandu

Yet when the conversation turns to the future, the people at the monastery do not speak about staying in Kathmandu. They speak about going home. Not necessarily to the Timure that existed before the flood. They know that the settlement has been destroyed.

Instead, they want to rebuild further uphill, in Khaidi, an old village about half an hour above Timure. Khaidi, they believe, could become an integrated settlement with several hundred houses.

“We want to return to our own place,” says Ghale. “We have our society there, our customs, our language, religion and culture.”

Without rehabilitation, he fears, more than homes will disappear.

“That culture will collapse.”

For the people of Timure, the desire to return is also tied to a sense of history and responsibility.

Kami Nurpu Tamang, president of the Cross-Border Traders Association and coordinator of the border management committee, describes the community as guardians of the frontier.

“We have our traditions. This is our birthplace,” he says. “We want to protect the history we have had since the Lichchhavi period, as well as the border and boundary pillars that our fathers and grandfathers protected.”

“We are the guardians of the border.”

His demand is simple.

“The government should arrange our rehabilitation as soon as possible.”

A home must be more than a house

Returning to Khaidi, however, will require more than permission. The survivors say the new settlement needs roads, electricity, drinking water, healthcare, education and security.

“There must be guarantees for health, education and security,” Ghale says. “Infrastructure has to be built first. There must be electricity, drinking water and roads.”

Only then, he says, can they begin again.

“We will go there, work there and build our lives there.”

For Chhiring Deki Tamang, staying in Kathmandu is not an option.

“We do not want to stay in Kathmandu. There is no work for everyone here. What will we do?” she asks.

Their livelihoods were tied to the border.

“The government first needs to open the road. Our old village is Khaidi, and that is where we will go.”

The desire to return is not simply about nostalgia.

It is about work, community and identity.

The people now sleeping on mats inside the monastery want to return to the mountains where their families lived, traded and maintained the border for generations.

‘The border must open’

They are also asking the government to reopen the Rasuwagadhi border point, coordinating with China if necessary. For Tamang, the border is more than a local commercial route.

“Damage to the Rasuwagadhi border point is not just a loss for the people of Rasuwa or Timure. It is a loss for the entire country,” he says.

“The border point must be reopened.”

Before the disaster, goods from Chinese companies could reach Kathmandu through the route in 10 to 12 days, he says.

“If they have to be brought by air now, it could take two or three months. The cost of goods will rise, and the burden on ordinary people will become even heavier.”

The flood has therefore taken away more than buildings. It has disrupted a community’s homes, livelihoods, rituals and connection to the border. At the Mustang Gumba, those losses are still being absorbed.

The prayers continue. The survivors wait for news of the missing.

They count the days left in the 49-day mourning period.

And beyond the grief, they are already talking about roads, houses, schools, water and electricity — the things they will need if they are ever to return.

For now, Timure exists mostly in memory. But for those sheltering in Kathmandu, it is still home. And they intend to go back.

title.rendered: Manaslu climbing season begins with record 466 climbers

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 17

Autumn climbing on Mount Manaslu has begun, with 466 climbers from various countries who obtained permits for the season starting their ascent from the base camp on Tuesday.

A total of 342 men and 124 women from 39 teams have set off from the base camp to climb the 8,163-metre mountain.

According to climber support staff Bis Bahadur Gurung, a Lama performed a traditional puja at the base camp before the climbers began their ascent.

Gurung said the climbers are expected to complete their summit attempts within the next two to three weeks.

The Department of Tourism said the government has collected Rs 212.448 million in revenue from Manaslu climbing permits this season.

Both the number of climbers attempting Manaslu and the revenue generated from climbing permits are the highest recorded so far.

Manaslu, located in Samagaun of Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1 in Gorkha district, was first successfully climbed on May 9, 1956.

Standing at 8,163 metres above sea level, Manaslu is the eighth-highest mountain in the world.

title.rendered: Supreme Court blocks two House rules on constitutional amendments

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

The Supreme Court has issued an interim order preventing the implementation of two provisions of the House of Representatives Regulations 2026 that it found inconsistent with the Constitution.

The order means that a constitutional amendment bill must be approved separately by a two-thirds majority in both the House of Representatives and the National Assembly before the amendment process can move forward.

The House had adopted the Regulations 2026 with provisions governing the procedure for constitutional amendments. The provisions had faced objections from opposition lawmakers, who argued that they undermined Nepal’s bicameral parliamentary system.

Nepali Congress National Assembly parliamentary party leader Kamala Pant and others filed a petition at the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Bench, arguing that certain provisions of the regulations were inconsistent with constitutional provisions governing the two chambers.

What was the dispute?

Article 274 of the Constitution sets out the procedure for constitutional amendments. Article 274(8) requires a constitutional amendment bill to be passed by at least a two-thirds majority of the total number of members currently in office in both houses of the Federal Parliament.

Under the constitutional arrangement, the amendment bill therefore has to secure the required majority separately in the House of Representatives and the National Assembly.

However, Rule 140 of the House Regulations 2083 included provisions on the procedure for constitutional amendment bills.

Rule 140(11) stated that when a constitutional amendment bill returned from the National Assembly with a message received the required two-thirds support based on the total membership of both houses, the Speaker could proceed with certification and send it to the President.

Opposition lawmakers argued that this effectively allowed the votes of the two chambers to be combined, contrary to the constitutional requirement that each house approve a constitutional amendment separately.

What did the Supreme Court order?

A five-member Constitutional Bench headed by Chief Justice Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma and comprising Justices Kumar Regmi, Dr Nahakul Subedi, Binod Sharma and Saranga Subedi ordered that Rule 140(11) and Rule 259 of the House Regulations 2026 not be implemented for now.

Rule 259 stated that, notwithstanding anything contained in prevailing law, the House regulations would apply as federal law and as a special law in matters concerning the House, its committees and its members.

The court’s interim order has placed both provisions in their existing state pending further proceedings.

The Constitutional Bench also considered constitutional provisions concerning Nepal’s bicameral Federal Parliament and the procedures governing the two chambers.

Article 83 provides for a Federal Parliament consisting of two houses, while Article 104 deals with the procedures for conducting the business of each house. Article 111(9) provides for circumstances in which a joint sitting of the Federal Parliament may be held.

The court noted that the constitutional provisions on joint sittings do not envisage consideration of constitutional amendment bills through a joint sitting.

Implications of the order

The Supreme Court’s order prevents the disputed provision from being used to treat the combined strength of the two houses as the basis for approving a constitutional amendment.

As a result, the constitutional requirement for a constitutional amendment bill to obtain a two-thirds majority separately in each chamber remains applicable.

The petitioners had also challenged provisions giving the House regulations the status of federal law, arguing that such a provision could conflict with the constitutional supremacy established under Article 1.

The court has not issued a final ruling on the underlying dispute. Its latest decision is an interim order preventing the two provisions from being implemented while the case proceeds.

title.rendered: Prithvi Highway reopens fully after 18 days as new track built at Krishnabhir

content.rendered:
Dhading, September 17

Two-way traffic has resumed along the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir in Dhading after authorities opened a new track, bringing relief to motorists after an 18-day disruption.

The highway had been blocked since August 30 after the Trishuli River flood washed away a section of the road at Krishnabhir. The flooding occurred four days after the devastating Bhotekoshi floods.

Authorities had tested the newly constructed track on September 13 by allowing several heavy vehicles to pass through. Work continued afterwards to complete and strengthen the track.

The District Administration Office, Dhading, had decided on Wednesday to fully reopen the highway from 6am Thursday.

Chief District Officer of Dhading Laxmi Pandey said the decision was taken after concerned agencies worked continuously to construct a new track at the damaged section.

According to the District Police Office, vehicles have been operating along the Prithvi Highway in both directions since early Thursday morning.

However, the administration has warned that several sections of the highway remain vulnerable to road subsidence, landslides and falling rocks and soil.

Authorities have urged drivers and passengers to exercise caution while travelling along the highway.

The reopening of the Prithvi Highway is expected to make travel to and from Kathmandu easier.

While the highway remained blocked, large and small vehicles travelling along the route had been using alternative roads to enter and leave the federal capital.

title.rendered: A Nepali’s journey into the microscopic world of computer chips

content.rendered:
When Basu Aryal was growing up in Jyamire, Makwanpur, advanced technology was still a distant idea.

The East-West Highway had brought some convenience to the settlement, but electricity and technology were developing slowly. For a boy who had grown up in a farming family, education became the route to a very different future.

Today, Aryal has a PhD in analytical chemistry from Brigham Young University in the United States and has worked in advanced semiconductor and processor technology.

His journey began in the village.

Aryal completed Grade 4 at Vyas Secondary School in Pakani. In 1993, his family moved to Jyamire in Manahari-9, Makwanpur, after floods displaced many people in Pakani.

He continued his education at Mahendrakiran Secondary School in Manahari and completed his SLC in 1999.

He had been an exceptional student from an early age.

Throughout school, Aryal regularly stood first in his class. He scored full marks in mathematics examinations and more than 90 in other subjects, according to retired Mahendrakiran Secondary School teacher Matrika Subedi.

He scored 86 percent in his SLC examination.

At the time, he was the only student in the district to score 86 percent from a community school. He had also stood first in the district in the Grade 8 examination.

After he topped the district, Kathmandu-based Siddhartha Vanasthali came to Mahendra Secondary School in Bhimphedi to honour him.

“At that time, Siddhartha Vanasthali used to award students who topped the district. I was called to Bhimphedi and honoured with an award,” Aryal recalls.

Inspired by his brothers

Basu Aryal’s parents, Badri Aryal and Bishnumaya Aryal, had only basic literacy. They supported their children’s education through farming.

The youngest of six brothers, Aryal also has a sister.

He says his older brothers helped him understand the importance of education from an early age.

His brothers Rajkumar and Jayaram Aryal were his main sources of inspiration. While Basu was still in school, both were studying in Kathmandu.

“Basu was an exceptional student from a very young age,” Jayaram says. “I have never heard of him scoring less than 90 in any subject. Some teachers even used to say that they had to deduct marks because they could not give him full marks.”

From a village to Kathmandu

After completing his SLC, Aryal moved to Kathmandu to study science at Tri-Chandra College. The transition was not easy. Having studied at a government school, he initially struggled with English-medium education.

“When I first came to Kathmandu to study, it was a little difficult for me. Since I had studied at a government school, studying in English was initially a problem,” he says.

But he worked hard and gradually overcame the language barrier.

“I worked very hard and was able to do well. Only the best students from across the country come here to study. Even then, I used to rank second or third in examinations while studying science,” he says.

Aryal completed his ISc from Tri-Chandra and then earned a BSc from Amrit Science Campus. He went on to complete an MSc in Chemistry from the Central Department of Chemistry at Tribhuvan University in 2009, scoring 82 percent.

Studying in Kathmandu itself was a challenge. He lived in a rented room and completed his MSc without a scholarship. After completing his studies, Aryal taught chemistry at Bagmati Modern College in Sukedhara until 2012. He then returned to Hetauda, where he taught at Hetauda School of Management until 2016. That year, he received an opportunity to pursue a PhD in the United States on a full scholarship. In August 2016, he left Nepal.

From chemistry to chips

His move to the US marked the beginning of a new chapter — one that would eventually take him into the world of processors and semiconductor technology.

Basu Aryal pursued a PhD in analytical chemistry at Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah. He completed his doctorate in 2021.

During his time at the university, he worked on research projects in professors’ laboratories and earned $2,200 a month.

Through a nanofabrication research project, he worked on developing new materials and objects using substances invisible to the naked eye.

From July 2021 to June 2024, he worked as a researcher in the Department of Chemistry at the University of Texas at Austin.

He then joined Intel Corporation in Hillsboro, Oregon, as a process engineer.

Intel is a major semiconductor technology company producing processors that power computers, laptops, mobile devices and advanced data centres. The company also works in areas including artificial intelligence, 5G networks, cloud computing and advanced chip manufacturing.

For Aryal, the transition from a rural school in Makwanpur to one of the world’s most advanced technology industries represents a remarkable change in his professional journey.

Working on smaller, more advanced processors

At Intel, Basu Aryal became involved in work related to the development of an 18A microprocessor, featuring 1.8-nanometre transistors.

He says smaller processors are generally associated with more advanced technology and can offer high performance.

“The smaller the processor, the more advanced the technology is considered to be. We work on its research every day,” he says.

He says continuous research and testing are carried out to make the microscopic technologies used in chip manufacturing more stable, faster and higher quality.

“Being able to work in processor production at a company like Intel is a matter of pride,” Aryal says. “I hope the country can also learn something from this.”

Intel’s Hillsboro facility in Oregon is one of the company’s locations involved in research and development of new processor technologies.

“The processors developed here are sent elsewhere for production. Production also takes place at other facilities of the company,” Aryal says.

Thinking about Nepal

Basu Aryal’s work in the semiconductor industry has also made him think about how his skills could eventually be useful in Nepal.

His annual salary at Intel was $131,000, equivalent to around Rs 20 million in Nepali currency. But he says his ambitions extend beyond personal financial success.

“We are always thinking about how these skills can be used in Nepal,” he says.

He does not believe large-scale chip manufacturing can be established in Nepal immediately. However, he says the country can begin by investing in research and basic technologies.

“Large-scale chip manufacturing industries are not immediately possible in Nepal. But research and the development of foundational technologies can be started,” he says.

Aryal says small-scale research efforts are already taking place at Tribhuvan University and Kathmandu University, but larger and long-term investment is needed.

Intel also has operations in countries such as Malaysia. Nepal, however, is not currently in a position to manufacture processors, he says, mainly because of the enormous investment required.

“I want my country to benefit. For that, a good team is necessary. We do have the idea of working in Nepal,” he says.

A journey beyond the village

Aryal’s journey began in a rural community where technology was still a distant concept.

He went from a government school in Makwanpur, where he regularly topped his class, to Kathmandu, where he had to overcome the challenge of studying in English. From there, he pursued postgraduate studies and research in the United States before entering the highly specialised world of semiconductor technology.

Today, his work is connected to the development of processors that serve as the “brains” of computers, mobile devices and other digital technologies used by millions of people around the world.

For his brother Jayaram, Aryal’s achievement carries significance beyond the family.

“A young man like him presenting his skills at the global level while living abroad is not only a personal achievement but also a way of enhancing the identity of the country,” he says.

title.rendered: Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle leaves for three-day India visit

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 17

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle left for India on Thursday morning for a three-day visit.

During the first day of his visit, Wagle is scheduled to meet his Indian counterpart Nirmala Sitharaman at 5pm on Thursday.

On Friday, the second day of his visit, Wagle will participate in a high-level diplomatic dialogue hosted by former Indian foreign secretary Shyam Saran at 9am.

He is scheduled to meet Indian Foreign Minister Dr S Jaishankar at 5pm the same day. Wagle will also attend a meeting hosted by Javed Ashraf, president of the Trade Promotion Organisation of India, at 7:30pm.

On the final day of his visit, Wagle will be the keynote speaker at a conference with prominent Indian industrialists organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry at 9:30am on Saturday.

He will then participate in an academic discussion on development economics organised by the Delhi School of Economics at 11:30am before returning to Nepal at 4pm.

Wagle is accompanied by Amrit Lamsal, joint secretary at the Ministry of Finance; Gehendra Rajbhandari, joint secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Dr Surendra Thapa, deputy chief of mission at the Nepali Embassy in New Delhi; and Economics Minister Taranath Adhikari, among others.

According to Wagle’s secretariat, the visit aims to strengthen cooperation between Nepal and India on various economic, political and diplomatic issues, including post-disaster reconstruction.

title.rendered: Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel will not travel to Japan for Asian Games

content.rendered:
Kathmandu: Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel will not travel to Japan to attend the 20th Asian Games, his secretariat has confirmed.

Pokharel had initially been listed as an official accompanying the Nepali delegation to the Asian Games. However, he has decided not to travel amid criticism over the planned visit and a heavy workload following the recent disasters.

“Minister Pokharel had said he would go if he could manage the time. But there is a heavy workload because of the disaster. The minister will no longer travel to Japan,” a member of his secretariat told Onlinekhabar.

National Sports Council (NSC) Member Secretary Ramcharitra Mehta has also decided not to travel to Japan for the Asian Games.

Mehta said preparations for the 10th National Games were the main reason behind his decision.

“If I go to Japan, it means postponing the 10th National Games. The National Games cannot move forward if I stay in Japan for 15 to 20 days without being present as member secretary,” Mehta said.

He said the Asian Games would go ahead even without his presence, but the absence could affect preparations for the National Games.

“That is why I have decided not to go to the Asian Games. The Games will take place even if I do not go, but the 10th National Games may not be held on time,” he said.

title.rendered: NOC takes action against fuel station, three oil tankers over alleged diesel theft

content.rendered:
Rupandehi, September 16

Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) has taken action against a fuel station, three oil tankers and their drivers and helpers after diesel was allegedly stolen from tankers before they reached the corporation’s Bhalbari depot in Rupandehi.

The incident came to light after police caught people allegedly extracting diesel from tankers inside the premises of Saraf Oil Stores in Bhairahawa.

The tankers were carrying diesel from NOC’s Madhesh Provincial Office in Amlekhgunj to its Lumbini Provincial Office in Bhalbari.

NOC has fined Saraf Oil Stores Rs 100,000 and suspended its sales, distribution and supply operations for six months under Regulations 29 and 33 of the Sellers Regulation 2018, as amended, for unauthorised purchase and sale of fuel.

The corporation has also suspended the three tankers involved — Lu 2 Kha 1544, Lu 1 Kha 6504 and Lu 1 Kha 66190 — for three months under Regulations 17 and 17(Gha) of the Transportation Regulation 2073.

The drivers and helpers of the three oil tankers have been permanently barred from entering any NOC depot or office. They have also been prohibited from driving tankers operating under NOC contracts.

According to NOC, the three oil tankers — Lu 1 Kha 6504 operated by Poudel Transport, Lu 2 Kha 1544 operated by BNS Transport Service and Lu 1 Kha 66190 operated by Trimurti Transport Pvt Ltd — entered the compound of Saraf Oil Stores before reaching Bhalbari and began extracting diesel.

A team from the Lumbini Province Police caught Lu 1 Kha 6504 and Lu 2 Kha 1544 while the alleged theft was taking place. NOC said the tankers’ mechanical security locking systems had been tampered with using a vehicle jack.

The third oil tanker, Lu 1 Kha 66190, was taken under control after it had already left the premises after allegedly extracting diesel.

Following the incident, police informed NOC, and a joint team of corporation officials and police inspected the fuel station.

The inspection found the manhole covers of all three oil tankers open, with around 30 litres of diesel from each tanker allegedly removed and stored in blue drums, according to NOC.

Saraf Oil Stores was subsequently sealed in the presence of police and NOC officials.

NOC has also filed a complaint with the District Police Office, Rupandehi, against the three oil tankers, their drivers and helpers, and the fuel station operator for further investigation and legal action.

NOC said it had previously received complaints of petroleum products being stolen through alleged collusion between tanker operators and petrol station owners.

Local residents have also alleged that the fuel station had constructed a gate designed to block tankers inside its premises and that fuel theft had been taking place there regularly.

NOC has a system of special seals and locking mechanisms on tankers transporting petroleum products to prevent theft and unauthorised sales during transportation. The seals can only be opened at designated loading and unloading points.

Tankers loaded at Amlekhgunj are required to reach the Bhalbari depot, where the quality and quantity of the fuel are checked before it is supplied to the concerned petrol stations.

Previous fuel theft case

Rupandehi has previously seen cases involving alleged theft and black-market trading of petroleum products.

In 2014, a case was filed against 18 people, including then-regional chief of NOC’s Bhalbari depot Nagendra Kumar Kurmi, over alleged fuel theft and black-market trading in Padasari and Madhawaliya.

Police had arrested Kurmi, transport operators, drivers and helpers after allegedly catching them stealing fuel from oil tankers on April 16, 2014.

They were accused of stealing and storing fuel in underground pits while transporting it from India’s Betalpur depot to NOC’s then-Western Regional Depot.

However, in 2016, District Judge Muraribabu Shrestha acquitted all the defendants, citing insufficient evidence.

NOC had also investigated 19 oil tankers operated by eight owners after finding alleged organised fuel theft and diversion involving tankers operating under its Bhalbari office. Those involved were also acquitted in the related customs and fuel leakage cases.

title.rendered: Nepal to host Bangladesh for historic three-match T20I series in March 2027

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Nepal will host Bangladesh for a three-match T20 International series in Kirtipur in March 2027 as part of a joint initiative by the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) and the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB).

According to a statement issued by CAN, the three matches will be played on March 26, 28 and 30, 2027.

The series will be historic for Nepal as it will be the first time a Test-playing nation visits the country to play a bilateral series. It will also be the biggest bilateral series hosted by Nepal to date.

The series will be dedicated to the memory of those who lost their lives in the devastating floods that recently hit Nepal. CAN and BCB said the matches will pay tribute to the deceased while expressing solidarity with bereaved families and communities affected by the disaster.

The two cricket boards described cricket as an important means of bringing the people of the two countries closer and said the series would carry a special message of friendship, humanitarian solidarity and cooperation.

The partnership between CAN and BCB will extend beyond the T20I series.

BCB has committed to supporting Nepal’s women’s cricket, age-group cricket and capacity-building programmes, according to CAN.

The two boards will also encourage future tours by the Nepal A team and bilateral A-team series.

CAN and BCB said they were committed to using cricket to convey a message of unity, empathy and solidarity between the two neighbouring countries during a difficult period, while strengthening long-term cooperation for the development of Nepali cricket.

title.rendered: Japanese ambassador meets PM Balendra Shah, pledges support for post-disaster reconstruction

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Japanese Ambassador to Nepal Maeda Toru held a courtesy meeting with Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers in Singha Durbar on Wednesday.

During the meeting, Prime Minister Shah expressed gratitude to the Japanese government for its goodwill, support and solidarity with the Nepal government and citizens affected by the recent floods.

Ambassador Maeda expressed condolences over the loss and suffering caused by the disaster and pledged that Japan would support Nepal in post-disaster recovery and reconstruction efforts.

The two sides also discussed various aspects of Nepal-Japan relations and ongoing cooperation between the two countries.

The meeting comes as Nepal continues recovery and rescue efforts following the recent floods and landslides that caused widespread damage and loss of life.

title.rendered: 364 bodies recovered in Chitwan after Bhotekoshi floods, 14 identified

content.rendered:
Chitwan, September 16

A total of 364 bodies have been recovered in Chitwan following the floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, with 14 of them identified so far.

DNA samples have been collected from 81 relatives of people who remain missing to assist in the identification process.

According to Rameshwar Paudel, superintendent of police at the District Police Office, Chitwan, most of the bodies recovered in the district were in a condition that made visual identification difficult.

He said the bodies were therefore managed through DNA testing and the required legal procedures.

The bodies that have been identified have been handed over to their families after completing the necessary legal formalities, Paudel said.

Of the 364 bodies recovered, 349 unidentified bodies have already been safely managed, according to police.

Only one body remains to be managed, while DNA samples from all the bodies that have been managed have been preserved for future identification.

Police have also prioritised collecting DNA samples from relatives of missing people to help establish their identities.

The collected samples have been sent to a forensic laboratory for testing.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

All-Party mechanism to be formed for post-disaster response

An all-party mechanism will be formed to address issues arising from the disaster caused by the Bhotekoshi River floods in Rasuwa. An all-party meeting held on Wednesday discussed forming the mechanism within the next seven days.

Prithvi Highway set to reopen after 18 days

Two-way traffic is set to resume on the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir from 6 am Thursday. Transport operators, who have incurred losses running into tens of millions of rupees after regular services along the major highway connecting the capital were disrupted for two and a half weeks, have expressed optimism following preparations to reopen the road after repairs.

Two bodies found inside Chilime Hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa

Two bodies have been found inside a tunnel of the Chilime Hydropower Project in Rasuwa during an ongoing search and rescue operation. Rasuwa Chief District Officer Kamal Prasad Pandey said the two bodies were found during the search operation around half an hour before the latest update.

9 banks and financial institutions offer Fonepay virtual credit cards

The number of users of virtual credit cards offered through Fonepay’s network has reached 50,000, reflecting the growing use of digital technology for accessing and making credit-based payments in Nepal. The virtual credit card service, launched two years ago, is currently available through nine banks and financial institutions connected to Fonepay’s network. The service allows customers to obtain a credit limit through their mobile banking applications and make payments by scanning QR codes, eliminating the need for a physical card or point-of-sale (POS) machine.

MrBeast joins global fundraising effort to help Nepal

World-famous content creator Jimmy Donaldson, known as MrBeast, has launched a fundraising campaign for those affected by the Bhotekoshi flood in Nepal. The American YouTuber, entrepreneur and philanthropist said via an Instagram story that he and his team are raising millions of dollars in relief funds for Nepal’s disaster victims, and called on people around the world to join the effort.

Digital Parliament launched

The Federal Parliament Secretariat has launched a new Digital Parliament platform aimed at making parliamentary information, services, records and activities more organised, accessible, effective and transparent.

title.rendered: Health ministry proposes major changes to safe motherhood law

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The Ministry of Health and Food Safety has begun the process of amending five laws related to the health sector, including the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2018.

The ministry has sent draft amendments to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for the next stage of the legal process.

Among the proposed changes is an increase in paid maternity leave from the current 98 days to at least six months.

The draft amendment to the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act also proposes up to 42 days of paid leave for fathers to care for their partners and newborn children.

The proposed changes would also require health institutions providing maternity services to ensure the availability of skilled health workers or trained birth attendants.

The draft includes provisions aimed at ensuring respectful maternity care and preventing physical and psychological violence against pregnant and postpartum women.

According to the secretariat of Health and Food Safety Minister Nisha Mehta, the amendment process seeks to move away from the idea that motherhood is solely a woman’s responsibility and ensure greater participation by fathers in parenting.

“Giving birth is a natural process associated with mothers. But raising a child is not solely the mother’s responsibility,” the ministry said.

It said the proposed provisions are intended to create an environment in which both parents can spend adequate time with their newborn and family during the critical period following childbirth.

The ministry said the amendments are being pursued to make legal provisions on safe motherhood more responsive to changing family structures, lifestyles and the health needs of mothers and newborns.

The proposed amendments will undergo further legal review before being taken forward through the legislative process.

  • Kshetra Prasad Kattel, Ram Prasad Bhattarai and Baburam Dahal, gazetted first-class officers of the Nepal Judicial Service, Judicial Group, have been promoted to the gazetted special class.
  • The Cabinet decided to issue an order allowing a Saudi Arabian lawyer to be granted power of attorney to pursue insurance and compensation claims on behalf of Nepali citizens who have died or been injured in Saudi Arabia.
  • The Revolving Relief Fund Operation Procedure, 2026 was approved.
  • Joint Secretary Kaliprasad Parajuli of the Nepal Administration Service was promoted to the post of Secretary in the gazetted special class.

Legal gap leaves Rasuwa flood families unable to register deaths of missing relatives

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Families who have lost hope of finding relatives missing after the Rasuwa floods have begun performing last rites by making symbolic bodies out of kusha grass, following Hindu religious traditions.

They are now approaching ward offices to seek official verification of their missing relatives or register their deaths.

However, local authorities have been unable to certify the deaths of people whose bodies have not been recovered or identified, citing a legal gap in the existing provisions.

Ward offices have asked the government to make a policy decision to address the issue and establish an alternative mechanism for registering such deaths.

The Rasuwa District Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committee decided last week to write to the Ministry of Home Affairs, saying the lack of clear legal provisions had created difficulties in dealing with people who went missing in the floods.

The committee said the existing process for registering deaths and other vital events involving people who remain missing is cumbersome, creating problems with insurance claims and official confirmation of deaths.

It requested the government to establish an alternative fast-track mechanism for registering such cases.

Rasuwa Assistant Chief District Officer Dipesh Rijal said the Home Ministry had been alerted after local governments across the district faced uncertainty over how to deal with the missing persons.

“Ward offices are currently finding it difficult to register deaths. Families of missing people have performed the last rites after giving up hope of finding them. Some have now come to register their deaths. But what should be recorded as the cause of death? How can we register the death of someone who remains missing?” said Jairam Upreti, chief administrative officer of Uttargaya Rural Municipality in Rasuwa.

“The families have completed the religious rituals even though the bodies have not been identified. But legally, we are in a difficult situation.”

Upreti said the issue had been raised repeatedly in the district disaster management committee.

“Except in cases where the body has been recovered and identified, ward offices are currently in no position to issue any documents for other missing persons,” he said.

Uncertainty extends beyond Rasuwa and Nuwakot

Nuwakot Chief District Officer Shambhu Prasad Regmi said uncertainty over how to deal with missing people was not limited to Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

According to him, another challenge involves verifying people from other districts who went missing in the floods.

“Families whose members have gone missing can only say that their relatives are missing. Until a body is found, there is always hope,” Regmi said.

“They also do not want to declare that their loved one is dead. There has been discussion about providing missing people with facilities similar to those available to deceased persons. The procedure for that also needs to be clarified.”

Regmi said there was no clear provision on whose information should be considered official when an entire family has gone missing or how such information should be recorded.

He said the problem could become wider because residents of more than half of Nepal’s 77 districts were affected by the floods, creating additional difficulties in managing documents for people who went missing away from their home districts.

What does the law say?

Section 40 of the National Civil Code Act, 2017 contains provisions concerning the declaration of death of missing persons.

Under the provision, a person may generally be presumed dead if they have been missing continuously for 12 years or if there has been no evidence of their being alive for 12 years.

The provision was introduced in the context of Nepal’s decade-long conflict, during which many people disappeared and their whereabouts remained unknown.

The law also contains alternative provisions for declaring a person dead when they have gone missing or their body cannot be recovered.

Section 40(4) allows a concerned person to apply to a court for a judicial declaration of death if an individual has gone missing without information or is believed to have died in a disaster or accident.

The court may issue an order declaring the person dead after examining evidence regarding the date, place, cause and basis of the disappearance or presumed death.

However, officials at the district administration offices in Rasuwa and Nuwakot say requiring families affected by the floods to go through a judicial process would be particularly painful.

They argue that the government should instead reach affected families and facilitate the registration process, rather than requiring grieving relatives to go through a legal procedure to have their loved ones declared dead.

Families may have to submit applications detailing the disappearance, establish the identity of the missing person, and collect documents related to requests made to government agencies to search for their relatives.

Local representatives in the flood-affected areas say the process could become even more burdensome because a judicial declaration of death may require witnesses and additional evidence.

Precedents from past disasters

Nepal faced a similar situation following the 2015 earthquake, when around 198 people went missing in landslides in the hills and avalanches in the mountainous areas.

However, officials say the situation was less complicated because houses had collapsed, bodies generally remained at the incident sites and identification was comparatively easier.

A similar case occurred during the Jure landslide in Sindhupalchok on August 2, 2014, when three settlements were buried after being swept into the river.

Of the 145 people reported missing, the bodies of only 33 were eventually recovered. The government later declared the remaining missing people dead.

A senior Home Ministry official said the government may need to make a decision to resolve the current legal difficulties.

“Even then, when there was no clear legal basis, the government declared the missing people dead. There are clearer grounds now compared to that time,” the official said. “The federal government will probably have to make a decision to resolve these difficulties.”

Nepal suffered a straight-sets defeat to Japan in their opening match of the women’s volleyball competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Wednesday.

Nepal lost 25–8, 25–12 and 25–11 against Japan, who are ranked sixth in the FIVB women’s world rankings and are the top-ranked team in Asia.

Japan dominated the match from the outset, leaving Nepal with little opportunity to challenge the hosts.

Nepal will play their second group-stage match against Indonesia on Thursday.

A victory against Indonesia would keep Nepal’s hopes of reaching the quarter-finals alive, while a defeat would send them into the classification matches.

In the Asian rankings, Indonesia are ninth while Nepal are 11th.

Nepal are competing in Group A alongside Japan and Indonesia. The women’s volleyball team is making its second consecutive appearance at the Asian Games.

title.rendered: Recruitment agencies seek institutional labour access to 186 countries

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies has urged the government to add new labour destination countries for Nepali workers and allow institutional recruitment in more countries.

The association submitted a memorandum to Deepak Kafle, secretary at the Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment, noting that Nepali workers have reached as many as 186 countries through individual arrangements, while the government has officially opened only 111 countries for institutional foreign employment.

Association General Secretary Hira Bahadur Dangi “Hari” said the government should identify promising and emerging labour markets among the countries where Nepalis are already working individually and establish mechanisms for sending workers there through recruitment agencies.

The association also urged the ministry to take diplomatic initiatives through Nepali missions to facilitate the verification of demand letters received from Sabah and Sarawak in eastern Malaysia.

It said the government should facilitate policy measures to explore new destinations and expand labour markets rather than relying solely on traditional destinations.

The association said policy reforms were underway to simplify procedures, including demand-letter verification, and stressed the need for active participation by recruitment agencies in promoting new labour markets.

It said expanding labour destinations would create additional employment opportunities for Nepali workers.

In recent years, Nepalis have increasingly sought employment in various European countries. However, institutional recruitment to those countries remains restricted.

Recruitment agencies have repeatedly called for demand-letter verification to allow institutional recruitment to European destinations, but the government has yet to facilitate the process.
