title.rendered: A beat, a bedroom and a dream that went global

content.rendered:
In 2025, Curtis Waters returned to Nepal with his family and travelled to the village in Lamjung where his mother was born. Standing there, he looked at the fields and forests where his mother had once cut grass. For a moment, the distance between that quiet Nepali village and the life he now leads in North Carolina seemed enormous. But for Waters, those two worlds are connected.

His journey has taken him from Kathmandu to India, Germany, Canada and finally the United States, where he has built an international career in hip-hop, pop and indie pop.

Born Abhinav Bastakoti in Kathmandu in 1999, he grew up moving between countries as his parents pursued their education and careers. Today, millions know him as Curtis Waters.

But before the name, the music and the global recognition, there was a boy who loved comics, drew cartoons and quietly made music late at night while his parents hoped he would concentrate on his studies.

A childhood across countries

Curtis Waters began his early education at Modern Indian School in Chobhar, Kathmandu. His childhood, however, was not confined to Nepal.

He moved with his parents to India and Germany, and when he was 10, the family moved to Calgary, Canada.

As a child, he loved reading comics and storybooks and spent time drawing cartoons.

Music entered his life almost by accident.

At 14, he returned to Nepal for three months for his bratabandha ceremony. Before coming, he had downloaded FL Studio onto his laptop. He began experimenting with beats. What started as curiosity soon became an obsession.

By the time he was studying at Winston Churchill High School in Calgary, making music and doing graphic design had become ways for him to deal with the loneliness and frustration that often came with adolescence.

His parents, like many immigrant parents, wanted to make sure their son received a good education.

His mother enrolled him in Kumon to strengthen his mathematics and academic skills.

But Curtis Waters was increasingly drawn towards music.

Mathematical formulas and piles of homework began to feel like another burden. Even the Kumon logo started reminding him of the frustrated boy he felt he was becoming. So he began making music secretly, often late into the night. He knew his parents were not particularly happy about it.

Still, he continued studying while trying to prove that his passion for music could become something more.

The competition that changed his confidence

Then he discovered that a beat battle was being held in Calgary. He was only 15 and approaching his 16th birthday. Participants had to be at least 18 to enter. That did not stop him.

He spent two or three days putting his studies aside to prepare for the competition and eventually managed to get into the venue through the back door.

He competed. And he kept winning. He reached the final, where he faced an established musician around his father’s age. He finished second. That was the day when he turned 16.

He went home carrying awards, gifts and two scholarships for music training. For perhaps the first time, his parents could see just how much the music meant to their son.

Seeing his face light up after the competition, they began to understand something themselves. Perhaps this was not simply a distraction from his studies. Perhaps music and creativity were what he was meant to pursue.

Another move, another challenge

In 2017, the family moved again, this time to North Carolina in the United States. Curtis Waters completed the rest of his high school education there. The transition was not easy.

Some subjects from his Canadian schooling did not align perfectly with the American curriculum. Friends he had grown up with in Canada were now far away. Once again, music became an outlet.

That same year, the Global Beat Battle was held in Toronto.

With his family’s support, he travelled from the United States to compete. He made it through a field of 65 contestants from around the world and reached the final eight.

The result gave him something he needed more than a trophy. Confidence.

How Abhinav Bastakoti became Curtis Waters

Around this time, Curtis Waters was posting his rap music online. But he felt that the name Abhinav Bastakoti did not quite fit the character he was creating through his music. He wanted another identity.

He took “Curtis” from Ian Curtis, the lead singer and songwriter of Joy Division, an artist he admired.

“Waters” came from another artist he liked — Frank Ocean.

And Curtis Waters was born.

At first, the name was almost a joke. Over time, however, it became something much more meaningful.

“For me, Abhinav is a person, while Curtis Waters is a character,” he says.

He began disappearing into that character when he made music. Eventually, the character became the artist the world came to know.

When the pandemic opened a door

By the time he finished high school, even his parents had begun to see his future differently. They no longer insisted that he pursue a conventional career. They encouraged him to study music.

Curtis Waters applied to the music programme at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and went for an interview carrying some of his own compositions. The professors recognised his ability and passion. But instead of simply offering him a place, they gave him something else — advice.

They told him that if he studied there, he would have to follow formal and theoretical music education. He might eventually become a professor like them. But if he followed his passion and created freely, they believed the world might one day know his name.

They even told him they would use his music as material to teach other students. The advice made both Curtis Waters and his parents reconsider his path.

He eventually enrolled at UNC Greensboro, living in a dormitory and developing his music alongside his studies. Then the COVID-19 pandemic arrived. The world shut down.

Concerts stopped. Music venues closed. Artists were left searching for new ways to reach audiences. For Waters, the internet became that stage.

Fifteen seconds that changed everything

In early April 2020, he uploaded a 15-second clip of his hip-hop/pop song Stunnin’ to TikTok. The video featured him dancing with his 16-year-old brother, Albert.

The caption was deliberately playful.

He said he would keep posting himself dancing to the song every day until it went viral.

It did not take long.

Within weeks, Stunnin’ exploded.

Millions of people began making videos using the song, while tens of millions watched them.

On YouTube, the song received more than two million views within a month.

The track reached No. 3 on Rolling Stone’s Breakthrough 25 chart. By July 2020, it had accumulated more than 35 million Spotify streams. Major record labels began approaching him. But Waters chose not to sign with a record label. He wanted to remain an independent artist.

He did, however, sign a licensing deal with BMG, while Chris Anokute — who had managed artists including Katy Perry and Rihanna early in their careers — became his manager.

The attention grew rapidly.

In June 2020, Rolling Stone published a detailed article about his breakthrough, describing the TikTok success of Stunnin’ as a challenge for major record labels.

A month later, The Guardian featured him in a lengthy article under the headline describing him as the “TikTok king” Curtis Waters and highlighting his sudden arrival in the music industry.

The teenager making music secretly at night was suddenly being interviewed by international media.

Beyond Stunnin’

The success of Stunnin’ opened doors around the world.

The song eventually passed one billion streams and earned certification from the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), including platinum certifications in Canada, Australia and Brazil and gold certifications in the United States, New Zealand, Mexico and India.

In 2021, Stunnin’ was also nominated for three Juno Award categories, including Fan Choice and Breakthrough Artist of the Year.

The song was used commercially by brands and organisations including Mercedes-Benz, Meta, the NBA, the Grammys and White Claw.

Curtis Waters began performing at festivals and events across North America.

He appeared at South by Southwest in Texas, Raleighwood in North Carolina, a music showcase in Colorado and the Northern Lights festival in Edmonton.

He has also performed solo in more than 15 major cities across the United States and Canada.

But he did not allow the success of one song to define his entire career.

Finding his own voice

After Stunnin’, Waters released System, a high-energy hip-hop track that reflected on the emotional ups and downs that followed his sudden fame.

In October 2020, he released his first album, Pity Party.

The album contained 12 songs, including Stunnin’ and System, many of which he had created while living in the UNC Greensboro dormitory.

His second album, Bad Son, followed in 2023.

It contained 14 tracks and explored his experiences and identity in greater depth.

Waters says he had been thinking about the album for around a decade and spent years putting it together.

“For me, it is not just music,” he says. “It is the whole life story of the son of an immigrant family — someone struggling with his identity and family responsibilities.”

The album also draws on his childhood, emotional experiences and cultural identity.

Now, he is working on the next stage of his musical journey, releasing songs he has been developing since 2023.

He says the new work will reflect what he has learned through his experiences.

For him, music is another form of storytelling.

“This time, my creations will include what I have learned and experienced so far,” he says. “I believe music is another artistic form of storytelling. These songs will essentially carry positive messages about life.”

More than a singer

Curtis Waters does not simply write and perform his songs.

He handles everything from lyrics, music and vocals to recording, mixing and mastering.

He has built a reputation as a DIY artist and is also taking on more of the visual art and creative work behind his music.

He has collaborated with artists from his generation and the generation that followed.

His collaboration with Ali Otto and Kim Petras on SugarCrash! became one of the notable collaborations of his career.

He is also working as executive producer on emerging singer Nafis’s debut album and has taken on the same role for songs by Rema, a South Asian-origin singer based in California.

For Waters, music is not simply entertainment.

It is part of how he exists.

“For me, music is the essence of life, the basis of living,” he says. “The joy of making songs and expressing myself is something I cannot stop, whether I want to or not.”

His music carries his experiences, culture and understanding of the world.

And perhaps that honesty is part of what has allowed listeners to connect with it.

Neither here nor there

Curtis Waters was born in Nepal.

He grew up across several countries. He was shaped by the internet. Today, he makes alternative music for an audience that is largely made up of people from his own generation. That audience crosses borders, ethnicities and communities.

Waters does not want his music to be confined by those labels either.

When he creates, he says he is not thinking of himself primarily as Abhinav, the son of Nepali parents.

He becomes Curtis Waters.

“I listen to the voice of my heart,” he says. “The more you put something inside boundaries, the more artificial the creation becomes.”

For him, authentic art requires freedom from those boundaries.

“The more free you feel from limits and restrictions, and the more you stay away from prejudices and biases, the more authentic your creation can be.”

It is an idea that perhaps explains the distance he has travelled — geographically as well as creatively.

Listening to his own voice

Before he became an internationally recognised musician, Waters had to make a difficult choice.

He grew up in a world where studying hard, getting a job and earning social respect were considered the safest paths to a good life. Choosing music instead meant going against those expectations. It was, in his words, a quiet rebellion. He faced uncertainty, disagreement and doubt. But he kept following his passion.

“The inner happiness you get from following your passion cannot be provided by any material comfort or social status,” he says.

Eventually, the world began to notice. His face appeared on billboards in New York, Toronto and other cities. His songs played on radio stations. Brands used his music in advertisements. International publications wrote about him. The anonymous child of an immigrant family had acquired a global identity.  Yet the lesson he draws from the journey is not simply about fame.

“I’m learning through life, and I put the truths I learn into my songs and music,” he says.

His message to young people who want to create is simple.

Listen to your heart. Trust it. Do not allow the approval or negativity of family and society to determine your worth.

“If we prove ourselves to ourselves, one day our family, relatives and society will believe in us too.”

After speaking with Waters, the influential music publication Complex captured that journey in the title of its own article about him: “Nobody believed in Curtis until everybody did.”

And perhaps that sentence says as much about Abhinav Bastakoti’s journey as any award, chart position or billion-stream milestone.

Before the world knew Curtis Waters, there was simply a young boy making music late at night — trying to find his own voice.

title.rendered: 7,000 broiler chicks seized near Morang border

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, September 16

The Armed Police Force has seized 7,000 broiler chicks from a border area in Sunbarshi Municipality-8 of Morang district.

A team deployed from the Border Outpost Sikti of the Armed Police Force recovered the chicks at around 2:50 am Wednesday while they were being transported in 14 loads.

The group carrying the chicks fled after spotting the security personnel while approaching through a path in a paddy field.

The chicks are believed to have been smuggled into Nepal through an unauthorised route by taking advantage of the open border. They are estimated to be worth around Rs 700,000.

SP Gehendra Bahadur Bhandari, chief of the Armed Police Force in Morang, said the team recovered 7,000 broiler chicks packed in 140 cartons in an abandoned condition.

Nepali farmers and poultry businesses have been facing problems due to the illegal entry of chicks and poultry products through the border areas.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

United School has inaugurated two new KUMON Labs equipped with 100 tablets, as part of its push toward technology-enabled mathematics education.

KUMON, a globally recognised mathematics learning programme, currently supports close to 700 students from grades 2 to 4 at the school.

The labs were inaugurated on Tuesday in the presence of United School Founder Director Nara Hang Rai, Principal Manoj Bishwokarma, KUMON Japan representative Yusuke Yoshiwaka, and Bikash Lama, CEO of IGC Business Holding, KUMON’s official partner in Nepal, along with school staff, teachers and students.

The two labs pair KUMON’s established teaching methodology with digital tools, aiming to make math learning more interactive while letting students progress individually at their own pace. The school says the setup is meant to build not just mathematical skills but also concentration, accuracy, confidence and independent learning habits.

title.rendered: Main accused in girl’s 19-day captivity and rape case sent to prison

content.rendered:
Janakpur, September 16

Tahir Rain, the main accused in a case involving the alleged abduction, 19-day captivity and rape of a minor in two hotels in Janakpur, has been sent to prison pending trial.

The Dhanusha District Court on September 11 ordered 23-year-old Rain to be remanded in custody for trial, according to the District Police Office, Dhanusha.

Rain had fled to Qatar after the incident and was arrested through Interpol. He was brought back to Nepal on August 10.

Meanwhile, Yakub Kawari, ward chair of Dhanauji Rural Municipality-5, who is accused of pressuring the survivor’s family to settle the case for Rs 2 million, has been released on Rs 100,000 bail.

The Dhanusha District Court ordered his release on bail on Monday. Police said Kawari was released after depositing the amount.

Kawari was arrested by Dhanusha police last Friday based on the survivor’s statement.

Two cases filed in Dhanusha District Court

The case concerns a 16-year-old girl from Dhanauji Rural Municipality who was allegedly abducted from her home on July 1, 2025, taken to Janakpur, and held captive in hotels for 19 days, where she was allegedly raped.

Two police officers are also among those accused in the case.

Two separate cases have been filed at the Dhanusha District Court in connection with the incident, involving around a dozen accused, including the two police officers. Most of the accused remain at large.

One case concerns alleged human trafficking, abduction and unlawful confinement, while the other relates to the alleged rape of the girl.

According to the case file, Rain, who ran a shop near the survivor’s home, allegedly abducted her on April 11, 2025, when her mother had gone to the fields, after luring her with a promise of marriage.

She was allegedly brought to Janakpur, where Rain and others are accused of sexually assaulting her and trafficking her between hotels, including allegedly arranging for customers to pay to sexually abuse her. The girl later escaped.

The survivor filed a complaint at the District Police Office, Dhanusha, on May 17, 2025. However, the complaint was allegedly not acted upon in time, allowing Rain to flee abroad.

Second abduction

The survivor was allegedly abducted again on July 1, 2025, at around 4am.

According to her complaint, she had stepped outside her home to tie up goats when three people, including Anjali Mahar, allegedly arrived in a vehicle, blindfolded her with a piece of cloth and abducted her.

She was allegedly held at Hotel CFC in Pidari Chowk, Janakpur, for two days before being taken to Madhesh Province Guest House in Murli Chowk, where she was allegedly confined for another 17 days.

The case file alleges that the accused, including hotel operators, raped the girl and also took money from customers to facilitate her sexual abuse.

The girl has remained in a safe house since the incident due to security concerns and continued pressure surrounding the case.

title.rendered: Expert panel formed to scientifically study Rasuwa Flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The government has formed a seven-member expert committee to scientifically investigate the causes and sequence of events behind the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation formed the committee on Wednesday under the coordination of water policy and governance expert Devesh Belbase.

The committee includes hydrologist Dr Narendra Man Shakya, glaciologist Dr Rijanbhakta Kayastha, remote sensing expert Dr Uttam Babu Shrestha, geologist Dr Megh Raj Dhital, hydropower infrastructure expert Dr Hari Pandit and disaster risk reduction expert Anil Pokharel.

The committee will conduct field studies from the flood’s source area to the downstream river corridor. It will examine the origin and progression of the flood, Himalayan geological and glacial risks, hydrological processes and the possible role of climate change.

The ministry said the flood would be studied as a potential “cascading disaster” involving interconnected geological, glacial, hydrological and other hazards rather than simply as a result of heavy rainfall.

A preliminary study by the Hydrology and Water Resources Research Center found insufficient scientific evidence to verify where the flood originated and how the physical processes spread through the Bhotekoshi-Lhende river system.

The study will be conducted in three phases, covering the event’s chronology and physical damage, immediate and underlying causes, and the extent to which human-induced climate change may have influenced the risks and their intensity. It will also examine measures to strengthen long-term disaster preparedness and hydropower resilience.

title.rendered: Federal government transfers Rs 71.12 billion to provinces and local levels through revenue sharing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The federal government transferred Rs 71.12 billion each to provincial and local governments through revenue sharing in the last fiscal year 2025/26.

According to the annual report of the National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission, the federal government deposited Rs 474.15 billion collected from value-added tax (VAT) and excise duty on domestic production into the Federal Divisible Fund during the fiscal year 2025/26.

Under the revenue-sharing arrangement, 70 percent of the amount remains with the federal government, while 15 percent each is allocated to provincial and local governments.

The commission recommends how much each province and local government should receive based on factors including population and demographic indicators, geographical area, human development index, expenditure needs, revenue collection efforts, infrastructure development and special circumstances.

The commission submitted its annual report to President Ram Chandra Paudel on Wednesday.

Provinces fall short of vehicle tax targets

The report also shows that most provinces failed to meet their targets for vehicle tax collection in the last fiscal year.

Koshi Province had set a target of collecting Rs 3.06 billion in vehicle tax but collected only Rs 2.66 billion, or 86.96 percent of the target.

Madhesh Province had set a target of Rs 5 billion but collected Rs 4.14 billion, or 83.33 percent.

Bagmati Province collected Rs 13.16 billion against a target of Rs 13.75 billion.

Gandaki Province collected Rs 2 billion against a target of Rs 2.30 billion, while Lumbini collected Rs 3.36 billion against a target of Rs 4.83 billion.

Karnali was the only province to exceed its vehicle tax collection target, collecting Rs 275 million against a target of Rs 240 million.

Sudurpaschim collected Rs 726.3 million against a target of Rs 929.4 million.

According to the commission, provincial governments are required to distribute the vehicle tax revenue they collect among local governments within their respective provinces on a monthly basis.

The commission said Madhes and Karnali failed to distribute such revenue regularly during the last fiscal year.

It also found that none of the provinces complied with the requirement to distribute the collected vehicle tax within the same fiscal year and settle the accounts accordingly.

Kathmandu, September 16

The government has reopened registration of public transport vehicles, effective from September 17.

According to the Department of Transport Management, registration has been reopened for now only outside Kathmandu Valley, with priority given to electric public transport vehicles.

Inside Kathmandu Valley, registration has been opened only for school buses and vehicles being registered as replacements for existing public transport vehicles. The department has instructed all provincial governments to register vehicles accordingly.

The government had halted public transport vehicle registration effective from May 21. Department officials have not disclosed why registration was suspended or what prompted the decision to resume it.

Department Director Maniram Bhusal said registration has been reopened only outside Kathmandu Valley to facilitate route and vehicle management within the valley.

The department had already reopened registration of cargo vehicles from August 3. Before that, it had also registered public transport vehicles for which letters of credit had been opened by June 22 and which had already arrived in Nepal.

title.rendered: Two bodies found inside Chilime Hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Two bodies have been found inside a tunnel of the Chilime Hydropower Project in Rasuwa during an ongoing search and rescue operation.

Rasuwa Chief District Officer Kamal Prasad Pandey said the two bodies were found during the search operation around half an hour before the latest update.

He said the tunnel had already undergone a “breakthrough”, allowing search teams to access the section where the bodies were found.

Search and rescue operations have been underway at various hydropower projects in Rasuwa following the devastating floods of August 26.

Authorities have been searching inside tunnels and other structures after receiving information that people may have been trapped inside hydropower project tunnels following the floods.

The identities of the two bodies found inside the Chilime Hydropower tunnel have not yet been confirmed.

title.rendered: All-Party mechanism to be formed for post-disaster response

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

An all-party mechanism will be formed to address issues arising from the disaster caused by the Bhotekoshi River floods in Rasuwa.

An all-party meeting held on Wednesday discussed forming the mechanism within the next seven days.

Rastriya Prajatantra Party lawmaker Gyanendra Shahi said the meeting discussed forming the all-party mechanism within seven days.

“There was discussion about forming an all-party mechanism within the next seven days. There was also discussion about investigating a parliamentary committee,” Shahi told reporters after the meeting.

According to Shahi, the meeting also discussed the possibility of introducing a “sunset law.”

A day after the devastating floods hit Rasuwa, Rastriya Swatantra Party Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane had proposed forming a high-level all-party mechanism for post-disaster rescue, relief and rehabilitation.

Following the devastating floods on August 26, Lamichhane had called an all-party meeting the next day. Top leaders from the Rastriya Swatantra Party, Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, Nepali Communist Party, Shram Sanskriti Party, Rastriya Prajatantra Party, Janata Samajbadi Party and Janamat Party attended the meeting.

At the meeting, Lamichhane proposed forming an all-party, parliamentary or broader multi-stakeholder committee to assist the government from rescue and relief to rehabilitation.

“Let us form an all-party, parliamentary or multi-stakeholder committee from rescue and relief to rehabilitation. This will make it easier for the government to make decisions,” he had said.

Other parties also agreed to Lamichhane’s proposal. The meeting issued a 10-point commitment that included the formation of a high-level all-party mechanism for long-term solutions.

The 10th point of the commitment stated, “We have agreed to form a parliamentary committee to continuously advise, assist and monitor post-disaster reconstruction, climate adaptation, timely reforms to the national disaster policy and the government’s activities.”

The proposed mechanism is expected to work not only during crises but also to build national consensus on disaster preparedness and sustainable development agendas and contribute to policy reforms.

The mechanism is now being formed accordingly. An all-party meeting held on September 1 had also agreed to form the mechanism, but it was not established.

Wednesday’s meeting set a seven-day deadline for its formation.

title.rendered: Prithvi Highway set to reopen after 18 days

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Two-way traffic is set to resume on the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir from 6 am Thursday.

Transport operators, who have incurred losses running into tens of millions of rupees after regular services along the major highway connecting the capital were disrupted for two and a half weeks, have expressed optimism following preparations to reopen the road after repairs.

The Federation of Nepalese National Transport Entrepreneurs has informed its member associations, committees, companies and private limited companies that they can resume their regular services via the Prithvi Highway once the road is reopened.

According to the federation, transport operators have suffered losses worth millions of rupees over the past 18 days due to the highway disruption. The closure has also made it difficult to transport passengers to their destinations on time.

A section of the highway at Krishnabhir collapsed on August 30, causing about 100 metres of the road to cave in. It took 18 days to construct a new track and prepare the route for traffic.

Although transport services were operated through alternative highways during the disruption, large vehicles and long-distance routes were significantly affected.

title.rendered: Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava bids farewell to Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava held a farewell meeting with Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal on Wednesday.

The meeting took place at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Singha Durbar.

During the meeting, Khanal congratulated Srivastava on the successful completion of his tenure and praised his contribution to deepening and broadening Nepal-India relations.

Khanal highlighted progress in energy cooperation, trade, infrastructure and connectivity between Nepal and India, as well as the close people-to-people ties between the two countries.

He also expressed gratitude to the Indian government for its solidarity with Nepal and its prompt support in search, rescue and relief efforts following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River.

Khanal wished Srivastava success in his future assignments and expressed confidence that he would continue to remain a good friend of Nepal.

During the meeting, Srivastava expressed his appreciation for the support and cooperation extended by the Government of Nepal throughout his tenure.

He expressed confidence that relations between Nepal and India would become deeper and more prosperous in the coming days.

title.rendered: Meta chief pushes back against calls to slow AI development

content.rendered:
San Francisco, September 16

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against growing calls to slow or pause artificial intelligence development, arguing that market incentives and legal liability can provide important safeguards against the technology’s risks.

“People won’t want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don’t do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned,” Zuckerberg wrote on X on Tuesday.

In AI development, “alignment” refers to efforts to ensure that an AI system’s goals and behaviour correspond with what humans intend.

The debate intensified in July after OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, disclosed that hundreds of AI agents had escaped their testing environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated a website during testing.

Zuckerberg argued that building trustworthy and reliable systems is becoming increasingly important for AI companies seeking to compete.

“Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind,” he said.

The debate has also expanded into questions over whether AI companies can be trusted to regulate themselves. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are among companies exploring the creation of a joint standards body.

At the same time, prominent technology figures, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have called for AI development to be slowed.

Zuckerberg points to Meta’s AI rollout

Zuckerberg said legal liability would ultimately encourage AI companies to take responsibility for the risks associated with their products.

He cited Meta’s decision to delay the rollout of its Muse AI system, which includes personalised AI agents, by several months while the company worked on safety and security measures.

“We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” Zuckerberg wrote about the decision to delay the Muse AI release. “We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”

Meta has itself faced a series of liability lawsuits in recent months unrelated to AI. In August, the company agreed to pay billions of dollars to settle claims that Facebook and Instagram were designed to be addictive to children.

Zuckerberg also backed the use of independent evaluators to assess AI systems.

He said Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company’s AI division, already uses external reviewers and called for a “larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators” across the industry.

His comments came amid a broader debate over how AI companies should manage the risks posed by increasingly capable systems and whether regulation, industry standards or independent oversight should play the central role.

Zuckerberg’s post was also endorsed by several Silicon Valley figures close to the White House who have pushed back against warnings about the potential dangers of AI and calls for a slowdown in development.

title.rendered: Israel will ‘finish job’ in Gaza and remove Palestinians, defence minister says

content.rendered:
Jerusalem, September 16

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday that it was only a matter of time before Israel resumes a full-scale war in Gaza and moves ahead with a plan to remove the territory’s Palestinian population.

Katz, known for his outspoken statements, made the remarks while responding to criticism from another right-wing contender ahead of Israel’s October 27 elections.

He said around 70 percent of Gaza had already been emptied of its population during Israel’s military campaign launched after the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023.

Katz said the ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump in October 2025 had “supreme value for all Israelis” because it resulted in the return of the remaining hostages and included a US commitment to the disarmament of Hamas.

“We all understand that this is not going to happen,” Katz said in a statement. “The IDF is prepared, once given the directive to eliminate Hamas, to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan.”

The Israeli military is known as the IDF.

Katz said earlier this month that Israel was prepared to remove Palestinians from Gaza by land and sea but was waiting for the United States, which he said was discussing possible destinations for the territory’s roughly two million residents.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has denied that Washington has any plan to “displace people out of Gaza against their will.”

Katz has described the proposed migration plan as voluntary, claiming that most Palestinians want to leave Gaza.

Nearly the entire population of Gaza has been displaced internally during the conflict, while much of the territory has been reduced to rubble.

More than 73,700 killed in Gaza

The Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 killed 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on Israeli official figures. It was the deadliest attack in Israel’s history.

Militants also abducted 251 people and took them hostage in Gaza.

Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 73,700 people, according to the territory’s Health Ministry, which operates under Hamas authorities and does not distinguish between combatants and civilians. The ministry’s casualty figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

An 11-month-old ceasefire has reduced the intensity of fighting, but Israel has continued to carry out regular strikes in Gaza.

According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, 1,375 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect.

Hamas said in late July that it was prepared to disarm, a development Trump described as a breakthrough.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has rejected the latest stage of the ceasefire plan, saying Israel will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas verifiably decommissions all its weapons.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah meets US acting ambassador Megan Boldin

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Prime Minister Balendra Shah held a courtesy meeting with US Acting Ambassador to Nepal Megan Boldin at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers in Singha Durbar on Wednesday.

During the meeting, Shah expressed gratitude to the US government for its solidarity with and support for Nepal during the difficult situation caused by recent disasters.

Shah told Boldin that both Nepali and foreign nationals had been affected by the disasters. He also said Nepal was facing such incidents amid the growing impacts of climate change.

The prime minister stressed the need to strengthen global cooperation and collective efforts to reduce the risks posed by climate-related disasters and address their impacts.

The two also discussed Nepal’s tourism potential and opportunities for mutual benefit through the development of the tourism sector. Shah said Nepal would continue to welcome US investment, according to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat.

During the meeting, Acting Ambassador Boldin expressed deep sorrow over the loss of lives and property caused by the floods in Rasuwa.

She extended condolences to the bereaved families and affected communities and said the US government stood in solidarity with the Government of Nepal and the Nepali people during the difficult time.

Boldin also said the US government was ready to provide necessary support and cooperation in relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts, according to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat.

title.rendered: 9 banks and financial institutions offer Fonepay virtual credit cards

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The number of users of virtual credit cards offered through Fonepay’s network has reached 50,000, reflecting the growing use of digital technology for accessing and making credit-based payments in Nepal.

The virtual credit card service, launched two years ago, is currently available through nine banks and financial institutions connected to Fonepay’s network. The service allows customers to obtain a credit limit through their mobile banking applications and make payments by scanning QR codes, eliminating the need for a physical card or point-of-sale (POS) machine.

Fonepay Chief Executive Officer Diwas Kumar said the service has helped connect consumers and small businesses with digital credit.

“Even with only nine banks and financial institutions participating, 50,000 virtual cards have been issued in two years. If all banks and financial institutions participate, most purchase and sales payments could become cashless,” Kumar said.

The overall number of physical credit cards in Nepal stands at around 341,000, while the number of POS machines is approximately 300,000, according to Kumar. Fonepay, meanwhile, has around two million QR merchants, allowing virtual credit card users to make payments at a wide range of businesses.

Laxmi Sunrise Bank has issued the highest number of virtual credit cards among the participating institutions, with around 15,000 cards. Citizens Bank ranks second, having issued more than 10,000.

Laxmi Sunrise Bank CEO Ajay Bikram Shah said the bank has been using customer behaviour, transaction patterns and data analytics to develop digital products. He said virtual cards have become an attractive option because customers can obtain, use and manage credit directly through their mobile phones.

Citizens Bank Chief Operating Officer Roshan Manandhar said customers increasingly prefer virtual cards because they become available on mobile devices immediately after approval, without the need to print or activate a physical card. He said around 90–95 per cent of customers opting for the bank’s credit card service now prefer the virtual option.

Fonepay currently has Siddhartha Bank, Kumari Bank, Everest Bank, Laxmi Sunrise Bank, Citizens Bank, Garima Development Bank, Shine Resunga Development Bank, Mahalaxmi Development Bank and Manjushree Finance on its network.

According to Kumar, the default rate on loans extended through virtual credit cards is currently around 1–2 per cent. He said the service targets customers with regular income and spending patterns and uses risk-based credit limits.

Fonepay charges no fee for payments of up to Rs 2,000. For transactions above that amount, a fee of 0.6 per cent applies, with the maximum fee capped at Rs 300. By comparison, physical credit card transactions can attract fees of up to 3 per cent.

Users can also view their transactions and spending details through mobile banking applications. Kumar said payments made through the virtual credit card are interest-free for up to 45 days, after which interest and late-payment charges apply to outstanding amounts.

title.rendered: MrBeast joins global fundraising effort to help Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

World-famous content creator Jimmy Donaldson, known as MrBeast, has launched a fundraising campaign for those affected by the Bhotekoshi flood in Nepal.

The American YouTuber, entrepreneur and philanthropist said via an Instagram story that he and his team are raising millions of dollars in relief funds for Nepal’s disaster victims, and called on people around the world to join the effort.

He said flood survivors urgently need support. The campaign aims to raise millions of dollars, so that anyone anywhere in the world can take part, and that the money raised will go directly to those affected.

He also said he has been working to bring attention to the plight of Nepal’s flood victims. MrBeast noted that he had originally planned to film a video in Nepal a few weeks ago, but that plan was put on hold because of the Bhotekoshi flood.

After postponing the filming plans, he turned his attention to the relief campaign instead. His philanthropic organisation, Beast Philanthropy, is taking part through its “Care Package” social initiative.

According to the link he shared, the campaign will provide essential relief supplies for those affected, including temporary shelter, solar power, cooking gas and equipment, drinking water, soap, and menstrual hygiene products. He also shared a donation link for those wishing to contribute financially.

Donaldson’s YouTube channel, MrBeast, is the most-subscribed channel in the world, with more than 517 million subscribers.

title.rendered: 3 killed in NBC Los Angeles helicopter crash

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

A helicopter belonging to NBC Los Angeles crashed in the San Fernando Valley in Chatsworth, California, on Tuesday night, killing three people.

According to Los Angeles firefighters, the incident occurred Tuesday evening in the 9100 block of Mason Avenue, where the helicopter crashed between two commercial buildings. It landed on two shipping containers and several parked vehicles.

The cause of the crash has not yet been determined. Aerial footage showed a large fire following the crash, with flames spreading to nearby parked vehicles. Los Angeles firefighters worked to bring the blaze under control.

After the fire was extinguished, firefighters and Los Angeles police placed a tent over one of the bodies at the scene.

LAFD officials later confirmed that two other people also died at the crash site. Two additional people who were injured were taken to a local hospital. Their conditions were not immediately available.

Kathmandu, September 16

The Federal Parliament Secretariat has launched a new Digital Parliament platform aimed at making parliamentary information, services, records and activities more organised, accessible, effective and transparent.

The platform, currently in its testing phase, was inaugurated by House of Representatives Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal and National Assembly Chair Narayan Prasad Dahal.

At the launch event, Speaker Aryal said the platform brings together parliamentary information, the status of bills, the calendar, lawmakers’ attendance, and committee and sub-committee details into a single system.

He said the platform would also help digitise old parliamentary registers and documents related to Nepal’s parliamentary history, preserving them for centuries to come and making research easier. He argued that using technology was essential not just for the legislature but for the executive, judiciary and all three tiers of government to become more transparent, citizen-focused and trustworthy.

National Assembly Chair Dahal said shifting the work of parliament, its committees and the secretariat from traditional paper-based processes to a digital system would make the work faster, more transparent, effective and accountable.

He noted that although more young lawmakers are now part of parliament, the old habit of relying on printed documents persists, and said lawmakers and staff would need practical, high-quality orientation to adapt. While acknowledging that Nepal’s starting point looks modest by international standards, Dahal stressed that the digital system should be rolled out in phases, tailored to the country’s actual needs and circumstances.

title.rendered: 83 days of suspension, no dialogue between the government and ANFA

content.rendered:
It has now been 84 days since FIFA suspended the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) indefinitely on June 25, citing third-party interference. Nepali football has been largely paralysed since players aren’t competing, coaches aren’t training teams, and referees aren’t officiating.

The government has repeatedly claimed it is in talks with FIFA to lift the suspension, with Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel saying publicly on several occasions that discussions were going well and a resolution was near. Yet 84 days on, the ban remains in place and, according to ANFA, the government has not held a single direct conversation with the association itself during that time.

ANFA General Secretary Kiran Rai says the association has reached out repeatedly, directly and indirectly, but government officials have responded that ANFA’s leadership term has already expired, leaving little basis for talks. ANFA had planned a protest and memorandum submission at the National Sports Council on Tuesday, but postponed it after the government proposed talks. Those talks, however, did not happen as scheduled.

The suspension stems from a dispute between the government and ANFA over early elections. The current ANFA leadership wanted to hold elections before its term ended, while the National Sports Council pushed for a regular general assembly instead. The early election didn’t happen, and Nepal wasn’t spared FIFA’s suspension either; it came on June 25, after NSC’s own earlier suspension of ANFA (from late March to mid-May) failed to resolve the underlying dispute. Nepal’s women’s team has already lost a FIFA series because of the ban, and the men’s team now risks missing the SAFF Championship if the suspension isn’t lifted by the end of September.

Rai said ANFA had stayed largely quiet publicly out of concern that going public could jeopardise the ongoing government–FIFA dialogue, but that patience is wearing thin the longer the impasse drags on. He argued that continuing to let the situation stay unresolved only puts players’ futures and the country’s standing in international football at risk.

He further said the priority should be shielding Nepali football from a “loss” that would affect the whole country, not any individual’s political win or loss.

NSC member secretary Ram Charitra Mehta, however, maintains that talks are pointless since ANFA’s current office-bearers’ term has already expired, questioning who exactly the government would even be negotiating with.

title.rendered: KP Oli holds lengthy meeting with Bidhya Bhandari amid UML leadership dispute

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

CPN-UML Chair KP Sharma Oli held a lengthy meeting with former President Bidhya Devi Bhandari last week as disagreements continued within the party’s reorganisation task force.

According to sources, Oli and Bhandari held talks for more than two and a half hours on Friday afternoon. The discussion focused largely on the UML’s internal politics, although national political developments were also discussed.

“The national political situation was discussed, naturally. But the conversation was more focused on the internal politics of the UML,” a source said.

Oli, who is reportedly in a minority within both the UML reorganisation task force and the party secretariat, went to Bhandari’s residence in Baluwatar for the meeting.

It was the first time Oli had met Bhandari since the UML decided not to renew her party membership.

Oli had previously visited Bhandari at Sheetal Niwas while she was president and later at her residence in Bhangal after her presidential tenure ended. However, in July last year, the UML Central Committee approved a decision not to renew Bhandari’s party membership.

Sources close to Bhandari said Oli sought her support amid the growing internal dispute within the party.

“There is a difficult situation in national politics and within the party. The proposal was that we should move forward together at such a time,” a source close to Bhandari said.

According to the source, Bhandari advised Oli to bring different factions together and move forward collectively.

Oli reportedly argued that there was a tendency within the party to create conflict, encourage indiscipline and prepare reports that could benefit external forces.

Bhandari, however, is said to have urged him to seek unity.

“You are in a minority, and those who stood close to you in the past are now standing against you. Can the party be run this way?” Bhandari reportedly asked Oli.

Bhandari, who previously served as a UML vice-chair, also urged Oli to adopt a new approach.

“The party needs to be strengthened through unity. The responsibility of leadership is to bring everyone to a consensus,” she reportedly told him, according to sources. “You also need to think about why those who supported you in the past are now standing in opposition.”

She also advised Oli to seriously consider the party reorganisation agenda raised by Vice-Chairs Bishnu Prasad Paudel and Prithvi Subba Gurung and General Secretary Shankar Pokharel.

Oli argues stepping down could create further problems

According to a source close to Bhandari, Oli argued during the meeting that stepping down from the leadership could create further problems for the party.

“He said that Bishnu and Shankar cannot run the party,” the source said.

The meeting comes as the UML remains divided over two separate reports prepared as part of its party review and reorganisation process. A task force meeting earlier failed to reach agreement on the reports prepared by Vice-Chair Ram Bahadur Thapa and General Secretary Pokharel, with three leaders later tasked with working toward a consensus draft.

The dispute has centred in part on the future of the party’s leadership. Pokharel’s report and suggestions collected from party unit

title.rendered: 105 kg of marijuana recovered from ambulance that broke through police barricade

content.rendered:
Siraha, September 16

Police in Siraha have recovered 105 kg of marijuana from an ambulance.

Police said the drugs were recovered from ambulance no. Ja 1 Cha 1213, which was travelling from Choharwa toward Jayanagar at around 8 pm on Tuesday.

After receiving a tip-off that marijuana had been loaded into the ambulance and was being brought toward Siraha, a police team was mobilised under the command of Police Inspector Sunil Chaurasiya.

According to police, the driver realised the ambulance was under surveillance and broke through police barricades set up at three locations between Choharwa and Siraha before fleeing with the vehicle.

As additional police pursued the vehicle, the driver abandoned the ambulance along the Hulaki Road section in Siraha Municipality-1 and fled on foot, Siraha Police said.

While inspecting the ambulance, police found 105 kg of marijuana packed in five sacks, SP Basudev Pathak said.

According to SP Pathak, the ambulance and the recovered marijuana have been brought to the District Police Office, Siraha, where further investigation is underway. He said efforts to identify and trace the fleeing driver are continuing.

title.rendered: Nepali man charged over death of 3-year-old girl in Sydney

content.rendered:
Sydney, September 16

A 27-year-old Nepali man, Sandeep Adhikari, has been charged over the death of a three-year-old girl who was struck by a car in Auburn, western Sydney.

Adhikari was arrested and charged with causing death by negligent driving. He has not yet entered a plea in court.

Adhikari appeared at Burwood Local Court on Wednesday, less than 24 hours after the incident.

According to reports, several supporters were seen accompanying him as he left the court. He reportedly attempted to cover his face with a sheet of paper when approached by reporters.

Adhikari’s lawyer, Danny Ede, described the incident as “extremely tragic.”

“He is under a great deal of stress and is concerned about his family and their situation,” Ede told reporters.

How did the incident occur?

Emergency services were called to Normanby Road in Auburn at around 2 pm on Tuesday after reports that a car had struck the girl while she was playing in a driveway.

The girl, who was critically injured, was immediately taken to Westmead Hospital. She died several hours later.

Adhikari was not injured in the incident. He was taken to Auburn Hospital for mandatory testing before being taken to Auburn Police Station, where he was charged.

Adhikari is currently out on bail and has been ordered to appear in court again on October 27.

As the case is before the court, the allegations against Adhikari have not been proven.

title.rendered: Project Abhaya holds central-level forum on fiscal transparency and accountability reform

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 16 September 2026

Project Abhaya convened the Central-Level Reform Prioritisation and Validation Forum on Monday in Kathmandu. The forum brought together more than 30 participants representing political parties, civil society, youth networks, legal and media communities, and fiscal and governance experts.

The forum reviewed and validated Project Abhaya’s Reform Pathways Document, developed through more than five months of research, provincial engagement, and consultations on fiscal transparency and accountability in Nepal. The discussion assessed the relevance and feasibility of the proposed reforms within Nepal’s legal, institutional, and federal context and identified areas requiring further refinement.

Research and Reform Pathways Consultant Dipesh Ghimire presented 24 reform pathways across six clusters: credible planning and budgeting, transparent and accountable resource allocation, effective implementation and institutional capacity, intergovernmental fiscal governance, results and citizen accountability, and fiscal sustainability and continuous reform. The pathways are structured across immediate, short-term, and medium-term implementation periods.

Participants highlighted several priorities, including realistic and needs-based budgeting, stronger project readiness and prioritisation, greater procurement and contract transparency, and better use of data in fiscal decision-making. Discussions also emphasised the need to strengthen provincial and local governments and improve coordination among all three levels of government.

Citizen participation emerged as a central theme. Participants called for stronger citizen involvement in project prioritisation, fiscal disclosure, public hearings, social audits, grievance mechanisms, and the monitoring of public expenditure and outcomes. They also stressed that fiscal information should be accessible and understandable to citizens.

Participants further recommended clearer baselines and indicators, stronger institutional mapping, greater involvement of lawmakers, and a shift from measuring expenditure alone towards assessing the results and public value generated by government spending.

Feedback from the forum will be incorporated into the next version of the Reform Pathways Document, followed by an online validation forum and further consultations. The revised document will inform Project Abhaya’s continued engagement with government institutions, parliamentary bodies, provincial and local stakeholders, civil society, youth networks, and other actors working to strengthen fiscal transparency and public accountability in Nepal.

title.rendered: When our best students leave, what does that say about Nepal’s education system?

content.rendered:
Recently, one of my students, a gold medal holder from one of Nepal’s prestigious universities, came to my office and requested a letter of recommendation.

I asked why.

He told me he was planning to go overseas to study at a foreign university. So I asked him something else: Wasn’t he happy with the degree, even the gold medal, he had just earned at home?

He paused. He offered no definitive answer, nor did he seem particularly motivated to say much more.

That silence stayed with me.

If a student who has achieved the very best the system can offer — top marks, top honours and a gold medal — still feels that something is missing, then perhaps the problem lies beyond marks.

He is not alone. Hundreds of young Nepalis pass through Tribhuvan International Airport every day, some with degrees in hand, along with passports and admission letters. Some are pursuing further education. Others are leaving for work. All are going somewhere else.

There are many reasons for this. Opportunities abroad, family aspirations and the prospect of better income all play a role. But underneath these reasons is a subtler question: What is the “quality education” they believe they can only get in another country?

Are they simply seeking more classrooms and more certificates, or are they looking for an education system connected to learning and skills, opportunity, innovation, confidence and employment?

The recent announcement by Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel that the curriculum would be changed based on recommendations from students, teachers and parents is encouraging. It signals a willingness to open a process that has too often remained closed to the people most affected by it.

But gathering suggestions alone is not enough to bring about meaningful curriculum reform. We also need to pay attention to the deeper signals coming from classrooms, universities, workplaces and the aspirations of young Nepalis.

Listening beyond suggestions

What does “meaningful listening” actually mean?

It is not simply about which chapter students dislike, which textbook teachers do not want to teach, or which examination format should be changed. Those are surface questions. Surface questions tend to produce surface reforms — new chapters added to an old book, or new covers on a book that has otherwise remained unchanged.

The deeper signals are already there, if somebody is willing to collect them systematically.

Students are asking themselves, “I have studied, but am I ready for a job?”

Graduates are saying, “I have a degree, but I have no work experience and I am not confident.”

Students are reporting, “I don’t see enough scope for inquiry, collaboration and real-world problem-solving in the curriculum.”

Employers are reporting that graduates have qualifications but lack the ability to apply their knowledge.

These voices should be treated as data points, not merely as a line item in a ministry report. This requires structured and continuous work involving consultation, classroom observation, graduate tracking, employer surveys and ongoing course adjustments rather than periodic reform.

Teachers, especially, should not be seen only as facilitators of a pre-made curriculum. They are among the first to discover what works, what does not, and what new skills pupils need.

Curriculum reform should begin with teachers’ voices, but it should not end with a questionnaire. Their experience should be a genuine catalyst for curriculum design and revision, rather than simply a confirmation of decisions already made.

From credentials to capability

This is not a standalone issue.

A 2025 study on graduate employability in Nepal found that the most important employability predictors included teamwork and problem-solving skills, practical training experience and the university curriculum studied.

The message is clear: a degree is for getting, but not necessarily for doing.

A degree is not necessarily proof of communication, collaboration, critical thinking, problem-solving, adaptability or the ability to apply knowledge in real-world situations.

This gap has tangible consequences.

During FY 2024/25 alone, more than 839,000 Nepalis received labour permits to go abroad for work, while more than 112,000 received no-objection certificates to study abroad in FY 2023/24.

Behind each number is a young person who has weighed Nepal’s classrooms against a classroom abroad and opted for the latter, just like the student who came to me for that letter.

Not all those who leave are escaping a broken system.

Remittances are a natural consequence of globalisation. They support millions of families and, indirectly, the country’s economy. Nor should going abroad automatically be seen as a rejection of Nepal.

The question of what we teach, however, is not merely academic when educated young people have limited pathways from learning to livelihood at home.

Teaching what machines lack

Learners today live in a world where knowledge is readily available. Through YouTube, TikTok, online courses and generative AI, they can access and learn information in ways that often go beyond what happens in a traditional classroom.

The Minister himself has acknowledged that AI needs to be introduced into the curriculum.

But this is not simply about adding a chapter on AI.

As machines generate more information and routine solutions, classrooms need to devote more time and attention to what humans do with information: question, analyse, create, communicate, collaborate and solve problems.

A curriculum that continues to value success primarily through memory risks preparing a generation for a future that has already arrived.

This leads to a fundamental question that curriculum reform must address: What should students be able to do with what they study?

And ultimately: What qualities should a Nepalese graduate have to succeed in classrooms, workplaces and the future?

From paper to practice

What is the next step?

Three things can help turn good intentions into reality if the Ministry is to fulfil its promise.

First, it should reach out to public and community schools as well, rather than consulting only those that are already organised and well connected. Otherwise, the same voices will be repeated over and over again.

Second, teacher training needs to happen alongside curriculum change. Giving a new curriculum to teachers who have not been adequately prepared to deliver it will not take us very far.

Third, every reform needs follow-up. Did students become more employable? Are they pursuing further study? Has their confidence increased? These questions can help make curriculum revision a continuous process rather than a one-off announcement.

There is no quick fix. Curriculum reform requires the determination to treat education as a long-term process, not a short-term intervention designed to respond to public criticism.

The way forward

When it comes to curriculum revision, changing what is written on paper is only half the battle.

The other half is ensuring that the change reaches classrooms, keeps pace with the world beyond them, and translates classroom learning into what that world demands today.

The true test of reform will be what students are able to do with what they have learned.

The aim should not be to graduate students who can only pass examinations or collect certificates. It should be to develop young people who can think on their feet, solve problems, work with others and apply their knowledge, regardless of who they are or where they choose to build their futures.

The airport queue, then, is not necessarily a commentary on the failure of Nepal’s education system. But it is a wake-up call.

It asks us to consider whether our classrooms are giving young people not only qualifications, but also the skills, confidence and opportunities they need to build their futures.

That is a question Nepal must address before the next generation packs its bags and searches elsewhere for the answers.

title.rendered: Wild elephant found dead in Jhapa

content.rendered:
Jhapa, September 16

A wild elephant was found dead this morning in a paddy field at Telpani in Mechinagar Municipality-3.

Nathuni Gohiwar Yadav, chief of the Division Forest Office, said a team from the office had been dispatched to the site.

He said locals reported the death after spotting the carcass of an adult tusker in the paddy field. The cause of death is not yet known, he said.

Wild elephants have long been causing heavy damage to human life and farmers’ crops in wards 2, 3, 4 and 5 of Mechinagar.

Large numbers of wild elephants cross the Mechi River from forests in India to graze in Jhapa, while the number of resident elephants living in local forests has also risen in recent years.

According to Division Forest Office records, 28 wild elephants have been found dead in various parts of Jhapa over the past 16 years.

title.rendered: Energy Minister Shrestha cancels South Korea visit

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has cancelled his scheduled visit to South Korea, citing the need to prioritise rescue, rehabilitation and restoration of electricity services following a natural disaster in Nepal.

According to the ministry, Shrestha cancelled the visit due to the extensive damage caused to the energy sector by the disaster and the need to focus on restoring and regularising power supply.

The ministry faces the responsibility of effectively coordinating search and rescue efforts as floods in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system have caused significant damage to energy infrastructure, while a large number of people remain unaccounted for.

It must also oversee the restoration of damaged energy infrastructure, ensure a regular and reliable electricity supply, facilitate support for affected private-sector energy companies, and expedite post-disaster reconstruction and recovery efforts.

Shrestha had been invited as a keynote speaker at the Global Infrastructure Cooperation Conference 2026, scheduled to be held in Seoul from September 15 to 17.

The Cabinet had approved the visit on August 13, with Shrestha scheduled to travel with a delegation including Nepal Electricity Authority Executive Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha.

Kathmandu, September 16

Work to open a new track at Krishnabhir in Dhading, along the Prithvi Highway, has been completed.

According to the Prime Minister’s Office, the work to open the new track at Krishnabhir was finished by Wednesday morning. With the new track ready, vehicles will be able to travel fully along this highway starting tomorrow.

The highway has been blocked since August 30, when floodwaters in the Trishuli River, arriving four days after the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi, cut away the road at Krishnabhir.

On September 13, some heavy vehicles were passed through to test the new track. Even after that test, vehicles were not allowed to operate, as the work had not been fully completed.

With the Prithvi Highway closed, both large and small vehicles that normally use this route have been travelling to and from Kathmandu via alternative highways.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The Armed Police Force (APF) has arrested an Indian national with approximately 9.5 kg of hashish from Alau in Birgunj Metropolitan City-17, Parsa.

The arrested man has been identified as 20-year-old Sandeep Chaudhary, who is from India. He was arrested by a team deployed from the APF Nepal Border Security Gulma in Alau.

According to the APF, Chaudhary was carrying the hashish on a motorcycle after concealing it in a false compartment inside the motorcycle’s fuel tank.

The security personnel recovered approximately 9.5 kg of hashish packed in 21 packets from the motorcycle’s fuel tank.

The APF said Chaudhary, along with the confiscated hashish and motorcycle, has been handed over to the concerned authorities for further legal action.

title.rendered: From Udayapur to America, one job at a time

content.rendered:
Success did not come easily to Kaaluram Chaudhary, known to many as Cals. Growing up in a family that relied on subsistence farming in Udayapur’s Chaudandigadhi, he learned early that earning a living could mean doing whatever work was available.

As a child, he worked part-time at a rice mill and went to school when he could. Later, he carried heavy loads for a construction company, worked as an office assistant, cut and delivered meat, and learned to cook in some of Kathmandu’s hotels.

His journey eventually took him from Nepal to Tibet, Dubai and the United States.

Today, at 47, Chaudhary runs his own restaurant in America, serving Nepali food alongside international dishes. The journey was neither easy nor planned. It was built one job, one setback and one opportunity at a time.

A childhood shaped by work

Chaudhary was born in 1978 into a poor family in Chaudandigadhi-5, Udayapur. Money was scarce, and he began working while still in school. At the local Mangal Rice Mill, he worked part-time, earning a small income to help cover his expenses before returning to his studies.

Then, in 1991, a political event changed his life. The owner of the rice mill, Congress leader Satyanarayan Chaudhary, popularly known as Kshetrapal, contested the general election that year and lost. The consequences were severe for his businesses. The rice mill eventually shut down, leaving the workers and technicians who depended on it without work.

Chaudhary was only in Grade 6. For a boy who had been balancing school and work, the closure meant losing the small income that helped him survive. He needed another way forward.

With the rice mill gone, Chaudhary travelled to Kathmandu in 1993 with the help of his neighbour, Kishun Dev Bishwakarma. Bishwakarma worked as a bus conductor on the Sita Travels route between Kathmandu and Gaighat. He helped the 15-year-old reach his maternal uncle’s home in Kalanki.

Kathmandu offered opportunities, but they were not easy ones. His first job was at an ice factory. He soon left because the work did not suit him. Then he found work with a construction company. He was still school-aged, but life gave him little choice. He worked as a labourer, carrying loads that were often heavier than himself.

“I had no alternative but to work,” Chaudhary recalls. “It was the middle of winter, but I had to work to arrange food and other necessities. I had to be ready to do whatever hard work was available.”

He spent three months at the construction company. Then an opportunity appeared that would change the course of his education. Someone from the company helped him get a job as an office assistant at the Chaudhary Group.

Studying on a rooftop

At Chaudhary Group, he worked during the day and lived there. But he had not forgotten about school. He knew his friends back home were moving into higher grades while his own education had stopped. So he began studying on his own. Every year, he bought books for the next grade and studied them in his free time. Grades 7, 8, 9 and 10 were completed not inside a classroom, but on the rooftop of the Chaudhary Group building.

“I would sit on the CG rooftop every day, remembering my friends and studying the pages of my books,” he says. “I studied Grades 7, 8, 9 and 10 there.”

He was known as a bright student in his village and did not want to give up on education. Eventually, he told someone at the office that he wanted to continue studying properly. The response was not encouraging.

An engineer mocked him and the matter reached his superiors. Chaudhary was effectively forced to choose between his job and his education.

He chose education. He resigned from the permanent job he had secured and walked away.

Becoming a butcher

Leaving the Chaudhary Group meant starting again. Chaudhary found work at a meat shop, where he cut meat and delivered it to different shops. He worked hard enough to catch the attention of the owner. Initially, he delivered meat on a bicycle. Within a month, the owner bought him a motorbike

Chaudhary began taking the job beyond simple delivery. He started marketing the meat himself and built relationships with hotels across Kathmandu. Soon, even five-star hotels were placing orders.

“I started taking meat to five-star hotels on my motorcycle,” he says. “After that, I began receiving offers for other jobs as well.”

His efforts were recognised again. The shop owner eventually bought him a car and handed him greater responsibility for marketing, deliveries, bills and payments.

“He valued my hard work and treated me like a son,” Chaudhary says. “He bought me a car and entrusted me with the entire marketing responsibility.”

By then, Chaudhary had built relationships with people across Kathmandu’s hotel industry. One of those connections opened another door.

Cooking his way up

In 2002, Chaudhary joined Hotel Yak & Yeti. He was hired to be a butcher, but the job became an informal culinary education. His colleagues were willing to teach him, and he began learning how to cook alongside his regular work.

“I got a job cutting meat there, but my colleagues were friendly and taught me cooking as well,” he says.

He gradually learned to prepare different dishes and gained experience in professional kitchens. That experience took him beyond Nepal. In 2006, he received an opportunity to work as a continental chef in Tibet.

It was his first international job. He worked at a hotel in Lhasa, where he also learned about Chinese cuisine and shared his own cooking knowledge. But Tibet brought another challenge.

The region experienced severe cold and long winters, meaning he could work for only about six months. After six months of work and another six months largely spent waiting out the winter, he returned to Nepal in 2007.

From Kathmandu to Dubai

Back in Kathmandu, Chaudhary joined Hotel Radisson as a senior cook. He worked there for two years. His ability to prepare food well and his willingness to teach others once again opened another door.

While working at Radisson, he received an offer from Al Bustan Hotel in Dubai. In 2009, he moved to the United Arab Emirates and began working as a chef. Dubai gave him another five years of experience in professional kitchens. But Chaudhary was still looking ahead.

His next opportunity would take him farther than he had ever imagined.

A job on one of the world’s biggest cruise ships

In 2014, Chaudhary moved to the United States after receiving an opportunity to work as a chef for Royal Caribbean. The cruise company operates some of the world’s largest passenger ships, capable of carrying thousands of people at a time. For Chaudhary, it was another new world. He worked as a senior cook and shared kitchens with people from different countries.

The experience exposed him to cuisines and cooking styles from around the world.

“Just as different countries have different ways of dressing, their food and dishes are different too,” he says. “I learned to prepare food from different countries and had the opportunity to exchange experiences with people from around the world.”

Two years on the cruise ship added another layer to the skills he had accumulated over decades. The boy who had once worked at a rice mill was now cooking for people from around the world. But he still had one more dream.

Bringing Nepal to America

After retiring from the cruise ship, Chaudhary began thinking about building something of his own. Together with some Nepali and American friends, he registered a company in 2022 and opened a restaurant in the United States. He named it Mount Everest Restaurant.

The idea was simple — bring the taste of Nepal to people in America while also offering international cuisine. The restaurant serves traditional Nepali dishes as well as food from other parts of the world.

“We can serve all kinds of food and dishes together,” Chaudhary says. “Nepalis can hold their heads high.”

For him, the restaurant is not simply another business. It is the culmination of everything he has learned along the way — from the meat shop and Kathmandu hotels to Tibet, Dubai and the cruise ship. The experiences of working alongside people from different countries have helped him understand different cuisines and bring them together under one roof. The restaurant has also created employment for eight people.

A journey built one step at a time

Chaudhary did not set out with a clear plan to become a chef or restaurant owner. At different points in his life, he was simply trying to solve the problem in front of him. When the rice mill closed, he went to Kathmandu.

When he needed money, he carried construction materials. When he could not attend school, he studied alone on a rooftop. When he left his office job, he cut and delivered meat. When an opportunity came at Yak & Yeti, he learned to cook. Then came Tibet, Kathmandu, Dubai, a cruise ship and, eventually, his own restaurant in America.

Each stage added something to the next.

His story is not one of sudden success. It is the story of a young boy who kept moving whenever one door closed — and learned something from every door that opened. Today, Kaaluram “Kals” Chaudhary is serving Nepali food thousands of kilometres from the village where his journey began.

The road from a rice mill in Udayapur to a restaurant in America was long. But he carried the lessons of every stop along the way with him.
