title.rendered: Federal Parliament launches Digital Parliament project

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The Federal Parliament Secretariat is launching the Digital Parliament project to make parliamentary information, services, records and activities more systematic, accessible and transparent.

A programme has been scheduled at Singha Durbar at 10 am today to formally introduce the project. The programme, organised by the Digital Parliament Project Coordination and Facilitation Committee, will provide detailed information about the concept and its implementation.

According to the Parliament Secretariat, the Digital Parliament platform has been introduced to make parliamentary activities more convenient, effective and transparent while ensuring integrated record-keeping and easier access to parliamentary information.

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal and National Assembly Chairperson Narayan Prasad Dahal are scheduled to jointly inaugurate the platform.

Prakash Chandra Pariyar, chief whip of the Rastriya Swatantra Party, said the implementation of the Digital Parliament concept is expected to make parliamentary activities more transparent and citizen-friendly.

“The Digital Parliament platform, which is being brought into operation on a trial basis from Wednesday, is expected to make parliamentary records, history, daily proceedings, lawmakers’ presentations, questions and procedures more effective,” he said.

According to Pariyar, the digital platform is being tested to modernise traditional parliamentary practices through greater use of technology and make the activities of the House of Representatives and parliamentary committees more organised, accountable, citizen-friendly and transparent.

He said the essence of the Digital Parliament is to modernise the activities, records and proceedings of the House, parliamentary committees and the Secretariat through extensive use of technology.

The digital platform will initially include a web page and an application, with the application expected to be expanded later. During the trial phase, access will be provided only to selected Parliament Secretariat employees and some lawmakers.

The existing parliamentary website already contains a large amount of information, including videos of lawmakers’ speeches. The new system aims to make such information available in text format as well.

The platform will also allow users to digitally access lawmakers’ attendance records and detailed profiles.

“It is an effort to digitally transmit issues raised by lawmakers to the concerned ministries and stakeholders and explore options for addressing them,” Pariyar said.

He added that suggestions will be collected during the first phase of the trial to make the platform more user-friendly and results-oriented, while experts will also be consulted for further improvement.

Kathmandu, September 16

The government has prepared a bill on waste management.

The bill covers the entire waste management process, including waste reduction, source segregation, collection, transportation to transfer stations, and reuse and recycling at processing centres. It also includes provisions for producing compost, gas and energy from waste, as well as the safe final disposal of residual waste.

Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam said the bill is ready.

“Nature has given us one of the most beautiful countries in the world. But today, the growing amount of waste on roads, rivers, settlements and public places is posing a challenge to our natural beauty, environment and public health,” she said. “With the objective of changing this situation, we are preparing to register a landmark waste management bill in the Federal Parliament.”

According to Gautam, the bill’s most important aspect is that it addresses waste management as a complete cycle, from waste generation to final disposal.

She said the bill also incorporates modern concepts such as zero waste, the circular economy and extended producer responsibility into the legal framework.

“Simply collecting waste is not the solution. This bill has organised the entire cycle, from waste generation to final management,” Minister Gautam said. “It is a historic legal step towards building a clean, healthy and beautiful Nepal.”

title.rendered: Nepal needs climate and disaster diplomacy as strategic foreign policy priority

content.rendered:
Nepal is mourning the catastrophic consequences of a massive rock-ice avalanche and subsequent debris flow. The disaster sent a devastating mud-rock slurry through transboundary river networks. Originating in the high-altitude reaches of the Lhende Khola, the deluge swept into the Purepu Tsangpo, Chhochen Khola, and Gyirong River in China before entering Nepal. It then funnelled violently down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river basins, compounding the devastation and worsening conditions for thousands of people.

Hundreds have been confirmed dead, thousands remain missing, and infrastructure worth billions has been destroyed. Amid this unimaginable tragedy, remarkable stories of rescue continue to emerge. The courage of local communities and the deep sense of solidarity demonstrated within Nepal and by the international community provide a glimmer of hope.

Yet this disaster has also raised existential questions for the nation: how much longer can a country that contributes almost nothing to global greenhouse gas emissions bear the catastrophic consequences of global heating?

The anatomy of a Himalayan crisis

Scientists working in climatology, meteorology, oceanography, and glaciology have long warned that climate change is accelerating glacier melt worldwide and increasing the risk of cascading disasters. The Earth’s “Third Pole”, the high-altitude Himalayan region, is warming at roughly twice the global average rate. This rapid warming is thawing ancient permafrost that acts as geological cement, holding steep and fragile mountain slopes together. As permafrost weakens, entire mountainsides can lose their structural integrity, creating conditions for rock avalanches, landslides, and glacial lake outburst floods.

This acute vulnerability recalls Elizabeth Kolbert’s eye-opening book, The Sixth Extinction: An Unnatural History (2014). Kolbert illustrates how human activities are driving a mass extinction event. Since the Industrial Revolution of the 1760s, human activity has rapidly increased the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. While natural processes such as solar fluctuations and volcanic eruptions have historically influenced the climate, contemporary global warming is overwhelmingly driven by human activities.

Compounding this crisis, modern regional wars and intense global competition for natural resources, from deep-earth fossil fuels to the rare earth elements required for advanced technologies, continue to contribute to greenhouse gas emissions and exacerbate global warming. Climate change is no longer merely an environmental concern; it is a complex web of destruction affecting life across land, sea, and atmosphere, from the local to the global scale. Over the past decades, increasingly frequent, intense, and extensive floods, storms, droughts, and heatwaves have heightened collective awareness of the scale of the crisis.

Redefining climate governance

One might naturally expect that, confronted with recurring disasters, politicians, policymakers, business leaders, the private sector, and citizens would align behind ambitious and binding measures to reduce future risks. Yet formal action frequently lags behind the scale and urgency of the challenge.

Traditional frameworks of climate governance often focus on political priorities such as combating domestic corruption, ensuring immediate economic well-being, maintaining political stability, and safeguarding national interests and defence. While these remain fundamental responsibilities of the state, the contemporary situation demands that governance extend beyond traditional boundaries. Climate change and human security have converged as among the greatest existential challenges facing humanity, with direct implications for economic development, sovereign stability, and sustainable peace.

For an ecologically fragile and socioeconomically stratified country like Nepal, this convergence is already a lived reality. Climate change acts as a severe threat multiplier, magnifying deep-rooted structural inequalities based on caste, ethnicity, and gender. Nepal’s economy relies heavily on climate-sensitive sectors such as rain-fed agriculture, which employs more than 40 per cent of the workforce. When erratic precipitation, droughts, or flash floods occur, marginalised communities often suffer first and most severely.

Women and girls bear a disproportionate burden. As access to clean water and fuelwood becomes more difficult, their daily workloads increase, while girls may be forced to leave school. When disasters displace families, existing vulnerabilities related to physical safety, reproductive health, and financial security can be severely aggravated in temporary shelters.

Therefore, modern climate governance cannot treat adaptation as a peripheral environmental project. It must become an integral part of national economic planning, development policy, and security architecture.

Climate diplomacy: A new era of foreign policy

Addressing these monumental challenges requires new thinking in foreign policy. Global negotiations under the Conferences of the Parties (COPs) establish emissions targets and carbon-market rules, but Nepal must approach these forums through the lens of active climate diplomacy. Climate diplomacy can connect global climate finance, adaptation mechanisms, technology transfer, and transboundary resource cooperation, providing an important framework for advancing Nepal’s foreign-policy interests.

Nepal contributes only a negligible share of global greenhouse gas emissions but remains one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries. This profound climate injustice demands that Nepal’s foreign policy transition from passive participation to active advocacy.

Nepal must, first, strengthen its institutional capacity for international climate negotiations; second, build strategic coalitions with other highly vulnerable mountain and developing countries; and third, assertively advocate for climate justice, technology transfer, and direct financing for loss and damage from the world’s largest emitters.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs should urgently elevate climate and disaster diplomacy as strategic national priorities. This requires a dedicated budget, a highly trained diplomatic corps specialising in environmental and climate law, and institutional mechanisms that can effectively connect local environmental data with international diplomacy and foreign relations.

Domestically, Nepal is attempting to address Himalayan vulnerabilities through a three-pronged approach: advocating for global climate justice; seeking to revive high-level global and regional dialogue platforms such as the Sagarmatha Sambad; and decentralising resource management to local governments under the federal system to ensure that resources reach affected communities.

Nepal’s intellectual capital in this field is also growing. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has increasingly drawn on the expertise of Nepali professionals, with 12 Nepali scientists and experts contributing directly to report-writing processes and helping shape global climate science. Similarly, work by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) highlights the close relationship between biodiversity loss and climate change.

Translating diplomacy into action: The Karnali framework

The tangible benefits of proactive climate diplomacy are illustrated by the recent success of the National Trust for Nature Conservation. In July 2026, the Green Climate Fund (GCF) approved an $8.5 million grant for a four-year climate-resilience project in Nepal’s highly vulnerable Karnali Province. The project, titled Building Climate Resilience of Forest-Dependent Communities through Enhanced Livelihood Opportunities and Local Capacity in Karnali Province, has a total mobilisation of Rs 1.29 billion.

The project demonstrates how global climate finance can be channelled to the local level. It targets forest-dependent communities by restoring degraded ecosystems, strengthening local capacity through participatory National, Provincial, and Local Adaptation Plans of Action, and creating climate-resilient livelihood opportunities.

By promoting high-value medicinal plants and non-timber forest products, the project aims to strengthen local economies against climate shocks. It also emphasises the establishment of community-based early warning systems to protect more than 100,000 direct beneficiaries.

This provides a framework that other provinces could adapt to maximise the benefits of Nepal’s climate diplomacy and access to international climate finance.

An urgent call for disaster diplomacy

While climate diplomacy addresses long-term systemic challenges, the immediate crisis in Nepal’s river basins provides an urgent warning about the need for disaster diplomacy. Nepal must strengthen its foreign-policy architecture through disaster diplomacy, which uses pre-disaster risk planning and post-disaster humanitarian response to facilitate international cooperation, strengthen regional and subregional relationships, establish bilateral agreements, and promote transboundary coordination.

Nepal cannot manage the risks associated with the Himalayan cryosphere and the Anthropocene alone. Disaster diplomacy requires formal protocols with China and India for the real-time sharing of satellite, hydrological, meteorological, and seismological data related to glacial movements, river flows, and lake levels. It also requires collaborative transboundary river-basin management to reduce the risk of downstream infrastructure, including vital hydropower facilities, being destroyed within minutes by cascading disasters.

Ultimately, Nepal’s resilience will depend on two interconnected imperatives: systemic global accountability and local human solidarity. Nepal must continue to demand that industrialised nations acknowledge and address their historical responsibility for greenhouse gas emissions and contribute to stabilising the world’s natural water towers.

At the same time, the government should establish a dedicated Department of Climate Diplomacy, along with specialised divisions for Disaster Diplomacy and Negotiations, Climate Finance and Trade, and Green Industrial Policy. These institutions should be linked across relevant ministries and established as an urgent national priority, particularly before the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister participate in the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

Nepal’s climate vulnerability is no longer a distant environmental concern. It is a matter of national security, economic resilience, human development, and foreign policy. The country’s response must therefore evolve accordingly—from reacting to disasters after they occur to using diplomacy, science, finance, and regional cooperation to anticipate and reduce the risks before the next catastrophe strikes.

title.rendered: Nepal government proposes six-month maternity leave, 42 days for fathers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The government is preparing to extend paid maternity leave for mothers from the current 90 days to six months and paternity care leave for fathers from 15 days to 42 days.

According to Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam, the ministry has prepared a draft amendment to the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2018.

The ministry is preparing to submit the amendment bill to the Cabinet before taking it to Parliament, she said.

The proposed amendment provides for at least six months of paid maternity leave for mothers and up to 42 days of paid paternity care leave for fathers.

“This is an important policy change in terms of safe motherhood and parenthood,” Gautam said.

The ministry said the proposal has been put forward against the backdrop of increasingly busy lifestyles, work pressures and changing family structures, with many families choosing to have only one or two children.

“The special period of motherhood and fatherhood comes only once or twice in a person’s life. It is also the responsibility of the state to ensure that parents have enough time for their newborn and family during this period,” Gautam said.

She said that while giving birth is a natural process associated with mothers, raising a child should not be considered the sole responsibility of the mother.

“Child-rearing is a shared responsibility,” she said.

caption.rendered: A newborn being fed breastmilk within the first hour of delivery. Photo Courtesy: UNICEF

image_meta.caption:
On 9 August 2022, at the Paropakar Maternity and Women's Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, Sunita Rai uses a spoon to feed her newborn son breastmilk. Sunita had come to the hospital to seek treatment after her son was born prematurely. Seeing that Sunita was unable to breastfeed her child, healthworkers quickly referred her to the hospital’s newly-launched 'Amrit Kosh', the first human milk bank to be established in the country, which provided Sunita’s baby with breastmilk donated by other mothers.  

In Nepal, only 42 per cent of children under 2 years of age are breastfed within one hour of birth and 62 per cent of children under six months are exclusively breastfed.

When expressed breast milk is not adequate or available, these newborns are usually given infant formula milk. However, feeding formula milk can often lead to a high risk of developing an infection (sepsis) as well as necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious disease that affects the intestines of premature infants. It typically happens within the first 2 weeks of life in babies who are fed formula instead of breast milk. Donor human milk, if made available to these babies, can save them from the adverse effects of formula milk.

The ‘Amrit Kosh' has the facilities to collect, pasteurize, test and store safe donor human milk from lactating mothers and then provide it to infants in need. The centre has been established in partnership with the European Union and UNICEF.  

Nepal’s Multi-Sector Nutrition Plan (MSNP) seeks to improve maternal, adolescent, and child nutrition throughout Nepal by promoting healthy, nutritious, and diversified diets for adolescents, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, infants, and young children. Since 2013, UNICEF has been supporting the Government of Nepal in implementing MSNP, with funding support from the European Union. Nepal.

title.rendered: Rain and snowfall likely across Nepal on Wednesday

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

Weather across Nepal is expected to remain generally cloudy on Wednesday, with rain, thunderstorms and snowfall forecast in several parts of the country.

According to the Meteorological Forecasting Division under the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, heavy rainfall is possible at one or two places in the mountainous, hilly and Tarai areas of Koshi Province, as well as in the hilly and Tarai areas of Bagmati and Gandaki provinces during the afternoon.

Moderate rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning, along with snowfall, is likely at a few places in the mountainous areas of Koshi and Bagmati provinces. Similar conditions are possible at a few places in the mountainous areas of Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

The department has also forecast moderate rainfall with thunderstorms and lightning at some places in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces and at a few places in the hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpaschim.

In the Tarai, moderate rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning is possible at some places in Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, and at a few places in Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Rain and snowfall likely at night

The country is expected to remain generally cloudy on Wednesday night as well.

A few places in the mountainous areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces and one or two places in the mountainous areas of Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces are likely to receive moderate rain with thunderstorms and lightning, along with snowfall.

Moderate rainfall is also likely at some places in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces and at a few places in the hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpaschim.

Similarly, some places in the Tarai areas of Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, and a few places in the Tarai areas of Lumbini and Sudurpaschim, may receive moderate rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning, according to the department.

title.rendered: Foreign Ministry finalises ambassador list, Balen-Rabi consensus still pending

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 16

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has finalised its list of candidates for ambassadors to 21 of the 22 vacant diplomatic missions, but consensus between Prime Minister Balendra Shah and Rastriya Swatantra Party chair Rabi Lamichhane is still pending on some of the proposed names.

A senior source said the ministry had submitted what it considered the final list, but names and countries were still being moved around during discussions at the political level.

The ministry has also proposed primary and alternative candidates for some countries to facilitate the decision-making process.

Prime Minister Shah’s Chief Adviser Kumar Ben has been holding discussions with Lamichhane and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal on the final list. According to a senior RSP source, Lamichhane has raised questions about some candidates and their backgrounds but has adopted a policy of not interfering once the government’s preferences are clear.

The RSP chair has reportedly emphasised that candidates should have credible previous relations or contacts with the country to which they are being appointed and should be able to work effectively there.

Ben has also been meeting some ambassadorial aspirants directly to assess their backgrounds and capabilities, according to sources.

Foreign Minister Khanal had earlier instructed officials to prioritise transparent and credible candidates. Following this, the ministry opened applications in the second week of Jestha, receiving around 4,400 applications. About 2,700 names were shortlisted.

Of the proposed appointments, 14 are political appointments and seven are career diplomats from the Foreign Ministry.

“We have prepared the list of ambassadors for recommending some names this week,” Khanal told Onlinekhabar. “Professionals and people who may not be prominent in Nepali politics but have expertise in their respective fields have been prioritised.”

India, China and US among key appointments

For neighbouring India, Nischal Nath Pandey is reportedly the leading candidate. Former chief secretary Shankar Das Bairagi is also under consideration.

Some former military officials had been included in earlier discussions but have reportedly been removed from the final list.

Former army chief Gaurav Shumsher Rana was considered for India, but concerns were raised within the party that his military background could prompt questions from the host country. He is now reportedly being considered for the ambassadorial post in the United Kingdom.

For China, Fudan University professor Kalyan Sharma is reportedly the RSP’s preferred candidate. However, sources say the Chinese side has indicated a preference for a career diplomat, putting Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai also in strong contention.

Three names — Chiran Jung Thapa, journalist Akhilesh Upadhyay and former secretary Krishna Gyawali — are reportedly in the final list for the United States.

Thapa, whose name has received relatively little public attention, is reportedly the government’s preferred candidate based on his professional background. Upadhyay and Gyawali are being considered as alternatives.

For Japan, Jijyan Thapa’s name is reportedly close to being finalised. Thapa previously worked as a language translator in Japan and is understood to have links with several companies there. His name was reportedly proposed by Speaker DP Aryal rather than the Balen or Rabi camps.

Other names under consideration include Saru Joshi, Sangam Shrestha and Chudamani Kharel.

Joshi, who has experience in the foreign employment sector, is reportedly being considered for a country with a significant number of Nepali migrant workers. Shrestha, a former dean at the Asian Institute of Technology in Thailand, is being considered for Malaysia, South Korea or Bangladesh.

Kharel was reportedly not among the initial applicants but has emerged as a possible candidate for Malaysia or a similar destination.

Career diplomats currently working in the government are being considered for Western Asian countries where foreign employment is a major component of Nepal’s bilateral relations. The government has said it will not repeat individuals who have previously served as ambassadors.

Political bargaining raises questions

The government had previously said it wanted to appoint ambassadors through a lawful and transparent process and had scrapped earlier political appointments as part of that approach.

However, the current process has raised questions about whether that commitment will be fully implemented.

Sources say the final list could still change as political discussions continue, while some names already settled for particular countries could be held back for some time.

Foreign Ministry officials have also expressed concern that candidates lobbying political leaders through private meetings could affect the process and potentially create difficulties in securing agrément from the receiving countries.

There are also concerns that political bargaining within the ruling party could influence the appointments, similar to the practice of dividing ambassadorial posts among coalition partners under previous governments.

The Foreign Ministry, however, says it wants to promote people who have achieved success in their professional fields but have had relatively little exposure in public life.

Khanal has not disclosed the names of the candidates but has urged the public to remain hopeful about the appointments.

A government source said at least half of the ambassadorial appointments would be recommended within a week.

The delay has come under increasing criticism as the government approaches six months in office without completing the ambassadorial appointments. The Foreign Ministry has now completed its list and is waiting for political consensus on the remaining issues.

“We will send people who can establish diplomatic access in the respective countries and further strengthen it,” a Foreign Ministry official said. “Consensus is still pending for some countries, but a good list has been prepared despite the delay.”

title.rendered: Sugar shortage deepens ahead of Dashain as prices climb to Rs 170 per kg

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Sugar consumption peaks during Dashain, Tihar and Chhath, but consumers have been struggling to find the essential commodity for more than two months as the festive season approaches.

Sugar that was available for around Rs 95 per kg until April is now being sold for Rs 110 to more than Rs 150, with some consumers reporting prices as high as Rs 170 per kg.

The shortage has affected households preparing everything from daily tea to festive sweets and other traditional dishes. Consumers say they are having to visit several shops to find sugar, while some retailers are allegedly hoarding supplies and selling them at inflated prices.

The situation is particularly striking because the government has approved large-scale sugar imports at a reduced customs duty, while state-owned companies have claimed they have sufficient stocks.

Consumers pay up to Rs 170

Pratikshya Khanal of Tokha said she recently had to visit three or four shops before finding a kilogram of sugar near her home. She eventually paid Rs 170.

“The shopkeeper said sugar was not available and that the sugar they had was expensive. Since I needed it, I had to pay Rs 170,” she said.

Radha Koirala of New Baneshwor said the price had risen sharply within just 15 days.

“I bought a kilogram for Rs 120 15 days ago, but yesterday I had to pay Rs 160,” she said. “Initially, the shopkeeper said there was no sugar, but later brought some out.”

Koirala also claimed the shopkeeper refused to accept payment through QR and asked her to pay in cash, saying the digital payment system was not working.

She normally consumes only around one kilogram of sugar in 20 to 25 days but expects her household’s demand to increase during Dashain and Tihar.

Jeevan KC, who runs a grocery shop in Shankhamul, said he could not obtain sugar from his regular wholesaler for around 20 days.

“The wholesaler said there was no sugar in the warehouse, so I could not sell it for 20 days,” he said.

KC said he eventually purchased three sacks from Salt Trading Corporation. Although the corporation sold the sugar at Rs 105 per kg, he said transportation costs meant he had to sell it at a higher price.

Private importers say sugar is too expensive to import

Large private sugar importers say they are unable to bring sugar into Nepal because of high international prices and India’s restrictions on sugar exports.

A major importer, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the government’s 15 percent customs-duty concession was not enough to make imports commercially viable.

“India has restricted exports. If we import from a third country, the price is more than $620 per tonne,” the importer said. “The cost by the time it reaches Nepal comes to around Rs 155 per kg. How can we import sugar at Rs 155 and sell it cheaply?”

According to the importer, Salt Trading is currently the only institution capable of easing the shortage.

He also said recent floods and landslides disrupted transportation to Kathmandu, with large cargo vehicles unable to enter the Valley. With roads gradually reopening, he expects supplies to improve.

Government approves 25,000 tonnes of imports

As complaints over shortages and price increases intensified, the government approved the import of 25,000 tonnes of sugar at a one percent customs duty on September 3.

The sugar is being imported by state-owned Salt Trading Corporation and Food Management and Trading Company.

The aim is to increase supply, provide sugar to consumers at affordable prices and prevent further price manipulation in the market.

Salt Trading says it already has substantial stocks and that consumers do not need to panic.

The corporation is currently selling sugar at Rs 105 per kg, significantly below the reported retail price of Rs 170.

Salt Trading spokesperson Kumar Rajbhandari said the corporation is providing four to six kilograms of sugar per household.

“We are currently selling sugar at Rs 105 per kg and providing up to six kilograms to consumers,” he said.

According to Rajbhandari, Salt Trading currently has around 6,000 to 10,000 tonnes of sugar across the country. It is selling sugar through branches in Kathmandu, Birgunj, Bhairahawa, Biratnagar, Dhangadhi and Nepalgunj.

The corporation had targeted purchasing 12,000 tonnes of domestically produced sugar and has already procured around 6,000 tonnes.

It is also expecting 22,500 tonnes of sugar from India. Of this, 2,500 tonnes have already arrived and are being cleared through customs, another 2,500 tonnes are coming through the Biratnagar border, and 7,500 tonnes are in the pipeline.

Rajbhandari said transportation remains a challenge because of road disruptions caused by floods and landslides.

“Large-capacity vehicles have not been able to come because of the road conditions, but we are transporting sugar using smaller 10-tonne trucks,” he said.

He expects supplies to become easier after the roads reopen from October 1.

Food Company has 1,200 tonnes in stock

The Food Management and Trading Company has also been selling sugar at subsidised prices.

Its information officer Madhav Mishra said the company has around 1,200 tonnes of sugar in stock, while 100 tonnes imported from India has already arrived.

The company is also purchasing sugar from domestic industries and mills.

To ensure subsidised sugar reaches more consumers, it has imposed purchase quotas. Consumers in Kathmandu Valley can buy two kilograms per person, while those outside the Valley can receive two to four kilograms depending on availability.

The company is selling sugar for Rs 109 per kg in Kathmandu and Rs 110 per kg elsewhere, including transportation costs.

Mishra said the procurement process for the sugar approved at one percent customs duty has already begun and the imported sugar is expected to arrive before Dashain and Tihar.

Wholesalers see signs of improvement

Wholesalers say the market has started to improve after Salt Trading increased the amount of sugar supplied to them.

Balaju-based wholesaler Ishwor Shrestha said Salt Trading increased its wholesale quota from Monday.

“Sugar is gradually becoming easier to obtain. Salt Trading has increased the quantity supplied,” he said. “The market should come under control within the next two to four days.”

However, Shrestha said private-sector sugar remains considerably more expensive. Wholesalers currently have to pay between Rs 128 and Rs 130 per kg when buying from private suppliers.

Supply problem or artificial shortage?

The contrasting claims from consumers, traders and government agencies suggest that Nepal’s sugar crisis is not simply a matter of insufficient national supply.

While state-owned companies say they have thousands of tonnes of sugar available and are selling it at around Rs 105 to Rs 110 per kg, consumers in ordinary neighbourhood shops are paying as much as Rs 170.

Government outlets are also limited, meaning most consumers cannot spend hours waiting in line to buy a few kilograms of sugar. Their main source remains local grocery shops.

Consumers have accused some retailers of withholding sugar, selling it only to selected customers and refusing digital payments to avoid leaving records of inflated transactions.

If such practices are taking place, increasing government stocks alone will not solve the problem.

Effective market monitoring and action against hoarding and black-market sales will be essential to ensure that the additional sugar being imported actually reaches consumers at reasonable prices before Dashain, Tihar and Chhath.

title.rendered: Rohit Paudel, two UAE players fined for code of conduct breaches

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Nepal batter Rohit Paudel and UAE players Adeeb Usmani and Khuzaima Bin Tanveer have been penalised by the International Cricket Council (ICC) for breaches of the code of conduct during the final of the ACC Men’s Premier Cup.

The ICC fined Rohit Paudel and Usmani 15 percent of their match fees under Level 1 of the code of conduct.

The two players were found to have failed to follow the umpire’s instructions while attempting to settle a dispute between them during the 31st over of Nepal’s innings.

UAE’s Tanveer was fined 10 percent of his match fee after striking the stumps with his bat following his dismissal during the 46th over of the UAE innings.

One demerit point has also been added to each of the three players’ disciplinary records.

As the incidents were their first offences under the ICC Code of Conduct in the past 24 months, no further suspension has been imposed.

According to the ICC, all three players admitted the charges and accepted the proposed sanctions, meaning no formal hearing was required.

title.rendered: Samagaun youths announce hunger strike against climate injustice

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Youth from Samagaun in Gorkha’s Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1 have announced an indefinite hunger strike at Manaslu Base Camp against climate injustice and the growing risks faced by Himalayan communities.

Local youth leader Dawa Norbu Lama said the hunger strike will begin on September 18 and continue until October 4, demanding measures to reduce the risks caused by climate change.

The youths have submitted an eight-point memorandum addressed to Gorkha Chief District Officer, as well as to Ward Chair Karma Chhewang Lama, the local office of the Manaslu Conservation Area Project (MCAP) and the Samagaun Police Post.

The memorandum calls for an assessment of the growing risks posed by glacial lakes in and around the Manaslu Base Camp and Samagaun area.

According to the youths, several new glacial lakes have appeared this year, raising concerns about possible glacial lake outburst floods.

They have urged the government to conduct aerial monitoring and inspection of lakes around Pungen at the foot of Manaslu, Birendra Lake, Kal Tal, the lake at Ghunsarphuk, and three large high-risk glacial lakes at Nyochuthan, as well as other lakes in the Manaslu and Chum regions.

They have also called for the depth of all these lakes to be measured and for detailed studies to assess the risk of possible future glacial lake outbursts.

The memorandum demands the installation of mechanisms to measure water levels in lakes and rivers, along with warning systems such as sirens to alert local residents when risks increase.

The youths have also called for joint study and monitoring of glacial lakes and glaciers in Nepal and China.

They urged organisations working in the Himalayan region, including MCAP, to regularly monitor rising water levels in mountain areas across the country and take measures to protect communities from the resulting risks.

The memorandum also calls for climate change impacts to be incorporated into the curriculum of schools in Himalayan areas.

The youths have highlighted Nepal’s relatively small contribution to global pollution, estimated at just 0.4 percent, and demanded that Nepal intensify efforts to secure climate compensation and justice from developed countries responsible for a larger share of global pollution.

They have also urged national and international governmental and non-governmental organisations to hold climate-related meetings and seminars in Himalayan areas rather than limiting such programmes to cities, allowing decision-makers to directly experience the impact of climate change on mountain communities.

The youths have further called for preparations to protect Himalayan settlements from worsening climate impacts, citing forecasts of a stronger El Niño effect in 2027.

Lama said he would initially begin the hunger strike alone, but many other young people have expressed their willingness to join him.

The protestors say their demands are aimed at ensuring greater government attention to the immediate climate risks facing Himalayan communities and securing stronger measures for their protection.

title.rendered: Banks to start dispensing Rs 100 notes through ATMs

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Banks and financial institutions in Nepal will now start keeping Rs 100 notes in ATMs after Nepal Rastra Bank directed them to make the denomination available for withdrawal.

At present, most ATMs dispense only Rs 1,000 and Rs 500 notes. Under the new arrangement, customers will also be able to withdraw Rs 100 notes from ATMs equipped to support the denomination.

The central bank said the decision was taken after the public repeatedly called for smaller denominations to be made available through ATMs. Banks and financial institutions have also informed the central bank that they can technically make Rs 100 available through their ATM networks.

However, the availability of Rs 100 notes will initially be limited to some ATMs because most machines currently in operation in Nepal are older models.

Traditional ATMs can hold only two denominations of notes, while newer and more advanced machines can hold up to four denominations. As many banks still operate traditional ATMs, only a limited number of machines will be able to dispense the notes.

Nepal Rastra Bank said making Rs 100 available through ATMs during the Dashain festival would help reduce crowds at bank branches, where customers typically line up to exchange larger denominations for smaller notes.

According to the central bank, banks consulted on the matter have confirmed that distributing Rs 100 notes through ATMs is technically feasible.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

Sher Bahadur Deuba calls proposed Nepali Congress general convention ‘illegal’

Former Nepali Congress president Sher Bahadur Deuba has described the general convention being pursued by the party’s establishment faction as illegal, warning that he will not remain a silent spectator if the process moves ahead. In an appeal issued on Tuesday, Deuba urged party leaders and cadres not to participate in the convention, calling the move against the interests of the Nepali Congress.

607 tourists from 34 countries missing since Bhotekoshi floods

A total of 607 foreign tourists from 34 countries remain unaccounted for following the Bhotekoshi flash flood that struck Nepal on August 26. Suraj Ghimire, information officer at the Department of Tourism, told that the 607 foreign tourists, who were travelling to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, Gosaikunda and Mustang on the occasion of the Janai Purnima festival, have been out of contact since the disaster.

Govt orders mandatory release of transferred civil servants within stipulated period

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation, Federal Affairs and General Administration has directed all ministries, commissions, secretariats, the offices of the chief ministers and councils of ministers of all seven provinces, and local governments to compulsorily release civil servants who have been transferred within the prescribed period.

Foreign Minister Khanal says government committed to national-interest-driven foreign policy

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has said the government is fully committed to conducting Nepal’s foreign policy with national interest at its core. Speaking at the House of Representatives meeting on Tuesday, Khanal said the government’s foreign policy would be guided by Nepal’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, national security and long-term national interests.

David Warner to play Nepal Premier League for Kathmandu Gorkhas

Australian cricket star David Warner is set to play for Kathmandu Gorkhas in the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL). Kathmandu Gorkhas announced Warner’s signing through its social media platforms. The 39-year-old becomes the biggest international cricket star to feature in the NPL so far.

Real estate transactions nearly double, Kathmandu Metropolitan City records highest growth

The value of real estate transactions nearly doubled in the last fiscal year compared with the previous fiscal year. A total of Rs 720 billion worth of real estate transactions were recorded in fiscal year 2025/26, compared with Rs 386 billion in fiscal year 2024/25.

Nepal moves to guarantee compensation for flight cancellations, delays and lost baggage

Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel said the government is seeking to ensure by law minimum compensation and passenger rights in cases of flight cancellations, delays and lost baggage, among other issues. Speaking during a theoretical discussion on the Bill on the Liability of Domestic Airlines, 2083, at a meeting of the National Assembly’s Legislative Management Committee in Singha Durbar on Tuesday, Minister Paudel said the bill seeks to establish in law the legal liabilities of domestic airlines, passenger rights and compensation-related provisions.

title.rendered: RSP lawmaker Sunar’s remarks against IGP Karki removed from parliamentary record

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Remarks made by Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Khagendra Sunar against Nepal Police Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki have been removed from the parliamentary record.

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal directed the Federal Parliament Secretariat to remove the relevant portion of Sunar’s remarks made during the House of Representatives meeting on September 11.

“I direct the Secretariat to remove from the parliamentary record the wording between the phrase ‘never’ and the phrase ‘the allegation is serious’ spoken by Hon. Khagendra Sunar at the meeting of September 11,” Speaker Aryal said.

Ekram Giri, joint secretary and spokesperson of the Federal Parliament Secretariat, confirmed that some words used by Sunar in connection with IGP Karki had been removed from the record.

During the zero hour of the meeting, Sunar had drawn the government’s attention to allegations of corruption involving the police chief and questioned why he had not been dismissed or investigated.

He claimed Karki had been accused of corruption amounting to millions of rupees and alleged that complaints against the IGP had been piling up at the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) and the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament.

Sunar had said that Karki was accused of misappropriating funds meant for lower-ranking police personnel’s shoes and socks, among other allegations.

He also questioned why the government was protecting Karki and why no investigation had been initiated against him.

Sunar further contrasted the allegations against Karki with the dismissal of three ministers over what he described as relatively minor allegations, claiming that serious corruption complaints involving Karki, his wife and other senior officials had accumulated at the CIAA and the Public Accounts Committee.

The remarks were subsequently ordered removed from the official parliamentary record.

content.rendered:
American writer, visual artist, and literary translator Daisy Rockwell is best known globally for bringing South Asian masterpieces to a wider audience, most notably through her English translation of Geetanjali Shree’s Tomb of Sand, which won the International Booker Prize in 2022.

Working primarily with Hindi and Urdu literature, Rockwell recently visited Nepal as a mentor for a literary translation workshop organised by the Department of Language and Mass Communication at Kathmandu University in collaboration with South Asian Literature in Translation (SALT) at the University of Chicago.

During her visit, Rockwell sat down with Onlinekhabar to discuss the impact of artificial intelligence on translation, her upcoming projects, and the nuances of preserving cultural voice across languages. 

Excerpts

You have spent years translating Hindi and Urdu literature into English. What first drew you to South Asian literature?

I started learning Hindi in college simply because I liked learning languages and wanted to study one I knew nothing about. Having previously studied French, German and Greek, Hindi felt entirely different, even if it is distantly related as an Indo-European language. In the U.S. university system, you can explore freely, so I thought I would just try Hindi out. I didn’t imagine I would get so deeply into it and spend the rest of my life working on it.

You conducted a literary translation workshop in Nepal. What potential do you see in Nepali literature reaching international readers through translation? 

It is difficult to get international publishers interested in South Asian literature in translation, but initiatives like the International Booker Prize are helping to make headway. Organisations like South Asian Literature in Translation (SALT) are doing a great job training translators and bringing Western publishers to South Asia to spark interest.

Nepali literature has a rich tradition spanning centuries that deserves to be known globally, not just in the UK or US, but across English-reading regions like Singapore and Nigeria. Beyond SALT’s efforts, prizes like the Armory Square Ventures (ASV) Prize, recently won by Rohan Chhetri for a Nepali translation project, Flowers of the Siris Tree, a translation of Shirishko Phool by Parijat, are creating direct pathways by guaranteeing publication with U.S. presses like Open Letter Books. 

A translator is often described as a bridge between cultures. What do you think gets lost when literature travels from one language and culture to another? 

Translators don’t usually think in terms of what is lost; we focus on what is being gained. If you really want to know what gets lost: everything. The original language, culture, and script are all gone. The translator’s job is to build something new that allows readers to feel as though they are experiencing the original work. In that sense, every translation is a kind of illusion.

What are some common mistakes that young or emerging translators make? 

Out of a fear of losing something, new translators often cling too tightly to literalism. But accuracy isn’t just about matching dictionary definitions word-for-word. Words together create a feeling and a world; true accuracy lies in recreating that feeling. In South Asia, emerging translators sometimes carry a fear rooted in colonial history, a worry of doing violence to the text by bringing it into English. I remind them that the original text remains untouched and intact; translation is simply an attempt to recreate its life in a new medium.

AI tools are rapidly changing the translation industry. How do you see AI changing literary translation in particular? 

AI is consistently wrong about 30 percent of the time, regardless of the task, whether it is solving a math problem, summarising history, or translating text.

The issue is that people now realise these outputs contain errors, so they hire human translators to fix them. Editing an AI-generated draft actually creates more work than starting from scratch. When a human translator makes a mistake, you can usually spot it immediately because the language feels awkward. AI, however, produces text that appears completely smooth and plausible on the surface, forcing an editor to meticulously compare every line against the original text to catch hidden mistakes.

For languages with smaller digital footprints—such as Nepali, Urdu, or Tamil—far less training material has been fed into these systems, making their outputs significantly worse. When AI encounters a word or concept it does not understand, it won’t flag the difficulty like a human translator would; it simply hallucinates and makes things up to maintain the illusion of a flawless translation.

What can a human translator understand that AI cannot? 

Feelings, culture, history, and vibes. AI can’t do a vibe check!

How much communication do you prefer to have with the author while translating their work? 

It depends on whether they are alive and whether they speak English. When working with Geetanjali Shree, who speaks English fluently, she had strong opinions and reviewed the translation closely. Her writing style is so idiosyncratic that her input was invaluable. However, it can occasionally be tricky when authors attempt to rewrite sentences in English that were already fine in translation.

Where does a translator need to draw the line and maintain independence from the author? 

At a certain point, you have to finalise the work for the publisher. Translator Maureen Freely, who translated several books by Orhan Pamuk, once told Pamuk directly: “I don’t work for you; I work for the publisher.” 

Ultimately, the translator’s primary responsibility is to the reader and the text in the target language.

How do you balance staying faithful to an author’s intentions with making creative decisions that you feel are necessary in the target language? 

Translators are almost like mediums, channelling an author’s voice. You have to ask yourself: “If this author were writing directly in English, how would they express this?”

You also have to ensure the text sounds compelling. If it doesn’t read well in the target language, the translation hasn’t succeeded, regardless of how literally accurate it might be.

What keeps you excited about translation after all these years, and what still surprises you about the process? 

Every book and author teaches you something new about writing. Translation involves immense drudgery, but there is a magical moment at the end when everything is polished and comes together, creating a finished piece of art in a new language. 

Lastly, what are you up to lately?

I am currently working on a collection of Urdu horror stories from the 1930s by Hijab Imtiaz Ali. Her work blends horror with romance.

Next, I am about to start translating Geetanjali Shree’s latest novel, which, as expected with her work, is a brilliantly wild piece of writing.

Finally, I am thrilled to share that I have secured the translation rights for Aag Ka Darya (River of Fire) by Qurratulain Hyder. Tracking down rights holders is a massive, behind-the-scenes effort that non-translators rarely see, so obtaining permission for this has been a long-time dream of mine.

River of Fire is considered the great Partition novel in Urdu, sweeping across 2,000 years of history. Hyder previously published her own English version, but she altered it significantly and cut nearly 200 pages from the original. I plan to produce a complete retranslation of the original text.

title.rendered: Foreign Minister Khanal says government committed to national-interest-driven foreign policy

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has said the government is fully committed to conducting Nepal’s foreign policy with national interest at its core.

Speaking at the House of Representatives meeting on Tuesday, Khanal said the government’s foreign policy would be guided by Nepal’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, national security and long-term national interests.

Addressing questions over his remark during his recent India visit that the “current government has no old baggage”, Khanal said the statement referred to freeing foreign policy and diplomacy from the internal political polarisation and narrow political use seen in the past.

He clarified that the phrase “old baggage” was not directed at Nepal’s history, national heritage, sovereignty, territorial integrity, independence, national interests or the preservation of historical documents.

He said interpreting the remark as being against continuity of the state and government or Nepal’s national heritage would be an exaggeration.

Khanal said the “baggage” he had referred to was the past practice of using relations with neighbouring countries as an instrument for domestic political gains and losses.

“The government is determined to abandon that practice and move forward,” Khanal said, explaining the message he intended to convey through his remark.

Khanal was responding to a question from lawmaker Sita Thapaliya regarding his statement during bilateral talks on his India visit.

The foreign minister also said the government wants to take Nepal’s relations with neighbouring and friendly countries in a transformative direction based on mutual equality, respect, trust and economic partnership.

He said the government would not allow prejudice, narrow-mindedness or unnecessary distrust to dictate its approach to foreign relations.

title.rendered: Govt orders mandatory release of transferred civil servants within stipulated period

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation, Federal Affairs and General Administration has directed all ministries, commissions, secretariats, the offices of the chief ministers and councils of ministers of all seven provinces, and local governments to compulsorily release civil servants who have been transferred within the prescribed period.

The ministry issued the directive after finding that transferred employees were being retained at their previous offices under various pretexts and were continuing to receive salaries and allowances from those offices even after their transfers had been decided.

In a circular issued on Monday, the ministry said the Civil Service Regulations require transferred employees to be released within the stipulated period. If an employee is not released within that period and continues to receive salary and allowances from the previous office, the amount paid beyond the prescribed joining period will be recovered from the concerned office chief and accounts chief responsible for the payment.

According to the ministry, employees have recently been denied release even after the expiry of the joining period set by the regulations. Some have continued working at their previous offices under various excuses, while their salaries and allowances have also continued to be paid from those offices.

The ministry said such practices have created serious problems in service delivery at the local level by contributing to shortages of human resources.

It has therefore instructed all concerned bodies to release transferred civil servants within the period prescribed by law, warning that failure to do so will invite action in accordance with the law.

The ministry has also requested the Office of the Auditor General to treat salary and allowance payments made to transferred employees without releasing them as arrears during audits.

Similarly, it has asked the Financial Comptroller General’s Office to direct subordinate Treasury and Accounts Controller Offices to assist in implementing the transfer decisions.

The ministry said the move is aimed at ending a long-standing situation in which transfer decisions were made but not implemented, and is expected to improve administrative stability and ensure more effective implementation of transfer decisions.

title.rendered: How one Nepali migrant turned hardship into hope

content.rendered:
When Keshu Thapa went to visit a Nepali in prison in Malaysia, he expected the difficult part to be the visit itself. Instead, what happened after he left stayed with him for years.

The prison was far from the city. When Thapa came out, there was no taxi or bus available to take him back. With nowhere to go, he eventually slept on the ground.

“I thought, if this happened to me, how difficult must it be for others?” he recalls.

That night became more than an unpleasant experience. It became a question that would eventually change the direction of his life.

On August 21, 2017, Thapa and a group of friends established Jan Uddhar Kendra Malaysia, an organisation dedicated to helping Nepalis facing difficult circumstances in the country.

Since then, the organisation has helped around 400 Nepalis return home.

Some were mentally unwell. Some were suffering from paralysis. Others were undocumented, stranded or simply had no one to turn to.

For Thapa, helping them is personal.

He knows what it means to arrive in a foreign country with little money, little understanding of the language and no certainty about what the future holds.

More than three decades earlier, he had been one of those migrant workers.

A young man looking for another way

Thapa grew up in a modest farming family in Galkot, Baglung.

His childhood was simple — school, farm work and playing with friends in the village. He passed his SLC examination in 2047 BS and moved to Butwal to continue his education.

He enrolled in an IA programme but failed one subject. He was unable to clear the backlog, and gradually his education came to an end.

“I studied in Butwal from 1991 to 1993. But I had a backlog in one subject in IA. I could not clear it, and it remained unfinished,” he says.

At the time, his family’s financial situation was not strong. Continuing his education seemed increasingly difficult, while finding a way to earn money had become a necessity.

Before leaving Nepal, Thapa worked as a schoolteacher in Butwal.

The work was respectable, but the salary was small and the demands were many. He began thinking about what his future might look like if he stayed.

He decided to leave.

Malaysia was not the destination he imagined

Around 1993–94, Thapa travelled to Malaysia with two or three friends.

Malaysia was not yet the familiar destination it would later become for thousands of Nepali workers. For Thapa, the journey itself was an adventure into the unknown.

He travelled through Singapore, where he stayed for about a week before continuing to Malaysia.

“At that time, we could get a visa on arrival. We stayed in Singapore for a week and then came to Malaysia,” he recalls.

The first days were difficult.

He could not understand the language. The culture was unfamiliar. Work was hard to find and even harder to understand. But there was one thing that helped Nepalis at the time. They were known as Gurkhas.

“Back then, people did not really know Nepalis. They knew us as Gurkhas,” Thapa says. “There were very few Nepalis, and the respect they received was different. Once people heard ‘Gurkha’, they would often give them work.”

Thapa found a job at a furniture company. He started at the bottom, working as a labourer for eight hours a day and earning 17.30 Malaysian ringgit. He remembers earning the equivalent of only around Rs 480 to Rs 500 a day. But he kept working.

Within four years, he had risen from labourer to supervisor. Then the 1997 global economic crisis disrupted his work, forcing him to return to Nepal.

Trying to build a life back home

Back in Nepal, Thapa turned to business. He began importing clothes from Malaysia and selling them in Nepal. For around five years, he tried to make the clothing business work. It was not easy.

Customs, taxes and credit sales created constant problems. He would pay for goods before bringing them into Nepal, only to sell them on credit. Getting the money back was another struggle.

“For small traders like us, it was difficult to sustain a business in Nepal,” he says. “We would bring goods by paying in cash but sell them on credit. There was no certainty about when the money would come back.”

His regular trips to Malaysia — sometimes every two or three months — had already kept him connected to the country. When the business failed to develop as he had hoped, he decided to return to Malaysia.

In 2003, he went back. This time, he began a cleaning services company in Kuala Lumpur. The business survived. It eventually gave him the stability he had been searching for and, perhaps more importantly, the freedom to think beyond his own livelihood.

Pain of others

Living in Malaysia for years, Thapa saw a different side of migration.

He encountered Nepalis who had ended up in prison, workers living without legal status, people who had fallen seriously ill and those who had become stranded without the means to return home.

For many, the problem was not simply a lack of money. It was the absence of someone to help. His own experience outside the prison made him understand that helplessness.

That is why, in 2017, he decided to do something about it.

Jan Uddhar Kendra began modestly. Within a few months of its establishment, Thapa and his friends had bought tickets for five Nepalis and helped them return home. The numbers grew. One person became dozens. Dozens became hundreds.

Since 2017, around 400 Nepalis have been rescued and sent back to Nepal.

Some journeys home are harder than others

Not every rescue ends with a flight home. Some Nepalis have died in Malaysia, leaving families faced with the painful question of how to bring their loved ones back.

In four cases, Thapa helped arrange cremations in Malaysia because the families or circumstances made it impossible to send the bodies to Nepal.

“We take permission from the embassy and the municipality and carry out the final rites according to Hindu or Buddhist traditions,” he says.

The organisation also helps sick Nepalis access treatment, manages the remains of deceased workers, assists with the immersion of ashes and provides financial support in some cases.

Jan Uddhar Kendra was formally registered with the Malaysian government in 2019. Yet its work has remained rooted in a simple idea — that a Nepali who is alone in a foreign country should not have to face a crisis alone.

Built from small contributions

Thapa does not describe himself as someone who became a social worker because he had great wealth. He says his own hardships pushed him towards the work.

“I had suffered myself. When I had to sleep on the ground after visiting someone in prison, that experience shook me,” he says. “I did not want others to go through the same hardship, so I started social work.”

He also believes that social service requires two things — money and genuine interest.

“Social service cannot continue without funds, and it cannot continue without interest either,” he says.

Jan Uddhar Kendra does not rely entirely on large donors.

Nepali workers themselves contribute what they can. Funds are raised through small contributions and activities such as selling Dhaka topis.

It is a fitting model for an organisation whose work is centred on ordinary Nepalis.

What life abroad taught him

Thapa left Nepal as a young man because he needed to earn. He arrived in Malaysia with little money and few certainties.

Over the next 32 years, he experienced almost every side of migrant life — the struggle of being a labourer, the satisfaction of rising through the ranks, the frustration of losing a job, the uncertainty of running a business and, eventually, the stability of building one that lasted. But his greatest sense of achievement does not come from the business he built.

It comes from the people he has helped.

Today, Thapa continues to run his cleaning services company in Malaysia while serving as the president of Jan Uddhar Kendra.

For thousands of Nepalis, his name has become associated not simply with business, but with help when there is nowhere else to turn.

“Earning money is for personal life,” he says. “But being able to do something for others — that is the real wealth.”

For a young man who once left Baglung hoping only to build a better life, that may be the most unexpected chapter of his journey.

title.rendered: 4 killed in EV accident in Makwanpur’s Indrasarowar

content.rendered:
Hetauda, September 15

Four people were killed when an electric vehicle (EV) travelling from Hetauda to Kathmandu met with an accident in Salle Sukoura of Indrasarowar Rural Municipality-2, Makwanpur.

According to the Area Police Office, Bhimphedi, four of the eight people travelling in the vehicle died at the scene, while the remaining four were rescued.

One of those rescued was taken to Hetauda Hospital, while the others were taken towards Kathmandu, the Area Police Office said.

The accident occurred at around 2 pm on Tuesday. The vehicle reportedly fell about 500 metres down a steep slope from the road.

Further details of the accident, including the identities of those killed and injured, have yet to be released.

title.rendered: Sher Bahadur Deuba calls proposed Nepali Congress general convention ‘illegal’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Former Nepali Congress president Sher Bahadur Deuba has described the general convention being pursued by the party’s establishment faction as illegal, warning that he will not remain a silent spectator if the process moves ahead.

In an appeal issued on Tuesday, Deuba urged party leaders and cadres not to participate in the convention, calling the move against the interests of the Nepali Congress.

“I cannot remain a silent spectator when actions are taken to weaken the Nepali Congress,” Deuba said in his appeal.

Expressing serious concern over the latest dispute and differences within the party, Deuba accused the group advocating the general convention of attempting to move ahead unilaterally in violation of the party’s procedures, statute, established practices and decisions of the Central Working Committee.

He argued that proceeding with the convention while its legality remains under consideration at the Supreme Court would go against established procedures, the party statute and legal principles.

Deuba also pointed to the Supreme Court’s decision to grant leave for a review petition, saying it demonstrates that serious constitutional and legal questions remain surrounding the proposed convention.

He accused the Gagan Thapa-led faction of attempting to move forward while ignoring experienced party leaders and a majority of party members.

Such a tendency, he warned, would not strengthen the Nepali Congress but instead weaken the party.

Sher Bahadur Deuba also said party leaders and the public had yet to receive a convincing answer as to why a special convention was necessary in the first place.

The former party president clarified that he had no personal desire for any party position or responsibility.

However, he said he would continue to serve if the party or the state felt that his experience was needed.

Deuba argued that, as the duly elected president of the 14th General Convention, he has a legal, political and moral responsibility to complete the 15th General Convention and hand over leadership.

He called for resolving the dispute through consensus and cooperation, while signalling that he would oppose any attempt to proceed with the proposed convention unilaterally.

title.rendered: Nepal moves to guarantee compensation for flight cancellations, delays and lost baggage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel said the government is seeking to ensure by law minimum compensation and passenger rights in cases of flight cancellations, delays and lost baggage, among other issues.

Speaking during a theoretical discussion on the Bill on the Liability of Domestic Airlines, 2083, at a meeting of the National Assembly’s Legislative Management Committee in Singha Durbar on Tuesday, Minister Paudel said the bill seeks to establish in law the legal liabilities of domestic airlines, passenger rights and compensation-related provisions.

He said the government has proposed increasing the existing insurance liability of around US$20,000 to US$100,000 in line with international standards. He said passengers should be prepared for the possibility that airfares could increase to some extent in the future as a result of the higher insurance coverage.

Minister Paudel said the government was also seeking, for the first time, to establish a legal basis for compensation if an aircraft accident causes death or property damage to people on the ground or at their homes who are not passengers.

He said issues concerning the separation of regulatory and service-provider functions and airport operations would be addressed through a separate bill concerning the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal.

title.rendered: UML chief whip objects to Home Minister walking across House while MP was speaking

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

CPN-UML Chief Whip Ain Bahadur Mahar has raised a point of order after Home Minister Sudan Gurung walked across the House while a lawmaker was speaking.

During Tuesday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, Gurung walked in front of Yubraj Dulal, chief whip of the Nepali Communist Party, while Dulal was addressing the House.

Mahar drew the attention of Speaker Dol Prasad Ghimire to the incident, saying it violated the rules of the House.

“When Honourable Yubraj Dulal was speaking, the Honourable Home Minister walked through the space between the Speaker’s chair and the member who was speaking,” Mahar said.

He referred to Rule 20(6) of the House of Representatives Regulations, which prohibits members from walking between the Speaker’s chair and a member who is addressing the House.

Mahar said former Prime Minister Balendra Shah had also violated the same rule in the past.

He urged members to follow parliamentary rules and maintain the dignity of the House.

What does Rule 20 say?

Rule 20 of the House of Representatives Regulations lays down rules of conduct that members must follow during a meeting.

Under the provision, members are required to stand and show respect when the Speaker enters the meeting hall.

Members may leave the meeting hall only after the meeting has been adjourned and the Speaker has left.

Members are required to speak only after being given permission by the Speaker.

When speaking, members must address the Speaker and, unless otherwise directed by the Speaker, speak while standing at their designated place.

The rules also state that members should not leave their seats while the Speaker is addressing the House and should listen attentively.

Members are specifically prohibited from walking between the Speaker’s chair and a member who is speaking.

The rules further prohibit members from sitting or standing with their backs turned towards the Speaker’s chair.

Members are also barred from engaging in any activity that obstructs a member who is speaking, disrupts the dignity of the House or creates disorder during the meeting.

title.rendered: Real estate transactions nearly double, Kathmandu Metropolitan City records highest growth

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The value of real estate transactions nearly doubled in the last fiscal year compared with the previous fiscal year.

A total of Rs 720 billion worth of real estate transactions were recorded in fiscal year 2025/26, compared with Rs 386 billion in fiscal year 2024/25.

In the fourth quarter of the last fiscal year alone, real estate transactions worth Rs 275 billion were recorded. In the same period of the previous fiscal year, transactions worth Rs 127.61 billion were recorded.

According to Nepal Rastra Bank, the total number of real estate transactions increased by 4.74 per cent in fiscal year 2025/26 compared with the previous fiscal year. The number of such transactions had declined by 1.84 per cent in fiscal year 2024/25.

In the fourth quarter of the last fiscal year, the total number of real estate transactions increased by 12.25 per cent compared with the same period of the previous fiscal year. In the same quarter of the previous fiscal year, the number had increased by 14.65 per cent.

The number of transactions involving deed registration increased by 12.28 per cent in the last fiscal year. In the fourth quarter of the previous fiscal year, such transactions had increased by 15.45 per cent.

The number of transactions involving relinquishment deeds increased by 22.88 per cent in the last fiscal year, compared with an 8.15 per cent increase in the fourth quarter of the previous fiscal year. The total area of land involved in transactions increased by 15.41 per cent in the last fiscal year, whereas it had declined by 2.98 per cent in the same period of the previous fiscal year.

Revenue collected from real estate transactions increased by 48.26 per cent in the last fiscal year. Such revenue had increased by 23.45 per cent in the previous fiscal year.

Capital gains tax collected from real estate transactions increased by 63.22 per cent in the last fiscal year, compared with a 29.98 per cent increase in the previous fiscal year. Bank lending to the real estate sector increased by 6.93 per cent in the last fiscal year, compared with a 5.86 per cent increase in the previous fiscal year.

Provincial real estate transactions

In the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025/26, Bagmati Province recorded the highest increase in the number of relinquishment transactions, at 69.38 per cent, while the number declined by 3.44 per cent in Madhesh Province. Such transactions increased in all other provinces.

The total area of land involved in real estate transactions increased by 50.24 per cent in Bagmati Province, the highest among the provinces, compared with the same period of the previous fiscal year. Madhesh Province recorded the highest decline, at 6.19 per cent.

The total value of real estate transactions increased in all seven provinces in the last fiscal year compared with the previous fiscal year. The highest increase was recorded in Bagmati Province, at 175.33 per cent, while Madhesh Province recorded the lowest increase, at 31.98 per cent.

Plots measuring 2.5 to 10 annas accounted for the highest number of transactions in all seven provinces in the last fiscal year. In the same period of the previous fiscal year, plots larger than 20 annas accounted for the highest number of transactions in Madhesh Province, while plots measuring 2.5 to 10 annas were the most commonly traded size in all other provinces.

Real estate transactions in metropolitan cities

In the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025/26, Kathmandu Metropolitan City recorded the highest increase in the number of real estate transactions, at 155.74 per cent. It was followed by Lalitpur Metropolitan City at 136.92 per cent, Pokhara Metropolitan City at 108.71 per cent, Bharatpur Metropolitan City at 63.04 per cent, Biratnagar Metropolitan City at 47.59 per cent and Birgunj Metropolitan City at 29.19 per cent.

The total area of land involved in transactions increased in all metropolitan cities in the last fiscal year compared with the previous fiscal year. Kathmandu Metropolitan City recorded the highest increase, at 208.22 per cent, while Birgunj Metropolitan City recorded the lowest, at 13.31 per cent.

The total value of real estate transactions also increased in all metropolitan cities compared with the previous fiscal year. Kathmandu Metropolitan City recorded the highest increase, at 217.40 per cent.

Real estate transactions in sub-metropolitan cities

In the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025/26, the number of real estate transactions increased in all sub-metropolitan cities except Kalaiya. Dhangadhi Sub-Metropolitan City recorded the highest increase, at 73.16 per cent, while the number of transactions in Kalaiya remained unchanged.

The total area of land involved in transactions increased in all sub-metropolitan cities. Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City recorded the highest increase, at 104.16 per cent.

Similarly, the total value of real estate transactions increased in all 11 sub-metropolitan cities compared with the previous fiscal year. Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City recorded the highest increase, at 186.80 per cent.
