title.rendered: UML criticises government’s disaster response, says ‘more could have been done’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The opposition CPN-UML has urged the government not to adopt an attitude that it can handle disasters on its own.

Speaking during Tuesday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, UML lawmaker Padma Kumari Aryal criticised the government for failing to carry out some of the immediate measures required following the floods.

Aryal said the government should have sought assistance through a public appeal, formal requests and diplomatic initiatives immediately after the disaster.

“The government should have sought support through an immediate public appeal, requests and diplomatic initiatives. We failed on that front,” she said.

She also said the government could have contacted and mobilised engineers and experts from schools, colleges and other institutions to support disaster response efforts.

Addressing Prime Minister Balen Shah, Aryal said all political parties share the same concern for the country and its people.

“The government should have learned from previous disaster experiences and immediately called an all-party meeting for discussion. That too did not happen,” she said.

“I want to say this — please do not have the arrogance of thinking that ‘I alone am enough’ during this disaster. Prime Minister, you cannot say that you love the country and its people more than we do,” Aryal said.

She clarified that her criticism did not mean the government had done nothing in response to the disaster.

“I am not saying that nothing has been done. I am saying that more could have been done,” she said.

title.rendered: Congress sets nomination fees for leadership positions from ward to central level

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The Nepali Congress has issued its election directive, specifying the nomination fees for candidates contesting leadership positions at various levels of the party.

According to the directive, a candidate seeking to become the party’s central president must pay a nomination fee of Rs 40,000. Candidates for the Congress presidency must also have 10 general convention representatives as proposers and 10 as supporters.

The directive also specifies nomination fees for candidates contesting positions from the ward level to the central office-bearers. The fees have been approved by a meeting of the Central Working Committee.

Candidates for central vice president and general secretary must have seven proposers and seven supporters. Candidates for central joint general secretary must have five proposers and five supporters, while candidates for central member must have three proposers and three supporters.

The nomination fee has been set at Rs 30,000 for vice president and general secretary, Rs 20,000 for joint general secretary and Rs 11,000 for central member.

For provincial positions, the Congress has set the nomination fee at Rs 20,000 for provincial president, Rs 15,000 for vice president and general secretary, Rs 10,000 for joint general secretary and Rs 5,000 for provincial members.

title.rendered: France hands over emergency relief supplies to Nepal following August floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The Embassy of France in Nepal has handed over emergency humanitarian supplies to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) to support relief and recovery efforts following the devastating floods of August 26.

The French government mobilised assistance to support Nepal’s emergency response mechanisms and communities severely affected by the floods.

The relief consignment includes floor mats, hygiene kits, kitchen kits, water purification tablets, solar lamps and urgent and general medicine kits.

The supplies were provided in response to requests from the Government of Nepal through the European Union’s Civil Protection Mechanism.

French Ambassador-designate Françoise Puig-Inza handed over the relief materials to Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun.

Speaking on the occasion, Puig-Inza said France stood in solidarity with the people and government of Nepal following the disaster.

“In the wake of this tragic disaster, France stands in solidarity with the people and Government of Nepal,” she said.

She added that the emergency assistance, along with further support planned by France, reflected the commitment of France and the European Union to supporting local authorities in their immediate relief efforts and helping vulnerable communities recover and rebuild.

In addition to the in-kind assistance, the French government will contribute to international relief efforts for people affected by the floods through UN agencies, the International Federation of the Red Cross and French international NGOs Action Contre la Faim and Triangle Génération Humanitaire.

The organisations are already deployed in affected areas and are supporting humanitarian operations on the ground.

The French Embassy also expressed its condolences to the families affected by the disaster and to the Government of Nepal.

title.rendered: Meera Rana to hold solo concert in support of cancer patients

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Veteran singer Mira Rana is set to perform at a solo musical evening on September 20, where she will present some of her timeless songs.

Proceeds from the event will be used to support cancer patients. Rana herself is a cancer survivor. After losing her husband to cancer, she established the Meera Rana Cancer Society to support people affected by the disease.

The 75-year-old singer will perform at the Nepal Academy in Kamaladi. The programme will feature around two dozen songs performed or composed by Rana. Other artists, including Shambhujeet Baskota, Ram Bhakta Jojiju, Kapil Lohani, Krishna Gopal Shrestha, Yogendra Upadhyay, Tshering Bhutia, and cancer-survivor singers Tara Thapa and Sangeeta Thapa, will also perform.

Nisha Deshar, Rupi Singh, Mandavi Tripathi, Sabina Karki, Itu Jojiju, Shital Thapa and Yunisha Deshar will also perform Rana’s songs.

Rana will perform songs she recorded with Swar Samrat Narayan Gopal, including “Timi Deu Ya Nadeu,” “Mero Jovan Laijau,” “Aankhaima Kasaiko Tasbir Basechha” and “Bainiko Daya Chha Bhane.”

She will also perform “Nachdeu Maichyang” and “Sindhupalchok Jilla Ma,” which she recorded with Baskota, as well as “Madal Ghanaghan Ghankaun Ki” and “Lek Phulyo Laligurans,” which she recorded with Kumar Basnet.

Rana’s solo songs, including “Makhamali Cholo Chahidaina,” “Mat Chadheko Sanjh,” “Nashalu Raat,” “Mero Pauma Aaja,” “Samda Sada Shiva,” “Birsiara Maile Pheri,” “Aajsamma Jasari Banera Aaye”, and “Mero Phullalai Basanta Bhayo,” will also be performed at the event.

title.rendered: Himalayan flood: When the dead are still waiting to come home

content.rendered:
The Himalayan flood came with the force of a tsunami, tearing through settlements with water, mud and debris and leaving behind homes without families, families without answers and communities struggling to understand the scale of what they have lost. The full number of people missing remains uncertain. Some may still be buried beneath layers of mud and debris, while others may have been trapped in tunnels or swept downstream by swollen rivers. As recovery teams continue their search, bodies have been carried far from the places where people lived and into areas such as Chitwan.

Chitwan, known for its forests, rivers and wildlife, has therefore become an unexpected destination for the dead. Bodies recovered from rivers are arriving from places hundreds of kilometres away, placing additional pressure on hospitals and temporary facilities that were never designed to manage such a large number of remains at once. Decomposition is also making identification increasingly difficult. At the same time, families continue to arrive with photographs, names and whatever information they have, hoping that one of the recovered bodies might finally tell them what happened to someone who has not returned home.

For these families, the disaster has not entered its aftermath. It is still unfolding.

This has left Nepal confronting a question that no disaster response system wants to face: What happens when there are more dead than our systems can hold?

An overwhelmed system is not an indifferent one

The decision to bury unidentified bodies is understandably painful for families still waiting for their loved ones. But it also comes at a time when hospitals and temporary facilities are running out of space, recovery teams are still bringing in bodies, and decomposition is making identification harder. In such circumstances, temporary burial may become necessary. The concern, however, is what happens to the identity of those buried.

Authorities say the bodies are being assigned identification numbers, documented, and subjected to DNA testing, with other evidence preserved before burial so they can be identified and returned to their families later. This is important, but it will only provide reassurance if these records are carefully maintained and can actually be used when a match is found.

What this situation really shows is that Nepal was not fully prepared to manage death on this scale. The challenge is no longer only recovering bodies, but also making sure that every person who is buried without a name can still be found later. A body may have to be buried, but its identity must never be lost. A grave may be temporary. The record must never be.

For families, identification is part of mourning

For the government, an unidentified body may become a case number. For a family, it is someone they love: a mother, father, child, spouse, sibling or friend. For families still waiting for missing relatives, finding an unidentified body may not bring relief. It can bring another painful question: Could this be my person?

That uncertainty makes it difficult to grieve or move forward. Families are left not knowing whether their loved one is dead, still missing, trapped somewhere or among the remains recovered in another district. This is why identification is more than a forensic or administrative process. It is part of humanitarian care. Giving a person their name back can also give a family the certainty they need to begin mourning.

This matters even more in Nepal, where death and final rites are closely connected to family, culture and religion. Families may fear that burying someone before identification could make it harder to recover the remains or carry out the final rites according to their wishes.

At the same time, authorities are dealing with a real capacity problem. Facilities designed for routine deaths cannot suddenly manage hundreds of bodies after a major disaster. There may be no simple answer, but the response must balance this practical reality with the basic dignity and rights of those who have died and the families still waiting for them.

Public health should protect dignity, not erase it

The government has pointed to decomposition, limited storage and health concerns as reasons for burying unidentified bodies. These are real concerns, but the public health argument should be placed in context. Dead bodies after natural disasters do not automatically cause epidemics. The greater immediate risks usually come from contaminated water, poor sanitation, overcrowding, injuries, displacement and disrupted healthcare.

This does not mean the management of human remains is unimportant. Decomposition, safe handling and the psychological impact on families all require proper attention. But public health cannot be reduced to controlling biological risks. It also includes dignity, mental well-being and the needs of affected families.

A response that protects the living while leaving families without answers about their dead is incomplete. Nepal does not have to choose between public health and human dignity. A responsible response must protect both.

Nepal is confronting a second disaster: identification

The first disaster was the flood itself. The second could be what happens when people disappear from the system even after their bodies have been recovered.

A person can disappear once when the flood carries them away. They can disappear again if their remains are never connected to a name, a family or a reliable record. That second disappearance is preventable.

Nepal has begun collecting DNA and other identifying information, but identification cannot stop there. Every unidentified person needs a proper record of where and when the remains were found, photographs, personal belongings, biological samples, an identification number and the exact place of burial. Families also need a clear way to report missing relatives, provide DNA samples and receive updates, even after the immediate disaster response has ended.

The government’s assurance that identified remains can later be exhumed and returned to families is important. But for families to trust that promise, there must be a system they can access and follow.

For someone standing in Chitwan with a photograph of a missing family member, reassurance from Kathmandu is not enough. They need to know that the person they are searching for has not been forgotten.

What does Nepal owe the families waiting for answers?

The government’s responsibility does not end once an unidentified body is buried. It continues until that person is identified or there is a documented and transparent conclusion to the search.

Families need clear information about where recovered bodies are being kept, how identification is being conducted, whether DNA samples have been collected, where unidentified remains have been buried and how relatives can provide information or biological samples. They also need to know what happens when a match is eventually found, who will coordinate exhumation and who will take responsibility for returning the remains to the family.

These may sound like bureaucratic questions, but for a grieving family, they are deeply personal. They determine whether a mother can finally perform the last rites for her son, whether a husband can know what happened to his wife or whether parents can finally stop waiting for a child who will never come home.

This is where the humanitarian dimension of disaster management becomes especially important. Families are not merely recipients of information. They are part of the response. Their knowledge, records, photographs, personal belongings and biological samples can all contribute to identification. They therefore need to be treated as participants whose rights and emotional well-being matter throughout the process.

What this disaster exposes about Nepal’s preparedness

The most uncomfortable lesson from this disaster is not simply that Nepal has had to bury unidentified bodies. It is that the country appears unprepared to manage death on this scale.

Disaster preparedness rightly focuses on search and rescue, evacuation, medical care and relief. But mass-fatality management is just as important. Nepal needs to ask whether hospitals can handle a sudden surge of bodies, whether temporary mortuary capacity can be created quickly, whether forensic and DNA services can be expanded during a crisis, and whether missing persons can be matched with unidentified remains across districts.

Most importantly, families must be part of this system.

Nepal needs a national mass-fatality plan connecting hospitals, police, forensic services, local governments and disaster authorities, with clear procedures for identification, documentation, storage, burial and later recovery of remains. These responsibilities must be decided before the next disaster, not while families are already waiting for answers.

Preparedness must include death just as seriously as it includes survival.

The dead are part of disaster response, too

Temporary burial may become unavoidable when facilities are overwhelmed and remains are deteriorating. But burial must not mean the end of identification. Nepal can recognise the limits of its emergency capacity while still ensuring that every unidentified person remains traceable and every family has a chance to find their loved one.

Disaster response should not be measured only by how many people are rescued, but also by how the state treats those it could not save. Their bodies must be identified, their families informed, and their dignity respected.

The flood may have taken away homes, livelihoods and lives. It must not take away names.

Nepal must prepare not only to save the living, but also to account for the dead. The real measure of a humanitarian response is not simply finding a place to bury the dead, but building a system that ensures they can still be found.

title.rendered: Can your smartwatch detect neurological disease?

content.rendered:
A few years ago, most people bought a smartwatch mainly to count steps, track exercise, or check messages. Today, the same small device can continuously monitor movement, physical activity, heart rate, and sleep. This has led neuroscientists to ask whether information collected from the wrist might also tell us something useful about neurological health.

A smartwatch cannot see the brain. It cannot perform an MRI, measure dopamine, or examine neurons. What it can do is repeatedly measure functions that the nervous system controls, including how we move, walk, sleep, and respond to our surroundings. Neurological diseases can gradually alter these functions, sometimes before the changes become obvious in everyday life. Researchers are therefore studying wearable devices as sources of digital biomarkers, objective measurements collected through digital technologies that may provide information about health and disease.

The brain leaves clues in movement

Walking across a room seems simple, yet it requires the brain to coordinate the legs, arms, muscles, posture, balance, and vision. When neurological disease affects these networks, walking can gradually change. Steps may become shorter, one arm may swing less, turning may slow, or the timing between steps may become less consistent. These subtle differences can be difficult to recognize during ordinary observation, but accelerometers and gyroscopes in wearable devices can convert movement into measurable data.

Parkinson’s disease is an important example. Tremor is its most recognizable symptom, but the disease can also cause slowness of movement, stiffness, reduced arm swing, postural changes, and difficulty walking. Studies suggest that walking speed, stride characteristics, stance time, and related gait measures can provide useful information about Parkinson’s disease severity, progression, and treatment response. Wearable sensors are also being studied for freezing of gait, when a person’s feet can suddenly feel stuck despite the intention to keep walking. A systematic review found considerable promise while emphasizing that further validation is still needed before these technologies become routine clinical tools.

The broader potential goes beyond Parkinson’s disease. Masurkar and Rikame reviewed 17 systematic reviews encompassing 308 primary studies and found substantial interest in using wearable technologies to assess gait, mobility, balance, and fall risk across neurological conditions. The attraction is easy to understand. Instead of observing someone walking for a few minutes every several months, researchers and clinicians could potentially study gradual changes during normal daily life.

Sleep, heart signals, and artificial intelligence

Movement is only one source of information. Sleep disturbances are common in neurological disorders and, in some conditions, can appear before more recognizable symptoms. A 2026 systematic review by Mijnsbergen and colleagues examined 70-studies using movement sensors for nighttime monitoring in Parkinson’s disease. The authors found potential for actigraphy and related sensors to assess sleep and nocturnal behavior, but they also highlighted major differences in methods and the need for greater standardization. A smartwatch is therefore not a replacement for formal sleep study, but repeated measurements over weeks or months may add another piece to the neurological picture.

Wearables can also measure cardiovascular signals such as heart rate variability, the small differences in time between heartbeats. Because this measure is influenced by the autonomic nervous system, researchers are interested in whether it could contribute to neurological monitoring. It must be interpreted cautiously because exercise, stress, sleep, medication, and illness can all affect it. Its value may ultimately come from combining it with movement, gait, sleep, and other signals rather than interpreting any single measurement in isolation.

This is where artificial intelligence becomes especially interesting. A slightly slower walking speed alone may mean little. A change in sleep alone may also have many explanations. But imagine a device collecting information about walking, arm movement, tremors, activity, sleep, and cardiovascular signals over months or years.

Artificial intelligence could search across these measurements for patterns that would be difficult for a person to recognize manually. More importantly, an algorithm could compare a person not only with a population but also with his or her own long-term baseline. If several measurements gradually changed together, the system might flag that something deserves attention. That would not be a diagnosis, but it could eventually provide a reason to seek medical evaluation earlier.

A neurological examination is extremely valuable, but it is also a brief snapshot. A person with Parkinson’s disease may see a neurologist every few months, while symptoms fluctuate from morning to evening and change with medication, fatigue, stress, and activity. Someone may walk relatively well in the clinic yet struggle more while shopping, climbing stairs, or moving around at home. Because wearable devices travel with the person, they could complement clinical examinations by showing what happens between appointments.

Why could this matter for Nepal?

This possibility is especially relevant in Nepal, where geography and the concentration of specialist services in major urban centers can make neurological care difficult to access. A patient living far from a specialist center may have to travel considerable distances simply for an assessment. In the future, some information about walking, movement, sleep, and activity could potentially be collected remotely and reviewed by health professionals. This would not replace a neurologist or an in-person examination. It could, however, provide additional information about visits and help clinicians decide when closer assessment is needed.

For Nepal, the promise of digital health should therefore be judged not only by technological sophistication but also by accessibility. A system that requires expensive devices, constant high-speed internet, or complex technical support may widen existing health inequalities. The more meaningful goal would be accurate and affordable tools that can function in real communities, including places where specialist neurological care is limited.

Your smartwatch is not a neurologist!

The excitement around wearable technology should not obscure an essential limitation: a consumer smartwatch cannot currently diagnose Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, or most other neurological disorders. Poor sleep, fewer steps, an unusual heart rate, or a change in movement can occur for countless reasons. Even in Parkinson’s disease, where wearable technology has been studied extensively, researchers use different sensors, algorithms, body locations, and measurement methods. Stronger clinical validation and greater standardization are still needed.

There is also a fundamental difference between detecting a pattern associated with disease and diagnosing the disease itself. A smartwatch may eventually recognize that something has changed, but understanding why it changed will still require clinical judgment, medical history, examination, and, when appropriate, further testing.

Privacy deserves equal attention. Continuous monitoring can generate years of information about sleep, movement, activity, and physiology. As these devices become more medically useful, societies will need clear answers about who owns that data, who can analyze it, how securely it is stored, and what should happen if an algorithm suggests increased neurological risk before symptoms are apparent.

Neurologists have always relied on careful observation: how a patient walks, moves the hands, balances, speaks, and coordinates movement. Those skills will remain essential. What wearable technology adds is the possibility of observing selected aspects of neurological function repeatedly during everyday life.

The real breakthrough may therefore not be a watch that suddenly announces that someone has Parkinson’s disease. A more realistic future is subtler. One day, a wearable device may simply recognize that a person is no longer moving, sleeping, or behaving quite like his or her usual self. That change may not provide a diagnosis, but it could provide something valuable: a reason to pay attention and begin an important conversation with a doctor.

title.rendered: Two tankers detained for alleged fuel theft in Bhairahawa

content.rendered:
Butwal, September 15

Police have detained two tankers after they were allegedly found stealing petroleum products being transported from India to the Nepal Oil Corporation’s Bhalwari depot in Rupandehi.

A team deployed from the Lumbini Province Police Office in Dang detained the two tankers while they were allegedly unloading petroleum products at Saraf Oil Centre in Bhairahawa on Tuesday.

According to police, the tankers had arrived at the oil centre after transporting petroleum products from India to the Bhalwari depot. The District Police Office, Rupandehi, said the tankers were found unloading fuel when police raided the centre at around 10 am. The tankers bore registration numbers Lu 2 Kha 1544 and Lu 1 Kha 6504.

Police said the seals on both tankers had been broken and petroleum products were being removed. The tankers and one co-driver have been taken into custody for further investigation.

Questions raised over depot

Some sources familiar with the matter have claimed that fuel has allegedly been stolen for a long time through collusion between tanker operators transporting petroleum products to the Bhalwari depot and petrol station operators.

According to the sources, the Bhalwari depot has not been regularly checking the condition of tanker seals or adequately measuring the petroleum products received from India.

There have been previous incidents of fuel theft involving tankers transporting petroleum products to the Bhalwari depot. The latest incident has raised questions about the system for transporting petroleum products, checking tanker seals and measuring fuel at the depot.

title.rendered: 607 tourists from 34 countries missing since Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

A total of 607 foreign tourists from 34 countries remain unaccounted for following the Bhotekoshi flash flood that struck Nepal on August 26.

Suraj Ghimire, information officer at the Department of Tourism, told that the 607 foreign tourists, who were travelling to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, Gosaikunda and Mustang on the occasion of the Janai Purnima festival, have been out of contact since the disaster.

Of those missing, 269 are men, 329 are women, and nine are unidentified. Most of the missing pilgrims are from neighbouring India, with 189 Indian nationals still unaccounted for, according to the department.

The department said 65 nationals from the United States, 55 from Malaysia, 54 from Ukraine, 37 from China, 33 each from Australia and Latvia, 32 from the UK, 30 from Canada, nine each from South Korea and Singapore, eight from Germany, six each from Russia and South Africa, five each from New Zealand and Japan, four from France and three from Kazakhstan are also missing.

Two nationals each from Belarus, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Estonia, Portugal, Spain and the Netherlands are unaccounted for, while one each from Finland, the Philippines, Vietnam, Hungary, Israel, Switzerland, Sweden and Lithuania remain missing.

The number of Nepali tourists who have been unreachable since the disaster stands at 188. The Nepali tourists had accompanied the foreign visitors as guides and helpers.

The government has continued search and rescue operations. A total of 310 foreign nationals have so far been rescued, including 258 men and 52 women.

Relief distribution has also been intensified by local governments and security agencies.

—RSS

title.rendered: India approves 18-hour daily power exports to Nepal until December 2026

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September

India has approved the export of electricity to Nepal for up to 18 hours a day from September 13 to December 31.

The Indian Ministry of Power has authorised the export of electricity to the Nepal Electricity Authority through the 400 kV Muzaffarpur-Dhalkebar double-circuit line and the 132 kV Tanakpur-Mahendranagar single-circuit line.

Under the approval, up to 600 MW can be exported through the Muzaffarpur-Dhalkebar line and up to 54 MW through the Tanakpur-Mahendranagar line, allowing Nepal to import up to 654 MW of electricity from India.

The approval covers an 18-hour period from midnight to 6 pm daily. The Indian Ministry of Power said the amount of electricity Nepal will require from January 2027 will be reviewed in December 2026.

Nepal’s electricity generation has declined following extensive damage to hydropower infrastructure caused by recent floods and landslides, creating a need for additional power to meet domestic demand.

The Indian ministry said the export approval was granted considering the damage to Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure caused by the floods and their impact on domestic electricity generation.

The approval is expected to help Nepal manage its electricity demand during the flood-affected period and further strengthen energy cooperation between the two countries.

title.rendered: Education minister falls ill, parliamentary committee meeting postponed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

A meeting of the Education, Health and Information Technology Committee of the House of Representatives was postponed after Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel fell ill and was unable to attend.

The meeting had been scheduled for 8 am Tuesday at Singha Durbar, with lawmakers in attendance. However, the meeting was postponed after the committee was informed that the minister was unwell.

The meeting had been called to discuss the measures taken and being taken by the Ministry of Education and Sports regarding the human and physical damage caused by the Bhotekoshi floods, as well as rescue, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts in the affected areas.

The agenda also included discussions on problems and challenges encountered in the ministry’s work and the strategies it plans to adopt in the coming days. Minister Pokharel and the ministry secretary had both been invited to the meeting.

After the committee meeting began, Minister Pokharel informed the committee that he was unwell. As he was unable to attend, committee chair Dr Ojaswi Sherchan announced the postponement of the meeting.

The committee had sought information from the minister and secretary on the impact of the floods on educational infrastructure and academic activities, the condition of students and teachers, and the ministry’s ongoing relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts in the affected areas.

title.rendered: House of Representatives moves ahead with digital Parliament concept

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The House of Representatives is moving forward with the concept of a digital Parliament. The issue was discussed at a meeting of the Business Advisory Committee on Tuesday.

The meeting, held at the Business Advisory Hall in Singha Durbar, focused on matters related to developing a digital Parliament system.

The proposed system seeks to digitally connect issues raised by lawmakers during the zero hour, special hour and emergency hour with the concerned ministries and government agencies.

The meeting also discussed developing a system to track how the government responds to issues raised by lawmakers, including what decisions have been made, the progress achieved and when the issues were addressed.

According to Prakash Chandra Pariyar, chief whip of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party, the Business Advisory Committee is holding discussions focused specifically on the concept of a digital Parliament. The discussions are ongoing, he said.

title.rendered: David Warner to play Nepal Premier League for Kathmandu Gorkhas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Australian cricket star David Warner is set to play for Kathmandu Gorkhas in the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL).

Kathmandu Gorkhas announced Warner’s signing through its social media platforms. The 39-year-old becomes the biggest international cricket star to feature in the NPL so far.

The announcement comes after Australian cricket organisation Sim Strike had earlier posted that Warner would play in the NPL. Warner had also liked the post.

Kathmandu Gorkhas had subsequently dropped hints about the identity of its marquee overseas signing, with the clues pointing towards Warner. Onlinekhabar had also reported on the possibility of the Australian opener joining the franchise.

David Warner is one of Australia’s most decorated modern cricketers. He has won two ODI World Cups, a T20 World Cup and the World Test Championship with Australia.

He was part of Australia’s World Cup-winning teams in 2015 and 2023, the T20 World Cup-winning side in 2021 and the team that won the World Test Championship in 2023.

Warner is also among the few Australian players to have scored international centuries across all three formats.

He played 110 T20 internationals for Australia, scoring more than 3,200 runs, including one century.

Across his T20 career, Warner has played 439 matches, scoring more than 14,000 runs with 10 centuries and 118 half-centuries.

The left-handed opener has extensive experience in franchise cricket around the world. He has played in the Indian Premier League (IPL), Australia’s Big Bash League (BBL), Pakistan Super League (PSL), The Hundred in England, Major League Cricket in the United States, Bangladesh Premier League (BPL), Caribbean Premier League (CPL) and Vitality Blast.

Warner’s arrival is expected to bring significant international attention to the upcoming edition of the NPL and Kathmandu Gorkhas.

title.rendered: Four arrested in Kathmandu with 2,770 illegal vapes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Police have arrested four people found in possession of illegal electronic cigarettes (vapes).

Those arrested are Purnalal Shrestha, 45, originally from Dhading and living in Chabahil, Kathmandu Metropolitan City-7; Shubham Gupta, 27, of Satungal, Chandragiri Municipality-16; Rajan Moktan, 19, originally from Ramechhap and living in Kathmandu Metropolitan City-3; and Saksham Shrestha, 19, originally from Panchkhal Municipality-9, Kavre, and living in Chyasal, Lalitpur.

The arrests followed intelligence from the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office, Teku, about the illegal storage and distribution of vapes across various parts of the valley. Police recovered 2,770 vape devices from the warehouses of RHS International Pvt. Ltd. in Kathmandu Metropolitan City-22 and Resha Collection in Chuchepati, Kathmandu Metropolitan City-6.

The four have been sent to the Tribhuvan International Airport Customs Office for further investigation and legal action.

title.rendered: 11 arrested for letting Nepalis gamble at casino

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Eleven people have been arrested on charges of allowing Nepali citizens into a casino to gamble.

The arrests were made at Garuda Casino in Taulung, Budhanilkantha Municipality-1, over allegations of letting Nepalis play card-based gambling games there.

Those arrested include Bikky Lama, 34, of Gokulganga Rural Municipality-6, Ramechhap; Nuwang Sherpa, 39, of Makalungla Rural Municipality-3, Solukhumbu; Pasang Sherpa, 39, of Dudhkunda Municipality-9, also of Solukhumbu; Jyoti Magar, 32, of Golanjor Rural Municipality-5, Sindhuli; and Narayan Khatri, 35, of Baiteshwar Rural Municipality-8, Dolakha.

Also arrested were Dil Lama, 44, of Kathmandu; Ashok Lama, 44, of Roshi Rural Municipality-1, Kavre; Sanjay Tamang, 32, of Dupcheshwar Rural Municipality-3, Nuwakot; Ashish Khadka, 40, of Umakunda Rural Municipality-4, Ramechhap; Sabin Man Shrestha, 49, of Lalitpur; and Sudip Adhikari, 30, of Jorpati Rural Municipality-4, Dhankuta.

They were arrested Tuesday afternoon in a joint operation by the Kathmandu Ring Road Police and the Budhanilkantha Police Circle. Police recovered Rs 1,085,600 in cash and some casino chips/coins from them. The District Administration Office has extended their detention by two days for further investigation.

title.rendered: Government’s reform package boosts stock market, NEPSE up 35 points in first hour

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The government’s capital market reform action plan appeared to have a positive effect on the stock market Wednesday.

Within the first hour of trading, the NEPSE index rose by 35 points (1.39%), bringing it to 2,620. Within just the first minute of trading, the index had briefly touched 2,679 before settling somewhat.

Turnover also jumped sharply, Rs 3.44 billion in trades in just the first hour, compared to Rs 4.68 billion across the entire four-hour session the previous day.

All sub-indices rose in the first hour, with banking, development banks, finance, hotels and tourism, hydropower, investment, manufacturing and processing, non-life insurance, microfinance, and trading all up more than 1%.

Prices rose for 255 companies, fell for 15, and stayed flat for 6. Joshi Hydropower, Unnati Sahakarya Laghubitta, and Sindhu Bikas Bank posted gains of 4–6%, while Api Power, Shivam Cement, Reliance Spinning Mills, Liberty Energy, and Laxmi Sunrise Bank led in turnover.

title.rendered: Kidnapped 15-month-old rescued after 11 Days in Dhanusha, woman arrested

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, September 15

Police have safely rescued a 15-month-old boy who had gone missing from Tinkoriya, Ward 6 of Bideha Municipality, Dhanusha, 11 days ago. A woman has been arrested on charges of kidnapping the child.

According to district police spokesperson Om Prakash Khanal, Sidhanta Mahato, son of Kamlesh Mahato, went missing while playing in his own courtyard around 4:40 p.m. on September 3. Police were mobilised immediately from the Giddha police post, and a 60-member team under Superintendent Rupesh Khadka later joined the search across the area, with the help of trained tracking dogs.

Investigators, a joint team led by Deputy Superintendent Khanal and Provincial Information Analysis and Investigation officer Babindra Nembang, determined that the boy had been abducted by Punita Devi Paswan, around 41, of Kamala Municipality-9, Hathalatwa.

Preliminary findings suggested she had repeatedly moved and hidden the child at various locations in both Nepal and India. Police then intensified round-the-clock monitoring at all border checkpoints in Dhanusha and stepped up technical investigation to track her down.

Once police closed in, the woman left the child by the roadside about 300 meters south of her home around 3:35 p.m. on September 14, before fleeing. Police recovered the boy immediately, had him medically examined, and handed him over to his family; his condition is reported as normal.

Paswan was later caught the same evening around 3:45 p.m. while attempting to flee toward India, near the Dashgaja border area in Mahinathpur, Ward 1 of Bideha Municipality. She is under investigation on charges of kidnapping, unlawful confinement, and human trafficking and transportation, according to the District Police Office, Dhanusha.

title.rendered: Opening of track at Krishnabhir in final stage

content.rendered:
File

Narayangadh, September 15

Efforts have reached the final stage to open a track as an alternative route for the damaged section of Krishna along the Prithvi Highway. The roadway was blocked after a landslide. Some vehicles passed through the track as a test run on Sunday.

With the successful test, preparation is being sped up to ensure full operation of the track. An engineer representing a company responsible for the construction, Ishwor Nepal, said that gravelling, slope cutting and drain construction were going on as part of the alternative route.

“We’ve made efforts to fully operate the route after two days, September 17,” Nepal said, adding that a dozen pieces of heavy equipment were mobilised for 10 days in the first phase of construction. In the final phase, nearly 50 workers, including a skilled workforce, were devoted to the construction.

“This section is a risky one. If there is no additional landslip, the vehicular movement is possible on the planned date,” he added. The track is nearly 300 metres long and 7 metres wide. Once the sub-base is finalised, regular transportation will be allowed.

—RSS

title.rendered: Why strengthening ties with the Global South was a top priority for Putin’s recent diplomacy blitz

content.rendered:
Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met with some 18 heads of state.

Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few.

The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks on Ukraine, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war.

Tellingly, however, the main thrust of discussions led by the Russian president had a different focus: fuel, trade and transit.

Here’s why Russia is deepening ties with many partners in the Global South – and what these meetings tell us about the impacts of Western efforts to isolate Putin.

Shoring up fuel and energy

Fuel and energy security is becoming a mutual concern for both Moscow and its partners in the Global South. Ukraine’s deliberate offensive campaign targeting Russia’s oil refining capacity has resulted in noticeable fuel shortages in the country.

It has forced the Russian government to import refined fuel from countries it has traditionally exported to, such as Belarus, Turkey and India.

At the same time, the Kremlin continues to push for the expansion of its energy exports. This includes finalising the contract to build the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which intends to deliver 50 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually from Russia to China via Mongolia.

Last week, Russia also signed a deal to establish a new strategic oil reserves hub in Vietnam.

Russia is also expanding cooperation on nuclear power, which was part of the discussion agenda with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Vietnam’s President To Lam (during his state visit to Russia), and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Deeper ties with the Global South

The ongoing sanctions war between Russia and the West has made its economic and trade relations with the Global South pivotal for the country’s survival and future development.

Two friendly interstate bodies, in which Russia plays core roles, are becoming especially important. The first is BRICS, a group of 11 economies including Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.

The BRICS economies now account for about 40% of global GDP. Last year, mutual trade turnover between BRICS member states exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time.

The second is the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). This is a political and security bloc spanning countries in Europe, Asia and the Indo-Pacific. According to Putin, Russia’s trade turnover with the SCO exceeded US$400 billion in 2025.

Overall, Asia accounted for 73.4% of Russia’s trade turnover last year. It’s no surprise that Moscow’s trade links with Asia featured in almost every conversation in Bishkek, Vladivostok and New Delhi.

Bypassing disruption in the Middle East

Despite its friendly ties with Iran, Russia and its clients aren’t immune from the ongoing disruption to transport and trade routes through the Middle East. To mitigate these risks, Russia is actively lobbying two relatively new transcontinental transit networks.

The first is the 7,200-kilometre combined rail-road-maritime International North-South Transport Corridor. This route connects Russia’s Baltic Sea ports with Mumbai in India, via the Caspian Sea and Iran.

Russia reportedly discussed this route with the Indian and Iranian delegations he met with this month.

The second is the 5,600-kilometre maritime Northern Sea Route, which connects Asia’s ice-free ports with Russia’s Arctic ports as part of the Northeast maritime passage across the Arctic Ocean.

In August, Beijing launched commercial operations along this route for the first time.

From business as usual to political signalling

Russia walked away from this month’s diplomatic blitz with some clear wins. In addition to securing US$7.7 billion worth of investments in Vladivostok, along with some lucrative deals with Vietnam, Putin could also claim some political success.

First, although challenging at times, Putin’s interactions with his counterparts showcased how Moscow’s relationship with major non-Western international players remains a geopolitical constant, even in the fifth year of the Ukraine war.

For leaders of emerging centres of global influence, whether India’s Modi, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto or Vietnam’s Lam, interacting with Russia forms part of their countries’ foreign policy approach based on the notion of “strategic autonomy”.

This sends a powerful signal to the United States and its allies, amid the latest round of high-level consultations involving the CIA and US Treasury chiefs and their Russian counterparts.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump sent his own personal envoys to Moscow and made a follow-up phone call to Putin.

Second, Russia and its core partners in Asia jointly signalled they will continue to maintain strategic partnership links. This includes the question of importing Russia’s fossil fuels, nuclear power and other goods and exporting processed fuel back to Russia.

Fuel security is particularly relevant to the Russian authorities’ attempts to stabilise the domestic situation. The Kremlin is under pressure to mitigate the aftershock of the escalating war with Ukraine amid upcoming parliamentary elections on September 18-20.

Why the Global South still has concerns

Still, many in the Global South remain concerned about the growing impact of what seems to be becoming a forever war in and over Ukraine.

The latest round of tit-for-tat attacks against merchant shipping in the Black Sea triggered fears of grain and wheat shortages.

In mid-November, China will host the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. This is tipped to be a possible venue for the first trilateral meeting between Putin, Xi and Trump.

Here, Moscow might feel increasing pressure to settle the war by political means from its partners. These countries don’t want to feel the effects of the sanctions war between the West and Russia, let alone be dragged into it.

title.rendered: Congress leader to urge Speaker to form all-party flood response mechanism

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Nepali Congress Parliamentary Party leader Bhishmaraj Angdembe is scheduled to meet Speaker DP Aryal on Tuesday to draw his attention to the need for forming a high-level mechanism for post-flood rescue, relief, reconstruction and long-term solutions.

According to Angdembe’s secretariat, during the meeting, Angdembe will urge the speaker to form a high-level parliamentary committee to oversee rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts following the floods, his secretariat said.

The proposal comes amid the failure to form an all-party mechanism proposed by Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chair Rabi Lamichhane shortly after the devastating floods in Rasuwa.

The ruling party leader had proposed forming a high-level all-party mechanism for post-disaster rescue, relief and rehabilitation. However, 20 days have passed, and the proposed mechanism has yet to be formed.

Angdembe’s secretariat said he will also urge Speaker Aryal to continue the question-and-answer session with the prime minister in Parliament.

title.rendered: Ropain Jatra celebrated in Panchthar’s Ranitar (Photos)

content.rendered:
Panchthar, September 15

Students entered the Baraju playground accompanied by traditional musical instruments and symbolically reenacted rice planting as part of the traditional Ropain Jatra festival in Ranitar, Panchthar.

The students portrayed farmers involved in various stages of rice planting, including transplanting seedlings, ploughing and other agricultural activities. Their performances not only entertained spectators but also helped preserve the local tradition.

The festival was held in Ranitar of Phidim Municipality-7 on the occasion of National Children’s Day. Students from Ranitar Secondary School presented the Ropain Jatra.

Dressed in traditional attire representing different ethnic communities, the students put on colourful performances. At the end of the rice-planting reenactment, they formed the national flag.

Ward Chair Rupendra Tamang said the festival has continued a tradition dating back to 2037 BS. He said the cultural display in traditional attire has become an important part of Ranitar’s identity, which is also known for its scenic beauty.

The festival was traditionally held on Bhadra 4 on the occasion of Children’s Day and was popularly known as Hile Jatra in Panchthar. The event was discontinued during the conflict period but was later revived. After the country became a republic, organisers began holding it on Bhadra 29, said Tank Gurung, chair of the Ranitar United Club, the organiser. The festival could not be held last year due to the Gen Z movement.

According to Ranitar Secondary School Principal Ganga Rai, students underwent four days of training to prepare for the rice-planting performance.

Various activities, including open and veterans’ football tournaments, a senior citizens’ race and dance performances, were also organised as part of the festival.

title.rendered: British veterans minister meets former Gurkhas in London talks

content.rendered:
London, September 15

Britain, the Nepal government, and former Gurkha representatives held informal talks in London on Monday.

The meeting took place at the Nepali Embassy in London between Calvin Bailey, the UK Ministry of Defence’s Minister for Veterans and People, and ten Gurkha representatives affiliated with the G10 group. It was the first such discussion between Minister Bailey and the G10 representatives, arranged through the efforts of Nepal’s Chargé d’Affaires to the UK, Bipin Duwadi.

During the roughly two-and-a-half-hour discussion, Bailey gave a positive response to the former Gurkhas’ call for a resolution by this December, and reportedly assured them he would bring forward an acceptable package that wouldn’t require the Gurkhas to resort to a hunger strike again.

Duwadi urged Bailey to work toward a responsible, sustainable, and fair solution as soon as possible. The meeting revisited earlier ministerial-level decisions, the Nepal Supreme Court’s ruling, the Gurkhas’ hunger strikes, and frustration over long-unresolved issues, including retrospective pensions and an affordable settlement.

Duwadi said Bailey seemed genuinely engaged, listened attentively to all the representatives, and pledged to pursue outcomes rather than more open-ended commitments.

“Today’s informal meeting brought all stakeholders together and created space for everyone to speak freely,” Duwadi said, adding that there was an understanding to continue the dialogue going forward. Bailey also expressed sympathy over Nepal’s recent floods and touched on the UK government’s support in that regard.

Dharma Tamang, vice-chair of the Gurkha Army Ex-Servicemen’s Organisation (GAESO), said the group presented its long-standing demands and pressed for concrete outcomes this time, noting that promises alone have come before without follow-through.

He said the Gurkhas made clear they want a proposal with real progress and a defined timeline before December, and warned that if no resolution comes within that window, they will move ahead with protest actions. The British side, he said, committed to preventing that scenario and to pushing for a quick resolution through further talks with the government.

Krishna Bahadur Rai, chief coordinator of the Gorkha Satyagraha Joint Struggle Committee, said the Gurkhas held firm with the new veterans minister that their demands must be met by December.

Also present were Alex Baker MP, chair of the UK Parliament’s All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Nepal, and Brigadier General Anoop Shah, the Nepali Embassy’s defence attaché in London. Gurkha representatives at the meeting included GAESO chair Krishna Kumar Rai, GAESO vice-chair Dharma Bahadur Tamang, Krishna Bahadur Rai of the Gorkha Satyagraha Joint Struggle Committee, Major (Retd) Tikendradal Dewan of the British Gurkha Welfare Society, Kesh Bahadur Gurung, and several others.

Trilateral talks resumed Monday after a long pause, following the resignations of then-Defence Secretary John Healey and Veterans Minister Louise Sandher-Jones from Keir Starmer’s cabinet. That gap had left many former Gurkhas feeling discouraged, especially after a cabinet reshuffle under Prime Minister Andy Burnham further delayed related discussions.

title.rendered: Kispang chair faces 10 banking offence cases

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Kispang Rural Municipality Chair Birbal Tamang is facing 10 cases related to banking offences, police said.

Tamang was arrested at the Singha Durbar gate on Monday while leaving after attending a meeting with Prime Minister Balen Shah. Police said 10 banking offence cases have been filed against him at various police offices.

The Kathmandu District Police Range has completed its investigation into a banking offence case involving Rs 30.4 million and submitted the case file to the District Government Attorney’s Office.

The Kathmandu police range has also forwarded another case involving Rs 10.33 million to the government attorney’s office.

Case files for two other banking offences, involving Rs 4.8 million and Rs 9.5 million respectively, have also been submitted.

According to Kathmandu Police Range SP Dan Bahadur Thapa, a fraud case involving Rs 25.6 million has also been forwarded to the government attorney’s office.

Police said a Rs 200,000 banking offence case has been registered at the Bhaktapur Police Range, while cases involving Rs 7.5 million, Rs 525,000, Rs 1.98 million and an unspecified amount have been registered at the Janasewa, Durbar Marg, Lainchaur and Maharajgunj police circles, respectively.

Prime Minister Shah had held discussions with local representatives from flood-affected areas. Tamang had gone to Singha Durbar to attend the meeting.

title.rendered: Nepal and Micronesia establish diplomatic relations

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Nepal and Micronesia formally established diplomatic relations on Monday, bringing to 185 the number of countries with which Nepal now maintains diplomatic ties.

The agreement was sealed through a joint statement signed by Nepal’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Lok Bahadur Thapa, and Micronesia’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Jim S. Lipwe. During their bilateral meeting, both ambassadors discussed matters of mutual interest and committed to strengthening bilateral and multilateral cooperation, including within the UN and other multilateral forums.

Micronesia is a Pacific island nation made up of more than 600 small islands, located east of the Philippines and north of Papua New Guinea. It comprises four states, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae, with its capital, Palikir, located on Pohnpei. The country has a total land area of just 702 square kilometres, making it one of the smallest nations in the world (roughly 210 times smaller than Nepal), and a population of around 114,000. The United States is responsible for its defence and security.

title.rendered: Devotees throng Risheshwar Temple on Rishi Panchami

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

A large number of devotees observing the Rishi Panchami fast gathered at Risheshwar Temple in Teku, Kathmandu, from early Tuesday morning.

Risheshwar Temple in Teku is considered one of the oldest temples in the Kathmandu Valley and has traditionally drawn large crowds of devotees on Bhadra Sukla Panchami.

Rishi Panchami is observed every year on this day. Women wake up early, complete their daily rituals and conclude their Teej fast before visiting nearby rivers, streams, lakes and ponds to perform ritual bathing. As part of the tradition, they brush their teeth with 365 sticks of datiwan and bathe after applying cow dung, soil and ash to their bodies.

As the fourth lunar day, or Chaturthi, falls immediately after the Teej fast this year, religious scholars say devotees should complete the Teej fast before performing the ritual bath and other rites associated with Rishi Panchami.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Skies will generally be cloudy nationwide today. According to the Weather Forecasting Division, isolated spots in the mountain and hill regions of Koshi, Bagmati, and Gandaki provinces could see heavy rain in the afternoon.

A few locations in the mountain areas of Koshi, Bagmati, and Gandaki, along with scattered spots in the mountains of Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim, may get moderate rain or snow with thunder and lightning. Some hill areas across the country could see similar conditions. Meanwhile, a few places in the Tarai belts of Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini, and scattered Tarai spots in Madhesh, Koshi, and Sudurpashchim, may see moderate rainfall.

At night, cloudy conditions will persist nationwide, with the division forecasting possible heavy rain in one or two spots in Koshi’s hill and Tarai areas. Moderate rain is possible in parts of the Tarai in Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini, and in scattered Tarai spots in Madhesh and Sudurpashchim. Mountain and hill areas of Koshi, Bagmati, and Gandaki, plus scattered mountain and hill spots in Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim, could again see moderate rain or snow with thunder and lightning.

Heavy rainfall was also recorded across the country in the past 24 hours, notably in Sankhuwasabha and Bhaktapur, the division said.

title.rendered: Ganesh Chaturthi: Devotees throng Ganesh temples across Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Devotees have been lining up since early morning at major Ganesh temples in Kathmandu and other parts of the country to worship Lord Ganesh, who is traditionally accorded the first place of worship in Hindu rituals as the remover of obstacles.

According to Hindu scriptures, Lord Ganesh was born on Bhadra Sukla Chaturthi. Ganesh Chaturthi is being celebrated today with special prayers at temples including Ashok Binayak, Chandra Binayak, Suryabinayak, Kamal Binayak and Kamaladi Ganesh in the Kathmandu Valley, as well as at Ganesh temples across the country.

Ganesh, the son of Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, is traditionally worshipped before other deities during religious ceremonies. Religious scholar Prof Dr Devmani Bhattarai said there is a scriptural tradition of observing a fast dedicated to Ganesh after completing the Haritalika (Teej) fast.

According to the Ganesh Purana, women observing the Teej fast on the third day pray for a happy married life, peace and prosperity, and worship Ganesh on the fourth day to seek protection from obstacles in their lives.

The day is also known as Mangal Chaturthi and is celebrated by the Newa community as Chatha. There is a tradition of distributing a special snack called ‘Chhusa-musya’ to children on the occasion. This year, the festival has fallen on a Tuesday, giving it added significance.

The National Religious Assembly Nepal has been celebrating Ganesh Chaturthi with various programmes since 2008. Assembly Chair Prof Dr Madhav Bhattarai said discourses have been organised at various Ganesh temples today alongside worship and prayers.

He said the assembly will also visit various Ganesh temples to perform worship on behalf of the organisation.

The National Religious Assembly has also been organising the Ganesh chariot procession since 2008.

title.rendered: Inside Rasuwa’s flood zone, a forensic doctor’s hardest case

content.rendered:
A forensic doctor sees bodies constantly. But nothing prepared Dr Salmali Yadav for what she found in Rasuwa’s flood zone.

After the Bhote Koshi flood on August 26, Yadav’s forensic team was deployed to identify the dead in Timure, Syafrubensi, and nearby areas of Rasuwa. She’d assumed bodies would be brought to a hospital for examination, as usual. But once she reached Dhunche, she learned there was no road; the team would have to work at Timure itself, the site of the worst destruction.

Flying in by helicopter on the morning of August 30, she recalled that the scene below looked like something out of a film; barely a building was left standing.

Working without a mortuary

There was no running water, no equipment, no proper space to lay out remains. The team had to carry buckets of water to wherever a body was found, just to clean it enough to examine. Many bodies were unrecognisable by face, so the team had to painstakingly note tattoos, scars, jewellery, and any scrap of remaining clothing, anything that might eventually help a family confirm identity.

On the first day, they processed seven cases. By the second day, the count of recovered bodies had reportedly reached around a hundred. The waterlogged ground made even walking to each site dangerous. At one point, Dr Yadav’s foot sank into the mud, and she had to be pulled out by army and police personnel.

Among the many cases, one affected her most — the body of a pregnant woman, her body badly damaged by the flood and decomposition, from which a roughly five-month-old fetus had emerged as the body deteriorated. Dr Yadav said the image still resurfaces in her mind and unsettles her even now.

Syafrubensi diaries

At Syafrubensi, the ground was marsh-like and unsafe even to land a helicopter on. The team sank in as soon as they stepped down, and for a moment worried about their own survival rather than the work ahead.

With no cold storage or permanent facility to preserve remains, and no safe ground to bury them either, the team pushed for the recovered bodies to be transported to Kathmandu instead. This was eventually arranged with coordination from local government, army, and security personnel.

The aftermath

Dr Yadav returned to Kathmandu but says her mind is still there, with one persistent question: will the details her team collected be enough to reunite these bodies with their families?

She noted how different this kind of frontline disaster work is from the controlled conditions of a hospital morgue.

As of the report, 1,388 bodies had been recovered from the Rasuwa floods, with around a hundred identified so far; DNA sampling continues for the rest, while 5,130 people remain missing.

title.rendered: ANFA postpones protest, memorandum submission and press conference

content.rendered:

All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) has postponed a programme planned for Monday to submit a memorandum, stage a sit-in and hold a press conference.

ANFA issued a notice on Monday stating that the programme scheduled for 11 am at the National Sports Council (NSC) has been postponed until further notice due to “special circumstances.”

ANFA had planned to mobilise a team comprising its staff, referees, coaches and other stakeholders to submit a memorandum to the NSC and draw the government’s attention to the need to lift FIFA’s suspension of the football governing body.

The group was also scheduled to stage a one-hour sit-in before holding a press conference.

FIFA suspended ANFA on June 25, citing third-party interference in the association’s affairs.

The suspension has affected Nepali football activities since then, with the country’s football administration and competitions facing uncertainty.

ANFA had planned Monday’s programme as part of its efforts to seek government support for resolving the issues that led to the FIFA suspension.

title.rendered: Asmita Ale’s journey to the Women’s Super League

content.rendered:
For Asmita Ale, football has become more than a career.

It has become a way of carrying her family’s story — and her Nepali heritage — onto one of the biggest stages in women’s football.

The 23-year-old defender is currently playing for Leicester City in England’s Women’s Super League, having previously represented Aston Villa and Tottenham Hotspur.

Born in Britain to a retired Gurkha soldier from Nepal, Asmita Ale has spent much of her life moving between two worlds. On the football pitch, she has risen through England’s youth system and into professional football. Away from it, her family has kept her closely connected to Nepal and its culture.

For her parents, seeing their daughter establish herself in one of the world’s most competitive women’s leagues is a source of immense pride.

“She has brought pride to our family and our country,” says her father, Amrit Ale. “That is what makes us proud.”

Ale is also studying for a bachelor’s degree in sports science at Loughborough University, balancing university education with a demanding professional football career.

A football journey that began at eight

Asmita Ale started playing football at the age of seven. A year later, she joined the Aston Villa academy, where she began developing the skills that would eventually take her into professional football.

Before that, she had spent some time playing for a local boys’ team. But Aston Villa became the foundation of her career. By the age of 16, she was playing in the Women’s Super League.

In 2019, shortly after turning 18, Aston Villa offered her a professional contract.

It was a significant moment. Ale had become the first footballer of Nepali heritage to sign a professional contract in England’s women’s league.

At the time, she described the opportunity as the fulfilment of a childhood ambition.

“Playing football professionally is my dream, and I’m really happy to be at this club,” she said.

Her contribution soon became important to Aston Villa’s ambitions. She played a key role as the club secured promotion to the Women’s Super League in 2020.

Her performances also began attracting wider attention.

In 2021, BBC Sport named her among the Women’s Super League’s five brightest young talents.

From Aston Villa to Leicester

Asmita Ale remained with Aston Villa until 2021, making 50 appearances for the club.

She then moved to Tottenham Hotspur, where she played from 2021 to 2024 and made 31 appearances.

Now at Leicester City, she is continuing her career in the Women’s Super League.

She has already made three appearances for Leicester this season.

Her progression through three English clubs has given her experience at the highest level of domestic women’s football in the country.

Sky Sports News reported last year that Ale was the only player of Nepali heritage competing in the Women’s Super League.

She was also described as the only footballer from the South Asian community playing in England’s top women’s league.

But her connection to English football goes beyond the club game.

From England’s youth teams to the European stage

Asmita Ale has represented England at several youth levels, playing for the Under-17, Under-18 and Under-19 teams.

She made her England Under-17 debut at just 16 during the 2018 European Championship, coming on in the second half against Italy.

She was also selected for England’s squad for the opening match of the European Under-23 League.

For Ale, representing England has been a dream since childhood.

“I love playing for England. It was my dream,” she told Sky Sports News last year. “For every little girl, playing for your country is probably a dream.”

She says representing a country feels different from playing for a club.

“You get that extra motivation,” she said.

Her development was also recognised early by those around her.

Gemma Davies, a former head coach who worked with Ale, said she had already demonstrated her ability and had significant potential ahead of her.

“She has already proved her ability,” Davies said. “She is still at the beginning of her career and I think she has a lot of potential.”

A Gurkha family and a sporting upbringing

Behind Asmita Ale’s football career is a family with a strong connection to both Nepal and sport. Her father, Amrit Ale, was born in Nepal and comes from Damauli in Tanahun. A former Gurkha soldier, he spent 19 years in the British Army. But the military was not his only sporting connection.

Amrit is also a squash player. While in Nepal, he competed for selection for the national squash team at the South Asian Games. His own sporting background, Ale believes, may have influenced her.

She has described her father as the source of her sporting genetics.

Her family’s circumstances eventually meant that Ale was born in Britain.

When her father had to return to his British regiment, the family travelled to the UK because her mother was nearing her delivery date. Ale became the first member of the family to be born in Britain.

Her parents, she says, have remained her biggest supporters throughout her career.

They travelled with her when she was young and continued to accompany her as she progressed through the Aston Villa academy.

When she began representing England, they travelled internationally to watch her play.

“When I was a child, they would take me to England,” Ale told Sky Sports News. “Even when I played at the Villa academy, they would take me along. When I played for England, they would get on flights and travel to different countries to watch me.”

Their support, she says, has been one of the most important parts of her journey.

Keeping Nepal close

Although Asmita Ale was born and raised in Britain, Nepal has remained an important part of her identity.

Her parents have always reminded her where the family came from and encouraged her to stay connected with Nepali culture.

Food, family gatherings and festivals remain important parts of her life.

“I love Nepali food. My mum is a really good cook,” she says. “We celebrate lots of festivals together.”

As a child and teenager, she also travelled to Nepal almost every year to visit relatives.

Many members of her extended family continue to live there.

Growing up in Britain also meant being part of a sizeable British-Nepali community, where weddings, parties and other cultural gatherings helped maintain that connection.

For Ale, her identity has never been something she needed to choose between.

She has grown up with both her British football career and her Nepali family heritage.

More than football

Football has also changed Asmita Ale beyond what happens on the pitch.

She says she was a quiet child growing up and lacked confidence in speaking up.

Her coaches pushed her to become more vocal.

“When I was a child, I was very quiet. My manager used to tell me many times that I needed to speak up,” she says.

Football gradually forced her out of that comfort zone.

It taught her to communicate, make decisions and deal with different situations.

People who knew her at school have noticed the difference too.

“People who knew me at school say I am much more confident now,” she says.

That transformation may be as significant as anything she has achieved on the football pitch.

At 23, Ale is still at the beginning of what could be a long professional career.

She has already played for some of England’s biggest clubs, represented the country at youth level and established herself in the Women’s Super League.

But for a young footballer whose roots stretch back to Damauli, her story carries another significance.

Her success has given a new generation of Nepali and British-Nepali girls another player to look up to.

And for the parents who watched their daughter grow from a seven-year-old kicking a football to a professional defender playing in England’s top flight, the pride extends far beyond the game.

Asmita Ale may have built her football career in England.

But she has never forgotten where her family began.

title.rendered: Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle to visit India on two-day trip

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle is set to visit India on a two-day official trip on September 18 and 19.

According to sources at the Ministry of Finance, Wagle will travel to India on September 18 (Asoj 2) and return on September 19 (Asoj 3).

During the visit, Wagle is scheduled to hold meetings with Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal.

However, according to ministry sources, there is currently no programme for Wagle to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

During his stay in India, Wagle will also participate in an event organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).

According to sources, discussions at the CII event will focus on attracting Indian investment to Nepal’s hospitality and wellness sectors.

Swarnim Wagle is also scheduled to address an event at the Delhi School of Economics.

The visit is primarily aimed at promoting investment in Nepal and exploring opportunities to attract greater Indian investment, according to sources.

The finance minister’s meetings with senior Indian officials are also expected to cover areas of economic cooperation and Nepal-India economic relations.
