title.rendered: Nepal probes 25 foreign employment firms selected by Malaysia under new worker recruitment system

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 15

The Nepali government has launched an investigation into 25 foreign employment companies selected by Malaysia as the main agencies for recruiting Nepali workers.

The Department of Foreign Employment has initiated an investigation into the licensed recruitment agencies affiliated with Malaysia’s Foreign Workers Centralised Management System (FWCMS).

Malaysia has recently introduced a system under which Nepali workers can be recruited through only 25 designated foreign employment companies. The arrangement has also brought around 250 other Nepali foreign employment companies affiliated with the 25 main agencies under scrutiny.

The Department is examining the transactions of the 25 main agencies, the basis on which they were selected, their past involvement in recruiting workers for Malaysia and the process through which they affiliated other foreign employment companies.

The department has also begun seeking clarification from the 250 companies regarding the basis and procedure for their affiliation with FWCMS and their relationship with the designated main agencies.

The 250 companies will not be allowed to obtain new pre-approval for recruiting workers for Malaysia until the investigation is completed.

The government, however, has clarified that the restriction applies only to new pre-approvals for Malaysia.

Workers who have already completed the recruitment process and obtained labour approval will not be affected and will be allowed to travel to Malaysia as planned.

The government’s move has nevertheless raised concerns over whether efforts to prevent a possible recruitment syndicate could end up affecting employment opportunities in Malaysia.

The recruitment of Nepali workers to Malaysia had remained suspended for a prolonged period in the past. With Nepal objecting to Malaysia’s decision to limit recruitment to a small number of foreign employment agencies, concerns have emerged that the process could again face disruption.

‘Malaysia needs workers, not agencies’

Rajendra Bhandari, former president of the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies, said Malaysia’s decision to give authority to only a limited number of foreign employment companies and place the other 250 firms under them as sub-agents does not conform to Nepal’s existing laws and system.

According to Bhandari, all licensed foreign employment companies in Nepal have equal legal status.

However, Malaysia’s arrangement of designating 25 agencies as principal agencies and the remaining 250 as supporting or sub-agencies could result in control over the recruitment process being concentrated in the hands of a limited number of companies, he said.

“Our foreign employment companies cannot be guided by an arrangement that goes beyond our acts, rules and laws,” Bhandari said.

He also argued that Nepal’s laws do not clearly envisage a system in which 250 foreign employment companies operate as sub-agents of 25 other companies.

Such an arrangement could create additional layers in worker recruitment and fee collection, increasing the risk of workers being charged more, he said.

Bhandari stressed that the solution should not be to stop recruitment for Malaysia, but to maintain a transparent and open system based on fair competition.

“Does Malaysia need workers or agencies?” he asked. “The Nepali government can send workers through any agency it has licensed.”

He said Nepal should not accept Malaysia’s position if it refuses to recruit Nepali workers through agencies other than the 25 designated companies.

Even if employment opportunities are temporarily affected, Nepal should prioritise its laws and the interests of workers, he said.

Government says it does not want Malaysia jobs to stop

The Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security said it is aware of concerns that the dispute could affect the deployment of Nepali workers to Malaysia.

A ministry official said the government was not seeking to stop employment in Malaysia but had raised legal and institutional questions over the limitations introduced through FWCMS.

According to the official, Nepal’s Foreign Employment Act, regulations and Constitution do not provide for restricting competition in foreign employment in such a manner.

The bilateral labour agreement between Nepal and Malaysia also does not contain the concepts of “principal agency” and “support agency”, the official said.

“Active foreign employment agencies have been given equal status under the Foreign Employment Act 2007,” the official said. “They have equal standing to send workers to any destination country.”

The government has therefore clearly communicated its position on Malaysia’s new arrangement and proposed that outstanding issues be resolved through bilateral discussions, the official said.

The ministry said Nepal had responded to Malaysia’s arrangement through official correspondence soon after it was introduced.

The official also rejected claims that the government had remained inactive diplomatically on the issue.

Instead, the government has made it clear that it does not agree with the arrangement favouring a limited number of foreign employment companies, while focusing its investigation and possible action on the companies involved, the official said.

‘It may stop for some time, but not for long’

Tik Bahadur Khatri, president of the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies, said Nepal and Malaysia need immediate high-level diplomatic dialogue to resolve the dispute.

He said a solution would not be possible without dialogue and called for an early meeting of the Nepal-Malaysia Joint Committee.

Khatri also raised concerns over the vacant post of Nepal’s ambassador to Malaysia.

He urged the government to appoint an ambassador without further delay, arguing that an ambassador would be better positioned to engage in high-level diplomatic discussions.

“An ambassador has the standing to meet even with ministers,” he said. “At present, officials can meet only counterparts at the same level, so there is a question over how much influence such discussions can have on decision-making.”

Khatri, however, does not expect employment in Malaysia to remain suspended for long.

Nepali workers remain a reliable labour source for major Malaysian employers and industries, he said. Even if recruitment is halted temporarily, pressure from Malaysian employers could lead to its resumption.

“It may stop for a little while, but I am confident it could resume after a month or two because of the interests of Malaysian industries themselves,” he said.

‘How was a company with no record of sending workers to Malaysia selected?’

Bishnu KC, head of Aakarshan International, which has been sending workers to Malaysia through ethical recruitment practices for years, has questioned the basis on which the 25 foreign employment companies were selected.

According to KC, at least one company on the list had not previously sent even a single worker to Malaysia.

He said the selection criteria for the 25 companies should therefore be made transparent.

“It has not sent even a single worker until today. How was it selected?” he asked.

KC also warned that giving recruitment authority to a limited number of foreign employment companies could increase the amount charged to workers.

He claimed that complaints had already begun emerging that workers were being asked to pay between Rs 800,000 and Rs 1 million to go to Malaysia.

KC also called for diplomatic initiatives by the government.

Although the recruitment process could be put on hold for some time, he said Malaysian employers prefer Nepali workers and therefore employment opportunities were unlikely to remain suspended for a prolonged period.

Jobs or syndicate?

The current dispute over recruitment to Malaysia revolves primarily around two issues.

The first is ensuring that Nepali workers continue to have access to employment opportunities in Malaysia. The second is preventing a limited number of agencies from gaining a monopoly over the recruitment process.

The government has prioritised the second issue by launching investigations into the 25 designated main agencies and the 250 companies linked to them.

Recruitment agencies, however, are calling for immediate high-level dialogue with Malaysia alongside the investigation.

The government says its investigation and diplomatic engagement with Malaysia are being pursued simultaneously.

Former association president Bhandari also argues that the government’s move against a possible syndicate should not be interpreted as an attempt to stop employment in Malaysia.

Even if recruitment is affected temporarily, he said Nepal should not compromise its laws and workers’ interests by accepting a monopoly for a limited number of companies.

The immediate challenge for the government is therefore how to prevent a recruitment syndicate while ensuring that employment opportunities in Malaysia continue.

The answer is likely to depend on discussions through the Nepal-Malaysia joint mechanism and high-level diplomatic engagement.

Recruitment agencies warn that delays in dialogue could affect employment for some time, while the government maintains that it will not compromise Nepal’s laws or workers’ interests.

The dispute, therefore, appears to be less about whether Nepali workers should continue going to Malaysia and more about whether Nepal will accept Malaysia’s proposed model of recruiting workers through a limited number of designated foreign employment agencies.

title.rendered: Who defines reconstruction after the Bhotekoshi flood?

content.rendered:
The Bhotekoshi Flash Flood of August 26 did not end when the water level receded. It has entered another phase that is slower, less visible and perhaps more consequential. The causes are being debated, damage is being assessed, and government agencies and other institutions are beginning to define recovery priorities.

According to the government’s latest rapid damage and needs assessment, 7,570 private houses were damaged and around 32,933 people were affected. About 55 kilometres of roads, 37 motorable bridges and 68 suspension bridges were damaged. The flash flood also affected 1,806 hectares of agricultural land and caused major losses to hydropower and transmission infrastructure. The estimated recovery requirement is around Rs 723.31 billion, with infrastructure accounting for the largest share.

These figures are necessary. Roads need to be restored, electricity generation has to resume, and damaged public services must function again. Yet converting a disaster into numbers, sectors, costs and projects is not simply a technical exercise. It gives institutional form to the disaster and creates the basis for later decisions.

Once damage is translated into tables, sectors and costs, institutions decide what requires immediate action, what can wait, which sectors should receive priority, who should lead and where limited resources should go. The flash flood itself does not make these decisions. They emerge through institutions, available knowledge, political priorities and different capacities to influence public action.

This is why the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood can be examined through two related ideas, the politics of disaster and the political economy of disaster. Political scientist Richard Olson argues that disasters are inherently political because they place pressure on governments, alter public agendas and raise questions of accountability. They also affect whose interests and voices enter public decisions. Disaster politics begins before an event through investments in safety, continues through emergency response, and extends into reconstruction because decisions made afterwards shape future opportunities.

The political economy of disaster takes this argument further. It considers how power, institutions, ownership and access to resources shape vulnerability before a disaster and recovery afterwards. Some losses enter budgets and projects more readily than others. Reconstruction can therefore redistribute public expenditure, risk, opportunity and future security.

Disaster scholars Ben Wisner and his colleagues have long argued that hazards become disasters through socially produced vulnerability. Exposure, access to assets, settlement conditions and institutional capacity shape who is affected and how severely. The hazardous event may be natural, while the distribution of loss and opportunities for recovery are not entirely natural. The central issue for Bhotekoshi is therefore not only what was damaged, but how the disaster itself will be defined for the purposes of recovery, including which losses are prioritised, whose knowledge matters, which institutions gain authority and where resources are directed.

Public attention to disasters fades quickly

The first political resource in this process is attention. A major disaster can bring issues into national debate within days that might otherwise struggle for recognition for years. Glacier and glacial lake risks, transboundary information, early warning systems, river-corridor development, hydropower risk and settlement safety have all gained renewed attention after the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood.

Political sceintist Thomas Birkland describes major disasters as “focusing events”. They concentrate the attention of the media, political leaders and policy communities, creating a window in which neglected problems can become visible and policy change becomes possible.

However, public attention is limited. Scholars Stephen Hilgartner and Charles Bosk describe public arenas as having a limited “carrying capacity”. Social problems compete for recognition, and even a major disaster can lose visibility when another crisis enters the public arena. Research on online news coverage after a major earthquake in Mexico found that coverage fell by roughly half every eight days after the initial surge. Intense attention is therefore not the same as sustained attention.

This matters because attention influences institutional behaviour. While a problem remains visible, it is more likely to generate meetings, data collection, policy reviews, budget discussions and administrative action. Once attention declines, there is no guarantee that the same issue will remain a priority.

The period immediately after a disaster should therefore be understood as both a political and policy window. Nepal can mobilise quickly through committees, meetings, studies and commitments. The harder task is to convert this mobilisation into durable institutions, regulations, budgets and implementation. Otherwise, governance can fall into a recurring pattern of shock, attention, response and forgetting.

Political incentives can reinforce this tendency. Andrew Healy and Neil Malhotra, scholars of political economy, found that voters in the United States rewarded post-disaster relief more than preparedness, even though their analysis suggested that one dollar spent on preparedness could reduce future losses by around fifteen dollars. Economists Tim Besley and Robin Burgess similarly found in India that stronger media reach and political accountability were associated with stronger government response to flood damage.

This produces a persistent contradiction. Strengthening a bridge before it collapses rarely becomes a political spectacle; while rebuilding it afterwards can become a visible achievement. Preventing settlement growth in a hazardous location attracts less attention than rescue from the same place. Prevention often creates greater social value, yet response is more visible. he political significance of attention therefore lies not simply in how much attention a disaster receives, but in what that brief period of visibility succeeds in placing on the institutional agenda before attention moves elsewhere.

Political urgency is not always negative

Yet the brevity of public attention does not make political urgency inherently problematic. Under certain conditions, the same pressure that encourages short-term responses can break institutional inertia, bring resources together and accelerate reforms that had remained stalled for years. A short period of public attention can become an important decision window.

The 2001 Gujarat earthquake provides a useful example. The earthquake struck on January 26. Only 13 days later, on February 8, the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, or GSDMA, was established. Reconstruction was linked not only with housing, but also with social infrastructure, livelihoods, risk reduction and longer-term institutional capacity. More than 202,000 houses were reconstructed and more than 908,000 were repaired. Owner-driven reconstruction became an important part of the housing strategy.

Political urgency helped create an institution that survived beyond the immediate disaster. Yet Gujarat also shows why speed and visible success are not sufficient measures of long-term recovery quality.

After the Gorkha earthquake, I was invited to CEPT University to speak on post-disaster resettlement. During that visit, I saw several post-earthquake resettlement sites around Bhuj. Rawalwadi particularly caught my attention. Its planned roads, new plots and housing created a strong impression of rapid and organised reconstruction. Yet the location raised an immediate concern about the movement of water and possible drainage problems during the monsoon.

Later research on post-earthquake development in Bhuj supported that concern. Studies found that micro-watersheds and natural drainage systems had not received sufficient attention in some relocation sites, and Rawalwadi had expanded across a seasonal drainage route associated with earlier flooding.

This does not justify describing Rawalwadi simply as a failed settlement. The more useful lesson is that politically necessary speed, visible physical reconstruction and long-term liveability are not always the same. A resettlement can appear successful when judged through completed roads, plots and houses while still carrying unresolved hydrological, ecological or livelihood risks.

Gujarat therefore illustrates two sides of disaster politics. Political urgency can create lasting institutions, while the same urgency can privilege speed and visible output over long-term habitability. The Bhotekoshi Flash Flood presents a similar challenge. The current momentum is also a moment to decide where reconstruction should occur, where it should not, what level of risk is acceptable, which families may require relocation and how livelihoods can be protected. These decisions will influence land, public investment, future exposure to risk and household opportunities. At this point, the politics of immediate response begins to become the political economy of reconstruction.

When the main question gets lost in a crowd of expertise

Political urgency shapes which problems receive attention. Knowledge shapes how those problems are understood. Institutions then determine which forms of knowledge become authoritative. This introduces another important dimension of disaster politics, the politics of expertise.

A complex Himalayan disaster such as the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood cannot be understood through a single discipline. Hydrologists examine river flow. Geologists study terrain, slope failure and sediment. Cryosphere and climate specialists examine high mountain systems. Engineers assess structures and infrastructure. Economists estimate damage and loss. Planners examine land use and settlements. Social scientists consider vulnerability, livelihoods and social relations.

All these forms of knowledge are necessary. Yet a room full of experts does not automatically produce decision-relevant knowledge. Interdisciplinary work becomes useful when the decision question is clear and the required expertise is organised around it.

Nepal has recognised the need to connect expertise with formal decision-making. The Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, 2074 provides for three experts, including at least one woman, to serve on the National Council chaired by the prime minister. This is important, but placing experts within a formal structure is different from creating a continuous system that connects multidisciplinary knowledge with policy, budgets and recovery decisions.

An expert dialogue organised by the National Planning Commission (NPC) after the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood illustrated this challenge from another angle. I participated in the discussion, which brought together more than sixty experts. The programme lasted around two hours, with a considerable part of the time devoted to institutional presentations by NPC itself. When the broader discussion began, much of the attention moved towards the physical causes of the flash flood, glacier monitoring, data systems and early warning technologies.

These issues are important. Nepal needs stronger scientific investigation, glacier and river monitoring, transboundary information and early warning. However, when the immediate purpose is to determine post-disaster damage, needs and recovery priorities, the questions are different. The process must establish what was damaged, how housing and livelihoods were affected, which settlements and groups suffered most, where reconstruction or relocation is appropriate and what resources are required.

This distinction explains the role of a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, or PDNA. It is not a substitute for scientific research into causes. It brings physical damage, economic losses, human impacts and recovery requirements into a common government-led framework. Build Back Better remains important because reconstruction should not reproduce earlier vulnerability. Even so, explaining why a disaster occurred and determining what affected people require for recovery remain different analytical tasks.

Nepal used this approach after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake. Around 755,000 houses required reconstruction or substantial repair, and the estimated requirement for housing alone was about US$3.27 billion, close to half of total recovery needs.

The institutional lesson is that expertise does not make decisions by itself. Institutions decide which knowledge becomes an official basis for action, which risks are acceptable, which needs receive priority and how resources are allocated. If the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood is defined mainly as a glacier-monitoring problem, investment may move towards sensors, modelling and data systems. If it is defined as a settlement and livelihood problem, land, housing, relocation and social protection become more prominent. If it is defined mainly as an infrastructure problem, roads, bridges, hydropower and transmission systems may dominate.

None of these framings is inherently wrong. Nor are they mutually exclusive. But the framing that acquires greatest institutional authority influences what becomes urgent, which organisations move to the centre of recovery and where resources are directed. The deeper challenge is therefore to connect the right forms of knowledge with the decisions that must be made.

Parallel worlds of knowledge

The problem, however, is not only how expertise is organised around a decision. The knowledge needed for recovery, the authority to act, the finance to implement and the capacity to deliver are often located in different institutions.

Government has the clearest legal and political authority. It can declare an area unsafe, provide or acquire land, allocate budgets, approve infrastructure, establish compensation rules and implement settlement decisions. Administrative authority, however, does not automatically provide technical depth in every field. The authority to make a decision and the knowledge required to make it are not always located in the same place.

Universities have a different strength. They train professionals, accumulate specialised knowledge and conduct longitudinal research that short project cycles rarely allow. Yet inviting individual academics to occasional meetings is not the same as creating a sustained institutional connection between universities and government decisions.

Independent research organisations and specialised centres can bring technical teams, GIS and data capacity, local networks and rapid mobilisation. Project-based financing, however, can influence what is studied, when it is studied and how long the work continues. Institutional memory may weaken when a project ends.

Development partners add finance, international experience, technical assistance and capacity support. Their contribution to disaster risk reduction in Nepal has been significant. At the same time, external agendas can influence national priorities and raise questions about ownership and unequal access to decision-making.

Development partners also work through country strategies, financing windows, project cycles and reporting requirements. A monitoring centre, data platform, bridge or school can be counted and reported. Restoring community relationships, resolving land arrangements or following displaced livelihoods for a decade is much harder to measure. What can be measured and reported is not always the same as what matters most socially.

This is where visibility can become a form of institutional currency. Political leaders, government agencies, universities and development partners all need to demonstrate relevance or results. These incentives are not inherently negative. The problem begins when what is easiest to see and count gains disproportionate influence over decisions and resources.

Political economy should therefore not be reduced to a search for bad intentions. Its purpose is to examine how authority, knowledge, finance, accountability and institutional incentives shape behaviour. Nepal’s deeper challenge lies in the disconnect between authority, knowledge, finance and implementation. Affected households, meanwhile, usually have far less capacity than institutions to convert lived experience into an official decision.

What did the Gorkha earthquake leave unfinished?

Nepal has already experienced this political economy of recovery after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake. Around 500,000 houses were completely destroyed and more than 250,000 were partially damaged. Overall, around 755,000 houses required reconstruction or substantial repair. Housing and human settlements alone accounted for an estimated US$3.27 billion, close to half of total recovery needs.

The scale of housing damage has already been well documented. The more important lesson for Bhotekoshi concerns what happened after housing reconstruction became an institutional programme. It concerns where and how families would resettle, how long public attention to these questions would persist, and what happened when government decisions and household decisions moved at different speeds.

The central challenge was not only how to rebuild structures. It was also where and how families would resettle. The earthquake created a rare planning opportunity because some communities became willing to reorganise inherited plots, access arrangements and ownership structures if this could produce safer and better planned settlements.

Jillu in Dolakha offered one such example. The community reorganised private land to improve roads, infrastructure and residential plots. In Nepal, a land ownership certificate, or lalpurja, represents more than an economic asset. It is tied to security, inheritance, identity and bargaining power. The post-earthquake period therefore created a short window in which collective decisions about land and settlement, normally very difficult, became possible.

However, this opportunity does not remain open indefinitely. Affected families cannot suspend everyday life while government plans are prepared. Children continue to attend school, farms and livestock require attention, families need income and loans must be repaid. When public decisions take too long, households create their own solutions. Some rebuild where they were, some migrate, and others return to risky locations because livelihoods remain tied to those places. The time of government planning and the time of household life do not move at the same speed.

The evolution of reconstruction priorities after the earthquake adds another dimension to this problem. The reconstruction of cultural heritage provides a revealing institutional comparison. Around 2,900 historic structures were damaged. In the immediate aftermath of the earthquake, unsafe settlements, relocation and resettlement received considerable political and public attention. As reconstruction progressed, however, heritage increasingly acquired institutional and political salience. Its relationship with national identity, tourism, World Heritage sites, international institutions and highly visible reconstruction projects helped it retain attention within the recovery agenda.

As attention and institutional momentum shifted, unresolved resettlement problems did not disappear. Their costs increasingly moved towards affected households. Families still had to decide where to live, whether to rebuild, how to sustain livelihoods and how to finance recovery even when public decisions remained incomplete. Delay could therefore become a private cost through additional borrowing, self-reconstruction, migration, livelihood disruption or continued dependence on locations exposed to risk.

This comparison is important because political priorities after a disaster are not fixed. A problem that is highly visible in the first months of reconstruction may lose institutional weight as other sectors acquire stronger political, symbolic or organisational constituencies. Yet households continue to live with the consequences of unfinished decisions long after that shift occurs.

Our own longitudinal research in Panipokhari and Jillu shows why these matters. Between 2021 and 2023, residential satisfaction remained relatively stable in Jillu, while it declined substantially in government-led Panipokhari. The difference was not explained by structural safety alone. Housing design, thermal comfort, drinking water, cultural suitability, participation, household economic capacity and the freedom to adapt a house to changing needs all shaped the longer-term experience of resettlement.

A structurally safe house is necessary for resettlement, but it is not sufficient evidence of successful resettlement. For the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood, the lesson is that the early period after a disaster can provide a rare opportunity to reconsider risky settlements, land, access, infrastructure and livelihoods together. Yet by the time institutions finish preparing a plan, households may already have reorganised their lives. The timing of decisions, meaningful participation and the integration of land, livelihoods and infrastructure are therefore as important as identifying a technically safe site.

Recovery happens inside the household

The Gorkha experience also reveals a further limitation of institution-centred recovery. Even when reconstruction progresses at the level of programmes and projects, recovery is ultimately experienced at the level of the household. For the state, a disaster appears through damage figures, sectors, projects and budgets. For a family, these disruptions occur within a single life.

Urban planning scholar Mariana Arcaya and her colleagues make an important distinction between the recovery of places and the recovery of people. A road may reopen, a market may function again and houses may be rebuilt, while the people living there do not necessarily return to their previous economic, social or psychological conditions at the same pace. Recovery varies according to income, assets, displacement, social position and access to institutions.

The same distinction is relevant to the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood. A road may reopen while a family remains economically displaced. A house may be rebuilt while its occupants continue to feel unsafe. A new settlement may be technically safer while placing a household far from its livelihood, neighbours and everyday support networks. Physical reconstruction and the restoration of life are related, but they are not the same.

Social capital is part of this difference. Political scientist Daniel Aldrich has shown how trust, mutual assistance and social networks help households gain information, labour, loans, childcare and emotional support during recovery. The cost of a road or house can be calculated relatively easily. The value of a neighbour who provides childcare or a relative who offers informal credit is much harder to capture in a damage assessment. Relocation may therefore reduce physical risk while creating new social vulnerability.

Place attachment also matters. People do not remain in hazardous locations simply because they fail to understand risk. Land, employment, ancestral memory, religious meaning, social identity and status may tie households to a place. Moving a family to a technically safer location can therefore create new economic, social and psychological costs.

Public-health research adds another dimension. Post-disaster mental health is connected not only with the event itself, but also with displacement, economic loss, loss of resources and prolonged uncertainty. Families may remain unsure whether land will be declared safe, whether they should rebuild or wait, how much compensation they will receive, where children will attend school and whether relocation will allow continued access to farms or employment. Officially, the emergency may have ended, while these uncertainties can continue for months or years.

Research in Nepal after the Gorkha earthquake found a similar pattern. A study following 400 households in four earthquake-affected communities showed that recovery varied according to displacement, livelihoods, hazard exposure, place attachment, mental health and institutional participation.

This is where political economy enters the home. Government may treat housing, roads, education, livelihoods, social protection and mental health as separate sectors. For a household, they are interconnected. The state separates these issues into administrative categories, while families experience them as one life. When institutional priorities change or public decisions remain incomplete, households do not escape those unresolved issues; they absorb them. Recovery must therefore be assessed not only through public budgets, but also through the costs that households are left to carry themselves.

Who controls the story?

Political economy operates not only through budgets and projects. It also operates through the way a disaster is explained.

Several explanations of the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood are currently in circulation. Preliminary technical assessments suggest that a large mass of rock and glacial ice collapsed on the Tibetan side, temporarily blocked the river and contributed to the formation and failure of a debris lake. At the broader policy level, the disaster can also be framed through increasing climate and cryospheric risk, weak transboundary information and early warning, the concentration of settlements and infrastructure within a narrow river corridor, or inadequate attention to infrastructure location and risk-sensitive planning. These explanations are not mutually exclusive.

Public policy scholar Deborah Stone describes such explanations as “causal stories”. Policy problems do not arrive with a single self-evident cause. Actors construct accounts of what happened, why it happened, who suffered and where responsibility lies. These accounts then influence which responses appear necessary and legitimate.

Nepal is fully justified in connecting the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood with climate justice. Nepal contributes very little to global greenhouse gas emissions, while Himalayan countries face disproportionate risks from climate change and changes in the cryosphere. The unequal global political economy that produces climate risk is therefore part of the Bhotekoshi story.

At the same time, climate change should not become a complete explanation for every domestic vulnerability. If the disaster is presented only as a consequence of global warming or an event originating in the high Himalaya, important domestic questions may be pushed aside. These include where infrastructure was built, how land use was regulated, why settlements expanded in particular locations, whether construction standards were sufficiently risk-sensitive and how effectively preparedness systems operated.

The opposite interpretation would also be incomplete. If the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood is explained only as a failure of planning or administration within Nepal, the unequal global political economy that produces climate risk disappears from the analysis. Demanding climate justice internationally should not weaken accountability at home. Recognising weaknesses at home should not make global climate injustice invisible.

Narrative power also matters. Government agencies, scientific institutions, development partners, project developers, the media and affected communities do not have equal access to data, public platforms, finance or institutional prestige. The explanation that becomes official is therefore shaped by evidence as well as institutional power.

A framing centred on high-mountain monitoring may direct attention towards sensors and data systems. A framing centred on infrastructure risk may favour standards and river-corridor management. A framing centred on settlements and livelihoods may bring land, housing, relocation and social protection to the forefront. These are not merely different explanations of the same event. Once institutionalised, they create different reconstruction agendas. The causal story therefore shapes not only responsibility, but also the direction of solutions, institutional authority and resources.

A mature response to the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood should therefore place global climate risk, natural processes and domestically produced vulnerability within the same analysis. Doing so allows responsibility to be understood across international, national and local scales rather than reduced to a single convenient explanation.

From attention to budgets

These competing explanations matter because causal framing does not remain at the level of public debate. Once an interpretation gains institutional authority, it begins to influence what is measured, which interventions are prioritised and where public resources are directed. This is the point at which attention and interpretation acquire material consequences. This is how public attention, interpretation and expertise eventually become budgets.

The estimated Rs 723 billion recovery requirement for the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood is therefore more than a financial figure. It is also an early representation of how the disaster has been institutionally classified and valued. Infrastructure accounts for around Rs 473.57 billion of the estimated recovery requirement, close to three quarters of the total. Given the scale of damage to roads, bridges, hydropower and other infrastructure, major investment in these sectors is clearly necessary.

The concern is whether other forms of loss enter the assessment with comparable clarity. Physical losses are generally easier to measure. Kilometres of damaged roads, destroyed houses, generation capacity and replacement costs can be estimated through established methods. Household and social losses are more difficult to quantify.

The dispersal of a neighbourhood has a cost. So does the additional travel time faced by a relocated farmer, the loss of informal childcare when extended families are separated, or the disappearance of a customer base for a small business. These losses are real even when they are difficult to monetise.

This difference can create a self-reinforcing cycle. Visible losses generate better data. Better data make it easier to define projects. Clearly defined projects attract finance. Financed projects produce measurable results, and measurable results are easier to present as political and institutional achievements. Less visible losses may remain weakly documented and therefore less competitive for public finance.

Attention, framing, expertise, institutional authority and budgets are therefore not separate domains. They form a sequence. What becomes visible influences how the problem is defined; the definition influences which knowledge becomes authoritative; institutional authority influences priorities; and priorities eventually shape where resources go.

That sequence is also why the question “who defines reconstruction?” matters. Whoever has greater capacity to define the problem also has greater capacity to influence what the state eventually recognises, organises and finances.

Keeping affected families in view

Ultimately, this entire sequence is tested in the lives of affected families. During the Bhotekoshi Flash Flood, those families became highly visible. Images of rescue, destroyed homes, blocked roads and displacement drew national attention. The more difficult test begins after the urgency of the event has passed.

Recovery takes place across different time horizons. The immediate period concerns safe shelter, basic services, income and access. The medium term brings decisions about permanent housing, land, settlement planning, common infrastructure and livelihoods. The longer term requires stronger river and mountain monitoring, early warning, infrastructure standards, land-use management and institutional reform.

All these levels are important. However, long-term technical solutions should not displace the immediate questions faced by displaced families. People need clarity about where they can live safely, what happens to land that can no longer be occupied, whether voluntary land readjustment is possible, how livelihoods will be restored, who will finance common infrastructure and how communities will participate in deciding the future of their settlements.

This is why a PDNA or RDNA is not simply a technical document. It creates an early institutional basis for determining which losses the state formally recognises, which needs receive priority and how recovery itself is defined. Its quality should therefore be judged not only by the total financial requirement it calculates, but also by the range of losses it succeeds in making visible.

The most meaningful measures of recovery may not be the easiest to publish. Five years from now, the stronger evidence will concern how many families have secure and legally recognised places to live, how many have restored stable livelihoods, how many carry additional debt because of reconstruction, how many relocated households continue to return to hazardous areas for farming or employment, and how many communities had a meaningful role in shaping their own resettlement.

No single discipline can answer these questions. Planners, engineers, economists, social scientists, psychosocial specialists and local governments all have roles to play. More importantly, affected families must be treated as sources of knowledge, not only as beneficiaries. They understand everyday risk, place-based livelihoods, social relations and which alternatives are practically workable.

The Bhotekoshi Flash Flood has made the state, experts, development partners and affected communities highly visible. The more difficult test of disaster governance begins when public attention declines, studies are completed, consultants submit reports, budgets are allocated and large infrastructure projects acquire their own institutional momentum.

By that stage, success should not be measured only by reopened roads, restored megawatts, improved monitoring systems or international assistance. These achievements matter, but they capture only part of recovery. A deeper measure is whether the people who are visible in disaster images today remain visible to the state when later decisions are made about land, livelihoods, settlements, budgets and future risk.

The experience after the Gorkha earthquake suggests why this matters. Political and institutional attention can shift, while unresolved recovery costs remain with affected households. Bhotekoshi therefore presents not only a question of how Nepal will reconstruct, but of who will retain the authority to define reconstruction as public attention, institutional priorities and financing evolve.

Which losses are recognised, whose knowledge becomes authoritative, who exercises decision-making power and where resources are directed will ultimately be reflected in the lives of affected people. Who defines reconstruction will, in the end, help determine whose recovery it becomes.

title.rendered: The Delhi BRICS Summit and what Nepal lost by staying away

content.rendered:
India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13. Leaders from Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, several newer members and partner countries came together under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”

It was a significant event. BRICS now represents more than half of the world’s population and accounts for almost 40 percent of global GDP, while its share of the global economy continues to grow. When such a group meets in our own neighbourhood, in a country with which we share a border and deep cultural ties, it is not a small event to watch from a distance. Yet Nepal was not part of the gathering.

In this brief article, I examine what Nepal’s absence means, why it happened, and what Nepal could have done differently.

BRICS started small, as a name for four fast-growing economies. Over the years, it has grown into something much bigger: a platform where countries outside the traditional Western-led system discuss trade, technology, development finance and global rules that affect their daily lives and the livelihoods of their people.

It now includes new full members and a widening circle of partner countries. Alongside the main summit, the host country often invites guest nations to an “outreach” session, allowing neighbouring and other relevant countries to have a seat at the table even if they are not members.

This is exactly what happened in 2016, when India hosted BRICS in Goa. At that time, India invited the leaders of BIMSTEC countries, including Nepal, to a special outreach meeting alongside the BRICS leaders. The then Nepali prime minister travelled to Goa and sat in the same room as leaders of some of the world’s major emerging economies.

It was a chance to be seen, to be heard and to raise Nepal’s concerns directly.

During the recent BRICS meeting on September 12 and 13, however, India chose a different guest list for its outreach segment. Nepal was not included this time. That is the real story behind the question of what Nepal has lost.

Many people may ask why Nepal’s absence from a major event in Delhi matters. Some may argue that since Nepal is not a BRICS member, there is little reason for its non-participation to be significant.

The answer is simple. Big international gatherings are not only about formal membership. They are also about visibility, relationships and the quiet diplomacy that takes place on the sidelines.

When leaders from member and partner countries sit together for two days, many smaller meetings take place outside the main hall. Ministers talk to ministers. Officials exchange views on trade and investment. Journalists from around the world report on which countries were present and what their leaders said.

A country that is present gets noticed. A country that is absent can easily be forgotten, at least for that news cycle.

For Nepal, situated between India and China, the two most powerful BRICS members, this matters even more. Both of Nepal’s neighbours were in New Delhi discussing issues that could influence trade routes, investment, connectivity and regional cooperation.

Nepal’s economy depends heavily on both countries for trade, transit, remittances, tourism and infrastructure projects. When the countries that shape Nepal’s economic future are discussing new opportunities and rules in the same city, it is natural for Nepal to want a voice in that room, even if it is a small one.

There is also a symbolic cost.

Nepal has long tried to present itself as an active and independent voice in South Asian and Asian diplomacy, rather than simply a country that reacts to decisions made by its neighbours. Being left out of a major regional gathering, particularly one held so close to home, does not help that image.

It raises a question that Nepali commentators have already started asking: has Nepal lost some of its diplomatic energy compared with a decade ago?

Many of us are accustomed to the blame game. It would be unfair, however, to blame India alone. Invitations to an outreach summit are the host country’s choice and are based on its political and diplomatic calculations at the time.

But it is also fair to ask whether Nepal did enough from its side.

Diplomacy is not only about waiting for an invitation. It is about building relationships and making a country’s case well before the guest list is finalised, so that its name naturally comes up when the host is deciding whom to invite.

In recent years, Nepal’s foreign policy has been affected by frequent changes in government and shifting political priorities at home. When leadership changes, policy often changes as well, making it harder to maintain steady, long-term engagement with international partners.

The Foreign Ministry, as well as other government ministries, must constantly adjust to new political leadership and priorities. This can leave less time to plan ahead for events such as BRICS outreach meetings, which require engagement months, or even years, in advance.

This is likely part of the reason Nepal was not on the list this time, even though it was included in 2016.

Nepal should have done a number of things.

The present government should have reviewed what previous governments had done, as well as their plans and commitments in the area of foreign policy. Nepal’s Foreign Ministry should have started reaching out to its Indian counterparts as soon as the 2026 BRICS Summit was announced, rather than waiting to see who would be invited.

The government should also have appointed ambassadors to vacant diplomatic posts on time. Early and repeated engagement at the political, diplomatic and official levels could have produced positive results.

Second, Nepal could have used its position as a BIMSTEC member and its close ties with both China and India to make a strong case for inclusion, pointing to the precedent set in Goa in 2016.

Third, even without a seat in New Delhi, Nepal’s leaders could have used the days of the summit to hold their own high-level meetings with visiting leaders passing through South Asia. They could also have issued clear public statements on the trade, connectivity and regional cooperation issues being discussed in Delhi, ensuring that Nepal’s views were at least part of the wider public conversation.

Fourth, and perhaps most importantly in the long run, Nepal needs a foreign policy that does not depend so heavily on which party or leader is currently in government.

Bilateral and multilateral relationships take years to build. They can be weakened when every change of government brings a change in policy and direction.

Despite all this, missing one summit is not, by itself, a disaster. Nepal will have other opportunities to engage with BRICS countries, both bilaterally and through other regional groupings.

But the Delhi summit is a useful reminder.

Neighbourhood diplomacy does not run on its own. It requires steady attention, clear goals and people working on it long before the cameras arrive.

If Nepal wants to participate in such events next time, the work to make that happen should begin now, not when the invitation list is being drawn up.

title.rendered: RSP says candidate club draws encouraging applications despite flood disruption

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) says its Candidate Club has received an encouraging number of applications despite the disruption caused by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods.

The RSP opened applications on August 17 for people interested in contesting local elections for positions in rural municipalities. Ten days later, on August 26, the Bhotekoshi flood forced the party to suspend all its official political and organisational activities.

A secretariat meeting held on the day of the disaster decided to suspend all pre-scheduled activities, saying the party needed to focus its attention and resources entirely on disaster management, rescue and relief.

However, the Candidate Club process has continued despite the suspension of other organisational activities, according to RSP General Secretary Bipin Acharya.

Acharya said the party was encouraged by the number of applications received so far.

“We are encouraged by the number of applications we have received from people interested in becoming rural municipality chairs, vice-chairs, ward chairs and ward members,” Acharya told Onlinekhabar.

The party has not disclosed the exact number of applications as the collection process is still ongoing.

The first phase of the Candidate Club process was opened for those seeking to become candidates in rural municipalities. The party plans to subsequently open applications for candidates in municipalities, sub-metropolitan cities and metropolitan cities.

The RSP has yet to decide how long applications for rural municipalities will remain open. It may either keep the existing application period unchanged or suspend it while opening applications for the other categories, Acharya said.

The party introduced the Candidate Club to identify qualified and capable candidates for local elections. However, the floods have affected efforts to explain the new system and conduct orientation programmes at the grassroots level.

RSP Koshi Province chair Chandra Rai said the floods had disrupted the party’s organisational activities and consequently affected the Candidate Club process as well.

Since the system is a new practice not previously adopted by Nepali political parties, there is a need to explain it to potential candidates and party members, Rai said.

“It is a new practice. It also needs to be explained from a technical perspective. Some people have already applied, while others are still in a wait-and-see situation,” Rai told Onlinekhabar.

The party had planned orientation programmes at the local level to explain the Candidate Club, its importance and the candidate selection process. Those programmes have been halted because of the floods.

RSP Gandaki Province chair Navin Tripathi said applications from people interested in contesting in rural municipalities in the province have also been encouraging.

Tripathi said the party had planned to visit local levels to explain the Candidate Club but had to suspend the programme because of the floods.

“We had planned to visit local levels and provide information about the system, but the floods forced us to suspend that plan,” Tripathi told Onlinekhabar.

The party plans to organise programmes in districts such as Tanahun, Parbat and Baglung, where extended meetings have not yet been completed, to brief party members and supporters about the Candidate Club.

Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading were among the districts most severely affected by the floods. The RSP has not yet decided whether a different process will be adopted for these districts.

According to Acharya, the party’s immediate priority in those districts remains relief and reconstruction, and no decision has been made regarding candidate applications there.

Bagmati Province chair Utsav Aryal said the party would need to adopt a separate approach for the flood-affected districts.

The Candidate Club is the first step for those seeking to become RSP candidates. Under the party’s candidate selection framework, aspirants must pass through four stages before being selected.

The party plans to select candidates through a primary election, with the primary vote carrying 40 percent of the total weighting. Local party members will have the highest weight in the primary election, accounting for 75 percent of the total weighting.

Those interested in becoming candidates must also attend classes at the party’s Leadership Academy after submitting their applications.

The party will additionally assess candidates’ “political proximity”, considering factors including organisational affiliation, previous roles and discipline, chances of winning, multidimensional popularity, educational and professional experience, and an impartial social assessment.

The RSP has also set eligibility requirements based on party membership and the time elapsed since leaving another political party.

People who have never been members of another political party can apply to the Candidate Club after completing 45 days of RSP membership. Those who have left another political party must have completed three months before applying.

For prominent, expert and publicly respected individuals with a clean image, the party has created a special application process subject to approval from designated committees and bodies.

The framework for selecting candidates was developed under the leadership of Acharya, who previously served as the RSP’s co-general secretary.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

Deuba camp rejects central office terms, sets own path for 15th convention

The non-establishment faction of the Nepali Congress has decided to move forward with the party’s 15th general convention process in its own way. This was concluded at a meeting of the faction held Monday at outgoing party president Sher Bahadur Deuba’s residence in Maharajgunj, where members determined they could not take part in the convention on the terms decided by the party’s central office.

Q&A with Prime Minister missing from House calendar

The House of Representatives has released its tentative calendar through October 1, outlining the dates on which meetings will be held and the likely agenda for each sitting. However, the calendar does not include the direct question-and-answer session with the prime minister.

Infrastructure Minister vows to restore flood-damaged roads by October

The government says it has stepped up work to restore damaged road networks in flood-affected areas and aims to bring them back into operation by October. The government is currently prioritising temporary alternative roads, suspension bridges and cable crossings in the affected areas. It plans to begin construction of permanent roads and bridges once immediate connectivity is restored. Speaking at a meeting with representatives from flood-affected areas at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers on Monday, Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal said the government had formed eight thematic task forces to accelerate the construction of roads and bridges.

Contracts for 10 road projects in Baitadi terminated

The Road Division Office, Baitadi, has terminated contracts for 10 road projects that had long remained unfinished. In a notice published Monday, the office said the contracts were terminated because the work had not been completed within the agreed timeframe and had not proceeded according to the contract terms.

PM Balen Shah assures no budget shortage for Bhotekoshi flood relief, reconstruction

Prime Minister Balen Shah has assured that there will be no shortage of funds for relief and reconstruction in areas affected by the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa. Speaking at a meeting with elected representatives from districts and local levels declared disaster crisis zones at Singha Durbar on Monday, Shah said all state agencies were working to address the situation and that the government would ensure adequate funding for relief and reconstruction.

RSP forms special team to resolve organisational dispute in Madhesh

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) has formed a special team to resolve organisational disputes in Madhesh Province, where party conventions have yet to be held in seven of the province’s eight districts. The RSP held its first general convention in Chitwan in late June. However, only Parsa has completed its district convention in Madhesh, while conventions in the other seven districts remain pending.

Gold and silver prices fall

The prices of gold and silver declined in the Nepali market on Monday. According to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association, the price of gold has fallen by Rs 1,200 per tola today.

Direct Pokhara–Dubai flights to start from September 23

Flydubai has announced its schedule for direct Dubai–Pokhara–Dubai flights, with the first flight landing at Pokhara International Airport at 6:15 pm on September 23. Pokhara Airport plans a water-cannon salute to welcome the arriving Flydubai aircraft and passengers. After disembarking arriving passengers, the plane will depart Pokhara for Dubai at 7:15 pm with a new set of passengers.

NEPSE rises 25 points as investors await market reform plan

Nepal’s stock market rose 25.55 points on Monday, the first trading day of the week, with the NEPSE index closing at 2,585.04 points. The index had gained 27 points in the previous trading session. With Monday’s rise, the market has gained 52 points over the past two trading days.

title.rendered: ANFA to stage protest at NSC seeking FIFA suspension lifted

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

All Nepal Football Association (ANFA), which has been suspended by FIFA, is preparing to stage a sit-in at the National Sports Council (NSC) on Tuesday, demanding that the suspension be lifted.

ANFA employees, referees and coaches, among others, will participate in the protest, according to ANFA General Secretary Kiran Rai.

“We have issues related to lifting ANFA’s suspension, including whether we will be able to participate in the SAFF Games. We are submitting a memorandum to seek a solution to the problems facing Nepali football,” Rai told Onlinekhabar.

ANFA plans to stage a one-hour sit-in at the NSC premises after submitting the memorandum, followed by a press conference.

The protest programme was decided following discussions between ANFA and its employees.

FIFA suspended ANFA on June 24, citing third-party interference in the football governing body. The suspension has effectively left Nepali football in limbo.

ANFA leadership has accused the government of failing to take any initiative to help lift the suspension.

title.rendered: RSP forms special team to resolve organisational dispute in Madhesh

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) has formed a special team to resolve organisational disputes in Madhesh Province, where party conventions have yet to be held in seven of the province’s eight districts.

The RSP held its first general convention in Chitwan in late June. However, only Parsa has completed its district convention in Madhesh, while conventions in the other seven districts remain pending.

Against this backdrop, the party’s Central Committee formed a Madhesh Province Organisation Audit Committee under the coordination of co-general secretary Hari Dhakal at its meeting on August 21.

The committee has been conducting discussions and consultations by visiting the districts directly. Besides Dhakal, the committee includes party leaders Surendra Chaudhary, Ashok Kumar Chaudhary, Pramod Neupane, Jagadish Kharel and Poonam Agrawal.

The team began its organisational audit in Parsa and has since completed discussions in Bara, Rautahat, Sarlahi, Janakpur and Mahottari. It is scheduled to hold discussions in Saptari on Monday.

The team plans to visit all seven districts, assess the organisational situation and identify ways to resolve the disputes before returning to Kathmandu.

According to an RSP leader, a power struggle between party lawmakers and the organisation at the district level has prevented the conventions from being held in Madhesh.

As a result, representatives from the previous organisational structure in all Madhesh districts except Parsa participated in the party’s general convention in Chitwan.

Even in Parsa, the district convention was held a day later than scheduled following an internal dispute. There had also been tensions between an elected lawmaker and the district organisation, with then-district chair Hari Pant eventually winning the contest.

The RSP is now working to resolve the disputes and pave the way for conventions in the remaining districts. The Central Committee formed the audit committee under Dhakal specifically for this purpose.

A member of the committee said the team is expected to return to Kathmandu on Wednesday after completing discussions in Saptari.

Party chair Ravi Lamichhane is then preparing to visit Madhesh Province.

During his visit, Lamichhane is expected to take initiatives to resolve the disputes based on the problems identified and recommendations put forward by the special team.

The government is currently prioritising temporary alternative roads, suspension bridges and cable crossings in the affected areas. It plans to begin construction of permanent roads and bridges once immediate connectivity is restored.

Speaking at a meeting with representatives from flood-affected areas at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers on Monday, Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal said the government had formed eight thematic task forces to accelerate the construction of roads and bridges.

Lamsal urged local representatives to coordinate directly with the task forces to avoid duplication and help speed up reconstruction efforts.

He also asked local representatives who were in Kathmandu for the meeting to coordinate directly with officials of agencies under his ministry. They should provide details of damaged infrastructure in their respective areas, help prepare plans, coordinate construction and follow up on progress, he said.

According to Lamsal, work is also underway to restore drinking water systems in the affected areas by December.

The government is also working on the reconstruction of health, education and other essential infrastructure in the flood-hit areas, he said.

Information and Communications Minister Bikram Timilsina, who is also a member of the House of Representatives from Nuwakot, raised concerns about non-governmental organisations making commitments to build houses for flood victims and provide protection to senior citizens and children without proper coordination.

He said such organisations should carry out their activities only in coordination with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Timilsina also suggested that local representatives collect comprehensive data on all affected people and submit it to the government on time to ensure that no victims are left out of relief and reconstruction programmes.

title.rendered: Q&A with Prime Minister missing from House calendar

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

The House of Representatives has released its tentative calendar through October 1, outlining the dates on which meetings will be held and the likely agenda for each sitting. However, the calendar does not include the direct question-and-answer session with the prime minister.

The House had previously scheduled a direct question-and-answer session with Prime Minister Balen Shah for August 26. The programme was disrupted after a devastating flood struck Rasuwa on the same day.

No new date has been fixed for the session since then.

The provision for the prime minister’s question-and-answer session is set out in Rule 56 of the House of Representatives Rules.

The rule states that the Speaker “shall” allocate the first hour of a sitting on any one day during the first week of every month for members to ask questions on important matters directly related to the prime minister or his area of responsibility.

The provision is mandatory, as it uses the term “shall”. It also specifies what should happen if the session cannot be held on the scheduled day.

“If, for any reason, the meeting cannot be held on that day, the Speaker shall allocate the first hour of the immediately following meeting,” states Sub-rule 1 of Rule 56.

However, despite this provision, no prime minister’s question session has been included in the parliamentary calendar through October 1.

According to the calendar, the House will meet on September 15 and 16, followed by sittings on September 17, 21, 22, 23, September 29 and 30, and October 1.

Meanwhile, preparations are underway to send bills currently before the House to thematic parliamentary committees for clause-by-clause discussions. The tentative agenda includes items related to this process.

title.rendered: After a global research career, Rajendra Pangeni plans his return to Nepal

content.rendered:
When Rajendra Pangeni looks back at the village where he grew up in Syangja, one memory stands out above everything else. Fire.

The house where he grew up was destroyed in a fire just as he was preparing to leave for Kathmandu to pursue higher education.

His books were gone. His clothes were gone. His family’s belongings were reduced to ashes. For Pangeni, the fire seemed to take his future with it.

“I felt that everything was over that night,” he recalls.

More than three decades later, Pangeni is preparing to return to that same village — this time after building a career in cancer research across three countries.

His journey has taken him from a rural community in Syangja to Mumbai, the United Kingdom and the United States, where he has worked on brain cancer and other areas of cancer research.

Now, he has resigned from his position as an assistant professor at a US university and is preparing to return home.

His plan is not simply to come back. He wants to help build a research culture in Nepal.

From working nights in Mumbai to studying cancer

Rajendra Pangeni’s route to scientific research was anything but conventional.

Growing up in Waling Municipality, Syangja, he was known as a curious child. His father taught at a local school, while his mother looked after the household.

While other children were playing football, Pangeni was often asking questions.

Why is the sky blue? How does rain fall?

The questions stayed with him, and so did the habit of looking for answers.

After completing his SLC in the first division in 1994, he dreamed of going to Kathmandu for college. At the time, for students from Nepal’s districts, studying in the capital was one of the clearest routes to a better future.

Then the fire changed everything.

Unable to afford college after the disaster, Pangeni eventually left Nepal. He travelled through Kanpur and Delhi before arriving in Mumbai with little money but a determination to continue his education.

He worked wherever he could.

At a petrol station. In hotels. In shops. At times, even in a dance bar. And he studied alongside the work.

“Sometimes I would work through the night and go to class in the morning,” he says.

After seven years in Mumbai, he graduated in microbiology from the University of Mumbai.

The experience also changed how he viewed his home country.

Compared with what he had seen in Mumbai, Nepal appeared to him to be decades behind in terms of opportunity, technology and coordination.

“I realised there was so much we needed to do,” he says.

In 2001, he returned to Nepal and began teaching. He later completed postgraduate studies through a college affiliated with an Indian university.

But returning to Nepal did not satisfy his appetite for learning. He wanted to go further.

The journey into cancer research

Rajendra Pangeni eventually moved to the United Kingdom to study at the University of Wolverhampton.

There, his interest in science became intertwined with his interest in people and institutions.

He contested and won an election for a non-political student union, giving him the opportunity to work with hundreds of students and understand the challenges they faced.

He also received a scholarship that opened the door to doctoral research into brain cancer.

His PhD focused on how breast cancer spreads to the brain and whether blood tests could help detect the disease at an early stage.

The research took him deeper into a question that would shape his career: how can laboratory science eventually become something that improves a patient’s chances of survival?

“Science helped me understand the deeper meaning of human suffering,” he says. “During the nights I spent in the laboratory, I realised that the purpose of research is to save lives.”

After completing his PhD, he moved to the United States.

At Northwestern University in Chicago, he carried out postdoctoral research into brain cancer, studying changes in cancer cells that can influence how effectively treatments work.

He later focused on glioblastoma, one of the most difficult forms of brain cancer to treat.

His research examined why existing treatments are often ineffective and how new approaches to treatment might be developed.

But after two years at Northwestern, Pangeni wanted to move beyond the laboratory.

He wanted to see how research could translate into actual patient care.

That took him to City of Hope National Medical Center, a major cancer treatment and research institution in the US.

There, he also became involved in research related to developing drugs for lung cancer.

The experience reinforced something he had increasingly come to believe.

“Science must create meaningful change not only in the laboratory but also in the lives of patients,” he says.

The question that kept following him

Despite building a career overseas, Rajendra Pangeni says he never stopped thinking about Nepal.

In fact, he says he had made a decision as early as 2010, when he went to the UK.

“I had decided that I would return to Nepal after completing my PhD,” he says.

But returning is easier said than done.

Through conversations with Nepali scientists and professionals living abroad, Pangeni noticed a common pattern.

Many wanted to return. Many wanted to contribute. But few wanted to make the move alone.

“Thousands of friends living abroad often expressed their desire to return to Nepal,” he says. “But they also felt that returning alone and working in Nepal would be difficult.”

That led to the Nepal Farkau Maha Abhiyan, an initiative aimed at bringing together Nepalis abroad who wanted either to return or contribute their expertise to the country.

The idea was straightforward: instead of asking individuals to solve the problem alone, create a network that could make returning and contributing easier.

The initiative has since attracted people from around the world, with some members already returning to Nepal.

But Pangeni wanted to go further. He wanted to create an institution.

Building a research network for Nepal

That vision eventually became NIRI Nepal — the National Institute for Research and Innovation.

The idea emerged through online meetings and discussions among Nepali scientists and researchers scattered across the world.

The ambition is to build a world-class, non-profit research institution that connects Nepali talent globally and directs that expertise towards research and innovation in Nepal.

It started with 27 people.

Today, Rajendra Pangeni says, 42 Nepali scientists from around the world are part of the network.

For him, the numbers matter less than what they represent. Nepal does not necessarily lack talented people, he argues.

It lacks the systems that bring them together.

“Nepal also has excellent minds,” he says. “What we lack is coordination and trust.”

NIRI Nepal is already working with Kathmandu Cancer Center through research projects involving cancer and other diseases.

One area of research is looking at why certain types of cancer appear more frequently among different ethnic communities in Nepal.

Research is also being conducted into cerebral palsy and other conditions.

Pangeni himself has published nearly four dozen research papers in international journals.

Now he is coming home

For years, the idea of returning to Nepal remained a plan for the future. Now it is becoming reality.

Rajendra Pangeni has resigned from his US university position and is preparing to move back to his village.

He plans to continue teaching remotely for the American university while living in Nepal.

For someone who once believed a fire had ended his educational dreams, the decision carries a certain symbolism.

He is going back to where it all started.

“I want the children in my village to understand that you don’t have to go abroad to dream,” he says.

That may be one of the most important parts of his return.

Pangeni does not want young Nepalis to see international universities and foreign countries as the only places where serious scientific work can happen.

Instead, he wants them to believe that Nepal itself can become a place where research happens, where difficult problems are studied and where young scientists can build careers.

His focus will be on attracting a new generation of researchers and working on problems rooted in Nepal.

It is a very different ambition from the one he had as a young student dreaming of Kathmandu.

Back then, Kathmandu represented opportunity because opportunity seemed unavailable at home.

Now, after spending years in some of the world’s leading research institutions, Pangeni wants to help create that opportunity at home.

Back to the hill where it began

There is an image Rajendra Pangeni returns to when he talks about coming home. Standing on the hill near his village and looking towards Mount Manaslu.

“When I stand on the hill in my village and look at Mount Manaslu, I feel that dreams can grow even from ashes, if you still have the confidence to believe in them,” he says.

The house where his childhood dream seemed to burn away is part of that story. So is Mumbai, where he worked nights while studying. So are the laboratories in Britain and the United States where he spent years studying cancer. And now, so is the village he once had to leave.

“I am returning to where the journey began,” he says. “I want to go there and do something new.”

For Pangeni, returning to Nepal is therefore not a retreat from the world.

It is an attempt to bring what he learned from the world back home.

The boy who once wondered why the sky was blue grew up to spend his life searching for answers to far more difficult questions.

Now he is returning home with another question in mind:

What can be built in Nepal if its scientists, researchers and young people begin to believe they do not have to leave to do their best work?
