title.rendered: Direct Pokhara–Dubai flights to start from September 23

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Flydubai has announced its schedule for direct Dubai–Pokhara–Dubai flights, with the first flight landing at Pokhara International Airport at 6:15 pm on September 23.

Pokhara Airport plans a water-cannon salute to welcome the arriving Flydubai aircraft and passengers. After disembarking arriving passengers, the plane will depart Pokhara for Dubai at 7:15 pm with a new set of passengers. Airport information officer Binod Singh Rawat said Flydubai will operate the route with an Airbus A319 or A320 depending on need — the A319 carries 140-150 passengers, the A320 160-180 — with the daily flight landing at Pokhara at 6:15 pm and departing for Dubai at 7:15 pm. He said the return leg will carry cargo along with passengers.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal granted Flydubai permission for the route in June. Officials say the direct link to Dubai, a major global aviation hub, will connect Pokhara to the international air network, something the airport hadn’t achieved in regular international service in the three years since it opened commercially. Flydubai’s Nepal-based general manager Nabaraj Shahi said tickets from Pokhara are up to Rs 5,000 cheaper than the equivalent Kathmandu departures, and that promotional discounts will be offered to passengers and partner agencies.

The service will run under a codeshare partnership between Flydubai and Emirates, allowing passengers from Pokhara to connect onward to Australia, Europe, or the US on a single ticket via Emirates’ hub at Dubai’s Terminal 3, which links to more than 140 countries.

Pokhara Tourism Council chair Hari Bhujel said the tourism sector stands to benefit directly and called for unity among local tourism operators to help make the route succeed. Nepal Tourism Board executive member Santosh Pokharel said sustaining the route is now a shared responsibility across stakeholders, noting Flydubai has taken a chance on Pokhara and everyone needs to support it in turn.

Pokhara Metropolitan City and Flydubai have also agreed to continue cooperating on tourism promotion, destination marketing, and expanding international air connectivity. The new route is expected to boost tourism, trade, and economic activity across Gandaki province, giving residents direct access to more than 250 global destinations including London, New York, and Tokyo, while making it easier for foreign tourists to fly directly into Pokhara.

Himalaya Airlines’ Pokhara–Lhasa service, launched in March 2025, has since been suspended due to low passenger numbers. The Pokhara–Dubai route will be the airport’s second scheduled commercial international service, following earlier charter flights to destinations in China, India, and Bhutan. Pokhara International Airport serves as Nepal’s third international gateway, amid ongoing calls to decentralise air traffic away from Kathmandu.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah assures no budget shortage for Bhotekoshi flood relief, reconstruction

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Prime Minister Balen Shah has assured that there will be no shortage of funds for relief and reconstruction in areas affected by the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa.

Speaking at a meeting with elected representatives from districts and local levels declared disaster crisis zones at Singha Durbar on Monday, Shah said all state agencies were working to address the situation and that the government would ensure adequate funding for relief and reconstruction.

During the meeting, Shah also sought information and suggestions on the post-flood situation, the current challenges, immediate measures needed and plans for recovery.

Representatives from the affected areas said damaged road networks had created major difficulties in relief distribution and reconstruction, urging the government to reopen the damaged roads as soon as possible.

Rajan Shrestha, mayor of Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot, said around 19 bridges over the Trishuli River and surrounding areas had been swept away. He said roads connecting Rasuwa, Dhading and Bidur had also been disrupted, creating difficulties in rescue and relief operations.

Shrestha said the municipality was preparing to relocate affected families from temporary holding centres to rented rooms to reduce overcrowding and the risk of possible disease outbreaks. The municipality also plans to provide each affected family with Rs 10,000 for six months, along with utensils, gas stoves and cylinders, and food supplies.

He said discussions were also held with the prime minister on immediately constructing a temporary pipe diversion and installing a Bailey bridge to reconnect settlements and the provincial-level hospital located across the Trishuli River.

According to Shrestha, Prime Minister Shah pledged that all three levels of government would work together to build the necessary infrastructure without delay.

Shrestha also said local representatives suggested developing settlements in safe locations through land pooling while preserving the cultural, historical and agricultural character of the affected areas.

Representatives and chiefs of 15 local levels from disaster-affected areas of Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun, along with members of the House of Representatives, attended the meeting.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood washed away 2,792 meters of bridges, report finds

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

The devastating flood that came down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers via the Rasuwagadhi border point has damaged a total of 37 motorable bridges. According to the government-formed “Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood 2083: Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment” report, 33 of these bridges were completely washed away.

The report states that the combined length of the fully washed-away bridges is 2,792 meters. By bridge length, the greatest damage occurred in Nuwakot.

In Nuwakot, 14 bridges were completely swept away, totalling 1,480 meters. In Rasuwa, 13 bridges were lost, but their combined length was only 566 meters. In Dhading, 5 bridges were washed away for a combined loss of 613 meters, while in Gorkha, one bridge was lost, amounting to 133 meters of damage.

Nuwakot alone accounts for about 40.5 percent of the damage among the washed-away motorable bridges. The report notes that Rasuwa’s bridges tended to be shorter, which is why, despite a similar number of bridges being damaged there as in Nuwakot, the total length of damaged bridges in Rasuwa district is lower. Four bridges were found to have suffered partial damage, totalling 240 meters.

The flood also damaged 68 suspension bridges, with total damage to suspension bridges amounting to 10,670 meters. As a result, the flood cut off access across river areas in various places, and suspension bridge reconstruction is currently underway at several locations.

title.rendered: NEPSE rises 25 points as investors await market reform plan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Nepal’s stock market rose 25.55 points on Monday, the first trading day of the week, with the NEPSE index closing at 2,585.04 points.

The index had gained 27 points in the previous trading session. With Monday’s rise, the market has gained 52 points over the past two trading days.

The recent gains come as Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle prepares to introduce an action plan aimed at improving the stock market. Expectations that the proposed measures could boost investor confidence have contributed to the recent rise in the market.

Trading turnover also increased on Monday. Shares worth Rs 4.68 billion changed hands, compared with Rs 4.35 billion in the previous session.

Of the companies traded, the share prices of 226 companies increased, while 47 declined and two remained unchanged.

All major sectoral indices closed higher. The banking sector rose 0.78%, development banks 0.87%, finance 1.67%, hotels and tourism 0.86%, hydropower 1.16%, investment 0.64%, life insurance 1.45%, manufacturing and processing 0.54%, microfinance 0.78%, non-life insurance 1.50%, others 1.39% and trading 1.38%.

title.rendered: ‘We promised to return with the trophy, and we did it’: Sandeep Lamichhane

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Nepali cricket team captain Sandeep Lamichhane said the team fulfilled the promise it made before leaving for Malaysia by returning home with the ACC Premier Cup trophy.

The Nepali team returned home on Sunday night after winning the ACC Premier Cup and securing a place in the Asia Cup.

Speaking to reporters at Tribhuvan International Airport, Lamichhane thanked the Nepali supporters who travelled to Malaysia to back the team as well as those who supported them from across the country.

“When we left, we had made a promise — to return to Nepal with the trophy. Today, we have been able to fulfil that promise. This is the result of the love and support of all Nepali fans,” he said.

Lamichhane also dedicated the team’s victory to Nepalis affected by the floods, saying the team was happy to have brought some joy to the country during a difficult period.

“We are all very happy. At a time when the country is going through sorrow, I feel we were able to bring some happiness to Nepalis through cricket,” he said. “This title and this achievement are dedicated to all those who lost their lives in the floods, as a tribute to them.”

Lamichhane said Nepal’s defeat against Hong Kong in the group stage was an exception and that the team performed strongly throughout the tournament.

Recalling Nepal’s semifinal against Oman, where the team successfully defended a target of 147 runs, he said the score did not reflect Nepal’s actual batting potential but the team’s collective effort made the victory possible.

“We focused on basic cricket. In the semifinal against Oman, our mindset was to treat every ball and every moment as if it were the final. Every bowler made an exceptional effort and every player played their role. That is why we were able to win,” he said.

He said a score of 180–200 could have been ideal on the wicket, but once Nepal had posted 147, the team knew it could get back into the game by taking two or three early wickets.

“We knew that if we could take two or three wickets early, we could get back into the game. Everyone gave their best,” he said.

Lamichhane, who was named Player of the Tournament, said the team’s success was more important than his individual award.

“This is not an individual achievement; it is a victory for the country. I am happy to be named Man of the Tournament, but Dipendra, Bashir, Gulshan, Karan, Aasif and Rohit all contributed equally. The credit goes to the entire team,” he said.

He also praised the coaching staff, physiotherapists, trainers, analysts, managers and other members of the support staff, describing them as the “heroes behind the scenes.”

According to Lamichhane, the team will resume preparations after a short break. With qualification for the Asia Cup secured, he said the Asian Games will also be one of the team’s major targets.

“We will rest for a day or two and then begin preparations again. The Asia Cup is there, but before that, the Asian Games are also a major target for us,” he said.

Nepal secured its place in the Asia Cup for the second time by winning the ACC Premier Cup.

title.rendered: Tribhuvan Highway section collapses in Makwanpur, traffic restricted to one lane

content.rendered:
Makwanpur, September 14

A section of the Tribhuvan Highway near Aghor Bazaar in Bhimphedi Rural Municipality-9, Makwanpur, has collapsed, disrupting traffic along the highway.

According to Makwanpur police, the lower section of the road gave way, forcing vehicles to operate on only one lane.

The road section collapsed at around 9:40 am on Monday. Police said efforts are underway to create a temporary track in coordination with the Department of Roads to resume two-way traffic.

A team of police personnel, including traffic police, has been deployed from the Area Police Office, Palung, under the command of Police Inspector Govinda Prasad Bhandari to facilitate the opening of the road for two-way traffic.

The Tribhuvan Highway has been carrying increased traffic in recent days as an alternative route between Kathmandu and Hetauda after the Trishuli River flood damaged the road at Krishnabhir along the Prithvi Highway.

The increased use of the Tribhuvan Highway has resulted in heavier traffic pressure on the route.

title.rendered: Why has Rabi Lamichhane’s proposed all-party disaster mechanism not been formed?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

The day after the devastating flood in Rasuwa, Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) chairperson Rabi Lamichhane proposed forming a high-level all-party mechanism to coordinate rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts.

The proposal came after the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26. The following day, Lamichhane called an all-party meeting attended by senior leaders from the RSP, Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, Nepali Communist Party, Shram Sanskriti Party, Rastriya Prajatantra Party, Janata Samajbadi Party and Janamat Party.

During the meeting, Lamichhane proposed forming an all-party, parliamentary or broader political committee to support the government from the rescue and relief phase through rehabilitation.

“Let’s form an all-party, parliamentary or broader committee from rescue and relief to rehabilitation. It would make it easier for the government to make decisions,” he had said.

Other parties agreed to the proposal. The meeting issued a 10-point commitment that included forming a high-level all-party mechanism to work on long-term disaster management.

The 10th point of the commitment stated that the parties had agreed to form a parliamentary committee to support and monitor reconstruction after disasters, climate adaptation, timely reforms to the national disaster policy and the government’s response.

The proposed mechanism was also envisioned as a platform for building national consensus on disaster preparedness and sustainable development, rather than functioning only during times of crisis.

However, 18 days after the agreement, the mechanism has yet to be formed.

Proposal also raised in Parliament

Lamichhane has continued to raise the issue in Parliament.

Addressing a meeting of the House of Representatives on September 9, he called for the Rasuwa flood to be declared a climate-related disaster of national importance and demanded the formation of an all-party parliamentary special committee to investigate its causes and damage and help take the issue to the international level.

“Let’s declare the current flood a climate-related disaster of national importance. Let’s form an all-party parliamentary special committee to investigate its causes and damage and internationalise the issue,” he said.

The proposal has also received support from opposition parties.

Speaking in the House on September 11, Nepali Communist Party lawmaker Barshaman Pun said disaster management was not the responsibility of any single ministry, government or level of government.

He called for a national mechanism bringing together political parties, security agencies, experts, local communities and other relevant stakeholders.

Pun also expressed his party’s support for Lamichhane’s proposal to form an all-party parliamentary special committee.

“We would like to express, on behalf of the Nepali Communist Party, our support for RSP chairperson Rabi Lamichhane’s proposal to form an all-party parliamentary special committee to deal with this disaster,” he said.

Despite the support, the process of forming the committee has not moved forward.

What kind of mechanism should be formed at the centre?

A second round of all-party discussions was held on September 1, focusing on the proposed high-level all-party mechanism.

The meeting, attended by second-tier leaders, agreed to coordinate with the government on rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts.

After the meeting, RSP spokesperson Jagadish Kharel said conditions had been created for forming all-party mechanisms at the provincial, district and local levels.

“The provinces, districts and local levels can form their own mechanisms. At the centre, discussions are still ongoing,” Kharel told Onlinekhabar on September 7.

According to Kharel, two options were being discussed for the central mechanism — a parliamentary committee or a high-level political mechanism outside Parliament.

A parliamentary committee would have a legal mandate but could also be seen as creating a structure parallel to the government, he said. Therefore, the possibility of forming a political mechanism outside Parliament was also being considered.

“There has been discussion about forming a mechanism comprising top leaders to provide political direction on policy issues. There has also been discussion about forming a task force under such a top-level mechanism,” Kharel said.

There was also discussion about establishing a permanent high-level political mechanism that could work on disaster-related issues over the long term, regardless of which political party is in government.

“It would be effective if we could establish a permanent, high-level political mechanism that could work on disasters in the long term, regardless of which party is in government,” Kharel said.

However, no decision has yet been reached on what kind of mechanism should be established at the centre.

‘A proposal made by the ruling party chair should be implemented’

Nepali Communist Party chief whip Yubaraj Dulal argues that the government and the ruling party itself should take concrete steps to implement the proposal because it was initially put forward by RSP chairperson Lamichhane.

“It has been almost a week since the RSP chairperson spoke about this issue in the House of Representatives. But there has been no formal decision to hold another meeting,” Dulal said.

Opposition parties have also held separate discussions on the matter.

On September 10, a meeting of opposition parties represented in the House of Representatives was held at Singha Durbar. According to Dulal, the meeting discussed the proposed committee’s terms of reference, legal status and authority.

“We discussed what the legal status of the committee would be. We discussed making its mandate effective, including a provision that after monitoring and issuing directions, the government should implement them,” he said.

The opposition parties also decided to draw the government’s attention to the need for a parliamentary special committee to make disaster management, relief, rescue, search and rehabilitation efforts more effective.

According to CPN-UML deputy parliamentary leader Padma Aryal, the opposition decided to urge the government to form a parliamentary special committee to monitor and inspect government rescue and relief operations, provide additional recommendations and facilitate necessary action through Parliament.

Opposition leaders have said they will continue to raise the issue in Parliament and press the government to form the committee.

However, the government has not formed such a committee so far.

Political leadership remains a question

An RSP office-bearer who has been involved in discussions over Lamichhane’s proposal says another question has emerged — who should provide political leadership to the proposed mechanism?

The RSP leader argues that the proposal should now move beyond discussion and into implementation.

“There would have to be a disagreement between the prime minister and the party chair. Otherwise, the ruling party chairperson himself proposed it. The chairperson also raised it in Parliament. It should be implemented,” the leader said.

The delay has left the fate of a mechanism that initially received cross-party support uncertain, even as the need for coordinated long-term disaster response remains on the political agenda.

title.rendered: Winning ACC tournament abroad proves Nepal’s cricketing standard, says Khadka

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

The Nepali cricket team, which won the ACC Premier Cup title and qualified for the Asia Cup, returned home Sunday night.

Welcoming the team, Nepal Cricket Association (CAN) Secretary Paras Khadka said reaching the Asia Cup was a matter of pride for Nepali cricket and should be seen as a major opportunity for the road ahead.

Paras noted that the Nepali team played excellent cricket throughout the tournament, saying that getting another chance to compete against strong sides like India and Pakistan was itself a major achievement.

He said the team could take pride in returning to the Asia Cup, adding that based on their recent experience playing India and Pakistan, this was another excellent opportunity, and that he hoped for an even better showing this time.

He noted Nepal had performed well overall in the Premier Cup group stage, aside from a single loss to Hong Kong.

He added that in a team sport like cricket, wins bring praise and losses invite fair criticism, but overall the team was moving in the right direction. While some aspects of the ODI setup still need improvement, he said the focus should be on the positives from this tournament.

According to Paras, winning the title in Malaysia wasn’t just a ticket to the Asia Cup; it was also proof of Nepal’s standing in associate cricket.

He said winning an ACC tournament away from home is itself a major achievement, noting that competition in Asia isn’t easy, yet the team performed excellently and won the title again, adding that the win has brought some joy to Nepalis amid the difficult situation the country has faced in recent weeks.

He also said CAN remains committed to its ongoing effort to unite the nation through cricket.

Paras said the Nepali team’s schedule for the next seven to eight months will be busy following Asia Cup qualification, with the team’s focus now shifting to the Asian Games, the Nepal Premier League (NPL), the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2, and various bilateral series.

He said the schedule through next monsoon is largely set, with a chance to win a medal at the Asian Games, followed by efforts toward the NPL, ODI cricket, and bilateral series, with details to be announced as each competition approaches.

This marks the second time Nepal has secured a spot in the Asia Cup by winning the ACC Premier Cup, having previously done so in 2023.

title.rendered: Deuba camp rejects central office terms, sets own path for 15th convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

The non-establishment faction of the Nepali Congress has decided to move forward with the party’s 15th general convention process in its own way. This was concluded at a meeting of the faction held Monday at outgoing party president Sher Bahadur Deuba’s residence in Maharajgunj, where members determined they could not take part in the convention on the terms decided by the party’s central office.

Earlier, the establishment side’s Central Working Committee had decided to allow all central members from the 14th general convention to take part in the 15th convention in the same capacity.

The non-establishment faction, however, said it was proceeding not for any position but as part of an effort to save the party, and has decided to move forward with the 15th convention schedule previously presented by Umakant Chaudhary.

After the meeting, leader Dr Prakash Sharan Mahat said informal discussions had taken place regarding the establishment side’s decision, and that a formal position would be set out at a press conference at 4 pm on Monday.

The Congress Working Committee meeting had earlier decided to welcome and assign responsibility, in the same capacity as central members, to any 14th-convention-elected central members wishing to take part in or serve as organisers of the 15th convention.

title.rendered: Investment in children is investment in nation’s future, says PM Balen Shah

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Prime Minister Balen Shah has said that investment in children is an investment in the country’s brighter future.

Issuing a message on the occasion of National Children’s Day 2026, Prime Minister Shah said protecting children’s present and ensuring their rights is essential to building a prosperous future for the country.

National Children’s Day is being observed this year with the slogan ‘Protect Childhood, Secure the Future.’

According to Shah, the slogan highlights the importance of creating a safe and rights-based environment for children as a foundation for the nation’s future.

Nepal, as a state party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, 1989, has made an international commitment to principles including non-discrimination, the best interests of the child, the right to life, survival and development, and the right to express views.

These principles have also been reinforced as fundamental and legal rights under Article 39 of Nepal’s Constitution, which guarantees children’s rights, as well as through the National Children’s Policy, 2080 and the Act Relating to Children, 2075.

Prime Minister Shah said the country’s key priority now should be to ensure that these constitutional and legal rights are actually experienced in the daily lives of every child.

He stressed the need for effective coordination, cooperation and accountability among the federal, provincial and local governments to achieve this goal.

According to Shah, the federal government should strengthen national policies and the legal and institutional framework, while provincial governments should focus on coordination and expanding services.

Similarly, local governments, as the level of government closest to children, should identify risks, provide protection and services, and create child-friendly environments, he said.

Shah said efforts by all three levels of government need to be brought together in a unified, results-oriented direction to ensure the protection and development of children.

title.rendered: 88-year-old man still missing 10 days after vanishing from Madhyapur Thimi

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

An 88-year-old man who went missing from Madhyapur Thimi, Bhaktapur, has still not been found after 10 days.

Jagat Lal Bade, 88, of Nagadesh Dhwakasi, Madhyapur Thimi Municipality-7, went missing on September 3. The elderly man, 5 feet 8 inches tall, has been missing from Madhyapur Thimi since 11 am that day.

His family filed a request with the Thimi Police Circle to search for him after he went missing, but he has not been found so far, according to the family.

The family says he was wearing a daura-suruwal, a dhaka topi, and a black coat at the time he went missing. He speaks the Newari language. The family has asked anyone who sees him to contact the nearest police station or the family at 9826519648 or 9749079270.

title.rendered: Resolution proposed in Parliament to end rape, sexual violence, and cyberbullying

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

A resolution aimed at ending rape, sexual violence, and cyberbullying has been introduced in Parliament.

The resolution was proposed by CPN-UML Chief Whip Nita Ghatani, with MPs Shraddha Kunwar Chhetri, Ambika Devi Sangraula, Renuka Kaucha, Khushbu Oli, Balawati Sharma, and Parwati BK as supporters.

The proposal notes that while Nepal’s constitution guarantees every citizen’s right to live with dignity, along with rights to freedom, equality, and specific protections for children and women, incidents of rape, sexual violence, and cybercrime against women and girls continue to rise in practice.

It points out that sexual crimes against girls and young women carry long-term psychological, physical, and future consequences, while the growth of digital technology has brought new forms of harm, such as cyberbullying and character assassination, that seriously damage women’s dignity and privacy.

The resolution states that despite the constitution’s guarantee of women’s right to live with dignity and to be protected from violence, such incidents keep occurring in practice, and calls for making state mechanisms more accountable for effective enforcement of the law, speedy justice, victim protection and rehabilitation, and controlling cyber violence.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah holds talks with representatives from disaster-affected areas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

Prime Minister Balen Shah is holding discussions with local representatives from districts and local levels declared disaster crisis zones following the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa.

The meeting began at 11 am Monday at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers in Singha Durbar, with representatives and lawmakers from 15 disaster-affected local levels in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun.

The discussions are focused on reviewing the situation following the floods, assessing the current conditions in the affected areas, identifying immediate steps to be taken and discussing recovery and rehabilitation efforts.

Representatives from Nuwakot attending the meeting include members of the House of Representatives Bikram Timilsina and Achyutam Lamichhane, as well as Bidur Municipality Mayor Rajan Shrestha, Belkotgadhi Municipality Mayor Jagat Bahadur Gurung, Kispang Rural Municipality Chair Birbal Tamang and Tarkeshwar Rural Municipality Chair Shiv Adhikari.

From Rasuwa, Uttargaya Rural Municipality Chair Madhav Prasad Aryal, Kalika Rural Municipality Chair Hari Krishna Devkota and Aamachhodingmo Rural Municipality Chair Buchung Tamang are participating in the meeting. Gosainkunda Rural Municipality Chair Kaisang Nurpu Tamang is attending the discussion virtually.

Representatives from Dhading include Galchhi Rural Municipality Chair Kedarnath Khatiwada, Siddhalek Rural Municipality Chair Parshuram Khatiwada, Gajuri Rural Municipality Chair Ganesh Lal Shrestha and Benighat Rorang Rural Municipality Chair Krishna Bahadur Thapaliya (Bibek).

From Tanahun, Devghat Rural Municipality Chair Til Bahadur Thapa and Aanbukhaireni Rural Municipality Chair Shukra Chuman are participating, while Gandaki Rural Municipality Chair Dipak Timilsina (Sakar) is representing Gorkha.

The meeting is expected to focus on the challenges faced by disaster-affected communities and the measures needed for relief, reconstruction and long-term recovery.

title.rendered: A borderless threat in a region governed by borders

content.rendered:
The political boundaries we draw across the map of the Himalayas are a dangerous fiction. They may make sense on a government map, but they mean very little to a mountain, a glacier or a river. While diplomats and governments dispute over lines, the mountains themselves operate on a completely different scale.

Natural hazards do not respect national sovereignty. They need no visa to cross borders, nor do they wait in the queue at immigration. A landslide does not stop at a checkpoint. A flood does not check which side of a river it is on. A collapsing glacier certainly does not care where one country’s territory ends and another begins.

If we continue to govern these hazards through the narrow lens of administrative borders, we are not merely failing to prepare for disaster. We are actively choosing collective disaster.

The terrifying velocity of the Bhotekoshi event in Rasuwa district of Nepal is a recent example of what this looks like in practice. Recent satellite images and publicly available videos show that a bedrock and glacial collapse originated on the Nepal side, near the China border, on the backside of the Langtang range. It triggered a cascading flood that surged northward across the international boundary.

That should force us to confront an uncomfortable reality that our traditional systems of disaster management are simply not designed for the speed and scale of the hazards we now face.

When a devastating mountain fracture can cross a border in the time it takes to make a cup of tea, our traditional, localised communication models are fundamentally outmatched by the catastrophic scale of modern disasters like the Rasuwa flood.

It is easy to blame these tragedies on a lack of bilateral data sharing. Better data sharing is certainly necessary, but that diagnosis does not tell the whole story. For sudden cryospheric collapses, the fundamental challenge is not simply the inability to share data. It is the physical limitation of knowing where and what to monitor in real time across a massive, inaccessible landscape.

It is, quite literally, like trying to pinpoint microscopic fractures across the vast Himalayan range.

That is the scale of the problem we are dealing with. And pretending otherwise will not make the mountains any safer.

We must also accept a reality that is uncomfortable but unavoidable: some of the damage to our mountains is already done, and it cannot be undone. We cannot unmelt a glacier. We cannot reverse every ecological change that has already taken place. And we cannot simply wish away the increasingly severe climate impacts that Nepal now faces every single year.

We have been seeing this at every global climate summit, like COP, where leaders endlessly debate the Loss and Damage Fund. For Nepal, however, this fund cannot remain a theoretical concept or another diplomatic talking point that disappears once the summit ends.

Nepal is now in a powerful position to demand Loss and Damage funds. And we should. This is not charity. It is a matter of survival.

Nepal contributes about 0.1% of global carbon emissions and yet is being forced to endure climate calamities year after year. We should not have to apologise for demanding resources to deal with destruction we did so little to create.

The global promises on climate finance must therefore become physical funding on the ground. They must rebuild communities, restore infrastructure and compensate people for damage that cannot simply be adapted away.

Nepal must strategically combine the global Loss and Damage Fund with international grants and loans to restore what has been lost and protect our future.

First, the Loss and Damage Fund must be used as direct, non-repayable compensation to cover what is permanently lost. This money must go directly toward rebuilding shattered communities in valleys and river basins, restoring destroyed public infrastructure such as roads and bridges, and compensating families who have lost their houses, land and livelihoods.

A developing nation should not have to take on debt to pay for damages it did not contribute to.

That is not simply an economic argument. It is a matter of climate justice.

Second, we must secure climate grants from wealthier nations to build long-term resilience. These funds should be prioritised for scientific research and technology, setting up transboundary monitoring systems and early warning systems along river basins, and conducting multi-hazard risk assessments.

This is no longer a luxury or an academic exercise. It is an absolute necessity for our new reality.

Finally, like any other developing country impacted by disaster, Nepal must utilise concessional soft loans from bilateral cooperation and development banks. But we must be clear about how this money is used. These funds should never be used simply for relief or cleaning up disaster damage. They should be strictly spent on building resilience to withstand devastating compound hazards in the future.

We cannot keep rebuilding the same roads, bridges and settlements after every disaster and call that resilience.

Yet our response to this escalating threat, and the scope of coordination required, remains characterised by a profound blindness toward the socio-economic drivers of vulnerability.

I reject the naive, detached notion that we can manage this crisis by simply ordering vulnerable populations to pack up and move away from active hazard zones.

It is an easy solution to propose from a distance. It is also a deeply unrealistic one.

People live, work and build in these dangerous valleys because of economic realities and the pursuit of their livelihoods. They are not living there because they have failed to understand the risks. They are there because this is where jobs, trade, transport and economic opportunity exist.

Rasuwa has served as a major transit point for more than a decade now, leading to rapid urbanisation and unplanned settlements. Aggressive hydropower development has pulled thousands of workers into intensive projects directly in the path of active landslides, floods and earthquakes.

We have seen workers trapped inside tunnels, demonstrating the devastating human cost of isolated infrastructure planning.

These are not simply unfortunate consequences of development. They are warnings about how we are developing.

It is vital to recognise that vulnerability and risk are not merely natural outcomes. They are systemic byproducts actively shaped by our economic choices.

We cannot halt development in these regions. Nor should we pretend that stopping development is a realistic or desirable answer for communities that depend on it. Our only ethical path forward is therefore to make development risk-informed.

If we are going to build in the mountains, we have a responsibility to understand the mountains.

To do this, we must stop treating one country, one settlement or one project as an individual entity. We must also stop treating one event as simply a flood, landslide or GLOF affecting several people or pieces of infrastructure.

A disaster occurring in one river basin can instantly devastate communities and assets downstream.

The watershed, not the administrative boundary, must therefore become the basic unit of planning, monitoring and coordination.

This requires us to think differently about disaster risk. We must replace single-hazard assessments with multi-hazard risk assessments that evaluate the combined forces of seismicity, shifting seasonality, climate change and population movement.

The government needs to proactively develop a framework that integrates national and local governments, authorities, scientific institutions, private developers and mountain communities into one cohesive planning structure.

The alternative is to continue planning in silos and then act surprised when the hazards refuse to do the same. Effective disaster management also requires mastering two operational timelines.

The first is long-term strategic planning. The second is immediate, real-time crisis response. These are not competing priorities. We need both.

Strategic resilience relies on sustained scientific research, multi-hazard assessments and basin-level diplomacy. Immediate response, meanwhile, hinges on rapid cryospheric monitoring and localised action.

We must aggressively finance early warning systems capable of operating during high-velocity mountain collapses.

When the warning window is exceptionally brief, even a few minutes of advance notice can mean the difference between life and death for downstream populations and workforce infrastructure.

Ultimately, we must recognise what the melting of our glaciers and the fracturing of our peaks really represent: a physical bill being handed to a country that is being forced to pay for it with the lives and livelihoods of its people.

We did not create this crisis, but we are living with its consequences.

While we fight to buy precious minutes of lead time through early warning systems, the global community must accept that some climate destruction is already too severe for traditional adaptation.

This is precisely why the Loss and Damage Fund cannot remain an empty diplomatic promise.

It must materialise on the ground.

It must pay for the irreversible damage done to our mountain valleys. It must help rebuild shattered communities, establish transboundary safety networks and protect the workers building our future.

And Nepal should not approach this as a passive recipient waiting for generosity. We should demand it as a matter of climate justice and survival.

The accelerating pace of climate-induced hazards can tempt observers into passive acceptance. It can make the scale of the problem seem so overwhelming that inaction begins to feel inevitable. It is not.

Giving up is not an option.

The crisis is urgent, but it is not hopeless. We have choices about how we respond, how we build, how we monitor our mountains and how we protect the people who live and work in them.

But those choices cannot wait.

If the international community finally acts on its moral obligation to fund our survival, and if Nepal finally treats disaster risk as a central part of development rather than an afterthought, the decisions we make today will decide who lives and who dies tomorrow in the shadow of the Himalayas.

title.rendered: AHZ Associates Nepal, DMH Foundation distribute relief to flood-hit families in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

AHZ Associates Nepal, in collaboration with Bangladesh-based Dr Mostofa Hazera Foundation (DMH Foundation), has distributed relief supplies to families affected by recent floods in Bidur, Nuwakot.

The relief initiative was organised to support families displaced by the floods, with essential food items and other basic necessities distributed directly to affected communities.

Financial support for the relief effort was provided by the DMH Foundation, while AHZ Associates Nepal’s employees and volunteers coordinated the distribution on the ground.

The AHZ team travelled from Kathmandu to Bidur and met with affected families to understand the challenges they were facing following the disaster.

“This was not simply about distributing food or basic necessities. It was about standing beside people who have suffered unimaginable losses, listening to them, and helping them feel that they are not alone,” said AHZ Associates Nepal Country Manager Shobin Thapa, who led the relief operation.

“Meeting the affected families in person reminded us once again of the importance of our collective responsibility,” he added.

DMH Foundation Chairman Captain A.K.M. Golam Kibria said the foundation’s support was guided by the principle that humanitarian assistance should not be limited by national borders.

“Humanity has no borders. When people are facing hardship and loss, our responsibility is not to ask where they come from, but to stand beside them,” Kibria said.

He said the foundation was pleased to support flood-affected families in Nepal and acknowledged the efforts of AHZ Associates Nepal in delivering the assistance directly to communities.

“We hope our contribution will provide families with some comfort, dignity and hope,” he said.

The relief operation was supported by AHZ Associates Nepal employees and volunteers, including Archana Yadav, Sajal Pokharel, Rishav Singh, Pragya Magar, Megha Bajracharya, Ambika Giri, Yogendra Saud and Dibesh Adhikari, alongside Thapa.

The initiative brought together a Nepal-based organisation and a Bangladeshi foundation to provide assistance to communities affected by the floods.

The DMH Foundation has continued to receive guidance from its founder and patron, Zahirul Islam, and Golam Mortuza, according to the organisations.

The organisations said the initiative was intended to provide both practical assistance and moral support to families as they begin recovering from the disaster.

title.rendered: The village they called home is now a place they never want to see again

content.rendered:
Uttargaya, September 13

Everyone loves their village. For the Thapa family, however, the thought of returning to theirs is unbearable.

They have survived an earthquake, been driven out by a landslide and, most recently, watched a flash flood erase their home—and take 15 members of their family with it.

In Lower Pairebeshi of Uttargaya-4, Rasuwa, five houses belonging to the Thapa family once stood in a row. On August 26, the flood swept them away.

It took 70-year-old Durgadevi Thapa; her 53-year-old middle son; his 47-year-old wife, Sarita; their 10-year-old grandson, Sanchit; and nine-year-old grandson, Nishan. Across the settlement, an entire family of 10 from Durgadevi’s daughter’s side was lost.

Their homes became riverbed. Their farmland, livestock and possessions disappeared. The Thapa family, which had spent years rebuilding after earlier disasters, was left with almost nothing.

Of the 28 family members who lived in the two households, 13 survived.

“We don’t want to go back there. We don’t even want to remember that place,” they say.

For a family that has repeatedly rebuilt its life after disaster, this time feels different.

They have loans they still need to repay. They have grief they cannot escape. And they have nowhere of their own to go.

Eleven years of displacement

The flood was not the first disaster to uproot the Thapas. In 2015, they lived in Kuwapani when the earthquake destroyed their home.

They moved to Tupche Sahugaun in Nuwakot, hoping to start again. But government resettlement rules tied reconstruction grants to rebuilding on the original site. They were eventually forced to return to Kuwapani.

“After six months, we returned to the same old place,” recalls 42-year-old Tara Bahadur Thapa. “At first, we built a tin shed.”

The reconstruction grant was not enough to build a concrete house. So the family borrowed more money. Some had laid foundations and completed the damp-proof course. Others were preparing to put on their roofs.

Then, in 2017, a landslide struck.

“The landslide took it before the house was even finished,” says 37-year-old Asmita Thapa, her voice breaking. “The roof wasn’t even on yet. The landslide destroyed everything. We were uprooted again.”

It was their second displacement.

For three or four months, they stayed in Colony of Bidur Municipality-9, Nuwakot.

The family again decided they could not return to Kuwapani. After discussions with the government, they became eligible for Rs 200,000 to purchase land and Rs 300,000 to build a house.

In 2018–19, they bought land in Lower Pairebeshi, roughly half an hour below their old settlement.

A soil test declared the land safe.

Five Thapa brothers built their homes side by side.

“We invested more than Rs 2 million in a single house. We took loans from organisations and microfinance institutions to build the settlement,” Asmita says. “We still haven’t paid them off.”

After years of displacement, they believed they had finally found somewhere they could stay. They were wrong.

“We didn’t even get to live in those houses for three or four years. The flood took everything.”

Fifteen family members gone

On the morning of August 26, Gita Thapa had cooked breakfast before going to the fields to cut grass.

Then she heard a sound she compared to a tyre bursting. It was a flash flood.

“It wasn’t raining. But suddenly, a flash flood was surging in. It felt like some kind of catastrophe. I started screaming for my daughters. The flood reached right where I was standing,” says the 47-year-old.

What happened next remains almost impossible for her to describe.

“Right before my eyes, it took all 10 members of my daughter’s family. And five from my own house.”

Among those swept away were people ranging from a 70-year-old grandmother to a four-month-old infant.

“My daughter’s daughter was two years old. My daughter’s sister-in-law had come to her parents’ home for postpartum care. There was a four-month-old baby boy. It took everyone right in front of our eyes,” Gita says.

“Even those trying to run away were caught by the surge. How could anyone bear it?”

None of those swept away was recovered.

“We saw them being swept away with our own eyes, so we began the funeral rites from the eighth day and completed them on the thirteenth,” says Tara Bahadur. “We’ve also given DNA samples.”

For Gita, the loss has made sleep almost impossible.

Her eyes remain wet as she remembers the children who were taken.

A phone call before the flood

Forty-year-old Khadga Bahadur Thapa has spent the past 15 years working in Dubai. On the morning of August 26, at around 6 am Nepal time, he spoke to his children and mother.

His children wanted money to go to the Lakhe festival. He sent Rs 10,000. He also told them he would come home for Dashain. Within hours, he was trying desperately to reach them.

No one answered.

“I sent that money saying I’d be home for Dashain, so they could buy what they needed to go to the festival. Everything here was swept away,” he says.

“My father never even got to withdraw the money I sent.”

Khadga eventually booked a flight and arrived in Nepal on the evening of August 27. The following day, he met the surviving family members in Kathmandu.

Only then did he learn that he had lost his mother, his son, his elder brother, his sister-in-law, his brother’s daughter and his granddaughter.

“Fifteen years of savings from abroad were gone in five minutes. How long would it take to build all that again?” he asks.

“I went abroad to fulfil my children’s dreams. My whole life has been destroyed.”

He has not returned to Pairebeshi.

“I haven’t gone to the site. I don’t want to go there. I hope I never have to go back. I’d rather beg and sift gravel and sand for a living here in Kathmandu. But I won’t go to Rasuwa.”

Swept away in his sleep

Twenty-one-year-old Sijal Thapa survived almost by chance. He had returned home after a night shift at a hydropower project and gone to sleep.m When the flood arrived, he was unconscious.

“At first, I thought I was dreaming about a flood. But when I woke up, I was already in the river.”

The flood carried away everything around him. Somehow, he survived.

Sijal suffered injuries to his head and leg. He was rescued and airlifted through Dhunche to Kathmandu’s Teaching Hospital. He has since been discharged, but has not fully recovered.

The family estimates that the five Thapa households lost property worth around Rs 100 million.

Homes, land, farmland and livestock were destroyed.

During the COVID-19 lockdown, Tara Bahadur had returned from Saudi Arabia with Rs 2 million in savings. He invested about Rs 1 million in a farm building and used the rest to establish a livestock farm.

The goats, along with the family’s cows and buffaloes, were all swept away.

“No cows, buffaloes or goats are left. Everything is gone,” he says.

Starting over—again

Tara Bahadur had been living in Hetauda, Makwanpur, for work when the flood struck. At 9 am on August 26, he called his elder brother.

“We talked for about five minutes, then the call dropped,” he recalls. “I waited for him to call back.”

He never did. The next morning, at 4 am, Tara Bahadur headed to Pairebeshi to bring back the surviving family members. They waited for two days, hoping for rescue. No helicopter came.

“We walked for nine hours and reached Suryagadhi Rural Municipality at around 7 pm,” he says.

They eventually reached Kathmandu on the fourth day after the flood. Now, all 13 survivors are staying with their niece in Hiletol Heights, Tarakeshwar Municipality. There are around 20 people in the house. The niece’s one-storey concrete home and an old mud-and-brick shed are both full.

There are a few mattresses, a small collection of cooking utensils and a wood stove. Smoke from the firewood fills the room where the displaced family sits together.

They cannot even eat at the same time.

“We have to take turns and wait. When it is time to eat, we look at each other’s faces, and tears fall from everyone’s eyes,” says 47-year-old Gita.

They have shelter for now, but no home. Their children need to return to school. They have no gas, little money and no place of their own. Returning to Pairebeshi is not an option.

“We hope the government resettles us quickly,” Tara Bahadur says.

But this time, they want a say in where they go.

“We’ve been through disasters three or four times. Even the first time, we wanted to stay in Makwanpur, but the rural municipality’s decision didn’t allow it,” the family says.

“We want long-term resettlement in a genuinely safe place.”

After 11 years of rebuilding, displacement and loss, the Thapas are asking for something that should never have been too much to ask:

A place where they can finally live without waiting for the next disaster.

“We don’t want to go through another disaster again.”

title.rendered: How Tarai industries are rerouting gas to Kathmandu after highway blockage

content.rendered:
With Kathmandu Valley’s cooking gas supply still falling short, gas-bottling plants across the Tarai are refilling cylinders around the clock to keep LP gas flowing to the capital. Fourteen plants in Makwanpur, Bara, Parsa, Chitwan, Mahottari, Dhanusha, and Nawalparasi are currently filling cylinders bound for Kathmandu.

After the August 26 flood on the Trishuli River triggered a landslide at Krishnabhir on the Prithvi Highway, blocking the road, gas tanker trucks importing from India have been stuck outside the Valley for lack of an alternate route. With tankers unable to reach Kathmandu directly, the government has arranged for gas cylinders to be brought in via small and large trucks along alternate roads instead.

Even so, the shortage in the Valley persists. Plants filling for 26 Kathmandu-marketed brands are having their cylinders refilled at Tarai gas plants and trucked in via the Tribhuvan Highway, with individual plants reportedly sending between 1,000 and 8,000 cylinders a day to Kathmandu for a single brand.

Sahara Gas Industry in Hetauda, which markets in Kathmandu, said it is filling 4,000 Everest Gas and 4,000 Sugam cylinders daily, running three shifts around the clock. Manager Khadga Thapa said the plant has ramped up production despite difficult conditions during the disaster.

“We’re filling at a rate of 8,000 to 12,000 cylinders a day, 2,500 of those go to the local market under our own Sahara brand, and we’re sending more than 8,000 to Kathmandu,” he said.

He added that gas is being routed to Kathmandu via the Palung road, with 5 to 7 small trucks plus vehicles belonging to Kathmandu dealers and parties carrying about 8,500 cylinders to the capital daily. He said the workload has meant 18-20 hour shifts, and that vehicles often have to wait their turn to load.

Manoj Gas filling 1,800 cylinders a day

Manoj Gas Udhyog Pvt. Ltd. in Parwanipur, Parsa, is filling cylinders for two Kathmandu-based brands, STC (Salt Trading Corporation) and Lokpriya, alongside its own. Staff member Sanjay Kumar Mishra said the plant fills its own gas from 9 am to 5 pm, then switches to filling and dispatching 1,600-1,800 cylinders of the two Kathmandu brands through midnight or 1 am, depending on demand.

Amber Gas in Bara is filling for Siddhartha and STC brands, with staff member Panna Lal Sah saying the plant fills up to 1,200 cylinders daily for the two companies combined.

Leo Gas Udhyog Pvt. Ltd., also in Bara, is filling for the Lokpriya and Shreemaya brands. Operator Nirmal Khatri, who also serves as treasurer of the LP Gas Industry Association, said supply has been increased out of a sense of duty to the public during the disaster.

He noted that gas imports from India have continued uninterrupted, with about half a dozen tankers arriving at his plant daily. The factory is now running two shifts, 7 am to 3 pm and 3 pm to 11 pm, and sending out 5,000 cylinders a day in total, of which roughly 2,000-2,500 go to the local market and the remaining 3,000 to Kathmandu.

Super Gas in Parsa is likewise filling cylinders for Kathmandu’s Himal brand.

Until the Prithvi Highway is fully restored, Tarai industries will continue filling and routing gas to Kathmandu via alternate roads in coordination with the Nepal Oil Corporation. While shortages persist in the Valley and some other districts, the Oil Corporation has stated that gas imports from India currently exceed market demand.

title.rendered: A Doctor, a dream and a cancer hospital for Nepal

content.rendered:
In a radiation oncology department at a university hospital in Bern, Switzerland, a Nepali doctor spends his days treating cancer patients with some of the most advanced technology available. But Dr Binay Kumar Shrestha’s mind often travels thousands of kilometres away, to Nepal.

For nearly two decades, Shrestha has worked in high-level cancer care in Europe. Since 2018, he has been a senior consultant at a university hospital in Bern, treating cancer patients, conducting research and training younger doctors.

Yet his ambition extends beyond his work in Switzerland as he yearns to build a modern cancer hospital in Nepal.

In Dhikurpokhari, Kaski, preparations are already under way. Land has been secured, a design is being developed with Dutch architect Prof Feenstra, and an agreement has been signed with the Cancer Centre at University Hospital Bern for knowledge transfer and training.

The project is expected to cost billions of rupees. Around Rs 50 million has already been invested by Shrestha’s team.

For Shrestha, however, the project is about more than constructing a hospital.

“Many people think that what we learn abroad should simply be shared,” he says. “But I am trying to do something with a bigger dream. This hospital will not just be a building. It will be a strong bridge between Nepal and Switzerland in healthcare.”

A childhood decision

Shrestha was born in 1973 in Mangalpur, Chitwan. His father, Chamunarayan Shrestha, was a teacher, and his mother was a homemaker.

Education was central to the family. Literature and learning were part of everyday life, and the family would often recite Muna Madan together.

But it was an illness in the family that first made Shrestha think about medicine.

When he was in Grade 4, his grandmother became seriously ill.

Even as a child, he began to understand what it meant to have the ability to protect someone’s health.

That experience eventually convinced him that he wanted to become a doctor.

He passed his SLC examination in first division from Balkumari Secondary School in Narayangadh and completed his ISc in first division from Nepal Science Campus in Ramshah Path, Kathmandu.

He later received a scholarship to study MBBS at the College of Medical Sciences in Bharatpur.

That opportunity would eventually take him far beyond Nepal.

The journey to Switzerland

After completing his internship at United Mission Hospital in Tansen in 2002, Shrestha initially focused on orthopaedic surgery. He began working as a resident doctor at HRDC Hospital in Banepa.

Around the same time, he applied for a position at a hospital in Switzerland. There was one problem. He needed to know German.

“I realised that without German, you couldn’t even move a leaf here,” he recalls.

The initial opportunity slipped away.

Instead of giving up, Shrestha used his time in Austria and Switzerland to pursue fellowships and training in orthopaedics and surgery while learning German.

He later worked in family medicine in rural Switzerland for two years, gaining experience by working closely with local communities.

During this period, he also completed a master’s degree in biomedical engineering from the University of Bern, adding another dimension to his medical and research background.

Then, in 2008, his career took an unexpected turn.

From surgery to cancer care

Shrestha had resigned from his previous position with the intention of pursuing orthopaedic surgery. But he was uncertain about what should come next.

He applied for an internal medicine residency at University Hospital Zurich, initially intending to improve his language skills before returning to surgery.

Instead, he encountered radiation oncology.

Working in internal medicine brought him into close contact with cancer patients and the radiation oncology department.

The experience changed his thinking.

“I realised that you don’t have to save lives only through surgery,” he says.

After about a year and a half of working closely with the field, Shrestha made a decision he had never originally imagined. He would specialise in radiation oncology.

At University Hospital Zurich, he gained experience in research, teaching and leadership within radiation oncology.

Although he later took some time away from Zurich for family reasons, his professional journey continued in Switzerland.

Since 2018, he has worked as a senior consultant at a university hospital in Bern, where he treats cancer patients using advanced technology while training and mentoring younger doctors.

A hospital for Nepal

For years, Shrestha had heard that doctors trained abroad should share their knowledge with Nepal.

But he felt that conferences and panel discussions alone were not enough.

That thinking eventually led to the Swiss-Nepal Cancer Hospital Project.

The plan to build the hospital in Dhikurpokhari, Kaski, has been developing for around five years.

“I have lived and worked in Switzerland for 20 years,” Shrestha says. “That experience has made me feel a responsibility. At this stage, my family and I feel that doing something for cancer patients in Nepal is more important than profit.”

He also sees the project as a way of giving back to the country where he received his medical education.

“If I had not received my basic education and skills from Nepal, this journey would not have been possible,” he says. “My responsibility is therefore not only to treat patients in Switzerland, but also to contribute to my homeland.”

His team has already invested around Rs 50 million in the project.

Over the past five years, work has continued on both sides of the Nepal-Switzerland relationship, including registering the organisation, building the team, purchasing land and reaching the final stages of leasing additional land.

The team includes businesspeople, technical professionals and doctors working in Nepal and Switzerland.

In October 2023, Dutch architect Prof Feenstra visited the proposed hospital site.

Shrestha and his team also invited Feenstra to Switzerland to study the cancer department at University Hospital Bern, including everything from patient facilities to equipment arrangements.

The initial cost estimate for the project was around Rs 2 billion, although Shrestha expects the final cost to be higher.

The plan is to develop the hospital in three phases, with an investment of around Rs 1 billion in each phase.

The project is currently being developed through private investment.

“We were worried that making the project public too early could affect the vision,” Shrestha says. “But this is not simply a private investment project. It is driven by a service-oriented vision.”

Two Swiss cancer specialists have also invested in the project, although they have described their contributions as donations. Shrestha says sending smaller amounts of foreign investment to Nepal has been difficult because of the country’s foreign direct investment rules.

Building a bridge between Switzerland and Nepal

The project has already moved beyond plans for a building.

On February 14, 2024, Shrestha’s team signed an agreement in Switzerland with the Cancer Centre at University Hospital Bern for knowledge transfer and training required to establish and operate the Swiss-Nepal Cancer Hospital.

The agreement is intended to give Nepali doctors and technical staff the opportunity to observe, learn and train in the operation of an advanced hospital in Switzerland.

“We can understand directly what the design should look like and what kinds of machines are effective,” Shrestha says.

Doctors, nurses and technicians from Nepal will be able to receive training in Switzerland, while Swiss doctors are also expected to travel to Nepal and participate directly in treatment once the project moves forward.

Shrestha says the partnership will also provide access to important cancer-treatment documents and expertise available at Swiss cancer centres.

His team is preparing to bring the head of the cancer centre, along with Swiss doctors who have invested in the project, to Nepal when the work there progresses.

For Shrestha, that exchange is at the heart of the hospital’s purpose.

It is intended to bring Swiss experience directly into Nepal rather than simply replicate a building.

Bringing health professionals together

While working on the cancer hospital, Shrestha has also been trying to connect Nepali healthcare professionals across Europe.

Last year, he took leadership of the Society of Nepali Healthcare Professionals in Europe.

The organisation aims to create a platform where Nepali healthcare workers can exchange experiences about different registration systems, examinations and professional challenges across European countries.

The organisation has also made information about registration and examination procedures available through its website.

“The idea is that healthcare professionals who have already gone through these processes can help those who are coming after them,” Shrestha says.

At the first annual convention in Amsterdam, Nepali doctors from across Europe discussed emerging trends, challenges and possible solutions in healthcare.

The conference also saw the Nepali Health Professional of the Year 2025 award presented to Prof Dr Ganesh Acharya.

Shrestha says the organisation plans to regularly recognise healthcare workers not only in Europe but also those working in remote areas of Nepal.

A long connection with Nepal

Shrestha’s connection with Nepal did not begin with the cancer hospital project.

He was also involved with the Swiss-Nepal Society, which was established by Swiss people who had worked in Nepal during the 1960s and 1970s.

He worked with the organisation from 2006 to 2015, an experience he says taught him a great deal.

He later became actively involved in the NRN movement in Switzerland, serving twice as president of NRN Switzerland and one term as an ICC member.

Those experiences helped him build connections among Nepalis living across Europe.

Today, those networks have become part of a much larger ambition.

A hospital in Nepal.

A professional network across Europe.

And a system through which knowledge can move in both directions.

A dream bigger than a building

For Shrestha, the cancer hospital is not simply another professional achievement.

It is an attempt to turn nearly two decades of experience in European healthcare into something that can serve patients in Nepal.

“My dream is not just a building,” he says. “It is about saving lives, giving hope and maintaining an unbroken connection with my homeland. Where there is determination, a plan and a commitment to service, nothing is impossible.”

He is proud to have specialised in both radiation oncology and general medicine.

But his ambitions have moved beyond his own career.

“I don’t want to simply be proud of what I have achieved,” he says. “I want to use it to do something for the country.”

For now, the hospital remains a work in progress.

The land is being prepared. The design is taking shape. Partnerships have been signed. Money has already been invested.

And thousands of kilometres away from Nepal, inside a cancer department in Bern, a Nepali doctor continues to treat patients—while working towards the day when the expertise he has spent decades acquiring can be put to work in his homeland.

title.rendered: Nepal in search of climate justice on the global stage

content.rendered:
Nepal did not create the global climate crisis. Yet Nepalis are increasingly paying an extraordinary price for its consequences—in lives lost, homes destroyed, livelihoods shattered and communities placed at growing risk.

The recent catastrophic flash flood in Rasuwa is a stark reminder that climate change is no longer a distant threat for Nepal. It is a present-day crisis.

And Nepal now has an opportunity to make the world listen.

As world leaders gather in New York for the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen, is expected to address the Assembly on September 24. The catastrophe gives Nepal an urgent reason to place climate justice, Himalayan vulnerability and global responsibility at the centre of that international conversation.

For Nepal, this is no longer an abstract debate about future climate scenarios. It is about people losing their lives today.

A disaster that began in the Himalayas

The catastrophe began on the morning of August 26 in the Himalayan border region. Reports indicate that a massive volume of glacier ice, rock and sediment collapsed at high altitude into the Lhende River system, temporarily obstructing the river. When the blockage gave way, a devastating surge rushed downstream through the Lhende Khola, Bhote Koshi and Trishuli River systems.

Within hours, a disturbance in one of the world’s most remote mountain environments had become a catastrophe for communities far downstream.

As of September 13, Nepal Government authorities reported at least 1,388 people confirmed dead, 13,676 rescued and 5,130 missing. Around 587 foreign tourists were also reported missing.

The economic damage is staggering. Nepal’s Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment estimates that Rs. 723.32 billion (USD 4.74 billion) will be required for reconstruction and recovery.

Thirteen hydropower projects, with a combined capacity of 759 megawatts, and five solar plants were affected. Roads and bridges were washed away, thousands of homes were damaged, and businesses, agricultural land, schools, health facilities and cultural heritage sites were destroyed.

The United Nations Development Programme estimates that the floods generated approximately 2.2 million tonnes of debris and affected more than 84,000 people across 17 municipalities.

But the human cost cannot be measured in dollars.

Behind these figures are families waiting for news of loved ones, communities buried beneath mud and debris, survivors who escaped with little more than the clothes they were wearing, and thousands confronting an uncertain future.

The Himalayas are sending a global warning

Nepal alone is home to more than 3,200 glaciers. Across the broader Hindu Kush Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau region are tens of thousands more, making it one of the world’s greatest concentrations of ice outside the polar regions.

These mountains are often called the “water towers of Asia.” The great river systems originating in the Hindu Kush Himalaya sustain more than 2 billion people across Asia.

What happens in the Himalayas, therefore, does not remain in the Himalayas.

Scientific research has documented accelerating glacier retreat and ice loss as temperatures rise. Retreating glaciers can contribute to expanding glacial lakes, destabilised mountain slopes, altered river flows and greater exposure to cascading hazards.

The Himalayas are sending a warning. The world cannot afford to ignore it.

Nepal’s case for climate justice

Nepal, like many developing and least-industrialised nations, has contributed comparatively little to greenhouse-gas emissions. Yet its people are increasingly exposed to retreating glaciers, unstable mountains, extreme precipitation, floods, landslides and unpredictable water systems.

That imbalance is what lies at the heart of climate justice.

Countries that industrialised earlier and accumulated wealth through carbon-intensive development carry greater historical responsibility for addressing the consequences. Today’s major emitters—developed and developing alike—also share responsibility for changing the world’s future trajectory.

But climate justice cannot remain an argument about blame while communities are suffering.

It must mean action.

Countries with greater financial resources, technological capabilities and institutional capacity should help climate-vulnerable nations such as Nepal strengthen adaptation, disaster preparedness and resilience.

That requires meaningful climate financing—not symbolic promises.

Nepal needs investment in glacier research, satellite monitoring, early-warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure, disaster communications, scientific cooperation and community preparedness.

And when vulnerable countries suffer catastrophic losses that reasonable adaptation could not prevent, the international community must take seriously the principle of loss and damage.

Those who contributed least to the climate crisis should not be left alone to bear its greatest human and economic costs.

From relief to resilience

Nepal has survived earthquakes, floods, landslides, avalanches and countless other hardships. Its people have repeatedly demonstrated extraordinary resilience.

But resilience cannot become an excuse for the world to expect vulnerable communities simply to endure catastrophe after catastrophe. This disaster must become a turning point.

Nepal needs humanitarian assistance today. Tomorrow, it will need reconstruction. Beyond reconstruction, it needs sustained investment in climate resilience and sustainable development.

That means continuous glacier and glacial-lake monitoring, cross-border hydrological cooperation, real-time early-warning networks, community evacuation systems, resilient roads and bridges, safer hydropower development, satellite and drone surveillance, expanded Himalayan research and sustainable land-use planning.

Rebuilding should not simply recreate what existed before. Nepal must rebuild safer and stronger.

At the same time, climate action cannot mean abandoning development. Industrialisation has lifted millions from poverty and produced extraordinary advances in medicine, science, technology and living standards.

The answer is better development: cleaner energy, climate-resilient infrastructure, sustainable cities, protected forests and watersheds, scientific innovation and economic systems that recognise environmental protection and human prosperity as inseparable.

PM Balen’s opportunity

Prime Minister Shah has already connected the recent tragedy with Nepal’s long-standing call for climate justice.

In a Facebook statement on September 5, he wrote:

“This disaster has been deeply painful for us. We are paying an enormous price despite having contributed very little to the problem. For a long time, we have been telling the world that climate change is having a profound impact on the Himalayan region and that our mountains and glaciers are melting. Its effects are not limited to the Himalayas; they extend all the way to coastal regions.

What we had long feared has now become a devastating reality in the form of the catastrophic flood in the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa. Nepal has endured a terrible tragedy. We must seek answers and accountability from the international community.

We believe that we will recover from this disaster soon.”

Now he has an international platform to turn those words into a stronger global demand.

Nepal cannot afford to remain on the sidelines of global climate negotiations. It must have a meaningful seat at the table when decisions affecting climate-vulnerable nations are made.

The Prime Minister has an opportunity to speak not only for Nepal, but for vulnerable mountain communities and developing nations facing the consequences of a crisis they did little to create.

But the message must be clear.

Nepal should not be asking for sympathy. Nepal should be asking for equitable climate justice.

The people who contributed least to global warming should not be asked to pay its highest price.

If Nepal fails to deliver that message clearly and forcefully to the world’s most powerful nations, its growing climate vulnerability risks being overlooked—and its call for justice left unheard.

The Himalayas may be geographically distant from the world’s great industrial centres. But their warning belongs to everyone.

And amid this enormous tragedy, Nepal offers another enduring message to the world:

When disaster strikes, Nepalis—at home and throughout the global diaspora—stand together.

Now the world must stand with them.
