title.rendered: Ignored study reports led to higher Rasuwa flood toll, experts say

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 14

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says the Rasuwa flood claimed at least 1,386 lives, with 5,130 people still unaccounted for.

According to the Authority’s rapid damage and needs assessment report, the flood caused more than Rs 408 billion in damage, and reconstruction and risk-reduction work is expected to cost around Rs 712 billion.

In his address to Parliament on September 2, Prime Minister Balendra Shah called the September 10 flood an “unimaginable disaster.” But was it really unimaginable, as the Prime Minister described it? Past study reports suggest otherwise.

Just 14 months before this devastating flood, another flood from the same Lhende (Bhotekoshi) river had already caused major damage in Rasuwa. In the flood of July 8, 2025, 18 people went missing, with damage exceeding Rs 1.8 billion at the time. A study prepared after that flood had warned that glacial lake outburst floods were likely to increase in the future.

That report, titled “Flash Flood of July 8 and 10, 2025 in a Transboundary River Lhende/Bhotekoshi/Trishuli: Its Nature, Losses and Damages” — noted that such floods can come in multiple waves, with water flow partially blocked and then bursting through again.

A separate report from Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Geography, Mahendra Ratna Campus, and the Nepal Mountain Academy warned that unplanned infrastructure expansion narrowing the natural river channel, as seen in areas like Rasuwagadhi and Timure, increases the risk of loss of life and property. The experts behind that report include geographer Prof. Dr Narendra Raj Khanal, Pashupati Nepal, Shaligram Sigdel, and Til Prasad Pangali Sharma.

According to the disaster authority’s rapid assessment, the hydropower sector alone suffered more than Rs 150 billion in damage, with reconstruction estimated to cost nearly Rs 400 billion. The report prepared after last year’s flood had specifically called for heightened caution in the hydropower sector, noting that delays in opening dam gates had contributed to damage, and recommending development of technology that allows faster gate operation.

At the Rasuwagadhi, Chilime, and Langtang Khola hydropower projects, the outlet structures for releasing water sit just below the normal flood level, meaning that during glacial lake outburst floods, high flows carrying mud and logs entered through the outlets and damaged the powerhouses. The report had recommended this be factored into future hydropower project design.

One of the report’s authors says the recommendations were never implemented; the government didn’t even take formal notice of it. This, they say, is just one example: nobody seems to track where such post-disaster studies on floods and landslides, from Thame, Sunkoshi, Melamchi, and elsewhere, end up filed away.

OnlineKhabar has previously reported that a similar report submitted to the Rasuwa District Disaster Management Committee after the 2025 flood, with recommendations on disaster management, compensation, relief, reconstruction, rehabilitation, preparedness, early warning systems, and cross-border coordination, was also shelved.

Experts stress that the government needs to incorporate evidence-based research findings into policy, implement them, and prioritise studies conducted through comprehensive, multidimensional approaches.

Former Water Resources Secretary Dr Dwarikanath Dhungel says that no matter how much research and how many recommendations are produced, nothing gets implemented because of a pattern of only reacting after disaster strikes.

“Everyone knows we’re sitting on something like an atom bomb, but those in Singha Durbar only seem to spring into action once something happens; I don’t see any report or research actually being implemented,” he said.

Dhungel says lessons haven’t been learned from past research on floods, landslides, glacial lake outbursts, and forest fires, and he doesn’t see much prospect of that changing going forward.

“Both the government and Parliament should be asking who studied what about the past floods on the Bhotekoshi,” he said. “But going by experience, we’ll likely forget about this flood too within a few days, and only really start discussing what should have been done after the Bhotekoshi flood once an even bigger one hits.”

title.rendered: 498 climbers obtain permits for Nepal’s autumn mountaineering season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

A total of 498 climbers had obtained permits to climb Nepal’s mountains for the upcoming autumn season as of Friday, according to the Department of Tourism.

The number of climbers seeking permits indicates continued interest in Nepal’s mountaineering sector despite the recent floods that have affected tourism infrastructure in parts of the country.

Among those who have obtained permits, the largest number are heading to Manaslu.

According to the Department of Tourism, 451 climbers, including 120 women, have received permits to climb Manaslu. They are part of 38 expedition teams.

The government has collected Rs 211 million in royalties from the climbing permits issued so far this season.

Climbers from 63 countries have obtained permits for the autumn season. Chinese nationals make up the largest group, with 100 climbers, including 29 women.

Russia has 53 climbers, followed by the United States with 37 and the United Kingdom with 28. France has 27 climbers, while Germany and Japan have 16 each.

title.rendered: The couple bringing Nepal to Australia, one product at a time

content.rendered:
When Bhushan Kakshapati first arrived in Australia around 16 years ago, he was looking for an opportunity. Today, from a warehouse and office in Sydney, he and his wife, Celina, run Sagoon Group, a business that has helped build a growing market for Nepali products across Australia.

Their company imports more than 200 types of Nepali products and distributes them through more than 250 outlets across the country.

But Sagoon is about more than selling food and consumer goods.

From pickles and noodles to beer and furandana, and from the utensils used during Dashain and Tihar to Nepali flags and other cultural items, the Kakshapatis have built a business around something larger than commerce: keeping Nepal connected to its diaspora.

For a growing Nepali community in Australia, Sagoon has become a way to find familiar tastes, traditions and objects from home.

And for the couple, it is also a way of introducing younger generations to a culture they fear could otherwise become distant.

Bhushan was born in Kathmandu. Celina was born in Kalimpong, India. Their relationship began almost by coincidence. Celina had travelled from Darjeeling to Kathmandu to stay with relatives. Bhushan happened to be there as well. Their families knew each other, and the meeting eventually developed into a relationship and later marriage.

Bhushan completed his schooling at Anand Kuti Vidyapeeth before finishing Grade 12 at United Academy. He then earned a bachelor’s degree in business from Everest College.

Celina completed Grade 12 in Kalimpong and later pursued her bachelor’s degree in Australia.

Both initially arrived in Australia as students. Today, the couple has built a business together, becoming an example of what can happen when two people combine their efforts and ambitions.

From car washes to a business of their own

Bhushan’s working life in Australia began far from the business he runs today. He worked at car washes, cut grass and eventually worked in restaurants.

Although he came from a business family in Nepal, starting out in Australia was difficult. After 2011, however, he began focusing on importing products from Nepal and selling and distributing them in Australia. The idea was simple: products that were familiar in Nepali homes could also find a market among Nepalis living abroad.

“We saw the demand in the market,” Bhushan recalls. “When we put products found in Nepali homes on sale here, it is not only about business. It also brings the country’s identity.”

The business initially began with friends before gradually developing into a separate, institutional operation.

For Celina, the appeal went beyond nostalgia.

“There are many products here that are extremely popular even though some younger people living in Nepal are beginning to forget them,” she says. “These products help preserve our culture and connect us with our identity.”

Today, Sagoon’s range includes traditional products such as kurkure nanglo, spices, pickles and chillies, as well as everyday food products and healthier options such as titaura, tofu and salad products.

The products are increasingly finding customers not only among Nepalis but also within Australia’s wider South Asian community.

Getting Nepali products through Australia’s strict borders

Building a market for Nepali products in Australia has not been easy.

One of the biggest challenges is Australia’s strict quarantine and biosecurity system.

Direct shipments from Nepal are limited, increasing the business’s dependence on routes through India.

Every shipment must meet stringent biosecurity requirements. Once a consignment reaches a designated location, government inspectors inspect it, and distribution can begin only after it has been certified.

Bhushan sees the strict regulations as a lesson rather than simply an obstacle.

“This strictness itself is a lesson,” he says. “If Nepal adopts strict testing before production, packaging, labelling and traceability at home, it will be easier to enter high-standard markets.”

Sagoon operates a warehouse-to-retail model from Sydney, managing demand forecasting, stock and transportation through cold and dry supply chains.

After strengthening its order-management system, the company expanded its partnerships with retail stores across Australia.

It has also sought to connect directly with consumers through Nepal-related cultural fairs, exhibitions and tasting events.

Building for quality, not just quantity

As the business has grown, so has the couple’s focus on quality and regulation.

Products exported to Australia need the required phytosanitary and food-safety documentation, appropriate labelling, allergen information and details such as “use-by” and “best-before” dates.

The couple say their experience has shown that preparing these requirements in Nepal before shipment increases the likelihood of consignments passing inspection.

Celina believes Nepal can make exports easier by creating a more integrated system.

“If the Nepal government and stakeholders could bring pre-export certification, grading centres, packing houses and traceability systems into one framework, export costs would fall and buyer confidence would increase,” she says.

A showroom and a bigger digital presence

The Kakshapatis are not stopping with their existing network. Their team plans to open a new experience centre, or showroom, in Sydney next year.

They also plan to strengthen their e-commerce capabilities, introduce real-time tracking and click-and-collect services, and add regional distribution partners.

The goal is to establish an omnichannel model and give Nepali products a more permanent place in Australia’s mainstream retail space.

Keeping culture alive far from home

Food is only part of what Sagoon brings to Australia.

The company has also expanded into products used during Nepali festivals and religious traditions.

Dashain, Tihar, Chhath, Nepal Sambat and Lhosar are among the festivals for which Sagoon supplies items to Nepali households across Australia.

The couple say the motivation is partly cultural.

“We believe Nepali culture should not disappear in the diaspora simply because people cannot find the materials needed for religious and cultural practices,” they say.

They believe this also helps second-generation Nepalis—those born and raised in Australia—learn about Nepali art, culture, festivals, traditions and religious practices.

Sagoon has therefore become not only a retail business but also a bridge between generations.

Two people, one journey

Bhushan and Celina describe themselves as two wheels of the same chariot.

If both wheels are strong, they say, the chariot can keep moving.

Their life in Australia has involved balancing business with raising two children while also supporting dozens of Nepali employees and participating in community events organised by the Nepali community.

Sagoon regularly supports and participates in Nepali community programmes across Australia.

“Our relationship and support are particularly dedicated to the Nepali community,” Bhushan says. “Their love and support have helped us move forward, so we feel that we should also support their programmes. We consider it our responsibility.”

A business built around a connection to Nepal

The Kakshapatis’ story is rooted in a mixture of struggle, practicality and a willingness to take risks.

Bhushan’s family business background gave him the confidence to take risks, but his Australian journey began with the same ordinary jobs taken up by many migrants.

“Starting a business and knowing where it will take you are two different things,” Bhushan says. “But the value of being connected to our culture is what motivates us.”

When asked whether they plan to return to Nepal, their answer is straightforward.

“For now, Australia is the place from where we can connect with Nepal and contribute the most,” they say. “But the connection and contribution continue to flow in both directions.”

For the Kakshapatis, Sagoon has become more than a company selling Nepali goods.

It has created a commercial market for Nepali products in Australia while carrying pieces of Nepal’s traditions, festivals and everyday life into homes thousands of kilometres away.

And in a market as tightly regulated as Australia’s, its growth also points to a larger opportunity for Nepal: the possibility of exporting more products to the world if quality, packaging, certification and traceability systems are strengthened at home.

For now, the Kakshapatis are continuing to build that bridge—from Nepal’s producers to Australia’s shelves, and from one generation of Nepalis to the next.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress opens door for Deuba-era central committee members

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

The Nepali Congress has opened the way for members of former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba’s central committee to return to the party’s Central Working Committee.

A meeting of the party’s Working Committee held on Sunday decided to include all members of the previous committee who were left out of the new committee formed after the special general convention.

“All of them will be invited to join the Central Working Committee. They can join the committee and remain as part of the organising committee for the general convention,” a party office-bearer said after the meeting.

“We appeal to them to participate in the general convention. Those who want to remain in the Central Working Committee can join. Those who do not want to may choose not to,” the office-bearer said.

The Nepali Congress has scheduled its 15th General Convention for October 2 to 5. Ward-level conventions have been scheduled for September 19 and 20.

The party establishment has also decided to recognise all active members whose membership was renewed by the party until last December.

title.rendered: China’s development model offers lessons for Nepal, says Khanal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Senior leader of the Nepali Communist Party and former prime minister Jhalanath Khanal has said Nepal should learn from China’s development experience and develop its own model of development and socialism based on the country’s unique circumstances.

Addressing the closing session of the third edition of the Kathmandu Dialogue in Kathmandu on Sunday, Khanal said Nepal could draw important lessons from the political stability and economic development China has achieved since the 1949 revolution.

He said China had treated political stability as the first and foremost condition for development and that establishing a foundation for sustainable stability remains a major challenge for Nepal.

According to Khanal, China did not simply copy development models from other countries but developed a path suited to its own political, economic, social, cultural and historical context.

He said Nepal should similarly develop its own model during its process of political change and transformation rather than directly imitating foreign systems.

Khanal said Nepal could learn from China’s political system and governance, but warned against copying the Chinese model outright. He also argued that China’s system was shaped by its long history and cultural, political, ideological and philosophical development.

“We need to think in the context of our own country,” he said.

title.rendered: Kathmandu Metropolitan City to launch ‘Recharge Kathmandu’ campaign to reduce urban flooding

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Kathmandu Metropolitan City is set to launch the ‘Recharge Kathmandu’ campaign to reduce the growing risk of urban flash floods in the capital.

The campaign aims to collect rainwater, recharge groundwater and promote better management of rainwater in the city.

Speaking at an event marking the 34th anniversary of the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Police Force on Sunday, Acting Mayor Sunita Dangol said the city was seeking long-term solutions to the increasing risk of flooding, noting that even relatively light rainfall can now cause flooding in Kathmandu.

“Three decades ago, unplanned development and construction in urban areas created the conditions for what we now call urban flash floods,” Dangol said. “In the past, we could sleep peacefully when it rained, but now we cannot sleep without worrying when rainfall begins.”

She said municipal police, disaster management teams and elected representatives often have to remain on standby to respond to emergencies, including during the night.

The metropolitan city is conducting studies on long-term measures to address urban flooding. However, Dangol said the city would not wait for the completion of the studies and would begin implementing measures that can be taken immediately.

Under the campaign, priority will be given to collecting rainwater, recharging groundwater and managing water resources effectively. The city aims to make Kathmandu safer and better prepared for flooding by starting with measures that can be implemented immediately.

title.rendered: Indra Jatra preparations begin as Guthi Sansthan team reaches Bhaktapur

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Preparations for Indra Jatra have begun with an auspicious ceremony marking the start of the traditional forest journey to select and cut a tree for the festival’s ceremonial linga.

Every year, on Bhadrapada Shukla Dwitiya, the Nepal Panchanga Nirnayak Development Committee sets an auspicious time for the forest journey to begin and for the tree to be cut for the ceremonial pole.

Janak Pokhrel, chief legal officer and spokesperson for Guthi Sansthan, told that the auspicious ceremony was performed at Basantapur Durbar Square at 9:53 am on Sunday.

Following the auspicious time set by the committee, the Guthi Sansthan team travelled to Nala Community Forest in Tanthali, located in Changunarayan Municipality-9 of Bhaktapur, to select and cut a tree for the Indra Jatra Linga.

According to Guthi Sansthan employee Ramesh Kafle, pine trees for both Indra Jatra and Bisket Jatra have traditionally been brought from the same community forest.

After reaching the forest, the tree, sword and khadga (ceremonial sword) will be worshipped before the tree is cut at 8:47 pm, the auspicious time set by the committee.

The tradition also includes Tantric rituals and a goat sacrifice before the tree is cut.

Guthi Sansthan signs an agreement with the community forest to obtain the tree for Indra Jatra. For Bisket Jatra, however, the tree is procured through a tender process, according to the Sansthan.

title.rendered: Month-long Gunla festival at Swayambhunath concludes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Around 200,000 devotees visited Swayambhunath, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, during a month-long festival organised by the Swayambhu Management and Conservation Federation.

Followers of Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism from Nepal and abroad attended the Gunla festival held at Swayambhunath. The festival, which began on August 13, concluded formally on Saturday night.

Chandraratna Buddhacharya, secretary of the federation, said Buddhists regard the month as sacred, believing that it was during this period that Buddha attained enlightenment and delivered his message for the welfare of humanity.

According to Buddhacharya, devotees traditionally visit nearby religious sites, including Shobha Bhagwati and Bijeshwari, after visiting Swayambhunath.

The conservation federation managed crowds visiting Swayambhunath and nearby monasteries and made arrangements for street lighting during the festival, he said.

Devotees believe that participating in the festival and visiting the religious sites helps accumulate religious merit.

Buddhacharya said devotees also attended the festival to listen to stories about Buddha’s life and teachings, which were recited throughout the month.

In Sanskrit, Swayambhu means “self-arisen land.” Buddhists believe that Bipashwi Buddha visited the site and worshipped there.

The site is particularly significant to Buddhists, and followers of various Buddhist traditions, including Hinayana and Mahayana, express their faith through religious activities there.

title.rendered: Teej begins with Dar feast ahead of fasting

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, September 13

The four-day Haritalika Teej festival begins Sunday with women across Nepal preparing to eat dar, a traditional feast consumed ahead of the fasting observed on Teej.

Dar is traditionally eaten on the second day of the bright half of Bhadra, a day before the main Teej fast. The tradition involves families, particularly parents and brothers, inviting daughters and sisters to their homes for the feast. Dairy-based dishes and other filling foods are commonly served.

According to religious scholar Toyaraj Nepal, wheat bread and ghee are considered particularly filling for women preparing for the fast.

Women who observe a strict fast on Teej eat dar to prepare themselves physically for the following day’s fast. Religious texts traditionally prescribe eating the feast by the second half of the night.

Teej is also regarded as an occasion for women to share their joys, hardships and grievances through songs and gatherings with friends and relatives.

However, sociologists and cultural scholars have raised concerns over the growing commercialisation of the festival. They say the practice of holding dar feasts weeks or even a month before Teej, along with excessive displays of jewellery and clothing, has contributed to the distortion of the festival’s traditional character.

The main Teej fast will be observed on Monday, followed by Ganesh Chauth on Tuesday and Rishi Panchami on Wednesday, marking the end of the festival.

The festival is traditionally associated with the Hindu goddess Parvati, who is believed to have observed a strict fast and performed penance to have Lord Shiva as her husband.

title.rendered: Flood survivors struggle to rebuild their lives (Photos)

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 13

The devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26 caused extensive destruction along the riverbanks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Thousands of people remain missing, while the bodies of more than 1,300 people have been recovered. Thousands of families have also been displaced.

Settlements around the river in Rasuwa, particularly Rasuwagadhi, Timure and Khalte, were devastated. In Nuwakot, settlements including Trishuli Bazaar, Betrawati and Devighat were badly damaged. Riverbank settlements along the Trishuli in Dhading, extending as far as Galchhi, also suffered extensive damage.

The government has introduced various relief packages for displaced people and has also begun rehabilitation efforts.

Meanwhile, residents of the flood-affected areas are struggling to rebuild their lives. During a visit to the market areas of Trishuli, Betravati and Devighat in Nuwakot on Saturday, locals were seen sifting through the rubble.

With heavy hearts, they were slowly trying to recover what remained of their homes and livelihoods.

Traffic along the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir in Dhading has partially resumed after the road was obstructed.

The road was partially reopened after two bulldozers completed levelling work and prepared the platform required for traffic movement.

According to Department of Roads Director General Dr Bijay Jaisi, only stranded gas tankers and vehicles carrying heavy equipment have been allowed to pass for the time being.

He said work to construct a drainage channel along the roadside remains to be completed and that two-way traffic will resume from Thursday after the work is finished.

Earlier, an empty gas tanker was driven along the road to test its load-bearing capacity and assess traffic conditions.

The road at Krishnabhir had been obstructed after the Trishuli flood on August 26 washed away part of the road.

Since then, large and small vehicles using the route have been travelling to and from Kathmandu via alternative routes.

title.rendered: Minister Pun: Work underway to free NAST from political interference

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun said work is underway to replace the existing law governing the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology (NAST) to free the institution from political interference and grant it financial autonomy.

Pun made the remarks at a discussion with subject experts and representatives of stakeholder organisations in Kathmandu on Sunday regarding the drafting of a bill to amend, consolidate and replace the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology Act, 1991.

He said NAST’s structure needs extensive reform to promote and develop science and innovation in the country. He said the government was moving to replace the law enacted in 1991 to address this need.

“Until 1991, the word ‘innovation’ was not even commonly used in Nepal. No one saw the need for it. If they had, Nepal would have made much greater progress in science and innovation by now. Therefore, while drafting the bill to amend, consolidate and replace the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology Act, 1991, we should first change its name,” he said.

According to Pun, the proposed bill will remove the existing provision that makes the prime minister the chancellor of NAST. He argued that the arrangement is inappropriate because the prime minister should be positioned at the highest level of the country’s science, technology and innovation sector rather than serve as the chancellor of NAST.

Pun said political interference in academies has hampered their institutional development and pledged that the new structure would prevent such interference.

“There is political interference in the academies at present. We will now create a structure that prevents political interference. Many people know that the academies have been weakened by political interference. Even if political interference improved some things, what do we call it when 20 things are damaged while 10 are improved?” Pun said.

He said the existing provision making the prime minister the chancellor would not be retained in the new bill.

“We need to place the prime minister at the highest level of science, technology and innovation. We have incorporated this provision in the act governing the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation. If the prime minister does not personally study the science and technology sector and provide proper direction, innovation cannot develop,” he said.

Pun added that the government was seeking to make NAST autonomous not only in its operations but also financially.

title.rendered: Flood causes Rs 172 billion in infrastructure damage, Rs 474 billion needed for reconstruction

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

The Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi flood caused nearly Rs 200 billion in damage to infrastructure alone, according to a government assessment.

According to the “Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood 2083: Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment” report prepared by a government-formed team, the flood caused infrastructure damage worth Rs 172.34 billion. An estimated Rs 473.57 billion will be required to reconstruct the damaged infrastructure.

The energy sector, including hydropower projects and transmission lines, suffered the most serious damage at Rs 134.69 billion. An estimated Rs 390 billion will be required to rebuild the sector. Renewable energy infrastructure suffered damage worth Rs 560 million.

The flood caused an estimated Rs 22 billion in damage to roads, while more than Rs 55.18 billion will be required for reconstruction. Bridges suffered damage worth Rs 11.35 billion, with an estimated Rs 18.06 billion needed for reconstruction.

The telecommunications sector suffered damage worth Rs 620 million and is estimated to require nearly Rs 1 billion for reconstruction.

Water supply and sanitation infrastructure worth Rs 1.38 billion was damaged, while irrigation structures worth Rs 1.64 billion were washed away.

The flood also caused an estimated Rs 67.84 billion in damage to private and public houses, schools, health posts and cultural structures. Nearly Rs 100 billion will be required to reconstruct these facilities, according to the assessment.

The total physical damage caused by the flood is estimated at Rs 274.48 billion. An estimated Rs 723.31 billion will be required for reconstruction.

Of the total reconstruction requirement, nearly Rs 9 billion is estimated to be needed for the immediate recovery programme covering the first six months. The remaining amount will be required for long-term recovery, according to the report.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi flood damages 7,570 homes across 5 districts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

The Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi flash flood that struck on August 26 caused damage to the highest number of houses in Nuwakot, according to a government assessment.

According to the “Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood 2083: Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment” report prepared by a government-formed team, a total of 7,570 houses were damaged by the flood. Of these, 3,977 were in Nuwakot alone.

The flood damaged 1,779 houses in Rasuwa and 1,451 in Dhading, the report shows. A total of 263 houses in Gorkha and 100 in Chitwan were also damaged.

Nuwakot also had the highest number of affected households. The flood affected a total of 8,317 households, including 4,418 in Nuwakot alone.

Similarly, 1,923 households in Rasuwa were directly affected by the flood, while 1,588 households in Dhading were affected. The flood also affected 274 households in Gorkha and 114 in Chitwan.

Nearly 33,000 people affected: How many in each district?

The flood affected a total of 32,963 people, according to the report. Nuwakot recorded the highest number, with 17,082 people affected.

The report states that 7,633 people in Rasuwa and 6,638 in Dhading were affected. A total of 1,096 people in Gorkha and 514 in Chitwan were also affected.

The flood affected 15 local government units across five districts.

title.rendered: Preparations underway to partially reopen Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir

content.rendered:
Dhading, September 13

Preparations are underway to partially reopen the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir in Dhading, where the road has remained blocked following flood damage.

Authorities are currently working to level the road and prepare a temporary platform for vehicle movement. Once the initial work is completed, an empty gas bullet will be driven through the section to test the road’s condition and load-bearing capacity.

A team led by the Dhading Chief District Officer has reached the site for an inspection, while various agencies and machinery have been mobilised to reopen the road.

Two bulldozers are currently being used to level and smooth the damaged section. However, graveling and compaction work is still pending before the road can be considered fully operational.

For the time being, authorities are attempting to make the road passable only for stranded gas bullets and vehicles carrying heavy equipment.

According to the project, if the weather remains favourable, gas bullets and heavy equipment-carrying vehicles could be allowed to move through the section partially from today.

Before allowing traffic, an empty gas bullet will first be driven through the road to assess its stability and capacity.

Although the road surface at Krishnabhir has been levelled and appears smooth, further work, including graveling and compaction, is required before it can be fully reopened to regular traffic.

The road has remained blocked since erosion caused by the Trishuli flood on September 26 damaged the highway section at Krishnabhir.

title.rendered: ‘Nailing’ technique to be applied on cliff as landslides continue unabated at Tuilkhola

content.rendered:
Narayangadh, September 13

The Road Division Office is turning to a specialised technique to find a long-term solution after landslides continued at Tuilkhola, on the Narayangadh–Muglin road section.

Since large boulders falling from above have caused blockages not just during the monsoon but through winter as well since last year, crews are now clearing the loose rock, shaping the slope, and preparing to apply “nailing”, driving rods or nails into the cliff face to stabilise it.

Road Division, Bharatpur, said a horizontal drain will also be installed alongside the nailing work to channel out seeping water, combined with bioengineering techniques.

Chief Engineer Narayan Prasad Lamichhane of Road Division, Bharatpur, said large boulders from above are currently being cut and cleared.

“For the past seven days we’ve been cutting and removing the large rocks from above. It’s difficult terrain, so only a small crew is working there right now,” he said. “Once the large boulders are cleared, we plan to bring in more workers and equipment to move the work forward.”

According to him, nailing will be the primary technique used to prevent landslides at the site. Depending on the nature of the slope, either two-dimensional or three-dimensional netting will be used alongside bioengineering measures.

Currently, workers are cutting into the landslide-prone slope and clearing rock to shape it, after which the nailing technique will be applied. Since standing and seeping water in the landslide zone weakens the terrain, a horizontal drain will also be set up to channel the water out.

“Nailing will mainly be used here. Depending on the slope’s condition, we’ll use dimensional netting and prioritise bioengineering,” he said.

Lamichhane added that nailing work is expected to begin within a month, and that once the large boulders above are cleared, the road should no longer face blockages.

On this stretch, vehicle movement is currently allowed for half an hour every two hours between 8:30 am and 6:00 pm, while vehicles run continuously from 6:00 pm to 8:00 am.

title.rendered: Government to provide monthly allowance to families displaced by Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

The government has decided to provide financial assistance to families displaced by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods on August 26 until they are able to return to permanent homes.

According to Communications Minister Bikram Timilsina, Thursday’s Cabinet meeting decided to provide funds to cover rent and other essential expenses for flood-displaced families until permanent housing is constructed.

Under the decision, families of up to four members will receive Rs 15,000 per month. Each additional family member will receive an additional Rs 2,000 per month.

Families that do not wish to receive the rental assistance will have the option of receiving temporary housing arranged by the government until permanent homes are built, Timilsina said.

The government has already sent forms to all concerned local governments to collect the details of eligible families, the minister said in a social media post.

Reconstruction to follow detailed assessment

Timilsina said the government has completed the preliminary assessment of the damage and losses caused by the floods, while a detailed needs assessment is underway.

“Based on the assessment, the necessary resources will be secured and reconstruction and rehabilitation work will be expedited,” he said.

The Bhotekoshi floods displaced a large number of families and caused extensive damage to homes and infrastructure in the affected areas.

Minister Timilsina said via social media that forms have already been sent to all relevant local levels to collect the necessary details.

He added that the government has completed its preliminary damage and loss assessment from the flood, while a detailed needs assessment process is still ongoing. He said reconstruction and rehabilitation work will move forward swiftly once the required resources are secured based on that assessment.

title.rendered: All four gates of Pashupati to open at 3 am tomorrow

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

All four gates of Pashupatinath Temple will open at 3 am tomorrow for Haritalika Teej. The Pashupati Area Development Trust has said special arrangements for worship and viewing have been made for this year’s Teej, which falls tomorrow.

For devotees visiting the temple, five queues will be set up outside the temple, with eight more inside the temple premises after entry.

Since a significant number of visitors are expected to be women, the Trust has requested the government to deploy additional female security personnel.

For traffic management, vehicles of VIPs will be parked within the Trust’s office premises, while other vehicles will be directed to designated parking areas at Bhandarkhal, Siphal Chaur, Bankali, Tilganga, and Umakunda.

title.rendered: AHZ Associates Nepal, Bangladesh’s DMH Foundation distribute flood relief in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

AHZ Associates Nepal, in partnership with Bangladesh’s Dr Mostofa Hazera Foundation (DMH Foundation), has distributed relief materials to flood-affected families in Bidur, Nuwakot, following the recent floods that devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot and left hundreds of families displaced.

A team from AHZ Associates Nepal’s Kathmandu office travelled to Bidur to meet affected families directly, hear their experiences, and hand out food and essential supplies. Funding for the initiative came from the DMH Foundation, while AHZ Associates Nepal’s staff and volunteers carried out the distribution on the ground.

DMH Foundation Chairman Captain A.K.M. Golam Kibria said humanity has no borders, adding that the organisation was proud to support flood-affected families in Nepal and hoped the contribution would bring them some comfort and hope.

The relief effort was led by AHZ Associates Nepal Country Manager Shobin Thapa, with a team including Archana Yadav, Sajal Pokharel, Rishav Singh, Pragya Magar, Megha Bajracharya, Ambika Giri, Yogendra Saud, and Dibesh Adhikari.

Thapa said the visit was as much about standing with people who had suffered major losses and helping them feel less alone as it was about distributing supplies.

title.rendered: Oli says oppressive rulers will eventually fall

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

CPN-UML Chair KP Sharma Oli has said rulers who suppress people’s voices and act in an oppressive and tyrannical manner will eventually face public resistance and fall.

Oli made the remarks on Sunday while addressing journalists from the print media after receiving their memorandum.

“Those rulers who are oppressive, who exploit people, who are anti-people and tyrannical, who suppress others’ voices and do not allow others to speak — such rulers will face opposition,” Oli said.

“People will oppose such rulers, and such rulers will eventually perish,” he added.

Oli said the principle that oppressive rulers cannot survive indefinitely is reflected in religious teachings as well and remains relevant today.

“That was the truth, and it remains true today. It is something the rulers of today also need to understand,” he said.

‘Anti-freedom moves cannot last long’

Oli also said recent regressive, narrow-minded and anti-freedom moves would not be sustainable for long.

“Regressive moves, narrow-minded moves and anti-freedom moves cannot continue for a long time,” he said.

He urged journalists in the print media not to give up their efforts and to remain patient while continuing to speak out.

“Have a little patience, but don’t just sit and wait,” Oli said, quoting poet Laxmi Prasad Devkota’s message that no one becomes a winner without fighting.

Oli said the issues raised by the journalists were legitimate and assured them that the UML would raise their concerns both inside and outside parliament.

He also said he had personally been involved in the struggle for equality and freedom for around six decades.

Oli recalled that he first read the UN Charter and Universal Declaration of Human Rights about 60 years ago, saying their emphasis on equality and freedom inspired him to continue advocating for those principles.

title.rendered: KMC to provide free burn treatment up to Rs 200,000 for the needy

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Kathmandu Metropolitan City (KMC) will provide free burn treatment up to Rs 200,000 for targeted groups.

The service will be provided to poor, violence-affected, and unidentified/unclaimed patients on the recommendation of the metropolitan city’s health education committee. An agreement has been signed between Kathmandu Metropolitan City and Kirtipur Hospital (Public Health Concern Trust) to provide this free burn treatment service.

The metropolitan city has also contributed Rs 20 million to the hospital to cover equipment and instruments needed for treatment and to run the free service. Of this, Rs 10 million will go into a dedicated “burn treatment fund,” from which up to Rs 200,000 per patient will be covered for the targeted group. Any amount from the fund not used within this fiscal year will carry over and continue to be used for burn treatment in future years.

At the event, metropolitan city acting chief Sunita Dangol said the agreement was made so that no one is denied burn treatment for lack of money, adding that the fund was set up so families don’t have to leave a patient at the hospital and go scrambling for money after finally getting them there.

title.rendered: Opposition parties register public importance proposal on safe motherhood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Opposition parties have registered a public importance proposal in the House of Representatives on safe motherhood and reproductive health.

The proposal has been registered with Nepali Congress lawmaker Sita Thapaliya as the proposer. CPN-UML lawmaker Bhumika Limbu Subba, Nepali Communist Party lawmaker Balawati Sharma, Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Radhika Ramthel and Rastriya Prajatantra Party lawmaker Saraswati Lama are supporting the proposal.

According to the proposal, women make up 51.2 percent of Nepal’s population. Around 8.7 million women aged 15 to 59 and nearly five million women aged 20 to 40 are in the reproductive age group.

The proposal states that women currently account for 30 percent of Nepal’s civil service, 27 percent of the teaching sector, 55 percent of health services, 25 to 30 percent of the banking sector and 18 percent of the garment industry.

Despite their growing participation in the workforce, the proposal says many women are delaying or giving up motherhood because of the social perception that “having and raising children is a woman’s responsibility.”

Article 38(2) of the Constitution guarantees every woman the fundamental right to safe motherhood and reproductive health.

To implement this right, the government enacted the Public Health Service Act 2018 and the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act 2018. However, the proposal argues that adequate policies have not been formulated to fully implement these provisions.

‘How is six months of breastfeeding possible with 98 days of leave?’

The proposal highlights what it calls a contradiction between government recommendations and maternity leave provisions.

“Nearly five million women aged 20 to 40 are of reproductive age. But due to the social belief that having and raising children is a woman’s responsibility, and the state’s inadequate provision of only 98 days of maternity leave, many women are being forced to delay motherhood,” it states.

It further questions how mothers can exclusively breastfeed their children for six months when they are entitled to only 98 days of maternity leave.

“The government says babies should be exclusively breastfed for six months and promotes the first 1,000 days as a crucial period, but gives mothers only 98 days of leave. How is six months of breastfeeding possible with 98 days?” the proposal asks.

The proposal also raises concern over Nepal’s declining birth rate. While the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) target a fertility rate of 2.1, Nepal’s rate has fallen to 1.68.

It argues that although the state once promoted the slogan “two children, God’s gift,” it has failed to introduce adequate policies to address the declining birth rate.

The proposal also states that women working in the private sector, banks, garment industries and informal sectors remain deprived of adequate safe motherhood protections.

“After 98 days, women are forced to leave their infants behind and return to work,” the proposal states. “Women involved in politics do not even have maternity leave. If they fail to attend, they risk being listed as absent.”

caption.rendered: A newborn being fed breastmilk within the first hour of delivery. Photo Courtesy: UNICEF

image_meta.caption:
On 9 August 2022, at the Paropakar Maternity and Women's Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, Sunita Rai uses a spoon to feed her newborn son breastmilk. Sunita had come to the hospital to seek treatment after her son was born prematurely. Seeing that Sunita was unable to breastfeed her child, healthworkers quickly referred her to the hospital’s newly-launched 'Amrit Kosh', the first human milk bank to be established in the country, which provided Sunita’s baby with breastmilk donated by other mothers.  

In Nepal, only 42 per cent of children under 2 years of age are breastfed within one hour of birth and 62 per cent of children under six months are exclusively breastfed.

When expressed breast milk is not adequate or available, these newborns are usually given infant formula milk. However, feeding formula milk can often lead to a high risk of developing an infection (sepsis) as well as necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious disease that affects the intestines of premature infants. It typically happens within the first 2 weeks of life in babies who are fed formula instead of breast milk. Donor human milk, if made available to these babies, can save them from the adverse effects of formula milk.

The ‘Amrit Kosh' has the facilities to collect, pasteurize, test and store safe donor human milk from lactating mothers and then provide it to infants in need. The centre has been established in partnership with the European Union and UNICEF.  

Nepal’s Multi-Sector Nutrition Plan (MSNP) seeks to improve maternal, adolescent, and child nutrition throughout Nepal by promoting healthy, nutritious, and diversified diets for adolescents, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, infants, and young children. Since 2013, UNICEF has been supporting the Government of Nepal in implementing MSNP, with funding support from the European Union. Nepal.

title.rendered: MCC completes 18-km transmission line in 9 months

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Millennium Challenge Account Nepal (MCA-Nepal) has completed the construction of an 18-kilometre transmission line within nine months of its groundbreaking. It is the first major infrastructure project to be completed under the MCC Nepal Compact.

Construction of the transmission line section from the New Butwal Substation under construction in Sunwal Municipality-13 of Nawalparasi (Bardaghat Susta West) to the Nepal-India border was completed on Sunday.

Then Finance Minister Rameshwor Prasad Khanal and then US Ambassador to Nepal Dean R Thompson had laid the foundation stone for the transmission line on Nov. 26, 2025 (Mangsir 10, 2082 BS). “We expedited the construction of this line in view of Nepal’s current needs,” said Khadga Bahadur Bista, executive director of MCA-Nepal.

MCA-Nepal had signed a contract with Indian company Transrail Lighting Limited on Bhadra 8, 2081 BS to construct the transmission line. The contract, worth $12.38 million, stipulated that the project be completed within 21 months.

However, implementation of the project was halted for some time after Donald Trump became US president and the US began reviewing foreign aid, temporarily suspending all foreign assistance.

MCA-Nepal constructed the 18-kilometre section of the Butwal-Gorakhpur transmission line on the Nepal side. With its completion, the Nepal section of the country’s second cross-border transmission line has been completed.

A total of 315 kilometres of 400-kV transmission lines are being constructed with an MCC grant. Contracts have already been signed for the construction of the remaining projects under three additional packages.

In addition, a 400-kV electricity substation and road improvement projects are also being implemented under the MCC Nepal Compact.

title.rendered: Passenger ship carrying 240 goes missing in Indonesia, loses contact in Java Sea

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

A passenger ship carrying 240 people went missing in Indonesia on Sunday after losing contact in the Java Sea.

The ship, identified as Virgo Transport 8, was travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province on the island of Borneo. Authorities have launched a search for the missing vessel.

According to the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, the ship’s communication system malfunctioned during the journey, after which authorities were unable to establish contact with the vessel.

Rescue officials said preliminary information showed that the ship’s last known location was in the Java Sea, about 148 kilometres from a port in Banjarmasin. Rescue teams are conducting an intensive search in the area. No information about casualties among those aboard the ship has been received so far.

Indonesia has witnessed several major maritime accidents in the past, with bad weather, storms, overloading and failure to comply with safety regulations often cited as contributing factors.

In 1981, the passenger ship Tampomas II sank in the Java Sea, killing around 430 people.

Similarly, the Senopati Nusantara ferry sank in the Java Sea in 2006 due to bad weather. More than 400 people were killed or went missing in the accident.

In 2007, more than 50 people died when the Levina I ferry caught fire and sank. In 2018, 36 people were killed when the Lestari Maju ferry sank off South Sulawesi.

Why is Indonesia at high risk of maritime accidents?

Indonesia has more than 17,000 islands, and a large proportion of its population of around 280 million lives across these islands. Ferries and passenger ships are therefore the main means of transportation between cities and islands, with large numbers of people travelling by sea every day.

As Indonesia lies in the tropics, it is frequently exposed to heavy rainfall, strong winds and high waves. Such weather conditions can make travel particularly difficult for small and medium-sized vessels.

Investigations into several past accidents have also revealed shortcomings such as overloading, inadequate safety equipment and failure to comply with safety standards properly. However, the causes of each accident may vary.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood: Over 3,000 DNA samples collected

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Efforts continue to collect DNA from relatives and from bodies recovered following the devastating flood on the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, which left many people missing.

According to Nepal Police, 1,846 DNA samples have been collected from relatives of missing persons.

Police spokesperson and DIG Abi Narayan Kafle said an additional 1,286 DNA samples have been extracted from bodies. In total, 3,132 DNA samples have been collected so far.

A total of 4,089 people remain missing from the flood. So far, 1,388 bodies have been recovered, of which 103 have been handed over to relatives, while 1,230 have been given last rites/managed on-site.

title.rendered: Nepal says no to Malaysia’s limited manpower plan despite support-agency compromise

content.rendered:
Nepal has reiterated that it will not accept the process Malaysia has moved forward with, under which only a limited number of manpower companies would be authorised to recruit Nepali workers.

Malaysia had earlier listed only 25 manpower companies as “registered recruitment agencies” in its Foreign Worker Centralised Management System (FWCMS) for bringing in workers from Nepal. After that drew widespread opposition in Nepal, Malaysia listed an additional 250 manpower companies as “support agencies” placed under those 25 companies.

However, the Nepal government has taken the position that even this structure- 25 principal manpower agencies with 250 support agencies under them is not acceptable.

The Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security informed Malaysia of this through a diplomatic note. Malaysia had listed 25 “principal agencies” empowered to bring in worker demand from employers and to send workers, with an additional 250 manpower companies placed under them as “support agencies.”

According to a ministry official, Malaysia was informed that this kind of monopolistic arrangement is not acceptable under Nepal’s constitution and existing legal framework. The official said Nepali law makes no provision for such a structure of principal and support agencies.

In its response to Malaysia, the ministry noted that Nepal’s Foreign Employment Act, its regulations, and the constitution give equal standing to all licensed foreign employment businesses. It also pointed out that the bilateral labour agreement between Nepal and Malaysia contains no provision for “principal” and “support” agencies, making clear that Nepal cannot accept such a system.

Under the Foreign Employment Act, 2064 (2007), all licensed and active foreign employment businesses are given equal standing for sending workers abroad. The ministry has concluded that existing law contains no provision limiting the right to send workers to a specific destination country to only a select few institutions.

The ministry’s stance is that no institution can be arbitrarily restricted under the Act, regulations, or constitution, and that the bilateral agreement likewise contains no such principal/support agency arrangement, so the government remains committed to its existing legal framework.

Ministry spokesperson Mira Acharya said that after Malaysia sent a letter outlining its plan to bring in workers through 25 principal and 250 support agencies, Nepal responded within a day or two through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, stating that the arrangement was unacceptable and that Nepali law does not envision sending workers through a limited set of manpower companies. As of now, Malaysia has not responded to that letter.

Earlier, once Malaysia made the list of 25 manpower companies public, the Nepal government had already made its objection clear, urging that any change to the existing system be settled through bilateral discussion. Malaysia then listed an additional 250 companies as “sub-agents” under the 25 main companies, a move the ministry also rejected, and it has since begun investigating and taking action against the companies on the list.

After the list of 25 companies was made public, Labour Minister Ramji Yadav had also called in Malaysia’s chargé d’affaires for talks. The ministry told Malaysia the arrangement was inconsistent with Nepal’s constitution, existing law, and the Nepal-Malaysia labour agreement, and urged a resolution through the joint technical committee and bilateral mechanisms. Some of the 25 listed companies subsequently asked to have their names removed, and after discussions with the ministry, all 25 agreed to be removed from the FWCMS list.

A ministry official said the government’s main challenge now is to keep Malaysian employment opportunities open while preventing a monopoly from being established among a limited set of companies, noting that demand for Nepali workers in Malaysia remains large, with thousands of positions still in process, so the government does not want to make any hasty decision that could disrupt employment. The official added that Nepal’s goal is not to halt employment in Malaysia, with 25,000-30,000 positions currently in process and more in the pipeline, but that Nepal is not obliged to accept a monopolistic system in the name of employment.

The government’s effort, the official said, is focused on removing the disputed structure rather than damaging the employment relationship with Malaysia. To that end, the ministry has directed the Department of Foreign Employment to investigate the basis on which the 25 principal companies were listed under the Malaysian system, and is preparing to seek clarification on how and on what basis the 250 support agencies were included. Following the ministry’s directive, the Department has suspended prior labour approval for the listed manpower companies.

The ministry said it has pursued the matter at both the legal and diplomatic level, not merely through a single letter, and stressed that Nepal responded promptly once Malaysia’s letter arrived, with the government’s position remaining clear that it will not accept any system falling outside the bounds of existing Nepali law and the bilateral agreement.

Nepal’s policy is to continue its employment relationship with Malaysia while refusing to accept any structure that unequally restricts Nepali foreign employment businesses.

title.rendered: Nepal Army Chief Ashok Raj Sigdel leaves for China

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Nepal Army Chief Ashok Raj Sigdel has left for China on an official visit. According to the Nepal Army Headquarters, Sigdel will be in China from September 13 to September 19.

During the visit, Sigdel is scheduled to attend the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum to be held in Beijing.

The visit is expected to further strengthen military relations between Nepal and China and contribute to Nepal’s foreign policy through military diplomacy, according to the Army.

During Sigdel’s absence, Lieutenant General Pradeep Jung KC will assume the responsibilities of the Acting Chief General of the Nepal Army.

title.rendered: Miss Nepal Deepmala reaches Dhunche and distributes relief materials

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Miss Nepal Deepmala Dhakal has reached Dhunche in Rasuwa to distribute relief materials to those affected by the Bhotekoshi flood. Dhakal, who also holds a position with the Non-Resident Nepali Association, is currently in Dhunche.

She had previously distributed relief in various flood-affected areas of Nuwakot as well. She had gone to Vietnam to support Luna Luintel at the Miss World finale, and travelled to Dhunche to distribute relief immediately after returning.

Having spent three days in Dhunche, she distributed four truckloads of clothing, food supplies, solar panels, and bedding materials to those affected. Photos she sent from the location show her interacting with affected children and the community.

title.rendered: 4 injured in auto-rickshaw accident in Palungtar, Gorkha

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 13

Four people were injured when an auto-rickshaw met with an accident on an inner road section at Chhapthok in Palungtar Municipality-4, Gorkha, on Sunday morning.

According to police, the auto-rickshaw (Ga 3-001 Ha 0210), travelling from Baddanda towards Thatipokhari, fell about 10 metres off the road at around 9:30 am and crashed.

The injured have been identified as 48-year-old Parmila GC, 45-year-old Gita Shrestha and 20-year-old Pragati Shrestha, all from Palungtar Municipality-4, and 31-year-old Menuka Giri of Palungtar-5, police said.

DSP Rajkumar Shrestha said all four injured people were in moderate condition.

They were given preliminary treatment at a local medical facility before being referred to Ampipal Hospital in Harni for further treatment, police said.

Police have taken the auto-rickshaw driver, 33-year-old Suresh Shrestha of Palungtar-4, into custody.

Further investigation into the incident is underway, police said.

Kathmandu, September 13

Machhapuchhre Bank has decided to distribute a 6 percent dividend to its shareholders. The decision was made at the 564th meeting of the bank’s board of directors, held on Friday afternoon, declaring a dividend of 6 percent (including tax) on paid-up capital.

Of this, the bank has decided to propose distributing 3 percent as bonus shares and 3 percent as a cash dividend. The bank stated the dividend will be distributed once it is approved by Nepal Rastra Bank and passed by the upcoming annual general meeting.

With the aim of delivering simple and convenient banking services to customers across every sector and class, the bank currently serves more than 1.8 million customers through 157 branches, 12 extension counters, 88 branchless banking service points, and 193 ATMs across all seven provinces of the country.

title.rendered: Nakkhu Prison escapee held in Gongabu, caught selling fake gold as real

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

A man has been arrested on charges of defrauding someone of NPR 1.39 crore by passing off fake gold as real.

The arrested man is 28-year-old Anish Thapa Magar, a permanent resident of Siddhicharan Municipality-1, Okhaldhunga, currently living at Naya Buspark, Kathmandu.

He was arrested by a team from the Gongbu Naya Buspark Police Circle.

Thapa Magar had defrauded a victim of NPR 1.39 crore by claiming fake gold was genuine.

Kathmandu District Police Office SP Danbahadur Thapa said 865 grams of fake gold were also recovered from him.

The Kathmandu District Court has remanded him in custody for five more days. He is a convict in a rape case and had escaped from Nakkhu Prison during the Gen Z movement.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi floods: Damage to 18 schools; Rs 4.23 billion estimated for recovery

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, September 13

A total of 18 schools from Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts were damaged in the Bhotekoshi flash floods that occurred on August 26. Among these, 11 schools were destroyed, recording a loss of Rs 937 million. The Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) report prepared by the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) showed the amount of damage incurred to schools.

A total of 56 buildings in 18 schools were affected. As many as 152 rooms received partial damage, and 156 rooms were destroyed. In Rasuwa, the schools damaged by the devastating floods were one from Gosaikunda Rural Municipality and three from Uttargaya Rural Municipality. Nine schools were damaged by the floods in Budur Municipality of Nuwakot. Galchhi Rural Municipality of Dhading suffered damage to three school buildings, while Benighat Rorang Rural Municipality from the same district suffered damage to a school.

A school in Siddhalek Rural Municipality in Dhading district also suffered loss, with its four buildings damaged in the disaster. For the reconstruction of the damaged schools, the government would require approximately Rs 4.23 billion.

—RSS

title.rendered: Flood affects 9,428 children in 32 schools across three districts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

The flood in the Bhotekoshi River has directly affected 9,428 children from 32 schools in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, according to the Children as Zone of Peace National Campaign (CZOP).

CZOP Chairperson Tilottam Poudel presented the figures at a discussion on “Impact of the Flood on Children and the Responsibility of Media” organised by the campaign on Friday.

According to Poudel, 1,373 children have been displaced and are currently staying in holding centres. A preliminary report shows that 488 students are still unaccounted for, while five students have been found dead.

Poudel said children, senior citizens, postpartum women and children with disabilities were among those most vulnerable during the disaster.

He said the government and concerned agencies should immediately prioritise the safety, protection and education of children affected by the flood.

He also stressed the need for greater sensitivity in protecting children who have lost their parents in the disaster.

Media urged to prioritise children’s issues

Former Federation of Nepali Journalists President Dharmendra Jha said the media should prioritise the voices of people who are unable to speak for themselves during disasters.

He said journalists reporting on children must pay particular attention to their rights, privacy and psychological well-being.

Irshad Ahmad Ansari, policy manager at Plan International, said the media should give special priority to children’s issues during disasters.

He also said Plan International was ready to coordinate and cooperate with CZOP as necessary in initiatives concerning children.

Journalists participating in the discussion said CZOP should publicly raise its voice if any media outlet, government agency or organisation carries out inappropriate activities involving children or disseminates inaccurate information.

They also called for more effective advocacy and lobbying with concerned authorities on issues affecting children.

title.rendered: Sikta Irrigation Project targeted for completion within five years

content.rendered:
Banke, September 13

Work on the national pride project, the Sikta Irrigation Project in Banke, has been accelerated with a target of completing the remaining infrastructure within the next five years.

Project Director Raju Acharya said construction has gained momentum following the government’s direction to complete the project within five years.

He said all remaining infrastructure could be completed within the deadline if there is no shortage of budget and human resources.

According to Acharya, the project has so far achieved 51 percent physical progress, while around Rs 24 billion has been spent on infrastructure development.

Although repair and maintenance works will continue regularly, efforts are currently focused on completing the remaining construction works within five years.

Sikta Irrigation Project started in 2005-06

The Sikta Irrigation Project was launched in fiscal year 2005-06 with the objective of providing irrigation facilities to 42,766 hectares of land.

Under the project, a 317-metre barrage is being constructed across the Rapti River at Agaiya in Rapti Sonari Rural Municipality of Banke.

The project aims to provide irrigation to 33,766 hectares through the West Main Canal and around 9,000 hectares through the East Main Canal.

At present, irrigation facilities have reached around 25,000 hectares, according to Sikta Irrigation Project Director Acharya.

The Sikta Irrigation Project was initially approved under a master plan in 2007 with an estimated cost of Rs 12.8 billion and a target for completion by fiscal year 2013-14.

During construction, the government expanded the project to cover an additional 9,000 hectares and added the East Main Canal and other infrastructure.

A revised master plan approved in fiscal year 2014-15 increased the estimated cost to Rs 25.02 billion and extended the completion deadline to fiscal year 2019-20.

However, the Sikta Irrigation Project was not completed within the revised deadline.

Under the latest master plan approved in 2022, the total project cost has been estimated at Rs 52.89 billion, with completion targeted for fiscal year 2029-30, according to Information Officer Manoj Kumar Sah.

Canal construction gathers pace

Sah said construction of branch and distributary canals is currently progressing rapidly, with tenders for 30 additional packages having been invited.

The 45-kilometre West Main Canal has already been completed. Its Sidhaniya, Akalgharwa and Guruwagaun branch canals are also nearing completion, while construction of the Duduwa branch canal is underway.

The Duduwa branch canal is designed to provide irrigation to around 16,000 hectares of farmland.

Construction of the canal had remained stalled for a long period due to a dispute involving contractor Coastal Pappu JV and a case pending in court. The dispute was resolved last year, allowing construction to resume through a new contractor.

According to Sah, tenders have also been invited for the construction of several other sub-branch and distributary canals under the West Main Canal.

In fiscal year 2025-26 alone, around 9.5 kilometres of canals were constructed under the Duduwa irrigation system, while nine kilometres of branch, sub-branch and distributary canals were built under the western canal system.

Similarly, around 9.5 kilometres of branch, sub-branch and distributary canals were constructed under the eastern canal system.

As part of irrigation-area protection and conservation works, 7.5 kilometres of embankments were constructed and 5.5 hectares of land were acquired during the same fiscal year.

Sah said the project achieved more than 96 percent physical progress and around 89 percent financial progress last fiscal year, out of the Rs 1.57 billion budget allocated to the project.

East Main Canal remains incomplete

The 53-kilometre East Main Canal is still incomplete.

Around 35 kilometres of the canal has been constructed from the barrage through Baisagaun. However, construction has been halted in the Narainapur Rural Municipality area.

Shalikram Dangi, chairperson of the Sikta Irrigation Water Users Committee, said farmers have been unable to receive irrigation when needed because the branch, sub-branch and distributary canals under both main canal systems have not yet been fully completed.

“Even though the main canals have been constructed in many areas, farmers cannot get irrigation when they need it because the branch and smaller canals are still incomplete,” Dangi said.

title.rendered: Excavation begins before permitted date at Siraha’s Gagane Khola

content.rendered:
Siraha, September 13

A contractor awarded a contract to extract riverbed materials from the Gagane Khola in Golbazar Municipality, Siraha, has reportedly carried out excavation several days before the permitted date.

Tirupati Construction secured the contract to extract riverbed materials from the stream for Rs 14.125 million. However, according to the municipality, the company is permitted to begin excavation only from September 17.

Despite this, excavation was reportedly carried out at the site a few days ago.

Golbazar Municipality Mayor Shyam Shrestha said he had asked officials to look into the matter.

“If permission has been granted from September 17, excavation cannot be carried out before then,” Shrestha said. “We had sent municipal police to inspect the river, but they did not find any vehicles there.”

He said the company had also been given permission to extract materials required for the construction of a road.

“The company has permission to extract materials needed for a road project here. I need to look into the other details as well,” Shrestha said.

Municipality Revenue Section Chief Rambriksh Mahato said excavation before the effective date of the agreement would be illegal.

Meanwhile, Rajendra Yadav of Tirupati Construction acknowledged that excavation had taken place for one day.

“I excavated for only one day. I have not excavated since then. Others may have done it; I don’t know,” Yadav said.

The municipality has said it is looking into whether any excavation took place in violation of the contract conditions.

title.rendered: Academic year at St. Xavier’s College concludes, releasing fifteen newsletters

content.rendered:
Students of St. Xavier’s College, majoring in Social Work and Psychology with a Journalism elective, as part of their writing project, wrapped up their academic year by releasing fifteen newsletters as their final academic deliverable. Working with 15 different groups, two of them produced Asha Awaaz and The Orchid Chronicles, the newsletters for the NGOs Asha Nepal and Orchid Garden Nepal, respectively. With this writing project, nearly 100 students stepped out of the classroom and engaged with the real-world, connecting classroom learning with the job market. 

Vice Principal Saluja Chand, Head of the Department of Major Arts Shishir Kumar Bhusal, representatives from the participating NGOs, and Faculty members joined the release ceremony. This project and pedagogies align perfectly with the Strategic Plan (2024-2029) of the University Grants Commission that envisages fostering employability with quality, project- and skills-based education. 

“Fostering communication, particularly persuasive written communication, is not just a fundamental skill for mass communication students, but essential for all learners, including Psychology and Social Work. We, at St. Xavier’s College, translate classroom learning into practice, engaging students in writing projects. Today, 91 future psychologists and social workers from the batch-2023 produced 15 newsletters, including Asha Awaaz and The Orchid Chronicles for two NGOs, which help them connect with future employers”, said Chun Bahadur Gurung, Faculty Lead of Journalism at St. Xavier’s College. 

The college leadership acknowledged this initiative. “Even at the micro level, engaging students in practical learning and real-world work is highly commendable. This initiative beautifully connects the classroom with the world of work, allowing students to turn their learning into meaningful work for the community. Hats off to the teachers for going the extra mile in guiding and enabling learners to learn at this level”. In a note, said Fr. Dr. Augustine Thomas, S.J., the principal of the college.

title.rendered: Elephants in the Fog to support flood victims in Nepal through special screening in France

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Nepali feature film ‘Tiniharu’ (Elephants in the Fog), winner of the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize 2026 at the Cannes Film Festival, will hold a special charity screening in France as part of its ongoing international journey and in solidarity with Nepal.

Directed by Abinash Bikram Shah, the film opens theatrically in France on September 23. Ahead of its French release, a special preview screening will be held at UGC Les Halles in Paris on September 17, 2026. Director Abinash Bikram Shah will be present at the screening, organised under the banner “In Solidarity with Nepal.”

The proceeds received by the French distributor from this special screening will be donated to a fund established by the Government of Nepal to support people affected by floods and natural disasters in the country.

Earlier, the team behind Tiniharu (Elephants in the Fog) also organised a special Fundraising Screening in Kathmandu on Bhadra 17 to support flood victims in Nepal. The entire amount raised from that screening was donated to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund for relief and support for those affected by the floods.

The special screening in France is being organised by the film’s French team and distributor as an expression of solidarity with families affected by the recent floods and natural disasters across Nepal. With the film currently playing in cinemas in Nepal, the initiative also extends the film’s efforts to raise support for Nepal internationally.

Representing Nepal, Tiniharu made history as the first Nepali feature film to be selected for the Un Certain Regard section in the 79-year history of the Cannes Film Festival, where it went on to win the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize. Since then, the film has continued its international journey, earning recognition and acclaim at film festivals around the world.

In Nepal, the film has been in theatrical release across the country since September 4, receiving an enthusiastic response from audiences and positive reactions from critics.

Director Abinash Bikram Shah said that having the film’s French screening become an opportunity to extend support and solidarity to flood victims in Nepal is deeply meaningful to the team.

The film stars Pushpa Thing Lama, Deepika Yadav, Jasmin Bishwakarma, Aliz Ghimire, alongside Gauri Malla and Maotse Gurung, among others.
