title.rendered: Tinkar raise Rs 134,211 for Rasuwa flood survivors in bid to put Tinkar on civic map

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 13

Residents of Tinkar village in Darchula have collected Rs 134,211 for survivors of the Rasuwa floods, bringing together Tinkaris from Darchula, Kathmandu, India and abroad in a rare collective initiative organised in the name of their village.

At a meeting with Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle on Friday evening, residents handed over the donation to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund. The contribution, residents said, was meant to stand with flood victims, while putting Tinkari on the government’s radar and bringing their overlooked community into Nepal’s civic space.

The initiative began on August 29, when Kamna Tinkari, from Byas Rural Municipality, Darchula, posted a proposal in the WhatsApp group used by Tinkari residents. What initially proved difficult was gradually brought together by Tinkaris living in Kathmandu, Darchula, abroad and even daughters of Tinkar married in India. 

The collection came as Tinkaris were watching the devastation in Rasuwa and thinking about their own vulnerability to floods.

Kamna, who started the campaign, had rarely seen Tinkaris come forward collectively on this large scale for a cause beyond their own community. “The experience made me think about how Tinkar is seen in Nepal, so often through adversity and remoteness, with even our distinctive culture sometimes becoming another fixed lens. These are realities, but I don’t want them to become our whole identity”.

Tinkar is in Ward no. 1 of Byas Rural Municipality in Darchula, Sudurpaschim Province. The village has roughly 70 households and is home to the Rung community. It lies in the far northwest of Nepal, at the tri-junction of Nepal, India and China. 

There is no road or foot trail connecting Tinkar with the district headquarters Khalanga on the Nepali side. People travelling between the settlements have to pass through the Indian territory. Tinkar is in fact the last village in the far north west Nepal.

The geographical distance has also shaped how Tinkaris are represented in the civic space and media.

According to Ranjana Tinkari, 28, one of the reasons she participated in this donation was to draw attention to Tinkar, a village that is largely unknown outside the community. She said Tinkaris often have to explain that their surname, ethnicity and language are part of Nepal too. The initiative, she said, was also a way to create a digital footprint of Tinkar’s existence and its people’s initiatives, rather than having the village appear in public discourses only during debates over border issues of Kalapani-Lipulekh.

For many Tinkaris, the decision to contribute was also shaped by their own experience with disasters.

According to Krishtal Budhathoki, 20 years old and from Tinkar, they have repeatedly suffered damaging floods every year but received little government attention. 

Every time after the floods, the little remaining roads get damaged, and with no attention from the government, residents had to rebuild themselves with one person from each household helping, said another 19-year-old resident, Juni Tinkari.

“Through this collective work, we hope the government recognises our vulnerability to disasters, lived experiences and also possibilities of Tinkar,” added Juni.

For Tinkaris, it is also a place whose traditions, Rung culture, natural temples and gumbas, unique natural landscape, tourism and trekking potential remain largely unseen by the government. And so, the importance of the donation goes beyond the Rs 134, 211 collected.

Tinkaris want the community to be seen beyond narratives of remoteness and victimhood.

“Yes, we are far, with limited resources and facilities, and we are in adversity but we are also much more than that,” Krishtal said, pointing to Tinkar’s agriculture, culture, and natural heritage. “Limiting a community to victimhood also takes away its voice and agency.”

For Tinkaris, the initiative is also a message to the state.

“Just because we are geographically far from Kathmandu, it doesn’t mean we have to be far or sidelined from national civic space too,” Kamna said. “It is our way of saying- though we are in one of the farthest places, we as a community have come forward to our fellow Nepalis, so the government too should reach out to us despite the distance.”

Kamna hopes the initiative will encourage attention to Tinkar, its basic facilities, lived experiences there and to its potential for tourism and trekking.

title.rendered: Korala border becomes revenue powerhouse, collects Rs 1.78 billion in 15 days

content.rendered:
Mustang, September 13

The Mustang Customs Office at the Korala border has collected Rs 1.78 billion in revenue in just 15 days, as the closure of the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border has increased the flow of goods entering Nepal through Mustang.

The Nepal-China customs office, located at Lomanthang-4, Nhechung, at the Korala border point, has witnessed a sharp rise in customs activity following floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa that disrupted the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border point.

According to Mustang Customs Office Chief Bidur Chudal, the complete closure of the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border has led to a significant increase in Chinese goods being imported through Korala.

The customs office collected Rs 270 million in revenue on a single day last Friday.

Chudal said the office has been collecting around Rs 300 million in daily revenue since September 7 and expects the trend to continue.

On Friday alone, customs officials processed 71 containers and 106 electric vehicles (EVs) bound for different destinations across Nepal.

Since the closure of the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border, a total of 434 containers and 641 electric vehicles entering Nepal through the Korala border have been processed by the Mustang Customs Office.

The increase in imports through Korala has turned the previously less-busy border point into a major revenue-generating customs hub for Nepal.

title.rendered: BRICS nations call for ‘maximum restraint’ in West Asia

content.rendered:
New Delhi, September 13

BRICS nations have called for “maximum restraint” in West Asia, urging countries to avoid actions that could further escalate tensions in the region.

In a joint statement issued Saturday during the BRICS summit in New Delhi, the 11-member group, which includes China, Russia, Iran and India, expressed deep concern over the continuing escalation of tensions in West Asia.

“We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint,” the statement said.

The group also urged countries to avoid actions that could further aggravate the situation.

BRICS foreign ministers had failed to reach agreement on a joint statement during their meeting in New Delhi in May, with members including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.

However, after intensive diplomatic efforts by India, the leaders managed to issue a joint statement at Saturday’s summit.

Concern over attacks on civilian and nuclear facilities

The BRICS leaders condemned attacks on civilian infrastructure and nuclear facilities.

“We express serious concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), in violation of international law,” the statement said.

The group stressed that nuclear safeguards, safety and security must be maintained even during armed conflicts to protect people and the environment.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, addressing the opening of the two-day summit, said the war in West Asia “does not serve the common interests of the international community”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are attending the summit.

The BRICS statement also called for greater international cooperation amid growing global polarisation and distrust.

“We note the current global context of polarisation and distrust and encourage global action to strengthen international peace and security,” it said.

The leaders also stressed the importance of maintaining the smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy in accordance with international law.

UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi are also attending the summit. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan is expected to join the meeting later Saturday.

BRICS was established in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in global institutions traditionally dominated by Western powers.

title.rendered: From earning a living in Qatar to building a business of his own

content.rendered:
For Mahendra Chaulagain, Qatar was never supposed to become home.

In 1996, he arrived in the Gulf country as an ordinary worker, driven by little more than the need to support a struggling family back in Jhapa.

He had no grand business plan. His elder brother was already in Qatar, and Mahendra followed him in the hope that two incomes would be enough to keep the family afloat.

Twenty-eight years later, the man who once arrived in Qatar as a worker runs a company employing between 1,500 and 2,000 people. More than half of them are Nepali workers.

He is now known as a businessman, social campaigner and prominent representative of the Nepali community in Qatar.

But his journey from a worker to a business owner did not happen overnight.

It began with an office-boy job, followed by work as a salesman, nearly seven years as a migrant worker, and eventually a small Nepali bookstore in Doha.

Today, Chaulagain owns 100 percent of the company he started expanding years ago—something he says is difficult to achieve for an older company with Qatari shareholders.

Behind that success, he credits three things: struggle, honesty and discipline.

From Jhapa to Qatar

Mahendra Chaulagain was born into a modest family in Barhadashi-7 of Jhapa, formerly Dangibari-3.

There were three brothers in the family, and money was scarce.

His elder brother had already gone to Qatar. Mahendra followed in 1996, hoping the two brothers could earn enough to support their family.

“We were three brothers and our financial situation was difficult,” he says. “My elder brother had already gone to Qatar. I went so that, with both of us earning, we could support the family.”

Qatar was very different then.

Nepalis were still few and far between. Coming across another Nepali could feel almost like being back home.

Over time, however, the Nepali community grew.

Chaulagain spent nearly seven years working as a labourer. Then he began thinking about what came next. He wanted to build something of his own.

A bookstore becomes a business

His first jobs in Qatar were modest. He worked as an office boy and later as a salesman. Then, in 2003, he opened what he describes as Doha’s first Nepali bookstore.

He called it Everest Book Shop.

The shop quickly became more than a place to buy books.

For Nepalis looking for newspapers, novels and other Nepali literature, it became a meeting point—a place where people could find not only reading material from home but also one another.

“I opened the first Nepali bookstore in Doha selling Nepali newspapers and novels,” he says. “There was no such shop in Doha, so it became a meeting place for many Nepalis. I used to bring newspapers and books from Nepal and sell them.”

Running the bookstore also exposed him to other possibilities.

In 2005, he established Woodland Import-Export Company and entered the clothing business, importing garments from Nepal, China and Dubai and selling them in Qatar.

Five years later, in 2010, he changed the company’s name to Woodland Contracting and General Services and moved into construction.

He started by employing 28 workers.

Today, the company employs between 1,500 and 2,000 people, more than 70 percent of them Nepali.

From worker to 100 percent owner

As the business grew, Mahendra Chaulagain began expanding further. One of his biggest milestones came only recently.

Foreigners owning companies outright in Qatar has not always been straightforward, particularly in older companies where Qatari nationals hold shares.

Chaulagain says he recently succeeded in bringing the entire ownership of Woodland Contracting and General Services under his control.

“I received full ownership of my company only a few months ago,” he says. “I believe I am probably the first Nepali businessman to have obtained 100 percent ownership of an existing company in this way.”

The company, which he has operated for the past 14 years, has a capital of 500,000 Qatari riyals.

He owns 90 percent of the shares, while his wife, Kanchan Chaulagain, owns the remaining 10 percent.

For Chaulagain, the achievement is not simply a business milestone. He sees it as evidence that his years of hard work and integrity earned the trust of the Qatari authorities.

“When Qatar saw that I was capable, it trusted me and gave me full ownership of the company,” he says.

‘It wasn’t luck. It was hard work’

Mahendra Chaulagain does not attribute his success to luck.

He points instead to the values that have guided him since his days as a worker: hard work, honesty and discipline.

“It wasn’t luck. It was hard work,” he says. “When I think that someone who left with 600 rupees now pays 200,000 riyals in rent, even I find it astonishing.”

His experience as a worker has also shaped the way he treats his employees.

He says he does not believe in being harsh with workers because he once stood where they do.

“I treat workers like family. I am someone who came through the same path,” he says.

For years, he worked within Qatar’s strict legal and competitive business environment. He believes his consistency and honesty eventually earned him the confidence of the authorities.

“When I left for Qatar, I was pushed by poverty and hardship at home,” he says. “I thought I would work for a few years and return. I never imagined I would establish my own company and come this far.”

Business became a platform for social work

As his business grew, Mahendra Chaulagain increasingly turned his attention towards the Nepali community.

He helped bring Nepali businessmen in Qatar together and established the Nepal Business Association, Qatar, becoming its founding president.

He claims it was the first Nepali organisation registered with the Qatari government.

Under his leadership, the association sent significant assistance to Nepal during the earthquake, floods and Covid-19 pandemic.

During the coronavirus pandemic alone, it sent oxygen cylinders worth more than Rs 10 million to Nepal.

More recently, Chaulagain was elected president of the International Jhapa Society, having previously served as its senior vice-president.

“We want to unite Jhapa residents around the world and contribute to the development of the district,” he says.

He has also served as an adviser to NRNA Qatar and as an honorary member of the NRNA ICC.

Qatar became a second home

For many Nepalis, Qatar is a place of work.

For Mahendra Chaulagain, it has become something closer to a second home.

He has spent much of his adult life on its roads, in its neighbourhoods and along its coast. His children grew up there and are now nearing the end of their education.

Yet his attachment to Nepal has never disappeared.

He increasingly feels the pull to return home, invest more in Nepal, create jobs and contribute to the country.

“I have never had to look back in my life,” he says. “Time took me along the path of success. I never imagined I would reach this point.”

He credits his parents’ blessings for much of what he has achieved.

“I am satisfied with what I have achieved through my hard work,” he says.

‘Qatar is a country built with Nepali sweat’

Mahendra Chaulagain believes the relationship between Qatar and Nepal should not end with Nepalis working there and sending money home.

Thousands of Nepalis have helped build Qatar, and millions of young Nepalis continue to work there.

He believes the skills, experience and capital accumulated in Qatar should eventually contribute to Nepal’s development.

“Qatar is a country that we Nepalis built with our sweat,” he says. “Now Nepal also needs to understand the value of that sweat.”

Under his leadership, the Nepal Business Association, Qatar, has worked with the Nepal Exporters Association to promote trade and business between the two countries.

But Chaulagain is critical of Nepal’s slow and complicated administrative processes.

“Qatar has a one-stop system. In Nepal, you have to visit 10 different offices,” he says. “If Nepal wants to attract foreign investment, the government must be stable and investment-friendly.”

A life-threatening illness changed his priorities

A few years ago, Mahendra Chaulagain faced a serious health crisis.

He spent a long period in hospital, caught between life and death.

“My life has had many ups and downs. This is my second life,” he says.

He remained unconscious in hospital for a long time.

“By God’s grace and because of my good deeds, I was brought back into society with renewed energy,” he says. “Life is like water on a taro leaf. I survived because of God’s grace and my family’s love.”

The experience changed his priorities.

He decided to devote the rest of his life to social service and nation-building.

Frustrated by Nepal’s slow system

His desire to contribute to Nepal is accompanied by frustration with the country’s bureaucracy.

“Opening a company in Qatar takes an hour. In Nepal, going from the ward office to the ministry can take six months,” he says.

He says investors coming to Nepal can become discouraged even at the airport.

He believes Nepal needs a toll-gate system and greater government-to-government cooperation to attract investment.

“Qatar’s roads and towers were built through toll-gate systems,” he says. “Nepal would not lose if it allowed roads to be built on 20- or 30-year leases.”

He is also concerned about frequent changes of ambassadors at the Nepali embassy in Qatar.

He says more than 10 ambassadors have changed since 1999 and believes an ambassador should serve for at least four years to ensure policy continuity.

The Nepali community in Qatar has also changed significantly during his years there.

Nepalis were once largely identified as labourers. Today, he says, thousands of Nepalis are involved in restaurants, salons, building materials, manpower supply and other businesses.

He believes Nepal needs to create an environment where the money earned by migrant workers in the Middle East can be invested productively at home.

“We are ready to help,” he says. “But the government needs a clear vision.”

Family and the road ahead

His wife, Kanchan Chaulagain, is a co-shareholder in his company.

Their son Durga and daughter Kamaksha are completing their education in Qatar.

Chaulagain plans to bring his children back to Nepal after they finish their studies.

He already has investments in Nepal, including a hotel, a school and a rice mill, and wants to expand them further.

He says he never imagined reaching the position he occupies today.

His explanation for the journey is simple.

“Those who have big dreams can turn difficulties into opportunities,” he says. “I am living proof that even someone who goes abroad to work can eventually become a leader.”

For Chaulagain, the formula remains unchanged: honesty, discipline and continuous hard work.

title.rendered: David Warner likely to play in Nepal Premier League, Australian source says

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 12

Australian cricket star David Warner is reportedly set to play in the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL), with speculation over his participation gaining momentum on social media.

According to information obtained from an Australian source, Warner’s arrival in Nepal for the NPL is almost certain. However, it has not yet been officially confirmed which franchise he will represent.

Social media speculation has linked the 39-year-old former Australian opener with Kathmandu Gorkhas.

Australian cricket page Seam Strike has also posted on Instagram claiming that Warner will play in the NPL. Warner himself has liked the post, further fuelling speculation about his participation.

If confirmed, Warner would become the biggest international name to feature in the NPL.

A T20 icon

Warner has enjoyed a highly successful international career with Australia, winning two ODI World Cups, a T20 World Cup and the World Test Championship.

He was part of Australia’s World Cup-winning teams in 2015 and 2023, won the T20 World Cup in 2021 and the World Test Championship in 2023.

Warner is also among the few Australian players to have scored centuries in all three international formats.

He played 110 T20 internationals for Australia, scoring more than 3,200 runs, including one century.

His record in franchise cricket is even more extensive. Warner has played 439 T20 matches, scoring more than 14,000 runs, including 10 centuries and 118 fifties.

He has featured in some of the world’s biggest T20 leagues, including the Indian Premier League (IPL), Australia’s Big Bash League (BBL), Pakistan Super League (PSL), The Hundred in England, Major League Cricket in the United States, Bangladesh Premier League (BPL), Caribbean Premier League (CPL) and Vitality Blast.

An official announcement from the NPL franchise and the league regarding Warner’s participation is still awaited.

title.rendered: Nepal beat UAE to win Premier Cup, qualify for Asia Cup

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 12

Nepal defeated the United Arab Emirates by 44 runs in the ACC Premier Cup final on Saturday to lift the title and secure qualification for the Asia Cup.

Chasing a target of 314 at the Bayuemas Oval in Malaysia, the UAE were bowled out for 269 in 49.1 overs despite an unbeaten century from Rahul Chopra.

Chopra remained unbeaten after scoring a century, while Tanish Suri made 42 and captain Harpreet Bhatia contributed 33. But the UAE could not sustain their chase against a disciplined Nepal bowling attack.

Karan KC was Nepal’s leading bowler with three wickets. Lalit Rajbanshi took two, while captain Sandeep Lamichhane, Rohit Paudel, Gulshan Jha, Basir Ahmad and Dipendra Singh Airee took one wicket each.

Aasif leads Nepal’s strong total

Earlier, Nepal posted 313 for nine after winning the toss and electing to bat.

Aasif Sheikh was the foundation of Nepal’s innings, scoring 102 from 106 balls with eight fours and four sixes. It was his second ODI century.

He put Nepal in control with a 97-run opening partnership with Arjun Kumal, who scored 43. Aasif then added 36 with Ishan Pandey before combining with captain Rohit Paudel for a 68-run third-wicket partnership.

Rohit scored 40, while Gulshan provided the late acceleration with 52 from just 38 balls, hitting three fours and four sixes.

For the UAE, Ibrar Ahmed took four wickets, while Khuzama Bin Tanvir claimed two. Haider Ali and Adib Usmani took one wicket each.

The victory also gives Nepal another significant result against the UAE in the Premier Cup. Nepal had defeated the UAE in the final of the 2023 edition as well.

title.rendered: International translation workshop begins at Kathmandu University

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 12

A three-day international literary translation workshop, ‘Literary Translation Workshop’, has begun at Kathmandu University, Dhulikhel campus, jointly organised by the Department of Languages and Mass Communication and South Asian Literature in Translation (SALT) at the University of Chicago, from September 11, 2026.

The intensive workshop focusing on the craft of translating literary prose from Nepali, Maithili, Tibetan and Nepal Bhasa includes twenty-five participants.

This workshop brings writers and translators to impart insights on literary translations to a new cohort of literary translators from Nepal.  

Jason Grunebaum, Daniel Hahn, and the Booker Prize-winning Daisy Rockwell and Deepa Bhasthi are among the translators mentoring the workshop. Rockwell received the 2022 International Booker Prize for her translation of Geetanjali Shree’s Tomb of Sand. Her translation was the first work originally written in Hindi to win the award. Bhasthi, the first Indian translator to win the International Booker Prize, received the honour in 2025 for her translation of Banu Mushtaq’s Heart Lamp.

Grunebaum, co-director of the SALT Project, has translated works like The Girl with the Golden Parasol and The Walls of Delhi. He is an Instructional Professor of South Asian Languages and Civilisations and Creative Writing at the University of Chicago. Hahn was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 2020 for services to literature, and is known for translating works by Pelé and José Saramago. He is also a co-director of SALT.

The SALT programme attempts to bring the rich literature from the South Asian region to the Anglophone markets. “One of the greatest successes of SALT so far is that we’re attending to every link in the system that you need for a book to start in a South Asian language and end up on the bookshelves in the Western Anglosphere,” Grunebaum said about the project.

“To have their literary pieces reviewed by mentors holding such a revered portfolio is a delightful opportunity for the new generation of Nepali translators wishing to hone their craft,” Dinesh Kafle, assistant professor at Kathmandu University and a member of the organising team, said.

The program will also include a publishers’ roundtable, editing workshop and a public reading session featuring the participants and the award-winning mentors along with James Tookey, co-director of Peirene Press, and Snigdha Koirala, editor at Faber. The event will be hosted at Yala Maya Kendra, Patan, on September 13.

title.rendered: Why Yatri and Sipradi joined hands to build a two-wheeler in Nepal

content.rendered:
Nepal’s automobile market has long been driven by imports. In the two-wheeler segment, Indian and Chinese brands have a particularly strong presence, with local companies largely involved in distribution and sales rather than designing and developing vehicles themselves.

The shift towards electric mobility, however, is creating some room for a different approach.

That is where the partnership between Nepali electric motorcycle maker Yatri and Sipradi Trading comes in.

The two companies have joined hands to develop and manufacture the Yatri P-2, an electric scooter designed and engineered in Nepal. For Sipradi, the project marks its entry into the two-wheeler market. For Yatri, it is an opportunity to take its experience in vehicle design and engineering into a new product and work with one of Nepal’s established automobile companies.

But the partnership did not begin simply with the idea of launching another electric scooter.

Sipradi had been looking to enter the two-wheeler market for some time. The company, which has been involved in Nepal’s automobile sector for more than four decades, had a presence across several parts of the automotive business but did not have a two-wheeler product.

The question was what kind of product it should bring to the market.

Rather than adding another imported brand to its portfolio, Sipradi decided to look at electric two-wheelers and, eventually, at the possibility of developing one in Nepal.

“We wanted to come into two-wheelers with a product that could contribute to the country,” Sipradi CEO Rajan Babu Shrestha said.

The decision was also influenced by the changing automobile market. Electric mobility was gaining momentum globally, while Nepal was increasingly moving towards electric vehicles. But there was another consideration.

Many electric two-wheelers available in Nepal were developed for markets outside the country. Sipradi believed there was an opportunity to develop a product with Nepal’s roads and riding conditions specifically in mind. That search led the company to Yatri.

Bringing two different strengths together

Yatri had already spent years building its identity around vehicle design and engineering. The company had developed electric motorcycles and built experience in areas ranging from vehicle architecture and software to battery systems and testing.

Sipradi brought a different set of strengths: decades of experience in the Nepali automobile market, distribution and service infrastructure, and an understanding of the local customer and market.

The two companies began working together, eventually agreeing to develop an electric scooter. The collaboration was important because neither company alone brought everything required for the project.

Yatri had the engineering and product-development experience. Sipradi had the scale, market knowledge and automotive business experience.

Together, they could attempt something that neither had previously done at this scale: develop a two-wheeler in Nepal and take it to the market.

The result was the P-2.

It starts with design, not assembly

Developing the scooter took more than two years.

The process began with design sketches before moving into computer simulations, component development, electrical testing, battery testing, chassis fabrication, assembly and road testing.

Yatri engineers simulated components such as the chassis and swingarm to understand how they would behave under stress and on rough roads. Physical components were then produced and tested, with data from road testing compared against the simulation results.

The electrical system was developed alongside the mechanical components. Yatri engineers designed the vehicle’s electrical architecture and developed a wiring harness containing more than 150 wires.

The company also developed the vehicle control unit, or VCU, which controls a range of functions within the scooter. The VCU board is manufactured in China but is programmed, tested and validated by Yatri engineers in Nepal.

The same approach can be seen across the scooter.

Not every component is manufactured in Nepal. Several technologically advanced components, including the motor and controller, are sourced from China. The batteries are currently assembled in Nepal using imported components under a semi-knocked-down model.

This is an important distinction when describing the P-2 as a Nepali-made vehicle.

It is not a scooter in which every component is produced domestically. Instead, its design, engineering, specifications, software, system development, testing and parts of its manufacturing process are being carried out in Nepal.

For an industry that has traditionally depended heavily on imported finished vehicles, that is still a significant change.

Why a two-wheeler?

There is a practical reason the project focused on two-wheelers.

Motorcycles and scooters are among the most widely used vehicles in Nepal. They are relatively affordable, easier to operate in congested cities and important for everyday transportation.

That makes the segment a useful starting point for local electric vehicle development.

It also gives companies like Yatri an opportunity to develop and test technology at a scale that is more achievable than trying to manufacture passenger cars from scratch.

The P-2 is available with three battery options—5.2 kWh, 3.7 kWh and 3 kWh—with the largest battery offering a claimed range of up to 157 kilometres.

Yatri has also been developing charging infrastructure alongside the scooter. The company says it has installed more than 20 charging stations across different parts of the country and is gradually expanding the network.

These are not just features intended to sell the scooter. They are also part of the practical challenge of making electric two-wheelers usable across Nepal.

What does it mean for Nepal’s automobile industry?

The significance of the Yatri-Sipradi partnership goes beyond the P-2 itself.

Nepal is still far from having a fully developed automobile manufacturing ecosystem. A large number of components have to be imported, and companies remain dependent on suppliers in countries such as China and India.

Manufacturing costs are also a challenge. Imported brands benefit from much larger production volumes and established supply chains, making it difficult for a relatively small Nepali manufacturer to compete on price.

There are regulatory challenges as well.

Developing a new vehicle locally can involve approval and certification processes that were not necessarily designed with locally developed vehicles in mind. Sipradi says these processes added time to the P-2 project.

But these are also the areas where the project could provide useful experience.

Developing a vehicle locally requires more than assembling parts. It requires engineers, testing systems, manufacturing processes, quality control and suppliers who can work to specific specifications.

The P-2 project is helping build some of that experience.

Yatri currently has production capacity of around 8,000 to 10,000 scooters a year and says it can increase capacity depending on demand. The company is also working towards greater local manufacturing, including plans to develop battery manufacturing infrastructure at Gajuri in Dhading.

That does not mean Nepal will soon stop importing automobile components or finished vehicles.

But it does provide a starting point.

A first step into a different kind of automobile industry

For Sipradi, the P-2 is the beginning of its two-wheeler business and its first major step into locally produced electric two-wheelers.

For Yatri, it is another stage in the company’s attempt to build vehicles in Nepal rather than simply sell into the Nepali market.

The partnership also reflects a broader change taking place in Nepal’s automobile industry.

The country is still heavily dependent on imported vehicles and components. But electric mobility is creating opportunities for local companies to participate in areas such as vehicle design, software, electronics, battery assembly and engineering.

The P-2 does not solve Nepal’s automobile manufacturing challenges. Nor is it completely independent of foreign supply chains.

What it does show is that a Nepali company can design and engineer a vehicle for local conditions, develop its systems, test it on Nepali roads and manufacture it locally with the support of an established automobile company.

The next question is how far that model can go.

If production volumes increase, more components can be localised and the supply chain around such vehicles develops, the impact could extend beyond one scooter.

For now, the P-2 is a relatively modest beginning.

But it is a beginning that puts design, engineering and manufacturing—not just importing and distributing vehicles—into the conversation about Nepal’s automobile industry.

title.rendered: Nepal’s flood recovery: What worked after the 2015 earthquake—and what didn’t

content.rendered:
In the aftermath of the devastating flash floods in Nepal on August 26, the immediate priority was to save lives and meet the urgent needs of victims. But the relief efforts must also begin laying the foundations for the future.

This requires a delicate balancing act. The early days after a disaster are crucial for ensuring a long-term recovery sets off in the right direction.

This means addressing challenging questions about how and where to rebuild homes, even while rescue efforts are ongoing and debris is being cleared. It also means ensuring aid agencies and policymakers are investing humanitarian funding in the right way and listening to communities.

After a 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck Nepal in 2015, killing nearly 9,000 people, I led a review of the recovery efforts of 15 of the largest international NGOs and their partners, which had received around US$100 million of funding from the United Kingdom’s Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) and the Canadian Humanitarian Coalition.

While that earthquake was very different to the recent flood catastrophe in terms of scale, spread and severity, there are still many lessons about what to do after a disaster – and what not to do.

Cash is important

Communities need cash after a disaster. Where markets are working, this money gives people greater control over what they need most. While this is derided by some as potentially wasteful (“What if they spend it on the wrong thing?”), the overwhelming evidence shows that it works.

In my review after the 2015 quake, I found the immediate transfers of cash to survivors by NGOs working with local banks was highly effective. These survivors were able to prioritise what to spend it on, such as medicine, food or rent.

Direct cash transfers was also at the top of the United Nations’ appeal to donors after the floods last month “to give families the dignity to buy essential goods while stimulating local economies”.

But one of the most important findings from our review is that all this money can’t just be allocated for short-term relief.

Several months after the 2015 earthquake, far too many NGO staff told me they were still operating in response mode, providing the basic necessities to victims. As one field worker said, “it is only about relief, there is nothing on development”, while a senior NGO manager said, “we’re still in delivery mode, the conversations [about the future] aren’t happening”.

Thinking about the future means supporting farmers to re-establish their livelihoods, for instance, or repairing water systems to ensure access to safe drinking water.

Big decisions on housing

Short-term temporary housing for victims can also be problematic, if not handled the right way. Shelter usually takes up much of the money spent in post-disaster recovery efforts. In 2015, this accounted for 55% of the funds provided by the DEC.

In my view, funds shouldn’t be spent on elaborate temporary shelters, which has unfortunately been a focus of too many misguided international design saviours following disasters. These types of projects should never be taken up by serious aid agencies or responsible governments.

If temporary shelters are needed, local materials and local skills work best. Permanent rebuilding as quickly as possible is the goal, especially for Nepalis now, given winter is arriving soon.

Our 2015 review found a mixed bag of housing responses. The best efforts involved training up local carpenters and masons to a proficient standard to build quality shelters quickly. In other cases, aid providers with little or no technical skills oversaw complex housing projects, with worse outcomes.

Where to rebuild is also important. Unlike the situation after the 2015 earthquake, where rebuilding tended to take place in the same location, riverside communities devastated by the floods in Nepal today may need to be rebuilt elsewhere, given further deluges from melting glaciers are a real possibility.

This will be a hard decision to make, given the strong connections many communities have to their villages and land. But these decisions need to be made very quickly, as temporary housing has a habit of becoming permanent.

Rebuilding also requires materials. After the 2015 earthquake, bureaucratic red tape and corruption hindered the recovery by delaying the arrival of much-needed supplies from overseas, such as corrugated iron sheets. Bribes were demanded at border crossings, for example, which slowed progress.

International NGOs and donors are well attuned to the risks of corruption following disasters and must resist the paying of bribes in Nepal today.

And when aid money is funnelled through government agencies, there is always misappropriation, even when auditing takes place.

This will undoubtedly be a concern during the flood recovery, given Nepal ranks 109 out of 181 countries in Transparency International’s annual perception of public sector corruption index.

Listening to communities

Finally, aid agencies need to listen to the people they seek to serve.

Affected communities need to be seen as agents of their own recovery – not the “helpless victims” that some newspaper headlines would have you believe.

In 2015, there were too many instances in which community engagement was limited due to speed or sacrificed because of needless donor contracting requirements.

One independent survey undertaken at the time asked residents if their particular problems were being addressed by aid agencies. A resounding three-quarters said “very little” or “not at all”.

Women, in particular, felt their specific needs weren’t being addressed – adequate shelter, financial support, health care, and clean water and sanitation.

The aid agencies on the ground in Nepal now will hopefully be undertaking needs assessments to tailor their support in the most effective manner. This must be a continuous process to make sure communities are heard.

David Sanderson, Professor and Inaugural Judith Neilson Chair in Architecture, UNSW

title.rendered: Licence Harayeko Manchhe: When the govt loses your licence, you pay the price

content.rendered:
I recently received a call from the hospital at midnight for an emergency surgical procedure. As a doctor and public health advocate, I know that every minute can matter when a patient needs urgent care.

But when I get on my bike in the middle of the night, I sometimes find myself worrying about something completely different. What will I say if the traffic police stop me and ask for my licence?

The reason is simple. My probationary driver’s licence (Licence number 01-10-01440401), issued on April 19, 2023, expired on April 18, 2024.

I had already done everything required to get a permanent licence. I completed the necessary process, submitted my application several years ago and paid the required fees to the Transport Management Office. As a citizen who had followed the rules, I expected my permanent licence to arrive soon after my probationary licence expired.

It didn’t.

As of September 2026, more than two years after my probationary licence expired, I still do not have my physical permanent licence.

Where did my licence go?

Frustrated, I approached officials at the District Transport Management Office in Tulsipur to find out what had happened. The answer was surprisingly casual. I was told that my licence was either missing or may have been destroyed in the fires during the September 2025 Gen Z protests.

That was when I realised this was bigger than my own missing licence.

Across Nepal, thousands of people have been left in a similar situation. They have paid for their licences, completed the required procedures and are now stuck between a government system that says their digital licence is valid and a system on the ground that often still demands a physical document.

Following the paper trail

After my probationary licence expired in 2024, I repeatedly contacted the District Transport Management Office in Tulsipur. I was given assurances that the matter would be resolved, but nothing happened.

Then came the September 2025 protests.

The Department of Transport Management’s central infrastructure in Kathmandu was damaged and set on fire. With the country’s main smart-licence printing facility affected, many licences that had already been printed but had not yet reached citizens were reportedly destroyed.

At that point, I gave up trying to chase my licence.

Recently, however, I decided to try one more time. I sent a formal complaint to the Department of Transport Management’s grievance-handling email address.

The response I received explained the government’s position. If a physical licence is unavailable, the government recognises the original bank revenue receipt together with the digital licence shown on the Nagarik App.

But there is a problem.

Once a licence has been marked as printed in the central system, it is treated as though the government has completed its part of the job. If that licence never reached the citizen, the system does not necessarily treat it as the government’s responsibility to replace it.

Instead, the citizen may have to apply for a duplicate licence through the provincial transport office, file a police report about the missing document and pay another fee.

In other words, even if the licence disappeared while it was still in the government’s hands, the citizen can end up being treated as though they lost it. That does not seem right.

A digital solution with a very real problem

The government’s response to the crisis has largely been digital.

The Nagarik App now allows drivers to display their licence digitally, and traffic police can verify the QR code through the relevant system.

This is useful. Digital services can make life much easier. But a digital licence cannot solve every problem.

In Kathmandu and other major cities, traffic police may be familiar with the system. But enforcement can be less consistent in districts, rural areas and at border points. Some drivers are still asked to show a physical licence.

For someone like me, who may have to travel long distances at short notice for work, that uncertainty is frustrating.

There is another problem too.

A digital licence that is accepted inside Nepal is not automatically accepted outside Nepal. If I need to prove my identity or driving credentials for an international process, an app on my phone may not be enough. A screenshot or an expired paper receipt certainly may not be accepted.

So the digital licence is helpful, but it is not a complete replacement for the physical document that citizens were promised.

Who is responsible?

This is where the problem becomes even more frustrating.

The Department of Transport Management controls the central database and the main printing system. Provincial transport offices, meanwhile, deal with many of the services citizens need at the local level.

When something goes wrong, the citizen is left moving between the two.

The federal system says the licence has already been printed. The provincial office says a replacement requires another process. And the citizen is left asking a very simple question.

If I paid for the licence and followed all the rules, why should I have to pay again because the government could not deliver it?

That is the real issue.

What should happen next?

The solution does not have to be complicated.

First, Nepal should have more decentralised licence-printing facilities. The country should not have to depend on a single central system to produce licences for citizens across all seven provinces.

Second, licences that were printed but destroyed before reaching citizens should be automatically reprinted. Citizens should not have to apply and pay again for something they never received.

Third, the government should make the legal status of the digital licence completely clear. Traffic police across the country should have the same instructions and the same system for verifying digital licences.

Most importantly, citizens should not have to figure out which level of government is responsible every time something goes wrong.

More than just a driver’s licence

My missing licence may seem like a small administrative problem. It isn’t. It is about whether a government can deliver a service after taking a citizen’s money and completing the required process.

The Nagarik App is an important step towards modernising public services. But digital technology should not become a substitute for fixing the systems behind it.

A government that can collect revenue from citizens within seconds should also be able to deliver the document they have paid for.

Until that happens, people like me will continue to face the same frustrating situation. We will carry an expired paper, show a digital licence on our phones, explain the situation to traffic police and hope that the next officer understands.

All because a licence that was supposed to reach us never did.

title.rendered: Two juveniles sent to child correction home in Garima Chaudhary murder case

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The Bara District Court has ordered two juveniles to be sent to a child correction home for trial in the abduction, rape and murder case of 12-year-old Garima Chaudhary of Simara, while releasing 10 other accused on bail.

A bench of Judge Prakash Kumar Adhikari issued the order on September 9, directing that the two juveniles be kept at a child correction home pending trial.

According to the court order, the decision was based on evidence including statements collected during the investigation, the post-mortem report, medical examination, DNA test and psychosocial counselling report.

The court said there were sufficient grounds to believe that the two juveniles could face punishment under the charges against them and ordered the case to proceed to trial.

The court has also ordered the concerned authorities to provide Rs 200,000 in interim compensation to the victim’s family from the Victim Relief Fund.

10 other accused released

On Thursday, the same court ordered 10 other defendants in the case to be released while proceedings continue.

Progresh (Purgesh) Chaudhary of Jitpur Simara Sub-Metropolitan City-1 was released on Rs 20,000 bail, while the other nine were released on general date.

Those released on general date include Progresh’s father Indrajit, mother Babita, wife Pushpa, sister Mamata, as well as Sabita Chaudhary, Bindu Chaudhary, Tek Bahadur Thapamagar, Nabin BK and Shesh Hasuddin.

The court said it did not find sufficient evidence establishing their involvement in the crime.

Police had filed charges against the accused based on a complaint lodged by Garima’s father, Manoj Chaudhary, accusing them of abduction, unlawful confinement, rape and murder.

Garima Chaudhary disappeared while playing

Garima Chaudhary went missing on August 16 after going to play at the house of Progresh Chaudhary in Jitpur Simara-1.

Her body was found two days later, on August 18, at a house in Bhaktinagar.

The case triggered widespread public outrage, with demands for severe punishment for those responsible. Following a three-point agreement with the government on August 23, Garima’s family received her body.

The family had named 12 people, including the two juveniles, as defendants in the case.

title.rendered: Supreme Court petition seeks action against ‘Green Army’ over military-style uniforms

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

A writ petition has been filed at the Supreme Court seeking action against Green Army Nepal, an organisation involved in rescue and relief operations following the Rasuwa floods, for allegedly using uniforms, ranks and insignia resembling those of the Nepali Army.

The petition, filed on Friday by advocates Sambharaj Aryal, Purna Bahadur Saud, Govind Ram Pariyar and Bishnuvar Singh Thapa, seeks cancellation of the organisation’s registration and an order preventing it from using military-style structures, uniforms, ranks and insignia.

The petitioners have named the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of Defence, Nepali Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, Social Welfare Council, Kathmandu District Administration Office, Gokarneshwar Municipality and the Office of the Company Registrar as defendants.

The first hearing of the petition has been scheduled for Monday.

Petition challenges ‘Green Army’ structure

According to the petition, Green Army Nepal is registered with the Office of the Company Registrar as a non-governmental organisation working in areas including environmental protection, youth leadership, social service and disaster management.

However, the petitioners argue that the organisation cannot be treated as an ordinary NGO because it presents itself as a “military-inspired” youth organisation.

They claim the organisation has divided its members into military-style ranks such as cadet, brigadier, marshal and chief marshal, while also using titles such as “Chief Marshal/Chairperson” and “Cadet” on its website.

The petition further alleges that the organisation uses the word “Army” and operates with military-style uniforms, ranks, insignia, boots and radio sets.

The petitioners say such practices could create the impression among members of the public that Green Army Nepal is affiliated with the Nepali Army or another state security agency.

Rasuwa flood response brings issue into focus

The petition specifically points to the organisation’s involvement in rescue and relief operations following the Rasuwa Gadhi disaster.

The petitioners said images and footage of Green Army members wearing uniforms and rank insignia similar to those used by the Nepali Army while carrying out rescue and relief operations had been publicly circulated through the media.

They argue that the incident has raised serious questions about the boundary between civilian organisations and the country’s security institutions.

According to the petition, allowing a non-governmental organisation to adopt a military-style identity could confuse the public and undermine the distinct institutional identity of Nepal’s security agencies.

The petitioners have also raised concerns over national security, civilian identification and the constitutional role of state security institutions.

Government approvals also challenged

The petition questions permissions and approvals allegedly granted to Green Army Nepal by government agencies for the use of its uniforms.

According to the petitioners, the Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of Defence and Kathmandu District Administration Office had provided permission or consent regarding the organisation’s uniforms.

They claim that although the Defence Ministry had given a favourable opinion on the grounds that the proposed uniform was different from those used by the Nepali Army and other security agencies, the organisation’s actual uniform, military-style structure and ranks could still create confusion among the public.

The petitioners have asked the Supreme Court to annul such government decisions, opinions and approvals if they are found to conflict with the Constitution and existing laws.

They have also challenged the registration and renewal of Green Army Nepal by the Office of the Company Registrar, arguing that its name, objectives and activities should have been subjected to greater scrutiny under the Company Act.

The petition seeks broader legal and administrative standards to ensure that no non-governmental organisation or local government body can use uniforms, insignia or military titles resembling those of Nepal’s security agencies.

title.rendered: UML weighs Parliament restoration amid public pressure

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The CPN-UML is preparing to formally discuss the possibility of restoring the dissolved House of Representatives, with party Secretary Mahesh Basnet saying growing public pressure and a case pending at the Supreme Court are creating an environment for Parliament to return.

Basnet said the issue would be placed on the agenda of the party’s upcoming Central Committee meeting following growing dissatisfaction with the current government and what he described as public demand to reverse the political course taken through the election.

Speaking to reporters on Friday after a meeting of the UML’s election review and party reorganisation task force, Basnet said the party sees a possibility of Parliament being restored through a combination of public pressure and the Supreme Court proceedings.

“An environment is developing for the restoration of Parliament through the strength of the people’s movement and the case under consideration at the Supreme Court,” Basnet said.

He argued that such a development could also provide an opportunity to correct what he called wrong practices adopted during the election.

Basnet claimed that public frustration with the government had intensified even though it has not yet completed six months in office.

“People have reached a state of mind where they want to take back their mandate,” he said, referring to what he described as growing dissatisfaction with the government’s actions.

He also alleged that international forces had used social media and algorithms to create confusion among younger generations and influence the formation of the current government.

According to Basnet, people have begun questioning the choice they made in the election after observing the activities of both the interim government led by former Chief Justice Sushila Karki and the current government.

UML to discuss the issue formally

Basnet’s remarks indicate that Parliament restoration could become a significant political issue for the UML as the party reviews its electoral defeat and reassesses its strategy amid changing political circumstances.

He said the party’s election review and reorganisation task force was not formed to remove UML Chairman KP Sharma Oli, dismissing reports to that effect as “misinformation.”

The task force, he said, has been assigned to conduct a rigorous review of the election, determine how the party should move forward under changing political circumstances and prepare a framework for necessary organisational restructuring.

Basnet said the UML would also seek to address its internal weaknesses, counter misconceptions among the public and maintain regular interaction with citizens.

He added that the party would seek to strengthen itself by focusing on social justice and social service.

title.rendered: Pressure builds on KP Sharma Oli as UML grassroots call for leadership change

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Pressure is mounting on CPN-UML Chairman KP Sharma Oli to step aside and make way for a new generation of leaders, with party cadres and organisational units across the country calling for leadership change as part of the party’s post-election review.

Recommendations collected by a UML task force show that most of the party’s provincial committees and affiliated bodies believe the party cannot continue in its current form and that its top leadership must take responsibility for the party’s electoral defeat.

The recommendations have been compiled in an annex to a report prepared by UML General Secretary Shankar Pokharel, who is the member-secretary of the task force reviewing the party’s performance and proposing its reorganisation.

Of the 13 bodies that submitted recommendations, only Madhesh Province, the Contact Coordination Committee and the party’s sister organisations stopped short of calling for a change in the leadership.

Most of the remaining bodies have either explicitly called on Oli to leave the chair or urged the existing leadership to make way for a generational transition.

The calls are particularly significant because they extend beyond Oli’s political opponents within the party. Even Koshi Province, his home province, has recommended that the leadership accept moral responsibility for the election defeat and be prepared to step aside.

“Leaders who have lost public support and failed should not run the party,” the Karnali Province committee said, urging leaders at all levels to be prepared to make sacrifices.

Calls for an orderly exit

Lumbini Province was more explicit, urging Oli to relinquish the party leadership and assume a guardian or patron role.

“Chairman KP Sharma Oli should put the party’s long-term future ahead of his personal position, pave the way for the new generation and remain in a guardian or patron role,” its recommendation said.

Lumbini has also proposed dissolving party committees from the centre down to the local level and forming convention organising committees, with new leadership to be elected within six months.

Gandaki Province called for a special general convention to facilitate a dignified leadership transition.

“Established party leaders or the chair should resign on moral grounds or pave the way through generational transfer,” the province said.

Karnali called on Oli to choose a “respectable exit”, arguing that the principal leadership should bear responsibility for what it described as an unexpected electoral defeat.

Sudurpaschim Province similarly said the party’s principal leadership should take responsibility and create an environment for a smooth transfer of power.

The call for change has also come from the UML’s central advisory bodies, commissions, departments and overseas organisations. The advisers have urged the party’s principal leadership to leave office with dignity in the interest of the party’s future.

Overseas chapters and commissions have called for capable and clean-image leaders from the second, third and fourth generations, including young leaders and women, to be brought to the forefront.

Bagmati offers only significant defence of Oli

Bagmati Province stands out as the only provincial committee to have submitted a mixed position on Oli.

Its recommendations include both calls for Oli to leave immediately and arguments against removing him.

The province argued that responsibility for the election defeat should not be placed solely on the party chair.

“Responsibility for the defeat should be taken collectively by the Secretariat, central leadership, provinces, districts, elected representatives and all levels of the party,” the recommendation said.

It also argued that a leadership elected by more than two-thirds of the party’s general convention should not be removed in violation of the party’s statute.

However, the same set of recommendations also states that Oli should be removed through due process if he does not voluntarily announce his departure.

The mixed position comes from Bagmati, where UML leader Mahesh Basnet, considered close to Oli, is the party’s in-charge.

Leadership model under scrutiny

The debate over Oli’s future is closely linked to wider criticism of the UML’s increasingly centralised decision-making structure.

The Kathmandu Valley committee argued that excessive concentration of power around the party chair had weakened collective decision-making within the UML.

It criticised changes made at the party’s second statute convention, saying they had created a structure in which lower levels were unable to act without the chair’s consultation or direction.

The recommendation went as far as comparing the organisational model to a “traditional Soviet-style” system and warned that excessive concentration of power could create risks of organisational fragmentation.

Another issue raised by several party units is the removal of the 70-year age limit and two-term limit for party positions.

The Kathmandu committee recommended restoring both provisions and enforcing them at every level.

The recommendations also criticised what Lumbini described as an “army-style” mode of party operation, in which collective leadership had been weakened and decisions were increasingly imposed from the top.

The task force is now set to deliberate on the recommendations as the UML weighs both the reasons behind its electoral defeat and a broader restructuring of the party—putting Oli’s leadership at the centre of an increasingly consequential internal debate.

title.rendered: Government investigates 25 agencies over Malaysia job recruitment, seeks explanation from 250 others

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The government has launched an investigation into the process of allowing only a limited number of recruitment agencies to send Nepali workers to Malaysia amid controversy over a list of 25 agencies selected for the job recruitment process.

The Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment has directed the Department of Foreign Employment to investigate the 25 agencies, including their transactions from the time they were established and the basis on which they were granted permission to send workers to Malaysia.

Malaysia had earlier published a list of 25 Nepali recruitment agencies authorised to send workers to the country. Following widespread criticism, Nepal suspended the pre-approval and document verification processes for workers travelling to Malaysia.

During the suspension, Malaysia’s Foreign Worker Central Management System (FWCMS) listed another 250 Nepali recruitment agencies as sub-agents of the 25 agencies.

Following the ministry’s directive, the department is preparing to seek explanations from the 250 agencies over the basis for their inclusion in the Malaysian system. It also plans to ask the Nepali Embassy in Malaysia to suspend pre-approval and document attestation for Malaysia-bound workers before issuing the notices.

Department Director General Navaraj Dhakal said action was being initiated in accordance with the Constitution and existing laws.

“This is not only against the law but also against the Constitution. Since the arrangement obstructs free competition, we are studying the matter for action under the existing legal provisions,” Dhakal said.

The Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies said limiting Malaysia recruitment to a small number of agencies could create a syndicate in the sector. Association President Dik Bahadur Khatri said Nepal has around 1,100 recruitment agencies and questioned the basis for allowing only 25 to send workers to Malaysia.

Khatri said the arrangement could also affect workers travelling under the employer-pay principle, who he claimed account for around 25 to 30 per cent of Nepali workers going to Malaysia.

The government’s investigation will cover the reasons the 25 agencies were selected and their transactions related to Malaysia-bound recruitment.

title.rendered: Nepal, UAE renew fierce rivalry in high-stakes ACC Premier Cup final

content.rendered:
Kuala Lumpur, September 11

In Associate cricket, there are matches that decide a trophy, and then there are matches that seem to carry the weight of an entire cricketing future. Nepal and the United Arab Emirates have become accustomed to the latter.

They have met in World Cup qualifiers, in Premier Cup knockouts and in matches where one team’s ambitions have ended with the other’s victory. The rivalry has acquired its own history: Nepal winning when UAE needed to advance, UAE responding when Nepal seemed poised to do the same.

On Saturday, they will meet again.

The occasion is the final of the ACC Men’s Premier Cup. The prize is the title. But the more consequential reward awaits beyond it: a place at the 2027 Asia Cup.

For Nepal, it would be another step into a competition they have appeared in only once before. For UAE, it would represent something new — their first qualification for the 50-over Asia Cup.

A rivalry without much room for sentiment

Nepal and UAE have spent the past several years interrupting each other’s plans.

In the 2022 T20 World Cup Qualifier, UAE defeated Nepal in a semi-final and left them outside the World Cup. Two years later, Nepal had their answer, beating UAE in the 2024 World Cup Qualifier to secure their own passage to the tournament.

Then came the Premier Cup.

When Nepal hosted the inaugural edition in 2023, the final ended with Nepal beating UAE and earning an Asia Cup place. In 2025, the balance shifted again. UAE defeated Nepal in the semi-final, and Nepal subsequently lost the third-place playoff to Hong Kong, missing the Asia Cup.

Neither team needs reminding of what the other is capable of taking away.

Their overall record is relatively close, too, though Nepal hold the advantage in ODIs, with 11 wins from 19 meetings. Yet statistics have never quite captured the character of this rivalry. Too many of their most important games have arrived at precisely the moment when a number on a scorecard matters least.

What matters is what it unlocks.

Nepal have the bowlers. They need the runs.

Nepal enter the final with a record that is impressive but slightly deceptive.

They have won four of their five matches in the tournament. Their only defeat came against Hong Kong in the group stage. In the semi-final against Oman, their batting produced only 147. And yet Nepal won.

Their bowlers turned a small total into a winning one, an outcome that said something encouraging about their attack but also exposed the narrow margin for error that awaits them against UAE.

There may not be another 147 to defend.

Nepal’s batting will therefore be under particular scrutiny. Aasif Sheikh’s start, Rohit Paudel’s ability to anchor an innings and Dipendra Singh Airee’s capacity to change the tempo could determine how competitive Nepal’s total becomes.

Airee, especially, has a history against UAE. He has been one of the players Nepal have turned to when these encounters have become less about accumulation and more about survival.

The younger Ishan Pandey could also be important if Nepal give him another opportunity near the top of the order.

UAE have arrived without a stumble

UAE have taken a simpler route to the final. They have won all five of their matches.

There has been no group-stage setback to recover from, no nervous semi-final to escape. They have simply kept winning, which gives them something Nepal do not have entering Saturday’s match: the quiet confidence of an unbeaten tournament.

Their batting has been built around players such as Adib Usmani and Harpreet Bhatia. With the ball, Ayan Afzal Khan and Haider Ali have offered the kind of control that can make an innings feel shorter than it actually is.

And then there are the conditions.

Bayuemas Cricket Oval can offer assistance to spin, something Nepal exploited against Oman. If the pitch again slows and grips, Sandeep Lamichhane could become central to Nepal’s plans, with Lalit Rajbanshi and Sher Malla offering further spin options.

But conditions can also change the calculation. A pitch that rewards patience may suit UAE’s consistency. One that offers early movement could give Nepal’s bowlers the opening they need.

The familiar ground, the unfamiliar prize

There is another layer to the final. Nepal have already beaten UAE twice in their most recent League 2 meetings in Kirtipur. But the last time these teams met in Malaysia, in 2018, UAE won.

The setting, then, offers no obvious advantage. Neither does the past. What remains is the opportunity.

Nepal are trying to return to the Asia Cup. UAE are trying to reach it for the first time in the 50-over format. Between them is a trophy, but more importantly, a door.

For one team, Saturday will confirm a place among Asia’s established cricketing nations. For the other, it will mean another season of wondering how close it came.

That is why this rivalry has endured.

Nepal and UAE do not need to dislike each other for their matches to feel personal. The stakes have done that work for them.

And on Saturday, once again, one of them will leave the field with a future that looks considerably brighter than it did that morning.

title.rendered: Government to reclaim land identified as encroached by Rawal Commission 31 years ago

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation and the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration have decided to register in the name of the Government of Nepal all government and public land identified as encroached upon by the Rawal Commission in its 2052 BS report.

A committee formed by the ministry to implement the report had submitted its recommendations. Based on the report, the ministry decided to collectively deduct the areas identified as having been encroached upon from the concerned land parcels and register them in the name of the Government of Nepal.

The ministry also decided to collectively register in the government’s name the land parcels whose entire area was identified in the report as government or public land.

The implementation committee is coordinated by Chief Survey Officer Ramesh Gyawali. Its members include an undersecretary from the Ministry of Home Affairs, an undersecretary from the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, the chiefs of the Land Administration Office and Survey Office in Dillibazar, the chief of the Local Level Coordination Section, a section officer from the Department of Land Management and Archives, and a survey officer from the Department of Survey, who serves as the member secretary.

title.rendered: Balen Shah to address UN General Assembly on Sept 24

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, September 24

Prime Minister Balen Shah is scheduled to address the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly on September 24.

Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai announced the prime minister’s speaking schedule during a regular press briefing on Friday.

“The high-level general debate of the 81st UN General Assembly will be held from September 22 to 28 at the UN headquarters in New York,” Rai said. “The Right Honourable Prime Minister is scheduled to address the General Debate on September 24.”

According to Rai, the UN has informed Nepal that heads of state from 81 countries and heads of government from 50 countries will attend the General Assembly.

He said the General Assembly would provide Nepal with an important opportunity to present the Gen Z movement that took place in Nepal last year, the successful election that followed, and the priorities of the current government formed with a strong popular mandate. Nepal will also call for continued and increased international support and goodwill.

Rai said Prime Minister Shah is expected to draw international attention to the significant loss of lives and property Nepal has repeatedly suffered from climate change and climate-induced disasters.

He said Nepal would also highlight that despite making a negligible contribution to global carbon emissions, the country continues to face severe impacts of climate change.

Shah is scheduled to call on the international community to ensure climate justice. Rai said Nepal would also highlight its contribution to global environmental protection through its nature-friendly lifestyle, more than 46 per cent forest cover, vast Himalayan region and extensive river systems.

Nepal will also host a high-level side event during the General Assembly, according to Rai. The event will focus on the adverse impacts of global climate change on the Himalayan region and the devastating consequences it has caused, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal is scheduled to attend ministerial-level meetings of least developed countries, landlocked developing countries, non-aligned countries and G7, China and other groups.

Khanal will also address other high-level discussions and side events organised by the UN and hold meetings with counterparts from neighbouring and other countries, as well as senior UN officials, Rai said.

title.rendered: Sanjay Sah, rescued from Trishuli 3A tunnel, discharged

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Sanjay Sah, who was trapped inside a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project for 10 days following the Rasuwa Bhotekoshi flood on August 26, has been discharged from the hospital.

Sah was rescued on the 10th day after being trapped inside the tunnel and was admitted to Birendra Army Hospital in Chhauni for treatment.

Nepal Army spokesperson and Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet said Sah was discharged on Friday after recovering from his injuries. He returned home after spending seven days in the hospital.

Sah was rescued safely by a joint team comprising the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police and technical experts. He is a mechanical foreman at the project.

Another person trapped inside the tunnel was also rescued along with Sah. Both were airlifted to Kathmandu by helicopter.

title.rendered: Apple’s Hollywood film Tenzing to be screened to help flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Tenzing, a film directed by Jennifer Peedom telling the story of the first successful ascent of Everest, is set to premiere as the opening film of the 22nd Zurich Film Festival.

Shot at various scenic locations across Nepal, the film stars Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Genden Puntsok. According to Variety, the film will screen on September 24.

Produced by Apple Original Films, the movie’s European premiere will see Hiddleston, Dafoe and director Peedom walk Zurich’s green carpet. The film follows the story of the first successful ascent of Mount Everest.

Festival CEO Christian Jungen said this year’s festival theme is Dream Big, calling Tenzing a fitting opening film for it.

“This year’s Zurich Film Festival theme is ‘Dream Big.’ Our thrilling opening film ‘Tenzing’ matches it perfectly, because it shows how, when the dream is big enough, people can rise above their own limits,” he said.

Based on true events, Tenzing tells the story of Tenzing Norgay (played by Genden Puntsok), who, together with New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary, achieved the first successful ascent of Everest in 1953.

The 22nd Zurich Film Festival will run from September 24 to October 4.

Meanwhile, the British Embassy in Kathmandu is organising a special screening of Tenzing in Kathmandu to raise funds for those affected by the Bhotekoshi floods. According to the embassy, proceeds from the screening will go to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

content.rendered:
Photos: NAFA

Kathmandu, September 11

An art exhibition featuring the works and stories of Binod Maharjan, a martyr of the Gen Z movement, and photojournalist Dipendra Dhungana has opened at the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA) in Naxal, Kathmandu.

Titled ‘Pratidhwani’, the exhibition was inaugurated on September 9 and will run through September 13.

According to a press statement, the exhibition brings together photographs captured by Dhungana before he was injured while covering the Gen Z protest in New Baneshwor on September 8, 2025. Dhungana, a senior photojournalist with Naya Patrika Daily, was struck near the neck by a rubber bullet while covering the violent demonstration.

The exhibition presents his photographs alongside news materials documenting the aftermath, tracing his experience from witnessing the protest as a journalist to becoming part of the event he was covering.

It also commemorates Maharjan, a versatile artist from Patan who was killed by gunfire while participating in the Gen Z movement.

Maharjan was skilled in sculpture, woodcraft, metalwork, painting and traditional arts. He had worked since 2013 as a specialist in facial detailing and finishing metal statues and had also practised gold and silver electroplating.

The exhibition presents the two individuals’ experiences as a visual record of the movement, highlighting both artistic expression and the personal costs of witnessing and participating in a historic event.
