title.rendered: Rabi Lamichhane was unaware of new minister’s appointment

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane was aware that Prime Minister Balen Shah was dissatisfied with outgoing Industry Minister Gauri Kumari Yadav, but he was not informed that the Prime Minister was preparing to remove her and appoint Deepak Sah as her replacement.

Yadav had previously become a minister from Lamichhane’s quota. Lamichhane has taken note of the fact that he was not consulted when she was removed and a new minister was appointed on Thursday.

Sources at both the Prime Minister’s Office and the RSP confirmed that Lamichhane was not informed about Sah’s appointment until shortly before the swearing-in ceremony.

An RSP source said Lamichhane had no objection to the prime minister’s authority to appoint or remove ministers, but argued that keeping the party chairperson uninformed about such an important decision was not appropriate.

The Prime Minister’s Office said Lamichhane had previously been informed about concerns over Yadav’s performance and had agreed that she should be removed following recent developments.

The office said Yadav had failed to adequately address the impact of the gas and petroleum crisis caused by the US-Iran war in West Asia, which also affected Nepal.

Sources close to Shah said efforts had been made to improve Yadav’s performance, including administrative changes, but her performance did not improve. They said her recent public remarks further prompted the decision to remove her.

The developments have also exposed growing differences over the balance of power between Lamichhane, the RSP chairperson, and Prime Minister Shah.

RSP leaders said Lamichhane had expected to be consulted on the appointment and was prepared to recommend Parliamentary Party Deputy Leader Ganesh Parajuli. However, the ministry that had been allocated to Lamichhane’s quota has ultimately remained with the Shah camp.

title.rendered: Don’t relocate flood-affected children without permission: Minister Badi

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Minister for Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, and Social Security Sita Badi has cautioned against relocating children from flood-affected areas without proper authorisation.

Speaking at Friday’s meeting of the House of Representatives’ Women and Social Affairs Committee, Minister Badi urged organisations to transfer children only through coordination with local child welfare officers and the recommendation of the National Child Rights Council, noting that children are at heightened risk of trafficking in such situations.

“Taking children from one place to another under the pretext of enrolling them in school or arranging other support carries a risk of trafficking,” Badi told the committee. “I therefore urge that no child be taken anywhere without coordination and recommendation from the local level and the Child Rights Council. We have seen many such incidents in the past.”

120 children without guardians

According to Minister Badi, 120 children currently without guardians are staying at holding centres in flood-affected areas. Initial assessment, protection, and efforts to trace their guardians are underway.

She said work was being expedited to set up a temporary protection centre under the National Child Rights Council at a government building in Khetso, Godawari Municipality-12, Lalitpur, to shelter these children.

She made clear that the government would prioritise reuniting children with their families wherever possible, and would take full responsibility for any child whose family could not be found or whose relatives were unable to care for them.

Checkpoints set up at sensitive border points

The ministry said surveillance has been stepped up at various points in coordination with Nepal Police to prevent human trafficking and gender-based violence that could occur during the disaster.

According to Minister Badi, special checkpoints have been established at sensitive locations, including Belkot, Galchhi checkpoint, Shivapuri, and Kajuri Bhanjyang, to ensure the safe transit of women and children.

Cyber Bureau to act against misuse of victims’ photos and videos

Minister Badi urged that victims’ suffering not be turned into cheap publicity on social media under the guise of relief and rescue efforts.

Emphasising the need to respect the dignity, privacy, and rights of flood-affected citizens, she said the ministry was coordinating with Nepal Police’s Cyber Bureau to prevent the unauthorised use of children’s photos and videos.

Single-window policy for relief coordination

Minister Badi said the government has implemented a single-window policy for disaster management and relief distribution, with coordination among the Social Welfare Council, the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, local levels, district administration, and security agencies.

According to ministry data, non-governmental support received for flood victims so far includes:

  • From international NGOs (54 organisations): relief assistance worth Rs 40,64,44,900
  • From national NGOs (30 organisations): relief assistance worth Rs 16,82,15,101
  • Additional deposits to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund from national and international NGOs: Rs 5,99,32,169

Minister Badi also informed the committee that, immediately after the floods, the ministry had convened a meeting of the “Protection Cluster” to activate mechanisms for child protection, response to gender-based violence, and psychosocial support.

title.rendered: Veel donates Rs 10 million to PM’s Disaster Relief Fund for flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

AI-Powered global video marketing platform Veel has donated Rs. 10 million to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support relief and rehabilitation efforts for communities affected by the recent floods in Nepal.

The contribution is intended to support the immediate needs of floodaffected families and communities, including access to essential supplies, emergency assistance, and other forms of relief. It will also contribute to ongoing recovery and rehabilitation efforts as affected communities work to rebuild and return to normalcy.

Veel expressed its condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and extended its solidarity to everyone affected by the floods. The company also recognized the efforts of government agencies, security personnel, volunteers, local communities, and other responders working on rescue, relief, and recovery efforts across affected areas.

Veel’s CEO and Founder Dileep Dhakal, also emphasized the importance of standing together and supporting those affected during this difficult time.

“During times like these, it is important for all of us to stand together and support the communities that need it most. We will also continue to look for meaningful ways, even in small ways, where we can make a positive impact and support those who need it most. In difficult moments like these, standing together and supporting one another matters,” the company said.

Veel also encouraged individuals, businesses, and organizations that are in a position to help to contribute to relief and recovery efforts and support communities affected by the disaster.

title.rendered: NCP calls for all-party parliamentary committee on post-disaster response

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The Nepal Communist Party (NCP) has called for the formation of an all-party parliamentary special committee to work on post-disaster issues, as proposed by Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane.

Speaking during a meeting of the House of Representatives, NCP leader Barshaman Pun said disaster management was not the responsibility of a single ministry, government or level of government.

He said a national mechanism should be formed by bringing together political parties, security agencies, experts, local communities and all other relevant stakeholders. Pun also called for an all-party parliamentary special committee based on Lamichhane’s proposal for addressing the situation following the disaster.

“I would like to express our party’s support for the proposal put forward by RSP Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane, who leads the government, to form an all-party parliamentary special committee to deal with this disaster,” Pun said.

He said the federal, provincial and local governments should work in effective coordination following the Rasuwa floods.

“The government could not coordinate and cooperate with the opposition parties, provincial governments and local governments to the extent required during such a major disaster,” he said.

What was Rabi’s proposal?

A day after the devastating floods on August 26, RSP Chairperson Lamichhane convened an all-party meeting attended by senior leaders from the RSP, Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, NCP, Shram Sanskriti Party, Rastriya Prajatantra Party, Janata Samajbadi Party and Janamat Party. The meeting adopted a 10-point resolution.

The 10th point called for the formation of a “high-level all-party mechanism” for long-term solutions.

The resolution said the parties had agreed to form a parliamentary committee to coordinate reconstruction after disasters, climate adaptation, timely reform of national disaster policies, and continuous consultation, support and monitoring of government activities.

It also said the mechanism would help build national consensus on disaster preparedness and sustainable development and play an important role in policy reform, not only during crises.

However, the proposed mechanism has yet to be formed.

Instead, a second all-party meeting was held on September 1, attended by second-tier leaders. The meeting agreed to coordinate with the government on relief, rescue and rehabilitation efforts.

Leaders said the meeting had paved the way for forming all-party mechanisms at the district and local levels. However, no such mechanism has been established at the central level.

Two options have been discussed for a central mechanism: forming a parliamentary committee or establishing a mechanism outside Parliament.

Against this backdrop, Pun raised the issue in the House, saying his party supports the proposal put forward by the chairperson of the ruling party.

title.rendered: Ministry takes Rajbiraj hospital incident seriously, Health Minister tells Parliament

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Minister for Health and Food Hygiene Nisha Mehta has said the government has taken seriously the incident in which a 30-year-old woman gave birth outside Gajendra Narayan Hospital in Rajbiraj, Saptari.

Responding to questions raised by lawmakers during a meeting of the House of Representatives, Minister Mehta said ensuring the safety of mothers and newborns, safe childbirth and quality healthcare remains a primary responsibility of the state.

“Since protecting the lives of mothers and newborns, ensuring safe childbirth and providing quality health services are the state’s primary responsibilities, the ministry has taken the Rajbiraj incident seriously,” she said.

Mehta said the government had taken serious note of the issues raised in Parliament. She said the ministry sought a 24-hour clarification from the hospital immediately after receiving information about the incident.

“The hospital has already submitted its clarification,” she said.

According to Mehta, a five-member team led by Nepal Medical Council Registrar Dr Suprabha Shrestha, along with Dr Ajay Shah from the council’s Ethics Committee, reached Rajbiraj on Thursday to conduct an on-site investigation into the incident.

Dr Pawan Jung Rayamajhi, chief of the Curative Services Division at the Department of Health Services, is also part of the team representing the ministry.

Minister Mehta also informed Parliament that the District Administration Office, Saptari, has formed a separate committee to investigate the incident.

She said the hospital had removed the staff members who were on duty when the incident occurred from their duties and that an investigation had already begun.

title.rendered: Nepal Police prepares to revise staff college course after high failure rate

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, September 11

Nepal Police has begun preparations to revise its Police Leadership and Staff Course (PLSC) after a large number of police officers failed the entrance examination, leaving seats in the course unfilled.

The Police Headquarters has formed a seven-member committee led by DIG Bishwa Adhikari to study the existing course and recommend possible revisions.

Nepal Police spokesperson DIG Abinarayan Kafle confirmed that the committee was formed on Bhadra 17 and has been given 15 days to submit its report.

“The committee has been formed as part of preparations to revise the course, and it has started its work. Further decisions will be taken after the committee submits its report,” Kafle told Onlinekhabar.

The committee will study the staff college course and recommend whether it should be revised and, if so, which subjects should be added, removed or modified. The admission process for the new batch has been halted pending the committee’s report.

The staff college course was formally launched in Baisakh 2082 after nearly two decades of preparations. It was considered a major project for Nepal Police and is linked to promotion to senior leadership positions.

The course has a quota of 35 officers per batch. However, only 17 of 131 officers passed the entrance examination in the first batch. In the second batch, 15 of 89 candidates passed.

Under the current rules, an officer can sit for the entrance examination only three times. Failure to pass the staff college course can significantly affect promotion prospects, with passing the course mandatory for promotion to DIG.

Police officials say the course is being reviewed partly because officers deployed extensively in the field often have limited time to prepare for the entrance examination. The review is also intended to prevent the course from adversely affecting officers’ careers because of difficulties in finding adequate study time.

title.rendered: Gen Z martyr statues rushed for unveiling before 40 per cent completion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The electoral government led by Sushila Karki had decided to construct a Gen Z Memorial Park in memory of those killed during the Gen Z movement.

An agreement reached between the then government and Gen Z had pledged to honour the sacrifice and contribution of those killed and injured through justice and meaningful memorialisation. The agreement stated that “reparatory measures, including meaningful memorialisation, would be ensured.” Bablu Gupta, a leader of the Gen Z movement and then Minister for Youth and Sports, had led the government’s initiative to build the memorial.

The construction of statues of 45 Gen Z martyrs at the swimming pool complex in Satdobato had begun during the previous government. Jagdish Kharel, spokesperson for the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) and then Minister for Communications, recalls that there had been difficulties in deciding the location for the statues. “Since there was also a sentiment among young people associated with sports, the location was finalised there after considering all aspects,” former minister Kharel told Onlinekhabar. He said Gupta had led the initiative to build the statues of the Gen Z martyrs.

Although the decision and process to build the statues had begun during the previous government, the work could not be completed. Gupta, who had led the initiative on behalf of the government, resigned from his ministerial post and turned his attention to the election.

“The plan was to complete them immediately. But while we were completing the government procedures, the election came around,” former minister Kharel said. “Those who were given responsibility for building the statues had to make sure the faces resembled the actual martyrs.” The unveiling had been scheduled to coincide with the first anniversary of the Gen Z movement. Home Minister Sudhan Gurung was scheduled to unveil the statues last Wednesday.

However, the statues were set to be unveiled before construction had been completed. Members of the martyrs’ families became angry after finding that the faces on the statues did not resemble those of the deceased. After family members objected to the lack of resemblance, Home Minister Gurung returned without unveiling the statues. Narayan Shrestha, president of the Gen Z Martyrs’ Family Welfare Society, said the unveiling was halted because the faces of the martyrs did not match those on the statues.

“We said the statues should not be unveiled because the faces did not match. We were told they would be remade and we would be informed once they were ready,” he said. According to Shrestha, the families of the martyrs were informed only a day before the unveiling ceremony that they were expected to attend.

Ravi Shakya coordinated the construction of the statues. Sculptors Manish Shrestha and Sujit Shrestha worked on them. Shakya, who coordinated the project, said problems arose because there was an attempt to rush the unveiling before the statues had been completed.

He said preparations had originally been made to show the statues, which were still under construction, to the families around Gen Z Day, but the sudden decision to unveil them led to the controversy. “Only 40 per cent of the work on the statues has been completed. Please look at their form once they are 100 per cent complete,” Shakya told Onlinekhabar.

Although the government provided the site for the statues, it did not provide funding for their construction. Shakya said the work had continued with funds raised through personal initiatives. “The Gen Z statues were not built with any government budget. We took the initiative because we felt they should be built and raised money little by little,” Shakya said.

According to Shakya, around Rs 2 million has been spent so far. He said construction of the statues would be completed within two months. Shakya expressed regret that the two sculptors, Sujit Shrestha and Manish Shrestha, had suffered a setback to their professional reputations when an attempt was made to unveil the statues before they were completed. “It has deeply affected them. Both are skilled sculptors,” Shakya said.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood affects around 150,000 people; 25 at holding centres suffer diarrhoea

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Around 150,000 people in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other districts are estimated to have been directly affected by the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26.

Health and Food Safety Ministry Secretary Dr Bikash Devkota presented the preliminary estimate at a meeting of the House of Representatives’ Education, Health and Information Technology Committee on Friday.

He said the estimate of the affected population was based on data collected through various mechanisms of the Bagmati provincial government and the ministry.

Secretary Devkota informed the committee that 25 people among those rescued from the affected areas and placed at holding centres had developed diarrhoea.

However, responding to questions raised by lawmakers, he clarified that no other serious outbreaks or infectious diseases had been reported so far apart from diarrhoea.

Master plan for climate-resilient infrastructure being prepared

Saying the health sector had learned important lessons from the latest flood disaster, Secretary Devkota stressed the need to make infrastructure built in the future climate-resilient.

He said building designs should take into account geographical conditions and temperature.

“It will now be important to consider the geographical conditions in which buildings or structures constructed by the Ministry of Health will be located. Structures built in areas with high temperatures should be different from those built in colder areas,” he said at the meeting. “All sectors now need to take this issue seriously.”

He also stressed that the availability of nearby health facilities should be considered when constructing new infrastructure so that people can easily access healthcare services during health emergencies.

Secretary Devkota said the ministry was preparing a master plan for rehabilitation and reconstruction that would incorporate climate-resilient infrastructure and pledged to submit the plan to the parliamentary committee once it was completed.

title.rendered: PM Shah vows closer cooperation with private sector to address economic challenges

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Prime Minister Balen Shah has said the government will make its cooperation with the private sector more effective to address the challenges facing the country’s economy.

Speaking at a meeting with entrepreneurs and business leaders at Singha Durbar on Friday, Shah said the government was committed to creating a favourable environment for investment and business expansion.

According to RSP lawmaker Vidushi Rana, who attended the meeting, Shah also sought information from businesspeople about the problems they have been facing while operating industries and businesses.

Rana said Shah told the meeting that investment by Nepali businesses should be prioritised, followed by investment from non-resident Nepalis, while foreign investment would remain the government’s third priority.

Business leaders said Nepali entrepreneurs have the capacity to undertake large infrastructure projects but stressed the need for policy and legal reforms to facilitate such investments.

They also emphasised the need for the state to create a favourable environment to boost the confidence of the private sector, which, according to Rana, contributes around 80 percent to the country’s economy.

The business leaders also complained that the practice of arresting and detaining businesspeople as soon as allegations are made against them has adversely affected the confidence of the private sector.

According to Rana, the meeting agreed to hold regular discussions between the Prime Minister’s Office and representatives of the private sector every three months to review issues facing businesses, necessary legal amendments and the overall investment environment.

Industrialists and business leaders Binod Chaudhary, Pawan Golyan, Umesh Shrestha and Chandra Dhakal were among those attending the meeting.

title.rendered: MPs demand accountability after woman forced to give birth on roadside in Saptari

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Multiple lawmakers raised the case of Babita Paswan, a woman from Rajbiraj Municipality-14, Parsahi, who was forced to give birth on a footpath near Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Saptari after the hospital allegedly turned her away for lacking sufficient money, during Friday’s sitting of the House of Representatives.

According to reports, Babita had only Rs 2,500 with her. The hospital refused to admit her on that amount, after which she gave birth on the footpath just outside the facility.

Dr Toshima Karki, an MP from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), raised the issue during the House’s emergency discussion segment.

She said the constitution guarantees the right to health and safe motherhood, but a wide gap remains between that guarantee and the healthcare citizens actually receive. She asked whether the woman had received timely triage and emergency clinical assessment on arrival, why the hospital had no record of when she left the premises, and why the hospital’s social service unit and the Aama Surakshya (Safe Motherhood) programme were not activated once it became clear she could not pay for a blood test.

She proposed implementing a “no denial in labour” protocol requiring immediate clinical assessment of any woman in labour regardless of ability to pay, expanding the Aama Surakshya programme to cover the full course of maternal care rather than just free delivery, keeping hospital social service units alert around the clock, and instituting detailed maternal care audits at every hospital.

RSP MP Lima Adhikari said the incident reminded her of her late father, former Finance Minister Bharat Mohan Adhikari, who had introduced the maternity allowance and helped advance the concept of safe motherhood in Nepal. She called it a matter of deep shame for the state that a pregnant woman was turned away from a hospital door for lack of a few thousand rupees, and demanded an immediate investigation into the hospital staff and administration involved, with strict action against anyone found responsible.

CPN-UML MP Bhumika Limbu Subba said the incident was not simply tragic but an example of the government’s irresponsibility, remarking that a “sad history of the state’s insensitivity and irresponsibility” had been born along with the newborn on the hospital footpath.

Nepali Congress MP Geeta Gurung demanded an explanation from the government, asking whether ensuring safe motherhood was the state’s responsibility or not, and pointedly asked whether, under the RSP-led administration, those without money are now expected to give birth on the streets.

“Similarly, Khusbu Oli, an MP from the Rastriya Prajatantra Party, sought accountability for the incident from the Prime Minister and the Health Minister.”

She asks, “Is it a crime to be poor in this country?”

Several lawmakers collectively questioned what had become of the constitutionally guaranteed fundamental right to free healthcare, given that a woman was compelled to deliver her baby on the road for lack of money.

title.rendered: Theatre practitioners demand collaboration with professional organisations in formulating theatre policy

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The Federation of Theatre Workers has demanded that relevant professional associations and organisations be consulted and involved when formulating policies, plans and programmes related to theatre.

Submitting a memorandum to the Music and Drama Academy, the federation emphasised the need to ensure the participation of stakeholder professional organisations when drafting policies and programmes concerning the theatre sector.

A team led by federation chair Rajendra Rimal submitted the memorandum to Academy Chancellor Brajesh Khanal at the Academy’s office.

The memorandum prioritised the need for necessary consultation, coordination and collaboration with relevant professional associations and organisations when formulating theatre-related policies, plans and programmes.

Accepting the memorandum, Chancellor Khanal expressed his commitment to being positive toward the federation’s demands and issues raised. He said continuous dialogue would be needed to take the necessary initiative and collaboration to address the federation’s demands.

The programme to submit the memorandum was also attended by the Academy’s Theatre Department Chief Jit Bahadur Deuja (Bijaya Bisphot) and Drama Department Chief Saraswati Chaudhary.

From the federation’s side, those present included Chair Rimal along with Vice-Chairs Sirjana Adhikari and Ram KC, General Secretary JB DC, Secretary Ashok Sivakoti, and Co-Treasurer Prabhan Bhusal, among others.

title.rendered: Proposal to remove the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders in the US

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The Trump administration has proposed eliminating the 60-day grace period that currently allows workers in the US to search for a new job or new sponsor after losing employment. The proposal also covers skilled workers on H-1B visas. This was disclosed in a government notice published online on Thursday.

Under the proposed rule published by the US Department of Homeland Security in the Federal Register, H-1B and other temporary work visa holders would be required to leave the United States as soon as their employment ends. The move could affect major American tech companies that rely heavily on foreign workers.

Since returning to power in January 2025, President Donald Trump has pursued this latest effort to restrict legal immigration. His administration has also decided to raise visa fees for skilled foreign workers.

In addition, as new training programmes are being rolled out, immigrant visa appointments at US missions worldwide have been temporarily suspended.

In its proposal, the Department of Homeland Security acknowledged that the change could have some impact on the operations of affected companies. However, it expressed the view that American workers could be placed in those positions instead.

title.rendered: An aircraft  landed at Dang’s Tarigaun Airport after one and a half months

content.rendered:
An aircraft landed at Dang’s Tarigaun Airport after a gap of one and a half months.

According to Pradeep Bhusal, a senior officer at the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, an aircraft landed at the airport on Thursday for the first time in one and a half months. Eight passengers from Kathmandu and four from Dang travelled on Thursday aboard Nepal Airlines’ 19-seat aircraft.

Senior Officer Bhusal said the Dang-Kathmandu air service, which had been irregular due to weather, would now become regular. “Weather had made the service irregular; now it will be regular,” he said.

According to him, the service will now operate four days a week — Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday. The current airfare is Rs 12,000. Bhusal said the flight would be available between 9 and 11 in the morning.

Tarigaun currently has a runway of only 750 metres, which can accommodate only 19-seat aircraft. Because only low-capacity aircraft can use the airport, and even that service is irregular, passengers from this region are often forced to travel via Nepalgunj or Bhairahawa instead. Although calls have repeatedly been raised to expand the runway to accommodate larger aircraft, this has yet to materialise.

The airport, established in 1954 AD, has not been expanded since. A budget of Rs 25 crore has been allocated in the current fiscal year for upgrading the airport.

title.rendered: Government suspends DAP fertiliser sales amid supply concerns

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The government has temporarily suspended the sale and distribution of diammonium phosphate (DAP) fertiliser, citing disruptions in the international supply chain.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment said the decision was taken to prevent a shortage of fertiliser for the upcoming wheat season.

On Bhadra 16, the Agriculture Inputs Management and Technology Section under the ministry’s Agriculture Development Division issued a letter directing Agriculture Inputs Company Limited and Salt Trading Corporation to suspend the sale and distribution of DAP fertiliser.

The letter, signed by ministry soil expert Rajanish Mishra, states that the Strait of Hormuz had been closed due to the war involving Israel, the United States and Iran. The ministry has claimed that the resulting disruption to the international supply chain of chemical fertilisers has created a situation of “force majeure.”

“Since the prospects of timely supply of DAP fertiliser for which purchase agreements have already been concluded appear weak, it has been decided to temporarily suspend the sale and distribution of DAP fertiliser in view of the possibility of a shortage for the wheat crop,” the ministry’s letter states.

The suspension was implemented based on a ministerial-level decision taken on Bhadra 15. To enforce the decision, the ministry has also suspended, until further notice, the provision under Subsection 6 of Section 12 of the Fertiliser Distribution Management Procedure, 2082.

Bishnu Prasad Pokharel, managing director of Agriculture Inputs Company Limited, said DAP fertiliser had been reserved for the wheat season because paddy currently requires only urea fertiliser.

“DAP is not in much demand for paddy in Bhadra and Asoj. If DAP is distributed now, there is a risk that cooperatives could take it to agro-vets or unnecessarily hold it,” he told Onlinekhabar. “Therefore, this decision was made through mutual consultation between the ministry and our company to ensure that DAP, which is mainly needed during the wheat season, does not become scarce.”

He said demand for urea fertiliser is currently high in the Terai-Madhesh and other areas for top-dressing paddy, and supplies are being maintained.

According to Pokharel, the company currently has 22,910 tonnes of urea fertiliser in stock, while around 33,000 tonnes are in transit from India and other countries.

He said the company has 14,645 tonnes of DAP in stock, with around 18,000 tonnes yet to arrive. He said fertiliser supplies have been affected globally by tensions in the Middle East.

Pokharel said it had become difficult to bring fertiliser on time because Iran had tightened restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz and shipping routes had been affected by attacks by Houthi rebels in the Red Sea.

“Production capacity for DAP has not been able to operate at full capacity because sulphur production from natural gas has declined in the international market,” he said. “As a result, the price of DAP has risen to more than $1,000 per tonne, while the price of urea has fallen somewhat to around $530 to $550.”

He said urea is relatively readily available in the international market, whereas DAP is extremely difficult to obtain and remains in high demand.

title.rendered: Parliamentary committee directs government to set up helpdesks for the safety of flood-affected women and children

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The House of Representatives’ Women and Social Affairs Committee has directed the government to set up helpdesks at holding centres to ensure the safety of women, children and other at-risk groups in flood-affected areas.

According to committee chair Akriti Awasthi, the committee’s meeting on Friday directed the government to establish helpdesks and designate contact persons.

She said there was a risk of people exploiting the sensitive disaster situation to lure, pressure or make false promises to victims under the guise of offering jobs, relief, transport home, or passage to a safer location.

The committee concluded that the safety of citizens staying at holding centres was particularly sensitive in areas including Betrawati and the Trishuli corridor, Timure, Khattekhola, Syafrubesi, Hakubesi and Mailung in Rasuwa.

The committee directed that effective safety and protection measures be put in place, noting that women, adolescent girls, children, persons with disabilities and other at-risk groups could face risks of sexual exploitation, gender-based violence, abuse, human trafficking and other forms of violence and oppression.

The committee has directed the Ministry of Women, Children and Senior Citizens, and the Ministry of Gender and Sexual Minorities and Social Security, to run helpdesks at relief camps targeting at-risk groups and to immediately mobilise local-level women’s cells actively and effectively.

Committee Chair Awasthi said the committee had also directed that a mechanism be ensured to maintain confidentiality of complaints and information received from victims, provide legal assistance, and make safe referrals to relevant agencies as needed.

The committee has also decided to form subcommittees along thematic clusters for study, research and coordination on issues concerning women, children, gender and sexual minorities, persons with disabilities, and senior citizens.

According to Chair Awasthi, the subcommittees are being formed to mobilise committee members with relevant expertise, leadership capacity and experience into the respective clusters so they can conduct studies and offer necessary recommendations.

She said the subcommittees would be formed on a party basis.

title.rendered: 4 new films hit theatres this week — which one should you watch?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Two Nepali films and two international films have opened in Nepal’s theatres since Friday. The Nepali films “Pension Patta” and “Behuli” have been released alongside Hollywood’s “Fall 2: Dead Point” and Bollywood’s “Hanuman Ansh.”

“Pension Patta,” directed by Maotse Gurung, is a socially themed film starring Dayahang Rai and Gaumaya Gurung in the lead roles. It portrays the struggle a wife faces trying to obtain her pension after the death of her Lahure (British/Indian Army veteran) husband.

The 128-minute film is said to be rooted in the customs and culture of the Gurung community. This is the second narrative feature from Mao Tse, who has already directed several Gurung-language films, following “Dayarani.”

“Behuli,” directed by Sashan Kandel “, Santosh,” has also been released since Friday. The film stars Paras Bam Thakuri and Divya Raimajhi in lead roles. This drama has a runtime of 175 minutes.

The Hollywood film “Fall 2: Dead Point” has also been released since Friday. The 98-minute English-language film is directed by Michael Spierig and Peter Spierig, and stars Harriet Slater, Ersema Thomas, Tom Britney and Grace Caroline Currey.

The story follows Jax Hunter, who is grieving the death of her sister Shiloh. During this time, she grows close to Shiloh’s daring friend Luce, and the two set out to climb Thailand’s dangerous Mount Kwan.

During the climb, a landslide leaves them stranded on a narrow platform four thousand feet above the ground. As Jax fights to survive, she must confront her own fears. The film is classified as an adventure-thriller.

Similarly, the Bollywood film “Hanuman Ansh” has also opened since Friday. The 150-minute film is directed by Vishal Chaturvedi and stars Shobhinav Satya, Chandan Anand and Purnima Tiwari in lead roles. It has been given a PG rating.

The film’s story centres on the life journey of a grieving boy who sets out in search of God in hopes of meeting his deceased mother. As he searches for God, he comes to realise that serving humanity is life’s most important purpose.

That same boy, who undertakes a spiritual journey of serving people through love, food and silent blessings, later comes to be known as “Hanuman Ansh”, Neem Karoli Baba. The biographical film presents the story of his spiritual journey and service to humanity.

title.rendered: Indian pharmaceutical company provides Rs 1.5 million in assistance to flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Indian pharmaceutical company USV Pharma has provided Rs 1.5 million in assistance for victims of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods. USV contributed to the Nepal Medical Association’s relief campaign.

The Nepal Medical Association said the funds would be used to provide essential supplies to individuals from severely flood-affected, poor families.

A memorandum of cooperation was exchanged between Nepal Medical Association President Dr Badri Rijal and USV Pharmaceuticals’ Chief Business Officer Mahidwaj Sisodia at a programme organised in Kathmandu on Thursday.

Dr Rijal, president of the Medical Association, said affected families would be provided with bedding, blankets, solar lights and mobile-charging facilities, and drinking water and sanitation supplies. He said essential household items, medicines and health-related supplies would also be distributed.

According to Dr Rijal, USV Pharma’s assistance is expected to directly benefit around 1,500 people from about 300 households in flood-affected areas.

Members of the Medical Association are visiting affected areas to identify local needs. Dr Rijal said relief programmes would be carried out based on recommendations from the monitoring team sent to the field. He also said there were plans to build around 300 temporary shelters for families that had been left homeless.

Mahidwaj S. Sisodia, Chief Business Officer of USV Pharmaceuticals, said supporting affected communities during times of disaster was an important part of the company’s social responsibility.

title.rendered: Rs 1.35 trillion of the financial system sits at the central bank; Rs 7.5 billion being withdrawn

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

With excess liquidity building up in the financial system, Rs 1.35 trillion has piled up at Nepal Rastra Bank. The surplus liquidity has accumulated at the central bank due to continuously rising deposits and falling demand for credit in the financial system.

When there is excess liquidity in the financial system, short-term interest rates, that is, interbank interest rates, fall. The central bank has adopted a policy of not letting the interbank rate fall below 2.75 percent. To manage this rate, the central bank has been both withdrawing and injecting liquidity as needed. However, in recent times, only withdrawal has been taking place because of the persistent surplus.

The central bank has been mopping up the excess liquidity in the financial system through deposit collection instruments, bonds, and the standing deposit facility. On Friday too, the bank moved to withdraw liquidity through a two-month deposit collection instrument worth Rs 7.5 billion.

The central bank had earlier issued a deposit collection instrument worth Rs 3.5 billion on Monday as well. The continuous improvement in remittance inflows has also contributed to the rise in liquidity in the financial system. In addition, sluggish demand for credit in the financial sector, caused by the slow economy, has further helped liquidity build up.

According to the central bank, as of Thursday, the financial system held about Rs 40 billion in liquidity. However, since money that banks and financial institutions had parked at the central bank through the standing deposit facility and deposit collection instruments was maturing, the deposit collection instrument was issued to draw it back in. Banks and financial institutions use the standing deposit facility to park excess liquidity at the central bank for the short term.

For the deposit collection instrument, the central bank prioritises allocation to banks and financial institutions that ask for the lowest interest rate.

When the central bank injects liquidity into the financial system, it charges interest at the bank rate, the upper limit of the interest rate corridor, and when it withdraws liquidity, it pays interest at the standing deposit facility rate, the corridor’s lower limit. The bank rate currently stands at 5.75 percent and the standing deposit facility rate at 2.75 percent.

title.rendered: Baluwatar food outlet fined Rs 300,000 for selling expired laddus

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Akash Foods in Baluwatar, Kathmandu, has been fined Rs 300,000 after it was found selling unsafe food products, putting consumers’ health at risk.

The Department of Food Technology and Quality Control under the Ministry of Health and Food Safety took action after an unannounced market inspection under its “rapid response modality” found spoiled potatoes and expired laddus at the outlet.

According to the department, the inspection found serious food safety violations at Akash Foods. Potatoes used as stuffing for pani puri were found to have an unusual foul smell.

Similarly, eight boxes of sugar-free laddus past their expiry date were found at the shop. The department said the laddus carried a production date of August 27, 2025, and were required to be consumed within 15 days (“best before 15 days”), but were still being sold after the recommended consumption period had expired.

Following the findings, the inspection team immediately destroyed around 100 grams of foul-smelling potatoes and eight packets of expired laddus.

The department has also instructed the business to strictly maintain food safety standards in the future in accordance with the Food Hygiene and Quality Act, 2081.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Sopan Pharmaceuticals Limited’s net profit has fallen by more than 82 percent within a year. According to the company’s unaudited fourth-quarter financial statement for FY 2025/26, the company posted a net profit of Rs 3.8289 crore.

In the same period of the previous fiscal year, the company’s net profit stood at Rs 21.7791 crore. This marks an 82.42 percent decline in profit. The company says the pressure on profit came from a decline in other income and a rise in selling, distribution, and administrative expenses, even though operating income saw modest growth.

The company’s operating income rose from Rs 50.05 crore to Rs 51.14 crore, a growth of about 2.18 percent. However, other income fell sharply from Rs 1.57 crore to just Rs 12.33 lakh, a decline of about 92 percent.

The company’s financial expenses fell during the review period, dropping from Rs 5.68 crore in the previous fiscal year to Rs 4.39 crore. However, even as financial expenses fell, operating expenses rose. The company’s selling and distribution expenses increased from Rs 4.07 crore to Rs 6.44 crore, a rise of about 58 percent.

Similarly, administrative expenses rose from Rs 4.27 crore to Rs 6.20 crore, an increase of about 45 percent. Thus, despite modest revenue growth, the sharp decline in other income combined with rising operating expenses appears to have significantly reduced the company’s profit.

Along with profit, the company’s earnings per share (EPS) also fell significantly, from Rs 18.33 in the previous fiscal year to Rs 2.23 in the review period, a decline of about 87.83 percent.

By the end of the review period, the company’s net worth per share stood at Rs 96.34, and total assets per share were valued at Rs 157.82.

The financial statement notes that the company’s reserves and accumulated fund stood at Rs 36.73 crore.

title.rendered: Government to hand over closed public enterprises to private sector after settling liabilities

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle has clarified that the government’s policy is to hand over the operation of closed and troubled state-owned enterprises to the private sector.

Addressing the 28th general meeting of the Society of Economic Journalists-Nepal (SEJON) on Friday, Minister Wagle said the narrative that the government was preparing to start operating industries itself was incorrect.

He said the assets and liabilities of state-owned enterprises would be managed and, after completing the required procedures, their operation would be handed over to the private sector.

DDA completed for seven enterprises

Finance Minister Wagle said detailed due diligence assessments (DDAs) had been completed for seven public enterprises, including Gorkharkali Rubber Industry, Hetauda Cement and Udayapur Cement. Based on the assessments, government-owned land and other assets would be managed to clear the way for the private sector to operate the enterprises, he said.

“There is a perception that the government has started running the industries, but we have only dusted them off,” he said. “We will take them to a certain point and hand them over to the private sector. Therefore, the premature narrative being created at this stage is not useful.”

‘Operational lease’ model to avoid disputes

Minister Wagle identified the management of accumulated loans, interest and other financial liabilities as the main challenge before handing the enterprises over to the private sector. He said the government was working diligently to settle liabilities accumulated over decades, including principal, interest and loans.

Recalling major disputes over land ownership during the privatisation process in 1992, he said the government would not touch similarly contentious issues this time.

“There are issues concerning land owned by the Nepali people, and we will not touch contentious matters like in the past,” Wagle said. “However, we are creating an environment to hand over the enterprises to those who come forward saying they can operate them under an operational lease.”

Minister Wagle also clarified that the government was not suspicious of legitimate profits made by the private sector but was focused on creating an environment of fair and healthy competition.

title.rendered: No one has been denied participation in the 15th General Convention: President Thapa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa has claimed that no leader has been barred from taking part in the party’s 15th General Convention. He said the convention would go ahead as per the scheduled timeline, and that all leaders and cadres would be able to participate in it.

Speaking at a programme organised in Kathmandu on Friday, President Thapa said the lower-level convention process would begin on September 20, with the central convention starting on October 2.

“No friend has been barred from taking part in the convention; all friends will participate in the convention, and there will be competition,” he said. “Whoever gets the responsibility will remain in leadership. We must also embrace those friends who don’t get responsibility through competition, and unite the party by taking everyone along.”

President Thapa pointed out that while internal competition would settle matters within the party, restoring the public’s broken trust remained Congress’s main challenge. He said the party was serious about the fact that dwelling only on internal problems would further weaken its relationship with the public.

“The convention will only sort out matters within the party for now. We will need to restore the public’s trust, and we are setting out on that journey of restoration,” he said. “As soon as the convention concludes, we will need to go across the country. We will reach all 77 districts, going village to village.”

President Thapa announced that immediately after the convention and Dashain, Congress would run a special nationwide campaign to improve its relationship with the public and win back their trust.

title.rendered: Solukhumbu’s Hunga River blocked by landslide, caution urged in downstream areas

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, September 11

The Hunga River in wards 2 and 4 of Mahakulung Rural Municipality, Solukhumbu, has been blocked by a landslide. The river was obstructed by a landslide that occurred on Friday morning.

According to Solukhumbu Police Chief DSP Nabinraja Budhathoki, a landslide roughly 35 metres high came down about 100 metres below the head office of Gaurishankar Hydropower, in the area falling under Ward No. 2, blocking the river. This has created an artificial lake in the river approximately 100 metres long and 15 metres deep.

He said water has been slowly flowing over the dam formed since morning, and caution has been advised because of flood risk in downstream areas.

Police have urged residents living along the riverbank, as well as two nearby hydropower projects, to remain alert.

The site is located about 10 kilometres southeast of the Ilaka Police Office in Bung.

Even though water has begun flowing over the artificial dam created by the landslide, the risk that it could burst at any time has not passed.

Officials say that if the dam breaches, water from the Hunga River could affect downstream areas through Sotang Rural Municipality and Thulung Dudhkoshi Rural Municipality, all the way to the Dudhkoshi River in Khotang and Okhaldhunga districts.

DSP Budhathoki added that since water has started flowing over the top of the landslide debris, the risk is not considered to be major at this time.

title.rendered: Foreign investors increasingly drawn to Nepal’s IT sector

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Foreign investors are increasingly showing interest in Nepal’s information technology sector, with the majority of projects receiving foreign investment commitments in the current fiscal year concentrated in IT.

According to the Department of Industry, 727 out of 1,116 projects for which foreign investment commitments were received in fiscal year 2025/26 are related to the information technology sector.

The department said foreign investors have committed around Rs 5.8 billion for the projects.

Among the other sectors, 63 projects are in manufacturing, four in energy, 18 in agriculture, 227 in tourism, 71 in services and two in infrastructure.

The Department of Industry said around Rs 6 billion was committed for 842 projects in the previous fiscal year, 2081/82.

According to department information officer Suresh Dahal, foreign investors tend to choose sectors based on their investment interests.

He said the volume of investment commitments varies because some projects require significantly larger amounts of capital.

“The investors choose the sectors in which they are interested. Some projects require large investments, so the total investment amount tends to be higher,” Dahal said.

title.rendered: US stocks fall for fourth straight session as oil prices, inflation fuel rate-hike bets

content.rendered:
New York, September 11

US stocks closed lower on Thursday for a fourth consecutive session as surging oil prices and stronger-than-expected wholesale inflation strengthened expectations of further interest rate hikes.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 316.56 points, or 0.60 percent, to 52,064.10. The S&P 500 dropped 44.66 points, or 0.58 percent, to 7,591.70, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 171.62 points, or 0.65 percent, to 26,081.73.

Nine of the 11 major S&P 500 sectors ended lower. Materials led the declines, falling 1.48 percent, followed by utilities, which dropped 1 percent. Communication services and consumer staples bucked the broader trend, gaining 0.25 percent and 0.24 percent, respectively.

Oil prices climbed sharply after US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that elevated fuel costs could persist through the upcoming midterm elections.

West Texas Intermediate crude for October delivery jumped $6.43, or 6.69 percent, to settle at $102.48 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange. Brent crude for November delivery rose $6.42, or 6.34 percent, to close at $107.63 a barrel on the London ICE Futures Exchange.

Inflation concerns also weighed on investor sentiment following the release of US wholesale price data on Thursday.

The US Department of Labor reported that the Producer Price Index (PPI) rose 5.4 percent year-on-year in August. The core PPI, which excludes food and energy prices, increased 4.6 percent over the same period.

Persistent inflation, combined with rising energy prices, prompted traders to increase their expectations of further monetary tightening.

According to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool, the probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate increase at the US Federal Reserve’s upcoming policy meeting rose to 73 percent, up from 64 percent before the PPI data was released.

In corporate trading, shares of enterprise software company Oracle fell more than 5 percent during regular trading but jumped nearly 7 percent in after-hours trading after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results.

Apple shares gained 3.56 percent following the launch of the company’s first foldable smartphone.

Investors are now awaiting Friday’s release of the August Consumer Price Index (CPI), the final major inflation indicator before the Federal Open Market Committee meets next week to decide on interest rates.

title.rendered: Suggestions to reduce curriculum load and include AI in national framework

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Suggestions ranging from reducing the curriculum load to incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) have been collected as part of the process to revise the National Curriculum Framework.

The suggestions were collected through workshops held in all seven provinces to revise the National Curriculum Framework, 2076 BS.

The Ministry of Education and Sports said participants suggested reducing the curriculum load, making education more employment- and entrepreneurship-oriented, and incorporating new technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), into the curriculum.

According to the ministry, participants at workshops organised by the Curriculum Development Centre, Sanothimi, Bhaktapur, in all seven provinces for the revision of the National Curriculum Framework, 2076, stressed the need to make the existing curriculum relevant to the times, practical, useful for everyday life and suited to local needs.

Discussions held in Koshi Province produced suggestions to link education with local production and make it employment- and entrepreneurship-oriented, while making learning student-centred, creative, practical and technology-friendly.

Participants said education should expand technical and vocational education while also promoting patriotism and morality and preserving traditional languages, scripts and culture. They also suggested making the curriculum flexible and giving schools and teachers some responsibility for its development and implementation.

In Madhesh Province, reducing the content and workload of the curriculum emerged as a major concern. Participants suggested incorporating knowledge and skills related to tourism, agriculture and other local and high-potential sectors into the curriculum. They also called for updating technology-related content and including knowledge about AI.

Participants from Madhesh also stressed the need for moral and spiritual education, assessment through students’ participation in social work, greater involvement of teachers in curriculum development, and prioritising teacher capacity development.

Suggestions were also made to ensure students gain proficiency in their mother tongue, Nepali and English, and to include content that can create employment opportunities through indigenous knowledge and skills.

Participants also suggested developing headteachers as educational leaders rather than administrators, giving local governments authority to develop local curricula, providing psychosocial counselling for students, and placing greater emphasis on parent education.

In Bagmati Province, emphasis was placed on entrepreneurship- and employment-oriented education, mandatory parent education, moral education, and the promotion of local knowledge, skills and culture.

Participants from Gandaki Province said education should be made practical, useful for everyday life, skills-based and employment-oriented. They suggested producing self-reliant and skilled human resources through pre-vocational, agricultural and technical education, while incorporating local geography, history, art, culture and diversity into the curriculum.

In Lumbini Province, participants suggested reducing the curriculum load and content, developing a curriculum that promotes patriotism, and using AI to foster creativity.

Participants said the curriculum should enable young people to become self-reliant and create employment opportunities within the country rather than forcing them to seek opportunities abroad.

In Karnali Province, participants suggested bringing early childhood development and education into the school structure as a two-year programme, making monitoring and evaluation of the actual implementation of the curriculum more effective, and ending the confusion caused by frequent curriculum changes. They also stressed the need to provide teachers with necessary support in various areas.

Although a programme was held at the Private and Boarding Schools’ Organisation Nepal (PABSON) Sudurpaschim and the Ministry of Social Development in Dhangadhi in Sudurpaschim Province, details of the main suggestions received from the discussion were not provided.

In line with a ministerial decision of the Ministry of Education and Sports, the task force formed to revise the National Curriculum Framework has been collecting suggestions and feedback from stakeholders at the field level in 28 districts across all seven provinces, with the objective of making the curriculum relevant to the times, practical, useful for everyday life and effective.

The task force has conducted direct interactions with teachers, students, headteachers, parents, experts, policymakers, local government representatives and other stakeholders in various districts.

According to Curriculum Development Centre Executive Director Mahendra Parajuli, suggestions will be collected from 28 districts in the first phase. Suggestions will then be sought from all 77 Education Development and Coordination Units, while feedback will also be collected through the centre’s website.

The suggestions received from workshops in all seven provinces indicate a common view that the National Curriculum Framework should reduce the curriculum load while linking education with local needs, employment, entrepreneurship, technology, morality and practical life skills.

The Curriculum Development Centre said it would move ahead with the necessary process to revise the National Curriculum Framework, 2076, based on the suggestions received.

title.rendered: PM Shah seeks New Zealand’s support for climate disaster financing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Prime Minister Balen Shah has sought New Zealand’s support in international forums to help Nepal secure financial assistance to address loss and damage caused by climate-induced disasters.

Prime Minister Shah made the request during a telephone conversation with New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon on Friday.

According to the Prime Minister’s Office, Shah said Nepal is highly vulnerable to climate-induced disasters and urged the New Zealand government to provide constructive support for Nepal’s efforts at international forums.

During the conversation, Shah also expressed gratitude for the NZ$2 million in humanitarian assistance provided by New Zealand following the Bhotekoshi flood.

Shah briefed Luxon on the government’s ongoing search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts following the devastating flood in Bhotekoshi, Rasuwa. He said the government has given high priority to locating all those who remain missing in the disaster.

Prime Minister Luxon expressed deep condolences, on behalf of the New Zealand government and people, over the loss of life and property caused by the devastating floods in Nepal.

He also expressed solidarity with Nepal during the difficult situation.

title.rendered: Devotees remember deceased fathers at Gokarneshwar on Father’s Day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Devotees across the country are observing Kushé Aunshi, or Father’s Day, on Friday by honouring their living fathers and remembering those who have passed away.

Kushé Aunshi, or the new moon day in the month of Bhadra, is traditionally observed as Father’s Day or Pitri Aunshi in accordance with the Sanatan Hindu tradition.

On this special day, children traditionally honour their living fathers by offering them their favourite dishes, fruits and sweets, presenting them with new clothes and seeking their blessings.

It is widely believed that receiving blessings from one’s father brings happiness and peace. Therefore, even children who live away from home for work make time to visit their fathers on this day.

Those whose fathers have passed away, however, visit various sacred pilgrimage sites to perform Shraddha, Tarpan and other religious rituals and make offerings in memory of their deceased fathers. On this occasion, the Gokarneshwar Mahadev Temple, a historic and religious pilgrimage site in northeastern Kathmandu, has been crowded with devotees since early morning.

Similarly, large numbers of devotees visit pilgrimage sites including Devghat in Tanahun, Bishnupaduka in Sunsari and Barahakshetra to bathe in the sacred waters and pray for the salvation of their deceased ancestors.

Onlinekhabar captured poignant scenes of devotees bathing, performing Shraddha and offering Tarpan at Gokarneshwar in remembrance of their deceased fathers.

title.rendered: Additional specialist doctors to be deployed to Rasuwa flood-hit areas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

An additional medical team, including specialist doctors, is being sent to Nuwakot to strengthen maternal and child health services in areas affected by the Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa.

According to the Ministry of Health and Food Safety, a team of specialist doctors from Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital and Kanti Children’s Hospital is being sent to Nuwakot as part of a decision to ensure continuity of health services and provide additional services based on needs in the flood-affected areas.

The ministry said another team was being deployed as specialist services related to maternal and newborn health, children and reproductive health were further needed, even though health teams had already been providing services in the affected areas.

The team includes Dr Bina Prajapati, a level-11 paediatric specialist at Kanti Children’s Hospital; senior obstetrician-gynaecologists Dr Harikumar Shrestha and Dr Shriram Khadka from Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital; and Dr Dhan Bahadur, an obstetrician-gynaecologist at the same hospital.

The team will visit flood-affected areas of Nuwakot and Rasuwa and provide specialist services related to maternal and newborn health, child health and reproductive health as required. Necessary medicines and medical supplies will also be sent with the team.

In view of possible disruptions to health services caused by floods and landslides, the ministry has been identifying needs and mobilising additional specialist health workers, medicines and medical supplies to the affected areas.

title.rendered: Private sector urges government to use respectful language towards business community

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Speaking in the presence of Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle, the heads of private-sector umbrella organisations have urged state and government representatives to use respectful language when referring to businesspeople.

President of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI), Kamlesh Agrawal, urged the government and political circles to use dignified language when addressing the business community. He made the remarks at a programme organised in Kathmandu on Friday to mark the 28th annual general meeting of the Society of Economic Journalists-Nepal (SEJON).

Agrawal said the economy had remained under pressure since the COVID-19 pandemic and that state-level initiatives were necessary to overcome the difficulties. He said competition was currently underway to contribute funds to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund following the government’s call for support.

On the occasion, Confederation of Nepalese Industries (CNI) President Birendra Raj Pandey suggested increasing capital expenditure. He also called for removing existing legal hurdles to boost private-sector investment, saying that the confederation had been continuously working towards this goal.

FNCCI President Anjan Shrestha said successive governments had consistently blamed the private sector for economic problems and urged the government to stop doing so. “Everyone has only criticised the private sector,” he said. “You have come with the idea of change, so please do not continue this practice.”

He also said the private sector would work together with the government in the recovery and reconstruction of flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: A Nepali father’s reflection on chasing dreams abroad

content.rendered:
Every time I video-call my children in Nepal, I ask the same questions.

Have you eaten? How was school? Did you finish your homework?

We talk for a few minutes. Sometimes they tell me about something interesting that happened that day. Sometimes they are distracted. Sometimes I am.

Then we say goodbye. The screen goes dark. And I am left with a question I do not always know how to answer: Am I building my children’s future, or slowly removing myself from their childhood?

My wife and I went to Australia with a dream shared by many Nepali parents: better education, greater financial security and a better life for our children.

Like many parents living abroad, we have repeated the same reassuring sentence to ourselves: We are doing all this for the children.

And perhaps we are.

But I have also begun to understand an uncomfortable truth: a decision made out of love is not automatically the right decision for a child’s emotional needs.

When the future becomes more important than the present

Adults are naturally drawn to the future. We plan careers, save money and think about education, visas, housing and financial security. We tell ourselves that the sacrifices we make today will benefit our children tomorrow.

Children experience time differently.

For a child, a year is not simply a year. It can be a significant part of a life. Adults may think, “We will be together soon.” A child may experience that same period as another birthday without a parent, another school event without them, another Dashain celebrated through a screen.

We measure the future in plans. Children, however, measure the present through presence.

Think about the small moments children remember: a friend’s mother picking them up from school, a father attending a parent day, a parent watching them perform on stage, someone being there on their birthday, or a hand placed gently on their head during the Dashain tika.

We can send new clothes from abroad. We can transfer money for a birthday cake. We can buy gifts and make sure school fees are paid. But a new dress sent from another country is not the same as sitting beside a child while they try it on.

Money for a birthday cake is not the same as standing beside them while they blow out the candles. Technology can bring our faces closer, but it cannot bring the warmth of an embrace.

What attachment tells us

Child-development research offers another way to think about this.

Attachment theory, developed through the work of John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth, stresses the importance of a reliable caregiver as a secure base from which children can explore the world.

That does not mean that every child separated from a parent will experience psychological problems.

Many Nepali children grow up happily with grandparents, relatives, or other caregivers. Our extended-family system can be an extraordinary strength. Grandparents and relatives often provide the love, stability and care that allow children to thrive.

But we should also acknowledge something more difficult: one kind of love does not completely replace another.

A grandparent can provide warmth and security. A relative can be deeply involved in a child’s life. A child can feel safe and loved while still missing their mother or father. These realities can exist at the same time.

Children may not always have the words to say, “I miss you.” Instead, their feelings may emerge in other ways: increased anger, unusual silence, changes in school performance, disrupted sleep, reluctance to talk on the phone or even physical complaints.

We should not automatically assume that parental separation is the cause. Children go through many changes as they grow. But persistent changes should not simply be dismissed.

Teachers, doctors, school counsellors and child psychologists can help when concerns continue.

There is also a danger in assuming that a child who seems unusually mature is necessarily unaffected. Sometimes, maturity is adaptation.

A child may simply have learned to hide their feelings because they do not want to make their parents worry.

The invisible debt children should never have to carry

There is another part of this conversation that deserves more attention.

Parents who migrate often make enormous sacrifices. They work long hours, live away from their families and endure loneliness because they believe they are securing a better future for their children. But when children repeatedly hear, “We sacrificed everything for you,” those sacrifices can sometimes become an emotional burden. A child may begin to feel that they owe their parents something in return — that they must study hard, succeed, fulfil the dreams their parents carried abroad and, perhaps most importantly, never complain.

But the decision to migrate was an adult decision. Our children do not have to repay our sacrifices, and they do not have to fulfil our dreams to deserve our love. Perhaps we should tell them instead: “We made this decision for our family. It is not your responsibility.” That distinction matters.

Whenever conversations like this arise, there is often another response: “It was your decision. Deal with it.”

There is some truth in that. Parents must take responsibility for the decisions they make. We cannot expect sympathy to erase the consequences of those decisions.

But responsibility and silence are not the same thing.

If thousands of Nepali families are making similar choices — parents going abroad while their children remain at home — then these experiences are no longer only individual stories. They are part of a wider social reality. Talking about that reality is not self-pity. It is a form of social self-reflection.

We should be able to ask difficult questions without turning them into accusations. A decision can be understandable, necessary or made out of love, and we can still ask whether its consequences are working for the child.

The purpose is not to condemn parents who leave. Nor is it to justify every decision simply because it was made out of love.

The question is simpler, and perhaps more difficult: What can we do differently now?

What can parents living abroad do?

There is no single solution to the pain of separation. Every family is different. Financial realities, immigration rules, education and caregiving arrangements all matter. But there are things parents can do.

Do not allow separation to become indefinite

“Next year.” “After the visa.” “After my studies.” “After we save a little more.”

Plans like these can quietly turn two years into five. If reunification is the goal, it requires more than good intentions. Families need a realistic plan, some sense of a timeline and regular moments when they can ask themselves whether that plan is still working. The future should not always be the reason the present is postponed.

Do not confuse phone calls with parenting

Calling your child every day is valuable, but the quality of those conversations matters too. Instead of always asking, “Did you eat?”, “Did you do your homework?” or “How were your studies?”, sometimes ask different questions: What made you happy today? Did anything upset you? What are you missing most these days? If I were there today, what would we do together?

Questions like these give children room to talk about their emotional world, rather than simply report whether they have completed their responsibilities.

Research on early childhood development often emphasizes the importance of responsive interaction — paying attention to a child’s signals and responding to them. In that sense, even a short conversation can become meaningful when a parent is genuinely present rather than distracted. Fifteen minutes of real attention can sometimes mean more than an hour of a distracted call.

Listen to each child individually

Families sometimes assume that the older child needs less attention because they appear more responsible. But an older child is still a child. They may be helping with younger siblings, doing well in school and appearing independent while quietly missing their parents. Maturity should not become a reason to overlook emotional needs.

Do not mistake anger for ingratitude

A child can be angry with you and still love you. They can appreciate everything you provide and still be unhappy that you are not there. Those feelings are not contradictions.

Parents still need to set boundaries around behaviour, but the feeling itself should not automatically be dismissed as disrespect. Sometimes the most helpful response is simply, “I understand that you are angry. Tell me why.”

Do not use gifts as a substitute for presence

There is nothing wrong with sending gifts. Children enjoy them, and gifts can be a meaningful expression of affection. But they cannot carry the entire weight of a relationship.

A handwritten letter, a story read together over a call, looking through old family photographs or simply talking about an ordinary day can create a deeper connection than an expensive toy.

Respect the people caring for your children

Grandparents and relatives who stay behind often carry the daily responsibilities of raising a child. They deal with school mornings, meals, illnesses, homework and discipline.

Parents abroad and caregivers at home should not compete over who knows the child better or who loves them more. They are on the same side. The child needs both.

Stay involved in the ordinary parts of your child’s life

Paying school fees is important. Sending money for food and clothing is important. But parenting is more than providing financially.

Know your child’s teacher. Join school meet

Nobody is perfect

Donald Winnicott’s idea of the “good enough parent” offers an important perspective here. Children do not need perfect parents. They need parents who are sufficiently reliable, who recognize when they have made mistakes and who are willing to reconnect and repair.

That matters to parents living abroad because guilt can easily become overwhelming. But guilt alone does not help a child. Learning does. Changing does. Reconnecting does.

We cannot undo every decision we have made. We cannot bring back every birthday we missed or every school event we could not attend. But we can decide what happens next.

I do not write this as a perfect father. I have been distracted. I have been tired. I have sometimes ended calls sooner than I should have. And I have used the familiar justification: “We are doing all this for the children.”

But I am beginning to ask myself what that sentence really means.

If we are truly doing this for our children, then their emotional needs cannot always be something we promise to address later. The future we are working so hard to build for them should not come at the cost of the childhood they are living now.
