title.rendered: Nepal to send 135 athletes in 21 sports to 20th Asian Games

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Nepal will send a 211-member contingent, including 135 athletes, to the 20th Asian Games to be held in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4.

The final size of Nepal’s delegation was announced at a farewell ceremony held at the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology in Singha Durbar on Thursday.

Nepal had earlier planned to participate in 22 sports with 137 athletes. However, the number was reduced after one athlete each was withdrawn from breaking and wushu.

Nepal’s sole breaking athlete, Sunil Bamjan, will not participate, resulting in the withdrawal of the sport from Nepal’s Asian Games participation.

Of the 135 athletes who will compete in 21 sports, 57 are women and 78 are men. The contingent will also include 29 coaches, 17 team managers and two technical officials.

Nepal’s athletes will compete in archery (2), athletics (6), badminton (4), boxing (7), cricket (15), cycling (2), golf (4), judo (6), kabaddi (24), karate (8), rafting and canoeing (2), skate and skateboarding (2), soft tennis (4), squash (2), swimming (5), table tennis (6), taekwondo (3), tennis (5), volleyball (12), wrestling (6) and wushu (10).

The Asian Games’ basketball competition has already begun, with matches starting on September 10. The formal opening ceremony of the Games is scheduled for September 19.

Nepal will be looking to improve its performance at the continental sporting event, with athletes from across the country set to compete in a wide range of individual and team events.

title.rendered: Thapa’s report defends Oli, rejects calls for him to step down as UML chair

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

CPN-UML Vice-Chair Ram Bahadur Thapa has prepared a separate report defending party Chair KP Sharma Oli and rejecting calls for him to step down amid the party’s ongoing debate over restructuring.

Thapa, who is also coordinator of the task force formed to collect suggestions on UML restructuring, has prepared a 39-page report that directly counters key conclusions in General Secretary Shankar Pokharel’s 65-page report.

Pokharel’s report, prepared after collecting suggestions from party leaders and cadres across the country, concluded that Oli should take moral responsibility for the party’s crisis and step down from the leadership.

Thapa’s report takes the opposite position, arguing that Oli should remain party chair.

According to sources, Thapa prepared the report with Oli’s support and in his defence.

Thapa has strongly criticised the attempt to link the party’s restructuring process with Oli’s removal. He argues that Pokharel’s report focuses more on creating grounds to remove the party chair than on objectively reviewing the party’s electoral performance.

“The draft report appears to be an attempt to establish grounds for restructuring by removing the party chair rather than reviewing the election,” Thapa wrote.

Thapa says Oli does not need to resign

A major argument in Thapa’s report is that losing an election does not automatically require a party chair to resign.

He cites examples from Nepal’s communist movement to support his position, including founding communist leader Pushpa Lal Shrestha’s defeat in the 1959 election. He also refers to Madhav Kumar Nepal’s resignation in 2008, arguing that it was linked to his political ambition to become president rather than simply a matter of moral responsibility.

Thapa further argues that the March 5 election should not be treated as an ordinary, isolated election result. He claims the election was a consequence of the political developments of September 8 and 9, 2025, and therefore should not be used alone as a basis for demanding Oli’s resignation.

He also points out that Oli was elected UML chair with around 75 percent of the vote at the party’s 11th General Convention.

“The mandate of the general convention cannot in any way be undermined by the result of a particular election,” Thapa wrote.

He argues that removing Oli less than six months after the general convention would be inappropriate.

Oli compared with Pushpa Lal, Madan Bhandari and Manmohan Adhikari

Thapa goes further in defending Oli by comparing his leadership with that of prominent figures in Nepal’s communist movement.

His report discusses the contributions of Pushpa Lal, Madan Bhandari and Manmohan Adhikari before arguing that Oli has also played a significant role in advancing the communist movement.

According to Thapa, Pushpa Lal provided leadership in Marxist philosophy, literature and organisation; Madan Bhandari developed political programmes and ideology creatively; and Manmohan Adhikari offered a new example of state leadership, experience and public service.

Thapa then argues that under Oli’s leadership, the Nepali communist movement was able to advance to a high point of unity, cooperation and progress.

He also recalls the historical removal of Pushpa Lal by a majority of the party’s politburo, arguing that the communist movement subsequently paid a heavy price for that decision.

Thapa warns that a similar attempt to remove Oli through a majority decision could have serious consequences for the party.

He also criticises what he describes as a tendency within the communist movement to insult or undermine leaders while they are in power and recognise their contributions only after they are gone.

Thapa defends Oli against criticism from UML leaders

Thapa has also challenged UML leaders who are demanding greater accountability from Oli despite having been elected to party positions on Oli’s panel at the 11th General Convention.

He argues that those leaders share responsibility for the party’s successes and failures and cannot place the entire blame on the party chair.

“Those elected as office-bearers after being on the panel of the party’s main leader cannot put all the blame on the main leadership and try to become champions of restructuring,” Thapa wrote.

According to Thapa, moral responsibility for the party’s performance should be shared by the entire leadership rather than imposed solely on Oli.

Rejects proposal for special convention

Thapa has also rejected Pokharel’s proposal to convene a meeting of the National General Convention Representatives Council within Ashoj to decide on party restructuring.

He argues that such a move would deepen internal disputes rather than resolve them.

Thapa has also defended the UML’s decision to remove the 70-year age limit and two-term limit for party leadership, rejecting claims that the changes were responsible for the party’s current difficulties.

He cites the Communist Party of China and Cyprus as examples of political parties that have changed leadership restrictions according to their circumstances.

While Thapa accepts some of Pokharel’s recommendations concerning the functioning and mobilisation of the party and its sister organisations, the central message of his report is clear: the UML’s restructuring process should not be used as a means to remove Oli from the party leadership.

One person was killed after an electric vehicle (EV) caught fire near Basanta Chowk in Bharatpur Metropolitan City-9, Chitwan, on Friday morning.

Police said an investigation is underway to determine the cause of the fire.

title.rendered: Ex-lawmaker Ichchha Raj Tamang sentenced to 5 years and 6 months in Civil Cooperative fraud case

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

The Kathmandu District Court has sentenced former lawmaker and businessman Ichchha Raj Tamang to five years and six months in prison in a case involving fraud at Civil Cooperative and organised crime.

A bench led by Judge Krita Bahadur Bohara handed down the sentence on Thursday, finding Tamang guilty of the charges. The court also fined him Rs 50,000.

Tamang, a former member of Parliament, was among 17 people convicted in the case. The court imposed different prison terms and fines on the defendants based on their respective offences.

Those convicted alongside Tamang include Prabin Prasad Pradhan, Keshalal Shrestha, Ram Krishna Poudel, Harihar Prasad Lamichhane, Danahira Tuladhar Kansakar, Sirjana Shakya Tamang, Lalkaji Gurung, Durga Prasad Sangraula, Jayandra Lal Shrestha, Khem Nath Dallakoti, Mukunda Prasad Neupane, Nagendra Bimali, Ram Raj Maskey, Hari Prasad Risal and Meena Gurung.

The case relates to allegations of fraud involving Civil Cooperative and charges of organised crime. The court announced the sentences after holding the defendants guilty of the offences.

title.rendered: The failure to stop 9/11 was a catastrophe. But even bigger mistakes were made in its aftermath

content.rendered:
The September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks were unlike anything the world had seen before.

For America, and the watching world, September 11 (or 9/11) seemed most like a Pearl Harbour moment – a devastating surprise attack by a distant enemy that demanded a response.

But here the distant enemy was not a nation state in the middle of war, it was a ragtag collection of rebels living in mountain hideouts, long underestimated and widely misunderstood.

It took Hollywood movies to convey the horror of Pearl Harbour. But hundreds of millions around the world watched, via live satellite TV feeds, in disbelieving horror as a fully laden commercial aircraft slammed into the first World Trade Centre tower in New York. Hundreds of millions more saw the second tower hit, then witnessed both massive skyscrapers collapsing faster and more completely than seemed possible.

At the time, this felt like a moment that changed everything – a hinge point in history on which so much would turn. Twenty-five years later, that devastating intuition has been confirmed through a cascading series of grim events and tragic mistakes.

Could the September 11 attacks have been prevented?

In September 2026 we live in a world of uncertainty and change. Geopolitics, technology and the physical world are experiencing rapid transformation that fascinates and terrifies in equal measure.

Much of this would have occurred without September 11, but there is a sense in which that day changed all these things.

The collapse of 80 years of global order cannot be said to have simply resulted from the world’s biggest terror attack, but it certainly played a role in triggering a series of responses that has changed all the nations involved.

Could the September 11 attacks have been foreseen and prevented? Absolutely.

Counterterrorism intelligence has evolved massively over the past 25 years. But international terrorism was not new in 2001, nor was al-Qaeda – the terrorist group responsible – completely unknown and operating without scrutiny.

Well before the 9/11 Commission report was published, it was clear there were multiple “if only” moments that may have prevented the attack. If only those sounding the alarm had been listened to. If only the FBI and the CIA had put aside their rivalries to trust each other, fully share what they knew, and act on it. If only the threat posed by al-Qaeda was taken more seriously. At all of these points, the attacks could have been stopped.

The September 11 attacks were audaciously ambitious, involving global orchestration of planning, training and execution on a scale never seen before. In the decades that followed, there have been dozens of mass-casualty terrorist attacks, first by al-Qaeda and then by its spinoff, Islamic State.

The biggest and most effective have been in conflict zones where explosive material is readily available and the tempo of violence makes stopping every attack impossible. But in stable states there have been multiple massive attacks that have killed hundreds at a time. One year after 9/11, in 2002, the October 12 bomb attacks in Bali took 202 lives, 88 of them from Australia.

Lessons have been learned

One area of lasting success in the past 25 years is the development of police lead intelligence. Police forces are now cooperating effectively across international agencies, which have developed remarkable capacity to intercept communications and disrupt planned terror attacks involving cells and networks.

In our region we have witnessed the remarkable results of close cooperation between the Indonesian police and the Australian Federal Police (AFP).

Thankfully, the ratio between attempted large-scale attacks that were detected and disrupted and those that have succeeded is large. Increasingly, the vast majority of terror plots are being thwarted at the planning stage.

The flip side of this is that lone actor attacks, with one or two gunmen acting alone without a cell or a network, remain a constant threat that is not easily countered. Australians were reminded of the horror of such attacks in the Bondi Beach shootings of December 2025.

Were it not for this welcome international cooperation and fast-evolving capacity, the past 25 years would have seen many thousands more lives lost.

However, this does not mean the threat posed by terrorist organisations seeking to inflict a mass casualty attack has been eliminated. Thankfully, it’s highly unlikely an attack of the scale and nature of September 11 could be repeated. But it is not impossible. The best intelligence systems in the world are only as good as the political frameworks in which they exist, and the leaders they serve.

A terrible recent reminder of this occurred on October 7 2023, when the al-Qaeda aligned Hamas terror group, based in the Gaza Strip and supported by Iran, succeeded in a mass attack on Israel.

Even more than was the case with the 2001 attacks, there were multiple intelligence reports and warnings given ahead of October 7. The attacks succeeded not so much because of an intelligence failure as a failure by Israeli leadership to listen to the intelligence.

Almost three years on, there has yet to be a proper reckoning of how Hamas managed to succeed beyond what anyone had dared think possible. Hubris and misplaced confidence in modern technology, a structural unwillingness to listen to junior intelligence officers, particularly women, and a complex web of political interests and cynical manipulation came together to defeat some of the world’s best counterterrorist intelligence.

The years since the October 7 attack by Hamas have shown the true potential of terrorism to provoke an angry, vengeful response that involves striking out without any plan, with catastrophic consequences.

The devastating impact of the response to the Hamas attacks, not just on the two million plus people living in the Gaza Strip but more broadly on Israel, the West Bank, Lebanon and the wider Middle East, is the topic for another discussion.

But it is that vengeful, angry response of understandable outrage that is causing the greatest lasting damage.

How the response to terrorism creates more terror

One clear way the September 11 attacks changed the world was as a catalyst for a decades-long global “War on Terror”. This war never had a clear strategic plan or an agreed endpoint. Instead, it saw first Afghanistan, then Iraq, drawn into destructive conflict that amplified threats and gave new opportunities to terrorist groups. Al-Qaeda had never been as effective as when the occupation of Iraq gave rise to Islamic State.

Incredibly, 20 years after a relentless military campaign by a global coalition fighting the Taliban in Afghanistan, the al-Qaeda aligned terror group is now running a cruel authoritarian state repressing tens of millions, particularly women and children. It presents a growing threat not just to its immediate neighbours but also to the wider world.

The great mistake made was not the failure to stop the September 11 attacks in the first place, although that should have been achieved. It was the failure to understand how terrorism can amplify its impact through our response to outrage.

To properly understand the way in which September 11 functions as a hinge point in history, we need to look back 50 years before 2001 to see the coalescing of the forces that gave rise to al-Qaeda.

Al-Qaeda’s origin story stems from the imprisoning and persecution of Muslim Brotherhood leaders in Egypt in the 1950s. The 1966 prison execution of visionary brotherhood leader Sayyid Qutb saw his brother and remaining Brotherhood leaders flee to Saudi Arabia, where their revolutionary political vision was fused with state-sponsored Wahhabi fundamentalism and the support of Osama bin-Laden. It fuelled the global resistance movement in Afghanistan and gave rise to groups such as Jemaah Islamiyah, the Southeast Asian terror network behind the Bali bombings.

Twenty-five years after September 11, the Salafi jihadi terrorist ideas first sketched out by Sayyid Qutb, then realised by al-Qaeda, remain an enduring threat.

Their impact in Afghanistan and central Asia continues to be underestimated. But it is in Africa where both al-Qaeda and Islamic State continue to expand and evolve, inflicting devastating violence across a dozen conflict zones.

Given the September 11 attacks were 50 years in the making, there’s every reason to believe the threat unleashed through the rise of al-Qaeda presents an enduring problem.

Sadly, the mistakes of the past 25 years seem set to produce more generations of angry young men drawn to the siren song of revolutionary jihad.

title.rendered: A 100-metre gap has cut Kathmandu off from one of Nepal’s most important roads

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

For 12 days, a roughly 100-metre stretch of one of Nepal’s most important highways has been missing.

At Krishnabhir, the Prithvi Highway has slipped into the Trishuli River, severing a crucial road connection between Kathmandu and much of the country. The collapse has stranded a highway that carries passengers, food, fuel and other essential goods into the capital.

The break in the road is small compared with the scale of the network it supports. But its consequences have spread far beyond the landslide site.

Kathmandu, a city of millions, has begun feeling the effects in its markets. The disruption has contributed to shortages of cooking gas, sugar and other essential goods, while prices and reports of black-market trading have risen. The crisis became severe enough that Gauri Kumari Yadav, the minister for industry, commerce and supplies, resigned.

The road closure has also disrupted travel between Kathmandu and Pokhara, Nepal’s tourism capital, severing one of the country’s most heavily used routes.

For infrastructure experts, however, the episode is less a story about one landslide than a warning about the fragility of Nepal’s road system.

The country has alternative highways, but many cannot accommodate the heavy vehicles that normally use the Prithvi Highway. When the main route failed, the alternatives were suddenly expected to perform a role for which they were never adequately built.

“This is not a problem that can be solved by an alternative route,” said Keshav Kumar Sharma, an infrastructure expert and former government secretary. The immediate effort to reopen the highway, he said, is essentially the only practical option available.

That effort involves cutting a temporary track through the same hillside where the highway disappeared.

A highway with few substitutes

The Prithvi Highway is one of the principal arteries connecting Kathmandu with the rest of Nepal. Its failure has demonstrated how much the capital depends on a single road corridor.

The government has designated the Kanti Lokpath, Tribhuvan Rajpath and BP Highway as alternative routes in previous emergencies. But none is a straightforward substitute for the Prithvi Highway.

Large freight vehicles cannot easily use them. That became particularly apparent when LPG tankers carrying cooking gas were unable to reach Kathmandu.

Instead, gas had to be filled into cylinders in the Tarai and transported to the capital, adding another layer of logistical difficulty to an already disrupted supply chain.

“The work being done now to reopen Krishnabhir has no real alternative,” Mr. Sharma said. “But it is also true that the problem has exposed the state’s excessive dependence on a single highway.”

The weakness of the alternatives is not new.

The Tribhuvan Rajpath, whose construction began around 1950, has become an important route for heavy vehicles when the main highways are blocked, but its infrastructure is in poor condition.

The BP Highway, which connects Kathmandu with eastern Nepal, has been damaged by repeated floods in recent years.

The Kanti Lokpath, another route between Kathmandu and Hetauda, is burdened by deteriorating infrastructure and congestion. At present, authorities have been directing freight vehicles from Hetauda toward Kathmandu through the Tribhuvan Rajpath and sending them back through the Kanti Lokpath.

Neither route, however, is designed to absorb the traffic of the Prithvi Highway for an extended period.

The Kathmandu-Tarai/Madhesh Fast Track was supposed to provide another major connection to the capital. The 70.97-kilometre road, being constructed by the Nepal Army, was inaugurated in 2017 and was expected under a revised schedule to be completed this year.

But its progress remains below 50 percent, and a dispute over its starting point on the Kathmandu side remains unresolved.

For years, Nepal has known that its major highways are vulnerable to landslides and floods. Yet the response has often been the same: an alternative route is sought after the main road has already failed.

The Krishnabhir landslide has exposed the consequences of that approach.

The road may reopen. The danger will remain.

The government is working to open a temporary track at the site, but reopening the road will not necessarily make the route safe.

Cracks have appeared higher up the slope above the new track, raising concerns that another landslide could occur during heavy rain. Even the dry season may not eliminate the danger.

Krishnabhir has been an active landslide area in the past.

A temporary track, therefore, may restore movement without resolving the underlying geological problem.

Mr. Sharma said the government would eventually have to consider a more permanent solution. One possibility would be to build two bridges and take the road along the opposite bank of the Trishuli River. Another would involve constructing a road along the river, supported by retaining walls. A third option would be a tunnel.

Each would take considerably longer than cutting a temporary track — somewhere between six months and two years, he estimated.

The government decided to open the temporary track three days after the highway collapsed. Mr. Sharma said a faster decision could have brought an earlier reopening.

Racing to restore the connection

The government now says it hopes to restore traffic within Bhadra, the current Nepali month, although it has not given a fixed date.

The Prime Minister’s Office said Thursday that workers have cut a track about 200 metres long through the hillside at Krishnabhir. Ten machines and 30 workers have been deployed.

The Armed Police Force has installed floodlights, allowing work to continue through the night.

Crews are also working to stabilise the slope above and below the new track. At five other locations, workers are clearing landslides and trying to restore two-way traffic.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah and Infrastructure Minister Sunil Lamsal have discussed the immediate repair of the highway. Technicians from the Department of Roads and the Nepal Geotechnical Society spent four days studying the site before recommending that the temporary track be built.

For Kathmandu’s residents, however, the technical work at Krishnabhir has become inseparable from a more immediate question: how long can the capital function when one road carrying so much of its supplies is cut?

A recurring warning

Nepal has seen versions of this crisis repeatedly.

When landslides close the Muglin-Narayangadh road, authorities routinely divert traffic through Hetauda and the roads connecting Hetauda with Kathmandu. Last year, a dry landslide near Tui Khola blocked the Muglin-Narayangadh section around the Dashain festival, forcing vehicles from eastern and western Nepal to take the Hetauda route.

There are several roads between Hetauda and Kathmandu.

The Tribhuvan Rajpath passes through Palung and Naubise. The Kanti Lokpath connects Hetauda with Thingan and Satdobato. Another road runs through Kulekhani and Pharping.

But two of those routes are largely suited to motorcycles and smaller vehicles, rather than the heavy trucks that keep Kathmandu supplied.

The same roads are called upon when the BP Highway is disrupted.

Each time, the country is reminded that having an alternative route on a map is not the same as having a functioning alternative highway.

That distinction has become painfully clear at Krishnabhir.

A 100-metre section of road disappeared into a river. Twelve days later, the effects are being felt hundreds of kilometres away — in Kathmandu’s markets, in the movement of fuel and food, and in the journeys of thousands of people.

The immediate priority is to put the road back.

But the larger question is harder: why does the failure of such a small section of highway have the power to disrupt so much of the country?

For Nepal, the answer may lie not in the landslide itself, but in the roads that were never built, strengthened or maintained well enough to take its place.

title.rendered: Nepal does not need another disaster portal

content.rendered:
Nepal’s experience with the 2015 earthquake reconstruction, the Earthquake Housing Reconstruction Program (EHRP) Management Information System (MIS), and the disaster information systems developed by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has given the country something far more valuable than technology: institutional learning. These experiences have helped Nepal build the knowledge, systems and institutional capacity needed to inform how it prepares for and responds to future disasters.

The question now is not whether Nepal can build another MIS. We already know it can. The more important question is what the next generation of disaster information systems should look like.

The answer should not be another standalone portal built around a single project or disaster-management function. Nepal now needs to move from project-based MIS platforms to a national, interoperable resilience information ecosystem.

Historically, reconstruction MIS platforms were designed to answer basic administrative questions: Who are the beneficiaries? Where are their houses? What stage of inspection has been completed? Is a grant payment authorised? Which grievances remain unresolved?

EHRP expanded on this foundation, while NDRRMA’s systems demonstrated the broader potential of digital platforms for disaster information, rapid assessment, response and decision-making. Yet these systems have largely evolved around individual programmes or specific functions, often in isolation from one another.

The crucial next step is to connect them.

Nepal should be able to follow the same household, settlement, infrastructure and community across the entire disaster-management cycle—from risk and preparedness, through disaster, assessment and response, to recovery, reconstruction and, ultimately, resilience.

This requires transforming the traditional MIS into a true Resilience Information System.

A future system should not merely report what has happened. It should help the government understand what is at risk, what has been damaged, who is affected, what assistance has been provided, whether reconstruction is safe, and whether a household or community has actually recovered.

To achieve this, the primary unit of information can no longer be limited to a project or an individual beneficiary. The system must instead centre on people, households, communities, infrastructure and place.

Connect what already exists

Achieving this vision does not require building another large, standalone portal. Nepal instead needs an interoperability layer—a National DRR/DRM Interoperability Hub—that allows existing government systems to communicate with one another.

Government databases covering disaster management, social protection, civil registration, health, education, land and local governance already contain enormous value. The problem is that these systems remain institutionally and technically fragmented.

Rather than replacing existing databases, an Interoperability Hub would allow them to exchange trusted information through common standards, application programming interfaces (APIs), shared identifiers and agreed governance arrangements.

In simple terms: do not build another database. Connect the databases we already have.

At the centre of this architecture, the household becomes a longitudinal resilience record.

Building on the lessons of the reconstruction MIS, a household affected by any hazard—whether an earthquake, flood, landslide or fire—could be tracked continuously through its risk exposure, disaster impacts, assistance received, reconstruction progress and remaining vulnerabilities.

Over time, and with strict privacy and security safeguards, this record could also integrate with broader social protection and local government systems.

That would shift a fundamental measure of governance. Instead of asking, “How much money did we spend?”, the system should help us ask, “What changed for this household and community because of that investment?”

That is a much more meaningful measure of recovery and resilience.

From dashboards to decision intelligence

The transition should also move Nepal beyond static dashboards towards dynamic decision intelligence.

A conventional dashboard tells us what is happening now. A modern resilience information system should help decision-makers understand what is likely to happen next.

By combining geographic information systems (GIS), remote sensing, artificial intelligence, climate data and predictive analytics, such a system could identify settlements exposed to multiple hazards, vulnerable infrastructure and concentrations of at-risk populations. This would allow limited mitigation and preparedness resources to be directed to the places where they are most needed.

The objective is not technology for its own sake. It is better decision-making.

Ultimately, disaster data should become a shared basis for action, giving federal, provincial and local authorities, as well as security and humanitarian actors, a single, trusted operational picture during a crisis.

A National Disaster Risk and Resilience Information Architecture

The proposed National Disaster Risk and Resilience Information Architecture (NDRRIA) can provide the framework for this transition.

At its core, the architecture would focus on improving disaster-risk intelligence, governance, coordination and resilience monitoring. It would connect information from national, sectoral, local and external systems, including those covering disaster management, health, infrastructure, weather and development.

A central data-exchange layer would allow different agencies and systems to share standardised information through common protocols and identifiers. This would make it possible to use the same underlying information to support risk assessment, early warning, preparedness, response, recovery, reconstruction and long-term resilience planning.

The architecture would also establish the governance arrangements needed for federal, provincial and local authorities to work from common standards and institutional mechanisms. This would need to be supported by stronger institutional capacity, appropriate legal and policy frameworks, public-private partnerships and meaningful community engagement.

Taken together, these elements would create a national information-sharing and governance architecture designed to turn disaster-related data into coordinated decisions that reduce risk and build resilience.

Six transitions for Nepal

Nepal’s path forward requires six fundamental transitions.

First, it must move from standalone MIS platforms to interoperable systems that can communicate across agencies and programmes. Data should no longer remain trapped within the boundaries of individual projects or institutions.

Second, it should move from project records to household resilience histories, allowing the experiences of people and communities to be followed across successive disasters and recovery efforts.

Third, it must move from construction monitoring to long-term outcome monitoring. Completing a house, road or infrastructure project is an output. Whether that investment has actually reduced vulnerability and improved people’s lives is an outcome.

Fourth, Nepal should move from historical reporting to predictive intelligence. Knowing what happened is important, but knowing where risks are emerging and what could happen next is far more useful for prevention.

Fifth, it should move from simple dashboards to decision-support systems that help authorities interpret information and determine where intervention is most urgently required.

Finally, Nepal must move from temporary, project-specific disaster MIS platforms to permanent national resilience infrastructure.

These transitions are not simply technological. They represent a shift in how the state understands and manages disaster risk.

The ultimate legacy of the 2015 reconstruction should therefore be more than the systems created to manage a single national crisis. It should be the institutional knowledge that Nepal can use digital information and coordinated systems to manage complex risks over the long term.

The country now has an opportunity to connect those foundations into a unified National Disaster Risk and Resilience Information Architecture.

When the next disaster strikes, the government should not have to ask, “Where is the data?” It should be able to ask the more important question: “What is the data telling us to do next?”

title.rendered: Who is the new Industry Minister, Deepak Kumar Sah?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Newly appointed Industry, Commerce and Supplies Minister Deepak Kumar Sah has taken a winding political route to the Cabinet, moving from a key role in the formation of the Janamat Party to becoming a lawmaker and minister from the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).

Sah, an engineer by profession, was appointed minister on Thursday after Gauri Kumari Yadav resigned from the post amid the government’s failure to resolve the shortage of cooking gas.

Elected to the House of Representatives from Sunsari-4, Sah entered Parliament for the first time in the 2026 election, defeating Nepali Congress leader Gyanendra Bahadur Karki by a wide margin. Sah secured 42,771 votes, while Karki received 16,587.

But Sah’s political career predates his entry into Parliament.

He was among the key figures involved in the formation of the Janamat Party and was initially a close associate of party chair CK Raut. The two had known each other for around three decades and were also connected by their engineering backgrounds.

Sah provided significant support to Raut during the early days of Janamat and later held two senior positions in the party—as vice-chair and chair of its Disciplinary Commission.

The relationship was close enough that, in Janamat’s early days, the party’s central office operated from Sah’s home in Suryabinayak-3, Bhaktapur.

Deepak Kumar Sah had also financially supported Raut when he was seeking admission to Pulchowk Engineering Campus, an episode Raut later mentioned in his book.

The close relationship, however, eventually broke down.

According to Janamat leaders in Madhesh familiar with the two, financial issues contributed to the growing differences between Raut and Sah. Their relationship also became strained over the party’s decision to remove Goma Labh from the House of Representatives.

Sah, who was then heading the party’s Disciplinary Commission, had urged the leadership to reconsider the decision. Raut, meanwhile, repeatedly wrote to then-Speaker Devraj Ghimire seeking Labh’s removal from Parliament. Ghimire did not act on the request.

The differences between Raut and Sah subsequently widened. Janamat sought clarification from Sah before suspending him and eventually expelling him from the party in August.

The party accused Sah of failing to fulfil his responsibilities as vice-chair, acting against Raut, violating the party statute and holding factional meetings aimed at splitting the party. Janamat also accused him of continuing to use the party’s name, flag and official stamp after his suspension.

Deepak Kumar Sah then sought to establish a political base of his own.

He formed the Janaswaraj Party and registered it with the Election Commission. However, the party faced a legal challenge from Raut, who opposed the recognition of a new party formed largely by former Janamat members.

The court ultimately did not recognise the Janaswaraj Party under Sah’s leadership.

Sah then registered another party, Sarvodaya, with the Election Commission. The party was given the corn cob as its election symbol, while many of its members were former Janamat leaders and cadres.

That political venture was also short-lived.

Shortly before the 2026 election, Sah joined the RSP, while Sarvodaya merged with the party. The move opened the way for him to contest the Sunsari-4 constituency on an RSP ticket.

The election marked Sah’s first electoral contest. He had not contested the 2022 election from Janamat.

His victory over Karki gave him his first parliamentary mandate and, within months, a place in the Cabinet.

Sah’s political journey has not been without controversy within the RSP either.

He came under scrutiny over a report he independently prepared concerning an incident in Kaptanganj, Sunsari, on July 25. The dispute, involving two communities, later spread to parts of Madhesh. Three people were killed in Sunsari and one in Siraha as tensions escalated.

Sah has said he prepared a separate report on the Sunsari incident following verbal instructions from Home Minister Sudhan Gurung.

Questions were nevertheless raised within the RSP over whether the report had been prepared without a formal party decision. He also faced criticism over the report’s contents, which allegedly implicated RSP lawmakers in the incident.

From helping establish Janamat and serving as one of its senior leaders to being expelled from the party, forming two political outfits and eventually joining the RSP, Sah’s political journey has taken several turns.

He now finds himself in the Cabinet, tasked with leading the ministry responsible for industry, commerce and supplies at a time when the government is under pressure to address the country’s cooking gas shortage.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

Loss and Damage Fund responds to Nepal’s request for emergency assistance

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has responded to Nepal’s request for emergency financial assistance following the devastating floods in Rasuwa. Nepal had written to the board of the UN climate change-related fund on September 1, arguing that climate change had contributed to the floods that struck Rasuwa on August 26 and requesting immediate financial support. Government officials said the board’s response was received a week later.

Nepal estimates Rs 723 billion needed to rebuild after Rasuwa floods

The Nepal government has estimated that Rs 723.31 billion will be required for reconstruction and recovery following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26. According to a Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment report prepared by a joint technical team involving the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, infrastructure recovery alone will require Rs 473.57 billion.

Industry Minister Gauri Kumari Yadav resigns amid controversial remarks on LPG shortage

Industry Minister Gauri Kumari Yadav has resigned from her post amid controversy over her remarks regarding the shortage of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) in the country. Yadav submitted her resignation to Prime Minister Balen Shah, according to her communications coordinator Kamal Chaulagain.

Cabinet approves PM Balen Shah’s US visit for UN General Assembly

The government has approved Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s upcoming visit to the United States to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. A Cabinet meeting held on Thursday approved the visit of the delegation led by Prime Minister Shah.

Opposition parties urge govt to form parliamentary special committee on disaster response

Opposition parties represented in the House of Representatives have decided to urge the government to form a parliamentary special committee to make disaster management, relief, rescue, search and rehabilitation efforts more effective.

Apple enters foldable era with iPhone Duo alongside iPhone 18 Pro lineup

Apple has officially unveiled its first-ever foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo, alongside the new iPhone 18 Pro series, Apple Watch Series 12, and AirPods 5 at its annual global hardware keynote on Wednesday night. The launch marks a significant shift for the Cupertino-based tech giant as it directly enters the foldable market, long dominated by rivals Samsung and Huawei.

Nepal beat Oman by 87 runs to reach ACC Premier Cup final

Nepal secured a convincing 87-run victory over Oman in the semi-final of the ACC Premier Cup being held in Malaysia, thanks to an outstanding performance by its spin bowlers. Chasing Nepal’s target of 148 runs, Oman were bowled out for 60 in 28.1 overs.

title.rendered: Cabinet approves PM Balen Shah’s US visit for UN General Assembly

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The government has approved Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s upcoming visit to the United States to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

A Cabinet meeting held on Thursday approved the visit of the delegation led by Prime Minister Shah.

According to Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel, who is also the government spokesperson, Shah-led delegation will leave for the United States on September 22 and return to Nepal on September 26.

Shah is scheduled to travel to New York later this month for the UN General Assembly, where Nepal is expected to raise issues including climate justice and the recent Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster.

This will be Shah’s first foreign trip since he assumed office as prime minister in March.

title.rendered: Kunwar and Khatri promoted to secretary

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The government has promoted two civil servants to the post of secretary.

title.rendered: Rebuilding flood-damaged energy sector to cost Rs 390 billion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The reconstruction of the energy sector damaged by the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers is estimated to cost Rs 390 billion, according to a rapid damage and needs assessment.

The Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) report prepared by a joint technical team comprising the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority found that hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 783 MW were damaged in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

The report identified damage to 13 hydropower projects and five solar power projects with a combined capacity of 24 MW. The energy and road sectors suffered the largest damage from the floods.

According to the report, Rs 390.623 billion will be required for the recovery and reconstruction of the energy and grid systems alone.

Among the damaged projects are the 216-MW Upper Trishuli-1, 111-MW Rasuwagadhi, 120-MW Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi, 20-MW Langtang Khola, 22-MW Chilime, 5-MW Mailung Khola, 24-MW Trishuli Hydropower Station, 14.1-MW Devighat Hydropower Station, 60-MW Upper Trishuli-3A, 37-MW Upper Trishuli-3B and 15.6-MW Middle Trishuli Ganga.

The 25-MW Nuwakot Solar Power Project and other solar projects were also affected.

The report said the floods damaged power-generation facilities, access roads, transmission systems and other infrastructure.

It also stated that 917 employees and workers of the affected projects remain unaccounted for. The Nepal Army, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police, foreign experts and technicians, and technical teams from the affected companies are involved in search and rescue efforts.

title.rendered: Nepal estimates Rs 723 billion needed to rebuild after Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The Nepal government has estimated that Rs 723.31 billion will be required for reconstruction and recovery following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26.

According to a Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment report prepared by a joint technical team involving the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, infrastructure recovery alone will require Rs 473.57 billion.

The infrastructure sector accounts for around 75 percent of the total recovery needs identified in the assessment.

Energy and roads suffered the most extensive damage among infrastructure sectors. Thirteen hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 759 MW and five solar power plants with a total capacity of 24 MW were affected by the floods.

The report estimates that Rs 390.62 billion will be required to restore the energy and power grid systems.

The floods also damaged 69 kilometres of roads. Thirty-three motorable bridges were washed away and four others suffered partial damage.

Of the 64 suspension bridges located in the affected areas, 53 were damaged.

The overall recovery of transport infrastructure in the affected areas is estimated to cost Rs 73.34 billion.

Rs 103.55 billion needed for social infrastructure

The floods also caused significant physical and economic damage to social and productive sectors.

A total of 7,570 private houses were damaged across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan. In addition, 48 public buildings, 18 schools, seven health facilities and 30 cultural heritage sites were damaged.

The government estimates that Rs 103.55 billion will be required for recovery in the social sector.

The productive sector—which includes businesses, banks and agriculture—will require another Rs 50.77 billion for recovery, according to the assessment.

The floods affected 1,806 hectares of agricultural crops, 17 bank branches and around 4,800 business establishments.

Among the 15 local units affected across the five districts, Bidur Municipality of Nuwakot recorded the highest number of damaged private houses, with 3,026 homes affected.

The report estimates that Rs 94.75 billion will be needed for disaster risk reduction and river management, while Rs 515.4 million will be required for the management of mud and debris generated by the floods.

Reconstruction divided into two phases

The assessment has divided the recovery and reconstruction process into two phases.

For immediate relief and short-term reconstruction over the next six months, the government estimates a requirement of Rs 8.74 billion.

Long-term reconstruction, meanwhile, is expected to cost Rs 714.58 billion.

The assessment provides the government’s initial estimate of the financial resources required to restore infrastructure, social services, productive activities and disaster management systems in areas affected by the August 26 floods.

title.rendered: 11 things to look out for in Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Apple has unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, bringing a new camera system, a more powerful chip, longer battery life and expanded AI capabilities.

The new Pro models were announced on September 9. Pre-orders will begin on September 12, with availability starting September 18 in more than 65 countries and regions.

Here are 11 things to look out for in Apple’s latest iPhones.

1. Variable aperture comes to the iPhone

The iPhone 18 Pro features a 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera with variable aperture — a first for the iPhone.

The camera can automatically adjust the aperture based on lighting and depth of field. Users can also manually choose from four aperture settings.

2. More control for photographers

Apple has added Pro controls to the Camera app, allowing users to adjust aperture, shutter speed and white balance.

A histogram has also been added to help users monitor exposure.

3. New camera features for video

The camera system gets several video upgrades, including the ability to apply Cinematic effects after recording videos at up to 60 frames per second.

Time-lapse videos can now be recorded in 4K Dolby Vision HDR, while Audio Mix gets new algorithms designed to improve voice quality and isolate music.

4. Apple introduces a tool to check photo authenticity

The iPhone 18 Pro introduces Apple Reference Image, which is designed to help determine whether a photograph has been edited.

The feature creates an unalterable reference image that users can compare with the main photo in the Photos app.

5. A20 Pro chip moves to 2nm

The new Pro models are powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, built using 2-nanometre process technology.

The seven-core GPU is up to 40 percent faster than the A19 Pro, while the chip offers twice the AI processing power of its predecessor.

6. A bigger cooling system

Apple has redesigned the iPhone’s thermal management system with a new vapor chamber that has three times the surface area of the system used in the iPhone 17 Pro.

Apple says this can deliver up to a 40 percent gain in sustained performance.

7. Battery life gets a major boost

The iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max reaches up to 45 hours.

Apple says five minutes of wired charging on the Pro Max can provide around seven hours of video playback.

8. Dynamic Island gets smaller

The Dynamic Island has been redesigned to occupy less space while providing more information.

It can now display three Live Activities at once, while continuing to support Face ID and other functions.

9. Siri gets an AI makeover

Apple is rolling out Siri AI in beta with iOS 27.

The new Siri can use personal context from messages, emails and photos, understand what’s on the screen and perform actions across apps.

It can also be used through the Camera app to provide information about what’s in front of the user.

10. eSIM-only models get a larger battery

In selected markets, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be available as eSIM-only models.

By removing the physical SIM slot, Apple says it has created additional space for a larger battery. The eSIM-only models get up to two additional hours of video playback.

11. The price starts at $1,199

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 in the US, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299.

Both models will be available with storage options ranging from 256GB to 2TB.

The phones come in four finishes: black, silver, glacier and burgundy.

Pre-orders begin September 12, with availability starting September 18.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Apple’s annual Apple Event unfolded in California with a series of massive hardware and software updates. Featuring executive presentations and product debuts, the event marked one of the biggest updates to Apple’s ecosystem in years.

If you missed the livestream, here are the seven biggest announcements and takeaways you need to know:

1. The iPhone Duo marks Apple’s entry into foldables

The biggest highlight of the event was Apple’s “One More Thing” announcement: the iPhone Duo. Unfolding like a passport, the device features a 5.4-inch outer cover screen that expands into a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR display inside.

Apple solved traditional foldable flaws by incorporating multi-layer flexible glass with a custom nano-texture finish to minimize the screen crease, a variable-torque titanium hinge, and an under-display FaceTime camera.

“We started with the experience that we wanted for ourselves — a larger display that feels as natural and intuitive as iPad, then we brought together thoughtful design with breakthrough engineering in a way only Apple can,” said John Ternus, CEO of Apple.

2. Apple Pencil support comes to iPhone for the first time

Alongside the folding screen, Apple confirmed that the iPhone Duo will support the Apple Pencil (USB-C) on both its outer cover screen and large inner display. Users can sketch, annotate PDFs, and take handwritten notes directly on an iPhone display for the first time.

3. iPhone 18 Pro introduces physical variable aperture

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max received major camera upgrades. The new 48MP Fusion main camera includes a custom 6-blade mechanical variable aperture system (f/1.8) that dynamically shifts to allow up to 50% more light into the sensor for low-light shots, deep landscape photos, and portrait mode background blur.

“Being able to change the aperture provides more control for light intake and depth of field, so iPhone 18 Pro has a new 48 megapixel fusion main camera with variable aperture for creative control that wasn’t possible before,” said Ternus.

4. Apple Silicon leaps to 2nm with A20 Pro & dual Neural Engines

At the core of the new iPhone 18 Pro series and iPhone Duo is the A20 Pro chip, built on an industry-first 2-nanometer architecture.

  • 32-Core Neural Engine: Features dual Neural Engines to deliver twice the AI processing power on-device.
  • Next-Gen Thermals: Paired with a redesigned 3x larger vapor chamber to sustain up to 40% higher peak performance during heavy workloads and AAA gaming.

5. Siri gets a deep AI overhaul and a standalone app

Powered by the A20 Pro chip, Siri AI gains context awareness across system and third-party apps. The assistant can now take action across over 300,000 apps—such as pulling recipe details from email threads to update your grocery list—and features a dedicated Siri App on the iOS 27 home screen for tracking past prompt conversations.

“Siri AI can find what you need and get more done than ever… It is personal intelligence that is actually personal,” said Ternus.

6. Active Noise Cancellation becomes standard across AirPods 5

Apple completely refreshed its open-ear audio lineup with the AirPods 5. For the first time, Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) comes standard across all models, delivering 50% improved noise reduction in an open-ear design. Apple also introduced stem-swipe volume controls and longer battery life on its step-up wireless charging model.

7. Apple Watch Series 12 introduces “Audio Intelligence” & 5-second heart tracking

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 featured significant health and audio upgrades:

  • Continuous Health Sensing: The sensor array takes background heart rate readings every 5 seconds (60 times more frequently) and HRV every 5 minutes.
  • Audio Intelligence: Powered by the S11 chip, the watch can now run Live Rewind (replaying and transcribing the last 15 seconds of audio) and Siri Recap for private ambient meeting note summaries.

title.rendered: Germany provides EUR 8.05 million to Nepal after Bhotekoshi Floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Germany has pledged EUR 8.05 million in assistance to Nepal to support communities affected by the recent Bhotekoshi floods and contribute to recovery and disaster-resilience efforts.

The Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany in Kathmandu said in a statement that the assistance combines emergency humanitarian aid, development cooperation and support channelled through European and multilateral mechanisms.

As part of the emergency response, Germany is providing more than EUR 500,000 worth of relief supplies through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism at the request of the Government of Nepal. The supplies include kitchen sets, tarpaulins, mosquito nets, drinking-water equipment and camp beds.

Germany is also providing EUR 200,000 in direct humanitarian assistance to two civil society organisations. The projects will support pregnant women, new mothers and newborns, while also creating income opportunities for affected households, supporting infrastructure recovery and improving conditions in displacement camps.

In addition, Germany has mobilised EUR 7.35 million in development assistance through the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Implemented by GIZ, the support will focus on health, energy and water supply while strengthening climate- and disaster-resilient infrastructure.

“Germany stands with the people of Nepal in this difficult time,” the embassy said, expressing solidarity with victims and their families.

—RSS

title.rendered: NNJS contributes Rs 14.14 million to Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Nepal Netra Jyoti Sangh (NNJS) has contributed Rs 14.14 million to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support the rescue, relief and rehabilitation of people affected by the recent Bhotekoshi River floods in Rasuwa.

NNJS General Secretary Bharat Bahadur Chand handed over the cheque to Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle on Wednesday.

Of the total amount, Rs 9,974,506 was collected institutionally through hospitals, eye care centres and district branches under the NNJS network, while Rs 4,166,635 was contributed by its employees and volunteers.

The Bhotekoshi floods on August 26 caused significant loss of life and property in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. In view of the disaster’s serious impact on the daily lives, health and livelihoods of affected communities, the Sangh collected the funds in response to the Government of Nepal’s call for contributions to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

NNJS said the contribution was made by consolidating donations from its hospitals, eye care centres, district branches, social workers, well-wishers, employees and volunteers.

Alongside financial assistance, the Sangh has been providing free healthcare services in affected areas. It has continued to provide eye examinations, treatment, consultations and other essential eye care services to people deprived of healthcare due to the disaster.

The Sangh said collective efforts by the government, civil society, private sector and various organisations were essential to protect lives, safeguard health and support the rehabilitation of disaster-affected communities.

It said it would continue providing humanitarian assistance and healthcare services based on the needs and circumstances of affected communities.

—RSS

title.rendered: Apple enters foldable era with iPhone Duo alongside iPhone 18 Pro lineup

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Apple has officially unveiled its first-ever foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo, alongside the new iPhone 18 Pro series, Apple Watch Series 12, and AirPods 5 at its annual global hardware keynote on Wednesday night.

The launch marks a significant shift for the Cupertino-based tech giant as it directly enters the foldable market, long dominated by rivals Samsung and Huawei.

The book-style iPhone Duo features a passport-style aerospace titanium frame with a 5.4-inch outer cover screen that unfolds into a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR inner display. Designed for heavy multitasking, the device runs on Apple’s newest 2nm A20 Pro chipset and carries a starting price of $1,999 (approx. NPR 268,000 before taxes).

It is also Apple’s first completely eSIM-only smartphone globally, eliminating physical SIM card slots entirely, and introduces high-density dual silicon batteries designed to sustain up to 44 hours of usage.

Hosting his first major product keynote as Apple’s new Chief Executive Officer, John Ternus framed the launch as a landmark moment in personal technology.

“The iPhone Duo represents the most radical leap in the history of the iPhone,” Ternus stated during the event. “By combining two decades of display engineering, custom silicon, and dynamic hardware design, we are delivering an entirely new form factor that gives users an unprecedented workspace without compromising on performance or portability.”

Alongside the foldable device, Apple introduced the flagship iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, featuring refined cameras with cinematic slow-motion support at 60 fps, upgraded Siri AI integration via iOS 27, and a new signature Burgundy color option.

In addition to smartphones, Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, both equipped with an advanced Health Sensing System capable of tracking Dynamic Readiness scores and calculating a user’s “Health Age.” The company also launched the AirPods 5, featuring upgraded Active Noise Cancellation and real-time Live Translation capabilities.

Global Pricing & Availability

Authorized Apple resellers in Nepal are expected to announce local pricing and official pre-order dates for the iPhone 18 series and wearable lineup in the coming weeks ahead of Dashain.

title.rendered: Lawmaker Thapa calls for early warning system linking mountains and glaciers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Nepali Congress lawmaker Sunil Bahadur Thapa has urged the government to develop an effective disaster early warning system that takes into account not only monsoon rainfall but also mountains and glaciers.

Speaking at the National Assembly meeting on Thursday, Thapa said the devastating Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa had raised serious questions about Nepal’s early warning systems, rescue capacity and infrastructure development model.

“Serious questions have been raised about Nepal’s infrastructure, disaster preparedness infrastructure, early warning systems, rescue capacity and reconstruction system,” he said. “We now need to develop an early warning system that considers not only rainfall but also mountains and glaciers.”

Thapa stressed that the government must address the basic needs of thousands of people who have gone missing in disasters, those who have lost family members and those whose lives have been severely affected. He said the destruction of homes, roads, bridges, schools, health facilities and drinking water infrastructure caused by the floods had seriously affected the national economy and called for international assistance.

Thapa said the state must firmly stand with people and families displaced by disasters. “Immediate priorities should be relief, rescue, safe shelter, food, drinking water and health services,” he said, drawing the government’s attention to the needs of the flood victims.

He said providing safe shelter and healthcare to flood victims should remain the state’s top priority alongside rescue efforts.

Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone, introducing a new design, larger display and several new features.

1. A 7.6-inch foldable display

The iPhone Duo opens into a 7.6-inch inner display — the largest screen ever featured on an iPhone.

2. A 5.4-inch display when folded

When closed, the phone has a 5.4-inch outer display and is designed to remain compact enough for one-handed use.

4. 48MP cameras and new photography features

Siri AI can understand what is displayed on the screen, work with information across apps and use personal context to assist users.

6. Titanium body and IP68 rating

Apple says the phone is built with grade 5 titanium, Ceramic Shield protection and a redesigned hinge. It is also rated IP68 for water and dust resistance.

7. It starts at $1,999

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the US for the 256GB model.

Pre-orders begin October 16, with sales starting October 23.

title.rendered: NC President Thapa pledges flexibility for party unity

content.rendered:
Waling (Syangja), September 10

Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa has said he is ready to be more flexible for the sake of party unity.

Addressing a condolence assembly organised by the Nepali Congress Syangja district chapter on the 45th day of the death of NC senior leader and former Deputy Prime Minister Gopal Man Shrestha, Thapa said he would move forward responsibly to strengthen the party.

“I pledge to be flexible for the sake of party unity. It is also necessary to take serious steps to address the shortcomings within the party,” Thapa said, adding that doing so would not be easy. “Some steps may have to be ruthless for the sake of the party’s welfare.”

Stating that the Nepali Congress had acted responsibly to resolve problems during difficult times in the country, Thapa said the party would work to regain the trust and confidence of citizens.

Thapa said the late Shrestha had played a significant role in strengthening the party. He also said it was not the right time to blame the government as the country had suffered massive destruction.

NC General Secretary Pradip Paudel, Gandaki Province Chief Minister Surendra Raj Pandey, NC Gandaki President Shukra Raj Sharma and other speakers recalled Shrestha’s contributions to the party and the political system.

content.rendered:

Nepali Congress lawmaker Mohan Acharya, who represents Rasuwa in the House of Representatives, has urged the government to introduce a special education package for children affected by the Bhotekoshi floods.

Speaking at the House meeting on Thursday, Acharya said many children who had lost their parents faced an uncertain future, while those whose parents survived were also struggling to see a way forward.

“Some children have lost their parents, and their future is already in darkness, while even those with parents are facing an uncertain future,” Acharya said. “I strongly urge the government to introduce a special education package and take action for these children.”

Acharya also urged the government to implement insurance provisions as soon as possible in areas affected by the floods.

He said around 90 per cent of employees and people engaged in various professions and businesses in Rasuwa had gone missing in the Bhotekoshi floods.

“Hydropower, tourism and the Rasuwagadhi border point were the main sources of income for Rasuwa,” he said, adding that many employees, entrepreneurs and professionals who had been working in the district were now unaccounted for.

He said those involved in businesses, industries and other professions in Rasuwa had lost almost everything, while survivors were struggling under the burden of loans after the floods swept away their property.

title.rendered: Woman sent to jail over alleged honey-trap scheme targeting government employee

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

A woman has been sent to jail for trial after being accused of honey-trapping a senior-level government employee and extorting money from him by threatening to make their private interactions public.

The woman, identified as 32-year-old Kusum Gubhaju of Ramechhap, was remanded to custody by the Kathmandu District Court on Wednesday.

A bench of Judge Jagat Bahadur Poudel ordered that Gubhaju be sent to jail pending trial. Police subsequently took her into custody in accordance with the court order.

According to the police investigation, Gubhaju allegedly developed a close relationship with a government employee after they met through social media. The two reportedly met in person, travelled together and stayed overnight at hotels.

The employee later approached the District Police Range, Bhadra Kali, Kathmandu, claiming that Gubhaju had repeatedly demanded money and threatened to expose their private conversations, photographs and meetings if he refused to pay.

According to the complaint filed by the employee, the two had also exchanged intimate messages on social media. Gubhaju allegedly began demanding money while threatening to make their photographs and details of their meetings and overnight stays public and send them to his family members.

The complaint states that their relationship, which began through social media, progressed to meetings at a cafe in Baluwatar, outings and eventually staying together overnight. The relationship reportedly deteriorated after Gubhaju began demanding money.

“I was threatened that everything would be made public if I did not pay Rs 5 million. I was forced to pay Rs 2.7 million, but the demands for money did not stop,” the employee stated in his complaint.

The employee claimed that he paid Gubhaju Rs 2.7 million after receiving repeated threats.

According to his complaint, he transferred Rs 1 million through ConnectIPS on May 29, 2026. He allegedly made another Rs 1 million payment through two cheques issued by Rastriya Banijya Bank—Rs 750,000 and Rs 250,000—on June 2. He also claimed to have paid Rs 700,000 in cash.

The employee said he eventually went to the police after the alleged threats and demands continued despite the payments.

Police arrested Gubhaju on August 12 following his complaint. She has denied the allegations.

In her statement to police, Gubhaju claimed that the government employee himself had sent her a friend request on Facebook and proposed a relationship. She also claimed that he had arranged a room for her to stay in as his wife.

She claimed that the employee voluntarily gave her Rs 2 million, while the remaining Rs 700,000 was provided to cover expenses related to accommodation, food and living costs.

According to her statement, the two lived together in a rented room in Basundhara for around a year.

Police records also show that the dispute between the two had previously reached the police before Gubhaju’s arrest. Following a dispute on May 21, the two had reached an agreement at the Kalimati Police Circle.

At the time, both parties agreed not to interfere in each other’s affairs and were handed over to their relatives. The employee does not appear to have made any further payments to Gubhaju after that agreement, according to the case records.

Gubhaju has been charged under two separate provisions: Section 253 of the National Penal Code, 2017, which prohibits obtaining criminal benefit, and Section 47 of the Electronic Transactions Act, 2006, concerning the unlawful publication of material in electronic form.

A person convicted of obtaining criminal benefit under Section 253 can face up to three years in prison and a fine of up to Rs 30,000.

Under Section 47 of the Electronic Transactions Act, a conviction can result in a fine of up to Rs 100,000, imprisonment for up to five years, or both.

The allegations against Gubhaju remain subject to determination by the court.

title.rendered: NEPSE falls 13.85 points as all sector indices decline

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

All major indicators of the Nepal stock market declined on Thursday, with the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index falling 13.85 points to close at 2,531 points.

The benchmark index had dropped 15.43 points on Wednesday.

Turnover also declined to Rs 3.99 billion from Rs 4.19 billion recorded in the previous session.

Shares of 69 companies gained on Thursday, while 201 companies recorded losses and eight remained unchanged.

The Manufacturing and Processing sector recorded the biggest decline, falling 1.14 percent. All other sectoral indices declined by less than 1 percent.

The Banking sector fell 0.47 percent, Development Bank 0.34 percent, Finance 0.66 percent, Hotels and Tourism 0.50 percent, Hydropower 0.55 percent, Investment 0.41 percent, Life Insurance 0.17 percent, Microfinance 0.56 percent, Non-Life Insurance 0.78 percent, Others 0.64 percent and Trading 0.27 percent.

title.rendered: Ministry, medical council team to probe woman giving birth outside Rajbiraj Hospital

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene has expressed serious concern over an incident in which a woman gave birth outside the premises of Gajendra Narayan Singh Sagarmatha Hospital in Rajbiraj.

A five-member team from the Nepal Medical Council, including Registrar Dr Suprabhat Shrestha and Ethical Committee member Dr Ajay Shah, will travel to Rajbiraj today to investigate the incident. Dr Pawan Jung Rayamajhi, chief of the Curative Services Division at the ministry, will also join the team in the investigation.

The ministry has sought an explanation from the hospital regarding the incident. It said an on-site investigation would be conducted to establish the facts and that those found responsible would face action in accordance with the prevailing law.

The hospital is also preparing to form a separate committee to investigate the incident.

The ministry said no person seeking treatment at a health institution should be denied healthcare services. It said it was taking the incident seriously and had initiated a detailed review and necessary investigation.

title.rendered: Lawmaker Awal says rescue teams in Rasuwa lack essential equipment

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Nepali Congress lawmaker Gangalakshmi Awal has said rescue teams deployed in the flood-affected areas of Rasuwa are facing a shortage of essential rescue equipment.

Speaking during the emergency session of the House of Representatives on Thursday, Awal said the teams involved in rescue operations lacked basic equipment.

She told the House that Arun Sainju of Bhaktapur, a member of the RN-A 16 rescue team, had informed her about the shortage.

“He called me from Timure this morning and informed me that the rescue team lacked equipment,” she said. “He said they do not have a meter to measure oxygen levels. He also said they do not have torches and that some of the ropes have snapped.”

According to Awal, Sainju has been in Rasuwa since August 26, working alongside security personnel to rescue people affected by the floods. “I would like to urge the government to immediately provide the rescue teams with the necessary equipment,” she said.

Awal also said she had received information from the District Administration Office that 25 people from Bhaktapur remained missing following the Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa, while one person had died.

title.rendered: Loss and Damage Fund responds to Nepal’s request for emergency assistance

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has responded to Nepal’s request for emergency financial assistance following the devastating floods in Rasuwa.

Nepal had written to the board of the UN climate change-related fund on September 1, arguing that climate change had contributed to the floods that struck Rasuwa on August 26 and requesting immediate financial support. Government officials said the board’s response was received a week later.

In its letter dated September 10, the fund’s board said consultations and coordination were underway to respond to Nepal’s request for immediate assistance as quickly as possible.

The letter, signed by the fund’s co-chairs Camila Minerva Rodríguez Tavarez and Georg Børsting, recommends that the board consider various options within the existing mandate, structure, framework, policies and procedures of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.

“In this process, we recommend that the Board consider various options within the existing mandate, structure, framework, policies and procedures of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, so that our response can be as swift and meaningful as possible,” the letter states.

The co-chairs also expressed their condolences to the people of Nepal over the loss of life and extensive damage caused by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, and expressed solidarity with the Nepali people.

Addressing Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle and Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Geeta Chaudhary, the letter also thanked the Nepal government for its readiness to provide preliminary assessments, official data, satellite information and estimates of the damage.

Dr Maheshwar Dhakal, head of the Climate Change Management Division under the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment and an alternate member of the fund’s board, described the response as a historic development.

“This letter is extremely important in the history of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. It will lay a foundation for addressing climate-induced loss and damage in developing countries around the world,” said Dhakal.

Nepal seeks $20 million initially

The Rasuwa floods on August 26 have so far claimed 1,377 lives, while 5,130 people remain missing, according to the figures cited by the government. More than 7,500 people have been injured.

A preliminary assessment by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has estimated that the floods caused physical damage worth around Rs 700 billion.

Nepal had sent its request after informal discussions at the international board of the Loss and Damage Fund following the Rasuwa disaster. The letter was signed by Finance Minister Wagle and Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Chaudhary.

According to alternate board member Dhakal, discussions at the informal board meetings focused on Nepal seeking more than Rs 3 billion—or $20 million—in compensation.

A government minister, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Nepal had initially requested $20 million in emergency assistance.

“We have asked for $20 million for now. Once the flood situation is over, we will assess the damage and seek additional funds,” the minister said.

A report published by The New York Times, citing board member Richard Sherman, said the fund could potentially provide Nepal with up to $20 million, equivalent to around Rs 3.04 billion.

Experts have argued that Nepal should receive financial support not only for losses and damages caused by climate-related disasters but also in recognition of its contribution to environmental protection.

Nepal is among the countries with very low carbon dioxide emissions, while it plays an important role in protecting its mountains, forests, vegetation and biodiversity.

Nepal plans to raise issue at UN General Assembly

The issue of the Rasuwa floods is also expected to be raised by Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the United Nations General Assembly scheduled for September 24.

Government ministers said Shah is preparing to travel to the General Assembly himself and raise the issue following the disaster. Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal is scheduled to lead Nepal’s delegation to the gathering.

One minister, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the government had decided that the issue should be raised at the highest political level as Nepal was suffering the consequences of a disaster despite having made a minimal contribution to climate change.

“We have reached the conclusion that the Prime Minister himself should raise this issue at the General Assembly because Nepal is suffering the consequences of something it did not cause. This is the time to strike while the iron is hot for climate justice,” the minister said.

The tenth meeting of the Loss and Damage Fund’s board is scheduled to take place in Manila, the Philippines, in December 2026. The eleventh meeting is scheduled to be held in Kathmandu from March 17 to 19, 2027.
