title.rendered: 4 arrested for stealing and buying stolen jewellery

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Police have arrested four people on charges of stealing gold and silver jewellery and purchasing stolen jewellery.

Those arrested have been identified as 29-year-old Sawan Kushwaha of Gaushala Municipality-5, Mahottari, currently residing in Jadibuti, Kathmandu Metropolitan City-32; 36-year-old Pabitra Limbu of Aathrai Rural Municipality-8, Tehrathum; 25-year-old Shrikrishna Bishwakarma of Gaurishankar Rural Municipality-5, Dolakha; and 43-year-old Ramila BK of Bhojpur Municipality-5, Bhojpur, currently residing in Narephat, Kathmandu Metropolitan City-32.

Police investigation found that Sawan was involved in stealing the jewellery, while Pabitra, Shrikrishna and Ramila were involved in purchasing it.

The four were arrested during an investigation into the theft of gold and silver jewellery from a house in Narephat, Kathmandu Metropolitan City-32, on August 3. A team deployed from the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office, Teku, arrested them during the investigation.

Police also recovered various gold and silver jewellery items from their possession.

The arrested individuals have been handed over to the District Police Range, Kathmandu, for further investigation and legal action.

title.rendered: 12 Federal hospitals to get morgues with capacity for at least 50 bodies

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The government has decided to build or expand morgues capable of accommodating at least 50 bodies at 12 federal hospitals and health science academies to improve the country’s capacity to manage mass casualties during disasters.

The Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene made the ministerial-level policy decision following difficulties in managing bodies during past disasters, including the recent Bhotekoshi floods.

Health and Food Hygiene Minister Nisha Mehta said hospitals needed adequate morgue facilities to prevent such difficulties from recurring and to strengthen disaster preparedness.

The ministry said the facilities would enable the safe preservation, identification and examination of bodies and help streamline necessary legal procedures. It said expanding morgue capacity was also essential to strengthen forensic medicine and medico-legal services.

Morgue capacity will be expanded or new facilities constructed at Koshi Hospital, Narayani Hospital, Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital, Bharatpur Hospital, Bheri Hospital and Dadeldhura Hospital.

Similar facilities will be developed at the National Academy of Medical Sciences, BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences, Patan Academy of Health Sciences, Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences, Rapti Academy of Health Sciences and Karnali Academy of Health Sciences.

The ministry said the initiative aims to make body management during disasters safer, more systematic, dignified and scientific while strengthening forensic and medico-legal services.

title.rendered: Cooperative federations barred from new savings and lending transactions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The Department of Cooperatives has barred cooperative federations from conducting new savings and lending transactions, implementing a provision of the Cooperatives Act that restricts such activities by federations.

The department issued the directive in accordance with Section 50(9) of the Cooperatives Act, 2017. District, provincial and central cooperative federations currently involved in savings and credit activities have been given three years to either jointly establish a cooperative bank or merge with an existing cooperative bank.

The federations have also been instructed to prepare and publish clear plans for returning members’ savings and recovering loans within the three-year period.

They must complete their audits and general assemblies by the end of Poush of the current fiscal year and determine their assets and liabilities. They must also prepare a strategic plan for either establishing or merging with a cooperative bank and submit it to the Office of the Cooperative Registrar and the National Cooperative Regulatory Authority after approval by their boards and general assemblies.

The government amended the Cooperatives Act through an ordinance in April and later converted the amendment into a bill, which was endorsed by the House of Representatives in June.

The department has directed federations to focus on cooperative development, member education, training, marketing, good governance and policy advocacy while complying with regulatory requirements.

title.rendered: Industry Minister Gauri Kumari Yadav resigns amid controversial remarks on LPG shortage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Industry Minister Gauri Kumari Yadav has resigned from her post amid controversy over her remarks regarding the shortage of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) in the country.

Yadav submitted her resignation to Prime Minister Balen Shah, according to her communications coordinator Kamal Chaulagain.

Yadav made the controversial remarks during a meeting of the Parliamentary Industry Committee on Wednesday, blaming LPG entrepreneurs for the ongoing shortage and saying the situation would not improve until the government “tightened the screws” on them.

She also said the licences of all 58 LPG companies currently operating in Nepal should be revoked, arguing that the country did not need so many gas industries and that two would be sufficient.

Her remarks drew strong objections from LPG entrepreneurs, who also brought the issue to the attention of the prime minister.

Kathmandu Valley is currently facing a severe LPG shortage, with consumers forced to queue for hours to obtain cylinders. Even when they manage to find gas, they are reportedly paying up to Rs 3,000 for a cylinder whose official price is Rs 2,060.

The shortage has been aggravated by disruptions along the road network. Since the road at Krishnabhir subsided on August 30, LPG supplies entering Kathmandu have remained inadequate. Supplies brought through alternative routes have also failed to reach consumers smoothly.

Meanwhile, Nepal Oil Corporation and the Ministry of Industry have been releasing data showing that LPG is being imported and supplied. However, the situation in the market remains markedly different, with consumers continuing to face long queues and shortages.

Yadav had also expressed frustration during the committee meeting, saying ministry officials had failed to cooperate with her efforts to take action against LPG entrepreneurs.

All 58 LPG bottling plants operating in Nepal are privately owned. The government has no infrastructure of its own for importing, storing or distributing LPG. Nepal Oil Corporation does not own a single LPG bottling plant.

Salt Trading Corporation, in which the government holds a 20 per cent stake, sells some LPG but lacks the capacity to meet market demand.

Nepal also does not have a single government-owned LPG bullet tanker. Even private LPG companies depend on Indian tankers to transport imported gas, resulting in an estimated annual outflow of Rs 6 billion in transportation costs.

Yadav’s resignation comes as the government faces growing pressure to address the prolonged LPG shortage and improve supply management.

title.rendered: Dhurmus-Suntali to release new comedy series from US on Friday

content.rendered:
Kathmnadu, September 10

The new comedy series Ma Ta Marchhu Ki Kya Ho, produced in the United States by comedy duo Sitaram Kattel ‘Dhurmus’ and Kunjana Ghimire ‘Suntali’, will be released to audiences from Friday.

Although the premiere date had been set two weeks ago, Dhurmus postponed the release following the Bhotekoshi floods, which caused extensive loss of life and property.

Produced by Dhurmus-Suntali Media, the series will be released every Friday at 8:15 pm Nepal time on the Dhurmus-Suntali YouTube channel, Sitaram said. In the United States, it will air at 10:30 am on Fridays.

The title Ma Ta Marchhu Ki Kya Ho is taken from one of Dhurmus’ popular dialogues and catchphrases from the past.

The series is based in the Raleigh area of North Carolina. According to Sitaram, who also directs the series, filming took place in Raleigh, Cary, Holly Springs, High Point, Greensboro and Charlotte, among other locations.

Directed by Sitaram and Kunjana, the series features veteran actor Mohan Mishra in a leading role. Dinesh Karki, Shankar Raj Wagle, Sanyam Lamichhane, Manika Chaulagain, Chuda Dhimal, Dharma Bharti and Shubhadra Acharya are also part of the cast. The series also marks the acting debut of Sitaram and Kunjana’s daughter, Subihani Kattel, as a child artist. Actor Jeevan Luitel will appear as a guest artist.

The series has cinematography by Raju KC, vocals by Ashish Abiral, lyrics by Prakash Punj, music by Rajendra Bajgain and editing by Rajendra Manandhar.

According to the production team, the series will not be limited to entertainment. Through comedy and satire, it will portray the struggles, successes, achievements, opportunities and challenges faced by Nepalis living in the United States, as well as their lifestyle, social and cultural environment, activities within the Nepali community and various aspects of life in the diaspora.

Dr Chandra Giri, a scientist and writer working for the US government, said the series is expected to bring real-life situations faced by Nepalis living abroad to audiences through humour.

Giri, who is also an adviser to the series, said it was not easy for artists living abroad to regularly pursue creative work and reach Nepali-speaking audiences around the world. “Starting regular artistic work from abroad is commendable in itself,” he said. “All Nepalis living abroad need to support and help this initiative.”

Sitaram and Kunjana have remained active in the arts since moving to the United States. During this period, they have also produced advertisements for around a dozen Nepali businesses and organisations. “Most importantly, audiences will now be able to watch our series regularly,” Sitaram said. “We want to convey the message that wherever we are, we can continue our art and creative work.”

title.rendered: Opposition parties urge govt to form parliamentary special committee on disaster response

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Opposition parties represented in the House of Representatives have decided to urge the government to form a parliamentary special committee to make disaster management, relief, rescue, search and rehabilitation efforts more effective.

A meeting of the opposition parties held at the Nepali Congress Parliamentary Party office in Singha Durbar on Thursday decided to press the government to form the committee to monitor and inspect relief and rescue operations, provide additional recommendations and facilitate necessary measures through Parliament.

CPN-UML Parliamentary Party Deputy Leader Padma Aryal said the opposition parties would continue to raise the issue strongly in Parliament and draw the government’s attention to the need for such a committee.

“We had demanded the formation of a parliamentary special committee to assist the government in disaster-related work, including relief, rescue, search and rehabilitation, and to monitor, inspect and review the government’s efforts while also providing additional suggestions and contributing actively from our side,” Aryal said.

She said the opposition parties would continue pursuing their demand as the government had not yet formed such a committee.

The meeting also thanked the agencies and personnel involved in search and rescue operations so far. However, the opposition parties concluded that shortcomings had emerged due to inadequate consultation, coordination and preparedness during the initial stages of the disaster response, according to Aryal.

She said the government must immediately accelerate temporary rehabilitation efforts to prevent people affected by the disaster from losing patience.

Aryal said opposition parties were committed to working with the government by putting aside partisan political interests and agendas during the national disaster.

“In this hour of national disaster, the opposition parties are committed to setting aside partisan political interests and agendas and working hand in hand with the government,” she said.

title.rendered: Nepal beat Oman by 87 runs to reach ACC Premier Cup final

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 11

Nepal secured a convincing 87-run victory over Oman in the semi-final of the ACC Premier Cup being held in Malaysia, thanks to an outstanding performance by its spin bowlers. Chasing Nepal’s target of 148 runs, Oman were bowled out for 60 in 28.1 overs.

Earlier, Nepal, having been invited to bat first after losing the toss, were all out for 147 in 45.4 overs. Dipendra Singh Airee was Nepal’s top scorer with 51 runs, while Basir Ahamad made 47. When Nepal were struggling at 36-4, Dipendra and Basir put together a 93-run partnership to steady the innings.

Dev Khanal scored 13, and Aasif Sheikh made 11, while none of Nepal’s other batters managed to reach double figures. Nepal lost their first wicket at 23 and slipped to 36-4 before recovering to 129-5 and eventually being bowled out for 147.

For Oman, Jay Odedra took three wickets while conceding just 26 runs in 10 overs. Hasnain Shah also claimed three wickets for 28 runs in 8.4 overs. Muhammad Imran took two wickets, while Shakeel Ahmed and Mujibur Ali claimed one each.

Nepal will now face the UAE in the final, which will be played on Saturday. If Nepal win the final, they will qualify for the Asia Cup.

By reaching the final, Nepal have also secured qualification for the ACC Emerging Teams Asia Cup.

title.rendered: 8-year-old snakebite victim dies after failing to receive timely treatment

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, September 10

An eight-year-old girl who was bitten by a snake died after she failed to receive timely treatment.

Aaswana Chauhan, the eight-year-old daughter of Asmita Chauhan of Itahari Sub-Metropolitan City–5, was bitten by a snake on Wednesday evening and died after being unable to receive timely treatment.

The girl was bitten on her left hand by a cobra while she was at home. Her family did not immediately realise that she had been bitten. They noticed only after seeing blood on her hand and took her to the Nepal Army’s snakebite treatment centre in Itahari.

However, the centre referred her to BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences in Dharan after administering antivenom, as she required intensive care. The Itahari treatment centre did not have an intensive care unit where she could be treated.

Treatment was started at BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences, but she immediately required admission to the paediatric intensive care unit (PICU). However, no PICU bed was available at the institute. All four PICU beds were occupied, making it impossible to admit her.

Her family then rushed her to Birat Teaching Hospital in Budhiganga, Morang. By the time she reached Dharan, her condition had already become critical, and it deteriorated further by the time she arrived at Birat. She died at around 8:30 pm, shortly after treatment began.

According to her uncle Maniraj Chauhan, Aaswana could have been saved if she had received intensive care in time. “When we were told that treatment was not available in Itahari, we rushed her to Ghopa [BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences]. Treatment was started there. They prepared the antivenom and put her on an IV. Then they told us she needed to be treated in a ventilator ICU, which they did not have,” Maniraj said. “We then rushed her to Birat Teaching, but we could not save her.”

Having lost a family member because she could not receive timely treatment, Maniraj said he does not want other families to suffer the same fate. “What happened at my home today should not happen to another family tomorrow,” he said. “The state must expand intensive care facilities and improve services at government hospitals.”

title.rendered: Schools await return of more than 500 students still unaccounted for

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

There is still no news of students caught in the floods. They have no textbooks or uniforms. Those who escaped the floods left their school bags behind on the way to safety. But now there is no alternative but to return to a normal routine.

Schools in flood-affected Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts are preparing to resume classes. They have urged their students to get in touch with the schools. “We need the data on how many students are available. That is why we have asked them to come to school once,” said Madhav Lamichhane, principal of Nilkantha Secondary School in Ward No. 5 of Uttargaya Rural Municipality, Rasuwa.

It is difficult to determine how many textbooks are needed until the students return. The school is preparing to resume classes from September 10. Roads have been cut off at several points, making it impossible to travel from one side to the other. “Students who cannot come to school should not panic. We will complete the course even if we have to repeat the lessons later,” he said, explaining the school’s preparations.

Most schools affected by the floods face similar problems. We spoke to the chiefs of the Education Development and Coordination Units in the affected districts about the damage to schools and when classes would resume.

Rasuwa: 285 students and 16 teachers unaccounted for

According to the Education Development and Coordination Unit in Rasuwa, 285 students have still not been accounted for. Of the 17 teachers reported missing, the body of one has been found. There are 39 students whose both parents remain unaccounted for.

“Relatives have taken in children whose parents are missing,” said unit chief Durgaprasad Silwal. According to him, four schools in Rasuwa have been completely destroyed. “Three community schools and one institutional school have collapsed,” he said. Classes have resumed at schools that were not affected. “Four to five schools have been turned into holding centres. Classes are not being conducted there,” Silwal said.

Classes resumed on August 27 in Naukunda Rural Municipality, September 9 in Uttargaya Rural Municipality, September 7 in Kalika Rural Municipality and September 9 in Aamachhodingmo Rural Municipality. However, preparations are under way to resume classes in Gosainkunda Rural Municipality from September 11. “Students from completely damaged schools will be taken to other schools to continue their education,” unit chief Silwal said. “There are plans to provide residential schooling.”

Nuwakot: 224 students and 11 teachers unaccounted for

In flood-hit Nuwakot district, 224 students and 11 teachers remain unaccounted for. According to unit chief Suryabahadur Khatri, 10 schools have been damaged, including two institutional schools. Ten schools have currently been turned into holding centres.

Classes have also resumed at schools in Nuwakot that were not affected by the floods. Schools in Bidur Municipality reopened on September 9. Plans have been made to provide alternative learning arrangements for students from damaged schools.

“Preparations are under way to continue learning with support from government and non-government organisations,” unit chief Khatri said. He said classes at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School are scheduled to resume from September 17. Preparations are also under way to restart damaged schools by providing them with buildings or land. “Local communities have offered community buildings, and the province has also said it will provide land. The Ministry of Education has asked us to submit a budget proposal for residential schooling,” he said.

The plan is to use schools serving as holding centres partly for classes and partly to accommodate displaced people. In Nuwakot, Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, Ramchandra Basic School, Chetana Basic School, Ganeshman Singh Basic School, Trishuli Boarding School and Uttargaya Boarding School have been completely damaged. Chandeshwori Secondary School and Chhetrapal Basic School have suffered partial damage.

Dhading: Three teachers unaccounted for, search for students underway

Three teachers remain unaccounted for in Dhading. According to the Education Development and Coordination Unit, the body of one teacher has been found. The bodies of four former teachers have also been recovered, while two others remain unaccounted for.

According to unit chief Krishna Kumar Shrestha, efforts are underway to collect data on the whereabouts of students. Ten schools in Dhading have been damaged. He said psychosocial counselling for students began today. “Classes will begin only after psychosocial counselling. We are collecting details of the students. Staff have been deployed for this work today as well,” he said.

The unit said Bageshwori Secondary School, Amleshwor Gurukul, Success Academy, Bhadrakali Gurukul, Jaleshwori Secondary School, Kalidevi Secondary School, Buddhi Bikas Basic School, Shankhadevi Secondary School, Rising Star and Dhusha Community Learning Centre have been damaged in Dhading.

Classes only after psychosocial counselling

The government has instructed schools to resume classes only after providing psychosocial counselling to students. In a circular, the Department of Education said students could experience fear, anxiety, stress and other psychosocial effects and instructed local governments to assess their psychosocial condition before regular classes resume.

Schools and local governments have been instructed to coordinate with health institutions and health workers to assess students’ psychosocial condition. “Schools must ensure that students are ready to attend regular classes. Only then should arrangements be made to resume regular teaching and learning,” the department said.

title.rendered: Deputy Speaker to donate one month’s salary to flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives Rubi Kumari has decided to donate one month’s salary toward the relief and rehabilitation of citizens affected by the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

Deputy Speaker Rubi Kumari has instructed the Administration Branch of the Federal Parliament Secretariat to deposit her one-month salary into the Government of Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

Her secretariat said the contribution was made with the aim of supporting relief, rescue, and rehabilitation efforts for flood-affected citizens.

Earlier, lawmakers from the Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, and Nepal Communist Party had written to the Parliament Secretariat requesting that specific amounts be deducted from their salaries to support flood victims.

This includes 38 Nepali Congress lawmakers from the House of Representatives and 24 from the National Assembly.

Congress parliamentary party leader in the House of Representatives, Bhishma Raj Angdembe, will contribute one month’s salary. Congress lawmakers Ganga Laxmi Awal, Rukmini Devi Koirala, Prakash Singh Karki, and Mohan Acharya will each contribute one month’s salary as well.

Congress lawmaker Tek Bahadur Gurung will contribute Rs 100,000. Since one month’s salary wasn’t enough to cover that amount, he asked that his full salary for one month be deducted, with the remainder taken from the following month’s salary.

The remaining Congress lawmakers will each contribute 15 days’ salary.

CPN-UML lawmaker Mohammad Ishtiyak Rai has written to the Parliament Secretariat pledging one month’s salary. The rest of the UML lawmakers will contribute 15 days’ salary each.

UML has 25 lawmakers in the House of Representatives and 10 in the National Assembly.

Nepal Communist Party lawmakers have also pledged to contribute 15 days’ salary.

In its letter to the Parliament Secretariat, the Nepal Communist Party also noted that, in addition to its lawmakers, its personal staff would contribute 15 days’ salary toward flood relief as well.

The Nepal Communist Party has 17 lawmakers in each of the House of Representatives and the National Assembly.

title.rendered: Blue Mountains Nepali community raises Rs 12,38,660 for flood victims in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The Nepali community living in the Blue Mountains region of New South Wales, Australia, has raised 1238660 (AUD $11,273) for families and communities affected by the recent devastating floods in Nepal.

The Blue Mountains Nepali Community, together with Blue Mountains Community, Katoomba locals, and the wider Nepali community, organised an evening fundraising event at a local hall in Katoomba. Volunteers cooked traditional Nepali dishes for attendees, while the event also featured Nepali music and cultural performances, offering local Australians a chance to connect with Nepali food, art, and culture.

The event drew around 200 people from both the local Australian and Nepali communities, far more than organisers had expected. Attendees enjoyed the food and music while generously donating to support flood victims back in Nepal.

The entire amount raised has been transferred to the Nepal government’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support relief and rescue operations for those affected by the floods.

Organisers said the event was more than just a fundraiser; it was a demonstration of how Nepalis abroad continue to hold on to their love, sense of responsibility, and unity toward their homeland. Many local Australians experienced Nepali food and culture for the first time, and the warmth and generosity toward flood victims thousands of kilometres away left a strong impression on the community, organisers said, adding that the event also helped strengthen ties between the Nepali and local Australian communities in the area.

The organisers extended their gratitude to everyone who attended, donated, volunteered in cooking and event management, performed, or contributed in any way to the event’s success, describing it as a collective achievement of the Blue Mountains community, Katoomba locals, and the Nepali diaspora working together.

title.rendered: Hotels recover from Gen Z protests, but Hilton still under reconstruction

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, September 10

Around two dozen hotels across the country were set on fire or damaged during the Gen Z protests on September 9 and 10, 2025. According to the Hotel Association Nepal (HAN), the hotels suffered losses worth around Rs 25 billion.

As of the first anniversary of the protests, the hotel industry as a whole is gradually recovering. Physical damage is being repaired, with some hotels already back in operation and others in the final stages of reconstruction, according to HAN Treasurer Yubaraj Shrestha. “Many hotels have already been rebuilt, are being rebuilt, or are in the final stage of reconstruction,” he said. The then interim government made continuous efforts to boost the morale of businesses in the immediate aftermath of the Gen Z protests.

A new government was formed following the peaceful completion of the elections. This has also raised hopes among businesspeople, Shrestha said. The tourism industry continues to face new challenges. Despite this, businesses are continuing to invest in the hope of a brighter future.

Hilton was among the hotels targeted by protesters. The Hilton hotel is also undergoing reconstruction. A hotel source said reconstruction of the structure, which was completely gutted by fire, is nearly complete, with additional work under way. “The civil construction work has been completed. The earthquake-resistant dampers need to be completely replaced, and they have already been ordered. The glass panels for the exterior have also been ordered,” the source said.

However, the source claimed that reconstruction has been affected because the hotel has yet to receive its insurance claim payment. “The reconstruction work will be completed within the next one to one-and-a-half years. In addition, expansion work is also being carried out simultaneously,” the source said.

The then government had introduced measures to revive businesses affected by arson and vandalism, including loan restructuring, loans at lower interest rates and an advance payment of 50 per cent of insurance claims. The deadline for tax payments was also extended. It also introduced customs exemptions on the re-import of goods damaged by arson and vandalism.

Meanwhile, to boost business confidence, then interim Prime Minister Sushila Karki and Finance Minister Rameshwor Khanal visited business establishments, met businesspeople, helped expedite damage assessments and encouraged those affected.

According to HAN President Binayak Shah, such visits provided immediate encouragement, but significant challenges remain in restoring businesses in the long term.

How did the Gen Z protests affect the hotel industry?

According to HAN data, hotels in Kathmandu Valley as well as Pokhara, Butwal, Bhairahawa, Jhapa, Morang–Biratnagar, Dhangadhi, Mahottari and Dang–Tulsipur were among those most severely affected. Hotel establishments were vandalised, set on fire and looted. Hilton Kathmandu, owned by business group Shanker Group, was set on fire. More than 2,000 jobs were directly put at risk at hotels damaged during the protests.

Another five-star hotel in Kathmandu that suffered significant damage was Taragaon Regency Hotels (Hyatt Regency). The hotel has repeatedly been recognised as one of the tourism industry’s major contributors to income tax and foreign currency earnings in Nepal.

Barnabas Museum Hotel, a five-star hotel in Kathmandu in which businessman and former Nepali Congress lawmaker Rajendra Bajgain has invested, was also vandalised and set on fire. The protests left hotels with little choice but to keep their rooms vacant at the time.

September is normally the beginning of the peak season for hotel businesses. The protests were called on September 8 last year, leaving around 80 per cent of hotel rooms vacant. According to President Shah, the biggest blow dealt by the protests was to business confidence.

How far has reconstruction of the fire-damaged hotels progressed?

Reconstruction of the Barnabas Hotel is progressing rapidly, with the hotel expected to resume operations in the near future. According to the company, the hotel suffered losses of more than Rs 300 million in the fire.

Hyatt Regency Hotel is also undergoing rapid reconstruction. Its operators aim to complete reconstruction and resume operations by December this year. Crown Plaza Kathmandu, which was damaged during the protests, has already completed reconstruction and resumed operations.

Pokhara, Nepal’s tourism capital, also suffered significant damage during the protests. According to HAN, Hotel Adam in Pokhara has resumed operations. HAN data also shows that Bar Peepal Hotel and Hotel Landmark in Pokhara have resumed operations. HAN Treasurer Shrestha said Bagaincha Resort in Pokhara has also resumed operations. According to him, reconstruction of Hotel Sarowar in Pokhara is still under way.

Dream International and Dreamland Gold Resort in Butwal have resumed operations. According to HAN data, two major hotels in eastern Nepal—Hotel Kingsbury in Jhapa and Mechi Crown—have also resumed operations.

Cable cars suffered heavy damage, but businesses bounced back quickly

Protesters also damaged and set fire to cable car facilities at various locations across the country. Businesses managed to restore those facilities relatively quickly.

Maulakali Cable Car in Nawalparasi resumed operations last December. Protesters had vandalised its lower station. The company brought in a technical team from Austria and resumed operations after completing repairs.

Meanwhile, the protests at Chandragiri Cable Car disrupted both the cable car and resort services.

Chandragiri Cable Car had to remain closed for two months because of damage caused by the protests. Its bottom station was completely damaged on September 10, 2025. The cable car service was restored after the company brought in technicians from Austrian manufacturer Doppelmayr and completed the necessary repairs, safety tests and further inspections. According to company data, more than 2,000 tourists visit Chandragiri Cable Car every day.

New government fails to restore confidence, businesses remain uncertain

The hotel industry is not the only sector dissatisfied with the current government; the broader tourism sector is also unhappy. The powerful government formed after an election held on the strength of the Gen Z movement began its tenure by pursuing a policy of detaining investors, while failing to focus on reforming its underperforming agencies. Nepal Airlines is on the verge of collapse, and the government has yet to find a capable person to lead the corporation. The Nepal Tourism Board has also been left without leadership.

Although the government’s policies and programmes contain attractive slogans, corresponding programmes have not been reflected in the budget. Businesspeople say the current government, which could remain in power for five years, lacks a vision and master plan for where the tourism sector should be in the next five years.

HAN President Shah said, “The government appears to be making efforts, but its vision is not clear.” Nepal’s hotels currently have the capacity to accommodate more than four million tourists annually. However, only around 1.2 million tourists visit the country each year. According to Shah, even this figure has been achieved largely through the private sector’s efforts.

“There is a big difference between the governments of yesterday and today. If this government wants to, it can solve any problem and take the country forward. Therefore, there is no alternative but to get down to work in tourism with a clear vision,” Shah said. Nepal, meanwhile, remains highly vulnerable to natural disasters. Shah said it was unfortunate that a disaster occurring in one part of the country could affect businesses across the country and that the state must play a leading role in addressing this vulnerability.

Businesspeople are also concerned that the longstanding problem of poor coordination among state agencies persists. The Ministry of Tourism is calling for tourists to visit Nepal, while the Ministry of Industry is unable to provide cooking gas. Hotels have been told to transport the gas themselves.

With two ministries pursuing different priorities, there is still uncertainty, as in the past, over which industries and businesses the state intends to prioritise. Businesspeople are concerned about this trend.

Current status of some hotels damaged during the Gen Z protests

Hilton Hotel: Under reconstruction

Hyatt Regency: Under reconstruction

Barnabas Museum Hotel: Under reconstruction

Crown Plaza Kathmandu: Operational

Hotel Adam, Pokhara: Operational

Bar Peepal Hotel, Pokhara: Operational

Hotel Kingsbury, Jhapa: Operational

Mechi Crown, Jhapa: Operational

Hotel Landmark: Operational

Hotel Sarowar, Pokhara: Closed

Bagaincha Resort, Pokhara: Operational

Dream International, Butwal: Operational

Dreamland Gold Resort: Operational

Sher Bahadur Magar, 25, from Khotang and working at Ambote in Melamchi Municipality-10 under the Melamchi Distribution Centre’s jurisdiction, was injured by an electric shock on March 24, 2026, while replacing a disc pin on a 15 kV transmission line.

title.rendered: Massive landslide, not earthquake, triggered deadly Lhende disaster, scientists say

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The devastating flood and debris flow in the Lhende Khola area along Nepal’s border with Tibet was triggered by a massive landslide rather than an earthquake, according to an analysis of seismic data by an international team of scientists.

The disaster has killed more than 1,300 people and left many others missing. Major towns and hydropower projects along the affected river corridors were also destroyed.

In the immediate aftermath, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and other agencies had suggested that a 4.4-magnitude earthquake may have caused rocks and ice to collapse, triggering the flood. Another possibility was that a glacial lake or dam had burst.

But an analysis of seismic data by an international team including geomorphologist Dr Kristen Cook of Grenoble Alpes University in France and seismologist Göran Ekström of Columbia University has challenged those early explanations.

Data recorded at a seismic station north of Kathmandu and by the Global Seismographic Network showed not the sharp, high-frequency shaking normally associated with an earthquake, but prolonged, low-frequency waves.

The pattern indicated a massive landslide.

Scientists estimate that the landslide generated seismic energy equivalent to a magnitude 5.7 earthquake, making it one of the largest landslides recorded anywhere in the world in the past decade or two.

What remains less clear is how such a large volume of water became part of the flood.

A glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, was initially suspected, but scientists have found no evidence of one.

Early satellite images from Planet Labs showed what appeared to be a glacier collapse at an altitude of around 5,200 metres, leading researchers to initially consider a glacial collapse as the likely trigger.

But calculations by Ekström and other scientists showed that the glacier alone was not massive enough to generate seismic waves equivalent to a magnitude 5 earthquake.

Clearer imagery from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and NASA-USGS’s Landsat-9 satellite later showed that a large rocky mountain had collapsed. The glacier was swept down with the landslide.

Dr Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of Tribhuvan University’s Centre for Disaster Studies, said the cause of the disaster was not immediately clear during the first three hours after the flood.

Subsequent drone footage and field investigations, however, confirmed that the event had been triggered by a landslide, he said.

According to Adhikari’s calculations, the energy generated by the landslide was greater than that released by the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima.

Scientists describe the disaster as a “cascading hazard”—a chain of disasters in which one event triggers another.

In this case, the landslide, debris flow and flood became part of a single destructive sequence.

Cook said similar cascading events occurred in India’s Chamoli disaster in 2021 and in Nepal in 2012, 2015 and 2017. But she estimated that the Lhende Khola event was about 10 times larger than those incidents.

Scientists are still trying to determine exactly how the flood acquired such a large volume of water.

One possibility is that the force of the landslide carried rocks, ice and debris into the river at such speed that it incorporated water from the river and old ice deposits in the lower part of the valley.

The disaster is also raising broader concerns about the stability of high-altitude mountain terrain.

Geographers including Alton Byers of the University of Colorado Boulder say rising global temperatures are causing permafrost—the permanently frozen ground that helps bind rocks and ice together in high mountain areas—to thaw.

As the permafrost weakens, mountain slopes can become increasingly unstable, potentially increasing the risk of large landslides.

For now, authorities are focused on rescue and relief operations in the affected areas, while attention is also turning to the need for more effective early-warning systems for communities downstream.

The Lhende disaster, scientists say, is a reminder that in the high Himalayas, a single destabilised mountainside can set off a chain of hazards extending far beyond the point where it collapses.

title.rendered: Human rights activists and lawyers demand Home Minister apologise over threatening remarks against journalists

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Human rights activists, senior lawyers, and civic campaigners have strongly objected to Home Minister Sudhan Gurung’s remarks, calling them threatening toward journalists. They have demanded that Home Minister Gurung retract his objectionable statements and issue a public apology.

Former National Human Rights Commission member Sushil Pyakurel, senior advocate Dinesh Tripathi, human rights activists Subodh Pyakurel, Shobhakar Budhathoki, and Som Niraula, women’s rights activist Shyam Kumari Sah, and youth activist Abhishek Adhikari issued a joint statement protesting the Home Minister’s remarks.

They stated that Home Minister Gurung’s remarks made on September 23 were, on the whole, objectionable, and expressed serious objection to the threatening language used against journalists.

According to their statement, the anarchic style and remarks of the Home Minister, who bears the primary responsibility for maintaining peace, security, and public order in the country and for disaster management, have diminished the dignity of the governance system itself.

“In the context where we have already treated the selection of the Home Minister and the ‘investigation’ into allegations against him with suspicion, Gurung’s aggressive comments toward journalists in general give us the impression that he does not understand the dignity, restraint, and seriousness required of the position and office he holds,” the statement states.

Reminding that a journalist’s primary duty is to question those in positions of state responsibility and hold them accountable, the rights activists noted that Nepal’s media has carried out its duty amid numerous challenges and threats since the Panchayat era.

They said the media played a responsible role from the anti-Panchayat movement, the armed conflict, the uncertainty following the royal palace massacre, and the struggle against Gyanendra Shah’s “Ashoj regime” all the way through the constitution-making process.

“Journalists will not be discouraged by threats”

Noting that Nepali journalists have previously confronted authoritarian-style rulers as well, the rights activists made clear that journalists would not back down in the face of fear, intimidation, or threats.

“We are confident that journalists who did not back down while exposing the truth in countless episodes in the past, such as the gold smuggling scandal, the fake Bhutanese refugee scandal, and the cooperative fraud scandal, will not be discouraged by the Home Minister’s threatening words,” the statement reads.

The activists also urged media professionals to report news responsibly within the bounds of the code of conduct, while once again drawing Home Minister Gurung’s attention to the demand that he immediately retract his words and apologise.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood shows why Nepal must rethink development in hazard-prone areas

content.rendered:
We have often heard, and repeatedly experienced, that Nepal is highly susceptible to natural hazards. The reasons are largely clear. Geologically, the Himalaya is a relatively young mountain system, and its mountain-building process remains active. The continuing convergence of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates produces uplift, seismic activity and ongoing changes in the terrain.

Steep slopes, fractured and weak rock, intense monsoon rainfall concentrated within a few months, and glacier-fed high-mountain catchments further expose Nepal to earthquakes, floods, landslides, avalanches, rockfalls and debris flows carrying rock, soil, ice and water at high velocity.

Within this sensitive geography, roads, hydropower projects, markets, settlements, tourism infrastructure and other investments have expanded rapidly in recent decades. Climate change is adding further uncertainty by altering rainfall, glaciers, snow and hydrological processes across a natural system that is already highly dynamic. Its effects can extend from the high mountains through the middle hills to downstream riverine areas.

Nepal contributes only about 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet the cost of climate-related risk is borne not only through lives lost during disasters but also through its long-term development. A World Bank study estimates that, without adequate action to address climate impacts, Nepal’s economy could be at least 7 percent smaller by 2050. In a country where major gaps in infrastructure and basic services remain, repeated destruction of roads, bridges, irrigation systems, homes and productive assets diverts scarce public resources from meeting new needs towards rebuilding what has already been lost. From the perspective of climate justice, it is difficult to regard as equitable a situation in which countries that contributed very little to global warming bear a disproportionate share of its consequences.

Yet the climate justice argument should not obscure the need to examine our own development decisions. Climate change can alter the probability, frequency or intensity of hazards, but whether a natural event becomes a major disaster also depends on where people live, where and how infrastructure is built, how development along rivers and steep slopes is regulated, and how seriously scientific knowledge influences planning and investment decisions. Disaster risk, in this sense, cannot be separated from the nature, pace, cost and sustainability of development.

The Rasuwa flood of August 26 brought this relationship into sharp focus along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli river corridor. Preliminary scientific assessments indicate that a large mass of rock and glacial ice collapsed in the high mountains, generating a powerful flow that entrained rock, soil, water and other debris before entering the river system. As it travelled downstream, it encountered roads, bridges, hydropower projects, settlements, trade infrastructure and other economic activities that had expanded along the corridor over decades.

The resulting losses were extraordinary. Understanding the Rasuwa flood therefore requires more than explaining how the physical event began and travelled downstream. It also requires examining where and how settlements, infrastructure and investment have expanded within risk-prone terrain.

What actually happened in Rasuwa?

The Rasuwa flood began in high Himalayan terrain and propagated far downstream through the river system as an extraordinary hazard cascade. Preliminary evidence indicates that a large, steep slope involving rock and glacial ice failed suddenly. As the material descended, it entrained more rock, soil, water and debris and transformed into a powerful debris flow and flood. Its effects travelled through Lende Khola into the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli system, reaching settlements and infrastructure far downstream. Initial scientific assessments estimated flow velocities of around 40 to 50 metres per second.

The human, physical and economic losses were extensive. According to the government’s preliminary damage and needs assessment available by 6 September, about 55 kilometres of roads, 37 motorable bridges, 68 suspension bridges, around 7,570 houses and 13 hydropower projects were affected. By September 8, 1,357 bodies had been recovered, while 5,326 people remained missing or unaccounted for. A total of 13,583 people had been rescued and 6,827 injured people had received medical treatment. Search, rescue, identification and verification were still continuing, so these figures remained provisional.

Early public discussion described the Rasuwa flood as a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF). The scientific evidence available so far, however, indicates a more complex process. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) has provisionally interpreted the event as a destructive debris flow and flood following the rapid failure of a steep slope involving a glacier within Langtang National Park. The collapse generated seismic energy equivalent to an earthquake of about magnitude 5.2, although it was not a tectonic earthquake. USGS estimates that the resulting flow travelled nearly 100 kilometres downstream. It remains uncertain whether the initial failure was primarily a rock collapse incorporating part of a glacier or whether a large section of glacial ice itself became unstable.

This uncertainty matters. As Stuart Dunning, Professor of Applied Geomorphology at Newcastle University, has explained, a collapse of rock and ice at high elevation can change character as it moves downslope. Fast-moving material can entrain sediment and water, temporarily block a river and later generate a much larger downstream flow. Such an event cannot be understood adequately as a landslide, avalanche or flood in isolation. One process can trigger or intensify another, creating a hazard cascade.

ICIMOD’s preliminary assessment points to the same complexity. Its scientists suggest that a large volume of ice and rock may have entered Lende Khola, followed by exceptional downstream water-level rises. At Galchhi, the river rose by about nine metres within roughly 30 minutes, while at Malekhu the increase was about seven metres. Whether debris temporarily blocked the river and later released a larger surge remains under investigation. ICIMOD has also cautioned that, although climate change is altering glaciers, snow and high-mountain slopes, its precise role in this particular event cannot yet be determined.

The initial sequence therefore remains unresolved. Scientific reconstruction may eventually provide a clearer account of how the physical event developed. But it cannot, by itself, explain why it became such a large disaster. That requires examining the risk conditions of the affected corridor, how settlements and infrastructure were developed, and how far available knowledge of risk influenced planning and investment decisions.

Hazard and disaster are not the same

A basic distinction is essential to understanding disaster risk. A hazard is a natural event or process capable of causing harm to people, property or the environment. But a hazardous event is not, by itself, a disaster. Exposure refers to the presence of people, settlements, infrastructure, assets or economic activities within an area that may be affected. Their vulnerability depends on their sensitivity and on the capacity and resources available to manage risk. The interaction among hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity creates the potential for loss, or disaster risk. When that risk is realised through serious human, physical, economic or environmental losses, it becomes a disaster.

Viewed through this framework, the Rasuwa flood involves two very different timescales. The first is measured in minutes and hours, during which a physical event in the high mountains transformed into a powerful downstream flow. The second extends over decades, during which roads were built, bridges added, hydropower projects developed, border-trade infrastructure established, settlements expanded and economic activity increasingly concentrated along the river corridor.

Put simply, the destructive flood developed within minutes, but the people, settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and other structures in its path had accumulated there through decades of development decisions. The scale of loss emerged where a rapidly developing natural process met a development pattern built over a much longer period. The risk exposed on August 26 was therefore not created that day. It had been accumulating through land-use, infrastructure and investment decisions.

The same river system experienced another major flood in July 2025. ICIMOD notes that Lende Khola experienced two major floods within fourteen months. This does not mean that both events had the same cause. Rather, it shows that the same corridor may be affected by different hazards and combinations of processes. It therefore needs to be understood as a dynamic, multi-hazard river corridor.

Whether the Rasuwa flood was technically a GLOF remains important for science, but it is not the only question that matters for planning. Equally important is how settlements, infrastructure and investment have expanded within a corridor exposed to different and potentially interacting hazards.

Not just a river, but an interconnected geo-system

Systems thinking remains weak in many urban and rural development plans and infrastructure decisions in Nepal. When a landscape is examined through isolated components, the relationships between them and the effects of change in one on another can be missed. Studying an unstable slope, analysing flow within a river reach, or designing a bridge are all necessary. But when an event travels through hillslopes, tributaries, the main river, roads, bridges, hydropower projects, settlements and administrative boundaries, overall risk cannot be understood by examining each element separately.

A river corridor is therefore more than a channel carrying water. It is a complex geo-system in which natural processes and human activities interact continuously. Topography and river processes are linked with roads, hydropower, settlements, livelihoods, land values, technology and public institutions. A new road does more than improve access. It can alter land values, attract markets and settlements, create demand for services and encourage further investment. Its effects extend beyond the project’s physical boundary.

The same interdependence appears in risk management. Embankments or river-control works may reduce flood or erosion risk up to a certain level, but they do not eliminate it. The risk remaining after protective measures is residual risk. If protection creates the perception that an area has become completely safe, additional settlement and investment may follow. Assessment therefore needs to consider how land use and investment patterns change after protection is provided.

Multiple development decisions also combine over time. A road, hydropower project or settlement expansion may appear technically acceptable when assessed independently. Yet as such decisions accumulate within the same corridor, accumulated exposure can increase and alter the overall risk. Planning must therefore consider the cumulative effects of infrastructure, land-use change and settlement expansion, not only the acceptability of individual projects.

Understanding these processes requires engineering geology, hydrology, cryospheric science, climate science and hydraulic engineering. Planning responsibility begins where this knowledge is translated into decisions. Planning must help determine where settlements and infrastructure can expand, where development should be regulated, where risk-reduction measures are necessary, and where further development should stop because residual risk exceeds an acceptable level.

The Rasuwa flood also exposes the limitations of a sectoral approach. Roads, hydropower, settlement development and river management may fall under different institutions, but their effects converge within the same geo-system. An integrated spatial land-use plan is therefore needed to connect these decisions and guide where infrastructure, settlements and investment may proceed, and under what conditions.

The problem is not a lack of risk-sensitive development policy

Nepal already has important policy and legal provisions for incorporating disaster risk into planning and construction. Frameworks exist for disaster risk reduction, safer settlement and building construction, climate adaptation, land use and local development control. The central issue is not whether policy exists, but how effectively it influences actual decisions on land use, settlement growth, infrastructure and investment.

The Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, 2017, the National Disaster Risk Reduction Policy, 2018, and the National Strategic Action Plan for Disaster Risk Reduction 2018–2030 provide a framework that goes beyond rescue, relief and reconstruction. They recognise the need to reduce existing risk, prevent new risk and integrate disaster risk reduction into development processes.

Following the Gorkha earthquake, Nepal introduced the Basic Construction Standards for Settlement Development, Urban Planning and Building Construction, 2015. These standards connected safer construction not only with individual buildings but also with settlement development, urban planning and development control.

The Local Government Operation Act, 20174 gives local governments authority to establish land-use standards based on geo-risk sensitivity, regulate building approval, oversee subdivision or plotting, and act on buildings considered unsafe from earthquakes or other hazards. Local governments therefore already possess legal instruments for linking risk information to development control.

The Land Use Act, 2019 and Land Use Regulations, 2022 provide a further basis for land classification, use and management. Their relevance extends to deciding what uses are appropriate in risk-prone terrain and where settlement and infrastructure expansion should be controlled.

Climate and urban policies reinforce the same direction. The National Adaptation Plan 2021–2050 calls for climate risk-sensitive land-use planning and mapping of risk-prone areas. The National Urban Development Strategy 2017 called for risk-sensitive mapping and a multi-hazard approach, while the National Urban Policy 2024 provides an updated urban policy framework.

Risk-sensitive settlement and spatial planning are therefore not new concepts in Nepal’s policy landscape. The principal weakness lies in integrated implementation. Policies, laws and standards are spread across institutions and levels of government, while their effects ultimately materialise in the same places. Their effectiveness should be judged by whether they actually produce safer settlements and infrastructure. The Rasuwa flood has made this implementation gap difficult to ignore.

When does risk enter the planning process?

The gap between policy and practice becomes clearer when we examine how plans are prepared. Many local governments prepare Integrated Urban Development Plans (IUDPs), physical development plans, transport plans, land-use plans and multi-hazard maps. These are necessary instruments. The critical issue is when risk information begins to influence actual planning decisions.

Consider an IUDP. It may contain maps of flood, landslide or earthquake hazards. But if future growth areas, major roads, economic centres, infrastructure priorities and the direction of expansion have already been decided before those maps are introduced, risk has not shaped the basic structure of the plan. The hazard map then becomes another thematic layer placed over an already determined development pattern.

Risk-informed planning reverses that sequence. Decisions on where settlements should expand, where roads should run, where major infrastructure should be located and which areas should accommodate future growth should not precede multi-hazard and risk analysis. Risk information should shape the location, form and direction of development from the outset.

This also broadens the meaning of preparedness. Early warning, evacuation routes, rescue equipment and emergency operation centres are essential, but they primarily help people and infrastructure already located within areas of risk. Land-use and development planning provide an earlier opportunity to limit new exposure before it is created.

Preparedness therefore begins when land uses are designated, road alignments chosen, infrastructure located, settlement-expansion boundaries set and future growth directions determined. Risk should not enter at the end of planning as a final check. It should be part of the decision framework from the beginning.

The question of where to develop

Once risk is incorporated from the outset, the next task is to determine where development is appropriate and what kind of development should be permitted.

Multi-hazard and risk analysis should provide the first screening. Areas where risk makes certain forms or intensities of development unacceptable should be identified first. Land within a high-risk debris-flow, flood or landslide zone cannot become suitable simply because it is close to a road, well connected to a market or inexpensive to service.

After such areas are screened out, the remaining land can be assessed through multi-criteria land suitability analysis. This should consider slope, geological conditions, river behaviour, agricultural productivity, environmental sensitivity, water availability, access to roads and services, existing settlements, infrastructure feasibility and local livelihood opportunities. These criteria are not fully interchangeable. Good accessibility, low infrastructure cost or high market value cannot compensate for an unacceptable level of risk.

The analysis can then identify different planning-suitability categories. Some areas may be appropriate for priority development. Others may allow limited development only under specified conditions and risk-reduction measures. Still others may be unsuitable for new settlement or major investment. These categories do not replace statutory land-use classifications. They clarify what type and intensity of development is appropriate within them.

Physical safety alone, however, does not determine suitability. Highly productive agricultural land should not necessarily be opened for urban expansion simply because it is relatively safe. Likewise, a safe location far from employment, schools, health services, markets and transport may not support a viable settlement. Safety, accessibility, livelihoods, environmental value, agricultural productivity and infrastructure efficiency must therefore be considered together.

Nor does development change direction simply because a map identifies suitable land. Public investment must reinforce the plan. Roads, water supply, drainage, public transport, schools and other services can help direct settlement and private investment towards safer locations. Where feasible, land pooling and land banking can support this process.

The reverse is equally important. If government continues to extend roads, electricity and services into high-risk areas, development control is weakened. Risk-sensitive planning therefore concerns not only where development should stop, but also where public investment should be prioritised, where it should be conditional and where further investment should not be encouraged.

Such decisions affect land values, development expectations and household assets. Land-suitability and development-control criteria therefore need a scientific basis, transparent procedures and explanations that communities can understand. Where major restrictions are necessary, due process, alternative development opportunities and appropriate incentives should also be considered. Even so, the planning system must retain clear authority to refuse further development where residual risk remains above an acceptable level.

Risk does not stop at local government boundaries

Natural systems do not follow administrative boundaries. A river does not stop at the edge of a municipality, and a slope may fail in one jurisdiction while its consequences extend far downstream. Yet authority over development and risk management is divided among federal, provincial and local governments and numerous sectoral institutions.

Local governments hold important powers over land use, settlement development, building approval and local infrastructure. Strategic highways, large hydropower projects, protected areas, hydrometeorology, geology, land administration and national disaster management involve provincial or federal institutions. Each has a legitimate mandate, but their decisions converge on the same landscape. A single municipality therefore cannot manage corridor-scale risk on its own.

Two forms of coordination are needed. Vertical coordination among federal, provincial and local governments must connect risk information, technical support, finance, regulatory authority and accountability. Horizontal coordination is equally necessary among institutions responsible for roads, energy, urban development, hydrology, geology, land, environment and disaster management.

The Nepal Disaster Report 2024 shows considerable institutional progress at the local level. All 753 local governments have local disaster-risk policies or legal provisions, more than 400 have Local Emergency Operation Centres, and 419 have prepared Local Disaster and Climate Resilience Plans. Yet technical capacity and the integration of disaster risk into development planning remain concerns. Institutional structures matter, but their effect on spatial decisions matters more.

A corridor such as the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli makes the limitation clear. No single local government can control all changes in the upper catchment, independently determine strategic infrastructure locations, or generate all the specialised cryospheric, geological and hydrological information it needs. Provincial government can play an important coordinating role across river corridors and catchments, while federal institutions remain essential for strategic infrastructure, national standards and specialised scientific information.

This does not mean decisions should be recentralised. Decisions should remain at the level where they are most appropriately made. But the understanding of risk that informs them must operate at the scale of the larger geo-system, and coordination must function before development decisions are made, not after a disaster has crossed several administrative boundaries.

Risk information and development decisions

Nepal’s base of risk information, data and technology has expanded considerably. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and national disaster-information systems such as BIPAD have strengthened the institutional basis for bringing information from different sources together. Satellite Earth observation, LiDAR, UAV surveys, InSAR, automated hydro-meteorological monitoring and spatial analysis now allow terrain change to be studied in far greater detail.

These technologies can help monitor glaciers, progressive slope movement, river channels and sediment patterns, changing flows, and the expansion of settlements and infrastructure. They can improve hazard understanding and support updated risk assessments.

But technology is not planning, and more data do not reduce risk by themselves.

The critical issue is whether risk information changes actual decisions. If a proposed growth area, road alignment or major infrastructure location remains unchanged after high risk has been identified, the link between information and decision-making remains weak. The value of a risk map lies not only in its technical resolution, but in whether it influences land use, infrastructure location, development approval and public investment.

A clear process is therefore needed to move from information to decision. It should specify what risk information is required for different development proposals, who reviews it, when plans or projects must be reconsidered, and how decisions change when risk exceeds an acceptable threshold.

Decision-makers must also understand uncertainty, return periods and possible consequences. Because land-use restrictions affect land values, construction expectations and livelihoods, their scientific basis must be communicated in language that affected communities can understand.

The political difficulty of prevention

One of the most difficult aspects of risk reduction lies in its political economy. Roads, bridges, hydropower projects and other major infrastructure are visible and can readily be presented as development achievements. By contrast, limiting development in a high-risk area, changing a proposed road alignment or choosing a safer but more expensive alternative produces less visible results. Prevention often succeeds through losses that never occur, and its political value may therefore be less immediate than that of visible construction.

This can distort development incentives. Restricting settlement growth or density may reduce future losses, but it can also affect land values and investment opportunities in the present. A safer alternative may be technically preferable yet more expensive, more distant or politically less attractive. Risk-sensitive planning therefore requires political and institutional commitment as well as technical analysis.

Responsibility for long-term risk needs to be understood in the same way. The exposure revealed by the Rasuwa flood was not produced by a single government, project or decision. Decisions made at different times accumulated within the same landscape. A government in office when disaster occurs remains accountable for decisions within its authority, but long-term risk should not be reduced to immediate political blame. The more consequential issue is whether land-use regulation, infrastructure approval, public investment and development-control practices actually change afterwards.

Prevention also has a social dimension. Development restrictions can affect landowners’ economic expectations, while directing settlement towards safer areas raises questions of livelihoods, employment, transport, schools, markets, services and social relationships. Experience from post-disaster resettlement repeatedly shows that a technically safe location does not automatically become a viable settlement. Risk-sensitive planning must therefore address physical safety and settlement viability together.

Prevention is not simply the prohibition of development. Where risk is excessive, development may need to be restricted. At the same time, infrastructure, services and opportunities need to be directed towards safer and viable locations. Development control and development incentives must operate within the same spatial strategy.

Learning must be reflected in development decisions

Scientific investigation of the Rasuwa flood should continue as new evidence emerges. Conclusions about the initial failure, the interaction between rock and glacial ice, possible river blockage and the role of climate change in this specific event should remain grounded in evidence. Acknowledging uncertainty is part of responsible investigation.

Planning, however, does not need to wait until every scientific question has been resolved. The issues raised here concerning policy, land use, multi-hazard analysis, site selection, accumulated exposure, public investment, institutional coordination and risk information can already be translated into practice.

The real test of learning is not the review conducted after the next disaster, but the routine development decisions made before it.

That change will be visible in whether growth can be redirected away from high-risk areas, whether road alignments and major infrastructure locations can be reconsidered, whether settlements and investment can be steered towards safer and viable areas, and whether further development can be refused where cumulative or residual risk exceeds an acceptable level.

The questions raised by the Rasuwa flood are not confined to Rasuwa. They apply to river corridors, hill towns, roadside settlements, rapidly urbanising areas and major infrastructure projects across Nepal.

Development decisions cannot be guided by access, cost and economic opportunity alone. Deciding where not to develop must become as integral to development planning as deciding where development should go.

title.rendered: Govt surveys flood-hit families to determine need for temporary housing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

The government has begun surveying people displaced by the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli floods to determine how many actually need temporary housing, as thousands remain in emergency holding centres across the affected districts.

Not everyone currently staying in a holding centre may require a separate temporary shelter, according to Prakash Aryal, deputy director general of the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction and coordinator of the Resettlement and Shelter Management Task Force formed by the Ministry of Infrastructure Development.

The survey is being conducted through local governments to establish the number of individuals and families who need temporary accommodation.

“Not everyone staying in the holding centres may need temporary housing,” Aryal said.

Local governments are collecting the required information through forms, after which the government will identify suitable sites and begin constructing temporary shelters. Aryal said the process would be carried out in coordination with local governments.

Sites are already being identified in areas including Galchhi and Bidur.

The Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers said flood victims staying in holding centres in different districts would be provided temporary accommodation according to their preferences.

The holding centres are currently serving as emergency shelters. From there, affected families will be moved into separate temporary accommodation, while longer-term resettlement will begin only after the government completes a detailed assessment of the damage and prepares a reconstruction plan.

Teams from the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction have been deployed to the affected districts since Tuesday to carry out the assessment.

The survey will collect details on affected individuals and families, including whether their homes were completely or partially damaged, the number of family members who died or remain missing, and whether they prefer government-provided temporary shelter or rented accommodation.

It will also record whether families have access to land, their preferred relocation options, and their needs for drinking water, sanitation and other essential services.

The department expects to complete the survey within a week.

The government also plans to survey affected families who are not currently staying in holding centres. Once the broader assessment is complete, the process of constructing temporary housing will move forward.

The need for safe long-term resettlement is expected to be a bigger challenge. The Rasuwa floods washed away not only homes but also land belonging to many affected families, leaving some without a safe place to return to.

Standards being prepared for donor-built homes

The Department of Urban Development and Building Construction is also preparing standards for temporary houses that donors and non-governmental organisations may want to build for flood victims.

Aryal said work was underway to establish the facilities and minimum requirements that each temporary shelter should provide.

NGOs and other organisations seeking to construct housing for flood-affected families will be able to use the same standards.

“We are preparing the standards,” Aryal said. “This will ensure that housing built by the government and non-governmental organisations follows the same standards.”

3,628 people in holding centres

According to the government’s latest figures, 1,367 bodies have been recovered so far, while 5,132 people remain missing. Of those missing, 1,393 are from Rasuwa and 651 from Nuwakot. A total of 13,646 people have been rescued.

The government has established 37 holding centres in different locations, where 3,628 people are currently receiving emergency accommodation.

Of them, 733 are in holding centres in Rasuwa, 2,699 in Nuwakot and 196 in Dhading.

The latest data from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority shows that 7,570 private buildings have been fully or partially damaged by the floods.

The government’s preliminary assessment puts the number of people directly affected at 32,933.

Government identifies land for permanent resettlement

The government had already taken steps toward permanent resettlement, forming a committee last Friday to identify safe land for families displaced by the Bhotekoshi floods.

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation, in coordination with the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration, formed the committee to identify suitable land for the safe resettlement and temporary accommodation of families affected and displaced by the floods in the Rasuwa–Bhotekoshi area.

The committee is headed by Prakash Joshi, director general of the Department of Survey.

Its members include representatives from the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration and the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, a director from the Department of Land Management and Archives, assistant chief district officers from the affected districts, chief administrative officers of the concerned local governments, district coordination officers, representatives of the Nepal Police and Armed Police Force, and chiefs of the district land administration and survey offices.

Damodar Wagle, an undersecretary, has been appointed member secretary.

The committee has been tasked with identifying families whose homes and land were damaged by the floods, those for whom returning to their previous locations is considered unsafe, and those still living in affected areas despite the risks.

It will assess potential land for resettlement, conduct field studies and preliminary disaster-risk assessments, and recommend the legal procedures required for temporary accommodation.

The committee will collect information on affected families in coordination with local governments. Land required for resettlement will be identified with the support of local governments, district land administration offices and survey offices.

Potential sites will then undergo field assessments with the help of subject experts.

The committee will examine the geographical condition of the land, flood and landslide risks, its suitability for settlement and the infrastructure required before making recommendations on where displaced families can be resettled.

title.rendered: The Project Beyond performs in Australia for Nepal flood relief

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

A Nepali music group, The Project Beyond, took the stage in New South Wales on Sunday, September 6, dedicating a special performance to Nepal in solidarity with communities affected by the country’s recent devastating floods.

The band performed as part of the Monsoon Mela event at FunHaus Factory, using the show to support the Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal. Alongside music and celebration, the group used its stage time to raise awareness about the hardship faced by flood-affected communities back home.

For the group, the show was more than a concert; it was a chance for young Nepalis and the broader Australian community to unite through music and express solidarity with disaster-affected communities. The Project Beyond says it plans to continue using music and community events to support meaningful causes in both Australia and Nepal.
