title.rendered: A hand pump in every yard, but no water anywhere in Betauna

content.rendered:
Chandardevi Mukhiya, 45, of Betauna in Golbazar Municipality–12, Siraha, has a hand pump right in her courtyard. But for the past several years, no water has come out of it. Since her own pump stopped working, she and other locals have depended on a submersible pump installed at the house of her neighbour, Mohan Jha.

Around 200 households in Betauna-Haripur face the same situation. Most have hand pumps in their yards, but since they’ve stopped drawing water, the entire village now depends on a single borewell. Long lines form in the morning and evening as people wait to fill water; locals say it can take hours just to fill two buckets.

Resident Ashadevi Mukhiya installed a special supersession motor to help draw water more easily from her hand pump. But she says even years after installing the motor, no water has come.

Ward chairperson Ganesh Mukhiya has two hand pumps on his property, one fitted with a supersession motor, yet even his pump has stopped drawing water.

According to resident Mohan Jha, the water problem in Betauna has been worsening over the past five years. In the past, sufficient monsoon rain would keep some water flowing into the pumps for a while, but this year’s prolonged lack of rainfall has made the situation far worse.

“We’ve had this water problem for the last five years. When there was good rain in June-August, we’d get a little water in the hand pumps until November-January,” Jha said. “But this year, with a long stretch of insufficient rain, the pumps have stopped giving water altogether.”

Jha says the added strain of running irrigation motors and pumps simultaneously to water paddy fields during the drought has put further pressure on groundwater levels. He added that since most locals also go to the fields to bathe and wash clothes, pressure on the village’s lone submersible pump is somewhat reduced.

“The motors and fire pumps in the fields are running for paddy irrigation. Since most people go to the paddy fields to bathe and wash clothes too, there’s some relief here,” Jha says. “If those motors over there weren’t running, this one submersible pump alone couldn’t sustain the whole village.”

He warned that without immediate alternative arrangements, Betauna residents will face an even bigger water crisis. Ward chairperson Ganesh Mukhiya acknowledged that a major water shortage now exists even for basic household use, but said the ward is not currently in a position to provide a separate submersible pump to every household.

“There’s a serious shortage of water even for everyday household use. But the ward is not in a position to give a submersible pump to every individual household,” Mukhiya says. “Due to the prolonged drought and the simultaneous operation of motors in the paddy fields, groundwater levels have dropped, causing the hand pumps to stop working.”

Although Golbazar Municipality spends millions of rupees every year in the name of drinking water and irrigation, former divisional drinking-water engineer Devnath Mahato says the practice of merely distributing hand pumps to individual households and scattering budgets across small projects will not resolve the long-term problem.

“Simply distributing hand pumps household by household will no longer solve the drinking water problem,” Mahato says. “Local governments need long-term plans, targeting a village or neighbourhood as a unit, to build shared borewells, small overhead tanks, and organised distribution systems.”

This year’s prolonged drought appears set to affect not just household water use in Betauna but agricultural production as well. Insufficient rainfall has increased irrigation demand in the fields, while excessive extraction of groundwater is drying up drinking water sources too.

Experts say the deepening drinking water crisis isn’t limited to Betauna; falling groundwater levels have worsened water shortages across various parts of the Tarai-Madhesh region in recent years.

Specialists note that uncontrolled extraction in the Chure region, erratic rainfall, prolonged drought, excessive groundwater use, encroachment on traditional ponds and reservoirs, and rising temperatures have all weakened the natural water-recharge system. With rising heat on one hand and falling groundwater levels on the other, the risk of a compounded crisis, affecting drinking water, agriculture, and the environment alike, is growing across the Tarai-Madhesh region.

title.rendered: NVL’s final three league matches today; here’s what each team needs

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Under the Nepal Volleyball League (NVL), the final three matches of the league stage are being played today. These matches will decide which team finishes on top and goes straight to the final, and which teams must go through the playoffs to reach it.

All six teams in the league will play their last league-stage match on the same day. Of the six participating teams, the top-ranked ones will remain in contention for the final, while the bottom three will be eliminated from the league stage.

Four teams are currently in the running for the top three spots: Annapurna Spiker Kings, Karnali Shivraj, Kathmandu Reds, and Sagarmatha Smashers. After four matches each, Annapurna leads with 9 points, Karnali and Kathmandu are tied on 8 points each, and Sagarmatha has 7 points.

Madhesh Warriors sit fifth with 4 points, and Khaptad Falcons are sixth with no points; both have already been eliminated from contention for the top three.

Result does each team need

The first match on Thursday will be between Annapurna and Sagarmatha, starting at 1 pm. Table-topping Annapurna is a strong contender to reach the final directly.

Riding a three-match winning streak, Annapurna will go straight to the final if they beat Sagarmatha in straight sets or by a 3–1 margin, in that case, they won’t need to wait for the results of the other matches.

If Sagarmatha wins instead, Annapurna will be pushed into the playoffs.

If Annapurna loses, their fate will depend on the results of the other matches. If Annapurna loses in a five-set match, they will still enter the playoffs.

For Sagarmatha, this match is do-or-die; if they lose to Annapurna, they will be knocked out of contention for the top three.

The second match, between Karnali and Madhesh, starts at 4 pm. This match is also crucial for Karnali; what result Karnali needs will become clearer once the first match concludes.

Currently second with 8 points, Karnali will move to 11 points with a win. For Madhesh, however, this match’s result won’t really matter, since their chances of finishing in the top three are already over.

The final league-stage match, between Kathmandu and Khaptad, starts at 7 pm. Since all other teams will have finished their matches by then, it will be clear exactly what equation Kathmandu needs to navigate.

If Annapurna beats Sagarmatha in the first match, Kathmandu will already be in the playoffs before their own match, and will need to win the playoffs to reach the final.

But if Annapurna loses in the first match and Karnali loses in the second, Kathmandu will have a chance to reach the final directly by winning their own last match.

title.rendered: Who brought the controversial religious leaders to the Gen Z memorial gathering?

content.rendered:
A memorial gathering held on Tuesday at the old Parliament Building premises in New Baneshwor, marking Gen Z Martyrs’ Day, has drawn criticism after two controversial “dharmagurus” (religious leaders) were made guests of honour. The organisers themselves gave stage prominence to Bijay Bhandari, who has been running fraud schemes for 15 years, and Shrinivas Acharya, who once tried to incite communal violence by having himself shot.

The event

The memorial for Gen Z martyrs on Tuesday, held in front of the old Parliament building in New Baneshwor, was attended by Home Minister Sudan Gurung as chief guest, along with Law Minister Sobita Gautam, Minister Mahabir Pun, Minister Sunil Lamsal, RSP (Rastriya Swatantra Party) lawmakers, former Home Minister Om Prakash Aryal, and others. Family members of martyrs and Gen Z leaders were also present.

Amid this gathering of martyrs’ relatives, injured Gen Z participants, and ministers, the two controversial religious leaders, Bijay Bhandari (who calls himself Balyogeshwar Vijay Krishnamurti) and Dinesh Pandit (who goes by Shrinivas Acharya), received notable prominence and hospitality. They even helped light the ceremonial lamp alongside Home Minister Gurung.

Shrinivas, seated in the front row on stage with the Home Minister, while some ministers and VIPs were pushed to the back rows, delivered an aggressive speech. He spared no effort in glorifying Home Minister Gurung, while challenging Prime Minister Balendra Shah directly and sharply criticising him for not attending the event.

Who invited them?

Following up on who brought these controversial figures to the stage, it appears they were invited directly by the organisers. Roshan Gautam, secretary of the organising body, the Gen Z Martyrs’ Family Welfare Society, confirmed this, telling Online Khabar: “We invited them ourselves.”

Asked why controversial religious leaders were invited, Gautam said the organisers were unaware of their background. “We didn’t think that just because someone is called a dharmaguru, they must be controversial,” he claimed.

He further claimed that, to keep the event apolitical, invitations had been sent to all religious institutions as well as the Office of the President, the Vice President, the Prime Minister, the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker, the Chair and Vice-Chair of the National Assembly, the Supreme Court, and all security agencies. However, despite this claim, no religious leaders from other faiths were present — though Gautam insists invitations were sent and those others simply didn’t show up.

The two religious figures also performed a “swasti-shanti” blessing ritual at the event. Organisers claim this was done only because the chief guests were arriving late, and that it was not a pre-planned part of the program. When asked why the religious leaders were seated alongside the chief guest ahead of a former minister, a lawmaker, and the Inspector General of Police, organisers explained that those who arrived earlier were simply seated in front. They also claim Shrinivas was given a turn to speak as part of allowing representative voices to address the gathering.

A controversial past

Both men have highly controversial histories.

Bijay Bhandari: Two years ago, he was the sole organiser of a month-long “Kotihom” religious ritual at Pashupatinath, which sparked major controversy over the funds collected. Journalists covering the event were reportedly denied entry and even attacked, drawing widespread criticism at the time.

A similar controversy arose over a “Mahayagya” (grand ritual) in Pokhara, where he was accused of cutting tree branches along roads and historic rest areas for the event.

Bhandari has faced numerous legal cases. For nearly a decade, under the guise of religion, he defrauded the public, running a fraud operation since roughly 2011 through an organisation called “Manav Kalyan Adhyatmik Paropakar Sangh, Nepal,” claiming he could arrange trips to America in exchange for money. Some victims paid as little as 100,000 rupees; others paid up to 1 million rupees.

Complaints were filed against Bhandari, his wife Sulochana Bhandari, and others. Police raided his residence in Chhauni Housing and recovered registers, cheques, and donation receipts as evidence. He was found to have opened a company under the name “Dynamic Derimerim Investment Pvt. Ltd.,” and police also treated receipt pads under the name “Aravind Yoga Mandir” as evidence of fraud.

Kathmandu Police arrested him and charged him with fraud amounting to 12.7 million rupees; he admitted in court to accepting the money, claiming it was all in the form of donations. The fraud case remained pending in the Supreme Court for five years before he reached an out-of-court settlement in November 2024 by returning money to victims.

Even after facing charges in Kathmandu, Bhandari continued his activities in 2019. He ran another Mahayagya in Gulmi, claiming it was to fund school building construction, collecting around 5 million rupees, then reportedly leaving with the funds without informing the school management committee.

He also faced a separate case related to foreign employment fraud, having taken 1.2 million rupees from three people under the pretence of enrolling them in religious programs abroad, then failing to return the money. Nepal’s Foreign Employment Tribunal sentenced him in June 2018 to one and a half years in prison plus a fine. He was arrested multiple times, in 2011, 2014, and 2019.

Shrinivas Acharya (Dinesh Pandit): His past is equally controversial. Police investigations revealed that in 2018, he had arranged to have himself shot in an apparent attempt to stir communal violence. He was subsequently arrested by the Morang District Police Office on weapons-related charges. It was found that he had asked a man named Madhav Chaudhary to shoot him, apparently to fuel a “Hindu nation” movement; the plot came to light after Chaudhary and Laxmiraj Adhikari were arrested.

His run-ins with law enforcement didn’t stop there. He once declared in a speech that “those who kill cows should be killed,” leading to his arrest in Sunsari in October 2023 on charges of disturbing public peace. He was arrested again in November/December 2023 after participating in a protest led by Durga Prasai at Gaushala, where he gave an inflammatory speech and, arriving with supporters carrying a trishul (trident), allegedly incited the crowd, leading to an attack on police.

Despite repeatedly being arrested and released, both controversial figures were seated with honour on stage at the Gen Z memorial, a decision that has drawn criticism even from leaders within the ruling RSP party itself.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood survivors face hidden health risks even after rescue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

When the first patients from the Rasuwa flood began arriving at the National Trauma Centre, some appeared to have survived the worst.

But one patient brought to the hospital in the early hours of the morning was in far more serious condition than initially apparent.

Dr. Saroj Kumar Gohiwar, an MDGP and emergency medicine specialist who was on duty that night, said 10 patients from the flood-affected areas arrived at the hospital in a single night. One was referred to Bir Hospital. The others were discharged.

The patient who arrived around 3 or 4 am was different.

His heart was beating extremely fast, and there were signs that his body was not getting enough oxygen or blood. An arterial blood gas test showed severe acidosis, while markers associated with infection and a serious systemic response were extremely high. His blood pressure was very low.

Doctors treated him in the intensive care unit. He died despite their efforts.

For Dr. Gohiwar, the case illustrated a danger that can be easy to miss after a disaster: surviving the flood does not necessarily mean the immediate danger has passed.

People who appear conscious, can speak and seem physically stable may still be suffering from serious internal problems. Dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, low oxygen and poor blood circulation, acidosis, kidney injury and damage to other organs can develop or become apparent only after rescue.

The risks became more apparent when Dr. Gohiwar and a team from the National Trauma Centre travelled to the flood-affected areas, visiting Dhunche, Lingling and Syabrubesi.

In Lingling, three houses had been washed away and eight to 10 people were reported missing. The local health post had little medicine available. Around 40 to 50 people came seeking medical care when the team arrived.

Many were not there because of injuries from the flood itself.

Patients with chronic illnesses said they had been unable to take their regular medicines. The medical team distributed the medicines that were available and coordinated for additional supplies.

For people displaced by the flood, the health threat was not limited to what the water had already done.

Some were staying in monasteries, sleeping together on black mats. Crowded conditions, contaminated water and inadequate sanitation can create an environment where infections spread quickly.

Doctors say diarrhoea, skin and wound infections and respiratory illnesses are among the immediate concerns. People exposed to cold for long periods can also develop hypothermia. Those who have spent extended periods without adequate food or water may suffer from dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

There are also risks that are less visible.

People who have been trapped inside tunnels or under debris can survive for long periods without food or water, but survival varies greatly from one person to another. Age, existing medical conditions, access to medicines, injuries, physical condition and temperature can all affect the outcome.

The survival of some people trapped for days, therefore, does not mean that everyone in a similar situation will survive.

And rescue itself is not necessarily the end of medical care.

Doctors recommend that people pulled from tunnels, debris or other dangerous locations undergo medical assessment even when they are conscious and able to speak.

One rescued patient treated by the medical team had an eye injury that raised concern about possible damage to the optic nerve. The patient was referred to Bir Hospital for further treatment.

The flood has also left another kind of injury that may not be visible in an emergency room.

Families of those who died or remain missing face the continuing uncertainty of loss. Doctors warn that psychological effects can emerge long after the immediate crisis has ended.

Intrusive memories, fear, nightmares, sleep problems, avoidance and a heightened sense of danger can make it difficult for survivors and families to return to ordinary life. Some may eventually develop post-traumatic stress disorder.

“The trauma is not only of an individual. It is a huge blow to the family, society and the country as a whole,” Dr. Gohiwar said.

The medical response to the Rasuwa disaster, therefore, is unlikely to end when the last person is pulled from the rubble or discharged from a hospital.

For those who survived, the consequences of the flood may continue to unfold—in their bodies, in their homes and in their minds—long after the water has receded.

title.rendered: Nepal seeks $20 million from loss and damage fund over Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 10

Nepal has sought more than Rs 3 billion ($20 million) in compensation from the international Loss and Damage Fund, arguing that the devastating Rasuwa floods were linked to climate change.

Nepal sent a letter to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage under the UN climate change framework last week. Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle and Agriculture, Forest and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary signed the letter.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said Nepal has made an initial claim of $20 million.

“We have made an initial claim of $20 million for now,” Khanal said in an interview with journalist Sudhir Sharma. “After assessing the damage caused by the disaster, we will present our case to the international community.”

Nepal is among the countries with very low greenhouse gas emissions but is highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

Climate experts say Nepal should receive support from the Loss and Damage Fund not only for disaster-related losses but also in recognition of its minimal contribution to global emissions.

The Fund’s international board makes decisions on financial support. Environmental experts say Nepal has a strong basis to seek assistance given both the scale of the Rasuwa disaster and its low contribution to climate change.

The devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on Bhadau 10 caused extensive loss of lives and property.

title.rendered: Deuba announces nationwide tour to reconnect with party members

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Former Nepali Congress president Sher Bahadur Deuba has announced that he will soon embark on a nationwide tour.

Addressing an interaction organised by the Nepali Congress Bhaktapur on Wednesday to mark the 133rd birth anniversary of BP Koirala, Deuba said he would travel across the country to meet party members and bring those who may have been confused or misguided back to his side.

“I will soon travel across the country, reaching out to friends in every district, village and place who may have been confused and bringing them to our side,” Deuba said. Deuba also said he was confident that he would receive justice from the Supreme Court. “While assuring you that I will travel across the country and once again stand with the people, I would like to sincerely thank those who have stood by us. I also express my confidence that we will receive justice from the Supreme Court,” he said.

Deuba said the love and support he received from the Nepali people after returning home following medical treatment abroad was not meant for him alone but for all genuine Nepali Congress workers. “When I returned to Kathmandu, I received such love, goodwill and support from the Nepali people. I did not receive it alone; all of you received it,” he said. “You received it. The genuine workers of the Nepali Congress received it.”

Deuba urged party members to move forward by considering the love and support given by the people as something they had all received collectively. “Therefore, we must all move forward together, considering the love given by the people as the love we have all received,” he said. Deuba also expressed sorrow over the loss of lives and property caused by the Bhote Koshi flood in Rasuwa on August 26.

title.rendered: Special Court releases German passport printer Veridos on regular date

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

The Special Court has ordered Veridos, the German company contracted to print Nepal’s passports, to be released on a regular date without requiring bail.

A bench comprising Special Court members Narayan Paudel and Dilli Ratna Shrestha ordered that Veridos be released on a regular date without requiring it to post any bail amount.

The Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) had filed a corruption case against Veridos, along with officials of the Department of Passports, alleging irregularities in the printing of passports.

After the case was filed, Veridos authorised a Nepali representative to appear on its behalf.

The authorised representative appeared before the Special Court.

Following statements and arguments on whether the accused should be detained, the court ordered the representative to be released on a regular date.

title.rendered: Cultural discrimination in the Gurkha regiments: From recruitment to a crisis of cultural identity

content.rendered:
Following the Treaty of Sugauli, a new phase of Gurkha recruitment into the British military began in 1816. Impressed by the fighting capabilities of Gurkha soldiers during the Anglo-Nepal War, the British began recruiting them into their own military forces. In the early phase, recruitment was largely drawn from communities such as the Gurungs, Magars, and Khas-Chhetris of western Nepal, and recruitment depots were developed in areas such as Gorakhpur. Later, with the expansion of British rule, recruitment also expanded towards eastern Nepal, including the Rai and Limbu communities, through the Ghum area of Darjeeling.

Alongside this recruitment process, the British increasingly classified certain communities as “Martial Races”—communities considered particularly suitable for military service. Gurungs, Magars, Rais, Limbus and others were consequently given a distinctive military identity within British recruitment policy. Yet while their martial qualities were recognised and institutionalised, their own traditions, cultural values and social identities do not appear to have been given equal recognition within the regimental structure.

Here, one important distinction needs to be made. Rai, Limbu, Gurung and Magar are not religious groups. They are Indigenous communities with their own histories, languages, rituals, social institutions, customary laws, worldviews and traditional knowledge systems. Their traditional religious and ritual institutions and specialists also differ from one community to another.

Among the Limbu, Phedangma, Samba, and Yeba/Yema have traditionally played important ritual and religious roles. Among the Rai, the Nakchho has an important religious role. Among the Gurung, Lamas and Ghyabring have traditionally performed important religious and ritual functions. Among different Magar communities, Jhankris and other traditional religious specialists have played significant roles.

Eden Vansittart’s Gurkhas (1915) provides an important historical observation regarding the traditional religious practices of the Gurung community. On pages 47–48, Vansittart describes the Gurungs in their homeland as being associated with Buddhist traditions and notes the role of Lamas and Giabrings as religious and ritual specialists within their communities. However, he also states that when serving in British Gurkha regiments, they accepted Brahmins/Pandits for priestly functions.

This raises a serious historical question: If Gurkha soldiers were recruited based on their martial qualities and community identities, why was their own traditional cultural and religious institutional structure not given equal recognition within the regiments?

This cannot simply be understood as an ordinary change in traditional and religious practice. It also raises important questions about the relationship between the state structure of the time, Hindu social hierarchy and colonial military administration.

Family, regiments and cultural transmission

In the early period, Gurkha soldiers were not regularly permitted to live with their families within their regimental establishments. Soldiers generally returned to Nepal during long periods of leave and, in many cases, spent extended periods with their families and communities.

After the Second World War, particularly as British Gurkhas were increasingly stationed for long periods in Malaya, Hong Kong and Brunei, the relationship between Gurkha families and military life gradually changed. Between 1948 and 1971, the movement and settlement of Gurkha families in Southeast Asia became increasingly visible.

However, even during the 1950s through the 1980s, not all soldiers had equal rights or opportunities to keep their families with them. Various restrictions existed concerning length of service, authorisation, and accommodation.

In Britain, formal “married accompanied service” was introduced in 1997.

Today, the presence of former Gurkha soldiers and their families in Britain continues to grow. Gurkha soldiers have also raised longstanding issues concerning unequal pay, pensions, benefits and other rights for their military service.

Yet beyond economic and administrative discrimination lies an even deeper question: the continuity of traditional cultural rights and identity.

Military success, but a crisis of cultural transmission

The children and descendants of Gurkha soldiers are now studying at universities in Britain. Some have reached prestigious institutions such as Oxford and Cambridge and have established themselves as teachers, professors, doctors, businesspeople and professionals in various fields. This achievement is undoubtedly admirable. But another question arises: How easily are they able to transmit the languages, rituals, religious traditions, indigenous knowledge and community lifestyles of their ancestors to the next generation?

Military service created new opportunities for economic and social mobility. At the same time, however, it could also create circumstances in which younger generations gradually became detached from the languages, religions, traditions and traditional knowledge of their ancestral communities. Particularly when families began living for long periods within military establishments or overseas, the social and cultural environment of younger generations increasingly differed from that of their ancestral communities. Seen from this perspective, the history of Gurkha recruitment is not merely a history of military mobility. It is also a history of cultural transformation and identity.

The question of religious equality within the regiments

In this context, the question of traditional, cultural and religious representation within the regiments becomes particularly important.

For Gurung and Magar communities, lamas or other religious figures are, in some circumstances, present for traditional and religious practices. But an important question remains: Have the Nakchho of the Rai community and traditional ritual specialists such as the Phedangma, Samba and Yeba/Yema of the Limbu community been given equal institutional recognition?

If soldiers from different Indigenous communities were recruited into the same Gurkha military structure, their cultural and religious rights should also be addressed on an equal basis.

For Gurungs, this could include recognition of Lamas/Ghyabring; for Magars, Jhankris and other relevant traditional religious specialists; for Rais, the Nakchho; and for Limbus, Phedangma, Samba and Yeba/Yema. Recognising and respecting these traditional religious and ritual institutions according to the needs of each community is not merely a religious matter. It is a matter of cultural rights and equality.

Hinduisation and the question of cultural inequality

The history of Gurkha recruitment cannot be understood solely as a history of military recruitment. The relationship between Nepal’s Hindu state structure, its social hierarchy and cultural influence, and the administrative structure of the British Indian Army may also have influenced the religious practices of Gurkha soldiers.

Despite the existence of distinct traditional cultural systems among communities such as the Rai, Limbu, Gurung and Magar, historical evidence indicates that Hindu religious rituals and Brahmin priests were given an important place within regimental life.

This therefore opens another possible way of looking at the issue: “Hinduisation within the military institution” or “the institutional influence of Hindu cultural dominance.”

However, an important distinction must be maintained. The British colonial administration and the Hindu state structure of Nepal at the time were not the same institution and did not necessarily pursue identical objectives. Therefore, it would be too simplistic to place the entire responsibility for cultural transformation or cultural encroachment directly on the British.

Rather, it is necessary to look at the interaction between the existing social and religious structures of Nepal and the administrative practices of the British military system.

Yet this interaction raises another fundamental question: If the British military structure protected and institutionalised the martial identity of Gurkha soldiers, why was their indigenous cultural identity not protected and institutionalised to the same extent?

From Brian Houghton Hodgson to Dr Campbell, Eden Vansittart, and H H Risley, British officials wrote extensively about the ethnic communities, histories, languages, religions, and cultural practices of the Rai, Limbu, Gurung, and Magar peoples. Much of the data used in these works came from Rai, Limbu, Gurung, and Magar men serving in the very regiments of the British Army.

Hodgson himself was one of the key advisers involved in organising and systematising the Gurkha regiments. Vansittart was an officer serving with the regiments, while Risley was an officer in the civil service. They were also aware that the religious traditions of the Rai, Limbu, Gurung, and Magar peoples were not simply Hindu.

Yet the British did not complain to the Gorkhali rulers about the traditions and cultural practices of the Magar, Gurung, Rai, and Limbu communities. Instead, they continued to document, study, and publish their observations. They did not tell these communities that their traditions were right or wrong, or that they should follow one practice rather than another.

So, does this suggest that British studies of different ethnic communities were primarily intended to develop political strategies and perhaps enhance the status, authority, or careers of the officials who conducted these studies?

The question today

Britain presents itself as a country committed to democracy, human rights, multiculturalism and religious freedom. Therefore, the protection of the cultural and religious identities of the communities that have served in the British Gurkha military tradition should also be understood as part of the principle of equality.

Gurkha soldiers should not be viewed only as fighters or military personnel. They should also be recognised as members of communities with their own histories, languages, religions, rituals, knowledge systems and collective identities.

Honouring their military contribution alone is not enough. Creating an environment in which their cultural heritage can survive and be transmitted to future generations is equally important.

The present need is therefore not only to secure economic or administrative rights for former Gurkha soldiers. Their cultural rights should also be established as an important dimension of the rights associated with their military service.

This requires serious discussion about: equal representation of traditional religious and ritual specialists from different Gurkha communities; the right to conduct community-specific religious and cultural rituals; language and cultural education; institutional support for preserving Indigenous knowledge and traditions; and creating opportunities for younger generations to remain connected with the heritage of their ancestors.

In this sense, the next chapter of Gurkha history should not be limited to “Gurkhas as Soldiers.” It should also become a history of “Gurkhas as Communities, Cultures and Peoples.”

Because Gurkha identity is not limited to the soldier carrying a rifle. It is also connected to language, land, memory, rituals, religion, ancestors and community.

title.rendered: SC dismisses writ against Former Chief Justice Rana, clears way for pension

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

The Supreme Court has dismissed a writ petition filed against former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana. With the Constitutional Bench’s ruling, the way has been cleared for Rana to receive pension benefits and other facilities.

Rana, who retired while suspended following an impeachment motion, had not received pension benefits or other facilities. A Constitutional Bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Manoj Kumar Sharma and justices Sapana Pradhan Malla, Kumar Regmi, Saranga Subedi and Binod Sharma decided to dismiss the writ petition against Rana.

Rana had retired as chief justice while an impeachment motion against him was pending. The term of the House of Representatives also ended before the impeachment motion against him could be concluded. Subsequently, Federal Parliament Secretary-General Bharat Raj Gautam sent a letter to the Supreme Court stating that Rana’s suspension would be lifted.

The Nepal Bar Association and Supreme Court Bar Association filed a writ petition challenging the letter. Following an immediate hearing, the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Bench issued an interim order preventing the implementation of the letter issued by the Federal Parliament Secretariat.

Rana has remained suspended until now because of the interim order.

title.rendered: Parliamentary committee questions surge in sugar prices to Rs 130 per kg

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Rahbar Ansari, chairperson of the Industry and Commerce, and Labour and Consumer Interest Committee, has expressed serious concern over the situation following India’s ban on sugar exports, rising market prices and consumer interests.

Ansari raised the issue during a meeting of the parliamentary committee.

He said questions had been raised over the sharp rise in sugar prices within a few months, despite assurances that there were sufficient stocks in the market and that prices would not increase after India halted exports.

The committee also questioned how the price of sugar had reached as high as Rs 130 per kilogram.

Ansari said sugar, which was previously expected to cost Rs 85 per kilogram and Rs 96 after adding VAT, is now being sold for between Rs 105 and Rs 130 in the market. He stressed the need to investigate why prices had increased despite adequate stocks.

The committee chairperson attributed the current shortage and price hike partly to the failure to import sugar from other countries promptly.

He also urged the ministry to promptly introduce bills and laws in Parliament to protect consumers and control cartelling and black marketing.

Ansari said market monitoring should be made more practical and rational, while measures should be taken to prevent opacity in the purchase of expensive software. He also called for consideration of practical problems such as increased transportation costs caused by infrastructure damage and fuel supply issues.

title.rendered: Nepal should go to the UN to demand fairness, not sympathy

content.rendered:
The devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system on August 26 was beyond just another natural disaster. Within hours, settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower projects, and other infrastructure were damaged or swept away. Many people lost their lives, while thousands were displaced and exposed to serious risks.

This tragedy is a stark reminder that climate change is no longer a future concern for Nepal. It is already affecting the country’s economy, environment, and development prospects. More importantly, it raises a fundamental question of fairness: why should a country that contributes only about 0.027 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions bear such a heavy burden of climate impacts?

This question lies at the heart of climate justice.

The timing of the Prime Minister’s visit to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly is therefore highly significant. As leaders from around the world gather in New York, Nepal has an opportunity to move beyond routine diplomacy and present a compelling case for climate justice, international support, and shared global responsibility.

Nepal contributes only a tiny share of global greenhouse-gas emissions, yet it is among the countries most vulnerable to climate change. Nearly 80 percent of the population is exposed to climate-related hazards such as floods, landslides, droughts, heatwaves, and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs). Rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, and increasingly frequent extreme weather events are already affecting agriculture, water resources, hydropower, tourism, biodiversity, and infrastructure.

The Himalayan region is particularly at risk. Nepal’s ice reserves declined by about 29 percent between 1977 and 2010, while the number of glacial lakes increased by 11 percent during the same period. Across the Hindu Kush Himalayan region, glaciers are melting at an accelerating rate, and scientists warn that up to 80 percent of glacier volume could disappear by the end of the century under high-emission scenarios. The result would be greater risks of floods, landslides, water shortages, and other climate-related disasters.

The economic consequences are equally serious. Climate change could reduce Nepal’s GDP by around 2.2 percent by 2050, while climate variability and extreme weather events already cost the country between 1.5 and 2 percent of GDP each year.

The injustice is clear. Countries that benefited most from fossil-fuel-driven growth are now better positioned to cope with climate change, while countries like Nepal are paying a disproportionate price. Climate justice therefore requires major emitters to take greater responsibility for supporting vulnerable nations through adaptation, resilience building, and recovery.

Nepal should remind the international community that the Himalayas are not Nepal’s concern alone. Often called the “Water Towers of Asia,” they support river systems that provide water, food, energy, and livelihoods to nearly two billion people. As glaciers retreat and glacial lakes expand, the risks of floods, landslides, and GLOFs continue to grow. These changes threaten not only Nepal but also millions of people living downstream across South Asia.

Protecting the Himalayas must therefore become a regional and global priority. Nepal should use the UN platform to call for stronger cooperation on glacier monitoring, scientific research, flood forecasting, early-warning systems, disaster preparedness, and information sharing.

For years, Nepal has raised climate concerns in international forums, but awareness alone cannot protect communities or rebuild what disasters destroy. Nepal must now turn concern into action.

The issue of loss and damage should be central to Nepal’s climate diplomacy. Climate-related disasters destroy lives, homes, livelihoods, and infrastructure, yet support for recovery remains inadequate. Assistance should prioritise grants, concessional financing, and dedicated loss-and-damage funding rather than loans that deepen the financial burden on vulnerable countries.

Nepal should also push for faster and easier access to international climate funds, as existing procedures are often slow and complex. At the same time, it must strengthen its capacity to access these resources by developing credible projects, improving institutions, and building technical expertise. Through mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund, Adaptation Fund, and Loss and Damage Fund, Nepal can mobilise greater resources for climate resilience and recovery.

In international forums, Nepal must make it clear that it is not asking for charity; it is asking for climate justice.

Under ordinary circumstances, Nepal could be represented at the United Nations by senior officials. However, the current situation calls for leadership at the highest level. The Prime Minister’s presence gives greater political weight to Nepal’s message and increases the likelihood of attracting international attention.

But speeches alone are not enough.

The Prime Minister should use the visit to hold strategic meetings with leaders from major development partners and economies, including India, China, the United States, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. Discussions with institutions such as the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, Green Climate Fund, and relevant UN agencies will be equally important.

These engagements should focus on securing commitments for climate finance, resilient infrastructure, disaster recovery, technology transfer, glacier monitoring, and early-warning systems. Their success should be measured by the practical partnerships, commitments, and resources Nepal brings home.

To strengthen its case, Nepal must present a clear, evidence-based agenda. The government should document the human, social, and economic costs of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster and clearly identify its financing and reconstruction needs.

Nepal should seek faster access to climate finance, emergency support, and dedicated loss-and-damage funding. It should also work more closely with other climate-vulnerable countries, particularly mountain nations and small island states, which face similar challenges despite contributing little to global emissions.

At the same time, Nepal must ensure that its graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category does not reduce access to the international support needed for climate adaptation, disaster resilience, and sustainable development.

Turning pain into action

The Bhotekoshi disaster has caused immense suffering, and recovery will take years. Yet Nepal can still use this tragedy to strengthen its voice in global climate diplomacy.

Nepal should tell the world a simple truth: it did not create the climate crisis, yet it is paying a heavy price for it. The country needs more than sympathy. It needs climate finance, technology, knowledge-sharing, and long-term partnerships to build resilience and protect vulnerable communities.

The Himalayas are not only symbols of natural beauty; they are essential to Asia’s water security, food systems, energy production, biodiversity, and environmental stability. Protecting them is therefore a shared regional and global responsibility.

The Prime Minister’s visit to the United Nations should mark a new phase in Nepal’s climate diplomacy, focused on results rather than rhetoric. Nepal must seize this opportunity to secure concrete commitments and place climate justice at the centre of the global conversation.

Nepal should go to the United Nations not to seek pity, but to demand fairness; not merely to highlight its losses, but to secure meaningful support that protects its people, its mountains, and its future.

content.rendered:
Bhaktapur, September 9

The Panchadan festival is being observed in Bhaktapur today, with five Dipankara Buddha idols being taken in procession around the historic city.

The festival is observed annually on Bhadra Krishna Trayodashi, known locally as Panchadan Chare, according to Buddhist tradition. Historical accounts attribute the beginning of the festival to Jayadev Bajracharya during the reign of Malla king Naresh Malla in Nepal Sambat 775.

The five Dipankara Buddha idols brought from five Mahavihars are taken to different parts of the city and Buddhist monasteries throughout the day. Devotees offer grains, fruits and other raw food items produced from the land according to their means.

The festival also features the traditional practice of giving alms to Shakya and Bajracharya priests and Buddhist monks. Devotees, from children to elderly people, participate in the procession and alms-giving rituals.

Panchadan in Bhaktapur has distinctive local traditions. Families traditionally prepare kwati, a mixed-bean soup, at home on the festival day. Traditional musical groups perform Gunla music, Dafa devotional songs and other forms of traditional music during the procession.

The festival begins at Adipadma Mahavihar in eastern Bhaktapur and traditionally concludes at Thathuwahi in the western part of the city.

title.rendered: Truck with 1,240 kg of marijuana found in Dhankuta, driver absconding

content.rendered:
Dhankuta, September 9

Police in Dhankuta have seized a truck carrying a large quantity of banned marijuana.

Police recovered 1,240.6 kg of marijuana from the truck. According to Hemant Bhandari Chhetri, information officer at the District Police Office, Dhankuta, the truck carrying the marijuana was intercepted during a checkpoint operation on the Koshi Highway at Phedi, Sangurigadhi Rural Municipality-7, last night.

A team deployed by the Armed Police Force Nepal’s Disaster Management Base at Mulghat had stopped truck number Na 4 Kha 527, which was heading from Dhankuta toward Bhedetar, for inspection. However, police said that as the team signalled the truck to stop, the driver suddenly jumped out and fled.

DSP Rajesh Phuyal, chief of Armed Police Force Nepal Battalion No. 6, Dhankuta, said that after the driver’s behaviour raised suspicion, the Armed Police called in a team from Nepal Police’s Mulghat police post, and a search of the truck turned up a large quantity of marijuana.

After the marijuana was found, police took the truck and its contents into custody and brought them to the District Police Office, Dhankuta. Police said the total weight of the marijuana, when measured at the district police office, came to 1,240.6 kg. Meanwhile, the District Police Office, Dhankuta, said a search is underway for the driver who fled after jumping from the truck.

Police said they have intensified surveillance and checkpoint operations based on recent information that large quantities of marijuana are being trafficked through the Dhankuta section of the Koshi Highway.

title.rendered: Industry Minister says licenses of all 58 gas companies should be revoked

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Minister for Industry, Commerce and Supplies Gauri Kumari Yadav has said the licenses of all 58 gas companies operating in Nepal should be revoked, accusing gas dealers of creating artificial shortages and defying the government.

Speaking at a meeting of the Industry Committee under the Federal Parliament on Wednesday, Minister Yadav said the government had been left with no option but to consider revoking the licenses of all 58 gas companies currently in operation if they continued to withhold cooperation.

Yadav said it was embarrassing for the country that consumers were unable to obtain cooking gas even after paying for it. She accused gas companies of no longer complying with directives from the government and Nepal Oil Corporation. “In a country like ours, we don’t need more than two gas companies. At most, two would be enough; all of them should be revoked,” Yadav said. “I have also pleaded with all of them to make gas supplies smooth. Even after bringing all the gas operators together and pleading with them, it seems nothing works.”

Yadav also said gas cylinders sent to Kathmandu Valley were disappearing before reaching the market. “We sent 48,000 cylinders to Kathmandu the other day, but no one here has received more than 19,000 or 20,000. Where did the rest go? No one knows,” she said. “They don’t provide them even when we ask. The Nepal Oil Corporation may have written to them 10 times, but they haven’t supplied even once. Is the Nepal Oil Corporation involved in this, or is the government involved?”

There are currently 58 private gas companies operating in Nepal, including Salt Trading Corporation, which holds a 20% stake. However, Yadav accused the companies of failing to cooperate during the current crisis. “If all 58 gas companies had sent 3,000 cylinders each to Kathmandu every day, we would not be facing this situation today. It is embarrassing to think about what kind of country this is if people cannot get goods even after paying for them,” she said.

Saying that relying on the private sector had resulted in a betrayal, Yadav said Nepal Oil Corporation should establish and operate its own gas companies.

title.rendered: Elephants in the Fog earns three Asia Pacific Screen Awards nominations

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Nepali feature film Elephants in the Fog (Tiniharu), directed by Abinash Bikram Shah, has received three nominations at the 19th Asia Pacific Screen Awards (APSA) in Gold Coast, Australia.

The film has been nominated for Best Film, Best Director for Abinash Bikram Shah, and Best Actress for Pushpa Thing Lama.

The nominations come shortly after another major achievement for the film: Elephants in the Fog won both the Best Film Award and the Audience Award at the New Zealand International Film Festival, adding to an extraordinary festival journey that began with its historic selection at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

At Cannes, Elephants in the Fog became the first Nepali feature film officially selected for the festival, premiering in the Un Certain Regard section, where it went on to receive the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize.

The film has since continued to travel extensively on the international festival circuit, with selections including Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), BFI London Film Festival, Busan International Film Festival, Hamburg International Film Festival and the Melbourne International Film Festival, among others.

Set in Nepal, Elephants in the Fog explores identity, belonging, family and resilience through the lives of Kinnar women. At its heart is a story about a chosen family and the bonds created by people who build communities of their own in a society that often refuses to see them on their own terms.

Director Abinash Bikram Shah says the continued response to the film has been deeply meaningful. “It has been an extraordinary journey for a film that comes from such a specific place and community in Nepal. To see it connect with audiences and filmmakers across the world is incredibly moving. The recognition from New Zealand, and now these three APSA nominations, means a great deal to all of us who made the film.”

For Pushpa Thing Lama, the APSA nomination adds another recognition to a performance that has been central to the film’s reception internationally.

The 19th Asia Pacific Screen Awards will take place on 30 October 2026 on the Gold Coast, Australia, celebrating outstanding cinema from across the Asia-Pacific region.

title.rendered: Supreme Court orders government to publish details of gifts received by public officials

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

The Supreme Court has ordered the government to prepare and publicly disclose a consolidated record of all gifts received by Nepal’s public officials in an official capacity.

A division bench of Justices Dr Manoj Sharma and Nripdhwaj Niraula issued the directive while hearing a petition demanding that gifts received by public officials during official meetings and foreign visits be brought under government ownership.

The court ordered the government to establish a system to regularly publish details of gifts received by public officials through government websites or other appropriate means.

It also directed the government to establish legal liability for officials who fail to submit details of gifts to the concerned authorities.

The court further ordered arrangements for classifying gifts and setting a minimum value if an official wishes to retain a gift personally. It said the government must determine whether such retained gifts constitute taxable income and that gifts above the prescribed threshold should have to be purchased from the government if the official wishes to keep them.

The court also directed the government to make immediate arrangements to fill the legal gap until specific legislation on gift management is enacted.

Nepal currently has no dedicated law governing gifts received by public officials. Such provisions have instead been included in directives and codes of conduct.

The 2015 directive on foreign travel, daily allowances and gifts required senior government officials to submit details of gifts along with their foreign-trip reports. The Diplomatic Code of Conduct, 2020, also requires gifts received by public officials to be published on the concerned office’s website and entered into its inventory records.

The Supreme Court studied gift-management laws in other countries while issuing its directive. In the United States, senior government officials generally cannot retain gifts received without complying with federal rules, while gifts above a specified value are treated as government property. In the UK, ministers and their family members are barred from accepting gifts or hospitality that could influence official decisions; ministers may retain gifts worth up to £140, with more valuable gifts required to be surrendered to the relevant department.

The court noted that countries including India and Pakistan also have legal provisions governing gifts received by public officials, and said Nepal needed similar arrangements.

Advocates Srijana Adhikari and Bhawesh Gautam, along with chartered accountant Shailendra Upreti, had filed the petition seeking monitoring of gifts received by public officials and legal arrangements for their management.

The Supreme Court’s full text of the judgment issued on December 28, 2025 was released this week.

title.rendered: LPG shortage pushes prices above government rate in Kathmandu Valley

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Consumers in Kathmandu Valley are being forced to pay up to Rs 3,000 for a cooking gas cylinder amid continuing shortages and disruptions to supply routes.

The government-fixed price of an LPG cylinder is Rs 2,165, but consumers say some dealers are charging Rs 2,500 to Rs 3,000. The shortage has worsened after landslides damaged the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir, disrupting the main supply route into the Valley following floods in Rasuwa.

To maintain supplies, LPG cylinders from industries in Kathmandu, Dhading and Kavrepalanchok are being transported through alternative routes to plants in Bara, Parsa, Makwanpur, Chitwan, Nawalparasi, Dhanusha and Mahottari for refilling before being brought back to the Valley.

LPG dealers say higher transport costs have pushed up their expenses. Gahas Bikreta Mahasangh Nepal First Vice-President Gehendra Prasad Rijal said dealers have had to travel to the Tarai themselves because industries have been unable to supply them.

He said transport costs can add Rs 325–450 per cylinder depending on the vehicle used. However, he acknowledged that charging Rs 2,800 to Rs 3,000 per cylinder was unjustified.

The Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection Department said it has received complaints of dealers charging above the prescribed price and has deployed two teams specifically to monitor LPG sales.

According to the department, some consumers have reported being charged Rs 2,600 or more, but enforcement has been difficult when complaints are submitted without the dealer’s name, address or other identifying details.

Demand in Kathmandu Valley is estimated at more than 100,000 cylinders a day, while current supply is reportedly below 20 percent of demand. Police data show around 169,530 cylinders entered the Valley through Nagdhunga between August 31 and Tuesday.

Consumers, meanwhile, say the shortage has left them with little choice but to pay inflated prices to keep their kitchens running.

title.rendered: NEPSE falls 15.43 points as trading turnover rises

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

All major indicators of the Nepali stock market declined on Wednesday, with the market index, NEPSE, falling 15.43 points to close at 2,545 points.

The market had risen for four consecutive trading days before declining on Wednesday.

Trading turnover increased slightly. Transactions worth Rs 4.19 billion were recorded on Wednesday, up from Rs 3.83 billion on the previous day. Share prices of 74 companies increased, while those of 192 companies declined and 11 remained unchanged.

The development bank sector recorded the steepest decline, falling 2.37%.

The banking sector fell 0.16%, finance 1.08%, hotels and tourism 1.38%, hydropower 0.49%, investment 0.82%, life insurance 0.20%, manufacturing and processing 0.28%, microfinance 0.25%, non-life insurance 1.57%, others 0.52% and trading 1.56%.

Upper Lohorekhola Hydropower recorded the biggest gain, with its share price rising 15%. Shubham Power gained 6.40%, Barahi Hydropower 5.79% and Ingwa Hydropower 3.66%.

Emerging Nepal, Sindhu Development Bank and Janaki Finance each saw their share prices fall 15%. The prices of Sindhu Development Bank and Janaki Finance have been declining since an agreement was reached for their acquisition by Muktinath Development Bank.

Kalinchowk Darshan fell 14.28%, Upakar Laghubitta 12.04%, Muktinath Development Bank 7.98%, Trishuli Hydropower 7.60%, Saptakoshi Development Bank 7.33%, Nepal Finance 6.44%, and Mailung Khola Hydropower 6.32%.

Companies with the highest trading volumes on Wednesday included Reliance Spinning Mills, Central Finance, NRN Infrastructure, Solu Hydropower, Shivam Cement, Sanima Middle Tamor and Emerging Nepal.

title.rendered: Lamichhane defends state response, says anger of flood victims is a cry for help

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) chair Rabi Lamichhane has defended the government’s response to the Rasuwa floods, saying the state mobilised its resources quickly for rescue, treatment and relief.

But speaking in the House of Representatives on Wednesday, Lamichhane also urged the government and his own party to be patient with flood victims who lash out in anger, saying their frustration should be understood as an expression of grief and an appeal for help.

“I don’t think we should look at the government’s work during this disaster through the traditional lens of government versus opposition,” Lamichhane said. “From the very first hours of the disaster, the government mobilised all its resources and began rescue, treatment and relief operations.”

He said thousands of security personnel had been deployed to the affected areas and described the scale of the government’s air rescue operation as unprecedented in recent times.

Lamichhane said he saw little reason to question the government’s immediate response in rescuing and treating the injured and arranging temporary accommodation and food for displaced people.

Responding to those asking, “Where is the state?” and accusing the government of doing nothing, he said the state’s presence should be demonstrated through its actions.

“The strongest rebuttal to the claim that the state did nothing is to show, with evidence and visibility, where the state was,” he said.

‘Don’t attack people who have lost everything’

Lamichhane, however, said anger from people who had lost everything in the disaster should not be met with ridicule or criticism.

“Let us stop, right now, the petty comments and sarcasm on social media and in public spaces targeting the natural anger of people who have lost everything in this disaster,” he said.

He urged the government to take action against anyone found abusing disaster victims.

“It is not enough for the government to issue a statement saying we will be ruthless against those who mistreat people in pain,” he said. “Show it in a way that citizens can actually feel that the state is serious and that it stands with the victims.”

He extended the same warning to members and supporters of his own party.

“The Rastriya Swatantra Party does not need blind supporters who belittle citizens crying in the middle of a disaster,” Lamichhane said. “We need members who stand with ordinary people in grief and pain and wipe their tears.”

He said action would be taken against anyone at any level of the party found making degrading comments or engaging in cyberbullying against disaster victims on social media.

‘Anger is not an attack on the state’

Lamichhane also asked the state machinery and his party ranks to accept the anger expressed by citizens during a time of grief.

“When people are deeply hurt and experience unexpected grief, they may even curse God. So what is this government? What is the RSP?” he said.

He said such anger should not be interpreted as an attack.

“We should understand the anger of citizens not as an attack against us, but as an expression of their expectations and their final cry for help from the state,” he said. “The true power of the state today is the ability to listen to that anger, endure it and wipe the tears of those people.”

‘This is not the time to play politics’

Lamichhane also called for political parties to work together in the aftermath of the disaster instead of using it to attack one another.

“There is a disease we see even after a devastating disaster and destruction: turning disasters into opportunities to play the blame game and looking for ways to bring each other down,” he said. “This is not the time to cook political rice on the fire of a disaster.”

The Bhote Koshi flood struck Rasuwa on August 26, leaving the country facing a major search, rescue and relief operation.

Lamichhane said the situation required political forces to move forward together.

The day after the disaster, he had called an all-party meeting attended by senior leaders from the RSP, Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, CPN, Shram Sanskriti Party, Rastriya Prajatantra Party, Janata Samajbadi Party and Janamat Party.

The meeting adopted a 10-point commitment, with the final point proposing the formation of a high-level all-party mechanism for a long-term response to disasters.

The commitment calls for a parliamentary mechanism to work on post-disaster reconstruction, climate adaptation, updating the national disaster policy and providing continued advice, support and monitoring of the government’s work.

It also envisions the mechanism working beyond immediate crises to build national consensus on disaster preparedness and sustainable development and to support policy reform.

Lamichhane did not elaborate on that proposal in his Wednesday address.

Opposition parties, however, praised the commitment they had made to stand with the government during the disaster.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa calls for action against all involved in September 8-9 violence

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has urged the government to conduct an impartial investigation into the incidents of September 8 and 9 and take action against everyone found to have been involved.

In a video message issued on the occasion of BP Memorial Day, Thapa recalled that his own house was set on fire on September 9. He said, however, that the suffering of young people who were killed or injured in the incidents was far greater than his own personal pain.

Thapa said those responsible for the state crackdown on the peaceful protest on September 8, 2025 must be identified, as should those who infiltrated the protest and incited violence. He also called for an impartial investigation into the destruction of public property, including Singha Durbar and the courts, on September 9, 2025.

“Reactions expressed in the heat of the moment should be forgiven. But those who exploited the situation to commit crimes should not be forgiven. They must be punished,” Thapa said.

Recalling the government’s commitment to conduct an impartial investigation into the September 9 incidents, he questioned how far the investigation had progressed. He also demanded the release of the full report of the study into the September 8 incidents.

Thapa said everyone responsible for the crackdown and incitement of violence on September 8, as well as those who committed crimes on September 9, must face legal action. “Only then can the state move forward on the path toward becoming an accountable state,” he said.

title.rendered: Mob targeted TU Cricket Ground during Gen Z protests, but it was saved

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Flames of anger were raging across the streets of Kathmandu. What had begun as a relatively ordinary protest by the Gen Z group on September 8 quickly turned violent that same day.

By the following day, September 9, the situation had spiralled out of control, taking an increasingly violent and chaotic turn. Government offices were engulfed in smoke, public infrastructure was being vandalised, and the homes of political leaders and party workers were being set on fire.

Amid the chaos, an unruly crowd made its way towards the Tribhuvan University (TU) Cricket Ground in Kirtipur—a venue where the future of Nepali cricket and the dreams of millions were taking shape.

At the time, the TU ground was undergoing a major transformation, with its upgrading work nearing completion. Modern stands built at a cost of millions of rupees, floodlights that were nearly ready to illuminate the ground and other infrastructure were briefly at risk of becoming targets of the angry crowd.

On one side was the raging unrest; on the other was a venue regarded as the heart of Nepali cricket. But at that critical moment, the vigilance of security personnel, awareness among residents and the sound judgment of those working at the construction site helped prevent the crowd from causing damage.

Had reason not prevailed that day and the wave of violence destroyed the infrastructure, it could have left a dark chapter in the history of Nepali cricket. Instead, the ground was saved—and thanks to that timely intervention, the TU Cricket Ground later came alive under bright floodlights during the Nepal Premier League (NPL).

Millions of rupees at risk

The decision to upgrade the TU Cricket Ground was taken by the Cabinet led by then-Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli in Asar, 2081BS. The government had set a target of installing floodlights and constructing spectator stands within 300 days.

Accordingly, construction of the stands began on Falgun 21, 2081 BS, following a religious ceremony. The initial plan was to complete the work by Baisakh 24, 2082 BS, but the project could not be completed on schedule. Prime Minister Oli subsequently directed that the work be completed by the end of Ashad, at any cost, leading to an extension of the deadline.

However, construction was delayed again due to natural conditions and technical reasons. Although the foundations for the floodlights had been completed, installation could not proceed because the required materials did not arrive on time. After the Ashad deadline passed, the construction company continued working while paying a daily penalty.

With construction of the stands in its final stage, the protests on September 8 and the circumstances they created placed the multimillion-rupee infrastructure at risk.

Security guard Manoj Bam recalls some people attempting to enter the ground, saying, “This was built by the KP Oli government, so it should also be burned.”

“There were other people here as well. We all tried to explain to them that this was national property and made them understand. They then moved towards another area,” Bam said.

Prem Poudel, operator of BKOI-KCDC-BG JV, the company constructing the stands, was also near the gate at the time. After being called by the security guards, he and several technicians came outside and tried to reason with the crowd. “If they had forcibly entered the ground at that time, there could have been significant damage. Thankfully, they listened to our appeal and did not enter,” Poudel said.

Journalist Rishi Khatiwada, who was also at the site, said the active efforts of those present helped prevent damage. “We were near the gate. We told them, ‘This is the future of our sports. There is nothing to gain by damaging it. Please leave.’ One person then said, ‘Let’s go, let’s go,’ and they headed towards Balkhu,” Khatiwada said.

Shortly after the crowd moved towards Balkhu, a plume of smoke could be seen rising from a nearby police post.

The TU ground lights up

Despite the delays, construction of the stands was completed before Dashain. Floodlight installation then proceeded, and the ground was prepared to host the Nepal Premier League.

Although the national cricket facility was caught in a moment of uncertainty for several minutes during the most violent phase of the Gen Z protests, it survived.

A year later, as the TU Cricket Ground takes shape as an international-standard stadium, memories of that day remain fresh.

The protests caused damage to numerous structures, but this important national sporting facility was spared thanks to the restraint of those present and the active intervention of locals.

The TU Cricket Ground was subsequently completed and illuminated for the long-awaited Nepal Premier League, with the second edition of the NPL held under floodlights.

title.rendered: Rasuwa floods, Krishnabhir road collapse hit customs revenue and supply

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

The devastating floods in Rasuwa and the collapse of the road at Krishnabhir have disrupted supplies from the northern border, causing a significant impact on customs revenue, the Ministry of Finance has said.

Finance Secretary Dr Ghanshyam Upadhyaya said the flooding at the Rasuwagadhi border point brought supplies from China to a standstill, with the disruption subsequently reflected in customs revenue.

Speaking at a meeting of the House of Representatives’ Finance Committee, Upadhyaya said the government had deployed additional staff at the Korala border point to facilitate imports as an alternative to Rasuwagadhi. But the situation became more difficult after the road at Krishnabhir collapsed, further disrupting the supply route, he said.

The flood completely destroyed 55 kilometres of the Betrawati–Rasuwagadhi road, according to Upadhyaya. Another four kilometres of the Galchhi–Devighat road suffered partial damage to its paved section.

The 10-kilometre Devighat–Trishuli–Betrawati road also sustained partial damage.

The disaster has also taken a heavy toll on bridges. Upadhyaya said 33 motorable bridges across four districts were completely destroyed, while another four suffered partial damage. A further 68 suspension bridges were damaged.

The total length of the damaged motorable bridges is estimated at 3,000 metres, he said.

The disruption has spread beyond transport infrastructure. In the financial sector, 17 branches of 12 banks have been either completely or partially damaged.

The disaster also affected 4,800 business establishments, according to the Finance Secretary.

The education sector has suffered major losses as well. Fifty-six buildings belonging to 18 schools, containing 308 classrooms, were completely destroyed.

A total of 7,570 private buildings were either completely or partially damaged, while 48 government buildings were damaged, of which 35 were completely destroyed.

Agriculture has also been affected, with 1,806 hectares of cultivable land damaged. Upadhyaya said 13 hydropower projects and 25 irrigation projects were also affected.

The detailed assessment shows the scale of the disruption across different sectors.

Flooding caused serious damage to 1,259 hotels and restaurants, 1,212 wholesale and retail businesses, and 345 electricity, gas and water-related projects. Similarly, 263 manufacturing industries and 227 other service-sector activities suffered serious damage, he said.

Upadhyaya also said contributions from within Nepal and abroad were continuing to arrive in the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.
