title.rendered: Nepal Volleyball League sparks a new craze

content.rendered:
Before 3 pm, the area around the covered hall at Dasarath Stadium in Tripureshwar starts getting busy. Fans holding tickets begin arriving at the venue.


By 4 pm, the match kicks off. Each point scored through a spike, block, or serve draws hooting and chanting from the stands. Even after the match ends, discussion of volleyball continues outside the hall, with fans crowding around their favourite players for selfies and photos.

At the centre of this new atmosphere in Nepali volleyball is the Nepal Volleyball League (NVL).

Nepal’s first-ever franchise league in men’s volleyball has fueled a volleyball craze both on and off the court, alongside thrilling competition within it.

The arrival of top foreign players, spirited performances by Nepali athletes, and enthusiastic crowds have kept the NVL in the spotlight since day one, further broadening the buzz around the sport.

Some spectators are watching volleyball for the first time, while others are regular followers of Nepali volleyball.

“I never imagined volleyball could generate this level of craze. It was a really fun atmosphere,” says one spectator of NVL. “The game is really fast-paced, and we got to see excellent performances from the foreign players too.”

Nepali fans, who previously watched only national team matches and major volleyball tournaments, have now become supporters of their region’s franchise team. Some are cheering for the team of their favourite player.

The different teams, players, and styles seen in the NVL have drawn spectators closer to the sport.

Organised for the first time by Kedia Group, the NVL features six franchise teams competing against each other. With more than half the league-stage matches completed, curiosity is building over which team will top the standings and qualify for the final, adding to the excitement on the court. Competition is intensifying in every match, making results increasingly hard to predict.

Organising the NVL was a challenge for the organisers given that the entire country was in mourning following the Rasuwa flood on August 26. But rather than deepen the gloom during a difficult time, the organisers decided to go ahead with the league as scheduled from September 4, aiming to send a positive message. They also decided to donate all ticket revenue from the first day’s two matches to the Prime Minister’s Natural Disaster Relief Fund to support flood victims.

NVL COO Bikas Khetan said the organisers contributed Rs 590,110, raised from first-day ticket sales, to the Prime Minister’s Natural Disaster Relief Fund.

Similarly, the Kedia family has contributed Rs 10 million to the fund.

Organiser Kedia Group said the league has received strong support from spectators and has performed better than expected.

Unbeaten Karnali

With 10 of the 15 league-stage matches completed among the six teams, Karnali Shivraj has won three matches in a row and remains the only unbeaten team.

Karnali defeated Annapurna Spiker Kings 3-1 in its first match and beat Khaptad Falcons in straight sets. In its third match against Sagarmatha Smashers, Karnali secured a 3-2 win that went to a fifth set.

Chasing Karnali are Sagarmatha and Annapurna Spiker Kings, each with two wins. Sagarmatha has played four matches while Annapurna has played only three.

Karnali tops the table with 8 points, followed by Sagarmatha with 7 in second place. Annapurna sits third with 6 points. Kathmandu Reds, who have won 2 of their 3 matches, are fourth with 5 points.

Khaptad Falcons, meanwhile, have yet to win a match, having lost three in a row. Madhesh Warriors, who lost their opening two matches, secured their first win by defeating Khaptad. Madhesh sits fifth with 4 points, while Khaptad remains at the bottom without a single point.

Foreign players add a new draw

Foreign players are another major feature of the NVL. This time, players from Mongolia to Brazil have appeared on Nepali courts. Previously, competitions held in Nepal saw a heavy presence of Indian and Pakistani players. But this time, the participation of players from a wider range of countries has made the league more competitive, exciting, and given it a more international character.

A total of 18 foreign players from 10 countries besides Nepal are playing in the NVL. Pakistan has the most, with 5 players, followed by India and Mongolia with 3 each. The remaining 7 players come from 7 different countries.

Of these, only 6 have played in Nepal before, while 12 foreign players are playing volleyball in Nepal for the first time.

Players from Mongolia, Russia, Brazil, Benin, and various European countries are playing men’s volleyball in Nepal for the first time.

Pakistani players who have played in Nepal before, such as Aimal Khan, Ahmad Mustafa, Fakhar Uddin, and Adnan Khan, are also delivering excellent performances in the league.

Meanwhile, players making their Nepal debut, such as Mongolia’s Uranbayar Munkhbayar and Enkh Erdene, Poland’s Emil Smetek, and Benin’s Bosco Deto, have also performed impressively.

The arrival of new foreign players has given Nepali spectators the chance to watch a different style and standard of volleyball. Their skill, physicality, and on-court presentation have also created learning opportunities for Nepali players.

The presence of foreign players has therefore both raised the level of competition and become a key draw, bringing spectators to watch.

Standout performances from Uranbayar and Mustafa

Among the foreign players, young Mongolian star Uranbayar Munkhbayar, playing for Annapurna Spiker Kings, has drawn special attention from Nepali fans. The 21-year-old outside hitter, playing in Nepal for the first time, has won over spectators with his standout performances on court.

Consistently impressive, Uranbayar has played a key role in two of Annapurna’s wins, being named Player of the Match in both. He has delivered strong performances for Annapurna in every match, contributing significantly through powerful spikes as well as blocks and serves.

After being named Player of the Match in his first game, he said, energised by the support of Nepali fans: “I am very happy for our victory. Thank you to everyone for supporting us.”

Uranbayar’s performance remained excellent in Annapurna’s second win as well, and after being named Player of the Match in the match against Madhesh Warriors, he once again thanked Nepali fans.

Uranbayar has scored 84 points across 3 matches, 29 points in his first match against Karnali Shivraj, 29 more against Kathmandu, and 26 in the win over Madhesh Warriors.

The sensational performances of this Mongolian player, making his Nepal debut, have made him one of the tournament’s biggest attractions. The crowd’s reaction to his every spike, block, and decisive point reflects his growing popularity.

Similarly, Pakistani spiker Ahmed Mustafa, already familiar to Nepali audiences and courts, has also been performing excellently, scoring 102 points across 3 matches. Mustafa and Uranbayar lead the league in points scored.

Jibin Sebastian, playing for Madhesh Warriors in his Nepal debut, has also performed well. Nepali fans have shown great enthusiasm for watching debutants like Uranbayar, Jibin, and Bosco Deto in action.

title.rendered: Scorpio driver arrested in Siraha with 123 bottles of narcotic drugs

content.rendered:
Siraha, September 9

Police in Lahan, Siraha, have arrested the driver of a Scorpio SUV with 123 bottles of suspected narcotic drugs. The driver was arrested during a joint inspection conducted by the Armed Police Force and Nepal Police on Wednesday morning at Thadi Road in Lahan Municipality-3, based on a tip-off.

An 11-member vehicle mobile team from the Armed Police Force Security Base in Lahan, led by an assistant sub-inspector, and a nine-member mobile team from the Area Police Office in Lahan, also led by an assistant sub-inspector, jointly stopped and searched the SUV, registration number Sa 1 Cha 1414.

During the search, police found 123 100ml bottles of Corex-C inside the vehicle. The arrested driver has been identified as 41-year-old Bijay Kumar Bisuke of Lahan Municipality-10.

SP Suman Jung Thapa, chief of the Armed Police Force in Siraha, said the joint operation was launched based on specific information. He said the driver was taken into custody after the drugs were found during the search of the Scorpio.

The seized drugs, the Scorpio SUV and Bisuke were handed over to the Area Police Office in Lahan at 10:24 am Wednesday for further investigation and legal action, according to the Armed Police Force.

Meanwhile, Siraha District Police Office Chief SP Basudev Pathak said an investigation into the case was underway. According to him, the drugs were seized and the driver taken into custody after the Armed Police Force and Nepal Police jointly conducted the operation based on information they had received.

“We have already initiated the legal process. We will seek an extension of the detention period tomorrow and begin further investigation,” SP Pathak said. Police said they are also investigating Bisuke’s possible involvement in drug trafficking, as well as the source and intended destination of the seized drugs.

title.rendered: Karnali Highway reopens to one-way traffic after landslide cleared

content.rendered:
Surkhet, September 9

The Dailekh section of the Karnali Highway has reopened to one-way traffic after a landslide at Bhallu Khola, Dullu Municipality-10, was cleared. The road, which had been blocked by the landslide since Tuesday evening, was reopened for one-way traffic from 10 am Wednesday after the debris was removed.

According to the District Police Office, Dailekh, vehicles are now being allowed to pass in one direction after the landslide debris on the road was cleared.

Vehicle movement on the highway had come to a complete halt for some time after the road was blocked by the landslide.

Road blocked since Tuesday evening

The Dailekh section of the Karnali Highway was blocked after a landslide struck Bhallu Khola in Dullu Municipality-10 on Tuesday evening. With the road blocked, vehicles travelling to and from Surkhet and various districts of Karnali via the highway were affected.

Soil and rocks piled up at the landslide site, completely covering the road and disrupting traffic. Since the landslide occurred at night, it was difficult to reopen the road immediately. The blockage caused difficulties for passengers and drivers trying to reach their destinations.

Clearing work began early morning

After the road was blocked, clearing work began in coordination with the relevant authorities. The District Police Office, Dailekh, said that after the debris piled on the road was cleared, vehicles were able to resume movement from 10 am Wednesday.

However, even after the landslide was cleared, the highway has not fully reopened to two-way traffic. Since vehicles are currently only permitted to travel one-way, drivers and passengers are urged to exercise caution while crossing the section.

Landslide risk during monsoon

The Karnali Highway is frequently blocked by landslides during the monsoon season. Since the road runs through hilly terrain, rain often triggers soil and rock slides from higher ground at various points, disrupting traffic.

When the highway is blocked, it affects not only passengers travelling between various Karnali districts and Surkhet and other districts, but also cargo vehicles transporting daily essential goods. Prolonged road blockages can also affect the supply of essential goods to local markets.

Drivers urged to remain cautious

Although the road is now open to one-way traffic, there remains a risk of further landslides in landslide-prone areas, including Bhallu Khola, especially during continued rainfall. Police have therefore urged caution while operating vehicles in the area.

Drivers have specifically been urged not to stop vehicles in landslide-affected areas or attempt risky crossings, particularly at night or during continuous rainfall. Full two-way traffic is expected to resume only once the road is deemed completely safe.

The Karnali Highway is a vital road connecting the hilly and Himalayan districts of Karnali Province with major markets, including Surkhet. Since even minor obstructions on the highway disrupt long-distance transport, regular monitoring and prompt landslide clearance are seen as essential during the monsoon season.

title.rendered: A year after Gen Z movement, insurers have paid just 38% of claims

content.rendered:
A full year after the damage caused by the Gen Z movement, insured claimants still have not received full payment. Property worth about Rs 23 billion was insured against losses from the Gen Z movement of September 8 and 9, 2025, but insured parties have received payment on only about Rs 9 billion of their claims so far.

According to the Nepal Insurance Authority, 3,390 insured parties who suffered losses in the Gen Z protest have filed compensation claims. Together, these claims amount to Rs 23.19 billion. But a full year after the movement, insurance companies had paid out only Rs 8.82 billion by July 6, just 38% of the amount claimed.

An Authority official said not all claimed amounts get paid in full. He explained that once an insured party files a claim, the company pays only after assessing the actual damage, and in the course of that assessment, some claims turn out not to warrant payment, or not the full amount requested. He added that payment is also sometimes delayed by litigation, since either party, the claimant or the payer, may seek court intervention if dissatisfied.

Arson and vandalism against government and private property occurred during the Gen Z movement, causing total damage estimated at Rs 84 billion. Of that, only property worth Rs 23.19 billion was insured, according to the Authority. Protesters targeted not only government property but also private businesses and enterprises.

Protesters vandalised and set fire to dozens of private homes and businesses, including the Chandragiri Cable Car, Bhatbhateni supermarket stores, several vehicle showrooms, bank branch offices, the Maulakalika cable car, CG Digital, Hotel Hilton, Ncell, and the Hyatt Regency Hotel, causing partial or total damage.

Bhatbhateni alone suffered damage of about Rs 12 billion and filed an insurance claim of Rs 8 billion. So far it has received only Rs 2.5 billion in payment. Bhatbhateni’s chief operating officer, Panu Poudel, said the delay in payment was due to the time taken to assess the damage.

He said the remaining claim is still in process and payment is expected in the coming days. Bhatbhateni’s claim breaks down into Rs 5 billion for stock losses and Rs 3 billion for building damage.

Similarly, Hotel Hilton, which was set on fire, has not even received an advance payment on its insurance claim. Hotel sources said that despite filing a claim of Rs 5 billion, it has not received a single rupee so far.

According to an Insurance Authority official, of the total Rs 23 billion claimed, only about Rs 15 billion is actually payable. An additional Rs 4–5 billion in claims is in the final stages of processing, which, once added, would bring the total to around Rs 13–14 billion. The remaining claims are still under process, the official said.

“The delay in payment is because surveyor reports are coming in late. Once an insured party files a compensation claim, the surveyor conducts a real assessment, and payment is based on that assessed damage,” the official said. “For instance, when goods are destroyed by fire during the protests, there’s no stock left to assess; the value has to be reconstructed and verified, and that fine-grained work takes time.”

Sunil Ballav Panta, secretary-general of the Non-Life Insurers’ Association, said claim payments for damages from the Gen Z movement have not stalled. He said survey reports for large claims have only recently started coming in, whereas smaller claims, including most vehicle claims, were easier to assess and have already been settled quickly.

He added that because large businesses suffered extensive arson and vandalism, damage assessment for them naturally takes more time.

Why are claim payments delayed?

When a loss occurs, the insured files a claim with the insurance company, which then has a surveyor conduct a full assessment and prepare a report. The claimant may request a larger sum than the surveyor finds justified, in which case the full claimed amount is not paid.

Determining the actual extent of damage requires careful, detailed assessment, which takes time, making insurance claim payment inherently slow. Gathering evidence appropriate to the nature of the damage also takes time, insurers say.

Delays also occur when insured parties are unable to submit required bills, receipts, police reports, or other legal documents on time.

In addition, large claims require approval and fund transfers from foreign reinsurance companies, which takes time. For large enterprises, the sheer volume of damage documentation to verify adds further delay.

Disputes also arise when the surveyor’s assessed damage amount doesn’t match what the insured party has claimed. Resolving such disputes, through negotiation or, at times, legal proceedings, further delays claim payments.

title.rendered: Home Minister leaves Gen Z Memorial Park without inaugurating it after martyrs’ families reject statues

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Home Minister Sudan Gurung left the Gen Z Memorial Park in Satdobato, Lalitpur, without inaugurating it after families of those killed during the Gen Z movement objected to the statues installed at the park.

Gurung had arrived at the swimming pool complex in Satdobato shortly before the scheduled inauguration of the park, which was built in memory of those who lost their lives during the Gen Z movement.

However, he returned without inaugurating the park after relatives of the martyrs expressed dissatisfaction with the statues, saying they did not resemble their loved ones.

The family members who had gathered for the inauguration objected to the statues, saying there had been negligence in their construction. “The statues do not resemble the martyrs who lost their lives during the movement. There was negligence in making the statues,” they said.

The Gen Z Memorial Park features statues of 45 people who were killed during the Gen Z movement on September 8 and 9 last year. The park has been built on two ropanis of land within the swimming pool complex.

According to the government, it was designed to commemorate the martyrs and promote national identity and collective remembrance.

title.rendered: Everest View Trail Race in Solukhumbu receives international recognition

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

The Everest View Trail Race, organised by Mapya Dudhkoshi Rural Municipality in Solukhumbu, has received international recognition.

The adventure race, which promotes tourism, nature conservation and sports development, has been officially recognised by the France-based international trail-running organisation Ultra-Trail.

The International Trail Running Association (ITRA) has also awarded the race three points. These points, which runners earn based on the difficulty of the distance and elevation of recognised trails, can help them qualify for other prestigious international trail races around the world.

Following the international recognition, Mapya Dudhkoshi Rural Municipality Chair Buddhikiran Rai said the campaign to connect sports with tourism, nature, culture and adventure travel had achieved its objective. He said the recognition would provide an additional opportunity to showcase the area’s natural and cultural heritage to the world.

The trail covers approximately 48 kilometres, with a maximum elevation of 3,181 metres and a minimum elevation of 1,803 metres. Runners have a maximum time limit of seven hours and 45 minutes to complete the race.

The race starts at the under-construction Korku Stadium and passes through Mahabhir, Siliguri, Kudham High Camp and Kailashnath Mahadev Temple before finishing at Korku Stadium.

During the race, runners can enjoy views of mountain ranges including Mount Everest, Kanchenjunga, Numbur, Thamserku and Mera Peak. Adventure destinations such as Blas Waterfall and Mahabhir are also among the attractions along the trail.

title.rendered: Kulman Ghising joins rescue efforts at Chilime Hydropower Project

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Ujyaalo Nepal Party chair and former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising has reached the Chilime Hydropower Project in Rasuwa to assist in the ongoing rescue operation inside the project’s tunnel.

According to his secretariat, Ghising went to Chilime at the request of the Nepal Army to help with necessary coordination and provide technical advice. A rescue team, including foreign experts, is attempting to make its way through the tunnel to reach the powerhouse.

Ghising had previously served as the executive director of the Chilime Hydropower Project. Based on his experience there, he was brought in to coordinate efforts to rescue those believed to be trapped inside the tunnel.

Earlier, Ghising had also conducted an on-site reconnaissance of the flood-affected areas, including the Chilime tunnel.

The Nepal Army said a joint team, including foreign experts, has prepared a passage inside the Chilime hydropower facility using four large pipes, each six metres long, that are large enough to allow people to walk through.

The Army said large rocks along the road from Syafrubesi to the Chilime Hydropower Project tunnel were blasted and cleared to allow heavy equipment to be transported to the site. Only 95 metres remain before reaching the main rock formation, it said.

Until Tuesday, travel to the Chilime area was possible only by helicopter. Preparations are now underway to open a temporary road to the rescue site. Authorities are also preparing to continue the rescue operation through the night.

The rescue team is attempting to reach the powerhouse, located about 200 metres inside the tunnel. As of Tuesday, the team had advanced approximately 90 metres into the tunnel.

The rescue team has intensified its search amid suspicions that six people may still be trapped inside the tunnel.

Kathmandu Valley is facing a severe shortage of cooking LPG gas after recent floods disrupted the supply system. The government, however, says it has made alternative arrangements to ensure adequate supply.

Minister for Industry, Commerce and Supplies Gauri Kumari Yadav has directed the concerned authorities to ensure that consumers have immediate access to cooking gas.

Under the directive, consumers in Kathmandu Valley who cannot obtain a cylinder from the company they normally use should be provided gas by exchanging their cylinder for one from another company at the same price.

The ministry said the measure has been introduced to immediately address supply disruptions caused by the floods and provide relief to consumers. The arrangement will, for the time being, apply only within Kathmandu Valley.

Minister Yadav has instructed the Nepal Oil Corporation and concerned LPG gas companies to implement the arrangement immediately and effectively.

She also warned that anyone found causing unnecessary hardship to consumers, creating artificial shortages or acting against government directives during the crisis would face strict legal action.

title.rendered: Bill proposing Law Minister as Nepal Law Commission Chair advances

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

A bill proposing that the Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs serve as the chairperson of the Nepal Law Commission has moved forward in the House of Representatives.

The bill to amend the Nepal Law Commission Act, 2006, was registered in the House of Representatives on August 13 and has now been taken forward by the lower house. On Wednesday, Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam is scheduled to present a proposal seeking permission to introduce the Nepal Law Commission (First Amendment) Bill, 2026.

Once permission is granted, the bill will be formally introduced in the House of Representatives. The bill will then proceed to discussions in the House.

If enacted, the proposed legislation will alter the current structure of the Nepal Law Commission. Under the existing law, the government appoints the chairperson from among former Supreme Court judges or individuals qualified to become Supreme Court judges.

The bill seeks to remove this provision and make the Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs the ex officio chairperson of the commission. This provision is included in Section 3 of the bill.

With the law minister serving as chairperson, the bill also seeks to establish clearer qualifications, duties and powers for the vice-chairperson and members.

Under the proposed bill, the vice-chairperson will be appointed by the Government of Nepal from among individuals who have either served in a special-class position after working in the field of legal drafting or have at least 20 years of professional experience in legal drafting.

Two members will be appointed by the government from among individuals with at least 15 years of experience in legal drafting. One additional member will be appointed from among individuals with at least 15 years of experience in teaching or research in the constitutional or legal fields.

The secretary of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs will also serve as a member of the commission, while the commission’s secretary will serve as its member-secretary.

The commission will thus have seven members. The law minister will serve as chairperson, while the ministry secretary will serve as a member and the commission secretary as member-secretary.

The government will appoint the remaining four members: one vice-chairperson and three members.

The existing law defines a “member” of the Law Commission as including the chairperson, vice-chairperson, honorary members and member-secretary. The proposed bill removes the provision for honorary members altogether.

Under the new definition proposed by the bill, the term “member” will refer to the vice-chairperson, members and secretary of the commission.

title.rendered: 341 km of roads blacktopped, 3,400 km of new tracks opened in Karnali in 9 years

content.rendered:
In the nine years since its establishment, the Karnali Province government has blacktopped more than 341 km of roads. In the same period, however, it has opened more than 3,416 km of new road track. This shows that the provincial government has prioritised opening new tracks over upgrading and blacktopping roads.

The provincial government had set a target of blacktopping 165 km of road in the just-completed fiscal year 2082/83. But by the end of the fiscal year, it managed to blacktop only 91.77 km. This is still higher than the previous fiscal year, when 72 km of road was blacktopped across the province.

Since the province’s establishment, a total of 341.37 km of road has been blacktopped. During this period, 3,416.05 km of new (dirt) road has been built. Similarly, 819.60 km of road has been gravelled, while 853 km of work has been done on road upgrading and drain construction.

Blacktopping fell short of targets

Looking at district-wise progress for the completed fiscal year, most districts failed to meet their blacktopping targets. Among Karnali’s 10 districts, Surkhet had a target of 59.7 km but completed only 29.9 km.

Dailekh exceeded its target, 17.1 km against a 10 km target. Dolpa managed 1.2 km against a 1.5 km target, Humla just 0.2 km against a 1 km target, and Jajarkot only 0.7 km against a 5 km target.

Jumla met its target of 2.5 km. Kalikot, despite a 5 km target, completed no work at all. Mugu achieved 0.9 km against a 1.3 km target, Salyan 16.6 km against 20 km, and Rukum West only 1.7 km against a 20 km target.

Progress on blacktopping has been even weaker in the Himalayan districts. Under the RCIP-AF project, only 21 km was completed against a target of 39 km.

New road excavation exceeded targets

The provincial government’s road data shows that progress in new road construction exceeded targets. Last fiscal year’s target was 216 km of dirt road construction, but about 37 km more than the target was actually opened as new track.

This pattern, failing to meet paved road targets while exceeding new-track targets, has raised questions about the province’s road development priorities. Even as new roads open, the lack of regular upgrading, gravelling, and blacktopping means roads get blocked during the monsoon and accident risk increases.

War and inflation cited as main causes

Prem Bahadur Oli, spokesperson and senior divisional engineer at the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Urban Development, said road construction work was affected by international circumstances.

According to him, the war in the Middle East disrupted the supply of bitumen and also raised petroleum prices. He said the rise in construction material costs forced contractors to halt work.

He added that other seasonal factors also affected road construction. He claimed that had the war not occurred, progress would have come close to the targets.

He said that although all three roads under RCIP were on track to be completed last year, around 25 km could not be blacktopped due to the war. Under that project, four paved roads worth about Rs 810 million are being built in Surkhet; the ministry says physical progress on the three roads under construction last year exceeded 70%.

“Paved roads are a priority, but the budget doesn’t allow it”

According to ministry spokesperson Oli, the large budget required for blacktopping is the main challenge; blacktopping 10 km of two-lane road costs nearly Rs 1 billion.

“Paved roads are indeed our priority, but our budget doesn’t allow it,” he said. He said that since vehicle traffic in rural areas is comparatively low, priority for now has to go to building dirt and gravel roads.

Infrastructure ministry’s budget execution only 48%

With road construction progress falling short, the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Urban Development’s overall capital budget execution has also been weak.

Last fiscal year, the ministry had a development budget of Rs 10.76 billion (10 arba 75 crore 59 lakh 32 thousand). Of this, only Rs 5.21 billion was spent, with capital budget execution limited to about 48%. Progress also fell short of targets for bridge and building projects. The government had prioritised suspension bridge construction under its goal of a “tuin-free Karnali” — but of a target of 52 suspension bridges, only 39 were built.

Similarly, of a target of 43 road bridges, only 21 were completed. Three buildings were constructed. Under the Janata Awas program, 211 houses were built, and under the housing program for the poor, 248 houses were built.

District office performance also weak

Capital budget execution by infrastructure development offices under the provincial government also fell short of expectations. Surkhet Infrastructure Development Office executed 46%, Jumla 61%, Mugu 73%, Rukum West 52%, Kalikot 69%, Salyan 50%, Humla 43%, Dailekh 56%, Dolpa 53%, and Jajarkot only 44% of their development budgets.

Despite repeated instructions from then Chief Minister Yam Lal Kandel to accelerate development works, performance by infrastructure development offices in most districts remained weak.

Only 389 of 772 projects completed

Last fiscal year, 772 projects, including roads, bridges, and buildings, were underway under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Urban Development. Of these, only 389 were completed.

The ministry has also left the liabilities of ongoing and multi-year projects for the incoming government, with multi-year project liabilities worth more than Rs 3 billion passed on to the new administration.

While large sums are being spent to expand Karnali’s road network, there is no balance between opening new roads and making completed roads durable and safe. Blacktopping only 341 km of road in nine years, against opening more than 3,416 km of new road track, shows that the province’s road-development pattern of “track first, upgrade later” persists.

title.rendered: Electricity restored in Bidur Wards 10 and 11 of Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

Electricity service has been restored in wards 10 and 11 of Bidur Municipality in flood-affected Nuwakot district.

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said the government has stepped up efforts to restore electricity services disrupted by the floods in Rasuwa.

According to the secretariat of Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, electricity service has also been restored in flood-affected wards 10 and 11 of Bidur. Similarly, electricity service has resumed in Tarkeshwar Ward 4, which was also affected by the floods.

According to the ministry, around 83 per cent of electricity services in Rasuwa and around 95 per cent in Nuwakot have so far been restored.

Meanwhile, efforts are underway to distribute 2-kilowatt solar systems through the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre for community shelters, as well as individual solar systems to households based on their needs in areas where electricity has yet to be restored.

Employees and technical teams from the Nepal Electricity Authority and staff from the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre have been continuously deployed in flood-affected areas to restore electricity services.

title.rendered: 5-year-old girl undergoes successful liver transplant at KIST Hospital

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

A five-year-old girl has successfully undergone a liver transplant at KIST Teaching Hospital in Lalitpur. The hospital said the girl underwent surgery on August 18. Her 33-year-old mother donated part of her liver to her daughter.

According to the hospital, the girl was brought to the hospital after her health condition became critical due to Wilson’s disease. Wilson’s disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by the accumulation of copper in the body.

The liver transplant was performed after specialist doctors stabilised her condition through coordinated treatment, intensive care and continuous monitoring for about a month.

The hospital said the girl’s mother, the liver donor, had been discharged a few days earlier, while the girl was discharged today.

content.rendered:

The price of gold fell by Rs 3,000 per tola on Wednesday.

The price of silver also declined today. Compared to the previous day, silver fell by Rs40 per tola to Rs4,750. The price of silver stood at Rs 4,790 per tola the previous day.

title.rendered: Reaching for a little warmth: Thoughts on Elephants in the Fog

content.rendered:
“Phul ko rang failina nyano chahinchha” 

A flower needs warmth to spread its colour, says Pirati to Apsara, as she drops some blue flowers, collected from deep in the forest, into a bucket of warm water. Perhaps people are not so different from flowers and we require warmth too.

In the Abinash Bikram Shah-directed Elephants in the Fog, before joining Pirati at her work, Apsara rubs her hand and holds her hands against Pirati’s face so she can feel its warmth. This is a small gesture but beautifully encapsulates their relationship. They are each other’s warmth. In each other’s presence, they are unafraid to laugh carelessly and throw their heads back, to sing about their desires and dreams, to just be. We see them braiding each other’s hair and making TikToks. Pirati not only rescued her but gave her a place where she can be herself without constantly having to watch herself. Something her birth family and parents couldn’t give. And in turn, Apsara gives Pirati something too: a glimpse of an ‘ordinary life.’ A little happiness. A little normalcy.

Another source of warmth for Pirati is the Drum Master. He sees what the rest of the world chooses to look past. With him, she finds a love she had never imagined for herself. He is ready to build a life with her. Suddenly, a life in which she is loved for who she is becomes possible.

But how could a society which is barely accepting her existence accept the possibility that she might want to love and live life like anyone else? 

Society is willing to tolerate trans people as long as they remain within the borders it has drawn for them. Early on in the film, when the villagers are on patrol, they shout at the elephants: Don’t cross the sacred boundary, or else we will crush, grind and destroy you. This reflects what society indirectly tells trans people. It is okay when they come to weddings, to childbirth, when they give blessings. But the moment they dare to think for themselves, the moment they ask for more, even the limited tolerance disappears.

The Kinnar community can offer a place to call home and a sense of belonging for those who are comfortable living within that community and its traditions. But there are rules, a particular way of life you are expected to follow. And if you do not want that life, there are very few places left to go. Outside the Kinnar community, a trans woman doesn’t get the same tolerance as she would when going from house to house, dancing and giving blessings. She is much more likely to be exploited or hurt. That’s why so many of them are pushed into sex work. And the same society looks down on them. Men seek them out, yet it is the trans women who are called immoral, who are accused of corrupting men’s minds. What are you supposed to do when you are given so few choices to begin with? They are not really being asked what kind of life they want but what kind of limitation they can live with.

Anything outside the options you’ve been dealt seems impossible. When you have been told all your life that it is not possible, you start believing it too. This can be seen in the scene on the tempo where they are returning from a wedding. There, they joke about opening different businesses. Chameli imagines Pirati expanding her herbal workshop, Joon starting a tailoring business and herself managing it all. Their faces light up. Even if it’s fleeting, there is colour in their faces. But they laugh it off. That scene is devastating precisely because all of their dreams are so ordinary. They are talking about making enough money to live with some dignity. Dreams that most of us would barely call dreams. But they laugh it off as if it is a far-fetched idea. 

Maybe their business would succeed. Maybe they wouldn’t. No one knows, but that is the point: they are never given the chance to find out. They aren’t allowed the luxury of making mistakes. They cannot afford it. It is as if society is waiting for them to make a mistake, so that it can use that mistake as proof that they never belonged there in the first place. Let alone respect, they don’t even get indifference; all they get is coldness.

When you grow up without warmth, you are very cautious with yourself, your body, your mannerisms, your desires, your dreams. You learn what parts of yourself are safe to show and what parts must be hidden. You stop talking about your dreams because you know what will happen if you say them aloud. You change the way you speak. You learn to look away. You learn whom you can love and how much of yourself you can reveal. Pirati, Apsara, Joon and Chameli have all lived through some version of that coldness. They have been pushed away from the families they were born into and forced to find warmth elsewhere. In each other, they find people who understand the parts that they keep hidden. With each other, they find some of the warmth that has been denied them. But it’s only a sliver of what so many others receive without having to ask for it.

Most of us grow up with this warmth without ever realising it is there. Our families love us without asking us to explain ourselves. We are allowed to be silly, difficult, ambitious, and embarrassing. We are encouraged to dream. We can fail and come home. We can fall in love. We can make mistakes, change our minds, try again. We are allowed to grow into ourselves. But queer people are denied this warmth. Even if they get it, it is conditional. And when you have lived in the cold for long enough, you fail to recognise warmth when it is right in front of you. You become afraid to reach for it. 

As a queer person, you learn to make yourself strong because you have been taught that nobody will be there for you. There is a scene where Chameli says to Maya, who is recovering from a self-inflicted wrist injury, “Afule aafulai baliyo bana. Jindagi ma koi pani hunna afno.” That is the voice of someone who has learned that the only person they can depend on is themselves. When the entire world treats you like an aberration, it becomes frighteningly easy to turn that hatred inward. You are forced to grow up too soon. You stiffen yourself, harden yourself. Because there is no other choice. You have to be soft with others but never with yourself.  Early in the film, Pirati tells Apsara, “hami milera basna parchha.” Even after being treated with coldness all their life, they are the ones most skilled at creating warmth for others.

A little warmth is all it takes to not hate yourself. A little bit of warmth is all it takes not to crush your dream. A little bit of warmth is all it takes not to run away from happiness. A little bit of warmth is all it takes for someone to keep living. Like a flower placed in warmth, slowly opening, releasing the colour and fragrance. 

And the warmth doesn’t have to be something grand. Meeting their eyes without accusation or disgust. Not running from them. Laughing with them, not at them. Giving them a shoulder to cry on. Listening when they talk about their dreams. Watching them fight for their dreams. Letting them be.

Kindness is not tolerating someone at the edges of society. It is helping them enter the centre of ordinary life; it is allowing them to work, to fail, to love, to dream, to come home.

I choose to imagine a world where Chameli is running a business, wearing an open-cut blouse and dancing. Someone says she is more beautiful than Katrina Kapoor. I see Joon with her own tailoring business. I see Apsara working in music videos, dancing and acting her heart out. I see Pirati with her lover, a bigger workshop, her daughters braiding her hair, their warm hands resting against her cheek as they laugh together. 

All of us are flowers, waiting to bloom, waiting to share our fragrance, waiting to let our colours show. All we need is a little warmth. A little kindness.

title.rendered: Oli calls September 9 a day of ‘horrific destruction’, questions why accused remain free

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

CPN-UML chair KP Sharma Oli has described September 9, 2025, as a day of “horrific destruction”, saying the violence that followed the Gen Z protests amounted to a major attack on the foundations of the state, democracy and the national economy.

In a video message issued on Wednesday, marking one year since the events, Oli said the Gen Z movement began peacefully on September 8 but was later infiltrated by criminal groups that, according to him, deliberately turned the protests violent.

He said young people had taken to the streets over issues including good governance and restrictions on social media, and that the Constitution guaranteed citizens the right to freedom of expression and peaceful protest.

“But criminal groups infiltrated the peaceful demonstration and deliberately incited violence,” Oli said.

He alleged that young protesters were deliberately surrounded and taken towards the Parliament building, where the situation escalated and gunfire resulted in deaths.

Oli remembered those who died during the protests, including young people and police officers killed while on duty, and offered condolences to their families. He also wished those still receiving treatment a full recovery.

According to Oli, however, the events of September 9 went far beyond the anger generated by the deaths on the previous day.

He pointed to attacks on the President’s Office, the Prime Minister’s residence, Singha Durbar, the Parliament building, the Supreme Court, political party offices and public and private property.

“The scale of vandalism, looting, arson and loss of life was not simply an emotional reaction to the human losses of the previous day,” he said.

Oli described September 9 as the culmination of what he called a “dangerous conspiracy” aimed at reversing what he termed Nepal’s progressive path of nationalism, democracy and constitutionalism and pushing the country towards authoritarianism and anarchy.

He also questioned why those responsible for the destruction have not been held accountable.

“Why are the accused in the September 9 destruction being given immunity? Why are the reports being kept secret?” he asked.

Oli said the concerns and intentions of the young protesters were genuine, but argued that other forces had taken advantage of the violence carried out in the name of the Gen Z movement.

He said frustration among young people remains widespread and urged that the events of last year should not be repeated.

Oli also criticised what he described as attempts to spread hatred and retaliation against democratic institutions and political parties.

He warned that such efforts could push the country further towards regression.

Calling for unity, Oli urged what he described as patriotic, democratic, progressive and left-wing forces, along with people seeking peace, to stand together in defence of democracy, the Constitution, national interests and Nepal’s sovereignty.

He called on the public to use the anniversary of September 9 to commit to opposing impunity and anarchy and to work towards national security and a prosperous Nepal.

title.rendered: What Nepal lost in two days of Gen Z unrest

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

A year after the Gen Z protests, the damage is still visible in some of Nepal’s most important government buildings.

The main building of the Prime Minister’s Office at Singha Durbar remains in ruins. Work on the Birendra International Convention Centre at New Baneshwor has yet to begin, while reconstruction of other government offices, police buildings and public infrastructure damaged during the two-day unrest is still underway.

The destruction was widespread. Government data puts the total physical damage caused during the protests at Rs 84.46 billion — equivalent to 1.38 percent of Nepal’s gross domestic product and 4.30 percent of the annual budget for fiscal year 2025/26.

The damage was not limited to government offices.

Political party offices, businesses, private homes, vehicles and community structures were also affected. In all, 2,671 buildings were damaged during the protests of September 8 and 9, 2025.

The government formed a committee under then National Planning Commission Secretary Rabilal Panth to assess the damage to public and private property and prepare a reconstruction plan.

The assessment showed that the government and public sector bore the largest share of the loss, accounting for 53 percent of the total damage. Private property accounted for 40 percent, while community and other property made up the remaining 7 percent.

Of the 2,671 damaged buildings, 79.8 percent were public buildings.

Some buildings still waiting for reconstruction

The government has carried out technical assessments of the damaged structures. Buildings that could still be used were repaired and repainted, while others were identified for reconstruction.

In fiscal year 2025/26, repair work had begun on 904 buildings, of which 494 had been completed and reopened.

But some of the most prominent structures remain unfinished.

The Parliament building at New Baneshwor, which was heavily damaged, is among them. According to Prakash Aryal, deputy director general at the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction, a decision has yet to be made on whether the building should be reconstructed or replaced.

The building is already around 30 to 35 years old, and the fire severely damaged its internal structure. Officials have therefore been considering whether constructing a new building would be more practical than rebuilding the existing one.

As a result, reconstruction work has not yet started.

At Bhaisipati, reconstruction of the ministers’ residence is underway. The former Home Ministry building in Singha Durbar is also being assessed, with a detailed project report being prepared.

Elsewhere, the design for the Godavari conference hall has been completed, while retrofitting work has started at the Kathmandu District Court. The design for the Kathmandu District Administration Office is also ready.

The Damak View Tower, which was heavily damaged, is being reconstructed.

Some reconstruction programmes were left out during the merger of ministries and now require Cabinet approval and fresh budget arrangements.

Damage went far beyond buildings

The destruction was not measured only in burnt walls and damaged offices.

Government figures put the damage to buildings at Rs 39.31 billion. Vehicles accounted for another Rs 13 billion, while damage to other physical assets stood at Rs 20.36 billion.

A further Rs 2.81 billion was recorded in losses involving cash and valuables.

Temporary and private property losses amounted to Rs 9.02 billion.

Within the private sector, businesses suffered Rs 27.49 billion in damage, while households suffered Rs 6.05 billion. Political parties and community organisations recorded another Rs 5.97 billion in damage.

The protests also disrupted the production of goods and services, resulting in an estimated Rs 13.87 billion in production losses.

The employment impact was also significant. A total of 2,999 jobs were affected, with 2,353 people losing their jobs entirely.

Many of the damaged buildings were relatively new

One of the striking findings of the government assessment is the age of the buildings that were damaged.

Nearly half — 46 percent — had been built within the previous 10 years. Another 48 percent were between 10 and 49 years old, while only 6 percent were more than 50 years old.

The assessment also identified 57 structures valued at more than Rs 100 million among the damaged buildings.

Of the total 2,671 buildings, 921 were valued between Rs 100,000 and Rs 1 million, 1,114 between Rs 1 million and Rs 10 million, and 312 between Rs 10 million and Rs 100 million.

The damage came only years after Nepal had spent billions rebuilding and repairing infrastructure following the 2015 earthquake, adding another layer to the cost of the destruction.

Insurance covered little of the loss

Insurance has done little to cushion the losses.

Of the 2,671 damaged buildings, only 130 were insured — 19 government buildings and 111 private buildings.

The government initially allocated money for essential repairs. Reconstruction has now been included in the current fiscal year’s budget, with plans to award contracts for a larger number of projects.

The National Planning Commission’s reconstruction and reorganisation action plan estimates that Rs 36.30 billion will be required for the reconstruction of public buildings, vehicles and other physical assets.

The government has adopted a three-year reconstruction strategy for damaged structures and physical assets. The plan, published by the National Planning Commission in March, aims to complete reconstruction over the previous, current and next fiscal years.

Projects are to be incorporated into the National Project Bank, the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework and the respective ministries’ budget systems.

Under the plan, the federal government is to allocate Rs 10 billion each in the current and next fiscal years, while provincial governments are expected to allocate Rs 1.5 billion annually and local governments Rs 3.25 billion annually.

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle has also announced that the government will prioritise the retrofitting and reconstruction of government buildings damaged during the protests. The Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport has allocated Rs 6 billion for reconstruction in the current fiscal year.

A year later, the numbers show how much was lost in just two days. But in places such as Singha Durbar and New Baneshwor, the damage is still easier to see than to count.

title.rendered: UML calls Gen Z uprising a ‘serious attack’ on democracy and national economy

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 9

The CPN-UML has described the events of September 8 and 9, 2025, as a “serious attack” on Nepal’s democracy, national economy and foundations of the state.

Issuing a statement on Wednesday, a year after the destructive events of September 9, the UML paid tribute to young people who were killed in police firing during the Gen Z protests on September 8, as well as police personnel killed while performing their duties.

The party wished those injured in the protests a speedy recovery and expressed solidarity with political and social figures and businesspeople involved in rebuilding after the destruction.

The UML said it was natural for citizens in a democracy to present their demands, grievances and expectations to the government. It noted that the Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression, peaceful assembly and the right to protest.

However, the party alleged that criminal groups infiltrated a peaceful youth demonstration on September 9, which was organised around demands including unrestricted access to social media and good governance, and turned it into an “uncontrolled, anarchic and violent” protest.

According to the UML, organisers had obtained permission for a peaceful demonstration and later announced that the programme had been suspended after the situation became chaotic. The party alleged that infiltrators then used young protesters as “human shields” and encouraged them to attack the federal parliament building.

The party said 19 young people were killed during police use of force to control the crowd.

The UML also recalled that the Cabinet subsequently decided to form a judicial commission to investigate the incident, lift the temporary restriction on social media, provide free treatment to the injured and compensate victims’ families. The then Home Minister also resigned, taking moral responsibility for the incident, it said.

The party has sharply criticised the events of September 9, when the Presidential Office, Prime Minister’s residence, Singha Durbar, Parliament building, Supreme Court, political party offices, monuments and public and private property were set on fire or vandalised.

Calling the destruction a planned attack on democracy, the UML said the events could not simply be attributed to anger over the deaths of young protesters the previous day.

“The tragedy of September 9 was not merely an expression of emotion or anger triggered by the deaths of young people the previous day,” the UML said. “It was the manifestation of a dangerous plan to reverse the progressive course of nationalism, democracy and the Constitution and push the country into authoritarianism, anarchy and geopolitical conflict.”

The UML called for a thorough investigation into how a demonstration that had been approved as peaceful became violent and who was responsible.

It also accused authorities of attempting to arrest and prosecute the then prime minister and home minister on what it called false allegations and political grounds.

The party said the report concerning the events and the role of security agencies had been kept secret. It further alleged that those accused of the September 9 destruction had been given impunity and that investigations and prosecution processes against them had been halted.

“This has institutionalised the criminalisation of politics,” the UML said.

The party also questioned why security agencies had failed to prevent attacks on major state institutions and symbols of democracy.

“It is necessary to find an appropriate answer to questions being raised in society over whether this was due to a lack of professional capacity or questions of integrity,” the statement said.

The UML warned against accepting violence and anarchy as instruments of democratic change, calling for an end to impunity and urging citizens to reject violence and anarchy.

It said changes of government must take place through the constitutional process and that political problems in a democracy must be resolved peacefully.

The party also sought to distinguish the Gen Z movement from the violence and destruction that followed.

“We are convinced that the concerns, expectations and intentions of the young generation were genuine,” the UML said. “Young people were not involved in the violence and destruction carried out in the name of the Gen Z revolt. Other forces benefited from it.”

The party said the role of those “beneficiaries” had contributed to growing frustration among young people.

The UML further claimed that efforts to undermine democratic institutions and constitutional structures had intensified since last year’s events. It said attacks on political parties and leaders associated with Nepal’s democratic movement, as well as on the presidency, parliament, judiciary, civil society and other pillars of democracy, were pushing the country towards a “regressive and undemocratic” path.

The party also said the economy had struggled to recover from the destruction and that business confidence had fallen sharply, while social harmony and tolerance were being weakened and the risk of Nepal being drawn into geopolitical conflict was increasing.

The UML called on “patriotic, democratic, progressive and leftist forces and individuals” to work together to protect democracy, the Constitution, national interests, sovereignty and peace.

content.rendered:

Both houses of Nepal’s Federal Parliament are scheduled to meet on Wednesday, with the House of Representatives set to consider two bills and a proposal related to membership in an Asian legislative body.

Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sobita Gautam is scheduled to present the Nepal Law Commission (First Amendment) Bill, 2026.

She will also present a proposal seeking consideration of the Mediation (Second Amendment) Bill, 2026.

According to the Federal Parliament Secretariat, Gautam is also likely to present a proposal concerning Nepal’s membership in the Council of Asian Legislative Institutions.

The National Assembly is scheduled to meet at 1:15pm.

National Assembly Chairperson Narayan Prasad Dahal will also inform the House about a letter received from the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers concerning the allocation of portfolios among Cabinet members.

title.rendered: Climate justice is still far away for Nepal

content.rendered:
By Surabhi Sharma

The Bhotekoshi flood has left Nepal confronting one of its harshest human tragedies. A massive rock-and-ice avalanche unleashed a devastating surge through the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli river system, destroying lives, homes and critical infrastructure within minutes. The catastrophe has become a powerful symbol of the new and unequal climate risks confronting Himalayan countries.

But Nepal cannot stop at condolences, relief and emergency assistance. Those are necessary in a crisis, but they are not enough. Nepal must now raise a louder, clearer and far more forceful voice for climate justice in international forums.

Countries like Nepal, which have contributed very little to global greenhouse-gas emissions but face some of the most severe consequences of climate change, cannot be expected to keep paying the price for a crisis they did little to create.

Nepal should not be asking for sympathy. It should be demanding justice.

Climate justice is about responsibility

Climate change is no longer simply an environmental problem. It is a humanitarian, economic and justice crisis. It threatens lives, health, homes, food, water and human security. It destroys infrastructure and livelihoods, erodes development gains and forces vulnerable countries to repeatedly spend scarce public resources responding to disasters.

At the heart of climate justice is a simple principle. Those who have contributed least to climate change should not be forced to bear the heaviest burden of its consequences.

Nepal contributes only about 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions, yet it is among the countries highly exposed to climate-related hazards. Nepal’s emissions were approximately 58.8 million tonnes of CO₂e in 2024, an extremely small or negligible share of global emissions.

The imbalance is difficult to ignore.

And yet the countries least responsible for the climate crisis are often the ones being asked to rebuild after climate-related disasters, borrow money to recover and divert scarce development resources towards coping with risks they did not create.

That is not climate justice.

Climate justice must therefore be guided by the Polluter Pays Principle (PPP). First articulated by the OECD in 1972, the principle establishes a straightforward idea: those responsible for environmental damage should bear an appropriate share of the costs of preventing, managing and remedying that damage.

Applied to the climate crisis, the logic is clear. Countries and corporations that have contributed disproportionately to historical greenhouse-gas emissions should accept greater responsibility for the costs imposed on vulnerable countries.

Nepal is not begging for charity. It is not asking the world’s wealthier countries for generosity.

It is demanding that those who have contributed most to environmental destruction and the climate crisis fulfil their responsibilities and help pay for the losses and devastation suffered by countries such as Nepal.

This is not charity. It is accountability.

The Polluter Pays Principle should not be limited to compensation after a disaster. It should also contribute to the costs of climate adaptation and resilience, disaster recovery and reconstruction, relocation and rehabilitation, protection of glaciers and ecosystems, early-warning systems, scientific monitoring, climate-related health services and compensation for irreversible losses, including loss of life, cultural heritage and ecosystems.

The international climate-finance system must reflect this responsibility.

For countries such as Nepal, climate finance should be adequate, predictable, accessible and additional to development assistance, with grants—not additional debt—given priority. Vulnerable countries should not be pushed into borrowing to recover from a crisis they did little to create.

A loan that deepens the debt burden of climate-vulnerable least developed countries like Nepal cannot reasonably be presented as climate justice.

You cannot call it justice if the victim is asked to pay the bill.

Nepal is on the frontline of a changing Himalaya

Nepal stands on the frontline of a changing Himalaya, where the majestic beauty of snow-capped peaks is increasingly overshadowed by the growing threats and vulnerabilities unleashed by a warming climate.

Nepal’s vulnerability is particularly profound because the Himalayas are threatening the entire world rapidly.

Nepal is home to more than 3,000 glaciers and more than 2,000 glacial lakes. These glaciers and snowfields sustain major river systems, providing water for millions of people, agriculture, ecosystems and hydropower.

The Hindu Kush Himalaya Water, Ice, Society and Ecosystems (HI-WISE) Report 2023 found that Himalayan glaciers lost ice 65 percent faster during 2011–2020 than during the previous decade. Glacier retreat, declining snow cover and permafrost thaw are accelerating, while expanding glacial lakes increase the risk of glacial lake outburst floods.

These are not distant scientific projections sitting in research papers. They are increasingly becoming realities experienced by mountain communities.

The Himalayas are not merely a scenic landscape or a tourism destination. They are a critical life-support system for millions of people across Asia. Their glaciers, rivers and ecosystems are connected across national borders. A disaster originating in the mountains can rapidly affect downstream settlements, infrastructure, economies and communities.

The international community therefore has a shared interest in protecting the Himalayas. But shared interest must mean shared responsibility.

Climate disasters are development disasters

Nepal’s climate vulnerability also has profound economic consequences. Climate-related disasters can destroy roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, agricultural production, tourism infrastructure and settlements. UNDP estimates that Nepal could face climate-related losses exceeding 2 percent of GDP by 2050 without urgent climate action.

Every major disaster can erase years of development gains, as the recent Rasuwa floods have so painfully demonstrated, potentially pushing communities and the country’s development progress back by decades.

This is where the injustice becomes particularly stark.

Nepal should not be expected to rebuild the same roads, bridges, settlements and infrastructure again and again with limited domestic resources while the world’s largest emitters continue activities that intensify climate change. A country cannot build its way out of a crisis if every disaster destroys what it has just built.

At this critical moment, when the devastating impacts of climate change are drawing unprecedented attention from global climate leaders, that attention must translate into action.

Climate finance must become faster, simpler and genuinely accessible to countries facing climate-induced disasters.

It must not only fund new infrastructure. It must also protect, retrofit and climate-proof existing infrastructure, so that hard-won development gains are not repeatedly destroyed by disasters that vulnerable countries did little to cause.

The Mountain Tsunami: A warning the world must hear

The Bhotekoshi–Rasuwa catastrophe of August 26 demonstrated how rapidly climate-sensitive mountain hazards can become humanitarian disasters. The rock-and-ice avalanche and resulting flood devastated communities along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli river system, leaving thousands dead or missing and exposing the extraordinary vulnerability of Himalayan communities.

The tragedy should therefore be understood not simply as a natural disaster, but as a stark warning about the intersection of climate change, fragile mountain environments, human vulnerability and global inequality.

The world should not look at Bhotekoshi–Rasuwa as another isolated Himalayan disaster.

It should see it as a warning.

Nepal has warned the world before

Nepal has repeatedly raised its voice about the climate risks facing the Himalayas.

In December 2009, Nepal’s political leadership held a Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar near Everest to draw international attention to the impacts of global warming on the Himalayas, particularly the accelerating loss of glaciers and snow, just days before the Copenhagen climate summit.

More than 15 years later, Nepal again brought the Himalayan voice to the global stage through the Sagarmatha Sambaad, held in Kathmandu in May 2025 under the theme “Climate Change, Mountains and the Future of Humanity.” Its call for action demanded urgent climate action, stronger international cooperation and greater support for vulnerable mountain communities.

Scientists warned us. The mountains warned us. Communities living on the frontline warned us through their suffering. Yet the world has still not acted with the urgency and scale required. The Bhotekoshi–Rasuwa disaster has made the consequences impossible to ignore.

What should Nepal demand at UNGA and COP31?

The upcoming United Nations General Assembly and COP31 provide Nepal with an important opportunity to move beyond statements of concern and make a clear political demand for justice.

Nepal’s highest political leadership should speak with one strong and united national voice.

The message should be simple. Nepal is not asking for sympathy. Nepal is demanding climate justice.

Nepal should demand international recognition of the Himalayas as a critical global climate-risk and water-security region. The protection of human life, dignity and the survival of vulnerable countries must be placed at the centre of international climate policy.

Most importantly, Nepal should call for the Polluter Pays Principle to become a practical foundation of international climate finance and loss-and-damage arrangements.

Those with the greatest historical responsibility must bear a fair share of the costs.

Nepal should demand:

  • Adequate, predictable and grant-based climate finance for adaptation, resilience, loss and damage, disaster recovery and climate-affected communities;
  • Direct and simplified access to international climate finance for vulnerable countries and local communities;
  • Recognition that climate finance must not become another source of unsustainable debt;
  • A stronger international mechanism for permanent scientific monitoring of glaciers, glacial lakes, permafrost, snow and unstable mountain slopes;
  • Internationally supported early-warning systems and transboundary disaster preparedness, including real-time information sharing and coordinated response;
  • Greater support for climate-resilient infrastructure, hydropower, settlements and ecosystems;
  • Long-term support for communities displaced or affected by climate disasters, including health care, psychosocial support, education and livelihood recovery;
  • Accelerated emission reductions by historically high-emitting countries and an end to continued fossil-fuel expansion;
  • Greater access for vulnerable countries to technology, scientific knowledge and capacity-building; and
  • A permanent international diplomatic agenda for the protection of the Himalayas and the communities that depend upon them.

Nepal should also build a stronger coalition with other climate-vulnerable countries, including least developed countries, small island states, mountain nations and some developed countries facing desertification, floods and extreme heat.

Nepal cannot afford to approach international climate negotiations only as a vulnerable country seeking assistance.

Vulnerability is not weakness.

Nepal has a legitimate moral, environmental and humanitarian claim.

The country has repeatedly demonstrated its commitment to climate action despite its very small contribution to global emissions. It is protecting ecosystems, adapting communities, managing disasters and investing in resilience while confronting risks generated largely beyond its borders.

That gives Nepal not just a reason to speak, but a responsibility to speak more forcefully.

Climate justice should therefore become a central pillar of Nepal’s foreign policy and international diplomacy.

The time for condolences is over

The question is no longer whether Nepal is vulnerable to climate change. The Bhotekoshi–Rasuwa disaster has shown the consequences in the most painful way possible. The question is whether the international community is prepared to accept its responsibility.

For decades, Nepal and other vulnerable countries have warned the world. The glaciers have retreated. Glacial lakes have expanded. Climate-related disasters have intensified. Communities have paid the price.

Still, the response has too often been predictable: condolences after disaster, promises during summits and inadequate action in between. That cannot continue. Climate justice is not charity. It is not generosity. It is not a favour. It is responsibility. It is accountability. It is fairness. And it is increasingly a matter of human rights and human dignity.

The world has heard warnings from the Himalayas for decades. It has seen the evidence. It has heard the scientists. It has witnessed the suffering of mountain communities.

After the Bhotekoshi flood, condolences alone are no longer enough. Nepal must raise its voice—loudly, clearly and collectively—at UNGA and COP31.

And that voice should carry one unmistakable message: Climate justice now. Polluter pays. Nepal will not pay for a crisis it did not create.

title.rendered: Landslide-blocked Kimrong Khola reopens, immediate risk subsides

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 9

The flow of the Kimrong Khola, which was blocked by a landslide in Annapurna Rural Municipality-11 of Kaski, has reopened.

The landslide blocked the river at around 8pm on Tuesday night.

According to Kaski Assistant Chief District Officer Chitrangal Baral, the blocked section of the river has opened naturally.

“The information was that a landslide had blocked the Kimrong Khola at around 8pm. But when we contacted locals early this morning, they informed us that the river had already reopened. The flow returned to normal overnight,” Baral told Onlinekhabar.

Baral said the immediate risk has now subsided as the river has returned to its normal flow.

A police team was also dispatched to the site at around 4am on Wednesday to assess the situation.

According to rural municipality chairperson Bishnu Bahadur KC, the river began gradually flowing again through one side of the landslide blockage at around midnight.

“The flow gradually opened through one side of the area blocked by the landslide from around midnight. It has now returned to its normal level. The immediate risk has passed,” KC told Onlinekhabar.

Residents living along the Kimrong Khola and Modi Khola riverbanks had been alerted and urged to remain cautious after the sudden landslide blocked the river on Tuesday night.

title.rendered: Landslide blocks Kimrong Khola in Kaski, residents urged to move to safety

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

A landslide has blocked the Kimrong Khola in Annapurna Rural Municipality-11 of Kaski, prompting police to urge residents in nearby settlements to move to safer locations.

According to Kaski District Police Chief SP Navin Karki, locals reported that the river has been blocked for around six hours after a landslide fell into the stream. The same river had been blocked by a landslide in the past, triggering flooding.

Police have been using loudspeakers in Nayapul, Birethanti and surrounding settlements to alert residents about the potential risk and advise them to move to safe locations.

“After the rural municipality chairperson and other local representatives informed us that the river had been blocked for several hours, we are now making announcements along the riverbanks,” Karki told Onlinekhabar.

The river has previously caused flooding in Birethanti, cutting roads and washing away a bridge. The road to Ghandruk remains blocked due to the damage, police said.

Rural municipality chairperson Bishnu Bahadur KC said the river was blocked from around 6am and that authorities had received information that the water level had since fallen.

“Very little water is flowing in the river now. It has been nearly three hours, and there could be a problem if the river suddenly breaks through,” he said.

A flood in the Modi Khola on August 18 had also damaged the road in the Birethanti area, disrupting transportation. The road has not yet fully reopened.

Following the latest landslide and blockage in the Kimrong Khola, police have also urged residents living around the Modi Khola to remain alert.

Police have warned that a sudden flood could occur if the amount of water trapped behind the blockage continues to rise. Residents have been advised to stay away from river and stream banks and remain in safe areas.

The Kimrong Khola flows through Annapurna Rural Municipality-11 before joining the Modi Khola. The Modi then flows through Parbat district and eventually joins the Kali Gandaki River.

title.rendered: Prachanda accuses government of hiding Gen Z movement probe report

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Nepali Communist Party coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’ has accused the government of withholding the investigation report into last year’s Gen Z movement.

Addressing a memorial gathering in Sindhupalchok, Prachanda said the truth about the events surrounding the movement had not been made public because officials in the government had kept the investigation report hidden.

“Responsible people in the government themselves have hidden the investigation report and have not allowed the truth of the incident to come out,” Prachanda said.

He said the intentions and demands of the young people who participated in the Gen Z movement should be understood separately from the destructive incidents that followed.

Prachanda also alleged that the movement had been infiltrated in an attempt to discredit the demands and objectives raised by the Gen Z generation.

“There needs to be an impartial investigation into the events of September 8,” he said. “Likewise, the truth about the destructive events of September 9 must be made public.”

He said it was necessary to establish who was involved in the arson, vandalism and other acts of destruction during the movement.

According to Prachanda, the facts and findings obtained through the investigation should be made public to establish responsibility for the incidents.
