title.rendered: What rescue teams found and how far they searched in hydropower tunnels today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Search and rescue operations are continuing for people who remain unaccounted for at various hydropower projects following floods in the Bhotekoshi River.

According to the Nepal Army, joint teams were deployed on Tuesday to several hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot to search for missing workers.

At the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, a joint team comprising Nepal Army personnel and project representatives reached the powerhouse and control point as part of the search operation.

At the Rasuwa Bhotekoshi Hydropower Project, a drone search of the cable tunnel at Ronga located one body, according to the Nepal Army.

Search and rescue operations are also continuing at the Langtang Hydropower Project.

At the Chilime Hydropower Project, teams have entered the tunnel to search for missing people. A joint team, including foreign technicians, has prepared an access route inside the tunnel using four large pipes, each six metres long.

A large rock blocking the road between Syafrubesi and the Chilime hydropower tunnel was blasted and removed to allow heavy equipment to reach the site. The Army said another 95 metres remained to be covered before reaching the “major rock.”

Inside the tunnel, teams are using winches and buckets to clear debris. The joint team has advanced about 115 metres into the tunnel during the search.

At the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project, a joint team including foreign technicians has entered about 400 metres into the main access tunnel to conduct searches.

At the Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, a joint team comprising 34 Nepal Army personnel, four Armed Police Force personnel and project representatives is searching the powerhouse and tunnel.

At the Upper Trishuli-3B Hydropower Project, 101 Nepal Army personnel and project representatives have been deployed for the search. Three excavators were used to dig to a depth of around 23 feet around the project office and residential areas, but no missing people were found there, according to the Army.

Large numbers of workers at hydropower projects have remained unaccounted for following the Bhotekoshi floods. Teams involving the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force, foreign technicians and representatives of the affected projects have been mobilised for search and rescue operations.

The operations have been complicated by buried structures, mud and debris inside tunnels and difficult terrain.

According to the Nepal Army, 919 employees and workers at 11 hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot remain unaccounted for.

title.rendered: GCEF launches national Teej cultural campaign to support flood relief

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

The Global Cultural Expedition Foundation (GCEF) has announced a national school and college cultural competition for Teej, combining student talent, Nepali cultural traditions and support for communities affected by recent floods.

The campaign, titled “GCEF Teej for Nepal 2026 — National School & College Cultural Championship,” will bring together students from schools and colleges across the country under the message “Celebrate Nepali Culture • Stand with Nepal.”

Students can participate in four categories: solo singing, group singing, solo dance and group dance.

As part of the campaign, participants will make a direct contribution to the government’s designated Prime Minister’s Relief Fund/Disaster Relief Fund. The contribution is set at Rs 1,000 for solo categories and Rs 4,000 for group categories.

GCEF said it will not collect the money in its own account. Instead, participants will deposit the applicable amount directly into the designated government relief fund and submit their official payment receipt or transaction proof to GCEF.

The campaign promotes the message: “Pay Directly. Send Proof. Support Flood-Affected Communities. Participate for Nepal.”

Performances to compete for national titles

Participating schools and colleges will select their representatives and publish their performances on social media.

According to GCEF, performances will be evaluated by a judging committee on talent and technical performance, cultural relevance and authenticity, creativity, presentation and overall impact.

The foundation said winners will not be determined solely on the basis of social media metrics such as likes, views or followers.

Selected performers will advance to a National Grand Finale in Kathmandu, where four national champions will be recognised with trophies and certificates.

GCEF said the initiative aims to use Teej as an opportunity to promote cultural identity while encouraging youth participation and social responsibility.

The foundation has invited schools, colleges, students, teachers, parents, artists, media organisations and the wider public to participate in the campaign and support flood-affected communities.

title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

Nearly Rs 12 billion deposited in Prime Minister’s relief funds

Nearly Rs 12 billion has been deposited in the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund and Prime Minister’s Relief Fund, according to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. As of 9am Tuesday, a total of Rs 11.77 billion had been deposited in the two funds, the office said.

PM Balen Shah to lead 15-member delegation to UN General Assembly

Prime Minister Balendra Shah will lead a 15-member Nepali delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, according to sources at the Prime Minister’s Office. The delegation will include Prime Minister Shah, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal and the Prime Minister’s Chief Adviser Kumar Ben, among others.

Researcher claims exceptional heat preceded glacier collapse that triggered deadly Rasuwa floods

The mountain glacier whose collapse triggered deadly floods in Nepal and China on August 26 experienced exceptionally high temperatures in the days before the disaster, according to an analysis of meteorological data by a researcher. Average temperatures at the glacier, located at an altitude of 5,200 metres, were estimated at around 5°C between August 21 and 26.

LPG supply falls in Kathmandu Valley as only 18,000 cylinders distributed

The supply of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for cooking has declined significantly in Kathmandu after landslides at Krishnabhir along the Prithvi Highway disrupted transportation. After the landslide blocked the main highway, gas companies have had to transport LPG trucks via the Tribhuvan Highway as an alternative route. Business operators say the longer and more difficult route has made it impossible to bring in enough gas to meet market demand.

Hong Kong beat Nepal to reach semifinals, Malaysia eliminated

Nepal lost to Hong Kong in their final group-stage match of the ACC Premier Cup. Hong Kong beat Nepal by 15 runs. Chasing a target of 262 set by Hong Kong, Nepal were all out for 246 in 49.1 overs. Ishan Pandey top-scored for Nepal with 90, but it wasn’t enough for victory.

3 Nepalis arrested in Japan over murder of Nepali woman

Three Nepalis have been arrested in connection with the murder of 25-year-old Nepali woman Laxmi Rajbanshi in Fukuoka, Japan. According to Japanese police, those arrested on murder charges are 28-year-old Sanju Tamang, who is studying at a vocational school in Hakata Ward of Fukuoka City; 25-year-old Amista Tamang, who lives in Tosu City, Saga Prefecture; and 22-year-old Prabin Lama, who also lives in Tosu City.

Nepal Gen Z Front seeks answers a year after the uprising

On the first anniversary of Nepal’s Gen Z uprising, the Nepal Gen Z Front has released a document questioning the government and political leadership over what has happened to the movement’s core demands a year on. The Front said the anniversary should be used to assess the progress made on the issues that brought young people to the streets last year, including good governance, accountability, transparency, institutional reform and digital rights.

title.rendered: 3 Nepalis arrested in Japan over murder of Nepali woman

content.rendered:
Tokyo, September 8

Three Nepalis have been arrested in connection with the murder of 25-year-old Nepali woman Laxmi Rajbanshi in Fukuoka, Japan.

According to Japanese police, those arrested on murder charges are 28-year-old Sanju Tamang, who is studying at a vocational school in Hakata Ward of Fukuoka City; 25-year-old Amista Tamang, who lives in Tosu City, Saga Prefecture; and 22-year-old Prabin Lama, who also lives in Tosu City.

Rajbanshi, a resident of Chandragadhi in Jhapa, was found dead in a river in Fukuoka on August 19. Police suspect that she was struck on the head, strangled with a rope and then thrown from a veranda into the river.

Police have not disclosed whether the three suspects have admitted to or denied the charges.

The investigation has also revealed that Prabin Lama, who was in a romantic relationship with Rajbanshi, had been living in the same house as Sanju, one of those arrested.

Police suspect that a dispute related to the romantic relationship may have been behind the incident and are conducting a detailed investigation into the events leading up to the murder.

title.rendered: Researcher claims exceptional heat preceded glacier collapse that triggered deadly Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

The mountain glacier whose collapse triggered deadly floods in Nepal and China on August 26 experienced exceptionally high temperatures in the days before the disaster, according to an analysis of meteorological data by a researcher.

Average temperatures at the glacier, located at an altitude of 5,200 metres, were estimated at around 5°C between August 21 and 26.

That is unusually high for the time of year. Temperatures at the site had not exceeded 4°C during the same period in more than 55 years of recorded data.

The localised temperature estimates were reconstructed by Robert Rohde, chief scientist at Berkeley Earth, an independent climate research organisation based in California.

Rohde’s analysis found that the average temperature at the collapse site during the six-day period has increased by about 1.8°C since the mid-20th century.

Without the additional warming associated with climate change, a comparable temperature pattern would probably occur only once in several thousand years, Rohde told AFP.

The collapse occurred during the Langtang region’s fourth-hottest summer on record, according to AFP’s analysis of data from Europe’s Copernicus climate monitoring programme dating back to 1970.

Possible role of heat

Scientists say the unusually warm conditions could have contributed to processes that weakened the mountain.

“These hot conditions can also explain permafrost thaw and combined slope and glacier collapse,” French climatologist Valerie Masson-Delmotte said.

Permafrost acts like ice cement, helping hold rock faces together. As it thaws, mountain slopes can become increasingly unstable.

Satellite imagery also showed substantial snowmelt in the days before the disaster.

The meltwater could have infiltrated cracks in the mountain and contributed to slope failure, according to Etienne Berthier, a glaciologist at France’s CNRS research agency.

Experts, however, caution against directly attributing the collapse to the heat.

“It’s not as straightforward as ‘high temperature equals collapse’,” Kristen Cook, a geomorphologist at Grenoble Alpes University in France, told AFP.

“If the temperature acted as a trigger, it seems that it needed to wait until the rock was right at the tipping point of collapse,” she said.

Researchers are now examining small movements detected in the mountain in the years before the collapse and how those movements interacted with changes in temperature.

Rohde said evidence that meltwater or permafrost thaw had significantly weakened the rock near the fracture plane would provide a strong link to climate change.

His temperature analysis used data from the European Union’s Copernicus programme and its ERA5 climate model, along with observations from 14 high-altitude weather stations located between nine and 140 kilometres from the collapsed glacier.

Applications have opened for Nepali workers seeking employment as caregivers for people of all ages with severe disabilities at long-term care centres in Israel.

Applicants must be at least 25 years old and not older than 45. Interested candidates can apply online from midnight on September 8 until 11:59 pm on October 12.

Applications can be submitted through the Department of Foreign Employment’s website at ferms.dofe.gov.np.

Workers will be required to work 42 hours per week and will receive one day off per week. Annual leave will be provided in accordance with Israeli law.

title.rendered: Iran conflict drives up fuel costs for US consumers

content.rendered:
Washington, September 8

The Iran conflict and disruptions to crude oil shipments through a key maritime route have pushed US gasoline prices to their highest level in years, increasing financial pressure on American households and affecting travel plans.

The average price of regular gasoline in the United States has reached $4.14 per gallon, nearly $1 higher than a year ago. The price has surpassed the previous record of $3.82 per gallon recorded in 2012. However, it remains below the all-time high of $5.02 per gallon reached in June 2022.

The surge has prompted some families to reduce long-distance travel as higher fuel costs strain household budgets. Rising gasoline prices are also increasing transportation costs, which could eventually push up the prices of food, industrial goods and other consumer products.

The increase has been linked largely to disruptions in crude oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for transporting oil and other energy products from the Middle East to global markets.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US government was taking measures to lower gasoline prices but did not provide a clear timeline for relief.

If disruptions continue, US consumers could face further pressure from persistently high fuel prices.

—RSS/AP

title.rendered: Gen Z upended the old order. A year later, what has changed?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

A year ago, Nepal was governed by a coalition between the Nepali Congress and the CPN-UML, the country’s two largest parties in the House of Representatives. By conventional parliamentary arithmetic, the government appeared difficult to dislodge.

That calculation changed dramatically after the afternoon of September 8, 2025.

A Gen Z-led protest against the social media ban, corruption and other grievances turned violent, leaving 21 people dead and many protesters and security personnel injured. Within 24 hours, the government that had appeared secure on paper collapsed.

Angered by the state’s crackdown on unarmed protesters, demonstrators on September 9 set fire to and vandalised major state institutions, including Singha Durbar, the federal parliament building and the Supreme Court, as well as party offices and the homes of political leaders.

Nepal’s politics has since moved through an interim government, dissolution of the House, a fresh election and the rise of a new political force.

September 8: A protest turns deadly

The Gen Z movement began from Maitighar in Kathmandu on September 8, with protesters demanding an end to the social media ban and corruption.

The situation spiralled after clashes between protesters and security personnel in the New Baneshwar area.

Police firing killed 19 people in Kathmandu. Two more people died in Sunsari on the same day.

Then-home minister Ramesh Lekhak resigned that evening, taking moral responsibility for the deaths. Before submitting his resignation at a Cabinet meeting, he had told a Nepali Congress office-bearers’ meeting that he should take responsibility for the incident.

September 9: The Oli government falls

The protests became more violent the following day.

Government buildings, including Singha Durbar, the parliament building and the Supreme Court, were attacked and set on fire. Party offices and the homes of political leaders were also targeted.

Police stations in several parts of Kathmandu were torched. Protesters seized police weapons and attacked security personnel, while police officers deployed on duty also lost their lives.

As the unrest reached its peak, then-prime minister KP Sharma Oli was forced to resign. He was evacuated by a Nepal Army helicopter to Chanaun Barracks near Hetauda in Makwanpur.

President Ram Chandra Paudel accepted his resignation but asked the outgoing Cabinet to continue running the government until a new one was formed.

Sushila Karki and the interim government

To manage the political vacuum and transition following the Gen Z uprising, former chief justice Sushila Karki was appointed prime minister.

Karki took charge of the interim government on September 12.

Her government was tasked with restoring normal state operations and holding a fresh election.

It declared those killed during the Gen Z protests martyrs, provided relief to their families and formed a high-level commission to investigate the violence.

House dissolved, election announced

The formation of the interim government opened the way for dissolution of the House of Representatives and a fresh popular mandate.

An election for a new House was scheduled for March 5, 2026.

Although some leaders of the major political parties opposed the dissolution, preparations for the election proceeded without major disruption. Voting was held peacefully across the country on March 5.

The dissolution, however, triggered a constitutional debate.

Political parties approached the Supreme Court arguing that dissolving an elected House was unconstitutional. The issue was particularly contentious because the Supreme Court had previously overturned House dissolutions.

Some argued that the political force generated by the uprising had effectively become greater than conventional constitutional mechanisms.

Former lawmakers from the Nepali Congress and UML separately filed petitions seeking restoration of the House.

But the Supreme Court itself had been damaged during the uprising, disrupting judicial services and delaying regular hearings.

Eight former Nepali Congress lawmakers filed a petition for restoration on December 9. The Constitutional Bench issued a show-cause order on December 17.

Former UML lawmakers also approached the Supreme Court after the party formally authorised then-chief whip Mahesh Bartaula and whip Sunita Baral to take the issue to court.

A total of 18 petitions seeking restoration of the House were filed. They remain under consideration at the Supreme Court.

March 5: A new mandate

The March 5 election marked the clearest electoral expression of Gen Z’s dissatisfaction with the established political parties.

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) won 125 of the 165 first-past-the-post seats, giving it a near two-thirds majority in the House.

The Nepali Congress won 18 constituencies, the UML nine and the Nepali Communist Party eight. The Shram Sanskriti Party won three seats, the Rastriya Prajatantra Party one, and an independent candidate also won.

No Madhesh-based party won a constituency. The Nepal Workers and Peasants Party and Rastriya Janamorcha also failed to send representatives to parliament.

The election also exposed deep problems within the Nepali Congress, which had been the largest party in the previous House.

The party held a special general convention to change its leadership, arguing that voters would not trust it to contest the election under then-president Sher Bahadur Deuba.

The change failed to rescue the party electorally. Congress president Gagan Thapa lost to RSP candidate Dr Amaresh Kumar Singh.

UML chair Oli was defeated by RSP senior leader Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen, by a huge margin.

Balen Shah becomes prime minister

Balen resigned as mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City in the first week of February and entered the parliamentary election.

After the election, the RSP chose him as its parliamentary party leader. President Paudel appointed him prime minister on March 27.

He became prime minister as the leader of the party commanding a majority in the House under Article 76(1) of the Constitution.

At 36, his rise was widely seen as the most significant political consequence of the new political mood created by the Gen Z uprising. He also became the first person from the Madhesi community to serve as prime minister.

But translating the support generated by the movement into effective governance has proved difficult.

Pressure from parliament, within his own party and from public opinion has confronted the government from its earliest days.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung resigned on April 22, less than a month after the government was formed, amid controversy over his business partnership with Deepak Bhatta, who was being held in connection with investigations into the source of share investments and money laundering.

The government later accepted a committee report into the matter and reappointed Gurung as home minister on June 9.

Earlier, on April 9, Prime Minister Shah had dismissed labour, employment and social security minister Deepak Kumar Sah on the recommendation of the RSP.

RSP chair Rabi Lamichhane had accused Sah of abusing his position by arranging for his wife to serve as a member of the Health Insurance Board and participate in its regular work despite the board having been inactive for a long period.

Questions over the Gen Z investigation

The government also formed a judicial inquiry commission led by Gauri Bahadur Karki to investigate the Gen Z uprising.

The commission recommended action against the then government and security leadership over the September 8 violence.

But questions had been raised about the commission’s impartiality from the beginning because of social media posts Karki had written on Facebook and X while the movement was underway. Its report therefore failed to become free of controversy.

The National Human Rights Commission also conducted its own study and recommended action against those responsible. Its report attracted significant attention even before the full text was released.

The government formed amid public anger against the old political parties and expectations that “the new” would govern better has consequently become the centre of political debate.

Reform first, but questions remain

The Balen government made governance reform one of its central priorities from the outset.

At its first Cabinet meeting, it introduced a 100-point governance reform agenda, setting targets for administrative reform, results-based performance, measurable service delivery and greater accountability within the state machinery.

In its review of the first 100 days, the government claimed 87.2 percent progress on the agenda.

Independently assessing that claim, however, gives a less clear picture. The reform agenda was a significant starting point, but its real success will ultimately be judged by results.

The government has also highlighted measures including an investigation into the assets of high-ranking officials, the cancellation of political appointments, recovery of public property and investigations into financial crimes.

It has pushed digital services to reduce the need for citizens to visit government offices, including expanding the Nagarik App, making certificates available online, decentralising some land administration services and introducing digital driving licences.

The government has also sought to distinguish itself through faster decision-making. It has moved quickly on policy decisions, legal amendments, administrative restructuring and service delivery.

But that “fast-track” approach has itself attracted criticism, particularly where institutional procedures, Parliament’s role and constitutional norms have appeared to be sidelined.

Despite having a near two-thirds majority, the government has used ordinances to advance important matters, including issues related to the Constitutional Council and cooperatives. Opposition parties and critics accused it of attempting to govern by bypassing Parliament.

Prime Minister Shah’s social-media-driven style has also generated controversy.

One prominent example was the three percent equity fee imposed in the education and health sectors. Following widespread criticism, Shah announced on social media that the fee would not be implemented immediately.

Critics pointed out, however, that because the charge had been introduced through the Economic Act, a Facebook announcement alone could not overturn it and that a formal legal process was required.

His parliamentary role has also come under scrutiny.

When President Paudel was presenting the government’s policies and programmes at a joint sitting of Parliament, Shah left the meeting. Opposition parties subsequently questioned his absence during discussions and his response to the policy programme.

Critics argue that the prime minister is not merely the leader of the government but also the centre of parliamentary accountability, making his presence in the House more than a matter of political convenience.

Squatter settlements and press freedom

The government has taken a hard line on removing squatter and informal settlements along the Bagmati river.

While the need to control encroachment and protect the river is widely recognised, the government has been criticised for removing settlements without a clear alternative housing or rehabilitation plan.

The issue became particularly contentious when settlements were cleared without a visible management or resettlement plan soon after the government took office.

Its relationship with the media has also raised concerns.

A government circular seeking to limit state advertising to government-owned media, warning statements by ministers and online pressure on journalists from groups supporting the government have prompted questions over press freedom.

The Supreme Court has also questioned the constitutional implications of the advertising circular in relation to freedom of communication and the press.

Gen Z leaders: The spirit of the movement remains unmet

The Gen Z uprising changed the government. But whether it has addressed the issues that brought young people onto the streets remains an open question.

Gen Z leaders who gathered in New Baneshwar on Tuesday to mark the first anniversary said they were not entirely disappointed with the government, but believed it had fallen short of expectations.

Gen Z leader Kiran BK said the government had not completely moved away from the spirit of the movement, but had “mishandled” some issues.

“The government has not been able to grasp the spirit of the Gen Z movement exactly as it was. But it has not gone completely off track either,” Kiran told Onlinekhabar. “Overall, the government is moving in a positive direction, but not in an exciting way. It is moving at a satisfactory pace.”

He described the government’s approach as a “loyal medium approach”, saying it appeared to be gradually moving towards the movement’s agenda.

Activist Kishori Karki said the government must do more for young people injured during the uprising and the families of those killed.

The movement, she said, had sought an end to corruption and “nepo kids”, the reopening of social media and greater youth participation in changing the country. But violence and repression had permanently altered the lives of many young protesters.

“We came onto the streets united, wanting to change the country, end corruption, stop the ‘nepo kids’ trend and reopen social media,” she said. “But the situation became such that the movement caused massive destruction. Younger brothers and sisters lost their lives and limbs at an age when they should have been learning and growing.”

Karki said the government should guarantee education, healthcare and employment for those injured.

She acknowledged that the Balen government could not be accused of having done nothing, especially since it had been in office for less than a year. But because it had emerged from the political mood created by Gen Z, she said it should give the movement’s demands greater priority.

Gen Z Muslim coordinator Mohammad Nayim Rain said the movement’s central demands had still not been fulfilled.

“Our position was clear. We came to the streets with slogans against corruption, nepotism and favouritism, and demanding accountability,” he said. “Even today, we have not achieved full success on those demands.”

He also questioned why those killed and injured during the movement had yet to receive justice and why the inquiry commission’s report had not been made public.

Rabi Kiran Hamal said the uprising should not be understood simply as a movement to change the government.

“The government has changed in one year. Nothing else has changed. There is still work to do, and we will continue working for it,” he said.

He described the movement as an ongoing political and social process aimed at raising political consciousness and building the nation.

Hamal also said both sides must take responsibility for the violence—the state for its crackdown and protesters for allowing the movement to become violent.

A test for the new political order

Political analyst Krishna Pokharel said the Gen Z uprising delivered a major political blow to leaders of the established parties.

“The Gen Z movement, in a sense, gave political punishment to the parties and leaders against whom young people were angry for exploiting the state,” Pokharel said.

He said the movement could ultimately be considered successful if the new leadership avoids repeating the mistakes of the old parties and delivers at least part of what voters expect.

The new leadership, he said, is still being tested for its political judgement, strategic skill and ability to govern.

There have not yet been many achievements that make people say “wow”, he said. But one important point is already visible.

“So far, they do not appear to have moved towards exploiting the state. For now, that itself is an important achievement,” Pokharel said.

That leaves Nepal’s political transition at a delicate point.

The Gen Z uprising changed who holds power. It broke the dominance of political figures who had occupied the centre of Nepali politics for decades and opened the door for a new generation.

But whether that amounts to a genuine change in politics—not merely a change in political faces—will depend on what the new guard does with the power it has inherited.

title.rendered: Karnali Highway reopens after landslide cleared at Gagane Khola

content.rendered:
Surkhet, September 8

The Karnali Highway, which had been completely blocked for three days due to a landslide, has resumed operation.

The highway reopened on Tuesday afternoon after the landslide at Gagane Khola along the Surkhet-Jumla road section in Kalikot was cleared.

The Karnali Highway was completely blocked after a landslide occurred at Gagane Khola on Bhadra 20. According to the concerned authorities, the road was cleared and reopened at 2:45 pm on Tuesday, Bhadra 23, allowing small and medium-sized vehicles to travel in both directions.

With the highway reopening, vehicles travelling from Surkhet and Dailekh toward Kalikot, Jumla and Mugu, as well as those travelling from these districts toward Surkhet, can now move more easily.

As landslides have become more frequent at various locations along the Karnali Highway during the monsoon season, travellers have been urged to exercise caution.

The concerned authorities said they are regularly monitoring the condition of the road due to the risk of further landslides causing another disruption.

title.rendered: A year after Gen Z movement, investigation reports remain unimplemented

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Just hours after Balen Shah was appointed prime minister and took the oath of office, former Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli and then-Home Minister Ramesh Lekhak were arrested in the early hours of Chaitra 14, 2082 BS.

They were arrested as part of an investigation into a complaint of culpable homicide. The allegation against them was that they had ordered the use of excessive force during the Gen Z movement, resulting in the deaths of teenagers.

After spending around 13 days in detention, Oli and Lekhak were released following an order from the Supreme Court. The court had ordered that their detention not be extended, but it had not directed authorities to stop the investigation against them. On Chaitra 26, 2082 BS, investigators and government attorneys released both men on a personal recognisance basis.

What additional investigation has the government conducted against them over the past five months? Did authorities gather evidence against either of them? If no evidence was found, why has no decision been made not to pursue charges? These questions remain unanswered.

Apart from transferring two political figures and taking action against some administrative officials, no further action has been taken against those accused of suppressing the movement.

Not only that, the government formed after the Gen Z movement and the subsequent elections has not considered it necessary to make public any progress on the investigation into the events of Bhadra 23, 2082 BS despite allegations that the then head of government and the home minister responsible for maintaining law and order were involved in the incidents that resulted in loss of life and property. The government has similarly remained silent on the report of the National Human Rights Commission.

Human rights activist Charan Prasai believes the same pattern has been repeated in the suppression of the Gen Z movement. “Several months have passed since reports were made public stating that human rights violations and repression took place during the movement,” Prasai said. “This government has also shown no initiative to take action against those responsible for human rights violations. Impunity appears to be something all those in power cherish. Whoever comes to power in our country seems to embrace impunity. Those in power themselves are nurturing and perpetuating it.”

Accident, use of force or murder?

In the immediate aftermath of the Gen Z movement, three broad narratives emerged in Nepali society about the incident in which 21 people were killed in front of the federal parliament building.

Those who were in power at the time claimed that the casualties occurred when the Special Task Force of the Nepal Police, which was regularly deployed in the area, attempted to prevent protesters from entering a sensitive area or “vital installation.”

Former Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli, as well as political leaders in power, administrative officials and security personnel, maintained the same position. They repeated this claim during proceedings before the inquiry commission and in their responses to the courts.

Human rights activists and other stakeholders, however, described the incident as the result of “disproportionate use of force.”

Studies and reports by various human rights activists also stated that the casualties resulted from an unusually lethal use of force and called for those involved to be held accountable. Protesters and leaders of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), meanwhile, have demanded that the incident be treated not merely as excessive use of force but as murder.

The inquiry commission led by former Supreme Court justice Gauri Bahadur Karki also recommended criminal prosecution, concluding that citizens had died due to negligence by those in positions of political leadership.

Based on the commission’s findings, Prime Minister Balen Shah, Home Minister Sudan Gurung and others directed the arrest of Oli and Lekhak the day after Shah took the oath of office. Although Oli and Lekhak were released about two weeks after their arrests, the criminal investigation against them remains pending.

However, police have not proceeded with questioning other people linked to the incident, collecting additional evidence or examining documents. The investigation has been virtually stalled since Oli and Lekhak were arrested. As a result, questions remain unanswered about the extent of the involvement of those implicated in the Bhadra 23, 2082 BS incident, how much evidence exists against them, and to what extent they should be held responsible and accountable.

Although the inquiry commission and the National Human Rights Commission investigated the incident, detailed documents identifying those involved in the use of force and analysing their accountability are not publicly available.

The inquiry commission formed by the government under the leadership of former justice Gauri Bahadur Karki had faced allegations from the outset that it was working with a political bias. The commission recommended that criminal investigations be initiated against those involved in suppressing the movement and that homicide charges be filed.

In the six months since the report was made public following the elections last Falgun, the government has formed one study team after another to examine the report but has shown little initiative in implementing its recommendations. There has also been insufficient public debate over how much criminal responsibility the political leadership of the time should bear, and to what extent, for the suppression of the movement.

The government led by then-interim Prime Minister Sushila Karki considered its responsibility fulfilled after sending the Karki Commission report to the library of the Federal Parliament Secretariat for public access. The post-election House of Representatives and its various parliamentary committees do not appear to have made studying the report or pursuing policy reforms a priority.

On Jestha 13, the National Human Rights Commission recommended departmental action against several officials over the suppression of the Gen Z movement. The commission held then-Inspector General of Police Chandra Kuber Khapung, current IGP Dan Bahadur Karki, Armed Police Force IGP Raju Aryal and then-chief of the National Investigation Department Hutaraj Thapa, among others, responsible.

Similarly, it recommended investigations into alleged human rights violations by DIG Om Bikram Rana, SP Bishwa Adhikari, Armed Police Force DIG Narayan Dutta Poudel, SP Jeevan KC, National Investigation Department Director Krishna Khanal and Kathmandu Chief District Officer Chhabilal Rijal. Some of these officials continue to hold key positions, while others have been transferred elsewhere. Apart from these measures, the government has not taken further action.

Human rights activist Charan Prasai witnessed the suppression of the 1990 People’s Movement and the 2006/07 People’s Movement firsthand. He has not only witnessed repression but also seen reports recommending action against those responsible and the bitter history of those perpetrators subsequently receiving impunity. An inquiry into the suppression of the 1990 People’s Movement was conducted under former justice Janardan Lal Mallik. The report of what came to be known as the Mallik Commission was never implemented. Similarly, another commission led by former justice Krishna Jung Rayamajhi was formed to investigate the suppression of the 2006/07 People’s Movement, but its report was also never implemented.

From the suppression during the Madhes movement to the Tikapur incident and the commissions formed for transitional justice, either the bodies were not allowed to function effectively or, even when they completed their work, their reports and recommendations were left in limbo. “Those who participated in past movements faced repression simply for taking to the streets, and some lost their lives. Those who came to power afterwards forgot their sacrifices and failed to take action against those responsible,” Prasai said. “This has been happening since 1990. This culture is not a good sign for democracy.”

Where is the investigation and scrutiny into the destruction?

Following the excessive use of force and loss of civilian lives on Bhadra 23, the homes of leaders from various political parties, police stations and government offices were set on fire and attacked on Bhadra 24. It has not yet been clearly established through investigation how many of these incidents were spontaneous reactions to anger, how many were acts of retaliation, and how many involved planned and organised groups.

In particular, apart from a limited number of people accused of carrying out deadly attacks on security personnel during the Bhadra 24 incidents, little action has been taken against others. Investigations into those who set fire to and destroyed documents at Singha Durbar, the Supreme Court and other government institutions have failed to gain momentum.

Although some people accused of attacking public institutions have been arrested and prosecuted, those involved in other, more serious incidents have largely escaped accountability. The interim government at the time itself failed to adopt a clear policy on how to deal with the Bhadra 24 incidents.

The government assigned the Karki Commission responsibility for investigating the events of the following day, but the commission effectively stepped outside its mandate, saying that the Bhadra 24 incidents required “further intensive and detailed investigation.”

Since the government led by Balen Shah came to power, it has not made investigation and prosecution of those involved in the Bhadra 24 incidents a priority. Gen Z rights activist Raksha Bam says the cycle in which people have repeatedly had to sacrifice their lives simply to demand answers to their questions must end.

She says the cycle of deaths in response to public demands will not stop until the government becomes responsible and accountable. “No government can be more valuable than the lives of the people,” she said. Prasai, who concludes that accountability has not been prioritised because those in power see greater benefits in accepting impunity, considers the lack of political will the main reason for its persistence. “Those who come to power have preserved the bad practices of their predecessors as if they were inherited property,” Prasai said. “Impunity, which has become a regular feature of Nepal’s political culture, has been repeated even after the Gen Z movement.”

title.rendered: Norway contributes to Nepal flood relief through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

On Monday, Norway, through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, handed over medical, energy and technical equipment to Nepal as relief for Bhote Koshi flood victims.

EU ECHO‘s Rapid Response Coordinator Asia and Pacific, Isabelle D’Haudt, formally handed over the shipment to Mahabir Pun, Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation.

“The arrival of this support reflects the continued commitment of European partners to stand with Nepal during this difficult time,” states the Delegation of the European Union to Nepal.

title.rendered: 10 Bangladeshis arrested for suspicious activities in Thamel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September

Police have arrested 10 Bangladeshi nationals on charges of residing illegally and engaging in suspicious activities in the Thamel area.

Police Superintendent Sharat Kumar Thapa Chhetri of the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office said the individuals were found to be residing illegally and carrying out suspicious activities at various hotels and guesthouses in the Thamel area of Kathmandu Metropolitan City-26.

According to police, those arrested are: 46-year-old Fahima Aktar Hasan, 48-year-old Mahamud, 45-year-old Mahbub Hasan, 49-year-old Repon Mehmud, 30-year-old MD-Keramot Alikhan, 30-year-old Shahidur Rahman, 50-year-old MD Khalilur Rahman, 28-year-old Arifur Rahman, 42-year-old MD Maruf Mridha, and 64-year-old Mohammad Hanif Miya — all residents of Thamel, originally from Gazipur, Gadbapur police station area, Bangladesh.

Police said they were taken into custody from locations including Hotel Dhaka Express, Hotel D Vedha, and Hotel Al Rahman. All those arrested have been sent to the Department of Immigration for further investigation and necessary action.

title.rendered: LPG supply falls in Kathmandu Valley as only 18,000 cylinders distributed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

The supply of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for cooking has declined significantly in Kathmandu after landslides at Krishnabhir along the Prithvi Highway disrupted transportation.

After the landslide blocked the main highway, gas companies have had to transport LPG trucks via the Tribhuvan Highway as an alternative route. Business operators say the longer and more difficult route has made it impossible to bring in enough gas to meet market demand.

Due to the supply disruption, a total of only 18,259 LPG cylinders from nine gas companies reached dealers in Kathmandu Valley on Tuesday.

Diwan Chand, president of the LPG Industry Association, said demand for LPG in Kathmandu Valley has risen to around 100,000 cylinders per day in recent days. Under normal circumstances, daily demand stands at around 35,000 to 40,000 cylinders, he said.

According to data provided by the LPG Department of Nepal Oil Corporation, Sagarmatha Gas supplied the highest number of cylinders on Tuesday, sending 4,699 cylinders of the Sagar brand to the market through 60 dealers.

Everest Gas distributed 3,475 cylinders through its 28 dealers, while Sugam Gas supplied 2,423 cylinders to 15 dealers. STC Gas, owned by Salt Trading Corporation, distributed 2,146 cylinders through 44 dealers.

Among other companies, Sitashree supplied 1,600 cylinders to 11 dealers, while Shree Gas sent 1,960 cylinders through 18 dealers.

Similarly, Shreemaya Gas distributed 1,291 cylinders through 14 dealers, while Shriram Gas supplied a total of 360 cylinders to nine dealers. Manoj Gas sent only 305 cylinders to six dealers, according to the Nepal Oil Corporation.

With transportation delays and gas supplies far below demand, the distribution system has been severely affected for the time being. Consumers have been waiting in long queues at dealers and gas plants day and night in the hope of obtaining LPG cylinders.

title.rendered: Brother searches for missing family after Rasuwa flood, still hopes they are alive

content.rendered:
Rolpa, September 8

Four members of a family from Rolpa have been missing since the Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa. The family of 40-year-old Kul Prasad Budha Magar of Thanekot, Ward 6 of Paribartan Rural Municipality, has been out of contact since the flood.

Kul Prasad, his 36-year-old wife Meena Gharti Magar, 21-year-old son Deep Budha Magar and four-year-old daughter Khushi Budha Magar have all been missing.

Kul Prasad’s family had been living in Timure Bazaar, Rasuwa, where they had been running a meat shop for around nine years.

After losing contact with his brother’s family following the flood, Kul Prasad’s younger brother Bhim Prakash Budha Magar has been desperately searching for them. Carrying photographs of his brother, sister-in-law, nephew and niece, Bhim Prakash travelled to Chitwan on Bhadra 13, hoping they might still be alive.

“I still hope I will find them alive until they are found. I spent eight days searching, hoping I might find them somewhere,” he said. During his search, he travelled to Nawalparasi, Chitwan, Nuwakot and Kathmandu, visiting hospitals, morgues, riverbanks, riverbeds and as many of the forested areas as he could, he said. “As I showed their photographs, I was shown many badly disfigured bodies. There was nothing recognisable among them. How could I identify them as my family members? How could I believe they were them?” he said.

After exhausting all possible avenues, he returned home empty-handed on the eighth day, Bhadra 20. However, he still cannot shake the hope that he might find his family somewhere. Before returning home, he left a DNA sample in Kathmandu.

“I gave a DNA sample before returning, hoping it might help identify them,” he said. “I was told it could take two or three months for the report to come.” Despite everything, Bhim Prakash still hopes to find his family alive. “How can I simply accept that they are gone? I feel they are still alive. I want the state to search for them,” he said.

Initially, 32 people from Rolpa were reported missing following the Rasuwa flood. Of them, eight have since been located, and contact has been established. Twenty-four people remain missing.

title.rendered: Hong Kong beat Nepal to reach semifinals, Malaysia eliminated

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Nepal lost to Hong Kong in their final group-stage match of the ACC Premier Cup. Hong Kong beat Nepal by 15 runs.

Chasing a target of 262 set by Hong Kong, Nepal were all out for 246 in 49.1 overs. Ishan Pandey top-scored for Nepal with 90, but it wasn’t enough for victory.

Asif Sheikh scored 44, Dipendra Singh Airee 25, Karan KC 21, and Gulshan Jha 20.

For Hong Kong, Ejaz Khan took 4 wickets, while Yasim Murtaza took 2, and Kinchit Shah, Nasrullah Rana, and Atiq Iqbal each took one.

Earlier, Babar Hayat’s brilliant unbeaten century helped Hong Kong post a total of 261 runs against Nepal.

Hong Kong scored 261 for 7 in 50 overs. At one stage struggling at 133-7, Hong Kong recovered as Babar Hayat scored a century and put on an unbeaten 128-run partnership with Ehsan Khan.

Babar remained not out on 117 off 127 balls, with 7 fours and 7 sixes, while Ehsan was not out on 34. Earlier, Shahid Wasif had scored 45.

For Nepal, captain Sandeep Lamichhane took 4 wickets for 44 runs in 10 overs. Sher Malla took 3 wickets for 27 runs in 10 overs.

Hong Kong’s victory eliminated hosts Malaysia from the tournament, while Hong Kong advanced to the semifinals.

title.rendered: WorldLink Communications Limited provides Rs 10.1 million for flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

WorldLink Communications Limited has provided Rs 10.1 million in aid for those affected by the Bhotekoshi flash floods on August 26. The internet service provider has deposited the amount into the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund. WorldLink’s CEO Keshav Nepal handed over the said aid amount to Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle on Monday.

He mentioned that WorldLink provided that amount with the aim of helping in the rescue, relief, and rehabilitation of the citizens affected during this difficult time of disaster. The recent flood has caused significant damage to WorldLink’s network and infrastructure. According to preliminary details, the company has reported a direct loss of around Rs 35 million.

Even though there was major damage to its own infrastructure, the company restored the affected network and resumed services within three days of the flood to ensure that customers and citizens were not left without internet for a long time, the company stated in a press release.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood: 1,357 bodies found, 5,326 still missing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Among those who went missing in the Bhotekoshi flood, 1,357 bodies have been found.

This latest data on the Bhotekoshi flood centred on Rasuwa, and the subsequent search, rescue and relief operations, was released by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

According to updated figures as of 1 pm on 23 Bhadra 2083, the death toll from the flood has reached 1,357. The authority says the largest number of bodies of those who went missing and died has been found in Chitwan district.

In Chitwan, 363 bodies have been found. Among other affected districts, 223 bodies were found in Nawalparasi East, 222 in Nawalparasi West, 197 in Nuwakot, 169 in Rasuwa, 75 in Gorkha, 70 in Dhading, and 38 in Tanahun.

So far, only 102 of the deceased have been identified and handed over to relatives. For the remaining unidentified bodies, the authority has requested that relatives submit photographs and proof of relationship, along with samples for DNA testing, at the relevant district police office.

5,326 people affected by the flood remain unaccounted for, of whom 2,860 are from Rasuwa district alone.

Among the missing are 587 foreign tourists, 45 Nepal Army personnel, 25 Nepal Police personnel, 12 Armed Police Force personnel, and 73 government employees. The authority noted that the list of unaccounted persons may still include people who have already been rescued or unidentified deceased, so the data is being cross-checked.

So far, 13,583 people have been successfully rescued. Of the 6,827 injured, 327 are currently receiving treatment in various hospitals, while 2,420 have been discharged after treatment. The Nepal Army and Armed Police Force have treated more than 6,500 injured people through their own mechanisms. Thirty-nine holding centres have been set up in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading for displaced people, currently housing 3,533 people.

21,402 security personnel have been mobilised for rescue and relief work: 9,287 from the Nepal Army, 7,912 from Nepal Police, and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force. Helicopters from the Nepal Army, private sector, and Armed Police Force have flown more than 1,400 sorties for rescue operations.

The government has also accelerated relief distribution. Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have each been provided Rs 10 million in cash relief, and Dhading Rs 5 million. In addition, Rs 135 million has been allocated for 15 affected local units. Helicopters and trucks are being used to transport food and non-food supplies.

On infrastructure, electricity has been restored to 99.8% of households in Dhading, 96.7% in Nuwakot, and 78% in Rasuwa. The authority says fuel stock in affected areas has been secured, and 457 gas cylinders have been sent as subsidised supplies.

title.rendered: Lichchhavi Cinema Festival to be held in Kathmandu; 10 world-famous films to be screened

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

The first edition of the Lichchhavi Cinema Festival will be held in Kathmandu from September 10 to 14. The arts and cultural centre Lichchhavi House is organising the festival with support from Kathmandu Metropolitan City and the European Union.

The festival aims to open a new dialogue between Nepali and international cinema. Ten feature films from Asian and world cinema will be screened, presented in a curated format using full DCP theatrical projection technology.

Organisers say the Nepali film “Elephants in the Fog”, which made history by winning the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, will also be presented here. Also on the list are Deepak Rauniyar’s “White Sun” from Nepal and Bhutanese director Khyentse Norbu’s acclaimed film “The Cup.”

Also being screened are Payal Kapadia’s “All We Imagine as Light” from India, “Ghost School” from Pakistan, and “The Red Phallus” from Bhutan. Landmark works by world-renowned directors, Andrei Tarkovsky’s “Stalker” (Russia), Mathieu Kassovitz’s “La Haine” (France), Wim Wenders’ “Perfect Days” (Germany/Japan), and Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s “Memoria” (Thailand), are the festival’s main highlights.

content.rendered:
Bajura, September 8

The Sanfe-Martadi road, which had been blocked for three days due to landslides, has now reopened. The road was completely blocked by landslides at various locations in Wards 6, 8 and 9 of Badimalika Municipality following continuous rainfall since Saturday.

According to Chief District Officer Dorendra Niraula, the road has been operational since earlier today. Two JCB excavators from the Department of Roads were deployed from Sunday to clear the landslides, and the road was reopened to traffic today, CDO Niraula said.

According to him, landslides occurred at several locations, including Karagar Mod near the district headquarters, Selagad, Suwakandh, Rapka and Birekhola. Continuous rainfall made it difficult to clear the debris, delaying the reopening of the road.

With the road now operational, long- and short-distance vehicles travelling from the district headquarters, Martadi, have started heading toward their respective destinations.

Power supply to be restored by this evening

Continuous rainfall also triggered landslides that toppled 32 electricity poles. Efforts are underway to restore electricity supply through the national transmission line across Bajura district by this evening. Chief District Officer Niraula said the 11-kV power line would be repaired and brought into operation by this evening.

He said that although the collapse of several poles along the 33-kV transmission line in the area was expected to take some time to repair, electricity would be supplied to Martadi through the 11-kV transmission line today.

title.rendered: 32 flood and landslide victims still receiving treatment in Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Of the 150 people injured in floods and landslides and brought to Kathmandu for treatment, 32 are still receiving medical care.

According to information obtained from hospital administrations, as of Tuesday, 19 patients are being treated at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, 10 at the National Trauma Center and three at Bir Hospital.

At Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj, 81 people injured in the floods and landslides had been admitted for treatment. According to an update released by the hospital administration as of 9 am Tuesday, 57 patients have been discharged after treatment. Nineteen patients are currently receiving treatment in various wards and intensive care units. The hospital said one patient is ready for discharge, while four others have been placed under “other” management.

The injured patients currently receiving treatment are being cared for in departments including orthopaedics, the high-dependency unit (HDU), intensive care unit (ICU), neurosurgery and plastic surgery.

According to the list released by the hospital, those still receiving treatment include Ashok Shrestha, Bal Bahadur Gharti, Min Bahadur Shrestha, Navalesh Sharma (India), Pabitra Karki, Pema Tamang, Rajendra Bhatta, Ram Prasad Tharu, Rita Dolcha, Ritu Dangol, Suruchi Rana Magar, Tej Bahadur Tamang, Maheshwar Shah, Nima Dorje Tamang, Sijal Thapa Chhetri and Sitar Tamang, among others.

At the National Trauma Center, 50 people injured in the floods and landslides had been admitted for treatment. According to Dr Rudra Prasad Marasini, the center’s chief medical superintendent, 38 patients have been discharged after treatment so far. One patient was referred to another hospital, while another died during treatment. Ten patients are currently receiving treatment, including two in the HDU.

Those currently undergoing treatment include Bhakta Bahadur Bhandari, Sita Bhandari, Nandalal Gharti, Shambhulal Shrestha, eight-year-old Joel Ghale, Subas Bhandari, Indramani Gaire, Ramji Bishwakarma, Nil Bahadur Sapkota and Bhakta Bahadur Nepali.

According to the hospital, some of the patients sustained injuries to their backs, limbs and heads, while others suffered injuries to various parts of their bodies, including internal injuries. Dr Marasini said the patients are receiving treatment in different wards based on the nature and severity of their injuries.

At Bir Hospital, 19 people injured in the floods and landslides had arrived for treatment. Most of them have since been discharged. According to Dr Anita GC, deputy director of Bir Hospital, only three patients are currently receiving treatment there.

Of the three, one is in the ICU, one is in the male medical ward, and one is in the female medical ward. The other injured patients have been discharged after treatment. Following the severe floods and landslides that struck various areas of Rasuwa, including Bhotekoshi, as well as Nuwakot, Gorkha and Dhading, on August 26, injured people were rescued and brought to Kathmandu for treatment. Some of the injured were also taken to other hospitals in Kathmandu.

title.rendered: Nation observes Memorial Day for Gen Z martyrs (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Memorial Day is being observed nationwide today in remembrance of the Gen Z martyrs.

As part of this, the Gen Z Martyrs’ Welfare Society has organised a memorial event on the premises of the old Parliament building in New Baneshwor.

Various government ministers as well as members of parliament are taking part in the program.

Those participating include Home Minister Sudan Gurung, Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam, Minister for Physical Infrastructure Sunil Lamsal, Health Minister Nisha Mehta, Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun, and Agriculture Minister Gita Chaudhary, among others.

The government has declared September 8 as the “Gen Z Martyrs’ Day” and given a nationwide public holiday today.

On September 8, 19 people died after being shot by police during a protest in the federal capital, Kathmandu. Protests took place across the country on September 9 in opposition to that incident.

Over the two days of protests, 76 people, including security personnel and protesters, died, and arson also occurred at government and private structures.

title.rendered: Rabi Lamichhane vows not to deviate from Gen Z movement’s path

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Rabi Lamichhane, chairperson of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), has described the Gen Z movement of a year ago as an eruption of a new awakening.

In a statement issued on Gen Z Martyrs’ Day, Lamichhane recalled how young people were compelled to take to the streets against the frustration created by decades of entrenched corruption, political patronage, institutional incompetence, restrictions on citizens’ fundamental rights and a lack of opportunities.

“For those of us who established a party without shedding a single drop of blood, seeing the blood of young people shed when they raised their voices for change was the most painful moment. What happened in this country on Bhadra 23 and 24 must never happen again. I pray that no mother will ever lose her child again in this country in the name of change,” he said. “I pay heartfelt tribute to all the immortal martyrs who lost their lives while raising their voices for citizens’ rights, the rule of law and a corruption-free society. I also extend my heartfelt tribute to the brave police officers who lost their lives in the line of duty.”

Lamichhane also wished those injured during the movement a speedy recovery. He said a generation that was often described as having no interest in politics took to the streets and rejected traditional political practices. He said the RSP has now been placed in a position to answer every question that young people raised from the streets. He also pledged that the party would not deviate even an inch from the path charted by the Gen Z movement. “Time has placed us today in a position where we must answer every question that young people raised from the streets yesterday. It has also reminded us that tomorrow, someone else will once again stand before us demanding answers,” he said.

title.rendered: How the Gen Z uprising changed Nepal’s political course

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

September 7, 2025, a day before last year’s Gen Z uprising, former Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli had amended the CPN-UML’s party statute in a move that would have allowed him to seek a third term as party chair.

The second Statute Convention of the UML, held in Godavari, Lalitpur, scrapped both the 70-year age limit and the provision limiting the party chair to two terms.

By amending the statute with a plan for an early general convention—and later deciding not to renew the party membership of former President Bidya Devi Bhandari, who had expressed interest in leading the UML—Oli had effectively secured the basis for remaining at the helm of the party.

Had the political course gone according to Oli’s plan, 80-year-old Sher Bahadur Deuba would have been Nepal’s prime minister today.

On June 29, 2024, Oli and Deuba had reached a seven-point agreement to take turns serving as prime minister. The agreement between the Nepali Congress, then the largest party in the House with 79 seats, and the UML, with 78 seats, had paved the way for Deuba to become prime minister for a sixth time.

Based on the leaders’ public statements and their political plans at the time, the rotation between Oli and Deuba could potentially have continued until 2032.

Oli had even told a UML Central Committee meeting that the Constitution would be amended in 2030. The proposed constitutional amendment was also seen as an indication that the power-sharing arrangement with the Nepali Congress could continue.

But two days after returning to Baluwatar from Godavari following the UML convention, Oli found himself in a very different situation. On September 9, he had to be evacuated by a Nepal Army helicopter to save his life.

Instead of Deuba becoming his successor under the earlier agreement, former Chief Justice Sushila Karki became the country’s first woman prime minister, heading an interim government tasked with holding elections.

Youth activist Ojashwi Bhattarai says one of the Gen Z movement’s major achievements was breaking the grip of ageing leaders over state power.

“The Gen Z movement proved that change is possible when people want it,” she said. “It also ended the musical chairs that had long been played among a handful of leaders over the prime minister’s post.”

Gen Z leader Uparjun Chamling makes a similar argument, saying the movement effectively transferred the opportunity to lead the country from the grandfather generation to younger people.

“The young people who used to stand in queues at Tribhuvan International Airport were brought to places where they could manage those very queues,” Chamling said. “That is one of the visible changes after the movement.”

The political developments that followed the Gen Z uprising appear to support their argument.

Had the Gen Z uprising not taken place on September 8 and 9 last year, Nepal’s next parliamentary elections would have been held in 2027. Political parties—old and new—were preparing accordingly, with “Mission 2027” campaigns becoming common.

As Gen Z protesters took to the streets in Kathmandu demanding an end to corruption and the lifting of the social media ban, the then CPN (Maoist Centre) was conducting a campaign focused on the Mid-Hill Highway. The UML, CPN (Unified Socialist) and other parties were also running election-oriented campaigns.

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which emerged from the 2022 election, was likewise preparing for its own “Mission 2027.”

But the Gen Z movement ultimately created circumstances that led to the dissolution of the very House of Representatives those parties had been preparing to contest.

Following the state crackdown on the peaceful Gen Z protests and the destruction witnessed the following day, the House elected in the November 2022 elections was dissolved and an interim government was formed to oversee elections.

UML leader Dr Binda Pandey says the former leaders of the three major parties—Deuba of the Nepali Congress, Oli of the UML and Pushpa Kamal Dahal of the Maoist Centre—bear much of the responsibility for creating the conditions in which the Gen Z movement altered Nepal’s political course.

“We abolished the Panchayat system and brought democracy, and later abolished the monarchy and established a republic,” Pandey said. “But the belief that three leaders could control everything created deep frustration among young people. That frustration eventually took the form of the Gen Z movement.”

Bhattarai believes the political course could have been different had the leadership of the time responded more prudently.

“There was already frustration among young people over the lack of visible change. But the incompetence of the government turned what was intended as a peaceful demonstration into something much more destructive,” she said. “People also wanted change, and that is why they ultimately supported young people through the elections.”

The trend changed, and so did the leadership

The transition triggered by the Gen Z movement came to an end with the House of Representatives election on March 5. The election also dealt a major blow to the parties that had built and shaped Nepal’s existing political system and Constitution.

In a peaceful election, the RSP won 182 of the 275 seats—close to a two-thirds majority. Balendra Shah, 36, the former mayor of Kathmandu, was appointed prime minister on March 27.

Shah’s rise to the premiership, along with several other records set by the election, left the parties that had carried the legacy of Nepal’s political transformation in a dramatically weakened position.

The Nepali Congress was reduced to 38 seats, the UML to 25 and the CPN to 17. The Rastriya Prajatantra Party, representing the former royalist establishment, won five seats, while Madhesh-based parties were wiped out.

The Shram Sanskriti Party led by former Dharan mayor Harka Sampang, meanwhile, won seven seats and emerged as another major talking point.

The result had not been widely expected in political circles. Even RSP leaders had not anticipated such a sweeping victory.

While unveiling the party’s election manifesto in Surkhet, RSP vice-chair Dr Swarnim Wagle had predicted that the party would win 155 seats.

“We need 138 seats to form a government. We will win 155,” Wagle had said.

The RSP eventually won nearly 30 more seats than Wagle had predicted.

The party’s victory also brought a strikingly different group of faces into parliament.

Around 93 percent of RSP lawmakers—169 out of 182—are first-time MPs. Only 13 had previously served in parliament.

The dominance of younger and new lawmakers has also produced a leadership profile unlike that seen in previous governments.

Shah became the country’s first prime minister from the Madhesi community. The home minister is 38, while Sasmit Pokhrel, the education and sports minister and government spokesperson, is under 30. Apart from Mahabir Pun, the other ministers are aged 50 or younger.

This represents a sharp break from the pattern that had characterised elections before the Gen Z uprising, when political records were often measured by how many times a leader had won elections or served as minister or prime minister.

Until the 2022 election, Deuba stood at the top of the list of repeat election winners, having won parliamentary elections seven times.

There was also a long list of politicians who had won six, five or four elections. KP Sharma Oli, Ram Chandra Paudel, Bijay Kumar Gachhadar and Prakash Man Singh had each won six times, while Pushpa Kamal Dahal, Madhav Kumar Nepal, Jhalanath Khanal and Upendra Yadav had won five times.

It had also become increasingly common for politicians defeated in one constituency to contest from another.

Dahal is perhaps the most prominent example. He has contested from Rolpa, Kathmandu, Siraha and Chitwan before eventually moving to Gorkha and later Rukum. Upendra Yadav, Narayan Kaji Shrestha, Barshaman Pun and even Gagan Thapa have also changed constituencies over the years.

Shrestha, who entered the first Constituent Assembly in 2008 through nomination and later served in the National Assembly, returned to contest the House of Representatives before completing his National Assembly term. He has contested parliamentary elections from Makwanpur, Gorkha and Sarlahi.

The list of politicians who benefited repeatedly from proportional representation was similarly long, stretching from Girija Prasad Koirala to Ram Bahadur Thapa, Balkrishna Khand, Shankar Pokhrel, Krishna Bahadur Mahara, Arjun Narsingh KC, Raghuji Pant, Kamal Thapa, Binod Chaudhary and DP Aryal.

The number of politicians repeatedly appointed as ministers also continued to grow.

Sharad Singh Bhandari, who has served as minister 20 times, became the most prominent example. Gachhadar, Bishnu Prasad Paudel, Prakash Sharan Mahat, Bhim Rawal, Krishna Bahadur Mahara, Janardan Sharma, Balkrishna Khand, Gyanendra Bahadur Karki, Ram Sharan Mahat and Top Bahadur Rayamajhi were among those who had held ministerial positions repeatedly.

Such patterns increasingly fuelled frustration among younger generations.

After the Constitution was promulgated in 2015, the same political figures continued to rotate through ministerial positions, while Oli, Deuba and Dahal repeatedly alternated as prime minister.

Coalitions were formed and dismantled largely around the question of who would control the government. Even after the 2022 election, four different coalitions had been formed and broken up.

As political parties focused on winning elections and capturing power by whatever means necessary, ideological differences increasingly appeared secondary.

Pandey argues that the Gen Z uprising grew out of a system in which democracy was increasingly controlled by the interests of a small group of political leaders.

“Democracy is not only about state power; it is also about power within political parties,” she said. “When parties carrying the political legacy failed to govern properly, the political course developed in a different direction.”

New concerns and a warning

The old parties suffered a crushing defeat largely because of the mistakes and weaknesses of their leadership, while the RSP secured enough seats to form a government.

But even before the first anniversary of the Gen Z uprising, questions have begun to emerge over the new government led by Balen Shah.

The government has faced criticism over its handling of squatters and landless communities, investigations into corruption, the prime minister’s absence from parliament and his public remarks.

Political economist and analyst Ghanshyam Bhusal says some of the same tendencies associated with the old political establishment are already visible among the new forces.

“When people said there should be something new, they meant there should be something better,” Bhusal said. “But the same tendencies seen in the old system are visible among those who came in promising to be new.”

“Gen Z was a sentiment—the desire for things to improve. But as soon as it reached the streets, the movement was hijacked. Those who came in as new forces have not been able to do better,” he said.

Bhusal describes the current situation as one in which the old system has died but a new one has yet to be born.

“The old has died, but the new has not been born. That is why we are seeing a lack of system, shortages and a state of things not being properly established,” he said. “This is a time of social meteors. Experiments will continue.”

Pandey reaches a similar conclusion.

“The central demand of the Gen Z movement was good governance. We have not seen governance that people can actually feel as good governance,” she said. “The current government needs to learn from history, but it appears to be failing to do so.”

According to Pandey, public trust in the old political establishment has already eroded, while dissatisfaction with those currently running the government is beginning to grow.

Gen Z leader Chamling, meanwhile, believes the future of the movement is closely tied to the performance of the current government and says it needs to be held accountable.

“If this government fails, it will create a narrative that September 8 and 9 were wrong, that the Gen Z movement was wrong and that Khadga Prasad Oli was right,” Chamling said. “No Gen Z activist wants the movement to fail.”

He also warns that failure by a government led by young people could damage public confidence in younger generations taking political leadership.

“If this government fails, people may start mocking the idea that young people were given an opportunity to lead,” Chamling said. “That could make it harder for young people to receive the courage and opportunity to lead in the future.”

“The government needs to understand this. Avoiding the mistakes made by the old political leadership would itself be one way of respecting the Gen Z movement,” he said.

title.rendered: Search intensified at Upper Trishuli-3 B with arrival of heavy excavators

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Search efforts for people missing after the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods have intensified at the 37 MW Upper Trishuli-3 B Hydropower Project following the arrival of three large excavators and a backhoe loader.

Of the 191 people working at the project who went missing in the flood on August 26, 13 employees of construction company Fewa Construction have since been accounted for, leaving 178 people still missing. Efforts to locate them continued on Monday.

According to the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), small excavators had previously been used to excavate the project’s residential and office areas. However, the search could not make the expected progress because larger heavy machinery could not be transported to the site.

After several days of effort to clear the project’s audit and main tunnels, it became possible to transport three large excavators to the flood-affected area containing the project’s office and residential facilities. Two of the excavators had previously been used in search and rescue operations at the Upper Trishuli-3 A project, while the third was arranged by the project developer.

Search teams are now using the large excavators and backhoe loader to remove mud, large rocks and piles of earth deposited by the flood and excavate the buried areas. The developer, Trishuli Hydropower Company, said it expects to determine the actual condition of the buried office and residential areas by Tuesday.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah also said on social media that search operations were continuing at the project site. According to him, efforts to locate the missing people began on August 26. A Chinese team conducted a reconnaissance of the project site on August 29, but search equipment could not be transported there because of the muddy terrain.

Prime Minister Shah said project employees and a team from the Nepal Army are currently continuing the search. The team entered 1.7 kilometres into the audit tunnel from its entrance after clearing mud and debris. During the operation, they found a vehicle inside the tunnel.

Six residential buildings and one office building at the project have been buried by the flood. Prime Minister Shah said excavation has already reached a depth of up to 15 metres in an effort to locate the buried structures.

Efforts are continuing to transport additional equipment to the project site. The search has been challenging due to the mud, large rocks and earth deposited by the flood, but authorities expect the arrival of heavy machinery to provide more information about the buried structures and the people who remain missing.

Prisoners at the local correctional facility have provided assistance to families affected by the Bhotekoshi floods.
