They provided 125 sets of relief items, including mattresses, blankets, bed sheets, bed covers, towels, nail clippers, soap, toothbrushes, toothpaste and combs.

The prisoners contributed between Rs 100 and Rs 2,000 each, as well as labour. On the occasion, it was reported that relief goods worth Rs 367,036 were purchased, while the mattresses and pillows were made by the prisoners themselves inside the prison.

Chief District Officer Aryal said the assistance provided by people serving prison sentences was exemplary and could serve as a model for others.

The prison currently houses 750 inmates, including 708 men and 42 women.

title.rendered: One year after Gen Z Movement, celebrities say hope remains in new government

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Tuesday marks exactly one year since the Gen Z generation staged protests that brought about a major political upheaval. In the year since, the country has witnessed numerous political twists and changes.

Analysts say the movement was an eruption of long-standing frustration over corruption and bad governance. Following the movement, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) came to power after securing nearly a two-thirds majority in the subsequent election, while the traditional political parties were pushed out of government.

Even now, the struggle for power between the forces that emerged and those that were displaced following the movement appears to be intensifying. We spoke briefly with several celebrities who expressed their views or participated during the Gen Z movement about how events have unfolded since the movement and whether its original objectives have been fulfilled.

Actor Deepak Raj Giri has frequently expressed his views on contemporary political developments. He was also widely discussed on social media as someone who participated in the protests and openly expressed his solidarity with the movement. We asked Giri how he views the year since the Gen Z movement.

Giri said major political changes require some time for their agendas to become institutionalised. He said a struggle for power between the forces that emerged and those that were displaced after the movement is still evident, and that there is no alternative to these two forces working together if the country is to move toward development.

“These two forces appear to be in psychological conflict. If we want to develop the country, they must move forward together. Otherwise, the country will head towards conflict. The established and displaced forces now need to move forward together,” Giri said. He added that he still has hope in the current government and the forces currently in power.

Giri said the established forces currently appear unlikely to bring the displaced forces along with them, adding that both sides need to understand why the Gen Z movement took place. “The established forces need to understand that public frustration had reached a very high level and eventually erupted,” he said. “The old forces also failed to understand the Gen Z movement, instead interpreting it as an attempt to seize power by diverting the issue.”

He said even the achievements of the republic secured after the deaths of 17,000 people during the conflict took time to become institutionalised. “It took more than one Constituent Assembly election to establish the republic. We had to hold another election,” he said. “After a major movement, the developments that follow take a year or two to normalise. A person who comes out of a revolution also needs time to learn.”

Giri said the public has accumulated enormous expectations. “There is not going to be a miracle overnight. There are problems,” he said. Singer Pramod Kharel said he remains optimistic about the current government. “Looking at the current situation, one group is dissatisfied while another considers things to be going well. People have expectations. They want change and want the country to improve. The results will tell us. We are optimistic,” Kharel said.

Actress Reecha Sharma said the new government that emerged a year after the Gen Z movement has given her reason for hope. “This year brought out the frustration that had been suppressed for a long time. A government came in with an understanding of the sentiments of Gen Z. Someone whom Gen Z likes became prime minister,” Sharma said. “But I am not a supporter of any political party. I have not taken membership in any party either. I am a citizen of this country.”

She said that, as a citizen, she feels entitled to tell the government what it has done right and what it has done wrong. “We have been able to tell this government that openly,” Sharma said. “But we should not give it the benefit of the doubt on certain issues. For now, let us trust the government. After the Bhotekoshi disaster, issues such as child and human trafficking and mental health may also emerge. The government needs to deal with these potential challenges. So, for now, let us trust the government.”

Sharma said the current situation is also a test for the government led by Balen Shah. “They do not have complete freedom either. They have to work under all kinds of constraints. Let us remain hopeful and support the government,” she said. Actress Niti Shah expressed a similar view. She appeared satisfied with the current government. “The changes brought by the new government are positive. The government’s response to rescue and assistance following natural disasters has been good,” Shah said. “The way funds have been raised for the Prime Minister’s Fund makes me feel that the country can be built. It is a matter of trust.”

Shah herself has been actively involved in providing relief to people affected by the Bhotekoshi floods. She said she remains hopeful because the current government is led by young people. “Instead of questioning the current government, we should support it,” said Shah, who is also a former Miss Nepal International.

title.rendered: Nepal Gen Z Front seeks answers a year after the uprising

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

On the first anniversary of Nepal’s Gen Z uprising, the Nepal Gen Z Front has released a document questioning the government and political leadership over what has happened to the movement’s core demands a year on.

The Front said the anniversary should be used to assess the progress made on the issues that brought young people to the streets last year, including good governance, accountability, transparency, institutional reform and digital rights.

The debate paper, released Tuesday, raises questions ranging from the implementation of the 10-point agreement between the government and Gen Z representatives to the cases against protesters, the rights of landless citizens, the role of parliament, health insurance, the investigation into the September 8 and 9 incidents and reform of the security agencies.

Nepal Gen Z Front has particularly questioned the continued detention and prosecution of Gen Z protesters despite the government’s commitment to withdraw cases and release those arrested in connection with the movement.

Under the headline “Gen Z in jail, leaders on the power train?”, it asks whether political leaders who claim the movement’s political achievements also accept responsibility for those who participated in it.

The paper also argues that several substantive commitments in the 10-point agreement remain largely unimplemented.

The agreement, signed on December 10, 2025, included commitments on free healthcare, education and employment for victims, institutional reform, investigations into the September 8-9 incidents, security-sector reform, ending political appointments, electoral reforms and protection of digital rights.

The Gen Z Front says visible commitments such as declaring victims martyrs and providing compensation and interim relief have moved forward, while issues involving structural reform, accountability and investigations remain stalled.

It has raised the following 12 questions:

1. Gen Z in jail, leaders in power?

Why are hundreds of protesters still facing cases or in detention despite the agreement to withdraw cases and release them? Does claiming the movement’s political gains also mean accepting responsibility for its victims?

2. Why are landless citizens repeatedly targeted?

Why does the state demolish settlements and evict landless and squatter communities without providing alternatives, despite constitutional guarantees of housing and land rights?

3. Is parliament for governing or bypassing?

Why is parliament increasingly being reduced to political theatre while important legislation is rushed through and governments increasingly rely on ordinances?

4. Why does the prime minister keep “slipping up”?

When the prime minister makes controversial or constitutionally and diplomatically sensitive remarks, who bears the consequences—the prime minister or the country?

5. Reform health insurance or let it collapse?

Why is a programme designed to provide affordable healthcare being weakened by funding shortages, unpaid hospital bills and management failures?

6. When will there be “Straight Talk with the Prime Minister”?

Why have politicians who once built their reputations by questioning those in power become reluctant to face questions from citizens, journalists and parliament after taking office?

7. When will the investigations happen?

Why are reports into the September 8-9 violence still not fully public, and why have those responsible not faced clear accountability?

8. How long will citizens keep being killed?

Why has excessive force against protesters continued despite repeated changes in governments, political parties and movements?

9. Where is the new party’s “filtration mechanism”?

What system do new political parties have to test the competence, integrity, ethics and democratic credentials of those seeking political and public office?

10. Is signing an agreement enough?

Why have the government and political leadership implemented the immediately visible parts of the 10-point agreement while leaving institutional reform, accountability, security reform, transparency and digital rights largely untouched?

11. What is the difference between Facebook likes and public opinion?

Does what trends on social media actually represent public opinion, or are citizens’ questions and priorities increasingly being shaped by algorithms?

12. Is the movement itself ready to question itself?

If the Gen Z movement was built around questioning those in power, is it equally prepared to examine its own leadership, internal democracy, divisions, transparency and accountability?

The Gen Z Front said the September 8-9 violence resulted in the deaths of 76 people, including 19 people killed on the first day of the protests. The government has previously declared 45 of those killed in the incidents as martyrs.

The Nepal Gen Z Front criticised both the interim government formed after the uprising and the current elected government for failing to adequately address the violence and implement the commitments made to the movement.

It said Nepal has gone through three governments with different political circumstances and objectives since the uprising, but has seen little fundamental change in the style of governance.

The organisation also acknowledged the current government’s efforts to respond to the devastating Trishuli-Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa, saying supporting citizens awaiting rescue and relief should remain a priority.

However, it argued that supporting the state during a disaster does not mean abandoning democratic scrutiny.

“Have we forgotten how to ask questions?” the Front asks in its paper, arguing that the core demands of the uprising—good governance, accountability, transparency and digital rights—must continue to be examined.

Nepal Gen Z Front concludes that the questions raised on the streets a year ago have not disappeared.

It argues that the state initially attempted to silence those questions with force, while it is now responding to them with silence.

For the Nepal Gen Z Front, the real test of the uprising will be whether the state eventually stops treating those who ask questions as adversaries and begins providing answers.

Until then, the Front says, it will continue to ask questions.

title.rendered: Rabi Lamichhane emerges as key diplomatic contact for India, China and US

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) chairperson Rabi Lamichhane has emerged as a key diplomatic contact for major powers including India, China and the United States, even as their ambassadors have also begun engaging with Prime Minister and senior RSP leader Balendra (Balen) Shah.

While diplomatic engagement with Prime Minister Shah has started, Lamichhane appears to have become more prominent in high-level communications with major powers, according to sources.

On Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a telephone conversation with Lamichhane and expressed condolences over the heavy loss caused by the floods in Rasuwa.

According to RSP sources, Rubio assured Lamichhane that US assistance to Nepal would continue to be provided on a priority basis.

Rabi Lamichhane thanked the US government for expressing concern over the damage suffered by Nepal and the difficult situation caused by the disaster.

Lamichhane has also held high-level discussions with Indian and Chinese officials in recent months.

On June 3, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi invited Lamichhane to New Delhi for a meeting. Lamichhane travelled to India with an RSP delegation and held talks with Modi as well as senior leaders of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal visited India shortly after Lamichhane’s visit.

At a time when Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava and other diplomats had not held separate meetings with Prime Minister Shah at the highest level, Lamichhane was engaged in high-level discussions with the Indian side.

Indian and Chinese ambassadors later held separate meetings with Prime Minister Shah.

The Chinese side has also invited Lamichhane to visit China. The visit, initially proposed for August, was postponed by Lamichhane to the second week of September citing domestic reasons.

An informal schedule had been prepared, but the visit was subsequently put on hold following the Bhotekoshi floods and other circumstances. RSP sources said the visit could take place soon when conditions are appropriate.

“The possibility of a meeting with the Chinese president, as well as preparations for some meaningful agendas, are among the reasons the visit has been put on hold. But the chairperson remains positive about travelling to Beijing,” an RSP source said.

A senior source said Lamichhane’s conversation with Rubio was possible because the US secretary of state wanted to establish communication at a level that carries significant political weight within the government.

Prime Minister Shah is preparing to travel to New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly. He is expected to present Nepal’s positions before world leaders and hold a number of bilateral and other meetings on the sidelines.

The complete schedule of those meetings has not yet been finalised.

The Nepali Embassy in Washington and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are understood to be working on the preparations for the Prime Minister’s US visit.

Diplomacy analyst and journalist Sudhir Sharma views the attention Lamichhane has received from major powers as a reflection of how powerful countries are adapting their diplomatic engagement to Nepal’s changing political landscape.

Sharma argues that Lamichhane’s position as the powerful chairperson of the ruling party, as well as his relatively direct access to Prime Minister Shah, are among the factors behind the increased engagement.

“It appears that not only the US but other major powers are also engaging based more on access, contact and where power lies than strictly on diplomatic protocol,” Sharma said. “The meetings and telephone conversations with Chairperson Lamichhane should be understood in that context.”

“Prime Minister Shah is not easily accessible. He is also preparing to travel to the UN General Assembly soon. Even if he does not travel to the US at the invitation of the American side, the General Assembly itself will be held on American soil, so it is natural that the US is currently communicating with Chairperson Lamichhane,” Sharma said.

Following the RSP’s landslide victory in the February elections, Indian Prime Minister Modi had spoken separately with both Shah and Lamichhane.

Other countries are also understood to be stepping up engagement with Lamichhane, who heads the ruling party, as Nepal’s new political leadership takes shape.

title.rendered: Car carrying 162 kg of marijuana intercepted in Makwanpur, 2 drivers arrested

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Police have arrested two people after recovering 162 kilograms of marijuana from an inner road section in Bhabar, Manahari Rural Municipality-9, Makwanpur. According to police, the marijuana was recovered from a car, registration number Ba Pra 01-025 Cha 0877, which was travelling from Bhabar towards Kharanga at around 2:45 am on Tuesday.

A patrol team from the Area Police Office, Manahari, acting on a tip-off, stopped and searched the vehicle while an SUV, registration number Ga 2 Cha 615, was escorting it. Police said they found 13 packets of marijuana wrapped in plastic on the car seats during the search.

When police attempted to stop the escorting vehicle, the people in both vehicles tried to flee. However, police managed to arrest 56-year-old Dev Narayan Mahato of Dhobaha, Madi Municipality-5, Chitwan, who was driving the car, and 48-year-old Tek Bahadur Dong of Bharatpur Metropolitan City-24, Chitwan, who was driving the SUV.

Police said preliminary questioning revealed that the jeep had been escorting the car carrying the marijuana. Further investigation into the incident is underway, police said.

title.rendered: No, Argentina’s sea did not dry up. What caused the water to recede?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Videos that have gone viral on TikTok, YouTube and Facebook have sparked concern around the world by claiming that the Atlantic Ocean in Argentina suddenly dried up overnight or dramatically receded. The dramatic footage shows a vast stretch of the seabed exposed, boats left stranded and what appears to be a mysterious “new island” emerging from the water. Some posts have even described the phenomenon as a “global catastrophe” or a sign of the apocalypse.

If you are wondering whether reports that the sea disappeared in Argentina are real or simply misleading claims, here are the facts.

The videos showing the sea receding are genuine. However, claims that the sea permanently “dried up” or disappeared into the Earth are false. Rather than being a global catastrophe, the phenomenon was a temporary natural event caused by weather-related forces.

What actually happened in Argentina?

The viral videos were filmed along the coast of Mar del Plata, a major seaside tourist city in Argentina’s Buenos Aires Province.

Over a period of several hours, the sea level receded significantly from the shoreline. According to Argentina’s leading daily newspaper La Nación, the receding water exposed a large, permanent rocky formation known as Restinga del Faro, which normally remains submerged beneath the sea.

Because the rock formation is usually underwater, its sudden appearance made it look to tourists as though a new island had emerged. However, after the normal tidal cycle was completed, the seawater returned to its usual level within the same day.

Why did the sea recede?

Several temporary natural forces combined to cause the unusual retreat of the seawater.

Strong offshore winds (wind setdown): According to local marine media outlet Pescare, prolonged strong winds blowing from the shore towards the open sea can push surface water away from coastal areas. This can cause the sea level along the coast to appear significantly lower.

Changes in atmospheric pressure: Significant changes in atmospheric pressure can cause temporary fluctuations in regional sea levels and push coastal water offshore.

Extremely low tide: The weather-related effects coincided with a naturally occurring period of low tide, making the retreat of the water appear even more dramatic.

When weather-related forces push seawater away from the coast in this manner, the phenomenon is scientifically known as wind setdown or a meteorological low tide. It is essentially the opposite of a storm surge, in which strong winds push seawater towards the land.

Is it a sign of a tsunami?

When seawater suddenly recedes, many people assume it is a warning sign of an approaching tsunami. Tsunamis, however, are generally triggered by events such as undersea earthquakes or landslides. In such cases, seawater can rapidly recede within minutes before a potentially devastating wave arrives.

The phenomenon observed in Mar del Plata, however, was caused by winds and weather conditions that persisted for several hours. It was not considered a sign of tsunami risk.

Similar weather-related phenomena have been observed in other parts of the world. For example, powerful storms can temporarily push water far back from some shallow bays and coastal areas.

Conclusion

The unusual retreat of the sea exposed stretches of sand and rocky formations that normally remain submerged. The weather-related phenomenon was temporary, ended within a short period, and the sea returned to its normal level the same day.

The sea in Argentina did not permanently dry up or disappear. The Earth did not crack open and swallow the ocean, nor was the event a sign of a global catastrophe.

title.rendered: One year of Nepal’s Gen Z uprising: What lies beneath the revolt and what comes next?

content.rendered:
It has been a year since Nepal’s Gen Z uprising. In the meantime, much like the blind men and the elephant in the popular folk tale, there have been different attempts to interpret what happened.

Was it an internal economic and political explosion, or was it the result of geopolitical manoeuvring from outside? What were the real forces beneath the surface? What direction could Nepal’s politics take in the future? And what are the major challenges ahead?

Nepal today truly stands at a crossroads of enormous possibilities and equally serious challenges.

A brief chronology

On September 8, 2025, a group of Gen Z youths spontaneously held a peaceful demonstration from Maitighar to the Federal Parliament building in New Baneshwor, Kathmandu. Their main demand was that the government lift its ban on several social media platforms. Corruption, nepotism and other issues were also raised.

On the surface, these were familiar issues in Nepali politics. But unexpectedly, the crowd grew in front of the Parliament building. A fierce confrontation followed. The youth tried to get into the Parliament building. To stop them, the state used force indiscriminately, killing 19 people. The situation soon went out of control.

The following day, a highly violent movement spread across the country.

In Kathmandu, symbolic state structures including the Parliament building, Singha Durbar, the Supreme Court and the President’s Office were set on fire. With only a few exceptions, virtually no police office or post was left untouched. Many prisoners escaped from jails. The private residences and rented houses of major political leaders were also not spared from arson.

A total of 76 people were killed across the country. The economic damage ran into billions of rupees.

Throughout the entire episode, the Nepal Army remained a silent spectator.

The prime minister resigned on September 9 itself. For three days, the country appeared to be without a central government. Rumours of various kinds became the subject of national and international discussion.

Finally, on September 12, an interim government comprising independent figures was formed under former Chief Justice Sushila Karki. On its recommendation, the House of Representatives was dissolved. New general elections were announced for March 5, 2026.

The Constitution, which had reached the edge of a cliff, was narrowly saved.

In the general election, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), formed only three years earlier, won nearly two-thirds of the seats with 48 percent of the vote. All the established old parties suffered a dramatic collapse.

At 36, young leader Balendra Shah assumed the post of prime minister. Nepali politics entered another new phase.

Meanwhile, an investigation commission led by former High Court judge Gauri Bahadur Karki had been formed by the interim government on September 22 to investigate the events of September 8 and 9 and submits a report with recommendations.

The commission submitted its report to the government on March 8. However, the report has not yet been officially made public.

An unofficial version of the commission’s 907-page report circulated through digital media. It provides a detailed account of the events of September 8 and recommends action against those found responsible.

Regarding the events of September 9, however, it provides only a general account and says further investigation is needed.

The report also briefly mentions the role of Discord in the violent protests. It refers to the technical aspects of preparations allegedly made by some individuals for violent activities in the days leading up to the protests.

Who are Gen Z?

There are now attempts to portray Gen Z youths as either heroes or villains. The term ‘Gen Z’ itself has become part of everyday political vocabulary.

But what exactly is Gen Z? Who are the Gen Z youths?

Generally, those born between 1997 and 2013 are described as Generation Z, or ‘Zoomers’. Since this is the generation that was born and raised alongside digital technology, the internet, social media and artificial intelligence, they are also described as ‘digital natives’.

Generational classifications are generally based on the period in which people are born. But there is no scientific standard for determining the ideological, cultural, political, economic or scientific character of an entire generation.

Nor is this something formally decided or declared by any official global institution. Such generational labels have emerged because terms used by journalists, writers, cultural figures and others gradually entered popular usage.

Thus, the generations following the Second World War came to be known as Boomers, followed by Generation X and Generation Y, or Millennials, and then Generation Z. The generation that follows is increasingly referred to as Generation Alpha.

Whatever the terminology, the scientific theory of evolution tells us that humanity itself has evolved over time. It is therefore natural for groups of people to develop certain distinctive ways of thinking, lifestyles, cultures and behaviours depending on their place and time.

Just as previous generations carried the distinctive imprint of their era, Gen Z is naturally influenced by developments in information and communication technology, science and knowledge, the global economy, politics and culture following the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

As a result, some of the common positive characteristics of the Gen Z generation include networking across the world through the internet and social media, including Discord; accessing knowledge from virtually every field instantly through tools such as AI; increasing their capabilities; developing broader, more inclusive and tolerant worldviews; and becoming more politically aware and active.

However, Gen Z youths living in nation-states at different stages of economic and social development cannot possibly possess identical qualities, tendencies and capacities.

The personal, social and national concerns of Gen Z in the so-called ‘Global North’, which has reached the peak of modernisation and is facing crises of that very model, can be—and often are—very different from those of Gen Z in the so-called ‘Global South’, which is only beginning its journey towards modernisation.

Even within the same nation-state, issues can differ along class, ethnic, gender and cultural lines.

Yes, during the uprising, there appear to have been attempts by certain anti-social elements and regressive forces opposed to the Constitution of the democratic republic to infiltrate the movement.

But that is a secondary factor.

Those who seek to ‘fish in troubled waters’ are active to some extent in almost every spontaneous uprising.

The diversity of recent movements in Bangladesh, Nepal, Indonesia, Mauritius, India and elsewhere also confirms this.

It is in this context that it is relevant to examine the underlying forces behind Nepal’s Gen Z movement and its possible future direction.

The underlying factors

Karl Marx wrote in his famous work The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte:

“Men make their own history, but they do not make it as they please; they do not make it under self-selected circumstances, but under circumstances existing already, given and transmitted from the past.”

Nepal’s Gen Z uprising, too, was neither the result of a carefully designed plan by Gen Z themselves nor, as some conspiracy theorists have claimed, the product of a web woven by foreign powers.

It was driven by crises that had been smouldering inside Nepali society for a long time, certain undercurrents of rapidly changing geopolitics, and some conscious efforts by young people who are highly skilled in the latest information technologies.

The political factor

In the concluding paragraph of my doctoral dissertation, which was more than 900 pages long and which I presented at Jawaharlal Nehru University in 1985 before it was later published as a book titled The Nature of Underdevelopment and Regional Structure of Nepal, I wrote:

“On the basis of this research, it can be concluded that Nepal’s problem of development/underdevelopment is essentially a problem of transforming a pre-capitalist society that has become a hybrid of a backward internal social structure and external capitalist/imperialist interests. … Therefore, unless society is radically restructured in a way that defeats these tendencies and the forces supporting them, there is little possibility of resolving the social and geographical problems of development/underdevelopment.”

In other words, my considered conclusion was that Nepal could not achieve economic development without ending the autocratic feudal state system rooted in the country for centuries and its externally dependent relationship with Indian and other foreign monopoly capitalism.

It is worth remembering that I was 31 years old at the time.

It was with the aim of achieving that goal that the Maoist armed conflict continued for a decade. The 2006/07 People’s Movement was built on its foundation. The Madhesh, Janajati and Tharuhat movements followed as complementary struggles.

Collectively, these movements resulted in Nepal’s sovereign people receiving, for the first time in the country’s history, a Constitution of a federal democratic republic through the Constituent Assembly on September 20, 2015.

But the younger generation, connected to contemporary global consciousness, saw no future for itself in such distorted and corrupt politics.

That is why a movement that began with the relatively simple demand to lift restrictions on social media turned into a massive uprising.

This is the principal political dimension of the Gen Z uprising.

In this sense, the political struggle for modern democracy that had begun around 1951 had essentially been completed in Nepal.

Looking back at world history, Nepal’s revolution in the 21st century can be seen as a later chapter in the modern democratic revolutions that began in Europe and America in the 18th and 19th centuries, particularly in countries that underwent modernisation relatively late.

Why have I repeated this long and perhaps tedious history here?

Because it is directly connected to the Gen Z uprising.

There are other dimensions to the uprising, which I will discuss later. Here, I am referring only to its political dimension.

Throughout world history, particularly in countries that underwent modernisation late, when the promises of ‘liberty, equality and fraternity’ made by political revolutions do not quickly translate into reality, people who participated in, witnessed or were born immediately after those revolutions eventually rise in revolt in different forms.

Philosophers including Friedrich Nietzsche and Hannah Arendt have developed interesting theories around this phenomenon.

The French term ressentiment is particularly well known in this context. In the absence of a precise Nepali equivalent, it refers to a deep psychological state in which, broadly speaking, everyone becomes angry with everyone else.

More recently, writer Pankaj Mishra discussed this tendency in his 2017 book Age of Anger, examining episodes of revolt from history to the present.

Something broadly similar happened in Nepal on September 8 and 9.

Everyone vented their resentment against everyone else.

Why did Gen Z youths and ordinary Nepalis become so angry with the old political parties and their leaders?

A serious self-review is essential.

The central problem was that after political change, the state and society should have undergone rapid transformation across all sectors so that ordinary people could experience meaningful improvements in their lives.

That did not happen.

A political revolution only opens the door to broader economic, social and cultural revolutions.

Instead, a large section of the parties and leaders who had led Nepal’s political revolution became absorbed in the politics of power after the revolutionary transformation.

In the decade following the promulgation of the Constitution, the three major parties and their three top leaders occupied the country’s political ‘musical chair’ eight times, taking turns in power.

Corruption, irregularities and cronyism knew no limits.

Although the parties called themselves Congress and communist, there was little difference in their policies and behaviour.

There was no significant improvement in public service delivery from top to bottom.

There were no serious efforts to fundamentally reform the administration, judiciary, security agencies or constitutional bodies.

Instead, all these institutions became increasingly politicised and corrupted.

Naturally, the younger generation connected to contemporary global consciousness saw no future in such distorted and corrupt politics.

That is why a movement that began with the demand to lift restrictions on social media turned into a massive uprising.

This is the principal political dimension of the Gen Z uprising.

Again, some anti-social elements and regressive forces opposed to the Constitution of the democratic republic appear to have infiltrated the uprising.

But this remains a secondary factor.

Those who seek to ‘fish in troubled waters’ are active to some extent in every spontaneous uprising.

The economic factor

Everyone must recognise that the country’s severe economic crisis lies at the heart of the Gen Z uprising.

All major and recognised macroeconomic and microeconomic indicators confirm that the Nepali economy has remained near the bottom of the global rankings for decades.

With growth proceeding at a tortoise’s pace, imagining that this situation will change quickly is little more than wishful thinking.

How can a young person carrying a smartphone and simultaneously connected to Silicon Valley, London, Tokyo, Dubai, Seoul and Sydney dream of finding decent employment within Nepal, living comfortably and building a secure future under such circumstances?

A young person may be unable to support a family through traditional subsistence agriculture in a village and therefore move to the city.

If there are not enough income-generating jobs in the city and the young person is forced to seek employment abroad, what else can they do but revolt against the state?

Nepal’s Constitution declares education and health to be fundamental rights and provides for free basic education and healthcare for all citizens.

But if the government, under various pretexts, creates a situation where people cannot easily access education and healthcare, why would those young people not join a revolt?

Historically, one of the biggest crises and contradictions of Nepal’s economy has been its entrapment in a cycle of exporting labour while importing goods and services—an inherently unequal and dependent economic structure.

Even after the political revolution, this cycle has not been broken. It has instead tightened further.

When young people see that they cannot secure decent employment in their own country, either for themselves or for their children, why would they not choose the path of revolt?

Is it surprising, then, that young people preparing to leave the country for foreign employment were among those at the forefront of supporting the Gen Z uprising and shaping public opinion against the old parties?

All these indicators clearly show that the fundamental cause of Nepal’s Gen Z uprising lies in the country’s economic condition.

As a student of political economy, I anticipated this and have been advocating alternative politics for the past decade under the slogan, ‘The way forward is economic development.’

The impact of digital technology

Over the past decade, the rapid expansion and reach of digital technologies, including the internet, social media and AI, have brought major changes in the thinking, skills, values, political inclinations and culture of Nepal’s younger generation.

I believe the role of the ‘digital native’ generation has become decisive in the Gen Z uprising and the politics that followed.

Traditional Nepali politics has generally operated through a mechanical hierarchy:

Party → Leader → Cadre → People

But the politics of the new generation, including Gen Z, is increasingly becoming network-based:

Individual → Smartphone → Network → Collective action

This represents a fundamental change in the arena of political power and struggle.

It has created a situation in which people who are not affiliated with any party or organisation can directly network with one another and potentially outperform traditional political parties and politicians in areas such as protest, organisation, elections and fundraising.

The decisive role played by Discord, particularly on September 9, during the Gen Z uprising has now become a matter of history.

No one can ignore it anymore.

The geopolitical factor

In today’s globalised and multipolar world, it is increasingly becoming an ‘open secret’ that different forms of ‘colour’ and ‘Gen Z’ uprisings can be influenced by centres of power according to their own strategic interests.

In that sense, there is still no basis for determining with certainty how much the major power centres influenced Nepal’s Gen Z uprising, or how much they attempted to influence it.

It is reasonable to assume that the visible and invisible manoeuvring of Nepal’s two major neighbours, both of which have declared or undeclared strategic interests in Nepal, as well as the global superpower United States, continues.

Among them, China, the northern neighbour, has traditionally worked by maintaining trust with established political forces. Therefore, there is no rational basis to conclude that China supported the Gen Z uprising.

India, the southern neighbour, has been visibly and invisibly involved in Nepal’s domestic politics since 1951. There may be some assumptions and suspicions about what role India played in the Gen Z uprising, but no concrete evidence has emerged.

There is widespread suspicion that the United States, the distant global superpower, may have played a direct or indirect role in the Gen Z uprising as it seeks to compete with its principal rival, China, in the future and establish its own foothold in Nepal beyond its engagement through India.

Other powers may also have played a greater or lesser role, but no concrete evidence has been found.

Whatever the case, there can be no doubt that the Gen Z uprising’s main roots lie within Nepal itself.

If there are secondary roots elsewhere, they should be investigated seriously.

All patriotic forces must remain extremely vigilant about this.

At the crossroads of great possibilities and serious challenges

From last year’s Gen Z uprising and the subsequent general election to this year’s devastating Himalayan disaster on August 26, the country now appears to stand at a crossroads of enormous possibilities and equally enormous challenges.

According to the laws of nature and social science, opportunities and risks—or possibilities and challenges—are inherently interconnected.

With favourable circumstances and the right leadership, risks and challenges can be transformed into opportunities and possibilities.

Otherwise, opportunities and possibilities can themselves turn into risks and challenges.

Let us look at some of these areas.

First: The political sector

The emergence of new political parties and a younger generation of leaders following the Gen Z uprising and the subsequent general election is historically significant for Nepali politics.

At the same time, it has created a positive environment for new political forces suited to the times to emerge as alternatives to traditional liberal democracy represented by the Congress and state-socialist democracy represented by the communist parties.

It has also created an opportunity for leadership to pass from the old and exhausted gerontocracy to a new generation.

The devastating Himalayan disaster on Bhadra 10 has also made climate change and the unimaginable crises it can bring not a distant issue but an immediate and urgent national concern.

For a new government that has not yet firmly established itself, managing this crisis will be a major litmus test.

But this is also where a major risk lies.

There remain numerous questions and uncertainties surrounding the political force and leadership that have suddenly come to power.

What are its concrete ideological and political commitments?

How strong is its commitment to the four major pillars of Nepal’s Constitution—republicanism, federalism, secularism and inclusive democracy?

How can we be confident that a force and individuals driven primarily by immediate issues and practical concerns, without clear and open ideological commitments, will not fall into right-wing or left-wing populism?

How sustainable will the internal unity of a party formed so suddenly by people from different backgrounds be?

These are only some of the questions.

On the one hand, there is a positive possibility that a force made up of different ideological currents, tendencies and capabilities could eventually evolve into an alternative political force reflecting Nepal’s diversity, like a rainbow.

On the other hand, there is a serious risk that it could fail to contain its internal contradictions, fall apart and push the country into another cycle of political instability.

Second: The economic sector

The country’s foremost challenge today is rapid economic and social transformation.

For this, Nepal must urgently create an average of 800,000 new jobs annually—500,000 new entrants and 300,000 returning from abroad.

It must transform an economy trapped in the cycle of exporting labour and importing goods into one that imports capital and technology while exporting goods and services.

It must achieve double-digit economic growth continuously for two decades.

It must provide quality education, healthcare and social security to everyone.

It must escape the growing trap of trade deficits and foreign debt.

And at the very least, it must become self-sufficient in food and energy security.

These tasks must be undertaken with a sense of urgency.

It is natural for people, particularly young people forced to leave the country, to have high expectations of the new political force and its leadership.

The examples of Singapore, China, South Korea and Malaysia before us show that, with a clear vision and strong political will, dramatic economic transformation can be achieved within a single generation.

Is our new leadership prepared for this?

Can it replace the development policy that has crawled like a snake for years with a take-off policy that flies like a plane?

As an economic philosophy, can Nepal—a country at our level of underdevelopment—move away from both ‘market fundamentalism’ and ‘state fundamentalism’ and adopt a model in which the state, market and community play balanced roles?

And instead of pursuing a one-dimensional policy focused solely on ‘growth’ or ‘distribution’, can it adopt a critical-modernist approach that incorporates four dimensions—growth, distribution, sustainability and happiness?

Can it also break free from the trap of external dependence that has continuously deepened since the Sugauli Treaty and move towards an interdependent economy?

These are the major possibilities and challenges facing the country’s economy today.

The ultimate test of the new political force and government that emerged from the foundation laid by the Gen Z uprising will be measured against these questions.

Third: Geopolitics

Another major opportunity and challenge for the new party and government that came to power after the Gen Z uprising will be managing growing geopolitical tensions.

In this projected ‘Asian Century’, Nepal will find itself at the centre of strategic tensions between its two major neighbours and the Western powers led primarily by the United States.

If we can manage this intelligently, Nepal can establish itself in the world as an independent and prosperous country.

If we fail to manage it, knowingly or unknowingly, we could become trapped in a prolonged cycle of conflict, potentially putting our national independence itself at risk.

It should be remembered that geopolitical interest and tension in Nepal have increased sharply, both visibly and invisibly, since the Gen Z uprising.

Whether in relation to the proposed seminar on Tibet, the search for the Dalai Lama’s successor or the recent Himalayan disaster, the signs are becoming increasingly clear.

The new government must remain alert.

It should remain firmly committed to a non-aligned foreign policy based on the principles of Panchsheel.

It should remain committed to the concept of making Nepal a ‘dynamic bridge’ between its two major neighbours.

Ultimately, it must move cautiously and skilfully towards the goal of making Nepal a ‘peace nation’.

Fourth: Climate change

Following the devastating Himalayan disaster on August 26, the question of climate change and the unimaginable crises it can bring is no longer a distant concern for Nepal.

It has become an immediate and serious issue.

For a new government that has not yet firmly established itself, managing this crisis has become a major litmus test.

Alongside immediate rescue, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction, the government now has the responsibility of effectively internationalising the issue of the climate crisis in the Himalayan region and demanding fair compensation for the damage Nepal has already suffered and could suffer in the future.

At the same time, it must take responsibility for systematically promoting a model of ‘green development’ in Nepal and mitigating the impending climate crisis.

In conclusion

Nepal’s politics has entered a new era following the Gen Z uprising.

Let us all recognise the objective reality that the country will—and must—move forward amid a combination of diverse possibilities and challenges.

The alternative to democracy is better democracy.

The alternative to a new political force is an even newer political force.

The continuous cycle of history moves forward through its many turns, disasters and catastrophes. It does not move backwards.

Let us all remain confident. Let us remain unwavering on the path of truth.

title.rendered: Cholera vaccine sent to Nuwakot; campaign to begin in Rasuwa on Thursday

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

With the risk of cholera infection rising in flood-affected areas, the Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene has stepped up efforts to manage vaccines and other essential health supplies.

On Tuesday, the ministry sent 80,523 doses of cholera vaccine (23 boxes) to Nuwakot, along with 10 freeze-free vaccine carriers, 220 ice packs with a capacity of 0.6 litres each, and eight fridge tags.

Vaccines had already been transported to Rasuwa by helicopter. The cholera vaccination campaign is scheduled to begin there on Thursday.

The ministry said the campaign is being conducted as a priority measure to prevent infections in flood-affected areas, where damage to drinking water and sanitation systems has increased the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases.

title.rendered: Gen Z Friends: Are we losing our humility in the name of change?

content.rendered:
Even before the month of Bhadra began, I had already started to feel that Bhadra 23 was approaching. Because when Bhadra 23 draws near, so do fear, anger, helplessness and grief. Above all, another question keeps troubling the mind and unsettling the heart: what really happened that day?

Bhadra 23, 2082 BS, was not merely a date on the calendar. It was a dark day etched into our collective memory. Young people had taken to the streets that day to break the chains of disorder and bad governance.

In fact, the young people had not gone to the streets merely to set things on fire. They had come with proposals for alternatives and to make their voices heard. They had come carrying their questions, frustrations and anger, ready to express all those emotions on the streets.

But instead of listening to those voices, the state turned the streets into a battlefield of brutality. The incompetence of those entrusted with running the state, and the cruelty that arose from it, consumed the very people who had taken to the streets. That day, it was not only bodies that fell on the streets; faith in the state also collapsed, while a deep sense of injustice took even firmer root in the hearts of an entire generation.

Although I was affiliated with a political party, the young person within me carried a consciousness of solidarity with that group. After all, isn’t that what politics is about—to raise one’s voice against injustice, stand on the side of truth, expect competent leadership, aspire to a well-governed state and remain hopeful for a brighter morning?

It was with that hope that I reached ‘Ground Zero’. But within a short while, the place before my own eyes was transformed into a scene of bloodshed. The uproar of angry young people and the storm of the state’s insensitivity shook even Singha Durbar.

I was at the forefront myself, trying to protect some of the young people. But the situation had taken such a horrific turn that we were already miles away from being able to bring it under control.

Within moments, an attempt was made to destroy the dignity of the nation. Mothers lost their children. Homes fell silent. The pillars of hope for families lay unconscious. It was not only blood that flowed on the streets; the dreams, trust and future of an entire generation were also stained with blood.

The whole country wept. And fear mingled with those tears. So did anger. So did helplessness. And out of it emerged an uncertain yet inevitable desire for change.

That uprising, and the change it brought about, came to be known as the Gen Z Movement.

But it was not merely the name of a movement. It was the voice of young people aged 13 to 28 who had risen for the sake of their future. They had taken to the streets carrying dreams of changing the system. Yet, ultimately, it was the sacrifice and blood of those very young people that wrote the final chapter of the movement.

The greatest irony of the Gen Z Movement was this: a generation that had taken to the streets demanding a future ended up losing its present.

Even today, I remain conflicted about how we should view the role of young people in the Gen Z movement.

Young people are often called the future pillars of the nation, and that is true. Today’s youth have greater access to knowledge from around the world. Older generations find it difficult to outpace them in technology. They are also more familiar with concepts of human rights. All of this is true.

But that does not necessarily mean that everything young people do, think or choose is right.

Youthful energy, by itself, is not synonymous with wisdom. And this is something young people must be particularly conscious of. Knowing what we are aware of is important, but knowing what we are unaware of is an even greater sign of awareness and wisdom.

Young people may be like a swelling river, but they should not remain confined to the flow of a river. They must become an ocean and connect with the wider sea. Because limited knowledge and limited awareness cannot sustain a long journey.

The process of learning must be continuous. Curiosity should arise not only about what we know but also about what we do not know. The ability to understand a world beyond our own perspective, learn from different experiences and ideas, and accept the possibility that we may be wrong is also part of awareness. If the depth of wisdom does not grow alongside the expansion of knowledge, knowledge itself remains incomplete.

In keeping with the spirit of the Gen Z Movement, young people’s presence and influence in state power have increased today. Efforts to establish stronger youth leadership in the opposition have also gained momentum. Yet, at the same time, the practice of hurling all kinds of abuse on social media is also increasing.

As access to advanced technology expands, is the creative power of our generation somehow weakening? Are serious study and intellectual discourse being displaced by superficial debates on social media? Instead of searching for solutions to problems, are our debates shifting from issues to personal criticism? Is ideological disagreement gradually turning into personal attacks? And in the name of development, are we sacrificing human sensitivity and empathy at the altar of progress? In our attempt to control this momentum, have we overlooked the democratic process itself?

Perhaps the most uncomfortable question is this: We questioned leaders of the older generation for their arrogance in believing that “we are the ultimate authority.” Are we, somewhere along the way, cultivating the same tendency within ourselves?

In the race to become leaders, are we forgetting society? Are we losing our humility in the name of change? Are we moving away from the patience to listen to criticism, the culture of respecting differing opinions and the ability to acknowledge that we, too, may be wrong?

Being young is not merely a description of age; it is also a responsibility of consciousness. The movement may have given us an opportunity to change those in power, but the real test will be whether we can change our thinking, our values and our behaviour. The decisive question is whether we are merely going to change the faces of the old leaders or whether we are going to change the political culture itself.

Because the greatest proof of change is not whom we removed, but what we ourselves became.

Perhaps what this country needs is a generation capable not merely of raising its voice in the name of patriotism, but of softening its own voice in the face of another person’s suffering. It needs a generation that does not merely demand power, but is capable of carrying the burden of power once it has it.

Because having power may be a measure of ability, but exercising power with restraint is a matter of character.

The true success of the Gen Z Movement will not be the day young people reach positions of power. It will be the day they reach positions of power and do not become like power itself.

I remain afraid. And that is precisely why I continue to care.

We questioned the older generation so casually: “Why didn’t you change?”

What if that very question eventually comes back to us?

What if, tomorrow, the brothers and sisters who gave their lives to open the path to change ask us: “How much have you yourselves changed?”

What answer will we have?

Will we have merely continued, under new faces, the very culture of power they sought to dismantle? Will our arrogance, intolerance and hunger for power once again stand where their dreams were meant to be? Or will we truly have succeeded in changing ourselves?

Because they did not merely give us an opportunity to lead. They also gave us the responsibility to prove ourselves.

May we live in such a way that tomorrow we can look into their eyes and answer their questions. For our generation, there can be no greater defeat than reaching a day when we have no answer to give.

title.rendered: Gold price rises by Rs 3,500 per tola

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

The price of gold increased by Rs 3,500 per tola in Nepal on Tuesday.

According to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association, gold is being traded at Rs 305,400 per tola today, up from Rs 301,900 on Monday.

The price of silver has also increased by Rs 100 per tola.

Silver, which was traded at Rs 4,690 per tola on Monday, has been fixed at Rs 4,790 per tola for Tuesday.

Gold prices in international markets also rose on Tuesday, with spot gold gaining amid a weaker US dollar and investor focus on upcoming US inflation data.

title.rendered: How Bhat-Bhateni rose again after the Gen Z protests

content.rendered:
It takes immense hard work, commitment, courage, investment, perseverance and patience to build a business from scratch. Few examples illustrate this better than businessman Min Bahadur Gurung.

Four decades ago, in 1984, Gurung rented a small shop in Kathmandu’s Naxal area with a different dream and started a business that would eventually set a distinct benchmark in Nepal’s business and entrepreneurship sector.

That business was Bhat-Bhateni Departmental Store.

What started from a single rented shop eventually became synonymous with investment, employment and the belief that it is possible to build something in Nepal itself. The scale of Bhat-Bhateni’s growth—with more than two dozen stores across the country—offers a glimpse of the effort that went into building it.

Over four decades, Gurung worked relentlessly to transform the small store he started in Naxal into a nationwide retail chain employing thousands of people.

He had been working towards his plan of gradually expanding Bhat-Bhateni across all 77 districts. But on September 9, 2025, that journey suffered a major setback.

The Gen Z protests that began on September 8, turned violent, with government property as well as private businesses facing vandalism, looting and arson. Among the major targets of the protests were Gurung’s Bhat-Bhateni stores.

As resilient as he is, Gurung did not give up.

He worked day and night. Tens of thousands of employees stood by the company, while millions of customers offered their support and encouragement. And, nearly a year later, Bhat-Bhateni has finally managed to rise again.

“We were able to rebuild Bhat-Bhateni because of the support of tens of thousands of employees associated with us and the backing, encouragement, trust, love, faith and inspiration of millions of consumers,” Bhat-Bhateni Super Store Chief Operating Officer (COO) Panu Poudel told Onlinekhabar. “We are proud to have reached this point.”

Poudel says there was a moment when the extent of the destruction made them wonder whether the stores could ever be rebuilt.

Of the more than two dozen stores established with billions of rupees in investment, almost all except one or two were vandalised, looted or set on fire.

“But the courage shown by Executive Chairman Gurung, along with the love and trust of tens of thousands of employees and millions of consumers, became the main source of motivation for rebuilding Bhat-Bhateni,” Poudel said.

According to Poudel, Bhat-Bhateni suffered losses of around Rs 11 billion during last year’s Gen Z protests due to looting, arson and vandalism.

Since then, the company has spent an additional 20 to 30 percent of the amount of the original damage on reconstruction. That amounts to another Rs 2.2 billion to Rs 3.3 billion.

In total, the reconstruction of Bhat-Bhateni has cost nearly Rs 14 billion.

‘We have upgraded the buildings’

Poudel says the reconstructed buildings are different, as many of them have also seen a major upgrade.

“We have made the buildings more robust and upgraded the materials used in them. We have also spent on improving their appearance and aesthetics.”

Of Bhat-Bhateni’s 27 stores, 23 are currently operational.

The Dharan store is scheduled to reopen on September 9, followed by the Tangal store in Kathmandu on September 21. Once these two stores reopen, 25 Bhat-Bhateni outlets will be fully operational.

The remaining stores in Damak and Hetauda are expected to resume operations after Dashain.

Despite the scale of the destruction, the company says it did not reduce its workforce.

“Even though most of the stores were completely destroyed, we did not cut our employees. We brought back the same people who had been working with us,” Poudel said.

“We did not cut salaries either. We even provided bonuses during last year’s Dashain. Employees and their families are also our families. Supporting them through good times and bad has always been our chairman’s first priority.”

Poudel does not want to dwell on the events of a year ago.

“We moved forward rather than remembering the incident,” he said. “It would have been difficult to rebuild if we had remained stuck in the past, remembering the incident and regretting what happened.”

“We forgot everything and moved forward. We have now managed to stand again on the same foundation. We have no animosity, complaints or lingering memories about it anymore.”

Where are Bhat-Bhateni’s stores operating?

Poudel said all 23 of Bhat-Bhateni’s currently operating stores are expected to be in operation by October, while the remaining two damaged outlets will resume operations by December.

In addition, four new Bhat-Bhateni stores are currently under construction.

According to Poudel, construction of all four has reached its final stages.

The stores in Tandi, Chitwan, and Lekhnath, Pokhara, are being prepared for operation within the current fiscal year. The company plans to bring its outlets in Satdobato and Bhaisipati, Lalitpur, into operation from the next fiscal year.

What happened to Bhat-Bhateni during the Gen Z protests?

Of Bhat-Bhateni’s more than two dozen stores across the country, 12 were completely burned down and destroyed. All of them were major and large outlets.

According to Bhat-Bhateni management, the company’s Naxal store, which also houses its headquarters, as well as the stores in Maharajgunj and Bouddha and its outlets in Koteshwor and the Baluwatar warehouse, were vandalised, looted and set on fire.

All of these facilities were completely destroyed.

Similarly, Bhat-Bhateni stores in Pokhara, Chitwan, Hetauda, Birtamod, Damak, Biratnagar and Dharan were also completely destroyed.

Around a dozen other stores were vandalised and looted.

In Kathmandu Valley, the stores in Kalanki, Balaju and Thimi were vandalised and looted. Outside the Valley, similar incidents took place at the stores in Janakpur, Butwal, Birgunj, Dhangadhi, Itahari and Bhairahawa.

However, the protesters did not manage to set fire to these outlets.

Fortunately, several other stores escaped damage. The outlets in Tokha, Satdobato, Anamnagar, Sanagaun, Tripureshwor and Patan inside Kathmandu Valley, as well as the Nepalgunj store outside the Valley, were spared after escaping the attention of protesters.

Poudel said the company could not even determine exactly how much cash had been kept at the counters of stores that were vandalised, looted and burned.

The protesters took away not only goods but also cash.

According to Poudel, Bhat-Bhateni conducts transactions worth around Rs 106.8 million every day across its stores nationwide.

“That means our annual turnover is around Rs 39 billion,” he said.

When the Gen Z protests began, Bhat-Bhateni stores across the country were operating normally.

But after 19 people were killed on the first day following the firing on protesters, vandalism, looting and arson began.

Even after the government imposed a curfew, looting, vandalism and arson targeting Bhat-Bhateni continued into the second day.

According to Poudel, each Bhat-Bhateni store provides direct employment to at least 500 people on average, with women making up a significant proportion of the workforce.

Across its warehouses and stores nationwide, Bhat-Bhateni provides direct employment to tens of thousands of people.

For a business that began four decades ago with a single rented shop in Naxal, the journey has now entered another chapter—one shaped not only by expansion and investment, but also by the determination to rebuild after one of the biggest setbacks in its history.
