title.rendered: What went wrong inside Nepal’s security apparatus before the Gen Z protests?

content.rendered:
A report published by The New York Times on July 13, titled “Inside Israel’s Secret Operation to Cultivate Ahmadinejad,” claimed that Israel’s intelligence agency Mossad had been running a covert operation to install former Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the country’s new leader.

The report, whether its claims are ultimately proven or not, offered a striking reminder of the reach of an intelligence apparatus: a foreign intelligence agency allegedly working to influence political leadership inside an adversary state.

Intelligence agencies are often described as the government’s eyes and ears. That raises a fundamental question whenever a major national crisis occurs. Where was the intelligence apparatus? What did it know, and what did it do with what it knew? A year after Nepal’s Gen Z movement, those questions remain unresolved.

When the executive, legislature and judiciary were engulfed in violence and key state structures were set ablaze, the roles of all four of Nepal’s security agencies—the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and National Investigation Department (NID)—came under scrutiny.

The most serious questions were directed at the NID, whose principal responsibility is to collect intelligence and provide early warning.

Information was available—but action was not

Intelligence officials reject the claim that they had no advance information about the Gen Z movement.

Hutaraj Thapa, who was the NID chief at the time, says information collected about the planned protest was reported in writing.

“We submit daily and weekly reports. At that time too, we submitted reports incorporating the information available to us,” Thapa, who has since retired, said.

The NID routinely sends reports to the Prime Minister’s Office, Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of Defence, the National Security Council and the Nepal Army. Some of these reports, officials say, are so sensitive that their envelopes are not even opened.

One such report, submitted on September 7, 2025, the day before the main protest, has been obtained by Onlinekhabar.

It contained six points on the Gen Z movement. The report said activists, organisations, groups and individuals were preparing demonstrations in Kathmandu Valley and other districts in opposition to the government’s ban on Facebook, YouTube, Instagram and other social media platforms.

It also recorded that a Gen Z group had held a discussion at Bhimsen Gola in Old Baneshwar, attended by around 10 to 12 people, including Amir Khanal and Khemraj Saud. The group had decided to march from Maitighar Mandala to New Baneshwar from 8 a.m. on September 7, wearing black masks and T-shirts.

The group had also approached the Kathmandu District Administration Office seeking security arrangements.

The intelligence report identified a number of people who could participate, including RSP leader Deepak Bohora, 100 Group’s Bablu Gupta, Khemraj Saud, Som Sharma, Ankit Malla, Routine of Nepal Banda’s Victor Paudel, Pathao’s Asheem Man Singh Basnyat, Nepal Students’ Union’s Binod Deuba and Durga Prasai.

It also noted that then Kathmandu Mayor Balen Shah had expressed support for the Gen Z protest on social media and warned that large numbers of his supporters could participate and that provocative or unruly activities were possible.

The report also identified preparations for protests in major cities including Jhapa, Makwanpur, Hetauda and Pokhara.

Former NID additional chief research director Devraj Bhatta says the information was there, but the analysis of what could follow was inadequate.

“There was general information, but there appears to have been a weakness in analysing it and assessing the risks that could arise,” Bhatta said.

The report did not contain much information that was not already publicly available. But Bhatta argues that the state still failed to take the report seriously enough.

“Even when reports named specific individuals and organisations, the government did not take them seriously. The country had to suffer a huge loss,” he said.

The NID’s own assessment, however, was not sufficiently detailed.

Thapa acknowledged that its reports did not contain an in-depth analysis of the preparations or the potential scale of destruction.

“The intelligence agency’s capacity is limited. But even when information is obtained within that limited capacity, failing to respond to or use it is not only yesterday’s problem; it remains a problem today,” Bhatt said. “Who is the consumer of which intelligence? That question still exists. Our misfortune is that there is no clear responsibility over who must act and when.”

A member of the Gauri Bahadur Karki Commission, which investigated the suppression of the September 8 and 9 protests, similarly said the NID had failed to effectively present the limited information it had, while the agencies receiving the information also appeared not to have examined it seriously.

The missing digital intelligence

The challenge was made more difficult by the fact that the movement was organised almost entirely online.

From September 6, Reddit, TikTok and Discord were filled with calls to protest over the “Nepo Baby” issue and the social media ban.

Yet the intelligence apparatus did not have the technological capacity to fully monitor or analyse the rapidly changing online environment.

Officials acknowledged that the NID lacked both adequate technical expertise and cyber-monitoring tools to track videos, triggers, inflammatory messages and other digital content.

The Kathmandu Valley had been divided into 32 sectors for intelligence collection, under the command of the Valley Operations Division. Its chief at the time, Krishna Khanal, told the Karki Commission that the intelligence assessment was that around 8,000 protesters could attend.

The NID collected information through open sources, its own personnel, undercover staff and informants. But officials acknowledged that the lack of cyber capabilities prevented deeper tracking of the online mobilisation.

The movement’s preparations were not taking place through physical meetings that security agencies could easily observe. They were happening across social media platforms.

According to security analyst Narayan Adhikari, the agencies failed to understand this shift, did not obtain the information in time and could not properly analyse it. Their estimates therefore failed to match what unfolded on the streets.

Reports that reportedly went unread

There was another problem: whether the intelligence reports reached the people who needed to act on them.

A Home Ministry official says the relationship between then Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli and NID chief Thapa had deteriorated badly.

Although the NID formally comes under the Prime Minister’s Office, the official said Thapa had difficulty even getting access to Baluwatar. His reports were allegedly viewed with suspicion, with some questioning his credibility because he came from Rolpa and was perceived as having a Maoist affiliation.

A person familiar with the relationship between Oli and Thapa said the prime minister’s personal assistant, Rajesh Bajracharya, also warned Thapa.

The pressure became so intense that Thapa reportedly responded to Bajracharya: “I may not be transferable outside the country. Send me wherever you want.”

The strained relationship was not limited to the intelligence chief, according to people familiar with the situation. Relations between Oli and other security chiefs were also reportedly poor.

One indication, they argue, was the events of September 9, when the army’s rescue of Oli began only after he resigned.

“Look at what happened on September 9. The Army did not even rescue Oli until he resigned. Relations with the security agencies had completely broken down by then,” one person familiar with the situation said.

No concrete decision at the security committee

The Central Security Committee, chaired by the home minister, includes the home secretary, defence secretary, a Nepal Army general, the chiefs of Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force, and the NID chief.

The committee met on the eve of the Gen Z protest.

But the Karki Commission found no written decision on a concrete security strategy for the protest.

The Commission reviewed decisions from Central Security Committee meetings held between September 5 to 10. Its report says that only attendance records were provided and that no written decision relating to the Gen Z movement was found.

The Kathmandu District Security Committee also met on September 7 and concluded that the overall security situation was normal, while calling for stronger coordination in the coming days.

On the eve of the protest, Oli also met security chiefs. He says he was briefed that around 6,000 to 7,000 protesters were expected and that the demonstration would be peaceful.

In testimony to the Karki Commission, Oli said no security agency had presented concrete information about widespread violence, arson or large-scale vandalism through platforms such as Discord, Reddit and TikTok.

Yet the army chief gave a different account.

Army Chief Ashok Raj Sigdel told the Commission that, during the Central Security Committee meeting on September 7, information had been received from the NID and other security agencies that the protest could become widespread.

Despite this warning, no National Security Council meeting was held before the protest.

The NID chief, meanwhile, assessed that between 3,500 and 5,000 people would attend.

The conflicting accounts point to a deeper problem: the state did not have a common understanding of the scale or nature of the threat.

Different assessments, weak coordination

On September 7, 3,441 police personnel were deployed in Kathmandu Valley, followed by another 505. A command post was established under the chief district officer. After the army was deployed, the command post was moved at around 4:30 p.m. to the Narasingh Dal Battalion in Singha Durbar, from where security coordination continued until the morning of September 10.

The police had prepared for a largely peaceful demonstration.

Former Kathmandu SSP, now DIG, Bishwa Adhikari told the Commission that the assessment had been for between 3,000 and 5,000 protesters. He acknowledged weaknesses in analysing advance intelligence.

Then IGP Chandra Kuber Khapung also said police had information that the demonstration would be peaceful.

But current IGP Dan Bahadur Karki, who was then an AIG, told the Commission that police had information about discussions on Reddit, Discord and X and that security plans had been approved accordingly, with 4,396 police personnel deployed.

Former AIG Siddhi Bikram Shah said he had informed the IGP after information about the movement began spreading rapidly on TikTok, Facebook, Reels and Discord.

The accounts were inconsistent.

The former acting chief of the Kathmandu Valley Police Office, DIG Om Rana, said the movement turned out differently from what had been expected.

The security agencies also struggled to coordinate on the ground.

DIG Bishwa Adhikari said there were sometimes delays in tactical movements between Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force and that command-clearance procedures created coordination challenges.

SP Rishiram Kandel, who was deployed with a special task force around Parliament, was more direct.

“Although the Armed Police Force was nearby on the September 8, it was not active as expected. On the September 9, a 10-to-12-member Army contingent became neutral after attacks intensified from the gate of the police headquarters. This clearly shows the lack of coordination among the security mechanisms,” he said.

Former Kathmandu police chief SP Apilraj Bohora also questioned the roles of the Armed Police Force and the Army.

“Both the APF and Army arrived in the later stages, but the expected professional support, institutional defence and collective coordination were not provided,” Bohora said.

Sigdel, however, told the Commission that he had instructed the security agencies to coordinate and make the necessary preparations after the security situation around Parliament became complicated.

A leadership vacuum inside the intelligence agency

The NID was facing another problem as the protest approached: an internal leadership contest.

Thapa had been appointed intelligence chief on September 13, 2022, and was due to complete his three-year term and retire on September 13, 2025—just five days after the Gen Z protest.

As is common among senior security officials nearing retirement, his activity had reportedly declined. At the same time, two AIGs, Tekendra Karki and Om Joshi, were competing to succeed him.

Joshi was then heading the Administration Department, while Karki led the Provincial Coordination Department and Intelligence Division.

An NID official said the leadership contest affected the agency’s ability to focus on gathering intelligence about the protest.

“The chief was almost on leave, while the two AIGs were competing over who would take over. The kind of effort needed to gather advance intelligence about the internal preparations for the Gen Z movement did not happen,” the official said.

The interim government led by Sushila Karki eventually appointed Tekendra Karki as NID chief on September 21.

Former AIG Bhatta said internal instability can affect intelligence collection.

“Not only the organisation but also the external environment affects intelligence gathering,” he said, adding that this was one reason discussions had begun about appointing intelligence chiefs a month before their predecessors retired.

Nepal Police faced a similar leadership transition. Chandra Kuber Khapung had assumed the post of IGP only on September 4, just days before the protest.

At the same time, the Kathmandu Valley Police Office in Ranipokhari, which commands police operations in the three districts of the Valley, was without a permanent chief. AIG Tek Bahadur Tamang had retired on September 4 and DIG Om Rana was serving as acting chief.

The result was a security apparatus facing simultaneous leadership changes, limited digital intelligence capabilities, weak analysis and poor coordination.

The Human Rights Commission also found that false information circulated through a fake Nepal Police Facebook page claiming that police could not use force against protesters wearing school uniforms. Despite the campaign spreading online, security agencies failed to counter the misinformation or identify those responsible.

A year later, the central question remains less about whether the state received any warning than about what it did with the warnings it had.

The intelligence agencies had information. Security committees met. Police and military leaders discussed the situation.

But there was no unified assessment of the threat, no clear written security strategy and, ultimately, no coordinated response proportionate to what unfolded.

The Gen Z movement exposed not simply an intelligence failure, but a wider failure of the state’s security architecture—from collecting and analysing information to sharing it, making decisions and coordinating those decisions on the ground.

title.rendered: One year on: Who really called Nepal’s Gen Z protest?

content.rendered:
Until September 6, 2025, there had been no public discussion about when Nepal’s Gen Z protest would take place. Yet preparations were already underway from the day the government shut down major social media platforms.

Who called the protest? Who decided the date? Why was September 8 chosen? And who took part in the discussions?

One year on, these questions remain largely unanswered. But the events of September 8, 2025, cannot be understood without looking at what happened in other countries—and how those events travelled through social media into Nepal.

From Indonesia and the Philippines to Nepal

Gen Z protesters surrounded Parliament as police tried to contain them with force. At the same time, a police van pushed through a crowd and struck 21-year-old Affan Kurniawan, a delivery worker who was not participating in the protest. The van did not stop and ran him over.

But the incident had not happened in Nepal.

It took place on August 28, 2025, roughly 4,500 kilometres away, outside Indonesia’s Parliament in Jakarta.

Affan’s death intensified protests in Indonesia. The following day, protesters set fire to a provincial parliament building in Makassar and targeted police and government buildings. Homes belonging to ministers and politicians were also vandalised and looted. CBC reported that 10 protesters had died and dozens had been injured as the unrest escalated.

The protests had already been building for weeks over taxes, the rising cost of living and a government decision to increase lawmakers’ allowances. Gen Z was at the forefront.

Videos contrasting the lifestyles of ordinary Indonesians with those of politicians and their families spread rapidly online. Hashtags including #GelapIndonesia, or “Dark Indonesia”, and #ResetIndonesia trended.

As violence escalated, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto appeared with political leaders on August 31, 2025, and announced that lawmakers’ allowances would be cut.

A similar movement was unfolding in the Philippines.

Around 1,400 kilometres from Indonesia, Filipino Gen Z protesters took to the streets after allegations of corruption in government flood-control projects. Their central question was: “Where did our tax money go?”

Large amounts of public money had been allocated for flood protection while people were still drowning in floods. Gen Z users searched for and posted photographs and videos of politicians and contractors, exposing their families’ luxurious lifestyles.

The hashtag #NepoBaby spread alongside slogans such as “It’s not floods drowning our country, it’s greed” and “We are drowning in floods while their children live luxury lives.”

The movement developed in stages. During the first week of August, information about alleged corruption in flood-control projects began circulating. The following week, videos documented deaths and property losses caused by flooding. In the third week, the lifestyles of politicians’ and contractors’ children came under scrutiny. By the fourth week, Gen Z and others were on the streets.

By the last week of August, international media were extensively covering the youth protests.

It was around this time that the Indonesian and Philippine “Nepo baby” trend suddenly appeared on Nepali social media.

Videos began highlighting the luxurious lifestyles of children of Nepali politicians and officials, juxtaposed with the hardships of ordinary people.

But how did the trend reach Nepal? Who made the first videos? And how did it spread so quickly?

The Nepo Baby trend reaches Nepal

One of the earliest Nepo baby-related videos found on TikTok was posted by an account called “Velvet Muffin” on September 2, 2025. The identity of the account holder is unclear.

The video received more than 350,000 views. Comments called for more such content, with some users writing, “Now it’s Nepal’s turn.”

The video showed the lifestyles of Jaiveer Singh Deuba and his wife, Shrinkhala Khatiwada and Smita Dahal, alongside images of people affected by floods and landslides in the Philippines. Although it appeared to have been uploaded from Nepal, it clearly drew influence from the Philippine movement.

The account had four videos. Three more, all focused on Nepo babies, were posted on September 6. One said, “We have to work and struggle here so their passports keep getting thicker.” Another said, “Our struggle, their enjoyment.”

A third said ordinary people in Nepal could not even exercise basic rights while the children of powerful people were posting photographs and videos of luxurious lives.

Other early accounts, including “Wakeup Nepal” and “Nepal GenZ,” also posted Nepo baby videos, although those accounts have since been deleted. Another account, identified by the number 7545709787246365908, was also active at the time.

After September 4, Nepo baby-related content began appearing across countless accounts.

The discussion, however, had started even before TikTok became the main platform.

Anger was already building on Reddit

Reddit had become a space for intense discussions about the protests in Indonesia and the Philippines. Because users can operate anonymously or under pseudonyms, it also became a place where Nepali young people could openly discuss the government’s decision to restrict social media.

On March 20, 2025, the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology had warned that social media platforms would be blocked if they did not register with the government within one month.

That same day, the Nepal Social subreddit carried a warning about the decision. One user questioned whether the government had made the decision for the public or for its own benefit.

The issue resurfaced on August 28, when the ministry issued another notice requiring social media platforms to register within seven days.

By September 3, none had registered. A Cabinet meeting the following day decided to shut down the platforms.

Based on the Cabinet decision, the Nepal Telecommunications Authority instructed mobile and internet service providers to block 26 platforms including Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, YouTube, WhatsApp, Twitter, LinkedIn and Snapchat. The decision triggered an immediate backlash.

Reddit remained accessible, and discussions intensified throughout the day.

At 11:05 am, a user named “Rosti” warned that the ban could destroy Nepali businesses dependent on Facebook and Instagram. At 12:20 pm, “Somaymoni” wrote that the government could not simply ban social media. At 4:05 pm, another user, “Aculithym”, insisted that the government would not shut the platforms down.

By 5:29 pm, the tone had changed. One user wrote that the shutdown had happened and that the time had come to “tie up all the thieves and burn them.”

The anger that was not obvious earlier in the afternoon was becoming increasingly visible.

Some people turned to VPNs. Others gathered in tea shops to discuss what was happening.

On Instagram, an activist using the name “iih” was among the early recognisable voices calling for action. In a post from Manang’s Yak Kharka, iih said most people relied on Messenger and WhatsApp to communicate with family, while some businesses depended on social media. The government’s decision, the post said, would disrupt communication and trade.

iih called for a campaign demanding the resignation of then Communications Minister and government spokesperson Prithvi Subba Gurung, and for a younger minister who understood the internet.

The post received around 3,000 likes. Comments included calls for a protest and comparisons with movements in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines.

Who actually set September 8?

Until September 6, there was no clear public announcement about the protest date.

Yet according to people involved in the early discussions, preparations had already begun on the day social media platforms were blocked.

Several people who later emerged as Gen Z leaders—including Miraj Dhungana, Tanuja Pandey, Anil Baniya, Yujanraj Bhandari, Dhiraj Joshi, Majid Ansari, Pradeep Gyawali, Monika Niraula, Manish Khanal, Rijana Rana Magar, Prakash Bohora, Amit Khanal, Bhawana Raut, Ojaswi Thapa, Nimesh Shrestha, Aditya Karna, Aakriti Ghimire and Rakshya Bam—said they did not know who had ultimately called the protest or fixed the date.

Their answer was broadly the same: they found out through social media.

On September 7, Sabal Gautam and Purushottam Yadav went to the Kathmandu District Administration Office seeking permission for a peaceful protest.

Gautam says the date—September 8, or Bhadra 23—was chosen by them.

According to him, six school friends, all under 20, discussed the date after the social media shutdown. Purushottam joined later.

Gautam had created the TikTok account “Wakeup Nepal” on the day the platforms were blocked and posted Nepo baby-related content. That night, they decided on September 8.

The Nepo baby trend had been circulating for three or four days. With social media blocked, they wanted to take the anger onto the streets.

Saturday was considered unsuitable because it was a holiday and they feared fewer people would attend, so Monday was selected.

But Gautam says the protest eventually became very different from what they had expected and went beyond their control.

A person active on Discord gave a slightly different account. According to the user, September 6 was initially discussed because Saturday was convenient for young people. But some felt it was too soon and that information would not reach enough people. The discussion then shifted towards Monday, September 8.

The user, who requested anonymity, said only around 15 or 16 people were involved in the Discord discussion that evening and that the names of those present were not remembered.

That night, AI-generated posters stating “Date: September 8, Location: Parliament Building” began circulating.

The following day, the Discord server suddenly grew to more than 10,000 users.

Some discussions became increasingly aggressive, including talk of “head hunting” and wearing full-face masks to prevent police from identifying protesters. Other users discussed how to remain safe during the protest.

Because TikTok had already registered in Nepal, it remained accessible while most other platforms were blocked. Many users therefore moved to TikTok.

Until September 5, there were relatively few posts about a September 8 protest. From September 6, however, TikTok was flooded with videos and posters announcing the date.

The protest call spreads

Gen Z participant Aditya Karna says that after seeing the posters, he organised a Zoom meeting on September 6 with activist iih and others.

Karna argued that Parliament at New Baneshwor was a prohibited area and that protesters should instead gather at Maitighar. He actively circulated information about the restriction and says many people were redirected to Maitighar, although many still went towards the original location.

Another incident also fuelled public anger.

On September 6, a vehicle carrying Koshi Province Minister for Economic Affairs and Planning Ram Rana Magar, who had come to Kathmandu to attend the CPN-UML statute convention, hit a girl in Harisiddhi, Lalitpur, and fled.

Locals briefly blocked the road and protested, angry that the minister’s vehicle had hit the girl without stopping to check her condition.

Then Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli defended the minister and urged people not to politicise the incident.

He said it was an unfortunate accident, that the girl had been taken to hospital and that the party would bear her treatment costs.

The response further fuelled anger among young people.

“Numbers were estimated, violence was not”

Before September 6, many popular TikTok creators were posting their usual content. From September 6, however, influencers began uploading videos calling on young people to join the September 8 protest at Baneshwor or Maitighar.

Ravi Chand Thakuri, who had around 140,000 followers, urged young people to gather at Maitighar, saying the country would not change unless they acted.

Ratan Karki, with more than 350,000 followers, also called for the protest but stressed that it should remain peaceful.

“Movement should begin from every part of the country,” he said, while urging protesters not to vandalise government offices or stop vehicles.

Suruchi Budhathoki, who had around 52,000 followers, called on young people to protest against the older political generation and demanded greater youth representation.

Thousands of other accounts also called for September 8, although there was no single, clearly defined agenda.

Their videos and banners pointed to opposition to the social media ban and corruption. Slogans included “The Final Revolution,” “We Are Punching Up,” “Stop Corruption,” “Time for Youth” and “Enough Is Enough.”

Even accounts with relatively few followers—including Brief Nepal, Save Nepal, Defector, Finding My World and Truth Talks—received hundreds of thousands or even millions of views.

The movement was clearly being framed as a Gen Z protest, but its leadership remained unclear.

Among the prominent voices were content creator Nimesh Shrestha and then Pathao Managing Director Asheem Man Singh Basnyat.

Basnyat posted on Saturday afternoon that he would go to Maitighar on September 8 and urged others to join him. He argued that digital support alone was not enough.

“Physical presence matters even more than digital presence,” he said, announcing that he would personally attend the Monday protest and calling for a peaceful movement.

At the same time, numerous fake accounts appeared. Many young women called for a peaceful protest, while some male users also expressed support. Others warned that the protest could turn violent and urged participants to remain safe.

Pseudonymous accounts posted provocative AI-generated videos showing Parliament being burned, gunfire and tear gas, and protesters occupying Parliament.

The YouTube channel InDepth Story (IDS), which had more than 600,000 subscribers and over 100,000 TikTok followers, also reshared an older video about Bangladesh ahead of the protest. The video referred to the student movement that forced then-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to leave and showed students occupying the prime minister’s residence.

Popular accounts such as Routine of Nepal Banda, NEB Result and News and No Next Question expressed support. Then Kathmandu Mayor Balen Shah, Deepak Raj Giri, Karishma KC, Ranju Darshana and other artists and politicians also backed the movement.

Royalist activist and medical businessman Durga Prasai said he supported the September 8 protest and would attend. Gen Z accounts subsequently asked him not to come, and Prasai said he would stay away.

Police prepare for unrest

Police were also watching the rapidly changing situation.

Then Kathmandu Police spokesperson SP Apilraj Bohora said security forces were on high alert and had received numerous videos calling for a peaceful protest but showing Parliament and Singha Durbar being burned.

He said security would therefore be strengthened around sensitive areas, with more police deployed than usual.

If the protest turned violent, he said, those violating the law would face action.

By September 6, therefore, the protest had acquired a date, slogans, online mobilisation and thousands of supporters—but no clearly identifiable central organiser.

What began with anger over the social media ban had absorbed the Nepo baby trend from Indonesia and the Philippines, grievances over corruption, frustration with Nepal’s political leadership and a growing sense among young people that they had little control over the country’s direction.

The call to protest was everywhere.

The people who made it, however, remained difficult to identify.

And who took part in the discussions? […]

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah to lead 15-member delegation to UN General Assembly

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 8

Prime Minister Balendra Shah will lead a 15-member Nepali delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, according to sources at the Prime Minister’s Office.

The delegation will include Prime Minister Shah, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal and the Prime Minister’s Chief Adviser Kumar Ben, among others.

According to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai, Chief of the UN Division Krishna Prasad Dhakal, Chief of Protocol Kumar Raj Kharel, two undersecretaries and a section officer will also be part of the delegation.

The Prime Minister’s Office will be represented by Chief Adviser Ben, Chief Personal Secretary Subash Sharma, Private Secretary Pradeep Pariyar and a personal undersecretary from the Prime Minister’s media team.

Two military officers from the Nepal Army assigned to the Prime Minister’s security team and one Nepal Police officer will also accompany the delegation.

Foreign Minister Khanal, Foreign Secretary Rai and officials from the UN Division will leave for New York on September 20. Khanal is scheduled to participate in various sideline meetings held on the margins of the General Assembly.

Prime Minister Shah, meanwhile, will leave Nepal on September 23.

Shah is scheduled to address the General Assembly on September 24. According to sources, his address will take place sometime between 3 pm and 9 pm local time.

A total of 24 heads of state, heads of government, or foreign ministers are scheduled to address the General Assembly that day, with Shah scheduled to speak 17th in the order.

The government had initially approved a delegation to attend the General Assembly under the leadership of Foreign Minister Khanal.

However, the government later decided to send Prime Minister Shah himself following the heavy loss of lives and property caused by the floods in Rasuwa.

The Prime Minister is expected to raise the issue of climate change and its impact on Nepal at the General Assembly. Government sources said Nepal plans to highlight the Rasuwa floods as an example of the increasingly severe consequences of climate change and press the international community for compensation and support for the losses suffered by vulnerable countries.

Nepal is also preparing to organise several sideline programmes focusing on climate change during the General Assembly. Prime Minister Shah, however, is not scheduled to attend those meetings.

Shah is expected to return to Nepal on September 25, a day after addressing the General Assembly.

title.rendered: Religion, democracy, and the making of a liberal republic

content.rendered:
Nepal’s debate over Hindu statehood is usually posed too narrowly: as a choice between the present constitutional arrangement and a return to formal Hindu privilege. The larger question is what kind of political community Nepal is becoming. Can religion remain culturally alive while citizenship remains equal and political authority non-confessional?

The Nepali term dharma-nirapekshata can carry an adversarial connotation of standing entirely apart from religion. Standard English usage does not necessarily convey this nuance. This semantic friction has sometimes been used to portray the post-monarchy state as actively anti-Hindu, including by projecting the more rigid, faith-exclusionary features of Western models such as French laïcité onto a constitutional order that does not share them.

Article 4 forecloses that reading on its own terms. Its definition is closer to a guarantee of liberty than to a negation of religion. This discussion therefore favors religious freedom, state neutrality, and non-establishment over secularism, using the latter when the constitutional category itself is at issue. For present purposes, “secular” means “the preservation of religion and culture handed down from time immemorial, including religious and cultural freedom.”

Religious freedom is not freedom from religion, and state neutrality is not hostility to belief. A devout citizen can support a neutral state, while a non-believer can defend religious freedom as a constitutional principle. Political neutrality limits the authority of the state, not the spiritual condition of the citizen. The central distinction is between protecting religion and giving it political privilege.

Religion, civilization, and the liberal problem of authority

Religion has been one of the deepest sources through which people understand moral obligation, community, and belonging. Religious institutions have also been major carriers of language, art, ritual, and historical memory. Any argument for neutrality that begins by dismissing these roles misdescribes the object it seeks to regulate. Religion has provided moral socialization, welfare and associational networks before the state supplied them, the transmission of ritual and craft across generations, and communal meaning in times of suffering. A liberal society still needs these functions because law cannot fully define the duties citizens owe one another.

These functions clarify what is at stake. The question is not whether religion belongs in public life, but whether it is better protected by establishment or neutrality. The case for restraint is not that religion is dangerous because it is powerful and therefore needs to be contained. It is almost the reverse. Religion can command forms of loyalty and mass mobilization that few institutions can match. For that reason, the state has particular reason to remain restrained toward it. A faith’s strength should come from conviction and community, not state patronage.

Will Durant’s Story of Civilization is not a treatise on religious freedom, but its historical narrative illuminates this problem. Religion appears throughout it as a formative civilizational force. The same history also shows what happens when religious authority becomes fused with coercive power. The Reformation is instructive. Breaking one religious monopoly did not by itself produce freedom. A Protestant state could be as intolerant as a Catholic one.

The more important achievement came later, when the state ceased to regard itself as guardian of a single religious truth. That is where liberal order begins: not with the absence of authority, but with authority sufficiently bounded that it cannot claim jurisdiction over conscience. Durant leaves another problem unresolved, and it deserves to be named. If religious authority no longer governs conscience, what provides the restraint a free society still needs? Religion has historically provided much of it. Yet religious authority, once coercive, can threaten the freedom it might otherwise sustain. The task is therefore not simply to free society from religious authority, but to preserve the moral resources freedom requires once such authority no longer commands by force.

B.P. Koirala, Durant, and the discovery of political neutrality

B.P. Koirala’s intellectual evolution is a case of a serious mind working through precisely this problem. In an interview, he expressed his profound happiness at completing Durant’s eleven volumes during his long imprisonment. This shows sustained and personally significant engagement rather than passing acquaintance. It would nevertheless overstate the evidence to say that Durant supplied B.P. with a doctrine. His democratic and socialist commitments, his reading of Gandhi, and his experience of authoritarian imprisonment drew on many other sources. The more defensible claim is that Durant gave him a framework in which religion, moral order, and political authority could be considered together rather than treated as separate subjects.

That framework helps clarify an otherwise puzzling turn in B.P.’s thought. An earlier rationalist, near-atheist B.P. became, in later life, a self-described spiritualist. Seen through the distinctions developed here, this was not a retreat from liberalism but a deepening of it. Religion is not the same as religious authority. Spirituality is not institutional power. Political neutrality is not philosophical rejection. His later spiritualism did not require the state to become spiritual, just as his respect for religion did not require it to become religious.

The earlier question was whether one can live without religion. The mature liberal question is why the state should decide whether anyone must. These are different questions. The liberal achievement is precisely that they do not need to have the same answer. His late advocacy of reconciliation with the monarchy is often read as political manoeuvre. It can instead be read as another expression of the same capacity for judgment: recognizing that means suited to one historical moment may become inadequate in another. That quality of mind, rather than any single political position, is what matters here. B.P. is more useful as a standard of intellectual seriousness than as political property to be recruited for a dispute he did not live to see.

What changes when religion becomes the religion of the state

State neutrality means refraining from officially privileging one tradition in law, public office, or public finance. It still protects belief and worship. Once religion becomes associated with the state, however, religious and political institutions acquire overlapping incentives. This does not necessarily result from insincerity. It happens because political power tends to instrumentalize whatever becomes politically useful, and an established religious identity inevitably becomes politically useful.

Three consequences follow. First, establishment invites capture. Access to the offices and patronage associated with an established religion becomes worth capturing. Because no religious tradition is internally uniform, the state must decide which interpretation deserves recognition. The question of what counts as authentically Hindu, or Buddhist, ceases to be purely internal and becomes political. This can narrow rather than enlarge the tradition’s own pluralism. Not every established religion is governed this way in practice; the degree of capture is an empirical question, not a necessary consequence. Second, establishment tends toward tiered citizenship.

Formally distinguishing one faith creates legal asymmetry in areas such as officeholding, family law, or representation, regardless of how liberally the arrangement is administered. The hierarchy is built into the category itself. Third, establishment can strain democratic accountability. It introduces the premise that political authority carries some form of religious sanction. Criticism of government can then be interpreted as criticism of the sanctioned faith. Laws justified chiefly by one tradition’s texts also narrow the reasons available to citizens outside that tradition for accepting, contesting, or revising them on shared terms.

None of this excludes religious conviction from democratic argument. Citizens may bring religious convictions into public debate on the same terms as other convictions. The distinction is between religious participation, which is an exercise of freedom, and religious establishment, which creates a hierarchy among freedoms.

The majority tradition and Nepal’s unfinished argument with itself

The case for neutrality applies with nearly equal force to the majority tradition itself. This is an argument that majoritarian confidence rarely wants to hear. Establishing whichever tradition holds the majority today is a wager against that tradition’s own future position. Demographic and religious composition are not fixed.

Establishment can also attract instrumental affiliation, with people seeking advantage rather than expressing belief. That can dilute precisely what sincere believers would value. Establishment also forces the state to decide which internal faction is authoritative, turning a tradition’s own disagreements into matters of state enforcement. A culturally confident majority should not need the coercive authority of the state to validate an inheritance whose vitality does not depend on it.

Nepal’s own history sharpens this point. Hindu civilization here cannot be reduced to caste hierarchy. Yet caste hierarchy was historically codified in Hindu-sanctioned law, most notably through the Muluki Ain of 1854. Its social consequences persist despite the constitutional abolition of untouchability. A comparable complexity concerns women. Hindu religious imagination contains some of the world’s most powerful images of female divinity. Alongside them are social practices, including menstrual exclusion, that have restricted women’s actual autonomy. Neither fact cancels the other.

The productive response is not to condemn the tradition, but to ask whether its own resources, including its exalted conceptions of the feminine, can be used to challenge the limitations that persist beside them. “The majority tradition,” in short, is not the settled and uniform thing that a constitution could safely elevate without inheriting its own unfinished argument with itself.

Nepal’s plural inheritance and the republican settlement

Establishment and exclusionary nationalism share a structural logic even though their content differs. Both draw a boundary around an ascriptive identity and attach different levels of standing to it. Both can recast dissent as betrayal. Both can also mobilize solidarity against one another at relatively low cost to political elites. This is not a claim of moral equivalence, but of a shared mechanism. The liberal alternative to both is not the abolition of identity. It is ensuring that no identity determines constitutional standing.

The republican transition changed not only institutions but also the symbolic relationship between state and society. For many conservatives, the monarchy and the Hindu Kingdom represented continuity and the protection of inherited values. Their disappearance is a genuine cultural loss. Those who feel that loss deserve to be taken seriously rather than dismissed as backward. But taking the loss seriously does not require restoring the guardian. The republic can instead demonstrate that tradition can survive without political restoration. This may be the harder half of the republican project.

Against this background, four constituencies help clarify what establishment would specifically cost. Dalit communities would not necessarily see caste hierarchy legally restored. They would, however, see the state once again identify with a religious order historically intertwined with that hierarchy. Women’s legal gains in inheritance and marriage would not automatically be repealed. Yet the symbolic basis of hierarchies whose social weight persists could be revived. Indigenous, Kirant, Bon, and animist traditions cannot be absorbed into a single Hindu category without losing what is distinctive about them. This is why Article 4’s protection of religion and culture should be read as protecting Nepal’s plural inheritance, not only that of the majority. Nepal’s relationship with Buddhism also exceeds its demographic share because it is the birthplace of the Buddha. That heritage should not be made constitutionally subordinate in the land associated with its own founding.

Religion, monarchy, and the changing political calculus

Hindu statehood was historically bound to monarchy. Before 1990 and before 2006, the political order combined the ideas of a “Hindu Kingdom” and monarchical rule as one package. In 2008, both were dismantled together. This gives contemporary Hindu-statehood advocacy a strategic asymmetry. Restoring the monarchy is an exposed institutional demand. Restoring the Hindu state, by contrast, can be presented as cultural continuity and can therefore provide a more resonant entry point into the same broader reversal.

This is not to claim that every advocate is secretly a monarchist or that every argument is merely strategic. The organizational overlap nevertheless deserves careful documentation rather than assumption. A society debating Hindu statehood is not always debating only what it appears to be debating. Nor can the historical fusion of these two symbols simply be dismissed. At the same time, the validity of other arguments for restoring the monarchy is a separate question, one that could be examined in a different but equally serious article.

A regional shift adds another dimension. The BJP’s rise and the RSS’s growing influence in India have made Hindu civilizational identity a more consequential political language across the region. This has changed the incentives surrounding religious symbolism in Nepal without impugning anyone’s sincerity. A politician can be genuinely devout while also recognizing that visible devotion now carries political advantages it once lacked.

What is notable is how widely this vocabulary has travelled across ideological lines. This suggests less a collective conversion than a changed political calculus available to all. The real question is not whether Hinduism has public space in Nepal. Plainly, it does. The question is whether that space is strengthened by making Hindu identity a constitutional attribute, or whether political usefulness itself is becoming an argument for changing the constitutional order.

The political economy of establishment

The persistence of establishment needs an explanation beyond religious sentiment. It offers a low-cost technology of political mobilization. Religious appeals are easier to organize than the sustained work of governing. Identification with a sanctioned order also supplies authority independent of competence. A government that cannot convincingly say “we govern well” may find it easier to say “we represent who you truly are.” This is powerful because identity often runs deeper than policy and can redirect attention from institutional performance toward cultural authenticity. Where Hindu statehood may serve as a vehicle for restoring a displaced institutional order, establishment can become a bridge between cultural nostalgia and a broader restoration than the religious question alone suggests.

A further and more contested claim is that neutrality carries an economic dividend because communal conflict can raise uncertainty and risk premiums. This is plausible given Nepal’s development needs, but it is weaker evidence than the constitutional argument. The case for neutrality does not need to rest on it. The less controversial point is broader. Societies that accommodate difference without turning it into existential conflict can devote more attention and resources to development. Social harmony is therefore not merely sentimental. It is part of the institutional environment in which economic confidence is built.

Equal belonging: The republican principle

Nepal’s democratic expansion has multiplied the identities seeking recognition. Federalism, migration, and education have widened horizons and expectations. This is not evidence of democratic failure. It is evidence that democracy has enlarged the number of people who expect to be heard. For that reason, what the republic owes its constituent identities cannot be settled once and for all. Equal belonging provides the organizing answer. The majority need not become a minority for minorities to become equal citizens. Minority equality does not require erasure of the majority.

Concretely, a Hindu-majority society can take pride in its inheritance without making the state Hindu. Buddhist heritage can be honoured without becoming a constitutional condition. Indigenous traditions can be protected without being absorbed into a single national narrative. Dalit citizens need not interpret symbolic restoration as a reopening of their own subordination. Minorities can belong fully without demonstrating cultural conformity. Women can reform inherited practices from within their own traditions without being told that doing so is an attack on civilization. Conservatives can mourn an earlier order without being excluded from its successor.

Citizens can also be as deeply religious as B.P.’s later life suggests is possible without surrendering the freedom that allows others to believe differently. This is not a reluctant compromise. It is part of what liberal democracy has been moving toward. It turns difference from a source of political insecurity into a condition of common life. A democratic order does not need to make every citizen agree about ultimate questions. It needs only to convince them that they need not agree in order to share one political community.

The case for a liberal republic

A serious version of this argument must concede real costs. Communities that have long organized themselves around a dominant tradition may genuinely experience neutrality as a loss of recognition. That is a real cost, not a grievance to be explained away. Neutrality also creates its own difficult boundary between public law and private practice. That boundary is not self-evident and must be renegotiated continually. Neutrality therefore substitutes a recurring dispute over boundaries for the different, and in this argument’s view worse, problem of formal hierarchy among traditions. A serious defense of liberal order should not pretend that neutrality solves everything or that every supporting claim is equally settled.

None of this is hostility toward Hinduism. It is closer to the opposite. Hinduism, like any tradition, deserves to flourish without becoming an instrument of the state. The strongest guarantee of Hindu religious life may be precisely the protection that applies to everyone else. The deeper point, reached through Durant and B.P. alike, is that a society need not choose between spirituality and freedom, or between respect for religion and liberal democracy. The mature liberal order does not ask citizens to abandon their convictions. It asks only that the state refrain from deciding those convictions for them. That is why Nepal’s constitutional principle is better understood not as dharma-nirapekshata in the sense of negation, but as a combination of religious freedom, equal citizenship, and state neutrality. These are three principles that Article 4 already holds together, if the political argument around it can be persuaded to do the same.

To continue B.P.’s legacy rather than merely commemorate him means several things. It means taking religion seriously without making the state religious. It means taking tradition seriously without making its inequalities sacrosanct. It means taking conservative anxiety seriously without granting it constitutional privilege. It means taking pluralism seriously enough that the republic does not dissolve into competing communities seeking the state’s endorsement. And it means taking development seriously enough to see social trust as one of its preconditions rather than an obstacle to it.

That, rather than the repetition of B.P.’s conclusions, is what taking him seriously today would mean. The danger in restoring Hindu statehood is not that Hinduism would become democracy’s enemy. The danger is that the state would again make religious identity part of the constitutional definition of belonging. In a society as layered and plural as Nepal, that could narrow rather than enlarge citizens’ freedom. If restoration also becomes a vehicle for reopening the question of monarchy, a dispute that presents itself as religious would become a dispute about the constitutional order itself.

The republic will be judged not by whether it eliminates Nepal’s civilizational inheritances. It should not want to do so. It will be judged by whether it builds institutions that allow those inheritances to coexist and evolve without any one of them having to govern the others in order to feel secure. The republic does not ask Nepal to choose between its Hindu inheritance and modern democracy. It asks the two to become compatible. It does not ask Nepal to forget its past. It asks Nepal to inherit that past without being governed by its inequalities. It does not ask Nepal to make religious citizens secular. It asks the state to remain neutral so that all citizens can live according to conscience. It does not ask Nepal to strip conservatives of memory. It asks the republic to show that continuity does not have to depend on restoration.

The deeper challenge is therefore neither secularization nor religious restoration. It is democratic maturation. The most fruitful reading of B.P. Koirala begins not by asking which contemporary position he can be recruited to endorse, but by asking what his intellectual development still allows Nepal to think about more deeply. The objective is a republic confident enough to let religion flourish, disciplined enough to keep political authority from appropriating it, and principled enough to insist that the republic belongs equally to all. This is not a rejection of Nepal’s civilizational past. It is one of the most consequential ways of carrying that past forward.

title.rendered: Mega dam is not a crazy idea. Nepal should debate it.

content.rendered:
In view of the massive Bhotekoshi flash flood and the immense suffering caused by the loss of life and property, a country like Nepal, situated in such a precarious position, has been compelled to ask itself a difficult question. Can Nepal afford to rebuild everything there, in the same place and in the same way, while carrying the same risks?

As an ordinary citizen, I cannot help but feel that this disaster may be nature’s warning to Nepal—a message urging us to rethink how we develop settlements, build infrastructure and use our enormous water resources.

The fact that this idea does not come from an expert or planner should not, in itself, be a reason to dismiss it. The value of an idea should ultimately be judged by its logic, merit and feasibility, rather than by the identity of the person proposing it. This proposal therefore deserves serious study and open public debate, with Nepal’s long-term national interest at the centre.

The central idea is straightforward: if a scientifically suitable mega dam and reservoir can be constructed in the disaster-affected area, a single multipurpose project could potentially generate enormous amounts of hydroelectricity. At the same time, regulated water flow could provide significant benefits in irrigation, flood control, drinking-water supply, fisheries and tourism.

If such a system is found to be technically, environmentally and socially feasible, Nepal could explore whether modern technology can reduce the risks posed by sudden glacial-lake outbursts. Water from such lakes could potentially be monitored and, where appropriate and safe, released in a controlled manner to regulate and augment the flow into the proposed project.

In other words, rather than viewing water solely as a source of risk, Nepal could explore whether some of that risk can be managed while turning an enormous natural resource into a national asset.

Developed countries have been building and operating large dams for decades and have derived substantial benefits from hydropower and regulated water management. Their experience also demonstrates that such projects involve considerable technical, environmental and social challenges.

Today, however, Nepal has access to far more advanced technology, engineering expertise, monitoring systems and risk-management tools than were available when many of the world’s major dams were first conceived. If scientific assessment concludes that the disaster-affected area should no longer be used to rebuild the same settlements and infrastructure, then Nepal must seriously examine whether a large reservoir and dam could provide a more resilient long-term alternative.

Unlike some countries where major dam projects have displaced enormous populations and had to contend with the immense forces of very large rivers, Nepal faces a different set of circumstances in certain locations. If the required relocation is minimal or manageable and the geological, seismic, hydrological and engineering conditions are favourable, the country may have an opportunity to think differently about how it develops its water resources.

What Nepal needs now is political courage, coupled with a willingness to examine solutions beyond conventional approaches.

If developed countries have historically extracted enormous amounts of natural resources and contributed significantly to global climate change, while countries such as Nepal are now facing some of its harshest consequences, why should Nepal hesitate to raise this issue on the international stage?

Nepal should seek international climate finance, loss-and-damage support and adaptation funding—and, where justified, argue that such resources should contribute to transformative, climate-resilient infrastructure and water-resource projects.

We should not be afraid to speak openly about the losses we are suffering. The more hesitant we are to articulate our interests, the greater the risk that those interests will remain unheard. A country must be able to speak clearly and confidently about what it needs.

If climate change has contributed to the increasing risks Nepal faces, then Nepal should have the courage to demand meaningful international support to build infrastructure capable of managing those risks. Such a demand would not necessarily be unreasonable or out of place. We simply need the courage to make it.

If Nepal fails to embrace bold thinking now, it may become increasingly difficult to imagine major hydropower projects in the country. If concerns over glacial-lake outbursts continue to grow, not only will new projects face greater challenges, but existing projects may also remain exposed to significant risks.

Insurance companies and financial institutions will inevitably pay greater attention to the location and climate-related risks of major infrastructure projects when deciding whether to insure or finance them. Similarly, if rebuilding the same settlements and infrastructure in the same vulnerable locations is no longer a sensible option, Nepal must look seriously at alternatives.

One such alternative could be a large, multipurpose reservoir protected by a properly designed mega dam—but only after rigorous scientific, environmental, geological, seismic and engineering studies establish that such a project is feasible, sustainable and safe.

The proposal, therefore, should not be understood as an argument for building a mega dam at any cost. It is an argument for asking whether Nepal can use this moment to reconsider its approach to disaster risk, water management and infrastructure development at a much larger scale.

So, the question before Nepal is clear:

Will we have the courage to explore whether a mega dam can turn water-related risks into national opportunities—or will we continue building small, risky “water mills” and remain satisfied with fragmented benefits?

A government with a two-thirds majority has a rare opportunity to think boldly, study this proposal seriously and make a decision based on the larger national interest.

Nepal does not necessarily need to rebuild exactly what nature has just destroyed. Perhaps this is the moment to rebuild smarter.

title.rendered: Trade pressure shifts to Korala as Rasuwagadhi and Tatopani border points remain disrupted

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Trade pressure between Nepal and China has shifted to the Korala border point in Mustang after the Rasuwagadhi border crossing suffered extensive damage in floods and the Tatopani border point was temporarily closed from the Chinese side.

According to officials, Korala, which previously handled relatively little commercial activity, is now bearing much of the trade pressure between the two countries and has become the only operational border point currently handling the flow.

After the Bhotekoshi floods devastated the Rasuwagadhi border point, hundreds of cargo containers carrying goods from China were stranded along the route to Nepal. The goods had already been cleared through Chinese customs, creating complications over administrative procedures, payment systems and refunds if the cargo were to be returned to China and imported through another border point.

Against this backdrop, the government directed cargo vehicles originally bound for Nepal through Rasuwagadhi (Timure) to be diverted to the Korala (Nechung) border point in Mustang as an alternative route.

As a result, a large number of cargo vehicles have begun arriving at Korala.

The Mustang Customs Office, which normally clears only a limited number of vehicles, is now facing additional pressure after effectively taking on traffic that would previously have been handled by three customs points.

Despite shortages of infrastructure and personnel, the customs and other government agencies are making emergency arrangements to keep customs clearance operations running.

According to Bidur Chudal, chief customs officer at the Mustang Customs Office, the workload increased sharply due to three consecutive public holidays and the influx of diverted cargo vehicles.

However, with banks and government offices fully reopening from Monday, traders have started submitting customs declarations in greater numbers and the clearance process has picked up pace.

On Sunday alone, 15 containers were cleared. Five were carrying fruits, while the remaining 10 contained ready-made garments and other goods.

Additional customs staff deployed

The Department of Customs has deployed additional personnel to Mustang to deal with the increased workload.

The Mustang Customs Office has a sanctioned strength of 18 employees but had only 12 working before the additional deployment.

The department has now assigned six additional employees, bringing the total to 18. The additional team comprises three officers and three non-gazetted first-class officials.

Chudal said the newly assigned employees were travelling to Mustang after receiving their transfer orders.

According to Mustang customs data, 175 containers have been rerouted towards Korala from the China side. Some have already started entering the customs yard.

The customs office has prioritised vehicles diverted from other border points for clearance.

“Let us think about the infrastructure issues later. For now, we are working around the clock, with the support of traders and container operators, to clear the vehicles that have arrived here and send them onward,” Chudal said.

He acknowledged that the border point continues to face long-term problems, including inadequate infrastructure, the poor condition of national highways and a shortage of bridges.

Quarantine services operating from a tent

While customs clearance has accelerated, plant quarantine services — mandatory for imports of agricultural and forest products — remain severely constrained.

Many of the vehicles diverted from Rasuwa are carrying perishable goods such as fruits, vegetables and herbs. In response, the Plant Quarantine and Pesticide Management Centre has sent a three-member team to Mustang led by senior crop protection officer Prakash Poudel.

However, although Korala has a government-owned quarantine building, officials are currently unable to operate from the facility.

The building had previously not been used for quarantine services because agricultural products were not regularly imported or exported through Korala. Following a decision by the local administration, the building is currently occupied by Nepal Police.

Poudel’s team, which travelled from Kathmandu, has therefore coordinated with Lomanthang Rural Municipality and set up a tent to provide emergency quarantine services.

“We have our own building, but as there was no work there in the past, it was given to the police,” Poudel said. “We are currently providing services from a tent. Because of the wind and cold, it is not possible to operate the chemicals required in the laboratory, so for now we are only checking documents and carrying out administrative work, including issuing release permits.”

According to Poudel, approval has so far been granted to divert 361 consignments from Rasuwa to Korala.

Of these, official requests have been received for around 68 vehicles. Ten vehicles are in the final stages of the diversion process, while four have already entered Nepal.

Government plans to strengthen Korala

With Korala currently serving as the only operational border point connecting Nepal with China, the government has identified strengthening its infrastructure, resources and human resources as a priority.

The government is working to ensure that the border point is better equipped to handle increased trade, officials said.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Environment has also prepared terms of reference (ToR) for a feasibility study aimed at developing a long-term management plan for the border point.

After repeated disruptions caused by natural disasters at the Rasuwagadhi and Tatopani border points, the government is now considering Korala as a more reliable and long-term trade route with China.

However, immediate challenges remain. Authorities must first create conditions for quarantine services to resume from their dedicated building and coordinate with the Chinese side to ensure customs clearance is managed according to international standards.

title.rendered: Tourism recovery is not the same as tourism resilience

content.rendered:
Each time disaster strikes Nepal, the tourism sector follows a familiar pattern: assess damage, reassure visitors, reopen destinations, and launch campaigns to restore confidence. Nepal has become remarkably effective at recovery. The more important question, however, is whether recovery will continue to rely primarily on reassurance and promotion, or whether future reopening decisions will be grounded in verified evidence, transparency, and preparedness.

Even though Nepal has become highly skilled at recovery, the institutionalisation of preparedness remains far less developed. After every major disruption, the national conversation understandably shifts towards rebuilding, reopening, and restoring visitor confidence. This instinct has helped many destinations, businesses, and communities recover from difficult periods. However, reopening infrastructure is not the same as reducing future risk, and restoring visitor numbers is not the same as strengthening resilience.

Recovery rebuilds economic activity, whereas resilience reduces vulnerability. This distinction matters because rebuilding exposure without addressing underlying risks simply recreates the conditions for future disruption. While reopening a destination may restore confidence in the short term, communities can face similar crises again unless the hazards they are exposed to are properly understood and managed. Nepal’s tourism sector has repeatedly demonstrated its capacity to recover and bounce back. The challenge now is to ensure that every recovery process leaves the country safer, more prepared, and more resilient than before.

The Lesson of the 2015 Earthquake

The 2015 earthquake demonstrated both the vulnerability and the regenerative capacity of Nepal’s tourism economy. The official post-disaster assessment estimated combined tourism damage and losses at approximately Rs 81.2 billion and warned of significant impacts on arrivals, employment, and foreign-exchange earnings. International arrivals fell from 790,118 in 2014 to 538,970 in 2015, representing a decline of roughly 32 percent. Yet the sector recovered rapidly, with arrivals increasing to 753,002 in 2016, reaching 940,218 in 2017, and approaching 1.2 million by 2019.

These figures demonstrate an important reality: tourism can recover. What they do not automatically demonstrate, however, is that Nepal became more resilient. This distinction is often overlooked when recovery itself becomes the primary measure of success. While the earthquake proved the strength, determination, and adaptability of Nepal’s tourism sector, it did not demonstrate that permanent mechanisms had been established to verify destination readiness, communicate risk consistently, or ensure that future reopening decisions were guided by evidence rather than urgency.

Recovery statistics should therefore be interpreted as evidence of economic resilience rather than proof that underlying institutional vulnerabilities have been resolved. The lesson from 2015 is not simply that Nepal recovered, but that recovery alone should not be mistaken for preparedness.

Tourism resilience is livelihood resilience

Tourism is far more than a collection of hotels and airlines. Nepal recorded more than one million international arrivals in 2023, while the sector comprised 1,416 registered tourist-standard and star hotels, 4,845 travel agencies, 3,191 trekking agencies, and more than 26,000 registered trekking guides. Tourism foreign-exchange earnings reached US$548.2 million in the same year.

Behind these figures are guides, porters, transport operators, restaurants, homestays, artisans, farmers, mountain communities, and countless small enterprises whose livelihoods depend on visitor spending. Tourism therefore functions as a nationwide livelihood system, meaning that when destinations are disrupted, the economic and social consequences extend far beyond the immediate disaster zone.

For this reason, tourism resilience is not solely about protecting visitor flows. It is also about protecting jobs, incomes, local businesses, and community wellbeing. When recovery efforts focus primarily on promotion without sufficient attention to preparedness, the livelihoods that depend on tourism remain exposed to recurring disruption.

Climate crisis, tourism resilience and climate justice

Climate change makes tourism resilience an increasingly urgent national priority. Although Nepal contributes only around 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions, it faces a disproportionate share of climate-related impacts. Climate impacts could leave Nepal’s economy at least 7 percent smaller by 2050, while annual climate-related damage to transport infrastructure alone could reach US$250 million. At the same time, the Himalayan environment on which much of Nepal’s tourism depends is changing rapidly. An ICIMOD assessment published in 2026 reported a 12 percent decline in glacier area across the Hindu Kush Himalayan region between 1990 and 2020.

For Nepal’s tourism economy, these trends translate directly into greater destination vulnerability. Climate-related hazards increasingly affect trails, bridges, roads, settlements, water systems, cultural landscapes, and local economies, while also influencing visitor safety and destination management. As a result, resilience can no longer be treated as a post-disaster concern; it must become an integral part of tourism planning and destination governance.

This is also a climate justice issue. Nepal has done little to create the problem, yet bears a substantial share of its consequences. That reality strengthens the case for increased international support for adaptation, resilient infrastructure, technical assistance, and loss-and-damage mechanisms, while also reinforcing Nepal’s responsibility to manage risk more systematically and to ensure that resilience investments are guided by evidence and long-term preparedness rather than reactive recovery alone.

The missing institutional link

Nepal is not starting from zero. The country already possesses disaster-management institutions, emergency frameworks, risk-information systems, and tourism authorities. The Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, the National Disaster Response Framework, BIPAD, the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, and the Nepal Tourism Board all play important roles within their respective mandates.

The challenge is therefore not the absence of institutions but the missing operational bridge between disaster information and destination management. A flood warning is not automatically a traveller advisory, a reopened highway does not confirm that connected trails, accommodation facilities, and communication systems are fully functional, and a structurally intact hotel does not establish that the broader community is prepared to receive visitors.

Likewise, a promotional campaign is not a substitute for a verified destination assessment. Visitors deserve transparency rather than assumptions, and confidence should be supported by evidence rather than urgency. The objective should not be to promote recovery as quickly as possible, but to ensure that reopening decisions are informed by credible information and demonstrable readiness.

A tourism resilience system as the solution

The answer is not another ministry, another agency, or another layer of bureaucracy. What Nepal requires is a Tourism Resilience System that connects the institutions already responsible for disaster management, infrastructure, tourism, and local governance. Its objective is simple: to place evidence before confidence and preparedness before promotion.

To achieve this, the system should focus on four core functions: assessing risk before disasters occur through continuous monitoring, hazard assessment, and preparedness planning; coordinating information during crises so that government agencies, tourism authorities, and local communities operate from a shared understanding of conditions on the ground; verifying reopening decisions through documented destination assessments that examine access, essential services, emergency capacity, and community readiness; and communicating transparently so that travellers receive accurate, timely, and evidence-based information about both affected and unaffected destinations.

Leadership and coordination should build upon existing institutional responsibilities rather than creating new structures. The priority is to ensure that disaster-management institutions, tourism authorities, and local governments are connected through a shared operational framework that supports informed and verifiable reopening decisions.

Prootion to preparedness

Financing should prioritise hazard mapping, early-warning systems, resilient infrastructure, destination assessment capability, interoperable information systems, and local preparedness. Nepal should also make strategic use of emerging climate-finance and loss-and-damage mechanisms to support investment-ready resilience programmes rather than relying primarily on post-disaster appeals.

Tourism confidence cannot be manufactured through promotional campaigns alone. It must be earned through verified safety, transparent information, and genuine preparedness. Nepal has already demonstrated that it can recover from disasters. The next challenge is ensuring that recovery becomes a pathway to greater resilience rather than a cycle of repeated vulnerability.The true measure of tourism resilience should not be how quickly Nepal asks visitors to return, but how confidently it can demonstrate, through evidence, that destinations, businesses, and communities are genuinely ready to receive them.
