title.rendered: Daily Digest: The biggest stories, developments and updates of the day

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

There is a lot happening every day. The Daily Digest brings together some of the most important stories and developments in one place—from Nepal’s latest affairs to international news, business, sports and stories that deserve a closer look.

PM Balen Shah to attend UN General Assembly in New York

Prime Minister Balen Shah is set to travel to New York on September 22 to attend the UN General Assembly. He is scheduled to return to Nepal on September 25. Shah is travelling to the United States primarily to address the General Assembly. Following the heavy loss of lives and property caused by the Bhotekoshi floods, he is expected to draw the international community’s attention to the growing impacts of climate change on Nepal.

Nepal seeks advanced rescue equipment from international community after Bhotekoshi floods

Nepal has asked the international community for advanced rescue equipment and specialised materials after technical difficulties intensified search and rescue operations following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River. According to the latest update issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday, the government has prepared a list of high-tech rescue equipment and appealed for international assistance to accelerate rescue operations and reduce risks in the affected areas.

US Secretary of State calls RSP Chairman; US ready to provide additional assistance to Nepal

A telephone conversation has taken place between Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chairman Rabi Lamichhane and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. According to information provided by the RSP, during the phone call, US Secretary of State Rubio expressed deep condolences for those who lost their lives in the Bhotekoshi flood and conveyed America’s solidarity with the government and people of Nepal.

131 federal lawmakers pledge part of salaries to flood victim

A total of 131 federal lawmakers have agreed to donate part of their salaries to support flood victims, according to data available as of Monday. The lawmakers have written to the Federal Parliament Secretariat requesting that specified amounts be deducted from their salaries and contributed to flood relief efforts.

Australian PM tells parliament Nepal is not alone in bearing this grief

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has expressed deep sorrow over the devastation caused by the catastrophic floods in Nepal and the Tibet border region of China, saying Nepal is not alone in this hour of disaster. Addressing the Australian parliament, he confirmed that 36 of the country’s citizens remain unaccounted for after the floods.

Army estimates 121 people trapped in hydropower tunnels

The Nepali Army has estimated that 121 people are trapped inside tunnels of various hydropower projects affected by the Rasuwa floods on August 26. Speaking at a press conference organised by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Monday, Brigadier General Subash Jung Thapa said the Army’s assessment showed that 121 people had entered the tunnels.

Indian team continues rescue efforts at Chilime hydropower project: Ambassador Srivastava

Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava has said rescue efforts are continuing at the Chilime Hydropower Project in Rasuwa in coordination with an Indian technical team. Srivastava said through social media that efforts to advance the rescue operation were continuing in coordination with the Indian team.

Police intensify crackdown on social media misinformation and rumours

Police have intensified monitoring of social media platforms to curb misinformation, rumours and misleading content that could undermine social harmony, particularly amid the ongoing crisis caused by the Bhotekoshi floods.

Himalaya TV secures NPL broadcast rights, NetTV gets OTT rights

Himalaya Sports (Himalaya Television) has secured the official broadcast rights for the Nepal Premier League (NPL), while NetTV has won the tournament’s over-the-top (OTT) streaming rights. Himalaya Sports secured the television broadcast rights with a bid of Rs 172.4 million, including taxes, when the Nepal Cricket Association opened the bids at its office on Monday. The company said its bid was more than five times the value of last year’s broadcast rights and nearly 2.5 times the minimum bid set for this year.

Flood-displaced Betrawati residents shelter in forest as tents and essentials run short

Flood-displaced residents from Betrawati in Nuwakot have been taking shelter in tents in the Swaradanda forest, about one kilometre uphill from Betrawati. Nineteen tents have been set up in a row, but residents say they will not be enough as more displaced families return.

NEPSE up 18 points, closes at 2,560

Nepal’s stock market rose 18.07 points on Monday, the first trading day of the week, with the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index closing at 2,560 points. The market has now closed higher for four consecutive trading days. On the previous trading day, the index had gained 4.66 points.

title.rendered: Disaster victims need state support and reassurance: President Ram Chandra Paudel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

President Ram Chandra Paudel has said people affected by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa are in deep pain after losing their homes, relatives, livelihoods and being displaced, and that they now need support and reassurance from the state.

Paudel made the remarks in an address to the nation on Monday after visiting flood-affected areas of Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

“The pain of citizens who have become homeless, lost relatives, been displaced and lost their means of livelihood in this natural disaster is extremely deep. Right now, they need the support of the state, they need reassurance,” Paudel said.

He said complaints and demands raised by disaster victims should not be viewed as criticism but as important signals for identifying and addressing their problems.

“We know that listening to the voices of citizens affected by disasters and being sensitive to their suffering is a fundamental duty of a democratic state,” he said. “I urge the government and all relevant bodies to view the complaints and demands of the victims not as criticism, but as important signals for finding solutions.”

Paudel said the government should continue making every effort to make search, rescue, relief, reconstruction and rehabilitation more effective by coordinating among all levels of government and relevant state agencies.

Search for missing to continue

The President reassured families still waiting for information about their relatives and friends that search and rescue operations would continue.

“I want to reassure everyone waiting for news of their family members and friends that search and rescue operations will continue. The whole nation truly feels the pain of this moment of uncertainty that you are going through,” he said.

He stressed that every rescued person should have access to food, clean drinking water, safe shelter, necessary medical care and psychosocial counselling.

Paudel also called for special attention to children, senior citizens, persons with disabilities, pregnant women and other vulnerable people requiring additional protection.

He said temporary shelters for disaster victims should be safe and dignified.

The President also stressed the need to provide accurate information to families of both Nepali and foreign nationals affected by the disaster and facilitate humanitarian support to help grieving families bring their loved ones home.

Those who lost their lives, he said, must be remembered and treated with dignity, respect and compassion.

“The procedures to identify the deceased should be carried out in a highly sensitive and accountable way,” Paudel said, calling on the government to preserve DNA samples and other evidence to ensure reliable identification.

‘Search and rescue must not be abandoned’

Paudel said the August 26 disaster, caused by a glacier collapse and avalanche along with rocks and debris, had caused unimaginable suffering and extensive damage to lives, livelihoods and critical infrastructure including roads, bridges and hydropower projects.

He paid tribute to those killed and expressed condolences to their families, while wishing those injured a speedy recovery and hoping for the successful rescue of those still missing.

The President praised the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, health workers, local representatives, government employees, volunteers and other individuals and organisations involved in rescue and relief operations.

He said many rescuers had entered extremely dangerous areas while risking their own lives.

“Their indomitable courage, dedication and sense of service represent Nepal’s exemplary humanitarian sentiments and national character,” he said.

However, Paudel stressed that difficult geography, damaged roads and unstable and hazardous conditions should not become reasons to halt or abandon search and rescue operations.

Foreign nationals also among victims

Paudel also paid tribute to foreign nationals who lost their lives in the disaster, including those working in Nepal, visiting as tourists, trekking in the Himalayas or undertaking spiritual journeys.

He said Nepal considers every person within its territory part of its own family and would coordinate with the governments and diplomatic missions of countries whose citizens were affected by the Bhotekoshi floods.

He thanked neighbouring countries, friendly nations and the international community for providing search and rescue personnel, technical experts, medical teams and equipment during Nepal’s difficult hour.

Calls for national unity and climate justice

Recalling that Nepal has faced earthquakes, floods and landslides in the past, Paudel said Nepalis had repeatedly confronted disasters with courage, patience and determination.

He called on political parties, elected representatives, civil society, humanitarian and rescue organisations, the private sector, business community and citizens to remain united.

“This is the time to show national unity and solidarity. It is a time for reconstruction, rehabilitation and economic revival,” he said.

Paudel also said the disaster presented an opportunity to rethink Nepal’s development model as the country enters a period of reconstruction and recovery.

He said the disaster demonstrated the deteriorating condition of the Himalayan environment and served as a warning about risks associated with rising global temperatures.

“I sincerely call on the international community not only to listen to the voices of ecologically affected nations including Nepal, but also to take concrete and effective steps to ensure climate justice for them,” he said.

title.rendered: Indian team continues rescue efforts at Chilime hydropower project: Ambassador Srivastava

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava has said rescue efforts are continuing at the Chilime Hydropower Project in Rasuwa in coordination with an Indian technical team.

Srivastava said through social media that efforts to advance the rescue operation were continuing in coordination with the Indian team.

According to the ambassador, a joint technical team from Nepal and India has established the necessary safety-rope connections to facilitate entry into the tunnel.

“High-capacity mud pumps and generators have also been brought to the site to remove the mud and sludge accumulated inside the tunnel,” he said.

Meanwhile, work to construct the road required to facilitate the rescue operation is also progressing, Srivastava said.

title.rendered: Nepal seeks advanced rescue equipment from international community after Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Nepal has asked the international community for advanced rescue equipment and specialised materials after technical difficulties intensified search and rescue operations following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River.

According to the latest update issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday, the government has prepared a list of high-tech rescue equipment and appealed for international assistance to accelerate rescue operations and reduce risks in the affected areas.

Nepal has sought assistance from foreign missions and friendly countries after its own technical capacity proved insufficient to rescue people trapped inside hydropower tunnels and search areas inaccessible to rescuers because of thick mud and debris.

The government has requested high-capacity drones and LiDAR technology to scan difficult terrain, landslide-affected areas and tunnel interiors in the search for missing people.

It has also requested mud/tunnel rescue suits designed to allow rescuers to safely enter areas filled with thick mud and hydropower tunnels.

Similarly, Nepal has sought high-capacity pumps to rapidly remove water and mud accumulated in flooded areas and tunnels.

The government has also requested Bailey bridges to quickly restore road connectivity by replacing bridges swept away by the floods, as well as DNA testing kits and laboratory freezers for the identification of victims.

Nepal has also appealed for materials to prevent outbreaks of infectious diseases in the disaster-affected areas. The government has requested medical and health supplies needed to control communicable diseases and possible epidemics following the disaster.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said tunnel rescue suits and LiDAR technology have become an immediate necessity because people may still be trapped inside tunnels and the thick mud has increased the safety risks involved in manual rescue operations.

The government believes that obtaining these technologies would make the search, rescue and identification of missing people significantly faster and more effective.

Specialised teams from five countries deployed

According to the ministry, specialised teams from five countries have been deployed to rescue people trapped inside tunnels.

In coordination with the Nepali Army, Nepal has mobilised specialised tunnel rescue teams from India, China, South Korea, the UAE and Malaysia.

The ministry said rescue operations are continuing at affected hydropower projects including Upper Trishuli 1, Upper Trishuli 3A, Upper Trishuli 3B, Chilime, Rasuwagadhi and Langtang.

Additional equipment and technical personnel are being deployed to sustain rescue operations at the affected projects.

Rescue equipment, high-capacity drones and heavy-lifting equipment received from neighbouring countries, friendly nations and the international community are being used in the operations.

For the search for missing people and identification of bodies, forensic teams from India, China, Japan, Singapore and South Korea are working with Nepal Police on DNA collection and analysis.

The ministry said Prime Minister Balen Shah and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal have been holding regular telephone conversations with their counterparts around the world to strengthen disaster response efforts.

On Monday, Khanal held a telephone conversation with Maldivian Foreign Minister Ibrahim Khaleel.

title.rendered: 131 federal lawmakers pledge part of salaries to flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

A total of 131 federal lawmakers have agreed to donate part of their salaries to support flood victims, according to data available as of Monday. The lawmakers have written to the Federal Parliament Secretariat requesting that specified amounts be deducted from their salaries and contributed to flood relief efforts.

The Federal Parliament consists of a 275-member House of Representatives and a 59-member National Assembly. Of these, 131 lawmakers have so far submitted letters requesting salary deductions for flood victims. According to the Parliament Secretariat, lawmakers from the Nepali Congress, CPN-UML and Nepali Communist Party have asked the secretariat to deduct specified amounts from their salaries and contribute them to flood relief.

The group includes 38 Nepali Congress lawmakers from the House of Representatives and 24 from the National Assembly. Bhishma Raj Angdembe, leader of the Nepali Congress parliamentary party in the House of Representatives, will donate one month’s salary. Congress lawmakers Gangalaxmi Awal, Rukmini Devi Koirala, Prakash Singh Karki and Mohan Acharya have also agreed to donate one month’s salary each.

Congress lawmaker Tek Bahadur Gurung has pledged Rs 100,000. As one month’s salary is insufficient to reach that amount, he has asked the secretariat to deduct his full salary for one month and the remaining amount from his salary for the following month. All other Nepali Congress lawmakers have agreed to donate 15 days’ salary.

CPN-UML lawmaker Mohammad Ishtiaq Rai has written to the Parliament Secretariat saying he will donate one month’s salary, while other UML lawmakers have agreed to donate 15 days’ salary. The CPN-UML has 25 lawmakers in the House of Representatives and 10 in the National Assembly. Lawmakers from the Nepali Communist Party have also agreed to donate 15 days’ salary. In a letter to the Parliament Secretariat, the party said that 15 days’ salary of lawmakers’ personal aides would also be contributed to flood relief.

The Nepali Communist Party has 17 lawmakers each in the House of Representatives and the National Assembly. Lawmakers from the Rastriya Swatantra Party have also said they will donate half a month’s salary, although their letter has not yet reached the Parliament Secretariat.

Based on the letters it has received, the Parliament Secretariat is preparing to deduct the pledged amounts from lawmakers’ salaries and transfer the remaining salaries to their bank accounts. Secretariat officials said deductions could also be made from the following month’s salary if additional letters are received later. As of Monday, 131 lawmakers from both houses had formally requested salary deductions, specifying the amounts they wished to contribute to flood relief.

title.rendered: When facts reach Gyirong, conspiracy theories begin to collapse

content.rendered:
On September 5 and 6, journalists from the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, India, Pakistan, Singapore, Brazil and other countries travelled to Gyirong in Xizang and entered the core area devastated by the August 26 mudslide. They did not have to imagine what had happened. They saw it.

Wearing a safety helmet at the disaster site, a journalist from the Press Trust of India praised China’s capacity to respond to such crises, noting the large number of professionally trained personnel and specialised rescue equipment deployed there. He paid tribute to the rescuers, saying their extraordinary efforts were deeply moving.

On September 6, foreign journalists also attended a press briefing held by the emergency rescue command in Gyirong County. Officials explained the disaster, rescue operations and reconstruction efforts, and took questions from the media.

This matters because only days earlier, some overseas commentators had already constructed a very different story: China was supposedly “hiding the truth,” restricting information and preventing outsiders from seeing what had happened.

Then the journalists arrived. And so did the facts.

By 6 p.m. on September 5, China had mobilised more than 2,500 rescue personnel, deployed more than 9,000 sets of rescue equipment and conducted more than 1,000 drone sorties. Helicopters, boats, engineering machinery and rescue teams were mobilised in a massive search operation.

Before damaged roads could be reopened, rescuers themselves had to reach the core disaster zone by water, helicopter and mountain detours, including routes requiring more than 12 hours on foot.

Yet according to some keyboard detectives thousands of kilometres away, the mystery was why foreign journalists were not immediately wandering around an unstable Himalayan disaster zone.

Seriously? Gyirong is not a television studio.

This was an active disaster site at high altitude. Roads had been destroyed. Electricity and communications were disrupted. Slopes remained unstable. Landslides, rockfalls, debris deposits and other secondary geological hazards persisted. Weather conditions were difficult and rapidly changing.

Under such circumstances, temporarily restricting access is not evidence of a cover-up.

It is called disaster management.

Would any responsible government knowingly send journalists into an area where rescuers themselves are struggling against broken roads, unstable slopes and continuing geological risks?

Journalists have every right to pursue the truth. Governments have an equally serious obligation not to turn journalists into additional rescue cases.

Once conditions permitted safer access, international journalists entered the disaster area, interviewed people on the ground, observed rescue operations and questioned officials.

That is a rather strange way to “hide” a disaster.

There is another inconvenient fact for the conspiracy theorists.

Among those reported missing were 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries. Chinese authorities communicated information through diplomatic channels to relevant foreign embassies and established a 24-hour hotline for families of missing foreign nationals. By September 5, that hotline had handled 509 calls from anxious families.

If the objective were really to “conceal” the disaster from the outside world, informing 23 countries through diplomatic channels and answering hundreds of calls from foreign families would be a remarkably inefficient strategy.

Facts can be terribly uncooperative with a good conspiracy theory.

None of this means China’s disaster response should be placed beyond criticism.

China is a developing country undergoing an extraordinary process of modernisation, and its emergency management system is still evolving. No government is perfect. No emergency response is flawless. No political leader anywhere possesses the power to eliminate natural disasters.

The serious question is whether a country learns from them.

Over the past several decades, China has endured devastating earthquakes, floods, typhoons, landslides and other natural disasters. Its response capacity has evolved through painful experience: professional rescue teams have expanded; helicopters, drones, satellites and specialised engineering equipment are increasingly deployed; geological monitoring and early-warning systems have improved; and coordination among different agencies has become more sophisticated.

The response in Gyirong demonstrates this accumulated capacity.

More importantly, it reflects a principle repeatedly emphasised by President Xi Jinping: “people first, life first.”

Thousands of rescuers have been working in dangerous conditions searching for the missing. Chinese media and officials have repeatedly stressed that China and Nepal must “overcome the difficulties together.”

Why? Because China is not some detached actor standing outside this tragedy. China is itself a victim country.

Chinese citizens have died. Hundreds remain missing. Families are grieving or desperately waiting for news. Roads, communications and infrastructure around an important China-Nepal border crossing have suffered devastating damage.

Yesterday, authorities announced an unbearable toll: 43 people confirmed dead and 519 still missing.

Those are not statistics for a geopolitical debate. They are fathers, mothers, sons, daughters, colleagues and friends.

Nepal, too, has suffered terribly. This was never supposed to be a contest between China and Nepal over who should be blamed. It is a shared Himalayan tragedy demanding a shared response.

And the work will continue long after television cameras leave: searching for the missing, identifying victims, comforting bereaved families, rebuilding homes and infrastructure, restoring the border area, improving geological monitoring, sharing hydrological and meteorological information, and strengthening cross-border disaster prevention. China and Nepal will never stop walking that road together.

Unfortunately, almost every international crisis now attracts the same peculiar army of online conspiracy theorists.

For them, uncertainty means concealment. A damaged communication network becomes “censorship.” A temporarily closed road becomes “secrecy.” Changing casualty figures become evidence of manipulation. A delay in access becomes proof that somebody must be hiding something.

The conclusion always arrives before the evidence. But disasters do not operate according to social-media deadlines.

Bodies have to be recovered. Identities have to be verified. Families have to be notified. Roads have to be cleared. Geological risks have to be assessed. Information changes because rescue operations continue.

Uncertainty is not secrecy. Caution is not censorship. And restricting access to an active disaster zone is not a cover-up.

There is an important distinction here. Questioning governments is journalism. Demanding evidence is journalism. Investigating inconsistencies is journalism. But deciding the answer first and forcing every incomplete fact into a predetermined political narrative is not journalism. It is prejudice wearing a press badge.

There is nothing new under the sun. More than two thousand years ago, Confucius said: “The gentleman is calm and at ease; the petty man is constantly anxious and troubled.” Two millennia later, the observation remains surprisingly relevant.

Some people seem almost disappointed whenever facts refuse to confirm their suspicions about China. But prejudice often begins exactly where knowledge ends, and arrogance rushes in to fill the space.

Today is not the moment for such games. Thousands of families are still waiting.

Chinese and Nepali rescuers and officials will have enormous work ahead of them. The families of victims will need answers and support. Communities will need reconstruction. Scientists and governments will need better cooperation on glacier monitoring, geological hazards, hydrology and cross-border early warning.

Those who genuinely care about the people of China and Nepal should contribute facts, compassion and constructive ideas. Those who prefer geopolitical point-scoring can keep typing. Those who specialise in conspiracy theories can keep guessing. But something has changed. The roads are reopening. The rescue continues. Foreign journalists have reached Gyirong. They have seen the disaster with their own eyes. They have spoken with the people doing the work. And the facts are beginning to speak louder than the rumours. Rumours stop with the wise.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Nepal’s stock market rose 18.07 points on Monday, the first trading day of the week, with the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index closing at 2,560 points.

The market has now closed higher for four consecutive trading days. On the previous trading day, the index had gained 4.66 points.

Market volatility remained relatively low on Monday, with the NEPSE index moving between a low of 2,542 points and a high of 2,565 points during the day.

Trading turnover increased slightly. Shares worth Rs 3.83 billion were traded on Monday, compared with Rs 3.46 billion on the previous trading day.

The prices of 195 companies increased, while 79 declined and four remained unchanged.

The non-life insurance sector recorded the biggest gain, rising 2.05 percent. The sector had been significantly affected by the floods of August 26.

With prices having declined in the past, investors showed renewed interest in the sector on Monday.

The banking sector rose 1.15 percent, development banks 0.13 percent, hotels and tourism 0.31 percent, hydropower 0.51 percent, investment 0.04 percent, life insurance 0.45 percent, manufacturing and processing 1.24 percent, microfinance 0.61 percent and the ‘others’ group 0.50 percent.

The trading sector declined 0.09 percent, while the finance sector fell 0.43 percent.

title.rendered: Police intensify crackdown on social media misinformation and rumours

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Police have intensified monitoring of social media platforms to curb misinformation, rumours and misleading content that could undermine social harmony, particularly amid the ongoing crisis caused by the Bhotekoshi floods.

Police arrested 24-year-old Birendra Madai of Surnaya Rural Municipality-7, Baitadi, currently residing in Balambu, Chandragiri Municipality-12, Kathmandu, on Sunday for allegedly posting videos on Facebook Reels targeting various ethnic groups, making derogatory and insulting remarks and expressing happiness over the loss of life and property caused by the Bhotekoshi floods.

Police say Madai is only one example of a growing problem involving the spread of false information, rumours and misleading news, as well as insensitive comments directed at people affected by the disaster.

Nepal Police central spokesperson DIG Abi Narayan Kafle said police were closely monitoring social media to prevent activities that could cause further distress, spread fear or undermine social harmony during the humanitarian crisis.

According to the latest data, 173 pieces of misinformation and rumour-related content were identified on social media, including 168 on Facebook, four on TikTok and one on Instagram. Of these, 83 pieces—79 from Facebook and four from TikTok—have been removed through cyber monitoring efforts.

A 10-member committee led by Cyber Bureau DSP Gajendra Acharya has been formed to monitor such content, identify those involved and coordinate with concerned police offices and authorities for legal action.

Acharya said the committee was working to bring those deliberately spreading misinformation, rumours and misleading news under legal scrutiny. He added that people who unknowingly posted or shared problematic content were being warned and asked to remove it after the seriousness of the material was assessed.

Police are also monitoring possible fraud conducted in the name of collecting relief for disaster victims and other crimes that could exploit the disaster situation.

title.rendered: Chinese Embassy lowers flag to half-mast in solidarity with Nepal flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

The Chinese Embassy in Nepal has organised a memorial event on the occasion of Nepal’s national day of mourning for those who lost their lives in Bhotekoshi floods.

The Chinese national flag at the embassy has been flown at half-mast in memory of the victims.

The embassy said China and Nepal would continue to stand by each other with hope and determination and work together to overcome the difficulties and rebuild their homes and communities.

The devastating Bhotekoshi flood on Bhadra 10 caused significant loss of life and property on both the Nepali and Chinese sides. The Kerung border point connecting Nepal and China was also completely damaged in the disaster.

title.rendered: Flood-displaced Betrawati residents shelter in forest as tents and essentials run short

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Flood-displaced residents from Betrawati in Nuwakot have been taking shelter in tents in the Swaradanda forest, about one kilometre uphill from Betrawati. Nineteen tents have been set up in a row, but residents say they will not be enough as more displaced families return.

According to local Milan Shrestha, around 80 people are currently staying at the site, with more expected to arrive by evening. Twelve tents were provided by the government and the rest by donors. Shashi Dangol, chairperson of the Betrawati Lakhe Club, said many residents are currently away attending funeral rituals and are expected to return after completing them. He said one tent would be needed for each family.

Residents say they urgently need blankets, mattresses, cooking utensils, vegetables and clothes. Medicines for people with chronic conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure are also lacking. There is also a shortage of cooking gas, while transporting supplies remains difficult because of damaged roads. Residents have been advised to collect dry wood from the nearby forest for cooking, but not to cut down trees.

Drinking water and electricity are also major concerns. Residents are currently using a generator, but diesel supplies are running low. Locals have requested solar power facilities.

The displaced community is also struggling with the loss of family members and homes. According to locals, 193 people from six settlements in Betrawati remain missing, 12 days after the flood. The area previously had 299 households with a population of 1,256.

Search operations are continuing in homes swept away or damaged by the flood. A 64-year-old woman, Chandika Shrestha, was rescued on Saturday, the 11th day after the disaster, after being swept away along with her house.

Meanwhile, efforts are underway to clear roads obstructed by mud and debris. An excavator became stuck during road construction, and another excavator is being used to retrieve it.

Photos: Milan Shrestha

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah to attend UN General Assembly in New York

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Prime Minister Balen Shah is set to travel to New York on September 22 to attend the UN General Assembly.

He is scheduled to return to Nepal on September 25.

Shah is travelling to the United States primarily to address the General Assembly. Following the heavy loss of lives and property caused by the Bhotekoshi floods, he is expected to draw the international community’s attention to the growing impacts of climate change on Nepal.

The government had earlier planned to send only the foreign minister to the General Assembly. However, following the devastating floods, Prime Minister Shah will now lead the Nepali delegation himself.

His participation is expected to place Nepal’s climate-related vulnerabilities and the consequences of extreme weather events on the international agenda.

title.rendered: Army estimates 121 people trapped in hydropower tunnels

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

The Nepali Army has estimated that 121 people are trapped inside tunnels of various hydropower projects affected by the Rasuwa floods on August 26.

Speaking at a press conference organised by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Monday, Brigadier General Subash Jung Thapa said the Army’s assessment showed that 121 people had entered the tunnels.

“We have evidence that only 121 people entered the tunnels,” he said. “We will continue search and rescue operations until all the tunnels have been cleared.”

Thapa said the Army also suspects that some other hydropower project workers may have been caught outside the tunnels.

Based on an assessment of the damage to the hydropower project tunnels, Thapa estimated that the floodwater and debris descended at a speed of around 180 kilometres per hour.

title.rendered: Himalaya TV secures NPL broadcast rights, NetTV gets OTT rights

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Himalaya Sports (Himalaya Television) has secured the official broadcast rights for the Nepal Premier League (NPL), while NetTV has won the tournament’s over-the-top (OTT) streaming rights.

Himalaya Sports secured the television broadcast rights with a bid of Rs 172.4 million, including taxes, when the Nepal Cricket Association opened the bids at its office on Monday. The company said its bid was more than five times the value of last year’s broadcast rights and nearly 2.5 times the minimum bid set for this year.

Meanwhile, NetTV secured the OTT rights after submitting the highest bid of Rs 180.4 million, excluding taxes. Digo Stream, the only other bidder, had offered Rs 170 million, excluding taxes. NetTV, which has WorldLink as an investor, and Digo Stream, backed by Dish Home, were the only two companies to submit bids for the OTT rights.

NetTV CEO Niran Rajbhandari confirmed that the company had submitted the highest bid. He said the Nepal Cricket Association had informed the company that it would provide formal confirmation by email after completing the required procedures.

The Cricket Association has authorised the OTT platform to charge subscribers up to Rs 400, including taxes, within Nepal, Rs 600 in Gulf countries and $10 in other countries.

Himalaya Sports said securing the broadcast rights was more than a commercial investment and reflected its long-term commitment to Nepali cricket. It pledged to provide quality and wider coverage of the NPL.

The company also said the rising value of the tournament demonstrates the potential for building a commercially sustainable sports competition and strengthening Nepal’s broader cricket ecosystem.

title.rendered: Army to continue tunnel search and rescue until breakthrough

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

The Nepali Army has said search and rescue operations inside tunnels of flood-damaged hydropower projects will continue until a breakthrough is achieved.

Speaking at a press conference organised by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Monday, Brigadier General Subash Jung Thapa said search and rescue operations inside the tunnels were being carried out intensively and would continue until the tunnels were cleared, unless the government decides to halt the operation.

The Army estimates that around 121 people may be trapped inside tunnels of hydropower projects affected by the floods. At the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, a search and rescue team, along with project representatives, has reached the powerhouse and control point and conducted searches, Thapa said.

At the Trishuli-3A project, Army personnel equipped with rescue gear have continued search operations in the powerhouse and tunnels. At Trishuli-3B, personnel entered through Audit 2 and exited through Audit 1, while work is underway to clear a route through the Audit 2 tunnel to transport excavators and other equipment.

Thapa said joint teams, including foreign personnel, were also removing mud from Chilime Hydropower and conducting further searches at the Upper Trishuli-1 project.

Based on assessments of damage to the hydropower tunnels, Thapa estimated that the floodwater and debris may have descended at a speed of around 180 km per hour.

title.rendered: Flood-Hit areas see restoration of most internet services

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Internet and telecommunications services disrupted by the recent floods in Rasuwa and surrounding areas have been restored in most affected locations, with service providers including WorldLink, Ncell and Nepal Telecom accelerating repair and restoration work.

WorldLink CEO Keshav Nepal said internet services had resumed in major areas including Betrawati and Dhunche. Around 11,000 WorldLink users were affected by the floods, and about 8,000 routers are now back online. Service remains unavailable to some customers whose homes were destroyed by the disaster. WorldLink has also restored major fibre connections linking Rasuwa and Nuwakot, while efforts continue to reach three wards across the Trishuli River.

Ncell said 92 per cent of its towers disrupted by the Bhotekoshi floods have been brought back into operation. Of its 27 affected towers, one in Ghattikhola, Timure, was completely destroyed, while restoration of another tower in Timure, Uttargaya, is being coordinated with helicopter support to transport equipment.

Nepal Telecom said fibre repair and restoration had reached the final stage, with most work expected to be completed by Monday evening. Three towers in Timure, Chilime Khola and Trishuli were completely damaged, but connectivity has been maintained through alternative networks. The company is also using generators and solar panels to maintain services in areas without electricity.

title.rendered: President Paudel to address the nation at 3:30 pm

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

President Ram Chandra Paudel is scheduled to address the nation at 3:30 pm today. According to his press adviser, Kiran Pokharel, the president will address the nation after returning from a visit to flood- and landslide-affected areas of Rasuwa and Nuwakot. His address will be broadcast live on Nepal Television.

President Paudel visited the disaster-hit areas earlier today to assess the situation. During the visit, he received briefings from the Nepal Army and other officials on the extent of the damage and the humanitarian crisis caused by the disaster.

The floods and landslides on August 26 caused extensive loss of life and property in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

According to the latest figures, 1,355 people have died in the disaster, while 4,996 remain missing.

title.rendered: Namuna Basti in Dailekh at high risk of landslide

content.rendered:
Dailekh, September 7

Namuna Basti in Narayan Municipality-1, Dailekh, is at high risk of landslides following continuous rainfall.

Eight families comprising 37 people have been displaced after a landslide began affecting the settlement on Sunday night following heavy rain. A team of police deployed from the District Police Office, Dailekh, under the command of Police Inspector Rishikesh Gautam Harijan, rescued the affected residents in coordination with local representatives.

The displaced residents have been sheltered at the vegetable collection centre in the same ward. The settlement, home to 65 Badi families and located on a steep slope, faces the risk of widespread damage if even one house is buried by a landslide. Residents remain fearful after Rupa Badi, her daughter Sapana and son Bishnu were killed in a landslide in the past.

One of the displaced residents, Kamala, said families have repeatedly been forced to take shelter at the jail, veterinary centre and vegetable collection centre whenever flooding and landslides occur. She said they would not return to the old settlement until they were permanently relocated.

Narayan Municipality-1 Ward Chairperson Sandesh Shrestha said the affected area was inspected and discussions were held with residents and community leaders. “Considering the current rainfall situation, we have discussed a long-term solution. The Badi community will be relocated elsewhere so that the landslide risk that has persisted for years can be eliminated,” Shrestha said.

He said the Badi families had already received identification documents from the Land Commission and that the process for their permanent resettlement would be expedited. Dailekh Chief District Officer Anand Sharu said the administration was ready to help permanently settle the Badi community if the local government moved the process forward quickly. “If they are landless, the municipality should expedite the process. We will help find land,” Sharu said. “Insisting that the Badi community must be given land only in a place of their choice is not consistent with state policy.”

Sharu said he had inspected disaster-affected areas across Dailekh and found that local governments had been slow in carrying out their responsibilities. He urged them to coordinate with the Land Commission to identify land for distributing land ownership certificates.

title.rendered: Relief has reached everywhere except helicopter-only zones, says disaster authority

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Dr. Dharmaraj Upreti, executive chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, has claimed that relief materials have already reached most flood-affected areas.

Speaking at a program organised at the Authority on Monday, Dr Upreti said relief has reached all areas except the most remote ones that require helicopter transport.

He made clear that airlifting relief is currently facing some difficulty, since helicopters are now mainly being prioritised for search operations for the missing and rescue of those trapped.

“We are in continuous contact with local governments. Relief materials have already reached many places,” Dr Upreti said. “Where helicopter operations are difficult, only search and rescue are being prioritised right now. That said, we’re trying to send food supplies not just from Kathmandu but also from stations closer to Trishuli or Rasuwa.”

“Fake videos on social media had negative impact”

Executive Chief Upreti also appealed to the public not to spread misleading and “fake videos” related to the disaster that are circulating on social media. He said that videos not actually from the affected sites are going viral, creating a negative impact and spreading fear among the public.

“We found that several fake videos, not from our actual field sites, are spreading rapidly on social media. We need to be alert to the misinformation this causes,” he said.

Security forces mobilised for rescue since day one

The Authority stated that all three security forces have been working around the clock on rescue and relief since the first day of the disaster.

He said the state has spared no effort in search, rescue, and relief, and that as soon as the names of missing persons are received, they are verified through security agencies and field teams are mobilised immediately.

Dr Upreti clarified that local complaints are being addressed progressively, and that the government is coordinating with neighbouring countries as needed for disaster management support.

title.rendered: Kathmandu to add 21 buses, 6 routes to night service

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Kathmandu Metropolitan City is preparing to expand its night-time public transport service by adding 21 buses and six new routes, following a three-month review of the pilot programme. The study found that 66,952 passengers used the service during the trial period, with each bus carrying an average of 142 passengers a day.

However, the service currently operates at a daily loss of Rs 1,690 per bus, as average revenue stands at Rs 3,134 against an operating cost of Rs 4,814. Passenger demand is highest between 8 pm and 9 pm, accounting for 41.56 per cent of total ridership, particularly among employees, workers and daily wage earners returning home late.

The study committee has recommended increasing the fleet from seven to 28 buses and expanding the service to six additional routes, including Godawari–Budhanilkantha, a two-way Ring Road service, Jagati–Thamel and Kirtipur–Nepal Airlines Corporation. The proposed routes would connect major hospitals, commercial centres and entry points across the Kathmandu Valley.

To improve financial sustainability, the committee has proposed a Rs 12 night-time premium fare, cost-sharing among eight municipalities and viability gap funding. It has also recommended CCTV cameras, GPS tracking and dedicated bus stops to improve passenger safety, particularly for women, senior citizens and tourists. The expansion is expected to reduce reliance on private vehicles and support the Valley’s night-time economy.

content.rendered:
Jhapa, September 7

A group of 22 elephants that had been camped out in various community forests across the district for the past month has headed back toward India this morning, elephant conservationist Shankar Luitel reported.

The herd, which included calves, had been causing near-daily disturbances in Bahundangi, Shantinagar, and surrounding areas. The elephants had been destroying residents’ homes, feasting on ripening paddy in the fields, trampling crops, and breaking betel nut trees, forcing residents of Jhapa’s northeastern region to live in fear and stress for a long time.

After a month, locals felt great relief once the large herd that had come from India returned to its natural habitat.

According to resident Neel Kantha Tiwari, fear among residents eased to some extent once the herd left. However, residents were startled again this morning when a lone elephant wandered into Birtamod Municipality-7. After the elephant was spotted right in a residential yard early in the morning, locals were forced to flee.

Journalist Pushpa Baral reported that the lone elephant, after roaming the settlement for about four hours in the morning, headed toward the tea gardens in Butabari. In Jhapa, elephants typically cross the Mechi River from forests in India’s Assam and West Bengal and enter Nepal via Bahundangi in search of food and shelter.

According to Tiwari, elephants are able to enter Nepal easily because the solar fencing (an electrified barrier meant to deter them) along the Nepal-India border has grown old and worn down. Every year in the district, people lose their lives to elephant attacks, alongside crop and property damage worth millions of rupees.

title.rendered: Powerful nations increasingly choose Lamichhane over PM Shah for diplomacy

content.rendered:
Rabi Lamichhane, chairman of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), has emerged as the preferred point of contact for major powers such as India, China, and the United States on diplomatic matters.

While ambassadors from these countries have also begun engaging with Prime Minister and senior RSP leader Balendra Shah, it is party chairman Lamichhane who has appeared more active in high-level conversations.

On Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a phone call with Chairman Lamichhane, expressed sorrow over the immense damage caused by the Rasuwa floods. According to RSP sources, the US Secretary of State assured continued, priority US assistance to Nepal.

RSP Chairman Lamichhane, in turn, thanked the US government for expressing sorrow over Nepal’s losses and the difficult time this has brought.

Earlier, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had invited Lamichhane to New Delhi on June 3 for a meeting. Lamichhane, leading a delegation on behalf of his party, held talks with Indian Prime Minister Modi and senior leaders of the ruling BJP.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal’s visit followed shortly after Lamichhane’s. Notably, while Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava and other diplomats did not get individual meetings with Prime Minister Shah, high-level talks did take place with Lamichhane. Only later did the Indian and Chinese ambassadors hold separate meetings with Prime Minister Shah.

Similarly, the Chinese side had also invited Lamichhane to visit in August. Lamichhane postponed it to the second week of September, citing internal reasons. After an unofficial schedule for the visit was drawn up, only formal confirmation remained. In the meantime, the visit has now been put on hold due to the Bhotekoshi floods and other factors. RSP sources say the visit is likely to happen soon, at an appropriate time.

“Confirming the meeting with the Chinese president, along with preparing some substantive agenda items, is what held up the visit, but the chairman remains positive about going to Beijing,” an RSP source said.

According to a senior source, the US Secretary of State’s wish to hold a conversation carrying decisive weight at the top level of government is what made the call with Chairman Lamichhane possible.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah, meanwhile, is preparing to travel to New York for the UN General Assembly session, where he is expected to raise Nepal’s concerns with world leaders and hold corresponding meetings, though the full schedule has not yet been finalised.

Nepal’s embassy in the US and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are reportedly making preparations for this. Diplomacy analyst and journalist Sudheer Sharma views the importance given to RSP Chairman Lamichhane as consistent with how major powers typically engage, based on access rather than protocol. He attributes this partly to Lamichhane’s position as the powerful chairman of the ruling party, and partly to Prime Minister Shah’s style of not being easily accessible.

“Not just the US, but other major powers too tend to engage based on access and where power actually lies, rather than strictly following diplomatic protocol. The meetings and calls with Chairman Lamichhane should be seen as a result of that,” journalist Sharma said. “Prime Minister Shah isn’t easily available, and he’s also due to travel to the UN General Assembly soon. Even if he doesn’t accept the US invitation to visit, since that trip will happen on American soil anyway, it’s natural that conversations are happening with Chairman Lamichhane right now.”

Earlier, right after RSP’s landslide victory in the March elections, Indian Prime Minister Modi had spoken with both Shah and Lamichhane. Several other countries are also understood to be advancing dialogue by giving importance to Chairman Lamichhane.

title.rendered: Landslides disrupt roads and power supply in Bajura

content.rendered:
Bajura, September 7

Rain-triggered landslides have disrupted road transportation and electricity supply in Bajura, affecting daily life across the district.

The Sanfe-Martadi road, the main road connecting the district headquarters Martadi with other areas, has remained blocked for two days after landslides occurred at several locations in Badimalika Municipality-9, including Karagar Mod, Binod Smriti Pratikshalaya, Selagad and Suwakandh.

According to the District Police Office, efforts to clear the debris began on Sunday using a JCB excavator but were halted after heavy rain resumed. Road clearance resumed Monday with a JCB and an excavator mobilised by the Department of Roads. Vehicles travelling to and from Martadi have remained stranded.

Electricity supply has also been disrupted after landslides brought down around 32 poles of the national transmission line. Seven poles were destroyed at Suwakandh, while another 25 fell at Birekhola in the Nunepani area.

The Nepal Electricity Authority has deployed technicians to repair the damaged infrastructure, with security personnel assisting the effort.

Meanwhile, landslides in Badimalika-8 and 9 damaged two houses and several sheds. Chief District Officer Dorendra Niraula has inspected the affected areas and is coordinating efforts to restore road and power services.

title.rendered: President Paudel visits flood-affected areas in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 7

President Ram Chandra Paudel on Monday conducted an on-site inspection of various areas of Nuwakot affected by the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

During the visit, he met with flood-affected residents and listened to their concerns. President Paudel received a briefing from the District Security Committee on ongoing efforts to search for and rescue people missing in the floods, as well as the loss of life and property caused by the disaster.

On the occasion, Chief District Officer Shambhu Prasad Regmi and other committee members presented details of the damage caused by the Rasuwa floods in the district. Regmi also briefed the president on ongoing efforts related to the search and rescue of flood victims, relief, resettlement and immediate reconstruction.

President Paudel also inspected a holding centre in Nuwakot where flood-affected residents are staying. The flood victims briefed the president on the loss of life and property caused by the unprecedented flooding in the Bhotekoshi River. Earlier on Monday, President Paudel also inspected a Nepali Army camp in Trishuli, Nuwakot, where flood-affected people were being assisted, as well as areas of Rasuwa affected by the floods.

title.rendered: 19 people arrested with drugs in Kapilvastu

content.rendered:
Kapilvastu, September 7

The District Police Office, Kapilvastu, has arrested 19 people up to September 6.

The individuals were arrested with drugs while attempting to cross the border on foot, some carrying the drugs strapped to their bodies.

From mid-July through September 6 of the current fiscal year 2026/27, police have registered 11 drug-related cases and arrested 19 people.

According to police, those arrested include 13 men and six women, all Nepali citizens. During this period, police recovered marijuana, hashish, heroin, opium, and Nitrovet tablets.

Police recovered 130 grams of marijuana, 5 kilograms 225 grams of hashish, 3 grams 150 milligrams of heroin, and 10 kilograms 364 grams of opium during this period.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Ripendra Kumar Singh of the District Police Office, Kapilvastu, said 10 Nitrovet tablets were also recovered. He said action was being taken against those involved in the drug trade in accordance with the law.

Surveillance in the border area has been further tightened in recent times

title.rendered: Bimalendra Nidhi calls for unity to tackle natural disaster

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Nepali Congress leader Bimalendra Nidhi has called on all sides to set aside political and partisan differences and unite to deal with the unprecedented natural disaster facing the country.

Addressing a Lions Club event in Janakpur, Nidhi stressed that rescue, relief and reconstruction should be prioritised in the wake of the disaster.

Nidhi said the recent floods and landslides across the country had caused significant loss of life and property.

He said the devastation in areas including Betrawati and Dhunge Bazaar in Rasuwa, as well as various parts of Nuwakot, had severely disrupted normal life.

Referring to the three stages of disaster management—rescue, relief and reconstruction—Nidhi said security agencies had been continuously engaged in rescue operations for the past 11 days.

He said the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force had done commendable work despite limited resources.

He also expressed gratitude for the assistance provided by the international community, including neighbouring India and China. “We have never faced such a massive disaster before. At such a time, we must rise above caste, ethnicity, gender, religion and politics and focus on humanitarian service,” he said.

Expressing concern over the damage to the hydropower sector, Nidhi said the loss of employees working at hydropower projects and the destruction of infrastructure represented an irreparable loss for the country.

title.rendered: Families wait for the missing at Trishuli 3B, 13 days on

content.rendered:
The floods that struck Bhotekoshi on August 26 caused massive damage to the 37-megawatt Upper Trishuli-3 “B” hydropower project. After the flood and landslide, 191 people working at the project went missing. Of them, 13 have since been reached, but the company says 178 remain unaccounted for.

Search and rescue efforts for the missing have been ongoing since the day after the flood. But even after 13 days, no concrete information about them has emerged.

On Sunday, work to clear the audit tunnel and bring in heavy machinery continued until evening. Search efforts were reportedly intensified further from Monday.

But with rescue still not accomplished after so long, the patience of the missing workers’ and staff’s families is wearing thin. Today they gathered at Maitighar Mandala to protest, saying the government’s rescue effort has been slow and demanding an immediate, effective operation.

13 days, and still no rescue

Among those missing at the Upper Trishuli-3 “B” project is senior geologist Sumesh Amatya, whose wife, Prismuna Shrestha, remains unaware of her husband’s condition.

She says that although she has heard her husband was inside the project’s camp, she still has no information on whether he is alive.

“It’s not enough to just say it’s hard, it’s hard,” she says.

According to her, the family has not been given any clear official information so far.

From Singha Durbar to Maitighar Mandala

Rina Amatya Shrestha, sister of the missing senior geologist Sumesh Amatya, came to Maitighar to draw the government’s attention, saying rescue has still not happened after 13 days.

“Today marks 13 days, and there’s still been no rescue,” she says. “We came here to tell the government to carry out the rescue as quickly as possible.”

According to her, the flood struck while her brother Sumesh Amatya and 41 others were in a meeting inside a building at the project camp.

“My brother and everyone with him are trapped,” she says. “We went to Singha Durbar; we went everywhere. But since no news came from anywhere, we came here.”

She said the Bhotekoshi disaster should not be understood merely as an ordinary landslide.

“This can’t be called a landslide at all. This is a Himalayan tsunami,” she says. She said their one demand to the government is for the immediate search and rescue of the missing.

“Rescue isn’t possible without a large excavator”

One relative of the missing accused the government’s rescue effort of being slow. According to him, the flood struck while 42 people were in a meeting inside a building at the project camp.

“That meeting building is completely buried. Today marks the 13th day, and the government still hasn’t been able to carry out the rescue,” he says.

He said a small excavator was initially brought to the site, but since it could not effectively clear the debris, a larger-capacity excavator is now needed.

“Only with a large excavator can work begin properly there. It’s not a situation where people can just go and look and expect something to happen,” he says.

He said the family understands that although the Nepal Army has reached the site, it has been difficult to proceed due to a lack of sufficient personnel and equipment. The family also considers the absence of a helicopter capable of transporting heavy machinery to the site a major reason for the delay.

“We should have asked neighbours for help immediately”

Family members have also accused the government of being slow to seek necessary assistance from neighbouring countries, India and China, for the rescue.

“If we don’t have a helicopter that can carry a large excavator, we should have asked our neighbouring countries for help,” the relative says. “If that had been requested, it wouldn’t still be this delayed today.”

According to him, the government should have sought help for the necessary heavy equipment and a helicopter to transport it on the very first day of the disaster.

“Work began after a week”

Another relative alleged that it took a long time for rescue work to even begin.

“It looks like work only barely began after eight or nine days. At an extremely slow pace,” he says.

He said the family understands the government has not made adequate effort to arrange the helicopter needed to bring a large excavator to the site.

“The government hasn’t paid proper attention. It hasn’t even been able to arrange a helicopter for the large excavator,” he says.

He said that although the home minister went to inspect the site in person, it failed to bring about the expected improvement in the pace of rescue.

“The home minister himself went to the field and came back. But that has just been something of a show,” he says.

Four members of one family missing

Upper Trishuli-3 “B” project engineer Somnath Paudel, his wife Tara Upadhyaya, and their children are also missing since the flood. They had been living in the project’s staff quarters.

According to Somnath’s cousin Sagar Paudel, the family had spoken with them as recently as the evening before the flood.

“We talked until the evening the day before. Then this happened in the morning, and since then there’s been no contact,” he says.

Somnath, whose home is in Basgadhi Municipality-3, Bardiya, is the eldest son in his family. His youngest brother is currently in Bidur, waiting for word of him. Their elderly father and disabled mother, along with other family members, are now waiting for news of their condition.

After 13 days without any concrete information about their relatives, families are now seeking results, not reassurances. Their question is: if there is reason to believe people are trapped in the project’s camp, quarters, or tunnel area, why hasn’t every available technology, equipment, and workforce been used to intensify the search?

And if moving large machinery is difficult, they ask, whose responsibility is it to arrange the helicopters and equipment needed to do so?

title.rendered: Landslides block Karnali Highway, road reopening may take days

content.rendered:
Surkhet, September 7

Traffic along various sections of the Karnali Highway has been disrupted after landslides triggered by incessant rainfall hit several locations along the highway. Damage to sections of the road has affected transportation since Sunday evening.

Although efforts are underway to clear the landslides and repair damaged sections of the road, it will take some time for the highway to fully reopen, according to the District Administration Office, Jumla. Given the condition of the road and the nature of the landslides, authorities said it would be difficult to restore smooth traffic immediately at all locations.

According to Jumla Chief District Officer Tej Prakash Prasai, landslides have blocked the road at several locations along the Karnali Highway. Coordination is underway with the concerned agencies to reopen the road, while necessary machinery and personnel have been mobilised to expedite debris removal.

“Landslides have occurred at several locations along the highway. Efforts are underway to reopen the road. However, as some sections have been damaged, it may take a few days for the highway to fully resume operations,” Prasai said. According to him, although efforts are being made to clear the landslides and reopen the road, the risk of further landslides remains due to continued rainfall. Authorities said weather conditions could therefore affect efforts to reopen the highway.

Authorities urge passengers and freight operators to exercise caution

The disruption has affected passengers and freight vehicles travelling to Jumla and other districts in Karnali. The administration has urged travellers to exercise caution, warning that vehicles could become stranded en route if people travel without first checking the road conditions.

As the risk of landslides is particularly high on the Karnali Highway during the monsoon, travellers have been advised to obtain updated information about road conditions from the concerned authorities before setting out.

Chief District Officer Prasai urged passengers and freight operators to coordinate with the Road Division Office in Jumla before travelling or transporting goods. He said vehicles should operate only after confirming which sections are open to traffic and where obstructions remain.

Machinery and personnel mobilised to clear road

The Road Division Office and other concerned agencies have mobilised necessary machinery and personnel to remove landslides from blocked sections. In addition to clearing debris, repair work is being carried out based on the condition of damaged sections.

However, authorities said the work has been challenging in some locations because sections of the road have been damaged and rocks and soil continue to fall from above. Travellers and drivers have been urged to remain cautious until the road is fully cleared and deemed safe, as the risk of further landslides remains even after traffic resumes.

Landslides have repeatedly disrupted the Karnali Highway during the monsoon in recent years. Traffic has previously been disrupted by landslides at locations including Gaganekhola, Pili, Molpha and S Mode.

According to the Road Division Office, Jumla, several locations along the road from Dahikhola in Dailekh to Jumla district headquarters, Khalanga, are vulnerable to landslides.

Travellers urged to check road conditions before departure

The District Administration Office, Jumla, has urged people travelling along the highway to check the latest road conditions before setting out. Authorities have advised travellers to proceed only in coordination with the concerned agencies, warning that attempting to force vehicles through blocked sections while clearance work is underway could be dangerous.

Freight operators and drivers have also been advised not to operate their vehicles until they receive confirmation that the road has reopened. Authorities have particularly urged long-distance freight operators to obtain advance information, as vehicles may otherwise be forced to remain stranded for extended periods en route.

Chief District Officer Prasai said the Road Division Office, District Administration Office and security agencies are coordinating to restore traffic along the highway. He said road clearance work has been prioritised and regular traffic would resume once conditions return to normal.

title.rendered: Australian PM tells parliament Nepal is not alone in bearing this grief

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has expressed deep sorrow over the devastation caused by the catastrophic floods in Nepal and the Tibet border region of China, saying Nepal is not alone in this hour of disaster.

Addressing the Australian parliament, he confirmed that 36 of the country’s citizens remain unaccounted for after the floods.

“We are hoping for a miracle”

Prime Minister Albanese said that although the floods triggered by the August 26 landslide caused massive destruction on both sides of the border, Nepal bore the brunt of the damage.

“Many have lost loved ones, homes, entire villages, and their livelihoods. With each passing day, the hope of finding those missing grows more like a miracle,” Albanese told parliament. “Thirty-six of our Australian citizens are still missing. The attention of the entire Australian people is right now focused on their families and friends.”

As Nepal observes a national day of mourning today, Prime Minister Albanese also expressed sympathy for those affected through social media.

In his parliamentary address, he said that last Friday he spoke by phone with Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah and conveyed Australia’s deep condolences.

“As Nepal observes national mourning today, I want to tell our Nepali friends, you are not alone in bearing the burden of this grief,” he said.

Praise for community coordination and support

Albanese said the Australian government has been in continuous coordination with the Nepali, Tibetan, and Indian communities in the country. He also urged all Australians not to lose hope, and to keep the affected in their prayers.

Praising the generosity and support shown by the Australian public in the emergency relief appeal for disaster relief, he said, “It sends a powerful message that we can face even the greatest disaster together, united by a shared sense of humanity.”

title.rendered: US Secretary of State calls RSP Chairman; US ready to provide additional assistance to Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

A telephone conversation has taken place between Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chairman Rabi Lamichhane and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

According to information provided by the RSP, during the phone call, US Secretary of State Rubio expressed deep condolences for those who lost their lives in the Bhotekoshi flood and conveyed America’s solidarity with the government and people of Nepal.

In response, Chairman Lamichhane informed him that the Government of Nepal is mobilising all available resources for post-disaster search, rescue, and relief operations.

He assured the US Secretary of State that Nepal remains equally committed to the safety of Nepali citizens as well as all foreign nationals residing in Nepal.

Lamichhane thanked the US government for the assistance provided during this difficult time.

During the telephone conversation, US Secretary of State Rubio expressed America’s commitment that it stands ready, at this hour of disaster, to provide further assistance to the Government of Nepal.
