title.rendered: How Nepal’s gods lose their place, identity and meaning?

content.rendered:
I have been working in heritage repatriation and restitution silently for almost 3 years. It was challenging in many ways, but I learned some important realities that deserve discourse when we talk about the theft of our gods, our history, our arts, and our heritage as a whole.  

As a researcher, I have always found archives to be one of the strongest foundations for any research, as they are for repatriation and restitution as well. As a researcher, I have always considered archives to be one of the strongest foundations of any serious research. The same is true for repatriation and restitution. Yet, sometimes, archives can also create an unexpected irony. A book titled Images of Nepal was published in 1984, and soon after, our deity Laxmi-Narayan was stolen from its home in Patko Tole, Patan. Was this simply a coincidence?

I am not blaming the author in any way. In fact, the book is an important and valuable piece of documentation. But the situation raises a question that is difficult to ignore. Books, photographs, and archival publications are essential for recording and preserving knowledge about heritage. At the same time, when Nepal’s sacred objects are photographed, identified, located, and described in detail, such publications also make information about them accessible to an international audience. In that sense, the very documentation intended to preserve the memory and knowledge of our heritage may, unintentionally, have also made vulnerable objects more visible to those who wished to remove them.

Before we question the security system through a colonised lens, we first need to understand the context in which Nepal’s heritage exists. In Nepal, small shrines and temples are there every other mile or half; it is because we did not believe in hiding our gods; we believed in celebrating them in every way possible by every community. This relationship with heritage is also closely connected to the constitutional protection of culture, including the right to language and culture guaranteed under Article 32 of the Constitution of Nepal.

Nepal have always been in attraction of western world in accordance to the heritage. The way the Western world has never been able to rise from the colonial mindset is the very reason they see our heritage and our gods as commodities, and as objects. Well, this brings me to the question of whether our laws were influenced by the very same mindset. If you look at the Ancient Monuments Act, 1956 A.D, section 2 (b) defines heritage with the particular word “object”.  The word object constrains the rich heritage of indigenous communities that they have been celebrating for generations; the living gods they worship every day are limited to objects of commodification. This problem is not confined to foreign museums. It also requires us to look critically at our own legal vocabulary.

Books such as “Art of Nepal” and “Nepal where the gods are young” have played an important role in introducing Nepal’s heritage to international audiences, but some of the narratives and visual choices in these publications can also be questioned. The cover of these books indicates the enticing of Nepal’s idols. This wrong narrative not only attracts the Western world; it also detaches the community from their heritage and their rituals. I find this much more absurd: propaganda of detaching the community from their gods so that, when our gods are taken away, the community avoids it.  And there persists the idea of tantric intimacy, which in reality does not exist.   

Our gods and history in many ways face an identity crisis. International museums, auction houses and so forth intentionally or unintentionally write the names of artefacts and paintings wrong, which not only misleads the audience but also hides the identity of the very artefact. Sometimes the origin of the artefacts is misleading; we can clearly see it is from Nepal but in the provenance it is written as Tibet or India to create the geographical dilemma.  For example, the National Museum of Asian Art has a painting from Nepal of Girvan Yuddha Birkam Shah but mentions its origin as India. 

Another heart-wrenching fact is that they always misguide our goddess. They have limited our goddess’s power to motherhood, beauty and consort. For example, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) has Nepal’s The Androgynous Form of Shiva and Parvati (Ardhanarishvara), where they have well described Shiva but have constrained Parvati as Shiva’s consort, which is demeaning to Nepal’s heritage. It mentions Siva and Uma; well, it’s either Siva-Parvati or Uma-Maheshwor, not Siva and Uma. 

Another example is the Chakrasamvara and Vajravarahi from C. 1500, which in collection of Philadelphia museum; the title in its provenance is “Chakrasamvara and Vajravarahi in Sexual Embrace”. While describing it depicts as, “dark blue-skinned Chakrasamvara stands locked in sexual embrace with his bright red consort Vajravarahi,” whereas we have always known this only as a union of enlightenment and wisdom. Well, they have admitted that this is the Newa style painting; however, they have left the geographical space empty in their object details. Our gods are taken to the market illegally and they are forced to lose their identity and are given a defaming identity to satisfy the market’s needs. 

Furthermore, the Metropolitan Museum of Art (MET) also has in its collection on the title “Plaque from a Tantric Ritual Apron (Chakrasamvara and Vajravarahi at Centre)”, dated around the 16th century. Another appealing word, “Tantric,” is used to mystify our heritage just to make it more saleable! The main problems arise with descriptions of “tantric intimacy” or other eroticised interpretations that do not reflect the actual beliefs, practices, or meanings understood by the communities themselves. This is another level of misinterpretation. Let us discuss the proved example: The Guardian’s 2026 editorial on the Upton Lovell Shaman may appear unrelated to Nepal, but it offers an important methodological lesson. For years, the high-status Bronze Age burial was assumed to be male. Ancient DNA analysis later identified the individual as female. The mistake did not arise because the evidence clearly proved the person was a man; rather, an assumption about gender and status became embedded in interpretation and was repeated until new evidence forced scholars to reconsider it.     

Institutions should take the same lesson seriously when interpreting cultures that are not their own. Labels can look authoritative even when they contain inherited assumptions. A museum may know the date, material and iconography of a Nepalese piece and still misunderstand its social life. A scholar may correctly identify a tantric motif but overstate sexuality because that is the category most legible to a Western audience. A collector may know the stylistic school while knowing nothing about the shrine from which the image disappeared. Expertise should therefore be accompanied by humility, and interpretation should be open to correction by source communities, ritual specialists and new research.  

The 2023 case involving Italian artist and teacher Tiziano Ronchi at the Taleju Temple area in Bhaktapur shows another dimension: the vulnerability of sacred heritage even in a highly significant protected place. Contemporary Nepali reporting stated that an eyewitness, Suresh Kawan, saw Ronchi apparently using a knife near a metal component of a sacred object and alerted Nepali Army personnel. Ronchi was arrested and investigated under heritage law. He disputed the allegation, and later Italian reporting stated that he was not found guilty of the alleged theft and that the matter concluded with a 50,000-rupee administrative fine. Any fair account must include both the allegation and the outcome.

What matters for the present discussion is the role of local vigilance. A witness noticed conduct that appeared suspicious, questioned it, and informed the guards. Heritage protection often fails when communities are treated as passive beneficiaries while all authority is placed in distant institutions. In reality, the person who walks past the shrine every morning may notice immediately what a centralised office will discover weeks later. Community custodians, residents, priests, guthi members, municipal staff, police and archaeological authorities should therefore be treated as part of one protective network, not as separate worlds. 

While we discuss the international market, we tend to delineate it from the organisations that are actually putting in an effort to help countries like Nepal; one is the Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA), ALIPH, and the Swiss Government in coordination with Namuna Foundation; even the Carabinieri,  Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, are of immense help. It has been a great help for the activists and Namuna Foundation itself to work in the field of heritage crime.  

“Our gods are living” If you wonder what that means, it means that they are living a dignified life within the community they belong to. They are woke up every morning by the community by lighting the diyo, ringing bell as an alarm and then cleaning them, feeding them with water and food, we share our sorrows to our gods, we cry in front of them, we share our happiness, we share secrets that we cannot share to others, this continues for the entire day and even during the evening they are again worshipped and fed. This is why our gods are living and they are meant to live a dignified life followed by a dignified death. We do not believe that our gods should be kept inside the glass box in a museum to be conserved; we are meant to live with them. 

When I see our gods in the museum, I feel like our gods are suffocating; they are inside ventilators. They are waiting for the community to take them back to where they belong. One thing I must clear out is our gods do not belong to museums, private collections or auction houses; they are not for someone’s gratification. They belong to the community. They belong to us, and anyone saying anything beyond that is influenced by the Western colonisation mindset.      

The theft of Nepal’s gods cannot be understood only through police files, customs records, auction catalogues or museum inventories. It is also a story about power: who has the authority to name, interpret, classify, possess and display the sacred life of another community. The market takes the deity physically. The museum can take it conceptually. The law can reduce it administratively. Scholarship can misunderstand it. And all of these processes can occur while the community that lived with the deity is treated as a secondary voice.

Our task is not to reject scholarship, museums, conservation or documentation. We need all of them. But we need them to work differently: with provenance, humility, consent, community knowledge and an understanding that some things called ‘objects’ are still living within relationships. The question is not whether the world may learn from Nepal’s heritage. It should. The question is whether learning requires possession, removal or control over meaning. It does not.

When a god is stolen, a space is left empty in more than a temple. A ritual is interrupted. A neighbourhood changes. Memory is wounded. And when that god returns, the real measure of justice is not that the object has crossed the border back into Nepal. Justice begins when the deity can once again belong, breathe and live within the community from which it was taken.

title.rendered: When everything is gone, where do families start again?

content.rendered:
When the Bhotekoshi River flash-flooded on the morning of August 26, families mainly in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts had little time to run and no time to save anything. Homes, livestock, land documents, bank cheques and ATM cards, and life savings kept in cash at home were gone within minutes.

So far over 1,300 lives have been confirmed lost, thousands remain missing, and more than 17,000 children are now in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. The immediate story, the one filling the news bulletins, is one of rescue and grief. But another crisis is already beginning, and it will unfold over the coming months largely out of the headlines: a household-level financial crisis, in which families with no savings, no insurance, and no documentation to prove what they owned are left to rebuild their lives with nothing to rebuild them on.

Approximately Rs 50 billion in aid support, including domestic and international pledges, has been collected for flood victims to sustain emergency response and support recovery. This aid is essential, and it is saving lives right now. But relief funding has a shelf life measured in weeks, while rebuilding a home, a hectare of farmland, or a small shop takes years.

Nepal’s own experience from the 2015 earthquake is instructive here: many households that lacked savings, insurance, or access to formal credit turned to informal moneylenders to rebuild, often at high interest rates that took years to repay. For many families, the financial struggle began exactly when the aid ended.

The cost of that gap is now being counted, and almost none of it will be paid by an insurer. According to a commentary published by the global insurance rating agency AM Best just days after the disaster, insured losses from this flood are expected to be modest relative to the scale of economic damage, largely because insurance penetration in Nepal remains among the lowest in Asia.

Whatever coverage does exist is concentrated in commercial risk — hydropower plants, infrastructure, cross-border trade — not in the homes, farmland, and small businesses of ordinary families in flood-prone valleys. Even large infrastructure isn’t fully protected: the flood damaged or destroyed 14 hydroelectric projects, wiping out 12 percent of the country’s generating capacity, much of it uninsured. Small shop owners, ordinary farmers, and daily-wage households are in a far weaker position. What’s left for them is debt, migration, or relief that won’t last.

It should not have been a surprise. Nepal has watched this pattern build for years. In 2021, a sudden debris-flow devastated Melamchi in Sindhupalchok. In 2024, heavy monsoon rains killed over 300 people and caused billions of rupees in damage nationwide, including in Kathmandu itself. In 2025, a glacial lake outburst flood in Rasuwagadhi swept away the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge and halted cross-border trade for months. Scientists have long warned that Langtang’s thinning glaciers make further collapses and outburst floods increasingly likely. The physical risk, in other words, was known. What was missing was financial readiness to absorb the shock, at both household and national level.

The case for financial preparedness literacy is not simply that disasters happen. It is that in developing countries like Nepal, a handful of structural weaknesses amplify disaster risk into something far more damaging than the disaster itself. Three stand out. First, the informal economy: a majority of Nepali households earn and hold wealth outside the formal financial system in the form of cash, land, livestock, or unregistered savings groups that vanish or lose all value the moment a flood hits. Second, the near-absent insurance penetration described above means the shock is absorbed almost entirely by the household itself, with no one to share the loss. Third, poor formal credit access pushes desperate families toward informal moneylenders at predatory rates, precisely when they are least able to negotiate. These are common features of most climate-exposed developing countries.

A household that has never been shown how insurance works, how to access formal credit, how to protect documents, or how to build even a small emergency reserve cannot reasonably be expected to make sound financial decisions in the middle of a crisis. That is not a failure of the household, but rather a failure of preparation. This is precisely what financial preparedness literacy addresses: building something more structural, well before the disaster. Call it the SHIEL approach: five pillars that turn a vague call for “financial literacy” into something a government or a cooperative can actually build.

  • Savings and community reserves. Grow cooperative and community-based emergency savings schemes, so households enter a disaster with a buffer they built themselves.
  • Hazard insurance for households. Expand affordable micro-insurance for homes, crops, and small businesses in known high-risk zones — not just hydropower and infrastructure.
  • Information and document protection. Help families digitize land records and identification before disaster strikes, so financial identity survives even when the paper doesn’t.
  • Efficient access to relief. Simplify relief packages and government’s compensation schemes so households can claim them without hassles.
  • Literacy and digital access. Teach basic budgeting and safe borrowing, backed by mobile savings that work when banks and roads don’t.

We can learn from international experiences. For instance, in Bangladesh, the long-running Cyclone Preparedness Program pairs early-warning systems with community-level organization, including guidance on protecting essential documents and valuables before a storm — a low-cost intervention that has measurably reduced both loss of life and post-disaster financial disruption over decades. Kerala (India) took a different piece of the puzzle: after catastrophic flooding in 2018, the state government and its banks introduced loan moratoriums and restructured repayment terms for affected borrowers, buying families time instead of pushing them into default. Likewise, in the Philippines, microinsurance distributed through cooperatives has given even low-income households modest payouts after disasters without depending on ad hoc charity.

Experts agree on one thing: glacial collapse and monsoon flooding are not going away in Nepal’s mountains, and a warming climate may only make them more frequent. Aid will always have a role in the first days after a disaster like this one, and no one should begrudge the families of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading the support reaching them now. But the real question is: what happens after the aid runs out? A model built around handouts leaves households waiting, after every disaster, for someone else to decide their financial future. We should build one around financial preparedness literacy instead, so that households walk into the next flood already knowing how to act.

title.rendered: Is Nepal’s climate money reaching the ground?

content.rendered:
Nepal is right to demand climate justice. The harder question is what happens to the money once it arrives in Kathmandu. On the morning of 26 August, a mass of rock and ice came off Langtang and a wave went down the Bhotekoshi River. It destroyed the Rasuwagadhi border post, bridges, hydropower stations and long stretches of the road to Tibet.

By the disaster authorities on September 7, 1342 people were confirmed dead in Nepal, and 4,996 were still listed as missing. Those figures are provisional, and they are still moving. Hold on to that shape, because it is the shape of the whole problem. In this country, climate impacts travel. Climate finance does not.

Nepal’s climate finance gap

Nepal has contributed only marginally to the emissions driving global warming; the figure our own government uses in its submissions to the UN climate process is about 0.027 per cent of the global total. Warming is increasing the instability of glaciers, permafrost and high-mountain slopes across the Himalaya, and while scientists are still establishing the precise trigger at Langtang, the direction of the risk is not in dispute.

Nepal is right to press that case at COP31 in Antalya in November. But there is a second question, and this one belongs entirely to us. When climate money does arrive, how far down the hill does it actually get? Our National Adaptation Plan is specific about what we need: 64 priority programmes across nine sectors, costed at USD 47.4 billion to 2050, of which Nepal expects to raise only USD 1.5 billion domestically.

The annual requirement, it states, is roughly USD 2.1 billion. Set that against the Green Climate Fund’s (GCF) own country page for Nepal, which lists six projects and USD 157 million in total approved financing, plus USD 5.9 million in readiness support. Approved, not disbursed. And one of those six is Nepal’s share of a multi-country regional programme rather than a project here.

The GCF is one fund among several. We also draw on the Adaptation Fund, the Global Environment Facility, bilateral partners and the new loss and damage arrangements, so the full picture is larger than that. But when the single biggest dedicated climate fund has approved, across its entire Nepal portfolio since 2019, slightly less than what our own plan says we need in a single month, the scale of the shortfall is not really arguable.

Volume, though, is the part Nepal cannot fix alone. The part we can fix is what happens next, and here our first GCF project deserves close study, precisely because it is not a failure. Building a Resilient Churia Region was approved by the GCF Board in November 2019 and became effective in May 2020. It carries a USD 39.3 million grant with government co-financing on top. FAO is the accredited entity; the Ministry of Forests and Environment executes it. It spans 26 river systems and is designed to work through some 750 community-based organisations and user groups. This is precisely the architecture the country says it wants. The GCF project page currently shows it around 60 per cent disbursed, running to 2027, after two opening fiscal years given over to preparation.

None of that is a scandal. An eight-year timeline for landscape restoration at this scale is normal, and arguably it is what careful implementation looks like. That is exactly the uncomfortable part. From board approval to results on the ground at scale, our best-functioning climate programme takes the better part of a decade.

Meanwhile, in July 2025, the GCF approved USD 36.1 million to protect lives and assets from glacial lake outburst floods in Nepal’s glacial river basins. Thirteen months later, the water came down the Bhotekoshi. No project could have prevented what happened in Rasuwa, and it would be dishonest to imply otherwise.

But the mismatch of clocks is real. Hazards here arrive in minutes. Our delivery systems are assembled in years. A forest would not have stopped a rock-and-ice collapse at 5,000 metres, and saying so plainly protects the argument that follows. Most of what climate change costs Nepal is not a cryosphere failure. It is the slower accumulation of monsoon landslides on cut and destabilised mid-hill slopes, gullies eating terraced farmland, springs that fail in March instead of May, a fire season that runs longer each year, riverbanks advancing on settlements. Those are losses that forests moderate.

For 15 years we have argued about our forests mainly in the language of carbon, through REDD+, registries and verification protocols. Carbon is a revenue conversation. Adaptation is the conversation our hills are actually having. But the claim has to be made precisely, because forests do not substitute for engineering.

Eco-engineering trials in the Panchase region tested what actually holds a failing road slope: drainage and civil works combined with deep-rooted vegetation, neither element sufficient on its own. Forests belong inside Nepal’s adaptation infrastructure alongside culverts and retaining walls, budgeted the same way, with a maintenance line and someone answerable for whether they still function in five years.

The most urgent place to apply that thinking is the road network. Nepal has more than 6,600 rural roads running to nearly 60,000 kilometres, much of it bulldozer cut without drainage or slope stabilisation, and peer-reviewed work in Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences has documented these informal roads as a significant and under-recognised driver of slope failure in the middle hills. Adaptation planning that does not reach the bulldozer is not adaptation planning.

Need to measure climate finance by results, not spending

What Nepal does not need is to invent a way of moving money to communities. More than 22,000 community forest user groups manage some 2.3 million hectares, about a third of the national forest estate, on behalf of close to three million households, with elected executives, approved operational plans, bank accounts and audits. Community forestry is not perfect, and pretending otherwise weakens the case rather than strengthening it.

Elite capture is real. Some groups distribute benefits unevenly. Women, Dalit and Indigenous members are not always meaningfully represented in decisions despite formal quotas. Capacity differs enormously between a well-run group in the Terai and a struggling one in a remote mountain ward, and very few user groups today would meet the fiduciary, procurement and safeguards standards that international climate funds require. But those are governance problems with known remedies. They are arguments for investing in a 40-year-old local institution until it meets the standard, not for routing around it and then complaining that the last mile in a mountain country is too difficult.

The 2019 Climate Change Policy commits at least 80 per cent of international climate finance to implementation at the local level, and it remains Nepal’s signature contribution to the global debate. The Climate Finance Mobilisation Procedure issued this February, which names the Ministry of Finance as focal point, defines implementing entities across all three tiers of government and opens eligibility to NGOs and private firms, is the first serious attempt to give that commitment machinery.

Yet notice how loosely the commitment is stated in practice. It is described variously as 80 per cent of international climate finance, 80 per cent of the climate budget, and 80 per cent of the funds of any climate project reaching the local community. Those are three different obligations, and compliance with all of them is demonstrated the same way as budget coded to local governments.

It is an accounting category, not a condition at a place. Follow the chain: ministry, province, palika, user group, forest, household. Every link reports upward on money moved. Almost none report on what changed. We can say how much was approved. We can rarely say how many hectares of degraded slope were planted and survived three monsoons, how many springs recovered their flow, how many households did not have to sell land after a bad year. Fixing that does cost something: baselines, field verification, remote sensing and community monitoring. But it does not require another institution. It requires the institutions we already have to measure something different.

So contract user groups as implementing entities rather than beneficiaries, and fund the fiduciary strengthening that makes them eligible. Build a permanent, staffed project preparation facility, because we forfeit finance we qualify for whenever nobody at provincial level has the time to write a bankable proposal.

Plan forestry alongside agriculture, water, disaster risk reduction and road construction instead of apart from them. Put maintenance into every restoration budget and measure survival at year five rather than seedlings at year one. And require every programme to answer four questions: where, for whom, what physically changed, and is that place measurably safer than it was. That is the moment to write the commitment so that it is measured where the money lands rather than where it is coded. Nepal’s resilience will not be settled by the size of the number we bring home from Antalya. It will be settled by how much of that number is still moving when it reaches the last village on the last ridge.

title.rendered: Bidur Municipality to provide Rs 10,000 rent aid to flood-displaced families

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 7

Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot has decided to provide Rs 10,000 per family as immediate rental assistance to residents displaced by the devastating floods that swept into the Trishuli River through the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

A meeting of the Bidur Municipal Executive held on Sunday decided to provide the assistance to municipal residents whose homes have become uninhabitable due to the floods so that they can rent accommodation.

The municipality will also distribute relief materials, including food, clothing, kitchen sets and hygiene kits, to affected families.

The municipality has also warned landlords against taking advantage of the disaster by increasing rents.

It said anyone found charging more than the prevailing or customary rental rates for rooms or houses will face strict action in accordance with the law.

content.rendered:

The price of gold has fallen by Rs 2,400 per tola in Nepal on Monday.

The Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association has fixed the price of gold at Rs 301,900 per tola for today. It was priced at Rs 304,300 per tola on the previous trading day.

The price of silver has also declined by Rs 35 per tola.

Silver, which was traded at Rs 4,725 per tola on the previous day, has been fixed at Rs 4,690 per tola today.

title.rendered: Indira Rana Magar meets UK House of Commons Deputy Speaker

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Former Deputy Speaker of Nepal’s House of Representatives Indira Rana Magar has met Caroline Nokes, Deputy Speaker of the UK House of Commons, in London.

The meeting focused on Nepal-UK relations and the devastating floods that have affected Nepal.

During the meeting at the House of Commons, Rana and Nokes discussed the longstanding relationship between Nepal and the UK, including the contribution of Nepali Gurkha soldiers to Britain. They also spoke about the flood disaster in Nepal and its impact.

Nokes expressed sadness over the situation in Nepal and conveyed the UK’s sympathy over the loss and devastation caused by the floods.

The two also discussed the exchange of parliamentary practices.

Rabindra Jung Lamichhane, a London-based fashion entrepreneur and philanthropist who serves as CEO of Gini London Ltd and R Famous Ltd (trading as Ravi Famous), was also present at the meeting.

Rana also met with other members of the House of Commons during her time in London and discussed Nepal’s flood situation and bilateral relations.

title.rendered: Volcanic eruption strands 170,000 passengers in Indonesia

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Around 170,000 passengers have been stranded at eight airports in Indonesia following a volcanic eruption. Flights from the affected airports have been temporarily suspended due to volcanic ash.

Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in the capital, Jakarta, was the first to be closed early Sunday after volcanic ash from Anak Krakatau was detected in the airspace around the airport.

According to Indonesia’s Ministry of Transportation, 1,558 flights have been delayed. The airports are expected to remain closed until 9 am local time on Monday.

Officials said the volcanic eruption began late Friday night. Continuous seismic activity was subsequently recorded in the surrounding areas, while fountains of lava and powerful explosions were heard.

Two additional eruptions occurred early Sunday morning. The Ministry of Transportation said flights to and from Singapore were among the most affected by the disruption.

Flights to other international destinations, including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur, have also been affected.

title.rendered: Rain expected to continue in Sudurpaschim for 3 more days

content.rendered:
Sudurpaschim, September 7

Rainfall is continuing in various parts of Sudurpaschim, including Kailali, and is expected to continue for another three days, according to the Office of Hydrology and Meteorology in Attariya.

The weather is expected to remain generally cloudy across the mountains, hills and Terai from today through September 9. Moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning is likely in several places during this period. Heavy rainfall has also been forecast in some parts of the hills and Terai, prompting authorities to urge people to remain vigilant.

Light rain is expected in the mountains this afternoon and tonight. Some areas of the hills and Terai are likely to receive moderate rainfall, while one or two places in the hills and Terai could experience heavy rain, according to the office.

Although rainfall is expected to ease on Tuesday, the weather will not completely clear. Several areas of the mountains and hills, as well as some parts of the Terai, are likely to receive moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning.

On Tuesday night, moderate rainfall is possible in a few places across all three regions.

title.rendered: Nepal did little to cause the climate crisis. Now it is paying for its consequences.

content.rendered:
On the morning of August 26, a slab of ice and rock broke away from roughly 5,200 metres on the flank of the Langtang massif, on the border Nepal shares with Tibet, and fell some 1,200 vertical metres into the valley of the Lhende Khola.

Seismometers registered the impact as the equivalent of a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. The debris dammed the river, then gave way. Downstream at Galchhi, the Trishuli rose about nine metres in thirty minutes, a wall of what one researcher called liquid concrete, travelling roughly a hundred kilometres through Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

By September 6, Nepali authorities had recovered 1,342 bodies. Some 4,996 people were still missing; 13,391 had been rescued.  It is Nepal’s deadliest disaster since the 2015 earthquake.

The event was not a glacial lake outburst flood, the hazard Nepal has spent two decades preparing for. It was the failure of frozen ground itself. Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado Boulder, describes high-altitude permafrost as the glue holding these slopes together. That glue is thawing: temperatures on Langtang Lirung have climbed since the 1980s, and four of the last five summers rank among the warmest recorded there.

The mountain gave notice

The most uncomfortable finding of the past week is that the collapse was visible in advance. A rapid hazard assessment by the HiRISK team, using Planet and Landsat 9 imagery, found indicators from August 24, two days out: the glacier’s surface changed, meltwater ran brown, water within the ice accelerated, and a crack propagated into the bedrock slope behind it.

No one was watching. “No early warning system for glacier-related hazards had been set up in the affected area,” the assessment concluded. Jakob Steiner, a geologist and co-author, put it bluntly: “We can’t say, oh my God, nobody knew.”

The alerting failed as well. Text warnings did go out on August 26. “People received SMS alerts about the event on the 26th,” said Saswata Sanyal, who manages disaster risk reduction at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development. “But people didn’t know what exactly to do with the warning or where to safely evacuate to.” Recipients read a routine monsoon notice and behaved accordingly.

The physics leaves almost no margin: settlements here get five to thirty minutes between detection and impact; a window only automated alerting can use. More than 200 Himalayan glacial lakes are rated high risk, and coverage is sparse. But the ice that failed was not a monitored lake at all, which is the deeper problem: Nepal’s hazard map was drawn around the wrong mechanism. The glacier also sits partly in Chinese territory, where no permanent mechanism for real-time hazard data exists.

Inside the tunnels

More than 500 of the missing were registered hydropower workers across nine projects with hundreds more informal laborers and truckers unaccounted for along the corridor. At Trishuli 3A, 42 are unaccounted for in a headrace tunnel more than four kilometres long. At Chilime, rescuers pushing into a 250-metre tunnel reached 130 metres before chest-high sludge stopped them. One survivor estimated that of roughly 1,000 workers at nearby sites, about 100 got out. Brigadier General Ujwal Rana warned that clearing the tunnels “may not even be completed in three to four months.”

These were mostly men working weeks from home and remitting wages to hill villages. After the 2021 Chamoli disaster in India and now this one, deep tunneling beneath thawing permafrost in a valley with a documented flood history is a foreseeable risk, yet Nepal has no regime for holding developers liable for such siting decisions and no compensation standard for the families.

The arithmetic of blame

Here is what makes this a story about somebody else’s power plants.

Nepal emitted 18.8 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2024, or 0.05 percent of the global total. Its cumulative contribution since 1850 is about 232 million tons, 0.013 percent of the 1,845 billion tons humanity has emitted in that span. Ten countries account for roughly 68 percent of the total. Nepal’s entire industrial history amounts to less than two days of current global emissions.

Who put the carbon there: cumulative fossil CO2, 1850 to 2024

World total 1850 to 2024: 1,844.6 billion tonnes. Calculated from the Global Carbon Project and Our World in Data series (ref. 33).

 What the water cost

Nepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Wagle, initially put losses above $4 billion; later estimates have run toward $7 billion. Reuters reported that rebuilding could consume up to a tenth of an economy of roughly $50 billion.

One flood, one balance sheet

Toll figures from Nepali authorities as of Sept. 6, 2026, and still moving. Generation losses are disputed.

Generation losses are still being counted, with published tallies ranging from about 280 to 550 megawatts of operating capacity destroyed or offline, plus roughly 390 megawatts under construction. In a system of some 4,300 megawatts that is more than 90 percent hydro, that is close to a tenth of the country’s electricity.

The timing is cruel. Nepal became a net electricity exporter in fiscal 2025-26, earning about 18.75 billion rupees, roughly $142 million, and its 2025 Energy Development Roadmap targets 15,000 megawatts of exports by 2035. The flood reversed the direction of the wire: flows to India have fallen from a monsoon peak of 950 to 1,000 megawatts to about 400, and Kathmandu has asked Delhi for advance import approvals from September. India’s grid absorbs the loss easily, since the Dhalkebar to Muzaffarpur link alone carries 1,000 megawatts. What is a rounding error in one grid erases an export revenue stream and creates an import bill in the other, in the same quarter.

The flood also severed Nepal’s only functioning road to China. The Rasuwagadhi and Gyirong crossing handled roughly $600 million a year, close to 30 percent of all China-to-Nepal trade; its customs complex, rebuilt after a July 2025 flood, is again under five feet of mud, and that earlier closure took five to six months. Beijing has offered emergency cash, supplies and two teams of tunnel-rescue specialists, without publishing a figure. Nepal is thus receiving help from the world’s first- and third-largest cumulative emitters as aid and electricity sales, while the mechanisms meant to deliver compensation as an obligation remain unfunded.

Madagascar: the same equation, a different ocean

Four thousand miles southwest, Madagascar runs identical arithmetic. Its 32 million people emitted 4.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide in 2024, 0.006 percent of cumulative global emissions and, by the World Bank’s accounting, 0.09 percent of current greenhouse gases. In two decades, it has absorbed 35 cyclones, eight major floods and five severe droughts. This year brought two cyclones eleven days apart.

Madagascar cyclone season 2026, so far

Source: UNICEF Madagascar cyclone response plan, February 2026 (ref. 36).

The World Bank projects that without adaptation, climate change will cut Madagascar’s economy by 5.8 percent by 2050 and push 1.68 million more people into poverty; the country needs $3.37 billion by 2030 for urgent adaptation and mobilised $416 million in 2020. The damage is cumulative: a cyclone in January takes the roof, a delayed rainy season in March takes the harvest, and the household sells livestock, then land, then sends someone north for work.

Madagascar also cautions against easy storytelling. When famine gripped the Grand Sud in 2021 and was called the world’s first climate-change famine, World Weather Attribution scientists found a roughly one-in-135-year drought whose likelihood human warming had not significantly increased; poverty, subsistence farming, pandemic restrictions and pests did the killing. A 2024 Harvard-led study found an anthropogenic fingerprint in the delayed onset of the rainy season. Both point the same way: vulnerability converts weather into catastrophe, and vulnerability is a product of history and income.

The funds that cannot pay

Global temperatures in 2025 averaged 1.44 degrees Celsius above the 1850 to 1900 baseline, and the last eleven years are the warmest in the 176-year record. Over three decades, Germanwatch counts more than 830,000 deaths and $4.5 trillion in direct damage from extreme weather. Two institutions are supposed to answer for that. Neither is close.

The Green Climate Fund is the largest dedicated climate fund in existence, and after eleven years it has approved $20.4 billion across 359 projects in 134 countries, disbursing about a third of it. Its second replenishment, covering 2024 to 2027, drew $10.64 billion in pledges, of which $9.64 billion was confirmed after Washington rescinded its outstanding commitments.

The bigger fund, and what it delivers

Portfolio figures read from the fund on Sept. 3, 2026.

The fund’s procedures are part of the problem. Accrediting a national institution has taken about 30 months on average, and some adaptation approvals have stretched beyond four years, according to Mukesh Ghimire, a researcher who previously coordinated Nepal’s climate fund proposals. The share of money flowing through developing-country institutions rather than international intermediaries has been stuck near 20 percent for a decade.

The distribution is the more awkward finding. The largest portfolios belong to India, at about $1 billion, Brazil at $756 million and Indonesia at $612 million, with Mongolia, Kenya, South Africa and Bangladesh each between $460 million and $500 million: substantial economies with the capacity to prepare bankable proposals. Nepal has been approved for $157 million across six projects in eleven years, Madagascar for $191 million. Set against a single morning in Rasuwa, Nepal’s lifetime receipts from the world’s flagship climate fund amount to between 2 and 4 percent of the flood damage.

The younger instrument is smaller still. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, created at COP27, has attracted $788.8 million in pledges since 2022, holds about $407 million and caps its startup phase at $250 million, with individual projects limited to $20 million. Estimated annual needs in developing countries run to about $395 billion.

The smaller fund

Sources: refs. 48 and 3. Analysts warn the fund could be exhausted by 2027.

On August 31, Finance Minister Wagle and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary asked the fund’s board co-chairs for emergency financing rather than waiting until December. “The scale of the damage caused by the floods is far beyond Nepal’s domestic resources,” said Maheshwar Dhakal, who heads the government’s climate change division. Even the fund’s largest possible grant would cover half of one percent of the low-end damage estimate, and of 176 proposals submitted, 129 are still stuck at eligibility screening.

So the reconstruction will be borrowed. Nepal’s public debt reached 2.975 trillion rupees by mid-July 2026, or 45.1 percent of GDP, with debt service at 5.85 percent. The mechanics deserve attention: of the 300 billion rupees added to the stock last year, more than half came not from new borrowing but from currency depreciation. Nepal’s obligations are in dollars and its earnings in rupees, so the debt grows on its own. Add several billion dollars of reconstruction loans and the arithmetic stops working.

There is now a legal alternative to waiting. On July 23, 2025, the International Court of Justice held that a state’s failure to take appropriate measures to prevent foreseeable climate harm can constitute an internationally wrongful act, that 1.5 degrees is the operative legal standard, that remedies include cessation, restitution and compensation, and that scientific evidence permits emissions to be attributed to individual states, subject to a sufficiently direct and certain causal nexus. Advisory opinions do not create a cashier’s window, and causation for a single ice avalanche is a formidable evidentiary problem. But the opinion converts loss-and-damage finance from a request into a claim, and it is the first instrument here that does not depend on a donor’s mood.

Build back better, or build somewhere else

The hardest question facing Kathmandu is not how to rebuild but whether to rebuild in the same valleys. Nepal’s development model routes national income through high-head hydropower in steep, glaciated, seismically active terrain, precisely the terrain that thawing permafrost is destabilising. Building for that risk is affordable: engineers estimate resilient design, through underground powerhouses, redundancy and evacuation protocols, adds 10 to 12 percent to construction cost. That is cheap insurance against losing a plant outright, and it was not bought.

Some answers are visible. Multi-hazard assessment should precede licensing rather than follow it, after years of what one environmental economist called haphazard permissions issued without accounting for glacial hazards. Shree Raj Shakya of Tribhuvan University argues the export-first strategy needs rethinking in favour of domestic supply. And diversification is now a resilience argument as much as an economic one: solar supplies under 3 percent of Nepal’s electricity but could reach 20 percent as costs fall, dispersed across the country rather than concentrated in a few vulnerable gorges.

None of this is free, which returns the argument to where it started. Nepal will pay for warning systems it should not have to fund alone, resilient turbines it can barely afford, and reconstruction loans denominated in the currency of a country that emits a hundred times more carbon per head. The question the Belem timetable leaves open is not whether the polluters can pay. It is whether they intend to before the ice moves again.

title.rendered: Traditional Falo festival begins in Mustang’s Thini village

content.rendered:
Mustang, September 7

The traditional Falo festival celebrated by the local Thakali community began on Sunday in Thini village of Gharpajhong Rural Municipality-3 in Mustang.

The festival is known as “Falo” in the local Thakali language because it is celebrated every year during the month of Bhadra (August–September).

Thini village, regarded as the ancestral homeland of the Thakali community, is considered significant for its historical, religious and cultural heritage. According to residents, the Falo festival has been celebrated in the village for generations, dating back to the time when a Thakali king ruled the area.

Various religious and cultural activities are held in Thini village over the two-day festival. On the eve of the festival, village lamas perform a special nature worship ceremony, after which residents receive their blessings.

As the lamas leave for the nature worship ceremony, local women traditionally bid them farewell by presenting khadas and placing flower garlands around them as a mark of respect.

According to local lama Shyam Prasad Thakali, the Thakali community worships the mountains as manifestations of the gods during the Falo festival. He said the nature worship ceremony is performed with prayers for the well-being of the village, protection from diseases, a good harvest, protection from natural disasters and peace throughout the world.

Recalling the increasing frequency of disasters in recent years and the heavy loss of life and property caused by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa, Thakali said prayers are also offered during the ceremony for such disasters not to happen again.

On the eve of the Falo festival, residents of Thini village travelled on horseback to the Namkhulek area to perform the nature worship ceremony. The village women traditionally bid farewell to the lamas participating in the festival with due respect.

The group that left for the nature worship ceremony will return to the village after two days. According to residents, the Falo festival will formally begin only after their return.

The festival features cultural performances and traditional dances, including the yak dance, Jogi dance and Tamaya dance. The two-day festival will conclude according to religious rituals and traditional practices.

title.rendered: Electricity restored to 99% of households in Dhading

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation has made significant progress in restoring electricity to areas severely affected by the recent floods.

Nearly all households in Dhading (99.8%) and a substantial majority in Nuwakot (96.7%) have had their electricity supply restored despite adverse weather conditions. Both districts were severely affected by the Bhotekoshi flash floods on August 26 and their aftermath.

A dedicated technical team from the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) is actively working to restore power to the remaining households in Rasuwa.

Search and rescue operations are currently underway at several hydropower facilities, including Upper Trishuli-3A and 3B, Chilime and Rasuwagadhi. To facilitate these efforts, essential equipment such as mud pumps and generators has been airlifted to the affected sites.

Rescue teams have successfully accessed the Rasuwagadhi powerhouse, while debris removal is ongoing at various locations. At Upper Trishuli-3B, mini excavators are being used to clear debris.

In addition to immediate restoration efforts, the Ministry is prioritising long-term energy solutions by dispatching solar power systems to the affected areas.

So far, 13 solar power systems for offices and 500 household systems have been sent, with plans to distribute additional systems to 1,268 households in Rasuwa.

The Ministry has coordinated the transportation of the solar systems by helicopter to the affected areas.

title.rendered: At least 5 killed as Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport

content.rendered:
Miami, September 7

At least five people were killed and five others injured after an Amazon cargo plane ran off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday and struck vehicles on a nearby road, authorities said.

The Prime Air aircraft overran the runway at around 2pm after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It crossed a road used by warehouse workers and businesses surrounding the airport before coming to a stop near two semi-trucks.

Five people were killed, while three of the injured were in critical condition. Two others were taken to hospital with less serious injuries, Miami-Dade County officials said.

It was not immediately clear whether the pilots survived or whether all those killed were inside vehicles when the plane crashed.

Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said the pilot and copilot were trapped in the cockpit following the crash, while several people were trapped in vehicles. Firefighters also had to rescue a person trapped beneath a vehicle.

The crash sent thick black smoke into the sky and halted flights at the busy airport for much of Sunday afternoon.

Around 200 emergency personnel responded to the scene. Firefighters found the aircraft engulfed in heavy flames and smoke from what authorities described as a complex engine-compartment fire.

Specialised airport firefighting units used foam to extinguish the blaze. Crews were still dealing with a fuel leak from the aircraft several hours after the crash.

Images from the scene showed the cargo plane lying beside a roadway near two semi-trucks. The aircraft appeared to have come to rest on its belly and remained largely intact despite the fire.

The cause of the crash had not been determined. It was also unclear whether weather conditions contributed to the accident.

The National Weather Service reported thunderstorms and wind gusts of up to 30 mph (48 kph) in the area around the time of the crash.

title.rendered: Narayangadh-Muglin road to face partial closures from today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

The Narayangadh-Muglin road section will face partial closures from this morning as authorities carry out landslide prevention work at Tuin Khola.

According to a notice issued by the Chitwan District Administration, soil-cutting work will be carried out under the Tuiin Khola project while repair work is underway at Krishnabhir in Dhading.

The notice said the authorities will use the period during which traffic remains affected by the Krishnabhir road repairs to carry out the work at Tuiin Khola.

The work will continue until the road repairs at Krishnabhir are completed and traffic resumes normally.

Authorities will periodically stop traffic to clear loose soil and debris from the upper section above Tuiin Khola, where landslides have been occurring frequently.

The Narayangadh-Muglin road will be open for traffic during the following periods:

  • 8:00am to 8:30am
  • 10:30am to 11:00am
  • 1:00pm to 1:30pm
  • 3:50pm to 4:00pm
  • After 6:00pm

Traffic will be stopped at the site outside these designated periods to allow the work to proceed, according to the administration.

title.rendered: The dogs helping rescuers search through the rubble

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Rocky and Jumbo have had a difficult few days.

The two Nepal Police canines have been working alongside their handlers in Timure and Ghattikhola in Rasuwa, areas badly damaged by the Bhotekoshi flood that struck on August 26.

Rocky, a Belgian Shepherd, and Jumbo, a German Shepherd, were deployed with Assistant Sub-Inspector Krishna Sen and Senior Head Constable Narayan Prasad Devkota on the very day the flood hit.

Since then, they have been searching through the damaged areas, following scents that can lead rescuers to places they cannot easily see or reach.

Their work has helped locate two bodies and a body part.

“The canines were fully equipped and deployed on the very day the flood came. They have proved to be very effective,” said Deputy Inspector General Abinarayan Kafle, central spokesperson for Nepal Police.

Rocky and Jumbo are trained in search and rescue and were brought in from the Nepal Police Canine Office in Kathmandu. But they are not the only police dogs working through the aftermath of the flood.

Three days after the disaster, on August 29, another team travelled from Kathmandu with two Labradors, Leo and Kalu.

Five handlers—Sub-Inspector Sudeep Thapa Magar, Head Constable Kishunlal Chaudhary, Head Constable Rishibahadur Thapa, Constable Sachin GC and Constable Sajindra Tamang—were deployed with them.

Leo and Kalu have been working across a wide stretch of the affected area, from Bidur, Archale and Shantibazar to Mailung Hydropower, Dhunge, Devighat, Betrawati, Bhainse and Battar.

At the employee quarters of Mailung Hydropower-3B, they helped locate a small body part. At Battar Solar House, they found part of a palm, according to police officials.

On the same day, another canine team was sent out by the Canine Branch of the Bagmati Province Police Office.

Deepsi, a German Shepherd, was deployed with four handlers—Assistant Sub-Inspector Ramesh Bahadur Singh, Senior Head Constable Anoj Adhikari, Head Constable Lok Bahadur Thapa and Assistant Head Constable Sagar Sinjali.

The team, operating from Chitwan, searched around the Narayani Bridge, Devghat and as far as Damouli Golaghat.

Deepsi helped locate two bodies at Damouli Golaghat, according to records at Nepal Police headquarters.

Together, five Nepal Police canines and 10 handlers have been deployed in the search and rescue operation following the Rasuwa flood.

The dogs work differently from the people searching beside them.

They are trained to locate bodies through smell. When a dog detects something, it signals its handler, who then decides how to proceed with the search.

That can make a difference in the kind of terrain left behind by a flood—places where debris is unstable, openings are too small for a person to enter, or something is buried beneath the surface.

The dogs can squeeze through small openings and use their powerful sense of smell to indicate whether someone is present.

Their signals have led rescuers to buried bodies.

The Armed Police Force has also deployed its own canine teams across the affected areas.

According to APF spokesperson Deputy Inspector General Netra Bahadur Karki, seven APF canines are working in the flood-affected areas: one each in Timure, Devighat, Betrawati, Trishuli Bazaar and Dhading, and two in Chitwan.

Fourteen handlers have been deployed with them.

The APF says its canines have helped locate and recover 19 buried bodies. Excavation teams found the bodies at locations indicated by the dogs.

Taken together, the canines of Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force have helped locate 26 bodies and body parts.

For the dogs, the work comes with its own limits. After working for a certain period, they have to be given time to rest before they can continue searching.

The handlers watch them closely, following their movements and acting on their signals.

It is work Nepal’s security forces have relied on before.

Police have used canines in search-and-rescue operations on numerous occasions, including after the 2015 earthquake.

The Nepal Army’s canines have not been deployed in the current operation. According to Army spokesperson Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, they have not been deployed in coordination with Nepal Police and the APF, although they remain on standby.

The search has also brought dogs from outside Nepal. A South Korean rescue team arrived with five canines and is working in the affected areas. Foreign rescue teams also brought canines to Nepal during the earthquake.

Nepal’s security forces have been training and using canines for decades.

The Nepal Army has maintained canines under a dedicated establishment since 1999, using them in search and rescue as well as for detecting explosives. The Armed Police Force has maintained canines since 2006 and has an establishment for 30 dogs, including those used for patrols at border points.

Nepal Police began keeping canines in 1970 after bringing two trained dogs from Malaysia. Since then, police dogs have been used in investigations, search and rescue, and the detection of explosives and drugs.

Some Nepali canines have also travelled abroad, serving in United Nations missions in conflict-affected countries.

But for Rocky, Jumbo, Leo, Kalu and Deepsi, the assignment at the moment is much closer to home.

The flood has left large parts of Rasuwa and surrounding areas buried beneath debris, and rescuers are still searching.

The dogs move through the rubble with their handlers close behind.

They stop, sniff and move on.

And when one of them finally gives a signal, the search team knows where to look.

title.rendered: National mourning observed today for victims of Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

Nepal is observing a day of national mourning today in memory of those who lost their lives in the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26.

A Cabinet meeting held on September 3 decided to observe a national day of mourning in honour of those who died in the unprecedentedly severe flooding in the Bhotekoshi River.

The national flag will be flown at half-mast today at government offices across Nepal, as well as at Nepali embassies and diplomatic missions abroad.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 1,342 people have so far died in the devastating floods, while 4,996 people remain missing.

A total of 6,083 people have been injured, while 21,465 security personnel have been mobilised for search, rescue and relief operations.

Authorities have rescued 13,391 people from the flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: Arnold Dix calls Nepal tunnel rescue his toughest challenge yet

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

International tunnel rescue expert Professor Arnold Dix, who gained global attention for leading the successful rescue of 41 workers trapped inside India’s Silkyara tunnel, has described Nepal’s ongoing efforts to rescue people from flood-hit tunnels as the toughest test of his career.

The Australian geologist and engineer, who is providing technical advice and field leadership for the rescue operations in Nepal, shared his experience and a message on social media on Monday morning.

“I have never experienced anything like this,” Dix wrote.

Dix said the situation in Nepal was fundamentally different from previous rescue operations, with several potential rescue sites being dealt with simultaneously.

“Here in Nepal, we are facing something I have never experienced before. This is not just one rescue. There are multiple potential rescues happening at the same time, in different locations, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved,” he wrote.

A test of duty and ‘dharma’

Dix reflected on the 2023 rescue operation at India’s Silkyara tunnel, where 41 workers remained trapped underground for 17 days.

“At Silkyara, there were 41 people underground and we had what seemed like an almost impossible responsibility to bring them home alive. We passed that test together,” he wrote.

“But passing one great test does not mean the test is over. Perhaps it means we have been entrusted with an even greater one.”

Dix contrasted the Western idea of “duty” with the Eastern philosophical concept of “dharma”.

In the Western tradition, he said, duty means doing what is right even when success is uncertain. Eastern traditions, he added, offer another powerful perspective through the concept of dharma.

“The test is not simply whether we succeed or fail. The real question is whether, as the path becomes harder, responsibilities increase and the outcome remains unknown, we continue to do what is right,” he wrote.

Dix said Silkyara taught him the difference between low probability and impossibility, while Nepal was teaching him something more.

“When multiple lives depend on us at the same time, we must turn hope into discipline and compassion into action, and duty must not depend only on certainty of success,” he wrote.

From Australia to Nepal’s flood-hit tunnels

Dix, a senior expert associated with the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association (ITA), initially provided technical advice remotely from Australia to the Nepal Electricity Authority during the early days of the Rasuwa floods.

Following his advice and coordination, two technicians were rescued alive from the flooded tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project 10 days after the disaster.

Dix subsequently travelled to Nepal and is now directly involved in field operations.

He has been guiding inspection and search efforts at several tunnels, including the Chilime Hydropower Project, based on the technical possibility that even structures completely buried by flood debris and mud could contain pockets of breathable air where people may still be alive.

Dix has vowed to continue the rescue effort to the end.

“Whether East or West, the principle is the same — we are not judged only by how many lives we save, but also by the lives we refuse to give up on,” he wrote.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood leaves a deep scar on Nepal’s economy

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

The devastating flood that swept through Rasuwa and Nuwakot on August 26 has struck one of Nepal’s most economically active river corridors, leaving damage that could reverberate across the country’s energy supply, tourism industry, foreign trade and government finances.

A preliminary Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) report has identified damage to 13 hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 783 megawatts.

A solar plant and two transmission lines have also been damaged, according to government data.

The physical destruction extends far beyond the energy sector. The flood has completely destroyed 7,570 private houses, directly affecting 32,933 people living in those households.

It has damaged 48 government structures, 35 of which have been completely destroyed. Eighteen schools have been damaged, including 11 that were completely swept away. Seven health facilities have also been affected, four of them completely destroyed.

The flood washed away around 55 kilometres of roads and 37 motorable bridges, while 68 suspension bridges were damaged. Fifty-five drinking water projects have suffered losses estimated at Rs 640 million.

Agriculture has also taken a major hit. Around 1,806 hectares of farmland have been completely destroyed, with an estimated reduction of 7,686 tonnes in food production.

Seventeen bank branches have also been damaged.

A blow to three pillars of the economy

The scale of the destruction has led concerns to move beyond immediate rescue and relief.

Rasuwa lawmaker and businessman Mohan Acharya says the flood has devastated three important pillars of the national economy—hydropower, tourism and the Rasuwagadhi trade route.

“Not just Rasuwa, but the country’s major economic foundations—hydropower, tourism and the border trade route—have been devastated,” Acharya said while presenting details of the flood damage at a Nepali Congress meeting on Sunday.

He said many economically active young people remain missing and entire villages have been emptied.

The human loss, he said, could prove to be the most consequential part of the disaster.

Acharya compared the impact with the 2015 earthquake, saying the two disasters caused fundamentally different forms of destruction.

“The earthquake damaged houses but did not destroy people’s land. This flood has left large numbers of people homeless all at once,” he said.

Many young people who had taken bank loans to start businesses have been affected, while in some villages mainly children have been left behind, he said. This could create a heavy economic burden for children at an early age and produce long-term psychosocial consequences.

Tourism faces a long road to recovery

Tourism has suffered another major blow. The Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation estimates that the flood has caused around Rs 50 billion in damage to the tourism sector alone.

Around 142 hotels along the river corridor are estimated to have been swept away, while 57 restaurants and 141 tourism vehicles have been damaged.

Twenty-seven cultural heritage sites have also suffered damage.

The trekking routes to destinations such as Langtang and Gosainkunda have been severely damaged. Some sections have been completely washed away and will have to be rebuilt from the beginning.

According to former Nepal Tourism Board CEO Deepak Raj Joshi, the damage could have consequences beyond the businesses and infrastructure directly hit by the flood.

The Langtang region attracts more than 50,000 tourists annually, according to Langtang National Park data. Gosainkunda also draws large numbers of religious visitors every year.

The corridor has another important tourism connection: the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route.

Joshi said the monsoon season, generally considered an off-season for Nepal, attracts relatively high-spending Indian and non-resident Indian visitors travelling to Kailash Mansarovar through Nepal.

“These are all high-spending tourists,” he said, adding that their contribution to employment and economic activity through Nepal’s tourism industry is significant.

Tourism has also lost business owners, guides and workers in the disaster.

“The loss of human lives has no price,” Joshi said. “On top of that, business owners and workers have been caught in this flood. They made an invaluable contribution to tourism.”

Tourism companies have reported deaths among tour guides, trekking guides and other workers.

Rebuilding the infrastructure may therefore be only one part of the challenge. Rebuilding the workforce and businesses that supported the tourism economy could take considerably longer.

Rasuwagadhi trade route disrupted

The flood has also disrupted Nepal’s trade with China after the structures and roads around the Rasuwagadhi border point were swept away.

The disruption has forced some trade to be diverted towards the geographically more difficult Korala border point, increasing transportation costs and creating concerns over prices inside Nepal.

In the last fiscal year, 2082/83, imports through Rasuwagadhi accounted for 2.18 percent of Nepal’s total foreign trade, according to government data.

Although the border point operated for only six months during the year, goods worth Rs 45.73 billion were imported through Rasuwagadhi, while exports amounted to Rs 894.6 million.

Its importance was even greater in fiscal year 2081/82, when imports through Rasuwagadhi amounted to Rs 85.23 billion and exports to Rs 2.04 billion. That represented 4.72 percent of Nepal’s total merchandise imports and 0.74 percent of exports.

From earthquake disruption to flood destruction

Rasuwagadhi has become Nepal’s most important operational land route for trade with China after prolonged disruptions at the Tatopani border.

According to Customs Department Director and Information Officer Kishor Bartaula, Rasuwagadhi has been the most reliable trade point between Nepal and China.

The border point lies around 132 kilometres from Kathmandu via Galchhi, with approximately 40 kilometres of the road on the Rasuwa side estimated to have been completely washed away.

The Department of Roads has begun assessing the condition of different sections.

More than two dozen bridges between the Friendship Bridge and Galchhi have also been swept away, raising uncertainty over the future operation of the customs and immigration points at Rasuwagadhi.

“The government will study all aspects and make a decision. The department will work accordingly,” Bartaula said.

Rasuwagadhi has served as an important trade and cultural route between Nepal and Tibet since ancient times. The Rasuwa Customs Office was established there in 2013 BS to facilitate trade and revenue collection.

China formally recognised Rasuwagadhi as an international border point in 2018, further increasing its importance.

Nepal imports electronic goods, ready-made garments, footwear, construction materials, agricultural products, telecommunications equipment, vehicles and industrial machinery through the route. Nepal exports carpets, handicrafts, woollen products, herbs, noodles, copper utensils and agricultural goods to China.

The border trade also supports thousands of jobs through hotels, transport operators, container loading and unloading services, customs agents and small businesses.

Billions invested in infrastructure swept away

The destruction at Rasuwagadhi comes after years of investment.

The Timure Dry Port was a project worth around Rs 3 billion, according to Ashish Gajurel, chair of the parliamentary Development Committee and former executive director of the Intermodal Transport Development Board.

Around Rs 2 billion had already been spent and most of the structures had been completed. The project was reportedly nearing its finishing stage.

The previous year’s flood had already caused substantial damage to the project, limiting further investment.

This time, however, many of the remaining structures have been completely destroyed.

The state has lost infrastructure and employees, while the extent of damage suffered by private businesses remains to be fully assessed.

The historic border and customs point now faces the daunting task of rebuilding almost from scratch.

Pressure on government budget and economic growth

The economic consequences could extend well beyond the affected districts.

Former National Planning Commission vice-chairman Dr Prakash Kumar Shrestha says the disaster could affect the government’s policies and programmes, the fiscal year 2083/84 budget, the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework and the targets of the 16th periodic plan.

The government will face greater pressure on its resources and may have to divert capital expenditure towards rescue, relief and reconstruction.

That, in turn, could make it difficult to achieve the government’s economic growth target.

The disruption to road infrastructure has already affected supply chains, potentially increasing pressure on prices.

“Disruption in an economically active corridor will also make it difficult for the government to meet its revenue targets,” Shrestha said.

As reconstruction becomes a priority, other government plans and development priorities could also be pushed back.

When taxpayers become aid recipients

Another less visible consequence is the sudden economic decline of people who were previously financially secure.

The flood has destroyed urban settlements and businesses along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor, pushing many people who once earned incomes, ran businesses and paid substantial taxes into dependence on others.

“People who were paying millions of rupees in taxes to the state yesterday have today been forced to depend on others,” Shrestha said. “This naturally deals a blow to our poverty reduction efforts.”

He said Nepal should now link its social protection system more closely with disaster management and urgently work to return families who have lost their homes to safe housing.

Loss of skilled workforce

The long-term impact could also be felt in Nepal’s labour market.

The disaster has taken a heavy toll on skilled workers in hydropower projects, while business owners and workers involved in border trade and tourism have also been affected.

Shrestha said the loss of skilled workers could affect the country’s labour supply for years.

Replacing experienced hydropower technicians, tourism workers, guides, traders and other specialised workers will take time.

Rebuild stronger, not simply faster

Former National Planning Commission vice-chairman Prof Dr Gobinda Raj Pokharel says the devastated corridor is one of Nepal’s most economically active areas, with hydropower, trade, tourism and agriculture all concentrated along it.

He argues that the government must move quickly towards a strong and safer reconstruction programme rather than simply restoring infrastructure to its previous condition.

The government should install early warning systems along river corridors and require disaster audits before major infrastructure projects are built, Pokharel said.

Such requirements should apply to hydropower projects, roads, bridges and other major infrastructure.

The flood has therefore exposed a challenge much larger than the repair of damaged roads and bridges.

For Nepal, the question is now whether this corridor will simply be rebuilt—or rebuilt in a way that makes its economy, communities and infrastructure more resilient to the next disaster.
