title.rendered: Nepal plans legal provision to relocate settlements in disaster-prone areas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 7

The government is preparing legislation that would allow the relocation of settlements considered vulnerable to natural disasters, amid growing concerns over people living along riverbanks, forests and other high-risk areas.

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation, in coordination with the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration, has drafted the Bill to Amend Some Nepal Acts Relating to Land, 2026.

The proposed bill seeks to amend the Land (Survey) Act 1963, which is 64 years old, and the Land Act 1964, which is 62 years old. If enacted, it would also amend provisions of the Guthi Corporation Act 1976, Land Revenue Act 1978 and Land Use Act 2019.

Mandatory relocation from high-risk areas

The bill proposes a new provision under Section 52B of the Land Act 1964 requiring authorities to arrange alternative settlements for landless Dalits and landless squatters living in high-risk locations.

The provision covers people living along riverbanks and lakes, inside national parks and conservation areas, in forests, within road rights-of-way and in other areas deemed vulnerable to disasters.

The use of the phrase “must be arranged” makes the proposed provision mandatory.

The government argues that the provision would help ensure the right to housing, promote planned settlements and contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals and climate adaptation.

Nepal’s Constitution already provides for the right of landless Dalits to receive land. However, many landless Dalits have yet to receive land under the constitutional provision.

Article 37 of the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to appropriate housing. Yet many landless squatters continue to live without secure homes or land.

The government categorises landless people broadly into two groups: those who own neither agricultural land nor a residential plot, and those without a permanent home who have been living temporarily on public or government land or for years along riverbanks, vacant government land and the edges of forests.

Nearly 1.1 million applications

The latest data from the Land Issues Resolution Commission shows that it has received 1,096,670 applications from landless squatters and unorganised settlers.

Of these, 87,995 applications are from landless Dalits, 166,060 from landless squatters and 842,615 from unorganised settlers.

However, there has been no separate comprehensive assessment of whether the areas where these people currently live are exposed to disaster risks.

The proposed legislation seeks to address this gap by requiring risk assessment before land is allocated to landless people.

Under the proposed amendment, land along rivers, streams and canals, land in high-risk areas, national parks and conservation areas, forest land and land within road boundaries would not be available for distribution.

There is an exception for certain areas that were identified as grazing grounds, fairs, markets or market areas during the initial land survey. If people have been living and cultivating such land for at least 10 years, they could still receive land ownership certificates, subject to specified conditions and a formal decision by the concerned local government.

Risk assessment before land distribution

Although the bill introduces the concept of relocating vulnerable settlements, it does not provide a detailed blueprint for how the process would work.

It does not clearly specify who will determine whether a settlement is in a high-risk area, where relocated families will be settled, how land will be acquired or allocated, or how housing, livelihoods and infrastructure will be provided after relocation.

The proposed legislation does, however, allow the government to establish committees or task forces at the federal and district levels.

Such bodies could identify landless Dalits, landless squatters and unorganised settlers, maintain their records, identify potential land, conduct field studies and collect evidence before facilitating land allocation.

They could also address problems related to ownership records, registration documents and maps of land previously distributed by various government commissions and task forces.

The bill does not explicitly state whether these committees would themselves have the authority to determine which locations are high-risk.

Government officials say these details could be clarified during the legislative process based on feedback from the public and stakeholders.

Bill now open for public feedback

The draft bill was published for public feedback on August 31, in accordance with the Legislative Act. The public has been given seven days to submit comments and suggestions.

After reviewing the feedback, the Ministry of Land Management will revise the bill if necessary and send it to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for legal review.

It will then return to the Land Management Ministry before being sent to the Ministry of Finance. Once approved by the Finance Ministry, the Land Management Minister will present it to the Cabinet.

If approved by the Cabinet, the bill will be registered in Parliament. It must then be passed by both houses and authenticated by the President before becoming law.

Officials at the Land Management Ministry say the provisions can be further clarified during this process.

The proposed legislation also seeks to devolve certain land-related services to local governments, including registration-related work, with the stated aim of reducing the time and cost for service users.

Why identify high-risk settlements?

A land-related bill was also introduced during the previous term of the House of Representatives to address issues involving landless Dalits, squatters and unorganised settlers.

The Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee of the previous House had discussed and endorsed the bill clause by clause. However, it became inactive after the House was dissolved on September 12, 2025.

The new bill retains many of the earlier provisions while adding a specific requirement to relocate people living in high-risk areas.

Ashok Kumar Chaudhary, chair of the current House Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee, says identifying high-risk settlements and relocating residents to safer locations is necessary.

“Identifying high-risk areas and protecting citizens’ lives and property is the constitutional responsibility of the state,” Chaudhary said. “Settlements at high risk from floods, landslides and river erosion should not be allowed to remain where they are.”

But he stressed that relocation must be based on scientific assessments, transparent criteria and protection of citizens’ fundamental rights.

“In particular, people who are landless, squatters or economically vulnerable must not be further displaced or made landless in the name of removing them from high-risk areas,” he said.

Chaudhary said the state must not remove people from one risk only to place them in another.

He called for relocation policies that guarantee safe and sustainable settlements, rehabilitation and resettlement, along with housing and livelihood opportunities.

‘Law must clearly define who decides what is risky’

Chaudhary said Parliament would examine the bill from multiple perspectives once it is introduced.

“Parliament should not look only at the objective of the government’s bill. It must also seriously examine how it protects citizens’ rights and how the provisions will actually be implemented,” he said.

He added that the concept of relocating settlements from high-risk areas could be positive, but the law must clearly address several questions: who determines whether an area is dangerous, on what basis, where people will be relocated, how land will be provided and how housing, infrastructure and livelihoods will be secured.

Chaudhary, who was also a member of the previous House, recalled that he had expressed dissent during discussions on the earlier land bill, arguing that provisions weakening the constitutional and legal rights of landless people and squatters could not be accepted.

He said those concerns would also guide his role in the current legislative process.

“If the state is going to restrict citizens’ rights in the name of land management, the legal basis, due process and alternative arrangements must also be clearly defined,” he said.

He added that Parliament and its committees should hold extensive discussions on the bill and amend provisions that remain unclear.

The proposed legislation comes as the government faces renewed pressure to address settlements exposed to floods and other disasters following the devastating Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods of August 26, which caused extensive loss of life, homes and infrastructure in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and surrounding districts.

title.rendered: Two bodies found inside Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Two bodies have been found inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa, on the 12th day since the devastating Bhotekoshi flood.

Project chief executive officer Giriraj Adhikari confirmed the discovery on Sunday, saying the bodies were recovered from the inner section of the tunnel.

The identities of the deceased have not yet been established, Adhikari told Onlinekhabar.

The discovery comes a day after rescuers pulled a Chinese national alive from the same tunnel. The individual was rescued from around 225 metres inside the tunnel.

Search and rescue operations are continuing inside the tunnel, with teams looking for other people who may have been trapped following the flood.

The Bhotekoshi River flood struck Rasuwa on August 26, causing widespread destruction across the district and leaving hundreds of people missing.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah thanks security forces for tireless flood response

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Prime Minister Balendra Shah has praised the security forces deployed in the response to the Rasuwa floods, saying their contribution during the crisis will be highly valued and that the government will not compromise on their safety, service and welfare.

In a message addressed to security personnel on Sunday evening, Shah thanked the Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force for their continued search, rescue and relief efforts in the flood-hit areas.

He particularly praised security personnel who managed to evacuate all 923 inmates from the Central Prison in Bidur Municipality-6 of Nuwakot after the Bhotekoshi flood struck on August 26.

According to Shah, 52 Nepal Police and Armed Police personnel deployed to guard the prison moved inmates from two buildings to a higher building as floodwaters carrying mud and debris entered the prison compound.

The flood damaged the prison’s administrative building, security posts and walls and reached the first floor of buildings where inmates had been held.

Shah said around 50 inmates took advantage of the situation to break through the prison wall and gate and flee as far as 100 metres. Security personnel later brought them back under control. Some security personnel were injured when inmates who had not escaped attacked them, he said.

The security personnel also helped protect the lives of nearby residents, according to the prime minister.

“Today, their barracks and offices are still covered in mud, access routes no longer exist and the water supply has been disrupted,” Shah said. “Yet they are carrying water from afar, using field embankments as roads, clearing routes and standing on duty with high morale. Their courage is remarkable.”

Shah said the prison response was only one example of the work carried out by security personnel during the disaster.

According to him, joint efforts by the Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force have so far rescued 13,391 people from the affected areas. Security personnel have transported injured people to hospitals by road, helicopter and, in some cases, by carrying them on their shoulders.

They have also been involved in managing bodies, preventing the spread of infectious diseases in affected areas and supporting survivors in temporary holding centres.

“Despite the difficult geography and adverse weather, our security personnel are still searching through the mud and debris left by the flood,” Shah said.

He acknowledged the emotional toll on security personnel, saying many were themselves grieving colleagues who had gone missing in the disaster.

According to Shah, 45 Nepal Army personnel, 25 Nepal Police personnel and 12 Armed Police personnel remain missing following the floods.

“Even while carrying this pain, you have hidden your tears and continued entering the mud, recovering bodies and standing guard day and night at holding centres,” he said.

Thousands deployed across flood-hit areas

Shah said the three security agencies have been working together in search, rescue and disaster management operations.

The Nepal Army has established a forward headquarters, emergency medical rescue team and forward air base at Maithil Barracks in Battar, Nuwakot. It has also established a tactical headquarters, forward medical team and additional air base at Dhunche in Rasuwa.

The army is leading rescue operations in difficult terrain and at hydropower tunnel sites, with specialised search-and-rescue teams from the Armed Police Force and dog teams from Nepal Police also involved.

The army has also accelerated the construction of Bailey bridges and the opening of blocked roads. At Devighat in Nuwakot, army engineers are installing an Acrow bridge to restore connectivity.

Around 9,287 army personnel are currently deployed in flood-affected areas, Shah said.

Nepal Police has been involved in search, rescue, relief distribution, body management and maintaining security in affected areas from the beginning of the disaster. Trained sniffer dogs have also been deployed.

Around 7,975 police personnel are currently working in the affected areas.

The Armed Police Force has deployed specialised divers, rope-rescue teams, drones and canine teams for search and rescue operations in the difficult terrain along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor.

The force had established disaster response posts, field command posts and 13 disaster response bases in the affected areas. It is also providing medical services.

Around 4,203 Armed Police personnel are currently deployed in the flood-hit areas.

Shah said the combined efforts of the three security agencies had given millions of people a sense of safety during the crisis.

“Your contribution will be highly valued,” he said. “The government will not compromise on your service, safety and welfare.”

He also expressed gratitude to the families of security personnel for encouraging them to continue working during the crisis.

Shah thanked experts from Nepal and abroad who have been supporting the security forces in disaster management.

“We will always remain grateful to you,” he said.

title.rendered: Search ends with 39 workers still unaccounted for at Langtang Khola hydropower

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The search for workers missing from the Langtang Khola Hydropower Project following the Bhotekoshi flood has been called off after rescue teams found only two bodies inside the project’s tunnel.

A joint team of the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force stopped the search after determining that further efforts inside the tunnel were no longer necessary.

According to details provided by the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), 39 people associated with the 20 MW Langtang Khola Hydropower Project remain unaccounted for.

Nineteen other people working at the project site were rescued after the flood.

The project, which had completed construction and was undergoing testing, is being developed by Multi Energy Development Pvt Ltd.

Langtang Khola Hydropower Project manager Bijay Mohan Bhattarai said the search inside the tunnel was suspended after Saturday following the recovery of two bodies.

The rescue team entered the tunnel by cutting through the penstock pipe. The two bodies were found inside, but they were badly damaged and have not yet been identified, according to IPPAN.

The bodies will be identified through DNA testing before being handed over to their families.

Bhattarai said the 39 missing people are believed to have been swept away by the flood. With no further signs of the missing workers found inside the tunnel, the search operation has now been stopped.

title.rendered: Govt forms committee to find land for resettling flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The government has formed a committee to identify land for the resettlement of people displaced or left at risk by the devastating flood that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26.

The 13-member committee, led by Survey Department Director General Prakash Joshi, has been tasked with finding suitable land to relocate settlements affected by the flood.

The committee includes officials from the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration, the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, the Department of Land Management and Archives, and the Survey Department, along with representatives from the affected districts.

District-level members include district coordination officers, assistant chief district officers, deputy superintendents of police, chief administrative officers of the concerned local governments, deputy superintendents of the Armed Police Force, and chiefs of the respective land administration and survey offices.

Identifying families requiring relocation

The committee will first establish the number of people whose homes have been destroyed or who are living in areas considered unsafe.

It will also determine whether families who have become homeless have land or houses elsewhere. Based on this information, the committee will coordinate with local governments and the land administration and survey offices in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading to identify potential sites for resettlement.

The committee has already begun coordination with local governments and district-level land and survey offices.

“We have already started coordinating with the land and survey offices and local governments in the concerned districts,” a committee member said.

According to the member, officials are currently collecting details on the number of houses damaged in each ward and determining how many houses and settlements need to be relocated.

Land to be assessed for disaster risk

After determining the number of families requiring relocation, the committee will search for suitable land and assess whether the proposed sites are exposed to disaster risks.

Only land considered suitable and safe for settlement will be considered for resettlement. The government will then begin the necessary legal process to facilitate the transfer or allocation of land to the affected families.

The committee will submit a report to the ministry containing data on families requiring relocation and recommendations on suitable locations for resettlement.

The August 26 flood caused extensive loss of life and property along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors. Search and rescue operations for those still missing are continuing.

title.rendered: Man arrested for harassing a woman in Thamel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Police have arrested a man accused of inappropriately touching a woman while she was walking along a footpath in Thamel, Kathmandu.

The arrested man has been identified as 30-year-old Salim Sah of Kabilasi Municipality-2, Sarlahi, who currently lives in Kathmandu. A team from the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office arrested him in Kalanki on Saturday night.

A video showing the alleged incident went viral on social media several days ago. Police said the incident took place at around 8 pm on September 1 on a footpath in Thamel.

Police launched an investigation after the video surfaced and identified Shah as the person allegedly involved in the incident.

SP Dan Bahadur Thapa said the District Police Range, Kathmandu, is investigating the case under the offence of indecent behaviour.

title.rendered: Energy Ministry runs rescue, power restoration and reconstruction efforts in parallel after Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation has been carrying out the search and rescue of workers trapped or missing at hydropower projects alongside efforts to restore electricity supply and rebuild infrastructure damaged by the devastating Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa.

The flood caused extensive damage to hydropower projects, transmission structures and electricity supply systems in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other districts.

The ministry has formed a high-level management mechanism (SMT) to coordinate the response. The mechanism includes the ministry secretary, heads of departments and divisions, and senior officials from the Nepal Electricity Authority.

The mechanism is coordinating rescue, relief, restoration of electricity services and management of damage caused by the disaster.

Since the day of the flood, the ministry has been maintaining records of the condition of affected hydropower projects, missing employees and workers, equipment deployed for rescue operations and progress made at different sites.

It has now begun developing a real-time update system to provide an integrated picture of rescue and restoration efforts.

The system will allow authorities to monitor which projects are being worked on, what equipment has been deployed and the status of rescue operations in real time, according to the ministry.

Rescue operations continue at hydropower projects

The ministry is coordinating with the Home Ministry, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, Nepal Army and other security agencies for rescue operations.

Technical personnel, excavators, drilling machines, vehicles and other equipment have been deployed at affected hydropower projects.

According to the ministry, the Nepal Army has so far rescued around 350 workers and local residents, including 25 workers trapped inside the tunnel of the Langtang Bhotekoshi Hydropower Project and people trapped in the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 project.

However, the search for people still missing inside tunnels and underground structures at several hydropower projects remains challenging.

At the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, the ministry is coordinating rescue efforts with the Nepal Army.

According to the project, an Army team reached the powerhouse area in four helicopters on Bhadra 20 with necessary equipment and began removing debris and searching the transformer cavern and different sections of the powerhouse.

However, the operation has so far failed to establish the whereabouts of the missing employees.

Electricity restoration also underway

Alongside rescue efforts, the ministry has prioritised restoring electricity supply to areas affected by the disaster.

Electricity has already been restored to around 90 percent of Nuwakot, while work is continuing to restore services in Rasuwa.

Alternative energy systems are also being arranged for remote and high-risk areas where power lines have been damaged, particularly to address immediate lighting and communication needs.

The ministry said it had initiated the process of sending institutional solar systems with a capacity of 2 kW and 500 solar sets of 20 watts each to affected areas.

More than 400 MW of supply affected

The flood affected more than 400 megawatts of electricity supply, equivalent to around 10 percent of the country’s supply, according to the ministry.

This has created a dual challenge for the government: restoring electricity services in the short term and repairing and rebuilding damaged energy infrastructure over the longer term.

The ministry is updating information on employees and workers at affected projects in coordination with project managers, the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), and Nepal Electricity Authority representatives.

To make night-time search and rescue operations more effective, 200 headlamps and 900 batteries have also been provided to security personnel.

Detailed damage assessment planned

The ministry is preparing to move beyond immediate rescue and restoration towards a detailed assessment of damage to hydropower projects, substations and other energy infrastructure.

In coordination with the National Planning Commission and the disaster management authority, it plans to assess the damage and identify the resources required for restoration, reconstruction and recovery.

The ministry said the immediate priority remains the search and rescue of missing workers and restoration of electricity services.

The next phase will focus on determining the full extent of damage and developing plans to bring damaged energy infrastructure back into operation and rebuild facilities that have been destroyed.

title.rendered: Bailey bridge installation begins over Tadi River in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The installation of a Bailey bridge over the Tadi River at Devighat Bazaar in Nuwakot began on Saturday, with the Nepal Army starting the construction work.

The bridge will reconnect Devighat Bazaar with Jiling, which have remained disconnected after a permanent bridge was swept away by a massive flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26.

The flood caused extensive damage to bridges and other infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, with around 100 bridges reportedly damaged.

Once completed, the Bailey bridge will provide a temporary transport link between Devighat Bazaar and Jiling and help ease movement in the flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: Pillar-less Bailey bridge proposed for Dhading’s Furke Khola

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The Department of Roads is consulting Chinese experts on installing a pillar-less Bailey bridge over Furke Khola in Dhading to restore traffic along the Prithvi Highway.

Department Director General Bijay Jaisi said the proposal was being discussed during an on-site inspection of the Prithvi Highway on Sunday.

“We are consulting Chinese experts about installing a pillar-less Bailey bridge across the 94-metre span at Furke Khola,” Jaisi said. “If the 100-metre bridge brought from China can be installed there, vehicular movement could resume within two to three weeks.”

Jaisi said the Department of Roads has the technical capacity required for bridge construction and pledged to restore damaged infrastructure as quickly as possible.

He said maintaining the country’s nearly 14,000-kilometre road network remained challenging, but the department was working around the clock with the resources available to it.

A team including a member of the National Planning Commission and the secretary of the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport also inspected the situation at Krishnabhir and directed officials to resolve the problem as soon as possible.

The Department of Roads has urged the public to remain patient, saying it is making every effort to ensure safe operation of the road network and restore disrupted transport links.

title.rendered: Expired food found among relief supplies for Bhotekoshi flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Serious negligence has been found in the relief supplies being prepared for distribution to victims of the Bhotekoshi floods. Food items including rice, flour, puffed rice and chips that were being prepared for delivery as relief were found to have expired and to be unfit for consumption.

The finding was made during a surprise inspection conducted at five storage and monitoring sites in Kathmandu by a joint team from the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control and the Food Technology and Quality Control Division Office, Kathmandu.

The inspection, carried out under the Food Hygiene and Quality Act 2081, found expired food items stored at locations ranging from government offices to a police training centre. The inspection team found irregularities particularly in relief supplies stored at the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction in Babarmahal, the Police Training Centre in Samakhusi and Radha Soami Satsang.

According to Dr Bal Kumari Sharma, senior food research officer at the department, expired items had been kept alongside usable goods at these locations where relief supplies were being collected and packaged for distribution. At the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction in Babarmahal, the team found expired “Current Chips” produced by Yashoda Foods Pvt Ltd of Rupandehi and “Bhuja” produced by Giridhari Food Products of Butwal among the items being prepared for relief packages.

The inspection team stopped 30 packets of Current Chips and 21 sacks of Bhuja from being distributed, placed them in a separate “expired zone”, and initiated further action. Similarly, at the Police Training Centre in Samakhusi, two packets containing 18 pieces of Chocofan and one five-kilogram packet of Chakki flour were found to have expired.

The team also found 59 packets of “All in One” dalmoth with only two days remaining before their expiry date. The department barred the distribution of both the expired items and the dalmoth nearing its expiry date and ordered them to be placed in the expired zone.

During an inspection at Radha Soami Satsang in Samakhusi, the team also found a 25-kilogram sack of Jayshree parboiled rice that had expired. The department said it had initiated action because distributing expired food as relief in such a sensitive humanitarian situation could seriously affect the health of already vulnerable and flood-affected people.

title.rendered: Bina Joshi’s book on traditional Newa masked dances wins Madan Puraskar

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The Madan Puraskar Guthi has awarded the 2082 Madan Puraskar to Bina Joshi (Rajbhandari) for her book Traditional Masked Dances of the Newa Community.

The Guthi announced Joshi’s book as the winner of the Madan Puraskar on Sunday.

The top 10 books shortlisted for the Madan Puraskar had already been announced. Among them, Joshi’s book on traditional masked dances of the Newa community was selected for the 2082 Madan Puraskar, said Kunda Dixit, chairperson of the Madan Puraskar Guthi.

Since 2072 BS, the Guthi has been selecting up to 10 works from among the books submitted to it and publishing a shortlist. Under the Guthi’s rules, books containing a substantial amount of previously unpublished material are considered among the selection criteria.

Established in 2012 BS, the Madan Puraskar Guthi first awarded the Madan Puraskar in 2013 BS to three works in the categories of prose, social sciences and science.

In its inaugural year, the award was presented to Satya Mohan Joshi’s Hamro Lok Sanskriti in prose, Chittaranjan Nepali’s General Bhimsen Thapa ra Tatkalin Nepal in social sciences, and Balaram Joshi’s Adhikvibhav Sthirvidyut Utpadak in science.

Since then, the award has been given to outstanding works published in the Nepali language.

The prize money has been Rs 400,000 since 2075 BS.

title.rendered: When disaster ends, grief has its own struggle

content.rendered:
Forty-year-old Hari Prasad Mainali went missing in the Rasuwa floods. His fate remained unknown after he was caught in the flood on August 26.

After many days of search operations with no results and hope of his return faded, the family had to give up hope that Hari Prasad would come back. Since his body was never found, the family performed his last rites using a symbolic effigy made of kush grass.

But amid the pain of losing a loved one, the Mainali family faced another problem: a lack of space to perform the mourning rites (kriya).

According to Hari Prasad’s brother Hem Chandra, most of the mourning-rite houses in Kathmandu’s Tarakeshwar area were full. The municipality then allowed the family to use an under-construction mourning-rite building temporarily, where they are now staying to complete the rites.

“There’s already the pain of losing someone close to us, and on top of that, finding a place to sit in mourning was a huge struggle. Most places were full. Right now we’re staying in an under-construction building to perform the rites,” Hem Chandra says.

Hari Prasad’s family’s situation has now become a common problem for many families who lost relatives in the disaster. After a large number of families lost loved ones at once following the floods in the Bhotekoshi and Rasuwa-Nuwakot areas, pressure has also mounted on Kathmandu’s mourning-rite houses.

Even the 42-room Kiryaputri Service Centre at Pashupati filled up, requiring alternative arrangements. According to an official at the Pashupati Area Development Fund, an approximately 80-room building in the Vanakali area, previously used for flower sales, has also been arranged for temporary use as a mourning-rite building. The official claims there is no longer an immediate shortage of space for mourning rites in the Pashupati area.

Similarly, Tarakeshwar Municipality has allowed an under-construction mourning-rite building to be used temporarily. Pressure has also increased on mourning-rite houses in Kathmandu’s Basundhara, Dhapasi, Bansbari, Nepaltar, and Kandaghari areas.

When the body isn’t found

When the body of someone missing in a disaster cannot be found, families face the added complication of how to perform last rites. As with Hari Prasad’s family, some families may eventually have to perform funeral rites using a symbolic kush-grass effigy after prolonged searching and waiting.

When a body is not found, it can take families a long time to even accept the death. On one hand, hope remains that the person might still be found; on the other, the uncertainty of searching and waiting leaves families mentally exhausted. In such situations, completing the last rites according to religious and social tradition can be emotionally significant for the family.

But even after deciding to proceed with the funeral, issues such as finding a place to sit in mourning, accommodation, food, toilets, sanitation, and financial arrangements can add further stress.

Grieving families shouldn’t face additional stress

Psychologist Grishma Paneru says that disaster or sudden death is itself a deep psychosocial trauma, and that grief becomes even more complicated when families then face further difficulties in body management, funeral, and mourning-rite processes.

“When families lose a loved one, they are already in a state of shock, disbelief, fear, guilt, and deep grief. At that very time, difficulty identifying the body, delays in receiving it, inability to manage it safely, or lack of arrangements for the funeral can increase their mental anguish,” Paneru says.

Psychologists say such circumstances can heighten traumatic grief, potentially causing problems like repeatedly reliving the event, nightmares, fear, or panic.

“Many decisions, body management, funeral, mourning rites, accommodation, financial arrangements, and informing relatives, must be made in a short time. Since family members themselves are in grief and under stress, disagreements can arise over what to do, who should do it, and where,” she says.

She noted that the feeling of not having been able to give the deceased a dignified farewell can make the grieving process even more complicated.

According to a relative of one deceased person who came to Kathmandu for the mourning rites, a grieving family’s first need is to steady themselves mentally and complete the funeral according to tradition, but when finding a place becomes difficult, families fall into further distress.

“We’re already struggling with how to cope with losing our own person. On top of that, having to call around and search for a place to sit in mourning makes it so much harder,” he says.

He said the problem is even greater for families who have come to Kathmandu from outside the city, unfamiliarity with the local area, not knowing where mourning-rite houses are located, and being forced to search elsewhere when one building is full all add to the family’s stress.

Grief management needed at the social level too

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, as of Sunday afternoon, 1,341 people have died in the Rasuwa floods.

Death and funeral rites are not merely personal or family matters; they are tied to social and cultural dimensions as well. In Nepali society particularly, mourning rites serve as an important social practice that expresses respect for the deceased and helps the family move forward through the grieving process.

Therefore, when large numbers of deaths occur during a disaster, there is a need to treat families’ grief management — alongside body management, as part of disaster management itself.

While rescue, treatment, relief, and body management are prioritised in disaster response, the social and psychological problems families face afterwards may not receive adequate attention. The lack of space for mourning rites is one example of this problem.

For disaster-affected families, arrangements are also needed for drinking water, toilets, sanitation, food, security, necessary information, and counselling alongside the mourning-rite site itself. Facilities become an even more sensitive a concern for families accompanied by elderly people, women, and children.

Funerals, too, are part of disaster management

In the view of disaster management experts and sociologists, ensuring a dignified funeral for the deceased during a major disaster is a humanitarian responsibility of both the state and the community.

In a situation like the Rasuwa floods, where many families are affected simultaneously, regular structures alone cannot meet the demand, making prior coordination necessary among local governments, hospitals, the Pashupati Area Development Fund, and social organisations.

For future disasters of this kind, the Kathmandu Valley could identify alternative mourning-rite sites in advance, prepare temporary structures, arrange drinking water and sanitation, and set up a mechanism to provide necessary information to families.

For families who have lost loved ones, a funeral is not merely a religious duty to complete; it is also an important psychosocial process of accepting the reality of death and gradually moving forward from grief.

Therefore, post-disaster management should keep at its centre not just the bodies of the deceased, but also the pain and needs of their families.

For families who have lost relatives, like Hari Prasad Mainali’s family, the current priority is not simply finding a room to sit in mourning. It is equally necessary that they be given an environment in which they can perform the funeral with dignity during this difficult time of grief, along with the social support and mental grounding they need to cope.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa urges PM Shah to take evidence-based climate case to UN

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6 

Nepali Congress president Gagan Kumar Thapa has urged Prime Minister Balendra Shah to present Nepal’s case on climate change and disaster losses at the upcoming United Nations General Assembly with scientific evidence, data and concrete claims.

Speaking at the party’s Central Working Committee meeting at Sanepa on Sunday, Thapa said Shah’s upcoming foreign visit should not be reduced to a formal trip or a “grand show”.

He urged the prime minister to consult climate experts, university researchers and specialists from relevant fields rather than relying solely on his secretariat while preparing for the visit.

Push for climate finance and compensation

Thapa said Nepal must make a stronger case internationally about the damage it is suffering from climate change despite contributing very little to global greenhouse gas emissions.

He cited disasters such as the devastating Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa as evidence of the disproportionate impact of climate-related disasters on countries such as Nepal.

“We have been raising the issue of being affected by climate change for years, but our claims now need to be based on scientific studies,” Thapa said. “Nepal must lobby strongly not only for loss and damage but also for grant-based climate finance.”

He also called for a review of the issues raised by previous Nepali governments and prime ministers at international forums.

Thapa said Nepal should build on earlier initiatives, including calls to link the “Himalayas to the oceans” and efforts to advance climate justice at COP28.

He said Nepal would be in a stronger position to establish its concerns internationally and secure concrete outcomes if its preparations were based on consultations with experts and skilled professionals both inside and outside the country.

Calls for change to law on missing persons

Thapa also called for an immediate amendment to the existing legal provision under which a person who goes missing in a disaster cannot be legally declared dead for 12 years.

He said the provision was creating additional uncertainty for families affected by the Bhotekoshi floods.

“The current legal provision that prevents a missing person from being declared dead for 12 years means families fear they will be unable to perform the final rites of their loved ones or access government benefits and rights,” Thapa said.

He called for the law to be amended to allow local governments to certify deaths in cases involving major disasters.

‘Tunnel rescue preparedness was inadequate’

Thapa also called for a serious review of disaster preparedness in hydropower projects and tunnels following the recent disaster in the Trishuli-Bhotekoshi corridor.

He said rescue operations inside tunnels during natural disasters had exposed significant challenges and that the government needed to examine whether existing project designs and technologies were adequate.

“We need to do more when it comes to rescuing people from tunnels during natural disasters,” he said. “We need technical clarity on whether this should be addressed during the design of projects or whether new technology is required.”

He said disaster preparedness, rescue equipment and appropriate technology should be incorporated from the infrastructure design stage itself.

Thapa said the country must learn from the latest disaster and improve preparedness and technology to reduce the risks of future disasters.

‘Service to disaster victims is the priority’

Thapa also said helping people affected by the floods and landslides should take precedence over the Congress’s internal political activities and dialogue.

He said the party’s organisational activities and convention-related discussions were part of a regular political process, but the current crisis required the party to focus on those affected in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Thapa, who recently visited some of the worst-affected areas, described the situation as devastating, saying communities had lost homes, family members and access to roads.

“This is not an ordinary disaster but a major catastrophe,” he said. “We will reach the last mile and remain with the affected citizens.”

He said relief and reconstruction were necessary, but affected people also needed compassion and solidarity.

Addressing questions about his recent meetings with senior Congress leaders, Thapa said his priority at present was the problems faced by disaster victims rather than internal political discussions.

“Meetings with Sher Bahadur Deuba, Dr Shekhar Koirala and Purna Bahadur Khadka naturally attract media attention,” he said. “But for me, solving the problems of victims in Dhading, Rasuwa and Nuwakot and communicating with them is more important right now.”

Thapa said Congress cadres were already working in the affected districts and that the party would formulate its next steps based on information collected from the ground.

He also pledged that the party would continue working with disaster-affected communities through the upcoming festival season.

“This time, the festivals will not touch us,” he said. “We will continue working alongside those who have lost everything.”

title.rendered: 193 missing in Betrawati as residents await search of destroyed homes

content.rendered:
Betrawati (Nuwakot), September 6

Twelve days have passed since the Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa, but those missing from Betrawati have yet to be found. Shashi Dangol, chairperson of the Betrawati Lakhe Committee, has been collecting data on the number of people missing from different settlements in the area.

According to Dangol, 193 people are missing from six settlements in Betrawati. “It has been 12 days today. We are going through a terrifying period, still hoping that our missing relatives will return,” he said. As hopes of finding them alive have faded, many families have performed last rites using symbolic bodies made from sacred kusha grass. “Families are also performing mourning rituals in memory of their loved ones,” he said.

Dangol has prepared a report on the extent of damage in Betrawati, which he provided to Onlinekhabar. “The settlements around Betrawati Bazaar, from Agitar to Satbise, Kaidletar and Naubise, have suffered massive loss of lives and property. The land, houses and other structures have been destroyed beyond use,” he said.

Betrawati lies on the border of Rasuwa and Nuwakot. Dangol said the data was collected through field visits to Betrawati, which falls under Uttargaya Rural Municipality-5 and Bidur Municipality-10.

Number of missing by settlement

  1. Agitar
    Households: 19
    Population: 80
    Missing: 15
  2. Betrawati, Nuwakot
    Households: 129
    Population: 528
    Missing: 119
  3. Betrawati, Rasuwa
    Households: 50
    Population: 199
    Missing: 11
  4. Satriphant
    Households: 15
    Population: 59
    Missing: 1
  5. Kaidletar
    Households: 76
    Population: 349
    Missing: 39
  6. Naubise
    Households: 10
    Population: 41
    Missing: 8

Although the Newa community makes up a large proportion of Betrawati’s population, the settlement had a mixed population. According to Dangol, the six settlements had a total of 299 households and a population of 1,256, of whom 193 are missing.

Families from various communities, including Dangol, Shrestha, Lawat, Nagarkoti, Magar, Tamang, Rijal, Dhakal, Acharya, Lamichhane and Adhikari, lived in the settlement. However, none of the houses remains intact. “I knew everyone in the settlements, so I remember each person. I collected the data myself, including who has made contact and who is missing,” he said. “There could be a slight variation in the figures, but not a significant difference.” Four injured people were rescued from Betrawati, one of whom later died while receiving treatment.

Hopes of survivors remain, residents call for searches

On Saturday, the 11th day after the flood struck Betrawati, 64-year-old Chandika Shrestha was rescued. She had been swept away along with her house. Following her rescue, residents have urged authorities to search houses that were swept away or destroyed by the flood.

“We need to search every house. We have asked the municipality to conduct searches,” he said. “There is still hope that someone may be alive. A search would at least give us some certainty.”

Where are those who escaped?

Sworadanda lies above Betrawati, where people who lost their homes are living in tents. Those who lost family members have travelled to Kathmandu to perform mourning rituals because it is not possible to do so in Betrawati.

According to Dangol, some people are also staying around Nilkantha School in Bogatitar on the Rasuwa side. “Some are staying in the Nuwakot Durbar area, while others are taking shelter with relatives in Kathmandu. There are currently around 20–22 households living in tents,” Dangol said. “After completing the mourning rituals, the villagers plan to gather there and stay until another arrangement is made.”

Residents are hoping the government will introduce a package, including policies and regulations, for their resettlement. “We hope the government will introduce the necessary policies and regulations and then make settlement arrangements accordingly,” he said. “For now, the focus should be on temporary housing in safe locations, medical treatment for the injured, care for senior citizens and ensuring children can continue their education.”

According to locals, relief supplies are reaching the area, but poor road conditions have caused difficulties. “Relief is arriving, but it appears to be delayed because of the road conditions,” he said.

Calls to preserve Betrawati and relocate the settlement to a safe area

Betrawati has historical significance and is also a site of religious importance, dating back to the treaty with Tibet. Residents have therefore stressed the need to preserve its heritage.

The area is known for Lakhe dances, Gaijatra and Uttargaya Dham. Betrawati is also considered a sacred site for performing ancestral rites and is an important commercial centre. “Since Betrawati provides the shortest route connecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, efforts should be made to build a paved road in the area and develop the settlement in a safe location,” Dangol said.

Betrawati residents had completed preparations to organise the Janai Purnima fair, Gaijatra and Krishna Ashtami chariot procession this year and to participate in the seventh National Lakhe Dance Competition scheduled for Asoj 9 and10 in Chitwan. However, all the programmes have been cancelled. Locals have stressed the need to preserve these historical and cultural traditions.

Plan to build a memorial

Residents are planning to build a memorial park in Betrawati in memory of those who went missing in the flood. “Betrawati will never be able to forget our relatives and loved ones, nor will we forget them. We will build a beautiful Betrawati Park and memorial in their memory,” Committee Chairperson Dangol said.

“We will carry out rehabilitation and reconstruction on either side of Betrawati, taking the geographical conditions into account, with the aim of establishing permanent settlements in safe locations.”

title.rendered: Missions abroad instructed to operate a separate account for depositing aid funds

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The government has instructed Nepali missions abroad to operate separate bank accounts for those wishing to contribute to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, missions have been told to use other accounts since it is not possible to send contributions directly to the fund, and doing so would create complications where transactions exceed a set limit.

“As per existing rules, missions have been instructed to use their various existing accounts or open new ones. Relief funds will be collected through these accounts from the Nepali diaspora, foreign nationals, local organisations, and community groups,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated in its daily press bulletin.

Missions will be required to maintain a daily record of funds collected in the prescribed format. The collected amount must be transferred each month to the designated relief account. Until now, the government had arranged for contributions to be deposited directly into the Disaster Relief Fund’s account.

The ministry and Nepali missions abroad have also informed that they are working in close coordination with all friendly nations to try to keep travel advisories limited only to the specific areas affected by the floods.

“It is also being clearly highlighted that other parts of the country remain open and safe for travel and tourism,” the ministry said.

title.rendered: Nepali lawmakers seek Bhutan’s support for compensation over Rasuwa flood damage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Nepali lawmakers have urged Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay to support Nepal’s efforts to seek compensation for the damage caused by the devastating floods in Rasuwa.

The Nepali representatives met Tobgay on the sidelines of the ongoing South Asian Regional Parliamentary Forum in Bhutan.

During the meeting, Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmakers Ashish Gajurel and Ashok Chaudhary briefed the Bhutanese prime minister on the loss of lives, property and infrastructure caused by the floods in Rasuwa.

Gajurel said Nepal’s contribution to global climate change is negligible, yet the country is bearing the severe consequences of climate-related disasters.

He argued that affected countries need more than sympathy and called for compensation and fair support.

Nepal has already formally approached the Loss and Damage Fund Board, seeking compensation for losses and damage caused by the Rasuwa floods. The government sent a formal letter to the board on August 31.

Gajurel and Chaudhary informed Tobgay about Nepal’s initiative and sought Bhutan’s support for Nepal’s efforts at the international level for climate justice and compensation.

Tobgay expressed his sorrow over the disaster in Nepal and pledged to take initiatives for necessary support.

He also emphasised the need to provide compensation to countries that have contributed little to climate change but are bearing a disproportionate share of its impacts.

The Nepali representatives said cooperation among South Asian countries would be important in pushing for greater climate justice and support for countries affected by climate-related disasters.

title.rendered: Nepal’s Bhawana–Sunita win silver medal in CAVA beach volleyball

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

In the women’s category of CAVA (Continental) Beach Volleyball, Nepal’s pair Sunita Rai and Bhawana Dangi have won the silver medal.

In the final match held in Thimphu, Bhutan, the Sunita–Bhawana pair had to settle for silver after losing to India’s Deepika–Pabitra pair.

The Nepali team won the first set 21–17, but lost the second and third sets, missing out on the gold medal. The Indian team took the gold by winning the second set 21–15 and the third set 15–5.

Nepal’s other pair, Kamala Pun and Kopila Rana, had already been eliminated by the same Indian pair, Deepika–Pabitra, in the semifinal.

In the men’s category, the title was won by Sri Lanka’s Dilipa Sadun Madusanka pair.

Nepal was represented by the pairs Mahendra Shrestha and Rajkumar Niroula, as well as Jhaman Singh Darji and Sharan Karki, but neither pair advanced to the semifinals.

title.rendered: Korean foreign minister: We will help in post-flood reconstruction, advocate for Nepal in international forums

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

South Korea has pledged to support Nepal in its post-flood reconstruction efforts following the Bhotekoshi disaster. Korea expressed this commitment during talks between Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal and South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun, held Sunday at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Singha Durbar.

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the two ministers held detailed discussions on the ongoing search, rescue, and relief operations following the devastating flood that struck the Bhotekoshi River on August 26, as well as on the search for missing Korean nationals.

The ministry said Minister Khanal thanked the South Korean government for deploying a Korean disaster relief team and an inter-agency rapid response team to the flood-affected areas.

Praising the humanitarian assistance and supply of relief materials, Minister Khanal said building disaster-resilient, sustainable, and strong infrastructure in the days ahead is a top priority for the Nepal government, and expressed hope for continued support from Korea toward this goal.

In response, Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said the Korean government stands fully ready to help Nepal with post-disaster reconstruction.

Pointing out that the international community bears historic responsibility for the damage suffered by countries like Nepal due to climate change, he stressed that Nepal and Korea should join hands to raise awareness on this issue at global forums such as COP.

He also pledged that South Korea would add its voice in support of the international financial assistance Nepal should receive from the global community.

At the end of the meeting, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that both ministers reaffirmed their commitment to work closely to further strengthen and elevate the long-standing friendship, mutual trust, and cooperation-based bilateral relationship to new heights.

Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun is in Nepal on a three-day visit.

title.rendered: Landslide blocks Karnali Highway for 19 hours

content.rendered:
Kalikot, September 6

A major mudslide at Gagane Khola in Shubh Kalika Rural Municipality-1 of Kalikot has completely blocked the Surkhet–Jumla section of the Karnali Highway. According to the District Police Office, Kalikot, the highway was blocked after a large landslide fell at Gagane Khola at around 6:30 pm on Saturday.

Vehicles travelling to Jumla from Surkhet via Dailekh and Kalikot, as well as those heading towards Surkhet from Jumla, have been stranded on the road. Passengers have also been left stranded. Some have turned back and taken shelter in Rakam and Khidkijiula in Dailekh. Passengers travelling from Jumla and Kalikot towards Surkhet and Nepalgunj have also turned back and spent the night in Hulma Bazaar.

DSP Him Bahadur Chhetri, chief of the District Police Office, Kalikot, said efforts have been underway since Sunday morning to clear the road, but the large volume of debris means the work will take time.

Police have urged travellers to check road conditions before setting out, as landslides and other road obstructions may occur at other points along the Karnali Highway.

title.rendered: Shekhar Koirala vows to make sacrifices for party unity

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Nepali Congress leader Dr Shekhar Koirala has said he is ready to make any sacrifices necessary from his side to maintain unity within the party.

During a meeting with party President Gagan Thapa on Sunday, Koirala said the country, democracy and national interests were currently facing difficult circumstances. “He made it clear that there is no alternative to keeping the party united and that he is ready to make whatever sacrifices are necessary from his side for this purpose,” Koirala’s secretariat said, describing his remarks during the meeting.

In response, President Thapa said he too was in favour of maintaining party unity. The two leaders discussed ways to resolve internal problems within the Nepali Congress as well as the situation in flood-affected areas. They also discussed the latest situation in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

title.rendered: Gorkha administration urges trekkers to avoid Manaslu and Larke Pass routes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The District Administration Office, Gorkha, has urged trekkers to avoid the Manaslu and Larke Pass trekking routes until further notice.

Issuing a public notice on Sunday, the administration asked trekkers who are preparing to travel or are already on the routes to suspend their trekking plans until another notice is issued.

A flood in the Therang Khola at Namrung on Sunday morning caused extensive damage to trekking trails, hotels and hydropower projects in the area.

According to the administration, the flood swept away the iron bridge connecting Chumnubri Rural Municipality wards 4 and 2, as well as the suspension bridge over the Budhi Gandaki River connecting the rural municipality with the Namrung forest.

The administration issued the notice following the flood, stating that trekkers preparing for or currently undertaking journeys along the Manaslu or Larke Pass trekking routes should refrain from trekking until further notice.

title.rendered: Nuwakot to hold meeting on management of Rasuwa flood holding centres

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 6

Authorities in Nuwakot will hold discussions with government and non-governmental organisations on the management of holding centres accommodating people rescued after the devastating Rasuwa floods.

The District Administration Office, Nuwakot has called a meeting for Monday at 4 pm to discuss the management of holding centres and other related issues.

Representatives of government and non-governmental organisations working in the district have been invited to attend the meeting, which will be held at the hall of the District Administration Office.

These centres have been established in Nuwakot and Rasuwa to accommodate people displaced or rescued following the August 26 floods. According to an earlier situation report from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 19 holding centres in Nuwakot were accommodating 2,653 people.

The centres have been providing temporary shelter and relief to people affected by the floods, which severely damaged settlements along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors.

The meeting is expected to focus on improving coordination among agencies involved in managing the centres and addressing the needs of people staying there.

title.rendered: Search for 93 missing Rasuwagadhi hydropower workers expands into forest

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 6

The search for 93 employees and workers missing from the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project has been expanded beyond the project’s powerhouse to nearby forests and difficult mountain terrain.

An eight-member team of experienced rock climbers has been deployed to search areas where workers may have fled to escape the flood, including forests around the Ghattekhola camp.

The project company said it mobilised skilled personnel associated with the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association through its own efforts. An eight-member team from Himalaya Summit Club Pvt Ltd is carrying out ground searches in the area.

According to company secretary Narnath Neupane, the team initially searched around Timure before being flown by helicopter to Ghattekhola, where it continued the search from 7:30 am on Saturday.

“We suspect that some may have fled uphill into the forest to escape the flood,” Neupane said. “Most of those who fled towards the forest have already made contact, but we are searching to see whether anyone was injured while fleeing and may be stranded somewhere, unable to walk.”

Some people who fled the project site during the flood and reached forests and higher ground have already been accounted for. However, the company said the search was being continued because some workers could have been injured and become trapped in the forest or other difficult areas.

The search team is focusing on possible escape routes, places where people could have taken shelter and hard-to-reach sections of the surrounding hills.

The expanded search follows an operation inside the project’s powerhouse on Saturday.

A Nepal Army rescue team, accompanied by former project employee and senior geologist and tunnel expert Bishnu Shiwakoti, reached the project site in four helicopters after conducting a reconnaissance of the area.

The rescue team entered the powerhouse after clearing debris and searched around the control room and other sections of the building. However, the control room was found completely buried under mud and silt.

Mud, debris and pieces of timber carried by the flood had reached above the level of the overhead travelling (EOT) crane, according to the company.

The company had estimated that between four and 14 people could have been trapped inside the powerhouse. However, Saturday’s search did not find anyone.

The rescue team has since left the powerhouse, while the focus has shifted to areas outside the building, particularly forests and surrounding mountainous terrain.

A total of 93 employees and workers involved in the project remain missing following the flood. Seven other workers who were at the project site have already been rescued.

title.rendered: Over 80,000 LPG cylinders brought into Kathmandu via alternative routes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Nearly 88,000 cooking gas cylinders have entered the Kathmandu Valley over the past three days through alternative routes after a landslide blocked the Krishnabhir section of the Prithvi Highway in Dhading.

According to the Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC), a total of 87,877 LPG cylinders were brought into the Valley between September 3 and 5 to prevent disruptions to cooking gas supplies.

The corporation said it had arranged for LPG cylinders to be refilled at industries in the southern plains and transported to Kathmandu through alternative routes after the highway was blocked.

Of the total, 24,494 cylinders arrived in Kathmandu on September 3, followed by 34,134 cylinders on September 4 and 29,249 cylinders on September 5.

The NOC said the arrangement was made after taking into account the possible impact of the road obstruction on LPG supplies to the Valley.

Under the alternative arrangement, cylinders belonging to gas industries in Kathmandu, Dhading and Kavrepalanchok are being transported to industries in Bara, Parsa, Makwanpur, Chitwan, Nawalparasi, Dhanusha and Mahottari for refilling. They are then being brought back to Kathmandu through alternative routes.

The cylinders entering the Valley through this arrangement include brands such as Shree, Surya, Om, Shriram, Sagar, Saibaba/Shreekrishna, Shreemaya (Kavsons), Lokpriya (Ugrachandi), Everest/Sugam, Nepal, HP (Himalayan), STC (Metro Kathmandu), Siddhartha, Himal (Gaurishankar), Sitashree and Namaste.

The NOC said LPG from 16 industries is being brought into the Valley continuously through the alternative routes.

The corporation said the alternative supply arrangement would remain in place until the Krishnabhir section of the Prithvi Highway is restored to regular operation.

The Krishna Bhir section has been affected by landslides and erosion, disrupting one of the main road links between Kathmandu and the rest of the country.

The NOC said it would continue monitoring the situation and maintain LPG supplies through the alternative route until normal road access is restored.

title.rendered: When the roads disappeared, helicopters became the lifeline for flood-hit Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Across parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, communities that had always depended on roads to reach markets, hospitals and neighbouring towns were suddenly cut off. The Bhotekoshi flood had erased much of the usual way in and out. There was, however, one way still open: the sky.

Within hours of the disaster on August 26, Nepal’s helicopter operators were called into action. Military and private helicopters began flying into some of the country’s most difficult terrain, carrying out people stranded by the flood and taking food, medicine and other relief supplies into places that could no longer be reached by road.

More than a week later, the operation continues.

According to the latest figures from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 1,341 people have died and nearly 5,000 remain missing. A total of 13,095 people have been rescued so far.

The Nepal Army has rescued 4,157 people, Nepal Police 4,068 and the Armed Police Force 4,870.

Among those airlifted by the Nepal Army were 273 foreign nationals and 3,684 Nepali citizens.

The numbers illustrate the scale of an aerial rescue operation that has unfolded across the mountains and river valleys of northern Nepal.

Flights coordinated by the Nepal Army have reached 881, while private helicopter companies have conducted another 129 flights. On Friday alone, 96 flights were made. But the helicopters have done more than evacuate people. They have become the bridge between isolated communities and the outside world.

When the roads disappeared

The destruction left behind by the flood explains why the helicopters have become so important.

Between Rasuwagadhi and Muglin, 41 bridges were damaged and 35 were swept away. Of the 64 suspension bridges along the same stretch, 53 were destroyed. The result was a huge break in Nepal’s transport network.

Much of Rasuwa, large parts of Nuwakot and some areas of Dhading were effectively cut off. For people living in these areas, the problem was not simply getting out of a disaster zone. It was getting anything in.

Food and relief materials had to reach communities. Rescue teams had to move. People with urgent medical needs had to be evacuated. Families searching for missing relatives needed access to places that could no longer be reached by road.

That was where the helicopters came in.

“The helicopter has once again demonstrated its importance during a crisis,” said Pratap Jung Pandey, president of the Airlines Operators Association of Nepal and managing director of Kailash Helicopter.

A fleet mobilised for a national emergency

The Nepal Army established helicopter bases at Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu and Battar in Nuwakot, creating two key points from which rescue operations could be coordinated.

The mobilisation began almost immediately after news of the flood reached the authorities on August 26.

Pandey said the government instructed all helicopter companies to remain on standby for rescue operations. Helicopters based in Kathmandu and nearby areas were then deployed to the affected areas.

Since then, the aircraft have been moving continuously between the capital and the disaster zone—bringing people out and supplies in.

For communities surrounded by destroyed roads and bridges, each flight has meant a connection that otherwise would not exist.

Flying where the geography is unforgiving

Getting a helicopter into the mountains is not as simple as flying from one point to another.

The affected areas are surrounded by steep terrain, narrow river valleys and rapidly changing mountain weather. This time, pilots also had to contend with unusually heavy air traffic over the disaster zone.

Mukesh Dangol, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, said the rescue flights are being conducted under what is known as a Class G operation.

Unlike controlled airspace, aircraft operating in Class G airspace are not under the direct control of an air traffic controller in the same way. Pilots must rely heavily on communication with one another and maintain constant awareness of other aircraft in the area.

Then came another complication: drones.

The destruction in Rasuwa and the rescue effort attracted intense attention from national and international media. Numerous drones were flown over the affected areas to capture images and video.

The increased drone activity posed an additional risk to helicopters operating at low altitude. The Civil Aviation Authority had to issue NOTAMs several times after drone flights began affecting helicopter operations.

Despite the difficult terrain, changing weather and crowded skies, aviation authorities say flight safety has been maintained.

Pilots accustomed to the mountains

Nepal’s geography, difficult as it can be for aviation, has also given its helicopter pilots years of experience in precisely the conditions they are facing now.

Helicopters regularly fly through narrow mountain valleys and river gorges. Pilots operating in Nepal are accustomed to weather that can change within minutes and landing sites where there is little room for error.

Pandey said most of the pilots involved in the current rescue operation are Nepali.

“This is the offseason, so we do not have foreign pilots,” he said.

He said Nepali pilots had been able to handle the demanding rescue operation because of their experience flying in challenging conditions.

The current operation, he said, is comparable in some ways to the intense helicopter activity seen around Lukla during the spring tourism season.

“Continuous flying has made our pilots accustomed to this,” he said.

The Nepal Army’s own pilots have also played a central role, flying into areas where roads and other forms of transportation have disappeared.

The first day set the pace

The intensity of the operation can be seen in the flight records from Tribhuvan International Airport.

On August 26, the day the flood struck, helicopters made 49 flights from Kathmandu to affected areas.

Sixteen flights were made between Kathmandu and Timure, six to Trishuli, six to Rasuwa and nine to Dhunche. There was also one flight to Mailung, two to Dhading and nine to Syafrubesi.

Nine flights had to be diverted.

Six Nepal Army helicopters and 10 private helicopters were involved that day.

The following day, another 40 flights were made from Kathmandu. Operations were particularly concentrated around Trishuli and Dhunche, with Dhunche alone receiving 17 flights.

On August 28, the third day after the disaster, 21 flights were made, including six each to Trishuli and Rasuwa.

The operation continued at a steady pace: 21 flights on August 29, 22 on August 30, 34 on August 31, 27 on September 1, 24 on September 2 and 28 on September 3.

The figures do not include flights operated from the Trishuli helicopter base.

A rescue operation against a staggering loss

The helicopters are operating against the backdrop of one of the country’s most destructive recent disasters.

The floods have damaged 7,570 private homes, according to the latest government figures, while the estimated economic loss has reached around Rs 400 billion.

Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan have all been affected, with the destruction particularly severe along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors.

For those caught in the disaster, however, the economic cost is secondary to the immediate human toll.

People are still searching for missing family members. Thousands have lost homes. Communities are waiting for food and other basic supplies. And in places where bridges and roads have disappeared, reaching those people remains a challenge.

The helicopters have filled that gap.

A small fleet carrying a huge burden

Nepal has around a dozen helicopter companies with a combined fleet of 32 helicopters, according to the Airlines Operators Association of Nepal.

The sector currently has around 45 helicopter pilots, with operators usually adding more pilots during the peak tourism season.

That is a relatively small fleet for a country with Nepal’s geography—and an even smaller one when confronted with a disaster of this scale.

Yet virtually the entire available capacity has been pushed into the response.

The helicopters have carried thousands of people away from danger, delivered relief supplies and kept isolated communities connected to the rescue operation.

They have also offered something less tangible but equally important: a way into places that, after the flood, appeared to have no way in.

When the Bhote Koshi swept away roads and bridges, it severed the physical links connecting northern Nepal.

The helicopters became the link that remained.

title.rendered: Krishnabhir track widened to facilitate road reconstruction

content.rendered:
Chitwan, September 6

A track opened above Krishnabhir along the Prithvi Highway to transport construction materials and equipment is being widened as preparations continue to reopen the road section blocked by a landslide.

The track was opened after trees and bushes were cleared from the upper section of the landslide site, allowing access for construction work.

According to Sachendra Mishra, an engineer with the western section of the Naubise-Muglin Road Project, a track about four metres wide has been opened in both directions along the top of the hill after continuous work above the landslide site. “Work has begun to widen the track that was opened yesterday,” he said.

Several tasks remain, including cutting the slope and roadside wall, widening and gravelling the road, adjusting the grade and managing the landslide according to the design. Mishra said it would still take some time before the road could be opened to public vehicles.

He said work was being expedited with the aim of making the road usable by public vehicles by the end of Bhadra. “An environment has now been created to proceed according to the design. There is no shortage of the technical equipment or manpower required for construction. The road will now be built according to the design, making it easier to carry out the work,” he said.

According to Mishra, the track currently being used is primarily for construction workers and the transportation of construction materials.

The new access track was opened by construction company Sharma-JIV JV. Site manager Engineer Ishwar Nepal said the track is about 20 metres above the main road and 350 metres long.

“After the track was opened, it has become easier to transport construction materials and fuel and for workers to travel to and from the site,” he said. “It is currently being used only for construction purposes. It is not a new road opened for the general public.”

According to Nepal, considerable work remains, including slope cutting, cutting the roadside wall, placing rocks and adjusting the road grade. He said the route had become passable on foot for the general public in emergencies.

He added that road construction would now proceed from both ends according to the approved design.

More heavy equipment was added to the site as of today. The number of excavators has been increased to seven with the addition of two more. One JCB, one loader and two bulldozers are also being used. Nepal said additional equipment would be deployed as required.

title.rendered: Nepal reach ACC Premier Cup semi-finals with third straight win

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Nepal advanced to the semi-finals of the ACC Premier Cup with a third consecutive victory, defeating Saudi Arabia by five wickets on Sunday.

Chasing a target of 191, Nepal reached 192 for five in 41 overs. Gulshan Jha remained unbeaten on 44, while captain Rohit Paudel scored an unbeaten 24. Ishan Pandey contributed 40 and Dev Khanal 39, while Aasif Sheikh and Arjun Kumal scored 20 and 15, respectively.

For Saudi Arabia, Istiyaq Ahmed and Muhammad Atif took two wickets each, while Mohammad Hisham claimed one.

Earlier, Saudi Arabia were bowled out for 190 in 49.2 overs after winning the toss and opting to bat. Abdul Waheed top-scored with 77, while Muhammad Atif made 30 and Mohammad Hisham Sheikh scored 18.

For Nepal, captain Sandeep Lamichhane took three wickets for 19 runs in 10 overs. Lalit Rajbanshi claimed two wickets for 26 runs, while Dipendra Singh Airee took three wickets and Sher Malla one.

Nepal had previously defeated Bahrain and Malaysia. The team will face Hong Kong in its final group-stage match on Tuesday, after which the group winner will be decided.
