title.rendered: Gagan Thapa holds separate talks with Purna Bahadur Khadka and Shekhar Koirala

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has held separate discussions with former Vice President Purna Bahadur Khadka and party leader Dr Shekhar Koirala.

A party leader said Thapa met former Vice President Khadka on Saturday and Koirala on Sunday.

According to a Nepali Congress office-bearer, Thapa held separate meetings with both leaders. “The president had already planned to meet Purna and Shekhar. The meetings have taken place. The president will brief the Working Committee on the issues discussed,” the leader told Onlinekhabar.

The party’s Working Committee is meeting today to discuss the upcoming General Convention as well as relief and reconstruction efforts following the flood.

The party is preparing to postpone the ward-level conventions by one week to continue dialogue with Khadka and Koirala. The lower-level conventions are likely to be rescheduled while keeping the date of the central General Convention—October 2 to 4—unchanged.

Khadka and Koirala do not appear to agree with the General Convention schedule proposed by the faction led by former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba, which has proposed holding the convention in November.

Neither Khadka nor Koirala attended the meeting at which the Deuba faction proposed its General Convention schedule. They also did not participate in the final day of the national gathering organised by the Deuba faction.

title.rendered: Eight arrested from casino, including police inspector and rural municipality chairman

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Eight people, including a Nepal Police inspector and a rural municipality chairman, have been arrested from a casino.

SP Pawan Kumar Bhattarai of the District Police Office, Parsa, said the eight were arrested from Pokhariya Area Police Office, Parsa, and included Nepal Police Inspector Pradeep Poudel and 36-year-old Jaswant Yadav, chairman of Sakhuwa Prasauni Rural Municipality.

They are accused of entering a casino called Golden Finger Gaming Zone Pvt. Ltd., located in Birgunj-14, Gandak, and gambling there.

Those arrested include Inspector Poudel; 36-year-old Jaswant Yadav of Sakhuwa Prasauni Rural Municipality-6, Parsa; 30-year-old Chandan Sahani from the same area; and 39-year-old Om Prakash Baitha of Birgunj Metropolitan City-11.

Also arrested were casino staff accused of letting Nepali citizens into the casino: 28-year-old Bijay Kumar Patel of Birgunj-14, 31-year-old Dinesh Kumar Patel of Birgunj-25, 49-year-old Jaydev Sah of Mahottari’s Pipra Rural Municipality-5, and 50-year-old Pradeshi Sah of Birgunj-12.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi flood: 244 bodies brought to TU Teaching Hospital

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The bodies of 244 people who died in the Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa on August 26 have been brought to Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj.

Dr Gopal Chaudhary, head of the hospital’s forensic laboratory, confirmed that 244 bodies of flood victims had been brought to the hospital.

Of the 244 bodies, 161 have been temporarily managed, while 24 identified bodies have already been handed over to their families and relatives, Dr Chaudhary said.

Fifty-nine bodies are currently at the hospital. The hospital said some of the bodies are yet to undergo postmortem examinations and will be managed after the examinations are completed.

—RSS

title.rendered: Four youths from same village working at Upper Trishuli-1 remain missing; village left in mourning

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Four young men from the same village in Kanchanpur remain out of contact more than two weeks after the devastating floods struck the Rasuwa–Bhotekoshi area.

All four worked at the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project in Rasuwa and hail from Dekhatbhuli village in Kanchanpur. The missing are Padam Singh Saud (43) of Lalajhadi Rural Municipality-5, and Kalu Rana (30), Rikesh Rana (29), and Kreshan Rana (23), all from Krishnapur Municipality-3.

According to family sources, the four had finished their night shift and were sleeping in the morning before the flood struck. There has been no contact with them since. Even after two weeks, their families say their whereabouts remain unknown.

None of them has been in touch with their families. Lalajhadi-5 Ward Chairperson Pahal Bahadur Thapa said the entire village has been plunged into mourning with four young men from the same community missing at once.

He said the affected families are extremely worried that there has been no contact so far, and have appealed to the government, local administration, and all concerned authorities to intensify search efforts and make their situation known publicly.

title.rendered: Third batch of gas cylinders sent to Bhotekoshi flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Gas entrepreneurs have sent a third batch of 75 Sagarmatha-brand LPG cylinders to Rasuwa as relief for victims of the Bhotekoshi flood.

According to Diwan Chand, president of the Nepal LPG Gas Industry Association, the cylinders were dispatched from the Nepal Oil Corporation premises in Babermahal on Saturday afternoon under the responsibility of the District Administration Office, Rasuwa.

The association had previously decided to provide a total of 1,250 gas cylinders to flood-affected communities. Of this amount, 232 Nepal Gas cylinders have already been delivered to the affected areas in two batches, Chand said.

He said the association had initially planned to send a large quantity of gas at once, but transportation difficulties caused by the closure of the Prithvi Highway forced them to send smaller quantities in several batches.

Similarly, another organisation of gas entrepreneurs, the LPG Gas Industry Association Nepal, has already provided 150 gas cylinders to flood victims in two batches—100 in the first and 50 in the second.

Dolpa, September 6

The Jajarkot-Dolpa section of the Bheri Corridor has reopened after a dry landslide blocked the road at Chhipredaha in Dolpa on Sunday morning. According to DSP Anil Raj Giri, the road was reopened after the landslide debris was cleared.

The landslide occurred at around 8:30 am at Chhipredaha in Tripurasundari Municipality-5, disrupting traffic and leaving vehicles travelling to and from Dolpa stranded at the site.

With the road reopened, the stranded vehicles have resumed their journeys to their respective destinations. Police have urged passengers and drivers to exercise caution as the road remains vulnerable to further landslides.

title.rendered: Palpa records 231 dengue cases in less than two months

content.rendered:
Palpa, September 6

Palpa has recorded the highest number of dengue infections among the 12 districts of Lumbini Province, with 231 cases confirmed in less than two months of the current fiscal year.

According to the District Health Office, Palpa, 231 people tested positive for dengue between the beginning of the fiscal year 2083/84 BS and Bhadra 20. The number is the highest reported from any district in the province during the period.

Dengue cases have been detected at four major hospitals in the district—Palpa Hospital in Tansen, Rampur Hospital, Lumbini Medical College in Prabhas and United Mission Hospital in Tansen. Cases are also increasingly being reported by other health facilities and private medical centres.

Health Office information officer Madhusudan Bhattarai attributed the rise to climate change and an expansion in dengue testing. He said a significant number of patients from outside the district treated at two major private hospitals in Palpa had also tested positive, contributing to the district’s high case count.

Palpa recorded 432 dengue cases in fiscal year 2082/83 BS, 510 in 2081/82 BS and 686 in 2080/81 BS.

Dengue is transmitted through the bite of infected female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, whose breeding increases during the rainy season. Health authorities have urged people to eliminate mosquito breeding sites and take precautions against mosquito bites.

title.rendered: As families disappear, children face a growing trafficking risk

content.rendered:
Nine-year-old Prabha (name changed) is a third-grader from Uttargaya Rural Municipality-5 in Rasuwa.

Before August 26, her days were ordinary. She went to school, played with her siblings and spent time with her family.

Her father worked at a nearby hydropower project. Her mother was a farmer. At home were her brother and sister. Then the flood came.

Since that day, Prabha has been unable to contact any of them. She is now alone.

Ten-year-old Ganga (name changed), a fourth-grader from Pairebeshi, Rasuwa, knows something of what that uncertainty feels like. She had been on her way to school when the flood struck. When her teacher heard that floodwaters were coming, she took Ganga to higher ground.

Ganga survived, but she does not know whether her family did.

Her father, who worked at a hydropower project, has been out of contact since the flood. Her mother is unreachable. Her grandfather and grandmother are unaccounted for. So are her maternal uncle and brother.

“My grandfather, grandmother, mom, aunt, and brother were all at home,” Ganga says, crying. “Where could they be now?”

For children like Prabha and Ganga, surviving the flood was only the beginning of their ordeal. More than a week after the disaster, authorities still do not have an official figure for the number of children who have been separated from their parents or remain unable to contact them.

As of September 3, Madhav Lamichhane, principal of Nilkanta Secondary School in Uttargaya Rural Municipality-5, said 74 school students from his rural municipality had already lost their parents. Many students had also lost their shelter. But the wider picture remains unclear.

The respective districts are still working to compile data on children who have remained out of contact with their parents, according to Nepal Police spokesperson Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Abi Narayan Kafle.

“It could take some more time to get the exact figure of children who haven’t been able to contact their parents,” Kafle says.

The police, he adds, are currently occupied with relief, recovery, security, rescue, investigation and transportation.

A UNICEF report published on August 31 offers another indication of the scale. It estimates that at least 107 children may have been separated from their parents or caregivers.

The report estimates that another 22,100 children require urgent child protection support, including mental health and psychosocial support, family tracing and reunification, case management and referral services.

The numbers point to a problem that goes beyond finding missing family members.

When children are suddenly left without parents, caregivers, shelter or the protection of familiar adults, they can become vulnerable to trafficking, exploitation, abuse and child marriage.

Tilotam Poudel, president of the Child Zone of Peace National Campaign (CZOP), says identifying these children must therefore be the government’s first priority.

“Nepal Child Rights Council should actively coordinate with the local level, prepare data, and take the necessary steps for their protection,” he says.

Poudel says Rasuwa’s history of human trafficking makes the situation particularly concerning.

“In times of crisis, particularly when children lack shelter and parental support, traffickers can easily take advantage and lure them,” he says.

CZOP, a child rights organisation, has also urged that children affected by the disaster receive priority attention, with safety, health, nutrition, protection and education treated as special priorities.

“During times like this, children can be at risk, including being vulnerable to trafficking and exploitation,” the organisation says, adding that child-friendly psychosocial counselling and support are essential to help children deal with fear, stress, anxiety and mental trauma.

For child protection workers, the concern is not simply what is happening to children today, but what could happen in the weeks ahead.

Narbada Soraili Magar, Protection Head at Anahat Nepal, an organisation working to prevent human trafficking, says previous disasters have shown how quickly children separated from their parents can become vulnerable.

“During the earthquake and Covid-19 pandemic, children who had lost their parents were found being transported from one place to another,” she says.

At the time, essential vehicles carrying vegetables, water and dairy products were allowed to travel, and children were found being transferred through such vehicles.

Magar fears similar risks could emerge as the immediate fear of the Rasuwa disaster begins to fade.

The presence of social activists in affected areas may decrease, while transportation is expected to resume. That combination, she says, could make it easier for vulnerable children to move without adequate monitoring.

Kathmandu could be a particularly important destination, she says, as many children may have relatives in the capital. Such movements have been seen after previous disasters.

Magar wants authorities to strengthen monitoring at checkpoints in Kathmandu.

“If there are any children, the authorities should ask who they are travelling with, what their destination is, and whether they have someone to receive them there,” she says.

“Children whose travel arrangements cannot be verified should be intercepted and handed over to their closest relatives, organisations, holding centres, or other trusted individuals.”

Nepal has seen the consequences of inadequate protection after disasters before.

Following the 2015 earthquake, children who had lost their parents became vulnerable to trafficking. In May 2015, authorities in India rescued more than 20 children from a human trafficking network targeting families who had lost their livelihoods in the earthquake.

UNICEF reported that at least 245 children were intercepted from being trafficked and unnecessarily or illegally placed in children’s care homes in the nearly two months after the first earthquake hit Nepal.

According to Children and Women in Social Service and Human Rights (CWISH), 104 children lost their parents in the 2015 earthquake.

The Anti-Human Trafficking Bureau (AHTB) of Nepal Police has continued to record child victims of trafficking. It recorded 163 trafficking cases in fiscal year 2022/23, with 81 children among the victims. In 2023/24, there were 170 cases involving 76 child victims. In 2024/25, 151 cases were recorded, with 80 children among the victims. In 2025/26, 214 cases were recorded, involving 85 child victims.

Magar says the lessons from previous disasters should prompt authorities to act before children begin moving out of affected areas.

She urges local governments in Kathmandu not to overlook children simply because they come from another municipality and calls for greater monitoring of vehicles entering the capital.

But trafficking is not the only danger.

Child protection experts also warn of the risks of child marriage, exploitation and abuse.

Anju Bhattarai, Urban Protection Coordinator at World Vision International Nepal, says the children affected by the floods are facing a major crisis.

“The current situation is a huge crisis for these affected children. If we cannot address this crisis immediately, it will have a long-term effect,” she says.

The challenge is made harder because the disaster has also affected the institutions expected to protect children.

Bhattarai says the child protection support system has become weak because local-level authorities themselves have been affected. At the same time, she says federal and provincial child protection systems have been significantly active.

The National Child Rights Council (NCRC) is conducting protection assessments.

For Bhattarai, protection also means giving children somewhere safe to be children.

She calls for child-friendly spaces where affected children can play and share their experiences, and says child protection should be mainstreamed throughout the disaster response.

She also stresses the importance of protecting children’s privacy.

“No photo, video, or anything that would reveal the identity of the affected children should be made public,” she says. “Before anyone takes their photo or video, they should obtain consent from the concerned people.”

Authorities say they are aware of the risks.

Rajan Limbu, Superintendent of Police and spokesperson of the AHTB, says police know that children who have lost or remained out of contact with their parents are particularly vulnerable to trafficking.

“Any family member or organisation taking care of children who are not in contact with their parents must inform the concerned authority whenever there is any kind of movement,” he says to Onlinekhabar.

“Since this is a critical time, and we are aware of the potential risk, we have been preparing ourselves accordingly,” Limbu adds.

The NCRC says it has also taken steps to mitigate the risk.

It has formed a committee to assess the condition of children and asked local governments to screen children to determine how many are with their parents and how many are not.

The council says the process of identifying and safely handing over children must be formal.

“We have strictly instructed the concerned authorities to hand over the children only after completing all the official procedures,” says Durga Prasad Chalise, member secretary of the NCRC. “The children should be handed over only through official channels.”

For Prabha and Ganga, however, the most immediate question remains unanswered.

They survived the flood.

They are still waiting to know what happened to the families they left behind.

Considering the privacy and safety of the children, their names have been changed.

title.rendered: Senior Maithili litterateur Revati Raman Lal dies at 83

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, September 6

Senior Maithili litterateur Revati Raman Lal (PhD) has died at the age of 83. He died while undergoing treatment at a hospital in Janakpurdham on Saturday evening, according to his family.

Lal, who held a PhD in Maithili, was a retired employee of Nepal Rastra Bank. He made significant contributions to various literary genres, including short stories, poetry, songs, essays, screenplays, interviews, travelogues and folk literature. His first published Maithili work, the song Saraswati Vandana, was published in 1960.

His major works include Sakshatkar, Madhav Nahi Aela Madhupursan, Hamar Bidesh Bhraman, Mahakavi Vidyapati and Khissa Pihani. He was also the writer of the television serial Vidyapati and editor of the Maithili quarterly Naimikanan.

For his contribution to literature, he received several honours, including the Mithila Ratna, Jyotirishwar Literary Award, Provincial Talent Award and Nepal Vidyapati Maithili Language-Literature Award.

Lal had been residing at his home in Janakpurdham Sub-Metropolitan City-11. He was born on March 2, 1943, in Khirkhiria village of the former Devadiha Village Development Committee-3 in Dhanusha.

title.rendered: 21,000 doses of cholera vaccine sent to Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

A total of 21,000 doses of cholera vaccine have been sent to Rasuwa in view of the risk of a cholera outbreak following the devastating Bhotekoshi flood on August 26.

The vaccines, received with support from the World Health Organization (WHO), were transported to Rasuwa by a Nepal Army helicopter on Sunday morning.

Health Minister Nisha Mehta has directed authorities to immediately provide medicines, vaccines, health supplies and necessary public health services in flood-affected areas to reduce the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases.

Health officials said that, in line with the minister’s directive, efforts have been launched to send vaccines and medicines to the affected areas, strengthen disease surveillance, pay special attention to safe drinking water and sanitation, and mobilise health workers as needed.

As the flood has damaged water sources and distribution systems, increasing the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases, priority has been given to prevention, early detection and treatment in the affected areas.

title.rendered: Congress prepares to postpone lower-level conventions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The Nepali Congress is preparing to postpone its ward-level conventions for its 15th General Convention by one week. The issue of rescheduling the lower-level conventions will be discussed at a meeting of the party’s Working Committee scheduled for today.

The party is planning to revise the schedule for the lower-level conventions while keeping the previously announced date for the central General Convention unchanged. Party President Gagan Thapa has called a meeting of the Working Committee for 1 pm today.

The 15th General Convention has been scheduled for October 2–4. The party had previously set the ward-level conventions for next Wednesday. A member of the Working Committee said the ward conventions would be postponed by one week. He said four factors had prompted the party to revise the previously announced schedule.

According to the leader, the delay is being considered due to the floods, road disruptions, internal consultations and the Teej festival. The Nepali Congress had decided to mobilise its party members and cadres in response to the devastating Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa on August 26. Roads in various places have been obstructed by the flood and subsequent rainfall. Leaders said internal consultations are also underway to build consensus within the party ahead of the General Convention.

The establishment faction is reportedly holding talks with former Vice President Purna Bahadur Khadka and leader Dr Shekhar Koirala. The schedule for the lower-level conventions also coincides with the Haritalika Teej festival. Party leaders said the festival celebrated by women is another reason for postponing the ward conventions. This year, Teej falls on September 14. Under the previously announced schedule, village/municipal-level conventions were set for September 12, while provincial assembly constituency-level conventions were scheduled for September 16.

Another faction of the Nepali Congress has set the date for the General Convention for November. A review petition is also currently pending in court. The establishment faction, however, is moving ahead with plans to hold the central General Convention on the previously announced dates.

A senior leader from the establishment faction said the General Convention scheduled for October 2–4 could be postponed only under one circumstance. “The two writ petitions would have to be withdrawn for a review. If the cases are withdrawn, the date of the central General Convention could also be postponed slightly to create an environment for consensus,” he said.

title.rendered: Nepal raises Rasuwa flood compensation at South Asian parliamentary forum in Bhutan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Nepal has called for stronger regional cooperation to address the impacts of climate change, including compensation for losses and damages suffered by countries that contribute little to global emissions.

The issue was raised at the South Asia Regional Parliamentary Forum being held in Bhutan, where parliamentarians from South Asian countries are discussing climate change, energy and environmental issues.

Representing Nepal at the forum are House of Representatives member and Development Committee Chair Ashish Gajurel, and House of Representatives member and Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee Chair Ashok Kumar Chaudhary.

During the discussions, Nepal highlighted the need for greater cooperation among South Asian countries to respond to the growing impacts of climate change.

The forum has brought together lawmakers from Nepal, Bhutan, India, Bangladesh, the Maldives and Sri Lanka to discuss the importance of climate action, energy security and sustainable development.

According to Gajurel, Nepal has emphasised the need to develop climate-resilient infrastructure, particularly in Himalayan countries that are increasingly exposed to climate-related disasters.

He also said Nepal’s potential in renewable energy and hydropower should be linked to broader regional energy cooperation.

“Nepal needs to learn from good practices and technologies adopted by other countries and improve its policy and institutional capacity accordingly,” Gajurel said.

Nepal seeks compensation for Rasuwa flood losses

Nepal also raised the issue of loss and damage in the context of the devastating flood in Rasuwa, arguing that the international community’s response should go beyond sympathy and include compensation for the damage suffered.

Gajurel said Nepal had formally written to the Loss and Damage Fund Board on August 31, seeking compensation for the losses and damages caused by the disaster.

The Nepal delegation also called for South Asian countries to work together to urge developed nations to provide compensation to countries affected by climate-related disasters.

The discussion comes after a devastating flood in the Rasuwa region caused widespread destruction along the Bhotekoshi corridor. The disaster affected settlements and infrastructure in Rasuwa and downstream areas, with deaths, disappearances and extensive damage to homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure.

Nepal has argued that countries with relatively low contributions to global greenhouse gas emissions are nevertheless facing severe consequences from climate change.

At the forum, participants pointed to Bhutan’s negative carbon emissions, while Nepal and Sri Lanka were described as making negligible contributions to global emissions.

Despite this, lawmakers from the participating countries expressed concern that countries with low emissions are among those bearing the consequences of climate change.

According to Gajurel, parliamentarians participating in the forum expressed sympathy over the disaster in Nepal and discussed the need for greater regional cooperation in responding to climate-related disasters.

Nepal has increasingly been calling for climate justice, arguing that vulnerable countries need greater access to finance, technology and other forms of support to adapt to climate change and recover from climate-induced losses.

The discussions in Bhutan have also focused on how South Asian countries can strengthen regional cooperation in climate adaptation, renewable energy and sustainable development.

title.rendered: Switzerland provides advanced drone to support search and rescue inside tunnels

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Switzerland has provided Nepal with an advanced drone to support ongoing search and rescue operations inside hydropower project tunnels following the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa.

The semi-autonomous drone, provided at the request of the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, was handed over to the Nepal Electricity Authority on Saturday. According to the Swiss Embassy in Nepal, a Swiss humanitarian aid expert who arrived in Nepal handed over the equipment to the authority.

The embassy said the drone was donated by Flyability, a renowned Swiss drone manufacturer. The drone is specifically designed to fly inside narrow, dark and hazardous tunnels and other areas that are difficult for people to access.

What is the Flyability drone and what can it do?

Swiss company Flyability primarily manufactures specialised drones from its Elios series for inspecting confined and hazardous structures such as tunnels, collapsed mines and industrial pipelines.

The drone can continue flying even after collisions. It is equipped with a strong spherical carbon-fibre cage around its exterior, allowing it to withstand impacts with tunnel walls or debris without crashing. It can regain its balance and continue flying after a collision.

The drone can also operate in complete darkness. Powerful LED lights and a thermal camera enable it to transmit clear video from even pitch-dark tunnels to a control room. As the thermal camera can detect body heat, the drone can be particularly useful in locating people trapped alive under debris.

Another key feature is 3D mapping. Advanced sensors and LiDAR technology on the drone can rapidly create a three-dimensional map of debris and damage inside tunnels.

Technicians say the equipment could prove highly effective in flooded or collapsed tunnels where it would be too dangerous for people to enter. The drone can be deployed to determine the condition and whereabouts of missing people while helping ensure the safety of rescue personnel.

title.rendered: 209 international flights affected after volcanic eruption in Indonesia

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Flight operations at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport have been affected by ash from the eruption of Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano.

Indonesia’s Ministry of Transportation said 209 flights, including international services, were affected after flights were suspended.

The volcano began erupting on Friday night, and the ash spread to Lampung in Sumatra and Banten Province on Java, disrupting daily life in the affected areas.

Several schools have been closed due to the ash, while fishing activities have also been suspended. The disaster mitigation agency, however, said there was no immediate risk of a tsunami.

title.rendered: Petroleum supplies to Kathmandu rerouted after Prithvi Highway blockage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) has started bringing petroleum products and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) into Kathmandu through an alternative route after the Krishnabhir section of the Prithvi Highway was blocked.

According to the corporation, petroleum products and LPG are currently being supplied to Kathmandu Valley and surrounding areas through the Tribhuvan Highway, also known as the Byroad.

The Prithvi Highway was damaged on August 30 after the Trishuli River eroded the road at the Krishnabhir section, leaving fuel tankers and LPG bullets stranded.

Following the disruption, the NOC began using the alternative route to transport LPG cylinders filled at industries in the Tarai to Kathmandu.

The corporation said around 24,500 LPG cylinders were brought into the Kathmandu Valley on September 3, followed by approximately 34,134 cylinders on September 4.

The NOC has also been supplying aviation fuel and LPG for ongoing search and rescue operations following the Bhotekoshi River flood that struck on August 26.

The flood caused extensive damage in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan, while search and rescue operations continue in several affected areas.

According to the NOC, helicopters deployed for rescue operations have so far been refuelled with 120,000 litres of aviation fuel from the Nepal Army barracks in Nuwakot.

The corporation has also sent 575 LPG cylinders to temporary shelters in Rasuwa and Nuwakot following a request from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

The rerouting of fuel and LPG supplies comes as authorities continue to deal with disruptions to road networks caused by flood damage, while ensuring the regular supply of essential petroleum products to Kathmandu Valley.

title.rendered: Landslide damages 7 houses and sheds in Badimalika, Bajura

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Seven houses and animal sheds were damaged after a landslide triggered by incessant rainfall struck Badimalika Municipality in Bajura.

According to the District Police Office, Bajura, continuous rainfall since 8 pm last night triggered a landslide that damaged the houses of Nare Rawal of Kothyara in Badimalika Municipality-8, and Kare Thapa and Dipak BK of Ward No. 9.

The landslide also damaged the animal sheds of Moti Okheda, Dhan Bahadur BK, Jang Okheda and Tule Lohar in Ward No. 9.

Police said food grains, clothing and livestock were damaged when the landslide hit the houses and animal sheds.

title.rendered: Nepali kickboxer Ghimire crowned world champion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

Nepali kickboxer Abiral Ghimire has once again achieved a remarkable feat, winning the world championship in kickboxing.

Ghimire made history by defeating French boxer Mathon Choinard in the main event of the Hit Kick Boxing – 59th International Sports Kick Boxing Federation World Championship, held on Saturday at Kariya Hall in Nagoya, Japan. Choinard was the reigning world champion, having won the title in 2025.

In a stunning display of skill, Ghimire delivered a powerful punch that knocked out Choinard in the second minute of the second round.

With 29 international bouts under his belt, Ghimire is the only Nepali athlete to have recorded 21 international victories, 20 of them by knockout.

Known as the “Himalayan Cheetah,” Ghimire has emerged as a prominent figure in Nepalese kickboxing, proudly representing the country on the international stage.

Following his victory, Ghimire told RSS that he was saddened by the loss of life in the recent Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa and expressed his commitment to supporting the victims.

Bajura, September 6

The Sanfe-Martadi road, which connects the district headquarters with other parts of the district, has been obstructed by landslides at several locations due to incessant rainfall in Bajura.

The road is currently impassable at Jelmode, Suwakandh and various other locations within Badimalika Municipality-9 in Martadi. Police Inspector Gagan Singh Bhatta of the District Police Office said landslides have also affected Rapka in Badimalika Municipality-8 and Jadanga in Ward No. 6.

A five-member police team led by Police Assistant Inspector Laxmi Dutt Bhatt has been deployed to the affected areas. According to the District Police Office, the team is clearing the landslides with the help of a JCB excavator provided by Badimalika Municipality and the Roads Department.

title.rendered: An elderly couple survived the flood. Now they must rebuild their lives

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 6

“It’s coming… it’s coming… the river is going to sweep everything away!”

People began shouting outside as residents of the old Trishuli Bazaar in Ward No. 1 ran for safety.

The Trishuli River was rising rapidly before their eyes. Water surged beyond its banks and towards the homes and streets where people had lived for generations.

“It came dancing,” 70-year-old Kanchi Shrestha recalls.

That day, Kanchi was at home with her 88-year-old husband, Siddhibahadur Shrestha, their son Shyam and grandson.

Before the flood reached their home, Shyam had urged his elderly parents to leave. He even tried to put them in a tempo and take them somewhere safe. But they refused.

This was where they had spent their lives. Their home held years of work, memories and the property they had managed to build.

“We will die if we have to. We will die here,” they told Shyam..

“My brother kept telling them to leave, but they would not listen,” their daughter, Sangita Tamang, recalls.

No one imagined that decision would soon become a matter of life and death.

She would not leave him behind

As the water surged closer, Kanchi realised they could no longer stay. But there was one problem. Siddhibahadur was frail and could not walk properly even under normal circumstances. His eyesight was also poor.

There was no time to think. Kanchi grabbed her husband and pulled him along.

“She somehow pulled him and brought him along. He still has injuries on his body from being dragged,” Sangita said.

Other villagers also came to their aid.

For Kanchi, surviving the flood meant refusing to leave behind the man with whom she had spent decades of her life.

‘I thought my parents were dead’

Shyam had already fled uphill with his son. He had tried repeatedly to convince his parents to leave.

“My parents said they would rather die there. I told them many times, but they insisted,” Shyam said over the phone.

Then another warning came: leave immediately.

His son had been sitting down to eat when news spread that the flood was approaching. They left without finishing their meal.

“We were about to eat rice, but we could not. We ran uphill, and as soon as we got a little higher, the river came,” Shyam recalled.

Within minutes, the flood reached the area they had just left. Water rushed along the road and towards the houses.

Shyam’s thoughts turned to his parents, but he could not return. He had reached higher ground with his son, while communication was intermittent.

In the confusion, he assumed the worst.

“I had already reached higher ground. I thought my parents must have been swept away. I felt guilty,” he said.

For some time, there was no word about his parents.

Then, several hours later, a relative brought news: someone had seen the elderly couple while fleeing the flood.

“As soon as I heard, ‘Your parents are over there,’ I ran to find them,” Shyam said.

By then, he had almost forgotten about his house and property.

He had only one question: Were his parents alive?

They were.

But Siddhibahadur was in poor condition. He could barely walk and had to be carried even to the toilet. He repeatedly became frightened, saying the flood was coming again.

Shyam kept his parents at a place of refuge for two days before arranging a helicopter to evacuate his father to Kathmandu.

The phone call at 6 am

Sangita lives in Kathmandu.

When the flood struck, she heard from her brother that there had been no word from their parents. She had begun to fear that they were dead.

Then, two days later, at around 6 am, her phone rang.

It was her brother.

“Didi, we are safe. Father is in a very difficult condition. We are arranging to take him to Kathmandu for treatment,” he told her.

Sangita travelled to the area. When she arrived around 10 or 11 in the morning, army personnel were carrying her father from a helicopter.

“The army personnel were carrying my father,” she recalled.

Seeing him alive brought relief, but another thought struck her.

How had her 88-year-old father survived?

And how had her elderly mother managed to save him?

“I was shaking when I heard about the flood. My elderly mother herself saved my father. Even now, when I think about it, I am amazed,” Sangita said.

Siddhibahadur was eventually brought to Kathmandu and admitted to Bir Hospital.

The struggle, however, had only changed form.

The flood is still with Kanchi

Kanchi survived, but the fear has not left her. Her daughter says she has become withdrawn and easily frightened. She trembles, cries and struggles to sleep.

“For two or three days after remembering what happened, my mother’s legs kept shaking. She could not sleep. She did not want to eat,” Sangita said.

Kanchi keeps asking the same questions: What if the flood comes again? What if the water rises again? What if everything is swept away again?

The family gave her a mobile phone to distract her.

But even that can trigger memories.

“When she sees videos of the flood on someone else’s phone, she starts crying,” Sangita said.

For others, those videos are images of a disaster.

For Kanchi, they are memories of the moment her world almost disappeared.

‘Where do we start again?’

The flood took much more than the couple’s sense of security.

Shyam had worked in Malaysia and used his savings to build a home for his family. He had gradually accumulated property, hoping life would become easier.

In a matter of minutes, much of it was gone.

“A flood I had never seen in my life destroyed everything. I built that house after years of hardship, going without things. Now that house is gone. What do I do?” Shyam said.

He had also been preparing to move into a new house in Trishuli’s old market area, in Ward No. 9.

“If we had been there, we would not even have had time to run. Even if we had gone to the roof, we might not have survived. At least our lives were saved,” he said.

His livelihood has also disappeared.

After returning from foreign employment, Shyam did not want to leave the country again. He borrowed money to buy a tempo, hoping to earn a living by driving it and repay the loan.

“I bought the tempo on loan because I wanted to do something here instead of going abroad. Now that is gone too,” he said. “The house is gone, the tempo is gone. I don’t know what to do now. Where do we start again?”

His wife is currently working in Kuwait, but Shyam says her income is not what they had hoped for.

He is now staying at a nearby relief camp while his father remains in Bir Hospital.

At 88, Siddhibahadur has other health problems as well. His family says he has kidney-related problems and gallstones and also needs dental treatment.

Beside his hospital bed, Sangita is struggling with the financial burden.

“The hospital may not charge for treating the external injuries, but how will we pay for treatment of his chronic illnesses?” she asked. “What do I have? I am also living in someone else’s house and barely managing. My parents are in such a difficult situation. I cannot afford to support them, but I also cannot bear to see them suffer.”

title.rendered: Banke collects DNA samples from 16 people to identify Bhotekoshi flood victims

content.rendered:
Ranjha (Banke), September 6

Sixteen people in Banke district have provided DNA samples to help identify bodies recovered after the Bhotekoshi flash flood.

Relatives of people who have been missing since the flood provided blood samples to help identify bodies that are in an unrecognisable state and have been recovered and kept at various locations across the country.

Many people from the district have gone missing since the flood swept away infrastructure, houses and settlements along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor on August 26.

DNA samples were collected from 16 people in the district, DSP Pratit Singh Rathaur confirmed.

For DNA matching with the recovered bodies, blood samples are collected from the biological father, mother and a son or daughter of the missing person. The samples are then sent to the Nepal Police Central Forensic Science Laboratory.

Anlal Rokaya, a resident of Nepalgunj-20, said he hoped to identify the bodies of his brother, sister-in-law and son after providing samples for DNA matching.

Rokaya lost his 19-year-old son Dipak, 53-year-old brother Sher Singh and 56-year-old sister-in-law Bishnumati. They went missing at the same time in the Bhotekoshi flood.

Banke district has reported 23 people missing in the flood. So far, three people from the district who were found dead have been identified, while 32 others were rescued alive, according to Chief District Officer Dil Kumar Tamang.

The district has contributed Rs 2.4 million to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund. Various social organisations, schools, business firms and individuals voluntarily contributed to the fund as humanitarian assistance for people in need following the catastrophic floods.

title.rendered: UK parliamentarian Lord Popat urges Britain to do more for Nepal flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

A British member of the House of Lords has urged the UK government to step up support for Nepal as the country continues to struggle with the aftermath of the devastating floods that swept through Rasuwa and several downstream districts.

Lord Popat, speaking in the House of Lords on September 1, said Nepal urgently needed food, medical supplies, emergency shelter and logistical support, as rescue teams continued searching for people missing in the disaster.

“What happened was tragic and I welcome the financial support that the Government are giving, but I think we need to give more,” Popat said.

He specifically pointed to the need for rescue operations, temporary reconstruction of homes and restoration of damaged infrastructure.

“While a lot of bodies are still under mud,” he said, there was a need for continued rescue and logistical support, as well as temporary housing and infrastructure restoration.

Popat also highlighted the longstanding relationship between Britain and Nepal, particularly the service of Nepali Gurkhas in the British Army.

“I am sure that we can do more than we have done so far to help Nepal in this difficult time,” he told the Lords.

Responding to Popat, Lord Wood of Anfield said the UK was already providing emergency assistance through several channels, while acknowledging that the needs created by the disaster were extensive.

The UK government has committed up to £750,000 through the Red Cross movement for emergency humanitarian assistance, including clean water, shelter, first aid and essential supplies.

A further £1 million has been allocated through Start Fund Nepal for local organisations providing life-saving assistance, while up to £250,000 is being provided to deploy UK humanitarian experts and strengthen coordination efforts.

Wood said the UK was also working with the Nepal government and authorities to identify areas where international support could complement existing relief efforts and fill emerging gaps.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The price of gold fell by Rs 3,100 per tola in Nepal on Sunday.

According to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association, fine gold is being traded at Rs 304,300 per tola today. The price stood at Rs 307,400 per tola on Friday.

Meanwhile, the price of silver also declined by Rs 40 per tola.

The federation has fixed the price of silver at Rs 4,725 per tola for Sunday, down from Rs 4,765 per tola on Friday.

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 6

A flood in the Namrung stream of Chumnubri Rural Municipality-4 in Gorkha swept away four houses and an iron bridge early Sunday morning.

According to Gorkha Deputy Superintendent of Police Raj Kumar Shrestha, the flood occurred at around 3am and swept away the houses of Nurbu Ongyal, Urgen Chhyoden, Lakpa Bhuti and Dorje Gyalzen in Namrung.

The flood also swept away an iron bridge connecting wards 4 and 2 of the rural municipality, police said.

No human casualties have been reported so far.

title.rendered: A voice in the rubble led rescuers to a woman trapped for 11 days

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 6

An armed police and Nepal Police team rescued a woman alive from a mud-filled house in Betrawati on Saturday, 11 days after the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River.

The woman, identified as Chandika Shrestha, was found trapped inside a four-storey house that had been swept away by the flood and deposited at another location.

So far, four people trapped in the flood-hit areas have been rescued alive. Three of them were rescued from tunnels.

The rescue team heard a woman’s voice while searching houses in the Betrawati area. The rescue operation was led by Armed Police Force Inspector Suman BK.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar, BK said the house belonged to Anand Shrestha and had been swept away by the flood on the third day. Three of its four floors had been buried in mud, with only part of the upper floor visible.

“As we were walking around the house, we heard a sound. We could not tell whether it was an echo or someone calling for help. But it sounded like a woman’s voice,” BK said.

After hearing the voice, the disaster-management-trained Armed Police team broke through a window that was partially visible above the mud and entered the house.

“We found her with about half of her body buried in mud. Only a small part of her body and her head were visible,” he said.

‘We heard the voice around 1 pm’

According to BK, the rescue team heard the voice at around 1 pm while carrying out a search operation.

“We have been going from house to house, calling out and checking inside. We have been doing this continuously,” he said.

Ten disaster-management-trained Armed Police personnel were deployed under BK’s command, while another team from Nepal Police was operating under the command of a police inspector.

It took the teams around 40 to 45 minutes to rescue the woman.

“She was buried in mud. We removed the mud, cut through the window and pulled her out. We then took her outside and sent her to Kathmandu,” BK said.

‘She could not walk’

BK said the woman was unable to walk when she was rescued.

“She had been pressed down by the mud. The upper part of her body was relatively safe, so she could speak a little. She was conscious and able to talk, but we did not allow her to speak much because her condition could deteriorate,” he said.

Asked whether rescue teams had reached the house earlier, BK said the security personnel had been searching the area for the past 10 days.

“We have been here and around this area for 10 days. From one house alone, we had recovered 22 bodies,” he said.

The search operation is continuing in the flood-hit area.

“Our search operation is continuing. We are deployed in the morning, afternoon and evening, at all times,” BK said.

title.rendered: Flood damages 55 drinking water projects in four districts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 6

The devastating flood in the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa on August 26 has affected 55 drinking water projects across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Gorkha districts.

According to the preliminary assessment of damage to drinking water projects, losses are estimated at around Rs 640 million.

The Department of Water Supply and Sewerage Management said Nuwakot was the worst affected, with 22 drinking water projects damaged. The estimated damage to these projects alone stands at Rs 41.15 million.

Department Director General Kamal Raj Shrestha said 20 drinking water projects in Dhading, five in Gorkha and eight in Rasuwa were also damaged.

The department said detailed assessment of the damage is still underway.

The department has launched both short- and long-term measures to restore drinking water services in areas where supplies have been disrupted. Shrestha said priority has been given to restoring services through alternative sources and repairing damaged infrastructure.

In the affected area of the Bidur Drinking Water Project, a 100 kVA diesel generator has been brought into operation to facilitate water distribution. The department said arrangements have been made to distribute around 500,000 litres of drinking water daily through the generator.

Likewise, seven one-horsepower pumps have been put into operation, restoring water services to around 500 households in the Battar area.

In coordination with the Kathmandu Upatyaka Khanepani Limited (KUKL), four water tankers have been distributing drinking water in various settlements of Bidur and Battar since August 28, according to Shrestha.

The department has also arranged necessary materials to expand drinking water services to the remaining affected areas of Trishuli Bazaar, Belkotgadhi, Kolputar, Galchhi, Gajuri and Bidur.

A total of 14 pumps—seven with a capacity of two horsepower and seven with a capacity of one horsepower—along with a 1,000-litre Hilltake tank and around 41.1 kilometres of HDPE pipes have been kept ready for the expansion of water services.

According to the department, preparations are underway to transport and install the materials in the affected areas.

Technical teams have been continuously deployed to repair and restore infrastructure damaged by the flood and ensure regular drinking water supplies to affected settlements.

The department said long-term rehabilitation and reconstruction work is being carried out alongside immediate relief measures to prevent a prolonged drinking water shortage.

Further reconstruction and rehabilitation programmes will be implemented based on the needs identified once a complete assessment of the damage is available.

title.rendered: Prithvi Highway section in Dhading to remain fully closed for repairs

content.rendered:
Dhading, September 6

The Parewabhir section of the Prithvi Highway in Gajuri Rural Municipality-2 of Dhading will remain fully closed for two hours on Sunday as authorities continue repair work on the flood-damaged road.

The road section was damaged by the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26. Following the damage, the highway had been operating on a one-way basis.

According to the District Administration Office, Dhading, traffic along the Parewabhir section will be completely halted from 6 am to 6 pm on Sunday to facilitate repair works.

All vehicles, except emergency services such as ambulances and hearses, have been barred from operating on the section during the repair period, according to the administration.

The administration had also completely closed the section from 6 am to 6 pm on Saturday for repairs. However, as the repair work could not be completed, authorities have decided to halt traffic again on Sunday to expedite the work.

The administration has apologised for the inconvenience caused to passengers and motorists and urged travellers to use alternative routes during the closure.

title.rendered: ANNFSU continues humanitarian campaign, distributes relief to flood-affected families in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 5

The All Nepal National Free Students’ Union (ANNFSU) has continued its Humanitarian Assistance Campaign to support citizens affected by floods and landslides. As part of the campaign, ANNFSU reached several disaster-affected areas of Rasuwa, distributing relief materials to affected families and handing over essential supplies to local authorities.

A team led by ANNFSU Central President Mahesh Shrestha reached Naukunda Rural Municipality–4, where relief materials were distributed door-to-door to 26 flood-affected families in the presence of Ward Chairperson Nokendra Tamang.

Similarly, in the severely affected Betravati area of Uttargaya Rural Municipality, ANNFSU handed over essential relief supplies to Rural Municipality Chairperson Madhav Aryal and Ward No. 5 Chairperson Yamanath Acharya.

The relief materials included food supplies, medicines, clothing, solar-powered equipment, lights, flashlights, kitchen utensils, and sanitation supplies, among other essential items.

According to ANNFSU, the campaign aims to provide immediate assistance to citizens affected by the disaster and stand in solidarity with families facing difficulties in the aftermath of the floods and landslides.

ANNFSU Vice President Ashok Thapa said that the humanitarian assistance campaign is not limited to the distribution of relief materials but represents the organization’s commitment to solidarity, responsibility, and humanity toward citizens affected by natural disasters.

“ANNFSU will continue the humanitarian campaign in the coming days and provide necessary support to disaster-affected communities to the best of its capacity,” Thapa said.

He also expressed gratitude to all individuals, well-wishers, and supporters who have contributed to the humanitarian initiative, reaffirming ANNFSU’s commitment to continuing its service and assistance to communities affected by natural disasters.

title.rendered: Himalayan hazards are becoming more complex. Our warning systems need to catch up

content.rendered:
The exact timeline of the recent Nepal flooding disaster is becoming clearer. At 8:37 am, instruments recorded what was initially interpreted as an earthquake near Nepal’s border with China. Seven minutes later, CCTV recorded the Gyirong Port border post being destroyed by a massive debris flow and flood.

Nepal’s flood authorities learned about the incident at about 9:00 am and sent out an emergency SMS alert at about 9:15 am. But by that time, Nepal was already deep into a major disaster.

The 38-minute gap between the tremor being detected and the emergency alert is striking. But it would be wrong to assume Nepal’s authorities could simply have acted on the initial signal: at the time, it appeared to be a small earthquake, rather than a much rarer mountain collapse. The flood also arrived too swiftly for water-level sensors: they went almost immediately from recording normal levels to being destroyed.

The more interesting question is what a better-integrated warning system might have made possible. Could seismic readings, satellite images and other observations have been combined quickly enough to recognise what was happening and alert people further downstream?

Existing early-warning systems have often been designed around particular hazards such as regular rain-caused floods or glacial lake outburst floods (Glofs). But this disaster was neither a Glof nor a regular flood. Instead it appears to have involved a rare, large-scale collapse of rock and ice, which turned into a devastating debris flow and flood.

As a recent study of a strikingly similar flood in India last year argued, this type of hazard is largely absent from existing warning frameworks. As warming destabilises glaciers and thaws permafrost, such events are likely to happen more often.

Cascading mountain hazards that cross borders

In July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least nine people and leaving around 20 missing in Nepal. Eleven people were also officially reported missing on the Chinese side.

After the flood, Nepal and China agreed in principle to share real-time information about floods, landslides and glacial lakes. However, despite Nepal’s foreign minister raising the issue during a visit to China in May 2026, no formal agreement has been signed.

Across the Himalayas and Hindu Kush mountain ranges, rivers, weather systems and infrastructure frequently span national boundaries. Our ongoing research shows a hazard that begins in one place can have lethal consequences – and create new warning requirements – far downstream.

A warming climate is increasing these risks by thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and destabilising slopes, even if climate change isn’t the sole explanation for every disaster. Meanwhile roads and hydropower projects are putting more people and infrastructure in threatened valleys.

Cooperation has to come before the disaster

Some cross-border early-warning arrangements already exist between Nepal and its neighbours, particularly for recurring floods. But sudden, cascading events such as the recent disaster pose a different challenge. A warning has value only if it travels the whole distance – from a sensor in the mountains, through scientific agencies, national and local authorities, to households in the valleys and plains below, in the minutes that matter.

Community-based flood warning already works in parts of Nepal’s Koshi basin, where upstream gauges and trained local volunteers buy downstream villages precious time. A regional early warning system would have to link these community-level systems with national and cross-border monitoring, so that information can move from the source of a hazard to the people at risk. That means agreeing in advance what should be shared, how warnings should be passed between countries and agencies, and what action they should trigger.

That requires institutional changes and political commitment, as much as new technology. The region’s existing water treaties were written to divide flows and manage dams and barrages, not to govern cascading hazards in the high mountains. Governments could establish permanent bodies responsible for Himalayan rivers and their associated hazards. Featuring both scientists and policymakers, and linked to counterparts in neighbouring countries, these public bodies would be mandated to share data, jointly monitor glaciers, lakes and slopes, and coordinate warnings across borders.

The aim would be to make cooperation routine and sustained between disasters, rather than improvised in a crisis when events may unfold too quickly for international debate. None of this requires neighbours to resolve their wider disputes; it asks only that disaster warning be ring-fenced as shared humanitarian infrastructure that keeps working unabated.

The technologies for predicting and monitoring high-mountain hazards are improving fast. We now need more international scientific and policy cooperation, and warning systems capable of turning these observations into rapid action.

title.rendered: The geotechnical trap inside Nepal’s hydropower tunnels

content.rendered:
On August 26, catastrophic debris flows swept down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors, exposing severe vulnerabilities in Himalayan hydropower infrastructure.

Several projects remain inundated, with workers still missing or trapped deep inside underground headrace tunnels and powerhouses.

Public frustration has understandably focused on how long rescue is taking—whether enough equipment is available, whether the right technology is being used, and whether machinery can reach the sites.

But there is another problem that deserves attention: the behaviour of the sediment itself.

The assumption that mud will eventually drain or dry enough to allow extraction does not necessarily hold inside a confined, flooded tunnel. The mechanics of saturated soil, hydraulic conditions and the interaction between trapped sediment and concrete tunnel linings can make extraction far more difficult.

Understanding this is important not only for the current rescue effort but also for how Nepal designs hydropower infrastructure in the future.

When a tunnel becomes a trap

Most Himalayan run-of-river projects have surface headworks, desilting basins, underground headrace tunnels and underground powerhouses. Putting critical infrastructure underground protects it from many surface hazards, but the same arrangement can become a serious liability during a major debris flow.

Underground structures behave differently from surface buildings. They are governed largely by the deformation imposed by surrounding rock and by the interaction between the tunnel and the ground around it.

During a major debris flow, however, surface intake portals and access adits can become entry points for enormous volumes of water, sediment and rock. A hyper-concentrated debris flow entering these openings can damage gates, scour tunnel floors and carry sediment deep into electromechanical areas.

Once the material enters an underground facility, access becomes difficult and drainage can become the biggest problem.

Tunnels and underground powerhouses are generally designed around the stresses of surrounding rock, internal water pressure and normal operating conditions. They are not normally designed to withstand the combination of massive sediment loads, debris impact and the confinement created when a debris flow fills the underground geometry.

The result can be an underground facility that is extremely difficult to enter, drain or clear.

Why waiting for mud to dry is not a solution

Trapped sediment inside a flooded tunnel is governed by saturated soil mechanics. It does not simply behave like wet soil left outside in the sun.

A mass of glacial till or alluvium can effectively seal a tunnel. Ventilation may be lost, while trapped air quickly reaches maximum relative humidity, severely limiting evaporation. Without an open drainage path and sufficient hydraulic gradient, pore water cannot escape easily.

The sediment therefore remains saturated and can behave more like a highly viscous, non-Newtonian fluid than ordinary soil.

In such conditions, waiting for the material to dry naturally could take months. For workers trapped underground, that is obviously not a viable rescue strategy.

Mechanical intervention is therefore essential.

This is not simply a pumping problem

Standard dewatering pumps are designed primarily for clear water. They are poorly suited to dense sediment containing gravel and abrasive quartz-rich silts. Such material can rapidly damage impellers and mechanical seals.

The equipment required is closer to what is used in deep mining and dredging operations. Submersible slurry pumps fitted with rotating agitators can break up dense sediment at the intake, reducing its apparent viscosity and allowing it to be moved as a fluid.

The sequence matters.

Heavy loaders cannot simply drive into fluid mud because they cannot gain traction. Slurry pumps may first need to remove the finer, mobile material. Once the level falls, loaders or other machinery can begin removing larger boulders that exceed pump clearances. High-pressure hydro-vacuum equipment may then be needed to break up compacted zones.

Conventional excavators can also create problems in the early stages. Cutting a trench through weak, saturated sediment may simply cause surrounding material to collapse back into it because gravity exceeds the mud’s low yield strength.

Pumping too fast can also be dangerous

There is another complication. The problem is not only finding extraction equipment; it is getting heavy equipment into steep mountain terrain where roads may have already been destroyed.

Even after machinery reaches the tunnel portal, extraction cannot necessarily proceed at maximum pumping capacity.

If the initial debris flow has damaged the concrete lining or scoured the tunnel invert, the dense mud inside may be providing temporary radial confinement to the surrounding rock mass. Removing that material rapidly can cause a sudden drop in internal hydrostatic and lateral earth pressures.

The surrounding rock cannot necessarily drain or adjust immediately. A severe inward hydraulic gradient can develop, potentially leading to hydraulic heave at the invert, inward buckling of tunnel walls or roof collapse.

Rescue teams may therefore have to advance incrementally, balancing pumping rates with pore-pressure dissipation, managing continuing water ingress and installing temporary support before moving deeper into the tunnel.

This is a geotechnical problem as much as a rescue operation.

How did the disaster become so destructive?

The disaster itself also shows why conventional hazard assumptions are no longer enough.

The event originated with a massive ice-rock collapse on the northern slopes of Langtang Lirung at nearly 5,200 metres. The trigger was thermal degradation of high-altitude permafrost rather than a tectonic earthquake.

In steep alpine terrain, ice can act as structural cement within rock fractures. Warming and meltwater infiltration can increase fluid pressures along structural planes, reducing the frictional resistance holding fractured rock together. As ice melts, the cohesive bond between rock blocks is also weakened.

Once gravitational forces exceed that degraded resistance, the rock face can fail.

But the scale of downstream destruction is determined not only by the initial collapse. As the avalanche accelerated down the steep gorge of the Lhende River, it scoured the channel and incorporated saturated moraine, alluvial deposits and river water.

Field investigations of recent cascading Himalayan hazards by the Chinese Academy of Sciences have shown that such entrainment can multiply the initial landslide volume by orders of magnitude.

The moving mass can therefore transform from a solid avalanche into a hyper-concentrated fluid-solid mixture.

This kind of non-linear volumetric bulking is often poorly represented in conventional hazard models. As a result, underground intake portals and surge chambers designed mainly around normal hydrostatic water pressures may be poorly prepared for the dynamic loads produced by a massive debris slurry.

What Nepal must change

The lesson is not that underground hydropower is inherently unsafe. It is that future Himalayan infrastructure must be designed around cascading geological hazards rather than isolated load cases.

Major projects should require dynamic debris-hazard assessments and incorporate redundant access corridors, independent ventilation routes and dedicated evacuation provisions as part of a multi-hazard strategy.

Surface portals and access adits should not be treated simply as entry points. In high-risk locations, they may need to function as defensive structures capable of routing, deflecting or withstanding major debris impacts.

The change must also extend to rescue preparedness.

The geomechanical challenges of clearing confined, flooded tunnels can exceed the capabilities of conventional civil defence agencies. Safe recovery requires pre-established access to international mining expertise and specialised equipment capable of mobilising viscoplastic mud under difficult underground conditions.

Nepal cannot wait until the next disaster to build those connections.

The immediate priority is, of course, the people still trapped or missing. Rescue teams are advancing carefully through compromised underground spaces, where even a seemingly simple operation can trigger a secondary collapse.

But once the immediate crisis passes, regulators and hydropower developers must confront what this disaster has exposed.

Nepal’s engineering codes have traditionally placed strong emphasis on seismic hazards and clear-water hydrostatic conditions based on relatively localised hazard assessments. The failures now unfolding in the Himalayan environment show the need to account for cascading multi-hazard events, including extreme volumetric bulking caused by debris entrainment.

Hydropower infrastructure must be designed not only to operate safely under normal conditions, but also to remain accessible, recoverable and safe when the mountains behave beyond conventional assumptions.

Hydropower tunnels must be designed as safe workspaces, never again allowed to become sealed traps during a surface disaster.
