title.rendered: Nepal needs the world. But Nepal must build Nepal.

content.rendered:
The recent floods in Rasuwa have once again reminded us how vulnerable Nepal remains to disasters. Families have lost homes and livelihoods. Infrastructure has been damaged. Communities are waiting for relief and, beyond that, the long and difficult process of recovery and reconstruction.

At a time like this, the generosity of people, organisations and countries around the world matters greatly.

Nepal needs help. We need financial resources, technical expertise, humanitarian assistance, technology, knowledge and experience. We need friends who can stand beside us when our own resources are stretched. And we should be grateful to everyone who comes forward.

But there is another side of disaster recovery that we must talk about—quietly, honestly and without pointing fingers.

When help arrives, influence can sometimes arrive with it.

Not everyone who comes with assistance has a hidden interest. Most people working in humanitarian and development organisations are genuinely committed to helping. But good intentions do not always mean that every approach is good for Nepal.

That is why, especially during a crisis, Nepal must be compassionate in accepting help—but careful in managing it.

The familiar scene in Singha Durbar

Walk through Singha Durbar and you will find a familiar development landscape.

In one room, a ministry is working with an international organisation. In another, consultants are discussing institutional reform. Somewhere else, a donor-funded team is developing a digital system. Another is preparing a policy document, workshop or training.

There may be one project for capacity building, another for resilience, another for digital transformation, another for disaster preparedness, and another for recovery and reconstruction.

Most have good intentions, and many have produced valuable results. But over time, something else can happen:

The project ecosystem can become bigger than the institution it was meant to support.

A new project brings a new team. The team brings consultants. Consultants bring recommendations. Recommendations bring new systems, which bring new reporting requirements. Before long, government officials may spend as much time responding to projects as they do strengthening the institution itself.

This is not necessarily anyone’s intention. But it is a risk Nepal must recognise.

A project should strengthen the government—not become a parallel government.

Haiti should make us think

There is an important lesson from Haiti.

When the devastating earthquake struck Haiti on January 12, 2010, the international community responded with extraordinary generosity. Governments, UN agencies, international financial institutions, NGOs, charities, consultants and volunteers came to help. Billions of dollars were pledged.

Haiti desperately needed that assistance. Yet the years that followed became an important lesson for the international development community. Despite enormous international assistance, sustainable recovery proved extremely difficult.

One challenge was the fragmentation of assistance: many organisations, many projects, different priorities and complicated coordination arrangements.

UNDP itself later noted that dispersed and uncoordinated external cooperation could be harmful to development and emphasised the importance of strengthening the Haitian government’s ability to coordinate and manage external assistance.

The lesson is not that the world should not have helped Haiti.

It is much simpler: A country can receive enormous assistance and still struggle to build strong national institutions.

After a disaster, a country needs homes, schools, hospitals, roads, jobs and functioning government. But if too many outside actors arrive with their own projects, systems, priorities and timelines, something unintended can happen: There may be projects everywhere, but ownership becomes unclear.

That is the lesson Nepal should learn before we become another case study.

Rasuwa should make us even more careful

The recent Rasuwa disaster comes at an important moment for Nepal. As relief reaches affected communities, recovery and reconstruction discussions will become larger.

More resources will come. More organisations will arrive. More projects will be proposed. More experts will be available. More promises will be made.

This is good.

But it is also when Nepal must be especially careful. Why? Disasters create urgency and that can weaken scrutiny.

When people are suffering, it is natural to accept help quickly. But emergency speed should not mean abandoning transparency, coordination or national ownership.

We need to ask: Who is coming? What are they bringing? What do they want to do? Where will the money go? Who will implement it? Who will own the data and systems? Who will maintain them after the project ends?

And most importantly: What will Nepal be left with when the project is over?

Help us—but please do not replace us

This should be Nepal’s message to international partners.

We are grateful for your support. Help us build our capacity, strengthen our institutions, train our people and bring technology and knowledge. Help us recover from disasters and build a more resilient Nepal.

But please do not replace the institutions that are supposed to lead Nepal.

An international organisation should complement government, not substitute for it. A consultant should advise, not decide and a donor should support, not govern.

A Project Task Team Leader should provide expertise and challenge our thinking when necessary, but also understand the limits of that role.

Ultimately, Nepal’s government must decide what Nepal should do and how Nepal should do it.

Let help enter through one door, open multiple windows, and empower multiple hands.

There will be times when Nepal’s approach differs from that preferred by a donor or consultant. That does not automatically mean Nepal is wrong.

Our geography, institutions, political and social realities are different.

What works in Washington, Geneva, Delhi or Singapore may not automatically work in Kathmandu, Jumla or Rasuwa.

Development cannot simply be copied and pasted.

And we must also look at ourselves

This conversation is not only about I/NGOs and donors. It is also about us.

Nepal’s bureaucracy has a responsibility to protect the national interest. Government officials should be open to learning from the world. Foreign exposure, training and study visits can be valuable.

But they should never become incentives for accepting projects or recommendations.

A foreign trip is not free. A five-star hotel is not free. A workshop is not free. A consultant is not free. A project vehicle is not free.

Someone is paying for it, and ultimately that money is being spent in the name of development.

So perhaps every public official should occasionally ask: “If this money were coming directly from Nepal’s national budget, would I still consider this expenditure necessary?”

If the answer is yes, proceed. If the answer is no, perhaps we should think again.

Our development partners may have money. But that does not mean we should stop asking whether it is being spent wisely.

Nepal’s experts must have a seat at the table

Nepal has many capable professionals—engineers, doctors, IT specialists, disaster management experts, economists, researchers, planners, administrators, academics and young innovators.

They may not always have the international title or the large consultancy behind them. But they understand Nepal. Their knowledge should not be treated as secondary simply because it is local. International expertise should add to Nepali expertise—not replace it.

We should bring the best of both together. This is particularly important in the digital age.

Every development project wants to create something: a portal, dashboard, database, assessment tool, mobile application or monitoring system. Each may have a valid purpose.

But if every project creates its own system, Nepal eventually ends up with systems that do not communicate with one another.

During a disaster, that becomes more than an IT problem. It becomes a governance problem.

A citizen should not have to wonder which government portal contains the correct information. A local government should not have to enter the same data five times. And a ministry should not have to maintain systems that disappear when project funding ends.

One government should mean interoperable systems, shared standards and one source of trusted information.

So what should Nepal do?

We do not need to close our doors to international cooperation. We simply need stronger doors.

Nepal should strengthen its policies and SOPs for I/NGOs and development partners. Every major project should clearly answer seven questions:

Who decides? Who owns? Who pays? Who implements? Who maintains? Who is accountable? What remains after the project ends?

Project expenditure should be transparent. Consultancy, travel, workshop, administrative and overhead costs should be visible and accountable.

And success should not be measured by the number of workshops, reports or meetings. It should be measured by one thing: Did Nepal become stronger?

We should be clever, not suspicious

Nepal should not become suspicious of every international organisation that comes to help. That would be unfair. Many organisations and individuals have stood beside Nepal during difficult times and continue to do excellent work.

We should appreciate them. But gratitude should not mean blindness.

We can be thankful and still be careful. We can welcome assistance and still ask questions. We can accept expertise and still make our own decisions. We can work with international partners and still protect national ownership.

That is not hostility. That is maturity.

The Rasuwa floods should remind us not only of the vulnerability of our mountains and communities, but also of how we manage the help that comes after a disaster.

Relief will come. Money will come. Organisations will come. Experts will come. Projects will come. Some will be excellent. Some may be less useful. Some may have interests beyond their stated project objectives.

We do not need to reject them all. We simply need to be clever enough to know the difference.

Let us welcome every helping hand. But let us also keep our hands firmly on the steering wheel.

Let international partners walk with Nepal, not ahead of Nepal. Let them help us build institutions that can eventually stand without them. Let every dollar and every rupee create lasting value for Nepali people.

And let the ultimate test of every development partnership be simple: When the project ends and the donor leaves, is Nepal stronger than it was before?

If the answer is yes, we have built a partnership.

If the answer is no, perhaps we need to rethink the way we receive and manage help.

Nepal needs the world. But Nepal must build Nepal.

title.rendered: The flood was natural, but was the disaster?

content.rendered:
The Bhotekoshi flash flood in Nepal cannot simply be called a natural disaster.

Extreme floods are commonly described using annual exceedance probabilities or return periods—such as 50-, 100- or 500-year events, or even rarer ones. These terms do not tell us when a flood will occur; they describe its estimated probability and magnitude. Even rare events, therefore, need to be considered when the consequences of failure are severe.

The real question is: were we prepared for it?

A natural hazard alone should not have resulted in this level of human casualties and economic loss. A river has its own right of way. It needs space to flow, expand and, during extreme events, sometimes change its course. But have our planners and decision-makers really respected that?

We continue to develop cities, roads, settlements and infrastructure in flood-prone and risk-sensitive areas. We know the risks, yet we often choose what is easier, cheaper and economically attractive today without seriously considering what may happen 20, 50 or 100 years from now.

Where is the science in our development decisions?

Where are the flood-risk maps, river corridors, historical evidence, future climate projections and risk-sensitive land-use plans? Even when these studies exist, are we actually using them to make decisions? Or are we simply hiring consultants to prepare reports, complete the paperwork and validate what has already been decided?

This is where our federal and local governments need to look inward.

Climate change is real, and it can increase the intensity and frequency of extreme events. But we cannot use “climate change” as a convenient explanation for every disaster and then walk away from the facts.

Why are we so quick to blame the global community in the name of climate change without first asking ourselves some uncomfortable questions?

Did we build inside floodplains? Did we allow settlements too close to rivers? Did we properly study flood hazards before approving development? Did we design our infrastructure with extreme events in mind? Did we enforce our own regulations? And did we listen to scientists, engineers and local knowledge when the risks were already visible?

If we failed in these areas, we have to accept that first.

Yes, climate change may increase the hazard, and global climate responsibility is an important issue. But climate change does not make poor planning disappear.

Our governments cannot escape accountability by pointing towards climate change or international responsibility. This is not about blaming one person or one institution. It is about questioning a system that repeatedly allows us to build vulnerability and then call the consequences a natural disaster.

Nature brings the hazard. Our decisions determine how destructive that hazard becomes.

This flood should not become another cycle of disaster, social-media outrage, international appeals, reconstruction, and then forgetting everything until the next flood.

We need to accept the facts. We need science-driven and evidence-based development. We need to respect rivers and their floodplains. We need governments, planners and communities that think beyond the next contract, the next project, the next funding cycle and the next election.

And, most importantly, we need accountability.

The river remembers its way, even when our planners forget it.

And to international agencies and development organisations: this disaster is not a desert waiting for your funding portfolios to bloom while communities are being buried under debris.

This is a time for humanity, coordination and genuine support—not competition for visibility, projects and funding opportunities.

If you are here to help, then help where communities actually need you. Listen first. Coordinate. Strengthen local capacity. Share knowledge. Support recovery that reduces future risk.

Do not turn people’s suffering into another project proposal or another line in an institutional portfolio.

And we, the public, also have a responsibility.

To social-media scrollers, content creators and curious visitors: a disaster site is not a tourism destination.

This is not the time to rush to affected areas simply to see what happened and become part of an already unmanageable crowd. Unnecessary visitors can block roads, interfere with rescue operations, create confusion and make an already difficult situation even harder.

If you cannot contribute to rescue, relief or technical support, sometimes the most responsible thing you can do is stay away from the affected area and allow responders to do their work.

Share verified information. Do not create panic for views and engagement. And do not make someone’s worst day of their life your social-media content.

content.rendered:
On the morning of August 26, Yogesh Dangol took one last walk around Betrawati without knowing it would become the last time he would see the town as he knew it.

He went to Uttargaya Dham, crossed the suspension bridge connecting Trishuli with Tupche, visited Maranghat Pati and watched the Lakhey. He also stopped by the building of the club he had chaired for eight years.

He was returning home and had just reached the middle of Betrawati Bazaar when someone warned him: “The flood is coming.”

It was around 9:20 am when the flood entered the settlement. Within 15 to 20 minutes, Betrawati had been devastated.

Dangol began looking for his son and his parents as the water swept through the town. Buses were being carried away. People were running across the fields on the other side of the river. The bridge was crowded with people and vehicles.

“I cannot imagine what happened to the people in that field,” he said. “There were people all over the bridge. Vehicles were running. Everything was swept away.”

Four or five large container trucks and cars parked in front of the Betrawati police post were carried away. Some of them had people inside. School buses were also swept away.

“It was a terrifying situation,” Dangol said, struggling to put what he witnessed into words.

He had barely crossed the Betrawati bridge when he saw his maternal aunt and her husband being swept away.

“When the flood reached my aunt’s house, panic began. A white torrent came down from the temple. After that, my mind stopped working,” he said.

Dangol had a five-storey house in the middle of the town. The flood reached the fourth floor.

His house was not an exception. Homes across Betrawati were swept away within minutes.

“Betrawati, this sacred place, was turned into ruins,” he said.

A town with a history

For Dangol, the loss is about more than homes.

Betrawati has long held historical and religious significance. Dangol says the area had a settlement even before the 1849 treaty with Tibet and that temples and guthis have existed there for generations.

The town was also home to generations of Dangols, as well as Tamang, Brahmin and Magar families.

“There were around 170 to 180 Dangol households alone,” he said. “There were also Tamang settlements, Brahmin families and Magar families on the other side.”

He estimates that around 230 to 235 households lived in Betrawati, with a population of between 700 and 800.

The town was also a trading centre, attracting people from surrounding areas to buy goods. It was home to Uttargaya Dham, an important religious site, and was known for its Lakhey and other festivals held throughout the year.

“It was a package in itself — fertile land, clean water, the confluence of rivers, the sacred land of Uttargaya and Lakhey festivals,” Dangol said.

Betrawati was also an important route towards Rasuwa and the Rasuwagadhi border point.

Now, there is nothing.

Dangol says 61 members of the Dangol community are believed to have been swept away. Others remain missing. Children are among those unaccounted for.

“There is no confirmed figure yet,” he said. “My aunt, my paternal aunt, my paternal aunt’s daughter, my sister’s daughter, and neighbours and brothers from around the area were swept away right in front of my eyes.”

He had come home to celebrate

Dangol had returned to Nepal from the United States just two weeks before the flood.

He had come home as preparations were underway for the local festivals. T-shirts had already been printed. The community was preparing for Ghode Jatra and Gaijatra.

“But the settlement itself is gone,” he said.

Betrawati had already been through one major disaster. The 2015 earthquake devastated the town. After the earthquake, Dangol was among those who worked to rebuild it.

“I started by saying I would build my own house first,” he said. “We had to save Betrawati and make it beautiful.”

He built a distinctive clock tower-like structure on top of his house, with clocks facing in different directions.

The clock had been made in Britain and brought from India. Dangol spent Rs 1.2 to 1.3 million on it around nine years ago.

Every morning at 6, it would begin chiming, continuing every hour until 9. It became part of the town.

“Now, the clock has stopped.”

‘Betrawati has to remain’

Dangol had built the house and then returned to the United States. He could not come back when his mother fell ill. After her health improved, the family finally returned to Nepal.

“I brought my mother to Nepal to show her the country after her treatment,” he said. “It feels like I brought her to see it for the last time.”

Even after building the house, Dangol spent only about five nights there — two nights initially and another three nights later.

Now, discussions have already begun about rebuilding Betrawati.

For Dangol, rebuilding is not simply an option. It is something that must happen.

“Betrawati has to remain. We will keep it there,” he said. “If we are told to leave Betrawati and settle somewhere else, that is not acceptable. Betrawati has to be there. We will build it again as it was.”

The town that survived an earthquake has been reduced to a riverbed again, only a decade after it was rebuilt.

But Dangol is already thinking about bringing it back.

“I have great hope that it will be built again,” he said.

title.rendered: A miracle from the tunnel gives Nepal hope after 10 days

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 4

For 10 days, there had been no word from the people believed to be trapped inside the Upper Trishuli-3A hydropower project tunnel.

Then, somewhere deep inside the darkness, a rescuer called out.

“Hello.”

A voice answered.

“Hajur.”

It was an ordinary Nepali response to an ordinary greeting. But after 10 days without knowing whether anyone was still alive inside, it was the sound the rescuers had been waiting for.

The rescue team had reached roughly 200 metres into the tunnel when they heard it. For a moment, the rescuers stopped.

Nepal Army personnel, Armed Police and Nepal Police officers, together with technical experts from the Nepal Electricity Authority, looked at each other in the darkness. Some were overcome with emotion. Then they moved.

There was still a wall of mud and broken rock between them and the people inside.

The team had been working its way through the debris since the flood devastated the area. Now, knowing that there were survivors somewhere beyond the blockage, every decision became more urgent—and more dangerous.

They discussed drilling through the debris, as they had done at other points while trying to locate the tunnel. If the rock could not be cleared that way, they would use controlled explosives to break it apart and widen a passage for rescuers. But there was a risk.

The people they were trying to save could be on the other side.

The Army’s Special Forces, Combat Engineers and Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue team had to spend hours assessing whether they could blast through without harming anyone inside.

Once they were satisfied that the operation could proceed safely, they called out again.

“Hello.”

“Hajur.”

The voice came back. The rescuers knew then that they were close.

They pushed oxygen cylinders further into the tunnel and brought in more lights. They moved through thick mud, careful not to become trapped themselves. A rope became a lifeline, helping the rescuers negotiate the treacherous passage.

Then they found Sanjay Sah. He was alive.

The team immediately informed those outside through their communication equipment and began preparing to bring him out.

But the rescue did not end there.

Another faint voice came from deeper inside. It was Kabir Maharjan, a supervisor at the project. He too was found alive and brought out.

For the rescue teams, the two men were more than two survivors. They were proof that the 10-day-old search still had a chance of producing more lives.

Lieutenant Colonel Ganga Baral of the Nepal Army, one of the officers involved in the operation, said the breakthrough was the result of sustained coordination between the different rescue teams.

“It took time, but ultimately we succeeded in rescuing two people alive,” Baral told Onlinekhabar. “We have shown that Nepalis can deliver a remarkable result even in a disaster rescue operation considered almost impossible.”

The rescue teams themselves had little time to savour the moment.

Keshav Dhakal, an engineer with the Nepal Army, has been at the site since August 27, the day after the flood. He credited the success to the entire team that had continued working despite the conditions.

For the rescuers, the job was not to celebrate the breakthrough but to use it.

They continued sending oxygen into the tunnel, hoping there could be others alive inside.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Amrit Thapa of the Armed Police Force said the condition in which the two men were found strengthened that hope.

“When we found them, they were able to open their eyes and look at us,” Thapa said. “When we heard them calling out, we became even more alert and intensified the rescue.”

The operation has required rescuers to cut through metal, concrete, rock and the debris that came down with the flood.

“Our team’s main contribution was cutting through metal and removing concrete,” Thapa said. “We have now cleared the mountain of debris and entered the tunnel, so the risk is not as high as before.”

The Armed Police team has been working around the clock in three shifts, with six personnel in each shift. For commanders, there has been no such thing as a shift ending.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung also spent time at the site as the rescue continued. He stayed near the operation, at a tent close to the tunnel entrance, while the teams worked underground.

When news came that two people had been rescued from about 200 metres inside, Gurung went to the tunnel entrance and helped carry an oxygen pipe.

The response has unfolded amid criticism that senior government officials were not spending enough time on the ground. But the rescue teams say that what mattered inside the tunnel was coordination, sustained effort and quick decisions.

The breakthrough at Trishuli-3A has now given fresh impetus to searches elsewhere in the disaster zone.

At the under-construction Trishuli-3B tunnel near Simle in Nuwakot, rescuers have advanced 426 metres inside, according to the Nepal Army’s Directorate of Military Public Relations and Information.

At Rasuwagadhi Hydropower, 93 people remain unaccounted for.

According to company secretary Narnath Neupane, those missing include 51 regular employees, one board member, two daily-wage workers and 39 workers employed by three contractor companies.

Search efforts there have been hampered by poor weather.

At Chilime Hydropower, a team including Nepal Army personnel has advanced beyond 150 metres into the tunnel.

At Langtang Hydropower, rescuers have drilled through several sections and created passages about eight feet long and three feet wide to continue the search.

At Rasuwagadhi, an Army team has advanced nearly 300 metres into the tunnel.

The Upper Trishuli-3A rescue is also being watched far beyond Nepal.

Ten days after what authorities have described as a “Himalayan tsunami” began in the Bhotekoshi area, the disaster remains a major international story. International media have gathered around the affected hydropower projects, following the tunnel searches and waiting for news of survivors.

Security officials have urged people not directly involved in the rescue to stay away from the sites, warning that unnecessary crowds could complicate an already dangerous operation.

Anil Pokharel, former chief executive of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, has described the crisis in the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors as a test extending beyond Nepal.

The region’s hydropower infrastructure has been badly hit. The powerhouse and other major structures of Upper Trishuli-3A are largely located in Kispang Rural Municipality-5 of Nuwakot, while its dam lies in Uttargaya Rural Municipality of Rasuwa.

One body has so far been recovered from the tunnels. The search for the others continues.

For the rescuers, the two men brought out of Upper Trishuli-3A have changed one thing after 10 days of darkness: there is now a reason to believe that someone else might answer when they call out again.

“Hello.”

“Hajur.”

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

The death toll from the devastating Rasuwa flood on August 26 has reached 1,294, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

The authority confirmed the recovery of 1,294 bodies during a press briefing on Friday evening.

NDRRMA spokesperson Shanti Maharjan said 5,053 people are still missing, while 13,095 people have so far been rescued.

According to Maharjan, 4,627 people are currently taking shelter in 37 holding centres across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

Preliminary assessments show that 7,570 houses have been completely destroyed by the floods, directly affecting an estimated 32,933 people.

The disaster has also damaged 48 government structures, 18 schools and seven health facilities, NDRRMA said.

Similarly, 55 kilometres of roads have been completely destroyed, while 37 motorable bridges and 68 suspension bridges have been damaged.

The floods have also destroyed 1,806 hectares of agricultural land. The authority estimates that this will result in a loss of around 7,686 metric tonnes of food production.

Three hydropower projects, one solar plant and two transmission lines have also been damaged, affecting electricity generation capacity of 783 megawatts, according to NDRRMA.

title.rendered: Rasuwa floods: What has the government done in the last 10 days?

content.rendered:
In the days after a devastating flood swept through Rasuwa and the Trishuli River corridor, more than 1,294 people have been confirmed dead, thousands remain missing and more than 12,000 people have been rescued.

The government says more than 21,000 security personnel have been deployed since the disaster struck.

But what exactly did the state do during those first 10 days—and where did its response fall short?

The answer is a mixed record: a rapid mobilisation of security forces, helicopters and medical services in the immediate aftermath; growing efforts to manage the dead and deliver relief; and, later, international assistance for increasingly difficult tunnel rescues.

At the same time, the disaster exposed major gaps in early warning, local preparedness, volunteer mobilisation and the government’s ability to rescue people trapped underground.

Here is what the government has done over the past 10 days.

Mobilised security forces and helicopters

The government moved security personnel into the affected areas immediately after the flood struck on August 26.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council held an emergency meeting within an hour of the disaster and directed security agencies to prioritise search, rescue and treatment.

The Cabinet subsequently authorised the Home Ministry to mobilise helicopters and other available rescue resources.

The Nepal Army deployed MI-17 helicopters for rescue and medical operations, while private helicopters were also kept on standby.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 21,402 security personnel have since been deployed for rescue and response operations.

The Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force have been involved in search and rescue, evacuation, body recovery and relief distribution.

The Armed Police Force also deployed trained sniffer dogs to search areas where people were believed to have been buried.

Expanded emergency medical response

The Health Ministry activated the health emergency system immediately after the disaster.

Hospitals in Dhunche and Trishuli were brought into the emergency response, while arrangements were made to transfer seriously injured people to Kathmandu.

Bir Hospital, the National Trauma Centre and Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital were prepared to receive patients from the affected areas.

The government says 5,384 people have received medical treatment since the disaster.

The scale of the deaths, however, created a separate challenge. Mortuaries across the country had capacity for only around 600 bodies, forcing authorities to look for additional locations to manage unidentified and unclaimed bodies.

The government subsequently made arrangements to manage unidentified bodies in Chitwan, Kathmandu, Kaski and other areas.

Sent relief supplies to affected areas

The government has also mobilised relief materials to communities affected by the floods.

On the first night alone, the Nepal Army sent eight trucks carrying mosquito nets, dignity kits, sleeping bags, blankets, plastic sheets, tents, solar lights and generators towards the affected areas.

The government has continued collecting and distributing relief materials, although complaints emerged that supplies were not reaching some affected communities quickly enough.

The response has also involved local governments, security agencies and volunteers in distributing relief and assisting displaced families.

Tried to rescue people trapped inside hydropower tunnels

One of the government’s biggest challenges has been the search for people believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels.

Search teams have been working inside the Upper Trishuli-3A, Chilime, Langtang and Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower tunnels.

Nepali security forces initially led the efforts, but the government later brought in specialised tunnel-rescue teams from China and India, with assistance from other countries.

Chinese and Indian rescue teams arrived after criticism grew over the delay in reaching people believed to be trapped underground.

Nepali and foreign teams have since entered several tunnels, reaching approximately 50 metres inside the Chilime tunnel, 150 metres inside the Langtang Hydropower tunnel and 200 metres inside the Upper Trishuli-1 tunnel.

Two bodies were recovered from the Chilime hydropower tunnel, while another two were later recovered from the Langtang Khola Hydropower Project tunnel.

The tunnel operation remains one of the most difficult parts of the government’s response.

Former executive chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority Anil Pokharel says the disaster exposed Nepal’s lack of specialised tunnel-rescue capacity.

“We have no knowledge, skills or capacity for rescuing people from tunnels,” he says. “That needs to improve.”

Former chief executive officer of the National Reconstruction Authority Yubaraj Bhusal also says international assistance should have been mobilised earlier.

Restricted movement and worked to restore connectivity

The government also imposed restrictions on movement towards affected areas as the flood damaged roads and bridges.

Traffic was stopped towards Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Chitwan and Dhading, while authorities also restricted movement along major highways and roads connecting the affected districts.

The disaster destroyed or damaged nearly three dozen bridges, cutting off communities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan.

The government has since begun temporary measures to restore connectivity. A cable crossing was installed at Battar in Nuwakot to provide an alternative crossing after the loss of a bridge.

The Prithvi Highway was also disrupted after the road sank at Krishnabhir along the Nagdhunga-Muglin section.

Introduced a single-window rescue system

As rescue operations expanded, the Home Ministry said it had introduced a single-window system to coordinate disaster response and avoid duplication among different agencies.

The government has been coordinating the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, local governments and foreign rescue teams through the mechanism.

Prime Minister Balen Shah has also held separate briefings with the chiefs of the Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force on the disaster response.

Sought international assistance

The government has sought and received support from several countries and international organisations.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to Prime Minister Shah and offered India’s humanitarian assistance.

China and India sent specialised rescue teams, while other countries and international organisations also expressed their willingness to assist Nepal.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres expressed condolences over the loss of life and pledged support.

The government has also been coordinating international assistance for rescue and relief operations.

Raised climate change and loss-and-damage concerns

The government has also sought to take the disaster beyond immediate rescue and relief.

Nepal has approached the United Nations’ loss and damage mechanism, arguing that climate change contributed to the disaster and seeking compensation through the international framework.

The move reflects the government’s effort to frame the Rasuwa disaster not only as a national emergency but also as part of the wider climate vulnerability faced by Himalayan countries.

Reported the scale of the disaster to Parliament

Prime Minister Shah briefed Parliament on the disaster on September 2, describing the tragedy as a national catastrophe rather than a disaster limited to Rasuwa, Nuwakot or Dhading.

Parliament has also raised concerns about the protection of women and children affected by the disaster.

The government has released its first situation report, estimating that 1.6 million people have been affected by the floods.

But what has the government failed to do?

The government’s response has been substantial in terms of the number of personnel and resources mobilised.

Pokharel, the former disaster management authority chief, says the rapid mobilisation of the state machinery and the large-scale deployment of security personnel and helicopters deserve recognition.

But the disaster has also exposed serious weaknesses.

The most immediate concern is the country’s early-warning system.

Geography professor Narendra Raj Khanal says the flood’s source was tens of kilometres upstream from the communities that suffered the greatest damage. Yet there was insufficient warning for people downstream to protect themselves.

Pokharel says Nepal’s existing early-warning system was not capable of dealing with an event of this scale.

“We had no advance information about the risk,” he says.

Local preparedness has also been questioned. Municipalities and rural municipalities lacked adequate warehouses, equipment and trained personnel for disaster response, according to Pokharel.

The shortage of trained volunteers was another problem.

Prabha Bogati, deputy mayor of Bidur Municipality, says local authorities struggled to find people who could reach places inaccessible by road or helicopter.

“There were places where helicopters could not land and roads could not reach, but we couldn’t even find manpower to walk five minutes to those places,” she says.

The government’s tunnel-rescue response has drawn the strongest criticism.

Both Pokharel and Bhusal say Nepal’s limited technical capacity meant it had to depend on foreign specialists, raising questions about why such expertise was not available earlier.

Ten days on

The first 10 days of the Rasuwa disaster show a government that mobilised quickly and at a significant scale once the disaster struck.

More than 21,000 security personnel have been deployed, over 12,000 people have been rescued and thousands treated. Helicopters, hospitals, relief supplies and foreign rescue teams have all been brought into the response.

But the same 10 days have also exposed weaknesses that existed before the flood: inadequate early warning, weak local preparedness, limited specialised rescue capacity and difficulties getting relief and volunteers to the hardest-to-reach communities.

With the immediate rescue operation still continuing, the government’s next test will be whether the lessons from these 10 days lead to changes that can prevent the next disaster from becoming another catastrophe.

title.rendered: 10 families relocated as landslide puts Darchula settlement at risk

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Ten families have been relocated from Bhattar settlement in Apihimal Rural Municipality of Darchula after a landslide put the area at high risk and temporarily blocked the Chaulani River.

The families have been moved to relatives’ homes as a precaution, while the rural municipality has provided them with essential supplies, including tents.

“The 10 families have been moved to relatives’ homes, and we have provided some necessary materials, including tents,” said rural municipality chair Bhakt Singh Thekare Bohara.

According to Bohara, the landslide is still falling and the settlement remains at risk. It has also caused extensive damage to roads and trekking trails in the area.

The landslide temporarily blocked the Chaulani River, affecting its flow. The river has now reopened, according to local authorities.

Darchula Chief District Officer Bartaraj Paudel said the disruption to the river’s flow has increased the risk of flooding in settlements along its banks.

“People living along the river have been alerted to remain cautious because the river’s flow has been affected,” Paudel said.

The District Administration Office, Darchula, has also issued a public notice urging people to remain alert to the risk of flooding and avoid going near the riverbanks.

title.rendered: Rescue at Trishuli-3B remains difficult as 191 workers remain missing

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 4

The search for 191 employees and workers missing at the Upper Trishuli-3B Hydropower Project in Rasuwa is proving increasingly difficult, with rescue teams still unable to locate the buried project building.

Three small excavators are working continuously at the site, removing debris and large rocks from the area buried by the flood and landslide. But the machines have so far been unable to reach the structures where the missing workers are believed to be.

“We are currently digging with three small excavators, but we have not even been able to locate where the building is,” said project deputy director Leela Aryal. “We are removing the large rocks.”

The biggest obstacle is getting a heavy excavator to the site. Landslides have blocked the road, while efforts to cut through the hillside and clear a route for the machine have yet to be completed.

The Upper Trishuli-3B project says effective debris removal will be difficult without a large excavator.

As an alternative, officials are considering dismantling a large excavator into several parts, transporting the pieces to the project site and reassembling the machine there.

Aryal said the project is coordinating with a mechanic team and the road division for the option.

“If we can somehow get the large excavator there, only then will we be able to see meaningful output,” she said. “With the small excavators, we cannot show any visible output.”

However, dismantling and transporting the excavator would itself take time and cannot be completed in a single day, she said.

Nepali Army and Armed Police Force personnel, along with the project team, are involved in the search and rescue operation. There is currently no foreign rescue team at the site, Aryal said.

Teams are also preparing to approach the buried area through an audit tunnel. They plan to remove timber and other obstructions inside the tunnel to clear a passage and use the route from the Audit-2 side to reach and remove debris.

For now, however, the immediate challenge remains reaching the buried structures. With 191 workers still unaccounted for, rescuers are continuing to clear the site with limited equipment while efforts are underway to bring in heavier machinery.

title.rendered: Nepal begins issuing permits for autumn mountaineering season

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Nepal has started issuing permits for the autumn mountaineering season, with hundreds of climbers already showing interest despite the devastation caused by monsoon floods across the country.

According to the Department of Tourism, 367 climbers from 32 teams had obtained permits to climb mountains in the upcoming season as of Thursday. Of them, 87 are women.

Manaslu has attracted the highest number of climbers so far, with 348 climbers from 29 teams receiving permits.

Three climbers from one team have obtained permits to climb Makalu, while 16 climbers from two teams have received permits for Danga Himal, which stands at 6,220 metres.

Chinese nationals account for the largest number of climbers who have obtained permits so far. The department said 55 Chinese, 39 Russian and 32 American climbers had received permits by Thursday.

Similarly, 27 climbers from France and 24 from the United Kingdom have obtained permits. Fifteen Nepali climbers have also received permits, while Poland, Canada and Germany have 14 climbers each.

The figures indicate that interest in Himalayan expeditions remains strong at the beginning of the autumn season, even as Nepal continues to deal with the aftermath of the monsoon floods.

title.rendered: Buddha Air’s new ATR 72-600 begins commercial operations

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Private airline Buddha Air’s new-series ATR 72-600 aircraft began commercial operations on Friday.

The aircraft, registered as 9N-AOS, made its first commercial flight from Kathmandu to Nepalgunj on Friday morning. Carrying 66 passengers, the aircraft departed Kathmandu for Nepalgunj at 8:06 am.

Buddha Air brought the aircraft to Nepal from Toulouse, France, on July 25, 2026. It took about a month to complete the necessary technical and regulatory procedures as well as repainting.

According to the airline, the ATR 72-600 is equipped with a fully glass cockpit, modern navigation systems, digital flight management and advanced safety systems.

The aircraft, designed for regional flights, is considered more environmentally friendly because it consumes comparatively less fuel. It is also equipped with an RNP-AR navigation system, which facilitates flight operations and landings in low-visibility conditions while meeting the required standards and procedures.

The company said the aircraft has larger passenger seats and overhead bins than those in its previous-generation aircraft. Its improved cabin design also significantly reduces cabin noise compared with the earlier series, according to the company.

Buddha Air is preparing to add another ATR 72-600 aircraft to its fleet in the near future. The airline currently operates 14 ATR 72-500s and one ATR 72-600.

The company recently retired two ATR 42-320 aircraft from service. It also sold another ATR 42-320, which had relatively few flight cycles, to an aircraft company in Europe for parts.

Buddha Air said it added the new-series aircraft to its fleet as part of its commitment to making air travel more convenient and efficient. The airline said the addition would help strengthen its flight operations and maintenance schedules.

Buddha Air currently operates more than 140 domestic flights and landings each day. Internationally, it operates flights from Kathmandu to Varanasi, India, three days a week and to Kolkata four days a week. It also operates flights from Pokhara to Bhairahawa and Nepalgunj.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Egg prices have reached a new record high after the Nepal Layers Poultry Farmers Association raised its farm-gate selling prices again. According to the new price list published by the association, which came into effect on Friday, the price of all egg varieties has been increased by Rs 15 per crate.

With the latest increase, farm-gate egg prices have reached their highest level ever. The association said the adjustment was necessary due to rising production costs and the need to maintain a balance between supply and market demand.

Under the price fixed on August 20, the farm-gate price of XL-sized eggs was Rs 590 per crate. It has now increased by Rs 15 to Rs 605. Similarly, the price of large eggs has risen from Rs 575 to Rs 590 per crate, while the price of medium-sized eggs has increased from Rs 535 to Rs 550.

The price of small eggs, however, remains unchanged. These are farm-gate prices. The consumer price has been set at Rs 25 per egg. Likewise, consumers will have to pay Rs 45 for two medium-sized eggs, or Rs 22.50 per egg. According to association secretary Madan Pokharel, the prices have been set nationwide based primarily on prices in Chitwan. The association has said that poultry farmers have been facing difficulties due to continued increases in the cost of chicken feed, medicines and transportation.

title.rendered: Nepal receives emergency relief and financial aid from 29 countries

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Nepal has received support from 29 countries and major international organisations following the disaster caused by the Bhotekoshi flood. While some countries have provided essential humanitarian assistance, others have sent financial aid as well as relief supplies.

According to a press briefing by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday afternoon, the countries that have expressed solidarity and provided timely assistance during the disaster are India, China, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United Kingdom, Japan, the United States, Qatar, Singapore, South Korea, Australia, Germany, Latvia, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Myanmar, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Norway, Israel, Canada, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Vietnam, New Zealand, Denmark, Switzerland, Ireland and the Czech Republic.

Likewise, the European Union, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank, the United Nations and other friendly countries and international organisations have also provided assistance. Individuals and social organisations have also announced support for Nepal. The Government of Nepal has expressed its gratitude for the assistance.

Forensic teams from 4 countries deployed to identify victims

Forensic teams from four countries have also been deployed in Nepal to help identify the bodies of those who died in the flood. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, forensic teams from India, China, Singapore and South Korea have arrived in Nepal to expedite the collection, analysis and identification of DNA from the bodies of the victims.

The teams are working in coordination with the Nepal Police and other relevant agencies to speed up DNA testing and the identification of the remains.

title.rendered: 93 still unaccounted for at Rasuwa Hydropower as bad weather hampers rescue efforts

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 4

Ninety-three people associated with the Rasuwa Hydropower Company Limited remain unaccounted for following the Bhote Koshi flood, with search and rescue efforts being hampered by bad weather, the company said.

According to company secretary Narnath Neupane, those missing include 51 regular employees, one board member, two daily-wage workers and 39 workers employed by three contractor companies.

The condition of employees who were inside the hydropower plant’s powerhouse remains particularly unclear, Neupane said.

The company had transported equipment needed to clear debris from the tunnel several days ago to the Maithali Army Camp in Battar, Nuwakot. The equipment included a mini excavator, a 30 kVA diesel generator, a submersible pump and hose pipes.

However, a reconnaissance by the Nepali Army rescue team found that the river had further eroded the area in front of the powerhouse, making it unsuitable for a large MI-17 helicopter to land, according to Neupane.

With the larger helicopter unable to transport the equipment, the company purchased a smaller generator and began preparing to send lighter equipment to the project site.

A 6.5 kVA diesel generator, submersible pump, hose pipes and electrical equipment had been scheduled for transportation from Tuesday, but adverse weather delayed the operation.

The company said the equipment was finally flown to Dhunche at 11:20am on Friday. However, it has not yet been possible to transport the equipment from Dhunche to the powerhouse.

Private teams also deployed

The company has also mobilised private-sector personnel to search for people who remain unaccounted for outside the powerhouse.

It has reached an agreement with Himalaya Summit Club Pvt Ltd to deploy skilled and experienced rock climbers associated with the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association. The team has been conducting searches in Timure.

The company had planned to send another helicopter to Ghatte Khola on Friday to search the area. However, the helicopter could not fly because of the weather, and the team was unable to reach Ghatte Khola.

The company has kept separate teams on standby in Battar, Dhunche and the powerhouse area to support the rescue operation.

Two personnel, including a senior engineer, are stationed in Battar. Two engineers are on standby in Dhunche, while an electrical overseer has been assigned to assist the powerhouse rescue team with electrical connections.

A specialised rescue team from the Nepali Army is also on standby in Dhunche with the necessary tools and equipment to be deployed towards the powerhouse.

However, the company said the team has not yet been able to fly to the powerhouse because weather conditions remain unfavourable.

Families kept informed through WhatsApp group

Meanwhile, the company has created a WhatsApp group for the families and relatives of the missing employees to keep them regularly informed about the situation.

The company said information gathered during search and rescue operations, including details of ongoing efforts and available updates, will be shared with the families through the group.

title.rendered: Father swept away in flood, 11-year-old daughter performs funeral rites

content.rendered:
Sindhupalchok, September 4

At an age when she should be holding her father’s hand on her way to school, 11-year-old Khusbu Karki of Bahrabise Municipality-3, Sindhupalchok, has been forced to perform the funeral rites for him.

Khusbu began observing the Hindu mourning rituals after her father, Padam Karki, went missing in the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The family’s elder daughter, 14-year-old Khushi Karki, was unable to perform the rites due to health problems, so her younger sister Khusbu stepped forward to undertake the rituals herself.

Khusbu, a sixth-grade student at Melamchi Ghyang in Helambu Rural Municipality, has been sitting in the mourning enclosure, crying as she remembers her father.

She is young, but the weight of her memories and grief is immense. Even as she observes the mourning rituals, a small hope remains alive in her heart that perhaps her father will return someday. “Although I am his daughter, I am performing the rites according to our social tradition because my father is missing,” she said emotionally. “It is my duty to complete the 13-day mourning rituals. I gathered the courage to do this because I believe that completing the rituals will help my father attain salvation. Even though I do not have a brother, I felt I had to fulfil my responsibility in mourning my father.”

Khusbu said that embracing the tradition and undertaking the rituals as her heart told her to has not been easy. “I am at an age when I should be carrying my schoolbooks and going to school. But after being burdened with this responsibility, I decided to complete it,” she said. “While sitting in mourning, I sometimes feel that my father might suddenly come home.”

Hoping that her father will return, she continues to look toward the road while sitting in the mourning enclosure. Having to perform the funeral rites without even finding her father’s body has left Khusbu both deeply distressed and confused. With no certainty about whether he is alive or dead, other family members are also in deep grief. Nevertheless, she chose to observe the mourning rituals herself, driven by the belief that she must fulfil her duty to her father according to Hindu tradition.

Padam was the family’s main breadwinner

Padam was the family’s primary source of income. He had been working as a van driver for nearly two decades. For the Karki family, which had modest financial means, his driving job was the main source of income for household expenses and the upbringing of his two daughters.

To his two daughters, Padam was more than just a father. He was the family’s main source of support and the foundation of their future. He had spent years behind the wheel, carrying the responsibility of educating his daughters, meeting household expenses and securing the family’s future.

The journey he undertook to provide for his family has now become the most painful journey of their lives. Padam went missing after the devastating flood on Bhadra 10 while he was transporting goods from Rasuwa to Kathmandu. For the family waiting for Padam to return home, each passing day has become increasingly difficult. Khusbu does not know what happened to her father, and his body has not been found. At her age, the absence of her father means far more to her than the meaning of performing funeral rites.

A daughter fulfils her duty

The decision to have Khusbu perform the mourning rituals even though her father’s death has not been confirmed was not an easy one for the family. But she says she is prepared to fulfil her duty to her father. Only 11 years old, Khusbu’s decision to perform the rituals in memory of her father has become an emotional moment for the entire family.

The floods have left many families without their loved ones. In many households, searches for missing relatives are still underway. Many families continue to wait day and night, hoping their loved ones will return. Khusbu has become a representative story of that grief.

Her father drove for years to provide for his family. He struggled to secure a better future for his daughters and put his own wishes aside for the sake of his family’s happiness. But Padam, who was once the family’s main support, has now become a memory and someone they can only wait for. Sitting in mourning, Khusbu keeps saying just one thing: “Father, please come back. I am waiting for you.”

title.rendered: NEA technicians enter Trishuli 3A tunnel to aid search for trapped workers

content.rendered:
Raswa, September 4

Technicians from the Nepal Electricity Authority have entered the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project tunnel alongside the Nepali Army to help search for people who may still be trapped inside.

The NEA technicians entered the underground powerhouse with the Army team to identify possible locations where workers and engineers could be trapped and assist in the ongoing search and rescue operation.

Two people were rescued alive from the project tunnel on Friday morning after nine days of continuous efforts.

The successful rescue of two people alive from the mud-filled tunnel 10 days after the flood has been described as a significant breakthrough in the operation. Rescuers have also recovered one body from inside the tunnel.

However, the NEA estimates that as many as 42 people may still be trapped inside the project.

A large number of workers are believed to have been inside the underground powerhouse when the flood struck. An NEA source said its technical staff entered the powerhouse alongside the Army to help determine where those workers may have taken shelter.

Project chief Awas Ojha said the two survivors are receiving treatment at the Nepali Army’s Military Hospital in Chhauni. The identity of the body recovered from the tunnel has not yet been established.

The two people rescued alive were Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman with the NEA, and Kabir Maharjan, a supervisor at the project.

The rescue operation has involved teams from the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police and the Nepal Electricity Authority.

The Nepali Army has said the health condition of both rescued workers is stable.

According to the NEA, an estimated 42 engineers and employees were trapped inside the tunnel and underground powerhouse of the Upper Trishuli 3A project. The largest number are believed to have been inside the powerhouse itself.

The search and rescue operation is continuing.

title.rendered: 155 more Nepalis stranded in China return home through Tatopani Border

content.rendered:
Sindhupalchok, September 4

Another 155 Nepali nationals who had been stranded in China following the devastating floods in Rasuwa returned home through the Tatopani border point on Friday.

The Chinese side safely brought them to the Liping area of the Tatopani border point and handed them over to Nepali authorities. As part of the ongoing effort to bring Nepalis stranded in China back home after the floods, 114 people returned to Nepal on Thursday, the first day, followed by 155 on Friday.

According to Sindhupalchok Chief District Officer Shashidhar Ghimire, 145 of the 155 people who arrived in Nepal on Friday are residents of Rasuwa. One is from Dhading, and nine are from Kathmandu. Chief District Officer Ghimire said the Chinese authorities also provided Nepali officials with necessary details of the returnees, including their passport numbers.

After completing the required procedures, the returnees will be taken to Kathmandu. On the first day, Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality arranged transportation to Kathmandu for those who returned. On the second day, the Sindhupalchok Chamber of Commerce and Industry arranged transportation for the returnees.

A large number of Nepali and foreign nationals were affected by the floods in Rasuwa. The district administration said efforts to safely repatriate Nepalis stranded in China are continuing. Around 800 Nepalis are reported to have been stranded in China due to the floods. They are being brought back to Nepal gradually through the Tatopani border point.

title.rendered: Goods entering through Korala can be cleared at Chobhar dry port

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Goods imported through the Mustang Customs Office can now be cleared at the Chobhar Dry Port Customs Office in Kathmandu.

For this purpose, the Department of Customs has designated specific road routes. As a result, goods entering Nepal through the Korala border point in Mustang can now be transported directly to Kathmandu for customs clearance without being cleared at the customs office in Mustang.

According to the department, the decision to allow inland transportation has been made until further notice, provided that all conditions, procedures and other requirements stipulated by the Customs Regulations are complied with.

For cargo vehicles, the designated route for vehicles entering through the Korala border point is Nechung–Chhusang–Kagbeni–Jomsom–Beni–Kushma–Pokhara–Damauli–Muglin–Kurinatar–Naubise–Kalanki–Chobhar Dry Port Customs Office.

If problems arise along this route, vehicles will be allowed to take an alternative route via Muglin–Narayanghat–Hetauda–Bhaise–Naubise–Kalanki–Chobhar to reach the dry port.

For new vehicles being driven into the country, the route via Hetauda has been designated for the time being.

Following the devastating floods that destroyed much of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, the Korala border point in Mustang is currently being used as an alternative entry point.

Poudel said authorities were preparing to alert settlements along the riverbank to remain vigilant as the river’s flow had been affected. “An official assessment of the damage at the landslide site has not yet been received. Police have been dispatched to the area,” Poudel said.

The District Administration Office, Darchula, issued a public notice on Friday warning that a landslide from above had buried part of the Chaulani River and that continued landslides could potentially block the river.

The administration has urged residents living along the riverbank to remain alert and take precautions against possible risks, including the possibility that a blocked river could suddenly burst through the blockage.

title.rendered: Chinese foundation brings 27 tons of relief supplies for Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

The China Foundation for Rural Development (CFRD) has arrived in Kathmandu with 27 tons of relief supplies for people affected by the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26.

The first phase of relief supplies arrived at Tribhuvan International Airport under CFRD’s “8.26 Nepal Mudslide Rescue Operation.” After fast-moving floodwaters carrying mud and debris damaged settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, CFRD’s Nepal office immediately activated its emergency response mechanism and began assessing the affected areas and distributing relief supplies.

The first batch of supplies brought from China includes 175 tents, 1,000 blankets, 1,000 warm cotton coats, 1,000 emergency humanitarian relief kits and 6,000 medical packing bags. The supplies, weighing around 27 tons in total, are worth more than 1 million Chinese yuan, according to CFRD. The organisation said the materials will be sent to flood-affected areas of Rasuwa in coordination with the Nepal government’s disaster management mechanism.

Similarly, CFRD has begun arrangements to provide 14 tents, 500 food packages, livelihood supplies for 500 families and 5,000 solar lights in Nuwakot. The food packages contain items including rice, cooking oil and lentils. CFRD said it will continue assisting in the coming days based on the changing needs and conditions of affected communities.

Chinese enterprises and partners, including Highflyer Quant, Beijing Tongxinyuan and Zhejiang Anjihui, contributed to the relief effort. CFRD’s humanitarian engagement in Nepal is not new. Following the 2015 earthquake, the organisation began its involvement in Nepal with emergency rescue and reconstruction efforts, which later expanded to community development, youth training, clean drinking water, agricultural development and disaster management. The organisation said it also assisted during the COVID-19 pandemic and disasters in Jajarkot, Sindhupalchok and Gorkha.

title.rendered: Rasuwa Flood: 180 people from Madhes still missing, 2 confirmed dead

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, September 4

As days pass since the devastating flood, despair is growing among families of people who remain unaccounted for. Meanwhile, more people have been reported missing by relatives in various districts of Madhes Province.

According to the Madhes Province Police Office in Janakpurdham, the number of people reported missing in the Rasuwa flood had reached 220 as of 10 am Friday. The provincial police office said only 195 people had been reported missing two days earlier.

According to SSP Prabhu Prasad Dhakal, spokesperson for the Madhes Province Police Office, 38 of those reported missing have since made contact with their families. The deaths of two others have been confirmed. SSP Dhakal said one person each from Saptari and Bara died in the disaster. A total of 180 people remain unaccounted for following the flood.

District-wise, Saptari has the highest number of missing people, with 52 reported cases. Of them, three have made contact, one has died, and 48 remain missing. In Parsa, three of the 46 people reported missing have made contact, while 43 remain unaccounted for.

In Bara, four of the 30 people reported missing have made contact, one has died, and 25 remain missing. Similarly, in Rautahat, six of the 20 reported missing have made contact, while 14 remain unaccounted for. In Sarlahi, six of the 27 reported missing have made contact, while 21 remain missing.

In Mahottari, seven of the 17 reported missing have made contact, while 10 remain unaccounted for. In Dhanusha, seven of the 14 reported missing have made contact, while seven remain unaccounted for, SSP Dhakal said. In Siraha, two of the 14 reported missing have made contact, while 12 remain unaccounted for.

The police compiled the figures based on applications submitted and information provided by family members and relatives over the phone.

title.rendered: Family celebrates Kabir Maharjan’s rescue after 10 days inside Trishuli 3A tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

For 10 days, Bidya Dangol did not know whether she would see her brother Kabir Maharjan again. Maharjan, from Lalitpur, was trapped inside the Trishuli 3A hydropower project tunnel after the devastating flood in Rasuwa on August 26 blocked the tunnel entrance.

On Friday, 10 days after the flood, he was finally brought out alive.

A Nepal Army-led rescue team, working with technical personnel, located and safely rescued Maharjan and another person trapped inside the tunnel. Maharjan was brought to Kathmandu and taken to hospital, where his treatment has begun.

His sister Dangol rushed to the Military Hospital in Chhauni after learning that her brother had been brought there. She was still waiting to see him when she spoke to reporters.

“We are very happy today. I heard that my brother has been brought here. I haven’t been able to see him yet, but I am relieved,” she said.

The relief, she said, was difficult to put into words.

“He is safe. That is all that matters. We are extremely happy. There is no limit to our happiness,” she said. “My brother had been in there for 10 days. All of us sisters came here to see him. We had almost lost hope. We never imagined that something like this could happen.”

On Friday morning, before she knew her brother had been found, Dangol had prayed for his safety.

“I performed puja in the morning. I was praying to God that nothing would happen to my brother,” she said.

After completing the puja, she checked her phone while having tea.

“I saw the news on my phone. I became extremely happy and immediately called my younger sister,” she recalled. “I told her, ‘Maya, this has happened, right?’ She said, ‘Yes, sister.’ We were so happy. I just said, ‘Oh God, thank you a million times.’”

Maharjan worked as a supervisor at the Trishuli 3A project.

His rescue has also brought a renewed sense of hope to families waiting for news about others still believed to be trapped or missing following the flood.

Dangol said she was now praying for the safe rescue of everyone still inside the tunnel.

Another person was also rescued alive from the Trishuli 3A tunnel on Friday.

title.rendered: Landslide-created lake below Langtang Lirung poses no immediate risk, authorities say

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

A lake formed after a landslide triggered by a falling ice-rock mass on the north face of Langtang Lirung is not considered a risk at present, according to Nepal’s Flood Forecasting Division.

The division’s chief, Binod Parajuli, said a Chinese team monitoring the area had informed Nepali authorities that although the water level in the upper lake had increased slightly, it had not reached a dangerous level.

Two lakes were formed after the ice-rock mass fell from the north face of Langtang Lirung. The first depression formed downstream, while a second formed higher up along the upper section of the Lhende Khola.

The Chinese team has referred to the lake near the stream as Barrier Lake One and the upper lake as Barrier Lake Two.

“Almost all the water from the lower lake has already flowed out, so there is no significant accumulation of water and there is not much of a problem,” Parajuli told Onlinekhabar. “The water level in the upper lake has increased somewhat, but we have been informed that it has not reached a dangerous level.”

According to Parajuli, the Chinese team has been observing the area on the Chinese side of the border and monitoring the Nepali side across the Lhende Khola. It has been regularly sharing information about the lakes with Nepali authorities.

The upper lake covers approximately 0.19 square kilometres. The water level there has risen by about two metres, with an estimated 600,000 cubic metres of water now accumulated in the lake.

“The Chinese team has been continuously providing information about the lake,” Parajuli said. “Based on the situation so far, their assessment is that there is no immediate risk from the water in the lake.”

Two lakes were formed near the Nepal-China border in the northern part of Langtang Lirung following the Rasuwa flood on August 26.

Four days later, the lower of the two lakes breached, sending water downstream and triggering another flood in the Bhotekoshi River.

Parajuli said the second flood caused the lower lake to drain, leaving the upper lake as the one currently being monitored.

title.rendered: Death toll from Bhotekoshi floods reaches 1,287, economic losses estimated at Rs 387.54 billion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

The death toll from the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa and the wider disaster has reached 1,287, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The authority’s latest update, released at noon on Friday, puts the preliminary estimate of economic damage and losses from the disaster at Rs 387.54 billion.

It said Rs 7.15 billion would be required for early recovery alone.

Chitwan records highest number of recovered bodies

Of the 1,287 bodies recovered by Friday noon, the highest number was found in Chitwan. Only 96 of the recovered bodies have so far been identified.

The district-wise breakdown is as follows:

More than 5,000 still unaccounted for

According to the authority, 5,083 people remain unaccounted for following the Bhotekoshi floods and landslides, including 583 foreign nationals.

The list includes 2,130 people from Rasuwa and 2,340 from Nuwakot. The authority said the list may also include unidentified bodies.

A total of 5,397 people have been injured in the disaster. They are receiving treatment at various hospitals and through medical teams from the Nepali Army and Armed Police Force.

Security agencies have so far rescued 13,093 people and taken them to safety, including 303 foreign nationals.

On Friday, two people were rescued alive from the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project.

For rescue and relief operations, the Nepali Army has conducted 830 helicopter flights, while the private sector has conducted 129 flights.

Thousands of homes and infrastructure damaged

The preliminary assessment shows extensive damage to homes and public infrastructure. A total of 7,570 private houses have been damaged, while 48 government structures, 18 schools and seven health facilities have suffered partial or complete damage. T

he disaster has also completely damaged 55 kilometres of roads, while 37 motorable bridges and 68 suspension bridges have been damaged.

More than 21,000 security personnel deployed

A total of 21,421 security personnel have been mobilised across the country for disaster management.

This includes 9,287 personnel from the Nepali Army, 7,931 from Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force.

Relief supplies have also been transported to affected areas. From Kathmandu, 69 trucks and 38 Boleros have carried food and non-food items.

The Armed Police Force has delivered relief to Nuwakot and Rasuwa through 163 air sorties.

The government has provided immediate cash relief of Rs10 million each to Rasuwa and Nuwakot, Rs5 million to Dhading and Rs135 million to 15 affected local governments.

Communication services gradually restored

Communication services disrupted by the floods are gradually being restored.

According to the authority, 116 of Nepal Telecom’s 120 towers and 75 of Ncell’s 78 towers are now operational.

Chinese meteorological authorities have been providing Nepal with weather monitoring, forecasting, early warning and impact-based services following a massive landslide at the Kerung-Rasuwagadhi border crossing between China and Nepal.

Following the disaster, China’s meteorological administration immediately held a video consultation with Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology on weather-related matters.

title.rendered: Body recovered from Trishuli 3-A Hydropower Project tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Rescue workers have recovered a body from the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli 3-A Hydropower Project, where two people were rescued alive.

According to Project Chief Awas Ojha, security personnel recovered one body from the tunnel. The identity of the deceased has yet to be established.

A rescue team comprising personnel from the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police and Nepal Electricity Authority had earlier rescued two people alive from the project tunnel. The two, Nepal Electricity Authority mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah and supervisor Kabir Maharjan, are receiving treatment at the Nepal Army hospital in Kathmandu.

The Nepal Army said their health condition is normal. The Nepal Electricity Authority estimates that 42 engineers and employees are trapped inside the powerhouse located within the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3-A project. Most of those trapped are believed to be inside the powerhouse itself.

Search and rescue operations are continuing in the underground powerhouse area to determine whether more people can be rescued.
