title.rendered: ‘Nepalis can do it too’: Nepal Army team pulls two survivors from Trishuli 3A

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Ten days after the Bhotekoshi flood blocked the entrance to a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, two people trapped inside were rescued alive on Friday.

The successful rescue has renewed hopes that others reported missing from the project may also be found.

A rescue team led by the Nepali Army, with personnel from the Armed Police Force, Nepal Police and technical staff from the Nepal Electricity Authority, had been working inside the tunnel for a week before locating and rescuing the two men.

For Lt Col Ganga Baral of the Nepali Army, who is commanding the rescue operation at Trishuli 3A, the successful rescue was the result of round-the-clock efforts by a team working against difficult conditions.

“We worked day and night. We kept at it. We have achieved an almost unbelievable success,” Baral said. “We have proved that Nepalis can do it too.”

He said the operation had provided a major learning experience in disaster management and that rescue teams were continuing their search because others could still be trapped inside the tunnel.

“We worked day and night and kept going. The Army, Armed Police, Nepal Police and employees of the Nepal Electricity Authority are working in coordination,” he said.

Two workers found alive

Sanjay Sah and Kabir Maharjan were rescued on Friday morning.

Sah worked in the project’s control room, while Maharjan was a supervisor at the project.

Maharjan was taken to the Military Hospital in Chhauni immediately after his rescue and is receiving treatment. Sah has also been kept under close medical observation.

After his rescue, Sah described how he became trapped inside the tunnel. He said that when floodwater entered the tunnel, he told others to escape. He was delayed in getting out and became trapped inside.

The rescue team has not stopped searching.

According to Baral, rescue personnel remain inside the tunnel and are continuing search and rescue operations.

‘We took time, but eventually succeeded’

Baral said specialised teams from the Nepali Army were deployed immediately after the flood.

“Soon after the flood, the Nepali Army’s Special Forces, Combat Engineers and Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue teams were deployed here,” he said. “Although it took some time to get the result, we eventually succeeded in rescuing two people alive.”

The rescue operation has involved a large number of personnel from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force.

Baral said coordination among the security agencies, together with technical guidance from engineers including Uday Neupane, who arrived from Kathmandu, had been crucial to the rescue.

“All the security agencies are working with excellent coordination in their respective areas. The guidance of the technical team, including engineer Uday Neupane, who came from Kathmandu, and effective coordination with other security agencies made this success possible,” he said.

Search continues inside the tunnel

As rescue teams continue searching for others who may be trapped, Baral said it was too early to provide detailed information about conditions inside the tunnel.

The teams are still assessing and working through the area, including the challenges posed by the conditions inside.

“The search and rescue operation is still underway inside, so it is not yet possible to provide detailed information,” Baral said. “The teams are deployed and the rescue operation is continuing.”

title.rendered: Rasuwa Flood: What is the rescue progress in each tunnel?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

The devastating flood that swept through the Bhotekoshi River into the Trishuli River in Rasuwa on August 26 caused extensive loss of life and property. Search and rescue operations are still underway.

People working at various hydropower projects in Rasuwa were also trapped by the flood. While the bodies of some have been recovered, the whereabouts of others remain unknown. Following reports that several people were trapped inside hydropower project tunnels, technical teams, including personnel from the Nepal Army, have continued focused search and rescue operations.

According to Nepal Army Colonel Jhabindra Bahadur Reshmi, the Army has so far rescued more than 3,200 Nepali nationals. The figure includes people rescued both from inside and outside the tunnels. He said the Army has also rescued more than 270 foreign nationals. “Our main priority is to rescue people alive. Search and rescue operations are continuing in all seven tunnels in the area,” he said.

According to Reshmi, the rescue progress at the various projects is as follows:

  • Trishuli 3-A: Rescue teams have entered up to 170 meters inside the tunnel and have rescued two people alive. Search and rescue operations are continuing.
  • Trishuli 3-B: Army personnel have entered up to 30 meters inside the tunnel. Work is currently underway to remove soil and sludge.
  • Chilime Hydropower Project: Army personnel have entered up to 150 meters inside the tunnel and are continuing search and rescue efforts.
  • Langtang Hydro: Openings measuring eight feet in length and three feet in width have been made at various points of the tunnel to facilitate rescue efforts. The rescue operation is continuing.
  • Upper Trishuli 1: The Army rescue team has entered up to 200 meters inside the tunnel.
  • Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project: Army personnel have entered up to 275 meters inside the tunnel.

Meanwhile, the Nepal Army has constructed a temporary rope crossing at Indreni Ghat. According to Colonel Reshmi, work has also begun on constructing a rope crossing and a Bailey bridge at Devighat. He said the Army is conducting rescue operations at 19 locations by land, in addition to carrying out aerial rescues.

title.rendered: Home Minister Gurung: Focus on results, not where I am

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Home Minister Sudan Gurung has responded to criticism over his physical presence in disaster management and the functioning of the state. Gurung said those who expect the old style of leadership, in which leaders remain seated in their offices holding documents, are “living in the wrong era,” describing the criticism as a “generation gap.”

In a statement posted on social media on Friday, Gurung clarified that the Disaster Response Command Center is fully operational with the participation of senior officials from the relevant ministries. “If you view leadership in the old way, associating it with sitting in a ministerial chair and holding documents, then you are in the wrong era—a generation gap,” he wrote.

He added, “The Disaster Response Command Center is fully operational with the participation of senior officials from the relevant ministries, so there is no need to worry. We are conducting command operations and strategic meetings online every four hours.” Gurung criticised the traditional working style, saying the country had suffered for years from the consequences of leadership from behind a desk without understanding the realities on the ground. “I am surprised to see some people still pressuring us to adopt the same old approach while expecting different and better results,” he wrote.

He claimed that the use of digital platforms has made administrative and rescue operations much faster and more effective than conducting them from behind a desk. Addressing his critics, he said, “Rather than worrying about where I am, I would like to request that you focus on the results.”

His clarification comes amid questions from some political circles and on social media about his working style and physical presence during the response to the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa and the subsequent rescue operations.

title.rendered: Oli prioritises direct relief to flood victims, questions ‘Green Army’ activities

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

CPN-UML chair and former prime minister KP Sharma Oli has said providing immediate relief directly to flood and landslide victims is his party’s top priority, arguing that government procedures can delay assistance reaching those affected.

Speaking on Friday while handing over relief materials collected by the party for flood victims in Rasuwa at the UML central office in Chyasal, Lalitpur, Oli said the party had chosen to deliver assistance directly to victims rather than relying solely on government funds.

“We have not said that we will not deposit money into the government fund. But considering that there can be delays in getting money deposited into the government fund to the victims on time, we have prioritised delivering relief directly into the hands of victims,” Oli said.

He said the party could also contribute to the government’s relief fund after immediate rescue and relief operations were completed, depending on the situation.

According to Oli, the UML has been collecting and distributing relief using its own resources and mobilising party members. The party had initially set a target of distributing cash and relief materials worth around Rs120 million, but the total value of assistance would exceed that amount, he said.

Oli criticises AI-generated images

Oli also criticised the use of artificial intelligence-generated images during the disaster, saying some people were attempting to gain popularity by creating artificial scenes and portraying themselves as public servants.

“At a time when thousands of lives have been lost and a large proportion of infrastructure has been destroyed, we should be focused on providing maximum service to the victims,” he said. “This is not the time to create artificial photographs and publicise them to portray oneself as a servant of the people.”

He urged individuals and organisations to focus on service rather than publicity, saying all available attention and resources should be directed towards rescue, relief and rehabilitation.

Oli questions ‘Green Army’

Oli also raised serious questions about the activities, training and financial sources of a group known as the ‘Green Army’, asking the government to clarify its identity and purpose.

Speaking during the same relief handover programme, Oli disputed the group’s claims that it had provided relief during the 2015 earthquake and the Covid-19 pandemic.

He also questioned the use of uniforms resembling those worn by the Nepali Army, with some members reportedly wearing rank insignia.

“This organisation did not exist in 2015, nor was it there during Covid. When floods hit Rasuwa last year or during other political developments in the country, no personnel from this group were seen in these uniforms,” Oli said.

“The army provides periodic training to NCC students, but how and through what process did this group receive training? Who paid for it? Why has my name been linked to it? There appears to be something suspicious here,” he said.

Oli questioned the source of funds for the boots, uniforms and mobilisation of the group, which is claimed to have around 70,000 members.

He called on the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Home Affairs, Nepali Army and Armed Police Force to provide the public with clear information about the group and its operations.

Responding to claims that the organisation was registered while he was prime minister, Oli said registering an organisation was not the responsibility of the prime minister but was handled through separate legal provisions and government offices.

He suggested that the mobilisation of opaque groups such as the ‘Green Army’ could pose challenges to security and legal norms.

‘It is unfortunate that the Army is being dragged into controversy’

Oli said it was unfortunate that the Nepali Army, which he described as a prestigious institution, had been drawn into political controversy.

He said the Army should remain a trusted and credible institution responsible for national security and should always remain above controversy.

“The Nepali Army is an institution that should never be dragged into political controversy. But efforts have been made to drag it into controversy since last year,” Oli said. “As the Army is a source of hope and trust for the Nepali people, it is appropriate for the institution to remain clean and operate within its boundaries.”

Oli also questioned the timing and effectiveness of the Army’s recent mobilisation in disaster management, saying it was unclear whether its presence in the name of rescue and relief had been effective.

He nevertheless praised the contributions made by the Nepali Army and Nepal Police to rescue and relief operations.

Oli said the immediate priority should remain relief and rehabilitation. He also said work was underway through provincial governments to replace suspension bridges with permanent footbridges in various locations and reopen roads that had been blocked by the disaster.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has expressed deep sorrow over the loss of life and destruction caused by the devastating floods in Nepal during a telephone conversation with Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah.

Albanese shared details of the conversation on social media, saying he had spoken with Prime Minister Shah and conveyed Australia’s deepest condolences following the disaster.

“Today I spoke with Nepal’s Prime Minister Shah to express Australia’s deepest condolences following the devastating floods and tsunami-like disaster,” Albanese wrote.

He said Australia was providing humanitarian supplies, equipment and specialised capabilities to areas where they were most needed.

“The loss of life and physical destruction caused by this disaster is heartbreaking,” he said. “We are providing humanitarian supplies, equipment and specialist capabilities to affected areas.”

Albanese also said Australian nationals had gone missing following the floods and that efforts were continuing to locate them.

He expressed his sympathy and condolences to the families and relatives of Australians who remain unaccounted for.

title.rendered: Across the Trishuli, an information vacuum leaves people at the mercy of rumours

content.rendered:
Trishuli, September 4

At the banks of the Trishuli, 86-year-old Bhuwan Prasad Ghimire leaned on his walking stick and stared across the river.

He has spent his entire life beside the Trishuli. He has watched it rise and fall through the seasons, lived through its quieter days and its angry ones. But what he saw now was beyond anything he had known.

The concrete bridge and the old suspension bridge that once connected the two sides had both been swept away.

“I have spent my whole life on the banks of the Trishuli,” Ghimire said. “I had never seen the river like this, nor even imagined it in my dreams. I had never heard my forefathers speak of such destruction.”

Then he fell silent.

For communities living along the river, the flood has destroyed much more than houses and bridges. It has broken the physical connections that allowed people to cross from one bank to another in minutes, to visit relatives, trade goods, attend school or reach a hospital.

It has also created something less visible but increasingly frightening: an information vacuum.

Without electricity, mobile connectivity or internet access, people cannot easily find out what has happened, what is happening or what might happen next. In that vacuum, rumours have begun to travel faster than reliable information.

And for people already traumatised by a catastrophic flood, some of those rumours are terrifying.

The Trishuli floods of August 26 destroyed or swept away 35 bridges between Miteri Bridge at the Nepal-China border and Muglin, cutting off movement between communities on either side of the river. More than 200 homes from settlements between Devighat and Betrawati were swept away, while more than 100 people remain missing or out of contact.

Flood victims, pregnant women and children are sheltering in cold classrooms at a holding centre in Bhairum Secondary School in Trishuli Bazaar.

The destruction is widespread, but the experience of it is not the same on both sides of the river.

The other side

Most ministers and lawmakers who have visited the flood-affected area have remained on the more accessible side of the river. From Kathmandu, the route through Tokha–Chhahare, or Kakani to Battar, Bidur and Betravati, is comparatively straightforward.

Crossing to the other side is another matter.

Almost every small and large bridge along the 82-kilometre stretch from Rasuwagadhi to Galchhi has disappeared.

Galchhi now has the only surviving bridge. On one side, the bridge does not rest on a conventional concrete span but directly on rock. Its engineering may explain why it survived the force of the flood.

Beyond Galchhi, however, there are few remnants of bridges at all. Some suspension bridges remain hanging limp and damaged. Others have vanished completely.

We crossed the only remaining bridge connecting the geography and lives of communities on both banks along this stretch, then travelled towards Uttargaya, following the stories of people living through the aftermath.

The affected settlements came one after another: Darshantar, Piplatar, Pipladanda, Sirkhali, Gauribesi, Kalikhola, Devighat, Trishuli Bazaar and Sole Bazaar.

The flood has brought down not only houses but people’s spirits.

Communities that once crossed the river in three minutes, sharing their celebrations, grief and everyday lives, have suddenly become strangers to one another. The river has swallowed the bridges, and with them the easy communication that once connected the two banks.

At Darshantar, Ghimire stood watching the settlement opposite him. For someone who has lived beside the river for 86 years, there was little left to say.

A project swept away

Directly opposite Darshantar is Ratmate, where the much-discussed MCC project substation was under construction.

The 400-kilovolt substation was designed to transmit about 3,200 megawatts generated by various hydropower projects. The project has an investment of USD 51.6 million, roughly Rs 7.25 billion.

Construction had only just begun in June 2026. It was scheduled for completion in 39 months. The flood swept away the project site.

Even after seven days, the Trishuli remains thick with mud and debris. The banks continue to erode, and residents fear that the river could reach homes that have survived so far.

The physical destruction is visible everywhere. But reaching the places where people are living through it is itself becoming a challenge.

The road on the far side of the river was never a major route. Vehicles generally travelled on the other bank, while people living on this side crossed the bridges. There had been little reason to prioritise paving an alternative road.

Now that dirt road is the lifeline of the entire side of the river.

It is narrow and covered in red mud. Rain and water make the journey slow and treacherous. Vehicles queue along the route. Sometimes passengers sit inside; sometimes they get out and push.

On August 13, it took us four hours to travel roughly 20 kilometres from Galchhi to Devighat.

Relief volunteers said that in the days that followed, the same journey could take nine or 10 hours because of the traffic.

At Devighat, it was difficult at first to tell whether one was looking at a market or a riverbed. The landscape was desolate.

Locals had gathered at chautaris — traditional communal resting and meeting places. In settlement after settlement, people were doing the same. There was no electricity. No internet. No Facebook or TikTok. There was little news and little entertainment. So people had returned to the chautari.

“It has been laid waste,” said 55-year-old Purna Bahadur Bhujel. “It feels like the Stone Age; we know nothing.”

When the government message arrived too late

Near Devighat stands a statue of Prithvi Narayan Shah, where the king died. The statue survived because it stands on higher ground. The bridge, however, did not. Neither did the settlements around it.

The Tadi River joins the Trishuli at Devighat. There were separate bridges over the Trishuli and Tadi at their confluence. Neither remains.

Images of an iron bridge being swept away by floodwaters travelled around the world. It was the bridge over the Tadi.

Below the chautari, a house stood with only its pillars remaining across two floors.

Lok Bahadur Pudasaini and his wife, Durga, were cleaning what remained.

The house belonged to journalist Shyam Sundar Pudasaini, an energetic journalist who died suddenly last year. Lok Bahadur lost his brother last year. This year, Durga’s brother is missing. He worked at Trishuli 3B and has been out of contact since the flood.

“Was he trapped by the flood inside the tunnel, or was he swept away while trying to escape?” Durga asked.

Her own maternal family is across the Trishuli. She has not even been able to sit with them and grieve. We suggested that she follow official information. She then showed us her phone, with barely any battery remaining.

“We sat on the hillside for two hours until the flood subsided, then came home and were doing household chores,” she said. “Then a message came: ‘A flood is coming in the Trishuli, please stay safe.’”

The message, rather than reassuring her, had only deepened her distress. “The government’s message came too late,” she said.

The warning had arrived after the danger had already passed.

The price of survival

More than 200 homes across both banks at Devighat were swept away. More than 100 people were swept away or remain missing. Some families, having found no bodies, made symbolic bodies from kusha grass and performed funerals. Others are still waiting and hoping.

Even people whose homes survived are struggling.

Cooking gas was already scarce. The market had been swept away. With the road damaged and goods unable to move easily, prices soared.

Petrol was reportedly selling for Rs 550 a litre in Trishuli.

At first, the price itself seemed like a story. But after travelling the road, the problem became clearer.

The road is so narrow that even ambulances struggle to pass. How, then, are oil tankers supposed to reach the area and keep fuel prices at a reasonable level?

There is a question for the government here, too. If helicopters are flying in to carry relief, could they not also transport fuel from the Nepal Oil Corporation so that people can obtain petrol at a reasonable price?

At the chautari, 77-year-old Krishna Prasad Aryal summed up the feeling of abandonment.

“Across the river, there is no state. We are alone,” he said. “Every resource has been spent there. It feels like everyone has abandoned us.”

A home, a shop and 30 years of work

A week after the flood, electricity had begun returning intermittently. Internet access, too, might gradually return. But that does not answer the bigger questions.

When will the roads reconnect these communities? When will the bridges be rebuilt? When will housing grants arrive? And even if the money arrives, where will people be allowed to build?

The disaster has raised a problem different from that faced after an earthquake.

After an earthquake, people could rebuild on the same foundations if the site and construction meet safety standards. But after a flood of this scale, where can the foundations be laid?

On the same riverbank, vulnerable to the next flood?

On the far side of the Trishuli is Bidur–Dhunge Bazaar. A journey that once took two minutes now requires a route from the Trishuli to Galchhi, then to Kathmandu and back towards Bidur. What once took minutes can now take as long as two days.

Helicopters can rescue people caught in a disaster. But how does an ordinary sick person reach a hospital in the city?

“It is even harder when someone falls ill,” one resident said. “If a patient is serious, taking them to Kathmandu is almost impossible.”

In Trishuli Bazaar, 62-year-old Beg Bahadur Bogati stood among the ruins of his six-storey house. For 30 years, he had run a television shop. On August 26, the flood swept away his home and the wealth he had accumulated over three decades.

“The damage is around Rs 50 million,” he said. “The house and business were financed with bank loans. I don’t know whether the bank will accept what has happened. I don’t know what to do.”

Many displaced residents stood along the embankment looking towards what remained of their homes. For many, there was little left to return to.

Four missing

At 9.30 pm on August 31, Bhairum Secondary School in Trishuli Bazaar had become a holding centre.

Heavy rain was falling.

Women, children, adults and elderly people lay on desks and benches inside the classrooms. Others sat or lay in rows along the verandah, using umbrellas to shield themselves from the rain.

Some had mats. Others lay directly on the cold floor.

Among those sheltering there was Suchit Joshi, from Bidur Municipality-1, who works at Tribhuvan Trishuli Multiple Campus.

He survived. Four of the eight members of his family are missing: his wife, Manju Shrestha; his seven-year-old daughter, Sumansi Joshi; his brother’s wife; and his brother’s son.

“I tried very hard to find them,” he said. “I repeatedly rode my motorcycle around the areas the flood had reached. I couldn’t find any trace.”

He kept searching.

“I have wandered around from morning until late at night. I shouted and called out, hoping they might hear me. I called their names in case they responded. I even walked around blowing a whistle, hoping the children would hear. But every attempt failed.”

Sumansi was a Grade 1 student at Gyankunj School. Her father remembered how she reacted whenever a helicopter passed overhead.

“When a helicopter came overhead, she would run out shouting, ‘Dad, a helicopter!’” he said. “Today the sky is full of helicopters. But my daughter is not here to watch them.”

During his search, Suchit found his nephew and uncle and helped get them rescued. He also found an elderly woman trapped by the flood and helped rescue her.

He also found three bodies, but they could not be identified. Around him, other families were waiting for answers.

Seven months pregnant

Srijana Nagarkoti, 27, is seven months pregnant. She was staying in a room at Bhairum Secondary School in Bidur Municipality-8. She had a house in Trishuli Bazaar.

“Our home in Trishuli Bazaar was swept away by the flood,” she said. “We have nothing left. I am staying in a cold classroom. I worry the cold in the room will affect the baby in my womb.”

She and her husband had run a meat shop in Trishuli. They also had a farm with 200 pigs. The flood has taken everything from them. Their home and their livelihood.

For people like Srijana, the disaster is not only about what has already been lost. It is about trying to imagine a life after the water has gone.

Rumours become another disaster

One week after the flood, electricity had started returning in some places, but not reliably. We brought battery backup equipment to charge their cameras. Locals were not so fortunate.

Even when electricity returned, it was sometimes only enough to provide what residents described as “half voltage”, insufficient to charge their phones. And even when a phone could be charged, there was still no internet. No internet meant no news.

Around the world, there is growing concern about misinformation and deepfakes circulating on social media. But in the villages along the Trishuli, something more basic — and in some ways more frightening — was happening.

Rumours were spreading without social media at all.

“More than the flood, the rumours have troubled us,” said Bhagwati Aryal of Tupche.

“They say China is going to open all the dams and lakes upstream. Sometimes they say Gosainkunda is about to burst. Yesterday there was a rumour that Manasarovar had tipped over and was coming this way. I haven’t been able to look at my mobile. How do we know which rumour is true and which is not? We have been terrified around the clock.”

For people already living through a catastrophe, uncertainty itself has become a source of trauma.

A fellow journalist took his father to Kathmandu overnight through Galchhi. But the rumours had so unsettled him that he continued to believe the flood was coming.

Even after reaching Kathmandu, he would wake everyone in the middle of the night, saying: “The flood has come.”

The problem is that people cannot simply dismiss the rumours. Last Sunday morning, another surge came.

“The river rose with a frightening sound,” one resident recalled. “I ran out of the house, and the whole village had already reached the higher slopes. The flood only became moderate at 6am.”

Once again, people fled uphill. And once again, the official warning came later.

They had spent two hours on the hillside before returning home. Only then did the government message arrive saying a flood was coming.

In an information vacuum, even a genuine warning can arrive looking like another rumour.

The rescue effort

The deployment of security personnel has been one of the more visible parts of the response.

Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force personnel have remained continuously in the field, moving almost constantly.

They carry relief supplies, bodies, generators and equipment. Excavators move through the damaged areas. Personnel travel back and forth along roads that are themselves barely passable.

We ate chowmein and instant noodles on the road for two days before returning home. Rescue workers have spent many days in the field, eating beaten rice and plain instant noodles. It is unclear how many more days they will have to continue.

From Tuesday, the government began installing a tuin — a cable crossing — to improve movement between the banks. When word spread that it was being installed, we rushed from the market towards the riverbank. Hundreds of people had gathered.

One end of the cable was tied to a pillar of a ruined house. The other was attached to a tree on the opposite bank. The first crossing carried three cartons of essential medicines for the District Public Health Office.

Then a woman who had been rescued on the near bank needed to be transported across. She was placed in the carriage. It moved rapidly over the river and then stopped suddenly in the middle.

Security personnel were waiting on the far bank, but there was no rope with which to pull the carriage across. The technical coordination had failed. An elderly man watching the scene became agitated.

“Is this how you play with people’s lives?” he said. “Is this a spectacle in the name of rescue and relief? Is this really a tuin? A tuin is supposed to be operated by the people themselves to cross from one side to the other. Is it possible to keep 15 people stationed here every time one person needs to be pulled across?”

Yet even amid such frustration, something striking remained: faith in the government had not disappeared. The same man continued to defend it through political reasoning.

“Would Sudan Gurung build such a tuin? Would Balen build such a tuin?”

When asked who had built it, he answered: “This must surely be the opposition party’s doing; they have done all sorts of things to defame the government.”

The exchange revealed another fracture running through the disaster zone. Thousands of people are directly affected — drowned, missing, homeless, injured or grieving. Yet beyond those immediate victims, people appear to have divided themselves according to whom they supported in the last election, rather than according to what the government has or has not done.

At a chautari in Devighat, the reporters asked residents about the state’s response.

One person said: “The state is nowhere here.”

Before he had finished, a young man behind him responded: “The state has done what it needs to do.”

The two views came from the same settlement, under the same government, in the same disaster. One saw abandonment. The other saw action.

The man criticising the government added that Nepali Congress president Gagan Thapa had only recently travelled along the same road.

“Except for him, no one has asked about us,” he said.

We did not ask which party he belonged to, nor which party the young man defending the government supported.

A settlement erased

Further upstream, near the confluence of the Betrawati and Trishuli, lies Sole Bazaar. On one side of the river is Paidhali Taar in Rasuwa. On the other is Sole Bazaar in Nuwakot.

Krishna Prasad Rijal, chair of the Red Cross Tumche sub-branch, explained how closely the two communities were connected.

Sole Bazaar once had around 100 homes. Now there is almost no trace of it.

“Sixty-eight people were swept away from one place in Sole Bazaar alone,” Rijal said. “Only one body has been found.”

From the riverbed at Sole Bazaar, the powerhouse of the Trishuli 3B hydropower project can be seen. Or rather, what remains of it can. Its powerhouse was swept away.

“There were 65 people inside,” Rijal said. “We do not know whether they were swept away or trapped inside.”

At Betrawati, a damaged building still stood with a tower and clock. The clock had stopped. It looked as though time itself had been stunned by the destruction.

Betrawati, also known as Uttargaya, was home to around 200 households and more than 1,000 people. The exact number of people missing is still unknown.

On the day we arrived, 24 bodies had been recovered from the ruins near the clock tower.

The place has long carried religious significance.

Betrawati lies at the confluence of the Betrawati and Trishuli rivers. It is known as Uttargaya — North Gaya — in contrast to Gaya in India, and is an important Hindu pilgrimage site for performing rites for ancestors. Locals say tens of thousands of people come during Poush Shukla Purnima.

The settlement had already been devastated by the 2015 earthquake. There had been doubts about whether people should resettle there.

Yogesh Dangol built the clock tower in an effort to encourage people to return. The settlement grew again. In barely a decade, the flood washed it away.

What comes after the water?

The immediate rescue effort will eventually end. The water will recede. The roads will, at some point, be repaired. Bridges will be rebuilt. Electricity and internet will return.

But the harder question is what happens to the people who have lost almost everything.

Where will they live? Where will they rebuild? What happens when the next flood comes? The disaster along the Trishuli raises a question that extends far beyond this river valley: how long can Nepal continue to absorb disasters of this scale?

The fever of the Earth is rising. Snow and ice are melting. The surface of the Himalayas is degrading. Mountains can collapse with ice, triggering disasters downstream.

Industrialisation and development, together with carbon emissions, are driving climate change.

Nepal, however, has contributed little to the emissions causing the crisis. Its share of global carbon emissions is stated at just 0.1 per cent.

And yet it is among the places paying a heavy price.

There is a Nepali expression for being harmed by something one did not consume: nakhayeko bish lagchha — to be poisoned by something you did not eat.

That is increasingly how the climate crisis feels in Nepal.

The people along the Trishuli did not create the conditions that are changing the climate. Yet they are watching their homes, bridges, businesses and communities disappear beneath increasingly destructive floods.

For now, many of them are still waiting for electricity, internet access, roads, bridges, relief and information.

But there is another thing Nepal must do.

It must speak.

And it is already taking too long to make the world hear what is happening here.

title.rendered: Sanjay’s brother says his rescue was ‘Happiness we never expected’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Thirty-year-old Sanjay Sah, who had been trapped inside a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3-A Hydropower Project following the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa, was rescued alive after 10 days.

A joint team of the Nepal Army and Armed Police Force rescued him safely on Friday morning, turning 10 days of anguish for his family in Saptari into tears of joy.

Sanjay, from Tilathi Koiladi Rural Municipality-4 in Saptari, worked in the project’s control room. His brother Sanjeev said their father, who had been in a state of near-unconsciousness, shed tears of joy as soon as he heard that his son had been rescued safely. “Father was almost unconscious. None of us in the family had slept last night,” Sanjeev said. “He is extremely happy now. He is heading to the airport in tears of joy.”

Sanjay’s uncle and aunt are also travelling to Kathmandu with his father to meet him.

Trapped while trying to rescue others

On the day of the flood, Sanjay became trapped inside the tunnel while trying to save the lives of others. He continued his efforts and managed to help several people get out of the tunnel. However, after night fell, he was unable to escape himself. Speaking to the Nepal Army after his rescue, Sanjay said, “I worked in the control room. Since I was there, it was my duty to save everyone’s life. Once the accident happened, I could not simply run away on my own; I had to save everyone.” He added, “I was helping everyone get out. In doing so, I ran out of time. I could not get out at night.”

Sanjay said that after becoming trapped inside the tunnel, he kept chanting a sacred Hindu mantra and believes that this helped save his life.

Happiness we never expected

Unable to bear the pain of her husband’s disappearance, Sanjay’s wife had gone to her parental home. The couple have a one-and-a-half-year-old daughter. On Friday morning, Sanjeev called his sister-in-law himself to deliver the unexpected news that Sanjay had been rescued. “She is extremely happy now too,” Sanjeev said. “This is happiness we never expected.”

On the morning of the flood, August 26, Sanjay’s family spoke to him for only about five seconds at around 7:45 am. When they learned about the incident through social media and news reports at around 1 pm and tried to call him, they could no longer reach him.

After 10 long days of anguish and uncertainty, the dark ordeal has finally given way to relief with Sanjay’s safe return.

Here is an excerpt from his brief conversation with Nepal Army officials:

How many people do you think are still inside?

I worked as an operator in the control room. Normally, there would be only four, five or six people at a time. But there were around 40 to 45 people there at the time. Since I was in the control room, it was my responsibility to save everyone’s life. When the accident happened, I could not just run away on my own. I had to save everyone. So, while trying to rescue everyone, I told them that there had been an accident in the Thamya area. I told everyone to get out. In the process, I ran out of time. In the end, I could not get out and became trapped myself.

How many people do you think are still trapped inside?

We were in contact with only three or four of our colleagues who were nearby.

There was a powerhouse inside. Could there be people inside the powerhouse as well?

There could be. Some people may not have been able to escape. The tunnel is long, and water may have entered it as well.

You have come out today after so many days. This is like a second life. Congratulations!

What date is it today?

Today is the 19th Bhadra.

So, it really is a second life. Many congratulations! I had been sitting inside chanting the Mahamantra.

title.rendered: Gold price rises by 2,500 rupees per tola

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

The price of gold rose by 2,500 rupees per tola on Friday.

The Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers has fixed the price for the day at 307,400 rupees per tola. The previous day’s trading rate was 304,900 rupees.

Over the course of a week, however, gold prices have actually fallen by 11,100 rupees; last Friday’s rate stood at 318,500 rupees per tola.

Similarly, the silver price rose by 40 rupees per tola today to reach 4,765 rupees, up from the previous day’s 4,725 rupees. Last Friday, silver had been priced at 4,965 rupees per tola.

title.rendered: Rescued alive after 10 days, Kabir’s brother says, ‘There are no words to describe our happiness’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Amir, the younger brother of Kabir Maharjan, who was rescued alive from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3-A Hydropower Project, said the family’s happiness knew no bounds after Kabir was rescued safely following 10 days trapped inside the tunnel.

Kabir had been trapped inside the tunnel after the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa. A joint team of the Nepal Army and Armed Police Force successfully rescued him on Thursday. Speaking to Onlinekhabar after learning of the rescue, Amir said the family was overwhelmed with happiness.

Sharing his feelings with Onlinekhabar, Amir said:

Kabir Maharjan, who was rescued safely from the tunnel after 10 days, is my elder brother. He has now been taken to Chhauni Hospital. We are on our way to see him, but we have not met him yet. We are extremely happy to hear that he has been rescued.
There are no words to describe how happy everyone in the family is. It is beyond anything we can express in words. We are all extremely happy. All our friends and relatives have supported and helped us.

We are especially grateful to the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and all the rescue experts involved in the operation. We learned through the media that our brother was trapped inside the tunnel. Even now, we are getting updates through the media. We were not in a position to go there ourselves and search for him. We are extremely happy that he is now safe. He is an employee there and used to work at the project regularly. That was his duty station. We never imagined that something like this could happen. It still feels unbelievable. We are eager to see him as soon as possible. The whole family is now heading to the hospital.

title.rendered: 2 rescued alive from Trishuli 3-A tunnel; how many remain inside?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Rescue teams have rescued two people alive from a tunnel of the Nepal Electricity Authority’s Trishuli 3-A Hydropower Project.

Mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah and supervisor Kabir Maharjan were rescued alive from the tunnel this morning, 10 days after they became trapped.

According to Trishuli 3-A Project Chief Awas Ojha, the two were rescued from a tunnel leading to the powerhouse. “They were found alive and rescued along the route leading to the powerhouse. The rescue team has yet to reach the powerhouse,” he said.

Ojha said it was not possible to determine how far from the powerhouse the two were rescued because the tunnel is dark.

The 60-megawatt project, which was in operation, had been shut down for a complete overhaul. As a result, the tunnel through which water from the river enters the powerhouse had been closed.

The Nepal Electricity Authority estimates that 42 engineers and employees are trapped inside the powerhouse tunnel. Most of them are believed to be inside the powerhouse itself.

Although Sanjay Sah, who was rescued first, said that everyone inside was alive, the exact number of people still inside remains unclear, Project Chief Ojha said.

title.rendered: Drones could be Nepal’s eyes in a crisis

content.rendered:
After a disaster, one of the first calls is often to someone who owns a drone.

The request may sound simple: Can you fly over the river? Can you check whether anyone is on that roof? Can you show us what remains of the road? The flight is rarely simple.

The August 26 flood in northern Nepal destroyed roads, bridges and communication links across already difficult terrain. The US Geological Survey says a glacial collapse probably triggered the flood and debris flow. The IFRC estimated that about 93,000 people may have been affected, while access problems continued to slow assessments.

I followed the response as a filmmaker and drone pilot, not as a member of the rescue operation. That distinction matters. I know how to fly in Nepal and how quickly mountain weather, altitude and signal loss can change a plan. I also know that experience on a film set does not qualify a person to run a search-and-rescue mission.

This is where our current gap begins. Nepal has aircraft. It has skilled operators. What it does not yet have is a dependable way to get the right pilot and equipment to an emergency on short notice.

A drone is not one kind of tool

People often talk about drones as though one aircraft can do everything. It cannot.

A high-zoom camera can inspect an opposite riverbank or a damaged building without sending rescuers across unstable ground. Thermal cameras can support night searches by picking up differences in surface temperature. The operator still has to compare that image with the normal camera because heated metal, animals and exposed rock can create misleading signals. Thermal imaging also cannot see through soil, concrete or heavy debris.

Mapping calls for a different setup. Photogrammetry, LiDAR and RTK systems can record the shape and position of a landslide, damaged road or unstable slope. Those files must then be processed into something an engineer or response commander can use.

Delivery is another job entirely. Heavy-lift aircraft can carry medicine, radios, food and first-aid supplies where the road has vanished. Smaller consumer drones are useful for quick visual checks, but they cannot replace the sensors or payload capacity of enterprise aircraft.

The model name matters less than the match between the aircraft and the assignment. Sending a camera drone for a thermal search wastes time. Sending raw LiDAR data to a command post with nobody ready to process it does not help either.

The pilot is part of a larger chain

In production work, I can postpone a flight, change the shot or return with another battery. Rescue work offers less room.

The pilot may be dealing with poor visibility and limited space to launch. Helicopters may be using the same valley. A ground team may be waiting for coordinates while the aircraft is losing power. The person holding the controller must know the search pattern, the flight boundary and exactly who receives the information.

This is why ordinary flying experience is not enough. Disaster pilots need practice in grid searches, thermal interpretation, airspace coordination and emergency communication. They must be able to report uncertainty without filling the gap with guesswork.

The aircraft also needs a support plan. Batteries must be charged where electricity has failed. Spare equipment has to reach the launch site. Live video and mapping data need a reliable route back to the people directing the operation.

We should not build the team during the emergency

The Nepal Drone Association mobilised members after the Rasuwa flood, including pilots with thermal and LiDAR systems. That willingness deserves recognition. It also shows how much the response still depends on professional networks and volunteers assembling after the damage is done.

Nepal needs a standing roster managed with the disaster-response authorities. It should record where trained pilots are based, which aircraft they can operate, what sensors are available and how quickly a team can move.

That registry would allow a control room to request a capability instead of searching for a familiar name. A thermal mission could go to a nearby thermal team. A mapping request could reach pilots and processors who already work together. Heavy-lift delivery would be assigned according to altitude, range and payload.

None of this works without joint training. Pilots need exercises with the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and local responders. Everyone should know who clears the airspace, divides the search area and receives the feed. These decisions are safer when they have already been practised.

Private experience can become public capacity

Much of Nepal’s drone experience sits outside the government. Filmmakers, surveyors, engineers and infrastructure companies own aircraft and use them in difficult places. That equipment should not be commandeered casually, and professional experience should not be mistaken for rescue certification.

There is still a useful role for the private sector. Operators who volunteer for emergency work could complete recognised training, take part in drills and join a deployable reserve. Some could also help teach government teams about flight planning, mapping and equipment maintenance.

The result would be a mixed system: public agencies providing command and accountability, with trained private operators adding capacity when the scale of an emergency demands it.

Nepal will continue to face floods, landslides and broken road access. We cannot predict every location or date. We can decide what happens after the call comes in.

The next response should begin with an assigned team and a tested procedure, not a last-minute search for somebody with a charged battery.

title.rendered: 252 containers pass through Korola border point in a week

content.rendered:
Mustang, September 4

Nepal-China trade through the Korola border point in Mustang has increased following the closure of the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border crossing after the devastating Bhotekoshi flood on August 26.

Before the disaster, an average of 8-10 containers passed through Korola daily. However, the number of containers using the route has increased since the disaster.

According to the Armed Police Force (APF) 33 Company Headquarters in Jomsom, 252 empty containers travelled to Korola via the Beni-Jomsom-Korola road between August 26 and September 3.

Similarly, trucks carrying goods from China have completed customs clearance at the Mustang Customs Office and proceeded to their destinations, according to APF DSP Deepak Koirala.

With the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border crossing disrupted by the disaster, containers originally scheduled to enter Nepal through that route have been diverted to Korola, he said.

However, Mustang Customs Chief Bidur Chudal said cargo diverted from the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung route to Korola had not yet arrived there.

NDRRMA estimates Rs 387.54 billion in losses from Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

The government has estimated losses of around Rs 400 billion from the Bhotekoshi flash flood that struck Nepal on August 26.

At a regular briefing organised by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) on Thursday, its Executive Director, Dr Dharma Raj Upreti, said the authority had made a preliminary estimate of Rs 387.54 billion in losses caused by the August 26 disaster. However, a detailed assessment is still awaited.

He said the country could require around Rs 8 billion over the next four months to restore various sectors affected by the disaster.

“It is essential to restore buildings, communications, energy and transport systems, health, nutrition, education, agriculture and livestock,” Dr Upreti said.

title.rendered: President Paudel extends greetings on Gaura Parba

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

President Ramchandra Paudel has said that indigenous Nepali festivals play an important role in fostering social harmony.

Extending his best wishes on the occasion of the Gaura festival, President Paudel said that folk traditions and cultural festivals have helped promote unity in diversity, social and cultural solidarity, and tolerance.

He said the Gaura festival contributes to strengthening national unity by bringing families and communities together, preserving cultural traditions, and fostering spiritual faith, happiness and peace in people’s lives.

The President expressed the belief that the festival helps reunite separated couples, promotes a sense of brotherhood, and strengthens the bond between husbands and wives.

Gaura Parba is celebrated with special significance every year in the western and far-western regions of Nepal from the fifth to the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhadra according to the lunar calendar.

During the festival, devotees observe fasts and worship Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, also known as Gaura. Biruda—a mixture of five types of grains and legumes, including wheat, paddy, peas, black gram and horse gram—is offered as prasad (sacred food) and consumed as part of the festivities. Devotees also offer prayers for human well-being, agricultural prosperity and family welfare.

On the occasion of Gaura, local communities gather to share their joys and sorrows through traditional folk songs and dances, including Deuda and Dhamari, performed in the local dialect.

title.rendered: Devotees across Nepal celebrate Krishna Janmashtami

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Followers of the Vedic Sanatana faith are celebrating Krishna Janmashtami across the country today with reverence and devotion, offering prayers to Lord Krishna.

Lord Krishna, regarded as the proponent of Jnana Yoga, Karma Yoga and Bhakti Yoga, is believed to have been born at midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhadra during the Dwapara Yuga. The day is therefore observed as Krishna Janmashtami, while the night is known as ‘Moharatri’.

On the occasion, temples across the country hold religious discourses and devotional singing and chanting, known as bhajan-kirtan. Devotees also observe fasts and stay awake throughout the night as part of the celebrations.

Regarded as the eighth incarnation of Lord Vishnu, Krishna is believed to have been born to protect humanity from injustice, oppression and evil. He championed truth throughout his life and inspired people to follow the path of righteousness.

The Shreemad Bhagavad Gita, believed to contain the teachings delivered by Lord Krishna to Arjuna, one of the five Pandava brothers, during the battle between the Pandavas and Kauravas at Kurukshetra, is revered as a sacred Hindu scripture. Commonly known as the Gita, the text is regarded as one of the world’s most widely translated works.

According to the Hindu Puranas, Krishna displayed extraordinary divine powers from childhood and defeated demonic figures including Putana, Kamsa, Jarasandha and Shishupala.

On the occasion of Krishna Janmashtami, a large fair is being held today at the famous Krishna Mandir in Mangalbazar, Patan. Similarly, large numbers of devotees are gathering at Navatan Dham in Kageshwari-Manohara Municipality in the northeastern part of Kathmandu.

Devotees are also flocking to Krishna temples across the country. Various religious organisations in Kathmandu traditionally organise cultural processions and chariot parades featuring tableaux depicting scenes associated with Lord Krishna.

The government has declared a public holiday today to mark the festival.

—RSS

title.rendered: Landslides, floods disrupt roads across Kathmandu Valley and Bagmati Province

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 4

Landslides and floods triggered by incessant rainfall have caused complete or partial blockages on major highways in the Kathmandu Valley and Bagmati Province.

According to a road condition update issued by the Nepal Police, the Prithvi Highway is completely blocked following a landslide at Krishnabhir in Benighat Rorang Rural Municipality-7, Dhading. However, small vehicles are operating on a single lane at Parewa Bhir in Gajuri Rural Municipality-2, while one-way traffic is in effect in the Jawangkhola and Kamere Bhir areas.

In view of the risk of flooding, time restrictions have been imposed on vehicles operating along the Kavre section of the BP Highway. Cargo vehicles weighing up to 10 tonnes will be permitted to operate between 7 pm and 5 am, while daytime operations will be allowed only after assessing road conditions.

Traffic has been completely halted after floodwaters damaged the road at Khalte in Uttargaya Rural Municipality-5 along the Trishuli-Mailung-Syaphrubesi road section in Rasuwa. Other major roads in Rasuwa also remain closed until further notice.

Similarly, vehicular movement has been prohibited from 10 pm to 5 am at Ghattekhola along the Tokha-Chhahare road in Nuwakot due to the risk of landslides. Police have also reported that the Pasang Lhamu road section at Simtar is completely closed.

One-way traffic has resumed on the Kathmandu-Dhading road section following the removal of a landslide at Chisapani in Chandragiri Municipality-2, a gateway to Kathmandu.

Meanwhile, police have urged the public to avoid travel unless necessary and to contact the traffic police or the police control room in the respective district to inquire about road conditions before undertaking long-distance journeys.

Police said a dozer and a technical team have been mobilised to clear blocked roads.

title.rendered: Feeling their homeland’s pain, Nepalis in the UK raise relief funds

content.rendered:
London: Whether it was the massive earthquake a decade ago, the Covid pandemic, or now the devastation of the Bhotekoshi flood, once again it has been proven that the Nepali diaspora in the UK cannot remain untouched by the pain their homeland faces during disasters.

On the morning of August 26, a massive flood in Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi River caused enormous loss of life and property. Areas along the riverbanks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and surrounding regions have been severely affected.

While the Nepal government and neighbouring countries mobilise for search, rescue, safe evacuation, and emergency relief, Nepalis in the UK have also opened their hearts to provide financial help for flood victims. Fundraising is ongoing, and since individuals and organisations are collecting separately, it is difficult to determine exactly how much has been transferred to Nepal or is still being raised.

The influential UK-based Nepali organisation Tamu Dhin UK has decided to provide over 10 million rupees in financial assistance to flood victims. Its executive committee, chaired by Jumkaji Gurung, decided at an emergency meeting on Tuesday evening to contribute 1,001,000 rupees in relief. This amount will soon be deposited into the Nepal government’s Prime Minister Relief Fund. Savings from last Sunday’s Nepali fair, along with funds to be raised through a charity trail-walk event from September 11–13, will also go toward flood relief.

Two active NRNA UK bodies in Britain are raising funds separately. The NRNA UK led by Rajendra Pudasaini has already collected nearly 5.2 million rupees through GoFundMe, with plans to send up to 10 million rupees to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund. The NRNA UK, chaired by Prem Gaha Magar, is also collecting through GoFundMe and separate fundraising; Gaha Magar said the organisation is acting as a “watchdog” to prevent misuse of the funds raised in the UK and plans to go directly to the affected areas to assist with relief and rehabilitation.

South West Nepali Samaj UK has deposited 1,035,000 rupees into the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund. Society chairperson Kisan GC said the amount was sent as part of fulfilling their social responsibility toward the homeland during this natural disaster.

The Nepalese Doctors’ Association UK (NDA UK) has also provided 1.1 million Nepali rupees to help the victims. Meanwhile, Kul Acharya, former president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA), contributed 1,111,111 rupees personally and on behalf of Holy Cow Company to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

International Educational Consultancy has provided 1,111,111 rupees to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund. London-based remittance company IME London has provided 1 million rupees; director Kamal Paudel said IME London does not charge any fee for sending money from the UK to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund. He added that the Nepalese British Community UK, of which he is a member, has already contributed 1 million rupees and is raising an additional 1 million.

OG Italian Restaurant in Leicester has contributed 555,555 rupees for Bhotekoshi flood victims. The amount, from the management team, staff, and director Dayanidhi Sapkota across all three OG Limited branches (OG Simply Italian, Bistro OG, and OG Kibworth), was deposited into the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund for disaster management and immediate rescue and relief work. Of this, Director Sapkota personally contributed 255,555 rupees.

“OG Limited has always stood together during every disaster and difficult situation in the past, and continues that social responsibility toward the country. We express heartfelt thanks to the management team members and all staff who contributed in solidarity to this campaign,” says director Sapkota.

Chitwan Aid Trust (CAT) UK has provided 500,000 rupees to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund to help natural disaster victims.

“This is not just financial help but a symbol of our solidarity, responsibility, and human compassion toward our Nepali brothers and sisters affected by the disaster,” says CAT UK chairperson Raju Acharya.

Meanwhile, a candlelight vigil in memory of those who lost their lives in the flood, along with a fund collection for victims, was held in Bexley, London. The Bexley Nepali Samaj held the event on Wednesday evening with participation from the local borough’s mayor, councillors and more than 160 others. The society announced it will immediately transfer the £6,500 (over 1.3 million rupees) collected so far through its fundraising campaign to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.

Galkot Samaj UK has contributed over 500,000 rupees. Chairperson Bishnu Chalise said 515,758 rupees from the society’s emergency fund had already been deposited into the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.

UK-based Hamro Guthi UK has provided 400,000 rupees to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund for the relief and rehabilitation of families affected by the devastating flood and landslides. The funds, raised through the initiative of coordinator Suman Kumar Kunwar, were deposited into the official relief fund account at Rastriya Banijya Bank’s Singha Durbar branch.

Global Parbat Samaj has deposited 325,000 rupees into the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund for Bhotekoshi flood victims. Society chairperson and London-based social worker Dadhi Acharya said the contribution reflects their embrace of social responsibility during this natural disaster in the homeland.

Pokhareli Manch UK has provided 500,000 rupees to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund aimed at helping victims’ relief and rehabilitation. Nepali Samaj Nottingham has contributed £2,500 (over 500,000 rupees) to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund for rescue and relief of flood-affected people in Nepal; the society said it sent this first round from its institutional fund and will raise further community contributions in a second phase.

Matrix Talents and Milanoyar Events, both operating under the same group in the UK, jointly contributed 200,000 rupees for relief and support of flood-affected families in Nepal, Matrix Talents giving 150,000 and Milanoyar Events 50,000.

Srijanshil Leicester Nepal UK, based in Leicester, has contributed 200,000 rupees for flood victims; chairperson Shiv Parajuli confirmed the amount has already been deposited into the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.

Shanti Nepali Samaj UK has immediately sent 250,000 rupees for Rasuwa flood victims.

Char Bhanjyang Tamu Samaj UK has decided to contribute 1.5 million rupees for relief and rescue of those affected by the devastating flood, a decision made at an emergency meeting Tuesday evening chaired by society president Durga Gurung. The society has already sent 500,000 rupees as immediate relief to Nepal through Bina Gurung, a daughter of Char Bhanjyang Tamu Samaj and local representative from the affected area. The remaining 1 million rupees will be raised through voluntary contributions coordinated by Captain Deu Bahadur Gurung, chairperson of the Char Bhanjyang Tamu Samaj International Coordination Council, across seven units in Nepal, the UK, Hong Kong, Europe, Japan and elsewhere, and will be deposited into the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.

Pasa Puchah Guthi UK has also decided to send 1 million rupees to the Prime Minister’s Fund.

Support Nepal UK has contributed £1,500 for flood victims. A-Star Financial Solutions contributed 100,000 rupees to support relief and rescue work, deposited into the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

The Nepalese Ladies Community Hounslow (NLCH), London, has turned this year’s Teej celebration into a charity event instead of pure festivity, organising it as “Charity Teej” to help those affected by the natural disaster in Nepal.

The Nepali Embassy in London has appealed to everyone to provide voluntary financial support for the relief, rescue, rehabilitation, and reconstruction of families affected by the devastating flood. In an appeal published on its official website, the embassy expressed solidarity with the disaster and called for contributions to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

Billions of rupees have now been collected from within Nepal and abroad into the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, established for the search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation of citizens affected by the devastating flood on the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa district.

UK announces £5 million in support

Immediately after the flood, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced £5 million to support relief and rescue efforts in Nepal. PM Burnham recalled the historic relationship between Nepal and the UK and the mutual support the two countries have given each other in difficult times, noting that Nepal had helped Britain when it was needed in the past, and that Britain now stands ready to help Nepal in its time of need.

title.rendered: 2 Indian nationals killed as car plunges into Phewa Lake

content.rendered:
Kaski, September 4

Two people died, and two others were injured when a car with an Indian license plate, travelling from Sedi towards Lakeside, plunged into Phewa Lake at 4:50 am at the Gairichautara bend in Pokhara-18 today.

According to Police Inspector Deepak Prasad Rijal, the Acting Information Officer at the District Police Office, Kaski, the deceased are 26-year-old Navdeep Kumar Yadav, a native of Raxaul in the East Champaran district of Bihar, India, and another Indian male whose identity has not yet been established.

Police Inspector Rijal said that the rescue team retrieved them in an unconscious state from the waters of the Phewa Lake and sent them to the Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences (Western Regional Hospital) for treatment, where doctors declared both of them dead.

Anmol Kumar Yadav (27) and Suraj Yadav (33), both from Raxaul in the Motihari district of Bihar, India, were rescued following the accident and taken to Gandaki Medical College for treatment. The car involved in the accident, bearing the Indian registration number BR 05 BB 6759, has been retrieved from Phewa Lake using a crane and is currently being kept at the Baidam Ward Police Office. Police Inspector Rijal stated that the police are conducting further investigations into the incident.

title.rendered: Nepal’s flood response must put children at its centre

content.rendered:
I have worked through several emergencies in Nepal. I have seen communities struggle through conflict and its aftermath, and I have seen families lose homes and loved ones in the 2015 earthquake.

Every disaster is different. But there is one lesson I have carried from each of them: when a crisis strikes, children often bear some of its deepest consequences, even when their protection is not immediately visible in the emergency response.

That is what I find myself thinking about as Nepal confronts another devastating flood.

The images from the affected areas are difficult to absorb. Homes have disappeared. Roads and bridges have been swept away. Schools and health facilities have been damaged. Families are searching for loved ones. Lives have been lost and people remain missing.

Behind every number is a human story. And behind many of those stories is a child.

UNICEF’s initial assessment estimates that at least 17,000 children have been affected by the recent floods. The figure will likely change as access improves and assessments continue. But even 17,000 can become an abstract number unless we ask what it actually means for a child.

It can mean waking up in an unfamiliar shelter after losing a home. It can mean not knowing where a parent or sibling is. It can mean losing a school, a friend or the routine that made life feel normal. It can mean being frightened and having no words for that fear.

A child does not stop being a child during a disaster

In the first hours of an emergency, our priorities are clear: rescue people, provide food and water, find shelter and treat the injured. They have to be. But child protection cannot be something we think about after the immediate crisis has passed.

A child who has survived a flood may have lost a parent, sibling, home or livelihood. They may have been separated from their caregivers during evacuation. They may now be living in an overcrowded shelter among people they do not know. And some children will say nothing at all.

That silence should not be mistaken for safety.

Emergencies can increase children’s exposure to violence, abuse, exploitation, trafficking, child labour and neglect. They can also leave children struggling with fear, grief and psychological distress long after the floodwaters have disappeared.

This is why protecting children must be part of the first response—not an activity added later.

A shelter is not necessarily a safe place

When we ask whether families have been given shelter, we should also ask a more difficult question: Is that shelter safe for children?

Can girls and boys sleep safely? Are sanitation facilities secure? Can a separated child be identified quickly? Is there someone a child can approach if they feel threatened? Are children with disabilities receiving the support they need?

These questions may appear less urgent when families are still struggling for food and clean water.

They are not.

A crowded shelter can provide a roof while creating new risks. A child who has become separated from their family can be physically protected from the flood but still remain deeply vulnerable.

This is why family separation must be treated as an emergency in itself.

During a disaster, communication networks fail, roads disappear and families are moved from one place to another. Children can easily become separated from the people they depend on.

Recently, nine schoolchildren who had been stranded at their school for two days were reunited with their families. Their story is a reminder that tracing and reunification are not secondary humanitarian tasks. For a frightened child, finding their family can be as important as finding food or shelter.

The school that was destroyed but whose children survived

The floods have also offered a powerful lesson in what preparedness can achieve.

In Nuwakot, a timely warning allowed a school principal to evacuate more than 1,600 students before floodwaters reached the school. The school was later destroyed. The children, however, survived. That distinction matters.

When we talk about disaster preparedness, we often focus on infrastructure, evacuation routes and early-warning systems. These are essential. But preparedness must also answer a more fundamental question: How do we protect every child when the warning comes?

For children, a school is more than a building. It is a place of routine, friendship, trusted adults and familiarity. When a disaster destroys it, children lose more than a classroom.

That is why continuity of education should also be part of disaster response and recovery. We know what to ask. We should know the answers.

Nepal has experienced conflict, earthquakes, floods, landslides and other emergencies. We have learned painful lessons from each.

Yet too often, preparedness becomes a conversation that begins after disaster has already struck.

Every municipality and rural municipality should already know where its most vulnerable children are, what happens if children are separated from their caregivers, where children can find safe spaces, who provides psychosocial support and how cases of violence, abuse or exploitation will be referred.

They should know how children with disabilities will be supported and how education will continue when schools are damaged.

They should even have plans for protecting or restoring essential documents such as birth registrations.

These are not questions for the aftermath.

We should have the answers before the water rises.

The real crisis begins after the headlines fade

There is another danger in the way we think about disasters.

We often measure the response by what can be seen: how many people were rescued, how many relief packages were distributed, how many roads were reopened and how many houses were rebuilt. Those numbers matter. But they do not tell us whether a child feels safe again.

When the floodwaters recede, some children will return to homes that no longer exist. Some will return to schools that have been destroyed. Some will return to families that have lost their livelihoods. Others may never return to the family members they were separated from.

And a child who appears physically unharmed may still be carrying fear, grief or trauma. So recovery must ask different questions, too.

Are children back with their families? Are they back in school? Do they feel safe? Are they protected from exploitation and violence? Are children who need psychosocial support receiving it?

These are not soft measures of recovery.

They are measures of whether recovery is actually happening.

And we need to listen to children

There is one more thing adults often forget in emergencies: children themselves know what they need. They know which places in their communities feel safe. They know what frightened them during the evacuation. They know what they have lost. They know what would help them feel normal again.

Yet children are often treated only as recipients of aid rather than people whose voices matter.

Listening to children does not mean asking them to solve a disaster. It means creating safe ways for them to tell adults what they are experiencing and what support they need. They are not simply beneficiaries. They are rights-holders.

Over the years, I have also seen something else repeatedly in Nepal: extraordinary community strength.

Teachers, local leaders, volunteers, security personnel, health workers, social workers and ordinary citizens step forward when others are in danger. Communities often become the first responders long before formal systems arrive. We should be proud of that strength.

But we should not build our disaster response around courage and goodwill alone.

We need systems. We need trained people. We need functioning referral mechanisms. We need local governments with child-sensitive disaster plans. We need preparedness that considers not only how to get children out of danger, but how to keep them safe once they are out.

Most importantly, we need to stop treating child protection as something that can wait until the rescue operation is over. It is part of the rescue operation. The floodwaters will eventually recede. Roads will be rebuilt. Houses will be reconstructed. Schools will reopen. But for some children, these days will remain with them for years.

Nepal has already learned difficult lessons from conflict, the earthquake and repeated disasters. The current floods are another reminder that those lessons cannot remain in reports and post-disaster assessments.

We have to turn them into preparedness. Because when the next emergency comes, a child should not have to depend on luck to survive. And surviving should not be the end of what we ask for.

Children deserve safety, dignity, family, education, care and hope—even in the middle of a disaster.

The water will recede. Our responsibility must not.
