title.rendered: Nepal moves to open payment market to foreign companies

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Nepal is moving to open its payment market to foreign companies, with Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle introducing a bill proposing a licensing framework for international payment institutions.

The Payment and Settlement Bill, introduced in the House of Representatives on Thursday, proposes allowing institutions established abroad and already conducting payment-related transactions internationally to apply for permission to operate in Nepal.

The existing Payment and Settlement Act, 2018 does not have a separate provision governing foreign payment institutions. The proposed amendment would, for the first time, create a legal basis for such institutions to apply for a licence to conduct payment transactions in Nepal.

Under Section 7 of the existing Act, anyone seeking to operate as a payment system operator or payment service provider must apply to Nepal Rastra Bank for a letter of intent, along with the required documents and prescribed fee, before establishing a company.

Section 8 requires an institution registered as a company under Section 7 to apply for a licence to operate a payment system or provide payment services within six months of receiving the letter of intent.

The existing law also states that no action will be taken on a letter of intent if the institution does not apply for a licence within the prescribed period.

The proposed bill seeks to add a separate provision for foreign institutions.

Section 6 of the bill states that an institution established abroad, conducting payment-related transactions internationally and meeting the eligibility criteria set by Nepal Rastra Bank may apply to the central bank for permission to conduct payment-related transactions in Nepal by submitting the prescribed documents and fee.

The application process would be carried out in line with Nepal Rastra Bank’s policy on licensing payment services and payment systems.

In effect, the bill seeks to create a separate legal route for foreign payment institutions to enter Nepal — something that is not provided for under the current law.

Foreign institutions to get continuing permission

The bill also proposes a separate provision concerning the duration of licences for foreign institutions.

Section 10 states that, when a licence is issued to a bank or financial institution under the Act, no specific validity period will be prescribed. The licence will be considered to remain valid continuously unless the institution is barred from conducting payment-related transactions or otherwise dealt with under prevailing law.

The proposed provision would make the process of maintaining permission to operate in Nepal more straightforward for foreign payment service providers.

The explanatory note accompanying the bill says one of its objectives is to allow foreign institutions to conduct transactions in Nepal and to organise the process for granting them permission.

According to the Ministry of Finance, the bill has been introduced with the broader objective of developing, expanding, promoting, monitoring and regulating the country’s payment, clearing and settlement system.

It also seeks to address practical difficulties that have emerged during implementation of the existing Act and clarify the definitions of certain terms used in the legislation.

The bill proposes allowing banks, financial institutions and payment service providers to appoint agents as well.

The entry of foreign payment companies into Nepal is also explicitly included among the reasons for amending the law.

Finance Minister Wagle said in the bill that the amendment was necessary to make the legislation more relevant to current needs, including organising the licence-renewal process for foreign institutions authorised to conduct transactions in Nepal and allowing Nepal Rastra Bank to provide loans to banks and financial institutions at specified interest rates.

title.rendered: Unregistered company produces substandard chocolates for 18 years, factory-sealed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

A company has been found to have been producing chocolates continuously for the past 18 years without being registered as a company. Following information received from the National Investigation Department, the Kathmandu District Police Range has sealed the chocolate factory.

The factory had reportedly been producing and distributing substandard chocolates under the label “Surya Confectionery” for the past 18 years. Security officials said the company is not registered with any government authority. The factory was sealed on August 25 and handed over to the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control for further action. According to security officials, the company had been producing and distributing chocolates in this manner since 2009.

Under the Food Hygiene and Quality Act 2024, food producers are required to register with the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control and can only distribute products after laboratory testing and certification that they meet the required standards. Surya Confectionery is said to have violated all of these procedures.

The company was found to have been distributing its chocolates across the country. The products were reportedly stored at locations including Gongabu New Bus Park, Kalanki, Koteshwar and Gaushala. The company was also found to be producing chocolates designed to resemble products made by foreign companies, apparently to mislead consumers. The prices also varied from one shop to another.

After Tekendra Karki became chief of the National Investigation Department, a Financial Intelligence Unit was established. The unit is headed by Deputy Investigation Director Uttam Khanal.

The unit collects intelligence and works to curb tax evasion, revenue leakage and other illegal activities. The unit has also gathered information on illegally operated dental clinics and hospitals, illegal tobacco warehouses and smuggling through border points in Kathmandu.

title.rendered: Fire breaks out at Supreme Court records section, minor damage reported

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

A fire broke out at the records section of the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court administration said the fire destroyed documents that had been kept for disposal and were no longer in use. “After we learned about the fire last night, security personnel and court employees arrived, called the fire brigade and brought the fire under control,” said Supreme Court spokesperson Arjun Koirala. “The fire broke out in an area where obsolete documents and copies of legal journals were stored.”

Court employees suspect that an electrical plug may have short-circuited and caused the fire in the records section of the newly constructed building. Spokesperson Koirala said no documents related to pending cases were damaged in the fire. According to him, the fire did not spread beyond the room housing the records section.

Courts maintain records sections to store files and documents related to cases that have already been decided. After a certain period, case files are destroyed while only the judgments are preserved. Koirala said that since the new building is still under construction, only obsolete and unused files and documents had been stored in the records section.

Following the arson at the Supreme Court on September 10, 2025, the court has been operating from its annex building. Some benches and administrative offices have now been moved to a section of the building currently under construction.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood halts power exports to Bangladesh, cuts supplies to India

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Nepal has halted electricity exports to Bangladesh and reduced exports to India after devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa caused extensive damage to hydropower projects. The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) said electricity generated by the Chilime and Trishuli hydropower projects, which were contracted for export to Bangladesh, can no longer be supplied after the floods damaged the projects.

Nepal had been exporting 40 MW of electricity generated by these two projects to Bangladesh. The exports have now been halted after the floods damaged power generation and transmission infrastructure. Nepal had received approval to export up to around 1,200 MW of electricity to India and Bangladesh combined. However, damage to hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot caused by the Bhotekoshi floods has reduced the amount of electricity available for export.

The floods damaged 12 hydropower projects operated by the NEA and private developers. Both operational and under-construction projects suffered damage. The NEA said the direct impact on power generation has forced it to reduce electricity exports to India as well. Export volumes are expected to come under further pressure until flood-affected projects resume generation.

Floods complicate rescue operations and power generation

The floods have not only damaged hydropower infrastructure but also complicated efforts to rescue workers and employees at projects under construction.

At the Langtang Hydropower Project, a joint 25-member search and rescue team, including foreign technicians, has entered the tunnel to search for missing people. The team has gone about 150 meters inside the tunnel and created small openings at two locations to assess the condition of people who may be trapped inside.

A joint team, including foreign technicians, is also conducting search and rescue operations at the Chilime Hydropower Project. Similarly, a 93-member joint rescue team is conducting search and rescue operations at the Upper Trishuli-3A Project. The team is using five excavators to clear mud, soil and other obstructions blocking the tunnel outlet.

While work continued until around 2 am, the opening at the tunnel outlet became too narrow. Blasting was therefore carried out in the crown area to widen and clear the opening. Opening the tunnel outlet to allow rescuers to enter and search for people who may be trapped inside has been given priority.

A joint team comprising Nepal Army personnel, civilian staff and project officials has also been deployed at the Upper Trishuli-3B Project. The team, comprising 89 Army personnel, three civilian staff and the project’s managing director, is identifying the project office and residential areas and working to clear access roads to those locations.

Excavators and bulldozers are being used to construct roads and remove soil in areas blocked by massive landslides and mud. A large number of workers and employees at hydropower projects affected by the Bhotekoshi floods remain unaccounted for. Hundreds of Nepali and foreign workers at the 12 affected projects have been out of contact since the floods.

A total of 974 people working at the affected projects remain unaccounted for. More than a week after the floods, authorities have yet to determine the status of people who may be trapped or remain out of contact in tunnels, underground powerhouses, offices and residential areas.

Although the government has mobilised search and rescue teams under the leadership of the Nepal Army, rescue operations have become extremely risky and challenging due to difficult terrain, landslides, mud and soil accumulated inside the tunnels.

title.rendered: Families wait for DNA results to bring flood victims home

content.rendered:
Bharatpur, September 3

For three days, Anil Yadav of Bhairahawa has barely let go of his phone.

On its screen is a photograph of a dead body. He looks at it repeatedly, showing it to people around him and telling them: “This is my person.”

Anil says he identified the body as that of his brother from the photograph on August 29. But he did not immediately tell the rest of his family, fearing it would cause them further pain.

He travelled to Chitwan with relatives to understand the process of taking his brother’s body home. Three days later, he is still waiting.

Anil says he is certain of the identification from the face. Police, however, have been handing over bodies to relatives only after DNA testing.

He repeatedly approaches police officers at the identification centre.

“I have been telling you since that day that this is my relative,” he says.

Other members of his family have also looked at the photograph and identified the body as his brother’s.

“My family is waiting at home to perform the last rites. I am here waiting for the DNA report,” Anil says.

For the family, the certainty that they have found their missing relative has not brought closure. Instead, the wait to take the body home has prolonged their grief.

‘Look at the face, the chin’

Man Bahadur Lama of Gorkha is facing a similar wait.

After learning that his son, who went missing from Timure in Rasuwa, had been found in Chitwan, he travelled to the body identification centre with his granddaughter.

Showing the photograph on his phone, Lama says the face is unmistakably his son’s.

“Look at the face, look at the chin. His lips are exactly the same,” he says.

But he has not been allowed to take the body home.

Confused about why, he has been trying to understand the procedure from police officers and volunteers working at the identification centre.

“Look at my son’s photograph. It matches exactly,” he said on Wednesday.

Families have been identifying bodies based on photographs, clothing, jewellery and other physical characteristics. But these forms of identification are not considered sufficient for the formal handover of the bodies.

Police say they are being particularly cautious because of the sensitivity of the situation. DNA testing has been made the final basis for identification to prevent a body from being handed over to the wrong family.

Police Sub-Inspector Hari Dhakal, who is working at the body identification centre, has been explaining the process to relatives such as Anil and Man Bahadur.

“Although a body may be identified initially, DNA testing is necessary for its formal handover,” Dhakal says.

He says the bodies cannot be handed over until the DNA reports are received.

The situation has created a painful gap between what families believe they already know and the scientific and legal process authorities say they must follow.

Hundreds of bodies, hundreds still missing

Of the 355 bodies recovered in Chitwan, only 12 have so far been formally identified.

Police say the number of families claiming to have recognised their missing relatives from photographs is also increasing.

So far, 836 people have registered with police in Chitwan as missing relatives.

As the number of affected families grows, authorities are facing increasing pressure to identify bodies, collect samples and manage the remains.

DNA sample collection began in Chitwan on August 31. The process is being carried out in coordination with the Bagmati Province Public Health Laboratory’s Bhaktapur unit office in Bharatpur, the District Public Health Office and Bharatpur Government Hospital.

According to Chitwan District Police Office information officer DSP Chandrabhushan Yadav, DNA samples from 25 people were collected over two days.

The samples will be sent to Kathmandu for testing, and the results will be returned after the testing process is completed there.

Yadav says the need to send samples to Kathmandu means the process may take some time.

For the families waiting to take their loved ones home, however, that “some time” can feel much longer.

Yadav says the reports could take two to three months to arrive.

Until then, families such as Anil’s and Man Bahadur’s remain caught between recognition and confirmation — convinced they have found their loved ones, but unable to bring them home for the final rites.

title.rendered: Experts dispute PM Balen’s claim that no country has expertise to rescue people trapped in mud-filled tunnels

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Experts have disputed Prime Minister Balen Shah’s claim that no country in the world has the expertise or technology needed to rescue people trapped inside tunnels filled with mud and debris following the Bhotekoshi flood.

Speaking in the House of Representatives on Thursday, Shah said the situation in Rasuwa was unlike previous tunnel disasters because the tunnels had been completely filled with floodwater, mud and silt.

Experts, however, say that while rescuing people from tunnels blocked by mud can be slow and technically difficult, it is incorrect to say that other countries lack the expertise or technology to undertake such operations.

They point to previous complex tunnel rescues in countries including India, China, Peru and Chile, where specialised equipment and techniques have been used to reach people trapped underground.

What did the prime minister say?

Shah described the Rasuwa disaster as an unusual type of tunnel emergency.

“Experts available around the world are capable of clearing landslides from tunnels and carrying out rescues. That expertise exists worldwide. But this is different because these are not tunnels blocked by landslides. Floodwater entered the tunnels and completely filled them with mud and silt. No country has extensive expertise in dealing with this kind of situation. We do not have it either. There is no technology available anywhere that can be used immediately,” he said.

Shah also suggested that rescue operations would only be possible once conditions inside the tunnels became suitable for people and equipment to enter.

He rejected criticism that more excavators should have been deployed simultaneously, saying the physical constraints of tunnel operations limited how many machines could work at once.

“You cannot operate four, five or 20 excavators in a single tunnel at the same time. Only one or two excavators can work inside a tunnel at a time. There is a limit,” Shah said.

What do the experts say?

Subash Chandra Sunuwar, an engineering geologist who has worked in Nepal’s hydropower sector for years, agrees that removing mud and debris from the tunnels will take time. But he disputes the prime minister’s claim that other countries do not have more advanced technology and expertise.

“Looking particularly at the tunnels of the Chilime and Upper Trishuli 3A projects, there is mud inside and it has to be removed gradually. That will take time. Rocks have also blocked the way, so you cannot simply go through at once,” Sunuwar said.

“But there are other technologies that have been developed around the world and have been used in rescues.”

He cited a 2012 incident in Peru, where nine workers became trapped about 200 metres underground after a tunnel collapsed. When it was found that opening the tunnel directly would not be possible, rescuers drilled from above using a small boring machine to reach them.

“Yes, Nepal doesn’t have these machines, but China and other countries do have them,” he said.

Sunuwar also pointed to tunnel rescues in India. At the Tapovan hydropower project, 12 of 20 people who went missing after a flood caused by a glacial lake outburst in 2021 were rescued. At the Silkyara tunnel in 2023, 41 workers trapped underground were successfully rescued.

In the Silkyara operation, rescuers were unable to reach the workers through the access tunnel because of rocks and mud. They used vertical drilling, horizontal pipe jacking and, eventually, manual “rat-hole” mining to reach and rescue the trapped workers.

Experts say China also has advanced equipment that can be used in such operations, including mobile dewatering pumps and micro-tunnel boring machines.

Sunuwar said the government should have considered bringing in private developers and specialists immediately if the initial rescue effort was proving inadequate.

“Once the government realised it could not carry out the operation, it should have immediately called in private developers and experts and moved to a Plan B. Different strategies could have been developed for each project,” he said.

“People are understandably angry when, after eight days without a rescue, such explanations are being given only now.”

He said private hydropower developers were given access to assist only after seven days.

“Too much time was lost. Once a tunnel is buried, it becomes completely dark. Even if people trapped in the mud are still alive, they cannot survive for many days. The rescue plan should have been prepared as quickly as possible, but that did not happen,” he said.

‘The technology exists’

Udayaraj Neupane, a geotechnical engineer currently working in the field on the rescue operation at the Upper Trishuli 3A project, also said the prime minister’s statement was incorrect.

He agreed that the scale and nature of the disaster may be unprecedented, but said this did not mean that the world lacked technology for tunnel rescue.

“It is true that this particular kind of destruction has not occurred in other countries. But saying that rescue can only be carried out after the mud dries, and that there is no rescue technology or expertise anywhere in the world, is wrong,” Neupane said.

He said the world has advanced technologies for tunnel rescue and that failing to explore ways of bringing such technology to Nepal was unfortunate.

“The rescue process is essentially the same here and elsewhere, but the technology and expertise make a major difference,” he said. “Some use equipment made manually, while others use machines. It is the same principle here. Modern equipment makes the process faster, while older methods take longer.”

Neupane said Nepal was currently relying heavily on improvised methods.

“The prime minister was completely wrong. What is different is how the tunnels became filled with mud. The process of rescuing people from a mud-filled tunnel is the same around the world, and both the expertise and technology exist,” he said.

He also disputed the argument that deploying more excavators would not have helped.

“Excavators cannot be taken inside the tunnel to carry out the work. But to reach the mouth of the tunnel, it would have been better to use as much equipment as possible,” he said.

‘A wrong and irresponsible statement’

Subash Chandra Baral, president of the Nepal Engineers’ Association, said engineering solutions exist for even highly complex situations.

“The prime minister’s statement that there is no such expertise anywhere in the world and that rescue can only be carried out when conditions become favourable is completely wrong and irresponsible,” Baral said.

He accused the government of delaying rescue efforts under various pretexts.

“They did not know how to carry out the rescue, they failed to prepare, they made mistakes and now they are shifting the blame to others,” he said.

Baral said engineers had sought from the day of the flood to bring in expertise and equipment available both in Nepal and abroad, but claimed the government did not listen.

“There seems to be a mindset that what they have done is right and that there is no need to seek help from others. It is deeply unfortunate that they are being irresponsible in an attempt to cover up their mistakes,” he said.

At the same time, Baral said those involved in the ongoing rescue effort, including security personnel, should be encouraged rather than blamed for the slow progress.

“Instead of saying this was not done or that was not done, all our institutions should focus on encouraging those who are working in the rescue effort,” he said.

‘The technology is there’

Bijayman Bhattarai, a promoter of the Langtang Hydropower Project, said it was particularly troubling for a young prime minister to make such a claim in a country with extensive hydropower development.

“It is fine to say that we do not have it, that it is new for us and that we have learned from it. But saying that such technology does not exist anywhere in the world is completely wrong. The technology is available in sufficient measure around the world,” he said.

Bhattarai said his technical team, working with the Nepal Army, had managed to cut through a penstock pipe in seven to eight hours to create access towards the area where workers are believed to be trapped.

Around 25 workers are estimated to be trapped inside the tunnel at the project.

“Now the Nepal Army can enter and find out what condition those people are in. We may know the situation by tomorrow afternoon,” he said.

title.rendered: Army chief Ashok Raj Sigdel visits Rasuwa, Nuwakot to monitor rescue efforts

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 3

Chief of Army Staff General Ashok Raj Sigdel has travelled to Rasuwa and Nuwakot to monitor ongoing search and rescue operations following the Bhotekoshi flood.

According to the Nepal Army headquarters, Sigdel visited the affected areas on Thursday to inspect the search and rescue operations underway inside hydropower tunnels.

He also inspected other affected areas and directed the agencies involved to maintain effective coordination and cooperation while continuing the search and rescue operations with high morale.

The Nepal Army has been leading search and rescue efforts at several hydropower projects where people are believed to have been trapped following the flood. International teams and technical experts have also joined the efforts.

Kathmandu, September 3

The bodies of two people have been recovered from the tunnel of the Langtang Khola Hydropower Project in Rasuwa.

A team of the Nepal Army deployed for search and rescue operations recovered the two bodies. According to project manager Bijay Man Bhattarai, the rescue team recovered the bodies from inside the tunnel.

Bhattarai said a team of hydromechanical engineers has now entered about 150 meters into the project tunnel to continue search and rescue operations.

Search operations were carried out up to 150 meters inside the tunnel on Wednesday. He said the search was intensified from early Thursday morning.

title.rendered: Teaching Hospital prepares to bury unidentified Bhotekoshi flood victims in Gokarna

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital is preparing to bury more bodies recovered from the Bhotekoshi flood in Gokarna on Thursday as authorities struggle to manage the growing number of unidentified victims.

The bodies are being temporarily buried as efforts continue to establish their identities.

According to the hospital’s Department of Forensic Medicine, 177 bodies have so far been brought to the hospital for management. Of these, post-mortems have been completed on 129 bodies. A total of 85 bodies have been sent for temporary burial, while 21 bodies have been identified and handed over to their families.

Use up and down arrow keys to resize the meta box pane.

Dr Gopal Chaudhary, head of the department, said many of the bodies were already in an advanced state of decomposition when they were recovered after a prolonged period.

“Some of the bodies have deteriorated to the point where even their faces cannot be recognised,” he said.

The condition of the bodies has made both identification and management increasingly difficult.

Authorities have now begun a scientific identification process for the unidentified bodies. DNA samples are being collected from the bodies at Teaching Hospital, while samples from possible relatives are being collected at the Nepal Police Hospital in Maharajgunj.

The bodies are being identified by matching their DNA with samples collected from close blood relatives.

The growing number of bodies has also placed considerable pressure on the hospital’s storage capacity. Teaching Hospital can accommodate around 150 bodies, but the number brought to the facility has exceeded that capacity.

The pressure has increased because decomposed bodies cannot be kept in open spaces and must be stored in the mortuary. With space running out, some bodies had previously been transferred to the cooling facility at Pashupati.

Bodies whose post-mortems have been completed but whose identities remain unknown are being sent to Gokarna for temporary burial after the necessary DNA samples have been collected and legal procedures completed.

Balen asks Kulman about rescue of people trapped in hydropower tunnels

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Prime Minister Balen Shah held a meeting with Kulman Ghising, chairperson of the Ujyalo Nepal Party, at the Prime Minister’s official residence in Singha Durbar on Thursday.

Ghising said he met Prime Minister Shah to share observations and recommendations based on his team’s field visits to flood-affected areas. “We met to provide suggestions on what we saw and understood during our field visits to various places in this disaster situation, and what needs to be done,” he said while leaving the Prime Minister’s Office.

A team led by Ghising provided the Prime Minister with recommendations on measures the government should take for rescue, relief and resettlement. “We have provided both written and verbal recommendations,” he said. “In the current disaster situation, we have provided the government with comprehensive suggestions, particularly on rescue, relief and resettlement.”

Ghising said Prime Minister Shah also asked how people trapped inside tunnels of hydropower projects could be rescued. “Primarily, they were concerned about how to rescue those trapped inside the tunnels,” he said. “We shared what we had learned and what needs to be done in this regard.”

After Ghising’s team briefed the prime minister on the measures needed to rescue those trapped inside the tunnels, Shah said the government would make every possible effort to carry out the rescue operation. “He said that the government would do whatever it takes in this regard. He said that no matter what the circumstances are, whatever resources and personnel need to be mobilised, they will be mobilised and the operation will be taken forward,” Ghising said.

title.rendered: Shishir, who went for an internship, is missing; family questions the university

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Shishir Giri, a civil engineering student at Kathmandu University, went to Rasuwa on August 13 for an internship at the Upper Trishuli 3B project. He was accompanied by fellow civil engineering students Sameer Poudel and Srishti Bastola. On August 26, when a sudden and devastating flood struck the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli area, Giri was among the thousands of citizens who went missing.

Shishir’s father, Ratna Prakash, works at the District Government Attorney’s Office in Dang. He was at work when his eldest son called that evening to tell him his younger brother was out of contact. Ratna Prakash immediately left for home and flew from Nepalgunj to Kathmandu the next morning.

After landing in Kathmandu, he tried contacting university representatives, but says he received only vague responses about going to the electricity authority or other offices. He went straight from the airport to the site, but couldn’t go past a barrack near the project area and had to wait there all day without further information. He returned to Kathmandu and began mobilising his personal network to help with the search.

Shishir’s family has been appealing to the government for help on social media. His mother, Sushila, posted a video on Facebook saying the foundation of their life has been destroyed, and appealed to the public for help finding her son, whether alive or not, so she could see him one last time.

Seven days after Shishir went missing, his situation remains unknown. Location tracking initially placed him in the project’s quarter area; later email-based location records showed conflicting data, one source placing him there until around 8:30, another until slightly after 9. The last known location was near a structure called an “audit tunnel,” which the family has since learned is now buried and further down than before. Ratna Prakash also expressed doubts about the reliability of the location tracking.

He has raised serious concerns that students weren’t warned in time despite the risky conditions, arguing that young, able-bodied people could have run to safety had they been alerted before the flood hit.

His biggest criticism centers on procedural failures by the university: the family was never informed about the decision to send students to the Upper Trishuli project as interns, no insurance appears to have been arranged for such risky work, and it’s unclear whether any formal agreement existed between the university and the project authority.

He also questioned the timing: the internship was scheduled during peak monsoon season, when flood and landslide risk is naturally elevated, and small floods had already struck the area on August 7 to 13, just before the disaster. He believes sending students despite this was a mistake.

Additionally, he says there’s a mismatch between the students’ field of study and the internship placement; hydropower-related work isn’t essential for a civil engineering curriculum, and he questions why civil students were sent specifically to a hydropower site at such a dangerous time. The university, for its part, maintains that hydro engineering is part of the civil engineering course content and that the internship was in line with the curriculum.

University response


Kathmandu University formed a Search, Rescue and Coordination Committee on August 27 to coordinate search, rescue, and support efforts for missing students and others in the affected area, and to mobilize resources. The university’s aid team from Dhulikhel Hospital has been active in the flood-affected area since Bhadra 10.

Committee member Mahesh Raj Bhatta said rescue work at the project quarters resumed as of yesterday, and that the university is positioned to assist the government further, including with equipment like excavators.

Another committee member, Manish Prakash, said the internship was conducted according to the university’s academic calendar, which has been in place since 2009, and that he doesn’t take the current criticism personally given the circumstances were caused by a natural disaster.

He added that out of sensitivity to the distressed parents, the university hasn’t said much directly to them, but maintains it followed its established calendar.

title.rendered: Rasuwa Flood: 1,252 bodies recovered, 4,216 still missing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

The bodies of 1,252 people who went missing in the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa have been recovered.

According to a bulletin issued by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) at noon, the bodies of 1,252 people reported missing in the floods have so far been recovered.

According to the authority, 127 bodies have been recovered in Rasuwa, 177 in Nuwakot, 60 in Dhading, 69 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 218 in East Nawalparasi, 208 in West Nawalparasi and 355 in Chitwan.

The authority said 4,216 people are still missing, while 11,993 people have so far been rescued.

A total of 5,135 people have been injured in the floods.

title.rendered: Risk of flash floods in Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems: Flood Forecasting Division

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

There is a risk of flash floods in Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems today also. Saraswati Bista, a flood expert at the Flood Forecasting Division, the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research, said that the water level in the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and nearby rivers is expected to rise today, as precipitation is taking place and there is a possibility of more precipitation in the upstream areas of the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The division urged residents in the riverbank areas in Rasuwa and Nuwakot to be highly alert in view of the flash floods in these river systems. According to Bista, there is a possibility that the water level may rise and there is risk of moderate flash floods today in rivers and streams flowing through districts like Taplejung, Panchthar, Tehrathum, Sankhuwasabha, Dhankuta, Bhojpur, Solukhumbu, Okhaldhunga, Khotang, Udayapur, Dolakha, Ramechhap, Sindhuli, Sindhupalchok, Kavrepalanchok, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur, Kathmandu, Dhading, Makawanpur, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahu, Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, Myagdi, Kaski, Syangja, Parbat and Dolpa, and nearby districts.

Similarly, the Division stated that the water level in even small rivers in districts like Rukum East, Rukum West, Salyan, Jajarkot, Surkhet, Dailekh, Kalikot, Mugu, Humla, Jumla, Achham, Bajhang, Bajura, Dadeldhura, Baitadi, Darchula, and Kanchanpur is expected to increase significantly, and there is a medium risk of sudden floods. The Division has suggested that the general public living in coastal areas and travelling along riverbanks stay alert, as there is a risk of flash floods in the small rivers and streams in those areas.

title.rendered: Flood sweeps away tree used to mark Nepal-India border in Susta

content.rendered:
Butwal, September 3

Flooding in the Narayani River has swept away a silk cotton tree that had long been recognised as marking the Nepal-India border in Susta Rural Municipality-5 of West Nawalparasi.

Locals said flooding entered the area from the same location after construction of a 132-meter embankment along the Narayani River was halted for two months following objections from India’s Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB). The government had begun constructing the embankment to protect Susta village from flooding.

Adam Khan, chair of the Susta Bachau Abhiyan and a ward member of Susta-5, said Wednesday night’s flood swept away the silk cotton tree that had been recognised as a border marker.

The tree, located in Tharu Tole across the Narayani River, had been agreed upon as a de facto border marker 18 years ago, in 2008, with the participation of district-level security officials from Nepal and India and residents.

Following the loss of the tree, residents of Susta have demanded that a permanent border pillar be installed immediately.

Tek Narayan Upadhyay, chair of Susta Rural Municipality, has urged the federal government to install a permanent border pillar, saying the absence of one has repeatedly led to disputes with the Indian side.

“Because there is no permanent border pillar, the Indian side has repeatedly encroached on Nepali territory and created disputes,” Upadhyay said.

Flooding two days ago also entered Tharu Tole in Susta, damaging sugarcane crops planted across around 20 bighas of land.

Susta-5, an area that has long been subject to a border dispute, is home to 1,457 people from 220 households.

Upadhyay stated that the Indian side gained an advantage in the Susta border dispute after Prime Minister Balen Shah, speaking from the parliamentary rostrum, remarked that Nepal had encroached upon India’s territory at several locations along the border.

title.rendered: GoPro Camera’ installed at Kankarbhitta border

content.rendered:
Jhapa, September 3

The Armed Police Force (APF) has installed a ‘GoPro Camera’ at Kankarbhitta, the eastern border of Nepal, to enhance surveillance and combat criminal activities.

The initiative, announced by the APF’s No. 2 Battalion Headquarters in Jhapa, aims to gather critical information and improve the transparency and effectiveness of investigations by providing direct evidence in cases of crime. Superintendent Sachin Karmacharya expressed optimism that the two activated cameras will help address issues such as illegal smuggling and theft in the border area.

The proactive use of technology by the armed police has contributed to a heightened sense of security among residents, who are increasingly supportive of the police’s efforts to maintain peace and security in the region.

title.rendered: Public holidays declared in seven municipalities of Kanchanpur

content.rendered:
Mahendranagar, September 3

A public holiday has been declared in seven municipalities of Kanchanpur district, including Bhimdatta, Dodhara Chandni, Shuklaphanta, Punarbas, Laljhandi, and Beldandi, in celebration of the Gaura festival.

The festival holds significant cultural importance in the far-western region. Mahesh Bahadur Bam, the Chief Administrative Officer of Bhimdatta Municipality, confirmed that this decision was made by local officials to honour the festival. Additionally, a two-day local public holiday has been announced in Raxirang and Kailash for the Nwagi (Chonam) festival, celebrated by the Chepang community.

This holiday will take place on September 8 and 9, with local councils closing government offices, public organisations, and educational institutions during this time. The Chepang community observes various traditions during this period, including Rakhi Puja and offerings to ancestors, emphasising their connection to new food crops and the worship of land and nature.

title.rendered: The roof of the world is collapsing: Nepal’s warning to a climate-delinquent world

content.rendered:
Within mere hours on August 26, a sudden deluge of mud, boulders, and roaring water tore through the high-altitude mountain communities of the Bhotekoshi region in Rasuwa, Nepal. Entire villages were destroyed overnight, vital transit corridors were severed, and families were cast into darkness, displacement, and absolute uncertainty.

The physical destruction was severe, but the true toll of the devastating flash flood extends far beyond what cold metrics, infrastructure audits, or financial damage calculations can reveal about the human cost.

Disasters are typically reported through numbers: lives lost, homes leveled, bridges snapped, and economic losses tabulated. Yet numbers cannot capture grief. A statistic cannot convey the silence inside a home after loss, a damage report cannot measure the trauma of a family waiting beside a swollen river for someone who may never return, and an economic assessment cannot reflect a community’s broken identity.

In Nepal, a sovereign nation home to approximately 29.6 million people, it is not aggressive industrial advancement or fossil-fueled factory outputs that are being disrupted; it is innocent human beings who are being killed, swept away, and buried under climate-induced debris.

The real impact of the Rasuwa tragedy is recorded in human struggle and silent grief: a family waiting anxiously beside a collapsed riverbank for news of missing loved ones, holding onto the smallest hope for a safe return; a parent carrying the unbearable grief of losing a child, sustained only by memories of shared laughter and love; a farmer watching years of hard work, dreams, and family security vanish as fields, livestock, and livelihoods wash away into a churning river; an elder standing before the ruins of an ancestral home that held decades of family celebrations; and a child forced to flee the only sanctuary they ever knew, facing fear and an uncertain future.

The Rasuwa flash flood is not an isolated natural mishap or an unavoidable fate of mountain geography. It is a human tragedy of intense suffering, loss of life, and displacement that underscores a dangerous, growing pattern of climate risk across the Himalayan arc.

Comprising a mere 0.1 percent of the Earth’s total land area, Nepal spans an extraordinary elevation gradient, rising from near sea level in the southern Terai plains to the top of the world at Sagarmatha, Mount Everest, standing at 8,848.86  meter . Within an average width of just 193 kilometers, the country has eight of the world’s fourteen independent mountain peak above 8,000 meters, serving as the crown jewel of global mountain geography and the primary headwaters for massive river systems that sustain over 1.6 billion people downstream.

Despite its small territorial footprint, Nepal harbors over 1.5 percent of global biodiversity. The country is home to nearly 8.9 percent of the world’s bird species. It protects roughly 3.96 percent of global mammal species, 3.72 percent of butterflies, and nearly 2.8 percent of global flowering plant species, including hundreds of endemic varieties found nowhere else on the planet.

Dense subtropical forests, temperate mountain woodlands, and alpine pastures provide critical sanctuary for iconic, globally endangered species such as the snow leopard, the red panda, the Royal Bengal tiger, and the greater one-horned rhinoceros. These ecosystems render Nepal a vital regulator of the regional climate system, water towers, and carbon storage.

However, rapidly rising global temperatures driven by external industrial emissions are destabilizing this delicate high altitude environment, turning peaks that once symbolized protection into landscapes of extreme peril.

Nepal stands as one of the clearest examples of global climate injustice. The nation contributes less than 0.1 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, while 77% of global emissions are shared by G20 member countries. Its annual per capita carbon footprint stands at a modest 0.63 tonnes of CO₂, a fraction of the global average of 4.7 tonnes per person, and a negligible drop compared to the massive per capita footprints of industrial world powers.

It has not waited for international prompts to practice progressive environmental stewardship. Through decades of community-managed forestry programs, Nepal increased its national forest coverage from 39.6 percent to 46.08 percent, reversing historical degradation and expanding vital global carbon sinks. More than 90 percent of Nepal’s national electricity is generated from clean, renewable hydropower. Policy incentives have driven the domestic sales share of electric vehicles (EVs) from 8 percent to approximately 73 percent.  

Here lies the painful paradox of the climate crisis: those who contributed the least suffer the most. Innocent communities who have actively protected their forests, powered their grid with running water, and adopted clean electric transport are bearing the catastrophic cost of environmental degradation caused by heavy emitters elsewhere.  

Nepal’s fragile high-altitude topography, reliance on climate-sensitive agriculture, and limited infrastructure compound its extreme vulnerability. For mountain farmers and rural families, climate change is not an abstract policy debate or a distant environmental metric; it is an everyday reality affecting whether crops can be harvested, whether children can safely reach school, whether pregnant mothers can access emergency medical care, and whether entire communities can survive once the floodwaters recede. Wealthy nations grew rich from fossil fuel-driven growth, whose emissions built the crisis Nepal is now suffering from.

The impact of a disaster does not end when the floodwaters retreat. Often, the most dangerous phase begins in the aftermath. The flash flood is far more than an immediate search and rescue mission; it is a severe threat to community health, safety, sanitation, and human dignity. Flooding destroys community Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) infrastructure, contaminating drinking water sources with municipal waste, silt, and agricultural runoff. These triggers immediate outbreaks of waterborne and vector-borne diseases, including cholera, typhoid fever, acute diarrheal illnesses, and severe skin infections.

Children, the elderly, pregnant women, and economically marginalized group bear the highest risk. When steep mountain roads collapse, pregnant women experiencing complex labor, infected infants, or severely injured survivors are cut off from regional health facilities. In rugged mountain terrain, a destroyed road transform a manageable medical concern into a fatal emergency, undermining even basic human dignity.

Extreme disasters also leave deep psychological wounds that linger across generations. Survivors cope with severe post traumatic stress, chronic anxiety, depression, and profound grief after losing their loved ones, homes, and economic safety nets. A house can eventually be rebuilt and a road repaved, but healing emotional trauma requires long term empathy, community support, and sustained psychosocial care to protect and safeguard vulnerable populations and restore basic human dignity. Protecting the environment is no longer just an act of conservation; it is a vital public health intervention to preserve human life.

When disasters strike vulnerable, low-emitting nations, the international community’s standard response is to offer humanitarian sympathy, international media coverage, and modest packages of discretionary emergency aid. However, sympathy does not rebuild destroyed highways, nor does charity compensate for lost lives, ruined harvests, and fractured identities. Frontline nations do not need pity; they demand climate justice and financial accountability. Nepal deserves climate restitution, not short term aid, donations, or charity.

Supporting nations on the frontlines of the climate crisis is not an act of international benevolence; it is a mandatory global obligation. Climate justice is anchored in established principle, primarily the Polluter Pays Principle and the foundational agreement of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

Under the Paris Agreement, Article 8 explicitly mandates global action to address loss and damage associated with the adverse impacts of climate change, while Article 9 establishes that developed countries must provide financial resources to assist developing nations in mitigation and adaptation.

The establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund at recent COP summits signaled formal global consensus that high-emitting economies carry a legal and financial liability to compensate vulnerable nations facing non-reversible climate impacts.

Yet, climate finance remains grossly inadequate and structurally flawed. A substantial portion of global climate assistance is still delivered in the form of high-interest development loans or conditional aid.

Forcing a low-emitting nation to accumulate sovereign debt in order to rebuild infrastructure destroyed by external global emissions is an unacceptable compounding injustice. Innocent nations that preserve their natural environment, expand their forest canopy, and maintain minimal emissions should never be forced to divert national fund away from public education, healthcare, and poverty alleviation to cover the costs of climate disasters. Major industrial emitters must fulfill their global commitments by providing direct, predictable, non-repayable grant compensation through loss and damage mechanisms. On the other hand, loss and damage are huge.

The establishment of the fund at COP28 in Dubai has resulted in a promised amount that falls painfully short of the necessary funds for recovery. While pledges hover in the hundreds of million, vulnerable societies face hundreds of billions in annual destruction. Rebuilding destroyed lives, homes, and local economies is not a matter of charity; it is a fundamental requirement for human dignity and social justice.

“We did our part. We barely caused this crisis. Why are we paying for it with our lives?” This question echoed across the mud caked valley of Rasuwa; it is not merely a localized cry of pain; it is a profound moral indictment of global climate governance.

Nepal has demonstrated that responsible environmental management, forest expansion, and renewable energy adoption is entirely possible even within a developing economy. Yet domestic action alone cannot hold back monsoons intensified by foreign industrial emissions, nor can local conservation stop glacial lakes from bursting their banks when global temperatures climb. Nepal’s devastating flash flood is a narrative of immense human loss, but it is equally a testament to community resilience and the enduring strength of mountain peoples. It serves as an urgent, unyielding warning that climate change is not a distant future scenario; it is happening right now, tearing through homes and killing innocent lives.

The Himalayas are speaking. The rivers are speaking. Mount Everest and the frontline communities living in its shadow are speaking to a delinquent global community.

Let this warning reverberate through the gilded halls of international summits, pierce the complacency of high-emitting capitals, and vibrate across every policy document that treats human lives as negotiable statistical trade-offs.

The critical question facing high-emitting nations is whether they will continue to offer empty declarations and token sympathy, or finally step up, take structural responsibility, and pay their climate liabilities. The time for promises and humanitarian pity has run out.

Global climate justice requires immediate action, rapid emission cuts by historical polluters, and direct financial compensation for the innocent communities defending Earth’s natural sanctuaries. No ifs, no buts: it’s an unequivocal warning to the world that it must pay its climate debt to the innocent lives for their justice. If the roof of the world collapses under the weight of global delinquency, the cascading shockwaves will inevitably engulf every nation on Earth

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood: Electricity service restored in 90 Percent of Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Following the devastating flood on the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, electricity supply that had been disrupted in Nuwakot has now been restored to about 90 percent of the district.

According to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, power supply has been restored in most areas of Nuwakot.

According to the details released by the Ministry of Energy, electricity supply has been restored in roughly 90 percent of Nuwakot’s area.

The Ministry stated that after the Chapali-Devighat right circuit was energised, power supply was restored to additional areas of Nuwakot. It noted that voltage has also improved as electricity supply has become more reliable than before in most parts of the district.

Areas where power has now been restored include Ward No. 6 of Bidur Municipality and roughly half of Ward No. 3 of Bidur Municipality, Wards No. 1, 5, and 6 of Tarakeshwar Municipality, Wards No. 2 and 3 of Tarakeshwar Municipality, and Ward No. 7 of Belkotgadhi Municipality. An additional 31 transformers have also been energised, according to the details.

However, the Ministry noted that power supply has yet to be restored in Ward No. 12 of Bidur Municipality, the remaining half of Ward No. 3 of Bidur Municipality, Kispang Rural Municipality, Ward No. 8 of Belkotgadhi Municipality, and Ward No. 10 of Bidur Municipality.

The Ministry of Energy said that following damage to electrical infrastructure in Nuwakot, repair and restoration work is underway to resume full supply.

title.rendered: Nepal beat Malaysia by six wickets for second straight ACC Premier Cup win

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Nepal continued their impressive start to the ACC Premier Cup by defeating hosts Malaysia by six wickets on Thursday, chasing down a target of 104 runs in 21.4 overs for the loss of four wickets.

Arjun Kumal remained unbeaten on 45, while Ishan Pandey scored 20 and Dipendra Singh Airee finished unbeaten on 12.

Earlier, Malaysia, after winning the toss and opting to bat first, were bowled out for 103 in 32.3 overs.

Captain Syed Aziz top-scored for Malaysia with 30 runs, while Akil Waheed made 24. Virandeep Singh scored 14 and Muhammad Syahadat Ramli added 13. None of the other Malaysian batters managed to reach double figures.

For Nepal, Karan KC was the standout bowler, taking four wickets for 23 runs in 7.3 overs. Lalit Rajbanshi claimed two wickets, while Hemant Dhami, Sandeep Lamichhane and Dipendra Singh Airee took one each.

Nepal had earlier defeated Bahrain in their opening match of the tournament.

Nepal will next face Hong Kong on Sunday.

title.rendered: Tree cutting begins to reopen Krishnabhir road

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Tree-cutting work has begun as part of efforts to clear a landslide and reopen the Krishnabhir section of the Prithvi Highway.

According to the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Development, 18 workers have been deployed from both sides of the landslide to cut down trees. The ministry said the necessary construction equipment has also been kept ready on both sides of the affected section to clear the debris.

The ministry said machinery will be mobilised to remove the landslide debris as soon as the tree-cutting work is completed. It said work is being carried out at a rapid pace, with reopening the road given top priority.

The subsidence of the road at Krishnabhir has disrupted supply chains to Kathmandu, while passengers travelling to and from the Kathmandu Valley have been facing difficulties. Taking advantage of the situation, artificial shortages have also begun to emerge in the market.

title.rendered: EU provides further Rs 89 million in humanitarian aid and relief supplies for flood-affected communities in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

The European Union (EU) is providing a further Rs 89 million in humanitarian aid to support communities affected by the devastating flash floods in Nepal. This brings the EU’s total emergency funding for the disaster to over Rs 445 million (EUR 2.5 million).

The new funding will support an International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) operation led by the Nepal Red Cross Society. The operation aims to assist up to 20,000 people – around 4,000 households – in Bagmati Province with emergency and transitional shelter, cash assistance, water and sanitation, healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support, protection and other essential assistance.

The funding comes as Nepal continues to respond to catastrophic flash floods that struck on 26 August, causing extensive loss of life and widespread damage to homes, infrastructure and essential services. Since that date, the Copernicus satellite service has been providing maps to support the response. 

The EU is also mobilising in-kind assistance. Through the EU’s Civil Protection Mechanism, Germany, Luxembourg, Latvia and Sweden are sending shelter and hygiene items, forensic equipment and other supplies. 

Furthermore, the EU is organising a Humanitarian Air Bridge to Kathmandu. A flight with over 80 tonnes of supplies from the EU’s emergency stock in Copenhagen is scheduled to arrive later this week.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa urges public to help Rasuwa flood victims, avoid harsh words

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has urged those who are able to help to come forward and support the victims of the Rasuwa floods.

In a video message posted on Facebook on Thursday, he also appealed to people not to use harsh words if they are unable to provide assistance. “I have one request: Those who can help should come forward and help. Even if we cannot help, let us at least not speak harshly,” he said in the video.

Thapa shared his observations from his visit to the flood-affected areas, describing the scale of the disaster, ongoing search, rescue and relief efforts, and the grievances raised by those affected. A few days earlier, he had visited several flood-hit areas in Dhading and Nuwakot for an on-site assessment.

“This is such a massive calamity, such a devastating disaster. It has destroyed so many homes and affected so many families and people. Only after going to the ground do you truly understand the scale of it,” Thapa said. “You simply cannot assess it from outside or comprehend what has happened there. Its scale is beyond measure.”

Thapa said everyone must work together during this time of disaster. “At this time, each and every one of us must work together,” he said. He also said the party would prepare and make public a detailed report based on what its representatives observed during their field visits, including recommendations on what the government should do and the steps to be taken in the next phase.

“Based on everything we saw on the ground, we will prepare and make public a detailed report on what the government needs to do and what we need to do in the next phase,” he said. Thapa also praised the work being carried out by local and provincial governments in the flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: With no bodies found, flood-hit families begin last rites for missing loved ones

content.rendered:
Photos: Chandra Bahadur Ale/Kamal Prasai

Rasuwa, September 3

For eight days, they waited and watched the roads, hoping their missing relatives would return. Whenever they heard that search teams had reached a particular area, a glimmer of hope emerged—perhaps their loved ones had been found.

But seven nights passed without any news. Now, many flood victims from Paharebesi in Ward No. 5 of Uttargaya Rural Municipality have begun to give up hope. They are preparing to make a decision that is difficult to accept: to perform funeral rites for their missing relatives, accepting that they are unlikely to return.

According to Ramchandra Thapa Magar of Paharebesi, many bodies have been recovered along the banks of the Koshi River. However, residents of Paharebesi were able to identify only one of them, and the body has already been cremated. There is no information about where the floods may have carried the others.

“Today marks eight days. After discussions among neighbours and community members, we have concluded that those who remain out of contact are unlikely to return, and we have begun preparations for the funeral rites,” Ramchandra told Onlinekhabar. The floods swept away 49 houses in Paharebesi, leaving only the ruins of some homes behind. More than 400 people are estimated to have lived in the village.

However, there is no confirmed figure on how many people were caught in the floods. According to information collected by locals, 54 people from Paharebesi alone are missing. Residents estimate that the number could exceed 70 when people from other places are included.

Even performing mourning rites is difficult

According to Uttargaya Rural Municipality Chairperson Madhav Prasad Aryal, families who have accepted that their missing relatives will not return have begun the process of performing the final rites. “Those who believe their relatives will no longer be found have started the necessary procedures,” he said.

However, the process has not been easy. First, there is a shortage of space in the village to perform the death rituals. Second, there is a shortage of priests to conduct the funeral rites. “Almost nothing remains of the old settlement. It is not possible for everyone to stay together while observing the mourning rituals,” said Deputy Chairperson Chameli Gurung. “Since there is no suitable place, some people have gone to stay with relatives to perform the rites, while others have travelled to Kathmandu.”

Displaced residents of Paharebesi have been divided between two camps, one in Majhgaun and another in Kuwapani. Around 50 people are staying at the lower camp, while about 25 are staying in Kuwapani. Under such circumstances, it has not been possible to provide separate spaces for families performing mourning rituals. The problem is even more serious for families that have lost several members.

On the eighth day, they are preparing to make symbolic effigies from kusha grass and perform the final rites, begin the mourning period, and continue other traditional funeral rituals. As all rituals must be completed within 13 days according to tradition, they say they can no longer afford to wait.

Therefore, they have concluded that the community must move forward with the rituals even if the bodies are never recovered. Families that have lost several members must perform separate mourning rites for each of them. Those observing the rituals require separate spaces, and because tradition requires them to wear white clothing and remain apart, it is not possible to accommodate many people performing the rites in a single room.

As a result, more than 20 families have left for Kathmandu and other places. When the Onlinekhabar team visited on Wednesday, around 20 more people were preparing to travel to Kathmandu. Following the deaths and disappearances of a large number of people in the floods and landslides, finding priests to conduct funeral rituals has also become difficult. Priests who previously performed such ceremonies are themselves mourning losses.

Entire families lost

People are missing from almost every household in Paharebesi. Some of the families who survived the floods are now staying in Majhgaun of Uttargaya Rural Municipality–5, where a school has been turned into a temporary camp. The camp is overcrowded. Some people sit on the floor, while others lean against the walls.

New mothers, sick people, children and elderly people are all staying there. They share the same concern: Where will they go now, and what will they do? The floods swept away their homes and, along with them, many of their loved ones. Some have lost their parents. Others have lost their husbands. Some have lost their children. In some cases, entire families have disappeared.

Two children from Paharebesi have lost their entire families and are now under the care of relatives. In one family, 10 members remain missing, leaving behind only one boy. In another family of four, three were swept away by the floods, leaving only a young girl alive. “Some are staying with relatives, while others have gone to Kathmandu. In some families, only small children remain. The floods swept away both their fathers and mothers,” Ramchandra said.

Such heartbreaking stories are not limited to Paharebesi. Similar tragedies can be found in households across Nuwakot and Rasuwa. “Two children have lost contact with their entire families,” Ramchandra said. “They have now been taken in by relatives.”

title.rendered: Special fundraising screening of ‘Elephants in the Fog (Tiniharu)’ held

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3, 2026 

The special fundraising screening of the Nepali feature film ‘Elephants in the Fog (TINIHARU)’, winner of the Jury Prize in the Un Certain Regard section at the Cannes Film Festival, was held on Wednesday in Kathmandu.

Organised to support relief and recovery efforts as the country continues to face the devastating impact of a natural disaster, the screening raised voluntary contributions from guests, along with funds from the film’s producers. The entire amount raised was directly deposited into the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

The screening was attended by the film’s cast and crew, alongside members of the media, journalists, artists, filmmakers, and guests from various fields. Following the screening, the film was met with a prolonged standing ovation and enthusiastic applause from the audience. Among those in attendance were actresses Manisha Koirala, Karishma Manandhar, Reecha Sharma, Keki Adhikari, and Usha Rajak, among others.

At the conclusion of the screening, the film was met with a roaring standing ovation and enthusiastic applause from the audience.

Member of the House of Representatives and businesswoman Vidushi Rana was visibly moved after watching the film and became emotional while speaking about it. She emphasised the importance of the film being seen by audiences, expressing that its story and themes make it especially important for people to engage with the film at this moment.

Speaking about the purpose behind the fundraising screening, Abinash Bikram Shah, writer-director of the film, said, “Our Nepal is in pain right now. We Nepalis are in pain. If this screening can, even in a small way, share in that pain and contribute something towards relief, I will consider it a success.”

Anup Poudel, producer of the film, also said that the fundraising screening was organised after reflecting on how the filmmakers could contribute, as members of the film community, during this difficult time of national crisis.

Following the fundraising screening, ‘Elephants in the Fog (TINIHARU)’ will be released in cinemas across Nepal from September 4.

Despite the country continuing to endure a period of grief and devastation, the film’s team has decided to proceed with the previously announced release date. The decision was made to continue the necessary process for the film’s Oscar submission. The filmmakers have also expressed their commitment to using the national and international platforms that come with the film’s theatrical and festival journey to bring Nepal’s stories, experiences, pain, and the issues surrounding climate change to audiences around the world.

In the coming months, ‘Elephants in the Fog (TINIHARU)’ will represent Nepal at international platforms including Toronto, BFI London, Taipei, Busan, and Rio, among others.

The film became the first Nepali feature film to be officially selected for the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival, where it went on to receive the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize. The film has also won Best Film and the Audience Award in New Zealand.

The film’s team extends its sincere gratitude to all members of the media, filmmakers, guests, and audiences who attended the fundraising screening and showed their support and solidarity.

title.rendered: Missing flood victims’ families called for DNA testing

content.rendered:
September 3, Kathmandu

Nepal Police has begun a DNA testing process to search for citizens who went missing in the Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa, and to identify unclaimed bodies and human remains that have been recovered.

Following the devastating flood on August 26, Nepal Police issued a notice asking blood relatives of the deceased to provide DNA samples to help identify bodies and body parts found along the riverbanks and surrounding areas.

According to the notice, first-degree relatives of missing citizens, whether based in Nepal or abroad, will need to complete the DNA testing procedure.

Things relatives in Nepal should do

One of the closest blood relatives (father, mother, son, or daughter) of a missing Nepali or foreign citizen must appear in person with two passport-size photos, as stated in the Nepal Police notice. They must provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling, either at the Pathology Lab of Nepal Police Hospital, Maharajgunj, Kathmandu, or at their nearest District Police Office.

Things families abroad should do

For foreign nationals or non-resident Nepalis abroad, one of the parents or children must get “autosomal STR DNA profiling” done through an official forensic laboratory in that country. Police have requested that a soft copy (digital copy) of this profile be sent to Nepal Police’s official email.

The email should include:

  • The full name and nationality of the missing person
  • Passport or official ID details
  • The date and probable location of disappearance
  • The DNA profiling report from a recognised laboratory
  • The family relationship between the person providing the DNA and the missing person

Nepal Police has designated two contact officers for coordination on DNA testing:

  • Police Inspector Shambhu Bahadur KC: 9841616095
  • Deputy Police Inspector (SI) Bishnu Ghimire: 9857091013

Police stated that since the flood swept away a large number of citizens and many bodies have been found in a badly damaged condition, this scientific identification process has been made mandatory to properly return the remains to families.

title.rendered: Locals risk lives crossing Taksugad after flood washes away bridge

content.rendered:
Surkhet, September 3

Residents and travellers have been forced to risk their lives to cross the Taksugad stream after floods washed away a bridge and a temporary causeway between wards 10 and 11 of Nalgad Municipality in Jajarkot along the Bheri Corridor.

Flooding on August 14 swept away a suspension bridge over Taksugad as well as a temporary causeway built to facilitate movement.

The destruction of the bridge and causeway has disrupted transportation along the Bheri Corridor, forcing locals to cross the stream at great personal risk.

With the regular route blocked by the floods, pedestrians and residents have found it particularly difficult to cross the stream, especially during the monsoon season.

The strong current has further increased the risk of accidents, as people are compelled to cross the stream under dangerous conditions.

As Taksugad lies along an important section of the Bheri Corridor, residents have urged the concerned authorities to reconstruct the bridge and causeway and immediately ensure safe passage.

title.rendered: The photo of his missing daughter that Suchit cannot bear to look at

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, September 3

Suchit Joshi of Bidur Municipality-1 was at work as usual on August 26.

A staff member at Tribhuvan Trishuli Multiple Campus, Joshi was busy helping enrol undergraduate students when he received a phone call from an elder relative warning him about a flood.

“A huge flood has come. Syabrubesi is about to be swept away,” the relative told him.

Joshi, who lives in the riverside area, initially thought it was another flood like those he had seen before. He did not expect the warning to mean anything on the scale that was about to unfold.

Then he heard the roar.

When he saw the flood surging towards them, he panicked.

“The flood is here. Run, run!” he shouted at everyone at the campus before rushing away on his motorcycle.

Amid the chaos, Joshi tried to find out what was happening to his family.

He saw his brother riding away on a scooter and assumed that meant the family was safe. If his brother had managed to get away, he thought, the others must have reached safety too.

They had not.

“I put a bank security guard on my motorcycle and headed uphill. I had no idea that my family was still down there,” Joshi told Onlinekhabar.

Of the eight members of his family, four remain missing.

His wife, Manju Shrestha; his seven-year-old daughter, Sumansingh Joshi; his brother’s wife; and his brother’s son have not been found.

Joshi has searched for them relentlessly. He has ridden his motorcycle through areas hit by the flood, returning again and again to places where he thought they might have been.

“I tried everything to find them. I went around the areas where the flood had entered on my motorcycle, again and again. But I couldn’t find them anywhere,” he said.

His brother’s infant child survived. The baby’s mother managed to carry the child with her to safety.

Since the flood, Joshi has searched almost everywhere he could think of—from early morning until late at night.

His face is worn from exhaustion and grief.

“I feel like my mind has gone blank. I search everywhere, but I can’t find them,” he said.

At one point, he even tried to enter the Trishuli River himself to search for his family. Police officers and friends stopped him.

There have also been moments that gave him reason to keep hoping.

While searching for his family, Joshi found his nephew and uncle. Two locals had rescued his nephew.

Finding him gave Joshi renewed courage.

“I kept searching to see if there was anyone else,” he said. “We found three more people.”

Among them was his uncle, Ram Joshi, whom he helped rescue.

His search gradually turned into a wider rescue effort. Five people joined his team, and they began helping others trapped by the flood. They rescued an elderly woman who had been stranded in the floodwater in front of her own house and took her to safety.

But every rescue brought him back to the same painful question: where was his own family?

Unable to find them, Joshi says he reached a breaking point.

“I screamed. I shouted. I called their names. I became almost like a madman,” he said. “There was no voice coming from anywhere.”

He even tried using whistles, hoping the children might hear them and respond.

Nothing worked.

“My every effort went in vain,” he said.

Joshi later joined security personnel in searching for his family.

During the search, they recovered three bodies from the Trishuli. They were badly damaged and could not be identified.

“We found three bodies in the Trishuli. They were in a condition where we couldn’t recognise them. There were insects on the bodies. Their heads had been crushed,” he said.

The bodies were recovered from behind his house. Jewellery was also found nearby.

Joshi believes the jewellery may have belonged to a neighbour who runs a jewellery shop.

But the hardest part of the search remains his daughter.

Seven-year-old Sumansingh was a Grade 1 student at Gyan Kunj School.

Joshi frequently breaks down when he remembers the things she used to say to him.

Whenever a helicopter flew overhead, she would point it out to him.

“Whenever a helicopter came from above, she used to say, ‘Dad, a helicopter has come,’” he recalled.

He also remembers the small gestures that once seemed ordinary.

“When I see other children scratching their fathers’ heads, I remember how my daughter used to scratch my head,” he said.

His daughter’s photograph is still the wallpaper on his mobile phone.

Every time he opens his phone, he sees her face.

And every time, the loss feels new.

Four members of his family remain missing, but Joshi has refused to stop helping others.

Even as he searches for his own loved ones, he has been trying to comfort other families caught in the disaster.

Drawing on his own experience, he urges them not to lose hope.

“My situation is like this, but I am enduring it and still continuing with the rescue work,” he said. “So please, don’t panic either.”

title.rendered: Electricity supply restored in 90% of Nuwakot after Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Electricity supply in Nuwakot, which was disrupted following the devastating Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa, has been restored in around 90 percent of the district.

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said electricity supply has resumed in most parts of Nuwakot.

According to the ministry, additional areas were brought back onto the grid after the Chapali–Devighat right circuit was charged.

Electricity supply has also become more reliable in most parts of the district, with voltage levels improving, the ministry said.

The areas where power has now been restored include Ward 6 of Bidur Municipality, around half of Ward 3 of Bidur, Wards 1, 5 and 6 of Tarkeshwar Municipality, Wards 2 and 3 of Tarkeshwar, and Ward 7 of Belkotgadhi Municipality.

An additional 31 transformers have also been charged, according to the ministry.

However, electricity supply remains to be restored in Ward 12 of Bidur Municipality, the remaining half of Ward 3, Kispang Rural Municipality, Ward 8 of Belkotgadhi Municipality and Ward 10 of Bidur Municipality.

The Energy Ministry said it has been carrying out repair and restoration work to resume electricity supply following damage to power infrastructure caused by the flood.
