title.rendered: The Bhotekoshi swept away Syabrubesi. Those left behind are still counting their losses

content.rendered:
Syabrubesi, September 3

Dawa Finjo Tamang is 91 and needs support to walk. Yet since the Bhotekoshi flood swept through Syabrubesi, he has been going from house to house in his neighbourhood, trying to comfort families who have lost loved ones.

When Onlinekhabar’s team reached the small village of Bharkhu in Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-5 on Tuesday afternoon, Dawa was returning from such a visit.

“A neighbour lost his son,” he said, drawing a long breath. “His daughter-in-law keeps crying, so I went to comfort her.”

The neighbour’s 24-year-old son, a driver, disappeared when the Bhotekoshi flood swept through Syabrubesi Bazaar. He had become the family’s main breadwinner. His mother has been unable to stop crying.

Dawa keeps going to comfort them, drawing on his age and experience. But he has his own grief to carry.

Standing beside his 86-year-old wife, Chenga Yangjen, he asked: “Should I walk around comforting others, or should I be comforting myself?”

A family built around a hotel

Dawa’s son, Furpasang, owned the Buddha Guest Hotel in Syabrubesi.

The hotel had grown over generations, built on ancestral property and four generations of family work. In recent years, Dawa’s grandson Tindu Chhiring had taken over its day-to-day operation.

Dawa was proud of him.

“My grandson knew so many people. Buses carrying pilgrims to Mansarovar used to fill the hotel,” he recalled. “People coming from Kathmandu would stay there by asking for my grandson by name.”

Travellers from China, India and other countries also stayed at the hotel.

Furpasang and Tindu would tell Dawa and Chenga to stay at the hotel and rest. With two great-grandchildren growing up around them, the couple enjoyed spending their later years in Syabrubesi.

“My son had the biggest hotel,” Dawa said. “Last year, my daughter-in-law was honoured as the owner of the number one hotel in all of Rasuwa.”

Dawa estimated that the hotel was worth at least Rs 25 crore.

For the couple, the journey from their ancestral home in the steep village of Bharkhu to a multimillion-rupee hotel business in Syabrubesi had been a source of immense pride.

Then age began to catch up with Dawa.

His eyesight deteriorated, and Furpasang took him to Kathmandu for treatment. After his latest treatment, Dawa and Chenga returned to Syabrubesi on August 21.

But a relative had died in Bharkhu, and instead of staying at the hotel, the couple decided to return to their ancestral home to offer their condolences. Furpasang himself accompanied his parents to Bharkhu.

Less than a week later, on August 26, the unimaginable happened.

The Bhotekoshi surged. Syabrubesi Bazaar was swept away.

“It sounded like a helicopter,” Chenga recalled. “When I came outside and looked, I saw the sky filled with clouds. It had taken everything.”

By the time they saw Syabrubesi again, the market was gone.

As Chenga recalled the family they had left behind, there was little chance of holding back her tears.

Dawa listed them one by one: his son Furpasang, daughter-in-law Chetin, grandson Tintu Chhiring, granddaughter-in-law Yangji, great-grandson Kalsang and a worker.

For four or five days, the couple held on to the hope that they might have been stranded somewhere in the forest. As the days passed, that hope began to fade.

“Furpa had said he would come to get us after a week,” Chenga said.

Young people from the village later showed the couple photographs of Syabrubesi, after the flood.

“The tall hotel is not there anymore,” Chenga said, giving up hope. “How could they have survived?”

The decision to stay in Bharkhu for a week had saved Dawa and Chenga. But surviving while losing three generations of their family has brought its own unbearable grief.

Their two sons, one living in Britain and the other in Australia, are preparing to return to Nepal. The couple has not yet been able to tell their youngest great-grandchild, who studies in Kathmandu, what has happened.

‘This time, it was a ghambal’

Dawa’s ancestors have lived in Bharkhu for 15 generations. He cannot remember the Bhotekoshi ever rising with such force.

“Our ancestors came here from Nuwakot 15 generations ago,” he said. “If a disaster like this had happened before, we would have left this place long ago.”

He remembers a major flood in 2018 and another last year. Neither, he said, swept away Syabrubesi.

His ancestors had always warned of the possibility of a flood powerful enough to carry away bridges, villages and roads if a glacial lake burst.

“I had heard that a ghambal — a flood caused by a glacial lake outburst — can pass over bridges,” he said. “That is what happened this time.”

The flood has touched almost every family in small Bharkhu.

Dawa’s neighbours, Mewang Tamang and Gangdhram Lhamo, have also lost sons.

“In this small village of Bharke alone, 35 people are missing,” Mewang said.

The figure was compiled by members of the Tamang community in Bharkhu. Unable to go out themselves to search, they have been counting relatives who have not made contact as missing.

“Where can we go to search? How can we go?” Mewang said. “Even when we hear the Bhotekoshi roaring, people in their homes are frightened.”

When the Onlinekhabar team left Mewang’s house, the family was still staring silently towards the river.

A village divided by the flood

The grief of Dawa, Mewang and Gangdhram is shared across Syabrubesi.

Dawa Mingmar Tamang, the ward chairperson of Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-5, is missing. Pratima Tamang, vice-chairperson of Gosainkunda Rural Municipality and a local resident of Syabrubesi, is also missing.

No reliable count has yet been established of how many people are missing, how many have been found alive and how many have been found dead. Families have been keeping their own lists of missing relatives.

“Thankfully, I survived, but all my relatives are missing,” Tharjen Dolmo Tamang said through tears.

An administrative assistant at the Chilime Hydropower Project, Tharjen had been preparing to leave for work when the flood struck.

“I managed to escape. My house was buried in mud. I cannot even bear to remember that day,” she said. “Six of my colleagues are trapped inside the powerhouse.”

Despite repeated efforts by the Nepal Army and the Nepal Electricity Authority, those trapped inside the powerhouse have not yet been rescued.

“Everyone from the office and from my family is missing,” she said. “We watched our settlement and our market disappear before our eyes.”

Where the market once stood, there is now only a riverbed. Tharjen’s sister’s son, her brother-in-law and her brother-in-law’s husband are also buried in Syabrubesi.

“I have lost hope now. So many days have passed,” she said.

According to Gosainkunda Rural Municipality, Syabrubesi has a population of 2,462, including around 450 elderly people. There is still no preliminary estimate of how many of them survived. Thats not all, the flood has also physically split Syabrubesi into four sections.

Crossing the Bhotekoshi is no longer possible. The flood also swept away the bridge over Bharkhu Khola at Dobhan, dividing the settlement further. People cannot simply walk from one part of the village to another.

Telephone networks, roads and bridges have all been severed, leaving even survivors unable to meet relatives who may still be alive.

“Even if there were a suspension bridge, a rough road or an environment where phones could connect, the survivors would at least be able to breathe a little easier,” Mewang said.

“We are in disbelief. We had never in our wildest dreams imagined that such a disaster could strike Syabrubesi”.

title.rendered: Trishuli-3A cable duct cleared of 20,000 cubic metres of debris after Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Efforts to clear the entrance to the 160-metre-long cable duct tunnel of the Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project have been intensified following the devastating Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa on August 26.

More than two dozen large boulders have so far been blasted away from the portal area as engineers and rescue teams work to remove mud, rocks and other debris accumulated after the flood, according to engineer Udayaraj Neupane, who is involved in the search and rescue operation.

Two excavators have been operating regularly since August 29. In five days, they have removed around 20,000 cubic metres of mud, sand, rocks, concrete slabs, beams, pillars and boulders as large as houses, Neupane said.

The clearance operation is continuing around the clock, with breakers and controlled explosives being used wherever necessary.

Neupane said workers have so far cleared a roughly 50-metre stretch of the portal area, reaching about 2.5 metres below the top face, or crown, of the tunnel.

The Trishuli-3A cable duct is 5.5 metres high. Work to construct an access and drainage passage through the remaining roughly three metres of debris must be completed before workers can begin clearing the mud accumulated inside the tunnel, he said.

Initial signs suggest no water has accumulated inside tunnel

Preliminary observations indicate that the section of the tunnel extending about one metre inward from the entrance is completely filled with mud.

However, water is flowing out of the tunnel at a rate of around two litres per second, with no signs of pressure, Neupane said.

This suggests that water has not accumulated inside the tunnel. At the outer portal, workers have found a gate slab, two large tree trunks and large boulders obstructing the entrance.

Based on the initial assessment, large rocks may not have entered the tunnel, apart from water and mud, Neupane said. The actual condition of the tunnel’s interior, however, has yet to be fully confirmed.

Tunnel structure believed to be intact

The 160-metre-long Trishuli-3A cable duct has a bend at around the 60-metre mark. The tunnel also rises towards the powerhouse, which has led engineers to make a preliminary assessment that its inner section is likely to be in normal and safe condition.

However, this can only be confirmed once the debris blocking the entrance is removed and the tunnel can be properly inspected, Neupane said.

The site has no road access, meaning machinery and materials needed to repair equipment have to be transported by helicopter.

This has caused some delays in bringing necessary materials to the site, but the overall rescue and debris-clearing operation is continuing without interruption, Neupane said.

title.rendered: ‘If the government can’t find him, let me’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

Rain falls steadily over the grounds of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital. People hurry in and out, some looking for shelter, others speaking urgently into their phones.

But there is another sound beneath the rain — a silence that seems to settle over the crowd and refuse to leave.

Along the hospital walls are dozens of photographs. They are faces of sons and daughters, husbands and wives, brothers and sisters, parents and children.

The people who put them there never imagined they would one day have to search for their loved ones this way. They do not know where those smiling faces are now, or even whether they are still alive.

Sabina KC stands in front of the photographs, scanning them one by one.

Her eyes linger on each face, moving from one photograph to the next, as though she might suddenly hear a familiar voice calling her name.

It has been eight days since her husband, Sohit BK, disappeared. Her 23-year-old brother-in-law, Amar BK, and their uncle, Narayan BK, are missing too. Three members of the same family have vanished.

And Sabina has only one thing left to hold on to: the possibility that they are still alive.

That is why she is here, looking at photographs on a hospital wall, searching for the faces she knows.

There is little family support around her now. Her mother-in-law is abroad. So is the wife of her missing brother-in-law. Sabina is left to wait, worry and search for answers herself.

Three days after Sohit disappeared without a word, she left her infant with a neighbour and came looking for him. She has another child, five years old, who suffers from seizures and sometimes loses consciousness. That child, too, is being cared for by a neighbour while Sabina moves from one place to another trying to find out what happened to her husband.

As she speaks, her eyes fill with tears. Her fingers tremble. She looks back at the photographs. Then towards the hospital entrance as an ambulance pulls in.

She has been doing this for days — looking, waiting, asking.

‘My husband and uncle ran towards the forest’

The BK family is originally from Surkhet. They had gone to Syabrubesi for work, while Sabina and Sohit lived with their family in a rented room in Imadol. Sohit worked as a driver, transporting goods from China.

On August 26, at around 6 am, Sohit and his uncle Narayan left together. They had barely reached Ronga when the flood came.

Three other people nearby began running for their lives.

One of them survived and eventually reached the area above Syabrubesi. He later told Sabina that he had seen Sohit and Narayan running towards the forest as the flood approached.

“Your husband and uncle ran towards the forest,” he told her. “I saw them running as the flood was coming.”

Those few words have become the foundation of Sabina’s hope.

She keeps wondering what might have happened after they disappeared from sight.

Are they somewhere in that forest? Are they hungry? Are they thirsty? Are they still waiting to be found?

Her brother-in-law Amar had been travelling from Timure in a vehicle. While coming from the Tatopani hill area, he made his final phone call to an elder brother.

“I have reached the checkpoint,” he said.

That was the last anyone heard from him.

‘They won’t let us go’

The account that Sohit and Narayan ran towards the forest has given Sabina a reason to believe they may still be alive. It has also left her frustrated by what she sees as the limits of the search.

She says search teams and helicopters have reached the tunnel and Timure, but that the forest where her husband and uncle are believed to have fled has not been searched.

“The forest where my husband Sohit and Narayan are said to have run has not been searched,” she says. “Neither drones nor helicopters have reached there. The family has not been allowed to go and search either. There has to be a search.”

Her relatives have tried to arrange a helicopter after speaking with the Army. Nothing has come of it. The family was also told that one of them would be taken there by helicopter. That did not happen either.

Sabina has asked to go herself. But she says she has been told she cannot.

“Even when I say I will go myself, whether they are dead or alive, they say I am not allowed to go,” she says.

She returns again and again to the same point.

“There has to be a search,” she says. “Even someone who is alive can die because of the government’s negligence.”

For Sabina, eight days of uncertainty have become a battle against time. She believes the search in the upper reaches has not been urgent enough and fears that every day without a proper search could reduce the chances of finding those who may still be alive.

A photograph on the wall, but no single list to follow

The photographs at Teaching Hospital have only made her more restless.

Her sisters came on Sunday and put up the photographs of the missing family members.

By then, Sabina had already spent days waiting for news.

“What is the point of staying in the room and crying all day?” she says. “I would rather search for my husband myself.”

She has called the police toll-free number, 100. She has used her TikTok account to circulate information about the disappearance. She has filed a missing-person report at the Imadol police post and contacted emergency numbers.

But another part of the process has left her frustrated: she says she has had to provide the same information repeatedly.

“Wherever I go, they write down the name again,” she says.

For her, the problem is simple. Once the name of a missing person is registered, it should be available to everyone involved in the search.

“Once it is registered, the name should be in the system,” she says. “We should not have to go somewhere else and register the same name again.”

For families waiting for missing loved ones, however, repeating a name is far more than an administrative inconvenience. It means telling the story of the disappearance all over again, taking out the photograph once more and hearing yet again that the person they are searching for has not been found. With every repetition comes the painful possibility that hope may slowly give way to despair.

That is why Sabina wants a properly managed central list of missing people—one that can be accessed and updated by all the agencies involved in the search.

Still, her most urgent demand is not about paperwork. It is about going into the places where she believes her husband and uncle may still be waiting.

“The government has to go into the forests and gorges in the upper areas,” she says. “It is not enough to search only where vehicles can reach or where there are tunnels. The government has to reach everywhere.”

She folds her hands as she makes one final appeal.

“I hope this reaches the government. They have to reach there, even if it means sending drones or helicopters. If the government cannot go, let the family go.”

Then comes the sentence that sums up the desperation of the past eight days:

“Otherwise, I will go myself to search for my husband.”

title.rendered: Langtang Lirung glacier was moving unusually fast before Bhotekoshi flood, Chinese study finds

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 3

A glacier on the northern face of Langtang Lirung had been moving at an unusually high rate in recent years, according to a preliminary study by a Chinese research institute.

The Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research under the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing found that the upper and middle sections of the glacier had moved relatively rapidly over the past two years.

Researchers analysed data from Sentinel-2 satellites and detected unusual movement in the glacier, along with changes in the slope. Their analysis suggests that cracks may have developed in the ice and that sections of the slope may have become increasingly unstable.

The findings, however, are preliminary. The researchers have not concluded that the glacier’s movement was a definite warning sign of the disaster.

‘There was activity before the landslide’

The study identified unusual signals at around 6:04am, 6:50am and between 8:15am and 8:19am Nepal time. Researchers classified these as seismic signals.

Some of the signals corresponded with the timing of landslide and dust activity reported by people in the area.

Rather than a single, sudden landslide, the researchers suggest that smaller-scale ice-rock movements may have begun before the major event.

But they have cautioned that there is not enough evidence to describe the signals as a “definite precursor” to the disaster.

The Chinese Academy of Sciences has also concluded that last week’s event cannot be explained simply as a conventional landslide or avalanche.

Researchers say an ice-rock avalanche that fell from Langtang Lirung, at an elevation of around 5,200 metres, caused much greater destruction further downstream than at the initial impact site.

The disaster grew as it moved downstream

The area where the glacier and rock fell is around 22 kilometres from Rasuwagadhi and about 3,400 metres higher in elevation, according to the study.

Researchers say the initial mass of ice and rock gathered river water, soil, sediment and other loose material as it moved downstream, increasing both its volume and destructive power.

By the time it travelled around 22 kilometres, the size and force of the flood had increased substantially.

The researchers say the key question is therefore not simply how large the initial avalanche was, but how much additional material it picked up on its way to Rasuwagadhi.

“The amount of ice and rock that initially fell was not the main factor determining the final scale of the disaster,” the report says. “The disaster grew progressively as soil, sediment, river water and unstable material from the riverbanks were incorporated along the way.”

The Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research is studying how an ice-rock avalanche in the high Himalayan region transformed into a destructive flood. Researchers used satellite imagery, seismic data and weather information in their analysis.

‘It was not caused by heavy rain’

The study found no evidence that rainfall triggered the ice-rock avalanche.

Researchers said rainfall in the area had been limited during the 72 hours before the event, with only 8.8 millimetres recorded during that period.

They therefore found no evidence to support the conclusion that heavy rainfall immediately before the disaster had triggered the avalanche.

At the same time, temperature data showed that the area had experienced warmer-than-average conditions.

The average temperature during the winter of 2026 was 0.38 degrees Celsius higher than the average, while the increase reached 0.58 degrees Celsius during the summer.

The study identifies climate change, long-term warming and glacier instability as important background factors. However, it does not conclude that climate change was the direct cause of the disaster.

Instead, researchers raise a question for further study: whether long-term warming is gradually destabilising the ice-rock system in the Langtang region.

Multiple factors may have triggered the avalanche

Researchers have identified six possible processes that may have contributed to the event and say there is not enough evidence to attribute it to a single cause.

Among the factors they identified are rapid glacier movement, cracks developing within the ice and meltwater entering those cracks.

They also point to weakening permafrost — permanently frozen ground — and the possibility of ice and rock falling from the upper slopes.

As temperatures rise, repeated cycles of freezing and thawing may have expanded cracks in the rock, the study suggests. Researchers also say ice and rock weakened by an earthquake a decade ago may have contributed to the collapse.

The study describes the disaster as a chain of processes rather than the result of one isolated trigger.

Above Rasuwagadhi, the Lhende River begins after the confluence of the Purepu Glacier and Chhochen Khola. The ice-rock mass that fell from an elevation of around 5,200 metres travelled about eight kilometres before striking the upper section of the Lhende River.

The avalanche then broke apart and transformed into a flood that travelled another 13 to 14 kilometres to Rasuwagadhi, where the Lhende and Kerung rivers meet.

Part of the powerful flow then entered another small valley along the Kerung River, around two to three kilometres upstream.

Even at that point, researchers found, the debris-laden flood still carried substantial energy and remained highly mobile.

title.rendered: Buddha Air freezes fares as Rasuwa disaster disrupts road travel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The disruption of major highways following the devastating floods in Rasuwa has pushed more travellers towards air travel, increasing pressure on domestic airlines.

With long-distance road travel disrupted and alternatives limited, airlines have been struggling to accommodate the surge in passengers.

Buddha Air, Nepal’s largest domestic airline by market share, fleet size and passenger volume, has announced that it will not increase airfares until road transportation returns to normal.

The airline currently carries more than 10,000 passengers a day. It says both passenger numbers and flight frequency have risen sharply since the Bhotekoshi floods.

“Road transportation has not been able to return to normal because of the impact of the Rasuwa floods,” Buddha Air Executive Chairman Birendra Bahadur Basnet told Onlinekhabar. “We will not increase airfares until the highways are accessible again. We will continue taking passengers to their destinations at the current fares.”

Basnet said the decision to maintain minimum fares would mean the airline is likely to incur losses of more than Rs 600 million in the current fiscal year.

 “When the country itself is facing a disaster, we have taken this decision as our contribution. Once things return to normal, we can make profits next year. This year, we will contribute to the country,” Basnet said.

The floods and landslides have disrupted the Krishnabhir section of the Prithvi Highway, a major road link connecting Kathmandu with other parts of the country. The alternative Tribhuvan Highway and Kanti Lokpath have also come under increased pressure.

“With the roads disrupted by a natural disaster, we are in a situation where we have to create an air bridge,” Basnet said. “No matter how much loss we incur in these difficult circumstances, our conscience does not allow us to raise fares.”

Fares to remain low during Dashain and Tihar

Domestic airlines often face criticism for raising fares during Dashain and Tihar, when demand for flights out of Kathmandu surges.

Buddha Air says it will maintain its minimum fares during this year’s festivals as well.

Basnet estimates that road transportation could take at least six months to return to normal.

“Until then, we will operate at the minimum fares and continue increasing the number of flights,” he said.

The airline has also extended its operating hours following the disaster, with its final flights now operating as late as 11pm.

Free transport of relief supplies

Buddha Air is also transporting relief supplies for people affected by the Bhotekoshi floods free of charge.

The airline says it transported 6,420 kilograms of relief materials to different destinations on Wednesday alone.

This included supplies bound for Bhadrapur, Bharatpur, Surkhet, Dhangadhi, Biratnagar, Bhairahawa and Simara.

Buddha Air currently operates 15 ATR 72-500 aircraft and one ATR 72-600, each with a capacity of 72 passengers. It operates around six dozen flights a day.

Meanwhile, aviation fuel prices have risen sharply. According to Buddha Air, the price increased 96 percent between February and August 2026, from $127 per litre to $249 per litre.

Despite the rise in fuel costs, the airline says it will maintain minimum fares while road connections remain disrupted.

On the Kathmandu-Bhairahawa route, fares rose from Rs5,700 in February to Rs6,500 in August, an increase of 14 percent.

title.rendered: CIAA files corruption case against five, including Rupaandehi land revenue chief

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) has filed a corruption case against five people, including Kumar Acharya, chief of the Land Revenue Office in Rupaandehi, for allegedly registering land belonging to a temple in an individual’s name.

The anti-graft body has sought a recovery of Rs453 million as damages from the accused, alleging that land subject to a landholding ceiling had been donated to the temple but was later registered in a private individual’s name.

The CIAA said the land had also been shown as belonging to the temple in the 2026 land survey.

The case has been filed against Acharya, who was the chief land revenue officer at the time, along with non-gazetted first-class officer (nayab subba) Laxman Neupane, Ajit Kumar Sahani, non-gazetted second-class employee (kharidar) Megh Bahadur Bhujel Magar, and landowner Parwatakant Mishra.

Acharya is a land revenue official who has repeatedly been embroiled in controversy.

While serving at the Bhaktapur Land Revenue Office, he faced allegations of taking a Rs2.4 million bribe. He was also involved in an attempt to register land belonging to the Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa in a private individual’s name.

‘Airport land’ controversy

Acharya was the chief land revenue officer at the Rupaandehi Land Revenue Office when he decided to register part of the land inside the Gautam Buddha International Airport, also known as Bhairahawa International Airport, in an individual’s name.

The land had already been acquired by the government.

Acharya’s decision was based on what was alleged to be a misinterpretation of a court ruling. He had argued that the court had issued a mandamus order directing the land to be registered in the individual’s name.

However, the Butwal bench of the Tulsipur High Court had actually ordered the authorities to examine the relevant matters and make an appropriate decision regarding the land registration.

In October 2023, while Acharya was serving as chief land revenue officer, the Land Revenue Office decided to register 4 bighas and 16 katthas of land in an individual’s name. The land was located inside the airport premises.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar at the time, Acharya claimed that he had made the decision only regarding 10 katthas of land and that decisions concerning the remaining land had already been made before he assumed office.

“I registered the land in the name of the person to whom it belonged,” he had said.

The controversial decision was halted after the District Administration Office, Rupaandehi, intervened following reports about the Land Revenue Office’s actions.

The administration sought an explanation from the Land Revenue Office, after which the further process was stopped.

The District Administration Office also investigated the decision, while the CIAA launched its own investigation into the matter.

The anti-graft body has now filed a corruption case in connection with that same incident.

title.rendered: Seven months pregnant, flood survivor has lost her home, livelihood and access to healthcare

content.rendered:
Bidur, September 2

Srijana Nagarkoti, 27, is seven months pregnant. Since the Bhotekoshi flood swept through her home, she has been living in a cold classroom at a school in Nuwakot, unsure of where she will live or how she will manage when her delivery approaches.

Srijana was at home when the flood struck. After receiving information about the rising water, people began fleeing. There was panic and chaos as the flood reached the settlement.

She ran for her life but fell while trying to escape.

“I fell the other day, and I haven’t felt the baby move since,” she said.

Srijana was due for her regular pregnancy check-up, but displacement has made it difficult for her to reach a hospital.

She is now staying at Bhairum Secondary School in Bidur Municipality-8, where families displaced by the flood have been taking shelter.

The school’s classrooms are filled with displaced families. Those who cannot find space inside are sleeping on the verandas outside.

Srijana says the cold conditions have made life particularly difficult.

“I had a house in Trishuli Bazaar, but the flood swept it away. There is nothing left. I am staying in a cold classroom. The cold in the room has made things even more difficult for the baby in my womb,” she said.

The family has lost more than its home.

Srijana and her husband ran a meat shop and a pig farm. Their farm, located below Macha Pokhari, had around 200 pigs. The flood swept them all away.

The couple also lost the money and valuables they had at home. Srijana said she had no time to retrieve them while fleeing.

“There was some money and gold. Everything was swept away. Now, I only have what I am wearing,” she said.

The family of three — Srijana, her husband and their daughter — is now dependent on the relief being provided at the school.

Displaced families have been receiving communal meals, but Srijana says the arrangement does not adequately address the needs of vulnerable people.

“There is no nutritious food. We have to stand in line to eat. I haven’t been able to go to the hospital. We are having a very difficult time,” she said.

Pregnant women, children and elderly people at the shelter face additional difficulties, she said. The temporary accommodation also lacks the comfort and basic amenities of a home, with displaced families sleeping in cold classrooms and relying on relief supplies.

For Srijana, the loss of her livelihood has compounded the uncertainty.

“Now we have problems with even food and shelter,” she said.

Her delivery date is approaching, but she has little left to fall back on. The money she had set aside for medical expenses was also swept away in the flood.

“My delivery date is getting closer. I have no idea where I will live or what I will do,” she said.

title.rendered: 133 bodies recovered from areas affected by Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Dhuche, September 2

The bodies of 133 people who died in the Bhotekoshi flood have been recovered from different areas of Rasuwa.

According to Deputy Superintendent of Police Ashok Thapa, 104 bodies were recovered from the Timure area, 18 from Syafrubesi and Ronga, and 11 from the Betrabati area.

Thapa said efforts are underway to airlift all the bodies to Bidur in Nuwakot by helicopter as they have started decomposing.

Meanwhile, rescue efforts have been hampered at the 111-MW Rasuwa Gadhi Hydropower Project, where people remain trapped.

According to Brigadier General Prajjwal Rana, commander of the Nepal Army’s No. 6 Brigade, it is currently not possible to open the tunnel because it is filled with mud.

The Nepal Army said rescue efforts are continuing for people trapped at the 20-MW Chilime Hydropower Project in Syafrubesi.

title.rendered: Nepal to lead South Asian task force on disaster-resilient electricity regulation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

A regional technical task force involving South Asian countries has been formed to study the risks natural disasters pose to electricity generation, transmission and cross-border power trade.

Nepal’s Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) will lead the task force, according to the commission.

The decision to form the regional technical group for technical studies and research on disaster-resilient electricity regulation was taken at meetings of the executive committee and board of directors of the South Asian Forum for Infrastructure Regulation (SAFIR).

The meetings were held in Manesar, Haryana, India, on Bhadra 14 and 15. The decision also provides for the active participation of regulatory bodies from India, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

The need for a regional study on disaster risk management in the electricity sector has become more apparent after the Bhote Koshi flood caused extensive damage to hydropower projects, transmission systems and other electricity infrastructure.

According to the ERC, a major natural disaster in a river basin does not affect only a single project or licensed entity. Its impact can extend directly or indirectly to electricity generation and supply, the stability of transmission systems, electricity trading, the financial obligations of projects and cross-border power flows.

The new task force will study regulatory standards to be adopted during natural disasters, risk-sharing mechanisms and procedures for ensuring the continuity of cross-border electricity trade even during disasters.

The commission said the study is expected to help develop a common regional regulatory framework for South Asian countries.

The Bhotekoshi flood has also shown that natural disasters cannot be treated merely as isolated problems affecting an individual project or company, the commission said.

With the interdependence between hydropower projects, transmission systems and electricity trade increasing, the commission said disaster risks need to be addressed from a regional and system-wide perspective.

title.rendered: Speaker urges government to ensure safety of women and children

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal (DP) has delivered a special address at a meeting of the House of Representatives, drawing the government’s attention to the need to ensure the safety and protection of women and children affected by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods.

The floods, which struck on August 26, caused extensive human and physical losses in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Tanahun and Chitwan districts.

Addressing the House on the disaster, Speaker Aryal urged the government to ensure the safety of women and children.

“I draw the serious attention of the government and concerned agencies to ensuring the safety and protection of women and children, as well as easy access to essential services, while remaining sensitive to the mental health and psychosocial well-being of citizens affected by the disaster,” Aryal said. Aryal recalled that the impacts of climate change have been a subject of continuous discussion for the past several decades.

“Temperatures are rising in the Himalayan region due to climate change, while glaciers and glacial lakes are undergoing changes,” he said. “The risk of avalanches is increasing, and incidents of unusual rainfall are also becoming more frequent.” He noted that Rasuwa had experienced several small and large-scale disasters in previous years as well.

Aryal said Nepal needs to firmly establish its concerns at the international level regarding national security challenges created by climate change. “Therefore, Nepal needs to raise its voice more clearly and strongly in the international debate on loss and damage caused by climate change,” he said. “I also draw the attention of the Government of Nepal to this issue.”

The Rasuwa disaster has also taught the country another important lesson, Aryal said. “We must now build a culture of preparedness, rather than focusing solely on post-disaster management,” he said. “Regular study and monitoring of glacial lakes and glaciers must be given priority.”

The Speaker also directed the government to maintain solidarity during this period of national mourning and mobilise all three tiers of government, political parties, civil society and all state mechanisms for search and rescue operations, the rehabilitation of displaced people and proper treatment of the injured.

Aryal said Nepal is highly vulnerable to both natural and human-induced disasters. “Nepal’s geographical diversity, fragile geological structure, unplanned and risky development, weak infrastructure, limited resources and climate change have caused various types of disasters to recur frequently,” he said.

He also noted that the government had mobilised security forces for rescue and relief operations for people affected by the latest disaster. On behalf of the House of Representatives, Aryal expressed gratitude to the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force Nepal, government agencies, provincial and local governments, health workers, the Red Cross, volunteers, journalists, local communities and rescue workers involved in search, rescue, treatment, relief and humanitarian services.

He also expressed appreciation for the technical personnel, relief assistance, support and solidarity provided by friendly countries and the international community.

title.rendered: What did the government do on the day of the Bhotekoshi flood?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

A massive flood entered the Trishuli River through the Bhotekoshi in Rasuwa on August 26, causing widespread loss of life and property along the riverbanks.

The flood swept away homes, damaged infrastructure and displaced families in several settlements. As the disaster unfolded, the government says it began a series of measures ranging from public warnings and emergency meetings to helicopter deployment, rescue operations and relief distribution.

Prime Minister Balen Shah presented the government’s response to the House of Representatives, providing a timeline of what authorities did from the time the first report of the flood was received.

The first information about the flood reached the government at 8:45 am. Fifteen minutes later, local administrations were instructed to urge residents in areas along the river to move to safer locations.

At 9:15 am, an emergency meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council was called, with a decision to begin rescue operations in the affected areas. Warning messages were then sent to mobile phone users through telecommunications companies.

The Nepal Army deployed a helicopter for rescue operations at 9:45 am, while private helicopters were kept on standby. The Army’s Monsoon Command Post also held an emergency meeting and decided to mobilise search-and-rescue teams and resources.

By 10:30 am, search-and-rescue and emergency response teams had been placed on standby at Tribhuvan International Airport. Security personnel from Kathmandu and other districts were also mobilised for search, rescue and relief operations.

At 11 am, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council met at the Prime Minister’s Office. According to Shah, security chiefs were instructed to prioritise search, rescue and medical treatment, while additional helicopters and drone teams were ordered to be mobilised.

The Cabinet held an emergency meeting at 12:30 pm, deciding to intensify search, rescue and medical treatment. It also declared 15 affected local units disaster crisis-hit areas for three months.

The Cabinet decided to provide immediate financial assistance to families of those killed and to rescue injured and stranded people using Army and private-sector helicopters.

The government then consulted federal lawmakers from the affected areas and contacted local representatives by telephone to gather information. At 3 pm, a team led by the Information and Communications Minister left for the affected areas by road.

Later that evening, at 7:40 pm, the government publicly appealed for donations to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund and the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.

By midnight, eight trucks carrying relief materials had been sent towards the affected areas. The government also said free voice, data and SMS services had been arranged for mobile phone users in the affected areas.

title.rendered: Dataram missed the bus while fetching water, and it saved his life

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 2

Seventy-five-year-old Dataram Devkota was among those scheduled to travel from Palungtar to Gosainkunda on a pilgrimage on August 26. His participation had been confirmed only the previous day.

Devkota had been told that the pilgrims would gather at 4 am and leave at 5 am. He spent the night packing his belongings and did not finish until around 1 am.

He had barely fallen asleep when he heard commotion outside. He stepped onto the veranda and saw that the bus had already arrived. “By the time I looked at the clock, it was already 3 am. I shouted, asking why they were leaving so early,” Devkota recalled. “I tried to stop the vehicle when it reached my house, but it did not stop. It drove straight to Mahadevatar and stopped there.”

He had told the people on the bus from the veranda that he would be joining them and asked them to wait. But the bus moved on without him. “The bus stopped at Mahadevatar for a while. I came out carrying my bags,” Devkota said. But just as he was about to leave, he suddenly remembered that he needed water. “I went into the kitchen to get a bottle of water. It took me some time to find it,” he said. “When I came back outside, the bus was no longer at Mahadevatar. It had already left.”

That brief detour to the kitchen to fetch a bottle of water meant Devkota missed the bus that was supposed to take him to Gosainkunda. That coincidence may have saved his life. “After missing the bus, I put all my belongings back inside the house and rested for a while. I kept regretting that I had missed the chance to go to Gosainkunda,” he said.

But after having breakfast that morning, panic suddenly spread through the village. “News came that the bus that had left without me that morning had been swept away,” Devkota said. “Until then, I had been feeling disappointed. After hearing that, I thought, ‘Thank God, I survived.’”

Devkota now feels that he was saved by divine intervention. “I feel that God blocked my way to save me,” he said. His son and daughter-in-law had also planned to travel to Gosainkunda that day, but they did not go either, he said.

Although Devkota survived by what he considers a stroke of luck, he remains devastated that 32 people from his village were swept away by the flood. The village of Naukhor is also mourning those who were carried away with the same bus.

title.rendered: Opposition slams government over Rasuwa flood response

content.rendered:
During Wednesday’s House of Representatives session, opposition parties sharply criticised the government’s handling of the Rasuwa flood disaster, even as search and rescue operations continued for thousands of citizens who remained uncontactable.

Congress: Government chased publicity, not rescue

Nepali Congress parliamentary party leader Bhishma Raj Angdembe accused the government of getting “tangled up in social media” instead of reaching at-risk communities in time.

“After hearing the cries of victims’ families waiting for site visits and rescue, I am compelled to say in this House today, the government got caught up in social media, and failed to reach the at-risk community in time,” he said. “It focused more on managing publicity than saving lives. There was more happening on Facebook than in the field.”

Angdembe contrasted this with the 2015 earthquake response, when international rescue teams from 34 countries arrived within 12 hours. He accused the current government of failing to coordinate with local governments, keeping hydropower project staff and the private sector out of affected areas, ignoring engineers and technical experts, and neither acting itself nor letting others act.

He was especially critical of the delayed tunnel rescue.

“After seven days had passed, the government raised its hands and said, ‘ Search inside the tunnel yourselves.’ What kind of sensitivity and responsibility is this? Isn’t this insensitivity, caused by delay, turning deaths inside that tunnel into something like killings? “

Angdembe also said families searching for missing relatives had faced verbal abuse and threats, and urged the government to make saving lives, searching for the missing, delivering relief, securing the displaced, and beginning rehabilitation and reconstruction its sole priorities.

“This is not a time to seek political points. It is a time for the nation to unite and save citizens’ lives,” he said.

3,916 people still uncontactable across 62 districts

In a separate address to the same House session, Angdembe called the delay in rescuing civilians trapped inside the tunnel “inhumane and serious.”

He informed lawmakers that 3,916 people across 62 districts remain out of contact, warning the number could still rise. He said that from the outset, rescue efforts should have brought together government agencies, the private sector, and, where necessary, international technology and expert teams.

Prachanda: Army mobilised, but not the people

Meanwhile, opposition Nepali Communist Party coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda) told the House that a real solution to the crisis remains impossible without mobilising ordinary citizens alongside the army.

“The army was mobilised, but the people were not,” Prachanda said, adding that he had repeatedly urged the government to bring in public participation and align federal, provincial and local governments, a call he said he had also made directly to ministers and ruling party leaders.

Despite his criticism, Prachanda praised the Nepal Army’s role in the disaster zone, noting the Prime Minister and ministers had been visibly active on the ground and that soldiers had taken major risks in rescue and relief work.

“We are thankful to them,” he said.

Prachanda questions PM’s style

In a separate, pointed remark, Prachanda questioned Prime Minister Balen Shah’s conduct in the House, saying the PM had failed to win the trust of all lawmakers, including members of his own side.

“He comes and leaves without looking at anyone’s face; what kind of attitude is this?” Prachanda asked.

He said Balen had been handed a major opportunity that should not be squandered, and that the country needed presence and leadership, not lengthy speeches or social media posts.

“You may have won the election through social media posts, but this crisis will not be solved that way,” Prachanda said. With the nation in crisis, he stressed that unity was the Prime Minister’s responsibility, and warned that if he failed to earn everyone’s trust, “time may not wait for him either.”

UML demands task forces for foreign aid and reconstruction

Separately, CPN-UML parliamentary party leader Ram Bahadur Thapa (Badal) called for the formation of two special task forces, one led by the Foreign Minister to coordinate international assistance and compensation, and another led by the Finance Minister to oversee reconstruction.

He also urged the Prime Minister to make a “qualitative change” in what he called a one-man style of governance, and to keep Parliament continuously updated on the government’s plans.

Thapa additionally proposed an immediate mechanism bringing together political parties, civil society and experts to tackle the ongoing crisis, along with a special parliamentary committee, led by the Speaker, to monitor, alert and support the government.

“To address the climate-driven crisis, the government must immediately move forward with a second edition of the Sagarmatha Dialogue to build international solidarity and strategy,” Thapa said.

title.rendered: UML calls for special task forces for disaster reconstruction, international coordination

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

CPN-UML parliamentary party leader Ram Bahadur Thapa has called on the government to form special task forces to coordinate international assistance and compensation and lead reconstruction efforts following the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26.

Speaking at the House of Representatives meeting on Wednesday, Thapa said the government should form a special task force under the leadership of the foreign minister to coordinate international support, compensation and other assistance related to the disaster.

He also called for a separate task force led by the finance minister to oversee reconstruction.

Thapa urged Prime Minister Balen Shah to make a qualitative change in what he described as his unilateral style of governance and to keep Parliament regularly informed about the government’s plans.

He also suggested that the government immediately initiate the formation of a mechanism bringing together political parties, civil society and experts to respond to the current crisis.

Thapa called for the formation of a special parliamentary committee under the initiative of the Speaker to monitor the government, caution it when necessary and provide support in addressing the crisis.

“To confront the crisis caused by climate change, the government should immediately move ahead with the second edition of the Sagarmatha Sambaad to build international solidarity and formulate a strategy,” Thapa said.

title.rendered: House of Representatives passes special resolution on Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The House of Representatives has unanimously passed a special resolution concerning the Rasuwa floods.

At Wednesday’s meeting of the House, Speaker DP Aryal presented the special resolution, which was unanimously endorsed by the lawmakers.

A devastating flood struck the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26. The disaster affected Timure, Syafrubesi and Betrabati in Rasuwa, Trishuli Bazaar and Devighat in Nuwakot, as well as settlements along the Trishuli River in Dhading, Chitwan and Gorkha districts.

A total of 1,114 bodies of people who had gone missing in the floods have been recovered.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the recovered bodies include 41 from Rasuwa, 155 from Nuwakot, 59 from Dhading, 348 from Chitwan, 66 from Gorkha, 38 from Tanahun, 217 from Nawalparasi East and 190 from Nawalparasi West.

A total of 3,916 people remain missing, while 292 have been injured. So far, 11,993 people have been rescued from flood-affected areas.

Prime Minister Balen also briefed the House on the situation on Wednesday. He said there was no time to take a break simply because one’s body was tired and that, even amid grief, there was no time to share it. He also informed the House about the measures taken by the government.

Political party leaders then addressed the House. Following their remarks, Speaker Aryal presented the special resolution, which was unanimously passed.

The National Assembly had also passed a special resolution on the Rasuwa floods on Tuesday.

The upper house also recommended that the government take various measures, including prioritising rescue, relief, rehabilitation and the search for missing people; providing free medical treatment to the injured; and scientifically managing the recovered bodies.

It also called for coordination among the three tiers of government during reconstruction, cooperation with local communities, civil society, the private sector, development partners and the international community, and the preservation of national unity in disaster management.

title.rendered: UK Ambassador pays courtesy call on Nepal’s Law Minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

British Ambassador to Nepal Rob Fenn paid a courtesy call on Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam on Wednesday.

During the meeting held at the ministry, they discussed the irreversible losses caused by climate change and the significant risks Nepal faces as a result.

Minister Gautam said Nepal would prioritise making development more disaster-resilient in the aftermath of the unexpected floods. She expressed confidence that friendly countries and development partners would continue their support for sustainable and resilient development.

On the occasion, Ambassador Fenn expressed condolences over the loss of life caused by the unexpected disaster triggered by the Bhotekoshi floods and stressed the need to make efforts to locate people who remain missing more effective.

Ambassador Fenn also expressed the UK government’s commitment to continuing cooperation and coordination in development and reconstruction efforts through financial, technical and human resources.

—RSS

title.rendered: Rescuers hopeful as blocked tunnel is cleared at Trishuli 3A

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Rescue efforts are continuing at the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project, where a large number of people are believed to be trapped following the massive flood that entered the Trishuli River through the Bhotekoshi on August 26.

A joint team of Nepali experts and security personnel is working to rescue those believed to be trapped inside the project’s tunnel.

According to geotechnical engineer Udayaraj Neupane, workers are currently focused on opening the tunnel and clearing the mud inside.

Neupane said the tunnel entrance appears to have been sealed by a slab, which may have prevented large rocks from entering the tunnel.

“The slab seems to have blocked the entrance to the tunnel. Because the entrance was closed, we believe other large rocks did not enter inside,” he told Onlinekhabar. “That is why we are hopeful.”

According to Neupane, seven large rocks inside the tunnel are being blasted one by one.

“We are working according to a plan to enter the tunnel today,” he said.

title.rendered: Joint secretary Sharma appointed acting chairman of Film Development Board

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The Ministry of Information and Communications has appointed Joint Secretary Rabi Lal Sharma as acting chairman of the Film Development Board, tasking him with overseeing the board’s work until a permanent chairman is appointed.

Ministry spokesperson Rabindra Paudyal said the ministerial-level decision assigning Sharma the responsibility was made on Tuesday. Sharma took charge of the position starting Wednesday.

“He has been given the responsibility to handle the work until a chairman is appointed,” Paudyal said.

Paudyal added that the process to appoint a permanent chairman will begin soon.

“The secretary is currently away. There’s been some delay due to the floods and other factors. The process for appointing a chairman through open competition will begin soon,” he said.

The chairman’s post has been vacant since Dinesh DC’s term ended on August 27.

title.rendered: Families hold mass cremations for missing Rasuwa flood victims (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Families who have lost hope of finding relatives missing in the Rasuwa floods are creating funeral effigies using kaas-kush (sacred grass) and performing their final rites.

On Wednesday, dozens of such effigies were cremated in a mass funeral at Pashupati Aryaghat. The cremation was carried out according to Hindu traditions by the families and relatives of those who remain missing, drawing a large crowd at the cremation site.

The scene was deeply emotional as grieving families performed the final rites in memory of their missing loved ones.

title.rendered: Insurance companies to make advance payments for Bhotekoshi flood damage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Insurance companies will provide advance payments to those affected by the August 26 Bhotekoshi flood, as full damage assessments for large losses like hydropower projects and major infrastructure will take time to complete.

The Finance Ministry announced the decision after discussions involving the ministry, the Nepal Insurance Authority, reinsurance companies, insurance companies, and surveyors, aimed at easing cash flow and enabling reconstruction to begin quickly.

Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle directed that insurance claim payments for flood-affected areas be made simple and smooth. Insurance companies had previously advanced up to 50 percent of confirmed damage claims following the Gen-Z movement in September 2025 (2082 BS), setting a precedent for this approach.

Scale of damage

The Bhotekoshi flood caused extensive damage to hydropower projects, physical infrastructure, vehicles, agriculture, and private property.

Hydropower projects in the Bhotekoshi area with a combined capacity of roughly 900 megawatts suffered losses totaling an estimated 180 billion rupees in investment. Preliminary estimates suggest significant additional damage to other infrastructure and vehicles.

Faster claims process

The ministry said it has decided to provide necessary advance payments to settle genuine, verified claims without bureaucratic delay and to allow reconstruction of hydropower and other major infrastructure to begin immediately. The Nepal Insurance Authority will coordinate to make surveyor deployment more transparent and impartial, and may bring in foreign expert surveyors if needed for damage assessment.

Given the extraordinary circumstances of the disaster, the Insurance Authority will simplify existing documentation requirements for claims. A special task force will be formed within the Authority to monitor the daily status of Bhotekoshi flood insurance claims and payments, manage company liquidity, and expedite reinsurance reimbursements.

“The country is in mourning because of this flood. Let’s join hands in this difficult time, let insurance companies help ease victims’ losses and make claim payments simple and smooth,” Minister Wagle said at the discussion, adding that the government stands ready to help if insurance companies face any difficulties.

Claims so far

According to the Nepal Insurance Authority, 583 insurance claims had been filed as of September 15, with a combined estimated value of 25.87 billion rupees. To prevent payment delays from paperwork bottlenecks, the ministry said procedures will be broadly simplified, with a system for faster processing of smaller claims prioritized.

Since full assessment of hydropower and other major infrastructure damage will take time, all parties in the discussion agreed to advance payments to ease policyholders’ cash flow. The Insurance Authority will also arrange for automatic surveyor deployment to make the process more efficient and transparent.

title.rendered: NID Inspector interviews delayed for three and a half months

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Recruitment, transfers and promotions at the National Investigation Department (NID), the country’s only intelligence agency, have come to a standstill.

The interview process for candidates who passed the written examination for inspector-level posts has been stalled for more than three months. The Public Service Commission conducted the written examination for the recruitment of investigation officers (inspectors) on March 28.

The commission published the results of the examination on June 7. However, even after three months, the interviews have yet to be conducted. The Public Service Commission Act, 2009, requires the date for the next stage of the examination and interviews to be announced when the results of the written examination are published.

However, three and a half months after the written examination results were made public, the interviews have still not been held. The NID is responsible for conducting the entire interview process. Officials at the agency say the delay is a result of the ongoing process of transferring the agency back and forth between the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Office of the Prime Minister.

During KP Sharma Oli’s tenure as prime minister, the intelligence agency, which was under the Ministry of Home Affairs, was brought under the Office of the Prime Minister. Later, during Sushila Karki’s tenure, it was transferred back to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The government is now once again in the process of transferring the agency from the Home Ministry to the Office of the Prime Minister. Officials say the ongoing administrative process has also stalled recruitment, transfers and promotions within the agency. Those who passed the written examination for investigation officer posts have been particularly affected.

One of the candidates said the prolonged delay in conducting the interviews has created uncertainty, adding that two candidates have already gone abroad.

title.rendered: Schools closed indefinitely in flood-hit Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Trishuli (Nuwakot), September 2

Schools affected by flooding in the Trishuli River following the Bhotekoshi flash flood have been closed indefinitely in Nuwakot district.

All schools in the worst-hit areas of Bidur Municipality and Kispang Rural Municipality have remained closed, while it remains uncertain when teaching and learning activities will resume in other flood-affected areas.

Bidur Mayor Rajan Shrestha said there are no immediate plans to reopen schools as students, teachers and parents are missing, while school buildings, roads and bridges have been damaged by the floods.

He said schools would be reopened only after daily life returns to some extent of normalcy and people can safely cross the rivers.

Education Section Chief of the municipality Nabraj Sapkota said the scale of the damage caused by the floods was far greater than anticipated, despite prior information about the approaching disaster.

However, some schools managed to avert major incidents by taking precautionary measures, he said.

“The current situation is not normal, and daily life has been disrupted. After some time, we will prepare a plan to conduct teaching and learning activities through alternative means,” he said.

Of the 83 schools in Bidur Municipality, around a dozen have been directly affected by the floods. According to the municipality’s Education Section, four school buildings have been completely damaged.

Preliminary data compiled by the Education Development and Coordination Unit in Nuwakot show that schools cannot resume classes at their previous locations because the floods have destroyed the structures of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, Ramchandra Basic School, Chetana Basic School and Trishuli Community Boarding School.

Similarly, three blocks and the hostel building of Uttargaya English Boarding School have been completely damaged.

Teaching and learning activities have also been disrupted after the hostel of Chandeshwori Secondary School, where visually impaired students were staying, was damaged. The premises of Shahid Jagat Prakash Jung Shah Sanskrit Secondary School and Pioneer English Boarding School have also been affected.

A school bus belonging to Ramchandra Basic School and two buses belonging to Uttargaya English Boarding School were washed away by the floods.

Although school buildings in Kispang Rural Municipality were not damaged by the floods, two school buildings have been converted into holding centres. One school building in Belkotgadhi has also been used as a holding centre.

Shila Devi Secondary School in Belkotgadhi-7 and Mahadev Secondary School in Belkotgadhi-5 have also been affected by the floods.

title.rendered: 200 trucks to transport LPG to Kathmandu via alternative routes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The government and transport entrepreneurs have reached a new agreement to facilitate the transportation of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and other petroleum products after the Prithvi Highway was disrupted when the Trishuli River eroded the road at Krishnabhir in Dhading.

A meeting chaired by Makwanpur Chief District Officer Basanta Adhikari, with representatives of relevant agencies and stakeholders, agreed to use alternative roads for transporting LPG and also fixed transportation rates.

According to Diwan Chand, president of the Nepal LPG Industry Association, arrangements have been made to safely transport trucks and LPG tankers under police escort.

He said the collection of empty cylinders and their refilling for supply to the Kathmandu Valley had already begun to prevent an LPG shortage following the road disruption.

“We had an important discussion with the CDO, SP, Nepal Oil Corporation and representatives of the Truck Entrepreneurs’ Association,” Chand told Onlinekhabar. “Truck operators have said they can immediately provide 150 to 200 vehicles for LPG transportation. Trucks have already started travelling from Kathmandu to Hetauda carrying empty cylinders from Nepal Gas and Everest Gas. The operation began on a limited scale today and will run at full capacity from tomorrow.”

Transportation rates and routes

The meeting designated Hetauda as the “base point” for LPG transportation and fixed the freight rate accordingly. The rate for a truck to bring empty cylinders from Kathmandu to Hetauda, refill them and transport them back to Kathmandu has been fixed at Rs 80,000 per truck.

“Using Sahara Gas in Hetauda as the base, the transportation charge to Kathmandu has been fixed at Rs 80,000, excluding VAT,” Chand said. “This rate applies to a 15-tonne load capacity, covering both the delivery of empty cylinders and the return of filled cylinders. If transportation is required from other industries or districts, the rate will be adjusted according to the distance, using Rs 80,000 as the base.”

The meeting also made concrete decisions regarding potential risks associated with using alternative roads and traffic management. Accordingly, the routes for LPG-carrying vehicles have been designated as one-way.

“Vehicles travelling from Kathmandu to Hetauda will use the Tribhuvan Rajpath, while those returning to Kathmandu after loading LPG will use the Kanti Rajpath,” Chand said. “There are currently no major problems on the Kanti Rajpath. The Department of Roads has fully committed to immediately clearing any landslides on the Tribhuvan Rajpath and reopening the road.”

The meeting was attended by the chief district officer, district police chief (SP), traffic police officials, officials from the Department of Roads, the head of the provincial office of Nepal Oil Corporation, a central-level director and representatives of the Truck Entrepreneurs’ Association.

The prompt response from the administration and transport businesses is expected to provide significant relief to consumers by helping address the crisis caused by the disruption of the highway.

title.rendered: New rules introduced as cooking gas supply is disrupted

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Nepal Oil Corporation has introduced new rules for LPG gas distribution after the Trishuli River eroded a section of the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir, disrupting supplies to Kathmandu Valley and surrounding districts.

Under the new rules, LPG distribution for commercial purposes — including hotels, restaurants and canteens — has been suspended for the time being. Gas will be supplied only to households and other essential users.

The decision was taken at a joint meeting of Nepal Oil Corporation officials and representatives of the Gas Sellers’ Federation on Wednesday, chaired by Deepak Baral, deputy executive director of the corporation’s market management division.

The meeting concluded that the road collapse at Krishnabhir on August 30 had severely disrupted the LPG supply chain and agreed on alternative arrangements to prevent a shortage in Kathmandu Valley.

As LPG bullets cannot currently reach Kathmandu through the blocked highway, LPG companies supplying the Valley will arrange to have cylinders filled at plants in the Tarai and transport them to Kathmandu through alternative routes.

The gas brought through these alternative arrangements must be distributed proportionately and efficiently, according to the new rules.

Corporation Executive Director Nagendra Sah said efforts were underway to arrange LPG supplies from the Tarai.

“Once gas arrives from the Tarai, it will be distributed by prioritising consumers who need it most,” he said.

Commercial users barred, essential groups prioritised

Under the new rules, gas sellers have been instructed to completely stop distributing LPG for commercial purposes for the time being.

The available gas will instead be prioritised for essential consumers, including students, people in need, patients, senior citizens, various shelters and care homes, people with disabilities, and centres established for flood victims.

Businesses must arrange their own LPG

Hotels and other businesses that use LPG commercially will now have to arrange their own supplies.

Large consumers and businesses must coordinate with the dealers or LPG companies supplying their preferred brand, transport their empty cylinders to plants in the Tarai, have them refilled and bring them back to Kathmandu.

Gas sellers to join market monitoring

The corporation has also decided to include two representatives from LPG sellers in its Quick Response Team (QRT) to prevent artificial shortages and black marketing.

Their participation is expected to strengthen market monitoring and help address consumer complaints more effectively.

The meeting was attended by Binita Mani Upadhyay, director of the corporation’s LPG and aviation department; Deputy Director Indu Sharma Adhikari; Bishnu Prasad Dulal, acting vice-president of the Gas Sellers’ Federation Nepal; Hem Bahadur Thapa, president of the Gas Sellers’ Association Kathmandu, among other stakeholders.

title.rendered: Who are the ‘Green Army’ seen in flood-hit Trishuli?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Videos and photos of the Green Army, a group wearing green uniforms that resemble those of the Nepali Army, have recently gone viral on social media.

The group was seen assisting in the Trishuli area following the recent flood, prompting questions and speculation among the public about who the group is and under whose authority it was operating.

Some social media users even linked the group to Prime Minister Balen Shah, calling it “Balen’s private army.” Others questioned the legality of the Green Army’s name, uniform and activities.

But the Green Army is not a force deployed by a political party or local government. The organisation describes itself as a youth campaign formed to engage students in environmental conservation, disaster preparedness and humanitarian assistance.

According to its chief marshal Sabin Sharma, the organisation grew out of the experience of disasters and the need to bring young people together during emergencies.

“We know the pain caused by disasters. The purpose behind this campaign was to come together again when emergencies strike,” Sharma said.

Green Army was formed after the 2015 earthquake

The Green Army says its roots go back to the devastating earthquake of 2015.

Sharma said some young people who were involved in relief and rescue work during the earthquake realised that young people needed to be organised not only to respond to disasters but also to work on disaster prevention and humanitarian assistance.

After losing family members in Kathmandu’s Sankhu area during the earthquake, they initially began working with school students on activities such as sanitation, toilet construction and relief distribution, according to Sharma.

The initiative was later institutionalised. On August 27, 2020, the Green Army was registered with the Office of the Company Registrar as a “company not distributing profits.” It was later affiliated with the Social Welfare Council.

Why is it called the Green Army?

The organisation initially worked with students from grades 6 to 9, encouraging them to participate in environmental conservation activities.

Sharma said the initiative initially used the term “Green Warrior” to motivate students and encourage them to take an active role in protecting the environment.

However, as students found the term “Green Warriors” less easy to grasp, the organisation adopted the name Green Army, which it says represents a force dedicated to protecting greenery.

The Green Army name, however, is not the only feature that has drawn attention. Its green uniform, which carries a tree-leaf emblem, also has a military-style appearance.

This has led to questions about whether the organisation had permission to use the name and uniform.

Sharma says the organisation obtained formal approval before using both.

“We sought clear opinions from the Home Ministry and Defence Ministry, as well as the Nepal Army headquarters, and obtained formal permission through the Kathmandu District Administration Office,” he said.

According to the Green Army, the Nepali Army’s Directorate of Management Policy and Planning concluded that its uniform did not resemble the uniforms of the Nepali Army or other security agencies and that it was appropriate for an organisation involved in environmental conservation.

Based on that opinion, the Green Army received formal approval through the Kathmandu District Administration Office on August 13, 2021.

The organisation says the Defence Ministry, Home Ministry and Kathmandu District Administration Office approved its activities and use of the uniform.

Green Army trains students in disaster response

The Green Army says it has reached around 400 to 500 schools across Nepal to provide training to students.

The training includes assembly management, discipline, basic first aid, and making compost and organic soap from waste.

Students and volunteers associated with the organisation have also received three-day basic disaster-response training from security agencies, including the Nepali Army and Armed Police Force.

Sharma said around 40 people are involved as Green Army trainers. Of them, 15 are full-time trainers who receive salaries, while the others work as part-time trainers.

Students who complete the training graduate as Green Warriors.

Sharma said around 30,000 students have so far received training through the organisation.

Students are not required to remain affiliated with the Green Army after completing the programme. However, Sharma said the organisation contacts those who are willing to volunteer during emergencies and mobilises them when necessary.

The Green Army also claims that it has not received any major external funding or donations so far. According to Sharma, schools provide between Rs 5,000 and Rs 15,000 per month to cover basic trainer expenses.

Former Nepal Police Inspector General Sarbendra Khanal and other retired security officials currently serve as advisers to the Green Army.

How did the Green Army reach the Trishuli flood zone?

The Green Army says it was not deployed to the Trishuli flood zone at the direction of Prime Minister Balen Shah or any political party, despite speculation circulating on social media.

Instead, the organisation’s team travelled to the flood-affected area voluntarily after its chief adviser, former IGP Sarbendra Khanal, considered whether the group could provide assistance to flood victims.

An 11-member team led by Khanal went to the area after informing the control room in Nuwakot.

The team helped rescue animals, including chickens and dogs, from some local homes.

The team reached the Trishuli area on the third day after the flood. The organisation says no formal Green Army rescue team is currently operating in Trishuli or elsewhere.

Students who had received Green Army training at school level have also returned home.

Khanal said the Green Army team had sought his advice before travelling to the flood-affected area. He then contacted the chief district officer and superintendent of police and suggested that the team could go there.

Khanal said he has been associated with the Green Army as an adviser for more than two years.

“People from outside come here and do various things. When young people from Nepal ask for advice, why shouldn’t I give it?” he said.

He said he also attends Green Army leadership development training sessions at schools when invited.

Green Army rejects political links

Sharma has rejected claims circulating on social media linking the Green Army to Prime Minister Balen Shah or any political party.

He said the organisation is a legally registered non-governmental youth campaign that emerged from the suffering caused by the 2015 earthquake and aims to raise awareness among schoolchildren about environmental protection and disaster management.

“It hurts us when we are tagged with others because we started this campaign after seeing the suffering in our own homes and villages. We also wear the uniform only after obtaining permission. So, we request people not to misunderstand us,” Sharma told Onlinekhabar.
