title.rendered: PM Shah calls Bhotekoshi flood a tragedy for the entire country

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Prime Minister Balen Shah has described the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa as a shared tragedy that has struck the entire country, while briefing the House of Representatives on the government’s response and the damage caused by the disaster.

“This pain is not just that of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. It is a shared tragedy that has struck the entire country,” Shah said while addressing the House on Wednesday.

A devastating flood hit the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26, affecting Timure, Syafrubesi and Betrabati in Rasuwa, as well as Trishuli Bazaar and Devighat in Nuwakot. Areas along the Trishuli River in Dhading, Chitwan and Gorkha were also affected.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the bodies of 1,114 people who had gone missing in the flood have been recovered.

Of them, 41 bodies were recovered in Rasuwa, 155 in Nuwakot, 59 in Dhading, 348 in Chitwan, 66 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 217 in Nawalparasi East and 190 in Nawalparasi West.

A total of 3,916 people remain unaccounted for, while 292 people have been injured.

Shah told the House that 11,993 people have so far been rescued from the flood-affected areas.

Of the 292 injured people, 182 have been discharged, while health workers are continuing efforts to improve the condition of those still receiving treatment.

Bhotekoshi flood severely damages hydropower projects

The Bhotekoshi flood has also caused extensive damage to hydropower projects operating or under construction along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridor, as well as solar projects, Shah said.

According to the prime minister, eight hydropower projects that were generating electricity have suffered damage affecting 281 MW, while four projects under construction have suffered damage affecting 388 MW.

“Only some of them appear repairable, and significant investment will be required,” Shah said.

He added that the Bhotekoshi flood had disrupted 4,031.1 MW of electricity generation.

The government has begun restoring electricity services in the affected areas. Shah said electricity had been restored to 85% of areas in Nuwakot through alternative transmission arrangements, while restoration had reached 98% in Dhading and 40% in Rasuwa.

Government response began immediately

PM Balen Shah said the government went on alert immediately after the Bhotekoshi flood struck.

A meeting of the National Council for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management was held under his chairmanship. The meeting instructed all concerned agencies to prioritise the search for affected people, rescue operations and relief efforts.

An emergency meeting of the Monsoon Response Command Post was also held immediately after the incident to coordinate the situation assessment, search and rescue, security management, health services and relief mobilisation.

Authorities urged local administrations and the public not to travel on the Galchhi–Nuwakot road, the Syafrubesi road in Rasuwa and the Mugling–Narayangadh road, given the risks created by the disaster.

Local administrations were instructed to completely halt transportation and other movement in high-risk areas, with the safety of citizens given the highest priority.

Nepali Army and private-sector helicopters were mobilised in Rasuwa and Nuwakot to accelerate search and rescue operations. Additional aerial and ground rescue resources were deployed according to the needs of affected areas.

The government also released an additional Rs 10 million each to the disaster management funds of Rasuwa and Nuwakot and Rs 5 million to the disaster management fund of Dhading.

Shah said the government’s entire focus remained on saving lives, search and rescue, treatment, relief and the safe relocation of affected people.

Cabinet decisions after the flood

The Cabinet met on the day of the disaster and expressed deep sorrow over the loss of life and property caused by the Bhotekoshi flood in the Rasuwa border area, Rasuwagadhi, the Bhotekoshi River and downstream areas.

It paid tribute to those who died and expressed condolences to bereaved families while wishing those injured a speedy recovery.

The government decided to provide free immediate medical treatment to those injured in the disaster through the Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene, the Nepali Army and government hospitals.

The Home Ministry and Defence Ministry were tasked with arranging the immediate rescue and relocation of injured and stranded people to safe locations, with Nepali Army and private helicopters to be mobilised for the operation.

The Home Minister was also instructed to mobilise all necessary rescue resources, including helicopters.

The government decided to arrange food and accommodation for people who had lost their homes by relocating them to safe areas. The responsibility was assigned to the Home Ministry, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the concerned disaster management committees.

The Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development was instructed to reopen roads disrupted by the Bhotekoshi flood and arrange drinking water in the affected areas as soon as possible.

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation and the Nepal Electricity Authority were tasked with restoring disrupted electricity supplies, while the Ministry of Information and Communications was instructed to restore telecommunications services.

The Cabinet also decided to provide financial assistance to the families of those killed in accordance with prevailing law.

The finance minister was tasked with coordinating the mobilisation of financial resources required for the immediate operation and reconstruction of damaged public structures and physical infrastructure.

The government also decided to declare flood-affected local levels in the affected districts as disaster crisis zones for three months under Section 32 of the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, 2074, and arrange for the declaration to be published in the Nepal Gazette.

The Cabinet called on provincial governments, local governments and various organisations to assist with the search, rescue and relief of affected people and the treatment of those injured.

Government coordinating with provincial and local authorities

Shah said the government had been coordinating continuously with provincial and local governments and elected representatives since the beginning of the disaster.

“From the very beginning, we have been in continuous dialogue with the provincial government, local governments and elected representatives. When we visited the affected areas, we also held discussions with a team led by the chief minister of Bagmati Province,” he said.

He said the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority subsequently held discussions and assigned responsibilities to provincial and local governments.

Shah said the government remained focused on coordinating these efforts while continuing rescue, treatment, relief and restoration work in the affected areas.

He also said there was no time to step back and rest simply because people were physically exhausted.

Even as the scale of the tragedy weighs heavily, he said, the priority now was to continue working together to respond to the crisis.

title.rendered: Rasuwa Floods: How is work being carried out inside the tunnels?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Search and rescue operations are still underway in the area devastated by the sudden and catastrophic flooding in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The operations are being carried out with the support and coordination of the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force, as well as rescue teams from other countries. Even a week after the floods, search and rescue efforts inside the tunnels remain challenging.

The Nepali Army, with assistance from foreign rescue teams, is working inside the tunnels, which are considered highly dangerous and difficult to access. According to the Army Headquarters, as of 11 am Wednesday, rescue teams had reached about 150 metres inside the Rasuwa Garhi Hydropower tunnel. The Army said large rocks had prevented further access, and search and rescue efforts were being resumed.

Similarly, a joint team of 25 rescuers, including foreign personnel, is working inside the Langtang Hydropower tunnel after entering approximately 150 metres into the tunnel. A joint team, including foreign rescuers, is also carrying out search and rescue operations at Chilime Hydropower, the Army said.

A Nepali Army team is conducting search and rescue operations at Upper Trishuli 1 in Haku. At Trishuli-3A, a joint team of 93 personnel, including Nepali Army personnel, is clearing debris with the help of three excavators and one Bobcat, according to the Army. After using a compressor machine, breaker and blasting operations, the team located the tunnel outlet. The team is also pumping out around 1.5 metres of water that accumulated inside the tunnel overnight due to rainfall.

At Trishuli-3B, a rescue team comprising 61 Nepali Army personnel, three civilians, and the project’s managing director is carrying out operations. According to Army Headquarters, the team identified the project office and residential area and used an excavator to construct an access route to reach the area.

title.rendered: Nepali Army: It could take 3–4 months to clear material trapped inside the tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Nepali Army officials say it could take three to four months to clear the mud, rocks, and other debris that has piled up inside tunnels following the devastating flood and landslide at Bhotekoshi in Rasuwa, to move rescue and search operations forward.

Ujjwal Bikram Rana, who is leading the Field Operations Command north of Dhunche, said the situation inside the tunnels is extremely complex, and clearing all the material for a smooth rescue within just two to three days is not realistic.

Based on the volume and condition of material lodged inside the tunnel, he estimated it could take three to four months to remove it completely.

“I don’t see any possibility of clearing everything from inside the tunnel within two or three days. I’ve seen for myself that it may not even be possible within three to four months,” he said.

According to him, there are four hydropower project tunnels within his area of responsibility. Rescue and search work at the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project tunnel has been halted after proving too difficult to continue. He said the decision was made in coordination with the project’s engineers, since the lower section of the tunnel is filled with water and debris and there is no longer a realistic chance of finding anyone alive there.

At the Chilime project tunnel, however, search and rescue efforts are continuing, with teams still deployed in the hope that survivors may be found.

The army had also entered about 64 meters into the tunnel toward Langtang, but officials said further progress became difficult as the tunnel narrowed to the point where it was hard even for a person to pass through. With only about two feet of clearance in places, requiring rescuers to crawl, the risk involved has increased significantly.

Rescue efforts resumed today at Tunnel No. 216 as well. Despite five earlier attempts to enter, teams were unable to proceed due to debris piled up to chest height inside.

The army says Timure and Syaphrubesi are the areas hit hardest by the flood and landslide. Officials reported that river flow caused damage up to five meters high in some areas, with more than half of the Syaphrubesi settlement washed away. Timure also suffered major damage.

With roads and other communication links severed, air rescue currently remains the primary means of reaching the affected areas.

“There’s a road problem; the river has swept away all the roads, which is why heavy machinery couldn’t be brought in. But even if machinery does get through, given the state of the material lodged inside the tunnel, this isn’t something that can be finished in two or three days,” he said.

title.rendered: High risk of flash floods in several districts, authorities urge vigilance

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The Flood Forecasting Division, the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research, has reported that the water levels in the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and nearby rivers are expected to rise today, and there is a high chance of flash floods.

Saraswati Bista, a flood expert at the Division, urged residents in the riverbank areas in Rasuwa and Nuwakot to be highly alert.
“A lake has been formed near the Nepal-China border area. Since this lake could burst at any time, we have been urging the general public to stay highly alert until further notice. With the possibility of rain, there is a high risk of flooding in those districts today and tomorrow,” she said.

According to Bista, there is a possibility that the water level may rise today in rivers and streams flowing through districts like Taplejung, Sankhuwasabha, Solukhumbu, Ramechhap, Dolakha, Sindhupalchok, Kavrepalanchok, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur, Kathmandu, Dhading, Makawanpur, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahun, Lamjung, Manang, Kaski, Syangja, Parbat, Myagdi, Baglung, Rukum East, Rukum West, Rolpa, Salyan, Surkhet, Jajarkot, Darchula, Baitadi, Dadeldhura, and Kanchanpur, and nearby districts.

The Division has suggested that the general public living in coastal areas and travelling along riverbanks stay alert, as there is a risk of flash floods in the small rivers and streams in those areas.

title.rendered: Two-year cooling-off period proposed for constitutional body officials

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

A proposal has been made to impose a two-year cooling-off period on officials of constitutional bodies, preventing them from taking up positions in private, non-governmental or commercial organisations directly associated with the body they previously served.

CPN-UML lawmaker Yashoda Kumari Baral has proposed the provision through an amendment to the Bill on Remuneration, Conditions of Service and Facilities of Officials of Constitutional Bodies (First Amendment), 2026.

The proposed provision states that an official of a constitutional body would not be allowed to work in any capacity at a private, non-governmental or commercial organisation having a direct interest in the same constitutional body for two years from the date of retirement or removal from office.

The proposal has been made as a new sub-section under Section 18 of the existing Act, which deals with pension and gratuity provisions for officials of constitutional bodies.

What does the proposed cooling-off period say?

The amendment proposed by Baral states an official of a constitutional body shall not be allowed to work in any capacity at any private, non-governmental or commercial organisation having a direct interest in the same body for two years from the date of retirement or removal from office.

A cooling-off period refers to a mandatory period during which a person leaving a public position is restricted from taking up certain appointments or roles.

The Bill currently has nine amendment proposals submitted by lawmakers in nine groups.

Bill seeks to address double benefits

Prime Minister Balen Shah registered the Bill in the House of Representatives on July 30, proposing changes to the existing law governing the remuneration, conditions of service and facilities of officials of constitutional bodies.

One of the stated objectives of the Bill is to prevent retired constitutional officials from receiving double benefits from the state.

The Bill notes that retired civil servants are often appointed to constitutional bodies. In such cases, officials may receive their retirement pension while also receiving facilities provided under prevailing law after being appointed to a constitutional position.

The government has argued that this can result in the same individual receiving two benefits from the state treasury.

The Bill also states that officials holding high public offices are expected to demonstrate a high level of ethical and moral conduct.

Prime Minister Shah has argued that such qualities should be visible in practice among people holding positions involving significant public accountability.

“If an official is seen receiving double benefits, it ultimately weakens public faith, trust and confidence in the institution associated with that person,” the Bill states.

It further argues that it is not appropriate for an official receiving salary, allowances and other facilities from the state treasury to also receive a pension from the same treasury.

The Bill is currently under consideration in a parliamentary committee.

title.rendered: China opens road to Kerung border, allowing heavy rescue equipment into affected areas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The road connecting to the Kerung border point linking to Rasuwagadhi has fully resumed operation as of Wednesday morning, 10 AM, according to China.

Chinese media reports say this will allow rescue workers, relief supplies, equipment, and heavy machinery to reach the main disaster-affected areas by road, enabling more extensive rescue operations.

Road-clearing efforts have now reached the core disaster zone, where search and rescue work is underway through coordination across multiple methods.

According to CCTV footage, the final stretch of road that had been blocked by water has been temporarily reopened, allowing heavy machinery to pass through as well.

Heavy machinery clearing the national highway near the main disaster-affected area of the Kerung border has now reached close to the main building at the Chinese-side Kerung border facility.

title.rendered: Gandaki CM reshuffles cabinet, swaps energy and physical infrastructure portfolios

content.rendered:
Pokhara, September 2

Gandaki Province Chief Minister Surendra Raj Pandey has reshuffled his Cabinet. Four ministers from the CPN-UML resigned on August 26 after the CPN-UML and Nepali Communist Party (NCP) allied at the federal level.

Pandey has once again appointed Phanindra Devkota, a lawmaker from the Nepal Socialist Party (NESP) who was elected on the Maoist Centre’s election symbol, as Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Drinking Water. Devkota had previously become a minister after voting in favour of Pandey’s confidence motion on June 3, 2024.

Nanda Prasad Neupane, who had been heading the Energy Ministry, has now been given responsibility for the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport Management, which had been retained by Chief Minister Pandey himself.

Devkota, who is associated with the NCP, had resigned on September 10, 2025, following the deaths of children and others during the Gen Z movement. The latest reshuffle was made in line with Devkota’s demand, with Devkota returning to the Energy Ministry and Neupane taking charge of the Physical Infrastructure Ministry. Devkota has already taken the oath of office.

Pandey was appointed chief minister on May 29, 2024, as leader of the largest party after filing petitions at the Supreme Court twice and securing the removal of then-Chief Minister Khagaraj Adhikari of the UML.

Pandey secured a vote of confidence with the support of two Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) lawmakers, independent lawmaker Rajib Gurung (Deepak Manange) and Phanindra Devkota, without the support of the UML or the Maoist Centre.

Only after Pandey secured the vote of confidence did the Nepali Congress and UML agree to cooperate at the federal level, following which the UML joined the provincial government.

After the UML and NCP again reached an agreement at the federal level, four UML ministers—Physical Infrastructure Minister Govinda Bahadur, Agriculture Minister Bhim Karki, Health Minister Laxman Pandey and Tourism Minister Yashoda Rimal—resigned on August 26.

Chief Minister Pandey had retained the ministries vacated by the UML ministers.

title.rendered: Alternative route opened on Prithvi Highway in Dhading

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

An alternative route has been opened at Parewa Bhir in Gajuri Rural Municipality-3 of Dhading along the Prithvi Highway.

The road had subsided due to erosion caused by flooding in the Trishuli River, bringing traffic to a complete halt. The District Police Office, Dhading, said an alternative track has now been opened at the site.

A 100-metre-long new track has been constructed, and vehicles have begun operating normally along the route, police said. However, they warned that travelling on the temporary track remains risky.

Earlier, traffic along the same highway had been completely disrupted after the road subsided at Krishnabhir due to flooding in the Trishuli River.

Following flood damage to the highway, vehicles travelling between the capital Kathmandu and other areas have been using three alternative routes from Narayangadh in Chitwan via Hetauda to Kathmandu.

title.rendered: Sonu Sood reaches flood-hit areas, calls for “Resolve to Build a Home” campaign

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Bollywood actor Sonu Sood arrived in Nuwakot on Wednesday to bring aid to those affected by the Bhotekoshi flood, accompanied by a relief team from Mumbai.

Before heading to Nuwakot, he met flood victims sheltering at a monastery in Kathmandu, sharing photos of the visit, including with children living there, on social media.

Upon arriving in Kathmandu on Tuesday, Sood spoke with Nepali journalists and proposed a “Resolve to Build a Home” campaign to provide housing for citizens left homeless by the floods.

“Nepal is going through an extremely difficult time right now. Coming forward to help as much as we can is a humanitarian duty for all of us,” Sood said. “The impact of showing up in person, holding a survivor’s hand and telling them we stand with you, is far greater than sending help from afar. I’m not here just to assist, but to fulfil my responsibility.”

His organisation, the Sood Charity Foundation, together with the Lions Club and Khalsa Aid, has formed a joint team that is assessing real needs directly on the ground.

He said 2,000 blankets, clothing, dry food supplies, and women’s health/hygiene items have already been sent from India to Nepal.

Sood said he plans to visit flood-affected areas, including Nuwakot, in person to develop a long-term support plan addressing education, health, and housing needs.

Praising the resilience and hardworking nature of Nepali citizens, he noted that most of the people who have worked with him in Mumbai over the past 25–30 years have been Nepali. He said the patience and smiles Nepalis have shown even amid this massive disaster have inspired him further.

He also expressed concern about climate change and environmental imbalance, saying that such disasters are increasing worldwide due to the exploitation of nature and deforestation, and stressed the need for serious conservation efforts now to protect future generations.

Sood said he came to Nepal in partnership with Lions Clubs International and Khalsa Aid to mobilise humanitarian assistance, and appealed to Nepali communities worldwide to help the country during this difficult time.

Recalling that his foundation built 257 homes after floods hit Punjab, India, he said housing construction would soon begin at identified sites in Nepal as well.

title.rendered: Big boulders placed to curb Narayani River erosion in Chitwan

content.rendered:
Chitwan, September 2

Work has begun to place large boulders along the Narayani River in Majhuwa of Bharatpur Metropolitan City-17, Chitwan, to control severe riverbank erosion in the area.

Dr Narayan Subedi, chief of the Irrigation and Water Resources Management Project in Bharatpur, said the Narayani River had eroded a stretch of nearly 300 metres in Majhuwa, prompting efforts to temporarily control the erosion by placing large boulders.

“It has been very difficult to find stones. We visited areas including Gaindakot and Rapti, along with the chief district officer, and requested local governments to help us locate and supply the stones,” he said. “More stones are still being brought in.”

According to Dr Subedi, the river has already eroded 25 to 30 metres inland.

Dr Subedi, also a disaster management expert, warned that continued erosion could risk splitting western Chitwan into two sections.

Project engineer Shailendra Bista said that 38 truckloads of stones had so far been delivered to the site. Of these, 23 truckloads were brought in on Tuesday alone, with some of the boulders already placed in the river to reduce the force of the current.

The secretariat of Law Minister Sobita Gautam also facilitated efforts to arrange the stones.

Boulders have now been placed along a stretch of more than 15 metres to divert or block the river’s main current, he said. Other protective measures, including the installation of RCC porcupines, are also planned.

The project has awarded an emergency management contract for work along this stretch in Asar (June/July). Pashupati Construction Service Pvt. Ltd. of Bharatpur-10 was awarded the contract for Rs 82.467 million and has begun work.

The company was contracted to carry out various river-control measures in areas vulnerable to erosion along the Narayani River, including locations where protective works had not previously been completed.

The construction company has been given until Jestha 25, 2084 BS to complete the project.

According to project officials, river-control work remains to be completed along around 10.5 kilometres of riverbank in western Chitwan, while various protection measures have already been carried out along the remaining sections.

title.rendered: Floods hit Nepal tourism as August visitor arrivals fall

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The impact of the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers has been reflected in tourist arrivals to Nepal.

Nepal welcomed 85,444 international tourists in August 2026, a decrease of 3,336 compared with the same month last year. Nepal recorded 88,680 tourist arrivals in August 2025, meaning arrivals fell by 3.6 per cent year-on-year this August.

In the final week of August, flooding that entered Nepal through the Rasuwagadhi border point on August 26 caused extensive human and physical losses in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, as well as other areas along the river system.

Domestic and foreign tourists travelling to Kailash Mansarovar and Gosainkunda were also affected by the floods. The disaster has had a direct impact on tourist arrivals. Following the floods, countries including the United States issued travel advisories warning their citizens about travel to Nepal.

According to the Nepal Tourism Board, India was the largest source market in August, with 26,373 visitors, accounting for 30.87 per cent of total arrivals. China was the second-largest source, with 10,304 visitors, a 36.78 per cent increase from 7,533 in August last year.

Similarly, Nepal received 8,710 visitors from Sri Lanka, a 46.24 per cent increase year-on-year. The country also welcomed 6,293 visitors from the United States, 4,487 from Bangladesh and 3,476 from the United Kingdom.

By region, South Asia accounted for the highest number of arrivals, with 41,422 visitors in August. Other Asian countries contributed 18,275 visitors, while Europe accounted for 10,875 visitors. Arrivals from Oceania stood at 2,529, an increase of 3.86 per cent.

A total of 7,473 tourists arrived from the Americas, up 2.47 per cent from the previous year. The Middle East contributed 1,010 visitors, marking a 6.99 per cent increase, while 338 visitors came from Africa, up 4.97 per cent year-on-year.

Several key markets recorded significant growth in August 2026. Nepal received 769 visitors from Russia, a 51.38 per cent increase from the previous year, while arrivals from Ukraine rose by 83.05 per cent to 216.

Similarly, arrivals from Cambodia increased by 277.78 per cent to 68 visitors. Nepal welcomed 1,288 visitors from Bhutan, up 49.25 per cent, while arrivals from Malaysia reached 1,618 and those from Thailand stood at 681, representing increases of 13.07 per cent and 19.89 per cent, respectively.

title.rendered: Flood-swept bridges leave Trishuli communities completely cut off

content.rendered:
Families separated by the river have had no contact with their relatives on the other side. No one knows what’s happening across the water, and no news travels the other way either. Since the flood struck on August 26, locals along the Trishuli River have been left without any word of their loved ones.

“Once the flood swept away both the suspension and concrete bridges, we’ve had no news from either side. All connection has been severed,” says Bhuwan Prasad Ghimire, 86, of Darshantar, Nuwakot. “We don’t know when the government will restore the connection.”

The flood on August 26 has left people deeply shaken; residents in the area remain in a state of fear.

“I’m 86 years old, and I’ve never seen anything like this. Whatever came this time, it came in a surge,” he says, adding that nothing like this had happened even in his father’s or grandfather’s time.

He recalled a flood in 1962 but said it was nothing compared to this one.

“Back then there was no bridge, and the settlement was higher up. After roads and bridges were built, the settlement moved down closer to the river. Now the flood has taken everything,” he says.

Bridges swept away

This is a shared crisis across numerous villages in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading. The flood destroyed 35 concrete bridges alone; the number of suspension bridges lost is still unclear. Only one bridge in Galchhi remains intact, and the alternate route through Dhading to reach the Nuwakot–Rasuwa border at Trishuli has become a “lifeline.”

In some places only the beams of a suspension bridge remain; some bridges dangle uselessly over the river; in others, not even the foundation of a former concrete bridge is visible. The river now flows far below where bridges once stood. Climbing uphill from Galchhi in Dhading, the team met Dhan Bahadur Adhikari, 78, whose home is on the Dhading side while his relatives live across in Nuwakot.

“Crossing used to take five minutes by bridge. Now it takes four to five hours on foot via Galchhi,” he says.

The Trishuli River has also washed through Wards 3 and 5 of Devighat in Nuwakot. Lokbahadur Pudasaini and his wife Durga Pudasaini of Devighat were cleaning out their flood-damaged home but still haven’t been able to cross to the other side. Durga’s parental family lives across the river; she has heard her brother was swept away but hasn’t been able to go check.

“My brother is unreachable. I haven’t been able to go there,” she says.

According to Lokbahadur, there were three bridges in the Devighat area.

“The iron bridge built in 1975 was washed away. The concrete bridges built in 2025 and 2007 (BS) are also gone,” he says. “Devighat connects three local governments, but now that connection is severed.”

Until roads and bridges are rebuilt, meeting relatives on the other side isn’t possible.

Years ago, a campaign helped phase out the old tuin (cable crossing) system in favour of proper suspension and concrete bridges.

“Now there’s neither a tuin nor a bridge. Even a temporary tuin would let people cross; the government should at least arrange that for now,” Dhan Bahadur says.

No power, no communication

In many places, floodwaters have destroyed electricity poles and wires, leaving areas across the river still without power. When the Onlinekhabar team reached Devighat via the alternate route, most locals were gathered outside their homes at communal rest spots.

“Since the flood took out the poles, there’s been no electricity. It’s hot, so we’re staying outdoors,” says Ambika Rimal, 65.

People now have to walk for hours just to charge a mobile phone.

Locals describe these areas as having become remote and hard to access.

“My relatives are across the river. I don’t know what happened to them; phones don’t connect, and I can’t go there. What used to take five minutes to cross now leaves us stuck on our own sides,” says Binda Adhikari, 48, of Devighat.

Daily life at a standstill

Households have paddy and corn stored, but no way to get it milled; the mill is across the river.

“The husked rice has run out. What do we eat now? It’s a disaster,” Adhikari says. “Even the vermilion for rituals has to be bought from the market across the river, but I hear there’s no market there either. I haven’t been able to go.”

People used to routine travel between the banks are now cut off even from basic news.

“We haven’t been able to watch TV. Mobile phones are off; it’s like a desert,” says Purna Bahadur Bhujel, 55. “Everything is deserted. It feels like the Stone Age; we don’t know anything.”

Daily life and trade have been disrupted broadly.

“Food used to be brought from one side to the other and vice versa. Now that’s completely stopped,” says Govinda Aryal, 55.

Once-bustling markets now lie in ruins, and locals can’t even buy daily essentials or transport their vegetable harvests across.

Students who used to cross to attend school on the other side are now unable to continue their studies, affecting students across all three districts along the Trishuli.

“Students up to Belkotgadhi Municipality used to come to Devighat for school. Now students on both sides can no longer attend,” says Krishna Prasad Aryal, 77.

No roads

Road connections between the three districts have also been severed, leaving no route for local travel except the single surviving bridge at Galchhi. Reaching Trishuli, Devighat, Dhunge, or Betrawati on the other side now takes hours via that detour. “The concrete road washed away. Now you have to go via Galchhi — it’s a narrow track, hard for two-way traffic,” Bhujel said.

No one knows when the road will be rebuilt. “It takes five hours to get from Bidur to Galchhi and then on to the other side of Betrawati,” said Ramhari Bogati, 32, of Bogatitar, Bidur-9, Nuwakot. “The road is unpaved and difficult.”

Relief supplies and local traffic have already begun causing congestion on this makeshift track.

Patients at risk

With no roads or bridges, essential services have been badly hit, and it’s proving especially dangerous for the sick. Getting patients to Kathmandu for treatment has become extremely difficult.

“For serious cases, patients need to go to Kathmandu. It used to take two hours; now, via Galchhi, it takes seven to eight hours,” Bogati says. “You have to call an ambulance, and it takes time just to reach here; by then, who knows what condition the patient will be in.”

Areas directly affected by the flood include Pimaltar, Tarukaghat, Pipaldanda, Kumaltar, Sirkhali, Multhala, Gauribensi, Kalikhola, and the upper reaches of the Trishuli.

content.rendered:

The government has postponed this round of the taxpayer reward programme, citing the floods and landslides that struck Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts.

The winners of the reward programme for the first 15 days of Bhadra were due to be announced on Tuesday. title.rendered: India sends fifth batch of aid to Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

India has sent its fifth batch of assistance to support rescue and relief efforts for people affected by the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

Indian External Affairs Minister Dr S. Jaishankar said on Wednesday morning that the fifth consignment of aid had been dispatched to Nepal by air.

He said the aircraft was carrying an 11-member rescue team equipped with specialised search and rescue equipment, along with 5.5 tonnes of essential medicines.

Earlier, on August 30, India had sent its fourth aircraft carrying 11 tonnes of relief supplies and a technical team for flood-affected communities.

Rescue and relief operations are currently underway at an accelerated pace in Nepal. India, along with various other countries and international organisations, has been assisting in the affected areas.

title.rendered: “I found new life after 20 minutes of struggle in the flood’s whirlpool”

content.rendered:
(This piece is based on an interview conducted by Onlinekhabar’s Lilu Dumre with Rasuwa Customs Officer Tilak Parajuli.)


It had been a month and a half since I was transferred to the Rasuwa Customs Office. I had to go to Kathmandu when my father fell ill, and I had only returned to my post on Tuesday.

We had 35 staff, including contract employees, at the office, and we regularly went on morning walks. On the day of the flood, Hari Khadka, who has been unreachable since the flood, and I had gone on our usual walk together. Afterwards, I was getting ready for the office and waiting for Hari on the third floor when I heard someone shout that an earthquake had hit. I never imagined a flood, let alone one this massive.

Suddenly there was a loud rumbling sound. At first I thought it was a landslide. People panicked and started running. Hari headed downstairs while I tried to get to another room, but by then, the muddy floodwater full of rocks had already reached us. Within seconds, the room was filled with mud pouring through the window; there was nothing to see anymore. I grabbed the hands of two others and held on.

The flood swept over us from head to toe. It felt like I couldn’t breathe, like this was the end. The force even broke through walls. The three of us holding hands were flung into a whirlpool. I spun around inside it, thinking I likely wouldn’t survive, but still tried to protect my head.

I went in and out of consciousness. Part of me thought it would be easier if the flood just took me. I kept praying: “God, I have a small child, save me for his sake, if nothing else.”

I spun in that whirlpool for what felt like 20 minutes. Containers and gas cylinders spun around with me; sometimes I struck a container, sometimes a cylinder, and sometimes rocks hit my body. I drifted between consciousness and unconsciousness, fighting to survive.

When the swirling finally stopped, I saw a green hillside nearby and tried crawling toward it, still fearing another wave might come or that I’d fall into a pit. As I crawled forward, I found myself grabbing someone’s head; I saw two or three people with head injuries. Even as I struggled to survive myself, I wished I could help them too.

Driven by the will to live, I dragged myself up the rocky slope. Two people who’d reached safety were searching for their own missing relative and may not have noticed me. With a battered body, I kept crawling up the rock face until I raised my hand; my friend Om Joshi spotted me. I had to tell him it was me, Tilak, since I was unrecognisable. He had been searching for his nephew, Rajendra.

Om helped me climb higher and tried to get me water by breaking open a pipe with a rock; only a little came out. There was also a young woman nearby whose forehead was badly cut; she drank some water too and was also trying to climb higher.

Still hoping for government rescue, I kept crawling upward until Bikram Shrestha spotted me; he’s the one who took the early photos that have since circulated. He recognised me and rushed over, then took me to a house. Aside from my lower clothing, nothing else covered my body; I was so covered in mud that I was unrecognisable. Bikram washed me off, which caused unbearable pain from all my injuries; I nearly passed out. Someone gave me clothes to wear.

Seeing that terrain, everyone wonders how an injured person made it that far up, but the hope of survival brings its own strength.

Once I escaped the whirlpool, I first hoped simply that I could survive. Then I hoped that if a helicopter came, I could make it. But the weather wasn’t favourable; the sun hadn’t come out. Still, after some time, I heard a helicopter, an army one, but it couldn’t land. I thought I wouldn’t survive after all; by then more than an hour and a half had passed since I’d been desperately awaiting treatment.

Once the helicopter finally came, I believed rescue was certain; even if I couldn’t stand, I thought they’d pull me up by rope if needed. On its last pass, the helicopter did land, but slightly below where I was. It picked up the injured there and flew off. Seeing my panic, Bikram tried to get me on that first flight, but the helicopter left anyway, worsening my situation. Since there was no landing space where I was, I had to climb back down; though I couldn’t be carried, there wasn’t a single part of my body without an outer injury.

With two friends’ help, I barely made it down to a spot where a helicopter could land. After being washed off, the pain intensified hugely. I’d survived this far through my own struggle; now I just hoped the government would complete the rescue.

After some time, a helicopter did arrive. The injured awaiting treatment were furious with the wait; one man with a head injury died while waiting for the helicopter, and people around him wept. Watching someone die while my own condition worsened was agonising. Kamal, a hotelier from Surkhet, and another man named Sanchit held onto me; even though Kamal’s own father and sister were unreachable, he still looked after me.

Eventually the helicopter came. I lost consciousness after boarding it, assuming I’d be flown straight to Kathmandu for treatment, but I was actually dropped at an army camp in Nuwakot, which I only realised while semi-conscious.

I dimly recall hearing that critical patients would be sent to hospital immediately. Once there, an army official asked if I could give a family member’s number. I gave my wife’s; it was off. I gave my brother Toran’s; no answer. Then I remembered my childhood friend Yuvraj’s number, which worked. I asked him to get word to my family quickly that I was alive; one of his friends came immediately to Chakradev Hospital.

Since helicopters were needed for the flood zone, I was given first aid and sent to Kathmandu by ambulance. I initially thought I’d been brought straight to a hospital, but later learned I was at Norvic Hospital. I’d arrived around 4 pm Wednesday. I was aware of some things around me, unaware of others. Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle came to check on my condition the same day I was rescued; I vaguely recall speaking with him. The Director General of the Customs Department also visited. I was admitted to the ICU, and by the next day (Thursday), my condition had improved somewhat.

According to doctors, there’s no internal damage. My right rib is broken, and I have external injuries all over, but no brain damage. Doctors say the rib will take some time to heal fully, but recovery is expected, just gradually.

title.rendered: Mahakali River flow exceeds danger level

content.rendered:
Dhangadhi, September 2

The movement of four-wheeled vehicles across the Sharda Barrage has been suspended after the water flow in the Mahakali River increased. According to police, four-wheeled vehicles have been barred from using the barrage since Tuesday morning after the river flow exceeded the danger level.

Although the water level, which reached 297,000 cusecs on Tuesday, has been gradually declining, the restriction remained in place on Wednesday as it had not fallen below the danger threshold, police said.

DSP Tek Bahadur Rawat of the Kanchanpur District Police Office said the water flow in the Mahakali had dropped to 255,284 cusecs by Wednesday morning.

According to him, four-wheeled vehicles are prohibited from crossing the Sharda Barrage, which connects Kanchanpur with Banbasa in India, when the river flow exceeds 100,000 cusecs.

Police said that as the water level continues to decline, the barrage could be fully reopened by the afternoon if there is no further rainfall in the hilly areas.

title.rendered: Nepal wants Loss and Damage funding. Will it get it?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Nepal has asked the UNFCCC-backed Loss and Damage Fund to consider providing financial support for losses caused by the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa, which experts have described as a climate-related disaster.

The government has written to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, arguing that Nepal is suffering the consequences of climate change despite contributing very little to global carbon emissions.

According to the World Bank, an average Nepali emits 0.54 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. That compares with 9.3 tonnes in China, 2.17 tonnes in India and 13.6 tonnes in the United States. The global average was 4.67 tonnes per person per year in 2024.

The figures highlight Nepal’s relatively small contribution to global emissions, while the country continues to face significant impacts from climate change, experts say.

Environmental experts have described the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa as a climate-related disaster.

Maheshwar Dhakal, chief of the Climate Change Management Division under the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment, said Nepal suffered major loss of life and property from an event in which the country had made little contribution to the underlying problem.

“The flood and landslides in Bhotekoshi caused the kind of loss of life and property that we would classify as a purely climate-related disaster,” Dhakal said. “Developed and industrialised countries have emitted large amounts of carbon, while Nepal’s contribution is negligible. We have suffered because of the actions of others rather than our own.”

It is against this backdrop that the government has approached the Loss and Damage Fund. The fund is intended to provide financial support to particularly vulnerable developing countries facing losses and damages caused by the adverse effects of climate change.

Environmental economist Arjun Dhakal said Nepal can make such a request, but it will need to establish the link between the disaster and climate change and provide a detailed assessment of the damage.

“Nepal can make such a claim and request support. But for further assistance, it must establish that the event was caused by climate change and carry out a detailed assessment of the losses,” he said.

Nepal has not put a figure on its request

Maheshwar Dhakal said Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary and Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle signed the request after informal discussions with the fund’s board.

“We had already held informal discussions with the board. We sent the request to discuss how the international community can respond to Nepal’s current situation,” he said.

Nepal has not specified a particular amount it is seeking in the letter addressed to the fund’s co-chairs.

Richard Sherman, a former co-chair and member of the fund’s board, has said Nepal could potentially receive around Rs 3 billion.

A New York Times report, citing the requests from other countries as well, estimated that Nepal could receive up to $20 million, equivalent to around Rs 3.04 billion.

For Nepal, however, that amount would cover only a small fraction of the damage caused by the disaster.

The Department of Roads has made an initial estimate that around Rs 50 billion will be needed just to rebuild damaged roads and bridges.

Nepal says it is also a contributor to climate stability

The government’s argument is not limited to Nepal being a victim of climate change.

Nepali experts say the country also contributes to global climate stability by conserving its mountains, forests, vegetation and biodiversity. Its mountain-fed rivers provide freshwater, while its forests absorb and store carbon.

“We therefore argue that Nepal should not be assessed only as a victim of climate change, but also recognised and compensated as a contributor to climate stability,” Maheshwar Dhakal said.

Nepal has already submitted three proposals to the fund, according to Dhakal.

“Our main request is that the Bhotekoshi incident, being so sudden, unprecedented and exceptional in nature, be considered by the board as a special case,” he said.

The fund itself faces a shortage of money

Whether Nepal receives the requested support remains uncertain, particularly because the Loss and Damage Fund itself has limited resources.

The fund had called for proposals ranging from $5 million to $20 million from 134 countries. More than 100 countries have already sought around $3 billion in support, according to those familiar with the process.

The fund has committed to providing a total of around $820 million, but only about $400 million has reportedly been deposited into its account.

The gap between the scale of requests and available resources raises questions over how much Nepal can ultimately receive.

Sherman told The New York Times that countries that have contributed the most to climate change are not paying the costs associated with it.

The United States, one of the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitters, had previously pledged $17.5 million to the fund. That commitment was withdrawn after Donald Trump returned to the White House.

‘Compensation is becoming more important than adaptation’

Climate adaptation refers to preparing people, infrastructure, agriculture, water systems, forests and other natural systems to withstand the impacts of climate change.

Experts say countries that have contributed more to climate change should bear a greater share of the cost of adaptation and loss and damage. But many of the countries responsible for high emissions are increasingly reluctant to take on that responsibility, they say.

Journalist and author Kunda Dixit said the growing emphasis on military spending, alongside declining resources for environmental protection, is directly affecting countries such as Nepal that have contributed relatively little to climate change.

“Earlier, the focus was on funding for adaptation. Now it appears that funding for compensation itself is needed,” Dixit said. “If Nepal receives such funding, it would also benefit other countries because it could help them prepare for and protect themselves from similar disasters.”

However, Dixit said Nepal cannot depend solely on international compensation.

“Whether or not the fund provides support, countries still have to prepare for their own safety,” he said.

Given the reluctance of major emitters to contribute to climate funds and rising military expenditure, countries such as Nepal need to remain prepared to deal with climate-related disasters on their own, he added.

title.rendered: Bodies of 1,114 people recovered from Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The bodies of 1,114 people who went missing in the devastating Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa on August 26 have been recovered, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The figure was released in the Authority’s 9 a.m. bulletin.

According to police, the bodies were recovered from eight districts: 41 in Rasuwa, 155 in Nuwakot, 59 in Dhading, 348 in Chitwan, 66 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 217 in Nawalparasi East and 190 in Nawalparasi West.

The Authority said 3,916 people remain unaccounted for, while 292 people have been injured.

So far, 11,993 people have been rescued from the flood-affected areas.

Seven bodies recovered after Bhotekoshi flood managed in Tansen

content.rendered:
Palpa, September 2

The bodies of seven people who died in the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa have been managed in Tansen.

The bodies were found in Nawalpur and brought to Palpa for management. Following a meeting of the District Disaster Management Committee, the seven bodies were managed at a community forest in Gorkhekot, Tansen-1.

According to Palpa Assistant Chief District Officer Shivaraj Sedhai, seven of the eight unidentified bodies brought to Palpa were managed in accordance with the prescribed standards after their DNA samples and identifying details were recorded.

The District Police Office, Palpa, said the bodies included those of three men, two women, a boy and a girl.

The body of one woman has been identified. It was handed over to her relatives who had arrived from Nuwakot.

title.rendered: Bibek, 12, is taping hope to a hospital wall

content.rendered:
At Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj, a wall is covered with papers bearing photos, names, ages, addresses, and contact numbers of people who went missing in the Bhotekoshi flood. Some are large colour photos, others small black-and-white ones. Anyone standing before the wall shows visible exhaustion, worry, and tears; some verify details on their phones, while others search for a spot to post a relative’s photo.

In the middle of this crowd is a boy carrying a roll of white tape, moving busily from person to person and asking anyone who looks like they might be a flood victim’s relative, “Do you have a photo to put up?”

Once handed a photo, he sizes it up, finds space on the wall, cuts tape, and sticks it in place, even climbing on others’ shoulders when he can’t reach the upper sections himself.

The boy is 12-year-old Bibek Pariyar.

He isn’t doing it for money. When people try to pay him, he shakes his head and says he won’t take it, though he says he sometimes accepts because people clearly want to give, joking that he even has some Indian currency to show for it.

Bibek is a fifth grader at Mahendra National Secondary School in Baluwatar, which is close to where he lives and close to the hospital too. Since the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26, his routine has shifted: school in the morning, helping flood victims in the afternoon, then home in the evening.

No one asked him to do this; he started it himself. The day after the Rasuwa flood, he noticed people posting pictures at the hospital and asked a man why. The man explained he was searching for a relative lost in the flood. Bibek had watched a YouTube video about the flood that morning, so he understood immediately. He recalled hearing that a glacial/ice collapse had caused the flood, and that many people had gone missing, so he thought helping put up photos might help someone be found.

By now the wall is nearly full, and Bibek estimates he personally put up about 80 percent of the photos there. He still returns daily; regulars now recognise him and ask him to help place photos higher up, which he does by climbing onto someone’s shoulders.

A mother finds out from the TV

His mother, Pramila, initially didn’t know what he was doing; she was busy caring for a patient in someone else’s home. Her employer called her to the television and pointed: her son was on screen, helping post photos of the missing at the hospital. She worried at first that he might have been begging for money, but learned he wasn’t; he’d simply started helping after hearing about the flood.

None of the missing was his own relatives, but he seemed to feel that behind every photo was a family. So he kept going back every day. When people offered him money, he initially refused; later, some began slipping money into his pocket anyway.

Once his mother learned of this, she was worried that a 12-year-old spending his days at the hospital among strangers could be at risk. She told him not to accept money or food from strangers, warning that someone could lure him away. Still, alongside her worry, she felt proud; he had seen others’ suffering and wanted to act.

“I didn’t teach him this,” she says. “Children learn these things on their own.”

Family background

Pramila, 42, is originally from Lamjung but has no permanent home there since her ancestral land sits on government property. She came to Kathmandu years ago for treatment after developing a health condition, and after recovering, chose to stay rather than return to a village with no work opportunities. She built connections doing domestic and caregiving work, eventually brought her family to Kathmandu, and the family found a room in the alley behind the teaching hospital.

Life was becoming more stable until, about a year and a half ago, her husband Hari suffered a sudden stroke. He was treated at Bir Hospital, partly free of cost given the family’s circumstances. He survived but can no longer work as before and cannot manage household responsibilities, so the burden has fallen on Pramila. She earns roughly 18,000–22,000 rupees a month between two caregiving jobs, most of which goes to rent, food, her husband’s medicine, and her children’s schooling. Some days there isn’t enough to eat.

Where is Bibek’s childhood?

While his peers play, use phones, and enjoy outings with parents, Bibek’s home has other pressing needs ahead of leisure. His father is unwell, his mother works all day, and three of his sisters are already married. Given the family’s financial hardship, Bibek seems to have grown up faster than his years, understanding early that money doesn’t come easily, that people should help each other in hardship, and that money others give isn’t always his to keep.

For Pramila, what her son is doing matters more than money or praise.

“Right now, flood victims need even five rupees,” she says. “Even a small snack given in kindness matters. If we can’t give money like others, maybe someone can find their family through the photo my son put up.”

She reflects that things might be different if he’d been born into wealth, but adds that he was born into a poor household; some days there’s food, some days there isn’t.

Even so, growing up amid hardship, Bibek has learned to see others’ pain. No one in his own family went missing in the flood, but other families’ loved ones did. He went to the hospital for them, put up photos, and helped in the search for people, seemingly hoping some family would find their missing person through his efforts- a lesson drawn from his own family’s experience of how much someone’s support matters in hard times.

title.rendered: Nagdhunga-Naubise road section sinks, traffic restricted

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

A section of the Nagdhunga-Naubise road has sunk near Patleban, close to Nagdhunga, the Department of Roads in Dhading said.

According to Arjun Prasad Aryal, an engineer at the Department of Roads, traffic is currently being operated in one direction after the road sank.

Only vehicles carrying petroleum products are being allowed to use the affected route, Aryal said.

Other vehicles travelling along the route are being prepared to be diverted through the tunnel, he said.

Aryal said the road may have sunk after an old retaining wall collapsed.

“The wall along the road was very old. The road may have sunk after the old wall collapsed. However, we will know the exact cause only after a technical team studies the site,” he said.

A technical team from the Department of Roads has already reached the site to assess the damage, Aryal said.

title.rendered: Ice mass that triggered Bhotekoshi flood estimated at 25 million cubic metres

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

Experts studying the glacier collapse believed to have triggered the devastating Bhotekoshi flood estimate that around 25 million cubic metres of snow and ice fell nearly 2,000 metres from the northern Langtang region.

The massive icefall is believed to have generated an impact comparable to a powerful explosion, contributing to the unusually destructive flood that swept through the Lhende Khola and the Bhotekoshi river system.

Prof Dr Ranjan Kumar Dahal, a geologist at Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Geology, is part of a team studying the glacier collapse and subsequent flooding.

“Even using a very conservative estimate based on satellite data, around 25 million cubic metres of snow and ice appear to have fallen,” Dahal told Onlinekhabar. “The energy generated when that mass fell about 2,000 metres would have had an impact similar to a bomb blast.”

According to Dahal, the impact was also recorded as equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake.

An unusually powerful ice avalanche

Dahal and scientists from Tongji University in Shanghai, the University of Cambridge, King’s College London and the University of Padua in Italy had already been studying changes taking place in the Himalayan region for about a year.

Their research included monitoring supraglacial lakes—small pools that form on glaciers—and other changes in the region above Rasuwa.

A supraglacial lake in the Pyurepu area had burst last year, contributing to flooding in the Bhotekoshi. The research team continued monitoring the region, and some of its members turned their attention to the glacier collapse after the latest disaster.

Satellite data indicates that the main ice avalanche was about 1.3 kilometres long and swept through an area measuring roughly 500 to 800 metres downhill.

The exact thickness of the collapsed mass is still being studied, but researchers estimate it may have been around 60 to 70 metres thick.

Based on different measurements, the total volume could be as high as 40 million cubic metres. Some preliminary estimates by other experts have put the figure at up to 100 million cubic metres.

Dahal, however, is using the more conservative estimate of 25 million cubic metres for now.

That volume would be enough to fill London’s Wembley Stadium around 22 times and is roughly 10 times the volume of Egypt’s Great Pyramid.

“This was not simply a block of ice falling downhill,” Dahal said. “It had effects similar to a powerful explosion. Witnesses themselves described it as sounding like an explosion.”

The force sent water, gases, rocks and ice rapidly downstream towards the confluence area near the Rasuwagadhi border point.

CCTV footage released from the Chinese side shows a powerful surge of water and debris rushing down from above, striking a hillside behind the Kerung customs and immigration office and damaging the structure.

Flood moved at different speeds

Some experts estimate that the flood travelled the roughly 12-kilometre stretch between the glacier collapse and the confluence at Rasuwagadhi at speeds of up to 120 kilometres per hour.

Unlike a conventional river flood, the event involved a rapidly moving mixture of water, rocks, debris and ice.

That unusual character led witnesses and others to describe it as an “aerial tsunami” or “Himalayan tsunami”.

Dahal says the speed and destructive potential of the rock-and-ice avalanche would have been difficult to anticipate.

There is little visual material from the upper section between Lhende Khola and Rasuwagadhi because of the lack of human activity in the area. Videos from areas downstream of Rasuwagadhi, however, show the flood moving with such force that the entire river corridor appears covered in mist and debris.

Dahal believes the flow began slowing after reaching Rasuwagadhi. The avalanche was moving at high speed after hitting the ground and generating a powerful surge, but its speed gradually decreased as it reached flatter terrain around Betrawati, Trishuli and Devighat.

Two new lakes formed

Satellite images show that a small lake has formed at the site where the main ice mass came crashing down. Chinese experts have referred to it as Barrier Lake-2.

Another elongated lake, known as Barrier Lake-1, formed alongside the Lhende Khola. It later filled and caused another flood in the Bhotekoshi two days ago. The Chinese government has since said that lake has emptied.

Dahal believes the initial ice avalanche may have swept up surrounding water and additional snow and ice as it moved downhill.

Videos of another landslide appearing to occur several hours after the initial event were also circulated on social media.

According to Dahal, another smaller landslide occurred at the same location two days later.

The research team is now analysing satellite and modelling data to determine the precise size and movement of the ice mass before the collapse.

“We plan to make some findings public over the next two or three weeks,” Dahal said.

Ground temperatures show sharp fluctuations

Researchers are also examining whether changing temperatures may have contributed to instability in the Langtang region.

Dahal says satellite data indicates that the ground surface around Langtang has been experiencing repeated periods of warming and cooling.

Data from the ERA-5 satellite system, which monitors temperature around two metres above the ground, shows temperatures in the past two years have been higher than the average recorded over the previous 25 years.

According to data released by Dahal, temperatures in the Langtang area have fluctuated by as much as 20 degrees Celsius—from around minus 12°C at some points to as high as 8°C at others.

There is currently no weather or environmental monitoring station in the area dedicated to continuously tracking conditions around Langtang. The lack of infrastructure has also limited the availability of ground-level data and early warning systems.

Researchers are therefore relying heavily on satellite observations to understand the changes taking place in the region.

“The data shows considerable fluctuations in temperature,” Dahal said. “We are studying what impact those repeated periods of warming and cooling may have had on the snow and glaciers, particularly their stability and movement.”

title.rendered: LPG shortage worsens as flood-hit roads disrupt supply to Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The shortage of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) in Kathmandu and several other parts of Nepal is worsening after the Bhotekoshi flood damaged key road links used to transport cooking gas into the capital.

The flood on August 26 caused severe damage along the Trishuli River corridor, including at Krishnabhir in Dhading, where a section of the Prithvi Highway was washed away. The highway is one of the main routes connecting Kathmandu with the southern plains, where LPG is refilled and transported to the capital.

With the main highway blocked, large LPG bullets have been unable to reach Kathmandu, disrupting the normal supply chain.

The shortage, however, predates the latest road disruption. Consumers in Kathmandu and other districts say they have been struggling to obtain LPG for weeks, with some reporting that they have gone without a cylinder for up to a month.

At dealers in areas such as Chabahil, Banasthali and Anamnagar, consumers say they are being told to wait without a clear indication of when new supplies will arrive.

“I haven’t got gas for 10-12 days,” Chabahil resident Shyam Dumre said. “They don’t even take our names at the dealer. They just say to come when the gas arrives.”

The shortage has particularly affected people living alone and students who rely entirely on LPG for cooking. A student in Bhaktapur said he had been without gas for a week and was now alternating between eating at friends’ rooms and restaurants.

In Gorkha, residents of Siranchok Rural Municipality-4 placed empty cylinders on the road in protest, saying they had been facing a shortage since June.

Alternative supply routes being used

Following the disruption, the Nepal Oil Corporation and LPG industry association have been trying to maintain supplies through alternative routes.

Empty cylinders from Kathmandu are being transported by small and medium-sized trucks to LPG plants in the southern plains, including Chitwan, Dhanusha, Bara, Parsa, Makwanpur and Nawalparasi. The cylinders are refilled there and brought back to Kathmandu.

The problem is that the alternative roads cannot handle the same volume of traffic as the Prithvi Highway.

The Tribhuvan Rajpath and Kanti Lokpath have been used to bring LPG into Kathmandu, but both are narrower and vulnerable to landslides. Authorities have introduced one-way, alternating traffic in some sections to manage congestion and reduce the risk of accidents.

Further landslides on the alternative routes have also disrupted movement.

Nepal LPG Industry Association president Diwan Chand said gas was available at plants but could not be transported efficiently to the market.

“Gas is being filled at plants in Chitwan, Nawalparasi and Parsa, but the roads are not yet in a condition to bring it here,” Chand said.

According to the association, a small truck can carry only around 400 to 450 cylinders. Kathmandu requires around 40,000 cylinders a day, meaning thousands of additional vehicle trips would be required to meet demand using smaller vehicles.

“If we bring only 10,000 cylinders a day, we need around 25 trucks. To take empty cylinders out and bring filled ones back, we would need around 50 trucks,” Chand said.

He said around 100 LPG bullets are currently stuck in Kathmandu, preventing them from returning to plants to collect new supplies.

Industry says shortage is also linked to earlier supply problems

Gas traders say the current crisis cannot be attributed entirely to the damaged roads.

Consumers have reported shortages for several months, while gas dealers in Kathmandu have increasingly been operating with little or no stock.

The LPG industry association says there had also been some disruption in imports from India earlier, although supplies have since improved.

At the same time, industry representatives say the immediate crisis is now transportation.

Nepal Gas operator Gokul Bhandari said the company’s Balaju plant has effectively stopped operating because LPG bullets have not been able to reach Kathmandu.

“There are no gas bullets coming to Balaju. Without gas, there is nothing to fill into cylinders, so the plant is currently closed,” Bhandari said.

The company is now trying to refill cylinders in Chitwan and transport them to Kathmandu.

Oil Corporation: Gas is available, roads are the problem

The Nepal Oil Corporation disputes the characterization of the current situation as a shortage of LPG itself.

Corporation executive director Nagendra Shah said there has been no disruption in LPG imports from India and that sufficient gas is available.

According to Shah, the main problem is the inability to transport the gas through damaged roads.

“Now the problem is not gas; it is the road and transportation,” Shah said, adding that LPG was previously being transported over relatively short distances but that damaged roads have made the journey much more difficult.

He said LPG is currently being refilled outside Kathmandu and that supplies are expected to begin reaching the capital through alternative routes.

The corporation says supplies in most provinces remain normal and that the disruption is concentrated around areas affected by the flood and road damage.

However, LPG traders warn that the alternative routes alone cannot meet Kathmandu’s daily demand.

For consumers, the distinction between a supply shortage and a transport problem makes little difference. With empty cylinders accumulating at homes and dealers unable to provide a clear delivery date, many households are already struggling to cook.

Unless the damaged road links are restored or a much larger alternative transportation system is put in place, consumers in Kathmandu and other affected areas are likely to face continued LPG shortages in the coming days.

title.rendered: New track to be opened above Krishnabhir to restore Prithvi Highway

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 2

The Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport has decided to open a new track above Krishnabhir to restore traffic along the Prithvi Highway.

A meeting held on Tuesday to discuss the immediate operation of the highway and short- and long-term solutions decided to begin work immediately to restore the supply chain between the disaster-affected areas and Kathmandu.

Under the plan, a structure will be built above the gabion breast wall at Krishnabhir to allow vehicles to pass. Sacrificial gabion boxes will also be installed, while boulders will be dropped down from the hillside as part of the effort to create a temporary route.

For a long-term solution, the Department of Roads will study options including a tunnel, soil nailing and sheet piling at Krishnabhir.

The ministry has also decided to immediately study the possibility of constructing a tunnel or bypass road as an alternative to the current section and establish an alternative road by the end of the current fiscal year.

The Nepal Geotechnical Society will provide technical expertise for the studies and, if necessary, sign a memorandum of understanding with the Department of Roads.

The highway section at Krishnabhir was severely damaged after the Bhote Koshi flood caused the Trishuli River to swell and eroded the road from below, disrupting a key route into Kathmandu.

title.rendered: Foreign rescue teams join efforts, but trapped Rasuwa workers remain out of reach after a week

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Seven days after a devastating flood swept through the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridor, rescue teams are still struggling to reach workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

Families and project officials say rescue efforts have been slowed by difficult terrain, mud and debris inside the tunnels, and delays in bringing the heavy equipment needed to clear access routes.

At the Trishuli 3B hydropower project, 198 employees and workers remain out of contact following the flood.

Bibek Pandey, whose father Kamal Pandey, a team leader and engineer at the project, is among those missing, said the family had been waiting for a stronger rescue operation since the disaster.

“We have been here since Friday, appealing to the government. The government is trying, but it does not feel like enough,” Pandey said.

According to him, the family and project officials had been trying to bring an excavator to the site since Friday, but the machine only arrived on Monday.

Officials initially said the area was covered in deep mud and could not be accessed. A reconnaissance on Monday, however, found a possible route into the site.

Pandey said a larger rescue operation was now needed, with 200 to 300 personnel and several excavators deployed simultaneously.

The first 72 hours after a tunnel accident are generally considered critical for rescue. However, a week after the flood, authorities have yet to successfully reach those believed to be trapped inside several hydropower tunnels.

Rescue teams face mud, debris and blocked access

At the Chilime Hydropower Project, project chief executive officer Bhairaja Maharjan said technical workers were still waiting to be rescued.

The Nepali Army and an Indian Army team entered the tunnel to assess the situation, but thick mud and debris have prevented further progress.

“The army teams went into the tunnel yesterday and today, but mud has entered the tunnel. Excavators and other equipment needed to remove it have still not reached the site,” Maharjan said.

He said only small amounts of mud and debris had so far been removed.

“There is an ocean of it there. The work done so far is like removing one litre of water,” he said.

A body recovered from the Chilime tunnel was also not that of any of the project’s missing employees, according to Maharjan.

At the privately operated Langtang Hydropower Project, the Nepali Army team entered around 100 metres into the tunnel on Monday before being stopped by a large boulder.

Project promoter Bijayman Bhattarai said the army had asked for equipment to clear the obstruction but the necessary machinery had yet to reach the site.

“We proposed a joint rescue operation once the equipment is taken there,” he said.

Bhattarai said it was unusual that no successful rescue had been carried out even seven days after the disaster.

Rescue at Upper Trishuli-1 also continues

At the 216 MW Upper Trishuli-1 project, 573 people remain out of contact, according to project sources.

The government gave permission on Tuesday for some rescue equipment to be transported from Kathmandu, but heavy machinery such as excavators has still not reached the project site.

Chinese and Nepali Army teams have entered through an access tunnel to assess conditions and search for missing workers.

Rescue teams have also been working at Upper Trishuli-3A, where they are trying to create an alternative route into the tunnel.

An engineer involved in the operation said a location had finally been identified where equipment could be taken inside.

A Bobcat machine is being brought to the site in an attempt to clear a path into the tunnel.

The flood damaged 12 hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. According to figures provided by the projects, 894 employees and workers remain out of contact, although it is not yet known how many are actually trapped inside tunnels.

Based on information from the projects, officials estimate that around 600 people could be inside the affected tunnel systems.

Calls grow for wider participation in rescue

Questions have also been raised over why the government did not bring in more domestic and international rescue expertise earlier.

India and China offered rescue personnel and equipment immediately after the disaster, while South Korea also prepared to send a rescue team.

However, foreign rescue teams were only allowed to begin operations several days after the disaster.

Domestic rescue groups and technical organisations have also complained that they were kept on standby despite offering assistance.

Tulsi Gurung, president of the Nepal National Mountain Guide Rescue Association, said his team had sought permission to participate in rescue operations from the day of the disaster.

He said the team had expertise in rope rescue, helicopter long-line rescue and accessing difficult terrain, and was ready with the necessary equipment.

“Every hour is important in rescue operations,” Gurung said, urging authorities to immediately mobilise Nepal’s available technical rescue and long-line rescue specialists.

The Nepal Engineers’ Association has similarly criticised the delay and said engineers and technical personnel offered by the association had not been adequately involved.

Association president Subash Chandra Baral said the organisation had been coordinating with the government to provide technical assistance but had not been given sufficient opportunity to contribute.

According to Baral, the government initially placed tunnel rescue at a lower priority while focusing on other rescue operations.

Private hydropower companies now allowed to join

The government had initially adopted a single-command system under which the Nepali Army led rescue operations at the affected hydropower projects.

Project operators were not allowed to independently conduct rescue operations.

After seven days without the expected results, however, the government has now asked hydropower companies to join the search and rescue effort with their own technical personnel and equipment.

Nepali Army spokesperson Rajaram Basnet said the army had not withdrawn from the operations and that private project promoters had been asked to work alongside the military.

“We have asked the private-sector promoters to join us,” Basnet said.

He said the army was continuing to coordinate with project officials at sites including Rasuwa­gadhi, Langtang and Chilime.

The continuing rescue effort comes amid uncertainty over the fate of hundreds of workers in the affected hydropower projects.

For families like the Pandeys, however, the focus remains simple: reaching the tunnels as quickly as possible and finding out whether their missing relatives are still alive.
