title.rendered: Nearly 1.6 million people affected by Bhotekoshi floods, first govt situation report says

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Nearly 1.6 million people have been affected by the August 26 glacial avalanche and subsequent floods near the Nepal-China border, according to the government’s first situation report on the disaster.

The report, released Tuesday by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said the floods caused extensive loss of life and property along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor.

Rasuwa and Nuwakot have been classified as the worst-affected districts, while Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan have been listed as moderately affected.

Deaths and missing people

The disaster has so far claimed 987 confirmed lives, according to the authority.

Chitwan has recorded the highest number of deaths at 321, followed by Nawalparasi East with 216, Nawalparasi West with 170, Nuwakot with 95, Gorkha with 65, Dhading with 55, Tanahun with 38 and Rasuwa with 27.

Reports from 62 districts put the number of people missing at 3,916.

Of those reported missing, 62 percent are domestic tourists and groups including Nepali nationals, 17 percent are government employees and 15 percent are foreign nationals.

More than 11,800 rescued

A total of 11,814 people have been rescued so far, including 253 foreign nationals, the authority said.

At least 3,702 people have been rescued by air, with 573 helicopter flights carried out as part of the operation.

A total of 21,011 security personnel have been deployed for rescue operations — 8,896 from the Nepali Army, 7,912 from Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force.

International teams from India, China and South Korea have also been deployed alongside Nepali teams for search and rescue operations.

A total of 279 injured people have received treatment at various health facilities. Of them, 79 remain under treatment, 168 have been discharged and three have died while receiving treatment.

The Nepali Army has also provided medical treatment to an additional 2,740 people in affected areas.

Roads, bridges and buildings damaged

The floods completely destroyed 41 concrete bridges, while four others were damaged.

In Nuwakot alone, 1,267 houses were completely destroyed and another 1,253 partially damaged, according to preliminary figures.

Satellite mapping shows that 4,689 buildings in the flood-affected areas of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor are at risk, the report said.

In Rasuwa, 3,702 households comprising 14,461 people in the worst-affected Gosaikunda and Aamachhodingmo rural municipalities have been cut off from roads, electricity and communications for six days.

All major highways in Rasuwa remain closed indefinitely. The Trishuli-Mailung-Syafrubesi road section at Khalte in Uttargaya Rural Municipality-5 is completely blocked.

In Nuwakot, traffic along the Tokha-Chhahare road at Ghattikhola has been halted from 10pm to 5am because of the risk of flooding and landslides.

The Pasang Lhamu highway section in Belkotgadhi Municipality-10 is also completely blocked.

The floods damaged 110 Nepal Telecom mobile towers and 78 Ncell towers, according to the report.

Hydropower projects affected

Several hydropower projects have suffered damage, including Rasuwa Gadhi, Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi, Chilime, Langtang Khola, Upper Trishuli-2, Upper Trishuli-1, Mailung Khola, Upper Trishuli-3A, Upper Trishuli-3B, Madhya Trishuli Ganga, Trishuli, Devighat and Super Trishuli.

Hydropower and solar projects with a combined installed capacity of 783.385 megawatts have been affected, along with substations and transmission lines.

Thousands of students affected

A total of 6,901 students at 19 schools in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading have been affected.

Eight schools were completely damaged and another eight partially damaged. Only three schools remain safe.

Health and water infrastructure damaged

The Syafrubesi Health Post, Timure Health Post, Timure Health Desk at Rasuwa Gadhi and Mailung Community Health Unit in Rasuwa were completely destroyed.

The Baireni Hospital in Galchhi and the Charaundi Basic Health Service Centre suffered partial damage.

Two wastewater treatment plants in Dhunge and Bidur, Nuwakot, were completely damaged.

Damage to the Bidur water supply project washed away around 4.5 kilometres of pipeline and three sump wells, affecting about 4,000 households.

The Trishuli Colony, Devighat and Betravati water supply projects were also affected, impacting another 465 households.

National park and agricultural offices damaged

Offices and buildings of Langtang National Park in Timure, Syafrubesi, Mailung and Bandare were either completely or partially destroyed.

The Agricultural Development Centre in Nuwakot and the Plant Quarantine Office in Timure were also damaged.

title.rendered: How rescue teams are searching for those missing in Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Search and rescue teams are continuing to look for people missing after the devastating Bhotekoshi flood, using a combination of tunnel operations, heavy equipment, air supply and specialist expertise.

Nepali security personnel are working alongside Nepali and foreign tunnel experts at several hydropower projects where people are believed to be trapped or remain unaccounted for.

At the Chilime Hydropower Project, rescue teams have entered about 50 metres into the tunnel and are continuing their search.

At the Langtang Hydropower Project, teams have advanced about 150 metres inside the tunnel, while at Upper Trishuli-1, they have reached about 200 metres.

The search is being carried out under difficult conditions inside the tunnels, with teams working to clear obstructions and reach deeper sections where missing people may be located.

At the Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, rescuers have located the tunnel head. A compressor is being used to pump air into the tunnel, while teams are also working to drain water from inside.

Three excavators are being used to create an alternative access route to the tunnel, allowing rescuers to approach the affected section from another direction.

At the Trishuli-3B Hydropower Project, a team including specialists has located the tunnel entrance and is using an excavator to dig through the area and create access for the rescue operation.

The operations come after a devastating flood swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river system in Rasuwa on August 26, causing extensive loss of life and damage to infrastructure.

With several people still missing, rescue teams continue to work inside the damaged hydropower tunnels, trying different approaches to reach areas that remain inaccessible.

title.rendered: Rs 6.5 billion in bank loans at risk after floods damage four hydropower projects

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Four hydropower projects financed by commercial banks were damaged by the floods of August 26, putting around Rs 6.5 billion in bank loans at risk, according to a preliminary assessment by the Nepal Bankers’ Association.

The association said the 5-megawatt Mailung Khola Hydropower Project in Rasuwa was among the projects damaged by the flood. A consortium led by NMB Bank has provided Rs 258 million in loans to the project.

The 20-megawatt Langtang Khola Hydropower Project was also damaged. Banks have Rs 2.5 billion in loans invested in the project, with Laxmi Sunrise Bank leading the consortium.

The 37-megawatt Trishuli Hydropower Project in Nuwakot was also damaged by the flood that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems. Nabil Bank has Rs 3.3 billion invested in the project.

The flood also damaged the Rasuwa Gadhi Hydropower Project, in which Nabil Bank has provided Rs 498 million in loans.

The association said several other projects with bank financing were not damaged by the flood. They include Blue Energy, Energy Engineering, Hiraratna Hydropower and Prime Hydropower.

Blue Energy, Energy Engineering and Hiraratna Hydropower are currently under construction, with investment from Nepal Investment Mega Bank. Prime Hydropower is a micro-hydropower project being developed with financing from Prabhu Bank.

Because multiple banks have invested in some of the damaged projects, the association said a detailed breakdown of how much each bank has invested is not yet available.

According to the association, there are eight hydropower projects with bank investment across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. Four of the larger projects have been damaged by the Rasuwa flood.

Banks face growing risks in hydropower lending

Banks and financial institutions have been increasing their lending to the energy sector after Nepal Rastra Bank made such investment mandatory.

The central bank requires banks and financial institutions to invest 10 percent of their total loans in the energy sector.

A banker said banks have been lending to the sector despite the risks because of the mandatory lending requirement.

“Hydropower projects require infrastructure to be built in geographically difficult locations, where there is always a risk of natural disasters. That also puts banks’ investments at risk,” the banker said.

The banker said lending to hydropower projects has generally remained limited because such loans are project-based and banks have little incentive to invest in the sector without the central bank’s mandatory lending provision.

The Rasuwa flood has made the risks associated with hydropower investment even clearer, the banker said, adding that lending to the sector could decline in the coming days.

title.rendered: A year before the Rasuwa disaster, a report had warned Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

On July 8, 2025, at around 3am, a sudden flood swept through the Bhotekoshi River — known as the Lhende River on the Chinese side — along the Nepal-China international border in Rasuwa.

The flood left 18 people missing and destroyed the Miteri (Friendship) Bridge. It also caused extensive damage to the Rasuwa-Gadhi Hydropower Project, the Rasuwa Customs Office yard, cargo containers and vehicles held for customs clearance, as well as the Syabrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road section.

Following the disaster, emergency meetings of the Rasuwa District Security Committee and District Disaster Management Committee formed a committee to assess the damage and prepare a preliminary report as soon as possible.

The report was submitted and remains part of government records. But its recommendations and conclusions were not implemented. Instead, the report was left in a drawer.

Within a year, a similar but far more powerful flood struck the same river system, causing an unprecedented loss of life and widespread destruction.

Ashish Gajurel, chairperson of the House of Representatives Development Committee and former executive director of the Nepal Intermodal Transport Development Board, said last year’s disaster had already served as a warning.

“Last year’s flood had already given a strong warning to the customs point and settlements in the surrounding areas. Perhaps we failed to take it seriously,” Gajurel said.

What did the report warn?

The report said the nature of last year’s flood showed the need to consider the possibility of sudden floods of this kind when building settlements and infrastructure along riverbanks.

It warned that modern technology and precautionary measures were needed to protect lives and property from floods triggered by glacial lakes, supraglacial lakes, rising temperatures caused by climate change, accelerated snowmelt, extreme rainfall and large landslides along rivers.

The report also said Nepal needed to develop the technology, infrastructure and early warning systems necessary to forecast such disasters and make them more predictable, which could help reduce loss of life and property.

Cross-border warning system, risk assessment recommended

The report called for cooperation between Nepal and China to establish a cross-border early warning system in high-risk areas along glaciers and rivers located near the two countries’ border.

Such a system could provide advance warning of floods, glacial lake outburst floods and other potential disasters, helping reduce casualties and damage, the report said.

It also recommended scientific mapping, monitoring and risk assessment of glacial lakes along both banks of the Bhotekoshi and its tributaries.

For high-risk glacial lakes, the report recommended long-term measures to reduce the risk of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), including water drainage structures and surveillance equipment.

Climate risk assessment for riverside settlements and infrastructure

For long-term risk reduction, the report recommended that the government adopt a policy requiring scientific assessments of potential risks from climate change, floods, glacial floods and other natural disasters before constructing any infrastructure, implementing projects or developing settlements along riverbanks.

It also recommended that hydropower projects under construction and in operation manage waste materials generated by their projects in a way that does not create risks in other areas, as required by their environmental impact assessments.

Assess risks before rebuilding the dry port

The report recommended that Nepal take up with the Chinese government the upgrading of the Syabrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road, a key northern trade route that was being prepared for upgrading with Chinese assistance.

It also called for a detailed geological and infrastructure study of the Rasuwa-Gadhi area, including an assessment of the post-flood situation, before reconstruction begins.

The report specifically recommended that reconstruction be started only after assessing the findings of such a study.

Plan relocation of settlements from Timure to Betrawati

The report recommended preparing and implementing plans to relocate settlements devastated by the flood.

It identified settlements along the river from Rasuwagadhi to Betrawati — including Timure, Syabrubesi, Mailung, Pairobesi, Shantibazar and Khalte — as being at high risk of flooding.

It called for scientific studies to assess the risks faced by these settlements and for relocation plans to be developed and implemented based on priority, moving people to safer areas.

Strengthen emergency response and install early warning systems

The report also called for strengthening the capacity of local administrations, security agencies, government offices, local governments and communities involved in disaster management, including by equipping them with adequate resources.

It recommended installing sirens in settlements and structures along rivers and establishing early warning systems using mobile messages, FM radio and other communication channels.

It also called for disaster risk reduction measures to be made mandatory in development and construction plans.

In addition, the report recommended government-supported insurance schemes targeting small businesses and farmers against natural disasters such as floods, landslides and glacial floods.

A warning left unheeded

The government had prepared the report itself and received it in July last year. Yet its recommendations remained unimplemented for a year.

Construction and other human activity continued around the river system without the recommended risk assessments and safeguards.

The consequences were seen in the latest Bhotekoshi flood.

The report, submitted last year, had concluded: “If these recommendations can be implemented from both immediate and long-term perspectives, it can be expected to build a disaster management system not only for Rasuwa district but for the entire Himalayan region.”

A year later, that warning has taken on a far more urgent meaning.

title.rendered: Rescue efforts continue across Rasuwa and Nuwakot as 2,251 remain missing

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 1

Search and rescue operations are continuing across Rasuwa and Nuwakot following the devastating Bhotekoshi flood on August 26, with security forces, Nepal Electricity Authority personnel and technical teams from friendly countries deployed at multiple locations.

The District Administration Office, Nuwakot, released an updated account on Tuesday outlining the progress of search, rescue, road clearance and relief operations.

Search continues at hydropower projects

At the Upper Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, around 90 personnel from the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Electricity Authority are involved in the search. After locating the tunnel head, teams drilled through around 10 metres of mud and created an opening into the inlet. However, a large volume of water began flowing through the opening, prompting teams to drill at another location.

At Trishuli-3B, 47 personnel have been deployed. An excavator was airlifted to the site, with 18 helicopter flights conducted so far.

At Upper Trishuli-1, foreign technical experts are working under the leadership and coordination of the Nepal Army. Search teams have advanced around 300 metres from the tunnel head at Haku and around 250 metres from the tunnel tail at Mailung. Progress has been hampered by three to four metres of thick mud inside the tunnels.

At the Chilime Hydropower Project, Nepal Army personnel, foreign technical experts and the CSSR team are conducting searches up to around 55 metres inside the tunnel.

Search efforts have also reached around 200 metres at Rasuwa­gad­hi Hydropower Project and around 150 metres in the Langtang area.

Roads remain a major challenge

Repair work is continuing along the Galchhi–Devighat road, including at the Big Khola bridge and areas covered by mud.

A survey has begun to reconnect the Bailey bridge at Tadi Khola, which was washed away by the flood. Repairs are also continuing along the Dhunge Bazaar–Tirtire Bhir section.

Around 2.8 kilometres of road near Betrawati remains to be repaired. Of that, around 300 metres was completely washed away by the river, prompting authorities to look for an alternative route.

Small vehicles are operating through Bahubesi–Lachyang–Parchyang–Dhunche and Dhikure–Fedibesi–Chogate–Borbanjyang–Betravati–Rasuwa.

Efforts are also underway to open the Chogate–Borbanjyang–Dandakhar­ka–Patikharka–Bhorle route to larger vehicles. Heavy machinery has been deployed along the Bidur-11 Thapatar–Betravati road.

The Colony–Budhisinghghat road is currently operational.

Relief reaches dozens of shelters

Dozens of holding shelters are operating in Bidur and Belkotgadhi municipalities.

Relief has reached 500 people at the Colony Covered Hall/Bhairum Secondary School shelter for those affected in Trishuli Bazaar, although no medical team is currently present there.

Other shelters have also received relief, including 272 people at Mahadev Secondary School in Belkotgadhi-7, 158 at the safe house/cremation building serving Trishuli Dhunge and Simchaur, and 159 at Chandrajyoti Secondary School in Devighat.

Relief has also reached 148 people at the covered hall in Battar, 100 at Trishuli Basic School in Bidur-9, 120 at Shukshana Secondary School in Bidur-9, 103 at the Ayurveda Alternative Medical Centre in Devighat and 93 at Sundari Kyaurini Secondary School in Betravati-Bhaise.

Other shelters receiving relief include Indrayani Basic School in Bidur-1, the Ranabhuwaneshwari Secondary School/Ward Office in Devighat Sitkhali, the library and health post in Tupche, and the health post at Betravati in the Nuwakot Durbar area.

The district administration said relief has reached most shelters, although only a limited number have medical teams.

Water and body management

Drinking water is being supplied in Devighat through a borewell using a generator, while tankers are being used to supply water at various locations in Bidur.

Relief distribution is being coordinated through a one-door mechanism involving the Home Ministry, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the District Administration Office, security agencies and local governments.

By August 31, relief had been collected through 219 organisations and distributed at 131 locations, according to the district administration. The figures for collections and distributions as of September 1 are still being updated.

Relief supplies were airlifted to 9 locations in 12 flights on August 31 and to another 8 locations in 11 flights by 10 a.m. on September 1.

Security agencies are continuing to search for bodies at 30 locations along both banks of the Trishuli, from Kolpu Khola to Mailung Shanti Bazaar.

3,162 rescued, 2,251 still missing

According to the district administration, 3,162 people had been rescued by 10 a.m. on September 1. They include 2,908 Nepali citizens—1,712 men and 1,196 women—and 254 foreign nationals, including 231 men and 23 women.

A total of 151 bodies, including partial remains, have been recovered. Of them, 51 have been identified, while the identities of 100 remain unknown.

The number of injured has reached 61.

Meanwhile, 2,251 people remain missing. The figure includes 1,615 Nepali men, 407 Nepali women and 55 people comprising foreign nationals and unidentified persons.

Compared with the period from August 26 to 31, an additional 23 people were rescued and 21 bodies recovered in the 24 hours up to 10 a.m. on September 1, according to the district administration.

title.rendered: Govt explores drilling from above to reach people trapped in hydropower tunnels

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Home Minister Sudan Gurung said the government is exploring whether drilling from above the tunnels could provide another way to reach people trapped inside hydropower projects following the Bhotekoshi flood.

Gurung made the remarks during a press briefing by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on the flood response in Rasuwa.

“Our new idea is to see whether we can dig from a point above and drill through to create another possibility of reaching them. The state is making efforts in that direction,” Gurung said.

He said the government had not given up hope of rescuing those trapped inside the tunnels.

“We have still not lost hope. We are also considering whether we can enter from above and whether they may have survived by drinking the water there. Our security agencies are still working at the site,” he said.

Search and rescue teams have been struggling to reach people trapped or missing inside hydropower tunnels after the Bhotekoshi flood.

title.rendered: Lamichhane, Chinese ambassador discuss support after Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) chair Rabi Lamichhane and Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming held a meeting on Wednesday to discuss the devastation caused by the Bhotekoshi flood and China’s support for Nepal’s response.

The meeting was held at Lamichhane’s residence in Budhanilkantha.

During the meeting, Ambassador Maoming expressed sorrow over the damage caused by the flood and said China was ready to provide Nepal with assistance in any way needed.

Maoming also conveyed that China would stand with Nepal through the search and rescue efforts and reconstruction. She said China was committed to helping strengthen Nepal’s early warning systems.

According to Lamichhane’s secretariat, Maoming said China had been providing necessary support, including rescuers and DNA experts, since shortly after the disaster and would continue such assistance for as long as needed.

Lamichhane thanked China for its ongoing support.

He also urged China to further strengthen and improve coordination in Nepal’s disaster early warning system.

title.rendered: Unidentified flood victims’ bodies being buried in Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Bodies of people killed in the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa and whose identities remain unknown are being buried in Kathmandu as authorities struggle to manage the large number of recovered bodies.

Several bodies were buried at a government forest area in Gokarneshwor, Kathmandu, on Tuesday afternoon. Forty-six bodies had also been buried at the same site on Monday night.

Bodies recovered between Fishling and Golaghat whose identities could not be established have also been managed in Chitwan.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 987 bodies had been recovered as of Tuesday afternoon, of which around 100 had been brought to Kathmandu.

The government is managing unidentified and unclaimed bodies in accordance with the Unidentified and Unclaimed Bodies Management Directive.

The directive requires authorities to prepare records of recovered bodies, conduct preliminary identification, use additional methods to establish identities, document confirmed identities, maintain records and place identifying markers before the bodies are buried.

title.rendered: South Korea to send 44-member disaster relief team to Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

A 44-member South Korean disaster relief team will arrive in Nepal on Wednesday to assist with search, rescue and relief efforts following the devastating floods.

The Korea Disaster Relief Team (KDRT) includes officials from South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), firefighters and other personnel, The Korea Times reported.

The team will depart South Korea on Tuesday night aboard a KC-330 transport aircraft and is scheduled to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday morning.

The team will bring 700 pieces of equipment and five search-and-rescue dogs to support operations in the flood-affected areas.

According to The Korea Times, the team will remain in Nepal for around 10 days to assist with rescue and relief operations.

Nine South Korean nationals remain missing following the floods.

title.rendered: Japan PM urges Nepal to step up search for 5 missing Japanese nationals

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held a telephone conversation on Tuesday over the devastating floods and landslides in Nepal’s border region with China.

The conversation lasted around 10 minutes, according to Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

At the beginning of the call, Takaichi expressed deep condolences for those who lost their lives in the floods and landslides on August 26, and extended her sympathies to bereaved families and those affected.

Recalling that both Japan and Nepal face high risks from natural disasters, Takaichi said Japan would stand firmly with its long-standing friend Nepal during the crisis.

She also urged Prime Minister Shah to provide maximum assistance in the immediate search and rescue of five Japanese nationals who remain missing.

Japan to send relief supplies and emergency team

Takaichi said emergency relief supplies, including tents and blankets that Japan has pledged to Nepal, would arrive soon.

She also said Japan was preparing to provide additional assistance through international organisations and send an international emergency relief team to Nepal, according to the Japanese Foreign Ministry.

In response, Prime Minister Shah briefed his Japanese counterpart on the extent of the disaster and the government’s ongoing search, rescue and relief efforts.

Shah expressed his deep gratitude to the Japanese government and people for their sympathy, assistance and solidarity, according to a statement issued by Japan’s Foreign Ministry.

title.rendered: Rights activists criticise federal government for sidelining local governments in flood response

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Thirty-one civil rights activists have criticised the federal government for sidelining local governments in rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts following the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers.

In a joint statement issued on Tuesday, the activists said disaster management and rehabilitation efforts could not be effective without the participation of local governments.

Criticism of federal role and one-door system

The activists accused the federal government of failing to play an effective coordinating and responsible role in search, rescue and relief distribution, while also pointing to administrative hurdles and delays.

They said the Nepal Army‘s controlling role in the collection and distribution of relief could further burden flood victims.

The statement also criticised the government’s “one-door system”, saying it had not been effective and that the system should not be used to restrict the role of civil society organisations.

Recalling the effective role played by local governments during the COVID-19 pandemic, they called for local governments to be given a leading role in the current disaster response.

Call for parliamentary and all-party mechanisms

The activists called for a special mechanism to ensure that funds collected in the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund are managed transparently, responsibly, accountably and fairly.

They also suggested that an all-party political mechanism could help make disaster management more effective and transparent.

They urged the Speaker of the House of Representatives to take the initiative to form a parliamentary committee to monitor the overall process.

Concerns over scale of damage and public health

The statement said the August 26 flood had killed hundreds of Nepali and foreign nationals, left thousands missing and caused damage worth billions of rupees.

Citing data from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the activists said that by the morning of August 31, around 900 bodies had been recovered, while thousands had been injured or remained missing.

Nearly 21,000 security personnel have been mobilised for rescue and relief operations, according to the statement.

The flood also swept away around a dozen hydropower projects with a combined capacity of about 900 MW, 50 kilometres of roads, thousands of houses and dozens of concrete bridges.

The activists said the government’s decision to bury unidentified bodies was understandable from a public-health perspective, but stressed that the right of grieving families to mourn must also be respected.

They urged the authorities to take immediate measures to prevent infectious diseases that could spread through contaminated water and decomposing bodies, and to pay particular attention to the health and psychosocial needs of women, children and senior citizens affected by the disaster.

Call for stronger Nepal-China information mechanism

The activists also called for an integrated information system to prevent the spread of misinformation and urged the government to ensure that domestic and foreign media can report from affected areas without unnecessary restrictions.

They further called for Nepal and China to strengthen the existing cross-border information-sharing mechanism and make it more scientific and effective, citing the risks posed by numerous glacial lakes across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.

The statement was signed by 31 civil rights activists, including Kanak Mani Dixit, Dr Bimala Rai Paudyal, Sushil Pyakurel, Subodh Pyakurel, Dr Gopal Krishna Siwakoti, Shobhakhar Budhathoki, Dr Padma Prasad Khatiwada and Asmita Sapkota.

title.rendered: 204 foreign workers at hydropower projects missing after Bhotekoshi floods, most of them Chinese

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

A total of 204 foreign workers employed at hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot remain out of contact following the floods in the Bhotekoshi River, with Chinese nationals accounting for the largest number.

According to available data, 898 workers employed at 12 hydropower projects affected by the floods remain out of contact. Of them, 204 are foreign nationals working with labour permits issued by the Department of Labour and Occupational Safety.

Department spokesperson Maninath Gop said the figure covers only foreign workers with valid labour permits. The department does not yet have details of foreign nationals whose work permit renewals are in process or those working while paying penalties during the renewal process. “Our records show that 204 foreign nationals have work permits. However, we have not yet received records of those whose permits are under process or those working after paying penalties,” Gop said.

According to the department, the largest number of foreign workers who remain out of contact are Chinese nationals employed at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project under the Power Construction Corporation of China.

The department had issued work permits to 121 Chinese nationals for the project, and none of them has been confirmed to be in contact since the floods, according to its records. Around 1,200 people, including Nepali workers, were employed at the project, of whom 557 remain out of contact.

Similarly, 26 foreign nationals working at Upper Trishuli-1 under Doosan Enerbility had obtained work permits. The department has received information that three of them were on leave, while the remaining 23 have not been contacted.

Among the foreign nationals working under Doosan, there is one South Korean, four Indian nationals, one American and one Canadian.

Likewise, 19 foreign nationals had obtained work permits to work on the construction of Nilkantha Model Secondary School in Rasuwa under China Jiangsu International Economic and Technical Cooperation. The department has not received information indicating that they have been contacted.

The department said it has also been unable to establish contact with 12 foreign workers employed at Salasungi Power Private Limited under China International Water and Energy Corporation.

Similarly, 11 Chinese nationals working at the Rasuwa Bhotekoshi Hydropower Project under Sinohydro Bureau 7 had valid work permits and remain out of contact.

Two foreign nationals—one Canadian and one American—working under a joint venture related to the Upper Trishuli-1 project and associated with Nepal Water and Energy Development Company are also on the department’s list of workers who remain out of contact.

The department said six foreign workers from another company, which has an office in Naxal, Kathmandu, and sends workers to field sites in the Trishuli area, are also out of contact. Gop said the company has not provided clear information on whether they had travelled to the field or are in a safe location.

Likewise, four foreign workers employed by HNAOC Shanghai JV are listed as being out of contact. According to the department, the figure of 204 announced so far includes only foreign workers with valid work permits recorded in the government system. Foreign nationals whose permits are being renewed or who are undergoing other administrative processes have not been included.

“Some foreign nationals are in Nepal while their paperwork is being processed. When the process is delayed, companies may continue employing them after paying penalties,” Gop said. “We have not yet received details of such individuals.” The actual number of foreign workers out of contact at flood-affected hydropower projects could therefore be higher than government records currently indicate.

According to the department’s records of valid work permits, Chinese nationals make up the largest number of foreign workers who remain out of contact. However, the exact status of all foreign nationals working at the affected projects remains unclear as updated information has yet to be collected.

title.rendered: Rasuwa floods: 28 missing Jumla residents re-establish contact

content.rendered:
Jumla, September 1

A total of 28 people from Jumla who had been out of contact following the Rasuwa floods have so far re-established contact.

Of the 76 people from Patarasi Rural Municipality who had travelled to Rasuwa for employment, only 23 have so far contacted their families, according to Rural Municipality Chairperson Purna Singh Bohara.

Chief District Officer Tej Prakash Prasai said the names and addresses of 99 people from Jumla who had travelled to Rasuwa for work have been confirmed based on information received from local governments.

Five additional people who had been out of contact have also re-established communication, although their addresses have yet to be verified, he said.

Most of the people from Jumla who travelled to Rasuwa for employment were men.

According to Chief District Officer Prasai, authorities are coordinating with relevant agencies to search for and rescue 71 Jumla residents who remain out of contact.

Relatives of those missing have been appealing through the local administration for intensified search efforts.

—RSS

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi flood estimated to have destroyed around 6,000 homes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The government estimates that around 6,000 private homes were swept away by the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26.

The estimate was made by the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction. According to information shared by departments under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport during a media briefing on Tuesday, damage to private housing alone is estimated at around Rs 12 billion.

The department also estimates that 45 government and public buildings were damaged by the floods. The figures are still being assessed and could change as further assessments are carried out.

The government estimates that at least Rs 900 million would be needed to immediately construct temporary shelters for around 6,000 households, with one temporary shelter required for each affected family.

The scale of the damage is still being assessed as authorities continue relief, rescue and reconstruction efforts in the flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: Government yet to decide how to reopen Krishnabhir section of Prithvi Highway

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Three days after a section of road subsided, the government remains undecided on how to reopen the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir.

The Department of Roads said at a press conference on Tuesday that no final decision had yet been reached on reopening the highway.

According to the department’s Director General, Dr Bijay Jaisi, extensive discussions were held on Tuesday on how to restore the road, but no conclusion has been reached.

The closure of the Prithvi Highway has disrupted road connectivity with western Nepal. An alternative route through the highway connecting Hetauda is currently being used.

Jaisi said a decision on the next course of action at Krishnabhir would be made only after consultations with a geotechnical team. He said authorities would then decide whether to open a new track on the other side of the Trishuli River or adopt another solution.

title.rendered: Salyan families caught between hope and grief after Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Salyan, September 1

For 23-year-old Birendra Rana, the search for his father has taken him from hospitals and police stations in Chitwan and Nuwakot to Rasuwa and Kathmandu. His father, 43-year-old Nim Prakash Rana of Gurudase in Kumakh Rural Municipality-3, has been missing since the devastating Bhotekoshi flood on August 26.

Birendra has searched everywhere he could. He has called relatives, checked lists of injured people and visited hospitals, hoping to find some trace of his father.

“We went to different hospitals thinking he might have been injured. We also went to Rasuwa and Nuwakot. We found nothing,” Birendra said. “Even without knowing whether he was alive, we went from hospital to hospital hoping we might find his body. Our relatives have gone as far as Chitwan and Pokhara. But there is still no information.”

He still hopes his father is alive. But as the days pass, that hope is increasingly mixed with fear.

Birendra’s family is not the only one in Gurudase waiting for answers. Six other men from the village — 60-year-old Durga Bahadur Rana, 40-year-old Ganesh Rana, 25-year-old Nabin Rana, 55-year-old Jhyase Rana, 27-year-old Nandaram Rana and 24-year-old Chitrabahadur Rana — have also been missing since the flood.

All of them had travelled to Rasuwa about a month and a half ago in search of work. Their families have been left waiting for news.

Five members of one family missing

For the family of Salleri in Sharda Municipality-13, Salyan, the flood has brought a particularly painful wait. Five members of the same family have been missing from Timure, Rasuwa, since the disaster.

They are 32-year-old Pramila Budhathoki, 28-year-old Laxmi Budhathoki, 17-year-old Prabin Budhathoki, 39-year-old Rita Budhathoki and 44-year-old Rimbahadur Budhathoki.

Some had been living in Rasuwa for as long as three years, while others had arrived only a year earlier. They had gone there in search of work and opportunities along the China border.

Nisha Khadka Budhathoki has been left without contact with five members of her family at once — her elder sister-in-law, aunt-in-law, younger uncle, younger aunt and brother-in-law.

“We feel that our people are still alive,” Nisha said. “But when we hear that so many bodies have been recovered, we are afraid that they too may have died.”

The family knows that the five had left the room where they were staying after the flood. Since then, however, there has been no word about where they went or what happened to them.

“We hoped they might be somewhere in the forest, but there has been no news for so many days,” Nisha said. “Even if they are alive, we are afraid of what may have happened to them after being exposed to so much water without food or water. It feels like a terrible tragedy has struck our family.”

The family has released their photographs in the hope that someone may have information about their whereabouts.

55 of 59 reported missing still unaccounted for

According to Salyan Chief District Officer Mahendrakumar Sapkota, details of 59 people from the district were reported to the District Police Office as missing following the disaster.

Of them, 55 remain unaccounted for. Four have since made contact.

Since the disaster, various reports have circulated on social media and through other channels claiming that missing people have been found, injured or identified among recovered bodies.

The district administration has urged families not to treat such information as confirmed until it has been verified by the authorities.

Sapkota has also urged families to immediately inform the police or administration if a missing person makes contact or if a body is identified. Such information will help authorities proceed with rescue, relief and compensation-related processes.

Ayush’s first government posting ended in the flood

For some families from Salyan, the wait for a missing relative has already ended in grief.

The body of 21-year-old Ayush Khadka of Bagchaur Municipality-10 was recovered.

But his family could not bring his body home for the final rites. As the body began to deteriorate, he was cremated on Monday at Devghat, at the confluence of the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli rivers.

Ayush had passed the Public Service Commission examination, and his first government posting was at the quarantine office in Timure, Rasuwa, in April.

He had plans for the future. He was preparing to return home to sit for his bachelor’s examination. He had planned to reach Kathmandu on September 3 and return to his home district for the examination on September 7.

The flood on August 26 brought those plans to an end.

A life that made it out of the darkness

While some families continue to search for their loved ones and others have begun mourning them, some survived experiences that could easily have ended differently.

Among them is Sabin Reule of Triveni Rural Municipality-4.

Reule was working inside a hydropower tunnel when conditions suddenly changed. A strong rush of air came through the tunnel, followed shortly by a power outage. The tunnel was plunged into darkness, and it became unclear whether it was safe to exit.

Local residents were also inside the tunnel. When they tried to get out after the lights went off, they discovered that one of the routes had already been blocked.

“While we were working, there was suddenly a rush of air and the power went out. The tunnel became completely dark,” Reule said. “There were local people with us. They had tried to get out as soon as the power went off, but one side of the tunnel had already been blocked. We managed to survive by entering through the other side.”

The Rasuwa flood has not only taken lives and disrupted the livelihoods of people who travelled there from Salyan for work. It has also left families across the district living with uncertainty.

The cooking fires continue to burn in their homes, but there is little peace inside them.

Some families still look toward the door, hoping their loved one might return.

title.rendered: Tunnel rescue efforts continue with little progress after Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Rescue efforts to reach people trapped inside hydropower tunnels following the devastating Bhotekoshi flood have continued, but authorities say there has been little progress so far.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Paudel Chhetri said Tuesday that no significant progress had been reported in the tunnel rescue operations.

Speaking at a press conference, Chhetri said Nepali rescue teams, along with tunnel specialists from India and China, were continuing their efforts despite the difficult terrain and conditions at the affected hydropower projects.

Two 24-member teams from India and a nine-member specialist tunnel rescue team from China have been deployed to the affected hydropower projects.

“The tunnel rescue team has been deployed from the beginning, and tunnel specialists from India and China are also assisting,” Chhetri said. “They are working day and night, overcoming the difficult geography and challenges there. But according to the information we had until a short while ago, there has been no significant progress. They are continuing their efforts.”

The Indian teams are working with the Nepali Army at the Chilime and Langtang hydropower projects, while the Chinese team has been conducting search operations in the Upper Trishuli-3A project area.

A rescue team from South Korea is also preparing to come to Nepal, Chhetri said.

Seven days after the flood, rescue teams have still been unable to reach those believed to be trapped inside tunnels at Chilime, Langtang, Upper Trishuli-3A and Upper Trishuli-3B hydropower projects.

The rescue operations have been complicated by water-filled tunnels, blocked entrances, debris and difficult terrain at the affected project sites.

title.rendered: Rasuwa floods highlight need for climate-resilient infrastructure: Minister Shrestha

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Birajbhakta Shrestha has said the recent Bhotekoshi floods have highlighted the need to prioritise climate-resilient infrastructure in the future.

Speaking at a discussion and assistance handover program with officials of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN) at the ministry in Singha Durbar on Tuesday, Minister Shrestha said future infrastructure must be designed to withstand climate-related disasters while taking the country’s geographical conditions into account.

He said the geographical terrain and adverse weather conditions along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor make the area highly vulnerable to disasters, adding that similar floods in other major corridors of the country could cause enormous damage.

“Considering what happened in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor due to the effects of climate change, one can imagine the scale of destruction if something similar were to occur in our other major corridors,” he said. “After visiting the area, it is clear that its geographical conditions are particularly challenging, along with severe adverse weather conditions. Therefore, we have reached a point where we must carefully consider everything, from climate-resilient structures to other factors, when building infrastructure.” Minister Shrestha said future infrastructure projects must anticipate the potential impacts of climate change and be designed accordingly.

Praising IPPAN for its coordination and cooperation with the government during the disaster, he said continued collaboration was also necessary for policy reforms and exploring future opportunities. “We may have ideological differences and other differences, but at a time like this, we need to send a message, not only nationally but also to the international community, that we are all together,” he said.

He added that the government had called on the private sector to assist in the search and rescue of people believed to be trapped inside tunnels of hydropower projects, stressing that the state’s priorities and response were being applied equally during the crisis.

title.rendered: With drone images, Chinese Ministry of Water Resources says: Glacier still at risk of collapse

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

China’s Ministry of Water Resources says the glaciers around the impact crater formed in Nepal’s Chochen (Bhotekoshi) River remain at risk of further collapse, which could pose a major danger.

Chinese state media CCTV News published this report on Tuesday, citing the ministry.

According to CCTV, the ministry continues consultation and monitoring to assess ongoing risks connected to the mudflow-flood disaster that struck Gyirong (Kerung) County in southwest China’s Xizang (Tibet) Autonomous Region.

According to a recent comparative analysis of remote-sensing images, no significant change has been observed in the water surface area of the 14 previously identified glacial lakes in the Gyirong Zangbo river basin. Those lakes remain largely stable overall.

Based on a drone image taken Tuesday at 5:45 a.m. Nepal time, most of the water that had accumulated in the impact crater at Nepal’s Chochen River has now drained out, and river flow in the downstream areas has returned to normal.

However, the report notes that the risk of the glacier or ice mass around the crater collapsing remains.

title.rendered: China closes Zhangmu port indefinitely, disrupting Nepal-China trade

content.rendered:
Sindhupalchowk, September 1

The Chinese government has informed Nepal that Zhangmu port, near Tatopani along the Nepal-China border, has been closed indefinitely.

According to Tul Bahadur Pandey, a customs officer at the Tatopani Customs Office, the Chinese side informed Nepali authorities of the closure through an email, citing the potential risk of a disaster. “We have received a brief email from the Chinese authorities regarding the closure of the port,” Pandey said. According to him, the email stated: “We have shut Zhangmu port for a while. We will inform you in another email when we reopen it.”

China is believed to have taken the decision amid concerns over possible river-related disasters following the recent floods in the Bhotekoshi River. It has been learned that the Chinese side has already relocated its administrative staff to higher and safer areas. A few days earlier, China had stopped sending containers until September 3, citing construction work in Khasa. Cargo transportation has also been suspended.

The Tatopani border point had been considered an alternative trade route following the devastation of the Rasuwagadhi customs point in the recent floods. The closure of Zhangmu port has further disrupted trade between Nepal and China. The local business community believes that the closure of Zhangmu port, located in Nyalam County of Tibet, could affect supplies to Nepal, particularly with the Dashain and Tihar festivals approaching.

Import and export through the Tatopani border point had remained largely suspended for around 40 days following landslides on the Nepali side on June 25, bringing cross-border supplies to a near standstill. The landslides damaged the road at several locations along the 26-kilometre Bahrabise-Kodari section of the Araniko Highway. The road was temporarily reopened after 40 days following repair work by a team deployed by the Department of Roads.

After the reopening, eight containers entered Nepal through Tatopani on August 28. However, following the closure of Zhangmu port, cargo containers bound for Nepal have reportedly been stranded in Nyalam.

title.rendered: Relief supplies and medicines transported by cable crossing in Nuwakot (Photos)

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, September 1

The devastating floods that swept through the Trishuli River after the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa overflowed on August 26 caused significant loss of life and property in both Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

Many people lost family members and homes, while many others were injured. Those affected are still waiting for relief supplies and medical assistance, along with ongoing treatment.

Floodwaters washed away bridges and roads that residents had regularly used for transportation, leaving many areas along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot resembling riverbeds.

With roads and bridges no longer available, a cable crossing has now been installed to facilitate movement. The cable crossing was set up over the Trishuli River to connect Ward 1 and Ward 9 of Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot.

The crossing was installed on Tuesday morning to make it easier for residents to travel between the two sides of the river. Relief supplies and medicines have also begun to be transported using the cable crossing.

title.rendered: Indra Prasad Gotame: Work is underway in Nuwakot, but not enough is being done in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Although rescue and relief efforts are underway for people affected by the floods in Rasuwa, difficulties have emerged in rescuing those believed to be trapped inside tunnels. The rescue of people believed to be trapped inside hydropower project tunnels has been hampered by a lack of adequate equipment and skilled technical personnel needed to assess conditions inside the tunnels, according to authorities.

Bagmati Province Assembly member Indra Prasad Gotame said more than 300 people are feared to be trapped inside six tunnels in different parts of Rasuwa. “The situation here is quite serious. We have been told that more than 300 people are inside six tunnels in Rasuwa,” said Gotame, who is currently in Dhunche. “The government does not have the technical personnel needed to enter the tunnels, nor does it have the necessary equipment.”

He said the biggest challenge in Rasuwa at present is rescuing those trapped inside the tunnels. “The Army has already rescued the people who survived the floods and were stranded outside. There is no major problem regarding relief here,” Gotame said. “The biggest problem is rescuing the people trapped inside the tunnels.”

Families of people who have been missing since the floods have been urging the government to immediately begin rescue operations to determine whether they are still alive. Gotame said the provincial assembly had also urged the government to deploy skilled technical personnel to assess the situation inside the tunnels. “We made a request to the federal government yesterday,” he said. “We asked it to bring skilled technical personnel along with the necessary equipment and assess the situation inside the tunnels.”

He stressed that efforts similar to those being made to rescue people from the tunnels of the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project should also be undertaken in the tunnels located elsewhere in Rasuwa. “The way they are working on Trishuli 3A and 3B, we want similar efforts to be made in the other five tunnels in Rasuwa,” Gotame said. He said residents and families of those missing in the floods were making the same demand. “Local people and relatives are demanding that those inside the tunnels be brought out so that we can know whether they are alive,” he said. “You could call it a hope or an assumption that they may still be alive, but it is the hope of their families.”

Excerpts from an interview with provincial assembly member Gotame:

The situation here is quite serious. In terms of rescue operations, the Army has already brought out those who survived and were stranded outside. The biggest problem here is rescuing those trapped inside the tunnels. “There is intense pressure from the families of those trapped inside the six tunnels to find out whether they are alive. The government does not have the technical personnel needed to enter the tunnels, nor does it have the equipment.

We requested the federal government yesterday. We asked it to bring skilled technical personnel along with the necessary equipment and assess the situation inside the tunnels. We have been told that more than 300 people are inside the tunnels. The way excavation and rescue operations are being carried out at Trishuli 3A and 3B, similar efforts should be made in the other five tunnels in Rasuwa. Work is underway in the Nuwakot area, but no rescue effort has yet been launched in the tunnels located in Rasuwa.

Residents here are demanding that work in Rasuwa also begin using the same approach adopted at Trishuli 3A and 3B. The relatives of those affected by the floods are making the same demand. There is no major problem with relief here. People who have made it out are not facing that problem. The pressure on the government is to bring out those inside the tunnels and determine whether they are alive. You could call it a hope, but it is the hope of their families.

This is not a problem of relief. The problem is that the government should bring the necessary equipment and skilled technical personnel and begin rescue operations in all five remaining tunnels. It has already been five or six days since the flood. We need to know what has happened to the people inside the tunnels. This is not the time to accuse the government of treating people unequally during a disaster. The government would not deliberately delay operations hoping that people would die. But there have been shortcomings in the way things have been handled, particularly in the division of responsibilities.

The government has assigned the responsibility mainly to the Army. Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force are also there but have not been fully utilised. If the three forces had been given separate responsibilities—for example, assigning the Armed Police Force to rescue operations, the Army to tunnel operations and Nepal Police to distribute relief materials—the problem could have been addressed more efficiently.

That would have helped resolve the major problems. Instead, the responsibility was concentrated in one place, resulting in a single chain of command. That is why there have been some shortcomings. This is the kind of problem we are seeing here.“The federal government has not really coordinated with local governments and the provincial government. We have been saying that during a disaster, it is everyone’s responsibility, and we should not sit back saying that this is someone else’s job.

There has not been much coordination. The responsibility has been given to the Army. Focusing efforts in one place may be appropriate, but there has been a problem with the division of responsibilities, making the response somewhat disorderly. If responsibilities had been divided properly, these concerns would not have arisen.

People suspect that there may be bodies inside houses that have been buried by the floods. They are saying that the buried houses need to be cleared because there could be bodies inside. The government does not have the necessary equipment for that either. Bodies found outside have been collected, but there are also problems managing them.

The government has done what it could for people who were outside. But rescue operations inside the tunnels have not been possible because of the lack of technical expertise. The government should have understood this. It should have brought in experts even from abroad if necessary.

If that had been done, the government could at least have said that it had made an effort but was unable to succeed. Instead, relatives are complaining that they lost their loved ones because the government did not make enough effort. Many of the workers inside the tunnels are not from Rasuwa. Most of them are from western parts of the country. As a result, their concerns have not received sufficient attention. In situations like this, there is also a problem where the loudest voices tend to get heard. Teams have gone there saying they will begin work on the tunnels from today. But they do not have the necessary equipment or skilled technical personnel.”

title.rendered: Stock market rises after 6 days, turnover below 3 billion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

After falling for six consecutive trading days, the stock market rose on Tuesday. Compared to the previous day, the NEPSE index rose 9.24 points today. Following this increase, the NEPSE index stood at 2,522 points.

Trading volume declined. While the previous day saw turnover of Rs 3.64 billion, today’s turnover was Rs 2.89 billion. The share prices of 182 companies rose, 84 fell, and 11 remained unchanged.

Following last Wednesday’s severe flood, the sectors that had been under pressure in the market until the previous day turned positive today as well. The hydropower sector rose the most, up 1.01 percent.

Manufacturing and processing fell 1.00 percent. All sector indices other than manufacturing and processing rose. Banking rose 0.18 percent, development banks 0.11 percent, finance 0.25 percent, hotels and tourism 0.66 percent, investment 0.61 percent, life insurance 0.89 percent, microfinance 0.05 percent, non-life insurance 0.87 percent, others 0.54 percent, and trading 0.10 percent.

Upper Mailung Khola Hydropower Company’s share price rose the most, up 7.15 percent. Emerging Nepal rose 4.85 percent, Sanjen Hydropower 3.81 percent, Menchhiyam Hydropower 3.69 percent, and Mandu Hydropower 3.61 percent.

Upakar Laghubitta’s share price fell the most, down 8.48 percent. Ghorahi Cement fell 5.53 percent, CYC Laghubitta 5.39 percent, and Bhagawati Hydropower 5.27 percent.

Today’s most actively traded companies were, in order, Solu Hydropower, Shivam Cement, Aankhukhola Hydropower, Ridi Power, Sanima Middle Tamor, and Chilime Hydropower.

title.rendered: Additional foreign technical team, including DNA experts, arriving in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 21

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says international technical assistance for disaster management continues to arrive from various friendly nations.

At a regular press briefing held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Poudel Chhetri gave information about international technical support being received in search and tunnel rescue as well as DNA identification.

According to him, a 24-member tunnel rescue team from India, coordinating with the Nepal Army, has been deployed in the Chilime and Langtang hydropower project areas, while a 9-member tunnel rescue team from China, also coordinating with the Nepal Army, has been mobilised in the Upper Trishuli 3’A’ project area. Spokesperson Poudel also said a rescue team from Korea has arrived in Nepal.

He said a 19-member DNA analysis expert team from India has been working in the field since August 29, and that coordination is underway to bring a 4-member forensic team from China as well as a disaster victim identification team from Singapore.

The ministry said DNA samples from bodies that could not be immediately identified are being preserved, and the bodies have been temporarily buried according to international standards.

Spokesperson Poudel said damage assessment will be carried out to prepare a “Post-Disaster Needs Assessment,” and long-term international assistance will be sought on that basis.

title.rendered: One person from Karnali dies in Rasuwa flood, 194 still unreachable

content.rendered:
Surkhet, September 1

One person from Karnali Province has died in the flood that struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26. The Province Police Office says the whereabouts of 194 people from Karnali who lost contact in the flood are still unknown.

According to police spokesperson, Senior Superintendent of Police Santosh Singh Rathaur, the man who died in the flood was from Salyan. As of noon on Tuesday, 270 people from Karnali had lost contact after the flood. Of them, 75 have since been reached.

Among the 194 still unreachable, the largest number, 81, are men from Jumla. This is followed by 54 from Salyan, 16 from Surkhet, and 11 from Mugu.

Police also say 9 people from Rukum West, 7 from Humla, 6 from Kalikot, 5 from Dailekh, 3 from Jajarkot, and 2 from Dolpa remain unreachable.

According to police, of the 194 still unreachable, 159 are men, 28 are women, and 7 are children. By district, this includes 40 men, 11 women, and 3 children from Salyan, and 15 men and 1 woman from Surkhet.

Police also report that 6 men, 4 women, and 1 child from Mugu, along with citizens from other districts, are still unreachable. Although 75 of those who lost contact in the flood have since been reached, the status of a large number of people is still unknown, making it necessary to intensify search and rescue efforts.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood: 12 discharged from Bir Hospital, 5 remain hospitalised

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Twelve of the 19 people taken to Bir Hospital after being rescued from the Rasuwa floods have been discharged following treatment, the hospital said on Tuesday morning.

According to Dr Anita GC, assistant director and spokesperson at Bir Hospital, 40-year-old Tshiring Chhumo Ghale, 3-year-old Dona Tamang and 3-year-old Paldung Tamang were discharged after receiving treatment for injuries sustained in the flood.

Similarly, 24-year-old Bibhushan Subedi, 32-year-old Narayan Krishna Shrestha, 96-year-old Siang Li Junon, 58-year-old Lizhi, 52-year-old Chen Fei, 35-year-old Krishna Bhatt, 34-year-old Kush Kumar Shrestha, 48-year-old Nurbu Ghale and 58-year-old Ritesh Bahadur Shrestha were discharged and sent home after treatment.

The hospital said 70-year-old Bharat Bahadur Nepali was referred to the Trauma Center for further treatment.

Five patients who require additional treatment are currently receiving care in different wards, according to the hospital.

Among them, 53-year-old Suman Mijar and 35-year-old Suman Khadka have been admitted to Bir Hospital for further treatment. Likewise, 26-year-old Utsav Pyakurel, who was initially receiving treatment in the emergency department, was admitted to the neurosurgery ward at 6 pm on August 31 and is continuing treatment there, according to the hospital.

The hospital said 75-year-old Guna Keshari Bohora is receiving treatment under medical supervision due to a chronic respiratory condition, while 53-year-old Tulsi Bahadur Bhandari is being treated for an ear injury.

Earlier, 38-year-old Biratman Tamang was referred to Nepal Eye Hospital for further treatment after sustaining an eye injury.

Meanwhile, one of the people brought to the hospital has died.

title.rendered: Unregistered doctors allowed to obtain temporary registration to treat Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Doctors who are not registered with the Nepal Medical Council can now obtain temporary registration to provide treatment to flood victims. The Nepal Medical Council announced this in a notice issued on Monday.

The council said domestic and foreign doctors, health volunteers and organisations wishing to treat people injured in natural disasters can obtain temporary registration from the council.

“Doctors and organisations not registered with the Nepal Medical Council may obtain approval or temporary registration from the council before providing treatment services, either individually or collectively, in accordance with Nepal’s prevailing laws, regulations and rules,” the notice said.

The council also said doctors and organisations involved in providing treatment must coordinate with the Disaster Management Division of the Ministry of Health.

They have also been requested to submit details of the personnel involved in providing treatment, the resources and medical supplies used, and accurate records of the people who received treatment to both the ministry’s Disaster Management Division and the council.

title.rendered: Kathmandu prepares site to manage unidentified flood victims’ bodies

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Bodies of people who died in the Bhotekoshi floods will also be managed in Kathmandu as authorities struggle to handle the large number of recovered bodies.

Kathmandu Chief District Officer Ishwar Raj Paudel said the authorities have identified a government forest area where the bodies will be managed.

“We have decided to manage them in a government forest area,” Paudel told Onlinekhabar.

Unidentified bodies recovered between Fishing and Golaghat had earlier been managed in Chitwan.

The volume of recovered bodies has overwhelmed existing mortuary capacity. On the third day after the August 26 floods, mortuaries were already unable to accommodate the bodies, with some at risk of decomposing along the corridor.

The Ministry of Health has said hospitals across the country have a combined capacity to hold around 600 bodies.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 987 bodies have been recovered so far. Around 100 of them have been brought to Kathmandu.

Paudel said identifying a suitable location in Kathmandu had taken several days of continuous effort.

“We were able to identify the site only after three to four days of continuous effort,” he said.

The government will manage unidentified and unclaimed bodies in accordance with the Unidentified and Unclaimed Bodies Management Directive, 2021.

The directive requires authorities to prepare records of recovered bodies, conduct preliminary identification, use additional methods for identification where necessary, establish identity, maintain records and place identification markers on the bodies.

title.rendered: MPs call for national mourning over Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Members of the National Assembly have urged the government to declare a day of national mourning following the devastating Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa.

The issue was raised during the zero hour of the National Assembly meeting, with lawmakers calling for the government to formally honour those who lost their lives in the disaster.

Nepali Congress lawmaker Yubaraj Sharma urged the government, through the chairperson of the National Assembly, to declare August 26 as a national day of mourning.

“We urge the government, through the respected chairperson, to declare August 26 a national day of mourning,” Sharma said.

He said all sides needed to come together during the disaster and called on the government to focus on search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation.

“What had to happen has happened. Now the government’s attention should be focused on search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation,” he said. “What is needed is result-oriented work and safe management, rather than publicity.”

NCP lawmaker Madan Kumari Shah Garima also called for a national day of mourning.

“I demand that the national flag be lowered for one day and that a day of national mourning be declared,” she said.

She also called for the issue of climate change and its impact on Nepal to be raised internationally, arguing that actions by wealthy and developed countries had contributed to climate change while countries such as Nepal were bearing its consequences.

The devastating floods struck on August 26 after the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa overflowed.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the bodies of 987 people had been recovered from areas affected by the Bhotekoshi floods as of 9am Tuesday.

The authority reported 27 bodies recovered in Rasuwa, 95 in Nuwakot, 55 in Dhading, 65 in Gorkha, 38 in Tanahun, 216 in Nawalparasi East, 170 in Nawalparasi West and 321 in Chitwan.

A total of 3,916 people remain unaccounted for, while 279 people have been reported injured. So far, 11,814 people have been rescued.

A total of 20,819 security personnel have been deployed for rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts. They include 8,722 from the Nepali Army, 7,894 from Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force.

NCP lawmaker Suresh Kumar Ale Magar also drew Parliament’s attention to the disaster, saying extreme weather events were becoming more frequent because of global warming and climate change driven largely by wealthy and developed countries.

He said poorer and less-developed countries such as Nepal were disproportionately suffering the consequences despite contributing far less to the causes of climate change.

Ale Magar called on the international community to take note of the impact of climate change on vulnerable countries such as Nepal.

title.rendered: Jhulaghat border area in Baitadi at high risk of landslides

content.rendered:
Baitadi, September 1

The Jhulaghat area of Baitadi, a border crossing connecting Nepal and India, is at risk of landslides. The area has been put at risk after landslides began falling from a road near the market due to continuous rainfall.

Locals said landslides have been occurring along the road near Jhulaghat market since last night as rain continues to fall. Baitadi Chief District Officer Mina Aryal said the market area and road are at high risk of landslides as debris continues to fall.

She said Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force have been deployed to facilitate movement in the area as the risk continues to increase. Authorities have urged residents to remain alert, warning that the risk of landslides could increase as rainfall continues.

title.rendered: Nepal sets a 9-step process for returning foreign flood victims’ bodies

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The Nepal government has set up the required process for returning the bodies of foreign nationals killed in last week’s devastating flood to their families.

The Indian Embassy in Kathmandu issued a press release on Tuesday explaining the procedure set by the Nepal government.

The 9 steps of body handover

According to Nepal government standards, the following nine steps must be completed before a foreign national’s body can be handed over to their family:

  • Preparing documentation related to the body.
  • Recording photographs and other details of the body.
  • Conducting a post-mortem examination.
  • Confirming the cause of death.
  • Establishing formal identification of the body.
  • Collecting fingerprints, DNA, or forensic samples.
  • Verifying the deceased’s passport or identification documents.
  • Completing embassy or consular coordination.
  • Completing the process of body handover and receipt.

The first four of these steps, from preparing documentation to confirming the cause of death, will be completed by Nepal government officials.

Identification and temporary management of bodies

According to the release, relatives or family members of the deceased can identify bodies based on photographs and details available on the Nepal Police website (udb.nepalpolice.gov.np). Once identification is confirmed this way, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu will coordinate with local authorities to help receive the body and send it back to the home country.

To prevent the public health risks that could arise from the large number of bodies, the Nepal government has managed them by temporarily and safely burying them. To identify such bodies, DNA matching with the deceased’s first-degree relatives will be required.

DNA matching process

For bodies that cannot be identified or have been temporarily buried, the Nepal government will facilitate DNA matching. Nepali authorities are collecting samples from the bodies to prepare DNA profiles of the deceased.

Relatives can send their DNA profiles to the Nepal Police email dnacodis@nepalpolice.gov.np or provide a blood sample.

Contact and helpline numbers

For more information on this and to understand DNA profiling, the Nepal Police helpline number +977 984-1616095 can be contacted.

title.rendered: Task force formed to expedite recovery in flood-hit Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The Ministry of Infrastructure Development has formed a task force to prepare an initial recovery and management framework and carry out measures to help people affected by the Bhotekoshi River floods in Rasuwa return to normal life within 21 days.

The task force will identify, coordinate and facilitate necessary work in areas including roads, bridges, drinking water, resettlement, suspension bridges, debris management, communications and health services in the affected areas. It will also mobilise relevant stakeholders and agencies and regularly monitor and report on the progress.

According to the ministry, the task force has been assigned responsibility for conducting a rapid technical and objective assessment of the damage and risks caused by the disaster. It will also identify emergency restoration measures and essential services that need to be resumed immediately and mobilise the relevant agencies accordingly.

The task force will classify affected areas, structures and families based on risk and priority and prepare immediate, short-term and long-term action plans.

It will also assess the need for human resources, equipment, materials and financial resources and coordinate and facilitate cooperation among the federal, provincial and local governments, security agencies, the private sector and development partners.

During reconstruction, the task force will apply the “build back better” principle by taking into account geological conditions, climate change, floods, landslides and other disaster risks. It will also use an integrated planning and information system to prevent duplication of investment, misuse of resources and unnecessary duplication of work.

The task force has also been assigned to recommend necessary policy, legal, administrative and budgetary decisions to the concerned agencies and the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. It will submit regular reports on progress, problems encountered and possible solutions.

The task force will monitor, evaluate and ensure the quality of work within its scope and provide policy recommendations for future disaster risk reduction based on experiences and data gathered during the recovery process.

The ministry said the task force would coordinate among all concerned agencies to expedite the recovery of affected areas, resume essential infrastructure services and help residents return to normal daily life.
