title.rendered: Seven days after floods, hydropower developers finally allowed to join rescue efforts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

With the chances of finding workers trapped inside hydropower tunnels alive diminishing, the government has finally allowed project developers to directly join search and rescue operations, seven days after the devastating floods.

Following the permission, hydropower companies and project developers are preparing to mobilise their technical teams and necessary equipment to search for workers who remain trapped or unaccounted for.

Until now, the government had followed a single-command approach to the rescue operation, with the Nepali Army leading efforts at the affected hydropower projects. Project companies had not been allowed to directly participate despite having technical personnel and specialised equipment.

However, the Army has been unable to rescue those trapped inside the tunnels despite seven days of efforts.

After the approach failed to produce the expected results, the government has now asked the respective project companies to join the search and rescue operation with their technical manpower and equipment.

Project developers have begun making arrangements to mobilise their teams.

Langtang Hydropower is preparing to send its technical team and necessary equipment to the project site, which has been buried by floods and landslides.

Project promoter Bijay Man Bhattaraisaid the government had now opened the way for the company’s technical team to participate in the search and rescue operation.

“The Nepali Army went around 100 metres into the tunnel and then told us they could not proceed further and asked us to bring our technical personnel and continue the work,” he said.

According to Bhattarai, project companies had been prevented from directly mobilising their technical personnel while the Army-led rescue operation was underway.

He said the situation had now changed, with the government mechanism and project teams expected to coordinate the operation.

“Our technical team was needed before as well, and it is still needed,” he said. “Now there needs to be coordination from our side as well. Helicopters and vehicles cannot reach the site, so they will need to arrange equipment for lifting and other requirements.”

He said the rescue operation would now have to adopt a different approach after the previous method failed.

“The previous approach did not work. So now we are working on a different approach,” he said.

The company’s team is currently in Kathmandu arranging the equipment and materials required for the operation. It plans to travel to the project site after purchasing and arranging the necessary technical equipment.

The Nepal Water and Energy Development Company (NWEDC), which is constructing the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 project, has also begun arranging technical personnel and equipment.

The company had sought to mobilise its technical team soon after several people at the project site went missing following the floods. However, it was not allowed to directly participate in the rescue as the government said operations were being conducted through a single command under the Nepali Army.

The latest decision has now cleared the way for project companies to use their own technical expertise, equipment and manpower in the search and rescue operation.

The decision comes as the status of many workers trapped or missing at the project sites remains unknown even a week after the floods, raising hopes that the involvement of specialised project teams could accelerate the search.

894 hydropower workers still unaccounted for

The August 26 floods damaged 12 hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. As of now, 894 employees and workers remain unaccounted for.

The largest number are from NWEDC’s 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 project in Rasuwa, where 573 people remain unaccounted for.

At the 111MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, 93 employees and workers are still missing. The Nepali Army has said its search inside the project’s underground powerhouse found no one. However, the company says three employees who were on duty at the time of the flood remain unaccounted for.

Another 41 people remain unaccounted for from the 20MW Langtang Khola Hydropower Project.

In Nuwakot, 42 employees and workers from the 60MW Upper Trishuli-3A project remain unaccounted for.

Rescue efforts continued at the project on Monday, with teams working for 24 hours inside the underground powerhouse, but they were unable to rescue anyone.

Teams worked to clear the tunnel portal, remove water and create an entry route into the tunnel. The Nepal Electricity Authority said the operation has been particularly challenging because the tunnel remains flooded.

On Monday, an engineering and drone team led by the Nepali Army also entered the tunnel to continue the search.

title.rendered: A social media call to help Rasuwa brought a community together

content.rendered:
As soon as entrepreneur Samaya Khadka landed in Kathmandu from the USA on August 26, he learned about the flash flood in Rasuwa. He immediately posted a status on social media urging people to help those affected, along with a list of items needed to send as relief.

A few of his friends then got in touch. Initially, they created a WhatsApp group with five members, including Khadka. The others were Sadikshya Thapa, Suraj Pandey, Dr Manu Karki and Sudarshan.

After landing in Kathmandu, Khadka had planned to go straight home and rest. However, things took a different turn. Instead, he found himself discussing with his friends what could be done to help those affected.

Gradually, more people began showing interest in volunteering and reached out to Khadka. The group grew from five to 10, then 35, 50 and now, as of this piece, has 65 members. They come from diverse backgrounds, with the majority being students.

Others are from sectors including medicine, hospitality and activism, among others. The group is not affiliated with any organisation or political party, a factor that makes it stand out. None of them is paid either.

“We are working entirely independently,” says Khadka.  

Initially, only individuals were reaching out to the group to hand over relief materials. Now, organisations are also contacting them for the same purpose.

There are six collection points where the group is accepting relief materials: Techspire College, Mandap and Moments, Yellow House, Ecosathi, Mirai Global and Cafe De Mandala. These locations cover all three districts of the Kathmandu Valley.

So far, the group has distributed relief to approximately 300 households.

“Initially, I didn’t think the group would be this huge,” says Khadka. “We are still receiving a lot of inquiries from people interested in volunteering and handing over relief materials.”

Members of Khadka’s group reached Dhunche, Rasuwa, after 36 hours of travel. They were “one of the first groups” to reach the area to distribute relief materials.

The group accepts only goods as relief. If anyone wants to provide financial assistance, they ask them to donate to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund.

Although the floods have also affected Nuwakot, the group has decided to focus its relief efforts on Rasuwa. Authorities in Nuwakot told them that the district had received sufficient relief supplies, while people in Rasuwa were still facing shortages.

The group is now heading to Mailung to distribute relief. There, they plan to set up a camp with a capacity of 400 people.

This is not the first time members of this group have been involved in relief distribution. They have also worked in relief efforts during the COVID-19 pandemic, which gave them an understanding of the importance of relief distribution and how to prioritise needs when distributing supplies.

“Currently, we are distributing food, sanitary pads, lights, surgical supplies and other materials required during an emergency,” says Suraj Raj Pandey, another member of the group.

The group has not faced many challenges in distributing the relief itself. However, poor road conditions remain a major challenge, raising concerns about whether they will be able to deliver the supplies to their intended destinations.

“As the government has implemented a single-door system for relief distribution, we are afraid that the goods may not reach everyone,” Khadka adds.

Among the group’s 65 members is activist Amy Ban, who learned about the group through friends before social media helped her learn more about its work.

Ban regularly spends 10 to 12 hours a day managing the goods to be sent as relief. She coordinates with different individuals and organisations to make sure everything is in place.

“Right now, the most important thing is to make sure that the relief is in the right hands and delivered at the right time, and we are giving our best to make that happen,” says Ban.

From five people in a WhatsApp group to 65 volunteers coordinating relief across Kathmandu and Rasuwa, the group has grown far beyond what Khadka initially imagined.

But the road ahead remains difficult. As they prepare to head deeper into Rasuwa, their success will ultimately be measured not by how many people joined the group, or how much relief they collected, but by whether the supplies make it through the difficult roads and into the hands of those who need them most.

title.rendered: Cable crossing installed over Trishuli River to reconnect two Nuwakot wards

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

A cable crossing has been installed over the Trishuli River to facilitate travel between Ward 1 and Ward 9 of Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot.

The connection between the two wards was cut off following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

The cable crossing was installed on Tuesday morning to make it easier for local residents to travel between the two sides of the river.

Following its installation, people have started using the crossing to travel between the two sides, despite the risks involved.

title.rendered: Rescue update: Search operations continue at hydropower projects as 23 bodies recovered

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Rescue and search operations are continuing in flood-hit Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, days after a massive flood swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26.

As of 11am Tuesday, the Nepali Army had evacuated the bodies of 23 people by helicopter, while search teams continued efforts to locate people still missing from several hydropower projects.

At the Chilime Hydropower project in Rasuwa, a joint search-and-rescue team including foreign personnel entered around 50 metres into the tunnel to search for those trapped inside.

At the Langtang Hydropower project, the team searched up to around 150 metres inside the tunnel, while at the Upper Trishuli-1 project, rescuers reached around 200 metres inside but have so far been unable to carry out any rescues.

At the Upper Trishuli-3A project, rescuers have located the tunnel head and are using a compressor to supply air inside. Water is being pumped out, while three excavators have opened an alternative route of around 15 metres.

Teams are also breaking rocks to create an entry point into the tunnel.

At Upper Trishuli-3B, security personnel and technical experts have located the tunnel entrance and are using an excavator to clear a path inside.

279 people rescued alive

During the initial rescue operation following the floods, 279 people were rescued alive from hydropower project areas.

They included two people from Rasuwagadhi Hydropower, 33 from Upper Trishuli-1, 221 from Upper Trishuli-3A, two from Upper Trishuli-3B, nine from Mailung Hydropower, four from Nuwakot Solar Power, three from Trishuli Hydropower and five from Devighat Hydropower.

The Nepali Army said more than 9,200 personnel have been deployed across affected areas from Timure in Rasuwa to parts of Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and Nawalparasi East.

They are involved in searching for and rescuing injured people, recovering and managing bodies, clearing blocked roads and providing emergency medical treatment.

The collection and management of bodies recovered from the flood-affected areas are also continuing.

title.rendered: Body of Timure Customs officer Nakul Sharma found in Gorkha

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The body of a customs officer who had been missing following the floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa has been found in Gorkha.

Nakul Sharma, an officer at the Timure Customs Office in Rasuwa, was found dead along the bank of the Trishuli River on the Gorkha side, according to DSP Raj Kumar Shrestha of the District Police Office, Gorkha.

Sharma was a resident of Tajakot Rural Municipality-2 in Humla. His family received the body after a postmortem examination.

So far, the bodies of 65 people have been recovered from the coastal area along the Trishuli River on the Gorkha side.

title.rendered: 894 people still missing from 11 hydropower projects after Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

A large number of people reported missing or out of contact at hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot following the Bhotekoshi River flood have yet to be rescued.

According to data from the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), 894 people remain unaccounted for across 11 hydropower projects.

The highest number is from the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa, where 573 people remain missing. Three people were rescued from the project on Monday, but a large number of others are still out of contact.

Around 300 of those reported missing at the project are believed to be workers who were working inside tunnels. It has not yet been established whether they were inside the tunnels when the flood struck or were preparing to enter them.

Around 1,400 people are estimated to have been working at the project on the day of the flood.

Rescue efforts continue inside flooded tunnels

Efforts to rescue people trapped inside the tunnel of the 60MW Upper Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project continued on Monday.

Rescue teams worked inside the project for 24 hours but have not yet been able to reach those believed to be trapped inside.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said teams are clearing the tunnel portal, removing water and creating an accessible route into the tunnel.

The presence of water inside the tunnel has made the rescue operation more difficult.

Rescue teams have also reached the Langtang Khola Hydropower Project, but those trapped inside the tunnel have yet to be rescued.

A team comprising personnel from the Nepal Army, Indian Army and technical experts reached the project site. The project said it would continue rescue efforts on its own on Tuesday.

Search efforts are also continuing for people missing from the 37MW Upper Trishuli-3B Hydropower Project since Sunday.

The flood swept away project structures, making the search and rescue operation more difficult. The 220kV Trishuli-3B Hub substation located alongside the project was also completely damaged, further complicating efforts to locate missing people.

93 missing from Rasuwagadhi project

A large number of people are also missing from the 111MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project.

According to the company, 93 people, including 49 employees, remain missing.

On Monday, a team led by the Nepal Army, along with engineers and drone operators, entered the tunnel to search for the missing workers.

The team used drones to inspect the inner section of the tunnel but found no people and subsequently ended the search and returned.

The search was conducted amid concerns that some workers could have been trapped near the far end of the tunnel.

Missing workers across Nuwakot projects

Several hydropower projects in Nuwakot have also reported missing workers.

According to IPPAN data, one person is missing from the 24MW Trishuli Hydropower Project and one from the 14.1MW Devighat Hydropower Project.

Another 42 people are missing from the 60MW Upper Trishuli-3A project, while 198 are missing from the 37MW Upper Trishuli-3B project.

Two people are also missing from the 15.6MW Middle Trishuli Ganga Hydropower Project.

IPPAN said the figures were based on information received from the affected projects as of Tuesday and that the number of people rescued could increase as search and rescue efforts continue.

Despite ongoing rescue operations, hundreds of people remain unaccounted for.

The flood has not only damaged major hydropower infrastructure but also left the whereabouts of hundreds of workers uncertain, making search and rescue operations particularly challenging.

title.rendered: Kathmandu faces challenge managing bodies as hospital morgues reach capacity

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The management of bodies recovered from the devastating floods along the Trishuli River has become increasingly challenging as the death toll continues to rise.

Bodies were previously placed on the ground for temporary management in Chitwan after the number of bodies exceeded hospital capacity. The same problem is now emerging in Kathmandu, where hospitals are also running out of space to store the bodies.

Discussions have begun on how to manage the bodies after they exceeded available capacity. The authorities are consulting the District Security Committee as well as medical professionals on possible arrangements.

A team led by the Kathmandu Chief District Officer is currently focused on discussions regarding the management of the bodies, according to the district administration.

Authorities are considering burying the bodies underground, similar to the arrangement made in Chitwan. However, no final decision has been made yet.

title.rendered: Forest Minister calls for climate change to be made a national priority

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Gita Chaudhary has said the government must make climate change and environmental issues a matter of national priority.

Speaking at a discussion with experts held at the ministry before her departure to attend a ministerial conference of least developed countries, Minister Chaudhary stressed the need to present climate change as a matter of Nepal’s rights and claims on international platforms.

She said it would be difficult to prioritise the damage and problems caused by the climate crisis at the national level unless the government succeeds in establishing climate justice as a right before the international community. Mentioning that she had been advocating for environmental and climate change issues even before entering politics, Chaudhary said the government is now committed to prioritising climate justice. She also emphasised the need to establish mountain issues on the global agenda, noting that Nepal is a mountainous country home to Mount Everest, the world’s highest peak.

“Previously, one of our concerns was that the government did not prioritise climate change and environmental issues. But now that I am at the ministry, I want to work to ensure that this agenda receives the highest priority in Nepal. Unless we can present this agenda as our right and our claim, we cannot give it the priority it deserves. We call ourselves the country of Mount Everest, home to the world’s highest mountain. Therefore, we must lead the mountain agenda and establish it globally,” she said. Minister Chaudhary said climate change should not be limited to one or two programs or international conferences.

Stressing that government efforts alone would not be sufficient, she called for cooperation and collaboration among civil society, experts, the media and all other stakeholders.

title.rendered: Water level in Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers below alert mark, but precaution advised

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Even though the water level and flow in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers are below the alert level, people are advised to remain alert. The Flood Forecasting Division of the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research said that after the flood in Bhotekoshi on August 26, the river flow is low, but people are still advised to remain alert.

The Division stated in its flood forecast bulletin issued today that there is a medium risk of flash floods as the flow of small rivers is likely to rise significantly in Taplejung, Sankhuwasabha, Solukhumbu, Khotang, Okhaldhunga, Ramechhap, Dolakha, Sindhupalchok, Kavrepalanchok, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur, Kathmandu, Dhading, Gorkha, Lamjung, and Dolpa and surrounding districts.

Similarly, the Division forecasted that the flow of small rivers in districts like Rukum East, Rukum West, Jajarkot, Darchula, Baitadi, Dadeldhura, Doti, Kailali, and Kanchanpur will increase significantly, with a medium risk of sudden flooding. Also, the flow of small rivers in Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts is expected to increase significantly, with a high possibility of sudden floods.

title.rendered: How rescuers found a 6-year-old girl alive after 62 hours under the mud

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The rescue of a 6-year-old girl who had been buried under mud on Friday in Timure, Gosaikunda Rural Municipality-2, Rasuwa, drew widespread attention.

Sixty-two hours after the flood struck Bhotekoshi, many had already begun to lose hope. It was at that moment that an Armed Police team on rescue duty heard a small voice from beneath the mud: “Mommy, mommy.”

That voice created a moment worth remembering in Nepal’s history of emergency rescue operations.

Inspector Sanju Khatri of the Armed Police Force’s 20th Battalion (Disaster Rescue Battalion), Sinamangal, Kathmandu, who led the rescue team, described his experience:

As soon as the incident happened, we were on standby within five minutes. We reached Dhunche in Rasuwa by helicopter from Kathmandu in about an hour, and from there we set out for Timure. Around 50 of us reached the site, including 9 personnel trained in special disaster rescue, and we were deployed for search and rescue work in Timure.

Our priority was to get out those who were still alive. In that process, we rescued about 350 people trapped there by helicopter and sent them to Dhunche. Among them were many people we brought to safety, ranging from Indian pilgrims headed to Mansarovar to Chinese nationals.

About 62 hours after the incident, while continuing the search, we heard a girl’s voice. As soon as our team heard the voice saying ‘Mommy, mommy,’ we immediately started searching in that direction. At that time, the area was buried under mud and wood, with nothing visible on the surface.

We searched using only the voice as our guide, and eventually we managed to bring the roughly 6-year-old girl out safely.

We immediately tried to inform our unit stationed at Dhunche, but since there was no communication signal there, we climbed up for about half an hour and sent the information by radio set. But because the weather was bad, the girl could not be taken out by helicopter that day.

We kept her safe and slowly began taking care of her. We assigned two members to look after her through the night. Gradually she became more alert and started talking back and forth, but she was very frightened.

Our biggest challenge was how to get her to a hospital safely. The weather remained bad the next morning as well. The helicopter was only able to fly around 1:30 in the afternoon, after which we brought the girl safely to a hospital in Kathmandu.

After we got the girl out, our entire team was overjoyed. Despite so many difficulties, we succeeded in saving her life.

title.rendered: Rasuwagadhi closure diverts Chinese imports to Korala, but Nepal’s alternative route is unprepared

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26 has wiped out the Rasuwagadhi–Kerung border point, the main lifeline for Nepal-China trade, forcing containers carrying imports from China to be diverted towards the Korala border point in Mustang.

The diversion comes just ahead of major festivals including Dashain, Tihar and Chhath, when demand for imported goods typically rises.

But Korala lacks the infrastructure, manpower and reliable road network needed to handle the sudden increase in trade.

This means importers are likely to face significant difficulties, while higher transportation costs could eventually push up prices in the Nepali market.

The number of heavy freight vehicles entering Mustang has already started to rise as cargo previously routed through Rasuwagadhi is diverted to Korala.

According to data from the Armed Police Force’s Jomsom checkpoint, 66 cargo containers carrying goods from China had entered Mustang by Sunday evening. The checkpoint said the number of containers heading towards Korala has been increasing.

However, the containers carrying the diverted goods have not yet reached the Mustang Customs Office.

According to Bidur Chudal, chief customs officer at the Mustang Customs Office, the diverted cargo is still on the way and customs clearance at Korala has not yet begun.

Empty containers are currently heading towards Korala to collect the goods.

“At the moment, only empty containers are going up. The diverted vehicles have not arrived yet,” Chudal told Onlinekhabar. “The empty containers are heading uphill to collect the goods. According to the information we have received, around 100 empty containers have already gone up.”

He said all the diverted goods would eventually have to enter through Korala if there was no other option, and customs clearance would be expedited once the vehicles arrive.

Customs short of staff and infrastructure

Although the government has promoted Korala as an alternative border point, its customs infrastructure remains limited.

The Mustang Customs Office, located at an altitude of around 4,650 metres, has a sanctioned strength of 18 employees, but only 12 are currently working there.

The lack of adequate infrastructure has also raised concerns about how the customs office will handle the increased workload.

Customs officials say they will work around the clock once the cargo containers begin arriving.

Despite its limited infrastructure, the Korala customs point collected Rs 6.92 billion in revenue in the last fiscal year 2025/26. It collected another Rs 290 million in the first month of the current fiscal year.

Businesspeople, however, complain that the government has failed to invest in manpower and road upgrades despite the border point’s strong revenue performance.

Chudal said discussions were underway with the Department of Customs about adding staff and infrastructure in anticipation of the sudden increase in traffic.

Although Nepal’s infrastructure is not as advanced as that on the Chinese side, Chudal said the customs office was continuing its regular operations using the resources available.

Food imports remain a problem

With Rasuwagadhi destroyed, Korala is now expected to handle a larger share of goods entering the Nepali market from China.

But while the border point can handle many types of imports, food and perishable goods pose a particular challenge.

Businesspeople say it is currently difficult to import fruits, vegetables and food products through Korala because of the lack of quarantine facilities and adequate manpower.

The road is the bigger problem

Bringing goods through Korala is not easy for either traders or truck drivers.

The road from Mustang to Kathmandu is narrow, rough and geographically challenging at several points, making it difficult for large containers to travel.

Chudal also acknowledged that road conditions could become a major obstacle.

“After you go uphill from Beni, there is a landslide risk along the Kaligandaki Corridor up to a place called Ghasa. Once you go above Jomsom, there is around 100 kilometres of unpaved road,” he said. “The road is currently usable, but there is a natural concern that it could deteriorate once vehicle and traffic volumes increase.”

Given these difficulties, traders have demanded that sealed containers arriving through Korala be transported directly to the Chobhar dry port in Kathmandu for customs clearance.

Customs officials, however, do not consider the proposal practical because of the additional travel time and security risks along the route.

There is another problem: heavy snowfall begins in Mustang soon after Dashain and Tihar, meaning Korala cannot operate at full capacity throughout the year.

Longer transport route, higher prices

The closure of Rasuwagadhi and the longer, more difficult route through Korala are expected to have a direct impact on the cost of goods.

According to Manoj Babu Shrestha, president of the Nepal National Business Federation, diverting goods stranded in Kerung towards Korala will significantly increase transportation costs.

Kathmandu is only around 110 kilometres from Rasuwagadhi. But goods travelling from Kerung to Korala have to cover an additional distance of around 1,100 kilometres.

“We have diverted goods that were sitting at transport warehouses in Kerung towards Korala, but the additional 1,100-kilometre distance will sharply increase transportation costs,” Shrestha said. “This will increase the cost of goods, and prices in the market could rise by Rs 100 to Rs 150 per item.”

He said the increase in freight charges would directly affect the prices of ready-made garments, shoes, raw materials, food products and fruits.

The country’s own road network is another major obstacle.

The main route connecting containers from Mustang to Kathmandu—the Muglin-Narayangadh section of the Prithvi Highway—has itself been repeatedly disrupted.

The Prithvi Highway has been completely blocked since Monday after the road subsided at Krishnabhir in Dhading.

“Small vehicles, vans or Tata Mobiles may be able to come through the Dakshinkali–Sisneri–Hetauda route, but large containers cannot use that road,” Shrestha said. “The lifeline connecting Kathmandu itself is damaged. Once that road is gone, it makes little difference whether the goods come through Korala or anywhere else.”

Although goods would normally be expected to arrive within five days based on distance, he said there was currently no certainty about how long transportation would take because of the poor condition of the roads.

For the immediate term, the government has arranged for all freight vehicles to travel towards Kathmandu via the Kanti Lokpath.

Goods on which taxes were paid also swept away

While traders face higher costs and difficult roads when using Korala, some businesses have already suffered losses after floodwaters swept away goods stranded in Kerung.

Traders complain that the government has remained a spectator as containers carrying goods that had already completed customs procedures were swept away.

They also say they have received little sympathy or support from the government.

“Around 50 to 70 vehicles carrying our goods were swept away in Kerung. The goods had been kept in the customs yard, customs duties and taxes had been paid, declarations had been filed and the vehicles were preparing to leave,” Shrestha said. “We are not even in a position to receive a refund or compensation for the taxes we paid to the government. We have been hit from every direction.”

Tatopani also remains an uncertain alternative

With Rasuwagadhi destroyed, the Tatopani border point in Sindhupalchok was also considered an alternative.

But bringing vehicles stranded in Kerung through Tatopani would require an additional detour of around 550 kilometres.

Traders say the route is also unreliable because of recurring landslides around Liping in the Tatopani area, and is unlikely to be dependable until the end of September.

The uncertainty surrounding the northern border points has already pushed around 40 percent of Chinese goods towards sea routes through Indian ports.

Such shipments take between one and three months to reach Nepal and eventually have to use the already deteriorated Muglin road.

At a time of crisis, Korala is serving as a lifeline for Nepal-China trade. But its narrow roads, landslide risks and reliance on just 12 customs employees make it difficult to see how billions of rupees worth of trade can be handled smoothly.

Stakeholders say the state must focus on constructing alternative tracks and repairing roads while the risk of further flooding remains.

They warn that unless the government moves at a war footing to expand Korala customs infrastructure and manpower and improve the Muglin–Narayangadh road, Nepali consumers could soon face severe shortages and sharply higher prices.

title.rendered: 24 bodies recovered from a single house in Betrawati

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Twenty-four bodies have been recovered from inside a single house in Betrawati, located in Bidur Municipality-10 of Nuwakot.

According to Nuwakot District Police Chief SP Bipin Regmi, the bodies were recovered from the building that housed Uttargaya Mini Mart in Betrawati.

“We have searched as much as our capacity allows and recovered 24 bodies. There are still other areas that need to be searched,” Regmi told Onlinekhabar.

He said the bodies are currently being documented and efforts are underway to identify them. None of the bodies has been identified so far.

Once the documentation process is completed, the bodies will be sent to Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj for postmortem examinations, Regmi said.

The victims were found inside the house following the devastating flood that swept through the Trishuli River after the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa flooded on August 26.

title.rendered: China’s new defence law allows mobilisation of civilian resources during war

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

China has made major changes to its national defence legislation, allowing the government to mobilise not only the military but also civilians, private companies and other national resources during war or a major crisis.

China’s parliament, the National People’s Congress, approved amendments to the National Defence Mobilisation Law on August 28. The revised law will come into force on October 1.

The new law provides not only for the requisition of resources but also for placing them under government control. Those who refuse to comply with orders or deliberately cause delays could face penalties and fines.

Major overhaul after 16 years

China’s National Defence Mobilisation Law was enacted in 2010 and has now undergone its first major overhaul. The revised law contains 14 chapters and 82 articles.

According to China, its main objective is to enable the country to rapidly shift from a peacetime footing to a wartime state in the event of any threat. Economic and social resources can also be mobilised for defence purposes.

The revised law covers the protection of China’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and security, as well as its “development interests.”

Military-civilian mobilisation mechanism under party leadership

According to Samantha Hoffman, an expert at the Jamestown Foundation, the new law introduces changes related to party leadership, organisational structures, reserve forces, recruitment, stockpiling of essential supplies and defence-related education.

Articles 3 and 17 place the national defence mobilisation system under the leadership of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party. Previously, the State Council and the Central Military Commission played the leading roles.

According to Hoffman, the party will be able to bring together military, civilian, economic and social resources to pursue its strategic objectives when necessary.

Hospitals, internet and transport services must also be prepared

Under the new law, sectors including transportation, postal services, telecommunications, cybersecurity, medical and pharmaceutical supplies, food supply and engineering must be prepared to fulfil national defence-related responsibilities.

Organisations in these sectors will be required to form specialised teams and provide them with training so they can be deployed immediately when needed.

Cybersecurity has been given particular emphasis. The law also calls for strengthening defence capabilities through the use of new and advanced technologies.

It also includes provisions for developing reserve forces, strengthening recruitment systems and increasing stockpiles of strategically important supplies.

Development now also a national security issue

Under the 2010 law, defence mobilisation could be activated when China’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity or security faced threats. The revised law now also includes the protection of “development interests.”

This means that threats to China may no longer be viewed only in terms of its borders or territorial security. Economic interests, access to essential resources, Chinese assets overseas and interests related to technological development could also be considered part of national security.

According to Hoffman, this change is also linked to China’s National Defence Law, which was revised in 2020 and included provisions for initiating defense mobilisation when the country’s development interests are threatened.

Is China preparing for war?

The new law has raised questions about whether China is preparing for war, although experts have differing views.

Theresa Fallon, director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies in Brussels, has expressed concern over the new law. In a post on X, she said the growing risk of war around the world was difficult to ignore.

She questioned whether factors such as declining US military stockpiles, the Russia-Ukraine war and the Israel-US conflict involving Iran could be leading Chinese President Xi Jinping to believe that a time of war is approaching.

Lyle Morris of the Asia Society Policy Institute, however, takes a different view. He said the law should not be interpreted as evidence that China has suddenly begun preparing for war, arguing that the country has been making such preparations for more than a decade.

Nevertheless, the new law indicates that China is not preparing only its military for a potential major crisis. It is also incorporating civilians, companies, essential services, technology and data into its broader national defence preparations.

According to experts, Taiwan and the United States could emerge as China’s principal potential military rivals in the future.

—With the assistance of agencies.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, this number of bodies had been found as of 9 a.m. Tuesday.

University Chancellor and Prime Minister Balendra Shah made the appointments based on the recommendation of the Vice-Chancellor.

According to a source at the Ministry of Education, Singh and Shiwakoti are scheduled to take their oath of office at 3 pm on Tuesday.

title.rendered: Rasuwa customs point’s future uncertain after floods wipe out key infrastructure

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The Rasuwagadhi customs point accounted for 2.18 percent of Nepal’s total imports last fiscal year, a relatively small share compared with its previous contribution to the country’s foreign trade.

The decline came after the Bhotekoshi (Lhende) River, which flows along the Nepal-China border, flooded on July 8, 2025, forcing the Rasuwagadhi border point to remain closed for six months.

Trade through the border point resumed after China brought a Bailey bridge into operation on January 1, 2026. In the six months following the resumption, goods worth Rs 45.73 billion were imported through Rasuwagadhi, while exports stood at Rs 894.6 million.

Nepal currently has three border points operating for cross-border trade with China. Rasuwagadhi is considered the most convenient and closest of the three.

In the last fiscal year, imports through the Tatopani border point amounted to Rs 47.48 billion, while there were no exports through the point.

Meanwhile, the Korala border point in Mustang, which has increasingly emerged as an alternative to the two traditional crossings, recorded imports worth Rs 14.40 billion and exports worth Rs 205.5 million during the same period.

The increase in trade through Korala was largely attributed to the closure of Rasuwagadhi following last year’s flood.

In the previous fiscal year, 2024/25, Rasuwagadhi recorded imports worth Rs 85.23 billion and exports worth Rs 2.04 billion. The figures accounted for 4.72 percent of Nepal’s total merchandise imports and 0.74 percent of total exports.

According to Kishor Bartoula, director and information officer at the Department of Customs, Rasuwagadhi is Nepal’s most reliable trading point with China.

Before the 2015 earthquake, China had made Tatopani its main customs point. The border was then closed for an extended period. Although it has not remained completely shut since, the Chinese side has not shown interest in operating it at full capacity, citing various reasons.

As a result, Rasuwagadhi gradually became the main gateway for Nepal-China trade.

Floods have repeatedly exposed the border’s vulnerability

A sudden flood in the Bhotekoshi at around 3 am in 2025 left 18 people missing and damaged major infrastructure, including the Miteri Bridge.

Ashish Gajurel, chair of the House of Representatives’ Development Committee and former executive director of the Nepal Intermodal Transport Development Board, says the previous year’s flood had already sent a strong warning about the vulnerability of the customs point and surrounding settlements.

“Last year’s flood had already given a strong warning to the customs point and the surrounding settlements. Perhaps we failed to take it seriously,” he said.

The disaster on August 26, however, has turned into a far more devastating episode. It has not only directly affected thousands of people but also washed away billions of rupees in state investment and potentially trillions of rupees in private investment.

Rasuwagadhi lies 132 kilometres from Kathmandu via Galchhi. Of that distance, an estimated 40 kilometres of road on the Rasuwa side has been completely washed away, according to a preliminary assessment by the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport.

The Department of Roads has begun assessing the condition of different sections of the road.

More than two dozen bridges between Miteri Bridge and Galchhi have also been washed away, raising uncertainty over the future operation of the Rasuwagadhi border point, customs office and immigration services.

Bartoula said decisions taken by the government would determine the future of the border point.

“This is a major cross-border trading point,” he said. “The government will study all aspects and make a decision. The department will work accordingly.”

According to the Department of Customs, 15 employees working at the customs point remain missing.

The department’s immediate priority is the search for and rescue of its missing employees. Teams have been deployed to the affected areas to determine their whereabouts.

A historic border point with seven decades of history

According to the Department of Customs, Rasuwagadhi has been known since ancient times as a major route for trade and cultural exchange between Nepal and Tibet.

The Rasuwagadhi Customs Office was established in 1956 with the aim of facilitating trade through the barter system between local residents of Rasuwa and people from Tibet’s Kerung area, while also generating government revenue.

China granted Rasuwagadhi international border status only in 2018, further increasing its significance in Nepal-China trade.

Nepal mainly imports electronic goods, ready-made garments, footwear, construction materials, agricultural products, telecommunications equipment, vehicles and industrial machinery through the border point.

Exports from Nepal to China have included carpets, handicrafts, woollen products, herbs, noodles, copper utensils and agricultural products.

The border point had also become a convenient route for Indian pilgrims travelling to Kailash Mansarovar.

Hundreds of tourists travelling for the pilgrimage this year have been left unaccounted for following the flood.

Rasuwagadhi has also been a major centre of employment and economic activity for local communities. Hotels, transport services, container loading and unloading, customs agents and other small businesses generated employment for thousands of people.

Dry port on which Rs 2 billion was spent washed away

The flood in 2025 had already caused billions of rupees in damage to infrastructure at the Rasuwagadhi customs point.

The newly constructed customs office building suffered damage worth Rs 8.159 million, while the dry port alone sustained damage estimated at Rs 912 million.

Goods and vehicles at the customs office and yard, along with containers, machinery and equipment, suffered an estimated Rs 705.1 million in damage.

This time, none of those structures have survived.

According to Gajurel, the Timure dry port was a Rs 3 billion project, of which Rs 2 billion had already been spent. Most of the structures had been completed and the project was preparing to begin finishing works.

No additional investment was made in the project after last year’s flood caused extensive damage.

Now, however, the state has lost billions of rupees in infrastructure that has been wiped out. Government employees are missing, while the extent of damage to private investment has yet to be assessed.

The historic border point and customs hub now face the daunting task of rebuilding from virtually nothing.

content.rendered:
Gorkha, September 1

Residents in Gorkha staged a protest by placing empty gas cylinders on the road, protesting a prolonged shortage of cooking gas.

Residents of Chorkate in Siranchok Rural Municipality-4 placed empty cylinders on the road on Tuesday as a symbolic protest.

“There has been a severe shortage of cooking gas here since mid-June,” said resident Madan Shrestha. “Even the gas that arrives is sent entirely to Gorkha Bazaar.”

He said the shortage had made it difficult for households to cook and warned that residents would launch a stronger protest if supplies were not restored.

“Today, we have only issued a warning. If we do not get gas, we will intensify our protest,” the locals said.

title.rendered: House of Representatives’ parliamentary calendar disrupted by indefinite adjournment

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

The House of Representatives’ parliamentary calendar has been disrupted after its meetings were postponed indefinitely.

According to the parliamentary calendar, meetings of the House of Representatives were scheduled for Monday and Tuesday. However, it is unclear when the House will convene next.

On August 26, the Federal Parliament Secretariat issued a notice announcing that the House of Representatives meeting had been postponed indefinitely.

Had the House meeting proceeded according to the calendar, Monday’s agenda would have included a proposal to consider the Employees Provident Fund (Tenth Amendment) Bill, 2083. The tentative agenda also included zero hour and the presentation of several annual reports.

Similarly, Tuesday’s agenda included a general discussion on the agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea concerning the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

The tentative agenda also included zero hour, special hour and a question-and-answer session with ministries.

However, the House meetings could not proceed as scheduled. A meeting of the House of Representatives’ Business Advisory Committee is being held on Tuesday to discuss issues including the disruption to the parliamentary calendar.

The meeting, to be held at Singha Durbar, will also discuss when to schedule the next meeting of the House of Representatives.

According to the parliamentary calendar, Wednesday’s tentative agenda includes a proposal to consider the Children (First Amendment) Bill, 2083, as well as zero hour.

The calendar also includes the dates of subsequent meetings and their tentative agendas. However, House of Representatives meetings have not been able to proceed according to the schedule.

title.rendered: Rasuwa all-party meeting prioritises ward-level relief, infrastructure repair

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Bagmati Province Chief Minister Kiran Thapa has said that the immediate priority following the devastating floods in Rasuwa is to rescue affected people and distribute relief assistance.

Addressing an all-party meeting chaired by Rasuwa Chief District Officer Narendra Pariyar, Chief Minister Thapa said the scale of destruction caused by the floods was unimaginable and that the entire government machinery had been mobilised effectively.

He said all concerned agencies had been strictly instructed to ensure there is no shortage of necessary manpower, equipment, food, medicines and other relief materials during this time of disaster.

The all-party meeting also made several important decisions to make rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts in flood-affected areas more prompt, systematic and effective.

What decisions did the meeting make?

Infrastructure repair and resumption of transport: Roads and other infrastructure damaged by the floods will be repaired immediately to resume transportation services. Necessary resources will be mobilised through coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments.

Relief distribution at the ward level: Relief materials will be collected from federal government offices, properly managed through the provincial government, and distributed directly to the ward level in coordination with local governments.

Local governments to manage bodies: Security agencies will be mobilised to identify and manage the bodies of those who died in the floods. The concerned local governments will be responsible for arranging the necessary locations and other logistical aspects of body management.

Long-term reconstruction and preparedness: Along with the immediate repair of damaged roads and bridges, concerned agencies will prioritise long-term reconstruction. Security and preparedness measures will also be strengthened to prevent further damage in potentially high-risk areas.

title.rendered: Hydropower worker escapes flood, spends night alone in cave

content.rendered:
When Shiva Giri of Ghorahi, Dang, left for work at around 7:30am on August 26, it was a routine start to his day.

Giri, a lab technician at the 216MW Upper Trishuli Hydropower Project, was heading towards Tunnel No. 3 when a dry landslide blocked the route.

He and his colleagues informed the office about the landslide and turned back towards their accommodation.

But before they could reach their rooms, Giri received another warning: A flood was coming from upstream, and everyone needed to be alerted.

Giri and his colleagues immediately ran towards their camp.

They managed to escape. But from a short distance away, they watched helplessly as the flood swept away vehicles, colleagues, a bridge, their camp and other project structures.

“Boulders as high as 50 metres were being tossed around as the flood came towards us, destroying the bridge and the camp,” Giri recalled. “We survived by jumping into the forest just two seconds before it reached us.”

The scene remains vivid in his mind.

“People were running on the road, and there were vehicles. It swept everything away. It left nothing behind,” he said.

All eight members of the lab team, including Giri, survived.

“There were eight of us in the group. Because we were warned on time, all eight of us survived,” he said.

But surviving the flood was only the beginning of their ordeal.

Waiting for a rescue that did not come

Around 10 or 11am, as the river began to subside, they moved a little further down. Helicopters soon began circling overhead to assess the situation.

“When the helicopter arrived, we felt there was hope of survival,” Giri said. “We lit a fire to signal them and called for help.”

But the helicopter left without rescuing them.

“We kept watching as some people on the other side were rescued,” he said.

By 3pm, however, there was still no sign of rescue for Giri and his colleagues.

They were running out of options.

“It became difficult even without water. When I could no longer walk properly, I called my family and asked them to send a helicopter at their own expense,” he said.

That effort also failed.

Through phone conversations, they were told that a village could be reached after walking for eight to 10 hours.

“It was already 3pm. What were we supposed to do by staying there? What would we eat? So we started climbing uphill,” Giri said.

As they climbed, the group split into two. Those who could walk faster went ahead, while Giri and some others fell behind.

Giri had injured his knee after falling while running to escape the flood.

“Darkness fell while we were walking. My phone had already switched off. I had no idea what time it was,” he recalled.

He eventually spent the night in a cave.

A dog that had followed him along the way became his companion for the night.

After walking for eight to 10 hours, Giri was exhausted. He had neither food nor water.

“I thought, if only it would rain, at least I could drink water,” he said. “And half an hour later, it started raining. I had an empty bottle, so I filled it with rainwater and drank it.”

Only then, he said, did he begin to feel that he might survive.

He could not sleep that night. As he lay awake thinking about what to do next, he decided it would be safer to return to where the flood had occurred rather than continue uphill.

“I thought a helicopter might come to where the incident had happened. It wouldn’t come all the way up there. There were no vehicles either. At least I might find some food there,” he said.

After spending around 10 hours climbing uphill, Giri turned back the next morning and spent another six hours walking downhill.

Three attempts to rescue him failed

Helicopters began arriving again after 10am.

Giri started signalling to them. At around 11am, one helicopter spotted him and attempted a rescue.

But the attempt failed.

When he tried to move towards the helicopter, he became stuck in the mud.

“They tried to pull me out three times, but they couldn’t,” he said. “After they failed, I signalled to them to drop some food and water.”

About half an hour after that helicopter left, a Nepal Army helicopter arrived.

“The ground sank wherever I stepped. The helicopter couldn’t land,” Giri said. “It held itself in the air and lifted me out.”

After being rescued, Giri was taken to Trishuli Hospital. Following initial treatment there, he is now receiving treatment at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu.

‘I told my family I might not survive’

Giri has survived to tell the story. But during those hours stranded after the flood, he said he repeatedly lost hope that he would make it out alive.

He called his family and recorded a video for his wife.

“I told her, ‘I don’t think I’ll survive. I haven’t even had water since morning,’” he said.

Now, after surviving what he describes as an experience that could easily have ended differently, Giri says his outlook on life has changed.

“It feels like my life has changed. I feel like I died once. But then I survived,” he said.

title.rendered: All-party meeting to discuss Bhotekoshi flood damage, rescue and rehabilitation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

An all-party meeting will be held on Tuesday to discuss the damage caused by the Bhotekoshi flood, as well as ongoing search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts.

According to Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) spokesperson Jagadish Kharel, the meeting will be held at 2pm at the RSP parliamentary party office in Singha Durbar.

The meeting will bring together representatives of various political parties to discuss the overall situation following the Bhote Koshi flood, including relief and rescue efforts and the rehabilitation of affected areas.

The parties are also expected to discuss the challenges facing affected communities and measures needed for their recovery.

title.rendered: Small vehicles to use separate routes on Hetauda–Kathmandu road amid rising traffic

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Traffic congestion has increased on the Hetauda–Kathmandu road after flooding in the Trishuli River blocked the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir in Dhading.

With traffic diverted through Hetauda, the local administration has introduced separate routes for vehicles travelling to and from Kathmandu from Tuesday.

According to a notice issued by the local administration, passenger vehicles with a capacity of fewer than 14 seats travelling towards Kathmandu will have to use the Bhimphedi–Kulekhani–Sisneri–Dakshinkali route.

Vehicles travelling from Kathmandu to Hetauda will have to take the Farping–Phakhel–Kulekhani–Bhimphedi route.

According to Santosh Subedi, administrative officer at the District Administration Office, Makwanpur, freight vehicles and large passenger buses travelling to Kathmandu will have to use the Tribhuvan Highway, while those returning to Hetauda will have to use the Kanti Highway.

Subedi said traffic using the Hetauda–Kathmandu route had increased after the Prithvi Highway was blocked at Krishnabhir in Dhading.

The administration has also asked fuel tankers and heavy freight vehicles not to use a Bailey bridge near the Tribhuvan Highway in Makwanpur, citing concerns over its load-bearing capacity. Such vehicles have been asked to use the diversion alongside the bridge.

The administration said the new traffic arrangement is expected to reduce congestion and prolonged vehicle stoppages on the alternative routes.

It has urged drivers, transport operators and passengers to follow the designated routes to keep traffic movement smooth, safe and orderly.

title.rendered: Bodies continue to be found in India, toll reaches 13 as Bhotekoshi flood link suspected

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, September 1

Six men and seven women have been found dead in the Gandak River in Uttar Pradesh, with Indian authorities coordinating with Nepal over identification and repatriation.

Bodies believed to have been swept downstream from Nepal following the devastating Rasuwa floods continue to be recovered from the Gandak (Narayani) River in India.

Kushinagar district authorities in Uttar Pradesh said 13 unidentified bodies have so far been recovered from the river. Of them, six are men and seven are women.

Six of the bodies have been kept at the mortuary of Kushinagar Medical College, while the remaining seven were sent to the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Gorakhpur after the mortuary ran out of space, according to the district administration.

Teams from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) are continuing search and rescue operations along the Narayani River amid concerns that more bodies could be recovered.

Kushinagar’s acting district magistrate and chief development officer, Vandita Srivastava, said authorities were following the required legal procedures for the recovered bodies.

The Kushinagar district administration is also coordinating with the relevant authorities in Nepal. Information about the recovered bodies is being shared with Nepal through India’s Ministry of External Affairs, according to the administration.

The bodies will be handed over to Nepal after post-mortem examinations and other required legal procedures are completed. Nepal will then begin the process of identifying the bodies and handing them over to their families.

Meanwhile, the Kushinagar administration has established a control room to assist Nepali citizens travelling to India and those reaching the district in search of missing relatives following the floods.

title.rendered: More than 20 bodies found inside a single house in Betrawati

content.rendered:
Betrawati, September 1

More than 20 bodies have been found inside a single house in Betrawati of Bidur Municipality-10, Nuwakot, following the devastating flood that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems August 26.

Superintendent of Police Bipin Regmi of the District Police Office, Nuwakot, confirmed that a large number of bodies had been found inside the house.

He said the exact number could not yet be established because of the rain and darkness.

“Yes, several bodies were found inside the same room of the buried house in Betrawati. However, because it is raining and it is already night, we have not yet been able to determine exactly how many bodies there are,” Regmi told Onlinekhabar.

A photograph obtained by Onlinekhabar from a trusted source shows around two dozen bodies lying inside a room of the house.

Mangal Tamang, a ward member of Bidur Municipality, said 22 bodies had been seen inside the house.

“Twenty-two bodies were found in the same house today. It is the house a little above Ghanti Ghar. It is a large house. We had asked that a drone be sent to inspect the area,” Tamang told Onlinekhabar.

According to Tamang, a security team including additional personnel reached the house on Monday and recovered several bodies.

“Five or six bodies were taken out of the house today. The others are still there. An attempt was made the day before yesterday but they could not do it. They tried again yesterday and could not. Today, the Armed Police Force also went there and many bodies were found,” he said.

He said around 16 bodies were still inside the house.

“Many of the bodies are in a condition where they cannot be identified,” Tamang said.

Police said search and recovery operations at the house would resume on Tuesday morning.

title.rendered: When the Home Minister becomes a rescuer, who leads the disaster response?

content.rendered:
Nepal’s disaster response is facing growing questions over command and coordination after Home Minister Sudan Gurung personally joined the search for missing people inside a tunnel in the Trishuli area, despite the Home Ministry’s broader responsibility for coordinating the country’s disaster response.

Under the Government of Nepal (Allocation of Business) Rules, 2026, the Home Minister is responsible for disaster-related functions including the development and dissemination of early warning systems, national disaster management policy and regulation, relief and rehabilitation of displaced people, and the operation of the national disaster fund.

These responsibilities effectively place the Home Minister at the centre of the country’s disaster command structure.

That means the Home Minister’s role during the devastating August 26 flood in the Bhotekoshi river should include coordinating the deployment of security personnel, setting rescue priorities, identifying shortages of equipment and resources, and directing relief and rehabilitation efforts across affected areas.

Instead, Gurung has spent several days at a tunnel site in the Trishuli area, personally participating in excavation efforts to search for people missing after the flood.

His hands-on involvement has been welcomed by many as a sign of personal commitment. But disaster management experts and former government officials have questioned whether the approach is appropriate for a minister whose primary responsibility is to coordinate the wider response.

“His eagerness to do something is clearly visible. I had openly praised him earlier. But it appears that he needs to improve his way of working,” a former home secretary told Onlinekhabar.

‘He can dig for 10 days, but that won’t solve the problem’

Families of people still missing after the flood have also expressed frustration.

Sobhit Pokhrel of Lamjung, who has been waiting for news of missing relatives at the Trishuli barracks in Nuwakot for six days, said Gurung’s personal involvement in excavation was not enough.

“The problem is that they built the tunnel, but there is no skilled manpower to carry out the rescue. The Home Minister himself went into the tunnel and worked. He deserves thanks for that. But even if he stays there and works for 10 days, it won’t solve the problem. Rescue requires skilled manpower,” Pokhrel said.

Pokhrel spoke to Onlinekhabar on August 29, when Gurung had gone to the tunnel to help with the excavation. Foreign rescue teams had not yet begun operations at the site. Chinese and Indian teams arrived later that evening and began work.

Gurung had travelled to the Bhotekoshi area on Friday and had remained there, focusing on the tunnel search.

At the same time, reports have emerged that relief supplies are not reaching some of the worst-affected communities in Rasuwa, even as large quantities of relief material remain stockpiled in Trishuli.

Critics say some of the problems could have been addressed through stronger coordination and instructions from the Home Ministry rather than requiring the minister to personally participate in excavation.

Security agencies have the manpower, but lack equipment

The concerns extend beyond the Home Minister’s role.

The Armed Police Force is legally tasked with rescuing people affected by disasters and epidemics anywhere in Nepal. The force has personnel trained in disaster response, including divers and teams trained to conduct search operations following floods, landslides and earthquakes.

But officials say the force lacks the equipment needed to make full use of that expertise.

Among the reported shortages are rescue equipment, drones and human-detection devices. Reaching remote disaster sites by helicopter is also a major challenge.

The Armed Police Force has repeatedly asked the government to provide it with a helicopter for disaster response. That request has yet to be fulfilled.

Gurung had promised to facilitate the purchase of a helicopter for the force when he visited its headquarters in Halchowk for an inspection during his first tenure as Home Minister. He subsequently left the ministry before the promise could be fulfilled.

He has since returned as Home Minister, but the helicopter has still not been provided.

As a result, the Nepal Army has largely taken the lead in helicopter-based rescue operations in difficult-to-reach areas following the Rasuwa flood. The Nepal Police and Armed Police Force have been assisting in areas accessible by road or on foot.

Different agencies, different figures

The disaster response has also exposed gaps in coordination between security agencies, with figures on personnel deployed, people rescued and those missing varying between agencies.

According to security sources, 8,399 Nepal Army personnel, 7,293 Nepal Police personnel and 4,203 Armed Police Force personnel are currently involved in search and rescue operations.

The sources say 2,974 people have been rescued by the Army, 2,699 by Nepal Police and 3,057 by the Armed Police Force.

Among the security personnel themselves, 45 Nepal Army personnel, 13 Armed Police Force personnel and 25 Nepal Police personnel are reported missing.

The August 26 flood in the Bhotekoshi caused extensive damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and surrounding areas. Over 900 bodies have been recovered, while nearly 4,000 people remain missing, according to the figures cited by security sources.

The government initially received praise for its response. A meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority was held soon after the flood, with a focus on rescue, search operations and relief. All three security agencies were mobilised following government instructions.

But as days have passed, criticism has intensified over the lack of progress in some searches, delays in bringing in international rescue expertise and questions over the Home Minister’s decision to personally participate in tunnel excavation rather than focus on overall command and coordination.

A decision reached at an all-party meeting facilitated by Rastriya Swatantra Party chairperson Rabi Lamichhane to cooperate in the disaster response has also failed to gain visible momentum.

The central question now is whether Nepal’s disaster response needs more ministerial presence at individual rescue sites — or stronger command, coordination, equipment and specialised manpower across the entire response system.

Heavy rain has been falling in Kathmandu since the evening, pushing up water levels in rivers and streams across the Kathmandu Valley.

The water level of the Bishnumati River has risen close to the danger mark, according to the Flood Forecasting Division. The Gongabu water measurement station recorded the river approaching the danger level.

title.rendered: Rescue team still unable to enter Trishuli-3A tunnel as mud, water block access

content.rendered:
Dhunche, August 31

A rescue team working at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project has been unable to enter the tunnel leading to its underground powerhouse, with mud and water continuing to block the way.

The team discovered a cable access tunnel on Sunday and had hoped to reach the powerhouse from there. But Nepal Electricity Authority Deputy Executive Director Madan Timsina said rescuers were still unable to enter the tunnel on Monday after finding it filled with water and mud.

Water has been seeping from the tunnel as rescuers excavate, while mud continues to accumulate inside. This has forced the team to cut further through the tunnel wall before it can proceed.

“We are working at the access tunnel, and the powerhouse is 183 metres inside from the point where we are cutting. If the employees are alive, we hope to find them in the powerhouse. That is why we are making every possible effort to enter,” Timsina said.

Seepage is common in underground powerhouses, with water normally pumped out to prevent damage to the facility. But after the flood shut down electricity generation at the project, the pumps stopped operating, allowing water to accumulate and flow out.

“We are continuing maximum efforts because we believe there is still a possibility of rescuing people alive,” Timsina said.

An official involved in the rescue said the operation was initially delayed because rescuers could not get sufficient equipment and manpower to the site.

“We could not initially bring an excavator from elsewhere. We repaired two excavators that were found nearby but had broken down and started work with them. The Army finally brought a third excavator on Monday,” the official said.

Other equipment also reached the site only after delays. The official said there is now no major shortage of equipment needed for the operation and expressed hope that rescuers could enter the tunnel soon.

He said the work could have progressed faster if more excavators had been available from the beginning.

The rescue team had been working continuously for three days before finding the cable access tunnel on Sunday.

Rescuers have attempted to use the tunnel to restore electricity and look for signs from anyone trapped inside. So far, however, no signs have been detected, according to sources involved in the operation.

The fact that water from the seepage is still flowing out of the tunnel has offered a small measure of hope. Sources involved in the rescue said people trapped inside could have access to water if they have survived.

“If the mud has not entered and buried the powerhouse, there is greater hope that people could still be rescued alive. There is enough oxygen in the powerhouse for around 15 days, and if they have been able to get water, there is a possibility they could still be alive,” a source said.

The source added that if there is not a large amount of debris inside, rescuers are hopeful of clearing the passage by Tuesday.

40–42 engineers were working inside

The 60MW Trishuli-3A project was already shut down for a complete overhaul when the flood hit.

Around 40 to 42 highly skilled engineers were working inside the underground powerhouse as part of the overhaul work.

The flood subsequently buried both the upper and lower tunnels of the project.

Rescuers are now attempting to reach the underground powerhouse through the cable tunnel used to carry electricity cables out of the powerhouse.

The search continues amid uncertainty over the fate of those who were inside when the flood struck.

title.rendered: 198 still missing from Upper Trishuli-3B hydropower project after Bhotekoshi flood

content.rendered:
Dhunche, August 31

As many as 198 employees and workers at the Upper Trishuli-3B hydropower project remain unaccounted for following the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

The flood affected the project site, where employees, construction workers, consultants, security guards and others were present. The project is being developed by Trishuli Jal Vidyut Company Limited.

According to the company, 201 people were initially reported missing or uncontactable after the flood. Three have since made contact, while 198 remain unaccounted for. A further 91 people from the project have been rescued and moved to safety.

Those unaccounted for include project employees and their family members, workers employed by civil construction contractors, electromechanical and hydromechanical personnel, consultants, security guards and students undertaking internships at the project.

Lila Aryal, deputy director of the company, said 21 of the project’s 48 employees remain unaccounted for.

“Twenty-one of the 48 employees at the project are unaccounted for,” Aryal said. “Those who were outside the project site are in contact with us. Everyone else was there.”

All workers inside tunnel reported safe

The company said all employees and workers who were inside the Upper Trishuli-3B project’s tunnel when the flood struck managed to get out safely.

“Everyone who was inside the tunnel managed to get out safely,” Aryal said. “Water initially entered the tunnel, so they moved higher up and waited. They came out after the water level went down.”

The project chief and the head of the consulting team have been at the site in recent days, coordinating search and rescue efforts. A team of 51 Nepali Army personnel has also reached the project site.

Search extends 1.5km into tunnel

As part of the search for those unaccounted for, a team including the Upper Trishuli-3B project chief entered the tunnel and inspected around 1.5 kilometres of its length.

The company said there was no indication that anyone was trapped in the section that was searched. However, the team could not proceed further because of darkness, mud and silt inside the tunnel.

“They went about 1.5 kilometres into the tunnel and came back after establishing that there was no one there,” Aryal said. “Beyond that point, it became dark, and there was too much mud and silt to proceed.”

The company is now preparing to bring additional equipment to expand the search inside the tunnel and at other possible locations.

Excavators need to be flown in

The flood destroyed or disrupted road access to the project, making it difficult to transport heavy equipment to the site.

The company is preparing to send excavators and other equipment by helicopter to support the search and excavation work. However, helicopter availability has caused delays.

“We are preparing to send an excavator and are also sending other supplies,” Aryal said. “We will start excavation after the equipment arrives. For now, people themselves are doing the digging.”

The excavator was initially scheduled to be transported a day earlier but could not be sent because of difficulties arranging a helicopter.

“The excavator was supposed to be sent yesterday, but it did not go. It is still being prepared today,” Aryal said. “There has been some delay because of the helicopter.”

The missing people are not limited to Upper Trishuli-3B project employees. A significant number of workers employed by consulting and construction companies are also unaccounted for.

According to the company, most of the personnel from the consulting side who were at the project site remain out of contact. One or two people who were away from the site have made contact, while another person reportedly escaped to safety.

Many workers employed by the civil construction contractor were also at their camp when the flood struck. The company said four Chinese nationals were among those staying at the camp.

“A lot of civil construction work was underway, and the workers, including four Chinese nationals, were at the camp,” Aryal said. “Those who were in the camp area, rather than the office area, may all have been affected.”

Search and rescue teams, including the Nepali Army, have been deployed at the project site since the flood. The project chief and the head of the consulting team are also there.

However, difficult terrain and the lack of necessary equipment have hampered the search. Workers are currently carrying out excavation and searches manually, with the company planning to accelerate the operation once excavators and other equipment arrive.

While everyone known to have been inside the tunnel has been reported safe, the fate of a large number of employees and workers who were in the project camp and other areas remains unknown.

The company said efforts are continuing to locate the 198 people who remain unaccounted for.

title.rendered: Nepal Army leads rescue efforts in flood-hit areas (Photos)

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 31

A devastating flood that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors on August 26 caused extensive loss of life and widespread destruction across Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

The full scale of the disaster is still being assessed, with the number of people killed and missing continuing to change as search and rescue operations remain underway. As of Monday, authorities had reported 903 deaths and more than 4,000 people missing.

Nepal’s security agencies were mobilised immediately after the flood, with the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force leading rescue and relief operations alongside local residents and other responders.

The Nepali Army has used helicopters and ground teams to reach people stranded in some of the worst-hit areas. By Sunday, the Army had rescued 2,697 people from Rasuwa alone, including more than 2,400 people evacuated by air.

Rasuwa’s Timure, Syabrubesi, Dhunche and Mailung areas have been among the key locations for rescue operations, while teams have also been working in Nuwakot and other downstream areas.

The destruction of roads and bridges has made many areas difficult to reach, forcing rescuers to rely heavily on helicopters and other emergency measures. Rescue teams are also continuing searches at hydropower projects and tunnels where workers remain unaccounted for.

The photographs captured by the Nepali Army show the scale of the destruction and the ongoing efforts to reach survivors and provide assistance in the flood-hit areas.
