title.rendered: Nepal asks Loss and Damage Fund for emergency financing after Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The government has asked the Loss and Damage Fund to provide emergency financing immediately following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River basin.

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle and Agriculture, Forest and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary jointly sent an official letter to the co-chairs of the fund’s board on Monday, requesting an urgent decision to release financial support.

The request was made after the government held a special meeting to discuss the extensive loss of life and property caused by the floods.

Dr Maheshwar Dhakal, chief of the Climate Change Management Division at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, said the government formally approached the fund through a special decision, citing the scale and urgency of the disaster.

The letter describes the Bhotekoshi floods as an extreme climate-related disaster originating in the high Himalayan region.

Dhakal said the government told the Loss and Damage Fund that the scale of the damage was far beyond Nepal’s domestic resources and its capacity to respond immediately.

“The scale of the damage caused by the floods is far beyond Nepal’s domestic resources and immediate response capacity,” Dhakal said. “The board’s regular 10th meeting is scheduled for December, but that would be too late for our needs. Our main request is for emergency support to be provided now through a special decision.”

The government has also highlighted the disaster’s impact on a sensitive transboundary Himalayan river system and its cascading effects on downstream communities far beyond the immediate flood-affected areas.

Search, rescue, relief and rapid damage assessments are still underway. Although a full assessment of the economic and non-economic losses is yet to be completed, preliminary information indicates that the impact is severe and beyond the country’s capacity to cope, according to Dhakal.

Nepal highlights climate justice

In its letter, Nepal has also emphasised the issue of climate justice, noting that the country contributes almost nothing to global greenhouse gas emissions but continues to face the disproportionate and devastating impacts of climate change.

The government said the Bhotekoshi disaster demonstrated how melting snow and other climate-related hazards in the high Himalayas can trigger sudden crises in densely populated downstream areas, affecting food, energy, health, infrastructure, ecosystems and overall human security.

The letter urges the Loss and Damage Fund’s board to take a “rapid, direct and effective” decision in accordance with its procedures, given the exceptional scale and severity of the disaster.

The government said immediate assistance would help protect affected communities, restore essential services and prevent further humanitarian suffering.

It also expressed confidence that timely support to Nepal could demonstrate how international solidarity with climate-vulnerable countries can be translated into concrete assistance during a crisis.

Nepal has told the Loss and Damage Fund it is ready to provide preliminary assessments, official data, satellite information and sector-wise damage details. It has also asked the board to coordinate with the government through a designated focal point.

title.rendered: Nepal Police warns against eating fish, drinking water from Bhotekoshi and Trishuli

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Nepal Police has urged people not to eat fish or other food products taken from the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers following the devastating floods in Rasuwa.

Police said floodwaters carried bodies, dead animals, waste and other contaminated materials into the rivers, potentially introducing harmful pathogens into the water.

People have also been advised not to drink water from the two rivers.

Police have asked residents living along the Bhote Koshi and surrounding riverbanks not to catch fish or collect other river products for consumption or take them home.

The consumption of contaminated water and food could increase the risk of diseases including cholera, diarrhoea and skin infections, police said.

The death toll from the Bhotekoshi flood has reached 939, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

Chitwan has recorded the highest number of recovered bodies, with 279. Eastern Nawalparasi has reported 216, while 169 bodies have been recovered in Western Nawalparasi.

The Nepal Army has also provided medical treatment to 2,700 people, according to the NDRRMA.

title.rendered: Six days after Bhotekoshi flood, some victims still waiting for relief

content.rendered:
Six days after the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River, Pemba Lhamu Tamang of Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-3 in Rasuwa has yet to receive any relief.

The food stored at her home is running out, leaving her increasingly anxious. She says the fear of being left without food has begun to affect her health.

Since the flood swept through settlements on August 26, Nepal Army helicopters have not reached the area where she lives.

Whenever she hears the sound of a helicopter, Tamang said she hopes relief is finally coming. But the helicopters have so far left behind only the sound of hope.

The lack of electricity has added to the hardship.

“We are surviving for now on whatever food we had at home. But if relief does not arrive soon, we will suffer a lot,” Tamang told Onlinekhabar. “There is no electricity and the entire village is in darkness. With all the roads washed away, it feels as if someone has locked us in a prison and left us to starve.”

Residents of wards 2 and 5 of Gosainkunda are facing a similar situation. With even rice and lentils running out, some residents are reportedly spending their days drinking water available at home.

Gosainkunda Rural Municipality chairperson Kaising Nurpu Tamang said that despite repeated efforts, not even a bottle of water had reached some areas in the municipality.

“Everyone calls just to ask whether relief has reached us. But no one is actually sending it,” he said. “Everyone is saying the state is neglecting us. I have also been trying day and night to arrange relief, but I have not been able to get it here.”

Meanwhile, Amachhodingmo Rural Municipality chairperson Buchung Tamang said some relief had arrived initially but had already run out.

The situation has become even more difficult because the lack of electricity has disrupted communication with residents.

“Because there is no electricity, we have not been able to remain in constant contact with everyone. Our village feels completely cut off,” he said. “We may somehow manage to get through today, but if relief does not arrive by tomorrow, there will be a crisis.”

Government says relief is being delivered

The government, however, says relief supplies have been continuously sent to the affected areas.

According to figures released by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Monday, 37 trucks and 35 Bolero vehicles had transported food and non-food relief supplies to affected areas. Eight helicopter flights had also been used to transport supplies.

The authority said that on August 30, five portable generators, along with food, non-food items, medicines and other health supplies, were sent to Rasuwa by road and air. Relief materials were also mobilised to Nuwakot through 13 vehicles and helicopters.

The Nepal Army has also posted photographs and videos on its Facebook page showing helicopters transporting relief materials, although it has not specified where all the supplies were delivered.

Prime Minister Balen Shah has also been providing updates on relief efforts through his social media accounts.

However, his updates have largely detailed where relief materials were collected and which military facilities they were taken to, rather than where they were distributed to affected residents.

According to Shah, relief materials collected at warehouses and government facilities in Kathmandu are being transported by air and road to the Nepal Army’s Maithil Barracks in Battar, Nuwakot, and to Uttargaya in Rasuwa.

He said the materials are then being distributed in affected areas by a committee coordinated by the assistant chief district officer and comprising security personnel and other stakeholders.

Shah also said an MI-17 helicopter transported food supplies from Tribhuvan International Airport to Dhunche on Monday, while essential food and non-food relief materials were sent to Dhunche and Uttargaya by road.

International assistance has also been arriving in Nepal. According to Shah, India, China, the United States and other countries have provided relief materials. India alone has sent 57.5 tonnes of humanitarian assistance and essential medicines in three phases.

Where is the relief going?

Despite the government’s figures, the situation on the ground raises questions about whether relief supplies are reaching those who need them most.

Most of the cargo vehicles travelling along the road towards Nuwakot are carrying relief supplies. But many appear to stop in Battar.

Local resident Rakesh Neupane said relief vehicles are often seen stopping around the Maithil Barracks of the Nepal Army.

“When people see those rescued by the army being brought to this barracks, many assume that relief will be distributed here. But as soon as distribution starts, there is a rush and people fight to get supplies,” Neupane told Onlinekhabar. “That is why genuine victims are not getting relief. Those who come to distribute it also choose places that are convenient for them, take photographs and leave. Without the government delivering relief further into the affected areas, it is impossible for it to reach the victims.”

Abhinav Joshi, who has been involved in collecting relief since the day after the flood, said poor road conditions are preventing supplies from moving beyond Nuwakot.

“Look at the condition of the vehicles carrying relief supplies even today,” he said. “Even if our relief has not reached them, government relief should at least have reached the victims by helicopter.”

The government’s own updates indicate that large quantities of relief have been taken to Battar, but do not clearly establish how much has subsequently reached individual communities in upper Rasuwa.

Asked where the relief was being distributed, Shanti Mahat, spokesperson for the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said 14 task forces led by joint-secretary-level officials had been formed to respond to the floods.

“You should probably ask the person in charge of relief for that information,” she told Onlinekhabar.

Joint Secretary Jagannath Tiwari, who heads the authority’s relief task force, said the supplies recorded in government figures are reaching affected people.

“We have not received information that relief has failed to reach anywhere. Where did this information come from?” he said.

title.rendered: NEA plans to operate Sanjen hydropower plant in isolated mode to restore power in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 31

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has begun preparations to operate the Sanjen Hydropower Plant in isolated mode to restore electricity supply in flood-affected areas of Rasuwa.

The NEA is working to operate the local electricity system separately and supply power to affected areas of the district. The authority said the necessary technical preparations and coordination are underway.

To generate electricity from the Sanjen Hydropower Plant and connect it to the local system, the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation is coordinating with a Chinese company through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to obtain the necessary assistance to reset the machine’s password.

Meanwhile, alternative energy sources are being prepared for areas where immediate reconnection to the electricity system is not possible.

The Alternative Energy Promotion Centre is preparing to provide electricity through solar power and other alternative sources in areas where the electricity infrastructure has been damaged by the floods.

The NEA said the strategy is to deploy alternative energy sources to meet immediate needs while repairs to flood-damaged electricity infrastructure and efforts to restore regular power supply continue.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi floods cause Rs 600 million in direct damage to bank branches

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Flooding in Rasuwa on August 26 caused an estimated Rs 600 million in physical damage to branches in the affected areas, according to the Nepal Bankers’ Association.

The association said 16 branches of 12 banks were operating in the flood-affected areas. Of these, 15 branches were completely destroyed, while one sustained significant damage.

The affected branches had a combined 78,204 depositors.

The banks also had eight ATM counters in the affected areas. Nine ATMs held a total of Rs 11.663 million in cash, while Rs 172.4 million was kept in cash vaults and Rs 11.7 million at cash counters, according to the association.

Anil Sharma, chief executive officer of the Nepal Bankers’ Association, said the cash held in vaults, counters and ATMs was insured and therefore was not included in the estimated physical losses.

“The physical damage to branch offices, excluding cash, appears to be around Rs 600 million,” Sharma said.

He said banks also face a separate risk from loans extended in the affected areas, as much of the collateral against those loans consisted of land in areas hit by the flood.

“Banks had extended loans against land as collateral in the affected areas. Now there is a situation where the collateral itself may no longer exist,” Sharma said.

The affected branches had 2,125 borrowers, with banks having extended a combined Rs 2.43 billion in loans in the area, excluding lending to hydropower projects.

The branches held total deposits of Rs 4.5 billion.

Agricultural Development Bank suffered the largest reported damage among the affected banks. Its Trishuli branch was completely destroyed, while 64 locker boxes used by customers were also damaged.

The association said losses to property kept inside the lockers have not been included because banks do not insure customers’ locker contents and do not know what customers have stored inside them. Gold pledged as collateral for loans, however, is insured and has also not been counted among the banks’ losses.

Branches of Agricultural Development Bank, Citizens Bank, Global IME Bank, Himalayan Bank, Laxmi Sunrise Bank, Machhapuchchhre Bank, NMB Bank and Sanima Bank each suffered damage.

Prabhu Bank had two affected branches, while NIC Asia Bank and Nepal Investment Bank had three affected branches each.

Meanwhile, 26 bank employees remain unaccounted for following the floods, the association said. The employees have been reported missing after several bank branches in the affected areas were completely destroyed.

title.rendered: Alternative road opens to flood-hit areas across Trishuli

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

A road has been reopened to reconnect parts of Nuwakot across the Trishuli River after bridges were damaged by the recent floods, restoring access to the district headquarters and easing the movement of relief supplies.

The Ministry of Infrastructure Development said the road has been brought into operation along the right bank of the Trishuli River under the Galchhi–Trishuli Highway.

The route runs from across the Trishuli bridge through Kalleritar, Koshikhola, Pipaltar, Darshantar, Chhatrekhola and Gauribesi before reaching Trishuli Bazaar.

The reopening has restored road access for many residents living across the river to the district headquarters, according to the ministry.

The road is also expected to make it easier to transport rescue teams, relief materials and other essential supplies to flood-affected areas.

Several bridges over the Trishuli River were damaged or swept away by the floods, cutting off communities on the other side of the river from the main road network. The newly opened route provides an alternative connection while those crossings remain affected.

title.rendered: How a vice-principal’s quick action got students out of the flood’s path

content.rendered:
It was breakfast time at Uttargaya Public English Boarding School when Pawan Sharma received the warning.

It was around 9:15 am. A huge surge of floodwater was moving downstream, the school was told, and people in the area needed to move at least a kilometre away from the Betrawati turn.

The hostel students were still eating.

Sharma did not wait.

“We stopped their food and took the children to the top of the hill, to a safer place,” he told Onlinekhabar.

For a school with more than 370 students, there was little time to think about what might happen next. There was only time to get the children out of the flood’s path.

What followed was a frantic effort to account for students, reunite them with their families and reach those who had become stranded as the flood swept through the area.

Sharma says around 95 percent of the students under the school’s care have since been handed over to their guardians or otherwise accounted for. But several children remain difficult to trace.

The school has records or information about roughly 40 to 45 percent of the students who were at the school during the disaster, he said. Around 10 percent were either on their way to other locations or staying at shelters elsewhere.

For some others, the school still does not know what happened.

“We have no record of them,” Sharma said. “We don’t know whether they left or stayed.”

Some of those children may have been with their guardians when the flood struck. That has made it difficult for the school to establish where they are.

The danger was not limited to the children.

As news of the flood spread, guardians began rushing towards the school to take their children home. Some came on motorcycles and in auto-rickshaws.

But even the journey to collect their children became dangerous.

“There were guardians who came to take their children, but they were caught along the way,” Sharma said.

Some managed to make their way uphill. Others were pulled to safety by people around them.

For Sharma and the school staff, the rescue did not end after the children were moved to higher ground.

Some students had become stranded in forested areas. The school arranged vehicles and sent staff, including managing director Suraj, to reach them.

The rescue continued late into the night.

“We were bringing them down until 10 at night,” Sharma said.

When help did not arrive as quickly as the school needed, staff members began arranging things themselves.

Sharma said he approached the municipality, a nearby security barracks and government officials, asking for food and medicines for students sheltering above the school.

They were told relief would be provided, he said, but the immediate assistance did not materialise.

So the school bought first-aid supplies itself.

School representatives then travelled to Nuwakot, where they received further help and arranged vehicles to reach students who were still stranded.

The vehicles were used to bring children to safety, and the school continued handing them over to their families.

For Sharma, however, the flood was more than a rescue operation.

He had joined Uttargaya Public English Boarding School only about five months earlier.

A veteran of the education sector with 28 years of experience, Sharma is originally from Darjeeling. Before coming to Nepal, he had worked in schools in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal.

He had arrived in Uttargaya expecting to build something new.

“A new family, a new life,” he said.

That is what makes the aftermath so difficult for him.

“I feel as if I have lost a family,” Sharma said.

The school community he had only recently begun to call his own had been torn apart by a disaster nobody expected to reach such a scale.

People had assumed that sending children home would keep them safer.

Instead, for some families, the journey home became the most dangerous part.

“People normally think the children will be safe at home,” Sharma said. “But it turned out the opposite.”

Now, after the rescue, comes the harder question: how does the school begin again?

“It feels like we have gone back to minus zero,” Sharma said.

He hopes the situation improves quickly and that the children who remain unaccounted for are found.

The school is also discussing relocating some students to safer places while continuing to establish the whereabouts of those it has not yet been able to contact.

For Sharma, the disaster has changed the meaning of the school itself.

He came to Uttargaya for work. In five months, he said, he had begun to see the students and colleagues as his family.

Now, as he tries to help the school recover, he is left wondering how that family can begin again.

“I pray that everything gets better as soon as possible,” he said.

title.rendered: Floods damage water supply systems in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, leaving thousands without drinking water

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The devastating floods of August 26 have caused extensive damage to drinking water systems in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. Government agencies have yet to determine exactly how many water supply systems were damaged or how many people have been deprived of access to drinking water.

According to Kamal Raj Shrestha, Director General of the Department of Water Supply and Sewerage Management, the biggest damage was caused to the water supply project serving Battar Bazaar in Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot.

More than 5,500 households had been benefiting from the water supply project managed by the Bidur Water Supply and Sanitation Users’ Institution.

“This water supply system was brought to Battar Bazaar from Betrawati along the road,” Director General Shrestha said. “Along with the road, all the structures of the project have also been damaged.” As a result, a large population has been deprived of drinking water. The disruption of electricity following the floods has also made it difficult to provide water through alternative arrangements in the affected areas, Shrestha said.

Shrestha and a high-level team are currently in flood-affected areas of Nuwakot and Rasuwa, assessing water supply systems and working on emergency management. “In settlements along the riverbanks, the water supply structures were washed away along with other infrastructure. Their damage is still being assessed,” he said. “The immediate impact has been on the water supply to Battar Bazaar.”

There is still no reliable electricity supply in Nuwakot and Rasuwa. Shrestha said the low-voltage supply has made it impossible to operate pumping systems to draw water from borewells. The department has therefore brought generators from Kathmandu and started working on an alternative pumping system. According to Shrestha, a pumping system with a capacity of 23 litres per second was brought into operation today using a 100 kVA generator.

In addition, arrangements have been made to distribute drinking water to shelters through Kathmandu Upatyaka Khanepani Limited and private water tankers, Shrestha said. The tankers are distributing water at locations including Rahul Dhara. Apart from Battar Bazaar, where demand for drinking water remains high, there is currently no immediate need to restore water supplies to all settlements along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli riverbanks in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, as many of those settlements were washed away by the floods.

However, ensuring clean drinking water and toilets for sanitation at shelters housing flood victims remains a major challenge. Shrestha said the department is currently focused on addressing these needs.

According to him, there is no major shortage of water sources during the monsoon season. However, the destruction of roads and bridges has created difficulties in distributing water. The department is also working to restore water supplies in affected areas of Rasuwa on a priority basis.

Rajendra Aryal, president of the National Federation of Drinking Water Consumers, said the source of Bidur’s water supply is Phalakhun Khola. The four-kilometre pipeline built to bring water from the source has been damaged.

Similarly, three borewells located in the Trishuli River were washed away, creating a drinking water crisis in Bidur, Battar, Inarpani and Majhitar. According to Aryal, water could potentially be pumped from Gangkate in Tadi Khola, but low voltage has made this difficult.

Water treatment plant washed away in Nuwakot, workers missing

The Department of Water Supply and Sewerage Management was constructing a water treatment plant in Nuwakot, where eight or nine employees were working. Director General Shrestha said the workers are missing.

“The plant was in the final stage of construction. The employees were swept away and the structure was also destroyed. The plant has suffered extensive damage,” he said.

Preliminary damage estimate exceeds Rs 600 million

The department has made a preliminary estimate that drinking water systems alone in the flood-affected areas of Rasuwa and Nuwakot have suffered damage worth more than Rs 600 million.

Shrestha said the estimate is still highly preliminary. In some areas, water sources remain intact while distribution systems have been destroyed. Restoring these systems will have to proceed alongside the reconstruction of roads and bridges.

Water shortage poses sanitation challenges

The Water Supply and Sanitation Division Office No. 6 in Nuwakot has begun collecting details from Nuwakot and Rasuwa on disrupted water supply projects in flood-affected areas.

According to engineer Kameshwar Das, the office is currently collecting data. Around 30 small and large water supply projects are estimated to have been affected in the two districts.

The department is concerned that failure to restore water supply projects on time could create additional challenges not only in providing clean drinking water but also in maintaining sanitation. “That is why we are working to restore the damaged systems as soon as possible,” Director General Shrestha said.

Infrastructure Ministry tasked with restoration

A Cabinet meeting held on August 26 following the floods decided that the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport would make arrangements as soon as possible for the restoration of roads and the provision of necessary drinking water supplies in the affected areas.

The ministry is currently responsible for water supply, urban development and infrastructure. It is preparing to install Bailey bridges at three locations immediately and operate alternative roads at other locations to facilitate transportation.

title.rendered: NRB warns of scams involving PM’s Disaster Relief Fund

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Nepal Rastra Bank has urged the public to be cautious when donating to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, warning of scams involving fake bank accounts and QR codes.

The central bank has advised people to use only QR codes and bank account numbers obtained from official sources to avoid fraud.

The warning comes after reports of unauthorised fundraising and fraud using fake QR codes and bank account details in the name of the fund.

The central bank has urged donors to verify the account name before transferring money through mobile banking, digital wallets, ConnectIPS or any other payment platform.

It has also advised people to carefully enter the amount they intend to contribute and verify the transaction before making the transfer.

According to Nepal Rastra Bank, donors can avoid scams by using only the official bank account details published on the websites of Nepal Rastra Bank, the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, or the Ministry of Finance.

The central bank has also warned people not to scan unauthorised QR codes shared through social media, email or messaging apps.

It has urged the public not to share their one-time passwords (OTPs), PINs or passwords with anyone.

Anyone who believes they have been defrauded while transferring money to the fund has been advised to immediately notify their bank or financial institution, payment service provider, the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau, or the Financial Consumer Protection Unit of Nepal Rastra Bank.

content.rendered:

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has visited flood-affected areas. He reached Bidur Municipality in flood-hit Nuwakot on Monday.

A resident of Bidur Municipality-3 complained to Thapa that rescue efforts for people who went missing or lost contact with their families during the floods were being delayed.

The resident said his relatives had gone missing in the floods, while some were reportedly trapped inside a tunnel.

Thapa visited Trishuli Hospital, a holding centre, Trishuli Bazaar, areas across the river from Devighat, Radbhumeshwori, the powerhouse and Tupche, where he listened to the concerns of flood victims. According to Nepali Congress leader Bijay Dhungana, who accompanied Thapa, he also visited Darshan Taar, Pipladanda, Kumaltar and Kolani, among other areas.

title.rendered: How can relatives provide DNA samples to identify missing loved ones?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Nepal Police have asked families searching for relatives missing in the floods to provide DNA samples to help identify recovered bodies and body parts.

Relatives who want to determine whether recovered bodies or body parts belong to their missing family members through DNA testing have been asked to contact the designated locations for sample collection.

Police have requested blood relatives of missing people to provide blood samples at the laboratory of Nepal Police Hospital in Maharajgunj or at the nearest District Police Office.

Those providing blood samples are also required to submit two passport-size photographs, according to police.

If a close relative of a missing person is living abroad, DNA profiling can be conducted in the country where they reside. Police said samples from the missing person’s father, mother, son or daughter can be used for the profiling.

A soft copy of the DNA profiling report conducted abroad can then be sent to Nepal Police at dnacodis@nepalpolice.gov.np.

The DNA testing process is intended to help families establish whether unidentified bodies or body parts recovered after the floods belong to their missing relatives.

More than 900 bodies of people who died in the floods have been recovered so far, while more than 4,000 people remain missing.

title.rendered: Syabrubesi devastated by Bhotekoshi flood (In Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The flood has left much of Syabrubesi in ruins, with residents still searching for missing loved ones and struggling to come to terms with the devastation.

Syabrubesi Bazaar in Rasuwa, one of the areas hardest hit by the August 26 flood in the Bhotekoshi River, has been largely devastated.

Rescue and relief efforts are continuing in the area, with the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force, Nepal Police and local residents involved in the response. Support is also arriving from individuals and organisations in Nepal and abroad.

But in Syabrubesi and other areas of upper Rasuwa, the situation remains difficult.

The devastation is visible across Syabrubesi. Homes and businesses have been destroyed, while residents remain frightened by the scale of the disaster.

For families who lost loved ones in the flood, the wait has been particularly painful. Tears continue to flow as they grieve those confirmed dead while holding on to hope that some of those still missing may be found.

Residents say they have never witnessed a disaster of such magnitude.

“We had never seen anything like this. This is a black day for us,” Syabrubesi residents said as they recalled the day the flood struck.

While rescue and relief operations have progressed in many parts of Nuwakot and Dhading, the response in upper Rasuwa—including Syabrubesi, Timure and Rasuwagadhi—continues to face challenges.

For the people of Syabrubesi, the flood has left behind not only physical destruction but also uncertainty, grief and the difficult wait for news of missing family members.

title.rendered: Relief distribution facing problems as government acts alone: Janamat General Secretary Singh

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Janamat Party General Secretary Chandan Singh, who recently returned to Kathmandu after visiting areas affected by the Rasuwa floods, has said that major challenges remain in search and rescue operations, relief distribution and the management of displaced people.

Singh, who travelled to the affected areas with relief supplies, said there were also difficulties in distributing assistance.

“There are four or five holding centres in Battar Bazaar where affected people are being accommodated. However, there has been no long-term arrangement for residents who have lost their homes,” he said. “People who have lost both their homes and businesses also need to be accommodated in holding centres and provided with food and shelter.”

Although helicopters are being continuously deployed for rescue operations in the Battar area, Singh said challenges remain in managing survivors after their rescue, coordinating with their relatives and identifying bodies.

According to Singh, families displaced by the floods are facing shortages of clothing and other essential supplies in addition to food.

“There are small children whose homes were completely washed away. Apart from the clothes they were wearing, they have nothing left,” Singh said. “They have been wearing the same clothes for five days. Therefore, not only food but also clothes, bedding and blankets need to be delivered immediately.”

Singh said that although there had been plans to form an all-party mechanism to involve all political parties in search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts following the floods, it had not been effectively implemented.

“There is no coordination between the political mechanism on the ground and the government,” he said, adding that problems had arisen because the government was trying to handle everything on its own.

title.rendered: From cooking to collecting donations, celebrities join flood relief effort

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Celebrities and artists have started travelling to areas affected by the Bhotekoshi flood to personally distribute relief supplies. Miss Nepal Deepmala Dhakal, singer Durgesh Thapa, and actor Paul Shah are currently in flood-hit Nuwakot.

Dhakal has been distributing relief materials at various locations in Nuwakot in collaboration with the Hami Nepal organisation. She said she has been visiting different camps with supplies, adding that not just victims but rescue workers too urgently need raincoats and boots.

Singer Durgesh Thapa has travelled to Bidur and other areas of Nuwakot to distribute food and clothing to those affected, personally serving rice and feeding flood victims.

Actor Paul Shah said he distributed relief to 400 households in Pipaltar, Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot, providing 200 households with quilts, mattresses, and blankets, and the remaining 200 with undergarments, shawls, noodles, biscuits, Jeevan Jal (oral rehydration solution), and sanitary pads.

Actress Priyanka Karki said she is preparing to distribute the clothing and donations she has received to areas that haven’t yet gotten relief supplies, sharing videos of the materials on social media.

Rapper VTEN has also travelled to Bidur, Nuwakot, to distribute relief. Singer Ekdev Limbu distributed a vanload of supplies, delivering vegetables to the affected area.

“There’s a special joy in returning after doing whatever small part I could,” Limbu wrote.

Singer Samikshya Adhikari said she provided relief materials for Rasuwa flood victims through the District Administration Office in Kaski.

Content creator Eva Giri has also begun distributing relief supplies in affected areas, posting videos on Instagram showing medicine, food, and clothing being provided.

Actress Reecha Sharma, who was on a visit to Gosaikunda, appealed for donations of clothing, noting it was urgently needed by stranded locals, especially women and children. Beyond these efforts, other artists have reportedly contributed money to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund according to their capacity.

title.rendered: Agni Group donates Rs 10 million to Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

At a time when corporate social initiatives are often widely publicised, Agni Group has taken a notably simple and understated approach to disaster assistance.

To support relief and rescue efforts for people affected by the recent devastating floods in Rasuwa, Agni Group Chairperson Cabinet Shrestha deposited Rs 10 million into the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund on behalf of Agni Group/Mahindra.

Despite making such a significant contribution, Agni Group did not issue an official press release or promotional advertisement about the donation. The company decided not to publicise the contribution, believing that humanitarian assistance during a crisis should not be used as a means of publicity.

The contribution reflects Agni Group’s sense of responsibility that the private sector should stand with citizens during times of national crisis, rising above commercial interests.

title.rendered: Govt says no one was found inside Rasuwagadhi tunnel. Where are the 3 workers on duty?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The Nepal Army says it found no one inside the tunnel of the 111MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, but three employees who were on duty inside when the Bhotekoshi flood struck remain unaccounted for.

The Nepal Army, project engineers and a drone team searched the tunnel up to its far end after concerns that people could have been trapped inside. The team said it found no human presence and returned to Dhunche after completing the search.

But the whereabouts of three employees who were reportedly on duty inside the tunnel when the flood struck remain unknown.

The apparent discrepancy has raised questions about what happened to the three workers and whether the search inside the tunnel was sufficient.

According to a project official, three employees were on duty inside the tunnel when the flood hit. The power plant was operating at the time, with employees working in two shifts—from 7am to 7pm and from 7pm to 7am.

“The plant was running. The night-shift employees went there at 7pm and were on duty until 7am,” the official said.

The three employees on duty inside the tunnel have been identified as Kishor Neupane of Palpa, Santosh Paudel of Pyuthan and Chhiring Tamang of Rasuwa. Their current whereabouts are unknown.

“There were three people inside the tunnel, and around 14 to 15 people in total outside,” the official said.

The three were responsible for tasks related to operating the power plant.

Employees were also working outside the tunnel, including at the switchyard, where staff had been deployed for the night shift.

According to the project, 93 employees and workers remain unaccounted for following the flood. Of them, 49 are employees of Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Company and two are daily-wage workers.

The company said 35 workers from Sherpa Hydro Construction, four from CWE and three from Venus Construction are also missing.

Army searched tunnel to its end

Search and rescue operations at the project did not begin immediately after the flood. The rescue team could not reach the project site until Saturday, and the search operation began only on Sunday. The Nepal Army then entered the tunnel along with project engineers and a drone team after concerns that workers could be trapped inside.

The team searched through the tunnel and reached its far end but reported finding no people. Project officials confirmed that their engineers had accompanied the Army team.

“Our engineers also went inside, and the Army team went as well,” the official said.

However, there is still no confirmed explanation of what happened to the three workers who were reportedly on duty inside the tunnel when the flood struck. Although the search team says it reached the end of the tunnel, authorities have not established whether the three workers managed to leave the tunnel before or during the flood, or whether they moved to another part of the project.

93 workers remain unaccounted for

The three workers inside the tunnel are among dozens of people whose whereabouts remain unknown after the flood.

According to the project, employees and workers were stationed both inside and outside the tunnel when the disaster occurred. Those working outside included two cleaning workers, two guards, two cooks and an engineer, in addition to employees assigned to the night shift.

“There were three people on duty inside the tunnel. Others were at the switchyard outside, while another employee assigned to the night shift was also on duty outside,” the official said.

The flood also trapped six people in the project’s underground desander. Four of them managed to make their way out on their own after spending two days in difficult conditions.

The Nepal Army later rescued them by helicopter and brought them to Kathmandu.

While those four survived by reaching safer areas, the fate of the three employees who were on duty inside the Rasuwagadhi tunnel remains unclear.

Work began today to install two CCTVs along the Nepal-China border in Rasuwa district.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi Flood: 33 of 48 injured patients discharged from Trauma Centre

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Thirty-three of the 48 people injured in the Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa on 10 Bhadra and brought to the National Trauma Centre in Kathmandu for treatment have been discharged.

According to Dan Bahadur Thapa, spokesperson and Superintendent of Police at the Kathmandu District Police Range, 48 people injured in the flood were rescued and brought to the National Trauma Centre for treatment. So far, 33 have been discharged after their health improved during treatment.

Fifteen injured people are currently receiving treatment at the National Trauma Centre, Superintendent Thapa said. According to the hospital administration, the condition of most of those receiving treatment is normal.

Nepal Police has established citizen assistance desks at Bir Hospital and the National Trauma Centre to provide necessary information to relatives of people injured or missing in the Bhotekoshi flood.

Family members of missing people have been visiting the assistance desks to obtain information about the health condition of injured relatives and to register details of those who remain out of contact, Thapa said. Relatives visiting the hospitals are also receiving updates on their family members’ health and treatment.

Police said search and rescue operations are still continuing in the affected areas following the extensive loss of life and property caused by the Bhotekoshi flood. Relevant agencies are coordinating with the injured, victims and families of missing people and providing necessary assistance alongside medical treatment for those rescued.

Rescue and relief operations have been intensified following the floods, with priority being given to searching for missing people, treating the injured and providing necessary support to affected families.

title.rendered: Nepal seeks technical assistance from Singapore to identify flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Nepal has requested assistance from Singapore in identifying flood victims.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri announced at a press conference on Monday that the government has sought technical assistance for victim identification.

He said Nepal has also requested DNA testing support from the United States and high-capacity equipment from China and Singapore.

The Ministry said additional specialised equipment is expected soon from Japan and South Korea as well.

According to Chhetri, rescue and relief materials have so far been received from India, China, France, the United States, the United Arab Emirates, South Korea, and other countries and partners. He said further supplies and support are also on the way from the United Nations, the World Health Organisation, and UNICEF.

The assistance includes rescue equipment, freezers, solar lights, testing kits, chains, blankets, sleeping bags, food, and medicine.

A special rescue team from India has been deployed to the affected area, and the Ministry said a South Korean team has also been mobilised on site.

Chhetri added that Nepal expects to need international support for post-disaster recovery and reconstruction as well.

The Ministry said the resources required to rebuild homes, roads, bridges, hydropower projects, and other infrastructure will be determined based on the extent of damage caused by the flood.

The meeting discussed the government’s ongoing search, rescue, relief distribution, and citizen-management efforts in areas affected by the flood on Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi River.

Discussions also covered the rescue and relief of affected citizens, as well as the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure.

title.rendered: Generator brings relief to Dhunche residents after 5-day power outage

content.rendered:
Dhunche, August 31

A generator has been brought to Dhunche, the district headquarters of Rasuwa, to provide mobile phone charging facilities. Electricity has been completely disrupted across Rasuwa for the past five days following the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

The Nepal Red Cross Society brought the generator to Dhunche with support from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

The prolonged power outage had cut off residents, flood victims and pilgrims in Dhunche from their families and the outside world.

The Nepal Red Cross Society’s Rasuwa chapter and the Tilganga Eye Centre jointly took the initiative to address the problem. With the generator now available at the district headquarters, arrangements have been made for people to charge their mobile phones free of charge.

More than 100 people are currently charging their phones at the same time, according to the Nepal Red Cross. The service has made it easier for people to send messages to relatives living far away to let them know they are safe.

The availability of mobile charging at the district headquarters has provided relief to residents and people who travelled to Dhunche from distant areas. After getting access to the charging facility, residents have been able to re-establish contact with their families.

“The phone calls have reconnected broken hopes and brought comfort to hearts filled with worry,” a resident said.

Technical teams are working to restore the electricity service disrupted by the floods, and efforts are underway to resume power supply as soon as possible.

title.rendered: NEPSE falls 43.89 points as flood-hit sectors remain under pressure

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index fell 43.89 points on Monday, the first trading day of the week, to close at 2,513 points.

Trading turnover also declined slightly. While shares worth Rs 3.78 billion were traded on the previous trading day, turnover stood at Rs 3.64 billion on Monday.

The market remained in the red throughout the trading session. The prices of only 21 companies increased, while 253 declined and four remained unchanged.

Three sectors have faced particularly strong pressure since the devastating floods last Wednesday, and the trend continued on Monday.

The non-life insurance sector suffered the steepest decline, falling 5.03%. The Others group dropped 3.30%, while the hydropower sector fell 2.94%.

More than a dozen hydropower projects have been severely affected by the floods. Non-life insurance companies have also come under pressure as they are expected to pay claims for vehicles, homes and hydropower projects damaged by the disaster.

The Others group includes Nepal Reinsurance Company and Himalayan Reinsurance Company.

Besides these three sectors, the banking sector fell 1.00%, development banks 0.96%, finance 1.41%, hotels and tourism 2.44%, investment 1.19%, life insurance 1.97%, microfinance 1.14% and trading 1.11%.

The manufacturing and processing sector was the only major sector to post a gain, rising 0.70%.

Cement companies saw positive movement amid expectations that demand for cement will increase during post-flood reconstruction.

Mailung Khola Hydropower fell 14.98%, Rasuwagadhi Hydropower 11.76%, Chilime Hydropower 10.49% and Mandu Hydropower 9.30%.

Police have seized a large quantity of marijuana from Shantiban forest in Banketar, Katari Municipality-6, Udayapur. Three people have been arrested on suspicion of transporting the marijuana.

Acting on a tip-off, a team from the Area Police Office, Katari, conducted a search of the Shantiban forest area at around 4 am on Monday. Police said they found 1,122.67 kilograms of marijuana concealed in 52 sacks.

Police also seized a Bolero pickup truck, registration number Ba 16 Cha 5269, which was allegedly used to transport the marijuana.

Those arrested on suspicion of involvement in the transportation of the marijuana have been identified as 55-year-old Ram Bahadur Magar, 21-year-old Nek Bahadur Magar and 46-year-old Prithviraj Magar, all from Dandagaun, Tapli Rural Municipality-1.

title.rendered: Tuin crossings revived after floods destroy roads, bridges in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Bidur, August 31

A traditional rope crossing is being reinstalled in Nuwakot’s Battar after the Bhotekoshi flood destroyed roads, motorable bridges, suspension bridges and footpaths across the region.

The sudden flood that swept into the Trishuli River through Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi caused extensive loss of life and property and destroyed critical transport infrastructure.

With roads and bridges washed away and movement between settlements becoming difficult, authorities have begun reinstalling a tuin—a rope-based river crossing that had previously been removed as part of efforts to eliminate such crossings.

Installation work is currently underway in Battar, Nuwakot.

Local resident Durgaraj Pathak said the disaster had made it clear how essential the tuin had become in the absence of other means of crossing the river.

“Time is powerful. Until recently, we were advocating for the removal of tuins. Now, this very tuin has become the most essential thing for us, and we are reinstalling it,” he said.

The flood has severely damaged transport links in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, with numerous bridges swept away and road connections disrupted.

Chandeswori Dapha Khalah of Tokha has raised funds for flood victims by organising a traditional Lakhe dance performance.

The Dapha Khalah, which has been active for many years, has made significant contributions to the preservation and promotion of Tokha’s Licchhavi-era culture and traditions.

title.rendered: Trishuli–Betrawati Road: 4 kilometres washed away, 6 kilometres remains usable

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Technical officials from the Department of Roads have conducted an on-site inspection of the 10-kilometre road section from Trishuli Bazaar to Betrawati Bazaar in Nuwakot.

The inspection found that the Trishuli River had completely washed away four kilometres of the road. Around six kilometres of the road remains usable and can be reopened to traffic after debris is cleared.

According to the department, the technical team travelled on foot from Trishuli Bazaar to Betrawati and is identifying a suitable location in Betrawati for installing a Bailey bridge.

The Department of Roads is preparing to install a Bailey bridge at Betrawati. Once the bridge is installed, it will reconnect the road to the Rasuwa national highway. Rasuwa is currently connected through an alternative route, but travel along the route remains difficult.

An estimated 40 kilometres of roads have been completely washed away in Rasuwa alone. The road from Betrawati to Rasuwagadhi has sustained extensive damage.

title.rendered: NEA employees urge PM Shah to speed up rescue of workers trapped in tunnels

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Nepal Electricity Authority employees have written to Prime Minister Balen Shah, warning that the lives of their colleagues and workers at several hydropower projects are at risk because of delays in rescue operations.

Fearing retaliation if they revealed their identities, the employees wrote the letter to the prime minister under pseudonyms. They said every minute is critical to saving the lives of people trapped inside tunnels, but the government has been slow to accelerate rescue efforts.

In the letter obtained by Onlinekhabar from a trusted source, the employees questioned why foreign rescuers and other groups ready to assist had not been granted permission and coordinated with in time.

They also questioned why rescue operations appeared to be taking place sequentially, with work at one location having to be completed before operations could begin at another.

“Why are we unable to conduct rescue operations simultaneously at all the locations where they are urgently needed?” they asked.

The employees said rescue operations inside the tunnels had already been delayed significantly and that every moment had become extremely critical.

“We sincerely request that necessary steps be taken immediately to accelerate the ongoing rescue operations,” they wrote in the letter to the prime minister.

Describing the situation as extremely serious, they said there was no time for lengthy administrative procedures or extensive formalities.

“The priority right now is only to save lives. Every minute of delay could mean losing someone’s chance of survival,” they said in the joint letter.

They urged the prime minister to intervene immediately to remove unnecessary administrative delays, grant immediate permission to all capable national and international rescue teams willing to help, and mobilise the necessary resources simultaneously at all critical locations.

“Please take action now. There is no time to wait,” they wrote.

Hundreds of employees and workers involved in projects operated by the Nepal Electricity Authority and its subsidiary companies have been reported missing following the Rasuwa floods.

The floods caused extensive damage to several hydropower projects, including Upper Trishuli 3A, Upper Trishuli 3B, Rasuwagadhi, Chilime, Trishuli, Devighat and Upper Trishuli 3B.

So far, the Nepal Army has managed to recover only two bodies from the tunnel of the Chilime Hydropower Project.

An army team also entered the tunnel at the Rasuwagadhi project but returned after failing to find anyone inside. However, a source at the Nepal Electricity Authority said at least three people had been working at the power house that day because it was in operation, and that the army team returned without reaching the power house.

Apart from Nepal Electricity Authority projects, hundreds of people working at projects including Upper Trishuli-1, Langtang, Mailung Khola, Rasuwa Bhotekoshi and Middle Trishuli have also been reported missing.

Families of the missing and other stakeholders have expressed anger over what they describe as delays by the government in carrying out search and rescue operations.

title.rendered: Exact number of people missing in Rasuwa floods still unclear: Authority

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has said it is still difficult to determine the exact number of people missing in the Rasuwa floods.

NDRRMA spokesperson Shanti Mahat said it remained difficult to establish the precise number of people missing in the disaster. She said authorities are currently collecting information from local governments, district administration offices, Nepal Police, the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force, national parks and hydropower projects, among other concerned agencies.

According to her, based on information received from official agencies as of 9 am Monday, 4,202 people are missing. Mahat said the figure could change as search and rescue operations are still underway.

“It is somewhat difficult for us to determine the exact number of missing people at the moment. We are collecting figures from local governments, the Chief District Officer’s office and various official agencies, including Nepal Police, the Nepal Army, the Armed Police Force, national parks and hydropower projects. We are referring to an approximate figure because we still do not know the exact number of missing people,” she said.

Meanwhile, rescue operations are continuing at various hydropower projects and tunnels. According to Mahat, 289 people have been rescued from hydropower tunnels alone. An additional 22 people—15 Chinese nationals and seven Indians—were rescued from hydropower project areas on Sunday. She said rescue operations were continuing on Monday as well.

Mahat said authorities had not yet received separate details regarding the damage at the Langtang Hydropower Project.

“Searches for missing people are continuing. There may be additional people to be accounted for, and it is difficult for us to say exactly how many of those reported missing are actually missing. We are trying to provide updates as much as possible,” she said.

So far, the bodies of 903 people who died in the Rasuwa floods have been recovered. More than 10,000 people have been rescued, while 267 injured people have returned home after receiving treatment. A total of 20,819 security personnel have been mobilised to search for people who remain unaccounted for.

The authority said road and communication services disrupted by the disaster have also been restored in most areas. NDRRMA spokesperson Mahat said alternative routes had been identified to facilitate road travel.

The authority has formed and mobilised around 14 separate task forces for disaster management. Mahat said separate teams have been working since Thursday on rescue operations, relief distribution, helicopter management, body management, and international assistance and coordination.

title.rendered: Relatives of workers trapped at Upper Trishuli-1 head to flood-hit site

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Relatives of people trapped at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project have headed to the project site after reaching an agreement with the company over search and rescue efforts.

The relatives had staged a sit-in at the Kathmandu office of Nepal Water and Energy Development Company (NWEDC) in Thapathali, demanding that the condition of their family members be made public.

Following an agreement between the company and the affected families, the relatives were taken to the site by two helicopters.

They will assess the condition of their family members, the progress of search and rescue operations and the damage caused to the project site.

The families had staged the protest after receiving no clear information about their relatives for five days. They had demanded that the company either rescue those who were alive or hand over their bodies if they had died, while also calling for immediate access to the project site.

Under the agreement reached between the company and the affected families, helicopters and rescue teams will be made available for search and rescue operations. The company will also arrange transportation required to reach the affected areas and cover the expenses of relatives travelling to the site for search and rescue efforts.

The company has also agreed to provide the families with details on the condition of all employees working at the project, CCTV footage from the day of the incident and its immediate action plan for dealing with the disaster. It will coordinate with government agencies as necessary.

The agreement also states that information related to the incident will be provided to the affected families and updates will be made public through social media.

The relatives had accused the company of failing to provide sufficient information about people at the project site since the day of the flood. They said the lack of clear information about the employees and workers had left them even more uncertain about their family members’ condition.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar earlier, relatives said the company had offered them assurances for five days without providing concrete information. With the condition of people inside the project tunnel and those at the Mailung site office still unclear, they had questioned the company’s responsibility.

According to the company, 576 workers were at the Upper Trishuli-1 project, while 75 people were at the Mailung site office.

The relatives had been demanding to visit the site themselves to find out where their family members were and what condition they were in.

The company had said a helicopter was kept ready for rescue operations but that it had not received government permission to fly. A Korean representative of the company had said five helicopters were on standby.

Following the agreement, the relatives have now been given an opportunity to see the situation at the site themselves. They were flown towards the project site on two helicopters.

According to the relatives, they will receive firsthand information from rescue teams and company representatives at the site and assess the condition of people working at the project. They will also inspect the areas affected by the flood and locations where search and rescue operations are underway.

The 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project is under construction in Rasuwa. The project’s tunnel and the Mailung area were affected by the flood.

Anger among the families had intensified over delays in the search and rescue of people believed to be trapped at the project.

title.rendered: No people found trapped in Rasuwa Hydropower Tunnel, army team returns to Dhunche

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

A Nepal Army rescue team has returned from the tunnel of the Rasuwa Hydropower Project (RHPL), which was affected by flooding in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s Secretariat said the rescue team, led by the Nepal Army, returned after finding no one inside the tunnel during the search operation.

The team had launched the search with engineers and a drone team after receiving reports that people might be trapped at the far end of the tunnel.

According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, the team reached the innermost section of the tunnel and used drones to conduct a thorough search but found no signs of human presence.

After confirming that no one was trapped inside, the Nepal Army team returned to Dhunche in Rasuwa.

title.rendered: Alternative route to Rasuwa hampered by narrow, muddy roads and traffic

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

An alternative route to Rasuwa has been opened after floods and landslides washed away highways and bridges. However, heavy traffic and the narrow road have made travel to the destination difficult.

Three days ago, the Kathmandu–Tokha–Chhahare–Gadkhar Bridge–Aapre–Narja–Lachyang–Sarmathali–Patikharka–Bogtitar–Kalikastan–Dhunche road was opened for small four-wheel-drive vehicles.

However, the narrow road is making two-way traffic difficult. The unpaved road has also become muddy due to rainfall. In some areas, road clearance has been easier where excavators operated by municipalities and rural municipalities are available. But vehicles are struggling to pass through sections where excavators have not reached.

As a result, vehicles carrying relief supplies have been getting stuck in long traffic jams.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah holds separate talks with security chiefs over Bhotekoshi flood crisis

content.rendered:
Kathmand, August 31

Prime Minister Balen Shah has begun discussions with the chiefs of the country’s security agencies over the crisis triggered by flooding in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, Shah is holding discussions with the heads of the security agencies on measures to address the crisis caused by the flooding.

Shah earlier received a briefing from Chief of Army Staff Ashok Raj Sigdel on the search, rescue, relief and management efforts carried out so far.

The prime minister is also scheduled to receive briefings from the chiefs of Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force on Monday.

According to his secretariat, Shah will shortly receive a briefing from Armed Police Force Inspector General Narayan Dutta Poudel, followed by a briefing from Nepal Police Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki.

title.rendered: Galchi bridge survives as floods destroy 35 bridges in 3 districts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 25 damaged 35 bridges in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts.

The floods swept away the pillars of some bridges, while others sustained partial damage.

Meanwhile, the bridge at Galchi in Dhading has survived the flooding. People are currently using the bridge to travel to villages across the river in Nuwakot, Rasuwa and Dhading.

Rescue and relief teams deployed to the affected areas are also using the bridge.

An alternative route via the Galchi Bridge is currently being used to reach various local levels in Nuwakot.

title.rendered: US travel advisory on Nepal: Avoid disaster areas, risk of unrest elsewhere too

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The US government has updated its travel advisory for Nepal, urging citizens not to travel for any reason to the Rasuwagadhi-Timure-Syafrubesi area of Rasuwa district or to the Nepal-China border crossing area.

According to the US government, following the major flood of August 26, roads, transportation, and communication services in the area have been disrupted, and search, rescue, and recovery operations remain ongoing, keeping risk levels high. The advisory also notes the possibility of further flooding and landslides.

The US has placed the affected area under “Level 4: Do Not Travel.” The affected zone includes settlements along the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and Narayani rivers.

The US government advises against going near riverbanks, low-lying areas, damaged bridges, and unstable slopes. It also urges compliance with any evacuation or relocation orders issued by Nepali authorities.

US citizens have been warned not to enter disaster-affected areas on their own, including to search for missing persons, and not to travel to the area for any reason.

Risk of unrest in Nepal

The US government has placed Nepal overall under “Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution,” citing civil unrest as the main reason.

The US assessment states that the nationwide protests that began in September 2025 have since stopped, and the security situation is currently stable. However, it warns that protests and local unrest, especially in cities, could resume.

Since protests can begin with little notice and sometimes turn violent, citizens are advised to stay away from large crowds and demonstrations and to follow the instructions of local authorities.

Limited health care

The US government notes that Nepal’s health and emergency services have limited capacity to manage both routine and emergency care.

While Kathmandu’s hospitals are generally better equipped than those elsewhere in the country, the advisory notes they can be overcrowded, may lack certain necessary equipment or medicines, and sometimes require payment before treatment.

The Nepal government does not cover treatment costs for foreign nationals. The US government therefore advises carrying necessary medications, obtaining travel health insurance that includes medical evacuation coverage, and being prepared to travel to another country for treatment in case of a serious health issue.

Risk of earthquakes, floods, and landslides

The US government notes that Nepal faces regular risks of earthquakes, floods, and landslides. It states that earthquakes can strike without warning in the Kathmandu Valley and other regions.

It warns that heavy rainfall during the monsoon season, particularly from June through September, can trigger flash floods and landslides, which may block roads, damage buildings, and complicate emergency rescue efforts.

Advice for US citizens travelling to Nepal

For those who decide to travel to Nepal, the US government advises enrolling in the Smart Traveller Enrollment Program to receive important updates and emergency alerts from the US Embassy or consulate, and to review Nepal’s security report.

title.rendered: Three brothers and two relatives from a Solukhumbu family lost contact in Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Three members of one family from Solukhumbu, along with two of their relatives, have been out of contact since the devastating flood in Rasuwa.

According to Ranjita Budhathoki Magar, a family member of those missing, her three older brothers are unreachable, along with two other relatives.

The three brothers and one relative had been travelling with Indian tourists on a Mount Kailash trip in Tibet. Another relative was preparing to travel to China and was in the process of obtaining a visa; his last known location was Timure. The other four’s last known location was in the border area.

Four of them had set out from Kathmandu on August 17 for the Kailash trip. According to Ranjita, a call connected around 8 a.m. on August 27, but they weren’t able to speak.

“After learning about the flood, I kept calling, but no one picked up. Around 11 a.m., the phone switched off,” she said.

With many days having passed without any word from her relatives, Ranjita has appealed: “Let the state tell us what has happened to the people who are out of contact.”

According to Ranjita, a list of uncontacted individuals has come from a China-based site.

“The missing list from the China site includes the names of my three brothers and one relative. The other relative’s name isn’t on it,” she said.

The devastating flood that struck the Gosaikunda Rural Municipality area of Rasuwa on August 27 caused massive loss of life and property. Debris accompanying the flood suddenly increased the flow of the Bhotekoshi River, damaging settlements, roads, bridges, and hydropower projects along its banks.

The flood affected not only local settlements and infrastructure but also tourists on the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route. Several Nepali and foreign tourists travelling through the area at the time have lost contact since the flood. Details are still awaited on the status of those who had gone through Rasuwa toward China for the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage, as well as other tourists.

Flood damage to roads, bridges, and communication infrastructure has made it difficult to establish contact.

Search and rescue operations are ongoing in the affected areas. The administration says it is collecting details on the status of uncontacted tourists.

title.rendered: Nepal begin ACC Premier Cup with seven-wicket win over Bahrain

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Captain Sandeep Lamichhane and Nepal’s bowlers put on a dominant display as Nepal began their ACC Premier Cup campaign with a seven-wicket victory over Bahrain.

Playing at the YSD-UKM Oval in Bangi, Malaysia, on Monday, Nepal chased down Bahrain’s target of 88 runs for the loss of three wickets.

Arjun Kumal remained unbeaten on 36, while Rohit Paudel was not out on 19 as Nepal completed the chase.

Bahrain’s Imran Javed took two wickets, while Nepal lost another wicket through a run-out.

Earlier, Bahrain were bowled out for 87 in 36.2 overs after being asked to bat first.

Captain Lamichhane was the star of Nepal’s bowling attack, taking five wickets for just 14 runs in his 10 overs. Lalit Rajbanshi claimed three wickets and Karan KC took two.

Fiaz Ahmed top-scored for Bahrain with 15 runs, while Muhammad Wasim made 13 and Ali Dawood scored 10.

Lamichhane made an immediate impact when he took a wicket with his first delivery. He then claimed another wicket with the fourth ball of the over.

He added another wicket in his fifth over before taking one each in his seventh and eighth overs to complete his five-wicket haul.

Nepal will play their second match of the tournament against hosts Malaysia on Thursday.

title.rendered: What progress has been made in rescuing those trapped in tunnels?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The sudden floods that struck Rasuwa and Nuwakot on August 26 morning caused widespread destruction along riverbanks and buried tunnels at several hydropower projects.

A large number of people are suspected to have been inside the tunnels when the floods struck. However, search and rescue operations inside some of the tunnels have yet to be completed, even on the sixth day after the disaster.

According to the Nepal Army headquarters at Bhadrakali, a controlled blast was carried out at the Trishuli 3A tunnel at 2am. Two excavators have also been used to create a hole by digging approximately 10 metres down.

The Nepal Army said workers are currently clearing water, mud and sediment from inside the tunnel.

Search and rescue operations are also underway at the Trishuli 3B tunnel, with security personnel deployed alongside technical experts.

A joint search and rescue team, including foreign personnel, entered approximately 100 metres into the Chilime Hydropower Project tunnel. Two bodies were recovered from inside the tunnel, where they were found buried under mud and soil.

At the Upper Trishuli-1 project, the search and rescue team entered approximately 300 metres into the tunnel, according to the Nepal Army. One body has been recovered from the tunnel.

Search operations have also begun at the Langtang tunnel. The Nepal Army said search and rescue personnel are using torchlights to search inside the tunnel.

title.rendered: 170 people from Madhesh still uncontacted; families cling to hope, plead for help

content.rendered:
Since the devastating flood struck Bhotekoshi in Rasuwa on August 27, engineer Ajay Prasad Singh, who worked at the Dosan Hydropower Project, has been out of contact. The 30-year-old from Dhanusha’s Kamala Municipality left behind an anxious wife, Puja Singh, who gave birth just a month ago.

Puja has been constantly scanning social media and news for any word of her husband, occasionally posting pleas for search-and-rescue teams to find him.

“Another day has passed, and still no news of my husband. Rescue teams still haven’t reached the area around his camp, especially the northwest side, and no information has come from there,” she wrote on social media Sunday evening. “I still believe he’s waiting to be rescued. May God keep him safe wherever he is. Please send a rescue team to him as quickly as possible.”

Ajay, who married Puja in an inter-caste marriage just a year ago, has a one-month-old daughter.

Ajay Kumar Yadav, an engineer from Saptari working at a school in Rasuwa’s Uttargaya Rural Municipality, has also been uncontactable since the flood. His older brother, Shyam Sundar Yadav, travelled to Rasuwa to search for him and has appealed on social media for help with search and rescue efforts, as the family remains anxious over Ajay’s unknown condition.

Their stories mirror those of 170 other people from Madhesh Province still uncontacted as of Sunday.

District breakdown

In total, 170 people across these eight districts remain uncontacted. Their families continue to hope for their return, much like the families of Ajay Singh and Ajay Yadav.

Relatives have kept up a steady stream of appeals to authorities, posting on social media, pleading with police, and in some cases travelling to the disaster site themselves to search for missing loved ones. As the days pass, hope is increasingly mixed with growing despair among these families.

Notable names still missing include Devraj Ishar, Anil Kumar Bishwakarma, and Ajay Marik from Saptari (though Marik has since been reached); Sarfaraz Miya and Sahabuddin Mansoori from Parsa; and Santosh Kumar Yadav, an NEA engineer, from Sirah. From Sirah, Tarzan Balampaki has been reached, and Umesh Yadav was rescued on August 29, but eight others remain missing.

Security personnel also affected

Among Madhesh Province police personnel deployed in Rasuwa, 9 lost contact; 6 have since been reached, leaving 3 still missing. From Parsa, Ojir Ansari has been reached while Shrawan Kumar Yadav remains uncontacted. Rautahat’s Nabin Kumar Singh remains out of contact with family, while Surendra Baitha is in contact and currently in Kathmandu; Mukesh Gosai reported a leg injury when he reached family on the evening of August 27.

From the Nepal Army, Rautahat’s Abhishek Gupta and Bara’s Suraj Kumar Sah remain uncontacted, while Bara’s Rowit Kumar Sah has been reached.

Police say the missing include Madhesh residents who were working in Rasuwa on hydropower projects, road construction, hotels, businesses, and trucking, as well as in Nuwakot’s Trishuli and Betrawati areas, at the time contact was lost.

title.rendered: This is the alternative route to flood-hit Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Some roads in the districts affected by the Bhotekoshi flood have reopened for traffic. With the main highway still not operational, the government has urged people to use alternative routes.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says those who don’t require emergency helicopter rescue can use these alternative routes.

The Authority has published the current alternative route connecting Rasuwa and Dhading. According to this route, travellers can reach Rasuwa via Nuwakot’s Bidur-Dhikure-Chaughada-Aapra-Narja-Lachyang-Sarmarthaley-Patikharka, continuing through Bogtitar (the Pasang Lhamu Highway to Rasuwa)-Kalikasthan-Dhunche. Four-wheeled vehicles are currently operating on this route.

In Dhading, however, the alternative route itself is now blocked. The Prithvi Highway section running through Dhadingbesi-Parewatar-Nepaltar-Gajuritar-Adamtar-Belintar-Keurinitar to Mastar (Hamlet Restaurant) had been operational, but the road has now been washed away at Parewatar. That stretch is currently blocked in both directions, and no alternative route has yet been identified.
