title.rendered: Gorkha landslide confirmed, river blockage rumours denied

content.rendered:
The District Administration Office, Gorkha, has said that rumours of a landslide blocking the Kaligandaki River in Gorkha are false. According to Assistant Chief District Officer Netra Prasad Sharma, while it is true that a landslide occurred in the Chum area, the river has not been blocked.

Sharma said the landslide occurred in the Chekampar area of Chumnubri Rural Municipality, at an elevation of roughly 3,500 meters.

“There was a landslide, but the rumour about the river being blocked isn’t true,” Sharma said.

He added that the administration is gathering further information about the landslide.

Rumours have been circulating on social media for some time claiming that a large landslide beyond Chekampar’s Chaurikharka blocked the Budhigandaki River, which flows from Chum.

Nima Lama, chairperson of Chumnubri Rural Municipality, said that although the landslide had blocked the river for some time, it has since started flowing again. According to Lama, the landslide at Chaurikharka in Chekampar had blocked the Syar Khola, a tributary of the Budhigandaki.

title.rendered: Government rescue portal can be misleading: How to identify official figures

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The Nepal government has launched a rescue request portal with a focus on people affected by the Rasuwa floods. Developed in coordination with the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure, the portal is managed by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). It allows users to submit details of people missing in the floods.

The government introduced the portal to facilitate rescue efforts. It includes contact numbers for Nepal Police, ambulance and fire services, the disaster authority, the Red Cross and other support organisations. Clicking the call button next to a number directly opens the phone dialler for mobile users. Below this is a QR code for the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, through which people can send financial assistance.

The portal also displays details of flood victims. However, the data displayed on the government’s rescue portal appears confusing and has created confusion among the public. Posts citing its figures have been circulating on social media, where the numbers have created an alarming impression.

At the time of preparing this report, the portal showed 17,098 reports of missing persons, while 12,819 people were listed as still missing. Many people have been sharing these figures as official statistics.

The figures labelled as reports of missing persons and those listed as people still missing have further added to the confusion. The data shown on the portal does not match the figures officially released by the government through the disaster authority.

Apart from missing persons, the portal also displays reports of people found, the number of people awaiting reunification with their families, and cases marked as resolved. It also shows a figure of 6,637 under “reports in the last 24 hours,” although it is unclear what type of reports this number refers to. It is not immediately clear whether the figure relates to people found, rescued or another category.

The portal also displays figures for missing children and senior citizens. While some people have shared these numbers as official statistics, others have questioned the unusually high figures.

However, a disclaimer below the data warns that the figures may differ from the actual situation.

“The data have been collected based on public complaints and reports. As the same person may be reported more than once in different circumstances, the actual number of individuals may be lower than the number displayed,” the notice states.

Anyone can upload details of a missing person to the portal. Members of the public can also submit information about people who have been found or stranded. This is one reason why the portal may display unusually high figures.

How does it work?

The government’s digital portal, launched to make rescue, search and relief distribution more effective during disasters, has in some cases created duplicate entries and statistical confusion.

According to an official at the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, differences in the figures displayed by the portal are linked to its technical system and the way data are collected.

Anyone who learns that someone is missing can easily upload the information to the disaster portal. If identical details are entered, the possibility of duplication is very low. However, even minor differences in the spelling of a name or other details can result in the same person being entered again as a separate case. If multiple people submit slightly different information about the same individual, the figures can therefore become inflated.

“If people who know the same person upload the details in their own way, multiple entries can be created for that individual. That is why the figures appear high,” the official told Onlinekhabar.

There is another source of information feeding into the portal: various groups operated under the government system. According to the Secretariat official, the government has created four WhatsApp groups involving local representatives and officials from responsible agencies. Members share information about missing people, people who have been found and other developments in these groups.

Information posted in the groups is automatically pulled into and updated on the rescue portal by the system. This also increases the possibility of duplicate data.

“The portal was developed at the initiative of the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure to make work easier during this period and enable faster data collection. Officials from the disaster authority and other agencies have access to its dashboard,” the official added.

Because the portal is based on publicly contributed information, its data are fundamentally different from verified statistics released by official agencies. Its dashboard uses colour indicators to show conditions in affected areas, with locations requiring rescue marked in red and areas needing relief assistance marked in yellow.

However, high numbers displayed on the portal alone do not confirm the actual scale of damage or the situation in a particular area. For example, if three people each report that 30 people are missing from the same location, the system could potentially count those reports separately, making the number appear three times higher.

The official urged the public to understand that the portal was created primarily as an emergency coordination and facilitation tool. The government later filters and verifies the information received through the portal before taking action where necessary.

Therefore, for immediate updates and official, verified statistics, the public should rely only on information released through the mechanisms and official channels of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

“Rather than relying on the figures displayed here, people should trust the statistics published by the disaster authority. The government created this system to make coordination easier and collect information quickly,” the official said. “The government filters the data before acting on it.”

Silver prices remained unchanged today, trading at the same rate as the previous day, Rs 4,780 per tola, according to the federation. On Friday, silver had been priced at Rs 4,965.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The road has been washed away at Parewatar, located in Dhading’s Gajuri Rural Municipality-3, along the Prithvi Highway.

Dhading Police say the road collapsed after continuous erosion of its base caused by the Trishuli River flood.

According to police, the base of that section has been steadily eroding since Sunday due to the Trishuli flood, and the road has now caved in, blocking traffic in both directions.

Earlier, the same highway was fully blocked when the road washed away at Krishnabhir, also due to the Trishuli flood.

Following the flood damage to that stretch, vehicles travelling to and from the federal capital, Kathmandu, have been using three alternate routes via Narayanghat in Chitwan and Hetauda as detours.

Nepal Police have safely recovered cash and gold worth millions of rupees from the flood-damaged Trishuli Dhunge branch of the Agricultural Development Bank.

After eight hours of continuous efforts on Sunday, police moved Rs 15 million in cash and gold, estimated at Rs 500 million, to a secure location.

Police also said they recovered several important documents safely from the bank.

title.rendered: Will insurance companies advance payments for Rasuwa flood as they did in the Gen Z movement?

content.rendered:
Insured parties are likely to receive advance payments for damage caused by the devastating August 27 flood. Stakeholders have suggested that advance payment is also necessary to help begin reconstruction of the unusual damage caused by the flood.

During the Gen Z movement on September 8-9, insurance companies similarly assessed losses and provided 50% advance payments. At the time, Nepal’s Council of Ministers had directly ordered advance payments, after which domestic reinsurance companies also provided advance payments to insurers, who then paid victims.

Sushil Dev Subedi, Executive Director of the Nepal Insurance Authority, said advance payments were easier at that time specifically because the Council of Ministers had made the decision.

“There will be no problem making advance payments to affected policyholders in the Rasuwa flood either,” Subedi says. “Under Section 10 of the Insurance Claim Payment Guidelines 2081, up to 50% of the estimated liability can be paid in advance; insurance companies can do this accordingly.”

Subedi said the Authority will provide necessary facilitation for advance payments, adding that a Council of Ministers decision would make the process even smoother.

If the government decides to direct the state-invested Nepal Reinsurance Company to act, that company would face similar pressure to make advance payments. Nepali insurance companies are required to reinsure 20% of their business with Nepal Reinsurance, which adds to that company’s responsibility in such situations.

In the case of the Gen Z movement, the Council of Ministers had directly ordered a 50% advance payment of liability, after which reinsurance and insurance companies paid policyholders up to that amount.

Sunil Ballav Panta, Secretary General of the Non-Life Insurers’ Association, said damage from the Rasuwa flood has been seen in hydropower projects, access roads to those projects, vehicles, transit facilities, and other means of transport.

“We still haven’t identified exactly what insured properties have been damaged by the flood,” Panta says. “There’s no information yet on livestock either. Insurance issues extend to bank-financed agricultural and other assets, and accident insurance for workers is also a major component.”

He said that because flood damage assessment follows a fairly standard process, insurance companies and surveyors need to work together going forward. If needed, reinsurers can also assist with assessment, so there shouldn’t be major problems. Panta noted that since human rescue and loss mitigation are currently the priority, property valuation and damage details haven’t yet been compiled.

Whether claims will be paid depends partly on assessing the condition of hydropower project machinery and equipment. Payment will also depend on whether a project was fully or partially destroyed, that is, whether only some equipment was damaged or the loss was total.

Since damage assessment requires mobilising experts, work begins as soon as insurance companies and surveyors reach the flood site. Panta noted that the Rasuwa flood is not the first such disaster Nepali insurers have handled.

“What insurance companies look at is evidence and process,” he says. “There must be evidence, the process must be followed correctly, and we need to make that easier.”

He added that procedural hurdles could cause some delays, and that in some cases, the person entitled to claim may not even be alive, which could further extend timelines.

Another insurer noted that because hydropower projects carry high risk, insurance companies keep their own exposure to such risk relatively low. According to this person, insurers can retain risk up to a maximum of 5% of their net worth and transfer the rest to reinsurance.

Per the “Insurer Reinsurance Directive 2080,” insurers must reinsure at least 20% of the value of policies they issue directly through Nepal Reinsurance Company, with the reinsurer taking its determined share as set by the Authority.

Under the same directive, insurers must reinsure based on their net worth according to policy type. For each policy or risk, a life insurer’s retention within Nepal cannot exceed 0.5% of its net worth, while a non-life insurer’s cannot exceed 5%.

Insurers must also obtain adequate catastrophe reinsurance for the portion of risk they retain under each policy. For catastrophe reinsurance agreements, the directive specifies that a life insurer’s net retention should not exceed NPR 100 million, while a non-life insurer’s should not exceed 10% of net worth.

After ceding the mandatory 20% of their business to the domestic reinsurance company, insurers retain part of the remaining 80% based on their capacity, and cede the rest, beyond what they can bear, to other reinsurers, domestic or foreign. This suggests that a large share of claims for hydropower project damage from the Rasuwa flood will likely come from foreign reinsurance companies.

title.rendered: Prithvi Highway closed after road subsides at Krishnabhir (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The Prithvi Highway has become deserted after a section of the road subsided at Krishnabhir along the Nagdhunga–Muglin road. With the movement of vehicles along the highway halted, hotels and shops along the route have also been affected.

Vehicles travelling from Kathmandu via the Prithvi Highway have been stopped at Kalanki. The Kathmandu–Muglin section of the Prithvi Highway, considered a vital lifeline connecting the capital with other parts of the country and external markets, has been completely blocked.

The Department of Roads has begun a technical assessment of the damaged road section at Krishnabhir on the Muglin–Kathmandu route. According to Department of Roads Director General Dr Bijay Jaisi, a technical team reached the site on Sunday and is conducting a detailed study of the area. Work to reopen the road will begin based on the recommendations of the team.

“This is already an area with difficult terrain,” Director General Jaisi said. “Moreover, the river is eroding the land from below, so we will make a decision only after assessing the risks.”

This means there is little possibility of the road reopening immediately. With a major transportation route cut off, consumers have begun to fear possible shortages and rising prices in the Kathmandu Valley.

The disruption of major road routes by floods is also expected to affect supplies to the Kalimati Fruits and Vegetable Market, the Kathmandu Valley’s main wholesale vegetable market.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi flood death toll reaches 903, more than 4,200 remain missing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

A total of 903 bodies have been recovered from the flood in the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) released the latest figures on Monday, saying the data is based on information collected as of 9am.

According to the authority, 4,227 people are still reported missing, while 10,451 people have been rescued so far.

Unidentified bodies have been kept at 21 hospitals in different districts.

Of the 267 people injured in the disaster, 156 have been discharged after receiving treatment.

A total of 20,819 security personnel have been deployed for rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts.

Of them, 8,722 are from the Nepali Army, 7,894 from Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force.

title.rendered: Cargo containers diverted to Mustang’s Korala border point after Rasuwagadhi closure

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

Cargo and containers that would normally enter Nepal through the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border point have increasingly started being diverted towards the Korala border point in Mustang following the complete destruction of the Rasuwagadhi crossing in the floods.

The Armed Police Force checkpost in Jomsom collected details of 66 cargo containers on Sunday evening.

The Jomsom checkpost said the number of containers being diverted to Korala for the import of goods has been increasing since the Rasuwagadhi border point was completely closed.

Kumar Devkota, a container driver heading towards Korala, said goods that would normally be imported through Rasuwagadhi have been diverted to Korala, prompting him to travel towards the border point to transport the cargo.

The government had brought Korala into operation as an alternative border point. The Mustang Customs Office at Korala collected Rs 6.92 billion in revenue in the fiscal year 2025/26.

The customs office collected a further Rs 290 million in revenue in the first month of the current fiscal year, according to the office.

Mustang Customs Office Chief Bidur Chudal said the office currently has 18 sanctioned positions, but only 12 employees are working there.

Uttargaya still has no count of missing as rescue efforts lag

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The government has declared 15 local units affected by the devastating floods of August 26 as disaster crisis-hit areas. Four of the five local units in Rasuwa are on the list.

Uttargaya, Gosainkunda, Kalika and Amachhodingmo rural municipalities have been designated as disaster crisis-hit areas. Among them, Uttargaya is the second-worst affected local unit in Rasuwa after Gosainkunda.

However, an accurate figure for those killed or missing in Uttargaya has yet to be established.

According to the 2021 census, Uttargaya has a total population of 8,555. No reliable figures have yet emerged on the number of local residents affected by the flood, or on workers employed at hydropower projects, labourers who had travelled to the area for work, and pilgrims who may have been caught in the disaster.

Elected representatives and chief administrative officers have been repeatedly urging the federal government to step up rescue and relief efforts.

According to Uttargaya Rural Municipality Chief Administrative Officer Jayaram Upreti, authorities have not yet been able to establish the condition of residents in Ward No. 1.

The area, known as the Tiru area, is still waiting for rescue. Tiru lies across the Trishuli River and at a higher elevation.

Major settlements in Uttargaya, including Mailung, Salletar, Simle, Pahirebesi, Betrawati, Kaidletar and Naubise, have also suffered damage.

Upreti said information had been received that around 150 flood victims were still waiting to be rescued.

“There is no phone contact there. With no electricity, people cannot charge their phones,” he said.

With all means of communication cut off, authorities have been unable to establish the exact number of casualties or determine how many people remain alive and safe.

Children used to trace missing parents

According to the 2021 census, Ward No. 1 of Uttargaya has a population of 1,176. Authorities have not been able to determine what happened to those who were at home when the flood struck.

“Since there are settlements where nothing remains and there is no communication, we have not been able to establish the number of missing people,” Upreti said.

Authorities have been trying to gather information about missing parents from children who survived the flood.

An attempt was made to trace missing family members by questioning children who survived in the Khalte area. So far, data has been collected showing that the mothers and fathers of 40 children in Uttargaya are missing.

There are 27 children who have only one of their parents accounted for.

“This is the data we have at present. The number could increase,” Upreti said.

Municipality left without offices

The flood swept away virtually all government offices in Uttargaya.

The municipality’s main office building and two ward offices have been completely destroyed. Two community schools and one boarding school have also suffered complete damage.

Buildings housing community health, veterinary and agricultural service offices were also swept away.

Although Uttargaya has been designated a disaster crisis-hit area, rebuilding government offices will not be straightforward. Construction cannot begin until the required procurement procedures are completed, meaning the rebuilding process is unlikely to move quickly.

“We are now left with only the people working in the office. We have been reduced to zero,” Upreti said. “To re-establish the local government, we have to complete the procurement processes all over again.”

Uttargaya’s elected representatives have begun approaching ministers and secretaries seeking assistance to construct new buildings and procure vehicles.

Holding centres operating

Holding centres have been established at four locations—Shivalaya, Shantibazar, Bhimsensthan and Kalika—to accommodate people rescued from flood-affected areas.

Two meals and snacks are being provided at the centres.

Ward chairpersons of Wards 2 and 3 have reached their respective wards and are staying there. Health workers, teachers and ward secretaries are operating the holding centres.

“After a disaster, we are following international practices on what needs to be prioritised first,” Upreti said. “We have made maximum efforts within the resources, knowledge, capacity and judgment available to the local government.”

Upreti said rescue and casualty verification have been difficult because ward chairpersons themselves have been affected by the disaster.

An alternative road route to Uttargaya has now been opened, and food supplies have started reaching Wards 4 and 5 since Monday. Authorities said only four-wheel-drive vehicles can currently travel along the route.

Hydropower projects add to concern

Uttargaya is home to several large and small hydropower projects under construction.

The 216-MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project is being built in the municipality, with more than 1,000 workers employed at the project.

With five days having passed without an effective search for missing workers, relatives of workers staged a protest at the project’s construction company on Monday.

Relatives of missing workers staged a sit-in outside the Kathmandu office of Nepal Water and Energy Development Company (NWEDC) in Thapathali.

Other hydropower projects in Uttargaya include Upper Mailung Khola, Mailung Khola, Upper Mailung ‘A’, Middle Mailung and Upper Mailung-B.

The growing concern among local authorities is that while relief and rescue resources are being concentrated in neighbouring Nuwakot, the scale of the disaster in Rasuwa—particularly in areas where communication and road links have been cut off—could leave some of the worst-affected communities without timely assistance.

title.rendered: Temporary shelters, relief centres set up at 26 locations for Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 31

The federal and local governments have jointly set up temporary shelters and relief distribution centres at 26 locations across Rasuwa and Nuwakot for people affected by the recent floods.

According to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, 3,454 people received temporary shelter and relief at these centres on Sunday.

In Nuwakot alone, 2,274 people were accommodated at 16 temporary shelters.

In Bidur Municipality, flood-affected residents from the Tupche area have been accommodated at a library camp, while those from the Trishuli Dhunge and Simchaur areas are staying at the safe house and the building used for families observing mourning rituals.

Residents affected in Betravati have been sheltered at the local health post, while those from the Battar area are staying at the covered hall. Flood victims from Devighat have been accommodated at the Ayurvedic Alternative Medicine Centre.

Similarly, residents affected in the Betravati-Bhaise area are staying at Sundari Kairyani Secondary School. Those from the Trishuli Bazaar area have been accommodated at camps set up at the Colony Covered Hall, Bhairum Secondary School, Rimal Danda and Indrayani Basic School.

Flood-affected residents from Sitkhali in Bidur-3, Devighat, have been accommodated at Ranabhuwaneswari Secondary School and the ward office.

Those affected in Bidur-9 are staying at Trishuli Basic School and Shulakshana Secondary School. Residents from the Ratmate-Jiling area of Belkotgadhi Municipality are staying at Mahadev Secondary School.

Similarly, people affected in Kispang Rural Municipality-5 have been accommodated at Karki Manakamana Basic School and Tribhuvan Secondary School, while some flood victims from Rasuwa are staying at Tamang Plaza in Battar.

Injured people rescued from the flood-hit areas are receiving treatment and accommodation at the safe house in Bidur-2, the Ayurvedic Alternative Medicine Centre in Devighat, Mahadev Secondary School in Belkotgadhi-7 and Shulakshana Secondary School in Bidur-9.

Meanwhile, 10 temporary shelters have been established in Rasuwa for flood victims, with 1,180 people taking shelter there, according to the Prime Minister’s Office.

Shelters have been set up in Dadagaun of Uttargaya Rural Municipality-2 and in Haku, Pangling and Gre of Amachhodingmo Rural Municipality-1 and 2.

Similarly, shelters are operating in Thuman, Dalphedi, Khaidi, Briddhim, Lingling and Syafrubesi in Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-1, 2, 3 and 5, as well as in Haku, Pangrang and Gre of Amachhodingmo Rural Municipality-1 and 2.

title.rendered: Children caught in Bhotekoshi flood wait for word from their families

content.rendered:
Uttargaya, August 31

Some children sit quietly, staring into the distance. Some are crying. Others are eating or playing.

When Onlinekhabar’s team reached the premises of Shivalaya Basic School in Uttargaya Rural Municipality of Rasuwa on Sunday afternoon, the human toll of the Bhotekoshi flood was difficult to miss.

A group of local leaders, civil society members, teachers and others who survived the flood were busy looking after the children. Around 100 students are currently staying at the school.

Whenever someone arrives at the school, the children gather around them. Perhaps, somewhere in their minds, there is still a hope that the person arriving could be a parent they have been waiting for.

The days are passing. But the children have not yet given up hope.

Among them is nine-year-old Bhujana Tamang, a third-grade student. Until the flood, her days were much like those of other children—playing and spending time with her family.

Now, the flood has disrupted that childhood.

On the day the Bhotekoshi flood struck, Bhujana had left home in Khalte of Uttargaya Rural Municipality-5 wearing her school uniform, just as she did every other day.

A school bus was on its way to pick her up. But before she could reach school, her life took a different turn.

Bhujana’s father worked at a nearby hydropower project, while her mother worked on a farm. She also lived with her five-year-old brother and 16-year-old sister. All four have been out of contact since the flood.

Recalling the moment the Bhotekoshi flood hit, Bhujana said police officers took her towards the forest after telling her that the river was rising.

At the time, her mother, brother and sister were on the road watching the flood. Bhujana has not seen them since. She is still hoping that her family members will return.

People around her believe that her parents, brother and sister may have been swept away by the flood. But nine-year-old Bhujana is not ready to accept that.

In a trembling voice, she said, “I haven’t seen anyone since the flood. Everyone says the flood swept away my father, mother, brother and sister. But I feel they will come back. I see them in my dreams.”

She continues to wait for her parents to return.

‘I am alone’

Ten-year-old Apsara Tamang is facing a similar uncertainty.

Apsara, who lives in Pairebesi in Rasuwa, is a fourth-grade student at Shri Malika Devi School. Before the Bhotekoshi flood, her daily routine was much like that of other children.

Wake up in the morning, comb her hair and go to school.

On Wednesday, she had also set out for school. After learning that the flood was coming, a teacher named Uma took her uphill to safety. Apsara survived.

But she does not know what happened to the family members who were at home.

Her father, Subba Tamang, worked at a hydropower project. He has been out of contact since the Bhotekoshi flood. Her mother is also unreachable. There is no information about her grandfather or grandmother either. Her maternal uncle, who worked with her father, is also missing.

Apsara’s 15-month-old brother is also missing.

“My grandfather, grandmother, mummy, aunt and brother were at home,” Apsara said through tears. “Where could they be now?”

When people tell her that her family members may have been swept away by the flood, she becomes even more distressed.

For a while, she cannot speak. Then, through tears, she repeats the same words: “I am alone.”

Alongside the worry over her family, she is also facing questions about what comes next.

What will she do now? Where will she live? Who will look after her?

Apsara is currently taking shelter at Shivalaya School. Other children are staying around her, while teachers and others are looking after them.

No home, no school

Mailung, Pahire Besi, Khalte, Kaidel Danda, Bogati and Betrawati areas of Uttargaya Rural Municipality have suffered extensive damage from the Bhotekoshi flood. After most houses were swept away, the settlements have been left in what was once their riverbed.

Hundreds of families have been displaced. Nearly 100 children have lost their parents, according to preliminary information.

According to Bharat Paudel, principal of Shivalaya Basic School, students had attended four schools in the Uttargaya area on Wednesday.

Teachers at Shri Nilkantha Secondary School, Ramchandra Basic School, Modern Trinity and Uttargaya Boarding School managed to take some students to safer places when the flood struck.

The displaced children were initially kept at Nilkantha Secondary School. However, as concerns grew over the possibility of further floods and landslides around the school, they were moved to Shivalaya Basic School, which was considered relatively safer, Paudel said.

Children are now staying at Shivalaya along with their parents and some flood-affected families from around Nilkantha Secondary School. Some children have been taken in by relatives.

According to Prakash Nepal, a teacher at Shri Nilkantha Secondary School in Uttargaya-5, the settlements that had been relocated after the earthquake were among those worst affected by this flood.

“After the earthquake, the displaced settlements were relocated along the riverbank,” Nepal said. “That is why there was such a heavy human toll this time.”

He said the residents of those settlements were originally from different areas of the former Haku Village Development Committee.

Instead of being relocated to safer areas after the earthquake, they had been resettled along the riverbank.

The same settlements have now been swept away by the Bhotekoshi flood.

Around 550 students were enrolled at Nilkantha Secondary School. Nepal said around 200 of them are currently out of contact.

Trinity, Ramchandra Residential and Uttargaya Public School, located within the school area, have also been completely destroyed by the Bhotekoshi flood. Preliminary information suggests that around 150 students from those schools are also missing.

“Nearly 200 students from Nilkantha alone have still not made contact,” Nepal said.

As the risk of flooding increased, the school had been conducting classes from 9 am for the past two years. Nepal said bringing students to school early had helped prevent an even greater loss of life this time.

“If the school had not been operating at that time, we could have lost nearly 80 percent of the students,” he said.

The school has also lost contact with four teachers and staff members following the flood. They include a computer engineering teacher, a Plus Two-level teacher, an early childhood teacher and the school nurse.

“We have lost hope. Even so, we still hope they will be found alive and come back into contact,” he said.

More than 60 students have lost parents in the Bhotekoshi flood

The school has begun collecting preliminary information about the family situations of students following the flood.

Nepal said the initial data suggests that around 100 students may have lost their parents.

“So far, we have registered the names of 60 students staying at this holding centre who have been left without parents,” he said. “We estimate that the number could reach around 100.”

With telephone and internet services disrupted, the full extent of the damage is still not known.

‘It did not feel like a river. It was like a storm’

Nepal said he was preparing to go to school on the day the flood struck.

After eating and putting on his school uniform, he received information that there were no settlements in the upper area but that settlements along the road in the lower area were at risk. He then began contacting students and relatives.

He also used Facebook to warn local residents, posting that the river was rising and asking people in the surrounding areas to stay safe.

But within minutes, the situation went beyond control.

“Within five to seven minutes of starting to make calls, we heard that the river had already reached Dhunche,” Nepal said. “It did not feel like a river. It was more like a storm or a strong wind.”

He said the scene after the flood was difficult to describe.

“It was something you could hardly bear to watch and something unimaginable,” he said.

Telephone and internet services remain disrupted following the flood, making it difficult to contact many students, parents and local residents.

But Nepal says the response cannot stop at addressing the immediate needs.

“Three schools no longer have any structure. The government needs to think about the long-term future of children who have lost their families,” teacher Nepal said.

title.rendered: Reconnecting Rasuwa could take weeks after floods destroy key bridges

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

At least 35 bridges between the Miteri Bridge at Rasuwagadhi and Muglin have been completely swept away by the devastating floods of August 26, severely disrupting road connectivity in the region.

Rasuwa, the district worst affected by the floods, remains effectively disconnected from the national road network. Although some alternative routes have technically been opened, transportation remains difficult.

With helicopter access to remote parts of Rasuwa also proving challenging for relief and rescue operations, the lack of a reliable road connection has added to the difficulties faced by flood victims.

There is growing pressure on the government to restore road connectivity immediately. However, the scale of damage means this is unlikely to happen quickly.

According to Department of Roads Director General Dr Bijay Jaisi, the floods completely destroyed several existing bridges, in some cases washing away even the ground and foundations around the bridge sites.

“As the entire structure of the existing bridges has been swept away, it is not possible to restore all of them immediately,” Jaisi said.

He added that authorities have not even been able to reach some damaged bridge sites to conduct detailed technical assessments.

“As a result, there is no immediate possibility of reopening the roads even by installing Bailey bridges,” he said.

Local authorities demand immediate alternative routes

Local representatives have been calling for faster restoration of road links.

Rasuwa Kalika Rural Municipality Chairperson Hari Krishna Devkota told Rastriya Swatantra Party Chair Rabi Lamichhane by phone on Sunday that the district needed to be reconnected to the national road network immediately.

Belkotgadhi Rural Municipality Chairperson of Nuwakot Jagat Bahadur Gurung has also called for an alternative road to be opened as soon as possible.

How long would it take to install a Bailey bridge?

According to Jaisi, a Bailey bridge can be installed in at least 15 days if the foundations on both sides of a damaged crossing remain intact.

The Nepali Army has previously installed Bailey bridges within about two weeks.

However, if new foundations have to be constructed on both sides, another 15 days would be required.

Given the extent of damage caused by the current floods, Jaisi said installing a Bailey bridge at a damaged crossing could take at least a month even with accelerated work.

Bailey bridges to be prioritised at three locations

The Department of Roads does not plan to install Bailey bridges at every damaged crossing.

“Our priority will be to reopen the national road network as soon as possible,” Jaisi said. “Bailey bridges will therefore be installed only at the most critical locations.”

At other locations, the department plans to upgrade alternative roads and use them to restore traffic.

The department has already resumed work on an alternative road connecting to Dhadingbesi.

According to Jaisi, preparations are underway to install Bailey bridges at three key locations.

The first is at Devighat, where the bridge over the Tadi Khola has been swept away.

The second is at Trishuli Bazaar, at the site of the old bridge.

The third is at Betrawati, which connects Nuwakot and Rasuwa.

“If Bailey bridges are installed at these three locations, the main highway can be brought back into operation,” Jaisi said. “The remaining bridges will then be rebuilt as permanent structures based on technical assessments and requirements.”

Nepal does not have enough Bailey bridges

Nepal currently has 11 Bailey bridge units with a combined length of 50 metres, according to the Department of Roads.

However, the floods have extensively eroded riverbanks and surrounding land, meaning longer spans will be required at many locations than were needed previously.

The government has therefore requested Bailey bridges from India and China.

According to the Ministry of Finance, Nepal has requested 30 Bailey bridges from China.

Bailey bridges are generally used as temporary structures to restore transportation across relatively narrow crossings. However, the extensive erosion caused by the floods means longer spans are now required in several locations.

Bridges damaged from Rasuwagadhi to Muglin

According to Department of Roads data, bridges along the corridor from the Miteri Bridge on the Nepal-China border to the old suspension bridge at Muglin have been affected.

The Miteri Bridge has been completely swept away, while the Muglin bridge remains intact.

In Rasuwa, two Bailey bridges at Timure have been washed away. The concrete bridge over the Bhotekoshi River and the concrete bridge at Chilime have also been destroyed.

A hydropower Bailey bridge at Syafrubesi has been swept away, along with the concrete bridge at the same location.

The Haku I and Haku II Bailey bridges in Rasuwa have also been washed away. The Bailey bridge at the Upper Trishuli hydropower project and the Mailung Bailey bridge have also been completely destroyed.

The concrete bridge near the Trishuli-3A dam at Mailung and another concrete bridge near Dam 2 have been swept away.

The concrete bridge over the Bhotekoshi River at Khalte, on the Rasuwa-Nuwakot border, has also been destroyed. Both the old and new concrete bridges at Betrawati have been swept away.

In Nuwakot, the concrete bridge at Trishuli-Tupche has been completely destroyed.

Both the old and new bridges at Trishuli Bazaar have been affected, while the concrete bridge over the Trishuli River at Simchaur has also been swept away.

The suspension bridge at Devighat has been destroyed, along with the concrete bridge over the Trishuli River there.

Both the old and new concrete bridges over the Tadi Khola at Devighat have also been swept away.

The bridge over the Trishuli River at Shrikhaali has been affected, while the bridge at Buddhisinghghat has been washed away.

The bridge over the Trishuli River at Ratmate and the bridge at Keureni have also been swept away.

In Dhading, the bridge over the Trishuli River near Galchhi remains intact. However, the bridge over the Trishuli River on the Baireni-Salyantar road below Galchhi has been swept away.

The concrete bridge over the Trishuli River near Hamlet Resort has been damaged, while bridges at Jare Bagaicha and Ghatbesi in Dhading have been washed away.

Both the new and old bridges over Kolpu Khola in Dhading have been damaged.

The Furkhe Khola bridge at Malekhu has also been swept away.

The bridges over the Trishuli River at Benighat and Fishling remain intact.

According to the Department of Roads, the Bailey bridge at Chumlingtar in Chitwan has also survived.

The new arch bridge and old suspension bridge at Muglin have likewise remained intact despite the floods.

title.rendered: Let us all help the government respond better to this Himalayan tsunami

content.rendered:
I am writing this after taking a short break from the campaign to support the government in this disaster.

What began in Rasuwa is not the kind of ordinary landslide or flood Nepal sees every year. It is something much bigger—a Himalayan tsunami that has shaken an entire region.

The disaster struck last Wednesday and may have caused more loss of life and property than the 2015 earthquake. It has also delivered a lesson that could take us decades to recover from.

We have repeatedly called it the “Rasuwa flood”. But that description does not quite capture what happened.

In a normal flood, water levels rise gradually in rivers and other water sources. People living along the banks have at least some time to move to safety. That was not what happened in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli region.

There had been no significant rainfall. The ground was not even wet. It was a bright sunny morning.

Suddenly, a violent snowstorm hit the Rasuwa-Tibet border area, producing something that looked more like an ocean storm than a conventional Himalayan flood.

Perhaps “Himalayan tsunami” is the more appropriate description.

And the threat has not gone away.

Nepal, China, India, Pakistan, Bhutan, Myanmar and other countries could face snowstorms and disasters of an even greater scale in the future.

There have been some encouraging signs in the response.

Prime Minister Balen Shah’s immediate messages on social media, followed by his visit to Bidur in Nuwakot, are worth noting. As far as I know, the visit was not part of a pre-planned programme. He simply travelled by road, without much fanfare, to one of the affected areas. That, in itself, is positive.

Nepali Congress president Gagan Thapa and other political leaders have pledged their support for the government’s efforts. The CPN-UML submitted an eight-point list of measures the government should take immediately on Sunday.

Across the country, government agencies, private organisations and communities have also been mobilising according to their capacity.

That is how it should be.

In a natural or human-made disaster, the responsibility of citizens and communities is not simply to support the government. It is to support the state. The government is, after all, one part of the larger state.

And supporting the government does not mean ignoring its failures.

The state did deserve credit for some of its initial response.

As soon as news of the Rasuwa disaster emerged on Wednesday, security personnel began making announcements through loudspeakers. The Cabinet called an emergency meeting. The House of Representatives took some time to get going, but Speaker DP Aryal eventually stopped other proceedings and gave the disaster the attention it demanded.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal immediately began coordinating with the international community.

The Nepal Army, which has developed considerable expertise in disaster response, launched emergency rescue operations. Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force were also deployed quickly.

These were the right first steps. They were also the steps one would naturally expect from the state.

But while the scale of this disaster could never have been completely avoided, the loss of life and property could have been reduced significantly.

We failed to do that.

Some of the reasons go back years—to our poor state of preparedness and our weak disaster-response capacity. Others have to do with the government’s own failures of coordination.

Before getting into the argument, look at the numbers.

Government figures show that by 6pm on Sunday, 781 people had been reported dead. Another 2,502 people were out of contact. The death toll is still rising.

The security forces have reported rescuing 9,435 people, while 267 people have been injured.

These are not just numbers. Behind each one is a family waiting for news.

Our Prime Minister and Home Minister may not be expected to operate exactly like Chinese Premier Li Qiang. But their urgency must show up in the results. Otherwise, all the running around risks becoming little more than another exercise in self-promotion and image-building.

The Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force deserve praise for their work in the immediate rescue and response.

But the Home Minister has a different responsibility.

If Home Minister Sudan Gurung had remained focused on the central chain of command instead of personally entering tunnels, his efforts might have appeared less like a race for visibility and more like a coordinated rescue operation.

Those with expertise in emergency rescue should be given the responsibility for operational command, while political leadership should remain focused on coordinating and clearing obstacles from the centre.

There is another major issue.

More than a dozen countries—including India, China, South Korea and the United Kingdom—have sought permission to send specialist emergency rescue teams. Yet the government has taken time to make decisions.

There have been discussions about the Army’s concerns and geopolitical interests.

But this is not the time to lose sight of the central issue.

This is about saving lives.

Information received so far suggests that construction companies from South Korea and other countries have also sought permission to rescue employees trapped inside tunnels in their project areas. They are reportedly frustrated by the delay in getting a decision.

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle’s remarks during his visit to Trishuli also shed light on the confusion and delay within the government.

If we manage to save as many people as possible, we will demonstrate not just the strength of the state but also what it means to be a country that stands by its citizens. Yet, so far, there has been little sense of that urgency.

This raises an uncomfortable question: does criticising the government during a disaster amount to being against the government?

Apparently, even well-intentioned advice is increasingly being treated that way.

Rastriya Swatantra Party chair Rabi Lamichhane and the party’s parliamentary whip Krantishikha Dhital issued an advisory to their lawmakers about what they should and should not do during the disaster. Yet Sagar Dhakal, Jwala Sangroula and Ashika Tamang, among others, do not appear to have followed it.

Tamang’s conduct in Dhading has also exposed the communication gap between the federal and local governments. In the race to make our videos go viral, we must make sure people’s lives do not become collateral damage.

Should politicians go to affected areas?

Of course they should. But there has to be some common sense about when to go, who should go and what they should do once they get there.

Ministers from affected districts such as Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, federal lawmakers, provincial and local representatives, and local political party units all have an important role to play.

So do elected representatives with relevant expertise, such as Shriram Neupane and Dhananjaya Regmi.

RSP lawmaker Shriram Neupane, for instance, is himself a tunnel expert and is currently involved in rescue efforts at the Upper Trishuli 3A project.

Other lawmakers, including Ganesh Karki, have urged politicians to stay home and support the response rather than crowd affected areas.

Yet the number of what can only be called “disaster tourists” does not appear to be falling.

There is a useful comparison right across the border.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang himself travelled as far as the area near Nepal’s border and took an active role in the response.

More importantly, there is evidence that his visit was not simply about appearances. The immediate priority given to rescue operations and the rebuilding of roads, electricity infrastructure and bridges is there for everyone to see.

A minister can certainly enter a tunnel and physically participate in a rescue. But people judge governments by results during a crisis.

The government may not have the luxury of comparing the Chinese premier’s style with that of our Home Minister. But the RSP and its supporters should be able to tell the government something very simple:

There is a difference between building an image and delivering results.

I keep coming back to one question.

Can a country like Nepal, with its limited capacity, really confront a disaster of this scale on its own?

Clearly not.

The burden created by climate change is also something this small Himalayan country cannot carry alone.

What we need is political will, a clear understanding of the scale of the crisis, and strong national and international lobbying and coordination.

Is our government capable of doing that?

And if it is not fully capable on its own, can it confidently approach countries and organisations that have the skills, resources and equipment we do not?

This federal government is led by young people. It should be capable of doing precisely that.

That is why we can—and should—expect more from it.

We should expect the government and its representatives not to turn this disaster into an opportunity to build their own image.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung may genuinely be giving everything he has to the response. There is no reason to doubt his commitment. But commitment alone is not enough.

Following him with cameras as he enters tunnels does not guarantee the rescue or safety of the engineers, employees and workers trapped inside them.

Engineers and workers are trapped inside tunnels at the Upper Trishuli 3A, Langtang, Upper Trishuli 1 and Chilime hydropower projects. Five days have passed, and we still have not been able to establish and publicly communicate their actual condition.

Imagine what their families must be going through.

At a moment like this, shouldn’t the Home Minister be running the central command properly? Shouldn’t he be taking the lead in immediately mobilising more than Rs5 billion in assistance?

When floods and landslides hit the mountains, a minister’s job is not to bang his head against a tunnel wall. It is to use the head—and the brain inside it—to run the central command.

That is why, despite wanting to support the government day and night, this is a point where we have to say something the minister may not want to hear.

If questioning the government’s approach and suggesting better, more practical ways of doing things is considered a failure to support it, then so be it.

We have to be willing to say it.

Because the priority now is simple: minimise the number of people who die, recover those swept away by the floods, find those missing inside tunnels, rescue foreign tourists and protect livestock and other animals.

Above all, we need to rescue as many people as possible, as quickly as possible.

Prime Minister Balen has spoken about protecting the life of every citizen. That commitment now needs to be felt on the ground.

There is no time to waste.

The Home Minister, other ministers and every arm of the state need to understand that. Every hour of delay means another life-saving opportunity is lost.

What is happening on the ground?

Information provided to the Onlinekhabar newsroom by reporting teams deployed to the affected areas at different stages paints a grim picture.

Some areas where people are trapped have no clean drinking water. Communication has been cut off and shelter and electricity are gone.

High-capacity helicopters such as the Mi-17 cannot easily land in many places. Rescue units that should be reaching victims are more heavily concentrated in the Nuwakot area.

The one-door system for relief distribution has also failed to ensure that assistance reaches people evenly.

Most bridges have been washed away.

Emergency Bailey bridges could make a significant difference in some locations, but the initiative has so far been limited. No one expects bridges to be built everywhere immediately. But even where vehicles cannot pass, people need walking routes and pedestrian bridges. At least some of them are urgently needed.

Who is supposed to lead and coordinate all of this?

The Ministry of Home Affairs and the units under it. That is where the leadership responsibility lies. Home Minister needs to lead.

There are plenty of ways for him to demonstrate that he remains connected with people on the ground. He can provide regular briefings. He can visit selected locations and offer reassurance.

But how much he sweats or how many calories he burns is completely irrelevant. His urgency and his ability to make decisions must be measured by the results.

Perhaps our Prime Minister and Home Minister cannot match the Chinese premier. They do not need to.

But their determination must be visible in what they achieve. Otherwise, all this movement will become another exercise in self-promotion and image-building.

This is bigger than politics

Nothing is more important than a citizen’s right to live. Certainly not the projection of any individual as a future prime minister.

Yet we are still seeing the danger that the Himalayan tsunami that began in Rasuwa—one of the most devastating disasters the country has faced—could become an opportunity to spend state resources building the glory of an individual.

Let us say it plainly.

Those who built and now lead this government must have the courage to remind Home Minister Sudan Gurung if he is using the disaster to burnish his image.

The rescue of people trapped in a disaster is not nearly as romantic as it may look from Singha Durbar.

It is difficult and it is painful. And the danger has not passed. More risks may yet emerge.

So what have we done with the time we have had?

Finding people swept away by floods is obviously not easy. But even a proper look at social media shows the desperate pleas coming from their families.

Climate change is no longer something to be discussed only in five-star hotels.

Glaciers melting and Himalayan ranges turning black are no longer issues limited to mountaineering expeditions and mountain flights.

For the poorest people living in these areas—and for indigenous and minority communities—the consequences are immediate. Their homes are being destroyed. Their children’s schools are being lost. Health posts, farmland and livelihoods are at risk. And yet, at a time like this, a section of the privileged appears more interested in promoting itself.

There is another side to Nepal, too.

A photograph posted on Facebook by Sonukumar Das and shared by RSP lawmaker Manish Jha offers a glimpse of it.

In Rautahat, 26 students collected Rs 470 for the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund by setting aside Rs1 0 to Rs 20 from their daily snack money. That small act says something important about Nepali society.

It is the same society that can put out the communal fire recently being stoked through Kaptanganj and Golbazar with tolerance and humanity.

There is something deeply pure about that gesture. The sentiment behind the money matters far more than how many zeros the amount has. Thank you, friends from Rautahat.

That same spirit is needed from citizens across the country. But this crisis also forces us to ask another uncomfortable question:

Are we genuinely sensitive towards other people and communities, or do we simply perform sensitivity on Facebook? We must make sure that crises like this do not become another form of preparation for the next election.

Let the government work

In March, a strong government was formed with a huge majority. But a strong government is not defined only by the number of votes it wins. It must also be able to make its citizens feel that the state is strong and that it will not abandon them.

So let the government work.

The blue jackets carrying “RAT” and the red-and-white promotional materials we have been seeing across Nepal are becoming a distraction. They are getting in the way of the work that needs to be done. And they risk repeating the same mistakes we have seen from governments in the past.

A political culture that thinks about the next election even during rescue and relief operations cannot be the politics of a modern, civilised state.

The voters are the very people suffering today. Winning their votes once is not enough. They have to be won over again and again.

For now, there is only one thing that matters; Let us all work together to help the government do its job—and do it well, effectively and with results.

title.rendered: Govt waits five days to bring in foreign tunnel rescuers as hundreds remain trapped

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Indian and Chinese tunnel rescue teams have finally begun operations in Rasuwa, five days after devastating floods swept through the district, as hundreds of people are feared trapped inside tunnels of hydropower projects.

Around 600 people are estimated to be trapped in tunnels of various hydropower projects affected by the floods, although authorities have yet to rescue those trapped underground.

Rescue operations began Sunday at the Chilime, Upper Trishuli-1 and Langtang hydropower projects after foreign rescue teams arrived in Nepal.

A nine-member Chinese tunnel rescue team has been deployed at the 216-MW Upper Trishuli-1 project, according to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The team arrived in coordination with China Railway, the Chinese contractor working on the project.

Around 600 people working at the Upper Trishuli-1 project are still unaccounted for, according to Giriraj Adhikari, chief executive officer of Nepal Water and Energy Development Company. Of them, around 400 are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.

Some 260 people who managed to escape the project area have already been rescued, including 10 South Korean nationals. However, those believed to be trapped inside the tunnels have yet to be rescued.

Of the estimated 400 people trapped underground, around 300 are believed to have been working inside the tunnel and about 100 at the headworks, Adhikari said.

A second Chinese tunnel rescue team also arrived in Nepal on Sunday morning, according to the Chinese Embassy in Nepal. It was not immediately clear where the second team had been deployed.

Meanwhile, an 11-member Indian technical team has been deployed to the Chilime Hydropower Project. The team includes doctors, paramedics and tunnel engineers. A separate 22-member Indian Army team has also been mobilised for rescue operations.

The Indian team conducted an aerial reconnaissance of the Chilime and Langtang areas by helicopter on Saturday before beginning rescue operations in coordination with Nepali security agencies.

The joint team of Indian and Nepali rescuers has already recovered two bodies from inside the Chilime hydropower tunnel.

Nepali Army spokesperson Assistant Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet said the rescue team had entered about 100 metres into the 250-metre-long tunnel but had not found any survivors.

The company estimates that six employees are trapped inside the Chilime tunnel.

The rescue teams are using specialised equipment to clear mud, sludge and debris that filled the tunnels after the floods and landslides.

Earlier, a mountain rescue team sent by Simrik Air had entered about 100 metres into a tunnel but was unable to proceed because it was completely filled with sludge. The team had reported that specialised equipment and tunnel rescue experts were required.

At the Upper Trishuli-3A project, rescuers on Sunday located a cable access tunnel after three days of continuous efforts. The tunnel provides a possible route for rescuers to enter the underground powerhouse area.

Nepal Electricity Authority Acting Managing Director Dirghayukumar Shrestha said the cable access tunnel can be used to enter the area where workers are believed to be trapped.

Five openings had earlier been drilled to send air into the tunnel and assess conditions inside.

Around 40–42 technical personnel, including highly skilled experts, had been working in the underground powerhouse for an overhaul when the flood struck, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority.

The rescue effort at the project began two days after the floods, but rescuers had been unable to reach the tunnel for several days.

Questions over delayed foreign assistance

The arrival of foreign rescue teams has also raised questions over the pace of Nepal’s response.

Hydropower companies have said they repeatedly requested government assistance to rescue employees and workers trapped underground.

Nepal Engineers’ Association President Subas Chandra Baral said the country lacked the specialised skills, equipment and capacity required for large-scale tunnel rescue operations.

He said foreign experts and equipment could have been brought in much earlier.

“The cost of the delay could be very high,” Baral said, adding that the association had repeatedly urged the government to speed up rescue efforts.

A senior Nepal Electricity Authority official also said the failure to bring in foreign experts and equipment earlier exposed Nepal’s limited tunnel rescue capacity.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, however, has denied that the government delayed permission for foreign rescue teams.

Foreign assistance has also been offered by South Korea, the United Kingdom and Australia.

Foreign Secretary Amrit Rai said a South Korean rescue team had arrived in Nepal, although it had yet to be deployed in the field.

The UK government has also announced that it would send a rapid deployment team to Nepal, primarily to assist British nationals and coordinate with Nepali authorities and the British Embassy.

According to sources, the British rescue team has arrived in Nepal and is on standby. However, the UK had also offered to send rescue personnel, but the Nepal government reportedly indicated that they were not required.

Australia had similarly offered to send a rescue team, but it did not come to Nepal after the government did not grant permission, according to sources.

The devastating floods triggered by the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26 caused widespread destruction across Rasuwa and neighbouring districts, damaging hydropower projects, roads and other infrastructure.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has reported that 589 foreign nationals were missing following the disaster, of whom 261 have been rescued alive. Among those missing, 167 are Indian nationals and 40 are Chinese nationals.

title.rendered: Why women and children need special care during flood rescue

content.rendered:
During floods, landslides, or other natural disasters, the priority is always saving lives. But rescue cannot treat everyone’s risk, needs, and physical condition the same way. Women, pregnant and postpartum women, infants, and children face heightened risk during disasters. That’s why they require special priority and sensitive care, “soft care” at every stage. 

Nepali Congress Chief Whip Basana Thapa said the “single-door system” implemented in flood-affected areas risks overshadowing the specific needs and rights of women and children. During her field visit to Rasuwa’s flood-hit areas, she found women and children’s conditions especially difficult, with a particular shortage of sanitary pads and hygiene kits.

She noted that centrally sent supplies were piling up in one place without reaching actual victims — showing that the single-door system alone isn’t enough; ensuring the right materials reach the right people is equally essential.

Life first, then special needs

According to Armed Police Force spokesperson DIG Netra Bahadur Karki, women and children are given special priority during rescue and management. Where possible, women are rescued by female security or rescue personnel, though this isn’t always feasible during fast currents or dangerous terrain; whoever rescuers encounter first gets rescued first, regardless of gender.

Prioritising women and children doesn’t mean neglecting men or others at risk. Whoever’s life is in immediate danger must be rescued first. But afterwards, attention must go to the specific needs of women, children, pregnant and postpartum women, senior citizens, and people with disabilities, including maintaining dignity and privacy for injured, semi-conscious, or soaked women during rescue.

Higher risk for pregnant and postpartum women

Pregnant and postpartum women are among the most vulnerable during disasters, since both mother and unborn child’s health are at stake. Gynaecologist Dr Deepa Chudal said rescued pregnant women should be moved to safety and healthcare providers notified as quickly as possible,  via helicopter if roads are blocked. Delays in reaching health facilities can turn situations critical.

Infection risk is also significant, as floodwater can spread cholera and diarrheal diseases; pregnant women need boiled or safe water, nutritious food, and medication. Standing water after floods also raises mosquito-borne disease risk, requiring bed nets and repellents.

Special care must be taken during rescue to avoid injury, since trauma can cause miscarriage in early pregnancy or internal bleeding and complications later in pregnancy. Beyond rescue, health checkups, nutrition, hygiene, mental health support, and access to maternity services must follow.

Menstruation as an “emergency need”

Relief typically prioritises rice, lentils, water, clothing, and medicine, but sanitary pads, underwear, soap, and sanitiser are equally essential for women. 

Lack of safe toilets and pads during menstruation raises infection risk. Dr Chudal says these items must be treated as basic necessities, not “extras,” with safe, private toilets and bathing facilities in shelters.

Children’s bodies show disaster’s impact faster

Paediatrician Dr Baburam Karki said children trapped in cold water or mud for extended periods face various health risks. Cold affects children’s bodies faster than adults, potentially causing dropped body temperature, cardiac issues, kidney problems, pneumonia, and metabolic disturbances. Dirty water entering through the mouth or nose can cause aspiration pneumonia.

Children trapped in mud, rocks, or debris risk fractures and injuries; since children’s bones are more fragile, extra care is needed during rescue. Afterwards, clearing water and debris from the mouth and nose, protecting against cold, providing first aid, and reaching healthcare quickly are essential.

“Soft Care” for children means understanding not just physical gentleness but also their fear, security, and emotional needs, says Dr Pandey. 

Child rights activist Gauri Pradhan emphasises reassuring language during rescue; phrases like “you’re safe, we’re here” help reduce fear in frightened, crying, or separated children. Rushed pulling from mud can cause further injury; situations must be assessed for safe extraction.

Protecting children separated from parents

Children risk separation from parents during disasters, making it risky to place them among general relief-seekers.

 The Armed Police Force prioritises health treatment for unaccompanied or separated children, managing them at holding centres while searching for families. 

If families aren’t found immediately, safe institutional care is required until reunification.

Shelters must be women- and child-friendly

Crowded camps can expose women and girls to sexual violence, abuse, or trafficking risks. 

Dr Chudal recommends safe spaces, adequate lighting, secure toilets and bathing areas, female health workers, and security arrangements in temporary shelters.

Tailored relief supplies

Distributing identical relief packages to everyone isn’t practical, says Pradhan.

 Children need diapers, nutritious food, and age-appropriate supplies; women need sanitary pads and hygiene kits; pregnant and postpartum women need additional nutritional and health support.

 Clearly labelled, need-based distribution ensures materials reach the right people.

Single-door system plus need-based distribution

While the single-door system prevents duplicate distribution and misuse, it shouldn’t mean identical distribution for everyone.

 Gender- and age-disaggregated data, needs assessment, and distribution monitoring are essential, requiring coordination between federal, provincial, and local levels.

Mental health matters equally

Losing homes, relatives, or witnessing destruction can cause serious psychological trauma, especially for children and women. 

Trauma counselling and psychosocial support are needed alongside food and medicine, with safe spaces for children to play, talk, and express emotions, particularly for those who lost parents or families.

Priority doesn’t mean neglecting others

Prioritising women and children doesn’t diminish other victims’ lives; disaster management’s core principle remains saving lives at immediate risk. 

But since women, infants, children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups face compounded risks, identifying and addressing their specific needs remains essential. Priority isn’t about excluding anyone; it’s about providing extra protection to those at greater risk.

title.rendered: Two bodies recovered from Chilime hydropower tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

An Indian team of tunnel experts and the Nepali Army have recovered two bodies from the tunnel of the Chilime Hydropower Project in Rasuwa.

The joint rescue operation began on Sunday after the Indian team arrived in Nepal. Nepali Army spokesperson Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet said the bodies were recovered from about 100 metres inside the tunnel.

“The joint team reached 100 metres into the 250-metre-long tunnel. We could not find any living people up to that point,” Basnet said.

According to Chilime Hydropower Project Chief Executive Officer Baburaja Maharjan, six employees are believed to have been trapped inside the project tunnel.

The rescue operation inside the tunnel began on Sunday following the arrival of the Indian team. The Indian experts had conducted an aerial reconnaissance of the Chilime and Langtang areas by helicopter on Saturday.

The Indian specialist team began the rescue operation on Sunday morning in coordination with an 82-member joint security team comprising personnel from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force.

The teams are using specialised equipment to clear the tunnel and search for workers believed to be trapped inside.

title.rendered: Krishna Bhir landslide blocks Muglin-Kathmandu road, repairs may take a month

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

A landslide at Krishna Bhir along the Prithvi Highway on Sunday has completely disrupted the Muglin-Kathmandu road after a section of the road was swept away.

Vehicular movement has come to a complete halt along the affected section.

According to Deputy Superintendent of Police Prakash Dahal of the District Police Office, Dhading, it could take at least a month to restore traffic.

“I went there for an on-site inspection this morning,” Dahal said. “Looking at the extent of the landslide, it will take at least a month to reopen the road.”

Gorkha route suggested as alternative

Authorities have suggested that vehicles travelling to Kathmandu via Muglin use routes through Gorkha for the time being.

One alternative route runs from Gorkha district headquarters through Bunkot, Namjung, Ghairung and Durbung to Siurenitar, from where vehicles can reach Benighat and continue towards Kathmandu.

Another route runs from Gorkha headquarters through Namjung and Bunkotghat before joining the road at Benighat.

These routes could particularly benefit vehicles travelling to Kathmandu from Pokhara, Gorkha and other western parts of the country.

Chief District Officer of Gorkha Tulsi Bahadur Shrestha said efforts were underway to restore connectivity between Muglin and Kathmandu through Gorkha.

He said the district administration was coordinating with the road office to identify the shortest and most suitable alternative route.

“We are coordinating with the road office to identify a short and suitable route,” Shrestha said.

He added that the identified road would be upgraded at necessary points to facilitate vehicular movement until the damaged section of the Muglin-Kathmandu road can be restored.

title.rendered: Teaching Hospital becomes a waiting point for families of Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Nearly 2,400 people remain unaccounted for nearly five days after a devastating flood swept through the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on August 26.

For their families, the uncertainty has become an agonising wait.

Relatives searching for loved ones who remain missing have urged the government to intensify search and rescue operations and reach those who may still be stranded in forests and other remote areas.

For Niru Tamang of Sindhupalchok, Sunday marked the fifth day since her husband, Ashish Tamang, went missing in Rasuwa.

With their two-year-old child, she has come to Kathmandu in search of her husband.

She has not given up hope that he may have survived by reaching a forest or another safe location.

“My husband, Ashish Tamang, has been missing since the flood. My child is only two years old. I have come this far hoping that I might find him,” she said.

“I want to request the government to speed up the search and rescue. I hope that he may have gone uphill into the forest when the flood came and survived. People who are still in the forests need to be rescued as soon as possible.”

Tamang is among many relatives who have been travelling from one place to another trying to find missing family members as rescue efforts continue in the flood-hit districts.

26 travellers missing after bus swept away

Dozens of people from Dhading who were travelling towards Gosainkunda for a pilgrimage are also still missing after the flood swept through the area.

According to Gopal Bishwakarma of Dhading, 26 people from Nilkantha Municipality wards 9 and 12 and other localities have been unaccounted for since the disaster.

The group was travelling by bus towards Gosainkunda when the flood struck.

Bishwakarma said one of the passengers managed to call a friend in Pokhara after reaching Betrawati and told him that the bus had already been swept away and that they feared they too could be swept away.

“My friends from Nilkantha Municipality-12, 9 and other areas of Dhading—around 26 or 27 people—went missing in the flood while travelling to Gosainkunda. They were travelling in a bus and have not been in contact since,” he said.

“After reaching Betrawati, one of them called my friend in Pokhara and said the bus had already been swept away and that they might also be swept away. He asked him to look after his family and children.”

Bishwakarma said at least one body from the group had been recovered, while others were still missing.

“One body has come here. I have also heard that more bodies are being recovered. But 19 people are still missing,” he said.

Families gather at hospitals

Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu has also seen a steady stream of relatives searching for information about their loved ones.

The hospital premises have remained busy with families who have come to determine the condition and whereabouts of people they have been unable to contact since the floods.

For many of them, the wait continues without an answer.
