title.rendered: He saved his family. The flood took everything else.

content.rendered:
Betrawati, August 30

At 8am on August 26, Santaman Lama of Betrawati took his son and daughter to school, as he did every day.

When he returned home, however, something made him stop outside rather than go in.

Lama owned a house in Betrawati, where he ran a shop selling religious items. He had also rented out a room to Ansari Motorcycle Workshop.

As he stood outside, the owner of a nearby hardware shop told him he had heard that a flood was coming to Betrawati.

“I heard that a flood was coming to Betrawati. They told us not to stay here,” the hardware shop owner told him.

Warnings about floods were not unusual for people in Betrawati, and Lama initially did not take the warning too seriously.

But the words—“they told us not to stay here”—stayed with him.

He repeated the warning to himself before calling his wife outside and telling her what he had heard.

“The hardware shop owner told us to go uphill and said he would go and check the river,” Lama recalls.

“I had barely told him, ‘Don’t go,’ when the river came. It hit us,” he says. “The first surge knocked him down and swept him away.”

What happened next remains vivid for Lama.

“My wife was behind me. I grabbed her first, but the river threw her away. Somehow, I lifted her and threw her uphill. Then I held on to some bushes and climbed up,” he says.

By then, the flood had reached his house. From higher ground, Lama watched as the water swept it away.

“I saw my neighbours lose not only their houses but also their family members. It was heartbreaking,” he says.

Ishwarlal Shrestha and Buddhilal Dangol were swept towards him, and Lama managed to pull both of them to safety.

“After that, I lost contact with them,” he says. “If I meet them, I want to tell them: it wasn’t only your everything that was lost. I lost everything too.”

Lama also saw two people calling for help from a rooftop but was unable to reach them.

Once he made it to higher ground, his thoughts turned to his children.

He borrowed a neighbour’s phone and immediately contacted their school. His son and daughter were safe at Nilkantha School, which is located on higher ground.

“I managed to save my family of four,” he says.

No home, and Rs 2.3 million in debt

Lama survived, as did his immediate family. But almost everything else he owned was lost in the flood.

The only house he owned was swept away. He now has to ask relatives staying in upper Keraghari for clothes to wear.

Wearing a torn shirt, Lama says he is struggling to understand what comes next.

“I have nothing to eat or nowhere to stay. I have been reduced to asking others for things. That was everything I had,” he says, visibly emotional. “It was property I had worked hard to build.”

The house was not only his home but also an investment he had built through years of work. Lama says he is now carrying a debt of Rs 2.3 million that he took to build it.

He has not been able to repay the loan, and the debt, along with concerns about his children’s future, weighs heavily on him.

“How am I supposed to repay the loan now? The bank does not understand my pain,” he says.

“If the government understands the situation of people like me who have lost everything and provides some relief, perhaps we can continue living. Otherwise, we may be forced to leave this world before our time.”

For now, Lama has one request.

“If you can, please take my story to the government,” he says.

title.rendered: Engineering, technical bodies urge govt to ease helicopter access for flood rescue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Engineering and technical professional organisations have urged the government to work with them in search, rescue and relief efforts in areas affected by the devastating floods.

Issuing a four-point appeal, the organisations called on the government to simplify the process of providing helicopter services to the private sector for rescue and relief operations.

They specifically urged the government to facilitate necessary permissions, coordination and administrative procedures so that private hydropower developers can use helicopters to reach remote disaster-affected areas and hydropower project sites.

“We request the government to make the necessary permissions, coordination and administrative procedures swift and easy so that private hydropower project developers can use helicopter services to conduct search and rescue operations and deliver essential relief to remote disaster-affected areas and hydropower project sites,” the appeal said.

The organisations have also offered technical support in preparing rescue plans and ensuring the participation of technical personnel in rescue flights.

The appeal was issued by organisations including the Nepal Engineers’ Association, Nepal Hydropower Association, Nepal Tunnelling Association, Independent Power Producers’ Association Nepal, Society of Consulting Architectural and Engineering Firms Nepal, Nepal Micro Hydropower Development Association and BTI Tradesmen Association.

The organisations said they were ready to coordinate with the government and contribute technical expertise to ongoing rescue and relief efforts.

title.rendered: In flood-hit Betrawati, even the dead are difficult to bring home

content.rendered:
Betrawati, August 30

When Biwash Shrestha and Bishwas Shrestha arrived in Betrawati on the day after the flood, they were looking for their parents.

The two brothers, who live in Kathmandu for work, had rushed to the settlement after learning that their 72-year-old father and 65-year-old mother had been swept away. They knew the chances of finding them alive were slim, but they still hoped they would.

Instead, they found themselves searching through mud and debris for their parents.

On Friday, they were informed by locals that their mother’s body had been found near their home. But even then, bringing her back proved difficult.

“We came after locals informed us that they had seen our mother’s body. But we could not retrieve it,” Bibash said from Keraghari, where the brothers had been staying about two hours uphill from Betrawati. “The administration has not come for rescue. There is no one left in the village.”

The brothers had tried to reach their home as soon as they arrived in Betrawati, but thick mud blocked their way.

“We moved towards our house as soon as we reached Betrawati to look for our mother, but we could not get there because of the mud. So we came back and stayed in Keraghari,” Bibash said.

They returned to Betrawati early the following morning. The body was still difficult to recover.

“On the fourth day (August 29), we retrieved our mother’s body ourselves,” he said. “We performed her last rites yesterday. My heart is still crying. I haven’t been able to sleep.”

For the brothers, recovering their mother was only part of what they had to confront. The flood had destroyed much of the settlement, leaving very few people behind.

“There were only four or five of us. The entire settlement has been swept away. There was hardly anyone to attend the funeral,” Bibash said.

His uncles and a cousin helped with the funeral, while another local resident brought firewood. But the flood had also destroyed the places where funerals were traditionally held.

“The river is now flowing where our house used to be. There is no road to take the body elsewhere. We could not cremate her on someone else’s land, so we did it in front of our own house and washed the place with river water,” Bibash said.

There was no house left in which the brothers could perform the mourning rituals, so they returned to Kathmandu.

The brothers began the mourning rituals for their mother in Kathmandu on Sunday. They also brought their uncle with them because, otherwise, he would have been left alone in the devastated settlement. Thier father is still missing.

Bodies remain as residents flee

The Shrestha brothers’ experience reflects a wider difficulty in Betrawati, where recovering bodies and performing funerals has become increasingly difficult as the settlement has been largely emptied by the disaster.

“Many people were swept away. The fear of the flood is still there. There are no houses to live in. Those who survived have scattered,” said local resident Narayanlal Dangol. “Bodies lying here and there in the river have started to smell.”

When an Onlinekhabar team reached Betrawati on the afternoon of the day after the flood, local resident Ashish Tamang was involved in rescue efforts.

Tamang had recovered his sister-in-law’s body from near the Betrawati clock tower and brought it to higher ground. But there was no one available to take the body away.

“When we informed the police, they did not come. They said they would come, but we did not know when,” he said.

His sister-in-law had worked at the NIC Asia Bank branch near the clock tower. While other employees managed to escape, she was caught in the floodwaters.

Her husband, Navaraj Tamang, arrived the following day and took the body for cremation.

“Her husband came and took the body. He took it to Keraghari the next day and performed the last rites,” said Dangol.

According to Dangol, the settlement, once densely populated, now has very few people left.

“It used to be a densely populated settlement. Now there are no houses. People have been swept away and there is still fear of another flood,” he said. “In almost every house—this one, that one, the house across and the one below—someone has been swept away.”

Local resident Yogesh Dangol said some families had lost every member, leaving no one to perform their last rites.

“In some houses, everyone has been swept away. We do not know who will perform their last rites,” he said.

The exact number of families in which all members are missing has not yet been established.

“They have all been swept away. Who will even report them as missing? I saw people being swept away with my own eyes. My legs are still shaking,” Yogesh said.

He estimated that more than 1,000 people lived in the settlement, which had more than 200 households, although no official figure is available.

“The settlement has become like a deserted cremation ground. It is in mourning. We are speechless,” Dangol said.

Those who survived have also been scattered, with many left without homes or food.

“Some have gone to Keraghari, some to Gerku and some to the district headquarters. They have gone wherever they have relatives. Some have come to Kathmandu,” said local resident Indramaya Dangol.

Residents say they were not prepared for the scale of the flood

Residents say they received warnings that flooding was coming, but did not receive information about the scale and severity of the disaster.

Bibash said the lack of a clear warning contributed to the loss of life.

“They should have told us how big the flood was going to be. For people here, floods were considered normal, so no one could have imagined this,” he said.

“If they had told us that Syafrubesi, Chilime, Timure and this place would also be swept away and that nothing would remain, this kind of loss would not have happened.”

Bodies swept downstream by the flood remain scattered around Betrawati, according to locals.

But with most residents displaced, there are few people left to recover them. Locals also say government rescue teams have yet to reach many areas.

“An APF team came on the afternoon of the third day. They did not bring relief supplies. They came with a dog and walked around. Then there was a rumour that another flood was coming, so they left without carrying out a rescue,” Dangol said.

“The smell is spreading because of the human bodies and dead animals. We are waiting for the government.”

title.rendered: Man survives flood by jumping from bus, but wife and fellow villagers missing

content.rendered:
Gorkha, August 30

When he saw several cargo containers turning back shortly after Galchhi in Dhading, 70-year-old Badriprasad Devkota began to sense that something was wrong. He had also heard rumours of flooding in the Trishuli River, leaving him increasingly worried.

Devkota, a resident of Naukhore in Palungtar Municipality-5, Gorkha, said there had been no visible sign of flooding in the Trishuli at that point. The river appeared normal, and other vehicles were continuing along the road. Assuming there was no immediate danger, the bus he was travelling on also continued its journey.

The driver gradually began increasing the vehicle’s speed. Before reaching Bhaisey, fellow passenger Baburam Devkota asked the driver to stop so he could relieve himself, but the bus did not stop. Instead, it began moving even faster.

As the bus continued, the driver suddenly spotted a massive wave approaching from upstream. He slowed down, apparently intending to turn the bus around. Baburam managed to jump from the bus, followed shortly afterwards by another passenger, Tularam Devkota.

Badriprasad became increasingly terrified. “I was sitting in a seat behind the driver. I looked through the upper window to see what was happening and saw a wave so enormous that it seemed to cover the whole world,” he said. Believing there was little chance of survival, he too decided to jump from the moving bus.

He rose from his seat and grabbed an overhead bar. A pile of bags was blocking the door. As he tried to climb over them, his wife, who was sitting beside him, grabbed his hand and pleaded with him not to jump. But at that moment, he said, he could think of nothing except escaping from the bus. He managed to free his hand and jumped from the moving vehicle. Moments later, the bus stalled and came to a stop.

Just then, the first wave struck the bus. The muddy floodwaters knocked Badriprasad, who was running for safety, into a drain. The wave briefly subsided, giving him a chance to get up and run. He eventually grabbed the branch of a small tree. “My younger brother Tularam was holding onto the same tree. The two of us clung to it,” he said.

Before their eyes, the flood swept the bus away. “We watched as the bus was carried away by the current. It was completely submerged and never came back up. My wife was inside, along with others. I loved them, but there was nothing I could do,” Badriprasad said, breaking down in tears.

The survivors then began searching for safer ground. Further uphill, they met fellow passengers Rabindra Devkota and Parbati Neupane. “The floodwaters had thrown them aside. They were covered in mud and looked like logs,” Badriprasad said.

The bus assistant, who had also managed to escape, later joined them. After finding one another, they broke down in tears and spent some time comforting each other. Meanwhile, the flooding continued, roaring down from upstream with tremendous force. They remained there for around two hours, waiting for rescue, but no one arrived. After more than two hours, they saw a helicopter in the sky, but they were not rescued.

“People on rooftops across the river were raising their hands and crying for help,” Badriprasad said. “Before our eyes, the flood swept them away along with their homes.” With no rescue in sight, the survivors continued on their own. By the time they reached Hilekharka, they were in a desperate condition. There, they received a cup of tea and some biscuits, although they did not know who had provided them.

They were later taken by vehicle to Suryagadhi Rural Municipality, where they received first aid for injuries sustained while escaping. On Friday, they were taken to Kathmandu via Hetauda and Kulekhani. Tularam, who also survived by jumping from the bus, expressed anger over what he described as the state’s failure in rescue and disaster response. He said the lack of timely warnings had contributed to the scale of the tragedy.

“If vehicles had been stopped at the Trishuli crossing as soon as information about the flood was received, perhaps such a huge loss could have been avoided. We would not have had to witness piles of bodies today,” he said. Although he survived, Tularam became emotional as he spoke about being unable to save his wife and the others travelling with him. “I survived, but my wife is gone, and my whole community has been devastated,” he said through tears. “My sisters-in-law and daughters-in-law were sent with me believing they would be safe, but I could not save anyone.”

He said they only realised the scale of the flood after the water reached their vehicle. He had returned to the area hoping to find his wife, relatives and neighbours who were swept away by the flood, but found no trace of them. The bus, carrying pilgrims from Palungtar to Gosainkunda, had 38 people on board from the same village, including the driver and bus assistant. Six people managed to save their lives by jumping from the bus.

Of the remaining 32 people who lost contact, the bodies of two have been recovered, while search efforts for the others are ongoing.

title.rendered: Rescue team locates tunnel leading to workers trapped at Trishuli 3A

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

A rescue team has located a tunnel that could provide access to workers believed to be trapped inside the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project tunnel in Rasuwa.

The team, which has been conducting rescue operations continuously for the past three days, located the project’s “cable access tunnel,” according to Acting Managing Director of the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha.

Shrestha told Onlinekhabar that a joint team of the Nepali Army, NEA personnel and tunnel experts found the tunnel used to take cables out of the powerhouse.

Rescuers are now preparing to send rescue experts through the tunnel to assess the situation inside and determine whether the trapped workers can be reached.

“People can enter through this tunnel, and it can also be used to rescue those trapped inside,” Shrestha said. “We made openings to send oxygen inside yesterday, so we hope those trapped are safe. We are making efforts to rescue them as soon as possible.”

The rescue team had earlier drilled five openings to send air into the tunnel and assess conditions inside.

Lawmaker and tunnel expert Shriram Neupane, who has been leading the rescue efforts at the site, said the team had been continuing drilling operations while trying to determine the condition inside the tunnel. He also confirmed that the access tunnel had been located.

According to the NEA, rescue efforts for workers trapped inside the project tunnel began only on Friday, two days after the floods struck.

Officials had grown increasingly concerned about the workers after rescue teams were unable to gain access to the tunnel for five days.

The NEA estimates that around 40 to 42 technical personnel, including highly experienced experts, were working on the overhaul of the underground powerhouse when they became trapped inside the tunnel.

title.rendered: Indian tunnel rescue team reaches Chilime to search for trapped workers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

An Indian technical and tunnel rescue team has reached Chilime in Rasuwa to begin search and rescue operations for workers believed to be trapped inside hydropower project tunnels.

The rescue team arrived in Nepal on Saturday and reached Chilime on Sunday to begin operations.

The 11-member technical team includes doctors, paramedics and tunnel engineers. A separate 22-member Indian Army team has also been deployed to support the rescue operation.

The initial team has already conducted an aerial reconnaissance of the Chilime and Langtang areas by helicopter. It has now begun operations focused on Chilime in Rasuwa and Trishuli in Nuwakot.

The team is working to rescue workers trapped inside tunnels of hydropower projects in the Chilime and Trishuli areas following devastating floods and landslides in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers.

The tunnels have been filled with thick mud, sludge, rocks and debris carried by the floods and landslides, making it extremely difficult for rescuers to enter.

According to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the Indian experts have begun working with an 82-member joint security team comprising personnel from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force. They are using specialised equipment to clear the tunnels and rescue those trapped inside.

The 22.1-megawatt Chilime Hydropower Project has suffered extensive damage from the floods and landslides.

Around 20 employees and workers associated with the project have been reported missing. Authorities estimate that six to eight workers are trapped inside the project’s powerhouse and tunnels, prompting the joint Nepal-India rescue operation.

The project’s structures have been buried under flood debris, while thick mud and sludge have filled the tunnel passages.

Power generation from the Chilime project has been completely halted due to the extensive damage to its infrastructure.

The flood also damaged the substation at the Trishuli-3B hub, which connects Chilime and other hydropower projects, disrupting the electricity transmission system in the area.

Along with the rescue teams, the Indian government has also handed over relief supplies to the Nepal government, including portable generators, food, water purification tablets and medicines.

title.rendered: Teaching Hospital nears capacity, only 10 more bodies fit

content.rendered:
Bodies of those who lost their lives in the devastating Bhotekoshi flood are continuing to be found in large numbers.

Meanwhile, the mortuary at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj, Kathmandu, is nearly full. According to Dr Gopal Chaudhary, a forensic expert at the hospital, 60 bodies from the Rasuwa flood have been brought in so far.

Of these, 8 have been identified, while postmortems are underway for 28. Dr Chaudhary said the mortuary can now accommodate a maximum of 10 more bodies.

“Our capacity is 150. 80 were already here before this, bodies whose identities hadn’t yet been established,” he said. “What we can still accommodate now is 70.”

He said that once 10 more bodies arrive, the hospital’s capacity will be full.

Dr Chaudhary has suggested that the relevant authorities move forward with a process for temporary body storage.

“A location needs to be identified through a proper process for temporary storage of bodies. This needs to happen at the government level,” he said.

He also said that most of the bodies brought in from the flood have arrived in a decomposed and severely damaged condition.

He noted that even keeping such bodies in refrigeration doesn’t solve the identification problem.

“There’s no point in just storing the bodies. The appropriate solution is burial. Keeping decomposed bodies in a freezer doesn’t help either,” he said. “The bodies coming in now are severely damaged. Most cannot be identified.”

title.rendered: Nepalis stranded in Kerung will be brought home via alternative route: Foreign Minister Khanal

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 30

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has said the Nepali people stranded in Kerung, China, due to the Bhotekoshi flash flood would be brought to Nepal via an alternative route. Foreign Minister Khanal said preliminary information was received that 1,000 Nepalis were said to be stranded in Kerung since the disaster.

So, they would be brought to Nepal via an alternative route, he added. The Minister said it during an inspection visit to the disaster-hit area at Dhunge of Bidur Municipality-1 today. He further informed RSS that the government had requested the Chinese side to resume the Tatopani check post (Sindhupalchowk) and Korala check post (Mustang) to ease cross-border movement and transport between the two countries.

The government had requested Chinese and Indian technical experts after it realised the need for foreign assistance to rescue those trapped inside the hydropower tunnels, he made it clear. “In case of further need, the assistance can be received from other countries as well. The international community has made a commitment to assistance. So, the assistance will be accepted based on need,” he explained.

title.rendered: Department conducts technical study of road washed away at Krishna Bhir

content.rendered:
The Department of Roads has begun a technical study of the road that collapsed at Krishna Bhir, along the Muglin-Kathmandu road section.

The road caved in after the river eroded it at Krishna Bhir, located in Dhading’s Benighat Rorang Rural Municipality. Because of this, Department Director General Dr Bijay Jaishi said technical experts are visiting the site today to study the area. Work to reopen the road will begin based on the recommendations of that team.

The road caved in after the protective wall built along the riverbank was eroded, leaving the Muglin-Kathmandu road completely blocked.

“For one thing, this is already a geologically complex area,” he told Onlinekhabar. “On top of that, since the river continues to erode from below, we’ll make our decision after a risk assessment.”

Following the August 26 flood, the Prithvi Highway had been blocked when the Galchhi area was submerged. Just two days after the blockage at Galchhi was cleared and the highway reopened, the Prithvi Highway has now been blocked again.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood death toll reaches 768; 160 injured discharged

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

The bodies of 768 people who died in the floods triggered by the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa have been recovered.

According to Nepal Police, 768 bodies had been recovered as of 2 pm Sunday.

The highest number of bodies, 264, were recovered in Chitwan. Similarly, 194 were recovered in East Nawalparasi, 100 in West Nawalparasi, 58 in Gorkha, 52 in Nuwakot, 50 in Dhading, 37 in Tanahun and 13 in Rasuwa.

Police said a total of 2,715 injured people, and others have been rescued so far.

Meanwhile, 160 injured people have been discharged from various hospitals in Kathmandu Valley after receiving treatment.

title.rendered: Only one bridge left to reach Dhunche, traffic piles up (Photos)

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, August 30

Since last Wednesday’s flood in the Bhotekoshi River washed away the main road connecting Rasuwa, reaching the Rasuwa district headquarters has become extremely difficult.

An alternative route from Kathmandu to Dhunche has been opened via Tokha–Chhahare–Gadkhar Bridge–Aapra–Narja–Lachyang–Sarmathali–Patikharka–Bogtitar–Kalikasthan. Within Rasuwa alone, on this side of the Miteri Bridge, the flood has completely swept away 13 bridges. Two bridges on the Nuwakot-Rasuwa border were also destroyed, cutting the district off from the road network.

The Pung Khola bridge has become the only remaining link connecting the Rasuwa district headquarters, Dhunche, to the transportation network. This bridge falls within Naikunda Rural Municipality.

Since it is a single-lane dirt road, travel is quite difficult. Many small vehicles can currently be seen heading toward Dhunche via this route, and there is heavy traffic congestion on the road.

Cargo vehicles and other small vehicles are also travelling toward Dhunche along this same road.

title.rendered: Alternative route ensures fuel and LPG supply to Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) has said there will be no disruption to the supply of essential goods, petroleum products and cooking gas to Kathmandu despite the closure of the main highway into the capital.

The announcement comes after the Muglin-Kathmandu road section was completely blocked when the Trishuli River eroded the road near Krishnabhir in Benighat Rorang Rural Municipality, Dhading, raising concerns about possible shortages of essential goods.

Immediately after the highway was blocked, the corporation began making arrangements to transport petroleum products and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) to Kathmandu through an alternative route.

NOC Executive Director Nagendra Sah said fuel would be transported to Kathmandu via the alternative route through Makwanpur (Hetauda).

“We are transporting fuel and gas through the Makwanpur route,” Sah said. “Most LPG plants are located in the Tarai, so we will load gas there and bring it to Kathmandu via the alternative route.”

According to Sah, the Amlekhgunj depot is the main backup for fuel supplies. Since oil is delivered directly to the depot through a pipeline, there will be no shortage of petroleum products in Kathmandu, he said.

“We can receive as much oil as needed through the pipeline. From there, we will transport it using 20-kilolitre and 12-kilolitre tankers operated by private transporters and dealers,” he said. “There may be a delay of an hour or two in the supply chain because of the road conditions, but there will be no disruption to supplies.”

The corporation said most tankers that had been held up due to continuous rainfall in recent days entered Kathmandu on Saturday, so there will be no immediate shortage of fuel in the market.

Amid concerns that the road closure could lead to fuel shortages, the corporation urged consumers not to panic.

“Supplies are continuing smoothly, and we have already made alternative arrangements,” Sah said. “We urge everyone to remain assured.”

The government is studying options to reopen the blocked road.

title.rendered: Five openings drilled to reach workers trapped inside Trishuli 3A tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

A rescue team has drilled five openings in an effort to send air into the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project, where dozens of employees are believed to be trapped following the devastating floods in Rasuwa.

According to lawmaker and tunnel expert Shriram Neupane, the rescue team has so far been drilling openings and trying to assess the situation inside the tunnel.

Neupane, who is at the rescue site, is leading the effort.

“We are using excavators to dig and locate the tunnel slab, but we have encountered rock while digging,” Neupane told Onlinekhabar. “If there is not much rock, we should be able to locate the slab soon. Otherwise, we are also considering using explosives to try to enter the tunnel.”

The rescue operation is being carried out by teams from the Nepali Army, Nepal Electricity Authority and other tunnel experts, Neupane said.

According to Nepal Electricity Authority engineer Suraj Dahal, if an opening large enough for one or two people can be created, Nepali Army rescue experts will enter to assess the situation inside.

“If we find that mud has not entered the tunnel, we will send more rescuers inside and try to bring the trapped workers out one by one,” Dahal said.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said the rescue operation at the project tunnel began only on Friday, two days after the floods struck.

Officials have expressed growing concern for the workers trapped inside as rescue teams have been unable to break through the tunnel even after five days of efforts.

The authority estimates that around 40 to 42 technical personnel, including highly experienced experts, were working on the overhaul of the underground powerhouse when they became trapped inside the project tunnel.

title.rendered: Nepal Telecom extends free services until further notice

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Nepal Telecom has decided to continue with free voice, data and SMS services it had earlier announced for the areas affected by the floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems until further notice.

Prior to this, the company had announced free voice call service, 2GB data and 50 SMS per day till August 30. According to NT spokesperson Kamal Lamichhane, such services were expanded to facilitate the relief and rescue operations in the affected areas.

People in the flood-hit areas have been urged to use the services on a need basis. The disasters caused damage to various telecom physical infrastructures, so the technical teams are at work to regularise telecommunication services as soon as possible in the areas, it is said.

The company said that most of the damaged structures in the flood-affected areas have been reinstated, and efforts are underway to operate the remaining structures as early as possible.

title.rendered: Parents of 6-year-old rescued alive after 60 hours in Rasuwa located

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

The parents of the six-year-old girl who was rescued alive after being trapped under debris for 60 hours in Rasuwa have been located and are receiving treatment, the Armed Police Force (APF) said.

The girl, identified as six-year-old Manisha, was rescued by a team from the APF’s Timure Border Outpost after rescuers heard what sounded like a child crying from beneath the mud.

According to APF spokesperson DIG Netra Bahadur Karki, Manisha’s mother, Gita, has been identified as an employee of Global IME Bank in Timure.

Manisha’s parents also survived the flood and told security personnel that they were thrown against a wall by the force of the floodwaters, which helped them survive.

Manisha’s health condition later deteriorated, and she was brought to Kathmandu for treatment. Her parents are also receiving treatment at the same hospital.

The parents have been informed that their daughter was found alive 60 hours after the flood.

According to Karki, most of Manisha’s body, except for her head, was buried under mud. A wooden structure had fallen over her, preventing her head from being completely buried. Rescuers heard her cries from underneath the structure and began digging, eventually rescuing her alive.

The APF team had initially provided her with first aid at the Timure Border Outpost. She was kept there overnight before being airlifted by an Army helicopter to Dhunche.

Nine APF personnel stationed at the same border outpost remain missing following the disaster.

The six-year-old was rescued on Friday evening from under the debris in Timure of Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-2, Rasuwa. The rescue team had been conducting search operations in the area when they heard her crying beneath the mud.

She was found in a critical and unconscious condition and was taken to the Timure border security post, where rescuers kept her warm and provided initial treatment.

Another team of Chinese tunnel rescue experts has arrived in Nepal and begun work to rescue people believed to be trapped inside tunnels in flood-hit Rasuwa.

The Chinese Embassy in Nepal said the team arrived in Nepal on Sunday morning and has already started rescue efforts at tunnels in Rasuwa.

The latest team joins a Chinese expert team that arrived in Nepal earlier and has already begun rescue operations.

China’s Ministry of Emergency Management had earlier dispatched five tunnel experts to Nepal at the request of the Nepali government to support rescue efforts at the Upper Trishuli 3 ‘B’ Hydropower Project tunnel. An additional four experts were also dispatched to provide further support.

The Chinese experts are working alongside Nepali rescue teams as authorities continue efforts to reach people trapped inside tunnels affected by the floods.

The devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems caused extensive loss of life and property in Rasuwa. Several people are believed to have been trapped inside tunnels following the disaster.

The specialised Chinese teams have been brought in to support the technically challenging rescue operation.

The Nepal LP Gas Industry Association has decided to provide 1,250 filled gas cylinders as relief for citizens affected by the devastating flood.

He said the association extended this support, recognising that disaster is not one person’s problem alone but a shared responsibility for everyone, keeping in mind the immediate needs and hardships of the affected citizens.

The 1,250 filled LP gas cylinders provided by the association will be distributed to the targeted groups through the Nepal Oil Corporation.

The association expressed sorrow over the loss of life and property in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and other districts caused by the devastating flood that struck the Bhotekoshi River on the morning of the 10th of Bhadra.

title.rendered: Alternative route reopens road to Dhadingbesi

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Road connectivity to Dhadingbesi, the headquarters of Dhading district, has been restored via an alternative route after the floods in Rasuwa swept away the Furke Khola bridge.

Following the destruction of the Furke Khola bridge, an alternative road has been opened via Mastar and Kuringtar, using the bridge over the Trishuli River and the road along its right bank to reach Dhadingbesi.

According to Sanjay Nepal, chief of the Federal Road Supervision Office in Kathmandu, road connectivity with the district headquarters was disrupted after the flood washed away the Furke Khola bridge.

He said an alternative route had subsequently been opened from Mastar through Kuringtar, using the bridge over the Trishuli River and the road along the river’s right bank to connect with Dhadingbesi.

“After the flood swept away the Furke Khola bridge connecting Dhadingbesi, our road connection with the district headquarters was disrupted. We have since been working to establish an alternative route to Dhadingbesi from Mastar via Kuringtar, using the bridge over the Trishuli River and the road on the right bank,” he said.

According to Nepal, small vehicles have now started operating to Dhadingbesi. However, work is underway to make the road suitable for larger vehicles by placing gravel on sections damaged by the floods and covered with mud and silt.

“Most of the work has now been completed. Machines were deployed from Friday. Road connectivity has been restored to the extent that small vehicles can now reach Dhadingbesi via this route. Efforts are underway to make the route more accessible,” he added.

He said stones had been arranged at stream crossings and other waterlogged sections to allow vehicles to pass.

Although some sections of the road remain in normal condition, he said vehicle movement remains difficult in areas washed away by the floods.

“We are placing gravel on difficult sections to make the route easier for small vehicles. Where streams cross the road, and culverts may be needed, we are arranging stones so that vehicles can pass safely,” he said. “Some sections require gravel. If a nearby source of gravel is available, we will use it to fill muddy and silt-covered sections and facilitate vehicle movement.”

He said two machines, along with a technical team from the Road Division Office, Nuwakot, have been deployed to put the alternative road into operation.

title.rendered: Immediate reopening of Furke Khola bridge unlikely after flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

The road connecting Kathmandu and Dhadingbesi through Furke Khola is unlikely to reopen immediately after the bridge over the river was swept away by floods, the Department of Roads said.

The department is exploring alternative routes to Dhadingbesi after the flood destroyed the bridge over Furke Khola, a key crossing on the route to Dhading district headquarters.

Department of Roads Director General Dr Bijay Jaisi said it would be difficult to install a Bailey bridge at the site immediately.

Inspecting the damaged bridge, Jaisi said officials were assessing whether a Bailey bridge could be installed to resume traffic. However, the length of the bridge and the condition of its piers pose significant challenges.

The department is studying the possibility of using a Bailey bridge as a temporary measure. However, Jaisi said one of the bridge’s piers had been swept away, and the available Bailey bridges may not be long enough to span the river.

The department is also examining other options to restore the crossing. Jaisi said a technical team would be deployed to carry out detailed measurements of the damaged structure.

“We are also sending a technical team to take exact measurements. If possible, our plan was to install a Bailey bridge and resume traffic immediately. But after the site inspection, it appears that a long-span Bailey bridge is not currently available here,” he said.

“Even if we connect short-span Bailey bridges to the piers on both sides, the required length appears to be greater than the Bailey bridges available to us. Therefore, it does not appear possible to install a Bailey bridge immediately,” he added.

According to Jaisi, the department is considering constructing a new deck using the existing structures or building a new bridge connected to the existing one.

Two options are currently under discussion.

Under the first option, the existing structures could be retained and a new deck constructed over them, potentially as a permanent structure.

The second option involves constructing a new bridge connected to the existing structure.

If neither option is feasible, an entirely new bridge may have to be constructed, Jaisi said. The department will begin the necessary process for a permanent bridge after completing the technical assessment.

“We will be able to say clearly how many days it will take and how traffic can be resumed after the technical assessment. This bridge has to be rebuilt. We will conduct the necessary technical study and make a decision soon to move ahead with the construction process,” he said.

Meanwhile, traffic has been diverted through an alternative route following the destruction of the bridge.

Jaisi said the bridge towards Mastar remains safe, allowing the road between Furke Khola and Mastar to be used as an alternative route.

title.rendered: Starlink offers free internet to flood-hit areas in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Elon Musk’s satellite-based internet company Starlink has offered to provide free internet services in areas affected by the devastating floods along the Nepal-China border.

Expressing deep sadness over the disaster, Starlink said it was ready to support the Nepal government and humanitarian agencies involved in relief and rescue efforts.

In a message posted on X on Saturday, the company said it was prepared to send Starlink equipment and provide free internet services as soon as it receives the necessary approval from the Nepali authorities.

“We are ready to send Starlink equipment and provide free service to the Government of Nepal and humanitarian partners as soon as we receive permission,” the company said.

Why is Starlink important during a disaster?

Starlink said its satellite-based communication service could be particularly valuable in areas where floods and landslides have destroyed roads, bridges and conventional mobile networks.

The company said the service could help rescue teams coordinate search operations for missing people, while also supporting health workers and medical teams treating those injured in the disaster.

It could also allow families in affected areas to communicate with relatives and loved ones who may have been cut off from communication networks.

How does Starlink work?

According to Starlink, its equipment can be set up and connected to high-speed internet within minutes of being taken out of the box.

The service requires two basic conditions: a power supply and a clear view of the sky for the equipment to connect to Starlink’s satellites.

The offer comes as rescue and relief operations continue in flood-hit areas along the Nepal-China border, where damage to transport and communication infrastructure has hampered response efforts.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa urges government to seek foreign help for rescue efforts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Nepali Congress President and leader of the main opposition Gagan Thapa has said the government should not hesitate to seek foreign assistance for rescue operations in tunnels, as domestic expertise alone appears insufficient.

Thapa made the remarks during a discussion held on Sunday at the Nepali Congress central office in Sanepa, Lalitpur, attended by party office bearers, central committee members and other stakeholders.

“We have received information that rescue operations in the tunnel cannot be carried out with our available expertise alone. After learning this, I contacted the foreign minister and urged him to seek assistance from other countries,” Thapa said.

He said it was natural to seek assistance from neighbouring and other countries during a disaster.

The Nepali Congress has decided to extend full support to the government during natural disasters, including floods, landslides and inundation, while also drawing attention to weaknesses in rescue and relief operations.

Thapa said supporting the government during a disaster is the duty of an opposition party, adding that pointing out gaps and shortcomings in the government’s response is not criticism but a form of assistance.

Emphasising the important role of local governments in disaster management, Thapa urged the federal government to coordinate with local authorities.

He argued that effective disaster management would not be possible by bypassing local governments. As the country remains in mourning and thousands of citizens have been affected, Thapa directed all levels of the party not to organise public celebrations or events.

He stressed that the party’s entire focus should now be on rescue efforts and the collection and distribution of relief supplies. “We can observe festivals such as Haritalika Teej in a normal manner, but I urge everyone not to organise public celebrations or extravagant events,” he said.

A disaster management team led by Thapa is scheduled to leave on Monday to inspect the directly affected areas and coordinate relief efforts. He said the team would provide further suggestions to the government and press the government for action based on information gathered from the field.

title.rendered: No shelter, no contact, no answers for Betrawati’s flood survivors

content.rendered:
No home to live in. No contact with family members. Only a faint hope that they might return. Locals of Betrawati are still searching, hoping to find a relative. Their bodies are caked in sand and mud. They have no clothes to change into.

When we arrived in the evening of August 27, those displaced by the Betrawati flood in Nuwakot were still searching for shelter.

“Yesterday we went and stayed at Keraghari. Today too, we’ll go there again,” says Indra Maya Dangol.

As evening fell, a group of 15–20 people set out for Keraghari, three hours away from Betrawati.

The Dangol family alone had more than 100 households in Betrawati. The flood swept away some; some are still reachable, and there’s no confirmed count. But on the day the flood hit, on August 26, around 50 people went to stay overnight at Keraghari. On the second day, about 30 stayed.

“Some left, saying they wouldn’t stay here and headed toward Kathmandu. Some have gone toward Bidur. We’re staying here because we have nowhere else to go,” Dangol says. “We’re sleeping under the open sky.”

More than shelter, she is worried about her son. Her son, seriously injured in the flood, was rescued and taken to Kathmandu.

“It’s been three days. I heard he’s being treated at the trauma centre. I haven’t been able to talk to him; the phone doesn’t connect,” she says, praying for his recovery.

Everyone who survived by fleeing has lost someone or something. Some are injured.

“We had more than 100 households. Whoever you see here now, that’s all that’s left. There’s no one else,” says Narayan Lal Dangol. “Some are said to be still in the jungle, but we haven’t been able to reach them. Most have been swept away.”

Betrawati had been preparing to celebrate Gai Jatra and Janai Purnima grandly today. But the flood left them homeless instead.

“We had prepared for a big festival procession. But now this place looks like a cremation ghat. We’re taking shelter in a villager’s house,” said Yogesh Dangol. “Just look at the state we’ve had to live in today.”

Even those who found shelter in a villager’s home remain haunted by memories of the flood.

“I can’t sleep. The moment I close my eyes, that’s all I remember. I couldn’t sleep last night either. How I escaped, how I got here, I don’t know. I can barely even walk,” Dangol says.

Resident Suna Tamang has been feeding the displaced morning and evening.

“On the first day there were 50–60 people. The gas ran out. I’ve been cooking over an open fire to feed them,” she said. “Everyone’s eyes are full of tears. Those who survived such suffering had to be fed.”

Since the flood buried everything, the displaced don’t even have food supplies of their own.

“There’s no house at all. Where would food supplies be? We don’t know how we’ll survive. For those who lived, it’s one hardship piled on another,” says Narayan Lal Dangol. “Relief is urgently needed here.”

The displaced are forced to spend the night in the courtyard of Suna Tamang’s house. They urgently need temporary shelter.

“We don’t know where to go tomorrow, where to stay. Will the government even look after us now that we’re homeless? The government hasn’t come here yet,” Indramaya says.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

A lake formed following a landslide in the Nepal-China border area is approximately the size of 14 football fields, according to Chinese media.

Chinese state broadcaster CGTN reported that monitoring conducted by the Anneng Group through August 29 found that the landslide-dammed lake covers an area of approximately 100,000 square metres.

Following the severe flooding on August 26, Chinese authorities have been continuously studying and monitoring the area for potential additional risks.

title.rendered: Was the Rasuwa flood really beyond prediction? What experts and studies say

content.rendered:
The devastating flood that swept through Rasuwa on August 26 has raised questions about whether such an event could have been anticipated.

While experts say it is generally impossible to predict the exact date, location or scale of many mountain disasters, decades of research have identified areas and conditions where the risks are higher.

Studies have repeatedly warned that Nepal’s glaciers, glacial lakes, landslides and downstream settlements require continuous monitoring and effective early-warning systems.

The Rasuwa disaster, however, has also highlighted an important limitation: monitoring glacial lakes alone may not be enough to understand all the hazards originating in the high mountains.

What experts had warned about

Environmental journalist Ramesh Bhusal says recent disasters across Nepal and the wider Himalayan region show that extreme mountain events can no longer simply be treated as unforeseeable.

Floods and debris-flow disasters have occurred in places including the Seti River in Pokhara, Melamchi, Roshi and Thame, as well as in other parts of the Himalayan region, including Uttarakhand, Pakistan and northeastern India.

“When similar events occur three times within five years, calling them unimaginable simply means we failed to anticipate them,” Bhusal says.

Experts estimate that around 83 percent of Nepal’s mountainous and hilly areas are exposed to risks associated with landslides and glacial lake outburst floods.

Disaster forecasting has evolved significantly over time. Researchers now use rainfall and river-gauge data, satellite imagery, remote sensing, geological studies and other technologies to identify areas exposed to different hazards. Artificial intelligence is also increasingly being explored as a tool for forecasting and risk assessment.

But forecasting a hazard does not necessarily mean predicting the exact moment when a disaster will occur.

Why glacial lakes are monitored

A glacial lake forms when water accumulates in or around a glacier, often behind a natural dam made of ice, rock or debris.

If the natural dam fails, a large volume of water can suddenly move downstream. This is known as a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF).

Such floods can travel long distances through mountain valleys, carrying rocks, sediment and debris and damaging settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and other infrastructure downstream.

Geography professor Dr Narendra Raj Khanal, who has studied glacial lakes and floods, says researchers have repeatedly highlighted the need for regular glacier monitoring and functioning early-warning systems.

“We may not be able to say that a particular glacial lake will burst on a particular date or that a landslide will occur at a particular location,” Khanal says. “But based on our studies, we have consistently said that regular monitoring of glaciers and the establishment and operation of early warning systems are essential.”

Which glacial lakes pose a risk?

A study by professors Narendra Raj Khanal, Pradeep Kumar Mool, Arun Bhakta Shrestha, Golam Rasul, Pawan Kumar Ghimire, Rajendra Bahadur Shrestha and Sharad Prasad Joshi assessed the potential human impact of glacial lake outburst floods.

According to an article published in the International Journal of Water Resources Development, a GLOF from Lumuchimi in the Bhote Koshi basin could potentially affect 16,313 people.

The study estimated that an outburst from Imja in the Dudh Koshi basin could affect 7,762 people, while an outburst from Tsho Rolpa in the Tamakoshi basin could affect 5,183 people.

A separate study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) also highlighted the potential danger posed by glacial lakes to downstream communities and infrastructure.

“Glacial lake outburst floods are an important problem for people living in the Himalayan region,” the 2020 report said, noting that lakes at high elevations can generate floods capable of travelling long distances downstream.

The report identified potentially dangerous glacial lakes as an important target for risk-reduction planning.

47 potentially dangerous lakes identified

The ICIMOD-UNDP study assessed 3,624 glacial lakes across Nepal’s Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins and identified 47 as potentially dangerous. Of these, 25 are in China, 21 in Nepal and one in India. The Koshi basin accounts for 42 of the potentially dangerous lakes, while three are in the Gandaki basin and two in the Karnali basin.

In Nepal, the potentially dangerous lakes are spread across several river systems, including four in the Tamor basin, five in the Arun, nine in the Dudh Koshi, one in the Trishuli, one in Mugu and one in the Tamakoshi basin. In China, 13 are located in the Arun basin, seven in the Tamakoshi, four in the Sunkoshi and one in the Trishuli basin. The remaining lake is located in India’s Kali (Mahakali) basin.

The study identified six lakes as being at particularly high risk: Tsho Rolpa, Lower Barun, Imja Tsho, Lumding, West Chamjang and Dona (Thulagi).

Why the Rasuwa flood is different

Experts now say the Rasuwa flood was not a conventional glacial lake outburst flood.

According to Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel, who is also the government spokesperson, glaciers appear to have collapsed, causing water to surge downstream while carrying large amounts of sediment.

Experts believe the flooding in the Bhote Koshi was triggered by the collapse of an ice-rock formation near the Lhende River, which flows from China.

This distinction matters because a GLOF and a glacier or ice-rock collapse can produce different warning signals and require different monitoring approaches.

Professor Khanal says the Rasuwa disaster has demonstrated that focusing only on glacial lakes leaves an important gap in understanding high-mountain hazards.

“The Rasuwa flood has sent a message that studying only glacial lakes is not sufficient,” Khanal says. “It appears that forecasting such risks requires detailed study of glaciers, snow and ice alongside glacial lakes.”

Why glaciers, snow and ice matter

Glacial lakes are only one component of a much larger mountain system.

Changes in glaciers, snow and ice can affect the stability of slopes and river systems. A collapse involving ice and rock can generate a sudden surge of water, sediment and debris even when there is no glacial lake outburst.

This means that risk assessments need to consider the entire chain of possible hazards—from changes in glaciers and snow to ice or rock collapse, debris flows and downstream flooding.

The Rasuwa disaster has therefore raised the question of whether Nepal’s existing monitoring systems are broad enough to capture these interconnected risks.

Can scientists predict exactly when a disaster will happen?

Not usually. Scientists can identify hazards, assess the likelihood of certain events, monitor changes and estimate which communities and infrastructure could be exposed.

But that is different from predicting that a particular glacier will collapse on a particular day or that a particular landslide will occur at a precise location.

This distinction is particularly important in the Himalayas, where terrain is difficult to access and mountain conditions can change rapidly.

The objective of monitoring and early-warning systems is therefore not necessarily to predict every disaster with certainty. It is to identify dangerous changes early enough to reduce exposure and give people time to act.

Monsoon can amplify mountain hazards

Glacial and ice-related hazards can become particularly dangerous during Nepal’s monsoon season.

Nepal’s monsoon generally begins around June 13 and continues until October 2, bringing around 80 percent of the country’s annual rainfall.

Heavy rainfall can increase river levels and destabilise slopes. When intense rainfall coincides with water released from a glacial lake, glacier collapse or other high-mountain event, the resulting flood or debris flow can become significantly more destructive.

Historical records show that glacial lake outburst floods have occurred between March and September, with nearly two dozen events causing significant damage in the wider Himalayan region.

Have warnings been turned into action?

Climate analyst Dr Ngamindra Dahal says studies have repeatedly identified the risks associated with glacial lakes and high-mountain hazards, but implementation has remained limited.

“We know there is a risk. Plans have also been prepared. But those plans have not been turned into projects,” he says.

A National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority official, however, says implementing every recommendation immediately is difficult.

“Not all the glacial lakes that can affect us are within Nepal,” the official says. “Implementation requires a large amount of money, which is not easy to secure.”

The cross-border nature of many Himalayan hazards adds another layer of complexity. Several potentially dangerous glacial lakes lie outside Nepal, meaning effective risk reduction can require cooperation between countries as well as monitoring within Nepal.

What the Rasuwa disaster has taught us

The Rasuwa flood does not necessarily show that scientists should have been able to predict the exact event.

Instead, it highlights the difference between predicting a disaster and understanding disaster risk.

Researchers have already identified potentially dangerous glacial lakes, assessed the number of people who could be affected and repeatedly called for monitoring and early-warning systems.

But the Rasuwa event shows that risk assessment must extend beyond glacial lakes.

Monitoring glaciers, snow, ice, glacial lakes, slopes and rivers together may provide a more complete picture of the hazards developing in Nepal’s high mountains.

The challenge now is turning that knowledge into continuous monitoring, effective warnings and practical preparedness—particularly for communities and infrastructure located downstream.

The precise timing of the next mountain disaster may remain impossible to predict. But understanding where the risks are, how hazards can cascade and who is exposed can make the consequences far less unpredictable.

The Nepal Army has rescued 54 people by helicopter from the Timure, Syafrubesi, and Mailung areas.

title.rendered: Foreign Minister’s visit to Serbia cancelled

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, August 30

Minister for Foreign Affairs, Shisir Khanal, has cancelled his scheduled visit to Serbia in the aftermath of the August 26 devastating floods in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

He was scheduled to leave for Belgrade, the capital city of Serbia, on Sunday, leading a three-member delegation to the High-Level Commemorative Meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM). The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has confirmed the cancellation of the Minister’s visit to Serbia. The NAM Commemorative Meeting is taking place in Belgrade on August 31 and September 1.

In the absence of the Minister, a two-member delegation led by Krishna Prasad Dhakal, the Chief of the UN and the Specialised Agencies Division, MoFA, will represent Nepal at the event. Belgrade hosted the first NAM Summit in 1961, and in commemoration of the same summit, it is organising the High-Level Commemorative Meeting.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Since the flood that struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on the morning of August 27, the Nepal Army has rescued 2,650 people as of now.

According to Army Headquarters, 54 people were airlifted from Timure, Syafrubesi, and Mailung on Saturday alone, including 46 Chinese nationals and 8 Indian nationals among them. Counting other locations, 550 people were airlifted on Saturday.

In total since the flood, the Army has rescued 2,650 people, 200 via ground rescue and 2,450 via air rescue. Among those rescued are 121 Indian nationals, 4 German nationals, 72 Chinese nationals, 2 American nationals, 2 Italian nationals, 1 Omani national, and 15 Korean nationals; the rest are Nepali citizens.

8,300 army personnel have been deployed for the rescue effort.

The Nepal Red Cross Society will provide free blood for the treatment of people injured in the floods.

Nepal Red Cross Society Chairperson Bishal Bhandari said patients injured in the floods on August 26 and currently receiving treatment at various hospitals will be provided blood free of charge.

Bhandari also said the Red Cross would arrange transportation of bodies for families facing financial difficulties whose deceased relatives have been identified.

According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 242 people are currently receiving treatment at various hospitals. So far, 734 bodies have been recovered.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

A man has been arrested on suspicion of defrauding people by falsely claiming to have donated to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

The arrested man has been identified as 32-year-old Bhagwan Karki of Gokulganga Rural Municipality-2, Ramechhap.

title.rendered: India sends fourth batch of aid to flood-hit Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

India has provided additional assistance for search, rescue and relief operations in flood- and landslide-affected areas of Nepal.

Indian External Affairs Minister Dr S. Jaishankar said that a fourth aircraft carrying 11 tonnes of relief supplies and a technical team had departed for Nepal.

In a social media post on Sunday morning, Jaishankar also reaffirmed India’s continued support and assistance for Nepal’s relief and rescue efforts.

According to the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu, a tunnel technical team equipped with search-and-rescue and disaster-management equipment arrived in Nepal aboard an Indian Air Force C-130 aircraft.

A team of forensic experts carrying equipment required for DNA analysis has also arrived in Nepal.

The embassy said the latest shipment also includes relief supplies such as blankets, sleeping bags, tarpaulins, plastic sheets and hygiene materials. This is the fourth batch of assistance India has sent to Nepal.

Bridge equipment also sent

With floods and landslides damaging roads and bridges, India has also sent infrastructure support to help restore transportation.

According to Jaishankar, 16 trucks carrying equipment for a 230-foot single-lane modular steel bridge have already departed for Nepal.

He added that equipment for seven more Bailey bridges, along with technical teams to install them, will also arrive in Nepal soon.

Nepal receives 68.5 tonnes of aid so far

India said it has so far airlifted a total of 68.5 tonnes of relief supplies to Kathmandu during the disaster.

According to India’s Ministry of External Affairs, earlier shipments included essential medicines, portable generators, ready-to-eat food packets, water purification tablets and other technical equipment.

The United States has announced more than $3.6 million in life-saving humanitarian assistance for people affected by flooding in Nepal.

title.rendered: Two Chinese Air Force planes arrive in Kathmandu with 50 tonnes of relief supplies

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

The Chinese government has provided Nepal with 50 tonnes of emergency relief supplies. Two large Y-20 transport aircraft of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force landed at Tribhuvan International Airport at around 7 am on Sunday carrying the relief materials.

According to the Chinese Embassy in Kathmandu, four Chinese tunnel rescue specialists also arrived in Nepal along with the emergency supplies and necessary rescue equipment.

The relief materials were handed over at Tribhuvan International Airport. Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun, Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming, and House of Representatives member Dharma KC were present at the handover ceremony. They also welcomed the Chinese rescue specialists who arrived in Nepal.

What do the Chinese relief supplies include?

The two aircraft departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport in China and arrived in Kathmandu after a flight of around three hours. They carried a total of 13,200 units of emergency relief supplies weighing 50 tonnes.

The supplies for disaster-affected people include tarpaulins, blankets, sleeping bags, dry food and biscuits, and first-aid kits.

China sent emergency assistance and a team of specialists to support Nepal’s disaster response following devastating floods and landslides in various parts of the country, including areas along the Nepal-China border.

title.rendered: 104 Nepali nationals missing in Tibet after flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

At least 104 Nepali nationals have gone missing after a massive flood hit the Kerung border point in China’s Tibet Autonomous Region.

Chinese state media CGTN reported the figure, citing information provided at a press conference held on Sunday morning.

According to CGTN, a total of 261 foreign nationals have gone missing in the disaster, with Nepalis accounting for the largest number.

Nationals of which countries are missing?

The figures released by Chinese authorities show that, besides 104 Nepalis, 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British nationals are missing.

Six nationals each from Australia and Canada, four from South Africa, and three each from Germany, Malaysia and Russia are also missing.

Similarly, two nationals each from Estonia, France, Ireland, the Netherlands and New Zealand have been reported missing.

One national each from Finland, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Lithuania, Portugal, Spain and Ukraine is also missing, according to CGTN.

Chinese authorities have informed the embassies and consulates of the respective countries in China about their nationals who remain missing.

Officials said at Sunday morning’s press conference that no foreign tourists are currently stranded in Kerung County.
