title.rendered: Nepal cannot keep rebuilding its way out of disaster risk

content.rendered:
We have policies for dead-body management. We have plans for search and rescue. We have flood forecasts, early-warning systems, hazard maps and disaster institutions. But perhaps we have not yet designed our development system for the scale and speed of disasters that are now becoming possible.

The devastation that unfolded along the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system on August 26 should force Nepal to ask a difficult question:

Are we actually reducing disaster risk — or are we becoming increasingly efficient at responding to disasters after they have already happened?

The distinction matters, and the numbers now emerging make it impossible to avoid.

What we now know

As of Saturday (August 29), four days after the event, Nepal Police had confirmed 669 deaths, while a provisional count put the number of people still unaccounted for at more than 2,500. NDRRMA’s own tally put the number of missing at 977 as of Thursday, illustrating how fluid—and contested—even the basic casualty picture remains this early in the response. By then, police had deployed more than 4,300 personnel and reported rescuing over 1,500 people, including hundreds from Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

This was not a conventional monsoon flood. Satellite imagery examined by scientists showed that the lower section of a glacier at roughly 5,200 metres elevation collapsed, falling about 1,200 metres onto the valley floor and entraining rock and sediment along the way. NDRRMA identified the event as an ice-rock avalanche on the Lhende River, about 20 kilometres northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing. The avalanche generated a debris-laden surge that tore through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. ICIMOD monitoring showed the river at Galchhi rising by as much as nine metres in just 30 minutes.

The surge did not remain contained to the mountains. It carried sediment and boulders all the way into the Narayani River, with bodies later recovered as far downstream as Chitwan. Twelve operating power projects, representing 431 MW of installed capacity—including a 25 MW solar plant—were damaged, out of 901 MW of energy infrastructure affected along the corridor. At the Upper Trishuli Hydropower Project alone, the Nepali Army rescued 350 workers and residents trapped inside a tunnel, with others still being searched for.

High alert remains in place across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan. The Prime Minister’s Office has confirmed major impacts in the first four districts, while the disaster has also crossed the border, with a mudslide reported in Gyirong county, Tibet, and casualties reported among trekkers and pilgrims travelling towards Kailash.

These are not just statistics for a news cycle. They are the data Nepal must now use to decide what needs to change.

The Melamchi lesson: we have already seen this movie

Nepal does not have to look very far back for a warning it failed to heed.

The 2021 Melamchi disaster demonstrated how a mountain catchment can suddenly transform into a destructive debris-flow system. It changed river morphology, destroyed settlements and infrastructure, and proved that downstream communities can be devastated by processes originating far upstream, out of sight and out of mind.

Five years later, the question is not what reports were written, how many meetings were held, or how many policies were approved. It is:

  • Which settlements were moved?
  • Which river corridors were protected?
  • Which infrastructure designs were changed?
  • Which extraction activities were stopped?
  • Which early-warning thresholds were revised?
  • Which communities were repeatedly drilled?
  • Which development approvals were refused because of unacceptable risk?

DHM continues to maintain hydrological monitoring infrastructure around the Melamchi system. But a sensor is not resilience. A sensor that produces information which does not reach a person in danger, in a form they understand, with a clear instruction about what to do, is not yet an effective early-warning system — and the nine-metre rise in thirty minutes at Galchhi this week is the clearest possible proof of that gap.

The riverbank settlement debate is not as simple as “people refuse to move”

Whenever a flood destroys riverbank settlements, the immediate response is often: “Why were people living there?”

That question is incomplete. For many families, the riverbank is ancestral land — where fathers and grandfathers lived, where social networks, temples, schools, markets and livelihoods developed. Relocation does not just cost a house; for many, it costs an entire social and economic system.

There is also an uncomfortable economic reality. Roads follow river valleys because they offer the easiest gradients. Markets follow roads. Hotels follow markets. Sand and aggregate extraction creates jobs. River-based tourism and hydropower depend directly on the same corridor. The result is a political economy that runs:

river → land → road → market → extraction → construction → employment → local revenue → provincial revenue → national economy

Disaster risk sits quietly inside that entire chain, all the way from Rasuwagadhi’s trading routes to the hydropower intakes that were damaged this week.

Who benefits today, and who pays tomorrow?

A local government may earn revenue from extraction. A business may benefit from a roadside location. A household may earn its livelihood from river-based activity. A contractor benefits from road construction. A municipality collects taxes. A province benefits from economic activity. The federal government benefits from national infrastructure and energy generation.

But when the river changes course and destroys the settlement, bridge, road or hydropower project it made possible, the family loses its home, the municipality loses infrastructure, the province requests support, the federal government mobilises the army and helicopters, and the national treasury pays for relief and reconstruction — as it is now doing across five districts and counting.

This is a classic case of risk externalisation: the benefit is decentralised and immediate; the cost is collective, delayed and enormous. Disaster risk cannot be addressed through awareness campaigns alone. It has to be addressed through fiscal policy, land-use planning, infrastructure regulation, environmental governance and accountability.

Climate change has changed the equation

Climate change does not care about administrative boundaries, ownership of a road, the age of a settlement, or who collects revenue from sand and gravel. It does not wait for the next five-year plan.

Warming is destabilising high-mountain environments. Glaciers are losing mass, slopes are becoming less stable, and cascading hazards — from ice or rock collapse, to debris flow, to river flooding — now have to be built into Nepal’s risk thinking as a single connected chain rather than separate hazards. That is precisely the sequence that unfolded on 26 August: a glacial collapse at 5,200 metres becoming a debris flood sixty kilometres downstream within hours.

The lesson is not that every riverbank settlement must disappear immediately. The lesson is that the historical behaviour of a river can no longer be treated as a guarantee of its future behaviour. A place that remained safe for a hundred years can become unsafe because the upstream system has changed — invisibly, and often irreversibly.

From “warning” to “action”

Nepal already has flood forecasting and monitoring infrastructure. DHM’s Flood Forecasting Division maintains real-time data. NDRRMA maintains national disaster information, alerts and coordination systems. Those systems functioned this week — Nepal Police and the Flood Forecasting Division did issue an urgent warning for communities along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani corridors, and high alert was declared for Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

The question is no longer “do we have an early-warning system?” It is:

  • Did the warning reach the right person, early enough?
  • Did they know exactly where to go?
  • Did the hydropower operator have an independent emergency protocol — the kind that got 350 people out of a tunnel alive at Upper Trishuli?
  • Did the trekking hub of Syabrubesi, full of transient tourists and pilgrims, have any evacuation register at all?
  • Did the warning automatically trigger action, or did it require another meeting first?

Nine metres of river rise in thirty minutes leaves no room for the second option.

What should change now

1. From hazard mapping to enforceable risk zoning. Flood-risk, debris-flow, GLOF and landslide-susceptibility maps must become development-control instruments that shape building permits, settlement expansion, road alignment, extraction permits, hotels, schools, hospitals and hydropower siting — not documents that sit inside a report.

2. River-corridor planning across government levels. A river ignores municipal boundaries. Local governments should manage land use and community preparedness; provinces should coordinate inter-municipal infrastructure and river corridors; the federal government should set national standards, run hydrological and glacial monitoring, and coordinate transboundary response with China and India, both of which were drawn into this week’s disaster.

3. Resettlement must mean livelihood relocation, not just housing relocation. A new house without new employment, markets, schools and access to services will not hold; people will drift back to the river corridor.

4. Make the economics of sand and gravel transparent. No revenue should count as “development revenue” if extracting it systematically raises disaster risk beyond acceptable limits.

5. Re-engineer infrastructure for cascading hazards. The 431 MW of hydropower capacity damaged this week shows that the design question can no longer be “will this survive the design flood?” It must be “what happens to the whole network if this single asset fails?” — water, rock, ice, sediment and debris together, not water alone.

6. Build a genuine last-mile early-warning architecture, combining rainfall sensors, river gauges, satellite data, glacier and lake monitoring, sirens, SMS/cell broadcast, police communication, hotel and tourism networks, and school registers — with every warning answering three questions: what is happening, who is at risk, and what must you do right now.

7. Drill the people who actually have to act, not only officials in a meeting room, and measure how many minutes it takes and how many people actually move.

8. Establish a national “safe settlement” programme with a transparent risk–cost–benefit framework: some settlements need relocation, some need in-situ protection, some need a hard stop on further expansion.

9. Change how preparedness is measured — not by how many plans exist, but by how many people can be evacuated within fifteen minutes, and how many critical facilities have independent emergency power and communication.

10. Make every reconstruction a risk-reduction opportunity. Rebuilding what was destroyed, in exactly the same place and the same way, is preparation for the next disaster, not recovery from this one.

Rethinking what we mean by “natural disaster”

The glacial collapse may be natural. The rainfall may be natural. But the scale of a disaster is shaped by human decisions — where we build, where we allow roads, where we extract, where we approve hotels and hospitals, how we design bridges, whether we enforce land-use rules, whether people trust a warning, and whether that warning becomes action in time.

So the question after Bhote Koshi–Trishuli should not simply be “what caused the flood?” It should be “what turned the hazard into a catastrophe of this scale?” That question moves us from meteorology to governance, from rainfall to land use, from glaciers to infrastructure, from policy to implementation, and from early warning to early action.

The real test of Nepal’s disaster governance

Nepal already has the institutions, the policies, the plans, the early-warning technology and the legislation. What it needs now is the political and administrative courage to connect them.

A disaster-management system is not successful because NDRRMA has an alert portal. It is successful when a mother in a riverbank settlement receives a warning, understands it, trusts it, and has enough time to take her children to safety before the river rises nine metres.

It is not successful because DHM produces an accurate forecast. It is successful when that forecast becomes an evacuation order before the water arrives.

And it is not successful because search-and-rescue teams can recover bodies efficiently, however necessary and courageous that work is right now across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan. Our ultimate measure of preparedness should be how many bodies we did not have to recover.

The Bhote Koshi–Trishuli catastrophe should become more than a tragedy to mourn. It should become a policy turning point — because climate change is not asking Nepal whether it is ready. It is already testing the answer.

title.rendered: 5 days on, families still wait for missing hydropower workers

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 30

Every time a helicopter lands at the Nepal Army’s No. 1 Military Training Centre in Trishuli, Nuwakot, families of people missing since the Rasuwa floods turn their eyes towards it, hoping their loved ones might be among those rescued.

But when the helicopter arrives without them, the families return to waiting.

They have been doing this for nearly five days.

Relatives of people who went missing after a sudden flood struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa early Wednesday say they are increasingly dissatisfied with the government’s search and rescue efforts.

Many of them are now staying at the Trishuli army barracks, waiting for news of their loved ones.

The families of those who have been rescued are relieved and happy. But for those whose relatives remain missing, the wait has become increasingly agonising.

Among them is Shobit Pokharel from Lamjung, who has been staying at the Trishuli barracks for three days. His cousin, a mechanical sub-engineer working at the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project, has been missing since the flood.

According to Pokharel, around 45 people were working at the site when the flood struck.

He last spoke to his cousin through a video call on the evening of August 25.

“She told me she had duty from 7 pm and would be working for 12 hours. She said we would talk again in the evening. It has been four days and we have not been able to contact her,” he said.

Her location was detected inside the tunnel at 9:18:56 pm that night. There has been no information since.

The Nepal Electricity Authority has told the family that the tunnel was designed in a way that could allow people to remain safe inside.

“But we have no information,” Pokharel said.

Like Pokharel, several other relatives have spent their days at the Trishuli barracks waiting for news.

They say they are not reassured by government claims that Home Minister Sudan Gurung himself has been involved in the rescue operation.

“The problem is that the tunnel was built, but there is no skilled manpower to carry out the rescue. We were told that the Home Minister himself went into the tunnel and worked. We thank him for that, but even if he stays there and works for 10 days, nothing will happen. Rescue requires skilled manpower. Experts need to be brought in,” Pokharel said.

He questioned the pace of excavation.

“An excavator is being used as if it were simply removing sand from a river. How can people be rescued that way?”

The families say a much larger operation should have been mobilised, with 15 to 20 excavators and specialised personnel working continuously.

They complain that the operation has instead been progressing at what they describe as office-hour speed.

“They work for eight hours as if it were office hours. The Army used night-vision equipment for operations 15 years ago, but now they stop work before 6 pm saying visibility is poor,” one relative said.

Some relatives have even risked their own lives to reach the tunnel sites themselves.

“Four people walked from the other side and reached the tunnel. But the work there is nowhere near what is being portrayed outside,” relatives said.

‘Give us their lives or their bodies’

Tapendra Bista of Kalikot has also come to the Trishuli barracks in search of his younger brother.

His brother is believed to be missing inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli 3B project.

Bista said his brother last spoke to the family at around 8 am on August 27, after completing his duty and saying he was heading to his room.

He has not been heard from since.

Another worker, Nepal Bista, who was with him, is also missing.

“Give us their lives or give us their bodies,” Tapendra said, expressing his frustration over the lack of progress.

The message from most families waiting at the barracks is the same: their relatives must be rescued as quickly as possible.

Hundreds still believed trapped inside tunnels

The frustration comes as hundreds of workers and employees remain missing or are believed to be trapped inside tunnels of hydropower projects along the Trishuli corridor, four days after the flood.

The 60 MW Upper Trishuli 3A, 216 MW Upper Trishuli-1, 20 MW Langtang and 22 MW Chilime projects are among those affected.

The concerned hydropower projects say full-scale rescue operations have been delayed by a lack of specialised manpower, expertise, equipment and government coordination.

At Upper Trishuli 3A, where Home Minister Gurung visited on Friday, authorities have so far been excavating to locate one of the access tunnels.

NEA Deputy Executive Director Madan Timsina said some of the equipment required for the operation reached the affected area only on Friday.

Two excavators and other equipment are now being used to dig towards the tunnel.

“It does not appear immediately possible to enter through the headrace or tailrace tunnels. There are also two access tunnels, both of which have been buried. Work has begun with the objective of locating those tunnels and entering through them, but they have not yet been opened,” Timsina said.

The project’s powerhouse is underground and the operational project had been shut down for an overhaul when the flood struck.

Timsina said around 42 employees were believed to be trapped inside the tunnel.

He said the Nepal Electricity Authority had provided available equipment and manpower, while the Nepal Army was also involved in the operation.

However, transporting equipment has been difficult because everything has to be flown in by helicopter, he said.

400 may be trapped at Upper Trishuli-1

The situation is also critical at the Upper Trishuli-1 project, the largest hydropower project under construction along the Trishuli corridor.

Giriraj Adhikari, chief executive officer of Nepal Water and Energy Development Company, said around 600 people working at the project remained out of contact, with around 400 believed to be trapped inside tunnels.

“Of those who managed to save their lives on the surface, 260 have been rescued, including 10 Korean nationals,” Adhikari said.

“But the rescue of those trapped inside the tunnel has not even started. We expect the work to begin tomorrow.”

A six-member Chinese tunnel expert team has arrived in Nepal to assist with the rescue operation.

China Railway is carrying out the civil construction work at the project, and the Chinese experts arrived in coordination with the company, Adhikari said.

Around 300 people are believed to have been working inside the tunnel and another 100 at the headworks when the disaster occurred.

The project expects the Chinese team to begin field operations on Sunday.

Langtang families have waited for four days

Around 25 people are believed to be trapped inside the tunnel of the Langtang Hydropower Project.

Project promoter Bijayman Bhattarai said 19 of the 60 people working at the project had been rescued, but those believed to be inside the tunnel had yet to be reached.

“Employees who managed to get out alive have also said that people are trapped inside the tunnel. I have repeatedly asked the concerned officials to rescue them, but the operation has not even started,” Bhattarai said.

“It has been four days. They keep saying they will do it today or tomorrow. Nothing has happened. I am exhausted.”

Chilime tunnel blocked by mud

Six employees trapped inside the Chilime Hydropower Project tunnel have also yet to be rescued.

Project chief executive officer Baburaja Maharjan said a mountaineering rescue team was flown to the site by Simrik Air helicopter on Saturday, but it could not reach those trapped inside.

“After going around 100 metres inside the tunnel, they found that it was completely blocked. They said they could not clear it and that a specialised team with special equipment was required,” Maharjan said.

An Indian rescue team that arrived in Nepal has conducted a reconnaissance of the area, and efforts are underway to deploy it for the rescue operation.

Experts question government response

Nepal Engineers’ Association President Subas Baral said there had been significant delays in rescuing people trapped inside the tunnels.

“Nepal has the capacity, equipment and skills for tunnel rescue. Even if any particular equipment was unavailable, it could have been brought immediately from neighbouring countries,” he said.

“The rescue of those trapped inside the tunnels should have been prioritised from the beginning. But there has been much more effort to rescue people outside than those trapped inside.”

Hydropower expert Surya Prasad Adhikari said the people trapped inside the tunnels should have been rescued within two days if the government had treated the situation with the required urgency.

He said the disaster had exposed Nepal’s lack of specialised expertise, equipment and technology for tunnel rescue.

He argued that the government should have immediately sought assistance from foreign teams with the required technical expertise.

The government finally decided on Saturday to allow foreign rescue teams to enter Nepal. A Chinese team and an Indian team have since arrived.

However, officials familiar with the operation said the teams were unable to begin field operations immediately because of a lack of government coordination.

898 people still out of contact

The Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), said 898 people from 11 hydropower projects remained out of contact following the Rasuwa floods.

The Upper Trishuli-1 project has the highest number, with 576 people still out of contact.

The Upper Trishuli 3B project has reported 201 people out of contact. The project said none of them were trapped inside its tunnel, and that the missing people included surface workers, office staff and employees staying at camps.

IPPAN said four people from the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Hydropower Project and 42 from the Langtang Khola Hydropower Project were missing. Eight people were missing from Chilime and seven from the Melung Khola Hydropower Project.

A further 42 people from Upper Trishuli 3A were out of contact, along with two from Middle Trishuli Ganga and one each from the Trishuli Hydropower Project and Devighat Hydropower Project.

IPPAN estimates that around 300 people are trapped inside the tunnels of Upper Trishuli-1, Upper Trishuli 3A and Upper Trishuli 3B.

So far, 361 people have been rescued from the affected hydropower projects, including 254 from Upper Trishuli-1, 18 from Langtang and 91 from Upper Trishuli 3B.

The floods struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa at around 8:45 am on August 27 after floodwaters entered from the Tibet side, causing damage in Rasuwa as well as downstream areas including Nuwakot and Dhading.

More than 15,000 security personnel have been deployed in search and rescue operations following the disaster.

For the families waiting at the Trishuli barracks, however, the priority remains unchanged: they want their loved ones brought home — alive if possible, and accounted for as soon as possible.

title.rendered: Kathmandu-Muglin road completely blocked by floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

The Kathmandu-Muglin road has been completely blocked after floods caused the water level in the Trishuli River to rise.

The flooding in the Trishuli was triggered by the increased flow coming through the Bhotekoshi River.

According to Dhading Chief District Officer Laxmi Pandey (Gautam), the rising Trishuli River eroded the road from below, causing the road section to sink and become impassable.

The road was briefly blocked earlier this morning but reopened after some time. It was completely shut again shortly afterward.

The closure has left passengers stranded along the route.

Authorities are monitoring the situation as the flood continues to affect the road section.

title.rendered: Kathmandu-Muglin-Narayangadh road section fully reopened after brief closure

content.rendered:
Chitwan, August 30

The Kathmandu-Muglin-Narayangadh road section, which was briefly closed on Sunday morning, has resumed full operation.

Police had halted all vehicles travelling to and from Narayangadh towards Pokhara and Kathmandu via Muglin after receiving information that the flow of the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa had increased.

The Chitwan District Police Office said traffic was allowed to resume after the Flood Forecasting Division under the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology reported that the Bhotekoshi flow did not pose an immediate risk.

All types of vehicles are now operating along the road section, according to police.

title.rendered: Trishuli water level rises 3 metres above danger mark amid heavy rainfall

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 30

Water levels in several rivers have crossed danger and alert levels following heavy rainfall in different parts of the country.

According to the Flood Forecasting Division, the level in the Trishuli River in Dhading is currently three metres above the danger level.

The rise in the Trishuli’s water level has been attributed to flooding from the Bhotekoshi River area of Rasuwa.

The division has also warned of rising levels in the Narayani River and its tributaries after heavy rainfall was recorded in several watersheds across Gandaki Province. Residents living along riverbanks have been urged to remain alert.

Meanwhile, the water level in the Sunkoshi River at the Khurkot hydrological station in Sindhuli has also crossed the alert level. Residents in areas along the river have been advised to exercise caution.

Very heavy rainfall was recorded in Sindhupalchok over the past 24 hours. The rainfall has resulted in rising levels in rivers downstream of the affected areas, according to the Flood Forecasting Division.

title.rendered: Rescuers and riverside communities urged to stay alert as water level rises in Bhotekoshi and Trishuli

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, August 30

The water level in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa has risen again since early Sunday morning, prompting authorities to urge rescuers and people living along the riverbanks to remain alert.

The warning comes as search and rescue operations continue for people affected by the flood that entered from the Tibet side on August 26.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) issued a notice urging caution after receiving information that the flood flow in the Bhotekoshi had increased further.

“Information has been received that the flood flow in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa has increased further. All those involved in search, rescue and relief operations in affected areas including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, as well as those living along riverbanks and all concerned, are requested to remain alert,” the authority said.

According to the Flood Forecasting Division, the water level in the Trishuli River in Dhading has risen three metres above the danger level.

The rise in the Trishuli’s water level has been attributed to flooding originating from the Bhotekoshi area of Rasuwa.

The division has also warned of rising water levels in the Narayani River and its tributaries after heavy rainfall was recorded in several watersheds in Gandaki Province. People living along the riverbanks have been advised to remain vigilant.

Meanwhile, the water level at the Khurkot hydrological station on the Sunkoshi River in Sindhuli has also crossed the alert level, according to the Flood Forecasting Division.

Authorities have urged rescue teams and communities in downstream areas to exercise caution as search, rescue and relief operations continue in areas affected by the earlier Bhotekoshi flood.

title.rendered: Over Rs 5 billion deposited in PM’s relief fund for Bhotekoshi flood response

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

More than Rs 5 billion has been deposited into the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund for the rescue and relief of people affected by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods.

Prime Minister Balen Shah said Rs 5.04 billion has been deposited into accounts maintained at nine commercial banks.

According to Shah, an additional US$1.8 million has been deposited into accounts at Himalayan Bank and Laxmi Bank.

The funds have been collected to support rescue and relief efforts for people stranded and affected by the floods.

Shah urged individuals and organisations wishing to contribute to use only the government’s officially published QR code and bank accounts to ensure transparency and prevent possible financial fraud.

“In this difficult disaster situation, we request everyone to provide financial assistance only through the government’s officially published QR code and accounts under the names ‘Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund’ and ‘Prime Minister’s Relief Fund’ to ensure transparent use and proper management of assistance and to prevent possible financial fraud,” Shah said.

title.rendered: Risk of lake burst in Rasuwa remains low, experts urge caution

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

The immediate risk of a lake burst from a water body formed after an ice-rock avalanche in Rasuwa has decreased, according to technical experts.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology said the possibility of the lake suddenly bursting has reduced after water began flowing out naturally. Experts have also warned that rumours of an imminent lake burst have affected ongoing search and rescue operations in downstream areas.

Binod Parajuli, chief of the Flood Forecasting Division at the department, said the risk of a sudden breach has declined as the newly formed lake has already started overflowing.

“Normally, unstable lakes burst soon after filling up. This lake has filled and started releasing water, and more than 24 hours have passed without a breach,” Parajuli said. “Once water begins flowing out, the possibility of the lake bursting decreases.”

Geologist Shri Kamal Dwivedi, who works at the Secretariat of the Water and Energy Commission, said the water body formed in a depression created after an ice-rock fall should not necessarily be considered a lake at risk of bursting.

“Water filling a depression and flowing out is different from a lake bursting,” Dwivedi said, adding that unnecessary rumours about a possible flood had affected rescue and search operations downstream.

After Wednesday’s devastating flood, a drone survey conducted by China in the northern region of Langtang Lirung identified two water bodies — one at around 4,000 metres above sea level and another in the upper section of Lhende Khola.

At the time, both water bodies were considered potentially risky as water levels were rising. However, recent images and data show that one outlet has opened and water is gradually draining, according to officials.

Experts estimate the two water bodies hold around 50,000 cubic metres of water. They said even in the worst-case scenario, a possible breach would not produce a flood as destructive as the one seen last Wednesday, when an estimated 20 million cubic metres of water and debris swept downstream.

Parajuli said the current concern is that fresh landslides could fall into the water bodies and trigger renewed flooding.

“The flood debris from Wednesday has already raised the riverbed. If another flood occurs, there could be risks along the riverbanks,” he said.

Experts said further monitoring of the water bodies, including their depth and volume, is ongoing through satellite images and drone data. While the immediate threat has decreased, authorities have advised continued vigilance.

title.rendered: 898 people still missing from hydropower projects affected by Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

At least 898 people remain unaccounted for after devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River swept through hydropower project areas in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

According to data provided by the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), 11 hydropower projects in the two districts have been affected by the floods. Rescue teams have so far evacuated 361 people from the affected project sites.

A large number of those rescued were employees and workers at the 216 MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project. IPPAN said 254 people have been rescued from the project alone.

However, around 300 people are still believed to be trapped inside the project’s tunnel.

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said a team of Chinese experts has also arrived in Nepal to assist in the rescue of those trapped inside the tunnel.

Similarly, 18 people have been rescued from the 20 MW Langtang Khola Hydropower Project and 91 from the 37 MW Upper Trishuli-3B Hydropower Project.

Seven hydropower projects affected in Rasuwa

According to IPPAN, seven hydropower projects in Rasuwa have been affected by the Bhotekoshi floods.

They are the 216 MW Upper Trishuli-1, 111 MW Rasuwa Gadhi, 120 MW Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi, 6.42 MW Upper Mailung-A, 20 MW Langtang Khola, 22 MW Chilime and 5 MW Mailung Khola hydropower projects.

The direct impact of the floods on these project sites has raised concerns about the safety of employees and workers.

With communication cut off with people at several project sites, search and rescue operations have been prioritised.

Six projects affected in Nuwakot

Six hydropower and energy projects in Nuwakot have also been affected.

The affected projects are the 24 MW Trishuli, 14.1 MW Devighat, 60 MW Upper Trishuli-3A, 37 MW Upper Trishuli-3B, 15.6 MW Middle Trishuli Ganga and 25 MW Nuwakot Solar Power Project.

Workers trapped inside tunnels pose major rescue challenge

Rescuing people trapped inside project structures, particularly tunnels, has emerged as the biggest challenge following the floods.

The estimated 300 people trapped inside the Upper Trishuli-1 tunnel highlight the complexity of the rescue operation. Additional technical expertise and specialised rescue teams are being mobilised to reach them.

The arrival of Chinese experts is expected to provide additional technical support for the tunnel rescue.

Search and rescue operations are continuing in the flood-affected areas, and further details on those still unaccounted for are expected as teams reach more project sites.

The latest figures indicate that while 361 people have been rescued, 898 remain unaccounted for.

The scale of the crisis shows that the Bhotekoshi floods have caused more than damage to hydropower infrastructure. They have created a major humanitarian emergency involving hundreds of workers and employees stationed at the affected projects.

The immediate priority remains establishing contact with those unaccounted for and rescuing them wherever possible.

title.rendered: Why is the govt temporarily burying unidentified bodies recovered from Rasuwa floods?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

The devastating floods in Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi River have killed more than 600 people, but most of the bodies recovered so far remain unidentified.

As bodies swept away by Wednesday’s floods continue to be recovered across several districts, authorities are facing a new challenge: there is simply not enough space to store them.

Some bodies have already begun decomposing in the heat, creating a growing risk of foul odour, infection and public-health problems. With morgues and available refrigerated storage unable to accommodate the large number of bodies, the government has decided to temporarily bury unidentified bodies until they can be identified and handed over to their families.

But why was burial chosen? How will the identities of the dead be preserved? And what happens if relatives come looking for a body later?

Here is what officials and forensic experts say.

Why are the bodies being buried?

The immediate reason is the lack of adequate facilities to store such a large number of bodies.

According to Nepal Police, bodies have so far been recovered in Rasuwa, Dhading, Gorkha, Nawalparasi East, Nuwakot, Chitwan, Tanahun and Nawalparasi West.

Chitwan has recorded the highest number, with 233 bodies recovered, followed by 158 in Nawalparasi East, 54 in Gorkha, 49 in Dhading, 47 in Nawalparasi West, 41 in Nuwakot, 31 in Tanahun and 13 in Rasuwa.

Relatives of many of the victims have also been unable to reach the recovery sites because roads have been destroyed or remain inaccessible.

The large number of bodies recovered at once has overwhelmed existing morgues and refrigerated storage facilities.

According to the Ministry of Health, government and private health institutions across Nepal have refrigerated capacity for around 600 bodies. However, much of that capacity cannot be used for the flood victims because the bodies have been recovered across geographically dispersed districts.

In Chitwan alone, health facilities have a combined capacity to store only around 50 bodies. Even that capacity has been strained, with some hospital freezers already occupied by unidentified bodies.

Authorities say there was not enough time or available infrastructure to immediately establish additional cold-storage facilities, temporary morgues or refrigerated containers.

As a result, temporary burial has been adopted as a last-resort preservation measure.

Police Inspector Anil Thapa says decomposition has already begun.

“The bodies have started decomposing. As decomposition progresses, the smell is spreading. We are burying them to prevent the risk of epidemics and infection,” Thapa said.

According to him, the smell has begun spreading up to 1.5 to two kilometres from some locations where bodies are being kept, affecting patients at nearby hospitals as well as local residents.

Why not simply keep the bodies in cold storage?

Refrigeration remains the preferred option when large numbers of bodies are recovered after a disaster.

International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) guidance recommends keeping bodies at around 2–4 degrees Celsius in refrigerated containers or other suitable cold-storage facilities wherever possible.

But when adequate refrigeration is unavailable, temporary burial in a safe location can be used to preserve the bodies until they can be identified and returned to their families.

Senior forensic expert Dr Gopal Chaudhary of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital says temporary burial is not the same as a final funeral.

“Temporary burial means documenting all the details of the deceased, taking photographs and DNA samples, and burying the body underground in a safe place until relatives come forward,” he said.

The objective, therefore, is not to dispose of unidentified bodies but to preserve them in a way that allows identification and recovery later.

Why couldn’t additional morgues or refrigerated containers be set up?

The scale and geographical spread of the disaster have made the problem more complicated.

Bodies have been recovered from several districts stretching from Rasuwa towards Chitwan and Nawalparasi. No single hospital or institution has enough capacity to store all of them for an extended period.

Hospitals normally have morgues designed for routine requirements, not for hundreds of bodies arriving simultaneously following a major disaster.

At the same time, authorities have to carry out postmortems, document bodies, photograph identifying features and collect DNA samples.

In Chitwan, Bharatpur Hospital has formed seven forensic teams to carry out postmortems and collect DNA samples, with forensic specialists from hospitals including Bheri Hospital and Lumbini also providing assistance.

With existing storage facilities overwhelmed and additional refrigerated infrastructure not immediately available, officials opted for temporary burial.

How will the bodies be buried?

Authorities say the bodies will not be dumped together in an unidentified mass grave.

Each body will be individually documented and assigned a unique identification number before burial.

The documentation includes photographs of the face, tattoos, injuries, scars and other distinguishing physical features. Clothing and other belongings found with the body will also be recorded.

A legal document will be prepared for each body, while DNA samples will be collected and preserved.

More than 100 bodies had already undergone DNA profiling by Saturday afternoon and were being prepared for burial.

Bodies began being buried on Saturday afternoon in a forested area between Ramnagar and Devghat in Bharatpur Metropolitan City-1, according to the authorities.

The graves are being dug to a depth of around 1.5 metres while avoiding damage to the surrounding sal trees. A gap of around 40 centimetres will be maintained between individual bodies.

The body bags will carry identification numbers, and corresponding markers will be placed at the burial sites.

Authorities will also photograph and record the burial process and maintain GPS coordinates and mapping data showing the exact location of each body.

The burial area will subsequently be fenced off or otherwise secured.

What happens if a body is later identified?

Temporary burial does not close the possibility of identification or recovery.

If relatives later come forward, authorities can compare information provided by the family with the records, photographs and other evidence collected before burial.

DNA testing can then be used to confirm the identity.

If a match is established, the body can be exhumed and handed over to the family for funeral rites according to their religious and cultural practices.

Inspector Thapa said the burial system has been designed specifically to make such future recovery possible.

“If a DNA match is established in the future and the family wants to perform the final rites according to their religion and culture, the body can be exhumed and handed over to them,” he said.

Dr Chaudhary said the same procedure can be followed by comparing DNA from relatives with samples collected from the bodies.

What happens to body parts recovered separately?

The floods have severely damaged some bodies, and body parts have been recovered separately from different locations.

These will also be documented and preserved in the same manner as complete bodies.

DNA samples and identification numbers will be assigned so that individual remains can potentially be linked to a victim later.

Will the bodies decompose underground?

Yes. Burial does not stop decomposition.

However, forensic experts say decomposition can be slower underground than when a body is exposed in the open.

According to Dr Chaudhary, the rate of decomposition is comparatively slower underground, meaning a body may remain in a relatively better state for a period of time.

The purpose of burial is therefore not to prevent decomposition indefinitely. Rather, it is to slow the process, control the immediate public-health and environmental problems caused by exposed bodies, and preserve the possibility of identification and future exhumation.

Why is location and record-keeping so important?

The entire process is designed to ensure that authorities can locate an individual body even years after burial.

Each body will have a unique identification number. The same number will be recorded in official documents, on a marker associated with the burial site and in forensic records.

GPS coordinates, photographs and videos of the burial location will also be preserved.

A concrete marker indicating the identification number will be placed near each burial site so that the location of a particular body can be traced later.

Has Nepal used temporary burial before?

Yes. A similar system was used following the 2015 earthquake when unidentified bodies had to be managed after existing facilities were overwhelmed.

According to Dr Chaudhary, 32 bodies were temporarily buried on the premises of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital following the earthquake.

Some foreign families came searching for their missing relatives years later. DNA testing helped identify two of the bodies, which were subsequently exhumed and handed over to their families.

Dr Chaudhary says around 30 bodies buried during the earthquake still remain on the teaching hospital premises.

How long must unidentified remains be preserved?

According to Dr Chaudhary, Nepal’s legal provisions require unidentified bodies and remains to be preserved for an extended period.

He says unidentified bodies and remaining bones or other remains are required to be preserved for up to 12 years.

“If relatives come looking for them within those 12 years, the remains must also be handed over,” he said.

After that period, legal provisions allow the person to be declared dead.

So, why bury the bodies now?

The decision is essentially the result of three immediate problems coming together: the unusually high number of bodies, insufficient refrigerated storage, and rapid decomposition caused by the heat.

Burial was not chosen as a substitute for identification or as a final disposal method. It was chosen because authorities needed a way to move the bodies away from overcrowded and unsuitable storage conditions while preserving every possible means of identifying them later.

Each body is therefore being documented, photographed, assigned a unique number, sampled for DNA and mapped before being buried.

For the families still searching for their missing loved ones, the crucial point is that burial does not mean the search for identity ends. The system is intended to ensure that a body can still be traced, identified and exhumed when a family comes forward.

title.rendered: Rescue team unable to reach trapped workers as sludge blocks Chilime tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

A search and rescue team deployed to Chilime Hydropower Project in Rasuwa has been unable to reach people trapped inside the tunnel due to heavy deposits of mud and sludge blocking access.

The team, comprising expert mountain guides from the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) and the Simrik Helicopter team, inspected the tunnel on Saturday as part of rescue efforts.

According to the team, the tunnel is completely blocked by deep muddy sediment and sludge, making entry extremely difficult. Using rope protection and maintaining rope contact, rescuers managed to move around 120–130 metres inside the tunnel.

However, the mud had risen up to their chests, preventing them from advancing further towards the blocked section.

The team said its next plan is to use hose pipes and a pump/motor system to remove the accumulated mud and sludge as quickly as possible. If the blocked section can be cleared, rescuers believe there may be a possibility of reaching those trapped inside.

During the operation, the team also recovered the body of one person outside the tunnel. The Nepal Army took control of the body and transported it from the site.

The rescue team said it would remain on standby and mobilise whenever requested by the Government of Nepal.

The operation was led by mountain guide Ashish Gurung and included Jenjen Lama, Dorji Sherpa, Sabin Thakuri, Tulising Gurung and Pasang Tendi Sherpa.

title.rendered: Chinese expert team deployed for rescue operation at Trishuli 3 ‘B’ tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

A six-member Chinese expert team has been deployed to rescue people trapped inside the tunnel of the flood-hit Upper Trishuli 3 ‘B’ Hydropower Project in Rasuwa.

The Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers said the team arrived in the Trishuli area by a Chinese helicopter after receiving approval from the Nepal government.

The deployment comes as authorities face a highly risky and technically challenging rescue operation inside the tunnel, which was affected by floods.

The Chinese experts will work in coordination with a technical team from the Nepal Army and conduct a technical reconnaissance of the tunnel to assess the situation and the possibility of rescue.

The Prime Minister’s Office said that if the initial assessment shows rescue operations are feasible, additional Chinese experts kept on standby near the Rasuwa border will be brought to the site immediately.

The joint team will begin work after assessing conditions inside the tunnel, where rescue efforts have been complicated by the extent of damage caused by the flood.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood death toll reaches 626, over 2,300 rescued

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

The death toll from the devastating floods in Rasuwa has reached 626, according to Nepal Police.

The police, updating the figures at 2:50 pm on Saturday, said bodies have been recovered from eight districts affected by the floods.The highest number of casualties has been reported in Chitwan, where 233 bodies have been recovered.

Similarly, 158 bodies have been found in Nawalparasi East, 54 in Gorkha, 49 in Dhading, 47 in Nawalparasi West, 41 in Nuwakot, 31 in Tanahun and 13 in Rasuwa, according to police data.Police said 2,301 people have been rescued so far from the affected areas.Among those rescued, 1,622 were from Nuwakot, 676 from Rasuwa and three from Dhading.

The police also said 140 injured people are currently receiving treatment or have been discharged from hospitals in Kathmandu Valley.

Authorities continue search and rescue operations in the flood-affected areas, with several people still reported missing.

title.rendered: Indian technical team deployed for tunnel rescue as Nepal seeks further foreign assistance

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

An 11-member specialist technical team from India has been deployed to assist in the rescue operation at a tunnel following the recent floods, while Nepal expects a specialised team from China to arrive soon.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said on Saturday that the Indian team had already been mobilised and that the government expected a Chinese team with expertise in tunnel rescue to arrive shortly.

Speaking at a press briefing organised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Khanal said the government was seeking necessary international technical assistance to make search and rescue operations more effective.

He said the government was prioritising technical assistance that could be provided by land because of the complex geographical conditions in the affected area.

“Because of the complex terrain and the impact the sudden flood has had on the ground, rescue operations have to be carried out with extreme caution,” Khanal said.

He added that bringing foreign rescue teams by helicopter could be even more difficult because of the challenging geography.

“Since this is unfamiliar terrain for foreign rescue teams, their safety also needs to be given priority. Therefore, the government is conducting rescue operations only on the basis of advice and field information from local security personnel who are already working there and understand the terrain well,” he said.

Khanal said Nepal had sought specialised assistance from friendly countries for the search and rescue of people trapped inside the tunnel.

He added that Nepal had also requested international assistance in identifying and locating people who may still be alive, including access to necessary technology, rapid DNA analysis and the long-term management of recovered bodies.

The government is seeking such international technical support as search and rescue operations continue in the aftermath of the devastating floods.

title.rendered: 187 tourists rescued or accounted for after Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

The number of tourists rescued from flood-affected areas or brought back into contact has reached 187, according to the Nepal Tourism Board.

The board said in its latest update that 184 tourists have been rescued, while three others have been accounted for after previously being out of contact.

However, 420 tourists remain out of contact, according to the board.

Many tourists travelling to Kailash Mansarovar via the Rasuwagadhi border point were reported out of contact after floods hit the area on August 26.

Among those rescued, Indian nationals make up the largest group, with 114 people, according to the Tourism Board.

The rescued tourists include 27 Chinese nationals and 20 South Koreans. Four each are from Germany and Malta, while three each are from the United States and Italy.

The Tourism Board said most roads across the country have resumed operation, except for some sections in flood-affected districts.

It has, however, advised tourists to check weather conditions before travelling, particularly in areas affected by the recent floods.

The board is continuing to monitor the situation and provide updates on tourists affected by the floods.

title.rendered: Want to help Nepal’s flood response? Map buildings from home

content.rendered:
Nepal’s flood response is turning to volunteers far beyond the disaster zone, asking people to map buildings and roads from satellite images to help responders identify affected locations.

The Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT), a global non-profit humanitarian mapping organisation, is working with the Prime Minister’s Office and other partners to map areas affected by the floods and provide geographic information that can support rescue and recovery efforts.

The work may look deceptively simple. A volunteer opens a satellite image, identifies a building and traces its outline on a digital map. Someone else may trace a road or another feature visible in the image.

But repeated thousands of times, those small contributions can produce a detailed map of an area where the landscape may have been radically altered by floodwaters and debris.

“The main goal is to support rescue and recovery operations by providing accurate data to the teams working on the ground,” said Kshitij Sharma, Product Owner at HOT, who said around 181 people are currently involved in the process.

HOT is working with local partners to identify priority areas for mapping. Volunteers from around the world can then work remotely on those areas, using satellite imagery to map buildings and other visible features.

The resulting maps are open-source and freely available to humanitarian organisations, government agencies, UN bodies and rapid-response teams.

Sharma said mapping has almost been completed along the upper corridor of the Bhote Koshi, from Rasuwagadhi down to around Bidur.

“The mapping of the lower corridor is now starting, and we need as many people as possible to join the process so that it is easier for responders and the government to use the information,” he said.

How the mapping works

Volunteers do not need to map an entire disaster-affected area. The mapping platform breaks the work into small tasks that can be completed individually.

Each task comes with instructions explaining how to identify and map features in the satellite imagery. Tasks are available at different levels of difficulty, allowing people with no previous mapping experience to begin with simpler assignments.

An easy task can take about 10 to 15 minutes.

Once a volunteer submits their work, experienced mappers review and validate it before it becomes part of the wider map.

“People don’t have to be on the ground to contribute. They can map small areas from home using satellite imagery, and those contributions can become useful information for responders,” Sharma said.

For people unsure where to begin, HOT has prepared a tutorial video that walks volunteers through the process. It explains how to sign up, choose a mapping task, map buildings and map roads.

The platform also provides a visual indication of the work still to be done. Areas that have already been mapped appear in blue, while areas that still require mapping appear in white.

The map is updated as volunteers complete and submit tasks, with the resulting data shared with rescuers and government agencies, who are provided with the latitude and longitude coordinates of mapped locations.

Why mapping matters after a flood

A flood can change a landscape in hours.

Buildings may be damaged or covered by debris. Roads and other familiar landmarks may become difficult to identify. For people trying to assess an affected area from the ground, knowing what stood there before the disaster can be crucial.

Satellite imagery provides one way of establishing that picture.

Mappers can compare imagery from before and after a disaster to identify buildings and other structures and document changes. They can then record the precise location of those structures using geographic coordinates, including latitude and longitude.

That information can help responders focus on particular locations rather than searching an entire affected area.

“We can tell responders, ‘This is where a building was located,’ and provide the coordinates so they can go and check that specific location,” Sharma said.

A mapped building does not by itself tell responders whether anyone is inside or whether a rescue is required. But it can give them a precise location to investigate — particularly in places where flooding and debris have altered the landscape.

The same information can later be used to assess the scale of destruction and support longer-term recovery planning.

A crowd working from thousands of kilometres away

The strength of the system lies in its numbers.

Volunteers can work on different tasks simultaneously, allowing large areas to be mapped without requiring everyone to be in the disaster zone. Experienced members of the international mapping community then validate the work.

“When more people work on the mapping at the same time, we can cover much larger areas and provide information more quickly,” Sharma said.

HOT has carried out similar humanitarian mapping operations following disasters in countries including Venezuela and Turkey. The organisation says its global community includes hundreds of thousands of contributors.

For someone sitting at home, tracing the outline of a building on a satellite image may seem like a small act.

But disaster response often depends on thousands of such pieces of information being brought together.

For people who want to support Nepal’s flood response but cannot travel to the affected areas, humanitarian mapping offers a way to contribute remotely.

All that is needed to start is a computer, an internet connection and about 10 to 15 minutes.

Want to help? Watch the tutorial, choose a task and start mapping Nepal’s flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: Nepal weighs foreign rescue offers as over 12 countries pledge Rasuwa flood aid

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

More than 12 countries have sought permission from the Nepali government to provide emergency assistance and participate in rescue operations for people affected by the Rasuwa floods.

India, China, the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Australia, Turkey, South Korea and Japan are among the countries that have offered assistance.

They have mainly proposed three types of support: emergency rescue operations, medical assistance and financial aid.

Bangladesh and Sri Lanka have particularly emphasized providing medical assistance, while the other countries have offered emergency rescue teams and other rapid-response support.

The Nepal government is prepared to accept the second and third types of assistance—medical and financial aid. However, it does not appear immediately willing to accept foreign involvement in emergency rescue operations.

The concerns expressed by the Nepali Army, which is leading rescue operations on the ground, as well as the government’s geopolitical considerations and past experiences, appear to be influencing this position.

According to government sources, Nepal wants to rely on its own capacity for two main reasons.

First, addressing the landslides and floods originating in the mountainous region near the Chinese border requires operations in deep gorges and narrow valleys.

Government officials say the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police possess the necessary geographical knowledge and expertise. In particular, the Nepali Army’s experience, courage and capacity in disaster response are considered key factors.

Second, officials say that some countries involved in disaster assistance in the past had displayed geopolitical interests, both directly and indirectly. While they initially appeared focused on humanitarian rescue, there were concerns that they might seek to prolong their presence even after their assistance was no longer required.

Government officials cite attempts to take control of the tower at Tribhuvan International Airport for security purposes following the April 2015 earthquake as one of the clearest examples.

“It may not be very difficult for anyone to travel from Bidur to Betrawati, but reaching the areas from Syabrubesi to Rasuwagadhi, where more extensive rescue operations are needed, is another matter. Instead, we may end up having to manage them,” a senior army official told Onlinekhabar.

“Our time could be spent coordinating with teams that are supposed to be working independently. That could also affect the rescue operations already underway.”

The military official said flying helicopters through narrow gorges and valleys is difficult and that there are no suitable landing areas for large helicopters such as the Mi-17. The official added that countries offering emergency rescue assistance may not be prepared to operate without helicopters and suggested that it would be better for them not to deploy under the current circumstances.

Government officials, however, said Nepal has requested assistance from two countries for rescue operations involving tunnels.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal told Onlinekhabar, “We have already sent timely requests to India and China for the assistance needed to rescue employees, workers and experts trapped in tunnels. We have received positive responses from both sides. Something may happen soon.”

Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said on Friday that India stands in solidarity with Nepal over the disaster and is ready to provide the necessary response and assistance.

He made the remarks after personally meeting Indian citizens who had escaped the flood risk while returning from Gosainkunda and Kailash Mansarovar.

At another meeting held at his ministry, Jaishankar said that Indian embassies in Kathmandu and Beijing were providing necessary information and developing strategies for rapid action. However, he did not specify what those actions would involve.

Nepali officials believe Jaishankar’s reference to rapid action may relate to rescuing employees and workers trapped inside tunnels.

The Nepali Army also appears more flexible about accepting assistance from the two neighbouring countries for tunnel rescue operations. Another government official indicated that emergency rescue teams from India and China could arrive soon.

“Teams also came during the earthquake, so this is nothing unusual,” the official said. “Humanitarian rescue is the first priority during a disaster.”

Nepali Army spokesperson and Director of the Directorate of Public Relations and Information, Assistant Rathi Rajaram Basnet, said the army had deployed its entire team for emergency rescue and search operations and that the government should decide matters concerning international coordination.

“All our teams are in the field. Even though I am the spokesperson, I am personally involved in rescue operations in the Trishuli area,” he said. “Whether those wishing to participate in rescue operations should be granted permission is not our decision. We are carrying out our responsibilities.”

Basnet said the army’s rescue teams were aware of the situation in the tunnels. However, complete information has not yet been consolidated because some tunnels remain blocked, some people who may have escaped have not yet made contact, and communication links have been disrupted.

“We have used our expertise as much as possible. On Friday alone, we opened an exit point of Trishuli Three A and rescued four people,” Basnet said.

“However, the floods have completely changed the terrain. There is no way to take bulldozers and cranes to the affected areas. Even though we have equipment, the mud has made it difficult to identify locations.”

Basnet said knowledge of the geography of the affected areas, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, was extremely important and indicated that those seeking to join emergency rescue operations should take this factor into consideration.

Some observers have expressed concerns that, despite disaster response being an area of expertise for the Nepali Army, the government could use the army’s role to demonstrate political activism. The army, however, has rejected such concerns.

The army said it had repeatedly carried out disaster response operations in the past and challenged critics to provide examples of instances where it had subsequently shown political interest.

Critics have often commented that Prime Minister Balen Shah and his government are particularly close to the military. They have cited Shah’s past remarks welcoming the army’s role during his tenure as Kathmandu mayor and during the Gen Z movement.

However, senior government officials have urged people not to view the matter with suspicion.

“Where our capacity is insufficient, we must use the skills of those who are good at disaster response,” a government official said. “We should make maximum use of the army and police. If it becomes too difficult, we must consider other options.”

However, the government has little time to consider alternatives.

Bodies swept away from Rasuwa and Nuwakot have begun to be found as far away as Chitwan and Nawalparasi and even along riverbanks in India. There are growing concerns about decomposing bodies and the possible outbreak of disease.

Those who have narrowly survived could also face further danger if they are not rescued in time or if another possible flood occurs.

According to official figures, 579 people have died so far in the floods that struck on Wednesday morning. Injured people, including those who have suffered permanent injuries, continue to arrive at hospitals, while others are receiving treatment. A complete list of missing persons has not yet been released, and the death toll continues to rise.

More than 500 of those affected by the Rasuwa floods are citizens of 33 countries. Their respective governments have also expressed concern about their nationals and sought permission from Nepal to participate in rescue operations.

The floods began after a mountain collapse on Nepali territory above the Lhende River in the Nepal-China border region. The disaster also caused heavy casualties on the Chinese side after the floods crossed the border.

The sensitivity of the area, given its proximity to the Chinese border, appears to have made Nepali authorities particularly cautious.

China is also believed to have taken note of international organizations depicting the area as Tibetan territory and foreign media referring only to Tibet rather than China.

According to a high-level source, China is unhappy with attempts to geopoliticize what it considers a humanitarian rescue issue. Analysts say this could also affect international emergency rescue assistance.

title.rendered: When disaster becomes a pretext for disinformation

content.rendered:
The devastating debris flow that struck the Nepal–China border region on August 26 has brought enormous human suffering to communities on both sides of the Himalayas. Lives have been lost, hundreds of people remain missing, roads and infrastructure have been destroyed, and rescue workers are risking their own lives in extremely difficult terrain to search for survivors.

At such a moment, the most basic human response should be sympathy for the victims, respect for the missing, support for rescue operations and cooperation across the border.

Unfortunately, alongside the disaster itself, another disturbing phenomenon has emerged: the rapid circulation of politically charged rumours and speculation attempting to blame the disaster on Chinese construction, Chinese infrastructure or even an alleged deliberate attempt by China to create an “ecological disaster.”

Such claims are not merely irresponsible. When presented without credible scientific evidence, they represent the insertion of geopolitical narratives directly into disaster reporting.

Science cannot be replaced by political imagination

One widely circulated narrative claims that Chinese construction activities in the Himalayan region caused an avalanche, which then triggered flooding and debris flows. Various versions point to road construction, settlements, border infrastructure, mountain excavation or changes to river channels.

But where is the scientific evidence?

Establishing the cause of a high-altitude cascading disaster requires serious investigation involving glaciology, geology, geomorphology, hydrology, meteorology, remote sensing and field surveys. Scientists need to determine where the initial collapse occurred, what material was involved, how much ice, rock and debris was mobilised, how the mass entered the river system, and how the disaster evolved as it moved downstream.

None of these questions can be answered by looking at photographs of construction projects and then drawing a politically convenient conclusion.

Correlation is not causation. Proximity is not causation. And political suspicion certainly is not causation.

To jump from “there is Chinese construction in the region” to “Chinese construction caused the disaster” is not scientific reasoning. It is speculation searching for evidence after the conclusion has already been chosen.

Even more astonishing is the description of the disaster as a “purposeful ecological disaster.” Such an accusation requires extraordinarily strong evidence. Without such evidence, it crosses the line from speculation into conspiracy theory.

Journalists spreading such claims might benefit from spending less time imagining geopolitical plots and more time reading basic books on geology, glaciology and hydrology.

The Himalayas deserve scientific respect, not political fantasy.

A natural dam is not a Chinese reservoir

Another misleading narrative circulating online concerns the word “dam.”

Reports referring to a “dam burst” or “dam collapse” have easily been transformed on social media into claims that a Chinese hydropower dam collapsed or that China deliberately released water from a reservoir.

This is a fundamental confusion of terminology.

In mountainous disaster environments, a “landslide dam” or “debris dam” can be formed naturally when rock, ice, mud or debris suddenly blocks a river valley. Water then accumulates behind this natural obstruction, creating a landslide-dammed lake. If the blockage becomes unstable, it may breach and produce severe downstream flooding.

That is entirely different from an engineered hydropower dam or reservoir.

Turning “landslide dam” into “Chinese dam,” and then turning “dam breach” into “China released water,” is not a minor translation problem. Once repeated in headlines and social media posts, it creates an entirely false causal narrative for ordinary readers.

Words matter, especially during disasters.

A journalist who cannot distinguish a landslide dam from a hydropower dam should first consult a geologist or hydrologist before publishing sensational claims to millions of readers.

“Most likely” is not evidence

Perhaps even more troubling is the tendency of some reports to place conclusions such as “most likely” directly into sensational headlines while providing no independent scientific evidence capable of supporting that probability.

Most likely according to whom? Which geological survey? Which satellite analysis? Which glaciological investigation? Which peer-reviewed assessment? Which team of scientists has established the causal relationship?

If the principal evidence consists of social media posts repeating allegations from other social media accounts, adding the phrase “most likely” does not transform speculation into fact.

Journalism has professional standards precisely because the public cannot independently verify every claim appearing on a screen.

A headline is not a laboratory. Repetition is not verification. Suspicion is not evidence. And “most likely” cannot be used as a rhetorical shortcut to manufacture certainty where scientific certainty does not exist.

To do so is deeply misleading to the public and contrary to the basic ethics of professional journalism.

Any media organisation willing to put such a conclusion into a headline without sufficient evidence should seriously reflect on its professional standards.

Do not turn human suffering into a geopolitical weapon

There is an even more important issue.

People on both sides of the Nepal–China border are suffering.

Families are waiting for news of missing relatives. Rescue personnel are entering dangerous areas covered by deep mud and unstable debris. Roads have been destroyed. Rivers remain dangerous. Mountain slopes are unstable. A landslide-dammed lake poses additional risks. Hundreds of rescuers are working against time while facing the possibility of further rainfall, landslides and flash floods.

Against this background, using the tragedy as an opportunity to manufacture hostility between China and Nepal is particularly disturbing.

Natural disasters should not become convenient raw material for geopolitical confrontation.

When every avalanche becomes a political conspiracy, every flood becomes evidence of another country’s malicious intentions, and every natural dam becomes a “Chinese dam,” disaster reporting ceases to inform. It becomes propaganda disguised as journalism.

This violates not only journalistic professionalism but also the humanitarian spirit that should guide public communication during a catastrophe.

Before asking how a tragedy can be exploited politically, we should be asking: Where are the missing? How can rescue teams reach them? What caused the disaster scientifically? Is another collapse possible? How can downstream communities be protected? What information should China and Nepal share? How can future cross-border early-warning systems be improved?

Those are the questions that matter.

The Himalayas need cooperation, not conspiracy theories

The Himalayas are one of the world’s most complex and fragile high-mountain environments. Glaciers, steep valleys, earthquakes, intense rainfall, landslides, ice avalanches, glacial lakes and rapidly changing river systems interact across national borders.

Nature does not recognise immigration checkpoints.

An avalanche does not carry a passport. A debris flow does not understand geopolitics. Floodwater does not distinguish between Chinese and Nepali territory.

That is precisely why the correct response to this disaster is cooperation.

China and Nepal need stronger cross-border disaster monitoring, hydrological information sharing, satellite and remote-sensing cooperation, geological risk assessment, emergency communication mechanisms and coordinated early-warning systems.

Scientists should investigate what happened. Rescue workers should be allowed to do their work. Journalists should verify before accusing. Governments should share information. And the international community should support, rather than politicise, disaster relief.

Above all, we should retain a sense of humility before nature.

The mountains are powerful enough without humans inventing conspiracies around them.

Rumours will not rescue a single missing person. Sensational headlines will not stabilise a landslide-dammed lake. Geopolitical manipulation will not prevent another debris flow.

And attempts to exploit a shared tragedy to sow suspicion between the Chinese and Nepali peoples will not destroy a friendship built through generations of exchanges across the Himalayas.

In the face of disaster, what is needed is not finger-pointing but helping hands; not conspiracy theories but scientific investigation; not political manipulation but humanitarian responsibility.

Respect nature. Respect science. Respect the victims. and work together. That is what this tragedy demands of all of us
