title.rendered: A mountain fell. A flood followed. Two nations bled.

content.rendered:
A glacier broke. A valley flooded. Two countries are burying their dead together. This is the truth of Langtang Lirung. Everything else — every rumor, every unverified claim, every attempt to turn grief into a geopolitical weapon — is noise the dead and the missing cannot afford.

Rescue teams are still digging. The final toll is not known. Families in Nepal and China wait by the same rivers for the same news. This is not the moment for blame. It is the moment for facts, for science, for solidarity. Nothing else serves the people still buried in the debris.

The facts

On August 26, a mass of ice and rock broke free near the summit of Langtang Lirung. It fell 5,200 meters into the Lhende Khola, a headwater stream on the Nepal-China border. The debris dammed the valley. The dam broke. A wall of mud and water tore down the Bhote Koshi and the Trishuli, and slammed into the Rasuwagadhi-Gyirong crossing twenty kilometers below.

This is the deadliest transboundary disaster the Himalaya has seen in years. By the afternoon of August 29, Nepal counted 616 dead, up from 390 a day before. China counted five dead. More than 2,000 people are still missing on both sides. A new lake had formed above the wreckage, at the meeting of the Chhochen Khola and the Purepu Tsangpo. It held 2 million cubic meters of water. Three million more will arrive within three days. China’s Ministry of Water Resources has warned it could breach. A second flood may follow the first. However, the dam has broken, and the flow was less than expected. Both Nepal and China are monitoring the flow.

These are not political facts. They are physical facts. A natural disaster struck two nations at once. Neither chose it. Neither controls it. Both are burying their people because of it.

The lie

Within hours, a claim spread online. A “geological disaster dam,” it said, had collapsed on the Chinese side and sent the flood into Nepal. China’s embassy in Kathmandu called it what it was: fake news. “An earthquake or earthquake-like glacier collapse occurred on the Nepali side of the border,” the embassy said, “triggering huge mudslides.” Then it added the only sentence that matters here: “Accusation helps nothing. Cooperation saves lives.”

The science backs this without qualification. USGS first logged a magnitude-4.4 seismic signal and mistook it for an earthquake. It corrected itself. The signal was a magnitude-5.2 landslide — the shockwave of ice and rock hitting rock, not tectonic plates shifting. Satellite images confirm the scar on Langtang Lirung’s Nepali flank. The flood ran downhill, from Nepal into China, not the other way. Water does not run uphill. Debris does not cross a border against gravity to blame the victim on the other side. This is not a matter of opinion. It is a matter of physics.

Let this be stated without hedging: spreading an unverified, geographically impossible claim about a neighbor’s infrastructure, in the middle of an active rescue operation, is not journalism. It is not analysis. It is a lie, and lies do not save lives. Whoever profits from that lie — in clicks, in outrage, in strategic advantage — profits off bodies still being pulled from mud. That should disqualify the claim from serious conversation, full stop.

Nepal and China have built roads and trade links across this same mountain range for years. Those links save lives when disaster strikes, because they move relief supplies and rescue teams across a border in hours, not weeks. Anyone spreading disinformation to poison that cooperation is not defending Nepal. They are undermining it. The Nepali people deserve solidarity and support in this dire hour, not a flood of falsehoods designed to serve someone else’s rivalry with China.

The real question

Not every question is a lie. Some are fair, and fairness requires saying so plainly.

Some Nepali journalists have asked, by name, whether China’s satellite capacity could have caught the danger sooner. That is a legitimate question. It deserves a real answer, not a dismissal.

Here is the honest answer. Nepal’s hydrology department and China’s meteorological agency had already agreed to share information more closely before this disaster hit. The failure was not a total absence of cooperation. It was scope. It was speed. No system yet exists built to catch a fast-moving ice avalanche, far upstream, hours before it reaches a village. The gap was not warning capacity. It was timing.

That is a solvable problem. Solve it, and this becomes the last disaster of its kind that catches both countries unprepared. Wave it away as propaganda, and it becomes the next one too.

China showed up

On August 28, President Xi Jinping sent a message of condolence to Nepal’s President, Ram Chandra Poudel. “On behalf of the Chinese government and the Chinese people,” Xi wrote, he offered deep condolences to the victims and sympathy to the bereaved, the injured, and the affected. China was doing everything in its power, he said, to search for the missing, resettle the displaced, treat the wounded, and prevent further disaster — a direct reference to the swelling lake above the valley. “China and Nepal are connected by mountains and rivers,” Xi wrote, “and share a common destiny.” China would help “within its capacity.” The two peoples, he said, would “join hands to overcome the disaster and rebuild their homes.”

The same day, Premier Li Qiang sent his own message to Nepal’s Prime Minister, Balendra Shah — 36 years old, a former Kathmandu mayor, now facing the defining test of his young premiership.

These were not just words. Vice Premier Zhang Guoqing went to Gyirong to see the damage himself. Li Qiang followed him there, in person, to direct relief work and meet the people who lost everything. China’s embassy in Kathmandu opened emergency channels and sent supplies and funds to Nepal — while its own people were still searching for their missing. India sent aircraft, heavy equipment, and medicine. The United States offered help. The World Bank pledged roughly 25 billion Nepali rupees. None of this required a villain. A flood born of a melting glacier does not check passports. Ambassador Zhang Maoming said it plainly on August 27: mountains and rivers connect us. That is not a slogan. It is a description of geography, and geography does not lie.

Turn grief into cooperation

Every disaster is also a choice. Nepal and China can let this one become another round of blame that fades in a week. Or they can let it become the moment the region finally builds what it should have built years ago.

Ambassador Zhang has already named the path. First, real cross-border monitoring of glaciers, weather, and geology, so a warning moves as fast as the danger does. Second, a standing joint emergency-response mechanism, with open channels ready before disaster strikes, not negotiated while it unfolds. Third, shared training and shared technology, so the knowledge held in Beijing and Kathmandu reaches the district officer standing closest to the next collapsing glacier.

None of this is new in theory. It has been discussed for years across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. What is new is the cost of not doing it — measured now in hundreds of lives, and in a lake still filling above the Bhote Koshi as this is written. Let Langtang Lirung be the disaster that finally forces the decision. Let it be the catalyst, not the casus belli. The people who live in these mountains — Nepali and Chinese and Indian alike — share the same glaciers, the same rivers, and the same warming climate. They deserve leaders and neighbors who treat this as one shared emergency, not a contest to be won. That is the only response equal to what has been lost, and the only one that will do any good the next time a mountain falls.

title.rendered: 616 bodies recovered from Rasuwa flood, 2,301 rescued

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

The bodies of 616 people reported missing after the devastating flood in Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi River on August 26 have been recovered, Nepal Police said.

As of 7 am Saturday, 616 bodies had been recovered from various locations, according to police.

Of the recovered bodies, 13 were found in Rasuwa, 41 in Nuwakot, 45 in Dhading, 233 in Chitwan, 48 in Gorkha, 31 in Tanahun, 158 in Nawalparasi East and 47 in Nawalparasi West.

Police said 2,301 people have so far been rescued from different locations affected by the flood.

Of those rescued, 676 were from Rasuwa, 1,622 from Nuwakot and three from Dhading.

title.rendered: Chaudhary Foundation, Nabil Bank announce Rs 150 million flood relief and rehabilitation plan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 29

The Chaudhary Foundation and Nabil Bank have announced a multi-phase relief and rehabilitation programme worth approximately Rs 150 million for communities affected by the devastating floods in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

The programme will focus on immediate relief, temporary housing, healthcare and long-term rehabilitation of flood-affected communities.

Under the first phase, the organisations will distribute food, drinking water, clothes, tarpaulins, personal hygiene products and other essential supplies to affected families. Relief supplies began reaching affected areas on August 27, with employees of the foundation and bank mobilised to support the distribution.

Two relief camps will also be established in Nuwakot and Rasuwa in coordination with local administrations. The camps will provide daily meals, clean drinking water, sanitation facilities and safe spaces for children.

The Chaudhary Foundation and Nabil Bank will also work with Dhulikhel Hospital to operate health camps providing primary healthcare and disease-prevention services in the affected areas.

The second phase will involve constructing 500 temporary housing units for families whose homes were completely destroyed or made uninhabitable by the floods.

The temporary shelters will be built in coordination with the federal and local governments and will provide affected families with safe and dignified accommodation until permanent reconstruction is completed. The organisations said the shelters will use technology previously deployed by the Chaudhary Foundation during earthquake relief efforts.

The programme will also support the construction of permanent shelters and essential community infrastructure in affected areas.

As part of its long-term health initiative, the foundation and bank will collaborate with Dhulikhel Hospital to establish a Center for Infectious Disease Prevention and Control. The centre will focus on disease surveillance, preventive healthcare, public awareness and strengthening institutional capacity to respond to infectious diseases and outbreaks following floods and other disasters.

Nirvana Chaudhary, chairman of the Chaudhary Foundation and Nabil Bank, said the organisations’ immediate priority was to protect lives and provide food, shelter and healthcare to affected families.

“Our responsibility should not be limited to emergency relief,” Chaudhary said. “Through this partnership between Chaudhary Foundation and Nabil Bank, we are committed to the entire journey from rescue and relief to temporary shelter, permanent rehabilitation, and strong public health preparedness.”

Officials from the foundation and bank will coordinate with the government, local administrations, security agencies, health workers, community organisations and volunteers to ensure assistance reaches the most affected and vulnerable families.

The organisations said the initiative is intended to support the government’s relief and rehabilitation efforts and help affected communities recover and become more resilient to future disasters.

title.rendered: As flood swept through Nuwakot school, teachers raced to save their students

content.rendered:
Uttargaya, Nuwakot, August 28

It was a normal morning at Uttargaya Public School in Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot, on August 26.

Students in school uniforms were making their way towards the school. Those staying in the hostel were eating breakfast in their uniforms. Some were playing on the school ground, while others had been attending early-morning tuition classes. Teachers were preparing for the day’s classes.

Then a loud cry suddenly echoed through the school.

“The flood is coming, and it’s taking everything on its way! Everybody run!”, somebody yelled.

At first, many students did not understand what was happening. Some teachers were left stunned.

But when they saw the torrent rising from the river and seemingly covering the sky, the teachers realised they had to get the students to safety.

Teachers and staff began rushing students towards the higher ground above the school. Students from Grades 7 to 10 ran on their own, while teachers pushed younger children towards the hill, carrying some of them in their arms.

But the efforts could not fully outrun the devastating flood that came from Rasuwa.

The flood reached students fleeing towards the nearby forest. Those who could not escape in time were swept away in seconds.

According to Uttargaya’s vice-principal Pawan Sharma, more than 370 students were enrolled at the school. But the school has so far been able to establish contact with only around 40 percent of them.

“About 25 to 30 percent have been handed over to their parents,” Sharma told Onlinekhabar. “We have also spoken to the parents of the remaining students.”

Sharma is still struggling to come to terms with what happened.

Parents of students who came to school that morning but have not returned home continue to contact him. But there is little he can offer them beyond reassurance.

“Relatives of students are contacting us from both inside and outside the country. But I don’t even have records of those children with me now,” Sharma said emotionally. “The relationship between students and teachers is always an intimate one. Losing even one student feels like losing an entire family.”

Another teacher, Somlal Dangol, said it was still impossible to determine exactly how many students were caught in the flood.

The flood struck around the time of the school’s morning assembly, leaving little time for students to react.

“Nobody had imagined that such a huge flood would come,” Dangol told Onlinekhabar. “That is why many did not run very far. By the time they saw the flood, they could no longer escape.”

Father swept away while rushing to save his son

As soon as Nawaraj Tamang learned that a massive flood was approaching, he rushed towards Uttargaya.

His only intention was to save his son, Ayush Tamang, a Grade 10 student at the school.

But Nawaraj was swept away before he could reach the school.

According to his mother, Mungsi Tamang, Nawaraj had been returning home from the market when he spoke to his son.

She said she became relieved when Nawaraj told her, “Mother, I have come to get Ayush.”

But moments later, she received devastating news.

“Your son has been swept away by the flood.”

“My son was swept away by the river,” Mungsi said through tears. “I had two sons. Now only one is left.”

Ayush said he did not know that his father was coming to get him. He had managed to escape towards the nearby forest after following his teacher’s instructions.

“Only a few of my friends ran with me. I don’t know what happened to the others,” Ayush told his grandmother, asking her not to cry.

Students who narrowly escaped

Grade 10 student Sujal Lama had just finished tuition and was heading to eat when the alarm about the flood spread.

At first, he continued towards the dining area, apparently not realising how serious the situation was.

Then he looked towards the river and ran straight towards the forest.

“When the teacher said the river was coming, I thought it wouldn’t be that big,” Sujal said. “But it was huge. If I had gone to eat, the flood would have caught me.”

He spent the night in the forest and was later given food by teachers.

“I will go home today,” he said.

Grade 8 student Rashmi Tamang also said she survived only because she managed to reach the forest in time.

“We climbed up even though we were covered in mud,” she said. “But many children couldn’t even run.”

title.rendered: Students escaped before flood destroyed Trishuli school; 15 still await rescue

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 28

The devastating flood in the Trishuli River swept away Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot on Wednesday. But the quick response of the school’s principal and staff ensured that all students were evacuated from the school before the flood struck.

No student was swept away inside the school premises.

However, a group of around 40–50 students and staff, along with Principal Rajendra Dawadi, became stranded after fleeing towards the hills. They remained there for three days, waiting for rescue after communication links were severed by the flooding.

Dawadi and the stranded students were finally rescued on Friday, the third day after the flood.

“I have also reached Battar now. When we fled the school, we climbed towards the hill. We stayed there, managing whatever we could. We were almost stranded,” Dawadi told Onlinekhabar.

“There were around 40–50 students and staff with me. We were all rescued today.”

15 more students waiting for rescue

Dawadi said around 15 other students who had also fled towards higher ground remain stranded in another location.

Some students who had left the school during the evacuation had sought shelter with relatives or elsewhere. After hearing that Dawadi and his group had been rescued, some of them also gathered at the same location.

“I have already asked the Army to rescue them,” he said. “They said it would not be possible today and that they would do it throughout tomorrow.”

Dawadi said only two or three students are believed to have not yet reached their parents.

However, in some cases, it has been impossible to establish contact because the homes where students had been sent were themselves swept away by the flood.

“If their houses and the entire market have been washed away, it is difficult to say what happened to those children and their parents,” he said. “There has been no way to contact them. But we are in contact with the others.”

Two school employees—teacher Santosh Pariyar and an office assistant—also remain out of contact, Dawadi said.

Three days without electricity or supplies

Dawadi said the stranded students and staff had to spend several difficult days on higher ground without electricity or easy access to food and other supplies.

“We are now in a relatively safe place. I have reached my own house near the barracks,” he said. “There was no electricity at the place where we stayed for the past two days.”

As the flood began sweeping away the market below, people who could escape climbed towards higher ground. But even there, conditions remained difficult as roads and bridges were cut off.

Local residents and clubs prepared food at a covered hall and distributed it to those stranded. Dawadi said they also stayed together at a church.

‘I don’t have many complaints about the rescue’

Dawadi said he did not believe the state had been slow in carrying out rescue operations.

“From what we could see, those who were visible outside their houses or in other exposed places had already been rescued,” he said. “There had not been much excavation work inside the affected areas.”

He said his group had deliberately remained at a higher elevation for safety, particularly amid reports that another lake upstream could burst.

“Considering the circumstances, I think the state’s response has been reasonable. I don’t feel that the rescue was delayed,” he said.

Dawadi, however, suggested that authorities prioritise people still trapped in places that are difficult to access.

“We survived and managed our food ourselves. But it would be better to prioritise people trapped in rivers, on roads and in places where bodies have been found,” he said.

“I don’t have many complaints. I feel the state is doing what it can with the resources available.”

Relief supplies reach Battar

After being rescued, Dawadi said those brought to Battar were receiving basic health checks before being handed over to their relatives.

“Those rescued are having their blood pressure checked and undergoing basic examinations before being handed over to their families,” he said.

Patients in serious condition have been flown to Kathmandu by helicopter, while ambulances are also transporting patients directly to the capital.

Large quantities of food and relief materials have also been stockpiled in the area.

“Yesterday, we were in a situation where we did not even have food,” Dawadi said. “If the relief materials arriving here could reach the people where we were yesterday, it would help them greatly.”

Remaining students are in Bidur

The remaining 15 students are believed to be staying in Bidur Municipality-9, near a hospital at an area locally known as the 3D Ground, where helicopters have been operating rescue and evacuation flights.

“Two or three of my teacher colleagues are with them,” Dawadi said. “I have already spoken to the administration here. They have said they will try to rescue them today if possible, or throughout tomorrow.”

He said the students may be under some psychological stress after spending days waiting for rescue.

“Otherwise, even if they are rescued by tomorrow, they should be fine,” he said.

The students are all Plus Two-level students, meaning they are aged 16 or above.

“They are reportedly sitting there watching the helicopters flying overhead,” Dawadi said. “I would urge everyone to make every effort to rescue all of them as quickly as possible.”

title.rendered: Flood bodies overwhelm Bharatpur Hospital as morgues run out of space

content.rendered:
Bharatpur, August 28

Bharatpur Hospital is struggling to manage a rapidly increasing number of bodies recovered from the Rasuwa flood, with its forensic department working under extreme pressure.

Four forensic teams have been conducting post-mortems continuously. While the hospital had yet to complete processing all the bodies that arrived on Thursday, another 50 bodies were brought in on Friday.

According to Dr Bishwabandhu Bagale, chief medical superintendent of Bharatpur Hospital, 137 bodies had reached the hospital by Thursday evening. The number was expected to reach around 200 by Friday evening.

But the hospital does not have the capacity to store such a large number of bodies.

“We have freezers that can hold only 24 bodies,” Bagale said. “Most of them are occupied by unclaimed bodies, with only two or four spaces usually available. We simply do not have the capacity to manage bodies on this scale during a disaster.”

The post-mortem building and its premises were already full on Thursday, forcing the hospital to keep some bodies outside the mortuary. Hospital staff had also been unable to move all the bodies from vehicles to designated areas.

“We are trying to complete the identification and legal procedures as quickly as possible,” Bagale said.

Intact bodies prioritised for identification

The bodies recovered from the flood are in varying conditions. Some can still be identified, while others have started decomposing or are severely damaged after remaining in water for a long time.

The hospital has prioritised bodies that are relatively intact and where identification is possible.

“We are first working on bodies that are intact and can potentially be identified,” Bagale said. “Once a body is identified, it can be handed over to the family for cremation.”

Forensic experts are conducting post-mortems and collecting fingerprints, photographs, videos and details of distinguishing marks on the bodies.

Initially, only two forensic teams were working at Bharatpur Hospital. As the number of bodies increased, the hospital sought assistance from other institutions.

Forensic experts from Bheri Hospital, hospitals in the Lumbini region and Nepal Medical College, among others, are now working alongside the hospital’s teams.

Bodies kept in corridors begin to decompose

With the hospital’s 24 freezers unable to handle the volume, alternative arrangements have been made to store the bodies.

Bodies that cannot be accommodated in the freezers have been kept in corridors and outside areas covered with tarpaulins. Police have cordoned off the areas and restricted public access.

“We have not been able to maintain the required temperature, but we have managed the security aspect,” Bagale said.

The high temperatures have caused some bodies to begin decomposing. Bagale said some of the bodies brought in on Thursday evening had already started to deteriorate.

“Not all the bodies have started decomposing at the same time, but the process has begun in some,” he said. “The extreme heat has accelerated decomposition.”

Bodies moved to temporary facility after post-mortem

Bodies that have undergone post-mortem and initial identification procedures are being moved to a government building near the Chitwan Industrial Association.

An air-conditioned temporary body management centre is being prepared there, with racks being installed to store the bodies.

By Friday afternoon, around 58 bodies had undergone post-mortem, fingerprint collection and other initial procedures and had been transferred to the facility.

Arrangements have also been made to help relatives identify missing family members.

Photographs, videos and distinguishing physical marks of the bodies have been displayed for relatives searching for their loved ones. If a person believes they have recognised someone, they can note the body number and inform the police.

The police then facilitate the process of showing the corresponding body to the relative.

“We are doing whatever we can in this disaster,” Bagale said.

553 bodies recovered, 977 still missing

As of the preparation of this report, 553 bodies had been recovered in connection with the Rasuwa flood.

Of these, 13 were recovered in Rasuwa, 38 in Nuwakot, 40 in Dhading, 44 in Gorkha, 134 in Nawalpur, 28 in Nawalparasi, 29 in Tanahun and 221 in Chitwan—the highest number.

Most of the bodies have yet to be identified.

The sudden recovery of a large number of bodies has overwhelmed mortuaries in several hospitals. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 977 people remain missing.

How are the bodies being examined?

A total of 25 bodies have so far been brought to Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu. Five have been identified and handed over to their families after post-mortem.

The remaining 20 bodies are undergoing data collection, documentation of identifying features and DNA sampling.

According to Dr Chaudhary, the hospital is recording physical characteristics and other information that could help establish the identities of unidentified bodies.

“Twenty-five bodies have arrived so far. Five have been identified and handed over to their families after post-mortem,” he said. “For the remaining 20, we are collecting data, identification markers and DNA samples.”

Forensic examination does not necessarily mean that every body must be cut open, doctors say.

Post-mortem is a detailed examination conducted after death. In this case, the external condition of the body, facial features, clothing, injuries and other distinguishing characteristics are also being documented.

“Not every body needs to be cut open,” Chaudhary said. “The cause of death in this incident is largely clear. The main challenge now is identification. Internal examination is carried out only when necessary for identification.”

Medical implants and other metal objects inside the body can also help identify victims. Plates, rods, prostheses or other materials inserted during previous medical treatment can provide important identification clues.

When a body has severely decomposed or the face can no longer be recognised, dental examination, fingerprints and, as a final option, DNA testing can be used.

The hospital is preserving DNA samples from unidentified bodies and collecting and storing other relevant information. These will be compared with information and scientific evidence provided by families and relatives.

“Bodies that are badly decomposed or damaged cannot be identified simply by looking at them,” Chaudhary said. “In such cases, dental records, fingerprints or DNA testing are necessary. A body should be handed over to the family only after identification is confirmed through DNA when required.”

Health Ministry preparing temporary mortuaries

According to Health Ministry spokesperson Dr Samir Adhikari, hospitals across the country have the capacity to accommodate more than 600 bodies combined.

However, much of that capacity cannot be immediately utilised because of geographical distances.

“If we add the capacity of all hospitals across the country, it is more than 600,” Adhikari said. “But that capacity is not available where it is currently needed. Capacity in Taplejung or Darchula cannot be immediately used to manage bodies here.”

The ministry has so far mobilised the capacity of 16 hospitals for body management and is preparing to use additional hospitals and other facilities if required.

Most bodies recovered from the flood have been found in Chitwan, Nawalparasi and other areas along the Trishuli river corridor. The ministry is also considering temporary facilities near the areas where bodies are being recovered.

Adhikari said transporting all bodies to Kathmandu or other distant locations would be difficult because of transportation and logistical constraints.

“Chitwan and Nawalparasi have a large number of bodies. Transporting all of them to Kathmandu or elsewhere creates logistical difficulties,” he said. “We are therefore focusing more on how temporary facilities can be established locally.”

The ministry is also considering the use of cold storage facilities, temporary mortuaries and containers.

Officials are searching for cold containers and other structures that can be brought into immediate use, while coordination with other government agencies is also being explored.

“We are looking for where such facilities are available,” Adhikari said. “We are working with other agencies on every option that can be brought into immediate use.”

title.rendered: Families scour hospitals across Nepal after Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Pokhara, August 28

Twenty-nine people from Palpa Dharapani and Sankosh in Nilkantha Municipality-9, Dhading, who had travelled to Gosainkunda on a pilgrimage, went missing after the devastating Bhotekoshi flood on Wednesday.

A reserved bus, registration number Ga 5 Kha 1250, went missing from Betrawati on Wednesday morning. Some pilgrims managed to contact their families after the flood and said they had survived by taking shelter on the roof of a house. But contact was subsequently lost.

Since then, their families and relatives have been moving from Kathmandu to Chitwan, Tanahun and Pokhara in search of their loved ones.

At the Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences, photographs of unidentified bodies have been displayed near the laboratory to help families identify them. The facility is currently holding 93 bodies.

“Neither their names are on the list of rescued people, nor can we identify them among the bodies at any one place,” Gokarna Lamsal, a relative waiting outside the mortuary, told Onlinekhabar. “Some family members are searching in Kathmandu, some in Chitwan, some in Tanahun and others here in Pokhara.”

As many as seven members of a single family are among the 29 missing pilgrims. Some families have lost four members, while others are searching for husbands, wives and children who travelled together.

“There is still hope until the bodies are found. But that hope is slowly fading, and we have started searching for the bodies,” said Balram Lamsal.

Families have been carrying photographs of the missing and visiting hospitals where bodies recovered from the flood have been taken.

‘I could identify him by his tattoos’

Among those searching in Pokhara is Sita, whose 38-year-old brother Ram Sharan Karki has been missing since Wednesday.

Karki, a resident of Aarughat in Gorkha, had returned home only three days earlier before leaving again for work in Rasuwa. He called his family from Mailung on Wednesday morning to say he was heading to work. Contact was lost shortly afterwards.

Karki worked as a driver for a Korean hydropower company.

Sita was outside the laboratory at Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences, calling relatives and looking through photographs of unidentified bodies.

“I don’t think I can find my brother here either. If I could see the body myself, I could identify him by his tattoos,” she said.

Karki has tattoos covering his arms. However, only parts of the faces and bodies of the unidentified victims are visible in the photographs displayed for identification, making it difficult for relatives to recognise them.

Of the 93 bodies currently kept at the academy, 75 have been washed and placed with identifying features recorded. The remaining bodies were yet to undergo the process when Sita arrived.

Her husband accompanied her to Pokhara, while other members of the family were searching hospitals in Kathmandu and Chitwan.

“My brothers have gone to Kathmandu. My sisters are searching in Chitwan. We are here in Pokhara,” she said, showing photographs that could help identify Ram Sharan.

Doctor among those missing

Dr Ayush Adhikari, who works at Kathmandu’s Grande International Hospital, had travelled to Gosainkunda as a medical specialist accompanying foreign tourists.

Adhikari, a resident of Tanahun, went missing from the Rasuwa border area. His brother-in-law, Matrika Dhungana, travelled to Pokhara to search among the bodies recovered from the flood.

“He had gone to Gosainkunda to provide medical assistance to foreign visitors in case anyone developed a health problem,” Dhungana said. “But he did not get the chance to save anyone. He himself became a victim.”

Adhikari’s family members are searching in Kathmandu and other locations, while Dhungana has been checking hospitals in Pokhara.

Most bodies remain unidentified

Relatives of missing people have been arriving at the Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences with photographs, hoping to identify their loved ones among the bodies recovered from the flood.

The academy is currently holding 93 bodies—41 from Nawalpur, 11 from Gorkha, 14 from Tanahun and 27 from Dhading.

Most of the bodies are badly damaged. The mortuary, which has a capacity of 75 bodies, is overcrowded, while photographs of the victims have been displayed in the laboratory to assist identification.

According to Kaski police chief Navin Karki, 102 bodies had been brought to Pokhara, but only one, from Bhaktapur, had been identified.

He said bodies would be handed over to families after identification and post-mortem examinations. Police are also collecting fingerprints as part of the identification process.

Nine additional bodies recovered in Tanahun are being kept at Manipal Teaching Hospital in Pokhara.

Families have been visiting both hospitals to examine the photographs displayed for identification.

“Wherever bodies have been taken for identification, we have to go there,” said Gokarna Lamsal. “We don’t know whether we will find them or not. This disaster has broken everyone’s hearts, and on top of that, families may not even be able to perform the final rites for their loved ones.”

He said the scale of the disaster meant it was not the time to blame anyone, but families needed help finding their missing relatives.

Bodies recovered across eight districts

The Bhotekoshi flood, which later swept into the Trishuli River, has caused extensive loss of life across multiple districts.

Nearly 500 bodies have been recovered so far from Rasuwa, Dhading, Nuwakot, Chitwan, Tanahun, Gorkha, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi.

Bodies recovered from the disaster have also been taken to Kathmandu, Pokhara, Palpa, Rupandehi and Kapilvastu for identification and further procedures.

For families of the 29 missing pilgrims from Dhading, the search continues from one hospital to another, with photographs of their loved ones in hand and hope of finding an answer.

title.rendered: ‘Rasuwa flood may have been triggered by a massive ice-rock fall, not a glacial lake outburst’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The devastating flood that swept through Rasuwa and along the Trishuli River on Wednesday may have been triggered by a massive ice-rock landslide in the Langtang Lirung rather than a glacial lake outburst, according to water resources and climate change researcher Santosh Nepal.

Nepal, who holds a PhD in the field, said satellite images indicate that a large mass of glacier ice, snow and rock fell from an elevation of around 5,000–5,500 metres on the northern slope of Langtang Lirung and plunged nearly 2,000 metres.

The impact generated enormous energy, which may have rapidly melted snow and ice and contributed to the sudden and massive flow of water into the Lhende Khola, he said.

“Such a huge ice-rock mass falling from that height would generate enormous energy,” Nepal told Onlinekhabar. “Our preliminary assessment is that this energy may have accelerated the melting of the glacier.”

Initial speculation had focused on a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), as the Himalayan region contains numerous potentially dangerous glacial lakes. However, satellite imagery obtained after the disaster has pointed researchers towards a different explanation.

According to Nepal, the satellite images show a major collapse on the northern side of Langtang Lirung, with glacier ice and snow apparently falling from around 5,000 metres to nearly 3,000 metres.

The falling mass may also have swept up rocks, debris and other material before reaching the river, he said.

“Once the snow and ice mix with water downstream, they can melt more rapidly. The temperature difference between 5,000 and 3,000 metres also means the lower elevation is roughly 12 degrees Celsius warmer,” Nepal said.

He cautioned, however, that the exact mechanism behind the flood has yet to be established.

“It is too early to conclude exactly what happened,” he said. “We need further satellite data and, when conditions allow, a field investigation.”

Similar to Chamoli, not Melamchi

Nepal said the Rasuwa disaster appears to resemble the 2021 Chamoli disaster in India’s Uttarakhand more closely than Nepal’s 2021 Melamchi flood.

In Chamoli, a large mass of glacier and ice-rock fell from the Nanda Devi mountain range, sweeping snow and debris downhill. The resulting rapid melting and massive flood caused extensive loss of life and damaged hydropower projects.

“The Rasuwa event appears similar to the Chamoli flood in terms of its characteristics and the mechanism involved,” Nepal said.

He said Nepal has experienced other multi-hazard disasters in the past, where heavy rainfall, landslides, river blockages and sudden floods have combined to cause extensive damage.

The current event, however, appears unusual because there was no exceptionally heavy rainfall in the area when the flood began.

Could the river have been temporarily blocked?

Nepal said one possibility being examined is that the Lhende Khola was temporarily blocked by the falling ice, rock and debris before suddenly releasing a large volume of water.

“If the river was completely blocked, the downstream flow would have stopped,” he said. “But if it was only partially blocked, water could still have continued flowing.”

He noted that some river monitoring and early-warning equipment may itself have been swept away, making it difficult to reconstruct the sequence of events using downstream measurements.

Researchers are continuing to analyse satellite images to determine the size and depth of the landslide, the amount of ice and snow involved and whether there had been recent snowfall in the area.

Small tremor may have followed the ice-rock fall

A small tremor was also recorded in the Langtang area around the time of the disaster, prompting speculation over whether an earthquake triggered the landslide.

Nepal believes the sequence may have been the other way around.

“My understanding is that the tremor was recorded after the large ice-rock mass fell and struck the ground at around 9:38 am,” he said.

He pointed to the Chamoli disaster, where a similar ground shock was recorded after a massive rock and ice fall.

Climate change increasing mountain risks

Nepal said the Rasuwa disaster should also be viewed in the broader context of climate change and increasing risks in Nepal’s mountain regions.

He said rising temperatures are weakening mountain rock through repeated heating, cooling, freezing and thawing.

“Water enters cracks in the rocks, freezes and expands, and this can create further cracks,” he said.

According to Santosh Nepal, Nepal’s mountainous terrain, concentrated monsoon rainfall and climate change are combining to create increasingly complex hazards.

“Climate change has made these risks greater,” he said. “We are now seeing events that our ancestors never witnessed or experienced.”

He said the country must prepare for “cascading hazards” in which one event triggers another—for example, an ice or rock fall leading to a river blockage, followed by a sudden flood and extensive downstream destruction.

Existing early-warning systems may not be enough

Santosh Nepal said Nepal’s existing early-warning systems are largely designed to monitor river levels and communicate flood risks to downstream communities.

But recent disasters, including the Melamchi and Rasuwa floods, have shown that conventional systems may not be sufficient for cascading hazards.

“Early-warning systems need to be upgraded,” he said, calling for greater use of remote sensing and artificial intelligence.

He also stressed the importance of real-time information sharing between Nepal and China, particularly because disasters originating in the upper reaches of rivers can quickly affect downstream areas in Nepal.

“Monitoring systems should be established in the upper reaches so that information can reach downstream areas in real time,” he said.

Nepal also called for a rethink of how infrastructure is designed in disaster-prone areas.

He said many structures are currently designed based on historical flood estimates, often considering events with return periods of around 40 or 50 years.

“But climate change is bringing larger and more unpredictable disasters,” he said. “We now need a policy-level debate on building infrastructure capable of withstanding these new kinds of risks.”

title.rendered: More than 400 container trucks, 1,000 people unaccounted for after Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River have caused unprecedented losses to the cargo container trucking business operating along the Rasuwa-Gyirong border and Trishuli corridor, transport operators said.

More than 400 container trucks and over 1,000 people working with them — including drivers, helpers, labourers and traders — are reportedly out of contact after being caught in the floods.

The trucks had travelled to the Rasuwa border point to transport goods for the upcoming Teej, Dashain and Tihar festivals.

Arjun Bahadur Sapkota, president of the Nepal Truck Container Transportation Service, said the whereabouts of the trucks and the people working with them remain unknown after they were swept away by the floodwaters.

According to Sapkota, 966 container trucks are registered with the association. Around 175 of them had travelled towards Kerung shortly before the floods to collect cargo.

More than 400 people associated with those trucks, including drivers, helpers and self-employed workers who own and operate their vehicles, are currently out of contact, he said.

When traders, customs clearance agents and other passengers who had travelled to collect goods are also taken into account, the number of people stranded or missing could exceed 1,000, Sapkota said.

“More than 400 drivers alone are missing. When helpers, traders and customs agents are included, the number is much higher,” he said.

Sapkota said vehicles belonging to transport associations from Narayani, Balkhu, Pokhara-Gandaki and other organisations were also stranded in the flood-affected areas, suggesting that the scale of the damage could be much greater than initially estimated.

Transporters blame customs, checkpoints

Sapkota blamed what he described as impractical rules and delays at customs offices and checkpoints along the route for contributing to the scale of the losses.

He alleged that trucks that had already completed customs procedures were prevented from travelling to their destinations at night and were forced to remain parked along the road.

“Rasuwagadhi Customs clears the vehicles, but the national park checkpoint in Dhunche only allows vehicles to operate from 7 am to 7 pm. After paying customs duties, 70 to 80 trucks were forced to line up along the highway for three or four days,” Sapkota said.

“It was those vehicles, parked unsafely along the road, that were swept away by the landslides and floods.”

He said the losses could have been significantly lower if customs authorities and checkpoints had allowed the containers to proceed to their destinations on time.

40 trucks swept away in Betrawati alone

The transporters have also been unable to determine the condition of containers that had travelled towards Kerung or were still on the Chinese side of the border.

In the Betravati area of Nuwakot, around 30 to 40 container trucks were swept away by the Trishuli River, Sapkota said.

Around 115 container trucks had been parked in the Betravati area before the flood.

“Our colleagues took risks and managed to move many containers to safety,” he said. “But 30 to 40 trucks were still swept away. Some tourist buses that remained there despite repeated warnings were also seen falling into the river.”

Transport operators have urged the government to immediately intensify search and rescue efforts for the workers who remain missing.

title.rendered: Rabindra Dhant advances to Road to UFC final after split-decision win

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Nepali mixed martial artist Rabindra Dhant has reached the final of Road to UFC Season 5 after defeating New Zealand’s Kasib Murdoch by split decision in the bantamweight semifinal in Shanghai, China.

Dhant secured the victory after all three rounds went to the judges.

One judge scored the fight 29-28 in Dhant’s favour, while another gave the same score to Murdoch. The third judge also scored it 29-28 for Dhant, handing the Nepali fighter the split-decision victory.

Dhant will now face Ryo Tajima in the Road to UFC final. Tajima advanced after defeating India’s Chungreng Koren in the other bantamweight semifinal.

The final will determine the winner of the Road to UFC bantamweight tournament, with a UFC contract at stake.

Rabindra Dhant had previously defeated Kimbert Alintozon by second-round TKO in the opening round of the tournament

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi floods severely damage hydropower projects in Rasuwa, Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 28

The devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River have caused severe damage to hydropower projects in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, leaving hundreds of workers at affected sites in distress.

According to the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), 13 hydropower projects have suffered direct damage from the floods and landslides.

A total of 933 workers at the affected projects were initially reported out of contact. Of them, 254 have been rescued, while some others have since made contact. However, a large number of workers remain unaccounted for.

IPPAN Senior Vice President Uttam Bhlon said both private and government-owned hydropower projects have been affected by the disaster.

“The damage is greater than expected. Right now, everyone’s focus is on rescue and relief,” he said. “Rescue and relief efforts are underway at most hydropower projects where immediate assistance is needed, but the situation remains critical at some locations.”

According to Bhlon, projects including Langtang Hydropower, Upper Trishuli, Trishuli-3 ‘B’ and Chilime require urgent rescue operations. Some workers at the projects are feared to be trapped inside tunnels.

Rescue efforts have been hampered by the disruption of road and communication links. With mobile and telephone services unavailable in many areas, authorities have been unable to determine the exact whereabouts and condition of workers at the projects.

Bhlon said attempts to use private helicopters for rescue have also faced difficulties due to the lack of suitable landing areas and other technical and safety concerns.

“We are only able to contact those who have made it out. There is no road to reach the upper areas and mobile phones are not working,” he said. “Even if we bring private helicopters, there is nowhere to land. The state needs to coordinate and carry out immediate rescue operations.”

576 workers unaccounted for at one project

According to IPPAN, the whereabouts of 576 workers at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project alone remain unknown.

Around 1,350 workers were employed at the project. While some have been rescued, a large number remain out of contact, IPPAN said.

Some workers from affected projects have been brought to safety, but the status of others remains unknown. IPPAN has said the immediate priority should be rescuing people who may be trapped inside tunnels and project premises.

“There are 576 people out of contact, and we do not have clear information about where they are,” Bhlon said. “If some of those trapped in the tunnels can be rescued, they may still be alive. That is why efforts to arrange helicopters are continuing.”

Hydropower sector relies on state for rescue

Although the private sector has been making efforts to rescue workers trapped at hydropower projects, IPPAN says the difficult terrain and lack of access have made immediate rescue operations impossible in some locations.

IPPAN said it has been regularly sharing information about the condition of workers at affected projects with the government, Nepali Army and Nepal Police.

The association is also preparing to mobilise institutional support for rescue and relief operations, Bhlon said.

The Ministry of Energy has held discussions with representatives of the affected projects and collected information on the damage and the humanitarian situation.

IPPAN has also nominated a civil engineer to a committee formed for post-flood reconstruction.

“We will provide whatever support we can for rescue and relief, and we are also working on mobilising support for the government’s relief fund,” Bhlon said. “The most important thing right now is rescuing people. Reconstruction can be done later.”

Completed projects also affected

The floods have affected not only projects under construction but also those that have already been completed.

Some project structures have been damaged, while others have been affected by disruptions to transmission lines and road access, hampering electricity generation and operations.

IPPAN said 13 projects have suffered direct damage from the floods. The number of indirectly affected projects could be significantly higher because roads, communication links and other access routes to several projects have been disrupted.

IPPAN is currently re-verifying information received from the projects. The details of people who have been rescued or re-established contact will be updated, while the actual number of people still missing will be determined.

The difficult terrain, disrupted roads and communication networks, and adverse weather have made rescue operations particularly challenging. IPPAN has called for urgent coordination among security agencies, helicopter operators and all relevant authorities to accelerate rescue efforts.

Additional helicopters deployed

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said rescue efforts for employees and workers stranded at various hydropower projects have been intensified.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said additional helicopters carrying necessary supplies, equipment and personnel have been sent from Kathmandu to the affected areas.

The helicopters were dispatched in coordination with security agencies and relevant authorities while following necessary safety measures, the authority said.

Rescue teams have been mobilised particularly to evacuate employees and workers stranded at various hydropower projects in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, as well as to relocate employees in the Shantibazar area to safer locations.

The safety and rescue of workers at flood-affected projects have been given high priority, the authority said, adding that rescue and relief operations will continue as necessary.

The authority has urged everyone to remain patient and calm during the crisis and to rely only on information issued by official agencies.

title.rendered: 48 flood victims brought to Teaching Hospital, 21 discharged

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The number of people brought to Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj for treatment after being rescued from the devastating Bhotekoshi floods has reached 48.

According to the hospital’s latest update, as of 4 pm Friday, 27 of the 48 flood-affected people were still receiving treatment.

Twenty-one patients have been discharged, while one person has died.

Of those currently undergoing treatment, six are in the intensive care unit (ICU) and one is on a ventilator, the hospital said.

The injured patients currently at the hospital range in age from five to 50.

title.rendered: Setu Rapid app launched to trace people missing after Rasuwa floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The ‘Setu Rapid App’ has been launched to help trace people who have been missing since the Rasuwa floods.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) launched the app, with technical teams from other agencies also working on the platform, according to NDRRMA Undersecretary Ram Bahadur KC.

According to KC, relatives of missing people can submit their details through the app. So far, around 1,500 people have submitted forms.

However, KC said the number of forms does not necessarily represent the actual number of missing people, as there may be duplicate submissions. Relatives may have submitted the form multiple times for the same person, while some people listed as missing may have already been rescued or their bodies recovered.

He said the forms received through the app are treated as raw data and must be verified before the authorities can confirm the actual number of missing people.

According to him, the authorities have so far confirmed 977 people as missing.

Verification of the remaining cases is underway. KC said data collected today is expected to be available by the evening.

title.rendered: Landslide debris completely buries Upper Trishuli-3 ‘B’ project camp in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The camp area of the Upper Trishuli-3 ‘B’ Hydropower Project in Nuwakot has been completely buried under landslide debris, according to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation.

The ministry said the site is currently in an extremely difficult and hazardous condition, making rescue operations and efforts to establish access to the site challenging.

Despite the risks, rescue and access-building efforts are continuing, the ministry said.

Helicopters have been conducting repeated aerial inspections of the site to assess the situation. Rescue and search operations are being carried out based on information gathered during the inspections.

Necessary equipment for rescue and establishing access to the site has also been transported by helicopter, and work has begun, according to the ministry.

The project said the rescue of people remains its top priority and that efforts will continue until everyone at the site has been safely rescued.

The project has also urged the public not to rely on unverified information or rumours given the sensitivity of the situation, and to follow only official updates.

title.rendered: Nepal Chamber hands over 17 surveillance drones to police

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The Nepal Chamber of Commerce has handed over 17 surveillance drones to Nepal Police Headquarters to support the rescue, relief and rehabilitation of people affected by the disaster.

Nepal Chamber of Commerce Senior Vice President and Chairperson of the Disaster Management Council Deepak Kumar Malhotra handed over the drones to Nepal Police at Police Headquarters on Friday.

The drones include two Mavic 4 Pro, five Air 3S FMC RC 2, two Mini 5 Pro Plus FMC RC 2, six Lito One Plus FMC R3 and two Lito X1 FMC R2 units.

IGP Dan Bahadur Karki, Nepal Chamber of Commerce Director General Devendra Lamichhane and Senior SP Damodar Kandel were present at the handover ceremony.

The Chamber said the surveillance drones are expected to help make search and rescue operations in disaster-affected areas more effective, faster and technology-driven. As access to people is limited in difficult terrain and high-risk areas, the drones are expected to assist in monitoring affected areas, assessing situations and coordinating rescue operations.

The Chamber had previously sent a drone with a 50-kilogram payload capacity and a surveillance drone to Bidur Municipality to support rescue operations. It has also provided 125 power banks to help maintain communications and operate essential electrical equipment in affected areas.

The Chamber has also launched a campaign to collect and distribute relief supplies for disaster-affected people. It provided immediate cash and material assistance to affected districts, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, on August 27, and said it would continue its relief campaign and support efforts.

title.rendered: Rasuwa Flood: 116 from Madhesh still uncontacted, 10 now in contact

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, August 28

Ten people from Madhesh Province who had lost contact due to the unprecedented flood on the Bhotekoshi River have since reached their families. 116 people from the province remain uncontacted.

According to Province Police Office spokesperson SSP Prabhu Prasad Dhakal, the 10 previously uncontacted individuals have now reached their families.

Police have not disclosed their identities.

Earlier, police had said 120 men, five women, and one child were uncontacted.

Of these, Saptari had the highest number with 31, followed by Parsa with 28, Bara with 19, Rautahat with 15, Sarlahi and Mahottari with 10 each, Siraha with 8, and Dhanusha with 5, according to police records.

SSP Dhakal said these figures were compiled based on applications and phone reports submitted by family members and relatives.

Police say the location for 91 uncontacted individuals is listed simply as “Rasuwa.” The rest are linked to various hydropower projects in Rasuwa, Betrawati and Trishuli Bazaar in Nuwakot, and other work or business activities.

Some are reported to be connected to projects including Upper Trishuli, Trishuli Hydropower, and Mailung Hydropower.

title.rendered: Nearly 2 billion raised for Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund in 36 hours

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

More than Rs 1.91 billion has been collected in the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund within 36 hours of the government appealing for donations, according to the Ministry of Finance.

The ministry said Rs 1.918 billion was deposited into accounts maintained at 10 commercial banks between noon on Wednesday and midnight Thursday.

A total of Rs 1.918 billion was deposited by donors during the period.

The government began receiving donations after a devastating flood swept through the Bhotekoshi River along the Nepal-China border on Wednesday morning, causing extensive loss of life and property. The Cabinet subsequently declared the affected areas disaster zones.

Individuals and organisations began contributing to the relief fund following the government’s appeal.

The government has designated the Ministry of Finance as the focal ministry for coordinating donations to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund. Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle is personally receiving institutional donations of Rs 10 million or more.

Individuals wishing to make cash contributions can also visit the ministry to hand over their donations.

With the latest contributions, the fund’s balance has reached Rs 4.091 billion. It had a balance of Rs 2.172 billion before the recent donations.

The ministry also received Rs 273.3 million in contributions from private-sector donors within six hours on Thursday.

The amount does not include funds pledged by various friendly countries.

title.rendered: Buddha Air to provide free air transport for relief supplies

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Private airline Buddha Air will transport relief supplies free of charge.

The airline said the free service has been arranged in line with a decision by the Ministry of Home Affairs to facilitate the collection and air transportation of relief materials.

The company also said it would maintain its regular airfares until road transportation becomes more accessible.

“Despite whatever commercial challenges may arise in the current difficult circumstances, we are committed to providing convenient and affordable fares,” the company said. “If you receive information about tickets being sold at excessively high prices anywhere, we request you to inform us. We will take necessary and strict action against such activities in accordance with the law.”

title.rendered: Army disposes of explosives found on Trishuli banks in Gorkha

content.rendered:
Gorkha, August 28

Explosive material found on the bank of the Trishuli River in Shahid Lakhan Rural Municipality-3, Silingtar, Gorkha, has been safely disposed of.

A team deployed from the Nepali Army’s Rudradhwaj Battalion carried out the disposal.

The explosive material was found on the riverbank around 2:30 pm on Thursday. An earlier disposal attempt the previous day had been unsuccessful.

Birodh Rijal, a company officer with the Rudradhwaj Battalion, said the explosive material may have been swept in by the flood that came down from Rasuwa.

title.rendered: Rasuwa reconnected to road network after devastating floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Rasuwa, the district worst affected by the recent floods, has been reconnected to the road network after an alternative route to the district was reopened for small four-wheeled vehicles.

According to the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, the road from Kathmandu via Tokha, Chhahare, Gadkhar Bridge, Aapre, Narja, Lachyang, Saramthali, Patikharka, Bogatitar and Kalikasthan to Dhunche has been opened for light four-wheeled vehicles.

Rasuwa had been cut off from the road network after the floods swept away 13 bridges within the district alone, on the Rasuwa side of the Mitir Bridge.

Two bridges along the Nuwakot-Rasuwa border were also destroyed, further disrupting road connectivity to the district.

The government has been prioritising the restoration of roads and bridges in Rasuwa following the devastating floods. The Bhotekoshi flood had destroyed around 40 kilometres of roads and 41 bridges in the district.

title.rendered: Chinese Embassy warns flood risk still high, urges vigilance

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The Chinese Embassy in Nepal says the risk created by the ice-and-rock avalanche along the Nepal-China border remains in place. Speaking Friday, an embassy spokesperson said officials from both countries are continuously monitoring the situation.

“In recent days, an ice-and-rock avalanche occurred on a tributary on the Nepali side of the upper reaches of the border river. The landslide blocked the river, forming a barrier lake alongside it,” the statement said. “The water level in that lake is now high and has begun overflowing, increasing the risk of further damage.”

The embassy said the situation remains at an extremely sensitive stage for both Nepal and China in terms of rescue and emergency response.

“Local communities and relevant personnel downstream of the barrier lake are urged to closely monitor changes in the river’s water level, remain highly vigilant, and prepare in advance for possible risk prevention and emergency response,” the statement said.

The statement added that the relevant agencies of both China and Nepal are continuing to monitor the situation.

It also urged the public to follow only official and reliable information, avoid spreading unverified reports, and refrain from creating unnecessary panic.

A total of 547 bodies have been recovered so far following the floods that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday, according to Nepal Police.

The bodies have been recovered from eight districts, with the highest number reported in Chitwan.

According to police, 13 bodies have been found in Rasuwa, 38 in Nuwakot, 40 in Dhading, 44 in Gorkha, 134 in Nawalpur, 28 in Nawalparasi, 29 in Tanahun and 221 in Chitwan.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said 977 people remain unaccounted for.

Of those reported missing, 28 are from Nepal Police, 45 from the Nepali Army, 13 from the Armed Police Force, 15 from customs offices and four from immigration offices. Another 162 people from Rasuwa and Nuwakot have also been reported missing.

According to Nepal Police, 1,473 people have been rescued so far.

title.rendered: Forgiveness puja performed at Palanchok Bhagawati Temple

content.rendered:
Banepa, August 28

A Kshama Puja — a ritual seeking forgiveness— was performed today at the Palanchok Bhagawati Temple after the idol was reportedly seen sweating during an evening aarti a few days ago.

Ward Chairperson Ram Kaji Shrestha said the ritual was performed after devotees noticed sweat appearing on the idol during the evening aarti.

Palanchok Bhagawati is a renowned Shakti Peetha, a sacred shrine dedicated to the divine feminine. The temple is located in Panchkhal Municipality-9. The idol was bathed, and special rituals and prayers seeking forgiveness were performed according to tantric traditions.

According to local religious beliefs and folklore, sweat appearing on the idol of Palanchok Bhagawati is regarded as a sign of an impending divine calamity or political crisis.

Locals say similar signs were observed before events including the 2015 earthquake, the floods and landslides of 2024, and the 2001 royal massacre.

Locals have viewed the flood in the Sunkoshi River on August 26 in the same context. A priest performed secret rituals as part of the Kshama Puja.

title.rendered: Families scan rescue lists, hoping to find missing loved ones

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 28

A list of flood victims rescued and brought to the Shree No. 1 Military Training Centre in Nuwakot has been posted on a wall outside the army facility.

Throughout the day, dozens of people gather around the list.

They scan the names carefully, searching for relatives who went missing in the floods. For many, the list represents a small but desperate hope of finding their loved ones.

A long queue forms as people arrive to check the names. At times, those gathered around the list can be seen jostling to get a closer look.

But many walk away disappointed after failing to find the names they are looking for.

The army has set up a help desk nearby. Those who cannot find the names of their missing relatives on the list have been asked to register their details at the desk.

The help desk, too, remains crowded.

The number of people gathered there offers a grim indication of the scale of those still missing following the floods.

title.rendered: Five-year-old flood survivor searches for family from hospital bed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Five-year-old Ishara Tamang lies quietly in a bed at the Paediatric Surgery Ward of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.

Her eyes remain closed for much of the time. A soft cervical collar supports her neck, medical equipment is attached to her body, and a cannula has been placed in her left hand. Bruises are visible on her face.

The fear of the flood has not yet left her.

At times, she opens her eyes and looks around before falling silent again.

But there is no family member beside her. Neither her mother nor father is there. Hospital staff are giving her medicine, feeding her, arranging her clothes and checking on her condition.

Ishara was rescued from the floodwaters in Khalte, Rasuwa, after she became trapped in a net. She was brought to Teaching Hospital on Wednesday and initially treated in the emergency department’s red zone. She is now receiving treatment in the Paediatric Surgery Ward.

At five, Ishara was too young to fully understand what a flood was. Yet she has experienced a disaster that has left both physical and emotional wounds.

She lost hold of her mother’s hand, was swept away by the current and survived after becoming trapped in a net.

Her physical injuries are being treated. But the questions that remain are harder to answer: Where is her mother? Where is her father? When will her family come to take her home?

When Ishara was brought to the hospital after being rescued, her condition was not normal. She remains psychologically affected by the trauma of the flood.

Dr Bivek Gurung, who is involved in her treatment, told Onlinekhabar that Ishara has not yet fully regained consciousness. However, as soon as she opened her eyes, she was able to give her name: Ishara Tamang.

That was how her identity was established.

Gradually, she began telling medical staff that she was from Rasuwa and had been with her mother when the flood struck. Her account, given in the language of a five-year-old, has also moved those involved in her treatment.

According to what she told them, Ishara was with her mother when the sudden flood swept her mother away. Ishara was also caught in the current. She tried to move forward using her hands but eventually became trapped in a net, where she was rescued.

“Mom was swept away. I jumped and moved forward, then got trapped in the net,” she said after regaining consciousness.

Those few words contain the story of the disaster she experienced. Doctors used the information to prepare her medical records.

‘For now, the health workers are her family’

At the Paediatric Surgery Ward, hospital staff are not only treating Ishara but also looking after her.

With no family member having made contact, doctors and other staff are caring for her as they would for a member of their own family.

They are providing more than medicine and treatment. They have arranged clothes, food and other necessities for her and continue to monitor her condition.

For hospital attendant Pavitra Magar, Ishara is not just another patient. With no family beside her, Magar says she is caring for the child as if she were her own.

“For now, the health workers are her family. From the doctors to all the staff, we are paying extra attention to her. We keep checking whether she needs anything and how her health is,” Magar said.

“No one from her family has been in contact. We don’t know whether someone will come looking for her. So, for now, we are doing our best to care for her like our own child.”

When Ishara was brought to the hospital, she did not even have clothes to wear. Most of her belongings had been swept away by the flood.

Hospital staff arranged clothes for her and took care of her food and other necessities.

A small gold earring

During her treatment, staff found a small gold earring in Ishara’s ear. It may be one of the few remaining belongings that could help identify her family.

Magar said the earring was noticed while Ishara was undergoing a CT scan.

“She had a gold earring in her ear when she was taken for a CT scan. I have handed it to the ward in-charge for safekeeping,” Magar said.

“Her family has not yet been identified, so her belongings also need to be kept safe.”

With no certainty about where Ishara’s family is or whether they are safe, ensuring her security and care has become as important as treating her injuries.

Search operations are continuing for people missing in the floods. Relatives are arriving at hospitals looking for their loved ones, while some survivors are receiving treatment for their injuries.

Ishara’s situation is different.

She is in a hospital, but the whereabouts of the people who should be looking for her remain unknown.

Father being searched for through Facebook

Efforts are now underway to locate Ishara’s father, including through social media.

A Facebook account under the name Chhiring Lama has appealed for help in finding her father. Ishara has told hospital staff that her father is in Kathmandu.

According to the Facebook post, Ishara is a student at Shree Ramchandra Secondary School in Satbise, Uttargaya Rural Municipality-1, Rasuwa.

Onlinekhabar also attempted to contact the school after learning about Ishara. However, it has so far been unable to establish direct contact with anyone at the school.

Kathmandu, August 28

The Nepal government has requested India and China to urgently build 42 Bailey bridges to restore transportation in flood-affected areas.

According to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nepal has asked both countries for assistance, specifying the number of Bailey bridges it urgently needs.

The government has made arrangements to receive foreign assistance based on the requirements identified by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. After the authority assessed that 42 bridges are urgently needed to restore transportation, the government approached both countries for assistance.

Indian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a regular press briefing on Thursday that India would provide Nepal with assistance, including Bailey bridges, whenever required.

Most bridges in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading were destroyed by the floods, bringing two-way movement of people and vehicles in the affected areas to a halt.

Four employees trapped inside the Rasuwa Hydropower Plant have been safely rescued.

Preparations are also underway for a possible rescue operation at the Trishuli-3B Hydropower Project.

Although adverse weather conditions have caused some delays, rescue operations in the affected areas are being continued as a high priority, according to the minister’s secretariat.

A dedicated helicopter equipped with necessary rescue materials has been deployed to rescue people trapped at the flood-affected Upper Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Home Minister Sudhan Gurung has pledged to ensure that relief supplies are delivered to disaster-affected people without delay. Gurung committed during a meeting with leaders including Nepal Communist Party leader Barshaman Pun, according to Pun’s secretariat.

Pun is currently conducting an on-site inspection of the Bidur area of Nuwakot, which was damaged by flooding in the Bhotekoshi River. During the inspection, Pun met with Home Minister Gurung and urged him to expedite the search and rescue of all people who remain missing in the Rasuwagadhi area.

He also urged the minister to immediately ascertain the whereabouts of missing people, including 21 residents of Rolpa, and make search and rescue efforts more effective. Pun also drew the home minister’s attention to the fact that although a substantial amount of relief materials donated by various organisations and individuals had been collected, they had not been distributed effectively.

In response, Gurung pledged to ensure the immediate delivery of relief supplies to affected people, according to Pun’s secretariat. Gurung also said he had instructed the concerned authorities to distribute the relief materials under the leadership of the District Coordination Committee so that they reach affected people without delay.

The Nagdhunga-Muglin highway, a major route connecting Kathmandu Valley with other parts of the country, has been completely closed following Wednesday’s flooding in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa. The Pasang Lhamu Highway, which connects to the Chinese border through Rasuwa, has also been closed after being severely damaged by the flood.

Cargo trucks that transport goods along these routes are now stranded in the capital. The roads from Kalanki to Balkhu are packed with large trucks, with trucks lined up along one lane of the road.

The trucks, which had been preparing to leave the valley, have been stranded since Wednesday afternoon.

title.rendered: Kathmandu power supply disrupted after two transmission circuits trip

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Electricity supply was disrupted in Kathmandu and parts of central Nepal on Friday after problems occurred in both circuits of the Khapti-Dhalkebar 220 kV transmission line while another transmission line was under a scheduled shutdown.

According to the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), the Hetauda-Dhalkebar 400 kV transmission line is currently under construction, and the 132 kV transmission lines were under a scheduled shutdown for stringing work. During this period, both circuits of the Khapti-Dhalkebar 220 kV transmission line developed problems, disrupting electricity supply to Kathmandu Valley and other parts of central Nepal.

The NEA said the Hetauda-Amlekhgunj and Kamane-Amlekhgunj 132 kV transmission lines had been under scheduled shutdown since 6:40 am. During that period, the power system was being operated through the Dhalkebar-Khurkot-Khimti-Bhaktapur-Syuchatar transmission route.

At 8:52 am, Circuit 1 of the Khapti-Dhalkebar 220 kV transmission line tripped after its conductor snapped. Circuit 2 of the same transmission line then tripped at 9:18 am, disconnecting the transmission link and disrupting electricity supply to Kathmandu Valley and other parts of central Nepal.

The NEA used an alternative transmission route to restore electricity supply as quickly as possible. Power was supplied through the Mainhiya substation via the Sampatia substation in Uttar Pradesh, India.

The NEA said electricity supply to Kathmandu Valley resumed at 9:44 am through the alternative arrangement.

A technical team is currently conducting an on-site inspection of the affected transmission system and carrying out necessary repair and maintenance work. The NEA said efforts are underway to identify the problem in the transmission line and restore the system to normal operation.

The flood that swept down the Bhotekoshi and into the Trishuli River on Wednesday has caused massive loss of life and property. Nepal Police say 489 bodies have been recovered so far.

Bodies have been found in Rasuwa, Dhading, Nuwakot, Chitwan, Tanahun, Gorkha, and Nawalparasi’s Bardaghat Susta East and West Nawalparasi districts.
