title.rendered: Health supplies, vaccines provided to prevent disease among flood-hit livestock

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

A technical team from the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment has reached Nuwakot to help prevent the spread of diseases among livestock affected by the floods.

The team visited the district to provide veterinary health services and necessary assistance in flood-affected areas and held discussions with the assistant chief district officer of Nuwakot.

During the meeting, the team briefed officials on ongoing efforts to rescue, provide relief to and treat livestock in the flood-affected areas.

The technical team also held discussions with officials at the Veterinary Hospital and Livestock Services Expert Centre in Nuwakot and handed over medicines, vaccines and other essential veterinary health supplies.

The ministry’s team said the supplies and vaccines were provided to help prevent and control infectious diseases, the risk of which is high among livestock following floods.

title.rendered: China to provide emergency aid to disaster-hit areas in Nepal

content.rendered:
KATHMANDU, August 28

The Communist Party of China (CPC) has decided to provide emergency assistance to disaster-affected areas in Nepal and advance international rescue cooperation following the floods and landslides in the Gyirong area.

The decision was taken at a meeting of the CPC Political Bureau chaired by Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, according to Xinhua.

The meeting assessed the flooding in the Gyirong area and discussed ongoing rescue and relief efforts following the devastating landslide. Xi instructed relevant authorities to make the necessary arrangements to strengthen the response.

At the beginning of the meeting, Xi, who is also chairman of the Central Military Commission, and other senior leaders observed a minute of silence in memory of those who died in the natural disaster at the Gyirong border crossing on Wednesday.

“Under the strong leadership of the Party Central Committee, emergency rescue operations have been carried out in an intensive, orderly and effectively coordinated manner,” Xinhua reported. “Comprehensive efforts are also being made for the resettlement of affected people and post-disaster management.”

The meeting noted that the disaster occurred in an extremely cold mountainous region characterised by steep valleys, changing weather conditions, numerous glaciers and glacial lakes, and potential geological hazards, creating significant challenges for emergency rescue operations.

It stressed that all relevant agencies and departments must take firm and effective measures to advance rescue efforts.

The meeting also called for search and rescue plans to be developed scientifically and for every possible effort to be made to locate and rescue all missing Chinese and foreign nationals.

Kathmandu, August 28

A 5.1-magnitude earthquake struck China’s southwestern Sichuan province on Friday, according to the China Earthquake Networks Centre.

The quake hit Longchang city in Sichuan, hundreds of miles from the flood-affected area near the Nepal-Tibet border. No immediate reports of casualties or major damage have been received.

The earthquake struck as rescue and relief operations continued in Tibet and Nepal following the devastating floods and landslides that hit the border region earlier this week. The disaster has killed hundreds of people, with hundreds more still missing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired a meeting with senior officials on Friday regarding the ongoing rescue operations in Tibet. Officials warned that risks from glacial lakes, glaciers, and geological hazards remain, further complicating rescue efforts.

Nepal has also issued a new flood warning after water levels rose again at the site of the earlier disaster.

Authorities have urged residents and rescue workers in at-risk areas to move to safe locations. China has warned that a newly formed barrier lake near the border could burst, raising fears of further flooding downstream.

Kathmandu, August 28

The government has made public the key decisions of Thursday’s Cabinet meeting. Government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmita Pokharel announced the decisions.

The Cabinet instructed the Ministry of Finance to prepare a relief and rehabilitation package, or business recovery package, for individuals and businesses affected by floods in Rasuwa, including the Rasuwagadhi area along the Nepal-China border, the Bhotekoshi River and downstream areas.

The Cabinet also granted in-principle approval to Agriculture Inputs Company Limited to purchase 25,000 metric tonnes of DAP fertiliser from the Government of India through a government-to-government (G2G) procurement mechanism.

Similarly, the Prime Minister and all members of the Council of Ministers will contribute one month’s salary and remuneration to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support people affected by the floods along the Nepal-China border in Rasuwa and the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

title.rendered: Government says no immediate major risk from glacial lake overflow

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The government has said glaciers broke off from a large lake formed near the confluence of the Chochen River and the Purepu Tsangpo River in China. However, government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmita Pokharel said there is no immediate major risk.

He shared the information while speaking to journalists following Thursday’s Cabinet meeting.

He also said the government is maintaining continuous communication with the Chinese government through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

“We are in continuous communication with the Chinese government through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. We have also been informed by the Chinese side that there is no such major risk. I would like to urge everyone to remain alert,” spokesperson Pokharel said.

He said there was no report of a dam bursting, but the breaking of glaciers had caused water mixed with mud to overflow in several areas.

“There is no information that a dam has burst anywhere. Since glaciers have broken off, water mixed with mud has overflowed in several places,” spokesperson Pokharel said. “No major immediate risk has been observed, but it is necessary to remain alert.”

Earlier, Rasuwa Chief District Officer Narendra Pariyar had said he received information from the Chinese side that the lake formed on the Chinese side had burst.

Security personnel are currently moving people living near the river to safer locations.

The prime minister and ministers will contribute one month’s salary and remuneration to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

Government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmita Pokharel said the decision was made at a Cabinet meeting held on Thursday.

According to the Cabinet decision, one month’s salary and remuneration of the Prime Minister and all members of the Council of Ministers will be deposited into the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund in response to the disaster along the Nepal-China border and the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

title.rendered: China monitoring lake formed after collapse near Chhochen and Purepu Tsangpo rivers confluence

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Chinese authorities are closely monitoring a large lake that formed after a lake near the confluence of Chhochen and Purepu Tsangpo rivers burst, according to information shared with Nepali officials.

According to government sources, the Chinese side has assessed that although water flow from the lake is increasing, the immediate risk of a major outburst flood remains low.

In a message sent to Nepali authorities, the Chinese side said water was continuously overflowing from the lake and that the lake was growing in size as the volume of water increased.

“However, under the current circumstances, the risk of a major explosive outflow of water is low,” the message said.

Chinese authorities have also reported an earlier incident in which ice and rocks fell in an area downstream of the lake. They said they were continuing to monitor conditions at the site.

The Chinese side has assured Nepali authorities that it will provide further information if there are any significant developments.

title.rendered: Health workers’ leave suspended, staff directed to assist in rescue and treatment

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The Ministry of Health has directed employees working in the health sector not to take leave except in essential circumstances amid the ongoing disaster situation.

The ministry has also instructed staff to remain on standby for search, rescue and treatment services, including on public holidays.

In a directive issued by the ministry’s Administration and Management Division on Friday, the ministry expressed condolences to those who lost their lives in the devastating floods and landslides triggered by the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa. It said search, rescue, medical treatment and relief operations are underway in the affected areas.

The ministry has instructed all employees under its jurisdiction to remain available for deployment in disaster management and not to approve leave or official travel assignments except for special reasons or urgent work.

Similarly, heads, focal persons and responsible officials of agencies involved in search, rescue and treatment have been instructed to remain present at their offices even on public holidays.

Other employees have also been directed to remain on standby to ensure essential services continue.

The ministry has requested health workers at hospitals to make necessary arrangements to treat people injured in the floods and landslides, including on public holidays.

title.rendered: Relatives of over 40 NEA employees trapped in Rasuwa tunnel reach Prime Minister’s Office

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Relatives of 40-45 employees of the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), said to be trapped in a tunnel in Rasuwa, have gathered at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.

According to Sita Adhikari of Kapilvastu, her husband had gone to the Rasuwa 3A Hydropower Project from Kulekhani III.

“We believe he’s trapped inside the tunnel, but there’s been no rescue effort. There are 40 to 45 government employees in there. Where are we supposed to go?” she said, speaking to journalists outside the Prime Minister’s Office.

She said she has no way of knowing whether any rescue attempt has been made, and complained that the response has been slow.

“They need to be rescued, even if it means bringing in help from abroad,” she said. “We’ve had no contact with them at all. It’s already been three days. What is the government doing?”

She said her husband works for the NEA.

According to her, the employees, including her husband, would typically eat breakfast at 7 am and head down into the tunnel to work, after which they would become unreachable. She said she was last in contact with him at 7 am on August 27, and has had no contact since.

She appealed to the government for rescue efforts, saying communication became impossible after the flood hit Rasuwa. She added that her husband had gone to Rasuwa on August 29 and had remained there since.

title.rendered: 24-hour hotline launched for rescue and treatment of livestock

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The Nepal Veterinary Association has launched a 24-hour hotline service to provide rescue and treatment support for livestock and poultry in flood-affected areas of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other districts hit by floods on Wednesday.

According to the association’s General Secretary, Dr Shankar Neupane, affected livestock farmers can call the hotline at 1159 for technical advice on the health condition, treatment and rescue of their animals and poultry.

Based on information received through the hotline, the association will coordinate with veterinarians and rescue and treatment teams deployed in the field and mobilise teams promptly as needed.

The association also deployed a veterinary team comprising Dr Pravesh Sharma, Dr Nishant Sharma Gelal, Dr Sudip Regmi, Dr Dinesh Aryal and Dr Keshav Kharel to flood-affected areas.

The association said it is coordinating with government agencies, including the Department of Livestock Services, to monitor and prevent diseases in view of the risk of infectious diseases and outbreaks following the floods.

The toll-free hotline 1159 is available for contact and coordination.

The association said people can also contact Dr Shankar Neupane at 9845440404, Dr Bishal Pokharel at 9843397587, and Dr Dinesh Aryal at 9840017076.

title.rendered: Sediment-laden flow rising in Bhotekoshi, Trishuli; NDRRMA urges caution

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has urged people living along the Bhotekoshi River and those involved in rescue and relief operations to remain on high alert after a fresh rise in the river’s water level raised concerns of another flood.

The authority said it had received information that water flow in the Bhotekoshi area, which was hit by a major flood on August 26, had increased again on Friday, with sediment-laden water flowing downstream.

The development has raised the possibility of another flood in the area, according to the authority.

NDRRMA has urged rescue and relief workers operating along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, as well as anyone in potentially vulnerable areas, to exercise extreme caution.

It has also asked people to move to safer locations immediately if signs of danger emerge.

In a notice issued on Friday, NDRRMA spokesperson and Undersecretary Shanti Mahat urged everyone to take necessary precautions in view of the potential risk.

The authority also urged people to take any changes in the river’s flow seriously and avoid staying unnecessarily in areas considered at risk.

Kathmandu, August 28

Former President Bidya Devi Bhandari has urged an immediate joint effort in rescue, relief, and recovery for citizens affected by floods and landslides in Rasuwa and the areas along the Bhotekoshi River.

Expressing sorrow over the loss of life and property caused by the natural disaster, Bhandari called on the government, security agencies, local governments, political parties, civil society organisations, and the general public to make the rescue of affected citizens their top priority.

She drew the attention of relevant authorities to the urgent need to deliver food, healthcare, temporary shelter, and other essential relief supplies to the affected areas, as well as to relocate at-risk residents to safer locations.

She stressed that, in this difficult hour of crisis, all sides need to unite in humanitarian service to provide the affected families with the support they need.

Former President Bhandari also said that greater coordination among relevant agencies is necessary to make the search and rescue of missing citizens more effective.

She paid tribute to those who lost their lives in the disaster and extended her condolences to their families.

title.rendered: World sports community sends solidarity after devastating Nepal floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

After the catastrophic flood on the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa caused massive loss of life and property across several districts of Nepal, the global sports community has expressed its solidarity.

From leading European football clubs to IPL franchises in India and international sporting bodies, organisations have shared messages of sympathy for Nepal’s flood-affected citizens on X (formerly Twitter) and Instagram.

Spanish La Liga champions FC Barcelona posted on their official X account, paying tribute to everyone involved in rescue and relief efforts and expressing solidarity with the Nepali people during this difficult time. A moment of silence was also observed before Barcelona’s match against Athletic Club.

Fellow Spanish club Atlético Madrid also shared condolences on X, expressing deep sorrow for families affected by the floods. The club’s message included the phrase “Stay strong, Nepal,” wishing strength and courage to affected communities.

Indian IPL clubs have shown similar concern. Rajasthan Royals posted sympathy messages on both X and Instagram, while Chennai Super Kings said they were saddened by the loss of life and property and issued their own message of support.

Kolkata Knight Riders expressed condolences to affected families on X and saluted security personnel involved in rescue and relief work. Sunrisers Hyderabad also wished for the safety of affected citizens and voiced solidarity with Nepal.

Beyond football and cricket clubs, various athletes and sporting organisations worldwide have also shared messages of prayer and support for Nepal on X.

The Bhotekoshi flood has caused widespread destruction along the banks of the Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Trishuli river areas, with confirmed reports of hundreds of deaths and a large number of people still missing.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood: Australia announces $5 million in aid, will also deploy technical team

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The Australian government has announced humanitarian assistance worth 5 million Australian dollars for those affected by the Rasuwa flood.

Australia stated on Friday that the funds will go toward immediate rescue, relief, and recovery efforts in the flood-affected areas.

According to the Australian government, at least 39 Australian nationals have been reported missing in the flood. The statement notes that Australian officials are working actively to confirm their status and provide necessary support to those affected.

Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has mobilised additional staff to assist affected Australian citizens. Along with embassy staff in Nepal, a member of the Crisis Response Team and a regional consular officer have been deployed to Kathmandu, with further regional and crisis-response staff expected to follow.

Australia says an initial team of three humanitarian experts will be sent to Nepal within the next 48 hours. Coordinating with Australian personnel already in Kathmandu, they will assist with assessing the humanitarian situation, management, communications, and relief planning. The team will be deployed under Australia’s “Australia Assists” program and will include specialists in humanitarian aid and disaster management.

Where will the funding go?

The $5 million will be channelled through established partner organisations to cover essential needs including food, emergency shelter, clean drinking water, and sanitation. 2 million will go to the World Food Programme (WFP), which Australia says has already begun providing emergency food and logistics support in Nepal. 2 million will be provided to Australian NGOs through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership, funding emergency shelter, sanitation supplies, blankets, medical treatment, and psychosocial support. 1 million will go through the Emergency Action Alliance to support locally led recovery and reconstruction efforts.

Australia noted that many communities remain cut off due to damaged roads and bridges, making access difficult, and said immediate humanitarian assistance is urgently needed.

title.rendered: China suspends rescue operation in Tibet amid increased flood risk

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

China has suspended an ongoing rescue operation in Tibet after the risk of further flooding increased due to a lake formed by a landslide.

Citing Chinese state-run broadcasters, Al Jazeera reported that the Chinese government had ordered rescue teams to move one kilometre away from the site. Hundreds of people remain missing in the Tibet region two days after the devastating landslide.

China suspended the rescue operation on Friday, citing a high risk of further flooding in Tibet. State-controlled media reported the development as hundreds of people remained missing two days after the devastating landslide.

According to China Central Television (CCTV), a lake formed by massive debris and mud deposited by the landslide along the China-Nepal border has filled up, causing water to flow towards the area where rescue teams had been operating. “All rescue teams have been ordered to remain on standby in a safe location and await further instructions,” CCTV reported. Emergency teams that had previously reached the area were also ordered to “withdraw one kilometre,” CCTV reported.

The lake was formed on Wednesday after a landslide carrying mud and debris struck Kerung, a border town in Tibet. Hundreds of people are reportedly missing following the incident. CCTV said continued rainfall is expected to cause the lake’s water level to rise over the next three days, with the level projected to peak around September 1.

This has increased the risk of the lake bursting its banks, potentially sending floodwaters into downstream areas and causing further damage to Kerung Port and other locations downstream, China’s state-run Xinhua News Agency reported late Thursday.

CCTV said emergency engineering teams are closely monitoring the situation. By Friday, 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreign nationals had been evacuated from the disaster-affected area to safety, CCTV reported. According to AFP, rescuers are continuing efforts to locate those still missing using drone-based 3D modelling and thermal imaging technology, as well as manual searches.

The rescue team retrieved the bodies from the river with the help of a motorboat, according to the report.

Workers, employees and security personnel from Sudurpaschim who had gone to Rasuwa for work were caught in the flood.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood raises questions over Nepal’s early warning system

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The devastating flood that tore through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi river corridor on August 26 has raised questions about whether the country’s flood early warning system is equipped to deal with sudden and extreme events.

According to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, the flood travelled about 36 kilometres from the Nepal-China border to Betrabati in roughly 40 minutes, an unusually rapid movement compared with previous floods.

Binod Parajuli, chief of the department’s Flood Forecasting Section, said a sensor near the Nepal-China border was transmitting flood data every 10 minutes. Data were received normally until 8:40am, but the 8:50am reading was not received.

Another sensor at Betrawati, about 36km downstream, continued transmitting data until 9:20am. Its 9:30am reading was also not received.

The timing suggests that the flood entered Nepal between 8:45am and 8:50am and reached Betrabati at around 9:25am.

“This means the flood was moving extremely fast compared with other floods in the past,” Parajuli said.

Previous floods have taken about 14 hours to travel from the Nepal-China border to Devghat, he said. The August 26 flood reached Devghat in about seven hours, with a recorded discharge of around 200 million cubic metres of water.

The extreme flow also destroyed flood monitoring equipment at Langtang, Rasuwagadhi, Betrabati, Syafrubesi and Malekhu. Only the stations at Devghat, Bhorle and Kalikhola near Muglin remain operational.

“We had installed most of the equipment on bridges, considering them relatively safe and strong structures,” Parajuli said. “But the bridges themselves were swept away, along with the equipment.”

The flood destroyed roads and bridges and reduced entire settlements and markets to ruins. The full scale of the human and economic damage is still being assessed.

Nepali and Chinese scientists are investigating the exact cause of the flood. Nepalese officials have so far confirmed that a large section of a glacier collapsed, although further investigation is needed to determine the age and other characteristics of the ice.

Was the warning system capable of detecting the flood?

The disaster has also triggered debate over Nepal’s flood early warning system.

Innovative Engineering Services Pvt Ltd installed the flood monitoring equipment in the Bhotekoshi area for the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

Anup Khanal, an engineer and head of the company, estimates that the flood travelled from Rasuwagadhi to Betrabati at an average speed of 15 to 20 metres per second.

Based on an estimated flood height of around 20 metres and width of around 40 metres, he estimates the peak discharge may have been between 12,000 and 15,000 cubic metres per second.

However, there was no recorded fall in the water level before the monitoring station was damaged, Khanal said. This raises the possibility that the flood may have resulted from a landslide temporarily blocking the river before the dam suddenly burst — a phenomenon known as a landslide dam outburst flood, or LDOF.

“If the river was blocked by a landslide for some time and then suddenly breached, the flood could behave differently from a normal flood, where the water level rises gradually,” Khanal said.

In such a situation, a system that transmits data at fixed intervals may not provide enough time to issue a warning before the flood reaches its peak, he said. However, he stressed that this remains a preliminary assessment that needs to be verified through detailed hydrological and hydraulic studies.

Experts call for sensors at different heights

Khanal said the incident highlights the need to rethink the design and operation of flood warning systems in extreme conditions.

One option would be to introduce threshold-based transmission, rather than relying solely on fixed-interval data transmission.

Under such a system, sensors could continue sending data every 10 minutes during normal conditions. But if the water level begins to cross a predefined risk threshold, the sensor could immediately transmit data instead of waiting for the next scheduled transmission.

This could reduce the time needed to detect a rapidly developing flood and issue warnings.

Khanal also suggested installing backup sensors at different elevations.

Instead of placing a single sensor at one level, one sensor could monitor normal and moderate floods near the lower river level, while another could be installed 20 to 30 metres higher to detect extreme flooding.

The higher sensor would normally remain inactive. If an exceptional flood exceeded the measurement range of the lower sensor, the upper sensor could continue monitoring the rising water and provide additional data for warnings.

‘System needs a comprehensive review’

Khanal said it would be premature to simply conclude that the early warning system “failed”.

Instead, he said authorities need to examine the entire system — including sensor capacity, data transmission, warning thresholds, sensor elevation, backup systems, the flow of warning information and whether equipment can continue operating during extreme disasters.

A technical investigation should determine how long each sensor transmitted data, when communication failed, when the stations were damaged, what the actual nature of the flood was and whether the available data provided enough time to issue warnings.

“The incident shows that Nepal’s flood early warning system needs to evolve beyond simply measuring water levels,” Khanal said. “It must be capable of surviving extreme floods, transmitting data rapidly, using backup sensors and issuing immediate warnings based on risk levels.”

He also stressed the need for continuous satellite monitoring of glacial lakes considered at risk of bursting.

title.rendered: Janai Purnima celebrated at Kumbheshwar Temple in Patan (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Janai Purnima, also known as Raksha Bandhan, is being celebrated across the country today. Every year, a fair is held at the Kumbheshwar Temple in Patan on the occasion.

The temple premises are crowded with devotees celebrating the festival. Some have lined up to offer prayers at the temple, while others are tying sacred threads as part of the Raksha Bandhan ritual. There is also a steady flow of people changing their sacred threads (janai).

Devotees can be seen bathing in the temple’s pond and water spouts. Some young people are enjoying themselves by diving and swimming in the pond within the temple premises.

Police personnel have been deployed to ensure security and manage the queues.

According to religious belief, Lord Ram shot an arrow at Kumbheshwar and brought water from Gosainkunda to the temple’s pond. Because of this belief, devotees from different parts of the country visit Kumbheshwar to bathe on the day of Janai Purnima.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood threatens Nepal’s festive season as China trade route lies in ruins

content.rendered:
Nepal’s biggest festivals — Teej, Dashain, Tihar and Chhath — are just around the corner, followed by the winter season.

Normally, this is when Kathmandu’s major commercial hubs would be buzzing with activity as traders stock up for the festive rush.

Instead, the mood in New Road, Bhotahity and Ranjana Galli is one of anxiety and uncertainty.

The reason is thousands of tonnes of goods meant for the festive season are now stranded, damaged or lost after Wednesday’s devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

Billions of rupees worth of clothes, footwear, electronic goods, garlic, onions, ginger and fruits, imported by traders on loans and credit, were being transported through the Rasuwagadhi border point with China. Hundreds of containers carrying such goods were swept away by the flood.

The disaster has also destroyed the Rasuwagadhi customs yard, while landslides have disrupted the road to the Tatopani border point in Sindhupalchok, leaving transit through that route halted for about a month.

The crisis is no longer only about lost goods and infrastructure. Customs officials, agents and truck drivers who had travelled to Rasuwagadhi to collect shipments are among those missing.

The flood has devastated infrastructure in the Rasuwagadhi area and caused a major human tragedy. The Rasuwagadhi dry port and customs yard, which held infrastructure worth billions of rupees, have been reduced to a riverbed. Hundreds of cargo containers parked there, along with newly imported expensive electric vehicles, were swept away.

For traders who had invested billions in preparation for the festive season, the losses have brought severe financial and psychological pressure.

‘There is nothing left’

Jayant Kumar Agrawal, secretary-general of the Nepal Overseas Exporters and Importers Association, said there was virtually no infrastructure left in the border area and that the humanitarian situation was deeply distressing.

“There is no possibility of opening Rasuwa or Tatopani for now. There is no infrastructure left there; everything has been reduced to a riverbed,” Agrawal said.

Fourteen customs officials remain unaccounted for, he said, while many customs agents, bank employees and truck drivers are also out of contact. Several containers and empty trucks have already been swept away.

Agrawal warned that traders were struggling to think rationally amid the scale of the disaster and that the situation could worsen unless the state immediately prioritised rescue and relief.

Parshuram Dahal, chairman of the RB Complex Business Association in New Road, said communication between traders in Kathmandu and drivers who had travelled to China had also been completely disrupted.

“Most drivers and helpers have their phones switched off, and it is difficult even to get basic information about their condition,” Dahal said. “Some traders’ goods intended for the festive season had already arrived at customs, but those goods have been damaged by the floods and landslides. CCTV footage shows that warehouses and the surrounding area have been destroyed, so a huge financial loss is certain.”

Tatopani offers little immediate relief

The government is also looking at reopening the Tatopani border point in Sindhupalchok, but the situation there remains difficult.

Although authorities have cleared landslides from the Nepal side and built a temporary road, Chinese authorities have not yet allowed containers to be released.

Deependra Prakash Giri, chief customs officer at the Tatopani Customs Office, said the Chinese side had not agreed to release the containers as previously discussed.

“We expected goods to come from there, but they have not released the containers, saying they have no higher-level order,” Giri said. “They say they are still working on the road and that it will take another two or four days. Vehicles can travel from the Nepal side, but the border is almost completely stalled because containers are not being released from the other side.”

Communication between the two sides is also limited.

“We can communicate with them only through messages at present. A nodal officer has been designated, and messages are exchanged through that person,” Giri said.

Chinese customs officials have moved elsewhere after floods and landslides damaged Liping and surrounding areas on the Chinese side.

Pressure grows on Mustang’s Korala crossing

With neither Rasuwagadhi nor Tatopani offering a reliable route, the Department of Customs has advised traders to consider the Korala border point in Mustang as an alternative.

Korala is located on relatively flat terrain and faces less flood and landslide risk. But traders say using the crossing is more a necessity than a genuine alternative.

The remote Korala border lacks the customs infrastructure, wide roads capable of handling large cargo trucks and warehouse facilities available at Rasuwagadhi and Tatopani.

Bidur Chudal, chief customs officer at the Mustang Customs Office, said cargo vehicles were currently operating through the border.

“We are working with basic infrastructure about 14 kilometres below the border,” Chudal said. “We do not have the sophisticated facilities available on the Chinese side, but the border is operating and vehicles are arriving.”

The crossing has already attracted importers of electric vehicles. According to Chudal, 100 BYD vehicles and 63 Foton electric vehicles recently entered Nepal through Korala, while vehicles from other companies are also on their way.

Ready-made clothes, shoes, bags and rolls of fabric are among the other major imports coming through the crossing.

As pressure has grown on the Rasuwa route, traders have increasingly turned to Korala.

“Earlier, one or two containers used to arrive. Now, as many as eight to 10 containers are arriving daily,” Chudal said.

But Korala cannot currently handle food and other perishable imports. The lack of quarantine facilities and adequate manpower means fruits, vegetables and food products cannot be brought through the crossing.

“Unless there is a quarantine facility, it does not appear possible to bring such goods through here,” Chudal said. “For now, Tatopani or other border points will have to be used.”

The Mustang Customs Office has a sanctioned strength of 18 employees, but only 10 are currently working there.

Dahal of the RB Complex Business Association said bringing goods through Korala was essentially a case of making do with what was available.

“It is better than having no option at all,” he said, adding that transportation through Korala would increase both costs and delivery times.

Transport costs could double

Ram Chandra Parajuli, secretary-general of the Nepal Himalaya Trans-Himalayan Commerce Association, said around 50 to 60 kilometres of road infrastructure on the Chinese side toward the Rasuwa-Kerung border had been completely destroyed.

“The physical condition of the Rasuwa border is extremely damaged. Rebuilding the road infrastructure will require a national-level budget and special efforts from the Chinese side,” Parajuli said.

Diverting shipments to Korala would sharply increase transport costs, he said.

“It takes around two days to reach Kathmandu from Korala. Changing the route in this way will significantly increase transportation costs,” Parajuli said. “As we had already estimated, the price of goods in the market could increase by as much as half.”

Another option is to import goods through the sea route via Kolkata in India. But traders say the route is too expensive, complicated and slow to meet demand during Dashain and the other major festivals.

According to Agrawal, the international geopolitical situation has also affected maritime trade.

“It takes a long time to bring goods from Kolkata. After the war in the Middle East, container waiting times have increased and charges have also risen significantly,” he said. “It takes around one and a half months for goods to reach Kolkata from a Chinese port and another 20 to 25 days to reach Nepal from there.”

A route that takes more than two months would increase bank interest costs for traders while potentially making the shipment arrive after the festive and winter seasons have already passed, he said.

Billions tied up in disrupted supply chains

The crisis is therefore not simply about shortages of essential goods. Traders warn that it could severely damage Nepal’s small and medium-sized business sector.

Thousands of traders who borrowed money at high interest rates and imported goods through letters of credit now face the loss of their capital while their shipments remain stranded or destroyed.

“The floods and landslides have destroyed not only goods and infrastructure but also traders’ capital. Many traders have lost their entire investment,” Parajuli said. “Some may even be forced to leave the business.”

He warned that shortages could emerge in the market because traders would struggle to raise new capital after losing goods they had already purchased.

Business representatives have called on the Chinese government to adopt flexible policies to help reroute stranded shipments by sea or air.

A recurring crisis

The disaster at Nepal’s northern trade routes is not without precedent.

Nepal has faced similar disruptions following the Jure landslide in 2014, the 2015 earthquake, the Bhotekoshi flood in 2020 and repeated monsoon disasters.

China formally declared the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border an international crossing on August 30, 2017.

Yet the road connecting Nepal to what is officially an “international” border remains far from the standard expected of a major trade route.

Every year, particularly around the festival season in August and September, floods and landslides disrupt the road network, leaving billions of rupees worth of goods stranded or destroyed. Traders, both large and small, have repeatedly suffered losses worth millions.

The scale of Nepal’s dependence on the route is significant.

In the first month of the current fiscal year 2083/84, in Shrawan alone, Nepal imported goods worth Rs 31.74 billion from China. In the previous fiscal year, imports from China exceeded Rs 400 billion.

Risk of shortages and higher prices

Trade and commerce expert Rabishankar Sainju said the government must take immediate steps to prevent shortages of essential goods in the market as the festival season approaches.

Although Korala is being considered as an alternative after the disaster, its transportation costs are significantly higher, he said.

“Korala is an option for bringing in goods, but compared with Kerung or Tatopani, its transportation cost could be almost double,” Sainju said.

He said transporting goods from Kodari (Tatopani) was already more expensive than through the Rasuwa route, and the cost would rise further if traders were forced to use Korala.

“From my preliminary analysis, the transportation cost through Korala is significantly higher,” he said. “Ultimately, the direct impact will be felt by consumers.”

Sainju estimated that around 200 to 300 containers of goods may have been swept away or damaged in the Rasuwagadhi area.

The resulting losses, he said, could run into billions of rupees and have severely affected traders’ confidence.

“Container drivers and traders themselves are missing or out of contact,” he said. “In such circumstances, it is difficult for traders to have the confidence to immediately bring goods through another border.”

With Rasuwagadhi itself blocked, he said traders may be forced towards more expensive options such as Korala or sea and air routes at precisely the time when import demand is at its highest ahead of the festivals.

Sainju urged the government to treat the situation as an emergency.

“The government needs to coordinate on a war footing to prevent artificial shortages and inflation during the festival season,” he said. “If the state can provide some form of subsidy or relief for the additional costs traders incur when using Korala or other alternative routes, it will provide relief to consumers.”

Economist Dr Dill Raj Khanal agreed that the disaster represented a major setback for Nepal’s broader economic development.

“This is a very serious loss for the country. Along with the loss of human lives, the billions of rupees in damage to roads, bridges and power generation will have a serious impact on the economy,” Khanal said.

The destruction at Rasuwagadhi, he said, would also undermine foreign trade and traders’ confidence.

With imports from China disrupted, supplies routed through India or other alternatives are likely to become more expensive. Khanal said the government should therefore consider special concessions or subsidies.

He also called for the government to coordinate with political parties, the private sector and development partners to prepare a time-bound and comprehensive recovery plan.

“Disaster management must move forward on a war footing,” he said. “The Rs 25 billion the World Bank is said to be providing, along with assistance from India, China and other countries, needs to be mobilised effectively.”

He stressed that the government must establish a rapid disaster management system to prevent shortages and control inflation.

For now, Nepal’s main supply chain from China has been severed just as demand for goods is about to surge.

The immediate consequences will be felt not only in warehouses and customs yards, but eventually in consumers’ kitchens and household budgets. If alternative routes prove significantly more expensive and supplies remain disrupted, the resulting price increases could hit low- and middle-income families hardest — and create a ripple effect across the wider economy.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood turns Devighat, Dhunge Bazaar into ruins

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 26

The shops are gone. So are the walls of homes and structures that had stood for decades.

Where Devighat Bazaar in Nuwakot once stood, there are now only rocks, mud and debris left behind by the flood.

The devastating flood of August 26 caused widespread destruction across Nuwakot, with the Trishuli and surrounding rivers swelling and tearing through settlements including Devighat, Dhunge Bazaar and Trishuli Bazaar.

An Onlinekhabar team visiting Devighat found a settlement barely recognisable. For locals, saying their shops were “damaged” does not come close to describing what happened.

“It’s not just that the shop was damaged. There is nothing left there. The house is gone. Everything in the shop is gone,” one shopkeeper said, staring at the rubble.

He had been running a business in Devighat for more than two decades. His wife taught tailoring while he ran an electrical goods shop. Years of work and savings disappeared within minutes.

But he has little time to count his losses. For now, he says, the biggest relief is that he and his family survived.

‘It came all at once’

The family was at a temple in Devighat when the flood began. After hearing that the Trishuli River was rising and had even swept away a bridge, they decided not to return home.

They received warnings that residents of Devighat needed to evacuate and immediately headed for higher ground.

“In the past, the river would rise gradually. This time, it came all at once,” the shopkeeper said. “After the Trishuli bridge was swept away, there was no way we could stay here. We left immediately.”

Their decision to flee saved their lives. But not everyone had the same chance.

The flood also inundated an ashram in Devighat, where rescue operations continued from the morning of Bhadra 10 until late at night.

For the shopkeeper, the destruction is more than a natural disaster. It marks the end of a chapter that had lasted more than 20 years.

He had never seen a flood like this before.

“I was told there was a flood like this in our grandparents’ time, in 2019 BS, and that it brought rocks down with it,” he said. “Now even that bridge is gone. The rocks are gone. Nothing is left.”

His voice broke as he spoke about the loss of Jalpa Temple, a site of archaeological and religious importance.

“Even a place with such historical importance, Jalpa Temple, has no trace left. You could say the very existence of this place has been wiped out.”

The flood has therefore taken more than houses and shops. It has damaged the history of a settlement, religious heritage and a way of life built over generations.

Flood reached as high as two-storey homes

According to Devighat residents, floodwater entered the settlement from the area below the statue of King Prithvi Narayan Shah.

Residents had only a short time to respond before rushing towards higher ground.

The floodwater reached from the area of an old-age home to the gate of a school across the river, locals said.

Many houses below the road were completely swept away. In some areas, signs of flooding can be seen as high as the second floors of buildings. Shop shutters and pillars have been damaged.

The bridges connecting Devighat have also been swept away.

Two bridges crossing the Tadi River were destroyed, while another bridge further downstream was also washed away, leaving Devighat largely cut off by road.

“It is completely disconnected now,” locals said.

Dhunge Bazaar: Where houses stood, there is now a riverbed

The destruction becomes even more severe further downstream at Dhunge Bazaar.

The nearby Trishuli Bazaar was also hit hard by the flood. Some three- and four-storey buildings have been buried under flood debris and mud, while a large part of the market has been damaged, according to residents.

Local resident Binay Rijal was in Kathmandu when the disaster struck, but remained in contact by phone with people in Trishuli Bazaar.

He said he had received reports that the water level around Betravati was becoming increasingly dangerous before the flood.

“We had seen smaller floods before, so perhaps we were a little careless too,” he said. “But nobody could have imagined this level of destruction.”

According to Rijal, around 80 percent of houses in the Dhunge and Trishuli Bazaar areas have suffered major damage. Some people who were in the market are still out of contact, locals said.

‘The shop is gone. My citizenship is gone too’

Sandeep Thakur, who ran a hair-cutting shop in Trishuli Bazaar, is no longer looking for his shop.

There is no shop left to find.

“My shop is completely gone,” he said. “We managed to run when the flood came. There were documents and some money inside, but we could not take anything. My citizenship certificate was also left there.”

Thakur is originally from Birgunj in Parsa district. He had moved to Nuwakot for work and was running the business while living there with his family.

After the flood warning, police, the Army and Armed Police Force used loudspeakers to alert residents.

He managed to get his entire family to safety.

“We warned my wife and children and managed to escape,” he said. “We survived. That is the most important thing.”

His house, shop, documents and money are gone.

But his family is alive.

For now, that is what matters most to him.

‘We don’t know where the three boys are’

Families displaced by the flood in the Dhunge-Trishuli area are now searching for their relatives.

Along the edge of Dhunge Bazaar, people stand staring towards the north. Some look silently at what remains of their homes. Others wait with a faint hope that missing relatives might somehow return.

According to one local resident, three young men who had left early in the morning for work remain out of contact.

“Two boys had gone towards the new bridge. We haven’t been able to find them,” he said. “Another had come towards Trishuli, and we have not heard from him either.”

His plea is simple: find the missing.

“If they are across the river, they need to be brought back from there,” he said.

Although the floodwaters have begun to recede, the anxiety among survivors has not.

Could their relatives still be buried beneath the rubble?

Could they have been swept far downstream?

Those questions continue to haunt the residents.

‘We lost the market, but we saved our lives’

The flood has almost erased the physical landscape of these Nuwakot settlements.

Hydropower projects, bridges, roads, homes, shops and government structures have all been damaged. Along the riverbanks, years of work and investment have been reduced to mud and debris.

Bagmati Province Chief Minister Kiran Thapa Magar, who inspected the flood-hit areas, said more than 40 small and large bridges had been damaged across Nuwakot.

For now, rescue and search operations remain the priority. The government plans to focus on restoring roads, bridges, health services and other infrastructure only after the immediate rescue operation is completed.

Reconstruction may eventually rebuild houses, reconnect bridges and revive the markets.

But how do you rebuild a life that was swept away in minutes?

The Devighat shopkeeper’s two decades of work will not return overnight. Thakur’s citizenship certificate and documents are gone. Jalpa Temple and the old structures that carried the history of the settlement will take years to restore, if they can be restored at all.

For now, residents of Devighat and Dhunge Bazaar are searching through what remains.

Some are looking for pieces of their homes.

Some are looking for shop shutters and documents.

Some are searching for missing relatives.

And some simply stand silently, looking at the places where their homes once stood.

The flood took almost everything.

title.rendered: 1,545 rescued after Rasuwa flood as 28 police officers remain missing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

A total of 1,545 people caught in the devastating Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa on Wednesday have been rescued, according to Nepal Police.

As of 7am Friday, 644 people had been rescued from Rasuwa, 898 from Nuwakot and three from Dhading, police said.

Meanwhile, 84 people injured in the disaster are receiving treatment or have been discharged from hospitals in Kathmandu.

Police said 4,348 personnel have been mobilised for rescue, relief and assistance operations in the flood-affected areas.

So far, 469 people affected by the flood have been found, according to police.

However, 28 police officers remain out of contact following the disaster.

Rescue and search operations are continuing in the affected areas.

title.rendered: 469 bodies recovered from Rasuwa flood across eight districts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The bodies of 469 people caught in the devastating Rasuwa flood have been recovered from eight districts, according to the latest police bulletin.

As of 7am Friday, 469 bodies had been recovered from Rasuwa and seven other districts affected by the disaster.

According to police, 12 bodies have been recovered in Rasuwa, 37 in Nuwakot, 33 in Dhading, 178 in Chitwan, 44 in Gorkha, 28 in Tanahun, 110 in Nawalparasi East and 27 in Nawalparasi West.

The recovery operations are continuing in the flood-affected areas as authorities search for those still missing.

title.rendered: ‘I thought I was dreaming. Then I opened my eyes and found myself in the river’

content.rendered:
For 21-year-old Sujal Thapa Chhetri, the first message he wants to send after surviving the devastating flood in Rasuwa is simple: do not build your home near a river.

Sujal is recovering at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, where he has been recounting the terrifying experience that nearly killed him.

Until a few days ago, home was where Sujal returned to rest after a long day.

He would usually finish his duty inside a tunnel at around 2am and return home to sleep. He did the same on the night before the flood.

At around 6am, he briefly woke up. Then he fell asleep again. That was when the river swept him away.

When he opened his eyes, Sujal realised he was not dreaming. He was in the middle of a raging river.

“At that moment, I felt as if sleep had been taken over by death. I thought I was dreaming that the river had swept me away. But when I opened my eyes, I was actually in the middle of the river,” he recalled from his hospital bed.

Water was surging violently around him. The current threw him from one side to another, repeatedly pulling him under before bringing him back to the surface.

He thought his chances of survival were almost gone.

Desperate to save himself, he tried to grab the edge of a field.

“I tried to hold on to the edge of the field. I kept trying to hold on and somehow managed to get out from there,” he said.

What happened next is unclear in his memory.

He does not know whether he lost consciousness or what happened after that. When he regained consciousness, he was somewhere else. Rescuers had taken him to his brother-in-law’s house higher up.

Sand in his ears and stomach

The flood left Sujal with injuries across his body.

He suffered a head injury and multiple wounds. One of his hands is difficult to move. Sand entered his ears, and the floodwater carried sand deep into his body.

“I vomited yesterday and it was all sand. Sand came out from my mouth and stomach,” he said.

Sujal is now receiving treatment in the red zone at Teaching Hospital.

His physical injuries may heal with time. The wounds in his mind, however, are harder to treat.

He survived. He does not know where his family is.

Asked whether he thought he would survive, Sujal shook off the question.

“I didn’t think I would. I thought I had died. I don’t know how I was lucky enough to survive,” he said.

For those few minutes, his life hung between survival and death. His desperate attempt to grab the edge of the field gave him a chance to reach safety.

But the news he received after regaining consciousness brought little relief.

He was alive. He did not know where his family was.

His father had been away in Gosainkunda when the flood struck. But Sujal has no answers about his mother, his brothers, his grandmother or his uncle.

“They say my grandmother was swept away. They say my two brothers were swept away. They say my elder uncle was swept away. They say my mother was swept away. I only just managed to survive,” he said.

His body is being treated in hospital, but his thoughts remain in his village.

When he thinks about what may have happened there, fear overwhelms him.

His own house has also been swept away.

It was a block-built house with a corrugated metal roof. Now, he says, there is no trace of it.

Sujal does not even have his mobile phone anymore. He has no clothes of his own and no phone numbers with which to contact relatives or ask about his family.

Friends have been coming to the hospital after seeing his name on the list of survivors released by the hospital.

‘I have learned my lesson’

After coming back from the brink of death, Sujal wants others to learn from what happened to him.

“People should not build houses on riverbanks or near rivers. Even if it is a small river, even if the river has dried up, even if you think water never comes there, you should not build a house near it,” he said.

“I have learned my lesson. I don’t know by what luck I survived.”

Waiting for news of his family

Sujal remains in hospital, receiving treatment. His physical wounds will gradually heal. But the questions haunting him have no easy answers.

Where is his mother? Where are his two brothers? Where is his grandmother? What happened to his uncle? That uncertainty is now his greatest pain.

His sister, who lives abroad, may or may not have received the full news of what happened. He does not know. He has no phone to call her and no numbers to reach anyone.

There is no home for him to return to either. Still, hope remains.

He hopes that one day he will hear news of the people he loves. Sujal survived death.

But the world he has returned to is no longer the one he left behind.

The flood did not only sweep away his home. It also carried away his family, his sense of security and the ordinary future he once imagined. From his hospital bed, Sujal carries two things with him: disbelief that he survived — and an aching wait for news of his family.

title.rendered: 27 bank employees remain missing after Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

At least 27 employees working at branches of seven banks near the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Rasuwa remain out of contact following the devastating Bhotekoshi flood.

The employees have been unreachable since the flood struck on Wednesday morning.

Santosh Koirala, president of the Nepal Bankers’ Association, said efforts to establish contact had continued but the employees had not been reached as of late Thursday.

“We are continuing our efforts from our side, but we have still been unable to establish contact,” Koirala said. “As of late Thursday, 27 employees working at branches of seven banks could not be contacted.”

He said nine bank branch offices in various locations have been completely damaged, including branches in Timure and Syafrubesi. The employees who remain out of contact are also from the affected areas, he said.

The highest number of missing employees are from Nepal Investment Mega Bank, with seven employees out of contact. Machhapuchchhre Bank has five, Sanima Bank two, Laxmi Sunrise Bank three, Himalayan Bank one, NMB Bank four and Prabhu Bank five employees who remain uncontactable.

Koirala said banks have not yet been able to assess the extent of physical damage to their branches because access to the affected areas remains difficult.

“We have not been able to assess the physical damage. We tried to do so on Thursday, but it was not possible,” he said, adding that the banks were still in the process of verifying the damage.

He said it was also too early to estimate financial losses, as banks have yet to determine whether the affected branches had lockers, how much cash was stored in their vaults and how much may have been swept away by the flood.

The Bhotekoshi flood has caused widespread destruction in Rasuwa, particularly around settlements and infrastructure along the river.

title.rendered: Govt orders universities to suspend exams from August 29 amid disaster

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The government has directed all universities in Nepal to suspend examinations scheduled from August 29, citing the disruption caused by natural disasters to the lives of students, parents and the general public.

Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel issued the directive to university vice-chancellors by exercising the authority granted under the respective university laws.

Under the directive, all examinations scheduled from August 29 must be postponed. Universities have been asked to publish revised examination schedules at an appropriate time.

Universities have also been instructed to arrange re-examinations at a suitable time for students who were unable to sit for examinations scheduled for August 28 due to various circumstances.

Minister Pokharel has also asked universities to suspend non-essential gatherings, workshops, seminars, assemblies and other collective events.

Universities have been directed to maintain regular contact and coordination with disaster-affected students and parents through the universities and concerned educational institutions, and provide necessary support and facilitation.

They have also been asked to arrange psychosocial counselling for affected students and, where necessary, their parents. Universities have been told to take necessary measures to ensure students can continue their education and receive appropriate academic support in light of the disruption caused by the disaster.

Pokharel urged university officials to take immediate decisions to implement these measures, citing the sensitivity of the current situation.

He also called on university authorities to give the highest priority to the safety and welfare of students, parents, teachers and staff during the difficult period caused by the disasters.

title.rendered: Rasuwa cut off from rest of Nepal as flood survivors face food, shelter shortages

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Rasuwa remains cut off from other districts and Kathmandu after Wednesday’s devastating flood, with roads, electricity and telephone services disrupted and local authorities warning of severe shortages of food, shelter and rescue capacity.

The worst-hit areas are Gosainkunda and Uttargaya rural municipalities, where survivors are struggling to access basic supplies.

“Nothing, nothing,” Gosainkunda Rural Municipality chair Kaisang Nurpu Tamang said when asked about the situation. The municipality’s vice-chair Pratima Tamang and ward chairs Kami Chhiring Tamang of Ward 2 (Timure) and Dawa Mingmar Tamang of Ward 5 (Syafrubesi) are among those reported missing.

Uttargaya Rural Municipality chair Madhav Aryal said the disaster had left people with a sense that the state was absent.

“All the connections are down. The electricity connection has been completely cut off, so there is nowhere to charge mobile phones,” Aryal said. “The minimum responsibility that the state should fulfil has not been met.”

He said rescue efforts remained severely limited, with roads cut off and helicopters unable to reach everyone in need.

Around 150 people who fled a hydropower project are stranded across the river and facing food shortages, Aryal said. Authorities have also been unable to reunite 36 students who are currently in Nuwakot with their families because the Trishuli River and damaged roads have cut off access.

The municipality is currently sheltering around 3,500 people, including students, survivors who have lost their homes and families, elderly people, pregnant women, new mothers and people requiring oxygen.

“We have two ambulances and one vehicle. We had an office. Now we have nothing,” Aryal said.

The scale of the deaths and disappearances also remains unclear. Aryal said the municipality was collecting data but estimated that around 750 people may be missing.

Workers at the under-construction Trishuli 3B hydropower project are also among those whose whereabouts are unknown, with some believed to be trapped inside tunnels. The condition of workers at other hydropower projects is also unclear.

Aryal said bodies had been swept downstream and some were lying along roads, creating a growing health risk as they began to decompose in the heat.

“There is no coordination mechanism from the state for managing the bodies,” he said. “It is a state of absence.”

He urged the federal government to immediately coordinate helicopter rescue operations with local representatives, saying authorities on the ground know where people are stranded and where help is most urgently needed.

“We need the state’s help and support. We need it immediately,” he said.

title.rendered: Prithvi Highway remains blocked as flood debris hampers traffic

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The Prithvi Highway, a key section of the Kathmandu–Muglin–Narayangadh road, remains blocked after a devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River deposited large amounts of mud and debris at several locations in Dhading.

The highway has been obstructed since Wednesday evening after floodwaters from the Bhotekoshi River swept mud onto sections of the road in Galchhi and Gajuri rural municipalities.

According to traffic police superintendent Dilli Narayan Pandey, debris remains to be cleared from three locations — two in Gajuri Rural Municipality and one in Galchhi Rural Municipality.

In Gajuri-5, mud has accumulated at Galoudi and Bahuni Bhir, while debris remains at Mahesh Dobhan in Galchhi Rural Municipality.

Authorities are using heavy equipment to remove the mud and debris and reopen the highway.

Pandey said the cleanup has taken longer because the affected sections are near settlements. “There are settlements where the mud has accumulated on the road. The deposited mud has to be removed and transported elsewhere, which has caused the delay,” he told Onlinekhabar.

He said equipment has yet to reach Bahuni Bhir in Gajuri-5. Work there can begin only after the debris at Galoudi and Mahesh Dobhan is cleared, he said.

Authorities are working to reopen the highway by the end of Friday, Pandey said.

title.rendered: Army rescues 350 people trapped inside Upper Trishuli hydropower tunnel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The Nepali Army has rescued 350 people who were trapped inside a tunnel of the Upper Trishuli Hydropower Project in Rasuwa following the devastating Bhotekoshi River flood.

The reports that hundreds of people were trapped inside the tunnel had sparked widespread concern as rescue teams faced difficult conditions in the flood-hit area.

The Prime Minister’s Secretariat said the Army successfully carried out the challenging rescue operation and brought 350 people to safety.

However, more than 100 people are still believed to be trapped inside the Upper Trishuli tunnel, according to the Nepali Army. Rescue efforts to reach them are continuing.

The Army said it rescued a total of 883 local residents and workers from various flood-affected areas of Rasuwa on Thursday alone.

The Bhotekoshi flood has caused widespread destruction in Rasuwa, damaging infrastructure and leaving people stranded in several locations. Rescue teams have been using helicopters and other resources to reach those cut off by the disaster.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood damages schools, leaves students and teachers stranded

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

The sudden flood that struck on Wednesday morning has damaged schools in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, disrupting classes and leaving authorities struggling to assess the full extent of the destruction.

In Rasuwa, where the flood entered Nepal from Tibet, the extent of damage to schools is still unclear because communication with several affected areas has been cut off.

Authorities in Nuwakot are also working to reunite students who were at school when the flood struck with their families.

Damage in Rasuwa still unclear

Preliminary information suggests that six schools in Rasuwa have been affected, with the Gosainkunda Rural Municipality reporting the most damage.

Timure Community School in Timure, Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-2, suffered major damage after floodwaters hit its building. The exact extent of the damage, including whether parts of the building were swept away or collapsed, has not yet been established.

A school in Uttargaya Rural Municipality was also damaged, with students reportedly escaping to safety.

Two boarding schools and two community schools in the Timure area have also been affected. Their names have not yet been confirmed.

Based on preliminary information, the four schools are believed to have possibly been swept away by the flood.

Durga Prasad Silwal, head of the Education Development and Coordination Unit in Rasuwa, reached Nuwakot after communication with the district was cut off.

He said it has been impossible to collect detailed information about the damage because all forms of communication have been disrupted.

“We have been unable to find out about the damage because there is no phone or internet. We cannot contact anyone. There is no electricity, telephone or internet,” Silwal told Onlinekhabar. “I had to come six hours away to Nuwakot before I could get connected.”

Preliminary reports indicate that Timure in Gosainkunda Rural Municipality-2 has suffered the most damage. Communication with the area remains cut off.

Pema Dorje Ghale, a ward member of Gosainkunda-2 who is currently in Kathmandu, said he had been unable to contact people in the flood-hit area.

“We have not been able to get information about the damage. The phone does not connect,” Ghale said.

Nuwakot struggles to reunite students with families

Schools in Nuwakot were already conducting classes when the flood struck.

Because the flood hit while students were at school, many children could not be taken home on Wednesday. With communication between students and their parents disrupted, authorities have struggled to reunite them.

Prabha Bogati, deputy mayor of Bidur Municipality, said the situation had become particularly difficult.

“It got late. The children were at school and the parents were at home. When you imagine the situation of the children and their parents, your heart breaks,” Bogati said. “Relief and rescue efforts are also difficult because the roads are blocked.”

She said authorities were asking schools and local residents around the affected areas to take care of the children.

The flood has damaged six schools in Nuwakot, four of them completely, according to Surya Khati, head of the district’s Education Development and Coordination Unit.

Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Bidur Municipality-5, which has 1,643 students, was completely damaged.

However, no human casualties were reported at the school because students had already been moved to a safe location before the flood caused major damage.

Principal Rajendra Dawadi said around 50 people, including teachers, staff and students, spent the day on higher ground above Trishuli Bazaar.

The flood also completely destroyed the hostel of Chandeshwar Secondary School in Tupche, Bidur-7.

The physical structures of Ramchandra Basic School in Betrawati, Bidur-10, and Uttargaya Boarding School were completely swept away.

Floodwater entered JD Boarding School and Pioneer School in Bidur-6.

Electricity has now been restored in parts of flood-hit Nuwakot that had been without power and telephone communication.

But damaged roads and bridges continue to make it difficult to reunite students with their parents.

“The roads in Bidur and Trishuli areas have been cut off,” Khati told Onlinekhabar. “We are currently using helicopters to take children to safe places and reunite them with their families.”

Schools in Dhading flooded, but no structural damage reported

Four schools in Dhading were flooded, disrupting classes, although no major physical damage has been reported.

Three schools in Galchhi Rural Municipality — Bageshwari Secondary School, Amaleshwar Gurukul School and Success Academy School — were affected.

Jaleshwar Secondary School in Siddhalek Rural Municipality was also flooded.

According to Krishna Kumar Shrestha, head of Dhading’s Education Development and Coordination Unit, the schools can only be cleaned and prepared for classes after the Prithvi Highway is cleared.

“Once the main road is cleared, transportation will be possible. Then the work of cleaning the school premises can begin,” Shrestha told Onlinekhabar.

Eight Dhading teachers missing after travelling to Gosainkunda

Eight teachers from Dhading who travelled to Gosainkunda have been out of contact since Wednesday.

According to Shrestha, the missing include three currently serving teachers and five former teachers.

The three serving teachers are Thakur Prasad Lamsal of Pashupati Secondary School in Nilkantha Municipality, Januka Khanal of Deurali Secondary School and Shivahari Lamsal of Palpa Samari Bhanjyang Secondary School.

Five former teachers from Dhading who travelled to Gosainkunda on pilgrimage are also out of contact.

They are Tulsi Timilsena and Ishwari Prasad Timilsena of Nilkantha Municipality, Hariprasad Silwal and Ghanshyam Bhatt of Siddhalek Rural Municipality, and former teacher Narayan Prasad Lamsal of Jwalamukhi Rural Municipality.

title.rendered: When disaster strikes before communities recover from previous climate extremes, crisis escalates

content.rendered:
Major flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have destroyed homes, roads, bridges and local hydropower projects. The flooding of the Bhote Koshi river is affecting 50,000 residents. More than 300 people are dead, with hundreds more, including international tourists, missing.

This region of the Himalayas had not yet recovered from the Bhote Koshi flooding in 2025 that killed nine people as it washed away a “friendship bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting trade and transport for months.

In Sri Lanka, recent floods and landslides struck affected communities that were still recovering from Cyclone Ditwah, which had caused widespread damage only nine months earlier. With little time to recover from the cyclone, communities had no protection from further flooding. More than 15,000 people have been directly affected and 6,800 people were displaced this August.

Disaster risk usually considers how severe the next flood, wildfire, cyclone or drought will be. But the Nepal and Sri Lanka examples show another dimension that is often overlooked: how quickly can a community recover and will it do so before the next disaster arrives?

A disaster rarely leaves a place exactly as it found it. Roads and bridges may remain damaged. Families may have spent their savings. Businesses may still be struggling. Governments can still be financing reconstruction, while hospitals and other public services remain under pressure.

If another hazard arrives before these systems have recovered, it does not encounter the same community that existed before the first disaster. It encounters a place with less resilience and a weakened infrastructure. Hundreds of travellers are missing after flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border.

A useful way to understand this is through the recovery gap: the relationship between how long recovery takes and how much time is available before another damaging disaster occurs.

Imagine two communities experiencing similar floods. In one, the previous major disaster occurred ten years earlier. Homes have been rebuilt, infrastructure repaired and emergency resources replenished. In the other, another disaster happened only six months ago. Roads remain under repair, families are still displaced or in debt, and public authorities are still paying for reconstruction. The new flood may be physically similar in both places. Its consequences may not be.

Incomplete recovery can substantially increase long-term losses. A 2025 study of recurrent flooding in the Philippines that losses increased by 40% between 2000 and 2018 because of incomplete recover. This suggests that repeated disaster losses are not always simply additive. The first disaster can change the conditions under which the next one occurs and the effects of subsequent disasters can be much more severe.

Recovery has many clocks

Recovery is often described as if a community is either recovered or not, a simplistic binary. It’s more of a sliding scale. Electricity and freshwater supplies may return within days. A damaged road may take months to repair. Rebuilding homes can take years. Businesses may reopen while still carrying substantial debt. Household finances, ecosystems and mental wellbeing can recover on entirely different timescales.

A place can therefore look recovered according to one indicator while remaining highly vulnerable according to another.

It took more than a decade for New Orleans in the US to achieve substantial physical and structural recovery following Hurricane Katrina in 2005. While basic emergency operations and power restoration took weeks to months, full neighbourhood rebuilding, population stabilisation and major flood protection system upgrades spanned 15 years or more. And this was in one of the richest countries in the world.

Recovery is also unequal. Wealthier households may have insurance, savings and access to credit. Poorer households often have fewer resources to repair homes, replace belongings or absorb lost income. In the case of Hurricane Katrina, many poorer households who had hurricane insurance were refused payouts as the damage was deemed to be flood-related because of the burst levees and not by the hurricane. So, it is not only the time between disasters that matters. It is also how much recovery can happen during that time.

This issue becomes increasingly important where climate change alters the frequency or severity of weather extremes. If reconstruction requires five years but another damaging event occurs after two, the interval between disasters starts competing with the time needed to recover. That should change how we manage disaster risk.

Measure recovery, not only damage

Governments are generally good at recording immediate losses: damaged buildings, displaced people, destroyed infrastructure and financial costs. But they also need to know what remains unrepaired months or years later. Recovery monitoring needs to include housing, infrastructure functionality, business activity, household finances, public services and displacement. The question should not stop at “how much did we lose?” It should continue with “how much vulnerability remains?”

Disasters are not isolated occurrences. Floods, wildfires, droughts and storms are often assessed separately. These assessments are essential, but communities experience these hazards through the same infrastructure, economy and population.

The road damaged by one event may be needed for evacuation during the next. An electricity system weakened today may be supporting hospitals or water services tomorrow. Risk assessments should therefore consider plausible hazard sequences and the condition critical systems may be in when another disaster hits. This does not mean predicting the exact order of future disasters. It means abandoning the assumption that every new disaster meets a fully recovered system.

Recovery should not be seen only as the final stage of the disaster that just happened. It is also preparation for whatever comes next. Restoring infrastructure, supporting households and reopening essential services quickly can reduce the vulnerability carried into the next event.

But simply rebuilding the same vulnerable systems recreates the same risks. Recovery should therefore combine speed with adaptation: stronger infrastructure, better redundancy, improved emergency planning and greater support for communities that would otherwise take the longest to recover. Recent research shows that the government plays a critical role in ensuring rapid, efficient and effective recovery.

While asking “how severe could the next disaster be?”, we should also ask “how recovered will we be when it arrives?” Because the next disaster does not start from zero. It inherits what the last one left behind.
