title.rendered: Rasuwa flood death toll reaches 389 as rescue efforts continue across eight districts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The death toll from the devastating Bhotekoshi flood that struck Rasuwa and swept downstream on Wednesday has risen to 389, with bodies recovered across eight districts, according to Nepal Police.

As of 9 pm Thursday, police had recovered 17 bodies in Rasuwa, 28 in Nuwakot, 33 in Dhading, 137 in Chitwan, 32 in Gorkha, 28 in Tanahun, 87 in East Nawalparasi and 27 in West Nawalparasi.

A total of 466 injured people have also been rescued, police said.

The latest figures came as search and rescue operations continued throughout the day in areas cut off by the flood. Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force personnel have been deployed alongside helicopters to reach stranded survivors and recover bodies.

The flood, which struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa on Wednesday morning, caused widespread destruction before moving downstream through the Trishuli and Narayani river systems. Roads, bridges, schools, settlements and other infrastructure have been heavily damaged, making access to several affected areas difficult.

In Rasuwa, communications remain disrupted in some of the worst-hit areas, complicating efforts to determine the full scale of the disaster. Families have meanwhile continued searching for missing relatives at hospitals, body identification centres and other locations where recovered bodies are being brought.

The disaster has also triggered a new warning downstream. Satellite analysis showed that a lake had formed upstream after a massive ice and rock avalanche blocked part of the Lhende River. Authorities have warned that the natural dam could breach and cause another flood, urging residents and rescue teams along the Bhotekoshi river corridor to remain highly alert.

Rescue operations have been further complicated by extensive damage to roads and bridges. In Nuwakot, authorities have also been working to reunite children who were at school when the flood struck with their families.

The scale of the destruction remains difficult to establish, with search teams still unable to reach some locations. Officials and local authorities have repeatedly called for more personnel and equipment to support field operations, including the recovery and management of bodies.

title.rendered: Lack of rescuers hampers search and body recovery after Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 28

Bidur Municipality Deputy Mayor Prabha Bogati has said a shortage of personnel on the ground is hampering rescue operations and the management of bodies following the Bhotekoshi flood.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar, Bogati said helicopters and relief supplies had reached the area, but blocked roads were making it difficult to deliver assistance to affected riverside settlements.

She said additional trained security personnel and volunteers were urgently needed to clear debris, search for survivors and recover bodies.

“Field teams have not been able to reach places that are just five minutes away because helicopters cannot land and roads are blocked,” Bogati said.

She said several bodies had been swept down the river, with reports of a large number of bodies in Belkotgadhi. Failure to manage them could create health risks for nearby communities, she warned.

Bogati also said authorities were trying to reunite children who were separated from their parents when the flood struck while they were at school, but a lack of resources was making the effort difficult.

She said access from Kathmandu to Bidur via Chhahare remains open, but reaching the flood-hit riverside areas from Bidur is difficult.

Rescue and medical teams are treating the injured at Trishuli Hospital, the Nepal Army training centre and private medical facilities, while seriously injured patients are being referred to Kathmandu.

title.rendered: Thermal drones to be deployed to locate people waiting for rescue in Rasuwa flood-hit areas

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

NagarikAlert is set to deploy drones to flood-affected areas to locate people waiting for rescue and help deliver relief supplies.

The organisation said it will send two thermal drones on Friday to search for people who may still be stranded in disaster-hit areas. The drones can detect the body heat of people and animals, helping identify whether survivors are present in areas that are difficult to access.

The drones are being deployed to help determine whether people waiting for rescue are still alive, according to NagarikAlert.

The organisation will also use drones to deliver relief supplies, said its CEO, Yujesh Maleku.

Two of the drones can carry up to 100 kilograms of relief materials each. Another drone can carry up to 50 kilograms, while two others can carry up to 15 kilograms each.

Maleku said two drone pilots, along with relief materials, will also be transported to the affected areas by helicopter on Friday.

The drone operation is aimed at reaching areas that remain difficult to access following the floods and helping authorities locate stranded people and deliver essential supplies.

title.rendered: Govt to map land damage caused by Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation and the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration have decided to collect details of damage to private and public land in areas affected by the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa.

A meeting of the ministry’s high-level management group decided to assign the Department of Survey the task of conducting a field assessment and collecting detailed information on damage to private and public land.

The Department of Survey will visit the affected areas to document damage to land and structures and carry out disaster mapping of the flood-affected areas, according to the ministry’s secretariat.

The ministry said the mapping will help establish the actual extent of the damage and facilitate relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts.

The ministry said accurate mapping of the damage to residents and physical infrastructure caused by the Bhotekoshi flood will be important for preparing plans for future management and reconstruction.

title.rendered: A new lake has formed above Rasuwa. Here’s what we know

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

A large lake has formed below a massive avalanche in the northern part of Langtang Lirung, raising concerns about another flood in Rasuwa.

Chinese media and experts who have analysed satellite images have concluded that the lake formed at the confluence of two small mountain streams.

Here is what is known so far about the new lake, how it formed and the potential risk it poses downstream.

How did the lake form?

A massive avalanche occurred in the northern part of 7,234-metre Langtang Lirung on Wednesday morning.

Water resources expert Santosh Nepal estimates that a mixture of ice, snow and rock fell from around 5,500 metres to about 3,000 metres.

“It appears that a mass of snow and ice fell from around 5,000 metres to an elevation of around 3,000 metres,” Nepal said. “Because it came crashing down from such a height, we estimate that it generated enormous energy.”

Experts believe the mass of snow and ice flowed downhill and turned into a flood, while a large depression was created below the avalanche site. Water then accumulated there, forming a lake.

According to Chinese media, the lake has formed below the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, whose waters eventually flow into the Lhende Khola. The Lhende Khola joins the Kerung Khola at Rasuwagadhi.

How large is the lake?

Citing China’s Ministry of Water Resources, China’s Global Times reported that around 2 million cubic metres of water had accumulated in the depression by Thursday.

Water has already begun flowing out of the lake.

Chinese state television has warned that another 1 million cubic metres could accumulate over the next two to three days, potentially bringing the volume to around 3 million cubic metres.

Chinese authorities have warned that the natural dam holding the lake could break.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has also confirmed the formation and expansion of the lake.

According to NDRRMA, Planet Labs and Landsat satellite images show that the flow of the Lhende Khola has been blocked around 18 kilometres north of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.

The lake covers approximately 0.11 square kilometres.

Could the lake cause another flood?

There is a risk.

NDRRMA said the natural dam could break and trigger another major flood downstream. The authority has urged residents in downstream areas and all concerned agencies to remain alert and take necessary precautions.

“The risk of the natural dam breaking and causing another major flood remains,” the authority said.

But experts say a possible flood from this lake would not necessarily be as large as Wednesday’s disaster.

How dangerous is it?

Ranjan Kumar Dahal, a professor at Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Geology, said the expanding lake has increased concerns about another flood.

However, he said the lake is relatively small.

“If the lake bursts, the flood from there will not be like Wednesday’s,” Dahal said.

Binod Parajuli, chief of the Flood Forecasting Section under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, said the Chinese side had informed Nepal that water was accumulating in the upper reaches of the Lhende Khola and that the lake was growing.

“The Chinese side appears to be monitoring the area closely. They may have issued the warning that it could burst after filling up based on their assessment,” Parajuli told Onlinekhabar.

“That is why we have urged people in the affected areas to remain alert.”

Parajuli said people in areas affected by the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli floods should remain cautious but did not need to panic.

According to him, the amount of water currently accumulated in the lake is only around 10 percent of the water involved in Wednesday’s flood.

“Even if all of it flows out, it does not appear capable of causing more damage than yesterday’s flood,” he said.

However, he stressed that the warning should not be ignored.

“That does not mean rescue workers can enter the riverside areas without concern. That is why we have asked them to remain alert,” Parajuli said.

Why is the lake still being closely monitored?

The lake is continuing to fill, and the natural dam holding it back remains a concern.

A Chinese team has been conducting continuous drone surveillance of the suspected source area of the Bhotekoshi flood since Thursday.

The team has been monitoring the avalanche area and the lake from close range.

Climate expert Ujwal Upadhyay said the continued flow of snow and muddy debris from the area was increasing the risk.

Upadhyay, who is also a visiting faculty member at Kathmandu University, wrote that water was continuing to accumulate in the natural reservoir, increasing the possibility of a sudden surge of water and further cascading disasters.

What does Nepal know about the site?

Professor Dahal said the Lhende Khola forms the Nepal-China border and that the lake is developing close to the border.

He said Nepal currently has limited possibilities for conducting a close aerial assessment of the site by helicopter.

Chinese teams, however, have been able to continuously monitor the area using drones.

“The Chinese team has provided information that has allowed us to learn that the lake is growing and that there could be another risk,” Dahal said.

For now, authorities are urging people along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors to remain alert.

Experts say there is no need for panic, but the possibility of a sudden release of water cannot be ruled out while the lake continues to grow and its natural dam remains unstable.

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 27

The wall of water slammed into the mountainside at Timure in Rasuwa before surging down towards the market.

Houses collapsed before people’s eyes. People ran in every direction. Some made it to safety. Others disappeared. No one knew who had survived and who had been swept away.

Among those caught in the chaos was Deepak Tamang of Sindhupalchok.

On Wednesday morning, the ground suddenly seemed to shake. At first, Tamang thought an earthquake had struck.

Then he saw it — a terrifying surge of mud, rocks and water racing towards the market.

“By the time I came out of the house, it had already arrived,” he recalled. “The wave of water hit the houses in front of us and they collapsed.”

There was no time to think. A mountain wall stood ahead of him. The flood was behind him.

He climbed. He climbed fast.

It became a race between life and death.

Tamang repeatedly fell as he tried to climb the slope. He grabbed at nettles and thorny bushes to pull himself higher while the flood roared below and people fled around him.

“When I fell, I thought this was it. This was the end for us,” he said.

He eventually made it to higher ground and survived. But what he saw from there continues to haunt him.

“I saw people being swept away right in front of my eyes. Some were reaching out their hands and shouting for help,” he said. “But there was no way to think about saving others at that moment. All we could do was watch our friends being swept away.”

At the time, Timure was crowded with foreign tourists, drivers, traders, police personnel, Armed Police Force personnel and Nepali Army staff. Many were caught in the flood. Even the police post was swept away, Tamang said.

But surviving the initial surge was only the beginning.

Those who escaped ran into the forest and eventually reached an old shed used for storing timber. Around 100 to 200 people crowded into the structure.

There was barely room to stand, let alone sleep.

“We stood in a line like that through the day and night,” Tamang recalled.

Then it started raining again.

People were crammed into the narrow tin-roofed shed. Some became dizzy. Others felt nauseous. But no one could go outside.

As they stood there, everyone thought if help would come the next day.

 “We were waiting for morning and wondering when the rescue would come,” Tamang said.

They were finally rescued after around 24 to 25 hours, when a Nepali Army helicopter arrived and flew them to Bidur.

But even after reaching safety, Tamang had no answers about the people left behind in Timure.

“There is no way to count the deaths there,” he said, his voice heavy with grief. “It is not even possible to search for everyone right now.”

‘There is almost nothing left in Timure’

Nischal Tripathi, from Kathmandu, had been in Timure for around 20 days for business.

He was at work yesterday morning when everything suddenly began shaking. He too thought it was an earthquake. He stepped outside and saw a massive wave of water mixed with mud approaching.

Tripathi was on the fifth floor. There was only one way out — the stairs.

He ran down and jumped from around the second floor before reaching the side of the mountain.

“Those who were on the side of the mountain managed to survive to some extent,” he said. “For those on the road side, it was very difficult to survive.”

After the flood, Tripathi and others also fled into the forest.

They spent the night there, surviving on noodles and biscuits they managed to find. Later, they moved to a goat shed.

Around 150 to 200 people gathered there, along with Nepali Army personnel.

But Tripathi was not thinking about his own safety. His brother was missing. So were five or six members of his team and seven truck drivers.

“My brother and five, six, seven truck drivers who worked with me are out of contact,” he said.

When he remembers the scene around Timure market, his voice grows heavy.

“Only one or two houses appear to have survived. Otherwise, there is not a single house left in Timure.”

The flood had erased the distinction between the customs yard, the road and the river, he said.

Where there had once been roads, shops and crowds of people, there was now only a riverbed.

‘If the current had hit us, none of us would have survived’

Rasuwa Customs Office accountant Hridayesh Neupane also escaped death. Neupane, originally from Dailekh, had reached the office at around 7:30am that morning.

The office stood beside the river. He was working on the lowest floor when he felt a slight tremor.

The buildings began shaking. Like others, he too suspected an earthquake. Then he heard a strange sound — almost like a siren.

“It was a very faint but very sharp sound,” he recalled.

Realising that something was wrong, he ran out of the office. When he reached the gate and looked north, he saw something far beyond what he had imagined a flood could look like.

Mud, dust and water were being thrown into the air, rising an estimated 100 metres. He knew immediately that he had to climb. And so he did and ran uphill.

After that, he remembers little.

“I only remember walking across the sheet of a roof,” he said. “After that, I don’t remember anything.”

When he regained consciousness, he was already higher up the mountain.

Looking down, he saw that Timure had been transformed into a barren riverbed.

“It cannot be described,” he said. “It was an unimaginable scene.”

Neupane believes they survived largely by chance.

The main force of the flood did not hit the side where they were standing. Instead, it slammed into the mountain wall opposite them.

“If the current had hit the side where we were, none of us would have survived,” he said.

Mud had been deposited 50 to 60 metres up the opposite slope. Large pine trees that had stood there had disappeared.

The situation in Ghattekhola market, further upstream, was even worse.

“Not a single person survived there,” Neupane said.

The survivors climbed higher as rescue operations began below. Then the weather deteriorated. Rain returned and the helicopter rescue operation had to stop. All the could do now was wait and hope.

They spent the night in a makeshift structure covered with sheets in an open pasture-like area. Around 50 to 60 people took shelter there.

At around 6:30am the next morning, helicopters began arriving again — including Nepali Army and private helicopters.

Neupane said they were among the last people to be rescued.

But several people were still waiting below.

Around two to two and a half hours after the flood, he said, a Nepali Army helicopter rescued eight to 10 people who had been partially buried in the Timure market and were still struggling to survive.

Rescue operation launched from Trishuli

The flood struck on August 26, turning settlements and markets along rivers in Rasuwa and Nuwakot into wastelands.

People living along the riverbanks in Rasuwa had barely seconds to escape.

Those who happened to be on upper floors or higher ground managed to scramble towards the forest and survive. But immediate rescue was difficult. Helicopters could not land safely in the affected areas. Communications were also disrupted.

After helicopter rescue was deemed impossible on Wednesday, a larger rescue operation began at around 6am on Thursday.

The Nepali Army and private helicopters were deployed at the No. 1 Military Training Centre in Trishuli, Nuwakot. From there, rescue flights carrying stranded and injured people were accelerated.

The same military training centre also became a gathering point for relatives of people missing in the flood. Every time a helicopter landed, families rushed towards it, hoping that the person they had been searching for was among those brought back to safety.

For the survivors, the flood was a matter of seconds. For those left behind, the waiting continues.

title.rendered: Rs 273.3 million raised for PM’s disaster relief fund in first six hours

content.rendered:

A total of Rs 273.3 million was collected in the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund within the first six hours, according to the Ministry of Finance.

The ministry said the largest contribution came from Gorkha Brewery, which donated Rs 100 million. Kumari Bank contributed Rs 30 million, while Ncell donated Rs 10 million.

NIC Asia Bank provided Rs 22.1 million, while NIFRA Bank contributed Rs 25 million.

Similarly, Rastriya Banijya Bank donated Rs 30 million and Nepal Bank contributed Rs 30.1 million.

Saras Beverages (Red Bull) provided Rs 20 million, while Shree Shakti Group donated Rs 5.1 million.

Reliance Sugar Mill and Chemical Industries contributed Rs 1 million.

According to the Ministry of Finance, the amount represents funds handed over to the finance minister for the disaster relief fund.

The contributions come as authorities continue relief, rescue and recovery efforts following the devastating floods in Rasuwa and other affected areas.

title.rendered: As flood toll rises, experts flag cholera, dengue and leptospirosis risks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

As of Wednesday evening, 359 bodies had been recovered from the Bhotekoshi flood, according to Nepal Police, with more than 900 people still out of contact, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Beyond the immediate loss of life and property, doctors warn that floods and landslides sharply raise the risk of infectious disease. Contaminated water, unsafe food, poor waste management, overcrowding, and rising mosquito populations can fuel outbreaks of cholera, diarrhoea, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, malaria, and respiratory illness in affected areas.

Nuwakot’s Bidur Municipality Deputy Mayor Prabha Bogati said bodies have been washing down the river, warning of serious health risks to nearby communities if not managed properly.

Cholera and diarrhoea risk is high

Public health expert Dr Baburam Marasini said infectious disease risk is elevated in flood-hit settlements like Timure, Syafrubesi, Betrawati, and Trishuli, as well as surrounding areas reliant on the same water sources.

Contact with cattle waste and contaminated water also raises leptospirosis risk, he said, urging health authorities to maintain active disease surveillance. He pointed to Pakistan’s devastating 2022 floods, after which the WHO reported rising cases of diarrhoea, cholera, malaria, dengue, skin infections, and respiratory illness, showing that health risks persist long after floodwaters recede.

Safe water and food come first

Infectious disease specialist Dr Sher Bahadur Pun said that since water sources are often destroyed or contaminated during floods, a lack of safe drinking water can become an even bigger problem than food shortages. Displaced people, having lost homes or family members, often cannot prioritise hygiene themselves, so relief workers must prioritise clean water and safe food first. Water should be boiled or purified using health-authority-approved methods, following recommended chlorine or tablet dosages rather than over-treating. Food touched by floodwater, spoiled, or left uncovered for long periods should not be eaten, and raw and cooked food should be kept separate.

Sanitation and toilets need urgent attention

With many toilets unusable, open defecation risks contaminating water and soil, spreading disease between people. Proper toilet facilities at temporary camps are essential.

Dr Marasini emphasised handwashing with soap before cooking or eating, after using the toilet, and after caring for the sick, as a simple but effective preventive measure. Camps should also prevent indiscriminate waste disposal and safely manage animal carcasses.

Mosquito-borne disease risk

Family physician Dr Bishwaraj Dawadi said stagnant water pooling after floods can boost mosquito populations, raising dengue and malaria risk, while mixing of sewage, dead animals, and contaminated food raises bacterial infection risk generally.

Children and elderly people face a higher risk of pneumonia and other infections, and those with existing conditions may worsen without regular medication. Precautions should include mosquito nets, covering the body, and preventing standing water near homes and camps.

Camps need extra caution

Crowded temporary camps make it easy for colds, flu, pneumonia, and skin infections to spread. Anyone with fever, persistent cough, breathing difficulty, diarrhoea, vomiting, or skin infection should notify health workers immediately.

Dr Pun advised isolating suspected infectious cases where possible, with special priority given to children, the elderly, pregnant women, and those with chronic illness.

Relief needs to include health supplies, not just food

Rice, lentils, and noodles alone aren’t enough; clean water, purification supplies, soap, mosquito nets, sanitation materials, and essential medicines are equally vital parts of relief efforts, experts say.

Dr Pun advised that anyone in flood-affected areas showing watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, fever, body aches, headache, breathing difficulty, skin infection, or unusual weakness should contact a health facility immediately. Severe diarrhoea, continuous vomiting, reduced urination, extreme weakness, or unconsciousness require immediate hospitalisation.

Experts stress that effective disease surveillance, alongside treatment, is critical after any disaster, so that outbreaks can be caught and controlled before they spread further.

title.rendered: Families crowd Kathmandu hospital in desperate search for Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Families searching for relatives who went missing in the Rasuwa flood have gathered in large numbers at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj, Kathmandu.

Many have been searching for loved ones since the Bhotekoshi River flood swept through Rasuwa and surrounding areas.

Some relatives have put up missing-person notices on the hospital walls, carrying photographs and details of those they are looking for. Others are checking official lists in the hope of finding the names of their missing family members.

They continue to hold on to the hope of finding their loved ones alive.

A large number of injured people rescued from Rasuwa, Nuwakot and other affected areas have been brought to hospitals in Kathmandu for treatment.

title.rendered: No power, no network, Rasuwa Hospital staff push through flood emergency

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The sound of helicopters echoed over Rasuwagadhi’s skies throughout the day on Wednesday. Some helicopters were arriving carrying the injured, while others were flying displaced people to safer locations.

As the pressure of rescue operations mounted following the destruction caused by the flood and landslides, health workers at Rasuwa Hospital remained fully occupied treating the injured.

According to hospital medical superintendent Dr Amit Prajapati, managing the sudden, large influx of injured patients on Wednesday was extremely difficult. Many of those brought in after being rescued from the flood were in serious condition.

“Suddenly, a huge number of injured people came in yesterday,” Dr Prajapati says. “There were patients who had been buried under landslides. Many had broken arms and legs, head and facial injuries, and severe injuries in various other parts of the body.”

He said the hospital treated 53 patients on Wednesday and 10 on Thursday. Among them, patients in serious condition were referred to Kathmandu, while some with minor injuries were treated and discharged. As of Thursday evening, four injured patients remained admitted at the hospital.

Most of the injured were “polytrauma” cases, patients with severe injuries to multiple parts of the body at once. He said patients with serious head injuries, in particular, were given primary treatment before being referred elsewhere for further care.

But managing the injured wasn’t the hospital’s only challenge.

There’s no electricity. No network. The hospital has been running on a generator, and the fuel needed to keep that generator running is now nearly exhausted.

“We’re running the generator right now, but the fuel is almost gone,” Dr Prajapati says. “We don’t know how many more days it will take for the power to come back. If fuel isn’t arranged, treatment services themselves could be affected.”

Mobile network service only began working from Thursday afternoon, and even then intermittently, about 10 minutes of connectivity before it cuts out again, he said.

With no electricity, battery backup can’t hold out for long either.

“The backup only lasts three to four hours,” he says. “Once the battery runs out, we need electricity again to recharge it. That’s why fuel has become the hospital’s biggest concern right now.”

On Wednesday, with the overwhelming number of injured, health workers barely had time to catch their breath.

“Nothing is easy in a disaster,” Dr Prajapati says.

“There’s no power, no network. It was hard to manage the injured coming in under these conditions, but everyone worked together and we managed.”

He said medicine, equipment, and staffing levels are currently adequate for immediate needs. Supplies have arrived from the Ministry of Health, along with support from the World Health Organisation (WHO), and a team from Bir Hospital has also reached the site.

“For now, we’re okay in terms of manpower, medicine, and equipment,” he said. “Our own staff and the teams that came from outside are working together.”

Still, the continuous workload has left health workers exhausted.

“We’re a bit tired from working nonstop since yesterday,” Dr Prajapati says, “But when the injured keep coming in, there’s no room to think about fatigue.”

Search operations for missing people were still ongoing on Thursday. He said more displaced people than injured people have been rescued so far.

“The exact number of rescues would be known to the army and rescue teams,” he says. “We just see the patients who come to the hospital. The search is still ongoing.”

The hospital’s patient load was somewhat lower on Thursday compared to Wednesday. But complete details of the damage caused by the flood and landslides are still not available. Several settlements remain out of contact, search operations continue, and there remains an equal likelihood that more injured people will be found during rescue efforts.

title.rendered: Supreme Court refuses interim order to halt Nepali Congress general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Supreme Court has refused to issue an interim order sought by Nepali Congress leaders Sher Bahadur Deuba and Purna Bahadur Khadka to halt the party’s general convention.

A bench comprising Justices Nahakul Subedi, Mahesh Sharma Paudel and Meghraj Pokharel issued the order.

Supreme Court spokesperson Arjun Koirala confirmed that the court had declined to issue an interim order on the petition filed by Deuba and Khadka.

“The supplementary petition had sought an order to stop the general convention. The three-member full bench has refused to issue an interim order as requested,” Koirala said.

The court’s decision means the Nepali Congress establishment faction can continue its regular party activities for now. The Supreme Court has said no interim order will be issued at this stage, although it may issue any order it considers appropriate when hearing the review petition.

The Deuba-Khadka faction has rejected the leadership of Gagan Thapa, who was elected through the party’s special general convention.

Thapa’s faction, meanwhile, has already begun preparations for the 15th general convention, scheduled to be held from October 2 to 5.

title.rendered: 215 staff from 5 hydropower projects out of contact, 212 awaiting rescue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

A total of 215 employees from five hydropower projects in the Bhotekoshi flood-affected area are out of contact.

According to the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), the workers have been unreachable since Wednesday’s devastating flood.

IPPAN said 76 employees of Andritz Hydro, the contractor working on the under-construction 216 MW Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, are out of contact, about half of them Nepali and half foreign nationals. Of these, 11 employees of project developer Nepal Water and Energy Development Company are out of contact, including 8 Korean nationals working on the project. Seven staff from project consultants Zed Consult and Lama Xavier’s JV are also unreachable.

IPPAN said 12 of the project’s employees working in the headworks area and more than 200 in the powerhouse area are awaiting rescue.

“There are unconfirmed reports that a first phase of rescue has taken place from the project site,” IPPAN stated in its statement.

At the Rasuwagadhi (111 MW) project, 51 employees are out of contact. Three people saved themselves by climbing to higher ground in Timure, but no communication has been established with anyone.

Eight employees at the powerhouse of the Mailung Khola (5 MW) project have been out of contact since Wednesday, IPPAN said, adding that efforts are underway to arrange a helicopter to survey the site.

“Two employees of Sinohydro are missing. Five have taken shelter in a nearby village — of these, 3 Chinese and 2 Nepali nationals are awaiting rescue,” IPPAN said.

Similarly, 60 people (25 staff and 35 workers) trapped in a tunnel at the Langtang Khola (20 MW) project due to the same flood remain out of contact, and their condition remains unknown. Although representatives of the developer company have attempted to reach the area for rescue, a helicopter has not yet been arranged.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood destroys 40km of roads and 41 bridges

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Bhotekoshi River flood has completely destroyed around 40 kilometres of roads in Rasuwa, severely disrupting transport links to the district.

The road connecting Betrawati to Syafrubesi and Rasuwagadhi via Mailung has been completely damaged. Around 10 kilometres of the Galchhi–Trishuli road is also closed.

Meanwhile, around 13 kilometres of the Prithvi Highway has been buried under mud and debris.

The Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport said clearing the debris and reopening the Prithvi Highway has been given top priority.

The flood has also completely destroyed 41 bridges.

The ministry said the government has seven Bailey bridges, each up to 50 metres long, and work is underway to identify locations where they can be installed. The governments of India and China have also committed to providing Bailey bridges as needed.

In the first phase, the government is prioritising the reopening of the Prithvi Highway and restoring road access to Rasuwa.

Preparations are underway to install a Bailey bridge at Betravati. Until the road to Betravati is reopened, it will not be possible to reach Syafrubesi via Dhunche, according to the ministry.

To speed up road clearance and reconstruction, 20 pieces of heavy equipment have been deployed — 10 provided by the government and 10 by the private sector.

The government has said restoration of damaged roads and bridges and the resumption of transport services are being treated as top priorities, with work being accelerated across the affected areas.

title.rendered: Every ambulance brings hope — and fear — for Rasuwa flood victims’ families

content.rendered:
Chitwan, August 27

The pain of families who lost loved ones in the devastating Rasuwa flood has now reached Chitwan.

Relatives of people missing after the Bhotekoshi flood have been moving between hospitals and the mortuary in Bharatpur, searching for any sign of those they have been waiting for.

Some clutch photographs of their missing relatives. Others sit with tears in their eyes.

They share the same hope and the same fear.

Since early Thursday morning, relatives carrying that uncertainty have gathered outside a newly established body identification centre in Bharatpur. Every time an ambulance siren is heard, they rush towards it. For a few moments, all eyes remain fixed on the ambulance carrying the bodies.

The doors open. A body is brought out. Relatives compare the face with photographs on their phones. For some, the search ends. For others, the wait begins again.

‘What do I tell my brother abroad?’

Yaman Banu, who lives in Tadi, Chitwan, arrived in Bharatpur looking for members of her family after 14 relatives went missing following the Bhotekoshi flood.

Time has become another source of pain for those waiting in Bharatpur. With every passing hour, their anxiety grows. Their eyes remain on the road and their ears tuned to the sound of ambulance sirens.

Yaman repeatedly shows a photograph of her relatives on her phone, her eyes filled with tears.

“What do I tell my brother who is abroad? Everyone from our home and my maternal family has been swept away,” she said.

She had been visiting hospitals and mortuaries in Bharatpur since early morning. After finding no information about her relatives, she was eventually forced to come to the identification centre and look for their faces among the dead.

On her phone, however, the face is still alive.

Holding on to the photograph, she continues to hope that one day she will see that face not on a dead body, but standing alive in front of her.

35 people from one village missing

Relatives who had travelled from Palungtar in Gorkha to Gosainkunda for a pilgrimage have also arrived in Chitwan.

Hari Baniya was waiting for his sister. He sat quietly until an ambulance siren suddenly broke the silence. He immediately got up and rushed towards the ambulance.

His sister was not among the bodies. Now he waits for the next ambulance.

After searching hospitals without finding any information, Hari and other relatives have been waiting for every ambulance carrying bodies from the flood.

According to Hari, 39 people from the same village who had travelled to Gosainkunda remain out of contact. Their disappearance has plunged the entire village into grief.

‘I’m at the border’ — then the call stopped

Chandra Lama is living through a similar wait.

His brother called in the morning and said he had reached the border. After that, the phone went silent.

Chandra came to Bharatpur after his uncle sent him to look for his brother.

The possibility that his brother could be among the bodies swept downstream by the flood brought him to the identification centre.

His wait now lies somewhere between two possibilities — the hope of finding his brother and the fear of finding his body.

Separate identification centre set up as mortuaries run out of space

As the number of bodies brought from Rasuwa to Chitwan increased, a separate body identification and preservation centre was established in Bharatpur.

The centre, located in the old building of the Industrial Enterprise Development Institute in Bharatpur-10, has the capacity to store around 250 bodies.

The mortuaries at Bharatpur Hospital and other hospitals can accommodate only around 50 bodies, prompting authorities to establish the additional facility.

Chitwan Chief District Officer Ganesh Aryal said arrangements had been made to preserve the bodies at controlled temperatures. Food and accommodation have also been arranged for relatives of those affected by the disaster.

Throughout the day, ambulances arrive carrying bodies. Relatives rush towards them. Then another siren sounds. And the same faces turn towards the road again.

The Nepal Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and municipal police have been mobilised for the search and management of the bodies.

Families identify loved ones through photographs

Chitwan District Police Office chief Rameshwar Paudel said special arrangements had been made both to preserve the recovered bodies and make identification easier.

“Bodies that arrive will be cleaned and preserved in dry ice. We are also preparing to photograph the bodies and display the photographs on boards,” he said.

A separate contact desk has also been established so that relatives can seek information more easily.

The arrangement is intended to reduce the need for relatives to open and inspect every body at the mortuary themselves, Paudel said.

But identifying a loved one from a photograph remains difficult.

The smiling face of someone they know from a phone screen has to be compared with a face changed by death — a process Paudel described as an extremely painful moment for families.

25 ambulances working continuously

Ambulance drivers have also been working around the clock to transport the bodies.

According to Navaraj Lamichhane, president of the Nepal Ambulance Drivers’ Association, 25 ambulances are currently on standby for transporting bodies.

The ambulances are bringing bodies to hospitals and the identification centre free of charge, he said.

The ambulances keep coming. The bodies keep arriving. And each siren sends relatives rushing towards the same place. Some are still hoping to find their loved ones alive. Others simply want the chance to see their faces one last time.

For everyone waiting, the search has narrowed to one place: the body identification centre in Bharatpur.

More than 130 bodies have been collected in Chitwan so far.

The flood has swept away homes, families and property. For hundreds of families, it has also carried away laughter, dreams and futures.

And in Bharatpur, time has become another form of suffering. Every tick of the clock brings more anxiety. Their eyes remain on the road. Their ears remain tuned to the ambulance sirens.

title.rendered: Two arrested for stealing earrings from bodies of Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Chitwan Police have arrested two men accused of removing earrings from the bodies of people who died in the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa.

Police launched an investigation after a video showing people removing earrings from a flood victim’s body went viral on social media.

The arrested men have been identified as 25-year-old Madan Gurung, a permanent resident of Binayi Tribeni Municipality-1 in Nawalparasi who has been living in Chitwan, and 38-year-old Umesh Chaudhary, originally from Sunsari and currently residing in Chitwan.

According to Chitwan Police, both men have been arrested after being identified from the viral video.

Police said further investigation into the case is underway.

title.rendered: New flood threat looms in Rasuwa as lake forms upstream

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

A new flood threat has emerged in Rasuwa after the flow of the Lhende Khola was blocked upstream, creating a large lake and raising fears that a natural dam could burst.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said a preliminary analysis of satellite images showed that a lake covering around 0.11 square kilometres had formed about 18 kilometres upstream of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.

The analysis was based on satellite images from Planet Labs and Landsat received at 11:44 am on Thursday.

The authority said the blockage of the river has created a natural dam whose stability remains uncertain. If the dam breaks, a large volume of water could rush downstream and trigger another major flood.

The warning comes a day after a devastating flash flood swept through Rasuwa, destroying settlements and infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi River. The cause and full extent of Wednesday’s disaster are still being assessed.

NDRRMA has urged residents and authorities in downstream areas to remain highly alert and take necessary precautions in view of the risk of a fresh flood.

The authority has also asked concerned agencies to closely monitor the situation and prepare for a possible sudden release of water from the upstream lake.

title.rendered: Govt forms emergency response team to search for foreign nationals missing in Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Ministry of Foreign Affairs has formed an Emergency Response Team (ERT) to coordinate the search and rescue of foreign nationals missing after the flooding of the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The ministry said on Thursday that it had received reports that several foreign nationals were among those missing following the flood in the northern district.

The ERT will serve as the ministry’s central coordinating body for the search and rescue of foreign nationals affected by the flood, verification of information and the provision of consular assistance.

According to the ministry, the team will collect information about foreign nationals affected or missing in the disaster, coordinate with relevant authorities and facilitate the sharing of necessary information with their families and diplomatic missions.

The ministry has urged foreign diplomatic missions, international organisations, families of missing people and the general public to share any information about foreign nationals affected or missing in the Rasuwa flood.

Information can be provided to the ERT through its emergency hotlines or WhatsApp numbers 9744441227 and 9744441228.

The ministry can also be contacted by email at emergency@mofa.gov.np.

title.rendered: Rasuwa Flood: 289 bodies recovered, lack of storage facilities hampers management

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The bodies of 289 people swept away by the Rasuwa flood have so far been recovered. The recovery of bodies is continuing. While the fact that bodies have been carried long distances has made the search operation difficult, a shortage of adequate cold storage facilities has created an additional challenge in managing the remains.

Health facilities in Chitwan have a combined capacity to store a maximum of 50 bodies. However, the number of bodies recovered has already exceeded several hundred. According to Dr Gopal Chaudhary, a senior forensic expert at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, bodies should not be cremated hastily as soon as they are recovered during a major natural disaster. There are international standards and guidelines for managing human remains during disasters.

Detailed information about each body, along with photographs and other evidence related to identification, must be collected and preserved before the remains are managed. “The first and most important thing is to ensure that the bodies are preserved safely,” Dr Chaudhary said. “All details must be systematically recorded, including where the body was found, the condition in which it was found, and what identifying features it has.”

According to Dr Chaudhary, most hospitals in Nepal do not have cold storage facilities capable of holding hundreds of bodies at once. “When a large number of bodies arrive, the regular infrastructure of hospitals cannot cope,” Dr Chaudhary told Onlinekhabar. “During a disaster, the state must make arrangements for alternative and temporary storage of human remains.”

Similarly, senior forensic expert Dr Harihar Wasti said the bodies must first be preserved safely and then identified through scientific procedures. “The bodies must first be kept safe. It is not possible to identify everyone immediately. It takes time. Relatives will also come looking for their loved ones. Therefore, the state must immediately arrange facilities to preserve the bodies,” Dr Wasti told Onlinekhabar.

Bodies can be temporarily buried for preservation

According to forensic expert Dr Chaudhary, when a large number of bodies are recovered, temporarily burying them in a safe location using scientific methods could be an effective way to preserve them. He said government-owned or other secure land located at a safe distance from water sources and settlements should be identified for this purpose. He suggested that the bodies could be systematically placed in pits dug to an appropriate depth.

“When bodies are kept underground, the decomposition process is slower than when they are exposed to the outside environment,” Dr Chaudhary said. “In a major disaster, bodies can be temporarily buried using scientific methods for preservation. Once relatives arrive and the bodies are identified, they can be exhumed, matched with the relevant records and handed over to the families.”

According to Chaudhary, each body must be assigned a separate number and tagged before burial. Photographs, the location and time where the body was found, clothing, jewellery and distinctive physical features must also be documented and preserved. There must also be a clear record of where and in what order the bodies were buried.

Bodies can decompose rapidly because of the hot weather. Identification becomes even more difficult when bodies have been severely damaged by the flood, when limbs have been separated or when the remains have been in water for a prolonged period. According to Dr Wasti, bodies can also be temporarily buried for preservation. However, he said this requires specific procedures and proper management.

“Bodies can be kept for some time by burying them. But a location must be arranged, and pits must be dug. Everything must be properly recorded,” Dr Wasti said. “Bodies cannot be managed in just any way. There is a specific protocol for this. Experts are needed.”

Refrigerated containers another option

According to Dr Chaudhary, if possible, large containers normally used to transport goods could also be converted into temporary cold storage facilities. “A temporary morgue can be created by installing the necessary refrigeration system in a container,” Dr Chaudhary said. “A large container can be arranged to hold around 50 bodies.”

However, he said it would not be easy to establish such facilities immediately everywhere, so areas where large numbers of bodies are likely to be recovered should prepare for temporary management of the remains at the local level.

Need for disaster victim identification team

According to Dr Wasti, who has extensive experience in the field, managing bodies after a major disaster cannot be handled by a single hospital, doctor or local administration alone. A separate Disaster Victim Identification (DVI) team should be formed for this purpose, he said.

Such a team should include forensic doctors, police personnel, dentists, fingerprint experts, DNA specialists and other necessary personnel, he said. “A specialised forensic team must be formed. A DVI team is necessary. How can one doctor, one individual or one hospital handle such work alone?” Dr Wasti said. “All bodies must be managed through a single-window system.”

The process of transporting bodies from the location where they are found to the morgue, assigning each body a separate number, collecting photographs and other details, and conducting necessary examinations should all be carried out through a single coordinated system.

Identified bodies to be handed over to families

Not all bodies recovered after being swept away by the flood are in the same condition. Some remain identifiable by their faces and physical features. Others may have begun decomposing after remaining in water for a long time or may be severely damaged. According to Dr Chaudhary, bodies that remain identifiable can be recognised directly by family members or identified based on tattoos, distinctive marks on the body, clothing, watches, jewellery or other personal belongings.

However, if the condition of the body has deteriorated or the face cannot be recognised, identification must be carried out through dental examination, fingerprints and, as a last resort, DNA testing. “A severely decomposed or badly damaged body cannot be identified simply by looking at it,” he said. “In such cases, dental records, fingerprints or DNA testing must be used. The body should be handed over to the respective family only after identification through DNA.”

Dr Wasti also said that conducting a post-mortem alone is not sufficient to identify a body. All available identifying information must be collected from the remains. “Information obtained from the post-mortem must be compared with the information available about missing people,” Dr Wasti said. “If fingerprints can be obtained, they should be collected immediately. Identification can then be made by comparing them with the records of missing persons.”

In the case of small tissue samples or unidentifiable human remains, a legal record must be prepared, and the process must proceed in accordance with the existing guidelines for the management of human remains.

Hasty cremation could lead to mistakes

Dr Chaudhary said identifying bodies after a major disaster is itself a lengthy and complex process. Therefore, he warned that handing over bodies without sufficient identification due to pressure from relatives or emotional circumstances could result in one family mistakenly taking the body of another person. “Families want to perform the final rites according to their traditions,” Dr Chaudhary said. “But if a body is handed over hastily without certain identification, there is a risk that one family could take the body of another person.”

According to Chaudhary, the identification of bodies after a disaster can sometimes continue for months or even longer. Citing examples from major disasters around the world where the identification of human remains has continued for extended periods, he said scientific procedures should also be given priority in the case of the Rasuwa flood. “The best approach is not to rush, to preserve all evidence and to hand over the body to the family only after certain identification has been established,” Dr Chaudhary said.

State must immediately establish safe temporary body storage facilities

As bodies from the Rasuwa flood have begun to be recovered in various districts stretching from Chitwan to Nawalparasi, it is no longer possible for a single hospital or institution to manage them all. Local hospitals also lack sufficient morgue and cold storage facilities, as well as forensic testing capabilities. In such circumstances, Dr Chaudhary has suggested that the federal government coordinate with local and provincial governments to establish safe temporary storage facilities for human remains.

Experts say secure government land should be identified, particularly in areas where large numbers of bodies are likely to be recovered, and temporary storage facilities should be established with the necessary security, record-keeping and forensic arrangements. “In my experience, when a large number of bodies need to be managed, temporarily burying and preserving them through scientific methods can be an effective solution,” Dr Chaudhary said. “The state must provide a secure location. Detailed information about every body must be recorded, and the remains must be preserved systematically.”

title.rendered: Police publish QR code to help identify Rasuwa flood victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Police have prepared a list of people who died in the floods in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The list, prepared by Nepal Police, includes bodies that have been recovered but have not yet been identified. To help families identify their missing relatives, police have included photographs showing the faces and physical descriptions of the bodies.

The list can be accessed by scanning a QR code.

Nepal Police has published the QR code on its official Facebook page. After scanning it, people can view the list of unidentified bodies and check the photographs and other identifying details.

Police said the list has been made public to make it easier for families searching for relatives missing since the flood to identify their loved ones.

title.rendered: Every helicopter brings hope for families waiting for the missing in Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Nuwakot, August 27

The helicopters arrive, and the crowd runs towards them.

For a few moments, the road outside the No. 1 Army Training Centre in Battar falls into a strange rhythm: people look up, rush towards the gate and wait for those being brought back from flood-hit Rasuwa.

Then they watch.

If the person they are waiting for is not among them, they slowly return to the roadside and wait for the next helicopter.

Since Thursday morning, families of people missing after the devastating flood have gathered here, searching for any news of their loved ones.

Among them is Sabita Adhikari. Her husband, who works at the Trishuli Hydropower Project, has been out of contact since the flood struck. Until then, they had been speaking regularly.

Now she does not know whether he was swept away or escaped and is stranded somewhere. Clinging on, she keeps asking people arriving at the Army training centre whether they have seen him. Whenever a helicopter lands, she hurries towards the centre. She waits until everyone has been brought out.

But the helicopters do not always bring survivors.

Some people are carried down on stretchers. Others are brought out in bundles. People in the crowd try to work out what they are seeing.

“It looks like they have brought only a head,” some say.

For Adhikari, each helicopter brings a brief moment of hope, followed by disappointment.

She returns to where she was sitting.

“What might have happened to him?” she asks, her eyes filling with tears.

Still, she has not given up.

She has heard that employees at Trishuli Hydropower may have taken shelter inside a tunnel. She has also heard that the army has reached the site with equipment to rescue them.

“People are saying the employees are inside the tunnel,” she says. “They say the army has already reached there for the rescue.”

Others nearby repeat the same thing.

“They say the army went there this morning with all the equipment. We heard that too.”

For a moment, the news gives her hope.

Then another thought comes.

“What if he has suffocated?”

Her husband had shown her the inside of the tunnel during video calls. She remembers how enclosed it was. Now she has heard that the tunnel’s opening has been filled with mud.

Then she hears that the owner of the hydropower project has arrived at the Army training centre.

She goes straight to the gate.

“Please let me meet him. I want to understand what happened there. I want to know what it is like inside. Please let me meet him,” she tells the soldiers, crying.

She is eventually allowed inside with a relative.

“If he is hiding inside the tunnel and that is why he cannot contact us, maybe he is still alive,” she says. “I pray that the army rescues them soon.”

‘The helicopter comes, but my person does not’

Adhikari is one of many people waiting in Battar.

A few metres away, 74-year-old Padam Bahadur Kandel walks around with an old bag over his shoulder.

His eyes are wet.

Sometimes he stops and looks towards the Army training centre. Sometimes he walks quickly, as if he cannot bear to stand still.

Kandel has come from Nahar Daha village in Nuwakot. His relative, Khal Prasad Timilsina, is stranded in Rasuwa.

He has come to Battar hoping that an army helicopter will find Timilsina and bring him back.

“The helicopter comes every two minutes, but my person does not come,” Kandel says, his voice breaking.

“At this age, why did I have to see something like this?”

He can barely speak.

Instead, he gestures towards two men nearby.

They are relatives of another victim.

One is Basudev Rijal, who has come from Tadi in Nuwakot.

His nephew, from Suryagadhi-5, had been travelling to Gosainkunda for trekking. He and about 10 friends were planning to travel by bus for part of the journey.

But when the bus reached Betravati, the flood from Rasuwa swept over it.

Rijal says his nephew and another friend managed to climb onto the roof of a house.

The nephew then called home.

“He called in a hurry and said, ‘If the house remains standing, I will survive. If it collapses, I will die.’ The flood took them away shortly afterwards, I think,” Rijal says.

“We came here yesterday and informed the army and police. We are hoping that he will be found. Even if it is his body, we want to see him.”

His voice falters.

“Now there is neither hope nor breath. We have lost all hope.”

Waiting has become a way of life

There are many families like them in Battar.

Some are crying. Some are pleading with security personnel. Others stand silently, watching each helicopter.

Battar has become a place where families come to look for people missing in the Rasuwa flood.

But the town itself has also been affected by the disaster.

People from communities on either side of the river remain stranded in one another’s areas.

The flood has also left schoolchildren shaken.

A group of students from Panchalinge Secondary School look distressed as they leave the Army training centre.

They had travelled to Bidur the previous day to play futsal.

Then the flood came.

They were stranded and could not return home that evening.

Some students from one side of the river are now stuck on the other. Others face the same situation in reverse.

The army has been using helicopters to move the students between the two sides.

“We had a game. We came here,” one student says anxiously. “Our families must already be very worried. We were lucky to survive. Now we just want to get home.”

The army has told them they will be taken home by helicopter.

So they wait.

The families wait too.

And when another helicopter appears over Battar, heads turn towards the sky.

For those standing outside the Army training centre, every helicopter carries the same possibility: perhaps this time, someone they love will come home.

title.rendered: 87 telecom towers disrupted in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading after flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Telephone and internet services have been disrupted in parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading following Wednesday’s devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River.

A total of 87 towers operated by Nepal Telecom (NTC) and Ncell have been affected, disrupting communications in several parts of the three districts.

According to the latest details, 60 Nepal Telecom towers and 27 Ncell towers are currently not operational.

Flood damage to telecom infrastructure, coupled with disruptions to electricity supply, has affected both telephone and internet services in several areas.

Nepal Telecom spokesperson Dr Kamal Lamichhane said 152 NTC towers had stopped working immediately after the flood, but most have since been restored.

“Currently, 60 towers are affected,” he said. “Work is underway to repair them as quickly as possible, and technical teams have already been deployed.”

Nepal Telecom has also airlifted generators, batteries and other equipment by helicopter to the Nyaupanechaur and Ramche repeater sites to restore services in Rasuwa.

Lamichhane said services have been restored in areas including Kispang (Kaule), Thulegaun, Tadi, Fikuri, Kalikasthan, Grang, Dadagaun, Mailung, Pangsang Danda, Langtang and Kyangjin.

Generators, fuel and personnel have also been deployed to restore services in Dhunche.

In Nuwakot, teams have been deployed with generators and fuel to restore services in Madanpur, Battar and Bidur Bus Park. Similar efforts are underway at Baireni and Thamel Danda in Dhading.

Lamichhane said generators, fuel and personnel have been sent to priority sites in affected areas to bring them back into continuous operation.

The company is also working to improve coverage and capacity at BTS sites that remain operational to ensure more effective service.

According to NTC, five sites in Chitwan, 13 of 36 sites in Dhading, 31 of 79 sites in Nuwakot and 13 of 32 sites in Rasuwa have been affected.

Ncell said 27 towers across the three districts have been affected, while fibre connections have also been cut at several locations.

The company said it has already deployed technical teams to flood-affected areas by road and helicopter to restore services.

Ncell said it expects telephone and internet services to be restored in most affected areas by Thursday evening.

In its latest situation update on the Bhote Koshi flash flood, NTB said the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, along with the Tourist Police and other tourism stakeholders, continues to work on verifying the whereabouts and safety of tourists and travellers who were in or passing through the areas affected by Wednesday’s devastating flood.

Four South Korean nationals were also rescued: Taeyoon Kia (41), Taehoon Yum (57), Jongho Lim (56), and Jaepok Yang (56).

Two Italian nationals, Lotumuw Stecano (30) and Valurntina Piccintui (37), were among those rescued, along with two American nationals, Anjana Raja (52) and Pattabiraman Venkatesan (55).

The largest group rescued was from India, with 13 nationals listed: Thiruma Bhaalan (62), Balani Yappan (69), Ratna Kumar (65), Rananaga Sawai (68), Raghunardan (56), Sima Ranjan (46), Naghu Kabir Dosh (54), Maran Gobinda Spanu (54), Satyai Dhakham (47), Bijaya Bakhu (54), and Panga Sawai (68), among others.

title.rendered: Cyber Bureau warns public of disaster relief scams

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Nepal Police Cyber Bureau has urged the public to remain alert to possible scams targeting people who wish to support those affected by the sudden flooding of the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The bureau warned that individuals with malicious intentions could misuse social media and other digital platforms to defraud people and misappropriate public donations during this sensitive period.

According to the bureau, possible scams may include soliciting money through personal bank accounts or e-wallets using the names of the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund or Prime Minister’s Relief Fund, as well as circulating fake QR codes on social media that imitate the logos, names or formats of official agencies.

The police have also warned the public to be cautious of fake pages or groups created on platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp, TikTok, Instagram and Viber in the name of different “relief funds” or “support campaigns.” Other potential scams include phone calls requesting personal and banking details under the pretext of “relief assistance registration,” phishing links designed to steal OTPs and passwords, and messages from unknown numbers asking for financial assistance with claims such as, “I am safe, please send me money.”

The Cyber Bureau has urged anyone who suspects that an individual or group is conducting or attempting to conduct a scam in the name of disaster relief to immediately contact the nearest police office or the Cyber Bureau.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Nepal Telecom has announced that it will provide free voice calls, data and SMS services to customers in flood-affected areas and surrounding regions for an additional three days.

Nepal Telecom had previously announced two days of free voice calls, along with 2 GB of data and 50 free SMS messages per day. The company has now extended the facility through August 30, covering August 28, 29 and 30.

The company said the services are being provided to help affected citizens stay in contact with their families, rescue and relief workers, and relevant authorities during the difficult circumstances.

Nepal Telecom said that although the floods have damaged physical infrastructure, its technical teams have been continuously deployed to keep services operational and repair the affected infrastructure.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood toll grows, Bharatpur Hospital holds 37 bodies and 27 body parts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Police have said 270 bodies have been found so far in connection with Wednesday’s devastating flood on Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi River. According to police, 108 bodies alone have been recovered in Chitwan district.

Bodies have been kept at hospitals and even at the premises of the chamber of commerce and industry across the district, according to Chiranjivi Sharma, spokesperson and Assistant Chief District Officer at the District Administration Office. Sharma said complete information on exactly how many bodies are where is not yet available.

Bharatpur Hospital at capacity

As of 3 p.m. Thursday, Bharatpur Hospital had 37 complete bodies brought in by the flood, hospital spokesperson Dr Ram Prasad Sapkota said. He added that the hospital also has 27 body parts, hands, feet, and heads belonging to different individuals.

Among the complete bodies are 13 women, 19 men, 4 boys, and 1 girl. Dr Sapkota said documentation procedures for the bodies are currently underway.

He said the hospital is facing difficulty storing the bodies, as its postmortem facility has capacity for only 24. Since 17 bodies were already at the hospital before the flood victims arrived, managing the additional bodies has been extremely difficult, he said.

Arrangements are now being made to keep bodies at the chamber of commerce premises instead. Sapkota said that after documentation, bodies will begin being transferred there starting this evening.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

A total of 289 bodies have been recovered so far from the devastating flood that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems on Wednesday.

According to data available as of 3 pm Thursday, three bodies have been recovered in Rasuwa, 12 in Nuwakot, 29 in Dhading, 29 in Gorkha, 16 in Tanahun, 121 in Chitwan, 65 in East Nawalparasi and 14 in West Nawalparasi.

The flood caused widespread destruction along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems, with a large number of people still reported missing or out of contact.

A joint team of the Nepal Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force is continuing search operations for those still missing.

The search and rescue teams are working across affected areas despite damaged roads, bridges and other infrastructure that have made access difficult.

content.rendered:

The Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) has decided to immediately provide financial assistance worth Rs 50 million toward the rescue, relief, and other support of flood-affected families.

An emergency meeting of the association decided to form a relief and rescue committee for those affected by the Rasuwa flood, coordinated by NRNA President Dr Hemraj Sharma.

A fundraising committee has also been formed, coordinated by Treasurer Krishna Timalsina, to collect financial contributions. The meeting further decided to mobilise essential medical and volunteer teams to the affected areas and appealed to NRNA officials and members to participate as volunteers in rescue and relief work.

content.rendered:

Electricity services have resumed in Battar and Trishuli Bazaar areas of Nuwakot following disruptions caused by the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River.

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) restored power supply through an alternative arrangement by charging the Balaju-Trishuli and Chapali-Devighat 66 kV transmission lines at 11 kV, bringing electricity back to the affected areas.

The NEA said it is accelerating repair and restoration work on electricity infrastructure damaged by the flood and continuing efforts to restore regular power supply across all affected areas.

content.rendered:

The District Administration Office, Kathmandu, has designated a contact person for those wishing to provide relief materials to flood victims.

The administration has said that organisations, individuals, companies, clubs and citizens based in Kathmandu district who wish to provide food, clothes, utensils or other household items needed by flood victims can do so through a one-door system for the collection of relief materials.

The District Administration Office issued a notice on Thursday asking individuals and organisations wishing to provide relief materials in Kathmandu to contact Administrative Officer Sujan Kumari Bardewa.

According to the notice, relief materials can be provided by contacting Bardewa at 9841798542.

The administration said the collected relief materials will be delivered to the victims through coordination and management involving the security agencies in the respective districts, security agencies based in Kathmandu that are directly involved in rescue and relief operations, and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Those wishing to provide cash assistance, however, can deposit funds directly into the account of the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund using the designated account number or the QR code provided by the government, the Kathmandu administration said.

title.rendered: Large lake forms near Nepal border, China warns of dam-break risk: Global Times

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

China’s Ministry of Water Resources has reported the formation of a large lake near the confluence of the Chhochen and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, close to the Nepal border.

The Chochhen and Purepu rivers are among the upper tributaries of the Trishuli River system.

Both rivers originate in China’s Tibet Autonomous Region and become part of the Trishuli River system after entering Nepal. The Purepu and Chochhen rivers flow from Tibet and join the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system near Rasuwagadhi.

By Thursday morning, around 2 million cubic metres of water had accumulated in the newly formed lake, while water had already begun flowing out of it, according to Chinese authorities.

China estimates that another 3 million cubic metres of water could accumulate in the lake over the next three days, raising the risk of the natural dam breaching, China Central Television reported on Thursday.

China’s Ministry of Water Resources is closely monitoring the lake’s condition to prepare for a possible dam breach and support emergency rescue operations, according to the Global Times.

Authorities are also conducting flood analysis to assess the potential extent and impact of flooding that could occur if the natural dam breaks.

The development comes as Nepal continues to deal with the devastating flooding along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system, which has caused significant loss of life and damage to infrastructure in several districts.

title.rendered: Bhotekoshi flood leaves Nuwakot towns, infrastructure in ruins

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River has caused extensive physical damage in Nuwakot, destroying riverside settlements, towns and critical infrastructure along the Trishuli River.

Several settlements along the Trishuli have been severely damaged, with homes and other structures swept into the river within moments. Buildings that survived the force of the flood are now left dangerously exposed, with large sections of land beneath their foundations washed away by riverbank erosion.

The flood has eroded the ground up to the foundations of several buildings, leaving the structures at risk of collapse. Once-bustling riverside areas of Trishuli, Dhunge Bazaar and Devighat have been transformed into stretches of debris and sand.

Major hydropower projects in the area have also suffered extensive damage. The uncontrolled flow of the river swept away project infrastructure, causing significant losses.

With hydropower infrastructure damaged, electricity services have been completely disrupted in Nuwakot, further worsening daily life for people in the flood-affected areas.

Army deploys more than a dozen helicopters for rescue

With road access disrupted by flooding and erosion, aerial rescue operations are being used to evacuate stranded residents.

The Nepal Army’s Maithili Barracks in Damki, Bidur Municipality-4, has been designated as a major base for the rescue operation.

More than a dozen helicopters are being continuously deployed to evacuate people stranded in affected areas and move them to safety. The rescue operation, led by the Nepal Army, has provided a vital lifeline to those cut off by the disaster.

Around 1,500 families displaced

The disaster has displaced thousands of people in Nuwakot.

According to Nuwakot Chief District Officer Shambhu Prasad Regmi, around 1,500 families have been displaced by the flood in the district alone.

Families who have lost their homes and belongings are now waiting for safe shelter and relief assistance.

Onlinekhabar journalist Shankar Giri captured the devastation in flood-hit areas including Trishuli, Dhunge Bazaar and Devighat, documenting structures reduced to rubble and major infrastructure destroyed by the flood.

title.rendered: Moderate to heavy rain likely in Gosainkunda and other religious sites during Janai Purnima

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology’s Meteorological Forecasting Division has issued a special weather forecast bulletin for major religious and tourist destinations across the country in view of the Janai Purnima festival.

In the bulletin issued at noon on Thursday, the division forecast moderate to heavy rainfall in various religious areas across the country on Friday and Saturday.

In the Gosainkunda area of Rasuwa, which was affected by the Bhotekoshi flood, moderate rainfall is likely in many places from the afternoon on Friday. At night, moderate rain is expected in some places, with heavy rain possible in one or two locations.

On Saturday afternoon, moderate rain is likely in many places from the afternoon, while moderate rain is expected in some places at night, with heavy rain possible in one or two locations.

In the Panchpokhari area of Sindhupalchok, moderate rainfall is likely in many places from the afternoon on Friday. At night, moderate rain is expected in many places, with heavy rain possible in one or two locations. On Saturday afternoon, moderate rain is likely in some places from the afternoon, while heavy rain is possible in one or two locations at night.

In the Jatapokhari area along the Dolakha-Ramechhap border, moderate rainfall is likely during the daytime on both Friday and Saturday. At night, heavy rain is possible in one or two locations, according to the Meteorological Forecasting Division.

In the Badimalika area of Bajura, moderate rainfall is likely in some places on Friday afternoon and at night. On Saturday, moderate rain is expected in some places during the afternoon and in one or two locations at night.

In the Manichud Daha area of Kathmandu, moderate rainfall is likely from Friday afternoon, with moderate rain also expected at night. On Saturday afternoon, moderate rain is likely in some places from the afternoon, while some areas may also receive moderate rain at night.

The division has forecast moderate rainfall in some places in the Dansadhu area of Jumla and the Trivenidham area of Nawalparasi during the daytime and nighttime on both Friday and Saturday.

In the Shailung area of Dolakha, moderate rain is likely in some places during the daytime on Friday and Saturday. At night, heavy rain is possible in one or two locations.

According to the bulletin issued by the Meteorological Forecasting Division, moderate rainfall is likely in some places in the Janakpur Dham area of Dhanusha during the daytime and nighttime on both Friday and Saturday.

In the Kumbheshwar Temple area of Lalitpur, moderate rainfall is possible in some places on Friday afternoon, with moderate rain also possible at night. Moderate rainfall is also expected on Saturday.

According to the division, rainfall of up to 10 millimetres is classified as light, rainfall of 10 to 50 millimetres as moderate, and rainfall of 50 to 100 millimetres as heavy.
