title.rendered: Banks to maintain services in areas hit by Bhotekoshi floods

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Nepal Bankers’ Association has said banks will make efforts to maintain banking services in areas affected by the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River.

The association expressed deep sorrow over the loss of lives and damage to property and infrastructure caused by the floods and other natural disasters, and said it would provide necessary support to affected customers.

The association paid tribute to those who lost their lives in the disaster. It said most bank employees working in the flood-affected districts were safe, although contact had not yet been established with 26 employees.

Several bank branches have also been affected by flooding and inundation, according to the association. Disruptions to electricity, internet and communication services have further complicated the operation of regular banking services in the affected areas.

Despite these challenges, banks are making maximum use of available resources and alternative arrangements to maintain service continuity, the association said.

The association said it was coordinating and cooperating with the Nepal government, Nepal Rastra Bank and other relevant authorities during the crisis.

It said Nepal’s banking sector remains fully committed to supporting the government’s relief, rescue and rehabilitation efforts.

The association also said banks would do their best to support affected employees, their families and members of the public.

In coordination with the government, the association said it was ready to work with member banks to provide necessary assistance and facilitate relief, rescue, service continuity and rehabilitation efforts.

title.rendered: Artists call off shows amid Nepal’s flood disaster

content.rendered:
With significant loss of life and property following the flood in Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi, an uneasy situation prevails across the country. More than 150 people have lost their lives, while hundreds of injured people are receiving treatment.

The government is engaged in rescue and relief efforts, with more than 800 people still reported out of contact. Amid this difficult situation, artists have been postponing entertainment and cultural events one after another.

Singer Prakash Dutraj had a program scheduled for Friday in his home district of Myagdi to announce a new musical group. The organiser, the Myagdi Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said the event has now been postponed in light of the country’s situation.

Dutraj had planned to mark the occasion of Janai Purnima by announcing “Prakash Dutraj and Lineup” as the country’s first folk music band. In a statement, the chamber said that since this is a time to focus on humanitarian service and relief, Dutraj’s event has been postponed for now.

Singer Rachana Rimal, who had travelled to Australia for a musical program, announced on social media that she is postponing her previously scheduled shows. Citing the tragic situation back home, Rimal said her programs in various Australian cities, scheduled from August 28 to September 12, have been postponed until further notice.

New dates will be announced soon, she said. Rimal also shared that she has contributed Rs 100,000 to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

Meanwhile, “Comedy Champion Season 4,” which had been preparing to hold its launch event today, Thursday, has also postponed its press conference announcement.

title.rendered: Nepal facilitates return of citizens stranded in China after Rasuwa flood

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The government has begun facilitating the return of Nepali citizens stranded in China following the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River that disrupted the Nepal-China border area.

The Nepali Embassy in Beijing issued a notice urging Nepali citizens stranded in China due to the disruption caused by the flood to contact the designated officials for assistance in returning to Nepal.

The embassy said the sudden and severe flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26 disrupted the Nepal-China border area, leaving some Nepali citizens stranded on the Chinese side.

“Due to the sudden and severe flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26, the Nepal-China border area has been disrupted, leaving Nepali citizens stranded in China. They are requested to contact the following officials for assistance in returning to Nepal,” the embassy said in its notice.

The notice has provided contact details for Yubaraj Chhetri of the Nepali Consulate General in Lhasa, and Sanju Maharjan and Rajkumar Sah of the Nepali Embassy in Beijing.

The embassy has urged Nepali citizens affected by the border disruption to contact the officials for necessary coordination and assistance to facilitate their return to Nepal.

title.rendered: Former PM Sushila Karki expresses grief over Rasuwa flood losses

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Former Prime Minister Sushila Karki has expressed deep sorrow over the loss of lives and property caused by the devastating floods that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.

In a statement, Karki expressed condolences to the families of those who lost their lives and prayed for the safe rescue of people who remain missing following the disaster on August 26.

She said reports that a large number of people remain out of contact had caused further distress and expressed hope that search and rescue teams would be able to locate and safely rescue those missing.

Karki also wished for the speedy recovery and safety of those injured and affected by the disaster, while urging families waiting for news of their loved ones to remain patient and strong.

“None of you are alone in this hour of grief. This is not the sorrow of just one family, community or district. It is the shared pain of all Nepalis,” Karki said. She added that support and assistance should reach wherever the disaster has struck and called for everyone to stand together to overcome the crisis.

Karki praised the efforts of security personnel, flight crews, civil servants, health workers, teachers, elected representatives, volunteers, social workers and others involved in search, rescue, relief, treatment and rehabilitation efforts.

She also appealed to Nepalis at home and abroad to contribute according to their capacity to support affected families.

“Even if we have to cut back on our own meals, let us help,” she said, urging people to reduce some of their festival spending where possible and contribute to saving lives and helping affected families rebuild their lives.

Karki said solidarity during a disaster was one of the country’s greatest strengths and that assistance and unity shown today would help build hope for tomorrow.

She also expressed concern over reports of significant losses on the Chinese side of the border. Karki called for effective coordination and cooperation between the relevant mechanisms of Nepal and China to advance search, rescue and relief efforts.

title.rendered: Celebrities rally behind PM’s Flood Fund as Maha Jodi urges Nepalis to set politics aside

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

With significant loss of life and property following the flood in Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi, an uneasy situation prevails across the country. More than 150 people have lost their lives, while hundreds of injured are receiving treatment.

The government is engaged in rescue and relief efforts, with more than 800 people still reported out of contact. The government has been appealing to citizens for help, sharing QR codes for various bank accounts.

Amid this situation, artists and celebrities have also been stepping forward with financial contributions. Madan Krishna Shrestha and Haribansha Acharya (the “Maha Jodi), Anmol KC, Biraj Bhatt, and many other artists have donated to the government account via QR code.

They have been sharing bank account details and QR codes on social media, urging others to contribute what they can to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

Hari Bansha Acharya wrote, “As the country weeps over the devastation of the flood, I sincerely request Nepalis both at home and abroad, regardless of political affiliation, to contribute what they can to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund. From us (Maha Jodi), we are contributing Rs 200,000, Rs 100,000 each, to the fund.”

Anmol KC wrote, “Today’s disaster has reminded us once again that suffering doesn’t knock on anyone’s door before arriving. Today it’s someone else’s father, mother, brother or sister in pain; tomorrow, any one of us could be. I’ve contributed what I could from my side. Now I humbly request the same of you. It’s not about how big or small the amount is; what matters is the spirit of giving. Let’s not let the affected families feel alone in this difficult hour.”

Other film industry figures, musicians, and TV artists have also been contributing to the government fund.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood damage details to be collected through local govts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The government will collect and update details of damage caused by the Rasuwa flood through the affected local governments.

A meeting of the high-level management group under the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation and the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration decided to collect details of damage to offices and other local-level infrastructure through the respective local governments.

The decision states that the ministry will “collect and update details of damage to the offices of affected local levels through the respective local governments.”

Local governments will also mobilise funds from their disaster management funds and other available sources, in accordance with existing regulations, for rescue and relief operations.

The Department of Survey will collect details of damage to private and public land in the affected areas and carry out disaster mapping.

The unexpected flooding originating from the Nepal-China border area has affected Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan, Nawalparasi and other districts along the Bhotekoshi and other river basins.

title.rendered: Chakradevi Hospital in Nuwakot struggles without electricity and fuel

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Chakradevi Hospital in Bidur has been operating in “emergency mode” to treat people injured in the flood that struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa. The hospital has been providing first aid to the injured and airlifting critically ill patients to Kathmandu by helicopter.

According to Dr Rakesh Pariyar of Chakradevi Hospital, the hospital is about one kilometre from the flood-affected area, so rescued victims have been brought there for treatment. The flood has caused extensive damage to settlements in Trishuli Bazaar, Betravati Bazaar, Dhunge Bazaar and Devighat areas of Nuwakot.

He said access to Trishuli District Hospital, the main treatment centre in the area, has also been affected after roads and bridges were swept away by the flood. With concrete bridges in the Dhunge area washed away, transportation has come to a standstill, making it impossible to send critically ill patients to Kathmandu by road, he said.

According to Dr Pariyar, 24 patients had been brought to the hospital as of Thursday, nine of whom were in critical condition. They were airlifted to Kathmandu in coordination with the Nepali Army. The other patients are receiving treatment at Chakradevi Hospital. Dr Pariyar said patients were still being brought to the hospital and that treatment was being provided under emergency conditions.

He said the number of injured people could increase further as search and rescue operations have only recently intensified. “Search and rescue operations have only just begun,” he said. “There is a possibility that a much larger number of patients could arrive.”

The 15-bed Chakradevi Hospital has also prepared to manage a large influx of patients at once through a triage system if necessary. However, Dr Pariyar said the hospital has limited human resources. According to him, a limited number of health workers, including two doctors, have been providing continuous services at the hospital.

Following the flood, the biggest challenge to the hospital’s medical services has been the disruption of electricity. The power outage has made it difficult to operate equipment needed for continuous monitoring of patients. The hospital is currently relying on a petrol-powered inverter to continue providing medical services. However, a shortage of petrol has made it difficult to sustain this arrangement for long.

Dr Pariyar said the flood also swept away a petrol station in the Dhunge area, while a shortage of petrol at another station in Battar has further aggravated the problem. “The main problem right now is electricity. Without power, it has become difficult to keep patients under continuous monitoring,” he said. “We have also run out of petrol to operate the generator.”

title.rendered: ‘Only helicopters can bring patients’: Rasuwa flood cuts off injured from hospital

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Treatment of people injured in the devastating floods in Rasuwa is continuing at Trishuli Hospital, but doctors say damaged roads and bridges have made it difficult to bring critically injured patients to the hospital.

According to Dr Rajendra Lama, director of Trishuli Hospital, 16 injured people were brought to the hospital for treatment on Wednesday. Three of them were in serious condition and have been admitted for further treatment.

On Thursday, rescuers brought another 21-year-old man to the hospital. He was also in serious condition and is undergoing treatment, including a CT scan, Lama said.

The disruption of road and bridge connections has become the biggest obstacle to transporting injured people from flood-affected areas, according to Lama.

“Right now, we are in a situation even more remote than Humla,” Lama told Onlinekhabar. “There is no way to bring patients here except by helicopter.”

The hospital has been able to receive injured people from areas within roughly five to seven kilometres of the hospital. However, bringing patients from settlements farther away has become extremely difficult.

“We were able to rescue and bring in the patients from nearby areas yesterday,” Lama said. “But it is not possible to bring those injured farther away to the hospital. They can only be brought here if they are rescued by helicopter.”

The flood has also disrupted drinking water, electricity and transportation services in the affected areas, Lama said. He stressed the need to immediately restore road connectivity between Bidur and Trishuli.

He said that even if major roads and bridges cannot be rebuilt immediately, temporary bridges or pathways that allow people to walk and motorcycles to pass could significantly improve rescue and medical services.

“Even a small bridge for pedestrians would allow us to carry patients across,” he said. “From there, it would also be easier to take them to Kathmandu.”

Lama urged the government to make immediate arrangements to bring injured people stranded in flood-affected areas to hospitals. He also called for safe drinking water, healthcare and sanitation facilities for people staying at relief centres.

title.rendered: Let us who survived help the victims of the Himalayan tsunami

content.rendered:
The devastation caused by the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, which began in the Syafrubesi and Timure areas, has been felt as far as the Terai region of central Nepal. Based on the damage reports, images and footage continuously collected by the Onlinekhabar team through Wednesday evening, as well as conversations with numerous local victims, we can say that the loss of life and property caused by this flood may be the worst since the 2015 earthquake.

Sudden storms that occur in the sea are known as tsunamis. The disaster witnessed in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli areas is similarly the result of climate change and various crises in the Himalayan region. The exact number of tourists missing in the area is still unknown. Security personnel and members of the general public are also missing. The actual figures were not available by the time this editorial was being written. The latest information puts the death toll at 78, with hundreds of people still missing.

Journalist Kedar Sharma has described this sudden and unimaginable crisis as a “Himalayan tsunami.” Drawing on several references, he has estimated that such Himalayan tsunamis are likely to become more frequent in the future.

Author Ramesh Bhusal, who has studied the flow of rivers originating in the Himalayan region, argues that Nepalis who have witnessed the Melamchi and Roshi floods, as well as the Seti flood a decade ago, cannot describe today’s disaster as entirely unimaginable.

He has said, “We should have been able to imagine that this could happen, and that is where we failed. For now, let us focus on rescue, but let us not create a situation where we once again sit helplessly and call another disaster unimaginable.”

For the time being, the focus must remain on emergency rescue, relief and search operations. The federal government appeared to have taken swift initiatives in this regard on Wednesday. All political parties, the private sector, professionals and communities of every kind need to join these efforts initiated by the government. Provincial and local governments can also help victims receive rescue and necessary assistance more quickly by moving forward in coordination with the federal government.

The scale of this crisis, which emerged in the China-Nepal border region, must have been understood by Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who themselves expressed concern about Wednesday’s disaster. China has decided to send its vice-premier to assess the situation in the border area. Indian Prime Minister Modi telephoned his Nepali counterpart, Balen Shah.

Anyone who sees the destruction caused by the Rasuwa flood in Nuwakot and Dhading would be alarmed. The Onlinekhabar team had already headed in that direction on Wednesday. We have published photographs, footage and initial reports of the damage and will continue to provide updates. We also appeal to all our readers to avoid the epidemic of misinformation and rely only on factual information.

At the same time, we remain committed to further strengthening the trust you have placed in us over the years. Let us recognise the reality that false and misleading information during a disaster can cause even greater suffering to victims and their families. Let us not turn disasters into spectacles or join the race to go viral by posting videos and photographs taken during the tragedy.

Instead, those of us who have survived by chance, and whose loved ones are safe, should put ourselves in the place of the flood victims and take part in rescue and relief efforts to the best of our ability. A crisis tests the extent of our humanity and our sense of solidarity. Nepalis must pass that test once again. We have survived this disaster, and that makes our responsibility even greater.

Several questions have come to the surface with this disaster. Was the flood caused by a glacial lake outburst in the Himalayan region? The Chinese side has assessed that the flood may have been triggered by an earthquake in the Tibetan region. Can an earthquake measuring less than magnitude 5 cause destruction on such a massive scale? These are questions on people’s minds. Some have suggested that this may have been a glacial lake outburst flood, or a GLOF, similar to those seen in the past.

Tribhuvan University geologist Ranjan Dahal said during a conversation with us, “I have never seen such a massive flood before. Nor had I imagined that a flood coming from the upper reaches could be this destructive. I have never witnessed a flood arriving on such a large, high and explosive scale.”

Although the flooding was seen in the Bhotekoshi, experts believe it may have originated from the Lhende River. Similarly, when a sudden flood occurred in Lhende in Asar 2082, nine people died, and 18 others went missing.

The Chinese side is also studying the disaster. They, too, have not yet reached a conclusion. The governments of Nepal and China have an agreement to exchange information promptly during disasters. However, it does not appear that the agreement was implemented reliably during this disaster. This will probably also be reviewed.

A disaster of a similar nature struck Kedarnath in Uttarakhand, India, in 2013. Since then, there has been broader debate about the causes and possible solutions to such sudden natural crises in the Himalayan region. Nepal is a country surrounded by mountains from east to west. We face greater risks than India and any other country in this region. The Himalayan region is Nepal’s wealth. But if we fail to use and manage this wealth properly, these very mountains can push us toward greater crises.

The immediate priority is to search for victims, rescue them and provide relief. Communities themselves have to come forward to support and sustain their own communities.

After that, let us call on researchers in Nepal and abroad to conduct in-depth studies. We cannot continue to face crises of this nature. It may take decades to rebuild the infrastructure that was swept away within just a few hours. The fact that an entire district has been cut off from communication is not an ordinary occurrence.

At the same time, the Nepali community is being tested. When attempts were made to ignite the fire of communalism from Kaptanganj in Sunsari, the people of the hills and mountains had also taken notice. In the Terai-Madhes region, disasters brought by floods are almost a regular problem. This time, the hills and mountains are bearing a similar disaster. At this moment, all three geographical regions, including the Madhes, must come together to support one another and extend a helping hand.

That is the collective strength of the Nepali community. It is during crises like these that this strength is needed most. Once again, we appeal to everyone: if there are differences or disputes among us, let us set them aside and join hands. At this moment, we have a great responsibility towards our own citizens as well as tourists who have come to Nepal from different countries.

Therefore, those of us who have survived must open our hearts and extend every possible help to all the victims of the Himalayan tsunami.

title.rendered: 26 injured in Rasuwa flood brought to Teaching Hospital; one dies during treatment

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

As of Thursday morning, 26 people injured in the devastating flood that swept from Tibet into Rasuwa have been brought to Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital for treatment.

The hospital said a 25-year-old man among them died during treatment.

According to Teaching Hospital spokesperson Dr Gopal Sedhain, six of the injured brought to the hospital are currently being treated in the ICU.

He said the hospital has received information that an additional 50 to 60 injured people from the flood-affected areas may arrive for treatment.

The hospital has already made necessary preparations in anticipation of this patient load, he added.

“We’re estimating that around 50 to 60 more patients could come in. We’ve made our hospital preparations accordingly,” spokesperson Dr Sedhain told Onlinekhabar.

He said that among the additional injured expected, the majority are anticipated to have general injuries rather than critical conditions requiring ICU care.

The hospital said it has kept its treatment teams and necessary services on standby to manage the potential patient load.

The devastating flood that came from Tibet has caused major loss of life and property in the Rasuwa area. As rescue and relief operations continue in the affected region, injured people continue to be sent to various hospitals for treatment. Relatives searching for those who have lost contact have also been arriving at hospitals.

title.rendered: 644 foreign and Nepali nationals reported missing in Bhotekoshi flood: NTB

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) has stated that a total of 644 travellers, including 127 Nepali nationals, have been reported missing following Wednesday’s devastating flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, affecting Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha.

In its “Situation Update – 3” issued Thursday, the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, NTB, Tourist Police, and other tourism stakeholders said they are working to verify the whereabouts and safety of tourists and travellers who were in or passing through the affected areas at the time of the flood, which struck around 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, August 26. Efforts to rescue and evacuate the injured and stranded are ongoing.

The preliminary figures, compiled from records submitted by trekking and travel companies, are still being cross-checked with travel agencies, guides, local authorities, and security agencies. NTB noted that only riverside areas of the four affected districts along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli have suffered severe damage, while other areas remain unaffected.

A separate breakdown released by NTB, current as of 12:00 p.m. on Thursday, August 27, lists missing persons by nationality. India tops the list with 178 missing, followed by Nepal with 127, Ukraine with 53, Malaysia with 51, the United States with 65, the United Kingdom with 33, Australia with 35, and Canada with 25.

Smaller numbers of missing nationals were also reported from countries including Germany (8), Russia (8), Singapore (9), South Africa (6), Latvia (6), France (4), Spain (3), Belgium (3), New Zealand (5), Japan (5), Portugal (2), the Netherlands (2), Italy (2), Ireland (2), Kazakhstan (2), and one each from Belarus, Bulgaria, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Serbia, Sweden, and Switzerland.

The board has asked the public to remain calm, stay informed, and follow official safety instructions, reiterating that tourist safety remains its priority.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah visits flood-hit Bidur for on-site inspection

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Prime Minister Balen Shah on Thursday reached Bidur in Nuwakot to inspect areas affected by the devastating floods and meet people injured in the disaster.

Shah, accompanied by Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal, travelled to Bidur by road and began an on-site assessment of the flood damage.

During the visit, the prime minister is assessing the extent of physical damage and meeting local officials, security personnel and elected representatives to discuss ongoing rescue and relief efforts, rehabilitation and the restoration of damaged infrastructure.

Bidur is among the areas in Nuwakot affected by the flood that entered the district through Rasuwa following the Bhotekoshi River disaster on Wednesday. Betrawati, Trishuli and Devighat areas were also affected, with significant damage reported in riverbank settlements.

The prime minister is also expected to issue instructions to accelerate relief distribution and reconstruction of damaged infrastructure in the affected areas.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood update: 177 bodies recovered so far

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Among those missing in the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa, 177 bodies have been recovered so far.

According to figures released by Nepal Police Headquarters, 177 bodies have been found to date.

Police say the bodies were recovered as follows: 2 in Rasuwa, 12 in Nuwakot, 27 in Dhading, 69 in Chitwan, 20 in Gorkha, 9 in Tanahun, 32 in East Nawalparasi, and 6 in West Nawalparasi.

The Nepal Army, Nepal Police, and Armed Police Force are currently mobilised for search and rescue operations. The injured have been rescued and taken to various hospitals for treatment.

title.rendered: Drone pilots called to join rapid response team for Rasuwa flood rescue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Drone pilots have been urged to come together to support intensified search and rescue operations in areas affected by the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa.

The Robotics Association of Nepal (RAN) has called on drone pilots to join a Drone Rapid Response Team (DRRT) to assist ongoing rescue and relief efforts.

The DRRT will coordinate directly with a team from the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, according to RAN.

The team will use drones to conduct aerial surveys of damaged riverbank areas that cannot be reached on foot or by vehicle. It will also help identify stranded communities and locate missing people using aerial technology.

Drone operators will also assist authorities in assessing the condition of washed-away bridges, damaged roads and settlements at risk, RAN said.

The team will provide rescue and relief personnel with real-time aerial photographs and videos to help speed up response and resource mobilisation.

Interested drone pilots can join the DRRT by filling out the registration form provided by RAN.

title.rendered: Home Minister Gurung briefs all-party meeting on post-disaster situation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Home Minister Sudan Gurung briefed an all-party meeting on the situation following the recent disaster. At the meeting held at Singha Durbar, Gurung said security agencies had been mobilised for rescue and security operations in tunnels and other sensitive areas.

“The scale of damage to infrastructure is extremely large, and collecting an accurate assessment of the damage has been challenging,” he said. He said efforts were underway through various channels and mechanisms to determine the exact number of casualties and people reported missing.

Gurung said the willingness expressed by all political parties and groups to mobilise volunteers was commendable and necessary. He further said, “It is necessary to form a special team to study, research and forecast risks that may arise from glacial lakes and mountainous areas in the coming days.” He also said a special team had been mobilised to restore communication and transportation links. The all-party meeting was held at Singha Durbar to discuss the situation following the devastating floods in Rasuwa.

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, RSP parliamentary party leader Ganesh Parajuli, RSP General Secretary Bipin Kumar Acharya, RSP Chief Whip Kabindra Burlakoti and RSP spokesperson Jagadish Kharel were also present.

title.rendered: All-party meeting adopts 10-point resolution over Rasuwa flood disaster

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

An all-party meeting has adopted a 10-point common resolution to respond to the human and physical losses caused by the unexpected flooding in the Bhotekoshi and other river basins along the Nepal-China border.

The meeting expressed deep sorrow over the loss of lives and damage reported in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan, Nawalparasi and other districts. It paid tribute to those who died in the disaster and extended condolences to their bereaved families.

The political parties also agreed that the state must take responsibility for the treatment and care of those injured in the disaster, as well as provide psychosocial counselling.

Describing the disaster as a test of national unity, the parties pledged to rise above political differences and prioritise the protection of citizens’ lives and the national interest.

The 10-point common resolution includes:

  1. Depoliticising relief efforts: Political parties will avoid competition in rescue and relief operations and work cooperatively. Party leaders and cadres will be mobilised solely as humanitarian volunteers.
  2. One-door system for financial assistance: Parties and individuals will be discouraged from collecting donations independently. Contributions will instead be deposited through the government’s official disaster relief fund or an account designated by the government.
  3. Responsible use of social media: Parties have called for verified information to be shared while avoiding misinformation, exaggerated content and material that could violate the privacy and dignity of disaster victims.
  4. Scientific study of glacial lakes: The government will immediately conduct scientific studies and mapping of Nepal’s high-risk glacial lakes. The parties also called for efforts to establish a joint scientific and technical mechanism with China to study high-risk glacial lakes on the Chinese side and reduce associated risks.
  5. Disaster diplomacy and early-warning systems: Nepal and China should institutionalise real-time data sharing and develop reliable, technology-based early-warning systems, taking into account transboundary river systems.
  6. National unity and inclusive rescue: The role of local governments as first responders should be strengthened, while rescue and relief efforts should prioritise women, children, senior citizens and persons with disabilities.
  7. Resilient reconstruction and zero tolerance: Damaged infrastructure should be rebuilt to higher safety and resilience standards. Those involved in black-marketing, artificial shortages and misuse of relief supplies should face strict legal action.
  8. Raising the issue of climate justice: Nepal should effectively raise the issue of climate-induced loss and damage at international forums and seek support from the international community and development partners based on climate justice.
  9. Appeal for international assistance: The parties called for humanitarian, technical and financial assistance from the United Nations, development partners, international non-governmental organisations, friendly countries and the Nepali diaspora for rescue, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction.
  10. Formation of a high-level all-party mechanism: A parliamentary committee should be formed to provide continued advice, support and oversight of government efforts related to post-disaster reconstruction, climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction and reforms to national disaster policies.

The meeting also highly praised the contributions of the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, health workers, civil servants and volunteers involved in the disaster response.

The parties expressed their commitment to turning the disaster into an opportunity to strengthen national unity, improve disaster preparedness and promote resilient reconstruction.

The joint statement was signed by Rastriya Swatantra Party chair Rabi Lamichhane, Nepali Congress president Gagan Thapa, Nepali Communist Party coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal, CPN-UML general secretary Shankar Pokhrel, Shram Sanskriti Party chair Dhruva Rai, Rastriya Prajatantra Party chair Rajendra Lingden, Janata Samajbadi Party chair Upendra Yadav and Janamat Party general secretary Chandan Singh.

title.rendered: PABSON and KUMON Nepal sign MOU to strengthen mathematics education

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Private and Boarding Schools’ Organisation Nepal (PABSON) and KUMON Nepal, a Japanese education program, signed a promotion partnership agreement on Wednesday in Kathmandu, with the objective of introducing KUMON’s student-centred self-learning method to PABSON member schools and supporting their efforts to improve the quality of education.

“Nepal’s private schools have been continuously exploring effective and innovative learning approaches that can improve educational quality and prepare students to face the demands of the emerging digital era. In this context, the need for a learning method that places students at the centre of the learning process and develops their ability to learn independently has become increasingly important,” reads the statement of KUMON.

KUMON, with over 70 years of history, operates in over 60 countries and supports around four million students worldwide. Its core philosophy is to develop the ability to learn independently, rather than simply teaching students what to learn.

According to KUMON, the self-learning method focuses on developing concentration, discipline, confidence, regular learning habits, problem-solving skills, and independent learning ability. It is designed to complement regular school education by strengthening students’ learning habits and encouraging them to take greater responsibility for their own learning.

Through the partnership, PABSON and KUMON Nepal will introduce and promote awareness of the KUMON student-centred self-learning method among PABSON member schools, enabling interested schools to explore the approach as part of their efforts to enhance educational quality.

The agreement was signed by PABSON President Krishna Adhikari and Ganesh Man Lama, Chairman of IGC Business Holding, in the presence of PABSON members and representatives from KUMON partner schools.

Sharing his personal experience with KUMON, PABSON President Adhikari said that he was first introduced to KUMON during a visit to the USA in 2008. He was impressed by how KUMON helped students, including his own children, develop strong academic skills, confidence, and independent learning habits. Nearly 18 years later, after learning that KUMON had been introduced in Nepal, he decided to introduce the program at his own school and expressed his happiness at being part of the KUMON journey.

The event brought together education leaders and representatives from different schools to discuss the future of mathematics education and the changing needs of students. The gathering emphasised the shared message: “Education is Evolving, and So Do We.”

Speaking at the ceremony, Ganesh Man Lama emphasised that education should not be limited to examination results and academic marks. He highlighted the importance of developing students who can learn, think, solve problems, and continue learning independently throughout their lives.

He further emphasised that the objective of introducing KUMON in Nepal is not simply to expand KUMON centres, but to provide more students with opportunities to develop self-learning habits through schools. He expressed his belief that the partnership with PABSON can help make this approach accessible to more schools and students across Nepal.

title.rendered: Ncell Foundation contributes Rs 10 million for flood rescue and relief

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Ncell Foundation has announced a contribution of Rs 10 million to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund to support rescue, relief, and rehabilitation efforts for those affected by Wednesday’s devastating flood on Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi River.

With significant loss of life and property along riverside areas in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and other affected districts, and an urgent need for rescue, relief, and rehabilitation of the affected population, Ncell announced the contribution in response to the government’s appeal.

Ncell expressed tribute to all those who lost their lives in the tragedy and deep condolences to the grieving families, while wishing for speedy rescue and relief for those missing and affected.

Ncell has also been supporting affected communities through its communication services during this difficult time. Starting Wednesday, Ncell customers in flood-affected areas have been given free voice and data services, and 100 SMS for three days.

This initiative is expected to help affected citizens stay in easy contact with their families, relatives, and rescue and relief teams.

Ncell’s Director of Corporate Communications, Marketing, and Sustainability, Bishakha Laxmi Khadka, said: “Standing with the affected people in this difficult hour of crisis is our shared responsibility. We have decided to make this contribution to support the government and relevant agencies in rescue, relief, and rehabilitation efforts.”

Ncell has previously supported rescue, relief, and rehabilitation efforts during various natural disasters.

title.rendered: Private helicopters told to coordinate with government in Rasuwa flood rescue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The government has asked private helicopters involved in search and rescue operations in areas affected by the Rasuwa flood to operate only under government coordination.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said uncoordinated helicopter operations could increase air traffic in the affected areas and raise the risk of accidents.

The authority has written to the district administration offices of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Gorkha, Dhading and Chitwan, directing them to ensure that helicopter-based search and rescue operations are conducted in an organised manner following decisions by the respective district security committees.

If a Nepali Army helicopter is required, the security committee has been asked to coordinate with the Army team in the respective district.

For private helicopters, authorities have been instructed to contact designated focal persons appointed by the NDRRMA to arrange rescue operations immediately when required.

The authority has designated Sachit Aryal of Heli Everest, Mingma Sherpa of Altitude Air and Balkrishna Pandit of Air Dynasty as contact persons for coordinating private helicopter operations.

The decision was taken to minimise the risk of helicopter accidents and other technical problems that could arise from uncoordinated flights in the flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: Chinese Ambassador links Rasuwa flood to earthquake on Nepali side

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

China’s Ambassador to Nepal, Zhang Maoming, has said preliminary information indicates that the devastating flood and landslide in Rasuwa were caused by an earthquake on the Nepali side.

The ambassador made the remarks in an interview with Nepal’s state television, NTV World.

According to details released by the Chinese Embassy in Nepal, China has expressed deep condolences to the Nepal government and people, paying tribute to those who lost their lives in the disaster.

Ambassador Zhang said preliminary information available so far shows that an earthquake struck the Nepal side on the morning of the disaster. The earthquake triggered a snow/rock avalanche, followed immediately by a flood carrying debris and mud. He said this natural event caused major human losses on both the Nepal and China sides of the Kerung–Rasuwagadhi border area, with many people reported missing.

Three areas of future cooperation

Ambassador Zhang pointed to three key areas where Nepal and China could cooperate to reduce the impact of such disasters in the future: information sharing and early warning, coordination in emergency rescue, and capacity building.

He said monitoring and early-warning systems for meteorological, hydrological, and geological hazards need to be strengthened, and that the cross-border disaster information exchange mechanism should be improved. He emphasised the need to strengthen communication and institutional development for coordinated response and rescue cooperation during disasters. He also said work should focus on staff training, technical knowledge exchange, and increased emergency supply support to build local-level disaster prevention and mitigation capacity.

Ambassador Zhang praised the resilience and response efforts shown by the Nepal government and people during this crisis. As a close neighbour connected by mountains and rivers, he reiterated China’s commitment to providing all possible support to Nepal to protect the lives and property of citizens of both countries.

The District Administration Offices of Morang and Sunsari said people who travelled to flood-affected areas for work may have lost contact, and asked that details of any such individuals be provided.

Morang’s Assistant Chief District Officer Pawan Raj Koirala issued a notice on Thursday requesting that families and other concerned parties provide the names, addresses, and contact numbers of anyone who went to the flood-affected areas for work and has since lost contact.

Sunsari’s Assistant Chief District Officer Rajmani Niraula also requested that information be provided about anyone from Sunsari who has lost contact.

title.rendered: Army team reaches Upper Trishuli-3A project to rescue stranded employees

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

A Nepal Army team has reached the site by helicopter to rescue employees stranded at the Upper Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, which was damaged by flooding in the Bhotekoshi River.

Although two landing attempts on Wednesday failed due to adverse weather conditions, the helicopter successfully landed at the project site on Thursday.

The Army team has begun an on-site assessment of the situation and the damage caused by the floods.

Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has directed authorities to expedite efforts to rescue employees stranded in the affected area and restore electricity services as soon as possible by taking all necessary measures.

Following the minister’s directive, a high-level team led by Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) Executive Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha has been deployed to the field. The team includes Deputy Executive Director Kirankumar Shrestha, Distribution and Customer Service Directorate chief and spokesperson Rajan Dhakal, and Chirantan Bikram Rana, chief executive officer of NEA Engineering Company, among other officials.

According to the NEA, the team is conducting an on-site assessment of the project, coordinating rescue efforts and carrying out the necessary technical evaluation for the restoration of the electricity infrastructure.

Meanwhile, efforts are underway to restore electricity supply through alternative means in flood-affected areas of Nuwakot where power infrastructure has been damaged.

The NEA has already restored electricity services in Kharanitar, Samundratar, Chaugada, Likhu and Panchakanya through an alternative line connected from the Sindhupalchok side.

In other affected areas of Nuwakot, authorities have identified the possibility of supplying electricity by charging the 66 kV lines at 11 kV. Preparations are therefore underway to charge the Chapali-Devighat 66 kV and Balaju-Trishuli 66 kV lines at 11 kV.

title.rendered: NEA restores power in flood-hit areas of Nuwakot through alternative lines

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has restored electricity supply to several areas of Nuwakot affected by power outages following the Bhotekoshi River flood by using alternative transmission arrangements.

The NEA said electricity has been supplied through an alternative line from Sindhupalchok to flood-affected areas including Kharanitar, Samundratar, Chaugada, Likhu, Panchakanya and Bidur.

NEA spokesperson Rajan Dhakal said work is underway to charge the Chapali–Devighat 66 kV line from the Chapali substation at 11 kV and charge the Balaju–Trishuli 66 kV line at 11 kV.

The authority is completing the necessary technical work and is attempting to bring the lines into operation by Thursday evening.

An alternative arrangement has also been made to supply electricity to some areas of the Trishuli region through the Salyanatar substation in Dhading.

The NEA said alternative sources are being used in areas where electricity supply through the regular system has been disrupted because of damage to power infrastructure caused by the floods.

The authority has deployed teams of skilled technicians, equipment and other resources from Kathmandu and surrounding areas to Nuwakot to restore electricity services as quickly as possible.

The teams are prioritising inspection and repair of damaged electricity infrastructure and arrangements for alternative power supplies.

Earlier, Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha had directed officials to intensify efforts to rescue employees who were out of contact or stranded in the flood-affected areas and restore electricity services immediately.

Following the minister’s directive, a high-level NEA team led by Executive Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha has been deployed to the affected areas.

The team includes NEA Deputy Executive Director Kiran Kumar Shrestha, Distribution and Customer Service Directorate chief and spokesperson Rajan Dhakal, and NEA Engineering Company Chief Executive Officer Chirantan Bikram Rana, among other officials.

The NEA said it is continuously assessing the condition of electricity infrastructure damaged by the floods and is prioritising alternative supply arrangements where possible and repairs to restore regular electricity services.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood: What happened and what we know so far

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

A sudden flash flood struck Nepal’s northern Rasuwa district on Wednesday, killing at least 165 people and leaving hundreds missing.

The disaster began near the Nepal-China border and sent a massive surge of mud, water and boulders down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.

Here are 10 things to know about what happened.

Where did the disaster happen?

Rasuwa is a mountainous district in northern Nepal, bordering China’s Tibet Autonomous Region.

The worst-hit areas include Timure and Syaphrubesi, near the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, an important route for trade and tourism between Nepal and China.

What happened on Wednesday morning?

At around 9 am on August 26, a huge surge of water, mud and rocks entered the Bhotekoshi River from the area near the Nepal-China border.

The flood rapidly swept through settlements and infrastructure before moving downstream into the Trishuli River.

What may have triggered the flood?

The exact cause is still being investigated.

Satellite imagery and preliminary analysis by experts suggest that a massive avalanche or landslide blocked the Lhende Khola, a river along the Nepal-China border.

Water then accumulated behind the blockage, forming a temporary lake. When the blockage failed, the stored water and debris surged downstream into Nepal.

Where does the earthquake fit in?

A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was recorded at 8:37am, shortly before the flood.

Scientists are still investigating whether the earthquake triggered the slope collapse or whether the enormous avalanche itself may have generated the seismic signal.

So far, it would be premature to say that the earthquake definitively caused the flood.

Why was the flood so destructive?

This was not simply a rise in river water. The flood carried enormous amounts of mud, rocks, boulders and debris, giving it tremendous destructive force.

Communities near the river had very little time to react as the surge moved rapidly downstream.

How far did the flood travel?

The flood began in the high mountains of Rasuwa but its impact extended far downstream.

It travelled through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, affecting parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading before reaching the Muglin area and eventually the Narayani River.

By the afternoon, floodwaters had reached Devghat, far from the original source.

How many people have been affected?

As of Thursday morning, 165 people had been confirmed dead and 826 people were reported missing.

Among those missing are 579 tourists, including 466 foreign nationals and 113 Nepali nationals.

Security personnel were also among those reported missing after several posts and facilities in the affected area were swept away.

Why were so many tourists in the area?

Rasuwa is not only a border district. It is also an important destination and gateway for tourism in the Himalayas, particularly those travelling to the Kailash Parbat and Mansarovar Lake.

The area provides access to the Langtang region, while Timure and Rasuwagadhi are located on the Nepal-China border.

The sudden disaster therefore struck both local communities and travellers who were in the region.

What has been destroyed?

The flood caused extensive damage to homes, hotels, roads, bridges, vehicles, hydropower projects, electricity transmission infrastructure and border facilities.

Around 19 bridges have reportedly been destroyed or swept away.

Several hydropower projects and transmission lines were damaged, while four hydrological monitoring stations were also swept away.

The Prithvi Highway, one of Nepal’s major road connections, was also blocked by flood debris further downstream.

Why does this disaster matter beyond Rasuwa?

The disaster highlights a growing concern in the Himalayan region: climate change is altering the stability of high-mountain environments.

Glaciers are retreating, glacial lakes are expanding, and permafrost and mountain slopes are becoming increasingly unstable. When landslides, avalanches or glacial lake outburst floods occur, enormous volumes of water and debris can move rapidly downstream across borders.

Wednesday’s disaster is therefore not only a story about one devastating flood in Nepal.

It is also a warning about the growing risks faced by communities living downstream of the rapidly changing Himalayas.

The search for survivors and missing people is continuing, while scientists and authorities investigate exactly what triggered the flood.

title.rendered: Chinese Embassy rejects allegations that China failed to issue timely warning

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Chinese Embassy in Nepal has rejected allegations that China failed to provide an early warning about the devastating floods and landslides in the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung area along the Nepal-China border, calling the claims misleading and untrue.

In a clarification issued publicly, the Chinese Embassy labelled two major allegations made in Nepal as “fake news” and dismissed them as false.

According to the embassy, two allegations—that the lack of a warning from China resulted in significant loss of life in Nepal, and that Nepal suffered major damage after a geological disaster dam on the Chinese side collapsed—are untrue.

What does the Chinese side claim?

Rejecting the allegations, the Chinese side said the actual sequence of events was different.

According to the embassy’s clarification, a landslide triggered by an earthquake or an earthquake-like tremor occurred on the Nepali side on the morning of August 26, 2026.

The resulting massive landslide caused significant loss of life and left people missing on both the Nepali and Chinese sides of the Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border area, the embassy said.

China urged both sides to focus on rescue and relief efforts rather than blaming each other during the sensitive situation.

“Blame solves nothing; cooperation saves lives,” the embassy said.

title.rendered: Prioritize information exchange with China, Prachanda tells all-party meeting

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

CPN coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal “Prachanda” has said that, in the context of the Rasuwa floods, information exchange with China should be made a priority.

He said this at an all-party meeting underway at Singha Durbar.

“What’s happening on information exchange from the China side? Let’s make this a priority,” Prachanda said.

Those present at the all-party meeting include RSP Chairman Rabi Lamichhane, Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa, CPN-UML General Secretary Shankar Pokharel, CPN Coordinator Pushpa Kamal Dahal “Prachanda,” RPP Chairman Rajendra Lingden, RPP parliamentary party leader Gyanendra Shahi, and JSP Nepal leader Mahantha Thakur, among others.

Also present are Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, RSP parliamentary party leader Ganesh Parajuli, RSP General Secretary Bipin Kumar Acharya, RSP Chief Whip Kabindra Burlakoti, and RSP spokesperson Jagadish Kharel, among others.

Speaking at the meeting, Prachanda urged that the public be kept informed: “What is the risk and possibility of further floods? Let’s keep the public informed.”

He also said that in the post-disaster situation, everyone should move forward together.

He said his side is ready for this, and that party leaders and cadres have already been mobilised for search and rescue as well as other humanitarian support.

He urged that, as in past disaster events, the parties should stand united.

Prachanda said: “Based on our experience from the Koshi dam breach, the Jure landslide, and the great earthquake, let all political parties stand together.”

At the meeting, RSP Chairman Lamichhane also called for setting aside party identity and uniting on relief, rescue, and reconstruction.

He also proposed forming an all-party committee covering everything from relief and rescue to rehabilitation.

Chairman Lamichhane said: “From relief and rescue to rehabilitation, let’s form an all-party or parliamentary or all-sided committee, one that makes it easier for the government to make decisions.”

He also urged that all parties stand together and contribute through the government’s relief and rescue fund as a single channel.

Police say that among those out of contact, Sarlahi residents Gyan Bahadur Thing and Shyamlal Moktan have come back into contact after being rescued. Search and rescue operations are underway to confirm the status of the remaining individuals.

The greatest damage has been reported at schools in Gosainkunda Rural Municipality, Rasuwa. Timure Community School in Timure has sustained extensive damage. Uttargaya School in Uttargaya Rural Municipality, Rasuwa, has also been damaged, with students reportedly fleeing to safety.

He said the Nepal Army’s rescue operation this morning successfully evacuated 116 people from Timure in Rasuwa, 95 Nepali and 21 Indian citizens, and that 7 more Nepali citizens were rescued from a tunnel.

title.rendered: Foreign exchange reserves rise 45.6%, enough to cover 23 months of imports

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Nepal’s total foreign exchange reserves rose 45.6 percent year-on-year to Rs 3.897 trillion by the end of the last fiscal year, according to Nepal Rastra Bank.

The reserves stood at Rs 2.678 trillion at the end of fiscal year 2024/25.

In US dollar terms, the country’s reserves increased 29.8 percent to $25.31 billion, from $19.50 billion a year earlier.

The central bank said the reserves are sufficient to cover 23 months of merchandise imports and 19.6 months of merchandise and services imports, based on imports recorded during fiscal year 2025/26.

Central bank holds most of the reserves

Of the total reserves, those held by Nepal Rastra Bank increased 43.8 percent to Rs 3.473 trillion from Rs 2.415 trillion a year earlier.

Foreign exchange reserves held by banks and financial institutions rose 61.4 percent to Rs 424.48 billion, compared with Rs 263.04 billion at the end of the previous fiscal year.

Indian currency accounted for 22.3 percent of Nepal’s total foreign exchange reserves as of mid-July 2026.

Reserves-to-GDP ratio rises

The central bank said foreign exchange reserves were equivalent to 63.8 percent of GDP at the end of fiscal year 2025/26.

Reserves were equivalent to 163.4 percent of total imports and 43.8 percent of broad money supply.

A year earlier, the corresponding ratios were 43.8 percent, 128.1 percent and 34.1 percent, respectively.

Net foreign assets rise

Nepal’s total foreign assets stood at Rs 4.263 trillion, while foreign liabilities amounted to Rs 2.446 trillion at the end of the fiscal year.

This left the country with a net foreign asset position of Rs 1.817 trillion, up from a surplus of Rs 779.77 billion a year earlier.

Authorities are working to reopen the Prithivi Highway connecting Kathmandu and Muglin by Thursday afternoon after the road was blocked by mud and debris following the Rasuwa floods.

According to Shubharaj Neupane, deputy director general and spokesperson for the Department of Roads, crews are working to clear the large amounts of mud deposited on the highway by the flood.

“The road from Muglin to Galaudi and from Kathmandu to Baireni is clear. Around 13 kilometres of road between Baireni and Galaudi have been covered with mud at several locations,” Neupane said.

title.rendered: Technical report details Bhotekoshi flood’s journey from Tibet to Devghat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Flood Forecasting Division has released a detailed technical report on the devastating floods that swept through the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers on Wednesday.

According to the report, a lake formed after the river was blocked in Tibet burst, sending a massive surge of water through the Bhotekoshi in Rasuwa and downstream along the Trishuli and Narayani river corridors.

The flood swept away four automatic hydrological monitoring stations along the river system. A preliminary technical assessment estimates that around 20 million cubic metres of additional water passed through the Devghat area alone during the flood.

Earthquake recorded before flood

The Department of Mines and Geology recorded a 4.4-magnitude earthquake at 8:37am on Wednesday. Shortly afterwards, a massive flood entered the Bhotekoshi from the Tibet side.

The Flood Forecasting Division said it began sending continuous alerts and SMS warnings to people living along the riverbanks and in vulnerable settlements after receiving information about the flood.

In coordination with Nepal Telecom and Ncell, a total of 679,295 early-warning SMS messages were sent to residents in vulnerable areas of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan.

The messages included 435,635 SMS sent through Nepal Telecom and 243,660 through Ncell.

The report said the timely dissemination of the warnings helped many people save their lives.

Flood’s journey from Bhotekoshi to Devghat

The report provides the following timeline of the flood:

  • 8:37am: A 4.4-magnitude earthquake was recorded by the Department of Mines and Geology.
  • 8:50am: Data transmission stopped from the Bhotekoshi-Syafrubesi hydrological station. Its last recorded water level at 8:40am was 1.62 metres, against a warning level of 6 metres and danger level of 7 metres.
  • 9:00am: Information about a major flood entering the Bhotekoshi from Tibet was received from the District Administration Office, Rasuwa, and staff at the Betrabati hydrological station.
  • 9:15–9:16am: The first early-warning messages were issued for communities along the Trishuli corridor up to Muglin, with 679,295 SMS messages sent.
  • 9:20am: The Betrawati hydrological station stopped transmitting data. Its last recorded water level was 3.55 metres, against a warning level of 4.1 metres and danger level of 5 metres.
  • 10:28am: The flood was reported to have reached the Galchhi area of Dhading. Further SMS alerts were sent to people along the Prithvi Highway, Muglin–Narayangadh road section and Trishuli river corridor.
  • 11:26am: Water level at the Fhurke Khola (Malekhu) hydrological station crossed the warning level.
  • 11:43am: The water level at the Fhurke (Malekhu) station crossed the danger level. Shortly afterwards, the station and the bridge were swept away by the flood.
  • 11:50am: The flood reached the Malekhu Bazaar area.
  • 1:00pm: The flood passed Muglin.
  • 1:35pm: Authorities again warned that the lake formed by the river blockage in China had not fully drained and that the risk remained.
  • 2:14pm: Water level at the Kalikhola hydrological station crossed the danger level of 12.1 metres and reached a peak of 12.3 metres.
  • 3:20pm: The flood reached the Narayani-Devghat area.
  • 4:00pm: Water level at the Devghat hydrological station peaked at 6.57 metres before beginning to recede.
  • 6:30pm: The water level at Devghat returned to around 4 metres, considered normal.

Four hydrological stations destroyed

The intensity of the flood destroyed four hydrological monitoring stations operated under the Centre for Water Resources and Hydrology.

The affected stations were the Rasuwa Bhotekoshi station, Rasuwa Syafrubesi station, Nuwakot Betrabati station and Dhading Malekhu (Fhurke) station.

The stations were swept away along with bridges, making it impossible to obtain direct water-level data from those locations, according to the report.

A technical assessment showed that approximately 20 million cubic metres of additional floodwater passed through the Devghat station during the event.

The division has mapped the area from the Rasuwagadhi border point to the Nepal-India border into very high-, high- and medium-risk zones and issued instructions to maintain heightened vigilance.

title.rendered: Helicopters to rescue flood-hit, injured people in Rasuwa from early morning

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Nepali Army and private helicopters will begin rescuing injured and at-risk people affected by the Bhotekoshi River flood in Rasuwa from early Thursday morning.

A meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority held earlier Thursday decided to evacuate injured people from the affected areas and provide initial treatment at camps being set up at Nepali Army barracks in Dhunche, Rasuwa, and Bidur, Nuwakot.

Ministry of Home Affairs spokesperson Anand Kafle said the decision was taken to ensure immediate medical care for those affected.

According to Kafle, critically injured people will be evacuated to Kathmandu immediately. Rescue and treatment efforts will be prioritised based on the severity of the injuries.

Meanwhile, relief materials required for the affected communities have started being transported by road to the Nepali Army barracks in Bidur.

The government has intensified rescue, medical and relief efforts following the devastating flooding in Rasuwa.

title.rendered: IFRC releases nearly CHF 1 million for Nepal flood response

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is releasing nearly CHF 1 million (around Rs 189.5 million) in emergency funding to support the Nepal Red Cross Society’s response to severe flash floods in Nepal.

The funding, provided through the IFRC’s Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF), will help the Nepal Red Cross respond to urgent needs as teams assess the extent of the damage and identify communities requiring assistance.

“The priority now is to reach affected communities and get assistance to people who have lost their homes, suffered injuries or have been cut off,” the IFRC said in a press statement.

The IFRC said it is closely monitoring the situation and is prepared to provide additional support if the needs increase.

The Nepal Red Cross has begun distributing drinking water and emergency supplies, including tarpaulins, blankets, sleeping mats, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.

The IFRC is supporting the Nepal Red Cross with emergency funding, operational coordination and technical assistance. Its regional and global teams are also on standby to provide additional capacity and international assistance if required.

title.rendered: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies – IFRC
Rasuwa flood: Rescuers push forward despite limited resources

content.rendered:
Around 9 AM on Wednesday, a sudden, severe flood originating in the Tibetan region of China caused massive loss of life and property in Nepal’s northern districts, including Rasuwa and Nuwakot. The flood, which came down through Rasuwa’s Bhotekoshi River, wreaked havoc across Timure, Syaphrubesi, Melung, Betrawati, Trishuli Bazaar, Dhungebazaar, and other areas. The flood swept away around 19 bridges, including the one leading to Dhading’s district headquarters.

As of this report, according to Nepal Police data, 157 bodies have been recovered so far. Positive identification of these bodies is still pending.

A large number of people remain missing. Nepal Police central spokesperson and DIG Abinarayan Kafle says that even the exact details of the missing are yet to be confirmed. According to him, 32 Nepal Police personnel alone are missing. Meanwhile, Armed Police Force co-spokesperson and DSP Shailendra Thapa says 9 armed police personnel remain out of contact so far.

Similarly, 44 army personnel are also out of contact. According to army spokesperson and Assistant Chief of Army Staff Rajaram Basnet, 44 soldiers have not been in contact so far; these were personnel deployed to secure Langtang National Park and hydropower facilities. This brings the total number of missing security personnel to 85.

Among Nepal Police and Armed Police Force combined, 41 personnel remain missing, including officers from the Timure, Syaphrubesi, Rasuwagadhi, and Melung police posts. On the armed police side, 9 personnel from the Timure Border Out Post (BOP) are missing. Assistant Sub-Inspector Santosh Rijal, who witnessed the event firsthand, says it is still not possible to assess the full extent of the damage.

Stationed at Betrawati Police Post, Rijal had been using a megaphone to warn people about the incoming flood when it suddenly struck, forcing him to flee to save his life. So far, 97 people have been rescued by air.

Following the sudden flood, the government and security agencies have shown active engagement in search and rescue. Prime Minister Balen Shah, upon learning of the incident, informed the public via Facebook that he had already directed agencies to mobilise for search and rescue.

He appeared to prioritise the Rasuwa flood from the outset, announcing that Nepal Army, Nepal Police, and Armed Police Force teams had already moved toward the flood-affected areas.

A Cabinet meeting was held following the incident, which decided to declare the flood-affected municipalities as crisis zones and focus on search and rescue. The meeting also authorised the Home Minister to mobilise all available resources, including helicopters.

The Home Ministry and Ministry of Defense were tasked with immediately rescuing the injured and those in distress and moving them to safe locations — further evidence that the government treated the Rasuwa flood with considerable seriousness.

Likewise, a meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority was held at the Prime Minister’s Office in Singha Durbar, where officials were briefed on the damage caused by the flood.

During the crisis, instructions were given for everyone to focus, from their respective positions, on rescuing, searching for, and providing relief to affected citizens in the flood zone.

Earlier, during flooding in the Nakkhu River within Kathmandu itself, citizens who had climbed onto a tin rooftop awaiting rescue were swept away, a case that drew criticism at the time for the state’s lack of urgency in rescue efforts. Similarly, the state mechanism was criticised for failing to act proactively in the Roshi River flood and the incident of buses buried in Dhading. However, experts believe the government has shown clear activeness in the search and rescue response to the current Rasuwa flood.

Home Minister Sudan Gurung himself went to the Kathmandu airport to oversee rescue preparations. Following government directives, all three security agencies were mobilised for search and rescue.

Nepal Army teams were deployed from the Dhunche and Trishuli barracks for search and rescue. Army spokesperson Basnet said a skilled disaster management team was also dispatched from the No. 6 Battalion headquarters in Gajuri, Dhading.

An Mi-17 helicopter along with the Nepal Army’s Emergency Medical Rescue Team was also deployed. Spokesperson Basnet said 97 people were rescued by air alone. Alongside the army, Armed Police Force teams were also deployed for rescue; according to the force, 1,100 personnel were mobilised. Nepal Police teams have also been deployed for search and rescue.

Ratindra Khatri, a retired Major General of the Nepal Army and an expert in crisis, emergency, and disaster management, says security agencies and the government have shown activeness in search and rescue during this disaster.

“Security personnel themselves are missing in large numbers. The flood risk persists. Yet, they remain active in search and rescue,” Khatri told Onlinekhabar. “This activeness should be viewed positively.”

However, the security agencies themselves have acknowledged a shortage of adequate resources for rescue operations. The Armed Police Force, which holds primary responsibility for disaster rescue, does not have a single air asset of its own for rescue operations. Personnel say they are often forced to travel on foot, which creates problems when that isn’t feasible.

While the Nepal Army was able to speed up rescue using its own helicopters, the Armed Police Force had to wait for private helicopters, something they themselves acknowledge caused some difficulty in their rescue efforts.

“We have made our best effort in search and rescue from our side. But the lack of air assets has been a problem,” said one security official. Nepal Police, too, lacks adequate resources, including air assets, for rescue work.

Space was cleared and kept on standby at the Armed Police Force’s APF Hospital, TU Teaching Hospital, and the National Trauma Centre to receive the injured brought in through search and rescue.

Teams from the Trauma Centre, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, and Nepal Army, including doctors, were sent to Trishuli. Those rescued and brought to Kathmandu are being treated at APF Hospital, TU Teaching Hospital, and the Trauma Centre.

A total of 15 helicopters, 7 from the Nepal Army and 8 from the private sector, carried out rescues. Ten ambulances were kept on standby at the airport to transport those airlifted to hospitals. This sequence of events also shows the government’s active role in post-rescue treatment and management.

Khatri believes the government has used its resources to the fullest extent possible. “Right now is the time to support search, rescue, and relief efforts, rather than picking apart shortcomings; we should unite and fight against this disaster,” he said. “It’s also evident that supplies from emergency warehouses have been put to use.

title.rendered: Nepal Army sends 8 tonnes of relief supplies to flood-hit Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

Around eight tonnes of relief supplies have been sent to flood-affected areas of Rasuwa through eight trucks operated by the Nepali Army.

The trucks carrying the relief materials were dispatched to the affected areas on Wednesday night.

The supplies include 500 mosquito nets, 1,000 dignity kits for children, 220 sleeping bags, 500 blankets, 10 plastic sheets, 100 tarpaulins, 500 solar lamps, 500 solar lamp panels and a 30 KVA generator, among other items.

The relief materials were transported overnight with the aim of providing immediate assistance and humanitarian support to people affected by the flooding in the Bhotekoshi River.

The materials were arranged and transported under the direct supervision of Home Minister Sudhan Gurung as the floods continue to disrupt daily life in the affected areas.

The government has said it is stepping up rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts in the flood-hit areas.

title.rendered: Remittances surpass Nepal’s annual budget as inflows hit Rs2.36 trillion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

Remittance inflows into Nepal surpassed the country’s total annual budget in the last fiscal year, according to data released by Nepal Rastra Bank on Wednesday.

Nepal received Rs2.36 trillion ($16.19 billion) in remittances in fiscal year 2025/26, a 37.1 percent increase from the previous year, the central bank said in its latest economic and financial report.

The amount is higher than the Rs1.964 trillion budget Nepal implemented during the same fiscal year.

Remittance inflows in June alone reached Rs242.33 billion, up from Rs189.11 billion during the same month a year earlier.

In US dollar terms, remittance inflows increased by 28.1 percent to $16.19 billion, compared with 16.3 percent growth in the previous fiscal year.

Net secondary income also increased significantly, reaching Rs2.581 trillion, compared with Rs1.874 trillion in the previous fiscal year.

The central bank said 406,519 Nepalis received institutional or individual labour approvals for foreign employment during the review year, while 385,783 received re-entry labour approvals.

The number of new labour approvals was lower than the previous year, when 505,957 Nepalis received such approvals. However, the number receiving re-entry approvals increased from 333,309 a year earlier.

title.rendered: US stands with Nepal after devastating floods, says Secretary of State Rubio

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has expressed solidarity with the Nepali people following the devastating floods and inundation in Nepal.

In a message posted on X, Rubio said the United States stands with Nepal during the disaster and expressed his sympathy for those affected.

“Following the devastating floods, we stand in solidarity with the people of Nepal, and our prayers are with the Nepali people,” Rubio said.

He also said the US Department of State stands ready to assist the Government of Nepal with necessary humanitarian assistance during the crisis.

The floods have caused widespread damage in several parts of Nepal, with rescue and relief operations underway in the affected areas.

title.rendered: No basis for reports of another major flood in Rasuwa, Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 27

The Flood Forecasting Division under the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has dismissed reports circulating about another major flood about to hit Rasuwa and Nuwakot, saying there is no official basis for such claims.

The division said its information and preliminary analysis so far do not indicate any credible possibility of another major flood in the areas.

It has urged the public to remain calm and not to follow unverified information or rumours.

Although rainfall is continuing in the affected areas and river levels could rise somewhat, the division said there is currently no indication of another destructive flood.

The division said that if there is any indication of a major flood entering Nepal, it will coordinate with security agencies stationed along the border and other concerned authorities and immediately inform the public.

In such an event, official early warnings will be disseminated through SMS and other available communication channels as soon as possible.

The division has urged people to rely only on official sources for flood-related information and take necessary precautions.
