title.rendered: Rasuwa flood: At least seven dead, dozens missing as rescue operations continue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

A massive flood that entered Nepal from the Tibetan side has caused widespread destruction in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, with at least seven bodies recovered and dozens of people still missing or out of contact.

The flood entered the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa early Wednesday morning, devastating riverside settlements including Timure, Syaphrubesi, Hakubesi, Mailung, Shantibazaar and Betrawati.

The full extent of the damage and casualties remains unclear as communication with several affected areas has been disrupted.

Seven bodies recovered

Bagmati Province Police Chief Deepak Regmi said seven bodies had been recovered so far—three from the riverbank in Nuwakot and four from Dhading.

He said the search for missing people and collection of bodies were continuing.

Local officials in Rasuwa have also reported that several people remain missing.

Uttargaya Rural Municipality Chair Madhav Aryal said local residents were recovering bodies from the river and described the situation as devastating.

He said the rural municipality office itself was swept away and some employees were missing.

Timure devastated

The flood struck Timure at around 8:30 to 9am, according to local representatives.

Ward member Pema Dorje Ghale said residents had little time to react before the flood swept through the settlement.

He said more than 100 houses had been in Timure and that many residents who escaped were waiting for rescue on higher ground.

Ghale said families had been left without food or basic supplies and were surviving on river water while waiting for rescue teams.

41 security personnel out of contact

A total of 41 security personnel—32 from Nepal Police and nine from the Armed Police Force—were initially reported out of contact following the flood.

Nepal Police spokesperson DIG Abi Narayan Kafle said some personnel had subsequently made contact, but 32 remained out of contact at the time of the latest update.

Police facilities in Timure, Syaphrubesi, Rasuwagadhi and Mailung were also damaged.

Nine Armed Police personnel stationed at the Timure Border Outpost were also reported out of contact.

12 people rescued by helicopter

The Nepali Army has so far rescued 12 people from different flood-affected areas of Rasuwa by helicopter.

Four Army helicopters and eight helicopters operated by private companies have been deployed for rescue operations.

Because helicopters could not land in some areas, people were rescued using baskets.

An Army medical team has also started emergency treatment services at the No. 1 Military Training Centre in Trishuli.

Injured people rescued from the affected areas are being airlifted to Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu and taken to different hospitals for treatment.

Hospitals placed on alert

The Ministry of Health has activated the Health Emergency Operation Centre and placed health facilities and medical personnel on alert.

Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital has activated its ‘Disaster Code’, preparing doctors and other staff for a possible influx of casualties.

The hospital has also sent two doctors and one paramedic to the affected area.

Bir Hospital has placed its emergency department, ICUs, ventilators, blood supplies and medicines on standby. A triage system has been prepared to treat patients according to the severity of their injuries.

The National Trauma Centre has sent seven doctors with medicines to the flood-affected area.

Trishuli Hospital remains safe and operational, although two injured people have already arrived there from Tupche. Both suffered leg injuries and are in stable condition.

Flood moves downstream

After devastating Rasuwa, the flood moved downstream through the Trishuli River into Nuwakot and Dhading and towards Chitwan.

In Nuwakot, the flood caused significant damage around Dhunge Bazaar in Bidur Municipality-1, as well as other riverside areas.

In Dhading, the Furke Khola bridge connecting the district headquarters with the Prithvi Highway was swept away. The Keurini-Fosretar bridge, an alternative route to Dhadingbesi, was also washed away.

Authorities have warned people living along the riverbanks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan to move to safer locations.

The flood has also reached areas around Chitwan, with authorities urging people to remain alert.

14 hydropower projects affected

The flood has affected 14 hydropower projects, including nine operational projects and five under construction.

According to preliminary figures from the Nepal Electricity Authority, the affected projects have a combined capacity of 748 MW.

Nine operational projects with a combined capacity of 354 MW and five under-construction projects with a combined capacity of 394 MW have been affected.

Earlier figures from the Energy Ministry showed that 431.1 MW of electricity had gone out of the system due to flood damage.

Affected projects include Rasuwagadhi, Chilime, Langtang, Upper Trishuli-3A, Trishuli and Devighat, among others.

The authority said the full extent of damage to dams, powerhouses, access roads, transmission structures and other infrastructure will only be known after detailed field assessments.

Government steps up response

Prime Minister Balendra Shah has convened emergency meetings to coordinate search, rescue and relief operations.

The Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have been mobilised, with additional personnel sent from other districts.

Private helicopters have also been kept on standby, while those involved in emergency rescue operations do not need separate permission to fly.

The government has instructed chief district officers to move people from vulnerable downstream areas to safer locations and is continuing to issue warnings through calls and SMS.

President Ram Chandra Paudel has also called on the government, security agencies, political parties, social organisations and citizens to intensify rescue and relief efforts.

The House of Representatives has suspended the scheduled direct question-and-answer session with the prime minister as the government focuses on the flood response.

Search, rescue and relief operations remain underway, while authorities continue efforts to establish the number of missing people and assess the scale of damage.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa directs party leaders and cadres to mobilize in flood rescue efforts

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has said the situation has turned serious and worrying due to the flood in Rasuwa, and has urged high alert in riverbank and surrounding areas.

Through social media on Wednesday, he urged residents living along the lower reaches and surrounding areas of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers to stay safe.

President Thapa requested the government to mobilize the entire state machinery during this disaster and coordinate with governments at all levels to focus on rescue and relief.

“The situation has turned serious and worrying due to the unexpected and sudden major flood in Rasuwa. In this disaster situation, I urge high alert and safety in the lower riverbank and surrounding areas of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers,” he said.

Thapa said the Nepali Congress stands in full support and cooperation with the government’s efforts in disaster management.

He appealed to all Congress committees, and particularly to the leadership and members in districts including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan, to immediately mobilize for rescue and relief work.

“I appeal to move families living in riverbank areas to safe locations, and to immediately mobilize and help with rescue and relief work,” President Thapa said.

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, August 26

A sudden and massive flood swept through Timure Bazaar in Rasuwa on Wednesday morning, leaving residents and government employees scrambling for safety as communication with several people remains cut off.

Rajendra Dhungana, chief of the Timure Customs Office, said the flood struck between 8:30 and 8:45 am while he and other employees were at the office.

Dhungana said the incident initially felt like an earthquake.

“We were at the Timure Customs Office. I had already reached the office. Suddenly, we felt as if there was an earthquake and everyone panicked,” he said.

“When we came outside, there was a huge rumbling sound. Before we could even think about what was happening, we saw the flood coming down from above like a volcanic eruption.”

Employees scramble to escape

Dhungana said the flood quickly approached the customs office, prompting employees to run for safety.

“The flood had already reached close to the office. We screamed and ran, telling everyone to get out,” he said.

Some employees managed to escape, but others did not have enough time, according to Dhungana.

“Some of our colleagues managed to get out, while others could not. Most of the people in the market could not escape,” he said.

The Timure Customs Office itself is located in Timure Bazaar.

“Nothing is left now. There were around 30 to 40 people at our office. Some are in contact, while we have not been able to reach others. No one’s phone is connecting at the moment,” Dhungana said.

Around 40-50 people sheltering in the forest

Dhungana said only around 15 to 20 employees have been able to maintain contact with one another.

“When I try to contact someone, their phone does not connect. Perhaps that is why mine also does not connect. Only around 15 to 20 of us are in contact with each other. We do not know where the others are,” he said.

The group has taken shelter in a forested area above the market.

“We are currently staying safely in the forest above the market. We have not met any rescue teams yet,” Dhungana said.

Although the water level in the river has now decreased, returning to the market to search for missing people is not possible, he said.

“The amount of water in the river has decreased now, but it is impossible for us to go back down to the market and search for others because everything has been completely devastated,” he said.

‘Our focus is on finding our colleagues’

Dhungana said the employees and some local residents who managed to escape are staying together.

“There is no possibility of us going out ourselves to conduct rescue or search operations. The employees we have found and some local villagers are all staying together. There are around 40 to 50 people in the group,” he said.

He said they have little information about what has happened further upstream.

“Nothing has been spared in Timure Bazaar. We do not know what happened further up or what the situation is there. Right now, our focus is simply on staying safe and trying to find our colleagues,” Dhungana said.

The government has mobilised the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police for search, rescue and relief operations following the flood. Two Nepal Army helicopters with medical teams have also been sent towards the affected areas, while private helicopters have been kept on standby.

“The flood has not reached the area where the cable car operates. However, since the water level could rise further, we have suspended the cable car service for safety reasons,” he said.

Vehicles travelling along the Prithvi Highway have also been halted due to the flood.

title.rendered: Flood leaves parts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot cut off

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, August 26

A massive flood originating from China has caused extensive damage in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, sweeping away settlements along the Bhotekoshi River and leaving many residents out of contact.

The extent of the damage is yet to be confirmed, with authorities currently unable to establish contact with people in several areas.

Several local levels, including Gosaikunda Rural Municipality in Rasuwa, have reportedly been badly affected. Many residents are out of contact, while others are waiting to be rescued.

Dawa Sirdar Waiba, chairperson of Gosaikunda Rural Municipality-6 in Dhunche, said authorities have been unable to establish contact with anyone from Syafrubesi to Timure.

“We are here in Dhunche, the district headquarters of Rasuwa. We have no information about how much damage has been caused down there,” Waiba said.

“We have not been able to contact anyone from Syafrubesi Bazaar down to Timure. We cannot go there either.”

A Nepal Army helicopter had recently flown towards the affected area, he said, adding that authorities may receive more information after it returns.

Communication cut off in affected areas

Waiba said there were reports that the flood had reached Syafrubesi Bazaar, but authorities had not yet been able to verify the situation.

“There is a rumour that the flood has reached Syafrubesi Bazaar,” he said. “We do not know why those below have lost contact. It could be because telephone towers have been damaged, or there could be another problem. We cannot say for certain at this point.”

He said further information would become available once rescue personnel reach the affected areas.

Meanwhile, the government has mobilised the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police for search, rescue and relief operations.

Two Nepal Army helicopters, along with medical teams, have been deployed towards the affected areas, while private helicopter companies have also been asked to keep aircraft on standby.

Authorities have urged residents in downstream and other high-risk areas to move to safer locations.

title.rendered: Timure devastated by massive flood, residents stranded on hillsides

content.rendered:
Rasuwa, August 26

A massive flood originating from China has caused extensive damage in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, with the Bhotekoshi River sweeping away settlements along its banks.

The full extent of the damage is yet to be ascertained.

A ward member of Gosaikunda Rural Municipality-2, Pema Dorje Ghale, said many residents in Timure are currently waiting to be rescued.

According to Ghale, the flood struck Timure at around 8:30 am with a loud rumbling sound, leaving residents with little time to respond.

“The flood came with a huge sound at around 8:30 in the morning. Before we could even think about what was happening, everything was devastated. There is nothing left of Timure Bazaar. The flood has destroyed everything,” Ghale said.

He said authorities currently have no clear information on the number of houses swept away or people who may be missing.

“There were probably more than 100 houses in Timure alone. Looking at the sound and the flood coming from above, it seems that nothing has been spared,” he said.

Residents stranded on hillside

Ghale said residents who managed to escape have taken shelter on higher ground.

“We have come up to the hillside and are staying here. We ran for our lives in whatever condition we were in,” he said.

He said residents, including young children, are now facing a shortage of food and basic necessities.

“What will we feed the small children? How will we keep them safe? We have nothing. We are surviving by drinking the floodwater,” Ghale said.

He said helicopters have been seen flying over the area, but rescue teams have yet to reach the stranded residents.

“We are waiting for rescue. Helicopters have been flying overhead, but they have not reached us yet,” Ghale said.

Ghale urged government agencies to establish contact with residents stranded in Timure and immediately arrange rescue operations.

“I am Pema Dorje Ghale, ward member of Gosaikunda Rural Municipality-2. If government agencies contact us and arrange our rescue, it would provide great relief,” he said.

The government has already mobilised security forces and emergency response teams for search, rescue and relief operations in the flood-affected areas.

title.rendered: Special meeting held as massive flood hits Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

A special meeting is underway at the Ministry of Home Affairs following a massive flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, as authorities step up search, rescue and relief operations in the affected areas.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority is also holding a meeting to assess the situation and coordinate the government’s response.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah has called a meeting of the National Council for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers to discuss further measures.

Two Army helicopters sent to affected areas

According to the Home Ministry, two Nepal Army helicopters equipped with medical teams have already been deployed to the affected areas for possible rescue and relief operations.

Private helicopter companies have also been asked to keep their aircraft on standby for search and rescue operations.

The government intensified its response after floods hit areas including Syafrubesi and Timure in Rasuwa on Wednesday morning.

Authorities have instructed the concerned Chief District Officers (CDOs) to relocate residents in high-risk and downstream areas to safer locations.

The government is also continuing to issue warnings to residents in other areas that could potentially be affected by the flood.

Travel warnings issued

Authorities have urged the public not to travel on several roads that could be affected by the flood.

People have been advised to avoid the Prithvi Highway, Galchhi–Nuwakot–Rasuwa–Syafrubesi road and Muglin–Narayangadh road until the situation becomes safer.

Nepal Police, the Armed Police Force, district administrations and other disaster-response mechanisms have been mobilised in the affected areas.

The Nepal Army has also intensified search and rescue operations, while the district-level disaster management authorities have been instructed to coordinate relief efforts.

The government is continuing to assess the extent of the damage and the need for additional rescue and relief resources.

title.rendered: Rasuwa flood damages hydropower plants and 220 kV substation, power supply disrupted

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

Flooding in Rasuwa on Wednesday has damaged several power plants and transmission structures of the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), affecting electricity supply in Rasuwa and surrounding areas, the authority said.

According to the NEA, the flood damaged the Rasuwagadhi, Chilime and Trishuli-3A hydropower plants, as well as the 220 kV substation at the Trishuli-3B hub. The Trishuli and Devighat hydropower plants and various distribution structures have also been affected.

The NEA said electricity supply has been disrupted in some areas after damage to infrastructure related to power generation, transmission and distribution. It said it is making every possible effort to restore regular supply and urged consumers to remain patient until the service is restored.

Preliminary information indicates that the flood has also caused significant damage to physical infrastructure, including houses, roads and bridges. A detailed assessment of the damage is currently underway.

The NEA has urged all relevant agencies to mobilise immediately and effectively for rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts in the affected areas.

As the risk of flooding remains, the authority has urged members of the public and NEA employees in river and stream corridors, riverbank areas and other vulnerable locations to remain highly alert. It has also urged people not to believe unverified reports or rumours and to rely only on official information.

Rasuwa has previously suffered major damage to hydropower projects and transmission infrastructure due to floods. The latest flooding has again affected energy infrastructure, raising concerns about disruptions across the power generation, transmission and distribution system.

content.rendered:

Sahan has scored 1,462 runs in 103 T20 matches and has also taken 54 wickets. He has previously won the Lanka Premier League title.

Sahan has played 5 ODIs and one T20I for Sri Lanka. He made his ODI debut in July 2023 against the West Indies in the World Cup Qualifier held in Harare. He has also captained Sri Lanka ‘A’.

He recently played a key role in helping Galle Gladiators win the Lanka Premier League title, scoring 240 runs across all 11 matches at a strike rate above 147 during their maiden LPL triumph.

Kathmandu Gorkhas’ cricket director, Sharad Veshawkar, said Sahan is a spirited player carrying a winning mentality, capable of consistent performances, and has delivered match-winning displays for Galle Gladiators and Sri Lanka ‘A’ even under pressure by sticking to the game plan. He said he is confident Sahan’s temperament and clarity of mindset will benefit the team’s batting lineup, and that his batting, bowling, and fielding abilities could prove valuable for Kathmandu Gorkhas.

Sahan has played in Nepal before, he featured for Pokhara Rhinos in the 2021 Everest Premier League.

title.rendered: Prophet Muhammad’s birthday being observed, public holiday declared for Muslim community

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

The 1,501st birth anniversary of Prophet Muhammad, the final prophet of Islam, is being observed today with various programmes across the country.

Known as the messenger of Islam, Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, and later moved to Medina. The Islamic Hijri calendar began 53 years after his birth, and the current year is 1448 in the Hijri calendar.

Mecca and Medina are considered among the holiest places in Islam. According to Islamic belief, the Quran was revealed to Prophet Muhammad while he was delivering his teachings. Following the revelation of the Quran, Mecca and Medina gradually became the principal pilgrimage centres of Islam.

Muslims traditionally seek to undertake the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca at least once in their lifetime if they are able to do so. The birth anniversary of Prophet Muhammad is observed to commemorate his teachings and contribution to Islam.

Various programmes, including rallies and gatherings, are being organised to mark the occasion. Special programmes are being held at the Nepali Jame Mosque, Kashmiri Jame Mosque and other locations.

The government has declared a public holiday today for the Muslim community on the occasion of Prophet Muhammad’s birth anniversary.

The Ministry of Home Affairs announced the holiday through a notice issued on Tuesday.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah orders emergency response as flood hits Rasuwa, Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

Prime Minister Balen Shah has directed authorities to step up rescue and relief operations following flooding in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, with security forces and emergency response teams being mobilised in affected areas.

In a statement on Wednesday, Shah said the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force (APF) and Nepal Police have been deployed for rescue and relief operations. Additional personnel from other districts have also been moved towards the affected areas.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has been activated to coordinate the response, while medical teams, Nepal Scouts and the Nepal Red Cross Society are being mobilised.

Shah said additional ambulances and medical personnel are also being sent to the affected areas.

Residents in downstream areas ordered to evacuate

The prime minister said Chief District Officers (CDOs) have been instructed to immediately relocate residents living in downstream areas to safer locations.

Authorities have also been asked to alert residents through SMS and phone calls and provide information about designated safe areas.

“All residents in downstream areas have been asked to move to safe locations immediately,” Shah said.

Helicopters kept on standby

Shah said all available helicopters have been instructed to remain on standby for possible rescue and relief operations.

Private helicopter companies have also been informed to keep their helicopters ready in case they are required for emergency operations.

A high-level meeting has been called to decide on further measures as the situation develops, according to Shah.

He urged residents to remain in safe locations and avoid unnecessary movement.

“If you are unable to contact your relatives, please wait for rescue updates from the concerned authorities,” Shah said.

The government has also provided 1234 as a contact number for information related to the disaster and relief operations.

title.rendered: Road project remains incomplete 10 years after a 2-year deadline

content.rendered:
Baglung, August 26

How long should it take to blacktop a road? The answer would normally be two or three years at most. However, 10 years after the contract was signed to blacktop the Baglung headquarters section of the Mid-Hill Pushpalal Highway, the work remains incomplete.

The authorities are preparing to award a new contract for the Baglung headquarters section. The process for a new contract has begun after the agreement with Bharat/Siddhisai JV, which was signed to complete the blacktopping work within two years, was terminated.

Ujjwal Sharma, information officer at the Mid-Hill Pushpalal Highway Project Office in Parbat, said the process of awarding a new contract had begun after the previous contract was terminated on January 1. The contractor failed to complete the work despite receiving five extensions, and the contract was subsequently terminated, with the process of recovering the amount due from the contractor also initiated.

The project office has sent documents to the Ministry of Finance through the National Planning Commission for evaluation of the new contract, a cost-estimate report and confirmation of funding. The road section has deteriorated further in recent days. Travellers using the road have been suffering from mud during the monsoon and dust during the dry season.

The condition of the road has continued to deteriorate since the contract was terminated, while some of the completed infrastructure has also been damaged.

“Based on a study of the work completed by the previous contractor and the additional infrastructure that needs to be included in the new contract, we have proposed around Rs 250 million to the Ministry of Finance for funding,” said engineer Sharma.

The study report shows that Rs 93.6 million needs to be recovered from the contractor whose contract was terminated.

“We are preparing to invite a new tender soon. It will probably be completed within four months,” Sharma said.

The 13-kilometre Baglung-Bihun section was contracted to Bharat/Siddhisai on January 28, 2017, for Rs 436.5 million, with a deadline of two years. The contractor has already received Rs 340.3 million in payments. The road has deteriorated further due to the monsoon, while potholes have developed in sections that have already been blacktopped.

title.rendered: RSP drafting Rabi’s Madhesh tour schedule, to hold conventions in 7 districts and the province

content.rendered:
Even after completing its first general convention, the RSP still has not held its Madhesh convention. To address this, party leaders gathered at party headquarters in Chamati on Tuesday to work out convention dates for 7 districts of Madhesh and a visit schedule for Chairman Rabi Lamichhane to those districts.

Co-general secretary Purushottam Yadav coordinated the effort. According to party sources, although it was said on Tuesday that the district conventions and the chairman’s travel plans would be finalized, the date has not yet been made public.

Because of disputes over party membership and representation, the general conventions of Madhesh’s 7 districts and its provincial committee could not be held before the RSP plunged into its central general convention.

At that time, a convention was held in Parsa, forming a new committee under Hari Panta’s leadership. However, district conventions could not be held in Bara, Rautahat, Sarlahi, Mahottari, Dhanusha, Siraha, and Saptari.

Leaders have cited factionalism in leadership selection and interference by lawmakers as reasons the conventions could not take place in these districts. They also say tension between the party’s old cadres and those who joined just before the elections, competing for leadership, contributed to the postponements.

Madhesh Province Chairman Tapeshwar Yadav says managing the situation has been difficult due to the surge of people joining the RSP from other parties before the elections. He said that people who once competed against each other in different parties are now in the same party, and rivalry over leadership has resulted from members of other parties joining and having to contest one another.

The competition for leadership positions reportedly escalated to physical altercations in some places. According to Provincial Chairman Yadav, conventions could not be held in 10 to 15 of Madhesh’s 136 local units, and ad hoc committees have been formed in those places instead.

Since Madhesh holds a large share of the population, party central leadership has taken the initiative after conventions failed to take place there. Chairman Rabi Lamichhane himself has said he will visit the districts of Madhesh Province to build an environment conducive to holding conventions.

Two days ago, while training central members, Chairman Lamichhane said he would go to Madhesh for the conventions. He said he is preparing to travel to Madhesh himself, within a week to ten days or two weeks, and that conventions need to be held there.

The party has assigned co-general secretary Hari Dhakal the responsibility of studying the disputes in places where conventions could not be held and submitting a report. Dhakal said he has been unable to focus on Madhesh due to family difficulties and work in his own constituency.

Madhesh leaders say a clear factional divide within the party is also a reason conventions have not been held smoothly there. According to one provincial-level leader from Madhesh, party ranks are polarized between the party chairman and Prime Minister Balen Shah’s camp.

According to Provincial Chairman Yadav, since having someone from Madhesh study the disputed areas could raise questions, the party assigned the responsibility to an outsider instead. He said giving the responsibility to a Madhesh native could invite controversy, whereas the party believes a report from an outside person is less likely to create problems.

The Madhesh convention has also been discussed in connection with the upcoming provincial and local-level elections. One Madhesh lawmaker said that cadres holding the mistaken belief that whoever leads the local-unit, municipal, district, and provincial structures will distribute election tickets is behind the friction seen around the conventions.

He said cadres have not been made to understand that the leadership sitting on party committees does not decide ticket distribution, the party has set up a “candidate club,” and cadres are not aware that becoming a candidate requires completing a set procedure. He added that many cadres believe that municipal, district and provincial chairs are the ones distributing tickets, which is the mindset that has made holding conventions difficult.

The RSP has opened applications, from August 17, for those wishing to become candidates at the rural municipality level. Registering with the candidate club is the first step in the selection process to become a candidate.

The RSP has devised a system under which candidates are chosen only after evaluating a person’s capability, organizational activity, public image, qualifications, and performance in a candidate academy presentation.

Chairman Lamichhane has reiterated that candidate selection cannot happen outside this system. He told central members two days ago that during the House of Representatives election, adjustments meant the party’s own selection system could not be fully implemented, and he urged party ranks not to believe anyone who promises to make them a local-level candidate.

Selecting representatives for the first general convention held in Chitwan proved most difficult in Madhesh. Because Madhesh’s representation could not be finalized in time, the voting process at the general convention could not start on schedule.

The general convention’s total number of representatives was reported at 4,211. It later emerged that the final representative count from Madhesh, the most disputed region, stood at 540.

According to Madhesh leaders, efforts are underway, as far as possible, to select leadership by consensus. Last week, some Madhesh leaders held internal discussions on matters that needed to be settled at both the provincial and district levels.

According to one leader, discussions on some names for potentially widely acceptable candidates took place from the provincial down to the district level.

Madhesh leaders say a clear factional divide within the party is also behind the difficulty in holding conventions smoothly there. According to one provincial-level Madhesh leader, party ranks are polarized between the party chairman and Prime Minister Balen Shah’s camp.

That leader claims that of Madhesh’s 39 lawmakers, 32 are close to Prime Minister Balen, and that at conventions, lawmakers naturally try to push forward those close to them.

The inability to hold Madhesh’s conventions even after scheduling dates has also been attributed to lawmakers exerting excessive influence. Leaders say disputes arose, and the convention process was disrupted, because of attempts to bring favored individuals into party structures.

Provincial Chairman Yadav sees the possibility of consensus-based leadership selection in some places but considers it unlikely in most. He said that pursuing consensus can create the appearance of favoritism toward a particular person, making an election the most appropriate method.

He said voting is ultimately the last resort, since it removes any allegation of who made whom leader. Provincial Chairman Yadav said he himself wishes to continue in the same post, adding that he did not contest at the general convention in order to continue as provincial chairman.

One Madhesh lawmaker said that since Chairman Lamichhane’s travel dates to Madhesh have not been finalized, and since co-general secretary Dhakal, tasked with studying the disputed areas, has not yet begun his work, it will be difficult to start the convention process soon. With festival season approaching, the lawmaker said the Madhesh convention will likely only be possible around mid-November to mid-December.

title.rendered: Flash flood from Tibet damages settlements in Rasuwa, reaches Nuwakot

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

A sudden flash flood entering Nepal from the Tibetan side has caused significant damage to settlements in the Timure area of Rasuwa, with authorities warning communities downstream along the Trishuli River to remain alert.

According to the Rasuwa District Police Office, a large volume of water suddenly entered the area at around 9 am on Wednesday, causing damage to settlements in Timure.

Police said details of the extent of the damage are still being assessed.

The Flood Forecasting Division has also urged people living along the Trishuli River downstream to remain on high alert following the sudden rise in water levels. Authorities have extended the warning downstream as far as Muglin.

Flood reaches Nuwakot

The flood has also reached Nuwakot, according to the District Administration Office.

Rupesh Prasad Nepal, information officer at the District Administration Office in Nuwakot, said authorities were currently unable to provide details of any damage caused by the flood.

Residents living along riverbanks have been urged to remain vigilant and move to safer locations if necessary.

A meeting of the District Coordination Committee is underway to prepare for possible rescue and emergency response operations.

Authorities have urged people living along the Trishuli River corridor to remain alert as the water level could rise suddenly.

title.rendered: Foreign tourist arrivals through Nepal’s western border increase

content.rendered:
Kanchanpur, August 26

The number of foreign tourists entering Nepal through the Gaddachowki border point in Kanchanpur has been increasing.

According to the Immigration Office, Gaddachowki, the number of tourists entering Nepal through the border point has risen in recent years.

According to the office, 1,753 foreign tourists entered Nepal through the border point in the last fiscal year. During the same period, the government collected Rs 10,518,119 in revenue, said information officer Navaraj Adhikari Bhatt. He said 1,534 tourists exited Nepal through the same border point.

Office data shows that 542 foreign tourists entered Nepal through Gaddachowki in 2022. The number increased to 983 in 2023 and 1,154 in 2024.

Although Sudurpaschim Province has significant tourism potential, tourists entering Nepal through the western border point often travel to cities such as Kathmandu and Pokhara.

Tourism entrepreneurs say that despite major tourist destinations such as Khaptad, Badimalika, Ramaroshan and Shuklaphanta National Park in Sudurpaschim, a lack of infrastructure and inadequate promotion has resulted in tourists entering through Gaddachowki travelling elsewhere.

“Gaddachowki is a major entry point for foreign tourists, and tourist cities in India are also nearby,” said tourism entrepreneur Jagadish Chandra Bhatt. “A tourism information desk should be established at the border point itself.”

He said arrangements should be made to provide tourists arriving through the border with information about tourist destinations in Sudurpaschim and other parts of Nepal through an information centre. He also stressed the need for coordination between the private sector and government to promote tourism.

Dinesh Malla, president of the Kanchanpur Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said tourists continue to travel elsewhere despite the tourism potential of Sudurpaschim because of inadequate infrastructure development and promotion.

“We lack convenient infrastructure and other facilities to reach the attractive destinations we have,” he said. “The tourist destinations here should be promoted and an environment should be created to encourage tourists to stay here for at least one night.”

title.rendered: Irrigation being restored via pipes in Jajarkot after flood destroys canal

content.rendered:
Jajarkot, August 26

Farmers of Roli Jiula in Nalgad Municipality-10, who faced difficulties after a flood in the Taksugad stream destroyed an irrigation canal, are set to receive immediate relief. With paddy crops at risk due to the lack of irrigation, the Drinking Water and Irrigation Office, Jajarkot, has resolved the problem by temporarily providing 500 meters of pipe.

The flood that struck the Taksugad stream, located between Nalgad Municipality wards 10 and 11, on August 14, completely destroyed the irrigation canal. The flood also damaged the road under the Bheri Corridor and swept away four houses entirely. After the canal was destroyed, irrigating the paddy planted in Roli Jiula became a problem.

Local farmers had been demanding an immediate alternative arrangement, warning that without timely irrigation, the paddy crop would dry up and yields would be severely affected. Since rebuilding the damaged canal right away was not feasible, providing water temporarily through pipes was proposed as an alternative.

Under the direction of Nalgad Municipality’s mayor, Dambar Rawat, and deputy mayor, Devaka Lamichhane, the municipality had prepared a cost estimate for the necessary structure after the canal was damaged. It then took the initiative to secure pipes through the Drinking Water, Irrigation and Energy Development Office.

Following the municipality’s initiative, the Drinking Water and Irrigation Office, Jajarkot, provided 500 meters of 110mm pipe. Preparations are underway to use this pipe as an alternative to the damaged canal to bring irrigation water to Roli Jiula.

According to the municipality, pipe installation will begin from Wednesday. Once installed, farmers are expected to receive irrigation facilities for the time being, providing relief for the paddy crop. The plan is to run irrigation through the pipes until the canal can be permanently rebuilt.

With the flood having damaged the canal as well as the road and homes, local residents’ daily lives have been affected. The flood in the Taksugad stream also damaged the road under the Bheri Corridor, causing transportation problems. Temporary reconstruction work on the flood-damaged structures has been completed.

The collapse of the irrigation canal has had its biggest impact on agriculture. Since Roli Jiula is an important agricultural area for Nalgad-10, urgent irrigation arrangements were needed to protect the paddy crop there. With the risk of major losses growing as farmers were unable to get water to their crops, the municipality took the initiative to arrange pipes as a temporary solution.

The municipality has also stated that while the pipes address the immediate problem, rebuilding the damaged irrigation canal is necessary in the long run. Preparations are underway to assess other flood-damaged structures and proceed with reconstruction and repair work in phases. Onlinekhabar had earlier reported on the problems caused by the lack of irrigation facilities.

title.rendered: DDC’s ghee export push faces questions over domestic supply and farmer payments

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

The ghee export drive of the state-owned Dairy Development Corporation (DDC) has gained momentum after the corporation sent its first 500-kilogram consignment to Dubai last Friday.

The shipment, sent via a Nepal Airlines flight, was presented as an important step in taking a Nepali dairy brand to international markets.

DDC now plans to expand its ghee export market to Japan, South Korea and Tibet in China, with the corporation saying it has already reached a commercial agreement to export 50,000 kilograms, or 50 tonnes, of ghee this year.

During a meeting of the House of Representatives on August 18, Agriculture, Forest and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary said sales of DDC dairy products had increased by 35 percent and that preparations were also underway to export DDC ghee to China.

DDC General Manager Dr Sharan Pandey said the corporation has signed an agreement with private company Rato Ra Chandra Surya International Pvt Ltd for the annual export of 50 tonnes of ghee.

He said exports to Japan, South Korea and Tibet are expected to begin from November.

“We have started by sending 500 kilograms of ghee to Dubai. An agreement has been reached to export 50,000 kilograms annually,” Pandey said on the day of the Dubai shipment.

The corporation plans to increase the volume of ghee export as domestic production grows.

However, behind the enthusiasm surrounding the export is a more complicated picture. DDC is currently under pressure to meet domestic demand while its stocks are gradually declining.

Ghee export begins during Nepal’s lean milk season

Milk production in Nepal follows a seasonal cycle commonly divided into the flush season and lean season.

Milk production generally rises from October to February, when weather conditions and the availability of green fodder are favourable. This is known as the flush season. Production falls from March to September during the warmer and drier months, creating the lean season.

Nepal is currently approaching the end of the lean season, when milk production is at its lowest.

DDC traditionally processes surplus milk collected during the six-month flush season into butter and milk powder and stores these products for use during the lean season.

DDC Information Officer Nilkantha Gautam described the Dubai shipment as a market test rather than a major expansion of its international business.

“The 500 kilograms we have sent is only a test in the international market,” Gautam said. “Demand for our ghee is already so high in the domestic market that our existing stock is expected to reach zero by October.”

Figures presented by Agriculture Minister Chaudhary also indicate that DDC’s stocks are limited. As of August 17, the corporation had around 150 tonnes of milk powder and 130 tonnes of butter worth approximately Rs 240 million.

Since butter contains around 20 percent moisture, DDC says only about 80 percent becomes pure ghee after clarification. Based on the current butter stock, this translates to roughly 100 tonnes of ghee.

With major festivals such as Dashain, Tihar and Chhath approaching, domestic demand for ghee is expected to rise significantly.

This raises questions over whether DDC can simultaneously meet domestic demand and sustain its planned ghee export of 50 tonnes annually to Dubai, Japan and South Korea.

DDC suspends plans for new outlets

The pressure on supply is also reflected in DDC’s decision to suspend plans to open new outlets.

The corporation had planned to open 30 new service counters across the country to clear old stocks and expand its market. However, after opening eight outlets, it has now suspended further expansion until further notice.

“We have stopped opening outlets for now because we have started facing a shortage of raw materials,” Gautam said. “There is no shortage of ghee at outlets across the country at present, but it will become difficult for us unless milk collection increases.”

The decision has raised questions about DDC’s simultaneous efforts to explore foreign markets while struggling to guarantee a consistent supply in the domestic market.

Gautam, however, said the Dubai shipment should not be interpreted as DDC aggressively pursuing international markets.

“DDC itself is not looking for foreign markets. A private exporter, Rato Ra Chandra Surya International, is taking the ghee from Nepal to test it in the market there,” he said.

He said the response from foreign consumers and Nepalis living abroad would determine whether demand develops.

Even if substantial foreign demand emerges, DDC currently lacks the capacity to meet it, according to Gautam.

“We are currently collecting only around 40,000 to 50,000 litres of milk daily across the country,” he said. “If collection from farmers does not increase, we will not be in a position to meet foreign demand. Our first priority will always be the domestic market and consumers here.”

Ghee export depends on farmers

Another major challenge for DDC’s ghee export ambitions lies at the foundation of its supply chain: dairy farmers.

DDC collects milk from around 1,200 dairy cooperatives across 45 districts. However, farmers supplying milk to the corporation have repeatedly complained about delayed payments.

DDC’s outstanding payments to farmers had previously reached around Rs 900 million. According to Gautam, the amount has now fallen to around Rs 450 million, but some farmers are still waiting for payments dating back three months.

Farmers argue that it is difficult for a corporation to build a sustainable export business when it cannot pay producers on time.

Delayed payments can force farmers to sell their cattle or reconsider dairy production, they say.

“If we stop producing milk, DDC’s machines alone cannot make ghee,” farmers have said.

Following Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s promotion of DDC products on social media and a subsequent increase in consumer interest, the corporation has begun selling its old stock and using the proceeds to clear outstanding payments to farmers.

But sustaining ghee export in the long term will depend on strengthening the domestic supply chain, particularly by ensuring farmers receive fair prices and timely payments.

Higher and more reliable payments could encourage farmers to increase production, creating the supply needed to support exports to markets such as Japan and South Korea.

Ghee export is a promising start, but not yet a breakthrough

DDC produces a wide range of dairy products, including fresh milk, standard milk, cow milk, yak cheese, yoghurt, buttermilk, ice cream and rasbari.

The corporation has also built consumer trust in the quality of its products, giving it an existing advantage as it explores opportunities among Nepali communities overseas.

DDC had exported small quantities of ghee and butter to Japan and Tibet five to seven years ago, but those efforts were not sustained.

The latest 500-kilogram shipment to Dubai is therefore a modest commercial beginning rather than a major breakthrough.

The ghee export initiative could eventually provide DDC with an opportunity to expand its international market and strengthen the value chain for Nepal’s dairy sector.

For that to happen, however, the corporation will first need to ensure adequate supplies for the domestic market, improve milk collection and settle farmers’ outstanding payments.

Until consumers at home can reliably find DDC ghee, farmers receive timely payment for their milk and the corporation substantially increases its milk collection capacity, the promise of large-scale ghee export risks remaining more publicity than a sustainable business strategy.

title.rendered: Bishwa Prakash sees little chance of interim order halting Nepali Congress convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

Nepali Congress Vice-President Bishwa Prakash Sharma has said he sees little possibility of the Supreme Court issuing an interim order to halt the party’s 15th general convention.

In a video message issued on Wednesday, Sharma outlined four main reasons why he believes an interim order is unlikely to stop the ongoing convention process.

Addressing concerns among party leaders and cadres following the filing of a petition at the Supreme Court, Sharma said the mere filing of a petition does not mean the court will necessarily issue an interim order.

His first argument was that the date for the general convention was not fixed as a new decision following the Supreme Court’s decision to grant leave for a review.

“The decision was taken by the Central Working Committee meeting held on March 25, following the election on March 5. This date was also mentioned in the court’s April 17 ruling,” Sharma said.

As his second reason, Sharma distinguished between filing a writ petition or supplementary petition and securing an interim order.

“Being in case review is one thing, while getting an interim order sought in the petition is another,” he said. “The court will have to consider whether simply having a case under review provides sufficient grounds for an interim order.”

Sharma said the court would also consider the right of dissenting leaders to participate in the general convention while respecting its previous order.

He pointed out that the scheduled date for ward-level conventions had already been postponed by 22 days, from August 18, providing additional time for dialogue, consensus-building and a possible resolution.

“Therefore, there is absolutely no situation where an interim order must be issued because someone is facing irreparable loss,” he said.

Nepali Congress term deadline

Sharma’s fourth argument concerns the constitutional and legal deadline for the party’s organisational terms.

He said the terms of the Nepali Congress Central Working Committee and all other party committees will expire simultaneously by December.

“Beyond that, neither the party statute nor the Constitution allows us to extend the term even by a single day,” he said.

Sharma said some may believe the party could extend its term by another six months after December, but argued that the Congress statute does not contain such a provision.

Article 269(4)(b) of the Constitution requires political parties to provide in their statutes for elections to federal and provincial-level office-bearers at least once every five years. It also allows for an additional six-month period in exceptional circumstances if elections cannot be held within five years.

Section 16 of the Political Parties Act, 2017 also allows a party to complete its general convention within an additional six months if such a provision exists in its statute and the Election Commission is informed, Sharma said.

However, he maintained that the Nepali Congress statute does not contain a provision allowing an additional six months after the five-year term.

According to Sharma, the party statute endorsed by the General Convention in 2018 states that the term of office-bearers and members at all levels is four years, with the Central Working Committee authorised to extend the term by up to one year in exceptional circumstances after stating the reasons.

The 14th general convention was held in December 2021. Sharma said both the original four-year term and the additional one-year extension will expire this December.

He said this constitutional and statutory deadline would be closely examined by the Supreme Court while deciding whether to issue an interim order.

Calls for internal dialogue

Sharma said resolving internal disputes within the party and selecting its leadership are ultimately matters for the party’s general convention representatives.

Addressing leaders who disagree with the ongoing convention process, he said the party does not oppose their right to approach the courts.

However, he urged them to seek solutions to internal party disputes through dialogue and consensus within the party rather than repeatedly turning to the courts.

“Let us take off the glasses of ego, sit together in the party office and find a solution,” Sharma said. “We are waiting with an open heart to move forward together.”

title.rendered: The Nepali scientist using mathematics to understand how diseases spread

content.rendered:
Before he was modelling viruses on computers in the United States, Dr Naveen Vaidya was a boy in Sindhuli studying under the faint light of a kerosene lamp.

His childhood was marked by loss. His father, a government employee, died when Vaidya was still young, leaving his mother as the family’s only support. She worked in the fields and took on small jobs to educate her children.

Every day, Vaidya walked for about an hour, up and down the hills, to reach school. At home, while his mother worked from morning until evening, he immersed himself in his studies.

The hardships, however, did not stop him. They pushed him forward.

Today, Vaidya is a professor at San Diego State University (SDSU) in the United States, where he uses mathematics to understand how diseases spread. His research has examined viruses including HIV, hepatitis and Covid-19, as well as diseases such as malaria, rabies, dengue and lumpy skin disease using mathematical models.

But his work has never been limited to laboratories in the US.

For years, Vaidya has worked to connect Nepal’s students and researchers with international scientific networks. He has helped establish research partnerships between Nepali institutions and SDSU, organised international programmes in Nepal and supported students pursuing PhDs and research careers.

His journey from a remote village in Sindhuli to the laboratories of North America began with a mother who refused to let hardship determine her children’s future.

A childhood shaped by loss

Dr Naveen Vaidya was born in Jhangajholi village of Ratmata in Sindhuli, surrounded by green forests, the Sunkoshi River and hills rising around the settlement.

His family struggled financially.

His father worked as an ordinary government employee but died while Vaidya was still a child. Losing his father meant growing up without the person whose hand he had once hoped to hold.

His mother became the family’s sole source of support.

She worked in the fields and took on whatever small jobs she could to keep the family going and ensure her children could study.

For Vaidya, education became a way forward.

He completed his early schooling in the village. The memory of reading books in a dim room filled with smoke from a kerosene lamp has stayed with him.

Getting to school meant walking for an hour through difficult terrain. But rather than discouraging him, the difficulties strengthened his determination.

He eventually began producing excellent results at school, becoming a source of pride not only for his own village but for neighbouring communities as well.

From Kathmandu to the world

After completing school, Naveen Vaidya moved to Kathmandu with bigger ambitions.

For someone from his village, the capital was another world. Surviving there was not easy, but he worked part-time while continuing his education.

He studied science at Patan Multiple Campus, completed his bachelor’s degree at Tri-Chandra College and earned a master’s degree in mathematics from Amrit Science Campus.

He also began teaching mathematics at schools and colleges in Kathmandu.

But he wanted to go further.

Vaidya realised that while Nepal provided a strong foundation in theoretical knowledge, pursuing research at an international level required opportunities that were difficult to find at home.

That ambition eventually took him abroad.

From Canada to the United States

Dr Naveen Vaidya enrolled at York University in Canada, where he pursued a master’s degree in industrial and applied mathematics before beginning his PhD.

His research focused on the mathematical modelling of membrane fusion between influenza viruses and human cells.

The research was distinctive enough to earn him York University’s prestigious Susan Mann Dissertation Award.

After completing his PhD, Vaidya went on to work at leading research institutions in the United States and Canada.

He completed postdoctoral research at Los Alamos National Laboratory and later became a fellow at the University of Western Research in Canada.

He then joined the University of Missouri-Kansas City as an assistant professor.

In 2017, he moved to San Diego State University, where he remains a professor.

Using mathematics to understand disease

Dr Naveen Vaidya studies disease from a different perspective.

He is not a doctor treating patients. He is a mathematician trying to understand what happens inside populations and bodies by turning disease processes into mathematical models.

His research has examined the dynamics of viruses including HIV, hepatitis and Covid-19.

He has also developed community-level mathematical models using data from Nepal to study diseases including Covid-19, malaria, rabies, dengue and lumpy skin disease.

For Vaidya, mathematical modelling is more than an academic exercise. It can provide important evidence for designing disease-control strategies.

His research has earned him four National Science Foundation grants, two Simons Foundation grants and more than 20 international research grants.

His work has appeared in more than 61 international journals, and he has delivered more than 125 research talks around the world, including keynote speeches.

Keeping Nepal in the equation

Despite building his career abroad, Dr Naveen Vaidya has remained closely connected to Nepal.

“Even though Nepal has limited resources and technology, its potential is unlimited. So wherever I am, I always think about contributing to the country,” he says.

That belief led to the 2019 CIMPA Summer School in Mathematical Biology in Nepal.

The programme was more than a short academic event.

Participants presented their work at the AMNS-2019 conference, while some went on to publish their research in prestigious journals. Others began long-term collaborations with scientists in the United States and Canada.

Perhaps most importantly, the programme helped strengthen cooperation between Tribhuvan University and San Diego State University.

The partnership eventually helped three students complete their PhDs under the supervision of Vaidya and Dr Kedarnath Upreti.

One of them, Dr Khagendra Adhikari, is now conducting collaborative research in Taiwan with support from a Taiwanese government scholarship.

Another eight students are currently pursuing PhDs at Tribhuvan University.

The collaboration also received funding from IMU’s Commission for Developing Countries (CDC), with each scholarship recipient receiving more than Rs 1.2 million in support.

During this period, the Nepal Health Research Council, the Central Department of Mathematics at Tribhuvan University and SDSU formally signed a research partnership.

It was an important step towards bringing mathematics into Nepal’s policy and public health discussions.

Building a scientific community

In 2023, Dr Naveen Vaidya and his colleagues established the Mathematical Biology Research Centre Nepal.

International programmes continued in the following years, including the SIMPA curriculum, AESIM School in Kathmandu and ICMB-2025 in Pokhara.

Researchers from 14 countries, including Nepal, took part in these programmes.

For Vaidya, the goal is not simply to bring international scientists to Nepal. It is to create a sustained scientific network in which Nepali researchers can collaborate, publish and develop opportunities beyond the country’s borders.

A weekly connection to Nepal

His connection with Nepal has also become part of his weekly routine.

“When it is 7am on Saturday in Nepal and Friday evening in San Diego, I join a Zoom meeting with my research group,” he says.

The meetings usually last two to three hours.

Researchers discuss ongoing work, exchange new ideas, debate recent findings and plan future projects.

Dr Naveen Vaidya has maintained these meetings for the past six years.

For Nepali students and researchers, the sessions offer direct exposure to international research practices. They also allow knowledge and skills to flow continuously between Nepal and its scientific diaspora.

Over time, the relationship has become more than a bridge between Nepal and the US. It has developed into a kind of living laboratory, where ideas can move freely despite borders and time zones.

Writing the mathematics of disease

Today, Dr Naveen Vaidya lives in the United States and works on the mathematics of disease.

But his story began thousands of kilometres away, in the dim light of a kerosene lamp in Sindhuli.

There was the loss of his father, the struggle of his mother, the long walks to school and the move from a village to Kathmandu. Then came the universities and laboratories of Canada and the United States.

Each stage added something to the scientist he would become.

Baidhya’s journey is a reminder that world-class scientific careers do not always begin in well-equipped laboratories. Sometimes they begin in ordinary villages, with limited resources, a determined parent and a child willing to keep studying.

And even after reaching the other side of the world, Vaidya has continued to look back—using the knowledge he has gained abroad to build opportunities for the next generation of researchers in Nepal

title.rendered: District committee urges PM Office to halt Barun River hydropower project

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

The District Coordination Committee (DCC) of Sankhuwasabha has urged the government not to grant permission for the construction of a hydropower project on the Barun River, citing concerns over religious significance, environmental impact and conservation of the protected area.

The committee has sent a letter to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers requesting that approval not be given for the 132 MW Lower Barun Khola Hydropower Project proposed at Syalshila in Bhotkhola Rural Municipality-4 of Sankhuwasabha.

DCC Chief Suman Shakya said the Barun River holds significant religious and cultural importance and needs to be protected.

The committee said Bhotkhola Rural Municipality’s 13th executive meeting had already decided to preserve the Barun River as a religious heritage site and oppose hydropower construction inside the Makalu-Barun National Park and Conservation Area.

Supporting the local government’s decision, the DCC has urged concerned authorities to follow the provisions of the National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act, 2029 and policies related to protected areas while considering approval for infrastructure projects.

According to the committee, Sankhuwasabha has the potential to generate around 6,000 MW of electricity from various rivers besides the Arun River. Around 75 MW has already been connected to the national transmission line, while projects with a combined capacity of around 3,576 MW are under development along the Arun River.

The committee warned that constructing the hydropower project on the Barun River could affect religious sentiments, the environment and the overall ecosystem of the region.

It has also requested the authorities to implement provisions under policies related to physical infrastructure development inside protected areas.

The Barun River is regarded as a site of religious and cultural importance by both Hindu and Buddhist communities. Locals associate several traditional beliefs with the river, while the annual Makar Mela held on January 15 along its banks serves as an important gathering point for residents from upper and lower regions of Bhotkhola.

Local residents have been demanding protection of the river, arguing that the hydropower project could alter its natural character and affect its religious significance.

Earlier too, locals had called for stopping hydropower development plans on the Barun River.

title.rendered: Yatri P-2: The making of a Nepali electric scooter

content.rendered:
An electric scooter does not begin its journey on an assembly line. It starts with a sketch.

For Nepal’s Yatri, the development of its latest electric scooter, the Yatri P-2, began in much the same way. More than two years of research, design, engineering and road testing went into developing a scooter that the company says is designed with Nepal’s roads and riding conditions in mind.

The Yatri P-2 has been designed and manufactured in Nepal in collaboration with Sipradi Trading. It is available with three battery options — 5.2 kWh, 3.7 kWh and 3 kWh.

According to the company, the largest 5.2 kWh battery can deliver a range of up to 157 kilometres on a full charge.

But the range is only one part of the development process. Behind the finished scooter is a series of computer simulations, electrical testing, battery testing, chassis fabrication, assembly and road trials.

From a sketch to an engineered product

According to Yatri Head of Product Krishna Prasad Shrestha, development of the Yatri P-2 began with a simple line sketch.

“The first form was a sketch,” Shrestha said. “It starts with a sketch and gradually develops into the final product.”

Once the initial design is ready, engineers begin testing individual components digitally before they are manufactured.

The chassis, swingarm and other critical components are subjected to computer simulations to determine how they will respond to stress, rough roads and other conditions.

Engineers check whether excessive pressure could develop in a particular component, whether the chassis could be damaged when riding over potholes and whether weld points could experience abnormal stress.

According to Shrestha, potential weaknesses can be identified months before manufacturing through these simulations.

Once a design passes the simulations, physical components are manufactured and subjected to durability testing. The scooter is then tested on actual roads, with data from road testing compared with the results of computer simulations.

The scooter’s electrical nervous system

The Yatri P-2 is not simply a combination of a chassis, motor and battery. Its electrical and electronic architecture is another major part of the vehicle.

Engineers first determine how the scooter’s electrical components will connect and communicate. The system is then converted into a physical wiring harness.

According to Shrestha, one harness developed by Yatri contains more than 150 wires.

The company tests the electrical system on a dedicated test bench before installing it on the scooter. Components including the display, combination board, vehicle control unit (VCU), horn and throttle are tested together.

Functions such as the stand switch, turn indicators and data transmission to the mobile application are also checked before the scooter reaches the road.

The VCU: the scooter’s ‘brain’

The vehicle control unit, or VCU, is another key component of the Yatri P-2.

Yatri designed the VCU board itself, while the board is manufactured in China. Once the boards arrive in Nepal, Yatri engineers program, test and validate them before they are sent to the production line.

Shrestha describes the VCU as the “brain” of the scooter because it controls and executes various vehicle functions.

An Internet of Things (IoT) device also connects the scooter to Yatri’s backend network, making software and connectivity an integral part of the vehicle.

Testing the battery beyond normal use

Battery performance is a critical aspect of any electric vehicle. Yatri has therefore subjected the Yatri P-2’s batteries to accelerated testing.

The company’s battery tester repeatedly charges and discharges batteries to generate data on their long-term performance in a shorter period.

The tests are designed to determine how long a battery can maintain its capacity, when degradation begins and how its performance compares with the company’s range and warranty expectations.

Yatri initially studied the range requirements before developing different battery sizes. The company eventually selected three options — 5.2 kWh, 3.7 kWh and 3 kWh — to offer different combinations of range and price.

The batteries are currently assembled in Nepal using imported parts under a semi-knocked-down (SKD) model. Yatri says it plans to manufacture batteries in Nepal in the future, with infrastructure being developed in Gajuri for the purpose.

Building a charging network

Alongside the scooter, Yatri has also been expanding its charging infrastructure.

The company says it has installed more than 20 charging stations in different parts of the country, including Kathmandu Valley, Bhairahawa and Chitwan.

It is expanding the network towards Pokhara, Butwal and Biratnagar and has also extended charging access to Mustang, according to Shrestha.

The Yatri P-2 uses a 3.3 kW charger. Under certain conditions, the company says the battery can be charged to around 80 percent in approximately 40 to 41 minutes.

The charging network is intended to reduce range anxiety, particularly for riders travelling longer distances.

Three stages of assembly

The Yatri P-2 assembly line is divided into three main stages.

The first station involves the installation of major components such as the motor, battery, chassis and wheel set. Electrical components are installed at the second station, while panels are fitted and additional testing is carried out at the third.

The completed scooter then undergoes dynamometer testing to assess various performance and functional aspects.

If a problem is identified, the scooter is not sent directly to the market. It is moved to a separate quarantine area for further testing and corrective work.

Yatri currently has an annual production capacity of around 8,000 to 10,000 scooters, according to Shrestha. The company plans to increase capacity depending on market demand.

Maintaining consistency in chassis production

Producing a component once is one challenge. Producing it repeatedly to the same specifications is another.

Yatri uses jigs and fixtures to maintain consistency during chassis production. The equipment holds different chassis components in fixed positions during welding, helping maintain uniform dimensions and welding positions.

The jigs and fixtures are designed by Yatri in Nepal but manufactured in India and brought to Nepal. The chassis itself is manufactured at the company’s facility in Gajuri, Dhading.

What ‘Made in Nepal’ means for the Yatri P-2

Although Yatri describes the Yatri P-2 as designed and manufactured in Nepal, not every component is produced domestically.

The company develops specifications for many of the components, which are then manufactured by overseas suppliers according to those specifications.

Yatri still depends on China for components such as the motor and controller. The VCU board is also manufactured in China before being brought to Nepal for programming, testing and validation.

Similarly, although the jigs and fixtures are designed in Nepal, their manufacturing requires reliance on suppliers in India or China.

“We cannot produce everything here, so there is some dependency,” Shrestha said. “We develop the specifications, and they manufacture the products for us accordingly.”

The Yatri P-2’s Nepali identity, therefore, extends beyond assembling imported components. Its design, engineering, system development, software, testing and parts of the manufacturing process involve Yatri’s engineers and designers in Nepal.

A step towards deeper local manufacturing

The development of the Yatri P-2 illustrates the complexity behind producing an electric two-wheeler.

From an initial sketch, the development process moves through computer simulations, electrical architecture, software development, test benches, VCU testing, accelerated battery testing, chassis fabrication, assembly, dynamometer testing and road trials.

While some components are designed and manufactured in Nepal, the company continues to rely on overseas suppliers for several technologically advanced parts.

For Yatri, the P-2 is therefore not just a new electric scooter. It represents an effort to expand Nepal’s capacity to design, engineer and manufacture electric two-wheelers.

Shrestha has been with Yatri for around eight years, while Manu Aryal, who leads the P-2’s finite element analysis (FEA) work, has been with the company for the past two to three years.

The Yatri P-2 now seen on Nepal’s roads is the result of thousands of hours of computer simulations, test-bench trials, battery testing and real-world data collected from Nepal’s roads.

What emerges from the factory is not simply a finished scooter, but the outcome of a development process that began with a sketch and evolved into a locally engineered electric vehicle.

title.rendered: Monsoon winds remain active, thunderstorms and rain likely across hills and Tarai

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

Monsoon winds remain active across Nepal, with rain and thunderstorms expected in several parts of the country on Wednesday, according to the Meteorological Forecasting Division under the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

The monsoon low-pressure line is currently around its average position, while most of the country is expected to remain cloudy throughout the day.

Light to moderate rainfall is currently being reported in some parts of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces.

The weather division has forecast moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning in several mountainous and hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, as well as some mountainous areas of Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Many hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces are also likely to receive moderate rainfall with thunderstorms. Similar conditions are expected in some hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Some areas of Madhesh and the Tarai belts of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces are also likely to receive moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning.

Heavy rainfall is possible at a few locations in the mountainous and hilly areas of Koshi and Bagmati provinces and the hilly areas of Gandaki and Lumbini provinces.

The weather division has forecast generally cloudy conditions across the country tonight as well. Several mountainous areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces and some mountainous areas of Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces are expected to receive moderate rain and snowfall with thunderstorms.

Many hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces and some hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces may receive moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning.

Some parts of the Tarai are also likely to receive moderate rain with thunderstorms.

Heavy rainfall is possible at a few locations in the mountainous and hilly areas of Koshi, as well as the hilly and Tarai areas of Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces.

The weather division has urged people in areas at risk of heavy rainfall to remain alert to possible debris flows, floods, landslides and soil erosion.

It also warned that rainfall could affect daily life, agriculture, health, tourism, mountaineering, road transport and air services in the affected areas, and advised people to stay updated with weather information.

title.rendered: MPs to question PM Balen Shah on border and government affairs today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 26

Prime Minister Balen Shah is set to face questions from lawmakers on issues including Nepal’s borders, nationalism and the government’s working style during a direct question-and-answer session in the House of Representatives today.

The questions have already been submitted to the Parliament Secretariat. However, their contents will not be made public until the question-and-answer session begins, according to the Secretariat.

The names of the lawmakers who will question the prime minister have been made public, but they have been asked not to disclose the subjects or details of their questions to the media or the public.

Parliament officials said the arrangement was made to ensure that the question-and-answer session remains substantive and spontaneous.

“Questions have been registered on nationalism, border-related issues, the government’s activities and its working style,” a source said. “The lawmakers have registered questions focused on specific issues.”

The direct question-and-answer session with the prime minister is provided for under Rule 56 of the House of Representatives Regulations. The rule allows the Speaker to allocate the first hour of a House meeting on one day during the first week of every month for questions on important matters directly related to the prime minister or his area of responsibility.

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal has scheduled the session with Prime Minister Balen Shah for Wednesday.

Aryal had invited lawmakers wishing to question the prime minister to register their questions by August 21. A total of 11 lawmakers have registered questions.

Among them are Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmakers Samikshya Baskota, Krishna Hari Budhathoki and Amaresh Kumar Singh.

From the main opposition Nepali Congress, Chief Whip Basana Thapa and lawmaker Gita Gurung are set to question the prime minister.

CPN-UML Chief Whip Ain Bahadur Mahar and lawmaker Ganesh Singh Thagunna have also registered questions.

Nepali Communist Party lawmakers Barshaman Pun and Prem Kumar Hamal are among those scheduled to question Shah.

Shram Sanskriti Party parliamentary leader Harka Sampang and Rastriya Prajatantra Party Chief Whip Khushbu Oli have also registered questions.

Rule 58 of the House regulations requires lawmakers wishing to question the prime minister to provide the Speaker with written information about the subject of their questions at least three days before the meeting.

The questions were therefore submitted by August 21, in line with the parliamentary procedure.
