title.rendered: Nepal’s creative talent deserves a system that can sustain it

content.rendered:
Nepal has never lacked creative people. The evidence is visible in films made with limited resources, music that travels far beyond its original audience, design rooted in local identity and young creators building communities through a phone screen. Talent appears everywhere. What remains uncertain is whether that talent is supported by an industry capable of sustaining it.

An industry is more than a collection of successful individuals. It is a system through which people can learn, work, receive fair payment, protect their rights, develop specialised skills and build careers that last longer than one successful project. Nepal has parts of that system. It does not yet have enough connection between them.

Talent is only the beginning

Creative careers are often described as if ability naturally produces opportunity. In practice, talented people leave the field because income is unpredictable, expectations are unclear, and growth depends too heavily on personal networks. A cinematographer may also have to produce. An editor may negotiate contracts, chase payments, and manage storage alone. A musician may be expected to understand branding, distribution and copyright without professional support.

This creates impressive generalists, but it can prevent specialisation. Industries mature when people can become exceptionally good at one part of the process and trust others to carry the rest. Directors need producers. Artists need managers. Productions need sound, styling, lighting, legal guidance, accounting and distribution. When these functions remain informal, the strongest people carry too much, and emerging people struggle to enter.

Audiences see the finished film, song or campaign. They do not see the contracts, production schedules, insurance, rights clearance, budgets, archives, training and professional standards behind it. Yet this invisible structure determines whether creative work can be repeated sustainably.

UNESCO’s recent work on Nepal’s cultural and creative industries recognises film, music, design, media arts and other fields as sources of cultural and economic value. Kathmandu’s designation as a UNESCO Creative City of Film and Lalitpur’s recognition as a Creative City of Music signal international acknowledgement. Designations, however, become meaningful only when they lead to practical opportunities for working creators.

Nepal needs reliable data on employment, business size, revenue, participation and barriers across the creative sector. Without it, public policy treats the field as entertainment rather than economic infrastructure. Banks struggle to understand creative businesses, investors struggle to assess them and institutions cannot see where intervention would have the greatest effect.

Professional standards protect everyone

Many creative projects begin with enthusiasm and vague expectations. The scope grows, the deadline remains fixed and payment arrives late. Because the sector is relationship-driven, people hesitate to insist on written agreements. The result is not flexibility; it is avoidable conflict.

Basic standards would improve the market for both clients and creators: written scopes, payment schedules, cancellation terms, ownership clauses, credits, overtime expectations and clear approval stages. These are not bureaucratic obstacles. They make creative ambition easier by reducing uncertainty around the work.

My experience building teams through production, music and artist-focused projects has shown me that creativity and business discipline cannot be separated. The work featured across my portfolio may be the visible part, but each finished frame rests on planning, communication, budgeting and people taking responsibility when conditions change.

Many emerging filmmakers learn cameras and editing through online tutorials. That access has transformed the field. But technical instruction rarely teaches how to price work, read a contract, pay taxes, manage intellectual property, lead a crew or create a safe set.

Film and media education should treat these subjects as central rather than secondary. Apprenticeships and paid assistant roles matter just as much. Creative work is learned through proximity: watching how decisions are made, how problems are solved and how experienced people respond when a plan fails.

The sector also needs stronger bridges between education and employment. A graduate portfolio is useful, but so is understanding real production pressure. Studios and agencies can contribute through internships with defined learning outcomes, open workshops, portfolio reviews and transparent entry-level roles.

From competition to collaboration

A small market can encourage secrecy. People protect contacts, equipment knowledge and client relationships because opportunity feels scarce. But industries grow when knowledge circulates.

Shared studios, rental systems, post-production resources, professional associations and regional networks can reduce costs while raising standards.

Collaboration does not remove competition. It creates a stronger field in which competition can happen. When crews know consistent practices and clients understand the value of specialised roles, good work becomes easier to commission and deliver. That benefits independent creators as much as established companies.

Many Nepali creatives believe they must leave the country to build a serious career. International experience can be valuable, but leaving should be a choice rather than the only route to professional growth. Nepal can retain more talent by improving payment reliability, access to equipment, production finance, distribution and intellectual-property support.

It can also export creative services. Remote post-production, animation, music, design and culturally distinctive storytelling are not limited by geography. But global clients expect consistency, clarity and dependable delivery. The same professional systems that protect local creators also make Nepal more competitive internationally.

Creative visibility is rising, but visibility alone is fragile. A viral video does not create health insurance. A successful song does not automatically build a label. One major campaign does not guarantee that a production crew can work safely next month.

Nepal already has the imagination. The next task is to build conditions in which imagination can become sustained work: better data, clearer contracts, practical education, investment, collaboration and respect for every role behind the finished product. Talent creates remarkable moments. An industry gives those moments somewhere to go.

title.rendered: Durga Prasai gets bank loan issues included in deal with microfinance victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

The government has signed separate agreements with three groups representing microfinance victims in the past two months, but the agreement with a group led by Durga Prasai goes beyond microfinance and includes provisions concerning borrowers of banks and financial institutions.

The government reached agreements with groups representing microfinance victims on July 31, August 13 and August 22, following protests, sit-ins and hunger strikes demanding solutions to problems faced by borrowers.

Although loan waivers were among the key demands raised by the groups, the government agreed to study the demand and provide an appropriate and implementable alternative.

All three agreements contain broadly similar commitments on loan rescheduling, blacklisting, collateral auctions and rehabilitation of borrowers.

However, the agreement with Durga Prasai-led Nagarik Bachau Abhiyan also covers borrowers of banks and financial institutions. Prasai has been campaigning against the repayment of bank and microfinance loans since the Covid-19 pandemic.

While two other groups focused primarily on microfinance borrowers, Prasai’s group managed to bring broader banking-sector issues into its 14-point agreement with the government.

What is different in Prasai’s agreement?

Under the agreement with Durga Prasai’s group, banks and financial institutions will be required to ensure that borrowers blacklisted by banks can continue to operate accounts receiving social security allowances, medical treatment payments, pensions and salary payments.

The government has also agreed to introduce provisions for rescheduling loans of borrowers who have been unable to regularly repay principal and interest due to circumstances beyond their control.

Another provision requires banks to provide borrowers with details when money from their savings account is used to adjust outstanding loans.

The government has also agreed to make savings held in accounts other than mandatory savings available to members when requested, while strengthening monitoring of the practice.

Prasai’s group had previously campaigned against repayment of loans taken from banks, financial institutions and microfinance institutions. Its protests had included warnings to the financial sector and opposition to loan recovery efforts.

The group had appeared to become less active after the Supreme Court opened the way for action against borrowers refusing to repay loans.

Similar demands for microfinance borrowers

Maniram Gyawali-led Struggle Committee Against Microfinance and Financial Exploitation signed a five-point agreement with the government, while the Microfinance and Financial Exploitation Farmers Workers’ Movement led by Ramesh Senchuri reached a seven-point agreement.

Both groups primarily focused on microfinance borrowers.

Their agreements include commitments to remove affected borrowers from blacklists, prevent collateral auctions and recommend implementable options for the rehabilitation of borrowers.

The government has also agreed to review existing provisions concerning blacklisting and collateral auctions by microfinance institutions.

The agreements further call for implementation of the recommendations of a task force formed to study solutions to problems faced by microfinance borrowers.

Government says implementation will take time

Mahesh Acharya, joint secretary at the Ministry of Finance, said it would take some time to assess the results of the agreements as they were reached only recently.

According to Acharya, the Finance Ministry and Nepal Rastra Bank are holding discussions on implementing all three agreements.

He also said the report prepared by the task force formed to recommend appropriate solutions to problems faced by microfinance borrowers has been made available to the concerned parties.

Under the agreements, the government has also committed to monitoring and ultimately prohibiting practices by microfinance institutions such as taking advance cheques as collateral and making borrowers sign blank promissory notes.

An online complaint system and toll-free hotline will also be established at Nepal Rastra Bank to address problems and complaints concerning banks and financial institutions.

The government has agreed to form a high-level committee comprising independent experts to address problems involving microfinance members, borrowers and employees.

It has also pledged action against illegal debt-recovery practices, including harassment, taking household goods from borrowers’ homes, keeping employees at borrowers’ homes until instalments are paid, and verbal abuse.

Collateral auctions and blacklisting

The government has agreed to make the collateral auction and valuation process more transparent by requiring borrowers to be informed before an auction notice is issued.

It has also agreed to make necessary legal arrangements to clear a loan and remove the borrower from the blacklist once the entire outstanding amount has been recovered through a collateral auction.

The government has further agreed to review the deposit and fees required from borrowers seeking to appeal to the Debt Recovery Tribunal and improve existing policies to address problems in collateral valuation.

Durga Prasai’s group also included the issue of landless squatters in its agreement with the government, while the other two groups focused on implementing the recommendations of the task force.

Representatives of the microfinance victims say they are confident that implementation of the task force’s recommendations could resolve many of the problems in the sector.

The agreement reached with the Struggle Committee Against Microfinance and Financial Exploitation on July 31 also overlaps with several provisions in the agreement signed with Durga Prasai’s group.

title.rendered: Man accused of assaulting on-duty police officer remanded for five days

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Court has remanded a 27-year-old man in police custody for five days for allegedly assaulting a police officer deployed on duty at New Baneshwor.

The suspect, Raj Kathayat, originally from Tatopani Rural Municipality-2 of Jumla and currently living in Kathmandu, was remanded for investigation on charges of obstructing a public servant in the discharge of duty and engaging in indecent behaviour.

According to SP Dan Bahadur Thapa of the Kathmandu District Police Range, the court granted police five days to investigate the charges against Kathayat.

Kathayat allegedly attacked a police officer on duty at New Baneshwor on Tuesday after the officer asked him to use an overhead pedestrian bridge to cross the road.

Police said Kathayat assaulted the officer instead of complying with the instruction.

The investigation into the incident is ongoing.

title.rendered: UML report identifies 6 reasons behind party’s humiliating election defeat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

CPN-UML General Secretary Shankar Pokharel has identified six major reasons behind what he describes as the party’s humiliating defeat in the recent election.

Onlinekhabar has obtained the report prepared by Pokharel for the Election Review and Party Restructuring Suggestion Collection Task Force. The report analyses the reasons behind the UML’s defeat and proposes measures for party reform and restructuring.

The report, prepared after collecting suggestions from 13 locations, including the seven provincial committees, concludes that the UML did not lose the election solely because of interference by external forces.

Instead, it identifies public dissatisfaction with the performance of previous governments, the party’s failure to address changing public aspirations, its inability to convince people of its interpretation of the Gen Z-led movement, and undemocratic practices within the party among the key reasons for the defeat.

The report also cites the decision to declare party chair KP Sharma Oli as the future prime minister following the Gen Z movement, the failure to attract young voters, and the party’s inability to understand social media algorithms and external influence.

The six reasons identified in Pokharel’s report are:

1. Public dissatisfaction and distrust

The report identifies public dissatisfaction with the performance of previous governments as the main reason traditional parties, including the UML, lost support.

It says a perception had developed that political parties were primarily interested in returning to power while failing to pay adequate attention to people’s needs.

“Failure to maintain good governance while in government, failure to appropriately address the demands of classes and communities engaged in protests, and the involvement of some ministers and elected representatives in allegations of corruption and irregularities, without taking timely action against them, contributed to growing public dissatisfaction,” the report says.

The report also says the UML’s alliance with the Nepali Congress was increasingly viewed as being driven by the pursuit of power rather than constitutional amendment.

It says the issue of constitutional amendment, which had been presented as a major agenda, was pushed aside with a decision to pursue it only after 2030, allowing the opposition narrative that the alliance was solely motivated by power interests to take hold.

The report also concludes that internal conflicts during the Nepal Communist Party period and subsequent alliances contributed to the fragmentation of the left-wing vote.

2. Failure to address changing public aspirations

The report identifies the UML’s failure to respond to changing public expectations as the second major reason for its defeat.

It says people’s living standards and aspirations had increased significantly, but employment and self-employment opportunities had not expanded accordingly, resulting in limited growth in their incomes.

The report also says the party failed to understand the consequences of educated people continuing to migrate from villages to cities and from cities abroad.

It points to the rapid expansion of private-sector education and healthcare and the declining quality of public services, which forced citizens to pay heavily for essential services.

“Failure to understand the growing public distrust of traditional parties and the state created an opportunity for populists to exploit public sentiment,” the report says.

3. Gen Z movement and Oli as prime ministerial candidate

The report says the UML was forced to participate in an election in which other traditional parties were unwilling to accept the UML’s proposal.

It says the party analysed the events of September 8 and 9, 2025, as a pre-planned conspiracy, but failed to convince either political circles or the general public of that interpretation.

The report also identifies a BBC documentary aired during the election silence period as a factor that worked against the UML.

It says the party leadership was accused of failing to demonstrate sufficient human sensitivity and sympathy towards young people who were killed or injured during the movement.

“The documentary broadcast by the BBC during the election silence period also contributed to turning public opinion against us,” the report says.

The decision to declare KP Sharma Oli, who was leading the government during the Gen Z movement, as the UML’s future prime ministerial candidate is also identified as a factor behind the poor result.

“With attacks coming from all sides and the entire party organisation being on the defensive, going into the election by declaring the party chair as the prime ministerial candidate made the party organisation even more defensive,” Pokharel wrote.

4. Geopolitics and algorithms

The task force also identified geopolitical manoeuvring and social media algorithms as factors behind the UML’s defeat.

The report specifically names several organisations in its discussion of the Gen Z movement.

“The suspicious role of groups with external links such as Barbara Foundation, Hami Nepal and TOB was directly visible in the events of September 8 and 9,” the report says.

It argues that the party paid a price for geopolitical manoeuvring allegedly triggered by what it describes as nationalist positions on issues including the trade and transit agreement with China, Nepal’s revised map, exploration of gas in Dailekh and the Dhauwadi iron mine.

The report also links the election result to the aggressive social media campaign of rival forces and the UML’s defensive position.

“Particularly during the election, our party organisation remained defensive while opponents were aggressive, and the significant presence of young people capable of using information and technology helped establish their agendas at the level of social media algorithms,” the report says.

5. Policy confusion and governance weaknesses

The report says the UML-led government also failed to adequately promote and implement the party’s policies and programmes.

It points to difficulties faced by party workers in meeting the prime minister, saying this contributed to further dissatisfaction.

“The policy of a prosperous Nepal, happy Nepalis could not be implemented in practice in line with public sentiment,” the report says.

The report also cites an inability to maintain balance in the budget, delays in public service delivery, dissatisfaction among teachers and government employees over unresolved demands, shortages of chemical fertilisers, and unpaid subsidies and sales proceeds owed to sugarcane and dairy farmers.

The government’s decision to require social media platforms to register before operating also increased anger among young people, according to the report.

It further says the government failed to properly understand and respond to what it describes as internal and external conspiracies against the party and government.

Other unresolved issues cited include problems faced by landless squatters and unorganised settlers.

The report says the failure to enact federal education, police and civil service laws created the impression that the government was negative towards federalism.

6. Internal problems

Pokharel’s report identifies internal problems within the UML as the sixth and final major reason for the party’s electoral defeat.

It points to candidate selection, factionalism and organisational indiscipline as major factors.

The report says the decision not to renew former President Bidya Devi Bhandari’s party membership contributed to divisions within the party.

It also criticises the lack of transparency in candidate selection and repeated changes to decisions.

“The lack of transparency in candidate selection, repeated changes to decisions, and the perception that those who stayed around leaders were given priority in receiving tickets rather than those deployed in the constituencies created dissatisfaction among sincere party workers,” Pokharel wrote.

The report also identifies the high cost of elections as a factor pushing sincere party workers away from politics and creating frustration.

It further says failure to take action against those involved in electoral sabotage encouraged organisational indiscipline and a mentality that “anything goes.”

title.rendered: UML report cites Bidya Devi Bhandari membership row as one reason for election defeat

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

A task force formed to collect suggestions on the restructuring of the CPN-UML has identified the dispute over former President Bidya Devi Bhandari’s party membership as one of the reasons behind the party’s electoral defeat.

The report prepared by UML General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel and submitted to task force coordinator Ram Bahadur Thapa lists six major reasons for the party’s defeat. Internal problems within the party have been identified as one of them.

The report begins its discussion of internal problems by referring to the dispute over Bhandari’s party membership.

“The dispute over the renewal of the former president’s party membership led to divisions within the party ranks,” the report states.

The UML’s decision not to renew the membership of Bhandari, who previously served as the party’s vice-chair, had sparked controversy within the party. A significant section of the UML had criticised the decision, arguing that revoking her party membership was inappropriate.

Because her membership was not renewed, Bhandari was unable to participate in the party’s 11th General Convention.

However, then-senior vice-chair Ishwar Pokhrel formed a panel with Bhandari’s backing and contested the 11th General Convention election. The report also identifies this internal contest as a factor contributing to the UML’s electoral defeat.

“On the eve of the election, the panel-based contest at the party’s 11th General Convention led to organisational divisions and the expansion of factionalism down to the grassroots level,” Pokhrel wrote in the report.

title.rendered: Cyberattacks by Chinese hackers using AI more than double

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Chinese government-linked hackers have more than doubled their cyberattacks by using artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as DeepSeek, according to Taiwanese cybersecurity firm TeamT5.

The use of AI has enabled hackers to complete tasks that previously required significant amounts of time much more quickly.

According to TeamT5, hackers have been using AI to identify potential targets on the internet, detect vulnerabilities in company websites, servers and computers, and find ways to gain unauthorised access.

The firm said a hacking group known as GrimFang used DeepSeek to develop code exploiting system vulnerabilities. Another group, TeleBoy, reportedly collected about 1,000 IP addresses from the internet and used them to gather information about a company’s websites and domains.

The investigation found that hackers used not only DeepSeek but also ChatGPT and Claude Code. In one attack on a Western think tank, hackers obtained files related to the Signal messaging application from an employee’s computer and used ChatGPT to develop a program capable of opening the files.

In another incident, Claude Code was reportedly used to automatically target 30 organisations and companies.

Researchers say AI is creating new challenges for cybersecurity by allowing hackers to scan and attack multiple systems in a shorter period. However, the AI systems did not initiate the attacks independently; hackers directed and connected them to specialised programs to carry out the operations.

title.rendered: Parliamentary committee questions use of procurement law to outsource workers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

A parliamentary committee has raised concerns over the use of procurement law to outsource workers in both the public and private sectors, warning that the practice is being used to evade responsibility and undermine workers’ rights.

The Industry and Commerce, Labour and Consumer Interest Committee of the House of Representatives held a meeting on Tuesday to discuss the management of workers through outsourcing.

Committee Chair Rahbar Ansari expressed serious concern over the practice of using procurement law to outsource labour and deprive workers of their rights.

Ansari said no government agency or private organisation should be allowed to avoid its responsibility towards workers by outsourcing labour under the cover of procurement law.

He also raised concerns about what he described as a nexus between politics and business, particularly in industrial corridors. He said ward chairs and local representatives of political parties were allegedly acting as outsourcing agents, recruiting workers for industries and benefiting from their wages.

Ansari called for strict action against such fake outsourcing agencies as well as industries and companies that allow political figures to exercise authority over worker recruitment.

He said a digital registry should be established to ensure transparency in labour management and protect workers’ rights. He also called for an end to the practice of employing workers for as little as Rs 10,000 to Rs 12,000 without paying the minimum wage.

Ansari further called for action against agencies that seize the citizenship certificates and other documents of domestic workers, effectively holding them hostage and subjecting them to financial exploitation.

He also criticised the emergence of practices such as “tighre allowance” and “mundre allowance” in the industrial sector. He expressed concern over the recruitment of thousands of workers from across the border, which he said was displacing local workers.

He also raised concerns over the lack of accountability when workers are injured or killed in workplace accidents.

Ansari urged the government to amend the Labour Act as necessary to address these issues and ensure workers’ rights are protected.

title.rendered: How a father’s dream took a mischievous boy from Siraha to Türkiye

content.rendered:
When Dr Binod Sah’s father became seriously ill, the doctor found himself in a role he was less accustomed to playing.

He was a son.

At 60, his father had developed a heart condition and kidney failure. Treatment was not possible in Nepal, so orthopaedic surgeon Dr Chakraraj Pandey gave Sah blunt advice: take him to Türkiye.

It was not an easy journey. His father was critically ill, needed oxygen and was not in a condition to take a long flight. Sah arranged an ambulance, oxygen cylinders, nurses and doctors. From Delhi to Türkiye, his father travelled on a stretcher.

“I held his hand and kept telling him, ‘Father, you will survive. You will survive,’” Sah recalls.

After they reached Türkiye, his father’s condition deteriorated further. He spent 25 days in intensive care, undergoing dialysis, ventilation and continuous monitoring.

Sah barely left the hospital.

“I was a doctor, but I was also a son,” he says.

Eventually, his father opened his eyes.

He smiled at his son.

“You saved me.”

For Sah, the moment carried a significance that went far beyond a successful medical treatment. Much of his life had been shaped by the same man lying in that hospital bed: a father who had once forced a reluctant, mischievous boy to become a doctor.

That boy had grown up in Golbazar, Siraha, with little interest in books and a preference for games and mischief.

His father had other ideas.

‘If you study, you will become a doctor’

Dr Binod Sah was the only son among his sisters. His father wanted him to become a doctor.

The boy himself had no such ambition.

“I was very mischievous when I was young,” Sah recalls. “I wasn’t interested in studies. I preferred playing and having fun.”

His father worried about him.

One day, he told his 13-year-old son: “If you study, you will become a doctor. If you don’t, you will become a thief or a thug.”

The words stayed with him.

His father decided that what the boy needed was discipline and sent him to St Joseph’s Boarding School in Biratnagar.

For Sah, accustomed to the freedom of village life, the school felt like a prison. So after two months, he ran away.

He returned to Golbazar, where his mother welcomed him. His father, however, did not.

“You cannot enter this house. Go back,” he told him.

That night, at around 11pm, his mother fainted. His father nevertheless arranged a vehicle and sent his son back to boarding school.

“That was the most difficult moment of my life,” Sah says. “My father’s strictness forced me to change direction.”

He says he has rarely had time to settle at home since.

“I left home at 13 against my wishes. My career and profession have always kept me moving. I don’t even remember having much free time at home.”

His father’s determination was rooted partly in his own experience.

The family was poor. In the village, Sah’s father earned a living by carrying sacks and goods from house to house. He saved money little by little until he could buy a horse, which he used to transport goods. That was how the family survived.

For his father, education offered a way beyond that life.

“Even if I have to sell my kidney, I will make you a doctor,” he would tell Binod.

Sah did not yet share the dream.

The first failure

Binod Sah passed his SLC examination in the first division in 1994.

He was an average student. He came to Kathmandu after SLC and lived with friends in Kalimati.

The city offered plenty of distractions. He spent time at Dasharath Stadium and with friends, and studying was still something he did largely because his father told him to.

He enrolled at Amrit Science Campus and began preparing for the MBBS entrance examination.

He failed on his first attempt.

“I thought everything was over,” he recalls.

His father, once again, refused to let him give up.

“You can do it. If you give up now, you will regret it for the rest of your life.”

Binod Sah prepared again, this time with his roommates Hemraj, Shivraj and Prabhakar. All three would eventually build medical careers in Nepal and Europe. But even then, Sah was uncertain about the path he was taking.

“For a long time, I felt this was my father’s dream, not mine.”

In 1994, he sat for the entrance examination again.

This time, he ranked 23rd on the MBBS scholarship merit list. In Golbazar, the news was celebrated with sweets.

The community had around 25,000–30,000 people, and Sah was the first person from the village to win such a scholarship. His achievement was reported in national newspapers.

The scholarship allowed him to study at any medical college in Nepal. His father, however, wanted something more.

“If you stay in Nepal, you will become a doctor, but you won’t become a complete person. Go abroad. Face challenges.”

Eventually, Sah received a full scholarship to study in Türkiye.

A night at the airport

He travelled to Türkiye with his friend Manju Shrestha. The country was unfamiliar. Neither knew the language and they had little money.

And they arrived on a Sunday, when the airport offices were closed. With nowhere else to go, they spent the night at the airport.

“My friend Manju became so frightened in the unfamiliar place that she developed a fever,” Sah recalls. “We were hungry and thirsty. It was Ramadan, so many shops were closed.”

Eventually, someone helped them reach the right place. Then Sah heard his name.

“In such a huge country, someone called my name for the first time. I felt I had finally reached the right place.”

The difficulties were only beginning.

Before medical school, Sah had to learn Turkish. He passed the language course with 97%. He could choose to study medicine in English or Turkish. He chose Turkish.

The decision immediately tested him.

During his first lecture, his professor spoke in an older form of Turkish that Sah could barely understand.

“In a 45-minute class, I understood only about 20 to 25 percent. I thought I had made the wrong decision. I thought my future was ruined. I sat in the first row and started crying.”

His friends reassured him. Even Turkish students, they told him, understood only about half of what the professor was saying.

For Sah, 25% was not failure. It was a beginning.

Medical school itself was fiercely competitive. Millions of students competed for limited places each year.

Binod Sah also struggled financially. His scholarship did not provide enough to cover his food expenses, so he applied for an additional food scholarship.

He got it.

For three consecutive years, he ranked first in his class.

After six years, he completed his MBBS and returned to Nepal. But Türkiye was not finished with him.

Becoming a pediatrician

At 27, Sah returned to Türkiye on a scholarship to pursue an MD in pediatrics.

He joined the Department of Pediatrics at Hacettepe University, considered among the world’s leading institutions in the field.

That same year, his research on neonatal medicine earned him recognition as one of the four leading researchers in the world in the field.

He subsequently completed a DM in neonatology.

His career continued to develop around some of the smallest and most vulnerable patients.

In 2015, the Turkish government honoured him with its Best Doctor of the Year presidential award for his contribution to child and neonatal healthcare.

In 2024, he received the Best Child Doctor award.

But the moments that stayed with him were not necessarily the ones involving awards.

One came on a cold night in 2011.

48 minutes

Binod Sah was on night duty at Hacettepe University Hospital when a mother gave birth to triplets.

All three were premature and two of them had died.

The third was also close to death. The baby had stopped breathing.

Medical protocol generally limited CPR to around 45 minutes.

Sah, however, continued for 48 minutes. Eventually, the tiny heart began beating again and the baby survived.

Two years later, the child returned to the hospital. This time, there was no medical emergency. The child was running and laughing and came straight into Sah’s arms. The mother had tears in her eyes.

“That was the most emotional moment of my life,” Sah says.

It was one of several moments that would shape how he understood his work.

Years later, another came in Nepal.

A child in Pokhara

The child of the South Asia bureau chief of Reuters suddenly lost consciousness while the family was visiting Pokhara.

The child was taken to hospital by helicopter.

Binod Sah had arrived in Nepal only two days earlier. It was around midnight.

The child was in critical condition.

The medical team was considering one course of treatment, but Sah’s experience suggested another.

He intubated the child, adjusted the settings and carefully balanced the insulin dose.

He worked through the night.

The child stabilised and was eventually discharged.

“For me, it was normal work,” Sah says. “But for the family, it was a miracle.”

The parents later told him that had he not been there, their child might not have survived.

By then, however, Sah was already thinking about something beyond individual patients.

He wanted to build something that would remain after he left.

Bringing intensive care to Nepal

In 2016, Sah decided to return to Nepal. Two things influenced him.

One was Dr Chakraraj Pandey, an orthopaedic surgeon who had also studied in Türkiye. Pandey told him that Nepal needed NICU and PICU services and encouraged him to return.

The other was the dream of the father who had pushed him towards medicine all those years earlier.

“If my father could dream of making me a doctor when there wasn’t even a doctor in our village, I should do something for the country,” Sah thought.

He joined Grand International Hospital in Kathmandu and led its pediatrics department.

At the time, Nepal did not have a dedicated pediatric intensive care unit.

Sah established the country’s first Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) at Grand International Hospital.

He introduced modern equipment, trained staff and protocols based on international standards.

“Child and neonatal mortality was high in Nepal. I believed a PICU could save many lives,” he says.

By 2018, the unit was fully operational after which Sah handed it over to the hospital.

“My goal was to create a system that would continue even after I left.”

Why Türkiye?

The question was not whether Binod Sah loved Nepal.

He returned every year during Dashain. He conducted health camps and awareness programmes. And he still hopes to establish a pediatric hospital in Nepal that can provide quality care to children from rural communities.

But he had also experienced the limitations of the country’s healthcare system.

“In Türkiye, hospitals have modern equipment, internationally recognised protocols, research funding and a medical system that is continuously updated,” he says.

When a patient dies unexpectedly, hospitals hold mortality and morbidity meetings. Doctors, nurses and technicians examine what happened, what went wrong and how procedures and documentation can be improved.

“Every incident is treated as a lesson. The system makes doctors accountable, but they are not afraid. They learn from mistakes.”

Nepal had fewer resources.

“There might be one ventilator, one incubator, and even then there were power cuts. There were administrative complications and budget problems.”

He says institutional interference was an even bigger challenge.

“It became difficult for doctors to focus on their work.”

At Grand International Hospital, Sah says, he fought to bring in equipment, train staff and introduce protocols.

But improving a healthcare system, he came to believe, could not be the work of one person alone.

“Doctors in Nepal are good. The system binds them. I tried many times to improve healthcare, but I realised it wasn’t possible alone.”

So he returned to Türkiye.

His professional life continued.

His connection to Nepal did not end.

Back to the beginning

By then, Sah had a modern pediatric clinic in Ankara. From 8am until 7pm, parents arrive with newborns, premature babies, children and teenagers.

Sah sees them one after another.

He listens to worried parents. He reassures them. He treats their children.

For a doctor who has spent decades caring for some of the most vulnerable patients, the routine remains demanding.

But his career has taken him a long way from Golbazar.

And then came the moment when his father became critically ill. His father spent 25 days in intensive care in Türkiye. The doctor who had spent his life saving other people’s children now sat beside his own father.

Eventually, the older man opened his eyes.

“You saved me.”

That same year, Sah received the Best Doctor of the Year award.

His father attended the ceremony in a wheelchair.

“I don’t have to worry even if I die now,” he told his son. “My son saved me. My dream has come true.”

Sah becomes emotional when he remembers those words.

“I couldn’t show my father that I had become a doctor. But I was able to show him that I could save him.”

He says every achievement is dedicated to his father.

“My father had the eyes that dreamed the dream. But I had the feet that carried that dream.”

From a boy who once ran away from boarding school to an internationally recognised pediatrician, researcher and healthcare pioneer, Sah’s life has travelled through poverty, scholarship, migration and medicine.

The boy who did not initially want to become a doctor eventually became one.

And the dream that began with his father did not end there.

It crossed borders—from Golbazar to Kathmandu, from Nepal to Türkiye—and eventually came full circle beside a hospital bed, where the doctor became a son.

title.rendered: Vaccination drive helps reduce livestock disease risk in Tanahun

content.rendered:
Damauli, August 25

A comprehensive livestock vaccination programme has helped reduce the risk of infectious diseases among cattle, goats and pigs in Tanahun district, according to the Veterinary Hospital and Livestock Services Expert Centre.

A total of 190,201 doses of vaccines against foot-and-mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, PPR and classical swine fever were administered across the district during fiscal year 2025/26.

According to centre chief Robinson Adhikari, 39,849 doses were administered against foot-and-mouth disease, 10,578 against lumpy skin disease, 131,471 against PPR and 8,300 against classical swine fever.

The programme covered around 50 per cent of eligible cattle and buffaloes against foot-and-mouth disease, 55 per cent of goats against PPR and 35 per cent of pigs against swine fever.

The vaccination campaign was conducted across all 10 local units, covering 85 wards and 1,113 settlements. A total of 93 vaccinators were mobilised to reach livestock farmers in coordination with local governments and relevant agencies.

Adhikari said no outbreaks of the targeted diseases had been reported in areas covered by the vaccination programme.

“Since the comprehensive vaccination programme was implemented, there have been no outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, PPR or swine fever in the district,” he said.

The programme had a budget of Rs 12 million, of which Rs 9.043 million was spent. Officials said preventive vaccination is more effective than treating diseases after they spread and helps protect livestock and reduce farmers’ financial losses.

title.rendered: Reward scheme drives surge in bill complaints and consumer participation

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

The government’s reward scheme for taxpayers has led to a sharp increase in consumer awareness about asking for bills, with the number of complaints against businesses refusing to issue bills also rising, according to the Inland Revenue Department.

Under the taxpayer incentive programme, every purchase bill can effectively become an entry into a government lucky draw, with consumers eligible to win prizes of up to Rs 1 million. The department says this has prompted more consumers to demand bills from businesses.

Keshav Raghuvanshi, director and information officer at the Inland Revenue Department, said the first month of the reward scheme showed a sharp increase in awareness among consumers about the importance of taking bills.

However, he said complaints that businesses are still refusing to issue bills remain common, even in major commercial centres such as New Road.

“Most of the complaints currently coming through Hello Sarkar are about shops refusing to issue bills,” he said. “This shows that market monitoring also needs to be increased.”

The department is preparing to step up monitoring, he said.

“After purchasing goods, consumers have the right to receive the original bill,” Raghuvanshi said. “Our objective through the reward scheme is also to create awareness about asking for bills.”

The department has received a particularly high number of complaints about businesses that are registered under PAN but still refuse to provide original or official bills.

Reward scheme participation surges

The Inland Revenue Department’s data shows a sharp increase in the number of consumers participating in the reward scheme during its first month.

The programme began on July 17. During the first 15 days, consumers uploaded 7,077 bills from cash transactions to participate in the scheme.

That number jumped to 357,149 between August 1 and 16.

A similar increase was seen in QR transactions.

The number of QR transactions automatically entered into the reward scheme stood at 25.608 million during the first 15 days. It increased to 32.086 million during the second 15-day period.

According to the department, the total number of transactions in the 16 days after July 31 reached 32.443 million.

Under the programme, the government has begun awarding Rs 100,000 every day after tax deductions, while a bumper prize of Rs 1 million is awarded every 15 days, also subject to tax deductions.

‘The state has invested in a campaign for aware consumers’

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle views the government’s reward scheme as an investment in consumer awareness.

Speaking at an event held at the Ministry of Finance last week to announce the second fortnightly prize, Wagle said the government had invested in consumers as part of an awareness campaign.

He said the campaign was launched to promote a culture of issuing and taking bills.

According to Wagle, the programme aims both to increase government revenue and bring more people into the formal economy.

He said the experience of the first month had generated excitement among consumers.

Wagle has also called on those who have won prizes to act as ambassadors for the government’s campaign.

“You have now become a symbol in your village, municipality and constituency. You can say, ‘I am the one who won the prize,’” he said, asking the winners to work as special ambassadors for the campaign.

What do the winners say?

Hemraj Joshi of Kailali won the Rs 1 million bumper prize after purchasing goods worth Rs 250.

He said the government’s reward scheme would encourage consumers and businesses to develop the habit of taking and issuing bills.

“If this habit continues among all consumers, it will also contribute to the economy,” he said at the event held at the Ministry of Finance last week.

Joshi also said he had stopped carrying cash since QR payments were introduced in Nepal. He said he generally relies on QR payments, although he has occasionally found himself in difficult situations when cash was unexpectedly required.

Himal Aryal of Gaindakot, who won Rs 100,000 in the first fortnight, said he initially thought someone with the same name might have won the prize when his name appeared on Facebook.

He realised the prize was his only after receiving a message on his phone.

Aryal won the prize after making a payment for ice cream with friends in the evening.

He said the government’s reward scheme could make a significant contribution to bringing economic transactions into the formal system.

After he won the prize, he said, his friends also started keeping their bills safely.

title.rendered: Deepak Khadka says he approached Supreme Court seeking justice over party disputes

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Nepali Congress leader Deepak Khadka has said he approached the Supreme Court seeking justice over what he described as unfair incidents within the party.

In a Facebook post on Tuesday, Khadka objected to what he called a campaign linking his name with claims that the court had been “set” after he registered a case at the Supreme Court.

He alleged that a planned campaign was being carried out to undermine confidence in the independent judiciary by portraying his decision to seek justice in court as an instance of “court setting.”

“I am seriously concerned about the campaign being carried out by certain individuals and groups, deliberately linking my name to claims of court setting with the intention of undermining the dignity of the independent judiciary and creating distrust when I have gone to court seeking justice,” Khadka said.

Khadka described the campaign as “misinformation” and expressed concern over what he called a deliberate attempt to undermine the dignity of the judiciary. He also urged the media to remain cautious about such claims.

Saying that he was a “soldier” fighting for justice and freedom, Khadka said he had equal faith and confidence in all courts. He also said he was fully confident that the Supreme Court would deliver justice in his case.

Earlier, Nepali Congress Central Committee member Kusum Thapa Magar had accused Khadka of claiming that he had “fixed” the court.

Thapa Magar alleged that Khadka had made statements suggesting that an order would be issued in his favor in a matter currently under consideration by the court.

In a social media post, Thapa Magar quoted Khadka as saying that he had arranged matters with the court to prevent a repeat of what happened when he was previously in jail.

According to her post, Khadka had allegedly said he had met certain Supreme Court justices at night and their people, and that a stay order and official recognition would be secured.

Thapa Magar also advised Khadka not to go around claiming that he had “managed” everyone from court employees to justices.

title.rendered: Government task force conducts on-site inspection of Birgunj Sugar Factory

content.rendered:
Birgunj, August 25

A government task force formed to assess the feasibility of reopening the long-shuttered Birgunj Sugar Factory conducted an on-site inspection of the factory premises on Tuesday.

The Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies formed the task force on August 18 to study the possibility of resuming operations at the factory. The team visited the factory to assess its current condition, existing structures and infrastructure required for reopening.

The task force will study the factory’s current status, past government decisions, previous studies and reports prepared on its possible reopening, and the steps that would need to be taken going forward.

During the inspection, the team examined buildings, structures, machinery, equipment and spare parts at the factory. It will also assess their current condition and determine whether they can be reused if the factory resumes operations.

The study will cover potential investment requirements, repair and reconstruction of infrastructure, and the condition of machinery and infrastructure required for production.

The task force is coordinated by Shrikant Yadav, a chief divisional engineer at the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies. Section Officer Jyoti Paudel and ministry adviser Shyam Sharma are members.

The task force has been given 15 days to submit its report to the ministry. Based on its study, including the site inspection, it will recommend whether the factory can be reopened, the procedures required and a possible action plan.

The Birgunj Sugar Factory has remained closed for years, causing its assets and infrastructure to deteriorate. Although reopening the factory has been discussed repeatedly, no concrete decision or implementation has followed.

The government is expected to make further decisions based on the task force’s report, which is expected to provide technical, financial and managerial grounds for determining the factory’s future.

—Safal Khatiwada

title.rendered: Nepal’s NEPSE falls for second straight day as turnover rises to Rs 4.1 billion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Nepal’s stock market fell for a second consecutive trading session on Tuesday, with the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index declining 5.30 points to close at 2,594 points.

The market had dropped 19.13 points on Monday.

Despite the decline in the index, daily turnover increased. Shares worth Rs 4.10 billion were traded on Tuesday, up from Rs 3.23 billion in the previous session.

Of the companies traded, 78 saw their share prices rise, while 187 declined. The prices of 12 companies remained unchanged.

Only the development bank and non-life insurance sectors recorded gains on Tuesday. The development bank index rose 0.08%, while the non-life insurance index increased 0.36%.

All other sectoral indices declined. The banking sector fell 0.03%, finance 0.91%, hotels and tourism 0.71%, hydropower 0.42%, investment 0.08%, life insurance 0.09%, manufacturing and processing 0.29%, microfinance 0.27%, others 0.18%, and trading 0.57%.

As usual, hydropower companies accounted for the largest share of trading activity. The sector contributed Rs 2.49 billion, or 60.66% of the total turnover.

Commercial banks recorded transactions worth Rs 320 million, while companies in the manufacturing and processing sector recorded turnover of Rs 380 million.

title.rendered: Bamboo trade begins in Bhaktapur ahead of Gai Jatra

content.rendered:
Bhaktapur, August 25

The sale of bamboo used to make Tahasa, a traditional structure carried during the Gai Jatra festival, has begun in Bhaktapur ahead of this year’s celebrations.

Bamboo vendors have started setting up near the Nyatapola Temple area to meet demand from families preparing to observe Gai Jatra. The festival will be celebrated in Bhaktapur on August 29.

Vendors are selling bamboo at around Rs 500 per piece. A completed Tahasa typically costs between Rs 2,000 and Rs 2,500, depending on the size and quality of bamboo used.

Jayaram Tamang, who brings bamboo from Ashapuri in Suryabinayak Municipality-8, said he has been selling bamboo near Nyatapola Temple every year, beginning about a week before Gai Jatra.

Bamboo sales are allowed only until 10 am, as the municipality does not permit the trade to continue during the day.

A Tahasa is traditionally made using four bamboo poles, each measuring around 15 to 20 feet. A representation of a cow is placed at the top before it is carried through the city during the festival.

Families who have lost a member during the preceding year use Tahasa to take part in Gai Jatra. As hundreds of families observe the tradition, demand for green bamboo rises sharply before the festival.

The tradition of making Tahasa for Gai Jatra has continued in Bhaktapur for generations. Preparations for the festival, including construction and decoration of Tahasa, have intensified across the city’s neighbourhoods as the festival approaches.

Gai Jatra is observed on the first day of the bright fortnight of Bhadra, the day after Janai Purnima. The festival honours and commemorates those who died during the previous year. According to tradition, a cow is believed to help guide the souls of the deceased to the afterlife.

title.rendered: Govt’s bill reward scheme is making Nepali consumers change the way they shop

content.rendered:
The government’s reward scheme for consumers who ask for bills is encouraging more people to demand receipts when making purchases, while also supporting efforts to curb tax evasion and make the market more transparent.

Introduced from July 17, the Taxpayer Reward Incentive Programme gives consumers a chance to win prizes ranging from Rs 100,000 to Rs 1 million when they obtain genuine bills for their purchases.

The government introduced the reward scheme to encourage consumers to obtain proper bills, discourage tax evasion and help control illegal transactions.

So far, winners have been announced twice.

Every day, consumers go to markets, buy goods, pay for them and return home. But many still do not make it a habit to ask for a bill, particularly when purchasing inexpensive items.

The new reward scheme is beginning to change that behaviour.

Rameshwar Acharya of Gothatar, Bhaktapur, is among those who have long made it a habit to ask for bills.

He was at Bhat-Bhateni Supermarket in Anamnagar on Monday, where he was collecting his bill after shopping.

“I have been taking bills for a long time,” Acharya told Onlinekhabar. “Now, it has become even more important to do so.”

Acharya is also aware of the reward scheme introduced through the government’s budget for the current fiscal year.

“Earlier, I only knew that I should take a bill when buying something,” he said. “Now that there is a reward, I am paying even more attention to it.”

According to Acharya, billing systems are well organised at large supermarkets and department stores such as Bhat-Bhateni and SalesBerry, where consumers generally receive bills automatically.

However, his experience is different at smaller grocery and retail shops.

“At larger stores, bills are issued automatically,” he said. “At ordinary grocery shops, they used to provide a simple bill when asked. Now, as consumers have started asking, they have also started providing VAT bills.”

Why does the reward scheme encourage consumers to ask for bills?

For some consumers, the chance to win up to Rs 1 million may be the biggest attraction of the reward scheme. But Acharya says asking for a bill is also important to protect consumers from being cheated.

“Taking a bill also protects you from being cheated,” he said. “I don’t check it immediately at the counter, but I go home and check it. That is why I always take a bill wherever I shop.”

A bill can help consumers identify instances where they have been overcharged, sold expired products or incorrectly charged for an item.

Consumers are now entering their PAN numbers

Ajay Lama, a manager at Bhat-Bhateni Supermarket, says the reward scheme has generated considerable interest among customers.

“After the taxpayer incentive programme was introduced, customers started asking for bills. They are quite excited,” Lama said. “They are also excited about the possibility of winning through the lucky draw, and this has increased the flow of customers.”

Some customers who previously paid for their purchases and left are now registering their personal details, including PAN numbers, to participate in the reward scheme.

“Even customers who pay through QR codes ask for a bill and provide their PAN number,” he said. “They want to be included in the lucky draw, so they ask for the bill and we provide it accordingly.”

From a business perspective, Lama says issuing bills is neither difficult nor burdensome.

“There is no difficulty in issuing bills. It is not a big deal,” he said. “Bills must be issued. It helps the government collect taxes and protects consumers from being cheated, so this awareness is essential.”

‘Customers who never cared about bills now ask because they could win Rs 1 million’

Monika Poudel, a supervisor at SalesBerry department store in Mid-Baneshwar, has also noticed a significant increase in customer awareness about bills.

“Previously, customers did not pay much attention to bills. But now, more people are asking for them,” Poudel said. “Many ask out of curiosity, saying they heard they could win Rs 1 million by taking a bill.”

Although she has not noticed a significant change in the number of customers since the reward scheme was introduced, she has seen an increase in questions and awareness about the programme.

According to Poudel, most customers now prefer digital payments over cash.

“People do not carry much cash these days. Most pay through QR codes,” she said.

When customers pay digitally, the transaction details are automatically recorded in the government system, making it easier for them to participate in the reward scheme. Customers who pay in cash, however, need to enter their bill details into the system themselves.

The habit of taking and checking bills has also benefited businesses by helping correct human errors at billing counters.

“Sometimes mistakes can happen when we are working in a hurry,” Poudel said. “But customers take the bill home and check it. If there is a mistake or they have been charged more than they should have been, they come back and we correct it. That helps us too.”

‘Ninety-five percent of customers now ask for bills’

Gyanu Tiwari, owner of Pokharel Store in Buddhanagar, says around 95 percent of her customers now ask for bills themselves.

“About 95 percent of customers ask for bills now,” Tiwari said. “Only those who are unaware or very young children generally don’t ask. Almost all informed and aware customers do.”

Although bills have traditionally been uncommon for small retail purchases worth less than Rs 100, she says digital payments have made the process easier.

“People don’t usually get bills for purchases below Rs 100, but these days payments are often made through QR codes,” she said. “Since QR payments are recorded, billing is also being done through that system.”

Tiwari says both sellers and buyers have a responsibility to ensure that transactions are properly billed.

Businesses must issue bills and consumers should ask for them, she said, because failing to do so increases the risk of tax evasion.

She believes the government’s reward scheme is a positive beginning.

“The government is doing something good. It is gradually getting started,” she said. “Eventually, I think the government will bring everyone into the billing system.”

Bini Khas, owner of Maya Cosmetics in New Baneshwar, has also noticed more customers asking for bills.

She says customers became more conscious about bills after the taxpayer incentive programme was introduced.

“Previously, there wasn’t much of a practice of asking for bills like this,” Khas said. “Now, those who know about the programme ask for bills themselves and take them.”

She said her shop started issuing bills more regularly after the government announced the programme and now provides VAT bills to customers.

More publicity needed for the reward scheme

Luma Basnet, who was shopping at a cosmetics store in New Baneshwar, was also seen asking for a bill.

A recent graduate working in sales and marketing, Basnet says she has always asked for bills because she believes in accountability.

“I strongly believe in accountability. I need to know where and how much I am spending, so I have always taken bills,” she said. “Whether it is groceries, cosmetics or clothes, I take bills for everything.”

She only recently learned about the government’s reward scheme, which offers consumers a chance to win up to Rs 1 million.

But she believes many consumers are still unaware of the programme.

“There are still many people who don’t know about it,” she said. “Whenever I meet people, I tell them about the programme and encourage them to participate because it is for our benefit.”

Basnet believes the government needs to do more to promote the reward scheme, particularly among people who do not use smartphones or are less familiar with digital technology.

“There needs to be much more advertising and awareness campaigns,” she said. “Some people are more traditional, don’t use smartphones and don’t spend much time on their phones. They need to be reached and encouraged personally.”

Many consumers still unaware of the reward scheme

Despite the government offering prizes of up to Rs 1 million to consumers who obtain bills for their purchases, many people are still unaware of the reward scheme.

Anisa Shrestha, who was shopping at Bhat-Bhateni, said the scheme was a good initiative but lacked sufficient publicity.

She has always made it a habit to ask for bills but only recently learned about the government’s reward scheme.

“I have always kept bills for all my purchases up to date,” she said. “But I only recently found out about the government’s reward scheme.”

She said she usually shops at Bhat-Bhateni, where bills are issued automatically, but has found that some smaller shops provide VAT bills while others do not.

Asking for a bill after making a purchase is both a consumer right and responsibility, she said. But for people to benefit from the government’s new initiative, they first need to know about it.

“This is a new programme, and it can be taken forward in an innovative and effective way,” she said. “If the government uses the right communication channels, it would be much easier for people to learn about it.”

More than just a chance to win

The government’s reward scheme is intended not only to encourage consumers to ask for bills but also to make the market more transparent and curb tax evasion.

The scheme can help consumers protect themselves from being overcharged while encouraging businesses to become more accountable and strengthening the state’s tax collection system.

The growing use of digital payments has also made the reward scheme easier to implement.

However, despite the chance to win up to Rs 1 million, many consumers remain unaware of the programme. Expanding and improving public awareness will be crucial if the reward scheme is to reach its full potential.

The government will also need to find ways to reach people who have limited access to technology and those who are less familiar with digital systems.

Ultimately, asking for a bill should not be seen merely as a chance to win a prize. It is also a simple act of consumer awareness and a small but important contribution to building a more transparent and accountable economy.

title.rendered: Deeprose Gurung’s ‘Samaya Yatra’ exhibition on display at Shashi Art Gallery

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Artist Deeprose Gurung’s solo exhibition, Samaya Yatra (Journey of Time), is currently on display at Shashi Art Gallery in Balaju, featuring paintings that explore women, relationships, memory and childhood experiences.

The exhibition, which runs from August 15 to 29, presents predominantly female figures alongside recurring motifs including parrots, moons, paper planes and paper boats. Red is a prominent colour throughout the works.

Gurung said his focus on women is influenced by the women around him, including his mother, sisters and friends.

“I am surrounded by women in such a way that I cannot separate myself from the feminine energy,” he said.

The artist uses parrots as a recurring symbol alongside female figures, associating the birds with communication, trust and emotional expression. He said he sees similarities between women and parrots in their ability to communicate openly when they feel comfortable and trust others.

The paintings also incorporate moons and childhood objects such as paper planes and boats. According to Gurung, the objects represent memories and the imagination associated with childhood, while the planes and boats suggest ideas of flying and travelling.

One of the works in the exhibition features a male nude figure, differing from the predominantly female subjects in the collection. The painting also incorporates the artist’s palette as part of the composition, highlighting the process of creating the work.

Samjhana Rajbhandari, mentor and director of Shashi Art Studio, described Gurung’s use of lines as one of the distinguishing features of his work. “The works of Deeprose are really profound, and the way he uses lines in his figures marks him as a distinct emerging artist of Nepal,” Rajbhandari said.

Gurung developed much of his artistic practice at Shashi Art Studio, which was established in 2010 and later evolved into a shared studio space for emerging artists.

The exhibition at Shashi Art Gallery provides a collection of Gurung’s recent works, bringing together recurring themes of femininity, communication, memory and personal experience.

title.rendered: Mocked Chinese animated film ‘Niu Lai’ becomes unexpected box office hit

content.rendered:
Chinese animated film Niu Lai, initially mocked online for its poor animation quality, has unexpectedly become a box-office and internet sensation in China and beyond.

According to Global Times, the film had earned more than 45 million yuan ($6.7 million) by Sunday. It was released in Chinese cinemas on August 5 and earned only 342 yuan on its opening day. Its total earnings stood at around 7,700 yuan during its first 10 days before ticket sales surged from August 14.

The film’s crude animation, stiff character movements and unusual storyline initially drew widespread criticism online. Some users described it as one of the most basic films ever released in cinemas, while others said they wanted to watch it simply to see how bad it was.

The online ridicule has since generated curiosity, memes and merchandise, helping drive audiences to cinemas. Fan-made posters have even appeared at theatres, while Douyin users have produced numerous clips and memes based on the film.

The trend has also spread outside China. Two independently organised screenings in San Francisco reportedly sold out, while distributors in Singapore are considering bringing the film to local cinemas. Hong Kong audiences have also called for its release.

Cultural researcher Zhang Peng said the film’s international popularity represents an unusual form of cultural export driven not by sophisticated production or traditional marketing, but by memes, curiosity and global internet culture.

title.rendered: Dhurmus-Suntali to launch new comedy series filmed in the US

content.rendered:
KATHMANDU

Popular Nepali comedy duo Sitaram Kattel ‘Dhurmus’ and Kunjana Ghimire ‘Suntali’ have produced a new comedy series in the United States.

Titled Ma Ta Marchhu Ki Kya Ho, the series has been filmed in and around Raleigh, North Carolina, including Cary, Holly Springs, High Point and Greensboro. Kattel, who has directed the series, said it will be released weekly through the Dhurmus Suntali YouTube channel.

The series is scheduled to air every Friday at 8:15 pm Nepal time and 10:30 am local US time.

Kattel and Ghimire will appear as Dhurmus and Suntali in the series. Veteran comedian Mohan Mishra also features in a leading role, marking his return to acting after a long break. Mishra is known for his work in popular comedy programmes including Hos Prasad and Mr. Fantus.

The series also features Dinesh Karki, Shankar Raj Wagle, Sanyam Lamichhane, Monica Chaulagain Chuda Dhimal and Dharma Bharti. The couple’s daughter, Subihani Kattel, will make her acting debut as a child artist.

According to the production team, the series will use comedy and satire to portray the experiences of Nepalis living in the United States, including their struggles, opportunities, achievements, cultural and social challenges, family relationships and efforts to preserve Nepali identity.

The title is derived from one of Kattel’s previously popular dialogues and catchphrases.

title.rendered: 5,068 new industries registered, 1,938 shut down in Madhesh last FY

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, August 25

A total 5,068 new industries were registered in the Madhesh Province last fiscal year 2082-83 BS (2025-26) during that period, 1,101 were officially listed in Parsa followed by 777 in Dhanusha, 639 in Bara, 636 in Sarlahi, 554 in Siraha, 533 in Rautahat, 514 in Mahottari and 314 in Saptari, said Province Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Tourism.

Upendra Kumar Mahato, Information Officer of the Ministry, said that last fiscal year, 7,540 industries underwent a renewal process. As Mahato said, in the last fiscal year, 6,122 private firms and 18 partnership firms were newly registered, and 11,144 were renewed. However, a total of 1,938 industries and business enterprises were closed or deregistered during the fiscal year. Of them, 1,117 were from the commerce sector.

The closures have been attributed to the ongoing economic slowdown and other challenges, including liquidity constraints and a shortage of investment capital. Information Officer Mahato said that Rs 52.649 million in revenue was generated from the registration and renewal of industries and business enterprises.

title.rendered: These 11 MPs will ask questions to PM in parliament tomorrow

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

A direct question-and-answer session with the Prime Minister will be held during Wednesday’s House of Representatives meeting, with 11 MPs set to question PM Balen Shah.

According to the Parliament Secretariat, ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) MPs Samikshya Baskota, Krishna Hari Budhathoki, and Amaresh Kumar Singh will ask questions.

Main opposition Nepali Congress Chief Whip Basana Thapa and MP Geeta Gurung are also set to question the PM.

CPN-UML Chief Whip Ain Bahadur Mahar and MP Ganesh Singh Thagunna have registered to ask questions, as have Nepal Communist Party (NCP) MPs Barsaman Pun and Prakash Kumar Hamal.

Shram Sanskriti Party parliamentary leader Harkaraj Rai and Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) Chief Whip Khushbu Oli will also participate.

The MPs have already submitted their intended questions in writing to the Parliament Secretariat.

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal had earlier fixed the schedule for this direct Q&A session during the House meeting on August 17.

Rule 56 of the House of Representatives Regulations provides for such a direct question-and-answer program, stating that the Speaker shall set aside the first hour of one meeting during the first week of every month for MPs to ask the Prime Minister questions on important matters directly related to his office. Accordingly, Wednesday’s session was scheduled.

Under Rule 57, such sessions may be broadcast live through government and other media.

Rule 58 requires MPs wishing to question the Prime Minister to submit written notice of their question’s subject to the Speaker at least three days before the sitting. Speaker Ghimire had given MPs until August 21 to register their questions, and 11 MPs did so.

Up to 15 MPs could have asked questions, but only 11 registered. The Speaker had allocated slots based on party representation, with one MP guaranteed per party and the remaining slots distributed proportionally. Under this formula, RSP could have had up to seven MPs ask questions, but only three registered.

Rule 59 stipulates that the Speaker will decide whether a submitted question is admissible, with other procedures for the session determined by the Speaker. Rule 60 states that no discussion will be held in the House regarding the Prime Minister’s answers under this chapter.

title.rendered: Nepal becomes finalist in Miss World’s Talent Round

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Miss World 2026 is currently underway in Vietnam, with 111 contestants competing across various categories. Nepal is represented by Miss Nepal Luna Luitel.

Nepal did not advance in the Head-to-Head, Top Model, or Sports categories. However, it has made the finals in the Talent round, where Nepal is among the 23 finalists. If Luna wins this category, Nepal will advance directly to the top 40, the country’s biggest achievement in the competition so far.

According to Miss World’s voting website, Luna currently ranks seventh in the Asia and Oceania region’s “People’s Choice” category with 25,319 votes. Nepal will need more votes to move up in this category.

As of this report, Cambodia leads the “People’s Choice” category. Results for the Talent and Top Model rounds will be announced on August 28.

As in every Miss World competition, Nepal’s main goal this year is to win the “Beauty With Purpose” category, a title Nepal has won several times before.

This year, Luna is presenting a project related to education, health, and entrepreneurship from Falebas in Parbat district. Built with an investment of nearly Rs 15 million, the project has Nepal hopeful of winning the “Beauty With Purpose” title, a hope Luna herself shares.

Nepal’s focus is now centred on this category, where it is seen as a strong contender. The Miss World 2026 grand finale will be held on September 5.

title.rendered: Traffic halted on 7 different road sections across country

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Roads have been obstructed in several places in the country due to flooding, landslides, deposition of debris and erosion by rivers following rains. According to police, different road sections have been affected due to this in Kavrepalanchok, Sindhuli, Makawanpur, Nuwakot, Ilam, Sindhupalchok, Rasuwa and Rukum West as of 10 am today.

Due to the potential risk of flooding on the BP Highway running through Kavrepalanchok via Khurkot–Nepalthok–Katunje Bensi–Sindhuli, all vehicular movement has been stopped from 6 pm to 4 am. However, vehicles will be allowed to operate from 4 am to 6 pm. Similarly, due to the rain, operation of all types of vehicles has been prohibited on the Kanti Lokpath in Makawanpur from 5 pm to 5 am.

Movement of public and private vehicles, except for vehicles on essential services, has been banned from 10 pm to 5 am on the Tokha-Chhahare road section in Nuwakot. The police have reported that the Mechi Highway in Rajduwali, Ilam Municipality-9, has been completely blocked due to the rain. Vehicles cannot pass because the road is muddy, and it has been mentioned that there is an alternative route at that place.

The road on the Araniko Highway in Liping Bazaar, Bhotechaur-2, Sindhupalchok, has been completely blocked due to a landslide, along with debris and stones deposited by the Khahare River on August 21. Similarly, the Trishuli–Mailung–Syafrubesi road section in Rasuwa’s Uttar Gaya Rural Municipality–5 Khalte has been completely blocked after the Trishuli River eroded the road from below.

The Jajarkot-Dolpa road section of the Bheri Corridor in Rukum West’s Aathbiskot Municipality-6, Rijegad Khola, is completely blocked after stones and soil mixed with debris fell onto the road. Nepal Police has advised taking precautions when travelling on these roads, as they are getting blocked and risks are increasing due to the rain.
