title.rendered: Months after mass removals, hundreds of key public posts remain vacant

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

The government removed 1,594 office-bearers from various boards, committees and public institutions in April, but only around 200 key public posts have been filled so far.

The positions were vacated after the government introduced the Special Provision Ordinance on the Removal of Public Office Bearers, 2026.

The prolonged vacancies have affected the functioning of various state bodies. Work at some commissions has come to a standstill, while institutions with vacant registrar positions have been left without budgets, policies and programmes.

Some appointments have also failed to meet the inclusive representation requirements prescribed by the Constitution and other prevailing laws.

Although the ordinance was introduced with the stated aim of ending political appointments and making public institutions free from political interference, the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) has faced allegations of appointing its own party workers to some of the key public posts.

Some appointments have also been overturned by courts over eligibility and procedural issues.

On August 20, the Supreme Court scrapped the appointment of Maheshwar Bhakta Shrestha as executive chairperson of Nepal Airlines Corporation. The court ruled that the decision to appoint a person who had exceeded the prescribed age limit was prima facie unlawful.

Candidates for appointment as executive chairperson are required to meet various qualifications, including being no older than 65.

A joint bench of Justices Sunil Kumar Pokharel and Balkrishna Dhakal overturned the Cabinet’s July 14 decision to appoint Shrestha as executive chairperson with responsibility for the duties of general manager, stating that the appointment did not comply with the relevant legal provision.

This is not the first appointment made under the government led by RSP senior leader Balen Shah to be overturned by the court.

Earlier, the Supreme Court also annulled the appointment of Dr Deepak Prasad Bastola as a member of the Nepal Airlines Corporation board.

On June 12, the court scrapped the decision to appoint Bastola, citing problems with his eligibility and the appointment process. The Minister for Culture and Tourism had appointed Bastola and four others to the corporation’s board on May 14.

Upendra Bahadur Karki had filed a petition challenging the appointment, arguing that the government had disregarded the selection committee’s recommendation, which had ranked him first. The court observed that the minister had made a baseless “pick and choose” decision.

The government has so far filled 198 of the positions that became vacant following the ordinance.

title.rendered: Kathmandu Valley Mayors’ Forum to meet PM over waste management issues

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, August 25

The Kathmandu Valley Mayors’ Forum is preparing to meet Prime Minister Balen Shah to brief him on issues related to waste management.

A meeting of the forum held on Tuesday decided to seek an appointment with Prime Minister Shah as soon as possible to draw his attention to waste management, management of streetlight charges, land-use rights for land being used by local governments, and arrangements for land needed for waste management, according to forum chair and Mayor of Lalitpur Metropolitan City Chiribabu Maharjan.

The forum said it would also raise concerns over the conduct of lawmaker Ashika Tamang towards its office-bearers and members during a meeting on waste management held at Singha Durbar on August 21.

The forum also discussed the implementation of an agreement reached between the then government and Nep Waste for waste management in the Kathmandu Valley when Shah was mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City. It also considered whether the agreement should instead be scrapped to clear the way for alternative waste-management arrangements.

The forum concluded that waste management in the Kathmandu Valley is a shared concern and responsibility of all three tiers of government.

title.rendered: Pokhara business leaders, UAE ambassador discuss regular Pokhara-Dubai flights

content.rendered:
Pokhara, August 25

Tourism and business leaders from Pokhara have held discussions with UAE Ambassador to Nepal Abdullah bin Saeed Mubarak Jarwan Al Shamsi on ways to make regular flights between Pokhara and Dubai successful and sustainable.

The participants said establishing regular flights from Pokhara to Dubai would be another important milestone for Pokhara, Gandaki Province and Nepal, as it would connect the city to a wider international network.

The business leaders told the ambassador that connecting Pokhara to Dubai would be historic for the city’s tourism sector and sought his support in making the flights successful.

Those participating in the discussions included former president of the Pokhara Tourism Council and former president of the Nepal Association of Tour and Travel Agents (NATTA) Gandaki Province, Pomanarayan Shrestha; former Nepal Tourism Board board member Basudev Tripathi; Hotel Association Pokhara President Laxman Subedi; Hotel Association Gandaki Province President Hari Sharma Gaire; Pokhara Chamber of Commerce and Industry President Gokarna Karki; NATTA Gandaki Province executive member Bijay Paudel; and NATTA central president Bharat Jung Pandey, among others.

Tourism entrepreneurs described the launch of regular flights between Pokhara and Dubai as a historic and significant achievement for the development of tourism in Nepal, Gandaki Province and Pokhara.

They pledged full support and cooperation from the private sector, Gandaki provincial government, local governments and other concerned stakeholders to ensure the flights continue and become successful.

During the meeting, the business leaders also urged the ambassador to immediately remove the requirement for Nepali tourists travelling to Dubai on tourist visas to obtain a police clearance certificate.

They acknowledged that it might not be possible to immediately remove the police clearance requirement for Nepali workers travelling to Dubai, but requested that the requirement for tourists be waived without delay.

The ambassador assured the business leaders that he would provide possible support and coordination on the matter.

title.rendered: Government begins study to set sugarcane minimum support price

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

The government has begun preparations to set the minimum support price for sugarcane for the current year with the aim of ensuring fair prices for sugarcane farmers.

The Department of Agriculture has started a field study in 11 Tarai districts where sugarcane farming is widespread.

A department team is collecting data on farmers’ actual production costs and other expenses in Sunsari, Morang, Siraha, Dhanusha, Mahottari, Sarlahi, Rautahat, Nawalparasi, Bardiya, Kailali and Kanchanpur.

Department Director General Prakash Kumar Sanjel said a new support price would be proposed based on the actual data collected through the survey.

He said the ongoing study would also closely assess changes in transportation, production and other miscellaneous costs compared with previous years.

After completing the study report, the department will submit it to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment for further discussion and consensus, Sanjel said.

The Cabinet will then make the final decision on the purchase price of sugarcane and the amount of subsidy the government will provide to farmers, he added.

The government sets minimum support prices for crops such as sugarcane and paddy every year to protect farmers from significant losses when agricultural commodity prices decline in the market and to safeguard their investments.

Last year, the government set the purchase price of sugarcane at Rs 620 per quintal and provided farmers with a subsidy of Rs 70 per quintal.

title.rendered: Country singer Jessica Lynn arrived Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

American country singer-songwriter Jessica Lynn has arrived in Kathmandu for a week of professional exchange, mentorship, and collaboration with Nepali musicians and music industry professionals.

The program, running from Aug 24 to 29, is part of “Arts and Music Envoy,” an initiative sponsored by the US State Department’s Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs.

Throughout the week, Lynn will engage with Nepali singers, musicians, songwriters, producers, artist managers, and other music professionals through interactive sessions on songwriting, the music business, digital platforms, copyright, and the broader music industry. Nepali artists and professionals will gain fresh perspectives on opportunities to collaborate with markets, audiences, and American music industry counterparts.

As Nepal’s music sector continues to grow, connecting its creative community with international industry perspectives could strengthen the sector’s ties to wider markets and audiences.

Acting US Ambassador Scott Urbom said the US-Nepal partnership extends into the arts, adding that the US is proud to share American cultural excellence this year as it marks 250 years of American independence.

He said music is a powerful medium connecting the people of both countries, and that the US is glad to contribute to the growth and creativity of Nepal’s expanding music industry by creating opportunities for American and Nepali artists and audiences to learn from each other, share perspectives, and build meaningful professional relationships.

The “Arts and Music Envoy” program will conclude with a public concert on Saturday, Aug 29, at The Plaza Convention Centre in Pulchowk, Lalitpur. Alongside Jessica Lynn, Nepali artists Raato Rani and Ujjan Shakya will also perform.

The evening will also feature a special fusion performance by Lynn and acclaimed sarangi player Kiran Nepali, a past participant in a US government exchange program.

title.rendered: Business confidence at 36-year low, says FNCCI President Shrestha

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Anjan Shrestha, president of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI), has said business confidence has fallen to its weakest level in the past 36 years.

Speaking at the opening ceremony of the 18th NADA Auto Show 2026, Shrestha said his 36 years of experience in the business sector had led him to conclude that business sentiment was currently at its lowest point.

He said the economy was facing challenges and the market remained sluggish.

“Overall demand has not increased, operating industries and businesses have become difficult, and businesspeople are facing difficult circumstances. Business confidence is at its weakest point in history,” he said.

Shrestha said the new government had failed to translate its budget commitments into action.

“The government has pledged through the budget to make the economy dynamic, increase per capita income to $3,000 within five to seven years, build a $100 billion economy and create 1.2 million jobs,” he said. “But the budget announcements have not moved forward.”

He said the government had failed to introduce strategies needed to implement those commitments and stressed that the time had come to restructure the economy.

Shrestha also highlighted the contribution of the automobile sector to government revenue. According to data he presented, Nepal imported automobiles worth Rs 106 billion in the last fiscal year, generating Rs 81 billion in revenue for the state.

“The government should prioritise a sector that alone contributes Rs 81 billion out of total revenue of Rs 1.2 trillion,” he said, calling for greater clarity in the government’s approach towards the automobile sector.

Shrestha said domestic industries should be established to reduce automobile imports and that such industries needed government protection.

“Some industries have been established, but the government has not paid attention to them or understood their problems,” he said.

He also criticised the government’s focus on reopening industries that have remained closed for decades, saying it had failed to pay sufficient attention to industries that are currently operating.

“While picking up what is on the ground, I want to caution the government that it should not end up dropping what it already has in its pocket,” he said.

title.rendered: NADA Auto Show kicks off, 53 brands of vehicles on display

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, Aug 25

With Nepal’s vehicle market expanding, NADA Auto Show 2026 has opened at Bhrikutimandap in Kathmandu, giving special priority to automobile parts and vehicles produced or assembled domestically.

Vice President Ramsahay Yadav inaugurated the 18th edition of the show, organised by the NADA Automobiles Association of Nepal.

The show features 53 brands across two-wheelers, four-wheelers, and commercial vehicles, with more than a dozen and a half new models being launched or displayed.

One of the main attractions this year is the “Yatri P-2,” an electric scooter manufactured in Nepal. Organisers say placing a Nepali-made vehicle alongside international brands in the same exhibition reflects the changing landscape of Nepal’s automobile industry.

Marking NADA’s 50th anniversary, this year’s show gives separate priority to vehicles and automobile parts made or assembled in Nepal, not just foreign brands.

A “Made in Nepal, Made for Nepal” pavilion has been set up at the venue, showcasing vehicles and automobile parts produced or assembled in Nepal.

According to NADA, around eight Nepali manufacturers are taking part in this section, including companies making electric motorcycles, automotive batteries, lubricants, and helmets. Alongside Yatri, Nepali producers such as Asian Wiring, Kohinoor Plastic Industries, Nepal Lube Oil, and Purwanchal Lube Oil will showcase their products.

NADA said the goal of giving Nepali products a dedicated space is to bring the country’s growing automobile manufacturing and industrial activity closer to consumers.

NADA President Surendra Kumar Upreti said the potential for domestic production in Nepal’s automobile sector is growing.

“The message we want to give is this: Nepal is no longer limited to just importing vehicles. We are gradually moving toward self-reliance and domestic enterprise,” he said.

He noted that over NADA’s 50-year history, its activities have expanded beyond vehicle sales, purchase, and servicing to include parts supply and manufacturing as well.

According to NADA, the organisation was established five decades ago to represent vehicle dealers, but has since grown into a representative body covering vehicle sales, assembly, financing, insurance, servicing, and parts supply businesses.

Brands on display

Passenger cars: Riddara, Aion, JMEV, Tata EV, Suzuki, Deepal, Avatr, Foton, Skoda, Nami, Changan, Proton, BYD, Geely, Omoda, Jaecoo, Jetour, MG, GWM, Leapmotor, MHero, Skywell, and Wuling, among others.

Light commercial vehicles: Foton, Sokon, King Long, Higer, Farizon, Jinbei, Tata Motors Commercial Vehicles, DFSK, Kama, New Gonow Auto, Aucwell, Diego, Skyworth EV, Dongfeng, Kawei Auto, Feidi, and Ekta Motors.

Two-wheelers: Royal Enfield, Yatri, Hero, Vida, Yamaha Racing, Vespa-Aprilia, Ampere, MetaEV, Zonsen, QJ Motor, Miche Auto, and Revolt, among others.

Beyond vehicles, more than 200 stalls will feature banks and financial institutions, insurance, auto parts, and garage equipment. The exhibition is divided into sections for four-wheelers, two-wheelers, financial institutions, auto parts and garage equipment, the “Made in Nepal, Made for Nepal” pavilion, and an international business pavilion.

Entry costs Rs 200 for the general public and Rs 150 for students, with tickets available online via the Khalti app. NADA said the venue also offers parking, traffic management, an information desk, a media desk, a cafeteria, and emergency health services.

With a large number of new foreign models displayed alongside Nepali-made products on the same platform, the show is being seen as a sign that Nepal’s auto market is moving beyond pure import dependence toward domestic production.

title.rendered: 250 girls under 10 raped in Nepal in a year, most perpetrators known to victims

content.rendered:
Kathmandu

A total of 250 girls under the age of 10 were raped in Nepal on average each year over the past five fiscal years, according to Nepal Police data. Most cases reportedly involved perpetrators known to the victims.

A recent case in Bara has once again highlighted the vulnerability of young children. A three-year-old girl went missing from a squatter settlement in Jitpur Simara Sub-Metropolitan City-1 on August 16. Her body was found two days later inside an abandoned house in Bhaktinagar.

Police arrested a 16-year-old boy in connection with the case after a trained sniffer dog helped investigators identify a suspect. Police said the teenager, who worked as a helper on a vehicle, confessed to raping and killing the girl after luring her with chocolate. The vehicle’s 24-year-old driver was also arrested.

According to Madhes Province Police chief DIG Om Adhikari, the accused teenager was acquainted with the victim. The girl frequently visited the driver’s house, where the teenager also went. Police believe the acquaintance was exploited to lure the child.

The Bara case is among several recent cases involving children. In Morang, a 31-year-old ward secretary was arrested and sent to prison on charges of raping a girl. In Rolpa, a teacher was arrested for allegedly raping a 12-year-old student after luring her to a secluded location.

Nepal Police data show that 268 girls under 10 were raped in fiscal year 2078/79 BS, followed by 259 in 2079/80 BS, 252 in 2080/81 BS, 217 in 2081/82 BS and 221 in 2082/83 BS.

Girls aged 11 to 16 constitute the largest group of rape victims. Police recorded 963 victims in this age group in fiscal year 2078/79 BS, 944 in 2079/80 BS, 1,009 in 2080/81 BS, 931 in 2081/82 BS and 966 in 2082/83 BS.

Overall, Nepal recorded 2,395 rape victims in fiscal year 2082/83 BS. Of them, 1,510 were girls under 18, while 885 were women aged 18 and above.

Police officials say most rape cases involving minors are committed by people known to the victims, including relatives, teachers, neighbours and acquaintances. Children are often lured through promises, gifts or other forms of persuasion.

Former DIG Hemant Malla said the pattern of perpetrators being known to victims is particularly common in cases involving minors.

Police have urged parents to remain vigilant about where their children go, whom they meet and changes in their behaviour.

The recent Bara case has also triggered calls for tougher punishment, including the death penalty. However, Nepal’s existing criminal law does not provide for capital punishment.

Under Section 219 of the National Penal Code Act, 2017, rape of a girl under 10, a person who is completely incapacitated or a woman above 70 carries life imprisonment. Rape of girls aged 10 to 14 carries 18 to 20 years in prison, while rape of girls aged 14 to 16 carries 12 to 14 years.

For victims aged 16 to 18, the punishment is 10 to 12 years in prison, while rape of women aged 18 and above carries seven to 10 years’ imprisonment.

title.rendered: India’s Vice President honours Nepali musician Saurav Sharma

content.rendered:

Young Nepali musician Saurav Sharma was honoured with the Youth Goodwill Ambassador Honour at MALHAR 2026 in New Delhi, India, on August 21.

Speaking at the event, the Vice President congratulated Sharma and said young people could serve as bridges of friendship between India and other countries through music and culture.

“Music is one of India’s greatest forms of soft power. It transcends language and borders and creates bonds between people without the need for translation,” he said.

The event was held under the patronage of Harsh Vardhan Shringla, a member of the Rajya Sabha and former Foreign Secretary of India.

Shringla also highlighted Sharma’s connection with India, noting that the Nepali musician has been a regular visitor to the Sri Sathya Sai Ashram in Puttaparthi, where he has performed on several occasions.

MALHAR 2026 brought together young audiences and prominent classical artistes, including vocalist Pt. Ulhas Kashalkar and Kathak exponent Pt. Rajendra Gangani.

The organisers said Sharma’s recognition reflected the role of young people, music and culture in strengthening the longstanding people-to-people and cultural ties between Nepal and India.

title.rendered: Medical report submitted to parliament saying PM Balen Shah needs to wear dark glasses

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

A letter accompanied by a medical examination report stating that Prime Minister Balen Shah needs to wear dark glasses has been submitted to the Federal Parliament Secretariat.

Ekaram Giri, joint secretary and spokesperson for the Parliament Secretariat, confirmed that the letter, along with the medical report recommending that Prime Minister Shah wear dark glasses, had been received.

Earlier, Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal (DP) had instructed lawmakers, through their chief whips and whips, not to wear dark glasses in Parliament. He had said that lawmakers would need to submit a medical report if they had a medical reason for wearing them.

Accordingly, the Prime Minister’s office has submitted the letter and medical report stating that Shah needs to wear dark glasses.

A direct question-and-answer session with the Prime Minister is scheduled to take place during Wednesday’s House of Representatives meeting, where 11 lawmakers will question Shah.

Rule 56 of the House of Representatives Regulations provides for a direct question-and-answer session with the Prime Minister. It states that the Speaker shall allocate the first hour of a meeting on any day during the first week of each month for questions on important matters directly related to the Prime Minister or his areas of responsibility.

In accordance with the provision, the session has been scheduled for Wednesday.

Rule 57 allows the direct question-and-answer session to be broadcast live through government and other media outlets.

Under Rule 58, lawmakers wishing to question the Prime Minister must submit written information about the subject of their questions to the Speaker at least three days before the meeting.

Accordingly, Speaker Aryal had given lawmakers until August 21 to register their questions for the Prime Minister. Eleven lawmakers subsequently registered their questions.

The letter containing the medical report was submitted to the Parliament Secretariat ahead of Prime Minister Shah’s appearance at the House for the session, stating that he needs to wear dark glasses while attending the programme.

title.rendered: Crisis deepens in Nepali Congress as 15th general convention nears

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

With the scheduled date for the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention drawing closer, the party has yet to resolve its political and legal disputes.

While one faction is waiting for the Supreme Court’s decision, another is calling for a political agreement to settle the dispute before the court ruling and create an environment for the general convention.

The Nepali Congress has scheduled ward-level conventions for September 9 as part of the 15th General Convention. However, the establishment-opposing faction has demanded that all convention activities be halted until the Supreme Court delivers its final verdict.

The faction has taken this position after the Supreme Court allowed a review of its earlier verdict in a case concerning the party’s official status.

Former vice-president Purna Bahadur Khadka said the Central Working Committee’s decision to move ahead with the 15th General Convention was against both the need for party unity and the Supreme Court’s decision to review the case.

“The decision recently taken by the Central Working Committee formed through the special general convention to move ahead with the 15th General Convention is clearly against both the historic need for complete party unity and the Supreme Court’s order to review the case,” he said.

Min Bishwakarma, coordinator of the publicity committee of the establishment-opposing faction, also said the convention process could not be unilaterally advanced while the case was sub-judice.

“When a case is pending in court, one side cannot naturally move the matter forward unilaterally,” he said. “But the process has been taken forward. Our side will file an application with the court on the matter.”

Little progress in dialogue

Although efforts are reportedly underway to resolve the dispute through dialogue, there has been little substantive communication between the leadership that emerged from the special general convention and the former leadership.

President Gagan Kumar Thapa has said he sought time for dialogue, but that it was not made available. Former president Sher Bahadur Deuba, meanwhile, appears to be waiting for the court’s final decision before engaging in discussions.

A conversation Deuba had with leaders who visited his Chundevi residence on Sunday also indicated his position on dialogue with Thapa. Nain Singh Mahar, who has recently taken on a mediating role, wrote on Facebook on Sunday that he had raised the need for a meeting between the two leaders.

“I also pointed out the need for a meeting and dialogue between President Gagan Kumar Thapa and him,” Mahar wrote. “He said he was making efforts to resolve the issue and suggested that we move forward after the court’s decision.”

The establishment faction expects former president Deuba to play a coordinating role in resolving the dispute.

General Secretary Pradip Paudel said efforts were being made to engage Deuba in dialogue and that the party was hopeful he would help with coordination.

“We are trying to meet and have a dialogue with the outgoing president. We are somewhat more hopeful about him,” Paudel told Onlinekhabar. “We expect that after meeting him, he will do something for coordination. We are also talking to others.”

Paudel stressed that the dispute should be resolved through political agreement rather than the courts.

“Our position is that we should resolve the party’s problems through mutual agreement and hold the convention at the scheduled time, rather than through the judicial process,” he said. “We will try to hold discussions and reach an agreement during the remaining 14 days.”

Paudel also said it was not appropriate for a political party to take its internal disputes to court.

“A party that advocates for the rule of law and the system of governance cannot naturally take its own internal problems to court,” he said.

Arguing that the party’s problems should ultimately be resolved through the general convention, Poudel said the establishment faction was ready to take any necessary steps to ensure a fair convention.

Nepali Congress leadership has recently appeared open to forming an organising committee to ensure the convention is conducted fairly.

Asked whether the party was prepared to form such a committee, Poudel said, “The leadership should be under the current president. We agree on everything else.”

‘A mechanism can be formed for management, not an organising committee’

Nepali Congress spokesperson Devraj Chalise said the party has no tradition of forming a general convention organising committee. However, he said a mechanism could be created for convention management and coordination.

“There is no provision for an organising committee in our party tradition. An organising committee will not be formed,” Chalise said. “But it can be given any name. The point is to seek advice and guidance from the leaders.”

He said any mechanism formed to facilitate an agreement would still have to operate within the party statute.

“If we use the provisions already in the statute, whatever name we give it, the issue ultimately concerns its role. We are ready to give that role,” he said. “Neither leaders nor cadres have the flexibility to amend or go beyond the statute.”

Chalise also said leaders and party workers who were left out during the membership update could be collectively included on the basis of a political agreement before the ward conventions begin.

‘General convention should be held under Deuba’s leadership’

The establishment-opposing faction has maintained that the 15th General Convention should be held under the leadership of former president Deuba as part of efforts to restore party unity.

The faction had also decided at a national gathering held in the final week of Shrawan to organise the convention under Deuba’s leadership.

NP Saud, a leader considered close to Deuba, said the current dispute should be resolved by using the 14th General Convention as the basis.

He said that because both sides had participated in the 14th General Convention, it should be recognised as the legitimate basis for moving ahead and creating an environment in which all sides could be included in the next convention.

“The case is before the court for review. Before it is settled, if an agreement is to be reached, both sides should be included since both participated in the 14th General Convention,” Saud told Onlinekhabar.

He also said holding the convention under Deuba’s leadership would provide a level playing field because the former president would not contest the upcoming election.

“Another important point is that Sher Bahadur Deuba, the president elected by the 14th General Convention, is not contesting himself,” Saud said. “Therefore, everyone gets an equal playing field. Everyone gets equal ground for competition.”

Saud said party unity could be achieved by recognising the leadership elected by the 14th General Convention. Otherwise, he said, the party would have to proceed according to the Supreme Court’s final decision on the party’s official status.

“The leadership elected by the 14th General Convention should be established. That will bring unity,” he said. “Otherwise, we will proceed according to whatever conclusion the review reaches.”

Three options proposed for unity

Nain Singh Mahar, who is leading the ‘Connecting Country and Congress’ campaign, believes the political leadership should take steps to resolve the dispute before the court delivers its decision.

He said he proposed three options to President Thapa during a recent meeting aimed at promoting party unity.

“I met Gagan in Gyaneshwar on the evening of the 20th. We spoke for around 25 minutes,” Mahar said. “I put forward three proposals to him.”

According to Mahar, Thapa expressed doubts about the possibility of reaching an agreement before the Supreme Court delivers its final decision.

“He kept saying, ‘What can happen before the court’s decision?’” Mahar said. “I told him it has to be done before the court’s decision.”

Mahar’s first proposal was to bring former president Deuba and President Thapa together for dialogue and resolve the party’s dispute.

“You two need to sit together. Whatever either of you has to give up, you should do it and unite the party,” Mahar said he told Thapa.

Mahar expressed optimism that direct dialogue between Deuba and Thapa could resolve the dispute.

“If the two of them sit together, they will reach an agreement. The dispute will be resolved,” he said.

His second proposal is to appoint a third person acceptable to both sides to oversee the general convention. His third is for both sides to publicly commit in advance to accepting the court’s decision and reach an agreement on the entire convention process.

“The second option is to give responsibility to a third person acceptable to both sides and hold the convention,” he said. “The third is to commit beforehand to accepting the court’s decision and reach an agreement on the entire convention process. That could also prevent a possible dispute after the court’s verdict.”

Mahar said the ‘Connecting Country and Congress’ campaign has continued discussions with various party leaders on party unity. He said he had also met former vice-president Purna Bahadur Khadka and leader Dr Shekhar Koirala to discuss the issue.

In Mahar’s view, the crisis in the Nepali Congress is linked less to a desire to split the party than to ego and mistrust among its leadership.

“No one appears to want the party to split. There is a little bit of an ego problem,” he said. “If a person or group works to reduce that ego problem, a solution can be found.”

He said the campaign was also engaging district presidents to build pressure from the grassroots for party unity.

Mahar stressed that the party should prioritise its institutional existence and future rather than who leads it.

“There is no alternative to uniting the party for the country and the people,” he said. “Even now, 99.9 percent of people want to see the party united. They want to see the party remain united.”

title.rendered: Parliamentary Committee seeks private sector input to cut legal, administrative hurdles

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

A parliamentary committee has sought suggestions from the private sector on ways to reduce legal procedures and administrative hassles involved in operating businesses.

The Infrastructure Development Committee of the House of Representatives is holding discussions on the current status and potential of public-private partnerships (PPPs) in Nepal’s infrastructure development, investment promotion, and problems encountered in project implementation, along with possible solutions.

Following an initial round of discussions, the committee decided to seek suggestions from stakeholders on the issue. It made three decisions in this regard.

First, the committee will seek written views and suggestions within 15 days from the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI), Nepal Chamber of Commerce, Confederation of Nepalese Industries (CNI), and Nepal-India Chamber of Commerce and Industry on problems faced by the private sector due to existing laws, regulations and procedures, and areas where they expect government facilitation.

The committee has particularly sought suggestions on implementing a one-window policy, reducing bureaucratic hurdles, facilitating investment inflows, and creating an environment that makes it easier to repatriate investment and profits and undertake reinvestment.

Second, the committee has asked the Investment Board to submit, within 15 days, details on the current status of hydropower and waste-management projects facilitated and approved under the PPP model. It has also sought information on the problems encountered in delivering these projects and the initiatives the committee could undertake to address them.

Third, the committee has asked for clear recommendations within 15 days on necessary reforms to the Investment Board Act and related legal provisions, as well as on the appropriate role of the Investment Board—whether it should focus on facilitating and coordinating investments or issuing permits.

title.rendered: Gandaki UML to recall Ministers; Phanindra Devkota likely to return as Minister

content.rendered:
Pokhara, August 25

The CPN-UML is preparing to recall its ministers from the Gandaki Province government. Chief Minister Surendraraj Pandey had urged the UML ministers to resign on moral grounds before the government removed them.

The decision to recall the ministers is expected to be taken at a meeting of the UML Gandaki parliamentary party board. Four UML lawmakers currently serving as ministers are Govinda Nepali, Minister for Physical Infrastructure and Transport Management; Bhim Karki, Minister for Land Management, Agriculture and Cooperatives; Yashoda Rimal, Minister for Industry and Tourism; and Laxman Pandey, Minister for Health.

Chief Minister Pandey reshuffled his Cabinet on April 15, replacing all ministers from both the Nepali Congress and UML before travelling to Kathmandu. A UML provincial leader said the parliamentary party board would decide on recalling the ministers while continuing discussions with other parties about forming a new government.

UML Chief Whip Devka Pahari said the meeting would discuss the government situation and make a decision. Another UML lawmaker said preparations were underway to ask the ministers to resign.

Earlier, Padma GC had served as agriculture minister, Krishna Pathak as health minister, Prakash Bahadur KC as physical infrastructure minister and Mitralal Basyal as industry and tourism minister from the UML.

From the Nepali Congress, Jit Sherchan replaced Dr Takraj Gurung as finance minister, Rekha Gurung replaced Bindukumar Thapa as social development minister, and Namdu Gurung replaced Bhesh Bahadur Paudel as forest minister. After Phanindra Devkota of the Nepal Socialist Party resigned as energy, water resources and irrigation minister, Pandey appointed Nandaprasad Neupane to the ministry. Devkota resigned following the loss of life during the Gen Z protests on September 8 and is now expected to be reappointed.

The UML parliamentary party board consists of party leader Khagaraj Adhikari, deputy leader Lil Bahadur Thapa, Chief Whip Devka Pahari, Whip Bhakta Kunwar, and lawmakers Sudhir Paudel and Sita Sundas.

Pandey was appointed chief minister on May 29, 2024, after the Supreme Court twice issued orders that resulted in the removal of the government led by Khagaraj Adhikari. In the 60-member Gandaki Provincial Assembly, 27 Nepali Congress lawmakers, two Rastriya Prajatantra Party lawmakers, Devkota and independent lawmaker Rajiv Gurung (Deepak Manange) had supported Pandey in a confidence vote. Manange has since been removed from office, while the others have not withdrawn their support.

About a month after the Nepali Congress and UML agreed to work together, Pandey finally brought four UML ministers into the government in September 2024. However, following a three-point agreement at the centre between the UML and the CPN, efforts to reshuffle provincial governments are now underway across the country.

In Gandaki and Madhesh, the UML and CPN have not yet decided because of their numbers. Even combined, the UML’s 22 lawmakers and the CPN’s six lawmakers in Gandaki do not have enough seats to form a majority government. The RPP remains the decisive force in the province and has not withdrawn its support for Pandey.

Former chief minister Khagaraj Adhikari had attempted to win over the RPP. However, the party has said it will remain neutral for now in line with the central decision. The RPP is also unhappy with the UML in Bagmati Province, where UML Chair KP Sharma Oli has been accused of trying to influence RPP lawmakers. The UML therefore plans to recall its ministers while continuing efforts to form a new government.

With the UML preparing to withdraw its ministers, leaders say Chief Minister Pandey has already held preliminary discussions with the party leadership in Kathmandu about appointing new ministers.

Phanindra Devkota of the Nepal Socialist Party (New Force), led by Baburam Bhattarai, is almost certain to return to Pandey’s Cabinet. Devkota had won the provincial election on the Maoist Centre’s election symbol. Discussions are underway to give him the Energy, Water Resources and Drinking Water Ministry again, although he is reportedly seeking the Physical Infrastructure Ministry.

Among Nepali Congress lawmakers, Ashok Shrestha of Tanahun, Dilliram Subedi of Baglung and Drona Kunwar, who had previously threatened to resign, are considered the leading contenders for ministerial positions. Mahesh Bhattarai of Syangja and Dilmaya Paubi of Baglung are also seeking ministerial posts. Congress leaders said two ministers from the party are likely to be appointed for now.

Proposals have also been made to appoint both RPP lawmakers as ministers. However, party leaders said they are unlikely to join the government because the RPP’s current policy is to stay out of power.

Chief Minister Pandey had repeatedly said that the UML ministers should resign on moral grounds and make way for changes before being removed from office. He had also said that the existing government could not continue for long after an agreement was reached at the centre. UML parliamentary party leader and ministers, however, had maintained that a coalition government could still be formed in Gandaki.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar, UML parliamentary party leader Khagaraj Adhikari said he was aware of the chief minister’s position. He said the stability of the provincial government remained the party’s priority regardless of agreements reached at the centre.

“Our primary concern is that the relevance of the provincial government should not be called into question. That is why our position was that we should move forward together,” Adhikari said. “It is not about the Congress, UML and Maoists fighting with each other. The situation requires us to prevent the government from doing wrong. We have to protect the country and the Constitution. That is where our main focus lies.”

Adhikari also said that if the chief minister believed UML ministers should resign on moral grounds, Pandey should also consider his own position from the same perspective. He said he was aware of the chief minister’s statements and that the UML would make a decision at an appropriate time.

title.rendered: Reconstruction begins in Jajarkot nearly 3 years after earthquake

content.rendered:
Jajarkot, August 25

Reconstruction of permanent homes for victims of the 2023 Jajarkot earthquake has begun from Bheri Municipality in Jajarkot, one of three districts severely affected by the disaster.

The reconstruction work formally began on Sunday from Ward No. 1 of Bheri Municipality, according to Suresh Sunar, undersecretary at the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

The foundation stones for the homes of earthquake victims Chandre Kami and Kaushila BK of Rawatgaun were laid to mark the start of the reconstruction, said Deepak Rana, ward chair of Bheri-1.

For families who have been living in temporary shelters for a long time, the start of permanent housing construction has renewed hopes of finally having a home of their own.

Kami’s family suffered both human and property losses in the earthquake. His four-year-old grandson, Bipin BK, died after being buried in the earthquake.

The reconstruction work began with the launch of the ‘Zero-Cost Reconstruction Programme’ for earthquake-affected residents of Jajarkot. Under the programme, earthquake victims in Jajarkot, Salyan and Rukum West will receive additional support and facilitation for reconstruction.

The programme, initiated by the NDRRMA, aims to facilitate the reconstruction of homes and other structures damaged by the earthquake, with economically vulnerable families and those facing difficulties rebuilding their homes expected to receive priority.

The earthquake, which struck on November 3, 2023, with its epicentre at Ramidanda in Jajarkot, caused extensive loss of life and property in Jajarkot, Salyan and Rukum West. Jajarkot suffered the heaviest damage.

188 homes listed for reconstruction in Bheri

In the first phase, 120 homes in Bheri-1 and 68 in Bheri-2 have been listed as beneficiaries for complete reconstruction, bringing the total to 188 homes.

The reconstruction of all 188 homes will be taken forward in the first phase, with priority given to families whose beneficiary selection and other required procedures have been completed.

Under the reconstruction arrangement, the NDRRMA will provide payments to the municipality for completed homes, while the municipality will make the payments to the beneficiaries.

Local governments will identify beneficiaries and forward their details through the District Administration Office to the authority, after which the reconstruction process will move forward.

Sunar urged other local governments to complete the beneficiary selection process for earthquake-damaged households and send the required details to the authority as soon as possible.

“Reconstruction will begin where beneficiaries have been identified and the required procedures completed. Other local governments also need to identify beneficiaries and send the details immediately,” Sunar said.

A team led by Sunar and Senior Divisional Engineer Sushilkumar Shrestha is currently in Jajarkot to facilitate the reconstruction process and provide technical support.

The team is coordinating with local governments across the district and gathering information on beneficiary details, required procedures, technical aspects and the progress of private housing reconstruction.

Reconstruction begins after a long wait

The earthquake caused extensive damage across Jajarkot, with thousands of homes affected and casualties reported in several local units.

Authorities initially built temporary shelters to provide earthquake victims with immediate protection. However, nearly three years after the disaster, many families are still living in temporary structures, tents and makeshift shelters because their permanent homes have not been rebuilt.

For families whose homes were completely destroyed, permanent housing has remained a major concern. The need to live in temporary structures during the monsoon, cold weather and other difficult conditions has added to their hardship.

Dipak Rana, ward chair of Bheri-1, said the existing procedures for reconstruction need to be changed, claiming that the current system is making it difficult to carry out the work.

With reconstruction now beginning in Bheri, authorities expect beneficiary selection and reconstruction work to gain momentum in other affected local units as well.

Earthquake victims in Nalgad still waiting for grants

Nalgad Municipality is among the local units worst affected by the earthquake. Many homes in the municipality were completely destroyed.

Although the government had arranged to provide Rs 50,000 per family for the construction of temporary shelters, some victims say they did not receive the amount on time.

Some victims have also complained that they have not received funds expected from the federal government or the second instalment from the municipality. They say the lack of funds has made it difficult to build temporary shelters and begin rebuilding their homes.

Victims who have not completed the grant process for temporary shelters are now demanding that they also be included in the beneficiary list for permanent housing reconstruction.

They have called for immediate resolution of problems in beneficiary selection, document collection and verification at the local level.

Although permanent housing reconstruction has now begun, authorities face the challenge of ensuring that all affected families are included and that the work progresses quickly.

Local representatives say identifying genuine victims left out of beneficiary lists, addressing delays in grant distribution, arranging adequate technical manpower and ensuring easy access to construction materials will be crucial to making the reconstruction campaign effective.

A total of 14 local units across Jajarkot, Salyan and Rukum West were affected by the earthquake. Sunar said work had previously been difficult due to a lack of manpower, but 30 to 40 technical personnel are now being mobilised to begin reconstruction work.

title.rendered: US preparing to cancel visas of nearly 200,000 foreigners

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, Aug 25

The US government is preparing to cancel the business and tourist visas of up to 200,000 foreign nationals. If carried out, it would be the largest single visa cancellation in American history.

The State Department could announce the cancellation of B-1 and B-2 visas in the coming weeks. The action will target holders of these visas issued between 2016 and 2026 who have applied, or are applying, for asylum in the US.

According to State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott, these individuals entered the US briefly as tourists or business travellers but later filed for asylum to settle permanently.

Visa cancellation does not mean immediate deportation

The State Department has declined to specify the exact number of people whose visas will be cancelled. Officials say the number could change as the process unfolds in phases.

A cancelled visa does not mean the person will be immediately deported. Those with pending asylum cases may see their status change, but their business or tourist visa status will end.

Visa rules tightened under Trump’s second term

The US has already tightened visa rules under President Donald Trump’s second term, requesting applicants’ social media information, imposing costly visa bonds, and barring visas for citizens of certain countries.

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said some people come to the US on tourist or business visas and then apply for asylum to stay. He added that asylum should not be used as a way to bypass immigration law.

Nearly 175,000 visas cancelled in the past 18 months

B-1 visas are typically issued for business travel, and B-2 visas for tourism, family visits, or medical treatment. It remains unclear how many of these visa holders have applied or are applying for asylum, or how many will be affected by the proposed action.

Over the past 18 months, the State Department has already cancelled roughly 175,000 visas, including some issued to people accused or convicted of crimes, as well as some who have publicly criticised US policies.

title.rendered: Average earners in Australia now spend more than half income on rent

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

A new report shows people earning an average income in Australia’s major cities must spend more than half of it on rent.

According to a Monday report by housing advocacy group Everybody’s Home, renting a unit in any Australian capital city costs more than 50% of the national average income.

Someone earning AU$70,000 a year must spend 56% of their income on the average rent. For those earning AU$40,000, housing costs reach 89% of total income, while even those earning AU$100,000 must set aside 41% for rent.

Across all eight capital cities, an average-income worker must spend at least 51% of their earnings on the average unit rent, the report concludes.

Sydney is worse still; someone earning AU$70,000 a year must spend 69% of their income on weekly rent, the highest ratio of any major city.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the average annual salary as of August 2025 was AU$74,100.

Housing advocate Maiy Azize said the government’s withdrawal from building public and community housing has caused a severe housing crisis, adding that Australia will need around 1 million such homes over the next 15 years.

— with inputs from Xinhua

title.rendered: Road to Tatopani border point opens after 40 days

content.rendered:
Sindhupalchowk, August 25

The Eco section linking the Tatopani border point along the Nepal-China border in Sindhupalchowk district reopened to traffic on Monday after 40 days of disruption.

The road was obstructed since July 15 after a landslide at Kodari in Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality-2. The traffic resumed on Monday after the Road Division Office opened a new track, it is said. Six tippers and two pieces of heavy equipment were mobilised to clear the debris for the resumption of vehicular movement.

Chief of Division Office, Narayan Dutta Bhandari, said that road maintenance will start soon in the Liping area too. Likewise, Chair of Sindhupalchowk Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Buddharaj Basnet, said that the containers stranded in Kodari bazaar have moved to the customs office after the traffic resumption. He, however, said that 85 more containers are still stranded in the Liping area.

The traders have complained of heavy losses from the vehicular disruption on the international highway for a long time and hoped that the highway will remain open in the upcoming days so that they could import goods unhindered for the festival season. Likewise, Chair of Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality-2, Kumar Shrestha, said that the Tatopani border point is not likely to operate unhindered until the road in the Liping area is maintained, though the road was cleared along the Eco area.

title.rendered: 325 households identified as landless in Pokhara Bus Park

content.rendered:
Kaski, August 25

Pokhara Metropolitan City (PMC) has identified 325 households from Pokhara Bus Park as landless people. The local government concluded the number after conducting a thorough investigation of the Dalit, landless, squatters and unorganised occupants at Pokhara Bus Park. PMC had sought applications for the management of landless people living in the Bus Park.

The applications filed by the occupants were cross-checked and investigated with facilitation from the ward level. PMC finally listed 242 households raising unorganised settlements, according to Mayor Dhanraj Acharya. In the initial phase, applications were received from 200 landless Dalits, 248 landless squatters and 116 unorganised settlers. The applications were verified by adopting the process of claim and objection.

An additional study was launched to verify details on the occupants. The final result showed 144 households as landless Dalit and 181 landless squatters totaling 325. Similarly, 242 families are categorised as unorganised settlers. Mayor Acharya further informed that with the identification of landless squatters, the local government would forward the process to manage these households well.

The ward committee had contributed well to preparing the report. “The local level will make a decision from its executive council and forward recommendation to the district committee for further action,” Mayor Acharya added. The issues of landless settlers have now reached a decisive stage.

Acharya underscored that local government was aware of the need to deliver justice to the victims. All seven district committees would be written after holding an executive council of PMC. The households were occupying the public land, Pokhara Bus Park, for years, thanks to the absence of strict intervention. Relocation of the identified households is the next step. In this regard, coordinator of Landless Squatters’ Concern Committee, Prem Gurung, said that landless people would not oppose the government’s move for development. However, before evacuation, we need proper management.

Gurung further argued, “It’s wrong to put the entire blame on us for not getting the Bus Park expanded. There are several reasons behind the sluggish expansion of the Bus Park.” He pledged that the settlers were ready to cooperate with PMC, but proper rehabilitation is imperative. PMC had acquired the land to develop a well-equipped bus park 50 years back.

But, for these years, no progress was made, thereby forcing the people to catch the long- and short-route vehicles for various destinations from a roadside at Prithvichowk. In addition to the landless people, some individuals had encroached upon the public land. Some months back, PMC had demolished the structures set up on the public land. It has made public its plan to build a modern bus park with the help of donor agencies.

title.rendered: Asian Games: Nepal’s long medal journey and the elusive gold

content.rendered:
Nepal has been part of the Asian Games journey since the inaugural edition in New Delhi in 1951. Seventy-five years later, the country is preparing for its 20th appearance at Asia’s biggest multi-sport event, still chasing a first gold medal.

From the first Asian Games in 1951 to the 19th edition in Hangzhou, China, in 2023, Nepal has competed in 17 editions. The country missed the 1954 and 1962 Games but has otherwise maintained a regular presence at the continental event.

Yet despite its long association with the Asian Games, Nepal’s medal tally remains modest: three silver and 23 bronze medals. No Nepali athlete has won an Asian Games gold medal.

Nepal is now preparing for the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, scheduled for September 19 to October 4. The country plans to send 137 athletes across 22 sports.

The Aichi-Nagoya Games are expected to bring together more than 11,000 athletes from 45 countries, competing in 43 sports, 71 disciplines and 469 events.

35 years for the first medal

When Nepal first competed at the Asian Games, athletics was the only sport it entered.

But the country had to wait 35 years for its first medal.

Nepal participated in seven of the first nine editions without winning a medal. The wait finally ended at the 1986 Asian Games in Seoul, South Korea.

Taekwondo player Bidhan Lama won Nepal’s first medal, while the country went on to claim an impressive eight bronze medals in that edition — four in taekwondo and four in boxing.

Dal Bahadur Rana Magar, Manoj Bahadur Shrestha, Sushil Pokharel and Tul Bahadur Thapa won bronze medals in boxing.

In taekwondo, Bidhan Lama, Raj Kumar Budhathoki, Raj Kumar Rai and Ram Bahadur Gharti Chhetri won bronze.

Seoul remains Nepal’s most successful Asian Games edition in terms of the number of medals won.

Four years later, Nepal won just one medal at the 1990 Beijing Asian Games, with boxer Chitra Bahadur Gurung taking bronze.

At the 1994 Hiroshima Games in Japan, Nepal won two bronze medals — through taekwondo player Man Bahadur Shahi and karateka Sita Rai.

Sabita’s historic silver

After winning only bronze medals in three consecutive editions, Nepal finally claimed its first silver at the 1998 Asian Games in Bangkok.

Taekwondo player Sabita Rajbhandari became the first Nepali athlete to win a silver medal at the Asian Games, nearly five decades after Nepal’s first participation.

Her silver remains one of the biggest individual achievements in Nepal’s Asian Games history and the highest medal Nepal has won in taekwondo at the Games.

Nepal also won three bronze medals in Bangkok. Taekwondo players Kishor Shrestha and Sapana Malla won bronze, while Sambhar Bahadur Gole added another bronze in karate.

The success of taekwondo continued at the following Games.

At Busan in 2002, Deepak Bista, Renuka Magar and Ritu Jimmy Rai won bronze medals in taekwondo.

At the 2006 Doha Asian Games, Nepal again won three bronze medals in taekwondo. Deepak Bista claimed another medal, becoming the first Nepali athlete to win medals at two consecutive Asian Games. That record still stands.

From Nepal’s strongest sport to a medal drought

Taekwondo has been Nepal’s most successful sport at the Asian Games.

Of Nepal’s 26 medals, 14 have come from taekwondo — one silver and 13 bronze.

After beginning its medal run in 1986, taekwondo continued to deliver at almost every Asian Games through 2006, with the exception of the 1990 edition.

Nepal won four taekwondo bronze medals in 1986, one in 1994, one silver and two bronze in 1998, and three bronze medals each in 2002 and 2006.

But that golden period eventually came to an end.

Nepali taekwondo has failed to win a medal in the last four Asian Games. The generation that followed Deepak Bista has yet to reproduce the medal-winning run of the past.

A sport that once became synonymous with Nepal’s international sporting identity is now facing questions about its decline.

Medal numbers also began to fall

Nepal’s strongest period at the Asian Games came between 1996 and 2006. Except for the 1990 edition, the country won more than one medal in each edition during that period.

Over roughly two decades, Nepal collected 21 medals, including one silver, mainly through taekwondo, boxing and karate.

After 2006, however, Nepal’s medal count began to decline.

At the 2010 Guangzhou Asian Games, boxer Deepak Maharjan won Nepal’s only medal — a bronze.

Four years later in Incheon, karateka Bimala Tamang won bronze in kata.

Nepal returned to the silver-medal podium at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and Palembang, where the men’s team cross-country paragliding team won silver.

Bijay Gautam, Bimal Adhikari, Sushil Gurung, Yukesh Gurung and Bishal Thapa finished second, just 27 points behind Japan.

It was Nepal’s first silver medal in two decades, although it remained the country’s only medal in that edition.

Arika brings new hope

Nepal’s medal tally improved at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, where the country won one silver and one bronze.

Karateka Arika Gurung won silver in the women’s kumite over-68kg category, while Nepal’s women’s kabaddi team won bronze in its first Asian Games appearance.

Arika became the first Nepali athlete since Sabita Rajbhandari in 1998 to win an individual silver medal at the Asian Games.

Her achievement also made her the third Nepali athlete or team to win an Asian Games silver, after Rajbhandari and Nepal’s paragliding team.

The women’s kabaddi team’s bronze was equally significant. The two medals meant Nepal had won more than one medal at a single Asian Games for the first time in 17 years.

75 years of participation, but gold remains elusive

Arika’s run in Hangzhou also offered Nepal a glimpse of what had long seemed out of reach.

She reached the final of the women’s over-68kg kumite but lost to Kazakhstan’s Sofia Berultseva.

For Arika, the silver was less about what she had won and more about the gold she had missed.

Her performance nevertheless raised a familiar question: When will Nepal finally win an Asian Games gold?

Nepal has now competed in 17 editions of the Asian Games over 75 years. It has won 26 medals but none of them gold.

The absence of gold is particularly striking because several Asian countries with comparatively smaller sporting resources than Nepal have already produced Asian Games champions.

After the Hangzhou Games, the National Sports Council launched the ‘Mission 2026’ campaign with the target of winning gold and reaching double figures in the medal tally at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. Athletes from 10 sports were initially included in the programme.

This time, Nepal is competing in 22 sports with 137 athletes.

But questions remain over whether Nepal has adequately identified its strongest medal prospects and prepared them accordingly. Training, international exposure, investment and preparation have all become part of the debate as the country pursues its first Asian Games gold.

Arika Gurung, who won silver in Hangzhou, is naturally among Nepal’s leading medal hopes. Nepal is also looking towards other martial arts disciplines and the women’s kabaddi team.

Whether those hopes can finally translate into gold — and whether Nepal can significantly improve its overall medal tally — will be decided when competition begins in Aichi-Nagoya on September 19.

After 75 years of participation, Nepal’s biggest Asian Games question remains unanswered: when will the country’s first gold finally arrive?

title.rendered: Jimmy Neesham returns to Janakpur Bolts for NPL 3

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

New Zealand all-rounder Jimmy Neesham has returned to Janakpur Bolts for the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL).

Janakpur Bolts announced the signing of the 35-year-old Neesham through social media on Tuesday.

Neesham played a key role in helping Janakpur win the inaugural NPL title in 2024. He scored 247 runs in nine matches at an average of over 35 and a strike rate of more than 196.

He was awarded the Best Strike Rate award for having the highest strike rate in the first edition of the NPL.

Neesham also took seven wickets while playing for Janakpur in the inaugural season. He became a popular figure among Janakpur supporters after representing the team as a ‘cap’ player.

“Jimmy has earned a special place not only on the field but also in the hearts of our supporters. His loyalty and connection with Janakpur Bolts is a beautiful story in itself. The hero who helped us become champions in the first season has returned home,” Janakpur CEO Niroj Khatiwada said.

Janakpur Bolts did not have a cap-player slot in the second season, after which Neesham joined Pokhara Avengers. He played four matches for Pokhara, scoring 99 runs, including a half-century, and taking five wickets.

Neesham will play for Janakpur Bolts this season under the Test-player quota.

He has represented New Zealand in 12 Tests, 76 ODIs and 105 T20Is. In February, he played for New Zealand in the T20 World Cup final against India.

Neesham has also been a regular in franchise cricket around the world. He has played in the Indian Premier League for Delhi Daredevils, Punjab Kings, Mumbai Indians and Rajasthan Royals.

He has also featured in the Lanka Premier League, Vitality Blast, Bangladesh Premier League, UAE’s ILT20, Pakistan Super League, South Africa’s SA20, The Hundred, Big Bash League and Caribbean Premier League.

Winning the NPL title with Janakpur two years ago was Neesham’s first franchise cricket title.

title.rendered: Nepal’s IT industry is booming. So why is the govt setting up its own software company?

content.rendered:
Nepal’s IT companies are estimated to export software and other IT services worth around Rs 150 billion, with more than 100,000 skilled workers employed in the sector. The IT industry also produces IT services worth more than Rs 100 billion for the domestic market.

Yet, instead of relying on this growing private sector, the government has decided to establish its own software development company.

The Cabinet recently approved the Software Development and Operations Committee Formation Order, paving the way for the establishment of a government office dedicated to developing, upgrading and maintaining software used by public agencies.

The new entity, called the Software Development and Operations Centre, will have six officials and 30 employees, according to the formation order.

The move has raised questions about the government’s approach to the country’s IT industry.

On one hand, government policies and budget statements have repeatedly described information technology as a strategic sector, promised incentives for software exports and announced plans to promote Nepal as a global digital economy hub.

On the other, the government has now chosen to develop software itself rather than depend on Nepal’s private technology companies.

Industry stakeholders say the contradiction exposes a gap between the government’s policy promises and its actions.

Policy promises, a different reality

The government has announced tax incentives for IT service exports, loans for new entrepreneurs and measures to promote software, digital services, cloud services, cybersecurity, green computing and AI-related exports.

Presenting the budget, Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle had said the government was providing a 50 percent tax exemption on income earned from exporting IT services as part of its plan to make the IT industry a new economic engine for the country.

The government also announced financial incentives for IT export businesses.

But only a few months later, the decision to establish a government-run software centre has left the private sector questioning those commitments.

Gauravraj Pandey, president of the Nepal Association of Software and IT Services (NAS-IT), said the decision shows that the government does not trust technology companies operating in Nepal.

He said the move could discourage the industry at a time when Nepali companies are trying to establish themselves in international markets.

“Making big promises is not enough. If the state itself does not trust its own citizens and private sector, how can foreign investors or other countries trust us?” Pandey said.

According to him, the government’s role should be to establish clear rules and quality standards and create an environment in which private companies can compete and provide services to the state.

“Instead, the government seems to have forgotten its role as a facilitator and is trying to directly compete with the private sector,” he said.

Government wants to build its own systems

The new centre will be based in Kathmandu Valley and will develop, upgrade and maintain software as requested by public agencies.

It will also be responsible for upgrading and maintaining software systems developed by the centre itself, as well as legacy systems currently being used by government agencies.

According to a senior official at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the initial concept behind the centre was for the government to become self-reliant in the software it needs.

Informal discussions had even considered employing around 200 software engineers at the centre, the official said.

“The purpose of this institution is to collect the technology requirements of government agencies and develop software accordingly. This could require hiring even more professional software engineers than those currently available,” the official said.

The government’s argument is that keeping software source codes, security systems and data within the state would help it remain sovereign over sensitive government systems.

But even officials within the government have questioned why the state does not trust Nepali companies with such work.

“I cannot understand why the government can give sensitive work such as licence and passport-related printing to foreign companies but does not trust companies here,” the official said.

“This either means the government believes Nepali companies do not have the capacity, or it does not trust them. Either way, it is harmful for us. I am not satisfied with this approach myself.”

The budget had promised something else

The government’s budget had not specifically promised to build software itself.

Instead, it had said the process for purchasing software for government agencies would be made more systematic.

The budget stated that arrangements would be made for software used by government agencies to be procured through a single agency.

Pandey said the government’s decision now appears inconsistent with that commitment.

He said NAS-IT has been working to promote Nepal’s IT industry internationally, including through road shows in Europe and other countries.

“We are going abroad and telling the world that Nepal is strong in technology service exports. But when our own government does not trust us, it naturally makes things difficult,” he said.

‘Government should not compete with startups’

Entrepreneur Alok Subedi said the government’s decision resembles an outdated model in which the state attempts to control the entire system rather than allowing the private sector to drive production.

He said the government’s responsibility should be to regulate the market and create standards rather than build software itself.

Subedi also questioned the timing of the decision, arguing that the rapid development of artificial intelligence has already made the global software business increasingly challenging.

“At a time when work coming from abroad is already declining, the government should be giving companies more work and creating an environment of trust. Instead, it is discouraging them further,” he said.

“Whatever the government says through its budget and policy programmes, its actions do not match. This is the opposite direction.”

Information technology researcher Amrita Sharma also questioned the government’s approach.

She said establishing a unit to set software standards, guidelines and quality assurance could be justified. But employing engineers to develop software and compete with startups and established technology companies would be a mistake.

“Having a regulatory unit for software standards, guidelines and quality assurance can be justified. But moving ahead with the intention of hiring engineers and competing with startups is wrong,” Sharma said.

She said the government risks focusing on managing employees within a small institution while losing sight of the larger goal of digital transformation.

Nepal already has established IT companies employing large numbers of skilled professionals, she said, and competing with them would send a message that the state does not trust its own technology sector.

“Such an inconsistent policy not only creates uncertainty for businesses within the country, but could also create distrust among foreign companies that outsource work to Nepal,” she said.

Who is responsible if government-built systems leak data?

Stakeholders have also raised concerns about security and legal responsibility.

If the government develops and controls software systems containing sensitive citizen information, including national identity data, questions could arise over who would be legally responsible if such information were leaked.

Subedi said the formation order does not clearly address such questions.

“When private companies do the work, they can be held accountable through laws, contracts and service agreements,” he said.

“But if sensitive personal information or national identity data leaks from systems developed by a government agency or committee, who will bear the legal responsibility?”

He also questioned the government’s ability to handle the security risks involved.

“We have not even been able to fully secure government website data. There are frequent reports of data being leaked onto the dark web,” he said.

“If the government now says it will handle everything itself, the risks could increase further. On one hand, businesses are discouraged; on the other, there are security risks. This approach does not appear mature or practical.”

For Nepal’s rapidly expanding IT industry, the debate is therefore no longer simply about who develops government software. It is also about whether the state sees the domestic technology industry as a partner in building the digital economy—or as a competitor.
