title.rendered: Nepal has a seat in global astronomy. Now it must build on it

content.rendered:
As the Nepal Astronomical Society (NASO) marks its 19th Foundation Day on August 25, there is good reason to reflect on how far Nepal’s relationship with the global astronomy community has come—and how much further it still has to go.

This year also marks two decades since Nepal first appeared at an International Astronomical Union (IAU) General Assembly in 2006, marking 20 years of steadily growing international presence. For a country whose relationship with the sky has always run deep—from the astronomical calculations of ancient calendars to the folklore built around eclipses and constellations—Nepal’s formal entry into the global astronomy community has been a long time coming.

Nepali astronomers first took part in an IAU General Assembly in 2006, marking the country’s first contact with the global astronomical community. It was also the year when Pluto was announced as a dwarf planet during IAU GA 2096.

NASO’s own story began a year later, in 2007, when a small group of enthusiasts began organizing stargazing sessions, school outreach programmes and public lectures with almost no formal support. Over the years, that grassroots effort grew into a nationwide network engaged in astronomy education, research and public outreach, reaching students, teachers and communities far beyond the Kathmandu Valley.

At the same time, Nepal continued participating in every IAU General Assembly since that first appearance in 2006. Along the way, the country built quiet but steady connections with the IAU itself.

In 2018, I was appointed as the IAU’s National Outreach Coordinator (NOC) for Nepal, a role later expanded to include Manisha Dwa as Co-NOC. Together, we coordinated public engagement activities in line with the IAU Office for Astronomy Outreach’s global network.

Outreach was only one half of the bridge NASO built toward the IAU. The other was education.

In 2020, the IAU’s Office of Astronomy for Education (OAE) launched a global network of National Astronomy Education Coordinators (NAECs)—volunteer teams tasked with documenting how astronomy is taught in their countries, organizing teacher-training workshops, and developing classroom-ready materials suited to local needs.

Nepal was among the earliest countries to join this network, with a NAEC team hosted at NASO. I am serving as Team Chair of the NAEC team for Nepal, currently appointed through August 2027, working alongside Manisha Dwa, who serves as the team’s contact person, as well as other education specialists drawn from across the country’s teaching and science communities.

That work fed directly into the establishment of the OAE Node Nepal, the first such Node in the OAE’s global network. It was formalized through a memorandum of understanding I signed in Kathmandu on July 8, 2021, as NASO’s Chairman, alongside then IAU General Secretary Teresa Lago and OAE Director Markus Pössel.

The Node, hosted by NASO, focused on citizen-science projects in low-resource settings, teacher training and preparation for astronomy Olympiads, while also building collaborative ties across the SAARC region.

The real inflection point came in 2024, at the IAU’s 32nd General Assembly in Cape Town, South Africa. There, NASO’s project coordinator, Manisha Dwa, presented our work, which we have been carrying out since 2009 through different NASO members, many of whom are now spread across the globe.

With the approval of Nepal’s membership status under the Observer category, we gained a formal foothold within the Union’s structure—a position Nepal continues to hold today. It was also a signal that years of outreach and education work had been noticed.

Nepal has held National Member status with the IAU since 2024, in the Observer category. The Observer category is not the end of the road. Within the IAU’s structure, it is understood as a stepping stone toward eventual Full Membership, a status that requires sustained institutional capacity, a growing base of professional astronomers and continued demonstration of Nepal’s contribution to the field.

Two years in, that remains the chapter NASO is still working to write. We are not there yet.

Alongside National Member status, the IAU has formally recognized Nepal’s National Committee for Astronomy (NCA), with myself serving as NCA Chair and Manisha Dwa as NCA Secretary.

The NCA now sits at the center of Nepal’s ongoing relationship with the Union, coordinating everything from individual membership applications to the country’s participation in IAU General Assemblies going forward.

The most tangible proof of what that status means arrived this year, when NASO completed its first cycle of a membership call inviting Nepali astronomers and researchers to apply for IAU Individual and Junior Membership.

Seven new members were admitted—five as Individual Members and two as Junior Members—bringing Nepal’s total to nine active members in the IAU’s official count. The other two are Manisha Dwa and myself, who hold IAU Associate Membership.

I became Nepal’s first IAU Associate Member in 2020, and Manisha became the country’s second in 2021, well before National Member status existed for Nepal.

Before Nepal held its own National Member status, there was no real way to reflect that on paper. Nepali members of the IAU were filed under “AA — Country Unknown” in the Union’s own system, with no option to select Nepal at all.

That has now changed.

Nepal has its own identity within the IAU, and every application that follows will be counted as what it actually is: Nepali.

This year’s seven new members—Sitaram Byahut, Daya Nidhi Chhatkuli, Sudarshan Karki, Min Prasad Khanal, Udayaraj Khanal, Janak Raj Malla and Sanjaya Paudel—were admitted as Individual or Junior Members, with several based in Nepal and others contributing from the diaspora in the United States and South Korea.

It is a small number today, but it is the beginning of exactly the pipeline sustained National Membership was meant to create. NASO intends to run further membership calls to keep growing it.

We continue to call on eligible Nepali citizens, both at home and abroad, to apply for individual IAU membership, recognizing that national recognition is only as strong as the individual talent it represents.

Practically, this opens doors that were previously closed.

Nepali students, academicians and researchers gain a clearer path to individual IAU membership, provided they meet the Union’s academic and professional criteria. Nepal’s participation in international scientific collaboration, conferences and joint research initiatives becomes easier to formalize.

And, crucially, the country’s young astronomers—many of whom have represented Nepal at International Astronomy Olympiads—now have an institutional bridge connecting their ambitions to a global professional community.

It would be easy to treat sustained National Member status as a finish line. It is not.

We are not a Full Member yet, and reaching that status will take a larger base of professional astronomers, deeper institutional capacity and years more of the same patient work that brought us this far.

That is the next chapter NASO intends to write.

For a country better known internationally for the peaks that touch its sky than for what lies beyond it, holding this standing reframes the conversation. Nepal is no longer only a place to look up at the stars from. It is now, formally, part of the global effort to understand them, even as it works toward a fuller seat at the table.

The most recent reaffirmation of that standing came through a certificate issued by the IAU Secretariat on July 8, 2026. Signed by Maria Rosaria D’Antonio, the Secretariat’s Head of Administration and Director, the certificate confirms that the Nepal Astronomical Society has been Nepal’s National Member, in the Observer category, since 2024.

For those of us who have spent years building astronomy from the ground up in Nepal—often with little infrastructure, minimal funding and even less institutional recognition—even a reaffirmation like this carries real weight. It is proof that our work has been noticed and sustained, not a one-time announcement forgotten the year after.

The work of 19 years—night-sky outreach in remote schools, Olympiad training for teenagers and patient correspondence with an international body many assumed was out of reach—has finally found its institutional home.

As NASO marks this Foundation Day, that work stands as the clearest answer to why we began: not for recognition alone, but because a country with Nepal’s scientific curiosity deserved a seat among the nations that study the universe together.

What comes next depends on whether we can turn this foothold into full standing.

title.rendered: Monsoon to bring rain across Nepal, heavy rainfall possible in three provinces

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 25

Monsoon winds continue to influence weather across Nepal, with the monsoon trough currently around its average position, according to the Meteorological Forecasting Division under the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

The country is generally cloudy, with light to moderate rain occurring in several parts of Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, as well as some parts of Koshi, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces. A few places in Madhesh Province are also receiving rain.

The division said most of the country will remain generally cloudy this afternoon. Some Himalayan areas are likely to receive moderate rain or snowfall with thunder and lightning.

Moderate rainfall accompanied by thunder and lightning is also likely in many hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces and in some hilly areas of Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Some areas of the Terai in Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces, as well as a few areas of the Terai in Madhesh and Koshi provinces, may also receive moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning.

Heavy rainfall is possible at one or two locations in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces.

The country will remain generally cloudy tonight as well. Some Himalayan areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces and a few Himalayan areas of Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces may receive moderate rain or snowfall with thunder and lightning.

Moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning is likely in some hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces and a few hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Some parts of the Terai in Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces, along with a few areas of the Sudurpaschim Terai, may also receive moderate rain with thunder and lightning.

Heavy rainfall is again possible at one or two locations in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces tonight.

The Meteorological Forecasting Division has urged people in areas at risk of heavy rainfall to remain alert to possible hazards including debris flows, floods, landslides and soil erosion.

It also warned that rainfall could affect daily life, agriculture, health, tourism, mountaineering, roads and air transport in the affected areas, and urged people to stay updated with weather information.

title.rendered: How Kamal Chaudhary turned hardship into a $7 million business in Dubai

content.rendered:
Kamal Chaudhary, 46, never imagined that he would leave Nepal for foreign employment, build a company abroad and eventually create jobs for others.

Growing up in Budhiganga Municipality-4 of Morang, Chaudhary dreamed of becoming a chartered accountant (CA) and building a career in Nepal. But his family could not afford the cost of CA studies, forcing him to abandon that dream and eventually seek opportunities abroad.

Today, the journey that began with financial hardship has taken him from a Rs 4,000-a-month accounting job in Kathmandu to senior positions in multinational companies and, ultimately, ownership of a Dubai-based company with an annual turnover of more than $7 million.

His story is one of persistence, professional growth and overcoming barriers as a Nepali professional in the international business world.

A difficult start

Born in 1979 in Morang, Kamal Chaudhary spent his childhood in his village. He studied at a boarding school until Grade 5 before moving to a government school because of his family’s financial difficulties.

He completed his SLC from Saraswati Secondary School in Duhabi in 1994. Reaching school itself was a challenge. He and his friends walked for about an hour each way, crossing several streams and travelling along dusty roads.

“Those days at the government school were difficult to describe. We would leave for school in the morning and return home only in the evening,” he recalls.

After SLC, Chaudhary studied at Mahendra Morang Adarsh Multiple Campus. He worked alongside his studies to support himself, taking jobs at Bhagwati Store, a battery company and later a soap factory.

He also taught at boarding schools and worked as a volunteer at his former school to cover his education expenses.

After completing his BBS, he moved to Kathmandu around 2000 in search of better opportunities.

The dream of becoming a CA

While studying at Mahendra Morang, Kamal Chaudhary had set his sights on becoming a chartered accountant.

But his family could not afford it.

“You would have to sell two bighas of farmland to pay for your CA studies. How would we educate your other siblings?” his father told him.

At the time, CA studies were not available in Nepal in the way he wanted, meaning he would have had to go to Delhi, India, where the cost was around six lakh Indian rupees.

Without the money to pursue the qualification, Chaudhary’s dream of becoming a CA came to an end.

“I had to put my CA dream aside. I came to Kathmandu looking for a better future,” he says.

From a Rs 4,000 salary to sleeping at the office

In Kathmandu, Kamal Chaudhary enrolled in a master’s programme at Shanker Dev Campus in Putalisadak in 2000.

But even finding a place to live was difficult.

Eventually, he found a small room in Chyasal, Lalitpur, which cost Rs 400 a month. He shared it with three friends while searching for work.

Around 2001, he found a job as an accountant at SCS Global Management Consultancy in Kamaladi. His monthly salary was Rs 4,000.

The salary barely covered his college fees and living expenses.

At one point, he could no longer afford his room rent and spent an entire year sleeping at his office.

“I couldn’t even afford the Rs 400 rent. With Rs 4,000, I had to decide whether to pay college fees, rent or cover my daily expenses. For about a year, I slept wherever I worked,” he recalls.

Food was another struggle.

He would often go to Ratna Park, where cheap food was available.

“There was bhutan (buffalo offal) for Rs 5. On days when I didn’t have enough money for food, I would eat that until I was full, drink water and go to college and the office,” he says.

“Those days still feel like yesterday.”

After leaving the consultancy, he worked as a senior accountant at Dalima Resort in Kurintar for a year and later became finance head at Daikin/Himal Air Conditioner.

But his income still did not meet his ambitions.

He began considering foreign employment.

Qatar changed the course of his career

In 2004, Kamal Chaudhary travelled to Qatar for the first time, joining Satco Trading as an accountant.

The company was involved in construction and imported construction materials from countries including China, Vietnam, Germany, Taiwan, India and Pakistan.

His starting salary was 1,200 Qatari riyals.

He was dissatisfied with the pay and resigned after six months. However, he could not immediately move to another company because of Qatar’s employment regulations at the time.

His employer eventually increased his salary to 3,600 riyals, and he continued working there for two years.

Still eager to advance, Chaudhary applied to Samko International in Doha and was selected in 2007.

The company was involved in mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) works and had been contracted for the Doha Tower project.

Kamal Chaudhary joined as a project controller.

He worked on the Doha Tower project for two years and helped complete it successfully.

“My salary at the time was 9,000 Qatari riyals,” he says. “When you go to Doha today, you can see the round tower. I worked on that project as a controller. Many other Nepalis also worked hard to build that tower.”

The project became an important milestone in his career.

The turning point: a multibillion-dollar project

Kamal Chaudhary’s next major opportunity came in 2008 when Australian company Kempe Engineering was looking for a project controller for a Qatar Aluminium project.

He applied despite having fewer formal qualifications than many of the other candidates.

Other applicants were foreign professionals with CA and CCA qualifications. Chaudhary had an MBS from Tribhuvan University and his experience working on the Doha Tower project.

“I had the lowest qualification among the candidates,” he says. “But I had the experience of working as a controller on the Doha Tower project.”

He was eventually selected.

Getting the required NOC was another hurdle, but he managed to obtain it and joined the company.

His role on the Qatar Aluminium project became what he describes as the turning point of his life.

The massive project had a multibillion-dollar budget, with Kempe Engineering handling work worth around $1.5 billion.

Chaudhary was responsible for project control and budget planning. He says he worked closely on aluminium processing and gained experience in handling large-scale industrial projects.

Around 700 workers were involved in the project, including Nepali, Indian and Filipino workers.

The project was completed successfully, and Chaudhary was promoted to management level.

From Qatar to Mozambique and the UAE

In 2011, Kempe Engineering sent Kamal Chaudhary to Mozambique as an assistant finance manager for an aluminium upgrade and modification project.

The project, undertaken with British multinational BHP Billiton, was worth around $460 million, according to Chaudhary.

After successfully completing the assignment, he returned to the UAE and was appointed regional finance manager.

He was responsible for operations across several branches in Dubai, Qatar, Oman and Saudi Arabia.

The company later merged with Australian and Finnish companies in 2014.

Chaudhary continued to rise through the corporate ranks.

Helping Nepalis rise with him

As his position grew, Kamal Chaudhary also began helping other Nepalis find opportunities in the companies where he worked.

He helped Nepali workers move from entry-level positions such as tea boys to clerks and supervisors.

“I helped many Nepali youths get jobs. I helped them move from tea boy positions to clerks and supervisors,” he says.

He also pushed for better salaries for Nepali employees.

According to Chaudhary, some workers who initially earned around Rs 100,000 eventually reached salaries of Rs 500,000–600,000.

But his own career eventually hit another obstacle.

When he was considered for promotion, he says the company required a CA qualification for the position.

Although he was among the most senior candidates, he did not have the qualification.

He also felt he was being treated differently because he was Nepali.

“I felt that I was being looked down upon because I was Nepali. My salary was around Rs 1.1 million a month at the time. I decided to leave the company,” he says.

Turning frustration into his own company

The experience became a motivation for Kamal Chaudhary to build something of his own.

In 2022, he established Clean World Management Consultancy in Dubai.

He brought Finnish national Pentti Korhonen on board as a partner, citing his decades of experience in marketing and international projects.

Chaudhary says the partnership was partly driven by the realities of the international business environment, where Asian entrepreneurs can still face difficulties in securing major projects.

His company now reports annual business of more than $7 million, equivalent to nearly Rs 1 billion.

Chaudhary says his company works on major projects and provides consultancy and related services.

Why he chose Dubai

Kamal Chaudhary says one of the major differences he has observed between the Gulf countries and Nepal is the enforcement of rules.

“In Dubai and Qatar, you don’t have to pay bribes to get work done. You have to complete the work properly and according to the rules, otherwise you face penalties,” he says.

He believes this discipline has contributed significantly to the development of countries such as Qatar and the UAE.

Nepal, he argues, needs not only better laws and policies but also stronger implementation and cleaner leadership.

Bringing experience back to Nepal

Despite building his career abroad, Kamal Chaudhary remains closely connected to Nepal.

He believes Nepalis working overseas have accumulated valuable skills, knowledge and international experience that can contribute to Nepal’s development.

For him, Nepal’s young people need to become more actively involved in development, while the country should also find ways to bring back the expertise of its migrant workforce.

He says the recent youth-led movement has created some hope for change, but argues that Nepal needs leadership committed to transparency and development.

“It’s not enough to have policies and laws. The intentions of those leading the country also need to be clean,” he says.

title.rendered: Nepal-made Yatri P-2 electric scooter launched with range of up to 157 km

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Nepali brand Yatri has launched its new electric scooter, the Yatri P-2, designed and manufactured in Nepal.

Sipradi Trading colaborated with Yatri to introduced the P-2 with three battery options: 5.2 kWh, 3.7 kWh and 3 kWh.

According to the company, the 5.2 kWh model can travel up to 157 km on a full charge. The 3.7 kWh version offers a range of up to 112 km, while the 3 kWh model can travel up to 90 km.

DC fast charging

One of the key features of the P-2 is support for DC fast charging.

Sipradi Yatri said it plans to install DC chargers at 35 locations across the country. The P-2 supports a 3.3 kW DC charger, which the company expects will make charging more convenient for customers travelling longer distances.

Android Auto and Apple CarPlay

The P-2 comes with several smart features, including support for Android Auto and Apple CarPlay.

It also features a real-time energy meter and a smart display.

The P-2 was tested in different geographical and road conditions across Nepal before being launched.

The company said the scooter was tested in areas including Jiri, Kathmandu, Mulkot, Katari, Bharatpur and Waling, covering routes from the plains to hilly and difficult roads.

The P-2 has been developed through a partnership between Sipradi Trading and Yatri Motorcycles. The company says the scooter has been designed, engineered and manufactured in Nepal.

Sipradi Yatri plans to invest around Rs 600 million in the production plant for the P-2 and aims to produce up to 50,000 units annually.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah skips local welcome in Mustang during private visit

content.rendered:
Prime Minister Balen Shah avoided a group of local women who had gathered outside a hotel in Jomsom to welcome him on Saturday, entering the hotel through a back door instead.

Members of the Puthang Women’s Group had gathered outside the Oms Home Jomsom carrying khadas, a traditional form of welcome in Mustang. After failing to meet the prime minister, they waited outside for some time before returning disappointed.

Shah was staying at the hotel during his private trip to Mustang. He later visited the Muktinath temple at around 8pm, travelling by an alternative route and reaching the temple premises by vehicle. He offered prayers at the main temple and returned to the hotel without meeting anyone.

The prime minister’s visit has drawn attention not only over his decision to avoid public interaction but also over the security arrangements made for the trip.

Shah travelled to Mustang by road and drove the vehicle himself. His private visit was coordinated primarily with the Nepal Army, while district administrations in Kaski, Baglung, Myagdi and Mustang said they had not been informed or involved in the visit in the usual manner.

The prime minister spent two nights in Pokhara and one night in Jomsom before returning to Kathmandu by air on Monday morning.

He stayed at Annapurna Eco Village in Machhapuchhre Rural Municipality on Friday and at Oms Home in Jomsom on Saturday. On Sunday, he stayed at Majheri Manzil Resort, owned by Tourism Minister Khadak Raj Paudel, before flying back to Kathmandu on a Buddha Air flight.

Shah had also stayed at the same resort during his visits to Pokhara while serving as mayor of Kathmandu.

District officials say there was little coordination

The prime minister’s security during the private trip was handled entirely by the Nepal Army, according to the information provided by district officials.

Baglung Chief District Officer Krishna Prasad Acharya said he was not particularly concerned about the visit because it had been described as a private trip.

Shah entered the Nepal Army’s 23 Brigade headquarters in Baglung, where he had a meal before leaving. Journalist Khemraj Gautam photographed him entering the barracks.

Mustang Chief District Officer Ajita Sharma said necessary security arrangements had been made but that, because the visit was private, there had been little emphasis on coordination.

Kaski Chief District Officer Kuman Singh Gurung likewise said the administration had not taken a greater interest because the visit was understood to be private.

Under the usual procedure for visits by very important persons, district security committees coordinate security arrangements. The procedure covers official, informal and private visits, but this time police and local administration were not involved in the same way because the trip was treated as private.

Normally, all four security agencies coordinate to establish separate security rings around the prime minister.

The Nepal Army’s specially trained team forms the innermost security ring, while Nepal Police personnel, including uniformed and plainclothes commandos and officers, operate in the next ring.

The Armed Police Force is responsible for outer security, crowd control, securing event venues and escorting the prime minister’s vehicle convoy. The National Investigation Department gathers and analyses intelligence about possible security threats in and around locations the prime minister is scheduled to visit.

Normally, an emergency meeting of the district security committee chaired by the chief district officer is held before the prime minister arrives in a district to assess potential security threats. Officials said this was not done in the same manner during Shah’s private trip.

A private trip that drew public attention

While some have praised Shah for travelling without a large entourage and avoiding excessive use of state resources, others have questioned whether the lack of coordination with local authorities was appropriate for a sitting prime minister.

Questions have also been raised on social media over whether a prime minister’s visit can be treated entirely as a private matter.

Locals had sought opportunities to meet Shah during his trip. In Mustang, residents waiting to welcome him were unable to meet him.

A similar situation occurred in Kaski, where local journalist Suresh Sunar said he was asked to delete a video he had recorded after learning that Shah was staying at Majheri Manzil.

“Since the prime minister had arrived, we were taking photos and videos. Someone came and asked us not to record the private visit and to delete it,” Sunar said. “When they asked me to coordinate and remove the video, I deleted it.”

Photos and videos were also reportedly not allowed at Oms Hotel and Annapurna Eco Village.

Shah’s decision to avoid public interaction during the trip has also prompted questions about the balance between maintaining his privacy and fulfilling the public responsibilities of a prime minister.

The photographs were provided by Sundarkumar Thakali from Mustang and Khemraj Gautam from Baglung.

title.rendered: Two killed, 10 injured in accident in Syangja

content.rendered:
Syangja, August 24

Two people were killed and 10 others, including the driver, were injured when an SUV met with an accident in Galyang Municipality-8 of Syangja district on Monday evening.

The SUV, bearing registration number Ga 1 Ja 6534, was travelling from Galyang towards Sangliya in Galyang Municipality-9 when it lost control while ascending a road at around 5:45 pm, according to police.

Two people died at the scene, said Deputy Superintendent of Police Ramesh Dutta Awasthi, information officer at the District Police Office, Syangja.

The injured, including the driver, have been taken to a hospital for treatment.

Police said they have yet to ascertain the exact number of people travelling in the jeep at the time of the accident.

title.rendered: NRB to be required to issue monetary policy on first day of fiscal year

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Nepal Rastra Bank will be required to issue its monetary policy on the first day of every fiscal year under a proposed amendment to the Nepal Rastra Bank Act.

The amendment bill currently under clause-by-clause discussion at the House of Representatives’ Finance Committee proposes that the central bank release its monetary policy every year on Shrawan 1, the first day of Nepal’s fiscal year.

The Finance Committee decided to include the provision during its meeting on Monday, committee chair Dr Krishna Hari Budhathoki said.

The committee also discussed and decided on proposed amendments to several provisions, including Sections 25 and 41 of the bill.

The committee also began discussions on provisions concerning the Nepal Rastra Bank’s authority to take general action against banks, including declaring individuals ineligible to hold banking positions.

However, officials from Nepal Rastra Bank suggested that the issue should instead be addressed through amendments to the Banks and Financial Institutions Act.

Officials from the Ministry of Law also said the committee could not discuss or amend provisions for which no amendment had been proposed.

Bankers seek changes to disqualification provision

Chair Budhathoki said the Nepal Bankers’ Association and chief executive officers of various banks had expressed serious concerns about Section 100 of the Nepal Rastra Bank Act.

According to him, bankers have demanded changes to the provision, arguing that it allows individuals to be declared ineligible for banking positions even on the basis of general disciplinary action.

The concern follows a recent Supreme Court ruling that individuals serving as directors of banks and financial institutions can be disqualified from holding their positions if they have faced action from Nepal Rastra Bank.

The ruling has created concerns in the banking sector because even individuals who have received warnings or written cautions from the central bank could be barred from continuing in their positions.

The bankers have therefore requested that the relevant legal provisions be amended.

The Supreme Court had ruled that such individuals could be considered ineligible under Section 18 of the Banks and Financial Institutions Act 2017. The ruling has raised concerns among chief executive officers and directors of banks and financial institutions.

title.rendered: Three-year-old’s rape and murder case raises questions over police probe, child privacy

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

The rape and murder of a three-year-old girl in Bara has shocked and angered the country, with widespread demands for strict legal action against the perpetrator.

But a video showing a minor arrested in connection with the case giving a statement while handcuffed has raised serious questions over police investigation, child rights, privacy and responsible information sharing.

In the video, which has gone viral on social media, the alleged offender is seen speaking about the incident while handcuffed. Police personnel can also be seen in the footage, while some individuals appear to be recording the statement on mobile phones.

The release of such a sensitive video during an ongoing investigation is not a routine matter. As the case has yet to reach a final court verdict, the circulation of footage that could reveal the identity of the minor could affect the investigation, judicial process and the child and his family.

The seriousness of the crime makes the need for a sensitive investigation and responsible flow of information even more important. Instead, the public release of the minor’s statement has itself become a serious concern.

Protection must come first, whether a child is a victim or accused

Psychiatrist Dr Sagun Ballav Pant says children require protection whether they are victims or accused of a crime.

According to him, releasing sensitive footage in a way that reveals a child’s face, name, voice or other identifying details goes against the basic principles of child protection.

This is particularly concerning in cases involving sexual violence and serious crimes, where the release of footage can cause further trauma to the victim’s family.

The accused minor and his family could also face long-term psychosocial consequences.

“Confidential material related to an investigation and judicial process should not be made public in this way. Spreading such material simply for views, likes or publicity is harmful to society,” Pant said.

He said repeated exposure to violent videos could increase fear, anxiety, insecurity, curiosity and psychological stress among children.

Children may also search for such content out of curiosity and experience psychological consequences from watching it. Such material can also increase anger, anxiety, suspicion, insecurity and sleep problems among parents and members of the wider public, Pant said.

Police investigation could also be affected

The unauthorised release of information that should remain confidential during an investigation does not only affect the victim and accused. It could also create problems for investigators, experts say.

“At present, this is still at the preliminary investigation stage. If the investigation takes a different direction tomorrow, the police could also face difficulties,” former Nepal Police DIG Hemant Malla said.

He said the public release of the accused’s statement could lead to questions over whether the investigation had been influenced.

“Technology is available to record statements. But it is not meant only to keep a record in case the accused says something different later. Such material should not be made public under any circumstances. This is plainly wrong,” Malla said.

Lawyer Rojina Shrestha also said confidential videos of this nature should not be made public.

Since the accused is a minor and the case has not yet been finally decided, publicly releasing his statement could affect his privacy, family life and future, she said.

There is also a risk that once someone is publicly labelled guilty on social media, public opinion could become stronger than the evidence-based assessment that must take place in court.

“Being accused and being proven guilty are not the same thing. The court must decide on the basis of evidence. Creating an environment where someone is declared guilty on social media before that process is a challenge to the justice system,” Shrestha said.

She said protecting privacy is not merely an ethical issue but an important part of children’s rights.

Consent does not mean unlimited publication

Even if a child is willing to speak or a family member agrees to a recording, that does not automatically mean the material can be widely published on social media, Shrestha said.

The child’s age, understanding and circumstances must be considered when determining whether consent is meaningful, she said.

In cases involving violence, sexual offences and judicial investigations, the best interests of the child must remain the priority.

Once such footage is circulated online, it becomes extremely difficult to control who uses it, how long it remains available and what impact it may have on the child’s future.

Pant said removing the sensitive video immediately, restricting its reach and discouraging further sharing should be priorities.

Because it is difficult to completely control a video once it has spread online, efforts should also be made to stop its redistribution through pages, groups and accounts, he said.

He also called for action against the deliberate circulation of sensitive material.

“Citizens need factual information on matters of public concern. But releasing confidential investigation material and creating a sensation is not the right to information. Protecting children from further pain and psychological harm is the responsibility of the state, media and society,” Pant said.

He added that the dignity and privacy of the deceased victim’s family must also be protected, while the age, psychological development, privacy and future of an accused minor must be considered from a child-rights perspective.

A viral video may fuel anger, but it does not deliver justice

The circulation of footage following a serious crime can quickly intensify public anger. People begin watching, sharing and commenting on the video in the name of finding out what happened.

But public anger and justice are not the same thing.

When opinions are formed on the basis of incomplete or unverified information, public outrage can grow and create pressure for punishment outside the legal process.

This can undermine evidence-based investigation and judicial proceedings.

Investigating crime is the responsibility of the police and judicial authorities. Creating a situation where social media crowds effectively deliver a verdict is not a healthy practice of justice.

‘An accused’s statement is not viral content’

Umesh Shrestha, chairman of the Press Council Nepal, said there should be no doubt that the truth must come out in serious crimes such as rape and murder and that anyone found guilty must face punishment according to law.

But publicly releasing a minor’s statement before a court has delivered its verdict is not justice, he said.

Journalism and information sharing also require restraint, sensitivity and adherence to professional standards. Regardless of the seriousness of an incident, the rights and human dignity of both the victim and the accused child cannot be ignored, Shrestha said.

“The victim’s suffering is not content. An accused’s statement is not viral material. Justice is needed, but through the justice system. Truth is needed, but with sensitivity. News is needed, but without compromising human dignity,” he said.

‘Do not forget responsibility in the race for likes and views’

Medical sociologist Madhusudan Subedi said the expansion of social media means almost everyone now has access to a camera and many people have begun producing and distributing content similar to journalism.

But the competition for likes, shares and views has encouraged people to overlook the social consequences of what they publish, he said.

This is particularly dangerous when dealing with sensitive issues such as rape, suicide and caste or communal tensions, Subedi said.

He urged people to ask themselves: “How would we think about this if it had happened to our own family?”

The fact that a piece of content goes viral does not prove that it is true, he said. The number of people sharing something cannot be treated as verification.

People should therefore rely on official information and facts obtained from credible sources when dealing with sensitive cases.

Those who receive such footage can choose not to share or download it for redistribution and can report it to the relevant social media platform, helping prevent further circulation.

Privacy is needed for both victim and accused

Child rights activist Tilottam Paudel said the matter should be taken even more seriously if the video was released by a government agency or someone working within the state mechanism.

Nepal’s Constitution, the concept of child-friendly justice, international child rights commitments and laws concerning children all place importance on children’s privacy and best interests, he said.

While demanding justice for the deceased girl is essential, violating the privacy and rights of another minor in the process is not a solution, Paudel said.

“Violating the privacy of an accused minor in the name of delivering justice to the victim is not a solution. The investigation must be impartial, scientific and child-friendly,” he said.

He called for effective mechanisms to ensure prompt investigation, legal proceedings and privacy protection in cases involving children.

Questions also raised over police investigation

The incident has raised questions not only for social media users but also for the investigating authorities.

If statements and evidence involving an arrested minor are supposed to remain confidential, questions remain over how the video was recorded and subsequently released.

Police have already arrested the police officer who allegedly recorded the video.

Pant said the release of confidential material during an investigation is a sensitive issue from both child protection and investigative perspectives.

In cases involving minors, investigators must give priority to the best interests and privacy of children, he said.

Paudel said responsibility must also be established if the footage was leaked by someone within the government system.

The leakage of sensitive investigative material could affect future investigations as well. Investigating agencies are responsible for protecting evidence, maintaining the confidentiality of statements and preventing unnecessary public pressure on the investigation.

Seeking justice without causing further harm

The alleged crime against the three-year-old girl is an extremely serious and painful incident. There have been widespread demands for the perpetrator to face strict punishment under the law.

The victim’s family deserves justice and the incident must be investigated fairly. The issue has also been raised in Parliament.

But even after a victim’s death, her dignity and her family’s privacy must be protected.

Likewise, protecting the privacy and rights of an accused minor does not mean minimising the crime or granting the accused impunity.

It means ensuring that the investigation is impartial, the truth is established through evidence and anyone found guilty is punished according to law.

According to Pant, the demand for justice and the protection of child rights are not contradictory.

A demand for justice for the victim does not require an accused minor to be publicly exposed or his video circulated. The search for justice should not result in damage to another child’s mental health, privacy and future.

Paudel said protecting the rights of both children — the victim and the accused — is the state’s responsibility.

Protecting the privacy of an accused minor is not about giving the person impunity, but about upholding the basic principles of child-friendly justice.

Experts say justice does not mean declaring someone guilty on social media. It means establishing the truth through evidence, punishing the guilty according to law and providing dignity and protection to the victim and her family.

The central question, therefore, is not whether the perpetrator should be punished. It is whether, in seeking justice, society is creating another lifelong source of harm by publicly exposing and stigmatising a child who has only been accused.

“This is a serious matter. Those responsible must also face action,” former DIG Malla said.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress chief whip meets Australian ambassador to discuss bilateral ties

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Nepali Congress chief whip Basana Thapa held a courtesy meeting with Australian Ambassador to Nepal Simon Ernst on Monday.

The meeting, held at the Nepali Congress Parliamentary Party office, focused on Nepal-Australia relations, parliamentary cooperation, education, people-to-people ties and matters of mutual interest.

Thapa said parliamentary cooperation should be prioritised to further strengthen relations between the two countries. She also stressed the need to increase regular dialogue and exchanges of experience between lawmakers from Nepal and Australia.

She called for the effective mobilisation of the Nepal-Australia Parliamentary Friendship Group to strengthen institutional ties between lawmakers of the two countries.

According to Thapa, the friendship group could serve as an important platform for cooperation and greater mutual understanding on issues of common interest.

Thapa also appreciated Australia’s longstanding support for Nepal’s social and economic development. She expressed gratitude for Australia’s contribution to Nepal’s human resource development through initiatives including Australia Awards scholarships, capacity-building programmes and training opportunities.

She noted that Australia remains a major destination for Nepali students pursuing higher education and said Nepali students and the wider Nepali community in Australia have played an important role in strengthening ties between the two countries.

During the meeting, Thapa also conveyed her greetings and best wishes to Australian House of Representatives Speaker Milton Dick through Ambassador Ernst.

Ambassador Ernst said parliamentary cooperation and people-to-people relations were important to further strengthening Nepal-Australia ties.

He expressed Australia’s continued commitment to expanding cooperation in areas including education, human resource development and parliamentary engagement.

title.rendered: Nepal A secure first win in Top End T20 Series

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Nepal A registered their first victory in the ongoing Top End T20 Series in Australia’s Northern Territory, defeating Hobart Hurricanes Academy by 39 runs on Monday.

Chasing a target of 155, Hobart Hurricanes Academy were bowled out for 115 in 18.3 overs.

Nitesh Samuel top-scored for Hobart with 37 runs, while Tim Ward made 23 and Nivethan Radhakrishnan contributed 20.

Narayan Joshi was Nepal’s leading bowler with three wickets. Pawan Sarraf and Shah Alam claimed two wickets each, while Bipin Khatri took one.

Earlier, Nepal A, after being asked to bat first, scored 154 for eight in their 20 overs.

Kushal Bhurtel was Nepal’s top scorer with 39 runs, while Anil Sah made 28 and Lokesh Bam remained unbeaten on 20.

For Hobart, Raph McMillan took three wickets for 18 runs in four overs. Marcus Bean claimed two wickets, while Bradley Hope and Nivethan Radhakrishnan took one each.

Nepal had lost their opening two matches of the tournament before securing Monday’s victory.

Nepal A will play their fourth match against ACT Comets on Wednesday.

title.rendered: Samsung Nepal announces monsoon offer with up to 23% cashback

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Samsung Nepal has announced a special monsoon offer on its TVs and home appliances, offering customers up to 23 percent cashback along with various gifts.

The offer covers Samsung’s latest range of TVs, washing machines and refrigerators, with the company saying it aims to make premium technology and features more accessible to consumers looking to upgrade their home appliances.

Under the offer, customers can receive up to 23 percent instant cashback on selected home appliances. Customers purchasing selected TV models will also receive gifts including up to 12 months of free NetTV subscription and a free soundbar, according to the company.

For washing machines, customers purchasing Samsung AI EcoBubble washer-dryer models ranging from 7kg to 12kg, as well as front-load, FATL and SATL washing machines, can receive up to 23 percent instant cashback.

Samsung is also offering up to 17 percent cashback on selected single-door, double-door and side-by-side refrigerators.

The company said the monsoon offer provides customers with options to upgrade their home entertainment systems, make everyday laundry smarter and replace essential kitchen appliances.

Samsung Nepal said the offer is intended to make it easier for customers to choose TVs and home appliances according to their needs and preferences.

title.rendered: NA chair urges Australian ambassador to help implement direct air service agreement

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

National Assembly Chair Narayan Prasad Dahal held a courtesy meeting with Australian Ambassador to Nepal Simon Ernst on Monday, discussing bilateral relations, mutual interests, cooperation and parliamentary exchanges.

The meeting took place at Dahal’s office in Singha Durbar.

During the meeting, Dahal urged Ambassador Ernst to take necessary initiatives for the implementation of the agreement to establish direct air services between Nepal and Australia.

Dahal expressed confidence that the longstanding friendly relations between the two countries would be further strengthened in the coming days.

He said Nepal and Australia have maintained cordial relations since establishing diplomatic ties and that there are no major differences between the two countries at either the bilateral or international level.

Dahal also said the trade and investment agreement signed between the two countries last year would give fresh momentum to economic cooperation.

Parliamentary ties

Dahal said the Federal Parliament has established the Nepal-Australia Parliamentary Friendship Group and stressed that exchanges of parliamentary experience, regular interactions and bilateral visits could further strengthen relations.

Referring to his meetings with the Speaker of the Australian Parliament on the sidelines of various Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) conferences, Dahal said parliamentary diplomacy should continue to be used to deepen ties between the two countries.

He also described people-to-people relations as an important foundation of Nepal-Australia ties.

Dahal noted that Australia has become a major destination for Nepali students pursuing higher education, with thousands of Nepalis studying there. He said the large Nepali community working and involved in various professions in Australia has further strengthened people-to-people relations between the two countries.

Ambassador Ernst thanked Dahal for the meeting and said he would continue working during his tenure in Nepal to bring the two countries closer and further strengthen bilateral relations.

Ernst said Nepal and Australia have strong ties not only at the diplomatic level but also between their people.

He said more than 60,000 Nepali students are currently studying in Australia and that the overall Nepali population in the country exceeds 200,000.

title.rendered: Raj Regmi went to Qatar with no big dream. He returned as an entrepreneur

content.rendered:
When Raj Regmi first landed in Qatar in 2003, he had a modest goal shared by thousands of Nepali migrant workers: find a job and support his family back home.

More than two decades later, the Baglung-born entrepreneur has become an employer of thousands of workers in Qatar, with around 70 percent of them Nepali.

Regmi, who is also a vice-president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) International Coordination Council, has built businesses in Qatar while investing in Nepal’s hydropower, banking, healthcare and real estate sectors.

His journey, however, began without a major business plan.

At 22 or 23, Regmi left Nepal amid political instability and limited employment opportunities. With the help of an uncle already working in Qatar, he arrived in the country for his first international flight and his first experience of working abroad.

From 2003 to 2006, he worked as a sales representative in the telecommunications sector.

The experience introduced him to Qatar’s market, business systems and working culture. It also exposed him to the challenges of living and working far from home.

“I did not come to Qatar with a big dream,” Regmi recalls. “But today, I have become a source of employment for thousands of Nepalis. That gives me the greatest satisfaction.”

From employee to entrepreneur

Raj Regmi returned to Nepal in 2006 with plans to start his own business in Qatar. However, restrictions on changing companies meant he had to spend about two years in Nepal preparing for the move.

In 2009, he returned to Qatar and established companies including Phidas Trading and Ocean, entering the construction and related service sectors.

He started with limited capital, focusing on road and building construction, oil and gas-related projects, housekeeping and maintenance.

His business expanded rapidly, particularly during Qatar’s preparations for the 2022 FIFA World Cup, when construction activity reached a peak.

His companies became involved in major infrastructure projects, including metro and stadium-related works. At one point, as many as 5,000–6,000 workers were working under his companies.

Today, his businesses employ around 4,000–5,000 workers.

Regmi says the experience taught him that business growth depends not only on capital but also on trust, discipline and the treatment of workers.

His companies adopted a policy of not charging workers recruitment fees and assisting them with visa processing and interviews.

For Regmi, the success of his business has also been closely linked to the contribution of Nepali workers.

Changing perceptions of Nepalis

Raj Regmi has witnessed a significant change in how Nepalis are perceived in Qatar.

Nepalis were once largely associated with construction and cleaning jobs. Today, he says, Nepalis are increasingly visible as doctors, engineers, managers and entrepreneurs.

He attributes this change to the community’s discipline, honesty and work ethic.

His own workforce reflects that shift, with Nepalis making up around 70 percent of his employees.

Regmi has also developed close ties with the wider Nepali community through his involvement in the NRNA and other business and social organisations.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, he worked through the NRNA to distribute food and medical supplies and support Nepalis who had lost their jobs.

Beyond business

For Raj Regmi, business is not simply a means of generating income.

He believes the experience and capital accumulated by Nepalis abroad can play a significant role in Nepal’s economic transformation if the government creates a more predictable investment environment.

He has invested in Nepal in hydropower, banking, healthcare and real estate but remains concerned about lengthy procedures and a lack of incentives for investors.

He believes Nepal needs clearer policies, easier access to investment and credit, and greater trust between the government and private sector.

“Foreign employment should not only be about sending workers abroad,” he argues. “The knowledge, skills, networks and capital they gain should also be brought back and invested in Nepal.”

Qatar as a learning ground

Raj Regmi describes Qatar as more than a destination for foreign employment. For him, it became a “university” where he learned about business, discipline, policy and development.

The early difficulties—from language barriers to understanding government procedures—gradually became lessons that helped him build his businesses.

He says Nepal can learn from Qatar’s development experience, particularly in areas such as policy clarity, infrastructure development and attracting investment.

He also sees potential for greater Nepal-Qatar cooperation in hydropower, tourism and industry.

Despite building a sizeable business empire abroad, Raj Regmi says his greatest achievement remains the employment his companies have created.

He left Nepal as a young migrant worker looking for a job.

More than 20 years later, his journey has taken him from being an employee in Qatar to becoming an entrepreneur, investor and employer of thousands—including many Nepalis who followed a path similar to his own.

title.rendered: 25 Nepali foreign employment companies to withdraw from Malaysia’s worker recruitment system

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Twenty-five Nepali foreign employment companies listed under Malaysia’s Foreign Worker Centralized Management System (FWCMS) have agreed to withdraw their names from the system.

The agreement was reached during a discussion at the Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment, according to Hari Bahadur Dangi, general secretary of the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies.

Malaysia had listed only 25 of around 1,200 licensed Nepali foreign employment companies in the FWCMS as “registered recruitment agencies” for recruiting Nepali workers.

The decision to include only 25 agencies had drawn opposition from foreign employment businesses, with the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies also suspending the membership of the listed companies and deciding to request government action against them.

Foreign employment agencies had argued that allowing only a limited number of companies to have direct access to Malaysian employers could create a syndicate and restrict competition in the recruitment of Nepali workers.

They said such an arrangement could leave access to employment opportunities in Malaysia concentrated among a small number of foreign employment companies.

Amid the controversy, the 25 companies listed in the FWCMS have now agreed to withdraw from the system themselves.

Dangi said the companies concluded that a system limiting recruitment opportunities to only them would not be in their long-term interest and agreed to leave the system collectively.

The 25 companies will also be required to submit a commitment to the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies.

The ministry had invited representatives of all 25 companies listed in the system for discussions.

During a separate discussion with Malaysia’s acting ambassador, Youth, Labour and Employment Minister Ramji Yadav said issues related to labour migration should be resolved through bilateral dialogue and agreement between the two countries.

title.rendered: Khushbu Oli calls for debate on death penalty for rape and murder

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) lawmaker Khushbu Oli has called for a debate on introducing the death penalty for heinous crimes such as rape and murder, arguing that the current criminal justice system may not be sufficient to deter such offences.

Speaking in Monday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, Oli said the debate should not be limited to how many years a convicted rapist should spend in prison, but should also address why capital punishment should not be considered for such serious crimes.

She also questioned the argument that Nepal’s constitutional and international commitments prevent the country from introducing the death penalty.

“Today, our mothers, sisters and daughters are on the streets demanding justice. So today’s debate is not about how many years to imprison a rapist; it is about why there should not be a death penalty for such heinous crimes,” Oli said.

She referred to the Constitution’s prohibition on laws providing for the death penalty and questioned whether international commitments should take precedence over the right to life of victims.

“Can any protocol be greater than the life of a Nepali daughter?” she asked, referring to cases including Nirmala, Anisha and the recent killing of a three-year-old girl.

Oli said the government should have the courage to review international commitments if they become an obstacle to justice.

She also questioned the focus on the human rights of accused and convicted criminals while victims are deprived of their fundamental rights.

“We talk about the human rights of criminals. But I want to ask this House a serious question: what about the human rights of those whose lives have been taken away?” she said.

Oli said the recent killing of the three-year-old girl had deprived her of the opportunity to experience life, relationships and the future.

She argued that the focus should therefore be on whether the state’s punishment system is adequate to prevent such heinous crimes.

Calls for rape convictions to carry ‘moral turpitude’ provision

Oli also called on the government to classify rape as a criminal offence involving moral turpitude.

She said rape constitutes a serious assault on a person’s body, dignity, freedom and life, and questioned why the law does not explicitly include rape among offences carrying such consequences.

“Why is there a provision of moral turpitude for other criminal offences but not for rape?” she asked.

Oli said people convicted of rape should not be allowed to misuse public office after serving their sentences.

She also called for a review of the statute of limitations for serious sexual offences, arguing that procedural time limits should not prevent victims from seeking justice.

“The door to justice should not be closed because a victim took too long to knock on it,” she said.

Oli urged lawmakers, courts and other stakeholders to review whether the existing limitation period for rape cases is appropriate and how it should be determined.

title.rendered: Supreme Court orders immediate payment of dues to dairy farmers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

The Supreme Court has ordered the government to ensure the immediate payment of outstanding dues owed to dairy farmers and establish a system for ensuring that farmers are paid regularly for their milk.

A division bench of Justices Nahakul Subedi and Sunil Kumar Pokharel issued the order, directing the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development to facilitate payment of all outstanding amounts owed to milk producers by the Dairy Development Corporation (DDC) and private dairy industries.

The court ordered the ministry to make “appropriate and necessary arrangements” to ensure that outstanding payments are made immediately and that milk producers are paid within a regular payment cycle in the future.

The court also directed the ministry to promote and develop the dairy sector.

Farmers owed around Rs 7 billion

The order came after lawyers Dr Punya Prasad Khatiwada and Dipak Bikram Mishra filed a writ petition seeking payment of the dues owed to dairy farmers.

At the time of the petition, dairy farmers were reportedly owed around Rs 7 billion, including approximately Rs 6 billion by private dairy industries affiliated with the Dairy Industry Association and Dairy Association, and around Rs 900 million by the government-owned DDC.

Around three million families are estimated to be directly or indirectly involved in Nepal’s dairy sector, keeping approximately 7.4 million cattle and 5.2 million buffaloes.

The petitioners argued that many dairy farmers had not received payment for milk supplied over three to four months, discouraging them from continuing livestock farming.

DDC had unsold dairy products

According to details submitted by the DDC to the government through the Ministry of Agriculture, the corporation had approximately 900 metric tonnes of milk powder, 700 tonnes of butter, three tonnes of paneer, three tonnes of mozzarella, 12 tonnes of yak cheese and five tonnes of Kanchan cheese in stock.

The DDC had prepared a plan to pay dairy farmers, citing around Rs 1.5 billion worth of dairy products that remained unpaid.

The issue had also been discussed between the Agriculture Ministry, DDC and representatives of farmers in February 2024. An agreement was reached at the time, following which farmers suspended their protests, but the outstanding payments were not cleared as expected.

Previous Supreme Court order also went unimplemented

The Supreme Court had issued a three-point directive around two and a half years ago, in February 2024, ordering authorities to address the dairy farmers’ problems within 15 days.

The court had directed the Agriculture Ministry, DDC, Dairy Cooperative Limited, Nepal Dairy Association and private dairy industries to submit a plan for clearing outstanding payments owed to dairy farmers.

It had also ordered authorities to determine why payments had not been made and prepare a realistic timetable for clearing the dues.

The court further instructed the Agriculture Ministry and the National Dairy Development Board to monitor implementation of agreements between dairy industries and farmers.

Despite those directives and an agreement between the government and farmer representatives, payment problems continued.

Government promises shorter payment cycle

Last week, Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary claimed that the maximum period for milk payments would be limited to 25 days by the final week of Bhadra.

She also said the DDC had paid Rs 600 million to farmers over the previous three months.

However, the Supreme Court has stressed that milk farmers in an agriculture-dependent country should not have to wait for long periods to receive payment for their produce.

The court said the state must take an active role in creating an environment in which farmers receive their payments on time.

The full text of the ruling, issued in December 2024, was made public by the Supreme Court on Sunday, around a year and a half after the judgment.

According to the court, the publication of the full text was delayed after case files were taken away following the events of September 9, 2025.

title.rendered: Koshi Chief Minister Karki receives vote of confidence

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, August 24

Koshi Province Chief Minister Hikmat Kumar Karki has received a vote of confidence. He won the vote at a Provincial Assembly meeting held on Monday.

57 votes were cast in his favour, while 22 votes were cast against.

Lawmakers from CPN-UML and the Nepal Communist Party voted in favour of the confidence motion, while Nepali Congress lawmakers voted against it.

The Koshi Provincial Assembly has 40 UML members and 17 Nepal Communist Party members.

RPP lawmakers remained neutral. RPP has 5 members in Koshi, including the Assembly Speaker. Nirmala Limbu, the sole lawmaker from the Janata Samajwadi Party, was absent.

Of the Provincial Assembly’s 93 seats, one member has resigned, leaving 92 current members. 83 members were present at Monday’s Provincial Assembly meeting.

title.rendered: 3 NCP ministers appointed to Lumbini Provincial Cabinet

content.rendered:
Butwal, August 24

Three ministers from the Nepali Communist Party (NCP) have been appointed to the Lumbini Provincial Government.

Chief Minister Chet Narayan Acharya recommended the names of the three ministers to the provincial chief. Dipendra Kumar Pun has been assigned the Ministry of Health, Indrajit Tharu the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Planning, and Krishna Kushma Tharu the Ministry of Agriculture, Land Management and Cooperatives.

The newly appointed ministers are scheduled to take the oath of office and secrecy at the Office of the Provincial Chief in Butwal at 3:25 pm on Tuesday.

Other members of the Cabinet have been recommended for the following portfolios: Tulsi Prasad Chaudhary for the Ministry of Forests, Environment and Tourism; Ramji Prasad Ghimire for the Ministry of Social Development; Santosh Kumar Pandey for the Ministry of Urban Development, Energy, Irrigation and Water Supply; Ratna Bahadur Khatri for the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development; and Bhandarilal Ahir for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Law, Industry and Transport.

Ghimire, who previously held the Health Ministry, has been assigned the Ministry of Social Development.

Chaudhary, who previously headed the Ministry of Agriculture, Land Management and Cooperatives, has been assigned the Ministry of Forests, Environment and Tourism.

Similarly, Pandey, who was serving as Minister for Social Development, has been proposed for the Ministry of Urban Development, Energy, Irrigation and Water Supply.

The Cabinet is being reshuffled in line with an agreement to have four ministers, including the chief minister, from the CPN-UML, three from the NCP and two from the Janata Samajbadi Party, Nepal, in the current provincial government.

title.rendered: Saroj Bhattarai’s book Gulabi Prem, Sapana ra Awashesh set to release on September 19

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Advocate and columnist Saroj Bhattarai’s new book, Kaleji Prem, Sapana ra Awashesh, is set to be launched on September 19.

Bhattarai’s new work blends legal argument, literary defiance, and unflinching social critique into a single ideological thread. The book goes beyond literature, posing sharp questions about power, politics, society, love, justice, and the unfulfilled dreams of ordinary people.

The book examines the harsh realities hidden behind political slogans, exposing how opportunism, self-interest, and power struggles trample the aspirations of common citizens. It gives voice to those left out of political rhetoric, people with broken dreams, unfinished love stories, and hopes crushed under the weight of power structures.

Drawing on his career arguing legal cases, Bhattarai brings life’s unresolved issues before the “court” of literature, addressing emotions society has condemned, voices power has silenced, characters history has forgotten, and remnants time has left behind.

In the book, love is portrayed not merely as sentiment but as rebellion, resistance, and a final act of courage in preserving human existence within a harsh system.

The author’s writing questions authority, holds a mirror to society, and confronts readers with their own silence. The book raises an uncomfortable question: what have we gained and lost in the name of change, and whose power stands today atop the ruins of our collective dreams?

The book is being positioned as an unflinching account of contemporary Nepali society, politics, and human emotion, an ideological challenge to the political darkness hidden beneath love’s rosy surface, and to the despair accumulated within the brightness of dreams.

title.rendered: Lawmakers call for death penalty for rape convicts

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Lawmakers speaking at Monday’s meeting of the House of Representatives called for laws imposing severe punishment, including the death penalty, on those convicted of rape.

They argued that although the death penalty may conflict with Nepal’s Constitution and its international human rights commitments, Parliament should have the capacity to address such legal constraints.

Lawmakers called for amendments to existing laws in line with current circumstances, citing the rape and murder of three-year-old Garima Chaudhary as well as several similar incidents in the past.

According to police, three-year-old Garima Chaudhary of Dasdhure Tol in Jitpur Simara Sub-Metropolitan City-1 went missing from her home on the morning of August 15. Her mother, Manmati, informed the Simara and Pathlaiya police after she had not seen her daughter for around three and a half hours. Police told her they would search for the girl.

The girl’s body was found two days later.

Raising the issue in Parliament, lawmakers said laws needed to be strengthened to ensure severe punishment for rapists.

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Prakash Pathak also raised the murder of 25-year-old Laxmi Rajbanshi, a permanent resident of Bhadrapur, Jhapa, who had gone to Japan for studies and was killed in her own room.

He also said that 12-year-old Rebika Bishwakarma, a seventh-grade student from Haldibari-2, Jhapa, had been missing for two days. He urged the Ministry of Home Affairs to immediately intensify efforts to locate her.

“Whether in Nepal or abroad, our daughters are unsafe everywhere,” he said. “Only those who experience it know what such pain feels like. How long must our daughters continue to become Laxmi Rajbanshi, Nirmala Pant and Garima Chaudhary?”

He suggested that authorities needed to examine whether flaws in existing policies and laws were contributing to the rise in such brutal incidents.

“Article 16(2) of the Constitution guarantees the right to live with dignity. But that does not mean criminals and murderers should be protected,” he said. “Unless murderers, rapists and other criminals are punished severely, our daughters will continue to fall victim to predators everywhere.”

He then called for the introduction of harsher punishments.

“Whether it is the constitutional restriction against introducing a death penalty law that conflicts with the fundamental law, or the human rights treaties and agreements to which Nepal is a party, these provisions now need to be reconsidered. This House must have the capacity to do so,” he said.

He proposed that the state should immediately introduce a law providing for the death penalty for convicted murderers and rapists instead of keeping them in prison at the taxpayers’ expense.

RSP lawmaker Ranju Darshana said efforts to address the problem should begin at the school level, noting that girls remain unsafe even in a society that traditionally worships daughters.

Nepali Congress lawmaker Shahjahan Khatun also called for measures to prevent such incidents from continuing.

Congress lawmaker Ninukumari Karn stressed that the state must be able to control such incidents.

Radhika Ramtel of the Shram Sanskriti Party demanded that the government provide answers on the issue. She urged the government to introduce strict punishments and take measures to prevent similar incidents.

RSP lawmaker Harimohan Bhandari said the government should not continue to provide for those convicted of serious and heinous crimes. “We are ready to make whatever law is necessary for this purpose,” he said, urging the government to introduce a stringent bill.

RSP lawmaker Ashika Tamang said the law should provide for the death penalty for rapists if possible. “If that is not possible, the law should provide for the amputation of the body part used to commit the rape,” she said.

title.rendered: Janmat Party to hold second general convention in September

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

The Janmat Party, led by Dr C.K. Raut, will hold its second general convention next month, in September. The convention will take place on September 25 and 25.

A secretariat meeting held on Monday set a schedule to complete ward- and municipality-level processes by September 6.

The meeting also decided to keep the active membership status intact for all members who remain on record as of September. Since only those who have renewed their membership by paying a set fee will be eligible to become convention delegates or candidates, party cadres have been urged to pay the fee and renew their membership.

A secretariat meeting has been called for September 7 to take further decisions regarding the convention.

title.rendered: Manish Jha raises concerns over demolition drive in Janakpur

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Manish Jha has raised concerns in Parliament over a demolition drive targeting structures built around public ponds in Janakpur.

Speaking during Monday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, Jha said bulldozers had been operating in Janakpur since Saturday as part of an effort to clear encroachments around public ponds.

“Around 65 houses have been cleared during the process,” he said.

Jha said the demolition drive had raised concerns among local residents, particularly over whether the campaign would disproportionately affect poorer communities.

“There is a kind of fear in Janakpur, and there is also a suspicion that perhaps only the settlements of poor people will be removed while the powerful will be left untouched,” he said.

Calls for action against powerful encroachers

Jha said he had coordinated with the Guthi Sansthan and had been informed that action would also be taken against structures belonging to influential individuals.

According to Jha, notices would be issued within 15 days to clear hotels built by encroaching on ponds, hotel parking areas constructed over ponds, hospitals and other structures built by encroaching on public ponds.

He also said action would be taken against land that had been encroached upon and leased out by private individuals who were collecting rent from it.

Jha said Janakpur was possibly among the sub-metropolitan cities in Nepal with the largest amount of public land.

He referred to a report prepared in 2005 under the leadership of Bhojraj Ghimire, which reportedly found that around 950 bighas of land in Janakpur had been encroached upon, acquired or misused.

Jha said the current demolition drive was being carried out on the basis of that report.

‘Do not target only the poor’

Jha thanked the federal government and Prime Minister for paying attention to the issue but urged the authorities to ensure that the campaign was not limited to demolishing the homes of poorer residents.

“We are grateful, on behalf of the people of Janakpur, for the attention of the federal government and the Prime Minister to the work currently underway,” he said. “But we would again like to request that this campaign and its action should not target only the poor.”

He called for equal treatment under the law and urged the authorities to ensure that the broader objective of protecting and reclaiming public land was achieved.

“All should be treated equally, and the campaign to protect and publicly reclaim the 950 bighas of land that have been encroached upon in Janakpur should succeed,” Jha said.

title.rendered: Spider-Man crosses Rs 160 million in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Spider-Man: Brand New Day has become the fifth-highest-grossing foreign film in Nepal. By Monday afternoon, the film had crossed Rs 160 million at the domestic box office.

The film’s total gross collection so far stands at Rs 160.2 million.

It is projected to overtake the Indian film Animal, starring Ranbir Kapoor, which has grossed a total of Rs 165.6 million, by this coming weekend.

Interestingly, “Spider-Man” is the only Hollywood film to feature in Nepal’s top 10 highest-grossing foreign films list.

title.rendered: Play on Ganesh Man Singh’s life to be staged at Sarwanam Theatre

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

A play based on the life of Ganesh Man Singh is set to be staged at Sarwanam Theatre. Titled Bir Ganesh Man, the play has been conceptualised, adapted and directed by Ashesh Malla.

The play will portray the life, struggles and convictions of Ganesh Man Singh, a prominent figure in Nepal’s democratic movement. Widely known as the “Iron Man” of Nepali politics, Singh devoted his entire life to establishing and restoring democracy in Nepal.

Born on November 24, 1915, into a Newa family in Kathmandu, Singh died on September 18, 1997. He was a founding leader of the Nepali Congress and the supreme commander of the historic 1990 People’s Movement.

The play, based on his life, will be staged regularly from August 30 to October 1, except on Thursdays.
