title.rendered: NEPSE falls below 2,600 as market sheds 19 points

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Nepal’s stock market fell below the 2,600-point mark on Monday, with the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index dropping 19.13 points to close at 2,599 points.

The market had declined by 10.67 points in the previous session, when turnover stood at around Rs 4.16 billion. On Monday, total turnover fell to Rs 3.23 billion.

The decline was broad-based, with 229 companies recording losses, while 47 gained and two remained unchanged.

All sectoral indices closed lower. The hydropower index recorded the steepest decline, falling 1.19 percent, followed by non-life insurance, which dropped 1.12 percent.

The banking sector fell 0.67 percent, development banks 0.47 percent, finance 0.80 percent, hotels and tourism 0.01 percent, investment 0.41 percent, life insurance 0.81 percent, manufacturing and processing 0.46 percent, microfinance 0.53 percent, others 0.78 percent and trading 0.50 percent.

As usual, hydropower companies accounted for the largest share of trading activity, with the sector recording turnover of around Rs 1.68 billion.

Manufacturing and processing companies recorded turnover of around Rs 320 million, while commercial banks accounted for around Rs 300 million.

The latest decline extends the recent weakness in the market. NEPSE had closed at 2,618.72 points on Friday after falling 10.67 points, and the index had already lost 25.11 points over the previous trading week.

title.rendered: SC orders authorities to appear with materials seized from Durga Prasai’s house

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

The Supreme Court has ordered the authorities to appear with materials seized from activist Durga Prasai’s residence in connection with a writ petition filed by him.

A bench led by Justice Nripa Dhoj Niraula issued the order on Monday, directing the concerned authorities to appear within 24 hours with the materials seized during a search of Durga Prasai’s house.

The court has also asked the authorities to explain within 24 hours why Prasai has been restricted from moving outside his residence.

The order directs the District Police Range, Bhaktapur, to submit a written response through the Office of the Attorney General and bring to the hearing the materials reportedly seized during the house search conducted on August 20 under a search warrant.

The Supreme Court order states that the authorities must provide the basis and reasons for why an order should not be issued against them and submit their written response within 24 hours, excluding the time required for transit.

The court has separately instructed the District Police Range, Bhaktapur, to bring to the hearing the items reportedly seized from Prasai’s residence during the search conducted under the warrant dated August 20.

The order was issued in response to Prasai’s writ petition challenging the restrictions imposed on his movement.

title.rendered: Lahan Municipality demolishes market structures, traders allege discrimination

content.rendered:
Siraha, August 24

Lahan Municipality has demolished houses and makeshift structures in Naya Bazar using a bulldozer, saying it was forced to take action after traders failed to vacate the structures despite repeated notices.

However, traders in Naya Bazar have accused Mayor Mahesh Prasad Chaudhary of acting selectively. They said there are more than 200 houses and makeshift structures in the market, but the municipality demolished only seven, alleging that the action was discriminatory.

The municipality had issued a notice asking occupants to vacate the structures within three days. Local trader Ramsundar Sah said they had been preparing to clear the structures after receiving the notice, but the municipality brought in a bulldozer early Sunday morning without informing the market committee or traders.

Trader Saraswati Devi Nayak said she had been living in Naya Bazar for around 35 years and that the demolition had destroyed her chiura and murhi business.

“All the goods inside the house were destroyed. I have suffered losses worth hundreds of thousands of rupees. Who will take responsibility for this?” she asked.

Nayak claimed that although the market has many houses and makeshift structures, only their structures were demolished. She alleged that structures operated by people close to the mayor and his supporters were left untouched.

Bhola Rai, chairperson of the Lahan Naya Bazar Committee, said the municipality demolished the structures without coordinating with the market committee. According to him, an agreement had been reached around four years ago to remove the structures as part of efforts to manage the market.

Rai said the market committee also supports development and a well-managed market, but Mayor Chaudhary had backed away from the agreement at the time.

After the municipality issued a notice a few days ago asking traders to vacate the structures, the market committee had scheduled a meeting with traders for 8 am Sunday. However, Rai said the municipality brought in a bulldozer at around 7 am, before the meeting began, and demolished seven houses and makeshift structures.

According to Rai, police detained some traders after they attempted to stop the demolition. He said those detained after burning tyres in protest were later released.

Rai said the market committee was collecting details of traders who suffered losses during the demolition and would file complaints with the concerned authorities and seek compensation for them.

Mayor’s response

Mayor Mahesh Prasad Chaudhary said the municipality had built three buildings with 72 rooms on around two bighas of municipal land and planned to relocate Naya Bazar traders by renting out the rooms to them.

He said the old houses and makeshift structures were removed because construction of the new buildings had reached its final stage. Chaudhary said the municipality had used a bulldozer as a last resort after occupants failed to vacate the structures despite repeated notices.

Asked why only seven structures were demolished when there are hundreds of such structures in the market, Mayor Chaudhary said the remaining structures would also be removed once orders were received from higher authorities. Chaudhary denied allegations of discrimination in the demolition drive, saying that all illegal and old structures would be removed gradually.

What did the municipality’s three-day notice say?

Lahan Municipality had asked all individuals living or operating shops in houses and makeshift structures built on the land of Gudri Hatiya in Lahan Bazaar, Ward No. 5—from the entrance of the Nepal Water Supply Corporation, Lahan, to the Hanuman Temple—to remove their structures and shop goods and vacate the area within three days of the notice.

The municipality said it planned to construct new structures and relocate the traders. However, the affected traders have demanded a proper assessment of their losses and compensation.

The market committee has also said it is preparing to collect details of the losses and seek compensation by filing a complaint with the concerned authorities.

title.rendered: Policeman arrested for videotaping statement of teenager involved in Bara incident

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

A policeman has been arrested on charges of recording and publicising a video of the statement given by the teenager involved in the rape and murder of a three-year-old girl child from Bara. The video, filmed in the statement room while the teenager’s statement was being recorded, has since gone viral on social media.

In the video, the teenager reportedly describes the entire assault in detail.

Questions had already been raised about the police after the video of the statement given before the police leaked it out.

The person believed to have recorded and leaked the video has now been arrested. According to Bara Police SP Narendra Kunwar, the policeman who filmed the video has been arrested and is currently in custody. Preparations are underway to proceed against him on criminal charges.

Five policemen were reportedly seen in the group involved in filming the video, and investigation into the others is ongoing.

title.rendered: RSP general secretary objects to videos of Garima Chaudhary’s parents, accused being made public

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) General Secretary Bipin Kumar Acharya has objected to a video of the parents of three-year-old Garima Chaudhary being recorded at the Ministry of Home Affairs, saying such practices should stop.

Speaking during Monday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, Acharya said the incident involving Garima should also prompt a broader discussion about the kind of society Nepal is creating.

“I have not said much about what happened in the Garima murder case. But something we all need to reflect on is what kind of society we are building,” he said.

“We have reached a situation where a video of the deceased’s parents saying thank you is recorded at a ministry. And when a medical examination is being conducted, things said by an accused are publicly released. This kind of society must be stopped,” he said.

Garima’s disappearance and death

According to police, three-year-old Garima Chaudhary of Jeetpur Simara Sub-Metropolitan City-1 went missing from her home on the morning of August 16.

Her mother, Manmati Chaudhary, informed police in Simara and Pathlaiya after she could not find the child for around three and a half hours.

Police reportedly told the family that they would search for her. Garima’s body was found two days later.

The case drew attention from the federal government after the body of the three-year-old, who had disappeared from her home, was recovered.

Garima’s father Manoj Chaudhary and mother Manmati Chaudhary were subsequently called to Kathmandu, where they held discussions with Home Minister Sudhan Gurung and officials from the Ministry of Home Affairs.

During the meeting, Manoj expressed satisfaction with the government’s initiative, saying that the authorities had listened to the family’s concerns.

Objection to public release of accused’s video

Acharya also objected to the public release of a video showing an accused person speaking about the incident.

A video of the person arrested in connection with Garima’s murder was made public, showing police questioning the accused during a medical examination at a hospital.

The footage shows the accused, who is handcuffed, being questioned by police officers.

“There is a situation where what an accused says is publicly released. This kind of society must be stopped,” Acharya said.

The public release of the video has also drawn the attention of the Nepal Police headquarters and the Madhesh Province Police Office, which have begun looking into the circumstances surrounding the footage.

Acharya raised the issue in Parliament amid growing concerns over the handling and public dissemination of material related to the case.

title.rendered: Artists paint and celebrate Tiniharu’s Cannes triumph in Bhaktapur

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Fifteen visual artists gathered amid the historic surroundings of Bhaktapur Durbar Square on Sunday for Paint and Celebrate, an artistic event celebrating the international acclaim and historic achievement of the Nepali film Tiniharu (Elephants in the Fog).

Directed by Abinash Bikram Shah, Tiniharu made history as the first Nepali feature film to be officially selected for the Cannes Film Festival, where it competed in the prestigious Un Certain Regard section and went on to receive the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize.

Supported by the British Council and Alliance Française Kathmandu, the day-long creative gathering brought together painters, printmakers, and conceptual artists to interpret the atmosphere, emotional world, themes, and landmark achievement of Tiniharu through their own artistic practices. The film’s lead actor Pushpa Thing Lama and producer Anup Poudel were also present, along with Nhooja Tuladhar from the British Council, interacting with the participating artists and encouraging them as they developed their works.

“Since the film itself was inspired by a photograph by American photographer Nan Goldin, we wanted to create a platform where different forms of art could come together. Paint and Celebrate was created as part of that effort,” said Anup Poudel, producer of the film.

The participating artists represent a dynamic cross-section of emerging and established visual artists, including creators associated with Tribhuvan University’s Lalitkala Campus and Kathmandu University School of Arts and Design. Coming from different parts of Nepal, including Sudurpaschim, Lumbini, Birgunj, and Pokhara, the artists brought a wide range of practices and perspectives to the event.

The resulting works span realism, surrealism, printmaking, textile art, and semi-abstract mixed media, transforming elements inspired by the film into distinct visual interpretations. Rather than reproducing scenes from Tiniharu, the artists were encouraged to respond freely to its themes, characters, emotions, and cultural resonance.

Paint and Celebrate also created an opportunity for artists and members of the film team to interact outside the conventional setting of a film screening, allowing the cinematic experience to become a starting point for a broader artistic conversation.

Hotel Dachi Bhaktapur served as the official venue partner, while Prisma Stationery served as the Official Stationery Partner and Dalai-la Hotel as the Official Gallery Partner. Selected artworks created during the event will be presented in an upcoming gallery exhibition at Dalai-la Hotel from 27 to 29 August.

Tiniharu (Elephants in the Fog) will be released in cinemas across Nepal on September 4.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Pothole repair work has been intensified on roads across Kathmandu, with the Road Division Office, Kathmandu, deploying a Road Maintenance Ambulance to speed up maintenance.

According to the office, pothole repair works are being carried out mainly at night when traffic volume is relatively low to minimise disruption to commuters.

On Wednesday, repair teams worked on potholes and damaged sections along the Tinkune–Gaushala–Airport–Gairidhara–Maitighar–Babarmahal–Bijulibazar–New Baneshwor road corridor, according to the Road Division Office.

The office said the maintenance ambulance is being used to respond quickly to damaged road sections and carry out necessary repairs.

The intensified maintenance comes as potholes and damaged road surfaces have remained a recurring problem on several major roads in the Kathmandu Valley, particularly during the monsoon season.

title.rendered: Poultry farmers protest, demand action against middlemen’s network

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Poultry farmers have launched a protest, demanding measures to prevent the displacement of small-scale farmers.

Farmers from various parts of the country staged a demonstration at Maitighar Mandala, calling on the government to break the network of middlemen and establish a direct link between farmers and consumers.

They also demanded an end to the grading system in the poultry sector, a crackdown on the smuggling of poultry from India, and transparency in the prices of poultry feed and chicks. They called for the introduction of a scientific pricing system and measures to ensure the quality of feed and chicks.

The farmers further demanded that their labour be respected and that their investments be guaranteed.

title.rendered: 2 killed, 3 injured as school bus collides with auto in Udayapur

content.rendered:
Udayapur, August 24

Two people were killed and three others injured when a school bus collided with an auto-rickshaw in Jahada, Belaka Municipality-5, Udayapur, on Monday.

According to police, the accident occurred at around 9:45 am when an auto-rickshaw (Ko. Pra. 05-001 Ha 0613) heading from Supade towards Lalbazar collided with a bus (Ko. 1 Kha 3516) belonging to Safal Adarsha English Boarding School, which was coming from the opposite direction.

All five people travelling in the auto-rickshaw were injured in the accident. They were immediately taken to BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences (BPKIHS), Ghopa Hospital, Dharan, for treatment.

Police said 34-year-old Mandira Magar of Belaka Municipality-5 and an unidentified woman travelling in the auto-rickshaw died during treatment. Doctors at the hospital declared both dead.

Auto-rickshaw driver Indra Thapa, 28, of Belaka Municipality-5, sustained serious injuries.

Similarly, 19-year-old Ajit Gurung of Biratnagar Metropolitan City-12 is in moderate condition, while 18-year-old Roshan Magar of Belaka Municipality-5 also sustained serious injuries. All three injured are receiving treatment at the same hospital.

Following the accident, a police team from the Area Police Office, Rampur Thoksila, was deployed to the scene.

Police said they have taken the bus involved in the accident and its driver, 36-year-old Bikram Thapa of Belaka Municipality-5, into custody.

Further investigation into the incident is underway.

title.rendered: Nagdhunga tunnel opens partially to public, small four-wheelers allowed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24:

The Nagdhunga Tunnel Road has been partially opened to the public from Monday, with small four-wheeled vehicles now allowed to use the tunnel.

The tunnel had previously been opened only to emergency service vehicles for testing. According to Department of Roads Director General Dr Bijay Jaisi, cars, jeeps and vans can now use the tunnel as part of the ongoing testing phase.

“The tunnel is still under testing. As part of that process, small vehicles have been allowed from today,” Jaisi said.

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal inaugurated the tunnel on July 27.

One-way traffic from 9am to 6pm

For now, the tunnel will operate for one-way traffic from 9am to 6pm.

Vehicles carrying highly flammable materials and two-wheelers will not be permitted to enter the tunnel.

Other larger vehicles will also be allowed to use the tunnel after the testing phase is completed.

Jaisi said that, depending on the initial operation, two-way traffic could be introduced within the next one or two days.

The authorities also plan to gradually extend the operating hours. The initial plan is to operate the tunnel from 7am to 8pm, before eventually extending the service from 6am to 10pm.

The Nagdhunga Tunnel Road is expected to provide an alternative route through the busy Nagdhunga section, where traffic congestion and difficult road conditions have frequently affected movement between Kathmandu and the western districts.

title.rendered: 30 killed as waste dump collapses in Guinea’s capital

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

At least 30 people have been killed and 22 others injured after a large pile of waste collapsed and buried nearby houses following heavy rainfall in Conakry, the capital of Guinea.

Six of the injured are in critical condition.

The incident occurred at around 2 am local time in the Dar-es-Salam area of the city. According to the Guinean government, a large pile of waste suddenly collapsed following heavy rainfall. Many people are feared to remain trapped under the debris.

The government has deployed a large number of security personnel, including members of the military, for rescue and relief operations.

Speaking to local media, a woman said, “Five of my children died.” Authorities fear that more people may still be trapped under the debris and that the death toll could rise.

Guinean Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah visited the site and assessed the situation.

Earlier, local leader Lancine Sylla told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that a large number of people were feared to have been affected by the incident.

He said 18 bodies had so far been recovered and sent to the morgue.

title.rendered: Foreign Minister Khanal to visit Serbia on August 30

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal is scheduled to travel to Serbia on August 30.

He will visit Serbia to attend the High-Level Commemorative Meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), which will be held in Belgrade, the capital of Serbia.

A three-member Nepali delegation led by Foreign Minister Khanal will participate in the commemorative meeting, scheduled to take place in Belgrade on August 31 and September 1.

A Cabinet meeting held on August 11 decided that Nepal would participate in the meeting.

The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held in Belgrade in 1961. The high-level commemorative meeting is being organized in Belgrade this year to mark the 65th anniversary of the first summit.

World leaders, delegations from various countries, and representatives of member states of the Non-Aligned Movement are expected to attend the event.

Nepal has adopted the principle of non-alignment as one of the fundamental pillars of its foreign policy.

Foreign Minister Khanal is scheduled to return to Nepal from Serbia on September 2.

title.rendered: Once a symbol of remoteness, Olangchung Gola is finding a new identity

content.rendered:
For years, “You might be transferred to Olangchung Gola” was a familiar expression among government employees, used to describe an exceptionally remote posting. Even in rural Taplejung, people would jokingly say a football kicked far outside the field had “reached Gola.”

The settlement, however, has always had an identity beyond its isolation.

Located around 75 kilometres from Taplejung district headquarters, Olangchung Gola is a historic Himalayan settlement known for its Walung community, yak and chauri herding, Tibetan trade and traditional wooden-roofed houses.

It is also the birthplace of renowned ophthalmologist Dr Sanduk Ruit, whose international reputation helped put the remote settlement on Nepal’s wider map.

But Olangchung Gola is changing.

A village once defined by distance

Olangchung Gola lies beneath the approximately 800-year-old Diki Chhyoling Monastery. Around 50 to 60 traditional houses remain in the settlement, built in a style reflecting the area’s Himalayan heritage.

The Tamor River flows through the valley after originating near the Tiptala Pass. The Singjema River, which grows substantially in volume downstream, eventually joins it.

The name Olangchung Gola itself is associated with an old story. According to local accounts, Tibetan pilgrims once lost their way while travelling through the area. A small animal resembling a mongoose is said to have shown them the route. The animal was called “Olung”, and the name is believed to have gradually evolved into Olangchung Gola.

For generations, however, the settlement’s defining characteristic was its isolation.

Before roads reached the area, helicopters flying above the Tamor were among the few visible signs of the outside world. Children would look up and say, “The helicopter has gone to Gola.”

That perception remained strong even outside Taplejung.

A student from Taplejung recalls arriving at Kathmandu’s Ratna Rajya Campus around 2015. When he introduced himself as being from Taplejung, a fellow student from Bajhang immediately asked how far his home was from Olangchung Gola.

The question reflected how deeply the name had become associated with a distant, difficult-to-reach place.

The road is changing Olangchung Gola

That reality is no longer the same.

The construction and upgrading of the North-South Highway, which connects Rani in Biratnagar to the Tiptala border, has brought Olangchung Gola into Nepal’s road network.

During winter, vehicles can reach the settlement.

The road was developed with the broader objective of connecting the area with China and developing Tiptala as an international trade point.

Mobile connectivity has also arrived. Nepal Telecom launched 4G service in the area in recent months, giving residents direct access to modern communications.

The changes are transforming not only how people travel to Olangchung Gola but also how the settlement is perceived.

A place once used as a metaphor for remoteness is increasingly becoming a destination in its own right.

From Tibetan trade to tourism

Olangchung Gola historically maintained close economic links with Tibet.

Yak and chauri products, wool and locally produced carpets were among the main items traded across the border. “Gola carpets” became a recognised product, with demand reaching Taplejung, Darjeeling, Kathmandu and even the United States.

That cross-border trade has, however, largely come to a standstill since China tightened border controls following the Covid-19 pandemic.

“The quarantine building is about seven kilometres from the Tiptala border. We have to stay there. Relatives come from Riu on the other side, and we meet there,” says Onga Sherpa, a ward member who runs a shop in Olangchung Gola.

For a community whose economy was historically tied to the border, the restrictions have been a major disruption.

Tourism, meanwhile, is offering a new possibility.

The lakes drawing visitors uphill

Beyond Olangchung Gola are two high-altitude lakes that have increasingly attracted attention in eastern Nepal: Singjema and Samdo.

The trek to the lakes begins above the settlement and takes visitors through an increasingly dramatic landscape.

Singjema Lake sits at around 4,700 metres above sea level. Before reaching it is Chhyer Valley, a natural camping area surrounded by rocky mountains, green pasture and the winding Singjema River.

Yak and chauri graze freely across the grasslands, their bells ringing through the valley.

After climbing for around an hour to an hour and a half from Chhyer, trekkers reach Singjema.

From there, the route continues towards a pass at around 5,100 metres. Only after reaching the pass does the pair of Samdo lakes come into view.

The landscape changes dramatically.

On one side, Singjema stretches across the highland pasture in blue. On the other, the two Samdo lakes sit quietly between rugged rock formations.

Clouds periodically cover and reveal the lakes, adding another layer to the landscape.

For visitors who make the demanding climb, the view from the pass can make the difficult journey worthwhile.

Staying with the Walung community

Visitors heading towards the lakes generally need to spend at least two nights in Olangchung Gola.

Many homes in the settlement now operate as small hotels, but accommodation remains closely connected to the traditions of the local Walung community.

Inside the traditional wooden-roofed houses are metal cooking utensils, Buddhist prayer spaces, burning lamps and broad hearths around which daily life takes place.

White flour is used to draw traditional Buddhist symbols on wooden beams.

Hospitality is equally distinctive.

Visitors are often welcomed with an invitation to sit down and have tea. Hosts may repeatedly offer more tea before presenting guests with a khada when they leave.

There is also a local tradition of placing the khada at Deurali, below Olangchung Gola, after returning from the settlement.

The warmth of that hospitality is becoming part of the experience for visitors as much as the landscape itself.

A community with a different political culture

Olangchung Gola’s distinctiveness extends beyond its geography and culture.

Many people originally from the settlement now live in Darjeeling, Kathmandu, France, the United States and elsewhere. Those who remain continue to maintain a Himalayan way of life while adapting to changing economic and social conditions.

The community has also developed an unusual approach to local politics.

Although residents may have different political affiliations, they have sought to avoid political divisions within the small settlement during local elections.

In the 2017 local election, residents selected Chheten Sherpa as ward chairperson by consensus without holding a formal vote.

Sherpa is known in Taplejung for his efforts to develop the ward.

The practice reflects the close-knit nature of a settlement where political competition can easily create divisions among families and neighbours.

Olangchung Gola beyond the old stereotype

For decades, Olangchung Gola was imagined from afar as a place at the end of the road—a difficult posting, a distant village and a destination reachable only after a long and arduous journey.

That image is increasingly outdated.

The road has arrived. Mobile connectivity has followed. Tourism is growing. The historic connection with Tibet remains important, even as cross-border trade faces restrictions.

And above the settlement, Singjema and Somdo are offering a new reason for travellers to make the journey.

Yet Olangchung Gola’s appeal lies not simply in becoming easier to reach.

Its traditional houses, Walung culture, yak and chauri pastures, Buddhist heritage, mountain landscapes and distinctive hospitality remain central to its identity.

The village may no longer be the symbol of remoteness it once was.

But perhaps that is precisely what makes Olangchung Gola worth discovering now: a Himalayan community opening up to the outside world without entirely losing what made it unique in the first place.

The price of gold increased by Rs 3,200 per tola on Monday.

The Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association has set the price of gold at Rs 322,700 per tola for the day, up from Rs 319,500 per tola on the previous day. The price of gold has increased by Rs 15,700 in a week. Last Monday, gold was priced at Rs 306,800 per tola.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa asks govt to immediately release Lal Commission report

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has urged the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers to immediately make public the report of the Lal Commission, which investigated incidents during the Madhes and Tharuhat movements.

Thapa made the demand through social media, while acknowledging that political parties have repeatedly failed to fulfil their commitments to release the report after coming to power.

He said political parties had been calling for the report’s publication almost every year since 2017, often promising to make it public before entering government.

“Since 2017, almost every year there have been calls to make the Lal Commission report public. Every time, we political parties promised to release the report before entering government, but after coming to power, we failed to implement that commitment,” Thapa wrote. “Now, almost a decade has passed.”

The high-level inquiry commission, formed in 2016 under former Supreme Court Justice Girish Chandra Lal, submitted its report after investigating incidents linked to the Madhes and Tharuhat movements.

Thapa said the continued failure to make the report public has prevented the truth about the incidents from coming out and left victims deprived of justice.

He said the shortcomings of previous governments should not be used as a reason to keep withholding the report.

“Previous governments also failed to do this. But the failures of the past cannot and should not become a reason for not releasing the report today,” Thapa wrote. “This time, the issue should not remain limited to a commitment.”

Thapa directly appealed to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers to release the report without further delay.

“My appeal to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers is this: release the Lal Commission report without any further delay. Citizens have the right to know the truth, and victims have the right to justice,” he said.

title.rendered: Man arrested for using stolen scooter in ride-sharing service

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

A man has been arrested for operating a ride-sharing service using a stolen scooter.

The arrested man has been identified as 39-year-old Saroj Khanal, a permanent resident of Damak Municipality-7, Jhapa, who had been living in New Bus Park, Kathmandu. He was arrested by traffic police.

Khanal reportedly became unreachable after a passenger travelling from Naxal to Bhaktapur Durbar Square accidentally left a laptop bag on his scooter.

The passenger informed traffic police and requested a search for the missing laptop. Police subsequently arrested Khanal at a hotel where he had been staying in New Bus Park.

According to police, questioning revealed that Khanal had been operating the ride-sharing service using another person’s ride-sharing account.

Police also found that he had allegedly stolen the scooter, bearing registration number Ba Pra 00-00 Pa 00, from Gongabu some time ago.

While searching for and returning missing motorcycles to their owners, Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police had found Khanal’s citizenship certificate inside the storage compartment of one of the motorcycles.

This has led police to suspect that Khanal had been involved in motorcycle theft for a long time and may have stolen other motorcycles as well. Further investigation is underway.

Traffic police have returned the recovered laptop to its owner.

title.rendered: 35 amendment proposals registered on Mines and Minerals Bill

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

A total of 35 amendment proposals have been registered on the Mines and Minerals Bill, 2083 BS.

Lawmakers have submitted the amendment proposals in 35 separate groups. The bill was introduced by Minister for Industry, Commerce and Supplies Gauri Kumari. The bill was registered in the House of Representatives on July 30, and lawmakers subsequently submitted 35 groups of amendment proposals.

The House of Representatives is scheduled to send the bill to a parliamentary committee on Monday for clause-by-clause discussion. The House meeting is scheduled for 1 pm.

According to the agenda, Minister Gauri Kumari will present a proposal to send the Mines and Minerals Bill, 2083, to the relevant committee for clause-by-clause discussion.

The government introduced the bill to clearly define the rights and responsibilities related to mines and minerals in line with the federal system of governance.

The bill, which aims to make the conservation, exploration and extraction of mines and minerals systematic, scientific and sustainable, contains 63 proposed clauses.

The Mines and Minerals Act, 1985, is currently in force. The new bill seeks to repeal the existing law and introduce a framework suited to the current context and the federal democratic republican system of governance. It includes special provisions concerning common construction minerals, minerals of strategic and security importance, and radioactive minerals.

The Constitution of Nepal divides powers concerning mines and minerals among the federal, provincial and local governments.

According to the Ministry of Industry, the existing Mines and Minerals Act, 1985, was enacted before the implementation of the federal system and is therefore inadequate to address the current constitutional framework, federal structure, modern mineral administration, environmental responsibilities, strategic mineral management and the need to promote investment.

The ministry said the bill has been introduced to ensure more scientific management of minerals and the mineral sector and to make the processes of conserving, exploring and extracting mines and minerals more systematic, transparent and accessible.

The bill states that it has been drafted to amend and consolidate laws related to mines and minerals with the objectives of regulating strategic, security-related and radioactive minerals; providing a legal basis for geological research and seismic monitoring; and clarifying the coordination and jurisdiction of the federal, provincial and local governments.

The bill’s core objectives are outlined in eight points:

  1. To ensure the scientific, sustainable and systematic use of Nepal’s mines and minerals, which are the property of the government of Nepal.
  2. To clarify the roles, coordination mechanisms and jurisdictions of the federal, provincial and local governments in accordance with the federal system of governance.
  3. To make the processes of conserving, exploring and extracting minerals transparent, competitive and accessible.
  4. To provide special protection and regulation for strategic, security-related and radioactive minerals.
  5. To use minerals while adopting environmental protection principles and reducing geological hazards.
  6. To establish a clear legal framework for attracting domestic and foreign investment in the mineral sector.
  7. To strengthen geological research, seismic monitoring and scientific studies.
  8. To introduce effective measures and penalties to control illegal extraction and illicit trade of minerals.

title.rendered: Nepal imports rice and paddy worth nearly Rs 1.8 billion in a month

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Nepal imported paddy and rice worth nearly Rs 1.8 billion in the first month of the current fiscal year 2082/83 BS.

According to data from the Department of Customs, Nepal imported 24,939 tonnes of paddy and rice worth Rs 1.78 billion in Shrawan, the first month of the fiscal year. The imports amounted to 24.94 million kilograms. Paddy and rice imports declined compared to the same month last fiscal year. In Shrawan of fiscal year 2081/82 BS, Nepal imported 57,083 tonnes of paddy and rice worth Rs 2.93 billion.

The data shows a decline in both the volume of imports and the amount spent on them during the first month of the current fiscal year compared to the corresponding period last year. A breakdown of the imports shows that the largest amount was spent on rice. In Shrawan, Nepal imported 11,852 tonnes of rice worth Rs 833.32 million. Almost the entire quantity—11,851 tonnes—was imported from neighbouring India, while a negligible 0.24 tonnes (240 kg) came from Italy.

Basmati rice ranked second in terms of import value. Nepal imported 4,125 tonnes of Basmati rice worth Rs 568.59 million in Shrawan, all of which came from India. In addition to milled rice, Nepal also imports a significant quantity of unmilled paddy. In the first month of the current fiscal year, 8,628 tonnes of paddy worth Rs 365.02 million were imported, all from India.

Similarly, Nepal spent millions of rupees importing broken rice. In Shrawan alone, 332 tonnes of broken rice worth Rs 13.31 million were imported from India. The customs data also shows that small quantities of brown rice and paddy seeds were imported, in addition to the larger volumes of paddy, rice and broken rice.

Nepal imported 625 kg of brown rice worth Rs 89,000 in Shrawan, of which 500 kg came from Thailand and 125 kg from India. Likewise, 67 kg of paddy seeds worth Rs 501,000 were imported during the first month of the current fiscal year. More paddy seeds were imported from China than from India.

title.rendered: For Lujendra Ojha, curiosity has always come first

content.rendered:
Dr Lujendra Ojha was 15 when he left Nepal for the United States. He arrived with little idea that the short trip would change the course of his life.

Raised in the narrow lanes of Kathmandu, with family roots in Doti in far-western Nepal, Ojha had grown up interested in music, theatre, mathematics and science. In the years that followed, that curiosity would take him into planetary science and eventually to research on Mars that attracted global attention.

Today, Ojha, 36, is an assistant professor of planetary science at Rutgers University. He has worked on more than 40 scientific papers, studying Mars and other planets in the solar system.

His advice, however, is surprisingly simple.

“Protect your curiosity. In life, education, career and struggle, put curiosity first. Money is not the only goal in life.”

Ojha’s story is not only about a scientific achievement. It is also the story of a teenager from Kathmandu who entered an unfamiliar country, adjusted to a different education system and culture, and slowly found his way into one of the most fascinating fields of science.

A childhood in Kathmandu

Dr Lujendra Ojha was born in Kathmandu in 1990. His ancestral home is in Doti, a connection he says has always been an important part of his identity.

He spent his childhood in different parts of Kathmandu but particularly remembers Mhepi, near Naya Bazaar.

“For many people, when they hear Mhepi, they think of the temple. For me, it is the centre of my childhood memories,” he says.

The memories are ordinary ones. Narrow streets, swings, firecrackers, cricket matches and the excitement of Dashain and Tihar.

His family initially lived in a rented house before his father built their own home. His mother worked at the Dairy Development Corporation, while his father, Tanka Prasad Ojha, worked in the Department of Mines and was a scholar of geology.

“I grew up in a middle-class family. There were struggles, but I was always happy,” Ojha says.

School, music and a rigid education system

Ojha began his schooling at Adarsha Yoghari Secondary School in Lainchaur, where he studied until Grade 3. He then moved to Galaxy Public School in Gyaneshwor, where he studied from Grade 4 to Grade 9.

The education system he experienced was strict.

“If a student crossed the line, beating was considered normal. Curiosity was treated as a violation of discipline,” he recalls.

He also remembers experiencing discrimination.

“Whenever someone with dark skin was seen, people would comment that they were Indian or from the Terai. It was surprising to see such behaviour even from teachers,” he says.

For Ojha, that experience also highlighted a larger problem with rote learning.

He felt that a system focused on memorisation could suppress creativity and independent thinking. Yet school was not all about textbooks. He played guitar in a band and took part in school plays.

“I was interested in music from a young age. I still play the guitar,” he says.

Science, however, gradually became the stronger pull.

Seven days in America that changed everything

In 2005, Ojha travelled to the United States with his father. The original plan was for him to stay for only seven days.

His father was already working with Americans, and his sister had received a full scholarship from a university in the US. Ojha was nearing the end of Grade 9 at the time.

“My father told me to attend school for a few days and see how I liked it. If I liked it, I could stay. Otherwise, I could return to Nepal and continue my studies,” he recalls.

He decided to stay.

It was not an easy transition.

Much of his clothing was still back in Nepal, and everything around him was unfamiliar. He was 15, in a new country, surrounded by a different culture and people.

“I didn’t see people of my own complexion, and there was no familiar environment. Starting over at 15 was a big challenge,” he says.

But the move also gave him access to opportunities that would shape his future.

He attended high school in Tucson, Arizona, where his interest in mathematics and science deepened. He later studied at the University of Arizona, where he also took courses in religion and philosophy.

“Religion and philosophy made my scientific perspective clearer. Science is not only about knowledge; it is also a way of thinking and developing curiosity,” he says.

Learning to work while studying

Dr Lujendra Ojha’s path through university was not simply about attending classes and conducting research.

He also worked.

After enrolling at university, he began working at a grocery store for 20 to 30 hours a week while remaining a full-time student.

“That routine taught me hard work, discipline and time management. Those skills later became very useful when I faced challenges in research,” he says.

At university, he also discovered that planetary science required knowledge from several areas of science.

“To understand planets, you need chemistry, physics and, in some cases, biology,” he says.

That interdisciplinary nature appealed to him.

It was also at the University of Arizona that he began working with data from the HiRISE camera, which had been sent to Mars to capture high-resolution images of the planet’s surface.

That work would eventually change his career.

His first step into NASA’s Mars mission

Dr Lujendra Ojha explains that working on a NASA mission does not necessarily mean being a NASA employee.

Researchers at universities can also become part of NASA missions if they demonstrate that they have the expertise and capacity to carry out the work.

“Plans are made based on how much money we have and what we want to do over the next 10 years. A team gets a contract only after demonstrating that it has the ability and credibility to do the work,” he says.

The Mars mission that would become important in Ojha’s career began in 2005.

“At that time, I was still in high school. The HiRISE camera had already been sent to Mars, and it began sending data from Earth after about eight months,” he recalls.

In 2009, Ojha joined the mission.

Initially, he worked as a data validator and data analyst. Much of the work was repetitive, but he wanted to go beyond simply processing data.

“I didn’t want to just look at data. I wanted to be involved in actual research,” he says.

He approached principal investigator Alfred McEwen with his ideas. McEwen agreed, allowing Ojha to begin additional research alongside his original work.

That decision would lead to one of the most widely discussed findings of his career.

The research that put Mars in the headlines

The existence of water on Mars was not new. Scientists had already established that large amounts of ice existed around the planet’s north and south poles.

But research published in 2011 suggested that water on Mars might not exist only in the form of ice, but could also occur in liquid form.

Dr Lujendra Ojha was part of the research team.

The conclusion came from analysing images captured by the HiRISE camera.

“We spent almost a year just testing and retesting. In science, the reliability of the evidence is more important than the result,” he says.

The paper was published in Science, one of the world’s leading scientific journals. Publication followed critical review by scientists from around the world.

“Writing a report and sending it does not mean it will be published. Researchers around the world critically review it. Only after passing that process can it be published,” Ojha says.

The research soon attracted international attention.

NASA issued an official press release, while CNN, BBC, Fox and other international media outlets reported on the findings. The story also received significant attention in Nepal, in part because a Nepali scientist was among those involved in the research.

For Ojha, however, the attention was only one part of a much longer scientific journey.

Still looking beyond Mars

More than a decade after the research that brought him international recognition, Ojha continues to work in planetary science.

His research is no longer limited to Mars. He has also been studying other planets in the solar system, including Jupiter and its moon Europa.

“I am not someone who stays on one subject continuously. New research, new curiosity and new challenges are what keep me moving into different areas,” he says.

He says the Mars research remains important, although there has not been a large amount of new data since the original study.

“There hasn’t been a new spacecraft there, so the updates are limited. But the HiRISE camera is still doing excellent work. Water-like activity can still be seen in those areas. Other technologies have not tested it in the same way, and humans have not gone there to test it,” he says.

Since that research, Dr Lujendra Ojha has worked on more than 40 other scientific studies.

“My current research is focused on planets other than Mars. That mission gave me a great deal of experience and recognition. Besides that, I have worked on more than 40 other scientific studies, and the details would be very long,” he says.

His interest in Mars is also connected to a larger question.

“My interest in Mars research is not only because of science. It is also because I am curious about how human civilisation might expand in the future. Searching for life beyond Earth is, in a way, searching for possibilities for our own future,” he says.

From Georgia Tech to Rutgers

In 2016, Ojha completed his PhD in planetary science at Georgia Tech in Atlanta. He received a full US government fellowship for his doctoral studies.

After completing his PhD, he spent three years as a postdoctoral researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

During that period, he published seven scientific papers covering research related to Mars and other planets, including their gravity, surface structures and geological history.

For Dr Lujendra Ojha, research is ultimately about asking questions that have not been asked before.

“The biggest challenge in science is having the courage to ask a question that nobody has thought of before. Research is not about memorising books. It is about having the confidence to search for new answers,” he says.

He is now an assistant professor of planetary science at Rutgers University in New Jersey.

His roots remain in Nepal

Despite spending around two decades in the United States, Dr Lujendra Ojha says he has never felt disconnected from Nepal.

“I was born and raised in Nepal. I came to America at 15, but my roots are here,” he says.

He does not see himself as a politician or policymaker.

“I am not a political person, nor am I at the level where I make policy. I am simply a scientist trying to understand the universe. I understand a little more every day. But that does not reduce my love for Nepal.”

Dr Lujendra Ojha does not completely reject the idea that young Nepalis leave because of limited opportunities, but he believes the issue is more complicated than a lack of resources.

“Nepal has universities and places where research can be done. The problem is more about priorities than resources,” he says.

He is particularly critical of how money is allocated and how education is approached.

“Money is not spent where it is needed, while spending increases where it isn’t needed. Rote learning is given more importance than research. In such an environment, curious students cannot move forward,” he says.

He believes Nepal itself has enormous potential as a place for research.

“Nepal is a laboratory in itself. The diversity of nature here is such that scientists from the US and Europe come to Nepal to understand its geography.”

He says the country’s education system also needs to do a better job of recognising different abilities.

“We don’t have a culture of identifying what each person is capable of. We put everyone into the same mould and expect them to become doctors or engineers. As a result, many students end up being average. Excellence is born only where curiosity is not killed.”

His father, Tank Prasad Ojha, also played a role in shaping his understanding of Nepal’s potential. As a geologist, he used to take foreign teams around Nepal to help them understand the country’s geological diversity.

“But we don’t take pride in the capabilities of our own country. The root of that problem is our mindset, not our resources,” Ojha says.

And after everything—from Kathmandu to the United States, from a grocery store job to university laboratories, and from analysing images of Mars to becoming a planetary scientist—his advice remains the same.

“Protect your curiosity, whatever happens. In life, education, career and struggle, put curiosity first. Money is not the only goal in life.”

For Dr Lujendra Ojha, Nepal remains home.

“Nepal is my original home,” he says. “But the world is our home too. When the mind is open, boundaries and limits have no meaning.”

title.rendered: 9 amendment proposals filed on bill seeking to end double benefits for constitutional officials

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Lawmakers have registered nine sets of amendment proposals on a bill seeking to prevent retired constitutional officials from receiving double benefits from the state.

The Remuneration, Conditions of Service and Benefits of Office Bearers of Constitutional Bodies (First Amendment) Bill 2026 was introduced by Prime Minister Balen Shah and has now moved into the parliamentary process.

Shah registered the bill in the House of Representatives on July 30.

The proposed amendment seeks to revise the existing Remuneration, Conditions of Service and Benefits of Office Bearers of Constitutional Bodies Act 1997 to regulate the remuneration and benefits provided to officials of constitutional bodies.

Bill seeks to end double benefits

The government has proposed the amendment after noting that retired civil servants are also appointed to constitutional bodies and, in some cases, continue receiving their retirement pension while also receiving benefits associated with their new constitutional position.

“The practice of appointing particularly retired civil servants to constitutional bodies exists. Officials appointed in this manner receive retirement benefits as well as facilities available under prevailing law after their appointment, resulting in a situation where the same individual receives double benefits from the state treasury,” the bill states.

Prime Minister Shah has argued that officials holding high public offices are expected to demonstrate a high level of ethical and moral conduct.

He said such standards should also be reflected in practice among people holding positions involving significant public accountability.

“If the situation continues in which an office bearer appears to be receiving double benefits, public faith, trust and confidence in the institution associated with that person will ultimately weaken,” Shah states in the bill.

He has further argued that it is not appropriate for an official receiving salary, allowances and other benefits from the state treasury to also receive a pension from the same treasury.

Nine groups of amendments

The bill was opened for amendments after lawmakers held a preliminary discussion on its principles.

Lawmakers have now submitted amendment proposals in nine groups, and the amendments will proceed alongside the government bill.

The proposals could lead to changes in the bill as it moves through the committee stage.

The House of Representatives is scheduled to send the bill to the concerned parliamentary committee for clause-by-clause discussion on Monday.

According to the parliamentary agenda, Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle will present a proposal on behalf of Prime Minister Shah to send the Remuneration, Conditions of Service and Benefits of Office Bearers of Constitutional Bodies (First Amendment) Bill 2026 to the concerned committee for clause-by-clause discussion.

The committee will consider the government’s proposal alongside the amendments registered by lawmakers before the bill returns to Parliament for further consideration.

title.rendered: Baburam Bhattarai urges govt to monitor social media over ‘misleading’ content

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 23

Former prime minister Baburam Bhattarai has urged the government to monitor social media accounts spreading misleading, threatening and hate-inducing content that could undermine religious and social harmony.

Issuing a statement through his secretariat, Bhattarai called on the public to remain cautious of manipulated videos, misleading images and posts aimed at creating religious hatred and social divisions.

He also urged the government to investigate individuals and groups involved in such activities and take action against their social media accounts in accordance with the law.

“While respecting freedom of expression and ideological freedom, the state must intervene effectively against activities that harm religious beliefs, personal security, reputation and social harmony,” Bhattarai said.

His secretariat said the statement was issued after attempts by some individuals and groups, allegedly driven by political interests, to portray Bhattarai as anti-Hindu by using the religious sentiments of Nepal’s Hindu majority.

It said old videos and statements had been taken out of context and circulated through manipulated images, posters and social media posts to create a misleading narrative about his views.

The statement stressed that secularism does not mean opposition to any religion. Rather, it said, secularism requires the state to treat all religions and beliefs equally while ensuring citizens’ freedom to follow a religion, hold a belief or choose not to have one.

It also said belief in science, adoption of a scientific outlook or atheism falls within an individual’s ideological freedom and should not be portrayed as hostility towards any religion or religious community.

Bhattarai’s secretariat further objected to what it described as prejudiced attempts to portray debates over caste practices, discrimination and social inequality within Hindu society as attacks on Hinduism.

“Questioning social practices within any religion, culture or tradition, engaging in critical debate and calling for reform are natural processes in a democratic society,” the statement said.

It argued that presenting debates on social justice and equality as hatred against a religion or religious community amounted to distortion of facts.

The statement also expressed concern over threatening posts and what it described as coordinated attempts to create misleading narratives around Bhattarai by separating his past statements from their broader context.

Such activities, it warned, could threaten not only an individual’s safety and reputation but also religious tolerance, social harmony and national unity.

title.rendered: Madhesh after federalism: Political gains, governance failures and a crisis of trust

content.rendered:
Madhesh is often described as the birthplace of federalism in Nepal.

The movement that began in the plains was not simply about creating another layer of government. For many in Madhesh, federalism was tied to a much larger promise: political representation, greater autonomy, better access to government and an end to the need to look towards Kathmandu for every decision.

The first Madhesh movement began in 2006/07 under the leadership of the then Madhesi People’s Rights Forum Nepal. Other Madhesh-based parties later joined, and the movement grew around demands for an autonomous Madhesh, federal governance, proportional representation and inclusion.

When the Constitution was promulgated in 2015, Madhesh was still protesting. Madhesh-based parties rejected the Constitution at the time, arguing that it did not address their concerns. Eventually, however, they accepted the Constitution and the federal system it established.

Eight Tarai-Madhesh districts were brought together to form Province 2, later renamed Madhesh Province.

For the parties that had led the federalism movement, this was the moment when years of political struggle turned into an opportunity to govern.

The 107-member provincial assembly gave Madhesh-based parties a majority. The then Federal Socialist Forum, led by Upendra Yadav, emerged as the largest party and joined the Rastriya Janata Party Nepal to form the government.

Lalbabu Raut became the province’s first chief minister.

At the time, the symbolism was difficult to miss. A leader from the movement that had demanded greater political power for Madhesh was now heading the government of the province created through that struggle.

And Raut knew what was expected of him.

Speaking at a programme organised by the Birgunj Chamber of Commerce and Industry shortly after taking office, he said development and prosperity would not be possible without good governance and promised that his government would leave no stone unturned to maintain law and order and good governance.

For many Madhesh residents, it was a moment of genuine hope.

Federalism begins to take shape

The first five years brought visible changes.

Roads were built and paved. Temples, mosques, party palaces and other public structures appeared across the province. New provincial institutions were established and laws were passed.

Federalism also created political opportunities that had previously been difficult to imagine. People from communities that had traditionally remained at the margins of power became provincial lawmakers and ministers.

The Madhesh-based parties deserved credit for much of this. So did their leaders, particularly Upendra Yadav, whose role in establishing federalism as a political agenda in Nepal remains significant.

But governing brought a different kind of test.

The question was no longer whether Madhesh could win political power. It was what its leaders would do with that power.

Some of the provincial government’s programmes initially appeared to offer an answer.

The ‘Chief Minister’s Beti Padhaun, Beti Bachhaun’ programme became particularly popular. Bicycles were distributed to girls, education insurance was introduced, cleanliness campaigns were launched and a Madhesh bus service was planned to connect the provincial capital with district headquarters.

The programmes were visible, practical and politically popular.

But gradually, questions began to emerge over how they were being implemented.

One of the clearest examples was the bicycle programme.

Around 10,000 bicycles were purchased for distribution to girls during Raut’s tenure. The bicycles were later found to be unnamed and substandard, and about 4,500 remain stacked in a government warehouse.

The CIAA filed a corruption case against eight people, seeking Rs 103.3 million in damages. The Special Court eventually convicted two officials, while acquitting the others.

The case became more than a dispute over a procurement process. The bicycles were supposed to represent the promise of a government investing in its daughters. Instead, thousands ended up gathering dust.

And the bicycle case was only the beginning.

From individual cases to a pattern

As Madhesh’s provincial governments changed, questions over governance continued.

Shailendra Prasad Sah, who served as both land management and agriculture minister and later finance minister under Raut, has been charged along with six others over alleged corruption in the construction of the Baghmati Municipal Park and Resort in Sarlahi. The CIAA has claimed that the project involved Rs 393.9 million in corruption.

Then came cases involving elected representatives themselves.

JSP Nepal provincial lawmaker Saroj Singh Kushwaha was convicted by the Special Court for taking bribes and commissions through consumer committees. He was sentenced to four years and one month in prison and fined Rs 3.85 million.

Vijay Yadav, another senior JSP leader who served as finance minister and later land management and agriculture minister under Raut, was also convicted in a corruption case involving a snake-venom project at the Jhalanath Khanal Health Sciences Academy in Sarlahi. He was sentenced to nine years and one month in prison and fined more than Rs 35.9 million.

The controversies were not confined to the first government.

A programme to establish public health laboratories in all 136 local units of Madhesh also became the subject of a corruption case. The CIAA alleged that Rs 520.9 million was misappropriated in the procurement of medical equipment.

The Special Court later convicted three people, including the then director of the Public Health Laboratory, while others were acquitted.

Then came questions over the provincial budget itself.

During the second provincial government, led by Saroj Kumar Yadav, the provincial assembly formed a special committee to investigate large-scale budget reallocations under then Finance Minister Sanjay Kumar Yadav.

The committee found that grants had been distributed unevenly among local governments and reported, among other things, that Rs 420 million had been reallocated using the letterhead of the personal secretary of the industry and tourism minister.

The provincial assembly passed the report and sent it to the CIAA.

But the report eventually returned to the provincial government and remains there.

No action has been taken on the irregularities formally identified by the provincial assembly.

The bigger question

Taken individually, these cases are about procurement, construction, grants, public laboratories, consumer committees and budget allocations.

Taken together, however, they tell a larger story.

When federalism arrived, many in Madhesh expected provincial government to mean something fundamentally different from the government they had known before. They expected power to come closer to them, development to become more responsive and public institutions to become more accountable.

Instead, the province has struggled with the same problems that have long troubled Nepal’s central government: political patronage, allegations of corruption, weak accountability and questions over how public money is spent.

That has gradually changed the conversation around federalism itself.

Federalism was supposed to be a means of transferring power and development closer to citizens. For critics, Madhesh increasingly offers evidence of how that promise can be undermined when political power is not accompanied by stronger institutions and accountability.

The JSP, of course, is not responsible for every problem in Madhesh or every failure of federalism.

But the party occupies a particularly important place in this story. It was among the principal political forces behind the Madhesh movement and was at the centre of the province’s first governments.

That means it receives the political credit for helping establish federalism. It also cannot completely escape responsibility for what followed.

And the political cost is becoming visible.

Political analyst Rojan Janakpur says Madhesh-based parties spent years benefiting from the political momentum created by the Madhesh movement.

“They had been living off the momentum of the Madhesh movement. That is no longer the case. Their very existence is now at risk,” he says.

The parties were reduced from national forces to regional ones in the election on March 5.

Now they are trying to rebuild their position through a new front.

But winning back political ground may prove easier than winning back public trust.

Madhesh affairs expert and senior journalist Chandra Kishore believes the parties lost credibility because of how they behaved while in power.

“If they improve their conduct, they can win some seats in the next election and preserve their existence,” he says.

There is an irony in where Madhesh finds itself today.

The region that once pushed hardest for federalism now has to defend the idea against some of the disappointment created by its own provincial governments.

The debate is no longer simply about whether Madhesh should have political power.

It is about what that power has delivered—and whether the people who fought for federalism still believe their leaders have used it well.

For many in Madhesh, federalism was tied to a much larger promise: political representation, greater autonomy, better access to government and an end to the need to look […]

title.rendered: Bagmati Chief Minister Thapa taking vote of confidence today

content.rendered:
Hetauda, August 24

Newly appointed Bagmati Province Chief Minister Kiran Thapa Magar is taking a vote of confidence from the Provincial Assembly today.

He is seeking the vote of confidence under Article 168(4) of Nepal’s Constitution and Rule 143 of the Bagmati Province Assembly Regulations, 2074.

A Provincial Assembly meeting has been called today at 1 PM for the vote.

Coalition partner CPN (Nepal Communist Party) has already issued a whip directing its 26 Provincial Assembly members to vote in favour of Chief Minister Thapa Magar. CPN Bagmati parliamentary party Chief Whip Ratna Prasad Dhakal has instructed lawmakers to attend the meeting without fail and vote in favour of the confidence motion.

Chief Minister Thapa’s own party, UML, has also issued a whip requiring mandatory attendance and a vote in favour.

However, disagreement persists within the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), which had also supported the government. RPP Chief Whip Kumari Tamang issued a whip on Sunday directing her party’s Provincial Assembly members to vote against the confidence motion.

The pro-government faction within RPP, represented by Water Supply Minister Raju Bista, has said Tamang was removed from the position of chief whip even before the government was formed. RPP Bagmati Province parliamentary party leader Uddhav Thapa had already removed Tamang from the chief whip position earlier.

Thapa was appointed Chief Minister in August 20 with the backing of UML, CPN, and RPP. However, a dispute erupted within RPP over its support for the government formation.

RPP has already taken action against Bagmati Province parliamentary party leader Uddhav Thapa, accusing him of supporting the Chief Minister against the party central committee’s decision.

The party’s Central Disciplinary Committee has also sought clarification from three RPP ministers serving in the government.

The attendance and voting decisions of RPP’s 12 Provincial Assembly members during the confidence vote have become the biggest point of interest right now.

title.rendered: Bhajan Sanjh to mark Krishna Janmashtami with devotional music evening

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Kathmandu is set to host a special devotional music event, Bhajan Sanjh, on the occasion of Krishna Janmashtami. The event will take place on September 4 from 5:00 PM onwards at Hotel Ananda Pashupati near Tilganga.

Billed as an intimate devotional music platform, Bhajan Sanjh brings together bhakti music, art, and shared cultural experiences in a warm, contemporary concert setting. The evening will feature live bhajan performances, mantra chanting (mantra ucharan), Pushpa Holi, a Kathak dance performance by Nritya Nidhi Dance Studio, Gopi Dots, and interactive stalls, alongside performances by Naman Band and rising artist Durlav.

According to Ravi Pandey, co-founder and organiser of Bhajan Sanjh, the initiative was originally launched through Yagyashala and has since grown into a dedicated platform for intimate devotional music experiences. The organizers say the event aims to bring people together for Krishna Janmashtami through devotion, music, art, and a shared cultural experience.

Registration is required for entry.

title.rendered: Manjil of Jumla wins first place in National Poetry Competition

content.rendered:
Bhimphedi, August 24

A poem titled Chhute Pachhi Desh has won first place in a national poetry competition held in Bhimphedi Rural Municipality.

The poem, presented by Hem Prakash Manjil of Guthichaur Rural Municipality-4 in Jumla, took first place and won a cash prize of Rs 50,000.

The national poetry competition was organised by Bhimphedi Rural Municipality to mark the memorial day of writer Tulsi Thapa, and featured poems touching on patriotism, contemporary society, and human sentiment.

Suman Ghimire of Lalbandi Municipality-4 in Sarlahi took second place with his poem Ma Desh Kasari Banaun?, winning Rs 30,000.

Yograj Paudel of Arjundhara Municipality-5 in Jhapa placed third with Matrigatha, winning Rs 20,000.

Chetana Sharma of Kathmandu’s poem Rato Canvas and Dhiraj Nath of Bhimdatta Municipality-18 in Kanchanpur’s poem Bagaicha received consolation prizes of Rs 10,000 each. Bhimphedi Rural Municipality Chairperson Hidam Lama distributed the prizes.

On the same occasion, a half-length statue of writer Tulsi Thapa was unveiled at Shree Krishna Secondary School in Bhimphedi Rural Municipality-2, Bhainse.

The program was chaired by Ganesh Lama, the first person from Makwanpur to earn a PhD, and was attended by writer Shrawan Mukarung and former District Development Committee chairperson Rameshwar Rana, among others.

title.rendered: Damachaur-Rampur bridge, supposed to be built in 3 years, completed in 15 years

content.rendered:
Syangja, August 24

A motorable truss bridge over the Kaligandaki River, connecting Chapakot Municipality-8 (Damachaur) in Syangja and Rampur Municipality-6 in Palpa, linking Gandaki and Lumbini provinces, has been completed. The project, which was originally targeted for completion within three years, took 15 years due to various technical problems.

According to the Road Division Office, Palpa, a construction agreement worth NPR 15,68,13,266 was signed with MS Elite ASBA JV, Kapan, Kathmandu, on July 10, 2011. The three-span bridge is 181.69 meters long and 11 meters wide.

Construction initially began based on a well-foundation design. Although pillars were completed on both riverbanks, work stalled after problems arose while building the middle pillar.

The design required the well foundation to reach a depth of 15 meters, but bedrock was encountered at around five meters, making construction as per the original design impossible, leading the construction company to halt work.

Later, in 2021, the Bridge Department decided to change the old design, replacing the well foundation with a pile foundation. Once the new design was approved, the same construction company was reassigned the work, after which construction picked up pace.

According to Pabitra Mani Acharya, officiating chief of the Road Division Office, Palpa, although the construction company had been granted an eighth deadline extension until Shrawan 30, the bridge construction has now been completed.

He said the design change increased the project cost by 22.05%. Originally targeted for completion in three years, the bridge — finished in 15- now has a total cost (including VAT) of NPR 21,62,61,368.

Shyam KC, a representative of the construction company, claimed that the long halt caused by the failed initial design led to losses of around NPR 70 million for the company.

Once operational, the bridge is expected to ease travel between Syangja and Palpa. It is also expected to serve as important infrastructure for the route from India through the Jhyagdi Khola corridor to the Andhikhola corridor, Parbat, and Muktinath, as well as for expanding connectivity with China to the north.

title.rendered: Five parliamentary committees to meet today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Meetings of five parliamentary committees are scheduled to take place today, with discussions ranging from tourism legislation and human-wildlife conflict to infrastructure development and livestock disease control.

According to the Federal Parliament Secretariat, the Agriculture, Cooperatives and Natural Resources Committee will meet at 9:30 am, followed by the Infrastructure Development Committee at 10 am and the International Relations and Tourism Committee at 11 am. The Legislation Management Committee will meet at 1 pm, while the Public Policy and Delegated Legislation Committee is scheduled for 2 pm.

The International Relations and Tourism Committee will discuss the Tourism Bill, 2025 with the Nepal Mountaineering Association and other stakeholders.

The Agriculture, Cooperatives and Natural Resources Committee will discuss a report prepared by a technical task force formed by the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment to address human-wildlife conflict.

The Infrastructure Development Committee will hold discussions on infrastructure development and public-private partnerships. Representatives from the Investment Board Nepal, Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Nepal Chamber of Commerce, Confederation of Nepalese Industries and Nepal-India Chamber of Commerce and Industry have been invited to the meeting.

The Legislation Management Committee will hold a theoretical discussion on the Contagious Animal Diseases (Control) Bill, 2026. The committee has invited the agriculture minister, secretaries of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment and the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs.

Meanwhile, the Public Policy and Delegated Legislation Committee will discuss pastureland policy with expert Dhan Prasad Lamichhane, who has been invited to the meeting.

title.rendered: Monsoon continues across Nepal, heavy rain possible in four provinces

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 24

Monsoon winds continue to influence weather across Nepal, with the monsoon trough currently positioned around its average location, according to the Meteorological Forecasting Division of the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

The country is currently experiencing generally cloudy conditions, with light to moderate rainfall reported in parts of Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, as well as a few places in Koshi, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces and one or two places in Madhesh Province.

The weather is expected to remain generally cloudy across the country this afternoon. Some parts of the mountainous region may receive moderate rain and snowfall accompanied by thunder and lightning, while many areas of the hills are also likely to experience moderate rainfall with thunderstorms.

The department has forecast moderate rain with thunder and lightning in some parts of the Terai areas of Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces, and in a few places in the Terai areas of Madhesh and Koshi provinces.

Heavy rainfall is possible at one or two places in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces.

Similar conditions are expected tonight, with generally cloudy skies across the country. A few places in the mountainous regions may receive moderate rain or snowfall with thunder and lightning.

Some hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, along with a few areas of the hills in Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces, may also receive moderate rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms.

Moderate rain with thunder and lightning is also possible in some parts of the Terai areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces and in a few places in Madhesh, Lumbini and Sudurpaschim.

The department has again warned of heavy rainfall at one or two places in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces.

Authorities have urged people in areas likely to receive heavy rain to remain alert to possible debris flows, floods, landslides and soil erosion.

The weather could also disrupt daily life and affect agriculture, health, tourism, mountaineering, road transport and air travel. The department has advised the public and concerned agencies to remain updated with its latest weather information.
