title.rendered: Nepal’s archers chase Asian Games medal amid crumbling facilities and equipment shortages

content.rendered:
The target boards are rotting away. The tarpaulin put up to provide shelter from the rain is torn. And beneath it, Nepal’s archers are training with a dream of winning a medal at the 20th Asian Games.

For athletes preparing to represent Nepal at the Asian Games, the training ground at the Nepal Police Academy in Maharajgunj is far from the setting one might expect for a national team preparing for one of Asia’s biggest sporting events.

The Nepal Archery Association does not have its own training facility in the capital, leaving the archers to train inside the Police Academy. But the lack of infrastructure is only part of the problem. The athletes also face a shortage of basic equipment.

Among those preparing for the Asian Games are Tilak Pun Magar and Gyanu Awale, who will compete in recurve archery. Both have had to buy equipment such as bows and arrows with their own money.

“We have problems even with the equipment. The things we need for training are not always available in Nepal, so we have to order them from abroad. It is expensive,” Tilak says.

Yet the shortage has not diminished his ambition.

Tilak is preparing for his third Asian Games, having previously represented Nepal at the 18th and 19th editions. This time, he says, his earlier experience has given him greater confidence.

“Let’s see what score we get there. We all go with the goal of winning a medal. You need confidence, but rather than just hoping for a medal, it is better to go with a clear target,” he says. “I am confident that I can set a better record than before.”

A medal has never come

Nepal will have two archers at the 20th Asian Games, scheduled for September. Tilak and Gyanu will compete in the 70-metre recurve events in the men’s, women’s and mixed categories.

Nepal’s archery team has participated in the Asian Games four times before, but has yet to win a medal.

Tilak says the current preparation is not something that began only in the final months before the Games.

“We have been training well so far. We have not been working on this for just these two months; we have been doing it for years,” he says.

Gyanu, who is also preparing for her second Asian Games, wants to improve on her previous performance.

“I will try to do better than before. We are somewhat different this time. Things were not as good previously, but this time my goal is to perform better,” she says.

Coach Prem Prasad Pun also believes the team is better prepared than it was for the previous Games.

“We have been preparing continuously for the past two years. Everyone has improved in terms of skills, technique and physical fitness,” he says. “The scores have also been very good.”

Competing against Asia’s best

For Prem Prasad, the Asian Games are not only about medals. They are also an opportunity for Nepal’s archers to compete against some of the strongest athletes in the world.

“Archery is like a powerhouse not just in Asia but in the world. The athletes winning medals at the World Cups and Olympics are also from Asia. Being able to compete against them is itself a major achievement,” he says.

But competing at that level requires equipment and preparation that Nepal’s athletes often have to arrange themselves.

Prem Prasad says the athletes are still buying their own equipment.

“Even now, they are buying their own equipment and competing. There is a shortage of arrows and other materials. Friends, relatives and others have been supportive, which has helped a lot,” he says.

‘We have a chance of reaching the quarter-finals’

Ramesh Siwakoti, general secretary of the Nepal Archery Association, believes Nepal’s archers have a realistic chance of reaching the quarter-finals this time.

He points to Tilak’s recent scores as a reason for optimism.

“Right now, the players’ performance is very good. An Olympic gold medallist in archery has scored around 695 or 697. Our player Tilak has scored 670. The requirement for an Olympic wild card is only 650,” Siwakoti says.

“If he can maintain the same form in Japan, there is a possibility of reaching the quarter-finals,” he says.

But behind those numbers is a training environment that the association says has received little government support.

Government neglect

Siwakoti says the archery association has not received meaningful support from the government.

He claims that the National Sports Council had even written to select athletes for the compound 50-metre event, but later cut the event after the selection process.

“Our target boards are rotten. The National Sports Council has not provided any equipment for the past seven years. We have had to arrange equipment by putting in our own money,” Siwakoti says.

He says the association has repeatedly sought support without success.

“We wrote 16 letters in five years, but none of them received any response. This time, I have heard that the National Sports Council has allocated a budget for archery,” he says.

Then comes his question: “How long are we expected to protect the national reputation by bringing the sport this far through our personal efforts?”

The shortage of equipment also creates a problem when athletes actually reach international competitions.

Tilak says Nepal’s team does not have the luxury of replacing equipment if something goes wrong during an event.

“We are short of arrows and bows. When athletes from other countries go to competitions like this, they take two bows each. But if our only bow breaks or something goes wrong, we have to withdraw. We don’t even get the opportunity to compete,” he says.

“Having two bows would make things much easier.”

The team also lacks exposure to international competition, according to Prem Prasad.

For now, however, the athletes continue to train beneath a torn tarpaulin, alongside ageing target boards, carrying equipment they have often paid for themselves.

The facilities may not match the scale of their ambition. But as Nepal’s archers prepare for another Asian Games, their target remains unchanged: to perform better than before and, if possible, finally bring home the medal the sport has never won at the Games.

title.rendered: Nepal’s Thermidorian Reaction: How the old political elite is trying to return

content.rendered:
September is on the horizon. Around this time last year, the lava of public anger and dissatisfaction had begun to boil beneath Nepali society, eventually erupting into the Gen Z uprising.

Nearly a year after that explosive youth revolt, an uncomfortable irony is becoming harder to ignore: the very political figures whose removal from power was at the heart of the movement are now moving, without much hesitation, to reclaim their parties and political influence.

At first glance, this may look like little more than the familiar ambition of three ageing politicians who refuse to leave the political stage. But something larger may be at work.

Nearly a century ago, political scientist Crane Brinton offered a framework for understanding precisely this kind of political reversal in The Anatomy of Revolution.

Brinton compared revolution to a fever.

As injustice and dissatisfaction accumulate, the fever rises. Citizens become restless, anger builds and eventually people take to the streets demanding change. But no society can remain indefinitely in a state of political fever. Eventually, exhaustion sets in.

Brinton called the stage that follows the “Thermidorian Reaction.” After the upheaval of revolution, society begins to crave stability and peace. The appetite for permanent confrontation weakens. The distinction between the “new” and the “old” can begin to blur, and with it the political energy required to question the return of forces that had once been rejected.

That is precisely the danger Nepal now appears to be approaching.

The revolutionary energy that demanded change is gradually being squeezed. The political environment is beginning to shift in ways that are increasingly favourable to the old establishment. And the old political elite is moving quickly to take advantage of that opening.

The same leaders whom the Gen Z movement pushed from the centre of political life towards the margins are once again attempting to reclaim their place.

The latest efforts of Sher Bahadur Deuba, KP Sharma Oli and Pushpa Kamal Dahal can, in many ways, be read as a Nepali version of the Thermidorian Reaction.

For a generation that expected accountability, if not outright political repentance, from these leaders, their apparent determination to return represents more than disappointment. It raises the possibility of political regression.

Nepali Congress’ internal wrangling, communists’ relief

There is little point in spending too many words on the communist parties that continue to operate through largely unchanged political structures despite the heat of the Gen Z uprising.

What is more revealing is what is happening inside the Nepali Congress.

The party had raised hopes of generational change and reform following the movement and the intervention of the Gen X generation. Yet the effort to turn the clock back appears to have gathered considerable momentum.

Deuba, who went abroad after coming under physical attack during the protests, has since returned through the windows of political opportunity.

His appetite for a political comeback appears so strong that he has refused to settle into the role of an elder statesman. Instead, he is once again moving actively through the political landscape, attempting to reclaim the old throne of party power.

Political manoeuvring is hardly unfamiliar territory for Deuba.

He once dissolved parliament in accordance with the wishes of the then king and did not hesitate to split his own party in the pursuit of political power.

Now, too, he appears unwilling to rule out anything—from a party split to religious issues—in his effort to regain influence.

His efforts have been helped by a section of his party and, seemingly, by the conduct of the state.

Recent developments suggest that Deuba’s return was not simply the result of a single day’s decision. As legal processes appear to weaken and the Nepali Congress’s legitimacy dispute has once again entered the courts, the party’s internal conflict has taken an increasingly consequential turn.

The sequence of events, from an arrest warrant to a security escort, has raised questions about whether his political return is simply coincidental or part of a broader preparation.

The same Home Ministry that had worked to secure an Interpol Red Notice to bring Deuba back to Nepal from abroad later escorted him to Chundevi.

The political symbolism is difficult to ignore.

There have also been discussions within judicial circles about alleged pressure from senior leaders of the ruling coalition regarding the Congress case.

Whether these developments are coordinated or merely coincidental is a question that deserves scrutiny.

But Deuba’s highly publicised rehearsal of a return to the “president’s chair,” even if staged at Chundevi, must certainly have offered some relief to Oli and Dahal.

The missteps of the new parties and the government have, in turn, brightened the prospects of the old political establishment. The space created by the Gen Z uprising is beginning to look less permanently closed to those who once occupied it.

Oli, Dahal and the resistance to generational change

Oli and Dahal, meanwhile, are confronting a different but related challenge: resistance to their leadership from younger generations within their own parties.

Within the CPN-UML, leaders who cautiously raise the question of party restructuring have faced Oli’s warnings and accusations.

Dahal, on the other hand, appears to have gone even further.

Less than a year after the Gen Z uprising, he has challenged the political consciousness and contribution of those who fought in the conflict by handing an important ministry in Koshi Province to his own son-in-law.

Oli’s intolerance toward political reform, Deuba’s hunger for power and Dahal’s embrace of nepotism may look like different political habits. But together they point to the same underlying problem: an old political elite struggling to restore the power it lost.

There is something deeply unsettling about watching old leaders perform a crude dance of power on political ground watered by the sacrifices of a generation that took to the streets demanding their downfall.

It is not merely disappointing. It deserves to be challenged.

The politics of fatigue

Brinton’s comparison of revolution to a fever offers another useful way to understand what may be happening in Nepal.

A society cannot remain in a permanent state of political mobilisation. Eventually, people become tired of upheaval and begin to value stability.

That fatigue is not inherently a rejection of change. But it creates an opening for those who were displaced by it.

There are already signs that Nepali society is becoming tired. And the old leaders are taking advantage of that exhaustion to replay a political game many believed had finally been discredited.

This, too, is not entirely new to Nepal.

After the political change of 1951, the Rana and royal establishments continued to occupy the centre of power in different forms.

After the 1990 democratic movement, elements of the old Panchayat establishment also found ways to return to political relevance.

The same pattern appeared after the Maoist insurgency and the 2006 movement that established the republic. Feudal structures and old political practices repeatedly found new forms in which to survive.

The lesson is not that revolutions inevitably fail. It is that revolutions do not, by themselves, guarantee that the structures and habits they challenged will disappear.

As the heat of a movement fades, old leadership and old political consciousness can begin to regain ground.

Nepal is not alone in this.

The Philippines offers a striking example. The People Power revolution drove Ferdinand Marcos into exile. Three and a half decades later, Filipinos elected his son to the country’s highest office.

In Egypt, the Arab Spring brought down Hosni Mubarak after three decades in power. Only three years later, Egyptians were living under the rule of military general Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, whose government became even more authoritarian.

Research into 123 movements between 1990 and 2015 and 98 counter-revolutionary challenges examined by Killian Clarke offers another important warning: the possibility of figures rejected by a movement returning to power increases not only when a new government is weak, but also when a new government is trying to institutionalise itself.

The reaction to a challenge against established power is rarely simple.

Sometimes, it is precisely the attempt to reform the existing system that forces the old rulers to fight back.

They make one final attempt to return.

The ‘lumpens’ versus the ‘incompetents’

Left-wing leader Ghanshyam Bhusal once offered a memorable description after the elections: the country had been in the hands of the “incompetent” and had now fallen into the hands of the “lumpens.”

The distinction is worth considering.

To be incompetent is to lack ability, judgement or expertise. To be a lumpen is to lack discipline, political culture and proper conduct.

An incompetent government can make mistakes. A lumpen political culture can damage not only governance but also the political environment in which governance takes place.

The warning is becoming increasingly relevant.

If the government, the new political parties and younger leaders within established parties fail to prove their worth, the voices of the old leaders will become louder and their political stature will rise again.

Every new generation claiming leadership—whether in government or in political parties—must work to prove Bhusal wrong.

Because when new parties and new governments fail to justify their existence, political space does not remain empty for long.

The old establishment fills it.

There is another point that must not be forgotten: the Gen Z uprising changed political faces, but it did not necessarily change the structure of power.

The arrogance that Oli displayed from the prime minister’s chair before the Gen Z movement—the tendency to place himself above rules, institutions and political norms—can now be seen in the behaviour of some leaders who came to power through the movement’s political opening.

The old leaders weakened internal democracy and promoted loyalists. Some of the new leaders appear to be reproducing the same practices once they acquire power.

They avoid dialogue with citizens, challenge institutions and procedures, and increasingly behave as though they themselves are exceptions to the rules.

That is slowly weakening the thread of trust between the new government and the public.

And it raises a fundamental question for the new generation:

Is political change simply about replacing old faces, or is it about changing institutions and political culture as well?

Why does a party that claims to represent the people gradually become the party of a handful of leaders?

The answer lies partly in internal democracy.

Unless democratic practices are institutionalised within political parties, changing faces will not necessarily change behaviour.

And if the new generation does not change its political style, the basis for resisting the old leaders waiting at the gates will become increasingly weak.

Put simply, when ordinary citizens have to stand in the rain for an entire day simply to obtain a cylinder of cooking gas, only to return home empty-handed because they lack political access, the voices of ageing leaders swimming comfortably in the syrup of power will inevitably become louder.

The risk and the responsibility

The political vacuum created when new forces fail to govern, communicate and institutionalise reform cannot last forever.

Sooner or later, someone fills it.

The old leaders will fill it with narratives of experience, organisation and past contribution.

That is why the growing desire of Deuba, Oli and Dahal to return to the centre of power—combined with the weaknesses and short-sightedness of the new political forces—could turn the Gen Z uprising into a political tragedy.

This is not only a challenge for the ruling party and government. It is an even greater challenge for the younger generations inside the old parties who claim to be working for political renewal.

For the third and fourth generations inside the communist parties, where internal democracy has still failed to take deep root, the question is particularly important.

The Rastriya Swatantra Party, too, needs to pay close attention.

The movement opened the door.

But opening the door is not the same as deciding who should walk through it.

Unless an organisation capable of making that distinction is built, the storm created by a popular movement can bring even worse characters and tendencies into power.

If political parties cannot stop or correct such figures, they themselves become the window through which citizens understand the state.

The ability to bring people onto the streets and the ability to govern a state are not the same thing.

A new generation that appears powerful on the streets must now demonstrate the institutional skill, political discipline and commitment required to preserve and deepen the change it demanded.

Otherwise, the sacrifices of the Gen Z uprising risk becoming a footnote in another cycle of Nepali political history.

The lesson of history is uncomfortable but clear: revolutions do not automatically destroy old political structures.

Sometimes, they merely push them temporarily out of sight.

The old order waits for fatigue. It waits for mistakes. It waits for disappointment.

And then it returns.

That is why vigilance cannot be the responsibility of one leader or one party.

It belongs to the generation that opened the door to change—and paid for it with its blood.

title.rendered: How ‘vibe coding’ is taking off in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

When Grade 9 student Pranav Paudel decided to give his sister a birthday present, he chose something she did not expect: a website.

The static website featured different birthday-themed designs. What surprised his sister was not just the gift itself, but the fact that her younger brother had built it without having taken any IT-related course.

Pranav, a student at Manakamana School in Narayantar, Kathmandu, had taught himself what is now popularly known as ‘vibe coding’.

He built the website in his spare time after developing an interest in technology. It was a simple project, but for his family, it was evidence of something more important—his curiosity and willingness to teach himself.

“We were happy to see that he is curious. Even afterwards, whenever he is interested in something, he tries to accomplish it through vibe coding and enjoys doing it himself,” Pranav’s sister said. “He has started dreaming of becoming a chess player as well as pursuing a career in IT. He is learning accordingly.”

Pranav is just 14, and he does not have deep technical knowledge. Yet, using AI, he is able to turn an idea into something tangible.

So, what exactly is ‘vibe coding’?

Vibe coding refers to a way of developing software in which a person describes in natural language what they want a computer programme or website to do, and an artificial intelligence tool generates the necessary code.

Instead of manually writing every line of code, users can give instructions such as, “I want a website with this design” or “I want this button to perform this action.” The AI tool then generates the code.

The process is iterative. Users run the generated code, identify errors or shortcomings, tell the AI what needs to be fixed, and repeat the process.

In other words, the person does not necessarily need to understand or manually write every line of code. They work with AI to turn an idea into a functioning product.

The term ‘vibe coding’ gained wider attention after AI researcher and OpenAI founding member Andrej Karpathy used it in a post on X on February 2, 2025.

Karpathy described it as a new kind of coding in which a person essentially gives themselves over to the process and focuses less on the code itself.

The phrase quickly entered the technology mainstream. Collins English Dictionary subsequently named ‘vibe coding’ its Word of the Year in 2025.

From students to government offices

What began gaining popularity among technology enthusiasts and developers around the world is now finding its way into Nepal’s software development ecosystem.

The practice is being used not only by students and individual developers, but increasingly in the development of internal software and government-related systems.

Nepal Telecom, for instance, has started developing several internal software systems using AI-assisted coding practices.

The company is developing a Procurement Management System to digitally manage its purchasing process, a Duty Chart Management System to manage employee shifts and responsibilities, and a Meeting Management System to record meeting agendas, participants and decisions.

It is also developing a Workflow Management System to make office files and decision-making processes paperless, as well as a Unified Ticketing System to manage network equipment and customer complaints in an integrated manner.

An engineer at Nepal Telecom told Onlinekhabar that the organisation is following the practice of vibe coding, using AI to create an initial version of the code based on requirements before technical teams test and modify it.

“We are following vibe coding and then modifying it in our own way. Security and other aspects are taken into consideration. It has made the process much easier,” the engineer said. “This is also the way software development is increasingly being done.”

The practice is also being adopted within the government.

An official at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers said the government has been giving priority to AI-assisted coding in the development of internal software, while its use is increasing in software being developed in other areas as well.

A member of the Nepal Association for Software and IT Services Companies (NAS-IT) said the use of vibe coding could also be observed in some newer government tools and websites.

According to the member, AI-assisted coding is being used to add new features, fix common user problems, modify forms and dashboards, and generate reports in systems related to driving licences and the Inland Revenue Department’s electronic lottery system.

“These things can be understood clearly by looking at the websites and systems. Anyone with software knowledge can identify the use of this process,” the member said.

But the growing use of AI does not mean the government is simply taking AI-generated code and putting it into operation.

The Prime Minister’s Office official said the government was not blindly deploying AI-generated software without understanding its implications.

Systems involving driving licences, tax information, payments and personal data are sensitive, the official said. Code generated through AI is therefore not deployed directly without testing.

According to the official, security testing, code reviews and access controls are carried out before AI-generated code is incorporated into critical systems.

“Previously, even for a minor change, a large portion of the code had to be typed manually. Now, we can give clear instructions about the requirement and use AI to create an initial structure of the code,” the official said. “The technical team and engineers then modify and test it according to the requirements of the government system. We do not build systems blindly.”

Faster development, bigger security concerns

The appeal of vibe coding is straightforward: it can make software development faster and allow people with limited programming knowledge to build things that would previously have required considerably more technical expertise.

But that speed comes with concerns.

As the popularity of vibe coding has grown worldwide, cybersecurity experts have raised questions about the risks associated with AI-generated code.

Reports published by technology publications have warned that vibe coding can create significant security vulnerabilities, including the risk of data leaks. AI-generated applications can potentially contain problems such as command injection vulnerabilities and exposed API keys.

An analysis published by Code by Melendez has suggested that evidence from 2026 indicates security vulnerabilities can be found in a significant proportion of AI-generated code when it is produced without adequate human supervision.

Other analyses have also pointed to problems such as insecure databases, weak authentication, exposed API keys and a lack of proper code auditing in applications created through vibe coding.

That does not necessarily mean the technology should be rejected.

Instead, experts recommend a hybrid approach: let AI generate the code, but have human developers review it, conduct security tests and make the necessary changes before deployment.

A growing global market

The rise of vibe coding is not limited to individual developers experimenting with AI. It is also becoming a growing global market.

According to a report by Future Market Insights, the global vibe coding market was valued at around $7.1 billion in 2026. The market is projected to grow at an annual rate of 17.1 percent over the next decade and reach $34.4 billion by 2036.

Technology companies including Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, Lovable and Vercel are developing tools and platforms designed to make AI-assisted software development easier.

Tools such as Cursor, Claude Code, Replit, Bolt and Lovable are allowing people with limited programming knowledge to create websites and applications.

The trend is becoming increasingly visible in Nepal as well.

But its adoption among Nepal’s established technology companies remains limited.

Gauravraj Pandey, president of NAS-IT, said vibe coding has yet to become widespread among large and established technology companies in Nepal.

According to Pandey, concerns about quality and long-term maintainability have prevented professional software companies from adopting it extensively.

“It is used less in professional work because of concerns about quality and long-term maintainability. It is more common in startups and freelancing, where quick results are needed,” he said.

Pandey identified three major challenges associated with vibe coding: security, system architecture and long-term maintainability.

Developers, he said, need to ensure that systems are built on a strong architecture capable of being expanded in the future, while also ensuring that the code can be maintained over the long term.

That does not make vibe coding inherently problematic, he said. If the process is properly managed and the code is reviewed and tested by experienced developers, it can still be useful.

‘Vibe coding cannot be rejected’

IT expert Vedvyas Pokharel believes vibe coding should not be viewed negatively as software development evolves.

The technology, he said, can significantly speed up developers’ work. He also uses it himself to develop software and provide services to clients.

“I use it myself and provide services to clients through vibe coding,” Pokharel said. “It has become very convenient recently. If you know how to use it carefully while paying attention to security, it makes the work easier and faster.”

Cybersecurity expert Naresh Lamgade also sees value in vibe coding, particularly in the speed it brings to software development.

He said it can make it easier for organisations to develop software according to their own requirements rather than relying entirely on external developers.

“It is very good because it increases the speed of work. But the main goal of AI is to complete the task. So when working at speed, less attention can be paid to security,” Lamgade said.

That trade-off is where much of the concern lies.

According to Lamgade, AI-generated applications can sometimes expose sensitive information such as API keys and secrets or leave connection mechanisms in plain text.

He said some platforms, including Lovable, have introduced security assessment as an additional paid feature, reflecting the growing concern around security in AI-assisted development.

The desire to build software quickly, he warned, can increase risks if security is treated as an afterthought.

“Secret keys should be stored securely before hosting and launching. At least one round of security testing should be conducted,” Lamgade said. “Depending on the commercial risk, manual testing of the code is also necessary. If these things are done, vibe coding cannot simply be rejected.”

For a student like Pranav, however, the technology represents something much simpler: an opportunity.

He did not need years of formal programming training to turn an idea into a birthday present for his sister. Curiosity was enough to get him started, and AI helped him build.

That same technology is now moving beyond personal projects and into Nepal’s businesses and government offices.

title.rendered: The Taliban has brought Afghanistan close to collapse, but resistance is growing

content.rendered:
Five years after returning to power in Afghanistan, the Taliban’s rule remains as ultra-extremist as ever.

Acting in the name of a self-centred version of Islam, the group has made no effort to modify its hardline ideological beliefs in favour of a more humane and inclusive approach to governing.

Nor has it refrained from hosting many like-minded violent extremist groups. The United Nations has issued repeated warnings about the resurgence of terrorism from Afghanistan.s

The Taliban is also facing growing security challenges from within its own ranks and a cluster of armed resistance forces. Relations with its former patron, Pakistan, have completely broken down, with the country’s defence minister declaring an “open war” on the group earlier this year.

Tightening its control

Prior to the takeover of Kabul in August 2021, Taliban leaders indicated they had changed. They claimed to have learned lessons from their draconian rule from 1996 until the US-led intervention in late 2001.

The Taliban also pledged to respect the rights of women and girls to be educated and to work. It said it would give amnesty to those who had worked with the previous US-backed government and establish an inclusive governing system. It took steps to ensure Afghanistan would never again become a nest for terrorism.

Yet, none of these promises has been met. If anything, the Taliban has only hardened its brand of Islam, which is not practised anywhere else in the Muslim world, and tightened its repressive, misogynist and regressive rule.

It has also taken advantage of the geopolitical rivalries in the region and globally to govern without any form of popular legitimacy or need for international recognition. Only Russia has so far formally recognised the Taliban government, but many others, including China, have boosted their diplomatic contacts with the country’s leaders and pursued economic and trade ties with them.

Taliban leaders were also invited to Brussels in recent months to meet with European Union officials over the outflow of Afghan refugees to the bloc – a visit heavily criticised by rights groups.

Millions of Afghans now live outside the country – most in neighbouring Iran and Pakistan. About half a million have applied for asylum in the EU since the Taliban came back to power, and many host countries have been keen to deport them.

Inside Afghanistan, meanwhile, most citizens are facing unprecedented poverty, mass unemployment, spiralling inflation and a severe lack of basic goods. Some families have found it necessary to sell a child to survive.

Threats on multiple fronts

The situation has only worsened with US President Donald Trump’s decision to shutter the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and Pakistan’s closure of transit roads into the country.

Washington has pursued an ambiguous policy towards the Taliban. Trump has demanded the return of the Bagram airbase in Kabul and US$7 billion worth of military assets left behind by departing US forces in 2021.

Yet, Washington has maintained dialogue with the militia. The UN has also indirectly delivered billions of dollars in funds from the US government to the Taliban’s coffers over the past five years.

Pakistan’s turn against the Taliban is rooted in the group’s support of the Pakistani Taliban (Tahreek-I Taliban Pakistan, or TTP). Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of providing TTP members with a base of operations to launch attacks across the border. It has retaliated by launching airstrikes on its neighbour.

Islamabad now seems determined to maximise pressure on the Afghan Taliban by bombing its bases – at a high cost of civilian casualties. It has also hosted meetings with some of the Taliban’s opponents.

This comes at a time of increased fighting in the northeastern province of Badakhshan between the Taliban and followers of a dissident commander, Juma Khan Fateh, over control of resources and local grievances against the group. Senior Taliban officials have been assassinated in the region.

There are a number of armed opposition groups operating there. These groups remain fragmented, though some reports indicate the resistance is expanding.

It is not clear where all this will lead. The Taliban is rattled, but these opposition forces have a way to go to demonstrate a sufficient degree of coordination and a united national agenda. The Taliban is also more deeply entrenched and much better equipped than the groups.

Most Afghans would be pleased to see the back of the Taliban. But for the opposition to be seen as a viable alternative, it will need to build trust with the people and provide hope for the future. The history of Afghanistan shows how hard this has been to achieve.

title.rendered: Nepal, India agree to strengthen surveillance at sensitive border points

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Nepal and India have agreed to strengthen security surveillance at sensitive points along their shared border by using modern technology, including CCTV cameras.

The agreement was reached at the 14th meeting of the Nepal-India Joint Working Group on Border Management, held in Dehradun, India, on Friday.

According to Nepal’s Ministry of Home Affairs, both sides agreed to use modern and advanced technologies and equipment to enhance security monitoring in sensitive areas along the border.

“Both sides agreed to increase security surveillance at sensitive locations in the border areas by using modern and latest technologies, including CCTV and other modern equipment,” the ministry said in a statement on the meeting’s decisions.

The two-day meeting, which began on Thursday, also discussed encroachment and unauthorised use of the no-man’s land, as well as the full operation and utilisation of Integrated Check Posts.

The two sides also held detailed discussions on mutual legal assistance and other issues related to border management.

“Detailed discussions were held on controlling encroachment and unauthorised use of the no-man’s land, the full operation and utilisation of Integrated Check Posts, mutual legal assistance and other important issues concerning border management,” the Home Ministry said.

title.rendered: Student killed after hostel dispute turns violent in Shankhamul

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

A student was killed after a dispute at Valley Boys Hostel in Shankhamul, Kathmandu Metropolitan City-10, turned violent on Friday morning.

The deceased has been identified as Basanta Kalathoki, a resident of Ghorahi Sub-Metropolitan City-17, Dang, who was staying at the hostel.

According to police, a group of youths attacked Kalathoki inside the hostel, using hostel furniture and a sharp weapon. The incident briefly turned the student hostel into a scene of violence.

Police from the New Baneshwor Police Circle reached the hostel after receiving information about the incident. Kalathoki, who had sustained serious injuries, was taken to Civil Hospital for treatment.

Doctors declared him dead at around 12:15 pm, according to Kathmandu District Police Range spokesperson SP Dan Bahadur Thapa.

“He was rescued and taken to the hospital. We were informed that he was declared dead at around 12:15 pm,” Thapa said.

Police said Kalathoki had injuries to his head and neck caused by a sharp weapon. They suspect he died as a result of a physical assault and sharp-weapon attack. The exact cause of death will be confirmed after the post-mortem examination.

Six initially detained

Police initially detained six people from the hostel as part of their investigation.

Among them, 18-year-old Shekhar Yadav of Kalaiya Sub-Metropolitan City-3, Bara, has been found to have been directly involved in the attack, according to police.

The identities of the other five detainees have not been made public. Police said they were detained for questioning as investigators tried to establish their involvement in the incident.

“We initially detained six people and investigated them. One of them, Yadav, appears to have been directly involved in the killing. Nothing has been established against the others so far,” Thapa said.

Police said those against whom no suspicious activity is found will be released after questioning.

Another suspect allegedly involved in the killing was arrested in Makwanpur while attempting to flee.

Pramit Patel, a resident of Kalaiya, was arrested from Bhaisey in Makwanpur with the coordination of the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office and Makwanpur police.

SSP Santosh Kumar Khadka of the Crime Investigation Office said Patel was being brought to Kathmandu.

“We arrested him in Makwanpur and are bringing him to Kathmandu,” Khadka said.

According to police sources, Patel was attempting to travel through Makwanpur towards Bara before crossing into India. Police intercepted and arrested him before he could leave the area.

Police are preparing to seek remand against Yadav and Patel on charges of murder and continue their investigation.

Murder weapon yet to be recovered

Although police suspect that a sharp weapon was used in the attack, the weapon itself has not yet been recovered.

Kalathoki had multiple injuries across his body and was reportedly unable to speak when he was taken to hospital.

“His injuries indicate that he died after being attacked with a sharp weapon. The weapon may have been hidden after the attack. We have not recovered it yet,” an investigating officer said.

Police are continuing their search for the weapon and gathering evidence from the hostel.

Police suspect dispute among friends

The preliminary investigation suggests that the killing followed a dispute among people who knew each other.

Police have not found evidence of an old personal rivalry between the victim and the suspects.

“We have not found an old enmity. It appears to have happened during an ordinary dispute between friends,” an investigating officer involved in the probe said.

According to police, the dispute escalated and the suspects attacked Kalathoki in a fit of anger.

However, investigators are yet to question all the suspects, including Patel, who was arrested in Makwanpur. Police say the exact motive behind the killing will become clearer after further questioning and investigation.

The incident has also raised concerns among police over the management and monitoring of hostels in the New Baneshwor, Buddhanagar and Shankhamul areas.

Police say they have increasingly received information about marijuana use and other suspicious activities in some hostels in the area.

Officers say incidents of noise, disputes and drug use have been reported from some hostels. Police have conducted searches from time to time, recovering marijuana and detaining some hostel residents.

According to police officials, inadequate monitoring by hostel wardens and the lack of proper supervision of young residents can contribute to students becoming involved in substance use and other risky activities.

Police suspect that disputes over drug use may also have contributed to conflicts in some hostels.

The latest incident has prompted renewed calls for better supervision and management of student hostels in the area.

title.rendered: Election Commission urges voters to update voter details

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The Election Commission has urged citizens to check and update their details in the voter list.

According to Narayan Prasad Bhattarai, joint secretary and spokesperson of the Election Commission, the commission regularly updates the voter list to make it accurate, updated, reliable and objective.

As part of the process, the existing voter list will be published on the commission’s website on September 17 for the purpose of updating the details.

The commission has urged voters to check the published list and play an active role in ensuring that their personal information is accurate and up to date.

Voters can request corrections if there are errors in their name, surname, age, address or other personal details.

The commission has also asked citizens to report cases in which someone has been registered on the voter list by providing false information.

If a voter’s name appears at more than one location, it can be retained at only one location. Voters who have changed their permanent address due to migration or marriage can also update their details accordingly.

The Election Commission said accurate and regularly updated voter lists are essential for maintaining the integrity, fairness and credibility of elections.

It expressed confidence that citizens would continue to cooperate in correcting errors, duplicate registrations and other inaccurate information in the voter list.

title.rendered: Deuba group withdraws petition seeking halt to NC general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The faction of the Nepali Congress led by Sher Bahadur Deuba has withdrawn a petition seeking an immediate halt to activities related to the party’s 15th General Convention.

The petition had been filed on behalf of Deuba and Purna Bahadur Khadka, challenging the party’s decision to proceed with the convention schedule.

The Supreme Court administration had said it would keep the petition for study and proceed with the remaining process on Monday. However, the Deuba-led faction withdrew the petition on Friday evening, saying it needed to make some corrections.

“The petition was submitted today. The administration had kept it for study. Later in the evening, they came and took it back, saying some corrections needed to be made,” Supreme Court spokesperson Arjun Prasad Koirala told Onlinekhabar.

Deuba and Khadka had submitted the petition through their representatives. Deepak Khadka represented Deuba, while advocate Shrawan Shrestha represented Khadka at the Supreme Court.

The faction has previously challenged the leadership of Gagan Thapa, who was elected from the party’s special general convention, by filing an appeal at the Supreme Court. The court has already ordered a fresh hearing in that case.

The latest petition was filed against what the Deuba faction described as the unilateral publication of the schedule for the 15th General Convention.

The Nepali Congress has scheduled its 15th General Convention for October 2–5.

title.rendered: Govt, local bodies discuss long-term solution to Kathmandu Valley’s waste problem

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The government has held a high-level inter-agency discussion on the existing problems in waste management in the Kathmandu Valley and measures for their long-term resolution.

The discussion was held at the Ministry of Infrastructure Development on Friday under the chairmanship of Information and Communications Minister and Nuwakot-1 lawmaker Dr Bikram Timilsina.

Mayors and representatives of local governments in the Kathmandu Valley, officials from the Department of Environment, heads of agencies involved in waste management, waste management experts and representatives of communities affected by the Bancharedanda landfill site participated in the meeting.

According to the Ministry of Communications, the meeting concluded that although waste management is primarily the responsibility of local governments, coordination among the federal government, local governments and other concerned agencies is essential for a long-term solution.

Timilsina said the government had given high priority to the problems faced by residents affected by the Bancharedanda landfill and the broader issue of waste management.

He said the government was serious about resolving the problems that have persisted in waste management for years.

“The government is ready to make every possible effort to address policy and practical problems. The federal government is very serious about resolving the waste management problem,” Timilsina said. “All municipalities and agencies must also contribute from their respective sides.”

Timilsina said the Constitution and existing laws assign waste management responsibilities to local governments and that each municipality should move towards managing its own waste.

He pledged that the federal government would facilitate and support local governments in doing so.

The minister also said the federal government would work to resolve issues related to acquiring land needed for waste management.

He said the government would also consider legal amendments if necessary and was discussing ways to make land available to local governments, including through leasing.

“The government is committed to resolving the problems related to land acquisition. Similarly, we are committed to resolving the issues surrounding Nepwaste, which has been stuck in legal disputes for years after an agreement was signed for waste management,” Timilsina said.

“We are ready to identify where the responsibility lies, who needs to do what and where problems arise during implementation, and make a breakthrough.”

Local governments said an agreement with Nepwaste and subsequent legal disputes have made it difficult for them to develop independent waste management systems. Nepwaste is a joint venture between Nepal’s Organic Village and Finland-based company Komunikation Oy.

Timilsina stressed that efforts to solve the waste problem should not create additional complications and that the government should proceed with a clear division of responsibilities.

Local governments say they are ready to manage their own waste

Local government chiefs participating in the discussion pledged to manage waste generated within their respective municipalities and called for necessary facilitation from the federal government.

Kathmandu Metropolitan City acting mayor Sunita Dangol said waste management had previously been politicised, with different levels of government blaming one another.

She said that approach should end and that the government should address the problem at its source.

Dangol said Kathmandu Metropolitan City was working responsibly on waste management but needed short-, medium- and long-term plans.

She also said resolving the issues related to Nepwaste would make waste management easier.

Lalitpur Metropolitan City mayor Chiri Babu Maharjan said the agreement with Nepwaste was still in effect, preventing the metropolitan city from independently managing its waste.

He called for the agreement, which he said falls outside the metropolitan city’s jurisdiction, to be scrapped and said Friday’s meeting could become a starting point for resolving the issue.

Budhanilkantha Municipality mayor Mitharam Adhikari said the municipality wanted to manage its own waste but had been unable to move forward due to various legal disputes and court orders.

Tokha Municipality mayor Prakash Adhikari said waste management was a shared responsibility and that the municipality was ready to provide financial and other support.

He said different technologies could be used for waste treatment and called for an integrated plan and long-term mechanism.

Dhunibesi Municipality mayor Balkrishna Acharya said various agreements had been reached on waste management in the past but had failed to resolve the problem.

He called for those agreements to be reviewed so that local governments could create systems to manage their own waste.

Kirtipur Municipality mayor Krishnaman Dangol said the municipality planned to implement a system to manage its own waste within the next six months.

He also said other municipalities could learn from the practices Kirtipur has adopted in waste management.

Dakshinkali Municipality mayor Mohan Basnet said the municipality had started waste segregation three months ago, which had reduced the volume of waste.

He called on elected representatives of all municipalities to commit to managing waste within their own jurisdictions.

Infrastructure Development Ministry Secretary Gopal Prasad Sigdel said all levels of government must take responsibility for finding a long-term solution.

He said blaming one another would not resolve the problem and called for a joint effort by all local governments and concerned agencies.

Kathmandu sends nearly half of waste to Bancharedanda

During the meeting, Kathmandu Metropolitan City Environment Department chief Sarita Rai presented a report on the current condition of the Bancharedanda landfill site and plans for its future management.

According to the presentation, 1,792 ropanis of land have been acquired for the Bancharedanda site. However, although the site is around 24 kilometres from Balaju, Kathmandu Metropolitan City has yet to receive official documents specifying the boundaries of the acquired land.

Of the waste transported to Bancharedanda from 21 local governments, Kathmandu Metropolitan City accounts for 48.8 percent, Lalitpur Metropolitan City for 10 percent and Budhanilkantha Municipality for 5 percent, according to the presentation.

The meeting proposed moving towards a decentralised waste management model, establishing technology within individual municipalities for the reuse and recycling of dry waste, producing organic fertiliser and energy from biodegradable waste, and installing resource recovery technology at Bancharedanda.

Improving waste collection and transportation services and increasing citizen satisfaction were also identified as priorities.

The Waste Management Act requires local governments to manage their own waste, and the meeting emphasised the need for municipalities to develop plans accordingly.

875 households directly affected by landfill

The meeting was informed that Rs 1.04 billion has so far been spent on infrastructure at the Bancharedanda landfill site, while contracts worth an additional Rs 516.3 million are currently underway.

According to the information presented, 875 households across 539 hectares have been directly affected by the landfill site, while areas within three kilometres of the landfill boundary are indirectly affected.

Residents of affected areas called for the establishment of a Waste Management Development Authority to address the problem on a long-term basis.

They also called for past agreements and commitments to be implemented, problems faced by affected communities to be addressed, and dependence on Bancharedanda to be gradually reduced.

Participants also proposed developing a plan to ensure that waste from the Kathmandu Valley no longer needs to be transported to Bancharedanda within the next four years.

To achieve this, they stressed the need to reduce waste generation, segregate waste at source, increase reuse and recycling, and promote circular economy practices.

They also proposed incorporating waste management, segregation, reuse and environmental protection into school curricula to increase public awareness.

title.rendered: Why is the government moving Nepal’s intelligence agency under the PM?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

A bill seeking to revive the provision placing Nepal’s intelligence agency under the prime minister’s office has moved forward in the National Assembly after being passed by the House of Representatives.

Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sobita Gautam, on behalf of Prime Minister Balendra Shah, presented the Bill to Revive the Existing Provision of the Nepal Special Service Act, 1985 at the National Assembly meeting on Friday.

The bill was subjected to a theoretical discussion in the National Assembly, with lawmakers questioning why the intelligence agency, currently under the Ministry of Home Affairs, should be brought under the prime minister.

Responding to the lawmakers, Minister Gautam said the provision placing the intelligence agency under the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers had been introduced through the Some Nepal Acts Amendment Act 2019.

She said the intelligence agency had been under the prime minister’s office at that time but was brought under the Ministry of Home Affairs during the government led by former chief justice Sushila Karki following the Gen Z movement.

Gautam said the government had introduced the latest bill because a replacement bill was not brought after the election and the provision amended through an ordinance had subsequently become inactive.

Asked why the intelligence agency had been moved between the Home Ministry and the Prime Minister’s Office at different times, Gautam said the issue was essentially a matter of principle.

“Previous governments also kept moving it from one place to another,” she said.

She said the government currently believes that it is appropriate for an intelligence agency dealing with national security to remain under the Prime Minister’s Office.

According to Gautam, the Ministry of Home Affairs is already heavily burdened with responsibility for the country’s internal security mechanisms, including disaster management, chief district officers, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force.

“The Home Ministry is already overloaded. It has to deal with all aspects of the internal security mechanism, from disasters and chief district officers to Nepal Police and Armed Police,” she said.

Gautam said the intelligence agency needs to provide regular information and intelligence to the government, while the home minister is already occupied with numerous responsibilities.

She argued that intelligence information related to regular law and order and national security should be directly available to the prime minister, who is the head of government.

“The Home Ministry is extremely overloaded, while intelligence goes beyond the regular internal security and law-and-order responsibilities. We are bringing the agency under the Prime Minister’s Office so that intelligence information can be directly delivered to the prime minister,” she said.

Gautam said it would be appropriate for the prime minister, as head of government, to receive such information directly.

Following the minister’s response, the National Assembly approved a proposal to consider the bill.

Lawmakers can now register amendment proposals on the bill within 72 hours.

title.rendered: Why did police search Durga Prasai’s house?

content.rendered:
Police raided medical businessman Durga Prasai’s house in Bhaktapur on Thursday. A team from Bhaktapur Police and the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office conducted the raid.

Police, who searched the house from afternoon until evening, seized his mobile phone, iPad, and other digital devices. A large contingent of plainclothes police was also deployed for the search, during which Prasai’s clothes and documents were left scattered around. Police have not yet issued any official statement about the search.

Asked about it, Bhaktapur District Police Range DSP Deepak Kumar Karki claimed he had no information on the matter.

The search lasted roughly three hours. It comes after Morang Police faced heavy criticism for an earlier search of Prasai’s house that turned up nothing. This time, police have remained silent about the operation.

Prasai was furious after the search, directing his anger at the prime minister and home minister. He said he is not a drug dealer, arms supplier, or human trafficker, that he pays taxes to the state and provides jobs to 5,000 people, and questioned why he keeps being targeted. He said the search happened suddenly while he had guests at home, calling it harassment.

Security sources, however, describe the reason for the search as quite sensitive. They allege that Prasai has recently been inciting protests among victims of microfinance institutions and loan-shark lending schemes, and that security agencies received information that some of these victims were preparing to resort to self-immolation if their demands weren’t addressed. A security official said the search followed intelligence that Prasai was instigating the microfinance victims.

Given how serious and volatile the situation was believed to be, the government had earlier formed a committee to hold talks with Prasai’s group, led by Joint Secretary Liladhar Subedi from the Prime Minister’s Office, with a 9-member team from Prasai’s side led by Bishnu Bohara Chhetri. Talks were held on Bhadau 2 but reportedly did not conclude, after which security agencies raided Prasai’s house. Sources say the matter remains under investigation.

title.rendered: Bulldozers to clear encroached Guthi land in Janakpur from Saturday

content.rendered:
Janakpur, August 21

Authorities will begin using bulldozers from Saturday to clear encroached Guthi land in Janakpur, starting with encroachments around ponds.

Janak Pokharel, member-secretary of the implementation committee formed to protect Guthi land and remove encroachments, said the first phase will focus on clearing encroached pond areas.

The committee had issued a notice on July 17 asking people to vacate encroached Guthi land. Public announcements are also being made in the areas concerned on Friday.

According to Pokharel, 50 ponds identified as having been encroached upon will be cleared in the first phase.

The committee has divided the eviction drive into phases, with ponds to be cleared first, followed by temple premises and other encroached Guthi land.

The committee is basing the drive on a report prepared by a task force led by Bhojraj Ghimire in 2005 to identify encroached Guthi land in Janakpur.

Bulldozers will begin clearing the encroached area around Gordhoi Pokhari from Saturday, marking the start of the first phase of the campaign.

title.rendered: Krishna Bahadur Damai: Dalit youth breaks caste barriers to become an ‘Acharya’

content.rendered:
August 8, 2024, thousands of devotees gathered at the historic Kotihom Mahayagya held on the premises of Pashupatinath Temple in Kathmandu. At the centre of the stage, a young priest sat on the Vyasasan, delivering religious discourses as devotees listened attentively. The young man seated on the Vyasasan was Krishna Bahadur Damai from Kanchanpur.

For a young man from the Dalit community to pursue higher education in Sanskrit and complete an Acharya (postgraduate) degree is remarkable. Once denied a tika at a temple because he was considered to be from a so-called lower caste, he was now sitting on the Vyasasan at the Pashupatinath premises, interpreting scriptures before the very society that had discriminated against him.

Determination born from temple humiliation

Born on October 7, 1991, in Tilakpur, Bhimdatta-3, Kanchanpur, Krishna spent his childhood in extreme poverty and deprivation. He is the third of nine children—four sons and five daughters—of Ran Bahadur and Kamala. Growing up in a low-income Dalit family, he faced both financial hardship and social discrimination from an early age. New school uniforms and adequate educational materials were almost a luxury for him. But an incident when he was in Grade 10 changed the course of his life.

While studying at the local Baijnath Secondary School, he once participated in a cleaning programme at a local Bishnu temple. All the students happily cleaned the temple together. After the cleaning was completed, the priest applied tika to the foreheads of all the students. But when it was Krishna’s turn, the priest refused after hearing his name and surname. The priest’s rebuke, accompanied by a caste-based remark telling him to “go over there,” deeply disturbed the young Krishna. That day, he silently resolved, “The priest who refused to put tika on me because I am a Dalit—I will not be inferior to him.”

Turning point of his life

After passing the SLC (School Leaving Certificate, now SEE) examination in 2064 BS, Krishna wanted to study science. But his family’s financial circumstances made that impossible. His old determination, however, remained alive.

The village had not only priests who practised caste discrimination but also teachers such as Ishwardutta Bhatt, who encouraged the oppressed. He not only encouraged Krishna but also provided him with Rs 500 in financial assistance. That money became the means through which Krishna began his journey into Sanskrit studies.

He began studying Sanskrit at Sharda Vidyapeeth at the Uttar Madhyama (plus-two) level. But he also had to bear the cost of his education and the responsibility of helping support his family. To look after six of his siblings, apart from two elder sisters, while continuing his studies, he began selling Janakranti Dainik, a newspaper published from Mahendranagar, in 2066 BS.

His daily routine involved reaching the market early in the morning carrying newspapers, finding customers, marketing the papers and spending the remaining time studying. “I covered my food, accommodation and education expenses with the money I earned from selling newspapers,” he recalls.

What some might consider an ordinary job of selling newspapers taught him discipline, self-reliance and the art of building relationships with people.

Social rebellion through priesthood

Overcoming numerous hardships, he completed his Shastri degree in literature from Nepal Sanskrit University and an Acharya degree from the university’s campus in Dang. By then, he had gained an in-depth knowledge of Sanskrit verses, the Vedas, the Upanishads and religious scriptures.

But society was still more concerned about his caste than his knowledge. “Can a Dalit know the scriptures?” he was repeatedly asked. Some people tried to discourage him. But Krishna wanted to prove himself through his knowledge and actions. Whenever he found an opportunity, he continued reciting the Vedas. Many people began to be impressed by his style and pronunciation.

Krishna proved his competence in various religious rituals, including weddings, Bratabandha, Nwaran and puja. Through his religious ceremonies, he promotes the message that all people are equal and seeks to challenge caste discrimination. For him, this is not merely a means of personal fulfilment but also a campaign to convey the message that all people are equal and that, if God exists, God loves everyone without discrimination. He wants to use religious rituals not merely as religious traditions but also as a means of campaigning against discrimination.

Impressed by his message and graceful style, members of the community now actively seek him out and invite him to conduct religious ceremonies.

Government service and social campaign

Krishna Bahadur Damai is no longer limited to performing religious rituals. This is part of his knowledge and social campaign. His main profession is government service. He works as a sixth-level officer as an inclusive education facilitator in the Education Section of Dhangadhi Sub-Metropolitan City.

The sub-metropolitan city assigned him the responsibility after assessing his educational qualifications and social struggles. Having gained confidence through education himself, Krishna Bahadur considers education the most powerful tool for transforming society. He believes higher education should be made accessible, particularly to children from Dalit, disadvantaged and marginalised communities.

Dream for the future

While pursuing his government career alongside his religious work, Krishna Bahadur wants young people from the Dalit community to study not only science, technology and economics but also Sanskrit and religious rituals. He dreams of establishing a “Dalit Karmakanda School” in his village.

Speaking about his plans, he says, “Society will not change just because I put tika on people at a temple. I want to create thousands of Krishnas who will ensure that the doors of temples remain open to everyone forever.”

Krishna Bahadur’s knowledge and dedication have challenged the centuries-old tradition of determining who can become a priest based on caste. His rebellion is not against any individual but against the social practice that creates divisions between people.

Today, Krishna Bahadur Damai is no longer simply an individual. He has emerged as a cultural activist working to end caste discrimination in Nepali society.

title.rendered: Bangladeshi national arrested with 150g gold concealed in stomach

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

A Bangladeshi national has been arrested at Tribhuvan International Airport after allegedly concealing gold inside his stomach.

The arrested man has been identified as Mohammad Russel Hawaldar. He was arrested by the Tribhuvan International Airport Security Police Office. He had arrived in Kathmandu on Flydubai flight FZ1133 on August 16 and was taken into custody by plainclothes police on suspicion.

He subsequently told police that he had concealed 150 grams of gold inside his stomach. A medical examination at Kathmandu Medical College in Sinamangal confirmed the presence of the gold. The gold remained inside his stomach even after he used the toilet.

According to SP Raj Kumar Silwal, he was admitted to the hospital and the gold was eventually recovered after five days through a bowel movement.

He was handed over to the customs office along with two capsule-shaped pieces of gold.

title.rendered: Nepal A lose by eight wickets to NT Strike in Top End T20 opener

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Nepal A have lost their opening match of the Top End T20 Series in Australia, going down to Northern Territory (NT) Strike by eight wickets in Darwin on Friday.

Chasing a target of 123 runs set by Nepal, NT Strike reached 126 for two in 15 overs at the DXC Arena. The match was the opening fixture of Nepal’s campaign in the tournament.

Douwtjie Hoogenboezem top-scored for NT Strike with an unbeaten 40 off 37 balls, while Jordan Silk remained unbeaten on 42. Pawan Sarraf took both wickets for Nepal.

Batting first after losing the toss, Nepal A scored 122 runs for the loss of eight wickets in their allotted 20 overs.

Pawan Sarraf was Nepal’s top scorer with 41 runs off 49 balls. Lokesh Bam contributed 16 runs, while Narayan Joshi scored 15.

For NT Strike, one of their bowlers took three wickets for 19 runs in four overs. Tom Menzies, Sam Barker, William Blair and D’Arcy Short took one wicket each.

Nepal will play their second match against Bangladesh High Performance on Saturday. The fixture is scheduled for Darwin as part of the Top End T20 Series.

title.rendered: Supreme Court holds off on registering petition against NC general convention

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The Supreme Court has decided to conduct further study of a petition seeking to halt the Nepali Congress’s 15th general convention scheduled for October.

The petition was taken to the Supreme Court by Nepali Congress leader Deepak Khadka and advocate Shravan Kumar Shrestha on behalf of former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba and former vice-president Purna Bahadur Khadka.

They had sought an immediate halt to all preparations and procedures related to the 15th general convention.

However, the petition has not yet been registered at the Supreme Court, according to a Nepali Congress leader.

The Supreme Court administration informed the petitioners that further study was required before the petition could be registered, the leader said.

The group had earlier filed an appeal at the Supreme Court challenging the leadership of Gagan Thapa, who was elected through the party’s special general convention. The Supreme Court has already ordered a fresh hearing in that case.

The latest petition was filed after the party announced the general convention schedule, which the group claims was made unilaterally.

The Nepali Congress has scheduled its 15th general convention for October 2-5.

title.rendered: Tribhuvan University budget held up as key appointments remain pending

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Delays in appointing rectors, registrars and Senate members have affected the approval of budgets and policy programmes at several public universities, leaving some institutions to operate on advance expenditure from the previous fiscal year.

At Tribhuvan University (TU), the new fiscal year has already begun, but its budget and annual policy and programmes have not yet been approved.

The university celebrated its annual day on July 23, but the Senate meeting could not be held due to the absence of newly appointed officials and Senate members.

“The registrar and rector have not been appointed. The budget is presented by the registrar, and the Senate has to approve it. Since the new appointments have not been made, the Senate meeting could not be held,” a Tribhuvan University central office employee said.

Tribhuvan University has been operating through advance expenditure since the beginning of the new fiscal year.

The delay has also affected the graduation process for thousands of students. According to TU, the graduation list of more than 90,000 students needs to be approved. The Examination Control Office has already prepared the list, but it cannot be endorsed until the Senate meets.

A Tribhuvan University professor said the Senate cannot convene without the required number of members.

“At least 50 percent of the members are required to hold the Senate meeting. But the senators have not been appointed. Without senators, the meeting cannot take place, and without the Senate, the university cannot function properly,” the professor said.

Tribhuvan University spokesperson Nabindra Bhandari, however, said preparations were underway to convene the Senate.

“Regular work is continuing. Preparations are being made to hold the Senate meeting,” he said.

The government appointed Tribhuvan University Vice-Chancellor Bhola Thapa on July 3 after university office-bearers were removed through an ordinance. However, nearly one and a half months after his appointment, the university is yet to get a full team of officials.

According to university officials, Vice-Chancellor Thapa has recommended names for rector and registrar, and the recommendations have been sent to the Office of the Prime Minister.

“The names have been recommended. We were told that the appointments would be made this week,” a Tribhuvan University official said.

Sources said the appointments have been delayed after disagreements emerged over the recommended names.

At present, Dean of the Faculty of Science and Technology Prof Dr Shankar Khanal is serving as acting rector, while Dean of the Faculty of Management Mahananda Chalise is serving as acting registrar.

The problem is not limited to Tribhuvan University. Several other universities are also functioning without permanent registrars, including Pokhara University, Purbanchal University, Mid-Western University, Agriculture and Forestry University, Nepal Sanskrit University and Far-Western University.

At Pokhara University, Vice-Chancellor Devendra Adhikari said the appointment process was underway.

“The names have been recommended and we have been told that the appointments will be made this week. The executive body has to make recommendations, while the Chancellor appoints the Senate members from different categories. Only after that can the Senate be convened,” he said.

Pokhara University is currently operating on last year’s budget. According to Adhikari, the university can spend up to 33 percent of the previous year’s budget under the existing arrangement.

Far-Western University, meanwhile, has already approved its budget through an acting registrar.

“We have an acting registrar at present. The process for a new appointment is underway and the recommendation has already been sent,” Vice-Chancellor Kishan Dutta Bhatta said.

Rajर्षि Janak University has also been affected by the absence of a registrar. Its budget has not yet been approved.

“The budget is stuck because there is no registrar. A name has been recommended, and once the appointment is made, the Senate will meet and approve the budget,” Vice-Chancellor Shyam Narayan Labh said.

Agriculture and Forestry University has approved its budget through its acting registrar. The university, however, has not yet recommended a candidate for the permanent position.

“We have not recommended a new registrar. Work has not stopped here, and the budget was approved by the end of June,” Vice-Chancellor Rishiram Kattel said.

Kathmandu University has also approved its budget. The budget was endorsed during a Senate meeting held in June for preparations for the university’s convocation. However, the university is yet to appoint a new registrar.

Meanwhile, Lumbini Buddhist University and Nepal Open University are still awaiting the appointment of vice-chancellors.

Most of the universities are currently relying on acting rectors and registrars to run their day-to-day affairs.

Professors and officials at the affected universities say the prolonged vacancies are beginning to hamper important institutional and long-term decisions.

Officials at the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology said recommendations made by university vice-chancellors for rector and registrar appointments have already reached the Office of the Prime Minister.

“The names are probably being studied at the Prime Minister’s Office. The rector and registrar are appointed by the Chancellor,” a ministry official said.

With appointments and Senate formation still pending at several universities, institutions face continued uncertainty over their budgets, policy decisions and other statutory processes at the start of the new fiscal year.

content.rendered:
Bajura, August 21

A total of 115 individuals from 14 disaster-prone households in Bajura district were shifted to safe areas as a landslide buried two houses at Katigaun in Gaumul Rural Municipality in the district.

The houses of Purnimal Bohara and Budi Bohara were destroyed in the Katigaun landslide that occurred on Thursday afternoon following heavy rain, according to District Police Office spokesperson Naresh Bahadur Shahi.
