title.rendered: Finance Ministry ready to facilitate regulated cannabis farming: Minister Wagle

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle has said the Ministry of Finance is ready to facilitate cannabis cultivation if it is regulated in accordance with the law.

Wagle made the statement during a question-and-answer session in the National Assembly on Friday.

National Assembly member Bishnukumari Sapkota had asked about the government’s plans for cannabis cultivation, noting that many countries have legalised cannabis and are using the plant for various purposes.

Responding to the question, Wagle said cannabis production and marketing was not simply a matter of income, employment and potential government revenue, but also involved controlled use for medicinal and narcotic purposes.

He said the matter required expert study and appropriate legislation.

“If the matter is studied and determined by relevant experts and is regulated in accordance with the law, the Ministry of Finance will be ready to facilitate it,” Wagle said.

The debate over legalising cannabis cultivation in Nepal has increasingly focused on its potential economic benefits, medicinal uses and the possibility of increasing farmers’ incomes.

Cannabis cultivation has been prohibited in Nepal under the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act. However, calls for legalising cultivation for medicinal and industrial purposes have increased in recent years.

Sapkota said different parts of the cannabis plant are considered useful in both Ayurvedic and modern medicine.

“Valuable medicines can be produced from it. Fibre from cannabis can also be used to make clothes, paper and ropes,” she said.

In a supplementary question, Sapkota recalled that although the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act 2033 BS prohibits cannabis cultivation, it contains provisions related to medicinal production. She also pointed out that Gandaki Province has already introduced legislation related to cannabis and asked when the federal government would enact a similar law.

Wagle said several Western and developed countries were also moving towards legalising cannabis for medicinal purposes.

“Legalisation for medicinal purposes is reasonable. Western and developed countries, under whose pressure we criminalised it here decades ago, are now moving towards greater openness,” he said. “In this context, we should also move forward positively on this issue.”

Wagle clarified that cannabis cultivation had not been specifically addressed in the current fiscal year’s budget.

He also said the issue primarily falls under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Home Affairs.

According to Wagle, the Finance Ministry would take a positive approach if further study and consultation with the Home Ministry leads to a decision to establish a legal framework for regulated cannabis cultivation.

He also expressed commitment to discuss the matter with the Home Ministry and work towards a conclusion on the issue.

title.rendered: Minister Shrestha emphasises preparedness to avert possible impacts of El Niño

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, August 21

Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, has highlighted the need to take prompt actions with preparedness in the fields of water, food, irrigation and disaster resilience. In his address at the inaugural ceremony of the national workshop ‘Super El Niño and Climate Risk: Impacts on Water, Food, Energy, and Disaster Resilience’ today, he stressed the urgency to take strides while keeping the potential impacts of Super El Niño into consideration.

The workshop was organised in Lalitpur by the Secretariat of the Water and Energy Commission and the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology. Minister Shrestha noted that the recent forecasts regarding El Niño indicate an increased likelihood of potential impacts on rainfall, temperature, hydropower production, irrigation, and food production in Nepal, so it has to be taken seriously.

“As Kulekhani-1 is only one seasonal reservoir project in the 4,120 MW electricity system currently operational in Nepal, there is therefore a need to increase storage capacity in the energy sector,” the minister stated. Nepal has made significant progress in energy trade. Although dependence on energy imports increases in dry seasons, developing reservoir projects and storage capacity is necessary for energy security, he argued.

Regarding irrigation, most projects are based on small and medium rivers, so there is an issue of insufficient water during the dry season. A long spell of drought has been impacting the country’s agricultural production. It now seems urgent to make agriculture climate-resilient.

In this connection, the ministry has already prepared the Tarai-Madhesh Drought Resilience Strategy. With the participation of the Department of Water and Meteorology, Department of Water Resources and Irrigation, Department of Drinking Water and Sewerage Management, Nepal Electricity Authority, and Department of Electricity Development, the ministry has set up a ‘Water-Energy Drought Monitoring’ mechanism to publish monthly information from October to March. The workshop offered a discussion on the possible impacts of El Niño on water, food, energy, and disaster resilience and measures for risk reduction.

title.rendered: Minister Timilsina, Kathmandu acting mayor discuss Bancharedanda waste management

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Nuwakot-1 lawmaker and Information and Communications Minister Dr Bikram Timilsina has discussed problems at the Bancharedanda landfill site, complaints from local residents and ongoing waste management efforts with Kathmandu Metropolitan City acting mayor Sunita Dangol.

During the meeting held at the Ministry of Communications, Timilsina said the federal government and Kathmandu Metropolitan City should allocate the necessary budget to upgrade and blacktop the road leading to the Bancharedanda landfill site.

Local residents in the Bancharedanda area have long complained about the poor condition of the road leading to the landfill, foul odours from the waste, uncovered waste-carrying vehicles, garbage falling from vehicles onto the road and vehicles returning to the Kathmandu Valley without being properly cleaned after dumping waste.

Residents have also complained that waste is not being adequately covered with soil after disposal at the landfill.

Timilsina held discussions with the acting mayor after receiving numerous complaints from residents in his constituency.

“I have received many complaints that locals are suffering because roads in some areas have not been blacktopped. People living around the road leading to the waste disposal site are genuinely suffering. There are complaints about foul odours and an increase in various infections,” he said.

He stressed the need for effective coordination among the federal, provincial and local governments to address problems at Banchare Danda.

Timilsina also said proper and timely soil capping of disposed waste was essential to control the spread of foul odours.

During the meeting, acting mayor Dangol said that although waste from Kathmandu Metropolitan City and other local governments in the valley is also transported to Banchare Danda, Kathmandu Metropolitan City has been bearing most of the financial burden of waste management.

“All municipalities had committed to sharing the cost of waste management. However, most of the expenses so far have been borne by Kathmandu Metropolitan City alone,” Dangol said. “If other municipalities also contribute financially, it will be easier to address the problems faced by local residents.”

Dangol said the metropolitan city has also been unable to acquire the land required for waste collection points and facilities to separate biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste.

The metropolitan city has adopted a decentralised waste management model and divided the city into seven waste clusters. It plans to promote the reuse and recycling of dry waste, but implementation has been delayed due to difficulties in acquiring the required land and completing other procedures, she said.

Although waste from 20 other local governments, in addition to Kathmandu Metropolitan City, is also transported to Banchare Danda, those local governments have not yet been effectively involved in sharing responsibility for waste management.

At present, Kathmandu Metropolitan City bears the primary operational, management and financial burden of the Banchare Danda landfill site.

The meeting also discussed long-term measures to improve waste management, including reducing the amount of waste reaching the landfill, segregating waste at source, and improving waste collection and transportation systems.

The Banchare Danda landfill site was constructed after the government acquired 1,792 ropanis of land. Waste disposal at the site began on May 24, 2022.

The landfill site is located along the border of Kakani Rural Municipality-2 in Nuwakot and Dhunibesi Municipality-1 in Dhading.

title.rendered: PM Balen Shah’s secretariat keeps his trips outside Kathmandu under wraps

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Prime Minister Balen Shah’s secretariat has been making efforts to keep details of his visits outside Kathmandu away from public attention.

The secretariat has generally not issued official information about the places Prime Minister Shah visits outside the capital or the people he meets during such trips.

Even after reports emerged that Shah would travel to Mustang via Pokhara, his secretariat did not provide information about his stay in Pokhara or his schedule there.

Shah left Kathmandu for Pokhara by road on Friday morning. The identities of the people accompanying him have also not been made public.

When contacted for confirmation about the prime minister travelling to Pokhara by road, a member of his secretariat told Onlinekhabar that the information could not be disclosed for security reasons.

“It is not possible to say whether the prime minister travelled to Pokhara by road or air due to security reasons,” the official said.

However, despite citing security concerns, a video showing a convoy of vehicles carrying the prime minister and security personnel was seen in Dhading on Friday.

The prime minister’s visit to Pokhara and Mustang had not been formally communicated even to the chief district officers of the two districts.

Mustang Chief District Officer Ajita Sharma said she learned about the prime minister’s planned visit through the media.

“We have been hearing since yesterday that the prime minister is coming to Mustang, but no formal information or programme schedule has reached us,” Sharma said.

Kaski Chief District Officer Kuman Singh Gurung also said he had not received any formal information, despite the place where Shah will stay in Pokhara having already been decided.

“We are also learning about it through the media. No formal information has arrived. Since the prime minister himself is coming, information will certainly come,” Gurung said. “We have learned that he is coming by road. We expect to receive other information as well.”

Annapurna Eco Village in Dhital Astam of Machhapuchchhre Rural Municipality, Kaski, has reportedly been booked for Shah’s stay. According to sources, all rooms at the resort have been booked.

However, security agencies said they had not yet received formal information about the prime minister’s visit.

The prime minister’s secretariat had similarly withheld information about his accommodation during his three-day stay in Chitwan during the RSP’s first general convention. Shah stayed at Lattauli Century Resort in Shaktikhor, Kalika Municipality-9, where 16 rooms were reportedly booked.

In the past, information about prime ministers’ visits was routinely shared with the press and the public.

However, the Prime Minister’s Office and the secretariat have increasingly withheld information about visits that would ordinarily fall within the scope of public information, including details about their purpose and schedules.

title.rendered: Commercial Bank CEOs eligible for NRB governor

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Chief executive officers (CEOs) of commercial banks will now be eligible to become governors of Nepal Rastra Bank, after the Finance Committee of the House of Representatives decided to open the path for them on Friday.

The committee is currently discussing the Nepal Rastra Bank Bill, 2083, registered by the government in Parliament. The government’s proposed bill had sought to remove the provision allowing commercial bank CEOs to become governors. Under the existing Nepal Rastra Bank Act, 2058, however, a person who has served as a commercial bank CEO is eligible to become governor.

The Finance Committee has been holding continuous discussions on the Nepal Rastra Bank Bill, 2083. During Friday’s discussion on the qualifications for governor, the committee decided to add provisions allowing commercial bank CEOs and individuals who have worked for international expert institutions to become eligible for the post.

Committee Chairperson Dr Krishna Hari Budhathoki said the committee had also introduced a provision requiring commercial bank CEOs to complete a two-year cooling-off period after leaving their posts before becoming eligible for appointment as governor.

“There was extensive discussion on the qualifications for governor, and they have largely been retained as they are,” Budhathoki said. “We have decided that commercial bank CEOs, who were not included in the bill, will also be eligible to become governor, subject to a two-year cooling-off period.”

He said Friday’s committee meeting also decided to include in the bill a provision allowing individuals who have worked at international expert financial institutions to become eligible for the post of governor.

The bill states that a person with at least a master’s degree from a recognised university in economics, monetary affairs, banking, finance, statistics or accounting, public administration, commerce, management or commercial law, and at least 10 years of experience at the gazetted special class level of the Nepal government, as an executive director of a bank, university professor, executive-level position at an international financial institution or an equivalent position, will be eligible to become governor.

The committee has added that a person who has served as a commercial bank CEO and completed two years since leaving the position will also be eligible for the post.

Under the existing provision, a person with at least a master’s degree in economics, monetary affairs, banking, finance, commerce, management, public administration, statistics, mathematics or law, along with professional experience in the fields of economics, monetary affairs, banking, finance or commercial law, can become governor.

Regarding work experience, the existing provision recognises experience at the gazetted special class level of the Nepal government or the bank, as a university professor, as the chief executive of a Class A commercial bank or financial institution, at the executive level of an international organisation or an equivalent position, or a position higher in rank or status.

Kalathoki, who sustained serious injuries in the incident, was taken to the Civil Service Hospital in Minbhawan for treatment. He was declared dead by doctors during treatment after suffering severe injuries to his head and neck, according to police.

Patel had fled following the incident. He was arrested from Bhaise in Makwanpur in coordination with the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office, Teku.

SSP Santosh Khadka of the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office said Patel is being brought to Kathmandu.

Further investigation into the incident is underway, police said.

The banking sector fell 0.04 percent, development banks 0.54 percent, finance 0.43 percent, hotels and tourism 0.10 percent, hydropower 0.66 percent, investment 0.19 percent, life insurance 0.37 percent, manufacturing and processing 0.46 percent, microfinance 0.44 percent, non-life insurance 0.04 percent and trading 0.68 percent.

Commercial banks recorded transactions worth Rs 330 million, while the manufacturing and processing sector saw turnover of Rs 420 million.

title.rendered: Meghraj Budhathoki: Taking Nepali wool products to the world

content.rendered:
Hundreds of hands work simultaneously inside a wool-processing factory in Dhobighat, Lalitpur. Some workers are shaping wool, others are making flowers, toys and decorative items. There is no deafening noise from machines. Here, the only tools for creation are hands, skill and patience.

These handmade products adorn homes in more than 40 countries around the world, including the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Japan and the Netherlands. Nepali handicrafts embody not only Nepal’s originality but also the labour, dreams and dignity of thousands of Nepalis.

Thirty-four-year-old Meghraj Budhathoki is the chairperson and chief executive officer of Om Sairam Felt Product Pvt. Ltd. Currently residing in Kirtipur, Meghraj’s business has gained recognition not only in Nepal but also internationally.

What began in a small room has now grown into one of Nepal’s leading handicraft export businesses under his leadership. The company has been listed among the country’s top handicraft exporters for five consecutive years and has now become the country’s largest handicraft exporter.

However, Meghraj prefers to define his identity not by the size of his business but by the employment it provides. “My greatest asset is not the company; it is my team,” he says.

Born in 2048 BS in Mayankhu village of Udayapur, Meghraj spent his childhood there. When he was in Grade 3, his family moved to Sarlahi. After completing his SLC (School Leaving Certificate, now SEE), he came to Kathmandu and began studying at Janamaitri Campus.

While studying at the plus-two level, most of Meghraj’s friends were busy getting passports and visiting consultancies, preparing to go abroad. But Meghraj’s mind was drawn elsewhere. His elder brother worked as a technician in a handicraft industry. While visiting various factories and workshops with his brother, he saw women weaving a variety of woollen products by hand. Having been interested in drawing and creative activities since childhood, he was fascinated by what he saw.

Around 2065/66 BS, he embarked on the risky journey of handicraft production with a team of three or four people, a small investment and a small flat. In the early days, he himself would sit on the floor and make woollen products.

At the time, they did not have their own brand. They made products and supplied them to large exporters. They also handled the packaging themselves. From delivering the goods to maintaining accounts, they had to shoulder every responsibility. Their capital was small and their experience limited, but their dream was big. “We kept working and kept learning. Our own factory became our university,” he says.

The international door opened by the earthquake

Soon after the devastating earthquake of 2015, Meghraj opened a small showroom in Thamel. A British customer who visited the showroom placed a small order. After Meghraj fulfilled the order honestly and on time, the customer’s trust grew, and the orders began to increase.

The international relationship that began with that customer has continued to expand, and today the company’s products are reaching more than 40 countries around the world.

Sheep wool brought from New Zealand is transformed into artistic products by the hands of Nepali women at the Lalitpur factory and exported to developed countries such as the United Kingdom, the United States, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan. Through this process, Meghraj’s business has continued to expand.

A source of livelihood for a thousand women

Meghraj’s factory is not merely a place for making profits. At present, up to 1,500 workers are employed on a regular or need-based basis, more than 1,000 of whom are women.

Women from marginalised communities and disadvantaged backgrounds, in particular, are learning skills here and earning an income with dignity. Even during major crises such as COVID-19, the blockade, the earthquake and floods, he did not shut down the factory or allow his workers to lose their livelihoods.

He has also provided employment at his factory to 15–20 young people who were cheated while seeking foreign employment or who returned home due to health problems.

Many of the women working with him had never previously ventured outside their homes for work. Now, many have educated their children with their own earnings, some have built houses, while others have reduced their financial dependence on husbands working abroad.

When he stopped his wife from going abroad

It is common for disagreements to arise when businesspeople struggle to find time for their families. In Meghraj’s case, however, his entire family is devoted to the same business.

He married Anuja, who is from Kathmandu, in 2068 BS. At the time, going abroad was a popular choice among young people. After getting married, Anuja also thought, “Most people are getting married and going abroad. Should I take the IELTS and go abroad too?”

But Meghraj persuaded her, saying, “Instead of going to another country to do the same work, let’s do it here in our own country. If we have a platform here, let’s not look for another one elsewhere.”

Anuja did not reject her husband’s request. Instead, she has been working alongside him for the past 15 years. Not only Anuja but other members of Meghraj’s family are also involved in the business.

Branding and quality audits

At a time when cheap, machine-made plastic products are dominating the market, Meghraj sees an even brighter future for Nepali handmade products. As environmental awareness grows around the world, foreign consumers are choosing organic and natural products made from 100 per cent wool, even if they are more expensive.

To meet international standards, Om Sairam Felt Product does not compromise on quality. The company has a separate quality-control unit. According to Meghraj, the company has successfully passed ISO testing and stringent international audits related to social responsibility every year. Foreign customers now visit the factory directly. The company also connects with customers through its website and international trade fairs.

However, the handicraft industry is run by people, not machines. It takes years to train workers in the required skills. But with the increasing trend of people going abroad, retaining skilled workers has become difficult. “The workers we spend years training leave for foreign countries. Then we have to train new people all over again,” he complains.

Challenges and state neglect

Running a business is not without challenges. In the past four or five months alone, the price of raw materials, wool, has nearly doubled due to the policies of the New Zealand government and the war in the Middle East, while transportation costs have risen sharply.

Ironically, there is no effective state policy to encourage export-oriented industries. The government even levies VAT on raw materials imported by industries that export 100 per cent of their products, while the refund process is highly cumbersome. The export incentive grants promised by the government have also been withheld. “Nepal’s indigenous sheep produce coarse wool, so it is not suitable for felt. But if the government and businesses work together to crossbreed improved sheep breeds and produce wool in Nepal, we can become self-sufficient in raw materials as well,” Meghraj says.

He says export-oriented industries need clear policies, tax incentives, measures to reduce energy costs and a long-term plan to produce quality wool within Nepal. “We have the market and the skills. What we lack is policy and facilitation.”

Creating jobs for Nepali youth in Nepal

Meghraj considers himself more of a social entrepreneur than a successful businessman. He arranges industrial visits for school students, provides free consultations to new entrepreneurs and conducts skills training at his company. He has also arranged for trainees to receive remuneration from their very first day of training.

His business journey, which began with a team of three or four people, has now reached the global market. But for Meghraj, this is not the final destination. He continues to pursue his dream of establishing Nepali handicrafts as a world-renowned identity.

title.rendered: Why does Nepal send so many officials to international sporting events?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

When Nepal sent its delegation to the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, three years ago, 253 athletes competed in 29 sports. Nepal won two medals at the Games.

But the country’s delegation was far larger than its contingent of athletes. Around 400 people, including athletes, coaches and officials, travelled to Hangzhou. That meant roughly 150 more officials and support staff than athletes were part of the delegation.

This is not an isolated example.

A similar pattern was seen at the 33rd Summer Olympics in Paris in 2024. Nepal sent just seven athletes to the Games, but more than three times that number of coaches and officials — 22 additional people — travelled to Paris. Nepal returned from the Paris Olympics without a medal.

The size of the delegation drew criticism at the time, particularly after then National Sports Council member-secretary Tanka Lal Ghising and then Sports Minister Tejulal Chaudhary travelled to Paris as observers, even though a badminton coach was unable to participate.

The same issue had surfaced at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. Nepal’s 26-member delegation included only five athletes and four coaches. The remaining members were officials and other representatives.

These are only a few examples. At major international events such as the Olympics, Asian Games and South Asian Games, Nepal has repeatedly faced criticism for sending more officials than athletes.

Travelling abroad in the name of sporting events and receiving allowances in the process is not a new practice in Nepali sports. Critics say priority is often given to the participation of officials rather than to the training, preparation and management needs of athletes.

The issue became particularly contentious ahead of the Paris Olympics, when the Ministry of Youth and Sports announced that it would not bear the expenses of people travelling to Paris who were neither athletes nor coaches.

Officials and employees of sports associations and the National Sports Council frequently travel abroad alongside athletes and coaches for international competitions. In some cases, people with no direct connection to the sport have also travelled as officials.

“The officials who travel in large numbers have little to do apart from sightseeing. When athletes need help, there is often no one to assist them. They go there mainly to watch the games and travel,” a former athlete said.

The government generally covers the airfare, accommodation, food and daily allowances of officials attending international competitions. Sending large numbers of officials to a single event therefore adds to the financial burden on the sports sector.

A smaller delegation for the 20th Asian Games

The 20th Asian Games are scheduled for October, raising questions over whether Nepal will once again send a large contingent of officials or limit the delegation to people directly involved in the competition.

The government has said it will not send unrelated individuals to this year’s Asian Games.

The National Sports Council has finalised the participation of 137 athletes in 22 sports. According to NSC member-secretary Ram Charitra Mehta, Nepal will send a total delegation of 218 people, including the athletes.

The number of athletes has also been reduced compared to the 19th Asian Games.

According to the NSC, the delegation will include 32 coaches, 18 managers, 11 headquarters officials, six members of the medical team, four journalists and five representatives from the Nepal Olympic Committee.

The delegation will also include one sports technical official, one chef de mission, one deputy chef de mission and one representative from the Ministry of Youth and Sports. Their names have not been disclosed.

Mehta said only personnel with necessary responsibilities would be sent to the Asian Games.

“Only people whose work is required will go. They will return as soon as their work is completed. No one is going there for sightseeing,” he said.

He said the delegation had been prepared with the aim of making the best use of limited resources.

The NSC has maintained that athletes and the coaches, managers, medical personnel and technical staff required for their participation have been prioritised.

Former NSC member-secretary Keshav Raj Bista, however, says sending unrelated people to international competitions is inappropriate.

“When many board members go and the Olympic Committee takes a large number of people, sometimes five to 10 people appear to be unnecessary,” he said. “Let’s see what happens this time. But sending people for sightseeing or simply to fulfil their wishes is not right.”

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The state-owned Dairy Development Corporation (DDC) has begun exporting its “DDC Ghee” to countries in the Middle East.

The formal launch of the export began on Friday with the shipment of 500kg of ghee to Dubai on a Nepal Airlines flight. DDC has signed a commercial agreement with private company Rato Ra Chandra Surya International Pvt. Ltd. to export ghee.

DDC General Manager Dr Sharan Pandey said the agreement covers the export of DDC ghee to all countries in the Middle East.

“We started today by sending 500kg of ghee to Dubai,” General Manager Pandey told Onlinekhabar. “We have already signed an agreement to export 50,000kg (50 tonnes) annually.”

Pandey said the agreement is limited to 50 tonnes in the first year due to the current low production of ghee, adding that export volumes will be increased as production rises.

The exports can also be made weekly depending on demand. DDC said it is accelerating efforts to expand its market beyond the Middle East.

According to General Manager Pandey, ghee exports to countries including Japan and South Korea will begin soon.

“We have just started, and we will gradually expand. For that, we also need sufficient raw materials,” he said. “From next Kartik, our products will also reach Japan, South Korea and Tibet in China.”

title.rendered: RSP Central Committee meeting to discuss candidate selection, party organisation (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Leaders of the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) have arrived at Ghanti Ghar in Banasthali to attend the party’s Central Committee meeting.

Party Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane and other leaders have reached the party’s central office, where the meeting is scheduled to begin shortly.

Other Central Committee members are also arriving at Ghanti Ghar.

According to General Secretary Bipin Kumar Acharya, the meeting’s agenda includes discussions on party documents, organisational management and nominations, plans, programmes and campaigns.

Under party documents, the meeting will discuss approving the Candidate Selection Framework 2083 for the local elections and preparing a document on the right to recall.

Under organisational management and nominations, the agenda includes nominating Central Committee members, office-bearers, Secretariat members, and departmental heads, as well as members of the Central Candidate Selection Committee for the local elections.

Under plans, programmes and campaigns, the meeting will discuss conducting orientation and training programmes on the candidate selection framework at the local level under the leadership of the Central Committee and members of the House of Representatives. It will also discuss publishing Swatantra, a monthly digital magazine as the party’s official publication.

title.rendered: Circular sent to local levels to ensure availability of free medicines

content.rendered:
The government has issued a directive to ensure the availability of free medicines and related supplies at health institutions at the local levels as part of basic health services. The Ministry of Health and Food Safety sent the circular to all local levels through the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration.

The ministry has shared with local levels a list of medicines and medical supplies needed to run basic health services, along with details on managing them. It said the move aims to ensure health institutions at the local levels distribute medicines free of charge and maintain their availability throughout the year, and has asked local levels to manage the supplies according to their responsibilities as outlined in the attached list.

The circular includes a detailed list of medicines and other medical supplies required for basic health services. Local levels have been asked to ensure the availability, storage, and free distribution of the necessary medicines at health institutions under their jurisdiction.

title.rendered: Parbat Kumar Karki appointed executive director of Citizen Investment Fund

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The government has appointed Parbat Kumar Karki as executive director of the Citizen Investment Fund. Karki, a permanent resident of Udayapur, was appointed by the Cabinet meeting of Bhadau 3 under Section 42(1) of the Citizen Investment Fund Act, 2047.

A retired executive director of Nepal Rastra Bank, Karki previously served as the fund’s executive director as well, having been selected for the post through open competition on January 17, 2024. He also has experience as CEO of Nepal Gramin Bikas Bank and Kisan Laghubitta Bittiya Sanstha.

Karki holds a Master of Banking and Finance (MBF) from Griffith University in Australia and a master’s degree in management from Tribhuvan University. He has also received international training in central banking, financial stability, and financial market analysis.

title.rendered: Karki and Jha win first Himalayan Open Golf titles

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Rijul Karki became the overall gross champion and Abhi Jha the overall net champion at the first-ever Himalayan Open golf tournament, held at Red Hawk Ridge Golf Course in Colorado, USA.

Held on August 8 and 9, the tournament drew more than 100 golfers from Nepal and the diaspora across the Himalayan region. Organisers said registration for the inaugural event, aimed at connecting the Nepali and Himalayan community through golf, had to close a month early due to demand.

Launched on the initiative of Nepali golfers based in Denver, the Himalayan Open brought together both experienced players and a younger generation, including Rijul Karki, Kashyap Raimajhi, Jaibir Pandey, and Suchit Sharma. On the women’s side, Nepal’s top-ranked amateur golfer Pratima Sherpa competed alongside Rihana Bhandari, Samara Pandey, and Shreya Sharma.

The two-day event featured competition in both gross and net categories, with a total prize purse of $41,200. Karki claimed the gross title with the best overall score, while Jha, who performed best relative to handicap, was crowned net champion.

Organisers plan to make the Himalayan Open an annual event, with future editions rotating through different US cities to draw more players. They also aim to hold the 2028 edition in Nepal itself, with a long-term goal of creating opportunities for young Nepali golfers as the sport develops.

She started the channel a decade ago with short dance and riding videos. In recent times, her moto-vlogs have won over viewers, particularly her videos from destinations like Manali, Nubra Valley, and Ladakh in India.

Surakshya, who hails from Myagdi, is married to fellow moto-vlogger Bibidh Jung Thapa, who has close to 1.6 million YouTube followers of his own.

title.rendered: RSP cadre confronts Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle over border tax crackdown

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

A Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) cadres from the Madhesh region has confronted Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle over the government’s increased enforcement of taxes on goods brought into Nepal from India.

The criticism came during a public interaction programme titled “Citizens, Policy and Leadership” held on Thursday evening, where ministers have been engaging directly with citizens.

A participant from Madhesh questioned Wagle over the government’s policy of tightening checks on Nepali citizens returning from India after shopping.

“You have formulated an economic policy. Is this Nepal’s policy or America’s? Is this the policy of the Himalayas, hills and Madhesh, or America’s?” the participant asked Wagle.

He claimed that the government’s crackdown at the border was making it difficult for the RSP to expand its organisation in the 22 districts bordering India.

“Why is it not possible? Because you have imposed taxes on everything. There is an open border across 22 districts, and we have a roti-beti relationship with India,” he said.

The participant said around 400,000 to 500,000 people cross the Nepal-India border every day from the border districts.

RSP General Secretary Bipin Acharya and Joint General Secretary Asim Shah were also present at the interaction.

The participant accused police and administrative authorities of harassing people in the border areas over small quantities of goods.

“People living along the border are being beaten by the police and administration even for bringing one kilogram of sugar. This is because of your policy,” he told the finance minister.

He also accused Wagle of becoming a finance minister focused only on Kathmandu and urged him to formulate policies addressing the needs of the hills, mountains and Madhesh alike.

The issue of harassment of Nepali citizens returning from India with small quantities of goods has also been raised by RSP leaders and lawmakers from the Madhesh.

Madhes lawmakers had raised the issue during a discussion chaired by RSP Chairperson Rabi Lamichhane with ministers and lawmakers.

Complaints have continued to emerge that police and administrative authorities are taking an impractical approach while enforcing tax provisions along the Nepal-India border.

The government has tightened checks in border areas as part of efforts to prevent tax evasion and regulate the movement of goods from India. However, the measures have drawn criticism from residents and political representatives in the border districts.

title.rendered: Nabin Nalbo’s ‘Temples, Nature and Pooches’ on display at Gallery Mcube

content.rendered:
Lalitpur, August 21

Artist Nabin Nalbo’s solo exhibition Temples, Nature and Pooches is on display at Gallery Mcube in Chakupat, began on August 7.

The exhibition, curated by Manish Lal Shrestha, features Nalbo’s latest body of work developed during his Mcube Young Artists Fellowship Residency 2025. It will remain on display until August 30.

The exhibition explores the relationship between heritage, spirituality, nature and everyday urban life through paintings inspired by the cultural landscape of Patan.

Nalbo’s works depict historic alleys, traditional houses, carved wooden windows, hidden shrines and sacred spaces, focusing on details of the city that often go unnoticed.

The exhibition also features street dogs observed by the artist in Patan’s neighbourhoods, presenting them as symbols of coexistence and belonging. Flowers and plants in the paintings represent resilience, growth and renewal, creating a dialogue between the natural and built environments.

The Mcube Young Artists Fellowship Residency is an extension of Gallery Mcube’s annual Young Artists Show. The fellowship provides selected emerging artists with an opportunity for research, experimentation and creative development through a dedicated residency.

title.rendered: Protest held in Kathmandu demanding justice for 3-year-old

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

A protest was held in Kathmandu today demanding justice for a three-year-old girl from Jitpur Simara Sub-Metropolitan City-1, Bara, who was allegedly raped and murdered.

Rights activists and the victim’s relatives staged the protest. Participants displayed placards.

Her family has also been staging protests in Bara, demanding justice. The Birgunj–Pathlaiya road section has remained blocked for the third consecutive day as her parents and other family members have been staging a sit-in on the road.

Although the administration reached an agreement with residents on Thursday night, the victim’s family has rejected the agreement, saying it was reached without their consent.

Her father, Manoj Chaudhary, has demanded that Home Minister Sudan Gurung and Law Minister Sobita Gautam personally come forward and commit to amending Nepal’s laws.

content.rendered:
The release date for actress Niruta Singh’s comeback film Saarthi has been set. The film will open nationwide on November 27.

This marks Niruta’s return to acting after seven years, with her last film, Dal Bhat Tarkari, having been released in 2019.

The film, directed by Kumar Gajurel, previously released its first look, stirring curiosity about the story. With the release date now announced, promotion is set to pick up pace.

Produced under the banner of Kimbhe Production and Dhiraj Film Infinity, with Tara Thapa as presenter, the film was shot in Gurja, a village in the northern Himalayan region of Myagdi.

The film reunites the pair from the once-hit film Darpan Chhaya, with Uttam Pradhan also starring. Other cast members include Mukunda Shrestha, Rajendra KC, Samrant Thapa, Giri Bishwakarma, Gayatri Joshi, Kalpana Thapa, Madan Thapa, Milan Khadka, Rashmi Gurung, Tulsi Rai, Asha Bishwakarma, Santosh Dhakal, Biplav Khadka, Sagar Kandel, Sudip Nepal, and Dhiren Karki.

Radip Shrestha and Pradip Rayamajhi are the investors, while Bek Bahadur Bishwakarma and Nabin Shrestha serve as executive producers.

title.rendered: RSP fully committed to federalism, says chief whip Burlakoti

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chief Whip Kabindra Burlakoti has said his party is fully committed to federalism and will move ahead with its full implementation.

Speaking at an interaction on “Federalism: Constitutional Amendment and Unbundling of Functions” on Friday, Burlakoti said the party had no compromise on federalism and democracy.

“We are fully committed to the Constitution, democracy and federalism. There is no compromise when it comes to democracy or federalism. We will move ahead with their full implementation,” he said.

The interaction was organised by the Federalism & Localization Centre.

Burlakoti also said the Constitution could be amended as circumstances and needs change, while stressing that democratic practices must also be strengthened.

He said any review of the Constitution should examine where democratic practices had fallen short and where the state had failed to deliver on the principles of public welfare.

“We need to strengthen these practices over time. I am personally and, as a party, we are committed to that,” he said.

Recalling his earlier involvement in campaigns for decentralisation of power, Burlakoti said political leaders across parties needed a better understanding of federalism and its implementation.

He said the contributions made by political parties to the Constitution and the federal democratic system should always be recognised.

“We were also part of this process,” he said.

Burlakoti recalled the 2006 People’s Movement and other movements, including the Madhes and Tharuhat movements, saying the achievements of those movements should be reflected in any constitutional amendment.

“I injured my leg during the 2006 movement, and my shoe was lost amid the rush,” he said, recalling his participation in the movement.

He said constitutional amendment could also incorporate new ideas and experiences that had emerged over time.

However, Burlakoti stressed that constitutional reform should be based on consensus and should not be treated as the agenda of any particular party or government.

“The Constitution concerns the entire nation. It concerns all forces within the country. The concerns of minorities must also be addressed, but they must also be acceptable to the majority,” he said.

He said discussions on federalism should take a broader perspective and focus on strengthening rights and autonomy at all three levels of government.

‘There is confusion over who does what’

Burlakoti said improvements were needed in the distribution of responsibilities among the federal, provincial and local governments.

He pointed to the confusion over which level of government should be responsible for development projects and other functions.

“Recently, what I have seen is that there is enormous confusion over who should do what in development and construction,” he said.

He said the problem was evident in the budget allocation of the previous fiscal year, with the federal, provincial and local governments spending money on projects in the same areas.

He questioned whether such duplication was consistent with the principles of federalism.

“We talk about federalism and brought federalism, but what is happening now is not even consistent with the decentralisation concept that existed before federalism,” he said.

Burlakoti said responsibilities should be clearly divided among the three levels of government.

“For example, the authority to remove a fallen tree should not remain with the federal government,” he said.

He acknowledged that necessary laws for implementing federalism had not yet been enacted and called for legislation to address the gaps.

Burlakoti also said lawmakers were ready to discuss reform proposals coming from local governments.

“If proposals for this kind of reform come from the local level, the chief whips and parliamentary leaders are here at the lawmaking level. We can sit together, discuss them and move them forward,” he said.

He said the RSP would approach the issue positively rather than through a partisan lens.

‘Local level should be strong, provincial level intelligent’

Burlakoti said Nepal’s federal structure should aim for strong local governments, capable provincial governments and a decisive federal government.

“The local level should be strong, the provincial level should be intelligent and the federal level should be decisive. Decisions at the federal level should be made properly,” he said.

With elections approaching, Burlakoti said reforms that can be implemented before the elections should not be delayed.

“We should not hold back the things that can be done before the elections. We should do what can be done. The longer we delay these issues, the longer the implementation will take,” he said.

He also urged political parties to play a role in resolving disputes rather than creating them.

He called on political leaders to take responsibility for resolving disagreements surrounding federalism and its implementation.

title.rendered: Deepal Nivo Q05 to arrive Nepal next week

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

MAW Vridhi AutoCorp is preparing to launch the all-new Deepal Nevo Q05 in Nepal next week. Established as the number-one SUV in its segment in China, the company claims the Q05 will offer Nepali buyers a “class above” experience through a combination of comfort, design, and technology.

The Q05 pairs a city-friendly exterior with a spacious, practical cabin. Its 2,735mm wheelbase gives generous rear legroom, while reclining rear seats add comfort and the 540-litre boot offers ample space for luggage and family travel gear.

Design is another highlight. The SUV was developed under Changan’s global design network, spanning 915 design professionals across 31 countries, led by Changan’s global design VP and former Volkswagen Group design chief Klaus Zyciora. It features a clean, aerodynamic profile, distinctive light signature, and commanding road presence, and has already won international recognition through the Golden A’ Design Award.

The electric SUV runs on a 51.9 kWh CATL lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery integrated with Changan’s Golden Shield 2.0 battery system, supporting 3C fast charging and up to 162 kW DC charging capacity.

The Q05 arrives in Nepal on the back of strong international sales, having crossed 100,000 cumulative units sold as of August 11, 2026, and having held the top spot in China’s compact SUV market for four consecutive months. With its spacious cabin, internationally recognised design, and advanced EV tech, the company expects the Deepal Nivo Q05 to set a new benchmark in Nepal’s compact electric SUV market.

title.rendered: Is Nepal’s cricket problem really a captaincy problem?

content.rendered:
Captaincy changes are nothing new in Nepali cricket.

When a team fails to perform as expected, changing the captain is often seen as one way of bringing about improvement. The Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) recently took that route, removing Rohit Paudel as Nepal’s ODI captain and handing the responsibility back to Sandeep Lamichhane.

Paudel had led Nepal for nearly four years, first taking charge of the T20I side and later the ODI team. His removal came after Nepal struggled for consistency in ODI cricket, particularly in overseas conditions during the World Cup League 2 campaign.

A new captain can bring a new mindset. Player roles can change, strategies can be adjusted and the team can approach matches differently. All of that can potentially translate into better results.

So, it would be difficult to call the captaincy change a wrong decision.

But given the state of Nepali cricket, a bigger question remains: Is changing the captain enough?

Nepal has been searching for consistency in ODI cricket for some time. The latest leadership change is expected to bring new energy and a different approach.

But if Nepal wants its results to change, it may need more than a change at the top. The team’s overall structure, preparation, selection process and player development will also need attention.

A history of changing captains

Nepal’s first national cricket captain was Uttam Karmacharya, who led the team when Nepal began playing international cricket in 1996.

After Karmacharya came a succession of captains including LB Chhetri, Ganesh Shahi, Pawan Agrawal, Paresh Lohani and Raju Khadka before the responsibility reached Binod Das.

Das captained Nepal from 2005 to 2008. From 2009 to 2019, Paras Khadka led the team through one of the most significant periods in Nepali cricket. Under Khadka, Nepal made major progress in international cricket and eventually secured ODI status.

After Khadka came Gyanendra Malla, followed by Sandeep Lamichhane. Rohit Paudel then took over at just 19 and led Nepal for around four years.

Now, the captaincy has returned to Lamichhane.

Nepal has gone through several captaincy changes over the years, but the latest one is notable because it has been directly linked to the team’s recent performance.

Paras Khadka stepped down voluntarily after almost 11 years as captain. Malla was removed by CAN as part of disciplinary action, while Lamichhane had to leave the captaincy amid legal problems.

Paudel’s case is different. His captaincy ended after a prolonged run of disappointing ODI results.

CAN cricket director Binod Das said the decision was made after assessing Nepal’s overall ODI performance.

“We have not been able to perform as expected in the ODI cycle. Overall, we have won only 11 matches. At home, we have won six of our last eight games. Apart from that, we have won only five of our other 24 matches. It shows that we have not been consistent in ODIs and that some changes were necessary. That result led CAN and the selection committee to take the decision,” Das had said.

What did Rohit achieve?

Paudel may have lost the captaincy, but his contribution to Nepali cricket cannot be overlooked.

Under his leadership, Nepal played 63 ODIs, winning 31 and losing 30, with two matches producing no result. In T20Is, Nepal played 59 matches under Paudel, winning 33 and losing 21. Three matches were tied and two ended without a result.

His individual record is even more significant.

Paudel is Nepal’s highest run-scorer in ODI cricket and became the first Nepali batter to reach 2,000 ODI runs. He also has two ODI centuries to his name.

His time as captain also included some of Nepal’s most important recent achievements. Under Paudel, Nepal won the 2023 ACC Premier Cup and qualified for the Asia Cup, where it played India and Pakistan in the ODI format.

That means Nepal has not simply changed its captain. It has changed the leadership of a player who has been one of the most important batters in the country’s ODI history.

Lamichhane, meanwhile, previously led Nepal in 14 ODIs. Under his captaincy, Nepal won four, lost nine and tied one.

The switch from Lamichhane to Paudel and now back to Lamichhane will certainly bring a different leadership style and tactical approach.

Whether it brings the stability Nepal needs remains to be seen.

A new captain, but the same challenges

The biggest positive of a captaincy change is the opportunity to introduce new ideas.

Former Nepal captain Raju Khadka believes Lamichhane could bring a different approach to the team.

“Leadership is about how you take the team forward and what strategy you use. A new captain has a different way of thinking. There could be a new style of play and they could bring something new,” Khadka told Onlinekhabar.

But Khadka does not believe changing the captain alone will solve Nepal’s problems.

“Captaincy change is one aspect, but it may not be the only solution right now. Analysing the opposition and selecting the team are also very important. I feel Nepal is still struggling in those areas,” he said.

That points to a bigger problem within Nepali cricket.

The captain can make decisions on the field, but many of the factors that determine a team’s long-term performance are outside the captain’s control.

Nepal has struggled with questions around team management, selection and preparation. The lack of a stable support structure can also affect the team’s performance.

The national team needs players ready to step in when key members are unavailable. It needs a stronger domestic system, a clearer pathway through Nepal A and more regular high-level matches and preparation specifically for ODI cricket.

“We are now at a point where our ODI status could come under threat. Captaincy change may bring an immediate change in results, but for the long term, structural development is also essential,” Khadka said.

Too much T20, not enough ODI focus?

Another issue is the growing focus on T20 cricket.

Nepali players are increasingly involved in franchise and T20 competitions. While that experience can be valuable, Khadka believes it has also meant that ODI cricket has not received enough attention.

He argues that Nepal may need to develop almost separate squads for the two formats, with players specifically prepared for the demands of ODI cricket.

The two formats require different skills, workloads and approaches.

A captain can redefine player roles. The batting order can change, bowlers can be used differently and decision-making under pressure can take a different direction.

A new captain can also create a fresh competitive environment within the squad.

But that requires time.

Lamichhane should not be judged solely on the results of his first few matches. His ability to build a balanced team, establish clear roles and create depth will be more important in determining whether the change actually works.

Nepal also needs to reduce its dependence on a handful of key players. A poor performance from one player should not be enough to derail the entire team. That requires a stronger bench.

Is the problem bigger than the captain?

Nepal has changed its captain. Naturally, there will be expectations that Lamichhane will bring better results.

But if captaincy change is treated as the solution to all of Nepali cricket’s problems, the team could simply find itself starting another cycle of change.

A good captain can provide direction, develop strategies and give players confidence.

But a captain cannot produce better players, provide them with regular high-level competition, organise long-term preparation or build a strong talent pipeline alone.

That responsibility also lies with CAN.

Nepal therefore needs to look beyond the captain.

The selection system, coaching and support staff, team management, analysts and player development structures all need to function effectively.

The latest change should therefore be seen not as the end of a problem, but as the beginning of another attempt to fix it.

Lamichhane may bring a new way of thinking. A new strategy may produce new results. But turning those results into sustained progress will require changes both on and off the field.

The real question is no longer simply whether Nepal changed its captain. Has Nepal also changed the way it approaches its cricket?

Lamichhane’s first big test

For the new captain, the first challenge will not simply be winning matches.

It will be keeping the team moving in the same direction over a sustained period.

Managing player roles, giving opportunities to those waiting on the bench, handling the workload of key players and making the right decisions under pressure will all test Lamichhane’s leadership.

His first major test will be the ACC Premier Cup.

Under Paudel, Nepal won the Premier Cup and qualified for the Asia Cup, where it got the opportunity to play ODI cricket against teams such as India and Pakistan.

Lamichhane has already made it clear that winning the ACC Premier Cup is his target.

Now comes the harder part: turning a change in captaincy into a change in Nepal’s cricket.

Minister for Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, and Social Security Sita Badi carried out an impromptu inspection of the Bhrikutimandap area today, accompanied by a team from the Social Welfare Council.

During the visit, Minister Badi inspected the various activities and structures operating on the premises, including the meat market, vegetable market, garden hall, various stalls and exhibitions, business areas, open and green spaces, parking, sanitation, public toilets, and pedestrian pathways, gathering firsthand information on each.

She also sought details from the relevant officials and management about how the different structures and areas are being used, the state of their management, the nature of the businesses and services operating there, and the income generated along with the benefits the state and citizens are receiving from it.

Calling Bhrikutimandap an important public property at the heart of Kathmandu, Minister Badi directed the concerned authorities to move forward with a study to develop it into a well-managed, safe, clean, green, inclusive, and citizen-friendly public centre, making the fullest use of the available space and structures rather than keeping it limited to its current form.

title.rendered: Pradip Paudel calls on NC leaders to resolve internal disputes through dialogue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Nepali Congress General Secretary Pradeep Paudel has urged all factions within the party to come to the table to resolve the ongoing internal disputes through political dialogue.

Issuing a statement on Friday, Paudel said disagreements within the party should be resolved through political discussions rather than by taking them to the streets or the courts.

He warned that the country could face a major political crisis if the Nepali Congress fails to remain alert and united at a time when the country is going through a challenging period.

Paudel urged dissatisfied leaders, party workers and supporters to come to the party headquarters in Sanepa and discuss their differences.

“This is not the time to take our differences outside the party or wait at the doors of the courts. I believe the disputes within the Nepali Congress are not, and should not be, matters for the courts to resolve,” Paudel said in his statement.

Paudel appealed to dissatisfied leaders, activists and supporters to bring their differing views to Sanepa, which he described as the party’s common home.

“I humbly request all respected dissatisfied leaders, committed party workers and dear supporters to come to the party’s common home in Sanepa with their differing views,” he said.

He also acknowledged that all sides share collective responsibility for the party’s past shortcomings and called for the differences to be addressed through dialogue.

“Let us sit together in Sanepa and engage in sincere dialogue. We all share collective responsibility for the mistakes of the past, and we must acknowledge that as we move forward,” Paudel said.

He called for the Nepali Congress to hold its upcoming 15th general convention on schedule and accept the leadership chosen by party members.

He said the party should remain united to strengthen democracy.

“Let us complete the 15th General Convention on time, accept the leadership entrusted by the general members and move forward together to further strengthen democracy,” he said.

Paudel also warned that division within the Nepali Congress would weaken both democracy and the country.

“At a time like this, dividing ourselves under various pretexts means weakening democracy and the country itself,” he said. “If we fail to correct our mistakes in time, history will not forgive us.”

title.rendered: Pokhara’s Annapurna Resort booked for PM Balen

content.rendered:
Prime Minister Balen Shah is travelling to Pokhara today, his first visit to the city since being appointed prime minister.

The Annapurna Eco Village at Dhital Astam in Kaski’s Machhapuchhre Rural Municipality has already been booked for his stay, though the security apparatus says it still has no formal information about the visit. According to sources, all rooms at the resort have been booked, and a security team from Kathmandu has already reached Astam to arrange checks and logistics for the PM’s stay.

It was announced Thursday that the PM would also visit Mustang, but Mustang’s Chief District Officer Ajita Sharma said she too had only learned of it through the media, with no formal schedule received yet. Kaski’s CDO Kumal Singh Gurung said the same, adding they only know the PM is travelling by road and expect further details soon.

The Annapurna Eco Village, run by the Adhikari family, blends nature, meditation, tradition, and hospitality, offering views of the Annapurna, Dhaulagiri, and Manaslu ranges. It has 15-20 traditionally built stone-and-wood rooms, runs on solar power and water-recycling systems, and grows its own organic produce for guests. The resort is popular with foreign visitors seeking yoga, meditation, and nature retreats close to the city, and is also known for its sunrise and sunset views and short hikes through nearby hills, forests, and villages.

title.rendered: Bancharedanda landfill crisis prompts Infrastructure Ministry to summon local representatives

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The Ministry of Infrastructure Development has summoned local representatives from Kathmandu Valley and other areas affected by the worsening situation at the Bancharedanda landfill site for discussions on waste management.

Mahesh Bahadur Singh, a senior divisional engineer and the ministry’s focal person for environment and premises sanitation, said local representatives have been called to Singha Durbar for a meeting at 1 pm on Friday.

“They have called us for a discussion on waste management at 1 pm,” Singh said.

The Bancharedanda landfill site lies on the border of Dhunibesi Municipality in Dhading and Kakani Rural Municipality in Nuwakot.

Dhunibesi Mayor Balkrishna Acharya also confirmed that he had been invited to the meeting.

“It is a discussion on waste management,” he said.

The meeting comes amid growing concerns over the condition of the Bancharedanda landfill site, which has been used for waste disposal from Kathmandu Valley for the past four years.

The sanitary landfill was constructed by the then Ministry of Urban Development at a cost of more than Rs 1 billion, with plans for it to serve as a scientific waste management facility for 20 years.

Bancharedanda was built to solve Kathmandu’s waste problem. Four years later, it is becoming another Sisdol

However, the site has already reached capacity just four years after waste disposal began.

Waste from 21 local governments, including those in Kathmandu Valley, is being dumped at Bancharedanda, which has increasingly turned into a conventional dumping site similar to the former Sisdole landfill.

Kathmandu Metropolitan City has been managing waste disposal at the site.

A large mound of waste has formed at the landfill, while leachate has started flowing from the accumulated waste. Local residents have also complained that the leachate has overflowed from the dam and entered nearby streams.

Residents of the affected areas have been demanding proper waste management and have called on authorities to ensure that people living around the landfill are not forced to live alongside unmanaged waste.

title.rendered: Jajarkot landslide victims seek safe, permanent shelter

content.rendered:
Jajarkot, August 21

Sixty-year-old Chandrakali BK of Risang in Bheri Municipality-2, Jajarkot, is currently living in a temporary shelter set up at Tribhuvan Secondary School. Staying there is not her choice but a necessity. After landslides damaged her house and farmland, she was forced to leave her home and move to the holding centre to save her life.

She does not even want to remember the day the landslide swept away her house. Whenever someone brings up the incident, tears fill her eyes and her voice chokes with emotion. Trying to compose herself, she says, “The government should create an environment where those who survived can live without fear. They should relocate us to a place where such incidents will not happen again.”

Chandrakali, whose problems have increased after her ailing husband was admitted to hospital, says, “We have lost our home and land. Where will we go, what will we eat and how will we live? We don’t even have clothes to wear.”

Her neighbours are in a similar situation. Everywhere they look, they see destruction. The settlements of Jajarkot, already weakened by the earthquake of November 2023, have become even more vulnerable due to landslides triggered by the monsoon rains. After cracks appeared in the ground and the settlements were deemed at risk, around 893 people from Risang have been living at the holding centre with their families.

Resident Parbati BK said spending the days in the school compound has been extremely difficult. According to her, accommodating a large number of people in one place has created numerous problems. She said they were struggling because they had been unable to save anything except the clothes they were wearing.

“We have no home, and we have small children. We have neither food nor a place to stay. We cannot remain at the school for long either. The government must relocate us to a safe place and arrange accommodation,” she said, crying.

Forty-five-year-old Sita BK, who says she survived the landslide “by sheer luck”, says the most important thing now is for the state to arrange a safe place for them to live. Saying that the landslide destroyed the house and land she had purchased with a loan, she said, “We don’t need much right now. We can even survive on half a stomach and struggle, but we want the whole family to be able to live together in a safe place.”

Shila of Risang is physically disabled. Although her house was not destroyed by the landslide, she feels unsafe because landslides have occurred all around it.

“I am constantly afraid and worried that my house could collapse at any time,” she says.

Residents of the landslide-affected areas expect the government to arrange permanent settlements where they can live safely without fear. The local government, meanwhile, says preparations are underway to provide immediate relief and temporary accommodation to the victims.

Bheri Municipality Mayor Chandraprakash Gharti said it would not be possible to keep the displaced people at the school for a long time, so alternative locations were being explored.

“We are looking for potential sites to build temporary housing for 40–50 families. We are also discussing the option of allocating a budget and constructing temporary shelters,” Mayor Gharti said.

The landslide triggered by incessant rainfall on August 15 caused extensive damage in Risang. Four people were killed and 11 others injured in the disaster. Although the victims urgently need food, clothing, medical treatment and temporary accommodation, they ultimately need to be resettled in a safe location.

Locals say the suffering of the displaced residents of Risang will not end until the vulnerable settlements are relocated to safe areas and permanent housing is arranged. Access to the affected area is also difficult because roads have not been constructed properly, making it challenging to reach the victims. The Lumbini–Rara road section is currently completely blocked. Although construction began five years ago, the lack of progress has continued to cause hardship for residents.

Geological study begins in landslide-affected areas

A team from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) reached the landslide-affected area of Risang in Bheri Municipality-2 on Wednesday and began a geological assessment.

The team includes NDRRMA Undersecretary Suresh Sunar, who is originally from Risang. According to House of Representatives member Parbati BK, an eight-member team comprising geologists Dr Prakash Pokhrel and Lekhraj Bhatt, Section Officer Niranjan Prakash Niraula, engineer Jagadish Bista and meteorologist Rajan Lamichhane, among others, has begun an on-site study and inspection of the affected areas.

Senior Major Govinda Thapa, chief of Bhawani Dal Battalion of the Nepali Army; Jajarkot District Police Office Chief Buddhi Sagar Puri; Gajendra Bahadur Chand, chief of the Jajarkot Garrison of the Armed Police Force; and local representatives from Bheri Municipality also visited the affected areas.

According to Chief District Officer Khadananda Adhikari, the team has begun on-site inspections of various landslide-affected and high-risk areas in wards 1, 2, 3 and 4 of Bheri Municipality. The team has also met residents to assess their immediate needs and the level of risk they face.

The team has been given a mandate to submit its preliminary report within two days.

Chief District Officer Adhikari said a concrete decision on whether to relocate the affected settlements or arrange for residents to live safely in their current locations could be made after the expert team submits its preliminary report.

“We will decide after receiving the expert team’s report whether the current location is suitable for temporary accommodation and, if relocation is necessary, where the safest place would be,” he said.

title.rendered: Supreme Court annuls Nepal Airlines executive chairman Shrestha’s appointment

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The Supreme Court has annulled the government’s appointment of Maheshwor Bhakta Shrestha as executive chairman of Nepal Airlines Corporation.

A bench of Justices Sunil Kumar Pokharel and Balkrishna Dhakal, conducting the final hearing on a writ petition filed by Upendra Bahadur Karki against Shrestha, ruled on Thursday that his appointment was not in accordance with the law. However, the court said Karki’s claim that he should be appointed chairman himself was not substantiated.

Shrestha’s appointment as executive chairman and general manager of the corporation was also found to have violated the government’s appointment procedures. Under the Standards on Appointment and Nomination of Members and Office-Bearers of Public Bodies, 2016, issued by the Ministry of Tourism, a person appointed as the executive head of a public body must be at least 30 years old and not more than 65 years old.

Karki had filed the writ petition arguing that Shrestha was over 65 years old and had been appointed 34 years after retiring from the corporation. With the Supreme Court’s ruling, Shrestha has been removed from the post, and the government will now have to appoint an executive chairman through a new process. He will, however, continue to serve as a member of the board of directors.

Shrestha was also among five board members whose appointments had previously been annulled by the Supreme Court. On May 14, five members were appointed to the corporation’s board of directors. The Supreme Court later annulled those appointments, with Shrestha among the five. The court had also annulled those appointments while hearing a writ petition filed by Karki.

title.rendered: Himalayan Rescue Association to operate health camp at Gosainkunda

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The Himalayan Rescue Association is set to operate a health camp at Gosainkunda in northern Rasuwa during the Gosainkunda fair held on the occasion of Janai Purnima, with a focus on the health of pilgrims visiting the site.

The association announced at a press conference that a seven-member team, including five doctors, had departed for Gosainkunda to provide medical services to pilgrims. The team, led by Dr Shivani Rayamajhi, comprises Dr Tapendra Dhakal, Dr Avinash Kumar Shah, Dr Uday Pandey, Dr Prajwal Luintel, medical student Namrata Adhikari and support staff member Prakash Khatri.

At the press conference, association Chief Executive Officer Govinda Basya said the medical team had been sent to Gosainkunda for the convenience and safety of pilgrims. The team will provide health services from Ekadashi to Purnima.

Association Chairperson Dambar Parajuli said the organisation has been operating a health camp at Gosainkunda continuously since 1997 after pilgrims began experiencing altitude sickness due to the site’s elevation of 4,380 metres above sea level.

Although altitude sickness can be completely prevented, some people have lost their lives due to a lack of awareness, the association said. Symptoms of altitude sickness include headache, nausea and vomiting, and pilgrims need to pay particular attention to these symptoms.

The association plans to distribute informational materials on altitude sickness this year to raise awareness among pilgrims. Last year, the association treated more than 500 patients.

title.rendered: Teacher, school staff pay hike to require Rs 4.69 billion

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The government’s decision to increase remuneration for teachers working under federal grants, early childhood development (ECD) facilitators and school employees will require an additional Rs 4.68983 billion in the current fiscal year. The Cabinet meeting on Wednesday decided to increase the existing remuneration grant for teachers working under the federal teaching support grant quota by 10 per cent.

Following the decision, the monthly remuneration of secondary-level teachers under the quota has increased from Rs 43,669 to Rs 48,058, while that of basic-level teachers has risen from Rs 34,730 to Rs 38,203.

Similarly, the federal government has increased the monthly remuneration grant for ECD facilitators, school employees and school support staff by Rs 5,000. Shree Prasad Bhattarai, spokesperson for the Ministry of Education and Sports, said an additional Rs 4.68983 billion would be required in the current fiscal year to implement the revised remuneration rates. He said the ministry had sought the Finance Ministry’s consent to arrange the additional budget in accordance with the government’s decision.

He said the pay increase would be implemented after the Finance Ministry provides its approval. Under the new arrangement, the monthly remuneration of ECD facilitators has increased from Rs 12,000 to Rs 17,000, that of school support staff from Rs 10,000 to Rs 15,000, and that of school employees handling accounting duties from Rs 15,000 to Rs 20,000.

Hansa Bahadur Shahi, president of the Nepal National Teachers’ Organisation, said a 10 per cent increase in line with the raise provided to other government employees was natural and positive. However, he said the monthly remuneration of ECD facilitators, school employees and school support staff should be increased to at least Rs 23,000.

Ganga Ram Tiwari, president of the School Employees Council, thanked the government for the pay increase and demanded that school employees be given the opportunity to serve in permanent positions.

title.rendered: Birgunj-Pathlaiya road blocked for third day over minor’s murder

content.rendered:
Bara, August 21

The Birgunj-Pathlaiya road section in Bara remains blocked for a third consecutive day as protests continue over the rape and murder of three-year-old Garima Chaudhary of Jeetpursimara Sub-Metropolitan City-1.

Garima’s family has been staging a sit-in on the road demanding justice, resulting in the disruption of traffic along the busy highway for the past three days.

Although the local administration reached an agreement with local representatives on Thursday night, Garima’s family has refused to end the protest, saying the agreement was reached without their consent.

Garima’s father, Manoj Chaudhary, said the agreement reached by the administration with political party representatives without informing the family was unacceptable.

“We were not informed about the agreement. We do not accept it,” he said.

Manoj has demanded that Home Minister Sudan Gurung and Law Minister Sobita Gautam visit the family and commit to amending Nepal’s laws.

He said the family would not feel that justice had been served unless those responsible for the rape and brutal murder of his minor daughter received the death penalty.

Local residents had initially demanded the transfer of Dilip Chhetri, chief of the Area Police Office, Simara, alleging negligence on the part of the police in connection with the incident.

After Chhetri was transferred, local representatives reached a five-point agreement with the administration. However, Manoj said the agreement was reached around midnight without the family’s knowledge or consent.

Meanwhile, the Bara administration has been attempting to reopen the Birgunj-Pathlaiya road since Wednesday.

Police and Armed Police Force personnel have been deployed as part of efforts to clear the road. However, local residents have warned the authorities against reopening the road by removing Garima’s family from the protest site.

A local resident said they were also in favour of reopening the road but insisted that the administration must first seek the consent of Garima’s family.

The dispute has kept one of the major road links in the Bara-Parsa corridor disrupted for a third day, as the family continues its protest demanding justice for Garima.
