title.rendered: Can we make Nepal’s traditional homes safer without replacing them?

content.rendered:
When the dust settled after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, thousands of Nepalis walked through villages that no longer looked like home. Stone walls that had stood for generations lay in ruins. Historic settlements that had survived centuries of harsh Himalayan winters had collapsed within seconds. Families searched through stones, broken bricks, and timber, not only for their belongings but also for memories.

Across the country, schools, monasteries, temples, and community buildings suffered extensive damage, while countless traditional homes were reduced to piles of rubble. The earthquake claimed nearly 9,000 lives, most due to the collapse of more than 600,000 houses, and hundreds of thousands of families were left without shelter.

The devastation understandably changed how many Nepalis thought about housing. Damaged traditional masonry houses were demolished and replaced with reinforced concrete buildings. For many families, reinforced concrete represented safety, progress, and a fresh start after unimaginable loss.

Yet, over the past decade, another question has quietly emerged: What are we losing in the process?

Traditional masonry houses in Nepal are far more than buildings. They represent centuries of accumulated knowledge, local craftsmanship, and ways of living that evolved to suit the Himalayan environment. Built using locally available stone, brick, timber, and mud mortar, these homes naturally stay cool during summer and retain warmth through the harsh winter months.

Their design also reflects generations of rural life. The Bhakari, traditionally used for storing harvested grain, helped preserve food naturally for extended periods. The attic provided dry, well-ventilated storage for crops and household goods, while the Pidi, a covered porch at the front entrance, served as a place where neighbours gathered, guests were welcomed, and families spent time together. The central Ageno, or fireplace, was not merely used for cooking; it was the heart of the home, where stories were shared and generations came together.

Replacing these houses with reinforced concrete buildings can therefore mean losing much more than traditional architecture. It can mean losing spaces and construction practices that have shaped the social and cultural fabric of Himalayan communities for centuries.

The issue also raises environmental and economic questions. Traditional masonry construction relies primarily on locally available materials and local craftsmanship, supporting rural economies while reducing the need to transport construction materials over long distances.

In contrast, reinforced concrete construction depends heavily on manufactured materials such as cement and steel, much of which would have to be transported into remote mountain regions. This can increase the environmental footprint of construction while placing a significant financial burden on families. For some, the cost of a reinforced concrete house could come at the expense of a child’s higher education, healthcare, or other opportunities.

Given the cost of materials, limited access to skilled labour, difficult transportation routes, and the dispersed nature of mountain settlements, wholesale replacement of traditional housing with engineered reinforced concrete construction may not be practical or economically feasible across large parts of the Himalayan region. Improving the seismic performance of existing vernacular housing may therefore offer a more practical and scalable pathway to reducing earthquake risk.

Post-earthquake research also points to the importance of looking more closely at traditional construction. A 2020 study by Rohit Kumar Adhikari and Dina D’Ayala highlighted socio-cultural and functional challenges associated with some newly constructed rural houses following the 2015 Gorkha earthquake.

Importantly, the researchers also documented an approximately 80-year-old traditional masonry house that had survived three major earthquakes, including the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, and identified traditional timber features that contributed to its earthquake resistance.

These findings are a reminder that, while many traditional masonry buildings remain highly vulnerable, not all performed poorly during past earthquakes. Understanding why some survived, and what can be learned from the local knowledge embedded in their construction, may be just as important as understanding why others failed.

From an idea to a research collaboration

Following the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, Associate Professor Helen Goldsworthy from the University of Melbourne closely followed post-earthquake investigations and developments, including through discussions with her Nepali students.

She became increasingly interested in whether modern earthquake engineering, combined with local knowledge and traditional construction practices, could improve the seismic resilience of vulnerable masonry houses across the Himalayas. This was particularly important as some traditional knowledge and skills have gradually been lost, while rebuilding efforts have increasingly focused on modern construction.

Several years later, during a discussion over lunch, Helen shared this vision with me. Having grown up in a traditional masonry house in Nepal, witnessed its collapse during the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, and later participated in post-earthquake building assessments and reconstruction activities, I had long hoped to contribute to Nepal through engineering research. It quickly became clear that we shared the same aspiration.

As our discussions developed, we recognised that addressing such a complex challenge would require a broader team with expertise in earthquake engineering, structural modelling, traditional masonry construction, and experimental research. This led to the formation of an international research collaboration focused on practical ways to improve the earthquake resilience of traditional Himalayan homes.

The newly established joint PhD project between the University of Melbourne and IIT Kanpur represents the first phase of this longer-term vision. It seeks to answer a simple but important question: What techniques are best suited to improving the earthquake resistance of existing traditional masonry houses in the Himalayan mountain region?

Rather than assuming traditional masonry construction should be replaced, the research will investigate how its seismic resilience can be improved while preserving its cultural, environmental, and social value.

The project will focus on traditional masonry buildings across the Himalayan region, including Nepal, northern India, and Bhutan, where millions of people continue to live in homes constructed using locally available stone, brick, mud mortar, and timber. There is unlikely to be a single solution for the entire region. Construction practices, available materials, seismic conditions, and local skills vary considerably between communities, so strengthening solutions will need to respond to local conditions.

The PhD research will combine field investigations, advanced numerical modelling, and large-scale experimental testing. Traditional buildings and construction practices will first be documented, including vulnerable buildings and historic structures that have survived major earthquakes such as the 2015 Gorkha earthquake.

These observations will help identify construction techniques, materials, and local knowledge that may inform future strengthening solutions. A range of techniques will then be investigated using advanced computer models, with the most promising solutions validated through laboratory testing. The aim is to identify practical solutions that can be implemented using materials and skills realistically available within different Himalayan communities.

The project brings together the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur (IIT Kanpur), combining complementary expertise and research facilities across Australia and India. The research is jointly supervised by Dr Elisa Lumantarna and Honorary Principal Fellow Helen Goldsworthy from the University of Melbourne and Professor Durgesh C. Rai from IIT Kanpur. Together, the supervisory team brings expertise in earthquake engineering, structural analysis, experimental testing, and traditional masonry construction.

For engineering graduates with either a bachelor’s or master’s degree who have a passion for structural or earthquake engineering, the PhD position offers an opportunity to contribute to the first phase of this longer journey. The successful candidate will undertake a fully funded joint PhD at the University of Melbourne and IIT Kanpur. Further information about the project, eligibility requirements, and application process is available through the University of Melbourne’s Research Degree Opportunities website.

Once suitable strengthening solutions have been identified and experimentally validated, the next phase would be to demonstrate selected techniques in a small number of publicly accessible buildings in Himalayan communities, such as libraries or community buildings. These projects would allow engineers and communities to observe the techniques in practice and help build public confidence that traditional masonry buildings can retain their character while being designed or strengthened to better resist earthquakes.

The longer-term ambition is to translate the knowledge gained from the research and demonstration projects into practical engineering guidelines and, where appropriate, building design codes. This would involve working with local engineers, governments, and communities to support wider adoption across the Himalayan region.

The ultimate goal is to ensure that future generations do not have to choose between preserving their traditional homes and protecting their lives.

title.rendered: Dhorpatan remains a top hunting destination for foreign hunters

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve, Nepal’s only legal hunting reserve, continues to attract foreign hunters seeking blue sheep and Himalayan tahrs.

During the last fiscal year, foreign hunters hunted 21 blue sheep and 11 Himalayan tahrs at the reserve, paying more than Rs 417 million in government revenue through competitive bidding.

Hunting at Dhorpatan is conducted in two seasons each year. The hunters paid Rs 303.05 million in revenue during the first season and Rs 143.74 million during the second.

According to reserve ranger Sagar Subedi, 11 blue sheep and eight Himalayan tahrs were allocated for hunting during the first season, which runs from September to November.

Foreign hunters who came through different companies hunted eight blue sheep and five Himalayan tahrs during the season. However, three blue sheep and three Himalayan tahrs could not be hunted despite the required revenue having been paid.

During the second hunting season, from February to April, permits were issued for 14 blue sheep and 10 Himalayan tahrs.

Hunters managed to hunt 13 blue sheep and six Himalayan tahrs during the season. One blue sheep and four Himalayan tahrs could not be hunted due to technical reasons, Subedi said.

Anannath Baral, chief conservation officer at the Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve Office, said several factors prevented hunters from hunting all the animals for which permits had been issued.

Problems with ammunition, hunters falling ill, changes in weather and missed shots were among the reasons, he said.

Dhorpatan is the only place in Nepal where hunting is legally permitted. Foreign hunters pay high fees through a competitive bidding process for permits to hunt blue sheep and Himalayan tahrs.

Hunters from countries including the United States, Spain, the Netherlands and Mexico visit Dhorpatan during the hunting seasons.

The reserve office deploys its staff and porters to the designated hunting blocks to provide logistical support and guide the hunters.

The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation determines the annual hunting quota based on the population of blue sheep and Himalayan tahrs.

The reserve is divided into seven hunting blocks: Seng, Barse, Surtibang, Fagune, Ghustung, Dogadi and Sundah.

Representatives of commercial foreign hunting companies and hunters generally travel to the reserve by helicopter. The hunters bear the costs of transportation, support staff, logistics and other expenses themselves.

According to the reserve office, a hunter spends between Rs 2 million and Rs 3.5 million during a 15-day hunting expedition.

Hunters, along with Nepal Army personnel and reserve staff, can remain in the forest for a maximum of 15 days.

The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation invites electronic bids for each hunting season to determine the hunting quota and revenue rates.

The cost of the animal, block reservation, licence, helicopter and other expenses means a hunting expedition in Dhorpatan can cost a hunter a substantial amount.

The reserve office said no Nepali hunter has so far participated in the bidding process for blue sheep and Himalayan tahrs.

Established in 1983, Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve covers 1,325 square kilometres across Baglung, East Rukum and Myagdi districts.

title.rendered: Bancharedanda was built to solve Kathmandu’s waste problem. Four years later, it is becoming another Sisdol

content.rendered:
Leachate is flowing from towering piles of waste at Bancharedanda. The dam built to collect it has filled up, and contaminated liquid has begun flowing into the Kalpu River.

When the wind blows, the smell of rotting waste reaches nearby homes. Crows and kites circle above the landfill and sometimes drop pieces of dead animals outside people’s homes.

For residents living around Sisdol and Bancharedanda, this has become part of everyday life.

“We are living a hellish life alongside the stench,” said 76-year-old Dhurva Prasad Upreti, describing the problems caused by the waste.

Located on the border of Dhunibeshi Municipality in Dhading and Kakani Rural Municipality in Nuwakot, the site began receiving Kathmandu Valley’s waste four years ago. The first cell was completed and waste disposal began on May 24, 2022.

The facility was built as a sanitary landfill, with plans to manage waste scientifically and keep people and waste separated. It was designed to last for 20 years.

But only four years after operations began, the landfill is already filled with massive piles of waste.

Waste from 21 local governments in and around the Kathmandu Valley is being taken to Bancharedanda. Instead of functioning as a properly managed sanitary landfill, it is increasingly resembling the dumping ground it was supposed to replace: Sisdol.

So how did a landfill designed to operate for two decades become overwhelmed in just four years?

An Onlinekhabar investigation based on a field visit to Bancharedanda found that a combination of poor waste segregation, inadequate infrastructure, irregular management and the failure of local governments to take responsibility for their waste has pushed the site towards crisis.

A Rs 1 billion landfill overwhelmed in four years

The sanitary landfill was constructed by the then Ministry of Urban Development at a cost of more than Rs 1 billion and handed over to Kathmandu Metropolitan City.

The federal government was responsible for constructing the facility, while the metropolitan city was expected to manage waste disposal at the site.

But according to officials at the federal government, the metropolitan city failed to follow the scientific waste management system for which the landfill was designed.

Madhav Katuwal, an engineer at the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction, said Kathmandu Metropolitan City was responsible for the landfill turning into a dumping site.

The facility was designed to receive only non-biodegradable waste after waste was separated at source. Even among non-biodegradable waste, only materials that could not be reused or recycled were supposed to reach Bancharedanda.

Instead, waste has largely been collected and transported in mixed form.

“The difference between a dumping site and a landfill was not understood,” Katuwal said. “Waste was collected and brought here in the same condition in which it was collected. Because it was dumped in an unmanaged way, a mountain of waste developed.”

When the Ministry of Urban Development handed over the landfill, it estimated that the facility could operate for 20 years. The government now says that if waste continues to be disposed of in the same manner, Bancharedanda may not last more than another four years.

Some recyclable materials are collected by scrap workers, but a large amount of biodegradable waste continues to arrive at the landfill.

“The infrastructure for biodegradable waste was not built,” Katuwal said. “The problem arose because all kinds of waste were brought together.”

And it is not just Kathmandu’s waste.

Waste from 21 local governments is being transported to Bancharedanda, with waste reportedly coming from as far as Panchkhal in Kavre.

“If local governments do not take responsibility for managing their own waste, there will be a disaster in four years,” Katuwal said.

About 1,400 tonnes of waste arrive every day

The scale of the problem can be seen in the amount of waste arriving at the site.

According to Kathmandu Metropolitan City, around 200 tipper trucks transport an average of about 1,400 tonnes of waste to Bancharedanda every day.

The original plan was very different.

After separating biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste, only around 15 to 20 percent of the total waste was expected to require disposal at the landfill. But workers at Bancharedanda say more than 60 percent of the waste arriving at the site is still mixed waste.

“Organic waste is arriving without being separated,” said a worker at the landfill. “Because there is so much waste, leachate cannot be properly managed.”

The excess organic waste is particularly problematic because it produces large quantities of leachate as it decomposes. The leachate was supposed to be collected in a dam, treated and then managed in a way that would allow it to be safely discharged.

Instead, the dam has filled up, and leachate has reached the Kalpu River.

“The dam has not been fully completed,” the worker said. “The dumping site was created before the construction was completed.”

He said the situation could be improved if the leachate were properly treated before being released.

Capping is also irregular

Proper landfill management requires waste to be covered regularly with soil. This process is known as capping. Workers at Bancharedanda say capping has not been carried out consistently.

“After waste is dumped, it should be covered with soil,” one worker said. “Sometimes capping is done and sometimes it is not. During the monsoon, it becomes difficult to cover the waste because of the rain.”

Without regular capping, flies and insects spread more easily. Authorities spray chemicals to control insects, but residents say the measures have not been effective.

Man Bahadur Tamang, ward chair of Dhunibeshi Municipality-1, said the situation has become particularly difficult during the monsoon.

“Capping has been inadequate during the rainy season. Because the waste is not being properly capped and the leachate is not being cleaned, the smell has spread throughout the villages,” he said.

Who is responsible?

Government agencies and local governments have largely been blaming one another for the failure to manage the landfill.

Kathmandu Metropolitan City, however, has acknowledged that it has struggled with waste segregation.

Sarita Rai, head of the metropolitan city’s Environment Management Department, said the biggest problem begins at the household level, where biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste is often not separated.

But the metropolitan city also says it does not have enough land to manage separated waste.

“If we separate the waste, where are we supposed to take it?” Rai said. “That is why the metropolitan city has been forced to dispose of waste in the same condition in which it is collected.”

Kathmandu Metropolitan City spends around Rs 650 million every year on waste management. Yet it has still not been able to establish an effective system for separating and processing biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste.

Living in hell

The landfill is located close to human settlements. In Dhunibeshi Municipality, wards 1, 3 and 4 are affected by the waste disposal site. Ward 1 is considered the worst affected.

According to ward chair Tamang, the ward has a population of around 4,500 and all residents are affected.

“One hundred percent of the people in Ward 1 are affected,” he said.

In neighboring Kakani Rural Municipality, wards 1, 2 and 3 are also affected.

Padam Balami, ward chair of Kakani-1, said around 1,100 affected households have health insurance.

“Even though waste was moved from Sisdol to Bancharedanda, the problems remain the same,” he said.

Kakani-2 has around 1,200 households, of which about 600 are considered highly affected, according to ward chair Krishna Ghimire.

“The situation is terrible. Citizens are suffering because the waste problem has not been solved,” he said.

In Ward 3, around 300 of the 900 households are considered highly affected, according to ward chair Ghananath Bajgain.

“This is the ward closest to Bancharedanda. The situation is difficult,” he said.

Residents report serious health problems

Residents say the waste has affected their health as well as their environment.

They report cases of cancer, heart and kidney disease, along with diarrhoea, typhoid, respiratory illnesses and skin diseases.

Senior cardiologist Dr Rajendra Koju said exposure to waste can cause biological and chemical contamination and affect the lungs and skin.

If the waste is highly contaminated, he said, it can also cause serious diseases, including cancer.

Local resident Badribahadur Ojha can list the names of people in the community who have died from cancer or are undergoing treatment.

“Everyone here seems to have become a cancer patient. Some have died at a very young age,” he said, pointing to lumps on his own body. “I also have these lumps. They itch and I have to keep taking medicine.”

Ojha said both his parents died of cancer.

“My father and mother died of cancer. My elder uncle and other relatives also died from cancer. Many people in the village have cancer,” he said.

Residents say the government has provided health insurance, but they have struggled to receive meaningful medical services.

“They have given us insurance, but when we go to hospitals, we are made to wait and sent from one place to another. We cannot even get medicines at the health post,” Ojha said.

Although health posts exist in the affected settlements, residents say there is a shortage of specialist doctors, laboratory facilities, medicines and regular health checkups.

“The government gave us disease, but not treatment,” Ojha said, his eyes filling with tears.

Residents describe the situation as “one sick person in every household.”

The government had once promised “one job per household” as part of its agreement with communities affected by the landfill. Residents now say they are facing the opposite reality.

“Earlier, we did not have to go to hospitals,” said Kamala Ojha. “Now, since the waste arrived, we have to keep visiting hospitals. Most households have cancer patients.”

Dead animals reach people’s homes

The landfill has also attracted large numbers of crows, kites, vultures and stray dogs.

Residents say bones, pieces of meat and parts of dead animals sometimes reach their rooftops and yards.

“Crows and kites drop the legs and pieces of meat from dead animals into our yards,” Badribahadur Ojha said. “This has spread disease throughout the village.”

Nepal’s Constitution guarantees citizens the right to live in a clean and healthy environment.

It also states that victims of environmental pollution and degradation have the right to compensation according to law.

Residents of Bancharedanda, however, say those constitutional guarantees have done little to improve their lives.

Farming has also suffered

The damage is not limited to human health. Agriculture, which has long been a major source of income for local families, is also suffering.

Standing near the Kalpu River, Dhurva Prasad Upreti recalled a time when the river was clean enough for people to swim and catch fish.

“We used to swim here. We could catch enough fish to take home in a bag in a day. There were large pools in the river,” he said.

“Now there is not even a place to take a dip. We used to drink directly from the Kalpu River. Now you cannot even step into it. The leachate has turned the Kalpu into a black river.”

Residents say the river’s pollution has also deprived them of access to clean water. The problem has been visible for nearly two decades.

“Waste and people cannot live in the same place,” Upreti said. “Either the waste must stop coming, or we must be relocated.”

Farm production has also declined.

“If leachate gets into the fields, rice does not develop grains. Only straw remains,” said local resident Khem Bahadur Thapa. “The fields, crops, animals and human health have all been affected.”

Before waste disposal began, families could largely support themselves through agriculture.

Residents say rice, wheat, maize, sugarcane, oranges, guavas, pomelos, peaches and pears were once produced in abundance.

“Earlier, even ordinary wheat cultivation produced 26–27 muri (1,600 kgs approx.),” said local resident Dipak Karki. “Now wheat does not grow. Even when we plant rice, the grains do not develop.”

With agricultural production falling, residents say they have become increasingly dependent on buying food from the market.

Livestock farming is also in crisis

Livestock, another important source of income, has also been affected.

Badribahadur Ojha said families once kept cows, buffaloes and goats and sold milk, yoghurt and ghee.

“Now livestock farming is not possible. If you keep goats, they become sick. Dogs attack them or they die. This is a problem in every household,” he said adding fruit production has also suffered because of insects and pollution.

The waste has even affected the social fabric of the communities.

Residents say dust, foul smells and pollution have made outsiders reluctant to visit the area. Some say this has made marriage relationships more difficult.

They claim families from outside are reluctant to marry their children into the affected communities.

“We married our daughter to someone in Kathmandu. She comes here, and the grandchildren come. But the son-in-law does not want to come,” one resident said.

Residents also say people have started moving away from the area because of the pollution.

Balen Shah’s unfulfilled promises

The problems at Bancharedanda have persisted despite repeated promises from federal and local governments.

After winning the 2022 local election as an independent candidate for mayor of Kathmandu, Balen Shah visited Sisdol and Bancharedanda.

He told local residents that he had come to solve the waste problem and promised not to accept ceremonial garlands until the issue was resolved.

Shah also visited the area with then-deputy mayor Sunita Dangol shortly after taking office and asked residents to cooperate with his efforts.

He argued that he had been mayor for only a few days and should not be held responsible for problems that had developed over decades.

“I have not been mayor for 17 years. It has only been four days. Can 17 years of problems be imposed on me?” he told residents. “You have to let me work here. If you let me work, the work can be done.”

Soon after, Kathmandu Metropolitan City announced a new waste segregation system.

Biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste were to be collected separately, with fines of Rs 500 for failing to separate them.

Under the plan, biodegradable waste would be collected on Sundays and Wednesdays and non-biodegradable waste on Mondays and Fridays.

The system was supposed to come into effect from July 17, 2022, but it was never fully implemented.

Before becoming mayor, Shah had frequently spoken about waste management and argued that waste could be turned into wealth.

He said Kathmandu produced around 600 metric tonnes of waste every day, with approximately 75 percent being organic.

If properly segregated, he argued, the waste could generate income and even electricity.

“From Kathmandu’s waste alone, 5 MW of electricity can be generated,” he had said, arguing that such infrastructure could be built within two years.

But the plans did not materialise during his tenure as mayor.

Plans that never took off

Shah’s then infrastructure adviser and waste management coordinator Sunil Lamsal also visited Sisdol and Bancharedanda.

In early 2023, Lamsal acknowledged to Onlinekhabar that the metropolitan city had not been able to fully implement its plan to collect biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste separately because it had not made sufficient preparations.

He said the city was preparing a waste segregation system and would implement it soon.

“If we continue dumping waste at the current rate, the site will fill up sooner than expected,” Lamsal said at the time. “We will not dump waste here in this way for a long time. Only waste that cannot be used after segregation should come here.”

The metropolitan city had plans to produce gas and compost from biodegradable waste, recycle reusable non-biodegradable materials and destroy other waste through incineration.

It had also planned processing centres for biodegradable waste and larger facilities for producing compost.

Those plans, however, were not implemented as announced.

Almost five years after Shah began taking an active role in waste management, he is now prime minister, having held the post for more than four and a half months.

Lamsal, who previously led the metropolitan city’s waste management efforts as Shah’s infrastructure adviser, is now the infrastructure development minister and has also been in office for more than four and a half months.

But for the communities around Bancharedanda, little has changed.

How the crisis began

The roots of the current crisis go back nearly two decades. In 2005, residents agreed to allow waste to be dumped at Sisdol after authorities promised one job per household, road upgrades and a hospital.

The agreement was for waste to be dumped at Sisdol for two years, after which Bancharedanda was supposed to become a scientifically managed landfill.

Japan’s international cooperation agency JICA had initially prepared to construct a landfill at Bancharedanda, around 2–3 km from Sisdol. But after disputes, JICA withdrew from the project. Construction was delayed, and waste continued to be dumped at Sisdol. What was supposed to last two years continued for 17 years.

In November 2018, the government again assigned the Ministry of Urban Development responsibility for developing infrastructure at Bancharedanda.

The government acquired 1,792 ropanis of land for the landfill, and construction of the sanitary landfill officially began in April 2019.

The project reached its final stages four years later. But waste began arriving even before construction was fully completed, triggering protests from local residents.

Following an 18-point agreement, residents eventually allowed waste disposal to continue.

They were promised that Bancharedanda would be different from Sisdol: waste would be properly managed, people and waste would be separated, and leachate would be treated before being released into the river.

Four years later, residents say those promises have not been kept.

“We had been saying from the beginning that the problems seen in Sisdol should not be repeated,” said ward chair Tamang. “We were told that waste would be properly managed, people and waste would be separated, and leachate would be treated before being released into the river.”

“But now the situation has become even worse than Sisdol.”

title.rendered: As Nepali football remains suspended, the toll spreads beyond the players

content.rendered:
Lately, the life of Nepali football players has completely changed. There is neither regular play nor practice. The passion they once had is nowhere to be found now. There is only one reason for this: they are not getting to play, either for the country or for their clubs.

This is supposed to be the time when Nepali football players would be busy preparing for the SAFF Championship in Bangladesh and other international competitions. But the reality is far from that.

With no matches being played on the field, Nepali football has not just reached zero but has slipped into the negative.

After FIFA, world football’s top governing body, suspended the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA), the national team players who became jobless made a public appeal through a video a few days ago, asking people to save Nepali football, a scene that was quite heartbreaking.

Right now the players have just one wish: to step onto the field and play again. But nobody knows when that wish will come true.

With no resolution in sight for a return to the field, not just the players but coaches, referees, and everyone else connected with the sport have effectively become unemployed, left with no option but to wait and see when football will resume regularly. Since ANFA’s suspension by FIFA, players have not been able to play, and no other football-related activities outside the field have taken place either.

For players, the game is not just a matter of income and career. They train for years, work hard, and prepare themselves for competition. That is why getting to play is more than a celebration for them. Stepping onto the field, playing for their team, and showing their ability is a player’s greatest motivation.

Right now, some footballers have reached a point where they are running academies, while others are choosing different paths altogether.

Around a dozen players from the women’s team are currently playing in leagues abroad. On the men’s side too, some players are playing in Bhutan and Bangladesh, though this is more out of necessity than choice.

Besides this, some players are playing local-level football in various parts of India.

This situation is especially serious for women’s football.

Regular competition is extremely important for advancing women’s football. The more they play, the more experience grows, new players emerge, talent develops, and the confidence of the new generation building careers in football also increases.

“In recent times, Nepali women’s football has been improving. Families were increasingly coming to believe that daughters could also play football and build their future through the sport. Family support was also gradually growing,” says one member of the women’s team.

But if domestic competition stops for a long time again, there is a risk of returning to the situation they faced in the past. The mindset of “what’s the point of a daughter playing football” could grow strong again. That could stop many talented players of the new generation from entering the sport.

So rather than assigning blame right now, the players believe all concerned parties should sit together and find a solution as quickly as possible.

This is not the problem of a single player alone. It is an issue tied to the future of Nepali football.

“For us players, football is not just a game. Football is our passion, our dream, and our celebration. Stepping onto the field to play for our country, our club, and our team is our greatest joy,” she says.

She adds, “All concerned parties must work seriously and urgently to create an environment where domestic football can resume soon. Players need the field, the new generation needs opportunity, and Nepali football needs continuity.”

Inactivity harms athletes

Physiotherapist Suraj Bhusal warns that extended inactivity or detraining severely weakens an athlete’s overall fitness.

“Under these conditions, cardiovascular endurance drops,” says Bhusal.

He adds that muscle flexibility and power deteriorate quickly. Furthermore, returning after a prolonged layoff significantly increases injury risks.

Research shows that 30% of sports injuries involve 1 to 3 weeks of inactivity.   

Research has also found that mitochondrial activity (energy production) in cells begins to decrease rapidly after roughly two weeks of training cessation. Eventually, it can harm body tissues, cause severe diseases, and lead to extreme tiredness.  

Football is an intermittent, high-intensity sport, requiring both aerobic and anaerobic processes for energy release, as well as relying on technical, tactical and psychological input. Aerobic capacity is known to be highly important and a major contributor (70-80%) of maximal capacity  

Within days of training cessation, aerobic capabilities can drop by 5-12%. As a result, the body becomes less efficient at taking in, transporting and using oxygen during physical activity, causing players to become fatigued and breathless more quickly than before. In practical terms, a person’s heart, lungs, blood vessels, and muscles can’t sustain exercise as easily as before.  

Left unaddressed, prolonged inactivity leaves athletes vulnerable to non-communicable conditions like hypertension, high blood sugar, and cardiovascular disease, he adds.

“A player’s duty is regular training and performance. Neglecting this routine also threatens mental health as well,” Bhusal explains.

Suspension’s hidden toll

Mental health experts say that for footballers, the sport has become an important part of their identity. People know them because of the sport they play, and being away from matches for a prolonged period can lead to an identity crisis.

“Sport is their priority, and the uncertainty created by others can provoke anxiety,” says clinical psychologist Hashana Shrestha. “If they do not have adequate support, they can become hopeless, which can affect their mental health.”

Women’s national team head coach and former national player Nabin Neupane notes that prolonged inactivity impacts not just players, but coaches and referees as well.

This hiatus takes a physical, mental, financial, and emotional toll on everyone involved.

“Coaching skills decline without active practice,” says Neupane. 

He further adds that football relies on teamwork. Long breaks erode coordination among players, ultimately affecting entire team performance. 

If the suspension continues, Nepal’s referees will also face a ban from international competition. The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) holds an annual referee course for the new elite referees each September, but Nepali referees will miss it if the suspension remains.

“The AFC course provides high-level training for the new elite referees. Missing it would be devastating for our referees,” says Prakash Nath Shrestha, football referee. 

This year, two new elite referees of Nepal are set to attend the course in Malaysia; however, due to the current situation, their participation is uncertain.

Nepali referee Prajwal Chhetri officiated the last SAF Games final. Without a lifted suspension, local referees cannot take part in future regional tournaments.    

Shrestha noted that an extended absence from officiating can affect a referee’s decision-making skills. He recalled that, “After the COVID-19 pandemic, returning to the field following a long break had hampered the decision-making ability of referees.”  

Research also backs Shrestha’s statement.  

Research on football referees during the COVID-19 pandemic suggests that prolonged interruptions affected their preparation, particularly decision-making training, and were associated with a perceived reduction in refereeing quality.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress Central Disciplinary Committee to meet today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 20

The Nepali Congress Central Disciplinary Committee has called a meeting for Friday.

Committee Secretary Dinesh Thapa Magar confirmed that the meeting will begin at 11 am at the party’s central office in Sanepa, Lalitpur.

The committee has not disclosed the agenda for the meeting.

The meeting comes amid heightened internal tensions within the Nepali Congress, with rival factions engaged in parallel activities ahead of the party’s 15th General Convention. The party has scheduled the convention for October 2–5 in Kathmandu.

The Central Disciplinary Committee has previously dealt with complaints and disciplinary matters involving senior party leaders.

title.rendered: Royal Enfield launches Gorkha Edition of the Classic 350 in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21 s

Alfa Automotive, Royal Enfield’s official dealer in Nepal, unveiled the Royal Enfield Gorkha edition in Kathmandu.

Retired Chief of Army Staff Rajendra Bahadur Chhetri chaired the unveiling event.

Alfa’s director, Meghraj Poudel, called the “Gorkha” name a symbol of Nepali bravery and discipline, not just a brand, and said the launch celebrates that identity alongside Royal Enfield’s legacy.

The edition keeps the standard Classic 350’s design and mechanicals largely unchanged, distinguished mainly by an olive-green “light military” color, special graphics, and a crossed-khukuri motif linked to the Gorkha Regiment identity.

It retains classic features like wire-spoke wheels, round mirrors, and chrome exhaust/headlight, with the same 349cc single-cylinder J-series engine (20.2 bhp, 27 Nm torque) and 5-speed gearbox, plus a semi-digital instrument cluster.

The Classic 350 Gorkha Edition starts at Rs 599,000 and became available in Nepal shortly after its launch in the Indian market.

title.rendered: The Nepali Congress does not need a new ideology. It needs a more capable state

content.rendered:
The ideological platform the party is mulling over

The Nepali Congress is presently weighing whether to continue on the platform of democratic socialism it adopted in 1955, or move toward a social democracy platform.

That choice is not primarily about which specific policy commitments the platform names; most of the modern commitments any contemporary platform would carry are, in one form or another, common to both options. What differs is the framework that undergirds them: whether these commitments are held together as expressions of an equalization mandate resting on state responsibility, or pursued as separate policy goals without that unifying commitment.

This essay takes up that choice by examining the record against which it should be judged: how far Nepal’s democracy has expanded since 1990, and how far the state’s capacity to act upon that expansion has kept pace. The position that record supports is worth stating at the outset, since the argument that follows is intended to substantiate it rather than discover it along the way.

Fiscal capacity has expanded, but its deployment has lagged; migration has produced substantial welfare gains without a corresponding productive transformation; and political inclusion has consistently advanced faster than socioeconomic equalization.

None of these findings requires treating redistribution as something that must await economic growth, nor do they justify retaining the classical instruments historically associated with democratic socialism—state ownership and centralized economic direction—for which Nepal’s record provides little support. They argue instead for retaining an explicit equalization mandate, the substantive commitment at the core of the democratic socialism the party adopted in 1955, while updating the instruments through which that commitment is pursued.

Nepal’s own Constitution already provides much of that update. Its Preamble commits the state to building a prosperous nation “with commitment to socialism based on democratic norms and values.” These democratic norms and values encompass—though are not limited to—a competitive multiparty democratic system, civil liberties, fundamental rights, human rights, adult franchise, periodic elections, full press freedom, and an independent, impartial, and competent judiciary along with the rule of law.

In substance, this preserves the same normative ideal the party adopted seventy years earlier, but within a democratic, rights-based and federal constitutional order. This is no coincidence. It fits a longer pattern: across the major constitutional transformations of Nepal’s modern history, the party has repeatedly helped shape the terms on which the state itself is organized. Set against that record, the continuity between the party’s original commitment and the present constitutional framework needs no further argument.

Stating a position, however, is not the same as settling the debate. A platform is easy to declare; building the capacity to deliver on it is not. The real question, therefore, is not simply what democratic Nepal has committed the state to achieve, but whether the state has built the institutional capacity to fulfil those commitments. This essay examines that gap—call it the authority-capability gap—domain by domain, drawing on the country’s broader experience to conclude with what democratic socialism should concretely mean within the existing constitutional framework.

Democratic transformation beyond the language of deficit

In the first years after the restoration of multiparty democracy in 1990, Nepal’s political course appeared relatively stable and hopeful. Over time, however, political fragmentation increased. Internal divisions within the Nepali Congress weakened governing cohesion, while the Maoist insurgency that began in 1996 created prolonged conflict and uncertainty.

The monarchy’s reassertion of executive ambitions added a further layer of institutional contestation. Nepal’s post-1990 experience has consequently often been described in terms of deficit: political instability, weak institutions, fragmented coalitions, corruption, poor governance, and incomplete development. These concerns are real. Nepal has experienced frequent changes of government, inconsistent policy implementation, administrative discontinuity, and weak institutional coordination. Yet this interpretation is incomplete because it gives insufficient attention to the transformation that occurred alongside these failures.

The Nepal that emerged in 1990 was highly centralized, fiscally constrained, and administratively narrow. Infrastructure was limited, territorial reach was uneven, and many social groups remained excluded from political and institutional life. Nepal in 2026 is structurally different. Political participation has expanded; historically marginalized communities have gained greater representation; public expenditure and state presence have increased; infrastructure and connectivity have improved; local governments now have constitutional authority; and education, health, and other measures of human development have advanced.

The central story of Nepal’s democratic development is therefore not simply failure or stagnation. It is transformation without full consolidation. Political inclusion has outrun administrative adaptation, fiscal resources have outrun implementation capacity, federalism has outrun coordination mechanisms, and social mobility has outrun productive economic transformation.

That pattern—expansion outrunning consolidation—recurs across every domain this essay examines, and it is worth naming before turning to the evidence. Four interrelated concepts organize the analysis that follows. Transformation without consolidation refers to a condition in which political, social, and economic change advances more rapidly than the institutional capacity required to absorb and stabilize it. Performance legitimacy captures the increasing dependence of democratic authority on demonstrable governance outcomes rather than on historical achievement or political affiliation alone. The coordination state highlights the growing importance of aligning authority, resources, and implementation across institutions and levels of government. Democratic stress denotes the pressures that arise when public expectations expand faster than institutional capacity.

Together, these concepts shift the analytical focus from the expansion of democratic authority to the institutional capacity required to govern an increasingly complex society. That is the shift this essay tests against the evidence—and the same shift on which the party’s platform choice ultimately turns.

Democratic expansion and the enlargement of state responsibility

The first domain in which the authority-capability gap appears is the state’s own fiscal reach. The democratic opening of 1990 changed the relationship between the state and society. Groups previously marginalized by geography, caste, ethnicity, class, language, gender, and region entered political life with increasing organizational and electoral significance. Democracy therefore changed not only how governments were selected but also what citizens expected from the state. As participation expanded, demands grew for infrastructure, public services, and economic opportunity. Political representation increasingly had to be matched by tangible improvements in everyday life.

State capacity also grew, particularly in the fiscal domain. In the early 1990s, limited domestic revenue restricted policy ambition and administrative reach. Improvements in taxation, customs administration, public financial management, and the monetization of economic activity over subsequent decades expanded the resources available to government. Public investment increased in roads, telecommunications, health, and hydropower, extending state presence into areas that had previously remained difficult to reach.

This was an important achievement, but it also changed the nature of the capacity problem: as resources and responsibilities grew, effective governance became increasingly dependent on implementation systems capable of managing larger budgets, more complex projects, and multiple institutions. The state’s ability to mobilize resources has therefore outpaced its ability to deploy them effectively, creating bottlenecks in procurement, project management, bureaucratic performance, and intergovernmental coordination.

Nepal’s challenge is consequently no longer simply to expand state capacity, but to translate expanded resources and responsibilities into effective and predictable outcomes. This is the authority-capability gap in its fiscal form—the version of it that each domain below will register in turn.

Remittances, household transformation, and deferred structural change

Labor migration has been one of the most important forces shaping Nepal’s recent development. Overseas employment has provided opportunities that the domestic economy could not offer to millions of Nepalis and has become a central household strategy for managing limited opportunities at home.

Remittances have transformed household life by financing education, healthcare, housing, land, consumer goods, and movement toward towns and cities. They have increased household incomes and resilience, contributed to poverty reduction, and expanded families’ ability to make choices about education, occupation, residence, and investment. Migration has also created new forms of social and economic mobility by linking households to transnational labor markets.

At the national level, remittances support consumption, foreign-exchange reserves, and the balance of payments and provide an important buffer during periods of economic difficulty. Yet their developmental effects are mixed: household incomes and consumption have both risen faster than domestic production, leaving domestic industries struggling to keep pace and a large share of demand to be met through imports, contributing to persistent trade deficits. Migration also reduces the labor available for agriculture, industry, and other productive sectors, particularly as large numbers of younger workers leave the country.

Remittance dependence has also altered the political economy of development. Because households receive income from abroad, pressure on governments to create employment at home may be weaker, even as rising incomes generate greater demands for infrastructure, services, and responsive government.

Migration has helped reduce poverty, improve living standards, and support macroeconomic stability—but the productive transformation that would make those gains more self-sustaining has not followed. Remittances have addressed many immediate constraints, but they cannot by themselves create a diversified and productive economy. Private income flows will not close this gap on their own; left to themselves, they can defer the structural transformation they help finance rather than produce it.

Inclusion, connectivity, and the transformation of democratic legitimacy

Nepal has experienced major advances in social inclusion, human development, and connectivity during the democratic era. Educational access has expanded, life expectancy has increased, maternal and child mortality have declined, and historically marginalized communities have gained greater political representation. Roads, telecommunications, migration, urbanization, and digital technologies have also reduced the distance between citizens and the wider world. Governance has consequently become a more direct part of everyday life.

This transformation has altered the basis of democratic legitimacy. During periods of democratic transition, legitimacy often derives from historical achievements such as the struggle for democracy, constitutional change, or institutional transformation. These sources remain important, but their capacity to sustain political support tends to diminish as democratic systems mature. Citizens increasingly judge governments by the outcomes they experience—whether public services function, infrastructure improves, and institutions respond to their needs. Political legitimacy thus becomes increasingly a matter of performance legitimacy, reinforced by the wider reference points that information access, migration, and global connectivity now give citizens for judging their own circumstances.

At the same time, political inclusion and socioeconomic equalization have not moved together: more groups participate in political life, but inequalities associated with geography, caste, class, gender, and region persist. As previously excluded groups gain political voice, claims on the state multiply. The result is a central tension of democratic development: the expansion of participation broadens political legitimacy while making governments more accountable to a larger and more demanding citizenry—a citizenry that, having acquired political voice, increasingly measures government against expectations of fair opportunity and redistribution rather than simply waiting for prosperity to arrive on its own.

Federalism and the emergence of the coordination state

The authority-capability gap also structures the institutional architecture through which any of this must be delivered. Federalism is one of the most consequential institutional changes in Nepal’s recent history. The federal democratic republic redistributed authority among federal, provincial, and local governments, creating new opportunities for political participation and bringing government closer to citizens. Local governments received constitutional authority, representation became more geographically dispersed, and citizens gained greater opportunities to participate in decisions affecting their communities. Federalism therefore changed not only the administrative structure of the state but also the relationship between citizens and government.

It also changed the nature of state capacity. Under a centralized system, governance depends largely on the effective exercise of authority within a hierarchical structure; under federalism, effectiveness increasingly depends on coordinating authority across institutions and levels of government. Decisions must be aligned among governments with different responsibilities, resources, political interests, and administrative capacities. Traditional measures of state capacity—revenue, bureaucratic competence, and administrative reach—remain essential, but federal governance adds another dimension: coordination capacity, or the ability to align planning, budgeting, implementation, monitoring, and accountability across levels of government.

Nepal is still developing this capacity. Jurisdictional overlaps, unclear responsibilities, uneven administrative strength, inconsistent planning, and fragmented implementation remain significant constraints. The constitutional framework itself was established relatively quickly; the administrative habits and institutional routines needed to make federalism work are taking much longer to build, which is why much of the difficulty lies not in decentralization itself but in running decentralized authority as a coherent system.

Nepal is consequently moving from an expansion state toward a coordination state: whereas earlier democratic development focused on expanding participation, services, infrastructure, and state presence, the next phase requires organizing these responsibilities across a multi-level system. Any mandate distributed across three tiers of government is only as credible as the coordination capacity that carries it from budget line to delivered service.

Democratic stress and electoral recalibration

Citizens register the accumulated effect of the gaps described above at the ballot box. This is where democratic stress stops being an analytical category and becomes a political fact. As democratic expectations have risen, elections have increasingly become mechanisms of political recalibration. Nepal’s recent electoral experience suggests that shifts in political support need not represent rejection of democracy itself; they can also reflect dissatisfaction with governance performance. Citizens assess governments through the quality and reliability of infrastructure, employment, and public services.

Yet electoral judgment does not necessarily correspond neatly to institutional performance. Responsibility for outcomes is dispersed across political leaders, bureaucracies, markets, different levels of government, and wider social conditions. Media, social networks, migration experiences, and international comparisons then shape how citizens interpret those outcomes. Elections therefore aggregate both lived experiences of governance and the narratives through which those experiences are understood.

This produces a distinctive form of democratic stress. Governments face pressure to demonstrate visible results within electoral time horizons, even though many reforms essential to long-term capacity—civil-service reform, procurement, intergovernmental coordination, professionalization, and organizational learning—require sustained effort and produce results slowly. The resulting tension is not simply between good and bad governance, but between the short political time horizon of electoral accountability and the longer time horizon required for institutional development.

Elections can expose the authority-capability gap in its electoral form and redistribute political authority, but they cannot by themselves resolve the institutional constraints underlying it. The more important question is whether electoral feedback can be converted into institutional learning and improved state capacity. Where that occurs, political competition can contribute to institutional adaptation; where it does not, governments may change while the underlying constraints persist.

What should democratic socialism mean today?

Nepal’s experience since 1990 neither suggests abandoning democratic socialism nor returning to its classical instruments. It instead points to retaining its core commitment—the acceptance of equalization as a direct responsibility of the state—while reinterpreting that commitment in light of the constitutional and institutional realities of today’s federal democratic republic. The analysis above makes the need for that rethinking clear: political inclusion has advanced further than socioeconomic equalization, while the responsibilities and resources of the state have expanded faster than its capacity to deploy them effectively.

This does not mean that the state simply needs to do more. It means that the state must become capable of doing effectively what democracy has already made it responsible for doing. Democratic socialism today must therefore concern itself not only with the distribution of resources, but also with institutional capacity, implementation, and coordination. Its credibility should be judged not by the commitments the state makes, but by whether it can translate commitments to equalization into reliable outcomes across different groups in society and across all three levels of the federal structure.

The argument stated at the outset need not be repeated here. But it is important to make clear that the argument alone is not sufficient. Making promises is easy; building the capacity to fulfil them is not. Rather than spending time debating the name of its platform, the party would do better to take up the more important question it has yet to address: how, within the state as presently organized, the authority-capability gap itself can actually be closed. Only by doing so can what the state promises and what it is actually capable of delivering be brought into alignment.

That leads to a more concrete question: what should democratic socialism mean in practice in today’s inclusive, empowered, federal democratic republic of Nepal? Five defining characteristics follow from the analysis.

First, it should be an explicit and committed project of equalization, accepting the reduction of inequality as a direct responsibility of the state rather than waiting for it to emerge as a secondary benefit of economic growth. Second, state spending and intervention in the social sectors need not be guided by traditional instruments such as state ownership or centralized economic direction; rather, they should be disciplined and guided by the Directive Principles of the Constitution of Nepal. Third, its test should not be what the state promises, but whether it has actually built the institutional capacity required to fulfil those promises—the authority-capability gap must be closed in practice, domain by domain, rather than merely acknowledged in name. Fourth, its benefits should be experienced equitably and reliably across all three levels of the federal structure—not as paper commitments confined to the federal capital, but as shared commitments carried by a coordinating state. Fifth, it must consciously and persistently address the gap between political inclusion and socioeconomic equalization, because the capacity to close that gap is what makes the state genuinely democratic and socialist. These five characteristics are a continuation of the ideal embraced seventy years ago; but connected to Nepal’s institutional realities today, they provide a clear and practical definition of democratic socialism for contemporary Nepal.

Democratic socialism, in this sense, need neither be defended merely as a historical doctrine nor abandoned as an outdated one. It can instead be understood as a continuing commitment to equalization, updated for a more inclusive, empowered, and federal Nepal, and made credible by the institutional capacity to translate that commitment into practice. That is both the continuity of the commitment adopted seventy years ago and its practical meaning in Nepal today.

title.rendered: 14 foreign doctors flagged as NMC uncovers questionable certificates

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

Nepal Medical Council (NMC) has suspended the registration process of 14 foreign doctors after questions were raised over the authenticity of documents they submitted to work in Nepal.

The doctors had come to Nepal to work at hospitals or take up faculty positions at medical colleges.

The issue came to light when the NMC began scrutinising the documents submitted by some of the doctors during the registration process. Among them were “good standing certificates” — documents that confirm a doctor is registered with the relevant regulatory authority in their home country and is eligible to practise medicine.

NMC Acting Registrar Dr Dipendra Pandey said the council became suspicious after examining the documents submitted by some of the newly arrived foreign faculty members.

“We reviewed the certificates and other documents submitted by the doctors for registration. Some aspects appeared suspicious, prompting us to conduct a further internal investigation,” Pandey told Onlinekhabar.

The council then sought verification from the relevant authorities in India regarding some certificates submitted by doctors who claimed the documents had been issued by Indian regulators.

The response raised further concerns: the Indian regulatory authority informed the NMC that it had not issued the certificates in question.

Pandey clarified that this does not necessarily mean the doctors themselves were not registered to practise medicine in India. Rather, the concern is that the specific “good standing certificates” submitted for their registration in Nepal may have been fabricated.

“We suspended the registration process after receiving a response that the certificates had not been issued by the concerned council,” Pandey said.

The NMC subsequently expanded its scrutiny and found other documents raising similar concerns. The registration process of 14 foreign doctors has so far been suspended.

The council has also sought written explanations from medical and dental colleges, health science academies and hospitals that recommended the doctors for registration without first verifying their documents.

The concerned institutions may also be required to bring the doctors before the council to verify their identities and documents.

NMC to examine records of around 500 foreign doctors

The discovery has prompted the NMC to widen its investigation beyond the 14 doctors.

The council has formed a five-member investigation committee led by Dr Chhabi Pant to examine the registration status, employment and professional activities of foreign doctors working in Nepal.

Around 500 foreign doctors are currently working in hospitals and medical colleges across the country, according to the NMC. A significant number are employed as faculty members at medical colleges.

The council plans to examine the files of all of them, including their academic qualifications, professional registration documents and good standing certificates.

“We are studying all around 500 files. We have currently suspended the registration process of 14 doctors. How many more will be identified will become clear after the investigation,” Pandey said.

The NMC has also informed the Medical Education Commission about the investigation.

But the investigation is not limited to the authenticity of certificates. The council is also looking into a wider concern over the use of foreign doctors as nominal or “dummy” faculty members at medical colleges.

Concern over ‘dummy faculty’ being used to secure medical seats

According to an NMC member, some medical colleges may be temporarily bringing foreign doctors into Nepal and showing them as faculty members during inspections conducted to determine student quotas.

The Medical Education Commission considers the number and qualifications of faculty members, among other criteria, when determining seats for MBBS, MD, MS and other medical programmes.

This has raised concerns that some colleges could be bringing in foreign doctors shortly before inspections to show that they meet the required faculty strength and then allowing them to leave once the inspection is over.

Such doctors are commonly referred to as “khadebaba” or dummy faculty.

“Doctors are brought from India, documents are allegedly prepared or falsified, and they are kept at the medical college for a short period so they can be shown as faculty during the commission’s inspection and help secure seats. They then return to India after staying for a few days,” an NMC member said.

According to the member, such practices may become more common as the deadline for determining MBBS seats approaches, with colleges seeking to demonstrate that they have the required number of faculty members before inspection teams arrive.

The NMC has now decided to investigate medical colleges to determine whether foreign doctors have been used in this manner.

“We had heard about the use of dummy faculty, but this incident has confirmed the concerns,” the member said.

The council has warned that medical colleges could also face action if the investigation finds that foreign doctors were listed as faculty merely to increase or retain student seats without actually carrying out their academic responsibilities.

The investigation into the 14 doctors is therefore expected to determine not only whether the documents submitted to the NMC were genuine, but also whether some medical colleges have been misusing foreign faculty to meet regulatory requirements on paper.

title.rendered: RSP Central Committee to meet today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 21

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) is set to hold a meeting of its Central Committee on August 21.

According to General Secretary Bipin Kumar Acharya, the meeting will be held at the party’s central office in Banasthali.

The meeting will discuss and decide on several issues, including the framework for selecting candidates for the upcoming local elections.

The party is also scheduled to approve the Local Election Candidate Selection Framework 2026 and work on a document related to the “Right to Recall” provision.

The meeting will also discuss the nomination of members to various party bodies, including the Central Committee, office bearers, Secretariat members, department chiefs and the central candidate selection committee for the local elections.

The meeting is expected to set out the party’s organisational approach and preparations for the upcoming local elections.

title.rendered: NIMB CEO Jyoti Prakash Pandey released on Rs 8 million bail

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 20

Kathmandu District Court has ordered Nepal Investment Mega Bank CEO Jyotiprakash Pandey to be released on Rs 8 million bail in a case related to the auction of Smart Telecom’s collateral.

Nepal Investment Mega Bank CEO Jyoti Prakash Pandey has been released on bail in a case concerning the auction of collateral belonging to Smart Telecom.

A single bench of Kathmandu District Court Judge Kamal Kant Joshi ordered Pandey’s release on Rs 8 million bail following a detention hearing on Thursday.

The order also clears the way for Pandey to return to his regular duties at the bank. Had the court ordered him to be detained, he would have faced the risk of being unable to resume his work.

Pandey was arrested in Sindhuli on May 12. The Supreme Court later ordered his release on a personal recognisance.

A bench of Justices Sharanga Subedi and Shant Singh Thapa ordered his release on May 20 after hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by his family.

The petition, filed by Pandey’s wife, Niru Dahal, had argued that he was being held unlawfully.

Following his release through the habeas corpus proceedings, the government filed a case against Pandey at the Kathmandu District Court. After Thursday’s detention hearing, the court allowed him to remain outside custody while facing the case.

Smart Telecom, which had obtained a basic telephone service licence from the Nepal Telecommunications Authority on April 15, 2013, failed to renew its licence as required.

Under Section 25(5) of the Telecommunications Act, 1997, the company’s licence was automatically revoked on April 16, 2023.

The government subsequently filed charges against Pandey, accusing him of fraud, organised crime and offences under laws governing banks and financial institutions.

The allegations relate to the sale of Smart Telecom’s assets and the recovery of loans. The government has accused those involved of selling the company’s assets without government approval through collusion.

title.rendered: Decisions by state institutions must be acceptable to people: Gagan Thapa

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 20

Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa has said decisions made by the government, Parliament, courts and constitutional bodies must not only be legally valid but also be justified and acceptable in the eyes of the public.

Speaking at a book launch programme organised by the Nandaprasad Januka Foundation in Kathmandu on Thursday, Thapa said the legitimacy of decisions taken by state institutions must be demonstrated to the people.

“Decisions made by the government, Parliament, courts or constitutional bodies cannot be considered sufficient merely because they are in accordance with the law. Their justification must be proven and accepted in the eyes of the people,” Thapa said.

He also warned lawmakers against developing an attitude that winning an election gives them unlimited freedom to say or do whatever they want.

Thapa said lawmakers must exercise seriousness, caution and full responsibility even when speaking during the one-minute Zero Hour in Parliament.

He urged political leaders to learn from history, recalling how two-thirds majorities held by the Nepali Congress-CPN-UML alliance and the then Nepal Communist Party eventually lost their political strength amid growing public dissatisfaction.

Thapa also urged newly emerging political parties not to repeat the mistakes of established parties and to address their own shortcomings as they move forward.

He said the country could not afford any further “political adventurism” and called for the five-year term to be used constructively and in an organised manner.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 20

The Embassy of Japan in Nepal has honoured the Nepal Mountaineering Association (NMA) for its contribution to the successful organisation of the “Manaslu Platinum Jubilee” programme marking 70 years since the first successful ascent of Mt Manaslu.

Japanese Ambassador to Nepal Maeda Toru presented the “Ambassador’s Commendation” to NMA President Phur Gelje Sherpa at a ceremony.

The honour was awarded in recognition of the NMA’s significant role in organising the platinum jubilee programme, which commemorated the historic first ascent of Mt Manaslu.

Accepting the award, Sherpa said the recognition from the Japanese Embassy was a major achievement for the NMA.

He said the association would continue to contribute to preserving the history of Manaslu mountaineering and strengthening the longstanding mountain-related ties between Nepal and Japan.

The ceremony was attended by NMA office-bearers and members, as well as representatives from the mountaineering and tourism sectors.

Mt Manaslu was first successfully climbed in 1956 by a Japanese expedition led by Toshio Imanishi and Gyalzen Norbu Sherpa.

Sankhuwasabha, August 20

The District Police Office, Sankhuwasabha, has arrested 11 absconding defendants in one month. The office said it made the arrests within the first month of the current fiscal year.

Police Inspector Meghraj Aryal of the District Police Office, Sankhuwasabha, said the arrests came as part of intensified efforts to track down and arrest fugitives wanted in criminal cases.

According to police, those arrested had been sentenced to a combined 22 years, two months and 23 days in prison. The District Police Office also said it recovered Rs 2,09,19,949 in fines from them.

title.rendered: Jai Nepal Party to launch nationwide signature campaign for constitutional monarchy, Hindu state

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 20

The Jai Nepal Party, led by Dhawal Shumsher Rana, has decided to launch a nationwide signature campaign to build public support for a constitutional monarchy and a Hindu state.

The decision was taken at the party’s first central working committee meeting held in Kathmandu on Thursday.

The party said the campaign would be conducted in phases to generate public opinion in favour of a constitutional monarchy and Hindu state and create positive pressure on relevant authorities, amid the government’s ongoing process of collecting suggestions for constitutional amendment.

The meeting also decided to organise pressure programmes in Bhadra to push the government and other concerned stakeholders to prohibit cow slaughter and the consumption of beef.

According to party chair Rana, the meeting also formed a dialogue committee to bring together parties, organisations, groups, campaigns and individuals that share the Jai Nepal Party’s political views.

The newly formed Jai Nepal Party had not made public the names of its central members when it registered with the Election Commission on August 14.

The party had submitted the names of 79 central members to the Election Commission. Except for Rana, who was designated chairperson, all were listed as central members.

At Thursday’s central committee meeting, minutes were prepared with the names of all 79 central members, although some members have not signed the document.

Jai Nepal Party central committee members

The central committee includes Dr Dhawal Shumsher Rana, Mukund Shyam Giri, Dil Vikas Rajbhandari, Narayan Prasad Koirala, Karna Bahadur Shahi, Keshav Raj Shrestha, Navaraj Simkhada, Sagun Sundar Lawati, Dhansur Shahi, Suresh Acharya, Prajwal Bohara, Chiragman Singh Kunwar, Shashank Shumsher Thapa, Ranjan Karki, Phaniraj Lohani, Prakash Jung Karki, Uday Raj Pokharel, Ram Raj Koirala, Lal Gopal Acharya, Khadka Bahadur Ghimire, Kalibahadur Shahi, Mahendra Jung Shah, Shashikumar Silwal, Kiran Dhungel, Prabhat Nath Yogi and Niraj Bam.

The party’s other central committee members include Kedar Bahadur Dhamala, Janak Bahadur Singh, Daman Basnet, Prem Deshar, Bikash Kapali, Yadav Raj Pandey, Thaman Singh Tamang, Pashupati Kathayat, Homanath Gautam, Jay Prakash Bagale, Ishwari Prasad Bhattarai, Mansur Sunar, Ram Naresh Yadav, Bhim Bahadur Shahi, Nabodit Giri, Prem Chand, Bishwadev Shah, Chet Nath Thapa, Krishna Bahadur Basnet, Sharan Kumar Singh, Pavitra Subba, Mina Hahi, Radhakumari Shah, Uma Shrestha, Laxmi Kumari Hamal, Radhika Joshi, Samriddhi Rajya Laxmi Rana, Sumira, Anjana Shah Rawal and Ramdevi Maharjan.

Other members are Bavina Moktan Lawati, Anjakumari Thapaliya, Reshma Rana, Sangita Silwal, Uguna Shahi, Sonisa Rijal, Sushma Rijal Regmi, Shanta Kumari Chand, Ramita Deshar, Pramila Thapa Shrestha, Babi Shah, Manmaya Bamjan Tamang, Govinda Bahadur Bogati, Anju Shrestha Khatri, Premnath Dulal, Kavita Acharya, Kasinda Yadav, Umesh Kumar, Nani Maya Acharya, Champadevi Adhikari, Bed Bahadur Shahi, Dr Govinda Prasad Acharya and Shaijan Sherpa.
