title.rendered: Astronomers uncover new clues about the cosmic mystery of ‘Little Red Dots’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu

Scientists have uncovered new clues about the mystery surrounding the small, red celestial objects known as ‘Little Red Dots’, discovered with the help of the James Webb Space Telescope. First observed in 2022, the nature of these objects has been the subject of extensive study.

An international team of researchers has published a new study on the subject in The Astrophysical Journal. According to the study, these red dots are not a distinct type of galaxy. Instead, they may represent a temporary stage in the evolution of a black hole.

To study the phenomenon, scientists examined a nearby spiral galaxy named ‘Saguarо’. At the centre of this galaxy is a small, red object that closely resembles the ‘Little Red Dots’ observed in the early universe.

Researchers conducted a detailed analysis by combining data from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes. Because the galaxies are extremely distant, their surrounding structures appear blurred, while only their bright central regions are clearly visible, making the objects appear isolated.

Observations with the Chandra X-ray Observatory confirmed the presence of an active black hole at the centre. The black hole emits only a small amount of X-ray radiation. The study is expected to contribute significantly to scientists’ understanding of black hole evolution. Researchers said they will continue searching for and studying similar galaxies.

title.rendered: Google to launch ‘Googlebook’ in New York on September 15

content.rendered:
Google has set a date to publicly unveil its new laptop, the ‘Googlebook’. The company said it will host a live media event in New York City, USA, on September 15.

At the event, Google will provide detailed information about the Googlebook’s software, its integration with Gemini AI, and its underlying Android codebase. Journalists attending the event will also be able to try out Googlebook devices developed by hardware partners, including Lenovo, ASUS and HP.

Earlier this year, at ‘The Android Show’, Google gave the first glimpse of its new premium laptop series. According to the company, the laptops have been developed from the ground up with Gemini AI at their core.

During the demonstration, Google highlighted features that allow users to create their own widgets with Gemini’s assistance, as well as ‘Magic Pointer’ and improved connectivity with Android smartphones.

However, the company did not release further details about the Googlebook after the event. Google also provided little information about the laptops during its recent Pixel 11 launch event.

The company had earlier said it would provide more information about the Googlebook in collaboration with hardware partners such as Lenovo, ASUS and HP.

Now, the date for an event to provide detailed information about the Googlebook platform has been confirmed. At the New York event, Google is expected to reveal more details about the Googlebook’s software, AI features and hardware developed by its partner companies.

Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth has arrived in Pokhara during his visit to Nepal.

Seth is scheduled to meet Indian ex-servicemen and their families at the Indian Pension Camp in Rambazar, Pokhara, where he will also deliver a brief address.

His visit comes days after former Indian soldiers staged a protest in Pokhara over the recruitment of Agniveers under India’s Agnipath scheme.

The former soldiers and their families have therefore been closely following the Indian Army chief’s visit.

Seth is also scheduled to distribute specially adapted scooters to former Indian soldiers who sustained disabilities while serving in the Indian Army.

Around 64,000 former Indian soldiers and their family members are affiliated with the Indian Pension Camp in Pokhara and receive their pensions through the facility.

Across Nepal, around 135,000 former Indian soldiers receive pensions, according to the figures provided.

title.rendered: 1 dead, 2 missing after 4 students swept away in Hetauda

content.rendered:
Hetauda, August 19

Four girls returning home from school were swept away by a river on August 18. One of them was found safe, while another was found dead. They were students at Nirmal Secondary School in Bastipur, Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City-19, Makawanpur.

Two girls are still missing, according to school Principal Prabodh Bidari, who informed police about the incident. The students were swept away by the Basudev River in Basudev, Hetauda-19, while crossing the river along the road leading from the school.

The body of Roshni, the eight-year-old daughter of Deep Syangtang, a resident of Bastipur, Hetauda-19, was found lodged in a tree about 600 meters from the incident site, said DSP Madhav Prasad Kafle, spokesperson for the District Police Office, Makawanpur.

Similarly, Seema Blon, the 13-year-old daughter of resident Sitaram Blon, was found safe. However, 11-year-old Sumitra Blon and 12-year-old Binita Blon remain missing, and a search operation is underway, police said.

As soon as they received information about the incident, a police team from the Area Police Office, Newarpani, was deployed to the scene. A team from the Armed Police Force and another from the Nepal Army, both part of the Bagmati Province Disaster Management Group, have also been deployed to search for and rescue the missing students.

title.rendered: Jajarkot hospital struggles with doctor shortage as illness rises among landslide-displaced people

content.rendered:
Jajarkot, August 19

Health services in Jajarkot have been affected as the number of patients continues to rise while the district hospital has been operating without sufficient doctors for an extended period.

The shortage has become a major concern as people displaced by floods and landslides have started reporting health problems, increasing pressure on the already understaffed hospital.

A request has been made to Chief Minister Mangal Bahadur Shahi to immediately arrange doctors for Jajarkot Hospital.

Dharmashila Basnet, a member of the task force and former chairperson of the hospital management committee, said the chief minister had been urged to send doctors to the hospital without delay.

The 50-bed district hospital has been facing difficulties providing daily services due to the lack of doctors.

Sunil Pun, chief of the Health Service Office, Jajarkot, said the shortage of doctors has severely affected service delivery.

Chief Minister Shahi, meanwhile, said he was serious about arranging doctors for the hospital.

The number of patients seeking treatment has increased in recent days, particularly following floods and landslides that have injured and displaced local residents.

Health workers said patients suffering from fever, common cold, injuries and other health problems have been arriving at the hospital in increasing numbers, but the shortage of medical personnel has made it difficult to provide effective treatment.

The lack of doctors has affected emergency and regular check-ups, specialist services and overall patient care. Patients have also complained of having to wait for long periods even for basic treatment.

The shortage has created additional difficulties for residents from remote settlements who travel to the district hospital for treatment.

Health workers have urged the authorities to immediately deploy additional doctors and health workers, warning that the number of patients could rise further during disasters.

They said failure to increase medical staff could make it difficult to provide timely and quality healthcare to people affected by floods and landslides.

Local residents have also called on the provincial and federal governments to ensure doctors are available according to the hospital’s sanctioned positions and to provide regular specialist services.

They have urged authorities to deploy additional doctors on a temporary basis if necessary, given the increased pressure on healthcare services during the disaster.

Fever, cold symptoms reported among displaced people

Health problems have also been reported among people displaced by floods and landslides and currently staying in temporary shelters.

Displaced residents from Bheri Municipality-2 and -3, who have been taking shelter in schools, have reported symptoms including fever and common cold.

Doctors said such symptoms were identified among 691 people during health assessments.

Chief District Officer Khadananda Adhikari said health problems had started emerging among people staying in temporary shelters.

On Monday, a team of doctors and health workers deployed by Bheri Municipality and Karnali Provincial Hospital, Surkhet, examined and treated 90 displaced people staying in shelters.

The health section of Bheri Municipality said symptoms of fever and common cold had become increasingly common among displaced people in recent days.

The municipality has also identified safe drinking water as a major challenge, with many local water sources contaminated following the disaster.

At least four people have died and 10 others have been injured in landslides that struck settlements in wards 1, 2, 3 and 4 of Bheri Municipality.

Hundreds of residents have been displaced and are currently taking shelter in schools and other safer locations.

Health officials have warned of an increased risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases, particularly because elderly people, children, pregnant women and new mothers are among those staying in the shelters.

Bheri Municipality has established health desks at shelters hosting displaced residents and is providing regular health check-ups and treatment services.

title.rendered: Geospatial study links lung cancer hotspots in Bagmati to air pollution

content.rendered:
Nepal’s lung cancer crisis cannot be understood by looking only at hospital records or individual risk factors; we must also ask a fundamental geographical question: where are people being exposed to the conditions that increase their risk? The air we breathe is not the same everywhere. Rapid urbanisation, traffic emissions, household air pollution, industrial activities, dust, biomass and solid-fuel use, and changing environmental conditions create highly uneven patterns of exposure across Nepal. Yet these spatial inequalities often remain invisible in conventional health statistics.

In recent years, cancer has stood as a major global public health challenge. Notably, the incidence of lung cancer is rapidly increasing in developing countries. According to the World Health Organisation, cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for nearly 10 million deaths in 2024, or nearly one in six deaths. The most common cancer is lung cancer, with 2.6 million cases. It is the most common cancer seen in men, primarily due to factors such as smoking, low air quality, haphazard industrialisation, and lifestyle changes. It is not distributed evenly across all geographical locations; the risks vary by place due to environmental conditions and social behaviours. It is also associated with access to healthcare services. In Nepal, there has also been a significant increase in the incidence of lung cancer in the last decade, highlighting the seriousness of this problem and the need for municipal-level analysis for a better understanding of its impacts.

In a country like Nepal, which has geographical diversity, the distribution of diseases is attributed to spatial characteristics. However, spatial studies are limited in our country. Many global and regional-level spatial studies indicated that the risk of lung cancer varies geographically. Various factors such as environmental and geographic exposures, population density, smoking rate, lifestyle, geographical structure, and dietary habits determine its risk, which has not been studied in our country. According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), there were 1,477 new cases of lung cancer reported in Nepal at a rate of 7.1 per million.

According to a study by Silpkars 2022, Nepal’s age-standardised incidence rate (ASIR) is 80.9, and the mortality rate (ASMR) is 54.8 per million, which is exceptionally high. The high mortality rate of lung cancer, especially among men in urban areas, poses a serious public health challenge. This rate is notably higher in the age group of 70 to 74, a high-risk demographic. In the Kathmandu Valley, the ASIR of lung cancer in men is 18.1 and 10.4 in women, indicating the severity of the disease in the capital. However, in rural areas like Rukum, this rate is only 13.2 and 5.2, respectively, demonstrating significant variation in lung cancer risk according to location.

Spatial health research is essential for studying complex and location-specific health issues. Geographic Information System (GIS), satellite data, and spatial statistical techniques are used to identify patterns of disease spread, risk areas, and associated geographic and environmental factors. Such spatial technology and methods play a significant role not only in disease control but also in policy-making. Unfortunately, spatial health research has not yet been given sufficient priority in Nepal.

This research on the relationship between lung cancer and PM2.5 in the Bagmati Province is one of the first studies expected to guide future research, health interventions, and policy-making by spatially mapping risk areas at the municipal level. Such research can serve as a practical tool for the scientific community, policymakers, public health advocates, and local governments.

 In this context, ‘Spatial Health Research’ is essential to understand the local distribution of diseases and to identify risk areas. Public health research focuses on individual or demographic details, but geospatial analysis makes it possible to clearly illustrate the interaction between disease, environment, and geographic features. The study of disease spread, risk areas, and potential causes such as pollution intensity, population density, and geographic barriers can be conducted using GIS and remote sensing technologies. Such analysis can contribute significantly to developing targeted and effective disease control policies.

For this reason, my recent research was conducted to identify the potential relationship between PM2.5 and lung cancer in the Bagmati Province. The study evaluated the spatial and temporal distribution of lung cancer cases from 2012 to 2021. It included a spatial mapping of high-risk areas and analysed the extent of PM2.5 impact at the municipal level. Factors such as demographic conditions, urbanisation, land use, and lifestyle were also included. In the context of Nepal, this type of localised health study has been conducted for the first time, representing an innovative effort in Nepal’s health research field. The findings of this research are expected to contribute to pollution control, formulating public health strategies, and reducing chronic diseases like lung cancer. Specifically, by providing clear information on the level of risk in local bodies of Bagmati Province, it will be possible to carry out evidence-based interventions targeting them.

Why lung cancer is 6 times higher in some municipalities

Bhaktapur Municipality faces a lung cancer rate of 24.39 per 100,000 people, which is six times the provincial average. Meanwhile, just 50 kilometres away in rural Raksirang, the rate sits at 3.85. The first-ever municipal-level disease mapping in Bagmati Province reveals how air pollution is silently creating cancer clusters across Nepal’s most populated region.

Nepal ranked 7th globally for air pollution in 2024, with toxic particle levels 8.5 times above World Health Organization safety limits. But this decade-long study of 2,183 lung cancer cases shows the danger isn’t spread evenly. The air you breathe depends entirely on your area, and so does your cancer risk. Between 2012 and 2021, lung cancer cases in Bagmati Province surged 128 per cent, jumping from 119 to 271 annual diagnoses. That’s roughly seven new patients every day. Among them, 60 per cent are men, reflecting global patterns linking male smoking rates to lung disease. But one statistic defies simple explanation: urban areas like Kathmandu Metropolitan City show lower rates than smaller municipalities despite worse air quality.

The answer lies in population density. High case numbers in the capital get diluted across millions of residents, lowering the calculated rate. Meanwhile, places like Panchkhal Municipality (14.64 per 100,000) and Sunapati Rural Municipality (12.96) show concentrated risk despite smaller populations. Raw numbers hide local crises.

Using satellite pollution data and decade-long hospital records, the study mapped cancer “hotspots” where cases cluster far beyond statistical chance. Bhaktapur, Sindhupalchok, and Kavre districts light up red year after year. These aren’t random; they’re areas where PM2.5 pollution (microscopic particles from vehicles, factories, and burning) reaches dangerous concentrations.

Figure 1. Municipal-level lung cancer risk presented on a map: (A) CIR for males, (B) CIR for females, and (C) total CIR.

The relationship between pollution and cancer appears to be growing stronger. In 2018, PM2.5 levels explained 59 per cent of cancer variation across municipalities, which is the highest correlation found in the decade. Earlier years showed weaker links, suggesting pollution’s effects compound over time. Residents breathing toxic air in 2012 may only develop cancer a decade later, making today’s pollution tomorrow’s epidemic.

Figure 2. Shows the municipal-level hotspot from 2012 to 2021 in Bagmati Province.

This data gap reveals a deeper problem: Nepal lacks coordinated cancer registries. Without comprehensive tracking, health officials can’t know the full scope of the crisis or target interventions effectively. Urban residents near major hospitals get counted; rural patients often don’t. Tiny particulate matter (PM2.5) penetrates deep into lungs and enters the bloodstream. Long-term exposure triggers inflammation, damages DNA, and provides pathways for cancer development. The 2018 hotspot analysis marked a turning point: cancer clusters aligned almost perfectly with pollution zones around the Kathmandu Valley.

This relationship shifted over the decade studied. Some years showed weaker correlations, reflecting pollution’s variable impact or the time lag between exposure and diagnosis. Cancer doesn’t appear overnight. A resident exposed to severe pollution in 2015 might not receive a diagnosis until 2021, complicating efforts to draw direct cause-and-effect lines.

This marks Nepal’s first municipal-level spatial health study, creating a roadmap for targeted intervention. Health officials can now see exactly which municipalities need immediate pollution controls, early cancer screening programs, and public awareness campaigns. The data removes guesswork from resource allocation.

The study’s broader message challenges one-size-fits-all policies. Average pollution levels across Bagmati Province mask extreme local variation. A provincial strategy that treats all municipalities equally wastes resources in low-risk areas while leaving high-risk residents underserved. Bhaktapur needs different interventions than Rukum, where cancer rates run half as high. Behind these statistics are families. Husbands diagnosed in their 60s, wives facing treatment costs that bankrupt households, children losing parents. The age group from 70 to 74 shows the highest risk, but working-age adults increasingly appear in cancer wards.

The hotspot maps also reveal environmental injustice. Wealthier residents can afford homes in cleaner areas, access better healthcare, and detect cancer earlier. Poorer communities concentrate in industrial zones with the worst air quality and fewest health services. Geography becomes destiny. The government now has evidence-based answers to critical questions: Where should mobile screening units go first? Which municipalities need emergency pollution reduction? Where will the next cancer cluster emerge?

Early detection programs targeting high-risk municipalities could catch cancer when it’s still treatable. Pollution controls in hotspot areas such as traffic restrictions, industrial emission standards, and construction dust management might prevent future cases. Both interventions require political will and funding. This study demonstrates that the burden of lung cancer in Bagmati Province is unevenly distributed, with municipalities experiencing substantially higher risks that closely align with long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5). These findings reinforce the importance of integrating spatial evidence into public health planning and environmental governance.

Geospatial health offers a powerful way to make these risks visible by bringing together lung cancer data, air-quality measurements, satellite observations, land-use patterns, population density, road networks, socioeconomic conditions, and healthcare accessibility. By mapping where environmental exposures overlap with vulnerable populations and where lung cancer cases are concentrated, we can move beyond simply counting patients toward understanding the places and environmental conditions that may shape disease risk.

This matters particularly in Nepal, where limited resources demand targeted prevention rather than a one-size-fits-all response. Geospatial evidence can help identify high-risk communities, guide environmental monitoring, prioritise screening and prevention, and support policymakers in directing resources where they are most needed. If lung cancer is partly a story of place, exposure, and inequality, then Nepal needs to put geography at the heart of its cancer prevention strategy. The question is no longer only how many people are developing lung cancer. It is also where, why there, and what can we do before exposure becomes disease? Lung cancer is no longer solely an individual health issue; it has become a geographic and environmental challenge that demands location-specific solutions.

Nepal can no longer rely on province-wide or national averages when designing cancer prevention strategies. Instead, policymakers should prioritise municipal-level interventions in identified hotspot areas. Strengthening air quality monitoring, enforcing stricter emission standards for industries and vehicles, improving urban planning, controlling construction dust, and promoting cleaner household energy sources are essential steps to reduce population exposure. At the same time, the health system should establish a comprehensive, nationwide population-based cancer registry integrated with GIS and environmental data to enable continuous surveillance of cancer patterns and emerging risks. Strengthening collaboration among the Ministry of Health and Population, the Ministry of Forests and Environment, local governments, and research institutions will be critical for translating scientific evidence into effective public policy.

title.rendered: Monsoon rains to continue across Nepal, heavy rainfall possible in five provinces

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 19

Monsoon conditions continue to prevail across Nepal, with the monsoon low-pressure line currently positioned around its average location, according to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

The weather is generally cloudy across the country, with light to moderate rainfall currently occurring in some parts of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

The Meteorological Forecasting Division said similar conditions are expected to continue this afternoon.

Some parts of the Himalayan region are likely to receive moderate rain and snowfall accompanied by thunder and lightning.

Many parts of the hilly region are also expected to receive rain, while some areas of the Tarai in Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces may experience thunderstorms and moderate rainfall.

A few areas of Madhesh Province and the Tarai region of Koshi Province are also likely to receive rainfall with thunder and lightning.

The weather office has warned of the possibility of heavy rainfall at one or two locations in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Strong winds are also possible in some parts of the Tarai in Koshi and Madhesh provinces.

Rainfall to continue at night

Tonight, the Himalayan and hilly regions are expected to remain generally cloudy.

The Tarai areas of Koshi and Sudurpaschim provinces will remain mostly cloudy, while the remaining Tarai areas will experience partly cloudy conditions.

Some parts of the Himalayan region are likely to receive moderate rain and snowfall accompanied by thunder and lightning.

Some areas of the hilly region may also experience moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning.

Similarly, some parts of the Tarai in Koshi and Lumbini provinces, as well as parts of Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki and Sudurpaschim provinces, are likely to receive moderate rainfall accompanied by thunder and lightning.

title.rendered: Landslide at Siddhababa tunnel section, Siddhartha Highway blocked

content.rendered:
Butwal, August 19

A landslide in the Siddhababa tunnel area of Tinau Rural Municipality-3, Palpa, has completely blocked the Siddhartha Highway. On Wednesday morning, the road was blocked when a landslide fell from above the road about 100 meters north of the point where the tunnel road begins from the Palpa side.

Bhim Lal Bhattarai, Deputy Superintendent of Police and chief of the District Police Office, Palpa, said that after the landslide stopped falling, work began using a dozer to clear the road, but it would take one to two hours.

Since the Siddhababa area faces a high risk of landslides, police have urged passengers and drivers to exercise caution.

With the highway blocked, traffic on the Palpa-Butwal road section has been affected.

title.rendered: Karnali Chief Minister Shahi to seek vote of confidence today

content.rendered:
Surkhet, August 19

Karnali Province Chief Minister Mangal Bahadur Shahi is set to seek a vote of confidence from the provincial assembly today. He is seeking the vote in accordance with the constitutional provision requiring a newly appointed chief minister to secure a vote of confidence from the provincial assembly.

Before the vote, the CPN-UML and CPN will hold discussions shortly. According to CPN leader Kalibahadur Malla, the two parties will discuss the vote of confidence, power-sharing arrangements, and the operation of the government in the coming days.

Following the discussions between the UML and CPN, they are also preparing to hold talks with other parties regarding the power-sharing arrangement and the vote of confidence.

Chief Minister Shahi has already registered a proposal seeking a vote of confidence at the Provincial Assembly Secretariat. The agenda has been set for the proposal to be discussed at the provincial assembly meeting scheduled for 3 pm today, after which Chief Minister Shahi will seek the vote of confidence.

If Chief Minister Shahi secures the vote of confidence, it will pave the way for the regular functioning of his government. Shahi has said that the government will then move forward by prioritising its policies and programmes, development projects, and contemporary issues facing the province.

Earlier, Yam Lal Kandel, who had become chief minister from the CPN-UML, resigned on July 25. Subsequently, on July 28, CPN parliamentary party leader Mangal Bahadur Shahi was appointed as the fifth chief minister of Karnali Province.

title.rendered: Pooja Chopra: I would love to work in Nepali cinema

content.rendered:
Pooja Chopra, Femina Miss India World 2009 and actor, is in Nepal for her third visit, a trip she says has left her with cherished memories of the country’s spirituality, food and warmth.

From attending the evening aarti at Pashupati Nath and visiting Boudhanath to enjoying Thakali food and momos, Chopra says Nepal feels “like home.”

In an interview with Onlinekhabar, she talks about her connection with Nepal, her admiration for the country’s young leadership, her journey from pageantry to cinema, and her hopes of collaborating with Nepali filmmakers.

Welcome to Nepal, Pooja ji. What brought you here this time, and what has your experience been like so far?

I had an appearance in Nepal a couple of nights ago and decided to take a day off to refresh my memories. This is my third time visiting- my first two trips were so beautiful and memorable that I just had to stay back for an extra day.

My experience has been amazing. Kathmandu has transformed so much since I was last here 13 years ago, in 2013, for an aviation academy appearance. Seeing the country’s growth and development during the drive from the airport to the hotel was wonderful.

We attended the Aarti at Pashupatinath Temple on Sunday. It was very crowded, but fortunately, my team and I met the chief Pandit ji and had a very peaceful darshan. After that, we went to Chandragiri and then had a full Nepali meal—Thakali thali, sel roti, and achar.

Later, I visited Boudhanath, where I tried laphing, soupy laphing, and keema noodles. These flavours are so unique and distinct from what we get in India; the very first bite of the soupy laphing was incredible and bursting with flavour.

I also reconnected with my Nepalese family. Manju Lama and her family have treated me like family since my previous visits, so I met Manju in the evening at Boudhanath Stupa before heading back to the hotel.

Did you get a chance to try some good momos while you were here?

Yes! When we ordered the Thakali thali at Jimbu Thakali, my driver recommended trying their chicken momos. They were delicious and so flavorful that we couldn’t finish them all, so I packed some for later. I was still too full from lunch to eat them in the evening, but I will definitely have them once more before I leave.

You can find good momos in India as well, right?

Not quite like these- the flavour profile is completely different. In India, momos are prepared differently. Here in Nepal, they aren’t overly spicy or heavy on masala, but they are rich in natural, delicious flavours.

You mentioned visiting Pashupatinath Temple yesterday. What did that experience mean to you personally?

As a spiritual person, I believe visits like this cannot just be planned; they are written in destiny. Sometimes trips get cancelled at the last minute, or weather disrupts your plans, but yesterday felt truly divine. We got darshan right at the front, and the Pandit ji explained the entire puja procession to me. It was deeply peaceful and enriching.

I am not much of a club person; I prefer visiting spiritual destinations. Just two months ago, I went to Haridwar for an event. My work often brings me to these sacred places, and I always return home with so many cherished memories. Nepal has always been exceptionally warm, beautiful, and kind to me. This was my third visit to Pashupati Nath, and during my previous trips, I also visited the Manakamana temple.

Nepal and India share deep cultural, spiritual, and cinematic connections. During this visit, what similarities or connections between the two countries have you personally felt?

The most intriguing part was working with the local hair and makeup team of four or five people. They were all speaking fluent Hindi and singing Hindi songs. When I asked how they spoke so fluently, they mentioned growing up watching Indian shows like Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi, Kasauti Jindagi Ki. While getting ready for the event, we played and sang along to songs like “Kabhi Alvida Na Kehna.” It was so much fun and did not feel like I was in another country at all. India and Nepal really are like siblings.

Even the written script looks a lot like Hindi. When I hear two Nepali people speaking, I can understand a lot of it, so it really feels like home.

You might know that Hindi cinema is extremely popular here in Nepal—in fact, some Hindi films earn more here than local films do.

Absolutely. Hindi cinema, daily soaps, songs—everyone here is updated on everything! It really doesn’t feel like I’m in another country.

Would you be interested in working in Nepalese cinema or collaborating with local filmmakers and artists if the right project came your way?

Of course! I can’t speak the language, unfortunately, but just as North Indian actors do in South Indian films, I would love to do it. It would give me a wonderful opportunity to stay in this beautiful country. I would love to collaborate, wear traditional Nepalese outfits, travel to places like Pokhara that I haven’t visited yet, and shoot songs there. It would be amazing.

Do you follow any artists in Nepal?

In Nepal, apart from my family friends, I’ve been following your new Prime Minister. Personally, I think he’s phenomenal. The changes he has brought about are impressive. I spoke to a few locals, including my driver, and they are all very happy with him. When you see a neighbouring country progress, it feels amazing. He is a hero of sorts—young, ambitious, with a great vision and heading in the right direction.

Whenever someone stands up for what’s right, people will support him, and he has that support. At 36, he is young, so the sky is the limit for him. I hope he continues on this path and that the country develops even more by the time I visit next. He is definitely someone I follow and admire.

You won Femina Miss India World 2009 and went on to represent India at Miss World. Looking back, how did that pageant transform your life and shape the person you are today?

Completely. Imagine being a regular middle-class girl studying in Pune, riding a non-geared scooter from home to college. Suddenly, you win Miss India, and your life transforms overnight. I remember the exact second I realised my life had changed: right after I was crowned, waved, and stepped down from the stage, seven or eight bodyguards suddenly surrounded me for protection. The media was crowding around with microphones, asking questions. They rushed me into a car; people were knocking on the windows, and as the car drove off, I thought, “My life has changed.” Going from an ordinary college student to someone the entire nation wants to know about happened in seconds. I couldn’t be more grateful; it’s the best thing that ever happened to me.

Your journey moved from beauty pageants to cinema, starting with films like Ponnar Shankar and Commando: A One Man Army. What was the biggest challenge in proving yourself as an actor rather than simply being known as a pageant winner?

Coming from a non-film background made it very challenging. I had taken acting courses, but I believe true acting can’t be taught—it has to come from within. I am naturally a spontaneous person, so understanding the mechanics of acting took some time. But when the audience accepts your work, it validates that you’re on the right path. Ponnar Shankar did well, and Commando was received wonderfully across the country. I was fortunate to work with great directors and talented actors like Neeraj Pandey, Manoj Bajpayee, Vidyut Jammwal, Sharman Joshi, and Sidharth Malhotra, learning a lot from each of them. The learning process is still ongoing.

By the way, my next film is Jeevan Bheema Yojana with Arshad Warsi, who plays a double role. It’s a fun, wholesome family film—I only do family films!

At this stage of your career, what kinds of characters and stories are you most interested in exploring?

I want to be part of stories that are realistic, inspiring, or leave the audience with a meaningful message. I’d love to do biopics and inspiring stories. I also really enjoy comedy! However, I can’t do horror films because I get scared far too easily. People try to convince me that shooting a horror movie isn’t scary in person, but I just can’t bring myself to do it. Similarly, if a role requires me to be extremely bold, I hesitate because I’m naturally quite shy.

Your TED Talk, Write Your Own Destiny: Journey of a Once Abandoned Girl Child, shares a deeply personal story of resilience. What message would you give to young women in India or Nepal who are pursuing ambitious dreams despite difficult circumstances?

My story has been unique. When I was born, my father refused to accept a second girl child since my elder sister was already born. My mother was asked to either abandon me or put me in an orphanage; otherwise, we couldn’t stay in his house. My mother chose me and walked away, raising my sister and me single-handedly.

Hats off to her—she is my true hero. Even at 72, she is still working. Growing up, I saw her work double shifts to support us alone. To this day, she gives me the motivation to work hard and make her proud. She deserves the world.

My advice to young people is to find your core motivation—understand why you want to achieve your goal, whether it’s entering the film industry, becoming a pilot, joining the Air Force, or anything else. Have a dream, stay motivated every day, work hard, and believe in yourself. Anything you can dream of can be achieved. If someone has done it before, you can do it too; if no one has, you can be the first.

That is wonderful advice. Having experienced Nepal and its people firsthand, what will you be taking back with you from this visit, and what message do you have for your Nepali fans?

First of all, I want to say a huge thank you to everyone in Nepal. People here are extraordinarily warm and welcoming. As I mentioned, it truly feels like home. I am taking back precious memories and prasad from Pashupatinath Temple. My heart was already full of fond memories of Nepal, and this trip has added even more.

title.rendered: NIMB officials to remain in office despite criminal case, legal provisions show

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 19

Nepal Investment Mega Bank (NIMB) Chairman, most board members and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) are set to continue in their respective positions despite the government filing a criminal case against them, as existing banking laws do not require their suspension merely because a case has been filed.

The government has filed a case at the Kathmandu District Court against NIMB directors and senior officials over the recovery of Rs 4.6 billion through the sale of collateral belonging to Smart Telecom.

The case has raised questions over whether the bank’s chairman, directors and CEO can continue in their positions.

However, provisions of the Bank and Financial Institutions Act (BAFIA) and directives issued by Nepal Rastra Bank indicate that the filing of a criminal case alone does not automatically suspend or remove a bank director or CEO.

Sections 16, 17, 18 and 19 of BAFIA set out the qualifications, disqualifications and circumstances under which a director of a bank or financial institution cannot remain in office.

Section 102 of the Act also provides for the suspension of a bank’s board of directors. However, none of these provisions state that a board or individual director must be suspended or removed simply because a criminal case has been filed against them.

Instead, Section 18(1)(tha) states that a person is disqualified from serving as a director if they have been convicted by a court in Nepal or another country and have not completed 10 years since serving the sentence for offences including theft, fraud, forgery, cheating, corruption, an offence involving moral turpitude or a banking offence.

This means the directors facing the current case would become ineligible for the position only if they are convicted, according to officials familiar with the legal provisions.

The Act also contains separate provisions governing the appointment and terms of service of a CEO.

Section 29 states that, among other qualifications, a CEO must not be disqualified from becoming a director under Section 18(1).

According to a Nepal Rastra Bank official, this provision also does not allow a CEO to be removed or suspended merely because a case has been filed before the allegations are proven.

Section 102 of BAFIA outlines the circumstances under which a bank’s board of directors can be suspended. Under the provision, only Nepal Rastra Bank can suspend the board.

The provision allows the central bank to suspend a board for up to three years and take the institution under its control if it is convinced that a licensed institution has violated the BAFIA, Nepal Rastra Bank Act, related rules or directives, failed or is likely to fail to fulfil its obligations, is not operating properly, or has acted against the interests of shareholders or depositors.

A Nepal Rastra Bank source said the provision does not provide for the suspension of directors simply because they have been accused in a criminal case.

A senior central bank official said NIMB’s chairman, directors and CEO therefore continue to perform their regular responsibilities unless a court establishes their criminal liability.

“Bank CEOs and directors can no longer remain in office only after a criminal offence is established,” the official said. “At present, NIMB’s chairman, board and CEO continue their regular work. The matter will be dealt with according to the court’s verdict.”

An NIMB official also said the bank had sought necessary legal advice and concluded that its directors and CEO do not need to step down.

“The board continues its regular work as before, and the CEO is also carrying out his responsibilities. There is no ambiguity on this matter,” the official said.

title.rendered: Six Nepali athletes eye national records and breakthrough at 20th Asian Games

content.rendered:
For Nepal’s athletics team, the 20th Asian Games will be about more than simply taking part. Six athletes will represent Nepal in athletics at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Japan from September 19 to October 4, with several arriving at the continental event carrying ambitions of breaking long-standing national records — and, if everything falls into place, challenging for a medal.

The six athletes — four men and two women — are currently training twice a day at Dasharath Stadium as part of their preparations.

The men’s team comprises Som Bahadur Kumal, Mukesh Bahadur Pal, Rajan Rokaya and Khadak Bahadur Khadka, while Santoshi Shrestha and Purnalakshmi Neupane will compete in the women’s events.

For Shrestha and Kumal, the Games will be a return to familiar territory. Shrestha will make her second Asian Games appearance, while Kumal will compete at the continental Games for the third time.

For Pal, Rokaya, Khadka and Neupane, however, Aichi-Nagoya will be their first Asian Games.

Nepal’s athletics athletes have been appearing at the Asian Games since the inaugural edition in New Delhi in 1951. Yet, despite that long history, the country has never won an athletics medal at the continental Games.

That record stands in contrast to athletics’ contribution to some of Nepal’s biggest international sporting achievements.

Jit Bahadur KC won Nepal’s first international athletics medal at the 1973 Asian Athletics Championships, taking bronze in the marathon. He repeated the feat in 1975.

Ajit Kumar Yadav later created history by winning gold at the 2019 Asian Youth Athletics Championships, while Deepak Adhikari won a historic gold at the 2022 Asian Cross Country Championships in Kathmandu.

Now, six athletes are hoping to add another chapter to that history.

Khadka chasing a record that has stood for nearly four decades

For Khadak Bahadur Khadka, the Asian Games debut comes with a very specific target: break one of Nepal’s most enduring athletics records.

The Nepal Army marathon runner will compete in the men’s marathon and has set his sights on the national record held by legendary runner Baikuntha Manandhar.

Manandhar ran 2 hours, 15 minutes and 03 seconds at the 1987 South Asian Games in Kolkata. The record has survived numerous attempts to break it over the years.

Khadka believes he is now close.

He has reduced his marathon time from around 2 hours and 18 minutes to approximately 2 hours and 15 minutes and wants to make the final jump in Aichi-Nagoya.

“Baikuntha Manandhar’s achievement has made us chase that time even today. I want to thank him. He also blesses us and tells us that we are getting close and should keep doing well,” Khadka said.

“If the weather, my health and everything else support me there, I believe I can break the record.”

Khadka, who is originally from Jajarkot, came to athletics through an unusual route. He first joined the Nepal Army as a soldier and spent 11 years in service before becoming involved seriously in competitive running.

“I was a soldier first and an athlete later. I did not even know that running was a sport,” he said.

His entry into athletics came through the army’s physical training and sporting activities. He eventually chose marathon running without competing in other events first.

For Khadka, simply making it to the Asian Games is already a significant achievement. But he wants to use the opportunity to chase a record that has survived for almost four decades.

Santoshi wants more than another medal

Santoshi Shrestha, the “Golden Girl” of Nepali athletics after her historic gold at the 2019 South Asian Games, will return to the Asian Games with two national records already under her name.

She will compete in the women’s 5,000m and 10,000m, events in which she holds the national records.

Her 5,000m record stands at 16:36.61, while her 10,000m record is 34:47.77.

Shrestha knows competing in two events will bring additional pressure, but she believes the preparation is similar for both.

“There is some pressure when competing in two events because if the event you have focused on comes later, it can create stress. But the training for both is the same. During the Games, you have to handle the pressure,” she said.

The 2019 South Asian Games champion is realistic about the medal challenge in Aichi-Nagoya. The gap between Nepal and the continent’s best runners remains, but she believes that gap is narrowing.

“We have to give our best. We don’t know whether that will result in a national record or a personal best. We have to be realistic about the medal,” she said.

“There is a gap, but we are working hard and that gap has become much smaller. If we break records, we can create a path for the next generation.”

For Shrestha, the goal is therefore not limited to the medal table. A strong performance and new records could help create a stronger foundation for athletes who come after her.

Mukesh wants to rewrite two national records

For Mukesh Bahadur Pal, the Aichi-Nagoya Games will be his first Asian Games, but the occasion itself is not new territory.

The Nepal Army middle-distance runner has already competed at the World Championships, Asian Championships and South Asian competitions.

He will race in the men’s 1,500m and 5,000m, with national records in both events firmly in his sights.

“I have competed at the World, South Asian and Asian Championships, but this is my first Asian Games. I am excited and have the goal of doing well,” Pal said.

His ambitions extend beyond simply participating.

In the 1,500m, Gopal Bahadur Adhikari holds the national record of 3:46.63, set at the 1993 South Asian Games. The mark has remained untouched for 33 years.

Pal is currently running around 3:49 and believes the record is within reach.

“I have been trying to break the national record in the 1,500m for a long time. I have worked very hard and suffered for it. I am getting closer. This time, I am determined to break it,” he said.

The 5,000m national record belongs to Rajendra Bhandari, who clocked 14:04.89 at the 2004 Athens Olympics.

Pal wants to challenge that record too.

He believes breaking the 1,500m mark could also have significance beyond his own career, potentially bringing Nepal closer to the Asian Games podium in future editions.

“If I can break the 1,500m record, there will be a possibility of a medal at future Asian Games. That is why I am working hard,” he said.

Pal also hopes to put Nepal on the international athletics map.

“The government has invested in us, and we are putting in our blood, sweat and effort. My attempt will be to give the country a medal. Even if I cannot win one, I want to show the world how much a Nepali athlete can achieve.”

Rajan shifts focus from marathon to 10,000m

Rajan Rokaya will have two events on his schedule — the 10,000m and marathon — but his attention is increasingly turning toward the shorter distance.

Like Khadka, Rokaya is a Nepal Army runner and has traditionally competed in the marathon. He also raced in the marathon at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou. This time, however, the 10,000m is his priority.

“My two events are the 10km and marathon. My focus will be on the 10km. I will also run the marathon,” Rokaya said.

Moving from marathon training to the faster 10,000m requires additional work on speed, he said.

“I am a marathon runner, so I have to work harder to adapt to the 10km. I have to struggle a little more. But my speed has been very good in the closed camp.”

Rokaya is following in the footsteps of fellow Nepal Army athlete Deepak Adhikari, who set the national record in the men’s 10,000m at the Hangzhou Asian Games.

Adhikari clocked 29:35.06 in Hangzhou.

With Adhikari not competing this time, Rokaya will take on the event.

He is reluctant to make a precise prediction about his result.

“Ninety-five percent is our effort and five percent is luck. Until the race starts and we reach the ribbon, you cannot say what will happen,” he said.

Purnalakshmi targets a national record on her debut

For Purnalakshmi Neupane, Aichi-Nagoya will be a first taste of the Asian Games. The Nepal Army athlete will compete in the women’s 1,500m and 5,000m, sharing the 5,000m field with Shrestha. Her main focus, however, is the 1,500m.

Neupane is targeting the national record in the event, currently held by Saraswati Bhattarai, who clocked 4:33.94 at the Rio Olympics.

A debut at the Asian Games will therefore come with a clear personal target: close the gap to a record that has stood for a decade.

Som Kumal has the podium in sight

Among Nepal’s six athletes, Som Bahadur Kumal has the most Asian Games experience. A third appearance awaits the middle-distance runner, who will compete only in the 800m this time.

Kumal competed in both the 400m and 800m at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and again in two events at the 2018 edition? No — at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou.

His biggest achievement came in Jakarta, where he set the national 800m record at 1:50.25.

Four years later in Hangzhou, he came close to improving it, finishing in 1:50.38.

This time, Kumal has decided to focus entirely on the 800m.

His recent training times have been around 1:49, giving him reason to believe he can lower his national record.

The bronze medalist at the previous Asian Games clocked 1:48.51.

That puts Kumal within striking distance, according to Nepal Athletics Association Secretary RK Bista, if the athlete can continue improving.

Three years of preparation behind the team

The six athletes are now training twice daily at Dasharath Stadium under coach Uttam Khatri.

They have been preparing under the Mission 2026 programme for around three years and are currently staying in a closed camp alongside athletes from other sports.

The National Sports Council and Nepal Athletics Association are supporting the preparation.

Unlike many team sports, athletics is ultimately measured in numbers — seconds, minutes and metres. The team is therefore using timing data to assess how close the Nepali athletes are to the level required to challenge for medals.

According to Athletics Association Secretary RK Bista, the athletes’ current performances are being compared with the timings of athletes who won bronze medals at the previous Asian Games.

The goal is not only to prepare them physically but to give them a realistic understanding of where they stand against Asia’s best.

The athletes are also expected to compete in the Indian Open World Athletics Continental Tour Silver-level event, beginning in India on August 22. The final number of Nepali participants has not yet been confirmed, although Bista said the Asian Games camp athletes are likely to be included, along with possibly one additional athlete.

For a country that has sent athletes to every Asian Games since 1951 without winning an athletics medal, Aichi-Nagoya represents another opportunity.

The six runners know the gap remains difficult to bridge. But they also know that records are there to be challenged — and that for some of them, the numbers are already getting close.

Nepal’s six athletics representatives at Aichi-Nagoya

Som Bahadur Kumal — Men’s 800m

Mukesh Bahadur Pal — Men’s 1,500m and 5,000m

Rajan Rokaya — Men’s 10,000m and marathon

Khadka Bahadur Khadka — Men’s marathon

Santoshi Shrestha — Women’s 5,000m and 10,000m

Purnalakshmi Neupane — Women’s 1,500m and 5,000m

title.rendered: What Shashank Koirala’s rise means for Purna Bahadur Khadka in Nepali Congress

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

A Supreme Court order has given fresh momentum to the faction of the Nepali Congress opposed to the party establishment. But the three-day national gathering that followed has also triggered a subtle shift in the faction’s internal power balance, with Dr Shashank Koirala emerging as its new political coordinator and Purna Bahadur Khadka’s role becoming less prominent.

The faction used the gathering, held in Kathmandu from August 14 to 16, to demonstrate its strength after the Supreme Court ordered a review in the dispute within the party.

Former Nepali Congress president Sher Bahadur Deuba, who returned to Nepal just a day before the gathering, became its chief guest. Senior leaders from the non-establishment faction were at Tribhuvan International Airport to welcome him.

His presence changed the dynamics of the gathering.

Had Deuba not returned, Koirala, who had been designated coordinator of the gathering, would have served as chief guest.

But the more consequential development was what happened to Khadka, a longtime Deuba loyalist who had been playing the leading role in the faction’s activities while Deuba was away from active politics.

Khadka agreed to attend after assurances party would not split

Khadka had initially been reluctant to participate in the gathering.

As acting Nepali Congress president, he had taken the position that he would not attend if the gathering was intended to pave the way for a split in the Nepali Congress.

The situation changed after the Supreme Court ordered a review of the earlier decision. With the immediate prospect of a party split receding, Deuba also decided to attend the gathering.

Koirala, accompanied by NP Saud, went to Khadka’s residence to persuade him to participate.

According to leaders familiar with the discussions, Khadka told them he would attend if the gathering was genuinely intended to preserve party unity and there was an assurance that the party would not split.

He eventually joined the opening session. But he did not attend the closing day.

That absence became significant because the gathering made a decision that effectively changed who would coordinate the faction’s activities going forward.

Koirala takes charge of convention preparations

The gathering decided that Koirala would lead the group’s activities until the 15th General Convention, working under Deuba’s direction.

The first point of the gathering’s decision states that the coordinator of the national gathering and convention will coordinate the party’s regular activities required until the 15th General Convention under the direction of the party president.

With that decision, Koirala effectively moved into the faction’s second position.

This is significant because Khadka had previously played the central role in calling meetings of the non-establishment faction, pursuing the legal process and setting the date for the national gathering.

The shift does not mean Khadka has formally lost his position as acting party president.

Non-establishment leader Guru Baral rejected that interpretation.

“Purna Bahadur is the acting president. We asked Shashank to lead the work related to the general convention,” Baral told Onlinekhabar.

But Khadka’s absence from the final day and the decision to place Koirala in charge of the faction’s future activities have nevertheless created speculation about his political position.

One leader from the faction said Khadka stayed away because he would not have authority to lead the group’s activities while serving as acting Nepali Congress president.

“When Sher Bahadur Deuba was not active in politics, it would have been natural for Purna Bahadur to lead the group,” the leader said. “But once the acting president was not given responsibility to lead the activities of our group, Purna Bahadur did not attend.”

The same pattern emerged over the faction’s contact office

The tension over roles within the faction had already surfaced when the group established a separate contact office at Chundevi.

Senior leaders including Bimalendra Nidhi, Krishna Prasad Sitaula, Prakashman Singh and Dr Prakash Sharan Mahat were involved in establishing the office.

Second-tier leaders including Min Bishwakarma, Mohan Basnet and Kanchharam Tamang also played an active role.

Khadka had initially taken the position that he would not visit the office if it was being established with the intention of splitting the party.

According to leaders, he agreed to attend its inauguration only after being assured that the initiative was not aimed at dividing the Nepali Congress.

The office formally began operating on July 6.

The leaders who took the initiative to establish the office also helped position Koirala as the leader of the faction.

Nidhi, Sitaula, Singh and other former office bearers gathered at the office and announced Koirala as the group’s leader.

“We have unanimously made him our coordinator and leader. We have chosen him as the leader of our group,” Nidhi had said.

From Deuba’s closest ally to a possible presidential contender

Khadka’s changing role is particularly notable because of his long association with Deuba.

He has served as acting party president, vice president, general secretary, joint general secretary and Central Working Committee member from Deuba’s faction.

Even during the current dispute, Khadka has repeatedly maintained that preserving Nepali Congress unity is more important than securing a position.

Nepali Congress leader Ramhari Khatiwada said Khadka’s decisions should be understood from that perspective.

“Purna Bahadur said he would not even go to the contact office if the Nepali Congress was going to split. Once it became clear that the party would not split, he went to the gathering. For him, unity is important, not the position,” Khatiwada told Onlinekhabar.

Khadka had, however, faced criticism from within the party while serving as acting president.

Critics accused him of failing to effectively perform his responsibilities when Deuba travelled to Singapore for medical treatment, with the Central Working Committee meeting continuing for around one and a half months without reaching a meaningful conclusion.

Khadka has defended himself by saying that he faced criticism precisely because he stood against a split and in favour of preserving party unity.

Khadka’s next move could be the general convention

The national gathering has now shifted the leadership of the faction opposed to the special general convention from Khadka to Koirala.

Khadka had earlier received the signatures collected for the proposed special general convention while serving as acting party president.

The faction subsequently approached both the Election Commission and the Supreme Court under Khadka’s leadership, seeking to invalidate the special general convention.

Following the latest gathering, however, Koirala has been given the mandate to lead the faction’s preparations for the 15th General Convention.

That could leave Khadka with a different political objective.

A leader from the faction believes Khadka may now focus on preparing to contest for the party presidency himself at the general convention.

“Whatever happened before has happened. Now Purna Bahadur will prepare to contest for party president at the general convention,” the leader said.

For now, Deuba remains the central figure around whom the faction continues to organise. But the national gathering has made one thing increasingly clear: as the Nepali Congress moves toward its 15th General Convention, the internal leadership of the faction is no longer as straightforward as it once was.

title.rendered: Balen camp holds back names for RSP nominations

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 19

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) is set to hold a meeting of its Central Committee on August 21.

The meeting will discuss several issues, including the nomination of Central Committee members, office-bearers, Secretariat members and heads of party departments. It will also discuss the nomination of members to the central committee responsible for selecting candidates for the upcoming local elections.

The party has yet to complete nominations that were required following its general convention in Chitwan. Although the issue has been included in the agenda for the upcoming meeting, leaders close to Prime Minister and senior RSP leader Balendra Shah have indicated that they may not submit names for the vacant positions yet.

According to a leader from the Shah faction, discussions have been held on not recommending names for vacant office-bearer and Central Committee positions at this stage. The faction is expected to submit its nominations to party Chair Rabi Lamichhane only after the party’s Madhesh provincial convention, the leader said.

The RSP has yet to complete its provincial convention in Madhesh, including in all eight districts of the province. The Madhesh convention had been postponed while the party proceeded with its central general convention.

Under the party’s statute, the chairperson has the authority to nominate one vice-chairperson, one general secretary, two joint general secretaries, one treasurer, one joint treasurer, one spokesperson, three deputy spokespersons and 51 Central Committee members.

title.rendered: Why a vote on taxing California’s billionaires is being watched around the world

content.rendered:
In November, California will vote on a proposal to levy a one-off 5% tax on the wealth of all billionaires in the state.

Google co-founder and billionaire Sergey Brin has already spent US$100 million on political donations to a group opposing the tax. Brin is hoping to avoid a potential tax bill of US$13 billion, a return of roughly 130 to 1 if that investment is successful.

Advocates of the billionaire tax claim it would raise US$100 billion in revenue, to be allocated directly to state-funded healthcare, food assistance and public education.

Supporters of the union-backed proposal also highlight that most billionaires currently pay lower marginal rates of tax than the average worker, and that the revenue is desperately needed to fill gaps in funding created by US President Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid.

Its critics, which include California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, argue the measure will drive billionaires and their tax revenue to leave the state.

Taxing the ultrawealthy

Similar measures targeting the ultrawealthy are currently under consideration around the world.

In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has proposed a 2% income tax increase for those earning over US$1 million, and passed a property surcharge tax on second homes. Other US states – including Washington state, Maine and Minnesota – have passed or are considering similar income or wealth tax measures.

In the United Kingdom, a group of 120 millionaires have launched a “Proud to Pay” campaign asking the government to levy an additional 2% tax on wealth over £10 million.

Spiralling global inequality

Behind the public discussion of California’s billionaire tax lies a much deeper debate about spiralling global inequality.

Recent data from the US shows the share of economic output flowing to workers has dropped to a record low of 52.9% in 2026. This means for every US$100 the economy produces, workers take home US$52.90 in pay, the smallest share since records began in 1947.

Similar trends have been observed around the world.

Conversely, the wealth of billionaires has accelerated rapidly. As of 2026, Forbes reports a global record 3,428 billionaires.

Perhaps most symptomatically, in June Elon Musk briefly became the world’s first trillionaire after the public launch of SpaceX. His wealth now sits at around US$800 billion.

The causes of inequality

Some blame globalisation for this explosion of inequality, but there are two other important related factors to consider as well.

The first is the global decline of the trade union movement. With union membership and power declining around the world, the ability of workers to negotiate for better wages has declined.

The second is a trend of corporate consolidation into a small number of large “superstar firms”. These companies, which include tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, and Uber, wield monopoly-like powers. This reduces competition and allows these firms to drive down wages.

The rise of artificial intelligence and automation will only accelerate these trends, enabling the largest firms to shed even more workers even as the firms’ output and profitability continues to climb.

Workers feel the crunch

For the last couple of decades, stagnating wages have been propped up by cheap access to credit. With central banks using unconventional policies to keep interest rates low, household spending has remained largely stable, funded by an increase in household debt.

However, with inflation rising, central banks around the world have pushed up interest rates from emergency lows during the pandemic, cutting off the source of cheap credit. With inflation rising faster than wages, the effect has been real declines in living standards.

Unsurprisingly voters are unhappy at this “cost of living” crisis, and all over the world have turned away from incumbents and established parties.

A jump to the left?

If the previous decade’s politics have been dominated by dissent on the right, many countries are now seeing the emergence of stronger dissent on the left.

After Mamdani’s headline-grabbing victory in New York, Democratic Socialists have ridden a wave of momentum to win a series of primary races. Beyond the US, we can note left-independent Catherine Connolly’s election as Irish president, the rise of the Greens in the UK, and the recent resurgence of left-wing Die Linke in Germany.

These different parties and leaders all share a focus on combating growing global inequalities of wealth and power. Billionaires, the most obvious and visible symbol of global wealth inequalities, are an obvious target.

However, as California’s proposal shows, attempts to rein in the wealth and power of billionaires should expect furious backlash from billionaires themselves.

In addition to Brin’s US$100 million, other billionaire donors including Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt and Chris Larsen have also spent significantly to oppose the tax. Brin’s campaign committee has also organised competing ballot propositions which, if passed, would nullify the tax.

For now, polling suggests the billionaire tax is supported by a majority of voters. More than 1.6 million Californians signed the petition to put the tax on the November ballot.

The future of wealth inequality

California’s coming election will serve as an important test of the political power of the billionaire class, and the broader health of American democracy.

Yet even if the tax is successful, taxing billionaires only treats a symptom of global inequality, rather than addressing its underlying causes.

A policy agenda for seriously addressing wealth inequality must also therefore include a much broader suite of measures. These might include improving workers’ bargaining power, breaking up monopolies and public ownership of AI technology.

Without these structural fixes, we should expect voter anger and the current political instability around the world to continue to escalate.

title.rendered: Aamir Akhtar and Nadeem Shahid join hands to launch T-10 League in Italy, 6 teams to compete

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal’s former international cricketer and Everest Premier League (EPL) founder Aamir Akhtar and former English cricketer Nadeem Shahid are set to organise a city-based franchise T-10 cricket league in Italy.

With the official backing of the Italian Cricket Federation, the first edition of “Italia T-10 Cricket” will be held in Rome from November 7 to 15. Six city-based franchise teams will compete in the tournament.

The league will be organised through Apex T-10 Limited. The company, founded by Akhtar and Shahid, aims to develop cricket in associate nations through T-10 franchise competitions.

Since a 10-over match finishes in roughly 90 minutes, the organisers say the T-10 format is being promoted as a means of bringing cricket to new audiences. The tournament’s matches will be broadcast live in more than 30 countries.

Shahid is co-founder and chief executive officer of Apex T-10. He played first-class cricket in England for Essex and Surrey for over two decades and also represented England A.

Akhtar is a former Nepali international cricketer who played a significant role in developing franchise cricket in Nepal by establishing the Everest Premier League there. He aims to apply that same experience in Italy to develop local players and raise the standard of domestic cricket.

The Italian Cricket Federation has said it is officially backing the league and will coordinate with the ICC on the approval process. As cricket prepares to return at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, this franchise league launching in Italy is being viewed as an important initiative for the sport’s expansion there.

title.rendered: 6,600 livestock receive artificial insemination in Syangja

content.rendered:
Syangja, August 18

The number of farmers opting for artificial insemination for livestock in Syangja has been increasing every year. Farmers have been increasingly turning to artificial insemination due to its role in improving breeds, reducing costs, and the declining number of farmers raising buffalo bulls and oxen.

The Veterinary Hospital and Livestock Services Office, Syangja, has been providing artificial insemination services at various locations across the district in coordination with local governments. According to office chief Dr Rupesh Shrestha, buffaloes account for the highest number of artificial inseminations in the district. The service has subsequently been expanded to cows, goats and pigs.

According to office data, artificial insemination was carried out on 6,695 livestock in the fiscal year 2082/83. Of them, 5,330 were buffaloes, 1,218 cows, 97 goats and 51 pigs. In the previous fiscal year, 2081/82, artificial insemination was carried out on 5,040 livestock. That year, the service was provided to 3,828 buffaloes, 1,018 cows, 116 goats and 15 pigs.

Similarly, 3,840 livestock received artificial insemination in fiscal year 2080/81. Dr Shrestha said the service was provided to 2,677 buffaloes, 1,122 cows and 41 goats that year. The three-year data shows a significant increase in the number of livestock receiving artificial insemination services in Syangja. In particular, 1,655 more livestock received the service in the latest fiscal year compared with the previous year.

Andhikhola records highest number

Among the local governments, Andhikhola Rural Municipality recorded the highest number of artificial inseminations in fiscal year 2082/83, with the service provided to 1,794 livestock. The lowest number was recorded in Biruwa Rural Municipality, where 56 livestock received the service, according to the office.

Similarly, artificial insemination was carried out on 1,127 livestock in Galyang Municipality, 813 in Waling Municipality, 777 in Putalibazar Municipality, 754 in Arjunchaupari Rural Municipality, 523 through the Veterinary Hospital and Livestock Services Office, 404 in Bhirkot Municipality, 152 in Chapakot Municipality, 115 in Fedikhola Rural Municipality, 95 in Harinas Rural Municipality and 85 in Kaligandaki Rural Municipality.

According to the office, the service is being operated in various local governments across the district, targeting livestock farmers. Office chief Dr Shrestha said artificial insemination services are being provided based on farmers’ demand in coordination with local governments.

Breed improvement also reduces costs

Dr Shrestha says improved livestock breeds are a major reason for the growing interest among farmers in artificial insemination. He said artificial insemination aimed at producing improved breeds can help increase productivity from livestock farming.

Similarly, the declining number of farmers raising buffalo bulls and oxen is another reason for the increased use of artificial insemination. The office said artificial insemination is comparatively more convenient for farmers when livestock farming costs and management requirements are taken into consideration.

In Syangja, artificial insemination services for pigs were introduced only from the previous fiscal year. Although the service had already been available for other livestock, it was newly expanded to pigs, Dr Shrestha said.

The increasing number of artificial inseminations indicates that farmers in the district are also becoming more interested in commercial livestock farming, according to the office. Increasing productivity through breed improvement could also help increase farmers’ income from livestock farming.

title.rendered: Nepal A begin second Top End T20 campaign with Asian Games in sight

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal are set to make their second consecutive appearance in Australia’s Top End T20 Series, with the Nepal A team heading to Darwin for the tournament beginning August 21.

Unlike last year, when Nepal sent its senior national team, the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) has selected a 15-member Nepal A squad for this year’s tournament. Anil Kumar Sah will captain the side.

The senior team’s commitments in the ACC Premier Cup have prompted CAN to send the A team to Australia.

The tournament will provide Nepal’s emerging players with exposure to Australian conditions and competitive opposition. Nepal will play six league matches against NT Strike, Bangladesh High Performance, Hobart Hurricanes Academy, ACT Comets, Kingsmen and Victoria CA XI.

Nepal will open its campaign against NT Strike on August 21 before facing Bangladesh High Performance on August 22. The team will then play Hobart Hurricanes Academy on August 24, ACT Comets on August 26, Kingsmen on August 27 and Victoria CA XI on August 29.

Building on last year’s experience

Nepal made its Top End T20 debut last year with the senior national team. It won two of its six league matches and lost four.

Nepal defeated Hobart Hurricanes Academy and Melbourne Renegades Academy but lost to Melbourne Stars Academy, NT Strike, Bangladesh A and Pakistan Shaheens.

Five players from last year’s squad—Kushal Bhurtel, Kushal Malla, Lokesh Bam, Rupesh Singh and Shah Alam—are returning for the tournament this year.

Bhurtel’s inclusion gives the A team an added boost. The regular national team member has been rested from ODI cricket for a period and has been included in the squad for the T20 tournament.

Captain Sah said the tournament would be a major opportunity for the players.

“Our preparations have been good. We have also spoken to senior players about the conditions there and learned how to prepare mentally,” Sah said. “Playing this tournament as Nepal A is a big opportunity and will provide valuable exposure.”

A test ahead of the Asian Games

The Top End T20 Series will also serve as an important preparation platform for players hoping to make Nepal’s squad for the Asian Games in Japan, which begin on September 24.

Several players involved in the tournament are part of Nepal’s preliminary Asian Games plans, although the final squad could change after the Australia tour.

Nepal can play at least six matches in the Top End T20. If it reaches the semi-finals and final, the team could play up to eight matches.

Nepal’s 15-member squad

Anil Kumar Sah (captain), Kushal Bhurtel, Lokesh Bam, Trit Raj Das, Mayan Yadav, Pawan Sarraf, Dipak Dumre, Kushal Malla, Rashid Khan, Narayan Joshi, Aakash Chand, Shahab Alam, Bipin Khatri, Yuvraj Khatri and Rijan Dhakal.

Nepal’s Top End T20 fixtures

August 21: vs NT Strike

August 22: vs Bangladesh High Performance

August 24: vs Hobart Hurricanes Academy

August 26: vs ACT Comets

August 27: vs Kingsmen

August 29: vs Victoria CA XI

The 2026 Top End T20 Series runs from August 21 to 30 in Darwin.

title.rendered: Nepal thrash Karnataka by 116 runs in first warm-up match

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal made an emphatic start to their preparations for the upcoming ACC Premier Cup, defeating Karnataka by 116 runs in their first practice match in India.

Batting first after winning the toss, Nepal were bowled out for 188 runs in 45 overs.

Aasif Sheikh top-scored for Nepal with 49 runs from 70 balls, hitting two fours and a six. Opener Dev Khanal contributed 27 off 43 balls with five fours, while Ishan Pandey scored 34 off 49 balls, hitting three fours.

Sundeep Jora added 27 off 37 balls with two fours, while Bashir Ahmed remained unbeaten on 19 from 27 balls.

Gulshan Jha scored 11 off 16 balls, while Rohit Paudel made four runs. Karan KC was dismissed without scoring, while captain Sandeep Lamichhane and Sher Malla scored two and one run respectively.

Nepal suffered an early setback when Arjun Kumal was dismissed for a duck after facing four balls. However, Aasif, Dev and Ishan steadied the innings and helped Nepal build a competitive total.

Karnataka’s Keerthi M was the standout bowler, taking five wickets for 20 runs from eight overs. Aditya Goel, Aravind Kumar Rai, Chirant Shivrudra, Sagar Gautam and Samarth Srinivas took one wicket each.

Karnataka collapse for 72

Chasing 189, Karnataka struggled against Nepal’s bowling attack and were bowled out for just 72 runs in 28 overs.

Sharath Srinivas was Karnataka’s top scorer with 32 runs from 65 balls, including three fours. Revanth Bairy scored 10, while Santosh Singh contributed nine.

The rest of Karnataka’s batting line-up failed to make an impact, with Lochan Gowda scoring two, Tushar Singh and Samarth Srinivas dismissed without scoring, and Sanjay Ashwin making one.

Ritesh Bhatkal scored six, Sagar Gautam was dismissed for a duck, Keerthi M made three and Aditya Goel scored six.

For Nepal, Karan KC led the bowling attack, taking two wickets for just nine runs in five overs.

Lalit Rajbanshi, Sher Malla and Bashir Ahmed also took two wickets each, while Sandeep Lamichhane claimed one.

The comprehensive victory gives Nepal a strong start to their warm-up campaign as they continue preparations for the ACC Premier Cup.
