title.rendered: Nepali Congress calls for constitutional amendment commission led by former chief justice

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Nepali Congress has called for the formation of a Constitutional Amendment Recommendation Commission headed by a retired chief justice of the Supreme Court to recommend reforms while protecting the fundamental values of the Constitution.

A meeting of the party’s Central Working Committee made the call, saying constitutional amendments should be pursued in line with contemporary needs while safeguarding the achievements of the Constitution.

Nepali Congress said it would continue taking initiatives to amend the Constitution to further strengthen democracy while protecting its achievements.

The party described the Constitution as a dynamic document that can be amended according to changing needs. It stressed that any amendment process must take into account public ownership, rights, representation and citizens’ trust in the state.

“Rule of law, inclusiveness and human rights are the fundamental values of the Constitution. No amendment can be made in a way that restricts these values,” Nepali Congress said in its decision.

The party also said that although the legal process for constitutional amendment falls within the jurisdiction of Parliament, public opinion must also be reflected in the process.

“For this, all-party political dialogue and participation are necessary,” the decision stated.

Nepali Congress said any constitutional amendment should therefore be pursued through broad political consultation and participation while maintaining the Constitution’s fundamental principles.

title.rendered: What is the Nepali Congress provision suspended to pave the way for its 15th General Convention?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Nepali Congress has suspended a provision in its party statute that requires local-level conventions to be completed well before the Central General Convention, clearing a procedural hurdle to its planned 15th General Convention.

The Central Working Committee, which concluded its nine-day meeting, decided to suspend Article 35(2)(d) of the party statute, spokesperson Devraj Chalise said.

So, what does the suspended provision actually say?

What does Article 35(2)(d) require?

The provision states that all local-level conventions and the formation of local-level party committees must be completed at least one year before the year in which the Central General Convention and provincial conventions are held.

It also sets a separate timeline for electing representatives.

According to the provision, representatives elected from local-level conventions for the provincial convention and Central General Convention must be elected at least three months before the respective conventions.

In other words, under the normal party statute, the Congress would have needed to complete its local-level organisational process significantly ahead of the Central General Convention.

Why did Nepali Congress suspend it?

The party has already decided to hold its 15th General Convention in Kathmandu from October 2 to 5.

With the time remaining insufficient to complete all the organisational processes required under Article 35(2)(d), the Central Working Committee decided to suspend the provision, according to Chalise.

The decision was made specifically to ensure that the general convention can be held within the scheduled timeframe.

The party’s decision states that the provision was suspended because it was necessary to do so under the prevailing circumstances to complete the 15th General Convention within the set timeframe.

What else did Nepali Congress decide?

The Central Working Committee has formed a 15th General Convention Management Committee under party president Gagan Kumar Thapa.

The committee will establish subcommittees responsible for accommodation, food arrangements, stage management, hospitality, health services and other convention-related preparations.

The party has also formed a 15th General Convention Publicity Committee under spokesperson Chalise.

Thapa will present the main political proposal at the convention, focusing on “The Coming Decade, Democracy and the Nepali Congress.”

Vice President Bishwa Prakash Sharma will present a proposal on the decline of political culture and the need for transformation, while Vice President Pushpa Bhusal will present a special proposal on provincial elections.

General Secretary Gururaj Ghimire will present a proposal on party organisation.

Nepali Congress has also formed a Statute Amendment Committee under General Secretary Pradeep Poudel. The committee will collect suggestions from different levels, bodies and members of the party and prepare proposals for amendments to make the statute more relevant to current circumstances.

title.rendered: House Committee summons CIAA officials for discussion on commission’s work

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The State Affairs and Good Governance Committee of the House of Representatives has summoned officials of the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) for discussions on the commission’s work and other related issues.

According to the committee secretariat, a meeting has been scheduled for 11 am on Thursday at the committee meeting hall in Singha Durbar.

The discussion will focus on issues raised in the CIAA’s annual report as well as the commission’s activities and performance.

The CIAA’s annual report was tabled in the House of Representatives on July 9.

On that day, Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam had tabled the 35th Annual Report of the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority for fiscal year 2024/25 on behalf of Prime Minister Balen Shah.

The committee secretariat said CIAA officials have been invited to discuss the issues highlighted in the annual report and matters concerning the commission’s overall functioning.

title.rendered: FDI commitment plunges to Rs 3.77 billion in first month of FY 2026/27

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal received foreign direct investment (FDI) commitments worth just Rs 3.77 billion in the first month of the current fiscal year 2026/27, a sharp decline from the same period last year.

According to the Department of Industry, a total of 191 industries and projects received FDI commitments in the first month of the fiscal year.

In the first month of fiscal year 2025/26, Nepal had received FDI commitments worth Rs 24.10 billion, meaning the commitment this year has fallen by more than 84% compared to the same period last year.

The number of projects receiving commitments, however, has increased. Last year, 127 projects received FDI commitments during the first month.

The sharp difference in the investment figures is largely due to a single major project approved last year.

A commitment of Rs 20.45 billion had been made for a processed cooked buffalo meat factory that was planned to export buffalo meat from Nepal to China.

No similarly large investment commitment has been recorded during the first month of the current fiscal year.

This year, FDI commitments have mainly come for small-scale industries, while only one large investment commitment has been recorded. Two medium-scale industries have also received commitments.

Automatic route attracts most commitments

The largest share of FDI commitments this year has come through the automatic approval route.

The government removed the upper limit on investments eligible for approval through the automatic route, resulting in an increase in the number of FDI approvals through the system.

The automatic route allows eligible foreign investments to receive approval without going through the conventional approval process.

IT dominates in number, tourism in investment

Information technology (IT) projects accounted for the largest share of approved projects in terms of number.

A total of 128 IT industries were registered during Shrawan, receiving FDI commitments worth Rs 569.8 million.

Tourism ranked second in terms of the number of projects, with 33 industries receiving commitments worth Rs 1.63 billion.

Service-sector industries ranked third, with 19 projects receiving FDI commitments worth Rs 682 million.

Manufacturing ranked fourth, with nine projects receiving commitments worth Rs 843.2 million.

Meanwhile, one industry each was registered in the agriculture and energy sectors. Each sector received FDI commitments of Rs 20 million.

The figures show that while IT dominates Nepal’s FDI pipeline by the number of projects, tourism continues to attract significantly larger amounts of foreign investment per project.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress forms committees for 15th General Convention, suspends party statute provision

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Nepali Congress has formed various committees to manage its upcoming 15th General Convention and suspended a provision of its party statute to facilitate the convention process.

A meeting of the party’s Central Working Committee decided to form the committees for the convention, which has already been scheduled.

According to party spokesperson Devraj Chalise, the meeting formed a 15th General Convention Management Committee under the coordination of party President Gagan Kumar Thapa.

The management committee will include other members as required.

The meeting also decided that the main committee will form various subcommittees to oversee arrangements including accommodation, food, stage management, guest reception and healthcare for the convention.

The party said the names of the coordinators and members of the respective subcommittees will be published later.

Nepali Congress suspends statute provision

The Nepali Congress has also suspended Article 35(2)(d) of its party statute.

The provision was suspended through the Central Working Committee meeting held from August 9 to August 17.

The party said the provision was suspended as it was deemed necessary to ensure that the 15th General Convention could be completed within the scheduled timeframe under the special circumstances.

“Since it is deemed necessary to complete the 15th General Convention within the scheduled timeframe under special circumstances, it has been decided to make the necessary suspension regarding Article 35(2)(d) in accordance with the statute,” the meeting’s decision stated.

Article 35(2)(d) requires all local-level conventions to be held and local-level committees formed at least one year before the year in which the Central General Convention and provincial conventions are held.

The provision also states that representatives elected through local-level conventions for provincial conventions and the Central General Convention must be elected three months before the respective provincial and central conventions.

The party has suspended these provisions to facilitate the timely completion of its 15th General Convention.

title.rendered: Govt prepares procedure to spend Rs 150 million on rescuing stranded Nepalis abroad

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has prepared a procedure to facilitate the rescue, relief and repatriation of Nepali citizens stranded abroad.

The Procedure for the Operation of Budget Allocated for the Rescue, Relief and Repatriation of Nepali Citizens Stranded Abroad has been sent to the Ministry of Finance for approval. It was submitted to the Finance Ministry on August 14 and is currently under consideration.

The government has allocated Rs 150 million in the current fiscal year for the rescue, relief and repatriation of Nepali citizens stranded abroad.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal informed the House of Representatives about the procedure while responding to a question raised by Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Ashika Tamang over the delayed repatriation of the body of Santosh Rai of Dhunibesi Municipality-7, Dhading, who died while receiving treatment in Cambodia.

According to Khanal, the government felt the need for a separate source of funding for rescuing Nepalis stranded abroad after it came to power. The Finance Ministry was subsequently requested to allocate funds, resulting in the Rs 150 million allocation for the current fiscal year.

The procedure proposes a maximum expenditure of Rs 1.2 million per person. It also includes limited provisions for cases involving Nepali citizens who require medical treatment.

Khanal said the Foreign Ministry will implement the procedure once it is approved by the Finance Ministry.

He said the delay in preparing the procedure was not due to negligence but because the government needed to carefully determine the circumstances and purposes for which public funds could be used.

“The delay was not because we were reluctant or unwilling to prepare the procedure. Since this is a serious matter, we had to carefully consider where and under what circumstances the funds should be used,” Khanal said.

Government faces difficulties in rescuing those who travel illegally

Khanal said the repatriation of Nepali citizens who travel abroad legally, particularly those who obtain labour permits, is comparatively easier because they are covered by insurance through the Department of Foreign Employment.

However, he said rescuing Nepalis who travel abroad through illegal channels presents legal and financial challenges.

“For Nepali citizens who go abroad through legal channels, particularly those with labour permits, insurance is provided through the Department of Foreign Employment, making the process of repatriating bodies and providing other relief and rescue relatively easier,” Khanal said.

“But the rescue process for Nepali citizens who have gone abroad through illegal channels is extremely complicated.”

The minister said the government has two major responsibilities: protecting its citizens and ensuring that taxpayers’ money is used properly and legally.

He said the government must also consider whether using state funds to rescue citizens involved in activities prohibited by law could inadvertently encourage illegal activities.

“There is a humanitarian need to rescue people, but we must also seriously consider whether legally collected public funds should be used in a way that encourages illegal activities,” Khanal said.

Body of Nepali who died in Cambodia yet to be repatriated

Khanal said Santosh Rai of Dhunibesi Municipality-7, Dhading, died while undergoing treatment at Calmette Hospital in Cambodia on May 14, 2026.

His body remains at a hospital in Phnom Penh.

According to information received from the Nepali Embassy in Bangkok, around US$1,000 is required to bring Rai’s body home, including outstanding hospital treatment bills, mortuary charges and airfare.

Khanal said the issue had been raised in Parliament by lawmaker Tamang, and he was providing clarification based on the Speaker’s ruling.

Around 160 bodies repatriated in four months

According to Khanal, around 160 bodies of Nepali citizens have been repatriated to Nepal in the past four months alone.

He also said around 860 Nepali nationals who had travelled to Cambodia on visit visas and were working in scam centres had been rescued and brought back to Nepal over the past few months.

Cambodia does not have a labour agreement with Nepal.

Khanal said the government has limited resources and therefore must carefully determine where and how they are used.

He stressed that while Nepali citizens stranded abroad should be assisted on humanitarian grounds, the government must also ensure the proper use of public resources and uphold its collective responsibility to citizens.

title.rendered: Gagan Thapa says NC’s 15th General Convention process formally underway

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa has announced that the process for the party’s 15th General Convention formally began on Tuesday.

Thapa made the announcement while addressing a programme organised for election officers appointed in various districts for the upcoming General Convention.

He said the party has limited time to complete the convention process as it is bound by the Constitution, party statute and a court ruling.

“We do not have the luxury of time. We are bound by the Constitution and the party statute. The court’s decision has also been based on the convention being held from October 2,” Thapa said.

According to Thapa, the use of digital active membership records will make organising this year’s convention easier than in the past.

“We have to conduct the convention in a way that leaves no room for questions. From today, our convention process has formally begun,” he said.

Thapa said everyone involved would have to follow the election schedule prepared by the Election Committee.

He also said the party’s Central Working Committee has already finalised the date and venue for the General Convention.

The 15th General Convention of the Nepali Congress will be held in Kathmandu from October 2 to 5.

title.rendered: Indian Army chief General Dhiraj Seth meets PM Balen Shah

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth held a courtesy meeting with Prime Minister and Defence Minister Balen Shah on Tuesday.

Seth met Prime Minister Shah at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers in Singha Durbar.

Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava also attended the meeting.

Seth arrived in Kathmandu on Sunday for a four-day visit at the formal invitation of Chief of the Army Staff Ashok Raj Sigdel.

On Monday, President Ram Chandra Paudel conferred the honorary rank of General of the Nepal Army on Seth.

Nepal and India have maintained a tradition since 1950 of conferring the honorary rank of General on each other’s army chiefs.

Seth also held bilateral talks with Chief of the Army Staff Sigdel on Monday.

title.rendered: Lalitpur District Court denies police request to arrest journalist Kishor Shrestha

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Lalitpur District Court has refused to grant permission to arrest journalist Kishor Shrestha.

The Lalitpur police had sought an arrest warrant from the court based on a complaint filed against Shrestha by Deputy Speaker Rubi Kumari Thakur at the District Police Range, Kathmandu, on Monday.

The court, however, declined to grant permission for his arrest.

Meanwhile, Shrestha on Tuesday filed a writ petition at the Patan High Court, seeking an order preventing authorities from arresting him or seizing his equipment.

Shrestha reached the High Court on Tuesday afternoon, saying he feared he could be arrested again based on the complaint filed by Thakur.

In his petition, he has sought an interim order against any attempt to detain him and seize his equipment.

Shrestha had been released only on Monday following a mandamus order issued by the Supreme Court.

The latest legal developments come a day after his release and following the complaint filed by Deputy Speaker Thakur.

title.rendered: Nepal Academy of Music and Drama reaches out to Kathmandu’s theatre community

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

On Thursday and Friday, a team led by newly appointed Vice-Chancellor Brajesh Khanal of the Nepal Academy of Music and Drama, along with Drama Department Head Academician Saraswati Chaudhary, Theatre Department Head Academician Jeet Bahadur Deuja, and academician council member Pariwartan, visited six theatre venues in the capital to hold consultations.

Senior director Ashesh Malla of Sarwanam Theatre, who has had a long journey in the field of theatre, along with performer and director Ghimire Yubaraj of Shilpee Theatre, celebrated actor Dayahang Rai of Mandala Theatre, and Suraj Tamu, who started running his own theatre after struggling with rented halls to stage plays, all expressed happiness that, for the first time in the Academy’s fifth term, the institution had come to their doorstep.

“Seeing the state come to our doorstep and recognise us as its own felt like an entirely new and deeply gratifying experience for us today,” they said.

Nabaraj Budhathoki of Shilpee Theatre, who has continued the children’s drama festival for 18 years, said this was the first time the Academy’s team had reached his doorstep, and that it made him feel proud to call himself a theatre practitioner.

During the consultation, theatre practitioners offered their suggestions for improving the Academy’s policies, planning, and immediate action plans. Theatre practitioners Akanchha Karki and Loonibha Tuladhar of Kausi Theatre advised that the Academy should become a “smart academy” friendly to women, persons with disabilities, and LGBTIQ+ communities. More than 200 theatre practitioners, both affiliated with theatre institutions and independent, active in Kathmandu, shared their concerns and experiences during the consultation. Suggestions included expanding theatre beyond its current capital-centric focus to the rest of the country; providing life insurance for technicians and performers involved in play production and staging; scholarships and writing grants for study; advance agreements with production teams to ensure a state-fixed minimum wage; artist identity cards with associated benefits and concessions; and fee waivers at state-owned theatre halls for staging plays.

Theatre practitioner Prabin Khatiwada said he had heard the government had allocated budget to build theatres in all seven provinces, which he said would help create an environment for independent theatre practitioners who lack venues of their own. Ghimire Yubaraj argued that the programme expenditure within the Academy’s overall budget should be increased. He also proposed that a policy be developed to protect private and community theatre institutions; that currently ad hoc theatre festivals and training programmes be organised systematically, grounded in multilingual and local cultural contexts; and that grants be given to each theatre institution on condition that it produces at least two plays.

Actor Dayahang Rai struck a somewhat different note. Noting that Mandala Theatre alone had produced more than 150 plays and over 200 performers, he requested that the Academy work to theorise and give conceptual grounding to the plays being staged by them and by others across the country.

Newly appointed Vice-Chancellor Brajesh Khanal had one consistent response: “The Academy has opened its doors today.”

He requested that all theatre venues regularly and transparently share their activities and programmes with the Academy, so they could be compiled and preserved in the Government of Nepal’s official database. He assured them that all the positive suggestions received would be addressed swiftly.

title.rendered: UML decides to appoint Kiran Thapa as Bagmati chief minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The CPN-UML has decided to appoint Kiran Thapa as the chief minister of Bagmati Province.

A meeting of the UML parliamentary party held on Tuesday decided to nominate Thapa for the post of chief minister.

The meeting also decided to retain Jagannath Thapaliya as the leader of the UML parliamentary party in the provincial assembly.

The decision comes amid growing differences among UML leaders over who should lead the Bagmati provincial government.

Under a new power-sharing arrangement between the CPN-UML and the Nepali Communist Party (NCP), the UML has been allocated leadership of the Bagmati provincial government.

Following the agreement, competition and internal disputes had intensified within the UML over the selection of the chief minister.

The parliamentary party meeting has now settled the issue by deciding to nominate Thapa as the next chief minister of Bagmati Province.

title.rendered: 5 reasons Nepali buyers may want to wait for the Deepal Nevo Q05

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepali customers planning to book a compact electric SUV may want to wait a little longer, with the Deepal Nevo Q05 set to make its Nepal debut at NADA Auto Show 2026.

The Q05 is arriving with a combination of cabin space, fast-charging capability, smart technology, international design credentials and a strong sales record in overseas markets.

Here are five reasons the Deepal Nevo Q05 could be worth the wait.

1. A surprisingly spacious cabin

The first reason to wait for the Deepal Nevo Q05 is its spacious interior.

The electric SUV has a 2,735 mm wheelbase, an important measurement when it comes to passenger space, particularly for those sitting in the rear.

Despite having an overall length of 4,435 mm, making it relatively easy to manoeuvre in urban environments, the Q05’s proportions allow a significant amount of its footprint to be used for passenger space.

It also claims a 540-litre standard boot capacity, offering additional room for family luggage, shopping and children’s belongings.

2. Fast charging

The second major attraction is its charging capability.

The Q05 is equipped with a 51.9 kWh CATL lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, Changan’s battery-system technology and 3C fast-charging capability.

Its peak DC charging capacity is rated at up to 162 kW.

According to Changan, under suitable conditions, the battery can be charged from 30 to 80 percent in around 15 minutes.

Actual charging times, however, can vary depending on the charger’s capacity, battery temperature and operating conditions.

3. Smart digital technology

The Deepal Nevo Q05 also brings a technology-focused cabin.

It features a 14.6-inch central touchscreen, a separate driver display and surround-view technology.

The system is designed to bring vehicle controls, supported connectivity features, camera views and entertainment functions together through an integrated interface.

The final list of features available in Nepal will be confirmed when the local variant is officially unveiled.

4. International design credentials

Design is another major selling point.

The Q05 was developed through Changan’s international design network, involving 915 designers from 31 countries and regions.

The team was led by Changan Global Design Vice President Klaus Zyciora, the former head of design at Volkswagen Group.

The Deepal Nevo Q05 features Changan’s ‘Inspired by Light’ design language, aerodynamic surfaces and a distinctive light signature.

The model has also received a Golden A’ Design Award.

5. A strong international sales record

Perhaps the most reassuring reason to consider waiting is the Q05’s sales performance.

Changan announced that cumulative sales of the Deepal Nevo Q05 had crossed 100,000 units as of August 11, 2026.

According to Gasgoo, the model recorded 18,871 deliveries in July, maintaining the top position in China’s compact SUV sales for four consecutive months.

The Q05 has also generated strong interest outside China. In Thailand, the model reportedly received more than 3,000 orders in less than two weeks of its launch.

These five measurable factors provide a strong case for Nepali buyers to wait before booking a compact electric SUV, particularly with the Q05 set to be unveiled at NADA Auto Show 2026.

title.rendered: Removing Nepal from EU Air Safety List a top priority: Tourism Minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel (Ganesh) has said that removing Nepal from the European Union’s (EU) Air Safety List is a top priority for the government.

Responding to questions from lawmakers in the House of Representatives, he said the government was pursuing both technical and institutional reforms as well as diplomatic initiatives to address the issue.

He said the government has also requested the EU ambassador and EU member states to support Nepal’s removal from the list. He also urged officials not to refer to the EU restriction as a blacklist.

Nepal’s aviation industry has been under EU restrictions since 2013. Paudel said further reforms would be carried out based on additional feedback from the EU.

He said work was also underway on bills to separate the regulatory and service-provider functions of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, as the two functions are currently handled by the same institution.

title.rendered: NEPSE falls 19 points as trading turnover declines

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal’s share market fell 19.34 points on Tuesday, extending the decline after the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) had dropped 2.25 points on the previous trading day.

Following Tuesday’s trading, the NEPSE index stood at 2,622 points.

The prices of 57 companies increased, while those of 217 companies declined. Shares of five companies remained unchanged.

Trading turnover also declined slightly. A total of Rs 5.07 billion worth of shares were traded on Tuesday, compared to Rs 5.52 billion on the previous day.

All sectoral indices except trading declined. The trading sector rose 0.41 percent, while the manufacturing and processing sector recorded the biggest decline of 1.40 percent.

The banking sector fell 0.59 percent, development banks 0.59 percent, finance 0.41 percent, hotels and tourism 0.84 percent, hydropower 0.92 percent, investment 0.83 percent, life insurance 0.76 percent, microfinance 0.39 percent, non-life insurance 0.57 percent and the others sector 0.97 percent.

The hydropower sector recorded the highest turnover at Rs 2.53 billion. Commercial banks recorded transactions worth Rs 440 million, while manufacturing and processing companies recorded turnover of Rs 450 million.

title.rendered: EU Ambassador Lorenzo pays farewell call on Foreign Affairs Minister Khanal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Ambassador of the European Union (EU) to Nepal, Veronique Lorenzo, paid a farewell call on Minister for Foreign Affairs Shishir Khanal at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs today.

On the occasion, they discussed various topics concerning Nepal-EU relations and mutual interests. Ambassador Lorenzo thanked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for the excellent relationship, saying that the ministry has been helpful, active, and responsive. She also expressed her happiness with the leadership and guidance of Foreign Minister Khanal. Foreign Minister Khanal thanked Ambassador Lorenzo for her openness, honesty, and support, and appreciated the assistance she has shown to Nepal and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

At the meeting, Ambassador Lorenzo said that the EU is interested in cooperating with Nepal on mountain and water-related agendas. Stating that mountain-related issues are the priority of the Government of Nepal, the Foreign Minister informed the EU ambassador that Nepal would be hosting the second edition of the ‘Sagarmatha Sambaad’ in the coming year. The ambassador said the EU has plans to cooperate with Nepal in the areas of safe, systematic and decent migration.

Welcoming such a proposal, the Minister requested detailed information on the proposed areas of cooperation for further study and to formulate Nepal’s views. He said that safe and decent migration is one of the key priorities of Nepal, adding that the government is committed to the protection of the Nepali diaspora abroad. The two also exchanged views on the suspension of the schedule of Nepal’s graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) to a middle-income developing country. The ambassador pledged the EU’s support towards that end, urging Nepal to submit substantive action plans and necessary details.

On the occasion, matters relating to the promotion of Nepali art, culture and civilisation, openness and freedom of expression were discussed. The ambassador urged the Ministry to support an exhibition relating to Newa art. In response, the Minister expressed the government’s commitment to the promotion of Nepal’s cultural heritage.

title.rendered: Over 70,000 receive labour permits for foreign employment in Shrawan

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

More than 70,000 Nepalis received labour permits for foreign employment in Shrawan, including renewals, according to the Department of Foreign Employment.

A total of 70,441 people obtained labour approval during the month. Of them, 60,472 were men and 9,969 were women.

According to the department, 42,693 people received new labour approvals, while 27,748 obtained re-entry labour approvals.

Of those receiving new approvals, 29,447 went through recruitment agencies, while 12,442 obtained individual labour approval. Another 712 people went abroad through government-to-government (G2G) arrangements.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) was the most popular destination for Nepali migrant workers in Shrawan, with 18,784 people receiving labour approval.

Similarly, 12,498 people received approval for Malaysia, 10,360 for Qatar, and 8,613 for Saudi Arabia.

In the previous month, Ashad, 69,362 people had received labour approval for foreign employment.

Meanwhile, a total of 792,187 Nepalis received labour approval to go abroad for employment in fiscal year 2082/83.

title.rendered: Home Minister Sudan Gurung receives probe reports on Sunsari, Siraha incidents

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The committees formed to investigate the incidents in Sunsari and Siraha have submitted their reports to Home Minister Sudan Gurung.

Ministry of Home Affairs spokesperson Rama Acharya confirmed that both committees submitted their reports on Tuesday.

“The committees submitted their reports today. Action will be taken after the reports are studied,” Acharya told Onlinekhabar.

Tensions had erupted between two communities in Kaptanganj of Dewanganj Rural Municipality-3, Sunsari, on the night of July 26. The ensuing clash and security forces’ firing left four people dead.

Om Prakash Mehta of Kaptanganj was initially killed after being shot by security personnel. Two others, Jay Prakash Mehta and Rabindra Mehta, who were receiving treatment for injuries sustained in the incident, later died.

The dispute subsequently spread to Siraha, where Ganesh Yadav was also killed after being shot.

The Ministry of Home Affairs had formed separate committees to investigate the two incidents.

A committee led by Home Ministry Joint Secretary Bhupendra Thapa was formed to investigate the Kaptanganj incident in Sunsari. Similarly, another committee led by Joint Secretary Pushparaj Shahi was formed to investigate the incident in Siraha.

Both committees submitted their reports to the Home Ministry on Tuesday.

title.rendered: Nepal Oil Corporation urges public not to stockpile LPG cylinders

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) has urged consumers not to unnecessarily stockpile cooking gas cylinders, saying the supply situation in the market is gradually improving and is expected to return to normal within a few days.

The corporation said the supply of LPG cylinders in Kathmandu Valley is currently higher than the average daily demand. “The average daily demand in Kathmandu Valley is 35,000 to 37,000 cylinders, but we are currently supplying an additional 5,000 to 8,000 cylinders on average,” said NOC Director Binit Mani Upadhyay.

According to the corporation, 22 gas companies in Kathmandu Valley are selling 47,388 cylinders on Monday. A total of 52,576 cylinders were sold in the valley on Sunday, around 15,000 more than the daily average.

The NOC said 309,553 cylinders were sold in the valley over the past week, from Shrawan 27 to the evening of Bhadra 2. This amounts to an average of more than 44,000 cylinders per day.

Industry operators said the current gas shortage is not due to supply problems. They said gas imports had declined in Falgun due to external factors, prompting the government to introduce the sale of partially filled cylinders to address the shortage. The effects of that measure are being felt now, but the situation is not expected to persist for long.

Krishnabhakta Shrestha, president of the LPG Gas Industry Association Nepal, said the situation has improved significantly since gas began being sold through dealers on Monday. He said the problems are expected to be resolved within a week.

According to the NOC, around 110,000 LPG cylinders are normally sold across the country each day. However, 57,316 metric tonnes of LPG, equivalent to 4,036,364 cylinders, were sold in Shrawan of the current fiscal year alone.

This was around 29.3 per cent higher than sales in Shrawan of fiscal year 2082/83, when 44,318 metric tonnes of LPG, equivalent to 3,120,986 cylinders, were sold.

Similarly, 45,735 metric tonnes of LPG, equivalent to 3,220,775 cylinders, were sold in Shrawan of fiscal year 2081/82 BS.

According to the NOC, 38,800 metric tonnes of LPG were imported in Chaitra last year, during which 5,464,789 partially filled cylinders were sold by various companies. In contrast, 48,327 metric tonnes of LPG were imported in Chaitra 2081 BS, when 3,403,310 filled cylinders were sold.

Similarly, 32,056 metric tonnes of LPG were imported in Baisakh this year, compared with 46,503 metric tonnes in Baisakh last year. Imports stood at 33,842 metric tonnes in Jestha this year, compared with 49,816 metric tonnes in Jestha last year.

In Ashad this year, 44,544 metric tonnes of LPG were imported, compared with 47,933 metric tonnes in Ashad last year.

title.rendered: Nepali Congress establishment rejects Deuba camp’s convention decisions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Leaders of the Nepali Congress establishment have strongly objected to proposals endorsed by a convention organised by the faction led by former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba, saying the decisions cannot be considered the official position of the party.

They argued that the proposals cannot override the party’s statute, institutional decisions or constitutional processes.

Nepali Congress General Secretary Pradip Paudel said leaders who had spent years in politics under Deuba appeared to be retreating from the political values and constitutional achievements they had previously championed.

“It appears they have moved away from what they struggled for throughout their political lives,” Paudel told Onlinekhabar.

He said it was inappropriate for leaders who had played a major role in promulgating the Constitution to now appear to be moving away from its achievements.

Paudel also rejected the documents endorsed by the Deuba camp as official Nepali Congress documents.

He said any group within the party has the right to meet, discuss issues and reach conclusions, but such decisions can become official party positions only after being endorsed through the party’s authorised forums.

“Those documents are not official. They have not been approved by an authorised forum of the party. They represent the views of those who participated in that gathering,” Paudel said.

The Deuba camp held a three-day gathering in Sukedhara and on Sunday endorsed proposals on politics, economic policy, organisation, contemporary national issues, and law and the party statute.

The group said the proposals incorporated suggestions and opinions collected through discussions among seven provincial-level groups.

The convention also decided to make Sanatan Dharma a national identity.

On the issue, Paudel said the Nepali Congress remains committed to the political principles it had advocated under Deuba’s leadership.

“We will continue to take forward the ideas that he himself taught and upheld,” he said.

‘We are not concerned about the faction’

Nepali Congress Joint General Secretary Farmullah Mansoor said there was no confusion over who leads the party.

“Gagan Kumar Thapa is the president of the Nepali Congress. This is a party under his leadership,” Mansoor said.

The Deuba camp has decided that the 15th general convention will be held under Deuba’s chairmanship, claiming it would be organised by the Central Working Committee elected by the 14th general convention.

It also decided that regular party activities until the general convention would be coordinated under the direction of Deuba by convention coordinator Dr Shashank Koirala.

Mansoor said such gatherings by former party leaders or factions would not affect the current leadership. He even mocked the Deuba camp’s convention, comparing it to a street performer displaying a monkey at a crossroads.

Joint General Secretary Dila Sangraula also said the party would not accept any of the proposals endorsed by the Deuba camp.

“The proposals passed by the national convention are not official. The party president has already made this clear,” she said. ‘We would have welcomed Deuba at the party office’

Joint General Secretary Yogendra Chaudhary said the party hoped Deuba’s return to Nepal would help strengthen institutional ties rather than deepen divisions.

He said the party would have welcomed Deuba at the party office if he had informed them of his intention to visit.

“We would have gone to the airport to welcome him, along with President Gagan Thapa,” Chaudhary said.

He expressed dissatisfaction that Deuba went to a contact office in Chundevi rather than the party headquarters in Sanepa.

According to Chaudhary, the Nepali Congress could have provided Deuba with a dignified office at the party headquarters in his capacity as a former prime minister and former party president. He said Deuba’s recent activities had created the impression that he was seeking to become the leader of only one faction.

“It appears that he is becoming the leader of only one faction. I am concerned that this could create a different chapter in Nepal’s political history,” Chaudhary said.

Nepali Congress Central Working Committee member Chandra Bhandari said the dispute should be viewed primarily through the lens of constitutionalism and institutional procedure.

He recalled that the Constitution was promulgated under Nepali Congress leadership and established separation of powers among the legislature, executive and judiciary.

Bhandari argued that senior political leaders should not themselves challenge constitutional processes.

He referred to the special general convention, recognition by the Election Commission and legal proceedings involving the party, questioning whether it was appropriate to challenge the current institutional arrangement after those processes had already taken place.

Bhandari warned that weakening established procedures could create more serious problems in the future.

“If rules, laws and the Constitution are not respected, what will we do tomorrow if armed people come and surround us?” he asked.

He said the Nepali Congress should serve as a school of democratic political culture rather than allow personal interests and egos to undermine its broader objectives.

“Nepali Congress is not just a political party; it is a school,” Bhandari said. “It is supposed to teach others.”

Thapa had already rejected the proposals

At Monday’s Central Working Committee meeting, Nepali Congress President Gagan Kumar Thapa had already said the proposals and decisions endorsed by the Deuba camp could not be recognised as official party policies.

Thapa said the party’s general convention, general assembly, special general convention and election manifesto are among the authorised mechanisms for establishing official Nepali Congress policies and decisions.

“The provisions of our statute clearly define the foundations for establishing the official position of the Nepali Congress,” Thapa said.

He maintained that ideas, reports or decisions presented or endorsed at gatherings outside these authorised forums do not become part of the party’s official policy or statute.

However, Thapa said the party respected the right of its members to gather freely and express their views.

“We respect the right to assemble freely. Our Constitution guarantees it, and it is also part of our party tradition,” he said. “We are open to constructive debate and discussion.”

title.rendered: 4 arrested for OTP fraud in bank KYC scam

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police has arrested four people for allegedly defrauding victims by obtaining their one-time passwords (OTPs) under the pretext of updating their bank KYC details.

Those arrested have been identified as 22-year-old Abhay Tiwari of Deutal Rural Municipality-4, Bara; 22-year-old Jaikumar Kewat of Ramgram Municipality-16, West Nawalparasi; 22-year-old Vidyasagar Kewat of Ramgram Municipality-17; and 27-year-old Kuber Thapa of Birgunj Metropolitan City-3, Parsa.

According to the bureau, the suspects were operating a gang targeting serving and retired government employees.

Investigators found that the suspects called victims, claiming to be bank representatives and telling them that their KYC details needed to be updated. They then persuaded the victims to share their screens through phone or WhatsApp calls and obtained their OTP codes. The suspects allegedly used the codes to gain access to the victims’ bank accounts and transfer money.

title.rendered: Old power infrastructure causing frequent outages: Energy Minister

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has said frequent power outages in Nepal are occurring because the country’s electricity infrastructure is old and unable to handle the increasing load.

Responding to questions raised by lawmakers during Tuesday’s meeting of the House of Representatives, he said the government has now prioritised improving and strengthening the electricity infrastructure.

He said the Nepal Electricity Authority has been working to improve the distribution system on a priority basis in coordination with the government. Accordingly, the authority has been carrying out maintenance work after issuing public notices about planned power disruptions, he said.

Shrestha said Nepal earned Rs 29.32 billion from electricity exports in fiscal year 2082/83. He said most hydropower projects in Nepal are run-of-river projects, and electricity production increases during the monsoon as river flows rise. As a result, only surplus electricity is currently being exported, he said.

According to him, Nepal imported electricity worth Rs 10.55 billion in the last fiscal year. He said electricity generation is no longer a major challenge for Nepal, while transmission and distribution remain the main challenges.

He said a committee had been formed to study voltage fluctuations in various parts of the country and that it had already submitted a report after examining tripping problems in different areas.

The minister said the Nepal Electricity Authority has been instructed to implement the recommendations of the report.

He said domestic electricity consumption is increasing rapidly, but frequent power outages remain a problem because old and low-capacity infrastructure is unable to handle the growing load.

title.rendered: Govt makes online business registration mandatory

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The government has asked all businesses operating through online platforms to register with the Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection.

The department has directed businesses selling goods and services through websites, mobile applications, social media and other digital platforms to mandatorily register through its online portal.

The department warned that businesses operating online without completing the required legal procedures could face action under the Electronic Trade Act 2024 and Electronic Trade Directive 2025.

The move comes amid growing complaints of consumer fraud and disputes related to online transactions. The government said it has tightened regulation to make digital commerce more transparent and organised.

According to the department, the registration requirement applies to all businesses conducting transactions using computers, mobile phones or similar devices through websites, applications, the internet, intranet, social media marketplaces and other digital platforms.

The department has urged all such businesses to complete the registration process as required by law.

title.rendered: Riders continue protest against inDrive over fare and labour concerns

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Riders and drivers affiliated with the Independent Drivers Foundation Nepal have continued their protest against ride-hailing company inDrive, demanding fair fares, better protection and recognition of their rights.

The riders have been organising peaceful protests and other demonstration programmes under the foundation’s call, seeking policy reforms in the digital ride-hailing sector and better working conditions.

The protesters are demanding a scientific and fair fare structure, reasonable remuneration for drivers and riders, and an end to what they describe as labour exploitation.

They are also pressing the authorities to introduce policy reforms for the digital ride-hailing sector and ensure adequate protection and fair pay for those working in the industry.

As part of Tuesday’s protest, riders also organised a motorbike rally.

The foundation said the protests would continue as part of its efforts to pressure concerned authorities and ride-hailing companies to address the issues faced by riders and drivers.

content.rendered:
For generations, Nepal has proudly told the world a simple story: We were never colonised, and we never colonised others. In a world shaped by empires, occupations, annexations and territorial expansion, Nepal’s place in history has been different. We defended our sovereignty fiercely, but we never built our national identity around taking somebody else’s land. This is not merely a historical fact; it is one of the foundations of modern Nepal and one of the few narratives that unite Nepalis across political, ethnic, regional and ideological lines.

It is also central to Nepal’s international identity. When foreigners think of Nepal, they think of the birthplace of the Buddha, the Himalayas, peacekeeping troops, and a nation that has preserved its sovereignty while navigating the interests of two Asian giants. Nepal has long projected itself as a bridge between India and China rather than a battleground between them, and as a country that respects others’ sovereignty because it deeply values its own. Countries spend centuries building such a reputation. Sometimes, however, a single statement can cast doubt on one of the very principles on which that reputation rests.

Recent remarks suggesting that Nepal has also encroached on a neighbour’s territory have done precisely that. The issue is no longer about who made the statement. The issue is what it communicated, how it was interpreted and what it means for Nepal’s credibility.

The Government subsequently clarified that the remarks referred to cross-border occupation and technical boundary-management issues rather than a formal admission that Nepal had encroached on another state’s sovereign territory. That clarification deserves acknowledgement because it distinguishes between complex boundary issues and sovereign territorial claims. Yet the episode also exposes a broader lesson in public administration and diplomacy: statements concerning sovereignty should be precise before they are delivered, not clarified afterwards. In international affairs, the first message often becomes the lasting message, while the clarification rarely receives equal attention.

If the original statement were interpreted literally, it would raise uncomfortable questions. What exactly have we been defending all this time? Nepalis have long supported institutions responsible for protecting national sovereignty, maintaining borders, producing official maps and representing Nepal’s interests internationally. If Nepal has indeed encroached on another country’s territory, the public deserves to know where, how, under what legal basis and since when. If that was never the Government’s position, as its subsequent clarification suggests, then the public deserves an equally clear explanation of how such an interpretation arose in the first place.

The implications extend well beyond domestic politics. Nepal has consistently advocated sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference, international law and the peaceful settlement of disputes. For smaller countries, these are not simply diplomatic principles; they are strategic assets. Unlike major powers, Nepal cannot rely on military or economic dominance to shape international opinion. It relies on something far more valuable: credibility.

Credibility gives small states influence disproportionate to their size. When Nepal speaks about sovereignty, it does so from a position built over generations. That moral authority carries obligations. A country cannot credibly condemn encroachment while appearing uncertain about its own position. Nor can it effectively defend international law if its own official messaging creates ambiguity about the principles it seeks to uphold.

If Nepal has indeed encroached upon another country’s territory, the response should be guided by evidence, law and diplomacy rather than emotion. The facts should be established, the legal position clarified, and any necessary corrective measures taken. If, however, Nepal has not encroached upon another country’s territory, as the Government’s clarification indicates, then equal effort should be devoted to correcting the public record and ensuring that no ambiguity remains.

This is where the issue moves beyond politics and enters the realm of national credibility. If we were uncertain about something as fundamental as territorial sovereignty, what else might become uncertain? Maps? Treaties? Diplomatic positions? Parliamentary resolutions? National security policies? Historical narratives? These are uncomfortable questions, but they are legitimate ones.

Nepal has spent decades arguing that maps matter, treaties matter and history matters.

If that is true, words matter too. Maps define territory. Treaties define rights. But words shape narratives. And narratives influence diplomacy.

The consequences of ambiguous statements extend far beyond the day they are made. Statements concerning borders enter the diplomatic record. They become future references, negotiation material, academic citations and political talking points. Future diplomats may one day be asked why a statement requiring clarification was made in the first place.

Small countries cannot afford strategic ambiguity on matters of sovereignty. Great powers may survive contradictory statements because their influence rests on military, economic and geopolitical weight. Countries like Nepal rely on something far more fragile: credibility. Once uncertainty enters the national narrative, restoring confidence becomes considerably harder than creating confusion in the first place.

History shows that words often outlive the circumstances in which they were spoken. A statement may later be clarified, corrected or withdrawn, but the original remark survives in public memory and diplomatic records. Negotiations, media reports and political debates can continue to refer to the original statement long after the clarification has faded from public attention.

Nepal itself offers a powerful reminder of this reality. More than a decade after the disruptions along the Nepal–India border following the 2015 earthquake and the promulgation of Nepal’s Constitution, public discourse continues to be shaped by the dominant narrative of a blockade, notwithstanding differing explanations and interpretations that have followed. Whether one agrees with that characterisation or not, the broader lesson is clear: first impressions often outlast subsequent clarifications.

This is why careful communication matters. Sensitive issues concerning sovereignty should not depend solely on political rhetoric. They should be informed by legal analysis, historical evidence, diplomatic consultation and technical expertise before they reach Parliament or the public. Governments invest in institutions precisely so that statements carrying diplomatic consequences are carefully prepared and rigorously scrutinised.

International experience demonstrates that even longstanding border disputes need not become permanent sources of tension. The peaceful implementation of the India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement showed that complex territorial questions can be resolved through political courage, technical expertise, evidence-based negotiations and mutual respect. Advances in satellite imagery, geospatial technologies and jointly verified digital mapping now provide tools that previous generations could only imagine. Nepal and India should continue strengthening technical cooperation so that outstanding boundary questions are resolved through evidence rather than ambiguity.

Nepal’s future does not lie in territorial rhetoric. It lies in economic transformation, education, innovation, connectivity, trade and regional cooperation. As a country strategically located between two rising powers, Nepal’s greatest comparative advantage has never been confrontation but credibility. It has long sought to serve as a bridge rather than a fault line.

Ultimately, this debate should not be remembered for one controversial statement. It should be remembered as a reminder that sovereignty demands precision. Governments have a responsibility not only to defend national interests but also to communicate them with clarity, consistency and care. When clarification becomes necessary on matters as sensitive as territorial sovereignty, institutions should ask not only whether the clarification is sufficient, but also why it became necessary in the first place.

Nepal has spent generations building a reputation as a nation that values sovereignty, its own and that of others. That reputation deserves to be protected with the same care that we devote to protecting our borders.

Because maps define territory. Treaties define rights. But words shape diplomacy. And for a country like Nepal, credibility may be the most valuable capital of all.

title.rendered: Acting Mayor Sunita Dangol backs Tiniharu ahead of theatrical run

content.rendered:
The film Elephants in the Fog (Tiniharu), currently preparing for release, is now in a rush of domestic promotion ahead of its launch. The film’s cast gave a special performance a few days ago at the recently concluded Naima Mobility Show.

The team performed to the song “Shaadi Ke Din Mein…” featured in the film. They then moved to another stall, where the cast danced to a song with the refrain “Balam.”

The Naima exhibition fair concluded a few days ago at Bhrikutimandap. The audience present for the team’s performance took part enthusiastically. Viewers reportedly expressed interest in the film and said they would head to theatres to watch it.

The team also gave a special performance at the Mahindra vehicle stall, entertaining the audience there as well. The film was recently honoured at the Cannes Film Festival in France.

Meanwhile, the film’s team also took part as chief guests at the K-pop Kathmandu Dance Festival, where they presented awards and honours to the competition’s winners and participants.

At the event, organised as a celebration of Korean pop dance, the film’s team encouraged and honoured the winning and participating performers.

The film was also honoured at the Infa Awards, held a few days ago. On that occasion, Kathmandu Metropolitan City Acting Mayor Sunita Dangol praised the film, recalling that she herself had attended its Cannes premiere.

Dangol urged audiences to watch the film and asked them to support and embrace it with love. Tiniharu is set to be released nationwide from September 4.

title.rendered: Ncell partners with BYD distributor to bring connected vehicle services to Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Ncell has partnered with Cimex Inc, the authorised distributor of BYD Auto Industry Company in Nepal, to provide connected vehicle services in the country.

Under the partnership, every BYD vehicle sold in Nepal will be equipped with an Ncell Internet of Things (IoT) SIM, giving customers a more digitally connected driving experience.

The partnership further strengthens Ncell’s position in IoT innovation in Nepal and reflects the company’s continued efforts to promote connected technology across different sectors.

With the IoT SIM built into the vehicle, customers will be able to access in-vehicle internet connectivity without requiring an additional device. The connectivity will support the BYD app ecosystem and connected infotainment features.

“Users will be able to access online services and digital entertainment such as YouTube, Spotify and karaoke directly through the vehicle’s system without connecting their phones or relying on a Wi-Fi hotspot,” Ncell said in a statement.

It added that the availability of such features would depend on the vehicle, software model and services available in Nepal.

Customers will also be able to benefit from Ncell’s nationwide network coverage through the IoT SIM. However, the user experience may vary depending on network coverage, location and vehicle configuration, similar to the experience of using Ncell’s network on a mobile phone.

The partnership is expected to bring features related to smart connectivity, infotainment, safety and intelligent mobility to BYD vehicles.

Speaking at the agreement-signing ceremony in Kathmandu, Ncell Chief Consumer Business Officer Upang Dutta said the partnership would provide direct vehicle connectivity for the BYD app and popular infotainment services.

“This will help users stay connected without depending on external hotspots or mobile data,” Dutta said. “Whether you are on the road or stuck in traffic, connecting directly to the local network will also help ensure more reliable navigation.”

The partnership marks another step towards expanding IoT-based connected mobility services in Nepal.

title.rendered: Government forms team to hold talks with Durga Prasai-led campaign representatives

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The government has formed a team to hold talks with representatives of the protesting “Nation, Nationality, Religion, Culture and Citizen Protection Grand Campaign,” led by Durga Prasai.

The Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers formed the negotiating team under the coordination of Joint Secretary Liladhar Subedi.

The members of the negotiating team are Home Ministry Joint Secretary Anand Kafle, Finance Ministry Joint Secretary Mahesh Acharya, and Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration Joint Secretary Dilaram Panthi.

Earlier, throughout Monday, discussions were held between representatives of the grand campaign and government representatives at the office of Chief District Officer Narahari Ghimire of the Lalitpur District Administration Office.

In the discussion, it was agreed that, as per the campaign’s demand, the Government of Nepal would formally form a negotiating team and invite the protesting side to talks.

Honouring the government’s call for talks, the campaign’s representatives accepted the letter inviting them to negotiations.

According to Prime Minister Balen Shah’s secretariat, the campaign’s representatives present at the discussion were Bishnu Bohara Chhetri, Raju Acharya, Sakuni Singh, Hardev Mahato, Tara Bajgain, and Bijay Thapa.

title.rendered: Harka Sampang accuses govt of failing to meet public expectations

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Shram Sanskriti Party Chair Harka Sampang Rai has criticised the government, accusing it of failing to deliver on public expectations and questioning the performance of ministers across key sectors.

Speaking during a special session of the House of Representatives on Tuesday, Rai raised serious questions about the government’s performance and accountability.

Rai said the prime minister and individual ministers had failed to fulfil their respective responsibilities.

He accused the government of failing on fundamental issues including border protection, law and order, the supply of fertilisers and food, job creation and controlling inflation.

Rai also demanded that Prime Minister Balen Shah attend Parliament and respond point by point to questions raised by lawmakers and the public.

Rai drew the attention of the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation to a land dispute in Ramdhuni-7 of Sunsari, where he alleged that land mafias had registered 64 bighas of land in their names.

He demanded that the government ensure justice for residents affected by the dispute.

Rai also raised the issue of depositors of Baraha Savings and Credit Cooperative in Dharan, saying billions of rupees belonging to depositors were at risk.

He urged the government to take steps to ensure that the depositors get their money back.

“Cooperative victims have not received their money, there is no justice in the courts, and people are not in a situation where they can receive treatment in hospitals,” Rai said.

“The government must be fully accountable to Parliament, and Parliament must be fully accountable to the people. Otherwise, there is no meaning to our debates.”

Speaking about development projects, Rai also called for the immediate advancement of the contracting process for projects in Sunsari-1 and other parts of the country.

He said delays in awarding contracts were holding back development and urged the government to move the process forward without further delay.

title.rendered: MP Pathak demands scientific management to stop wild elephant terror

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Rastriya Swatantra Party MP Prakash Pathak has drawn the government’s attention to the need for scientific management to control the terror caused by wild elephants.

Speaking during the House of Representatives meeting, he said the lives of residents in the Jhapa-3 constituency have been affected by wild elephants entering in large numbers from India, and he urged the government’s immediate attention toward controlling and managing the problem.

He said herds of elephants have been destroying paddy crops planted by farmers, damaging homes, and raising the risk of attacks at any time.

He demanded that the government adopt a policy of scientific management to control the elephants. He also drew the government’s attention to installing high-capacity transformers in elephant-affected areas and arranging solar streetlights along the roads.

Stressing that the state needs to focus on preparedness and effective management to prevent potential damage, he said the state should work to prevent damage altogether rather than merely expressing condolences and sympathy after damage has already occurred.

He said residents are living in fear for the safety of their children and elderly due to the elephant terror, adding that some citizens have been forced to relocate because of it.

Saying the measures currently used to control elephants have not been effective, he added that the presence of security mechanisms in the affected areas is also weak.

He said that when power supply is weak, homes lack adequate lighting, and without streetlights on roads, the risk from elephants increases further.

title.rendered: RSP creates Google Form to monitor MPs’ attendance and activities

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) has introduced a Google Form to monitor and document the activities and attendance of its lawmakers in Parliament.

According to RSP Whip Krantishikha Dhital, the form has been created to systematically record MPs’ attendance and reasons for being absent or leaving parliamentary meetings.

Under the new arrangement, MPs who cannot attend a parliamentary meeting must fill out the form and upload evidence explaining the reason for their absence.

The requirement also applies to MPs who arrive more than 30 minutes late, leave a meeting midway after attending, or leave the parliamentary premises during a meeting and later return.

RSP Chief Whip Kabindra Burlakoti said MPs must provide their name, constituency, contact number, reason for absence and reason for leaving a meeting midway through the form.

MPs who are absent because of illness must provide details of where they are receiving treatment.

Similarly, MPs travelling to their constituencies must submit a schedule showing their departure and return. Those attending formal invitations or programmes abroad must also provide details of the event.

For overseas programmes, MPs will have to submit information about the organising institution and the programme, along with the approval letter obtained from the relevant authority.

According to RSP leaders, the main purpose of the Google Form is to make MPs more accountable for their presence in Parliament.

The party plans to maintain a consolidated record covering MPs who fail to attend meetings, arrive late, leave meetings midway or leave the parliamentary premises and return.

RSP leaders say parliamentary attendance should not be treated merely as a matter of marking presence, but as part of an MP’s responsibility and accountability.

Move follows failure to meet quorum

The RSP’s decision comes against the backdrop of a recent parliamentary meeting that had to be postponed after failing to meet the required quorum.

On August 11, a meeting of the House of Representatives was adjourned after the required number of lawmakers was not present. The failure also halted the process of advancing government legislation.

The RSP has 182 lawmakers in the House of Representatives, making it the largest force in Parliament. As the ruling party, it carries a major responsibility for ensuring that parliamentary business proceeds smoothly.

However, during the August 11 meeting, even the required 69 lawmakers needed to table the proposal for a decision on the Mines-related Bill were not present.

It was against this backdrop that the RSP moved to introduce a formal system for monitoring its lawmakers’ parliamentary attendance and movements.

According to Chief Whip Burlakoti, MPs have been instructed to submit a parliamentary absence application form under four circumstances to make parliamentary proceedings more organised and effective:

1. When they cannot attend the parliamentary meeting in full.

2. When they arrive more than 30 minutes late.

3. When they have to leave the meeting midway after attending.

4. When they leave during a meeting and return later.

The party has sent the instruction to all its lawmakers.

The instruction states that MPs must mandatorily submit the parliamentary absence application form if they cannot attend a meeting for any reason, arrive more than 30 minutes late, leave the meeting midway after attending, or leave the meeting temporarily and return.

title.rendered: Election Commission urges update of deceased voters’ records

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The Election Commission has urged family members and other concerned individuals to update the voter records of deceased voters.

Election Commission Joint Secretary Narayan Prasad Bhattarai made the request through a press statement. The commission has been regularly updating the voter roll to keep it accurate, up to date, reliable and objective.

After the death of a voter, a family member or any other individual can notify the concerned election office as soon as possible, along with the death registration certificate, to have the voter record updated.

“Updating the voter roll is the basis for ensuring the integrity, fairness and credibility of elections,” the statement said.

The collection and updating of voter lists has been ongoing since Chaitra 22, 2082 BS, following the election held on Falgun 21, 2082 BS.

Individuals with a National Identity Card can register their names on the voter roll online using their national ID details. Nepali citizens who are not enrolled in the National ID system must fill out an online form through the Election Commission’s pre-enrolment system and physically visit the concerned provincial or district election office to provide their biometric details, including a photograph and fingerprints.

The commission has also made arrangements for online applications to correct names, surnames and addresses in the voter roll; transfer a voter’s name to a more convenient polling location when there are two or more polling stations within the same ward; correct voter details according to their citizenship certificate; and remove duplicate entries.

title.rendered: Minister Lamsal’s helicopter evacuation sparks heated exchange in Parliament

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The use of a helicopter to evacuate Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal after he fell ill has triggered a heated exchange among lawmakers, with ruling party MPs defending the minister and opposition lawmakers questioning the government’s priorities.

The issue was first raised in Parliament on Monday and continued to dominate discussions on Tuesday, with lawmakers trading arguments both in support of and against Lamsal’s use of the helicopter.

Lamsal, who was inspecting highways and infrastructure projects in Sudurpaschim, fell ill after reaching Baitadi. He was flown by helicopter to Dhangadhi and later brought to Kathmandu on a Nepal Army Sky Truck.

He has since been discharged from hospital.

‘The government can spend millions to bring a minister, but not Rs 300,000 to help people’

Nepali Congress Chief Whip Basana Thapa criticised the government over the incident, saying ordinary citizens were still struggling to access basic services.

She said people were not receiving relief, medicines such as paracetamol or even transportation to hospitals when they needed to go for childbirth.

“Ministers who have grown up drinking mineral water and jar water in Kathmandu are taken to Kathmandu by helicopter at a cost of millions when they cannot adjust to the water and food in Karnali,” Thapa said.

“The government can spend Rs 30–35 million to bring a minister back to Kathmandu, but cannot spend Rs 300,000 to provide relief to the people.”

She also raised the issue of people struggling to obtain even a single cylinder of cooking gas.

“Listen carefully, government. The life of a citizen in Karnali is just as valuable as the life of a minister,” she said. “A helicopter reaches a minister, but an ambulance does not reach a sick citizen. Is this equality? Is this the government of the people?”

Thapa also questioned the government’s emphasis on building expressways while people in Karnali continue to face shortages of medicines.

RSP MP defends Lamsal

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Bharat Prasad Parajuli came to Lamsal’s defence soon after Thapa’s remarks.

He began by recalling Prime Minister Balen Shah, saying people who attempt to bring change often face criticism.

“In our country, people who want to do something are criticised. The present government has also become a victim of this criticism,” Parajuli said.

He said Prime Minister Shah had been working day and night with the aim of changing the country’s face but was facing criticism from all sides.

Turning to Lamsal, Parajuli said the minister had been travelling across the country to understand infrastructure and connectivity problems rather than for ceremonial purposes.

“As a representative of a responsible government, Minister Sunil Lamsal has been working day and night, driving himself from the eastern part of the country to the far west, reaching remote areas during the monsoon to understand what the connectivity problems are and what problems people are facing,” he said.

“He did not go there to cut ribbons. Yet he is criticised.”

Parajuli called for a political culture in which good work is supported and negative work is criticised, rather than criticising simply for the sake of criticism.

RSP lawmakers had questioned ministers’ frequent tours

Interestingly, another RSP lawmaker had raised concerns about ministers’ frequent field visits just a day earlier.

Speaking in Parliament on Monday, RSP MP Paras Mani Gelal had urged ministers not to spend excessive time travelling outside their ministries.

“Do you want to travel around the country, or are you driven by the urgency to solve problems?” Gelal had asked. “Instead of behaving as though you are travelling on holiday, stay in the ministry. Make policies, take decisions and boost the morale of the employees.”

Gelal said lawmakers from the country’s 165 constituencies could provide information about problems in their respective areas and suggest solutions.

He also said the government did not need to spend state resources maintaining a large number of advisers for this purpose.

Instead, he urged ministers to pay attention to what people actually need.

“Today, people are struggling for gas, fertiliser, communication services, electricity and basic healthcare,” he said.

He questioned whether the conduct of ministers reflected these realities.

“A helicopter is available when a minister has a common cold, but when a citizen is dying, there is no means of getting them to a hospital. There are no doctors in hospitals,” Gelal said.

The debate over Lamsal’s helicopter evacuation continued in Parliament on Tuesday, with lawmakers putting forward contrasting views on the minister’s extensive field visits, the use of state resources and the government’s responsibility to ensure basic services for ordinary citizens.
