title.rendered: Promised ‘blue buses’ still off the road as govt approval remains pending

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The government’s plan to operate free blue buses for women across all seven provinces remains on hold, months after the Cabinet formally approved the initiative as part of its governance reform programme.

The Cabinet meeting on March 27 approved a 100-point governance reform plan. Point 97 of the plan stated that free blue bus services would be operated in all seven provinces to ensure women’s safe mobility.

The plan also set a first-phase target of putting at least 25 buses into operation within 100 days.

Had the government followed that timeline, the blue buses should have been running by July 17 (Shrawan 1) at the latest.

In June, numerous news reports carried headlines saying that the blue buses would begin operating from July 17. Had the buses started running as announced, Tuesday would have marked exactly one month since the service began.

It has not happened.

The initiative has also been included in the budget for the current fiscal year presented by Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle.

The budget states that arrangements will be made to operate a modern blue bus service equipped with CCTV cameras to ensure women’s safe transportation.

The Ministry of Infrastructure Development has allocated Rs 45 million for the programme.

Technical preparations completed, approval still pending

According to the ministry, most of the groundwork required to launch the service has already been completed.

Ministry Joint Secretary and Spokesperson Er. Ramhari Pokhrel said the technical preparations have been completed and an agreement has already been reached with Sajha Yatayat.

The file is now awaiting political approval.

“The agreement with Sajha Yatayat has been signed and approval has already been received from the Ministry of Finance,” Pokhrel said. “The day a decision is made by the political leadership, this announcement will be implemented.”

He said the ministry is ready to launch the service as soon as it receives a high-level go-ahead.

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal had also included the blue bus programme in his 100-day progress report released on July 4.

The report said preparations were underway to operate free blue bus services across all seven provinces for women’s safe transportation.

According to Lamsal, the ministry had coordinated with Sajha Yatayat to operate at least seven blue buses in Kathmandu Valley.

A draft proposal covering the operating procedure, timetable, action plan, cost estimate and responsibilities has already been prepared.

The ministry’s progress report said an operating proposal, including alternatives, had been sent to the Ministry of Finance for its comments and consultation.

The ministry says the Finance Ministry has already approved the proposal.

Lamsal’s report also stated that Rs 45 million had been allocated in the fiscal year 2026/27 budget for operating and managing blue bus services across all seven provinces.

An annual action plan, milestones and key performance indicators for the service have also been prepared, according to the minister’s report.

However, another senior ministry official said the file has reached Minister Lamsal’s secretariat and is currently stuck there.

The official said there was no clear information about why the file had stalled.

Election promise

The blue bus plan has also generated controversy over the colour and branding of the buses.

The Rastriya Swatantra Party had introduced the concept of blue buses in Chitwan, where buses painted blue were operated.

Sajha Yatayat, however, uses green as its brand colour.

The government’s plan to operate Sajha’s green buses as “blue buses” triggered criticism on social media, with some questioning whether the government was simply rebranding existing Sajha buses.

Sajha Yatayat later clarified that it would not change the colour of its buses.

Under the initial plan, Sajha Yatayat and the government were preparing to operate two buses on the Budhanilkantha-Lagankhel-Godawari route in Kathmandu Valley.

Two buses were planned for the Nagdhunga-Airport route, while four electric buses were planned for the Ring Road.

The social media debate has since died down.

But the government appears to have missed an opportunity to answer its critics through action.

At a time when it had made a written commitment and set a specific timeline for implementation, actually putting the blue buses on the road could have sent a positive message about the government’s ability to deliver on its own announcements.

Sajha Yatayat, however, says there has been no concrete decision or agreement on the operation of the blue buses yet.

“We have not moved ahead with further work related to the blue buses,” Sajha Yatayat Chief Executive Officer Bhupendra Aryal said. “We are currently working on the operating modality.”

title.rendered: Suspension bridge constructed at Kailatar, Ilam

content.rendered:
Ilam, August 18

Locals of Ilam Municipality Wards No. 8 and 10 are elated following the construction of a suspension bridge over the Mai River at Kailatar. The 179-metre-long bridge, which connects the two wards, was constructed for eight million 471 thousand and 460 rupees with financial support from the Koshi Province government. Ranjay Singh, head of the Infrastructure Development Office, Ilam, said the bridge, constructed along the Tilkeni-Silpur road, has made travel easier and reduced commuting time for residents.

Locals said the bridge has eliminated the need to make lengthy detours via Rajduwali and Simalgolai roads, particularly during the rainy season when crossing the river becomes difficult. Santosh Gole of Ilam Municipality-8 said the bridge has significantly eased travel between the two wards. “In winter, it was easy to cross the river as the water level remained low. But during the rainy season, even short trips required a long detour through either Rajduwali or Simalgolai.

Now, we no longer face that problem,” he said. Gole added that the bridge has also become a popular spot for visitors, with increasing numbers of people coming to the area to spend time, make TikTok videos and take photographs. Dalman Tamang, ward chairperson of Ilam Municipality-8, said the bridge has also been used as an alternative route between Ilam and Jhapa by motorcyclists after the Ilam-Rajduwali section of the Mechi Highway was blocked by a landslide. The new bridge is therefore serving not only as a vital link between the two wards but also as an important alternative transportation route for residents of the area.

content.rendered:

Four people have been arrested on charges of snatching a pedestrian’s chain in Lokanthali, Madhyapur Thimi Municipality-1, Bhaktapur.

Those arrested are 32-year-old Yogendra Tamang of Ramprasad Rai Rural Municipality-2, Bhojpur; 40-year-old Milan BK of the same rural municipality, ward 6; 36-year-old Debendra Thapa Magar, known as “Kale,” of Doramba Rural Municipality-3, Ramechhap; and 40-year-old Indian national Sanjit Samnat. They were arrested by a team from the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office.

Police said the group snatched the chain of a person walking near Lokanthali around 2 pm on August 11. A similar robbery had also occurred in Lokanthali on July 15 using the same method.

Police said the group specifically targeted women and elderly citizens for chain snatching. According to police, two of them would ride up on a motorcycle, snatch the chain, and flee.

Among those arrested, Yogendra was the one driving the motorcycle. Kale was the person who sat on the back and snatched the chains. Milan and Sanjit, police said, were the ones who bought the stolen gold.

title.rendered: Landslides affect 19 families in Nalgad, Jajarkot

content.rendered:
Jajarkot, August 18

Nineteen families have been affected by flash floods and landslides triggered by incessant rainfall in Nalgad Municipality-13, Jajarkot. With continuous rainfall causing the ground to crack, sink and erode at various locations in the ward, several settlements are at risk.

According to preliminary details collected by the ward office, 19 families in areas including Fumda and Khatigurtal have been affected. Some houses and sheds have been completely damaged, while even houses without visible damage are at risk as the ground beneath them has become unstable, according to locals.

Preliminary details show that the house of Bhade Damai in Fumda has been completely damaged. The houses and sheds of Datte Damai, Chandraprakash Singh, Khimbahadur Gurung, Nabin Singh, Bhaktabahadur Singh, Prembahadur Singh, Chandrabahadur Damai, Raju Budha, Dhanraj Shahi, Dilli Budha, Lile Damai, Kalibahadur Shahi, Binod Shahi, Manbahadur Malla, Saroj Malla, Gopal Shahi and Rambahadur Shahi have either been damaged or are at risk. Karne Damai’s house has also been damaged.

The toilets of Chandrabahadur Damai, Raju Budha and Lile Damai have been completely damaged. The sheds of Gopal Shahi and Rambahadur Shahi have been damaged, while their houses are also at high risk, according to the ward office.

Damage to monsoon crops as well

The flash floods have damaged not only houses and settlements but also farmland and monsoon crops. Locals said crops including maize have been damaged after floodwater entered agricultural fields.

Locals said the ground has also been increasingly cracking, sinking and eroding in areas including Fumda, Dharachaur, Majhabara, Chaulapani, Kolpella, Puderi Gaira, Panikhala, Shantibe, Tharigaun and Hale settlements. Fear has grown among residents as some settlements are becoming increasingly uninhabitable.

As the ground continues to erode, some families have left their homes and taken shelter in neighbours’ houses. Even families whose homes have not been directly damaged have been forced to remain there despite the risks.

Concerned that further damage could occur as the rain continues, locals have demanded immediate inspection of vulnerable settlements and relocation of residents to safer areas. They have also urged authorities to provide relief and essential food supplies to affected families.

Flash floods and landslides have also damaged drinking water pipelines at various locations. Locals said water supply problems have begun to emerge in some areas after the pipelines were damaged.

According to locals, minor damage had occurred at various locations during road and trail construction in fiscal year 2082/83 BS, when soil and rocks fell from higher ground. With continuous rainfall, the risk of landslides and flash floods has now increased in those already weakened areas.

Locals have demanded that families at risk be immediately relocated to safe areas, a detailed assessment of the damage be carried out, and essential relief supplies, including drinking water and food, be provided.

title.rendered: Safety orientation conducted for Asian Games participants

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

A safety orientation programme has been organised for participants heading to the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, set to take place in Japan this coming September-October.

The Nepal Olympic Committee (NOC) says the National Olympic Academy (NOA), in coordination with the NOC, organised the safety orientation programme on Tuesday at the NOC building for athletes and officials preparing for the Asian Games.

Olympic Academy Chairman Tej Bahadur Gurung stressed the importance of creating a safe, respectful, and inclusive environment for everyone involved in sports.

At the orientation, Academy Director Sujan Lal Shrestha, along with members Pratibha Joshi and Dr Pramila Thapa, gave presentations on related topics. They discussed the principles of safety in sports, prevention of harassment and abuse, protection of athletes’ rights and welfare, and the collective responsibility of athletes, coaches, managers, and officials in promoting a safe sporting environment.

At the event, it was also announced that NOC Joint Secretary General Ramji Bahadur Shrestha has been appointed as Nepal’s Safety Officer for the upcoming Asian Games.

The first session of the programme was attended by coaches, managers, and athletes from swimming, badminton, archery, kabaddi, and table tennis. The second session included representatives from judo, taekwondo, table tennis, volleyball, boxing, and squash. According to the NOC, similar sessions will be held for the remaining sports as well.

The NOC stated that the purpose of this orientation programme is to thoroughly familiarise every member of Nepal’s team with safety policies and practices before departing for the Asian Games.

title.rendered: Nepal’s ODI status at stake as World Cup League 2 race enters final stage

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 17 August

The race in the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 has become increasingly intriguing and challenging for Nepal following the results of the recently completed series involving Scotland, Canada and the UAE.

In the series held in Scotland, the hosts won three matches while the UAE won one, with two matches ending without a result.

Rain prevented the matches between Scotland and the UAE and Canada and the UAE from producing results. Scotland won both its matches against Canada, while the UAE defeated Canada in one match but lost to Scotland by one wicket.

Canada failed to win any match in the series. After earning one point from a no-result match, Canada moved one place above Nepal in the League 2 standings, pushing Nepal down to seventh.

Nepal is currently seventh with 24 points from 32 matches. Its chances of finishing in the top four and qualifying directly for the World Cup Qualifier have already become extremely difficult.

However, Nepal remains in a relatively strong position in the race to finish in the top six and retain its One-Day International (ODI) status.

Nepal now has only four matches remaining in League 2, with two matches each against Oman and Canada. The upcoming series will be Nepal’s final series in the League 2 campaign.

If Nepal fails to finish in the top six after the series, it could be locked into seventh or eighth place in the final standings and face the prospect of losing its ODI status.

Following Nepal’s poor performance in the previous series, the team has also undergone a captaincy change. Sandeep Lamichhane has replaced Rohit Paudel as captain.

Several key players have also been left out of the squad for the upcoming ACC Premier Cup, including Sompal Kami, Kushal Bhurtel and Bhim Sharki. The squad for Nepal’s final League 2 series has not yet been confirmed.

With a new captain at the helm, Nepal’s immediate challenge will be to win its remaining matches and preserve its ODI status. Captain Lamichhane has said the team will learn from its mistakes and move forward with better planning.

“We could not play the way we should have in our last two tours. We gave our best effort, but we fell short for various reasons,” he said. “Now we will correct our mistakes and move forward with better plans for the upcoming tour.”

League 2 standings

Scotland currently lead the standings with 45 points from 36 matches after completing all their games. The United States are second with 43 points from 32 matches, while the Netherlands are third with 38 points from 32 matches. All three teams are mathematically out of Nepal’s reach.

Oman are fourth with 31 points from 28 matches, followed by Namibia with 28 points from 32 matches and Canada with 25 points from 32 matches.

Nepal are seventh with 24 points from 32 matches, while the UAE are eighth with 18 points from 28 matches.

After the upcoming series involving Oman, Canada and Nepal, the United States, Namibia and the UAE will play a series, followed by a series between the UAE, Netherlands and Oman.

Slim chance of finishing in top four

Nepal’s only remaining route to a top-four finish and direct qualification for the World Cup Qualifier is to overtake fourth-placed Oman. However, Nepal would need to win all its remaining matches and rely heavily on results involving other teams.

Nepal must win all four of its remaining matches — two against Oman and two against Canada — to reach a maximum of 32 points. Even one defeat would end Nepal’s top-four hopes.

Oman, which currently has 31 points from 28 matches, has eight games remaining. Even if Nepal beats Oman in both of their upcoming matches, Oman would still have six matches left.

For Nepal to finish fourth with 32 points, Oman could collect no more than one additional point from those six matches, meaning Oman would have to lose at least five of them.

If Oman wins even one of its upcoming matches, Nepal would be eliminated from the top-four race.

Similarly, Namibia, which currently has 28 points, cannot collect more than four points from its remaining four matches if Nepal is to have a chance of overtaking it. Nepal would also need to beat Canada in both remaining matches and keep Canada below 29 points.

Race to retain ODI status

With direct qualification for the World Cup Qualifier now almost out of reach, finishing in the top six and retaining ODI status has become Nepal’s main and more realistic objective.

If Nepal fails to break into the top six after the series against Oman and Canada, its route to retaining ODI status will effectively be closed.

If Canada remains seventh after the series, Nepal’s main concern will be the UAE, which still has eight matches to play and could theoretically reach 34 points.

Nepal has several possible routes to the top six.

If Nepal wins three or all four of its remaining matches against Oman and Canada, it will finish with between 30 and 32 points. In that scenario, Nepal would move ahead of Canada and Namibia, although Namibia still has matches remaining and could potentially overtake Nepal.

If Nepal beats Canada in both matches but loses both games against Oman, it will finish with 28 points. Canada would remain behind Nepal if Nepal wins both matches against Canada and Oman also beats Canada at least once.

The UAE, currently on 18 points, has eight matches remaining and could theoretically reach 34 points. If the UAE produces an exceptional run and overtakes Nepal, Nepal could drop to seventh and Canada to eighth, although such a scenario remains difficult.

Therefore, beating Canada in both matches and reaching at least 28 to 30 points would be Nepal’s safest route to retaining ODI status.

The simplest route for Nepal is to win all four remaining matches. If Nepal fails to beat Canada and Oman, finishing in the top six will become extremely difficult.

Even if Nepal reaches the top six with a maximum of 32 points, its position would be secure unless the UAE wins all its remaining matches. If Nepal finishes on 26 or 28 points, however, it will have to depend on results from other teams.

title.rendered: RSP members active since party’s formation more likely to get local election tickets: Rabi Lamichhane

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chair Rabi Lamichhane has said party members who have been actively working since its formation are more likely to receive tickets to contest the upcoming local-level elections.

Lamichhane made the remarks while launching the application process for the party’s ‘Rural Municipality Candidate Club’.

He said those who have remained active in the party from its early days would have an advantage in the candidate selection process.

“We have not forgotten those who faced cases, were beaten, abused and humiliated while carrying the bell,” he said.

Lamichhane also sought to reassure existing party workers that they should not become discouraged by the possibility of new faces receiving election tickets.

However, he said existing party members would have to make way if a more capable candidate came forward.

He added that the RSP would keep its doors open for “lateral entry” to bring in capable new faces.

“There is a possibility that someone exceptionally capable may come along, and it is true that many people have been prevented from joining the party because we were waiting to see whether such candidates would emerge,” Lamichhane said. “The Candidate Club will put an end to that practice.”

The RSP has opened applications from people interested in contesting local-level elections as representatives of rural municipalities.

In the first phase, applications have been invited for rural municipality chairpersons, vice-chairpersons, ward chairpersons and ward members.

The party expects to select 460 candidates for rural municipality chairperson and vice-chairperson positions through the process.

Applications have also been invited from those interested in contesting for 3,685 ward chairperson positions and 14,740 ward member positions.

title.rendered: Spider-Man earns 156.3 million in Nepal, 2 billion dollars worldwide

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is setting one record after another, both in Nepal and around the world. It has earned more than 2 billion dollars worldwide through its third weekend.

Variety magazine reported that the Tom Holland-starrer film earned 785 million dollars from North America and 1.23 billion dollars from international markets.

Its total earnings stand at 2.022 billion dollars. With this haul, Spider-Man: Brand New Day has become the eighth highest-grossing film of all time. It is the first Spider-Man film to cross the 2-billion-dollar mark.

In Nepal too, its earnings show no signs of slowing. As of Monday afternoon, the film’s gross earnings in Nepal exceed 156.3 million rupees. With this, the film has become the fifth highest-grossing foreign film in Nepal to date.

title.rendered: Federal Government offices to pay salaries every 15 days

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The government will now pay salaries every 15 days to employees working in all offices under the federal government.

The Office of the Financial Comptroller General informed all Treasury and Accounts Controller Offices, the Pension Management Office, and the Kumari Chowk and Central Tahasil Office about the provision through a letter.

The Ministry of Finance had decided in Baisakh to introduce semi-monthly salary payments for employees working under federal government agencies. However, the decision had not been implemented because the necessary system had not yet been developed.

The office decided on August 17 to make salary payments every 15 days after the completion of each 15 days. Allowances will also be paid on a semi-monthly basis.

The office has instructed the Treasury and Accounts Controller Offices to make arrangements for such payments when federal agencies within their jurisdictions request the release of funds.

The government initially launched the programme at the Ministry of Finance. Although it was planned to expand the system to all federal agencies from the current fiscal year, implementation was delayed by one month.

title.rendered: Athlete Santosh Rai achieves success at Ironman Leeds

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

London-based runner Santosh Rai has achieved success at the Ironman Leeds competition. In Sunday’s race, Rai finished second in his age group and 51st overall.

This is one of Ironman’s toughest courses, featuring a 3.8-kilometre swim, 180-kilometre cycle, and a 42.195-kilometre marathon run. The route’s uphill-downhill terrain adds to the challenge as well.

Due to water safety concerns, the swim leg was cancelled, and the event included only cycling and running.

“The most important thing is that my first attempt to qualify for the Ironman World Championship in Kona, Hawaii, has succeeded,” he said.

He said he felt immensely proud to become the first Nepali, and the first London bus driver, to qualify for the Ironman World Championship in Kona.

Qualifying for the Ironman World Championship in Kona, Hawaii, to be held on October 10 this year, is an extremely difficult feat. Only about 3 percent of triathletes across all age groups manage to secure a spot.

To do so, one must either win their age group outright or, to have their name entered into the “ballot” (selection process), must have completed 12 Ironman races in their lifetime and have participated continuously over the past two years.

It is considered a dream and an ultimate destination for triathletes around the world.

“I hope this journey of mine will inspire others to believe that anything is possible with dedication, hard work, and persistence,” Rai said.

Rai first represented Nepal in 2024 at the World Championship Long Distance Triathlon, where he finished in the top 13.

He competed in the elite category at that World Championship, held in Townsville, North Queensland, Australia.

Last year, Rai represented Nepal again at the World Championship Long Distance Triathlon held in Spain. Competing in the 40-44 age group at the event in Pontevedra, Spain, Santosh secured a top-17 finish.

Rai, founder of Nepal Run UK, set a Guinness World Record by running the prestigious London Marathon’s 45th edition dressed in Nepal’s national attire, the daura-suruwal.

Rai began running in 2009. He is the first Nepali to complete six of the world’s major full marathons: London, Berlin, New York, Chicago, Boston, and Tokyo.

Nepal Run UK has also launched a “7 marathons in 7 provinces in 7 days” event in Nepal, in which Rai has participated twice.

title.rendered: Bhat-Bhateni Supermarket to operate select stores 24 hours a day, starting with Radhe Radhe

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal’s largest retail chain, Bhat-Bhateni Supermarket, has begun round-the-clock operations at its Radhe Radhe outlet in Bhaktapur from Monday.

The company says the move is aimed at making shopping more convenient for consumers who may not have time during regular business hours.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar at the Radhe Radhe outlet, Bhat-Bhateni Chief Operating Officer (COO) Panu Paudel said the 24-hour service was introduced to provide greater flexibility to customers.

“This concept is new in Nepal, but it is already common internationally,” Paudel said.

According to Paudel, Bhat-Bhateni plans to operate one 24-hour outlet in each of the three districts of Kathmandu Valley.

The service began at the Bhaktapur outlet on Tuesday. The company plans to introduce the same service at its Krishna Galli outlet in Patan, Lalitpur, and its Tangal outlet in Kathmandu.

The Tangal outlet is scheduled to begin 24-hour operations from September 9, Paudel said, adding that the company is preparing to start the service from that day if possible.

He said the experience from the first day would help the company determine how much the 24-hour model should be expanded.

As the outlets will also operate through the night, the company has informed local governments and security authorities about the new arrangement.

“We have informed the concerned authorities as well,” Paudel said. “There are no security concerns from that perspective.”

Government spokesperson welcomes move

During reporting at the Radhe Radhe outlet, Onlinekhabar met government spokesperson and Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokhrel, who also praised the initiative.

“This was necessary for nightlife in Kathmandu Valley. It is also good from an economic perspective,” Pokhrel said.

He said the government would provide support wherever necessary, describing Bhat-Bhateni’s decision as a positive development.

‘We don’t have time during the day’

Consumers also appeared pleased with the new service.

Several customers interviewed at the Radhe Radhe outlet said they often struggled to find time for shopping because of their daytime work schedules.

The 24-hour service, they said, gives them the option of shopping after dinner or later in the evening.

One customer who had travelled from Bouddha to shop at Bhat-Bhateni said the new arrangement had made things easier.

“I couldn’t manage it during the day because of work. Now it’s much easier,” he said.

He added that he would be even more comfortable with the service if security and other arrangements were further improved.

According to Bhat-Bhateni management, only the first floor of the stores operating around the clock will remain open overnight. Only grocery items will be available on that floor.

Paudel said the company plans to introduce 24-hour operations at one of its Pokhara outlets after the three Kathmandu Valley stores begin operating around the clock.

“We believe this will further improve customer convenience,” he said.

27 stores across the country

Bhat-Bhateni Supermarket was started by businessman Min Bahadur Gurung in Tangall, Kathmandu, 42 years ago. The company now operates 27 stores across Nepal.

The retail chain generates annual revenue of around Rs 32 billion and provides direct employment to more than 22,000 people across its stores.

Most Bhat-Bhateni outlets were set on fire, looted and vandalised during the Gen Z protests on September 8 and 9, 2025, causing billions of rupees in losses to the company.

Despite the scale of the damage, Bhat-Bhateni says it did not lay off a single employee. The company reinvested and has already brought almost all of its outlets back into operation.

title.rendered: Floods, landslides disrupt construction of hydropower projects in Myagdi

content.rendered:
Photo: RSS

Myagdi, August 18

Construction of hydropower projects in Myagdi district has been affected by floods and landslides. Two hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 20 MW have also been forced to shut down. Four hydropower projects under construction in Dhaulagiri Rural Municipality have been affected due to difficulties on the roads, which have disrupted the transportation of construction materials, equipment and fuel.

Construction of the 53.5 MW Upper Myagdi-1, 37 MW Upper Myagdi, 65 MW Myagdi Khola, 14 MW Mudikhola and 6.5 MW Darkhola hydropower projects has been affected. Similarly, road access to the construction site of the 9.14 MW Super Ghalemdi Hydropower Project under construction in Narchyang, Annapurna Rural Municipality-4, has been cut off.

The 6 MW Rele Khola Hydropower Project has been shut down since the last week of Ashad after floodwaters from the Relekharka area of Narchyang accumulated at the dam. Power generation at the 14 MW Gharkhola Hydropower Project in Annapurna Rural Municipality-6 has also come to a halt after a dry landslide buried the powerhouse on August 11. One person died, and another was injured in the landslide.

Jyotikumar KC, project chief of Upper Myagdikhola-1, said vehicles carrying construction materials such as cement and steel rods, as well as equipment, have been unable to reach the project site since Ashad due to landslides at Ghumawne (Phaparkhet), Bangepahiro and Ilpu, and flooding in the Shivaratri Khola.

“We have continued work by using the available equipment and existing construction materials,” he said. “However, we have been unable to work at the expected pace because floods and landslides have disrupted the transportation of construction materials.” Construction of a motorable bridge over the Shivaratri Khola under the Infrastructure Development Office has also been delayed, making it difficult for vehicles to cross the river during the monsoon.

Buddhiraj Adhikari, public relations officer of the Myagdikhola Hydropower Project, said construction work has been affected by rising water levels in the river and landslides along the access road. “We have had to use alternative measures and available materials, which has affected the pace of construction,” he said. “We have been forced to use excavators to help vehicles carrying materials cross the river and clear landslides to allow vehicles to pass.”

The Upper Myagdi Hydropower Project, which has achieved 60 per cent physical progress and is in the process of increasing its capacity from 37 MW to 46.25 MW, has also reported that construction has been affected by floods and landslides. Resham Bhandari, chairman of Darkhola Hydropower, said the company has been unable to transport construction materials due to landslides at Thapachaur, Gauthali and Dachaur Bhir along the Beni-Darbang and Darbang-Dharapani-Takam-Muna roads.

—RSS

title.rendered: Swastima Khadka turned down an engineering career to lead Nepali cinema

content.rendered:
Swastima Khadka, who studied architecture, stepped into the silver screen almost as a side pursuit. But her journey from Bulbul to Lalibazar made her a leader in the Nepali film industry. Strong across both commercial and arthouse currents in an eleven-year career, she has won two National Awards. She has also led the debate on equal pay between male and female actors in the Nepali film industry.

Eleven years ago, when I met 19-year-old Swastima Khadka at the workshop for her debut film Hostel Returns, the eagerness and curiosity for acting were clearly visible in her eyes.

When the film was released, she rose as a “star” right from her very first movie. Since then, the storytelling and craft of the domestic film industry have changed a great deal. In light of that change, Swastima is now among the most in-demand actresses in the Nepali film industry.

From Hostel Returns to Laalibazaar, Swastima has established herself not just as an actress but also in film production and social intervention. Her greatest strength is her ability to carry both commercial and arthouse films on her shoulders and move forward in balance.

On one hand, she worked in films like Bulbul, Chiso Manchhe, and Dimag Kharab, which examine society closely; on the other, she proved equally accomplished in commercially successful films such as the Chhakka Panja series, Nai Nabhannu La 5, Bhasme Don, Hari Bahadurko Jutta, and Lalibazar.

Over her eleven-year cinema career, she has worked in a total of 21 films, all of which are either box-office hits or critically acclaimed.

A desire to become an “architect,” a journey into acting

Coming from a military family background, Swastima’s childhood was spent in a military environment. Having studied while living in the hostel of an Army Public School, she grew up amid social expectations that she should “become a doctor or a pilot when she grew up.” At one point, she even dreamed of becoming an air hostess.

But when she started watching the series featuring Madan Krishna and Hari Bansha (Mahajodi) on TV and began feeling the characters they portrayed within herself, that was the point from which the seed of acting sprouted in her heart.

Having graduated in architectural engineering from Thapathali Campus, Swastima initially wanted to keep acting as only a side pursuit.

“I thought my permanent job would be in engineering,” she recalls.

That thinking remained in place through her debut film “Hostel Returns” and her second film “Love Love Love.” But when she worked in the blockbuster “Chhakka Panja 2” (2074 BS), her thinking changed completely. After that, she decided to make acting her permanent profession. Time pulled her in such a direction that she came to stand among the country’s top actresses.

Deep characters of ordinary people

Whether it’s Madhubala of Lalibazar, or Pushpa of Chiso Manchhe, or Rankala of Bulbul, these deep characters that Swastima has lived on screen will always remain in the archive of Nepali cinema.

For her role as Rankala, a tempo driver, in Bulbul, she won Best Actress at the SAARC Film Festival held in Colombo within a week of each other, along with Nepal’s National Film Award. Likewise, for Dimag Kharab, she once again won the National Film Award for Best Actress.

Notably, her recently released film “Laalibazaar” is the biggest solo hit of her career. Earning close to 100 million rupees, the film brought a suppressed reality of Nepali society into public debate.

Swastima, who played the character of Madhubala, a rebellious mother, is being widely praised for her effort.

“These characters made it easy for me to connect quickly with audiences,” she says. “The reason ‘Bulbul’ resonates is that it was the story of an ordinary person. For ‘Chiso Manchhe,’ I went to the far-west and spent about ten days there meeting the local people and learning from them. If I had only been an architect, I would never have had this learning.”

This “learning” is itself the biggest achievement of this decade of her career. “Once you’re an actor, you can look at society from many angles. If I weren’t an actor, I would never have experienced or seen this,” she feels. She adds with a laugh, “Now there’s a path to study and then come into acting. It wasn’t like that in our time. I’ve been earning money and learning at the same time for ten years.”

Equal pay and the power of cinema

Swastima’s personality is not limited to being an actress. She was likely the first in the Nepali film industry to start the debate on equal pay between male and female actors. Other actresses in the domestic film industry are now also joining the debate she initiated and raising their voices for equal wages.

Having come to this position, I must also be able to say ‘no.’ I should make things easier for the girl who comes with a dream of becoming an artist,” Swastima says.

“I chose this path so that when I say ‘no,’ it becomes easier for the next generation to say ‘no’ too.”

Having reached this height of stardom, the audience’s love, awards, and box-office earnings alone are not enough for her.

“It’s not enough if the film does well commercially but isn’t critically acclaimed,” she says. “Working with a good creative team and achieving something meaningful, that’s what gives me real happiness.”

Last year’s release, Dimag Kharab, made her realise just how powerful cinema can be. Based on a story of youth leadership and intervention, the film’s release coincided with a heated atmosphere ahead of the Falgun 21 parliamentary election. Some leaders even criticised it, saying it had “manipulated voters’ minds by screening the film on night buses.”

“We start from a blank page, but it makes people cry and laugh too,” she says. “If you can change people’s minds positively without even meeting them, how powerful is the power of cinema! It was said that ‘Dimag Kharab’ even influenced the election results. This process of filmmaking keeps me very excited.”

Last year, she also stepped into production with the film Behuli from Meghauli.

Going forward, she wishes to bring to the screen more challenging characters who occupy an important but often-overlooked place in society.

Her one piece of advice to the new generation: “Do come into this field, but don’t stop being honest. Above everything else, honesty toward your craft is what matters.”

title.rendered: Why is Infrastructure Minister Sunil Lamsal constantly on the road?

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal has travelled to 55 districts in the four-and-a-half months since the formation of the Balen Shah-led government, according to ministry sources.

His latest tour took him to Sudurpaschim. After visiting Darchula, however, Lamsal fell ill upon reaching Baitadi.

He was airlifted from Baitadi to Dhangadhi in a Nepal Army helicopter and brought to Kathmandu by Sky Truck on Monday. His secretariat said he underwent tests at Chhauni Hospital that night and was diagnosed with a urinary infection.

He was discharged the same night and is currently resting at his residence on doctors’ advice.

The minister’s extensive travel across the country comes against the backdrop of a remark made by Prime Minister Balen Shah at the first general convention of the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).

“Our vehicle will not travel on local roads. It will speed through on an expressway,” Shah had said.

Lamsal’s travel record appears to have given that remark a literal meaning.

Why is Lamsal travelling so extensively?

There is a practical reason for at least part of the minister’s frequent travel.

After the formation of the new government, the then ministries of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, Water Supply, and Urban Development were merged to create the Ministry of Infrastructure Development.

The ministry has the largest budget allocation for the current fiscal year 2026/27, with Rs 302.83 billion allocated for implementation. It is also responsible for a large number of major infrastructure projects, many of which are facing various problems.

A ministry official said Lamsal and his team have been travelling to project sites to assess their condition, monitor progress and understand problems at the local level.

Lamsal’s approach has also changed over time.

Initially, he focused on bringing contractors to the ministry through the police and having them questioned through his secretariat. More recently, he has shifted his attention to field inspections.

The minister is generally accompanied by the ministry secretary and director generals of agencies responsible for implementing road, urban development and water supply projects. Lawmakers from the concerned constituencies and leaders of the ruling RSP have also joined some of his visits.

But the scale of the travel has raised another question: is there a political dimension to the minister’s district tours, particularly with local and provincial elections approaching?

That question has gained traction because Lamsal has been making commitments during his visits even though the annual budget has already been allocated and approved by Parliament.

He has been promising new projects, assuring locals that their demands will be addressed and, in some cases, directing officials to terminate contracts on the spot.

From project inspections to controversial remarks

Lamsal’s tours have attracted attention not simply because of how frequently he travels, but also because of what he says and does once he reaches the project sites.

In late May, locals protested during his inspection of the Kamala Bridge in Siraha. They said ministers had repeatedly visited the project without making tangible progress.

Lamsal was reportedly the 18th minister to inspect the bridge.

A joint interaction held by Lamsal and Law Minister Sobita Gautam in Sindhuli in early August also became controversial.

Gautam said the two ministers were responsible for the country’s budget and laws and that “the country will develop” as both were present.

The remarks drew criticism in light of the RSP’s own political rise.

The party had gained significant public support in the last election by strongly criticising the practice of ministers and lawmakers visiting districts and distributing projects according to their political interests.

Critics now say Lamsal is making similar promises during his own district tours, assuring locals that projects they demand will be completed immediately.

Some have accused him of making promises as though he could allocate funds from his own pocket.

One such remark came during his inspection of the Bahrabise-Tatopani road in Kavre in early August.

Asked about the 42-household Panthali settlement, Lamsal responded: “Just relocate the village.”

The remark went viral.

Former Sindhupalchok-1 lawmaker Madhav Sapkota criticised it, saying it reflected a tendency to “cut off the entire hand when only a finger is injured.”

According to Sapkota, instead of seeking sustainable solutions, the minister was offering irresponsible options such as closing roads or simply relocating settlements.

Lamsal also came under criticism in early June over the Naubise-Malekhu road.

After learning that the contractor responsible for relocating electricity poles had failed to complete the work, he directed officials to find and bring in the contractor. He then threatened that the contractor’s “legs should be broken” if the work was not completed.

A similar controversy followed his visit to Gulmi in late July.

Lamsal directed officials to terminate the contract for Gulmi Hospital, even though the project had achieved around 91 percent physical progress.

He ordered the cancellation, saying the project had failed to make sufficient progress even five years after construction began.

His approach of directly ordering contract termination rather than exploring other measures to improve project implementation has also drawn criticism.

A minister constantly on the road

The scale of Lamsal’s travel becomes clearer from the list of projects he has inspected since taking office.

He has inspected all three sections of the Kakarbhitta-Laukahi road project.

He has also inspected the East-West Highway expansion project from Kanchanpur in Saptari to Kamala in Siraha, including the Kamala-Kanchanpur bridge.

The Nagdhunga-Sisnekhola Tunnel is another project he has inspected and inaugurated. He has also visited the Siddhababa Tunnel.

Under the Kaligandaki Corridor, Lamsal has inspected the Beni-Jomsom-Korala road project. He has also inspected the Saljhandi-Sandhikharka-Dhorpatan road.

On that tour, he travelled from Saljhandi in Rupandehi through Sandhikharka in Arghakhanchi and Madane in Gulmi before reaching Dhorpatan in Baglung.

In Gulmi, he also inspected sections of the Madan Bhandari Highway.

The Karnali Highway has also been on his itinerary. Lamsal spent a week in Karnali in early August, travelling from Bangemsimal in Birendranagar to Kalikot.

Another major tour took him to the road network connecting Hilsa on the Nepal-China border with Simkot in Humla. He visited eight districts during that tour alone.

He has also inspected the Butwal-Narayangadh road, Daunne section, as well as both the eastern and western sections of the Muglin-Pokhara road project.

The Madi Bridge is among the other projects he has inspected.

Lamsal has also travelled with Law Minister Gautam to Sindhuli, Dolakha and Sindhupalchok to inspect infrastructure projects.

In just four-and-a-half months, the infrastructure minister has therefore covered 55 districts.

Whether the unprecedented pace of these tours translates into faster project implementation—or remains a defining feature of Lamsal’s tenure—is likely to be judged by the progress of the projects he has been visiting.

Kathmandu, August 18

Four of the six people injured in an SUV accident at Jurikhet in Bhimphedi Rural Municipality-6, Makwanpur, have been brought to Kathmandu for treatment.

The injured were airlifted by a Nepal Army helicopter to Birendra Army Hospital, Chhauni.

According to police, the Scorpio, registration number Province 3-01-002 Jha 5183, was travelling from Kathmandu to Birgunj at around 7 a.m. on Tuesday when it went out of control and fell about 100 metres off the road into a ravine.

Six people, including Gokarna Dangi, Chief Judge of the Birgunj Bench of the High Court, were travelling in the SUV. Four of the injured, who were in critical condition, were airlifted to Kathmandu.

title.rendered: Heavy rainfall predicted in few places

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Heavy rainfall has been predicted in a few places of hilly region in Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim Provinces. The Meteorological Forecasting Division has informed that moderate rainfall coupled with thunder and lightning would occur in most of the places of the hilly region and some places in the Tarai region across the country today.

Even a storm is likely in the Tarai belt of Koshi Province and some places of Madhes Province. Currently, the monsoon wind is active across the country. The low-pressure belt of the monsoon is situated in its average range in the east and to the north of its average range in the west, or near Nepal. It is causing rainfall at present in the western belt of Nepal.

It will be generally cloudy across the country today. Some of the mountainous places are forecasted to have light to moderate rainfall/snowfall along with thunder and lightning. Similarly, the weather service added that moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning is predicted in a few places of Madhes Province tonight. Similar weather features in Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim Provinces.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

The death toll from Japanese encephalitis (JE) across the country has climbed to 16 so far this year. According to the Family Welfare Division of the Department of Health Services, the JE virus has so far infected 63 people across 50 local levels in 22 districts.

The Division confirmed 63 JE cases from among 878 cases of acute encephalitis syndrome. Nine new cases of JE were reported in the last five days alone. As per the report shared by the Division, 34 men and 29 women were infected with the JE virus, and 31 of them are undergoing treatment. Likewise, all 16 dead people, including nine women who died of JE infection, were not inoculated. The prevalence rate of JE is high among the senior citizens.

The officials said that Jhapa reported five deaths, two each from Sunsari and Saptari and one each from Morang, Ilam, Rautahat, Dhanusha, Parsa, Kavre and Dang districts. More cases were reported in the eastern region of the country, but the disease has gradually spread to the west late.

Officials stated that most of the JE-infected individuals were residing near paddy farms and piggery. The first JE case in Nepal was reported in 1978 and the infection has since become a pressing public health concern.

title.rendered: Water recharge programme to protect sources in Kavrepalanchok

content.rendered:
Kavrepalanchok, August 18

Roshi Rural Municipality in the district has launched a scientific management of water sources and watershed conservation in a bid to ensure sustainable drinking water and irrigation facilities. The local government has forwarded the initiative in the wake of climate change impacts- drying up of water sources and shortage of drinking water.

Various international organisations working in the sector of climate change have extended support to the local government to run the programme under the integrated climate adaptation solution for Hindu Kush. The initiative would help reduce climate change impact and boost resilience of the local community. Chair of Roshi Rural Municipality, Dinesh Lama, informed that a concept paper on climate action was signed by the Rural Municipality, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and the Centre for Environmental and Agricultural Policy Research, Extension and Development (CEAPRED).

As per the concept paper, the activities for the programme include conservation of water sources, scientific management of watersheds, social inclusion through gender mainstreaming, gender equality, upliftment and empowerment of women, nature-based adaptation, and promotion of clean and renewable energy. A survey report has stated that 22 per cent of water sources and watersheds dried up in Roshi Rural Municipality. The multi-year project would run with the support of Global Affairs Canada.

title.rendered: Monkey menace leaves Bhojpur farmers struggling with crop losses

content.rendered:
Bhojpur, August 18

Farmers in Bhojpur district are facing growing difficulties due to increasing monkey attacks that have damaged crops and fruits throughout the year.

Farmers say it has become extremely difficult to protect crops once troops of monkeys enter maize fields. The animals destroy plants and consume harvested crops within a short period, causing significant losses.

Areas near forests and settlements far from human habitation have been particularly affected by the problem.

Kumar Raut, a resident of Bhojpur Municipality-4, said authorities need to find a long-term solution to control the growing monkey population.

“Monkeys destroy crops cultivated through months of hard work. We have to stay in the fields to chase them away,” Raut said, questioning why government agencies have failed to address farmers’ concerns.

The problem is not limited to maize fields. Farmers say vegetables and fruits grown in gardens are also being destroyed. Many families have been forced to build temporary shelters in their fields and assign two to three family members daily to guard against monkey attacks.

Chief of the Division Forest Office, Bhojpur, Khudrus Minya, said local governments and farmers have been provided devices to chase away monkeys. However, he acknowledged that such measures only offer temporary relief and that more effective long-term solutions are needed.

The continued crop damage has created both economic and social challenges for farming communities. Some farmers have even considered leaving their settlements due to repeated losses.

Farmers have urged local governments and concerned agencies to coordinate and develop a long-term strategy to control the monkey menace, reduce crop damage and protect agricultural livelihoods.

title.rendered: Juri Khet SUV Accident: Identities of all injured revealed

content.rendered:
Hetauda, August 18

The identities of all those injured in the SUV accident at Juri Khet in Makwanpur have been revealed.

The injured have been identified as Gokarna Dangi (57), Chief Judge of the High Court Birgunj, who is a resident of Tulsipur Sub-Metropolitan City-9, Dang; Registrar Taradatta Badu (57); Badu’s wife Laxmi Badu (49); his son Ritendra Badu (25); and his sister Rita Badu (31).

Chhunilal Chaudhary, around 32, a jeep driver from Rapti Municipality-8, Dang, was also injured.

The accident occurred on Tuesday morning when a Scorpio SUV, registration number Province 3-01-002 Jha 5183, travelling from Kathmandu to Birgunj, fell approximately 50–60 metres off the road into a ravine at Jurikhel in Bhimphedi Rural Municipality-6.

All those injured in the accident were rescued and taken to Bhimphedi Hospital for treatment. Police said preparations were underway to transfer the seriously injured, including Laxmi Badu, to better-equipped hospitals for further treatment.

According to police, a team led by SP Shyambahadur Khatri of the District Police Office, Makwanpur, also reached the accident site.

Police said further investigation into the cause of the accident is underway.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

A year after proudly embracing the label ‘jhole’—a term used by critics to describe blind followers—CPN-UML chair KP Sharma Oli is now calling some of his former loyalists ‘awara’, or aimless and irresponsible people.

The change in language reflects a deeper shift inside Nepal’s largest communist party.

Several leaders who once stood firmly behind Oli are now questioning his leadership and calling for organisational reform. Some of those who participated in last year’s ‘I am a jhole’ campaign are now among those demanding a change in the way the party is led.

Oli, meanwhile, has responded by questioning the credibility and intentions of those challenging him.

The latest confrontation has brought an old question back to the centre of the UML debate: Can a party built on dissent and internal debate accommodate criticism of its own chair?

From ‘jhole’ to ‘awara’

The irony in Oli’s latest remarks becomes clearer when viewed against what happened a year ago.

On May 29 last year, the UML organised a separate Republic Day celebration in Kathmandu while the party was leading the government.

The event attracted considerable attention on social media, where critics repeatedly described UML supporters as ‘jholes’.

Oli, who was then serving as prime minister as well as party chair, soon turned the insult into a political slogan.

At the 11th general convention of the UML Nepal Intellectual Council in Tokha on June 2, 2025, he said he had no problem being called a ‘jhole’.

“I am a jhole who carries the bag of the people’s interests, the bag of their welfare and the flag of change,” Oli said.

His remarks quickly became a social media campaign.

An ‘I am a jhole’ campaign was launched from Oli’s own social media page, with senior leaders and hundreds of party cadres posting photographs carrying the slogan.

Vice Chair Bishnu Paudel, General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel, then Deputy General Secretary Prithvi Subba Gurung and Bishnu Rimal were among those who joined the campaign. So did younger leaders including Samik Badal and Kshitij Thebe.

But a year later, the political equation inside the UML has changed dramatically.

Some of the same leaders who once defended Oli are now discussing whether the party needs a change in leadership.

And Oli has responded by calling some of those questioning him ‘awara’.

At a meeting of the party-affiliated Democratic Indigenous Nationalities Federation in Ilam on Saturday, Oli criticised those discussing his removal as party chair.

“Drinking tea at a canteen, these awaras are talking about removing the chair,” he said.

The remarks triggered a backlash, with some UML leaders and cadres launching an ‘I am awara’ campaign on social media.

Those who once defended Oli are now questioning him

The leadership-reform debate is significant not simply because it challenges Oli, but because many of those involved were once considered his political allies.

Vice Chair Bishnu Paudel, General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel and Secretary Hikmat Karki are among the senior leaders involved in discussions about reorganising the party leadership.

Leaders including Ishwar Pokhrel, Surendra Pandey, Gokarna Bista, Yogesh Bhattarai, Binda Pandey, Gokul Baskota and Karna Bahadur Thapa have also been raising questions about the party’s direction.

The debate intensified after Paudel and Pokhrel began arguing that the party cannot move forward in its current form. To explore future path, Vice Chair Ram Bahadur Thapa has been given responsibility for preparing a proposal on leadership reorganisation.

For Oli, the challenge is particularly significant because much of the pressure is coming from within his own political camp.

Young UML leader Samik Badal, who participated in the earlier ‘jhole’ campaign, says the circumstances have changed.

“We risked our lives to defend the leadership. What we did at that time was right. But now we have to stand up to protect the party,” Badal said.

He says criticism should not be equated with disloyalty.

“We have the right to criticise in order to protect the party’s soul. We have the right to demand answers,” he said. “The leadership should also behave appropriately.”

The leadership dispute is spreading to the provinces

The struggle over Oli’s leadership is not confined to the UML’s central organisation. It is also playing out in provincial governments.

In Koshi Province, Oli had previously sought to replace Chief Minister Hikmat Karki with Til Kumar Menyangbo following a power-sharing agreement with the Nepali Communist Party.

Karki, who is also a UML secretary, is now among those calling for leadership reform.

Oli had reportedly mobilised another party secretary, Sher Dhan Rai, to work on replacing Karki. Karki, however, insisted that any decision to remove him should be made through the party’s formal process and challenged the move.

Oli eventually had to continue with Karki as chief minister.

A similar dispute has emerged in Bagmati Province, where Oli reportedly wants to replace parliamentary party leader Jagannath Thapaliya with Kiran Thapa Magar.

But there too, party leaders have not simply followed his wishes.

These disputes point to a broader change inside the UML: leaders who once readily followed Oli’s decisions are increasingly prepared to challenge them.

‘Harsh language’ becoming a problem for the left

Oli’s ‘awara’ remarks came under scrutiny just a day after General Secretary Shankar Pokhrel spoke about the language used by leaders in Nepal’s left-wing politics.

Speaking at a discussion on the future of Nepal’s leftist movement on Sunday, Pokhrel said hostile language used during political disputes was contributing to growing distrust in the left.

“Harsh language itself has become a factor that is driving away the left-wing electorate,” Pokhrel said. “When they agree, they speak in extremely friendly language, but when disputes arise, they use extremely hostile language.”

His remarks are particularly notable because Pokhrel himself is now involved in the debate over UML leadership.

The language of internal communist disputes has historically included terms such as opportunist, revisionist, reactionary, traitor, broker and anti-revolutionary.

‘Awara’ is now the latest addition to that vocabulary.

A party whose history was built on dissent

The dispute has also revived questions about the political culture that has developed inside the UML.

The party’s history was built around debate, dissent and criticism.

At the fifth general convention, leaders with differing views were allowed to present their own political documents. At the sixth general convention, Oli himself presented a separate political proposal challenging the prevailing leadership line.

In other words, dissent was once a normal part of UML politics.

Oli’s own political rise was also partly built on questioning the leadership and political practices of his time.

Critics now argue that this culture has changed, with loyalty to the chair increasingly being treated as the ultimate measure of commitment to the party.

Left-wing analyst Jhalak Subedi says the change represents a departure from Oli’s own political history.

“Oli himself became a leader by questioning established values and practices. Until he reached power, he talked about democratisation. After reaching power, he abandoned it,” Subedi said. “Now he is calling his own leaders and cadres awara.”

Election defeat has intensified the leadership debate

The demand for leadership reform gained further momentum following the 2025 general election.

Oli had secured a strong mandate at the UML’s general convention. But the party subsequently suffered a major electoral setback.

Oli himself lost from Jhapa-5, while the UML was reduced to 25 seats in the House of Representatives.

For leaders demanding a review of the party’s leadership, the election result, declining public support and growing dissatisfaction within the organisation are reasons to reassess its direction.

The question now confronting the UML is whether such a review should be treated as a normal exercise in internal democracy—or as an attempt to undermine the party chair.

Much of that debate is taking place informally over tea at the UML’s Chyasal headquarters, as well as inside formal party committees.

According to Subedi, the problem is not that questions are being raised, but that the leadership is increasingly unable to listen to and absorb them.

From an individual’s brand to a party’s future

Critics argue that the UML has spent much of the past decade strengthening the political brand of an individual rather than its ideology.

The party, they say, prioritised power management over organisational development, placed personal loyalty above criticism and often attributed electoral setbacks to external factors instead of conducting a deeper internal review.

The result is now visible in the growing demand for leadership reform.

The debate is no longer simply about whether KP Sharma Oli should remain party chair.

It is increasingly about what kind of political culture the UML wants to have—and whether disagreement with its chair can once again be treated as part of the party’s democratic life rather than as disloyalty.

A year ago, many UML leaders proudly called themselves ‘jholes’ in defence of Oli.

Today, some of them are being called ‘awaras’ by the same leader.

The words have changed. The underlying question has not: what does loyalty to a political party really mean?

The damaged Scorpio remains at the accident site, while traffic along the road has resumed, police said.

title.rendered: Nepal’s PUBG team qualified for the Asian Games. A dispute took them out.

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Nepal’s PUBG team secured a place at the 20th Asian Games after a strong performance in the qualification tournament in Vietnam. But the team will now miss the Games after esports bodies and the government failed to resolve a dispute over which organisation should represent the country.

The Nepali PUBG team qualified for the Asian Games on June 21 after finishing seventh in the qualifier held in Vietnam from June 13 to 21.

The team consisted of Samir Costello (Zyo), Rohit Tamang (Zordy), Deepesh Gurung (Delta X), Saurav Tamang (TMG-8) and Sonu Karki (Biabia).

The qualification had raised hopes that Nepal could win a medal in Japan. Nepal’s PUBG team had finished fifth at the 19th Asian Games in China, narrowly missing out on a medal.

However, the National Sports Council (NSC) announced on August 11 that Nepal would participate in 22 sports at the Asian Games, with esports, including PUBG, excluded from the final list.

The decision has left the qualified players unable to compete despite having secured their place through the official qualification process.

The players recently held a press conference questioning why they were being denied the opportunity to compete after qualifying for the Games. They have now been forced to seek legal intervention.

One game, two associations

At the centre of the dispute is the existence of two esports associations in Nepal.

The Nepal Esports Association (NESA) is recognised by the Asian Electronic Sports Federation and has been involved in sending Nepali players to international competitions.

The Esports Association of Nepal (ESAN), meanwhile, is registered with the NSC and claims official recognition to conduct esports activities in Nepal.

The National Sports Development Act 2020 provides for only one association for each sport. However, both organisations currently exist and claim authority over esports in Nepal.

According to ESAN president Anjan Dhamala, the NSC initially received a long list of players recommended by ESAN. However, the list did not include the players who had qualified in Vietnam.

“We submitted the names of the teams that had won the previous competition as the long list to the Ministry of Sports,” Dhamala said. “NESA did not inform the government that the team had qualified.”

ESAN later informed the NSC that it would not participate in the Asian Games after the players it had recommended were not selected.

The NSC says the decision not to include esports in the Asian Games was made based on ESAN’s letter.

The council has also claimed that it attempted to coordinate with NESA but did not receive a response.

NESA, however, has rejected the allegations and accused the government of preventing qualified players from representing Nepal.

NESA president Suraj Dangol said the team selection and subsequent procedures had been completed according to international requirements and protocols.

Government, associations trade blame

The dispute intensified over the deadline for registering athletes for the Asian Games.

Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel has said NESA failed to submit the players’ names by the June 15 deadline.

“We cannot directly submit names without the recommendation of the sports association. We had kept a place open for esports until the last day and were ready to submit the names as soon as they arrived. But the names never came,” Pokharel said.

He claimed NESA contacted the government only after the deadline had expired.

NESA president Dangol disputed the minister’s claim, saying the association had repeatedly tried to contact the government.

“We continuously followed up. When we tried to meet the minister, we were not given an appointment,” Dangol said.

He also claimed that even when the players themselves approached the NSC, officials refused to register them.

“We went for registration even before leaving for the qualifiers, but they refused to register us. They behaved as if they did not recognise NESA. Even when the players went themselves later, they were not registered,” he said.

ESAN president Dhamala, meanwhile, blamed NESA for the situation.

“The players are the ones who have suffered because they cannot participate in the Asian Games, and that is unfortunate. But NESA is primarily responsible for this,” he said.

Players caught in the middle

NESA says it made several attempts to ensure that the qualified players could participate, including offering to send the team at its own expense.

“Our main concern is the players. We wanted them to be able to compete. There was a strong possibility of winning a medal in PUBG this time,” Dangol said.

“We even told the government that we would bear the expenses ourselves and only needed approval to participate, but our request was not heard.”

ESAN says a compromise could have been reached if both organisations had worked together.

“No one was supposed to go through ESAN alone. The state could have made a decision and both sides could have sat together to select and send the team in the interest of the players. But NESA was not flexible on that,” Dhamala said.

For the players who qualified through competition, however, the dispute between the two organisations has come at a heavy cost. Their Asian Games dream now hangs in the balance, despite Nepal having already secured its place on the field.

title.rendered: Government plans industrial security force, declares industrial areas ‘Peace Zones’

content.rendered:
The government has prepared a Private Investment Protection and Promotion Strategy that includes provisions for establishing an Industrial Security Force and declaring areas housing industries as “peace zones.” According to the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, the strategy was formulated following incidents of vandalism, looting, arson and theft at private industries, business establishments and commercial structures during the Gen Z movement on September 8 and 9, 2025.

A report prepared by the National Planning Commission estimates that public and private establishments suffered physical damage worth around Rs 84 billion during the movement. The government had announced, in its governance reform action plan approved on March 26, that it would formulate and implement a strategy for the protection and promotion of the private sector.

The government expects the implementation of the strategy to ensure the security and protection of industrial and commercial investments, boost confidence in the private sector and make a significant contribution to overall economic development. Nepal’s productive sector has been affected not only by political movements but also by natural disasters every year. According to the ministry, natural and human-induced disasters cause annual losses equivalent to around 3 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product.

The ministry has said that such losses pose a serious challenge to the national goal of achieving sustainable economic development. The strategy has been formulated to address these challenges.

Aim to boost private sector confidence

The government says it has prepared the strategy with a long-term vision of encouraging private-sector investment to promote economic prosperity. One of its key objectives is to boost confidence in the private sector and promote investment. The strategy aims to create a safe, stable and reliable environment for operating industries and businesses. It also seeks to establish physical and legal security arrangements to promote industries and businesses and protect investments.

The strategy aims to discourage all forms of unwanted and illegal activities—including vandalism, arson, closures, strikes and looting—that may occur at industrial and commercial establishments, while reducing risks to industrial and commercial investments.

Industrial security force, peace zones

In response to demands from the private sector, the government has made it clear in the strategy that an Industrial Security Force will be established to protect the physical assets of industrial and commercial establishments. Existing laws governing industrial security will be reviewed and amended as necessary. Industrial areas, industrial corridors, special economic zones and industrial villages will be declared “peace zones.”

Arrangements will also be made to prevent any form of unwanted activity at industrial establishments. Under the new strategy, the government will classify industrial and commercial establishments based on their security risks and provide security accordingly. Rapid-response security teams will be mobilised based on the risk of damage to industries, businesses and private property.

A designated contact person will be assigned at the nearest security unit to coordinate security for industries and businesses. The government will also adopt a zero-tolerance policy toward attacks, vandalism and arson targeting the physical assets and operations of industrial and commercial establishments.

A zero-tolerance policy will likewise be adopted against attacks, vandalism and arson targeting the private property and residences of industrialists and businesspeople.

Security patrols on highways to ensure smooth supply

The strategy includes continuous security patrols along highways and strategic highways to ensure the uninterrupted supply of goods and services and the smooth operation of services. The government also plans to launch a special search operation to recover goods looted from industrial and commercial establishments during the protests.

In addition, the hotlines operated by district emergency operation centres in every district and provincial emergency operation centres will be operated 24 hours a day as industrial security hotlines.

Relief and concessions for damaged businesses

The strategy proposes simplifying and facilitating regulatory procedures to promote private-sector investment. Private industrialists and businesspeople whose businesses were damaged by arson or vandalism during the movement will be provided exemptions, facilities and concessions for one fiscal year or for a specified period, in accordance with existing laws and provisions in the government’s annual budget.

Businesses affected by vandalism will also receive exemptions when renewing their business registrations or licences. The strategy allows for possible exemptions on building permit fees, electricity and drinking-water connection charges, and integrated property tax. Concessional loans will also be provided through banks and financial institutions.

Tax incentives to remain stable for five years

The government also plans to integrate the electronic information systems of the Department of Industry, Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection, and Office of the Company Registrar to simplify procedures related to the registration of industries, businesses and companies.

To make service delivery easier and more efficient, the strategy proposes interconnecting electronic systems operated by different government agencies so that documents submitted to one agency will not have to be submitted again to another. To promote industrialisation and job creation, the strategy also proposes maintaining at least a two-tier difference in customs duty rates on industrial raw materials and finished goods, based on an impact assessment of the relevant sectors.

It further states that tax exemptions, facilities and concessions granted under tax policies and relevant laws will remain stable for at least five years.

Private sector to be included in coordination committee

The government will establish a Coordination and Facilitation Committee to oversee implementation of the strategy, with representation from the private sector. The committee, to be coordinated by the Minister for Industry, will include presidents of umbrella organisations representing the private sector as members.

The committee will also identify problems and obstacles faced by entrepreneurs and investors and take initiatives to resolve them promptly.

title.rendered: Five parliamentary committees to meet today, here’s the agenda

content.rendered:

The committee has invited the Minister for Agriculture, the ministry secretary and other officials to respond to issues raised during the discussion.

The Infrastructure Development Committee, meeting at 10 am, will discuss the problems faced by the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN).

The Public Policy and Delegated Legislation Committee will meet at 10:30 am to discuss various issues, including a field observation visit to the Madan Puraskar Guthi.

Meanwhile, the Federalism Strengthening and National Concerns Committee will meet at 11 am to discuss ways to ensure inclusive and proportional representation in appointments to government bodies, among other issues.

The agenda of the Legislation Management Committee was not specified in the information released for the day.

title.rendered: Heavy rain likely in parts of hilly areas, strong winds possible in Tarai-Madhesh

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 18

Several parts of Nepal are likely to receive heavy rainfall on Tuesday, while strong winds are possible in some areas of the Tarai and Madhesh, according to the Meteorological Forecasting Division.

The country is currently under the influence of monsoon winds. The monsoon low-pressure line is around its average position in the east and slightly north of its average position, close to Nepal, in the west.

The weather will remain generally cloudy across the country this afternoon. Some areas of the Himalayan region are likely to receive moderate rain and snowfall accompanied by thunder and lightning.

Most parts of the hilly region and some areas of the Tarai are expected to receive moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning.

Heavy rainfall is likely at one or two places in the hilly areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Strong winds are also possible in some areas of the Tarai in Koshi Province and Madhesh Province.

At night, some parts of the Himalayan and hilly regions are likely to receive rain and snowfall accompanied by thunder and lightning.

Some areas of the Tarai in Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces, as well as a few areas of Madhesh Province, are also likely to receive moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning.
