title.rendered: RPP to remain neutral in trust votes of Chief Ministers Baniya and Acharya

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 17

The chief ministers of Bagmati and Lumbini provinces are set to seek votes of confidence today. Chief Minister of Bagmati Province Indra Bahadur Baniya and Chief Minister of Lumbini Province Chet Narayan Acharya are preparing to seek votes of confidence at meetings of their respective provincial assemblies today.

As the two chief ministers prepare to seek votes of confidence, the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) has decided to remain neutral. The RPP has instructed its provincial assembly members in both provinces to remain neutral. The party directed the leaders of its parliamentary parties to instruct their provincial assembly members to remain neutral until another decision is made regarding government formation in the provinces.

In the Bagmati Provincial Assembly, the Nepali Congress is the largest party with 36 seats. The CPN has 26 seats, while the CPN-UML has 25 seats, including the deputy speaker. The RPP has 12 seats, the Nepal Workers’ and Peasants’ Party has three, and Hamro Nepali Party has two seats. A majority of 53 provincial assembly members is required to form a new government in Bagmati.

The Lumbini Provincial Assembly has 87 seats, but only 83 members are currently in office after four members resigned to contest the election held last February. Based on the current number of members, 42 votes are required for a majority in the provincial assembly. The assembly has 29 members from the CPN-UML and 13 from the CPN, including the speaker.

Kathmandu, August 17

Nepali and Nepal Bhasa senior poet Durgalal Shrestha (Khwobilu) has passed away. He was 91. He died at his residence in Budhanilkantha on Sunday night, according to his family.

His body will be kept at the Nepal Bhasa Manka Khala office premises for paying last respects today, and the last rites will be performed tomorrow at Shobha Bhagawati. He is survived by his spouse, a daughter and two sons.

Born in 1992 BS, Shrestha was a teacher for a long time at the Kanya Mandir Vidyalaya at Chhetrapati. Shrestha’s first poem, ‘Santwana’, was published in the Dharmodaya magazine. He was conferred the title of ‘Janakavi’ by the Nepal Bhasa Parishad in 2060 BS.

Shrestha, the writer, became a member of the Nepal Academy in 2061BS.

Seven people have died in a stampede at Ashokdham Temple in Lakhisarai, Bihar, India. Lakhisarai Sub-Divisional Police Officer (SDPO) Shivam Kumar told the BBC that the incident occurred at Ashokdham Temple on Monday morning.

According to Kumar, seven people have so far died and six others were injured in the incident. The injured have been admitted to the Sadar Hospital. Lakhisarai District Officer Shailendra Kumar visited the Sadar Hospital to meet the injured and briefed journalists about the incident. According to him, all seven people who died were women.

“There was a long queue stretching from directly in front of Ashokdham Halt railway station to the temple. At the same time, two trains arrived at the station. Meanwhile, a rumour spread that an electricity pole had fallen, when in fact only an electric wire had snapped,” he said. “Following this, pressure increased in the queue of women on the left side, causing them to fall on top of one another.”

title.rendered: Geological study to be held of landslide-hit areas of west Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 17

The government is planning to carry out a geological study of the landslide-affected areas of the western region of the country. A meeting of the Monsoon Response Command Post of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) held Sunday decided to conduct a preliminary geological study of the landslide-hit areas at Thawang and Sunchhahari rural municipalities in Rolpa, Triveni municipality in Bajura and Bheri municipality in Jajarkot district.

The command post has also decided to deploy a study team in the field within three days under the leadership of NDRRMA, including representatives from the concerned agencies. The team will have participation from the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology. Likewise, the Monsoon Response Command Post has directed the concerned agencies to effectively advance the search, rescue, relief and rehabilitation works as the monsoon-induced disasters have caused havoc in different districts, according to the NDRRMA.

The NDRRMA has expressed its serious concern over the loss caused due to the landslides in some districts, and has urged that rescue and relief operations target the affected households. Today’s meeting of the command post has asked the concerned district administration offices, district disaster management committee and local levels to ensure treatment for the injured ones for free and provide relief materials to the affected households based on a rapid assessment of the disasters.

Similarly, the NDRRMA has directed the construction of temporary housing for those affected by the disasters and to initiate processes for retrofitting of the private houses and provide grants for the reconstruction and rehabilitation at the earliest possible time. The NDRRMA has also urged the people to exercise high alertness during the monsoon season as the risk of landslides has increased due to torrential rain in the hilly and mountainous regions in the country. Furthermore, the residents have been advised to avoid non-essential travel as the risks of inundation, flooding, flash floods, and debris flows remain high in different parts of the country.

title.rendered: Foreign employment agencies withdraw protest after government agrees to address demands

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 17 August

The Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment has agreed to address various demands raised by foreign employment agencies.

Following talks on Monday, the government and the agencies agreed to address the demands within 45 days, according to Hari Dangi, general secretary of the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies.

With the agreement, foreign employment agencies will resume operations from Tuesday, Dangi said.

The agencies had put forward 15 demands, including fixing the service fee charged to workers and withdrawing action taken by the Department of Foreign Employment. They had announced that they would close their offices and stop sending workers abroad from Monday if their demands were not addressed.

Following Monday’s talks, all protest programmes have been withdrawn, Dangi said.

The Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies had been organising protests and other pressure programmes since August 7, putting forward 15 demands concerning the foreign employment sector.

The meeting was held at the Ministry of Labour in the presence of the minister and secretary, along with the association’s chairperson, advisers and other office bearers. The ministry said the meeting held detailed discussions on all 15 demands raised by the association.

According to the ministry, most of the demands are related to policy changes. As the issues are also being considered as part of the ongoing process to amend the Foreign Employment Act and Regulations, the ministry and the association agreed to make maximum efforts to address them through the amendment process.

The ministry said it is moving ahead with amendments to the Act and Regulations to make the foreign employment sector more transparent, safe and dignified.

The two sides also agreed that foreign employment agencies can submit issues related to their demands to the Department of Foreign Employment along with the necessary evidence and documents, while the department will provide the required administrative facilitation.

The ministry said that if an issue cannot be resolved by the department, the law provides for an appeal to the ministry. The meeting also discussed resolving such issues through the established legal process.

content.rendered:
Bajura, August 17

The Badimalika Puja has officially commenced today at the Badimalika Temple in Bajura, marking the beginning of festivities and worship at this significant religious and tourist site. An all-party meeting organised by the District Coordination Committee led to the decision to start the worship earlier than usual, anticipating a large influx of pilgrims, particularly on the main puja day scheduled for August 27.

Last year, over 45,000 devotees visited the temple, with many travelling from various districts and neighbouring India as well. The temple’s appeal has been enhanced by the recent construction of a new temple by the Nepali Army, which is expected to attract even more visitors this year. Local authorities, including Mayor Amar Bahadur Khadka, have confirmed that comprehensive arrangements for the puja and fair management are in place.

Preparations involve collaboration among the district administration, local authorities, and security agencies, with 14 measures established to ensure safety and order during the festivities. Additionally, to maintain the sanctity of the site, there will be prohibitions on alcohol, drugs, and meat products, along with the installation of signs and information boards along the route to the temple. The Badimalika Puja has commenced, with District Coordinating Officer Dipendra Pandey assuring that the district administration, security agencies, and local authorities are prepared to provide emergency assistance to pilgrims in need.

Collaboration with the district hospital and health office is planned, while the Nepali Army will manage additional support alongside health workers. Efforts are being made to activate a 4G tower by Telecom to improve communication during the fair; however, construction has faced delays due to adverse weather affecting material transportation. Minister for Information and Communication Dr Bikram Timilsina previously urged Nepal Telecom to expedite the expansion of telephone and internet services in the area.

The lack of a road network has further complicated the delivery of necessary equipment, which is valued in the millions. Ishwar Singh, Head of the Nepal Telecom Telecommunications Office, indicated that a technical team had recently returned after spending a week on-site, but their work was interrupted by inclement weather and the delayed arrival of equipment.

Despite the initial arrival of technicians, they had to leave when the equipment did not arrive as planned, resulting in stalled progress on the tower’s construction. Chief District Officer Dorendra Niraula has confirmed that a team from Badimalika municipality is actively transporting goods to the tower construction site, with plans to ensure communication facilities are operational before the upcoming fair.

Amar Bahadur Khadka noted a significant increase in tourist activity in Badimalika, particularly as the fair approaches and the puja has commenced. The region has gained heightened attention following Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s characterisation of Badimalika as the ‘Switzerland of Nepal’ during a recent election campaign.

Bhu-Swarg (earthly paradise) Badimalika, located at an elevation of 4,200 meters, is celebrated for its natural beauty and spiritual significance, attracting visitors year-round, especially during the main puja on the eve of Janaipurnima. The site is believed to fulfil wishes and heal ailments, drawing both domestic and international devotees.

Key attractions within the region include the picturesque Triveni area, vibrant flora, and significant sites such as Kehitibeti, Bishnupani, and Dharmadwar. Local legends enhance the area’s allure, particularly the tale of the unchanged paddy from an ancient battle. The region is also home to diverse wildlife, including rare bird species, making it a compelling destination for those seeking both spiritual and natural experiences.

title.rendered: Govt moves to revive Udayapur Cement Industry

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 17 August

The government has begun preparations to resume operations at Udayapur Cement Industry.

As part of the preparations, the Cabinet has renewed the licence to extract limestone for the state-owned cement factory. The licence had been cancelled in September 2024 during the tenure of then Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli.

In a letter sent to Udayapur Cement Industry on February 13, 2025, the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies had informed the company that its limestone extraction licence had been cancelled and removed from departmental records.

The current government led by Prime Minister Balen Shah has now moved to revive the industry and has renewed its limestone extraction licence.

The Cabinet decided on July 2 to renew the licence. Two decisions were taken for this purpose.

First, the Cabinet approved the Department of Mines and Geology to reissue the previously cancelled licence for the extraction of limestone and red soil to Udayapur Cement Industry Limited under Section 12(3) of the Mines and Minerals Act, 1985.

Second, the Ministry of Finance will provide Rs 7,497,331.95 in outstanding dues that Udayapur Cement Industry owes to the Department of Mines and Geology.

This means the government has decided to cover the outstanding amount owed by Udayapur Cement Industry to the department as part of the process of reviving the factory.

According to sources, the Ministry of Finance has already provided the amount to the Department of Mines and Geology in line with the Cabinet decision.

The government is now preparing to appoint a general manager and operate the industry at full capacity. Udayapur Cement Industry currently has a production capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day.

Built in 1987 with financial and technical assistance from the Japanese government, Udayapur Cement Industry became Nepal’s largest cement company in fiscal year 2016/17.

The industry is located in a forest area in Jaljale, Triyuga Municipality-11, Udayapur. Infrastructure was built to transport the limestone required for production from Sukoura in the northern part of Udayapur through a ropeway.

The government is now preparing to bring the cement industry, which has been described as one of the largest of its kind in Asia, back into full-capacity operation.

title.rendered: Seeds of prosperity: China–Himalaya food security

content.rendered:
As climate change, geopolitical uncertainty and disruptions to global supply chains continue to test the world’s food systems, agriculture has grown into far more than a domestic economic sector. It has become a vital instrument of diplomacy, sustainable development and international cooperation. Among the countries advancing this vision most consistently is China, which has drawn on four decades of agricultural modernisation to build partnerships spanning Asia, Africa and Latin America. Nepal, bound to China by a shared Himalayan border and centuries of cultural exchange, stands today as one of the clearest examples of how agricultural cooperation can strengthen food security, uplift rural livelihoods and deepen bilateral ties.

China’s agricultural transformation ranks among the most remarkable achievements of the modern era. With less than ten percent of the world’s arable land, the country feeds nearly one-fifth of humanity, having become a global leader in grain, vegetable, fruit, aquaculture, tea and livestock production. This success reflects sustained investment in agricultural research, mechanisation, irrigation, hybrid seed technology and digital farming, policies that have lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty while steadily raising productivity.

Rather than keeping this experience to itself, China has chosen to share it. Unlike conventional foreign assistance, which often centres on financial aid alone, China’s agricultural diplomacy emphasises technology transfer, technical training, scientific research, infrastructure development and mutually beneficial trade. This model rests on a simple conviction: that global food security, technological innovation and sustainable farming are inseparable from peace, resilience and shared prosperity — principles at the heart of China’s vision of a community with a shared future for mankind.

Nepal: A natural partner in the Himalayas

Nepal has emerged as a significant partner within this expanding framework of cooperation. Agriculture remains the backbone of the Nepali economy, sustaining millions of livelihoods, yet the sector continues to face fragmented landholdings, climate stress, inadequate irrigation, limited mechanisation, post-harvest losses and restricted market access. These shared challenges — familiar to China from its own development journey — have created strong incentives for the two neighbours to deepen collaboration in agricultural modernisation.

One of the most visible results of this partnership is the transfer of modern farming knowledge directly to Nepali communities. The Chongqing–Nepal Vegetable Training Centre in Khokana, Lalitpur, has become an important platform for equipping Nepali farmers, women entrepreneurs and young agricultural professionals with skills in greenhouse cultivation, climate-smart farming and integrated pest management. Initiatives such as this demonstrate how practical, hands-on knowledge exchange can lift productivity while promoting environmentally sound farming practices.

Scientific collaboration has likewise become a defining feature of the relationship. The Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC) and the Sichuan Academy of Agricultural Sciences (SAAS) have built research cooperation aimed at strengthening Nepal’s capacity in maize, potato and sweet yam production. Through researcher exchanges, joint field experiments and technical training, Nepal is steadily adapting modern agricultural technologies to its unique mountain ecosystems while cultivating homegrown scientific expertise.

A shared challenge: Climate change impacts

Climate change has added urgency to this cooperation. The Himalayan region faces mounting risks from erratic rainfall, glacial retreat, floods, droughts and landslides that threaten both food production and rural livelihoods. In recognition of these shared vulnerabilities, Nepal and China — working alongside the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) as part of South-South cooperation funded via CIDCA — have launched joint projects promoting climate-smart agriculture, digital advisory systems and resilient food production in vulnerable hill and mountain communities. These efforts show how agricultural cooperation can address food security and climate adaptation as two sides of the same coin.

High-value agriculture represents another promising frontier. Chinese expertise in greenhouse farming, protected cultivation, orchard management, irrigation efficiency and value-chain development has offered practical lessons suited to Nepal’s diverse ecological zones. Demonstration farms and farmer training programs have introduced cultivation techniques that raise yields while conserving water, innovations of particular value in Nepal’s hill and mountain regions, where climatic conditions often limit year-round production.

Trade bridges built on trust

Trade has become an equally important pillar of this partnership. As of December 2024, China extended zero-tariff treatment to 100 percent of taxable items from least-developed countries, including Nepal — building on an earlier scheme that had already covered roughly 98 percent of Nepal’s tariff lines since 2019. Bilateral agreements have opened the door to exports of citrus fruits, medicinal herbs, silage and other agricultural commodities, while private-sector partnerships have created new opportunities for processed buffalo meat exports through modern meat-processing infrastructure. These measures give Nepal meaningful opportunities to diversify its exports and narrow its trade imbalance with one of the world’s largest consumer markets.

Improving cross-border connectivity holds further promise for Nepal’s premium agricultural products — tea, coffee, honey, large cardamom, and Himalayan medicinal and aromatic plants — even as imports of Chinese agricultural machinery, irrigation equipment, fertilisers and farming technology help accelerate Nepal’s own modernisation. Transparent regulatory standards, efficient customs procedures and improved border infrastructure will be essential to realising the full potential of this trade relationship.

Building capacity through people-to-people ties

Education and professional exchange have further strengthened bilateral cooperation. Nepali students, researchers and agricultural professionals have benefited from advanced training and study opportunities at Chinese universities and research institutions, while Chinese scientists have worked closely with Nepali universities and technical organisations. These exchanges build institutional capacity and foster long-term scientific partnerships that support innovation across the Himalayan region — the kind of people-to-people bond that gives diplomacy its lasting strength.

This partnership also reflects the broader philosophy of South-South cooperation. Rather than a donor-recipient relationship, China and Nepal increasingly approach agricultural development as a process of mutual learning. China contributes decades of experience in rural modernisation, poverty reduction and agricultural innovation, while Nepal offers internationally recognised expertise in mountain agriculture, community forestry, biodiversity conservation and indigenous farming systems. This balanced exchange shows that effective cooperation is built on respect for local knowledge as much as on technological advancement.

Charting the road ahead

Challenges remain. Differences in phytosanitary standards, customs procedures, transport infrastructure, quarantine systems and market regulations continue to limit the full potential of bilateral agricultural trade, while climate change continues to threaten food production across the Himalayan region through increasingly unpredictable weather. Overcoming these obstacles will require sustained policy dialogue, scientific collaboration, investment in resilient infrastructure, and stronger partnership among governments, researchers, private enterprises and farming communities.

Looking forward, the prospects for China-Nepal agricultural cooperation appear bright. Emerging fields such as digital agriculture, artificial intelligence in farming, precision agriculture, biotechnology, renewable-energy-powered irrigation, cold-chain logistics, food processing and agricultural e-commerce offer considerable room for expanded collaboration. Joint investment in agricultural innovation and climate resilience could transform Nepal’s rural economy while contributing to food security across the wider region.

As the international community searches for sustainable solutions to hunger, climate change and rural poverty, agriculture has become one of the most powerful bridges connecting nations. The partnership between China and Nepal illustrates how cooperation rooted in practical results can improve livelihoods, strengthen food systems, encourage scientific innovation and build lasting trust between neighbours. Ultimately, the success of this relationship will be measured not only in trade volumes or investment figures, but in the prosperity of farmers, the resilience of rural communities, and a shared commitment to building a more secure, sustainable and interconnected future in the Himalayas and beyond.

title.rendered: Over 180,000 visitors attend NAIMA Nepal Mobility Expo 2026

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 17

The NAIMA Nepal Mobility Expo 2026, organised by the Nepal Automobile Importers and Manufacturers Association (NAIMA), has concluded with more than 180,000 visitors attending the six-day event.

The expo, which began on August 11 at Bhrikutimandap in Kathmandu, attracted more than 30,000 visitors on its final day alone, according to NAIMA. The association said 29,000 people visited on the opening day, 26,000 on the second day, 22,000 on the third, 31,000 on the fourth and more than 42,000 on the fifth day.

NAIMA had expected around 150,000 visitors over the six days. However, the expo attracted more than 30,000 visitors, above the initial estimate.

More than 55 brands, 53 new products

NAIMA President Ritu Singh Vaidya said the participation of more than 55 brands, attendance of over 180,000 visitors and the launch of 53 new products were among the expo’s major achievements.

She said efforts were made to develop the expo not merely as a platform for showcasing new vehicles and technologies, but also as a platform for knowledge and learning. Saying, “This is not the end, but the beginning,” Vaidya said NAIMA aims to organise an even larger and stronger expo in the future.

Bookings and inquiries exceed expectations

Organisers said customer interest in vehicles, as reflected in inquiries and bookings, also exceeded expectations. Auto Show Planning Committee Chair Gaurav Sharda said more people than expected visited the expo and that inquiries and bookings were also higher than anticipated.

NAIMA board member Cabinet Shrestha described the large turnout as a positive sign for the automobile industry. Akash Golchha, chair of NAIMA’s Strategy and Membership Affairs Committee, described the expo as a “superhit.”

Discussions and dialogues alongside vehicle displays

This year’s expo was not limited to vehicle displays, with discussions and interactive sessions held on a range of topics.

The NAIMA Mobility Dialogue was held on the closing day, August 16, featuring House of Representatives member Bidushi Rana, NAIMA board member and Padma Jyoti Group Chairperson Saurabh Jyoti, Padma Kanya Campus Assistant Professor Bhagwati Sedain and Thapathali Engineering Campus Assistant Professor Lochan Kendra Devkota.

Throughout the expo, discussions were held on artificial intelligence and automotive technology, battery recycling, ethanol blending, finance and insurance, the present and future of mobility, investment and foreign direct investment, among other topics.

Focus on sustainable and technology-friendly transport

According to NAIMA, the second edition of the expo was organised with the objective of promoting a sustainable, green and technology-friendly transportation system in Nepal. Domestic and multinational vehicle manufacturers and importers participated significantly in the expo.

NAIMA Executive Director Raj Kumar Dulal said the organisers focused on learning sessions, collaboration and demand-driven management alongside the large-scale exhibition. According to him, visitor satisfaction was the key measure of the expo’s success.

Various banks, insurance companies, technology and charging companies, educational institutions, ride-sharing companies, and organisations from the health and safety sectors also partnered in this year’s expo.

NAIMA said the large turnout and strong interest in new products demonstrated that consumer interest in Nepal’s automobile and mobility market remains strong.

title.rendered: Horaa finishes eighth in PUBG Mobile World Cup, wins nearly Rs 20 million

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 17

Nepal’s Horaa Esports has finished eighth at the PUBG Mobile World Cup, part of the Esports World Cup held in Paris, France.

The “smash rule” was in effect on the final day of the finals, and the outcome wasn’t settled until the very last match. Horaa secured eighth place after totalling 109 points across 18 matches.

With the eighth-place finish, Horaa took home a combined $127,500 in prize money, $57,500 earned during the group stage plus $70,000 for the finals. At today’s exchange rate, $127,000 works out to roughly Rs 1.94 crore (about 19.4 million rupees).

On the first day of the finals, Horaa scored 19 points across 4 matches; on the second day, 39 points across 8 matches; and on the third day, the team put in a strong showing, adding 51 points. In the first match of day three, Horaa scored nothing, but bounced back with 21 and 14 points in the second and third matches. Without support in the fourth match’s zone, the team managed just 1 point, followed by 4 points in the fifth match and 11 in the sixth.

On the first day, Horaa opened with 6 points in the first match, then 10 points (5 kills, 5 placement points) in the second, and 3 points (2 kills, 1 placement point) in the third, before failing to score in the fourth. On the second day, Horaa earned 7 points in the first match, 15 in the second, and 6 in the third, before a rough stretch from the fourth through seventh matches, including a scoreless fourth match, 1 point each in the fifth and sixth, and 3 points in the seventh. The team closed day two with 6 points in its final match, finishing that day in 11th place overall with 58 points across 12 matches.

Horaa advanced directly to the grand finals from the group stage, finishing among the top five of Group B’s 16 teams after last Sunday’s group matches, placing fourth overall with 98 points, including one chicken dinner. That fourth-place group finish had already guaranteed the team $57,500 in prize money.

Turkey’s IHC Esports (referred to in the source as ESTG Esports) won the grand finale, taking home $500,000. All 16 teams competing in the PUBG Mobile grand finals received prize money: the champions earned $500,000, the runner-up $250,000, and third place $150,000. Fourth place received $120,000, fifth $100,000, sixth $90,000, seventh $80,000, and eighth (Horaa) $70,000. Teams finishing ninth through 16th received $60,000, $55,000, $50,000, $45,000, $40,000, $35,000, $30,000, and $25,000, respectively.

In last year’s edition of the World Cup, Horaa finished ninth and won over $127,500 in prize money.

title.rendered: Heavy rain likely in several provinces today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 17

Monsoon winds currently affect the entire country. The monsoon’s low-pressure trough runs roughly through its average position in the east, while in the west it sits north of its usual position, closer to northern Nepal.

According to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, this pattern is bringing rain to western Nepal, with Baitadi, Kanchanpur, Kailali, and Bardiya recently seeing extremely heavy rainfall, and Syangja and Nawalpur also recording very high totals.

This afternoon, moderate rain with thunder and lightning is likely at many hilly and mountainous locations in Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim provinces, along with a few hilly and mountainous spots in Koshi and Bagmati. The same kind of moderate rain is expected across many Terai locations in Gandaki, Lumbini, and Sudurpashchim, throughout Madhesh province, and at a few Terai spots in Koshi and Bagmati. Heavier rain is possible in hilly areas of Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim, as well as at a few Terai locations in Lumbini and Sudurpashchim, with one or two spots in Lumbini’s Terai belt likely to see heavy rain specifically.

Tonight, rain and snow accompanied by thunder and lightning are expected at a few mountainous and hilly locations. In contrast, moderate rain with thunder and lightning is likely at a few Terai locations in Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, and Sudurpashchim, along with a few spots in Madhesh province.

title.rendered: Home Minister Sudan Gurung tells voters to ‘take back their votes’ after questions over election promises

content.rendered:
Gorkha, 17 August

Home Minister Sudan Gurung has told voters in Gorkha to “take back their votes” if they expect him to transform the area within four months.

Gurung made the remarks during an interaction with voters in Shahid Lakhan Rural Municipality-9 of Gorkha on Sunday.

Gurung, who was elected to the House of Representatives from Gorkha-1, had met voters in Bhimsen Thapa Rural Municipality on Saturday and Shahid Lakhan Rural Municipality on Sunday as part of his previously announced programme to visit his home district every month.

During Sunday’s meeting, local residents reminded Gurung of promises he had made during the election campaign, including a commitment to allocate a budget for a laboratory in the ward.

Rastriya Swatantra Party ward secretary Khopendra Lamichhane reminded Gurung that he had promised to allocate funds for the laboratory when he visited the area during the election campaign. Gurung acknowledged the commitment.

When asked why the budget had not been allocated as promised, Gurung said voters should not expect results within four months and told them to “take back their votes” if they were dissatisfied.

A video of Gurung’s remarks has gone viral on social media.

During the interaction, a participant wearing a cap asked Gurung about the budget for the laboratory, reminding him that he had even called the ministry secretary from the area during the election campaign.

“You had said that you would arrange the budget for the laboratory according to the needs here in the upcoming budget. But it is nowhere to be seen in the budget,” the participant said.

Gurung responded that there were many small budget demands and said it would be impossible to include all of them.

“We have asked for a list from here. We need a list of what should be included,” he said.

Another participant sitting beside Gurung said the issue had been discussed with the ministry secretary only recently.

However, the questioner remained unconvinced and said local residents were increasingly frustrated.

“People in the village are about to kill us. Sudan Gurung said this yesterday, and now they are asking where it is,” he said.

Gurung then said his government had only recently brought its first budget and that he could not transform everything within four months.

“It has only been four months since the first budget came from our side. You just need the work to be done, don’t you? I cannot transform everything in four months. Take back your votes,” Gurung said.

The remark prompted laughter among participants.

One participant responded, “You should have said this before. We already elected you.”

Gurung then said he had been clear about his position and asked voters to judge him over his full five-year term.

“If you cannot trust me, don’t elect me. Watch me for five years. At least I have had the courage to say this,” he said.

Gurung added that only around 15 to 20 days had passed since the budget process began and said immediate demands could not necessarily be fulfilled.

title.rendered: CAN to purchase cricket ground equipment with ICC funding

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 17 August

The Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) is set to purchase various cricket ground equipment using funds received from the International Cricket Council (ICC).

CAN issued a notice on Monday inviting international competitive bids for the purchase of various ground equipment. CAN said part of the funds received from the ICC will be used for the procurement.

The equipment will be purchased through a “single-stage, two-envelope” bidding process. Companies and firms participating in the tender will have to submit their technical and financial proposals separately.

Eligible bidders can purchase the tender documents from CAN’s office in Mulpani until September 15, 2026. Applicants must submit a written application along with a copy of their company or firm registration certificate. The tender document fee has been set at Rs 10,000.

Those wishing to submit bids electronically can download the documents free of charge from CAN’s website.

Bids must be submitted to CAN’s Mulpani office by noon on September 16, 2026, either in person, by courier or electronically.

The bids will be opened at 1 pm the same day in the presence of representatives of the bidders. The bids must remain valid for 120 days.

CAN has made a bid security of at least Rs 1.5 million mandatory. Those submitting bids electronically can submit a scanned copy of the bid security in PDF format. The security must remain valid for an additional 30 days beyond the expiry of the bid validity period.

CAN said that if the deadline for purchasing or submitting bids falls on a public holiday, the first working day thereafter will be considered the deadline.

title.rendered: Kulman Ghising calls for review as Nepal Electricity Authority’s profit shrinks

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 17 August

Ujyalo Nepal Party Chair Kulman Ghising has called for a serious review and reforms at the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), saying its profits are shrinking.

Ghising made the remarks in a Facebook post on Monday while extending his wishes to the NEA on the occasion of its 41st anniversary.

“The shrinking of the authority’s profit — from Rs 12 billion in fiscal year 2024/25 to only around Rs 5 billion in pre-tax profit in fiscal year 2025/26 — requires a serious review and improvement,” he wrote.

“However, the solution is not to weaken the authority, but to make it more capable, stronger, professional, transparent and accountable to the people.”

Ghising expressed confidence that the NEA would play an increasingly effective role in providing reliable electricity services, achieving energy self-sufficiency, expanding electricity exports and contributing to the national goal of building a prosperous Nepal.

He recalled how the authority, once known as an institution responsible for imposing load-shedding, transformed its identity after fiscal year 2015/16.

“From ending load-shedding to achieving almost 100 percent electrification, from becoming a net electricity exporter from a net importer, and from a loss-making institution to a profitable one making a significant contribution to the national economy, this journey is itself an inspiring story of transformation,” he wrote.

He described fiscal year 2015/16 as a “turning point” in Nepal’s energy history.

“Before that, there was a story of darkness, scarcity and losses; after that, a new chapter of light, confidence and possibilities began,” he wrote.

According to Ghising, the NEA’s transformation also demonstrates that public institutions are not merely a burden on the state.

“With capable leadership, honest management and clear objectives, public institutions can become strong drivers of national prosperity,” he wrote.

title.rendered: Rahul Bisunkhe: Nepali teenagers turning plastic waste into furniture

content.rendered:
While solving math equations in a Kathmandu classroom, a boy could hardly have imagined that one day he would work in a village far from his own roots, doing work that most people would turn away from as mere garbage. But in a settlement in Dhading, Rahul Bisnukhe, chasing after waste, is sketching a map toward a sustainable future. It marks the start of his business, but he sees it as the result of a consciousness formed far from Kathmandu’s comfortable urban life, in a remote village.

Rahul’s ancestral home is in Jilu, Bhimeshwar Municipality, Dolakha, but he grew up in the lanes of Kathmandu’s Baphal neighbourhood. Raised in a lower-middle-class family, he represents the first generation to receive formal education, something his parents constantly emphasised the importance of.

From math to management

Rahul enjoyed working with numbers, so when he chose management over science after high school, many people asked why. He explains that most of his friends were headed into management, so he followed the same path. After finishing school at Harbour International School in Baphal, he enrolled at Greenfield College (affiliated with Tribhuvan University) to study Social Work and Mass Communication.

There, an orientation talk by teacher Sanjita Thapa Magar on “why social work matters” completely changed his outlook on society.

From Chepang settlements to Humla

Around 2018, during his first year of undergraduate studies, Rahul visited a Chepang settlement in Shaktikhor, Chitwan, for the first time. The local reality was starkly different from what he studied in his Kathmandu classroom. The scarcity and terrain made it hard for him to adjust; he recalls wanting to go straight back home. But once he spoke with the local people and closely observed their hardships and hopes, he realised this was the “real Nepal.”

It was in that Chepang settlement that he learned empathy, the ability to put himself in others’ shoes, a lesson reinforced by his mother’s teaching that life gains meaning only through helping others.

That visit was just a glimpse; it left him hungry to understand Nepal as a whole. Setting a goal of visiting a new, remote place every year, he went on to travel to Syangja, Dolpa, Rukum, and Humla.

In Taksera, Rukum, he stayed with a school friend, Ripendra Ghartee, observing traditional village life, and in Humla’s remote settlements of Chaugad Fya and Syada, he engaged in conversation with local youth and children. He felt that what these regions needed wasn’t sympathy but a sustainable initiative, though he realised he couldn’t do it alone.

From a hackathon to Paramendo Nepal

In December 2021, another turning point arrived. A Makeathon, a competition to solve real-world problems within a set time, was held in Kathmandu. At Impact Hub, Rahul met Bishal Damodar and Isal Tamang from Rigau, Dhading. The pair had brought their village’s problem to the competition: plastic waste. As in much of Nepal, plastic consumption in Rigau was rising with no proper management system; locals either burned it or dumped it in rivers, damaging both the environment and farmland.

Mechanical engineer Sujit Shrestha was also at the forum. Sujit brought technical know-how, Bishal and Isal understood the community, and Rahul brought experience and drive from his social work. Together, the four founded Paramendo Nepal, where Rahul now serves as CEO.

The company mainly processes plastic waste into tiles and boards, though it took them several years to develop the right technology and model.

A “circular economy” that turns waste into value

The team has set up collection and recycling centres in Rigau and Tawal, Dhading. In Rigau, 115 households have been trained to sort their waste; organic waste is managed by households themselves, while non-biodegradable plastic is collected in baskets provided by the company. Twice a week, company staff collect the waste from the village and bring it to the centre; in Tawal, the local municipality’s vehicle handles collection.

They mainly recycle LDPE, HDPE, PP, and multi-layer plastic (MLP). The collected plastic is shredded, cleaned, and then heat-pressed into “plastic boards,” which Rahul says are stronger and more durable than ordinary wood, resistant to insects and water damage. They also make mobile stands, tables, chairs, and other furniture from the material.

Even in a remote place like Rigau, about 40 tonnes of plastic waste are generated annually, and not all of it can be recycled. The team is still searching for new technology to handle the remaining plastic and rubber. International partners, including Cambridge University, Fab Lab Nepal, and Impact Hub, are providing technical support; Cambridge has helped with machinery design and quality, while the local government has provided land for the recycling centre.

The team is currently working on this circular-economy model with funding from the European League Race grant. A circular economy is an economic model in which materials are reused cyclically rather than discarded after a single use. Their goal, in Rahul’s words, is for whatever they use not to end up as waste but instead be transformed back into new products for consumers.

The company now employs 14 people, including its founders. At their office in Jhamsikhel, Kathmandu, the team focuses on research and innovation, with plans to expand the model to other municipalities across Nepal through a franchise-style approach.

title.rendered: Indian Army chief Dhiraj Seth to receive honorary rank of General from Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 17 August

Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth will be conferred the honorary rank of General of the Nepal Army on Monday.

President Ram Chandra Paudel will confer the honorary rank insignia on Seth at a special ceremony at Sheetal Niwas.

Seth arrived in Kathmandu on Sunday for a three-day official visit to Nepal at the invitation of Nepal Army Chief General Ashok Raj Sigdel.

His visit is being seen as a continuation of the traditional military ties between Nepal and India and an effort to further strengthen bilateral defence cooperation.

India’s Ministry of Defence has also said the visit is aimed at strengthening defence cooperation and military-to-military relations between the two countries.

Seth is the highest-ranking Indian official to visit Nepal since Prime Minister Balen Shah took office. He has also chosen Nepal for his first foreign visit since assuming charge as the Indian Army chief, making the visit significant from both diplomatic and strategic perspectives.

During his stay in Kathmandu, Seth is scheduled to pay a courtesy call on Prime Minister and Defence Minister Balen Shah. He will also hold bilateral talks with Nepal Army Chief General Ashok Raj Sigdel.

The discussions are expected to focus on Nepal-India military relations, mutual assistance and ongoing cooperation between the two armies.

Seth is also scheduled to visit the Army Pavilion at Tundikhel to pay tribute to fallen soldiers. He will then hold bilateral talks with General Sigdel at the Nepal Army headquarters.

Seven-decade-old military tradition

The tradition of conferring the honorary rank of General on the army chiefs of Nepal and India began in 1950. It is regarded as a symbol of the friendly relations, mutual respect and military cooperation between the two countries.

Nepal Army Chief General Ashok Raj Sigdel has also received the honorary rank of General of the Indian Army. Indian President Droupadi Murmu conferred the honorary rank on Sigdel at a special ceremony at the Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi on December 12, 2024.

General Dhiraj Seth assumed office as Chief of the Indian Army on June 30, 2026. He previously served as Vice Chief of the Indian Army.

India’s Ministry of Defence has said Seth’s visit to Nepal will last three days. The high-level meetings and military discussions during the visit are expected to further the long-standing defence cooperation between Nepal and India.

title.rendered: Nepal Oil Corporation to resume regular LPG distribution through authorised sellers

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 17 August

Nepal Oil Corporation (NOC) will no longer distribute cooking gas through the special arrangements used on Saturday and Sunday.

From Monday, the corporation has asked consumers to purchase LPG through sellers appointed by the respective gas companies under the regular distribution process.

The NOC had distributed LPG through five locations on Saturday and seven locations on Sunday.

Consumers have been urged to contact the gas seller most convenient to them and purchase LPG through the regular system from Monday.

The corporation has also instructed gas companies and sellers to provide various details to make LPG distribution more organised.

Consumers without gas can contact Quick Response Team

Consumers who are unable to obtain gas from a nearby seller for any reason and urgently need LPG can contact the Quick Response Team (QRT) operated by the NOC.

The corporation has provided two numbers for the QRT: 9851455124 and 9851455128.

The NOC has introduced a five-point system to make LPG distribution more organised and effective.

According to the corporation, gas companies must provide the NOC, by 9 am every day, with details of the sellers and distributors making sales that day, including their names, addresses, contact numbers and the number of cylinders available.

Similarly, LPG sellers and distributors must maintain daily records of the quantity of gas sold, along with consumers’ names and contact numbers, and provide the details to the respective gas companies.

The gas companies must then submit the details to the NOC every seven days.

The NOC has also directed gas companies to give priority to consumers who use LPG for essential household purposes.

The corporation said it has requested the concerned district administration offices, through the Ministry of Home Affairs, to facilitate the safe transportation and distribution of LPG.

A joint team comprising NOC personnel and representatives of the Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection will also monitor LPG distribution.

The NOC has urged all concerned parties to comply with the prescribed arrangements to ensure smooth distribution of LPG.

title.rendered: Naag Panchami today: Religious, cultural and environmental significance

content.rendered:
Naag Panchami, observed every year on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Shrawan, is being celebrated today by worshipping snakes as tradition dictates. Although there are 12 names of Naags, the tradition of worshipping eight Naags representing eight clans has been followed since the Vedic period.

The eight Naag—Ananta, Vasuki, Padma, Mahapadma, Takshaka, Kulika, Karkotaka and Shankha—are worshipped by Brahmin priests today, and their images are then placed above the main entrance of homes. It is traditionally believed that after an image of a Naag is placed at the entrance, people should refrain from ploughing or digging in the fields and should not kill snakes, Naags, or other reptiles.

According to religious belief, placing and worshipping an image of a Naag at the main entrance protects the household from snakes and scorpions throughout the year, as well as from the fear of fire, storms and lightning. According to Vedic beliefs, the Naag is regarded as the king of snakes. Religious scholars say the tradition of worshipping Naags developed from the belief that misfortune could occur if they were angered, and that worshipping them would appease them.

From early morning today, special worship is being performed at Nagpokhari and Taudaha in Kathmandu, Siddhapokhari in Bhaktapur, and various Naag ponds, water bodies and sacred sites across the country. Milk, rice grains, dubo grass, kheer, roti and other offerings are presented as a mark of respect to the Naags. It is also believed that ancient sages established the tradition of worshipping snakes after recognising their ecological role in consuming harmful organisms and helping prevent the spread of poisonous substances in nature.

Religious significance

In Sanatan Hinduism, the Naag is regarded as a powerful and sacred creature. Various mythological stories feature serpent deities, particularly Shesha Naag, Vasuki, Takshaka and Kaliya. Lord Vishnu is traditionally depicted reclining on Shesha Naag, while Vasuki is believed to adorn Lord Shiva’s neck.

Naag Panchami is considered particularly significant because Vasuki is associated with Lord Shiva and the festival falls in the month of Shrawan, which is sacred to Shiva. According to mythology, when King Janamejaya began a snake sacrifice, the sage Astika stopped the ritual to save Takshaka Naag.

There is a religious belief that worshipping Naags on this day protects people from the fear of snakebites, brings prosperity to the family lineage and earns enduring spiritual merit. According to astrology, worshipping Naags on this day is also believed to pacify Sarpa Dosha, a condition associated with the lunar nodes Rahu and Ketu.

Cultural significance

According to Nepali tradition, an image of a Naag is placed at the main entrance of a house by a family priest or by family members themselves. The image is worshipped with offerings such as milk, rice grains, popped rice and dubo grass, with the belief that it protects family members from snakebites and other calamities.

There is also a popular belief that worshipping Naags brings rainfall and ensures good agricultural yields. Traditionally, placing the symbol of a Naag at the entrance of a house is believed to protect the household and ward off disasters.

The practice of worshipping at Naagpangar, or traditional mounds associated with Naags in rural areas, remains alive. This tradition has contributed to the preservation of indigenous cultural practices. Nag worship can therefore be seen as a practice that helps preserve Sanatan traditions, culture and customs.

Environmental significance

Naag Panchami is also a festival that raises awareness about the conservation of wildlife, particularly reptiles and snakes. Snakes play an important role in maintaining ecological balance. By feeding on rats, frogs and other animals, they contribute to natural pest control.

The religious belief that snakes should not be killed because they are sacred also promotes the protection of biodiversity.

Naag Panchami encourages respect for nature and wildlife while fostering gratitude toward the natural world and awareness of conservation. Scientifically, snakes play an important role in ecosystems by controlling populations of other organisms and maintaining ecological balance.

Naag Panchami is therefore not merely a religious festival. It is an important occasion that brings together religious faith, cultural tradition and environmental awareness. By encouraging respect for creatures such as snakes, the festival contributes to the protection of both nature and cultural heritage.

title.rendered: Manpower agencies to shut down nationwide from August 17

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 17

The Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies has announced that manpower agencies across the country will shut down from today. The decision comes after talks with the government failed to reach an agreement within the deadline set by the association. Manpower operators will stop sending workers abroad for employment from today.

The association has put forward a 15-point list of demands, including a revision of the service fees charged by manpower agencies. The agencies are set to close their offices nationwide, saying the government has failed to address their demands. Association President Dik Bahadur Khatri said the association is pursuing negotiations with the government while continuing its protest programs.

“We are now going to the Ministry of Youth and Employment for discussions,” Khatri told Onlinekhabar.

The association also held preliminary discussions with the ministry on Friday. During the meeting, representatives of the agencies briefed officials on their demands and presented their position. Ministry officials, meanwhile, shared updates on the progress and work being carried out by the ministry.

On July 22, the association held a special gathering of foreign employment business operators and submitted a 15-point list of demands to the government. The demands include setting the service fee that workers going abroad for employment must pay to manpower agencies and withdrawing disciplinary action taken by the Department of Foreign Employment, among others.

title.rendered: 120 families in Sangurigadhi at high risk of landslides (Photos)

content.rendered:
As the monsoon sets in, around 120 families in Sangurigadhi Rural Municipality of Dhankuta are at high risk of landslides. More than a dozen families in the area have already been displaced due to the threat of landslides.

Dadhuwa village in Ward No. 7 of Sangurigadhi Rural Municipality is one example of the landslide risk. The village, home to around 27 families, is surrounded by landslides on both sides. According to locals, the landslide on the eastern side began in 1999. As it expanded, seven families were forced to leave the village. Although the landslide on the eastern side has come under some control in recent years, the threat to the remaining residents has not disappeared.

The situation became more concerning after another landslide began on the western side of the village in 2018. Several families have already been displaced because of the western landslide, while others are in a situation where they may have to leave their homes at any time. Resident Jite Rai said the landslide has been expanding because of the steep terrain and erosion caused by streams and rivers on both sides of the village.

Rai said residents face the monsoon with fear every year because the landslide becomes more active as the flow of water increases. He added that the risk remains even during the dry season, as landslides continue to occur even when there is no rainfall. The situation in Dadhuwa is no different from that in other settlements across Sangurigadhi. Several areas of the rural municipality, which has 10 wards, are at risk of landslides.

According to Dipak Rai, a technical officer at the rural municipality, landslide problems are comparatively more severe in Wards No. 1, 5, 6, 7 and 8. Data collected by the rural municipality shows that around 120 families across the municipality are currently at risk of landslides. More than a dozen families have already been displaced, while several others are at risk of displacement.

Providing new homes for families displaced after their houses were threatened by landslides is a major challenge. For families dependent on agriculture, having to abandon not only their homes but also their farmland has also affected their livelihoods. The rural municipality said it has begun the process of relocating families at the highest risk to safer areas. However, Rural Municipality Chairperson Jitendra Rai said immediate relocation of all at-risk families is difficult because of the area’s geographical remoteness, limited resources and lack of suitable safe locations.

Chairperson Rai said the rural municipality has been carrying out various measures to reduce the risk of landslides. These include planting trees and constructing retaining walls in vulnerable areas to control landslides and soil erosion. According to Rai, a team including geologists has conducted a study of the affected areas to assess the actual level of risk. Based on the findings, the rural municipality is working to formulate plans for risk reduction and the safety of affected families. The process of relocating families severely affected by landslides has also been initiated. However, Chairperson Rai said the process has been delayed due to what he described as negligence by the provincial and federal governments.

Weak terrain and unplanned roads

The landslide problem in Sangurigadhi is linked to both natural and human factors. The area’s fragile hills, steep terrain and erosion caused by rivers and streams have made the land vulnerable to landslides. Technical officer Rai said haphazardly constructed roads in recent years have further increased the risk.

Rai said cutting into hills during road construction disturbs the natural stability of the terrain. Poor drainage of rainwater has also contributed to soil erosion and landslides in areas around roads. Sangurigadhi Rural Municipality, located in the southern part of Dhankuta district, lies within the Mahabharat mountain range.

Technical officer Rai said the area’s geological structure is relatively weaker than that of the higher mountainous areas of the district. He said landslide problems are becoming increasingly complex because of unplanned road construction and inadequate water management in an already naturally fragile landscape.

title.rendered: Chanira Bajracharya: From Patan’s Kumari House to an Australian Corporate Office

content.rendered:
In Chaitra 2057 BS, Chanira Bajracharya was just five years old when she was selected as the Kumari, the living goddess. Shortly after becoming Kumari, she met then-King Birendra during the Bhoto Jatra festival of Rato Machhindranath.

It was nine days before the Narayanhiti Palace massacre. Yet, four days before the massacre, tears began to flow continuously from Chanira’s eyes.

“My family tried to comfort me, thinking I was crying because I had just become Kumari and had to stay at home after leaving school,” Chanira recalls. But nothing they did could stop her tears. Seeing this, priests and elders took the Kumari’s crying as a bad omen.

Four days later, news of the Narayanhiti Palace massacre spread. “The news came just as my family was preparing to perform a ritual of forgiveness, thinking that perhaps the goddess had been defiled in some way,” Chanira says. In another strange coincidence, she had stopped crying only a short while before the news arrived.

In Nepali tradition, the living goddess crying or becoming angry is associated with the belief that something unfortunate is about to happen in the country. After spending 10 years at the centre of such mysterious traditions and beliefs, Chanira is now living her “second life” as an ordinary, independent young woman.

The struggle of coming down from the throne

When introducing herself, Chanira never gives only her name. “I am a former Kumari, and that is the biggest part of my identity,” she says.

She does not consider her 10 years as a living goddess a burden. She still vividly remembers thousands of people bowing in reverence as she was carried around the city in a palanquin during festivals. But when she returned from the Kumari throne to ordinary life, her real struggle began.

What was the most difficult thing about becoming a former Kumari? Her answer is unexpected: “Learning to walk.”

After spending 10 years being carried by others at public events, walking on the streets on her own feet was an entirely new experience. “At first, I even wondered why they weren’t carrying me anymore,” she says with a laugh.

Then came the struggle of adjusting to school, friends, classrooms and social interaction. Because her contact with the outside world had been limited while she was Kumari, she was extremely shy in the beginning. Once, when she stood up to give a presentation in class, she could not utter a word for two minutes. “I just stood there silently and then sat down again,” she recalls.

Even wearing ordinary clothes felt strange. Having been accustomed to red attire for years, clothes of other colours did not feel like her own. Some habits from her Kumari days remain even today. She has never worn leather shoes and does not use leather products. She is still not accustomed to sharing food that someone else has already eaten from. These are no longer imposed rules but have become part of her personality.

A dream of space and an educational gap

As a child, Chanira dreamed of studying space science. Planets, stars and the universe fascinated her from an early age. But studying science required access to laboratories, an opportunity that was not readily available to her because of her life as a Kumari.

Teachers used to come to her home to teach her while she was a Kumari. But there was no laboratory or extracurricular activities. The lack of classmates also had a significant impact on her social development. “It was very difficult for me to adjust to the outside educational environment at first,” she says.

This experience has now compelled her to speak up for the next generation of Kumaris. She believes the government should ensure the same standard of education for Kumaris, whether they are from Kathmandu, Patan or Bhaktapur. She says Kumari houses should have facilities for computer education, music, art and sports.

A love for numbers and a corporate journey

When the path to studying science became difficult, she turned to another interest—numbers and accounting. Her life as a Kumari, which was governed by routine, discipline and precision, had taught her to think in an organised manner.

After her time as Kumari ended, the school where she had studied invited her to work as a volunteer teacher. The aim was to help her gradually adjust to the social environment. Initially, she stayed outside the classrooms, checking homework and handling administrative tasks.

Impressed by her organised and meticulous approach to work, the school moved her into administration and accounting. She worked in the school’s accounts department for around eight years while completing her undergraduate and postgraduate studies.

While looking for new challenges, she applied to several companies. On her first attempt, she received an opportunity from an international company. Today, she works as a Senior Credit Analyst at an Australian company, where she analyses financial risks and assesses the financial condition of clients.

Interestingly, when applying for jobs, she did not mention anywhere on her CV that she was a former Kumari. “I wanted my work to speak for me first,” she says. Her colleagues learned only later that she had once been Nepal’s living goddess.

Breaking misconceptions, preserving culture

After she started college, people often asked her the same question: “You must know the Kumari dance, right?”

There is no separate dance form called “Kumari dance.” But the question eventually led her to Charya dance. She has been studying Charya dance for nearly a decade and is now also an instructor. “When I dance dressed as a Kumari or Tara, I feel as if I am reconnecting with my past,” she says.

Negative comments and references to “child exploitation” that she encountered about the Kumari tradition on the internet always disturbed her. To challenge such misconceptions, she engages directly with foreign tourists, journalists and researchers.

In collaboration with various travel agencies, she has shared her experiences with thousands of foreign tourists. “If the tradition needs reform, it should be based on facts. Reform should be based on facts, not misconceptions,” she says firmly.

Through the Vajra Dance Mandal, she teaches Charya dance to children. As secretary of Ratnakar Dha Baja Khalah, she is also actively involved in preserving traditional Newa musical instruments.

For Chanira, women’s empowerment is not merely an ideal to talk about. “Women must be financially independent. Only when you have your own income do you gain the confidence to make your own decisions,” she says.

A girl who once stood silently in front of her classmates for two minutes, unable to utter a single word, is now an analyst at an international company and teaches culture to hundreds of people.

Life gave her two identities—a goddess and an ordinary citizen. Today, she has transformed the honour she once received from the Kumari throne into a commitment to society and culture, while standing firmly on her own feet.

title.rendered: Akanchha Karki asks the questions society avoids

content.rendered:
In the latest generation of Nepali theatre, Akanchha Karki is a name for whom drama is never merely a vehicle for acting or entertainment. For her, theatre is a means of engaging in dialogue with society, questioning inequality, and searching for the possibility of change.

The founder of Kausi Theatre, Akanchha’s identity doesn’t stop there; she is also an actor, writer, counsellor, and trainer.

Drawn to literature, poetry, and art from an early age, Akanchha began acting on stage from grade four. But it was only after reaching college that she realised art was not just an interest but her life’s identity.

She went to India for higher education, earning a bachelor’s degree in performing arts and a master’s in counselling psychology. Her time in India became the decisive turning point of her theatre journey.

Recalling that period, Akanchha says, “I wasn’t a competitive person by nature, but India’s theatre culture made me competitive and combative.”

When others in college projects were reluctant to take the lead, she began taking on directing responsibilities herself.

Plays she directed, such as “Face Hooked” and “Rat Race,” even won awards at various competitions. “Face Hooked” addressed the theme of social media addiction, while “Rat Race” satirised modern society’s obsession with the race for success. Akanchha, who enjoys the combination of music and drama, also experienced India’s street-theatre (nukkad natak) culture up close.

Nepali adaptation of “The Vagina Monologues”

Akanchha returned to Nepal in 2015. Soon after, she began working as a psychologist at Ullens School with an attractive salary. Outside office hours, she also offered personal counselling.

Life was comfortable. But her heart remained fixed on theatre. Around that time, she got the opportunity to participate in a workshop organised by Mandala Theatre for women theatre artists. After the workshop ended, she proposed staging “The Vagina Monologues,” which she had performed in India.

Staging this play was itself a challenge in a Nepali society where open conversation about women’s bodies and sexuality is often considered indecent. On the other hand, presenting the play entirely in English risked reaching only a limited audience. So Akanchha, working with friends, translated about 80% of the play into Nepali, and it was first staged at Mandala Theatre.

The play received a bigger response than expected. Beginning at Mandala, its journey extended to Trisara and the Nepal Tourism Board, and it continued to be staged through 2019. It sent a message that Nepali society was ready for open, rational dialogue even on sensitive subjects.

The foundation of Kausi theatre 

During the staging of “The Vagina Monologues,” Akanchha came to a new realisation. The story they were performing was based on the experiences of an American writer. But during rehearsals, Nepali women began sharing their own deep, painful, and never-before-public experiences.

At that point, a question arose in her mind: why weren’t they bringing their own stories to the stage?

That very question inspired her to create original plays based on the experiences, pain, and struggles of Nepali women. As a result, “Private is Political” was staged in 2019, co-written with Saurav Karki and Suraj Subedi.

At the time, debates related to the #MeToo movement were also surfacing in Nepali theatre. Akanchha wanted to create a safe, respectful creative workplace with equal opportunity for artists, especially women and members of marginalised communities. This vision gave rise to the founding of Kausi Theatre.

Kausi Theatre’s first production was Dayalu Rukh, an interesting coincidence, since Akanchha had also directed this same play back when she was a student in India.

“When I was in college, I put together an entire production on a budget of just one thousand rupees,” she recalls with a smile. “But years later, when we staged the same play professionally at Kausi, the budget had grown a hundredfold to one hundred thousand rupees.”

After Kausi’s founding, Akanchha directed play after play. To date, she has directed over 15 plays, including notable works such as “Wedding Album,” “Animal Farm,” and “Play the System.”

Working together with artists with disabilities, she has also directed plays such as “But Still We Rise,” “Sick Room,” and “Prima Facie,” reflecting her commitment to inclusive theatre.

Risk, regret, rebirth

Akanchha Karki is now known as a theatre director, actor, writer, and counsellor. But she prefers to identify herself, most comfortably, simply as a “theatre director.” That identity, however, did not come easily.

In 2015, she acted in the play “Look Back in Anger,” directed by Che Shankar, a significant turning point in her acting journey. Around the same time, she received an offer to act in a commercial film.

She left her attractive job for the film. She lost weight. She devoted herself to acting full-time. Although she had no particular dream of becoming a “heroine,” she dedicated around six to seven months to the project because of the director’s persistent request and trust in her.

But after about 40% of filming was complete, the film was halted altogether due to technical and internal issues.

That event had a profound effect on her life.

“Everything had been going well. Why did I quit my job? Why did I take such a big risk? This question haunted me for a long time,” she recalls.

As soon as the film stopped, she battled depression and anxiety for about eight months. A persistent sense of regret over her decision followed her constantly.

But over time, she began to view that event from a different perspective.

“Looking back now, I feel that if the film had actually been made, I might have become merely an actor, but the director within me would never have been born.”

For her, that failure wasn’t an ending but a new beginning. It was from that very experience that the realisation emerged that she needed to build her own vision, her own stories, and her own creative space. The result was Kausi Theatre.

That said, her relationship with film hasn’t broken entirely. She has worked as an assistant director and actress in the Nepali film Elephants in the Fog, which won a jury prize in the “Un Certain Regard” category at the world-famous Cannes Film Festival.

Proving herself repeatedly

Even after directing more than 15 plays, every new production still feels as challenging to Akanchha as her very first. 

“As a director, I still feel I have to prove myself every single time,” she says.

That feeling isn’t only about creative pressure; it’s also tied to the experience of being a woman director.

“If a man had done work at this same level, I feel he would receive a different kind of respect,” Akanchha says. “When a woman does it, somehow it doesn’t seem to be taken quite as seriously.”

In her experience, there remains a large gap between the recognition a male director gets after directing just two plays and the respect a female director earns after years of consistently producing quality work.

“If a man does one good piece of work, he’s considered ‘great’ forever. But a woman has to prove her ability all over again with every new project,” she says.

According to her, the film industry still hasn’t fully freed itself from a male-centred narrative. Theatre, by comparison, is more inclusive; an environment has developed there featuring women-centred stories, the participation of women artists, and sensitivity toward gender equality.

However, at the level of direction and creative leadership, women’s presence remains low. While some women directors have begun their journeys, many are unable to continue due to financial instability, family responsibilities, and long-term insecurity.

Speaking about her own journey, Akanchha says, “Because my partner, Sudam CK, is also in this field, I’ve been able to continue with theatre to this day. Also, I don’t have children. From the outside, these might seem like ordinary details, but for a woman artist, such family circumstances make a huge difference in being able to stay in this field.”

Questions from Kausi’s stage

Despite an extreme lack of resources, Nepali theatre continues to spread its vibrant identity, earning praise even on international stages. But that praise hasn’t changed the daily reality of the artists working here.

For many artists and directors, theatre still hasn’t become a sustainable livelihood. Akanchha herself remains active in other professional work alongside theatre.

“If I were to give up everything else and depend on theatre alone, neither my life nor this theatre would survive,” she says. Still, her deeper concern isn’t financial hardship; it’s about which stories theatre should tell, whose experiences it should voice, and why those stories need to be told.

For Akanchha, a play is born from an uncomfortable question. She draws on her own experiences, society’s inconsistencies, and especially the uncomfortable experiences women go through, as the foundation for her plays.

“Whatever shakes me from within, whatever angers me, that’s the script I choose,” she says.

To the new generation entering theatre, she offers the same message, “If a piece of work doesn’t come from your very soul,  from the soles of your feet, never do it.”

Amid numerous social barriers, economic challenges, and systemic discrimination, Akanchha Karki has carved out her own distinct place in Nepali theatre. But perhaps her greatest achievement isn’t that.

The plays she creates don’t offer audiences easy answers; instead, they ask uncomfortable questions. For Akanchha Karki, that, perhaps, is success itself.
