title.rendered: Earthquake in Indonesia: Death toll rises to 51, 5,000 displaced

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 16

At least 51 people have been killed and around 5,000 displaced after a powerful earthquake struck eastern Indonesia on Saturday. According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck at 5:58 am local time on Saturday. Its epicentre was about 68 kilometres north-northwest of Ende, a city on Flores Island in East Nusa Tenggara province. The earthquake occurred at a depth of 10 kilometres.

Officials said around 341 aftershocks were recorded following the earthquake. It is being described as one of Indonesia’s deadliest earthquakes in recent years. Deputy Health Minister Benjamin Paulus Oktavianus said in a televised statement on Sunday that 36 people were seriously injured, while 77 others sustained minor injuries.

According to Indonesia’s disaster management agency BNPB, more than 3,300 people have been displaced from their homes in Sikka Regency, one of the areas worst affected by the earthquake. They remain stranded after roads were blocked. Some displaced residents have been temporarily sheltered in sports stadiums.

In the port city of Maumere, some residents have erected tarpaulins outside their damaged homes and are staying there. Some injured people have been treated at temporary medical camps set up outside local hospitals. According to BNPB chief Lieutenant General Suharyanto, at least 157 houses were destroyed, and around 200 others were damaged. In Nagekeo Regency, the area closest to the earthquake’s epicentre, around 2,000 villagers have been moved to temporary shelters.

Officials said rescue and relief operations have been challenging because of the region’s geography, which consists of numerous small islands. Three helicopters and a rescue vessel have been deployed for emergency rescue operations. East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudy Darmoko said buildings had collapsed and extensive property damage had been reported in several parts of the province.

Rescue teams have yet to reach all affected areas of Nagekeo. Fathur Rahman, head of the local search and rescue agency, said landslides had blocked roads and disrupted communication services, making rescue operations difficult. According to Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya, more than 3,500 soldiers and police personnel have been deployed from across the country for rescue and relief operations.

A tsunami warning issued immediately after the earthquake was later lifted. However, authorities have advised residents in some areas of the northern islands to move to safer locations, warning that aftershocks could continue for several days. According to Al Jazeera, the same coastal region was struck by a powerful earthquake in December 1992. Indonesia’s geological agency said more than 2,500 people were killed in Flores in the disaster, including by the tsunami that followed the earthquake.

With a population of around 290 million, Indonesia is spread across nearly 17,000 islands. Located along the Pacific Ocean’s “Ring of Fire,” the country is among the world’s most seismically active nations.

Nepal expresses condolences

Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has expressed sorrow over the loss of life and property caused by the earthquake on Indonesia’s Flores Island.

Saying that Nepal, which has experienced devastating earthquakes itself, understands the pain and suffering caused by natural disasters, Khanal expressed solidarity and sympathy with the Indonesian government and people on behalf of the Government of Nepal and the Nepali people.

He also extended heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families of those killed in the earthquake and wished a speedy recovery to those injured.

He further expressed hopes for the safety, rescue and relief of all those affected, missing or displaced by the earthquake, as well as their swift rehabilitation.

title.rendered: Preparing Nepal’s youth for the digital future

content.rendered:
Education is the foundation of a nation’s development. In Nepal, it is more important than ever to modernise education to keep pace with a fast-changing, technology-driven world. Today’s children are growing up in the digital age, and their future success will depend on how well our education system prepares them with the skills, knowledge, and opportunities needed for tomorrow.

The digital generation

Today’s children are growing up in a digital world. For many of them, a mobile phone is one of the first technologies they encounter, and screens have become a regular part of daily life. Unlike previous generations who mainly learned through classrooms, textbooks, and lectures, today’s learners are exposed to technology from an early age. Tools such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), virtual reality, and interactive multimedia are changing how people explore, learn, and understand the world.

Education expert Sugata Mitra, known for his famous “Hole in the Wall” experiment, observed that “Children can learn to use computers on their own, regardless of who they are or where they come from.” This is especially relevant for Nepal’s young generation. Given the right opportunities and support, they are naturally curious, quick to adapt, and eager to use technology to learn, create, and grow.

Skills for the next decade

The jobs and opportunities of the future will require more than just reading and writing skills. Students need practical knowledge, technical skills, and the ability to solve real-world problems. Across the world, countries such as South Korea and Finland have introduced digital learning and vocational training into their education systems, helping young people prepare for a competitive global economy.

Nepal also needs a clear long-term vision for education and development. Along with modernising agriculture, making better use of water resources, and improving infrastructure, the country must invest in quality education at every level. Skills such as critical thinking, digital literacy, coding, creativity, and problem-solving are no longer optional. They are essential for success in the 21st century.

Programs like India’s Skill India initiative show how education can be linked directly to employment through practical, job-oriented training. Nepal can learn from such approaches to help students gain relevant skills and reduce the gap between education and labour market demands.

Personalised learning and the role of AI

The future of education lies in personalised learning, where students can learn at their own pace and explore subjects that match their interests and strengths. Around the world, schools are increasingly using videos, simulations, interactive tools, and digital technologies to make learning more engaging and effective.

Artificial Intelligence is accelerating this transformation. Schools and universities are increasingly using AI-powered tools to support teaching, personalise learning, and improve student outcomes. China is already using AI-powered platforms that adapt lessons to each student’s individual learning needs, helping them learn more effectively.

For Nepal, AI presents both opportunities and challenges. AI-based learning tools can help address teacher shortages, provide personalised support to students, and expand access to quality education, particularly in remote areas. However, successful adoption will require reliable infrastructure, internet connectivity, digital resources, and continuous teacher training. If implemented thoughtfully, AI can make learning more accessible, engaging, and effective for all students.

Personalised and lifelong learning

Countries like Singapore have embraced the concept of lifelong learning by encouraging people to continuously upgrade their knowledge and skills throughout their lives. This approach helps individuals remain relevant in a rapidly changing world.

Nepal can benefit from a similar model by promoting creativity, adaptability, critical thinking, and ethical values. Education should not end with graduation but continue as a lifelong journey of learning and growth. As UNESCO notes, “Education is not only about economic growth, but also about building responsible citizens.” This vision is vital for Nepal’s long-term social and economic development.

Nepal’s policy push

Recognising the growing importance of digital education, Nepal has begun adapting its education system through the School Education Sector Plan (2022–32). The plan incorporates digital skills into the curriculum and encourages local and provincial governments to provide computers, internet connectivity, smart boards, and teacher training. Similar efforts have been seen in India through initiatives under the Digital India program, which promotes smart classrooms, digital infrastructure, and online learning platforms.

Making digital literacy a national priority is an important step toward ensuring that every child has access to modern learning opportunities. However, turning policy into practice remains a major challenge. Many rural schools still lack reliable internet access, technological resources, and the infrastructure needed to support digital learning. At the same time, teachers require continuous professional development to integrate technology effectively into their classrooms.

To achieve inclusive and equitable digital education, Nepal must bridge the gap between urban and rural schools through sustained investment in infrastructure, teacher capacity building, and digital resources.

Challenges and opportunities

Despite progress in education, Nepal continues to face challenges such as political instability, unemployment, limited research opportunities, and gaps in governance. However, education remains one of the country’s most powerful tools for transformation and long-term development.

Many talented Nepali students pursue higher education and career opportunities abroad due to limited facilities and opportunities at home. Creating a supportive environment for research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and skills development can encourage young people to remain in Nepal and contribute to national progress.

As education philosopher John Dewey famously said, “Education is not preparation for life; education is life itself.” His words remind us that education must be practical, adaptable, and closely connected to the needs of society.

Conclusion

Nepal stands at a critical moment in its educational journey. As technology, AI, and digital innovation reshape the world, the country must ensure that its education system equips young people with the skills, knowledge, and mindset needed for the future. By investing in digital infrastructure, teacher development, lifelong learning, and innovation, Nepal can turn its youthful population into a national strength.

title.rendered: Provincial Public Health Laboratory service suspended

content.rendered:
Narayangadh (Chitwan), August 16

The Provincial Public Health Laboratory in Chitwan has suspended all services, except for tuberculosis and certain viral load tests, due to a shortage of essential materials. The closure, which began on August 12, was prompted by the depletion of supplies from the previous fiscal year and the failure to receive new materials for the current fiscal year.

Ramesh Singh Dowal, the laboratory’s information officer, confirmed that a notice regarding the service suspension has been issued to inform users. Despite ongoing procurement processes, the lack of necessary materials forced the laboratory to halt operations entirely after a gradual reduction in services.

The laboratory previously conducted over 100 health tests daily, attracting patients with its affordable and reliable services. Dowal noted that the closure has compelled patients to seek alternatives, undermining the laboratory’s reputation for cost-effective healthcare. The public health laboratory service unit was established on 1 July 2023.

title.rendered: Sukepokhari: A mesmerising confluence of nature

content.rendered:
With the first rays of the morning sun, a distant mountain range appeared from Sukepokhari in Panchthar. Within moments, the mountains disappeared behind the mist. The clear sky was soon covered by clouds again. This playful hide-and-seek between mist and sunlight made the landscape around Sukepokhari even more enchanting.

Sukepokhari takes on a unique charm during the monsoon. Lush greenery stretches in every direction, clouds drift across the hills, cool mountain air blows through the area, and colourful flowers bloom here and there, compelling visitors to pause and admire nature. Located near Pauwa Bhanjyang Bazaar along the Mechi Highway, Sukepokhari is an attractive tourist destination in Panchthar. Its landscape changes with the seasons.

While Sukepokhari is covered in mist and greenery during the monsoon, the mountain ranges, including Kanchenjunga and Kumbhakarna, become clearly visible after a few weeks. In Chaitra and Baisakh, the same area bursts into bloom with rhododendrons. The wide-open meadows around Sukepokhari are currently lush and green. The sky is reflected in ponds of various sizes. Clouds racing over the hills and mist drifting across the landscape make the scenery look like a painting. As a high-altitude area, Sukepokhari also enjoys a cool and refreshing climate.

The rural lifestyle here is equally appealing. Farmers remain busy working in their fields, while others are preparing to plant radishes in fields where potatoes have recently been harvested. Agriculture and livestock farming are also important sources of livelihood for residents. Various species of trees, plants and seasonal flowers reflect the rich natural diversity of Sukepokhari.

Visitors to Sukepokhari can enjoy local delicacies alongside the natural scenery. According to resident Ajay Rai, the number of homestays and hotels has been increasing as the number of domestic tourists continues to grow. Along with Sukepokhari, areas such as Lohakil are also emerging as attractive tourist destinations. The Falgunanda Trail passes through this area, further expanding its tourism potential. The trail has been promoted as an important tourism project in Koshi Province.

“The scenery changes with the season, but it remains attractive throughout the year,” says resident Suresh Rai. Locals say the number of domestic tourists visiting Sukepokhari during the monsoon has increased in recent years, particularly as road access to the area has become easier.

Sukepokhari is not a destination where visitors have to wait for the perfect weather to see the mountains. Sometimes the mist conceals the mountains; at other times, sunlight illuminates the hills. Clouds race across the ridges, while flowers bloom amid the greenery. This ever-changing landscape, shaped by the shifting weather, is what makes Sukepokhari especially captivating during the monsoon.

title.rendered: Japanese encephalitis cases on rise in Jhapa

content.rendered:
Bhadrapur (Jhapa), August 16

The onset of the rainy season in Jhapa has led to an increase in Japanese encephalitis (JE) cases, with a recent report confirming a new infection in Mechinagar. The total number of infections so far has reached 10 in the district. Five individuals have succumbed to the disease, including three men and two women.

According to the Public Health Office, of the total infected, four are from Mechinagar, while others are from Haldibari, Bahradashi, Kachankawal, Birtamod, and Arjundhara. Currently, two patients are undergoing treatment, and three have recovered and been discharged. Notably, one of the infected individuals is a seven-month-old baby.

Public Health Inspector Bishwanath Shrestha has emphasised the importance of preventive measures during the rainy season, particularly the elimination of stagnant water around homes, to mitigate the risk of JE transmission through mosquito bites.

title.rendered: Jajarkot landslide: One killed, three missing

content.rendered:
Karnali, August 16

One person died in a landslide in Bheri Municipality-2, Risang, in the district last night. According to Police Inspector Sudhir Kumar Khadka of the District Police Office, 52-year-old Kedar Karki of Risang died in the incident.

In the incident, 54-year-old Umasinh Khatri, 70-year-old Bhim Bahadur Karki and 87-year-old Rati Khatri of the same ward went missing while nine others were injured. One of the injured is being treated at Nepalgunj Nursing Hospital, two at Kohalpur Medical College, and three at local Daurikanda Medical Centre.

Three others have recovered and returned home. According to the police, in view of the risk of landslides, 200 people from that ward have been transferred to the building of Tribhuvan Basic School. Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and Nepali Army have been mobilised at the accident site

title.rendered: 4 UML ministers take oath in Sudurpaschim Province

content.rendered:
Dhangadhi, 14 August

Four ministers from the CPN-UML, including a Minister of State, have taken the oath of office in Sudurpaschim Province.

They took the oath before Province Chief Nazir Miya on Friday afternoon. Earlier, Chief Minister Khagaraj Bhatta had taken the oath of office.

Santosh Sharma Thapa took the oath as Minister for Social Development, Chakra Bahadur Malla as Minister for Economic Affairs, Daman Bhandari as Minister for Land Management, Agriculture and Cooperatives, and Janaki Air Bam as Minister of State for Economic Affairs.

Bhatta, who has been appointed Chief Minister, is the parliamentary party leader of the Nepal Communist Party (NCP) in the provincial assembly. He became Chief Minister as part of an alliance between the CPN-UML and the NCP under a three-point agreement reached between the two parties.

On Thursday, Nepali Congress parliamentary party leader Kamal Bahadur Shah resigned as Chief Minister.

Following his resignation, Province Chief Miya appointed Bhatta as Chief Minister on Friday.

title.rendered: Government sets new salaries for constitutional officials

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, 14 August

The government has set new salaries for officials of the judiciary and other constitutional bodies. The Ministry of Finance published the new salary scale in the Nepal Gazette through a notice issued on July 22. The new salary scale will be effective from July 17 (Shrawan 1), 2026.

The Chief Justice will now receive a monthly salary of Rs 112,522, while Supreme Court justices will receive Rs 93,547. Members of the Judicial Council and the Attorney General will also receive the same salary as Supreme Court justices.

The salaries and benefits of the Chief Justice and Supreme Court justices are determined in accordance with the Remuneration, Benefits and Conditions of Service Act, 2017.

The Chief Justice is provided with an official residence in Baluwatar, while other Supreme Court justices have been residing in government quarters in Pulchowk for the past few years. Justices who are not provided with official accommodation receive a lump-sum housing allowance.

They are also entitled to allowances and facilities for electricity, water and telephone services, transportation and fuel, daily and travel expenses, clothing, and other benefits. Justices of the High Courts and District Courts receive similar benefits, although at lower rates.

The salary of the Chief Judge of a High Court has been increased to Rs 90,640, while High Court judges will now receive Rs 84,590 per month. The salary of District Court judges has been increased to Rs 77,110.

The government has set the salaries of heads of constitutional bodies at Rs 93,547, equivalent to that of Supreme Court justices. Other officials of constitutional bodies will receive Rs 85,426 per month.

The Secretary-General of the Federal Parliament will now receive Rs 84,932 per month, while its secretaries will receive Rs 79,290.

title.rendered: Tribhuvan University to introduce formal Theatre Studies program

content.rendered:
Tribhuvan University is set to formally introduce theatre studies as an academic program. The university will offer a Postgraduate Diploma in Theatre Studies.

The one-year program will be offered under the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences. According to Dean Prof Dr Dhrubanand Dhakal, the course is expected to begin in Magh, provided all necessary preparations are completed. The program will be operated under a self-sustaining financial model.

The curriculum for the program, titled Theatre Studies, has already been prepared. The Standing Committee of the University Academic Council approved the curriculum on August 3. According to Dhakal, the curriculum covers the history of theatre, theatre theory, traditions, theatre pedagogy, research, and practical theatre exercises.

Kedar Shrestha, chairperson of the Nepal Centre of International Theatre Institute and a theatre practitioner, said the initiative would be significant in institutionalising Nepali theatre and fostering a stronger theatre culture in the country.

This will be the first time a university in Nepal has formally offered theatre as an academic subject. Cinema and music are already being taught at universities in the country.

title.rendered: Gunla festival celebrations begin in Kathmandu (Photos)

content.rendered:
The Gunla festival, a month-long festival celebrated by the Newa community from the first day of the bright fortnight of Shrawan to the first day of the bright fortnight of Bhadra according to the lunar calendar, began on August 13 this year.

The festival is observed with particular significance in Kathmandu Valley and various other parts of the country. It is traditionally celebrated by observing certain rules and practices aimed at promoting religious devotion, good deeds and a disciplined way of life. According to the Nepal Sambat calendar, the tenth month is known as Gunla.

The term Gũ refers to performing virtuous, beneficial and good deeds, including helping others. During the festival, devotees observe practices believed to contribute to a better life. Throughout the month, people traditionally refrain from sleeping on high beds, avoid entertainment and eat their meals on time. They also make donations wholeheartedly according to their means.

As a special fair is held at the Swayambhunath Mahachaitya throughout the month, devotees begin visiting Swayambhunath early in the morning.

Every year during Gunla, large numbers of devotees from different parts of Kathmandu travel to Swayambhunath while playing traditional Gunla musical instruments. Many devotees also visit Swayambhunath while playing Shingabhedi, a traditional instrument made from a buffalo horn, in memory of people who died during the year.

title.rendered: Madan Subedi, the Nepali researcher tracing grasshoppers’ family tree

content.rendered:
Growing up in the rural hills of Parbat, Madan Subedi was close to nature from his school days. After passing his SLC in 2009, he studied science for his plus-two at Golden Gate College in Kathmandu. He then completed his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in agriculture at the Agriculture and Forestry University in Rampur, Chitwan.

A government officer whose heart stayed in research

It was during his undergraduate studies that he first got a close look at entomology. While most students focused on how to control crop pests, his interest moved in a different avenue, toward identifying and classifying insects rather than eliminating them. He pursued a master’s in entomology, with his thesis in taxonomy, a field with only a handful of active researchers in Nepal at the time.

While still studying for his master’s, he applied for and was selected as a permanent agriculture officer at the Agriculture and Forestry University. Since December 17 2019, he has been posted at the Agriculture Science Centre under the university in Ghyalchok, Gorkha, where he still works today. Alongside his official duties, he began devoting his spare time to research, not on crop production, fertilisers or pest control like most others, but on the tiny creatures hopping through the grass. His master’s thesis examined the diversity and taxonomy of grasshoppers found in paddy fields at different elevations across Nepal, around 258, 758, 1258 and 1758 metres, revealing that species varied by altitude. That study opened the door to a whole new world for him.

Research from scratch

Although entomology had seen considerable study in Nepal, taxonomy remained a largely neglected field, with no experts available to correctly identify insects or explain the science behind identification. The work itself wasn’t easy either; distinguishing between two species that look identical to the untrained eye can come down to a single tiny spine, the pattern of wing veins, or the shape of genitalia, requiring specialised microscopes that were scarce in Nepal.

DNA sequencing facilities were also inadequate, and legal restrictions meant samples couldn’t be sent abroad for testing, though he learned that PCR products (amplified copies of a sample’s DNA) could legally be sent out. Even so, the cost of outsourcing PCR work made research difficult.

“There are a few limited labs in Nepal that offer gene sequencing. I understood that one lab does the PCR and sends it to Korea for gene sequencing,” Subedi says. “There were many such reasons that made the research complicated, but I didn’t give up.” Resources, funding and mentors were all scarce, but his curiosity to learn and discover kept him going. Interestingly, he has named the “ground hoppers” he’s discovered after notable Nepali figures, the mentors who supported his research, and specific places.

An email that reached Germany

With no local support available, he began seeking out international researchers, eventually coming across the name of a well-known German orthoptera researcher, Sigfrid Ingrisch, who had conducted extensive research on Nepal’s grasshoppers from 1987 to 2006 and alone had documented around 311 species, having discovered roughly 60 of them himself.

Madan wrote Ingrisch an email, not expecting much of a reply, but the response came within days. Ingrisch sent him research papers, discussed samples, and taught him the finer points of classification. A small piece of research that started in Nepal became connected to Germany. Later, Madan also got in touch with another German researcher, Tömring, who had compiled a checklist of Nepal’s ground hoppers.

Through the Orthopterists’ Society, Subedi reached out to the wider international research community and found support from Croatian researchers Josip Skejo and Niko Kasalo, among others. He also received a $1,500 grant from the Orthopterists’ Society for his grasshopper research.

“That was around 2019. I spent about 145,000 rupees from that fund to buy a Canon camera. I didn’t even know how to use a camera; I taught myself,” Subedi told Onlinekhabar. “I used that camera instead of a microscope for my grasshopper research. I still keep it safe today.”

He continued his research with the help of video calls with mentors abroad and Google Docs. At the time, just over 65 species of ground hoppers were on record in Nepal; his research has since pushed that number past 80.

New genera and species discovered — and given Nepali names

During his master’s, he travelled from Koshi to the far west collecting grasshoppers, carrying a net and transparent plastic containers, gathering anything that looked unfamiliar, studying its life cycle, and publishing his findings in science journals once confirmed as new.

“In the beginning I used to collect all kinds of grasshoppers and give them grass to feed on. Later I focused only on ground hoppers within the Tetrigidae family,” Subedi says. “I’ve given the Nepali name ‘bhuinphadke’ to ground hoppers in the Tetrigidae family, because they didn’t have a Nepali name before.”

For example, around 2020 he first found a new ground hopper near Netrajyoti Basic School in Ghyalchok, Gorkha, and named it “Skejotettix netrajyoti,” combining the names of Josip Skejo, who supported his research, and the school. It took a year to confirm it as a new species, and he published a research paper on it in 2022.

He found a second new species near his own home in Bajung, his home district of Parbat, and named it “Skejotettix kasalo” after another supporter of his research, calling it “Bajung’s bhuinphadke” in Nepali.

A third species, found near Tirtire Khola in Ghyalchok, Gorkha, was named “Aryalidonta itishreea” after Bhairav Aryal, a towering figure in Nepali satirical writing. “I’ve read Bhairav Aryal’s essays and drawn inspiration from his life, so I named this in his honour,” Madan says.

Similarly, he named another new species “Aryalidonta rochaki,” combining it with the name of Rochak Ghimire, Bhairav Aryal’s friend and a writer and journalist, “so that their names would always stay together,” he says.

Likewise, he has named species after King Mahendra Bir Bikram Shah (“Skejotettix mahendrai”), the comedy duo Madan Krishna and Haribansha Acharya (“Skejotettix mahajodi”), folk singer Jhalakman Gandharva (“Lamellitettigodes jhalakmani”), and eye specialist Sanduk Ruit (“Hebarditettix sanduki”).

“I named them this way so the world would come to know these people,” Subedi says.

Another new species found near Brijtal while visiting Kapilvastu to celebrate Holi with friends was given the local Tharu name “Motbotwa”, “mot” meaning fat and “botwa” meaning grasshopper in Tharu.

“I discovered this one two years ago, and its research paper was published about a month and a half ago,” Subedi says.

Another species found in Ramaroshan, Achham, was named “Hedotettix samitae” after his wife, Samita, who currently works as an agriculture extension officer in Kankai Municipality, Jhapa.

His search for grasshoppers has taken him from Kapilvastu, Chitwan, Parbat and Gorkha to Ramaroshan in Achham. In Shivapuri Nagarjun National Park alone, 11 species of ground hoppers have been found, five of which he discovered himself — the species named after King Mahendra, the comedy duo, Jhalakman Gandharva, Sanduk Ruit and Rochak Ghimire were all found within this park.

So far, Subedi has discovered 12 new species and 3 new genera of grasshoppers, introducing them to the world. In recognition of this contribution, a newly discovered grasshopper species in Australia was named after him.

His most recently discovered species of ground hopper has been named “Hyboella rampuriana,” after the Rampur area of the Agriculture and Forestry University campus where it was found. Another species was discovered at a herbal processing centre in Tamaghadi, Bara district, and named “Thotebhutle bhuinphadke.”

The new genera he discovered are Skejotettix, Aryalidonta and Ingrischana. His new species include Skejotettix netrajyoti, Skejotettix kasalo, Aryalidonta itishreea, Hedotettix samitae, Aryalidonta rochaki, Hebarditettix sanduki, Lamellitettigodes jhalakmani, Skejotettix mahajodi, Skejotettix mahendrai, Ingrischana motbotawa, Ingrischana aspinosa, and Hyboella rampuriana, most recorded from various locations in Gorkha, Parbat, Achham, Kapilvastu, Kaski, Sankhuwasabha and Chitwan.

He has also recorded nine grasshopper species for the first time in Nepal, including Phlaeoba antennata, Bibracte burmana, Caryanda cachara, Gonista bicolour, Acanthalobus curticornis, Acanthalobus inornatus, Coptotettix problematicus, Euparatettix balteatus and Bolivaritettix insignis.

The first two new species he found are preserved at the Annapurna Natural History Museum in Pokhara, with others kept at his office in Ghyalchok, Gorkha. His work has significantly expanded the scientific record of Nepal’s grasshopper diversity and contributed to the country’s insect taxonomy research.

A new Australian species carries Subedi’s name

In recognition of this contribution, a newly discovered grasshopper species found in Australia has been named after Madan Subedi. Croatian researchers discovered the new species in an Australian forest and named it Peraxelpa subedi.

“I’ve never even been to Australia, but hearing that a species bearing my name is roaming some corner of the world makes me feel happy and amazed,” Subedi says.

Croatian researchers Josip Skejo and Niko Kasalo discovered 11 new species in Australia, one of which was named after Subedi.

Balancing challenge and satisfaction

According to Subedi, ground hoppers are usually found in damp areas, near water sources and in paddy fields, feeding on fertile soil, algae and moss. They don’t harm crops; rather, they become food for spiders, frogs and birds.

“These ground hoppers aren’t enemies of crops; they’re important bio-indicators of the ecosystem,” says Subedi, who has travelled from Koshi to the far west researching them.

During his master’s thesis work, his bag always held a camera and transparent plastic containers. Whenever a grasshopper looked new, he’d place it in a container, occasionally feeding it the grass species grasshoppers typically eat, and cover the opening with breathable cloth secured with a rubber band, letting the grasshoppers get oxygen and survive longer. He used a net to collect larger numbers, one woven for him by the Magar community near his village in Parbat.

Now he follows a more scientific process. During his thesis, he mainly studied larger grasshoppers, most from the Acrididae and Pyrgomorphidae families. Now he focuses on ground hoppers of the Tetrigidae family, which are much smaller, typically under 2 centimetres.

“I currently use a ‘killing jar’ with a chemical called ethyl acetate, which helps kill the insects painlessly,” Subedi says. “The dead insects are then pinned with rust-proof insect pins and preserved, and their morphology, external structure, is studied.”

He devotes his time outside office hours and on public holidays to research. This year, he plans to conduct research in national parks and has applied for permission from park offices. The path of research, especially on grasshoppers, isn’t easy, but because it’s his passion, he remains active in it. Despite all the difficulties, he says he finds more joy in the process of discovery than in the results themselves.

While serving farmers as an agriculture officer in Ghyalchok, Gorkha, Madan Subedi is also adding new facts to the world’s understanding of grasshopper classification, contributing, brick by brick, to Nepal’s biodiversity record. In his own words, he sums himself up simply: “I am just a ground person searching for ground hoppers.”

title.rendered: Roads blocked due to landslides and flooding in various places

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 14

Landslides and floods triggered by continuous rain have blocked roads in various parts of the country. According to the information shared by the Nepal Police, until 9 am today, traffic has been affected on some highways and road sections in different districts due to this. Considering the possibility of flooding on the Khurkot–Nepalthok–Katunje Bensi road section of the BP Highway connecting Kavrepalanchok and Sindhuli, traffic has been stopped from 6 pm to 4 am.

It has been announced that vehicles will be allowed to operate from 4 am to 6 pm on this road section. Vehicular movement has also been stopped at Kanti Lokpath in Makawanpur at night. The police have informed that traffic on this road has been banned from 5 pm to 5 am, police said.

The Mechi Highway is completely blocked at Rajduwali, Ilam Municipality-9, because the road got muddy due to the rain. However, an alternative road is operational in that area. Landslides have completely blocked the road at Charkilo in Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality-4 along the Araniko Highway in Sindhupalchok. In Ekuma, Kodari of Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality-2, a landslide of stones, mud, and debris has blocked the road.

Also, in Liping of the same Municipality-2, the road collapsed, causing the Araniko Highway to be blocked as well. The dirt road from Trishuli–Mailung–Syaphrubesi in Khalte, Ward No. 5 of Uttargaya Rural Municipality, Rasuwa, is completely blocked after the Trishuli River eroded it. The Bheri Corridor road from Jajarkot to Dolpa at Rijegad Khola in Aathbiskot Municipality-6, Rukum West, is blocked due to a landslide. The Mid-Hill Highway in Bhume Rural Municipality-4, Kadabagar and Bhume Rural Municipality-5, Dhaulapahira, in Rukum East is also completely blocked because of a landslide.

Similarly, the mid-hill highway has been blocked by landslides at Bimirebhanjyang in Lamjung’s Madhyapur Municipality-10, and the Besisahar-Manang road has been completely blocked by a landslide at Kharkhare in Besisahar Municipality-6. The police have reported that the Beni–Jomsom road is completely blocked due to a landslide at Baiseri in Raghuganga Rural Municipality-2 and at Mahabhir in Annapurna Rural Municipality-7 of Myagdi.

title.rendered: Divorce Law in Nepal: Legal provisions, jurisdiction, and contemporary trends

content.rendered:
Marriage has long been regarded as the cornerstone of family life in Nepal, built on love, trust, mutual respect, and shared responsibilities. While most marriages are intended to last a lifetime, not every relationship can withstand the challenges that arise over time.

When differences become irreconcilable and living together is no longer possible, divorce serves as a legal means of ending the marital relationship. Divorce is the dissolution of a relationship. When two spouses differ from each other is known as divorce. The Black dictionary of law has defined divorce as ” the legal separation of husband and wife effected by the judgment of a court and either totally dissolving the married relations or suspending its effect so far as concerns the combination of the parties.

In recent years, Nepal has experienced a noticeable rise in divorce cases, influenced by changing social attitudes, increased awareness of legal rights, greater economic independence, and evolving family relationships. Against this backdrop, it is important to understand the legal framework governing divorce. It is time to explore the legal provisions, jurisdiction, and contemporary trends in divorce cases in Nepal.

Legal concepts and provisions relating to divorce in Nepal

The legal concepts relating to divorce are provided under Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074. When discussing divorce, it is first necessary to understand marriage as a legal institution that permits a man and a woman to establish a family life. A marriage is legally valid when it is solemnised in accordance with all applicable legal requirements. According to Section 73 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, if the legal requirements for a valid marriage are not fulfilled, the marriage may be considered void or voidable, depending on the circumstances prescribed by law. Where a marriage has been concluded through misrepresentation as referred to in Section 71(2), the person who does not accept such a marriage may seek to have it voided. However, where the woman is pregnant or has given birth to a child as a consequence of the marriage, the marriage may be voided only with the consent of the woman.

Section 93 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074 provides for divorce by mutual consent. If both the husband and wife desire to obtain a divorce, they may do so at any time. Thus, Nepali law recognises the right of both parties to seek divorce by mutual consent. In addition, either spouse may initiate divorce proceedings without the consent of the other spouse, provided that the legally prescribed grounds are fulfilled. Sections 94 and 95 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074 establish the grounds on which a husband or wife may seek divorce without the consent of the other spouse. If the prescribed legal grounds are not met, a divorce petition may not be maintainable on those grounds.

Section 94 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074 provides that a husband may seek divorce without the consent of his wife under certain circumstances. These include situations where the wife has been living separately for three or more consecutive years without the husband’s consent, except where the parties have been legally separated after obtaining their partition share or separating bread and board; where the wife deprives the husband of maintenance costs or expels him from the house; where the wife commits an act or conspiracy likely to cause grievous hurt or severe physical or mental pain to the husband; or where the wife is proved to have sexual relations with another person.

Similarly, Section 95 provides that a wife may seek divorce without the consent of her husband under certain circumstances. These include situations where the husband has been living separately for three or more consecutive years without the wife’s consent, except where the husband and wife have been legally separated after obtaining their partition share or separating bread and board; where the husband deprives the wife of maintenance costs or expels her from the home; where the husband commits an act or conspiracy likely to cause grievous hurt or severe physical or mental pain to her; where the husband concludes another marriage; where the husband is proved to have had sexual intercourse with another woman; or where the husband is proved to have raped the wife.

Jurisdiction and limitation

As provided under Part 3, Section 18(3) of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, jurisdiction for filing a complaint lies with the district court serving the district in which either the plaintiff or the defendant is located. Limitation is equally important because the law requires a person to approach the court within the prescribed period. Under Section 104 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, a person seeking a divorce-related remedy must generally institute the case within three months from the date of knowledge of the relevant act or cause of action. Therefore, timely access to the appropriate court is essential to ensure that a person’s right to seek legal protection is not lost because of delay.

Status Quo

According to the records of the Kathmandu District Court, a total of 4,280 divorce cases were filed during the reporting period. Of these, 4,140 cases were decided by the court, while 2,953 cases were successfully resolved through mediation.

The majority of divorce cases were filed by women. These data indicate that mediation continues to play a significant role in resolving divorce disputes alongside judicial adjudication. The relatively high number of cases resolved through mediation also demonstrates the importance of alternative dispute resolution mechanisms in reducing the burden on courts and facilitating mutually acceptable settlements between spouses.

Conclusion

Divorce represents the legal dissolution of a marital relationship and serves as an important legal mechanism for protecting the rights, dignity, and well-being of spouses when a marriage has irretrievably broken down. The provisions of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074 establish a comprehensive legal framework governing marriage, divorce, jurisdiction, and the rights and obligations of both husbands and wives.

The available data further reveal that the majority of divorce petitions were filed by women, indicating increased awareness among women of their legal rights and a greater willingness to seek judicial protection in cases involving marital disputes and injustice. While judicial intervention remains essential in contested divorce cases, the significant number of cases resolved through mediation demonstrates its potential to preserve the dignity of the parties, reduce emotional and financial burdens, and promote mutually acceptable outcomes. Ultimately, an effective divorce framework should not merely provide a legal means of ending a failed marriage; it should also safeguard the rights, dignity, and future welfare of the individuals and families affected by marital dissolution.

title.rendered: Dharan Sub-Metropolitan City approves annual budget of Rs 2.76 billion

content.rendered:
Sunsari, August 14

Dharan Metropolitan City has passed its annual budget of Rs 2.76 billion for the current fiscal year. The 19th municipal assembly held on Thursday approved the current fiscal year’s budget, which has given much priority to building road networks and physical infrastructure, drinking water supply, education, health care, tourism facilities, agriculture, employment creation and disaster management.

Acting Mayor of Dharan Sub-Metropolitan City, Ayindra Bikram Begha, tabled the budget allocating Rs 2.47 billion for the municipal executive and Rs 287 million for 20 ward offices. Begha shared that Rs 1.40 billion in revenue will be collected from the sub-metropolitan city and Rs 862 million will be received from federal grants; Rs 91.6 million will be received in grants from the provincial government, Rs 328.89 million from revenue sharing and Rs 10 million from the Road Board. Likewise, the city has a deposit of Rs 70 million from the last fiscal year, according to Acting Mayor Begha.

title.rendered: One missing, two injured in Bajura landslide

content.rendered:
Bajura, August 14

A person has gone missing, and two others were injured after a landslide buried a house following torrential rain at Tamsu in Triveni Municipality-9 in Bajura district. The Information Officer of the District Police Office, Naresh Bahadur Shahi, confirmed that two people were injured in the incident.

The landslide buried the houses of Dharma Thapa and Karna Bahadur Thapa of Tamsu in the municipality. Ward Chairperson of Triveni Municipality-9, Nanda Thapa, shared that they have faced difficulties in carrying out a search for the missing person and rescuing the injured people, citing torrential rain.

Currently, a team of police personnel under the command of the Chief of the District Police Office, Shaileshwori Bohara, reached the site for rescue operations.

title.rendered: Rolpa landslide death toll rises to 7, 5 still missing

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 13

The death toll from a landslide triggered by incessant rainfall in Rolpa has risen to seven, while five people remain missing.

Seven people were killed, and five others are still missing after a landslide struck Kotlabara in Thabang Rural Municipality-5 of Rolpa on Wednesday night.

According to Armed Police Force DSP Shailendra Thapa, the deceased have been identified as 18-year-old Shanti Pun Magar, 65-year-old Kamal Bahadur Pun Magar, 40-year-old Junkumari Pun Magar, nine-year-old Ashim Pun Magar, six-year-old Ashok Pun Magar, 75-year-old Dal Bahadur Pun Magar and 71-year-old Manrakhi Pun Magar.

Twenty-two-year-old Himal Pun Magar and 25-year-old Sanjay Gharti Magar were injured in the landslide. Both have been referred from Thabang Health Post to Butwal for further treatment.

The bodies of one woman and two men among the deceased were recovered along the banks of the Madi River in Swargadwari Municipality and Mandavi Rural Municipality of Pyuthan.

Those missing have been identified as 80-year-old Ajambar Pun Magar, 78-year-old Bal Bahadur Pun Magar, 72-year-old Lil Bahadur Pun Magar, 71-year-old Mani Pun Magar and 67-year-old Hastakala Pun Magar.

A joint team of the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police has been deployed to search for the missing people. However, ongoing rainfall and continuous mud-laden landslides have made rescue operations difficult, Thapa said.

title.rendered: Deuba returns to Nepal after five and a half months (Photo Feature)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 13

Former Nepali Congress President Sher Bahadur Deuba has returned to Nepal. He arrived at Tribhuvan International Airport at around 12:30 p.m. on Thursday. Deuba had travelled to Singapore with his wife, Arzu Rana Deuba, for medical treatment after being seriously injured during the Gen Z protest on September 9 last year.

He returned to Nepal after five and a half months. A large number of leaders from the non-establishment faction of the Nepali Congress gathered at the airport to welcome him.

Deuba was seen waving from his vehicle and accepting traditional khada garlands from supporters.

title.rendered: EU marks International Youth Day in Nepal with a day of opportunity, innovation and youth leadership

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 13

The Delegation of the European Union to Nepal marked International Youth Day 2026 with full-day activities at Hotel Malla, Kathmandu, bringing together students, Erasmus scholars and alumni, entrepreneurs, civil society organisations, innovators, private-sector partners and youth leaders. The programme connected three events: the Erasmus Mundus Pre-Departure Orientation, EU Youth Fest 2026 and EU Youth Alumni Day, highlighting opportunities for young people in digital skills, innovation, and entrepreneurship.

EU Ambassador to Nepal H.E. Véronique Lorenzo felicitated 42 Nepali students who have secured the coveted Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degree scholarship to study at universities across the European Union. The scholarship recipients, including 22 women and 20 men, met representatives of EU Member States, Erasmus alumni and fellow scholars ahead of their studies. The students will pursue subjects including public health, cybersecurity, journalism, renewable energy and sustainable construction.

More than 1,500 young people attended the EU Youth Fest 2026, where they received guidance and mentorship from seasoned professionals and had the opportunity to learn about emerging industries such as animation, robotics and artificial intelligence, alongside hands-on experiences including 3D modelling and printing, drone simulations and AI-powered games.

At the Youth Fest, the EU Delegation also marked the launch of two new grants worth a combined EUR 1.91 million: Creating Opportunities for Youth in Digital Economy (CODE) and Unleashing Digital Acceleration and Ambition of Nepali Youth (UDAAN). The implementing partners are Swisscontact, Restless Development and Robotics Association of Nepal for CODE; and Youth Innovation Lab, Women in Animation, Heifer Project Nepal and the Nepal Applied Mathematics and Informatics Institute for Research (NAAMII) for UDAAN. The initiatives will engage young people across all seven provinces, with a focus on digital skills, employability, entrepreneurship and innovation, particularly for young women, rural communities, and vulnerable and marginalised groups.

“One of Nepal’s greatest resources is its youth. Young people are dynamic, energetic, and full of potential. But this potential must be matched by investment in skills, opportunity, and employment. That is what the new EU initiatives are about. They aim to help bridge the digital divide and ensure that the benefits of technology reach those who have too often been left behind,” Ambassador Lorenzo remarked.

Alongside the Youth Fest, the EU marked EU Youth Alumni Day, bringing together EU Youth Alumni, youth organisations and partners to showcase youth-led initiatives across the EU’s areas of action, including circular economy, green growth, quality education, climate action and youth participation. The gathering offered alumni a platform to share success stories and discuss future cooperation.

The day reflected the EU’s continued commitment to working with young people as partners in Nepal’s future, spanning education and mobility, digital skills and jobs, innovation and entrepreneurship, and civic participation.

title.rendered: Mid-hill highway blocked by landslide in Eastern Rukum, passengers stranded

content.rendered:
Eastern Rukum, August 13

The Mid-Hill Highway has been blocked in Eastern Rukum following heavy rainfall on Wednesday evening. The highway was obstructed after debris-laden runoff and landslides fell at Kadabagar and Dhaula Pahiro in Bhume Rural Municipality-4. Passenger buses and other vehicles travelling from Kathmandu towards Eastern Rukum, Western Rukum and Dolpa have been halted along the route, leaving passengers stranded.

Efforts are underway to clear the blocked road using excavators and other equipment. However, continuous rainfall has made it difficult to remove the landslide debris, according to Eastern Rukum Chief District Officer Kopila Rai. According to Rai, JCB excavators from Sisne and Bhume rural municipalities have also been mobilised to reopen the road. She said it could take some time to fully resume traffic as the landslide is large and the road itself has also been damaged.

The district administration has urged travellers to exercise caution, warning that further landslides could occur as long as the rainfall continues.

title.rendered: FNJ to protest Kishor Shrestha’s arrest

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 13

The Federation of Nepali Journalists (FNJ) is staging a sit-in outside the Kathmandu Police Complex today, demanding the release of journalist Kishor Shrestha. The FNJ has also called on all supporters of press freedom to participate in the protest. FNJ General Secretary Ram Prasad Dahal issued a notice calling for the sit-in.

Nepal Police arrested Shrestha, editor-in-chief of Jan Aastha weekly, on Wednesday. A police team also raided and searched the Jan Aastha office early Thursday morning.

The FNJ has condemned both Shrestha’s arrest and the search of the Jan Aastha office. On Wednesday night, a team of journalists, including FNJ President Nirmala Sharma, staged a protest outside the Kathmandu Police Complex. The FNJ has warned of stronger protests if Shrestha is not released unconditionally.

Police have said Shrestha was arrested on allegations of committing an offence under the Individual Privacy Act, 2018, and that an investigation is underway. Shrestha is also the senior vice president of the World Press Council. He is a former chairperson of the Press Council Nepal and former general secretary of the FNJ. He has established a distinct identity in investigative journalism and is known as a forthright and fearless journalist.

title.rendered: Rising meat and egg prices squeeze consumers, leave farmers struggling

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 13

In Nepal, some people traditionally refrain from eating fish, meat and eggs during the month of Shrawan. With demand generally lower during this period, meat and egg prices would normally be expected to fall. But the market has shown exactly the opposite trend this year. Since the beginning of Shrawan, egg and chicken prices have risen. Consumers complain that their household expenses have increased due to repeated price hikes within a short period.

With egg and meat prices seemingly out of reach, one might assume that farmers are making good profits. But the rising price graph has brought neither happiness to farmers nor relief to consumers.

Stakeholders allege that middlemen and traders operating between farmers and consumers are making excessive profits by controlling the market. This raises a fundamental question: What kind of market mechanism is this, where farmers fail to receive even their production costs while consumers cannot buy the products at reasonable prices?

Egg prices rise four times in Shrawan

The Nepal Layers Poultry Farmers Association, which has been setting the farm-gate support price for eggs, has issued four notices announcing price increases in Shrawan alone. According to the figures, on August 2, the farm-gate price per crate of the largest, or XL, eggs was Rs 465, while large eggs cost Rs 450 and medium eggs Rs 420.

By August 11, however, the prices had surged to Rs 560 for XL eggs, Rs 545 for large eggs and Rs 500 for medium eggs. Prices had also been increased on August 6 and 13. Thus, within less than a month, the farm-gate price of eggs had increased by as much as Rs 95 per crate.

But this is where a clear picture of consumers being overcharged emerges. Whether the farm price was Rs 465 or had risen to Rs 560, every notice issued by the association continued to set the consumer price at Rs 25 per egg. Yet consumers are currently paying as much as Rs 30 per egg at retail shops.

Although egg prices vary according to size, once they reach the retail market, eggs of different sizes are often placed in the same basket and sold at Rs 30 each. Traders and dealers also do not necessarily pay farmers according to egg size when purchasing directly from farms. Instead, they buy the eggs in bulk.

Consumers and stakeholders have long accused middlemen and retailers of buying eggs from farmers at low prices, sorting them by size and selling them to consumers at higher prices, thereby pocketing substantial margins.

Consumers face similar pressure over chicken prices

The problem is not limited to eggs. A similar form of market control can be seen in chicken prices. The National Chicken Sales Business Association increased the prices of live chickens and meat on August 7. Just four days later, on August 11, another price increase came into effect.

The price of live chickens, which previously stood at Rs 240 per kilogram, has been raised to Rs 250. Similarly, the association says the wholesale price of processed chicken has increased from Rs 330 to Rs 345 per kilogram. However, the wholesale price loses its meaning by the time the product reaches consumers. In Kathmandu’s retail shops, consumers are currently paying between Rs 380 and Rs 410 per kilogram of chicken. So, why are prices rising?

Bird flu and its impact on production are being cited as the main reasons. According to the Department of Livestock Services, 835,563 birds have been culled due to bird flu infections over the past four months. In addition, 1,225,536 eggs and 264,213 kilograms of poultry feed have been destroyed.

According to Binod Pokharel, president of the Nepal Layers Poultry Farmers Association, around one million to 1.2 million layer chickens producing eggs have been destroyed across the country due to bird flu. “We used to produce 4-4.1 million eggs a day across the country. Now production has fallen to 2.9-3 million,” he says. “Production has declined significantly while market demand is increasing.”

Although market prices have risen, farmers themselves are still operating at a loss, Pokharel says. “The production cost of one crate of eggs for farmers is Rs 573, but farmers are still receiving only Rs 545 for large eggs,” he said. “Farmers have not made profits simply because consumer prices have increased. They are still suffering losses.”

A poultry entrepreneur also agrees. According to him, farmers sold chickens at a loss during the bird flu outbreak, and many poultry sheds are now empty. The government has restricted the smuggling of Indian chickens and eggs across the open border. According to the businessman, the market has faced shortages after the supply of cheaper Indian products stopped and domestic chicken production declined.

However, he argues that claims that prices have risen because feed and raw materials have become more expensive are unfounded. “Feed prices have remained stable. We don’t need to import corn from India at present, as locally produced corn can meet demand for the next five to six months,” the businessman said. “Therefore, the current price increase is not primarily due to higher production costs but to shortages in the market and the activities of middlemen.”

The chicken market also under the grip of middlemen

Another poultry businessman says the biggest problem lies in the structure of the market. “The chicken and egg market has now become just like the vegetable market. Just as consumers buy cauliflower for Rs 40 after farmers sell it for Rs 5, suppliers, dealers and retailers are making excessive profits from chickens and eggs that leave farms at much lower prices,” he said.

Because farmers cannot transport their products to markets themselves, and eggs can spoil if stored for too long, they are forced to sell at whatever price dealers offer. He says the role of commodity associations in this system, which exploits consumers and squeezes farmers, is particularly questionable.

Can the Layers Poultry Farmers Association or meat traders’ associations legally issue notices setting prices?

Consumer rights activist Madhav Timalsina considers such practices by the associations illegal. He says Nepal’s existing laws do not authorise commercial or commodity associations to set prices. “The practices of the Fruit Traders Association setting juice prices, the Egg Traders Association setting egg prices, the Poultry Farmers Association setting meat prices and the Gold and Silver Traders Association setting gold prices are completely illegal,” Timalsina says.

According to him, determining how much a commodity should cost in the market is not the responsibility of such associations. “No farmer in the country can receive a fair price. Middlemen within these associations determine prices, forcing consumers to pay more,” he says. “The same middlemen create projections that prices are going to rise, engage in cartel-like practices and attempt to charge new, higher prices even for old stock. This has led to the current situation.”

Government inaction emboldens traders

Consumer rights activist Timalsina blames the government’s weak monitoring mechanism for the overall disorder. According to him, the government lacks a scientific mechanism to regulate, analyse and determine market prices. The Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection has never conducted an in-depth investigation into whether the prices set by such associations are justified.

“Until the authorities responsible for market intervention monitor and regulate prices, our market will remain trapped in the grip of traders,” he says. “Since the prices set by these associations are themselves illegal, the government must first stop this practice.”

He says the current situation in the chicken and egg market is essentially a cartel. Even if farmers are suffering losses, he argues, that does not give middlemen the right to exploit consumers.

He has called for immediate government monitoring and action against associations that raise prices overnight through cartel-like practices under the pretext of declining production, as well as retailers who buy eggs cheaply from farmers and sell them at inflated prices.

Poultry Business Forum Nepal also claims that suppliers and middlemen are exploiting both farmers and consumers by taking advantage of the bird flu outbreak and resulting shortages in the market. Jairam Mahat, secretary of Poultry Business Forum Nepal, says middlemen are taking advantage of the current shortage of chickens and eggs.

“There is currently some shortage in the market. Although dealers and sub-dealers purchase products from farmers in cash, the intermediaries are keeping slightly higher margins,” Mahat said. “It appears that middlemen are charging consumers more by using farmers as an excuse.”

Although chicken prices have increased in the market, he says broiler farmers are still not receiving prices that cover their production costs.

“A day-old chick itself costs Rs 75-80. On top of that, the cost of feed, electricity, water, labour and rent makes production very expensive,” he said. “It would have been easier for farmers if prices had been maintained according to production costs to provide relief to those who suffered losses for a long time because of bird flu.”

Mahat says the current shortage in the market is the result of the large number of chickens destroyed during previous bird flu outbreaks. Under existing rules, poultry sheds affected by bird flu must be disinfected and kept empty for three months. Mahat said farmers have been reluctant to place new chicks in their sheds because continuous rainfall has made disinfection difficult.

Although demand for meat appears to have increased slightly recently, the forum says meat consumption will decline during Shrawan and the subsequent 16-day period of Sorah Shraddha.

“Meat sales virtually come to a standstill during Sorah Shraddha,” Mahat said. “Therefore, farmers are hoping they will receive better prices during Dashain rather than in the coming month of Bhadra.”
