title.rendered: Onlinekhabar unveils third edition of ‘40 Under 40’

content.rendered:
In celebration of International Youth Day on August 12, Onlinekhabar.com has unveiled its list of 40 Under 40 Influential Youths in Nepal. The list honours 40 young individuals under the age of 40 who have made significant contributions in diverse fields, including politics, society, culture, art and literature, youth and sports, knowledge and science, entrepreneurship and the diaspora.

2024 marked the first time Onlinekhabar published its 40 Under 40 list, establishing an annual tradition of recognising exceptional young talents. This time, it is the third edition, honouring 40 young individuals for their contributions to society.

List of 40 Under 40 – 2026

Madan Subedi – Entomologist

A boy who loved collecting old coins and leaves has grown into a determined entomological researcher. Madan Subedi of Parbat has identified 12 new species and three new genera of grasshoppers and is introducing a new genus and species of groundhopper to the world. A new grasshopper species discovered in the forests of Australia has also been named after him.

Chanira Bajracharya – Former Kumari / Credit Analyst

Chanira Bajracharya spent 10 years as the living goddess Kumari in Patan, where she did not have to walk on her own feet and was carried during processions. After stepping down from the throne, she had to learn to walk on her own. Overcoming significant academic and social challenges, she has become a senior credit analyst at an Australian company. Beyond the corporate world, she remains active in cultural preservation, reconnecting with her roots. She was included in the BBC 100 Women influential women list in 2016.

Dr Saroj Kumar Aryal – Diplomacy Scholar

Saroj Kumar Aryal worked as a hotel receptionist in Kathmandu while pursuing higher education. He moved to Poland in 2013 and earned a PhD on a scholarship in 2019. He is an assistant professor of international relations at the University of Warsaw and is involved in three international research projects. His primary research focuses on the diplomacy of small states amid the global balance of power. During this period, he has received the Rector’s Award for three consecutive years as well as Poland’s Outstanding Young Scientist Award.

Saurav Subedi / Prajjwal Sharma – Technology Entrepreneurs

The Nepali startup Edex, launched in 2022, attracted an American company with its rapid growth and reached an agreement to be acquired for $2.4 million just three years after its establishment. Having secured a rare exit for a Nepali startup, its founders now have another ambition: empowering citizens through technology. Through the launch of Pratipakshya.com, they have begun digitally monitoring government promises, actions and decisions.

Saigrace – Storyteller

The storytelling skills Saigrace learned from his father during nights when the electricity went out found an outlet in a room in Barcelona during the silence of the lockdown. He turned digital platforms into his stage, where stories of love, pain, memories and human relationships have touched millions of people around the world. For him, stories are not merely words but bridges that connect people.

Akanksha Karki – Theatre Artist / Director

A failed film project pushed her into deep disappointment, but that turning point gave rise to Kaushi Theatre and helped shape her as a director. Having directed more than 15 plays, Akanksha Karki is not a director who seeks to provide society with answers. Rather, she is a powerful voice that asks uncomfortable questions, challenges the status quo and seeks change.

Majid Ansari – Gen Z Activist

Questions remain even after a change in power. Some questions are uncomfortable, while others are unpopular. Yet the health of democracy depends on the ability to ask such questions. Majid Ansari is a young activist who continues to raise those uncomfortable questions, viewing the movement not as a temporary wave of excitement but as a continuing journey of scrutiny and accountability.

Rahul Bisunkhe – Social Entrepreneur

Having witnessed the hardships of Chepang settlements and the struggles of Himalayan communities, Rahul Bisunkhe saw an opportunity for change in plastic waste. Through an initiative led by Rahul and his friends, waste in Rigaun, Dhading, is being transformed into plastic boards, chairs and furniture. By turning a persistent waste problem into a solution, they are pioneering a new practice of the circular economy in Nepal.

Nishkal Rai – Member of Parliament, House of Representatives

Nishkal Rai returned to his village to support his widowed father and later came back to Kathmandu carrying the voice of his constituents. After becoming involved in Nepal Students’ Union politics, he moved into academia. He not only challenged the entrenched hierarchy within his own party but also opened the door for the Nepali Congress in a traditional leftist stronghold. In Parliament, his style is expressed through pointed questions rather than a loud voice. By calling for a moment of silence for martyrs from the parliamentary floor, he even compelled the ruling side and the Speaker to engage with his agenda. He continues to remind a powerful government of democratic values.

Sahas Bhandari – Esports Player

Sahas Bhandari, known as Killer YT, once played PUBG secretly to avoid his parents’ attention. He is now one of Nepal’s highest-earning esports athletes. Having once been willing to sell his beloved bicycle to raise money to buy a phone, he has now gifted a car to his parents. As a member of DRS Gaming, he helped change Nepali society’s perception of esports after finishing second in the world at PMGC 2022.

Swastima Khadka – Actress

Swastima Khadka, who studied architecture, entered the film industry while initially treating acting as a part-time profession. But her journey from Bulbul to Lalibazar has established her as a leader in the Nepali film industry. Over an 11-year career, she has demonstrated strength in both commercial and arthouse cinema and has won the National Film Award twice. She has also led the debate over equal pay for male and female actors in Nepal’s film industry.

Saroj Kumar Mahato: Blood Donation Activist

Saroj Kumar Mahato once travelled from Dhanusha to donate blood to a child with cancer, only to learn upon reaching a hospital in Chitwan that the child had already died. Deeply affected by the experience, he refused to remain silent. Determined to ensure that blood reaches patients on time, he launched a campaign that has so far provided 25,000 pints of blood. Patients’ families still struggle enormously to secure every pint they need. That is why the national ‘Blood for Nepal’ campaign, led by Mahato, continues.

Sompal Kami – Cricketer

Sompal Kami once played street cricket in Patiala, India, wearing slippers. Today, he is the only Nepali cricketer to have played in three T20 World Cups. He is also Nepal’s leading wicket-taker in the T20 World Cup, with 10 wickets. An aggressive pace star on the field, he is known off the field as a “dog father” for his efforts to rescue and care for stray dogs.

Meghraj Budhathoki – Handicraft Entrepreneur

When New Zealand wool is transformed into art through Nepali craftsmanship, it finds its way into homes across developed countries. Along with the products comes recognition of Nepali labour, skills and creativity. Meghraj Budhathoki, who has led this journey, sees business not merely as a means of making profit but as a source of dignified employment for thousands of Nepalis.

Krishnabahadur Damai – Sanskrit Scholar

There was a time when Krishnabahadur Badi (Damai) was denied a tika at a temple because of his caste. Today, he is challenging discrimination from within the same religious tradition. After earning an Acharya degree from Nepal Sanskrit University, he has even delivered religious discourses from the Vyasasan at Pashupatinath. His goal, however, is not simply to become a priest but to turn religious rituals into a cultural campaign against caste-based discrimination.

Yash Puri – Fish Feed Entrepreneur

A business idea born during the COVID-19 pandemic has grown into an industry challenging the dominance of Indian products in Nepal’s fish-feed market. Established in Chitwan using modern technology, the industry has not only helped reduce farmers’ production costs but has also captured 33 per cent of the market within three years of its establishment, raising hopes that Nepal can become self-sufficient in fish feed.

Kanchhalal Jimba – Chairperson, Mahabharat Rural Municipality

Kanchhalal Jimba once joined the Maoist insurgency carrying a gun on his shoulder. Today, he is serving his second term as chairperson of Mahabharat Rural Municipality in Kavre. The rural municipality was once without roads, electricity or effective government services. Jimba has brought changes through roads, electrification and coffee farming while also presenting a model of good governance by maintaining zero outstanding audit irregularities for three consecutive years, according to the Office of the Auditor General.

Maya Basyal – Auxiliary Nurse Midwife

Maya Basyaal is an auxiliary nurse midwife who rushes to assist pregnant women on a motorcycle with her husband whenever she receives a call at night, and has even donated her own blood to save a woman after childbirth. Her dedication has contributed to three consecutive years without a maternal death in Janaki Rural Municipality, Banke. However, she remains troubled by the reality that some fathers still leave hospitals after learning that their newborn is a daughter.

Dipesh Nepal – Agricultural Entrepreneur

It is easy to campaign against the use of chemical fertilisers in farming, but what are the alternatives? That question, raised by disadvantaged Chepang farmers in Chitwan, kept Dipesh Nepal awake at night. It eventually gave birth to Chhahari Farm. Started as a small vegetable farm with his friends from the agricultural college, the initiative has now grown into a commercial enterprise. Through the Agriculture for Food campaign, it has also completed an organic farming awareness journey across 22 districts.

Namrata KC – Associate Professor and Kathak Artist

What distinguishes Namrata KC is her dual identity as an associate professor at Lalitkala Campus and an established performer of Nepali classical dance. After training in Kathak in Lucknow, she returned to Nepal with a mission to transform dance from mere entertainment into a medium of dialogue with society. By bringing historical figures such as Rajendra Lakshmi to the stage, she is also helping popularise dance drama in Nepal.

Alok Khatri – AI Trainer 

From serving as president of the India chapter of the global youth leadership organisation ‘AIESEC’ and representing at the UN General Assembly, to post-earthquake reconstruction campaigns. From being a gym trainer in Kathmandu to successfully finishing an ‘Iron Man’ marathon in Frankfurt. Having studied industrial engineering, what hasn’t he done? After his health startup failed, he turned to deep learning, and now teaches AI to human resources at Commercial Bank and various institutions at home and abroad.

Deepa Khadka – Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM)

While statistics showing that 25 per cent of children under five in Nepal are stunted, 19 per cent underweight, and 8 per cent wasted are deeply troubling, the warmth of healthcare workers like Deepa offers equal relief. From bathing malnourished children and counselling mothers on nutrition, to paying bus fares and buying medicine out of her own pocket, her dedication has made the ANM profession itself exemplary.

Dhiraj Jha – Entrepreneur 

During the chaos of the 2005–06 movement, he fell from a rooftop and suffered severe injuries to his spine and legs. He attended school in a wheelchair through grade 10 but could not continue his studies further. Yet the company built through his determination and dedication now does business worth billions of rupees annually and has enabled more than three hundred workers to stand on their own feet.

Mingma David Sherpa – Mountaineer and Member of Parliament 

A journey that began as a porter took him to the summit of Everest 10 times. He has completed more than three dozen climbs of peaks above 8,000 meters. Mingma David, who led the record-setting team that summited Pakistan’s K2 in winter 2021, recently lost his climbing partner Nims Dai in Pakistan. He has been active in mountain rescue efforts for the past decade and has now entered parliament carrying the cause of the mountains.

NJ Subedi – Tech entrepreneur

A young man who dropped out of computer engineering studies midway and returned to Pokhara faced numerous failures. But the ‘Ludo’ game created by his startup ‘Yarsa Labs’ during the COVID period has now been downloaded more than 200 million times worldwide, while users across another dozen-and-a-half games have reached 500 million. NJ, an engineering college dropout, now runs a company with 200 engineers, built together with friends.

Dilisha Shrestha – Women’s health entrepreneur 

Sanitary pads used by women are thrown away every month, but that waste, made from non-biodegradable plastic, remains in the environment for years. On the other hand, sanitary pads carry their own problems: burning, rashes, and increased infection risk. This dual concern gave birth to ‘Period Panty Flowy.’ This product has changed the daily lives of about 50,000 women and reduced the environmental impact of roughly 500,000 sanitary pads.

Nadish – Poet 

Poet Nadish is emotional, but not a prisoner of emotion. He is philosophical, but doesn’t put philosophy on display. He is modern, but doesn’t get swept up in the fashion of modernity. He is not a trader of words; he is a silent seeker.

Prakash Bohara – Gen Z protester 

Prakash Bohara’s blood-stained shoe became an icon of the movement. After the RSP made him a proportional representation candidate, he campaigned for the party day and night on crutches. But his name didn’t make it onto the list of elected MPs. He also lost the election for the party’s central committee. Yet even without holding any formal position, he remains confident that his shoe will continue to hold the government accountable.

Badri Panta – Ward Chair, Nalgad-4 

Having first attended adult classes before starting school at age 13, who could understand the value of education better than him? Badri Panta, who spent 12 years in journalism, is now the ward chairperson of Nalgad in Jajarkot. He has mobilised support and budgets from home and abroad to improve local school infrastructure. Carrying a spade, he built roads through community labour and introduced an “allowance program for postpartum buffalo” to support farmers.

Aditya Subedi – AI entrepreneur 

A national-level tennis player, Aditya Subedi had earned a generous scholarship to Harvard University. But he left his studies unfinished to go to Silicon Valley, where he founded the AI company ‘Architect Labs.’ Having raised $24 million in investment, the company aims to automate the world’s chip design process. His technology will also make the work of companies like Google and Amazon easier.

Deepak Kafle – Entrepreneur 

Carrying the dream of freeing his family from financial hardship, Deepak came to Kathmandu from Dang at the age of 16 and opened a tea shop, but failed. He then went to India, returned and ran a clothing business in Kathmandu that also collapsed. To make ends meet, he worked as a loader carrying liquor cartons, then went to Qatar for manual labour. After returning to Nepal, he opened a momo shop in Dang, which also failed. But he picked himself back up and started a cake business in Dang, and this time failure gave up before he did. Today, ‘Rani Cake’ is one of the biggest brands in western Nepal, with branches in various cities employing more than 60 people.

Rabindra Dhant – Mixed martial arts fighter 

Having broken stones in Pithoragarh, carried electric poles, and made tea in a Delhi office, Rabindra Dhant has now become the Nepali fighter who reached the semifinals of the UFC selection. Unable to afford bus fare, he trained by walking every day from Kirtipur to Jhamsikhel and delivered Nepal’s first historic win on ‘Road to UFC.’ Once seen crying while cleaning stairs with a bucket as he watched boys his own age go to school, he is now an inspiration to millions of young Nepalis.

Khusbu Oli – Member of Parliament 

Once Miss Teen Nepal, Khusbu Oli now serves as chief whip of Rastriya Prajatantra Party in parliament. Having continuously raised her voice in parliament to bring back Sharmila Darji, who was trafficked to Kuwait, she has established herself as a vocal MP who consistently raises questions on such socio-political issues. Her style of speaking with preparation and following up on issues she raises has lent her debates real weight.

Jenny Khadka – Burn survivor counsellor 

The acid her husband threw at her caused her pain, but society’s treatment of her burns caused even more. Jenny Khadka, who initially covered her face with a scarf to hide her scars, has now turned that very identity into strength, counselling other burn survivors. Burn patients coming to Kirtipur Hospital draw the most encouragement from her story and resolve.

Amigo Khadka – Entrepreneur 

Amigo Khadka had a job at JP Morgan Chase on Wall Street, but was drawn instead to the dream of running delivery vans through the streets of Nepal. After shaping and accelerating ‘Upaya Logistics,’ he went on a scholarship to the London School of Economics, then returned to Nepal once again to industrialise the country’s tea culture, turning ‘Nepal Tea Collective’ into a global brand. The company’s revenue has grown fivefold in four years to reach $2 million.

Ajar Rajbhandari – E-commerce entrepreneur 

What to do with clothes returned by customers at the family shop? Ajar Rajbhandari’s mother had the idea of selling them cheaply online. In the US, he followed his mother’s same approach to institutionalise e-commerce on Amazon. His startup ‘Herd,’ with just seven employees and reliance on AI, did about $15 million in business in its very first year. The products he sells on Amazon consistently remain bestsellers.

Priya Rai – Trail runner 

Twenty-six-year-old Priya Rai from Khotang, who came to trail running via taekwondo and rugby, has set a record by winning the ‘Asia Trail Master’ title twice in a row. Flying Nepal’s flag from Thailand to Europe and dominating world trail running, her beginnings were far from easy. There was no one to teach her what shoes to wear or how to run. She learned to run by watching videos of ultra-runners online, and today she is an inspiration to many she has never even met.

Dr Yadav Prasad Kandel – Quantum scientist 

Having grown up cutting grass and firewood in the hills of Gulmi’s Shringa, Dr Yadav Prasad Kandel now works as a ‘Staff Scientist’ at IBM, a leading global tech company. IBM aims to build a large quantum computer named ‘Starling’ by 2029, capable of self-correcting errors in complex calculations and delivering reliable results. As a staff scientist on that very project, his plans also include opening a new quantum technology company in Nepal and building a research team at a university there.

Dr Suman Giri – Data scientist 

Pfizer, the vaccine manufacturer, became well known in Nepal too during COVID-19. The Senior Vice President and Head of AI at this company, which supplies over 600 products across 140 countries, is Dr Suman Giri. Having grown up in the narrow alleys of Ason, he is now responsible for developing and implementing data science and AI strategy to further expand Pfizer.

Archana Tuladhar – Churpi entrepreneur 

A background in chartered accountancy combined with a fondness for dogs gave birth to Actent Exports. This company, which produces Himalayan Dog Treats, has today become Nepal’s largest churpi industry. Eighty per cent of this export company’s income goes directly into the accounts of more than a thousand farmers across districts including Ilam, Panchthar, and Taplejung in eastern Nepal. The factory in Kathmandu’s Kapan employs 87 workers, 80 per cent of whom are women.

title.rendered: Tiger that killed man in Chitwan captured and caged

content.rendered:
Narayangarh, 12 August

A tiger that killed 65-year-old Mangle Bote of Jitpur, Bharatpur Metropolitan City-28, has been captured and taken to a holding cage at the Sauraha-based facility of Chitwan National Park.

According to police, Mangle had gone for a morning walk with 55-year-old Jeevan Bote, also from the same area, on Tuesday morning. After Mangle went missing, a search team comprising police and the Nepali Army found him dead in the Rapti Hariyali and Bethari Buffer Zone Community Forest area.

His body was found with signs of a tiger attack.

Following the discovery of the body, the search for the man-eating tiger was intensified. During the search, the tiger was spotted in the same area and was darted and captured by wildlife technicians working with the National Trust for Nature Conservation.

According to Avinash Thapamagar, information officer at Chitwan National Park, a search for both the man and the tiger was launched immediately after authorities were informed of the attack.

He said the search for the tiger was intensified after the man was found dead, and that the combined efforts of the search team successfully led to the tiger being darted and captured.

“The tiger appears to be a male, around seven to eight years old. It appears healthy, and its canines are also in good condition,” Thapamagar said.

According to him, the captured tiger has been taken to the holding cage in Sauraha. Although its external physical condition appears normal, its internal health condition will be known only after medical examination and monitoring, he said.

With the latest capture, the number of tigers held in cages at Chitwan National Park for various reasons has reached seven. Of them, five are male and two are female.

Most of the tigers were captured after they became man-eaters. One was brought from Banke, while the others were captured in Chitwan National Park and its buffer zone.

title.rendered: Onlinekhabar to unveil ‘40 Under 40’ 2026 list today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 12

On the occasion of International Youth Day, Onlinekhabar is releasing this year’s list of 40 influential young people under the age of 40 today. President Ram Chandra Paudel will present awards to the 40 honorees at a ceremony in Lalitpur.

Onlinekhabar began publishing the list of 40 young people three years ago with the aim of highlighting youths who are quietly driving change in society, even amid several negative national indicators. This is the third edition. Onlinekhabar has previously published the “40 Under 40” list in 2024 and 2025 as well.

The selection committee, comprising former Supreme Court Justice Anil Kumar Sinha, researcher Dr Uttam Babu Shrestha, researcher Dr Amrita Sharma, and Onlinekhabar Editor-in-Chief Basanta Basnet, finalised the list of 40 individuals. Editor-in-Chief Basnet said the 40 Under 40 list recognises the dedication, diligence and significant contributions made by young people in their respective fields, and helps guide society towards progress. Basnet, who is also a member of the judging panel, credited his team and readers for the continued success of the search for 40 young people under forty, now in its third year.

“The primary job of the press is to expose the problems and ills facing the nation and society. At the same time, it is also our job to share the country’s successes with everyone and encourage potential,” he said. “For three years now, we have continued this work by publishing a list of forty young people under the age of forty. In the days ahead as well, we will continue this search, fairly and effectively, for young people who show society the way forward.”

Basnet also extended gratitude to the newsrooms, bureaus, sponsors and all readers who have supported this initiative. Onlinekhabar’s team worked for nearly four months to prepare the list of 40 influential youths. From around 1,500 names received through online applications and recommendations, a preliminary list was submitted to the judging/selection committee, from which 40 were to be chosen.

The final list of 40 influential young people was drawn up based on the committee’s selection and recommendations.

title.rendered: Nepal Police moves to establish anti-cyber scam centre

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 12

The process of establishing an ‘Anti-Cyber Scam Centre’ has been initiated in response to a sharp increase in cyber scams. The initiative comes amid a rise in incidents of hacking funds from mobile banking, digital wallets, and accounts such as eSewa and Khalti through various schemes, phishing, and other fraudulent methods.

Nepal Police spokesperson DIG Abinarayan Kafle said discussions have been held on the matter and work is underway to prepare a possible framework for the centre. Representatives from all relevant agencies will be involved in the centre, according to Kafle. Representatives from Nepal Police, Nepal Rastra Bank, the Nepal Bankers’ Association, digital wallet service providers, payment service providers (PSPs), payment system operators (PSOs), the Nepal Telecommunications Authority and internet service providers will be assigned as authorised contact persons.

They will be co-located at the Cyber Bureau and work through a case management system to coordinate responses to cyber scam cases, according to Nepal Police.

title.rendered: Int’l Youth Day being observed today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 12

International Youth Day is being observed around the world, including in Nepal, today with various programmes highlighting the important role of young people in shaping society and the future. The theme for this year’s celebration is “Different Contexts, Shared Aspirations,” focusing on the common aspirations of young people despite differences in their social, cultural, geographical and economic circumstances.

International Youth Day has been observed on August 12 since 2000 at the initiative of the United Nations. The Day aims to promote youth-centred discussions and advocacy, increase young people’s participation in policymaking and implementation, and encourage greater investment and partnerships for youth development. A special programme is being held at Nepal Academy in Kamaladi, Kathmandu, featuring an exhibition on information technology and startup businesses.

A youth awareness run is also being organised from Bhrikutimandap to Kamaladi in the federal capital, Kathmandu. The main event will feature a high-level panel discussion on promoting youth entrepreneurship and employment in Nepal. Similarly, six businesses will receive national awards for information technology and startups, while young entrepreneurs from all seven provinces will also be honoured on the occasion.

It may be noted that a meeting of the National Youth Council, chaired by its Chairperson and Minister for Youth, Labour and Employment Ramji Yadav on July 17 this year, decided to celebrate International Youth Day grandly. According to the 2021 National Census, 12,412,173 people aged 16 to 40 accounted for 42.56 per cent of the country’s total population.

title.rendered: New mining law after 4 decades proposes fines of up to Rs 10 million

content.rendered:
The government is preparing to amend the Mines and Minerals Act to impose fines of up to Rs 10 million on anyone who explores or extracts minerals without obtaining a licence.

The government is moving to amend the Mines and Minerals Act after four decades. The Mines and Minerals Bill formulated to amend and consolidate laws relating to mines and minerals, presented by the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies in the House of Representatives, will replace the Mines and Minerals Act 1985.

According to Industry Minister Gaurikumari Yadav, the new law will address the scientific, sustainable and systematic utilisation of mines and minerals. The Act will clarify the roles, coordination mechanisms and jurisdictions of the federal, provincial and local governments in accordance with the federal system. It will also make the process of conserving, exploring and extracting minerals more transparent, competitive and accessible.

The bill also proposes special protection and regulation of strategic, defence-related and radioactive minerals, the use of minerals in line with environmental protection principles, and measures to reduce geological hazards.

Provinces to get greater role in mineral exploration

The proposed law provides that the authority to explore mines and minerals will be exercised in accordance with provincial law. Under the existing law, the Nepal government has exclusive authority over all activities related to minerals. Under the new provision, exploration of mines and minerals extending across two or more territories will be carried out with the mutual consent of the concerned provincial governments. In case of a dispute, exploration will be conducted through the Department of Mines and Geology, according to the bill.

However, the authority to extract minerals will remain with the Nepal government. For this purpose, the government may conduct extraction through the department itself or grant a company a licence to carry out mining activities. The bill also states that the Nepal government may, by publishing a notice in the Nepal Gazette, delegate certain mining and mineral extraction-related responsibilities to provincial and local governments. The concerned local governments will be responsible for the conservation of mines and minerals. All authority over activities involving radioactive minerals will remain with the Nepal government.

Special provisions for strategic and defence-related minerals

Under the proposed law, the Nepal government may designate any mineral as strategic or defence-related based on its use, availability and national interest. The government will have the authority to set necessary conditions, impose restrictions and prohibit specific activities at locations where such minerals are found.

The authority to conduct or commission activities involving such minerals will also remain with the Nepal government. Work involving these minerals will have to be carried out through companies fully owned by the Nepal government.

Under the bill, companies seeking to explore or extract mines and minerals must obtain a licence. However, a licence will not be required to collect and use ordinary construction materials such as stone, gravel, sand, soil and slate found on privately owned land for personal use.

Exploration licence periods specified in the Act

The bill proposes to specify the duration of exploration licences in the Act itself. The existing Act does not prescribe a fixed period. Under the proposed law, an exploration licence for major minerals will be valid for three years. The period will be two years for important minerals and one year for ordinary minerals.

The validity of licences issued before the new Act comes into force will also be maintained in accordance with the new provisions. Extraction licences will be valid for a maximum of 30 years. Under the proposed bill, licences for the extraction of very small, small, medium and large-scale mineral deposits will be valid for 10, 15, 20 and 30 years, respectively.

If extraction cannot be completed within the prescribed period, the licence may be extended. The extension periods will be two, three, five and seven years, respectively. Licence holders will be required to begin extraction within two years of obtaining a licence. Mining companies will also have to comply with environmental protection laws. The authorities may suspend mining activities if the prescribed conditions are not met.

Fines increased

No person may explore or extract minerals without obtaining a licence under the Act. Under the proposed bill, anyone who conducts or commissions exploration in violation of the law may be fined up to Rs 500,000. For extraction-related offences, the fine will be based on the nature and quantity of the mineral extracted.

Where the value of the illegally extracted mineral can be determined, the offender will have to pay the assessed value as well as an additional fine equal to that amount. If the value cannot be determined, the fine will range from Rs 2.5 million to Rs 10 million.

Under the existing law, the maximum fine is only Rs 100,000. The new law proposes that, when determining the value of illegally extracted minerals, the amount will be calculated at 50 times the prescribed royalty rate for the relevant mineral. Anyone who conducts or commissions mining activities in violation of prescribed conditions will face a fine ranging from Rs 500,000 to Rs 1 million and imprisonment for five to 10 years.

According to the bill, if a licensed company extracts more minerals than the annual quantity specified in its licence, or conceals the actual quantity extracted and submits a false statement showing a lower quantity, the company may be required to pay the assessed value of the excess or concealed quantity and an equivalent fine. If the value cannot be determined, a fine ranging from Rs 100,000 to Rs 1 million may be imposed.

Under the proposed law, anyone who obstructs or interferes with an inspector in the discharge of official duties may be fined up to Rs 10,000 immediately by the inspector. If extraction is carried out outside the approved mining area, the licensed company may be required to pay the assessed value of the minerals extracted and an equivalent fine. If the value cannot be determined, the company may be fined between Rs 500,000 and Rs 1 million.

Anyone or any organisation involved in the export, extraction, transportation or sale of prohibited minerals may be required by the director general to pay the assessed value and an equivalent fine. If the value cannot be determined, a fine of Rs 200,000 to Rs 500,000 may be imposed, and equipment used in the offence may be confiscated.

For the purpose of determining the value of minerals in such cases, the bill proposes using an amount equivalent to 10 times the prescribed royalty rate for the relevant mineral. In another provision concerning valuation, the amount will be calculated at 15 times the prescribed royalty rate.

A licensed company that fails to comply with prescribed conditions may be fined Rs 500,000. Anyone who obstructs or interferes with mining activities carried out under the Act, or commits any other act in violation of the Act, may be fined up to Rs 200,000. The bill states that fines imposed under this section will be recovered from the concerned individual, organisation or company as government dues.

In the case of minerals falling under the jurisdiction of provincial and local governments, enforcement action and fines will be governed by the laws of the respective province or local government.

title.rendered: Gol Bazaar shops reopen after a week as protest damage tops Rs 740 million

content.rendered:
Preliminary estimates show that vandalism and arson during the protests of July 30 in the Gol Bazaar area of Siraha caused damage worth over Rs 740 million.

According to SP Basu Dev Pathak, chief of the District Police Office, Siraha, the damage details were made public after analysing on-site reports prepared based on complaints received from victims.

Police say that during the protests, 64 structures were vandalised or set on fire in the Gol Bazaar area, including 15 private homes, 18 shops and businesses, 28 vehicles, and religious and educational sites.

According to police, the damage breaks down as follows: private homes and commercial structures suffered the highest loss at Rs 340.559 million, shops and businesses at Rs 331.712 million, vehicles at Rs 10.2 million, and religious and educational sites at Rs 58.19 million.

Shops in Gol Bazaar, which had remained closed for nearly a week due to the unrest, resumed operations from 10 am on Tuesday. Before this, on Monday, MP Purushottam Yadav held discussions with Muslim community business owners in Golbazar Municipality-11, Balkawa, urging them to maintain social harmony and resume their businesses.

During the discussion, Yadav committed to raising the issue of damage to shops, malls, and private homes in parliament and before the government, and to pressuring the government to take the matter seriously and provide compensation to the victims.

During the protests on July 30, 15-year-old Ganesh Yadav of Aurahi Rural Municipality-2, Tulsiyahi, Siraha, was killed after being shot by security personnel. Following Ganesh’s death, the protests intensified, leading to vandalism and arson targeting various shops, businesses, and private structures in the Gol Bazaar area.

Since the incident, local authorities, the administration, political parties, and representatives of various communities have been working to restore social harmony and normalise daily life in the affected area.

title.rendered: What AI means for the future of filmmaking in Nepal

content.rendered:
Every major change in filmmaking begins with a period of uncertainty. Digital cameras were once treated as inferior to film. Editing software made physical cutting rooms unnecessary. Smartphones placed capable cameras in millions of pockets. Each shift created the same fear: that technology would make existing skills, equipment and even people irrelevant. Artificial intelligence has brought that fear back, only louder.

Today, AI can generate images from a sentence, create video from a prompt, remove unwanted objects from a frame, imitate voices, translate dialogue and build a rough storyboard before a camera has been switched on. Tasks that once took days can sometimes be completed in hours. For a country like Nepal, where filmmakers regularly work with limited budgets, small crews and tight deadlines, this creates a genuine opportunity. It also raises difficult questions about work, ownership and truth.

AI is already part of the production process

The public conversation often imagines AI as a machine that receives a prompt and produces an entire film. That possibility receives attention because it is dramatic, but it is not how most working filmmakers currently experience the technology. AI is entering production through smaller, less visible tasks.

During pre-production, it can help organise research, produce early visual references, create draft storyboards, and break scripts down into locations, characters, and props. In post-production, it can assist with transcription, subtitles, footage organisation, noise reduction, object removal and the creation of multiple versions of the same video. McKinsey has identified applications across development, production and post-production, including pre-visualisation, editing, audio synchronisation, tagging, subtitling and dubbing.

Production companies are also experimenting with leading AI video generators such as Higgsfield, Runway, Kling and Seedance, as well as tools such as Google Veo, Adobe Firefly and OpenAI’s Sora. Depending on the platform, these systems can turn text or reference images into short clips, test camera movement and visual styles, extend or alter footage, and help build concept films or pre-visualisations before a full shoot. For a production company, their most practical value may be less about generating a finished film and more about communicating an idea quickly, testing creative directions and identifying what still needs to be achieved by a real crew on location.

Used responsibly, these tools can reduce repetitive work and give filmmakers more time to focus on decisions that require judgment. That distinction matters. AI can produce options, but a filmmaker still has to know which option serves the story.

What AI could mean for Nepal?

Filmmaking in Nepal is often an exercise in adaptation. A location becomes unavailable. The weather changes. Equipment cannot reach the place where it is needed. A small crew performs several roles. The ambition of a project is frequently larger than its available budget. AI cannot remove these realities, but it can help teams prepare for them.

A director can test the visual direction of a scene before committing resources to it. A production team can compare approaches to a location or sequence. An editor can search hours of footage more efficiently. A small organisation can subtitle a documentary for international viewers without beginning from zero. For independent filmmakers, students and emerging creators, this may lower some barriers to entry.

This is especially relevant outside the Kathmandu Valley, where access to specialised production resources can be limited. AI-assisted tools could allow more creators to experiment, learn and participate. But cheaper production does not automatically produce better films. Making images easier to generate may increase the quantity of content while making original thinking even more valuable.

The camera was never the storyteller

The availability of technology has never been the same as the ability to tell a story. A camera does not decide where to stand during an intimate moment. Editing software does not understand why silence may be more powerful than music. An image generator does not carry lived memories of a place, language, ritual or relationship. Those decisions come from observation and experience.

Through my work as a producer, director, photographer and editor, I have seen projects with modest resources create a lasting impact because they understood their subject. I have also seen technically polished productions fail to connect because they had no clear emotional centre.

AI may help us produce a shot. It cannot decide whether that shot belongs in the story. If we use AI only to imitate visual trends from somewhere else, we may create work that appears sophisticated but says very little about us. Nepal does not need cheaper copies of international advertising or cinema. It needs tools that help Nepali creators express ideas rooted in their own experiences.

The risks cannot be an afterthought

Many generative systems are trained using enormous collections of existing creative work. A filmmaker may generate an image in seconds, but the visual language behind it may come from photographers, illustrators and designers who were neither consulted nor compensated. Synthetic voices and faces create another problem. If a person’s likeness can be reproduced without meaningful consent, the damage affects dignity, identity and public trust.

Employment is also a legitimate concern. Production companies may be tempted to use AI simply to reduce the number of people they hire. Editors, assistants, designers and junior crew members do not only complete tasks; they learn through them. If every entry-level responsibility is automated, where will the next generation gain experience? Nepal’s creative sector needs an honest discussion about consent, copyright, disclosure and fair credit before harmful practices become normal.

A responsible approach

AI should be treated as a production tool, not an invisible replacement for human contribution.

Filmmakers should obtain permission before recreating a face or voice; never present synthetic documentary material as a real event; check output for cultural and factual errors; disclose meaningful generative use to clients; protect confidential footage; and credit the people responsible for final creative decisions.

These principles will evolve with technology. The goal is not to reject experimentation. It is to ensure that experimentation does not come at the cost of trust.

The future still needs filmmakers

AI will change jobs inside filmmaking. Some tasks will become faster, some roles will evolve and new specialisations will appear. The filmmakers who remain valuable will not simply be those who know the latest software. They will be the ones who can ask better questions, recognise truthful moments, guide collaborators and understand the people whose stories they tell.

For Nepal, AI could make ambitious visual storytelling more accessible. It could help smaller teams plan carefully, reach international audiences and make limited resources travel further. But its greatest value will not come from generating more content.

It will come from giving filmmakers more space to think. Technology may change how an image is produced. The responsibility for deciding what that image means still belongs to us.

title.rendered: 5 Nepali agencies win 17 awards at Flame Awards Asia 2026

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 11

Five Nepali marketing and advertising agencies have won 17 awards at the Flame Awards Asia 2026 held in New Delhi, with Outreach Nepal, Lemon and DigitalIn securing the largest share of the honours.

The awards ceremony was held on August 7 at Taj Vivanta, Dwarka. The Nepali agencies collectively won 13 Gold, three Silver and one Bronze award for campaigns created for brands including Vaseline, Samsung, Mountain Dew, Ncell, Mero Khukri, Gorkha and Zyn.

Outreach Nepal, together with its activation and digital agencies Lemon and DigitalIn, secured 17 awards. Storm Communication Nepal and D20 Labs were the other Nepali agencies recognised at the event.

The Flame Awards Asia, instituted by the Rural Marketing Association of India (RMAI), recognises marketing and communication campaigns across India and emerging Asian markets based on strategy, innovation, execution, technology, community participation and measurable impact.

The 2026 awards featured agencies and organisations from several Asian countries, including India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Vietnam, the Philippines and Sri Lanka.

The jury was chaired by Santosh Desai, Founder and Director of Think9 Consumer Technologies. Ernst & Young (EY) served as the tabulation partner for the awards.

Ujaya Shakya, founder of Outreach Nepal and first vice-president of the Advertising Association of Nepal, described the performance as an indication of the growing talent and potential of Nepal’s marketing communications industry.

title.rendered: Egg support price increased as demand rises

content.rendered:
Chitwan, August 11

Poultry businesses have increased the support price of eggs following a rise in demand. The Nepal Layers Poultry Farmers Association has revised the support price, effective from today.

According to the association, the support price has been set at Rs 560 per crate of 30 XL eggs, Rs 545 for large eggs, Rs 500 for medium eggs, and Rs 3,000 per box of small eggs, with each box containing seven crates. Association Chairperson Binod Pokharel said market demand has increased significantly following a decline in egg production after the bird flu outbreak subsided and a large number of chickens died. He said the support price was determined based on the rates provided by poultry farms.

Despite the price increase, farmers are still unable to recover their production costs, Pokharel said. The cost of producing an egg is Rs 19.12, which puts the cost of a crate of 30 eggs at Rs 573.60. Farmers have suffered heavy losses due to bird flu. As they have been unable to recover their production costs, many farmers have started leaving the poultry business in recent years.

Business operators say declining production, poultry diseases and other factors have increasingly forced farmers to rely on bank loans to sustain their businesses. Pokharel said some farmers recently lost chickens to bird flu, while those who managed to keep their poultry suffered significant losses because they were unable to receive a fair price for their eggs.

content.rendered:
Every year, Nepal celebrates another graduating class of young doctors and nurses. Families gather with pride. Parents celebrate years of sacrifice. Universities produce another generation of highly trained healthcare professionals ready to serve their communities. Yet, for many of these graduates, another journey soon begins. Not to a district hospital. Not to a rural health centre. But to an international airport. Within months or years, many leave Nepal to build careers abroad in Australia, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States or Gulf countries. Nepal loses some of the very people it has invested years in educating. Among many reasons, an important one is sole dependency on relatively low salaries from their medical practices. Whenever we discuss this problem, we usually ask one question. How do we stop doctors and nurses from leaving? Let’s ask a different question. How do we make staying in Nepal a better choice? No healthcare system can become stronger while continuously losing its most valuable resource. Buildings can be constructed. Equipment can be purchased. Technology can be installed. But experienced healthcare professionals cannot be replaced overnight. Healthcare ultimately depends upon people.

One uncomfortable reality deserves honest discussion. Many doctors and nurses in Nepal are not undertrained. They are underutilised, and many are underpaid. The years required to become a physician or a specialist are long and demanding. Nurses likewise carry enormous responsibility for patient care. Yet many healthcare professionals struggle to earn incomes that reflect their expertise and contribution. Some take on multiple jobs to support their families. Others conclude that the only practical path to financial security is to leave the country. This is not simply a workforce issue. It is a healthcare issue. Every doctor or nurse who leaves takes knowledge, experience and capacity with them.

Traditionally, earning additional income has required taking on another hospital appointment, opening a private clinic or working longer hours in the same physical location. Digital healthcare allows us to imagine another possibility. Instead of tying professional opportunities to a single building, why not connect healthcare professionals directly with patients who need their expertise? Imagine a physician finishing work at Patan Hospital. Rather than ending the working day, she chooses to make herself available for two hours that evening through a secure national digital care network. Patients request consultations at times that suit their schedules. The physician accepts consultations or other services within his/her area of expertise at their own convenient off-duty time. The consultation is not a random video call. It is informed by the patient’s authorised medical history, previous investigations, medications and recent clinical information. The doctor earns additional income. The patient receives timely specialist advice. No unnecessary travel is required. Everyone benefits.

Now imagine this happening across Nepal. A paediatrician in Kathmandu advises families in Humla. A psychiatrist in Pokhara supports patients in Bajura. An endocrinologist in Bharatpur follows patients with diabetes living hundreds of kilometres away. An experienced nurse provides postoperative counselling from home. Professional knowledge begins moving around the country instead of requiring patients to do all the travelling.

This is not simply about creating a “gig economy” in the conventional sense. Healthcare is fundamentally different. Clinical practice requires professional licensing, ethical standards, accountability and patient safety. Those principles must never change. What changes is access to opportunity. Healthcare professionals gain the flexibility to contribute beyond the walls of a single institution. Patients gain access to expertise that would otherwise remain out of reach. The platform becomes a professional marketplace built on quality, trust and continuity of care, not casual work. 

One of the greatest opportunities may lie with healthcare professionals whose careers do not fit traditional models. Many highly trained women doctors reduce clinical practice after starting families because hospital schedules can be difficult to balance with caregiving responsibilities. Retired specialists often possess decades of clinical wisdom but no longer wish to work full-time. Experienced nurses may prefer flexible schedules while continuing to practice. A connected digital healthcare system allows these professionals to remain active, continue serving patients and generate additional income while maintaining flexibility. Healthcare does not lose its expertise. It gains new ways to use it.

There is another opportunity that deserves national attention. Thousands of Nepali doctors and nurses now practice overseas. Many continue to care deeply about Nepal. Imagine if they could contribute selected teleconsultations, specialist opinions, teaching or mentoring through a secure national platform. The experience gained abroad would no longer be entirely lost to Nepal. Instead, it could strengthen the country’s healthcare system while maintaining professional careers overseas. The healthcare workforce would become global, while still contributing locally.

This broader philosophy is reflected in the vision behind MEDeCLOCK. Beyond creating patient-centred digital health records, the platform envisions a secure national network where registered doctors and nurses can provide telemedicine services based on their expertise and availability. Combined with longitudinal health information and continuity of care, this approach could expand access for patients while creating additional professional opportunities for healthcare workers. In a country where low remuneration contributes to workforce migration, such opportunities may help some professionals build more sustainable careers while remaining in Nepal. 

This idea should not be viewed as a substitute for fair salaries, better working conditions or continued investment in public healthcare. Those remain essential; rather, it is a complementary strategy. A way to unlock additional professional opportunity without asking doctors and nurses to leave the communities they serve.

Throughout this series, we have argued that healthcare should follow the patient. Perhaps another principle deserves equal attention. Opportunity should follow expertise. A doctor should not have to leave Nepal simply because opportunity is concentrated elsewhere. A nurse should not have to choose between serving her country and providing for her family. If digital health can help create meaningful new opportunities for healthcare professionals while expanding access for patients, then its benefits extend far beyond technology. It becomes an investment in Nepal’s most valuable healthcare resource. Its people!

title.rendered: Gathamuga: Interesting stories behind strange rituals of Kathmandu’s annual monsoon festival

content.rendered:
Today, the Newa community is celebrating Gathamuga, also spelt as Gathemangal, a local festival. Every year, Shrawan Krishna Chaturdashi (the 14th day of the waning moon in the Shrawan month) marks the festival. It is also known as Gathamuga Chahre or Ghantakarna Chaturdashi.

This is also considered the festival of keeping one’s house or surroundings clean and performing puja to ward off evil spirits.

It is yet to be ascertained when the festival started being marked. However, the earliest mention of the festival being celebrated has been found in the Gopal Raj Vamshavali, a handwritten manuscript that mentions the festival started in the Lichhavi era.

For the occasion, people in various communities gather together to burn a straw effigy of a demon, Ghantakarna. That is the most basic part of the festival. However, there are other interesting pieces of information about the demon and the festival.

Here are a few key things:

What happens on the day of Gathamuga

People make a human-sized effigy out of straws/hay, and bamboo, in the form of a demon. The demon is put up at crossroads and burnt at the end of the day. 

People offer cooked rice or beaten rice along with rice husk and raw buffalo lungs as well as a special kind of flower called dronapushpa (Leucas cephalotes). Some also hang up dolls to burn along the effigy. Some people take the burning of an effigy as the burning of the demonic presence or the end of the yearly duty of the helpful demon.

In the evening, a person also roams around the community with paints all over his body, taking the form of a demon. He is flanked by a person holding a torch and many others who follow him around. He goes around the locality to beg for food or donation.

People give him dahi chiura (a mixture of yoghurt and beaten rice). After that, the man reaches near the effigy and goes around it three times. Once he is done, the people then pull the effigy to the nearest river, burn it and throw it into the river. The ritual is known as ‘aaju dya ha’. 

Inside the houses, people perform a small puja and prepare a lit makal (earthen utensil) with coal and other herbs, three-headed nails and squared charms with mantras to ward off the evil spirits. A paper is nailed down at the top of the entrance of the house and rooms, followed by the fanning of makal inside the room. Homeowners also put together rice, spices, garlic, raw meat, and flower, to offer to the spirits and keep them outside the home. This is called ‘bau wayegu’.

On Gathamuga, people also wear iron rings on this day as they believe iron keeps evil spirits away and eat samaybaji.

Some other communities also worship Kumar Kartikeya, the firstborn of Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati. 

Stories around the Gathamuga festival

There are a few variations of stories around the Gathemuga festival.

1. It is said that in ancient times, the Kathmandu valley saw a decline in the number of farmers working in the field. In one monsoon season, a group of people performed some tantric rituals and prayed for supernatural help. But, the demons who came to help needed a lot of food and started wreaking havoc in the village. So the villagers collectively chased the demons away to the river. 

Now, at the end of the plantation season, the people performed the rituals to chase the evil spirits away from the house. In another version, people mark the day to thank the demons for their help.

2. In the heart of the city, there was a demon that was terrifying the residents there. The demon was known as Gathamuga or Ghantakarna for it wore a pair of bells dangling from its ears.

Another local version of the story famous in Itumbahal of Kathmandu also refers to the demon as Gurumappa. Because the demon was invited to the community and told to eat whatever was available on the roof of the houses, it started eating the children sleeping on the roof. 

The people wanted to get rid of him and hence they prayed to the gods. As if hearing their prayers, a group of frogs came to the locality and then started croaking to irritate the demon. The demon ran after them and when the frogs jumped into a swamp, the demon followed and then drowned in the swamp itself. So, Gathamuga is celebrated as the day people got rid of the demon.

The frog, in another version of the same story, has been believed to be a tantric who takes the form of a frog and saves people from the demon’s violence.

Based on this story, another festival byaa jaa nakegu (feeding rice to frogs) is also observed on the next full moon day where people offer frogs rice from their harvest. Others also offer panchamrit (five elements of elixir/nectar), flowers, kwati, and beans.

3. In another story related to Gathamuga, the demon is considered a protector of the people. In this version, it has been renamed Sambar Bhairav, one of Lord Shiva’s warriors. Here, Gathamuga or Ghantakarna has been defined as a protector of the Kathmandu valley, who saves the inhabitants from tantric influences. And for that, the people worship him and offer him food he likes so that he continues to protect them. It is believed that the demon had died this day, and people perform all the funeral rites for him. 

4. In Bhaktapur, Gathamuga is not a demon but a man who sat at the crossroads and took money from the rich and gave it to the poor. When the rich people refused, he killed them. When the man died, he had bells hanging from his ears. Then, people collected money for his cremation as an acknowledgement of his work.

5. According to historian Hari Ram Joshi, Gathamuga refers to the work of tying strong knots around junctions of pillars of the houses and keeping the foundation strong too. The ritual of tying the knots around the wooden pillars to make the chariot of the Rato Machhindranath is also called Gathamuga. 

His interpretation of the story also says that the festival gives the message to stay united and live in harmony for the well-being of an individual, society and the nation.

Other things to know

1. Gathamuga or Gathemangal ends the seven-week period starting from Sithi Nakha when the musical instruments are barred from playing.

2. The end of Gathamuga also marks the start of other yearly festivals too, starting from Gunlaa, Panchdaan, Indra Jatra and so on.

3. The men of the Navadurga Gana or Devgana who become deities for the Navadurga Naach wear ceremonial masks again this day. On Gathamuga/Gathemangal, the lifecycle of Navadurga starts by wearing the masks and ends on the day of Bhagashthi. In the end, the masks are burned and turned into ashes at Brahmayani near the Hanumante river.

4. Starting this day, lakhe is taken out for various processions in different places, including Milpu Lakhe of Tokha.

5. Children are made to pass over the burning fire with the belief that it will keep them safe from evil spirits.

title.rendered: Senior literary figure Rajendra Bimal dies at 79

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, August 11

Senior literary figure Prof Dr Rajendra Bimal has died at the age of 79. Bimal died at around 12:45 am, his youngest son, Bibhas Labh said. According to Labh, Bimal suddenly fell ill at around 11:30 pm on Monday while they were talking. He was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, but died during treatment.

His body has currently been kept at his residence in Devichowk, Ward No. 10 of Janakpurdham Sub-Metropolitan City, for people to pay their last respects. Bimal wrote extensively in Nepali, Maithili and English across various literary genres. He held a PhD in linguistics and master’s degrees in Nepali, Maithili and Hindi.

He had been involved in teaching Nepali at Tribhuvan University since 1972. Bimal received numerous honours, including the Jagadambashree Award and Madhyapark Award. Bimal’s last rites will be performed at Swargadwari in Janakpurdham at 3 pm today.

title.rendered: Heavy rain likely in several parts of Nepal, authorities urge caution

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 11

The monsoon is currently affecting the entire country. The monsoon low-pressure line is positioned slightly north of its average location, closer to Nepal, over the western part of the country and around its average position over the eastern region.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology said most parts of Koshi and Lumbini provinces, as well as the mountainous and hilly areas of Bagmati, Gandaki, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces, are generally cloudy.

The Madhesh Province and the Tarai areas of Bagmati, Gandaki and Sudurpaschim provinces are partly cloudy. Light to moderate rain is currently occurring in some areas of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces.

According to the department, the weather will remain generally cloudy across the country this afternoon. Some areas of the mountainous region may receive moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning, with snowfall also possible. Many areas of the hilly region are likely to receive moderate rainfall.

The department said the mountainous and hilly areas of Koshi and Bagmati provinces, along with Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces, will remain generally cloudy, while the Tarai areas of Madhesh, Koshi and Bagmati provinces will remain partly cloudy.

According to the department’s weather bulletin, some areas of the country’s mountainous region may receive moderate rain and snowfall accompanied by thunder and lightning. Many areas of the hilly regions of Karnali and Sudurpaschim provinces, as well as some areas of the hilly regions of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces, are likely to receive moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning.

Some areas of the Tarai regions of Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces, as well as one or two areas of the Tarai regions of Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, may receive moderate rainfall. Heavy rainfall is possible in some areas of the hilly region of Karnali Province and in one or two areas of the hilly and Tarai regions of Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces.

Tonight, the country will remain generally cloudy. Some areas of the mountainous region may receive moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning, with snowfall also possible. Many areas of the country’s hilly regions and the Tarai areas of Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces are likely to receive moderate rainfall accompanied by thunder and lightning.

Some areas of the Tarai regions of Madhesh and Koshi provinces may receive moderate rainfall. Heavy rainfall is likely in some areas of the mountainous and hilly regions of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, the hilly region of Karnali Province, and the hilly and Tarai regions of Lumbini and Sudurpaschim provinces. Very heavy rainfall is possible in one or two areas, according to the department.

The department has urged residents in vulnerable areas to take necessary precautions, warning that heavy rainfall could increase the risk of debris flows, floods, landslides and soil erosion.

The weather could also affect daily life, agriculture, health services, tourism, mountaineering, and road and air transport services, the department said, urging people to remain alert.

title.rendered: Transport entrepreneurs demand concession on electric vehicles

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 11

An umbrella organisation of transport entrepreneurs has demanded that Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle provide a concession on customs duty when importing parts of electric vehicles. It would help encourage an environmentally friendly transport system, they argued. A team led by the chair of the Nepal National Federation of Transport Entrepreneurs, Punya Prasad (Saroj) Sitaula, submitted an 11-point memorandum to the Finance Minister on Monday.

The delegation requested the Minister to take immediate measures to address the existing problems in the transport sector. The Federation reminded the government that the transport sector had an investment worth Rs 13 billion and four million families depended on it. The transport entrepreneurs also urged the government to enforce the report submitted by the probe commission led by former government secretary Dipak Subedi, ensure timely revision of the Motor Insurance Rate Directive 2073, and give direction to the Insurance Authority accordingly.

The government is also proposed to establish an ‘accident relief fund’ by imposing an additional fee of one rupee per litre on fuel (diesel/petrol) and one rupee per unit on electric vehicles. The fund can be further reinforced with the allocation of one per cent of the insurance premium and an additional amount from the government. The Federation advocated for making a strict provision on imports of vehicles, abolishing the 72-hour facility given to Indian freight and passenger vehicles, amending the Company Act, and implementing a uniform tax system.

The Minister suggested forming a powerful ‘transport authority’ for effective regulation and development of the transport sector, and reconsidering the operating hours of tippers in the Kathmandu Valley. Receiving the memorandum, Finance Minister Dr Wagle assured that the genuine demands of the transport sector. The Ministry would conduct a necessary study on the transport entrepreneurs’ demands and take appropriate steps accordingly.

title.rendered: Dry landslide damages Gharkhola hydropower project; one goes missing

content.rendered:
Santosh Gautam/Myagdi, August 11

A person has gone missing, and another one got injured when a dry landslide occurred at Pokharebagar of Annapurna Rural Municipality-6 in Myagdi. The landslide occurred this morning and also damaged the powerhouse of Gharkhola Hydropower Project.

A worker at the powerhouse, Dipak Baruwal, 55, went missing in the landslide while another, Surendra BK, 31, was injured, according to the District Police Office. Baruwal is from Annapurna-6 and BK from Gauriganga Municipality-5. The search for the missing one is continuous with the joint effort of police personnel, Nepali Army staff, the Armed Police Force, people’s representatives and locals.

The injured one has been sent to Province Hospital, Beni after rescue and general treatment, according to Police Inspector Sagar Timilsina. Equipment in the hydropower with a capacity of 14 MW received damage, resulting in disruption of power production.

title.rendered: Powerful earthquake strikes Colombia, killing at least 111

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 11

A powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, killing at least 111 people and damaging numerous buildings. Several people are feared to be trapped under the rubble, and authorities have warned that the death toll could rise. The government has declared a state of emergency in the affected areas following the earthquake.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake struck at 7:34 am local time on Monday, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó province. The earthquake occurred at a depth of around 103 kilometres. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) also confirmed a 7.4-magnitude earthquake in western Colombia. According to the USGS, the epicentre was about three miles east of San José del Palmar and approximately 280 kilometres west of the capital, Bogotá.

Pereira suffers major damage, no casualties reported near epicentre

Pereira, one of the major cities in Colombia’s coffee-producing region, has suffered the most significant impact from the earthquake. Located about 55 kilometres from the epicentre, the city has reported collapsed buildings and extensive damage. Videos verified by the BBC showed a building collapsing in Plaza Bolívar, Pereira’s main square. Rubble and dust spread across the square following the collapse. A large number of people were reportedly present in the square when the earthquake struck.

The earthquake also had a significant impact on surrounding cities and the Valle del Cauca region. However, local officials said there were surprisingly no reported casualties in the village of San José del Palmar, where the earthquake was centred. According to village mayor León Fabio Marín Moncada, roads leading to and from the village were damaged by the earthquake, but no deaths or injuries had been reported so far.

The tremors were felt in various parts of the country, including the capital Bogotá. People took to the streets for safety after buildings shook in the capital, and alarms were reportedly triggered in some buildings. Bogotá Mayor Carlos Galán said on social media that no casualties or major structural damage had been reported in the capital so far. He said some buildings had developed minor cracks.

Full extent of damage yet to be assessed

Rescue and search operations have been intensified following the earthquake. Authorities fear the number of deaths and injuries could rise as people may be trapped under collapsed structures.

Seismologists are reanalysing the earthquake’s preliminary magnitude and other details. The USGS said the magnitude and intensity estimates could be revised as additional data become available.

title.rendered: Five bodies found at Yalung-Ri base camp identified

content.rendered:
Kavrepalanchok, August 10

The five bodies found at the base camp of Yalung-Ri Mountain in the Rolwaling region of Gaurishankar Rural Municipality-9, Dolakha, have been identified as those of two Nepali and three foreign climbers.

District Police Office Dolakha information officer Police Inspector Santosh Kumar Khadka said the five bodies recovered on Sunday belonged to Nepali mountain guides Padam Tamang of Gaurishankar Rural Municipality-9, Dolakha, and Mer Karki of Mapya Dudhkunda Rural Municipality-5, Solukhumbu.

According to Khadka, the bodies of the foreign climbers have been identified as Marco Di Marcello of Canada, Markus Karchiller of Italy and Kyakob Iseriver of Germany.

Khadka said the bodies of the three foreign climbers and one mountain guide have been sent to the Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu for post-mortem examinations, while the body of Tamang from Dolakha will undergo a post-mortem examination in Charikot.

title.rendered: Mandala Theatre stages The Age of Darkness (Photo Feature)

content.rendered:
The staging of “The Age of Darkness” has begun at Mandala Theatre in Thapagaun. The production is based on Dharamvir Bharati’s celebrated play “Andha Yug.”

Translated into Nepali by Rajendra Salab, the play is directed by Sudip Khatiwada. Khatiwada had made his acting debut through this very play 11 years ago.

The play tells the story of how the violence, revenge and mental emptiness caused by the Mahabharat war engulf its characters. Through the mindset of characters living through the aftermath of war, it explores themes of violence, power struggles, revenge, moral conflict, and human responsibility.

The cast includes Jinlop Dong Waiba, Aabhushan Ghimire, Milan Panta, Indra Kumar Limbu, Joheb Shah, Sujit Malla Thakuri, Samata Rai, Bijay Dong, Saugat Shrestha, Raju Shrestha, Nitya Poudel, and Bishwajit Dhakal, among others.

Music for the play has been composed by Saurav Chalise, Salina BK, Jeevan Rai, and Kumar Lama.
