title.rendered: Kathmandu’s parking nightmare continues: Unplanned bans, unaffordable parking fees

content.rendered:
Across the Kathmandu Valley, navigating the regular streets in a vehicle is very frustrating. The city’s ambitious policies, strict parking bans, and mandated construction requirements indicate that we have improved in regulation, but the day-to-day reality that the residents have been facing tells a very different story.

Over the past few years, local authorities have introduced several parking regulations. Kathmandu metropolis mandated that newly constructed houses and commercial buildings allocate 20 per cent of ground-floor area strictly for parking. Furthermore, the metropolis also designated specific parking zones and standardised fee structures across key zones. However, implementation remains deeply flawed.

Unnecessary hassle

Banning roadside parking in major commercial areas such as New Road, Durbar Marg, and Baneshwor was expected to be a step towards cleaner streets. Yet, the metropolis failed to create sufficient off-street facilities before enforcing these bans. Many cities around the world have a system of short-term parking. This allows citizens to pull over, run into a store for a quick purchase, and leave without wasting time.

    In Kathmandu, roadside parking is strictly banned, and yet there are no quick-stop alternatives. If you need to pick up a fast-food order or buy a single item, you cannot just stop near the shop. You are forced to drive around searching for a private parking space, which is far from the shop, pay a full, unreasonably expensive fee, and walk back to the store. A task that should take 5 minutes will eventually cost you nearly an hour of lost time and unnecessary stress.

    Also, the current parking charge places a heavy financial burden on drivers with cars and larger vehicles who are hit up with charges like Rs 80 to Rs 100 per hour. The issue is made worse by this: even if someone stops for 5 to 10 minutes, parking operators force them to pay the full 30-minute or 1-hour rate, making a simple stop unnecessarily expensive.

    For drivers who must stay parked for 4 to 5 hours for work or personal matters, parking costs rapidly convert into a huge daily expense. This fee structure highlights an urgent need for municipalities to move towards a more reasonable and fair fee. The government must step in to mandate fair, minute-based pricing and introduce affordable prices so that vehicle owners are not penalised unnecessarily.

    Another problem is that during peak weekend shopping hours and major festival seasons, the designated parking zones overflow almost instantly, leaving commuters subject to heavy municipal fines. It is very evident that Kathmandu’s population and vehicle density are growing, but when compared to major international metropolises handling far higher traffic volumes, the Valley’s traffic problem is entirely manageable with competent infrastructure planning.

    Undue burden on taxpayers and solution

      It is unfair to the citizens if the government imposes a ban on parking on public roads without providing adequate alternatives at a fair price. By just focusing heavily on enforcement, wheel-locking, and fines while lagging on infrastructure development, local authorities are placing an undue burden on taxpayers. The government cannot criminalise everyday commuting without offering a solution. The government should be answerable to the following questions:

      • Why isn’t the public infrastructure budget being utilised to construct public, high-capacity, multi-story parking garages in major commercial centres? Private operators can be fully replaced by the metropolis.
      • Why is short-term and regulated street parking not an option, or is it absent?
      • Who is regulating parking operators, and how are they being regulated?

      Moreover, to move from a broken system to a functional and modern parking system, the government and the urban engineers should go hand in hand. Here are some modern solutions that the government could easily adopt:

      • Mandate a minute-based and digital parking system: A strict municipal rule for minute-based parking and a free grace period of about 15-20 minutes for quick pick-ups and drop-offs. Engineers should focus on developing an automated ticketing system. We can build a system similar to this: when a car enters, its plate is scanned; when it exits, the system calculates the exact minutes elapsed and automatically deducts the fee via digital wallets (e.g., eSewa, Khalti, or mobile banking), completely removing human attendants from charging higher, unfair and unregulated rates.
      • Design quick stop zones: Allowing short-term parking facilities right outside commercial shops in the public streets works. But to encourage a fast turnover, charge a higher per-minute rate after 15 minutes. This can be helpful where drivers need to run quick 5-minute errands. Engineers can also contribute to integrating overhead AI cameras into road spaces and outside lanes that detect when a car parks and alert city police automatically if a vehicle exceeds its 15-minute limit.
      • Smart parking navigation App: The major problem is that drivers endlessly circle busy areas like New Road, Thamel, or Baneshwor searching for parking spots, creating too much frustration. We can build a single app where drivers can view live available spots in nearby lots before arriving 15 mins in advance and navigate straight to the lot. The government can mandate open parking data, urging all commercial buildings and private parking lots to inform about their live parking availability in a single public database. 

      We are not asking for free parking everywhere; all we are asking is for predictable, affordable and accessible urban management.

title.rendered: Nepal’s football academies struggle to feed young players amid FIFA suspension

content.rendered:
Nepali football is at a standstill after the country was suspended by the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA). Not only have football activities come to a halt, but people dependent on the sport have also been affected.

Four football academies in Nepal are being operated under FIFA’s Goal Project. With the All Nepal Football Association (ANFA) suspended, more than 100 children at these academies are facing uncertainty. “Students who used to eat chickpeas and eggs before going to training now have to make do with tea and biscuits. We are running everything on credit, from school fees to groceries,” an academy employee said.

There are 21 students at the academy located at ANFA headquarters in Satdobato, Lalitpur. The children had previously been based in Sisneri, Makwanpur. However, after six players died in a flood and landslide two years ago, they were moved to Hetauda and later relocated to Satdobato.

With funds no longer being received from ANFA, the academy is now struggling to provide food and education for the children. ANFA spokesperson Suresh Shah acknowledged that the association has been unable to provide players with the supplies they require.

“The players have a routine, including their diet and meals, but things are not the same as before. There are some problems. Nevertheless, we are still running the academies,” he said. Shah said it costs around Rs 200,000 a week to operate the Lalitpur academy alone, but funds cannot currently be transferred due to the suspension. The situation is similar at other academies. The Butwal academy has 30 students, two coaches and four to five staff members. Acting director Shankar Malla said he has been running the academy by taking loans.

“Schools are now saying they need the fees before Dashain. It has also been more than three months since we paid the grocery store. They will no longer extend credit. The problem is serious. The children are constantly falling ill,” he said. “The staff are also complaining because they have not received their salaries.”

Despite the shortage of funds, Malla said the academy was still meeting the students’ basic needs. “Training is continuing. They are also attending school. We have not cut back on anything. We are trying to manage things as best we can. We have not allowed the children to see the problems we are facing. Since we are responsible for the academy, we are finding ways to manage,” he said.

Malla fears the situation could become more serious if the problems are not resolved by September. “When we call ANFA, they tell us there is nothing for now and ask us to keep things running. They say we will receive our pending bills once the suspension is lifted,” he said. The academy in Rautahat, which has 29 children, is facing a similar situation. With no funds coming from ANFA, its operators have been forced to take loans in their own names to keep the academy running. Bhagwan Darlami, coordinator of the academy, said it is also operating entirely on credit.

“Everything is on credit. We are running it by assuring people in the market that we will pay them,” he said. “We hope the government can resolve the situation as soon as possible so that the children can quickly receive the services and facilities they are entitled to. It would also help Nepali football regain momentum.”

According to Kishor Rai, president of the Dharan academy, the academy there has not faced the same difficulties as the other three. Local partnerships have helped the academy, which has 30 players, continue operating without major problems.

“Our municipality allocates a regular budget. The provincial government also provides some funding, and we have supporting donors. We are managing by getting a little from everyone,” Rai said. “ANFA also provides us with a small amount of money through a partnership.”

‘The government has asked us not to conduct any activities’

ANFA, which has been responsible for providing resources to the academies, says it has been unable to support them because the government has instructed it to halt its activities. ANFA spokesperson Shah said the suspension has prevented the association from providing financial support to the academies. He said the academies have not received funds for the past two to three months.

“Since everything ANFA was supposed to send, including funds, has been stopped, there has been no question of sending money. The government has also told us not to carry out any activities,” he said. Tika Lama, an ANFA central member and president of the Makwanpur District Football Association, said the government needs to take the operation of the academies seriously.

“The government needs to think seriously about this. Players should not go hungry. Once you take responsibility, you have to fulfil your obligations. This is my question to the prime minister and the sports minister,” he said.

title.rendered: Teaser of the documentary Road to Everest released

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 10

The first glimpse of “Road to Everest,” a documentary about the world’s highest peak involving a Nepali technical crew, has been released.

The documentary is based on the story of a journey from sea level to the summit of Everest. In a press release, the producers said the story explores the courage, mystery, and curiosity of climbing Everest, along with the impact of climate change there.

The documentary follows the inspiring journey of a person over 50 who chases the dream of climbing Everest while challenging age, time, and their own limits.

The release states that the film presents not just the grandeur of Everest but also, in depth, the risks of climbing, the tireless contribution of the Sherpa community, human courage, and the changing mountain environment due to climate change.

Directed by Nirmal Shrestha, the documentary features record-holding climbers Phurba Tenjing Sherpa and Nima Gyalzen Sherpa. Phurba has successfully summited Everest 18 times, while Nima has done so 10 times, including all 14 of the world’s highest peaks.

The documentary’s Nepal premiere will be held in Kathmandu on August 22, with the international premiere in Hong Kong on September 13. Following that, screenings are planned across various international platforms and theatres alongside Nepal.

Written by journalist Santosh Acharya and director Shrestha, who is also a journalist, the film comes after two years of research, filming and production. The documentary, narrated by Bhushan Dahal, has been made in both Nepali and English.

Produced by the social organisation Be Will Rise Foundation, the documentary is expected to help promote Nepal’s tourism worldwide. Its runtime is over 50 minutes.

title.rendered: Charting the history and growth of actuarial science in Nepal

content.rendered:
While watching Gilmore Girls, I came across an interesting scene where Lorelai is introduced to an actuary by her mother. During the episode, the actuary discusses how he can predict the probability of death with great accuracy and mentions the use of actuarial models to do so. As a student of actuarial science, this scene really caught my attention. I was excited to see a television series from the 2000s that discussed actuaries, life tables, and their importance in insurance.

The history of actuarial science dates back to more than three centuries. Its origins lie in the growing interest in statistics and probability theory in the 17th century. At that time, governments and business people were interested in understanding population trends, mortality rates, and economic risk. But there existed no systematic way to measure how long people would live or how likely they were to die at a given age.

One of the earliest figures to address this problem was the English statistician John Graunt. In 1662, he studied the London “Bills of Mortality,” or records of births and deaths. Although his work may seem simple by modern standards, it was revolutionary for its time. For the first time, scholars attempted to quantitatively analyse patterns of human life and mortality using real data. Graunt’s research laid the foundation for demography, epidemiology, and ultimately actuarial science. A few decades later, the famous astronomer Edmond Halley (whom we know today best for Halley’s Comet) developed Graunt’s ideas further. In 1693, he studied the birth and death records of the city of Breslau (now Wrocław, Poland) and produced the first mortality table suitable for pricing life annuities

Halley’s contributions were not limited to collecting mortality data. He showed how to use mortality data to calculate the fair value of a life annuity. For the first time, insurance companies and financial institutions could mathematically determine how much money a person would have to pay based on their age and life expectancy. This is widely regarded as the birth of modern actuarial science. Mathematicians such as Blaise Pascal, Pierre de Fermat, and Jacob Bernoulli developed probability theory rapidly. Their work provided a mathematical basis for analysing uncertainty and transformed actuarial calculations from estimates to scientific and quantitative models.

By the 19th century, the actuarial profession had matured significantly for specialised professional bodies to emerge. The Institute of Actuaries was founded in London in 1848, and thereafter the Faculty of Actuaries was established in Scotland in 1856. These bodies formalised actuarial education, examination systems, and professional standards, and played a significant role in the development of the modern profession.

During the Industrial Revolution, the need for actuaries grew exponentially as life insurance expanded throughout Europe and North America. Actuaries became responsible for setting premiums, valuing reserves, analysing pension plans, and ensuring the financial stability of insurance companies. Their role thus expanded beyond calculating life expectancy.

Actuarial science experienced another major transformation in the 20th century. The field expanded from life insurance to health insurance, pensions, investments, banking, social security systems, and enterprise risk management. The development of computing technology made it possible to build advanced models for analysing big data and complex financial systems. In India, L. S. Vaidyanathan became the first Indian Fellow Actuary in 1926, a significant achievement for South Asia. In the following decades, actuarial education and professional institutions began to be established throughout Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

Today, actuaries work not only in insurance, but also in climate risk, healthcare financing, disaster modelling, investment management, artificial intelligence (AI), and public policy. Despite the great advances in technology, the core purpose of the profession remains the same as that envisioned by Halley in 1693: to use mathematics and statistics to understand uncertainty and help make informed decisions about the future.

Despite its long global history, actuarial science is a relatively new discipline in Nepal. Until the 2010s, Nepal had neither a formal actuarial education program nor a qualified actuary resident. In fact, formal actuarial education in Nepal only began in 2016 when the School of Mathematical Sciences of Tribhuvan University (SMSTU) launched the country’s first B.Math.Sc. (Actuarial Science) program.

Before that, Nepali insurance companies used to outsource all actuarial work to foreign consultants, and most students had never even heard of the actuarial profession. The SMSTU itself has noted that “there is a serious shortage of actuaries in the country due to a lack of actuarial education.”

A 2018 report found that there were no qualified actuaries living in Nepal and that the number of Nepali students studying in the field was very low.

A student entering SMSTU in 2016 was joining a profession that virtually did not exist in Nepal. After 2016, the situation gradually changed. The Actuarial Society of Nepal (ASN) was established in 2019 and the first actuarial graduates were produced from SMSTU in 2020. During this period, most actuarial work was being done by experts from other countries, including India. Fellow Actuary Prechhya Mathema, who trained in the UK, returned to Nepal in 2018 and became the founding president of ASN. She is widely regarded as the first fully qualified actuary to reside in Nepal.

The regulatory framework also gained momentum with the development of education and the professional community. In May 2024, the Nepal Insurance Authority (NIA) issued a landmark directive mandating the appointment of at least one actuarial analyst in every insurance company. Life insurance companies and reinsurance companies were asked to implement it immediately, while non-life and micro insurance companies were given a specific deadline. This decision is considered a significant achievement for the insurance sector in Nepal.

As of 2026, actuarial science in Nepal is still in its infancy, but it is no longer an unknown subject. SMSTU continues to produce graduates and ASN is now an Associate Member of the International Actuarial Association (IAA). Nepal currently has 37 insurance companies (14 life, 14 non-life, 2 reinsurance and 7 microinsurance), but insurance penetration remains low, with roughly 90 percent of the population lacking insurance coverage. This suggests that demand for actuaries will continue to grow as insurers develop new products, refine premium pricing, and strengthen risk management.

When Edmond Halley published his mortality tables in 1693, he probably never imagined that more than three centuries later, students in Nepal would be using the same concepts to price insurance products and assess financial risk. Actuarial science, which has a history of over 330 years worldwide, has only been in Nepal for a decade. In this short period of time, the profession has evolved from an unknown field of study to become a key pillar of regulatory requirements and the insurance industry. If current trends continue, the next decade may no longer be about introducing actuarial science to Nepal. Rather, it may be the time for Nepal to shape the future of the profession by producing world-class actuaries.

title.rendered: Ward offices at risk due to landslides in Solukhumbu, 11 families displaced

content.rendered:
Solukhumbu, August 10

Ward offices in Solukhumbu are facing a serious threat from landslides, resulting in the displacement of 11 families due to the relentless heavy rainfall. The affected ward offices are located in Tamakhani and Sotang Rural Municipalities in the district. Chief District Officer Kamansing Thapa Margar shared that a landslide struck last Saturday night, jeopardising the Solududhakunda Municipality-3 office, while another landslide hit the Sotang Rural Municipality-4 office just days earlier.

The ongoing rains have also caused minor damage to other government buildings in the area. Notably, a landslide has taken out the toilet facility at the Tamakhani ward office, putting the nearby administration building in jeopardy as well. Ward chair Lhakpagelu Sherpa emphasised the gravity of the situation, noting that a large landslide from the upper hill has already compromised surrounding infrastructure, including roads, and poses a risk of further damage.

He voiced concerns that if the landslide continues to worsen, it could threaten both the ward office and the local health post, making the area increasingly perilous. In Rural Municipality-9, five households have been forced to evacuate and are now staying in a nearby school due to the landslide threat. Additionally, in Likhupike Rural Municipality-3, another family has been relocated for their safety after their home was put at risk. In total, 11 families have been affected by these dangerous conditions.

title.rendered: Nepal’s first tied-arch bridge completed in Ramdi

content.rendered:
Syangja, August 10

Nepal’s first tied-arch motorable bridge has been completed over the Kali Gandaki River at Ramdi, on the border of Syangja and Palpa districts, connecting Gandaki and Lumbini provinces.

With the main construction work completed, the bridge is expected to be opened to traffic after some minor finishing works are completed and obstructions at both ends of the bridge are removed.

According to the Pokhara Bridge Sector, the bridge constructed at Ramnadi (Ramdi) is based on the concrete-filled steel tube arch bridge, or tied-arch, technology. The bridge was designed by Thai designers. Although bridges using similar technology have been constructed in Bhutan, China and Dubai, this is the first of its kind in Nepal.

The single-span bridge is 120 metres long and 11 metres wide. According to Krishna Prasad Adhikari, chief of the Pokhara Bridge Sector, the new bridge is 27 metres longer than the old truss bridge, which was constructed in 2028 BS.

A contract was signed with Him Sagarmatha Pvt. Ltd., Chitwan, on Asar 30, 2079 BS, with a three-year completion deadline. However, construction could not be completed within the stipulated period due to delays in preparing the design and the failure to receive construction materials from India and the required technical experts from China on time.

The contract was signed for Rs 277.109 million. Adhikari said only some minor construction work on both sides of the bridge and painting remain to be completed.

According to him, the old truss bridge had been deteriorating, creating difficulties, particularly for the operation of heavy vehicles. The new bridge has a load-bearing capacity of 70 metric tonnes, allowing even large cargo vehicles to cross it with ease.

Although the initial construction period was set at three years, the deadline was extended by one year until Asar 27 to complete the work.

However, some houses at both ends of the bridge still need to be removed before it can be brought into operation. Adhikari said preparations are underway to begin regular vehicular movement on the new bridge within about a month after the structures are cleared.

The old truss bridge at Ramdi was started in 2022 BS with the construction of the Siddhartha Highway. It was completed about six years later in 2028 BS and inaugurated by then-Prime Minister Kirti Nidhi Bista.

For more than five decades, the bridge served as a major transportation link between Gandaki and Lumbini provinces. However, as it gradually deteriorated, the need for a new bridge became increasingly apparent.

Authorities expect the new bridge to make transportation between Gandaki and Lumbini provinces safer, easier and more efficient. It is also expected to end the long-standing dependence on the deteriorating truss bridge.

title.rendered: US Embassy selects 55 youth for USYC 2026

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 9

The US Embassy in Nepal has selected 55 youth from across the country for the US Embassy Youth Council Nepal (USYC Nepal) 2026 cohort.

The embassy held the new group’s inaugural session with participants chosen from more than 1,600 applicants.

Chargé d’Affaires Scott Urbom congratulated the selected participants, expressing confidence that they would play an important role in driving innovation, economic growth and positive change in their communities.

According to the embassy, over the course of the one-year term, members of the group will develop leadership skills while expanding their network of contacts with peers and experts across various sectors. The program also aims to prepare them for future opportunities that benefit Nepal, the embassy said.

Noting that the United States is marking 250 years of independence, the embassy said programs like USYC Nepal demonstrate America’s commitment to working with Nepal’s next generation of leaders across various professional fields.

The embassy said a prosperous Nepal would create new opportunities for trade, innovation and long-term cooperation, benefiting both Nepal and the United States.

title.rendered: Sat-Chit-Ananda gathering to promote mental wellbeing in Sydney

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 9

Project Beyond, in collaboration with NRNA NSW, will organise Sat-Chit-Ananda – An Intimate Kirtan Gathering on August 14 at The Granville Centre, 2A Memorial Drive, Granville, NSW 2142.

According to the organiser, it is a community wellbeing event featuring music, meditation and spiritual connection. The event will offer participants an opportunity to relax, reflect and connect with others in a peaceful environment.

The programme will feature Vedic chanting, guided meditation, live devotional music and collective singing.

“The gathering is open to people of all cultures, beliefs and backgrounds. This initiative aims to support mental wellbeing, encourage personal growth and strengthen community connections,” said Bharat Poudel, event lead of Sat-Chit-Ananda.

The event will feature various artists, including Aadesh and Anjuli Hamal on vocals, Sabin Ghising on flute, Rozan Subedi on keyboard, Om B. Shrestha on drums, Nischal Bista on bass guitar, Aantariksha Dahal on guitar, and Avi on tabla.

Admission is free, but registration is required.

Project Beyond also plans to support talented but underprivileged classical music students in Nepal through future proceeds from the initiative.

title.rendered: Ovarian cysts: Key facts, symptoms, and treatment options

content.rendered:
An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled sac that forms on or within an ovary. These cysts come in different sizes and can arise from various causes. Although numerous ovarian cysts are benign and might remain asymptomatic, certain cysts can produce symptoms or lead to complications, necessitating medical assessment and intervention.

While most ovarian cysts are benign and pose no threat, their size and origin can vary. While some ovarian cysts remain asymptomatic, they can become problematic if they enlarge, rupture, or cause discomfort.

These cysts are frequently observed in women of childbearing age, often forming during the ovulation process. Their incidence tends to decline post-menopause. Many times, they dissipate on their own without evident symptoms or necessitating intervention. Yet, in certain situations, they might signal an underlying medical issue and could require surgical removal.

Although it’s challenging to entirely prevent ovarian cysts, certain precautions can mitigate the risk. These include maintaining a healthy weight, opting for contraception, and undergoing routine pelvic exams.

Incidence of ovarian cysts in Nepal

The exact prevalence of ovarian cysts in women remains uncertain, largely because many cases are asymptomatic and go undiagnosed.

By the age of 65, about 4 out of every 100 women will have been hospitalised due to ovarian cysts. In a study involving 335 asymptomatic women aged 24 to 40, 8% were found to have an adnexal lesion. An adnexal lesion refers to a growth, either fluid-filled or solid, located around the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or adjacent connective tissue.

Among postmenopausal women, 2.5 out of every 100 have a simple unilocular adnexal cyst, typically benign and often resolving on its own.

In a comprehensive survey of 33,739 women spanning both premenopausal and postmenopausal stages, nearly half displayed an adnexal cyst on transvaginal ultrasound. Of these, approximately 63.2% (or 9,958 women) showed cyst resolution upon subsequent ultrasounds.

Types of ovarian cyst

Women possess two ovaries situated on either side of the uterus in the pelvic region, integral to the reproductive system. If a cyst emerges on the left ovary, it’s termed a left ovarian cyst; conversely, if it arises on the right ovary, it’s called a right ovarian cyst. Occasionally, cysts, known as bilateral ovarian cysts, can manifest on both ovaries simultaneously.

Ovarian cysts can be broadly classified into two categories:

1. Functional ovarian cysts

These are the most prevalent benign ovarian cysts, typically transient and indicative of a healthy ovulatory cycle. Typically, they diminish within approximately two months without intervention.

– Follicular Cysts: These arise when a follicle, intended to release an egg during ovulation, doesn’t do so and instead accumulates fluid, enlarging in the process.

– Corpus Luteum Cysts: Post-ovulation, the follicle becomes the corpus luteum. On occasion, fluid accumulation within the corpus luteum can give rise to cysts.

Both follicular and corpus luteum cysts can occasionally transform into hemorrhagic cysts due to ruptures, injuries, certain medications, or ovulation-related factors. Treatment options encompass rest, pain relief, and surgical intervention if the cyst is substantial and symptomatic.

2. Pathological Cysts:

These are less common and stem from various medical anomalies.

– Dermoid Cysts: These are unique growths containing diverse bodily tissues like skin, teeth, hair, and occasionally, brain matter. Symptoms may be absent until the cyst reaches a considerable size. Their origins can be attributed to infections, genetic anomalies, or developmental irregularities.

– Endometriomas (Chocolate Cysts): These cysts are replete with endometrial tissue, mirroring the tissue shed during menstruation. Manifestations include intense menstrual cramps, non-menstrual pelvic discomfort, and potential infertility.

– Cystadenomas: These growths surface on the ovary and can contain either a watery or a thicker, mucoid fluid.

– Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): This hormonal imbalance prompts the formation of numerous small cysts on the ovaries, leading to their enlargement.

– Ovarian Cancer Cysts: Distinct from the aforementioned conditions, these are solid formations comprising malignant cells, not fluid-filled sacs.

Symptoms of ovarian cysts

Many women may harbour ovarian cysts without evident symptoms. Typically, symptoms manifest when a cyst ruptures, enlarges significantly, becomes twisted, or impedes ovarian blood flow. When symptomatic, manifestations can range in intensity and might comprise:

  • Pelvic Discomfort: Ovarian cysts often induce sensations of pressure or pain in the lower abdominal region. This can vary from a mild, persistent ache to intense, intermittent sharp pains. A ruptured cyst may result in pronounced, acute pain, while a hemorrhagic cyst can present with sudden, intense pelvic discomfort on its affected side.
  • Abdominal Distention: Certain women might feel a consistent or sporadic sensation of abdominal fullness, swelling, or bloating due to ovarian cysts.
  • Menstrual Irregularities: Cysts that secrete hormones can disrupt the menstrual cycle. Notably, endometriomas or “chocolate cysts” associated with endometriosis can exacerbate menstrual pain.
  • Unexplained Weight Fluctuations: Ovarian cysts, notably in conditions like PCOS, can be correlated with weight changes and challenges in weight management.
  • Fertility Challenges: While the presence of a singular cyst typically doesn’t impact fertility, conditions like PCOS, characterised by multiple cysts, can potentially diminish fertility prospects.
  • Organ Displacement: Enlarged cysts can exert pressure on neighbouring organs like the bladder or rectum, leading to heightened urinary urgency, dysuria, constipation, or altered bowel patterns.
  • Painful Intercourse: Particularly sizable cysts, when ruptured, can cause acute pain during sexual activity, often due to penile pressure.
  • Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A cyst’s torsion or rupture might induce nausea, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort.
  • Concerning Signs: Symptoms suggestive of a malignant cyst include persistent bloating, pelvic discomfort, altered bowel movements, early satiety, and irregular menstrual bleeding.

Causes of ovarian cysts

The precise origin of many ovarian cysts remains elusive. However, several factors, including menstrual cycle regularity, may influence their formation.

  • In premenopausal women, the predominant causes of ovarian cysts encompass:
  • Hormonal Imbalances: Disturbances in hormones governing the menstrual cycle can pave the way for cyst development.
  • Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): This condition is marked by excessive production of hormones like testosterone, fostering the emergence of multiple ovarian cysts.
  • Thyroid Disorders: Both hyperactive and underactive thyroid conditions can disrupt ovulation. The resemblance between the alpha subunit of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and hCG might promote ovarian cyst growth in hypothyroidism.
  • Endometriosis: Advanced stages of endometriosis can lead to the formation of endometrioma cysts, colloquially termed “chocolate cysts.”
  • Pregnancy: In early gestation, ovarian cysts may develop to sustain the ovary until placental formation, occasionally persisting into later pregnancy stages.
  • Pelvic Infections: Severe infections can extend to the ovaries and fallopian tubes, resulting in cysts filled with pus in proximity to these structures.
  • Medications: Certain fertility treatments and hormone replacement therapies can elevate the propensity for ovarian cyst development.
  • Genetic Factors: Some ovarian cysts may have genetic underpinnings, with individuals having a familial predisposition to ovarian cancer being at an augmented risk.
  • Ovarian Cancer: While rare, some ovarian cysts in premenopausal women may be indicative of ovarian cancer, albeit accounting for less than 1% of ovarian growths.
  • For postmenopausal women, the leading causes of ovarian cysts include:
  • Non-Malignant Growths
  • Accumulation of Fluid within the Ovary
  • Ovarian Cancer: New growths in or around the ovaries are more likely to be malignant compared to menstruating counterparts.

Diagnosis of ovarian cyst

The assessment of an ovarian cyst typically encompasses a thorough review of the patient’s medical history, a physical examination, and specialised diagnostic procedures by an experienced Gynaecologist. Here’s a breakdown of the diagnostic steps for ovarian cysts:

1. Medical History: Gathering detailed information about the patient’s symptoms, menstrual cycle, previous medical conditions, and family history.

2. Imaging Studies: Ultrasound – Abdomen & Pelvis, Transvaginal Ultrasound (probe is inserted into the vagina for closer examination). Pelvic MRI also provides a comprehensive view of the pelvic region, aiding in the identification and characterisation of ovarian cysts.

3. Pathological Tests: Complete Blood Count (CBC), Pregnancy Testing beta HCG, Urinalysis, Swab Test, Cancer Antigen 125 (protein often elevated in ovarian cancer, cysts, or in other related conditions).

Treatment of ovarian cyst

Non-surgical Treatment Options for Ovarian Cysts: Treatment approaches for ovarian cysts are tailored based on factors such as the patient’s age, menopausal phase, cyst size, and any suspicious characteristics indicating possible malignancy.

Here are some common strategies for managing ovarian cysts:

  1. Watchful waiting (Observation): Many cysts in reproductive-age women, such as follicular or corpus luteum cysts, are benign and often disappear within a couple of months. While they might rupture and cause discomfort, they usually resolve spontaneously. A gynaecologist might advise regular monitoring without immediate intervention.
  2. Pain management: For cyst-related discomfort, medications like Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or stronger pain relievers may be prescribed to alleviate symptoms. Make sure medicine is taken under the gynaecologist’s guidance.
  3. Oral contraceptives (Birth Control Pills): To minimise the risk of functional ovarian cysts, contraceptive pills can be recommended. By regulating hormone levels and preventing ovulation, they can deter the formation of such cysts. For those experiencing recurrent cysts or seeking preventive measures, oral contraceptives might be a suitable option.
  4. Cyst drainage/surgical intervention: In cases where a cyst is particularly large or painful, it can be drained using a needle or a minor surgical procedure. However, it’s important to note that this method may not offer a permanent solution, as the cyst could reform over time.

For patients with simple ovarian cysts, aggressive treatment isn’t always necessary since these cysts often resolve independently.

Ovarian cyst prevention:

While it’s challenging to completely prevent ovarian cysts, adopting certain practices can potentially lower the risk of their development:

  1. Regular Health Checkups: Periodic visits to a gynaecologist can aid in overseeing reproductive health and facilitating early detection and management of any cysts.
  2. Maintaining a Healthy Weight: Obesity is linked to an increased risk of ovarian cysts. Thus, embracing a balanced diet and engaging in regular physical activity can mitigate this risk.
  3. Balanced Diet: Consuming a nutritious diet not only supports weight management but also guards against other chronic ailments like cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and type 2 diabetes.
  4. Regular Exercise: Engaging in consistent physical activity can bolster both physical and hormonal health.
  5. Avoiding Harmful Habits: Steering clear of smoking and limiting alcohol intake is pivotal, as these habits can compromise ovarian health and elevate cyst risk.
  6. Cautious Hormone Use: Be careful with hormone therapies, as their excessive use can influence the onset of ovarian cysts.

Additional Recommendations:

  • Incorporate Fruits and Veggies: These foods are teeming with antioxidants and essential nutrients that shield cells from harm.
  • Moderate Processed Foods and Sugary Beverages: These items, rich in calories, unhealthy fats, and sugars, can contribute to obesity and other health issues, including ovarian cysts.
  • Prioritise Sleep: Adequate sleep is vital for overall well-being. Inadequate sleep can escalate cortisol (stress hormone) levels, potentially heightening health risks.
  • Stress Management: Chronic stress can disrupt hormonal balance, increasing susceptibility to ovarian cysts. Implementing stress management techniques is pivotal for holistic health and cyst prevention.

Ovarian cysts and pregnancy

Ovarian cysts can manifest during early pregnancy, even in the absence of menstrual cycles. Typically, these cysts pose no significant threat, mirroring the benign nature of most ovarian cysts.

Nevertheless, if these cysts persist and enlarge during pregnancy, potential complications such as rupture, torsion, or childbirth challenges could arise. Hence, maintaining regular consultations with a gynaecologist throughout your pregnancy and beyond is crucial.

For those with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), there’s an elevated likelihood of encountering complications like gestational diabetes, hypertension during pregnancy, miscarriage, or preterm birth.

Engage in a discussion with your gynaecologist regarding your specific risks and available treatment avenues. They will offer comprehensive guidance and tailor recommendations to ensure the most optimal and healthy pregnancy outcome for you.

title.rendered: What the 72-hour emergency contraceptive pill does to a woman’s body

content.rendered:
“I took the 72-hour emergency contraceptive pill. Can it harm my body?”

This was a question a friend sent to obstetrician and gynaecologist Dr Dija Khanal through a message. The woman admitted that she had taken the pill on several previous occasions as well and had been experiencing irregular menstrual cycles over the past year.

Similarly, another 32-year-old woman told Dr Khanal that she developed health problems after taking the emergency contraceptive pill. “I noticed four or five drops of chocolate-colored blood five days after taking the 72-hour pill,” she said. “It’s been 10 days since the spotting started.”

She also reported feeling physically weak. “I even bought a pregnancy test kit,” she said. “It came back negative. Why is that?” An ultrasound examination revealed several small ovarian cysts, a thin endometrium (the lining of the uterus), and clear signs of hormonal imbalance. According to Dr Khanal, this is a common issue among many married women and one she encounters almost every day.

“Many women tell me they had to take the pill due to unavoidable circumstances,” she said. “However, they often don’t realise that repeated use can lead to significant complications.”

What is the 72-hour pill?

The 72-hour pill is an emergency contraceptive, commonly known as the “I-Pill.” Even when pregnancy is not desired, unprotected sexual intercourse can sometimes result in conception, especially when no contraceptive method has been used. Pregnancy may also occur if a woman forgets to take her regular birth control pill or if a condom breaks during intercourse.

In such situations, emergency contraceptive pills are available to reduce the risk of pregnancy. These pills should be taken within 72 hours of unprotected sex. “The sooner the pill is taken, the more effective it is,” Dr Khanal says.

Why is it called an emergency contraceptive?

Dr Khanal explains that emergency contraceptive pills contain a high dose of the synthetic hormone levonorgestrel, a form of progestin. “The dose is much higher than that found in regular birth control pills,” she says. “Because it acts quickly, it is recommended only for emergencies.”

Obstetrician and gynaecologist Dr Upama Basnet compares it to a fire extinguisher. “Many women see the 72-hour pill as an easy solution,” she says. “But it is not meant to provide regular contraception. It’s like a fire extinguisher—you use it to put out a fire, not to start one. Likewise, it should not be used repeatedly.”

She emphasises that it is an emergency safety measure, not a long-term family planning method.

How does it prevent pregnancy?

Pregnancy depends on three biological processes: ovulation, fertilisation, and implantation. The emergency contraceptive pill interferes with these stages in different ways.

What happens if the pill is taken repeatedly?

1. Delays or Prevents Ovulation

Around the middle of the menstrual cycle, the pituitary gland releases a surge of luteinizing hormone (LH), which triggers ovulation—the release of an egg from the ovary. According to Dr Khanal, the high dose of progestin in the emergency pill signals the brain that the body already has sufficient progesterone. As a result, the LH surge is delayed or prevented. “If there is no LH surge, the egg is not released,” she explains. “Without an egg, fertilisation cannot occur.” The pill is most effective if taken before ovulation.

2. Makes Fertilisation More Difficult

If ovulation has already occurred, the pill can still reduce the chances of pregnancy. Dr Khanal says the high-dose progestin thickens the cervical mucus. Normally, when estrogen levels are high, cervical mucus becomes thin and slippery, allowing sperm to travel easily to the egg. “Thicker mucus slows the movement of sperm, making it more difficult for them to reach the egg,” she explains. The hormone may also reduce sperm mobility and lifespan, further lowering the likelihood of fertilisation.

3. Changes the Uterine Environment

In rare cases where fertilisation has already occurred, the pill may affect the endometrium, or uterine lining. Normally, balanced estrogen and progesterone make the endometrium thick and receptive to embryo implantation. However, the high dose of progestin may thin the lining. “When the endometrium becomes thinner, it is less suitable for implantation,” says Dr Khanal. “However, if an embryo has already implanted, the pill cannot remove it.”

Possible side effects

Most side effects after taking the emergency contraceptive pill are mild and temporary. Dr Khanal says the high hormone dose temporarily disrupts the body’s natural hormonal cycle, which can cause symptoms that differ from normal. Common side effects include:

  • Irregular menstrual periods
  • Nausea
  • Mild vomiting
  • Headaches
  • Breast tenderness or heaviness
  • Lower abdominal pain or bloating

“Some women may get their period within ten days, others may experience delays, and some may notice prolonged chocolate-colored spotting,” she says. She explains that this brown spotting is usually a hormonal response to the medication rather than a menstrual period. “These symptoms usually resolve on their own within a few days. However, women should seek medical attention if they experience heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or if menstruation does not return for two to three months.”

Repeated use can increase the risk of hormonal imbalance. According to Dr Khanal, the high dose of progestin can repeatedly disrupt the body’s natural estrogen-progesterone balance, resulting in irregular menstrual cycles. Possible effects include:

  • Irregular periods
  • Prolonged spotting
  • Missed periods for two to three months
  • Lower abdominal pain or a feeling of heaviness
  • Mood swings
  • Fatigue

She says ultrasound scans may also reveal small ovarian cysts. These are usually temporary but may indicate that the body has experienced repeated hormonal disruption. Another concern is that if the pill is taken more than 72 hours after unprotected intercourse and pregnancy has already occurred, there is a higher risk of an ectopic pregnancy, in which the embryo implants in the fallopian tube. “If the embryo grows inside the fallopian tube, the tube may rupture, creating a life-threatening emergency,” Dr. Khanal warns.

Can it cause permanent infertility?

Dr Upama Basnet says many women ask whether repeated use of the emergency contraceptive pill can permanently affect fertility. According to current scientific evidence, it does not cause permanent infertility. Using the pill once or twice in genuine emergencies is very unlikely to have a lasting impact on a woman’s ability to conceive.

“The problem arises when women use it repeatedly instead of regular contraceptive methods,” Dr Basnet says. “The repeated high doses of progesterone can temporarily suppress ovulation, disrupt menstrual cycles, or even stop periods for several months.”

She adds that if menstrual periods remain absent for a long time or hormonal problems persist, women should undergo medical evaluation, as underlying conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), thyroid disorders, or other health issues may be responsible. Dr Khanal agrees. “There is no evidence that the emergency pill causes permanent infertility, but repeatedly exposing the body to high doses of synthetic hormones is not considered good practice.”

What are safer alternatives?

There is no single contraceptive method that is best for everyone. The ideal choice depends on a woman’s age, health, future pregnancy plans, breastfeeding status, and lifestyle. According to Dr Khanal, women who want reliable ongoing contraception and can remember to take a daily pill may choose oral contraceptive pills. When used correctly every day, they are up to 99 per cent effective and can also help regulate menstrual cycles and reduce menstrual pain. For women seeking longer intervals between pregnancies, Dr Basnet recommends long-acting reversible contraceptives such as:

  • Copper IUD: A small device inserted into the uterus that can protect for 5 to 10 years.
  • Contraceptive implant (Norplant/Implant): A small rod inserted under the skin of the arm that protects for 3 to 5 years and can be removed whenever pregnancy is desired.
  • Depo-Provera injection: A hormonal injection given once every three months.

“These methods eliminate the need for daily worry and do not expose the body to repeated hormonal shocks like emergency contraceptive pills,” Dr Basnet says. Experts therefore recommend using the 72-hour pill only in genuine emergencies and choosing a regular contraceptive method after consulting a healthcare provider.

Can the 72-hour pill cause ovarian cysts?

According to Dr Basnet, the high dose of levonorgestrel suppresses the release of luteinizing hormone (LH), preventing ovulation. Without ovulation, follicles stimulated by follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) may continue to fill with fluid instead of releasing an egg. These enlarged follicles can appear as small ovarian cysts.

Repeated use of emergency contraceptive pills may increase hormonal imbalance and may contribute to the development or worsening of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in susceptible women. Although these cysts are usually temporary, experts warn that frequent misuse of emergency contraceptive pills may increase the risk of longer-term reproductive health problems. For this reason, gynaecologists recommend using the 72-hour emergency contraceptive pill only in genuine emergencies and avoiding repeated or routine use.

The woman admitted that she had taken the pill on several previous occasions as well and had been experiencing irregular menstrual cycles over the past year. […]

title.rendered: Healthcare should no longer be confined to hospitals

content.rendered:
For generations, hospitals have been the centre of healthcare. When people become ill, they travel to a clinic or hospital. A doctor examines them. Medicines are prescribed. Treatment begins. Then patients return home, and healthcare largely waits until they come back again. It is a model that has served medicine well for more than a century. But it is also a model built around a simple assumption: Healthcare happens inside hospitals. The twenty-first century invites us to challenge that assumption.

In my previous article, I argued that healthcare should not stop caring when patients leave the clinic. If that is true, another question naturally follows.

Where should healthcare happen?

The traditional answer is obvious. Hospitals. The future answer may be very different. Healthcare should happen wherever people need it. Sometimes that will be inside a hospital. Often, it will not. Consider a child who develops a fever in Humla. Before a doctor is seen, important decisions have already been made. Should the family wait another day? Should they begin the long journey to the nearest health facility? Can they afford the travel? Is the illness serious enough to justify leaving work and school? By the time the child reaches a hospital, the most important barrier has already been crossed. Not the hospital door. The distance. Distance has always shaped healthcare in Nepal. It determines how quickly people seek care. How much they spend. Whether they complete follow-up visits. Whether they receive specialist advice. Whether they survive emergencies. Geography should never determine the quality of healthcare a person receives. Yet too often, it still does.

Hospitals are indispensable. No digital technology can replace emergency departments, operating theatres, intensive care units or skilled clinicians. Nor should it. The goal is not to replace hospitals. It is to extend their reach. A hospital should no longer be viewed as the place where healthcare begins and ends. It should become the centre of a much larger network of continuous care. Imagine a patient returning home after treatment for pneumonia. Two days later, breathing becomes more difficult. Today, that patient often faces an impossible decision. Should they wait? Should they spend an entire day travelling back to the hospital? Or should they hope the symptoms improve? A patient-centred healthcare system offers another possibility. The patient reports worsening symptoms through a simple digital follow-up. The treating clinician reviews the information. Perhaps reassurance is all that is needed. Perhaps medicines need to be adjusted. Perhaps new investigations should be arranged before the patient begins travelling. Or perhaps immediate referral is essential. Healthcare reaches the patient before the crisis reaches the hospital.

Nepal presents this question more clearly than almost any other country. We are a nation of extraordinary geography. Communities are separated by mountains, hills, remote valleys, rivers, weather and difficult roads. For millions of Nepalis, reaching healthcare is itself a major challenge. Sometimes the first obstacle is not disease. It is distance. Every unnecessary journey carries a cost. Parents miss work. Children miss school. Families borrow money. Elderly patients endure exhausting travel. For many, a routine follow-up appointment becomes an entire day’s journey. Sometimes much longer.

We often measure access to healthcare by counting hospitals. Perhaps we should instead ask a different question. How much travelling should a patient need to do to receive good healthcare? Modern technology allows us to rethink that question. Instead of asking patients to travel whenever expertise is needed, we can increasingly allow expertise to travel instead. That simple shift changes everything.

Imagine a dermatologist in Kathmandu. Today, patients from every corner of Nepal travel long distances for consultations that may last only fifteen minutes. Now imagine that many of those consultations could be performed remotely after appropriate triage. Patients travel only when procedures or direct examination become necessary. The specialist spends more time practising medicine. Patients spend less time travelling. Healthcare becomes more efficient without compromising quality.

The same principle applies across many specialities, including mental health, rehabilitation, nutrition, medication counselling, diabetes education, and post-operative follow-up. Not every medical interaction requires physical presence. Some require expertise. Those are not always the same thing. This is where telemedicine becomes transformative. Its greatest contribution is not replacing hospital visits. Its greatest contribution is reducing unnecessary hospital visits. Hospitals remain available for patients who genuinely need hospital care. Many of the routine consultations, specialist advice, medication reviews, and patient education can safely occur much closer to where patients actually live.

A truly connected healthcare system also changes the role of local health facilities, such as health posts, primary care clinics, and community health workers. Instead of functioning independently, they become connected to district hospitals, teaching hospitals and specialists. A nurse in a rural municipality can consult a specialist when necessary. A community health worker can receive guidance without referring every patient to an urban hospital. Knowledge begins moving through the healthcare system instead of patients carrying the entire burden. This approach strengthens, not weakens, local healthcare. People often assume digital health centralises medicine. The opposite can happen. When local providers remain connected to specialists, they become more capable of managing patients within their own communities. Only those requiring advanced care need referral. Healthcare becomes distributed. Expertise becomes shared. Patients remain closer to home whenever possible. This broader philosophy also changes how we think about healthcare infrastructure.

Traditionally, governments improve access by constructing additional hospitals. Hospitals will always remain essential. Digital infrastructure can extend the value of every hospital already built. One specialist can support multiple districts. One teaching hospital can strengthen dozens of rural facilities. One consultation can eliminate an unnecessary journey. Healthcare capacity grows not only by building more buildings but by connecting the ones we already have.

This philosophy is reflected in MEDeCLOCK. Rather than treating hospitals as isolated institutions, it proposes a connected healthcare ecosystem in which hospitals, health posts, clinics, diagnostic centres, pharmacies and patients can interact through a shared digital infrastructure. Telemedicine becomes one component of that ecosystem, not an isolated service but an extension of coordinated care supported by longitudinal health information and secure communication.  Whether this approach ultimately becomes part of Nepal’s healthcare future will depend on evidence, careful implementation and public trust. One principle already seems clear. Healthcare should no longer be defined by where hospitals stand. It should be defined by how effectively expertise reaches people. Perhaps the most important hospital of the future will not be the one with the tallest building. It will be the one whose knowledge reaches the greatest number of people. The true purpose of healthcare is not to bring patients to hospitals, but it is to bring health to people.

title.rendered: Tourists’ arrival increases by 13k in Dhorpatan

content.rendered:
Baglung, August 9

The number of tourists coming to enjoy Dhorpatan has been on the rise of late. More than 37,000 tourists have reached Dhorpatan in a year, with most of them including domestic tourists, according to the Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve Office, Baglung. The number of tourists visiting Dhorpatan in the fiscal year 2082/83 reached 37,520, of which 37,270 were Nepali tourists.

A total of 23,692 tourists had reached Dhorpatan in the fiscal year 2081/82 and 15,573 in the fiscal year 2080/81. Ranger Sagar Subedi of the office shared that the number of tourists reaching Dhorpatan, the only hunting reserve in Nepal, has increased by 13,000 in a year. The number of tourists is increasing every year due to the construction of tourist infrastructure, publicity and development of well-managed hotels and homestays in Dhorpatan.

The increase in the number of tourists has also led to a rise in revenue collection. A total of Rs 4,768,405 was collected from tourist entry fees in the fiscal year 2082/83 and Rs 3,121,500 in the fiscal year 2081/82. According to Ranger Subedi, the reserve has been charging Rs 100 for domestic and Nepali tourists to enter Dhorpatan, Rs 1,500 for tourists from SAARC countries and Rs 3,000 for foreign tourists.

Similarly, the reserve has collected Rs 10 million from stones, gravel and sand in the fiscal year 2082/83, which is Rs 4.6 million more than the previous fiscal year. While foreign tourists used to come to Dhorpatan only to hunt, domestic tourists have been coming here to observe the Dhorpatan Valley, Nisheldhor and Dhorbarah Temples, Bukipatan and Jaljala. Dhorpatan Valley is 2,900 meters above sea level, while Bukipatan lies at an altitude of over 4,000 meters.

title.rendered: Himalaya Roadies returns with Season 8, ‘Attitude vs Altitude’

content.rendered:
Kathmandu

Nepal’s longest-running youth adventure reality show, Himalaya Roadies, is returning with its eighth season on Himalaya TV, with the theme ‘Attitude vs Altitude.’

The new season will once again bring together adventure, competition, physical challenges and the search for young talent, while placing greater emphasis on contestants’ attitude, personality and ability to perform under pressure. Himalaya Roadies has established itself as one of Nepal’s most popular youth-oriented reality shows and is also the country’s longest-running reality show.

With Season 8, the makers are preparing to introduce new challenges and a fresh set of contestants. Yamaha has joined the eighth season as the title sponsor, while Mountain Dew is the ‘ In Association With ’ sponsor. There will also be some changes among the gang leaders this season. While some familiar faces will return, new faces are also expected to join the show. Host Remon Das Shrestha will continue to lead the show, while Anup and Laure will also return as gang leaders. The remaining gang leaders will be announced in the coming days.

The talent hunt for Season 8 will begin with a city tour. The show will conduct physical auditions across five major cities in Nepal, with the auditions scheduled to begin within the next two weeks. The new theme, ‘Attitude vs Altitude’, is expected to reflect the show’s focus on both physical endurance and mental strength. Contestants will be tested not only on their ability to overcome physical challenges but also on their attitude, determination and ability to perform under pressure.

“This season will be even more thrilling as the Gen Z young talent will have to prove themselves in the high-altitude terrain of Nepal’s mountainous region,” said Shyam Kadel, Executive Director of Himalaya TV.

Himalaya Television is producing and broadcasting the eighth season of Himalaya Roadies. The broadcaster has built a strong portfolio of international-format reality shows in Nepal, including The Voice of Nepal, Shark Tank Nepal, Nepal’s Next Top Model and MasterChef Nepal.

With the Season 8 auditions set to begin soon, the latest edition of Himalaya Roadies is preparing to embark on another nationwide search for young people ready to put their attitude to the test at altitude.

title.rendered: Rain causes road blockages, affects traffic on various highways

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 9

Heavy rainfall has led to significant road blockages across various regions in the country, severely impacting traffic on multiple highways. The police reported that roads such as the Mid Hill Highway in Tehrathum, the Araniko Highway in Sindhupalchok, the Mechi Highway in Ilam, and the Trishuli-Mailung-Safrubensi road in Rasuwa are among those affected by landslides and erosion.

In response to the heightened risk of flooding, authorities have imposed vehicle bans on certain road sections, including the BP Highway connecting Kavrepalanchok and Sindhuli, from 6:00 PM to 4:00 AM, while allowing traffic from 4:00 AM to 6:00 PM. The situation is particularly dire on the Mechi Highway, where traffic has been completely halted due to slippery conditions.

Landslides have also caused complete blockages on several sections of the Araniko Highway, particularly in areas such as Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality and Chautara Sangachokgadhi Municipality. Additionally, the Trishuli-Mailung-Safrubensi road has been rendered impassable due to erosion, and the Bheri Corridor’s Jajarkot-Dolpa section is blocked by landslides. The police have urged travellers to check road conditions with relevant agencies before embarking on journeys, as the rainy season poses ongoing risks of landslides, floods, and road erosion.

title.rendered: International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples observed today

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 9

Today marks the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples. It’s estimated that there are around 476 million Indigenous Peoples spread across 90 countries. While they represent less than 6 per cent of the global population, they make up at least 15 per cent of the world’s poorest individuals.

According to the UN, these communities speak a vast majority of the estimated 7,000 languages worldwide and embody about 5,000 unique cultures. Indigenous Peoples are the guardians of rich traditions and distinctive ways of connecting with both people and the environment. They have preserved social, cultural, economic, and political traits that set them apart from the dominant societies surrounding them.

Despite their diverse backgrounds, Indigenous Peoples face shared challenges when it comes to safeguarding their rights as unique communities. For years, Indigenous Peoples have fought for recognition of their identities, lifestyles, and their rights to traditional lands, territories, and natural resources. Unfortunately, their rights have often been overlooked throughout history. Today, they are considered some of the most disadvantaged and vulnerable groups globally.

The international community has begun to acknowledge that special measures are necessary to protect their rights and sustain their unique cultures and ways of life. To highlight the needs of Indigenous Peoples, every August 9 is observed as the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples, a date chosen to honour the first meeting of the UN Working Group on Indigenous Populations, which took place in Geneva in 1982.

title.rendered: Doctors trained abroad record higher failure rate in medical licensing exam

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 7

A higher number of medical graduates from foreign institutions failed the Nepal Medical Council’s Special Licensing Examination compared to graduates from Nepali medical colleges. The Nepal Medical Council (NMC) has published country-wise results of the Special Examination conducted on July 23 and 24 (Shrawan 7 and 8). A total of 1,013 candidates who studied at medical institutions in Nepal and abroad appeared for the examination.

According to a notice issued on August 7 by Acting Registrar Dr Dipendra Pandey, 947 candidates (93.48 per cent) passed the examination, while 65 failed. Among the 919 candidates who graduated from Nepali medical institutions, only 15 failed the exam. Among graduates from foreign institutions, candidates who studied in India performed comparatively better. Of the 17 candidates from India, 13 (76.47 per cent) passed.

In contrast, only eight out of 37 candidates (21.62 per cent) who studied in China passed, while 28 failed. Among those who studied in Egypt, eight of the 19 candidates (42.11 per cent) passed. Two out of five candidates each from Kyrgyzstan and the Philippines passed, giving both countries a 40 per cent pass rate.

All nine candidates who graduated from Pakistan passed the examination. The sole candidate from the United States also passed, while the only candidate from Belarus failed. Medical graduates in Nepal are required to pass the Nepal Medical Council’s licensing examination before they are allowed to practice medicine. The council conducts the licensing examination twice a year.

Acting Registrar Dr Dipendra Pandey said the results of the Special Examination should not be used to conclude that doctors educated in Nepal are better than those trained abroad. According to him, the council published the country-wise results solely to disclose the examination outcomes and not to assess the quality of medical education in any country or institution.

“This is only the result of one examination. It cannot be used to conclude that medical education in Nepal is superior or that education abroad is inferior,” Dr Pandey said. He added that the examination results will also be forwarded to the Medical Education Commission, which is responsible for conducting a detailed analysis, evaluating the quality of medical education, and making any necessary policy decisions. “We have published the results for administrative transparency. It is the responsibility of the Medical Education Commission to analyse the overall findings and draw conclusions about the quality of medical education,” Dr Pandey said.

title.rendered: Consumer wins Rs 1,000,000 million bumper prize in Taxpayer Incentive draw

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 7

The government has announced the results of the first fortnightly bumper draw under its Taxpayer Incentive Reward Program for the first 15 days of the Nepali month of Shrawan.

A consumer who purchased goods worth Rs 250 from Shiva Krishna General Store in Punarbas, Kanchanpur, has won the Rs 1 million bumper prize. The winning coupon number is 007 315 254 493. The purchase was made on Shrawan 7.

Another 15 consumers have each won Rs 100,000. The Inland Revenue Department (IRD) announced the winners during a program held at the Ministry of Finance on Friday.

The incentive scheme aims to encourage consumers to ask for invoices when making purchases and to strengthen the country’s tax system.

The government introduced the program in the budget for the current fiscal year, and Friday marked the first prize announcement. Under the scheme, 15 consumers receive Rs 100,000 each every 15 days, while one consumer wins a Rs 1 million bumper prize.

To facilitate participation, the IRD launched a new website, prize.ird.gov.np, on Saturday. Consumers who make cash purchases of goods or services worth more than Rs 100 in a single transaction for personal use within Nepal and obtain an original invoice can upload their bill to the website to enter the draw.

The department said that QR code payments are automatically included in the reward system, meaning users who pay digitally do not need to upload their invoices manually.

According to the IRD, consumers who purchase goods or services worth more than Rs 100 using a bank or digital wallet QR payment should keep a copy of the payment transaction, as the transaction number itself will serve as the qualifying entry for the prize draw.

In the Fiscal Year 2026/27 budget, Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle announced the Taxpayer Incentive Reward Program to bring more taxpayers into the formal tax system and promote a culture of requesting invoices. Following the announcement, the Ministry of Finance approved the program’s operating guidelines in the final week of Asar.

Under the guidelines, one consumer will receive a cash prize of Rs 100,000 (after applicable tax deductions) every day, while two consumers each month (through fortnightly draws) will receive a Rs 1 million bumper cash prize.

title.rendered: Electrical transformer theft cases rising in Madhesh

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, August 7

Cases of electrical transformer theft are increasing in different districts of Madhesh Province. Administration Chief of Nepal Electricity Authority Madhesh Province Office, Janakpurdham, Kali Charan Yadav told that 99 electrical transformers were stolen in the last five years.

Yadav added that the theft cases have increased as the copper wire used in transformers fetches a high price in the market. The highest number of transformers was stolen from Mahottari in five years, standing at 35, followed by 14 in Dhanusha, 10 in Rautahat, nine each in Sarlahi and Siraha, three in Saptari and two in Parsa. The stolen transformers had a capacity of 15-200 kV. Farmers in those districts have been facing problems irrigating their land due to the missing transformers, as the power supply is disrupted due to this.

The farmers have demanded that the concerned bodies install new transformers by arresting those involved in stealing transformers. Deputy Inspector General at Madhesh Province Police Office, Janakpurdham, Om Prasad Adhikari, shared that activities are underway to search for the stolen transformers.
