title.rendered: 7 most-effective social media and internet safety tips in Nepal’s context

content.rendered:
With the rise of digital media, internet safety and privacy have been a topic of concern for everyone. According to the global scenario, the leaking of data and increasing cybercrimes have been widespread. In the context of Nepal as well, cyberattack cases are increasing daily.

With numerous reports concerning cybersecurity, it is hard to assume that social media usage is safe, secure and private. One cannot control all the things that will happen to you, but you can take some basic measures to make your online presence secure. So, in this article, we have some tips that you can use to ensure social media and internet safety.

1. Use strong and unique passwords

Using poor credentials risks your internet safety and makes it easy for hackers. Hackers have high-performance computers and advanced tools which help them get into your computer or any device in under an hour. They have various ways to get into your systems, like phishing, DOS (denial of service) attacks, dictionary attacks, fake WAPs (wireless access points), and many more. And, if your password is easily predictable, they get access to the applications in seconds.

In summary, a strong password:

  • Must not contain the username
  • Must not use known words
  • Must include uppercase characters (A-Z), lowercase characters (a-z), numbers (0-9), and symbols (!, #, %, etc.)
  • Must be ten or more characters in total (the longer, the better)

This does not mean you should make one password super strong and have the same one for all your social media accounts. Repeated passwords in multiple platforms can be risky. So, have strong passwords, many strong passwords. It can also be problematic to remember all the strong passwords all by yourself. In that case, you can also use encrypted vaults to save your passwords. But make sure you are using only the certified ones.

2. Do not click anything suspicious

Do not click everything that is on your screen. With one click, you will give the entire system access to the hackers. Also, there are various websites made to disturb your privacy on the web. Some of the websites are so refined with a similar interface to some renowned websites, which can confuse anyone, even professionals. But they may ask you to enter your username and password to go further. When you do it, your login credentials will directly be in the hands of the hackers. This form of taking your credentials is called phishing, and the website is called a phishing website.

So, be cautious when someone random or someone you know shares any kind of links with you from now on. Many people are becoming victims of cyberbullying as a result. For prevention and to ensure your internet safety, be selective with the friends’ requests you receive on your social media. Clicking malicious links is the direct way others hack into your social media accounts or your device as a whole. So, do not click on any malicious links you get in front of you.

3. Never skip reading websites’ privacy policy

Something people often just tick the “I accept the terms and conditions, and I have read the privacy policy” or something similar without even reading the terms and conditions. One directly scrolls down to the bottom of the page and clicks the ‘I AGREE’ button. But this habit has been proven to be detrimental. It concerns your privacy and your security on the website/application. So, you need to read it. Next time, make sure you have read and are aware of the terms, conditions and privacy policies before signing up for anything on the internet.

4. Customise the privacy settings of your social media accounts

The social media applications also allow you to customise your default privacy settings. Things like who can see your photos, who can access your contact details and who can send you messages can be changed as per your requirement. You can get this option inside the privacy or security section of your social media application settings.

Use your fingerprints to get access to your device. Face unlocks are good but not as secure as fingerprint locks. One of the important privacy settings to enable is two-factor authentication. It is a setting that requires you to use it. Besides, you can also use an app lock or other password protection for your social media individually and your phone. With this, no random individual can get into your phone or device and do anything without your consent.

5. Be careful as you use digital wallets and mobile banking applications

Making transactions has been way easier with the help of digital payment methods, whether it is utility bill payment, internet bills, TV bills, school fees or broker payment for collateral deposit, fund transfer to friends/family, mobile top-up, etc. Payments for the various applications have been way easier with digital wallets like Global IME Pay, eSewa, Khalti, ConnectIPS, etc and mobile banking applications like EBL Touch 24 (Everest Bank Pvt Ltd), NIC Asia Mobank (NIC Asia Bank Pvt Ltd), etc. But you need to be extra cautious with these digital transaction applications.

The most crucial thing for your internet safety is to NEVER share your 4-digit pin of those applications (or 6-digit pin like in the case of ConnectIPS) with anyone. And, like any other application, use a lengthy, strong and unique cloud password. Choose your own phone number and email as the authorisation, not others’. 

Similarly, log in to only one of your devices and enable two-factor authentication from security settings. Keep your mobile phone and message display private so that the OTP code you receive on your mobile phone and email is secure. Many of these applications already have secure settings by default. But still, check out all the settings inside the application. Also, do not forget to read the privacy policies.

6. Keep all the applications updated

Ensure all your applications are updated regularly for your internet safety. When a company/owner of an application like social media, software, etc gives an update, they do not only add interesting features to the program or upgrade their interface and design. Along with interesting features, companies fix their applications’ drawbacks, bugs, and other security issues through their updates. 

So, keep all your applications, browser, operating system, and software updated. And, most importantly, update your antivirus software. In the first place, you should install and use anti-virus software if you do not have any. It can be beneficial for protecting against malicious attacks and safe social media and other online digital media usage.

Another thing that is very popular in the country is using APK files to get premium features of the software for completely free. The software may give you features that may cost you more for free but may also add malicious software to your device that can harm your internet safety, including the system and your privacy. Do not use third-party software and do not install software from third-party sources. The disadvantage of using third-party software is that you do not get updates, and your device will be at risk of getting infected and badly affected.

7. Be self-aware

Self-awareness is the most essential aspect when it comes to your online privacy and internet safety. The number of cyberattacks is increasing, and new cases are reported every day. There are also authorities in Nepal like the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and the Nepal Telecommunications Authority that are working for it and have even succeeded in many cases. But, since the saying ‘prevention is better than cure’ is never wrong, you should be self-aware on your own. Watch out for the language your friends on social media use for sharing/posting content or asking you for a request.

Do not share your personal information with anyone; it cannot be stressed enough. It can be your home address, financial information, contact number, or anything personal relating to you. So, stay lowkey on social media. This does not mean that you are completely off social media, but do not be too revealing about yourself. Also, when someone recommends installing an application or following a link, be extra cautious. Likewise, make sure your device is not public property and only accessed by you. Stand by and watch when you give someone else your device to use, even for seconds.

Originally published in 2022.

title.rendered: Customers lose thousands to a TikTok store that never delivers

content.rendered:
On July 23, Nanu Maya B.K. of Hupseykot, Nawalparasi (East), ordered a T-shirt and a skirt for her daughter from a TikTok account called Laxmi Collection Store. She was asked to pay Rs 900 in advance and was told that her order would be delivered the following day.

After she transferred the money, the store claimed it had not received the payment due to a technical issue. It then asked B.K. to send a seven-day bank statement. She complied, unknowingly revealing all her financial transactions for the past week.

The store later called her and asked her to resend the payment, this time by entering a specific code in both the remarks section and the amount field. She followed the instructions. Soon after, Rs 27,000 was withdrawn from her bank account.

“I tried to call them immediately, but they had already blocked me,” says B.K.

A week later, she received a call from an unknown number. The caller identified himself as a police officer and told her, “We have your money. We will return it to you, but you have to share your screen with us.” She complied. The caller then instructed her not to use her mobile banking app for at least 24 hours.

Soon afterwards, she began receiving SMS notifications that money was being withdrawn from her account. When she tried to access her mobile banking app, she found that she could no longer log in. This time, the store had also compromised her mobile banking account.

B.K. has filed a police complaint against the incident.   

According to Yubaraj Khadka, SP at the District Police Office, Nawalparasi (East), the case is under investigation. Similarly, he also informed that the cases of online scams via social media accounts are increasing. 

However, B.K. is not alone. Another victim, Chiring Limjom Lama of Boudha, was also scammed by the same store. Lama’s sister had ordered a shirt and a skirt from the store, but due to a technical issue, Lama made the payment on her sister’s behalf.

The store used a similar method to defraud Lama. In total, Rs 53,000 was withdrawn from her bank account. Unlike in B.K.’s case, however, the store did not gain access to Lama’s mobile banking account.  Recently, the store has been contacting Lama again, claiming they will return her money if she enters a code into her mobile banking app. Suspecting another scam attempt, she has not complied. 

The TikTok account of Laxmi Collection Store has more than 35,000 followers and regularly posts videos showcasing women’s and children’s clothing, giving the impression of a legitimate online business. Some of its videos have garnered millions of views, and many users in the comments express interest in purchasing the advertised products.  

There are also comments from users sharing their negative experiences with the account and urging others to stay away from it.

One comment by a user named Biren Lama reads, “They are frauds. Do not fall into their trap.”

Similarly, another comment by a user named Christian Girl reads, “Please, everyone, do not order anything from here. They will scam you. They looted my Rs 28,000. Stay away from this page.” 

One tactic they use is communicating with customers through different phone numbers, even though all customers initially contact the store using the same number listed on its TikTok page. 

These are just two representative cases. Under many of the store’s videos, several users have commented that they were scammed, while others have warned people not to buy anything from the account.

Another woman from Kathmandu, who requested anonymity, also said she was scammed by the same store. She said the store asked her to make an advance payment of Rs 900, which she did. Later, the sellers claimed they had not received the payment and asked her to send a bank statement. She shared only the section showing the transaction she had made to the store, rather than her full bank statement.

After receiving the document, the sellers stopped responding. Recently, however, they contacted her again, asking her to make another payment through a message on WhatsApp.

Onlinekhabar attempted to contact the store using the phone number listed on its TikTok account, but received no response. 

According to recent official data from Cyber Bureau, total reported complaints involving cybercrime and fraud peaked at 20,526 cases in fiscal year 2025/026, up from 18,926 cases in FY 2024/025 and 19,730 cases in FY 2023/024. Cybercrime applications consistently formed the vast majority of all registered complaints over the three years, registering 15,576 cases in FY 2023/024, 11,186 in FY 2024/025, and rebounding to 13,230 in FY 2025/026. 

Meanwhile, fraud complaints rose significantly from 4,154 cases in FY 2023/024 to 7,740 cases in FY 2025/025, remaining high at 7,296 cases in FY 2025/026. 

Cyber Bureau’s spokesperson and Police Superintendent (SP) Dilip Giri says that the one who does pre-payment are mostly found to be scammed. 

“While ordering anything online, pre-payment should be totally avoided,” says Giri. “ One should always do cash on delivery.”

title.rendered: Consulate General of Nepal in San Francisco to provide services until August 31

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 7

The Consulate General of Nepal in San Francisco, United States, has announced that it will discontinue its services from September 1, 2026. Consular services at the consulate general would remain available only until August 31, as the Consulate General of Nepal there is in the process of being permanently closed.

The Consulate General has urged all service recipients to obtain services before September 1, stating that the San Francisco-based Consulate General will be permanently closed after August 31. Issuing a notice today on the closure of passport and consular services, the Consulate General said that passport and consular services, including visa services, will no longer be available from September 1 onwards.

Similarly, the Consulate General has asked applicants who applied for passports at the Consulate General office or its passport mobile service centres before July 6 this year to collect their new passports soon from the Consulate General office.

title.rendered: Weak data protection exposes Nepal to growing cybersecurity risks

content.rendered:
Tribhuvan University’s first-year undergraduate examinations are currently underway. Last week, colleges across the country were busy distributing admit cards to students. However, while institutions focused on making admit card distribution more convenient, they largely overlooked data security and privacy.

Padma Kanya Campus in Bagbazar publicly exposed the personal data of 1,364 students by posting their admit cards on social media. The post was removed after media reports highlighted the issue. By then, however, students who had scanned the QR code had already gained access to other students’ symbol numbers, registration numbers, and academic records.

Despite the seriousness of the breach, the campus administration appeared to treat it lightly. Campus Chief Jayalakshmi Pradhan said the intention was simply to make the process easier for students. Some staff members even dismissed the concern, commenting that “it’s just a photo and a name.”

The administration further claimed that Padma Kanya was not alone in adopting this practice, arguing that other educational institutions also distribute admit cards in the same manner. “We are not the only ones. I won’t name them, but other colleges are doing the same. You just happened to find Padma Kanya,” one administrative staff member told Onlinekhabar.

The incident reflects the limited understanding of data privacy and sensitivity among leaders of Nepal’s educational institutions.

A few weeks earlier, another major incident raised concerns about Nepal’s digital security. Software developer Nirdesh Subedi was found to have cloned the Nepal government’s official Nagarik App web portal and hosted it on his personal domain.

He used an older version of the Nagarik App interface on his personal website. When users searched for “Nagarik App login,” Subedi’s website appeared among the top search results on Bing. Google Chrome, however, flagged the site as dangerous and warned users before allowing access.

The Nagarik App contains highly sensitive personal and government records, including citizenship certificates, passports, PAN cards, and educational certificates. Unauthorised cloning of such a platform significantly increases the risk of data theft. The incident prompted widespread criticism of the government’s cybersecurity practices and its handling of sensitive data.

Experts warned that cloned websites are commonly used in phishing attacks to trick users into revealing login credentials, making such incidents a serious cybersecurity threat. Cyberattacks targeting Nepal’s government digital systems are not new. Security weaknesses have repeatedly been exploited because lessons from previous incidents have not been adequately implemented.

Government websites have increasingly become easy targets due to weak security infrastructure. On February 13, 2025, hackers gained unauthorised access to 21 subdomains under the Koshi Provincial Government. A hacking group known as YNR claimed responsibility by publishing evidence of the breach on the Zone-H portal.

Exactly one month later, on March 26, 2025, the government’s Hello Sarkar website, operated under the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, was also compromised. A group calling itself Ghudra claimed it released data through the “Breach Forums” platform after alleging that the government had ignored its attempts to establish contact.

The attacks continued.

On April 23, 2025, the Nepal Police Headquarters website also suffered a security breach. A hacking group known as Kaju reportedly obtained citizenship records of around two million Nepali citizens and offered the data online for US$7,000. The recent cloning of the Nagarik App’s web version is viewed as another example in this continuing pattern of cybersecurity failures.

Concerns over data misuse are not limited to online platforms. Physical businesses, including supermarkets and cafés, are also collecting customers’ personal information without adequate transparency. Major supermarket chains such as Bhatbhateni and Big Mart routinely ask customers for their names and phone numbers when processing bills or offering membership programs. Many customers complain that they receive little or no meaningful benefit in exchange for providing sensitive personal information.

Similarly, many cafés and restaurants require customers to submit their phone numbers before granting access to Wi-Fi. Instead of simply providing a password, many establishments use captive portals that force customers to enter their mobile numbers before accessing the internet.

Collecting personal information in exchange for basic services raises significant privacy concerns. Most businesses do not clearly inform customers that they are collecting and storing their data. If these businesses suffer software vulnerabilities or data breaches, the personal information they have collected could easily be exposed or misused.

Moreover, few businesses explain how they secure the personal data they collect in exchange for free Wi-Fi or minimal discounts. Cybersecurity experts warn that weak data protection practices directly threaten citizens’ privacy. Using personal information without consent often causes unnecessary inconvenience and harm.

A recent example involved the widely discussed “SG Update” incident.

Last Baisakh, at 10:11 p.m., around 4,000 mobile users received unsolicited promotional messages from the “SG Update” shortcode asking them to subscribe to a YouTube channel. Recipients criticised the late-night advertisements on social media, questioning how their personal phone numbers had been obtained despite never sharing them with the sender.

Following widespread criticism, YouTuber Sagar Chhetri, who operates the channel, issued an explanation, attributing the incident to a technical error. “While sending updates to participants of our event, a technical issue caused unnecessary contacts to be added to the system,” Chhetri wrote on LinkedIn. “One employee’s personal phone contacts were accidentally synchronised, resulting in messages being sent to people who had never given permission.”

Similar concerns arise during election periods, when political parties and candidates frequently send bulk campaign text messages to voters without obtaining prior consent. Cybersecurity expert Naresh Lamgade says weak data protection practices make it easy for voters’ phone numbers to end up in the hands of campaign organisations.

Lamgade, founder of cybersecurity firm Bugv, said, “Once a database is breached, everyone’s data can leak. People often don’t realise the value of their own data, so they don’t pay attention. In many countries, companies face heavy fines after data breaches, and affected citizens can sue for compensation. In Nepal, however, regulators and responsible institutions show little concern, and public awareness remains very low.”

According to him, misuse of personal data is becoming increasingly common across many industries. “We once heard from a celebrity whose contact information was leaked from a delivery company’s database. The person received so many unwanted calls and messages that they eventually had to change their SIM card. That’s just one example.”

Ride-sharing and delivery companies, he added, possess highly sensitive information such as customers’ home addresses and phone numbers, making stronger data protection essential. Information technology expert Dobhan Rai identifies three main reasons behind Nepal’s weak data protection practices.

First, Nepali society has not yet developed a strong culture of respecting privacy and personal space. Second, public awareness remains low regarding how digital data—including sensitive personal information—can be misused and what consequences such misuse can have. Third, many institutions lack professional accountability and a culture of responsibility.

According to Rai, numerous incidents clearly demonstrate the risks created by this combination of negligence and poor awareness. She noted that in developed countries, citizens are highly conscious of their data privacy rights, while governments enforce strict data protection laws that impose substantial fines on organisations responsible for data breaches. Victims also have legal avenues to seek compensation.

Nepal, by contrast, lacks clear and robust legal regulations governing data protection, allowing organisations that possess citizens’ personal data to escape accountability. Rai argues that safeguarding citizens’ privacy in the digital age requires strong legal frameworks, institutional accountability, and greater public awareness.

The growing lack of data security has also contributed to a rise in cybercrime. According to statistics provided by Nepal Police’s Cyber Bureau to Onlinekhabar, 20,526 cybercrime complaints were registered during the last fiscal year. Of these, 13,230 involved electronic offences, while 7,296 were related to cyber fraud.

In fiscal year 2081/82 (2024/25), authorities received 18,926 complaints, including 11,186 electronic offence cases and 7,740 cyber fraud complaints. In fiscal year 2080/81 (2023/24), the total number of complaints stood at 19,730, comprising 15,576 electronic offences and 4,154 cyber fraud cases.

Although the yearly figures fluctuate, both the statistics and recent incidents indicate that cybersecurity and data protection are becoming increasingly critical issues in Nepal.

title.rendered: 43.8 million fish hatchlings grown in Janakpur

content.rendered:
Janakpurdham, August 7

The Fisheries Human Resource Development and Technology Validation Centre, Janakpurdham, has grown 43.8 million fish hatchlings in the fiscal year 2082/83 BS.

Chief of the Centre Dr Gyan Bahadur Jirel shared that the Centre produced 43.8 million fish hatchlings, 3.2 million fry, 1.38 million fingerlings and 2,053 kilograms of fish in the fiscal year 2082/83 BS. The Centre earned Rs 3.45 million from the sale of fry during the period.

The fry reared in the Centre are being sold out in the districts across the Madhes Province and some districts of Bagmati and Koshi provinces too. The Centre grows fish species of common carp, silver carp, bighead carp, grass carp and some others. The Centre also conducts training targeting the fish farmers and the hatchery businesspeople on technical know-how of commercial value.

title.rendered: 20 founders from across Nepal to showcase ventures at U.S. Embassy Capstone Accelerator finale

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 6

Twenty emerging entrepreneurs selected from more than 200 participants across seven cities will gather in Kathmandu on Friday for the finale of the U.S. Embassy Entrepreneurship Skill Development Program – Capstone Accelerator.

The event marks the culmination of a nationwide entrepreneurship initiative that has equipped founders across Nepal with practical business skills in marketing, storytelling and communication, AI readiness, export orientation, and investment readiness. Following a competitive national selection process, twenty founders were invited to Kathmandu to participate in a three-day residential accelerator before presenting their ventures to investors, business leaders, and ecosystem partners.

The day will begin with an Investment and Global Market-Focused Pitching Session, where founders will present their businesses before an expert panel. Instead of a competition, the session is designed to provide constructive feedback to help entrepreneurs strengthen their market positioning, scalability, export readiness, innovation, and investment potential.

The program will conclude with the Capstone “Main Street” Showcase, an interactive marketplace inspired by the traditional American Main Street model. Founders will exhibit their products and services through live demonstrations and conversations with guests, creating opportunities to receive market feedback, build professional networks, and explore future collaborations. Throughout the program, the 20 finalists benefited from masterclasses, mentoring, and coaching from AmCham Nepal and other American firms.

“Strong economic partnerships are built by investing in people. By equipping emerging Nepali entrepreneurs with the skills, networks, and global perspectives they need to grow, this initiative reinforces the longstanding partnership between the United States and Nepal while creating new opportunities for trade, investment, innovation, and private-sector collaboration,” said Mike Harker, Public Affairs Chief at U.S. Embassy Nepal.

The Capstone Accelerator is the final stage of the U.S. Embassy Entrepreneurship Skill Development Program, supported by U.S. Embassy Nepal and implemented by the International Development Institute (IDI) in partnership with Aadyanta Advisory.

Earlier this year, the program reached more than 200-plus entrepreneurs through regional workshops in Nepalgunj, Dhangadhi, Biratnagar, Janakpur, Hetauda, Bhairahawa, and Pokhara. Participants then continued their learning through virtual sessions on legal compliance, export readiness, AI-enabled growth, and digital marketing.  Twenty founders were selected for the national Capstone Accelerator.

The 20 founders represent a wide range of sectors in Nepal’s entrepreneurial landscape, including agriculture and agri-processing, food and beverage, technology, manufacturing, creative industries, consulting, digital services, natural products, handicrafts, cooperatives, and social enterprise. Together, they reflect both emerging and growth-oriented businesses from across the country, united by a commitment to innovation, market expansion, and building enterprises with significant potential to create jobs and contribute to Nepal’s economic development.

title.rendered: Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth to visit Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 6

Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth is set to visit Nepal later this month. According to a high-level government source, General Seth is scheduled to arrive in Nepal on August 16. He assumed office as the Chief of the Indian Army on June 30, 2026.

It is a long-standing tradition for the serving Chief of the Indian Army to be conferred the honorary rank of General of the Nepal Army. Likewise, newly appointed Army chiefs of Nepal and India traditionally pay official visits to each other’s countries.

During his visit, General Seth is also expected to pay a courtesy call on Prime Minister Balendra Shah. Although a proposal for the meeting has been sent to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, it has not yet been confirmed.

The Nepal Army and the Indian Army share a long-standing historical relationship. For nearly 75 years, the two countries have maintained the tradition of conferring honorary general ranks on each other’s Army chiefs.

According to the Nepal Army Headquarters, the practice of awarding the honorary rank dates back to 1950.

The current Chief of the Nepal Army, Ashok Raj Sigdel, has also received the honorary rank of General of the Indian Army.

On Dec. 12, 2024 (27 Mangsir 2081 BS), Indian President Droupadi Murmu conferred the honorary rank on General Sigdel during a special ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi.

title.rendered: Arya Nishaant wants the world to see Nepal’s sociable spirit

content.rendered:
Madhesh Province has won the “Miss Nepal” title for the second time. A few years after Nikita Chandak became “Miss Nepal World,” Arya Nishaant was declared “Miss Nepal International 2026” last week.

Soft-spoken and easygoing, Arya Nishaant is a fashion model and education activist. She will represent the country at the international “Miss International” pageant to be held in Japan on November 25.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar, she said that after winning the “Miss Nepal” crown, a weight of responsibility has been added to her shoulders. She says her duty to raise the country’s prestige on the international stage has grown.

“After the crown came onto my head, for a moment I felt like I was in a dream,” she says. “I felt a big responsibility had been added. I will be known as Nepal on the international stage. There’s pride in that, and it’s also a bigger responsibility.”

She says she entered the competition determined to give her best.

“I went in telling myself I’d give my best without comparing myself to others and without expecting anything. It’s a matter of fortune. I didn’t focus on the result; even if I hadn’t won, I wouldn’t have gone home sad. I’m happy that I won,” she says.

She believes that becoming “Miss Nepal” will expand the audience that wants to listen to and watch her. She says winning the title won’t change her personal nature, but it does add the responsibility of representing the country.

She says the “Miss Nepal” crown isn’t just a crown studded with diamonds; the expectations of every Nepali are tied to it too.

“It’s not merely a diamond-studded crown; every Nepali’s expectations will be attached to it. When I go to the international stage, I’ll have to represent in a way that satisfies everyone,” she says.

On the “Miss International” stage in Japan, she said she would try to convey that Nepal is not only the land of Everest and Buddha but also carries certain values.

“I want people to understand that Nepal isn’t just the land of Everest and Buddha, that we Nepalis are sociable, that we treat guests as gods, and that it’s also the land of the Gorkhas,” she says. “I’ll try to reflect those values in my own personality too.”

She says she has been influenced and inspired by the personalities of past “Miss Nepal” titleholders.

“Certainly, Miss Nepal is the biggest platform among the country’s beauty pageants. Whoever becomes Miss Nepal, it shows in her personality that she is Miss Nepal. That’s why I joined pageantry,” she said.

She believes the biggest lesson she learned on the journey from auditions to winning the crown was not to give up.

“Sometimes life brings a lot of challenges. If you make a mistake, if something goes wrong, you shouldn’t let it hurt you. Get up every day and try to give your best,” she advises.

She recounted stumbling on stage in the round after the audition, saying that falling isn’t the problem.

“Falling isn’t the problem; what matters is getting back up after falling. Being able to get up and keep walking is the real victory,” she says.

Arya Nishaant says the work of former Miss Nepal titleholders, including Nikita Chandak and Shrinkhala Khatiwada, has inspired her.

“The love they received and the name they made for themselves on international platforms, their journeys have inspired me,” she says.

A business finance student, Arya Nishaant wants to move forward with work that brings equal access to education.

“Besides Miss Nepal, my dream is to work toward equal access to education. I want to run a business in a non-profit way,” she says.

She says she plans to raise the agenda of quality education, one of the UN’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals, at the Miss International competition. Finally, she offered advice to today’s younger generation: “Draw your own life’s path, seize opportunities, don’t give up, dreams do come true.”

title.rendered: Service providers begin organising overhead utility cables in Kathmandu (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 6

Work is progressing rapidly to organise the tangled overhead utility cables across the Kathmandu Valley. Internet and other service providers are clearing and reorganising the disorderly cables in major urban areas of the valley. The government had instructed concerned agencies and service providers to properly manage the overhead internet, telephone, television, and other cables hanging haphazardly from electricity poles.

According to officials, the tangled cables not only spoil the city’s appearance but also increase the risk of accidents. Service providers are currently organising the overhead cables along the Kalimati–Kalanki road corridor.

In the first phase, unused cables are being removed and managed along six major routes in the Kathmandu Valley: Tripureshwor–Kalimati–Kalanki, Jadibuti–Pepsicola, Tripureshwor–Lazimpat, Samakhushi–Town Planning–Gongabu, the Kirtipur area, and Old Baneshwor–Gaushala–Chabahil.

title.rendered: Approval granted to four hospitals as teaching hospitals

content.rendered:
Sudurpaschim, August 6

The government of Sudurpaschim province has officially approved four provincial hospitals to function as teaching hospitals for the Martyr Dasharath Chand University of Health Science (MDCUHS). During a meeting of the Provincial Council of Ministers today, it was decided that Seti, Lamkichuha, and Tikapur hospitals in Kailali, along with the Mahakali Provincial Hospital in Kanchanpur, will be utilised for the university’s educational programmes starting this year.

Prayagraj Khanal, the Chief Private Secretary to Chief Minister Kamal Bahadur Shah, shared that the provincial hospitals will be used as teaching facilities in line with the University of Health Sciences’ guidelines. They will now move forward with the necessary legal and administrative steps after reaching agreements with the relevant agencies.

According to Section 20 of the Act, 2082 concerning MDCUHS, there is a provision for these hospitals to be used under an agreement. The Act states, “The University can conduct educational programmes in such hospitals or utilise them as teaching hospitals by entering into an agreement with the hospital in coordination with the government of Nepal, the provincial government, or the local level.”

title.rendered: Petrol tanker catches fire in Rautahat

content.rendered:
Rautahat, August 6

A petrol tanker caught fire on the East-West Highway near Dhansar Bridge in Ward No. 3 of Gujara Municipality, Rautahat, on Thursday morning. The tanker was destroyed in the blaze following a road accident.

According to police, the incident occurred at around 5:30 am when the petrol tanker (registration number Madhesh Province 03-001 Kha 7811) was travelling from Amlekhgunj in Bara to Sarlahi. The vehicle reportedly overturned onto its right side after the driver lost control while trying to avoid a deer that had suddenly crossed the highway.

The tanker caught fire immediately after overturning, the Rautahat District Police Office said.

Police teams from the Chandranigahapur Area Police Office and the District Traffic Police Office in Chapur, along with fire engines from Chandrapur and Nijgadh municipalities, responded to the scene and brought the fire under control.

Although the tanker was destroyed, no human casualties were reported, according to DSP Basanta Gautam of the Rautahat District Police Office.

Traffic on the Mahendra Highway, which was temporarily disrupted following the accident, has now resumed normal operation.

Police have taken the tanker driver, 25-year-old Samir Gurung of Simara Sub-Metropolitan City-11 in Bara, into custody and are conducting further investigation into the incident.

content.rendered:
For many of us, the day does not truly begin until we take that first sip of coffee. It wakes us up, sharpens our focus, and makes the morning a little easier. But could your daily cup of coffee be doing something more? Could it actually help protect your brain as you grow older?

Scientists have been trying to answer this question for decades. Their findings suggest that coffee is much more than a source of caffeine. While it is certainly not a cure for neurological diseases, growing evidence indicates that moderate coffee consumption may lower the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease. It may also help reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia. At the same time, researchers emphasise that coffee is only one piece of a much larger picture. No single food or drink can prevent these complex diseases.

More than just a source of caffeine

Coffee contains hundreds of naturally occurring compounds. Along with caffeine, it is rich in antioxidants, chlorogenic acids, and plant compounds known as polyphenols, many of which help reduce inflammation and protect cells from damage.

Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain. Adenosine is a chemical that gradually builds throughout the day and makes us feel tired. When caffeine blocks these receptors, we feel more alert and focused. Researchers have also discovered that this process influences dopamine, one of the brain’s most important chemical messengers.

A landmark review published in Pharmacological Reviews by Fredholm and colleagues showed that caffeine affects brain signalling, dopamine activity, blood flow, and communication between nerve cells. Later studies by Cunha and other neuroscientists demonstrated that these same pathways are involved in inflammation, oxidative stress, and the gradual loss of brain cells seen in many neurological disorders. These discoveries provide a biological explanation for why coffee could influence brain health.

The strongest evidence is for Parkinson’s disease

Among all neurological diseases, the evidence linking coffee to a lower risk of disease is strongest for Parkinson’s disease. Parkinson’s disease develops when dopamine-producing nerve cells in a small region of the brain called the substantia nigra gradually die. As dopamine levels decline, people begin to experience tremors, muscle stiffness, slower movements, and balance problems. Many also develop constipation, sleep disturbances, depression, and loss of smell years before movement symptoms appear.

One of the first major studies to attract worldwide attention was published in JAMA in 2000 by Ross and colleagues. Following thousands of participants over many years, the researchers found that people who regularly drank coffee were significantly less likely to develop Parkinson’s disease than those who rarely consumed it.

The finding has since been confirmed repeatedly. In 2010, Costa and colleagues combined results from numerous studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. Their analysis showed that people with higher caffeine intake had approximately a 25 per cent lower risk of developing Parkinson’s disease.

A comprehensive review published in The Lancet Neurology by Ascherio and Schwarzschild reached a similar conclusion. After reviewing decades of research, they identified caffeine as one of the most consistent lifestyle factors associated with a lower risk of Parkinson’s disease.

Scientists believe this relationship makes biological sense. Caffeine blocks adenosine A2A receptors in the same brain circuits that control movement. By doing so, it may improve dopamine signalling while reducing inflammation and stress within vulnerable brain cells.

Can coffee treat Parkinson’s disease?

Although people who regularly drink coffee appear less likely to develop Parkinson’s disease, clinical studies have not shown that caffeine can significantly improve symptoms once the disease has already developed. In a randomised clinical trial published in Neurology, Postuma and colleagues tested whether caffeine could improve movement symptoms in patients with Parkinson’s disease. Despite promising observational evidence, the researchers found that caffeine did not produce meaningful long-term improvements. This is an important distinction.

Something that lowers the risk of developing a disease does not necessarily become an effective treatment after the disease begins. Coffee should never replace proven therapies such as levodopa, exercise, physical therapy, or deep brain stimulation when recommended by a neurologist.

What about Alzheimer’s disease?

The evidence for Alzheimer’s disease is encouraging, although it is not as strong as it is for Parkinson’s disease. Alzheimer’s disease develops through a combination of abnormal protein accumulation, inflammation, damage to blood vessels, and changes that occur with ageing. Scientists believe that many lifestyle factors influence this process, including diet, exercise, sleep, cardiovascular health, and education.

Several large studies have found that people who drink moderate amounts of coffee tend to have a lower risk of dementia. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis published in Nutrients concluded that drinking about two to four cups of coffee each day was associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

Even more impressive was a large study published in JAMA in 2026. Researchers followed more than 131,000 adults for as long as four decades and identified over 11,000 cases of dementia. They found that participants who drank about two or three cups of caffeinated coffee each day had a modestly lower risk of developing dementia and maintained slightly better cognitive performance over time. Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

Still, these findings should be interpreted carefully. Observational studies cannot prove that coffee itself prevents dementia. People who drink coffee may also exercise more, eat healthier diets, receive better medical care, or have other lifestyle habits that contribute to healthier ageing. Although researchers adjust for many of these factors, no observational study can eliminate every possible source of bias.

Moderation is important

When it comes to coffee, more is not always better. Most studies suggest that moderate consumption, roughly two to four cups each day, is associated with the greatest potential benefit. Drinking excessive amounts of coffee may increase anxiety, interfere with sleep, raise heart rate, or cause digestive discomfort.

Sleep is especially important because poor sleep has been linked to memory decline and several neurodegenerative diseases. Drinking large amounts of coffee late in the day may reduce sleep quality and potentially offset some of its benefits.

Both the United States Food and Drug Administration and the European Food Safety Authority state that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally safe for most healthy adults. This amount is roughly equivalent to three or four regular cups of coffee, although caffeine content varies depending on how coffee is prepared.

Coffee is only part of the story

Although coffee has received considerable attention, it should not distract us from lifestyle habits that have much stronger scientific evidence for protecting brain health.

According to the 2024 Lancet Commission on Dementia Prevention, controlling blood pressure, exercising regularly, treating hearing loss, avoiding smoking, managing diabetes, staying socially connected, and continuing to learn throughout life are among the most effective ways to reduce the risk of dementia. Coffee may provide an additional benefit, but it cannot replace these well-established habits.

The bottom line

Current research suggests that moderate coffee consumption may help lower the risk of Parkinson’s disease and may also contribute to a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease and dementia. The evidence for Parkinson’s disease is particularly strong and has remained consistent across decades of research. For Alzheimer’s disease, the findings are promising but less definitive because they rely mainly on observational studies.

The message is both simple and reassuring. If you already enjoy coffee, there is little reason to give it up unless your doctor advises otherwise. For most healthy adults, two or three cups each day can comfortably fit within a healthy lifestyle.

At the same time, coffee should not be viewed as a miracle drink. Protecting the brain depends on the choices we make every day, including staying physically active, eating a balanced diet, sleeping well, controlling blood pressure, remaining socially engaged, and continuing to challenge our minds.

Your morning cup of coffee may offer more comfort and energy. It may give your brain a small advantage. But lasting brain health is built through a lifetime of healthy habits, not from a single cup.

title.rendered: Health assistance desk set up for devotees at Manakamana temple

content.rendered:
Gorkha, August 6

Devotees visiting the Manakamana Temple will now have access to primary healthcare services within the temple premises. A Health Assistance Desk has been established through a joint partnership between the Manakamana Area Development Committee and the Shahid Lakhan Rural Municipality.

The facility, which is equipped to provide primary medical care, including ECG services, was inaugurated on Wednesday. The Health Assistance Desk was officially opened by Rural Municipality Chairperson Ramesh Thapa during a special ceremony.

Anjan Basnyat, Executive Director of the Manakamana Area Development Committee, said the desk was established in view of the health risks faced by devotees waiting in long queues to pay their homaage in the temple.

“Millions of devotees visit Manakamana every year,” he said. “Some have suffered serious health complications, and there have even been deaths while waiting in fasting conditions. This facility has been established to address such emergencies.”

Basnyat added that the Health Assistance Desk will also provide emergency treatment to elderly and physically vulnerable residents.

The rural municipality will provide the required healthcare personnel, while the committee will be responsible for overall management of the facility.

Medical equipment for the Health Assistance Desk has been donated by Manakamana Darshan Pvt. Ltd.. Temple chief priest Insan Thapa Magar has also pledged to contribute monthly financial support for the operation of the facility.

title.rendered: Nepali coach Sudarshan Simkhada proves stature is no barrier to excellence

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 5

Nepali karate coach and international referee Sudarshan Simkhada is a living example that success in sports is measured not by physical height, but by ability, confidence, and dedication.

Standing at approximately 152.4 centimetres (5 feet) tall, Simkhada has brought international recognition to Nepal in Kyokushin Karate while setting several rare milestones of his own.

In 1996, at just 20 years of age, he served as a referee at an international Kyokushin Karate tournament, becoming one of the youngest international referees in the sport.

A year later, at the age of 21, he was appointed head coach of the Nepali team at the First World Weight Category Kyokushin Karate Championship held in Tokyo, Japan. This made him one of the youngest and shortest head coaches at the championship.

Also in 1997, during the 7th Asian Kyokushin Karate Championship in India, he officiated as an international referee at the age of 21, achieving yet another historic milestone.

Throughout his sporting career, Simkhada has demonstrated that ability and self-confidence matter far more than physical stature. Representing Nepal alongside some of the world’s most experienced athletes, coaches, and officials, he has played a significant role in establishing Nepal’s presence in international Kyokushin Karate.

Over the past 35 years, Simkhada has remained active as a coach, training between 8,000 and more than 10,000 athletes. Hundreds of his trainees have gone on to represent Nepal in both national and international competitions.

Beyond sports, Simkhada has also been actively involved in social service and has become an inspiration to today’s younger generation. By turning what many might perceive as a physical limitation into a source of strength, he has shown that even seemingly impossible goals can be achieved through determination, perseverance, and hard work.

His accomplishments are regarded as important milestones in the history of Nepali karate.

title.rendered: Project Abhaya concludes youth dialogue on financial governance in Bagmati

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 5

A three-day “Youth-CSO Provincial Dialogue on Financial Governance” concluded in Kathmandu, bringing together youths, civil society representatives, and technical experts to discuss fiscal federalism, budget transparency, and citizen oversight in Bagmati Province.

The dialogue was organised by Project Abhaya through its Youth Fiscal Accountability Network (YFAN). It opened with a session introducing participants to the program’s national fiscal governance themes, led by Ishika Panta and Nipuna Neupane of Project Abhaya.

On the second day, Roshan Shrestha, Deputy Director General at the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction, led a session on fiscal federalism, the provincial budget cycle, and revenue generation.

This was followed by a session on identifying the root causes of local fiscal problems, facilitated by Ishika Panta, founder of Project Abhaya, and Nipuna Neupane. Participants worked in small groups to trace issues such as procurement delays and poor coordination between government levels back to their underlying causes.

Narayan Adhikari, Co-founder and South Asia Representative of Accountability Lab, then led a session helping participants narrow these issues down into a ranked list of top priorities for the province.

On the final day, Binod Bhattarai of Transparency International led a session on citizen oversight, public hearings, social audits, and the Right to Information (RTI) process.

Participants then practised applying the RTI process through a short exercise led by Rakshya Bam, a youth political activist and coordinator of the Nepal Gen Z Front. The dialogue closed with a session facilitated by Ishika Panta, in which participants turned the province’s prioritised issues into concrete advocacy goals for the short, medium, and long term. Findings from the dialogue will be included in Project Abhaya’s upcoming publication, “Provincial Perspectives on Financial Governance.” Project Abhaya, established in 2024, is a youth-led civil society organisation.

title.rendered: From Hong Kong to Miss Nepal, Deepmala Dhakal carries a message for the diaspora

content.rendered:
Miss Nepal made history in more ways this year. Anushka Shrestha became the first Miss Nepal to be elected to parliament, where she has been raising issues of art and entrepreneurship.

Deepmala Dhakal added a different chapter to that story this week. Born and raised in Hong Kong, she is the first non-resident Nepali to become Miss Nepal. She currently serves as the “Second Generation Coordinator” from Hong Kong on the Non-Resident Nepali Association’s (NRNA) sitting executive committee.

The 24-year-old Dhakal, who has been working through the NRNA to connect the diaspora’s second generation with their homeland, now wants to carry that cause forward through the Miss Nepal platform. She says she entered the pageant with a vision of linking the diaspora to Nepal, and wants to send a message to the second generation about returning to work in the country.

“I wanted to inspire second-generation NRNs. Even though we were born and raised abroad, I wanted to show that we can still make a place for ourselves here and give something back to the country,” she says of her reason for competing in Miss Nepal. “I came to show that the second generation can come to Nepal and do something — and that they should.”

She also wants to push back against the perception that people who go abroad stop caring about or helping their country. “A lot of people say we don’t help either. That’s simply not true,” she says.

Since becoming Miss Nepal, she wants to use a cancer-awareness campaign to connect the country with the diaspora. She has taken this forward as an ambassador for Nepal Cancer Hospital, and her team recently held a cancer screening programme in Birgunj.

She hopes to bring the diaspora on board with this cancer-awareness project as well, not just people in Nepal.

“This isn’t just my project; it belongs to the whole Nepali diaspora. I want everyone to come together and do something for Nepal, to help the Nepali community,” Dhakal says.

Following the death of a cousin from cancer, Dhakal became even more determined to pursue the project. A one-day charity walk she recently organised in Hong Kong raised NPR 600,000 for the cause. The project also won her the Beauty With a Purpose title at Miss Nepal.

She now plans to take the same project to Miss World’s Beauty With a Purpose segment, to be held in Tanzania in 2027.

“For me, this felt like an international project. Through this win, I was able to bring joy not just to the Nepali community in Hong Kong, but to the entire NRN community,” she told Onlinekhabar.

She says that because more people will now listen to what she has to say as Miss Nepal, she intends to use the platform well.

“My focus will be on using this spotlight to advance cancer awareness on a much bigger scale,” she says.

Legacy, the number 17, and the country

Dhakal was born and raised in Hong Kong. Since childhood, she has faced the same recurring, and often stressful, question. “In Hong Kong, people would ask where I was really from. When I came to Nepal, I’d get asked the same thing,” she says. “After a lifetime of having to prove I was Nepali, now I finally feel like Nepal has chosen me.”

She says the Miss Nepal crown has given her a chance to introduce the country to the world.

“That’s why I feel truly proud to be a daughter who can genuinely represent Nepal through this crown,” she says. “I also had to live up to the value of this crown; my main goal is to go to Miss World, participate well, and not come back empty-handed.”

Dhakal’s win also carries her mother’s legacy. Her mother, Roshani, competed in Miss Nepal 1994 wearing sash number 17. By coincidence, Deepmala Dhakal also won her title wearing sash number 17, a moment that let her both fulfil her mother’s unfinished dream and carry forward her legacy of participation.

That confidence shows clearly on her face. Perhaps that’s why Dhakal didn’t just win the Miss Nepal World title; she also won four sub-titles, setting another Miss Nepal record.

title.rendered: Ensuring the independence of Nepal’s anti-corruption commission

content.rendered:
Constitutional bodies are institutions whose existence, functions, duties, and powers are established by a nation’s constitution. The constitution protects these bodies, and any significant changes to their powers, functions, or duties require a constitutional amendment.

The Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) is an independent constitutional body established to minimise corruption in Nepal. It is responsible for investigating and prosecuting corruption and abuse of authority. The commission carries out its responsibilities through punitive, preventive, promotional, and institutional capacity-building strategies.

To safeguard its independence and autonomy, the Chief Commissioner and Commissioners are appointed by the President of Nepal on the recommendation of the Constitutional Council.

Why the CIAA needs to be independent

An independent and autonomous anti-corruption agency is a crucial mechanism for controlling corruption in any country, whether developed, developing, or underdeveloped. As a constitutional body, the CIAA must exercise its powers and functions as provided by the Constitution of Nepal while remaining free from unlawful influences that could hinder its operations within the constitutional framework.

An independent CIAA prevents arbitrary government interference and enables the commission to function without political influence. It ensures that laws are applied equally to all individuals and institutions while upholding the rule of law through impartial investigation and prosecution of corruption cases.

An independent anti-corruption commission is also essential for the effective investigation and prevention of corruption through practical and responsive approaches. Corruption remains one of the greatest obstacles to good governance. Independence enables the commission to exercise its authority without fear of political retaliation. It allows the CIAA to function as a watchdog rather than a political instrument used against the opposition. Such independence ensures that its work is not dependent on political favour, allowing investigations to be conducted impartially. Furthermore, it strengthens institutional integrity by enhancing transparency and accountability while encouraging the public to report wrongdoing without fear.

De facto and De jure independence

Both de facto and de jure independence are fundamental to the effective functioning of the CIAA.

De facto independence develops through the commission’s continuous interaction with political parties, public officials, interest groups, and citizens. De jure independence, on the other hand, is guaranteed through constitutional provisions, laws, and regulations that formally establish the commission’s autonomy. In simple terms, de facto independence exists in practice, whereas de jure independence exists in law.

Both legal and functional independence are essential for the CIAA’s effective performance. De facto independence enables the commission to perform its duties without undue pressure or interference, while de jure independence provides the legal authority necessary for its functioning. However, the two often diverge. Even where laws guarantee independence, legitimate and illegitimate political influence may still undermine the commission’s ability to function effectively.

The Constitution of Nepal (2015), the Prevention of Corruption Act (2002), and the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority Act (1991) provide the legal framework for the CIAA’s independence. Nevertheless, interference from governments and ruling-party leaders has continued to hinder the commission’s effective functioning.

Anti-corruption efforts as political weapons

Nepal was declared a federal democratic republic in 2008. Since then, coalition governments led by major political parties have largely governed the country. However, the results of the 2026 election showed that the Rastriya Swatantra Party secured a majority and formed a government without coalition partners.

Despite ideological differences, anti-corruption has remained a central commitment in the election manifestos of almost every political party. Governments since 2008 have consistently pledged to prioritise anti-corruption. Political parties have often interpreted corruption according to their own political philosophies, raising new public expectations during every election cycle. However, Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index has shown little significant improvement in Nepal’s corruption levels.

One reason for this limited progress is the perception that anti-corruption mechanisms are frequently used as tools of political revenge. Although strengthening anti-corruption institutions has been a major political agenda, their implementation often appears selective rather than impartial.

Political leaders deny allegations that anti-corruption campaigns are politically motivated. Nevertheless, actions against opposition leaders frequently create the perception of a political vendetta. Filing corruption cases or reopening investigations involving opposition leaders primarily for political publicity reinforces concerns that anti-corruption institutions are being used as political tools.

A comparison between previous governments and the current administration reveals recurring patterns with only minor differences. Earlier governments were criticised for overlooking corruption involving members of their own or coalition parties while reopening cases against political opponents in the name of good governance. The current government appears to be following a similar path.

Major corruption scandals—including the Bhutanese refugee scam, gold smuggling, Maoist cantonment fund misappropriation, the Nepal Airlines wide-body procurement case, the visit visa extortion scandal, the Sudan scam, and the COVID-19 procurement scandal—were often alleged to have been delayed or inadequately pursued because of political interests.

Similarly, cases involving cooperative fraud, financial crimes, and money laundering against former minister Rabi Lamichhane, as well as the land misappropriation case involving former Prime Minister Madhav Kumar Nepal, gained momentum only after the individuals were no longer politically aligned with the ruling coalition. Such developments have raised concerns about the selective enforcement of anti-corruption laws.

The current government has faced similar criticism. Allegations include withdrawing money laundering charges, overlooking claims of business conflicts of interest, budget information leaks, tax manipulation, the call bypass case, the Smart Telecom case, and the use of private red number plates by ministers’ advisers. Meanwhile, opposition leaders have reportedly faced investigation and arrest based on limited evidence. This disparity reinforces concerns that anti-corruption measures continue to be used selectively rather than impartially.

Political will and anti-corruption effectiveness

Countries with strong political commitment have generally achieved greater success in implementing anti-corruption strategies. Singapore and Hong Kong, for example, have established highly independent anti-corruption agencies supported by sustained political will. Their experiences demonstrate that legal provisions alone are insufficient; genuine political commitment is equally essential.

In Nepal, limited political will continues to hinder the effectiveness of anti-corruption institutions. Frequent interference in their work illustrates the government’s inadequate commitment to protecting institutional independence.

Recent reports concerning the alleged conduct of the Prime Minister’s advisers toward the Chief Commissioner and senior officials of the CIAA have generated significant public debate. Summoning the Chief Commissioner and senior officials has been viewed as a threat to the independence of the constitutional body. Such actions have been described as ultra vires and as undermining the commission’s institutional autonomy.

Similarly, public remarks reportedly made by the Prime Minister Balendra Shah regarding summoning CIAA officials for several hours have raised further concerns about the commission’s independence. Public statements suggesting interference in the affairs of a constitutional body risk undermining its institutional autonomy and reinforce perceptions that the government seeks to maintain influence over the commission. In this regard, the current government’s approach appears to reflect continuity rather than a departure from the practices of previous administrations.

For the CIAA to function effectively as Nepal’s constitutional anti-corruption body, both de facto and de jure independence are indispensable. Although the Constitution of Nepal and related legislation define the commission’s powers, functions, and responsibilities, legal guarantees alone are insufficient. Government interference, pressure from ruling-party leaders, and both legitimate and illegitimate political influence continue to undermine the commission’s independence and its ability to fulfil its constitutional mandate. Therefore, strong political will to uphold both legal and practical independence is essential to ensuring the CIAA can perform its duties impartially, effectively, and in the public interest.

title.rendered: Government, social activist Ranabhat ink 19-point deal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 5

Activist Jyoti Ranabhat, who was on a hunger strike to press for the fulfilment of various demands, has broken her fast. She terminated the hunger strike this morning after she and the government negotiation team reached an agreement on 19 points.

Ranabhat, who is also a nurse, had been on a hunger strike since July 30. Krishna Shrestha, Additional Secretary at the Ministry of Health and Food Safety, Senior Medical Superintendent Dr Hemanta Chandra Ojha, and Legal Officer Jaya Prakash Subedi have signed the agreement. Under the points of agreement, the Ministry of Health and Food Safety is to form a task force within seven days to determine the pay, decent service, conditions, and facilities for healthcare workers, including nurses and midwives working in government, institutional, private, community hospitals, medical colleges, and teaching institutes, with the work expected to be completed within at least six months.

An understanding has been reached where the Ministry of Health and Food Safety has to amend the Guidelines, 2072 for the mobilization of doctors and health workers who have received scholarship from the government within 30 days as well as the Ministry of Education and Sports has to make necessary arrangement to ensure scholarship to midwives for the study of PCL Nursing and Midwifery in accordance with Health and Midwifery Strategy 2077/78-2087-88.

Similarly, the deal also mentioned that the Ministry of Health and Food Safety, through the Ministry of Education and Sports, would request the Council for Technical Education and Vocational Training within two days to determine the date for the entrance examination for the coming academic session for admission to the PCL Nursing and Midwifery Programme.

Likewise, nursing processes, nursing care plan, nursing documentation and nursing evaluation, medicine management, infection control, patient safety, adverse incident management, routine nursing and midwifery practices would be mandatorily implemented in all hospitals. The Health Ministry would send a circular to all health institutions within a week to make arrangement of audit of RMC and strictly implement it as per the Safe Motherhood and Reproductive Health Rights Act, 2075 as well as the Nepal Nursing Council would monitor it.

title.rendered: 5 bathing habits that can harm your skin

content.rendered:
Many people believe that bathing frequently or scrubbing the body thoroughly with soap makes the skin healthier. However, the opposite can be true. Certain common bathing habits can strip away the skin’s natural oils and weaken its protective barrier.

As a result, the skin may become dry, tight, rough, and more sensitive. To keep your skin healthy and soft, it is important to bathe correctly, use a suitable cleanser, and apply a moisturiser promptly after bathing.

1. Bathing with very hot water

Many people enjoy taking long, hot showers, especially during cold weather. However, this habit can cause significant damage to the skin.

Hot water removes the skin’s natural oils, leaving it dry, tight, and sometimes flaky. Those who already have dry skin are particularly vulnerable to these effects.

A study published in the Journal of Clinical Medicine in 2022 found that prolonged exposure to very hot water weakens the skin’s protective barrier, increases water loss through evaporation, and contributes to dryness and redness.

2. Using harsh soaps and heavily fragranced products

Not all soaps are equally beneficial for the skin. Harsh chemical soaps, antibacterial soaps, and heavily fragranced body washes can weaken the skin’s protective barrier.

Regular use of such products may increase the risk of skin irritation, dryness, and allergic reactions. People with sensitive or dry skin are advised to choose mild, fragrance-free, skin-friendly cleansers.

Research published in Contact Dermatitis in 2021 found that fragranced skincare products are associated with a higher risk of allergic reactions, particularly among women and individuals with sensitive skin.

3. Scrubbing the skin too hard

Some people scrub their skin vigorously with a loofah, brush, or scrubber while bathing. Others rub their skin aggressively with a towel to dry it quickly.

This can cause minor damage to the outer layer of the skin, leading to irritation, redness, and dryness. Instead, dermatologists recommend gently patting the skin dry with a soft towel.

A study published in the Journal of Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nursing also reported that repeated vigorous scrubbing can damage the skin’s protective barrier.

4. Bathing too frequently

During hot weather, many people bathe two or three times a day because of excessive sweating. While this may provide temporary freshness, it also removes the skin’s natural oils more frequently.

Using soap every time can further reduce the skin’s moisture. If frequent bathing is necessary, use a mild cleanser and apply a moisturiser after every shower.

5. Skipping moisturiser after bathing

The skin retains some natural moisture immediately after bathing. Applying a moisturiser at this stage helps lock in that moisture and keeps the skin hydrated for longer.

If you wait too long to apply moisturiser, much of the skin’s moisture will already have evaporated. Therefore, applying a moisturiser within a few minutes after bathing is considered the most effective approach.

A 2022 study published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology found that moisturisers help maintain skin hydration and reduce excessive water loss.

Who should take extra care?

The following individuals should pay special attention to their bathing habits:

  • People with eczema
  • People with psoriasis
  • People with diabetes
  • Individuals with naturally dry skin
  • People with sensitive skin
  • Older adults, whose skin naturally loses moisture with age

Tips for healthy skin while bathing

A few simple changes to your bathing routine can help keep your skin healthy and well-hydrated:

  • Limit bathing time to 5–10 minutes.
  • Use lukewarm rather than very hot water.
  • Choose a mild, fragrance-free soap or cleanser.
  • Avoid scrubbing your skin aggressively with a loofah or brush.
  • Pat your skin dry gently with a soft towel instead of rubbing it.
  • Apply a moisturiser within 3–5 minutes after bathing.
  • If you need to bathe frequently because of excessive sweating, use a mild cleanser.
  • Make it a habit to apply moisturiser after every bath or shower.

title.rendered: Nepal Liquors CEO named Asia’s CEO of the Year

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 5

Nepal Liquors Pvt. Ltd. Chief Executive Officer Avanish Bir Singh Tuladhar has been honoured with the prestigious ‘CEO of the Year’ award at the Asia Business Leaders Awards held in Singapore.

The company said the recognition is a significant achievement for both Nepal Liquors and Nepal’s corporate sector, highlighting Nepalese executive leadership on an international platform. The annual awards recognise business leaders across Asia for visionary leadership, strategic innovation and transformational contributions to their industries.

Tuladhar assumed the role of CEO after serving as the company’s Director of Operations. According to Nepal Liquors, his leadership has combined the company’s longstanding legacy with innovation and a modern business approach. He studied at the University of Richmond and ESSEC Business School and has played a key role in introducing new market strategies and strengthening the company’s operations.

Expressing gratitude for the recognition, Tuladhar said the award belongs to the entire Nepal Liquors team whose dedication has driven the company’s success. He also dedicated the honour to the legacy of his late grandfather, Bhakta Bir Singh Tuladhar, and thanked his family for their continued support.

Founded in 1979, Nepal Liquors Pvt. Ltd. manufactures, blends and distributes alcoholic beverages in Nepal. The company is a franchise partner of global spirits producer Diageo and produces brands including Signature Whisky and Smirnoff Vodka.
