Kathmandu, August 2

Deepmala Dhakal has won the Miss Nepal 2026 title. She was crowned Miss Nepal World at the grand finale held on Saturday at The Plaza, Pulchowk, Lalitpur.

Arya Nishaant was named Miss Nepal International, and Kashis Subba was named Miss Nepal Cosmo. Miss Cosmo Yolina Lindquist was among those on the judging panel. The Hidden Treasure organised this year’s Miss Nepal pageant.

Dhakal also holds the title Miss Nepal Hong Kong International 2026. She works as an investment strategist at BlackRock, the globally renowned investment management firm.

She is also a black belt taekwondo athlete, runway model, international event host, and marathon runner.

Dhakal became the youngest-ever elected member in the history of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA).

She additionally serves as a goodwill ambassador for Nepal Cancer Hospital.

She has said her goal is to take her cancer-awareness campaign to an international level through the Miss World platform.

Her mother had also taken part in the first-ever Miss Nepal pageant, held in 1994.

title.rendered: Aman Karna’s “One Continuous Dream” concludes at Moksh

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, August 2

Musician and music producer Aman Karna’s show “One Continuous Dream” concluded on Friday at Moksh, Lalitpur.

The 95-minute show featured 21 songs, along with a live electronic audiovisual session of original, unreleased music. Karna was accompanied by other artists including Nattu Shah, Shailu Rai and Uttam Ghosh, Bikash SJB Rana and Adhishree Kaspal.

“Organising something like this as an independent artist takes a lot. Every ticket helps bring this to life with the amazing artists and team behind it,” Karna said. “I did this for the love of music, art and our creative community.”

Know more about Aman Karna

Aman Karna is a Kathmandu-based music producer who has worked across genres for more than two decades. He is known for his work with Fuzz Factory Productions and Jazzmandu, as well as with the Kathmandu-based indie band Phosphènes.

In 2020, he took a significant step in his solo career by releasing two EPs. His live performances have taken him across South Asia and Europe, with notable appearances in London, Berlin, Mumbai and Kathmandu.

With a rich background in diverse genres and a continued interest in pushing musical boundaries, Karna has been creating live sonic experiences with a multidisciplinary team of artists. “One Continuous Dream” grew out of sessions held earlier this year, in January and May, under the names “Body” and “Sketches.” The show has been in the works for several months and is billed as the first of its kind in the valley to be independently produced.

title.rendered: Bodies of Nirmal Purja and other climbers to be brought to Camp 1 today

content.rendered:
The team recovering the bodies of late Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja and other climbers who died in the avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak is preparing to descend to Camp 1 today.

According to the ground rescue team, the first phase of the operation involves bringing the bodies of those who lost their lives in the avalanche down to Camp 1. They are then expected to be moved to the Japanese Camp on Monday.

The ground team said that if weather and mountain conditions remain favourable, helicopters will be able to transport both the recovery team and the bodies from the Japanese Camp to a safer location.

The recovery team said every effort is being made to retrieve the bodies safely and repatriate them to their home countries with dignity.

Purja and nine other climbers had gone missing after the avalanche. Of the 10 victims, six were Nepali mountaineers. Purja’s death was officially confirmed only on Saturday.

The avalanche struck Broad Peak, the 8,047-metre mountain in Pakistan’s Karakoram, around midday on Thursday (July 30). Ten climbers, including six Nepalis, were caught in the avalanche. Purja was leading the expedition.

title.rendered: 18 suicides a day: Nepal’s overlooked public health crisis

content.rendered:
Recently, the country watched Ganesh Nepali die. A 25-year-old ride-hailing driver, carrying debt, supporting a family, preparing for foreign employment, fined Rs 1,000 over a wheel-locked motorcycle. He died at Bir Hospital a day after setting himself on fire outside the passport office. Since then, the argument has been about accountability: the municipal police, the metropolitan city, the Home Ministry. That argument matters and should continue.

But I keep sitting with a different question. How many people reach that same point in this country without a camera nearby? By police count, about 18 a day. Last fiscal year, 6,866 Nepalis died by suicide. The number was down slightly from the year before, and I have seen that reported as good news. Eighteen families a day is not good news.

Here is the statistic I want every policymaker in Singha Durbar to hold. The last time Nepal seriously studied why women of reproductive age die, suicide emerged as the single leading cause. Not childbirth. Not road accidents. Suicide. A fifth of those deaths were girls under 18. That study is from 2008/09, and researchers who have reviewed the evidence since have found no reason to believe the picture has improved. Sit with the second scandal inside the first: the finding is old enough to vote, and we have never repeated the study.

I have spent more than eight years working with women and children in Gandaki, and I can tell you what those numbers look like up close. The girl in our office living with violence at home. The survivor whose legal case will grind on for years while her community whispers. Suicide among Nepali women is rarely a separate problem from the ones we already know about. The research says what our case files say: it travels with domestic violence, with early marriage, with debt, with the particular loneliness of a young wife in a house where she has no allies. Young married women are among those most at risk in this country. That should reorganise how we think about both suicide and marriage.

And yet the official numbers, grim as they are, are almost certainly an undercount. Police data are what we have, and families have every reason not to report. For generations, attempting suicide was treated as a matter of shame and, in practice, punishment. The stigma has outlived the statutes. When a woman dies, communities often find a quieter story to tell. Researchers have been saying for years that the real burden, especially among women, is higher than the record shows.

To be fair, this is not a story of pure government neglect. In December, the Ministry of Health launched the National Mental Health Campaign with UNICEF and WHO, aimed at reducing stigma and helping families know where to seek support. The national suicide prevention helpline, 1166, is free and operational. A national strategy exists on paper. These are real steps, and the people behind them deserve credit.

But I work at the level where policy either arrives or does not, and I want to describe what has actually arrived. Nepal spends less than one per cent of its health budget on mental health. The country has roughly 0.2 psychiatrists per 100,000 people, nearly all of them in cities. More than 90 per cent of people with mental health conditions receive no treatment at all. In most of the municipalities where we work, there is no psychiatrist, no clinical psychologist, and no budget line for the community psychosocial workers who are, in practice, the entire mental health system for a rural woman in distress. When our counsellors visit a ward, we are frequently the first mental health service a woman has ever encountered. That is not a boast. It is an indictment of how thin the safety net is.

So, in the spirit of a government that likes measurable asks, here are three.

First, put the campaign’s money where the districts are. A national campaign that normalises help-seeking is only ethical if help exists when people seek it. Every municipality should have at least one trained, certified psychosocial counsellor with a protected budget line, not a project-funded post that vanishes when the donor cycle ends. We have watched trained counsellors leave the field twice because of funding gaps. Each departure costs exactly the trust that takes years to build.

Second, connect the systems that already touch the same person. The health post treats a woman’s injuries, the police register her complaint, the ward office’s judicial committee handles her case, and none of them screens for suicide risk or refers her to anyone who can help. Ganesh Nepali’s last interactions with the state were enforcement interactions: fines, a wheel lock, an argument. Every frontline official, municipal police included, is a potential first responder to despair, and almost none of them has been given even an hour’s training or a number to call. Judicial committees, one-stop crisis centres, and yes, city enforcement units should have referral protocols to services as standard, not as an NGO’s improvisation.

Third, count better, and count women. A suicide prevention office that relies solely on police mortality data will keep designing policy for a fraction of the problem. Commission a successor to the 2008/09 maternal mortality study. Add community-level surveillance and attempted-suicide data from hospitals. Honest research into why young married women are dying would give the new mental health office something it currently lacks: an accurate map less than two decades old.

Nepal’s young government talks fluently about execution rates and digital dashboards. Good. Then measure this: eighteen a day. The country saw one of those deaths recently and has not stopped talking about it. The other seventeen that day belonged to families who will mostly stay silent. Of all the numbers in this country’s ledgers, this is the one most worth driving down.

If you or someone you know is struggling, the National Suicide Prevention Helpline is 1166. The call is free.

title.rendered: Kathmandu Metro: Shaping the Future of Nepal’s capital city

content.rendered:
Thousands of Kathmandu residents’ morning journeys to either work or school are caught in some of the most horrendous congestion and painfully slow-moving traffic that never seems to go anywhere. As the city’s population continues to grow by 3%, according to numerous online reports, it shows that if we are already facing these issues now, and the roads can no longer accommodate the increasing traffic, can Kathmandu truly continue to rely on its roads alone?

Take a moment to truly think and examine the situation. Have you ever had a pleasant journey on your way to work?

One solution to address Nepal’s current road and transport issues is to build a metro system. As the chairperson of the Society of Nepalese Engineers and the owner of a project management consultancy that has worked in the metro industry, I have always reflected on Nepal’s public transport industry. Especially between my meetings in Kathmandu, when I get stuck in traffic, I can’t help but think: in a city with over one million people living, why isn’t there a Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) system? It’s something nearly all major cities with a high population have incorporated.

Hence, I remember that after returning to Kathmandu in 2023, I decided to create a proposed metro route map. My approach was to adopt a phased construction strategy, making the project more practical and financially achievable. The initial proposal centred around five strategically located stations: Sinamangal/Koteshwor, Kalanki, Narayan Gopal Chowk, Lagankhel, and Bhrikutimandap.

Based on my estimates, the metro would have cost approximately US$1.5 billion with a 19.65km route. In an interview with Nepali Link UK on 24 September 2025, I outlined this vision for a phased metro system and explained why these five stations were selected as the foundation of the network. You can see the proposed route plan in the image attached to this article.

You might be wondering why I chose these five stations first. First and foremost, I strongly believe that a phased construction approach is essential. It allows Nepal to identify and address challenges as they arise. While we can certainly learn from other countries’ experiences, Nepal faces unique circumstances, including differences in the availability of construction materials, engineering capabilities, and the local workforce.

Secondly, these five stations were carefully selected because they serve the areas experiencing the highest levels of traffic congestion. Together, they provide coverage across the Valley, connecting the central, eastern, western, northern, and southern parts of Kathmandu. This ensures that the first phase delivers the greatest possible benefit while laying the foundation for future expansion.

I often hear critics ask, “Why not simply widen the roads?” It is a reasonable question, but after speaking with a plethora of engineering institutions and transport professionals in Nepal, the consensus has been clear: Kathmandu’s road network has already been stretched close to its practical limits. In many parts of the city, there is simply no room for further expansion without significant social, environmental, and economic consequences.

I remember discussing this very topic with my family over dinner. My daughter suggested, “Why not build a tram system like the ones in Manchester?” It was an interesting idea, and one that prompted a thoughtful conversation. However, Nepal’s geographical and geological conditions present unique challenges. As a country highly susceptible to earthquakes, any damage or displacement of tram tracks could compromise safety and disrupt the network.

A metro system, particularly one designed with modern seismic engineering standards, offers a more resilient and reliable long-term solution. Also, a tram cannot carry as many passengers per day as a metro, which can serve 250,000-350,000 passengers per day if the metro is fully functioning. But in the proposed route of mine, with five stations per day, it can definitely house 50,000-75,000 people. Even if a modest number of Kathmandu residents shifted from private vehicles to the metro, peak traffic volume could decrease by 10-15% according to transport modelling studies.

It is also important to recognise that a metro is not built solely to combat traffic congestion. While reducing congestion is one of its greatest advantages, a metro also improves connectivity, shortens travel times, stimulates economic growth, reduces air pollution, and provides a safe and dependable form of public transport for future generations.

Now you may be wondering how we may begin? How will we get the finances? What other benefits are we getting besides environmental benefits, i.e., reduction of carbon emissions?

First and foremost, to begin the metro project, we must clearly define the scope and establish how we will secure the necessary funding. I have been following multiple news outlets reporting that the Government of Nepal has opened discussions regarding the development of a metro project. Therefore, I believe defining the scope from the very beginning is essential to ensure the project has a clear direction and realistic objectives.

From the information I have gathered through the news outlets, the Honourable Minister for Infrastructure Development, Sunil Lamal, has highlighted Nepal’s development goals and mentioned that the government plans to rely heavily on private sector participation and foreign investment rather than depending solely on internal state budgets.

Hence, it will be imperative for the government and key stakeholders to establish a clear funding structure for the project. The latest major metro project in South Asia was the Dhaka Metro Line, which had a construction cost of approximately US$2.71 billion. The project was funded through a combination of support from the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), which contributed around 58% of the funding, while the remaining portion was provided by the Government of Bangladesh.

Nepal could consider adopting a similar funding model. However, given the scale of investment required, it is important to recognise that the current government may not have the capacity to independently provide hundreds of millions of dollars towards the project. Therefore, a strong partnership between the public and private sectors through a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model could be essential in securing the required funding.

Under such a model, the government could take responsibility for areas such as land acquisition, utility relocation, and administrative infrastructure, while the private sector could contribute financial capital, technical expertise, and project management capabilities.

Some critics may argue that PPP partnerships and foreign-funded infrastructure projects have not always been viewed positively, particularly following concerns surrounding projects such as Pokhara International Airport, which has raised discussions about financial sustainability and the burden placed on Nepali taxpayers. To prevent similar challenges, it is vital that the Government of Nepal, if it is serious about delivering this project, establishes strong oversight mechanisms. This could include appointing independent international watchdogs and experts to critically review the design, costs, feasibility, and long-term sustainability of the project.

Once the financial framework has been established, the Government of Nepal may also need to remain flexible regarding the proposed route during the design phase. As engineers and stakeholders, we may not always be able to identify every challenge at the initial stage. Detailed studies and consultations are essential to identify potential issues and ensure that the final design is practical, efficient, and sustainable.

Once the financial structure and implementation strategy are established, it is equally important to consider the wider economic benefits that a metro system could bring to Nepal. As I have been involved in several charitable organisations, serving as the Chairperson of SONEUK and a Trustee of the Subodh Foundation UK, I have had the opportunity to speak with many Nepali students and young professionals. During these conversations, one message has been consistent: if there were a major infrastructure project in Nepal where they could apply their skills and contribute to the country’s development, many would return without hesitation.

In 2022, The Kathmandu Post reported that approximately 500,000 Nepalis moved abroad, with roughly 80% doing so permanently. A large-scale infrastructure project such as the Kathmandu Metro would not only strengthen Nepal’s transport network but also encourage talented members of the Nepali diaspora to return home and contribute their expertise. It would create opportunities for engineers, planners, architects, lawyers, project managers, and countless other professionals, while also allowing skilled construction workers who have gained valuable experience overseas to apply their knowledge in Nepal.

The economic benefits extend beyond employment. According to the Journal of Economic Impact Nepal, traffic congestion costs the country approximately US$165 million each year. By providing a fast, reliable, and efficient alternative to private vehicles, a metro system has the potential to significantly reduce these losses while improving productivity and supporting long-term economic growth.

I have witnessed the value of investing in young professionals in the United Kingdom. At Heathrow Airport, a significant proportion of the workforce is made up of millennials and younger generations, bringing fresh ideas, increased productivity, and a culture of innovation. Empowering young people to take part in transformative infrastructure projects has not only benefited the organisation but has also strengthened the wider community. Nepal has the same potential. What is needed is the opportunity to harness the talent, ambition, and dedication of its young people through projects that shape the nation’s future.

I often imagine a young person twenty years from now. Instead of walking from Ason to Pulchowk Engineering Campus, enduring a two-hour journey by car, or asking a friend for a lift on their scooter, they simply board the metro and arrive at university in just twenty minutes.

That is what a metro truly delivers. It is not merely a means of transport; it provides a safe, reliable, and peaceful way to travel. It gives people something increasingly precious in modern life. Time to study, time to work, and time to spend with family rather than sitting in endless traffic.

A metro does far more than stimulate economic growth. It improves the quality of everyday life. By encouraging people to shift from private vehicles to efficient public transport, it reduces congestion, lowers stress on our roads, improves air quality, and creates a more connected and productive city. Ultimately, investing in a metro is not simply investing in infrastructure; it is investing in the future well-being of the people of Kathmandu.

As of mid-2026, Kathmandu has reached a crossroads. The city’s population shows no signs of declining. Instead, with the growing optimism surrounding Nepal’s future, it is encouraging to see more young people and members of the Nepali diaspora expressing a willingness to return and contribute to the country’s development in whatever capacity they can. As Kathmandu continues to grow, the demand for a modern and efficient public transport system will only increase. This makes the metro not merely an ambitious proposal, but an essential project for the future of the capital.

Therefore, I believe the time to make the Kathmandu Metro a national priority is now. Delaying such a project will only result in higher construction costs, greater congestion, and increased pressure on an already overstretched road network. I know I have heard critics argue that Kathmandu’s soil conditions are not suitable for a metro system. To that, I would say that these are engineering challenges, not engineering barriers. Modern techniques such as ground improvement technology, detailed geotechnical investigations, and advanced tunnelling methods have enabled metro systems to be successfully constructed in some of the world’s most challenging environments.

If countries such as Japan and Chile, both highly susceptible to earthquakes and complex geological conditions, can safely design and operate metro systems, there is no reason Nepal cannot do the same. The challenge is not whether it can be built, but whether we have the vision and determination to build it.

title.rendered: All 10 climbers killed in Broad Peak avalanche, including Nirmal Purja

content.rendered:
August 1, Kathmandu

The deaths of all 10 climbers, including renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja, have been officially confirmed following Thursday’s avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan’s Karakoram mountain range.

Four bodies were recovered on Friday, while the remaining six climbers had initially been reported missing. On Saturday, Nimsdai Foundation and Elite Exped, both founded by Purja, officially announced through social media that all 10 climbers had died.

Among the victims were six Nepali climbers, including former British Gurkha Nirmal Purja, popularly known as Nimsdai, who was born in Dana, Myagdi. The other Nepali victims are Pur Bahadur Gurung, Nima Sherpa, Kili Pemba Sherpa, Gyalu Sherpa, and Nawang Thindu Sherpa.

The four foreign climbers who died were Sohel Shakhi of Pakistan, Wang Zhong of China, Nadira Ahmad of Oman, and Mallory Geis of the United States.

Purja rose to global prominence in 2019 after setting a world record by climbing all 14 peaks above 8,000 meters in just six months and six days. He went on to achieve several other notable mountaineering records.

The avalanche reportedly swept the climbers nearly 800 meters downhill from an altitude of more than 6,000 meters. Rescue efforts were severely hampered by poor weather conditions.

House of Representatives member Mingma Gyabu (David) Sherpa, who was also Purja’s business associate, left for Pakistan on Friday.

Among the deceased Nepali climbers, Pur Bahadur Gurung was from Gorkha, Kili Pemba Sherpa from Dolakha, Gyalu Sherpa from Okhaldhunga, and Nawang Thindu Sherpa and Nima Sherpa were from Sankhuwasabha.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Balendra Shah has expressed his heartfelt tribute to Nirmal Purja and all the climbers who lost their lives in the tragedy.

title.rendered: Microfinance borrowers say debt trap left them landless

content.rendered:
Photos: Bikash Shrestha

For the past several days, an unusual scene has unfolded near Maitighar in the federal capital.

A large crowd of women from Nepal’s Tarai region has gathered along one side of the road. Most are dressed in yellow saris and green blouses, giving passersby the impression that they may be attending a religious event.

But the women have come from various Tarai districts after abandoning their homes and livelihoods, hoping the government—not pedestrians—would understand their suffering and deliver justice.

Even after arriving in Kathmandu, they saw little sign of progress, and they say the government has largely ignored them. Left with no alternative, the women, most of them small-scale farmers from low-income households, began an indefinite hunger strike on Tuesday.

The monsoon has made their protest even more difficult. Whenever it rains, they seek shelter under plastic sheets and tarpaulins. Protesters say security personnel have prevented them from erecting proper shelters, forcing them to cover themselves with plastic during downpours. They cook, eat and sleep on the roadside at Maitighar.

The women, from districts including Siraha, Saptari and Dhanusha, say they were pushed into financial ruin by microfinance institutions and have come to Kathmandu demanding justice.

They say they initially took group-guaranteed loans from microfinance institutions to start or expand small businesses and improve their financial condition. Instead, mounting debt has left many of them landless, forcing them to resort to an indefinite hunger strike as their final option.

One protester said she chose the hunger strike because she would rather fight for justice than take her own life. According to her, around 1,500 victims of microfinance-related debt have died by suicide since 2018.

“Microfinance institutions, which were supposed to improve the lives of the poor, drove us into the hands of loan sharks. The loan sharks made us landless,” she said. “What kind of government cannot even implement a Supreme Court order?”

Many protesters share similar stories.

Shilam Yadav of Bardibas, Mahottari, says she has been dealing with microfinance institutions since 2018 and has now become landless.

A mother of three, Yadav previously ran a cosmetics shop. She says that after borrowing to expand her business, she eventually lost not only her home and farmland but also the shop itself.

She said Divya Microfinance Financial Institution had recently begun operating in Bardibas and was issuing loans based simply on citizenship certificates. After employees told her she qualified, she applied for a loan of Rs 50,000.

“They promised Rs 50,000 and said they would increase the amount if I repaid regularly,” Yadav said. “They never asked about my income, source of earnings or business. They only took a copy of my citizenship certificate and a photograph. A few days later, they called me to the office and handed me Rs 46,000.”

According to Yadav, the institution deducted Rs 4,000 as service and insurance fees but calculated interest on the full Rs 50,000.

Although she invested the money in expanding her shop, business did not improve as expected.

“My monthly sales were only around Rs 5,000 to Rs 10,000, just enough to support my family. Then I had to pay a monthly instalment of Rs 5,000 to the microfinance institution. My income was no longer enough to cover the repayments,” she said.

At the same time, new microfinance institutions continued opening branches and encouraged residents to become members. To repay one loan, she began borrowing from another institution and eventually became a borrower at nearly a dozen microfinance companies.

Yadav says borrowers are often accused of deliberately avoiding repayment.

She said the institutions organised borrowers into groups of 10. If one member failed to pay an instalment, the savings of the other nine members were deducted.

When she was unable to make repayments, fellow group members allegedly came to her house and took valuables, including jewellery, a television, cupboards, tables, beds and chairs. Even her livestock was not spared, she said.

“I did borrow money, and I also repaid it,” Yadav said. “But to repay one institution, I had to borrow from another. Eventually I borrowed from eight to ten institutions. In the end, I took loans from loan sharks to settle the accounts. Microfinance institutions created the loan-shark problem. If I borrowed Rs100,000, I had to pay Rs10,000 every week.”

Yadav says she borrowed a total of Rs1.5 to Rs1.6 million. She still owes around Rs1 million. She claims the loan sharks eventually locked her shop.

“My shop remained closed for six months. I also owed Rs 50,000 in rent, and the landlord locked the room,” she said.

She says she lost seven tolas of gold, sold one and a half katthas of land, and now lives in a landless settlement. She also had to sell her shop for just Rs 30,000.

“I have already repaid Rs1.8 million to loan sharks and another Rs700,000 to microfinance institutions, yet I still owe Rs1 million. That is why I joined the protest.”

The experience of Yubraj Rasaili of Mahottari is similar.

He said he borrowed from several institutions, including Asha Microfinance, Forward Microfinance, Mero Microfinance, Bijaya Microfinance, Naya Nepal and Infinity Microfinance, to buy a Tata Sumo vehicle.

Soon after purchasing the vehicle, Nepal entered a COVID-19 lockdown. Rasaili invested his remaining money in vegetable farming, but the lockdown prevented him from operating the vehicle or selling his produce.

“For six months I could not operate the vehicle. I could not take my vegetables to market, and the crops rotted in the fields,” he said.

After the lockdown, he says microfinance institutions stopped issuing new loans and instead pressured borrowers to repay, threatening to seize vehicles, lock homes and even telling them to prepare death certificates.

“I borrowed from loan sharks to keep making repayments,” Rasaili said. He alleges that because of the system, borrowers who take Rs1 million from loan sharks end up repaying as much as Rs10 million through weekly interest payments.

Unable to repay both the loan sharks and the microfinance instalments, he says his house was locked. He eventually sold both his vehicle and his 10 dhur plot of registered land to repay debts.

Tara Pandey of Palpa says she also fell victim to what she describes as deceptive lending practices.

According to her, microfinance institutions prepared loan agreements for Rs100,000 but handed borrowers only Rs80,000 while charging interest on the full amount.

Although the institutions advertised interest rates of around 15 per cent, she says borrowers effectively paid between 36 and 52 per cent.

She initially borrowed Rs100,000 but eventually found herself dealing with 13 different institutions in an effort to repay earlier loans.

Pandey said she sold her residential plot five years ago to clear her debts and has been living in rented accommodation ever since.

“I lost the money I had saved to build a house, and I lost my land as well,” she said.

She had originally borrowed to raise goats. She says loan officers visited her home to issue the loan but returned to collect monthly instalments before a full month had even passed.

According to Pandey, the institutions also used her goat farm as an example while extending loans to others. She believes their main objective was simply to issue as many loans as possible.

Talks between the protesters and the government have been described as positive but ended without a conclusion. The Ministry of Finance said negotiations would resume on Friday, and discussions are continuing.

The protesters say they launched the indefinite hunger strike because the government has failed to implement a Supreme Court mandamus ordering authorities to address the grievances of microfinance victims.

The Supreme Court had directed the government, Nepal Rastra Bank and the Microfinance Bankers’ Association to implement an agreement aimed at resolving the problems faced by borrowers. Protesters say that despite the court’s order and implementation directive, the government has shown little interest, leaving them with no option but to continue their protest despite the rain.

title.rendered: Bodies of Sunsari police shooting victims released after government-family agreement

content.rendered:
Biratnagar, July 31

The bodies of those killed in the Dewanganj incident in Sunsari have been removed from Neuro Hospital in Biratnagar.

According to police, the bodies of Om Prakash Mehta and Jai Prakash Mehta were released after their relatives arrived to claim them.

The bodies will be taken to Koshi Hospital for post-mortem examinations. After the autopsies are completed, they will be handed over to the families.

Om Prakash and Jai Prakash Mehta, both residents of Kaptanganj, Ward No. 3 of Dewanganj Rural Municipality, were killed after being shot by police on Sunday night.

The families agreed to receive the bodies after reaching a seven-point agreement with the government earlier on Friday morning.

title.rendered: Mountaineer Pur Bahadur Gurung passes away on Broad Peak

content.rendered:
The death of well-known mountaineer Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta) during an attempt to climb Pakistan’s 8,047-metre Broad Peak has been confirmed. The Alpine Club of Pakistan confirmed the news. According to the club, the bodies of four people were found, among them an Omani climber, Nadhira Al Harthy, and Nepali climber Pur Bahadur Gurung, both of whom were identified. The Alpine Club of Pakistan is the official body overseeing mountaineering in the country. The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association has also confirmed that Yukta lost his life in an avalanche on the peak.

Who was Yukta?

Born in Lapu Village, Dharche Rural Municipality-4 in northern Gorkha, he spent his childhood in the shadow of the Himalayas. Born in 1989, he had once dreamed of joining the British Army. With that dream cut short by the armed conflict, he left home at a young age to work at a hotel in Manang, where he came into contact with trekking guides and, drawn to the idea of becoming one himself, moved to Kathmandu.

“He started as a porter in 2009,” said his colleague Tulsi Singh Gurung. “Gradually he began working as a kitchen helper for camping groups.”

From there, he moved up to assistant guide, then trekking guide, and eventually planning guide, Tulsi Singh said. According to him, Yukta had passed the International Mountain Guide certification only this past December.

“He had qualified as an International Mountain Guide through the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, but today we had to hear this tragic news,” he says. Tulsi Singh, who is also from Lapu, serves as the association’s president.

Yukta had summited Everest more times than anyone from the Gurung community, with ten successful ascents to his name. He first climbed Everest in 2011. He had also successfully climbed 12 of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks.

“There are 14 peaks in the world above 8,000 metres, eight of which are in Nepal,” Tulsi Singh says. “He had climbed all but two of them.”

He had also set a record by summiting Pakistan’s K2 within 24 hours. He was regularly involved in rescue operations for tourists stranded in the mountains.

Having grown up in the mountains, he met his end there too, at the age of 37. He had left Nepal three weeks earlier to attempt Broad Peak in Pakistan, a journey from which he would never return.

title.rendered: Grieving father of teen killed in Siraha protest demands justice

content.rendered:
Siraha. Shrawan 15

Fifteen-year-old Ganesh Yadav was killed on Thursday during protests that erupted in Siraha over the Sunsari incident. He died after being shot by police in Golbazar. Ganesh was a resident of Tulsipur-Motipur in Aurahi Rural Municipality-2.

His death has plunged his family into grief. His father, Rambriksh Yadav, says those responsible for killing his son must be identified and brought to justice.

Sitting at his home in Tulsipur-Motipur, Aurahi Rural Municipality-2, the grieving father repeatedly asks, “Where is my son? Who killed him?”

Forty-two-year-old Rambriksh has worked as a driver at a local brick kiln for the past eight years. He says he does not want financial assistance in exchange for his son’s life but only legal action against the person who pulled the trigger.

“We are poor people. I don’t want anything. I don’t want money. The person who shot my son should be identified, made public, and prosecuted according to the law. That is my only demand,” he said emotionally.

Rambriksh had previously spent four years working at a plastic factory in Malaysia. After falling ill, he returned to Nepal and has since supported his family by working as a driver in his village.

He has two sons and a daughter. His elder son, Kamlesh, and younger son, Ganesh, were both students at Mount Everest Secondary Boarding School in Golbazar. For the past two years, the brothers had been living in rented accommodation in Golbazar to attend school.

On the day of the incident, Ganesh called home. His mother repeatedly urged him not to go near the protests. He reassured her, saying, “I won’t join the protest, Mom. I’ll only go to watch.” But the teenager who went “just to watch” became a victim of gunfire.

Rambriksh said residents informed him that Home Minister Sudhan Gurung was expected to visit the family.

“I’ve heard the Home Minister is coming, and I’m waiting for him. I will ask him too: Where is my son? Who killed him? Where is the culprit? When will those responsible be brought before the law? When will we get justice? What harm had my son done to anyone?” he said.

The family’s youngest child, 11-year-old Manisha Kumari Yadav, is a fourth-grade student. Rambriksh, the family’s sole breadwinner, is now burdened not only with supporting his family but also with the unbearable grief of losing his son.

Residents Phooljhari Devi Yadav and Shanti Devi Mandal said the death of an innocent teenager has left the entire village in mourning. They have urged the government to conduct an impartial investigation, identify the person who fired the fatal shot, and make that information public.

They are also demanding legal action against those responsible, adequate compensation for the bereaved family, and employment for one member of the family.

The family says its anguish has been compounded by the lack of clear information about the condition of Ganesh’s body and the full circumstances surrounding the incident.

title.rendered: Nepali national killed in drone attack in Kuwait

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 31

The Embassy of Nepal in Kuwait has confirmed the tragic death of an innocent Nepali national in a drone attack in northern Kuwait. The deceased is Som Kumar Tamang, 44, of Tehrathum district.

Likewise, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has condemned this indiscriminate attack against civilians and has called upon all parties concerned to engage in dialogue and diplomacy, exercise the utmost restraint and to ensure the safety, security and protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with their obligations under international law.

The Ministry has underscored the imperative of full respect for and strict adherence to the Geneva Conventions and applicable rules of international humanitarian law under all circumstances. In a press release, the Ministry extended deep condolences to the bereaved family of the deceased and expressed commitment to providing all necessary assistance, including facilitating the earliest possible repatriation of the mortal remains of the deceased.

title.rendered: ‘Miss Menuka’ opens at Shilpee Theatre (Photo Feature)

content.rendered:
The play Miss Menuka: A Sensitive Sex Worker has begun its run at Shilpee Theatre in Battisputali. The Nepali adaptation of the French play La Putain Respectueuse has been staged since Shrawan 13 (July 29).

The original play was written by Jean-Paul Sartre. The Nepali adaptation has been translated by Kalpana Ghimire Nourisson, while the production is directed by Pabitra Khadka.

The story follows Menuka, a sex worker who witnesses an incident while travelling on a bus. To protect the real culprit, influential figures attempt to coerce her into falsely accusing an innocent man of trying to rape her. The police also side with those in power and pressure her to give a fabricated statement. Later, the innocent man approaches Menuka for help in saving his life. What unfolds next forms the central plot of the play.

The production explores how communal discrimination, cultural prejudice, social injustice, gender discrimination, political corruption, and the abuse of power undermine truth and justice.

The cast includes Sarita Giri, Ghimire Yubaraj, Rupesh Mandal, Prabhakar Dev Sharma, Dhanraj Sunar, and Govinda, among others.

The play will continue its run until August 22.

title.rendered: Chhurpi export up by 27 per cent; transaction reaches Rs 1.79 billion in a year

content.rendered:
Bhadrapur (Jhapa), July 31

Chhurpi amounting to over Rs 1.79 billion and 2.8 million has been exported from the Mechi Customs Office in the last year alone. With the rise in demand for Nepali Chhurpi products in the international market, the export in the last fiscal year has increased by around 27 per cent compared to the previous fiscal year.

title.rendered: Four bodies recovered after avalanche strikes Nirmal Purja’s expedition team on Broad Peak

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 31

Ground rescue teams have recovered four bodies following a devastating avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak (8,047 m), which hit a 10-member international climbing expedition led by world-renowned Nepal-born mountaineer Nirmal Purja, popularly known as “Nims Dai.”

The recovery was confirmed in an Instagram update by Irfan Khan, President of the Alpine Club of Pakistan. Khan stated that while four bodies have been retrieved from the avalanche site so far, authorities have not yet confirmed their identities. The entire 10-member team lost contact after being caught in the disaster.

Rescue helicopters carrying specialised personnel and high-altitude equipment are currently operating on the mountain alongside ground teams to locate the remaining climbers.

The missing 10-member team includes high-profile international climbers alongside experienced Nepali high-altitude guides:

  • Nirmal Purja “Nims Dai” (Nepal – Expedition Leader)
  • Pur Bahadur Gurung “Yukta” (Nepal)
  • Kili Pemba Sherpa “Kilu” (Nepal)
  • Nima Sherpa (Nepal)
  • Nawang Thindu Sherpa (Nepal)
  • Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy (Oman)
  • Sohail Sakhi (Pakistan)
  • Wang Zhong (China)
  • Mallory Geis (USA)

“Rescue helis are on Broad Peak with rescuers and equipment. Meanwhile, four bodies have been found by ground rescue teams so far,” Khan shared in his post.

title.rendered: Nirmal Purja-led team loses contact after avalanche on Broad Peak

content.rendered:
A 10-member international climbing team led by world-renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja alias Nims Dai has lost contact after being caught in an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.

According to the BBC, an avalanche struck the 8,047-metre Broad Peak in Pakistan’s Karakoram range around midday on Thursday. Pakistani mountaineering officials said there has been no contact with the team since then.

The team includes one American, one Chinese, one Omani, and five Nepali citizens. Team leader Nirmal Purja set a world record in 2019 by summiting all 14 of the world’s peaks above 8,000 metres in just over six months.

Officials said preparations are underway to deploy helicopters for search and rescue if weather conditions permit.

Broad Peak, the world’s 12th-highest mountain, is considered one of the most challenging peaks to climb.

The Alpine Club of Pakistan issued a statement saying efforts are underway to launch an immediate search and rescue operation in continuous coordination with government agencies. The club said every effort is being made to mobilise all available resources, including helicopters, as quickly as possible.

The club wished for the safe rescue of all the climbers and expressed solidarity with their families and the international mountaineering community during this difficult time.

Nirmal Purja joined the British Army in 2003 and became a Royal Marine in 2009. He became drawn to mountaineering during a 2012 trek to Everest Base Camp; although he initially planned to return after reaching base camp, he changed his mind and went on to successfully summit Everest. In 2019, he climbed the world’s 14 tallest peaks in just six months – the shortest amount of time anyone has done that. Since then, he has established himself as one of the world’s best-known mountaineers.

Banana farmers not benefited despite price hike in local market

content.rendered:
Sudurpaschim, July 30

The farmers in Kailali and Kanchanpur districts have urged the government for market monitoring, citing an unusual rise in product prices in the retail market. At a press conference organised today by the Banana Producers’ Association, Kailali, and the Banana Producers and Business Association, Kailali, they called for stronger market monitoring, stating that they are selling bananas at Rs 60 to Rs 65 per dozen, while consumers are being charged higher prices in the local market.

Issuing a press statement after the media briefing, the associations expressed confidence that the government’s decision would contribute to banana production, safeguard farmers’ interests and strengthen food security. Banana farming is carried out on around 2,000 hectares of land in Sudurpaschim Province, producing nearly 72,000 metric tonnes of bananas annually.

title.rendered: In Dewanganj’s tense hours, the Home Minister stays away

content.rendered:
Sunsari’s Dewanganj area has been tense since Sunday night, after a dispute over a flag placed at a local intersection turned into a clash. Local administration has deployed a large number of security personnel to calm the tension at the village level. While no unpleasant incident has occurred so far, both sides remain dissatisfied and tense, according to the local administration. The effects of the tension seen in Dewanganj have also spread to some other districts in Madhesh.

To normalise the situation in Dewanganj, locals have demanded the presence of political leadership. According to Dewanganj Rural Municipality Chairperson Bechan Prasad Mehta, locals have demanded that the home minister come to the site himself to address the problem.

Shiva Kumar Yadav, a resident of Dewanganj-3, also said locals expect the home minister and prime minister to visit in order to normalise the situation in the village.

However, Yadav says locals are unhappy that Home Minister Sudan Gurung, who has gone to border points and hotels in the name of monitoring, did not come to the site during this sensitive time.

Although the home minister has not visited the site so far, he has sent his chief personal secretary (PA), James Karki, to Dewanganj. Along with Karki, Paras Chhetri, personal secretary to Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal, has also gone there.

They arrived in Sunsari on Tuesday evening and reached the Dewanganj area along with a drone. Their team also monitored the site on Wednesday.

At an all-party meeting held Wednesday evening, Karki represented the home minister and presented the government’s position. He said the home minister and Prime Minister Balen Shah were serious and concerned about the incident, and that the government was committed to resolving the problem.

At the meeting, however, Chairperson Mehta argued that the central leadership needed to come to the village itself to understand the real situation.

“They need to come to the village and understand the real situation. It’s not enough to stay in Kathmandu; they must go to the site and talk,” he says. “It’s been four days; what facilities have people received from the ministry? What has the government done?”

He expressed dissatisfaction, alleging that the Home Ministry’s representative and the Chief District Officer had not answered his calls at the time of the incident.

“If the Chief District Officer doesn’t even pick up when the municipality chair calls, how are people supposed to feel the government’s presence?” he asks.

He urged government representatives to go to the site itself and talk with locals. In response, Karki said he had come precisely to have that dialogue, and that the focus now needed to shift toward a solution.

At the all-party meeting, Chairperson Mehta demanded that the deceased be declared a martyr, that the injured receive free treatment, that the madrasa in Kaptanganj be properly managed, and that those responsible for the incident be prosecuted. He said these demands needed to be addressed by the home minister in person in Dewanganj.

In response, the home minister’s chief personal secretary, James Karki, said the government was ready to move forward with the demands, including the martyr declaration, through the legal process. He said the home minister would also visit Dewanganj once all sides reached agreement.

Although clashes and tension persisted from Sunday night through Tuesday night, the situation in Dewanganj has been comparatively calm since Wednesday. A large security presence has been deployed given the potential risk. The curfew remains in effect until Thursday morning, with further decisions to be made based on an assessment of the situation, according to the local administration.

Five-point collective commitment

To normalise the situation following the clash in Kaptanganj, the all-party meeting reached a five-point decision.

The meeting, attended by political parties, security agencies, and stakeholders, paid tribute to the deceased and urged all sides to exercise restraint.

Expressing regret over the communal tension and unrest seen in various parts of the district following the Dewanganj incident, the meeting decided that all sides would take initiative from their respective positions to prevent anarchy and unwanted activity from spreading in society.

The public has been urged not to post or share misleading or provocative content on social media, and to trust only official information.

Similarly, parents have been asked to instruct their children not to go out unnecessarily, not to take part in any clash or crowd, and to exercise restraint.

Since the curfew order issued by the local administration remains in effect, gatherings, processions, and demonstrations are banned.

DSP Chandra Bahadur Khadka, spokesperson for the District Police Office, Sunsari, said the district’s situation is improving but has not yet fully returned to normal.

title.rendered: Passport seekers crowd Kathmandu’s Passport Department (Photos)

content.rendered:
A long queue of people has formed in Kathmandu to issue passports.

The crowd has gathered at the Department of Passports in Tripureshwor, Kathmandu, with young men and women making up most of the line.

The department said the arrangement was made to make services more accessible after the number of applicants for South Korea’s EPS program rose sharply over the past week.

According to the department, the first shift will run from 7 am to 2 pm and the second from 2 pm to 9 pm, from July 30 to August 7.

Similarly, the department said it would provide electronic passport services on Saturdays, Sundays, and other public holidays. On public holidays, services will run from 10 am to 4 pm, according to the department’s notice.

The rise in passport seekers has come alongside the increase in EPS applicants, since a passport is mandatory to proceed with the employment process in South Korea, a trend the department says has driven the surge in demand for passport services over the past week.

The department said the extended hours and two-shift system were arranged to manage the growing crowd and ensure timely service.

title.rendered: Trapped behind the scam: The new face of human trafficking

content.rendered:
A dream job abroad. A free air ticket. A salary several times higher than what a young person could earn in Nepal.

For a growing number of youth, that dream has ended behind the locked gates of scam compounds in Cambodia, Myanmar and elsewhere in Southeast Asia. Their passports and phones are confiscated, and they are forced to work long hours carrying out online fraud. Those who resist reportedly face threats, violence, starvation and torture.

The trafficking of Nepali youth into online scam operations has emerged as a rapidly growing form of transnational crime. Most victims travel on tourist visas, bypassing Nepal’s official foreign employment system and its screening mechanisms, allowing traffickers to operate with less scrutiny. The rise in Nepali tourist arrivals in Cambodia, from 101 in 2021 to 9,676 in 2025, illustrates the growing scale of this route.

This is the disturbing reality behind this year’s World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, observed on 30 July under the theme “Trapped Behind the Scam”. It draws attention to organised criminal networks that use digital technology to recruit, transport and exploit people in online scam centres.

Scam trafficking combines human trafficking with cyber-enabled fraud on an unprecedented scale. It generates enormous profits for criminal networks while devastating the lives of thousands of youths. It is not only a technology-facilitated crime, but also a failure of prevention, protection and accountability. It is a serious transnational crime that requires stronger international cooperation. 

According to INTERPOL’s 2025 Global Crime Trend Update, as of March 2025, victims from 66 countries had been trafficked into online scam centres, with 74% taken to compounds in Southeast Asia. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) estimates that online scam operations generated between US$88.3 billion and US$114.1 billion across the Asia-Pacific region in 2025. These criminal enterprises are closely linked to human trafficking, cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering and other forms of transnational organised crime, making them one of the fastest-growing global security threats.

Scam trafficking and Nepali youth

On December 10, 2025, 47 Nepalis, including two women and a 17-year-old, were rescued from scam compounds in Myanmar and repatriated to Kathmandu. Many had completed high school, and some had information technology backgrounds. On 25 March 2026, another 51 Nepalis trafficked to Cambodia through fraudulent job offers were repatriated with support from the Nepali Embassy in Thailand, the Cambodian government and Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) Cambodia. They had been lured by promises of well-paid jobs in customer service, digital marketing and information technology, then forced into online scams and casino-linked fraud. Some had also lost or had their passports confiscated.

Nepal Police data show that 422 Nepalis, including 400 men and 22 women, had been rescued from scam compounds in Cambodia by 2026. The Nepali Embassy in Thailand assisted in the rescue of 390 of them, comprising 372 men and 18 women. The figures illustrate both the growing scale of scam trafficking and the increasing burden it places on Nepal’s law-enforcement agencies and diplomatic missions. Their stories mirror those of thousands of victims from around the world.

However, nationwide prosecution data show that only 29 online scam-related cases have so far been filed under human trafficking or smuggling charges. These include 12 cases linked to Myanmar, 14 to Cambodia, seven involving trafficking and seven smuggling, and three to Laos.

According to Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Nakul Pokharel, Chief of the Nepal Police Anti-Human Trafficking Bureau (AHTB), most victims identified are young men aged 20–35.

“Young people are lured through social media and informal networks with promises of well-paid jobs in the digital or hospitality sectors. They often travel on tourist visas through India, Thailand or Vietnam,” SSP Pokharel said.

Traffickers contact potential victims through Facebook, Telegram, WhatsApp, TikTok, LinkedIn and online job portals, offering attractive salaries, free accommodation and visa support. These offers are designed to appear genuine. He urged young people to verify overseas employment offers through official channels and immediately report suspicious recruitment. He also emphasised the importance of intelligence sharing and joint investigations among countries to dismantle criminal networks.

The anti-trafficking systems in Nepal were designed primarily to respond to sexual exploitation and forced labour in conventional industries. Today, trafficking increasingly intersects with cybercrime, digital technology, cryptocurrencies and cross-border organised criminal networks. Investigations now require digital forensics, financial intelligence, cyber expertise and international evidence-sharing that extend well beyond conventional policing.

Condition of victims after they are trafficked

After arriving in Myanmar, Cambodia or Laos, victims often have their passports and phones confiscated and are confined in heavily guarded compounds. Instead of the well-paid jobs they were promised, they are forced to work 12 to 18 hours a day under constant surveillance, carrying out romance scams, fraudulent investment and cryptocurrency schemes, phishing, online gambling and other illegal activities. They must meet daily targets, and those who fail or resist may face threats, beatings, deprivation, extortion, blackmail, torture and severe psychological abuse.

Although victims may be involved in online fraud, many were deceived, trafficked and forced to participate under threat or violence. This distinction is essential. Survivors should be recognised and treated as victims of trafficking, with access to protection, support and justice, rather than punished for crimes they were compelled to commit.

SSP Pokharel says, “Those who fail to meet their targets are often subjected to physical and psychological abuse. Many victims face a painful dilemma: they are victims of human trafficking but were also forced to commit online fraud”. As a result, many are afraid to report their experiences to the police after returning home, making investigations and prosecutions more difficult.

Who is most vulnerable and why?

Young men aged 20–35 are the group most vulnerable to scam trafficking. Nepal Police data show that 37 of the 41 identified victims – 90.2% are male, while only four are female. This represents a significant shift from the traditional pattern of trafficking in Nepal, which has often been associated mainly with women and girls.

Criminal networks deliberately target educated but unemployed young people who have basic English, computer and typing skills. Many are actively looking for better employment opportunities abroad and may be under financial or family pressure to earn an income. Recruiters exploit these hopes by advertising fake overseas jobs through Facebook, TikTok, Telegram and other online platforms.

The advertised positions often include roles such as “computer operator”, “customer service representative” or “digital marketing assistant”, with promised salaries of USD 800 – 1,500 per month, along with free accommodation and visa support. Because the offers appear professional and attractive, many young people do not realise that they are being recruited into scam compounds until they arrive in the destination country.

From prevention to protection

Prevention begins with awareness. Jobseekers and their families need practical guidance on verifying overseas job offers, spotting fraudulent recruitment, recognising warning signs and reporting suspicious activity. Schools, universities, local governments, recruitment agencies, civil society and the media all have a role in raising awareness. Digital literacy has therefore become an essential tool in preventing human trafficking.

Technology companies also have responsibilities. Online platforms should respond more quickly to fraudulent job advertisements, fake recruiter accounts and organised recruitment networks that exploit their services to target vulnerable job seekers.

Governments must act urgently by strengthening prevention, improving regulation and international cooperation, protecting survivors, and holding traffickers accountable.

When trafficking occurs, safe repatriation is only the first step. Survivors often return with psychological trauma, financial loss, debt, social stigma and fear of retaliation or arrest. They need comprehensive support, including legal aid, psychosocial counselling, medical care, compensation, livelihood opportunities and long-term reintegration services. Laws and procedures must recognise the coercion they experienced and ensure that authorities treat them as victims rather than criminals.

The legal process is also difficult. Crimes span several jurisdictions, victims may be treated as suspects abroad, and evidence is often held on encrypted platforms. Successful prosecution requires effective legal assistance, intelligence sharing and close cross-border cooperation among law enforcement agencies.

Human rights advocates argue that people trapped in scam compounds should be recognised first and foremost as victims of organised crime. Although they may be forced to carry out online scams, they have often been deceived, trafficked and exploited through threats, coercion and violence. They deserve protection, rehabilitation and the opportunity to rebuild their lives, while governments work together to dismantle the criminal networks responsible for their exploitation.

Challenges 

  • No Dedicated Law: Nepal has no specific law on scam trafficking. Cases are prosecuted under the Human Trafficking and Transportation (Control) Act, 2064, making it difficult to make appropriate charges and convictions.
  • Evidence Abroad: Key digital evidence, including Telegram chats, payment records and crime scenes, is usually located in Myanmar, Cambodia or Laos. International legal cooperation is often slow or ineffective.
  • Limited Victim Cooperation: Many victims travelled on tourist visas and fear being treated as offenders because they were forced to take part in scams. This discourages reporting and testimony, limiting investigations.
  • Weak Coordination: Coordination among the Anti-Human Trafficking Bureau, relevant departments and Nepalese embassies remains limited. There is no shared information system, and border screening is not designed to detect fraudulent job recruitment.
  • Limited Resources: The AHTB faces budget constraints, frequent staff transfers and limited digital forensic capacity. Without a dedicated rescue and repatriation fund, it relies heavily on embassies and partner organisations.

On this World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, the message is clear: We must modernise our response to technology-facilitated trafficking, strengthen international collaboration and ensure that every survivor is treated with dignity, protection and justice. Criminal networks operate across borders. Our response must do the same. Nobody should leave home in search of a better future only to end up imprisoned behind a computer screen in a foreign country.

title.rendered: Government, doctors reach agreement; Nationwide medical protest ends

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 29

The Government of Nepal and the Nepal Medical Association (NMA) have reached an agreement, leading to the withdrawal of the nationwide protest launched by doctors.

The two sides signed a five-point agreement to resolve the dispute that arose following recent incidents in which healthcare workers were assaulted and mistreated. The agreement was signed on Wednesday after discussions at the Ministry of Health and Food Safety, attended by representatives from the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, and officials of the Nepal Medical Association.

Under the agreement, the government has committed to effectively enforcing the Health Workers and Health Institutions Security Act, 2009 (2066 BS). It also agreed to promptly prepare the necessary implementation guidelines, strengthen legal action against those involved in vandalism at health facilities and attacks on healthcare workers, and improve coordination among the relevant ministries.

The agreement further states that the government will develop an action plan to ensure the security of health institutions. A joint task force will be formed in collaboration with the Nepal Medical Association to oversee implementation, and progress will be reviewed on a regular basis.

Following the agreement, the Nepal Medical Association announced that it has immediately suspended all protest programs and will resume regular healthcare services across the country.

title.rendered: Nepal Army conducts aerial patrol in Sunsari

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, July 29

The Nepal Army has conducted an aerial patrol in Sunsari after the security situation in Kaptanganj, Ward No. 3 of Devanaganj Rural Municipality, and surrounding areas became tense.

According to Nepal Army spokesperson and Assistant Rathi Rajaram Basnet, the aerial patrol was carried out to assess the security situation and monitor conditions on the ground. He said that, as of Wednesday, the situation in Sunsari remained peaceful.

Following the imposition of a curfew, the Nepal Army was deployed to assist with security operations. Basnet said that, in addition to ground patrols, the army also carried out aerial surveillance on Wednesday as part of its efforts to maintain law and order.

Meanwhile, the Nepal Police also used drones to assess the situation in Kaptanganj.

The unrest began after a dispute between two groups in Kaptanganj, Devanaganj Rural Municipality–3. During efforts by security personnel to bring the situation under control, 24-year-old Om Prakash Mehta of Kaptanganj was fatally shot on Sunday night.

According to security authorities, the clash broke out after one group refused to remove a flag while the other played loud music through a DJ sound system. They claim that warning shots were fired into the air to control the situation, during which one person died.

Tensions escalated after one person was killed and nine civilians were injured. The violence flared up again on Tuesday evening, with incidents of vandalism, arson, and clashes. However, authorities say that the situation in Sunsari is now gradually returning to normal.

content.rendered:

The Koshi Provincial Government has announced financial assistance of Rs 200,000 for the families of those who lost their lives in the incident that occurred in Devanaganj, Sunsari.

Chief Minister Hikmat Kumar Karki announced this during an all-party meeting held on Wednesday.

The government also announced that each injured person will receive Rs 50,000 in relief assistance. In addition, families whose homes, shops, or other properties were damaged by arson will also receive Rs 50,000 each.

The all-party meeting adopted an eight-point resolution in response to the situation that arose following the incident on July 25. Organised by the Koshi Provincial Government, the meeting focused on maintaining social harmony, peace, and security.

The government decided that political leaders, social organisations, and administrative authorities would work together to preserve social harmony and communal unity. It also resolved to hold all-party and all-stakeholder meetings at the local government level and implement programs aimed at strengthening social cohesion.

To promote reconciliation and harmony at the community level, the government will coordinate with local authorities to organise goodwill marches, public awareness campaigns, and other related activities.

The meeting also decided that organisations representing all religious communities should issue a joint appeal for peace and play an active role in coordination and facilitation. It further called for heightened security vigilance against any undesirable activities that could occur along the border. It requested the federal government to support the treatment of the injured and provide relief to the families of those who died.

title.rendered: Tiger Census-2026: Tiger population reaches 429 in Nepal

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 29

The population of tigers has reached 429 in the country, as per the latest census. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment made public the recent tiger census today on the occasion of Global Tiger Day. Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment, Gita Chaudhary, launched the Tiger Census Report-2026.

As per the census report, the population of tigers has reached 429 across the country, including 145 tigers in Chitwan National Park, 112 in Bardiya National Park, 71 in Parsa National Park, 51 in Banke National Park and 50 in Shuklaphanta National Park. It is said that the population of tigers has increased following improvements in protected areas and habitat in recent periods.

Tiger census is conducted every four years in Nepal. In the tiger census conducted in 2022, the number of tigers was 355 in the country. The highest population of tigers was in Chitwan National Park with 128, while 125 were in Bardiya National Park, 41 in Parsa National Park, 36 in Shuklaphanta National Park and 25 in Banke National Park in 2022.

The Ministry has been carrying out tiger census every four years since 2009. Nepal was home to 121 tigers in 2010, 198 in 2014 and 235 in 2018. Global Tiger Day is observed every year on July 29. With the rapid decline in tiger populations, the Tiger Summit held in St. Petersburg, Russia, in 2010 declared the observance of the Day on July 29 with an objective of stopping such situations and protecting their natural habitat.

title.rendered: Ashad Shukla Purnima: Guru Purnima, Vyasa Jayanti being observed

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 29

Guru Purnima, also known as Ashad Shukla Purnima, is being observed across the country today by honouring and expressing gratitude towards mentors and teachers alike. The festival also holds religious and cultural significance, serving as a day to honour the gurus- traditionally revered as those who impart wisdom and guide their followers on the path of knowledge and enlightenment.

Academic institutions observe the day as Teachers’ Day, with students honouring their teachers in recognition of their invaluable contributions to learning, academic growth, and excellence. In Sanskrit, ‘Gu’ means darkness, while ‘Ru’ means light, symbolising Guru as one who dispels the darkness of ignorance with the light of knowledge.

Today is also observed as Vyasa Jayanti, commemorating the birth of Ved Vyasa, who is credited with dividing Vedas into four parts- Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda-and composing 18 Purans and Upapuranas in simple Sanskrit language, making the teachings of the Veda more accessible. Since Veda Vyasa is believed to have been born on the full moon day of the month of Asar, Vyas Jayanti is celebrated on this day.

On this occasion, Nepal Maharishi Vedic Foundation is organising a special Guru Purnima programme at Brahmananda Saraswati Gram in Champadevi today. Former minister and foundation chairman Deepak Prakash Baskota told the RSS that the programme will be observed by highlighting the significance of Guru Purnima.
