title.rendered: CAVA Men’s Volleyball Championship: Nepal enters world rankings, but medal dream remains unfulfilled

content.rendered:
When Nepal departed for Islamabad, Pakistan, to play the CAVA Men’s Volleyball Championship, its goals were clear: enter the FIVB world rankings and win a medal for the senior men’s team for the first time in nearly a decade.

Since the tournament carries world-ranking recognition, Nepal entered the world rankings as soon as it played its first match. But the second goal went unfulfilled.

Despite competitive performances, Nepal lost all five of its league-stage matches and failed to reach the semifinals. With the semifinal berth out of reach, the medal target also remained incomplete.

Nepal last won a medal, bronze in the Central Zone back in 2017, and has not won one since at the senior level, though it did win a medal at the CAVA U-20 age-group level.

This time, apart from host Pakistan, the other four teams were considered roughly on par with Nepal, so the goal was to reach the semifinals and at least “touch” a medal. But despite performing well in every match, Nepal fell short on results, losing all its league-stage games and missing out on the semifinals.

Having lost all five consecutive matches, Nepal was defeated in three of them after going the full five sets. Because those matches went to five sets, Nepal earned 1 point per match from them, ending with 3 points overall.

Nepal also lost against Kazakhstan for fifth place by 3-0.

This time, under the captaincy of setter Hari Hajur Thapa, the Nepali squad was dominated by young and new players. Six of the twelve players were representing the national team for the first time. Four players had only played one previous international tournament, last year’s CAVA Nations League. Only setter Harihazur and libero Binod Chand had somewhat more international experience.

However, the spirited performances of the new players could not be sustained throughout the matches. Despite playing well overall, Nepal lost due to a lack of international experience, an inability to hold up under pressure in decisive moments, and the greater experience of opposing teams.

Nepal’s Performance

Against a strong Kazakhstan side, Nepal put in an outstanding performance in its very first match. Although it lost a competitive contest, Nepal’s comeback drew widespread praise. After losing the first two sets, Nepal fought back to win the next two and level the match 2-2.

But Nepal could not maintain that momentum in the fifth and decisive set, losing 3-2 overall. Kazakhstan defeated Nepal 25-19, 25-21, 32-34, 19-25, 15-9.

In the second match against Sri Lanka, Nepal again went the distance to a fifth set before losing. After dropping the opening set, Nepal fought back to take a 2-1 lead by winning two sets in a row, but again could not hold the momentum.

Having lost the first set 25-18, Nepal took control by winning the second 25-21 and third 25-19. But losing the fourth set 25-21 sent the match to a decider, where the same pattern from the first match repeated. Unable to hold a 9-8 lead, Nepal saw Sri Lanka take the set 15-10 to win the match.

In the third match, against tournament favourites Pakistan, Nepal could not offer the expected challenge and lost comfortably, 25-14, 25-18, 25-10. For a Pakistani side featuring players who had come to play in Nepal, the match against Nepal posed little challenge.

After three straight losses, Nepal needed to win both remaining matches to reach the semifinals. But the fourth match, against Bangladesh, followed a similar pattern.

Nepal made an excellent start, taking the first set 25-18. But Bangladesh fought back to win the second 25-19, levelling the match 1-1.

In the third set, Nepal again started strong, winning 25-21 to take a 2-1 lead — needing just one more set to win the match. But Nepal could not maintain control and ultimately lost in the fifth set.

Bangladesh won a competitive fourth set 25-23 to force a decider, then took the fifth and final set 15-11 to win the match.

In the fifth league match, against Uzbekistan, Nepal again played competitively but lost in straight sets. Nepal had previously beaten Uzbekistan, but that result did not repeat on Monday.

In a competitive first set, Nepal led 24-23, just one point from winning the set, but fell short — Uzbekistan scored three points in a row to win the set in a tiebreak, 26-24.

Uzbekistan then led from the start of the second set to win it 25-20, and again led throughout the third set to take it 25-22.

Weaknesses and areas for improvement

Across all six matches, apart from the game against Pakistan and Uzbekistan, Nepal lost matches even while in strong positions.

Nepal played competitively in four of its six matches but could not convert that into results, including two matches where it held a lead but failed to turn it into a win. Weaknesses in blocking, reception, and experience were evident in decisive moments. While opposing teams made fewer errors under pressure, Nepal lost crucial points at key moments and struggled to handle pressure in decisive sets.

With a squad heavy on new players lacking international experience, and with blocking and reception, both essential in volleyball, being relatively weak, Nepal came close to victory several times but could not close it out.

For Nepali men’s volleyball, the CAVA tournament served as a means to enter the world rankings, identify weaknesses, and prepare well for future international competitions.

Through this tournament, Nepal entered the FIVB world rankings. After its first match, Nepal reached the 83rd rank, and after six matches settled at 109th.

Six new faces were included in the Nepali squad for this tournament — Himal Sunar, Rajendra Dhami, Suraj Chunara, Dipesh Kunwar, Santosh Bik, and Saroj Bardewa, all of whom made their debut in the very first match, against Kazakhstan.

These six new players were given their first opportunity with the senior national team and showed they are capable of competing at the international level, raising hope for the future of Nepali men’s volleyball.

It has shown that investment in Nepali volleyball, along with continuous training and international matches, could lead to much better performances.

According to head coach Jagdish Bhatta, if Nepal receives long-term planning, regular training, and international competition, it could establish itself as the fourth-strongest team among the 14 nations of Central Asia.

“If we plan and prepare well and play international competitions, we will be right behind Iran, India, and Pakistan,” he says.

Iran is a strong team not just in Asia but globally, ranked in the top 20. In South Asia, India and Pakistan are strong teams that play international competitions regularly and are also investing in age-group categories.

Coach Bhatta said that if Nepal also builds a good plan from the grassroots to the age-group levels and moves forward, the national team could improve significantly in the coming years.

“A franchise league is also starting now. If we keep identifying good talent from age-group and grassroots levels and provide continuous training, Nepal’s team can become much better,” Bhatta says.

The results at the CAVA men’s volleyball championship exposed Nepal’s weaknesses, but the performances also revealed potential. Going the distance to five sets in three of five matches, an outstanding comeback in one match, holding leads in two matches, and six new players debuting with confidence are all positive signs for Nepali men’s volleyball.

If these experiences can now be paired with organised preparation, domestic competitions, and regular international exposure, there is a foundation for Nepal to turn its medal ambitions into reality in the future.

title.rendered: Organisations gathered to advance inclusive menstrual education through resource-sharing dialogue

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 29

More than 25 representatives from organisations working in menstrual health, disability inclusion, education, and youth engagement gathered in Kathmandu for the Inclusive Dialogue on Menstrual Education on Monday. The event brought together founders, activists, educators, parents, and disability advocates to exchange resources, build partnerships, and reimagine how menstrual education can reach everyone.

The dialogue was jointly organised by Global Action Nepal, Dignity Without Danger, Liverpool John Moores University and Down Syndrome Society, Nepal. In response to a common challenge: while many organisations have developed valuable menstrual education resources, these materials often remain within limited communities, limiting their reach and impact.

Rather than creating new resources, participants explored how existing tools could be shared, adapted, and made more accessible across different communities, including people with intellectual and physical disabilities. Organisations including Blind Youth Association Nepal, Aina Foundation We Craft Nepal, Autism Care Nepal, and others showcased their educational materials while other organisations exchanged feedback and identified opportunities for future collaboration.

Sila Thapa, Founder of Down Syndrome Society Nepal, emphasised the importance of ensuring that menstrual education reflects the lived experiences and needs of persons with disabilities, as inclusion is needed to change the narratives inside the home. 

Professor Sara Parker stressed the need for all organisations to work together across different sectors and work with all to share the excellent resources and expertise that are in Nepal and ensure that everyone has a happy and healthy period free from shame.

“We all must speak publicly about this issue to continue to break the silence for periods,” said Parker.  

The dialogue also highlighted the leadership of women working at the intersection of menstrual health, disability, research, and education, while reinforcing that inclusive menstrual education requires collective action from educators, caregivers, advocates, organisations, and policymakers alike.

The event concluded with a shared commitment to strengthen partnerships, increase resource accessibility, and continue collaborative efforts so that no one is left behind in menstrual education. The collective resources can be accessed at the Global Action Nepal Resource Centre, and anyone can add their resources.

title.rendered: Jolene blends music, mystery and emotional turmoil

content.rendered:
When Geoffrey Chaucer wrote that “love is blind all day, and may not see,” in his collection The Canterbury Tales,  he was indicating how falling in love completely skews a person’s judgment, making them oblivious to reality, red flags, or obvious flaws. Some real-life events often make it hard to argue with his point. 

Audiences might be even more convinced by Chaucer after they watch Jolene, a play being staged at the Kausi Theatre.

Directed by Rishav and co-written with Buddhi Pokharel, the play centres on an extramarital affair between Madhav (Anoj Pandey) and Jolene (Tara), while Madhav remains married to Meera (Meera Khadka).

Meera is a housewife convinced she is pregnant, constantly talking with her unborn child. She desperately loves Madhav, regardless of the time and effort Madhav gives to her. 

The way Madhav talks to Jolene and shares everything with her reveals that he is more emotionally committed to Jolene than to Meera. 

When Meera finds out about Madhav’s affair with Jolene, an unexpected incident occurs, which creates a conflict in the play. The thriller begins afterwards. The play incorporates thriller elements in a unique style, going beyond dark music and a suspicious tone. To investigate the unexpected incident, a group of four police officers is deployed. Their investigation unfolds in a deliberately theatrical and unconventional manner rather than through a realistic police procedural. 

Rather than relying on dialogue, the officers investigate through a musical number that cleverly outlines the crime’s motive and method. The way they sing the song for several minutes, as a part of the investigation, deserves appreciation because when it comes to singing a song, it is not only about remembering the lyrics, but also maintaining a melody that should be performed with the right timing.  

The standout element of this play is its music, which includes both live and recorded tracks. The audience can enjoy music ranging from slow ballads and rap to hard rock. These stellar performances showcase the raw talent of Vitamin Sex, the live band featured in the show.

In one striking scene, the guitarist steps onto the stage, plays a distorted heavy riff, and headbangs, making the audience feel like they are attending a metal gig.

The acting overall is commendable, with every character maintaining impressive consistency in their dialogue and expressions. In particular, Anoj Pandey and Tara prove their versatility. Featured together in May’s Lucifer Rising as aggressive, loud junkies, they take a complete turn in Jolene with calm and serious performances. However, from the third row from the back, Madhav’s voice projection occasionally felt weak, making some of his lines difficult to hear.  

The play has a decent setting featuring an apartment with a bedroom, kitchen and a living room. Most of the incidents occur in the living room. They have cleverly made the same setting as a different apartment, one belonging to Madhav and Meera and another of Jolene.  

As the play approaches its conclusion, a cage appears in Madhav and Meera’s bedroom with Madhav inside, turning the space into a prison. This visual symbol shows how overcomplicating life can make someone a prisoner of their own choices. It also highlights how unresolved mistakes and ignored problems eventually invite karmic consequences. 

Despite its many ups and downs, the play leaves key questions unanswered: Why couldn’t Madhav confess his affair to free Meera? And why do both women continue to love him despite his disloyalty? These unanswered questions may frustrate some viewers. Then again, the artists perform a song that says, Maya Ma Kasko K Kabu, suggesting that once you fall in love with someone, it is hard to stop. This makes Chaucer’s saying, “Love is blind all day, and may not see,” particularly relevant.  

Jolene will run through August 14 every day (except Tuesdays) at Kausi Theatre, Teku, at 5:15 pm. There will be an additional show on Saturdays at 1 pm.

title.rendered: Nepal’s healthcare has a memory problem

content.rendered:
An elderly farmer from Rolpa arrives at a hospital in Kathmandu after travelling for nearly two days. He has visited his local health post, a district hospital, and a private clinic over the past several years. He has been treated for diabetes, high blood pressure and, more recently, chest pain. He has undergone blood tests, X-rays and an ECG. Somewhere along the way, medicines were changed. New diagnoses were added. Old reports disappeared. Now, sitting across from a doctor, he hears a question familiar to millions of Nepalis.

“Do you have your previous medical records?”

He slowly opens a plastic bag filled with folded prescriptions, fading laboratory reports and handwritten notes. Some documents have been damaged by rain. Others were left at home. A few have simply been lost.

The doctor studies the papers, but the story is incomplete. Unable to see the patient’s full medical history, the physician orders another round of tests, not because the previous tests were unnecessary, but because the information cannot be trusted, verified or accessed.

The patient pays again. Another day is lost. Treatment is delayed. This scene plays out every day across Nepal. It is so common that we rarely stop to ask an important question.

Still depending on paper and memory

For decades, Nepal has invested in hospitals, medical colleges, diagnostic centres and specialist services. These investments have undoubtedly improved healthcare and saved countless lives. Yet one critical part of healthcare has remained fragmented, which is the information about the patient’s medical records. Every hospital maintains its own records. Every laboratory stores its own reports. Every pharmacy keeps its own dispensing information.

Some hospitals have adopted electronic medical record systems, while others continue to rely on paper files. But regardless of the technology used, one reality remains unchanged: medical information rarely moves easily from one institution to another. The result is that every hospital remembers only the care delivered within its own walls. The patient becomes the only connection between them. Healthcare has become institution-centred rather than patient-centred.

Imagine if Nepal’s banking system worked this way. Suppose every time you travelled from Pokhara to Kathmandu, your bank account remained behind. Suppose you had to carry years of transaction records in a folder simply to withdraw your own money. No one would accept such a system. Today, banking works because the account belongs to the customer, not to the individual branch. Healthcare should work the same way. A person’s medical history does not belong to a hospital. It belongs to the patient. The hospital contributes one chapter. The clinic contributes another. The laboratory adds another. Together, they tell the story of one human life.

The consequences of fragmented healthcare extend far beyond inconvenience. Repeated investigations increase healthcare costs for families already struggling financially. Doctors make important clinical decisions without complete medical histories. Emergency physicians may not know a patient’s allergies or current medications. Patients living with chronic illnesses must repeatedly explain the same medical history to every new healthcare provider. In rural Nepal, where specialist services are often separated by long distances and difficult terrain, these problems become even more severe. Continuity of care disappears precisely where it is needed most. The challenge becomes even greater when we consider how Nepalis actually receive healthcare. For instance, a pregnant mother may begin her care at a local health post, deliver her baby in a provincial hospital, and later seek specialist care in Kathmandu. An elderly man with heart disease may receive medicines from one hospital, laboratory investigations from another, and emergency treatment somewhere else. Children receive vaccinations at one facility, treatment for infections at another, and nutritional support through community programs. Each institution sees only one part of the story. No one sees the whole patient.

This is not a criticism of doctors. Nor is it a criticism of hospitals. Doctors can only make decisions using the information available to them. Hospitals can only manage records created within their own systems. The problem lies deeper. It lies in how we have organised healthcare itself. For more than a century, healthcare systems around the world have been built around institutions. Hospitals became the centre. Medical records remained inside hospitals. Patients travelled from one institution to another carrying pieces of their own medical history. That model made sense when paper records were the only practical option. The world has changed. Healthcare has been slower to change with it. We have designed healthcare around institutions. It is time to redesign it around people. 

Today almost every Nepali carries a smartphone. Families separated by thousands of kilometres communicate instantly. Financial transactions occur digitally. Businesses operate across continents. Information moves around the world in seconds. Yet healthcare often remains fragmented into disconnected islands. Perhaps the question is no longer how we build better hospitals. Perhaps the more important question is whether healthcare itself should continue revolving around hospitals.

Many countries are now confronting this challenge. Ageing populations, rising chronic disease, increasing healthcare costs and growing expectations for continuity of care are forcing governments to rethink long-established assumptions. The conversation is gradually shifting. The goal is no longer simply to digitise hospitals. It is to redesign healthcare around patients. That distinction matters. Digitising existing systems may make hospitals more efficient. Redesigning healthcare changes how patients experience care throughout their lives.

Nepal stands at an important crossroads. We can continue building healthcare, one institution at a time. Or we can begin asking a different question. What would a healthcare system look like if it were designed around the patient rather than around the hospital? The answer to that question could shape the future of healthcare in Nepal for generations to come. It is a conversation that deserves the attention not only of doctors and policymakers, but of every citizen because healthcare is not simply about hospitals; it is about people. Perhaps the first step toward building a better healthcare system is recognising a truth that has remained hidden in plain sight. Our hospitals remember patients. Our healthcare system does not.

title.rendered: Senior Nepali Congress leader Gopal Man Shrestha passes away

content.rendered:
July 28, Kathmandu

Senior Nepali Congress leader Gopal Man Shrestha has passed away at the age of 83. He died on Tuesday while undergoing treatment at Helios Hospital in Jawalakhel.

Former Gandaki Province Minister Mekhlal Shrestha confirmed the death of the former Deputy Prime Minister. He said that Shrestha’s body will be kept at the Nepali Congress central party office from 8 am to 11 am on Wednesday for party members, supporters, and the public to pay their respects.

“Afterwards, a funeral procession will accompany the body to Pashupati Aryaghat, where the final rites and cremation will be conducted,” Mekhlal Shrestha wrote on Facebook.

On July 23, Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa announced that Gopal Man Shrestha had been appointed as the party’s Senior Leader.

title.rendered: Protests continue in Sunsari–Morang; East–West highway blocked sgain

content.rendered:
July 28, Biratnagar

A protest group opposing the recent incident in Kaptanganj, Ward No. 3 of Dewanganj Rural Municipality, Sunsari, has once again blocked the East–West Highway on Tuesday.

Protesters burned tires and blocked traffic at several locations along the Sunsari section of the highway. Demonstrations are also taking place in Biratnagar, where groups of young people have gathered in market areas to protest against the government.

According to DSP Chandra Bahadur Khadka, spokesperson for the Sunsari District Police Office, there are roadblocks at multiple points between Pakali and the Koshi Barrage. He said crowds have gathered at major intersections, staging demonstrations.

As the protests intensified, the local administration stopped vehicles traveling west from Itahari. Meanwhile, the situation in Dewanganj itself is gradually returning to normal.

The unrest began after a clash between two groups in Kaptanganj on Sunday. During efforts to control the violence, police opened fire, resulting in the death of one person and injuries to nine others.

Following the incident, the local administration imposed a curfew in five locations in the southern part of the district to restore order. Despite the curfew, protesters continued demonstrating throughout Monday. The curfew remains in effect on Tuesday.

According to a notice issued by Chief District Officer Ishwari Prasad Aryal, a prohibitory order is in force from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. on Tuesday across the entire areas of Dewanganj Rural Municipality and Harinagar Rural Municipality.

A full curfew remains in place in the market areas of Harinagara, Bhutaha, Kaptanganj, Ghuski, and Dewanganj.

The curfew boundaries are as follows:

  • Harinagara Market: From Nuniya Tol in the east to West Khuniya Dhar in the west, from the Harinagar Rural Municipality Office in the north to Basantpur Junction in the south.
  • Bhutaha Market: From Moriya Dhar in the east to Idgaha Field in the west, from the Sunsari River in the north to the Harinagar Rural Municipality Office in the south.
  • Kaptanganj Market: From Yadav Tol in the east to Panchau Simal Secondary School in the west, from Krishna Secondary School in the north to the Nepal–India border in the south.
  • Ghuski Market: From Kasamiya Madrasa in the east to the Ghuski Police Post in the west, from Isha Hardware in the north to Hilal Public School in the south.
  • Dewanganj Market: From Musahar Tol on the road to Biratnagar in the east to the Moriya River in the west, extending north to the Chiura (beaten rice) Mill.

The administration has urged the public not to organize or participate in any gatherings, rallies, demonstrations, or other activities that could disrupt peace, security, or public order within the curfew areas.

title.rendered: Rising arrivals demand a national tourism dashboard

content.rendered:
Visitor arrivals have nearly recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Nepal’s next challenge is to measure, track, and distribute tourism value through receipts, local retention, workforce development, destination competitiveness, and a National Tourism Digital Dashboard.

Nepal’s tourism recovery is no longer a matter of hope; it is visible in the numbers. In 2025, Nepal received 1,158,459 international visitors, recording 0.95% growth over 2024 and reaching 96.8% of 2019 levels, according to Nepal Tourism Board’s Tourism Insights. The momentum has continued into 2026. Nepal welcomed 91,363 international tourists in June 2026, a 19.5% increase from June 2025 and 22.01% higher than June 2019, according to figures from the Nepal Tourism Board and the Department of Immigration.

These figures confirm an important national achievement. After years of disruption, uncertainty, and slow recovery, international confidence in Nepal has returned. Tourists are again choosing Nepal for the Himalaya, trekking, mountaineering, culture, spirituality, wildlife, and increasingly diverse travel experiences.But recovery alone is not the destination. It is only the starting point. The central question for Nepal is no longer whether visitors are returning. The real question is whether Nepal can convert this returning demand into higher economic value, stronger local retention, better jobs, improved service quality, wider regional benefit, and long-term competitiveness. That question cannot be answered by arrival numbers alone. For that, Nepal now needs a National Tourism Digital Dashboard.

Arrivals do not measure value

Tourist arrivals tell us how many people crossed the border. They do not tell us how much value was created, where that value went, who benefited, or whether the tourism economy became stronger as a result.The 2024 statistics show this gap clearly. Nepal received 1,147,548 tourists in 2024, an increase of 13.07% over 2023. The average length of stay rose slightly from 13.2 to 13.3 days, while tourism earnings increased from US$548.2 million to US$623.4 million. Yet average daily visitor spending declined marginally from US$41.0 to US$40.8.

This is the most important signal hidden within the recovery story. Nepal earned more largely because more visitors arrived, not because each visitor generated significantly higher daily value. That distinction matters. A country can receive more tourists and still fail to capture enough value. It can fill airports, hotels, trails, and vehicles while leaving local enterprises underpaid, municipalities underprepared, workers undertrained, and destinations under-managed. In such a situation, growth becomes visible, but value remains weak.

Nepal must therefore move from a narrow arrival-counting mindset to a broader value-measurement system. The country needs to know not only how many tourists arrive, but how long they stay, how much they spend, which regions they visit, what services they use, how much income remains locally, and whether tourism growth is strengthening the wider economy. This is where a National Tourism Digital Dashboard becomes essential.

Tourism must become a national industry

Tourism should not be treated as a narrow service sector limited to hotels, travel agencies, trekking companies, and airlines. Properly managed, it is a national industry with strong multiplier effects across transport, agriculture, food supply, handicrafts, culture, conservation, construction, digital services, education, local governance, and small enterprise development. When a visitor spends in Nepal, that spending can support many layers of the economy: hotel workers, guides, drivers, porters, restaurants, farmers, artisans, homestays, shopkeepers, community groups, conservation areas, municipalities, and local suppliers. But this does not happen automatically. It depends on how tourism products are designed, how supply chains are connected, how destinations are governed, and how much spending is retained within local economies.

This distribution question is becoming more important as tourism capacity expands. In 2024, the number of star hotels increased from 182 to 214, non-star hotels from 1,234 to 1,364, and total bed capacity from 54,370 to 62,642. These investments show confidence in Nepal’s tourism future. However, the policy question is not only whether capacity is growing, but whether that capacity is being used effectively across seasons, regions, and market segments. If hotel capacity expands without stronger year-round demand, better market positioning, improved visitor experiences, and higher-value tourism products, Nepal risks creating underutilised assets rather than stronger competitiveness. The objective should not be simply to attract more visitors. Nepal needs visitors who stay longer, spend more, travel beyond saturated destinations, and engage with a broader range of services and local experiences.

This is also why tourism value must be measured geographically. Kathmandu, Pokhara, Chitwan, Everest, Annapurna, and Lumbini will remain important, but Nepal’s tourism future cannot depend only on familiar destinations. Emerging, rural, and marginalised destinations must also be visible in national tourism data. Without that visibility, policy attention, infrastructure investment, marketing support, and enterprise development will continue to concentrate in already established areas. A National Tourism Digital Dashboard can help make this wider tourism economy visible.

A national tourism digital dashboard

Nepal already counts arrivals. Now it must measure tourism performance. A National Tourism Digital Dashboard would provide a unified system for tracking how tourism growth translates into real economic and social outcomes. It should integrate data on arrivals, receipts, visitor spending, length of stay, hotel occupancy, regional distribution, employment, enterprise growth, visitor satisfaction, service standards, sustainability indicators, and local value retention.

Such a dashboard would help policymakers answer practical questions that arrival numbers alone cannot answer. Which destinations are receiving visitors but generating low spending? Which regions have hotel capacity but weak occupancy? Which tourism products create higher value? Where are workforce shortages emerging? Which municipalities are benefiting from tourism growth? Which communities remain outside the tourism economy? Where is visitor satisfaction rising or falling? Which areas require better connectivity, training, waste management, safety systems, or destination branding? These are not abstract questions. They are governance questions.

A national dashboard would allow tourism policy to become more evidence-based, timely, and targeted. Instead of relying mainly on annual statistics and broad assumptions, Nepal could monitor tourism performance across destinations and sectors. It could identify gaps earlier, support weaker regions, strengthen high-potential products, and align investment with actual market behaviour. This would also help reduce the gap between national-level tourism ambition and local-level tourism reality. Many municipalities want to develop tourism, but they often lack reliable data on visitors, spending, product performance, service quality, and economic benefit. A dashboard could support federal, provincial, and local governments by making tourism data more accessible and actionable. In this sense, the dashboard should not be seen merely as a technical platform. It should be understood as a national tourism governance instrument.

Measuring what matters

Tourism Policy 2082 arrives at an important moment. It seeks to align tourism with federal governance, digital transformation, climate resilience, global competition, product diversification, sustainability, quality, and trust. Its priorities including integrated tourism data systems, a Tourism Satellite Account, e-visa expansion, connectivity improvements, and improved tourism governance—provide a strong foundation for modernising Nepal’s tourism information architecture.

A National Tourism Digital Dashboard can become the operational tool that translates these policy ambitions into measurable outcomes. It can also support the long-term ambition of building a Tourism Satellite Account by improving the quality, consistency, and usability of tourism data. If Nepal wants to understand tourism’s real contribution to national income, employment, investment, and local development, it must strengthen the way tourism data is collected, connected, and interpreted.

Workforce development is one area where better data is urgently needed. Official statistics show that Nepal had 4,963 travel agencies, 3,252 trekking agencies, 5,269 tourist guides, and 27,128 trekking guides in 2024/25. These figures demonstrate institutional depth, but numbers alone do not guarantee quality. High-value tourism requires skilled human resources, professional management, safety awareness, digital communication, service discipline, and stronger destination-level coordination.

Tourism education and training systems already exist. Nepal Tourism Statistics 2024 reports that Nepal Mountain Academy trained 1,468 students in tourism and adventure-related programmes during 2024. This contribution is important, but future demand will be much larger if Nepal wants to compete in higher-value tourism segments.

A dashboard could help identify where workforce gaps exist, which destinations need trained guides or hospitality workers, where service quality needs improvement, and where training investment should be directed. This would connect tourism growth with human capital planning. The same logic applies to sustainability and visitor satisfaction. Nepal cannot build a stronger tourism brand through promotion alone. A credible brand is built when visitor expectations match actual experiences on the ground. Clean destinations, reliable services, professional guides, safe adventure operations, responsible waste management, climate resilience, and meaningful local engagement all shape the country’s competitiveness. If these dimensions are not measured, they are easily ignored.

Counting visitors converted to creating value

Nepal should celebrate its tourism recovery. The return of international visitors is a real achievement and a sign of renewed confidence in the country. But celebration should not become complacency. The next phase of Nepal’s tourism development must be guided by a more serious question: how much value does tourism create, where does that value go, and how can it be distributed more widely across the country?

A National Tourism Digital Dashboard can provide the analytical foundation for this transition. It can help Nepal move beyond counting visitors and toward managing tourism as a national industry. It can connect arrivals with receipts, spending, employment, local enterprise growth, workforce development, hotel utilisation, destination performance, visitor satisfaction, sustainability, and local value retention. This is the reform Nepal now needs.

Tourism recovery is real. But recovery is not enough. The future of Nepal’s tourism success should not be measured only by how many tourists arrive, but by how much economic and social value tourism creates, retains, and distributes throughout the nation. Arrivals are only the first number. National value creation is the real measure of tourism success.

title.rendered: Health Ministry urges not to obstruct services at hospitals

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 28

The Ministry of Health and Food Safety has urged one and all not to obstruct health services, which are essential for round-the-clock. Joint Spokesperson at the Ministry, Dr Samir Kumar Adhikari, reminded everyone concerned not to obstruct the services at hospitals.

Adhikari’s appeal came in response to the announcement of medical and health persons to halt services except emergency. “Health service is essential and sensitive. So, the doctors must realize its significance, prestige and social responsibility,” Dr Adhikari mentioned in the press statement issued today. He appealed to all hospitals to ensure services without any hindrances and inconvenience to the patients.

According to him, it is the rights of every medical person to provide sensitive and life-saving service to the people, while medical persons also have the right to work at safe and respectable atmosphere. The Ministry also reminded the responsibility of every citizen to cooperate in creating safe atmosphere at hospitals. The Ministry expressed serious concern over the attack and misbehaviour meted out against hospital, health workers and health institutes.

Those involved in such incident would be taken stringent action, Adhikari warned. The Nepal Medical Association had announced closure of health services except emergency reasoning the attack on doctors and health workers at Narayani Hospital of Birgunj on Saturday.

title.rendered: WordCamp Kathmandu 2026 Set for September, bringing together 500 global WordPress professionals

content.rendered:
July 27, Kathmandu

WordCamp Kathmandu 2026, Nepal’s flagship conference for the WordPress community, will be held on September 18–19 at Alice Receptions in Gairidhara, bringing together more than 500 participants from Nepal and abroad.

Organized by WordPress Kathmandu, the two-day event will feature over 30 speakers and delegates from countries including the United States, India, Bangladesh and several European nations. The conference will be held under the theme, “Where Ancient Culture Meets Open Source,” highlighting the connection between Kathmandu Valley’s cultural heritage and the collaborative nature of open-source software.

The opening day, designated as Contributor Day, will focus on collaborative efforts to improve the WordPress platform by allowing participants to contribute to its development, security and accessibility. The second day will feature keynote sessions and technical presentations on emerging topics such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, search engine optimization (SEO) and digital marketing.

Organisers said the event aims to strengthen Nepal’s growing technology sector by providing developers, entrepreneurs and digital agencies with opportunities to exchange knowledge and connect with international experts. With WordPress powering around 43 per cent of websites worldwide, the conference is expected to help local professionals expand their global reach.

The event also continues the Ujwal Thapa Memorial Scholarship, which supports the participation of students from marginalised communities in the technology sector. Organisers said the initiative is intended to promote digital inclusion while helping build skilled human resources for Nepal’s expanding IT industry.

WordCamp Kathmandu follows similar regional events previously held in Butwal, Pokhara and Bharatpur, which organisers say contributed to expanding Nepal’s WordPress community beyond the capital.

title.rendered: 7 children’s books give voice to marginalised communities

content.rendered:
Photo: Sushila Tamang

July 27, Kathmandu

Seven children’s books promoting gender equality, inclusion and the voices of marginalised communities were launched in Kathmandu on Sunday under the British Council’s Gender Arts: Equal Together 2025 programme.

The books were unveiled at the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts in Naxal by educationist Kedar Bhakta Mathema, veteran children’s writer Ganga Karmacharya, former Nepal Academy of Fine Arts Chancellor K K Karmacharya, children’s literature critic Pramod Pradhan, rights activist Gauri Nepali and the authors.

Published as part of the Aparajita Story Project, coordinated by journalist Sushila Tamang, the titles include Aitiko Bihe by Tamang, Namko Katha by Bina Thing, Indreni by Hansawati Kurmi, Mitini by Shanti Sapkota, Mummyghar by Sanjog Thakuri, Haitamako Himmat by Asmita Badi and Surjiko Ujyalo by Sangita Uranw. The project was supported by the Centre for Children’s Literature and Research and Hami Dajubhai.

The project aims to use children’s literature to encourage girls’ empowerment, gender equality and social inclusion by highlighting the lived experiences of communities often absent from mainstream narratives. Rather than portraying marginalised groups as objects of sympathy, the stories emphasise their resilience, identities and cultural heritage.

Speaking at the event, Mathema stressed the importance of encouraging children to read books of varying complexity to broaden their intellectual horizons. Project coordinator Tamang said children’s literature should increasingly reflect diverse social realities and community experiences, while reviewer Gauri Nepali noted that the books depart from traditional moralistic storytelling by presenting realistic accounts that challenge patriarchal and discriminatory social norms.

Speakers, including children’s literature experts, authors, illustrators and British Council representatives, said the collection could make a meaningful contribution to Nepal’s children’s literature by fostering diversity, equality and inclusion through storytelling.

title.rendered: DDC to open 30 dedicated retail outlets across Kathmandu Valley

content.rendered:
July 27, Kathmandu

The state-owned Dairy Development Corporation (DDC) has unveiled a market expansion strategy and plans to open 30 dedicated retail outlets across the Kathmandu Valley by the end of Shrawan (mid-August) to improve consumer access to its products.

According to DDC General Manager Dr Sharan Kumar Pandey, the outlets will sell only DDC products.

“We are opening our own dedicated outlets to provide convenient services to our consumers. These stores will stock only DDC products,” he said.

The outlets will be established in major commercial and residential areas, including Budhanilkantha, Banasthali, Kalanki, Koteshwor, New Baneshwor, and Shankhamul. DDC is currently identifying suitable locations in densely populated areas.

Pandey said around 15 outlets are expected to become fully operational between Shrawan 20 and 25 (early to mid-August), while the remaining outlets are in the final stages of preparation and interior setup.

The stores will offer DDC’s full range of dairy products, including milk, curd, ghee, butter, paneer, cheese, khoa, ice cream, lalmohan, rasbari, and buttermilk.

As part of the same expansion strategy, DDC has already opened a newly renovated outlet at Basantapur Dabali, which was inaugurated by Pandey on Sunday. A similar outlet has also begun operations in Ekantakuna, Lalitpur.

Alongside its physical expansion, DDC is introducing a digital marketing and online delivery service. Within the next few days, consumers will be able to order DDC products online and receive home delivery through a subscription-based system.

“We are moving towards digital marketing. Consumers who subscribe will be able to order DDC products online and have them delivered to their homes,” Pandey said. “Our goal is to make our products more accessible by delivering them directly to consumers’ kitchens.”

Milk collection declines during Shrawan

While expanding its market presence, DDC is also closely monitoring milk collection. Pandey said milk procurement typically declines during Shrawan because many farming households consume more milk at home instead of supplying it through formal collection channels.

“Farmers tend to use more milk for household consumption during Shrawan, so collection has dropped slightly. It will return to normal once Bhadra begins,” he said.

DDC is currently collecting around 65,000 litres of milk daily from across the country.

If the dedicated outlet model proves successful in the Kathmandu Valley, the corporation plans to expand it to other major cities across Nepal in the near future.

title.rendered: TU warns of exam cancellation for code of conduct violations

content.rendered:
July 27, Kathmandu

Tribhuvan University (TU) has warned that students found violating the examination code of conduct will have their examinations cancelled. TU Registrar Prof Dr Mahananda Chalise said around 17,000 students from the Faculty of Management are currently appearing for examinations and urged students to immediately report any misconduct to the police.

“About 17,000 students are taking the examinations today. If anyone is seen engaging in inappropriate activities, responsible students should immediately inform the police,” he said.

The examinations are being conducted for bachelor’s, master’s and MPhil programmes under the Faculty of Management, Office of the Dean. TU has also issued a six-point notice outlining examination rules for students.

According to the notice issued by the Office of the Controller of Examinations, students must bring their valid admit cards on the examination day and sit only in their assigned seats. They are not allowed to leave their seats or the examination hall without permission from the centre superintendent or invigilator.

Students are also prohibited from leaving the examination hall within the first hour after the examination begins.

The university has banned the entry of mobile phones, smartwatches, electronic devices, cheat sheets, books, and any other prohibited materials into examination halls.

Acts such as cheating, assisting others in cheating, impersonating another candidate, disrupting the examination process, or behaving improperly toward examination staff are strictly prohibited.

Students are required to fully comply with the instructions of the centre superintendent, supervisors, invigilators, and examination staff throughout the examination period.

TU has warned that any violation of the examination rules and code of conduct may result in the cancellation of the examination, disqualification from future examinations for a specified period, and, if necessary, legal action in accordance with university regulations.

title.rendered: Nagdhunga–Sisnekhola tunnel inaugurated, initially open only to essential vehicles

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 27

The Nagdhunga–Sisnekhola tunnel has been formally inaugurated. Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal inaugurated the tunnel in the presence of Japanese Ambassador Maeda Toru and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) President Tanaka Akihiko.

According to Deputy Project Director Sanjay Panthi, the tunnel will not immediately open to all vehicles. Initially, only ambulances, fire engines, security agency vehicles, and other vehicles providing essential services will be allowed to operate through it.

Following a trial period of about three months, during which safety and traffic management will be assessed, other vehicles will be allowed entry in phases.

The tunnel’s foundation stone was laid by then Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli, while the main tunnel’s breakthrough was achieved under another Prime Minister, Pushpa Kamal Dahal “Prachanda.” The formal inauguration has now taken place during the tenure of Prime Minister Balen.

Fees based on vehicle type

The project has said no charges will be levied on vehicles using the tunnel during the trial period; fees based on vehicle type will apply after regular operations begin.

According to the Department of Roads, cars and vans will pay Rs 65 to enter Kathmandu and Rs 60 to exit. Minibuses, trucks, and tippers will pay Rs 115 to enter Kathmandu and Rs 80 to exit. For buses and large trucks, the fee is set at Rs 260 for entry and Rs 200 for exit. The Cabinet had earlier fixed fees ranging from Rs 60 to Rs 600 depending on vehicle type.

Pedestrians, motorcycles, scooters, three-wheelers, and vehicles carrying flammable substances such as diesel, petrol, or gas, or explosive materials, are barred from entering the tunnel.

Coming into operation roughly 80 months after construction began, the tunnel is being seen as a new chapter in Nepal’s physical infrastructure development.

The tunnel begins at Dahachok Totipakha- 1 of Chandragiri Municipality, Kathmandu, and ends at Sisnekhola in Dhunibesi Municipality, Dhading. By bypassing the traffic jams, steep climbs, and winding road of the current Nagdhunga section, it is expected to save around an hour of travel time.

The project cost approximately Rs 25 billion, funded through a concessional loan from the Government of Japan and investment from the Government of Nepal. Of this, about Rs 17 billion was spent on construction, an additional Rs 2 billion arose from exchange rate fluctuations and rising construction material costs, and around Rs 6 billion was spent on land acquisition and compensation. A total of 480 ropanis of land was acquired for the project.

Although the tunnel was originally targeted for completion within 42 months, the project was delayed well beyond schedule due to the COVID-19 pandemic and other technical complications.

title.rendered: Koshi Province Scout members slam dissolution of Nepal Scout Councils as unlawful

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 27

Elected members of the National Council of Nepal Scout from Koshi Province have issued a joint press statement calling the government’s dissolution of Nepal Scout’s National, Provincial, and Local Councils illegal and against due process.

The statement comes after Nepal Scout’s official Facebook page announced on the night of Shrawan 8 that the Prime Minister, as Patron of Nepal Scout, along with the Minister for Education and Sports, as Chief Scout, had dissolved all elected councils and executive committees of the organisation.

The signatories say the councils were formed through elections held in Magh 2080 B.S. after a 12-year gap, under a process overseen by an Election Committee formed by the Ministry of Youth and Sports. They note that observers from the World Organisation of the Scout Movement (WOSM) monitored the polls and found them free, fair, and democratic.

According to the statement, the four-year term of the National Council members, elected on Magh 27, 2080 B.S., is protected under the Nepal Scout Act 2050 and its accompanying Regulations, making their removal before the end of their tenure unlawful. The members also argue that neither the Prime Minister nor the Education Minister has legal authority under the Act to dissolve elected bodies, and that only the respective appointing authorities—provincial ministers and local mayors or chairs—can act on Provincial and Local Committees.

The statement further claims that the formation of an “Interim National Executive Committee,” reported to have been sworn in on Shrawan 8, violates a Supreme Court mandamus order issued in the case Lok Bahadur Bhandari v. Ministry of Youth and Sports (Writ No. 078-WO-0484), which had barred the formation of ad-hoc committees within Nepal Scout.

Calling the move an obstruction to a youth development movement spread across all 753 local units and seven provinces, the signatories have urged the Prime Minister and the Education Minister to withdraw the decision immediately. They have also appealed to provincial chief ministers, social development ministers, and local mayors and deputy mayors to intervene, warning that Scouters nationwide will launch protest programs if the decision is not reversed.

The statement is signed by National Council members Nawal Prasad Upadhyay, Nirmala Adhikari Bhandari, Kiran Giri, Durga Bahadur Bista, and Ravi Khanal.

title.rendered: Nepal weighs its role as SCO prepares for Bishkek summit amid leadership transition

content.rendered:
As the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation gears up to mark its 25th anniversary with a Council of Heads of State summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, later this September, Nepal finds itself approaching the gathering under a markedly different government than the one that represented it at last year’s summit, a shift that adds a new layer of uncertainty to how, and at what level, Nepal will engage with the bloc this time around.

A summit still taking shape

Kyrgyzstan assumed the SCO’s rotating chairmanship after the 2025 Tianjin summit, adopting the motto “25 Years of the SCO: Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity.” Bishkek is expected to host the Council of Heads of State meeting in September 2026, though the exact dates have not yet been formally announced by the Secretariat, contrary to some earlier reports that had pencilled in August 31–September 1.

Preparatory work has been underway for months. The Council of National Coordinators met in Beijing in late January, defence ministers from nine member states finalised a 2026–2027 cooperation roadmap in April, and a “Civilisations Dialogue” cultural forum was convened in Bishkek in mid-July. Kyrgyz officials have repeatedly framed their chairmanship around a shift from the SCO being an “organisation of agreements” to one of “implementation,” with proposals reportedly on the table for a dedicated centre to counter new threats and challenges, alongside a push, long championed by Bishkek, for an SCO Development Bank and investment fund.

Notably, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has indicated that the SCO plans to consolidate its outer ring of engagement: the current 15 dialogue partners and two observer states would be merged into a single “partner” category ahead of the Bishkek summit. If confirmed, this would directly affect Nepal’s formal standing within the organisation.

Nepal’s standing: Dialogue partner, not member

In the past, Nepal has held SCO Dialogue Partner status since 2015, formalised through a memorandum signed in Beijing in March 2016. It shares this tier with 14 other countries, including Turkey, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt and, most recently, Laos. The SCO’s ten full members, China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Iran and Belarus, retain the organisation’s decision-making authority; dialogue partners like Nepal participate in a consultative, not decision-making, capacity.

Nepal has for several years pushed to be elevated to observer or full member status, arguing this would guarantee its presence at every summit and give it direct diplomatic access to the bloc’s major powers. That aspiration was reiterated by then-Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli when he attended the 2025 Tianjin summit, where he addressed the “SCO Plus” session and called for a shift from isolation to connectivity and from confrontation to consultation among member states. The upgrade, however, has not materialised, and geopolitical sensitivities among existing members are widely seen as the main obstacle.

A new government in Nepal

The political backdrop to Nepal’s SCO engagement has changed dramatically since Tianjin. The Gen Z-led protests of September 2025 brought down the UML-Nepali Congress-led Oli government, and the country subsequently held general elections in March 2026 that delivered a landslide to the Rastriya Swatantra Party under Rabi Lamichane and Balendra Shah “Balen”, the former Kathmandu mayor turned prime minister. Shah, sworn in as Nepal’s youngest-ever head of government, now leads a cabinet that has only recently marked its first hundred days in office, with a stated focus on trimming the size of government and delivering on reformist campaign pledges.

This transition means Nepal’s SCO posture for Bishkek will be shaped by an administration with a very different political character than its predecessor, one built on an anti-establishment mandate rather than the traditional party alliances that previously managed Nepal’s foreign policy portfolios. Whether Prime Minister Saha personally attends Bishkek, or whether Nepal is represented at a ministerial level, has not yet been publicly known, and will likely depend on the final invitation list the SCO Secretariat circulates to dialogue partners, as per its usual practice of sharing a “Plan of Main Events.”

What’s at stake for Nepal

Regardless of the level of representation, I think  Nepal’s approach should remain pragmatic rather than symbolic, treating SCO engagement as a channel for economic diplomacy rather than a signal of geopolitical alignment. The SCO’s cooperation framework with Nepal already spans trade, transit, investment, transport, energy, agriculture, disaster management, science and technology, tourism and education.

Five broad interests  should frame Nepal’s engagement if it participates:

Economic diplomacy — deepening trade linkages with Central Asian economies and courting investment in hydropower, tourism, ICT and agriculture, while diversifying export destinations beyond traditional markets.

Regional connectivity — positioning Nepal as a bridge between South and Central Asia, and exploring feasible multimodal transport and cross-border logistics links, even though large infrastructure commitments through a body where Nepal has no voting power remain unlikely in the near term.

Energy cooperation — Nepal’s substantial hydropower potential remains its strongest card for attracting technology transfer and investment partnerships, alongside discussions on regional electricity trade.

Security cooperation — dialogue on terrorism, cybercrime, organised crime and disaster response, calibrated carefully to avoid compromising Nepal’s constitutionally rooted non-aligned foreign policy.

Strategic balance — maintaining equilibrium in ties with China, India, Russia and the Central Asian republics without appearing to tilt toward any bloc, a posture Nepal has historically guarded closely given its geographic position between two larger neighbours.

Preparation across four fronts

I see that, if Nepal choose to send a high-level delegation, preparation would need to happen simultaneously on diplomatic, economic, political and business fronts. On the diplomatic side, this would mean finalising bilateral meeting schedules with counterparts likely to be present, China, Russia, India, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan among them, alongside issue-specific briefing papers coordinated across the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Finance, Energy and Industry within the country.

Economically, Nepal would benefit from arriving with an investment-ready project portfolio: hydropower schemes, transmission infrastructure, industrial parks, special economic zones, dry ports, tourism facilities and digital connectivity projects that could be pitched directly to potential investors on the sidelines.

Politically, a consistent national position is expected to underpin any Nepali statement at the summit: support for multipolar cooperation, adherence to the UN Charter, non-participation in military alliances, and an emphasis on peaceful regional cooperation, messaging largely consistent with Nepal’s post-1990s non-aligned foreign policy tradition regardless of which government is in power.

On the business side, participation from apex bodies such as the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI), the Confederation of Nepalese Industries (CNI), the Nepal Chamber of Commerce, and the Investment Board Nepal could help translate summit visibility into concrete business-to-business engagement.

Realistic outcomes

Given Nepal’s dialogue-partner status, expectations for Bishkek should be calibrated accordingly. Realistic outcomes include greater political visibility in the Eurasian space, fresh bilateral meetings with major regional powers, exploratory investment conversations in infrastructure and energy, tourism promotion, and expanded cooperation on disaster management and digital technology. Binding financial commitments are unlikely, since decision-making authority rests solely with full members.

Nepal’s likely talking points would be sustainable Himalayan development, glacier and mountain ecosystem protection, hydropower investment, cross-border connectivity, digital economy growth, tourism recovery, food security, disaster resilience and youth exchanges, which align closely with the cooperation areas already covered under its SCO partnership framework.

Headwinds facing the summit

The Bishkek summit itself will not be immune to the structural tensions that have periodically complicated SCO consensus-building: India-Pakistan friction, China-India strategic competition, Russia-West sanctions disputes, and Iran-related Middle East tensions have all, at various points, made it harder for the grouping to move beyond broad declarations. Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship has explicitly sought to counter this by pushing an implementation-focused agenda, though translating declarations into action has long been the SCO’s central institutional weakness. There is no indication of any organised effort within the bloc to specifically undermine China at Bishkek, though differences over regional security priorities and connectivity initiatives may be considered likely, consistent with the SCO’s pattern of managing disagreement through negotiation rather than open rupture.

For Nepal, the recommended posture should remain a development-first, strictly non-aligned approach: prioritising economic cooperation over geopolitical positioning, and presenting itself as a stable, reliable partner invested in regional peace and sustainable development — a strategy consistent with Nepal’s long-standing foreign policy principles, and one that offers the clearest path to turning summit participation into tangible national benefit, whoever leads the delegation to Bishkek.

title.rendered: 1.2 million tourists entered Nepal in one year, 25 percent Indian

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 26

In fiscal year 2025/26, 1,209,357 foreign tourists entered Nepal. According to the Nepal Tourism Board, the largest number, 311,531, came from India, while 111,325 tourists came from the United States and 109,892 from China.

According to international tourist arrival data released by the Nepal Tourism Board, India has become Nepal’s largest source market, accounting for about 25.76 percent of total arrivals. After India, the United States (111,325) is the second-largest source market, and China (109,892) is the third.

They were followed by 58,163 tourists from Bangladesh, 56,649 from the United Kingdom, 53,195 from Australia, 43,211 from Sri Lanka, 36,289 from Bhutan, 30,737 from Myanmar, 29,296 from Germany, 27,201 from Thailand, 25,762 from Japan, and 25,640 from Malaysia.

In the last fiscal year 2025/26, the highest number of foreign tourists, 124,829, arrived in mid-October to mid-November 2025. This was followed by 119,390 in mid-March to mid-April 2026, 114,152 in mid-February to mid-March 2026, and 111,780 in mid-September to mid-October 2025, according to the data.

The Nepal Tourism Board said it has intensified promotional programs in its closest source markets, India and China. In fiscal year 2025/26, more than 12 promotional events were held in various Indian cities including Pune, Hyderabad, Chennai, Mumbai, and New Delhi. In total, more than 40 tourism promotional events for Nepal were held in international markets.

Similarly, in the last three months of fiscal year 2025/26, various cross-border tourism marts and fairs were held from Jhapa in the east to Kanchanpur in the west, to safeguard investment in tourism infrastructure in Nepal’s Tarai region bordering India. The Board’s analysis shows this led to a notable rise in the number of tourists entering Nepal through the border areas.

Nepal Tourism Board Acting Chief Executive Hikmat Singh Airee said Nepal’s tourism has grown positively due to international market promotion, expanded air access, and cooperation with the private sector.

He said, “Tourist arrivals in fiscal year 2025/26 clearly indicate that Nepal’s tourism industry is moving from recovery toward sustainable growth. Alongside our major source markets, we will continue making targeted promotion in new, promising markets more effective, in our ongoing effort to establish Nepal as an attractive year-round destination.”

Acting Chief Executive Airee pointed out that although China has enormous potential for tourist arrivals, sales missions targeting that market need to be made more effective to expand business-to-business (B2B) contacts.

He said, “To strengthen our presence further in new, high-potential source markets such as the US, Australia and Bangladesh, alongside China, we need to run regular international sales missions. To make tourism promotion more results-oriented, the Nepal Tourism Board is moving to expand such programs immediately in cooperation with the private sector through the fiscal year 2026/27 budget.”

Noting that the Government of Nepal has declared this year the Wellness Tourism Year 2027, Acting Chief Executive Airee said tourist arrival numbers are expected to rise further in the current fiscal year. The Nepal Tourism Board said it will work in the coming days to attract high-spending tourists, increase length of stay, and further strengthen Nepal’s tourism promotion in both traditional and new international markets.

title.rendered: Fires in Parsa, Kathmandu and Dang cause damage worth millions

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 26

Fire incidents in Parsa, Kathmandu, and Dang have caused damage worth millions of rupees.

A fire at a clothing shop in Birgunj Metropolitan City-6, Parsa, caused damage worth Rs 1.2 million.

The fire broke out on Saturday night due to an electrical wire short circuit at Durga Ready-Made Suppliers, run by Raj Kumar Sah of Parwanipur Rural Municipality-4, Bara.

Police said clothes inside the shop were burnt. The fire was brought under control with the help of fire engines and locals.

Fire at a clothes stitching centre in Kathmandu

A fire at a clothes stitching centre near Radha Krishna Temple in Ward 16 of Kathmandu Metropolitan City caused damage worth Rs 350,000 the previous night.

The fire broke out at around 12:15 am at the clothes stitching centre operating on the ground floor of Jagrit Khanal’s house.

The cause of the fire has not been determined, though it is suspected to have been caused by an electrical wire short circuit.

Police Circle Balaju said the fire was brought under control with the help of locals and police.

Fire in Dang as well

Similarly, a fire broke out due to an electrical short circuit at the house of Ramesh Kumar Gupta in old Bhaluwang Bazaar, Rapti Rural Municipality-1, Dang.

Police said the fire broke out around 9 pm on Saturday when wires in the house’s meter box short-circuited, burning and destroying clothes, a refrigerator, and other household items inside the house.

title.rendered: French company IN Groupe wins National ID contract without competition

content.rendered:
The government is set to purchase the Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS) needed for national identity cards from IN Groupe, France’s state-owned company.

The Council of Ministers meeting decided to purchase the Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS) through a government-to-government (G2G) arrangement, without competitive bidding. The system, to be procured for around 10 million units, will make it easier to distinguish between individuals’ identities.

ABIS helps store personal records of millions of individuals and detect matches among the stored data. Once personal details for the national ID are collected, this record is used for criminal investigation, personal identification, security, and other purposes. The system contains fingerprint, facial, and eye-retina identification data. The license the government is purchasing will help detect and check this data for duplication.

The proposal prepared by the Department of National ID and Civil Registration was endorsed by the Council of Ministers meeting on June 12. Department Director General Krishna Poudel said approval had been given to obtain a license for 10 million units from IN Groupe, which is wholly owned by the French government’s Ministry of Economy.

According to him, the mandate is to negotiate and sign the contract without exceeding the amount agreed in the fiscal year 2018/19 deal. He said the rate at that time was set at 0.0995 euros per unit, which comes to about Rs 17.49 at the current exchange rate.

The government initially began collecting biometrics and issuing national ID cards for government employees in Taplejung and at Singha Durbar, and later planned to distribute national ID cards to 20 million Nepalis. Director General Poudel said preparations are now underway to obtain a license for about 10 million units from the French company IN Groupe for the remaining roughly 10 million people.

Director General Poudel said that although the contract is with France’s IN Groupe, Idemia, which holds the passport contract, has no role in it. He said the rate is determined through negotiations between government representatives of both countries, with no agent or commission involved, calling some of the circulating claims baseless.

He said, “The company called Idemia is not connected to that process in any way.”

France’s Idemia Group has three main divisions, Idemia Secure Transactions, Idemia Public Security, and Idemia Smart Identity. Idemia Smart Identity, which works on passports, national ID cards, driving licenses, and digital identity solutions, merged into IN Groupe two years ago, and it is from this entity that the government is purchasing ABIS.

The Council of Ministers decided that 1.5 million units would be purchased directly at first, with the remaining 8.5 million to be purchased through the G2G arrangement. After the Council of Ministers’ decision on June 12, government spokesperson Sasmit Pokharel did not comment on the agreement decision.

title.rendered: Rethinking grazing in community forests in Nepal

content.rendered:
Livestock rearing through grazing has been one of the major livelihoods for centuries; however, feeding patterns have changed with time and circumstances. Born from the urgency of the 1960s and 1970s afforestation drives, when young saplings needed protection and degraded hillsides desperately needed cover, the blanket stopping grazing became gospel. It has been helpful during massive afforestation. Forests came back. But that success story may now be obscuring a quieter crisis unfolding on the forest floor.

Nepal’s community forestry programme is, by any measure, one of the world’s great conservation achievements. In 1992, forests covered just 26 per cent of the country’s land area. By 2016, that figure had climbed back to 45 per cent, nearly double, thanks largely to more than 22,000 Community Forest User Groups (CFUGs) that today collectively manage close to three million hectares across Nepal, directly benefiting roughly half of all rural households. The programme has been lauded globally as a model of participatory resource governance.

But decades of successful protection have created a new problem in many mature forests: dense, impenetrable undergrowth. Without periodic disturbance, shrub layers thicken, fire risk rises, and the conditions that allow natural seedling regeneration deteriorate. In these forests, not the young or actively managed ones, but the mature, well-stocked community forests of the hills, the old logic of total exclusion may be working against forest health.

“There was a time when we used to say no livestock in the forest. It seems that was a mistake. Now we say grazing needs to be open for the health of the forest,” says Chairperson, District FECOFUN, Dolakha, Jagnath Basnet. This view is gaining ground among forest practitioners and ecologists alike.

In mature forests without intensive management, controlled grazing can suppress dense understorey growth, reduce accumulated dry fuel, and help maintain a healthier, more diverse forest floor. Well-planned rotational or seasonal grazing is increasingly recognised not as a threat to forests, but as an ecologically valuable tool for managing them.

Crucially, the legal framework does not stand in the way. Neither Nepal’s Forest Act nor its regulations impose a blanket grazing prohibition. CFUGs retain full autonomy to set rules according to local conditions. What has persisted is not a legal mandate but an institutional habit, a conservation narrative that outlived its original context.

The human cost of rigid rules

The persistence of that narrative carries real costs for those who remain in Nepal’s hills. Livestock rearing- goats, cattle, buffalo- remains central to hill economies, providing milk, meat, manure, and cash income. Community forests are the primary source of fodder and grazing land for most rural families.

A Chauri herder in Kalinchowk Rural Municipality shares, “Every time we (herders) are blamed for forest degradation in community forest meetings, we have started to skip the CF meeting”. The narrative of negative impacts of grazing inside the forest is deeply rooted in common people.

A goat rearer in Bhimeshwor Municipality put it simply: if grazing were permitted, she could expand her herd from 30 to 60 goats. The alternative, stall-feeding, which requires cutting and carrying fodder by hand, is exhausting work, and it is growing harder. With young people leaving for Kathmandu, the Gulf, or beyond, it is increasingly the elderly who shoulder this burden alone.

Nepal’s 2021 census confirmed what many in the hills already knew: the country’s population growth rate has fallen to its lowest in eight decades, at just 0.93 per cent annually. The hill and mountain regions have seen absolute population decline. Over 29 per cent of people from the hill regions have migrated internally in the last decade alone, and Nepal’s net migration figure remains deeply negative. The villages that once needed rules to manage pressure on forests are now facing the opposite problem: too few people, and too little economic activity to sustain rural life.

A 2021 study by Jefferson Fox of the East-West Center, published in the Journal of Peasant Studies, tracked this shift across middle-hills communities between 1992 and 2017. In 1992, the average hill household owned four cows and buffalo and five-and-a-half goats and sheep. By 2017, those numbers had roughly halved. The pressure on forests from livestock has diminished substantially, yet the rules designed to address that old pressure have largely remained unchanged.

Nuance, not a free-for-all

Rethinking grazing does not mean opening all forests to all animals at all times. Context is everything. Regeneration felling areas, where mother trees are retained to promote natural seedlings, require temporary fencing and exclusion, as do newly planted forests in their early years. These protections remain as necessary as ever. What is outdated is the default assumption that grazing is always harmful everywhere.

The path forward is adaptive management: zoning forests by ecological condition and management stage, developing seasonal grazing calendars that protect regenerating areas while opening mature sections, and building monitoring systems that allow CFUGs to track impacts and adjust rules accordingly.

Nepal’s CFUGs already have the institutional capacity for this; the same deliberative structures that produced one of the world’s most successful conservation programmes can produce nuanced, locally appropriate grazing policies too.

A new definition of success

Nepal’s forest recovery is a story worth celebrating. Forest cover has nearly doubled in three decades. Biodiversity has returned to once-degraded hillsides. Community institutions have been strengthened. These gains must be protected.

But the next chapter of Nepal’s community forestry story cannot be written with the rulebook of the 1970s. A country whose hill villages are emptying, whose remaining residents are older and more dependent on livestock than ever, and whose mature forests increasingly need management rather than simply protection, requires a more adaptive approach.

The ideal for Nepal’s hills is no longer just dense forest. It is forests that also sustain resilient rural economies and the communities that have spent generations caring for them. A thoughtful re-examination of long-standing grazing practices, grounded in ecological evidence, local knowledge, and the legal autonomy that CFUGs already possess, can help achieve both.
The fence, in other words, has served its purpose. It may be time to open the gate.

title.rendered: Flood inundates settlement in Bajura, 13 families rescued

content.rendered:
July 24, Dhangadhi

Floodwaters entered a settlement in Badimalika Municipality-9 of Bajura after the Selagad River and Bauli Khola overflowed near their confluence, prompting the evacuation of 13 families to safer locations.

According to Bajura DSP Shaileshwari Bohara, the affected families were rescued along with their belongings on Thursday night and moved to safety.

The evacuees have been temporarily sheltered in the homes of nearby residents located in safer areas, DSP Bohara said.

Of the 13 affected households, three remain at high risk from further flooding.

According to the Disaster Preparedness and Response Plan 2083, recently released by the District Disaster Management Committee, more than 100 villages in Bajura are at high risk of floods and landslides.

Roads blocked by landslides

Meanwhile, continuous rainfall has triggered landslides that have blocked roads at two locations in the district.

Police said roads have been obstructed after landslides occurred in Badimalika Municipality-6 and behind the District Prison.

Efforts are underway to clear the blocked roads and restore traffic, police said.
