title.rendered: Bodhichitta harvest season brings spike in theft and disputes in Kavre

content.rendered:
The harvesting season for Bodhichitta (Buddha seed), an increasingly lucrative cash crop, has begun, but with it has come a familiar wave of thefts, disputes and conflicts in Kavrepalanchok district.

More than a dozen incidents related to Bodhichitta have already been reported this season. The crop’s high market value has fueled disputes among orchard owners and traders, and among traders themselves, creating growing security concerns.

Between June 3 and July 10 (Jestha 20 to Asar 25), Bodhichitta thefts were reported from several parts of the district, including Dhulikhel, Panauti, Panchkhal, Bhumlu, Mandandeupur and Roshi Rural Municipality. In some cases, thieves cut down entire trees to steal the seeds, while in others, they allegedly used motorcycles to carry out nighttime thefts, according to police investigations.

District Police Office Kavrepalanchok Information Officer DSP Rabin Bista said more than a dozen Bodhichitta-related incidents have occurred during the current harvesting season alone. Seeds were stolen directly from trees at eight different locations, he said.

On June 27 (Asar 13), the trunk of a Bodhichitta tree belonging to Kulman Tamang in Anekot, Panchkhal Municipality-1, was cut in half before its seeds were stolen. Police have yet to identify those responsible.

On the same day, seeds worth an estimated Rs 500,000 were stolen from the orchard of Janak Bahadur Khatri in Pinale, Bhumlu Rural Municipality-4. Preliminary investigations suggest the theft was carried out by individuals who arrived on motorcycles.

Similarly, on July 5 (Asar 21), Bodhichitta seeds belonging to Suman Lama of Kamrang Tol, Bhumlu-5, were stolen.

Also, on July 5, a Bodhichitta garland belonging to Sanukanchha Tamang of Dadagaun, Mandandeupur-1, was stolen. On July 8 (Asar 24), another garland was stolen from the orchard of Akkal Bahadur Tamang in Chitle, Mandandeupur-2, while on July 9 (Asar 25), police recorded the theft of Bodhichitta belonging to Manorath Bhurtel of Rajbas, Roshi-9.

Earlier, on June 21 (Asar 7), Bodhichitta owned by Surya Kumar Tamang of Balthali Pallodanda, Panauti-11, was stolen. On June 3 (Jestha 20), about one pathi (traditional measure) of Bodhichitta garlands belonging to Ajay Tamang of Mitinchhap, Dhulikhel-1, was also reported stolen.

On June 13 (Jestha 30), a police team from the temporary police post at Kavrebhanjyang, Dhulikhel-9, arrested two individuals during a security check while they were carrying Bodhichitta seeds.

Disputes over harvesting rights

Police say theft is not the only concern. Disputes over the right to harvest Bodhichitta seeds have also intensified.

The District Police Office deployed 16 police personnel at four locations to maintain security after conflicts erupted over harvesting rights.

According to police, security was provided at orchards owned by Krishna Kumari Badal of Dhulikhel-8, Mohan Bahadur Rayamajhi of Roshi-11, Aitesing Thing, Dhawa Thing and Jenising Thing of Lurpung, Roshi-5, and Sher Bahadur Tamang of Roshi-6 after disputes arose over who had the legal right to harvest the seeds.

DSP Bista said police even had to guard a Bodhichitta tree in Dhulikhel-8 because of a dispute between a husband and wife.

“The couple had been living separately and had independently signed agreements with different buyers to sell the seeds from the same tree. A dispute later arose over who had the right to harvest the seeds, prompting a request for police protection. The matter even reached the court. Eventually, the husband won the case, harvested the seeds and sold them. We provided security until the sale was completed,” Bista said.

In another case, police provided security in Roshi-11 after business partners who had jointly purchased a Bodhichitta garland became involved in a dispute. In Lurpung, Roshi-5, security was deployed after three owners of a single Bodhichitta tree separately signed agreements to sell the same harvest, leading to conflict.

Bista said police provide protection only when requested by orchard owners or traders.

“As the price of Bodhichitta continues to rise, disputes recur every year because some orchard owners attempt to break earlier purchase agreements and sell their harvest to other traders offering higher prices,” he said.

Arrests made in theft cases

Of the nine theft cases reported so far, police have arrested suspects in two.

Three men—Fursang Tamang, Rose Tamang and Phurba Tamang, all from Dhulikhel-1—have been arrested for allegedly stealing Bodhichitta seeds worth around Rs 700,000 belonging to Kanchhi Tamang.

In another case, Samrat Kami and Kumar Kami of Bhumlu Rural Municipality-6 have been charged with stealing Bodhichitta seeds worth approximately Rs 500,000 from Sun Bahadur Tamang of Mandandeupur Municipality-12.

High-Value crop with growing security concerns

Temal and Roshi Rural Municipality are considered the main Bodhichitta-producing areas of Kavrepalanchok. Encouraged by its rising market value, cultivation has expanded to other local governments across the district in recent years.

Although production and trade have increased, disputes over harvesting rights, purchase agreements and recurring thefts continue to pose security challenges every harvest season.

The collection and processing season for Bodhichitta, highly valued by Buddhists for making prayer beads, runs from Asar (mid-June) to Ashoj (mid-October).

Driven by strong demand from China, traders often purchase the harvest directly from farmers before the seeds are picked. The seeds and prayer bead garlands are mainly exported to Tibet in China and Bodh Gaya in India.

The value of Bodhichitta depends largely on the size and the number of natural “faces” or grooves on each seed. According to traders, a high-quality prayer bead garland made from 108 seeds can fetch anywhere between Rs 30,000 and Rs 800,000.

title.rendered: 17-year-old girl’s ovum extracted in Lalitpur after Rs 50,000 lure

content.rendered:
Another case of ovum trafficking has come to light, echoing an earlier episode that was quietly buried without prosecution under state protection.

During Sushila Karki’s tenure as prime minister, then-Attorney General Sabita Bhandari had decided not to pursue the ovum -trafficking case. The Hope Fertility and Research Centre, in which Bhandari herself had an investment, received a clean chit in that case.

Now a similar case of ovum trafficking has surfaced again.

A 17-year-old girl, a grade 11 student, has become a victim of an attempted ovum -trafficking scheme. According to the victim, she was first told by a friend that nothing would happen if she had her ovum extracted.

“My friend told me, ‘I’ve already given ovums two or three times myself. This is something that just goes to waste every month anyway. Nothing happens. And you get money too,'” the victim told Onlinekhabar.

After being told she’d get money and that nothing would happen to her, she says she agreed. She was then connected with an agent, who convinced her further.

After being lured with promises, the girl agreed.

“I was told nothing would happen, there’d be no pain, and it wouldn’t harm my body at all,” she says. According to her, she was then taken to B&B IVF in Gwarko, Lalitpur.

“First they gave me an injection. About a week to ten days later, the ovums were extracted,” the victim says.

The injections are used to stimulate ovum development, and once the ovums are mature, they are extracted. Initially, she was only given the injections.

Once the ovums had developed, they were extracted from her on June 28. After that, her body suddenly began to change. She became so weak she was at the point of collapsing.

After her health deteriorated, she told her family everything. She was then admitted to and treated at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj.

Ovum from other women is used to help infertile couples have children. The collected ovum is used to produce a child through IVF.

Although she was initially told she would receive Rs 50,000, she was only given Rs 30,000. The victim says that when her health worsened and she needed treatment, she instead ended up short of money.

After her health complications and subsequent treatment, the victim’s family filed a complaint with the police. They lodged the complaint at the District Police Range, Lalitpur. SP Gautam Mishra, spokesperson for the Range, confirmed that the complaint had been received.

“We have received the complaint. We are investigating the matter,” Mishra informed Onlinekhabar. Police have arrested one middleman in connection with the case and are investigating further. According to SP Gautam, the person arrested is 21-year-old Radhika Gotame, originally from Lamjung and currently residing in Lalitpur. She was arrested by police on July 17.

Police say the investigation against her is proceeding under human trafficking charges. However, the victim’s family has complained that police have not arrested the doctor involved in the ovum extraction.

“If the doctor who extracted the ovum is the main culprit, why hasn’t he been arrested yet?” the family asks.

Police, for their part, claim the investigation is ongoing and that those involved will be arrested.

“The victim has said the ovum was extracted at B&B. We are gathering all the evidence and investigating. Whoever is found involved or guilty will be arrested,” SP Gautam says.

Earlier, in June 2025, the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) of Police had arrested people involved in a similar ovum -trafficking case.

Investigators had found that ova were being trafficked through the Hope Fertility and Research Centre in Babarmahal and the Angel Fertility Clinic in Maharajgunj.

The investigation found that victims were given only Rs 8,000–10,000, while the ovum s were sold for as much as Rs 2 million.

After completing its investigation, the CIB recommended in Bhadra last year that seven people, including Dr Swasti Sharma, Pratyusha Baral, Asim Adhikari, Malini Chaudhary, Alisha Oli, and Justina Pradhan, be prosecuted under Section 66 of the Children’s Act, 2075.

However, then-Attorney General Bhandari decided in October 2025 not to pursue the case. Pratyusha, who had been recommended as a defendant, is Bhandari’s own daughter, and Swasti is also a family member.

After it came to light that ova were being illegally bought and sold, the government prepared new standards. To regulate infertility treatment (IVF) services, the government issued the Standards for Operating Infertility Management Services, 2082.

The ministry issued the standards under the authority granted by Section 64 of the Public Health Service Act, 2075, to give practical effect to the reproductive rights guaranteed by the constitution and bring uniformity to infertility treatment services.

Under the new standards, ovum donation must now follow set limits, confidentiality, and health-safety protocols. A woman may not donate ovum more than six times in her lifetime.

There must be a gap of at least three months between each donation. Donors must be between 20 and 35 years old, and must undergo physical examination and lab tests to confirm they are free of communicable diseases before donating.

Women donating ovum must be informed of the possible immediate and future health complications from the procedure, and informed consent is mandatory. In this case, however, a 17-year-old girl had her ovum extracted after being lured with false promises.

title.rendered: Nepali space innovator Jagriti Luitel to speak at International Astronautical Congress

content.rendered:
Nepali space innovator Jagriti Luitel will represent the country on the “Emerging Space Nations” panel at the International Astronautical Congress 2026 in Antalya, Turkey. She is the first Nepali selected as a speaker for this global conference.

During the event, Luitel will present research from her work with the MIT spin-off Aurelia Institute. Her presentation focuses on space architecture for disaster resilience, using the 2015 Nepal earthquake as a case study.

The conference runs from October 5 to 9, with Luitel’s panel scheduled for October 7 alongside speakers John Leur Labrador, Jakub Masek, Linda Ngozwana, and Alex Shi.

“A decade ago, I was sleeping under the open sky after Nepal’s earthquake. This October, I’ll be speaking about how space can help build a more resilient future for countries like ours,” Luitel shared on Instagram.

A human spaceflight trainee, Luitel previously worked at the Canadian Space Agency and represented Nepal on a zero-gravity flight.

title.rendered: Mcube Young Artists Show 2026 to spotlight emerging voices in Nepali contemporary art

content.rendered:
July 23, Lalitpur

Gallery Mcube has presented the Mcube Young Artists Show 2026, bringing together works by 10 emerging artists whose practices engage with themes ranging from gender, identity and memory to urbanisation, indigenous histories and environmental change. Curated by multidisciplinary artist and curator Manish Lal Shrestha, the annual exhibition aims to provide a platform for young contemporary artists to engage with the public and Nepal’s broader art community.

The exhibition features works by Amisha KC, Amisha Maharjan, Kripa Shakya, Kritika Manandhar, Rujan Maharjan, Saijal Sthapit, Sharmila Devi Tamang, Smarika Maharjan, Sonam Chamling Rai and Spandan Pyakurel (KEKI), employing media such as painting, installation, drawing, photography, performance, video and mixed media. According to the gallery, the exhibition reflects the diversity of contemporary artistic practices among Nepal’s younger generation.

Curator Shrestha said the exhibition seeks to nurture new artistic voices while creating opportunities for dialogue between emerging artists and the wider art community. He noted that each participant presents a distinct visual language shaped by personal experiences as well as broader social realities.

Many of the featured works examine pressing social and cultural issues. Amisha KC’s oil paintings question the objectification of women and the role of the viewer’s gaze, while Amisha Maharjan’s installation Uprooted reflects on the disappearance of agricultural land and the social consequences of rapid urbanisation. Kripa Shakya explores the significance of everyday rituals through fabric and thread, and Kritika Manandhar’s performance installation To Inherit investigates maternal lineage and inherited memory.

Other artists draw inspiration from cultural traditions and environmental concerns. Rujan Maharjan revisits the Newa festival Sithi Nakha through terracotta reliefs inspired by Paubha and Thangka symbolism, while Sharmila Devi Tamang documents birds adapting to Kathmandu’s urban landscape through photography. Saijal Sthapit’s paintings use fish as metaphors for memory and desire, and Smarika Maharjan’s performance work examines grief as an evolving emotional process.

The exhibition also highlights issues of migration and indigenous identity. Sonam Chamling Rai explores intergenerational displacement and the preservation of indigenous cultural memory through two projects centred on migration and the traditional Dangam bamboo jaw harp. Meanwhile, Spandan Pyakurel’s surreal paintings reflect on family, travel and inherited memories rooted in childhood journeys to his ancestral home.

Gallery Mcube said the annual exhibition continues its long-running commitment to supporting emerging artists through exhibitions, educational programmes, residencies and international collaborations. Established in 2011, the gallery says it has sought to strengthen Nepal’s contemporary art scene by fostering dialogue between established and emerging practitioners.

The exhibition continues till July 31.

title.rendered: Nepal defeated by Sri Lanka in CAVA Championship match

content.rendered:
File

Kathmandu, July 23

Sri Lanka defeated Nepal in today’s match of the Men’s Central Asian Volleyball Association (CAVA) Championship. This is Nepal’s second consecutive drubbing in the tournament. In the first game yesterday, Nepal was defeated by Kazakhstan in sets of 3–2.

In a match held today at the Liaquat Gymnasium in Islamabad, Pakistan, Nepal was defeated by Sri Lanka 3–2 in sets. Sri Lanka won the first set 25–18. Then, Nepal took the next two sets, winning the second set 25–21 and the third set 25–19. Sri Lanka grabbed the fourth set 25–21.

In the final set, Sri Lanka also won 15–11 to win the match. Nepal will now play their third match on Friday against the host, Pakistan. After the single round-robin league, the top four teams will enter the semifinals. The tournament includes the host Pakistan, along with Nepal, Kazakhstan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and Uzbekistan.—RSS

title.rendered: Rabi Lamichhane to visit Beijing for high-level meetings

content.rendered:
July 23, Kathmandu

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Chair Rabi Lamichhane is preparing to visit China. According to a high-ranking government source, a four-member RSP delegation led by Lamichhane is scheduled to travel to Beijing in the second week of August.

Although the names of all Chinese officials he will meet have not been disclosed, meetings with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and senior leaders of the Communist Party of China have been confirmed.

“The visit is being organised under the framework of party-to-party relations. Chairperson Lamichhane had actually received an invitation from China during the previous parliamentary term. This time, however, we expect more substantive discussions,” a senior government official told Onlinekhabar.

“There will be talks at a high level. The main agenda is to further deepen and strengthen Nepal–China relations,” the official said.

The visit is expected to last five days. The identities of the other members of the delegation have not yet been made public.

No government representatives will be part of the delegation.

According to RSP sources, the Beijing visit will be similar in nature to Lamichhane’s previous visit to New Delhi, where he held a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

content.rendered:
Chitwan, July 22

The price of eggs, which had decreased due to the impact of bird flu, has started to rise. Prices have begun to increase because production has dropped and demand has gone up. The Nepal Layers Poultry Association sets market prices based on the rates determined by big farms. According to the association, starting today, the price of large eggs has increased from Rs 450 to Rs 500 per crate (30 pieces).

The price of medium eggs has gone up from Rs 420 to Rs 470, while that of small eggs has now reached Rs 415. The price has gone up by Rs 50 for all sizes of eggs. Binod Pokharel, the central president of the Nepal Layers Poultry Association, said that prices have started to rise as the demand for eggs has increased. He mentioned that daily egg production, which used to be around 4.5 million eggs, has dropped to about 2.8 million due to bird flu.

At the end of Jestha (June 14), a crate (30 eggs) was sold for Rs 550, but the price had dropped to Rs 450 after the detection of bird flu. The cost price of one crate of eggs comes to Rs 573.60. Each egg costs Rs 19.12. Pokharel mentioned that the price has started to rise as egg consumption has increased.

Even though the prices have gone up, farmers still haven’t been able to get the cost price. Chairperson Pokharel said that farmers are now hoping to get the cost price soon after the rise in egg prices. He said that farmers have suffered huge losses due to bird flu and that the government should provide relief to the affected farmers

title.rendered: MRB: The inspiring journey of a vlogger driven to put Myagdi on the map

content.rendered:
Ever since childhood, Bibid Jung Thapa from Myagdi has loved riding bicycles, motorcycles, and exploring new places. That passion eventually led him to become one of Nepal’s most recognised moto vloggers, but not before overcoming setbacks that taught him resilience.

In 2016, he participated in Pulsar Dareventure Season 2, an adventure reality show. However, he was eliminated early because he struggled to express himself confidently in front of the judges.

Rather than giving up, Bibid returned home, bought a mirror, and spent months practising speaking in front of it every day. A year later, he competed in Season 3, where his improved communication skills helped him reach the Top 4. Although he was eliminated after failing to secure enough votes from fellow contestants, he won the Most Popular Award through public voting.

“That was when I truly realised the strength of my village,” he recalls. People began calling him “Myagdi” wherever he went—a nickname he wore with pride. “I love introducing Myagdi to people. The support I received from my hometown was unbelievable. While others received a few dozen votes, I would receive two or three thousand,” he says.

He believes his experience proved a simple truth: “In cities, houses are close together, but hearts are far apart. In villages, houses are far apart, but hearts are close.”

Promoting Myagdi through YouTube

Since then, Bibid has made it his mission to promote Myagdi. He initially named his YouTube channel “Myagdi Rider Bibid”, but later shortened it to “MRB,” a name by which he is now widely recognised. “I realised many people knew Mustang and Baglung, but very few had heard of Myagdi. That bothered me. So I decided I would use Myagdi’s name to introduce it to the world,” he says.

Today, his YouTube channel has 1.54 million subscribers. He has travelled across the United States, the Maldives, Thailand, India, and nearly 70 districts of Nepal, carrying the name of Myagdi wherever he goes.

A student more interested in machines than books

Bibid admits he was never particularly interested in academics. Instead of studying, he enjoyed repairing radios, wiring electronics, and riding bicycles—sometimes secretly borrowing friends’ bikes without permission. Frequent moves between his village, Kathmandu, and Beni also disrupted his education.

While in Grade 9, he was expelled from school and almost abandoned his studies altogether. A turning point came when a neighbour promised to buy him a motorcycle if he passed the School Leaving Certificate (SLC) examination. “I studied with determination after that,” he says.

He eventually passed with a first division. The promised motorcycle had become old by then, so he persuaded his family to buy him a new one instead. “I didn’t dream of becoming anything through education. I simply wanted the motorcycle,” he says with a laugh. Just days after taking his SLC exams, he travelled to Kathmandu to obtain a motorcycle license.

While studying in Grades 11 and 12, he regularly rode to college—but often skipped classes with friends to ride to Mustang. “We used to bunk college just to have coffee in Mustang,” he recalls. During the monsoon, they also helped pilgrims heading to Muktinath cross swollen rivers and find their way. His passion for motorcycling eventually inspired him to enter Pulsar Dareventure.

Inspired by YouTube

Bibid had never seriously considered becoming a YouTuber until he watched videos produced by the SMZ YouTube channel. Seeing riders receive appreciation for riding on paved roads, he thought, “If people enjoy watching that, why wouldn’t they enjoy watching me ride off-road?”

Without a camera of his own, he asked his uncle in Japan to send him an action camera that could be mounted on his helmet. He began uploading riding videos, but they attracted little attention.

Later, he discovered rapper Girish Khatiwada’s vlogs. “I realised talking to the audience made videos much more enjoyable. He inspired me to speak on camera.” At first, he could not even afford a microphone and often borrowed one from friends. “I used to wonder whether I should buy a microphone or spend the money on fuel to keep riding,” he remembers.

From few views to millions

Bibid started uploading videos in 2017. For the first couple of years, his channel attracted very few viewers. Everything changed in 2019, when one of his videos went viral. “I had been used to seeing just two or three views. Suddenly, every time I refreshed the page, another thousand views appeared. Imagine how that felt.”

Even after his channel became monetised, earning a meaningful income took time. “I didn’t understand YouTube’s algorithm, and there was nobody to teach me.” He continued uploading consistently. Today, his channel has 1.54 million subscribers. Bibid says he has never viewed YouTube as merely a profession.

“It doesn’t feel like hard work. Creating videos is as natural to me as breathing. I do it because it makes me happy.” His first YouTube earnings amounted to Rs 11,000, which he gave entirely to his parents, grandfather, and sisters. “When I received my first YouTube income, I felt like I had conquered the world.”

During the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020, while most people stayed indoors, Bibid explored villages and forests to create content, helping his channel grow even faster.

Nepal remains his favourite destination

Despite travelling internationally, Bibid believes no destination matches Nepal. “In Nepal, you can reach the Himalayas, the hills, and the plains all within a day. I think that’s why foreigners love this country so much.” He recently completed a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar.

Having already explored nearly 70 districts, he now hopes to travel to the remote regions of Sudurpashchim Province and highlight local challenges to the government through his videos.

A life and career shared

Bibid has also found a partner in both life and content creation. He is married to fellow moto vlogger Surakshya KC from Pokhara, whom he met while vlogging. Surakshya’s YouTube channel has more than 927,000 subscribers.

“Travelling together allows us to support each other. She knows things I don’t, and I know things she doesn’t. We divide the work, and together we create better content.” Although many fans regard him as Nepal’s leading moto vlogger, Bibid avoids such labels.

“I have never claimed to be number one. That’s something supporters say. More important than subscriber numbers is winning viewers’ hearts.” He has no plans to stop vlogging. “I will never stop travelling, making vlogs, and entertaining my audience.”

For aspiring vloggers, his advice is simple, “Don’t worry about making a huge investment in the beginning. Focus on creating good content first.”

title.rendered: The price of dissent: From JNU to Kirtipur

content.rendered:
Modern authoritarianism does not always announce itself through the suspension of elections, the dissolution of Parliament or the arrival of soldiers on the streets. It can grow inside formally democratic systems, through the gradual redefinition of who is entitled to democratic rights.

Its politics is apocalyptic. Society is repeatedly told that it faces an exceptional danger: anti-nationals, urban extremists, infiltrators, foreign agents, disorderly students, politically motivated activists or people supposedly obstructing the state’s work. The identity of the enemy may change, but the political requirement remains constant. Power needs an internal adversary against whom extraordinary conduct can be presented as necessary governance.

The cases of Indian activist Umar Khalid and Nepali activist Majid Ansari are not identical in scale, duration or legal circumstances. Khalid has spent years incarcerated under India’s Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act in the alleged conspiracy case concerning the 2020 Delhi violence. Ansari’s detention at the Kirtipur Holding Centre is a recent and still-developing incident involving disputed accounts of police conduct. To equate the two cases completely would be analytically careless.

But comparison does not require equivalence. It requires identifying a common political method: first diminish the dissident’s standing, then treat the demand for rights as evidence of guilt.

Manufacturing the public enemy

Long before a court determines criminal responsibility, political communication can produce a social verdict.

Umar Khalid experienced this process after the 2016 JNU controversy. In 2018, following an alleged attempt to shoot him outside New Delhi’s Constitution Club, he described a sustained campaign in which ruling-party spokespersons, television anchors and online trolls had branded him “anti-national.” At that stage, he argued, public condemnation had preceded formal legal proof: allegations were repeated as settled facts, debate was displaced by trolling, and political disagreement was converted into threats against his life.

This was not merely Khalid’s subjective description of hostile coverage. In 2022, India’s News Broadcasting and Digital Standards Authority found that several television broadcasts had crossed the line between reporting allegations and presenting an accused person as already guilty. The authority objected to sensationalist headlines portraying Khalid as the mastermind of the Delhi riots and ordered the relevant channels to remove the broadcasts, finding violations of impartiality, objectivity and neutrality.

The political function of labels such as “anti-national” is therefore larger than insult. They reduce a citizen’s legal and cultural standing. Once a person is placed outside the imagined national community, constitutional safeguards begin to look like undeserved privileges. Arrest becomes accountability. Prolonged imprisonment becomes prevention. Violence becomes a response to provocation rather than an abuse requiring investigation.

In Kirtipur, the language was different, but the method was recognisable.

According to reports, Majid Ansari and other activists had gone to a holding centre where families displaced by squatter evictions were living amid serious flooding and waterlogging. Police said the activists obstructed rescue work and refused instructions to leave. Eyewitnesses disputed that account, alleging political favouritism and excessive force. Photographs subsequently showed injuries on Ansari’s face, while police maintained that only the minimum force necessary to manage resistance had been used.

A video circulated from the incident shows Ansari asking, “Give me an arrest warrant.” The response was not a clear explanation of the legal basis for his detention. Instead, a police officer reportedly addressed him through the language of hierarchy and infantilisation: “Your father sent you to study, and you are doing politics? He was then told, “Do not do politics.”

This language matters. It converts a citizen into a disobedient child and a political question into a disciplinary problem. Ansari was not answered as someone invoking legal rights. He was lectured as a student who had supposedly crossed the boundaries assigned to him.

The message was not simply “you may have committed an offence.” It was: politics is not your domain.

Due process is most meaningful when the person invoking it is unpopular, disruptive or accused of wrongdoing. A right that exists only for respectable citizens is not a right. It is social approval disguised as law.

In Khalid’s case, the media environment frequently blurred accusation and conviction. The current legal position must nevertheless be described carefully. Courts have treated the prosecution’s allegations as prima facie sufficient to trigger the restrictive UAPA bail standard. In rejecting bail, the court expressly clarified that its observations were limited to the bail inquiry and should not influence the trial on its merits. A prima facie determination at the bail stage is not a conviction after trial.

That distinction disappears in a media trial. The public does not hear “an accusation has met the preliminary threshold governing bail.” It hears “terrorist,” “mastermind” or “enemy.” The legal presumption of innocence survives on paper while political communication administers punishment in advance.

In Majid Ansari’s case, the constitutional question is similarly broader than whether a physical warrant existed. Nepal’s Constitution prohibits detention without informing the person of the grounds for arrest. It guarantees access to a legal practitioner from the moment of arrest and requires production before the relevant authority within 24 hours, excluding travel time. It also prohibits physical or mental torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.

Nepal’s criminal procedure law permits different forms of arrest depending on the offence and circumstances. It also requires that, before an arrest under the relevant provisions, the person be informed of the cause necessitating arrest. Therefore, the decisive issue is not merely whether police displayed a particular piece of paper. It is whether Ansari was told the legal grounds for depriving him of liberty and whether the force used against him was lawful, necessary and proportionate.

Ansari later alleged from hospital that he had been dragged and beaten, had not been informed of the reason for his arrest and had not been shown a warrant. These remain allegations requiring an independent and credible investigation. The police account must also be examined rather than dismissed in advance. But constitutional government requires more than competing statements. When an injured detainee alleges abuse, the state carries a duty to explain, document and investigate its own use of force.

A government cannot answer a demand for legality with “do not do politics.” Asking why one is being arrested is not insolence. It is citizenship.

Who belongs to the democratic universe?

The religious identity of Umar Khalid has been central to the political imagination constructed around him. Opposition to the Citizenship Amendment Act was frequently represented not as a constitutional disagreement but as a Muslim conspiracy against the nation. Peaceful assembly could consequently be described through the vocabulary of jihad, communal mobilisation or civilisational threat.

This is how minorities are expelled from what may be called the democratic universe: the shared political space in which citizens are presumed entitled to speak, organise, disagree and demand accountability. A majority-community activist may be portrayed as idealistic, misguided or passionate. A Muslim activist expressing the same dissent is more readily interpreted as sectarian, radical or disloyal.

Majid Ansari is also a young Muslim activist. But intellectual honesty requires an important qualification: the publicly available reporting on the Kirtipur incident does not yet establish that the police explicitly targeted him because he was Muslim. The strongest documented evidence concerns his political activity, the police’s disciplinary language, disputed allegations of obstruction and force, and his claim that he was not informed of the legal basis of his detention.

The comparison with Khalid should therefore not depend upon asserting an unproven motive. Its value lies in showing how existing social identities can deepen vulnerability once a dissident is marked as troublesome. A Muslim name does not prove religious targeting. But neither can a society ignore the wider environment in which Muslim political participation is often viewed with greater suspicion.

The question is not only whether an officer uttered a communal slur. It is whether public institutions and political audiences find it easier to suspend empathy when the dissident belongs to a minority already associated with danger.

The crowd as an auxiliary institution

The state’s coercive power does not operate through police and prosecution alone. It is reinforced by television studios, anonymous accounts, partisan influencers and ordinary spectators trained to see suffering as entertainment.

Dehumanisation reaches its most dangerous point when a bruised face provokes ridicule instead of concern. The “Haha” reaction made by Home Minister Sudan Gurung on a post about Majid Ansari’s arrest transforms what might otherwise seem like a trivial social-media gesture into an alarming political message. When the minister responsible for the country’s security apparatus appears to mock the suffering of an injured citizen, that person is no longer treated as a rights-bearing human being, but as someone whose humiliation and pain are considered acceptable. It is not merely laughter directed at Majid; it is a public display of state indifference and a signal to supporters that his rights need not be defended and his suffering may be mocked.

This is why the “public enemy” must be manufactured before force is used. Without prior vilification, an image of a bleeding student might create outrage. After vilification, the same image is treated as proof that the troublemaker received what he deserved.

In this environment, even demands for due process are manipulated. Asking for a warrant becomes arrogance. Seeking legal counsel becomes obstruction. Questioning police conduct becomes hostility to law enforcement. Refusing to obey an unexplained command becomes proof of dangerous radicalism.

The term “efficient governance” then acquires a sinister meaning. Institutions are praised for acting quickly precisely because they have avoided the delays associated with evidence, hearings, explanations and review. The inconvenience of constitutional procedure is presented as weakness; the spectacle of immediate punishment is marketed as strength.

This is the logic of rule by force: the belief that order can be created by disregarding the law. Its appeal lies in its simplicity. It tells the public that complex social problems do not require careful governance, accountable institutions, or respect for due process. All that is needed is a powerful authority and a convenient enemy against whom that power can be displayed.

The price paid by everyone

A society may convince itself that the suspension of rights will remain confined to controversial figures. It never does.

The machinery created for the “anti-national” can be used against the journalist. The powers normalised against the minority activist can be used against the opposition worker. The contempt shown toward a student asking for the grounds of arrest can later be directed at a labourer, a displaced family, a comedian or an ordinary citizen recording police misconduct.

The ultimate danger is not that every dissident will become Umar Khalid or that every detention will reproduce the Kirtipur incident. It is that the public will lose the capacity to recognise a constitutional violation when it occurs.

Democracy is not tested when the state respects citizens it admires. It is tested when an accused, unpopular or confrontational person invokes the law and the state restrains itself.

On a hospital bed lies Majid, his eye injured. Inside a Delhi prison, the label “anti-national” remains attached to Umar’s name. Between them stands a citizen’s question: “What is the legal basis for my arrest?” surrounded by the words “Rohingya,” “serves him right,” and the digital echo of HaHa React. The promise of equal protection still remains written on the pages of the Constitution.

The danger does not begin only when rights are erased; it begins the moment society hears a citizen’s name and stops believing that person deserves those rights.

title.rendered: Bird flu outbreak brought under control, government says

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 23

The bird flu outbreak that spread across several parts of Nepal and severely affected poultry farmers has now come under control, according to the Department of Livestock Services.

The department said no new cases of bird flu have been detected anywhere in the country since Shrawan 1 (July 17). Director General Dr Umesh Dahal stated that the disease is now fully under control.

The most recent case was confirmed in Sundarijal, Gokarneshwor-1, Kathmandu. Since then, no additional infections have been reported. To minimise any remaining risk, the department has intensified laboratory testing by collecting samples from areas surrounding previously affected sites.

The latest outbreak was first confirmed on March 17, 2026 (Chaitra 4, 2082) in Urlabari-8 and Sundarharaicha-4 of Morang district before spreading to 11 districts across the country.

According to the department, the disease has now been completely contained in all seven affected districts outside the Kathmandu Valley. Within the valley and neighbouring Kavrepalanchok district, infections had been detected at a total of 119 locations—32 in Kathmandu, 15 in Lalitpur (including the Central Zoo), 45 in Bhaktapur, and 27 in Kavrepalanchok.

As part of the containment effort, the government culled 835,563 birds nationwide. Senior Veterinary Officer Dr Mukul Upadhyay said authorities also safely destroyed 1,165,663 eggs and 245,035 kilograms of poultry feed.

In the Kathmandu Valley and Kavrepalanchok alone, 367,835 birds were culled. Commercial layer chickens were the hardest hit, while broilers, local chickens, ducks, turkeys, and pheasants also suffered losses.

To support affected farmers, the government allocated Rs. 520 million in compensation. According to Dr Dahal, about Rs. 507.1 million has already been distributed to 104 farmers and poultry farms whose birds were destroyed.

Dr Upadhyay attributed the successful containment of the outbreak to the government’s prompt response, expanded laboratory testing, and the full cooperation of poultry farmers. He said the likelihood of further transmission is now very low.

With the outbreak under control, consumption of chicken meat and eggs has begun to recover. The department said poultry farmers, who had suffered heavy losses due to falling prices and unsold chicks during the outbreak, are now starting to receive fair market prices as demand returns.

title.rendered: Beyond the canvas: Sagar Manandhar on process and perception

content.rendered:
For artist Sagar Manandhar, a painting does not begin when colour touches the canvas. It starts much earlier—with the rhythm of a space, the sound of a scraping tool, the silence of a studio and an ongoing dialogue between the artist and his materials. His latest exhibition, Dialogue and Perception, which began on July 16 at The Kala Salon, Thamel, shifts the focus from the finished artwork to the creative process itself, inviting viewers to experience abstraction as a language rather than a puzzle.

In this conversation, Manandhar speaks about why sound is as important as colour, how experimentation reshaped his practice, living under the legacy of celebrated artist Kiran Manandhar, and why art should first move people before trying to change the world.

Q. Why did you choose the title Dialogue and Perception for this exhibition?

The title emerged from my belief that we often become obsessed with the final artwork and forget how it came into existence. Every painting begins with a process. Throughout that journey, I am constantly in conversation—with my thoughts, my materials and the work itself.

This exhibition is about that dialogue rather than the outcome. While my previous works explored melody, this series is more deeply concerned with the experience of making a painting. The scratching of surfaces, the layering of textures, the mixing of pigments, even the sounds created while preparing colours—all these become part of the artwork. I want viewers to experience not only what they see but also the invisible conversations that happen before an image is born.

Q. How do sound, colour and silence influence your paintings?

People usually think colour is purely visual. For me, colour also has a sound. Every material produces its own vibration. The scrape of a palette knife, the resistance of a textured surface or the sound of pigment being mixed all influence my emotions while I work.

I usually paint late at night because silence allows me to hear these subtle sounds more clearly. Even the sound of a falling leaf becomes meaningful. Those vibrations become part of my thinking, and eventually they become part of the painting itself.

Q. Your recent works show a noticeable shift in technique. What has changed?

The biggest change is that I have challenged my own materials. Earlier I knew how much water to use or how a line would behave. This time I deliberately stepped outside that comfort zone.

I introduced new materials, accepted unpredictability and allowed the paintings to surprise me. Some textures appeared unexpectedly, tonal values changed naturally, and the paintings developed their own identity. Instead of trying to control everything, I learned to listen to what the materials wanted to become.

Q. Many people find abstract art difficult to understand. How do you respond?

I think abstraction is simply another language. We enjoy songs in languages we do not understand because we connect with their rhythm and emotion. Abstract painting works in a similar way.

Viewers don’t need to decode every meaning. They simply need to spend time with the work. Even someone saying, “I don’t like this painting,” has already entered into a dialogue with it. That response itself is valuable. To me, abstraction is reality deconstructed. It explores what exists beneath appearances rather than merely describing what we already know.

Q. Why has abstraction remained central to your artistic practice?

Because it never truly ends.

A realistic painting often reaches a point where it feels complete. Abstraction keeps opening new possibilities. Even after I sign a painting, I sometimes look at it the next day and imagine another direction it could have taken.

That sense of infinity keeps me curious. Every completed work becomes the starting point for another journey rather than the conclusion of one.

Q. Nature seems to play an important role in your work.

Absolutely. My paintings are deeply inspired by natural soundscapes—the rhythm of rainfall, the movement of water, the colours of landscapes and even intangible sensations found in nature.

Living in Nepal also shapes my colour palette. The reds of religious rituals, the greens of our landscape and the colours found in everyday cultural life naturally become part of my visual memory. Even when I paint abstractly, these experiences remain present beneath the surface.

Q. Your father, Kiran Manandhar, is one of Nepal’s leading artists. How has that influenced your career?

My greatest inheritance from my father isn’t his paintings—it’s his discipline and energy. Growing up, I constantly watched him working. That commitment inspired me far more than his fame.

Of course, being known as Kiran Manandhar’s son came with challenges. Early in my career, people often assumed my achievements came because of him. At first that was frustrating, but eventually I realised that I could only answer those assumptions through consistent work. Rather than escaping my father’s legacy, I learned to build my own voice alongside it.

Q. Besides your father, who has inspired your artistic journey?

Uttam Nepali has been a tremendous inspiration. As a young student, I visited his exhibition, and he encouraged me to paint without fear. He even gave me one of his brushes, which I still treasure today.

That simple gesture gave me confidence at a formative stage of my career. My father gave me the energy to keep working, while Uttam Nepali inspired my artistic direction. Both remain central to who I am as an artist.

Q. Who gives you the most honest criticism?

Without question, my mother.

If she says a painting isn’t finished, I don’t sign it. Her observations often make me rethink a work more deeply than formal criticism does.

Today, my daughter and my wife also play an important role. My wife says she doesn’t understand art, but her comments often reveal something I had overlooked. Art may appear to be an individual practice, but my family is deeply woven into my creative process.

Q. What role should art play in society?

I don’t believe art changes society overnight.

What it can do is create a moment of relief. If someone walks into my exhibition carrying worries and forgets those worries for even a few seconds while looking at a painting, then the artwork has already done something meaningful.

A gallery is a place of celebration. My exhibition is my celebration, and if visitors can make it part of their own celebration, then I feel I have succeeded. Small emotional shifts eventually lead to larger changes in people’s lives.

Q. Finally, what does art mean to you?

Art is a reflection of myself.

People often describe art as a reflection of society, but I believe my paintings first reflect who I am—my experiences, my questions and my way of seeing the world.

Every painting in this exhibition also carries a memory. That is why I now record not only the year but also the completion date of each work. Each painting reminds me of a specific moment, a particular studio atmosphere and the dialogue that unfolded while it was being made. In that sense, every canvas becomes both an artwork and a memory preserved in colour, sound and time.

title.rendered: Money laundering probe widens to include inspector Gurung’s boyfriend in APF School fraud case

content.rendered:
Police have launched a money-laundering investigation against an inspector and her boyfriend, who were arrested in connection with the embezzlement of funds from the Armed Police Force School in Kirtipur.

The investigation targets the school’s chief accountant, Inspector Kalpana Gurung, and her boyfriend, Lila Bahadur Lama, on charges of money laundering. Police had initially investigated them for fraud and criminal proceeds, but after uncovering large-scale embezzlement, the probe was expanded to include money laundering.

The District Police Range, Kathmandu, has moved forward with the money-laundering investigation after the APF Headquarters wrote to it, alleging financial irregularities at the school, prompting the range’s team to arrest and investigate the pair.

During the investigation, it was found that Inspector Gurung had given the school’s money to Lila Bahadur. SP and spokesperson Pawan Kumar Bhattarai said vehicles, a house, and land were found registered in Lila Bahadur’s name.

“We have seized two vehicles registered in Lila Bahadur’s name and brought them to our office. A house and land have also been found,” SP Bhattarai says. Police say a third vehicle is also registered in his name, though it has not yet been seized.

Given the scale of assets found under Lila Bahadur’s name, police suspect they may have been purchased with the embezzled school funds and are investigating accordingly. However, police sources say the accused, Lila Bahadur, claims he had acquired the house and land before the embezzlement took place.

Inspector Gurung has reportedly admitted to keeping funds that should have been in the school’s account in her personal account and handing them over to her lover. No embezzled funds have been found in her own name.

“Accountant Gurung has said she gave all the money to Lila Bahadur. Vehicles, a house, and land have been found in the lover’s name,” SP Bhattarai says.

More than 100 million rupees are reported to have been embezzled so far. The matter has been communicated to Armed Police Force Headquarters, though a formal letter is still awaited, and SSP Dilip Ghimire of the range says it will take more time to determine the exact amount embezzled.

Lila Bahadur accused in six prior cases

A check of the Criminal Record System revealed that Lilabahadur, Inspector Gurung’s boyfriend, has been named in six separate criminal cases. The most recent was a banking offence case in 2022.

He also faced a citizenship-related case in 2005, along with three theft cases the same year, one in Lalitpur and two in Kathmandu, and another theft case in Kathmandu in 2004. Despite his record spanning theft, citizenship, and banking offences, Gurung made her boyfriend and is found to have funnelled the school’s money to him.

Lilabahadur has reportedly also been running a travel agency in recent times. Police have now seized two of his vehicles and are proceeding with the investigation.

Accountant’s post held in violation of norms

Under regulations, an accountant’s position should be rotated every two years. However, Gurung had held the accountant post at the same school for six years. She joined the Armed Police Force as an Assistant Sub-Inspector and became the school’s accountant while still holding that rank.

Notably, even after her promotion to Inspector, she was posted back to the same school. This has raised questions about the role of the transferring authority.

“Normally, an accountant is transferred every two years, but she stayed at the same office for six years; this is a clear violation of the transfer norm,” an APF official says.

Previously, the Kirtipur school was headed by a DSP-level commandant; SSP Bhupendra KC was the first to be posted as commandant at that level, and it has since been run by SPs. SP Ramjung Pandey was the most recent commandant before being recalled to headquarters once the investigation began; Lekhnath Khanal has since replaced him.

title.rendered: KMC Haatbazar showcases student entrepreneurship through 32 business stalls

content.rendered:
KATHMANDU

Kathmandu Model College (KMC) on Thursday organised KMC Haatbazar 2083, bringing together hundreds of students to showcase entrepreneurial ideas, business skills and creativity through a student-led marketplace.

Organised by the KMC Entrepreneurship Club and the KMC Media Reachout Club under the coordination of the KMC Student Quality Circle, the event was held under the theme “Learning Hands, Courage to Earn” and aimed to bridge classroom learning with practical business experience.

Former Miss Nepal 2018, entrepreneur and Member of the House of Representatives Anushka Shrestha inaugurated the event alongside KMC College Chief Surendra Subedi and Kathmandu Model Secondary School Principal Dr Nagendra Aryal.

Addressing the gathering, Shrestha described entrepreneurship as a necessity for today’s generation rather than merely a career option. She encouraged students to develop innovative solutions to real-world problems and said practical initiatives such as the Haatbazar help build leadership, teamwork, financial management and risk-taking skills.

The event featured 32 stalls operated by students from Kathmandu Model College and other institutions under the KMC Educational Network, including KMC Bagbazar, KMSS Bagbazar, KMSS Lalitpur and MIT College. Students displayed and sold food, clothing, handmade jewellery, handicrafts, home décor items and other products.

Around 2,000 students and visitors attended the day-long event, giving many participants their first opportunity to market products, interact directly with customers and gain hands-on business experience.

At the closing ceremony, organisers recognised outstanding participants with cash prizes and certificates. Studio Chrome won the Most Innovative Stall award with a cash prize of Rs. 5,000, while Tech Hub from KMC Bagbazar received the People’s Choice Award and an equal cash prize. A Mehendi competition organised by the Art and Literature Club also honoured winning students for their artistic performances.

Organisers said the annual event seeks to foster innovation, leadership and an entrepreneurial mindset among students while encouraging them to turn academic learning into practical enterprise.

title.rendered: Over 1,100 residents receive home Passport Delivery Service in Gulmi

content.rendered:
July 22, Gulmi

More than 1,100 residents in Gulmi have received their passports through a home delivery service, which has now been expanded to all 12 local governments in the district.

The service has been rolled out across Gulmi’s two municipalities and 10 rural municipalities, with passports delivered directly to applicants’ homes.

The initiative is part of the government’s policy of providing public services at citizens’ doorsteps, eliminating the need for applicants to make repeated trips to government offices. The Home Passport Delivery Service, operated through the Department of Postal Services, is now available in all local governments in the district, according to Bhuvan Pandey of the District Post Office, Gulmi.

Chief District Officer Badrinath Gaire said the programme, which began in Resunga Municipality, has now been extended throughout the district. He said 1,110 people have so far received passports through the home delivery service.

The service was introduced to improve access to government services across the district. Residents said it has been particularly beneficial for people requiring passports for foreign employment, higher education and other purposes, as it has reduced the need to travel to the district headquarters.

Recipients said the home delivery service has saved both time and travel expenses. Previously, applicants had to return to the District Administration Office or another designated office to collect their passports after they were issued.

Khet Bahadur Khatri, chief of the District Post Office, said the Department of Postal Services now coordinates with local governments to deliver passports directly to citizens’ homes. Chief District Officer Gaire added that efforts would continue to make the service more effective, particularly for people living in rural areas.

title.rendered: More than 2,300 medieval copper coins discovered in Kapilvastu

content.rendered:
July 22, Kapilvastu

A copper vessel containing more than 2,300 medieval copper coins has been discovered in Babhani, Ward No. 5 of Kapilvastu Municipality.

The archaeological find was made by local farmer Rajaram Yadav while working in his field.

After residents informed the police, the artefacts were recovered by a team comprising local representatives, elected officials and staff from the Kapilvastu Museum. The copper vessel and the coins have since been transferred to the museum for preservation and further study.

Kapilvastu District Police Chief SP Manohar Prasad Bhatt said the artefacts had been handed over to the museum for detailed examination.

Shanti Sharma, chief of the Kapilvastu Museum, said the discovery is believed to date back to the 12th or 13th century, placing it in Nepal’s medieval period.

“The unearthed artefacts are estimated to belong to the 12th or 13th century,” Sharma said.

According to her, museum officials are continuing to remove the coins from the copper vessel. So far, 2,314 copper coins bearing Arabic inscriptions have been recovered. The copper vessel measures approximately 23 centimetres in height.

title.rendered: Congress establishes Rs 1 million humanitarian welfare fund, first assistance to go to landless families

content.rendered:
July 22, Kathmandu

The Nepali Congress has established a Humanitarian Welfare Fund using a portion of the party membership fees collected from its members. The announcement was made by party General Secretary Gagan Thapa during the Green Run programme held on Wednesday to mark the memorial day of BP Koirala.

According to Thapa, the fund has been launched with an initial allocation of Rs 1 million. The first phase of assistance will be directed towards displaced landless families, with particular priority given to single women and children who are unable to attend school.

“From today, we have decided to establish the Humanitarian Welfare Fund using a portion of the membership fees contributed by our party members,” Thapa said during the event.

He said volunteers from the Nepal Women’s Association would be mobilised to manage the fund. Representatives of the organisation will visit affected settlements to assess needs and help distribute assistance. Thapa also invited volunteers from the Tarun Dal and other interested groups to join the campaign.

Thapa said the Green Run was organised not only to raise public awareness about climate change but also to mark the beginning of a concrete social responsibility initiative. He added that the Nepali Congress would pursue policies and programmes aimed at making climate change one of Nepal’s key development priorities.

Recalling the legacy of BP Koirala, Thapa said the late leader had advocated inclusive democracy and equitable access to natural resources during his time, adding that those ideas remain relevant today.

Acknowledging that turnout at the event exceeded expectations, Thapa admitted there had been shortcomings in its management and apologised to the young participants. He pledged that future events would be better organised.

Thapa also announced that the Nepali Congress would launch a new nationwide campaign beginning Thursday, with further details to be made public the following day.

title.rendered: Bagmati coalition collapses as UML withdraws support

content.rendered:
July 22, Hetauda

All six ministers from the CPN-UML serving in the Bagmati Provincial Government have collectively resigned, formally withdrawing the party from the ruling coalition.

The ministers submitted their joint resignation to Chief Minister Indra Bahadur Baniya.

In a letter addressed to the Chief Minister, UML Bagmati Provincial Parliamentary Party leader Jagannath Thapaliya stated that, in accordance with Article 168(2) of the Constitution of Nepal, the party had decided—considering the current political situation—that all UML ministers would resign with immediate effect. The letter also requested the Chief Minister to accept the resignations and proceed with the necessary constitutional and legal processes.

Speaking to Onlinekhabar, Thapaliya confirmed that the UML had also withdrawn its support for the Bagmati Provincial Government.

The resigning ministers are:

  • Madhusudan Paudel, Minister for Agriculture, Livestock, Forests and Environment;
  • Dr. Dinesh Chandra Devkota, Minister for Physical Infrastructure Development;
  • Jayaram Thapa, Minister of State for Transport under the Ministry of Industry, Tourism, Labour and Transport;
  • Bharat Bahadur KC, Minister of State for Forests and Environment under the Ministry of Agriculture;
  • Kiran Thapa, Minister of State for Health under the Ministry of Health and Social Development; and
  • Bindu Shrestha, Minister for Industry, Tourism, Labour and Transport.

The ministers had returned to Kathmandu after attending a Cabinet meeting on July 16 (32 Asar) and arrived in Hetauda on Tuesday night, five days later, to formally submit their resignations.

According to Minister Paudel, the party leadership issued a clear directive to resign after UML Chairperson KP Sharma Oli and CPN (Maoist Centre) Chair Pushpa Kamal Dahal “Prachanda” held discussions on Monday regarding power-sharing arrangements in the provincial governments.

The Nepali Congress–UML coalition has governed Bagmati Province since August 2024 (Shrawan 2081). After nearly two years in office, the UML’s withdrawal of support has reduced Chief Minister Baniya’s government to a minority.

Under the Constitution, Chief Minister Baniya must now seek and secure a vote of confidence from the Provincial Assembly within 30 days.

title.rendered: The reconciliation we still owe B.P. Koirala

content.rendered:
Today, on Shrawan 6, Nepal marks the forty-fourth anniversary of the death of Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala. It comes at an unusually painful moment for the party he founded: a Nepali Congress reduced to thirty-eight seats in the House of Representatives; its president defeated in his own constituency; a widening divide between its old guard and a younger generation pressing for change, each drawing sharply different lessons from the same electoral debacle; and the word split uttered within its ranks with a seriousness it has not carried in years. Moments like these naturally invite political parties to seek refuge in the memory of their founders. Institutions in decline often invoke those who established them, less as standards by which to judge themselves than as sources of borrowed legitimacy. The temptation is understandable. But it is also misleading. B.P. Koirala deserves better than to be quoted. He deserves to be read.

To read Koirala is to discover something more demanding than the familiar outline of his life—an outline so familiar it has almost become political furniture: the revolutionary who helped end a century of Rana oligarchy; Nepal’s first democratically elected prime minister; the leader whose government King Mahendra overthrew in 1960; the prisoner who spent nearly eight years in detention rather than recant; the exile who, through those years, continued to write political essays, prison memoirs, and novels of remarkable literary quality, revealing a mind as interested in the complexities of human character as in the exercise of political power. Yet the outline conceals what made him exceptional. Koirala did not confuse steadfastness with rigidity. The same leader who refused to bend during years of imprisonment later undertook the one political act many of his own followers found harder to understand than his resistance itself: he sought reconciliation with the very monarchy that had overthrown his elected government and imprisoned him. That decision revealed the defining quality of his statesmanship—not reconciliation as a virtue in itself, but the political judgment from which it arose.

Act that should be harder to invoke

By the mid-1970s, Koirala had reached a sobering conclusion. Released from prison and living first in exile and then back in Nepal, he no longer believed that continued frontal confrontation with the Panchayat state was moving the country towards democracy. It had settled into a stalemate that exhausted the democratic movement without bringing democratic restoration any closer. His answer was the policy of ‘National Unity and Reconciliation.’ The formulation itself was his own. At its heart lay the idea of engaging the very monarchy that had overthrown his elected government and imprisoned him, in pursuit of a negotiated path back to multiparty democracy that confrontation alone had failed to secure.

It is tempting, with the benefit of hindsight, to mistake this policy for moderation—or to imagine that reconciliation itself was its objective. It was neither. What Koirala demanded was considerably harder: that a democratic leader subordinate the desire for vindication to the larger imperative of restoring democratic politics itself. He was not asking that the past be forgotten, only that it not become a prison from which the country’s democratic future could no longer escape.

The proposal carried an immense personal and political cost. Many within his own party regarded it as capitulation—a repudiation of everything his years of imprisonment were thought to have proved about his commitment. Even Ganesh Man Singh, his lifelong comrade-in-arms, who returned from exile with him despite the personal risks involved, harboured serious doubts about its wisdom. Koirala persisted nonetheless. He believed the historical moment demanded something different from what political emotion demanded, and he was prepared to disappoint even his closest allies if that was the price of giving Nepal’s democratic movement a chance that confrontation alone could not provide. It is a rare leader who is willing to pay that price—not for personal vindication, but for the future of the cause he serves. Koirala was one of them.

History’s verdict

History ultimately rendered a more generous verdict than many of Koirala’s contemporaries were prepared to give, and two developments proved especially revealing. The first followed with surprising speed. Koirala’s return to Nepal and his policy of national unity and reconciliation fundamentally reshaped the political environment. Within little more than two years, under mounting pressure from a nationwide student movement and within the altered political climate Koirala had helped create, the monarchy announced the 1979 national referendum. For the first time since the royal coup of 1960, the Nepali people were offered a choice between a reformed Panchayat system and the restoration of multiparty democracy. The referendum did not restore democracy. It did something more fundamental: it irrevocably changed the terms on which the struggle would thereafter be conducted. The Panchayat system could no longer plausibly present itself as the nation’s uncontested political settlement.

The second development came after Koirala’s death. Within seven years, Ganesh Man Singh—the very colleague who had once questioned the wisdom of reconciliation—led the nationwide people’s movement that peacefully restored multiparty democracy in 1990. In recognition of his leadership, he came to be revered as the nation’s Supreme Leader.

History, in other words, vindicated not merely a political strategy but a political judgment. What many contemporaries had dismissed as accommodation gradually revealed itself to have been an act of strategic foresight, expanding rather than narrowing the democratic possibilities available to Nepal. It was this quality—perhaps less celebrated during Koirala’s own lifetime than his courage or sacrifice—that ultimately secured his place among Nepal’s foremost statesmen. He consistently placed the nation’s democratic future above personal ambition, partisan advantage, and even his own political standing. That is the part of his legacy most likely to endure, because it rests not upon the circumstances of one historical moment but upon a standard of political leadership that transcends it.

Question before the Nepali Congress today

Forty-four years after Koirala’s death, Nepal confronts a democratic question very different from the one he faced. The central challenge today is no longer the restoration of democracy but the restoration of public confidence in democratic politics itself. For that reason, it would be mistaken to search Koirala’s life for ready-made answers. His policy of national unity and reconciliation belonged to a particular historical moment; the habit of judgment that produced it does not. That distinction matters. Koirala’s authority never rested on fidelity to inherited positions. It rested on his willingness to re-examine inherited assumptions whenever he believed Nepal’s democratic future required it. No serious political tradition survives by mechanically repeating the answers of another age. The more searching question is whether it still possesses the habits of judgment that enabled those answers to be discovered in the first place.

That question cannot be avoided by diminishing the scale of the Nepali Congress’s present predicament. A party reduced to the largest—but still marginal—opposition in the House of Representatives has suffered more than an electoral defeat. It has suffered a crisis of confidence that cannot be explained away as a temporary fluctuation or overcome simply by waiting for political fortune to turn. Nor has the election resolved the question of leadership. If anything, it has sharpened it. The party’s old guard and the younger generation pressing for change have drawn strikingly different conclusions from the same defeat. One locates the problem principally in organisational erosion and declining discipline; the other in the failure to renew leadership, methods, and the party’s relationship with a changing electorate. Neither diagnosis is implausible. Neither is sufficient. Yet each increasingly treats the other not as an indispensable interlocutor but as the principal obstacle to recovery.

It is precisely here that Koirala’s example ceases to be an object of commemoration and becomes a measure of leadership. His deepest insight was never simply that reconciliation with a monarchy was possible. It was that even legitimate grievances become politically disabling once the desire to be proved right outlives its usefulness. The divisions within today’s Congress are not divisions of irreconcilable principle. They are divisions of generation, authority, and competing interpretations of a shared failure—the kinds of divisions that exist within every living democratic party. They become dangerous only when the desire to prevail over one another begins to outweigh the responsibility to preserve the institution itself. History offers no guarantees, only standards. No historical analogy is exact. Yet every political generation must eventually answer some version of the same question: what, given its own circumstances, is worth sacrificing to preserve something larger than itself?

Judgment over vindication

Whenever a political party enters a period of uncertainty, there is a natural temptation to seek refuge in the memory of its founder. The instinct is understandable. Founders represent moments when a party appeared united in purpose, confident in direction, and certain of its place in history. Yet memory can become a substitute for reflection. Institutions often honour their founders most lavishly when they are least willing to confront the standards those founders established. The Nepali Congress has never ceased to commemorate Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala. But commemoration, however sincere, is not the same thing as fidelity. The truest tribute the party can pay its founder is not to invoke his words more frequently, but to recover the habits of judgment that gave those words their authority. Koirala understood that politics was never simply a contest in which moral seriousness consisted in defeating one’s adversaries or proving oneself right. At decisive moments, he believed, the higher obligation of leadership was to preserve the conditions under which democratic politics itself could endure.

That conviction led him to advocate national unity and reconciliation with the very monarchy that had overthrown his elected government and persecuted him. It was not an act of forgetfulness, still less of surrender. It was an act of political judgment. The reconciliation Koirala sought belongs to history. The reconciliation the Nepali Congress still owes him does not. It lies in recovering the standards of judgment, restraint, and magnanimity that his example embodied—the willingness to place the long-term interests of nation and democracy above the immediate satisfactions of personal vindication and partisan triumph. That remains the most demanding part of his legacy because it asks something difficult of every generation that claims him: whether it can distinguish between winning an argument and serving the larger democratic purpose the argument was meant to advance.

Those questions do not confront only the Nepali Congress. They confront every democratic party that hopes to outlive the circumstances of its own founding. But they confront the Congress with particular force, because no other party can claim Koirala as its founder while exempting itself from the discipline of his example. History rarely remembers political leaders for the positions they defended alone. More often, it remembers them for the quality of judgment they brought to moments when no position was without cost. Koirala’s greatest legacy was not that he showed Nepal how to reconcile with an adversary. It was that he showed democratic leaders when reconciliation becomes a higher duty than vindication. That, ultimately, is why B.P. Koirala still deserves better than to be quoted. He deserves to be read.

title.rendered: Under pressure, government drops 3 percent tax on education and health

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 21

Prime Minister Balendra Shah (Balen) has said a decision has been made not to implement the 3 percent tax imposed on health and education.

In a social media post on Tuesday, PM Shah said that implementing the 3 percent equity tax imposed on the private education and health sectors as currently framed would mean the general public having to bear additional expenses and hardship.

“Implementing the 3% equity tax imposed on the private education and health sectors as it currently stands would mean ordinary people facing additional costs and distress. Therefore, after consultation with Honourable Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, a decision has been made not to implement the education equity fee and health equity fee for now,” the Prime Minister said. “This government is a people-oriented government formed on the trust and expectations of the citizens. Our main objective is to ensure good governance while providing all citizens with a quality standard of living.”

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle had announced, through the budget statement for fiscal year 2026/27, a 3 percent “equity fee” on the education and health sectors.

The government planned to collect an additional 3 percent charge on the service fees taken by private schools, colleges, hospitals, medical colleges, and nursing homes, and use that revenue to improve the quality of public education and health services and expand access for disadvantaged citizens.

However, as soon as the budget was made public, operators of private schools, colleges, and hospitals had been protesting the provision. They argued that imposing additional charges on basic services like education and health would ultimately burden students, guardians, and patients, making these services more expensive. Various umbrella organisations had been continuously pressuring the government to scrap the fee.

As a result, Prime Minister Balen has announced the decision not to implement the education equity fee and the health equity fee.
