title.rendered: MetLife Foundation Supports WWF Nepal’s JEEWAN Project

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 21

MetLife Foundation has awarded a grant of US$ 120,000 to WWF Nepal to implement the “Joint Efforts for Ecosystem, Wellbeing and Alternative Livelihoods of Local Communities Based on Nature (JEEWAN)” project in Rajapur Municipality, Bardiya District.  The initiative will support marginalised Sonaha and Tharu communities living along the Lower Karnali River basin, where recurring floods, riverbank erosion, and declining fish populations continue to threaten livelihoods and food security.  

The one-year project is designed to strengthen climate resilience and improve economic opportunities for around 140 low-income households.  WWF Nepal will implement nature-based solutions, including bio-dykes, green belts, and stream restoration, to reduce flood risks and protect agricultural land and settlements from inundation. 

Alongside ecosystem restoration, the project will promote diversified and sustainable livelihoods by strengthening homestay-based eco-tourism, supporting livestock and poultry activities, and improving access to markets.  MetLife associates are also expected to contribute through volunteering engagement, particularly in financial literacy, budgeting, and small business management training, further enhancing community capacity and long-term resilience. 

By reducing dependence on declining fish stocks, the initiative will also contribute to the conservation of the Karnali River’s rich biodiversity, including endangered species such as river dolphins and gharials. The partnership reflects MetLife Foundation’s commitment to building resilient communities and enabling low-income populations to achieve greater financial security and well-being.

“As a company rooted in risk protection, we understand that real impact comes from prevention and preparedness. MetLife Foundation’s partnership with WWF Nepal allows us to go beyond our traditional role and support flood-prone communities in Karnali with solutions that protect lives, restore ecosystems, and create sustainable livelihoods,” said Nirmal Kajee Shrestha, Vice President and General Manager of MetLife Nepal.

“We are delighted to partner with MetLife Foundation on the JEEWAN project. Having just concluded a project that strengthened community stewardship to protect otters and their riverine habitat in the same stretch of the Karnali River, where Nepal’s first fish sanctuary is also established,” said Ghana Shyam Gurung, Country Representative of WWF Nepal. Through JEEWAN, we are thrilled to continue working with the Sonaha and Tharu communities of Rajapur to reduce flood risk through bio-dykes and green belts, while opening new livelihood pathways through eco-tourism, livestock support, and market access. We’re grateful to MetLife Foundation for investing in solutions that protect both people and the rich biodiversity of the Karnali River.” s

title.rendered: NepalHRM launches HR and payroll software built for Nepali businesses

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 21

NepalHRM, a human resource (HR) and payroll software designed specifically for the needs and regulations of Nepali businesses, has officially launched. The company says the platform allows businesses to manage employee records, attendance, leave, recruitment, onboarding, and Nepal-compliant payroll all from a single system.

Unlike foreign HR software, NepalHRM comes pre-configured with the latest tax slabs for PF, CIT, SSF, eTDS, and the Inland Revenue Department (IRD). The company claims the system updates automatically whenever the government changes regulations, removing what it describes as one of the biggest compliance headaches for Nepali HR and finance departments.

Free for small teams

One of NepalHRM’s most notable features is its pricing model. The platform is free forever for teams of up to 10 employees, with no card required and no minimum commitment. This gives Nepali startups and small businesses a way to digitise their HR and payroll operations at no cost.

The system is also available for larger organisations, where most companies can become fully operational within two to four weeks with the help of a dedicated onboarding specialist.

Integrates with biometric devices and mobile apps

NepalHRM connects easily with popular biometric attendance devices, including ZKTeco, Anviz, Realand, and Hikvision. Its Android and iOS mobile apps let employees check in themselves, submit leave requests, file reimbursement claims, download pay slips, and view company announcements.

The company also says the system is built with strong security standards, with all data encrypted using TLS 1.2+ and AES-256, along with role-based access control and standard daily backups.

Built for Nepal

NepalHRM’s co-founders, Sujan Thapaliya and Rajnita Bhetwal, say Nepali businesses have long struggled with foreign software that doesn’t understand local regulations. According to them, many companies in Nepal still manage payroll and attendance on Excel, or purchase foreign tools that don’t account for PF, SSF, or eTDS requirements, which is why they built a system tailored to Nepal’s own rules, so that small businesses too can digitise their HR without cost.

Support in English and Nepali

NepalHRM provides customer support in both English and Nepali via email, phone, and WhatsApp. The platform is currently available at nepalhrm.com.

NepalHRM is an HR and payroll software platform built around the regulations, language, and working style of Nepali businesses, helping organisations automate attendance, leave, recruitment, onboarding, and payroll management while ensuring full compliance with Nepal’s PF, CIT, SSF, and eTDS regulations.

title.rendered: Lugum: A village where the rhythm of the drum and sacred chants still lives (Photos)

content.rendered:
Rukum East, July 21

People gather in the open ground at the heart of the Himalayan village of Lugum. Before long, the resonant beat of the dhyangro (traditional shamanic drum) echoes across the settlement, while the fragrance of incense fills the air. One after another, shamans—adorned with feathered headdresses, bronze bells, traditional ornaments, and colourful attire—enter the gathering ground.

While shamanic traditions have gradually disappeared from many parts of Nepal with the march of modernity, they remain remarkably alive in Lugum, Ward No. 1 of Bhume Rural Municipality in Rukum East.

Modern medical science does not recognise or validate shamanism, ritual healing, or spiritual incantations as medical treatment.

For the people of Lugum, however, the shamanic tradition has endured not primarily as a form of healthcare but as an important expression of their cultural identity. The annual Shaman Festival, held on the first Tuesday of the Nepali month of Shrawan, celebrates a way of life passed down through generations.

For the local community, the festival is an opportunity to honour their ancestors, strengthen social bonds, and keep their cultural heritage alive.

On the day of the festival, Lugum is filled not only with residents but also with relatives and visitors from various districts. Shamans dance together to the rhythmic beat of the dhyangro, transforming the village’s atmosphere. For the community, the occasion is far more than entertainment—it is a day to remember ancestral wisdom, beliefs, and identity.

More than four dozen shamans remain active in Lugum today. One distinctive feature of the village is that women perform the role of shamans alongside men on equal footing. Sacred chants, rituals, and practices continue to be handed down from teacher to disciple, often within the same family.

According to local belief, shamans are more than ritual healers. They are regarded as custodians of the village’s spiritual life, social values, and cultural heritage. The festival also brings together masters and their disciples, allowing elders to pass on sacred chants and ritual knowledge. Shamans review one another’s spiritual practices and conduct religious ceremonies seeking the well-being of the community while addressing both auspicious and inauspicious signs.

Perhaps the most striking feature of the festival is the sisno (stinging nettle) ritual. Shamans’ close relatives, nephews and nieces, village youths, and other participants playfully strike one another with stinging nettles. While the practice may appear unusual to outsiders, the local community regards it as a cultural rite of purification. They believe it helps cleanse the body of impurities, protects against illness, and wards off negative forces.

The shamans’ attire itself serves as a living cultural record. Wearing feathered crowns, strings of bronze bells around their necks, traditional ornaments across their bodies, and carrying dhyangro drums, they dance in unison across the village square, turning it into what resembles an open-air cultural museum. Every face, every costume, and every rhythm tells a story of traditions preserved through generations.

As science and technology continue to advance rapidly, many indigenous cultures around the world face the risk of disappearing. Lugum, however, has safeguarded its unique identity for generations.

Even more encouraging is the active participation of the younger generation, who continue to learn from their elders and embrace the tradition. This continuity has ensured that Lugum’s shamanic heritage is not merely a memory of the past but a living cultural legacy that continues to thrive today.

As the final beat of the dhyangro fades, the festival comes to an end. The village square gradually empties. Yet the rhythm that echoes through the hills of Lugum lingers in the community’s memory, waiting to return with the first Tuesday of Shrawan next year.

title.rendered: E-library to be established in Hetauda

content.rendered:
Bagmati, July 21

The Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City has announced that an e-library will be operated in the sub-metropolis. It has been announced in the local government’s policies and programmes for the fiscal year 2083/84 (2026-27). It is said the facility named ‘City E-Library’ will be launched for the purpose of building a knowledge-based society.

According to Mayor Meena Kumari Lama, review of teachers’ quotas, merging schools or downsizing them will be continued in this fiscal year, too. Likewise, it has to uphold the provision of the ‘teachers’ bank system’ implemented to address the vacuum in teaching and learning activities when teacher posts turn vacant. Similarly, the local government is to continue with the provision of the maternity substitute teacher system to compensate for the learning loss while female teachers are on maternity leave.

Mayor Lama said that the arrangements will be made for ensuring health check-ups of all students through the mobilisation of health posts, urban health centres, urban health promotion centres, hospitals and school nurses. The local government has pledged to make institutional arrangements required for ensuring the learning of children with special conditions and diverse needs due to anxiety, autism, intellectual disability, and Down syndrome.

The Sub-Metropolitan City has stated that the scholarship distribution process provided by institutional schools will be made more systematic and transparent. In addition, scholarships, along with educational material support, will be provided to students from marginalised communities to help them continue their studies.

title.rendered: Annapurna area welcomes visitors from 169 countries in last fiscal year

content.rendered:
Gandaki, July 21

Tourists from 169 countries visited various destinations in the Annapurna Conservation Area in the last fiscal year. During that period, a total of 508,476 foreign tourists visited this area. Among them, 384,145 were from South Asian countries and 124,331 from other countries.

Indians accounted for the highest number of tourists visiting the Annapurna area last fiscal year from July 17, 2025, to July 16, 2026. The area received 375,797 Indian tourists. Coming in second were 12,539 Chinese tourists, and third were 9,884 Americans. Similarly, 9,859 tourists from the UK, 7,939 from France, 7,848 from Malaysia, 7,634 from Germany, 7,448 from Bangladesh, 7,095 from Australia, and 6,398 from Israel visited this area in the last fiscal year.

Dr Rabin Kadariya, the Head of the Annapurna Conservation Area Project, said that more than double the number of foreign tourists visited here last fiscal year compared to FY 2081/82. According to him, 278,113 people visited the Annapurna area in FY 2081/82. Dr Kadariya said that the number of tourists from South Asian countries, including India, increased by nearly three hundred per cent in Jeth month (May 15 to June 14). This is the first time so many Indian tourists have come. The increase in Indian tourists is due to the promotion of destinations in this area like Pokhara and Muktinath, easy transportation, and publicity through social media.

During this season, Indian tourists have been coming to Pokhara and nearby destinations to escape the heat. In the months of Baisakh–Jestha, hotel occupancy in Pokhara, the tourism capital, had reached up to 90 per cent. Among the Indian tourists coming to Pokhara, about 40 per cent visit Muktinath, Dr Kadariya said.

The Annapurna region is considered a world-famous destination for trekking tourism. Through the Annapurna Circuit trekking route, tourists reach destinations like the Annapurna Base Camp, Mardi Himal, Ghorepani, Tilicho Lake in Manang, Thorong La Pass, Upper Mustang, Muktinath area, and Ghodepani in Myagdi, among others. The Annapurna Conservation Area, which spreads over 7,600 square kilometres, is famous for its natural beauty, biodiversity, Himalayan lifestyle, culture, and more. It includes 87 wards from 15 local units in Kaski, Lamjung, Manang, Myagdi, and Mustang districts. This area is considered one of the best tourism destinations for trekking and exploration thanks to its attractive destinations, tourism-friendly infrastructure, hospitality, and service facilities.

title.rendered: Beyond mountains and lakes, Pokhara builds a future in education

content.rendered:
Pokhara is known worldwide for its stunning lakes, majestic mountains, and breathtaking scenery. But the city is now building a new identity beyond tourism. It is steadily emerging as a centre for education, research, and intellectual development. With its natural beauty, cultural diversity, and social harmony, Pokhara has long been a source of national pride. In recent years, the rise of universities, growing interest in research, and international academic partnerships have begun steering the city toward knowledge-based growth.

Safe surroundings, quality education, and a comfortable lifestyle are making Pokhara increasingly attractive to students from across Nepal and abroad. What was once celebrated only as Nepal’s premier tourist destination is now evolving into a vibrant “Student City” where learning and innovation thrive alongside natural beauty.

A proud educational legacy

Pokhara’s journey in education goes back centuries. In 1524 B.S., King Kulmandan Shah of Kaski granted land near Barpatan to Padmapani Padhya of Myagdi Rakhukhola to begin traditional “Pindi” education. This made Kaski a centre for Sanskrit studies and inspired the saying: ‘If you lose knowledge, go to Kaski.’ 

Pathsalas, monasteries, temples, and gurukuls taught Vedas, Sanskrit, astrology, philosophy, and ethics, laying the foundation for a culture of learning. During Prime Minister Dev Shamsher’s tenure, the first language school was established in Bindhyabasini in 1958 B.S., later evolving into a Sanskrit secondary school. By 2004 B.S., another Bindhyabasini school was established in Batulechaur, while schools in Bhairavtol, Nadipur, and other areas expanded access to education. The small primary school at the public inn (pauwa) in Nadipur later developed into Gyan Bhumi School.

In 2006 B.S., the establishment of Public Middle School in Nadipur gave new momentum to modern education in Pokhara. Just three years later, the school was relocated to Tundikhel and evolved into National High School. Soon after, institutions such as Bhadrakali School, Aranyajyoti Library, and Soldiers Board School (later Amar Singh School) emerged, further strengthening the city’s academic foundation. By 2014 B.S., schools like Barahi, Talbrahi, and Kanya School were founded, with Kanya School playing a pioneering role in advancing women’s education.

By 2016 B.S., nine schools had already been established. The founding of Prithvi Narayan College in 2017 B.S. ushered in a new era of higher education, producing thousands of graduates and positioning Pokhara as western Nepal’s leading educational centre. Gandaki Boarding School (2023 B.S.) added a new dimension to school education. Later, institutions such as Manipal College of Medical Sciences (1994 A.D.), Pokhara University (1997 A.D.), Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences (2072 B.S), and Gandaki University (2019 A.D.) accelerated higher and health education, giving Pokhara international recognition.

From Sanskrit gurukuls to modern universities, Pokhara’s educational legacy reflects resilience, vision, and progress. What began as a centre for traditional learning has grown into a vibrant hub of higher education, research, and global collaboration making Pokhara not just a tourist paradise, but a proud city of knowledge.

Pokhara emerging as education hub

Pokhara’s education sector is expanding rapidly. According to statistics from 2082 B.S., Kaski district has 634 schools, 375 communities and 259 institutions with 452 located within Pokhara Metropolitan City. The district also operates 377 early childhood centres, serving nearly 141,000 students, of whom about 128,000 are in Pokhara. In addition, more than 51 colleges function under various universities, further strengthening the region’s educational landscape.

Pokhara has also become a higher education hub. The city hosts Pokhara University, Gandaki University, Prithvi Narayan Campus, Manipal Medical College, and the Academy of Health Sciences. These institutions offer programs in medicine, engineering, IT, management, tourism, agriculture, and forestry. International collaborations, such as Informatics College’s partnership with London Metropolitan University, add to Pokhara’s global appeal.

Colleges like Janapriya, Janaprakash, Kanya, Kalika, Gaurishankar, and Gupteshwar provide accessible education, while specialised institutes including Western Engineering Campus, Institute of Forestry, Gandaki College of Engineering and Science, Gandaki Medical College, Nursing Campus, and Polytechnic Institutes are producing skilled manpower for Nepal and beyond.

Pokhara is no longer just a tourist paradise. It is steadily shaping its identity as Nepal’s ‘Student City,’ where schools and universities drive knowledge, skills, and innovation.  

Pokhara’s promise as a student city

According to the QS 2026 rankings, Seoul, Tokyo, London, Munich, Melbourne, Sydney, Berlin, Paris, Montreal, and Toronto stand among the world’s top student cities. In India, Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore, and Chennai have also emerged as important hubs by linking education with technology and modern lifestyles. These examples highlight the strong connection between education and urban development.

Pokhara holds strong potential to emerge as one of South Asia’s leading student destinations. Its peaceful surroundings, affordable living, and unmatched natural beauty create an environment that nurtures creativity and focus. Beyond lifestyle advantages, the city’s diverse geography offers vast opportunities for academic research. Fields such as Himalayan studies, climate change, biodiversity, sustainable tourism, agriculture, water resources, and disaster management provide rich ground for exploration. With the establishment of modern laboratories, digital learning hubs, and startup ecosystems, Pokhara could transform into a vibrant centre of innovation and knowledge.

The ‘15-minute city’ concept, where education, healthcare, transport, and essential services are accessible within short distances, aligns perfectly with Pokhara’s vision. Student-friendly infrastructure, combined with collaboration among universities, the private sector, and local communities, can establish the city as a hub of knowledge and opportunity.

Already renowned for its natural charm, Pokhara has the potential to evolve into South Asia’s most inspiring ‘Student City,’ where education, innovation, and beauty come together to shape the future.

Linking education with economy

Education in Pokhara must connect directly with employment and entrepreneurship. Establishing IT parks, innovation centres, and startup programs can give students the practical skills they need to succeed. 

Collaboration across tourism, health, agriculture, and information technology would strengthen the local economy while opening new opportunities for graduates. By blending education with Pokhara’s natural beauty, the city could also promote “educational tourism,” attracting international conferences, student exchanges, and research seminars. 

Pokhara’s future lies in connecting classrooms with careers, linking education to innovation and industry, and positioning itself as a dynamic “Student City.”

The role of Pokhara Metropolitan City

Pokhara Metropolitan City has a vital role in shaping the future of education. It must see education not only as a social service but as a key driver of urban growth and prosperity. Student-friendly planning is essential. Safe roads, reliable public transport, affordable housing, libraries, cultural centres, and 24-hour study spaces all help create an environment where young people can truly thrive. 

With smart investment and strong commitment, the metropolis can turn the vision of a true ‘Student City’ into reality, making Pokhara both a tourist paradise and a proud hub of knowledge.

From tourist city to student city

Pokhara is globally renowned as a tourist paradise, but its future potential extends far beyond tourism. 

With a long-term vision, quality education, and student-friendly infrastructure, the city can emerge as a leading educational hub in South Asia. 

While tourism defines Pokhara’s present, education can shape a more sustainable and prosperous future.

title.rendered: Landslides and floods block main highways at 9 locations, night driving banned on BP and Kantilokpath

content.rendered:
Due to floods and landslides in various districts across the country, the main highways were blocked at nine locations as of 6:55 am Monday. According to details released by the Nepal Police, some roads are completely closed, while others have one-way traffic.

In Koshi Province, one-way traffic is running on the Mid-Hill Highway in Bhojpur due to flooding. The Mechi Highway in Ilam (Rajduwali–Talchajung road) is completely blocked due to continuous rainfall. Police have said an alternative route can be used for this road.

Similarly, under the Mid-Hill Highway in Khotang, the road is completely closed in the Mattim area of Diktel Rupakot Majhuwagadhi–6 due to a landslide.

In Bagmati Province, on the BP Highway’s Khurkot–Nepalthok–Kavrebhanjyang section in Kavre, vehicle movement has been completely halted from 6 pm Monday to 4 am Tuesday due to the risk of possible flooding. Police say that from 4 am to 6 pm on Tuesday, traffic will resume after the situation is assessed.

In Sindhupalchok, there is complete blockage at two locations due to landslides — on the road to Tatopani in Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality-4, and at Kodari in Ward No. 2 on the Araniko Highway.

On Kantilokpath (Hetauda–Bhimphedi–Bagmati–Lalitpur section) in Makwanpur as well, all types of vehicles are barred from operating between 5 pm and 5 am due to the risk of possible flooding and landslides.

Similarly, one-way traffic is operating in the Bogtekhola area of Gosaikunda Rural Municipality-4 in Rasuwa’s Pasang Lhamu road section due to a landslide.

Nepal Police has also reported that transportation is completely blocked due to landslides on the Kaligandaki Corridor road section in Baglung, Gandaki Province, and on the Mahakali Highway in Darchula, Sudurpaschim Province.

Police have urged people to check road conditions before travelling and to exercise caution in risk-prone areas.

content.rendered:
July 20, Kathmandu

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) has said that rainfall is expected to gradually decrease from Wednesday onward. According to the department, the country is currently under the influence of monsoon winds, while the monsoon trough remains north of its average position, resulting in widespread rainfall.

Senior Meteorologist Min Kumar Aryal said rain is likely across various parts of the country today and tomorrow, but precipitation is expected to gradually subside from Wednesday. He said there is a possibility of moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning this afternoon at a few places in the Himalayan region and at many places in the hilly region.

The department has forecast moderate rainfall in many areas of the Tarai districts of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, and Sudurpashchim provinces, as well as at a few locations in Madhesh Province. Light to moderate rainfall is also likely at a few places in the hilly and Tarai areas of Koshi and Sudurpashchim provinces.

Heavy rainfall is likely at one or two locations in the hilly regions of Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim provinces. Tonight, moderate rain accompanied by thunder and lightning is expected at many places in the hilly and Tarai regions of Madhesh, Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini provinces.

Similarly, a few places in the hilly areas of Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces are likely to receive moderate rainfall with thunder and lightning. Heavy rainfall may also occur tonight at one or two locations in the hilly and Tarai regions of Koshi, Bagmati, Gandaki, and Lumbini provinces. The department has urged residents in vulnerable areas to remain alert due to the risk of floods, landslides, inundation, and debris flows.

title.rendered: Two killed in 62 disaster incidents in last 24 hours

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 20

Sixty-two disaster-related incidents were reported across the country in the last 24 hours, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). NDRRMA spokesperson Shanti Mahat said two people have died and 15 were injured in those incidents. During this period, natural disasters such as floods, landslides, drowning, and snake bites occurred in different parts of the country.

“Two people have died due to snake bites and 11 others have been injured. Nine districts have been affected by the disaster-related incidents. Two people were injured due to a landslide, and 11 districts are affected,” she said. NDRRMA said 11 roads have been blocked in the past 24 hours due to landslides and floods. According to the daily disaster bulletin released by the authority today, the estimated economic loss due to the disaster is about Rs 1 million and 227 thousand.

Six livestock were also lost in the incident. The NDRRMA bulletin recorded 26 landslide incidents in 18 districts, 13 snakebite cases, eight fires, seven instances of continuous rain, five animal attacks, and three flood incidents in the last 24 hours. It stated that 47 districts were affected by those incidents and 267 personnel from security agencies were deployed for rescue. NDRRMA had made extensive preparations for disaster response in view of the moderate, heavy, and very heavy rainfall in different parts of the country on Saturday and Sunday, warning the public to take precautions against floods and landslides.

title.rendered: Women reportedly missing inside Shuklaphanta National Park contact families

content.rendered:
Mahendranagar, July 20

Groups of women who were reportedly missing after entering the Shuklaphanta National Park (SNP) in Kanchanpur to collect mushrooms have been found safe. Following the reports that 14 women from Bagphanta of Bheemdutta municipality-19 had gone missing inside the park area since Sunday evening, the Nepali Army (NA) Shuklaphanta unit had launched a search operation, it is said.

According to Prakash Ghimire, Battalion Chief of Ranasingh Battalion deployed for the park security, the women have reportedly come into contact with their families. “We mobilised all available mechanisms for a comprehensive search operation and received reports a short while ago that they had come into contact with their families.

All of them are said to be safe,” he said. Earlier, a group of three women from Beldadi rural municipality-2 who had reportedly gone missing inside the park since Sunday evening were rescued by a security team led by Captain Suman GC. The group had also been inside the park without official permission to harvest wild mushrooms. The NA, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, city police and CNP administration were involved in the search operation, it is said.

title.rendered: Rs 30 million loss to Central Zoo due to bird flu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 20

The Central Zoo at Jawalakhel, Lalitpur, incurred a loss of Rs 30 million after it had to close for 27 days following the confirmation of bird flu at the country’s main zoo. After bird flu was detected in birds at the zoo, the National Trust for Nature Conservation had closed the facility to the public from June 19. Now that the infection is under control, the zoo has reopened from July 17.

The zoo’s information officer, Ganesh Koirala, said that regular cleaning, treatment of infected animals, and necessary precautions were taken after the infection was detected at the zoo. After that, a joint meeting of senior officials from the Department of Livestock Services and the Epidemiology and Disease Control Division of the Central Animal Disease Research Laboratory decided to reopen the zoo.

According to him, on a regular day, about 1,700 to 1,800 visitors used to visit the zoo. On Saturdays, 5,000 to 7,000 people and on Sundays, 3,500 to 5,000 people used to spend time at the zoo. On the first day after reopening, on July 17, only 800 people visited the zoo. The zoo has been charging Rs 100 for children and senior citizens, Rs 150 for students, and Rs 250 for other visitors. Last fiscal year, the zoo earned about Rs 180 million. Even though the target was to collect Rs 210 million in the fiscal year 2082/83 from entry fees, the zoo administration has stated that the prolonged closure due to bird flu has made it more challenging to meet the goal.

title.rendered: Want to build a house in the city? Soon you’ll need an insurance policy first

content.rendered:
One line buried in the FY 2026/27 budget can potentially change how cities in Nepal construct – and who pays when disaster strikes. A proposed budget provision would make insurance mandatory during building-map approval in urban areas, linking construction permission with risk protection.

The budget season in Nepal year after year follows a script. Income taxes, salaries, roads, hydropower, subsidies – these typically grab the headlines, and this year was no different. When Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle presented the budget to the Parliament on May 29, the newspaper headlines splashed with income tax rebates, an effort to promote artificial intelligence, reforms in the electricity sector, and a smaller civil service.

But one easy-to-miss line may end up being far more important to everyday city dwellers than perhaps half of all headline declarations put together: insurance is to become a pre-condition before a municipality approves the blueprint of building construction in urban areas. It is in the Budget Speech 2026/27, under section 60 ‘e’. Insurance, Securities, and Cooperatives. The exact provision says: “We will make insurance mandatory while approving building construction maps in urban areas.”

The thought behind it may sound very procedural. It is not. If subtle, this indicates a paradigm shift in Nepal’s risk perception – a move from being a reactive post-disaster cleaner-upper to a country attempting to put a price on danger before construction work begins. What does this mean for a hypothetical family?

Let’s say a family wants to build a home in a municipality; beyond obtaining land permits, engineering plans, municipality authorisation and a tax clearance, a policy that insures the building would become mandatory. This is not an insignificant obligation. It means one more added expense for homeowners before they even start constructing a home, one more criterion for municipalities to check for approving a building. It means a significantly larger market for insurers and, potentially, fewer government payout needs every time an unfortunate event such as a fire, flood, or building collapse destroys homes.

Not entirely new, but a step further

This is not a leap in the dark. The budget last year already hinted at plans to include natural disasters and accidents into property insurance and extended insurance to rural areas as well as proposing cybersecurity insurance. These were about spreading, extending an existing network. The budget this year takes it further, by tethering insurance to the building-map approval process. In other words, this isn’t simply about one more document to sign on the side – your ability to build will now have to first get an insurance stamp.

This is where the action is needed. Nepal’s cities are urbanising much faster than the structures designed to manage them. Houses rise on less and less space; roads shrink while climate risks grow, even as earthquakes, floods, fires and landslides keep erupting at ever greater cost in money and lives. Nepal continues to largely depend on disaster relief. It still means that when disaster strikes – and it will, and it does – the first casualty is families and their homes. Family help will come, perhaps then banks and cooperatives, then aid groups, local government, finally federal funds, if the scale of the damage warrants it.

Mandatory building insurance will turn the entire cycle around; risk is no longer addressed post-disaster, but is factored in like any other upfront construction cost.

The good part, and the catch

Done properly, insurance does something valuable: it spreads the cost of bad luck across many people instead of bankrupting one family. It can also push builders towards safer construction — if insurers actually do their homework, a poorly built structure should cost more to insure, which is a quiet but real incentive to follow the building code.

But housing in urban Nepal is already expensive. Land costs a fortune, materials keep getting pricier, and most middle-class families build their homes slowly — savings, a loan, money sent home from abroad, stitched together over years. Adding a mandatory insurance requirement adds another cost to that pile. And if it’s designed badly, it could turn into exactly the kind of thing Nepalis are used to seeing: a certificate you buy to get past a counter, not protection you can actually rely on when your house is underwater or on fire.

That’s really the question this whole policy comes down to — will it actually protect people, or just give them one more form to collect?

It’s bigger than just buildings

It’s not just the buildings on the line. The same budget increases third-party motor insurance cover to Rs 1 million, mentions plans to add accident-detecting devices to vehicles, and makes accident, critical illness and transportation insurance mandatory. Placed side by side, they are not small modifications – they show a government that wants to transfer more of the nation’s day-to-day risk to formalised insurance, rather than leaving it to be handled piecemeal, post-fact, in the informal sector. This is larger than it seems. 

For decades, the state, in effect, played insurance for citizens without collecting a rupee from them. When a house burns, a bus falls off a cliff, the season’s crop floods – the people go to the state for relief because nowhere else can they turn. But relief is fickle. It depends on a state subject to politicking, attention and the scrutiny of the public. Rarely does it compensate fully for the damage incurred. 

Insurance, provided all works as it ought, should be more predictable than relief. Provided all works as it ought – a key qualification – insurance covers people’s risks. But this is not the default for any developing country; it comes only if premiums are affordable, claims are paid smoothly and promptly, insurance policies are easy to read and understand, and people believe in the institution enough to sign up. That belief requires trust. That trust must be patiently built.

What still needs answering

To really do this, and do it in a way that doesn’t create yet another headache, there needs to be more clarity:

  • What needs to be insured? Earthquakes?Fire?Floods?Just construction defects?
  • Who will determine and enforce insurance rates?
  • Is there a subsidy for smaller homeowners?
  • Will a homeowner be assured their claims will actually be paid in a timely way?
  • Will a municipal building inspector actually verify that insurance exists, or only that it is documented somewhere?

The government hasn’t even scratched the surface of those questions. Unless it does, the “reform” risk becoming an expensive piece of paper that doesn’t actually protect anybody when disaster strikes. But the underlying concept shouldn’t be dismissed. After all, Nepal’s a frequent site for natural disasters, so including insurance in its urban planning is not as out-of-the-box as it might seem; quite the contrary, it is somewhat overdue.

That one-liner on the budget might seem like nothing, but the question underlying it is anything but trivial: as Nepal’s cities continue to expand, who bears the ultimate financial risk? Traditionally, and historically, in much of the country the ultimate financial risk is borne first and foremost by individual households, then if, and only if, the government can absorb it. But this new proposal is a bid to shift that to a regime that insures before construction, not after the inevitable devastation. 

Do this correctly, and the government has in its grasp the means to effectively insure the homes of its citizens, stimulate Nepal’s largely stunted insurance industry to play a larger role in managing these risks and relieve the strain on long-term government spending when crises hit. 

Do it incorrectly and, like so many bureaucratic initiatives, the reform will amount to just another piece of paper in a cumbersome process that can barely cope as it is. Nevertheless, this sentence in the long budget speech is worth far more attention than it is likely to get because it goes beyond an insurance product and asks the real question: who really pays to live, build, and endure life in a Nepalese city?

title.rendered: Devotees throng Pashupatinath on first Monday of Shrawan (Photos)

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 20

Today, the first Monday of the month of Shrawan this year, has drawn crowds of devotees since early morning to the Pashupatinath Temple and Shiva temples across the country.

According to Tirtha Shrestha, Member Secretary of the Pashupati Area Development Trust, arrangements have been made for darshan by opening all four gates of the Pashupatinath Temple from 3 am. Having opened from 3 am, all four gates of the temple will remain open until 8 pm at night, after the evening aarati. The special puja, however, will run from 8:30 am to 12 noon.

Devotees are lining up to worship at the Pashupatinath Temple. The Trust says it has made the necessary arrangements to ensure smooth, safe, and well-managed darshan and the special puja for devotees. However, Member Secretary Shrestha said that due to delays in appointing officials and a shortage of manpower, not all the required work could be carried out as needed.

To make the darshan management effective, the Trust’s officials and staff have been mobilised along with the Temple Security Group, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, the Nepal Army, Traffic Police, the Kathmandu Metropolitan Police, and various religious and social organisations.

Along with Pashupatinath, crowds of devotees have also gathered since early morning at other Shiva temples in the Kathmandu Valley, including Gokarneshwar, Nageshwar, Doleshwar, and Makhan Mahadev, known as the “Sano Pashupatinath” (Small Pashupatinath), located in the Basantapur Durbar area. Likewise, devotees have also gone to Shiva temples across the country for worship and darshan.

There is a religious belief that observing the fast and puja on Shrawan Mondays brings family happiness and peace, and helps one find a suitable spouse.

title.rendered: Spain ends 16-year wait, wins second World Cup title

content.rendered:
Sixteen years after first bagging World Football glory in South Africa, Spain has once again established its dominance over the world.

On the strength of young talent, attractive passing football, and collective performance, Spain has won the FIFA World Cup 2026 title, achieving the distinction of becoming world champions for the second time.

Beating defending champions Argentina 1-0 in the final at New York-New Jersey Stadium, Spain ended a 16-year wait. Lifting the World Cup for the first time since 2010, Spain has also sent a clear message that its new generation is ready to lead world football.

Under coach Luis de la Fuente, Spain introduced itself as the most attractive and balanced footballing side throughout the tournament. A blend of ball control, high pressing, sharp attacking, and disciplined defence carried Spain to the title. After impressively beating a contender like France in the semi-final, Spain maintained its rhythm in the final too, defeating former champions Argentina.

Spain created more than a dozen chances while playing continuous attacking football against Argentina in the final. However, the win had to wait until extra time.

Golden new generation

The Spain that was once ruled by the generation of Xavi, Iniesta, Casillas, and Puyol has now reached the summit again with new faces.

A balanced blend of young players like Lamine Yamal, Pau Cubarsí, Pedro Porro, Ferran Torres, and experienced players like Rodri, Fabián Ruiz, and Aymeric Laporte made Spain world champions.

Spain’s Pau Cubarsí was named Best Young Player, while Spain’s captain Rodri, named the tournament’s best player, won the Golden Ball award. The Golden Glove also went to Spain’s goalkeeper Unai Simón.

Having already become European champions before the World Cup, Spain has signalled it will maintain its dominance in world football for some years to come.

Impressive winning journey

Spain didn’t have as smooth a start in the group stage as expected. After a surprising 0-0 draw with Cape Verde in the opening match, it beat Saudi Arabia 4-0. It then secured a 1-0 win over Uruguay in the final match, topping the group and advancing to the knockout stage.

After an easy 3-0 win over Austria in the round of 32, Spain went on to beat Portugal 1-0 and Belgium 2-1. Mikel Merino scored the decisive late goal in both matches. In the semi-final, Spain delivered its best performance of the tournament, keeping France completely under pressure. By controlling possession for long stretches and neutralising France’s attack, Spain secured an impressive win to reach the final.

Experience steadied it, youth won it

Collective performance was at the heart of Spain’s success. Rodri controlled the midfield throughout the tournament while Fabián Ruiz set the tempo of play. The Laporte-Cubarsí pairing was excellent in defence, while goalkeeper Unai Simón conceded just one goal in the entire tournament.

Although young sensation Lamine Yamal didn’t contribute much directly to goals or assists, he consistently pressured opposition defences. Among the players with the most successful dribbles in the tournament, he showed his influence in the final as well.

Different players stepped up in different matches for Spain. In the group stage, players like Mikel Oyarzabal, Dani Olmo, and Lamine Yamal scored goals. In the knockout stage, from Mikel Merino shining off the bench to Pedro Porro and Ferran Torres, goals came from various players, showing that every player in the Spanish squad gave their full effort. In defence too, alongside Laporte’s experience, young players Pau Cubarsí, Pedro Porro, and Marc Cucurella excelled.

New era of Spanish football

After winning the World Cup in 2010, followed by disappointments in 2014 and 2018, and an underwhelming performance in 2022, Spanish football has returned to the top of the world once again.

This title doesn’t just mean winning the World Cup; it also signals that Spain’s new generation has begun leading international football. With this win, Spain has started a new golden chapter in world football, holding both the European and World champion titles simultaneously. Spain had also won the Euro 2024 title, and two years later, succeeded in winning football’s highest-status trophy as well.

Story of the final

Tactically, the final appeared one-sided. Spain attacked continuously from the start but couldn’t find the breakthrough. Argentina, busy defending against Spain’s attacks, couldn’t build much of an attack of its own.

With neither side scoring in the regulation 90 minutes, the match went to extra time. There was no goal in the first half of extra time either. Right at the start of the second half of extra time, in the 106th minute, Ferran Torres scored to put Spain ahead. Argentina tried to find an equaliser in the remaining 14 minutes plus 5 added minutes but couldn’t succeed, and Torres’s goal proved decisive.

title.rendered: Halftime show at World Cup final aims to unite world through music

content.rendered:
If the match between Spain and Argentina is the World Cup final, then the “halftime show” is the symbolic final of world pop music. As Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal face off for the title at MetLife Stadium in New York, the heavyweight of world music, Madonna, Shakira, BTS, and Justin Bieber will give their performance in a nearly 30-minute halftime show.

This unprecedented convergence of football and music is creating a unique chemistry between sports fans and music lovers alike. At a time when geopolitics is causing upheaval across the world, the World Cup final and its halftime show could become a formula that unites divided minds.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino made this message clear at a pre-final press event, delivering remarks in front of President Donald Trump himself, a moment carrying diplomatic weight, given that the FIFA chief’s message of global unity was delivered directly before Trump.

The halftime show will be performed in front of Trump. Notably, Trump, who is often seen as unfriendly toward Hollywood and celebrities, will witness this musical performance, and other figures from the global entertainment world are also expected to be present at the same time.

FIFA’s choice of performers for the show appears deliberate. By bringing pop stars from different continents onto a single stage, FIFA seems to be aiming to send a message of global unity and cooperation, an unprecedented gathering across continents, generations, languages, and musical cultures.

Madonna is one of the most influential names in global pop culture. Shakira has built a strong connection between Latin music and football celebrations. Justin Bieber is among the most popular pop stars of the digital era. BTS has brought K-pop into the global mainstream, while Burna Boy represents the growing international influence of African music.

First time in World Cup

This will be the first-ever halftime show at a World Cup, a format similar to America’s Super Bowl. Alongside the headliners, Nigerian singer Burna Boy, Venezuelan music director Gustavo Dudamel, and Coldplay, along with the PS22 Chorus, will also perform, with the show coordinated by Coldplay’s Chris Martin.

According to FIFA, the televised musical segment will run 11 minutes, though international media reports suggest the halftime break, including time for stage setup and removal, could stretch to around 25 minutes.

Since a football match’s halftime is normally capped at 15 minutes, there has been debate over whether this extended break could affect players’ readiness and the game’s rhythm. FIFA, however, has stated there will be no compromise on the fairness of the game or players’ welfare.

The halftime show is being organised in support of the FIFA/Global Citizen Education Fund, which aims to raise $100 million to provide quality education and football opportunities to children around the world. More than $50 million has already been raised, with one dollar from every World Cup ticket contributed to the fund.

Support and Criticism

The gathering of famous pop stars representing different geographies, cultures, languages, and generations on one stage isn’t limited to entertainment value alone; it sends a message that football and music can rise above political and cultural boundaries to unite the world.

The participation of Madonna, Shakira, BTS, Justin Bieber, and Burna Boy reflects an effort to bring together audiences from North America, Latin America, Asia, Europe, and Africa in a single global event. Since the performance is tied to raising funds for children’s education, it also represents an effort to convert fame into social impact.

Meanwhile, debate continues over whether the World Cup is increasingly being turned into an American-style entertainment and commercial “mega-event.” There is criticism of the halftime show, though it amounts more to ongoing debate among football fans, analysts, and media than any organised boycott.

Critics worry that extending the halftime break to 25 minutes could pose health risks to players, their bodies cooling down during a long period of inactivity, increasing the risk of injury in the second half. Under International Football Association Board rules, halftime cannot exceed 15 minutes, and any change requires the referee’s approval, raising questions about how the proposed extended break would be reconciled with the rules.

There are also concerns about disrupting the game’s rhythm, with critics arguing that a musical performance could affect players’ concentration and the game’s natural flow. Some have complained that football is being “Americanized,” while some supporters have accused FIFA of following the Super Bowl model and turning football into more of an entertainment and advertising spectacle than a sport.

Supporters, however, see this as an opportunity to connect with new audiences. They believe the participation of globally famous artists could draw younger and new viewers, even those with limited interest in football, closer to the World Cup. The argument goes that music makes the final feel like a bigger cultural occasion than an ordinary match, and that as audience expectations for major sporting events grow, the world of sports needs to experiment with new formats too.

Supporters argue that bringing together artists from different regions- Madonna, Shakira, BTS, Justin Bieber, and Burna Boy, will further broaden the World Cup’s international character. Organisers, meanwhile, insist there will be no compromise on the fairness of the game or players’ health.

Ultimately, the debate centres on one question: will the music make the World Cup final even more special, or will it overshadow football’s core appeal and the players’ wellbeing? A practical answer will likely become clearer only after the event and match are over.

Given its popularity, cultural influence, and potential global audience, the halftime show could become one of the largest musical gatherings ever held. Since the World Cup final itself is among the most-watched sporting events in the world, its stage will be far larger than any ordinary concert.

title.rendered: Several highways affected by rain; some highways closed for traffic at night

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 19

Highways in various parts of the country have been affected by floods and landslides triggered by continuous rain. Some road sections are completely blocked, while in others, vehicular traffic is disallowed at night. According to the Nepal Police, considering the potential risk of floods, all types of vehicles are banned from operating on the Khurkot–Nepalthok–Katunjebesi road section of the BP Highway connecting Kavrepalanchok and Sindhuli every day from 6:00 pm to 4:00 am until further notice.

However, the road section will be open from 4:00 am to 6:00 pm. Similarly, all types of vehicles are prohibited from operating on Kanti Highway from 5:00 pm to 5:00 am until further notice. Traffic has been stopped on the Mechi Highway in Rajduwali, Ilam Municipality-9, after the road became muddy. Similarly, the Saljhundi–Dhorpatan road section has been completely blocked after rocks fell from above in Dhungekhola, Ward 2 of Panini Rural Municipality in Arghakhanchi.

Traffic is also halted at the Belbagar area, Jaimini Municipality-8, Baglung, along the Kaligandaki corridor highway after a landslide occurred at the place. The Araniko Highway has been completely blocked after landslides and rocks mixed with mud fell in Jirokilo of Bhotekoshi Rural Municipality-4 and the Kodari area of Ward No. 2 in Sindhupalchok. The BP Highway is completely blocked due to landslides at Ghumaune, Ward No 7, at Ward No 8 Gimdi, and at Ward No 9 Biruwadanda and Pinthali areas of Roshi Rural Municipality in Kavrepalanchok district.

title.rendered: Mandala Theatre welcomes third batch of Mandala Drama School

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 19

Mandala Theatre Nepal organised the Welcome Program for the students of the Mandala Drama School (MDS), Third Batch (2026–2027), at Mandala Theatre on Friday. The program marked the formal commencement of the 18-month intensive residential theatre training program implemented under Project RANGA (Reclaiming Advocacy through Narratives, Debates, Grassroots Theatre and Arts), funded by the European Union.

Mandala Drama School is a flagship initiative of Mandala Theatre Nepal that aims to nurture a new generation of socially conscious playmakers, theatre educators, writers, directors, and cultural leaders from across Nepal. The Third Batch brings together 15 students selected through a competitive nationwide selection process.

The Welcome Program was chaired by Buddhiram Tamang, Chairperson of Mandala Theatre-Nepal, with Véronique Lorenzo, Ambassador of the European Union to Nepal, attending as the Guest of Honour. The event was graced by distinguished guests representing government institutions, academia, development partners, and the theatre community.

The 18-month residential program is designed to equip students with the knowledge, skills, and experiences required to become socially engaged and independent theatre practitioners capable of contributing meaningfully to their communities and the broader cultural landscape of Nepal.

The program featured a keynote speech by Nand Kishor Yadav, representative from GIZ Civil Peace Service, who shared his experiences with the previous batches of Mandala Drama School and reflected on the transformative role that theatre education has played in shaping young theatre practitioners. He highlighted the growth, achievements, and contributions of former students and expressed their continued support for nurturing emerging artists committed to social engagement and creative excellence.

The program also featured a keynote address by Véronique Lorenzo, who highlighted the importance of theatre as a powerful medium for dialogue, cultural preservation, and social transformation. Appreciating Mandala Theatre Nepal’s continued efforts to nurture emerging theatre practitioners from diverse communities across Nepal, she encouraged the students to remain curious, courageous, and committed to using art as a force for positive change. She further inspired the young theatre-makers to embrace their creativity, amplify diverse voices, and contribute meaningfully to building a more inclusive and compassionate society through theatre.

The students and guests also witnessed a welcome performance by the Mandala Alumni Circle, celebrating the spirit of creativity, collaboration, and artistic excellence that lies at the heart of the Mandala Drama School.

Following the Welcome Program, the selected students will formally begin their academic journey at Mandala Drama School and participate in an intensive residential learning experience designed to prepare them as independent, socially conscious, and community-engaged theatre-makers.

The program formally concluded with a vote of thanks delivered by Buddhiram Tamang, who extended his sincere gratitude to the European Union, consortium partners, Debate Network Nepal (DNN) and Campaign for Change (CfC), all distinguished guests, and everyone whose continued support and collaboration have made this initiative possible.

title.rendered: Chitwan National Park sees more tourists but less revenue

content.rendered:
The number of tourists visiting Chitwan National Park has risen by 41,594 compared to the previous fiscal year. In FY 2025/26, 272,923 tourists visited the park, up from 231,329 in 2024/25.

According to the park office, last fiscal year’s visitors included 161,375 Nepalis, 22,883 tourists from SAARC countries, and 88,665 from other countries.

The number of Nepali tourists rose significantly compared to the previous fiscal year; 117,206 Nepali tourists had visited the park in FY 2024/25, along with 24,800 from SAARC countries and 89,323 from other countries during that period.

While the number of Nepali tourists rose by 44,169 last year, the number of tourists from SAARC and other countries actually declined slightly.

According to the park, the highest number of visitors, 32,252, arrived in the month of October/November, while the lowest, 7,073, came in July/August. Tourist numbers typically remain high from Sepember/October through May/June. Although in the past visitor numbers tended to drop after March/April, the park noted that last year the increase continued through May/June.

According to park information officer Abinash Thapa Magar, the largest numbers of Nepali tourists arrived in October/November (19,109) and April/May(18,046). SAARC tourists came in greatest numbers in May/June(5,863), while tourists from other countries peaked in October/November (10,326) and February/March (11,809).

The highest number of tourists in the park’s history came in FY 2023/24, when 306,837 tourists visited and the park collected revenue of Rs 36,72,92,807. In FY 2022/23, 299,412 tourists visited the park.

According to the last 10 years’ data, the fewest tourists, 87,39, came in FY 2015/16. During FY 2020/21, when the Covid-19 pandemic was having an impact, 98,228 tourists visited the park.

Tourists up, but revenue down

Even though tourist numbers rose, the park’s revenue declined.

According to information officer Thapamagar, the park collected Rs 31,01,64,551 in revenue in FY 2025/26, down from Rs 33,86,00,000 collected in FY 2024/25.

He said the decline in revenue was due to the drop in the number of foreign tourists, adding that the Gen-Z movement and the Iran-US conflict kept foreign tourist arrivals below expectations, which directly affected Chitwan National Park as well.

The park’s entry fee is set at Rs 150 per person for Nepalis, Rs 1,000 for SAARC nationals, and Rs 2,000 for other foreign tourists. A fee of Rs 5,000 applies for jeeps entering the park.

The park has six entry points for tourists, of which the Sauraha gate sees the highest number of visitors; 237,025 tourists entered through Sauraha alone last fiscal year.

Chitwan National Park is known for its rare one-horned rhinoceros, Bengal tigers, bears, elephants, spotted deer, gharial crocodiles, and various species of birds, plants and reptiles. Tourists here observe wildlife through jeep safaris and jungle walks.

Every year, jeep safaris are suspended from the third week of the first week of July to the third week of September due to the monsoon.

Areas including Sauraha, Meghauli, Patihani, Madi, Devghat and Siraichuli in Chitwan district are the main attractions for domestic and foreign tourists.

title.rendered: Sixteen years later, Nepalis in Spain await that same joy

content.rendered:
Barcelona (Spain): Andrés Iniesta’s extra-time goal in the World Cup final in Johannesburg, South Africa, made Spain world champions for the first time. But the joy of that historic moment wasn’t confined to South Africa alone. Thousands of kilometres away, Spain’s streets, squares, bars and public spaces stayed awake all night. Among that crowd were Nepalis living in Spain, who celebrated that history-making moment alongside Spanish fans.

Sixteen years later, history has arrived at a similar turning point. In today’s FIFA World Cup final at a stadium in New York-New Jersey, USA, Spain faces Argentina for a second title. The Nepalis who were working in bars while watching the match back then are now running their own businesses. Some recall the victory march in Bilbao, others the night spent with thousands of fans at Barcelona’s Plaça d’Espanya. Some are currently in Belgium or Germany, but their hearts are still waiting for Spain’s win.

Akkal Bohara, a social worker, businessman and Everest climber who runs the “Rara Restaurant Coffee Bar” in Alfaz del Pi in Costa Blanca, still gets emotional remembering the 2010 final. He said he was working in a bar at the time, and the moment of Iniesta’s extra-time goal that made Spain world champions for the first time still comes vividly before his eyes.

Bohara, who watched that final 16 years ago while working at a restaurant, is now preparing to watch the game with customers at his own restaurant. He said his support is entirely for Spain because of the opportunities and sense of belonging Spain has given Nepalis, adding that out of this same affection he had even flown Spain’s flag atop Everest’s summit. He mentioned that many customers from Norway, the Netherlands and Belgium who visit his restaurant are also supporting Spain, so he expects today to be busier than usual.

Tulasi Gurung, who has been living in Bilbao in Spain’s Basque region, was also a direct witness to the victory march after the 2010 World Cup win.

“The Nepali community was quite small back then, whereas now there are many more Nepali friends around,” says Gurung to Onlinekhabar. “I even took part in the victory march after Spain’s win, it was an unforgetable moment.”

This time too, he plans to watch the match at Bilbao’s public fan zone, saying his wish is simply for Spain to win the World Cup again.

Yagya Narayan Poudel, currently on summer vacation in Germany, recalled watching the 2010 final on a big screen with thousands of fans at Barcelona’s Plaça d’Espanya. He said the excitement and joy of that night still can’t be forgotten, and that even though he’s in Germany now, he’ll watch the final with his family.

Gopal Regmi, who watched the 2010 final on a public screen in Barcelona, now lives in Belgium. Despite the distance, his support remains with Spain. He said the celebrations after Spain’s 2010 win remain one of the unforgettable moments of his life, and that he believes Spain will repeat that same joy this time.

Ram Krishna Pudasaini still keeps a special memory from watching the 2010 final at the Hyundai Fan Park at Cibeles in Madrid. He said he still has a bag he received as a gift after the match, with which he has travelled to more than 25 cities across 15 countries, mending it and reusing it whenever it wears out, calling it his lucky memento.

Recalling that he’d had the chance to sit and watch the match alongside well-known TV presenter Kiko Matamoros back then, he said this time he’ll watch the final with his family in Nepal, adding that wherever he is, his support will be for Spain.

All of Spain in football mode

It’s not just Nepalis, the whole of Spain is awaiting the World Cup final. Large public screens have been set up in major cities including Barcelona, Madrid, Valencia, Seville and Malaga. Dozens of municipalities in Catalonia have arranged live broadcasts of the final in parks and public squares.

Anticipating a bigger-than-expected turnout, Barcelona’s city government moved the large screen it had initially planned to place at Les Corts to the Marina del Fòrum platform at the last minute. Municipalities including L’Hospitalet, Badalona, Tarragona, Reus, Salou, Gavà, Cornellà, Terrassa and Sabadell have also arranged public viewings.

After Spain reached the final, Madrid’s streets echoed with red-and-yellow flags, music, car horns and chants of “España” until midnight. Plaza de la Cibeles, the fans’ main gathering spot, is expected to fill again with thousands of supporters on Sunday.

Excitement for the final is also visible at restaurants and bars, with table bookings rising in many places days in advance. According to business owners, the night of the final will be far busier than a typical Sunday.

Contest between two generations

This final is also being viewed as a contest between two generations: on one side, 39-year-old Lionel Messi aiming for a second consecutive World Cup, and on the other, 19-year-old Lamine Yamal leading Spain’s bid for a second World Cup title.

Messi spent his golden club career at Barcelona, and Yamal too is a product of Barcelona’s “La Masia” academy, which is why many see the Spain-Argentina final as more than just a match: a contest between two generations, two footballing cultures and two eras.

Sixteen years ago, after Iniesta’s goal, Spain’s streets stayed awake all night. On Sunday night, those streets hope that history repeats itself. For Nepalis living in Spain too, this isn’t just a World Cup final; it’s another special night tied to the joy of the country they consider their second home.

title.rendered: Spain and Argentina set for World Cup final showdown

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 19

Forty-eight teams, 104 matches, and finally one champion. The 23rd edition of the World Cup, spanning 96 years of history, has reached the point where new history is once again being written.

One team is aiming for a rare achievement in football history, winning back-to-back World Cups, while the other steps onto the field carrying the dream of returning to football’s highest throne after 16 years.

On one side is Argentina, playing in its eighth World Cup final, still centred around Lionel Messi. On the other is Spain, which has impressed the world with youthful energy, sharp attacking play and attractive football, and is now seeking its second World Cup title.

Monday morning’s FIFA World Cup 2026 final at the stadium in New York-New Jersey, USA, won’t just be a title clash between two teams, it will be a decisive contest between two generations, two styles, and two footballing philosophies.

The experienced Messi will try to add another golden chapter to his historic career, while 18-year-old Lamine Yamal will aim to usher in a new era of world football. So this final won’t just decide who takes the trophy; it will also answer the question of who holds the future of football.

Unbeaten since the group stage, both teams have shown why they are top contenders for the title. Argentina has reached the final for a second consecutive time by navigating a difficult knockout run. At the same time, Spain has built a reputation as one of the tournament’s most impressive teams by playing possession-based, attacking football throughout.

Now only 90 minutes remain, or extra time, if needed. After that, World Cup football will have its champion for the 23rd edition.

Spain’s impressive run

European champions Spain reached the final by keeping title favourites France fully under control in the semi-final. Their long spells of possession and clinical finishing have made them the tournament’s most balanced team.

Spain didn’t have an easy start in Group H. After a surprising goalless draw with Cape Verde, they beat Saudi Arabia 4-0 and then defeated Uruguay 1-0 to win the group.

Spain then beat Austria 3-0 in the round of 32, before defeating Portugal in the round of 16 and Belgium in the quarter-final, both matches decided by late goals from Mikel Merino. Spain has conceded just one goal in the tournament so far.

Playing in the World Cup final for the first time since 2010, Spain is now aiming to become world champions for the second time.

Argentina’s difficult road

The Copa America champions and defending World Cup champions Argentina had a far tougher journey than Spain.

Under Messi’s captaincy, Argentina won all three group matches; a hat-trick from Messi against Algeria, two goals against Austria, and another strong performance against Jordan saw them cruise through the group stage.

But Argentina had to fight in every round after that. They beat Cape Verde 3-2 in extra time in the round of 32, then staged a historic comeback in the round of 16 against Egypt, overturning a 2-0 deficit as late as the 79th minute.

Argentina beat Switzerland in extra time in the quarterfinal, then came from behind again against England in the semifinal to reach the final. After falling behind to an Anthony Gordon goal, goals from Enzo Fernández and substitute Lautaro Martínez sent Argentina to a second consecutive final.

Argentina is now looking to turn its chance into reality, becoming, after Brazil, the first team to win two consecutive World Cups.

Second World Cup meeting

Spain and Argentina have met only once before at a World Cup.

In that 1966 match, Argentina beat Spain 2-1, with both Argentine goals scored by Luis Artime.

Outside the World Cup, the two teams have played 13 friendly matches, with Spain winning 6, Argentina winning 5, and two ending in draws.

Their most recent meeting was in 2018, when Spain beat Argentina 6-1.

Players to watch

For Argentina, all eyes will once again be on Lionel Messi. With eight goals, he remains in contention for the Golden Boot and is one of the tournament’s most influential players.

For Spain, young star Lamine Yamal, captain Rodri, Dani Olmo, and the centre-back pairing of Aymeric Laporte and Pau Cubarsí could prove decisive.

For Argentina, alongside Messi, Julián Álvarez, Lautaro Martínez, Enzo Fernández, and goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez will also be key players.

title.rendered: 893 scrub typhus cases recorded in Chitwan last fiscal year

content.rendered:
Chitwan, July 17

Among the patients who came to various hospitals in the district in the last fiscal year, 893 were found to be infected with scrub typhus. Out of the 11,419 patients who visited the district’s hospitals in the fiscal year 2082/83, 893 were found to be infected with scrub typhus during testing.

According to Ram KC, the vector control officer at the Chitwan Public Health Office, 621 of the infected people are from Chitwan. Among the infected found in the district, 246 are from Ratnanagar Municipality, 117 from Khairahani Municipality, and 90 from Bharatpur Metropolitan City.

Likewise, KC said that 82 of the infected are from Rapti Municipality, 69 from Kalika Municipality, seven from Madi Municipality, and 10 from Ichchhakamana Rural Municipality. In the fiscal year 2081/82, out of 7,095 people tested, 1,055 were found to be infected with this disease. In the current fiscal year, one person has died from this disease.

title.rendered: Poor drainage system to blame for inundation problem in Kathmandu

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 17

Different areas in the federal capital city of Kathmandu, including Anamnagar, New Baneshwor, Jamal, Raniban, and Singha Durbar, become waterlogged even during light rainfall. Road traffic was badly affected on Thursday afternoon after these areas were waterlogged following the afternoon downpour. Passengers had to face long traffic delays due to the obstruction.

Though such a problem recurs every year, no long-term solution has been found so far. Spokesperson at the Kathmandu Upatyaka Khanepani Limited (KUKL), Prakash Kumar Rai, shared that as Maitighar is situated on a downward slope, rainwater accumulates here. He mentioned, “Though the drain pipes of the Maitighar area drain into Tukucha rivulet, the drain water cannot flow easily once the water level in Tukucha rivulet rises during the rainy season.

So this area gets waterlogged every year even in light rain in this season.” “The main problem is with the drainage system. Most of the drainage pipes in these areas are old and narrow. Their capacity is insufficient to handle the rainwater flow,” he added. Although discussions were held for the integrated improvement of the sewerage management system around Maitighar, New Plaza and Singha Durbar areas, a comprehensive plan has not been implemented yet. Rapid urbanisation, lack of a separate system for rainwater outlets, and rivers that have steadily lost their capacity to carry floodwater are major reasons behind inundation in Kathmandu Valley.

title.rendered: 3,296 disaster incidents claim 160 lives in last three months

content.rendered:
Kathmandu, July 17

The country recorded 3,296 incidents of natural disasters in the last three months of the last fiscal year, in which 160 people lost their lives. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, two persons went missing, and 945 people sustained injuries in such incidents that took place from April 14 to July 16. Similarly, 4,375 families were affected during the period. The highest number of incidents of fire took place in three months, which stood at 897, where 17 people died, 109 were injured, and 990 families were affected, added the Authority.

Likewise, 514 incidents of snakebite were recorded during the period, killing 38 people, leaving 479 injured and affecting 517 families. Thirteen people lost their lives in incidents of storms, 68 sustained injuries and 1356 families were affected during the period. A total of 477 incidents of storms had taken place. The country recorded 433 incidents of landslides, where 12 people died, 15 were injured, and 351 families were affected, while 24 people died, 120 were injured, and 262 families were affected in 223 incidents of lightning.

As per the details published by the Authority, 181 incidents of wildlife attack took place, killing 17 people, leaving 103 people injured and affecting 287 families. According to the Authority, nine people died, two went missing, nine were injured, and 396 families were affected in 161 incidents of flood while 153 incidents of heavy rainfall took place, where four people lost their lives, one sustained an injury, and 132 families were affected. Likewise, 21 people died due to high-altitude sickness, two died when a stone fell upon them, one died, and two were injured in wildfire incidents, and one died and another was injured in avalanches in three months.

Lalitpur, July 17

The Central Zoo has been reopened to the general public from today. The zoo, located at Jawalakhel in Lalitpur, was closed from June 19 after bird flu was confirmed in crows, vultures, ducks and other birds on the zoo premises. The central zoo has been reopened after the ‘environmental samples’ of birds tested negative for the bird flu virus.

The zoo administration has urged the visitors to maintain distance from animals and birds. Similarly, the general public has been requested not to consume food brought with them in open areas, to dispose of waste properly in the dustbins, and to mandatorily wear a face mask.
